title: #2185 Discovery of a rare vitamin D receptor defect as an inherited cause of kidney stones in Malta
authors: Julian Delicata; David Farrugia; Edith Said; Shabbir Moochhala
abstract:
Background and Aims
Loss of function variants in the CYP24A1 gene, encoding the inactivating vitamin D 24-hydroxylase enzyme, are known to cause a variety of clinical phenotypes ranging from infantile hypercalcaemia to adult-onset kidney stones.
Treatments to reduce kidney stone formation have focused on controlling serum and urinary calcium levels (steroids and loop diuretics), by targeting the cytochrome system (rifampicin, fluconazole) or by reducing vitamin D levels (avoiding supplementation and prolonged sun exposure).
Method
Patients from the metabolic kidney stone clinic at Mater Dei Hospital were selected for genetic testing on the basis of a history of bilateral kidney stone disease before 40 years of age and hypercalciuria of unknown cause. A metabolic work-up, which included blood analysis and at least two sets of 24-hour urine tests, had already been performed. Thirteen unrelated adult patients with monoallelic or biallelic CYP24A1 variants, all of Maltese ethnicity, were identified for further analysis.
Results
Genetic testing identified the same pathogenic variant (c.1186C>T, p.[Arg396Trp]) in all thirteen patients. Ten patients were homozygous for this variant and two patients were found to be heterozygous for this same pathological variant in the CYP24A1 gene. One patient was compound heterozygous for the c.1186C>T, p.[Arg396Trp] and the c.1508C>T, p.[Pro503Leu] variants in the CYP24A1 gene.
The two heterozygous patients first presented with kidney stones aged 27 and 35 years respectively. The median age of presentation of the other patients was 17.
Results are shown in Table 1. All ten patients carrying two (homozygous) CYP24A1 variants demonstrated suppressed PTH levels ranging from <6 to 22 ng/L (median 10 ng/L; normal range: 14–51 ng/L) whereas the two heterozygous patients had normal PTH levels (median 36 ng/L) (Fig. 1). One homozygous patient was diagnosed with hyperparathyroidism and is awaiting excision of a parathyroid adenoma.
The median urine calcium levels in the ten patients with two (homozygous) CYP24A1 variants and no evidence of hyperparathyroidism was 9.1 mmol/24 h as opposed to 15.7 mmol/24 h in the two heterozygous cases. Two of the homozygous patients subsequently became pregnant and developed severe hypercalcemia in the second and third trimesters respectively. This was managed by intravenous hydration, oral steroids and furosemide.
Another two homozygous cases had been started on fluconazole with a reduction of 2.7 mmol/24 h in urine calcium appreciated after four weeks in one patient. Bendroflumethiazide was started in both heterozygous and in two homozygous cases. One year after starting Bendroflumethiazide, one homozygous patient's urine calcium plummeted by 5.5 mmol/24 h and repeat renal imaging showed stable stone burden.
Conclusion
This study confirms that patients with heterozygous CYP24A1 pathogenic variants can present with kidney stones. Heterozygous cases may have normal serum PTH levels despite severe hypercalciuria and kidney stones, and therefore this diagnosis may explain some cases of “idiopathic” hypercalciuria. Cases with two pathogenic variants in the CYP24A1 gene present with suppressed PTH levels and sometimes an association with hyperparathyroidism as seen in other case reports. Pregnancy poses a challenge particularly in homozygous cases. Fluconazole (by inhibiting 1α-hydroxylase) and thiazide diuretics (by reducing hypercalciuria) can both play an important role in treatment.

title: #2706 Genetically determined reduction of renal carbonic anhydrase 12 is associated with decreased kidney function and increased serum urate
authors: Amber Emmett; David Scannali; Xiao Jiang; Xiaoguang Xu; Shadi Hames-Fathi; James Eales; Yong Sun; Abigail Lay; Ewa Kasprzak-Miller; Bernard Keavney; Fadi Charchar; MacIej Tomaszewski
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) affects 10% of the world's population and is the third fastest growing cause of death globally. Hyperuricemia and gout are frequent comorbidities of CKD and are associated with worse prognosis and increased mortality. We conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) of four CKD-defining traits (estimated glomerular filtration rate from creatinine—eGFRcr; eGFR from cystatin C—eGFRcys; blood urea nitrogen—BUN; and urinary albumin creatinine ratio—UACR) in the joint analysis of UK Biobank and CKDGen. We zoomed in on the novel candidate Carbonic Anhydrase 12 (CA12) given its role in renal acid-base and electrolyte balance, as well as treatment of several diseases through its inhibitor acetazolamide. Hypothesizing that CA12 is a causal contributor to kidney function, we aimed to characterise the effects of regulatory and loss-of-function CA12 alleles on CKD-defining traits and urate levels.
Method
We performed GWAS of four markers of kidney function in up to 327,689 UK biobank (UKB) participants, and meta-analysed the results with associations from CKDGen in up to 567,460 individuals. This identified a total of 508 unique independent genetic signals of associations with eGFRcr (424), eGFRcys (235), BUN (198) and UACR (51). A common CA12 variant rs1043256 showed strong consistent associations with eGFRcr, eGFRcys and BUN. We then tested rs1043256 association with its kidney mRNA (n = 645) and protein product (n = 83) in 2 collections of human kidney tissue. This was followed by Bayesian colocalization analyses to detect shared causal associations between gene/protein expression and kidney function biomarkers. To fully characterise the phenotypic effects, we tested a common CA12-reducing allele for association with 193 quantitative traits in 337,350 UKB participants by linear regression. A multi-trait colocalization analysis was performed to identify shared causal genetic associations. To investigate effects of CA12 loss-of-function, we tracked carriers of a rare allele causing the recessive monogenic disorder Hyperchloridhidrosis (HYCHL) in UKB (n = 1,038) and Million Veterans Program (MVP; n = 844). We tested this pathogenic variant for association with electrolytes, altered in HYCHL, and renal phenotypes. Associations were meta-analysed across the two cohorts when possible. The analyses were conducted in participants of European ancestry.
Results
The common CA12 rs1043256-C allele was associated with reduced kidney function (eGFRcr: P = 1.5 × 10−16, eGFRcys: P = 7.8 × 10−13, BUN: P = 1.1 × 10−9) and decreased expression of renal CA12 (mRNA: P = 1.2 × 10−5, protein: P = 1.5 × 10−3). The rs1043256-C allele was associated with increased serum urate in UKB (P = 4.5 × 10−6). Our multi-trait colocalization analysis confirmed a shared causal variant for indices of kidney function, urate and CA12 renal expression. In the fixed-effect meta-analysis conducted in UKB and MVP, we found that 1,882 heterozygote carriers of the CA12 loss-of-function allele (rs148438059-T) had decreased eGFRcr (P = 0.01), increased BUN (P = 0.03) and increased risk of gout (odds ratio = 1.5, P = 1.5 × 10−7). Serum urate was increased in UKB (P = 5.5 × 10−4).
Conclusion
We demonstrate that genetically determined CA12 reduction is associated with decreased kidney function and increased serum urate. Our findings suggest that pharmacological CA12 inhibition by acetazolamide may mimic the renal effects of genetic CA12 reduction, including a drop in GFR and increase in serum urate (with the latter not a well-recognised side effect of this treatment).

title: #123 Exploring the role of polygenic risk scores in aneurysm risk among ADPKD patients—a collaborative study
authors: Tomas Visser; Shohdan M Osman; Kane Collins; Matti Sentürk; Elhussein A E Elhassan; Omid Sadeghi-Alavijeh; Daniel P Gale; Aarno Palotie; Teemu Niiranen; Peter J Conlon; Patrik Finne; Daniel Gordin
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cerebral aneurysms in patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) carry significant risks, with genetic and environmental factors contributing to their development. Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS) have emerged as a method for quantifying genetic predispositions to complex diseases. This study evaluated the associations of PRS for hypertension (HTN-PRS) and intracranial aneurysms (IA-PRS) with aneurysm development in ADPKD patients.
Method
This study analysed the diagnosis of cerebral aneurysm in a cohort of 2458 ADPKD from Ireland (n = 474), Finland (the FinnGen Study, n = 779) and the United Kingdom (UK Genomics England GEL, n = 1205). Finnish and Irish patients were combined and analysed together as a combined cohort, while the GEL cohort was analysed separately. Patients were stratified into low (bottom 20%), intermediate (60%), and high (top 20%) risk groups based on their PRS for HTN and IA. Multivariate proportional hazards models were used to assess associations between PRS groups and the diagnosis of cerebral aneurysm. Hazard ratios (HR) were adjusted for the first ten principal components of genetic ancestry to account for population stratification.
Results
Among the Finnish and Irish cohorts, 48% were males, compared to 51% in the GEL cohort. The lifetime risk of hypertension was 85% for the Finnish and Irish cohorts and 71% for the GEL cohort. The risk of cerebral aneurysm was smallest in the group with low HTN-PRS (FinnGen and Ireland 6%, GEL 6%), intermediate (FinnGen and Ireland 13% and GEL 3%) and high (FinnGen and Ireland 14%, GEL 3%) (P = 0.005 for high versus low HTN-PRS in FinnGen and Ireland cohorts) (Figs 1 and 2). The mean age at aneurysm diagnosis was similar across PRS groups within the Finnish and Irish cohorts: 63 years (GEL 50 years) for low HTN-PRS, 60 years (GEL 54 years) for intermediate HTN-PRS, and 61 years (GEL 53 years) for the HTN-PRS groups (P > 0.2). The HR for developing an aneurysm was 2.04 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.09–3.82) for the high HTN-PRS group compared to low HTN-PRS (GEL = 2.36; 95% CI 0.66–8.42). Additionally, high HTN-PRS group had a higher lifetime risk of HTN (87.6%, GEL 69%) than low HTN-PRS (80.1%, GEL 70.8%) (P = 0.029). For the IA-PRS, aneurysm risk was highest in high IA-PRS within the Finnish and Irish cohort (18%, GEL 4%) compared to low IA-PRS (8%; GEL 1.2%) (P = 0.001) (Figs 1 and 2). The high IA-PRS group also experienced a younger age of aneurysm diagnosis (59 years; GEL 52 years) compared to low IA-PRS (64 years; GEL 57 years) (P = 0.003). Compared to low IA-PRS, HR for developing an aneurysm was 2.20 (95% CI 1.26–3.84; GEL: 3.21, 95% CI 0.85–12.13) in the high IA-PRS group.
Conclusion
Higher HTN-PRS and IA-PRS were associated with increased aneurysm occurrence and earlier disease diagnosis in ADPKD patients in the combined Finnish and Irish cohorts. However, these results were not replicated in the GEL cohort. These findings highlight the potential of PRS as a tool for identifying high-risk ADPKD patients. Further research integrating PRS with clinical and imaging data is warranted to optimise risk stratification and preventive strategies. We are currently working on a meta-analysis of the three cohorts (Finnish, Irish, and GEL) to validate these findings or determine if consistent results can be achieved across all cohorts.

title: #3418 Genealogical analysis in the Era of big data: implications for biomedical research
authors: Mirella Aurora Aceto; Teresa Serra Cassano; Ersilia Paparazzo; Gemma Antonucci; Davide Lagrotteria; Pierluigi Mercatante; Silvana Geracitano; Antonella La Russa; Loris Belcastro; Giuseppe Passarino; Paolo Trunfio; Alberto Montesanto
abstract:
Background and Aims
The use of extended families from genetically isolated populations with high consanguinity has proven effective in identifying genetic risk factors for rare and common disorders. Church and civil records, dating back to the 16th century, have enabled genealogies and databases to be reconstructed. However, no tools for visually representing AI-based reconstructed pedigrees for entire populations existed. Progeny-AI was developed to bridge this gap. Using AI algorithms, this tool links historical birth, death, and marriage records to reconstruct genealogies and databases. It was applied to a Calabrian municipality with Fabry's disease cases, a Mendelian disorder that is often underdiagnosed. Progeny-AI automatically reconstructed a family of 228 members spanning five generations, going back to the 18th century. This helped identify undiagnosed family members at risk of developing Fabry's disease, enabling earlier diagnosis and better management.
Method
Data sources and data collection
The main data sources used include church and civil status registers (baptism, birth, death, and marriage records) from the area under investigation from 1734 to the present day. The information from these records was first imported into IND-DB, which contains data extracted from birth and death records. Simultaneously, a second database, MAR-DB, containing only marriage data, was created. Data pre-processing, including eliminating spelling errors, duplicates, and typos, improved the quality of databases. Using record-linkage methods, the pedigree generation algorithm processed individual records in IND-DB to reconstruct family trees (Fig. 1).
Family tree inference
Family trees were inferred by matching information about parents from IND-DB to corresponding marriage records in MAR-DB. A similarity score was calculated for each potential pair of parents. If the score was below a predefined threshold, the search was extended to IND-DB records. In this case, both parents were individually matched, ensuring that their marriage status aligned with the information from the other parent.
Matching score
A deterministic linkage procedure was used to match records from IND-DB with those in MAR-DB. The process began by estimating matching similarities for multiple candidate marriage records in MAR-DB. Similarity values were calculated using specific measures. For string comparisons (e.g., names, surnames), Jaro-Winkler similarity with a threshold of 0.9 was applied. For numerical data (e.g., ages, distances), a transformed Euclidean distance was used. A family tree of over 11,000 individuals, built by genealogists, served as training data to optimize thresholds and parameters for family tree inference.
Implementation
Progeny-AI first employs a deterministic data-matching approach implemented in Python. An efficient layout algorithm for drawing and navigating genealogical graphs is then implemented using the Neo4j graph database.
Results
We reconstructed the entire pedigree and linked most past generations in a large genealogical tree, reaching back to the population of the area under investigation in the mid-1700s. Progeny-AI was also used to infer a genealogical tree starting from a family with several members affected by Fabry's disease (Fig. 2). Progeny-AI enabled rapid reconstruction of a large family, now including 228 individuals with descendants spread across several municipalities of Calabria. Extending the investigation area enabled the identification of potential patients for screening for Fabry's disease.
Conclusion
Progeny-AI improves genealogical research. While evidence for a founder variant in this region remains to be demonstrated, the results highlight Progeny-AI's relevance in accelerating genetic diagnosis of younger or mildly affected patients, especially those with ancestors from the area under investigation.

title: #769 Urinary myeloid bodies as a biomarker for early diagnosis and monitoring of enzyme replacement therapy in Fabry disease
authors: Junlan Yang; Bin Wang; Xiao Liang Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fabry disease is a rare X-linked disorder caused by mutations in the GLA gene, leading to a deficiency in α-galactosidase A (α-Gal A) and lysosomal dysfunction. This results in the accumulation of lipid substances, such as globotriaosylceramide (GL-3) and globotriaosylsphingosine (Lyso-GL-3), in organs like the kidneys, heart, and nervous system, causing organ dysfunction. Renal involvement, including proteinuria and renal dysfunction, is a major contributor to disability and mortality. Early detection and treatment, such as enzyme replacement therapy (ERT), are critical; however, ERT is less effective in patients with severe proteinuria. Identifying novel biomarkers for early kidney damage is essential.
Myeloid bodies, multilamellar myelin figures observed under electron microscopy, are a hallmark of Fabry disease and are crucial for diagnosis. First identified in urine sediment in 1977, their role in disease progression was confirmed in 2018. However, the prevalence of urinary myeloid bodies and their link to disease progression are not fully understood. This study aims to analyze urinary myeloid bodies in Fabry patients, assess their prevalence, and explore their potential as a non-invasive biomarker for monitoring ERT effectiveness and disease progression.
Method
This single-center, retrospective study included 25 patients with Fabry disease and 27 controls (2 healthy individuals and 25 patients with other renal diseases). We analyzed 24-hour urine samples for the presence of urinary myeloid bodies and evaluated clinical data, including serum creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), 24-hour urinary protein levels, α-Gal A, and Lyso-GL-3. Seven Fabry patients underwent analysis of urine samples before and after one year of ERT.
Results
Urinary myeloid bodies were detected in 21 Fabry patients (84%), while no myeloid bodies were observed in the control group (Table 1). The median age of the Fabry patient cohort was 43 years, with a male-to-female ratio of 44% to 56%. None of the Fabry patients had a history of cationic amphiphilic drug use. Urinary myeloid bodies were detected in 21 patients (84%) (Fig. 1A–F). Comparison between Fabry patients with and without urinary myeloid bodies revealed no statistically significant differences in age, gender, serum creatinine, eGFR, 24-hour urinary protein, α-Gal A, or Lyso-GL-3 (Table 1).
Based on the presence of urinary myeloid bodies and proteinuria, patients were divided into four groups (Fig. 1G). Two patients exhibited neither condition, while fourteen patients presented with both. Seven additional patients showed urinary myeloid body excretion despite the absence of proteinuria. Among the Fabry patients with myeloid bodies, 48% had no proteinuria, and 52% were in CKD stage 1, G1 (Fig. 1H–K). Furthermore, urinary myeloid bodies were detected in four patients under the age of 20, despite the absence of or only minimal proteinuria, and these patients all exhibited a substantial number of myeloid bodies. After one year of ERT, significant reductions in both the count (P = 0.043) and area ratio (P = 0.028) of myeloid bodies were observed (Fig. 1L and M).
Conclusion
Urinary myeloid bodies are specific to Fabry disease and are associated with early renal injury, even in the absence of proteinuria. These findings suggest that urinary myeloid bodies may serve as a non-invasive biomarker for the early diagnosis of Fabry disease and for monitoring the efficacy of ERT.

Background and Aims
Fabry disease is a rare X-linked disorder caused by mutations in the GLA gene, leading to a deficiency in α-galactosidase A (α-Gal A) and lysosomal dysfunction. This results in the accumulation of lipid substances, such as globotriaosylceramide (GL-3) and globotriaosylsphingosine (Lyso-GL-3), in organs like the kidneys, heart, and nervous system, causing organ dysfunction. Renal involvement, including proteinuria and renal dysfunction, is a major contributor to disability and mortality. Early detection and treatment, such as enzyme replacement therapy (ERT), are critical; however, ERT is less effective in patients with severe proteinuria. Identifying novel biomarkers for early kidney damage is essential.
Myeloid bodies, multilamellar myelin figures observed under electron microscopy, are a hallmark of Fabry disease and are crucial for diagnosis. First identified in urine sediment in 1977, their role in disease progression was confirmed in 2018. However, the prevalence of urinary myeloid bodies and their link to disease progression are not fully understood. This study aims to analyze urinary myeloid bodies in Fabry patients, assess their prevalence, and explore their potential as a non-invasive biomarker for monitoring ERT effectiveness and disease progression.
Method
This single-center, retrospective study included 25 patients with Fabry disease and 27 controls (2 healthy individuals and 25 patients with other renal diseases). We analyzed 24-hour urine samples for the presence of urinary myeloid bodies and evaluated clinical data, including serum creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), 24-hour urinary protein levels, α-Gal A, and Lyso-GL-3. Seven Fabry patients underwent analysis of urine samples before and after one year of ERT.
Results
Urinary myeloid bodies were detected in 21 Fabry patients (84%), while no myeloid bodies were observed in the control group (Table 1). The median age of the Fabry patient cohort was 43 years, with a male-to-female ratio of 44% to 56%. None of the Fabry patients had a history of cationic amphiphilic drug use. Urinary myeloid bodies were detected in 21 patients (84%) (Fig. 1A–F). Comparison between Fabry patients with and without urinary myeloid bodies revealed no statistically significant differences in age, gender, serum creatinine, eGFR, 24-hour urinary protein, α-Gal A, or Lyso-GL-3 (Table 1).
Based on the presence of urinary myeloid bodies and proteinuria, patients were divided into four groups (Fig. 1G). Two patients exhibited neither condition, while fourteen patients presented with both. Seven additional patients showed urinary myeloid body excretion despite the absence of proteinuria. Among the Fabry patients with myeloid bodies, 48% had no proteinuria, and 52% were in CKD stage 1, G1 (Fig. 1H–K). Furthermore, urinary myeloid bodies were detected in four patients under the age of 20, despite the absence of or only minimal proteinuria, and these patients all exhibited a substantial number of myeloid bodies. After one year of ERT, significant reductions in both the count (P = 0.043) and area ratio (P = 0.028) of myeloid bodies were observed (Fig. 1L and M).
Conclusion
Urinary myeloid bodies are specific to Fabry disease and are associated with early renal injury, even in the absence of proteinuria. These findings suggest that urinary myeloid bodies may serve as a non-invasive biomarker for the early diagnosis of Fabry disease and for monitoring the efficacy of ERT.

title: #3118 PCK1 loss contributes to kidney disease progression by altering mitochondrial fitness through its cataplerotic function
authors: Delal Dalga; Anna Rinaldi; Anna Faivre; Quentin Gex; Deborah Paolucci; Alban Longchamp; Joseph Rutkowski; Pietro Cippà; Thomas Verissimo; Sophie Deseigneux
abstract:
Background and Aims
During chronic kidney disease (CKD), renal gluconeogenesis is impaired, leading to metabolic dysfunction. Among the enzymes involved in gluconeogenesis, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 1 (PCK1), which facilitates the conversion of oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate, is rate-limiting. In this study, we hypothesize that the alteration of PCK1 expression in kidney proximal cells contributes to metabolic alterations during CKD and renal dysfunction, through modifications of acid-base balance and cataplerosis.
Method
Using kidney tubular-specific knockout (KO) and knock in (KI) PCK1 mice models, we assessed the influence of PCK1 expression changes on renal function and kidney metabolism under physiological and pathological conditions. We utilized models of AKI (ischemia) and CKD (proteinuria and platinum toxicity).
Results
Under physiological conditions, PCK1 deletion leads to a loss of renal function and hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. PCK1 inhibition also induces significant alterations in mitochondrial structure and function, as evidenced by Seahorse analysis and electron microscopy. Additionally, metabolomic analysis revealed that the loss of PCK1 results in decreased cataplerosis, leading to the accumulation of TCA cycle. Additionally, the accumulation of TCA metabolites likely promotes inflammation. In models of AKI and non-diabetic CKD, PCK1 deletion exacerbated renal dysfunction and mortality. Conversely, in two models of non-diabetic CKD, restoration of PCK1 in kidney tubular cells improved renal function, reduced tubular injury, and slowed fibrosis progression. Similarly, PCK1 restoration mitigated mitochondrial damage by promoting TCA cataplerosis.
Conclusion
PCK1 is essential for maintaining renal tubular acid-base balance, metabolism and mitochondrial energy production through cataplerosis. Restoring PCK1 could be a crucial target for preventing mitochondrial dysfunction and the progression of kidney disease during CKD.

title: #3146 Genetic heterogeneity of ADPKD: A total of 21 different genes identified in a population-based ADPKD cohort
authors: Nikola Zagorec; Marie-Pierre Audrezet; Jean-Michel Halimi; Frank Bridoux; Augusto Jean François; Jacques Dantal; Yannick Le Meur; Emilie Cornec-Le Gall
abstract:
Background and Aims
A significant number of individuals presenting with an ADPKD-like phenotype either harbour pathogenic variants in other cystic genes or genes that mimic ADPKD, or remain genetically unresolved (GUR). Understanding this variability is a key research priority emphasized in the 2025 KDIGO guidelines on ADPKD.
Method
Genkyst is a population-based cohort including all patients with ADPKD or ADPKD-like phenotype followed in 28 nephrology centers in northwestern France. Inclusion criteria were: 1) Pei-Ravine radiologic criteria in patients with positive family history or proven pathogenic variant in PKD1/PKD2 (N = 3122); 2) >10 bilateral kidney cysts (N = 263). A gene panel including 25 known or candidate cystogenes was employed, and whole exome sequencing (WES) was performed in majority of GUR families.
Results
Total of 3385 individuals from 2326 families were included (47.8% males) at the median age of 54.8 (16–94). Likely pathogenic or pathogenic variants (LP/P) compatible with cystic phenotype were identified in 91.2% and 87.6% of individuals and families, respectively. While PKD1 and PKD2 LP/P variants were identified in 64.7 and 18.5% of families, respectively, 4.4% of families had atypical forms of ADPKD caused by variants in 19 different genes, the most common being IFT140, ALG8, DNAJB11, COL4A4 and HNF1B (Fig. 1). WES was performed in 266 GUR families leading to precise genetic diagnosis in 56 (21%) of them and revealing some important ADPKD-differentials like heterozygous COL4A4, OFD1 or even biallelic TULP3 with significant clinical implications. Pathogenic variants in a recently identified ADPKD candidate gene, IFT172, were identified in four unrelated patients, further supporting its role in atypical PKD. After this systematic genetic analysis including WES, a total of 299 individuals remained still GUR. Compared to PKD1-PKD2 patients, GUR individuals were more often males (65% vs 46%, P < 0.001), significantly older (65.05 vs 53.0, P < 0.001), more often diagnosed incidentally (40% vs 24%, P < 0.001), less commonly had positive familial history (24% vs 74%, P < 0.001) and developed kidney failure (16% vs 42%, P < 0.001) and had better renal survival [84.6 y (81–91.8) vs 53.9 y (53.1–55) in PKD1-truncating or 78.4 y (73.5–84) in PKD2 individuals]. Of interest, monoallelic predicted loss-of-function variants were detected within 34 different known ciliopathy genes in 58 GUR individuals from 55 families, and causality is being investigated.
Conclusion
ADPKD is a genetically heterogeneous disease, with in our cohort 12 ADPKD-associated genes and 9 phenocopies. Further genetic heterogeneity is likely, with new candidate genes identified by WES being currently characterized.

title: #1977 Deep phenotyping predicts genotype and refines prognosis in lower risk ADPKD genotypes
authors: Eugene Chen; Jie Han Chong; Albert Ong
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is characterized by the progressive development of kidney cysts which eventually lead to kidney failure. Effective management of ADPKD necessitates accurate risk stratification and tailored monitoring strategies. Although individual kidney outcomes are highly variable, genotype is a major determining factor of kidney life-span with a PKD1-T genotype conferring the highest risk of earlier kidney failure. Nonetheless genotyping remains costly and is not widely available globally outside developed health systems. Here, we report baseline factors that are predictive of the major genotypes and determine prognosis in lower risk genotypes in a large, unselected ADPKD cohort.
The primary aim of this study was to identify what baseline factors could predict the presence of the major gene variants (PKD1 and PKD2) compared to minor gene variants (non-PKD1 or PKD2). A secondary aim was to identify prognostic factors associated with more rapid disease progression in patients with lower risk genotypes, specifically those other than PKD1-T variants.
Method
A cross-sectional analysis was conducted in 763 ADPKD patients followed-up in a specialist PKD clinic between 2010 and January 2024. Data collected included genotype (n = 641), baseline height-adjusted mean kidney length (HtMKL) (n = 504), family history (n = 763) and baseline ultrasound (USS) liver cyst counts (n = 667). Rapid disease progression was defined as an annualized eGFR decline (∆eGFR) of >2.5 ml/min/year by linear regression over 3 years. Genotyped patients were classified into those with PKD1 (T: truncating; NT: non-truncating), PKD2, other genes (non-PKD1 or PKD2), NMD (no mutation detected), variants of uncertain significance (VUS) or complex gene inheritance (CGI).
Results
Among those genotyped, PKD1 variants (50%) was most common, followed by PKD2 (17%). Of PKD1 variants, 59% were truncating (T) and 41% non-truncating (NT). Of the minor genes (7%), IFT140 was the predominant variant (75%). 3% had VUS, 2% had CGI and 21% had NMD. Compared to patients with PKD1-T or PKD2 variants, those with IFT140 variants had significantly smaller HtMKL, lower frequency of positive family history, lower frequency of liver cysts and are more likely to be asymptomatic at presentation. Multivariate logistic regression identified age ≤43 years, HtMKL >9.5 cm/m, presence of liver cysts as independent predictors of a major gene variant (PKD1 and PKD2) after excluding those referred due to a positive FH. The presence of at least 1 liver cyst on USS alone had a positive predictive value (PPV) of 99% and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 25%, with NPV increasing to 59% in patients aged ≥50 years. The combination of HtMKL >9.5 cm/m increased the PPV to 100% but reduced NPV to 14% (increasing to 29% in older patients aged ≥50 years).
Conclusion
We identified three independent factors highly predictive of major gene variants (PKD1 or PKD2): age at presentation, baseline HtMKL, and the presence of liver cysts. Strikingly, a history of UTI in PKD2 patients (n = 41) and NMD patients (n = 67) were significantly associated with more rapid disease progression in our cohort. In contrast, no specific features could distinguish between PKD1-NT patients (n = 59) with slow and rapid progression. Where genotype testing is not available, deep phenotyping can predict major gene variants to inform individual treatment decisions. Where a lower risk variant has been identified, careful phenotyping can also refine individual prognosis such as in patient with PKD2 variants and NMD subgroups.

title: #3174 Monoallelic IFT172 variants as a genetic contributor to the ADPKD spectrum
authors: Nikola Zagorec; Doaa Elbarougy; Marie-Pierre Audrezet; Hana Yang; Laurence Michel-Calemard; Pierre André Massard; John Sayer; Peter Harris; Emilie Cornec-Le Gall
abstract:
Background and Aims
PKD1 and PKD2 are the two major genes in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Up to 15% of patients with ADPKD-like phenotype are genetically unresolved (GUR) or carry variants in minor cystogenes including IFT140. Here, we describe features of an ADPKD-like phenotype linked to monoallelic predicted loss-of-function (pLoF) variants in a new candidate cystogene, IFT172. The IFT172 protein is part of the IFT-B subcomplex and plays a role in protein trafficking within primary cilia. Biallelic variants in IFT172 cause a severe ciliopathy.
Method
A total of ∼3200 unrelated individuals with cystic kidney disease (CyKD) underwent genetic testing employing whole-exome sequencing (WES) or massive-parallel-sequencing (MPS) gene panels in Brest, Lyon and in Rochester, MN. In addition, 185 individuals ICD coded as CyKD from Mayo Clinic Biobank (MCBB) underwent WES. Clinical and genetic data of individuals with predicted loss-of-function variants of IFT172 were collected and analyzed. Also, the Genomics England 100kG Project cohort was screened for pLoF variants in IFT172.
Results
In the CyKD population, 18 patients with a monoallelic pLoF variant in IFT172 were identified. In the MCBB CyKD cohort, 3 individuals had IFT172 pLoF variants. We describe the clinical presentation of these 21 affected individuals (15 males). Median age at CyKD diagnosis was 67 (range 34–88) years. Family history for CyKD was positive in 10 (48%), negative in 9 (42%) and not known in 2 (10%) individuals. Arterial hypertension was present in 9 (45%) patients, in three of them diagnosed before age of 50 years and in 6 at a later age. Hypertension status was not known in 10 of them. A majority of the patients presented with multiple bilateral cortical kidney cysts with moderate kidney enlargement or normal-sized kidneys with large, exophytic kidney cysts and were classified as Mayo Imaging Class 2A. In one patient, unilateral CyKD was present with >10 cysts. Liver cysts were present in 4 (19%) and gout in three (15%) patients. None of the three patients who underwent screening were found to have intracranial aneurysm. Median eGFR at diagnosis (N = 19) was 53 (range 29–119) ml/min/1.73 m2. Of 15 patients older than 60 y, one had CKD stage G1, 5 stage G2, 3 stage G3a, 5 stage G3b and one G4. Only one patient of African descent (APOL1 G1/G0) reached kidney failure at age of 43 y, likely due to additional contribution of uncontrolled hypertension and poorly controlled diabetes. In addition, in two patients, the IFT172 pLoF variant was identified alongside a pathogenic variant in PKD1 (p.Gln2519*) or PKD2 (c.844-1G>T). Both progressed to kidney failure at an earlier age than typically observed with PKD1 or PKD2 alone, at 29 and 52 years, respectively. Familial segregation is ongoing. Of the total of 94,799 patients recruited in “rare disease program” within 100kG Project, 51 carried monoallelic pLoF variants in IFT172 (genetic prevalence: 5.38 [0.95 CI 3.9–6.86] per 10,000). Four of them (7.8%) had CyKD.
Conclusion
Carriers of monoallelic pLoF variants in IFT172 are likely to develop cystic kidney disease (CyKD) that is atypical of classical ADPKD, generally associated with a favorable kidney prognosis. Nonetheless, individuals over the age of 60 may have an increased risk of progressing to CKD stage G3 or worse. Disease penetrance in IFT172 pLoF variant carriers appears to be incomplete, similar to what is observed in IFT140.

title: #3430 Enhancing diagnostic precision for inherited kidney diseases: the importance of databases
authors: Leonor Fayos de Arizón; Rafael Leon; Elizabeth Romelia Viera Ramírez; Monica Furlano; Pedro Arango; Víctor Alfonso López Báez; Erknet Expert Centers; Alexandre Perera; Roser Torra
abstract:
Background and Aims
Inherited kidney diseases (IKDs) are the leading cause of early-onset chronic kidney disease but remain underdiagnosed. Clinical diagnosis is extremely complex due to high phenotypic variability, frequent lack of familial history, and their ultra-rare nature. Although artificial intelligence (AI) could advance both clinical diagnosis and genetic testing, existing ontology-based tools have not been widely adopted, partly due to inaccuracies in addressing certain disease groups, including IKDs. Currently, no tool specifically targets IKDs. The study aimed to demonstrate the potential of a curated, domain-specific database in improving diagnostic precision for these diseases.
Method
Development of a curated database built upon the Mondo Disease Ontology which uses annotations from the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO). Over 150 IKDs and thousands of HPO annotations were exhaustively reviewed and refined by nephrologists in collaboration with international experts. This process incorporated deep phenotyping details and renal-specific terminology. A pilot study was conducted using a cohort of real patients (n = 339) with 12 genetically confirmed IKDs (Alport syndrome (AD, AR, XL), ADTKD (MUC1, UMOD), HNF1B-related disease, Fabry disease, Von Hippel-Lindau disease, tuberous sclerosis complex, AR polycystic kidney disease and nephronophthisis). Clinical data was collected and represented using HPO annotations, subject to informed consent. The new curated, domain-specific database was compared with the present MONDO ontology by calculating similarity scores using 3 existing tools (Phenomizer, Phrank, and Phen2Disease). For data description, paired permutation and Mann-Whitney tests were applied to show initial differences in similarity scores between the newly curated database and MONDO. A Mixed-effects Model accounted for biases from disease and clinical level variability. Ranking performance was assessed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and Discounted Cumulative Gain (DCG) to evaluate top-ranked diagnostic results and confirm whether higher similarity scores translated into better diagnostic prioritization.
Results
Initial comparisons between the curated database (CURATED) and MONDO revealed that CURATED aligned more closely with real patient phenotypes across the three tools (Phenomizer, Phrank, and Phen2Disease). Mean similarity scores increased significantly when using CURATED: Phenomizer from 0.574 to 0.674 (p = 0.01), Phrank from 28.11 to 34.79 (p < 0.001), and Phen2Disease from 0.844 to 1.017 (p = 0.007). Mixed-effects model confirmed that the improvement remained robust despite biases in diseases and annotating clinicians: the estimator for Phenomizer was 0.1296 ± 0.0411 (p = 0.01), for Phrank was 7.104 ± 1.291 (p = 0.001), and for Phen2Disease 0.1695 ± 0.0433 (p = 0.007). Positive estimators mean that CURATED scores are significantly higher than MONDO scores. Diagnostic rankings also improved markedly with CURATED. The proportion of patients correctly ranked in the top position (Top 1) increased from ∼18% to ∼42% with Phenomizer, ∼18% to ∼38% with Phrank, and ∼20% to ∼52% with Phen2Disease. Furthermore, DCG scores were consistently higher in CURATED (0.651 vs. 0.577 for Phenomizer, 0.628 vs. 0.555 for Phrank, 0.730 vs. 0.597 for Phen2Disease), indicating more accurate prioritization of correct diagnoses. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test further demonstrated a significant difference in rankings for Phrank (p = 0.037) and Phen2Disease (p < 0.001), while the differences between CURATED and MONDO in Phenomizer were not statistically significant for now (p = 0.066).
Conclusion
These findings underscore the potential of an improved ontology to enhance diagnostic accuracy for inherited kidney diseases. A high quality, domain-specific database can be a game changer in advancing AI diagnostic tools that may improve the clinical diagnosis of inherited kidney diseases in the near future.

Clinical data was collected and represented using HPO annotations, subject to informed consent. For data description, paired permutation and Mann-Whitney tests were applied to show initial differences in similarity scores between the newly curated database and MONDO. A Mixed-effects Model accounted for biases from disease and clinical level variability. Ranking performance was assessed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and Discounted Cumulative Gain (DCG) to evaluate top-ranked diagnostic results and confirm whether higher similarity scores translated into better diagnostic prioritization.
Results
Initial comparisons between the curated database (CURATED) and MONDO revealed that CURATED aligned more closely with real patient phenotypes across the three tools (Phenomizer, Phrank, and Phen2Disease). Mixed-effects model confirmed that the improvement remained robust despite biases in diseases and annotating clinicians: the estimator for Phenomizer was 0.1296 ± 0.0411 (p = 0.01), for Phrank was 7.104 ± 1.291 (p = 0.001), and for Phen2Disease 0.1695 ± 0.0433 (p = 0.007). Positive estimators mean that CURATED scores are significantly higher than MONDO scores. Diagnostic rankings also improved markedly with CURATED. The proportion of patients correctly ranked in the top position (Top 1) increased from ∼18% to ∼42% with Phenomizer, ∼18% to ∼38% with Phrank, and ∼20% to ∼52% with Phen2Disease. Furthermore, DCG scores were consistently higher in CURATED (0.651 vs. 0.577 for Phenomizer, 0.628 vs. 0.555 for Phrank, 0.730 vs. 0.597 for Phen2Disease), indicating more accurate prioritization of correct diagnoses. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test further demonstrated a significant difference in rankings for Phrank (p = 0.037) and Phen2Disease (p < 0.001), while the differences between CURATED and MONDO in Phenomizer were not statistically significant for now (p = 0.066).
Conclusion
These findings underscore the potential of an improved ontology to enhance diagnostic accuracy for inherited kidney diseases. A high quality, domain-specific database can be a game changer in advancing AI diagnostic tools that may improve the clinical diagnosis of inherited kidney diseases in the near future.

title: #623 SGLT2 inhibitors in adult patients with Alport syndrome: a single center Italian experience
authors: Diego Toso; Valeria Cinquina; Letizia Zeni; Laura Econimo; Roberta Cortinovis; Gianfranco Savoldi; Cinzia Mazza; Chiara Dordoni; Francesco Scolari; Federico Alberici; Claudia Izzi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Alport syndrome (AS) is the most common inherited glomerular disease, caused by pathogenic variants in COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5 genes, leading to distinct inheritance patterns. Structural disruption of glomerular basement membrane due to collagen IV gene variants leads to a clinical renal spectrum characterized by microhematuria, glomerular proteinuria, and progressive chronic kidney disease (CKD), often culminating in kidney failure (KF). Proteinuria is a recognized key prognostic marker for KF in AS, and combination therapy with renin-angiotensin system (RAS) blockers and SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) has recently been recommended in an AS guideline [1] to slow CKD progression. However, a randomized control trial is ongoing, and a retrospective study have evaluated its effect in a young cohort with short mean follow-up period [2]. Thus, this study aimed to evaluate the impact of SGLT2i therapy on proteinuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in an older AS patients cohort.
Method
A retrospective, single-center, observational study involving adult patients with a confirmed genetic diagnosis of AS, treated with the maximum tolerated dose of RAS blockers and SGLT2i, following Italian regulatory agency criteria (eGFR 45–90 mL/min with uACR ≥200 mg/g, or eGFR 20–45 mL/min with or without albuminuria). Clinical, histological, and laboratory data were retrospectively collected from 5 years prior to treatment initiation until December 2024, excluding data from the first month of therapy to avoid biases related to the known initial eGFR drop upon SGLT2i initiation. Genetic diagnosis was performed using a next generation sequencing targeted glomerular genes panel. Statistical analyses included Shapiro-Wilk test, paired t-test, linear regressions, and linear mixed model, conducted using R version 4.1.2.
Results
Out of a cohort of 140 adult patients with AS, 20 received RAS blockers and SGLT2i treatment, and 5 of them were excluded due to a lack of post-treatment data. Baseline characteristics of the remaining 15 patients are summarized in Table 1. All patients were over 40 years of age, with a mean age of 60.4 ± 9.6 years, an eGFR of 54.5 ± 19.5 mL/min/1.73 m², and median proteinuria of 910 mg/day (IQR 340;1610). Most patients (11/15) carried heterozygous variants in COL4A3 or COL4A4 genes. The mean observation period was 17.9 ± 7.4 months, ranging from 6.1 to 32.7 months. Four patients discontinued SGLT2i due to different reasons: diarrhea, symptomatic hypotension, severe eGFR impairment, and KF.
As described in Fig. 1a, eGFR slope reduced after treatment initiation (−0.19 mL/min/month before and −0.02 mL/min/month after SGLT2i, p = 0.204). Similarly, while the reduction in proteinuria did not reach statistical significance, a trend toward improvement was observed, with an estimated reduction of 19.5% from baseline (Fig. 1b, p = 0.204).
Furthermore, consistent with known SGLT2i effects, haemoglobin levels increased (from 13.9 ± 1.2 to 14.3 ± 1.4, p-value: 0.060) and serum uric acid levels decreased (from 5.9 ± 1.1 to 5.4 ± 1.2, p-value: 0.060), although these changes were not statistically significant.
Conclusion
This study supports the potential antiproteinuric and nephroprotective effects of SGLT2i in a real-world cohort of older AS patients compared to those reported in literature, predominantly carrying heterozygous COL4A3/COL4A4 variants. Despite a relatively high discontinuation rate, no serious adverse events were observed, and symptoms resolved promptly after treatment cessation.
The restricted sample size and single-center design limited the statistical power of the analyses. Nonetheless, randomized control trials (such as DOUBLE PRO-TECT Alport) are essential to better define optimal treatment strategies and timing for SGLT2i initiation in AS.

title: #3265 Pegcetacoplan treatment effect in patients with nephrotic range proteinuria: results from the VALIANT Phase 3 study in patients with C3G or primary (idiopathic) IC-MPGN
authors: Marina Vivarelli; Andrew S Bomback; Gema Ariceta; Antonio Mastrangelo; Carla M Nester; Giuseppe Remuzzi; Nicole Van De Kar; Zhongshen Wang; Johan Szamosi; Dima Decker; Lucia Quintana Gallardo; Fadi Fakhouri
abstract:
Background and Aims
C3 glomerulopathy (C3G) and primary (idiopathic) immune complex membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (IC-MPGN) are rare diseases where uncontrolled C3 activation results in excessive glomerular deposition of C3 breakdown products. Current treatments, such as mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) and corticosteroids, are used off-label, primarily targeting inflammatory changes rather than the underlying disease mechanism. These treatments are associated with adverse effects and lack robust clinical evidence of efficacy. As a result, up to 50% of patients progress to kidney failure within 10 years.
Pegcetacoplan (PEG) binds selectively to C3 and C3b to strongly block C3 activation by classical/lectin/alternative pathways, C3/C5 convertase activity and activation of downstream effectors. PEG targets the pathogenic process in C3G/primary IC-MPGN with the aim of stopping kidney damage.
In the Phase 3 VALIANT study (NCT05067127) in pts aged ≥12 years with native or post-transplant recurrent C3G/primary IC-MPGN, PEG led to a 68.1% relative proteinuria reduction vs placebo (PBO), glomerular C3 clearance in 71% of pts and stabilization of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR).
Pts with native or post-transplant recurrent C3G/primary IC-MPGN who present with nephrotic range proteinuria (urine protein-to-creatinine ratio [UPCR] ≥3 g/g) are at high risk of rapid disease progression to kidney failure, constituting a patient population with a high unmet medical need. The aim of this analysis was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of PEG vs placebo (PBO) in pts presenting with nephrotic range proteinuria at baseline.
Method
VALIANT study participants were randomized 1:1 to receive PEG (subcutaneous infusion twice weekly) or PBO for 26 weeks as add-on to their stable treatment regimen. The primary endpoint was the log-transformed ratio of UPCR at Week 26 vs baseline. Secondary endpoints included the proportion of pts achieving a reduction in C3c staining on kidney biopsy, change in eGFR from baseline vs PBO, and normalization of serum albumin.
Results
Overall, 124 pts were randomized in VALIANT (63 PEG; 61 PBO). At baseline, there were 24 (38.1%) and 16 (26.2%) pts in the PEG and PBO arm, respectively, who had UPCR ≥3 g/g. Baseline characteristics are shown in the Table.
At Week 26, PEG-treated pts with baseline UPCR ≥3 g/g achieved a significant and clinically meaningful 72.1% relative reduction in proteinuria vs PBO (p < 0.0001). 66.7% (16/24) of pts in the PEG group vs 0% (0/16) in the PBO group had a ≥50% reduction in proteinuria from baseline (p < 0.0001). Furthermore, 66.7% (10/15) of PEG-treated pts with baseline UPCR ≥3 g/g and low baseline serum albumin achieved normalization of serum albumin at Week 26 vs 0% (0/12) for PBO.
84.6% (11/13) of pts achieved a reduction in glomerular C3c staining with PEG vs 0% (0/9) with PBO (p = 0.0002). PEG-treated pts experienced a mean change of +4.7 mL/min/1.73 m2 in eGFR, showing a relative improvement of +16.2 mL/min/1.73 m2 (p = 0.0046) vs PBO.
Rates of treatment-emergent adverse events were comparable between PEG vs PBO pts with UPCR ≥3 g/g, similar to the overall study population, with no study discontinuations or deaths.
Conclusion
In the VALIANT trial, C3G/primary IC-MPGN pts presenting with nephrotic range proteinuria demonstrated robust reductions in proteinuria and glomerular C3, eGFR stabilization, and serum albumin normalization, confirming a disease-modifying effect of PEG in this severe subpopulation. PEG was well-tolerated and the safety profile was consistent with previous reports.

title: #1365 NOX2-independent NETosis enriched in oxidized mitochondrial DNA via cGAS/STING pathway as a therapeutic target for inflamed acute kidney injury in chronic granulomatous disease mice
authors: Tetsuya Abe; Yukihiro Wada; Emiko Takeuchi; Masashi Satoh; Takayuki Imanishi; Makoto Otsu; Tadahiro Suenaga; Yasuo Takeuchi
abstract:
Background and Aims
NADPH oxidase (NOX2) is essential for NETosis that is a program to induce neutrophil extracellular trap (NET). Involvement of NETs in inflammatory renal diseases (IRDs) is highlighted. Meanwhile, unusual NETs were determined in chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) that is unable to form the NOX2-dependent NETosis. Hence, two different types of NETosis according to NOX2-dependency were present, but dissimilarity of the two NETosis on IRD remain elusive. In this study, we focus on the two different NETosis and elucidate the influence of unusual NOX2-independent NETosis on inflamed acute kidney injury (AKI) after ischemia reperfusion injury (I/R).
Method
We compared the severity and progression of AKI at 8 and 24 hours after unilateral I/R for 24 minutes between wild type (WT) of C57BL/6 (B6) mice and gp91phox deficient X-linked CGD (X-CGD) mice. At each time after I/R, WT mice (male, 6-week-old, n = 5–15) and X-CGD mice (male, 6-week-old, n = 8–15) were sacrificed. Age matched male B6 mice (n = 3) received sham operation were used as normal control (NC). In vitro, bone marrow (BM) neutrophils derived from WT and X-CGD mice were stimulated with PMA, TLR ligands (zymosan, LPS, and R848), and ribonucleoprotein (RNP)-containing components such as small nuclear RNP antigen (sn-RNP-Ag) and sn-RNP-anti-snRNP antibody immunocomplex (RNP-IC) to induce NETosis. Moreover, X-CGD mice (male, 6-week-old, n = 9–13) were administrated either an inhibitor of cGAS/STING pathway (C-176, S6575, Selleck chemical, 750 nM/body) or vehicle via intraperitoneally 4-hour before I/R to evaluate the effect of its pathway on NOX2-independent NETosis in inflamed AKI.
Results
Compared to NC mice, WT and X-CGD groups showed remarkable tubulointerstitial damages with infiltration of inflammatory cells and elevation of Kim-1 transcripts at each point after I/R. At 8-hour after I/R, degree of AKI and accumulation of intrarenal NETosis demonstrating double positive for Ly6G and citrullinated histone H3 (CitH3) by IF analysis were comparable among the study groups. However, FACS analysis showed significant increase of 7-ADD positive dead neutrophils in damaged kidneys of X-CGD mice than WT mice. At 24-hour after I/R, AKI in WT mice were spontaneously healing, meanwhile X-CGD mice showed significant aggravation of AKI with elevated Kim-1 transcript (p = 0.0068). Compared to WT mice, intrarenal accumulation of NETosis was significantly higher in X-CGD mice (p = 0.0022) with increased mRNA levels for chemokines (CXCL2, CXCL3, CCL2, and CCL3) and chemokine receptors (CXCR2, CCR1, and CCR2). In addition, intrarenal 8-OHdG positivity, reflecting oxidized mitochondrial DNA (ox-mtDNA), was significantly higher in X-CGD mice (p = 0.012) with apparently elevated transcripts for PAD4 and inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, TNFα, and IL-6. In vitro, stimulation with sn-RNP-Ag and RNP-IC apparently increased the sytox green expression and ox-mtDNA positivity by IF analysis in BM neutrophils derived from X-CGD compared to those from WT mice (Fig. 1). In contrast, stimulation with LPS or PMA did not induce apparent NETosis or ox-mtDNA expression in BM neutrophils of X-CGD. Furthermore, in the evaluation of extracellular DNA by measuring sytox intensity and mt-ROS production by FACS using MitoSox dye, NETosis with ox-mtDNA were remarkable in BM neutrophils from X-CGD after stimulation with RNP components rather than TLR-ligands. Regarding the involvement of cGAS/STING pathway on I/R-induced AKI of X-CGD mice, pretreatment with C-176 significantly attenuated AKI at 24 hour (Fig. 2) with suppressing intrarenal accumulation of NETosis, positivity of ox-mtDNA, and mRNA expressions for Kim-1 and PAD4.
Conclusion
Aggravated AKI in X-CGD mice was attributable to accumulation of intrarenal NOX2-independent NETosis enriched in ox-mtDNA which exacerbates inflammation via activated cGAS/STING pathway. In contrast to usual NETosis, unusual NOX2-independent NETosis in X-CGD might complementarily exacerbate inflammation instead of inability to eliminate debris or damaged cells. We suggest that NOX2-independent NETosis could be a therapeutic target for acute active IRD.

title: #56 Development of a multiple biomarker model to predict the tubulointerstitial fibrosis area in patients with primary IgA nephropathy
authors: Jorge González Rodríguez; Elías Jatem Escalante; Jose Manuel Valdivielso; Mercè Borrás Sans; Andrea Muijsenberg Alcalá; Miquel Pinyol Ribas; Elena Ostos; Jacqueline Del Carpio; Alfons Segarra Medrano; Maria Luisa Martín Conde
abstract:
Background and Aims
Previous studies have highlighted the utility of individual urinary biomarkers excretion in the prediction of interstitial fibrosis (IF) in IgAN patients so it has not been possible to compare each of them to know exactly which is the biomarker/combination of biomarkers providing a more accurate estimation of renal IF surface (IFS). Here we have measured the urinary excretion of a set of seven tubular biomarkers in a cohort of patients with primary IgAN and analyzed their utility as non-invasive estimators of the IFS found on the kidney biopsy.
Method
Our study included 247 adults with primary IgA nephropathy diagnosed by kidney biopsy and a control group of 50 healthy volunteers. We measured the urinary excretion of EGF, MCP-1, NGAL, KIM-1, L-FABP, β2-microglobulin and DKK-3 the day the renal biopsy was performed. eGFR was measured by CKD-EPI formula. IFS was quantified using a quantitative morphometric procedure and graded according to Oxford classification. Predictive multivariate models were developed to estimate the IFS.
Results
Patients with primary IgA nephropathy showed significantly higher urinary levels of DKK-3, L-FABP and β2-microglobulin and lower EGF levels than healthy controls. IF was negatively correlated with urinary EGF levels and positively with age, proteinuria, eGFR and urinary DKK-3, L-FABP and β2-microglobulin. The best model to predict IFS accounted for >60% of its variability and included age, eGFR, proteinuria, DKK-3, EGF, L-FABP and β2-microglobulin.
Conclusion
Our study provides a model to estimate the IFS in IgA nephropathy which could be useful to monitor the progression of chronic kidney injury.

title: #494 NPT2b deficiency mitigates tubulointerstitial fibrosis via mitochondrial restoration and suppression of partial epithelial-mesenchymal transition in renal tubular cells
authors: Chi-An Hsieh; Ruo-Jie Liu; Cheng-Hsueh Lin; Sheng-Chu Chou; Shu-Wei Chang; Ya-Chien Yang; Tzu-Ming Jao
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects approximately 13% of the global adult population and often progresses to end-stage renal disease due to the lack of effective treatments. Dysregulated energy metabolism plays a pivotal role in CKD progression, particularly in the high energy-demanding proximal tubular cells. title: #3345 Nefecon provides kidney benefit irrespective of baseline eGFR in patients with IgAN: a subanalysis of the NefIgArd study
authors: Jonathan Barratt; Richard Lafayette; Heather Reich; Jens Kristensen; Russell Jones; Jürgen Floege; Vladimir Tesar; Hernan Trimarchi; Hong Zhang; Brad Rovin
abstract:
Background and Aims
Immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) is a chronic immune complex-mediated kidney disease characterized by galactose-deficient immunoglobulin A1 (Gd-IgA1) deposition in the glomeruli. The Peyer's patches of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue are a major site of Gd-IgA1-producing B cells. Nefecon is an oral targeted-release formulation of budesonide that targets drug release into the distal ileum. Nefecon has been shown to reduce the loss of kidney function in adults with primary IgAN who are at risk of disease progression. Results from the Phase 3 NefIgArd study demonstrated that nefecon 16 mg/day reduced proteinuria and preserved estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) over 9 months of treatment. Proteinuria and eGFR benefit were sustained for up to 15 months of observational follow-up in patients with primary IgAN. Results showed similar treatment effect in those with baseline eGFR <60 or ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m2. Here, we present results from a subanalysis of the NefIgArd study evaluating the efficacy of nefecon 16 mg/day by baseline eGFR deciles, with a focus on the upper and lower eGFR ranges.
Method
NefIgArd study design and endpoints have been previously described. Briefly, eligible patients were aged ≥18 years with biopsy-confirmed primary IgAN, eGFR 35–90 mL/min/1.73 m2 (calculated using the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration formula), proteinuria ≥1 g/24 hours despite optimized renin–angiotensin system (RAS) inhibition, and well-controlled blood pressure. Patients received nefecon 16 mg or placebo daily for 9 months (n = 182 per treatment group) in addition to supportive care (RAS inhibition), followed by a 15-month off-drug observational period on supportive care only. For this subanalysis, patients were divided into eGFR deciles based on the overall population at baseline (defined as the geometric mean of the two most recent measurements before randomization). This subanalysis reports urine protein–creatinine ratio (UPCR) and eGFR results across the subgroups of patients in the upper and lower deciles of kidney function at baseline in the NefIgArd study.
Results
Median eGFR was 55.49 mL/min/1.73 m2 (IQR: 45.93–69.84 mL/min/1.73 m2) in the overall population and was balanced across nefecon and placebo groups. Patients from the full analysis population were divided into groups based on the decile boundaries of baseline eGFR: above and below 38, 43, 47, 51, 55, 60, 66, 72, and 82 mL/min/1.73 m2. In general, UPCR reduction at 9 and 12 months and eGFR benefit at all time points was observed with nefecon relative to placebo (Table 1). UPCR and eGFR benefit with nefecon relative to placebo was also observed in patients within the lower and higher baseline eGFR decile boundaries, specifically at 9, 12, and 24 months (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
This NefIgArd subanalysis demonstrated that the efficacy of a 9-month nefecon treatment course in reduction of proteinuria and preservation of kidney function was independent of baseline eGFR, both at the end of 9 months of treatment and throughout the remaining 15 month off-drug observation period.

title: #1320 Immune phenotyping of checkpoint inhibitor-induced acute interstitial nephritis uncovers distinct profiles associated with clinico-biological features, treatment response and outcome
authors: Idris Boudhabhay; Hélène Lazareth; Julie Oniszczuk; Mathilde Burki; Alaeddine Redissi; Anne Grunenwald; Stéphanie Chhun; Jacques Fourgeaud; Marie-Sophie Meuleman; Marion Rabant; Lubka Roumenina; Pierre Isnard
abstract:
Background and Aims
Checkpoint inhibitor-induced acute interstitial nephritis (ICI-AIN) is the most common histopathological finding in ICI-associated AKI potentially leading to irreversible loss of renal function and impacting therapeutic strategies and responses to the underlying malignancy. Our objective was to characterize the immune infiltrates in kidney biopsies of ICI-AIN patients and explore their association with clinical features, biological markers, and therapeutic outcomes.
Method
We conducted a multicentric retrospective study of 39 patients with biopsy-proven ICI-AIN. Using multiplex immunofluorescence, we quantified key immune cell populations infiltrating the kidneys (macrophages, neutrophils, B cells, T cells and plasma cells). Unsupervised clustering was performed to identify patient subgroups. Baseline characteristics, ICI-AIN events, and outcomes were compared between clusters. Finally, we evaluated the role of the C5a/C5aR1 axis in neutrophil recruitment.
Results
Three distinct immune phenotypes of ICI-AIN were identified based on immune infiltrates. Cluster 1 was characterized by a low level of mononuclear cell infiltration, with significantly fewer macrophages and plasma cells compared to clusters 2 and 3 (p = 0.005 and p = 0.001 for macrophages; p = 0.009 and p = 0.01 for plasma cells). Cluster 2, on the other hand, displayed a high level of mononuclear cell infiltration, primarily driven by significantly elevated T cell numbers compared to clusters 1 and 3 (p = 0.02 for both). Finally, cluster 3 was distinguished by a predominant infiltration of neutrophils, with significantly higher neutrophil counts compared to clusters 1 and 2 (p < 0.001). On standard histological analysis, cluster 3 was distinguished from the other groups by a higher prevalence of granular casts and neutrophilic tubulitis (p < 0.0001 for both).
While baseline characteristics were similar across the three clusters, notable differences emerged in clinical and biological parameters during ICI-AIN events. Cluster 3, the neutrophil-rich group, demonstrated a higher peak CRP levels (127 [30–131] mg/L versus 20 [4–49] mg/L in cluster 1 and 27 [19–63] mg/L in cluster 2; p = 0.01) and an elevated neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (7.2 [5.4–8.6] versus 2.8 [2–3.9] in cluster 1 and 2.3 [1.9–4] in cluster 2; p = 0.0002). Patients in this cluster also experienced worse renal outcomes, with higher peak serum creatinine levels (330 [263–548] µmol/L versus 232 [200–271] µmol/L in cluster 1 and 221 [166–259] µmol/L in cluster 2; p = 0.001) and more pronounced proteinuria (p = 0.02).
Therapeutic outcomes also varied, with renal response rates at 12 months reaching 100% in cluster 2, compared to 68% in cluster 1 and only 34% in cluster 3 (p = 0.01). Furthermore, relapses during corticosteroid tapering were more frequent in cluster 3, affecting 38% of patients, compared to 7% in cluster 1 and none in cluster 2 (p = 0.02).
To better characterize the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of the neutrophil-rich cluster, which morphologically mimics acute pyelonephritis, we performed metagenomic sequencing on kidney biopsies to exclude any infectious agent as a potential cause. Secondly, to better define the molecular mechanisms behind this neutrophilic infiltrate, we performed complement pathways analysis in relation to its known role in neutrophil chemotaxis. We identified elevated urinary levels of C5a in ICI-AIN patients compared with healthy controls (p = 0.03), with a trend towards higher levels in group 3 compared with group 2 (p = 0.06). Importantly, C5a levels correlated with the infiltration of neutrophils expressing C5aR1 in the kidneys of ICI-AIN patients.
Conclusion
We identified distinct ICI-AIN subtypes with varying clinico-biological presentations and outcomes, including a neutrophil-rich cluster associated with complement activation. These findings highlight the importance of immune phenotyping in understanding ICI-AIN pathophysiology and suggest their potential predictive ability for diagnostic and therapeutic strategies to optimize personalized care in ICI-treated patients.

title: #1408 Early-onset lupus nephritis: insights into clinical, laboratory and prognostic characteristics of monogenic forms
authors: Giulia Palazzini; Carmela Errichiello; Marco Allinovi; Andrea Angeletti; Francesca Becherucci; Marta Calatroni; Samuela Landini; Gabriella Luisa Moroni; Francesco Peyronel; Giovanni Rossi; Paola Romagnani; Augusto Vaglio
abstract:
Background and Aims
7%–10% of patients with early-onset systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) underlie a monogenic cause and lupus nephritis (LN) is one of the earliest and more severe complications affecting long-term prognosis. In this study we analyze the clinical, laboratory and prognostic differences between monogenic and non-monogenic LN and the predictors of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD).
Method
In this Italian multicenter retrospective study we enrolled patients with kidney biopsy-proven early-onset LN (biopsy performed ≤18 years old) and analyzed the data at disease onset and last follow-up. Whole exome sequencing was only performed in a fraction of patients. We defined patients with monogenic LN as patients with mutations in genes known to cause monogenic SLE.
Results
We collected data from 84 patients with a median age at diagnosis of LN of 14 years and a median follow-up of 10.6 years. During follow-up more than 50% of patients had at least one renal flare, 12% developed severe adverse effects from immunosuppressive therapy (mainly osteoporosis and cataracts), one patient died for sepsis and 26.2% developed stage 3 or more chronic kidney disease. Thirty patients underwent whole exome sequencing and a monogenic cause was found in 9 patients (30%). Genetic data of these patients are shown in Table 1. Patients with monogenic LN showed, compared to non-monogenic LN, an earlier age of SLE onset (6 vs 14 years) and LN (9 vs 15 years) diagnosis, a more balanced M:F ratio, a more severe renal presentation (eGFR 43 ml/min/1.73 m vs 70 ml/min/1.73 m), a different percentage of ANCA (43 vs 15%), anti-dsDNA (38 vs 76%) and anti-ENA (14 vs 48%) positivity, a higher prevalence of renal thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) at biopsy (40 vs 7%) and a higher probability of ESKD. 56% of patients with monogenic LN reached ESKD (after a median of 5.3 years) compared to 14% of non-monogenic patients (median 7.5 years). The renal survival analysis is shown in Fig. 1. Lower age and a lower eGFR at LN diagnosis, the presence of renal TMA, involvement of the nervous system and monogenic cause were predictors of ESKD at Cox univariate regression model (Table 2).
Conclusion
Early-onset LN is a severe disease, with a substantial risk of ESKD. Monogenic LN is a distinct pathological entity that differs from non-monogenic LN for its severity, renal prognosis, autoantibody profile and histopathology. The genetic study in early-onset LN provides relevant prognostic implications and allows for further knowledge of disease pathogenic mechanisms.

title: #3413 Targeted treatment with pegcetacoplan for adolescents with C3G or primary (idiopathic) IC-MPGN in the VALIANT Phase 3 trial
authors: Antonio Mastrangelo; Marina Vivarelli; Gema Ariceta; Yael Borovitz; Bradley P Dixon; Christoph Licht; Nabil Melhem; Nicole Van De Kar; Dean Wallace; Li Li; Luis Lopez-Lazaro; Carla M Nester
abstract:
Background and Aims
C3 glomerulopathy (C3G) and primary (idiopathic) immune complex membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (IC-MPGN) are rare diseases where uncontrolled C3 activation results in excessive glomerular deposition of C3 breakdown products, which may lead to kidney damage and ultimately kidney failure.
Both C3G and primary IC-MPGN are frequently diagnosed in adolescence or early adulthood. At onset, children with C3G or primary IC-MPGN present with varying degrees of proteinuria (ranging from mild to nephrotic), hematuria (ranging from microscopic to macroscopic), and sometimes low serum C3 levels. Current treatments are associated with significant side effects and approximately 20% of children progress to kidney failure within 10–15 years of diagnosis, despite treatment.
Pegcetacoplan (PEG) binds selectively to C3 and C3b to strongly block C3 activation by classical/lectin/alternative pathways, C3/C5 convertase activity and activation of downstream effectors. PEG targets the pathogenic process in C3G/primary IC-MPGN with the aim of stopping kidney damage.
In the Phase 3 VALIANT study (NCT05067127) in patients (pts) aged ≥12 years with native or post-transplant recurrent C3G/primary IC-MPGN treated with a stable regimen, PEG led to glomerular C3 clearance in 71% of pts and achieved significant and sustained reduction in proteinuria across pt subgroups with stabilization of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Here, we report results for the subgroup of adolescent pts (12–17 years).
Method
VALIANT study design and pt population have been previously described. Pts were randomized 1:1 to receive PEG (subcutaneous infusion twice weekly) or placebo (PBO) for 26 weeks as add-on to their standard of care regimen.
Adolescent pts had a biopsy-proven diagnosis of C3G or primary IC-MPGN with evidence of active renal disease. Active disease was defined by either biopsy at baseline (optional for this subgroup) or, in those not providing a baseline biopsy, at least one of the following: elevated plasma sC5b-9 concentration, low serum C3 concentration, presence of active urine sediment, or presence of C3 nephritic factor.
The primary endpoint was the log-transformed ratio of urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) at Week 26 vs baseline. Key secondary endpoints were proportion of pts achieving a composite renal endpoint (≥50% reduction in UPCR and ≤15% reduction in eGFR at Week 26 vs baseline) and eGFR reduction.
Results
Overall, 124 pts were randomized in VALIANT including 55 adolescent pts (28 PEG, 27 PBO; Table 1).
Among adolescent pts at Week 26, PEG treatment led to a significant and clinically meaningful relative reduction in proteinuria of 74.5% (relative change: −73.6% PEG vs 3.7% PBO, p < 0.0001; Table 1). In the PEG group, 16/28 pts (57.1%) achieved the composite renal endpoint, compared to 1/27 pts (3.7%) in the PBO group (p = 0.0016). Additionally, 20/28 pts (71.4%) in the PEG group achieved a ≥50% reduction in proteinuria at Week 26 from baseline vs 1/27 (3.7%) in the PBO group (p = 0.0002). Improvements in proteinuria were accompanied by stabilization of eGFR, with a +9.7 mL/min/1.73 m² relative difference compared to PBO. Mean change in proteinuria from baseline to Week 26 is shown in the Fig. 1.
Among 6 adolescents with serious treatment-emergent adverse events (PEG, n = 3; PBO, n = 3), 1 event (pyrexia of undetermined origin) was considered PEG-related.
Conclusion
Results from VALIANT demonstrate that PEG, a C3/C3b inhibitor that blocks C3 overactivation, is the only treatment to induce clinically meaningful proteinuria reduction and eGFR stabilization compared with placebo in adolescent pts with C3G or primary IC-MPGN. The treatment was well-tolerated.

title: #288 Pegcetacoplan demonstrates clinically significant responses in C3G and primary (idiopathic) IC-MPGN Patients with or without concomitant immunosuppression in VALIANT
authors: David Kavanagh; Andrew S Bomback; Gema Ariceta; Antonio Mastrangelo; Carla M Nester; Giuseppe Remuzzi; Marina Vivarelli; Zhongshen Wang; Johan Szamosi; Dima Decker; Lucia Quintana Gallardo; Fadi Fakhouri
abstract:
Background and Aims
C3 glomerulopathy (C3G) and primary (idiopathic) immune complex membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (IC-MPGN) are rare diseases where uncontrolled C3 activation results in excessive glomerular deposition of C3 breakdown products, which may lead to kidney damage and ultimately kidney failure. These treatments are associated with adverse effects and lack robust clinical evidence of efficacy. As a result, up to 50% of patients progress to kidney failure within 10 years.

Participants were permitted to continue pre-existing MMF, glucocorticoids (maximum dose 20 mg prednisone daily or equivalent) and other immunosuppressive therapies, provided that the doses of these, as well as other drugs impacting proteinuria, remained stable throughout the randomized controlled period and preceding 12-week screening period.
The aim of this analysis was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of PEG versus PBO in VALIANT patients with and without concomitant immunosuppressants (IS) (IS-treated vs non-IS treated).
Method
VALIANT study participants were randomized 1:1 to receive PEG (subcutaneous infusion twice weekly) or PBO for 26 weeks as add-on to their stable treatment regimen. The primary endpoint was the log-transformed ratio of urine protein-to-creatinine ratio at Week 26 vs baseline. Key secondary endpoints included the proportion of pts achieving a reduction in C3c staining on kidney biopsy and change in eGFR from baseline for PEG vs PBO.

Overall, 124 pts were randomized (63 PEG, 61 PBO). At baseline, 48 (76%) PEG and 42 (69%) PBO participants received concomitant IS (Table 1). Baseline characteristics of these 90 pts did not differ from those not receiving concomitant IS.

In this pre-specified analysis, C3G/primary IC-MPGN pts receiving stable concomitant IS achieved robust proteinuria reduction, glomerular C3 reduction, and eGFR stabilization with PEG treatment, with outcomes similar to pts without concomitant IS treatment. title: #1596 Stopping eculizumab treatment safely in atypical HUS: a multicentre, open-label, prospective, single-arm trial of the safety and impact of eculizumab withdrawal
authors: Neil Sheerin; Sally Johnson; Michal Malina; Emma Montgomery; Edwin Wong; Andy Bryant; Thomas Chadwick; Luke Vale; Sarah Dunn; Ciara Kennedy; Giovany Orozco Leal; David Kavanagh
abstract:
Background and Aims
Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (aHUS) is a rare disease which without treatment is associated with high morbidity and mortality. Eculizumab, a monoclonal complement inhibitor, is an effective treatment but the optimal way to use this high-cost medication has not been determined. The SETS aHUS trial aimed to establish the safety of eculizumab withdrawal and the effectiveness of a monitoring protocol to detect disease relapse and safe reintroduction of treatment if disease relapse occurs.
Method
The SETS aHUS multicentre, open label, prospective, single arm trial enrolled participants from 15 UK hospitals with embedded qualitative and health economic analyses. Patients over two years of age with aHUS who were receiving eculizumab therapy for at least six months were eligible to withdraw from treatment, replacing it with monitoring to assess disease activity with re-introduction of treatment if relapse occurred. The primary outcome measure was harm to a participant as a consequence of eculizumab withdrawal during the 2-year trial period. Participants met a primary outcome if there was a permanent reduction in estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR), requirement for kidney replacement therapy or significant extra-renal manifestation of disease. The Bayes factor single arm binary model was used to monitor and analyse the trial data, applying pre-trial stopping rules. The trial is registered with the European Union Drug Regulating Authority (EudraCT 2017-003916-37).
Results
One of 28 participants (3.6%) who withdrew from treatment met a primary outcome. Four participants relapsed, all of whom had pathogenic genetic variants in complement proteins. Only participants with an identified cause of complement dysregulation relapsed. It was possible, by monitoring and rapid participant access, to successfully reintroduce eculizumab treatment. Based on the pre-trial analysis plan, withdrawal from treatment is not associated with a greater risk to patients compared to remaining on treatment. Most patients welcomed the opportunity to withdraw from treatment but identified concerns about monitoring and the risk of relapse, informed by initial experience at presentation. Withdrawing a patient from treatment saves £4.2 million in health care costs.
Conclusion
Withdrawal of eculizumab treatment with monitoring of disease activity was not associated with an increased risk of harm compared to continuation of eculizumab. The presence of an identifiable cause of complement dysregulation predicts a higher risk of relapse. This study adds to the growing evidence for time limited periods of anti-complement therapy in patients with aHUS.
