title: #2559 High-resolution nanoliquid chromatography-mass spectrometry of circulating IgA1 glycosylation provides novel insight in the pathogenesis of IgA nephropathy
authors: Anastasia Tzasta; Tomas Post; Anna Wasynczuk; Steinar Gijze; Ilse Rood; Elmar Pieterse; Alain van Gool; Jonathan Barratt; Nils Rother; Joannes Jacobs; Manfred Wuhrer; Raphaël Duivenvoorden
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is a progressive kidney disease that can eventually lead to renal failure. Although the exact pathogenesis of IgA nephropathy is not yet fully understood, it is believed that abnormal O-glycosylation of the IgA1 HYT peptide in the hinge region, also known as galactose-deficient IgA1 (gd-IgA1), is a prerequisite for the development of the disease. Gd-IgA1 is considered Hit 1 in the “multi-hit” hypothesis of IgAN pathogenesis. However, limited information is available regarding glycosylation of immunoglobulins in IgAN patients. Here we present the first high-resolution molecular characterization of protein-specific O- and N-glycosylation of circulating immunoglobulins in IgAN patients compared to age- and kidney function-matched controls.
Method
We used nanoliquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) for the glycopeptide analysis of circulating IgA and IgG of 41 IgAN patients that were not treated with corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants, and 41 age- and eGFR-matched controls. Gd-IgA1 was measured in plasma with the monoclonal KM-55 antibody using a commercially available ELISA assay (MBS109533). Comparisons between IgAN patients and controls were made using Student's t-tests and were corrected for multiple testing using FDR correction. Correlations were assessed using a linear regression model with age and sex included as covariates.
Results
The average age of IgAN patients and controls was 39 (SD 15) and 40 (SD 15) years, respectively, with an eGFR of 60 (SD 27) and 61 (SD 29) ml/min/1.73 m². Using LC-MS analysis, we identified 92 O- and N-glycopeptides derived from different peptide backbones and quantified 30 glycosylation traits (Fig. 1A). Focusing on the IgA1 hinge-region O-glycopeptide (HYT), we found that the galactose content on this peptide was lower in IgAN patients compared to controls (Fig. 1B). Interestingly, the LC-MS measured galactose content of 40 (98%) IgAN patients fell within the range observed in controls. ELISA-measured gd-IgA1 levels were, on average, higher in IgAN patients than in controls, with 33 (80%) IgAN patients having values within the control range (Fig. 1C). ELISA-measured gd-IgA1 correlated with LC-MS measured terminal GalNAc content on the IgA1 HYT peptide (Fig. 1D), while there was no correlation with LC-MS measured terminal galactose on the HYT peptide (Fig. 1E), indicating that terminal GalNAc on the IgA1 HYT peptide is the epitope for the ELISA-measured gd-IgA1 (Fig. 1F). Interestingly, two specific glycopeptides, HYT_H3N6S1 and HYT_H5N5S4, and their ratio, were significantly correlated with the level of circulating gd-IgA1, with HYT_H3N6S1 being increased and HYT_H5N5S4 being reduced in IgAN patients (Fig. 1G–I). These two glycopeptides and their ratio also significantly correlated with ELISA-measured gd-IgA1 levels (Fig. 1J–L).
Conclusion
Our high-resolution LC-MS data show that, on average, IgAN patients have more terminal GalNAc on the IgA1 HYT peptide compared to age- and kidney function-matched controls. This allowed us to identify HYT-specific traits that strongly associated with IgAN. We confirm that terminal GalNAc on the IgA1 HYT peptide is the epitope for the ELISA-measured gd-IgA1. Interestingly, the level of terminal GalNAc on the IgA1 HYT peptide for most IgAN patients falls within the range observed in their age- and kidney function-matched controls, suggesting that for most patients it could be considered a naturally occurring epitope rather than the result of aberrant glycosylation. The next step is to further analyse our LC-MS O- and N-glycosylation data of IgA1, IgA2 and IgG in this patient population. In this regard we have already identified specific glycosylation features associated with kidney function for both patients and controls. Furthermore, we aim to relate these features to longitudinal follow-up of renal endpoints.

title: #1835 Glomerulonephritis-induced changes in epithelial lipid composition reveal a signature of prominent proximal tubules metabolic switch
authors: Lucia Martin Saiz; Charlotte Sierra; Léa Resmini; Ibai Calvo; Marion Rabant; Alexandre Karras; Olivia Lenoir; Olatz Fresnedo; Jose Andres Fernandez; Pierre-Louis Tharaux
abstract:
Background and Aims
Glomerulonephritis (GN) is characterized by inflammation of the glomeruli, leading to impaired kidney function and, in some cases, chronic kidney disease (CKD). This process can result in global fibrosis beyond the site of initial glomerular injury.
Peroxisome proliferator-activator receptor γ (PPARγ), a nuclear receptor involved in lipid and glucose metabolism, has been implicated in modulating the inflammatory response in renal fibrosis and has been suggested as a potential therapeutic target for this condition. Dysregulation of lipid metabolism has been associated with inflammation and fibrotic processes in the kidney. Thus, a better understanding of the specific lipidome changes associated with renal fibrosis and CKD could provide relevant information to tackle this pathology best.
Method
Here, we present an in-depth renal lipidome study assessed mainly by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-image mass spectrometry (MALDI-IMS) of control and GN mice. We used the nephrotoxic serum (NTS)-induced crescentic GN as a transition model from glomerular insult to CKD progression and mainly focused on tubular epithelial cells (TECs) lipidome.
GN was induced on male mice with C57BL6/J background by retroorbital injection of sheep anti-mouse GBM NTS. Mice were euthanized at day 21 post-injection, at the stage of CKD progression, and snapped frozen kidney sections of 15 μm thickness were prepared in a cryostat. MALDI-IMS analyses were performed at 10 µm of spatial resolution using a MALDI-LTQ-Orbitrap XL.
Renal biopsy specimens for MALDI-IMS analysis after the completion of diagnostic workup were obtained from patients diagnosed with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis and GN or normal kidneys. They were used after informed consent and approval from and following the guidelines of the local ethics committee (IRB00003888, FWA00005831).
Lipid assignment was based on comparing the experimental m/z and the species in the software's LIPID MAPS database. After MALDI-IMS, immunofluorescent staining of the different tubular segments was performed over the same tissue section to correlate each structure with its lipid fingerprint. Additionally, key enzymes involved in lipid metabolism were assessed by RT-qPCR for the two study groups.
Results
Sixteen lipid families were identified by MALDI-IMS, accounting for 167 different lipid species in all the samples. The control and GN kidneys confirmed up to eight different lipid fingerprints. GN condition was associated with increased phosphatidylcholine (PC) and ether/vinyl ether phosphatidylethanolamine (PE-O/P) levels and decreased HexCer and PS species. These results were consistent with the modification in some enzyme expressions involved in phospholipid biosynthesis.
We also observed a marked loss of PPARγ expression in epithelial cells in GN samples, especially highlighted in proximal tubules. Some features point to the proximal tubules as the most affected kidney region in GN: A higher number of modified individual lipid species were accounted for in proximal tubules. This region had a positive correlation between the increase in PC/PE ratio and the urea and creatinine sera levels. In agreement with these results, similar profiles were observed in proximal tubules of ANCA GN kidney biopsies. A higher concentration of carnitine, a biomarker of proximal tubule injury, was found in the urine of GN mice.
Conclusion
MALDI-IMS characterized the lipid composition of different kidney regions and identified GN-CKD-related changes. Modification in the expression of enzymes involved in lipid biosynthesis is consistent with some of the changes in lipid composition observed in GN. Our results identify a lipidomic signature of GN-induced CKD progression in the proximal tubule, including loss of PPARγ.

title: #1026 Persistent isolated low C3 (PILC3) predicts long-term eGFR decline in lupus nephritis: a linear projection of total eGFR slopes from BLISS-LN trial data
authors: Paride Fenaroli; Michelangelo Tesi; Francesco Peyronel; Lucio Manenti
abstract:
Background and Aims
The dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, hallmarked by isolated reduction of the serum C3 fraction, has been recently recognized as an additional feature of lupus nephritis pathogenesis. Moreover, PILC3 (i.e., persistent isolated low C3, that is not accompanied by C4 hypocomplementemia, 6 months after treatment) is associated with a higher risk of ESKD in these patients.
Methods
We conducted a secondary analysis on 425 patients included in the BLISS-LN trial. The total eGFR slope (weeks 0–104) was derived using a linear mixed-effects model consisting of time of visit (weeks), PILC3 status, and treatment group (belimumab vs placebo). PILC3 status and treatment were considered as fixed effects, including their interaction with time, whereas patients were considered as random effects.
Results
Of the 446 patients included in the BLISS-LN trial, only 425 had sufficient data for the definition of PILC3 and were therefore considered for the analysis. Of those, 102 (24%) were identified as PILC3. Table 1 shows the annual rate of eGFR decline, which appears to be steeper in PILC3 patients, despite having a higher eGFR at baseline, and in the belimumab-treated group. When considering the trial period (i.e., 2 years), PILC3 does not add any significant difference to eGFR decline (p = 0.517), whereas belimumab provides a 5.12 ml/min/1.73 m2 per year gain (difference vs placebo 0.62 ml/min/1.73 m2 per year; p < 0.001). However, a long-term linear projection of the total eGFR slopes shows that PILC3 patients reach ESKD (i.e., eGFR = 10 ml/min/1.73 m2) at least 15 years before patients who cannot be categorized as PILC3 (Fig. 1).
Conclusions
The results of our post-hoc analysis confirm the efficacy of belimumab in the treatment of lupus nephritis. Even if not significant in the short term, PILC3 seems to predict long-term kidney disease progression. The linear projection of total eGFR slopes provides an intriguing perspective on the role of chronic overactivation of the alternative pathway of the complement system in lupus nephritis.

title: #541 Single urinary extracellular vesicle proteome analysis reveals CD35 as novel biomarkers of sepsis-associated acute kidney injury
authors: Ning Li; Lin-Li Lv
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SA-AKI) is strongly associated with unacceptable morbidity and mortality, while early identification of patients at risk of AKI is still challenge. Urinary extracellular vesicles (uEVs) are increasingly recognized as mirror of the pathophysiological status for urogenital system disease. However, uEVs are derived from various cell types and organs, with unrelated uEV subpopulations potentially confounding the identification of disease-specific uEV subclusters. This can significantly impair the diagnostic specificity and sensitivity. Therefore, the precise identification of key disease-associated uEV subclusters is crucial for enabling non-invasive pathological assessment of cellular stress and injury. Recent developments in single-vesicle analysis have facilitated the process of searching biomarkers from those heterogeneous populations of EVs. This study aims to utilize proteomic analysis of single uEVs to identify novel biomarkers for SA-AKI patients, providing valuable insights for the non-invasive early diagnosis and prognostic assessment of SA-AKI.
Method
We employed a proximity-dependent barcoding assay (PBA) to profile the surface proteins of individual uEVs using antibody-DNA conjugates and next-generation sequencing. This study was conducted in a screening cohort of SA-patients, with or without AKI (n = 8 per group). The data were subjected to PCA for dimensionality reduction, followed by K-Nearest Neighbors clustering. The candidate single uEV biomarker was identified and subsequently validated in 2 independent multicenter cohorts: a sepsis-associated AKI cohort (SA-AKI cohort, n = 134, comprising septic patients with or without AKI) and a prospective cohort of subclinical AKI (S-AKI cohort, n = 72). To elucidate the origin of the candidate biomarkers, single-cell transcriptomics and spatial transcriptomics were also integrated.
Results
PBA analysis of individual vesicles identified thirty-two distinct subclusters of uEVs originating from tubular epithelial cells, lysosomes, complement receptors, endothelial cells, and other sources which displayed remarkable different distribution in SA-AKI compared to SA patients. Notably, the cluster expressing CD35 was significantly diminished in patients with SA-AKI and demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy for SA-AKI (AUC: 0.98). In the validation SA-AKI cohort, CD35 expression on single uEVs (sCD35-uEV) was significantly reduced in SA-AKI compared to SA patients. Impressively, sCD35-uEV levels correlated with the stage and duration of AKI. During follow-up, sCD35-uEV levels predicted mortality (AUC: 0.70) and the development of subsequent acute kidney disease (AKI lasting for seven days) (AUC: 0.66). In the S-AKI cohort, sCD35-uEV levels at 24 h after onset of SA significantly decreased in patients who later developed AKI compared to those who did not (p < 0.001, AUC: 0.84), the predictive capacity outperformed traditional AKI markers TIMP2*IGFBP7 (AUC: 0.75). By integrating single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, we established that the reduction in sCD35-uEV levels was attributable to decreased CD35 expression in injured podocytes during SA-AKI. In SA-AKI, podocytes exhibit a state of injury and dedifferentiation, suggesting that sCD35-uEV may serve as a non-invasive liquid biopsy biomarker for podocyte injury.
Conclusion
Through single-EV proteomic profiling of uEVs, we revealed the vast heterogeneity of uEV populations and identified uEVs secreted by various intrinsic cells, immune cells, and other cell types. Among these, we highlighted CD35 at single uEV as a promising biomarker of SA-AKI, with prominent accuracy for risk stratification, early diagnosis as well as prognostic assessment. Integrated -omic analysis revealed that reduced level of sCD35-uEV represents a non-invasive indicator of podocyte injury, suggesting a critical renal histological damage of SA-AKI which may explain the dissociation of renal tubule necrosis from renal dysfunction in the traditional concept.

title: #2029 The incidence and prevalence of IgAN from 2002–2023 in Denmark
authors: Ina Ystrøm; Simon Kok Jensen; Ina Trolle Andersen; Per Ivarsen; Christian Fynbo Christiansen
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA Nephropathy (IgAN) is the most frequent form of primary glomerulonephritis. The clinical presentation and course of disease is very heterogeneous but accompanied by a significant risk of progression to end-stage kidney failure. Supportive care aiming at decreasing proteinuria is the cornerstone of treatment. Estimates of incidence and prevalence of IgAN show large geographical and ethnic variations across worldwide. In Denmark data on the IgAN occurrence is limited. This study elucidates the current landscape of IgAN by examining the incidence, prevalence, treatment modalities, and prognosis in Denmark during the last twenty-two years.
Method
This population-based cohort study included all adult patients with a first pathology-verified diagnosis of IgAN in Denmark between 2002–2023. The study utilized Danish health registries and medical databases. SNOMED-codes from kidney biopsies registered in the Danish Pathology Register were used to define the study population. Comorbidity at the time of diagnosis was based on hospital diagnoses up to 10 years before the time of diagnosis derived from the Danish National Patient Registry. The use of medical therapy was assessed at the time of diagnosis and during follow-up. For a subset of the population laboratory values were available depending on the coverage in the registries, with more patients covered in the recent years of the study period.
Incidence and prevalence of IgAN were computed as crude and as age- and sex-standardized to the Danish population at the beginning of the study period. To further describe changes over time, the study period and time of diagnosis were divided into three time-periods. Cumulative incidence of end stage kidney disease was computed treating death as competing risk.
Results
The study population included 1,298 incident adult patients with the diagnosis of IgAN. The median age at the time of diagnosis was 42.7 years and the median follow-up time was 6.0 years (IQR 2.6–10.9). At the time of diagnosis 37% had hypertension, 36% had cardiovascular disease and 54% of the population had filled a prescription for a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor (RASi) within a one-year period before diagnosis. For patients with available laboratory values the median estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 (IQR 40.0–85.0) at time of diagnosis (75% of the cohort included). For patients with available urine albumin/creatinine ratio (UACR) 59% had a UACR above 1g/g (50% of the cohort included).
The crude annual incidence of IgAN was 13.3 (95% CI 9.8–16.5) per 1,000,000 and did not change significantly upon standardization (Fig. 1a). The annual incidence increased during the study period, which was also reflected in the prevalence which reached an annual prevalence of 213 per 1,000,000 (95% CI 200–266) in the latest time-period (Fig. 1b). There was a tendency towards an increased use of RASi and a decreased use of corticosteroids during the study period.
The 5-year and the 10-year risk of end stage kidney disease was 21.6% (95% CI 19.2–24.2) (Fig. 2) and 33.1% (95% CI 29.9–36.4) respectively with no significant changes during the study period. The 5-year and the 10-year all-cause mortality was 9.5% (95% CI 7.8–11.3) and 16.4% (95% CI 13.9–19.1) respectively.
Conclusion
The annual incidence of IgAN in Denmark was higher than the pooled incidence known for Europe and was increasing during the study period. At the time of biopsy Danish patients had preserved kidney function and significant albuminuria. The course of disease, however, was very variable with one third of patients progressing to ESKD within 10 years of diagnosis. Overall, the prognosis for Danish IgAN patients remained unchanged over the last two decades with the effect of improved treatment yet to be anticipated.

This study is financially supported by CSL Vifor, Nordics.

title: #2883 Kidney outcomes and effects of proteinuria in Alport syndrome: a longitudinal analysis of 1175 patients from the UK National Registry of Rare Kidney Diseases (RaDaR)
authors: Katie Wong; David Pitcher; Dane Rogers; Sascha van Boemmel-Wegmann; Klaus Francke; Julie Lin; Shiguang Liu; Susie Gear; Alex Mercer; Bruce Hendry; A Neil Turner; Daniel P Gale
abstract:
Background and Aims
Alport syndrome (AS) is often characterised by pathogenic variants in type IV collagen genes COL4A3/4/5. Previous genotype-phenotype studies have shown patients with certain genotypes reach kidney failure (KF) at a younger age. However, more detailed understanding of the trajectory of eGFR decline for AS patients, and whether this differs by genetic or clinical factors such as genotype or proteinuria control is lacking. Here, we examine KF and eGFR slope and describe associations between proteinuria and kidney outcomes in a large cohort of AS patients, using data from the UK National Registry of Rare Kidney Diseases (RaDaR).
Method
RaDaR has data linkage with the UK Renal Registry for Kidney Replacement Therapy initiation data, renal units for laboratory results and regional genetics hubs for clinical genetic reports. For analyses relating to mutation type, patients with variants reported by accredited clinical labs as “Pathogenic” or “Likely Pathogenic” by American College of Medical Genetics criteria were included. eGFR slope was estimated for each CKD stage using multi-level linear models to account for individual patient trajectories, and included a covariate to test for differences between mutation types categorised as “Classical” (Male X-linked AS, Digenic and COL4A3/4 homozygous/2x mutations) vs. “Heterozygous” (Female X-linked AS, COL4A3/4 heterozygous) genotypes. Proteinuria progression was investigated by modelling each patient's uPCR by age using linear mixed models, stratified by genotype. Kaplan Meier analysis was used to estimate time from eGFR 90/60/45 mL/min/1.73 m2 to KF or death and compared using logrank statistics. Results were stratified by proteinuria level in the year prior to eGFR 90/60/45 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Results
The cohort comprised 1175 patients, 584 (50%) female. Clinical genetic reports were available for 535/1175 (46%) patients, of whom 459 (86%) had Pathogenic or Likely Pathogenic variants identified, 198 classical (n = 45 COL4A3/4 homozygous/2x mutations, n = 151 Male X-linked AS, n = 2 Digenic), and 261 heterozygous genotypes (n = 116 Female X-linked AS, n = 145 COL4A3/4 heterozygotes).
Overall, median uPCR increased until CKD stage 5: Stage 1: 84.7 mg/mmol (IQR 25.0–231.4), 2: 132.5 (37.0–298.0), 3a: 132 (41.0–301.0), 3b: 187.3 (69.0–385.0), 4: 237.9 (121.9–426.5) and 5: 211.1 (118.8–336.4), however results from the linear mixed model, stratifying by genetic mutation type demonstrated that only patients with autosomal recessive (p = 0.005) and Male X-linked (p < 0.0005) disease experienced a significant progressive increase in proteinuria. Median uPCR in the year prior to reaching eGFR 90/60/45 ml/min/1.73 m2 was 158, 254 and 268 mg/mmol respectively. Compared to those with below median uPCR, patients with above median proteinuria had significantly worse kidney survival with hazard ratios of 5.3 (95% CI 1.5–19.0, p = 0.0097), 3.6 (95% CI 1.5–8.7, p = 0.0048) and 6.5 (95% CI 3.0–13.9, p < 0.0001) from eGFR thresholds of 90, 60 and 45 ml/min/1.73 m2 respectively (Fig. 1).
Patients with classical genotypes had higher annual eGFR loss during each CKD stage compared to those with heterozygous genotypes (Fig. 2), most markedly in CKD stage 4 (Classical vs Heterozygous genotypes: −9.1(95% CI −10.9 to −7.3) vs −3.8 ml/min/1.73 m2/year (−5.5 to −2.1)). For patients with heterozygous genotypes, mean eGFR loss was similar throughout CKD stages 1, 2 and 3a at −0.9 ml/min/1.73 m2/year, increasing in later CKD stages.
Conclusion
These analyses demonstrate differences in eGFR trajectory by genotype in AS: compared with those with heterozygous genotypes, patients with classical genotypes exhibited rising proteinuria levels early in disease and had faster eGFR loss throughout their clinical course. eGFR loss accelerated in both groups on reaching CKD stage 4 and lower proteinuria levels were strongly associated with better renal outcomes at all eGFR thresholds. These findings could inform design and interpretation of clinical trials in AS.

title: #3256 Quality, power and fragility of randomised controlled trials in ANCA-associated vasculitis
authors: Vanja Ivkovic; Annette Bruchfeld; Lauren Floyd; Andreas Kronbichler; Jae Il Shin
abstract:
Background and Aims
Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) make up the backbone of high-grade clinical evidence. A number of recent RCTs have been published, changing the landscape of therapy in ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV). However, not all RCTs are of high quality and they can be underpowered to detect the outcomes which might translate to sub-optimal therapeutic strategies. Using three key metrics—quality, statistical power and fragility (reversal of trial findings if the outcome of a small number of patients is changed)—we evaluated the robustness of all RCTs in AAV.
Method
We have searched PubMed for RCTs published from beginning of indexation to May 2024 on granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis RCT quality was assessed using modified Jadad 8-point scale which takes into account randomization, blinding, inclusion and exclusion criteria, withdrawal/drop-outs, adverse effects and statistical analysis. It stratified RCTs according to score (mJS) to poor (3 points or less), moderate (4 or 5 points) and high quality (6 to 8 points). RCTs were further assessed for reporting of statistical sample size calculation or power analysis. Lastly, fragility index (FI) was calculated representing the number of patients switched from event to non-event needed to change the RCT result from statistically significant to non-significant. Conversely, for studies reporting a non-significant result, reverse FI was calculated. This represents the number of patients needed to be switched from a non-event to an event to shift the results towards statistical significance. For example, if the FI is 3 then this means that if 3 or more patients did not experience trial outcome, the results would no longer be significant.
Results
A PubMed search resulted in 572 hits which were filtered through several rounds to include only original (main) RCTs of which 56 were found. The RCTs enrolled 5,336 patients (45.26% women, mean age 57 ± 7 years). The median sample size was 69 patients (IQR 43 to 121 patients, min-max: 17 to 704 patients), with a median of 33 events (IQR 20 to 72 events, min–max: 4 to 235 events). RCTs had a mean mJS of 5.7 ± 1.4 (min-max 3 to 8). Three (5%) RCTs were of poor quality, 17 (30%) had moderate quality, while 35 (63%) were of high quality. RCT quality increased over time (B = 0.08, p < 0.001, Fig. 1). Quality was also associated with larger RCT size (B = 0.004, p = 0.039, Fig. 2).
A total of 36 (64%) RCTs reported sample size or power calculation with 35 of these providing details on calculation. Twenty RCTs (56%) reporting sample size or power analysis did not enroll a sufficient number of patients.
FI was calculated for 12 RCTs while reverse FI was calculated for 33 RCTs. RCTs had a mean FI of 4.0 ± 3.3 (min-max: 0 to 10). A total of 5 (42%) RCTs had number of patients lost to follow-up, withdrawn or dropped out higher than the FI. Median reverse FI was 5.0 (IQR: 2.8 to 6.0, min-max: 0 to 15). A total of 15 (45%) of RCTs had number of patients lost to follow-up, withdrawn or dropped out higher than the reverse FI. Mean FI and reverse FI of RCTs published in the last 10 years (2015 or later) were 5 and 6.7, respectively. Reverse FI was associated with RCT size (B = 0.02, p < 0.001, Fig. 3) and quality (B = 1.1, p = 0.01, Fig. 4). There was no temporal trend of FI or reverse FI (both p > 0.05).
Conclusion
The quality of RCTs in AAV is rising, but they are frequently underpowered and highly fragile. On average, shifting 4 or 5 patients from event to non-event or vice versa, which is frequently less than the number of patients lost to follow-up, is enough to change the whole outcome of the trial which shows that results from these trials should be interpreted with caution.

title: #2708 Baseline C3 levels improves the predictive capacity of ANCA kidney risk score in patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis

This study included 169 patients from 3 tertiary referral hospitals diagnosed with AAV with a histological confirmation and measured serum C3 levels at diagnosis. Baseline data and outcomes were compared and multivariate logistic regression analysis was applied to assess the risk of renal failure for each group. Cox regression analysis was performed to evaluate the impact of C3 at diagnosis on ESKD risk.

title: #2626 Effect of iptacopan discontinuation on proteinuria and complement biomarkers in patients with immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN): a post hoc analysis from a Phase II trial
authors: Jonathan Barratt; Dana Rizk; Hong Zhang; Bart Maes; Naoki Kashihara; Brad Rovin; Hernan Trimarchi; Dmitrij Kollins; Manasi Desai; Olympia Papachristofi; Evanthia Koukouli; Vlado Perkovic
abstract:
Background and Aims
Studies have shown involvement of the alternative complement pathway (AP) in glomerular inflammation and tubulointerstitial damage in IgAN. AP inhibition with iptacopan, a potent oral complement factor B inhibitor, demonstrated a significant reduction in proteinuria, leading to its accelerated approval by the US FDA. The effect of iptacopan discontinuation on relevant IgAN characteristics are of clinical interest. Herein, we report proteinuria and AP biomarker data from a Phase II (PhII) study that included an observational period after iptacopan discontinuation, and preliminary data from the ongoing open-label extension study (OLE; NCT04557462), in which iptacopan was reinitiated.
Method
The PhII randomized, double-blind, placebo (pbo)-controlled study recruited adults with confirmed IgAN and urine protein–creatinine ratio (UPCR) ≥0.8 g/g or urine protein ≥0.75 g/day on stable renin–angiotensin system inhibitors to receive pbo or iptacopan (10, 50, 100 [in Part 2 only] or 200 mg twice daily [bid]) for 90 days in Part 1 or 180 days in Part 2 (Fig. 1). After stopping iptacopan treatment in either part, patients (pts) were followed for a 90-day off-iptacopan phase. Eligible pts could restart iptacopan 200 mg bid in the OLE (time from PhII study end [EoS] to OLE start varied). In this post hoc analysis, data were pooled in the iptacopan dose arms >10 mg bid (which showed effective AP inhibition) to compare the change from baseline (BL) in proteinuria between the on- and off-iptacopan phases. Data from the approved iptacopan dose 200 mg bid arms were also pooled from both parts. OLE data were pooled in all analyses up to Month (M) 12 (cut-off date: 15 August 2023). Mixed models for repeated measures were used to assess UPCR (from first morning void) during the PhII study and OLE. Descriptive analyses were conducted for AP biomarkers (urine soluble C5b-9 [sC5b-9], serum Wieslab and plasma Bb) in pts who received iptacopan 200 mg bid during the PhII study; AP biomarker data were not collected in the OLE. The PhII BL was considered the BL for all analyses.
Results
PhII data were used from 67 pts (Part 1: n = 23; Part 2: n = 44), 40 of which joined the OLE. In the pooled PhII study cohorts, the relative reduction in UPCR (95% CI) from BL in Part 1 was 30.0% (13.5, 43.4%) at Day (D) 90 (Fig. 2A) and in Part 2 was 35.4% (17.5, 49.5%) at D180 (Fig. 2B). In pts from Part 1 who had a shorter duration of iptacopan treatment relative to pts in Part 2, UPCR returned to BL levels within 30 days of iptacopan discontinuation (Fig. 2A). In pts from Part 2, UPCR remained below BL 30 days after iptacopan discontinuation but was higher compared with the end of treatment (EoT) visit (Fig. 2B). Upon iptacopan reinitiation in the OLE, UPCR decreased again for pts entering from Parts 1 and 2 (Fig. 2A and B). Similar trends were seen in the iptacopan 200 mg bid arms (n = 26); there was a relative reduction in UPCR (95% CI) of 27.0% (10.8, 40.3%) at D90 and 23.2% (−0.8, 41.5%) at EoT (D180). In the first off-iptacopan visit, UPCR increased to near PhII BL values, before decreasing after treatment reinitiation in the OLE.
Iptacopan 200 mg bid inhibited the AP in pts pooled from both parts of the PhII trial (n = 26), as shown by a decrease in AP biomarkers (median [interquartile range (IQR)] reduction from BL to D90 in urinary sC5b-9: 97.2% [89.3, 98.4%]; serum Wieslab: 81.4% [72.9, 92.5%]; plasma Bb: 24.5% [13.6, 40.6%]). AP biomarkers increased at the first off-iptacopan visit, with a median (IQR) increase from BL of 18.3% (−77.8, 168.8%) for urinary sC5b-9 and 3.3% (−12.7, 11.2%) for plasma Bb, and a serum Wieslab reduction from BL of only 10.3% (0, 19.7%).
Conclusion
The data indicate that iptacopan discontinuation leads to quick reactivation of systemic and renal complement to near BL levels. Renal complement reactivation is associated with an increase in proteinuria. Notably, proteinuria decreased again after reinitiation of iptacopan, indicating continued sensitivity to complement inhibition. Limitations of this analysis include the short duration of PhII treatment, low pt numbers, and varying duration and lack of knowledge of other treatments or disease progression between the PhII EoS and the OLE.

title: #940 Effectiveness and remission predictors of obinutuzumab in primary membranous nephropathy
authors: Zhenbin Jiang; Song Wang; Yue Wang; Danxia Zheng
abstract:
Background and Aims
Obinutuzumab is a more humanized and more potent efficacy in basic research, and it has a different epitope anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody compared with rituximab. We conducted an exploration to investigate its effectiveness in primary membranous nephropathy (PMN) and present the results here.
Method
A total of 66 PMN patients who received obinutuzumab from March 2022 to December 2023 were retrospectively enrolled. The patients had an age of 50 ± 13 years, among whom 48 were male (72.7%). They were grouped into the clinical remission group and the non-clinical remission group. Data was expressed by median (25%, 75%) or mean ± SD.
Results
One month after the first administration of obinutuzumab, the anti-phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) antibody decreased by 84.7% (64.9%, 94.0%), urinary protein decreased by 37.4% (7.3%, 57.9%), and serum albumin increased by 13.8% (8.1%, 22.5%) (all P < 0.05) (Fig. 1A). The anti-PLA2R antibody and urinary protein continued to decrease, and serum albumin continued to increase (all P < 0.001 from the second month, not shown in Fig. 1A). During the follow-up period (with an average of 15.1 ± 6.5 months), 58 cases (87.9%) achieved clinical remission, among which 29 cases (43.9%) achieved complete remission (CR). The median time to the first (recorded) response was 4 (2, 7) months for partial remission (PR) and 11 (8, 15) months for CR (Fig. 1B). After the first administration of obinutuzumab, the serum anti-PLA2R antibody and proteinuria decreased significantly and maintained a downward trend. The serum albumin level increased significantly and continued to rise to the normal level, and the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) remained stable (Fig. 1 C–F). The decrease rate of the anti-PLA2R antibody one month after obinutuzumab was higher in the remission group than in the non-remission group [88.2 (72.0, 94.3)% vs 62.5 (14.2, 82.9)%, P = 0.063]. Multivariate logistic analysis showed that the decrease rate of the anti-PLA2R antibody was associated with clinical remission (OR = 1.058, 95% CI 1.012–1.105, P = 0.012). The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve indicated that it had a predictive value for complete remission (AUC = 0.796, 95% CI 0.685–0.908, P < 0.001), and patients were more likely to achieve complete remission when the decrease rate was >85%.
Conclusion
Obinutuzumab showed a rapid and long-acting effect in reducing the serum anti-PLA2R antibody levels in PMN patients, and finally led to good clinical remission. The decrease rate of the anti-PLA2R antibody one month after administration has a predictive value for the clinical remission of PMN.

title: #1721 Proteinuria as a clinical trial endpoint in focal segmental glomerulosclerosis: validation of PARASOL findings in RaDaR
authors: Abigail Smith; David Pitcher; Margaret Helmuth; Alex Mercer; Laurel Damashek; Tobias B Huber; Howard Trachtman; Matthias Kretzler; Laura Mariani; Daniel P Gale
abstract:
Background and Aims
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is a rare condition that affects children and adults, lacks any approved therapy, and has a high risk of progression to kidney failure (KF). The PARASOL consortium was set up to establish evidence to inform adoption of feasible and clinically meaningful surrogate endpoints for FSGS clinical trials.
Method
PARASOL combined 9 registries of biopsy-proven or genetic FSGS patients from North America and Europe. Eligible participants required: (1) UPCR ≥1.5 g/g at any time post-biopsy or diagnosis or up to 3 months prior (index UPCR); (2) eGFR ≥30 ml/min up to 3 months prior to index UPCR; (3) ≥1 additional UPCR and eGFR measurement 3 to 24 months post-index; and (4) no evidence of KF (kidney replacement therapy, eGFR sustained <15 ml/min) prior to the first post-index measurements. Relationships between change in eGFR and proteinuria response (across various thresholds) in the first 24 months post-index and subsequent probability of kidney failure beyond 24 months were assessed using Cox proportional hazards models, using a landmark approach with a landmark time of 24 months post-index. Validation was performed among participants fulfilling the same criteria in the UK National Registry of Rare Kidney Diseases (RaDaR).
Results
PARASOL contained 1626 eligible participants, with median (IQR) follow-up time from kidney biopsy of 64.2 months (35.2, 103.1). At biopsy, median age was 19 years (IQR 7, 43), median UPCR was 3.8 g/g (IQR 2, 7.2) and median eGFR was 81 ml/min (IQR 54, 109). eGFR and the rate of eGFR decline were associated with KF hazard but were highly variable: sample size requirements for clinical trials using eGFR endpoints ranged from 500–1000 individuals per arm. Proteinuria reduction was strongly associated with reduced KF hazard. Using a UPCR responder threshold of 0.7 g/g, achieved in 406 participants, responders had an 85% lower hazard of kidney failure (HR = 0.15, 95% CI = 0.09–0.26) and a survival difference of +0.27 (95% CI 0.22–0.32) compared to non-responders, consistent in incident and prevalent subpopulations and in subgroups based on age and index proteinuria or eGFR level. Estimated sample size requirements for trials using this proteinuria endpoint was 100–200 per group.
The findings were validated in RaDaR, which included 465 eligible participants. At index, RaDaR participants were older, median age 36 (14–55), with lower kidney function, median eGFR 71 ml/min (46–106), and higher proteinuria, median UPCR 5.3 g/g (2.7–8.9). Responder status based on UPCR at 24 months was similar to PARASOL. Stratifying by index UPCR into 1.5 to <3.5 g/g, 3.5 to <7.0 g/g and ≥7.0 g/g, in PARASOL 32%, 31%, and 34% achieved <0.7 g/g by 24 months compared with 25%, 42% and 29% in RaDaR (Fig. 1). At the 0.7 g/g threshold, adjusted hazard ratios and survival differences were similar to PARASOL at 0.07 (0.02–0.27) and 0.29 (0.22–0.36) respectively (Fig. 2), consistent in all subgroups analysed.
Conclusion
For most therapeutic effect sizes, variability in eGFR within and between patients with FSGS means that sample size requirements for trials using eGFR or eGFR slope endpoints are unfeasibly large. In contrast, there was consistent and strong association of proteinuria reduction (a biologically plausible parameter) with higher KF-free survival. Proteinuria reduction is therefore a potential surrogate endpoint for FSGS clinical trials that is both feasible and clinically meaningful.

title: #3553 Predictors and long-term impact of sustained complete renal response in lupus nephritis patients over a 10-year follow up
authors: Ioannis Michelakis; Eleni Kapsia; Ioannis Boletis; Smaragdi Marinaki; Petros Sfikakis; Maria Tektonidou
abstract:
Background and Aims
Complete renal response (CRR) is a major goal in lupus nephritis (LN) management and is associated with favorable long-term renal outcomes. Growing evidence suggests that the duration of CRR is more important than CRR achievement per se. However, the definition of sustained CRR (sCRR) varies significantly among studies.
We aimed to assess the prevalence and duration of sCRR and identify the factors associated with its achievement, evaluating the impact of sCRR on flares, severe kidney function loss (≥30% reduction in eGFR at the last follow-up compared to baseline), organ damage accrual measured with SLICC/ACR Damage Index (SDI), and overall survival. Furthermore, we aimed to determine the minimum sCRR duration required for favorable long-term prognosis and examined whether sCRR can be achieved and maintained with reduced immunosuppressive (IS) and glucocorticoid (GC) therapy.
Method
Data from an inception cohort of 142 patients with biopsy-proven LN [71% proliferative (PLN), 29% membranous (MLN)] were analyzed over a median follow-up of 121 (IQR: 90) months, using linear, logistic, and Cox regression models. CRR was defined according to the 2012 EULAR/ERA-EDTA guidelines and the 2021 KDIGO recommendations and sCRR as a CRR maintained for ≥12 consecutive months. The time to sCRR was measured from LN diagnosis and a composite unfavorable outcome was defined as progression to end-stage kidney disease or death.
Results
Among 118 patients (83%) achieving sCRR, 56% and 20% of them maintained it for ≥5 and ≥10 years, respectively, with a median time to achieve sCRR of 20 (IQR: 9) months post-LN diagnosis. Achievers of sCRR were more likely to have received maintenance therapy with mycophenolic acid derivatives compared to non-achievers (74% vs. 52%, p = 0.01), had a slightly better baseline eGFR (99 vs 82 ml/min, p = 0.09), and less severe interstitial fibrosis/tubular atrophy (9% vs 21%, p = 0.08). Persistent hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) use (≥2/3 of the follow-up) (adjusted HR: 1.7, p = 0.01) and absence of renal flares (adjusted HR: 0.33, p = 0.01) were independently associated with a shorter time to achieve sCRR, whereas there was a trend for non-nephrotic levels of baseline proteinuria (adjusted HR: 1.51, p = 0.06) (Fig. 1a–e). Among patients with PLN, subgroup analysis revealed similar results, with non-nephrotic proteinuria reaching statistical significance (adjusted HR: 2.30, p = 0.01).
Renal flares occurred in 44 patients (37.3%) post-sCRR, in a median time of 43.5 months following CRR. The risk of renal flares 5 and 10 years after sCRR was 20% and 26.2%, respectively. Notably, the risk of flares decreased progressively per additional year on sCRR. A longer duration of sCRR, rather than its achievement per se, significantly predicted a preserved kidney function (adjusted OR: 0.81, p = 0.015) and improved overall survival (adjusted HR: 0.75, p = 0.001) during follow-up. Achieving sCRR was a strong predictor of reduced organ damage (adjusted β-coef = −1.08, p < 0.001). Among patients with extended follow-up (≥100 months), the minimum sCRR duration required to protect against several unfavorable outcomes was four years (Table 1). At 4 years of sCRR, 26% of patients were on full IS treatment, 44% on reduced IS dosage and 30% had discontinued IS, while in 78% GC treatment was also withdrawn. Fifteen patients experienced a renal flare after achieving sCRR for 4 years, with a median time to flare of (IQR: 27) 25 months.
Conclusion
Achieving sCRR is a feasible goal in LN patients, which significantly improves long-term survival and reduces damage accrual. Non-nephrotic baseline proteinuria, persistent HCQ use, and absence of flares were associated with shorter time to sCRR, while maintaining sCRR for at least four years was essential for long-term protection against adverse outcomes.

title: #1722 Serum C3 levels are associated with glomerulosclerosis in membranous nephropathy and ANCA associated vasculitis
authors: Martina Tedesco; Chiara Bedognè; Martina Uzzo; Marta Salti; Anisa Idrizi; Dario Trebeschi; Elisa Delbarba; Stephen McAdoo; Mark Little; David R W Jayne; Federico Alberici; Federica Mescia
abstract:
Background and Aims
Complement dysregulation plays a pivotal role in sustaining glomerular injury in many glomerular diseases, including membranous nephropathy (MN) [1, 2]. In MN, urinary levels of terminal complement products and C3 deposition in kidney biopsies correlated with disease severity and poorer kidney outcomes [1, 3] Clinically, the most widely available laboratory markers of complement activation are C3 and C4 serum levels. In MN and other glomerular diseases, low serum C3 levels have also been linked to a more severe presentation and poorer outcomes [1, 2, 4]. Our study aimed to investigate the relationship between serum complement levels and the clinical and histological features of adult patients with primary MN at disease onset.
Method
This study included a monocentric retrospective case series of patients aged ≥18 years diagnosed with primary MN between 2010 and 2023, with an available serum C3 and a follow-up >6 months. Patients were stratified into two groups based on C3 and C4 levels at diagnosis: above and below the median (respectively, “complement-high” and “complement-low”). Clinical features at disease onset, along with light microscopy and immunofluorescence findings from diagnostic kidney biopsies, were collected and compared across groups. Correlations between complement levels and histopathology features were also assessed. The findings were replicated in a cohort of patients with ANCA-associated Vasculitis collected within the EUVAS group.
Results
A total of 48 patients with MN were identified. The mean serum C3 levels were 138 ± 10 mg/dL in the C3-high, and 105 ± 14 mg/dL in the C3-low group. The mean C4 levels were 34 ± 5 mg/dL in the C4-high, and 22 ± 4 mg/dL in the C4-low group. No significant association between serum C3 or C4 levels and baseline proteinuria, serum creatinine, microhematuria or anti-PLA2R titer was observed. Baseline serum albumin was higher in the C4-low group compared to the C4-high group (Table 1). Notably, patients in the C3-low group exhibited a greater degree of glomerulosclerosis; a trend towards lower C4 levels and glomerular deposition of IgG was also observed (Fig. 1, Panel A).
To further explore the possible link between renal histopathology features and serum complement levels, we looked into an independent cohort of ANCA associated vasculitis (AAV) patients with biopsy-proven kidney involvement, grouped according to Berden's classification [5]. In the subset with available complement levels (n = 200), serum C3 levels were significantly lower in patients with the sclerotic class, compared to those categorized as focal and crescentic. Conversely, no significant differences in C4 levels were observed across Berden classes (Fig. 1, Panel B).
Conclusion
Patients with MN and AAV with glomerulosclerosis had lower levels of circulating C3, further confirming the role of the alternative complement pathway in contributing to renal damage. Further studies with larger cohorts are required to validate these observations and to understand how to translate this finding into a better therapeutic approach to patients.

title: #3255 3-months short course of avacopan in ANCA vasculitis with severe clinical involvement. A real-life experience
authors: Pierre Braud; Charles Ronsin; Antoine Neel; Simon Ville
abstract:
Background and Aims
Over the last decade, seminal studies allowed the implementation of rituximab as induction therapy (instead of or in addition to cyclophosphamide) and the decrease of cumulative steroid doses in the treatment of ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV). However, uncertainties persist in patients with severe renal involvement. Indeed, patients with serum creatinine $ \ge $350 µmol/L were excluded from the RAVE trial and a recent real-life study showed an increased risk of a composite outcome of death, renal failure and disease progression before remission or relapse within 12 months of induction in patients receiving the reduced-dose steroid regimen of the PEXIVAS trial, especially in patients with serum creatinine $ \ge $300 µmol/L induced with rituximab. (Nagle, Ann Rheum Dis, 2024).
Otherwise, avacopan emerged as a glucocorticoid sparing agent in AAV as demonstrated in the phase 2 CLEAR study, where it was shown to be non-inferior to glucocorticoids in inducing remission at 12 weeks. These results were then confirmed in the ADVOCATE study, in which patients received avacopan as induction (along with steroids which were discontinued at weeks 4) and maintenance therapy for a total period of 12 months. The ADVOCATE study's maintenance regimen was criticised because azathioprine was used rather than rituximab.
Method
Based on these considerations and medico-economic concerns, and with the assumption that the window for the beneficial effect of avacopan is over after 3 months especially when rituximab is used as maintenance therapy, we designed a regimen in which patients with severe involvement, received a short course of avacopan (3 months, then tapered over 2 weeks (40 mg for one week, then 20 mg, then stopped) in combination with rituximab and reduced dose glucocorticoid (PEXIVAS scheme).
Results
A total of 12 patients with severe AAV (MPO n = 10/PR3 n = 2), mostly incident (7/12), 58% male, mean age 63 years (±16) were included in the analysis. All had renal involvement, proven by biopsy in 9/12, with a mean baseline creatinine of 477 μmol/L (±535) and a mean urine protein/creatine ratio of 2.58 g/g (±2.3). Initial renal replacement therapy was required in 3 patients, two of whom received plasma exchange. The most common extrarenal involvement was the lung in 5/12 patients, with mechanical ventilation required in one patient. All patients received rituximab alone as induction therapy (1 g × 2 n = 4/12, 375 m2 × 4, n = 8/12) on top of glucocorticoid boluses (mean dose 1416 mg), followed by oral prednisone according to the PEVIVAS low-dose regimen (Fig. 1a), with a mean dose of 5 mg or less achieved at 126 days. Avacopan was initiated at a mean of 3.6 days (±5.7) and discontinued at a mean of 99 days (± 25).
Mean follow-up was 249 days (± 116). One patient died of a haemorrhagic stroke at week 16 post-induction while avacopan was discontinued.
Clinical remission, defined as the absence of active disease (BVAS v 3 = 0) was achieved in all patients at month 3 and in the nine patients who reached month 6, with prednisone doses of 5 mg in 8/9 patients and 10 mg in one. At month 12, remission was maintained in 4/4 patients, with two patients weaned off prednisone and two others on 5 mg. Importantly, no patient experienced disease progression before remission or relapse.
In terms of renal outcome, dialysis was discontinued in the 3 patients who initially required it. As shown in Fig. 1b, serum creatinine and proteinuria decreased continuously from induction to month 6.
Avacopan was well tolerated except in two patients who had to discontinue before month 3 due to liver test abnormalities. Half of the patients experienced infectious complications, only two were severe (hospitalization requirement).
Conclusion
In a series of severe AAV with renal involvement, the combination of rituximab with a 3-month short course of avacopan and a PEXIVAS low-dose glucocorticoid regimen was safe and allowed remission without progressive disease in patients with severe renal involvement and no relapse was observed when rituximab was used as maintenance therapy. Whether such a regimen preserves the putative renal recovery benefit of avacopan requires further investigation.

title: #2209 A novel monoclonal antibody against PAPP-A significantly inhibits disease progression in three mouse models of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
authors: Georgios Koukos; Quaisar Ali; Florian Schmid; Matt Sooknah; Xiaomeng Zhang; Ho-Lan Peng; Romica Kerketta; Reuben Sana; Byounghoon (Brian) Hwang; Neha Murad; Ana Basso; Yuliya Kutskova
abstract:
Background and Aims
Pregnancy associated plasma protein-A (PAPP-A) and the IGF signaling pathway have been implicated in the pathogenesis of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). We generated a human monoclonal IgG1 antibody, ABBV-CLS-628, that binds to PAPP-A neutralizing its proteolytic activity, and evaluated its therapeutic potential in preclinical models of ADPKD.
Methods
Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and in vitro potency assays were used to characterize ABBV-CLS-628. To conduct in vivo studies, a mouse chimeric version of ABBV-CLS-628 (anti-PAPP-A) was generated and characterized. The efficacy of anti-PAPP-A was investigated in three different mouse models of ADPKD, the pcy (a fast-progressing non-orthologous disease model), the Pkd1flox/flox;Pax8rtTA; TetO-Cre (Pkd1fl/fl, an inducible and fast-progressing disease model) and the Pkd1RC/RC (a slow-progressing orthologous disease model) by monitoring the total kidney volume (TKV, by MRI), and the kidney function, by transdermal evaluation of the glomerular filtration rate (tGFR, by MediBeacon®). Pcy, Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd1RC/RC mice were treated weekly with anti-PAPP-A or isotype control antibody for a total of 22, 12 and 62 weeks, respectively. Plasma and kidney tissues were collected for further analysis.
Results
ABBV-CLS-628 binds PAPP-A with high affinity and inhibits the cleavage of its substrates, IGFBP-2, IGFBP-4 and IGFBP-5, resulting in suppression of IGF signaling, in vitro. In mouse models of ADPKD, treatment with anti-PAPP-A significantly suppressed TKV enlargement by 480 mm3 (or 52%), 1436 mm3 (or 62%), and 164 mm3 (or 45%), in the pcy, Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd1RC/RC mice, respectively, compared to isotype control (Fig. 1). The effect of anti-PAPP-A treatment on TKV change was associated with amelioration of kidney function decline and increase in the survival rate. Transcriptomics analysis of kidney tissues identified modulation of ADPKD-related pathways (such as oxidative phosphorylation and TGF-beta signaling) from anti-PAPP-A treatment, compared to isotype control, in all three mouse models of ADPKD (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
ABBV-CLS-628 is a novel human monoclonal antibody that acts as a specific and potent inhibitor of PAPP-A. Treatment with anti-PAPP-A provided a significant benefit in clinically relevant endpoints (TKV and GFR) and modulated disease relevant pathways, in three different mouse models of ADPKD. ABBV-CLS-628 is under clinical development for the treatment of ADPKD.

title: #800 The effect of canagliflozin dose on cardiovascular and renal outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk
authors: Elias Elenjickal; Frederic Baroz; Abhinav Sharma; Thomas Mavrakanas
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors have revolutionized the management of chronic kidney disease (CKD). As shown in large randomized clinical trials, they reduce the incidence of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and heart failure and they delay CKD progression. There is evidence from pharmacokinetic studies that their effect on surrogate endpoints, such as albuminuria or blood pressure, might be dose dependent. However, the effect of SGLT-2 inhibitor dosage on hard clinical endpoints has not been adequately studied. This analysis investigates whether the effects of canagliflozin on cardiovascular and renal endpoints are dose dependent.
Methods
The CANVAS trial (Canagliflozin Cardiovascular Assessment Study) randomly assigned 4,330 patients with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk to receive canagliflozin 100 mg, canagliflozin 300 mg, or placebo in a 1:1:1 ratio. Results from this trial were reported together with CANVAS-R in the CANVAS program but have not been published independently [1]. Our post-hoc analysis evaluates the impact of each dose of canagliflozin on cardiovascular and renal outcomes. Our primary endpoint was a composite of non-fatal myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death. Secondary endpoints included the individual components of the primary outcome, hospitalization for heart failure, all-cause mortality, a composite renal endpoint (including doubling of serum creatinine, end-stage kidney disease or renal death), sustained 40% reduction in estimated glomerular filtration rate, and albuminuria progression or regression. Safety outcomes included acute kidney injury and serious hyperkalemia. Hazard ratios (HR) were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models. Kaplan-Meier survival curves were compared across groups using the log-rank test.
Results
The study enrolled 4330 participants with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk. Median age was 61 years and 66% of patients were males. Baseline characteristics were similar across all treatment groups. Median follow-up was 74 months. In the adjusted analysis for age, sex, and history of cardiovascular disease, canagliflozin at 300 mg significantly reduced the incidence of the composite cardiovascular endpoint, compared with placebo: hazard ratio (HR) of 0.83, 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.68–1.00 (p = 0.049). In contrast, no difference was identified between canagliflozin 100 mg, compared with placebo, for the composite cardiovascular endpoint: HR 0.96 (95% CI 0.80–1.15, p = 0.64). Both doses of canagliflozin were associated with a significant reduction in the incidence of the composite renal endpoint, compared with placebo: HR 0.50 for canagliflozin 100 mg (95% CI 0.25–0.96, p = 0.039) and HR 0.42 for canagliflozin 300 mg (95% CI 0.21–0.86, p = 0.017). Albuminuria progression to a higher stage (A1 to A2 or A2 to A3) was less common with the 300 mg dose, compared with placebo (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.73–0.95, p = 0.006), but not with 100 mg dose (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.83–1.07, p = 0.326). All-cause mortality was significantly lower with the 300 mg dose compared with placebo (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.63–0.97, p = 0.027). In addition, a trend towards lower mortality rates was seen with the 100 mg dose. The incidence of acute kidney injury was comparable across the three treatment arms. A trend towards fewer severe hyperkalemia episodes was seen with the 300 mg canagliflozin dose. Results for all secondary and safety endpoints are shown in Table.
Conclusion

title: #1836 Mesangial cell injury-aggravated CKD in Jak2-mutated myeloproliferative neoplasms
authors: Florian Siegerist; Tina Schnöder; Florian Perner; Tim Lange; Philipp Jost; Elke Hammer; Völker; Karen Lopez-Cayuqueo; Kai Schmidt-Ott; Maike Buettner-Herold; Florian Heidel; Nicole Endlich
abstract:
Background and Aims
Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) are clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorders characterized by excessive production of mature blood cells. In most cases, MPNs are caused by the JAK2 V617F mutation leading to constitutive activation of JAK2 signaling. Besides cellular proliferation, JAK2 V617F leads to increased expression of proinflammatory cytokines causing tissue remodeling and the development of fibrosis. Recently, an analysis from 1420 MPN patients reported significant chronic kidney disease (CKD, eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2) in up to 29% of patients. In the general European population, the CKD prevalence varies between 3.3% in Norway and 17.3% in northeast Germany. Herein, we aimed to assess for pathophysiologic correlates of kidney dysfunction and the pathogenesis of MPN-associated CKD.
Method
We used established mouse models of Jak2-V617F-mutated MPN (Jak2V617F/Vav-Cre, Jak2-VF). Morphological evaluation was performed using electron microscopy, super-resolution microscopy-based PEMP analysis, and standard histology. Multiplex immunofluorescence-processed sections were imaged with confocal laser scanning microscopy. For morphometric and single-cell expression analysis, tissue compartments and single cells were virtually microdissected using custom-trained Deep-Learning networks. Bulk-proteomic analysis of isolated glomeruli was performed using tandem mass spectrometry and bulk transcriptomic analysis of cultured mesangial cells (MCs) incubated with VF-conditioned medium with mRNA sequencing.
Results
Jak2-VF animals displayed severe glomerular hypertrophy (difference of glomerular tuft area 840.7 ± 64.5 µm2; p < 0.0001) and glomerular capillary dilatations (WT n = 6; 1.9% versus VF n = 7; 61.2%; p = 0.0012). Electron microscopy and super-resolution microscopy showed an unchanged morphology of glomerular endothelial cells, the glomerular basement membrane, and podocytes. Jak2-VF animals had significantly fewer MCs (ITGA8+intraglomerular cells per 1000 µm2 WT n = 34; 4.86 vs. VF n = 30; 3.81; p = 0.0021). In Jak2-VF animals, MCs deposited significantly more fibronectin-dominant extracellular matrix. MCs were activated as demonstrated by Ki67-expression of ITGA8-positive cells (2.12% vs. 4.16%; p = 0.021) and de-novo α-SMA positivity. Jak2-VF animals showed increased serum creatinine and albuminuria (p = 0.01). Cre-mediated induction of Jak2-VF in residential kidney cells as a potential confounder of the phenotype was excluded using the mT/mG reporter strain. Pharmacologic Jak-inhibition with enteral Ruxolitinib for 8 weeks resulted in a potent reduction of proinflammatory cytokines, rescue of the glomerular phenotype, and kidney dysfunction.
Global proteomic analysis was performed on isolated glomeruli to assess pathways contributing to kidney dysfunction. Compared to the wildtype controls, 479 out of 4954 proteins were differentially abundant in Jak2-VF animals. Consistent with the structural data, functional enrichment analysis revealed an accumulation of extracellular matrix proteins (p = 1.55 × 10−8) like fibronectin, nidogen, and multiple laminins (alpha 1, 2, 4; beta 2, and gamma 1). In line with the prosclerotic phenotype indicating MC activation, a significant enrichment of actin-regulating proteins (p = 2.16 × 10−46) and proinflammatory signaling pathways including necroptosis could be detected. Bulk transcriptomic analysis of Jak2-VF-conditioned medium-treated MCs showed enrichment of terms related to cytokine signaling, oxidative phosphorylation, and cellular metabolism. Histological analysis of kidney biopsies of JAK2 V617F-mutated MPN patients revealed a Jak2-VF-similar histological phenotype including glomerular capillary dilatations.
Experiments integrating the activated signaling network of MCs, in-depth single-cell analysis of murine kidneys, and spatial proteomic analysis of kidney biopsies are currently underway.
Conclusion
Taken together, the kidneys of mice with Jak2-mutated hematopoiesis show mesangial cell injury and chronic kidney disease due to local activation of inflammatory cell signaling and matrix production.

title: #407 Patient and carer treatment preferences for chronic kidney disease (CKD): a discrete choice experiment (DCE) across eight countries
authors: Simon Fifer; Ciro Esposito; Ricardo Correa-Rotter; Mai-Szu Wu; Helmut Reichel; Hesham Elsayed; Juan Jose Garcia Sanchez; Surendra Pentakota; Thames Kularatne; Richard Hull; Steven Chadban
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a widespread and progressive global health issue affecting over 850 million people worldwide. It can lead to kidney failure, severely diminishing patients’ quality of life and imposing a significant burden on caregivers. Although various treatment options are available, there remains limited insight into how patients and carers make treatment choices and prioritise treatment attributes. This study aimed to investigate treatment preferences through a discrete choice experiment (DCE) conducted across eight countries, reflecting diverse regional contexts. The goal was to provide evidence that supports more patient-centred decision-making in CKD management.
Method
This large, multi-country, non-interventional cross-sectional study included CKD patients and carers at all stages of the disease, with a total of 2,324 participants—1,511 patients and 813 carers—across 8 countries: Australia, Egypt, Germany, Italy, Mexico, Taiwan, the UK, and the US. Participants were identified via online research panels and patient advocacy groups and were required to have personal or informal caregiving experience with CKD for at least three months. A minimum of 30% of respondents in each country were receiving dialysis. Data was collected between 2022 to 2024.
The experiment presented participants with 7 hypothetical scenarios, each offering two unlabelled treatment options (Treatment A and Treatment B) and an option to opt out or to choose “neither”. Five treatment attributes were assessed: (1) delay in the need for dialysis or transplant; (2) life extension; (3) reduced risk of heart failure hospitalisation; (4) risk of side effects; and (5) monthly out-of-pocket costs.
Data were analysed using mixed multinomial logit (MMNL) models. Patient and carer models were estimated for each country, resulting in 16 models. To make comparisons between countries, relative attribute importance was estimated by taking the maximum difference in utility between the attribute's levels and expressed as a percentage of the sum of all maximum differences.
Results
The study revealed diverse treatment preferences among patients and carers:
Model results can be used for scenario analysis (mapping real treatment attributes to the model parameters) through a dashboard, enabling country comparisons of preference shares and predicted treatment uptake (comparison of treatments based on patient values, otherwise referred to as patient value mapping).
Conclusion
This research represents the largest DCE conducted to date on CKD treatment preferences, both in sample size and geographic representation.
It provides valuable insights into how patients and carers prioritise treatment attributes in CKD management across diverse settings. Differences in preferences (represented as preference heterogeneity) suggests that patients and carers should be included in the process of shared decision-making to pursue treatments that are in line with patients’ goals and values. By addressing regional and individual variations in preferences, this research advances the understanding of patient-centred CKD care and highlights the need for further exploration of caregiver priorities, which remain under-researched.

title: #2440 Impaired renal progenitor regeneration and polyploid tubular cell progression underlie physiological kidney tubule aging
authors: Elena Lazzeri; Giulia Antonelli; Giulia Carangelo; Benedetta Mazzinghi; Carolina Conte; Antea Di Lorenzo; Letizia De Chiara; Paola Romagnani
abstract:
Background and Aims
Aging is associated with a natural decline in nephron mass and number, leading to progressive kidney function loss and an increased risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD). With individuals over 65 years old being the fastest-growing demographic in developed nations, understanding the mechanisms driving CKD in this population is of critical clinical relevance. CKD often remains undiagnosed in up to 90% of patients due to the kidney tubule's remarkable compensatory capacity to maintain function despite nephron loss. However, these compensatory mechanisms are poorly understood. Aging in most organs is frequently linked to a loss of stem cell pools or impaired progenitor cell proliferation. In the kidney, we have revealed that a population of renal progenitor cells (RPC), interspersed among tubular cells (TC), are key to regenerating kidney tubules after acute kidney injury. Additionally, TC undergo polyploidization, acquiring extra genome copies, enabling them to sustain kidney function during stress. This is a key mechanism underlying kidney's ability to buffer against TC loss. This study investigates these two adaptive responses during physiological kidney aging.
Method
To trace RPC (Pax2⁺ cells), we used inducible Pax2/Confetti mice, where RPC are labeled with one of four fluorescent reporter genes. To study polyploid TC, we used inducible Pax8/FUCCI2aR mice, identifying polyploid TC by cell cycle fluorescent proteins and DNA content analysis. Mice aged 2, 5, 12, and 20 months were analyzed, and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was performed at 2 and 20 months of age.
Results
Aging was associated with a natural decline in nephron number, progressive kidney function decline, fibrosis, and accumulation of senescent TC, culminating in CKD. In Pax2/Confetti mice, we observed a gradual loss of Pax2⁺ RPC and a decrease in their regenerative capacity starting from 12 months of age. scRNA-seq revealed an age-dependent signature in RPC characterized by DNA damage, TGF-β signaling, senescence markers, and enrichment of stress response pathways, which collectively underlie the impaired regenerative capacity of aged RPC. In Pax8/FUCCI2aR mice, tubular polyploidy progressively increased, accumulating additional chromosome sets as evinced by octaploid TC (8C DNA content), throughout aging. Polyploid TC showed elevated DNA damage and were detected in urine, suggesting ongoing loss. scRNA-seq of polyploid TC showed the increment of hypertrophy- and maladaptive-associated genes in aged mice and expression of fibrotic and senescent genes in polyploid TC expressing DNA damage markers. Additionally, we revealed the polyploid characteristic pathways, which were associated with tubulointerstitial fibrosis, including TGF-β signaling and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, TNF-α signaling, DNA damage responses, and mitochondrial dysfunction. These findings highlight the dual role of polyploid TC in acquiring a profibrotic/proinflammatory phenotype to buffer against DNA damage throughout aging, while driving fibrosis and CKD progression.
Conclusion
Aging-related kidney decline is characterized by:
These age-related changes likely compromise the kidney tubule's capacity to compensate for nephron loss, increasing the susceptibility to CKD in the elderly population.

title: #3314 Estimated GFR in clinical practise: rolling the dice
authors: Sergio Luis Lima; Patricia Isabel Delgado Mallén; Beatriz Escamilla Cabrera; Sara Estupiñán Torres; Domingo Marrero Miranda; Ana González Rinne; Carlos Alayón; Pablo Jorge Pérez; Coriolano Cruz; Federico Gonzalez Rinne; Laura Díaz Martin; Esteban Porrini
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal function is evaluated in clinical practice by creatinine- and/or cystatin-C-based formulas. Several studies reported that cystatin-C-based formulas improves the performance of those based on creatinine. More than 50 formulas have been published in the last 70 years, and the most commonly used are aMDRD and CKD-EPI. Recently, EKFC equation has been published, improving the performance of the former. However, the reliability and real error of formulas is still a matter of debate. Our objective was to evaluate the error of all the formulas published to date in a cohort of 5128 patients (2015 with measured cystatin-C) with different clinical conditions and to study whether cystatin-C-based formulas really improve those based on creatinine.
Method
At the Renal Function Laboratory (https://lfr.ecihucan.es/en/renal-function-lab), in Tenerife, we establish the use of measured GFR by the plasma clearance of iohexol using dried blood spots (iohexol-dbs) in clinical practice and research more than 10 years ago. For this analysis we selected all measurements done between July 2013 and June 2024. For each subject we estimated GFR using 54 formulas based on creatinine and/or cystatin-C. The agreement between measured and estimated GFR was tested with the total deviation index (TDI), concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) and coverage probability (CP) and the P10% and P30%.
Results
A total of 5128 GFR measurements were evaluated in 2903 patients. In all we calculated a large group of formulas using creatinine and/or cystatin-c. The latter was available in 2021 determinations. TDI averaged 69%, 67% and 51% for formulas based on creatinine, cystatin-C and the combination of both respectively, meaning that 90% of the estimates of GFR showed an error ranging from −69 to +69%, −67 to +67% and −51 to +51% when compared with measured GFR. CCC averaged 0.876, 0.877 and 0.915 for the formulas based on creatinine, cystatin-C and the combination of both markers, respectively, showing poor and moderate concordance, respectively. No formula showed a CCC >0.95 that is considered good agreement. CP averaged 23%, 24% and 29% for the formulas based on creatinine, cystatin-C and the combination of both respectively, indicating that 77%, 76% and 71% of the GFR estimations had an error greater than ±10% with respect to the mGFR. Likewise, the creatinine-based formulas showed a mean P10 of 26%, being 27% for those based on cystatin-C and 32% for the equations that use both markers, indicating that only one fourth or one third of the estimations showed an error lower than 10% for different type of equations. Also, P30 were 66%, 68% and 75% for creatinine, cystatin-C and the combination of both markers respectively, meaning that about one third or on quarter of estimations showed and error higher than 30% with respect to measured GFR for all type of equations.
Conclusion
In conclusion, no formula for GFR estimation showed acceptable agreement with respect to measured GFR by iohexol-dbs. Moreover, cystatin-C-based formulas did not improve those based on creatinine, but the combination of both markers seem to improve it, although modestly and without clinical significance. Thus, no formula is reliable in assessing the real renal function in patient with and without CKD. Therefore, measured GFR should be used in clinical situations where a reliable measurement of renal function is crucial, such as living kidney donors, renal transplantation, pre-dialysis patients, ADPKD, adjustment of potentially nephrotoxic drugs or dosing of drugs that are adjusted by GFR.

title: #2198 Effect of finerenone on eGFR slope across different levels of baseline albuminuria: insights from FINEARTS-HF
authors: Finnian R Mc Causland; Hiddo J L Heerspink; Muthiah Vaduganathan; Brian L Claggett; Akshay Desai; Pardeep Jhund; Meike Daniela Brinker; Adriaan Voors; Faiez Zannad; Bertram Pitt; John McMurray; Scott Solomon
abstract:
Background and Aims
Finerenone did not modify the risk of kidney outcomes or eGFR decline among patients with heart failure (HF) in the FINEARTS-HF trial, who were generally at low risk for kidney disease progression. However, whether the effect of finerenone on eGFR slope differs according to baseline urine albumin:creatinine ratio (UACR) is not clear.
Method
FINEARTS-HF was a global, randomized clinical trial of finerenone vs. placebo among patients with HF with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction (N = 6,001). title: #1352 A multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 3 study in patients with idiopathic IC-MPGN: APPARENT protocol amendment
authors: Marina Vivarelli; Andrew Bomback; David Kavanagh; Junhao Liu; Udaykiran Veldandi; Rafael Levitch; David Lawrence; Chang Liu; Deborah Keefe; Richard Smith
abstract:
Background and Aims
Immune complex-mediated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (IC-MPGN) is a rare, fast-progressing kidney disease that may be idiopathic (primary) or secondary to chronic infection, autoimmune disorders, or monoclonal gammopathies. Idiopathic IC-MPGN has a comparable clinical course to complement 3 glomerulopathy (C3G). Iptacopan (LNP023) is an oral, proximal complement inhibitor that targets Factor B to selectively inhibit the alternative pathway (AP) of the complement cascade. Based on the learnings from the Phase 3 APPEAR-C3G study evaluating iptacopan 200 mg twice daily (b.i.d.) in patients with C3G, and to strengthen the evaluation of the treatment effect on preservation of kidney function, the APPARENT Phase 3 study design has been amended by extending the double-blind treatment period from 6 months to 12 months, introducing ‘inadequate response criteria (to enable participants to receive open-label iptacopan after 6 months of double-blind treatment)’, while the recruitment of adult patients is ongoing.
Methods
APPARENT (NCT05755386), a randomized, double-blind, multicenter, placebo-controlled Phase 3 study, is the first study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of iptacopan on top of supportive care in patients with idiopathic IC-MPGN. Approximately 106 adult and adolescent participants with biopsy-confirmed IC-MPGN, proteinuria (urine protein–creatinine ratio [UPCR]) ≥1 g/g, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m2 will be enrolled in the study. All participants will have received maximally recommended or tolerated dose of renin angiotensin system inhibitors and vaccination against encapsulated bacteria. Participants with any cell or organ transplant, rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis, or kidney biopsy with >50% interstitial fibrosis/tubular atrophy, as well as secondary IC-MPGN, will be excluded. Eligible participants will be randomized 1:1 to receive either iptacopan 200 mg b.i.d. or placebo during the double-blind period, followed by open-label treatment with iptacopan 200 mg b.i.d. for all participants. The study consists of two Cohorts. Cohort 1 (Fig. 1A) includes adult participants enrolled in previous protocol versions who completed the Day 180 (6 months) visit and/or those who have not yet reached Day 180 and choose to continue with the 360 days (12 months) treatment period when the amended protocol is implemented. Cohort 2 (Fig. 1B) includes the newly enrolled adult participants after the implementation of the amended protocol along with those who enrolled in the previous protocol versions but have not yet reached Day 180 visit and have consented to the amended 540 days study period, as well as the adolescent participants (adolescent recruitment will start based on the amended protocol). Results
Recruitment is ongoing, and study is expected to complete in Q4 2028.
Conclusion
This study will provide evidence towards the efficacy and safety of iptacopan in idiopathic IC-MPGN in adult and adolescent patients.
