title: #693 Hospitalization for congestive heart failure following treatment with roxadustat in patients with or without a history of CHF: pooled post hoc analysis of phase 3 studies
authors: Gabriel Choukroun; Alina Jiletcovici; Arianne Schild; Ernesto Paoletti
abstract:
Background and Aims
Roxadustat, a hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor, is approved in multiple countries for the treatment of anemia of chronic kidney disease (CKD). Previous pooled analyses have reported that roxadustat was non-inferior to erythropoiesis-stimulated agents (ESAs) for time to first major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE) and MACE plus congestive heart failure (CHF) or unstable angina requiring hospitalization in patients with dialysis-dependent (DD) or non–dialysis-dependent (NDD) CKD; however, these analyses were not stratified by history of CHF. The current post hoc analysis was conducted to evaluate time to first hospitalization for CHF in patients with DD or NDD CKD with or without a history of CHF treated with roxadustat compared with ESA.
Method
Patients with anemia of CKD from four phase 3, multicenter, randomized, open-label, active-comparator studies (HIMALAYAS, ROCKIES, SIERRAS, and PYRENEES) were pooled for the DD CKD group, and patients from a phase 3, multicenter, randomized, open-label, active-comparator study (DOLOMITES) were analyzed as the NDD CKD group. Data were analyzed for the time to first occurrence of hospitalization for CHF during and up to 7 days after the treatment period (ie, on-treatment plus 7 days) using a separate model for each of the four groups (DD CKD with a history of CHF, DD CKD without a history of CHF, NDD CKD with a history of CHF, and NDD CKD without a history of CHF). Hazard ratios (HRs) were estimated with a Cox proportional hazards model adjusted for baseline age as a continuous covariate. The non-inferiority margin was set at 1.8, as recommended by industry guidance provided by health authority bodies regarding the assessment of cardiovascular risk in clinical studies.
Results
Of the 4714 patients with DD CKD (roxadustat: n = 2354; ESA: n = 2360), 1122 had a history of CHF (roxadustat: n = 562; ESA: n = 560). title: #3574 Predicting absolute time to kidney failure in chronic kidney disease patients using machine learning
authors: Tamas Szili-Torok; Michele Provenzano; Roberto Minutolo; Lilio Hu; Rosita Greco; Carlo Garofalo; Silvio Borrelli; Gianluigi Zaza; Martin H de Borst; Luca De Nicola
abstract:
Background and Aims
In patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), timely preparation for kidney replacement therapy requires adequate prediction of the absolute time until kidney failure. To date, no algorithm exists to perform such prediction. This study therefore aimed at predicting the absolute time to kidney failure in CKD patients.
Method
A machine learning model was developed, based on data from a multi-center Italian cohort study including 3,599 adult patients followed for at least 6 months in nephrology clinics across Italy with CKD stages G3-G5. To predict the absolute time to kidney failure, defined as dialysis initiation or kidney transplantation, a bootstrap aggregating extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) model with the accelerated failure time objective was used. After performing hyperparameter tuning and feature engineering using 5-fold cross validation, model performance was externally evaluated in an independent national cohort (Nephro FED II, n = 346) as well as an international validation cohort from The Netherlands (n = 297). Model output was explained by Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) values.
Results
In the training data, during a median follow-up of 37.3 (interquartile range, IQR, 25.2–54.9) months, 728 (20.2%) patients developed kidney failure. Median patient age was 70.1 (IQR, 60.6–76.6) years; 1434 (39.8%) were females. Baseline eGFR was 32.5 ± 13.0 mL/min/1.73 m2. Estimated GFR (CKD-EPI), proteinuria, age, plasma phosphorus, plasma calcium, body mass index (BMI) hemoglobin and total cholesterol were selected as features contributing to the final model. External validation showed that the model had excellent discrimination (concordance index: national validation = 0.849, international validation = 0.878) and the model had good performance across time (Fig. 1). By comparing the predicted and real times to kidney failure, the model showed acceptable calibration in both external validation sets (Fig. 2). SHAP values revealed that eGFR, proteinuria, BMI, and age were the most impactful features for predicting time to kidney failure.
Conclusion
We developed a machine learning model that predicts the absolute time to kidney failure in CKD patients with excellent discrimination. This model may be used during clinical care to timely plan kidney replacement therapy, and it may also serve as an outcome for clinical trials aimed at investigating the effect of CKD treatment strategies.

title: #3510 Outcomes of canagliflozin in patients with type 2 diabetes with and without progressive renal function decline: insights from the CREDENCE trial
authors: Frederic Baroz; Elias Elenjickal; Abhinav Sharma; Thomas Mavrakanas
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors have become a cornerstone of management for patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). However, pivotal clinical trials with SGLT-2 inhibitors have largely excluded individuals with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <20–30 ml/min/1.73 m², leaving a critical gap in understanding the risks and benefits of these agents in advanced CKD. Post-hoc analyses have attempted to address this gap by focusing on patients with an eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m² at baseline. Nevertheless, the limited sample size of this subgroup has reduced the statistical power and precision of these findings. Emerging evidence suggests that SGLT-2 inhibitors may retain their efficacy as kidney function declines, raising the possibility of extending their therapeutic role to patients with advanced CKD. We hypothesize that these agents will continue to protect against cardiovascular and renal events in patients whose eGFR drops below 30 ml/min/1.73 m² after treatment initiation.
Method
This is a post hoc analysis of the CREDENCE trial, a double-blind, randomized controlled study, investigating the effect of canagliflozin, an SGLT-2 inhibitor, at the dose of 100 mg daily on renal and cardiovascular endpoints in patients with diabetic kidney disease. The CREDENCE trial enrolled 4401 participants with an eGFR of 30–90 mL/min/1.73 m² and a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 300–5000 mg/g. The study protocol allowed for continuation of the study drug in patients with eGFR decline until the initiation of renal replacement therapy. In this analysis, we compared renal and cardiovascular outcomes between canagliflozin and placebo in two subgroups: patients whose eGFR dropped below 30 mL/min/1.73 m² during follow-up and those whose eGFR remained above this threshold. The primary outcome was a composite of end-stage kidney disease (dialysis, transplantation, or a sustained eGFR of <15 mL/min/1.73 m²), a doubling of the serum creatinine level, or death from renal causes. Secondary efficacy endpoints included non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, cardiovascular death, hospitalization for heart failure, all-cause mortality, and the individual components of the primary endpoint. Safety endpoints included acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia. We used a time-updated Cox proportional hazards model to account for time-varying covariates. P-values for interaction were used to study the differential effect of canagliflozin on clinical endpoints in patients with and without eGFR decline.
Results
Among a total of 4401 patients, 665 (15.1%) experienced a deterioration of eGFR below 30 ml/min/1.73 m² during the follow-up period. Patients with a decline in eGFR had higher blood pressure at baseline, were more likely to have severely increased albuminuria, and were more frequently treated with loop diuretics and insulin. The incidence of hard clinical endpoints was higher in patients with eGFR decline with the exception of stroke. Canagliflozin was associated with a significant reduction in the primary outcome among patients who did not experience eGFR decline below the 30 mL/min/1.73 m² cutoff: hazard ratio (HR) 0.58, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.45–0.74. In contrast, no benefit was seen in those with eGFR decline: HR 1.01, 95% CI 0.43–2.40. However, there was no significant interaction between the treatment arm and eGFR decline for this endpoint (p for interaction 0.21, Fig. 1). Similarly, point estimates for the effect of canagliflozin were comparable for most secondary endpoints, while P-values for interaction were all above the 0.20 cutoff. In addition, there was no evidence of harm from canagliflozin with respect to the safety endpoints in the subgroup of patients with eGFR decline.
Conclusion
In this subgroup analysis from the CREDENCE trial, there was no evidence of a differential treatment effect from canagliflozin on hard clinical endpoints in patients with and without eGFR decline below the 30 mL/min/1.73 m² cutoff. In addition, there was no evidence of harm from canagliflozin who progressed to advanced CKD during the follow-up period.

title: #795 Associations between sodium gradients and all-cause mortality in maintenance hemodialysis patients
authors: Karin Bergling; Felix Maralescu; John Larkin; Yue Jiao; Jochen Raimann
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sodium loading is a hypothetical process in which sodium is transferred during hemodialysis (HD), this can occur when the dialysate sodium concentration exceeds the blood concentration. The impact of the magnitude and direction of such gradient on patient outcomes remains uncertain. We here investigated the association between sodium gradient exposure and all-cause mortality in HD patients across four geographical areas.
Method
In this retrospective study, we analysed HD treatment records from 543 169 patients in the ApolloDialDb™ database, collected between January 2018 and March 2021. Countries contributing fewer than 200 patients were excluded. Eligible patients had at least 100 treatment records during a baseline period spanning 3 to 15 months after dialysis initiation, with HD accounting for at least 90% of sessions, and provided sufficient data for at least three sodium gradient evaluations. All-cause mortality was assessed during a subsequent two-year follow-up period. We employed region-specific Cox proportional hazards models with a penalized spline function to examine associations between sodium gradient exposure and mortality risk, adjusting for albumin, age, diabetes mellitus, gender, and exclusively in the USA cohort, interdialytic weight gain.
Results
A total of 63 609 patients from 8 countries met the inclusion criteria. The mean age was 61.7 ± 14.6 years (mean ± 1 SD), 57.7% were male, and 44% had diabetes. The mean serum sodium concentration was 137.5 ± 2.6 mmol/L (Fig. 1A), dialysate sodium concentration 137.4 ± 1.2 mmol/L (Fig. 1B), and average sodium gradient −0.1 ± 2.8 mmol/L (Fig. 1C). We observed an all-cause mortality rate of 8 deaths per 100 patient-years. In the United States cohort, hazard ratios (Fig. 2A) indicated that a slight negative sodium gradient was associated with lower mortality compared to positive gradients, while similar trends were seen in the three other cohorts with smaller sample sizes, they did not demonstrate statistically supported associations (Fig. 2B–D).
Conclusion
Our findings demonstrate potential associations between the magnitude and direction of the sodium gradient and all-cause mortality. However, due to the limited range of dialysate sodium prescriptions in our dataset, we could not determine whether these associations are driven by low serum sodium levels, a known risk factor for mortality among HD patients. Further studies are needed to elucidate potential underlying mechanisms and causality.

title: #291 Prevalence and patterns of intradialytic arterial oxygen saturation instability: observations in a large U.S. hemodialysis cohort
authors: Andrea Nandorine Ban; Lin-Chun Wang; Peter Kotanko; Len Usvyat; Hanjie Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Intradialytic hypoxemia is a common yet underrecognized condition among maintenance hemodialysis (HD) patients, potentially contributing to adverse outcomes (Meyring-Wösten et al., CJASN 2016). One potential etiology is sleep apnea, a condition characterized by intermittent “saw-tooth patterns” (STP) of arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2). Identifying STP during HD may offer insight into the prevalence of intradialytic sleep apnea and its implications for patient care. The objective of this study was to analyze the prevalence of SaO2 STP at treatment and patient levels using artificial intelligence.
Method
We extracted intradialytic SaO2 measurements from a large U.S. HD population. In these patients, intradialytic SaO2 was continuously monitored using the Crit-Line Monitor (CLM; Fresenius Medical Care North America), a device approved by FDA for the measurement of oxygen saturation and hematocrit in the extracorporeal dialysis circuit. The CLM reported SaO2 data at 10-second intervals. The data were subsequently transmitted to a cloud-based platform for analysis. We extracted data between January 14, 2021, and July 30, 2023.
To develop our one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D CNN), a random subset of HD sessions was selected. The time series data from each session were divided into consecutive 5-minute segments, which were visually reviewed and independently classified by a physician and a researcher as either displaying a saw-tooth pattern (STP) or not. The trained 1D CNN was then applied to the entire dataset to classify each segment as exhibiting an STP or not. Figure 1 provides a visual example of SaO2 measurements during a HD session, highlighting segments classified as STP by the 1D CNN.
Results
After rigorous data cleaning, we retained over 3 million HD sessions from more than 49,000 patients receiving HD across 731 clinics. 11% of the 5-minute segments were classified as STP, while 89% were classified as non-STP. For each HD session, we calculated the proportion of STP segments relative to all 5-minute segments. For instance, in the example shown in Fig. 1, 21 segments were classified as STP out of a total of 48 segments (240 minutes), yielding an STP rate of 43.8%.
The treatment-level distribution of STP rates across all HD sessions is depicted in Fig. 2A and B. More than half of the sessions contained no STP segments, while 4.29% of sessions exhibited STP rate between 50% and 75%. Specifically, 137,423 HD sessions fell into this range, reflecting substantial variability in STP occurrence during dialysis.
At the patient level, we assessed the proportion of HD treatments containing at least one STP. For each patient, we calculated the ratio of their STP-positive sessions to their total number of sessions during the study period. This analysis identified two distinct patient clusters: (a) patients who experienced STP in nearly all HD sessions and (b) patients who exhibited few or no occurrences of STP. Specifically, 5,499 patients had no STP across all treatments, while 5,820 patients experienced STP in every HD session (Fig. 2C and D).
Conclusion
This study represents the largest analysis of intradialytic SaO2 measurements in maintenance HD patients to date, leveraging a comprehensive dataset from a diverse U.S. HD population. The identification of SaO2 STP provides a novel avenue for investigating the interplay between intradialytic hypoxemia, sleep apnea, and patient outcomes. Further research is expected to elucidate the clinical significance of STP, including its relationship to sleep apnea, morbidity and mortality. Insights gained from such studies can inform strategies to improve patient care and optimize HD treatment protocols.

title: #3394 Plasma endothelin-1 concentration before hemodialysis is related to the direction of blood pressure changes during hemodialysis
authors: Leszek Pstras; Simon Correa; Finnian R Mc Causland
abstract:
Background and Aims
While most patients experience a decline in blood pressure (BP) during hemodialysis (HD), in a subset of patients BP remains relatively stable or even increases during HD. Both excessive decreases and increases in BP during HD may be associated with adverse outcomes. In this study, we set out to investigate whether pre-HD and intra-HD concentrations of plasma endothelin-1 (ET-1), a potent vasoconstrictor, are associated with the direction of BP changes during HD.
Methods
We performed a secondary analysis of data collected in a prospective study of 50 patients on maintenance, thrice-weekly HD admitted to Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston, MA, USA. A single HD session was studied in each patient. Plasma ET-1 was measured in blood samples drawn before dialysis, at 30, 60, and 120 minutes during HD, and post-HD. BP was measured before and every 15 min during HD using an automated BP cuff. 16 patients were excluded from the analysis due to missing data, very low pre-dialysis BP (below 85/55 mmHg), dialysis sessions lasting less than 3 hours, or lack of a clear intradialytic BP pattern. The remaining 34 patients (16 females, median age 65 years) were divided into two groups based on the trend in systolic BP (SBP) in the first 2 hours of HD, determined by the slope of the linear regression line of SBP values relative to pre-HD SBP (expressed in percentage change per hour): 1) patients with a relatively stable SBP or with an increasing trend in SBP (slope >−1%/h), and 2) patients with a decreasing trend in SBP (slope <−1%/h).
Results
11 patients were classified into Group 1 (median slope of SBP 0.6%/h, range from −0.9 to 7.5%/h), and 23 patients were classified into Group 2 (median slope of SBP −8.6%/h, range from −1.9 to −21.4%/h). Median ultrafiltration was 2.0 L in both groups (P = 0.81). In Group 1, there was no significant change during HD in median SBP (152 vs 146 mmHg, P = 0.40) or median DBP (73 vs 72 mmHg, P = 0.71). In Group 2, the median SBP decreased during HD from 144 to 125 mmHg (P < 0.001), while the median DBP decreased from 67 to 65 mmHg (P = 0.02). No difference between the two groups was observed in median pre-HD SBP (146 vs 144 mmHg, P = 0.70) or median pre-HD DBP (72 vs 67 mmHg, P = 0.58). Patients from Group 1 had a significantly higher median pre-HD ET-1 compared to patients from Group 2 (3.41 vs 2.17 pg/mL, P = 0.006). Pre-HD ET-1 was positively correlated with the slope of SBP changes during the first 2 hours of HD (Spearman's rho = 0.46, P = 0.01). During HD, median ET-1 decreased in Group 1 from 3.41 to 2.40 pg/mL (P < 0.001), whereas it did not change in Group 2 (2.14 vs 2.17 pg/mL, P = 0.29).
Conclusion

title: #2296 Blood pressure-lowering effects of hydrochlorothiazide in chronic peritoneal dialysis patients with residual urine output
authors: Gordon Chun Kau Chan; Kit-Chung Ng; Cheuk Chun Szeto; Kai Ming Chow
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hypertension is common in patients with advanced kidney disease. However, the blood pressure-lowering effect of thiazide diuretics in patients on chronic peritoneal dialysis with residual urine output remains unknown. This study aims to evaluate the blood pressure effects of thiazide diuretics.
Method
This single-center crossover study examined patients on long-term peritoneal dialysis with residual urine output greater than 500 mL per day. After recruitment and consent, patients received oral hydrochlorothiazide tablets 25 mg once daily for 3 months, followed by a 2-day washout period and a 2-week drug-free observation period. Blood pressure measurements (systolic [SBP], diastolic [DBP], and mean arterial pressure [MAP]), residual urine volume, and body composition via bioimpedance spectroscopy (total body water [TBW], extracellular water [ECW], intracellular water [ICW], and overhydration volume) were assessed on days 30, 60, and 90 during both treatment and drug-free periods.
Results
Ten patients participated in the study—7 males (70%) with a mean age of 64.4 ± 11.4 years. The group had a daily urine output of 0.9 ± 0.6 L. Baseline blood pressure readings showed SBP of 164.0 ± 9.5 mmHg, DBP of 87.6 ± 15.1 mmHg, and MAP of 111.9 ± 13.7 mmHg. Patients were taking a median of 4 antihypertensive drugs (interquartile range 3–4). Their baseline body weight was 70.9 ± 13.3 kg, with an overhydration volume of 5.6 ± 2.6 L.
With treatment, SBP decreased over time, showing a 16 ± 9 mmHg reduction by day 90 (P = 0.004). No patients experienced hypotension during treatment. Daily urine volume remained stable during drug treatment (P = 0.9). However, we observed a slower decline in residual urine volume (pre-treatment -0.9 ± 1.1 L/year vs. during treatment −0.1 ± 1.0 L/year; P = 0.04).
After discontinuing hydrochlorothiazide, SBP increased by 11.4 ± 10.5 mmHg at Day 30 (P = 0.02) and remained elevated through Days 60 and 90 (Fig. 1). Daily urine volume declined from 0.9 ± 0.7 L/day to 0.5 ± 0.3 L/day. The annual decline in urine output worsened after stopping hydrochlorothiazide (from −0.1 ± 1.0 L/year during treatment to -0.8 ± 1.3 L/year after discontinuation).
Body weight increased by 0.8 ± 1.7 kg after hydrochlorothiazide discontinuation, accompanied by a 0.6 ± 0.7 L increase in overhydration volume (Fig. 2). Body composition analysis showed increases in TBW, mainly in the ICW (Fig. 2).
During the study period, two subjects were hospitalized—one for herpes zoster and one for influenza A respiratory infection. Neither hospitalization was related to the study medication.
Conclusion
Thiazide diuretics effectively lower blood pressure in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease who are on long-term peritoneal dialysis with residual urine output. The treatment reduces both overhydration volume and total body water volume, with the decrease occurring predominantly in intracellular water volume.

title: #1554 The increase in ultrafiltration volume correlates strongly with an increase in sodium removal during steady concentration peritoneal dialysis with the Carry Life UF system
authors: Olof Heimbürger; Jörgen Hegbrant; Charlotte De Leon; Ola Carlsson; Martin Wilkie
abstract:
Background and Aims
Achieving adequate ultrafiltration (UF) as well as adequate sodium removal is a challenge in patients treated with peritoneal dialysis (PD), especially during automated PD (APD) as a result of sodium sieving. Carry Life UF is a novel PD system, using the concept of steady concentration peritoneal dialysis (SCPD), where glucose is added continuously during the PD dwell to maintain a stable intraperitoneal glucose concentration, thereby enabling effective UF throughout the whole duration of the dwell. During the entire treatment with the Carry Life UF system a small portion of the intraperitoneal fluid is repeatedly transferred to the device, where it is mixed with a small volume of a 50% glucose solution, and then returned to the patient. The aim of this study was to investigate ultrafiltration, sodium removal and glucose efficiency using the Carry Life UF system.
Method
Eight stable adult patients (2 females) treated with continuous ambulatory PD (CAPD) were included in the study. The participants underwent three 5-hour Carry Life UF treatments using different glucose doses (11, 14, 20 g/h). An initial fill with 1500 ml, 1.36% glucose PD solution was used. A standard 4-hour 2.27% glucose CAPD dwell was used as the control. UF volume, sodium removal, and glucose absorption was calculated as well as glucose efficiency for UF (mL UF volume/g glucose absorbed), and for sodium removal (mmol sodium removed/g glucose absorbed). Data are expressed as mean ± SD, statistical analysis using one-way ANOVA, *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001.
Results
The results from control and Carry Life UF treatments are shown in the Table 1 and Fig. 1. Compared to the control treatment, there was an increase in UF volume (4–5 times) for the Carry Life treatments, as well as a proportional increase (4–5 times) in sodium removal. Glucose absorption increased during the Carry Life UF treatments compared to the control, however, the glucose UF efficiency was increased (2–3 times) with the Carry Life UF treatments. Further, increased sodium removal per absorbed gram of glucose (2–3 times) was noted, which was statistically significant for the Carry Life UF 11 g/h and the 14 g/h glucose doses. There was a strong positive correlation (r = 0.98) between UF volume and sodium removal for the Carry Life UF treatments.
Conclusion
The simultaneous increase in UF volume and sodium removal with SCPD performed with the Carry Life UF system compared to the control is a clinical benefit. The increased UF volume with the Carry Life UF treatments compared to control, was associated with an increase in glucose absorption, which, however, was not proportional to the increase in UF. Hence, glucose UF efficiency was significantly higher with the Carry Life UF treatments compared to control. Furthermore, also glucose sodium removal efficiency was increased with the Carry Life UF treatments. The strong correlation between UF volume and sodium removal with SCPD is in contrast to the situation with APD, where an increased UF volume does not result in a proportional increase in sodium removal.
In summary, SCPD performed with the Carry Life UF system resulted in higher UF, greater and predictable sodium removal and more efficient use of glucose, both with respect to UF and sodium removal, and is potentially a suitable therapy to improve volume management in PD patients.
Trial registration number: NCT03724682 (ClinicalTrials.gov).

title: #2571 Role of sildenafil and SB204741 in suppressing fibrotic potential of peritoneal fibroblasts obtained from PD patients
authors: Harshit Singh; Saurabh Chaturvedi; Narayan Prasad; Vikas Agarwal
abstract:
Background and Aims
Peritoneal fibrosis (PF) results in technique failure in peritoneal dialysis (PD) patients. Peritoneal fibroblasts are characterized by increase in the ACTA2 gene, responsible for alpha smooth muscle actin (α-SΜΑ), extracellular matrix (ECM) production, and inflammatory cytokines production, which are the are key mediators in the pathogenesis of PF. 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT; serotonin) induces ECM synthesis in fibroblasts in a transforming growth factor-beta 1 (TGF-β1) dependent manner. The aim of the study was to identify the potential mechanism and role of sildenafil and 5HT2B receptor inhibitor (SB204741) combination in attenuating PD-associated peritoneal fibrosis.
Method
Studies were performed to determine the effect of TGF-β1, sildenafil, and SB204741 on human peritoneal fibroblasts (HPFBs) isolated from the parietal peritoneum of patients in long-term PD patients (n = 6) and controls (n = 6). HPFBs were incubated with TGF-β1 (10 ng/mL) for 1 h and later with TGF-β1 (10 ng/mL)/[sildenafil (10 µM) or SB204741 (1 µM)] and their combination for 24 h (post-treatment strategy). In the pre-treatment strategy, HPFBs were pre-treated with sildenafil (10 µM) or SB204741 (1 µM) and a combination of the two for 1 h and later with only TGF-β1 (10 ng/mL) for 24 h.
Results
The anti-fibrotic effects of the combination of sildenafil and SB204741 were greater than that of each drug alone. In TGF-β1-stimulated HPFBs, pro-fibrotic genes (COL1A1, COL1A2, ACTA2, CTGF, FN1, and TGFB1) exhibited higher expression than in controls, which are crucial targets of sildenafil and SB204741 against peritoneal fibrosis. The synergistic approach played an anti-fibrotic role by regulating the pro- and anti-fibrotic gene responses as well as inflammatory cytokine responses. The combination treatment significantly attenuated peritoneal fibrosis, as evident by the almost complete amelioration of ACTA2 expression, restoration of anti-fibrotic genes (MMP2/TIMP1), and, at least, by reducing the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IFN-γ, IL-4, IL-17, IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, and TGF-β1) along with an increase in IL-10 levels.
Conclusion
Taken together, the above research evidence that the combination of sildenafil and SB204741 may have therapeutic potential in suppressing peritoneal fibrosis due to peritoneal dialysis.

title: #2979 Impact of phase angle on mortality in hemodialysis patients
authors: Andrea Basantes Delgado; Elisabet Coll Piera; Jonas El Bachouti; Ricardo Gabriel Zules; Lluis Guirado Perich; Alejandra Ramos Gali; Silvia Benito; César Ruiz
abstract:
Background and Aims
Despite advances in hemodialysis (HD), mortality rates are still high in this population. Bioimpedance evaluates body composition and helps in the management of hydration and nutrition. The phase angle (PA), obtained with this technique, reflects cellular integrity and tissue composition, and it is associated with muscle quality, nutritional status, and mortality. This study aims to evaluate the phase angle as a prognostic indicator of mortality in HD patients.
Method
This is a retrospective observational study performed in a HD Unit in Barcelona, Spain. Patients on a chronic HD program for at least 6 months who were in our Unit between January 2023 and December 2024 were included. All of them had a Bioimpedance measurement performed before HD using the Fresenius Body Composition Monitor (BCM). Descriptive and bivariate analyses were performed, comparing the phase angle with variables related to mortality, using proper statistical tests. A Kaplan-Meier survival analysis was also conducted.
Results
The mean age of deceased patients was 76 ± 10 years, while that of survivors was 70 ± 13 years, with comparable groups. 70% of dead patients were male, compared to 60% of survivors (P: 0.41). 66.67% of deceased patients had cardiovascular disease, compared to 43% of survivors (P: 0.69). Diabetes was present in 46% of dead patients, compared to 53.5% of survivors (P = 0.60). Cancer history was present in 45% of deceased patients, compared to 54% of controls (p: 0.59).
The underlying cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD) in all patients was: 40% unknown, 20% glomerular, 16% urological, 10% diabetic nephropathy, 6% hereditary, and 3% tubulointerstitial. 20% of deceased patients presented glomerular CKD, while the predominant cause in the controls was urological (23%), with no significant differences. There were also no significant differences in the type of vascular access used.
The average phase angle in deceased patients was 3.1° (SD 0.83°), and it was 4.3° (SD 0.91°) in survivors, being statistically significant (P = 0.00). A significant correlation was found between the phase angle and mortality with creatinine (P = 0.003), potassium (P = 0.01), and albumin (P = 0.008) in deceased patients, and with ferritin (P = 0.01), albumin (P = 0.007), and creatinine (P = 0.008) in survivors. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and Cox regression showed that when phase angle increased in one unit, the risk of death decreased by 38.8% (HR 0.61, P = 0.005). The area under the ROC curve adjusted for the Cox model was 0.84, showing that the phase angle had an 84% probability of correctly classifying patients according to their outcome.
Conclusion
The phase angle obtained through bioimpedance is a good marker of muscle mass and nutritional status in HD patients. A low phase angle (<4°) is associated with a higher risk of mortality. Although it should not be considered in isolation, it can be useful as a prognostic marker in association with other factors. Detecting a low phase angle can alert us to intensify surveillance and treatment in these patients.

title: #3321 Which patients benefit most from hemodiafiltration compared with hemodialysis: prediction of the individualized treatment effects
authors: Robin Wm Vernooij; Michiel L Bots; Peter J Blankestijn
abstract:
Background and Aims
Randomised trials showed that (high dose) hemodiafiltration (HDF) compared to hemodialysis (HD) reduces mortality risk. No differences in treatment effects were found in subgroup analyses for specific patient populations when defined on a single characteristic. Yet, it is unclear to what extent individual patients, characterized by a combination of clinical characteristics, may benefit from HDF. Therefore, we aimed to develop and internally validate a treatment effect prediction model based on a combination of individual clinical characteristics to determine which individual patients would benefit most from high-dose HDF, compared with HD, in terms of survival.
Method
Individual patient data from five European randomized controlled trials (CONTRAST, ESHOL, Turkish HDF study, French HDF study, CONVINCE) comparing HDF with HD on all-cause mortality were used. The 4153 patients included in the trials were aged 18 year or above and at least three months on (low or high flux) hemodialysis before randomisation. Patients were randomised to HDF or continue with (low or high flux) HD. Routine clinical patient characteristics were obtained at baseline, notably age, biological sex, body mass index, diabetes mellitus, history of cardiovascular disease, creatinine levels, and c-reactive protein levels. High-dose HDF was defined as a convection volume of at least 23 liters per session. Royston-Parmar models were derived for exploring the prediction of absolute treatment effect of HDF in terms of survival based on pre-specified patient and disease characteristics. Internal validation of the model was performed using internal-external cross validation with discrimination and calibration metrics.
Results
Among 4153 participants, with a median follow-up of 30 months (Q1–Q3: 24–36), 558 patients (27.2%) died. The median predicted survival benefit of HDF compared with HD was 6.9 (Q1–Q3: 5.6–9.0) months, with a range of 2 to 42 months. Thus all patients on HDF had survival benefit. Those benefiting most from HDF (i.e., estimated survival >12 months more than when treated with HD) were younger, less likely to have diabetes or a cardiovascular history and had higher serum creatinine levels. The predicted gain in median survival was higher when HDF was delivered as high-dose (Fig. 1). Internal-external cross validation showed adequate discrimination and calibration.
Conclusion
Our results suggest that with readily available patient and disease characteristics, the clinician is able to identify those dialysis patients who are estimated to especially benefit from HDF than from HD in terms of survival. The absolute length of survival benefit is likely to be (much) bigger, since follow up was truncated in this dataset, due to the design of the trials. Hence, long-term effectiveness of HDF, within a real-world setting, will have to be determined.

Our results suggest that with readily available patient and disease characteristics, the clinician is able to identify those dialysis patients who are estimated to especially benefit from HDF than from HD in terms of survival. title: #1097 Delivered hemodialysis treatment time and mortality risk: a retrospective analysis
authors: Rachel Lasky; Linda Ficociello; Priya Desai; Benjamin Hippen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Shorter dialysis treatment time has been shown to increase mortality in hemodialysis (HD) patients [1]. Treatment time is a modifiable factor of the dialysis prescription and extending it may be more under the purview of the care team than factors such as interdialytic weight gain. This study investigates the impact of mean delivered treatment time on mortality risk in a large cohort of in-center HD patients.
Method
A retrospective cohort analysis was performed on adult, chronic in-center HD patients dialyzing at Fresenius Kidney Care (FKC) clinics any time from 1/1/2022 to 7/1/2023. The date of first dialysis treatment from 1/1/2022 to 7/1/2023 was defined as the start of a 30-day period during which baseline characteristics were assessed. Mean delivered treatment time was calculated for each patient during a 30-day exposure period following the baseline period. After the exposure period, patients were followed until death, censoring (received transplant, left FKC, or changed dialysis modality) or end of 1 year. A Cox proportional hazards model adjusted for age, sex, race, BMI, and access type was used to estimate hazards ratios for each treatment group.
Results
152,921 patients were included in the analysis. Patients were stratified into 7 treatment time groups at 15-minute intervals based on their mean delivered treatment time (hours). The most frequently delivered treatment time was 3:45–3:59 hours (23.2%), followed by 3:30–3:44 hours (21.6%) and 4:00–4:14 hours (19.9%). When compared to patients with a mean delivered treatment time between 3:00-3:14 hours, patients in the 4:00–4:14 group experienced a 19% (HR 0.81 [0.77–0.86], P < 0.0001) reduction in mortality. Patients in the 3:30–3:44 and 3:45–3:59 groups also experienced a reduction of 10% (HR 0.90 [0.86–0.95], P < 0.0001) and 8% (HR 0.92 [0.87–0.97], P < 0.0001) respectively, while there was no difference in mortality in the 3:15–3:29 or 4:15+ hour groups. There was an increase in mortality in the <3:00 hour group.
Conclusion
Patients with delivered treatment times between 3:30 and 4:14 hours experienced a significant reduction in mortality when compared to patients with delivered treatment times 3:00 and 3:14 hours. This effect was most pronounced among patients with an average delivered treatment time between 4:00 and 4:14 hours. Additional information is needed to assess the impact of treatment time and mortality for patients in the <3:00 and 4:15+ groups, as these treatment times are not typically prescribed.

title: #3713 Integrated conservative therapy-low dose peritoneal dialysis in patients with severe CKD (I-COPE CKD): multicentre prospective controlled study in Italian Nephrology Units
authors: Carlo Garofalo; Silvio Borrelli; Chiara Ruotolo; Gianfranca Susanna Cabiddu; Roberto Russo; Valerio Vizzardi; Adamasco Cupisti; Loris Neri; Vincenzo Bellizzi; Gaetano Alfano; Roberto Minutolo; Luca De Nicola
abstract:
Background and Aims
The effectiveness of nutritional and pharmacological treatment in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) decreases with worsening of renal function due to the onset of resistance to the conservative management (CM). The integration of CM with a “low-dose” dialysis may allow better control of CKD complications and postpone the need for “full-dose” dialysis.
Method
We designed a prospective, multicentre, observational study, enrolling all consecutive adult patients with complicated CKD stage 5, despite regular nephrology care, who met the current indications on dialysis start. Primary endpoint was to test the effects of add-on therapy (I-COPE arm) with peritoneal dialysis (PD) at low dose (continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis-CAPD 1–2 exchanges/24 h or automated peritoneal dialysis-APD ≤4 sessions/week) compared with CM alone (control arm—in patients that refused starting dialysis therapy) on the time to renal death (a composite of full dose dialysis defined as CAPD ≥3 exchanges/24 h, or APD ≥5 sessions/week; shift to haemodialysis and all-cause death).
Results
We included 405 patients from 24 Nephrology Units in Italy, with advanced CKD and at least 2 complications unresponsive to medical treatment. 205 and 200 patients completed the follow-up in I-COPE and control arm respectively. No statistically significant difference at baseline was found between arms regarding age, baseline eGFR, comorbidities and number of CKD complications unresponsive to medical treatment. The length of nephrology care before at baseline dated back 64 months (IQR, 19–143]. The initial modality for low-dose PD was CAPD in 91.8% of enrolled patients with 54% of these performing only one exchange/die. Kaplan-Meyer survival analysis showed a significant greater renal survival rate (longer time to renal death) in I-COPE vs control group (Fig. 1, P < 0.001). Overall median time to renal death was 23 months [95% CI, 18–27] in I-COPE and 10 months [95% CI, 9–12] in control arm (P < 0.001). The risk of renal death is significantly reduced of 67% in I-COPE arm vs control group (HR: 0.34, 95% CI: 0.26–0.44; P < 0.001, Fig. 2). No difference in mortality was found. The overall rate of peritonitis in I-COPE arm was 0.15 episodes/per patient year. No patient had the need of full dose PD or switch to HD for malnutrition.
Conclusion
I-COPE CKD study has evidenced, for the first time, in patients with advanced CKD and complications unresponsive to medical treatment, the effectiveness of integrating CM and low-dose PD with a significant improvement of renal survival that is associated with a low risk of mortality and a very low rate of peritonitis, suggesting also the good safety of this innovative approach.

title: #2597 Gallic acid carbon dot-supported heparin-like polymer as an optimized membrane-anchored antioxidant and anticoagulant for hemodialysis treatment
authors: Yi Wang; Teng Xiao; Qiang Zhao; Jianhua Zhou; Yu Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hemodialysis, a common renal replacement treatment for end-stage kidney disease, exacerbates thrombosis and oxidative stress by exposing the blood to low-biocompatibility dialysis membranes. Here, we developed a functionalized hemodialysis membrane with excellent anticoagulant and antioxidant properties, and simultaneously explored the mechanisms of antioxidation and anticoagulation of gallic acid carbon dots (GA-CDs).
Method
This study utilized a traditional Chinese medicine extract, gallic acid, as the main raw material and synthesized non-metallic nitrogen-doped GA-CDs through a hydrothermal reaction with ethylenediamine. The antioxidant and anticoagulant performance of GA-CDs was evaluated by measuring reactive oxygen species(ROS) clearance rate and antioxidant enzyme expression, and macrophage procoagulation experiments and tissue factor expression respectively. Subsequently, GA-CDs were co-deposited with polydopamine and heparin-like polymer on the polysulfone (PES) membrane surface to produce functionalized membrane. Finally, the bio-compatibility of the functionalized membrane was assessed by detecting cytotoxicity, ROS clearance rate, anticoagulant effect, hemolysis rate and complement activation. One-way ANOVA was used for statistical significance analysis between multiple groups and statistical analyses were performed by GraphPad Prism 9.5 and Origin 2021.
Results
The synthesized GA-CDs possessed superior cytocompatibility and antioxidative cytoprotection, 100μg/ml GA-CDs could effectively eliminate 94.7% ROS and 37.2% O2− production, increasing the cell survival rate in the oxidative stress state from 76.9% to 90.9% (P = 0.0304). Mechanistic investigations revealed that GA-CDs predominantly activated the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor2 (Nrf2) signaling cascade, enhancing the expression of antioxidant proteins, most notably heme oxygenase-1 (Ho-1), to induce cytoprotective effects. After inhibiting Nrf2 expression, GA-CDs could only eliminate 39.3% of ROS production, indicating that the activated Nrf2-Ho-1 pathway is crucial for the ROS clearance ability conferred by GA-CDs. Besides, GA-CDs also upregulated the mRNA expression of the antioxidant enzymes Cat (P < 0.0001) and Sod1 (P = 0.0042), facilitating the clearance of intracellular ROS. On the other hand, the GA-CDs exerted anticoagulant effects by inhibiting the activation and up-regulation of tissue factors on the surface of endothelial cells and macrophages caused by oxidative stress. Endothelial cell tissue factors mRNA expression was upregulated after the co-culture with macrophages under oxidative stress state (P = 0.0014), and the pro-coagulation time of endothelial cells was shortened by 50.0 seconds, corroborating our hypothesis that oxidatively stressed macrophages activate endothelial cells. And when oxidatively damaged macrophages and activate endothelial cells were treated with GA-CDs, the level of tissue factors mRNA expression declined (the P-values were 0.0405 and 0.0034 respectively), and the coagulation time was prolonged by 16.6 seconds and 53.4 seconds respectively compared to that of the control group. Finally, the functional PES membrane by GA-CDs-supported heparin-like polymer exhibited excellent antioxidant and anticoagulant properties. The DPPH and ABTS+ radical scavenging rates of the modified membrane were 83% and 97%, respectively, and the APTT can reach 420 seconds. In addition, the hemolysis rate of modified membrane was also much lower than 5%, and the rate of complement C3 activation was significantly inhibited (P = 0.0002), substantially increasing the biocompatibility of the blood dialysis membrane.
Conclusion
We developed a highly biocompatible hemodialysis membrane with superior anticoagulant and antioxidant capabilities by surface modification using a GA-CDs-supported heparin-like polymer, offering considerable potential for clinical blood purification applications.

title: #160 A novel system to continuously estimate blood pressure in real time during haemodialysis: comparison against standard brachial cuff blood pressures
authors: Daniela Viramontes Hörner; Paul Stewart; Maarten Taal; Nicholas Selby
abstract:
Background and Aims
Intradialytic hypotension (IDH) is a common complication of haemodialysis that is associated with recurrent episodes of myocardial and cerebral ischaemia, and increased mortality. Current clinical practice involves measuring blood pressure (BP) periodically during haemodialysis using brachial cuff measurements, which makes management of IDH largely reactive (i.e., interventions are implemented after BP has already fallen). Conversely, continuous BP measurement during haemodialysis may allow earlier detection and intervention for IDH episodes. However, this approach has relied on techniques that are unsuitable for clinical environments and are restrictive for patients. Therefore, we have developed a new non-invasive approach to continuously estimate systolic blood pressure (SBP) in real time during haemodialysis using pressure wave sensors in the extracorporeal circuit. In this study, we sought to compare the performance of our continuous real-time SBP estimator against brachial cuff BP measurements.
Method
This was a single-centre, observational study conducted in 21 participants receiving haemodialysis with a functioning arteriovenous fistula who were studied throughout two 4-hour haemodialysis sessions and had continuous BP monitoring via the real-time SBP estimator, and brachial cuff BP measurements every 20–30 min. To determine if the real-time SBP estimator was able to track changes in intradialytic SBP, we compared the time-averaged value generated by the estimator from the 5-second period immediately prior to each SBP cuff measurement from both study sessions for each participant. Analyses of the association and agreement between the brachial cuff SBP and the real-time SBP estimate were conducted. IDH was defined as brachial cuff SBP of ≤100 mmHg.
Results
Mean age was 71 ± 11 years and median dialysis vintage was 20.0 months (IQR 12.5–63.5). From 42 completed monitored haemodialysis sessions, 522 BP comparison data points were generated. Average brachial cuff SBP and real-time SBP estimate were 121.8 ± 27.1 mmHg and 123.7 ± 27.9 mmHg, respectively. Brachial cuff SBP and real-time SBP estimate were significantly associated (r = 0.825; P < 0.001). There was a low absolute mean difference between the brachial cuff SBP and the real-time SBP estimate of −1.9 ± 16 mmHg, and no evidence of systematic bias between measurements (Fig. 1). Across all comparison points, 95% of SBP estimator values were within 30% of the matched brachial cuff value, and 66% within 10% of the cuff value. A total of 131 (25%) of the brachial cuff SBP measurements were categorised as IDH of which the SBP estimator was able to recognise the majority.
Conclusion
We have developed a BP estimator that runs in real time during haemodialysis using pressure wave sensors in the extracorporeal circuit and avoiding additional sensor-burden on patients. When compared against regular brachial BP measurements, it has good performance in tracking intradialytic SBP and this supports its further development and larger scale testing. Planned next steps are to develop a computer algorithm to predict IDH in real time and to assess the impact of using this approach to enable pre-emptive interventions to prevent IDH.

title: #570 The clinical evaluation of an antimicrobial impregnated catheter for the prevention of peritoneal dialysis catheter-related infections—initial results
authors: Maarten Taal; Hari Dukka; Zoe Pittman; Waheed Ashraf; Cemile Aksoy; Kelly White; Karen Jones; Carol Rhodes; Andrea Junor; Katie Belfield; Roy Harris; Roger Bayston
abstract:
Background and Aims
Despite the implementation of numerous preventative strategies, catheter-related infections (CRI) remain the most important complication of peritoneal dialysis (PD) and have multiple adverse consequences including additional clinic visits, antibiotic treatment, hospital admissions, emergency catheter removal and, in severe cases, death. Building on technology successfully applied to neurosurgical catheters, we have developed a process for impregnating peritoneal dialysis catheters with three antimicrobial compounds as a novel strategy for preventing infections. Here we report our initial experience of a Phase 1 (first in human) study designed to assess the safety and participant acceptability of these catheters.
Method
We developed peritoneal dialysis catheters impregnated with three antimicrobial compounds: rifampicin, sparfloxacin and triclosan. In keeping with the “two-drug” principle to prevent antimicrobial resistance, the three agents were chosen to provide cover by at least two drugs for the gram positive and gram negative bacteria that most commonly cause CRI. Catheter processing was performed by the research team in a “clean room” facility. Antimicrobial-impregnated catheters were packaged and sterilised (using ethylene oxide) by a commercial provider. Quality assurance checks confirmed expected antimicrobial concentrations and safe residual solvent and ethylene oxide concentrations. All patients scheduled to have elective catheter placement (percutaneous and surgical) for PD are eligible for this observational study, except for those with known allergy to the antimicrobials, pregnancy or expected pregnancy. Standard protocols for insertion, follow-up and monitoring of new PD catheters are followed. We aim to enrol 40 participants, and each will be followed for six months. The primary outcome measure is adverse events. Secondary outcomes include participant acceptability, health related quality of life, infection rates and technique failure.
Results
The study opened for recruitment in September 2024 and to date 20 of 25 (80%) people invited to participate have agreed. To date, 19 catheters have been placed, 15 percutaneously and 4 surgically. Baseline study population characteristics are as follows: median (range) age 58 (19 to 77) years, 11 (58%) female, 10 (53%) with diabetes, BMI 29.6 (20.9 to 44.8) kg/m2. We have observed nine serious adverse events, but none have been attributable to the antimicrobials or catheter processing. No local tissue reactions have been observed. After a median observation of 89 days, one episode of peritonitis has occurred, but this was clearly related to a surgical wound (mini-laparotomy) infection rather than CRI. No episodes of exit site or tunnel infection have been observed. Participant feedback has been universally positive. Our recruitment target is 40 participants by September 2025 and updated data will be presented at the conference.
Conclusion
We have observed a high initial participation rate, suggesting that patients starting PD perceive benefit from the antimicrobial impregnated catheter. Initial experience has been positive and no adverse events attributable to the antimicrobials or impregnation process have been observed.

title: #840 Therapeutic approach to the management of intradialytic complications: from combating hypoxemia to improving hemodialysis tolerance
authors: Stella Kushnirenko; Liubov Savytska; Oksana Lysianska
abstract:
Background and Aims
Prolonged intradialytic hypoxemia (PIH) is a common complication arising during hemodialysis (HD), characterized by a drop in oxygen saturation (SpO₂) below 94% during more than one-third of the session duration. PIH is associated with a significantly increased risk of cardiovascular complications, higher hospitalization rates, and increased all-cause mortality in patients.
The aim of this study is to evaluate the feasibility of using intradialytic oxygen therapy to correct hypoxemic conditions (SpO₂ <94%), intradialytic hypertension (iHTN), and reduced HD tolerance that is resistant to treatment.
Method
A prospective cohort study included 35 patients with PIH and iHTN, 10 of whom had low HD tolerance (mean session duration was 210.6 ± 32.5 minutes). Patients were prescribed oxygen therapy (2–4 L/min) for 80% of the total dialysis time. Parameters assessed included SpO₂, blood pressure (BP), heart rate (HR), and quality of life—using the EQ-5D questionnaire. The study consisted of three periods: a control period (1 week without oxygen therapy), a therapeutic period (1 week with oxygen therapy), and a post-therapeutic period (2 weeks without oxygen therapy). Data were statistically processed using Cohen's d effect size to assess the therapeutic effect on the following parameters: SpO₂, the number of iHTN episodes, fatigue assessment, and quality-of-life indicators.
Results
The median age of patients with PIH was 58.5 years (IQR [42.6–62.8]). Before the start of the treatment, the mean value of SpO₂ was 92.1 ± 1.25%. During oxygen therapy, SpO₂ increased to 98.04 ± 0.40%, showing a statistically significant improvement of 6.04% (P = 0.0004). The low standard deviation (±0.40) indicates stability of these parameters during treatment. title: #1762 Thirst in peritoneal dialysis patients
authors: Vítor Fernandes; Andrew Davenport
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fluid overload adversely impacts on peritoneal dialysis (PD) patients, and fluid restriction is often advised. Thirst is a prevalent and distressing symptom in patients with end stage kidney disease (ESKD). Thirst determinants in PD patients are poorly understood, so we wished to evaluate thirst and its determinants in this population.
Method
We report a cross-sectional study of 387 adult PD patients attending a dialysis center in London from January 2020 to December 2023. Patients completed a visual analog scale for thirst, and clinical, biochemical and multifrequency bioelectrical bioimpedance data were reviewed. Based on thirst intensity scores, patients were categorized into three groups: 121 patients (0–3; low thirst), 136 (5–6; moderate thirst) and 130 (6–10; high thirst).
Results
Higher thirst scores were associated with female gender (P = 0.03); lower median of total weekly urea clearance (1.92 vs 1.97 and 2.09, lower and moderate thirst groups respectively; P = 0.04); and higher daily net sodium removal (136 vs 123 and 115 mmol, lower and moderate thirst groups respectively; P = 0.009). On bivariate analysis, body mass index (BMI) showed a weak inverse correlation with thirst score (P = 0.046). However, there was no association with measured serum osmolality.
Conclusion
We found that patient self-reported higher thirsts scores were associated with female gender, higher daily net sodium removal, suggesting greater dietary sodium intake, and lower weekly total Kt/V. BMI showed a weak inverse correlation with thirst scores. This study highlights the complex mechanism and determinants of thirst in PD patients warranting further study.

title: #2105 The proinflammatory CD14++CD16+ monocytes and lymphocytes subsets are independently associated with technique failure in peritoneal dialysis patients
authors: Christos Georgopoulos; Maria Triantafyllidou; Ioannis Alekos; Georgios Markopoulos; Lefkothea Dova; Maria Pappa; Gerasimos Baxevanos; Vasileios Tatsis; Michalis Mitsis; Athanasios Kitsos; Anila Duni; Evangelia Ntounousi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Technique survival in peritoneal dialysis (PD) is one of the five core outcomes identified by the SONG-PD initiative. The unified definition of technique failure includes a composite end point of death or transfer to hemodialysis for more than 30 days. Chronic inflammation is a hallmark of kidney failure and appears to adversely affect cardiovascular risk, technique and patient survival in PD patients. The associations of immune cell subsets as potential markers of inflammation, with specific modality related and clinical outcomes remain to be determined in PD patients. Thus, the aim of our prospective study was to investigate the prognostic value of a selected panel of immune cells with respect to technique failure development in a cohort of PD patients.
Method
30 stable PD patients were enrolled. Exclusion criteria included a history of malignancy, autoimmune disease, liver disease, acute or chronic infections, treatment with immunosuppressive medications and/or recent hospitalization (<1 month). The peripheral blood immune subsets CD14++CD16−, CD14++CD16+ and CD14+CD16++ absolute values and percentages out of total monocytes and NK cells (CD3+CD16+CD56+), CD3−CD19+ B lymphocytes, CD3+CD4+ T cells, CD3+CD8+ T cells and Tregs (CD4+CD25+FoxP3+) absolute values and percentages out of total lymphocytes were measured by flow cytometry. Simultaneously, clinical, laboratory and echocardiographic data were assessed. Logistic regression analysis was used to identify predictors of technique failure among various cell subtypes. Comparison of the prognostic accuracy of various models was performed using area under the curve (AUC) analysis. Based on the appropriate cut-off points predicted by the ROC curves, we performed survival analysis for the same endpoint and Kaplan–Meier curves were generated and compared by a log-rank test for each of the immune cell subsets of interest.
Results
The mean age of our cohort was 72 ± 14.6 years and 58.6% were males. More than half of patients had diabetes (55%), 17% had heart failure and coronary artery disease was present in 24% of patients. During a mean follow up of 30.5 ± 19.8 months, 20 patients (67%) developed technique failure (15 patients transferred to hemodialysis and 5 patients died). At binary logistic regression analysis, immune cell subsets that correlated with the development of technique failure included the CD14++CD16+ monocytes number (P = 0.01, exp(B) = 1.279), the CD4+ T cells number (P = 0.011, exp(B) = 0.978), the CD8+ T cells number (P = 0.011 exp(B) = 0.981) and the Tregs number (P = 0.029, exp(B) = 0.595). In contrast, no such associations were found for age, eGFR, dialysis vintage, cardiovascular comorbidities and the rest of clinical or laboratory indices. The diagnostic capacity of specific immune cells to identify PD patients experiencing technique failure was assessed by separate ROC analyses. CD14++CD16+ monocytes count provided an AUC of 0.8 (95% CI: 0.63–0.96, P = 0.000), while the AUCs of T cell subsets were 0.83 (95% CI: 0.68–0.99 P = 0.00) for CD4+ T cells, 0.92 (95% CI: 0.82–0.99 P = 0.01 for CD8+ T cells and 0.84 (95% CI: 0.71–0.99 P = 0.000) for Tregs. Kaplan–Meier technique survival curves according to the immune cell subsets levels below versus above cut-off points predicted by ROC curves are shown in Fig. 1. Increased CD14++CD16+ monocytes count above 40/μl (p log-rank test = 0.011) and reduced counts of CD4+ T cells numbers below 650/μl (p-value log-rank test = 0.022), of CD8+ T cells numbers below 500/μl (p log-rank test = 0.004) and of Tregs number below 25/μl (p log-rank test = 0.000) were associated with development of technique failure.
Conclusion
Our results indicate that increased proinflammatory CD14++CD16+ monocytes and decreased T cells subsets are associated with technique failure in PD patients. Further research is needed to clarify potential underlying pathophysiological mechanisms. Finally, studies with larger cohorts are required to specify the utility of immune subpopulations monitoring in the identification of PD patients at risk for technique failure.

title: #3445 Association of incident dialysis modality with patient survival: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Luca Nardelli; Matteo Passerini; Anna Sikharulidze; Carlo Maria Alfieri; Dalia Zubidat; Mohammad Murad; Giuseppe Castellano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Although the choice of dialysis technique is based on several factors, patient survival is undoubtedly one of the most relevant. In a context where randomization to either peritoneal dialysis (PD) or hemodialysis (HD) proved to be extremely challenging, previous meta-analyses were greatly limited due to the inclusion of historical studies.
Method
We performed a systematic review by searching multiple databases up to April 22nd, 2022. We included studies meeting the following criteria: adult patients (>18 years) with end-stage kidney disease on dialysis; comparison of PD versus HD; reporting mortality data via intention-to-treat analysis; initiation of dialysis after 2000; patient classification by dialysis modality at 90 days post-initiation; and ≥50 patients per group (Figs 1 and 2). The primary outcome was the association between dialysis modality (PD vs HD) and mortality assessed via hazard ratios (HR) [Fig. 3]. Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore potential sources of heterogeneity, including sex, age, diabetes, dialysis vintage, geographical location, HD access, and study cohort inclusion period [Figs 4 and 5].
Results
Database search yielded 5317 citations, from which, 27 observational studies met the eligibility criteria, including 1 033 362 incident dialysis patients [Figs 1 and 2]. The pooled mortality HR for PD versus HD was 1.01 (95% CI 0.93–1.10 [Fig. 3]). Heterogeneity was substantial (I2 = 94%) and was largely explained by different baseline features of the included populations. A statistically significant subgroup effect was demonstrated for age (>65 vs.<65 years; P = 0.01), geographical location of the studies (Oceania vs. Europe vs. Asia vs. North America; P < 0.01), and HD vascular access (central venous catheter vs. arteriovenous fistula; P < 0.01, only one study included) [Figs 4 and 5].
Conclusion
This meta-analysis suggests that overall PD and incentre HD likely carry equivalent survival benefits. However, differences were detected among subgroups based on age, geographic location, HD access type, but not on sex, diabetes status, dialysis vintage and study cohort inclusion period.

title: #3561 Peritoneal dialysis outcomes in relation to ultrasonographic peritoneal thickness, IL-6, and MCP-1 levels: a prospective study
authors: Saliha Yıldırım; Mesudiye Bulut; Sevim Gönen; Özant Helvacı; Hadim Akoğlu; Ulver Derici
abstract:
Background and Aims
Peritoneal dialysis (PD) is a widely used renal replacement therapy; however, its long-term success is influenced by peritoneal membrane integrity and function. This study aims to investigate the relationship between ultrasonographic peritoneal thickness, inflammatory markers, and clinical outcomes in patients undergoing automated peritoneal dialysis (APD) and continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD).
Method
Demographic data and clinical parameters were recorded. Ultrasonographic peritoneal thickness was measured for all patients from four different quadrants of the abdomen. Inflammatory markers, including intraperitoneal and blood IL-6 and MCP-1 levels, were analyzed. Correlations between peritoneal thickness, inflammatory markers, and clinical outcomes were assessed. Additionally, patient outcomes over a two-year follow-up period, including kidney transplantation, switch to hemodialysis due to peritoneal dialysis failure, and mortality were recorded.
Results
A total of 106 adult peritoneal dialysis patients were included in the study, with 53 undergoing APD and 53 undergoing CAPD. The demographic characteristics of the included patients are presented in Table 1. Analyses revealed that the mean ultrasonographic peritoneal thickness was correlated with intraperitoneal IL-6 (r = 0.211, P = 0.031) and peritoneal fluid MCP-1 levels (r = 0.252, P = 0.010), as well as with blood IL-6 levels (r = 0.320, P = 0.001). However, no significant correlation was found between blood MCP-1 levels and peritoneal thickness (r = −0.009, P = 0.930). In patients with a history of peritonitis, ultrasonographic peritoneal thickness (0.45 (0.20–0.77) vs 0.29 (0.22–0.73), P < 0.001), intraperitoneal IL-6 levels (136.61 (16.21–694.40) vs 19.85 (5.80–1781.00), P < 0.001) and blood Il-6 levels (106.65 (20.12–601.70) vs 55.55 (10.20–372.25), P = 0.001) were found to be significantly higher. Additionally, ultrasonographic peritoneal thickness was observed to increase significantly with decreasing peritoneal permeability in PET testing (Fig. 1) (P = 0.046) and correlated with longer duration on peritoneal dialysis (r = 0.469, P < 0.001).
During the two-year follow-up period, 5 patients underwent kidney transplantation, 24 transitioned to hemodialysis due to peritoneal dialysis failure, and 7 patients died from cardiac causes. A significant association was observed between ultrasonographic mean peritoneal thickness and switch to hemodialysis due to PD failure (PD group: 0.29 (0.20–0.67), PD failure group: 0.36 (0.25–0.77), P = 0.002).
Conclusion
Ultrasonographic peritoneal thickness is significantly associated with intraperitoneal IL-6 and MCP-1 levels, peritoneal permeability, and clinical outcomes in PD patients. The lack of correlation between systemic MCP-1 levels suggests that peritoneal inflammation may be governed by local mechanisms distinct from systemic inflammation. Increased peritoneal thickness correlates with reduced peritoneal permeability, longer PD duration, and history of peritonitis. Furthermore, it is linked to PD failure and adverse patient outcomes. These findings suggest that ultrasonographic peritoneal thickness may serve as a valuable non-invasive marker for monitoring peritoneal membrane integrity and local inflammatory processes and predicting long-term PD outcomes.

title: #1233 Iron deficiency and mortality risk in patients starting peritoneal dialysis
authors: Vladimir Rigodon; Brianna Hartley; John Larkin; Yue Jiao; Len Usvyat; Dinesh Chatoth; Franklin Maddux; Peter Kotanko; Thyago Moraes; Murilo Guedes; Roberto Pecoits-Filho
abstract:
Background and Aims
Iron deficiency is an anemia-independent mortality risk in people with chronic kidney disease who do not require dialysis. Less is known regarding this association in dialysis dependent kidney failure, particularly in peritoneal dialysis (PD). Transferrin saturation (TSAT) and ferritin are commonly assessed in dialysis care to evaluate iron stores. This study investigated the risk of death in incident peritoneal dialysis patients based on iron stores and IV iron therapy.
Method
We evaluated data from incident adult PD patients treated between 2004 and 2011 at a large US dialysis provider network. Patients were included if they were on PD for ≥180 days, had no modality change for ≥90 days, and had at least one measurement of TSAT, ferritin, hemoglobin, and albumin during the 180-day baseline period after initiation of PD. Adjusted Cox proportional hazards model with smoothing splines were used to investigate the hazard ratio for death across continuous values of TSAT and ferritin. Analyses were assessed by IV iron administration status during the baseline period. Adjustments were made for demographic characteristics (age, sex, race, dialysis vintage, and history of hemodialysis before PD start), comorbidities (gastrointestinal bleeding, peripheral vascular disease, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, heart failure, acute myocardial infarction, diabetes mellitus and cancer), laboratory values (albumin, hemoglobin, white blood cell (WBC) counts), and erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA) usage.
Results
Out of the final cohort of 11,013 patients (mean age of 55 years, 54% male, 70% Caucasian, albumin of 3.6 g/dL, TSAT of 31%, and ferritin of 445 ng/dL), 34% received IV iron therapy during the 180-day baseline period after starting PD. Majority (90.5%) of the cohort received an ESA dose during baseline. Patients with TSAT levels <25% were observed to have higher risks of death as compared to higher levels (Fig. 1). This pattern was consistent in the subgroup of patients who did not receive IV iron and was independent of hemoglobin levels. Despite this, the impact of low TSAT on mortality was attenuated in patients who received IV iron. High ferritin was associated with increased risk of death among those who did not receive any IV iron, yet the risk of death was not present in those who received IV iron.
Conclusion
Our analysis revealed that iron deficiency is associated with mortality risk among patients starting PD treatment. This effect was independent from hemoglobin and restricted to those not treated with IV iron. High ferritin levels were associated with an increased mortality risk in those who did not receive IV iron; there was no association between ferritin and mortality risk in patients who received IV iron. These findings suggest a duality in how ferritin can be an indicator of functional iron deficiency and inflammatory-driven mortality risk, which could have potential implications for managing iron therapy in PD patients.

Adjustments were made for demographic characteristics (age, sex, race, dialysis vintage, and history of hemodialysis before PD start), comorbidities (gastrointestinal bleeding, peripheral vascular disease, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, heart failure, acute myocardial infarction, diabetes mellitus and cancer), laboratory values (albumin, hemoglobin, white blood cell (WBC) counts), and erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA) usage.
Results
Out of the final cohort of 11,013 patients (mean age of 55 years, 54% male, 70% Caucasian, albumin of 3.6 g/dL, TSAT of 31%, and ferritin of 445 ng/dL), 34% received IV iron therapy during the 180-day baseline period after starting PD. Majority (90.5%) of the cohort received an ESA dose during baseline. Patients with TSAT levels <25% were observed to have higher risks of death as compared to higher levels (Fig. 1). Despite this, the impact of low TSAT on mortality was attenuated in patients who received IV iron. High ferritin was associated with increased risk of death among those who did not receive any IV iron, yet the risk of death was not present in those who received IV iron.
Conclusion
Our analysis revealed that iron deficiency is associated with mortality risk among patients starting PD treatment. This effect was independent from hemoglobin and restricted to those not treated with IV iron. High ferritin levels were associated with an increased mortality risk in those who did not receive IV iron; there was no association between ferritin and mortality risk in patients who received IV iron. These findings suggest a duality in how ferritin can be an indicator of functional iron deficiency and inflammatory-driven mortality risk, which could have potential implications for managing iron therapy in PD patients.

title: #1600 Stronger together: sodium and chemical displacers combine to improve uremic toxin clearance beyond individual effects
authors: João Brás; Emma Sünnen; Jeroen Vollenbroek; Fokko Wieringa; Karin Gerritsen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Current hemodialysis techniques do not efficiently remove protein-bound uremic toxins (PBUTs), which are highly bound to plasma proteins (e.g. albumin). This leads to PBUT accumulation in end-stage kidney disease, causing complications such as cardiovascular diseases and cognitive impairment. Therefore, developing a method that increases the toxins’ free fraction (FF), which allows higher dialytic removal, is crucial. Currently, various PBUT removal strategies such as adsorbents, increased ionic strength (i.e. high sodium concentration), chemical displacers (e.g. drugs and fatty acids [FAs]), or pH variations, are explored. Displacers compete with PBUTs for the same binding sites on albumin while sodium alters the electrostatic toxin-protein interactions. Using sodium requires removing the excess amount after infusion such that safe concentrations are recirculated back into the patient, as done by Krieter et al. [1], and most studies on chemical displacers focus on the effect of a single displacer. However, these strategies still require further research and safety evaluations before reaching clinical use. In this work, we investigated whether combining PBUT removal methods (chemical displacers and increased ionic strength) resulted in a synergistic increase in toxin free fraction. This strategy aims to increase toxin removal with a lower dose of each displacer and thus with reduced adverse effects.
Method
PBUT FFs were determined with static in vitro “rapid equilibrium dialysis” (RED) protein binding assays (Fig. 1). An albumin solution (40 g/L) was spiked with three toxins at uremic concentrations: indoxyl sulfate (IS), p-cresyl sulfate (pCS), and hippuric acid (HA) (150 µM, 200 µM, and 400 µM, respectively). This solution was combined with NaCl (0.8 M) and displacers (400 µM) including ibuprofen (IBU), furosemide (FURO), caprylic acid (CA) and oleic acid (OA), both individually and combined, to measure their effect on PBUT FF. These solutions were incubated for 4h at 37°C and PBUT concentrations were measured with HPLC. Statistical analysis was performed with 2-way ANOVA.
Results
Figure 2A–C shows the effect of single displacers and the combination with NaCl on the FF of 3 toxins (IS, pCS, HA). IBU increased the FF of IS and pCS by ±2-fold, while FURO affected HA the most (1.7-fold). CA was most effective for IS and pCS.
Adding only NaCl did not affect the FF of the 3 PBUTs. Combined with IBU or FURO, NaCl had no significant effect on IS and pCS. Interestingly, this same combination decreased the FF of HA by 1.2-fold. The synergistic effect was more pronounced with NaCl and FAs. The addition of NaCl to CA increased the FF for all 3 PBUTs compared to CA separately, whereas NaCl with OA increased only that of IS and pCS. The synergistic effect was most visible for pCS FF using NaCl and CA. Their combination showed a 3-fold increase, 1.4 times more than the sum of the individual effects (1.2- and 2-fold, respectively).
The comparison of single component strategies versus the synergistic strategy of adding drugs and FAs is shown in Fig. 2D. There is no significant difference in FF of either IS or pCS when using single displacers or combinations. For HA, a 50:50 combination of IBU and FURO increased the FF compared to the IBU-only group. Notably, with the FAs, the free fraction of HA increased when there was an uneven ratio (1:3 and 3:1) of CA and OA compared to either their separate use, or a 50:50 combination.
Conclusion
We have shown the synergistic use of displacers and increased ionic strength to enhance PBUT release from albumin. Fatty acids showed the most potential due to (1) a strong displacement effect on all three uremic toxins, (2) a positive synergy with NaCl (3-fold increase), and (3) being primarily metabolized by the liver, thus with less risk of systemic accumulation in kidney failure.

title: #3384 Effect of remote ischemic preconditioning on hemodialysis adequacy, hematological, and cardiovascular parameters in hemodialysis patients: a randomized controlled trial
authors: Ahmed Mohamed Naguib Attiya; Hoda Mahmoud Mohammad Abdulaziz; Salwa Elwasif; Samir Sally; Mohamed A Sobh
abstract:
Background and Aims
Remote ischemic preconditioning (RIPC), characterized by transient cycles of ischemia-reperfusion, has demonstrated organ-protective effects against ischemic injury. Hemodialysis (HD) is associated with microcirculatory disturbances, endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and systemic inflammation, which may exacerbate tissue ischemia. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of RIPC on dialysis adequacy, hematological parameters, and cardiovascular outcomes in HD patients.
Method
In this single-blind randomized controlled trial, 55 patients on maintenance HD (>1 year) were allocated to an intervention group (n = 30) receiving RIPC (three cycles of 5-minute ischemia at 200 mmHg via sphygmomanometer cuff on the non-access arm, followed by 5-minute reperfusion) prior to each HD session for 12 weeks, or a control group (n = 25). Dialysis adequacy was assessed via single-pool Kt/V and urea reduction ratio (URR). Hematological parameters (hemoglobin, hematocrit, neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio) and cardiovascular metrics (trans-thoracic echocardiography) were evaluated
Results
Baseline demographics (age: 41 ± 10 vs. 36 ± 12 years; sex, dialysis vintage) were comparable between groups (P > 0.05). Post-intervention, intragroup analysis revealed a significant increase in Kt/V within the RIPC group (1.24 ± 0.23 to 1.36 ± 0.23, P = 0.04), though between-group differences in Kt/V (P = 0.6) and URR (P = 0.5) were nonsignificant. Hemoglobin levels were higher in the RIPC group versus controls (11.7 ± 1.2 vs. 11.1 ± 1.0 g/dL, P < 0.05), with no significant changes in hematocrit, platelets, or inflammatory markers. Echocardiography demonstrated a reduction in intraventricular septal diameter post-HD in the RIPC group (1.39 ± 0.34 to 1.17 ± 0.30 cm) versus controls (1.33 ± 0.29 to 1.32 ± 0.26 cm; P = 0.01), suggesting cardioprotective effects.
Conclusion
RIPC may offer potential benefits in anemia management and cardiovascular remodeling in HD patients, though its impact on dialysis adequacy remains inconclusive. These findings warrant further investigation into RIPC as an adjunctive therapy to mitigate HD-associated complications.
