title: #3115 Serological extracellular matrix fragments may serve as early kidney damage biomarkers in children with defects in Alport genes
authors: Solveig Groen; Federica Genovese; Christoforos Anagnostopoulos; Rebecca Preston; Rachel Lennon
abstract:
Background and Aims
Alport syndrome is a genetic disorder caused by variants in COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5, which encode type IV collagen, a critical component of basement membranes (BMs). The clinical features of Alport syndrome include progressive kidney disease, hearing loss and eye problems. While microscopic haematuria can be present from birth, the condition remains asymptomatic during the early childhood, despite a significant risk of kidney failure. Timely therapeutic intervention with ACE inhibition is crucial, as initiating treatment at an earlier stage can delay the progression to kidney failure by over a decade. However, the lack of diagnostic tools for detecting early BM damage in Alport syndrome remains a major clinical challenge. In this study, we aim to identify blood-based protease-mediated fragments of the extracellular matrix (ECM) as potential early biomarkers of BM damage.
Method
ELISAs (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays) quantified ECM turnover biomarkers in baseline and six months follow-up serum samples from 41 pediatric patients with variants in Alport genes, who were recruited from the Royal Manchester Children's Hospital, Manchester, UK, along with 30 age- and sex-matched healthy pediatric controls (Discovery Life Sciences; Los Osos, CA, USA). The selected biomarkers reflected type I (nordicC1SIG™), III (nordicC3M™), IV (nordicC4M™), and VI (nordicC6M™) collagen degradation, type III (nordicPRO-C3™) and VI (nordicPRO-C6™) collagen formation, type IV collagen turnover (nordicPRO-C4™) and nidogen (nordicNIC™) and laminin (nordicLG1M™) degradation. The patients with Alport were divided into two groups based on absence or presence of proteinuria (urine protein creatinine ratio (uPCR) <30 or >30 mg/mmol).
Results
C4M, LG1M, NIC reflecting BM degradation were reduced in both Alport groups compared to healthy controls (Fig. 1A and B: C4M and NIC P < 0.0001; Fig. 1C: LG1M P = 0.0006, P = 0.0004), while PRO-C4 reflecting BM turnover was elevated in the Alport groups compared to healthy controls (Fig. 1D: PRO-C4 P < 0.0001). PRO-C3 and PRO-C6, reflecting interstitial matrix formation, were reduced in both Alport groups compared to healthy controls (Fig. 1E: PRO-C3 P < 0.0001; Fig. 1F: PRO-C6 P = 0.0068, P = 0.0051). Among the biomarkers reflecting interstitial matrix degradation, C3M was reduced in Alport group with uPCR >30 (Fig. 1G: C3M P = 0.0231), C6M was elevated in the Alport group with uPCR < 30 (Fig. 1H: C6M P = 0.0130), and C1SIG was elevated in both Alport groups (Fig. 1I: C1SIG P = 0.0003, P = 0.0111) compared to healthy controls. No significant differences were observed between the two Alport groups for any of the biomarkers.
Conclusion
The decrease in C4M, LG1M and NIC (BM degradation), PRO-C3 and PRO-C6 (interstitial matrix formation), along with the increase in C1SIG and C6M (interstitial matrix degradation) and PRO-C4 (BM turnover), indicate a significantly altered turnover of both BM and interstitial matrix in pediatric patients with defects in the Alport genes. Since these biomarkers were already altered in patients with no detectable proteinuria, they may indicate early BM and kidney damage, and their use could enable earlier initiation of kidney-protective treatments in children with Alport syndrome.

title: #31 Identification and characterization of genetic founder effects in Chuxiong-Yi populations with extremely high local incidence of Gitelman syndrome
authors: Jian Han; Jinghua Gao; Lanxin MA; Dezhen Zhang; Ling Wang; Xueli Yang; Yiyi Luo; Yanqiong Wang; Heng Luo; Yagang Xie
abstract:
Background and Aims
Gitelman syndrome is a rare, autosomal recessive, salt-losing tubulopathy characterized by hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesaemia, and hypercalciuria. Incidence of GS in European population is 1 in 40000, but the one in Chinese remains unknown. Loss of function in both copy of SLC12A3 is thought to be the cause of GS, and the affected patients were either homozygous for two causative SLC12A3 alleles with loss of function or heterozygous for one causative SLC12A3 allele with loss of function plus one large genomics rearrangement containing the SLC12A3. While the spectrum of causative SLC12A3 alleles exhibits heterogeneity in GS, some of them show ethnicity specificity. In this study, we identified and characterized a genetic founder's effect in a Yi population with an extremely high local incidence of GS in rural Chuxiong area of China.
Method
Whole exome sequencing (WES) was used to etiology study the first two probands with suspicion of GS, and the capillary sequencing was used to confirm the results from WES. Diagnosis of GS was confirmed by identification of two mutant alleles of SLC12A3. The pedigrees were built based on information from family surveys. Targeted sequencing was used to diagnose new patients and to detect all carriers. The MassARRAY System was used to genotype the selected tagSNPs, and the Haploview 4.2 software were to construct haplotypes in the region of SLC12A3. Incidence of GS was calculated based on the total patients and the total local populations, and the allele frequency was predicted by targeted sequencing 500 randomly selected health individuals from the local population.
Results
As part of etiology study on rare diseases, we identified homozygous variants of SLC12A3: c.1262G > T (p.C421F) from 2 patients with clinical suspicion of GS by using WES, and these results were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. In a data bases searching, we noted that the C421F variant had previously been reported in two patients with GS, including one Chinese (compound heterozygous) and one Japanese (homozygous). Thus, the diagnoses of GS were confirmed in both patients. Family studies revealed that the both patients are all Yi ethnic but from two unrelated Yi families in the same rural community, where 98% of the population are Yi. In further local clinical studies, we found additional 20 patients with clinical suspicion of GS from 12 unrelated Yi families. By using targeted sequencing, all of these patients were confirmed to be homozygous for C421F, so all patients were diagnosed with GS All parents and other available family members were then screened for carriers, and 31 asymptomatic carriers including all parents were detected. All of these suggests that homozygous C421F should be the cause of GS in all patients, and that the high local incidence of GS may be due to genetic founder effects. To support this hypothesis, we genotyped 30 tagSNPs selected from internal and flanking sequences (1.5 MB region) of SLC12A3 in all patients and carriers using the MassARRAY System and built their haplotypes using Haploview 4.2 software analysis. The results showed a same mutation-carrying haplotype in all patients (homozygous) and carriers (heterozygous), which supported that the causative variant find in the local should be derived from the same ancestor (genetic founder). Based on the total patients (22) and the total local population (appr 20000), we estimate that the local incidence of GS is close to 1 in 1000, which is 40 times of the incidence reported in the European population. By screening the C421F variant in 500 local randomly selected individuals, we calculated the allele frequency of p.C421F in local was 3%. Currently, the screening of the founder variant in an expending population is underway to identify more patients and all carriers.
Conclusion
We reported a Yi population with an extremely high incidence of GS (1 in 1000) in rural community of Chuxiong and determined the homozygous C421F variant of the SLC12A3 is the causative in all phenotypic patients. Haplotype study suggests that the C421F variant is the genetic founder of GS in local, and the extremely high incidence of GS should be resulted from the genetic founder effect.

title: #17 Serum metabolic profiling analysis of Gitelman syndrome by untargeted metabolomics
authors: Jian Han; Lanxin MA; Jinghua Gao; Honghan Zhang; Jin He; Dezhen Zhang; Meifen Yang; Yagang Xie; Heng Luo
abstract:
Background and Aims
The early clinical signs of Gitelman syndrome (GS) are often non-specific, making diagnosis primarily dependent on genetic testing methods. Identifying potential biomarkers linked to GS is crucial for the early diagnosis and treatment of the condition. This study aims to examine the changes in serum metabolite levels in GS patients and to validate their potential as diagnostic biomarkers.
Method
This study analyzed 5 GS patients from Yunnan's Yi community and 7 controls from the same area. Serum samples were collected and analyzed using UHPLC-Q-TOF for untargeted metabolomics analysis. PCA and OPLS-DA were used for statistical evaluation, and metabolites' pathways were explored with HMDB and LMSD. Differential metabolites were identified using heat map significance (P < 0.05), fold change (FC > 1.5 or FC < 2/3), and VIP > 1 criteria. ROC curves were applied to evaluate these metabolites as potential biomarkers.
Results
Serum metabolomics analysis revealed a strong association between differential metabolic pathways and lipid metabolism in patients with GS. This study identified 27 differentially expressed metabolites through screening and enrichment processes. A pathway enrichment analysis was conducted on these metabolites, identifying 10 metabolic pathways related to GS. The results indicated that the most significant metabolic pathways included glycerophospholipid metabolism, linoleic acid metabolism, and the biosynthetic metabolism of pantothenic acid and coenzyme A. Hexanoylglycine (HG) and PE (P-18:0/19:1) were primarily noted among the differentially expressed metabolites. Additionally, we measured serum total cholesterol (TC) levels and body mass index (BMI) in patients with GS. The findings showed that GS patients had significantly lower serum TC levels and BMI values compared to the healthy control group. This suggests that their lipid metabolism function may be impaired, aligning with our untargeted metabolomics analysis results.
Conclusion
This study highlights the potential significance of lipid metabolism in the development of GS. HG and PE (P-18:0/19:1) could be novel biomarkers for diagnosing GS.

title: #1471 A novel CT-based radiomics approach for kidney function evaluation in ADPKD
authors: Luca Calvaruso; Pierluigi Fulignati; Luigi Larosa; Huong Elena Tran; Claudio Votta; Carla Cipri; Luigi Natale; Viola D'ambrosio; Giulia Condello; Francesco Pesce; Luca Boldrini; Giuseppe Grandaliano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Management of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) might take advantage of the use of new tools to predict risk of progression towards end stage kidney disease. The aim of this study is to explore the potential of radiomic features obtained from computed tomography (CT) scans for the prediction of kidney function decline over time of ADPKD patients.
Method
We retrospectively selected a cohort of 58 ADPKD patients who routinely underwent CT scan for total kidney volume (TKV) assessment from February 2020 to March 2021. An expert radiologist generated a region-of-interest segmentation for cystic kidneys from which we extracted 217 radiomic features. In a subgroup of 51 patients with at least 3 serum creatinine measurements, on the basis of eGFR we identified 26 rapid progressors to ESKD (>3 ml/min/year), and we developed a radiomic model to discriminate rapid from not rapid progressors. Area under the curve (AUC) of the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) and sensitivity were employed to evaluate models’ performance.
Results
The most statistically significant radiomic feature (F_cm.corr) (p-value = 0.04) associated with rapid progression showed an AUC (95% CI) of 0.78 (0.65–0.90) and a sensitivity of 0.92 (0.78–0.98). On the contrary, the logistic regression model based on the ht-TKV presented a lower AUC (95% CI) of 0.65 (0.49–0.80), with a sensitivity 0.62 (0.42–0.78).
Conclusion
We developed a model based on the radiomic feature F_cm.corr that was able to discriminate rapid progressors. Further studies on larger cohort are warranted to validate our findings and to confirm the role of radiomics in ADPKD management.

title: #3623 Lanthanum carbonate does not reduce urinary oxalate excretion in hyperoxaluric kidney stone formers
authors: Els Van De Perre; Dieter De Clerck; Pozdzik Agnieszka; Patrick D'haese; Philippe Durieux; Sophie Boesmans; Simon van Hooland; Christian Tielemans; Frédéric Cotton; Karl Martin Wissing
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyperoxaluria is an important metabolic risk factor for kidney stone formation. Currently available treatment options for idiopathic hyperoxaluria have limited efficacy and are difficult to maintain in the long-term. Pre-clinical data suggested that Lanthanum Carbonate (LaCa), a non-calcium phosphate binder might effectively bind oxalate. We performed a multicentre interventional, open-label, dose-response study to assess the efficacy and safety of LaCa in the reduction of urinary oxalate excretion in kidney stone formers with idiopathic hyperoxaluria.
Method
Kidney stone formers with urinary oxalate excretion >45 mg/24 hours were treated with LaCa at a dose of 750 mg daily during a first 14-day treatment period, followed by a second 14-day treatment period with LaCa treatment at a dose of 1500 mg daily (Fig. 1). The study was powered for the primary efficacy endpoint of detecting a ≥20% reduction of urinary oxalate excretion after the first treatment period. Secondary endpoints were the incremental reduction of urinary oxalate excretion with LaCa dose increase to 1500 mg during the second treatment period and the effect of LaCa on serum phosphate and urinary phosphate excretion.
Results
Forty-four patients started the study of whom 42 completed the two months follow-up. LaCa treatment with both the 750 mg and 1500 mg dose had no effect on urinary oxalate excretion (52.0 mg/24 h at BL, 49.1 mg/24 h AFTP and 52.6 mg/24 h ASTP) (Table 1). Urinary phosphate excretion, expressed as urinary phosphate/creatinine ratio and as fractional excretion of phosphate decreased significantly after treatment with 1500 mg LaCa (from 17.1 mmol/g at BL to 15.2 mmol/g ASTP for urinary phosphate/creatinine ratio and from 16.6% at BL to 14.7% ASTP for fractional excretion of phosphate), while LaCa treatment had no effect on serum phosphate levels (0.97 mmol/L at BL and 0.95 mmol/L ASTP) (Table 1).
Conclusion
Short-term treatment with LaCa at doses up to 1500 mg did not reduce urinary oxalate excretion in kidney stone formers with idiopathic hyperoxaluria. Urinary phosphate excretion decreased slightly without effect on serum phosphate levels. LaCa in its current formulation is not a good treatment for the reduction of urinary oxalate excretion in kidney stone formers with idiopathic hyperoxaluria.

title: #197 A phase 4 study to evaluate the safety and tolerability of higher infusion rates of agalsidase beta to shorten the infusion duration in Fabry disease—Preliminary data
authors: Maryam Banikazemi; Ozlem Goker-Alpan; Khan Nedd; Mrinalini Sarkar; William Wilcox; Chase Lee
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fabry disease is an inborn, chronic disorder caused by mutations in the gene encoding the lysosomal enzyme, α-Galactosidase A (α-Gal A). These mutations cause αGAL A deficiency, which leads to the buildup of glycosphingolipids, especially globotriaosylceramide (GL3), in various cells and tissues. Such accumulation impairs organ function, increasing the risk of renal failure, cardiovascular issues, and stroke in patients with Fabry disease. Fabry disease is typically categorized as classical, or later-onset. Classical has little or no α-Gal A activity due to GLA variants, whereas later-onset retains higher α-Gal A activity. Agalsidase beta (1 mg/kg biweekly) is an enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) for Fabry disease. It has been shown that treatment with agalsidase beta preserves kidney function and delays progression to severe clinical events among adult patients with Fabry disease. The present study was conducted to evaluate the safety and tolerability of agalsidase beta at the approved dose at an increased infusion rate with a reduced total infusion volume.
Method
This phase 4 (NCT06019728) study is an open-label, single-arm, multi-center study conducted in the US. The infusion durations were reduced by 20 or 30 minutes from the initial duration for each subsequent infusion until reaching 20 minutes as defined in the protocol. All patients were given acetaminophen and diphenhydramine as premedication before each infusion. The primary endpoints were percentage reduction of infusion duration from prestudy mean of the most recent three infusions and from an initial 120 minutes, along with the shortest infusion duration each participant can tolerate.
Results
Eight patients (3 females, 2 non-classic males, and 3 classic males) who had been previously treated with agalsidase beta for at least 3 months without any infusion-associated reactions (IARs) during at least 3 most recent infusions were enrolled. The age, body weight, prestudy duration of agalsidase beta treatment, and prestudy average duration of infusions were 19–62 years, 62.5–100.0 kg, 43–244 months, and 90–222 minutes, respectively. The duration of the first infusion in the study was 120 minutes for 6 patients, 90 minutes for 1 classic male patient, and 60 minutes for 1 non-classic male patient. All patients have reached 20-minute infusions. No IARs have been observed during the study. The plasma lyso-GL3 levels remained low and stable, except a transient mild elevation in a patient after skipping an infusion. Antidrug antibodies to agalsidase beta remained negative in 7 patients. Only 1 patient (non-classic male) was seropositive at baseline. The titer was low (1:800) and remained in the range of 1:400–800.
Conclusion
The results demonstrate that agalsidase beta infusions can be safely administered in as short as 20 minutes in ERT-experienced patients without IARs. These findings will help establish a protocol to reduce the duration of agalsidase beta infusions and minimize the resulting treatment burden.

title: #2556 Exploring exosome-mediated effects on renal pathology in Anderson Fabry disease
authors: Livia Lenzini; Maria Lina Massimino; Monica Vettore; Elisabetta Iori; Anna Olena Kalmykova; Giulia Annesi; Giorgia Gugelmo; Gianni Carraro; Alessandro Bertoli; Federico Nalesso; Gian Paolo Fadini; Nicola Vitturi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Despite substantial progress in understanding the molecular basis of genetic lysosomal storage diseases, the systemic mechanisms linking lysosomal defects in specific cells to widespread organ damage remain unclear, particularly in Anderson-Fabry disease (AFD). This project introduces a novel perspective by investigating the role of exosomes as mediators of intercellular communication and contributors to the spread of pathology in AFD.
The aim of this study is to explore exosome-mediated renal cell damage mechanisms in AFD progression.
Methods
Urinary exosomes were isolated from adult patients with AFD and from age- and sex-matched healthy controls by ultracentrifugation. Quality and quantity were checked by cytofluorimetry using p63 and p81 markers. Renal cells (HEK293) were incubated with the same amounts of exosomes for 48 and 72 hours and, then, autophagic flux and endoplasmic reticulum stress were assessed by western blot analysis. Cell respiration was monitored using the SeaHorse system (Agilent Technologies).
Results
Incubating healthy renal cells (HEK293) with exosomes isolated from the urine of AFD patients (male: 3; female: 4) caused a disruption of autophagic flux after 72 hours. This was evidenced by an increase in the LC3-II/LC3-I ratio (A.U. at 48 h: 0.68 ± 0.19; at 72 h: 1.14 ± 0.42, P < 0.05), a marker of autophagy, along with the lack of p62 degradation (A.U. at 48 h: 0.07 ± 0.03; at 72 h: 0.05 ± 0.04, P > 0.05), a protein typically degraded during properly functioning autophagy.
No significant effects were observed when HEK293 cells were incubated with exosomes derived from the urine of healthy volunteers (male: 3; female: 2) (LC3-II/LC3-I ratio: A.U. at 48 h: 1 ± 0.23, at 72 h: 1 ± 0.38, P > 0.05; p62: A.U. at 48 h: 0.05 ± 0.03, at 72 h: 0.04 ± 0.02, P > 0.05).
No differences were observed in other cellular processes (e.g. cell respiration and endoplasmic reticulum stress) after 24, 48, and 72 hours of incubation with exosomes from either experimental group.
Conclusion
These findings demonstrate that exosomes derived from AFD patients disrupt normal autophagic processes, providing a potential novel mechanism for the pathogenesis of the disease. Furthermore, the effect of exosomes on autophagic flux appears to be specific, as no alterations were detected in other cellular processes (e.g. cell respiration or endoplasmic reticulum stress).
This study offers novel insights into the potential role of exosomes in AFD progression, challenging the traditional understanding of this disease as a primarily localized disorder characterized by substrate accumulation confined to cells expressing the genetically altered enzyme. Instead, it suggests that the systemic, multi-organ manifestations of AFD may arise, at least in part, from the active dissemination of toxic metabolites and signaling molecules via exosomes.

title: #2522 KDASDB: a comprehensive and user-friendly database for alternative splicing in kidney diseases
authors: Yalan Kuang; Yilong Chen; Haopeng Yu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney disease has been a major public health concern for many years, and understanding its causes, mechanisms, and progression is crucial for developing effective prevention and treatment strategies. Alternative splicing (AS), a key gene regulatory mechanism, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of kidney diseases. Although the role of AS in kidney diseases is increasingly recognized, there is currently no dedicated database for alternative splicing associated with kidney diseases. To address this gap and facilitate a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying kidney diseases, as well as the identification of potential therapeutic targets, we developed the Kidney Diseases Alternative Splicing Database (KDASDB, http://www.hxdsjzx.cn/KDASDB).
Method
Human and mouse sequences were downloaded from the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) and Sequence Read Archive (SRA), and we also collected data from papers using PubMed and Google Scholar. Trim Galore was used to perform quality control on the raw sequencing data using the default parameters. To eliminate the bias of assembly tools, we initially assembled sample by sample using both the HISAT2-StringTie pipeline and the Star2-Cufflinks pipeline. To make better use of biological replicates while reducing interference from other studies, we employed a two-step assembly strategy. We first merged the transcripts on a study-by-study basis using Cuffmerge, and then reassembled them using the “merge” function within StringTie to obtain uniform transcripts. We used rMATS to primarily identify and quantify alternative splicing events (ASEs). Additionally, we annotated AS events that may affect protein domains.
Results
KDASDB includes a collection of 90,273 alternative splicing events identified from 2,608 samples, 29 types of kidney diseases, and 126 projects, covering both humans and mice. We identified 3,354 novel alternative splicing events in humans and 5,638 in mice. KDASDB offers user-friendly query and visualization interfaces, enabling researchers to quickly access AS data and explore its biological functions. As an example, we use VEGFA to demonstrate how to leverage our database to identify disease-associated ASEs.
Conclusion
By providing comprehensive insights into the roles of ASEs in kidney disease, KDASDB will help researchers gain a deeper understanding of the pathogenesis of kidney diseases and aid in the search for new treatment strategies.

title: #1726 Effect of tyrosine kinase inhibitors on hyperfiltration response and renal functions in nephrectomized renal cell carcinoma patients
authors: Muhammed Furkan Yeşil; Guldehan Haberal; Bulent Altun; Yunus Erdem
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is a disease that is resistant to classical cancer treatments such as systemic chemotherapy and radiotherapy and is instead treated with surgery, ablative methods, immunotherapy, and targeted agents. Nephrectomy is frequently used and causes dramatic nephron loss. The hyperfiltration response that occurs after nephron loss appears as a compensatory mechanism. In this study, the effects of Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (TKIs), used in the treatment of RCC, on the hyperfiltration response and renal functions were investigated.
Method
A total of 248 patients who were either followed up without treatment or received TKI within 12 months post-operatively, among those who underwent surgery for RCC at Hacettepe University Hospitals between January 2015 and June 2023, were included in the study. Five-year follow-ups of the patients were examined. To investigate the effect of the timing of TKI initiation on the hyperfiltration response, the patient group who started the medication was divided into two subgroups: early (0–3 months) and late (0–12 months). The inclusion and exclusion processes of the patients are shown in the flowchart (Fig. 1).
Results
Basic clinical and demographic data of the patients are summarized in Fig. 2. No difference was observed between the preoperative estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and proteinuria values of the groups that did not receive TKI and those that received early or late treatment (P = 0.24, P = 0.145). The postoperative eGFR course was similar in patients who received and did not receive TKI. In the group that started TKI early, following the decrease in eGFR in the first month postoperatively, it was observed that the eGFR values stabilized between the 1st and 6th months with the initiation of TKI. In the late-start group, after a rapid decrease between the 0th and 3rd months, the eGFR values were found to be clinically and statistically lower than the other group at the 3rd month (P = 0.03). In this group, it was observed that eGFR values increased after the 3rd month with the initiation of TKI, and the difference between the two groups became statistically significant at the 24th month (P = 0.04) (Fig. 3). When proteinuria values were compared between the three groups, proteinuria values in the group that started early treatment at the 1st, 6th, 12th, 18th, and 24th months were found to be statistically significantly higher than in the other groups (P < 0.05). It was shown that the presence of hypertension before diagnosis was associated with lower eGFR in the preoperative period and up to the 24th month postoperatively, independent of TKI use (Fig. 4).
Conclusion
Although eGFR loss was observed in all patients after nephrectomy, no significant difference was shown between the groups that received and did not receive TKI (Fig. 5). In the group that started TKI after nephrectomy, regardless of whether the drug was initiated early or late, no negative impact of starting the drug on the hyperfiltration response could be demonstrated. It was determined that the decreased eGFR after nephrectomy remained stable or did not decrease further with early treatment in advanced-stage patients and with late treatment in low-stage patients. In light of these findings, it is suggested that TKIs may be safe and beneficial for renal survival in the presence of the necessary indications, even in patients with low eGFR.

title: #925 Genotyping and phenotyping early and very early autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease onset
authors: Maria Varveri; Myrto Kostopoulou; Tsielestina Poulli; Angeliki Poula; Niki Markou; Emmanouil Kanavakis; Eleni Frangou; George Tsirpanlis
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is usually diagnosed in adults. Early (18 months–15 years) and very early (<18 months) onset (EO and VEO) forms of the disease are rarer. Genetic and clinical characteristics may be of importance. This study investigates genetic and phenotypic profiles in a group with EO and VEO ADPKD patients.
Method
From a total of 135 ADPKD patients with genetic analysis followed in the outpatient ADPKD clinic at our hospital, 27 were diagnosed before the age of 15 (4 VEO and 23 EO). All patients underwent genetic testing, including targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) of over 600 clinically relevant genes, Sanger sequencing, and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed in 14 EO and VEO patients at study entry, revealing more than 10 renal cysts. Younger children with a positive family history (FH) displayed at least one cyst on echography, while two without FH had multiple renal cysts.
Results
The median age at diagnosis for the 27 EO and VEO patients (15 females, 12 males) was 4 years (IQR: 3–7 years), and the median age at study entry was 13 years (IQR: 4–17 years). Twenty-one (77.8%) patients had positive FH and 6 did not. The ADPKD parent of 9 VEO and EO patients developed end stage renal disease (ESRD) at a median age of 43 (42–48) years. Among the 12 remaining EO and VEO patients with positive FH, 6 had ADPKD parents with an e-GFR lower than expected for their age (<90 ml/min for 40–44 years old, <75 for 45–49 years old and <60 for 50–55 years old) while the other 6 did not. At study entry, 46% of the 27 patients had hypertension and among the 14 patients with MRI data, 36% were classified in Mayo Clinic Imaging Category 1C, 29% in 1D, 14% in 1A, 14% in 1E and 7% in 1B). Their e-GFR was 120 (118–120) ml/min at study entry. The predicted time to ESRD, calculated using the Irazabal MV et al formula (JASN 2015), was 37 (25–42) years. Genetic testing confirmed a diagnosis in 26 out of 27 patients. Variants in PKD1 were detected in 23 (85%) and in PKD2 gene in 2 (7%) patients. Two patients had 2 pathogenic variants, the first in PKD1 and SLC7A9 genes and the second in PKD1 and PKHD1 genes, while 1 revealed negative result. Twenty-one (81%) of the PKD1 patients had truncated variants (38% nonsense, 31% frameshift, 4% splicing and 8% CNV-large deletions) while 19% had non-truncating (all were missense, 3 pathogenic and 2 likely pathogenic). Among the 4 VEO ADPKD patients, one had a large deletion (PKD1 exons 25–33 del), one had a frameshift PKD1 variant, one had the above-mentioned double variants (in PKD1 and SLC7A9 genes), and the last one (with multiple renal cysts, normal kidney size and no hepatic cysts) had negative genetic testing.
Conclusion
Truncating pathogenic PKD1 variants, large deletions and double genetic injuries predominate in VEO and EO ADPKD. Family history and phenotype are also emphasized, together forming a distinctive genetic and phenotypic profile that may indicate early ADPKD onset.

title: #427 Not a cluster of grapes, but bananas: cord-like three-dimensional structure of cysts in ADPKD supports tubular obstruction hypothesis
authors: Ming Yang; Xiu Yang; Ming Cheng; Shuai Han; Changlin Mei
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is a progressive genetic kidney disease and one of the leading causes of end-stage renal disease. Despite the identification of the causative genes, the pathogenesis of ADPKD remains unclear and hampers the development of effective treatments. The present study aims to elucidate the three-dimensional structure of the kidneys of polycystic kidney disease (PKD) mouse models and its implications for the disease mechanism.
Method
We performed histological observations on the kidneys of rapid-onset and chronic-onset mouse models of PKD, and also transparentized the kidneys for three-dimensional imaging.
Results
We discovered that the cysts had a cord-like three-dimensional structure resembling a cluster of bananas rather than a bunch of grapes, suggesting tubular obstruction as the initiating event. Furthermore, the presence of epithelial cell bridges within the renal tubules, as observed in both three-dimensional images and two-dimensional pathological sections, was identified as a potential causative factor for the obstruction. In addition, a comparative analysis of Ki67 staining in kidney tissue at various developmental stages was conducted with wild type mice. This analysis revealed no significant differences, suggesting that there was no additional cell proliferation.
Conclusion
The findings of this study provide robust support for the obstruction hypothesis and significantly challenge the proliferation hypothesis for ADPKD. These results offer novel insights that could lead to the development of more effective treatment strategies.

Furthermore, the presence of epithelial cell bridges within the renal tubules, as observed in both three-dimensional images and two-dimensional pathological sections, was identified as a potential causative factor for the obstruction. In addition, a comparative analysis of Ki67 staining in kidney tissue at various developmental stages was conducted with wild type mice. The findings of this study provide robust support for the obstruction hypothesis and significantly challenge the proliferation hypothesis for ADPKD. These results offer novel insights that could lead to the development of more effective treatment strategies.

title: #2399 Evaluation of eGFR slope and ht-TKV after one year of treatment with dapagliflozin in ADPKD patients: a retrospective case series analysis
authors: Giulia Condello; Pierluigi Fulignati; Viola D'ambrosio; Chiara Tacente; Ilaria Mariani; Luca Calvaruso; Francesco Pesce; Giuseppe Grandaliano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) patients have been excluded from recent trials demonstrating the nephroprotective and cardioprotective effects of SGLT-2 inhibitors (iSGLT-2). However, in ADPKD, these drugs may have additional benefits: cystic epithelium exhibits a strong dependence on glycolysis compared to oxidative phosphorylation. By inducing a metabolic switch toward ketogenesis, iSGLT-2 could potentially slow renal cyst growth. Evidence from animal models is conflicting, and limited studies in ADPKD patients report variable results, including an increase in kidney volume after dapagliflozin administration and inconclusive nephroprotective effects. A recent trial showed beneficial effects of dapagliflozin on eGFR and kidney volume, but only when combined with tolvaptan. Current studies have not incorporated baseline predictions of renal function and volume changes based on the Mayo classification. This study aims to describe changes in height-adjusted total kidney volume (ht-TKV) and eGFR after one year of dapagliflozin treatment and compare them with expected changes according to each patient's Mayo classification.
Method
This retrospective study was conducted at the A. Gemelli Hospital in Rome, involving six ADPKD patients. All patients underwent abdominal imaging with ht-TKV calculation and Mayo class determination, along with blood tests for eGFR assessment (CKD-EPI 2021 formula) at baseline (T0) and after 12 months (T1) of dapagliflozin treatment (10 mg daily). The observed eGFR slope was calculated as the difference between eGFR at T0 and T1 and compared to the expected annual eGFR decline according to each patient's Mayo class. Similarly, the observed change in ht-TKV was compared to the expected annual increase for each Mayo class. Statistical comparisons assessed deviations from predicted outcomes.
Results
Table 1 summarizes the clinical characteristics and Mayo classifications of the patients. In the patient with Mayo Class 1C (Fig. 1a) a reduction in ht-TKV was documented (from 1255 to 1173 ml/m). For the patient with Mayo Class 1D (Fig. 1b), the observed ht-TKV increase was 3.8%, lower than the expected increase (4.5%–6%). In the remaining four patients (one with Mayo Class 1A and three with Mayo Class 1E), observed ht-TKV changes were consistent with expected outcomes. Regarding eGFR slopes, the three patients with Mayo Class 1E experienced slower declines (−2.2, −2.8, and −4.4 ml/min/1.73 m², respectively) than expected (−4.7 ml/min/1.73 m²). The patient with Mayo Class 1C exhibited an eGFR decline matching the expected slope, while patients with Mayo Classes 1A and 1D showed a greater decline than predicted.
Conclusion
To our knowledge, this is the first study to report reduction in renal volume and slower-than-expected ht-TKV increase in two ADPKD patients after dapagliflozin therapy. In the remaining patients, dapagliflozin had no discernible effect on renal cyst growth. However, among the three patients with Mayo Class 1E (at high risk for rapid progression to ESRD), dapagliflozin demonstrated a nephroprotective effect by slowing eGFR decline. While these findings require validation in larger cohorts, they suggest potential benefits of dapagliflozin in specific subgroups of ADPKD patients.

title: #2395 Association of renal diameters with ADPKD gene variants: focus on PKD2 truncating mutations
authors: Giulia Condello; Pierluigi Fulignati; Viola D'ambrosio; Chiara Tacente; Ilaria Mariani; Luca Calvaruso; Giuseppe Grandaliano; Francesco Pesce
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common monogenic inherited nephropathy, caused by mutations in the PKD1 or PKD2 genes. The disease primarily affects the kidneys, leading to an increase in kidney volume and progressive decline in renal function, potentially culminating in end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Kidney size is a key factor in the prognostic evaluation of ADPKD patients. Studies on the phenotypic variability of the disease have shown that genetic variants significantly influence clinical outcomes. It is well established that PKD1 mutations (ADPKD type 1) are associated with a more severe clinical phenotype than PKD2 mutations (ADPKD type 2), with PKD1 truncating mutations, in particular, linked to worse outcomes. However, the phenotypic impact of different PKD2 gene variants has not been thoroughly investigated. Therefore, this study aims to evaluate whether PKD2 truncating mutations are associated with a more severe clinical phenotype compared to non-truncating mutations, similar to observations for PKD1 mutations.
Method
This single-centre, retrospective study was conducted at the A. Gemelli Hospital in Rome, involving a cohort of 112 ADPKD patients (Table 1). All participants underwent genetic testing, haematochemical evaluations, abdominal ultrasounds, and renal diameter measurements. The cohort was divided into four subgroups based on the type of mutation: non-truncating PKD2, truncating PKD2, non-truncating PKD1, and truncating PKD1. The primary objective was to determine statistically significant differences in renal diameters, particularly between the PKD2 truncating subgroup and the other groups. Statistical analyses used the average bilateral renal diameter for each patient, employing linear regression models and Spearman's correlation tests to assess associations and correlations. Statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05.
Results
Patients with PKD2 truncating mutations had significantly larger renal diameters than those with non-truncating mutations of the PKD2 gene, a difference that remained significant after adjusting for gender and age (P = 0.03, Beta = 2.54). However, no statistically significant differences in renal diameters were observed between the PKD2 truncating group and the PKD1 non-truncating group, even after adjusting for gender and age. The median average renal diameters were as follows: 13 cm (11.50–15.40 cm) in the non-truncating PKD2 group, 14.15 cm (11.10–17.90 cm) in the truncating PKD2 group, 14.70 cm (12.20–17.10 cm) in the non-truncating PKD1 group, and 16 cm (13.60–18.90 cm) in the truncating PKD1 group (Fig. 1). Additionally, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) showed a strong negative correlation with renal diameter (Beta = −0.612, P = 9.81E−13).
Conclusion
To our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate that in ADPKD type 2, truncating mutations in the PKD2 gene are associated with a more severe clinical phenotype, characterized by larger renal diameters, compared to non-truncating PKD2 mutations. Notably, the renal phenotype of patients with PKD2 truncating mutations was not significantly different from that of patients with PKD1 non-truncating mutations. While larger studies are needed to validate these findings, our results suggest that distinctions based on genetic variants may have prognostic value even within ADPKD type 2.

title: #2357 Kidney volume based on multi-dimensional orthogonal ultrasound measurements is more accurate than kidney length in evaluation of kidney growth in paediatric ADPKD
authors: Luc Breysem; Frederik De Keyzer; Djalila Mekahli
abstract:
Background and Aims
Monitoring kidney growth is crucial in paediatric autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). While kidney length is often used as a surrogate for kidney growth, its accuracy in reflecting dynamic volume changes, especially during growth spurts, is unclear. In addition to kidney length, this study investigated the value of measuring kidney width and depth on ultrasound to estimate total kidney volume (TKV) in a cohort of paediatric ADPKD patients, focusing on the contribution of each dimension to overall kidney growth during childhood.
Method
All 2D ultrasound measurements of patients included in the international ADPedKD registry extracted in November 2024 were evaluated. A total of 1506 patients and 6648 entries (see Fig. 1) were analysed. Of these, only a subset of 611 patients with 1625 evaluations (∼2.7 evaluations per patient) had completed data for length, width, and depth of both kidneys, allowing for TKV estimation using the 2D ellipsoid formula. Regression analysis was performed to assess the growth rates of kidney length, width and depth, averaged over both kidneys, as well as estimated TKV before and after the age of 10 years.
Results
The 611 patients (309 females, 302 males) with complete imaging data had proven genotypes of PKD1 (n = 292), PKD2 (n = 29), GANAB (n = 1), and no genotyping in the remaining cases (n = 289). Regression analysis demonstrated a marked acceleration in TKV growth after age 10 years (30.5 mL/yr) compared to before (10.9 mL/yr), representing a nearly threefold increase. However, when looking at kidney length growth rates, this substantial increase in TKV was not present at all; they even decreased slightly in the second decade (0.33 vs 0.31 cm/yr). In contrast, both width and depth exhibited similar increased growth rates after age 10, with width increasing from 0.09 to 0.18 cm/yr and depth increasing from 0.09 to 0.14 cm/yr. Although these increases were smaller in magnitude than the change in TKV, they demonstrate that width and depth contribute significantly to the observed volumetric growth acceleration in ADPKD patients after 10 years of age.
Conclusion
Our results indicate that, in paediatric ADPKD patients, incorporating kidney width and depth measurements in routine ultrasound assessments provides crucial kidney growth information not adequately captured by kidney length alone. This allows to provide a kidney volume estimation and as such a more accurate and comprehensive assessment of disease progression.

title: #3530 Prenatal ultrasound features and long-term prognosis of very-early-onset autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
authors: Eleonora Superchi; Viviana Palazzo; Laurence Heidet; Samantha Innocenti; Paola Romagnani; Olivia Boyer; Francesca Becherucci
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) has a highly variable phenotye, with its most severe manifestations being an early (EO) or very early (VEO) onset of the disease. EO and VEO definition implies the occurrence in infancy of ADPKD-related chronic kidney disease (CKD), defined as the contemporary presence of bilateral nephromegaly and one sign of initial kidney function impairment. We argue that, even if not in the presence of such a severe phenotype, it is still worth recognising in utero ADPKD to address the affected patients to early nephrological care.
The aim of our study was to describe prenatal characteristics of patients with an in utero diagnosis of ADPKD and define their long-term prognosis in terms of incidence of hypertension and CKD.
Method
This was a multicentre retrospective observational study. All patients with in utero characteristics of VEO-ADPKD from 1981 to 2024 were enrolled at two centres in France and Italy, namely Hôpital Necker Enfants Malades, Paris, and Meyer Children's Hospital IRCCS, Florence. The definition of VEO-ADPKD was the in utero ADPKD diagnosis due to (i) multiple bilateral cysts and/or (ii) enlarged kidneys at prenatal ultrasound. A cohort of patients with in utero diagnosis of other cystic kidney diseases (i.e. ARPKD, RCAD) was included as control group, together with a cohort of paediatric patients with ADPKD not fulfilling either VEO or EO criteria.
Results
We enrolled 33 VEO-ADPKD patients. Of 38 patients initially labelled as VEO-ADPKD, 5 were reclassified after genetic testing. The median follow-up was 18 (range 1–38) years.
Univariate logistic regression demonstrated that a known familial history of cystic disease before diagnosis (OR 28.846, 95% CI 2.933–210.464) and birth weight (OR 1.001, 95% CI 1.000–1.002) were positively correlated with ADPKD diagnosis, while the presence of microcysts had a strong negative correlation with ADPKD diagnosis (OR 0.042, 95% CI 0.005–0.373). Multivariate analysis confirmed only the predictive role of familiarity.
Figure 1 shows Kaplan-Meier curves comparing incidence of hypertension and CKD among patients with VEO-ADPKD, ARPKD, RCAD, and non-VEO-ADPKD patients. For all investigated outcomes, VEO-ADPKD had an event-free survival falling between that of patients with non-VEO-ADPKD and patients with ARPKD, the latter showing the worst renal prognosis (log-rank P < 0.001). Of note, of the four examined patients with RCAD, none developed hypertension, whereas all of them developed CKD (eGFR <90 mL/min/1.73 m2) and one had a sever kidney function impairment (eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2).
Conclusion
Our study demonstrates that: in patients with prenatal ultrasound features of VEO-ADPKD, a known family history of cystic kidney disease represents a strong predictor of ADPKD diagnosis, whereas the presence of microcysts suggests a diagnosis of ARPKDgenetic testing is a cornerstone of VEO-ADPKD diagnostic workup, since a consistent number of patients might have a complex genetic backgroundeven considering our extended definition criteria for VEO-ADPKD, these patients show a worse long-term renal prognosis than non-VEO-ADPKD patients. Our findings strongly support the need for careful evaluation of prenatal manifestations of polycystic kidney diseases through a detailed family history, genetic testing and early nephrological assessment to guarantee the timely recognition and management of early disease complications.

title: #1358 Development and characterization of 3D models based on urine derived renal epithelial cells
authors: Valeria Pizzuti; Emma Balducelli; Sofia Bin; Elisa Gessaroli; Anna Mistretta; Eleonora Chisena; Angelodaniele Napoletano; Valeria Corradetti; Giorgia Comai; Gaetano La Manna
abstract:
Background and Aims
Three-dimensional (3D) culture techniques represent a significant evolution from traditional monolayer culture methods for cell biology and regenerative medicine studies. These cell models provide a more accurate representation of human tissues, allowing a higher reliable simulation of cell-cell and cell-extracellular matrix (ECM) interactions and of the biological processes occurring in both physiological and pathological conditions. Different cell types can be combined into hybrid and multicellular 3D structures, to study how they interact and distribute. Urine derived renal epithelial cells (URECs) are a heterogeneous cells population voided in urine from the upper urinary tract, and particularly from proximal tubule; these cells are rarely detected in healthy subjects, while their number increases in presence of acute kidney damage and after kidney transplant as a response to ischemia reperfusion events and the increased cell turnover. In particular, we previously described URECs derived from kidney transplanted patients, focusing on their phenotype and their immunomodulatory properties in traditional monolayer culture [1, 2]. Here, we aimed to establish a 3D model combining URECs derived from kidney transplanted patients with Wharton's jelly mesenchymal stromal cells (WJ-MSCs), to evaluate structure, cell distribution and viability of the newly generated spheroids. For a functional characterization of the 3D model, the immunomodulatory properties were analysed by coculturing spheroids with peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs); the proliferation of CD4 and CD8 T cells, as well as the percentage of Treg cells and Granzyme B positive cells were evaluated after coculture.
Method
URECs and WJ-MSCs were combined to obtain spheroids by seeding cells in ultra low attachment (ULA) plates, allowing cell aggregation in 24 h Different condition and ratio were tested: URECs or WJ-MSCs only, URECs:WJ-MSCs 1:1 and 2:1 ratio. Spheroids formation and cell distribution were analysed using Incucyte, and by staining URECs and WJ-MSCs with different fluorochromes. The viability was assessed by Live/Dead assay at different time point. Spheroids were then cultured with PBMCs, and after 72 h immune cells were analysed by flow cytometry, comparing the results with activated PBMCs set as control.
Results
Stable spheroids were obtained combining URECs and WJ-MSCs (Fig. 1a and b), with a higher viability compared to WJ-MSCs spheres, while URECs alone could not self-aggregate (Fig. 1a, b and d). URECs were mostly located in the core of the 3D model, while WJ-MSCs were in the outer layer (Fig. 1c). During coculture with activated PBMCs (Fig. 2a), hybrid spheroids in both 1:1 and 1:2 ratio, significantly reduced CD4 and CD8 T cell proliferation (Fig. 2b), while WJ-MSCs only spheroids do not affect the proliferation rate, compared to activated PBMCs cultured without spheroids. For what concerns specific T cell subsets, hybrid spheroids reduced the percentage of Granzyme B producing cells, while increasing the CD4+CD25+FoxP3+ regulatory T cell subset (Fig. 2c).
Conclusion
The date obtained in our study indicate a long term stability and viability of UREC:WJ-MSCs spheroids, with a specific cell distribution into the 3D structure. Moreover, these 3D models showed promising immunomodulatory properties during coculture with PBMCs, which need to be further assessed by evaluating their effect on other immune cell subset including B cell and monocytes. These findings may provide the background for studies testing unknown effects of this new hybrid 3D cell model for cell therapy and regenerative medicine applications.

authors: Corentin Tournebize; Thomas Robert; Nadia Abid; Aurelie De Mul; Maxime Schleef; Laurence Derain-Dubourg; Flora Lefèvre; Marine Dancer; Emmanuel Letavernier; Sandrine Lemoine
abstract:
Background and Aims
Medullary sponge kidney (MSK) is characterized by precalyceal dilatation of the renal tubules and recurrent kidney stones (KS). Although etiopathogenesis is unknown, genetic origin is suspected since familial cases have been reported with autosomal dominant segregation, incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity. Some authors suggested that pathophysiology may involve disruptions in renal organogenesis with defective interaction between GDNF (glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor), RET (REarranged during Transfection) and GFRα1 (GDNF family receptor alpha-1). The aim of this study was to describe the genetic findings and diagnostic yield with whole exome sequencing (WES) in MSK.
Method
WES was performed between January 2023 and June 2024 in 42 patients diagnosed with MSK. MSK was diagnosed on CT or after an ureteroscopy. The pathogenicity was assessed using American College of Medical Genetics guidelines. We constituted 3 groups of patients according to WES results: positive WES group, variants of interest group, and negative WES group.
Positive WES was defined by one or more “likely pathogenic” or “pathogenic” variants in agreement with the mode of inheritance and a urolithiasis and/or cystic kidney phenotype (MSK-like phenotype).
Variants of interest group brought together monoallelic/heterozygous LP/P variants either in agreement with a MSK-like phenotype but not for the mode of inheritance, variants of unknown significance (VUS) and variants with conflicting interpretations in genes predisposing to MSK-like phenotype.
In parallel, we searched for rare variants in the RET, GDNF and GFRα1 gene from a variant datastore of some 8000 WES results. We then checked whether the patients identified had a recurrent KS phenotype.
Results
In total, 10 patients were identified as WES-positive (24%). These P/LP variants were found in 9 genes: IFT140 (n = 1); PRKCSH (n = 1), PKHD1 (n = 1), SLC34A3 (n = 1), SLC34A1 (n= 2), SLC26A1 (n = 1), UMOD (n = 1), COL4A3 (n = 1), MT-TL1 mitochondrial (n = 1).
Furthermore, 13 patients (31%) were found to have variants of interest in 16 different genes.
The presence of liver cysts was associated with the presence of a pathogenic variant and should be considered for WES analysis in MSK patients. No other clinical or biological abnormality was significantly associated with positive WES.
A total of 140 rare P/LP or of unknown significance variants of RET (n = 107), GDNF (n = 11) and GFR α1 (n = 22) were identified in the variant datastore. None of these variants were associated with recurrent KS and MSK phenotype.
Conclusion
Our findings expand the genetic landscape of MSK, revealing its association with a diverse set of genes related to KS diseases and/or cystic kidney diseases which underscore the heterogeneity of MSK, both in its presentation and its underlying genetic basis. This broadens our understanding of MSK as a possible polygenic trait and raises important considerations for genetic screening in clinical practice.

title: #2763 Dysregulated ion channel distribution promotes cyst formation in hereditary cystic kidney diseases
authors: Susanne Hahnenstein; Fatima Hassan; Dieter Haffner; Wolfgang H Ziegler
abstract:
Background and Aims
Pathogenic variants of the polycystic kidney and hepatic disease 1 (PKHD1) gene alter epithelial water and ion transport, and lead to renal collecting duct dilatations and to liver cysts formation, hallmarks of autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD). In the context of epithelial models using ARPKD genetics, loss of fibrocystin/polyductin (FPC) protein function results in a change from absorptive to secretory epithelial phenotype, thus reflecting one major pathophysiological mechanism for cyst growth. Our aim is to understand the molecular aspects of defective epithelial homeostasis by identifying channels that mediate aberrant electrolyte transport and promote cystic fluid accumulation. Here we employ a monolayered, three-dimensional (3D) epithelial model, allowing us to control cystogenic signals, determine channel distribution and test therapeutic targets.
Method
To model ARPKD conditions, Pkhd1 knockout clones were established using CRISPR/Cas9 in a principle-like Madin-Darby canine kidney (pl-MDCK) cell line. Single cells seeded into matrigel were allowed to form polarized spheroids with a lumen and stimulated by forskolin to enhance cAMP levels inducing secretory cystic epithelia. Measurement of cyst pressure and determination of the proportional lumen (i.e. ratio of lumen to spheroid area) confirmed enhanced water and ion transport across the epithelial barrier, as observed in ARPKD. The involvement of chloride channels in ARPKD disease progression was addressed by pharmacological inhibition, and subcellular distribution of water and ion channels was tested. Impact of FPC function was determined expressing functional domain constructs.
Results
Besides significantly enhanced cyst pressure, which is represented also by increased proportional lumina of pl-MDCK spheroids, FPC deficiency results in a prominent re-localization of the ion channels ENaC and CFTR from the apical to the basolateral membrane domain. In wild type cells, enhanced cAMP-levels mimic this phenotype and correlate with increased pressure values, whereas tight junctions (ZO-1) and the water channel aquaporin-2 remain apical in control and disease conditions. Both, treatment with selective chloride channel- inhibitors as well as controlled expression of the FPC cytoplasmic domain allowed us to suppressed cAMP-induced cyst formation in Pkhd1-KO cell lines, and controls.
Conclusion
A secretory phenotype of cyst-lining epithelia in disease conditions, as represented by enhanced cAMP-signals, mimics disturbed epithelial homeostasis in ARPKD and associates with altered ion channel distribution. Targeting of mis-localized ion channels represents a strategy to test for therapeutic options. Reconstitution of a functional c-terminal domain of FPC was sufficient to correct aberrant ion flux in our 3D in vitro model, suggesting that the cytoplasmic tail may function as a natural inhibitor of cyst growth and disease progression.

title: #781 Genetic fingerprinting of inflammation in Anderson–Fabry disease: the role of NLRP3 polymorphisms
authors: Gemma Antonucci; Antonella La Russa; Rosita Greco; Alberto Montesanto; Ersilia Paparazzo; Mirella Aurora Aceto; Simona Granata; Gianluigi Zaza
abstract:
Background and Aims
Anderson–Fabry disease (AFD) is a genetic disorder due to mutations in the GLA gene that result in a deficiency of the enzymatic activity of a-galactosidase A and in a consequent accumulation of glycosphingolipids in various tissues and organs. Historically, AFD was primarily regarded as a disorder driven by substrate accumulation. However, more recent insights into its pathophysiology have highlighted the contribution of secondary mechanisms, including inflammatory responses. Among these, the Nod-like receptor protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome has emerged as a key player in regulating inflammatory pathways. Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome can lead to the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and interleukin-18 (IL-18), contributing to tissue damage and fibrosis. Aberrant activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome has been implicated in exacerbating inflammation and triggering the production of inflammatory cytokines. Genetic polymorphisms of NLRP3 are associated with susceptibility to a variety of autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, including CKD. NLRP3-rs10754558 is associated with regulation of inflammasome activity, with specific alleles being associated with increased inflammatory reaction. Similarly, the NLRP3-rs4612666 polymorphism has been implicated in the modulation of NLRP3 expression and inflammasome activation, with an influence on susceptibility to inflammatory conditions. The aim of this study is to investigate whether these genetic variants of the NLRP3 gene can act as genetic modifier of inflammation in AFD and influence the progression and severity of the disease.
Method
Study Population
A total of 33 patients were recruited from Anderson-Fabry Reference Nephrology Centres. Patients included carried both classical and non-classical mutations. The control subjects (n = 20) were recruited after a detailed visit. All control subjects had an eGFR >60 mL/min/1.73 m2 and were negative for GLA gene mutations.
SNP Genotyping
Genomic DNA was extracted from whole blood (QIAmp DNA Blood kit, QIAGEN) and quantified by a Nanodrop Spectrophotometer. Genotyping was carried out by Polymerase Chain Reaction followed by digestion reaction using restriction enzymes (PCR-RFLP). PCR was performed to amplify fragments overlapping rs10754558 and rs4612666 in the NLRP3 gene. 100 ng of DNA was used in a PCR reaction containing 1× PCR buffer, 2.5 mM MgSO4, 0.25 mM dNTP, 0.5 mM of each primer and 0.5 U Taq-polymerase. After PCR amplification, 10 μl of PCR product was digested by restriction enzyme for 3 h at 37°C and subsequently evaluated by gel electrophoresis on a 3% agarose gel.
Statistical Analysis
Statistical analyses were performed using the R programming environment (v 4.3.3, https://cran.r-project.org). Genotype and allele frequency distributions were calculated using four different models of inheritance (codominant, dominant, recessive, and overdominant) and the SNPassoc package was used for fitting the relevant regression models. A p-values of 0.05 was used as a cut-off for statistical significance.
Results
Association analysis revealed that rs4612666-C allele was significantly associated with AFD risk (P < 0.005). Specifically, the frequency of the CT + CC genotypes (dominant model) was higher in AFD patients (60.7%) compared to controls (9.1%) with a corresponding odd ratio of 20.0 (95% CI 2.26–176.75). The genetic variability of rs10754558 was not significantly associated with AFD risk.
Conclusion
This study shows that the NLRP3-rs4612666 polymorphism is associated with AFD risk and contribute to the high phenotypic heterogeneity observed in patients within the same families. This suggests that the variability of NLRP3 rs4612666 should be taken into account in genetic screening of AFD patients. These preliminary results may contribute to the understanding of the pathophysiology of the disease and to explore the mechanistic links between these polymorphisms and AFD-related inflammation, potentially opening new avenues for targeted therapies.

title: #3756 Fabry or not Fabry? This is the problem: a clinical case
authors: Antonella La Russa; Rosita Greco; Gemma Antonucci; Alberto Montesanto; Ersilia Paparazzo; Simona Granata; Gianluigi Zaza
abstract:
Background and Aims
Glycosphingolipid accumulation is a common feature of Anderson Fabry disease (AFD), a lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient activity of α-galactosidase A encoded by the GLA gene. Over 1000 mutations in the GLA gene have been described, including missense and nonsense mutations, rearrangements and splicing defects, which have been identified as causes of AFD. The GLA gene has seven splice variants, and aberrant splicing accounts for approximately 5% of AFD mutations, but information on pre-mRNA splicing is available for only a limited number of patients. Many polymorphic GLA variants have been described, but it is unclear whether complex intronic haplotypes (CIH) formed by combinations of these variants are associated with disease onset, although several studies report cases of patients with classical forms of AFD with only haplotypes. We present a case of Fabry disease in a man with the CIH mutation and classic manifestations.
Case presentation
A 64-year-old male patient was admitted to our nephrology unit because of an elevated serum creatinine level (sCr 1.8 mg/dL) and proteinuria of 2 g/24 h. The anamnesis reported a previous diagnosis of hypertension at the age of 50 years treated with antihypertensive drugs, episodes of nephrolithiasis, sensorimotor peripheral polyneuropathy evaluated by electromyography in the lower limbs and, in the last year, hands acroparesthesias. The patient was ineligible for percutaneous kidney biopsy for bilateral parapelvic and voluminous left polar cysts. In addition, immunological evaluations reported antinuclear antibody (ANA) positivity (1:320), negative serum and urine immunofixation, normal free light chains ratio (dFLC), normal C3 and C4, normal serum immunoglobulin levels (IgG-IgM-IgA), and glycosylated Hb. A cardiac left hypertrophy (increase in SIV and PP) and mitral/aortic valve insufficiency was demonstrated by echocardiography and cardiac RMN. Based on the previous clinical data and a family history of CKD and cardiovascular disease (mother died of ischaemic stroke), we decided to test for Fabry disease.
Method
DNA was extracted from dried blood spots and sequenced for all GLA exons and up to 50 base pairs upstream and downstream of the intron-exon boundaries at both sites. Total RNA was extracted from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) for functional haplotype characterization (CIH). The RNA was reverse transcribed into cDNA and the mRNA expression was analyzed by qPCR. Total proteins were extracted from the PBMCs and the expression of alpha-Gal protein was determined by Western blotting analysis.
Results
Genetic analysis revealed the presence of 3 variants within (CIH): c.370-81_370-77delCAGCC, c.640-16 A > G, and c.1000-22 C > T. In addition, qPCR results show a higher expression of GLA mRNA levels in the patient compared to a healthy subject (control) (Fig. 1), suggesting a possible activation of cryptogenic splicing. Conversely, western blot analysis revealed lower alpha-Gal protein expression in the patient compared to the control (Fig. 2). This could explain the clinical Fabry phenotype in our patient.
Conclusion
Thus, our clinical case reports a specific genetic combination of SNPs in a patient with a multisystemic clinical alteration that, according to biomolecular analysis, could be associated with alpha-Gal protein deficiency. Although we cannot consider these mutations as classical AFD genetic features and further studies are needed to elucidate how inheritance of complex intronic haplotypes affects GLA regulatory mechanisms, genetic analysis of the entire GLA gene sequence and multiple ligation dependent probe amplification (MLPA), the study of GLA expression could be extremely useful tools to explain the clinical phenotype of these patients and define a possible treatment. Moreover, our clinical report demonstrated the importance of strengthening the collaborative network between clinicians and other technical figures (genetists, biologists) in our nephrology centres to better diagnose and treat fragile patients with rare kidney diseases.

title: #1896 Discoidin domain-containing Receptor 2 in pericyte plays a crucial role in AKI–CKD continuum
authors: Hui-Chiun Tseng; Yu-Hsiang Chou; Shuei-Liong Lin
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a major cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD). Mechanisms of AKI-CKD continuum needs to be further investigated for the development of promising pharmacologic agents. Discoidin domain receptors (DDRs) including DDR1 and DDR2, which are receptor tyrosine kinases that bind to and activated by collagen in the extracellular matrix (ECM). While the role of function of DDR2 in the process of AKI-CKD continuum is less clearly understood.
Method
We evaluated the DDR2 expression in the whole kidney and isolated pericytes during AKI-CKD continuum. In vivo study, we used IRI (ischemia-reperfusion injury) as AKI model in C57BL/6 mice model to monitor DDR2 expression level. In vitro study, we used collagen 1 as DDR2 stimulator and WRG-28 as DDR2 inhibitor in the NIH/3T3 cells to measure the expression level of fibrosis-related genes and proteins in this cell line.
Results
Our results demonstrated that DDR2 was expressed mainly in pericytes. DDR2 expression increased in the whole kidney and isolated pericytes during AKI-CKD continuum. In experiments of cell lines, 200 μg/ml of collagen-1 treatment for 4 hours could activate the fibrosis-related genes. In addition, DDR2 inhibitor WRG-28 impeded collagen-1-induced DDR2 activity and fibrosis-related gene expression levels. Furthermore, WRG-28 inhibited collagen-1-induced cell migration and proliferation.
Conclusion
DDR2 expresses in pericytes and increases during the AKI-CKD continuum. In vivo, AKI activates DDR2 and enhances pro-fibrotic genes in the whole kidney. In vitro, collagen-1 activates DDR2 and promotes pro-fibrotic genes in pericytes. Inhibition of DDR2 ameliorates pericytes activity and collagen production. Regulation of the DDR2 is a crucial factor for the therapeutic strategy for the AKI-CKD continuum.

title: #1805 Mechanosensitive cation channel Piezo1 regulates AQP2 expression in collecting ducts of the kidney
authors: Meng Li; Xiaoduo Zhao; Weidong Wang; Chunling Li
abstract:
Background and Aims
Water reabsorption in the renal collecting duct, mediated by aquaporin-2 (AQP2), is essential for body fluid balance. Piezo1, a mechanosensitive cation channel, is highly expressed in the collecting ducts to sense mechanical and osmotic stress. The signal recognition particle 54 kDa subunit (Srp54), a key regulator of protein translocation, modulates protein transcription and translation. The present study aims to investigate whether Piezo1 activation affects intracellular trafficking and expression of AQP2 in the principal cells and the potential involvement of Srp54.
Method
In vitro, mpkCCD cells overexpressed AQP2 and primary rat inner medullary collecting duct (IMCD) cells were treated with Piezo1 agonist Yoda1, mechanical stretch or hypoosmotic stress, respectively. AQP2 distribution and cell volume were assessed by super-resolution fluorescence imaging, Western blot, and qRT-PCR. Transcriptomic analysis and bioinformatic tools (catRAPID, JASPAR) were used to examine gene expression and molecular interactions. In vivo, C57BL/6 mice were subjected to dehydration and expression levels of protein and mRNA in the kidney inner medulla were analyzed. Statistical significance was assessed using one-way ANOVA (P < 0.05).
Results
Piezo1 activation with Yoda1 increased protein expression and plasma membrane distribution of AQP2 in renal collecting duct principal cells and mpkCCD cells, which was associated with enhanced trafficking of AQP2 in endoplasmic reticulum. Hypoosmotic stress or mechanical stretch upregulated AQP2 protein expression, which was markedly inhibited by GsMT×4, a Piezo1 antagonist. EGTA, a calcium chelator, significantly inhibited hypoosmotic stress-induced upregulation of AQP2 protein in mpkCCD cells. In Piezo1+/− mice, AQP2 expression was moderately decreased in the renal inner medulla, compared to wildtype mice. These data indicate a role of Piezo1 in modulating expression of AQP2 protein. In mpkCCD cells, Yoda1, hypoosmotic stress, or mechanical stretch activated CREB and YAP signaling pathways. Transcriptomic analysis showed increased Srp54 mRNA levels and enhanced AQP2 processing in mpkCCD cells treated with Yoda1. title: #3329 Autonomic modulation in normotensive ADPKD patients
authors: Daniel Rocha; Ana Carolina Anauate; Milene Subtil Ormanji; Ana Cristina Matos; Cássia Bergamaschi; Ruy Campos Júnior; Bruno Silva; Ita Pfeferman Heilberg
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common monogenic kidney disease, leading to progressive loss of kidney function. Arterial hypertension (AH) is one of the most common and early-onset extrarenal manifestation, whose pathogenesis is multifactorial. Autonomic dysregulation is associated with an increased risk for all cardiovascular events in the general population, having already been described among ADPKD patients with AH and reduced renal function. The present study aimed to investigate cardiovascular autonomic regulation in ADPKD before the development of AH.
Method
Cardiovascular autonomic modulation parameters at rest, baroreflex sensitivity (BRS), and cardiovascular reactivity were evaluated in young patients (18 to 40 years old) with ADPKD, normotensive, and with preserved renal function. The control group consisted of healthy individuals, matched by age, sex, and body mass index (BMI). Heart rate (HR), blood pressure (BP) variability (HRV and BPV), and spontaneous BRS during the 5-minute rest were determined. The analysis of BRS during the Valsalva maneuver (VM) and cardiovascular reactivity during and after sympathoexcitatory maneuvers using the Stroop test, Cold pressor test (CPT), and Handgrip (HG) were also evaluated. Cardiovascular monitoring was performed using the Finapres device. ADPKD patients were classified according to Mayo Clinic imaging criteria (MIC) as between slow or rapid progressors.
Results
A total of 37 individuals were evaluated, 18 with ADPKD (11F/7M, 27.7 ± 6.4 years) and 19 controls (9F/10M, 25.7 ± 3.8 years), with no statistical differences in the distributions of sex, age, and mean BMI and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). HRV and BPV did not reveal statistical differences in either the time or frequency domains, demonstrating that the sympathovagal balance was similar among groups. Cardiovascular reactivity during sympathoexcitatory maneuvers revealed no differences between groups. The results of all these tests also did not show statistical differences between subgroups of ADPKD patients with slow versus rapid progression. Serum markers of inflammation, endothelial function, and hormones, such as neuropeptide Y and angiotensinogen did not differ between ADPKD and controls. However, urinary angiotensinogen and albuminuria levels were significantly higher in ADPKD.
Conclusion
In summary, the present study did not demonstrate cardiovascular autonomic dysregulation in normotensive ADPKD patients with preserved renal function, nor in those patients with ADPKD who were rapid progressors according to the Mayo Clinic Classification in relation to slow progressors. Serum markers of endothelial function and inflammation were not different between ADPKD patients and controls, nor between those with rapid or slow progressors. These findings suggest a complex interaction between the RAS and sympathetic nervous system in the regulation of albuminuria, although further studies are needed to clarify the exact mechanisms underlying this interaction in ADPKD.

title: #1182 Impaired renal function in patients with spinal muscular atrophy: a longitudinal cohort study
authors: Fay-Lynn Asselman; Sabine Meijvis; Renske Wadman; Inge Cuppen; Robin Wm Vernooij; Lina Vermeer; Leonard Van den Berg; Ewout Groen; Ludo van der Pol
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hereditary proximal spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a severe motor neuron disease caused by loss-of-function of the survival motor neuron 1 (SMN1) gene and the resulting deficiency of the ubiquitously expressed SMN protein. Adequate SMN protein levels are critical for many generic cellular functions. SMA differs in severity, classified as SMA types 1–4. Classification is based on age at onset and achieved milestones with SMA type 1 as most severe and earliest onset and SMA type 4 as relatively mild. The recent introduction of genetic SMN protein-augmenting therapies has allowed partial rescue of motor units and improved prognosis of patients with SMA, but the consequences of SMN-protein deficiency for function of other tissues and organs have not been studied in detail. Kidney tissue, especially tubular, expresses high levels of SMN protein comparable to brain and spinal cord. This may suggest that the kidney is particularly vulnerable to low SMN protein concentrations. To explore clinical consequences of SMN deficiency in kidney, we longitudinally assessed renal function in a large cohort of patients participating in a cohort study on SMA in the Netherlands.
Method
We collected baseline data before the start of SMN-augmenting therapies (nusinersen and risdiplam) and during follow-up (maximum range 18–30 months). We assessed renal clearance by analysing serum creatinine and serum cystatin C and tubular function through serum potassium levels and urine protein concentrations.
Results
We enrolled 266 patients with SMA. Median age was 32 years (IQR: 22.2–49.1). Fifty-four (21%) patients had serum cystatin C based eGFR rates <90 ml/min/1.73 m2, 10 (4%) patients had eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2) and 2 patients showed end-stage renal failure based on eGFR <15 ml/min/1.73 m2. Abnormal low serum potassium levels (<3.8 mmol/L) and proteinuria as symptoms of tubular dysfunction were present in 144 (51.1%) and 55 patients (22%), respectively. Forty-four (16.5%) patients had a history of kidney stones or nephrocalcinosis. Treatment with nusinersen or risdiplam resulted in reduction of the number of patients with hypokalemia (55.1% to 26.1% among patients treated with nusinersen and 56% to 42.4% among those treated with risdiplam), but not of those with proteinuria. Cystatin C eGFR declined during follow-up in both treatment groups.
Conclusion
Assessing renal clearance with cystatin C shows that patients with SMA are at risk of impaired renal function, which does not improve after 1–2 years treatment with SMN2-splicing modifying therapies. Tubular function may improve partially following the start of treatment. These data indicate that SMN protein deficiency not only affects motor neurons but also affects peripheral tissues with high expression levels and that the incomplete functional rescue during treatment indicates health risks in later life.
