title: #63 Long-term prognosis of lupus nephritis comparison between pediatric, adult, and advanced age onset
authors: Marta Calatroni; Simeone Andrulli; Federico Doti; Federica Bello; Giovanni De Vivo; Antonio Mastrangelo; Nicoletta Del Papa; Tommaso Schioppo; Laura Locatelli; Francesco Reggiani; Gabriella Luisa Moroni
abstract:
Background and Aims
Lupus nephritis (LN) presents with varied outcomes depending on the age at diagnosis. We aimed to evaluate long-term kidney survival across three age groups.
Method
Patients were categorized based on their age at lupus nephritis diagnosis: ≤18 years (childhood), >18 to <45 (adulthood), ≥45 years (elderly). The three groups' chronic kidney disease (CKD, eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2 for at least 3 months) or death-free survival was estimated using Kaplan-Meier curves and compared with the Log-RANK test. To evaluate the independent prognostic role of age, adjusted for other predictors of CKD or death, we used multivariate Cox regression analysis.
Results
This retrospective cohort study analyzed 260 patients followed for a median of 14.8 years. Of them, 46 (17.7%) were <18, 173 (66.5%) >18 and <45, and 41 (15.8%) >45 years old. Baseline demographics and clinical features are reported in Table 1a. Forty-six percent of elderly vs 32.6% of children and 24.3% of adults had acute kidney disease (AKD) at diagnosis (P = 0.02). Children had more active SLE, while elderly had more chronic damage and hypertension. Renal response at one year after the start of therapy is reported in Table 1b. At 5, 10, and 20 years, CKD or death-free survival rates were 95.3%, 92.5%, and 88.4% in children; 98.2%, 90.1%, and 82.6% in adults; and 87.5%, 67.8%, and 53.5% in the elderly. Survival in elderly patients was significantly worse compared to children and adults (P = 0.001), whereas survival rates between children and adults were comparable (P = NS) (Fig. 1). At multivariate analysis, when chronicity index was excluded from the model, older age emerged as an independent predictor of CKD or death (Relative Risk, RR: 3.278; CI: 1.402–7.662; P = 0.006), with AKD (RR:2.930; CI: 1.674–5.130; P < 0.001), arterial hypertension (RR: 3.692; CI: 1.844–7.389; P < 0.001), SLICC >0 (RR: 1.824; CI: 1.155–2.881; P = 0.01), and failure to achieve complete remission at one year (RR: 4.784; CI: 2.355–9.716; P < 0.001) (Table 2).
Conclusion
While children and adults demonstrate comparable long-term kidney survival, elderly patients face significantly worse outcomes due to advanced chronicity and systemic damage. These findings highlight the need for tailored interventions in late-onset LN. Older-onset LN, in fact, was an independent predictor of CKD or death together with AKD, arterial hypertension, SLICC >0, and no remission at one year.

title: #2566 Urinary markers of inflammation and damage in anti-GBM disease before and after treatment with Imlifidase
authors: Linnéa Tyrberg; Thomas Hellmark; Mårten Segelmark
abstract:
Background and Aims
Anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease is a rare autoimmune disease presenting with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and in some cases also lung hemorrhages. Urinary markers of inflammation and damage are of great interest as they could present easily accessible information about prognosis with the possibility of repeated measurements to monitor disease progression and response to treatment. However, despite the large number of known urinary markers, the potential in clinical practice remains largely unknown. Imlifidase is a new treatment option in anti-GBM disease for rapid removal of autoantibodies and showed promising results in the phase II trial GOOD-IDES-01.
Method
In that trial, 15 anti-GBM patients from five European countries were treated with a single dose of imlifidase in addition to standard treatment and monitored for six months. Urine samples from these patients and 28 healthy controls were analyzed for urinary markers already in clinical use (creatinine, albumin, IgG, κ, λ and protein HC), measured at the Department of Clinical Chemistry, Skåne University Hospital, Lund, Sweden, and preclinical markers of renal damage and inflammation (KIM-1, Clusterin, Ngal, sCD163 and MCP-1), measured using ELISA. All markers were corrected for U-creatinine.
Results
We found that all measured urinary markers were elevated in the anti-GBM patients as compared to established reference values or healthy controls, and though all markers decreased during the trial, they remained elevated at the end of the trial in most patient (Fig. 1). We saw trends to higher levels of albumin, IgG, protein HC, κ, λ, clusterin, Ngal, sCD163 and MCP-1 in patients where anti-GBM autoantibodies rebounded 5–21 days after removal by imlifidase (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
In conclusion, in our study the urinary markers indicate both glomerular and tubular inflammation and damage which despite improvement persists for six months in patients with anti-GBM disease. Furthermore, patients with a rebound of anti-GBM autoantibodies displayed a tendency to have elevated levels of several urinary markers. These urinary markers could therefore help predict in which patients rebound is likely to occur to allow for adaptation of treatment strategies.

title: #1247 Prognostic significance of Soluble urokinase-type plasminogen activator receptor (suPAR) in patients with glomerulonephritis: association with renal outcomes
authors: Ji-Young Choi; Jeong-Hoon Lim; Mingyu Kim; Jieun Yoo; Youn-Sik Oh; Seong-Wook Lee; You-Hyun Jeon; Hee-Yeon Jung; Jang-Hee Cho; Chan Duck Kim; Yong-Lim Kim; Sun-Hee Park
abstract:
Background and Aims
Studies determining the relation between soluble urokinase-type plasminogen activator receptor (suPAR) levels and clinical outcomes in glomerulonephritis (GN) are limited. In this study, we aimed to investigate the association between suPAR levels and renal outcomes in patients with GN.
Method
A total of 96 patients diagnosed with primary GN on renal biopsy in two tertiary hospitals between 2013 and 2020, who underwent both baseline and follow-up sampling and consented to participate, were included. Serum suPAR levels were measured at the time of biopsy and during follow-up. The association between serum suPAR levels and the reduction of renal function and proteinuria was analyzed.
Results
The most common GN was IgA nephropathy, followed by focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, membranous nephropathy and minimal change disease. The median follow-up duration was 2.3 years. Ln(suPAR) levels, logarithmically transformed on a natural log of suPAR showed no significant difference according to the type of GN at the time of biopsy (P = 0.42), but there was a significant difference at follow-up (P = 0.018). Ln(suPAR) levels were significantly higher in patients with an eGFR less than 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 compared to those with an eGFR of 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 or higher at both baseline (P = 0.02) and follow-up (P = 0.001). There was a significant difference in the change in Ln(suPAR) per year (%/year) among GN groups (P < 0.001). Higher baseline Ln(suPAR) levels were significantly associated with eGFR decline in the Cox proportional hazards model (HR 1.760, 95% CI 1.101–2.813, P = 0.018), although they were not significantly associated with a reduction in the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) (HR 1.540, 95% CI 0.988–2.386, P = 0.057). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed that patients in the highest tertile of Ln(suPAR) at the time of biopsy exhibited a faster eGFR decline (P = 0.019). However, there was no statistical significance for reduction of UPCR (P = 0.065). Multivariate regression analysis identified Ln(suPAR) (P < 0.001) and UPCR (P = 0.043) at the time of biopsy as independent factors influencing Ln(suPAR) levels at follow-up. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses demonstrated a modest improvement in predictive power for eGFR and reduction of UPCR when incorporating suPAR into models that included age, sex, hypertension, diabetes, type of GN, UPCR and the presence or absence of eGFR less than 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 at baseline.
Conclusion
Higher suPAR levels at the time of biopsy are associated with eGFR decline in patients with GN, although they are not significantly associated with the reduction of proteinuria. suPAR could be suggested as a potential marker for renal outcomes in GN.

title: #2215 Development and validation of nomograms for predicting the activity index of lupus nephritis
authors: Zishan Lin; Bingjing Jiang; Fan Wu; Wenfeng Wang; Shidong Xie; Yufeng Liang; Jianxin Wan; Hong Chen; Caiming Chen; Yanfang Xu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Lupus nephritis (LN) is a common and severe complication of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The initial treatment strategy for LN is guided by pathological features, with the activity index (AI) being a key predictor of renal outcomes and prognosis. The objective of this study was to develop and validate clinical data-based nomograms for assessing AI in LN patients, thereby aiding clinical decision-making and reducing reliance on invasive kidney biopsies.
Method
This multicenter study enrolled 266 LN patients diagnosed through renal biopsy, divided into a training cohort (n = 213) and a validation cohort (n = 53). Patients were stratified into high AI (AI > 4) and low AI (AI ≤ 4) groups. Demographic data, medical histories, renal pathology reports, and results from blood and urine analyses were collected. A logistic regression model was developed integrating lymphocyte count, hematuria, leukocyturia, albumin (ALB), serum creatinine (Scr), complement C4, and anti-histone antibodies. Nomograms for individualized assessment were constructed based on the regression equations. Model performance was evaluated using ROC curves, calibration plots, Decision Curve Analysis (DCA), and the Hosmer-Lemeshow test.
Results
A total of 266 patients were enrolled, with 84.21% being female and a median age of 33.5 years. The most common pathological type was proliferative LN (Classes III, IV, and III/IV + V), with Class IV + V accounting for 34.59%. The median AI was 8.00 (IQR 4.00, 11.00), and 71.8% of patients had an AI score above 4 (Table 1). A nomogram for individualized assessment of AI was constructed based on the logistic regression model (Fig. 1). The model, integrating key clinical factors, demonstrated strong predictive power, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.867 (95% CI 0.816–0.918) in the internal validation cohort and 0.882 (95% CI 0.778–0.986) in the external validation cohort. It passed the Hosmer-Lemeshow test (P = 0.563 for the training cohort and P = 0.568 for the validation cohort), confirming good calibration. Decision curve analysis (DCA) showed significant net benefits in predicting high AI (> 4), confirming the model's clinical utility (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
The developed nomograms provide a reliable and user-friendly tool for predicting high AI in LN patients. The models demonstrate strong predictive performance and good calibration, offering valuable support for clinical decision-making and reducing the need for invasive kidney biopsies.

title: #0910 Using national hospital discharge data to estimate the clinical and economic hospital burden and care pathways of patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis in Italy
authors: Helen Banks; Giovanni Fattore; Claudio Jommi; Luca Quartuccio; Federico Alberici
abstract:
Background and Aims
Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV) are rare autoimmune disorders of heterogeneous clinical presentation. Studies have shown high clinical and economic burden, especially for hospitalizations. However, few studies have examined outcomes, resource use, care patterns using national-level data on rare diseases.
Method
Using 2010–2019 Italian nationwide hospital discharge records, we developed algorithms to identify granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) and microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), estimating prevalence, resource use, hospital mortality, regional differences. Regression models identified cost and hospital mortality determinants.
Results
The 3,763 GPA and 1,206 MPA patients identified averaged 6.9 (±5.6) and 8.6 (±6.5) admissions/patient over 10 years, with 20.3% and 21.4% hospital mortality especially during the first year after diagnosis (respectively 47% and 39% for GPA and MPA). In GPA, 1665 patients (44%) showed renal involvement at any point of the follow-up available defined as the occurrence of acute kidney disease or chronic kidney disease or end-stage renal disease while this was recorded in 100% of the MPA patients. Cardiovascular conditions, e.g. coronary artery disease or atrial fibrillation, affected at least 1 in 7 patients. Diabetes was observed in 17% for GPA and 21% for MPA patients. Osteoporosis or fractures were recorded respectively in 16% and 13% of the GPA and MPA patients while cancer in 14% of the GPA and 12% of the MPA patients. In GPA and MPA respectively, infections as a primary diagnosis were observed for 14 and 16% of patients, while 29% and 34% had at least one infection among primary and secondary diagnoses. The interregional mobility for all the admissions was higher in the center regions of Italy (respectively 9.3% for GPA and 6.1% for MPA) and the south ones (respectively 19.9% for GPA and 15.9% for MPA) compared to the north ones (6.6% for GPA and 5.6% for MPA). Mean total hospital costs/patient were €28,275 for GPA, €36,462 for MPA over the 10-year period, or €8,954 for GPA and €9,730 for MPA per patient-year. Roughly 60% of costs occur in the diagnosis year ±1. In regression analysis, commonly associated comorbidities (infections, renal diseases, coronary artery disease) were significant determinants of increased overall costs and mortality, particularly infections impacting on the diagnosis year for +€4,146 [95% CI 2.723–5.570], on total costs for +11,152€ [8,948–13,356], on mortality with an OR 1.818 [1.50–2.20] for GPA; in MPA the same figures were +€5,522 [2,846–8,198], +€14,127 [10,018–18,237] and OR 2.311 [1.66–3.21]. In GPA patients, the development of CKD was associated with an increase in total costs +4,729€ [95% CI 2.200–7.258] and mortality OR 1.409 [1.139–1.745]. For MPA patients the development of ESRD was associated with an increase in costs in the diagnosis year of +€7,405 [95% CI 3.648– 11.162], total costs +17,490€ [95% CI 12.388–22.592] and mortality OR 2.546 [1.816–3.568]. Seeking AAV-related care in numerous hospitals (poor loyalty) raised costs by >€4000. Geographically, 60% of GPA and 53% of MPA were followed in hospitals located in the North regions of Italy. Of the top 10 hospitals in terms of volume of admissions, 90% for GPA and 80% for MPA were located in the North.
Conclusion
Italian nationwide results showed elevated hospital resource use and mortality with care patterns indicating difficulties in obtaining a diagnosis and specialized care, especially in southern regions. Comorbidities and poor access to continuous specialized care raise costs and mortality, highlighting the importance of early, effective management to prevent disease progression.

title: #3848 CD163+ macrophages: a prognostic marker in ANCA vasculitis?
authors: Silvia Benito-García; Beatriz Bardaji; Yolanda Arce; Patricia Moya; Xoana Barros Freiria; Helena Marco; Lluis Guirado Perich; Montserrat Mercedes Diaz Encarnacion
abstract:
Background and Aims
Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV) is a necrotizing vasculitis characterized by inflammation of small blood vessels, with the kidneys being one of the most affected organs. Its pathogenesis is a complex and multifactorial process involving both inflammation and fibrosis, with macrophages playing a key role. Macrophages are plastic cells capable of changing their phenotype in response to environmental cues. In kidney biopsy the infiltration of CD163+ macrophages (anti-inflammatory) is observed in the interstitium and glomeruli of patients with AAV.
Our objective was to investigate the clinicopathological significance of CD163+ macrophages in AAV, their association with interstitial fibrosis, and potential differences between PR3-AAV and MPO-AAV.
Method
This was a retrospective, single-center study that included 79 patients with AAV (66 MPO-AAV and 13 PR3-AAV) diagnosed by renal biopsy with at least one year of follow-up. Renal tissue samples (62 in total: 13 PR3-AAV and 49 MPO-AAV) were stained with trichrome and immunohistochemestry with CD163 to assess the degree of fibrosis and M2 macrophage infiltration. Histomorphometric quantification was performed using MetaMorph® software in both cases. The results were correlated with clinical and pathological data. Statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05.
Results
Furthermore, a positive and statistically significant correlation was identified between the intensity of M2 macrophage infiltration and renal function at both the time of diagnosis (P = 0.005) and the end of follow-up (P = 0.02). However, macrophage infiltration did not demonstrate a significant correlation with interstitial fibrosis,.CD163+ macrophage infiltration in the interstitial space was significantly higher in MPO-AAV than in PR3-AAV (P < 0.001), with higher levels observed in patients over 50 years of age.
Conclusion
CD163+ macrophage infiltration is significantly higher in MPO-AAV than in PR3-AAV, independent of age. However, this disparity becomes more pronounced with increasing age. These findings suggest that age plays a key role in macrophage activation through the reparative pathway, potentially contributing to fibrogenesis, which is also a differentiating element between MPO and PR3.
However, no significant correlation with fibrosis at diagnosis was identified, potentially due to macrophages representing a precursor stage in the fibrotic process. Likewise, based on the observed results, CD163+ macrophage interstitial infiltration could serve as a prognostic predictor of long-term renal function in AAV.
Further studies with larger cohorts, particularly including a greater number of PR3-AAV patients, are required to validate these findings and refine their clinical implications.

title: #2162 Temporal trends of severe infections in patients with lupus nephritis and CKD: a nationwide study
authors: Charikleia Chrysostomou; Francesca Faustini; Iva Gunnarsson; Franz Peter Barany; Marie Evans; Anne-Laure Faucon
abstract:
Background and Aims
Little is known regarding the excess infection risk of patients with lupus nephritis (LN) and moderate and advanced chronic kidney disease (LN-CKD). There is a need to identify LN-CKD patients at risk, who might benefit from prevention strategies, and to assess whether temporal trends of severe infection have changed, considering the evolution of corticosteroid- and immunosuppression therapies in LN over the last two decades.
Method
We included all patients with LN and non-dialysis CKD stages G3–G5 from the Swedish Renal Registry (SRR) 2006–2021. Study outcomes included death due to infection and all-cause infection-related hospitalization. We excluded hospitalization due to Covid-19 in order to be able to compare recent with early time-periods. Patients were followed until the first occurrence of an infection-event, kidney failure, death, or end of follow-up. Cause-specific Cox models were used to explore factors associated with infection-related hospitalization. Incidence rates were calculated per 100 person-year (PY), and temporal trends of infection were analyzed using cause-specific proportional hazard models. Time was considered in 4-year blocks, 2006–2009 being the reference category.
Results
We identified 317 patients with LN (median age 61 years, 76% women, eGFR 30 mL/min per 1.73 m²). Across more recent calendar periods, age (from 55 to 63 years), percentage of women (from 68% to 79%) and prevalence of comorbidities increased, baseline albuminuria decreased (from 74 to 29 mg/mmol), while eGFR (30 mL/min per 1.73 m²) and baseline corticosteroids (60%) remained comparable across the four timeblock-patient-groups.
Older age, lower eGFR, serum albumin levels, and baseline corticosteroid therapy, but not sex or baseline non-steroid immunosuppressive therapy, were independently associated with infection-related hospitalization (Table 1).
Over a median follow-up of 4.0 [3.6; 4.6] years, 123 (39%) patients were hospitalized for infection and 21 (7%) died from infection. Between 2006 and 2021, while incidence rates of infection-related hospitalization increased by 48% (from 8.7 [5.8–12.5] per 100-PY to 16.8 [10.3–25.5] per 100-PY, P for trend = 0.03), rates of death due to infection decreased by 33% (from 2.1 [1.0–4.0] to 1.4 [0.2–4.9] per 100-PY, P for trend = 0.34) (Fig. 1). Compared to 2006-2009, the period 2018-2021 was associated with a 26% increase in the rate of infection-related hospitalization, but 57% decrease in the rate of death due to infection (although non-statistically significant, probably due to a lack of power). After adjustment for age and sex, the strength of the association slightly decreased, but remained in the same magnitude.
Conclusion
In this nationwide study conducted in patients with LN-CKD, our findings show that, although the rate of death due to infection markedly decreased, that of infection-related hospitalization substantially increased—with older age, lower eGFR and corticosteroid use being the most important factors. This highlights the need for prevention strategies and a tailored prescription of steroids and immunosuppressive therapies in this high-risk population.

title: #1839 Renal cysts in ADPKD patients can be distinguished by low and high sodium concentrations in vivo using 23Na magnetic resonance imaging
authors: Christoph Kopp; Judith Schirmer; Anke Dahlmann; Peter Linz; Silke Härteis; Bernd Wullich; Mario Schiffer; Michael Uder; Bjoern Buchholz; Armin Nagel
abstract:
Background and Aims
In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) cysts can arise from all compartments of the nephron and collecting duct. Identification of the cellular origin would improve our understanding of cyst development and allow to target cyst growth in a more specific and potentially personalized way. However, no imaging technique is currently able to classify cysts according to their origin. Ex vivo data of cyst fluid suggested variations of Na+ concentration probably linked to cyst development. We hypothesized that cyst Na+ concentration can be measured by 23Na magnetic resonance imaging (23Na MRI) in vivo and that cysts of ADPKD patients can be characterized and distinguished by their Na+ concentration.
Method
We conducted 23Na MRI measurements combined with anatomical 1H MRI sequences of the kidney using an ultra-high-field 7Tesla MRI scanner (Siemens, Magnetom Terra.X, Erlangen, Germany). Initially, polycystic kidneys of four ADPKD patients (three on dialysis/one kidney transplant patient) were assessed ex vivo after nephrectomy. Correspondent cyst fluid was obtained by aspiration and electrolyte concentration was determined by ion selective electrodes. title: #1968 Native kidney biopsy in lateral position compared to prone position: technical aspects, diagnostic yield and complications
authors: Francesco Fontana; Camilla Ferri; Gaetano Alfano; Gabriele Donati
abstract:
Background and Aims
Ultrasound (US) guided native kidney biopsy is traditionally performed by nephrologists with patient in prone position, targeting the lower pole of left kidney scanned in longitudinal US section. With this approach the distance between the kidney and skin surface can be considerably high; moreover, with most widely used bracket guides the resulting needle path lays perpendicular to kidney capsule, crossing cortical tissue and often reaching medulla. A lateral approach to native kidney biopsy has been proposed as an alternative (especially in obese patients), but it is scarcely reported in the nephrology literature. A cortical tangential approach of the needle path, which is best obtained with transversal kidney US scanning, has been described only in transplant kidney biopsies.
Method
We designed a single-center retrospective and prospective cross- sectional study comparing depth of biopsied kidney, diagnostic yield and risk of complications in patients who received native kidney biopsy in lateral position (LP) with transversal kidney US scanning compared to prone position (PP) with longitudinal kidney US scanning. The study received approval from local Ethical Committee. We collected: demographic, clinical and laboratory data; US-measured skin-kidney distance in LP e PP; data on biopsy adequacy (total number of glomeruli in tissue allocated for light microscopy [LM] and immunofluorescence, percentage of included medullary tissue) and presence of big-size parenchymal (arcuate) arteries in LM; occurrence of complications defined as major (red blood cells transfusion, need for selective arterial embolization, surgical revision, nephrectomy) or minor (drop in hemoglobin >2 g/dl, bladder tamponade, macrohematuria, need for angio-CT scan, hematoma >3cm).
Results
After exclusion of patients with inadequate data collection, we considered 101 subjects: 47 who received biopsy in LP and 54 in PP. Demographic, clinical and laboratory characteristics were similar between groups. Kidney depth at biopsy was significantly lower in LP group (Fig. 2); considering the whole population, the average difference in skin-kidney distance in LP compared to PP was significantly higher in patients with BMI >25 (26 mm with IQR 18–32 mm vs 20 mm with IQR 6.83–30.48 in patients with BMI < 25, P = 0.03). Total number of glomeruli in biopsy sample was significantly higher in the LP group (Fig. 2); moreover, the proportion of samples containing less than 10 glomeruli was significantly lower in LP (2.13% vs 14.82%, P = 0.034). The proportions of biopsies with more of 30% of the LM sample containing medulla and of those containing arcuate arteries were significantly higher for the PP group (Fig. 2). At the univariate binary logistic regression we identified two significant predictors of “ideal kidney biopsy” (defined as a sample containing more than 10 glomeruli, no medullary tissue and no big-size arteries): skin-kidney distance (OR 0.968, 95% CI 0.946–0.991, P = 0,006) and biopsy in LP (OR 2.739, 95% CI 1.22–6.173, P = 0,014). There were no major complications in our cohort; we encountered no significant differences in the proportion of minor complications between the LP and PP groups.
Conclusion
a lateral position for native kidney biopsy can significantly decrease kidney depth compared to PP, leading to a better visualization and enhancing operator comfort; the LP approach aiming for a cortical tangential needle path can promote a more adequate tissue sampling, minimizing the inclusion of medulla tissue and big-size vessels, resulting in an improved diagnostic yield.

title: #808 Targeted release budesonide (TRB) can effectively reduce proteinuria when active lesions are present in IgA Nephropathy (IgAN) patients: A multicenter study
authors: Christodoulos Keskinis; Eleni Moysidou; Eleni Kapsia; Christos Bintas; Maria Styliani Trivyza; Michalis Christodoulou; Georgios Lioulios; Stamatia Stai; Panagiotis Pateinakis; Marios Papasotiriou; Smaragdi Marinaki; Maria Stangou
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA Nephropathy (IgAN), the most dominant primary glomerulonephritis worldwide, is associated with a variety of histological lesions, which are classified and graded according to the MEST-C classification system. This classification tool can provide information regarding to prognosis, but it cannot guide treatment strategies.
The recurrent nature of the disease often leads to frequent relapses, which require multiple rounds of corticosteroid therapy, posing challenges for long-term management. Recent evidence shows that targeted release budesonide (TRB) can effectively inhibit the first immunological steps taking place in Peyer patches in distal ileum, but also healing glomerular damage due to the minor absorption in systematic circulation causing no life-threatening side-effects.
Method
Adult IgAN patients, diagnosed the last 10 years, maintaining eGFR >30 ml/min/1.73 m2 and Uprotein >750 mg/24 hr, despite standard supportive treatment for at least 6 months, commenced on a 9-month TRB treatment, 16 mg/d with 1 month tapering, and followed regularly in the outpatient clinic. Renal biopsies were re-evaluated and scored according to Oxford classification. Parameters of renal function were monitored during TRB administration in a 3 month basis, at 0, 3, 6, 10 months, T0, T3, T6, 10, respectively.
Results
Thirty-three IgAN patients, M/F:25/8, Median age: 45 (38.5–65) years, from four different departments, included in the study. During the period between diagnosis and the initiation of treatment, [37 (22–87) months] eGFR declined from 64.99 ± 24.95 ml/min/1.73 m2 to T0, 58.93 ± 24.83 ml/min/1.73 m2, P = 0.063, and Uprot (2.87 ± 1.96 gr/24 hr) presented a minor decline to Uprot = 2.76 ± 1.7 gr/24 hr, P = 0.309 (T0).
After commencing on TRB, T0–T3: 2.76 ± 1.7 − 2.31 ± 1.82 gr/24 hr, P = 0.225, T3-T6 2.31 ± 1.82 − 1.85 ± 1.69 gr/24 hr, P = 0.048, T6-T10 1.85 ± 1.69 − 1.67 ± 1.18 gr/24 hr, P = 0.052 and from T0 to T10: 2.76 ± 1.7 − 1.67 ± 1.18 gr/24 hr, P = 0.004. (Fig. 1) Simultaneously, eGFR remained stable during follow up. (56.01 ± 26.04 ml/min/1.73 m2) has been decreased since treatment initiation (eGFR -T0 = 58.93 ± 24.83 ml/min/1.73 m2), P = 0.244.
Despite significant improvement in the severity of proteinuria, only 10/33 patients managed to reduce Uprot <1 gr/24 hr at the end of the study. This group of patients were characterized by the presence of endocapillary hypercellularity (E1) and crescent formation (C1), P = 0.015 and P = 0.041, with Phi's value of 0.438 and 0.367, respectively, indicating that IgAN patients presenting these lesions are more likely to respond to treatment.
Conclusion
A 10-month TRB administration can effectively reduce proteinuria in IgAN patients. The presence of E1 and/or C1 in kidney biopsy can be considered favorable prognostic indicators when TRB is administered. Both of these lesions are indicative of ongoing immunological activity and TRB can effectively reduce proteinuria.

title: #2093 Targeted-release budesonide (TRB) treatment may have different effects on the inflammatory process in IgAN patients with recent and old diagnosis
authors: Christodoulos Keskinis; Eleni Moysidou; Stamatia Stai; Michalis Christodoulou; Georgios Lioulios; Sotirios-Spyridon Vamvakas; Maria Styliani Trivyza; Panagiotis Pateinakis; Marios Papasotiriou; Maria Stangou
abstract:
Background and Aims
Targeted-release budesonide (TRB) constitutes the first approved agent aiming at early stages of pathogenetic cascade in IgA nephropathy. The direct impact of this new regimen on anti-inflammatory and pre-inflammatory biomarkers is still under investigation.
Method
In this prospective study we included Caucasian adults, with IgAN, diagnosed during the last 5 yrs, with eGFR (CKD-EPI) ≥30 ml/min/1.73 m2, Uprot/24 hr ≥1 g/day and being on Sodium-Glucose Co-Transporter 2 inhibitors (SGL-2i) and maximal tolerated dose of Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone axis inhibitors (RAASi) for at least the last 6 months.
All patients were commenced on 16 mg/d of TRB and followed in the outpatient clinic, in a 3-month basis. Kidney function and proteinuria (Uprot) were recorded at the initiation of TRB (T0) and at 3, 6 and 10 months (T3, T6, T10, respectively). ELISA was applied to evaluate urinary Clusterin (CLU), Monocyte Chemotactic Protein-1 (MCP-1) and Matrix MetalloProteinase-2 (MMP-9) levels at T0 and T3. Patients were divided in two groups, those with recent diagnosis (RD, n = 8, t ≤ 6 months), and patients with old diagnosis (OD, n = 6, t > 6 months).
Results
At T0, urinary levels of biomarkers in the whole cohort of patients (Mage 53.24 ± 12.76 yrs), were CLU = 93.73 (46.41–147.54) pg/ml, MCP-1 = 274.47 (173.2–391.36) pg/ml, MMP-9 = 0.4 (0.21–0.86) pg/ml.
Changes in eGFR and Uprot during follow up are depicted in Table 1.
Patients in RD group showed an increase in CLU, from T0 to T3, 48.38 (28.02–139.77) vs 94.92 (31.85–214.11) pg/ml, P = 0.036, and MCP-1 levels 307.23 (174.99–715.93) vs 417.55 (257.63–727.10) pg/ml, P = 0.917, while urinary MMP-9 levels were decreased (0.59 (0.24–1.07) vs 0.50 (0.26–12.85) pg/ml, P = 0.123.
In OD group, urinary CLU levels were reduced from T0 to T3, (130.70 (63.28–286.45) vs 115.96 (71.19–302.70), P = 0.917, yet, both urinary MCP-1 and MMP-9 levels were increased, 307.23 (174.99–715.93) vs 417.55 (257.63–727.10) pg/ml, P = 0.917, and 0.27 (0.19–13.48) vs 0.45 (0.24–11.23) pg/ml, P = 0.753, respectively.
Conclusion
Urinary excretion of pre-inflammatory, MCP-1 and MMP-9, and anti-inflammatory mediators, CLU, were differently affected following TRB treatment, depending on the time passed since initial diagnosis of IgAN, with recent diagnosis favoring a more prominent anti-inflammatory effect.

title: #860 Clinical and biological characteristics predictive of immune checkpoint inhibitors-induced acute tubulo-interstitial nephritis
authors: Thomas Kondolff; Mathis Michel; Pierre Isnard; Antoine Max; Alain Wynckel; Vincent Vuiblet; Zeinab Awada; Arnaud Stolz; Benjamin Savenkoff; Hélène Lazareth; Hervé Sartelet; Adrien Flahault
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal toxicity from immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) is considered rare (1%–2%). Risk factors for acute kidney injury (AKI) includes pre-existing chronic kidney disease (CKD), proton pump inhibitor use. Kidney biopsy was performed in a minority of patients reported in the literature, and acute tubulo-interstitial nephritis (ATIN) accounts for over 90% of cases. Use of ICI combination and ICI association with chemotherapy has been associated with a higher rate of adverse kidney events, especially in patients treated with ICI and pemetrexed combination. Kidney biopsy was seldom performed in these reports, but AKI mainly resulted from ATIN and acute tubular necrosis (ATN). While ATIN is believed to respond well to steroid therapy, ATN does not. Furthermore, steroid therapy has been associated with decreased overall and progression-free survival in patients treated with ICIs. Although kidney biopsy provides a formal diagnosis, logistical and clinical challenges often delay or preclude timely renal biopsy in real-world settings. We aimed to identify if clinical and/or biological parameters could predict ATIN, versus ATN and other kidney injuries, in patients with AKI receiving ICI.
Method
NEPHROTOX is a retrospective, multicenter study, including patients treated with ICI who were referred to the nephrology clinic for AKI five French centers (CHRU Nancy, Hôpital Européen Georges Pompidou, GHT Verdun Saint Mihiel, CHR Metz-Thionville, CHU Reims) and who underwent kidney biopsy between January 2018 and December 2024. We collected clinical and biochemical data, kidney function outcome and steroid use from hospital file. Histopathological data was obtained from biopsy reports. Ethical approval was granted by the CHRU Nancy Ethics Committee on April 2, 2024 (Ref. 2023PI178).
Results
We obtained 95 kidney biopsies of ICI-treated patients with AKI. ICI combination was used in 13 (14%) cases, and association with pemetrexed was used in 44 (46%) cases. Median [25%, 75%] baseline (pre-immunotherapy) and biopsy eGFR were 73 [63, 89] and 27 [16, 43] ml/min/1.73 m2, respectively. Urine protein to creatinine ratio was 369 [170, 830] mg/g, and urine albumin to creatinine ratio was 67 [3, 229] mg/g. AKI stage according to the KDIGO classification was 1 (n = 33, 35%), 2 (n = 22, 23%) or 3 (n = 35, 37%) while AKI did not meet criteria for stage 1 in 5 (5%) cases. ATIN was diagnosed in 70 (74%) cases. ATN was found in 64% and 68% of ATIN and non-ATIN cases, respectively. ATIN, versus non-ATIN-related AKI, was associated with a more severe AKI (Fig. 1, eGFR decrease from baseline, 64 [51, 81] % vs 42 [38, 50] %, P < 0.001), and with leukocyturia (found in 69% of ATIN versus 35% of non-ATIN, P = 0.006). Proteinuria, eosinophilia and other immune related events did not differ between ATIN and non-ATIN cases. Immunotherapy combination and use of pemetrexed were not associated with ATIN diagnosis. Steroids were given in 90% cases of ATIN. Kidney function improvement was better in ATIN cases, compared to non-ATIN (eGFR increase at 3 months, 18 [10, 28] versus 3 [−3, 8] ml/min/1.73 m2). In patients with AKI under ICI monotherapy, French national guidelines suggest ICI withdrawal and steroid therapy in case of AKI stage 2-3 KDIGO; in our study, this would have resulted in excess treatment in 3 (9%) cases where no ATIN was identified. In contrast, these guidelines recommend no treatment and ICI continuation, with close kidney function follow-up, in stages 0–1 KDIGO; this would have resulted, in our study, in insufficient or delayed treatment in 11 (52%) of cases where ATIN was identified.
Conclusion
Although ICI-related AKI was most often related to ATIN, one in every four cases was not attributable to ATIN. Leukocyturia and a more severe AKI were the only factors associated with ATIN diagnosis, and these were neither specific nor sensitive. ATIN diagnosis is associated with specific treatment and better outcome. Given diagnosis uncertainty, empiric steroid therapy without kidney biopsy should be avoided when possible in the treatment of ICI-related AKI.

Steroids were given in 90% cases of ATIN. Kidney function improvement was better in ATIN cases, compared to non-ATIN (eGFR increase at 3 months, 18 [10, 28] versus 3 [−3, 8] ml/min/1.73 m2). In patients with AKI under ICI monotherapy, French national guidelines suggest ICI withdrawal and steroid therapy in case of AKI stage 2-3 KDIGO; in our study, this would have resulted in excess treatment in 3 (9%) cases where no ATIN was identified. In contrast, these guidelines recommend no treatment and ICI continuation, with close kidney function follow-up, in stages 0–1 KDIGO; this would have resulted, in our study, in insufficient or delayed treatment in 11 (52%) of cases where ATIN was identified.
Conclusion
Although ICI-related AKI was most often related to ATIN, one in every four cases was not attributable to ATIN. Leukocyturia and a more severe AKI were the only factors associated with ATIN diagnosis, and these were neither specific nor sensitive. ATIN diagnosis is associated with specific treatment and better outcome. Given diagnosis uncertainty, empiric steroid therapy without kidney biopsy should be avoided when possible in the treatment of ICI-related AKI.

title: #110 Association between relapse and long-term kidney outcomes in IgA nephropathy
authors: Xue Shen; Pei Chen; Jicheng Lv; Hong Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Relapse in IgA nephropathy (IgAN) remains under-researched. This study investigates the incidence of IgAN relapse, its association with adverse outcomes, and its risk factors within a prospective cohort.
Method
We analysed data from a prospective cohort of 1,069 patients who achieved remission after treatment. The study assessed relapse incidence, its correlation with kidney endpoint events, and identified clinicopathological predictors of relapse using Cox regression analysis.
Results
Among the 1,069 patients, 348 (33%) experienced 411 relapses, the overall relapse free rates at 1, 5 and 10 years were 83%, 31% and 9% respectively. Relapse patients had a significantly higher incidence of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) and composite kidney endpoint events compared to non-relapse patients. In addition, patients with two or more relapses had a higher incidence of ESKD compared to patients with one relapse. The relapse group also exhibited a more rapid decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) compare with non-relapse group (2.3 vs 1.0 mL/min/1.73 m²/year). After adjusting for confounders, significant predictors of relapse included 24-hour urine protein excretion rate (24-h UP) at remission, eGFR at remission, and medications used for inducing remission. Notably, patients with corticosteroid-induced remission had a higher likelihood of relapse within 3 years. Controlling 24-h UP at remission to below 0.3 g/d was associated with a significantly improved relapse-free rate.
Conclusion
Relapse is prevalent in IgAN and is associated with an increased rate of kidney endpoint events and accelerated eGFR decline. Predictors of relapse encompass various clinical indicators and treatment modalities, with stricter control of proteinuria at remission being crucial for reducing relapse rates.

title: #1777 Primary renal bilateral diffuse large B cell lymphoma: a case report
authors: Samara Guadalupe Padilla Barragán; Yair Alejandro Hernández Rea; Miguel Medina Perez; Claudia Mendoza Cerpa
abstract:
Background and Aims
Primary renal lymphoma (PRL) is defined as a non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the kidney without primarily extra renal lymphatic disease. It is rare, as the kidney is an extranodal organ and does not contain lymphatic tissue. The incidence of PRL is 0.7% of all extra nodal lymphomas. The present study reports the case of a young man with PRL in both kidneys.
Method
He is a 21 year old man, healthy, with occasional consumption of proton pump inhibitors and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. The patient was admitted due to headache, nausea, vomiting and back pain. The blood work reported serum creatinine of 4 mg/dl. Urine analysis without hematuria or leukocyturia and immunological panel within normal range. The abdominal computed tomography (CT) reported bilateral nephromegaly, with kidney length of 15 cm with diffuse hyperechogenicity. The physical examination was normal. It was considered an acute kidney injury (AKI) due to Acute Interstitial Nephritis (AIN) and he was administered 3 IV methylprednisolone bolus, however, 72 hours after AKI got worse, with hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, starting hemodialysis. Kidney biopsy showed 7 normal glomeruli. Immunofluorescence without deposits. Light microscopy showed obliteration of kidney parenchyma by a mixed lymphoid infiltrate composed large lymphoid cells with abnormal nuclei. Immunohistochemistry was positive for CD20, CD10, BCL2 and CD3, and negative for MUM1 and BCL6, suggestive of diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL) of the germinal center B cell. The Ki-67 proliferative rate was 70%. The neck, chest and abdominal (CT) did not show evidence of systemic invasion. Due to the high risk score in the International Prognostic Index (IPI) and Central Nervous System International Prognostic Index (CNS-IPI), it was decided to administer DA EPOCH R regimen, for six courses. The CT scan after treatment showed a complete response, returning to normal kidney size and improvement of kidney function, with serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dl.
Results
Lymphomatous infiltration of the kidney is a frequent complication of hematologic disorders, presenting in 34% of lymphomas. However, PRL is rare, comprising less than 1% of all renal masses and extranodal lymphomas.
The diagnosis can be challenging due to the clinical presentation, ranging from silent kidney masses, kidney abscesses or kidney tumor metastasis, to symptoms as flank or pelvic pain, hematuria, AKI or weight loss. Our patient debuted with AKI and bilateral kidney enlargement. The presumptive diagnosis was drug induced AIN. AIN is characterized by an interstitial infiltrate associated with edema and tubulitis. Imaging studies may show normal or enlarged kidneys. The management include cut off the harmful medication and steroid therapy. Our patient´s kidney function got worse after steroid therapy, behaving as a tumor lysis syndrome.
The usual presentation of PRL is as a unilateral, solitary mass. Bilateral presentations are rare and can cause nephromegaly. The incidence of AKI is 0.5%, more commonly in bilateral cases.
Other radiological findings are multiple renal masses and diffuse renal infiltration. The kidney biopsy from our patient showed infiltrating cells diffusely positive for B cell marker CD20. These was consistent with DLBCL, the most common histopathological lymphoma subtype involving the kidney. As the CT scan did not show evidence of systemic invasion, it was considered as Primary renal lymphoma. The prognosis will depend on the tumor stage. Early diagnosis and treatment may improve survival. Hematology considered him as high risk patient, deciding the DA EPOCH R regimen. After 6 courses, a complete response was achieved. Our patient has been followed for a complete year, showing a complete response by CT scan and improvement in kidney function.
Conclusion
Even PRL is rare, it should be considered between the differential diagnosis when a kidney mass is presented, or like in this case, a bilateral involvement without any other possible cause. An early diagnosis and prompt management can make the difference and improve the patient's survival.

title: #2444 Patients with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) achieved low proteinuria targets earlier and more often with sparsentan (SPAR) vs irbesartan (IRB) in DUPLEX
authors: Vladimir Tesar; Hernan Trimarchi; James Tumlin; Laura Kooienga; Radko Komers; Jula Inrig; Edward Murphy; Eva Rodríguez García
abstract:
Background and Aims
Previous research supports that reductions in proteinuria are associated with a lower risk of progression to kidney failure (KF) in patients with FSGS. The phase 3 DUPLEX trial examined the efficacy of SPAR, a non-immunosuppressive, dual endothelin angiotensin receptor antagonist (DEARA), vs IRB in patients with FSGS and showed that SPAR led to sustained proteinuria reduction. Expanding on earlier findings from this study, we investigated the comparative effects of SPAR vs IRB on varying low proteinuria targets, including complete and partial remission of proteinuria, and the effect of remission on progression to KF in DUPLEX.
Method
DUPLEX (NCT03493685) was a randomized, double-blind, phase 3 study evaluating the efficacy and safety of SPAR vs IRB in patients with FSGS (without secondary causes). Patients received SPAR (n = 184) or IRB (n = 187) for 108 weeks at target doses of 800 mg/d and 300 mg/d, respectively. Study endpoints were defined as follows: (i) partial remission of proteinuria, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) of ≤1.5 g/g and a >40% reduction from baseline; (ii) complete remission of proteinuria, UPCR of <0.3 g/g; and (iii) KF, estimated glomerular filtration rate of <15 mL/min/1.73 m2 or kidney replacement therapy. We investigated the impact of SPAR vs IRB on achieving partial and complete remission and varying levels of proteinuria reduction (UPCR of <0.5, 1.0, or 1.5 g/g) at any time during the 108-week double-blind treatment period. Post hoc analyses using pooled data from all treatment groups examined the risk of KF among patients who achieved partial or complete remission of proteinuria vs those who did not.
Results
Patients achieved all proteinuria thresholds earlier and more frequently with SPAR vs IRB. The median time to partial remission was 14.1 weeks with SPAR vs 109.0 weeks with IRB, with 64.7% of patients achieving partial remission at any time with SPAR vs 43.9% with IRB. Additional results are shown in the Table 1. Irrespective of treatment arm, patients who achieved partial or complete remission at any time during the 108-week study period were less likely to reach KF than those who did not (Fig. 1). Among patients who achieved partial remission, 3.0% reached KF vs 15.9% who did not. Among patients who achieved complete remission, 2.1% reached KF vs 9.9% who did not. SPAR was generally well tolerated, with no new safety concerns.
Conclusion
Clinically meaningful low proteinuria thresholds and partial and complete remission definitions were achieved earlier and more often with SPAR vs IRB. In DUPLEX, the risk of KF was lower among patients who achieved partial or complete remission of proteinuria vs those who did not. Taken together, results support the nephroprotective benefit of SPAR in patients with FSGS.

title: #1610 Long-term patients and kidney prognosis of pure membranous compared to mixed lupus nephritis: an Italian multicenter study of 195 patients
authors: Martina Uzzo; Marisol Bracalenti; Marta Calatroni; Luca Iaccarino; Francesco Reggiani; Barbara Trezzi; Roberto De Pascale; Giovanni Maria Rossi; Renato Alberto Sinico; Gabriella Luisa Moroni; Andrea Doria
abstract:
Background and Aims
Membranous lupus nephritis (MLN, Class V ISN/RPS) represents a distinct subtype of lupus nephritis (LN) accounting for 15%–20% of the histological forms, with unique clinical and histopathological features. Traditionally regarded as less aggressive than proliferative lupus nephritis (Classes III and IV ISN/RPS), MLN is commonly characterized by nephrotic syndrome at presentation, with lower extra-renal disease activity. Emerging evidence suggests a potential for MLN to cause significant kidney damage and long-term complications.
This retrospective study aimed to analyze and compare baseline characteristics, short- and long-term clinical outcomes and response to therapy between patients with pure MLN (Class V ISN/RPS) and those with mixed forms (Classes V + III or V + IV ISN/RPS).
Method
A large cohort of 195 patients with MLN (pure or mixed) was gathered from three Nephrological Italian centers (IRCCS Humanitas Research Hospital, Milano; IRCCS San Gerardo Hospital, Monza; Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria di Parma) and one Rheumatological center (Azienda Ospedale Università di Padova).
Outcomes were evaluated over an extensive follow-up period spanning more than five decades. A multivariable Cox regression model was employed to identify predictors of renal and patient prognosis within the overall cohort.
Results
At baseline, mixed MLN patients exhibited more severe disease activity, as evidenced by higher activity and chronicity indices on kidney biopsy (activity index: 6 [IQR 4, 8] vs 0 [0, 2), P < 0.001; chronicity index: 2 [IQR 1, 4] vs 1 [IQR 0, 2], P < 0.001), lower complement levels (C3: 66.50 [IQR 49.25, 79.00] g/L vs 73.25 [IQR 56.62, 92.50] g/L, P = 0.039; C4: 10.00 [IQR 6.00, 15.00] g/L vs 13.05 [IQR 9.25, 21.75] g/L, P = 0.002), higher rate of dsDNA positivity (n = 84 (84.8%) vs n = 64 (66.7%), P = 0.008) and a greater prevalence of nephritic syndrome at presentation (n = 14 (14.3%) vs n = 1 (1.1%), P < 0.001). Conversely, pure MLN patients were more likely to receive less aggressive treatment, often limited to steroid monotherapy (n = 22 (22.9%) vs n = 8 (8.1%), P = 0.002).
Both groups achieved similar rates of complete remission over time (P = 0.11), although mixed MLN patients showed a trend toward faster remission (Fig. 1). While CKD-free and relapse-free survival rates were comparable between groups, crude survival rates for the composite outcome of kidney failure and death were significantly lower in the pure MLN group (P = 0.026), with the difference becoming evident after 10 years of observation (Fig. 2). In the best predicting model including baseline eGFR and the use of immunosuppressive therapy beyond steroids as induction therapy, the histopathological class was confirmed as a significant predictor of prognosis (HR 0.21 (CI 95%: 0.05–0.95), P = 0.041). Of note, baseline eGFR emerged as the strongest determinant of prognosis (HR 0.98 (CI 95%: 0.96–0.99), P = 0.009), together with the use of immunosuppressive therapy beyond steroids as induction therapy (HR 0.28 (IC 95%: 0.10–0.79), P = 0.016).
Conclusion
This study challenges the long-standing perception of pure MLN as a generally benign condition, demonstrating that it carries significant risks for CKD, kidney failure, and death over the long term. These findings underscore the importance of personalized treatment strategies tailored to clinical and histological features.

title: #1987 Single-nucleus multi-omic profiling identified different extent of podocyte injury and podocyte-parietal epithelial cell communication in podocytopathy
authors: Yitao Lin; Ying Wang; Lubin Xu; Zheng Huang; Saifu Yin; Yixin MA; Yun Li; Yu-Bing Wen; Wenling Ye; Tao Lin; Lan Jiang; Limeng Chen
abstract:
Background and Aims
The mechanism underlying podocyte disorder in primary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and minimal change disease (MCD) remains unclear. This study aimed to identify the potential pathogenesis of podocytopathy using single-nucleus RNA (snRNA) and assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (ATAC) sequencing.
Method
We applied snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq on kidney biopsy tissue from patients with primary FSGS (n = 4), MCD (n = 10), and healthy controls from time-zero biopsy in renal transplantation (HC, n = 14). Cell types were annotated through reference mapping. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and differential peaks in the diseased conditions were identified. We further performed enrichment analysis, calculated degenerative podocyte gene signature score, and inferred cell-cell communication pattern.
Results
We identified a total of 242,744 high-quality nuclei, with 1,843 podocytes by reference mapping. DEGs in podocytes per condition were identified. Down-regulated genes in FSGS podocytes were enriched in pathways related to actomyosin structure organization and integrin-mediated signaling. Up-regulated genes in MCD podocytes were enriched in pathways related to protein localization to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and protein folding. The podocyte damage or stress represented by the degenerative podocyte signature score was significantly higher in FSGS than in MCD podocytes and healthy controls. Through CellChat, we noticed remarkable changes in podocyte-parietal epithelial cell communication and the increase in outgoing Notch signaling from parietal epithelial cells sent to podocytes in FSGS.
Conclusion
This is the first single-nucleus multi-omic analysis on kidney biopsy tissue from patients with FSGS and MCD. Our results provided direct evidence of actin cytoskeleton reorganization, cell-extracellular matrix interaction, ER stress, and different extent of podocyte injury in the pathogenesis of podocytopathy at single-cell resolution, and shed light on the precise cellular crosstalk in patients with FSGS and MCD.

title: #2627 Adult renal progenitor cells can decrease the inflammatory and immunological triggering in IgA nephropathy patients at renal tissue level
authors: Francesca Montenegro; Angela Picerno; Francesca Giannuzzi; Antonella Cicirelli; Vincenzo Di Leo; Loreto Gesualdo; Fabio Sallustio
abstract:
Background and Aims
Recent investigations have explored the complex ways in which progenitor and stem cells impact renal disorders. In fact, the connection between stem/progenitor cells and the kidney's microenvironment has been the subject of extensive research, providing insight into the intricate cellular interactions and signaling pathways involved in the pathophysiology of renal illness.
Overall, adult renal progenitor cells (ARPCs) have a variety of roles in kidney disorders, including immunological regulation, tissue regeneration, and renal homeostasis maintenance.
In this study, we isolated the renal stem/progenitor cells from IgA Nephropathy (IgAN) patients and compared them with renal CD133− cells to identify, for the first time, genes and biological processes that are specifically activated in IgAN patient ARPCs and that can affect the disease.
Method
Urine-derived cells were collected from 5 IgAN patients and 5 Healthy Subjects (HS), ARPCs were isolated, characterized for the CD133 and CD24 markers by Cytofluorimetric Analysis and separated from the CD133− portion by immunolabeling. RNA-Seq through PromethION 2 Nanopore technology was performed on both cell fractions from IgAN patients and HS. Differential analysis, Over Representation Analysis (ORA) and Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) were performed across the four sample types. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were corrected for FDR using BH method.
Results
We found 39 genes that were exclusively expressed in ARPCs from IgAN patients and 140 genes specifically expressed in CD133− cells from IgAN patients, whereas only 14 genes were in common between these two cell types. The ORA and GSEA analysis showed that in IgAN, and not in HS, ARPCs modulate genes involved in immunomodulatory mechanisms such as the regulation of leukocyte migration, regulation of T cell proliferation, regulation of T-reg cells, and response to molecules of bacterial origin (FDR 0.0238, Fig. 1). This is interesting, considering previous studies showing the ARPC capacity to induce Tregs and CD3+ CD4− CD8− double-negative (DN) T cells. Noteworthy, in ARPCs from IgAN patients we found some genes known as involved in the disease that were downregulated compared to CD133− cells from the same patients such as IL6 (logFC −3.35, FDR 0.0002), CXCL1 (logFC −2.87, FDR 0.0178), CXCL8 (logFC −4.12, FDR 0.0007), whereas TNFRSF14 was upregulated (logFC 2.67, FDR 0.0295).
Conclusion
Our results suggest a role of ARPCs in decreasing inflammatory and immunological triggering in IgAN at renal tissue level. Background and Aims
Recent investigations have explored the complex ways in which progenitor and stem cells impact renal disorders. In fact, the connection between stem/progenitor cells and the kidney's microenvironment has been the subject of extensive research, providing insight into the intricate cellular interactions and signaling pathways involved in the pathophysiology of renal illness.
Overall, adult renal progenitor cells (ARPCs) have a variety of roles in kidney disorders, including immunological regulation, tissue regeneration, and renal homeostasis maintenance.
In this study, we isolated the renal stem/progenitor cells from IgA Nephropathy (IgAN) patients and compared them with renal CD133− cells to identify, for the first time, genes and biological processes that are specifically activated in IgAN patient ARPCs and that can affect the disease.

title: #2548 Long-term stabilization of kidney function (estimated glomerular filtration rate) with iptacopan in patients with native C3 glomerulopathy
authors: David Kavanagh; Christoph Licht; Serge Smeets; Rubeen Israni; Deborah Keefe; Soudeh Ansari; Junhao Liu; Carla M Nester
abstract:
Background and Aims
C3 glomerulopathy (C3G), is an ultra-rare primary glomerulonephritis caused by overactivation of the alternative complement pathway (AP). Iptacopan (LNP023) is an oral, proximal complement inhibitor that targets Factor B to selectively inhibit the AP of the complement cascade. The estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) slope (i.e. the rate of decline over time) is accepted as a surrogate endpoint in glomerular diseases. We have previously reported stabilization of eGFR parameters with iptacopan treatment across Phase 2 and 3 studies. This pooled analysis aims to demonstrate the long-term stabilization of eGFR observed with iptacopan treatment in patients with native C3G.
Method
In this pooled exploratory analysis, data spanning up to 57 months were combined for all patients with native C3G from Study X2202 (Phase 2), APPEAR-C3G (Phase 3), and Study B12001B (Phase 3b, roll-over extension; Table 1). Improvement in kidney function through long-term stabilization of eGFR was evaluated by comparing the change in eGFR slope from prior to treatment with iptacopan to post-iptacopan treatment initiation (200 mg b.i.d.) in the overall study population and subgroups of participants with baseline eGFR <90 mL/min/1.73 m2 versus ≥90 mL/min/1.73 m2 (normal range). Historical serum creatinine data (collected up to 2 years before randomization) were used to calculate eGFR using the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) formula. Pooling the data allowed for more precise eGFR slope reporting. Before iptacopan treatment, a common eGFR slope was assumed for all treatment arms.
Results
A total of 90 patients with native C3G were included in the pooled analysis (baseline eGFR ≥90 mL/min/1.73 m2, n = 47; <90 mL/min/1.73 m2, n = 43). In the overall study population, an improvement in post-iptacopan treatment initiation eGFR slope was observed (change in slope: 7.62 mL/min/1.73 m2/year, P < 0.0001; Table 2). Subgroup analyses demonstrated an improvement in post-iptacopan treatment initiation eGFR slope in participants with baseline eGFR <90 mL/min/1.73 m2 (eGFR slope change: 12.98 mL/min/1.73 m2/year, P < 0.0001) but not in participants with baseline eGFR ≥90 mL/min/1.73 m2 (eGFR slope change: 0.57 mL/min/1.73 m2/year, P = NS; Table 2). In the subgroup with eGFR ≥90 mL/min/1.73 m2, the eGFR slope was only minimally negative in the prior to treatment with iptacopan period and remained unchanged post-iptacopan treatment initiation. These pooled data are consistent with eGFR slopes from the individual studies.
Conclusion
The findings from this pooled analysis indicate that in patients with native C3G, treatment with iptacopan 200 mg b.i.d. resulted in the stabilization of eGFR trajectory, with significant change observed in patients with at least mild renal impairment from C3G disease at baseline (<90 mL/min/1.73 m2) and maintenance of stable eGFR in those with normal baseline eGFR (≥90 mL/min/1.73 m2). eGFR slope analysis has demonstrated valuable utility in monitoring kidney function over time, and these data suggest iptacopan treatment results in a long-term, clinically relevant positive impact on kidney function.

title: #3832 Predicting disease progression in IgA nephropathy Portuguese patients: the role of inflammation and vascular damage markers beyond the IgAN PT
authors: Vítor Fernandes; Rafael Henriques de Figueiredo; Roberto Silva; Luís Carlos Ferreira Mendonça; Bernardo Faria; Ines Alencastre; Isabel Brandão; Manuel Pestana; João Paulo Oliveira; Jorge Reis Almeida
abstract:
Background and Aims
The International IgA Nephropathy Prediction Tool (IgAN PT) is recommended by KDIGO guidelines to assess disease progression in IgAN. This study aimed to identify clinical and histological parameters, at diagnosis, associated with disease progression, in a northern Portuguese population over an extended follow-up period and compare them with the established IgAN PT.
Method
This retrospective cohort study reviewed all kidney biopsies performed at São João University Hospital Center from 2003 to 2018. We included patients with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy and an eGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m² at biopsy. Exclusion criteria included unavailable histological material for review, secondary causes, and age <18 years were excluded. Clinical and histological data were reviewed retrospectively at the time of the biopsy. The risk of progression at 5-years after biopsy was calculated using the IgAN PT. Two groups were defined according to the rate of decline: if eGFR <2 ml/min/year patients were classified as slow decliners; if ≥2 mL/min/year as rapid decliners.
Results
Of the 783 kidney biopsies, 141 IgA cases were selected, and we achieved a cohort of 52 cases of IgAN after applying exclusion criteria. The mean follow-up duration was 7.3 ± 5.0 years. At diagnosis, median age was 40.1 years, median eGFR was 84.5 mL/min/1.73 m², median proteinuria was 1.0 g/day. Hypertension was present in 46% of patients, and 67.3% were treated with RAASi. Based on yearly eGFR decline, 23 patients were classified as slow decliners and 29 as rapid decliners. Compared to slow decliners, rapid decliners, at time of biopsy, had significantly higher age (P = 0.03), hypertension prevalence (P = 0.01), RAASi use (P < 0.01), dyslipidemia prevalence (P < 0.01), eGFR 30–59 mL/min frequency (P < 0.01), segmental sclerosis (P = 0.02), higher serum IgA levels (P = 0.03) and higher ferritin levels (P = 0.01). Presence of arterial hyalinosis approached statistical significance (P = 0.05). Median proteinuria or IgAN PT score showed no significant difference. In univariate binary logistic regression, dyslipidemia prevalence (OR 18.20; P < 0.01), eGFR 30–60 mL/min/1.73 m² (OR 7.41, P = 0.02), hypertension (OR 4.64; P = 0.01), and segmental sclerosis at biopsy (OR 3.74; P = 0.03) were more strongly associated decline, whereas IgAN PT score (OR 1.10; P = 0.02) and age (OR 1.05, P = 0.04), although significant, had a weaker association.
Conclusion
The IgAN PT includes variables associated with eGFR decline, such as age, eGFR, RAASi use, and segmental sclerosis. However, in this cohort, the diagnosis of dyslipidemia and hypertension were stronger predictors of rapid decline than IgAN PT score or proteinuria at biopsy. These findings suggest that vascular damage and inflammation play a crucial role in disease progression, highlighting the need to address these factors beyond the IgAN PT.

title: #0181 Efficacy and safety of apixaban in patients with nephrotic syndrome: a prospective longitudinal cohort study
authors: Iryna Mykhaloiko
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with nephrotic syndrome (NS) face a higher risk of venous and arterial thromboembolism due to altered clotting factors, reduced natural anticoagulants, and increased platelet activation, which correlate with hypoalbuminemia severity. While warfarin, low-molecular-weight heparin, and aspirin have been used to manage this risk, the efficacy and safety of newer direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) remain largely unknown. Apixaban, a direct FXa inhibitor, is appealing due to minimal renal clearance and evidence suggesting its safety and efficacy in reduced glomerular filtration. However, hypoalbuminemia may affect the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of apixaban, although this aspect is insufficiently considered in routine clinical practice.
The aim of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of apixaban in the prevention of thromboembolism in patients with NS associated with primary glomerulonephritis (GN).
Method
A single-center prospective longitudinal cohort study was conducted between October 2021 and November 2024, including 76 patients with primary GN and NS who had an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) >60 ml/min/1.73 m². In all 76 patients the diagnosis of GN was confirmed morphologically as follows 23 patients (30.3%; 95% CI 20.2–41.9) were diagnosed with mesangioproliferative GN, 21 patients (27.6%; 95% CI 18.0–39.1) had membranous nephropathy, 14 patients (18.4%; 95% CI 10.5–29.0) had focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, 11 patients (14.5%; 95% CI 7.5–24.4) had minimal change disease, and 7 patients (9.2%; 95% CI 3.8–18.1) was confirmed membrane proliferative GN. The patients were divided into two groups: The first group (38 patients) received prophylactic anticoagulation with warfarin, while the second group (38 patients) received anticoagulation therapy with apixaban at a dose of 5 mg twice daily. The cohorts were balanced by age, gender, morphological diagnosis, and renal function. Both groups of patients received immunosuppressive therapy for NS based on their underlying primary disease. Prophylactic anticoagulation was indicated in cases of severe hypoalbuminemia, defined as less than 25 g/L in membranous nephropathy and less than 20 g/L in other types of GN. The anticoagulation therapy lasted between 1 and 6 months, depending on how quickly remission of NS was achieved. Instances of thrombosis and bleeding were monitored.
Results
No thromboembolic events were recorded in both groups. In contrast, bleeding episodes were observed in 6 patients (15.8%; 95% CI 7.4–30.4) from first group and in 4 patients (10.5%; 95% CI 4.2-24.1) from second group (P = 0.497). All classified as minor as per ISTH criteria (e.g. epistaxis, gingival hemorrhage, menorrhagia, and subcutaneous hemorrhage), and did not require medical intervention and discontinuation of the drug.
Conclusion
This study found apixaban to be as effective as warfarin in preventing thromboembolic events in NS patients, with a similar rate of minor hemorrhagic complications. Further large multicenter randomized, controlled trials should be conducted to confirm these encouraging results. Additionally, the guidelines for prophylactic anticoagulant therapy, including its optimal duration and timing of discontinuation, remain unclear.

title: #920 Effects of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors on proteinuria and kidney function in glomerulonephritis and glomerulopathy of different etiologies undergoing induction immunosuppression therapy
authors: Britta George; Stephanie Damm; Thomas Schachtner; Fabrice Benz
abstract:
Background and Aims
Glomerulonephritis (GN) and glomerulopathy (GP) have a high risk of progressing, which affects about 10% of the world's population and has become a leading cause of mortality. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) have emerged as a promising option to prevent progression in chronic kidney disease.
Besides for IgA nephropathy and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis out of sub-analyses of EMPA-Kidney and DAPA-CKD there is less known about treatment with SGLT2i in different types of glomerular disease (GD) [1, 2].
A retrospective study showed a significant reduction in proteinuria across all underlying GD. The effect on proteinuria was greater in patients with higher body mass index (BMI) [3].
We aim to provide more information about the antiproteinuric effect of SGLT2i in different types of GD. We additionally present for the first-time data on the progression of proteinuria and renal function in patients with active GN (including deterioration of kidney function) undergoing induction immunosuppression therapy (IIT).
Method
This is a retrospective, observational, single center cohort study at the university hospital of Zurich. Between 01/2000 and 02/2024 patients with biopsy proven GD treated with an SGLT2i and 2 outpatient visits since 01/2000 were included.
The primary outcomes were change in proteinuria and change in glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) at 1, 2, 3–4, 5–7 and 9–12 months after SGLT2i initiation. For patients undergoing IIT adverse events (infections, hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis) were investigated.
Results
Out of 450 patients with biopsy proven GD 114 patients treated with SGLT2i were identified. 73 patients were included. 17 patients were undergoing IIT. The disease etiologies are shown in Fig. 1. Mean age was 47 years, 38% were female, mean BMI was 26.6 kg/m2, mean renal function was 64 ml/min/1.73 m2 and mean urine protein creatinine ratio (UPCR) was 850 mg/mmol. All patients except 4 were on an additional therapy with renin-angiotensin system blockers. The median change in UPCR for all patients was −14%, −24%, −13%, −18% and −27%, whereas the median change in urine albumin creatinine ratio (UACR) was −21%, −5%, −26%, −48% and −40% at the defined timepoints after SGLT2i initiation, respectively. The median change in delta eGFR in ml/min/1.73 m2 for all patients enrolled was +/−0, −1, −2, −2 and −2 after SGLT2 inhibitor initiation, respectively. 73% had a proteinuria reduction of at least 30% in either UACR or UPCR, 25% did not respond to treatment and for 3% of patient's data were unavailable. The results for eGFR and proteinuria were consistent in all disease etiologies (Fig. 2).
Patients undergoing IIT did not experience frequent infections, especially no urinary tract infections, hypoglycemia or lactic acidosis and the decline in eGFR was comparable to patients without immunosuppression. All patients receiving IIT had residual proteinuria at 12 months (Fig. 3).
Conclusion
The use of an SGLT2i in GN and GP is associated with a reduction in proteinuria and stable renal function, irrespective of the underlying disease. In particular, the early use of an SGLT2i in patients undergoing IIT appears to be safe and has no negative effects on renal function and seems to be beneficial according to proteinuria.

title: #2789 Rituximab in treating steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome in children—experience from Uzbekistan
authors: Komiljon Khamzaev
abstract:
Background and Aims
Steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome (SSNS) and steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) significantly affect children's quality of life. While the majority of children with nephrotic syndrome respond to corticosteroids, half of these patients develop frequent relapses (FR) and/or steroid dependency (SD) and require multiple immunosuppressive agents, either in sequence or in combination, to prevent relapse. These children are at high risk of significant medication side effects such as short stature, Cushing syndrome, infection, and calcineurin inhibitor-associated nephrotoxicity. Rituximab (RTX), a chimeric anti-CD monoclonal antibody, has emerged as an effective therapy in children with FR-SD-NS to induce long-term disease remission and avoid steroid toxicities. Considering the challenges and adverse effects of previous treatments, rituximab has evolved into a therapy that can be used in different forms of nephrotic syndrome to induce long-term immunosuppression. The aim of this study is to find out the response of rituximab in idiopathic nephrotic syndrome and to look for response at 6, 9, 12, and 24 months after therapy.
Method
We conducted a prospective observational study in the Department of Paediatric Nephrology, National Children's Medical Centre, Uzbekistan, from May 2021 to December 2024, involving 86 children aged 3–18 with SSNS undergoing 3 years of continuous RTX therapy. The primary outcome was complete remission (CR), as defined by IPNA/KDIGO guidelines, at 6, 12, 18, and 24 months on RTX; secondary outcomes included adverse events. Kidney biopsies were performed in 65% of patients. RTX was administered every 6–12 months, depending on CD20 levels, IgG levels, and the presence of infections. The effectiveness of RTX was evaluated using eGFR (Schwarz formula) and proteinuria (ACR). The efficacy of RTX was assessed at three intervals: immediate (6 months post-therapy), short-term (12 months), and long-term (24 months).
Results
86 children were selected for RTX treatment. Overall, 1 experienced a severe allergic reaction. 72% of children with SSNS achieved and maintained complete remission within 2 years. Remission rates in SSNS children ranged from 60% (RR 0.78; 95% CI: 16.4–61.4%) at the 6th month. At the end of 12 months, in the FRNS category, 90% of patients were in remission; in the SDNS category, 91.6% of patients were in remission. The total number of relapses in 1 year before giving rituximab and one year after giving rituximab was assessed, and it was seen that the number of relapses was significantly reduced after giving rituximab in each category with p-values of 0.000 and 0.000 in FRNS and SDNS. The median duration of RTX use was 26.1 months, with a median cumulative dose of 2950 mg/m². Adverse reactions and complications were presented by mild infusion-related reactions in 3 children (3.49%), severe allergic reactions in 1 child (1.16%), hypogammaglobulinemia in 4 children (4.65%), and infections in 2 children (2.32%).
Conclusion
RTX was tolerated well and proved highly effective as a steroid-sparing agent, offering potential in terms of stopping relapses and minimising steroid-related side effects. It also demonstrated efficacy in slowing progression in SRNS, indicating potential for use in ACR reduction and renal function restoration, but requires careful use given potential severe allergic reactions and infectious complications. While the majority of children with nephrotic syndrome respond to corticosteroids, half of these patients develop frequent relapses (FR) and/or steroid dependency (SD) and require multiple immunosuppressive agents, either in sequence or in combination, to prevent relapse. title: #2284 Long-term efficacy and safety of telitacicept in the treatment of IgAN
authors: Liangxiang Xiao; Mengjiao Lin
abstract:
Background and Aims
Telitacicept is a recombinant fusion protein that combines the B lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS) receptor with an antibody, effectively inhibiting the abnormal activation of B cells and plasma cells. This mechanism significantly reduces the production of galactose-deficient IgA1 (Gd-IgA1) and subsequently decreases the deposition of immune complexes in the kidneys of patients with IgAN. Therefore, this study aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of telitacicept in the treatment of IgAN.
Method
Two high-risk progression IgAN patients confirmed by renal biopsy from March 6 2023 to May 29 2023 were included. Both patients received methylprednisolone 12 mg daily combinate with telitacicept at a dose of 160 mg weekly, and were followed up over 15 months. The primary endpoint was the mean percentage change in 24 h urinary protein (UP) from baseline at 1, 3, 6, 9, 12, and 15 months. Secondary endpoints included changes in serum creatinine, eGFR, and serum albumin at the same time points, along with a detailed recording of adverse events throughout the follow-up period.
Results
The baseline clinical characteristics of the two patients are summarized in Table 1. By followed-up12th month, patient 1 showed an 88.5% decrease in 24 h UP from 5.42 g to 0.62 g, and reduced telitacicept dose to 80 mg weekly. By followed-up 9th month, patient 2 exhibited a 76.8% reduction of 24 h UP from 3.28 g to 0.76 g, and reduced telitacicept dose to 80 mg weekly. After follow-up 15 months, patient 1 demonstrated a 90.87% reduction in 24 h UP compared to baseline, a 5.95% increase in serum albumin, a 93.96% decrease in urinary red blood cells, and a 21.13% reduction in serum creatinine, and then reduced telitacicept dose to 80 mg every 2 weeks. At the 15th-month follow, patient 2 experienced an 89.20% reduction in 24 h UP, an 11.05% increase in serum albumin, a 93.70% decrease in urinary red blood cells, and stable serum creatinine levels. Both patients tolerated telitacicept well, with no adverse events reported throughout the follow-up period.
Conclusion
Telitacicept could be an effective and safe treatment for high-risk progression IgAN patients.
