title: #1468 What characteristics are associated with a positive genetic study in patients suspected of Alport syndrome?
authors: Andrea Cifuentes-Talavera; Shehab Sayed; Patricia Torres Martínez; Teresa Bada Bosch; Amir Shabaka; Gema Maria Fernandez Juarez; Eduardo Gutiérrez Martínez; Manuel Praga Terente; Ángel Manuel Sevillano Prieto
abstract:
Background and Aims
Type IV collagen is the main component of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), configured in the form of α3α4α5 heterotrimers. These collagen chains are encoded by the COL4A3-5 genes. Pathogenic variants in any of these genes result in Alport syndrome (AS). Therefore, the definitive diagnosis of AS is established through confirmatory genetic test (GT). Despite this disorder remaining underdiagnosed, increased knowledge of its milder phenotypes has led to a higher level of suspicion for the disease in patients with a compatible clinical presentation. Understanding whether there are clinical or analytical characteristics associated with a greater pre-test probability of a positive GT can help identify which patients would benefit from undergoing testing, thereby reducing costs and minimizing inconvenience.
Method
This retrospective study included 206 patients who underwent GT at our center due to clinical suspicion of AS between 2018 and 2023. The clinical and analytical characteristics of this cohort were recorded and compared based on the positive or negative result of the GT. Patients who were undergoing kidney replacement therapy (dialysis or kidney transplantation) prior to the GT were excluded. Baseline was defined as the time when GT was performed, and multicystic phenotype was defined as five or more cysts detected on kidney ultrasound.
Results
Of the 206 included patients, 79 (38.3%) presented variants in type IV collagen genes, with 15 cases (19%) classified as variants of uncertain significance. Among the 64 patients with pathogenic variants, 23 (36%) had variants in COL4A3, 30 (47%) in COL4A4, 9 (14%) in COL4A5, and 2 (3%) were digenic. Table 1 shows the baseline characteristics of patients with and without AS according to the GT result. Both groups were similar; however, patients with AS had a higher frequency of multicystic phenotype (44% vs. 21%, P < 0.01).
As presented in Table 2, patients with AS more frequently had a family history of hematuria (78% vs. 20%, P < 0.01), chronic renal failure (54% vs. 15%, P < 0.01), and end-stage kidney disease (39% vs. 11%, P < 0.01) compared to those with a negative result. The follow-up time in our cohort was 55 (SD 86.9) months. At the end of follow-up, patients with AS showed higher serum creatinine levels and hematuria than those without the disease (1.7 ± 1.6 vs. 1.2 ± 0.7 mg/dl, p 0.01; 18 ± 20 vs. 10 ± 17 red blood cells per field, p 0.01, respectively). There were no differences in proteinuria.
Conclusion
Among patients with clinical suspicion of AS, the presence of a multicystic phenotype and a family history of hematuria and kidney disease are more frequently found when the GT is positive. Further investigations are needed to validate our results.

title: #3909 Are there differences in the impact of induction immunosuppression on kidney outcomes according to ANCA renal risk score in patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis?
authors: Ruth Martínez Galindo; Deborah Roldán; Marina Pujol Pujol; Antolina Rodriguez-Moreno; Maria Maldonado-Martin; Afroditi Konstantouli; Gema Maria Fernandez Juarez; Amir Shabaka
abstract:
Background and Aims
ANCA renal risk score (ARRS) is a clinical tool developed by Brix et al that uses 3 clinicopathologic parameters that predicts renal survival at 36 months in patients with newly diagnosed ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV). This clinical tool has been widely validated in different population cohorts worldwide. The impact of induction immunosuppression according to the ANCA renal risk score remains unclear. The aim of our study was to evaluate whether there were differences in the clinical outcomes of patients receiving different induction immunosuppression regimens according to ANCA renal risk score.
Method
We performed a retrospective observational study that included 173 patients diagnosed with AAV who underwent a renal biopsy. We calculated their ARRS and stratified the cohort as high, medium, or low risk for developing ESKD. We compared the differences in reaching end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) at each risk group between patients that received 3 different induction immunosuppression regimens (Cyclophosphamide [CfA], Rituximab [RTX] or combined Cyclophosphamide-Rituximab [CfA-RTX]).
Results
A total of 173 patients were included in the study (low risk n = 31, medium risk n = 75, high risk n = 67). We confirmed the differences in clinical outcomes between the different risk groups by using adjusted Cox proportional hazard models, with the low risk group as the reference (High risk group HR 8.8, 95% CI 2.1–36.9, Medium risk group HR 2.1, 95% CI 1.04–9.4). Within the low risk group, 57.1% of patients received CfA, 35.7% received RTX and 7.1% received CfA-RTX, and only 1 patient (who received RTX) reached ESKD. On the other hand, in the medium and high risk groups patients received CfA, RTX or CfA-RTX in 62.5%, 22.2%, 15.3%, and 71.9%, 9.4% and 18.8% respectively. Renal survival was 82.2%, 93.8%, 81.8% and 45.2%, 50% and 64.7% respectively. In the multivariate Cox proportional hazard model for risk of ESKD, after adjusting for baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate at presentation, proportion of normal glomeruli and interstitial fibrosis, using CfA as the reference we found that there were no differences in renal survival compared to receiving RTX or CfA-RTX neither in the medium risk group (RTX HR 0.99, P = 0.99 and CfA-RTX HR 0.34, P = 0.42) nor in the high risk group (RTX HR 2.26, P = 0.17 and CfA-RTX HR 1.93, P = 0.50).
Conclusion
ARRS is a useful clinical tool that predicts well renal survival in patients with AAV and offers clinicians additional prognostic information. There were no differences in renal survival between different induction therapies within each risk group.

title: #810 Efficacy and safety of telitacicept in IgA nephropathy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Piyush Ratan; Fnu Kritika; Kumar Ratan; Neelam Kumari
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA nephropathy is most common form of primary glomerulonephritis worldwide. Current treatment options include supportive therapy, including blood pressure control, renin-angiotensin system inhibitors, lifestyle changes, and steroids for high-risk patients. Telitacicept, a dual-target fusion protein, inhibits B cell maturation and differentiation by targeting B lymphocyte Stimulator (BLyS) and A Proliferation-Inducing Ligand (APRIL). We aim to perform a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the efficacy and safety of Telitacicept in patients with IgA nephropathy.
Method
PubMed, Cochrane Central, and Embase databases were searched from inception till 25 December 2024 for studies that compared Telitacicept with placebo or standard therapy in IgA nephropathy patients. We computed mean difference (MD) for continuous outcomes and odds ratio (OR) for binary outcomes, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) based on random effects model. Heterogeneity was assessed using Higgins’ I² statistic, and statistical analyses were performed using Review Manager 5.4.1. The results were represented in forest plots.
Results
Three studies including a phase II randomised controlled trial (RCT), with a total of 162 patients were analysed. Of these, 97 (59.8%) received Telitacicept, and 65 (40.2%) received placebo or standard treatment. The median time from diagnosis to treatment initiation was 51.8 months. After 24 weeks of Telitacicept therapy, patients had significantly lower 24-hour proteinuria (MD: −0.51; 95% CI: −0.84, −0.17; P = 0.003; I2 = 11%) (Fig. 1A). Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) remained stable between both groups (MD: −1.74; 95% CI: −13.47, −9.99; P = 0.77; I2 = 0%) (Fig. 1B), and no significant difference in adverse events was observed (OR: 0.78; 95% CI: 0.18, 3.42; P = 0.74; I2 = 69%) (Fig. 1C).
Conclusion
Telitacicept was associated with a significant reduction in proteinuria after 24 weeks of treatment, suggesting its potential efficacy in managing IgA nephropathy. Renal function as estimated by eGFR, and adverse events were comparable between groups, supporting the safety profile of Telitacicept. These findings suggest that Telitacicept may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for IgA nephropathy.

title: #130 Novel Bruton's tyrosine kinase inhibitor EVER001 in Chinese patients with primary membranous nephropathy: preliminary results from a phase 1b/2a study
authors: Zhao Cui; Lihua Wang; Caili Wang; Zuying Xiong; Guangbiao Xu; Luandi Yao; Bei Wang; Yiwen Xu; Lisa Ying; Kehua Wu; Zhao Minghui
abstract:
Background and Aims
Primary membranous nephropathy (pMN) is an autoantibody-driven glomerular disease. Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) is a key mediator of B-cell receptor signaling and a promising therapeutic target for autoimmune diseases. EVER001, a highly selective, reversible, covalent BTK inhibitor, is being developed for the treatment of proteinuric autoimmune glomerular diseases. This phase 1b/2a study aims to evaluate the safety, tolerability, efficacy, pharmacokinetics (PK), and pharmacodynamics (PD) of EVER001 in patients with pMN (NCT05800873).
Methods
This ongoing, open-label, single-arm study enrolled patients with anti-phospholipase A2 receptor (anti-PLA2R)–positive, biopsy-proven pMN, and nephrotic-range proteinuria (≥8 weeks) on top of supportive care. The total study duration includes a treatment period of 36 weeks and a follow-up period of up to 68 weeks. Patients were enrolled in two cohorts: patients in cohort 1 received EVER001 100 mg once daily for 4 weeks, escalating to 100 mg twice daily for 32 weeks, while patients in cohort 2 received EVER001 200 mg twice daily for 36 weeks. The primary endpoints were safety and tolerability. Secondary endpoints included changes in anti-PLA2R autoantibodies and proteinuria, percentage of patients with immunological complete remission (ICR) (anti-PLA2R <20 RU/mL), percentage of patients with complete remission (CR) (proteinuria <0.3 g/24 h) or partial remission (PR) (proteinuria ≥0.3 g/24 h but <3.5 g/24 h and a decrease of >50%), and PK/PD analyses.
Results
Thirty-one patients (13 in cohort 1 and 18 in cohort 2) were enrolled at 19 sites in China. By December 17, 2024, the median durations of exposure in cohorts 1 and 2 were 253 days and 190 days, respectively; 11 patients in cohort 1 completed 36 weeks of treatment, with 10 of these patients followed to 52 weeks; in cohort 2, 17 and 10 patients completed 12 and 24 weeks of treatment, respectively. Four patients discontinued early. The median age was 44.5 years and 63.3% were male. At baseline, the median (range) values were: anti-PLA2R autoantibodies 85.4 (18.3–296.8) RU/mL; proteinuria 5.2 (2.4–10.8) g/24 h; serum albumin 31.2 (21.6–37.7) g/L; and estimated glomerular filtration rate 93.8 (62.5–135.9) mL/min/1.73 m2. In the safety‑evaluable population (n = 31), treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) occurred in 76.9% (10/13) of patients in cohort 1 and in 44.4% (8/18) of patients in cohort 2. Four patients had Grade 3 TRAEs whereas the others all experienced Grade 1–2 TRAEs. Serious TRAEs occurred in 15.4% (2/13) and 11.1% (2/18) of patients in cohorts 1 and 2, respectively. title: #1151 An observational study of treatment on IgA nephropathy with telitacicept and immunosuppressive regimens in a single center
authors: Xuehong Lu; Jia Lv; Ping Nie
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is currently the most prevalent primary glomerular disease in the world, and 20%–40% of IgAN can progress to end-stage renal disease (ESRD). At present, there is increasing evidence that the pathogenesis of IgAN is closely related to autoimmunity. In recent years, a few of studies have shown that B cell activating factor (BAFF/BLyS) and A proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL) are extremely important for the activation of autoimmune signaling pathways, which have also become key targets for the treatment of IgAN. As a dual-target biologic, Telitacicept can inhibit two cytokines at the same time, BLyS and APRIL, thereby improving renal immune complex deposition and reducing clinical symptoms such as hematuria and proteinuria, which is extremely important for studying the pathogenesis, treatment and long-term prognosis of IgAN. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the clinical efficacy and safety of telitacicept in the treatment of IgAN.
Method
Patients who underwent renal biopsy pathological biopsy in our hospital from October 2021 to September 2023 and were still ≥0.5 g on the basis of 3-month optimized supportive treatment were selected as the study subjects and were divided into the treatment group (n = 20) and the control group (n = 21) according to whether they received telitacicept treatment. The treatment group received 160 mg of telitacicept subcutaneous injection in combination with methylprednisolone (MPS) (0.3–0.5 mg/kg) and/or mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) (≤1.0 g/d), and the control group received MPS (0.5–0.8 mg/kg) and/or MMF (≤1.0 g/d), and both groups received optimized supportive care [maximum tolerated dose of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibition], the entire study lasted 24 weeks. The 24-hour proteinuria change at week 24 was the primary endpoint, and the change in eGFR was the secondary goal. The collected data were analyzed and plotted using statistical software such as SPSS27.0 and Origin2024.
Results
Week 24 saw a 58.66% (mean difference −2.27, 95% confidence interval, −0.72 to −3.82, P = 0.004) decrease in 24-hour proteinuria in the treatment group, and 22.92% (mean difference −1.93, 95% confidence interval, −2.68 to −1.17, P < 0.001) decrease in IgG, 44.61% (mean difference −1.20, 95% confidence interval, −1.70 to −0.73, P < 0.001) decrease in IgA, and 46.79% (mean difference −0.51, 95% confidence interval, −0.73 to −0.29, P < 0.001) decrease in IgM in the treatment group. The change in 24-hour proteinuria in the control group was observed to be 39.13% lower than the baseline at week 24 (mean difference −0.63, 95% confidence interval, −1.01 to −0.25, P = 0.002) (Fig. 1). Both before and after therapy, the eGFR in both groups stayed comparatively constant. Both groups experienced similar adverse events; no serious adverse events were reported.
Conclusion
To a certain extent, telitacicept can slow the progression of IgAN by reducing the levels of 24-hour proteinuria, IgG, IgA, and IgM.

title: #2683 Characterizing the NIH activity and chronicity indices in two independent lupus nephritis cohorts: a critical analysis
authors: Valentina Querin; Natasha Jordan; David P D'cruz; David Isenberg; Suzanne Wilhelmus; Terry Cook; Augusto Vaglio; Ingeborg Bajema
abstract:
Background and Aims
The inclusion of National Institutes of Health (NIH) activity and chronicity indices (AI and CI) in the International Society of Nephrology/Renal Pathology Society (ISN/RPS) classification of lupus nephritis (LN) aims to provide a more precise characterization of the amount of active and chronic lesions next to the lupus histological class. These indices were based on expert opinion over 40 years ago and their clinical usefulness today is uncertain. The NIH AI is based on six lesions (range 0–24) and the NIH CI on four lesions (range 0–12). The aim of this study is to investigate how the NIH AI and CI scores are represented in two large international LN cohorts; which lesions mostly determine the value of the indices; and what their relation is to LN histological class.
Method
We collected renal biopsies of patients diagnosed with LN, confirmed by light microscopy and immunofluorescence. Cohort 1 included 90 patients from Italy and The Netherlands, while cohort 2 comprised 104 patients from the UK (Table). We excluded biopsies that had fewer than 10 scorable glomeruli, those from transplanted kidneys, or with a concomitant glomerular disease. We calculated the NIH AI and CI according to the 2018 ISN/RPS classification revision. We used the Spearman coefficient to explore correlations among the NIH indices and the active and chronic lesions. Mann Whitney U test was used to investigate differences in NIH AI and CI distribution between classes III and IV and other classes (I, II and V), and between adult and pediatric populations.
Results
The NIH AI score was usually medium-low, reaching a maximum value of 16 in both cohorts, while the NIH CI had a more even distribution and reached a maximum value of 10. The NIH AI score was significantly higher in classes III and IV compared to the other classes (P < .001); the latter mostly had a NIH AI score of 0. The NIH CI showed higher scores in classes III and IV only in cohort 2 (P < .001). Despite the lack of significant difference in the distribution of histological classes, adults presented a higher NIH CI compared to pediatric patients in both cohorts (P < .001). Endocapillary hypercellularity was present in more than 70% of biopsies and showed a strong correlation with neutrophils/karyorrhexis (rs = 0.842, P < .001); both categories were also strongly correlated, especially in cohort 2, with cellular/fibrocellular crescents (rs = 0.610 and 0.635, P < .001). Fibrinoid necrosis was quite rare to encounter (13.3% and 8.7% of the biopsies, in cohorts 1 and 2, respectively) and showed a correlation with cellular/fibrocellular crescents (rs = 0.302, P = .004 in cohort 1). Among chronic lesions, total glomerulosclerosis, tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis were present in about half of the renal biopsies and had a strong correlation with each other (P < .001); fibrous crescents were less frequently encountered and had the strongest correlations with NIH CI (rs = 0.390, P < .001), NIH AI (rs = 0.256, P = .009) and cellular/fibrocellular crescents (rs = 260, P = .008) in cohort 2.
Conclusion
This study revealed key limitations of the NIH indices, such as the restricted range of attainable NIH AI scores, the strong relationship between the NIH AI and histological classes, the major role of the endocapillary hypercellularity in driving the NIH AI, and the likely independent value of the NIH CI across different classes. All these aspects raise doubts about their effectiveness in accurately reflecting the extent of activity and chronicity in LN biopsies and predicting patient outcomes. It is crucial to further investigate whether potential modifications to these indices could lead to a more balanced and reliable scoring system.

title: #3596 Biomarkers of lupus nephritis histopathology: Where do we stand?
authors: Valentina Querin; Leonardo Palazzo; Agnes Fogo; Mark Haas; David R W Jayne; Liz Lightstone; Brad Rovin; Surya V Seshan; Augusto Vaglio; Ioannis Parodis; Ingeborg Bajema
abstract:
Background and Aims
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is characterized by a complex and variable disease course, necessitating continuous clinical and laboratory assessments to monitor organ involvement and disease progression. Lupus nephritis (LN), the most common organ-threatening manifestation of SLE, is commonly monitored using kidney biopsies, alongside blood and urine parameters. While kidney biopsy remains the gold standard for diagnosis, it is an invasive procedure and provides only a snapshot in time. Therefore, there is growing interest in non-invasive biomarkers that could improve clinical management of LN, aiding in diagnosis, prognostic assessment, and treatment decisions. By critically assessing the quality of existing studies on potential biomarkers—urinary, serum-based, or others—correlating with histological findings, we here explore the challenges in implementing these biomarkers in clinical practice and identify promising candidates for future validation.
Method
A systematic literature search on LN biomarkers was conducted, extending a previous review by Palazzo et al. [1]. Studies in English, published between 2012 and 2024, and involving adult patients with biopsy-proven LN were included. The search focused on studies demonstrating significant correlations between biomarkers and histological findings, particularly the National Institutes of Health (NIH) activity index (AI) and chronicity index (CI), the International Society of Nephrology/Renal Pathology Society (ISN/RPS) histological classes, and specific active or chronic lesions. From this search, 96 articles were selected, investigating the potential utility of over 100 biomarkers, which were categorized into groups. The quality of each article was assessed by a multidisciplinary panel of experts utilizing the scoring system by Guyatt et al. [2].
Results
The 96 publications were stratified into various biomarker categories: autoantibodies (n = 6), complement factors (n = 4), cytokines, chemokines, growth factors (n = 26), cell adhesion and surface molecules (n = 8), immune cells (n = 8), markers of kidney damage (n ≈ 20), micro-RNA (n ≈ 10), others (n ≈ 30). The biomarkers were tested against various lesions, both individual and combined, as well as measurements such as NIH AI and CI, and ISN/RPS classes. In quality assessment, over 50% of the articles were weak, 17% were very weak (score <5), and only 1 was deemed robust (score >8). Considering the scores of the respective articles, transforming growth factor beta 1 (TGF-β1) emerged as the biomarker deriving from the most robust study, followed by pentraxin 3 (PTX3), CD163, CD11b, hemopexin, and interleukin 16 (IL-16) (Figure 1).
Conclusion
Our findings highlight the challenges in translating biomarker research into clinical practice for LN. Methodological heterogeneity across studies is a limitation to the interpretation of results. Furthermore, by focusing on selected markers, many studies oversimplify the intricate landscape of histological findings in a kidney biopsy. All clinical trials in LN should store samples for biomarker assessment and validation, prioritizing their ability to accurately reflect specific histological features, evolve with biopsy parameters over time, and demonstrate predictive value for long-term outcomes. Until substantial progress is made in the development of new biomarkers for LN, their clinical applicability will remain limited.

title: #847 Impact of SGLT2 inhibitors on kidney function and proteinuria in patients with membranous nephropathy
authors: Bogdan Sorohan; Bogdan Obrisca; Stefan Lujinschi; Camelia Achim; Gener Ismail
abstract:
Background and Aims
The current management of membranous nephropathy (MN), based on immunosuppressive therapy and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system blockade, is insufficient in certain cases to control proteinuria and the progression of chronic kidney disease. Data on the use of SGLT2 inhibitors in this context is lacking. We aimed to evaluate the impact of sodium-glucose transporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) on kidney function and proteinuria in patients with MN.
Method
We performed an observational prospective study on 22 patients with MN. Among them, 11 received standard-of-care (SOC) therapy and 11 received SOC along with one SGLT2i (either dapagliflozin or empagliflozin). All patients had an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) >15 ml/min, albumin-creatinine ration >300 mg/g at baseline and received immunosuppressive therapy. Follow-up period was 6 months. Primary outcome was to analyze the mean change of eGFR as adjusted mean difference (AMD) between the two groups. Secondary outcomes consisted of AMD of 24 h proteinuria and average percentage decrease of proteinuria at 6 months.
Results
The mean age was 47.64 ± 9.85 years, and 59.1% of patients were males. Mean baseline values for eGFR, serum albumin, and 24 h proteinuria were 55.83 ± 23.16 ml/min, 2.04 ± 0.24 g/dl, and 9.61 ± 2.22 g/24 h. Adjusted mean difference (AMD) in eGFR at 6 months of follow-up, between the 2 groups, was significantly favorable for SGLT2i group [+6.16 ml/min (95% CI: 0.16 to 12.16), P = 0.04]. AMD of proteinuria was significantly lower in SGLT2i group [−1.21 g/24 h (95% CI: −2.19 to −0.23), P = 0.01] and also average percentage decrease of proteinuria at 6 months was significantly higher in patients treated with SGLT2i than standard of care (72.72 ± 13.07 vs 59.02 ± 9.59%, P = 0.01).
Conclusion
SGLT2i have a significant favorable impact on kidney function and proteinuria in patients with MN.

title: #1077 Predictors and long-term outcomes of glucocorticoid discontinuation in an inception cohort of lupus nephritis patients with a 10-year follow-up
authors: Ioannis Michelakis; Alexandros Panagiotopoulos; Eleni Kapsia; Ioannis Boletis; Smaragdi Marinaki; Petros Sfikakis; Maria Tektonidou
abstract:
Background and Aims
There is no consensus on optimal glucocorticoid (GC) treatment duration for lupus nephritis (LN). The updated 2023 EULAR [1] and 2024 KDIGO guidelines [2], recommend reducing GC to ≤5 mg/day (prednisolone equivalent) within 3–6 months after diagnosis and considering discontinuation (D/C) after maintaining complete renal response (CRR) for 12 months [2]. This study examined the frequency and factors affecting GC D/C, predictors of flares during tapering and post-D/C, long-term outcomes, and damage accrual by the end of follow-up (EFU) in patients achieving GC D/C compared to those who did not.
Method
We analyzed data from an inception cohort of patients diagnosed with LN between 1992 and 2021 and used regression models to identify predictors of GC D/C and long-term outcomes, assessing baseline characteristics, Lupus Low Disease Activity State (LLDAS), definitions of remission in SLE (DORIS), and the SLICC/ACR damage index (SDI). To evaluate GC exposure across decades, patients were categorized by diagnosis period: 1992–2005 (period 1) or 2006–2021 (period 2).
Results
The study included 137 patients (83.1% females), with 71% having proliferative (PLN) and 29% membranous (MLN) LN. Median age was 32.5 years (IQR: 19) and follow-up 121 months (IQR: 89). title: #3501 The immunomodulatory role of neuroendothelial cells in lupus nephritis
authors: Lena Peresztegi; Audrey Izuhara; Alejandra Becerra Calderon; Georgina Gyarmati
abstract:
Background and Aims
There is an unmet medical need for specific, mechanism-based therapies for lupus nephritis (LN), the major organ complication and cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). A newly discovered subtype of endothelial cells (EC), termed neuro-endothelial cells (NECs) in renal resistance arterioles plays key roles in the maintenance of vascular health and immune balance. Importantly, NEC localizations and functions are consistent with the vascular mechanisms in LN. Cytokine-like 1 (Cytl1) is the top NEC specific secreted factor with anti-inflammatory properties. The aim of the present study was to test whether NEC-derived Cytl1 controls the local peripheral tissue specific immune response in LN. The main hypothesis is that NEC/Cytl1 maintains vascular integrity and immune balance in the local tissue microenvironment via both local endothelial effects and effects on circulating immune cells.
Method
A comprehensive experimental approach used NEC specific, AAV2-QUADYF- Cytl1 shRNA mediated genetic silencing and overexpression of Cytl1 in vivo, acute treatment with mouse recombinant Cytl1, endothelial and immune cell cultures in vitro, chemotaxis assay, and in vivo multiphoton microscopy (MPM) of the mouse kidney.
Results
Intravital MPM imaging after NEC specific genetic silencing of Cytl1 found multiple severe and segmental, sphincter-like vasoconstrictions along all resistance vessels, and marked reductions in blood flow in NEC-Cytl1 KD mice compared to NEC-WT. In addition, NEC-Cytl1 KD mice featured increased glomerular vascular permeability to plasma albumin compared to NEC-WT (Albumin GSC: 0.249 ± 0.027 vs. 0.006 ± 0.001, P < 0.0001, n = 8), and capillary density and vessel diameters were reduced in both NEC-Nos1 KD and NEC-Cytl1 KD compared to NEC-WT. In addition to these hemodynamic changes, MPM imaging of the plasma marker observed numerous negatively labeled cells sticking and rolling in the vascular lumen in Cytl1 KD animals. Specific labeling of all immune cells found high density of homing CD45+ immune cells in the arteriolar/capillary/venule lumen in NEC-Cytl1KD mice(17.13 ± 2.36/glomerulus) in contrast to NEC-WT (4.750 ± 0.73/glomerulus, P < 0.01, n = 8). Glomerular EC damage and inflammatory activation were evident by the upregulation of EC inflammatory markers including ICAM, VCAM, and PLVAP in the glomerulus of NEC-Cytl1 KD mice compared to NEC-WT. Further, acute mrCytl1 treatment (iv. 20 ug/kg) reduced immune cell homing in NZM.2328 BAFFTg+ mice, a human-like mouse model of LN. mrCytl1 reduced chemoattractant (Ccl19) induced directed migration (chemotaxis) of immune cell freshly harvested from NZM.2328 lupus mice.
Conclusion
In summary, our studies identified novel Cytl1 mediated anti-inflammatory and vasoprotective molecular-level mechanisms of a new EC-subtype that are highly relevant to lupus and have clinical therapeutic potential.

title: #1876 Time to diagnosis in patients with rare kidney diseases: findings form the European Rare Kidney Disease Registry
authors: Franz Schaefer; Aude Servais; Olivia Boyer; Francesco Emma; Kathleen Claes; Justine Bacchetta; Valentina Capone; Francesco Trepiccione; Michal Maternik; Victor Perez Beltran; Adrian Catalin Lungu; Dario Roccatello
abstract:
Background and Aims
Limited expertise of healthcare professionals and late referral to specialist care may cause delays in establishing the correct diagnosis and initiate appropriate treatment in rare diseases. The European Rare Kidney Disease Reference Network (ERKNet) aims to improve awareness and knowledge of rare kidney diseases in the nephrology community. ERKNet collects prospective information about the diagnostic and therapeutic management of rare kidney diseases in the European Rare Kidney Disease Registry (ERKReg). Here, we present an analysis of the diagnostic delay in adult and pediatric patients with rare kidney diseases.
Method
The date of first signs and symptoms was available in 17,016 (61.8%) out of 27,503 patients enrolled in the European Rare Kidney Disease Registry (ERKReg) from October 2018 to January 2025 in 20 European countries. The largest contributing countries were Italy (32.8%), France (21.1%), Germany (10.4%), Belgium (8.4%), the Netherlands (4.6%), Spain (3.7%), Poland (3.2%) and Romania (2.4%). 58% of patients were male and 75% exhibited disease onset during childhood. A total of 211 individual rare and ultrarare kidney diseases defined by Orphacode were observed in the cohort.
We analyzed factors associated with time to diagnosis, defined as time from first signs and symptoms to diagnosis established by kidney biopsy, genetic testing, ultrasound or clinical presentation as appropriate.
Results
The distribution of time from first symptoms to diagnosis in the total population was markedly skewed with the 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentiles at 0.0, 1.2, 10.8, and 60 months, respectively.
Diagnoses were made with greater delay in hereditary glomerulopathies (75% diagnosed within 48 mo.), autosomal dominant kidney disorders (35 mo.), metabolic nephropathies (28 mo.) and tubulopathies (24 mo.) than in immune-mediated glomerulopathies (6 mo.), kidney congenital malformations (7 mo.) and thrombotic microangiopathies (<1 mo.).
Among the 60 most commonly reported rare kidney disorders, the greatest diagnostic delays were observed for Fabry disease (n = 72, 75% diagnosed within 167 mo.), Bardet Biedl syndrome (n = 65, 148 mo.), Alport syndrome (n = 629, 91 mo.), ADTKD (n = 141, 68 mo.), Tuberous sclerosis complex (n = 219, 50 mo.), Cystinuria (n = 408, 46 mo.) and Dent disease (n = 78, 41 mo.).
Time to diagnosis was considerably longer in patients with adult vs. childhood disease onset (75% diagnosed within 18 v. 8.4 months). This difference was consistent across all disease groups: (e.g., 75% diagnosis time in adult v. pediatric patients 120 v. 40 mo. for hereditary glomerulopathies, 12 v. 3.6 mo for immune-mediated glomerulopathies, 25 v. 6 mo. for metabolic and stone disorders, 16.8 v. 3.6 mo. for tubulopathies).
Furthermore, substantial differences were noted between countries: The 75% diagnosis time was 18 mo. in Italy and Spain, 12 mo. in Romania, 7.2 mo. in France, 6 mo. in Germany, 4.8 mo. in Belgium, and 3.6 mo. in Poland. These differences were largely consistent for patients with pediatric and adult disease onset (Table 1) and disease category.
Conclusion
A considerable fraction of patients with rare kidney diseases is diagnosed with major delay. The time required to establish the correct diagnosis differs by the type of kidney disorder. The diagnostic delay is greater in patients with disease onset at adult as compared to pediatric age and differs between European countries. Our findings underline the need to raise awareness and optimize referral pathways and diagnostic procedures for patients with suspected rare kidney diseases.

title: #999 Minimal change disease: a novel regimen of glucocorticoids-induced remission and then rituximab as maintenance remission therapy
authors: Wang Ling; Xiao Fei; Dai Huanzi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Frequent relapse or glucocorticoids (GCs) dependence hampers maintenance treatment of minimal change disease (MCD). We investigated the efficacy and safety of rituximab (RTX) in maintaining remission in patients with MCD.
Method
A single-center retrospective cohort study was conducted on patients hospitalized from January 2020 to July 2023. Patients with renal biopsy-confirmed MCD, all of whom had achieved complete remission (CR) with GCs, were enrolled. They were assigned to groups A (GCs maintenance remission) or B (RTX maintenance remission). After matching of propensity scores, 13 patients were brought into each group. Primary endpoint was relapse prevalence at 48 weeks.
Results
All patients achieved CR with full-dose GCs treatment. The median time to CR was 19 (range, 14–26) days. Seven patients had acute kidney injury (three in group A and four in group B) but all patients had rapid recovery of renal function. GCs accumulation in group A was 9105.7 ± 3375.7 mg, and that in group B was 4468.2 ± 864.6 mg. Cluster of differentiation (CD)19+ B cells were undetectable in group B after using RTX twice. At 48-week follow-up, seven (53.9%) patients in group A relapsed, and the median duration of relapse was 35.7 (26.1–45.7) weeks. In group B, one (7.7%) patient relapsed at 26.7 weeks. The prevalence of drug-related adverse events in group A was significantly higher than that in group B.
Conclusion
We demonstrated the marked efficacy and safety of RTX in maintenance remission of MCD, and it was significantly superior to that of GCs.

title: #3560 Biochemical changes in ?-glutamyl cycle and their relevance in systemic lupus erythematous
authors: Corina-Daniela Ene; Ilinca Nicolae; Cristina Capusa
abstract:
Background and Aims
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease with a complex pathogenesis. Many molecules have been evaluated in SLE, but there is still the need to establish a panel of biomarkers in order to identify as early as possible the patients at risk for SLE progression. The present study focused on the characterization of biochemical changes in γ-glutamyl cycle induced by oxidative damage and their relevance in SLE subjects.
Method
We developed a prospective, case control study that included 58 SLE subjects with cutaneous-mucosal, hematological and renal determinations, with stable treatment in the last six months, and 40 healthy subjects. All subjects with renal determinations of SLE underwent renal biopsy. In each subject, we evaluated the γ-glutamyl cycle activity (GSH, GSSG, GSH/GSSG ratio); oxidative stress (ImAnOx, Albumin), nitrosative stress (Direct Nitrite, Total Nitrite, Nitrate), carbonyl stress (4-HNE, Pentosidine), inflammation (IL-17A), angiogenesis factors (HIF1a, HIF2a, VEGF).
The exclusion criteria were age younger than 18 years old, pregnancy, tobacco use, vitamin or antioxidants use, or stage 5 chronic kidney disease; any cardiovascular, hepatic, thyroid, gastrointestinal, or oncological disease; hyperhomocysteinemia and any viral or bacterial infections in the previous three months.
Statistical analysis. All the results were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics 2015 and were presented as average value ± standard deviation. P < 0.05 was considered with statistical significance.
Results
We detected in SLE subjects compared to control: high levels of GSSG, nitrosative and carbonyl stress parameters, inflammation, angiogenesis related factors and low levels of GSH, GSH/GSSG. GSH was with 33.6% higher, while GSSG was with 28% lower in lupus nephritis compared with SLE subjects without renal impairment. In SLE group, negative correlations between GSH and electrophile metabolites levels (nitrite, nitrate, 4-HNE, pentosidine), angiogenesis markers (HIF1a, HIF2a, VEGF) and inflammatory parameters (IL-17A) were determined. Positive correlations were detected between GSH and studied antioxidants markers (ImAnOx, albumin).
Conclusion
γ-Glutamyl cycle metabolism was dysregulated in SLE. γ-Glutamyl cycle acts as a redox active metabolic mechanism that plays an important role SLE pathology by inactivating electrophile metabolites, cytoprotecting, hypoxia regulation, inflammation, angiogenesis.

title: #2835 Kidney injury molecule–1 and beta-2-microglobuline significance in lupus nephritis
authors: Corina-Daniela Ene; Ilinca Nicolae; Buturca Corina; Cristina Capusa
abstract:
Background and Aims
Lupus nephritis (LN) is a major complication of systemic lupus erythematous (SLE). Several new molecules have been investigated for their role in LN. Recent studies showed molecular abnormalities of kidney injury-1 molecule (KIM-1) and beta-2 microglobuline (β2MG) in systemic lupus erythematous. We aimed to examine the relation betwen serum and urinary levels of KIM-1, respectively β2MG and lupus nephritis activity.
Method
We developed a prospective, case control study that included 80 SLE subjects grouped by cutaneous-mucosal, hematological and renal determinations, with stable treatment in the last six months, and 30 healthy subjects. All subjects with renal determinations of SLE underwent renal biopsy. In each subject, we determined the serum and urinary levels of KIM-1 by ELISA method, respectively β2MG by immunoturbidimetry. Their levels were analyzed in relation with urinary albumin to creatinine ratio (UACR), eGFR, SLEDAI and clinical features of SLE.
The exclusion criteria were age younger than 18 years old, pregnancy, tobacco use, vitamin or antioxidants use, or stage 5 chronic kidney disease; any cardiovascular, hepatic, thyroid, gastrointestinal, or oncological disease; and any viral or bacterial infections in the previous three months.
Statistical analysis. All the results were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics 2015 and were presented as average value ± standard deviation. P < 0.05 was considered with statistical significance. The relation between the studied markers was evaluated using Pearson coefficient.
Results
Serum and urinary levels of KIM-1 and β2MG were significantly different between SLE and control, respectively between SLE subgroups (Table 1).
Urinary KIM-1 was positively associated with albuminuria, hematuria, and negatively with eGFR. Serum levels of KIM-1 were correlated with eGFR, albuminuria, but not with SLEDAI. Serum and urinary levels of KIM-1 were correlated when UACR was over 300 mg/g and decreased eGFR. Serum and urinary β2MG were associated with albuminuria; urinary β2MG correlated negatively with eGFR and hematuria. Serum β2MG is positively associated with SLEDAI, cutaneous-mucosal, hematological determinations of SLE. Serum and urinary levels of β2MG were correlated only at high levels of SLEDAI.
Conclusion
Serum KIM-1 was associated with lupus nephritis disease activity, while β2MG mostly with mucosal, cutaneous and hematological determinations of SLE. Though, KIM-1 could define the renal phenotype, while β2MG could configure the clinical and biological expression of SLE.

title: #749 Plasma apixaban concentrations and their effect on thrombin generation in nephrotic syndrome
authors: Sarah Kelddal; Erik Grove; Camilla Duus; Louis Nygaard; Tilde Kristensen; Frank Mose; Jon Waarst Gregersen; Anne-Mette Hvas; Henrik Birn
abstract:
Background and Aims
Nephrotic syndrome is characterised by elevated thrombin generation and an increased risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE). Current guidelines recommend preventive anticoagulant therapy with low molecular weight heparin or warfarin. Apixaban with no need for therapeutic monitoring and potentially lower bleeding risk, presents an alternative option. However, data on apixaban's pharmacokinetics and effects on thrombin generation in patients with NS remain limited. To explore its potential as an alternative anticoagulant strategy in nephrotic syndrome, we evaluated steady-state apixaban concentrations and the impact on thrombin generation in patients with nephrotic syndrome due to primary glomerular diseases.
Method
A Danish multicentre, open-label, interventional trial comparing apixaban concentrations in nephrotic patients with healthy individuals, both receiving apixaban 5 mg twice daily. Eligibility criteria included plasma albumin <25 g/L, urine albumin-creatinine ratio >2,200 mg/g, age ≥18 years, hemoglobin A1c <65 mmol/mol, and biopsy-confirmed minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, or membranous nephropathy. Exclusion criteria were estimated glomerular filtration rate <30 mL/min/1.73 m2, current anticoagulant treatment, thrombophilia, prior VTE, current infection, malignancy, or pregnancy. Plasma apixaban concentrations and thrombin generation markers were analysed using linear mixed-effects regression models to compare groups across multiple time points, Fig. 1.
Results
We included 11 nephrotic patients (mean plasma albumin 19 g/L; median urine albumin-creatinine ratio at 5,029 mg/g), and 10 healthy individuals (Table 1). In nephrotic patients, in vivo thrombin generation markers, such as prothrombin fragment 1+2, decreased significantly on apixaban treatment compared to healthy individuals (nephrotic: mean 223 µg/L, CI 95% 175–268; healthy: mean: 145 µg/L, CI 95% 98–191; P = 0.02). Conclusion
Nephrotic patients demonstrated significantly lower steady-state plasma apixaban levels than healthy individuals. Despite this, there were no significant differences in endogenous thrombin potential, yet a substantial reduction in prothrombin fragment 1+2 suggesting effective anticoagulation. The findings support apixaban as a potential alternative to traditional anticoagulants in this high-risk population.

title: #2649 Investigation of the Rac1-SGK1 pathway and therapeutic effects of finerenone and Rac1 inhibition in a Fabry disease podocyte model
authors: Kultigin Turkmen; Sedef Akcaalan; Canan Eroglu Gunes; Ercan Kurar
abstract:
Background and Aims
Podocyte injury is a central feature of Fabry nephropathy characterized by proteinuria, glomerulosclerosis, and progressive renal decline. The small GTPase Rac1 plays a pivotal role in cytoskeletal dynamics, podocyte structure, and function. Dysregulation of Rac1-SGK1 pathway contributes to cytoskeletal disorganization, oxidative stress, and increased susceptibility to podocyte injury. 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 (11βHSD1) is an enzyme expressed by kidney, that plays a significant role in converting inactive cortisone into its active form, cortisol excessive cortisol activation due to heightened 11βHSD1 expression may contribute to podocyte injury. We aimed to analyze the role of Rac1, SGK1, NOX, 11βHSD1 and effects of finerenone which is a non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and Rac1 inhibition in Fabry podocytes.
Method
A Fabry disease model was established by suppressing GLA gene expression using shRNA in a commercially purchased human podocyte cell line. The control group (wild type; wt) and GLA-suppressed cells (Fabry podocytes) were treated with finerenone and Rac 1 inhibitor (NSC23766). To determine the highest non-toxic dose of finerenone in podocyte cells, a CCK8 assay was performed. Changes in the expression levels of RAC1, SGK1, 11-β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 (11β HSD1), and NOX5 genes were evaluated by RT-qPCR in the experimental groups. Additionally, the RAC1 protein levels were assessed using the ELISA method. To confirm the establishment of the Fabry model, suppression of GLA mRNA and protein levels was demonstrated in shRNA groups by RT-qPCR and Western blot analyses, respectively (Fig. 1). Based on the results of the CCK8 assay, 10 nM finerenone was applied, while 50 µM NSC23766 was selected based on literature data and applied separately to specific experimental groups.
Results
In Fabry podocytes, compared to wt podocytes, increased gene expression levels of RAC1, SGK1, NOX5, 11β-HSD1, and mineralocorticoid receptor (NR3C2) were observed (Fig. 2). The RAC1 ELISA levels measured in the supernatant were also elevated in Fabry podocytes compared to wt podocytes (Fig. 3). Upon the application of finerenone to Fabry podocytes, a reduction in the gene expression levels of RAC1, SGK1, NOX5, 11β-HSD1, and the mineralocorticoid steroid receptor was detected, along with a decrease in Rac1 ELISA levels (Figs 2 and 3). A decrease in these values was also observed with the Rac1 inhibitor (NSC237666) (Fig. 2). The concurrent increase in NOX5 gene levels along with Rac1 and SGK1, as well as the reduction in NOX5 following finerenone treatment and Rac1 inhibition, demonstrates that oxidative stress—one of the major cause of Fabry podocyte damage—occurs through the RAC1-SGK1 pathway.
Conclusion
This study is the first in the literature to demonstrate the involvement of the RAC1-SGK1 pathway including increased mineralocorticoid receptor, 11β-HSD1 and NOX5 gene expression and Rac1 protein levels in Fabry podocyte damage and to show the therapeutic effectiveness of finerenone, a non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, as well as Rac1 inhibition. We believe that finerenone therapy, as a podocyte-protective treatment, may be effective in preventing Fabry nephropathy in the future.

title: #2154 Imlifidase a new treatment for severe minimal change disease?
authors: David De Saint Gilles; Simon Leclerc; Tomoko Takano; Tobias B Huber; Laurent Mesnard; Laure Calas; Khalil El Karoui; Emmanuel Esteve; Paul Gabarre; Cyril Mousseaux; Nastassia Liaukouskaya; Nicola M Tomas; Jean Jacques Boffa; Felicitas E Hengel; Cédric Rafat
abstract:
Background and Aims
Minimal change disease (MCD) is an immune-mediated podocytopathy recently characterized by the presence of circulating and kidney-bound anti-nephrin antibodies in a significant subset of patients. Imlifidase (Hansa Biopharma, Lund, Sweden) is an IgG-degrading enzyme that cleaves all human IgG subclasses, producing [F(ab′)2] and Fc fragments. It shows promise in treating autoimmune diseases like anti-GBM disease. Herein we report a case of MCD treated with imlifidase.
Method
An 82-year old patient with no significant prior medical history was admitted in our renal intensive care unit for a nephrotic syndrome complicated with acute kidney injury. On admission his blood pressure was measure at 190/120 mmHg with evidence of volume overload. Biologically, severe KDIGO stage 3 AKI was noted, with a creatinine level of 319 µmol/L (eGFR 16 ml/min/1.73 m²), along with a nephrotic syndrome defined by low levels of plasma albumin at 18 g/L and proteinuria at 20.8 g/L, of which 16 g/L was albuminuria (77%). Urinary biochemistry was consistent with prerenal azotemia with restricted natriuresis (NaU < 20 mmol/L) and elevated urinary creatinine (20 mmol/L).
The patient was started on hemodialysis 12 hours following admission for life-threatening hyperkalemia. A kidney biopsy performed on day 5 revealed no glomerular lesions upon optical microscopy. Immunofluorescence showed fine granular podocytic staining, consistent with anti-IgG antibodies consistent with anti-nephrin deposits. A diagnosis of minimal change disease was posed.
The patient was immediately started on prednisone 1 mg/kg. Two weeks after starting corticosteroid therapy, the patient remained severely oliguric (100–200 mL per day), requiring repeated hemodialysis, with while heavy proteinuria. (Fig. 1).
Serum sampling was performed for anti-nephrin antibody testing at various time points but the results are expected soon.
Results
Imlifidase was administered intravenously at a dose of 22 mg (equivalent to 0.30 mg/kg) on the 14 days after initiation of cortisteroid therapy.
Following the injection, a rapid and significant increase in urine output was observed without any changes to the diuretic treatment, allowing for the discontinuation of renal replacement therapy. By the fourth day post-injection, urine output exceeded 1.5 liters per day. Kidney function plateaued 48 hours after the administration of imlifidase and improved rapidly from the fourth day onward.
By 10 days after the imlifidase injection, kidney function had returned to baseline level with a serum creatinine at 88 µmol/L (ie., an eGFR at 76 ml/min/1.73m²), and antihypertensive medications including diuretics were discontinued.
A 50% reduction in proteinuria levels was observed 48 hours after the injection (4 g/L vs. 8 g/L), plummeting to less than 1 g/L by the fourth day. By day 7 post-imlifidase, total proteinuria was below 0.5 g/L.
Imlifidase injection was well tolerated. Rituximab was administered 5 days after imlifidase.
Thirty days after imlifidase injection, the patient remained in remission from MCD with a kidney function at baseline level plasma creatinine at 99 µmol/L (eGFR: 66 mL/min/1.73 m2) normal plasma albumin (39 g/L) and albuminuria within physiological range (19.1 mg/L).
Corticosteroid therapy was gradually tapered down to 5 mg two months after its initiation.
Conclusion
Imlifidase may offer a potential add-on therapeutic option for minimal change disease (MCD) patients when used in combination with other anti-B cell targeted therapies. Methodologically rigorous studies are needed to confirm these findings.

title: #1764 Evaluation of the proposed clinical and histological prognostic scores in patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis: a single-center retrospective study
authors: Amirreza Manafzadeh; Imola Krisztina Fejes; Ábrahám György István; László Bitó; Dóra Bajcsi; Sándor Turkevi-Nagy; Bela Ivanyi; Péter Légrády
abstract:
Background and Aims
This study aimed to evaluate the usefulness and prognostic ability of 4 different histological scores—EUVAS/Berden classification, Mayo Clinic Chronicity Score (MCCS), Renal Risk Score (RRS), and Improved ANCA Kidney Risk Score (AKRiS)—for kidney survival or death in anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis.
Method
Clinical and histopathologic characteristics of 48 patients with ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis proven by biopsy from January 2012 to December 2023 were analyzed in this retrospective cohort study. The primary outcome was the time to end stage kidney disease (ESKD) defined as persistent (≥6 months) requirement of dialysis or kidney transplantation and death.
Results
Of the 48 patients, 41 had MPO-ANCA and 7 had PR3-ANCA positivity. During the median follow-up of 57.5 months [IQR: 28.5–114.0], 12 patients progressed to ESKD and 4 patients died. According to the Berden classification, the sclerotic group had the worst outcome compared to the other groups (focal, crescentic, and mixed). The Harrell's C statistic was 0.657 (95% CI: 0.524–0.790), 0.708 (95% CI: 0.607–0.809), 0.710 (95% CI: 0.599–0.822), and 0.697 (95% CI: 0.547–0.847) for Berden classification, MCCS, RRS, and AKRiS, respectively.
Conclusion
Our study supports that the MCCS, RRS, and AKRiS had better performance and ability to predict renal outcomes compared to the Berden classification.

title: #2924 Complement 3 (C3) staining and glomerular inflammation in immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN): real-world biopsy data in the United States (US)
authors: Clarissa Cassol; Briana Ndife; Helen Trenz; Sean Bartlett; Hamid Moradi; Titte Srinivas
abstract:
Background and Aims
The clinical presentation and disease course of IgAN, the most common primary glomerulonephritis globally, vary considerably among patients. IgAN is diagnosed by kidney biopsy; histopathology findings of prognostic value are summarized and scored using the Oxford MEST-C classification system (mesangial [M] and endocapillary [E] hypercellularity, segmental glomerulosclerosis [S], interstitial fibrosis/tubular atrophy [T], and cellular crescents [C]). Studies show that higher M, E, and C scores are associated with increased glomerular inflammation. Overactivation of the complement system, especially the alternative pathway, plays an important role in the pathogenesis of IgAN. Studies have demonstrated an association between the intensity of glomerular C3 staining on kidney biopsy, and poor clinical outcomes in patients with IgAN. Despite this, the MEST-C classification system does not incorporate complement activity. This study evaluated the association of glomerular C3 staining intensity with demographics, proteinuria, hematuria, markers of glomerular inflammation, and MEST-C scores, in a US cohort of patients with IgAN.
Method
This retrospective cross-sectional analysis of adult patients (≥18 years of age) with biopsy-confirmed IgAN, used biopsy data (January 2016–December 2016) from Arkana Laboratories, a national and international nephropathology reference laboratory. Patient demographic and clinical characteristics at the time of kidney biopsy were stratified by intensity of C3 deposition, assessed by immunofluorescence staining (from 0 [negative staining] to 3+ [high-intensity staining]). Glomerular inflammation was defined as patients with either M1 or E1 or C1/C2 scores. Between-group differences were assessed using Kruskal–Wallis tests for continuous variables and chi-square tests for categorical variables. The association between glomerular C3 deposition intensity and MEST-C scores was assessed using multivariable ordinal logistic regression models and reported as odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI).
Results
Kidney biopsy data from 470 patients with IgAN were included; 63.8% were male, and the mean age ± standard deviation was 46.9 ± 16.0 years. Patient demographics and clinical characteristics stratified by C3 deposition are presented in Table 1. A C3 deposition intensity score of ≥1 was present in 77.7% of patients and there was an association between C3 deposition intensity and hematuria (P = 0.01). There was evidence of some association between C3 deposition intensity and individual MEST-C scores: M1 (P = 0.05), E1 (P = 0.45), and C1/C2 (P = 0.08). C3 deposition intensity was associated with the presence of any MEST-C score M1, E1, or C1/C2, indicative of glomerular inflammation (P = 0.04) (Table 2). When adjusted for patient age and sex, patients with M1 or E1 or C1/C2 scores had 55% higher odds of greater C3 deposition intensity compared with patients without M1 or E1 or C1/C2 scores (OR: 1.55, 95% CI: 1.11–2.15; P = 0.009).
Conclusion
In this study, >75% of patients with IgAN had C3 staining intensity ≥1. Furthermore, in our model, glomerular inflammation (M1 or E1 or C1/C2 score) was associated with higher odds of C3 deposition intensity when adjusted for patient age and sex. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and assess whether including the degree of glomerular C3 deposition, as indicated by staining intensity, can be of additional prognostic value.

title: #3573 Frailty as a proxy measure for infection risk and mortality in ANCA glomerulonephritis
authors: Joshendra Durailingam; Kavita Gulati; Gavin Chapman; Emma Barrett; Nina Brown; Neeraj Dhaun; Stephen McAdoo; Silke Brix
abstract:
Background and Aims
Frailty is a functional term referring to a decline in physiological function that leads to dependency, vulnerability and a high risk for poor health-related outcomes. Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) vasculitis affects the elderly and often results in a rapid decline in general health. We aimed to better understand the interaction between rapidly evolving ANCA associated inflammation and the impression of frailty to improve prediction modelling for adverse outcomes. Here, we investigated the clinical frailty scale (CFS) at the time of diagnosis for its association with clinical outcomes.
Method
We performed a multicentre retrospective analysis of newly diagnosed ANCA glomerulonephritis (GN) patients across 4 centres in the UK with CFS assessment at the time of diagnosis. Wilcoxon-Rank-Sum, Kruskal-Wallis and Fisher-Exact testing were used to analyse the relationships of age, CFS and infections, end stage kidney disease (ESKD) and death.
Results
Working on a complete data basis, 253 patients were included in the analysis. There was an association between CFS at the time of diagnosis and the occurrence of severe infections during the first 6 months of induction therapy (P = 0.0027). Patients did suffer more often from infections with rising scores (CFS 1–2 12.8%, CFS 3–4 26.5%, and CFS 5–7 41.4%, respectively).
In patients with infections, 16.7%, 22.2% and 44.8% died according to CFS with CFS 1-2, 3-4 and 5-7, respectively. An association was detected between CFS score and mortality (P = 0.0358), with 19.1% of patients dying with an initial CFS of 1–2, 30.1% with CFS of 3–4 and 41.4% with CFS of 5–7.
There was an association between the comorbidity diabetes and mortality (P = 0.0137) but no association between diabetes and infection (P = 0.129). No association was found between the comorbidity lung disease with mortality (P = 0.056) or infection (P = 0.154).
Using a logistic regression model investigating the influence of infection and diabetes on mortality, CFS (P = 0.016, OR = 3.01) and diabetes (P = 0.013, OR = 2.41) independently associated with mortality.
Conclusion
Frailty assessment at the time of diagnosis associates with infection risk and mortality. While the presence of diabetes associates with mortality, diabetes did not influence the risk factor frailty in predicting severe adverse events. Frailty might be able to assist in stratifying infection risk and guiding the intensity of induction therapy in ANCA vasculitis patients.

title: #1989 Dapagliflozin in inactive lupus nephritis: a randomized cross-over trial
authors: Gisele Vajgel; Braziliano Silva Junior; Carlos Miranda Filho; Camila Oliveira; Denise Maria Costa; Camilla Lima; Lucila Valente; Paula Sandrin-Garcia
abstract:
Background and Aims
Lupus nephritis (LN) patients under immunosuppression were excluded from the main trials with SGLT2 inhibitors. This trial aims to assess the effect and safety of dapagliflozin in inactive LN patients with residual proteinuria.
Method
We include adult patients with LN class III, IV (+/−V) without active LN but with proteinuria >500 mg/24 h and eGFR ≥20 ml/min, in the maintenance treatment with a RAAS and MMF <2 g/day in stable a dose for at least 4 weeks. We excluded patients with other etiologies of CKD, those with active LN lesions on the recent biopsy (AI >2), use of induction therapy in the last 12 mo. Those included were randomized to receive dapagliflozin 10 mg on top of standard of care therapy (SoC) or not. After 24 weeks the groups were switched and those without dapagliflozin received it for the next 24 weeks. Primary endpoint is reduction of proteinuria compared to baseline at 6 and 12 mo. Exploratory endpoints were RNA expression and cytokines levels with and without dapagliflozin. The sample size was calculated for 28 patients enrolled providing 80% power to detect a 25% relative risk reduction in proteinuria (α 0.05). Exploratory analysis included gene expression assays performed with TaqMan® fluorogenic probes to the target genes IL1B, IL18 and NLRP3, (Thermo Fisher, Madison, WI, USA). The reference genes ribosomal protein P0 (RPLP0) and elongation factor 1-alpha 1 (EF1A) were used for data normalization. The experiments were performed on the ABI7500 real-time PCR system (Thermo Fisher, Madison, WI, USA).
Results
From 97 screened class III, IV (+/−V) LN patients, we excluded 67 due to active LN, low proteinuria or low eGFR. We included 30 patients that were randomized 14 to start the treatment with dapagliflozin on top of SoC and 16 to remain with the usual therapy for 24 weeks. Nine patients were excluded from the analysis due to new LN flare or lost to f/u. Patients in initial dapa group had a significant decrease in proteinuria after 6 months 1018 to 609 mg/day; P = 0.017 but increased to 984 mg/day 6 months after the drug withdrawal. Final analysis shows a significant reduction in the proteinuria of –36.1% in patients after 6 mo of dapagliflozin as opposed to a –3.5% for those in the SoC therapy at the end of a 6 mo period, P = 0.03 (Fig. 1). There were more reported hypotension symptoms in the dapa group (33%), but no drug withdrawal and no significant changes in blood pressure or weight in the follow-up between the groups. There was one case of urinary infection in each group, but in the same patient. And there was no pattern of inflammatory genes expression, namely IL1B, IL18 and NLRP3, with or without use of dapagliflozin (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
We demonstrate a significant reduction in residual proteinuria in patients with inactive LN with dapagliflozin without an increase in infections. However, changes in expression of IL1B, IL18 and NLRP3 do not seem to be associated to use of dapagliflozin in these patients.

title: #3749 Safety and mid-term efficacy of switching from eculizumab to ravulizumab in a cohort of adult patients with atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome
authors: Daniela Palazzetti; Lucrezia Dimartino; Gianfilippo Di Liberato; Francesca Bruno; Rocco Baccaro; Giuseppe Grandaliano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) is a rare form of thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) caused by an uncontrolled complement activation, characterized by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. Before the availability of treatment with C5 complement inhibitor drugs, the prognosis of aHUS in both pediatric and adult patients was unfavorable despite the use of plasmapheresis or plasma infusion, with a mortality rate during the acute phase of 25%. In fact, the advent of Eculizumab (ECZ), humanized monoclonal antibody directed against the C5 complement factor, has drastically altered the natural history of aHUS, improving prognosis and ensuring rapid recovery of renal function.
Although highly effective for the treatment of patients with aHUS since its approval in 2011, ECZ requires intravenous infusions every two weeks, increasing infusion burden, in-hospital visits, patient journey and limiting patients’ and caregivers’ quality of life. Therefore, through targeted modifications of ECZ to enhance antibody recycling, a new anti-C5 monoclonal antibody called Ravulizumab (RVZ) was developed. RVZ presents a optimized halflife in comparison with ECZ, allowing intravenous infusions every 8 weeks.
The clinical efficacy and safety of RVZ in adults and pediatric patients with aHUS has been demonstrated in several clinical trials. Although RVZ has been approved for the treatment of aHUS in the United States, Europe, and Japan there is currently no large real-life evidence of the mid- and long-term effects of therapy switch from ECZ to RVZ.
Method
From June 2023 to January 2025, 15 patients followed at our center for aHUS on ECZ therapy made the switch to RVZ. RVZ was administered via intravenous infusion based on bodyweight. Patients received a first loading infusion of RVZ on day 1, which was 14 days from the last dose of ECZ, followed by maintenance doses administered on day 15 and every 8 weeks thereafter. Patients were followed regularly during follow-up with baseline hematochemical examinations performed on day 1 and then approximately every 8 weeks (preinfusion). t-test for paired data was used to analyze data.
Results
Patients have a median age of 50.5 (SD 9.4) years and are predominantly female (9 patients). Four patients are on hemodialytic replacement treatment for ESKD, seven patients are on conservative therapy for chronic kidney disease (CKD), and four patients are normal renal function. All patients underwent genetic testing, showing mutations in complement genes in 9 patients. The test was negative in three patients and was still ongoing in three patients. The mean follow-up was 390 (SD 168) days. Baseline and post switch lab values are summarized and compared in Table 1. No patient required hemodialytic treatment at any time during RVZ therapy, and renal function, as measured by eGFR values, remained constant throughout follow-up. No signs of disease recurrence. All patients preserved the same stage of CKD observed at baseline. Throughout the observation period, hematological parameters and indices of hemolysis (platelets, hemoglobin, haptoglobin, LDH) remained stable. Spaghetti Plot image shows the trend of laboratory values for each individual patient. Two adverse events of post-infusion asthenia (unrelated to CPK increase or otherwise) were recorded during follow-up. No other unexpected adverse events were recorded.
Conclusion
RVZ represents an important therapeutic option for aHUS patients. Long-term treatment with RVZ was well tolerated and associated with stable renal function and hematological parameters. In addition, the reduced infusion frequency of RVZ reduces the therapeutic burden and, as a result, may improve the quality of life for patients and their caregivers.

title: #3697 Integrating crescent characteristics, vascular lesions, and podocyte injury into the MEST-C framework: enhanced risk stratification in IgA nephropathy
authors: José Soares; Andreia Carnevale; Ana Rita Pereirinha Ramos; Rodolfo Almeida; Madalena Borges; Fernando Caeiro; Mário Ventura Góis; Helena Sousa; Cristina Rego de Freitas Mendes Jorge
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA Nephropathy (IgAN) remains a leading cause of chronic kidney disease and end-stage kidney disease globally. While the MEST-C framework has significantly advanced risk stratification, certain histopathological features, including crescent characteristics, vascular lesions, and podocyte injury, might warrant further exploration. The aim of this study was to evaluate the clinical significance of crescent type and extent, vascular lesions and podocyte injury as predictors of renal function and proteinuria.
Method
A retrospective, multicenter cohort study was conducted involving 125 adult patients with biopsy-confirmed IgAN who underwent kidney biopsy between January 1st 2015 and December 31st 2022. Patients with IgA Vasculitis or secondary causes of IgA deposition were excluded. Demographic and clinical data, including kidney biopsy findings, were collected from electronical records. Statistical analysis was done using SPSS software (Version 30).
Results
The mean age was 45.54 ± 16.03 years, with 72.0% (n = 90) male, 72.8% (n = 91) hypertensive, and 9.6% (n = 12) diabetic. The considerations for biopsy included hematoproteinuria (n = 48, 38.4%), nephrotic- range proteinuria (n = 20, 16.0%), and worsening kidney function (n = 12, 9.6%). The mean glomeruli count was 11.4 ± 6.3. Basal median protein/creatinine ratio was 3039.7 ± 9817.2 mg/g, and mean eGFR was 50.7 ± 30.1 ml/min/1.73m2. Histopathology showed podocyte injury (n = 27, 21.6%), mainly hypertrophy (n = 27, 21.6%), and vascular lesions (n = 66, 52.8%) such as hyalinosis (n = 32, 25.6%) and intimal thickening (n = 24, 19.2%). Crescents were observed in 32 patients (25.6%), specifically cellular (n = 17, 13.6%), fibrous (n = 10, 8.0%), and fibrocellular types (n = 11, 8.8%), present in ≥25% of the glomeruli in 10 patients (8%). Therapies included ACEi/ARB (n = 101, 80.8%), SGLT2i (n = 16, 12.8%), and corticosteroids (n = 42, 33.6%). At 12 and 24 months serum creatinine variation was slightly increased (0.1 ± 1.4, P = 0.013; 0.2 ± 1.2 mg/dL P = 0.002), while proteinuria decreased by 1969.0 ± 1538.2 and 2195.1 ± 1578.9 mg/g, respectively (both P < 0.001). Oxford MEST-C parameters E and S were significantly associated with proteinuria reduction, both at 12 (P = 0.006) and 24 months (P = 0.033). Crescents correlated with higher baseline proteinuria (3212.5 ± 2428.8 vs 1880.0 ± 1698.7 mg/g, P = 0.044), but also with greater reductions at 12 and 24 months, particularly cellular crescents (P < 0.001). Patients with hyalinosis (n = 32, 25.6%) had significantly higher baseline proteinuria (5531.9 ± 18944.7 vs. 2186.8 ± 2008.0 mg/g, P = 0.008), but exhibited a pronounced reduction at 12 (P = 0.009) and 24 months (P = 0.005). Those with elastic lamina duplication (n = 9, 7.2%) had higher baseline creatinine (3.9 ± 2.8 vs. 2.0 ± 1.3 mg/dL) and were associated with a serum creatinine increase at 12 months (1.5 ± 4.3 mg/dL, P < 0.001) althought not at 24 months (P = 0.896).
Conclusion
IgA nephropathy demonstrates significant heterogeneity, with crescents, vascular lesions, and podocyte injury playing key roles in disease progression and treatment response. In our population, cellular crescents were linked to severe proteinuria but showed the greatest improvement over time, suggesting potential reversibility. Vascular pathology strongly influenced outcomes, with hyalinosis linked to higher proteinuria yet also demonstrating significant improvement with treatment, whereas elastic lamina duplication correlated with worsening renal function and disease progression over time. These findings support integrating crescent type and vascular pathology into risk stratification models, as they could enhance predictive accuracy beyond the current MEST-C framework. This may optimize treatment approaches, particularly for aggressive or atypical disease phenotypes.

title: #3063 Real-world utility of the International IgA Nephropathy Prediction Tool in a tertiary referral centre of nephrology
authors: Iulia Diana Florescu; Tudor Sergiu Niculae; Otilia Ciurea; Nicoleta Petre; Mariana Lipan; Cristina Capusa
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is the commonest glomerulonephritis worldwide, affecting mainly young adults. Since its course is variable from asymptomatic urinary abnormalities to rapidly progressive disease, and more than half of the patients reach end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) during a decade, predicting the outcome in an individual case is essential. Therefore, the International IgAN prediction tool (IgAN-PT) was developed and validated in various conditions. We aimed to investigate its utility in a real-life setting within a tertiary referral centre of Nephrology from Eastern Europe.
Method
Subjects with biopsy-proven primary IgAN were retrospectively selected from all patients who underwent a biopsy in the hospital over a ten years period (01.01.2008–31.12.2018). Those with inadequate histologic sample, repeated or graft biopsy, secondary IgAN missing data, and lost from evidence were excluded. The main outcome of interest was the start of kidney replacement therapy (KRT—either dialysis or transplantation). Follow-up period ended on December 31st, 2023. Data from the time of the biopsy were used for obtaining the 5-year scores of the IgAN-PT. Performance was assessed by receiver-operating characteristic (ROC) curves and calibration plots.
Results
The investigated cohort comprised 184 subjects, mostly men (68.5%), with a median age of 44 years, median glomerular filtration rate of 47 ml/min/1.73m² (49% - chronic kidney disease stage G3), and median proteinuria of 1.2 g/day. More than two third were on an anti-angiotensin II drug and 42% were treated with immunosuppressive regimens. Histological findings showed a high proportion of chronic lesions (glomerular sclerosis and interstitial fibrosis/tubular atrophy being found in 26.6% and 37.5% of subjects, respectively).
During the follow-up, 24 subjects (13%) died, and 58 subjects (31.5%) started KRT within 5 years. The median 5-year prediction tool score was 20.9%. The area under the ROC curve at 5 years was 0.780, supporting a good discrimination performance in predicting ESKD (Fig. 1).Overall, the calibration plot for IgAN-PT displayed a close alignment between the predicted and observed risks, except for the median part of the cohort, suggesting an underestimation for cases with a moderate risk (i.e. between 30%–50%) (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
The international IgA nephropathy prediction tool appears useful in predicting 5-year kidney outcome in this single-center cohort of Eastern European adults, but its accuracy seems limited for those with moderate risk of progression.

abstract:
Background and Aims
Vancomycin, a glycopeptide antibiotic, is clinically used but causes nephrotoxicity through direct tubular damage and vancomycin-uromodulin casts, lacking effective therapeutic strategies to date. Given that vancomycin's solubility is pH-dependent, the effects of urinary pH modulation are not well understood. Moreover, vancomycin is excreted via glomerular filtration and proximal tubular secretion, particularly through the anion (OAT) transport system. This study investigates the effects of urinary pH modulation and OAT blockade with probenecid on vancomycin-induced renal lesions in a murine model.
Method
Eight-week-old male C57Bl/6J mice were intraperitoneally administered vancomycin at a dose of 0.5 mg/g daily for two consecutive days to induce acute kidney injury. Urinary pH modulation began 24 hours before vancomycin administration, with 0.2 M bicarbonate in drinking water for alkalinization or 2% ammonium chloride mixed in the food for acidification. Probenecid was administered intraperitoneally at a dose of 0.15 mg/g, 30 minutes prior to each vancomycin dose. Mice were euthanized and tissues collected on the third day. A chronic model was also developed to evaluate the effectiveness of probenecid: both doses of vancomycin were administered on two consecutive days, comparing vancomycin alone versus vancomycin with probenecid, with transcutaneous GFR measurements on days 3, 8, 15, 21, and 30. Half of the mice in each group were euthanized at Day 8 for an interim analysis, and the remainder at day 30. Renal function tests, histological analysis, and intravital microscopy were used to assess outcomes.
Results
At early time points (day 3), urinary acidification significantly reduced plasma urea levels (29.48 ± 15.48 vs. 46.19 ± 13.31 mmol/L, P = 0.0013) and improved histological scores for tubular necrosis (ATN score P = 0.0054) and cast formation (cast score P = 0.0326). Probenecid treatment led to notable reductions in plasma urea (16.14 ± 4.013 vs. 46.19 ± 13.31 mmol/L, P < 0.0001), acute tubular necrosis (ATN score P = 0.0315), and intraluminal casts (cast score P = 0.0274). Notably, intravital microscopy confirmed a substantial reduction in cast formation with probenecid treatment (P = 0.0002). In the long-term follow-up, at day 8, plasma urea levels were significantly lower in the probenecid group (15.48 ± 4.013 mmol/L vs. 29.48 ± 15.48 mmol/L, P = 0.0003), with histological improvements in tubular lesion scores (P = 0.0447) and cast scores (P = 0.047). Additionally, transcutaneous GFR measurements indicated significantly improved renal function in the probenecid group compared to the control, (P = 0.0321). At day 30, further reduction in plasma urea was observed (12.14 ± 3.312 mmol/L vs. 25.19 ± 13.31 mmol/L, P = 0.0162), along with significant histological improvements in tubulointerstitial fibrosis scores (P = 0.0368).
Conclusion
The study demonstrates that urinary acidification and anionic transporter inhibition through probenecid significantly mitigate vancomycin-induced renal injury. These findings suggest potential preventive strategies for reducing nephrotoxicity in clinical settings where vancomycin is essential.

title: #2851 Clinical and histological response of proliferative, crescentic IgA nephropathy to 6-month methylprednisolone course: a repeat biopsy study
authors: Kirill Komissarov; Olga Krasko; Tatjana Letkovskaya; Margarita Dmitrieva; Viktoria Savosh; Aliaksandr Shpakouski; Valery Pilotovich
abstract:
Background and Aims
The use of repeat biopsy histology as a surrogate endpoint or guide to ongoing immunosuppression has not been adequately studied in adult patients with IgA nephropathy (IgAN). The aim was to evaluate the clinical response and reversibility of proliferative, crescentic IgAN by performing a repeat kidney biopsy after 6-month course of methylprednisolone (MP).
Method
We conducted a prospective multicenter open-labelled trial of 15 (11 men; 32 [28; 41] years old) patients with IgAN had been confirmed by histological examination of biopsies using the Oxford classification (MEST-C) and the presence of histopathological proliferative changes (M1 and/or E1) and/or cellular crescent (C1) with glomerular filtration rate (GFR) >50 ml/min and proteinuria (PU) >0.75 g/day after 3 months course of maximal tolerated dose of ACE inhibitors or ARBs and then treated with intravenous MP 1 g per day for 3 consecutive days at the beginning of months 1, 3, and 5, plus oral methylprednisolone 0,4 mg/kg on alternate days for 6 months. Exclusion criteria were secondary forms, rapidly progressive course, nephrotic syndrome, T2 according to MEST-C, previous treatment of corticosteroids, pregnancy, active infection and decompensated chronic disease. All calculations were performed using the R statistical package, version 4.2. The significance level (alpha) was set at 0.05 for statistical inference. When examining laboratory data, it was calculated the differences between the baseline value (at the start of the study) and the final value (after 6 months), which were considered the effect size of the changes in response to the treatment administered.
Results
Clinical and laboratory parameters improved significantly after 6-month MP treatment: PU (P = 0.003) and hematuria (P = 0.001) decreased, serum albumin increased (P = 0.003). A repeat kidney biopsy was performed in all treated patients. Endocapillary proliferation were eliminated in 5 from 10 patients with E1, cellular crescents were disappeared in 8 from 11 with C1, while mesangial proliferation (M1) remained unchanged. During our observation, no specific side effects of steroid therapy were noted.
Conclusion
We concluded that 6-month MP treatment reduces PU and hematuria, stabilizes serum albumin and attenuates endocapillary proliferation and cellular crescents in patients with proliferative and crescentic forms of IgAN with PU and preserve renal function.
