title: #2642 Effects of Nefecon on hits 1, 2, and 3 of the pathogenic cascade of IgA nephropathy: a full NefIgArd analysis
authors: Ishika Khan; Nadia Nawaz; Amal A A Jama; William Barratt; Róisín Thomas; Russell Jones; Jonathan Barratt
abstract:
Background and Aims
The pathogenesis of immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) is commonly described as a multi-hit paradigm characterized by an increase in circulating levels of poorly O‑galactosylated IgA1 (Gd-IgA1) (referred to as “Hit 1”), which leads to the presence of IgA and IgG antibodies that bind to the Gd-IgA1 (“Hit 2”), and the formation of circulating IgA-containing immune complexes (IgA-IC) (“Hit 3”). These immune complexes have a propensity to accumulate in the mesangium, driving inflammation and scarring in the kidneys (“Hit 4”), leading to progressive nephron loss. To avoid kidney failure in the lifetime of patients with IgAN, there is a pressing need for disease-modifying therapies capable of targeting these pathogenic Hits, inhibiting mesangial IgA-IC accumulation and kidney damage. The gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) is considered to be a major site for Gd-IgA1 production in patients with IgAN; Nefecon is an oral, targeted‑release formulation of budesonide that is designed to inhibit Gd-IgA1 production in the GALT. NefIgArd (NCT03643965) was a Phase 3, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial in patients with IgAN at high risk of disease progression despite optimized supportive care. Patients received 9 months of treatment with either placebo or Nefecon 16 mg/day, before entering a 15-month off-drug observational period. Nefecon stabilized estimated glomerular filtration rate decline and was associated with a significant and durable reduction in proteinuria versus placebo. Here, we present data for all of the exploratory biomarker time points (baseline, 3, 6, 9, 12, and 18 months) from all consenting patients in the NefIgArd trial, looking in detail at changes in markers of Hits 1, 2, and 3 of the IgAN pathogenic cascade with Nefecon versus placebo.
Method
Gd-IgA1, IgG anti-IgA antibody, and IgA-IC levels were measured using serum samples collected at baseline and at 3, 6, 9, 12, and 18 months from 216 consenting NefIgArd participants (n = 108 per treatment group). Gd-IgA1 levels were assessed using a commercial assay, while IgG anti-IgA antibody and IgA-IC levels were measured using in‑house sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Comparisons between the placebo and Nefecon-treated groups were made using robust regression with multiple imputations, and with a significance threshold set at P < 0.05.
Results
Statistically significant reductions in circulating Gd-IgA1 levels were observed with Nefecon versus placebo at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months; however, levels were not significantly different at 18 months (Fig. 1A). Nefecon was also associated with significant reductions versus placebo in IgG anti-IgA antibodies at 3, 6, and 9 months of treatment, with levels approaching baseline by 12 months (i.e., 3 months post-treatment) and remained non‑significant at the 18-month time point (Fig. 1B). Additionally, treatment with Nefecon resulted in a significant reduction versus placebo in IgA-IC levels at 3 months, with numerical reductions maintained at 6 and 9 months in the Nefecon group (Fig. 1C).
Conclusion
Nefecon 16 mg/day was the first fully approved treatment for IgAN based on the Phase 3 NefIgArd trial findings. The 18-month NefIgArd biomarker data represent the most complete analysis to date of the effects of a drug on the IgAN pathogenic cascade, showing clear reductions in markers of Hits 1, 2, and 3 with Nefecon compared with standard of care alone. These findings, coupled with other previously published data, demonstrate that treatment with Nefecon has a direct disease-modifying effect in IgAN.

title: #3452 Real-world effectiveness of ravulizumab in adults with aHUS who switched to ravulizumab within 3 months of eculizumab treatment (aHUS IMPACT)
authors: Shruti Chaturvedi; Yan Wang; Moh-Lim Ong; Arpita Nag; Rui Song; Lynn Huynh; Jordan A Burdeau; Mei Sheng Duh; Ramy Magdy Hanna
abstract:
Background and Aims
Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (aHUS) is a progressive rare disease caused by complement dysregulation that, if untreated, can lead to severe organ damage and death. Ravulizumab, a next-generation terminal complement C5 inhibitor, has demonstrated immediate, complete, and sustained terminal complement inhibition in clinical trials. Real-world evidence supports ravulizumab effectiveness in patients (pts) already stable on eculizumab; however, evidence of ravulizumab effectiveness following short-term eculizumab treatment (≤3 months) is limited.
Method
This was a retrospective, longitudinal, physician panel-based chart review of adults (aged ≥18 years) with aHUS in the USA who switched from eculizumab to ravulizumab between 1 November 2019 and 30 September 2022, and with ≤3 months of eculizumab treatment. Physicians with medical and laboratory records for ≥1 pt(s) with aHUS randomly selected ≤5 pts with ≥6 months of medical records after ravulizumab initiation; pts with <6 months of medical records could be included if the pt died during these 6 months. Laboratory parameters (platelet count, lactate dehydrogenase [LDH], and serum creatinine [SCr]) were collected at eculizumab and ravulizumab initiation (or at the point closest to eculizumab or ravulizumab initiation, respectively, within the prior 6 months), and at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months after ravulizumab initiation. Complete thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) response was defined as having platelet count normalization (≥150 × 109/L), LDH normalization (≤246 U/L) and ≥25% reduction in SCr levels compared with the last measure before eculizumab initiation, determined based on laboratory data or physician-reported complete TMA response. The proportion of pts requiring dialysis during the baseline period (12 months before and up to 2 weeks after ravulizumab initiation) and during follow-up (2 weeks to 12 months post-ravulizumab initiation) was also analysed.
Results
Overall, 54 pts with aHUS (enrolled by 33 physicians) were included in the analysis; 35 (64.8%) were male, 39 (72.2%) were White, 9 (16.7%) were Black or African American and 6 (11.1%) were Asian. Median (range) age at ravulizumab initiation was 43.0 (32.5, 57.0) years. Mean (standard deviation [SD]) time from diagnosis to eculizumab initiation was 1.8 (3.7) month(s), and from eculizumab initiation to ravulizumab initiation was 1.7 (0.9) months. Complement genetic testing was performed in 21 pts (38.9%); of those, 10 pts had variants identified in: C3 (n = 3); CFH, CFHR1, CFHR3, CFI (n = 2 each); and CFB, CFHR5 (n = 1 each). Two pts (3.7%) had a kidney transplant prior to eculizumab initiation, and 6 pts (11.1%) received acute (n = 4) or chronic (n = 2) dialysis during the baseline period. Platelet count, LDH level and SCr level improved following ravulizumab initiation up to Month 12 post-ravulizumab initiation (Fig. ). Statistically significant changes in platelet count, LDH level and SCr level from on or before ravulizumab initiation occurred as early as Month 1 after switching to ravulizumab following short-term eculizumab treatment (Table). Among 46 pts (85.2%) who did not receive dialysis during baseline, 2 (4.3%) initiated dialysis during follow-up (mean [SD] 5.3 [4.0] months after ravulizumab initiation; duration of 4.9 [6.5] months by Month 12 post-ravulizumab initiation). Among 6 pts (11.1%) who reported receiving dialysis during baseline, 5 required dialysis during follow-up (mean [SD] duration of 5.7 [5.3] months by Month 12 post-ravulizumab initiation) and one pt did not require dialysis during follow-up. Complete TMA response was achieved in 30 pts (55.6%) and 33 pts (61.1%) within 6 and 12 months, respectively, of early switch to ravulizumab from eculizumab; median (interquartile range) time to complete TMA response was 5.5 (2.9, not reached) months.
Conclusion
This study provides real-world evidence that switching to ravulizumab after short-term eculizumab is achievable in pts with aHUS and can result in significant haematological and renal improvements in this cohort. This was demonstrated by both an early response and continued improvement through 1 year after ravulizumab initiation.

title: #2164 Nine-year experience of severe ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis treatment: a single-center retrospective study
authors: Anastasiia Zykova; Elena V Zakharova; Natalia Chernyshova; Galina Thakohova; Tatyana Makarova; Eugenia Leonova; Elena Nikitina; Eugeny Shutov
abstract:
Background and Aims
Severe ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis (ANCA-GN) remains challenging in the real-world practice. Such patients were excluded from most of the landmark trials, while some of the observational studies reported the patients with different disease phenotype, including those with severe kidney damage. We aimed to assess the outcomes of severe ANCA-GN in the real clinical practice.
Method
This single-center retrospective study included patients, diagnosed with the new-onset severe ANCA-GN from January 2016 to January 2024. According to the KDIGO 2021 Guidelines definition, we considered ANCA-GN as severe if serum creatinine level at presentation exceeded 354 µmol/L. Disease activity was assessed according Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score version 3 (BVAS v3). Initial treatment included glucocorticoids, combined with intravenous cyclophosphamide (CYC) or rituximab (RTX).
Results
The study group consisted of 63 patients, mean age 55.2 ± 13.8 years, 27 (42.8%) female, 45 (71.4%) with microscopic polyangiitis, 19 (30.1%) with kidney-limited disease. Median serum creatinine was 540 [461; 712] µmol/L, 30 (47.6%) patients required dialysis at presentation, 49 (77.7%) patients underwent kidney biopsy, in the rest 14 (22%) biopsy was not performed due to the disease severity. Median ANCA Kidney Risk Score was 14 [11; 18], median Mayo Clinic Chronicity Score was 7 [5; 8]. CYC sub-group included 52 patients, and RTX sub-group—11 patients. The median follow-up was 18 [6; 63.5] months.
There was no differences in the disease activity, serum creatinine median levels, need for dialysis at presentation, histological scores and kidney function recovery rate between the sub-groups of patients, treated CYC or RTX (Table 1). A single patient in the RTX sub-group progressed to kidney failure within 15 months, and 14 in the CYC sub-group progressed to kidney failure within 16 [2.25; 33.5] months (log-rank test, P = 0.844). Kidney survival did not significantly differ between the treatment sub-groups: (log-rank test, P = 0.697), mortality was also compatible (Table 1); in the CYC sub-group 5 patients died of infection, 2 of severe lung vasculitis and 1 of stroke, two of them were dialysis-dependent; in the RTX sub-group 3 patients died of severe COVID-19, none of them were dialysis-dependent.
Twelve (19%) patients—10 (19.2%) in CYC and 2 (18.1%) in RTX sub-groups with the most severe vasculitis, namely with significantly higher disease activity, higher median serum creatinine and higher need for dialysis at presentation (P = 0.001, P = 0.043, and P = 0.009, respectively, Table 1) received plasma exchange (PEX) in addition to initial treatment. Kidney survival tended to be better in PEX sub-group compared to non-PEX, but the difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.602); mortality was similar.
Conclusion
In our cohort of patients with severe ANCA-GN, compatible for the disease activity, need for dialysis and histological scores, kidney survival and mortality in the sub-groups treated with CYC and RTX were similar. In the sub-group of patients with significantly higher disease activity and worse kidney function, PEX used in addition to CYC or RTX was beneficial and ensured kidney outcomes compatible to only immunosuppressant's usage. The study limitation is the lack pathology data for the patients, who received PEX, only three of them underwent kidney biopsy.

There was no differences in the disease activity, serum creatinine median levels, need for dialysis at presentation, histological scores and kidney function recovery rate between the sub-groups of patients, treated CYC or RTX (Table 1). title: #3696 Characterizing IgAN and assessing the role of International IgAN Prediction Tool in our population

abstract:
Background and Aims

Patients with IgAN display heterogeneity in epidemiology, clinical manifestations, renal progression, and long-term outcomes. Given these facts, treatment options are highly variable, and it is believed that, rather than being a single entity, IgAN may include different entities that lead to mesangial IgA deposition.
There are clinical and histological factors associated with worse prognosis but, due to its variable presentation, it is very difficult to estimate the specific prognosis for each patient. Therefore, the aim of this study was to characterize IgAN and to associate the risk estimated by I-IgAN-PT with the decline of GFR in our population.
Method
A retrospective observational study was performed including patients diagnosed with IgAN by kidney biopsy in our hospital. Clinical, analytical, and histological parameters were collected at the time of kidney biopsy. I-IgAN-PT and GFR were calculated at 12, 24, and 60 months after kidney biopsy. The statistical software utilized was Jamovi v2.3.
Results
This study included 89 patients diagnosed with IgAN by kidney biopsy, mostly men (66.3%). The median age was 47.8 years old (IR: 30.8–58.3), and mean body mass index (BMI) was 27.5 ± 5.4 kg/m2. Secondary causes of IgAN were found in 14.6% of patients. The median decline of GFR was: 3.8% (IR: −10.9–13.7) at 12 months, 3.75% (IR: −6.2–19.5) at 24 months, and 11.9% (IR: 2.1–34.2) at 60 months.

A positive correlation between proteinuria and age was found, and a negative correlation between proteinuria, hemoglobin, and albumin was observed. Albumin was negative correlated with BMI, and positive correlated with hemoglobin. These correlations were statistically significant (P < 0.05).
A significant association was observed between the risk estimated by I-IgAN-PT and the presence at the onset of high blood pressure, nephrotic syndrome, AKI, and nephritic syndrome. Other parameters, such as crescents, secondary IgAN, and CKD, were not associated with that risk. Regarding these mentioned parameters, only AKI and baseline GFR were statistically significant associated with decline in GFR at 12, 24, and 60 months.
When the decline in GFR was analyzed at 12, 24 and 60 months, no significant correlations were found with the risk estimated by I-IgAN-PT at 12, 24 and 60 months.

IgAN is an extremely variable disease and it is difficult to predict single patient outcomes. This study showed the heterogenicity of this disease in our population. I-IgAN-PT did not demonstrate a significant correlation with GFR decline over time. However, some factors at diagnosis were associated with changes in these parameters. Although the tool's ability to predict GFR decline was limited, these findings demand new prognostic tools, and individualized management strategies in IgAN. Further prospective and larger studies may redefine predictive models and enhance risk stratification in this heterogeneous population.

title: #1916 Concomitant sparsentan and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors in adults with IgA nephropathy in the phase 2 SPARTACUS trial
authors: Isabelle M Ayoub; Sydney Tang; Laura Kooienga; Priscila Preciado; David Lee; Radko Komers; Bruce Hendry; Alex Mercer; Stephanie Moody; Brad Rovin
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sparsentan (SPAR) is a non-immunosuppressive, dual endothelin angiotensin receptor antagonist (DEARA) approved in the US and Europe for adults with immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN). In patients with IgAN, SPAR showed sustained proteinuria reduction and preservation of kidney function in the phase 3 PROTECT trial. In a subgroup analysis from DAPA-CKD and EMPA-KIDNEY, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) reduced proteinuria and the risk of progression to kidney failure in patients with IgAN. The combination of SPAR added to stable SGLT2i treatment led to further reductions in proteinuria in patients with IgAN in an interim analysis of the phase 2 SPARTACUS trial. Here we report results from the final analysis of SPARTACUS.
Method
SPARTACUS was a 28-week, open-label, multicenter study of the efficacy and safety of SPAR added to a stable SGLT2i in patients with IgAN at risk of disease progression. Patients had biopsy-proven IgAN, a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) of ≥0.3 g/g, and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of ≥25 mL/min/1.73 m2 despite a stable SGLT2i and maximum tolerated dose of renin-angiotensin-system inhibition (RASi) for ≥12 weeks. Endpoints included change in UACR from baseline to week 24 (primary); achievement of UACR of <0.2 g/g, or a ≥50% or ≥30% reduction in UACR at week 24 (secondary); change from baseline in UACR, eGFR, and blood pressure (BP) at each visit (secondary); and adverse events.
Results
A total of 48 patients (mean [SD] age, 48.9 [13.9] y) received ≥1 dose of SPAR, of whom 41 completed the study. At baseline, patients (male, n = 28 [58%]; female, n = 20 [42%]) had a median (IQR) UACR of 0.70 (0.49–1.01) g/g, median (IQR) urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 1.24 (0.88–1.74) g/g, and mean (SD) eGFR of 57 (26) mL/min/1.73 m2. At week 24, SPAR added to a stable SGLT2i led to a 56% reduction in UACR (median [IQR] UACR at week 24, 0.33 [0.16–0.72] g/g) (Figure and Table); 12 patients (31%) reached a UACR of <0.2 g/g, and 20 (51%) and 30 (77%) patients showed a ≥50% or ≥30% reduction in UACR from baseline, respectively. eGFR remained relatively stable through week 24, with slight decreases in BP (Table). Thirty (63%) patients had a treatment-emergent adverse event, the most common of which was hypotension (15%). No patients experienced abnormal liver function test results >3 × the upper limit of normal.
Conclusion
Switching from RASi to SPAR treatment on a background of an SGLT2i allowed for further reduction in proteinuria in adult patients with IgAN, lowering their risk for disease progression. SPAR combined with an SGLT2i was generally well tolerated, with no unexpected safety signals.

title: #2686 Free light chains in light chain proximal tubulopathy: de novo sequencing and resistance to lysosomal proteases
authors: Xin Wang; Shuang Wang; Xiaojuan Yu; Fude Zhou; Yi Liu; Minghui Zhao
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with light chain proximal tubulopathy (LCPT) typically overproduce abnormal immunoglobulin-free light chains (FLCs). They easily pass through the glomerulus into the proximal tubules. When the endosomal system fails to catabolize abnormal FLCs, it results in their accumulation in cytoplasm of proximal tubule cells (PTCs), forming inclusions or numerous lysosomes. Particular types of abnormal FLCs have been implicated in the onset of tubulopathies, suggesting that the amino acid (AA) sequence of FLCs may play a crucial role in the pathogenesis. This study aimed to determine the AA sequences of patient-derived FLCs and try to explain its relationship with intracellular crystal formation.
Method
The complete amino acid sequences of FLCs from five patients with LCPT were detected using an innovative de novo protein sequencing workflow. One patient (κPWL) did not exhibit crystalline histopathological lesions, whereas the other four patients showed crystalline lesions (κDEH, κWJJ, κWWJ, and κZGN). In this study, the degradation of FLCs in LCPT by human CtsB, CtsD and CtsL was tested under ideal in vitro conditions. An AI model AlphaFold3 was used to compare the structural variations of different FLCs, providing insights into the underlying crystallization mechanism.
Results
All pathogenic FLCs were highly homologous to the same germline counterpart, IGKV1-33. Kinetic studies of FLC digestion by the lysosomal enzyme CtsD revealed the production of a protease-resistant ∼12 kDa fragment in FLCs associated with crystalline LCPT. The CtsD-digested fragments of κ FLCs causing tubular crystallization corresponded to the VJ regions, whereas the λ FLC leading to tubular crystallization was linked to the C region. Site-directed mutagenesis in the variable domain may suppress the formation of intracellular crystals, which likely resulted from a change in hydrogen bonds leading to an alteration in folding.
Conclusion
The generation of a proteolysis-resistant fragment from FLCs in crystalline LCPT by CtsD may be a common feature of this class of FLCs. Key amino acids may determine intracellular crystallization.

title: #3363 Diagnostic gaps in C3G and ic-MPGN: findings of the CompCure study cohort
authors: Giulia Bassanese; Joanna Sladowska-Kozlowska; Enrique Morales Ruiz; Marina Vivarelli; Andrea Pasini; Aude Servais; Enrico Vidal; Nele Kanzelmeyer; Giulio Del Vecchio; Rita Santarsiere; Francesca Lugani; Franz Schaefer
abstract:
Background and Aims
C3 glomerulopathy (C3G) and immune complex-mediated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (ic-MPGN) are chronic kidney disorders characterized by abnormal activation of the alternative complement pathway. The etiology of the conditions is heterogeneous and variably involves C3 activating auto-antibodies, alterations in complement regulating genes and activation of the terminal complement pathway. Classification by diagnostic biomarker panels has been proposed to improve outcome prediction. While currently available non-specific immunosuppressive and antiproteinuric therapies yield highly variable long-term disease outcomes, new treatments targeting individual components of the complement system are in development. These emerging novel therapeutic options increase the need for standardized, comprehensive diagnostic evaluation of C3G/ic-MPGN to empower rational, personalized treatment approaches.
The European Rare Kidney Disease Reference Network (ERKNet) and the CompCure Association for complement-mediated diseases have recently established a large prospective registry study following adults and children with C3G/ic-MPGN. The CompCure project aims to explore the association of diagnostic biomarkers with treatment responsiveness and disease outcomes. Here, we analyzed the completeness of available complement diagnostic features and the detection rate of abnormalities in the study cohort.
Method
A total of 236 patients were analyzed, including 157 with C3G (141 C3GN, 16 DDD) and 70 with ic-MPGN, registered across 36 European nephrology referral centers (30 pediatric, 11 adult). Disease onset was during childhood in 70% of the patients. 77% of patients were enrolled within 6 months of diagnosis. The diagnosis was established by kidney biopsy with immunofluorescence and electron microscopy in all cases.
Results
At time of diagnosis, global CH50 and AP50 complement tests were conducted in 26% and 15% of cases, respectively. While serum C3 was tested in 71% and C4 in 69% of patients, other complement proteins were rarely assessed: Factor H in 17%, C5 in 3%, and Properdin in 2%. The membrane attack complex (sC5b-9) was measured in 32%, and Bb in 4%. Among autoantibodies, C3Nef was tested in 33%, anti-FH in 31%, anti-FB in 9%, anti-C3b in 11%, and C5Nef in 5% of patients. Genetic testing was performed in 56% of C3GN, 75% of DDD, and 15% of ic-MPGN patients.
The assessment of core diagnostic features increased with time during the observation period:
Conclusion
The diagnostic evaluation of patients with C3G/ic-MPGN in European referral centers primarily relies on histopathological findings and serum C3 levels. Essential tests such as sC5b-9, C3Nef and other autoantibodies as well as complement gene screening are still performed in a minority of patients. Reasons for the incomplete diagnostic assessment may include the low number of specialized complement diagnostic laboratories in Europe, a lack of standardized diagnostic panels, high cost and long processing times. This gap in diagnostic practices hampers accurate disease classification and patient stratification for personalized treatment protocols. The CompCure cohort study will support participating sites to obtain standardized diagnostics in newly diagnosed patients with C3G/ic-MPGN.

title: #3432 Real-world evidence for efficacy and safety of iptacopan and pegcetacoplan in patients with primary membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)
authors: Giulia Bassanese; Maddalena Marasa; Federica Maritati; Luis Fernando Quintana Porras; Federico Alberici; Anne-Els van de Logt; Franz Schaefer; Marina Vivarelli
abstract:
Background and Aims
C3 glomerulonephritis (C3GN), dense deposit disease (DDD) and immune complex-mediated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (IC-MPGN) are chronic glomerulopathies characterized by abnormal activation of the alternative complement pathway. While disease remission can usually not be achieved with the currently available non-specific immunosuppressive and antiproteinuric therapies, novel drugs specifically targeting C3 activation have shown promising results in recent clinical trials. Additional treatment experience with proximal complement inhibitors (PCI) is obtained under real-world conditions in patients who were either found uneligible for the clinical trials or are followed at centers that do not participate in the trial programs. Here, we collected such cases to provide complementary efficacy and safety information on the new therapies.
Method
Anonymized data of patients treated with Iptacopan or Pegcetacoplan outside clinical trials were collected through an online survey among the members of the European Rare Kidney Disease Reference Network (ERKNet). Twenty-four patients were reported by 12 centers (5 adult, 8 pediatric) in 5 European countries. uPCR and eGFR were recorded at baseline and after 1, 3, 6, and 12 months of therapy. The % change of uPCR from baseline at 6 months was used as the primary efficacy endpoint. In case of shorter treatment duration, uPCR and eGFR at 1 month (n = 4) or 3 months (n = 2) were carried forward. In one case, 3- and 12-month entries were used to interpolate 6-month values.
Results
Twenty-one patients with primary C3GN, 2 with DDD and 1 with IC-MPGN treated with a PCI outside clinical trials were evaluated. Fourteen patients received Iptacopan and 10 Pegcetacoplan. The drugs were either made available through compassionate use agreements (n = 16) or prescribed off-label (n = 8). Mean (SD) age at start of treatment was 23 (14) years, ranging from 10 to 66 years. Preceding therapies included steroid pulses (n = 11 patients), oral prednisone (n = 15), MMF (n = 21), calcineurin inhibitors (n = 3) and RAS inhibitors (n = 23). On these treatments, temporary remission of proteinuria was attained in only 1 of the 24 patients. The mean (SD) lowest uPCR achieved prior to treatment was 1.6 (1.3) g/g and the mean uPCR at start of PCI was 5.1 (3.8) g/g. PCI treatment was started with ongoing RAS inhibition in 21, MMF in 11, oral prednisone in 3 and CNI in 1 patient. Mean (SD) PCI treatment duration was 11.9 (10.2) months. During treatment mean uPCR declined steadily, from 5.1 (3.8) at baseline to 3.1 (3.0), 2.8 (2.4), 2.2 (2.2) and 1.9 (2.0) at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months respectively. At 6 months, proteinuria had decreased on average by 59(26)%. eGFR remained stable in most and increased in some patients, with a mean 6-month mean (SD) change of 11.3 (17.1) ml/min/1.73 m2. During a cumulative exposure time of 254 months, two adverse events were reported as potentially related to PCI, i.e. one case of pneumonia and one case of asymptomatic, reversible increase of pancreatic enzymes. Neither case led to hospitalization or drug discontinuation.
Conclusion
Our real-world findings confirm impressive antiproteinuric and potentially GFR stabilizing effects of PCI in patients who demonstrated limited responsiveness to conventional immunosuppressive and nephroprotective treatment. The drugs appear to have a highly favourable safety profile.

title: #2049 Exploring the mechanism and clinical validation of mitochondrial dynamics-related genes in membranous nephropathy based on Mendelian randomization study and bioinformatics analysis
authors: Qiuyuan Shao; Nan Li; Humin Qiu; Min Zhao; Chun-Ming Jiang; Cheng Wan
abstract:
Background and Aims
Membranous nephropathy (MN) is a prevalent glomerular disease characterized by immune-mediated damage to the glomerular filtration barrier. Despite extensive research, the interplay between MN and mitochondrial dynamics remains largely unexplored. Recent advances in bioinformatics have opened up new avenues for understanding the molecular underpinnings of various diseases, including MN, thereby providing a solid foundation for further investigation into the genetic and environmental factors contributing to its pathogenesis.
Method
This study aims to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms underlying mitochondrial dynamics-related genes (MDGs) in the context of MN using a comprehensive bioinformatics approach. We conducted a systematic analysis to identify differentially expressed genes associated with mitochondrial dynamics in MN. Subsequently, a nomogram model was constructed to assess the diagnostic value of these key genes. Additionally, immune infiltration analyses were performed to explore the relationship between MN and immune cell composition.
Results
Our analyses identified four key genes—RTTN, MYO9A, USP40, and NFKBIZ—that are significantly implicated in mitochondrial dynamics regulation in MN. The enrichment pathways of these genes predominantly pointed toward olfactory transduction and related processes. Notably, seventeen immune cell types exhibited significant differences in infiltration levels between the MN cohort and the control group. Furthermore, significant regulatory relationships were uncovered, including ATF2 being co-regulated by RTTN and MYO9A. Pseudo-time analysis indicated variable expression trends for these key genes, revealing distinct patterns in their regulation over time. RT-qPCR confirmed that expression levels of the four identified genes were significantly decreased in the MN group compared to normal controls.
Conclusion
This study provides new insights into the role of mitochondrial dynamics-related genes in the pathogenesis of MN, highlighting the potential for RTTN, MYO9A, USP40, and NFKBIZ as biomarkers for diagnosis and targets for future therapeutic intervention. Our findings underscore the importance of further research into the intricate molecular interactions involved in MN, paving the way for innovative strategies in the management of this challenging disease.

title: #3242 Long-term outcomes in IgA nephropathy: findings from the ERKNet patient registry (ERKReg)
authors: Eyal Rahmani; Licia Peruzzi; Jürgen Floege; Dario Roccatello; Enrique Morales Ruiz; Olivia Boyer; Loreto Gesualdo; Kathleen Claes; Peter J Conlon; Marina Vivarelli; Francesca Lugani; Franz Schaefer
abstract:
Background and Aims
In IgA nephropathy, kidney function gradually declines, but at a highly variable pace. A study of IgA nephropathy patients followed in the UK nationwide RaDaR registry recently depicted a generally poor long-term prognosis, with only few patients likely to avoid kidney failure during their lifetime. In this study, we explored the relationships of proteinuria and eGFR slope with the lifetime risk of kidney failure in patients followed in European reference centers and recorded in the European Rare Kidney Disease Registry (ERKReg).
Method
Data were analyzed on 31.12.2024. At that time, the IgA nephropathy cohort within ERKReg comprised 884 adults and 385 children from 10 European countries and 49 units, all with a biopsy-proven diagnosis of IgA nephropathy. Kidney failure was defined as the first occurrence of kidney replacement therapy (dialysis or transplant) or eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m². Kidney survival was analyzed from the time of diagnosis to kidney failure using Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression models.
To compare the findings with those of the RaDaR study, a matched “RaDaR Inclusion subcohort” was created by including only patients with proteinuria >0.5 g/d or eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m² at any time.
Results
The median (interquartile range (iqr)) age at diagnosis for the total cohort was 33 (17, 49) years, the median age at first recorded centre visit 43.7 (24, 60) years and the median follow-up duration 6.0 (2.3, 14) years from diagnosis. During the observation period, 240 (18.9%) patients progressed to kidney failure and 7 (0.6%) died. The overall median kidney survival following diagnosis was 35.9 (95% CI: 29.0 to NE) years.
For patients with manifestation at adult age, the median age at diagnosis was 41.8 (31, 57), median kidney survival time 35 years (95% CI: 27 to NE), and 10- and 20-year kidney survival rates 75.7% (71.9% to 79.1%) and 64.2% (59.0% to 68.8%) respectively. By comparison, disease manifestation during childhood was diagnosed at a median age of 13.2 (9, 16), with an estimated 10- and 20-year kidney survival of 86.7% (80.6% to 91.1%) and 79.1% (69.6% to 86.0%), respectively.
Disease manifestation at adult age was independently associated with a higher risk for kidney failure as compared to disease manifestation during childhood, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.0 (95% CI: 1.4 to 2.8, P < 0.001) (Fig. 1).
Time-averaged proteinuria was strongly associated with worse kidney survival, with about threefold higher risk for kidney failure in patients with 0.5–1.0 g/d time-averaged proteinuria compared to patients with <0.5 g/d (Table 1).
The RaDaR Inclusion subcohort, consisting of patients with more severe disease, had a median kidney survival of 28.3 years (95% CI: 22.0 to 35.7). These outcomes were notably better than those reported in the RaDaR study, which showed an overall median survival of 11.4 years from diagnosis.
Patient sex and the region of residence in Europe had no significant impact on kidney survival.
Conclusion
In this large European IgA nephropathy cohort, poorer kidney survival was associated with disease manifestation at adult age and greater time averaged proteinuria. Even mild proteinuria had a notable impact on kidney function prognosis. The outcomes observed in this registry cohort indicate a more favorable prognosis for most patients compared to the findings of the British RaDaR study.

title: #2900 Lupus nephritis outcomes in patients with acute kidney injury and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis presentation—cohort of a tertiary center
authors: José Oliveira Da Costa; Natália Marchão; Iolanda Godinho; Marta Sofia Henriques Pereira; Cristina Resina; José António Lopes; Estela Nogueira
abstract:
Background and Aims
Lupus Nephritis with acute kidney injury (AKI) and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) presentation represent a spectrum of severe lupus nephritis that are more prone to long-term worse outcomes.
Method
The authors retrospectively analyzed all systemic lupus erythematous (SLE) patients with lupus nephritis that presented with AKI and RPGN at presentation followed at a tertiary center between 2005 and 2025. According to the established definition by Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) 2024 lupus nephritis guidelines, we evaluated complete (CRR) and partial renal response (PRR) as well as primary efficacy renal response (PEER) at 1 year, and the risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD) at 5 years in this specific population.
Results
We evaluated 107 patients, 93 female (87%), 23 black African (21%), 79 caucasian (74%), 5 other ethnicities (5%).
Presentation with AKI (5; 21%) or RPGN (19; 79%) occurred in 24/107 patients (22%) with a mean age at diagnosis of 36.5 +/− 14.3 years [19–76], 17 female (71%), 16 caucasian (67%), 7 black african (29%), 1 other ethnicity (4%). Mean and SD proteinuria of 3.63 +/− 2.73 g/day [0.33–11], mean and SD creatinine 2.61 +/− 2.67 mg/dL [1.23–12.98] with urinary red blood cells (uRBCs) being present in 21 patients (88%). Regarding LN classes, this group of patients presented with class I (1; 4.16%), class II (1; 4.16% with lupus podocytopathy), class III (6; 25%), class IV (14; 58.33%) and class V (2; 8.33%). The severity of renal lesion led to the need of transient hemodialysis in 2/24 patients (mean time 17 days). Regarding AKI and RPGN etiology, 4/24 patients (17%) developed acute tubular necrosis and 2/24 prerenal AKI (8%) related to severe nephrotic syndrome or sepsis, and in 18/24 patients (75%), renal injury was linked to the gravity of proliferative nephritis, with 2 patients having crescentic glomerulonephritis, defined with more than 50% of crescents. Patients with RPGN universally presented with active urinary sediment with mean and SD proteinuria of 3.57 +/– 2.98 g/day [0.33–11] and mean and SD creatinine 2.24 +/− 1.67 mg/dL [1.23–8.00], contrasting with the group of AKI patients in which only 2/5 (40%) had positive URBCs and presented with mean and SD proteinuria of 3.87 +/− 1.68 g/day [1.5–5.54] and mean and SD creatinine of 5.03 +/− 4.02 mg/dL [1.27–12.98].
For the proliferative LN (20; 83.33%) chosen induction therapy was mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) and glucocorticoids (GC) (12; 60%); Cyclophosphamide (CYC, Eurolupus regimen) and GC (3; 15%); high-dose CYC (NIH regimen) and GC (3; 15%); Rituximab, CYC (3 g) and GC (1; 5%); Rituximab, MMF and GC (1; 5%). Methylprednisolone pulses were administered in 8 patients (40%).
Maintenance therapy consisted in MMF and GC (13; 54%); MMF, azathioprine (AZA) and GC (5;21%); GC and AZA (1;4%); belimumab, MMF and GC (1;4%) patients, respectively.
Regarding outcomes, in the group of patients with proliferative LN, we found that at one year, 16 patients (80%) achieved CRR, 19 (95%) PRR and 17 (85%) PERR. Conversely, patients with LN classes V and II with podocytopathy achieved CRR and PRR in 66.67%/100% of the patients at one year.
Mean up of the overall AKI/RPGN group of patients was 8 years with mean serum creatinine (SCr) at last follow-up of 1.27 +/– 0.92 mg/dL (median 0.95 mg/dL). Renal relapse occurred in 9(37.5%) patients. We found that 19 patients completed 5 years of follow up and of them 35% reached CKD stage 3–5 (5 CKD stage 3; 1 CKD stage 4; 1 CKD stage 5), being one of them on dialysis.
Conclusion
Presentation of lupus nephritis with significant renal function deterioration and a high incidence of renal relapse can explain such a high incidence of CKD at 5 years of follow up in this specific LN population. Being excluded from most clinical trials due to kidney injury severity, the best treatment of these patients remains to be defined, but probably should be treated in more aggressively to decrease the risk of kidney failure.

title: #3500 Exploring the interaction between the complement system and ANCA vasculitis
authors: Lina María León MacHado; Irene Vázquez Raso; Maria Maldonado-Martin; Daniel Jimenez Gutierrez; Laura Lucientes; Elena Goicoechea De Jorge; Gema Maria Fernandez Juarez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Activation of the complement alternative pathway (AP) is involved in the pathogenesis of ANCA vasculitis. Recently our group described some genetic variants were associated with disease susceptibility (CFB32Q/W) or severity of renal damage in AAV (CFH-H1, CFH-H2 and ΔCFHR3/1), and that plasma levels of complement components were significantly different between active and remission cohorts, confirming the role of AP in ANCA vasculitis with renal involvement.
Our aim is to identify different profiles of dysregulation of AP in ANCA vasculitis patients and evaluate the association with renal outcomes.
Method
We conducted an analysis of the cohort included in the previous study of 55 patients with active and histologically confirmed renal involved ANCA vasculitis.
All patients were followed-up for 12 months after diagnosis. All patients received only inmunosupressive treatment (prednisone-rituximab-cyclophosphamide)
Plasma levels of different components of complement (FH, FB, Properdin (FP) and urine c5b9 ) were determined by ELISA assays at diagnosis.
Using a multiple regression model and supervised clustering model we selected the optimal cut-off of the levels of component of complement to predict the kidney outcome at 12 months.
Results
The mean age of the patients was 67 ± 15 years, eGFR of 23 ± 19 ml/min/1.73 m2 and proteinuria 0.85 g/24 h (IQR 0.5–1.5), the 59% were male, the BVAS index was 16 ± 5, most of them had mixed histological class, the 16% required chronic hemodialysis and 25% have no remission during follow-up.
Using the optimal baseline cut off of FH (173 ug/ml) and urine C5b9 (1476 ng/mmol) to predict response to inmunosupressive treatment, the cohort was divided into three groups: profile 1 (n = 31 with FH >173 ug/ml, uC5b9 <1476 ng/mmol), profile 2 (n = 9 with FH >173 ug/ml, uC5b9 >1476 ng/mmol) and profile 3 (n = 13 with FH <173 ug/ml, uC5b9 >1476 ng/mmol) .
From clinical point of view, the profile 3 compared with profile 1 and 2, showed worse renal function at diagnosis (eGFR 12 ± 13 vs 19 ± 11 and 24 ± 15, P < 0.02 (Profile 3 vs profile 1) and P = 0.06 ( profile 3 vs profile 2), and higher acute hemodialysis at diagnosis time (75% vs 25% ans 18%, P < 0.001 and P = 0.06). The levels of the other complement factors were significantly different for profile 3 vs 1 and 2: C3 (90 ± 28 vs 105 ± 30 and 67 ± 18 , p 0.013 and p 0.008), FB (130 ± 69 vs 223 ± 67 and 218 ± 68, P < 0.001 and P = 0.013), FHR1 (174 ± 80 vs 248 ± 88 and 244 ± 126, p 0.015 and P = 0.1), FHR5 ( 3 ± 0.7 vs 4 ± 1.5 and 3.6 ± 1.8, p 0.005 and P = 0.2) and properdin 4.6 ± 2 vs 6 ± 2 and 6.5 ± 1.7, p 0.022 and P = 0.06)
The probability of response to treatment at 12 months of profile, 1, 2 and 3 was: 90%, 87 % and 16 % (Log rank P = < 0.001 ), respectively, (Kaplan Meier Fig. 1).
In the multiple regression model the risk of achieve clinical remission of profile 3 was significantly worse than profile 1 (OR 48, IC95% 7-332, p 0.0001) and profile 2 (OR 35, IC 95% 2.6-465, p 0.0071).
Conclusion
There are multiple AP dysregulation profiles in patients with ANCA vasculitis with renal involvement. These different profiles show different clinical presentation and different response to immunotherapy. Patients with more profound dysregulation (lower levels of FH and higher levels of uC5b9) have a more aggressive renal clinical presentation and have a lower response to immunotherapy. This study proposes that different AP dysregulation profiles may help identify patients with different clinical courses, as well as those in whom immunotherapy is sufficient to achieve remission and those in whom additional AP blockade may be necessary.

title: #897 Rapid diagnosis of membranous nephropathy based on serum Raman spectroscopy combined with deep learning methods
authors: Chen Lu; Li Zhang; Wenjun Yang; Shun Wang; Guoqiang Zhu; Xueqin Zhang; Shuo Wu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Membranous nephropathy (MN) is a leading cause of nephrotic syndrome. Although PLA2R has diagnostic specificity, only 70% to 80% of patients typically test positive for PLA2R. Therefore, this study aims to develop a rapid, accurate, and non-invasive diagnostic technique for MN.
Method
Serum samples were collected from 60 biopsy-confirmed MN patients and 60 healthy controls at the First Affiliated Hospital of Xinjiang Medical University. Raman spectra of the samples were acquired, and three deep learning models—ResNet, GoogleNet, and AlexNet—were constructed for classification analysis of the spectral data.
Results
Analysis of serum Raman spectroscopy signals revealed significant differences between the membranous nephropathy (MN) group and the healthy control group at wavenumbers of 728, 842, 980, 1316, 1439, and 1650 cm⁻¹. Three deep learning models were applied to classify the serum Raman spectra data of MN patients and control subjects, achieving classification accuracies of 93.33%, 96.67%, and 98.33%, respectively. These accuracies were notably higher than the 73.33% accuracy obtained using PLA2R-based diagnostic methods. The results suggest that Raman spectroscopy combined with deep learning models holds great potential as a non-invasive diagnostic tool for membranous nephropathy.
Conclusion
Raman spectroscopy combined with deep learning can rapidly identify membranous nephropathy, showing significant potential for non-invasive MN diagnosis.

Background and Aims
Membranous nephropathy (MN) is a leading cause of nephrotic syndrome. Although PLA2R has diagnostic specificity, only 70% to 80% of patients typically test positive for PLA2R. Therefore, this study aims to develop a rapid, accurate, and non-invasive diagnostic technique for MN.
Method
Serum samples were collected from 60 biopsy-confirmed MN patients and 60 healthy controls at the First Affiliated Hospital of Xinjiang Medical University. Raman spectra of the samples were acquired, and three deep learning models—ResNet, GoogleNet, and AlexNet—were constructed for classification analysis of the spectral data.
Results
Analysis of serum Raman spectroscopy signals revealed significant differences between the membranous nephropathy (MN) group and the healthy control group at wavenumbers of 728, 842, 980, 1316, 1439, and 1650 cm⁻¹. Three deep learning models were applied to classify the serum Raman spectra data of MN patients and control subjects, achieving classification accuracies of 93.33%, 96.67%, and 98.33%, respectively. These accuracies were notably higher than the 73.33% accuracy obtained using PLA2R-based diagnostic methods. The results suggest that Raman spectroscopy combined with deep learning models holds great potential as a non-invasive diagnostic tool for membranous nephropathy.
Conclusion
Raman spectroscopy combined with deep learning can rapidly identify membranous nephropathy, showing significant potential for non-invasive MN diagnosis.

title: #723 Predictive value of Gd-IgA1, poly-IgA in the treatment of IgA nephropathy with targeted−release formulation budesonide
authors: Chen Qinlan; Jicheng Lv; Hong Zhang; Chen Pei; Jincan Zan; Xue Shen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Targeted release formulation (TRF)-budesonide (Nefecon), targeting the production of galactose-deficient IgA1 (Gd-IgA1) and IgA immune complex formation, has been approved for the treatment of IgA nephropathy (IgAN). In this study we aim to investigate whether these biomarkers can predict the clinical response to Nefecon therapy.
Method
Plasma samples from eight Nefecon-treated IgAN patients were collected at each regular clinic follow-up visit. We measured the levels of Gd-IgA1 and poly-IgA, analyzing the association between their baseline levels or changes and proteinuria reduction.
Results
Nefecon treatment significantly reduced proteinuria with a notable reduction after 5 months of therapy. The alterations of proteinuria were 18%, −33%, −36%, and −39% at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months, respectively. While plasma levels of Gd-IgA1, poly-IgA and total IgA decreased within the first 2 months with changes in Gd-IgA1 of −6%, −34%, −17%, and −34%; in poly-IgA of −8%, −24%, −13%, and −18%; and in total IgA of −3%, −21%, −16%, and −29% at 1, 2, 3, and 9 months, respectively. Poly-IgA reductions correlated with proteinuria alterations (P = 0.01). Importantly, the early reduction in poly-IgA during the first 2 months was associated with proteinuria reduction at the final visit (R2 = 0.59, P = 0.07). Similar trends were observed for Gd-IgA1 or total IgA while not reaching statistical significance.
Conclusion
The early changes in Gd-IgA1 or poly-IgA during the first two months, especially poly-IgA, were associated with future proteinuria reduction. These findings suggest that Gd-IgA1 and poly-IgA may serve as biomarkers for Nefecon response.

title: #3267 The effect of immunosuppression based on corticosteroids on arterial stiffness in patients with glomerulonephritis
authors: Adamantia Bratsiakou; Marios Papasotiriou; Areti Alafaki; Antonios Chalvatzis; Themistoklis Paraskevas; Georgia Andriana Georgopoulou; Evangelos Papachristou; Dimitrios Goumenos
abstract:
Background and Aims
Most types of glomerulonephritis are characterized by inflammatory stimulation. Chronic inflammatory diseases are associated with subclinical atherosclerosis and endothelial dysfunction as chronic inflammation accelerates the vessel ageing process and subsequently increases cardiovascular risk, just as metabolic syndrome, obesity, diabetes mellitus and chronic renal insufficiency. The aim of the present study was to determine the effect of corticosteroid based immunosuppressive treatment in patients with glomerular diseases on endothelial function according to arterial stiffness indices.
Method
In this prospective open label cohort study, we included 141 patients (93 males) with a medical history of primary or secondary glomerulonephritis. These, were divided into three groups according previous, concurrent or no prescription of corticosteroid based immunosuppressive treatment. Participants were followed as outpatients every three to six months for 2 years. At each visit, central blood pressure (cBP) and pulse wave velocity (PWV) measurements were performed with mobli-O-graph device, as well as basic laboratory testing.
Results
Overall, 38 patients (M:F = 22:16) were actively receiving immunosuppressive treatment with corticosteroids, 59 (M:F = 41:18) had received corticosteroids in the past, while 44 patients (M:F = 30:14) had never received corticosteroids. The three groups did not differ in terms of median age [52.0 (39.7–64.3) vs 57.0 (49.0–67.0) vs 58 (43.2–65.0) years, respectively, P = 0.420], the presence of diabetes mellitus, arterial hypertension, or heart failure. Accordingly, PWV was higher in the group receiving corticosteroids during the study compared to the group that had received corticosteroids in the past, while patients who had never received corticosteroids had the lowest PWV values; however, differences were did not reach statistical significance [7.9 (6.5–9.6) vs 7.8 (6.4–9.6) vs 7.5 (6.3–9.2) m/sec, respectively, P = 0.586]. Regarding cSBP, there was no difference between the three groups [118.5 (109.1–130.9) vs 118.5 (109.4–131.0) vs 117.0 (108.0–128.5) mmHg, respectively, P = 0.541].
Conclusion
Immunosuppressive therapy based on corticosteroids is a mainstay of treatment in most types of primary glomerulonephritis with a proven benefit on reducing inflammation, but does not appear to have a significant effect on arterial stiffness.

title: #2104 Prevalence and associated factors of sexual dysfunction in female patients with lupus nephritis: a cross-sectional study at AIIMS, New Delhi
authors: Arpana Limbu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Lupus nephritis, a severe complication of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), predominantly affects women of childbearing age (15–44 years). Chronic diseases like SLE often negatively impact sexual function, an essential aspect of quality of life, yet this issue is frequently overlooked in clinical care. Many patients feel that physicians focus only on the disease, neglecting their emotional and psycho social needs.
Aim
To evaluate the prevalence of sexual dysfunction and identify its causative in women with lupus nephritis, to promote more holistic and patient-centred care.
Method
A cross-sectional study was conducted among 100 female patients, aged 18–45 years, diagnosed with lupus nephritis, who attended the nephrology outpatient department (OPD) at AIIMS, New Delhi. Participants were selected using purposive sampling based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data collection involved a demographic questionnaire, the Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21), the Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI), and the Brief Illness Perception Questionnaire (BIPQ). Statistical analyses were performed using the t-test, Pearson & Spearman correlation, binomial exact test, Chi-square test, rank-sum test, and logistic regression.
Results
The study revealed that 68% of the participants experienced sexual dysfunction, as indicated by an FSFI score below 26.55. A mild negative correlation was observed between depression and sexual function. Additionally, weak negative correlation was observed between sexual function and anxiety, stress, participant's age & illness perception. A weak positive correlation was found between sexual function and socioeconomic status of the participants. Logistic regression analysis further confirmed that sexual function was significantly influenced by depression and anxiety levels with the p value< 0.006 & 0.001, respectively.
Conclusion
The findings highlight the significant burden of sexual dysfunction among females with Lupus Nephritis, underscoring the profound impact of sexual health on overall well-being. This critical aspect of health is often overlooked in clinical practice, undermining holistic patient care. The study emphasizes the need for a compassionate, multidisciplinary approach to care that address both the physical and psychological needs of female SLE patients.

title: #3482 Targeted treatment with pegcetacoplan for post-transplant recurrent C3G or primary (idiopathic) IC-MPGN in the VALIANT phase 3 trial
authors: Michiel Js Oosterveld; Jessica Kaufeld; Daniel Zecher; Kathleen Claes; Julien Zuber; Irene L Noronha; Andrew S Bomback; Zhongshen Wang; Johan Szamosi; Li Li; Luis Lopez-Lazaro; Ondrej Viklicky
abstract:
Background and Aims
C3 glomerulopathy (C3G) and primary (idiopathic) immune complex membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (IC-MPGN) are rare diseases where uncontrolled C3 activation results in excessive glomerular deposition of C3 breakdown products, which may lead to kidney damage and ultimately kidney failure.
Following kidney transplantation, most patients (pts) with C3G/primary IC-MPGN experience disease recurrence (∼89%), often resulting in high rates of premature allograft loss and an increased risk of mortality. At present, no effective treatment is available to prevent or treat disease recurrence after kidney transplantation.
Pegcetacoplan (PEG) binds selectively to C3 and C3b to strongly block C3 activation by classical/lectin/alternative pathways, C3/C5 convertase activity and activation of downstream effectors. PEG targets the pathogenic process in C3G/primary IC-MPGN with the aim of stopping kidney damage.
In the Phase 3 VALIANT trial (NCT05067127) in pts aged ≥12 years with native or post-transplant recurrent C3G/primary IC-MPGN treated with a stable regimen, PEG led to glomerular C3 clearance in 71% of pts and achieved significant and sustained reduction in proteinuria across pt subgroups with stabilization of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Here we report the results for the subgroup of pts with post-transplant disease recurrence.
Method
VALIANT study design and pt population have been previously described. Pts were randomized 1:1 to receive PEG (subcutaneous infusion twice weekly) or placebo (PBO) for 26 weeks as add-on to their standard of care regimen. Randomization was stratified by transplant status (post-transplant recurrent vs native disease). The primary endpoint was the log-transformed ratio of urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) at Week 26 vs baseline. Key secondary endpoints included proportion of pts achieving a composite renal endpoint (≥50% reduction in UPCR AND ≤15% reduction in eGFR at Week 26 vs baseline), reduction in C3c staining on kidney biopsy, and eGFR reduction.
Results
Of 124 pts in VALIANT, 9 pts (PEG, n = 5; PBO, n = 4) had post-transplant recurrent C3G or primary IC-MPGN. Baseline characteristics are shown in the Table.
At Week 26, pts receiving PEG achieved a significant 64.9% reduction in UPCR compared to PBO (95% CI: −85.9, −12.9; P = 0.0241). Three of 5 pts (60%) in the PEG arm achieved the composite renal endpoint vs 0/4 in PBO. All four PEG-treated adult pts with available biopsy data had a reduction in C3c staining vs 1/4 pts (25%) in the PBO arm. Stabilization of eGFR was also achieved (+9.3 mL/min/1.73 m2 relative difference vs PBO). There were no safety concerns, with no deaths, rejection episodes, or graft losses.
Conclusion
Results from VALIANT demonstrate that PEG effectively halts the disease mechanism underlying C3G/primary IC-MPGN, indicating a profound disease-modifying effect. PEG, a C3/C3b inhibitor, is the first therapy to achieve significant and clinically meaningful improvements in the three key efficacy measures of proteinuria reduction, C3 renal deposit clearance, and stabilization of eGFR in pts with post-transplant recurrent C3G or primary IC-MPGN. The results of this subgroup analysis confirm that PEG is equally safe and efficacious in treating post-transplant recurrent or native C3G/primary IC-MPGN.

title: #3023 Efficacy and safety of telitacicept treatment for proliferative sclerosis IgA nephropathy: a real-world retrospective study
authors: Yang Yun; Meng Yuan; Xiaomin Zhang; Xin Feng; Detian Li; Xiaohui Bian
abstract:
Background and Aims
Besides proteinuria, histological scores also serve as robust predictors of kidney outcomes in IgA nephropathy (IgAN). There is ongoing controversy concerning immunosuppressive therapy for patients with focal or diffuse proliferative sclerosis in IgAN, primarily due to the challenge of balancing treatment efficacy with the risk of immunosuppressant toxicity. Telitacicept has been demonstrated to safely and significantly reduce proteinuria in patients with IgAN in a randomized phase Ⅱtrial, however, this trial did not account for the severity of kidney pathological lesions in the two groups. Therefore, we conducted a real-world study to assess the efficacy and safety of telitacicept compared to traditional treatments in patients with proliferative sclerosis IgAN classified as Lee's grades IV and V.
Method
We retrospectively analyzed the clinical data of patients with IgAN classified as Lee's grades IV and V at shengjing hospital affiliated China Medical University, between September 2022 and December 2024. In the telitacicept group, 20 patients were treated with telitacicept with or without half-dose corticosteroids for at least 12 weeks. In the tradition group, 35 patients received treatment with corticosteroids and/or other immunosuppressive agents (cyclophosphamide or mycophenolate mofetil, etc). All patients received optimized supportive care, including ACE inhibitor or ARB, and SGLT2 inhibitor. The primary end point was the mean change in 24-hour proteinuria from baseline (%), while the secondary composite outcome was the mean change in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) from baseline (%). The efficacy evaluation was determined based on complete remission (24 h proteinuria ≤0.3 g) and effective remission (a ≥ 50% reduction in 24 h proteinuria compared to the baseline).
Results
There was no statistically significant difference in baseline data between the two groups, with 24 h-proteinuria ranging from 1.80 to 2.47 g/d and eGFR between 61.93 and 68.11 ml/min/1.73 m² (Table 1). Compared to the traditional group, the telitacicept group significantly reduced the mean change rate in 24 h-proteinuria from baseline (%) at 12w (−65.59 [−77.18, −36.88] vs. −29.70 [−70.19, −8.97], p = 0.0021), 24 w (−74.60 [−86.18, −50.93] vs. −59.85 [−76.11, −27.98], p = 0.0332), 48 w (−85.29 [−93.97, −68.97] vs. −44.23 [−80.67, −12.93], p = 0.0001) (Fig. A). The mean change rate in eGFR from baseline (%) at each follow-up point showed no statistically significant difference between the two groups (Fig. B). Specifically, the mean change rate in eGFR from baseline (%) remained stable over time in the telitacicept group (1.01% [12 w] vs. −1.95% [24 w] vs. −1.93% [48 w]), while it exhibited a downward trend in the tradition group (0.00% [12 w] vs. −5.98% [24 w] vs. −5.81% [48 w]) (Fig. B). The telitacicept group exhibited significantly higher complete remission rates compared to the tradition group at 24 w (31.58% vs. 6.45%, p = 0.041) and 48 w (40.00% vs. 6.67%, p = 0.011) (Table 2). Additionally, the effective remission rate was notably higher in the telitacicept group compared to the tradition group at 12 w (68.42% vs. 31.25%, p = 0.019) and 48w (100% vs. 46.67%, p < 0.001) (Table 2). There is no significant difference in the occurrence of severe adverse events between the two groups; however, one case of severe pneumonia was identified in the traditional group.
Conclusion
In patients with proliferative sclerosis IgAN (Lee's grades IV–V), treatment with telitacicept resulted in a clinically significant reduction in proteinuria while maintaining stable eGFR without any severe AEs, compared to traditional immunosuppressive therapies. Our study suggested that telitacicept may be a novel treatment option for proliferative sclerosis IgAN.

title: #2613 Reduction of hematuria and albuminuria with iptacopan in C3G: findings from APPEAR-C3G study
authors: Fernando Caravaca Fontan; Minghui Zhao; Richard Smith; Rubeen Israni; Yaqin Wang; Junhao Liu; Serge Smeets; Deborah Keefe
abstract:
Background and Aims
C3 glomerulopathy (C3G), is an ultra-rare primary glomerulonephritis caused by overactivation of the alternative complement pathway (AP). Hematuria is a common manifestation of kidney damage in patients with active C3G; while albuminuria is a prognostic biomarker for many types of glomerulonephritis, including C3G. Iptacopan (LNP023) is an oral, proximal complement inhibitor that targets Factor B to selectively inhibit the AP of the complement cascade. We previously reported data from the Phase 3 APPEAR-C3G study (NCT04817618) showing iptacopan treatment for up to 12 months resulted in a statistically significant and clinically meaningful proteinuria reduction, estimated glomerular filtration rate stabilization and a reduction in C3 deposition within the glomeruli. Here, we report the efficacy of iptacopan 200 mg twice daily (b.i.d.) in reducing hematuria and albuminuria compared to baseline in participants with C3G over 12 months in the APPEAR-C3G study.
Method
APPEAR-C3G was a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo (PBO)-controlled, pivotal Phase 3 study that treated adult patients with biopsy confirmed C3G. The study comprised a 6-month randomized double-blind treatment with iptacopan vs PBO followed by 6-month open-label iptacopan treatment, as previously described. Two of the key exploratory endpoints were to evaluate reduction of urine albumin-creatinine ratio (UACR) and incidence of hematuria with iptacopan and PBO at 6 and 12 months compared to baseline. The proportion of participants without hematuria (≤5 red blood cell [rbc]/ high power field [HPF] using central laboratory data), mixed model for repeated measures analysis of the log-transformed ratio to baseline (BL) in 24-hour (h) UACR (g/g) and change from BL in first morning void (FMV) UACR (g/g), at both 6 and 12 months are reported here.
Results
Seventy-four participants were randomized 1:1 to either iptacopan (n = 38) or PBO (n = 36). At BL, the proportion of participants without hematuria were notably lower in the iptacopan arm vs PBO (13/38 [34.2%] vs 18/34 [52.9%]). The proportion of participants without hematuria at Month 6 increased in the iptacopan arm (22/36 [61.1%]; 95% CI: 45%, 77%) in comparison to no improvement in the PBO arm (18/32 [56.3%]; 95% CI: 39%, 73%) compared to baseline. The proportion of participants without hematuria increased further at Month 12 in the iptacopan arm to 28/36 (77.8%; 95% CI: 64%, 91%). title: #3469 Socioeconomic and psycho-emotional impact of C3 glomerulopathy and immune complex membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis in adult patients in Spain
authors: Fernando Caravaca Fontan; Álvaro Madrid Aris; Marta Moreno; Marian Vidal Jorge; Julieta Nafissi; Manuel Praga Terente
abstract:
Background and Aims
C3 glomerulopathy (C3G) and primary immune complex-mediated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (IC-MPGN) are rare diseases with overlapping pathogenesis. We present the sociodemographic and clinical characteristics, signs and symptoms (S&S) and the psychoemotional and economic burden of adult C3G and IC-MPGN patients.
Method
Cross-sectional, market research collaborative study conducted in Spain, in cooperation with the National Federation of Patient Associations for the Fight Against Kidney Diseases (ALCER, as per the Spanish spelling). Data were collected through online questionnaires from patients with a biopsy-confirmed diagnosis of chronic primary GN invited to participate by 81 clinical nephrologists and 15 pediatric nephrologists of 52 hospitals across all Spanish regions. The questionnaires covered 5 domains: sociodemographic and clinical characteristics, impact of the disease (emotions and daily activities), patient journey, treatment, and economic impact.
Results
Sociodemographic and clinical characteristics: A total of 360 patients participated, including 30 adults with C3G and 46 adults with primary IC-MPGN. Mean (SD) age was 44.4 (17.5) years for C3G and 49.2 (16.9) years for IC-MPGN. Of the total patients, 20.0% of those with C3G and 23.9% of those with IC-MPGN have been on dialysis for a mean (SD) of 24.3 (26.1) and 22.0 (38.3) months, respectively. Additionally, 13.3% of C3G and 15.2% of IC-MPGN patients received a transplant, with 50.0% and 28.6% of these patients, respectively, having received two or more transplants.
S&S: The signs and symptoms (S&S) and their distribution at diagnosis and at the time of completing the questionnaire are described in the Table.
Burden of disease in daily activities: 80.0% of C3G patients and 67.4% of IC-MPGN patients reported that the disease had psycho-emotional impact. Most patients experienced an impact on self-esteem due to C3G and IC-MPGN (70.0% and 56.5%), anxiety (45.8% and 29.0%) and sadness (33.3% and 22.6%). The most concerning aspect of the disease was the loss of quality of life, reported by 90.0% and 60.9% of patients, respectively, followed by the need for dialysis (53.3% and 54.4%), the inability to carry out personal or professional plans (50.0% and 45.7%), and the need for a transplant (40.0% and 41.3%).
Work status: 53.3% of C3G patients and 43.5% of IC-MPGN patients were active workers; 10.0% and 10.9% were unemployed; and 16.7% and 26.1% were retired, respectively.
Economic burden: Over the past 12 months, patients with C3G made a mean (SD) of 5.8 (4.8) visits to the nephrologist, while patients with IC-MPGN made a mean (SD) of 7.7 (14.9) visits. Additionally, C3G patients had a mean (SD) of 0.9 (1.8) emergency visits, and IC-MPGN patients had a mean (SD) of 1.0 (1.6) emergency visits. Times hospitalized averaged (SD) 2.1 (1.0) times for C3G patients and 1.7 (0.9) times for IC-MPGN patients.
Conclusion
The present study reveals a significant burden of the disease in patients with C3G and IC-MPGN, particularly relevant as these diseases are diagnosed at young ages and impact patients in their productive working days. Despite 7.8 years and 11.8 years, respectively, having passed since disease diagnosis, most patients continue to experience severe symptoms such as proteinuria, edema, hypertension, and fatigue. These symptoms persist over time, impacting daily life and psycho-emotional well-being. The burden of GN is profound, notably affecting self-esteem, anxiety levels, and overall quality of life. Additionally, the economic burden is substantial, with frequent healthcare visits, hospitalizations, and a significant number of patients requiring dialysis. This is especially critical for young adults, highlighting the urgent need for innovative treatments and comprehensive care strategies to mitigate the disease's impact and improve patients outcomes.

title: #3435 Burden of illness in chronic primary glomerulonephritis: the patient perspective
authors: Fernando Caravaca Fontan; Álvaro Madrid Aris; Marta Moreno; Marian Vidal Jorge; Julieta Nafissi; Manuel Praga Terente
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic primary glomerulonephritis (GN) significantly impacts patients on physical, emotional, and economic levels due to its symptoms and prognosis. The existing literature on the subject is scarce. Thus, this collaborative study with the National Federation of Associations for the Fight Against Kidney Diseases (ALCER, according to Spanish spelling), aims to describe the impact on the psycho-emotional and economic well-being of GN from the perspective of the patient and their caregivers. To our knowledge, this is the first report to comprehensively assess the burden of the disease in several domains in a large GN population.
Method
Market research study conducted through online questionnaires to patients with a biopsy-confirmed diagnosis of GN, including immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathy, IgA vasculitis, lupus nephritis, complement 3 glomerulopathy, immune complex-mediated membranoproliferative GNs, monoclonal gammopathies of renal significance, membranous nephropathy, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, minimal change podocytopathy and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies associated vasculitis, aged ≥12 years and their caregivers (for <18 years patients). Two questionnaires were developed with the collaboration of a multidisciplinary scientific committee: (1) targeting adult patients (≥18 years); (2) designed for adolescent patients (between 12 and 17 years) and their caregivers. Patients were invited to participate by nephrologists (81 clinical nephrologists and 15 pediatric nephrologists) across 52 hospitals representing all regions of Spain, with confirmed GN diagnosis. Questionnaires included questions grouped into 5 domains: sociodemographic and clinical characteristics, impact of the disease (psycho-emotional well-being, daily life activities, relationships, academic and work environment), patient journey in the health system, treatment, and economic impact.
Results
360 patients participated: 337 adult and 23 adolescent patients with their respective caregivers. 50.8% of the total patients were men with a mean (SD) age of 44.8 (18.3) years, being 46.9 (17.1) years for adults and 14.3 (1.2) for adolescents.
Overall, 71.9% of the patients reported an impact on their psycho-emotional well-being related to GN; this was more prominent in transplanted patients (81.5%). The primary concern among patients was the loss of quality of life (73.1%), followed by the need for dialysis (51.7%), the need for a transplant (40.6%) and risk of early death (38.1%).
Patients experienced a fluctuating psycho-emotional journey throughout the different stages of the disease (Fig. 1), predominantly characterized by concern and sadness prior to being placed on the transplant waiting list, which shifted to hope after being listed.
Beyond the described psycho-emotional impact, GN significantly affects patients' work and family life: 34.4% of adult patients have given up or postponed having children due to GN, 56.2% of working patients reported an impact on their work environment, and up to 38.9% of post-transplant patients were unable to fully develop their careers. Additionally, GN impacts other aspects of patients' lives, including leisure activities (83.1%), diet (84.2%), sports (77.0%), sleep (70.3%), and relationships (31.1%).
Conclusion
This study underscores the significant and multifaceted burden of chronic primary GN on patients’ physical, emotional, and economic well-being. The high prevalence of psycho-emotional distress, coupled with substantial impacts on daily activities, work, and family life, reveals a clear unmet need for these patients. The findings highlight the urgent need for innovative measures and therapies aimed at reducing the disease burden.

title: #3462 Characteristics of IgA nephropathy patients treated with mycophenolate mofetil in the real world
authors: Efrain Tatis; Sara Núñez-Delgado; Juan León Román; Marina López Martínez; Sheila Bermejo Garcia; Irene Agraz Pamplona; Tiffany Alvarez; Natàlia Ramos Terrades; María Alejandra Gabaldón; Federico Yandian; Ehimy Marcela Suárez Barajas; Maria Jose Soler Romeo
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA Nephropathy (IgA) is the most common primary form of glomerulonephritis. Up to 50% of patients with IgA reached kidney failure or died within 10 years of the diagnosis. There is little evidence of the use of mycophenolate in IgA Nephropathy in the non-Chinese population. The aim of this study is to evaluate the efficacy of mycophenolate mofetil or mycophenolic acid (MMF) in the management of IgA.
Method
We did a retrospective cohort study of patients diagnosed with biopsy-proven IgA in our hospital between 2013 and 2024 with at least 6 months of follow-up. Patients were classified based on the treatment received during the first 6 months post-biopsy. (1) MMF. (2) Oral steroids without MMF. Patients in these first 2 groups were allowed to receive another immunosuppressor before the MMF or steroids, based on the treating physician's criteria. (3) Conservative management. Data were collected at the time of the kidney biopsy and the follow-up visits at approximately 3 and 6 months, and each year after the initiation of the treatment with a maximum of 2 years. The patients were censored at the time of death, last follow-up, kidney failure, transplant, or initiation of an additional treatment. Clinical outcomes were assessed to determine the treatment efficacy, including changes in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), serum creatinine (sCr), the persistence of hematuria, changes in the number of red blood cells in the urine (RBC/HPF), and proteinuria levels.
Results
Between 2013 and 2024, 120 patients were diagnosed with IgA. After an initial screening, 64 patients were selected. Of the 64 patients included, 19 were in the MMF, 14 in the steroids, and 31 in the conservative treatment group. In the MMF, 17 patients also received steroids at the start of treatment. Additionally, 8 patients in the MMF and 2 patients in the steroid group also received cyclophosphamide before initiating the treatment. Patients in the MMF and steroids group presented with a more severe clinical profile (higher sCr, hematuria, proteinuria, and lower eGFR) (Table) compared to those in the conservative group. In terms of pathology findings, the MMF and steroids group had higher s and c scores. Almost all patients with a C1 score and all the patients with a C2 score were in the MMF group.
At baseline MMF group patients had significantly higher hematuria than the other two groups combined (P = 0.002). A significant percentage reduction in hematuria and UPCR were observed from the third month in the MMF group, with a statistically significant difference compared to the other two (98.6% P = 0.002, 81.9% P = 0.048).
At baseline median UPCR was significantly higher in the steroid (1138.9 mg/g) and MMF group (858 mg/g) and lowest in the conservative (545 mg/g). (P = 0.032) (Table). Interestingly, at 24 months median UPCR was lowest in the MMF (173.1 mg/dl), and similar in the steroid (409.7 mg/dl) and conservative group (403.4 mg/dl) (P = 0.868)
At 2 years, the mean sCr and average eGFR were similar in the MMF (1.18 mg/dl and 72 ml/min/m²) and the conservative treatment (1.07 mg/dl and 83 ml/min/m²), while being higher in the steroids group. (1.75 mg/dl and 51.1 ml/min/m²). Patients treated with MMF showed a significantly greater improvement of the eGFR from the third month compared to supportive care. (P = 0.002).
There was no difference in outcomes (eGFR <15, Dialysis, transplant, death, initiation of additional immunosuppressant) between the three groups. (P = 0.212)
Conclusion
Our patients with IgA treated with MMF have a baseline more severe clinical and kidney biopsy profile as compared to the conservative and steroids treated ones. In our clinical setting the initiation of MMF by the nephrologist is based on the baseline severity of the disease. The MMF group achieved greater UPCR reduction, eGFR improvement compared to the supportive care group and more hematuria reduction compared to the other groups, despite having more severe baseline disease. Our results suggests that MMF may be a valid treatment for severe IgA.

title: #2543 Effect of desmopressin on post-kidney biopsy bleeding: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study
authors: Narayan Prasad; Jeyakumar Meyyappan; Ravi Sankar Kushwaha; Manas Ranjan Behera; Manas Ranjan Patel; Anupma Kaul; Monika Yachha; Brijesh Yadav
abstract:
Background and Aims
Percutaneous ultrasound-guided kidney biopsies are the gold standard for diagnosing native and transplant kidney parenchymal diseases. Despite advancements in biopsy techniques, post-biopsy bleeding remains a concern. Desmopressin acetate, a selective V2 receptor agonist, has shown transient hemostatic benefits by increasing von Willebrand factor (VWF) and factor VIII levels. While desmopressin is proven effective in uremic bleeding, evidence in the context of kidney biopsies is conflicting. Few randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have addressed its role in reducing post-biopsy bleeding. This study evaluates the efficacy and safety of intranasal desmopressin in reducing bleeding risk in kidney biopsy patients with varying eGFR levels.
Methods
This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial was conducted between February 2020 and January 2023 at a tertiary nephrology center in India. Adults aged 18–65 years undergoing kidney biopsy for glomerular hematuria, proteinuria, or unexplained renal failure were included. Exclusions were coronary artery disease, CKD with small kidneys, congenital anomalies, coagulopathies, pregnancy, or refusal to consent. Dialysis patients were included if dialysis was performed ≥24 hours before biopsy without heparin.
Patients were randomized (1:1) to desmopressin (300 µg intranasal) or placebo, stratified by eGFR >30 or ≤30 ml/min/1.73m². All biopsies were percutaneous, ultrasound-guided, and performed using automated biopsy devices. Blinding was maintained for participants, investigators, and nephrologists. Outcomes included bleeding incidence, hematoma formation, hemoglobin drop >1 g/dL, hypotension, gross hematuria, transfusion, or interventions.
