title: #3306 Lupus nephritis treated with belimumab: experence in Canary Islands
authors: German Perez Suarez; Ana Gloria Montesinos; Fayna González Cabrera; Patricia Isabel Delgado Mallén; Katia Toledo Perdomo; Sara Afonso Ramos; Ana Jarque; Patricia Perez; Cesar García Canton; Domingo Hernandez; Manuel Luis MacÍa Heras
abstract:
Background and Aims
Nephritis, the most severe manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), affects up to 50% of patients. The current treatment for proliferative lupus nephritis (LN) involves intensive immunosuppression with standard therapies such as mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), cyclophosphamide–azathioprine, and glucocorticoids. Belimumab, a recombinant human monoclonal antibody that inhibits B-cell activating factor, has shown promising results when added to standard therapy for active lupus nephritis, leading to significant primary renal efficacy responses. The aim of this study was to evaluate kidney function, as assessed by glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), proteinuria, and the rates of partial renal response (PRR) and complete renal response (CRR), in patients with LN treated with standard immunosuppression combined with Belimumab.
Method
This was a retrospective study conducted across five hospitals in the Canary Islands. The study included 32 patients (25 women, 78%) with a mean age of 41.1 ± 14 years. LN diagnosis was confirmed by kidney biopsy (class III = 5, class IV = 11, class V = 8, class III+V = 6, class IV+V = 2). Induction immunosuppressive therapy consisted of MMF and steroids (n = 16, 50%), cyclophosphamide + steroids (n = 13, 40.6%), or tacrolimus + MMF and steroids (n = 3, 9.4%). Belimumab was added to the treatment regimen in all patients, with 72% receiving subcutaneous Belimumab at 400 mg/week for 4 weeks, followed by 200 mg weekly, and 28% receiving intravenous Belimumab at 10 mg/kg body weight. The mean follow-up period was 21.7 ± 15 months. Kidney function was assessed using creatinine levels, eGFR (estimated by the CKD-EPI formula), and proteinuria. PRR was defined as a urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) ≤0.7, an eGFR no more than 20% below the pre-flare value, or ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m², with no use of rescue therapy. CRR was defined as a UPCR <0.5, an eGFR no more than 10% below the pre-flare value, or ≥90 mL/min/1.73 m², with no use of rescue therapy. Clinical, demographic, and analytical data were recorded, as well as the use of ACE inhibitors, aldosterone antagonists, and SGLT2 inhibitors.
Results
At 12 months, 42.1% of patients achieved CRR, and 47.4% achieved PRR. Baseline mean creatinine was 1.02 ± 0.5 mg/dL, decreasing to 0.9 ± 0.4 mg/dL at 12 months (P = NS). Baseline eGFR was 80.8 ± 23 mL/min/1.73 m², improving to 84.2 ± 29 mL/min/1.73 m² at 12 months (P = NS). Proteinuria decreased from 2.5 ± 3.4 g to 0.6 ± 0.5 g (P = 0.023). Additionally, there was a significant reduction in steroid dosage, from 24.3 ± 9.9 mg to 4.5 ± 5.1 mg at 12 months (P = 0.000). At 12 months, 90.5% of patients had inactive urinary sediment (P = 0.012). A low infection rate was also observed.
Conclusion
The addition of Belimumab to standard immunosuppressive therapy was associated with improved renal outcomes, including a reduction in proteinuria, decreased steroid requirements, and a favorable renal response at 12 months of treatment.

title: #3740 Ultrastructural patterns in membranous nephropathy: a scanning electron microscopy study
authors: Davide Viggiano; Michelangelo Nigro; Scognamiglio Mariarosa; Giuseppe Gigliotti; Pierluigi D'angiò; Ernesto Reverchon
abstract:
Background and Aims
Treating renal diseases requires precise localization of pathological features that cannot be resolved by optical microscopy. A critical diagnostic challenge is determining whether immunoglobulin deposits are located in the subendothelial or subepithelial space of the glomerular basement membrane—a distinction that is crucial for differential diagnosis yet remains difficult to achieve with conventional light microscopy. Other ultrastructural details essential for diagnosis include podocyte foot process effacement, alterations in basement membrane thickness, presence of fibrils, and Fabry's intracellular inclusions. While transmission electron microscopy (TEM) provides the necessary resolution for these assessments, its high costs and time-consuming nature limit its routine use. Here, we report our experience with scanning electron microscopy (SEM) on paraffin sections from standard pathology specimens as a potential alternative.
Method
We analyzed paraffin sections from renal biopsies of 10 patients with membranous nephropathy. The paraffin sections were processed according to standard procedures (fixation, paraffin embedding), with a thickness of 3–4 µm. Sections were deparaffinized, stained with PASM (periodic acid Shiff + methenamine), mounted in aqueous mounting medium and imaged with 40x and 60x objectives. Sections were then unmounted, washed to remove glycerol, dehydrated in absolute alcohol, and air-dried. Finally, they were gold coated ("sputtering") and analyzed in a scanning electron microscope (Zeiss).
Results
For the interpretation of SEM images, correlative analysis has been used, imaging precisely the same region of the section using standard optical microscopy and SEM. Our analysis revealed characteristic subepithelial immune deposits beneath podocytes, accompanied by extensive foot process effacement. In areas of tissue fibrosis, we observed the distinctive periodic banding pattern of collagen fibers. The interpretation of the images required knowledge of fixation artifacts and careful recognition of cellular structures, particularly nuclei with their characteristic peripheral chromatin condensation.
Conclusion
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) proves to be a valuable tool for studying kidney diseases, providing nanometric-scale details not visible with optical microscopy. Our findings demonstrate that SEM can effectively identify key ultrastructural features critical for diagnosis, including immune deposits and podocyte alterations. Compared to transmission electron microscopy (TEM), SEM offers several practical advantages: simpler sample preparation, lower operational costs, and the ability to archive specimens for future review. These benefits, combined with the quality of ultrastructural visualization, suggest that SEM could serve as an efficient alternative to TEM in routine nephropathology practice.

title: #3131 Multi-center study of anti-nephrin antibodies in minimal change disease and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
authors: Clara Maria Cases Corona; Patricia Alonso; Beatriz Sanchez Alamo; Elena Martin Garcia; Laura Garcia-Bermejo; Gema Maria Fernandez Juarez
abstract:
Background and Aims
In recent years, progress has been made in studying the immunological mechanisms of primary podocytopathies, such as membranous nephropathy (MN). However, in minimal change disease (MCD) and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), these mechanisms are still not well understood.
Nephrin is a structural component of the filtration slit, and mutations in its gene are responsible for congenital Finnish nephrotic síndrome. Recently, the presence of anti-nephrin antibodies has been described in a cohort of patients with minimal change disease and in recurrent cases of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.
The aim of this study is to investigate the presence of anti-nephrin antibodies in the serum of patients with MCD and primary FSGS and determine whether they are found at a similar percentage to what has been reported in the literature.
Method
We evaluated serum samples from patients with MCD and FSGS in an active disease state from hospitals within the GLOSEN network, searching for circulating autoantibodies against nephrin. These were compared to a control group of healthy patients and another group with MN. The presence of these antibodies in serum was determined using ELISA techniques, and the measurement was normalized by protein levels.
Results
A total of 136 serum samples were studied: 56 from MCD patients, 33 from FSGS patients, 21 from MN patients, and 15 from controls.
The threshold for considering anti-nephrin autoantibody levels as positive was 3,872, the highest value observed in the control cohort without renal pathology (n = 15). Based on this threshold, the presence of anti-nephrin antibodies was confirmed in 18% of MCD samples and 12.1% of FSGS samples. However, in the MN group, they were found in one case (4.8%). It was also observed that the maximum levels of autoantibodies were higher in MCD and FSGS than in MN (MCD: 38,181; FSGS: 31,279; MN: 5,740).
No significant differences were found in biochemical parameters between patients with and without anti-nephrin antibodies.
Conclusion
We confirm the presence of anti-nephrin antibodies in MCD, although at a slightly lower percentage than previously reported in the literature (18% vs. 29%).
In FSGS, we also found the presence of anti-nephrin antibodies, but at a lower percentage than in minimal change disease (12% vs. 18%).

title: #1899 Cardiorenal outcomes and long-term kidney function decline in IgA nephropathy compared with chronic kidney disease patients with and without diabetes—FinnGen study
authors: Matti Sentürk; Tomas Visser; Laura Pyle; Phoom Narongkiatikhun; Petter Bjornstad; Tapio Hellman; Ye Ji Choi; David Cherney; Krzysztof Kiryluk; Teemu Niiranen; Patrik Finne; Daniel Gordin
abstract:
Background and Aims
Long-term cardiorenal outcomes and decline of kidney function in IgA nephropathy (IgAN) are incompletely characterized. We examined kidney and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) along with eGFR decline in patients with IgAN in the FinnGen study which covers approximately 10% of the Finnish population (n = 520210)
Method
We compared 775 IgAN patients with at least three eGFR measurements during a minimum of six months and baseline eGFR of 30 ml/min/1.73 m2 or higher to diabetes patients and CKD patients without diabetes as controls. IgAN, CKD, and diabetes patients were matched for eGFR, age and sex (with a ratio 1:4:4). The outcomes of interest were annual eGFR decline, kidney replacement therapy (KRT), and MACE identified by ICD-codes. Multivariable-adjusted Cox regression and mixed-effects models were used to compare the groups.
Results
The mean baseline eGFR was 67 ml/min/1.73m2 for IgAN, 68 ml/min/1.73 m2 for diabetes, and 69 ml/min/1.73 m2 for CKD patients. The maximum follow-up time was 9.5 years. Change in eGFR was −2.36 ml/min per year (95% CI −2.55 to −2.16) among IgAN, −2.39 (−2.44 to −2.34) in CKD and −0.53 (−0.59 to −0.48) in diabetes patients. Altogether, 37%, 23% and 4% of patients with IgAN, CKD and diabetes, respectively, started KRT during follow-up. IgAN patients had a higher risk of entering KRT than CKD patients (HR 1.80, 95% CI 1.57–2.07) and diabetes patients (HR 9.91, 8.00–12.27). However, the risk of MACE was lower in IgAN patients than in those with CKD (HR 0.64, 0.54–0.76), or diabetes (HR = 0.72, 0.60–0.85).
Conclusion
In this large register cohort, patients with IgAN demonstrated faster decline in eGFR compared to diabetes patients and exhibited greater risk for KRT compared to both CKD and diabetes patients. Notably, the risk for MACE was lower in IgAN compared to CKD and diabetes patients.

title: #1483 Anti-phospholipase A2 receptor antibody IgG4-to-IgG ratio predicts remission of PLA2R-associated primary membranous nephropathy
authors: Yuting Liu; Zhenling Deng; Zihan Wang; Danxia Zheng; Song Wang; Biao Huang; Yue Wang
abstract:
Background and Aims
PLA2R-associated primary membranous nephropathy (PA-PMN) was classified as IgG4-associated autoimmune disease in which anti-PLA2R antibody is predominantly IgG4 subclass. Our objective was to establish the anti-PLA2R antibody IgG4-to-IgG ratio (IgG4/G) as a novel indicator for forecasting remission in PA-PMN patients.
Method
143 patients with anti-PLA2R IgG level ≥14 RU/ml were biopsy-confirmed as PA-PMN. Serum samples collected at the time of renal biopsy were tested for anti-PLA2R IgG and anti-PLA2R IgG4 using time-resolved fluoroimmunoassay. The anti-PLA2R IgG4/G was calculated as the anti-PLA2R IgG4 level (ng/ml) divided by anti-PLA2R IgG level (RU/ml). Based on the cutoff value of 31.5 ng/RU determined by the maximum Youden Index from the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, patients were divided into low ratio and high ratio groups. Patients were also stratified into low-moderate risk and high risk groups according to 2021 KDIGO guideline. Cox proportional hazard regression analysis was conducted to assess the relationship between the anti-PLA2R IgG4/G and prognosis.
Results
Compared to the low anti-PLA2R IgG4/G group (n=30), patients in the high ratio group (n = 113) were significantly younger (52 [40–60] vs. 58 [51–61], p = 0.035), had a higher eGFR (102 [88–111] vs. 94 [72–100] ml/min/1.73 m2, p = 0.004) and obtained higher 6-month partial remission (64.6% vs. 30.0%, p = 0.001) and 1-year complete remission (38.3% vs. 7.7%, p = 0.003) despite the similarity in treatment options between the two groups. The higher remission persisted across both low-moderate risk and high risk subgroups stratified according to 2021 KDIGO guideline. In a multivariable Cox proportional hazard regression analysis adjusting for gender, age, smoking status, drinking status, haematuria, proteinuria, serum albumin and eGFR, a high anti-PLA2R IgG4/G was significantly associated with partial remission (HR [95%CI] = 2.093 [1.266–3.463], p = 0.004). The Kaplan-Meier curve demonstrated a significant higher probability of partial remission in the high ratio group. Our results indicate that anti-PLA2R IgG4/G may have additional abilities beyond urinary protein and anti-PLA2R antibodies in outcome evaluation of PA-PMN.
Conclusion
An elevated anti-PLA2R IgG4/G may be an independent predictor of remission in PA-PMN.

title: #1577 Insights into early crescentic glomerulonephritis via single-nuclei sequencing
authors: Jessica Alam; Sidrah Maryam; Marc Buse; Evangelia Ntounousi; Marcus Johannes Möller; Viktor Sterzer; Ina Verena Martin; Rafael Kramann; Tammo Ostendorf; Sikander Hayat; Eleni Stamellou
abstract:
Background and Aims
Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN) is a life-threatening disease characterized by a rapid decline in kidney function and the appearance of glomerular cellular crescents consisting of T cells, macrophages, and intrinsic glomerular cells. Activated parietal epithelial cells (aPECs) and podocytes play critical effector roles in the pathogenesis of crescentic glomerulonephritis. De novo CD44 expression on PECs serves as a hallmark of their activation, reflecting their proliferative and migratory capacity. This study aims to investigate the key pathways implicated in PEC activation and their interaction with other glomerular and tubular cells.
Method

title: #2190 The protective effects of a ketogenic diet in experimental glomerulonephritis are independent of the Hca2 receptor

abstract:
Background and Aims
Ketogenic diets (KD) have gained attraction across various medical disciplines for their therapeutic potential. Recently, we demonstrated the benefits of a therapeutic KD in an experimental murine model of immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis (GN). However, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we investigated signaling through the HCA2 receptor (HCAR2) and its ligand ß-hydroxybutyrate using the nephrotoxic serum nephritis (NTS) model to assess their contribution to the renoprotective effects of KD.
Method
To investigate Hcar2 expression in an experimental model of GN, we first re-analyzed available single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from Chung et al. [1] Based on these findings, NTS was induced in Hcar2-KO mice and littermate wild-type (WT) controls. Three days post-induction, mice were either switched to KD or maintained on SC. Short-term outcomes were assessed 21 days after NTS induction. For long-term outcome assessment, a subset of mice was transitioned back to SC after 18 days on KD for further five weeks. Spot urine samples were collected to measure the albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR). Total renal RNA was extracted for real-time PCR quantification of genes involved in extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling. Additionally, immunohistochemistry was performed to assess immune cell infiltration within the kidney.
Results
scRNA-seq analysis of the glomerular compartment revealed 12 distinct cell clusters, each defined by unique marker gene signatures. By further subclustering the immune cell population, we annotated nine discrete immune cell subtypes. Among these, Hcar2 expression emerged predominantly in neutrophils. Gene expression levels increased over the GN time course. Mice subjected to 21 days of NTS and maintained on KD showed significantly increased Hcar2 expression compared to those on SC, whereas no regulation of Hcar2 was observed without GN. Interestingly, an increase in neutrophil infiltration was observed in the kidneys of WT mice on KD. At day 21 after induction of NTS, WT mice fed KD exhibited a significant reduction in albuminuria and a significant downregulation of ECM genes, specifically Col3a1, Col1a1, and Acta2 as compared to WT mice fed with SC. Interestingly, Hcar2-KO mice also showed an improved phenotype when subjected to NTS and treated with KD comparable to the KD-response in WT mice. Additionally, there were no differences in ECM gene expression or neutrophil infiltration between WT and Hcar2-KO mice following KD treatment. Furthermore, kidney fibrosis was assessed at day 56, revealing that WT mice and Hcar2-KO on KD displayed a significant reduction in fibrosis compared to those maintained on SC.
Conclusion
Our recent work showed that KD significantly reduces albuminuria and downregulates ECM genes in WT mice with immune complex-mediated GN. These renoprotective effects were not mitigated in Hcar2-KO mice. By indicating that KD's protective mechanisms extend beyond HCAR2 signaling, this work potentially transforms the landscape of treatment for glomerular inflammatory diseases.

title: #3391 Pegcetacoplan treatment appears to halt disease progression in C3G and primary (idiopathic) IC-MPGN patients: results from the phase 3 VALIANT study
authors: Daniel P Gale; Andrew S Bomback; Christoph Licht; Carla M Nester; Matthew C Pickering; Giuseppe Remuzzi; Nicole Van De Kar; Zhongshen Wang; Johan Szamosi; Dima Decker; Lucia Quintana Gallardo; Fadi Fakhouri
abstract:
Background and Aims
C3 glomerulopathy (C3G) and primary (idiopathic) immune complex membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (IC-MPGN) are rare diseases where uncontrolled C3 activation results in excessive glomerular deposition of C3 breakdown products. Current treatments, such as mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) and corticosteroids, are used off-label, primarily targeting inflammatory changes rather than the underlying disease mechanism. These treatments are associated with adverse effects and lack robust clinical evidence of efficacy. As a result, up to 50% of patients progress to kidney failure within 10 years.
Pegcetacoplan (PEG) binds selectively to C3 and C3b to strongly block C3 activation by classical/lectin/alternative pathways, C3/C5 convertase activity and activation of downstream effectors. PEG targets the pathogenic process in C3G/primary IC-MPGN with the aim of stopping kidney damage.
In the Phase 3 VALIANT study (NCT05067127) in pts aged ≥12 years with native or post-transplant recurrent C3G/primary IC-MPGN, PEG led to glomerular C3 clearance in 71% of pts and achieved significant and sustained reduction in proteinuria across all pt subgroups with stabilization of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR).
Change in proteinuria has been proposed as a predictor of progression to kidney failure [1]. Registry data show that a ≥50% reduction in proteinuria over time correlated with a significantly lower risk of kidney failure in C3G pts [1]. Pts with urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) of <0.88 g/g 12 months after diagnosis have an 87% [2] reduction in kidney failure risk over 20 years.
The aim of this analysis was to investigate the indicators suggesting a potential long-term protective effect of PEG in preventing kidney failure.
Method
Pts were randomized 1:1 to receive PEG (subcutaneous infusion twice weekly) or placebo (PBO) for 26 weeks as add-on to their stable treatment regimen. The primary endpoint was the log-transformed ratio of UPCR at Week 26 vs baseline. Secondary endpoints included the proportion of pts achieving a reduction in C3c staining on kidney biopsy and change in eGFR from baseline vs PBO.
We present a pre-specified analysis on the effect of PEG on complement dysregulation and a post-hoc analysis on changes in proteinuria across the VALIANT population.
Results
Overall, 124 pts enrolled in VALIANT (63 PEG, 61 PBO). After PEG treatment, there was a rapid response in serum complement C3 and sC5b-9 from Week 4 that was maintained through 26 weeks. On treatment, C3 increased in all pts with a mean (standard deviation [SD]) change of 308.7 (94.7) mg/dL and soluble C5b-9 decreased with a mean (SD) reduction of 612.3 (614.7) ng/mL at Week 26 vs baseline, while no change was observed in PBO pts. Improvement in circulating complement biomarkers was associated with 25/35 (71%) PEG pts achieving 0 glomerular C3c staining at Week 26. Significant proteinuria reduction was observed as early as Week 4 in the PEG arm and remained stable up to Week 26 with no discernible change in UPCR over time in the PBO arm.
Pts were categorized by proteinuria range at baseline and Week 26, and shift in proteinuria was evaluated. In the PEG arm, pt distribution across proteinuria ranges shifted towards lower values with 50.8% (32/63) achieving UPCR <1 g/g, including 31.7% (20/63) <0.5 g/g, and a decrease in proportion of pts in all higher UPCR ranges >1.5 g/g. In contrast, in the PBO arm at Week 26, there was no increase in the number of pts in the low proteinuria ranges while the proportion of pts in higher ranges either stabilized or increased, as expected (Figure).
Conclusion
PEG treatment led to an increase in serum C3 levels, a reduction in serum sC5b-9 and clearance of glomerular C3 deposition. Further, PEG treatment resulted in a significant and clinically meaningful decrease in UPCR to <0.5 g/g. These findings demonstrate a profound disease-modifying effect, regardless of baseline proteinuria levels. Based on registry data, the observed reduction in proteinuria across the cohort at 26 weeks suggests PEG treatment is likely to significantly lower the long-term risk of patients progressing to kidney failure.

title: #3428 Phenotypic analysis of the oral and intestinal microbiome reveals microbial signatures for disease classification and potential drivers of autoantibody production in IgA nephropathy
authors: Robin Kempkens; Lennard Ostendorf; Adrian Schreiber; Sofia K Forslund; Toni Sempert; Lisa Budzinski; René Maier; Gi-Ung Kang; Shazia Malik; Hyun-Dong Chang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathy (IgAN) is caused by immune complex deposition in the kidneys and subsequent inflammation. Increased production of galactose-deficient IgA1 (gd-IgA1) and autoantibodies targeting exposed N-Acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) in the hinge region of gd-IgA1 leads to the formation of pathogenic immune complexes. Their glomerular deposition eventually leads to fibrosis and chronic inflammation. The microbiome is hypothesized to play a role in IgAN by influencing mucosal IgA production and triggering the production of carbohydrate-specific autoantibodies. Reliable biomarkers are needed for non-invasive diagnosis and in particular to identify patients at risk for progression. In this project we use a phenotypic-driven analysis of the oral and intestinal microbiome to stratify IgAN patients and identify microbiota influencing antibody production in patients to elucidate the underlying cause for the development and origin of IgAN.
Method
We apply multiparameter microbiota flow cytometry (mMFC) to analyze the phenotypic composition of the intestinal and oral microbiome of IgAN patients as well as to identify microbiota with distinct phenotypes potentially influencing the antibody production in IgAN patients. We use machine learning to analyze the phenotypic composition of a microbiome sample, integrating various phenotypic parameters—such as host immunoglobulin coating and bacterial surface carbohydrate structures—at the single-cell level. This generates a multi-parametric profile, enabling sample-wise comparison and disease classification. Additionally, mMFC combined with 16S rRNA sequencing enables the sorting and taxonomic identification of bacteria with distinct phenotypes that may influence antibody production in IgAN patients. Specifically, we investigate whether GalNAc-positive bacteria potentially induce gd-IgA1-specific autoantibody production and whether (gd)-IgA1-coated microbiota contribute to (gd)-IgA1 overproduction.
Results
Using mMFC and machine-learning, we determine a phenotypic signature in both the salivary (Bray Curtis, Adonis R2 = 0.2, P = 0.001) and fecal (R2 = 0.22, P = 0.001) microbiome, which discriminates IgAN patients from healthy controls. Moreover, IgAN patients stratify into two subgroups based on salivary microbiome composition (R2 = 0.26, P = 0.02). One group, characterized by an enrichment of Neisseria (log2 fold change (FC) = 2.3, P = 0.02), is associated with a more severe decline in kidney function (Creatinine 2.5 vs 1.3 mg/dl, P = 0.03; GFR 33 vs 66 ml/min, P = 0.03). The other group, exhibiting a microbial composition more similar to healthy controls, is enriched for Veillonella (FC = 1, P = 0.01) and Prevotella_7 (FC = 2, P = 0.03). To build a connection to the increased (gd)-IgA1 and autoantibody production in IgAN patients we perform fluorescence-activated cell sorting of (gd)-IgA1-coated and GalNAc-positive bacteria. This reveals that Akkermansia (FC = 3.55, P < 0.01) and Ruminococcus (FC = 1.63, P < 0.01) in fecal samples, as well as Rothia (FC = 1.5, P = 0.02) in salivary samples, are significantly enriched among GalNAc-positive bacteria in IgAN patients, but not in the respective bulk samples.
Conclusion
In this study we show that IgAN patients not only harbor a distinct microbial signature different from healthy subjects, but that the oral microbiome stratifies IgAN patients according to kidney function. The identification of bacteria enriched for GalNAc surface expression in patients suggests a potential link between these bacteria and the production of gd-IgA1-specific autoantibodies. The fact that these microbiota are not enriched in the respective bulk samples indicates the presence of a different, GalNAc-positive bacterial phenotype and highlights the strength of our phenotype-driven approach. Overall, these data suggest an intimate link between the salivary and fecal microbiota and IgAN.

title: #3041 A PK/PD analysis and population PK modeling of ravulizumab using data from the phase 2 trial in adults with IgA nephropathy (SANCTUARY)
authors: Narayan Cheruvu; Katherine Garlo; Andreas Kateifides; Joyce Chen; Kara Rice; Jonathan Monteleone
abstract:
Background and Aims
The phase 2 SANCTUARY study was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (NCT04564339; EudraCT No. 2020-001537-13) which evaluated treatment with the second-generation complement C5 inhibitor, ravulizumab, in adults with IgA nephropathy (IgAN). Rapid and clinically meaningful proteinuria reduction was observed. Change from baseline to week 26 in 24-hour urine protein was 41.9% with ravulizumab and 16.8% with placebo (30.1% treatment effect; P = 0.005) [1]. The aim of this analysis was to develop a population pharmacokinetic (PopPK) model to characterize the pharmacokinetics (PK) of ravulizumab in patients with IgAN and determine the impact of potential covariates (intrinsic and extrinsic factors) on exposure. Furthermore, the developed PopPK model was used to perform dose simulations to confirm dosing regimens for the phase 3 I CAN trial (NCT06291376; EU CT 2023-507851-31-00).
Method
The phase 2 trial enrolled 66 patients with biopsy-proven primary IgAN. Patients were randomized 2:1 to ravulizumab (n = 43) or placebo (n = 23) during the 26-week initial evaluation period. All patients received ravulizumab during the subsequent 24-week extension period. Patients received weight-based dosing, with loading dose on Day 1 followed by maintenance dosing on Day 15 and every 8 weeks thereafter. A previously developed PopPK model for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome was used as the base model for developing an IgAN-specific model. The NONMEM® software (ICON Development Solutions, Hanover, MD) was used to perform nonlinear mixed effects regression analyses to assess if potential covariates (demographics, laboratory assessments, and concomitant medications) identify PK parameter source and magnitude of inter-patient variability in drug exposure. Qualification of the PopPK model was performed by comparing observed and predicted concentration-time profiles using a Visual Predictive Check (VPC).
Results
In total, 926 blood samples were obtained from 61 of 66 patients with IgAN at baseline and in follow-up visits (female 44.3%, age ranged from 21 to 64 years, body weight ranged from 48 to 129 kg). Inhibition of terminal complement was assessed by free C5 levels and showed immediate, complete, and sustained C5 inhibition following dosing with ravulizumab: a precipitous drop in free C5 from ∼100 µg/mL at baseline to <0.5 µg/mL following the end of infusion after the first dose. For PK characterization, a two-compartment model with linear clearance (CL) described the serum ravulizumab concentration-time data. A covariate analysis identified body mass index (BMI), hemoglobin, and proteinuria as significant factors that helped explain inter-patient variability, thus reducing overall variability in the dose-concentration relationship among patients. The observed median, 5th, and 95th percentiles of ravulizumab concentrations were consistent with model-predicted values. For the final PopPK model, the ravulizumab systemic CL, intercompartmental CL (Q), apparent volume of distribution in the central compartment (Vc), and apparent volume of distribution in the peripheral compartment (Vp) were 0.00388 L/h, 0.0087 L/h, 3.37 L, and 1.44 L, respectively, given a typical 70-kg patient with a BMI of 25.5 kg/m2, hemoglobin of 134 g/dL, and proteinuria of 2.3 g/day. Relative standard error for CL, Q, Vc, and Vp were 2.37%, 31.9%, 2.11%, and 6.88%, respectively. The inter-patient variability of CL and Vc were 15.9% and 9.98%, respectively. The mean (standard deviation) terminal elimination half-life of ravulizumab was 38.1 (7.7) days.
Conclusion
A two-compartment linear PK model described the dose-concentration relationship in adults with IgAN. Our findings describe the PK/PD characteristics of ravulizumab and support the rationale for dose selection in the ongoing phase 3 trial in IgAN (NCT06291376, EU CT 2023-507851-31-00).

title: #3060 A phase 3, open-label, multicenter study of ravulizumab in pediatric patients with IgA nephropathy or IgA vasculitis-associated nephritis
authors: Andreas Kateifides; Katherine Garlo; Youssef Farag; Stephen Nolan; Huma Wasim; Christine Ulysse; Narayan Cheruvu
abstract:
Background and Aims
In immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN), immune complex formation and deposition leads to activation of the complement system. Complement activation leads to glomerular damage and is implicated in tubulointerstitial fibrosis [1]. IgA vasculitis-associated nephritis (IgAVN) is an autoimmune disease with similar pathogenesis to that of IgAN [2]. Currently, there are no approved treatments for children and adolescents with IgAN; treatment recommendations are largely informed by evidence generated in adults [3]. Similarly, there are no treatments specifically for IgAVN. Ravulizumab, a complement C5 inhibitor, is currently approved to treat atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (including pediatric), paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (including pediatric), generalized myasthenia gravis, and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. In a phase 2 trial in adults with IgAN, a rapid and clinically meaningful reduction in proteinuria was observed with ravulizumab [4]. A phase 3 trial of ravulizumab in adults with IgAN (I CAN study, NCT06291376; EU CT 2023-507851-31-00) is ongoing. Here, we describe the design of a phase 3 study of ravulizumab in pediatric patients with IgAN or IgAVN.
Method
This phase 3, open-label, single-arm, multicenter study evaluates the pharmacokinetics (PK), pharmacodynamics (PD), efficacy, and safety of ravulizumab in pediatric patients (N≈18) with IgAN (cohort 1, n = 12) or IgAVN (cohort 2, n ≈ 6). Patients with a diagnosis of IgAN or IgAVN based on kidney biopsy, an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m2 during screening, and a urine protein to creatinine ratio (UPCR) of ≥0.5 g/g from first morning void (FMV) during screening will be included (Table 1). The study consists of a 6-week screening, a 34-week primary evaluation, and a 72-week extension period. Patients will receive weight-based loading dose of ravulizumab intravenously on Day 1, followed by weight-based maintenance dose on Day 15, and every 8 weeks (if body weight ≥20 kg) or 4 weeks (if body weight <20 kg) thereafter up to Week 106 (Fig. 1). Formal sample size calculation and statistical hypothesis testing will not be performed due to the descriptive nature of the study.
Results
The primary endpoints (PK and PD) are ravulizumab maximum serum concentration, trough serum concentration, and change in serum free C5 concentration through Week 34. Secondary endpoints include change from baseline in UPCR up to Week 34, partial remission (≥50% reduction in UPCR from baseline and UPCR <3 g/g) at Week 34, and change from baseline in eGFR up to Week 106. Safety, tolerability, and immunogenicity will also be evaluated.
Conclusion
IgAN and IgAVN may lead to kidney failure and need for dialysis or transplant if left untreated. This study aims to characterize the PK, PD, efficacy, and safety of ravulizumab in pediatric patients with IgAN or IgAVN. Data from this study could inform future management of these conditions in the pediatric population.

title: #3020 Health-related quality of life in patients with lupus nephritis: a cross-sectional survey based study
authors: Zohreh Gholizadeh Ghozloujeh; Amir Abdipour; Sayna Norouzi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Lupus nephritis (LN) is a severe manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus, with significant implications for health-related quality of life (HRQoL). While studies on HRQoL in LN are increasing, many have relied on generic instruments that may not fully capture the nuanced physical, emotional, and psychosocial challenges faced by LN patients. Disease-specific tools offer a more comprehensive understanding by addressing aspects unique to LN.
This study aimed to evaluate HRQoL in LN patients using the LupusPRO questionnaire, a validated disease-specific tool, and identify demographic, clinical, and socioeconomic factors influencing HRQoL to inform patient-centered interventions.
Method
This cross-sectional study included 35 adult patients aged ≥18 years with biopsy-confirmed LN, recruited at Loma Linda University Medical Center. HRQoL was assessed using the LupusPRO questionnaire, which provides domain scores ranging from 0 to 100 (higher scores indicate better HRQoL). Demographic, clinical, and socioeconomic data were collected during routine clinic visits. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) at Loma Linda University Medical Center and funded by GlomCon. It represents an ongoing investigation assessing HRQoL in LN patients, with findings presented as an interim analysis.
Statistical analyses included descriptive statistics and Shapiro-Wilk tests for normality. Gender differences were analyzed using Mann-Whitney U or independent t-tests, while Kruskal-Wallis tests and one-way ANOVA assessed outcomes by employment and disease severity, with LSD post-hoc tests for significant findings. Multiple linear regression models evaluated predictors of HRQoL, including gender, disease activity, and employment status.
Results
As part of this interim analysis, data from 35 lupus nephritis patients were analyzed. The study population was predominantly female (n = 30, 85.7%), with a mean age of 40.9 years (SD = 12.9). Over half of the patients were unemployed (n = 19, 54.2%), while smaller proportions were employed full-time (n = 6, 17.1%) or part-time (n = 3, 8.5%), or were students (n = 5, 14.2%). Disease activity, assessed using SLEDAI, was predominantly mild-to-moderate (n = 27, 77.1%), with severe disease observed in 22.8% of the cohort (n = 8). Pain, fatigue, and body image were the most affected HRQoL domains, with mean scores of 56 (SD = 24), 61 (SD = 28), and 54 (SD = 26), respectively. In contrast, satisfaction with care remained consistently high (mean = 88, SD = 21).
Male patients reported significantly better fatigue scores (mean = 81, SD = 18) compared to female patients (mean = 57, SD = 29; p = 0.037). Full-time employed patients demonstrated significantly higher physical health (mean = 89, SD = 11; p = 0.009) and fatigue scores (mean = 96, SD = 6; p = 0.026) compared to other groups. Disabled patients, despite poor fatigue outcomes (mean = 38, SD = 18), exhibited high body image (mean = 85, SD = 15) and cognition scores (mean = 100). Patients with mild disease activity reported significantly better physical health scores (mean = 76, SD = 19) compared to those with severe disease (mean = 51, SD = 25; p = 0.038). A declining trend in HRQoL was observed across most domains with increasing disease severity.
Multivariate regression identified disease activity as a significant predictor of physical health (β = −0.474, p = 0.003) and fatigue (β = −0.417, p = 0.013). Full-time employment was strongly associated with better physical health (β = 0.488, p = 0.003) and fatigue scores (β = 0.490, p = 0.005), while being a student negatively predicted coping scores (β = −0.555, p = 0.005).
Conclusion
Lupus nephritis significantly impairs HRQoL, with pain, fatigue, and body image identified as the most affected domains. Employment status and disease activity were key predictors, with full-time employment linked to better HRQoL and higher disease activity associated with poorer outcomes. These findings highlight the need for interventions addressing the physical and psychosocial challenges of LN to improve patient outcomes.

title: #2450 Predictors of disease activity in ANCA-associated vasculitis subtypes: a statistical and predictive analysis
authors: Sonja Golubović; Vladimir Veselinov; Siniša Živković; Milica Popović; Tatjana Ilić; Nikola Glogonjac; Violeta Knežević
abstract:
Background and Aims
ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) is a systemic autoimmune condition that frequently leads to kidney impairment and systemic inflammation. This study aimed to evaluate and compare inflammatory markers, renal function, and prognostic outcomes in patients with anti-MPO and anti-PR3 AAV.
Method
Seventy-three AAV patients were analyzed, focusing on age, hematological parameters, renal function, inflammatory markers, and disease activity scores (BVAS and FFS). Predictive regression models were applied to assess kidney function (eGFR and creatinine) at six months, and T-tests and correlation analyses were used to compare group differences.
Results
The regression models demonstrated that baseline eGFR and creatinine were the strongest predictors of kidney function at 6 months (P < 0.001). The model explained 91.9% of the variability in eGFR for anti-PR3 patients and 88.7% for anti-MPO patients, when using these parameters with age and hemoglobin. Older age (t = 3.28, P < 0.05) and lower hemoglobin were associated with worse kidney outcomes. Baseline creatinine was also a significant predictor (P < 0.001).Group comparisons revealed significant differences in inflammation markers and disease activity. CRP levels were higher in anti-PR3 patients (52.82 vs. 32.7 mg/L, P = 0.09), suggesting more systemic inflammation. Anti-PR3 patients also had a higher BVAS (16.89 vs. 14.97, P = 0.06), indicating greater disease severity. Platelet counts were higher in the anti-PR3 group (351.31 vs. 317.56), although this difference was not statistically significant.Age was significantly different between groups, with anti-MPO patients being older on average (62.85 vs. 54.54 years, P < 0.05). Despite these differences, kidney function remained comparable between the groups. Baseline creatinine levels were elevated in both anti-MPO and anti-PR3 patients (290.21 vs. 366.59 µmol/L), and eGFR was similarly reduced (37.47 vs. 32.46 mL/min). Although both groups had impaired kidney function, the Five-Factor Score (FFS) was higher in the anti-PR3 group, reflecting a worse prognosis. Predictive modeling identified C3 (33.4%), SE (15.8%), and albumin (13.5%) as the strongest predictors of BVAS. The model explained 62% of the variance in BVAS (R² = 0.62).
Conclusion
Patients with anti-PR3 AAV exhibit more pronounced inflammation and disease severity than those with anti-MPO AAV, despite similar degrees of renal dysfunction. C3, SE, and albumin levels are key predictors of disease activity in AAV. These findings highlight the importance of individualized therapeutic approaches informed by predictive modeling.

title: #2130 Evaluation of objective nutritional indexes as predictors of renal progression in IgA nephropathy patients
authors: Yan Yang; Bixia Yang; Min Yang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) is a clinical and pathological syndrome with heterogenous manifestation and progression. The prognostic nutritional index (PNI) and the controlling nutritional status (CONUT) score, indicators of nutritional status and systemic inflammation, are associated with poor prognosis in dialysis patients. This study was aimed to investigate the predictive value of the objective nutritional indexes (PNI and CONUT) for renal progression in IgAN patients.
Method
A multicenter retrospective study was conducted in biopsy-proven IgAN patients. Baseline characteristics were obtained within 1 week before renal biopsy. The renal composite endpoint was defined as eGFR decline greater than 50%, doubling of baseline serum creatinine, or the occurrence of end stage renal disease (ESRD). The receiver operating characteristic curve analysis was conducted to determine the optimal cut-off value of PNI and CONUT. The Kaplan-Meier curve estimated the cumulative renal-survival rate. Univariate and multivariate Cox regression models were preformed to investigate the association between objective nutritional indexes and renal outcomes.
Results
A total of 659 IgAN patients participated in this study. During a median follow-up period of 45 months, 68 patients (10.32%) achieved the composite endpoint. The Kaplan-Meier curve revealed that renal-survival rate was significantly higher in high PNI group (PNI > 46.5; P < 0.001) and low CONUT group (CONUT ≤2; P < 0.001). Even after adjustment of traditional risk factors, including sex, age, mean arterial pressure, hemoglobin, uric acid, eGFR, tyriglycerides, 24-hour urinary protein, E score, T score, and treatment with ACEI/ARB, low PNI [hazard ration (HR) = 2.337, 95% confidence intervals (CI) = 1.123–4.863, P = 0.023] and high CONUT (HR = 2.050, 95% CI = 1.041–4.034, P = 0.038) remained independent risk factors for poor renal outcomes.
Conclusion
This study suggested that low PNI and high CONUT were significantly and independently correlated with poor prognosis in IgAN patients. The PNI and CONUT are inexpensive and straightforward indicators to help clinicians improve IgAN management.

title: #2503 Clinical significance of punctate podocyte IgG staining in primary diffuse podocytopathy
authors: Qiyu Wang; Ayman Aljurdi; Claire Avillach; Anushya Jeyabalan; Nicole Bowman; Andy Watts; Astrid Weins
abstract:
Background and Aims
The recent discovery of anti-nephrin autoantibody has established the role of antibody-mediated pathogenesis in diffuse podocytopathy. Punctate podocyte IgG colocalizing with nephrin has been identified as the tissue marker for anti-nephrin mediated injury; however, its clinical significance remains unclear. We aim to evaluate the association between podocyte IgG staining on kidney biopsy and corticosteroid responsiveness and risk of relapse in adult diffuse podocytopathy.
Method
Retrospective cohort study including adult patients with new biopsy diagnosis of minimal change disease or primary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) at Mass General Brigham from 2014 to 2023. Two pathologists independently reviewed the immunofluorescence images and adjudicated the cases into +podocyte IgG vs. -podocyte IgG if not already interpreted on the biopsy report. Cases with non-diffuse podocyte foot process effacement, advanced diabetic nephropathy and <6 months of follow-up were excluded. Remission is defined as attainment of at least partial remission (≥50% reduction of proteinuria and UPCR ≤ 3.5 g/g). Acute kidney injury (AKI) is defined as ≥1.5-fold increase in creatinine from baseline. Continuous and categorical data were compared using Wilcoxon rank-sum and Fisher's exact test, respectively. Kaplan-Meier curves and multivariate Cox regression models were used to assess association between podocyte IgG staining and co-primary outcomes (time-to-remission, time-to-relapse). Logistic regression was used to identify risk factors for corticosteroid resistance.
Results
61 patients were included. Median age was 61 (IQR 46–70) years, 64% (39/61) were male, and 75% (46/61) were white. 59% (36/61) had +podocyte IgG. 34% (21/61) presented with AKI, of which 33% (7/21) required temporary dialysis. +podocyte IgG was associated with white race, lower serum albumin at diagnosis, and lower rate of FSGS on biopsy (Table 1). Earlier time-to-remission was observed in patients with +podocyte IgG compared to -podocyte IgG (median time-to-remission 47 vs. 123 days, P = 0.011, log-rank test, Figure 1A). In a multivariate Cox regression model, +podocyte IgG and upfront rituximab therapy were both associated with earlier time-to-remission (HR 3.3, CI 1.62–6.84; HR 2.56, CI 1.27–5.20, respectively; Table 2). There was a trend towards earlier relapse in patients with +podocyte IgG though not statistically significant (P = 0.09, log rank test, Figure 1B). 15% (9/61) patients did not respond to initial course of corticosteroids. -podocyte IgG was associated with higher odds of corticosteroid resistance (OR 6.7, CI 1.8–37.8, P = 0.032). 4 patients who were corticosteroid-resistant developed end stage kidney disease at last follow-up (range 94–1806 days).
Conclusion
In adult patients with diffuse podocytopathy, presence of punctate podocyte IgG on biopsy at diagnosis is associated with earlier response to immunosuppression. Lack of podocyte IgG staining is associated with increased risk of corticosteroid resistance.

title: #2772 Long-term safety and efficacy of the combination of belimumab and rituximab in the treatment of severe and refractory SLE: a preliminary report
authors: Mieke van Schaik; Eline Arends; Marjolein Wetzels; Tineke Kraaij; Stephanie Verbruggen; Sandra van der Kooij; S W A Kamerling; Tom Huizinga; Robbert Goekoop; Cees van Kooten; Ton Rabelink; Y K Onno Teng
abstract:
Background and Aims
Combination therapy with rituximab and belimumab is a novel treatment strategy for severe systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and lupus nephritis (LN). Phase 2 studies have shown promising results, although long-term data are currently lacking. To address this, we analyzed outcomes of patients with severe treatment-refractory SLE who previously participated in the phase 2 Synbiose study, with a particular focus on immunological parameters.
Method
Eight patients continued belimumab treatment beyond the two-year duration of the original trial. We conducted a descriptive study to evaluate the course of treatment and immunological parameters over an extended follow-up. Our analyses include blood cell counts, immunoglobulins, autoantibodies, complement markers, and clinical disease activity parameters. Additionally, we examined long-term effects on the B cell compartment employing high-sensitivity flow cytometry.

title: #451 The effects of early or late empagliflozin, liraglutide & combined therapy on the a-Klotho/autophagy pathway in renal and pancreatic-ß cells in diabetic db/db mice model
authors: Farid Nakhoul; Offir Ertracht; Wisal Swaed; Atar Shaul
abstract:
Background and Aims
Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) can lead to kidney and pancreatic cells damage, causing diabetic nephropathy (DN) and pancreatic failure, receptively. The sodium-glucose transporter type 2 inhibitors, like Empagliflozin (EMPA) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, like Liraglutide (LIRA) are new T2DM medications which prevent diabetes progression and improve renal and pancreas function. However, their exact mechanisms of action are not fully understood. It is known that α-Klotho and autophagy proteins play a key role in tubule-glomerular injury, have anti-oxidative, and anti-inflammatory effects.
We hypothesized that EMPA, LIRA and their combination will attenuate T2DM progression, and preserve renal and pancreatic structure and function, by affecting the α-Klotho and autophagy pathway.
Method
We used BKS.Cg-Dock7m +/+Leprdb/J (db/db) leptin-deficiency mutated T2DM mouse model. These mice exhibit T2DM within 4–5 weeks post-partum, characterized with blood glucose level >300 mg/dL, and considerable obesity (>35 gr). EMPA (30 mg/kg/day) was administered through drinking water, while LIRA (0.2 µg/gr/day) was administered subcutaneously. Blood glucose was measured weekly by stick, and 24 hrs urine collection took place three times along the experiment for urine albumin and electrolytes excretion, and urine glucose and creatinine. Mice were treated either at 7-weeks-old or 16-weeks-old mice for early phase or late phase, respectively, for four weeks at each phase, followed by sacrifice and organ harvesting. At sacrifice renal and pancreas samples were collected for histological and biochemical analyses.
Results
The preliminary results show that only EMPA+LIRA combination attenuated mice weight gain, while both EMPA and EMPA+LIRA combination reduced blood glucose levels. At the early phase, EMPA and the EMPA+LIRA combination, increased water intake, and reduced urine production. LIRA alone, attenuated water intake, decreased urinary glucose level, but did not affect urine production or urine protein level. At the Late phase, all treatments increased water intake, and reduced urine glucose level, but only the EMPA+LIRA attenuated urine production, and none affected protein urine level. All treatments moderated glucose tolerance test results.
2. Histological T2DM pancreas samples display characteristic pathological changes, including altered islets’ structure and possible signs of inflammation.
3. α-Klotho, LC3 and ATG5 immunofluorescence staining of renal tissue show reduced expression compared to the healthy specimens. LIRA prevented α-Klotho and LC3 expression reduction, while EMPA preserved ATG5 expression, in T2DM mice kidneys.
Conclusion
There are different effects for EMPA, LIRA and their combination when given at different time points (early phase vs. late phase). At early phase, EMPA and EMPA+LIRA combination significantly reduces T2DM mice blood glucose level and proteinuria (Microalbuminuria). At late phase all treatments affected urinary glucose level. EMPA, LIRA and their combination upregulate α-Klotho, LC3 and ATG5 proteins renal expression. These treatments alone or in combination, may delay the onset of hyperglycaemia and T2DM, preserve renal structure, and function, thus may potentially use to prevent T2DM complications such as DN, probably through their effect on both α-Klotho and autophagy pathway.

title: #1928 Anti-drug antibodies are common in membranous nephropathy and affect response to rituximab: a multicenter study
authors: Micaela Anna Casiraghi; Maxime Teisseyre; Matteo Accinno; Cecilia Finocchi; Vincent L M Esnault; Marion Cremoni; Vesna Brglez; Leonardo Caroti; Calogero Cirami; Alessandra Vultaggio; Barbara Seitz-Polski; Marco Allinovi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Primary membranous nephropathy (pMN) is an autoimmune glomerular disease characterized by immune system dysregulation leading to podocyte damage through auto-antibodies and complement activation.
According to KDIGO guidelines, rituximab is recommended as a first-line immunosuppressive therapy for pMN with proven efficacy and safety. However, the use of therapeutic monoclonal antibodies (such as rituximab) can lead to the formation of anti-drug antibodies (ADA) able to interfere with the therapeutic efficacy. As a matter of fact, around one third of patients with pMN treated with rituximab develop ADA.
Understanding the correlation between ADA and clinical outcome, as well as evaluating the clinical relevance of ADA titer and the most appropriate timing of detection would be pivotal in patients with pMN treated with rituximab.
Method
We included 74 patients with pMN treated with rituximab at Careggi University Hospital, Florence, Italy and at Nice University Hospital, France in a retrospective international multicenter study. Rituximab was administered according to KDIGO guidelines (1000 mg x 2, two weeks apart or 375 mg/m2, one week apart) and ADA were detected by using a commercially available ELISA kit (cut-off: 5 ng/mL). Evaluation of clinical and laboratory data, including ADA, were performed at baseline and every three months after rituximab administration, for at least 12 months.
Results
In our cohort, 35 out of 74 (47%) patients developed ADA. Antibodies were detected after a median of nine months (IQR, 6-12) following rituximab administration. Monitoring at month-9, month-12 and prior to rituximab re-administration, identified 88% of patients with ADA.
ADA positivity increased progressively with exposure to subsequent rituximab courses, as showed in Fig. 1.
Remission rate at 6 and 12 months after rituximab administration was significantly lower in patients with ADA (31% vs 56%, P = 0.03 and 54% vs 87%, P = 0.0017, respectively).
ADA were associated with a significantly higher rate of relapse (63% vs 29%, P = 0.036), and relapse occurred earlier in patients with ADA (mean 22 months vs mean 32 months, P = 0.01).
Patients who developed ADA had a significantly higher anti-PLA2R1 antibody titer than ADA negative patients (mean 167 vs 70.5 RU/mL, P = 0.029). Unlike anti-PLA2R1 antibody titer, which correlates with patient prognosis, ADA titer was not associated with clinical outcome.
Conclusion
In accordance with literature data, our study confirmed that: (1) up to 50% of patients with pMN treated with rituximab develop ADA; (2) ADA are associated with a higher relapse rate in patients with pMN.
Furthermore, for the first time we demonstrated that (3) ADA are significantly associated with a reduced remission rate in patients with pMN, making these antibodies one of the most important prognostic factors; (4) standardized monitoring of ADA at both 9th- and 12th-month following rituximab infusion, in addition to the monitoring of ADA prior to rituximab re-administration, would allow the identification of about 90% of ADA positive patients. In this subgroup of patients, alternative therapies with obinutuzumab or ofatumumab should be considered.

title: #1765 Plasma endothelial biomarkers in relation to albuminuria, kidney function and CKD progression in IgA nephropathy
authors: Karin Bergen; Sigrid Gertrud Gisela Lundberg
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is the most common primary glomerulonephritis in the world and a significant proportion of patients develop kidney failure within 30 years. Circulating undergalactosylated IgA, a key driver of IgAN, has been shown to induce endothelial damage. Glomerular endothelial activation is believed to contribute to complement activation and potentially contribute to disease progression. However, the clinical utility of plasma endothelial biomarkers in IgAN is unclear and no study has analyzed the relationship between endothelial biomarkers and loss of kidney function over time in IgAN. We aimed to study the association between plasma endothelial biomarkers at time of kidney biopsy and CKD progression over time, assessed using eGFR slope. We also wanted to compare biomarker levels between patients with IgAN, healthy controls, and disease controls at baseline.
Method
We conducted a single-center prospective cohort study including 44 patients with IgAN and 19 disease controls, 11 membranous nephropathy (MN) and 8 hypertensive nephropathy (HN), recruited as part of BIONEF-DS, a biomarker study which has consecutively recruited patients undergoing a kidney biopsy at Danderyd Hospital, Stockholm, Sweden, since 2019. We also included 40 age-matched healthy controls (HC). Plasma levels of VCAM-1, ICAM-1, E-selectin, VE-cadherin, and Syndecan 1 were measured at time of biopsy using Meso Scale® (Meso Scale Diagnostics, Maryland, USA), a highly sensitive multi-array assay based on electrochemiluminescence. First, we compared plasma biomarker levels between the four groups and their relation to albuminuria, eGFR and clinical parameters at baseline using Spearman's Rank Order correlation and Kruskal Wallis ANOVA. Secondly, we used linear regression to analyze the association between biomarker levels and eGFR slope amongst patients with IgAN.
Results
Baseline characteristics of the patients and controls are shown in Table 1. There was no significant difference in age between IgAN patients and HC, whereas patients with IgAN were significantly younger than disease controls (P < 0.0001). Blood pressure was similar in all groups. Kidney function and albuminuria did not differ between IgAN and disease controls, whereas HC had significantly better-preserved kidney function (P < 0.0001) and no albuminuria. Patients with IgAN had significantly higher levels of ICAM-1, VCAM-1, Syndecan-1 and Thrombomodulin compared to HC (P = 0.02 for ICAM-1; P < 0.001 for others) but similar levels to disease controls. Amongst patients with IgAN, there were weak positive correlations between U-ACR and E-selectin, VCAM-1 and Syndecan-1 (P < 0.05 for all). There were significant negative associations between all biomarkers and eGFR at baseline (P < 0.05 for all). ICAM-1 levels were significantly lower amongst IgAN patients treated with RAASi (P < 0.01). We found no significant association to MEST-C score. Only three patients were on cortisone at baseline. For the longitudinal part of the study, median follow-up was 3.3 years (2.1–4.1) and median eGFR slope was −1.4 mL/min/1.73 m2/year (−4.1–0.9). There was a significant positive association between E-selectin and eGFR slope (P < 0.05) (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
We found a significant elevation of key endothelial and glycocalyx biomarkers amongst patients with IgAN compared to healthy controls, with the highest levels found amongst patients with high-grade albuminuria and decreased kidney function. Importantly, patients with IgAN had similar levels of plasma endothelial biomarkers as patients with HN and MN, despite the disease controls being significantly older and with more cardiovascular comorbidities. IgAN patients with the highest levels of E-selectin at baseline improved their kidney function over time, likely as an effect of treatment. Future studies should assess the association between baseline endothelial biomarkers and CKD progression in a larger and more ethnically diverse patient population. It would also be of interest to conduct serial biomarker measurements to study the effect of different therapies on endothelial biomarkers in IgAN.

title: #745 Sex differences across treatment response to corticosteroids and kidney outcomes in IgA nephropathy: insights from the TESTING trial
authors: Dana Kim; Mark Woodward; Jicheng Lv; Michelle Hladunewich; Vivekanand Jha; Lai Seong Hooi; Helen Monaghan; Vlado Perkovic; Hong Zhang; Muh Geot Wong
abstract:
Background and Aims
The Therapeutic Effects of Steroids in IgA Nephropathy Global (TESTING) study found that, compared to supportive care, 6–9 months of methylprednisolone reduced the risk of major kidney events in people with IgAN at high risk of disease progression but resulted in a greater number of serious adverse events (SAEs). As new treatments for Immunoglobulin A Nephropathy (IgAN) emerge, it is crucial to identify which patient populations are likely to receive treatment benefit and which are more at risk of disease progression. Few studies have examined the impact of sex on kidney outcomes and treatment response in IgAN, with limited and conflicting data. This post-hoc analysis of the TESTING study aims to (1) evaluate the effect of sex on treatment response to corticosteroids and (2) explore sex differences in the risk of kidney and safety outcomes in IgAN.
Method
Participants with IgAN and proteinuria >1 g/day, despite 3 months of maximal renin-angiotensin system blockade, were randomised to full- or reduced-dose oral methylprednisolone (0.6–0.8 mg/kg/day or 0.4 mg/kg/day) versus (vs.) placebo. The mean follow-up period was 4.2 years. Cox proportional hazards models were used to analyse the effects of methylprednisolone on kidney outcomes in males compared to females. The primary outcome was a composite of 40% decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), kidney failure or death due to kidney disease. Analyses were also conducted to assess the interaction between sex and the treatment effect of methylprednisolone, compared to placebo, on the relative change in proteinuria from baseline at 12 months and the absolute difference in total eGFR slope over 2 years. The number of females and males who experienced at least one serious adverse event (SAE) and adverse event of special interest in each treatment arm was reported to assess safety outcomes by sex. To investigate the association between sex and kidney outcomes, Cox models, adjusted for randomised treatment, were used to estimate the risk of kidney outcomes in males vs. females. The absolute sex difference in total eGFR slope over 2 years, adjusted for treatment, was also estimated for both sexes using a two-slope, mixed-effects, linear spline model with a knot at month 3.
Results
There were 503 (39% female) participants in the TESTING study. Males were younger, more likely to have hypertension or a history of smoking, had a greater systolic blood pressure and more tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis on kidney biopsy at baseline, compared to females. Methylprednisolone lowered the risk of the composite primary outcome, compared to placebo, in both males (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.74) and females (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.09), with no heterogeneity (P-interaction = 0.47). Similarly, methylprednisolone reduced proteinuria from baseline at 12 months compared to placebo, and slowed the rate of total eGFR decline, regardless of sex (P-interaction = 0.28 and 0.81, respectively). In the methylprednisolone vs. placebo arms, the number of males who experienced at least one SAE was 20 (13%) vs. 4 (3%), whilst for females, it was 8 (8%) vs. 3 (3%). All 4 fatal SAEs occurred in male participants receiving methylprednisolone.
Taking the two trial arms together, males had a greater risk of the primary outcome compared to females (HR 1.42, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.96, P = 0.03), with no heterogeneity observed across all pre-specified baseline characteristic subgroups. The difference in total eGFR slope over two years in males compared to females was 3.13 mL/min/1.73 m2/year (95% CI 0.92 to 5.34, P = 0.006).
Conclusion
A 6–9-month course of methylprednisolone improves kidney outcomes in high-risk IgAN, regardless of sex. However, a higher proportion of males experienced SAEs with methylprednisolone therapy compared to females. Overall, males also experienced poorer kidney outcomes compared to females. Achieving adequate female and male recruitment for clinical trials in IgAN and assessing the impact of sex on both treatment response and kidney outcomes, is critical in future prospective studies.

title: #2645 Serum inflammatory biomarkers in IgA nephropathy: insights from a Swedish cohort with 25 years of follow-up
authors: Jacqueline Haller; Inga Soveri; Mazdak Sanaei Nurmi; Katja Gabrysch; Niclas Eriksson; Anders Larsson; Bengt Fellström; Sigrid Gertrud Gisela Lundberg
abstract:
Background and Aims
Immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) and IgA vasculitis with nephritis (IgAVN) are inflammatory diseases that frequently progress to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). Biomarkers for early detection and monitoring of disease progression or interventions are needed. Inflammation-related proteins, including cytokines and chemokines, play a crucial role in the initiation and maintenance of kidney inflammation and have been implicated in IgAN development. We aimed to detect potential new serum biomarkers for the prediction of disease progression and treatment response in IgAN and IgAVN.
Method
A Swedish single center cohort with biopsy-proven IgAN or IgAVN was studied. Serum samples were collected at the time of kidney biopsy and during the follow-up period (1994–2019), with sample collection completed by 2015. The median clinical follow-up time was 10.7 years, and the median eGFR slope was −1.6 mL/min per year. Samples were analyzed using the OLINK Proximity Extension Assay (PEA) Inflammation panel, a multiplex immunoassay technology designed to detect and quantify 96 inflammation-related proteins. title: #1875 Physician-directed nudge for glycemic and lipid management in older patients with glomerulonephritis treated with immunosuppressants
authors: Jovan Sim; Felicia Loo; Lydia Lim; Hui Zhuan Tan; Tung Lin Lee; Irene Mok; Jason Choo; Chieh Suai Tan; Cynthia Lim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Glomerulonephritis and its treatment may be associated with cardiometabolic disease. Hence, optimizing glycemic and lipid control is important to reduce adverse health outcomes. We implemented an electronic medical records (EMR)-based physician prompt to nudge nephrologists on guideline-based glycemic and lipid optimization. We aimed to evaluate the impact of the prompt on glycemic and lipid management among older adults with glomerulonephritis receiving immunosuppressive therapy.
Method
This was a single-center, single-arm, implementation study with a pre-post design. We included adults ≥40 years old with active glomerulonephritis treated with immunosuppressants who had received the physician prompt as part of the ConFIRM (Cardiovascular, Infection and Frailty Risk in Older Adults with Immune-Mediated Renal Disease treated with Immunosuppressant: Recognition, Intervention and Self-Management) program. Demographic and clinical data at 6-monthly intervals were obtained from the EMR. We compared the prevalence of glycemic and lipid evaluation during follow-up visits before and after the intervention using mixed effects logistic regression models to account for variability across patients and repeated measures over time. The models adjusted for age, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR), and treatment with prednisolone and calcineurin inhibitor.
Results
Among 137 patients with 856 visits, we compared 478 visits between Jan 2021 and June 2024 before intervention, and 378 visits between July 2022 and December 2024 after intervention. The median age at the visits was 55 (interquartile range: 48, 68) years and 58 (48, 69) years in the pre- and post-intervention groups, respectively. Table 1 shows that age, kidney function and degree of proteinuria were similar in the two groups.
Glycemic evaluation was 51.8% pre-intervention and 70.0% post-intervention (unadjusted odds ratio [OR] 2.56, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.66–3.07). Fasting glucose was evaluated in 22.2% pre-intervention and 44.6% post-intervention, while HbA1c was evaluated in 44.7% pre-intervention and 52.5% post-intervention. Table 2 shows that glycemic evaluation was significantly associated with the intervention (adjusted OR 2.10, 95% CI: 1.52–2.90, P < 0.001), lower eGFR (adjusted OR 0.99 per 1 mL/min/1.73 m² increase, 95% CI: 0.98–0.998, P = 0.02) and prednisolone use (adjusted OR 1.65, 95% CI: 1.11–2.45, P = 0.01).
Lipid evaluation was 43.6% pre-intervention and 43.2% post-intervention. Lipid evaluation was not associated with the intervention (adjusted OR 0.91, 95% CI: 0.67–1.23, P = 0.55), nor with age, kidney function, proteinuria or use of prednisolone or calcineurin inhibitor.
Conclusion
A physician-directed nudge significantly increased glycemic evaluation but not lipid evaluation in older patients with glomerulonephritis treated with immunosuppressants.

title: #3004 Repurposing disulfiram to target neutrophil extracellular traps in experimental ANCA associated vasculitits
authors: Kim Maree O'sullivan; Angela Vu; Lu Lu; Timothy Gottschalk; Kathryn Lawlor
abstract:
Background and Aims
Myeloperoxidase anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis (MPO-AAV) is characterized by small blood vessel inflammation in the kidney, leading to glomerulonephritis (GN). This disorder is driven by MPO autoimmunity and the pro-inflammatory effects of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) formed via a distinct cell death program called NETosis. Although NETosis is critical to disease progression, no current therapies specifically target it, and standard-of-care treatments are associated with severe infection risks, the leading cause of mortality in AAV patients. Gasdermin D (GSDMD), a key mediator of NETosis, is a promising therapeutic target. We aimed to test the therapeutic potential of disulfiram (DSL) a FDA approved drug for alcohol addiction to inhibit GSDMD and subsequent NET formation both in vitro and in an experimental model of MPO-AAV.
Method
In this study, we evaluated the therapeutic potential of disulfiram (DSL) which inhibits GSDMD to prevent NET formation using mouse and human neutrophils for in vitro assays and confocal imaging. A well published in vivo 20-day murine experimental model that replicates human disease in terms of histological damage to the kidney and systemic autoimmunity to MPO was utilised to test DSL in vivo. DSL was given daily after establishment of autoimmunity to MPO and triggering of GN with a sub-nephritic dose of anti GBM Ig. Draining lymph nodes, spleen, blood, urine and kidneys were collected to assess reductions in inflammation and clinically relevant endpoints (renal histology, proteinuria and ANCA titre.)
Results
In vitro, DSL significantly reduced NET formation regardless of the inducing stimuli (LPS, TNFα, ionomycin, or C5a) in both mouse and human neutrophils. This indicated the role of GSDMD in different biochemical pathways both canonical and non-canonical which result in NETosis. In vivo, DSL-treated mice demonstrated marked reductions in kidney injury (segmental necrosis), glomerular neutrophil infiltration, macrophages, and CD4+ T cells when compared to the vehicle control group (P < 0.05). Confocal imaging of NETs revealed a significant reduction in NETs within kidney glomeruli of the DSL group compared to vehicle controls (P < 0.05). DSL effectively reduced MPO specific IL17A and IFNɣ producing cells from the draining lymph nodes and spleens but had no effect on the production of MPO-ANCA. DSL effectively disrupted downstream inflammation by preventing NET formation, thereby reducing MPO deposition as an autoantigen and via direct injury to surrounding epithelial and endothelial cells.
Conclusion
These findings highlight DSL's ability to selectively modulate innate immune pathways, mitigate glomerular injury, and prevent glomerulonephritis in MPO-AAV. Collectively, this study underscores the therapeutic potential of DSL as a novel steroid-sparing option for MPO-AAV by disrupting critical immunopathological mechanisms and providing a rationale for further investigation into its clinical application.

title: #1974 Obinutuzumab alone may be an effective option for the initial therapy of adult minimal change disease
authors: Qiong Bai; Danxia Zheng
abstract:
Background and Aims
Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody (such as rituximab) has proven effective and safe in pediatric and adult minimal change disease (MCD) in recent studies. Obinutuzumab, a novel type II humanized anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, has demonstrated superior efficacy in inducing faster and more sustained B-cell depletion compared to equivalent doses of rituximab. Whether obinutuzumab alone could be used as initial therapy of MCD remains uncertain. We aimed to explore the efficacy and safety of obinutuzumab alone as the initial treatment for adult MCD patients.
Method
A retrospective study was conducted at Peking University Third Hospital between January 1, 2020 and December 31, 2024, and included adult patients with MCD. MCD was diagnosed through kidney biopsy. Exclusion criteria encompassed secondary nephrotic syndrome, malignancy, a history of severe adverse events during rituximab treatment, serologic evidence of active hepatitis B infection, known history of human immunodeficiency virus infection, and active cytomegalovirus infection. The patients subsequently received either obinutuzumab or glucocorticoids (GC). The primary endpoint was treatment response, which was defined as complete remission (CR) of nephrotic syndrome. The secondary measures included infection and relapse.
Results
Among the 37 participants, 15 received obinutuzumab and 22 received GC. The median age was 49.0 years (IQR, 26.5–66.5), and the median duration of MCD was 20.0 days (IQR, 13.0–60.0). The median level of proteinuria was 8.7 g/day (IQR, 5.8–12.0), the median serum albumin level was 19.6 g/l (IQR, 17.7–23.4), and the median serum creatinine level was 73.0 µmol/L (IQR, 64.0–117.5). The mean eGFR was 84.3 ± 34.1 ml/min/1.73 m2.
There were no significant differences in proteinuria levels, serum creatinine levels, eGFR, diabetes mellitus and hypertension at baseline between two groups. Participants in the obinutuzumab group were older than participants of GC group, 67.0 (34.0, 72.0) vs. 43.0 (23.0, 56.5), P = 0.044. Duration of MCD in obinutuzumab group was longer than that of GC group. Participants in the obinutuzumab group had higher level of serum albumin and HbA1c.
In the obinutuzumab group, 11 the of 15 participants (73.3%) achieved CR during a median follow-up of 28 days (IQR 20.0–40.0). In the GC group, 20 the of 22 participants (90.9%) achieved CR, during a follow-up of 21 days (IQR, 14.0–42.0). There were 5 participants (22.7%) relapsed in GC group. Meanwhile, none patient was observed relapse in the obinutuzumab group. The relapse rate of GC group was significantly higher than the obinutuzumab group. The infection rate of the GC group was higher than that of the obinutuzumab group (40.9% vs. 13.3%, P = 0.072), but the difference did not reach statistical significance.
Kaplan-Meier curves demonstrated that there was no significant difference in the CR rate between the obinutuzumab group and the GC group (log rank χ2 = 1.639, P = 0.200; Fig. 2). Univariate regression analysis showed that duration of MCD and obinutuzumab treatment were significantly associated with CR rate (P < 0.05). Hypertension and proteinuria levels were also associated with CR rate (P < 0.1), which were put in the multivariate Cox regression analysis. Multivariate Cox regression showed that the treatment of obinutuzumab or GC was not independently associated with CR rate after adjusting for covariates.
Conclusion
In this study, we compared the effectiveness of obinutuzumab versus GC as an initial treatment for adult MCD patients. The results of this study showed that the induction regimen of obinutuzumab alone can achieve clinical remission in MCD patients, especially those with previous steroids resistant/dependent, longer duration of MCD, elderly, high levels of BMI and HbA1c, avoid the side effects of steroids, and reduce the relapse in MCD patients. This retrospective study is the first study demonstrated that obinutuzumab alone as the initial therapy can effectively induce and maintain remission and can be applied as an alternative to GC therapy in adult MCD patients.
