title: #3257 Urinary metabolomics in nephrotic syndrome: the experience of “Fondazione Policlinico Universitario A. Gemelli”
authors: Martina Ambrogio; Rocco Baccaro; Federica Urciuolo; Jacopo Gervasoni; Lavinia Santucci; Stefano Costanzi; Francesco Pesce; Giuseppe Grandaliano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Metabolomics is an emerging discipline which aims to systematically study the profile of metabolites present in a biological system. It offers an integrative view of biochemical changes associated with different physiological and pathological conditions, providing critical information for diagnosis, prognosis and therapeutic monitoring. Metabolomics uses advanced technologies that enable high-resolution analysis of a wide range of metabolites in different biological matrices. The objective of this study is to identify a systematic panel of biomarkers for primary nephrotic syndromes from urine samples by applying nontarget metabolite profiling, and to validate their utility in independent sampling and analysis by multiplex statistical approaches. Nephrotic syndrome (NS) is a nonspecific renal disorder, mainly represented by minimal change disease (MCD), focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), and membranous glomerulonephritis (MGN). Because urine metabolites may reflect disease-specific functional perturbations in renal damage, we examined urine samples for distinctive metabolic changes to identify biomarkers for clinical applications.
Method
We collected urine samples of 41 patients with FSGS, MCD or MGN from October 2021 to April 2024 in Fondazione Policlinico Universitario A. Gemelli. Table 1 shows baseline clinical characteristics of study population. In this protocol a mass spectrometry-based targeted metabolite approach was used, with assays covering 1019 metabolites belonging to 39 metabolite classes, using MxP Quant 500 XL Kit. Specifically, a group of 107 small molecules was measured by ultraperformance liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) operating in both positive and negative ion modes, while a group of 912 lipids was measured by flow injection analysis coupled to tandem mass spectrometry (FIA-MS/MS) operating in both positive and negative ion modes. For exploratory data analysis in comparing nephrotic and non-nephrotic patients, we used MetaboAnalyst 6.0 to provide Fold Change (FC) analysis, t-tests, and volcano plot analysis.
Results
Fold change analysis identified 44 metabolites significantly downregulated, and 23 metabolites significantly upregulated in nephrotic patients. At the t test, 74 significance characteristics were demonstrated in nephrotic patients. The Volcano Plot showed 17 significantly metabolites downregulated, and 8 significantly metabolites upregulated in nephrotic patients. Figure 1 shows box plots with some of the details of these features. Next, we included the most significant metabolites in a pathway analysis, which showed several related pathways altered in nephrotic syndromes such as glycerophospholipid and glycosylphosphatidylinositol metabolism.
Conclusion
Our study showed the streamlined analytical and statistical processes for the authentication biomarker discovery for different nephrotic syndrome. The multi-step statistical confirmation with realistic sample duration maximizes reliability and robustness of biomarkers proposed in this study. Determining the integrated concentrations of the common metabolites could be crucial for future clinical applications and the development of feasible methods. Taken together, our findings will expectantly help diagnose and guide therapeutic plans in adult patients with NS.

title: #1294 Albuminuria predicts GFR-decline in patients with Alport syndrome
authors: Jan Boeckhaus; Mira Choi; Annika Jens; Andreas Leha; Sima Jami; Jan Halbritter; Oliver Gross
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) significantly impacts health and lifespan, but its progression remains difficult to predict. Therefore, there is a crucial need for biomarkers that can identify adults at high risk for rapid CKD decline. Alport syndrome (AS), the most common inherited glomerular kidney disease, exemplifies this challenge. While some patients experience rapid progression, others exhibit a more gradual decline in kidney function. This study investigates the potential of routinely measured urinary proteins as predictors of kidney function decline.
Method
This observational, non-interventional, retrospective study investigated 127 patients with AS at two German centers at different stages of the disease. Receiver operator characteristic (ROC) curves were drawn for the discrimination of fast vs not fast eGFR decline. title: #1520 Chronic kidney disease in Sjögren's syndrome: key predictive factors revealed in a 133-patient cohort
authors: Paula Milhazes Guimarães; Nuno Moreira Fonseca; Vera Bernardino; Heidi Gruner; Sofia Pinheiro; David Navarro
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sjögren's Syndrome (SSj) is an autoimmune disease that primarily affects exocrine glands. The renal manifestations of SSj are diverse, with tubulointerstitial nephritis being the most common form of kidney damage. Although renal involvement is rare, it can lead to chronic kidney disease (CKD). Understanding the factors that predict renal impairment in SSj is crucial for early intervention and improving patient outcomes. This study aims to investigate the prevalence of CKD stages in SSj and identify the factors associated with worse renal outcomes in a retrospective cohort.
Method
This retrospective study reviewed patients diagnosed with SSj at an autoimmune outpatient clinic in a Portuguese center from 2013 to 2024. Data on clinical symptoms, immunological markers, and kidney function parameters were collected. The prevalence of CKD stages was assessed using estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) values. Univariate statistical analyses were performed to assess the association between clinical and laboratory variables, including the presence of autoantibodies and comorbidities and CKD progression. Multivariate analyses were performed, including variables that theoretically impact the outcome of interest and variables which had statistical significance in the univariate analyses.
Results
Out of 158 identified SSj patients, 133 were included after excluding those lost to follow-up or deceased. The cohort predominantly comprised women (96.2%) with a mean age of 67 ± 14 years and an average disease duration of 11 ± 7 years. The most commonly reported symptoms were xerophthalmia (97%), xerostomia (82%) and arthritis (46%). The Chisholm-Mason biopsy scores showed that 36 patients scored below 2, 15 scored 3 and 21 scored 4; 61 patients had no biopsy records. Positive autoantibodies were frequently found, with ANA positivity in 114 patients(86%), anti-SSA positivity in 80 patients(60%), and anti-SSB positivity in 39 patients(29%). Hypergammaglobulinemia was present in 29 patients, and hypocomplementemia was identified in 14 patients. Comorbidities were present in 48.8% patients, including hypertension (43.6%), dyslipidemia (48.1%) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (10.5%). Systemic immunosuppression was used in 81 patients (60%).
Four patients were under nephrology follow-up: three cases were related to SSj, including one with tubulointerstitial nephritis and two with end-stage CKD of unknown etiology. No other types of renal involvement were documented. Pulmonary involvement was found in three patients. Among the cohort, 86 patients (64.6%) had no other associated autoimmune diseases. The mean eGFR was 85 ml/min/1.73 m². The CKD staging is presented in Table 1. Proteinuria above 30 mg/g was observed in 31 patients, with only one patient presenting a urine protein/creatinine ratio greater than 500 mg/g.
We performed univariate correlation analysis for eGFR. We found associations with hypocomplementemia (r:0.2097; P = 0.0158), the presence of SSA (r:0.1775; P = 0.0418) and with the presence of hypertension (r:0.2826; P = 0.0010). We found no associations with clinical manifestations of SSj, the presence of other antibodies, or with any treatment. In multivariate analysis, in a model which included the presence of hypertension, diabetes, xerostomia, xerophthalmia, SSA, SSB, ANA, hypocomplementemia, proteinuria, and disease duration, only hypocomplementemia remained statistically significant (B = 12.25 [0.67–23.84]; P = 0.038). When analyzing CKD stages, proteinuria and proteinuria stages, univariate correlations did not persist when evaluating in multivariate models.
Conclusion
Chronic kidney disease is a rare but significant manifestation of sjögren's syndrome. Early stages of CKD are often asymptomatic, making it crucial to identify at-risk patients before irreversible damage occurs. Hypocomplementemia is a risk factor for decreased eGFR, suggesting that ongoing inflammation has a detrimental effect on kidney function.

title: #2264 Decoding podocyte effacement: a high-resolution approach using STED microscopy and spatial transcriptomics
authors: Johannes Pospiech; Ricardo Castro-Hernandez; Tobias Bohnenpoll; Anna Guhl; Carolin Wiechers; Menglin Zheng; Janne Schoening; Kristina Liebe; Florian Grimm; Christian Wurm; Gerald Donnert; Philipp Skroblin
abstract:
Background and Aims
Podocyte injury and foot process effacement are early events that precede proteinuria and podocyte detachment in focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and other glomerular diseases. Despite their clinical relevance, the cellular and molecular mechanisms driving these processes remain poorly understood, largely due to the limited resolution of conventional microscopy and transcriptomic methods. Stimulated emission depletion (STED) is a super-resolution light microscopy technique that provides a powerful tool to examine podocyte foot process morphology in exceptional detail. By combining STED microscopy with high-resolution spatial transcriptomics, we can map cellular morphology and gene expression at the tissue level in parallel. In this study, we characterized kidney biopsy samples from the NURTuRE patient cohort to explore the cellular and molecular mechanisms involved in podocyte injury and effacement.
Method
Kidney biopsies from the NURTuRE cohort were selected to represent a range of disease stages to capture variations in kidney function and proteinuria. Adjacent paraffin sections of formalin-fixed samples from FSGS and other glomerular diseases and control samples from healthy living donors were analysed using STED microscopy (Infinity line, Abberior) and spatial transcriptomics (Visium HD, 10x Genomics). Podocyte foot processes and slit diaphragms were labeled with synaptopodin and nephrin, and super-resolution images were collected for deep learning-based morphometric analysis and histopathology expert assessment. Spatial transcriptomes associated with individual glomeruli were aggregated into pseudobulk samples to allow integration of transcriptomic and morphometric profiles.
Results
Unbiased clustering and dimensionality reduction of glomerular pseudobulk transcriptomes revealed a molecular gradient defined by cell type and mechanistic signatures linked to podocyte depletion and glomerulosclerosis. This pseudotime trajectory, which integrated glomerular transcriptomes from different patient samples closely aligned with conventional H&E-based histopathology, including mesangial expansion and varying degrees of sclerosis, suggesting a molecular axis of disease progression. Notably, dimensionality reduction revealed substantial molecular variation early along the disease continuum, that was not reflected by conventional histopathology and light microscopy features. Integration of STED microscopy data showed that this early molecular variation in disease progression was strongly associated with podocyte foot process effacement, marked by molecular signatures of cytoskeletal remodelling and epithelial dedifferentiation.
Conclusion
By combining high-resolution morphometry and spatial transcriptomics, this study enhances our understanding of the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying podocyte injury and effacement. Further exploration of the identified molecular disease trajectory has the potential to provide valuable insights into the progression of kidney diseases and pave the way for novel therapeutic interventions.

title: #1075 Cancer incidence and risk factors in PLA2R-associated membranous nephropathy
authors: Ilario Russo; Maria Vargas; Francesca Annese; Jing Miao; Loreto Gesualdo; Fernando Custodio Fervenza; Ladan Zand
abstract:
Background and Aims
Malignancy is commonly seen in patients with membranous Nephropathy (MN) with a prevalence up to 22%. M-type phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) antigen and its associated antibody account for up to 80% of the cases but its association with malignancy is less clear. To date, no study has specifically evaluated cancer incidence and risk factors in patients with PLA2R associated MN as most studies were conducted in an era before many MN antigens were identified. Here, we report cancer incidence, types of cancer, and effect of immunosuppressive therapy and clinical parameters in a cohort of patients with PLA2R-associated MN.
Method
A single center retrospective cohort study in adults with diagnosis of PLA2R associated MN from 1/1/1996 to 12/31/2021. Follow-up was defined as the time from MN diagnosis to the last follow-up or if the patient initiated dialysis or underwent transplantation. The primary outcome in this study was the incidence of cancer events reported as cancer incidence/1000 patients/year. The cancer events were compared to the age-adjusted United States (U.S.) general population using Centers for Disease Control (C.D.C) data. The standardized incidence ratio (SIR) was calculated by dividing the cancer rates in our cohort to the cancer rates in general population. Time-to-event analysis was conducted using the Kaplan-Meier method. The log-rank test compared age, sex, smoking habits, hypertension, diabetes, body mass index (BMI), previous immunosuppression (IS), remission of the MN, PLA2R titers at the time of diagnosis. Cox proportional hazards regression was used to evaluate the associations between baseline characteristics and cancer incidence. For the multivariate model of cancer incidence, we evaluated variables clinically relevant for the outcome.
Results
We identified 239 patients with PLA2R-associated MN, with mean (±SD) age of 52 (±13) years, with 72.8% male (n = 174), median [IQR] BMI of 29.8 [26.3, 33.6] kg/m2, median eGFR of 68 [45, 94] ml/min, median proteinuria of 8.2 [5.1, 11.2] g/24h, and median PLA2R titers of 38 [9, 122] RU/ml. Common comorbidities included hypertension (60.2%), and diabetes (17.1%). Majority of patients drank alcohol (90.7%) and 32.6% were smokers (active or former). Of 239 patients, 15 had a history of cancer before the MN diagnosis. But in all these patients, cancer had been treated and was considered to be in full remission. A diagnosis of cancer was made in 37 patients (15.4%) during a median follow-up of 60 [27.5, 145.5] months. Incidence of cancer in our cohort was 22.6 [95% CI, 15.9 to 31.1] per 1000 persons/year. In comparison, age adjusted U.S. general population has a lower cancer incidence of 15.9 [95% CI, 15.9 to 16.1] cases per 1000 person/year. The resulting SIR of cancer in our cohort was 1.42. This SIR is lower than the one reported by Bjørneklett and al. (2007) in a Norwegian cohort that included all patients with MN and was not limited to PLA2R-positive MN. The cumulative incidence of cancer diagnosis is shown in Fig. 1. Mean age at cancer diagnosis was 66 (±10.2) years old. Prostate cancer was the most common (n = 11) type of cancer, followed by skin cancer (n = 9), followed by cancer of the urinary tract (n = 5). In univariate and multivariate analysis (Table 1), only older age (>65 years) and tobacco use were associated with statistically significant increased risk of cancer. Other clinical parameters such as sex, eGFR, baseline proteinuria, BMI, hypertension, diabetes, alcohol use, anti-PLA2R antibody titer, type of immunosuppression, remission status (partial, complete, no response) were not associated with a significant increased risk of cancer.
Conclusion
Patients with PLA2R associated MN are at increased risk of developing cancer following diagnosis compared to general population and routine age-appropriate cancer screening in this population is essential. The increased incidence of cancer is independent of IS therapy, response to therapy or other comorbidities. These data suggests that there are likely mechanisms beyond the traditional risk factors at play that may be unique to the presence of PLA2R antibodies.

title: #2027 Antiproteinuric effect of SGLT2 inhibitors in non-diabetic glomerulopathies is dependent on body mass index
authors: Maria Vargas; Ilario Russo; Anila Cara; Gian Marco Berti; Joaquim Milheiro; Thongprayoon Charat; Sanjeev Sethi; Paola Romagnani; Fernando Custodio Fervenza
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) are emerging as an essential part of the new standard of care for proteinuria, alongside renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors in patients with proteinuric chronic kidney disease (CKD). Subgroup analysis of EMPA-KIDNEY and DAPA-CKD trials done in patients with glomerular diseases [IgA Nephropathy (IgAN) and focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)] showed these agents are less effective in reducing proteinuria compared to other agents like Sparsentan, or Double RAS Blockade. Also, the antiproteinuric effects of SGLT2i in patients with glomerular diseases is not well understood. To date, no study has specifically evaluated the effects of body mass index (BMI) on the antiproteinuric efficacy of SGLT2. Here we report the impact of BMI on the antiproteinuric efficacy of SGLT2i in non-diabetic patients with glomerular diseases.
Method
Single-center retrospective cohort study. Inclusion criteria (1) adult patients with a biopsy-proven glomerular disease or genetic diagnosis [i.e., Collagen IV mutations] from January 1st, 2019, to December 31st, 2023, (2) no Diabetes Mellitus, (3) proteinuria more than 0.75 g/24 h at the time of initiation of treatment despite optimized blood pressure control with renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibition at maximum tolerated dose (5) no concomitant use of induction immunosuppression therapy—stable maintenance immunosuppression was allowed. Patients with active neoplasia, no follow-up available after initiation of therapy or kidney transplant were excluded. Baseline was defined as the time of the initiation of SGLT2i. Laboratory values, including proteinuria, serum creatinine, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), were obtained at baseline and 6 months. Changes in laboratory values over time were analyzed using the paired t-test and the signed-rank test, depending on the distribution. Weight status was classified based on BMI in three categories: regular (BMI < 25 kg/m2), overweight (25–29.9 kg/m2), and obese (>30 kg/m2).
Results
We identified 115 non-diabetic patients with glomerular diseases. Median age [IQR] at the time of SGLT2i initiation was 49.1 [35.4, 61.5] years; 74 (64.3%) patients were male, and 96 (83.5%) patients were white, with the second most common ethnicity being Asian with 10 (8.7%) patients. Median BMI for the entire cohort was 28.2 [26.0, 33.1] Kg/m2. Fifty-three (46.1%) patients had IgAN, 22 (19.1%) had secondary FSGS (sFSGS), 3 (2.6%) primary FSGS (pFSGS), and 12 (10.4%) genetic FSGS (gFSGS), with collagen IV mutations as the most common cause of gFSGS. Kidney function and proteinuria over time are presented in Table 1. Significant declines in eGFR [−1.77 ml/min/1.73m2 95% CI: (−4.2, −1.19)] and proteinuria [−0.58 g/24h 95% CI (−0.91, −0.44)] were observed at 6 months in the entire cohort compared to baseline. However, in the subgroup analysis by BMI strata, i.e., <25, 25-29.9, ≥30, the reduction in proteinuria was statistically significant only in overweight and obese patients. The expected early drop in eGFR was not observed in patients with a normal BMI. However, the decline in eGFR progressively increased and was statistically significant in the obese group (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
The principal finding of the present study is the lack of significant proteinuria reduction in patients with BMI<25 kg/m², which contrasts with the significant reductions observed in overweight and obese patients. SGLT2i's main antiproteinuric mechanism of action involves reducing glomerular hyperfiltration, which is commonly seen in patients with diabetes and obesity. In non-diabetic patients with glomerulopathies, proteinuria may be sustained by mechanisms not dependent on glomerular hyperfiltration, especially in those patients with normal BMI. These findings are crucial to advocate a personalized approach to treatment, challenging the “one-size-fits-all” strategy.

title: #3876 Macula densa cell targeting kidney tissue regenerative therapeutic approaches
authors: Georgina Gyarmati; Audrey Izuhara; Alejandra Becerra Calderon; Janos Peti-Peterdi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Recent studies using intravital imaging in combination with a multiomics approach identified the neuronal differentiation, novel key sensory and regulatory functions, and an endogenous kidney tissue remodeling and regenerative program of the understudied renal cell type of the macula densa (MD). Molecular-level understanding of new MD cell functions revealed the high, MD-specific expression and secretion of several angiogenic, cell growth, patterning and extracellular matrix remodeling factors including cell communication network (CCN1), and the tissue hypertrophy regulator pregnancy-associated plasma protease A2 (PAPPA2) in both the mouse and human kidney. The present study aimed to provide initial pre-clinical validation of the specificity and efficacy of in injectable MD targeting new therapeutic approaches.
Method
Treatment with either MD cell secretome from freshly harvested and conditioned MD cell culture media, or human recombinant CCN1 protein, or AAV9-mediated MD targeting gene therapy with shRNA-mediated CCN1/PAPPA2 overexpression or knockdown specifically in MD cells was performed in vivo in WT and Cdh5-Confetti mice (for genetic cell fate tracking of endothelial cells at the single-cell level) and in Adriamycin-induced focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS).
Results
Chronic administration of hrCCN1 for 5 consecutive days (5 ug/animal/day iv) in Cdh5-Confetti mice induced substantial proliferation and clonal remodeling of endothelial precursor cells at the glomerular vascular pole that propagated to glomerular and peritubular capillaries. In the ADR-BalbC mouse model of FSGS, chronic treatment with either MD cell secretome or hrCCN1 significantly improved GFR, albuminuria (ACR), glomerulosclerosis histology index, and increased podocyte number confirmed by weekly follow-ups for 4 weeks. Systemic iv injection of AAV9-GFP (10^9 GC/animal iv, tissue harvest 1 week later) resulted in highly MD-specific (76.6±2.7%) and efficient (80.2±2.8%) GFP expression in the mouse kidney. Treatment with AAV9-PAPPA2/CCN1 RNA/shRNA (10^9 GC/animal single-dose iv) resulted in highly MD-specific and efficient overexpression/knockdown of PAPPA2/CCN1, improved glomerular and renal blood flow and tissue remodeling.
Conclusion
The novel MD program for endogenous kidney tissue remodeling and regeneration can be manipulated and targeted pharmacologically and genetically in pre-clinical mouse models of glomerular and kidney diseases. Short-term MD cell therapeutic targeting in CKD can improve kidney structure and function by regression of pre-existing pathology, opening the doors for the future development of MD mimetics as a new class of renoprotective therapies.

title: #1545 Efficacy and safety of low-dose telitacicept in patients with primary IgA nephropathy: a retrospective cohort study
authors: Chenxi Liu; Ming Xia; Juanyong Zhao; Xiaomiao Hao; Di Liu; Xia Tan; Lingshan Zhou; Haiyang Liu; Hong Liu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Most IgA nephropathy (IgAN) patients will progress to end-stage renal disease within 10-15 years of diagnosis. Telitacicept is a B lymphocyte stimulator/A proliferation-inducing ligand dual-target fusion protein that has recently been used in autoimmune diseases. A phase II clinical trial with a small sample size indicated the efficacy of Telitacicept treatment with 160 mg or 240 mg once a week in reducing proteinuria in patients with IgAN. This study assessed the efficacy and safety of low-dose Telitacicept in IgAN patients.
Method
Biopsy-proven IgAN patients with 24-hour proteinuria > 0.5 g/day or UPCR > 500 mg/g who received low-dose Telitacicept (80 mg qw) were recruited in this study. This study included 15 IgAN patients who received Telitacicept treatment, forming the ‘Telitacicept group’. Additionally, 15 patients selected to match historical controls received immunosuppressive (IS) therapy (IS agents with or without corticosteroid therapy) and were classified as the ‘IS group’. These patients were matched 1:1 with the Telitacicept group based on age, sex, eGFR, and UPCR levels to enhance the comparability between groups (as detailed in Table 1). Telitacicept was partially used with the supplement of hydroxychloroquine or IS agents (but without corticosteroids) in different doses. Among the Telitacicept group, 6 patients showed severe renal impairment, with eGFR < 35 mL/min/1.73 m2, which was the exclusion criteria in the Telitacicept phase II clinical trial. The primary outcomes were the changes in UPCR and eGFR over time. This study analyzed changes from baseline in UPCR and eGFR through 4 months using a mixed-effects model for repeated measurements.
Results
The median duration of follow-up was 126 and 130 days for the Telitacicept and IS groups, respectively. As for reducing proteinuria, reductions in UPCR in the Telitacicept group were observed in month 2 (P = 0.036) and persisted until month 4 (P = 0.010). In the fourth month, the Telitacicept group showed a change in UPCR from a baseline of −44.65% compared with 5.63% in the IS group, despite no statistical difference between Telitacicept and IS group over the current observation (P = 0.180). Additionally, Telitacicept was superior to reducing proteinuria among patients with severe renal impairment (P = 0.022), with a change in UPCR from baseline at 4 months of −30.38%, compared with 111.17% in the conventional IS group (P < 0.001). At 4 months, the eGFR change from baseline was 0.57 mL/min/1.73 m2 in all participants who received Telitacicept treatment, compared to −1.57 mL/min/1.73 m2 in IS groups. Compared with the IS group, Telitacicept exhibited a kidney protection effect according to the values of eGFR change from baseline over 4 months of observation (P = 0.037), while the percentage change of eGFR from baseline showed no difference between groups during observation. Telitacicept was generally well-tolerated during the research period, with the most common adverse event in the Telitacicept group assessed as related by the study investigator was blood IgG decrease (4/15 [26.7%]).
Conclusion
This study indicates that low-dose Telitacicept alone or assisted with IS therapy can significantly and safely reduce proteinuria and protect eGFR in patients with IgAN. Additionally, Telitacicept showed superior kidney protection efficacy compared with IS agents during the 4-month follow-up.

title: #1738 Exogenous ketosis increases renal function and sodium excretion in healthy subjects
authors: Trine Züricho Lyksholm; Steffen Nielsen; Henrik Thomsen; Jesper Bech
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renewed interest in the physiological role of ketone bodies (KB) has emerged. Several beneficial effects are related to ketosis including improved exercise capacity and improved cardiac function. Animal studies have suggested that ketosis is renoprotective due to anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects. However, only few clinical studies have examined renal effects of ketosis, and there is a paucity of clinical studies investigating the effects of ketosis on sodium- and water balance.
We aimed to examine the effects of exogenous ketosis on renal function and sodium excretory capacity in healthy subjects.
Method
We conducted a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blinded, crossover study. Sixteen healthy participants received a ketone monoester drink and a placebo drink three times a day for five days in a randomized order. There was a washout period for two weeks in between each treatment period. The participants followed a standardised diet during the study periods.
At the end of each treatment period, we performed a 99mTc-DTPA-clearance estimation to determine glomerular filtration rate (GFR) along with fractional excretion of sodium (FENa), and fractional excretion of potassium (FEK+). We also performed a 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure measurement including a cuff-based determination of vascular stiffness and peripheral resistance.
We employed a linear mixed model to analyze the effect of ketosis on GFR and sodium excretion incorporating treatment, time and treatment sequence as fixed effects and participant ID as random effect. The models were checked for a treatment-by-time interaction.
Results
Thirteen healthy participants completed both study periods. Baseline characteristics are displayed in Table 1. Intake of ketone monoester drink successfully increased plasma concentration of beta-hydroxybutyrate above 2 Mmol/L half an hour after intake. Ketosis significantly increased GFR compared with placebo resulting in a mean difference of 6 mL/min (95% CI: 2.4, 9.7; P = 0.007). Also, ketosis increased FENa with a mean difference of 0.4% (95% CI: 0.23, 0.55; P < 0.001). FEK+ was significantly decreased with a mean difference of −7.9% (95% CI: −10.1, −5.7; P < 0.001) during ketosis. There was no change in systolic or diastolic blood pressure. However, peripheral vascular resistance was decreased with a mean change of −49 dyn*s/cm5 (95% CI: −95, −3; P = 0.04) while heart rate was increased by 9% (95% CI: 4, 14; P = 0.002).
Conclusion
Ketosis increases GFR and sodium excretion, whilst decreasing potassium excretion. Furthermore, ketosis reduces peripheral vascular resistance. The findings suggest potential advantages for kidney health, but further research is needed to assess its therapeutic efficacy in chronic kidney disease prior to formulating clinical recommendations.

title: #2240 Exploring the second line agent of choice in the management of chronic kidney disease-associated pruritus: a global cross-sectional study of clinician experience and preference
authors: Sarah Nestor; Frank Brennan; Aoife C Lowney
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic Kidney Disease-associated Pruritus (CKD-aP) in the setting of End Stage Kidney Disease (ESKD) is prevalent [1] and contributes to reduced quality of life for this patient cohort. For years, the most common initial treatment approach included antihistamines, even though the aetiology of CKD-aP isn't thought to be histamine-mediated. [2] Recently, the use of Gabapentinoids has become a widely accepted first line management strategy, supported by Grade A evidence. [3] Although the literature includes several alternatives, [4] there doesn't appear to be consensus on a second line option.
The aim of this study was to determine the preferred second line agent for the management of CKD-aP.
Method
Full ethical approval was received from the Clinical Research Ethics Committee of the Cork Teaching Hospitals. Sixty eight international experts across Nephrology and Palliative Medicine from eight different countries were surveyed using a web-based tool.
Results
A response rate of 72% was achieved. 61% reported to be working in a high-income region. 83.3% of respondents were medical consultants. 53% were Nephrologists, 22% were Palliative Medicine Consultants and 25% worked across both. 90% confirmed either gabapentin or pregabalin as their first-line in treatment of CKD-aP in line with best practice and current evidence.
30% (n = 9) use topical menthol as preferred second-line option with 20% (n = 6) prescribing either Evening Primrose Oil or topical steroid preparations for the same indication. Other second line options includes first-generation antihistamines 13% (n = 4) and Difelikefalin (7%). 3% (n = 1) of respondents reported to use either UV-B phototherapy, oral Sertraline or topical Capsaicin cream respectively. Only 43% had access to Kappa opioid agonists (such as Difelikefalin) in their region with the majority administering it parenterally.
Conclusion
Gabapentinoids continue to be the mainstay of CKD-aP treatment. This study highlights marked heterogeny in preferred second line option in management of this debilitating condition. Further research is required to develop guidance in CKD-aP symptom management.

title: #720 SMART stone MDT and patient care recommendations: the nephrologist's role in optimizing the adult high-risk kidney stone patient pathway
authors: Pietro Manuel Ferraro; Esteban Emiliani; Thomas Knoll; Giorgia Mandrile; Gill Rumsby; Bhaskar Somani
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney stone formers are at risk of loss of kidney function over time and have substantial morbidity as well as reduced quality of life (QoL) [1,2]. There is a need for earlier diagnosis, alongside metabolic investigation, to determine suspicion of secondary stone disease to enable earlier intervention and prevent progressive kidney damage [2]. Currently, there is a lack of best practice recommendations for forming a multidisciplinary team (MDT) to aid patient management of high-risk adult recurrent kidney stone formers. We propose a ‘SMART’ Stone MDT that aims to provide guidance on the role of an MDT, including Nephrologists, in the early identification, referral and assessment of adult high-risk kidney stone formers to advance patient care.
Method
Recommendations were developed by the expert Steering Committee (SC, 1 Nephrologist, 3 Urologists and 2 Biochemists/Geneticists) from the UK, Spain, Germany and Italy. These recommendations were voted on by invited specialists to determine their level of agreement, from ‘strongly agree’ to ‘strongly disagree’, via an online survey. With an agreement threshold set at 70%, the SC reviewed the survey results, additional comments and any areas of disagreement, before finalising the recommendations.
Results
A total of 44 recommendations were developed by the SC, designed to support the structure of an ideal MDT including team composition, patient identification and referral, planning and coordination, patient assessment, decision-making, communication, onward referral and care integration. Thirteen core recommendations were chosen as being the highest priority for the activities of an MDT. Of the 48 additional invited specialists, 29 voted on the core recommendations (5 Nephrologists, 22 Urologists and 2 Biochemists/Geneticists) from 19 countries across Europe, Canada, East Asia, South/Southeast Asia, and the Middle East. All 13 core recommendations reached the 70% agreement threshold.The remaining 31 recommendations were voted on by those specialists who opted-in to partake in an extended questionnaire (n = 15/21; 3 Nephrologists, 10 Urologists and 2 Biochemists/Geneticists). All 31 extended recommendations reached the 70% agreement threshold.
93% (n = 27/29) of responders agreed or strongly agreed that an MDT is required to improve the patient journey and provide the best outcomes for patients with complex stones. 100% (n = 29/29) of responders agreed or strongly agreed that the Nephrologist should be included in the MDT as a core team member. The main recommended roles and responsibilities of the Nephrologist from the perspective of an ideal MDT reached an agreement level of 80% (n = 12/15, extended questionnaire). Roles and responsibilities include but are not limited to, leading cases relating to patients on a medical pathway, metabolic assessment and interpretation of laboratory tests to establish a diagnosis and/or suspicion of secondary stone disease, medical management and follow-up and kidney function monitoring, and management of reduced kidney function. While the recommendations focus on the ideal situation, location-specific nuances, including healthcare setting, infrastructure and resource availability, should be taken into consideration.
Conclusion
An ideal MDT process can achieve comprehensive, high-quality, and coordinated patient care, which is especially useful for patients with complex stone diseases. The role of the Nephrologist is important in the formation of an ideal MDT, to establish a correct diagnosis and/or suspicion of secondary stone disease, as well as medical management and follow-up to name a few. A high level of agreement was reached on core and extended recommendations relating to the implementation of an ideal MDT in identifying and managing high-risk stone formers.

title: #3715 Burden of chronic kidney disease and related urinary disorders on healthcare utilisation in Ireland: a national inpatient analysis
authors: Leonard Browne; Meera Tandan; Austin Stack
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease and related urinary tract disorders (CKD-RD) significantly impact healthcare systems worldwide. In Ireland, there is little data on the burden and impact of CKD-RD on healthcare utilisation, thus limiting opportunities for intervention. This study determined the national burden, length of stay (LOS), associated costs, and in-hospital mortality of CKD-RD in the Irish health system.
Method
We analysed data from the national Hospital In-Patient Enquiry (HIPE) in 2022, to identify all hospitalisations with a primary or additional diagnosis of CKD-RD defined by ICD-10 codes. We excluded infant admissions and cases where dialysis or kidney transplantation was the principal diagnosis. Major outcomes included hospitalisation rates, LOS, healthcare costs, and in patient mortality. We utilised general linear modelling (GLM) to estimate the effect of demographic and clinical characteristics on total costs and LOS and multivariable logistic regression to examine associations with in-hospital mortality.
Results
In 2022, CKD-RD accounted for 225,164 hospitalisations (13.1% of total), incurring €427 million in costs. After excluding dialysis and transplant admissions, 35,409 hospitalisations from 24,110 patients accounted for 422,738 bed days (€320.3 million in costs), with a mean LOS of 11.9 days. Diabetic kidney disease (49.3%), Tubulointerstitial kidney disease (9.1%), Other kidney and ureter disorders (6.7%), and Glomerular diseases (4.3%) were the most frequent contributing conditions to CKD burden. The most common principal diagnoses when CKD-RD was recorded as an additional diagnosis were Urinary system disorder (6,442/100,000 admissions), Acute kidney injury (3,764/100,000), Diabetes (Type 1: 2,540/100,000; Type 2: 2,489/100,000), Heart failure (2,362/100,000), Other sepsis (2,199/100,000), Acute lower respiratory infections (1,831/100,000) and Unspecified pneumonia (1,710/100,000). Emergency admissions accounted for 71.1% of cases, with 69% of patients eligible for free or reduced-cost healthcare. Advancing age, increasing Elixhauser comorbidity score, and acute kidney injury were strongly and significantly associated with increased LOS (P < 0.001), cost (P < 0.001), and in-hospital mortality (P < 0.001).
Conclusion

title: #3835 Influence of age and GFR thresholds on kidney failure and death in the Irish health system
authors: Leonard Browne; Meera Tandan; Austin Stack
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is commonly diagnosed using a fixed estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) threshold, which may lead to excessive nephrology referrals, particularly in older adults where kidney function decline is often age-related. This study determined the impact of an age-adapted versus a fixed GFR threshold on CKD identification and major outcomes in an Irish cohort in order to inform national policy and strategy.
Method
We assembled a cohort of 125,890 adult patients, age 20 years or more from the National Kidney Disease Surveillance System (NKDSS), recruited between January 1, 2005, and December 31, 2010, and followed until December 31, 2013. Kidney function was estimated with the CKD-EPI 2012 equation and CKD was defined as sustained reduction in GFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m² (fixed threshold) or an age-adapted threshold (75, 60, and 45 mL/min/1.73 m² for individuals <40 years, 40–64 years, and ≥65 years, respectively). The primary outcome was end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) [defined as GFR < 10 ml/min1.73 m², dialysis, or kidney transplant] or all-cause mortality modelled as competing events. Patients were censored at date of dialysis initiation, kidney transplantation, death, loss to follow-up, or the end of follow-up (December 31, 2013). Absolute risks of kidney failure and death were estimated using the Aalen-Johansen method and relative risks using the Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard model.
Results
125,890 participants, mean age of 54.1 (SD: 17.7) years, 55 %women were followed for a median 7.8 years (IQR: 6.33–8.55). The prevalence of CKD at baseline in the fixed CKD and age-adapted CKD cohorts was 19,864 (15.8%) and 11,714 (9.3%) respectively. During follow-up, 243 patients (0.19%) progressed to ESKD, and 14,179 patients (11.26%) died. The fixed-threshold cohort incurred lower absolute risks of ESKD (1.1% vs 1.8%) and higher risks of death (34% vs 28%) than the age-adapted cohort did. The absolute risks for ESKD were age and GFR dependent with the highest risks observed for age group <55 years at GFR threshold of <60 ml/min/1.73 m² and lowest for age >75 years at GFR threshold <45 ml/min/1.73 m² (Fig. 1).
Compared to the referent group (GFR 60 to 89 ml/min/1.73 m²), GFR values between 45–59 mL/min/1.73 m² were associated with higher risks of ESKD in adults <55 years (sHR = 26.3, 95% CI: 11.1–62.3, P < 0.001) and 55–64 years (sHR = 14.2, 95% CI: 3.56–56.9, P < 0.001), but not for 65–74 years (sHR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.27–3.64, P = 0.98) or >75 years (sHR = 1.82, 95% CI: 0.52–6.46, P = 0.35).
Similarly, mortality risks were greatest for adults with GFR values 45–59 mL/min/1.73 m²) and age <55 years (sHR = 2.13, 95% CI: 1.64–2.77, P < 0.001), followed by 55–64 years (sHR = 1.38, 95% CI: 1.20–1.60, P < 0.001) and 65–74 years (sHR = 1.18, 95% CI: 1.09–1.28, P < 0.001), with only a modest increase for >75 years (sHR = 1.08, 95% CI: 1.02–1.15, P = 0.006) compared to the referent group.
Conclusion
A fixed GFR threshold may overestimate CKD burden and inaccurately classify prognostic risk leading to unnecessary interventions for older patients in the Irish health system. An age-adapted approach better reflects the risks of kidney failure and death, reducing over diagnosis while ensuring timely identification of high-risk individuals. These findings support the use of an age-specific GFR threshold for optimal CKD management.

title: #3901 Impact of adoption of European Kidney Consortium equation (EKFC) equation compared to CKD-EPI equations on CKD prevalence and staging in Irish adults
authors: Meera Tandan; Leonard Browne; Jennifer Bragg-Gresham; R Saran; Austin Stack
abstract:
Background and Aims
The Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) equation tends to overestimate glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in younger and older age groups. In contrast, the European Kidney Function Consortium (EKFC) full-age spectrum (FAS) provides a more accurate estimate of CKD burden across the age spectrum thereby providing a more accurate estimate of disease burden. We conducted a comparative analysis of the EKFC-FAS equations with the CKD-EPI equations on CKD prevalence and staging in Irish adults age 50 and over.
Method
We utilised data from The Irish Longitudinal Study on Ageing (2009–2011), for participants aged 50 to 79 years with kidney function assessment. Estimated GFR was calculated using the EKFC-FAS and CKD-EPI equations, with CKD defined as eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m². We compared median eGFR values, CKD prevalence, concordance correlation coefficient (CCC)s across a panel of estimating equations. We then evaluated the impact of the EKFC-FAS equations [FAS 2017Scr-CysC, EKFC 2021Scr and FAS 2021CysC] on eGFR category reclassification of CKD staging, using CKD-EPI 2012Scr-CysC and 2009Scr as referent equations.
Results
A total of 5,092 participants (53.3% women, median age 61 years) were included. CKD prevalence weighted to the population was significantly higher using the FAS equations as compared to the to the CKD-EPI -based equations and ranged from 7.53% [6.78%–8.35%] using CKD-EPI 2021Scr (race-free) to 18.14% [16.96%–19.39%] using FAS 2023CysC equations, P < 0.001 for each category. Median eGFR was 74.5 ml/min/1.73 m² for EKFC-FAS 2017Scr-CysC and 82.1 ml/min/1.73 m² for CKD-EPI 2012Scr-CysC, leading to a 5.9% difference in CKD prevalence [10.8% vs. 16.7%, P < 0.001]. The reclassification discrepancy towards a more severe CKD stage varied from 20.7% to 26.6% when the EKFC-FAS equations were compared to the CKD-EPI 2012Scr-CysC, and varied from 17.9% to 32.9% when compared to CKD-EPI 2009Scr. The CCC ranged from 0.82 to 0.89 (EKFC-FAS vs CKD-EPI 2012Scr-CysC) 0.61 to 0.82 (CKD-EPI 2009Scr).
Conclusion
The prevalence of CKD in Irish adults differs significantly according to eGFR equation with higher prevalence predicted by EKFC-than the CKD-EPI derived equations. Discrepancies in CKD staging and lack of concordance are a cause for concern at the individual level and population level as these influence clinical decision making, care delivery, healthcare planning, resource allocation, and referral to nephrology services in Ireland.

title: #2052 Hypocalcemia and other bone and mineral disorders associated with denosumab across the spectrum of kidney function: the Stockholm CREAtinine Measurements (SCREAM) project
authors: Ruowei Xiao; Dongze Ji; Anne-Laure Faucon; Yang Xu; Juan-Jesus Carrero
abstract:
Background and Aims
Denosumab is a treatment commonly used for osteoporosis, and often preferred to bisphosphonates in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Given its antiresorptive properties, denosumab could potentially lead to hypocalcemia, with compensatory elevation of parathyroid hormone levels which lead to a decrease in serum phosphorus. These adverse effects may be magnified in patients with impaired kidney function, but evidence on the safety of denosumab in patients with CKD is limited. Here, we compared rates of hypocalcemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism (sHPT) and hypophosphatemia among users of denosumab versus zoledronate, a common intravenous bisphosphonate agent, across the spectrum of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR).
Method
We used data from the SCREAM project, a healthcare utilization cohort from Stockholm, Sweden. We conducted an active-comparator, new-user cohort study of older adults (65 years or older) who started therapy with denosumab (60 mg) or zoledronate (5 mg). The primary outcomes were the first occurrence of any hypocalcemia (defined as having a clinical diagnosis, total calcium or albumin-corrected calcium <2.0 mmol/L, or ionized calcium <1.0 mmol/L) and severe hypocalcemia (defined as having a hospital diagnosis, total calcium or albumin-corrected calcium <1.75 mmol/L, or ionized calcium <0.9 mmol/L) within the first 6 months of treatment. Secondary outcomes included sHPT and hypophosphatemia. We used Cox proportional hazard regression models with inverse probability of treatment weighting to estimate hazard ratios (HRs), and the weighted Aalen-Johansen estimator to estimate 6-month absolute risks (ARs) and their differences. Restricted cubic splines evaluated treatment safety across the spectrum of underlying eGFR.
Results
We identified 4,592 new users of denosumab and 2,889 new users of zoledronate. New users of denosumab were older (mean 80 versus 76 years) and with lower eGFR (mean 68 versus 76 mL/min/ 1.73 m2) than zoledronate users. Compared with zoledronate users, denosumab users had a higher risk of hypocalcemia (HR 2.24, 95% CI: 1.28–5.07; AR difference 0.74%, 95% CI: 0.24–1.24). Similarly, they had higher risks of sHPT (HR 2.79, 95% CI: 1.80–5.47; AR difference 1.29, 95% CI: 0.76–1.87) and hypophosphatemia (HR 1.66, 95% CI: 1.10–2.91; AR difference 0.62, 95% CI: 0.12–1.17). Risks of hypocalcemia events were greater with lower eGFR (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
In routinely-cared older adults, compared with zoledronate, initiation of denosumab treatment was associated with higher rates of hypocalcemia, sHPT and hypophosphatemia. Observed hypocalcemia rates were higher with lower kidney function. Our findings suggest the need to closely monitor phosphor-calcic biomarkers in patients with CKD on denosumab therapy.

title: #1659 Underestimate of the diagnosis and treatment of chronic kidney disease for in-hospital cardiovascular disease patients—a nationwide cross-section study in China
authors: Yibo He; Yihang Ling; Xiaozhao Lu; Tian Chang; Xianlin Ruan; Jingru Deng; Zeliang Li; Shiqun Chen; Yong Liu; Jiyan Chen
abstract:
Underestimate of the diagnosis and treatment of chronic kidney disease for in-hospital cardiovascular disease patients—A nationwide cross-section study in China
Background and Aims: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is common and prognosis-related in patients with existing cardiovascular disease (CVD). We aim to understand the gap between clinical practice and guideline recommendations on the diagnosis and treatment of CKD in CVD patients.
Method: We performed a nationwide, multicenter, cross-sectional study, enrolling CVD patients with in-hospital cardiology department records from the past year who met the CKD criteria. CKD was defined as having an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of ≤60 mL/min/1.73 m² on two separate occasions or a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR) of ≥30 mg/g, with measurements taken at least three months apart.
Results: From July 2023 to June 2024, 2000 eligible patients from 25 centers were enrolled. Serum creatinine was measured for all patients, while urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR) was measured only in 400 (20%) patients during their hospital stay. The CKD diagnosis rate for the overall patient population was 54.7% (95% CI: 52.5%–56.9%). Only 40.1% of patients in Stage 3a, but 80.8% of patients in Stage 4, were diagnosed with CKD. Patients with diabetes (63.4%) and heart failure (58.9%) were more likely to be diagnosed with CKD. The usage rate of SGLT2 inhibitors (37.8% vs. 35.3%, P = 0.28) was low but similar in patients regardless of CKD diagnosis, while the use of ACEI/ARB was lower in hypertensive patients diagnosed with CKD (56.8% vs. 63.8%, P = 0.002). Additionally, traditional Chinese medicine was more likely to be prescribed to patients with a CKD diagnosis (23.86% vs. 4.42%, P < 0.001).
Conclusion: The diagnosis and guideline-recommended treatment of CKD remain underestimated among CVD patients in China.

title: #1723 A positive functional modulator of ABCC6 decreases vascular calcification and improves kidney function in a rat adenine diet model of chronic kidney disease
authors: Daniel Crawford; Yong Ren; Patrick Stoiber; Darius Shubert; John Miller; Pui Yee Ng; Nathan Fuller; Robert Hughes
abstract:
Background and Aims
Vascular calcification (VC) is one consequence of the ionic and metabolic imbalance observed in chronic kidney disease (CKD). Greater VC content is demonstrated in advanced CKD stages and leads to significantly higher rates of cardiovascular events and mortality. Multiple factors influence the progression of VC, including the levels of inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi), which inhibits VC. Several proteins maintain the homeostatic balance of anti-calcific PPi with pro-calcific inorganic phosphate (Pi). Among these, ABCC6, which is expressed on the basolateral membrane of hepatocytes, facilitates ATP release into circulation where it can be broken down into AMP and PPi by enzymes such as ENPP1.
Rectify has developed an efficient platform capable of delivering small-molecule, positive functional modulators (PFMs) which enhance the function of proteins. We hypothesized that an ABCC6 PFM may increase ATP release from hepatocytes, leading to increased PPi levels and subsequent slowing or prevention of VC progression in the context of CKD.
Method
Rectify's proprietary small molecule library was screened to identify PFMs that increased ABCC6 expression. These PFMs were assessed in primary human hepatocytes (PHH) for their potential to impact ABCC6 protein levels using a novel AlphaLISA assay. In parallel, secreted PPi levels were measured from the media using an assay adapted from the literature. Additional SAR optimization provided ABCC6 PFM analogs with improved in vivo pharmacokinetic properties. One such potent and selective PFM, RTY-822, was dosed orally at 30 and 100 mg/kg once daily for 6 weeks in a rat adenine diet VC model with modified diet composition and supplemented with calcitriol dosing 3x/week. Calcium levels were assessed in the aorta and femoral artery using mass spectrometry and calcification was visualized via von Kossa histological staining. PPi levels were measured in terminal plasma samples and liver ABCC6 expression was measured by western blot. Kidney function was assessed using serum creatinine, urea, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). KIM-1 levels were determined in plasma and in kidney tissue lysates.
Results
RTY-822, a potent and selective ABCC6 PFM, was identified using the Rectify platform. RTY-822 demonstrated significant and correlated increases in ABCC6 protein and PPi levels in PHHs. Rats on the modified adenine diet for 6 weeks showed decreased kidney function and significant VC in both the aorta and femoral artery. 100 mg/kg RTY-822 significantly reduced VC in both vascular beds as determined by both types of calcium measurement. RTY-822 also dose-dependently decreased serum creatinine and urea levels and increased eGFR, indicating improved kidney function. RTY-822 dosing led to reduced KIM-1 levels in the plasma and increased KIM-1 in the kidney, consistent with less kidney damage and corroborating the improved kidney function measurements.
Conclusion
Rectify's platform enabled rapid identification of compounds with the potential to increase ABCC6 protein and PPi levels in vitro, including in translationally relevant PHHs. Compound dosing in vivo led to a significant reduction in VC and significant improvements in kidney function in a modified CKD model, thereby demonstrating the importance of ABCC6 in the progression of VC-associated with CKD.

RTY-822, a potent and selective ABCC6 PFM, was identified using the Rectify platform. RTY-822 demonstrated significant and correlated increases in ABCC6 protein and PPi levels in PHHs. title: #2123 Impact of a plant-based food basket on uremic toxins, dietary patterns and carbon footprint in patients with chronic kidney disease
authors: Valeria Cecchini; Olof Heimbürger; Alice Sabatino; Bengt Lindholm; Peter Stenvinkel; Carla Maria Avesani
abstract:
Background and Aims
Plant-based diets (PBD) have been recommended to patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) stages 3 to 5, due their potential metabolic benefits. Among these is the reduction in the production of uremic toxins by the gut microbiota, including trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO), p-cresyl sulfate (PCS), and indoxyl sulfate (IS). Additionally, evidence suggests that higher consumption of ultra-processed food (UPFs) is associated with elevated levels of circulating PCS and IS, likely due to their influence on gut microbiota composition and activity. Another important benefit of adopting a PBD is lower greenhouse gas emissions (GHGEs), which is aligned with environmentally sustainable diets. Given these benefits, we aimed to evaluate changes in UPF consumption, uremic toxins’ concentration and UPF metabolomic markers in plasma, including caffeine and saccharin, and GHGEs before and after a medically tailored meal intervention with plant-based food baskets. This is a sub-analysis of a feasibility clinical trial conducted in patients with CKD and hyperkalemia at inclusion who received sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) to achieve acceptable plasma potassium levels.
Method
Data were derived from a six-week feasibility one-arm clinical trial (HELPFUL Trial, ID: NCT04207203) involving 26 patients with CKD (stages 4 and 5), not on dialysis and with baseline plasma potassium between 5.1 and 6.5 mmol/L. During the initial 3 weeks, patients followed a low-protein, low-potassium diet alongside SZC administration. From week 3 to 6, patients received plant-based food baskets once a week delivered to their homes. Dietary intake was assessed using 24-hour food recalls collected at baseline (week 0), week 3 and week 6, and classified according to the NOVA classification. Food intake was further categorised into plant-based (e.g., starches, cereals, fruits, vegetables, beans, nuts, and seeds) and animal-based (e.g., red and processed meat, poultry, eggs, fish, and dairy) components. The associated GHGEs were estimated using the RISE food climate database. The uremic toxins, TMAO, PCS and IS and metabolomic markers of UPFs (caffeine and saccharin) were assessed at week 0, 3 and 6. Statistical analyses were performed using Friedman's test for repeated measure to evaluate changes over time.
Results
A significant reduction in UPF consumption (P = 0.024) was observed over the intervention period. Post-hoc analyses revealed a significant change between week 0 and 6 (P = 0.008). GHGE analyses showed no significant changes in the consumption of either plant-based or animal-based foods (Table 1). However, a non-significant decrease in GHGEs from animal-based food consumption was observed between weeks 3 and 6. No significant changes were observed in levels of TMAO (P = 0.23), PCS (P = 0.76) and IS (P = 0.24) over time. Similarly, no significant differences were found in UPF metabolomic markers (caffeine P = 0.96; saccharin P = 0.20).
Conclusion
The implementation of a plant-based food basket in patients with CKD led to a significant reduction in UPF intake, highlighting the potential for dietary interventions to encourage healthier food choices. However, no significant changes were observed in GHGEs, uremic toxins’ and UPF metabolomic markers’ levels. As this is a feasibility trial, the findings suggest dietary modifications improved quality, but larger samples and additional strategies may be needed to reduce GHGEs and uremic toxins. Future research should explore long-term adherence and gut microbiota modulation to better clarify its role in kidney health.

title: #303 Unraveling the biology of adversity: proteomic and metabolomic insights into socioeconomic disparities in kidney disease
authors: Insa Schmidt; Aditya Surapaneni; Lawrence Appel; Casey Rebholz; Tessa Novick; Eugene Rhee; Josef Coresh; Sushrut S Waikar; Morgan Grams
abstract:
Background and Aims
Socioeconomic deprivation is a key contributor to chronic kidney disease (CKD), and both disproportionately affect people of color. The mechanisms linking socioeconomic deprivation to adverse health outcomes in CKD remain underexplored.
Method
We tested associations of 4,091 plasma proteins and 605 metabolites with measures of socioeconomic status (SES), including education and income, in individuals from the Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC) study. Cross-sectional associations were conducted using race-stratified (Black and non-Black) multivariable-adjusted linear regression models in 3,247 participants with available proteomic (SomaScan) and 1,800 with available metabolomic (Broad Institute) data. Cox proportional hazard models assessed the relationships between SES-associated proteins and metabolites and adverse clinical outcomes, including kidney disease progression, cardiovascular disease (CVD), congestive heart failure (CHF), and death.
Results
Among participants with proteomic and metabolomic measurements, 59% (40% female, mean eGFR 46.0 ± 16.2 ml/min/1.73 m²) and 58% (39% female, mean eGFR 46.1 ± 16.6 ml/min/1.73 m²), respectively, self-identified as Black. After Bonferroni correction, higher levels of protein C (PROC) and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), along with lower levels of transcobalamin-1 (TCN1), adenosine deaminase CECR1 (CECR1), and triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 1 (TREM1), were associated with higher SES in both Black and non-Black individuals (Fig. 1A and B). The directionality was consistent across groups for all proteins, although CECR1 did not reach statistical significance in non-Black individuals (Fig. 1B). Among metabolites, higher levels of phosphatidylethanolamines (PE) C34:0 and C38:2, as well as sphingomyelin (SM) C14:0, were associated with higher SES in Black individuals (Fig. 1C), while C34:0 PE and C14:0 SM also showed concordant associations in non-Black individuals (Fig. 1D). In outcome analyses, proteins and metabolites associated with SES showed opposite associations with risks of outcomes (kidney disease progression, CVD, CHF, and death); proteins and metabolites associated with lower SES were associated with higher risk and vice versa (Fig. 1E).
Conclusion
Large-scale omics investigations reveal proteins and metabolites involved in inflammation, lipid metabolism, and vascular health that are associated with SES and future disease risk, providing insights into the biological pathways linking socioeconomic deprivation to adverse health outcomes in CKD.

title: #2319 Brain changes in a long-term rat model of chronic kidney disease (CKD)
authors: Irene Cortijo; Juliana Boukhaled; Jonas Laget; Pascaline Fontès; Seniha Pehlivan; Marie-Christine Lebart; Flore Duranton; Françoise Trousse; Fabrice Raynaud; Nathalie Gayrard; Anne Marcilhac; Angel Argiles Ciscart
abstract:
Background and Aims
An increasing number of studies demonstrate a significant association between chronic kidney disease (CKD) and a higher risk of cognitive impairment. This involves several interconnected mechanisms between kidney and brain, particularly evident in end-stage renal disease. Uremic toxin accumulation, including neurotoxic compounds like indoxyl sulfate, could contribute to oxidative stress and cellular dysfunction in the brain. This can lead to modifications in glial cells that can impair their protective functions and potentially exacerbating neuronal damage. The blood-brain barrier can be disrupted, allowing harmful substances to infiltrate brain tissue, thus further promoting neurological dysfunction. The aim of this study was to evaluate brain morphology changes and pathological processes induced by CKD, using a long-term 5/6 nephrectomy rat model to investigate potential mechanisms involved in such pathology.
Method
Twelve-week-old Sprague Dawley rats were randomly assigned to undergo either 5/6Nx or sham surgery. Twenty-four weeks after surgery, renal function and brain histopathological changes were assessed. Plasma and brain tissue levels of indoxyl sulfate were measured using high performance liquid chromatography coupled with Triple Quad mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Brain modifications were evaluated through western blot analysis of tight junction protein Claudin-5, Perls’ Prussian blue staining for cerebral microbleeds, and immunostaining for GFAP and Iba1 to assess perivascular astrocytes and microglial cell densities, respectively.
Results
5/6Nx rats developed CKD, evidenced by increased plasma levels of creatinine (P = 0.0402) and urea (P = 0.0043) (Fig. 1). The presence of macrophage infiltration in 5/6Nx rats, highlighted by CD68 staining, was noticed as a sign of inflammation of the renal tissue. Indoxyl sulfate levels were elevated in both plasma (P = 0.0519) and brain tissue (P = 0.0063) of the 5/6Nx group compared to the sham group. Notable brain modifications, including disruption of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) were observed in CKD group: (i) reduced expression of the tight junction protein Claudin-5 (P = 0.0087), (ii) appearance of cerebral microbleeds, (iii) decreased density of perivascular astrocytes (P = 0.0442) and microglial cells (P = 0.0029).
Conclusion
Our results demonstrate significant CKD-induced brain tissue alterations. This provide evidences in favor of an increased risk of cognitive impairment associated with CKD. To further investigate these findings, potential cognitive deficits should be evaluated using behavioral tests, which would help to determine whether the observed brain tissue changes can be linked to specific cognitive impairments as observed with patients.

title: #2823 Association between nephrotoxic drugs and the development of chronic kidney disease based on french real-world data
authors: Camille Boissiere; Sahar Bayat; Astrid Bacle; Guillaume Bouzille; Mathilde Bories
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is primarily associated with cardiovascular conditions such as hypertension (HTN) and diabetes. However, the impact of nephrotoxic drugs on the development of CKD remains difficult to assess due to multiple factors, including the slow progression of the disease, polypharmacy, particularly in elderly patients, and a lack of data.
Given the constant increase in CKD prevalence and the growing trend of polypharmacy, our objective is to explore the iatrogenic impact of nephrotoxic drugs on the onset of CKD using real-world data.
Method
This retrospective study is based on the linkage of hospital data alias PMSI (Program for the Medicalization of Information Systems) and the French National Health Data System (SNDS). The SNDS provides information on outpatient drug consumption, while hospital data include biological test results. These two datasets were matched using common information from the PMSI, such as ICD-10 (International Classification of Diseases) diagnoses and medical procedures.
We included non-dialysis adult patients hospitalized between 2015 and 2018 who had at least one creatinine measurement. Patients were categorized based on their renal status: healthy patients (without CKD or acute kidney injury) and patients who developed CKD (normal GFR at least once followed by an ICD-10 diagnosis of CKD or three months of clearance < 60 mL/min/1.73m²). Age and sex were identified, along with other comorbidities influencing CKD, such as HTN, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and obesity, identified using ICD-10 codes and the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classification of outpatient medications.
The nephrotoxic drugs studied included drugs known to induce CKD, such as lithium, antiretrovirals (ARVs), fluindione, tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), triptans, tolvaptan, proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Drug exposure was assessed in a binary manner (exposed/unexposed) over the year preceding the first clearance measurement for healthy patients and over the year preceding the onset of CKD for patients who developed chronic kidney disease.
Comorbidities by renal status were analyzed using logistic regression. Subsequently, the impact of each nephrotoxic drug was assessed using logistic regression adjusted for significant comorbidities, with an alpha risk of 5%.
Results
The study included 244,937 healthy patients (mean age: 63.5 years, 55% female) and 238,676 patients who developed CKD (mean age: 71.6 years, 40% female).
According to the preliminary results, comorbidities were more frequent among patients who developed CKD, including HTN (82%), dyslipidemia (48%), diabetes (25%), and obesity (7%). Age was a significant risk factor for CKD development, with a notably higher risk in patients over 75 years old (OR = 10.31 [95% CI: 9.6-11.1]). The total number of nephrotoxic drugs was a significant factor in renal function decline (OR = 1.1 [95% CI: 1.0–1.1]). Among the studied drugs, those with a significant impact on CKD development included ARV 2 (OR = 5.4 [95% CI: 3.9–7.4]), ARV 1 (OR = 3.2 [95% CI: 2.5–4.1]), TKIs (OR = 2.6 [95% CI: 2.2–3.0]), fluindione (OR = 2.2 [95% CI: 2.1–2.3]), lithium (OR = 1.9 [95% CI: 1.6–2.4]), and PPIs (OR = 1.2 [95% CI: 1.1–1.2]). However, in this study, certain drugs such as NSAIDs and triptans were not significantly associated with CKD development. The complete results of the statistical models are presented in Table 1.
Conclusion
Thanks to full visibility of the patient pathway from outpatient care to hospital settings, we conclude that the significant factors contributing to CKD development include comorbidities such as age, HTN, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and obesity. The nephrotoxic drugs with a significant impact are ARVs, TKIs, lithium, fluindione, and PPIs, which are widely prescribed on a population level. Ongoing studies aim to investigate the relationship between CKD development and drug exposure quantified using the cumulative Defined Daily Dose (DDD), which represents the assumed average maintenance dose per year for a drug used in its primary indication.

title: #1921 The shadow of renal dysfunction on guideline-directed medical therapy in HFrEF: insights from a cardio-nephrology perspective in Eastern Europe
authors: Adelina Mihăescu; Viviana Ivan; Luciana Marc; Felix Mihai Maralescu; Lazar Chisavu; Nicu Olariu; Bernadett Csomai; Adrian Apostol; Andreea Gostian; Adalbert Schiller
abstract:
Background and Aims
Although guideline directed medical therapy (GDMT) in HFrEF, consisting of the 4 pillars of treatment (ARNI/RAASi, B-blockers, MRAs, SGLT2i) which significantly reduce cardiovascular mortality and hospitalisation is accepted by the cardiologist as mandatory, the real-world data show a lesser use of the forementioned medication. Severe kidney dysfunction can be an impediment for using 3 out of 4 of the HFrEF pillars (a.i. ARNI/RAASi, MRAs, SGLT2i) although the same medication classes are the mainstay of nephroprotection.
The AIM of our study was to evaluate the impact of renal dysfunction on the choice of treatment, the inhospital mortality and the outcome of a cohort of consecutive patients with known HFrEF admitted in the cardiology ward of an emergency hospital in Romania, between Jan 2022 and Dec 2023.
Method
We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study on all patients diagnosed with HFrEF who were consecutively admitted to the cardiology clinic of the Emergency Clinical Hospital in Timișoara for heart failure decompensation between Jan 2022 and Dec 2023. We collected data from the medical records: demographic, medical history, lab tests (creatinine at discharge, serum K, CRP, serum albumin, LDLc, TGL, glycaemia), in-hospital mortality, hospitalization days and treatment at discharge on which we performed statistical analyses.
Results
In the entire cohort of 439 patients with HFrEF we found high prevalence of CKD (34,2%), diabetes (37%) and stroke (18,2%). AKI was present in 12,8% of the entire cohort and in 57,1% patients with previous CKD. The cardiac insufficiency was severe, with a mean ejection fraction (EF) of 29. Overall in-hospital mortality was 3,6% (16 subjects), and 4% among the CKD patients.
Main variables, calculated as mean ± SD, are: age 70 ± 12, hospitalisation days 7.3 ± 3.8, 13 ± 2.3 Hb mg/dl, creatinine 1.3 ± 0.97 mg/dl, eGFR 66± 27 ml/min, K 4.2 ± 0.62 mmol/l, serum Albumin 3.7 ± 0.67 g/dl, CRP 34 ± 52 mg/dl, LDL 91 ±38 mg/dl, TG 117 ± 60 mg/dl, glycaemia 122 ± 42 mg/dl.
Between 2022 and 2023 there was an obvious increase in the number of patients treated according to GDMT, from predominantly 2 pillars (betablockers and spironolactone) to 3 pillars (increase in RASi/ARNI use). The proportion of patients treated by each class of medication changed from 2022 to 2023 as follows: bblocker 92,8 to 89,3%; RASi/ARNI 50,4 to 54%; SGLT2i 14,4 to 55,3%; sprinolactone 72,7 to 80,7%.
We split the study population in 2 groups, CKD patients and non-CKD patients, and we analysed if there are any significant differences between them. (Table 1).
Conclusion
In our cohort of HFrEF patients we emphasized the high rate of chronic renal involvement. Although 3 (RAASi, MRA, SGLT2i) of the GDMT pillars recommended for these patients are the same type of medications that offer nephroprotection, our real world study proved that the presence of CKD is the main factor that prevents cardiologists from prescribing them.
Hyperkalemia was not significantly higer in th CKD patients, neither was in-hospital death, but CDK patients had a higher risk of AKI. There was an obvious increase in the number of pillars of GDMT for HFrEF from 2022 to 2023, mainly on the base of SGLT2i use. The presence of chronic kidney dysfunction should be a signal for the mandatory use of cardio-nephroprotective drugs and not a hindrance in the treatment of HFrEF patients.

We split the study population in 2 groups, CKD patients and non-CKD patients, and we analysed if there are any significant differences between them. (Table 1).

title: #1942 Novel therapeutic for diabetic kidney disease through targeting Lp-PLA2 in immune cells and damaged renal parenchymal cell
authors: Ruting Zheng; Hongyan Shi; Meihua Huang; Li Wang; Xiafei Huang; Lanyun Jin; Fei Wang; Shuai Li; Haowen Huang; Jie Zhou; Li You; Jun Xue
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diabetic kidney disease (DKD), a highly prevalent form of chronic kidney injury, is characterized by intricate mechanisms involving inflammation, metabolism and haemodynamics. Currently, the available therapeutic interventions fall short of effectively halting the progression of patients towards end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Lp-PLA2 (Lipoprotein-associated phospholipase A2) is an enzyme that participates in regulating the immune response, cellular senescence and metabolism. Under the pathological conditions of DKD, significantly elevated levels of Lp-PLA2 have been detected in the blood, and these levels are positively correlated with the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR). In this study, we provide a series of comprehensive evidence supporting Lp-PLA2 as a promising potential therapeutic target for DKD. Our analysis draws upon three distinct perspectives including preclinical studies using animal models, renal biopsy section analysis, and an investigator-initiated clinical trial.
Methods
The efficacy of the proprietary Lp-PLA2 inhibitor SR1375 on renal function were tested in a mice model of diabetic nephropathy (HFD-Unx-STZ-DKD model) and a rat model of hypertensive nephropathy (DOCA-salt-HTN model).
Localization and quantification of Lp-PLA2 were analyzed in renal biopsy samples (n = 6) from DKD patients. The results were then correlated with renal function indices.
A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled investigator-initiated trial (IIT) involving 3 multiple dosing cohorts (1, 3, 10 mg) of SR1375 for patients with DKD is currently underway in Huashan Hospital in China. An interim analysis was conducted in 12 subjects who completed 12 weeks of drug administration and data collection.
Results
In the animal models of both diabetic nephropathy and hypertensive nephropathy, elevated plasma Lp-PLA2 enzyme activity was detected. After administration of SR1375, a significant inhibition of plasma Lp-PLA2 enzyme activity was achieved. Concurrently, the UACR and UAE were substantially reduced in both models, with the highest remission rate reaching up to 65.5%.
In the kidneys of DKD patients, the mRNA levels of renal PLA2G7(Lp-PLA2) were elevated. PLA2G7 was localized not only in infiltrating immune cells but also in damaged renal parenchymal cells. Moreover, the levels of PLA2G7 in the kidney showed a positive correlation with UACR.
The interim analyses of the IIT revealed the following key findings: SR1375 demonstrated a favorable safety and PK profile in DKD patients, and in subjects with UACR >100 mg/g*Cr at baseline, those who received SR1375 treatment for 12 weeks showed an average 49.7% reduction in UACR (n = 5). In contrast, only an average 17.5% reduction was observed in the placebo group (n = 2).
Conclusions
Our results suggest a functional role for Lp-PLA2 in the pathogenesis of DKD, providing preclinical and clinical proof-of-concept for Lp-PLA2 inhibitors as a novel therapeutic approach for patients with DKD. A Phase 2 clinical trial in DKD patients is scheduled to be conducted in the second half of 2025.

title: #436 Discordant results between creatinine- and cystatin C-based equations for estimating glomerular filtration rate: the equation matters
authors: Pierre Delanaye; Hans Pottel
abstract:
Background and Aims
Discordant results between cystatin C and creatinine to estimate glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) are an important medical issue. It remains unresolved which equation should be used when eGFR estimations are discordant.
Method
In this cross-sectional analysis, we included 15,485 participants from 17 studies (including White Europeans, n = 12; White Americans, n = 1, Black Europeans, n = 2; Black Africans, n = 2) with measured GFR by clearance of an exogenous marker (reference method), serum creatinine, and cystatin C. We studied the proportion of discordant results defined as an absolute (>15 mL/min/1.73 m²) or relative (>20%) difference between creatinine-based eGFR (eGFRcrea) and cystatin C-based eGFR (eGFRcys) using different equations (Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology (CKD-EPI), European Kidney Function Consortium (EKFC), and re-expressed Lund-Malmö (r-LMR)). We also researched for the best estimating equations to be used in subjects with concordant or discordant results to estimate measured GFR.
Results
In the total cohort, the proportion of subjects with discordant results (absolute or relative) was larger for CKD-EPI (35.1 and 40.6%) than for EKFC (21.9 and 31.7%) or r-LMR (22.8 and 32.8%) equations. Among discrepant results, the proportion of eGFRcys<eGFRcrea was significantly higher than the proportion of eGFRcrea<eGFRcys for the CKD-EPI equations, whereas the occurrence of discrepancy was similar in the two discrepant groups for EKFC or r-LMR (Fig. 1). For EKFC and r-LMR equations, but not for CKD-EPI, the equation combining creatinine and cystatin C was consistently closest to measured GFR in discrepant groups.
Conclusion
Based on the lower discrepancy proportion, the better balance between eGFRcrea and eGFRcys, and the better concordance with measured GFR, the EKFC and r-LMR equations should be preferred over the CKD-EPI to estimate GFR.
