title: #1491 Low rate of infusion-related reactions and high treatment adherence with obinutuzumab in patients with active lupus nephritis: analysis of the NOBILITY and REGENCY studies
authors: Rachel B Jones; Brad Rovin; Himanshi Sehgal; Petra Kirchner; Bongin Yoo; Imran Hassan; Thomas Schindler; Elsa Martins; William F Pendergraft; Jay Garg; Edward Vital; Liz Lightstone
abstract:
Background and Aims
The randomised, placebo-controlled Phase II NOBILITY (NCT02550652) and Phase III REGENCY (NCT04221477) studies demonstrated superiority of obinutuzumab plus standard therapy over placebo plus standard therapy in achieving complete renal responses in patients with active lupus nephritis (LN) while maintaining an acceptable safety profile. Obinutuzumab is approved in certain haemato-oncology indications, and infusion-related reactions (IRRs) are a known risk (Table 1). Here, we characterised the IRR profile of obinutuzumab in participants from the NOBILITY and REGENCY studies.
Method
NOBILITY and REGENCY randomised adults with biopsy-proven active LN 1:1 to receive placebo (physiological saline) or obinutuzumab plus standard therapy (mycophenolate mofetil plus glucocorticoids). All patients met the 1997 American College of Rheumatology classification criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus and had biopsy-proven proliferative LN. To reduce the risk of IRRs, patients were premedicated with methylprednisolone (80 mg intravenously [IV]), acetaminophen (650–1000 mg) orally and an antihistamine orally or IV.
IRRs were defined as any adverse event occurring during or within 24 hours after IV infusion of obinutuzumab or placebo and judged by study investigators to be related to the infusion. Systemic IRRs were considered adverse events of special interest (AESIs). NOBILITY randomised patients 1:1 to placebo or obinutuzumab (1000 mg: Day 1, Weeks 2, 24, 26) plus standard therapy. REGENCY randomised patients 1:1 to placebo or obinutuzumab (1000 mg: Day 1, Weeks 2, 24, 26, ± 50, 52) plus standard therapy. In NOBILITY, the primary endpoint was at Week 52 and patients were followed up until Week 104; in REGENCY, the primary endpoint was at Week 76. NOBILITY and REGENCY IRR data were pooled through Week 76 for safety assessment.
Results
Overall, 200 patients received obinutuzumab for a total of 944 infusions. AESIs of IRRs were numerically greater in the obinutuzumab arm (30 patients [15.0%]) compared with the placebo arm (21 patients [10.9%]) (Table 2). In the majority of cases, IRRs were mild to moderate (Grade 1–2) and managed by slowing or temporarily halting the infusion. IRRs in both arms primarily occurred at the first infusion, with decreasing incidence of IRRs at subsequent infusions (Table 2). All Grade 3–4 IRRs (n = 4) occurred during/after the first or second infusion (Table 1). IRRs led to a temporary interruption of the infusion in more patients in the obinutuzumab arm (13 patients [6.5%]) than the placebo arm (2 patients [1.0%]). Only 1 patient in the obinutuzumab arm had an IRR leading to discontinuation of study treatment, which was a serious Grade 4 event related to respiratory distress that resolved after ≈1 hour without any reported intervention. All other IRRs in both arms were nonserious.
Conclusion
Although the incidence of IRRs was higher in patients receiving obinutuzumab compared with placebo, the overall risk of IRRs was low, and IRRs also occurred in the placebo arm. In the majority of cases, IRRs were mild to moderate and managed by slowing or temporarily halting the infusion. IRRs primarily occurred at the first infusion in both arms and only 1 patient in the obinutuzumab arm had an IRR leading to discontinuation of study treatment. Furthermore, the rate of IRRs and high-grade IRRs associated with obinutuzumab in patients with active LN was considerably lower than what was previously observed in patients with haematologic malignancies. These observations suggest that infusions were related to cell killing rather than immunogenicity, with patients with LN having lower numbers of CD20-positive target cells. These data, along with the acceptable safety profile of obinutuzumab, support the possibility of increased treatment adherence in patients with LN.

abstract:
Background and Aims
The quadruple therapy has become the cornerstone of treatment for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). It consists in the introduction of treatment with angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRA) and the sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, with the aim to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death and worsening HF in patients with HFrEF. However, there is limited evidence to guide the medical treatment in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (ACKD) (FG < 30 ml/min), often excluded in clinical trials, and due to the challenges that a reduced kidney function represent.
We aim to analyze the changes in kidney function and left ventricular ejection fraction, after starting the quadruple therapy as prognostic modifying treatment in patients with ACKD and HFrEF.
Method
Single-center, observational, prospective study assessing clinical and analytical parameters, mainly renal function, and echocardiographic parameters in patients with ACKD and HFrEF visited in our Cardiorenal Unit for one year (June 2023-June 2024). Medication titration was performed according to clinical criteria and following our titration protocols. Each visit included clinical and analytical assessment and echocardiogram was performed at least once before and after introducing the prognostic modifying drugs.
Results
22 patients were included, 4 of them did not complete the titration (2 due to rejection of the proposed treatments, and 2 died of cardiac causes). From the remaining 18, 15 (83.3%) were men aged 73 (40–89 years, SD 11.51). Heart disease main etiologies were non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (8, 44%) and ischemic heart disease (7, 38.9%). CKD etiologies were: attributed to a combination of hypertension and cardiorenal syndrome (12, 66.7%), glomerular diseases (3, 16.7%), and diabetic kidney disease (2, 11.1%). Six participants were on renal replacement therapy (hemodialysis: 3 patients, kidney transplant: 2 patients and peritoneal dialysis: 1 patient). Upon titration, 83.3% received ARNI, 100% beta-blockers, 94.4% iSGLT2 and 61.1% MRA. The most frequent adverse events were hypotension (16.7%), hyperkalemia (11.1%) and the combination of both (11.1%). Ten patients (55.6%) experienced no adverse events. The mean initial FEV was 34.89 (20–40, SD 4.66) and the final one was 46.50 (34–58, SD 6.28). (P ˂ 0.001). There was no statistically significant difference between initial and final renal function (P = 0.413)
Conclusion
We found that despite the challenges, it is possible to introduce quadruple therapy even in patients with ACKD with a good safety profile and without significant changes in kidney function, achieving an improvement in left ventricular ejection fraction. Cardiorenal units are necessary for the close monitoring and follow-up of these patients and thus guarantee the results.

title: #3895 Exploring the impact of medication adherence, beliefs, perceptions, and psychological factors on blood pressure control in elderly CKD patients
authors: Bülent Demirelli; Murat Tugcu; Mehmet Koc
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a prevalent clinical issue in elderly patients, contributing to increased morbidity and mortality. As life expectancy continues to rise on a global scale, there is an increasing prevalence of comorbidities and risk factors, such as hypertension. The present study aims to investigate the relationship between medication adherence, beliefs, and perceptions, the frequency of somatic symptoms, depression, and anxiety, and their role in blood pressure control in elderly CKD patients.
Method
The demographic data of 95 old patients diagnosed with chronic kidney disease were collated. The Medication Adherence Report Scale (MARS-5), the Beliefs About Medicine Questionnaire (BMQ), the Brief Illness Perception Questionnaire (B-IPQ) and Patient Health Questionnaire–Somatic, Anxiety, and Depressive Symptoms (PHQ-SADS) was employed to assess medication beliefs, illness perception, and somatic and psychiatric symptoms. Furthermore, kidney function tests from one year prior to and one year following the administration of the questionnaires were recorded.
Results
Of the 95 patients, 29 (30.5%) were female, and the mean age was 68.9 ± 6.1 years. According to PHQ-SADS, 34 patients (35.8%) exhibited moderate-to-severe somatic symptoms, 49 patients (51.6%) displayed symptoms of depression, and 23 patients (24.2%) demonstrated moderate-to-severe anxiety. Blood pressure control was achieved in 56 patients (59%). In patients with blood pressure control, fewer somatic symptoms (69.5% vs. 30.5%, P = 0.011), less depression (71.1% vs. 28.9%), and fewer instances of polypharmacy (28.9% vs. 71.1%) were observed. No significant correlation was identified between medication adherence, medication beliefs, illness perception, and blood pressure regulation. Furthermore, the patients with a decrease in GFR of less than -1 mL/min showed better blood pressure control (Table 1).
Conclusion
Despite the high rate of non-compliance with medication observed in this study, it is crucial to note that factors beyond medication adherence, illness perceptions and beliefs about medications, such as psychological health and somatic symptoms, may play a pivotal role in the management of blood pressure in elderly CKD patients. It is important to pay attention to polypharmacy and drug interactions, to control somatic symptoms such as pain, fatigue, nausea and to prevent depression in order to control blood pressure in this demographic.

title: #1855 Hemoglobin increases faster at high altitude in CKD patients treated with SGLT2 inhibitors: the SGaLTitude study
authors: Mabel Aoun; Michel Jadoul; Maize Ducret; William Hanf; Christopher Loens; Magdalena Madero; Hans-Joachim Anders
abstract:
Background and Aims
SGLT2 inhibitors increase hemoglobin levels and may cause erythrocytosis. We hypothesize that patients living at high altitude might be more prone to this effect. This study aims to understand the hematological response of patients with CKD living at altitude and treated with SGLT2 inhibitors.
Methods
This is a retrospective multicenter study that included patients with CKD living in the Alps Mountains, compared to a control group living at sea level. Patients were included if they were treated with SGLT2 inhibitors for more than 3 months between October 2022 and October 2024. We excluded patients who did not have hemoglobin measured before and after initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors, or if they had their hemoglobin measured during a hospital admission. Erythrocytosis was defined as Hb>16 g/dL. We used independent t-test to compare the change in hemoglobin from baseline to 3, 6 and 12 months between the altitude group and the control group. Chi-square test was used to compare categorical variables. Multivariable linear regression analysis was used to assess the association of altitude with hemoglobin change after adjustment for demographics, diabetes, baseline ferritin and ESA and iron intake. This study got the approval of the IRB of Foch Hospital.
Results
A total of 118 patients were included, 59 at sea level and 59 living at ≥500 meters (min 500, max 1800, median 700 m). Mean age was 72.5 years and 79.7% were males in both groups. Diabetes was present in 62.7% at sea level and 49.2% at altitude, RAS inhibitors were used in 95% at sea level and 91.5% at altitude. Anticoagulants or antiplatelets were used in 64.4% at sea level and 67.8% at altitude. Median eGFR at baseline was 37 (33, 47) mL/min/1.73 m2 at sea level and 38 (30, 47) mL/min/1.73 m2 at altitude. Median proteinuria at baseline was 550 mg/g of creatinine at sea level and 470 mg/g at altitude. Mean hemoglobin at baseline was 13.4 ±1.7 g/dL at sea level and 13.6 ±1.9 g/dL at altitude. Median ferritin at baseline was 136 (71, 219) ng/mL at sea level and 138 (79, 243) ng/mL at altitude. Erythrocytosis at baseline was present in 10.2% of patients at sea level and 8.5 % at altitude. During follow-up, 4 patients at sea level and 2 patients at altitude needed ESA and 12 patients at sea level and 9 patients at altitude received iron therapy. Ferritin <100 ng/mL was significantly more prevalent at 6 months at sea level compared to altitude (P = 0.003). The progression of hemoglobin over 12 months is illustrated in Fig. 1. Using multivariable linear regression analysis, living at altitude was an independent risk factor for a more significant change in hemoglobin levels at 6 months (Table 1). Erythrocytosis at 6 months was found in 10.2% at sea level and 16.9% at altitude (Fig. 2). There was no thrombotic event among all patients.
Conclusion
Based on this study, patients with CKD, treated with SGLT2 inhibitors, have a faster increase in hemoglobin levels at 6 months if they are living at ≥500 m compared to patients at sea level. Further investigation is required to understand the hematological response of patients living at higher altitudes.

title: #1813 High glucose worsens calcium deposition and osteoblastic differentiation induced by high phosphate treatment in human aortic endothelial cells
authors: Paola Ciceri; Martina Molinaro; Mario Gennaro Cozzolino
abstract:
Background and Aims
Vascular calcification (VC) is one of the main causes of arterial stiffness that is responsible for the high morbidity and mortality risk due to cardiovascular disease in diabetic and chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients.VC in diabetes and CKD affects tunica media, nevertheless endothelium seems to be involved as endothelial dysfunction has been identified as a non-traditional risk factor in CKD. We therefore studied the effect of high-phosphate and high-glucose on endothelial cells dysfunction and calcification.
Method
Human aortic endothelial cells (HAECs) were treated with, high phosphate (Pi) (3 or 3.5 mM), and/or high-glucose (10 mM, 20 mM, 30 mM) for 7 days. Alizarin Red staining and de-staining was performed to highlight calcium deposition. RT-PCR and WB were performed to evaluate gene and protein expression.
Results
High-Pi induced calcium deposition in HAECs that was further exacerbated by high-glucose concentration-dependently after 7 days (fig. 1A). High-Pi induced a significative elevation in gene expression of osteoblastic markers RUNX-2, BMP-2 and MGP (Fig. 1C) further significantly increased by co-treatment with high-glucose (1.8 ± 0.2 vs 2.3 ± 0.2; 1.9 ± 0.2 vs 2.8 ± 0.2; 1.9 ± 0.2 vs 2.9 ± 0.4; Pi vs Pi+high-glucose; RUNX2, BMP2, MGP; rel.exp.; Fig. 1B). Preliminary data on endothelial to mesenchymal transition (EndMT) showed that it was induced by high-Pi further exacerbated by high-glucose both at gene and protein level at day 3, before osteoblastic differentiation and calcium deposition occurred.
Conclusion
High phosphate levels induce endothelial calcification with deposition of calcium phosphate crystals and osteoblastic differentiation further exacerbated by high-glucose. Moreover, preliminary data showed that high-Pi induces EndMT, anticipating calcification, a process exacerbated by high-glucose.

title: #1807 Tumor necrosis factor alpha and high phosphate increase platelet adhesion, by modifying endothelial anti-thrombotic properties
authors: Paola Ciceri; Martina Molinaro; Claudia Ghali; Antonella Fioretti; Mariangela Scavone; Gianmarco Podda; Mario Gennaro Cozzolino
abstract:
Background and Aims
Endothelium constitutes an antithrombotic barrier that promotes the blood flow, but when endothelial balance is disturbed, vascular disease may initiate favouring platelet adhesion, the process underlying the thrombotic disease. It is known that inflammation can impair antithrombotic endothelial features, whereas the role of high phosphate load and hyperglycemia have not been investigated yet. Therefore, we investigated the role of inflammation and high-phosphate (Pi) induced alterations on endothelial cells in the platelet adhesion process.
Method
We incubated primary human aortic endothelial cells (HAEC) treated either with 50 ng/ml TNFα (18 h) or 3 mM Pi (7 days) with platelet-rich plasma (30 min) of healthy volunteers. Adhesion was quantified by fluorescence, staining platelets with an anti-CD-61 antibody and HAEC with the vital dye Orange tracker
Results
We set up a static model of platelet-endothelium adhesion, where we found that platelets adhered significantly more on TNFα treated cells compared to control endothelium (0.093 ± 0.023 vs. 0.189 ± 0.039; ctr vs TNFα; % platelet coverage; P < 0.05). These data were further confirmed in parallel microfluidic experiments. Moreover, high glucose (30 mM) was able to exacerbate platelet adhesion both in static and microfluidic experiments. High-Pi treated HAEC became able to deposit calcium phosphate crystals, thus inducing endothelial cells calcification. We incubated calcified HAEC with PRP finding a 2-fold increase in platelet adhesion compared to control HAEC (0.64 ± 0.10 vs 1.12 ± 0.18; ctr vs Pi; % platelet coverage; P < 0.05). Moreover, by scanning and transmission electron microscopy, we could observe platelet activation on inflamed and calcified endothelial cells.
Conclusion
In this study we found that in an in vitro cellular model TNFα and high phosphate are able to modify the antithrombotic endothelial cell features, resulting in increased platelet adhesion. Moreover, adhesion on inflamed endothelial cells is exacerbated by hyperglycemia. These findings may pave the way to better elucidate the mechanism responsible for an increased thrombotic risk driven by microinflammation, and hyperphosphatemia in diabetic and chronic kidney disease patients.

title: #532 Optimal timing for dialysis preparation in CKD; modeling with multiple linear regression
authors: Geo Neul Park; Seon Min Kim; Yoon Won Choi; Jin Kuk Kim; Mooyong Park; Soo Jeong Choi; Byung Chul Yu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Determining the optimal timing for preparing dialysis is a clinical challenge. The complexity arises because the progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD) to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) is influenced by diverse factors, requiring consideration of both kidney function and clinical findings. Despite extensive research over the past decades to predict for dialysis initiation, emergency hemodialysis (HD) using a catheter is still the most common way to start renal replacement therapy (RRT) in ESKD patients. Unplanned dialysis initiation is associated with increased morbidity and mortality compared to planned initiation with prior preparation. Therefore, predicting the optimal timing for dialysis preparation is highly important.
This study aimed to develop a predictive model for determining the appropriate timing for dialysis preparation in CKD patients by conducting a retrospective cohort study.
Method
We included patients followed at the nephrology clinic for at least 1 year for CKD who progressed to ESKD and initiated HD from January 2011 to June 2024. Patients with prior RRT history (HD, peritoneal dialysis, or kidney transplantation) or those who discontinued HD within 3 months due to kidney function recovery, transition to another RRT modality, or death were excluded (Figure 1).
Baseline demographics, anthropometric data, comorbidities, laboratory findings, echocardiography results, and chest X-ray findings were collected. A multiple linear regression (MLR) model was developed to predict the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) 6 months before dialysis initiation (eGFR_6M), which is considered the appropriate time to prepare for dialysis, such as vascular access formation.
Results
A total of 507 patients (299 males, mean age 61±14 years) were included. The mean duration from the first nephrologist visit to the initiation of HD was 69.0 ± 52.7 months. Significant variables identified in the univariate analysis were selected for the MLR model (Table 1). The intercept for predicting eGFR_6M was 19.936 (95% CI 13.581, 26.291; SE 3.225; p-value <0.001). Female patients, or those with higher EF or elevated BUN levels, should be prepared for dialysis in relatively lower eGFR levels. Conversely, patients with impaired mobility (requiring complete assistance for ambulation), a history of diuretics use, or elevated hemoglobin levels need to be prepared for dialysis at comparatively higher eGFR levels. Our predictive model is based on the following equation (Table 2):
eGFR_6M = 19.936 − 1.161*(female) + 2.405*(impaired mobility) − 0.069*(EF) + 1.110*(diuretics use) + 0.601*(hemoglobin) − 0.151*(BUN)
The adjusted R² of this model is 0.406. The Durbin-Watson statistic is 2.097, indicating that the assumption of independence was satisfied. The scatter plot and the Q-Q plot demonstrated that the assumptions of normality, homoscedasticity, and linearity were met (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
The predictive model developed in this study may serve as a valuable tool for clinical nephrologists in planning dialysis preparation and vascular access formation, thereby improving patient outcomes.

abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) imposes a significant burden on quality of life and healthcare utilisation. Early identification can benefit patients by enabling risk factor modification and timely intervention, potentially slowing disease progression. Understanding the current and future prevalence of CKD is also critical for informing healthcare resource allocation. However, robust insights into CKD epidemiology require reliable population-level data. This is the first study to estimate CKD prevalence from real-world Irish primary care data and aims to identify practical challenges of CKD diagnosis through electronic health record (EHR) in Irish primary care.
Method
We analysed data from Centric Health Ireland Primary Care Database, an EHR network covering 66 general practices in Ireland. Three definitions of “indicative CKD” were utilised based on estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and urinary albumin-creatinine ratio (uACR) values, of which the ‘strict definition’ followed KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline (Table 1). Crude prevalence of CKD was estimated in overall study population and in the subgroup aged 50 and above, and was standardised by age groups and sex according to Irish Population Survey 2024. The prevalence was compared to published data from The Irish Longitudinal Study on Ageing (TILDA), a nationally representative longitudinal study of the population of Ireland aged 50 years and above. CKD stage was defined using the latest eGFR reading.
Results
By January 2025, 470,433 adult individuals aged 20 and above are active in the dataset: 46% of them were men and 39% were aged 50 years and above (16.6% 50–59 years, 11.8% 60–69 years, 6.5% 70–79 years and 4.1% 80 years and above). Overall crude prevalence of indicative CKD was 3.2% to 4.7% based on the three definitions, and standardised prevalence was in the range of 3.9% to 5.5% (Table 2).
Direct disease coding markedly underestimates the true prevalence, with a median of 98.7%, 100% and 100% patients with indicative CKD uncoded at stage 3, 4, and 5 separately across the practices. In the subgroup of individuals aged 50 years and above, the standardised prevalence using expanded definition was 10.6%, distributed by stage as follows: 3%–8.7%, 4%–0.4% and 5%–1.5% (Table 2).
Compared to published TILDA data, real-word primary care data showed 2.2% higher in the prevalence estimation in the 50–59 age bracket (2.4% vs.4.6%), 1.2% higher in the estimation for 60–69 year olds (6.7% vs. 7.9%) and 5.1% lower in the estimation for 70–79 year olds (24.2% vs. 19.1%).
Conclusion
In Irish Primary Care Practice, CKD is a significant burden, with a standardised adult prevalence ranging from 3.9% to 5.5%. Our study demonstrates the potential use of primary care EHRs for monitoring CKD prevalence and staging but highlights limitations such as the critical need for improvements in coding accuracy and standardisation within Irish primary care to enhance the reliability of EHRs for population-level studies. Utilising eGFR and uACR to supplement CKD diagnosis codes can be used to identify more patients and identify them earlier. The discrepancies between our data and TILDA prevalence substantiated that considerable work remains to accurately estimate the true prevalence of CKD in Ireland, particularly among older age groups. Recognising these limitations can enable the smarter use of EHRs to effectively aid in improving CKD detection and management, with downstream effects on improved healthcare service delivery.

title: #1731 Artificial intelligence in the prediction of congenital urological anomalies from perinatal characteristics
authors: Helvécio Neves Feitosa Filho; Rian Vilar Lima; João Filipe Cavalcante Uchoa Furtado; Eduardo Correia Eulálio; Pedro Vianna Caldas Ribeiro; Lucas MacÊdo Aurélio Paiva; Isabela Diógenes Feitosa; Elizabeth De Francesco Daher; Geraldo Bezerra Da Silva Junior
abstract:
Background and Aims
Congenital anomalies of kidney and urinary tract are the most common causes of chronic kidney disease in children. The aim of this study is to develop an artificial intelligence (AI) model to predict the occurrence of congenital urological malformations (CUMs) in newborns (NBs) and identify the most relevant variables for this prediction.
Method
Fourteen sociodemographic, clinical, and obstetric variables were collected from NBs registered in the Brazil National Live Birth Information System (SINASC). Newborns with CUMs (ICD Q600-Q649) and healthy newborns were selected in a 1:2 ratio. A supervised Machine Learning model based on the Support Vector Machine (SVM) architecture was used. The sample was randomly divided into 70% for training, 15% for testing, and 15% for validation. The results were compared with a traditional logistic regression model. A subanalysis for renal agenesis and hypoplasia (Q600-Q605) was also performed.
Results
A total of 7,864 healthy NBs and 3,932 with MUCs were included. The mean gestational age was 37.8 weeks, with a mean weight of 3,099.0 g and 58.01% of newborns were male. Among the MUCs, the following prevailed: congenital hydronephrosis (24.72%), polycystic kidney (8.92%), Potter syndrome (6.40%) and epispadias (6.07%). The SVM model showed sensitivity of 85.81%, specificity of 67.52% and AUC of 0.834. Logistic regression obtained sensitivity of 89.54%, specificity of 62.09% and AUC of 0.838. In the sub-analysis, SVM presented sensitivity of 90.20%, specificity of 73.95% and AUC of 0.897 and logistic regression obtained sensitivity of 89.89%, specificity of 69.61% and AUC of 0.872.
Conclusion
The models were equivalent in predicting CUMs, demonstrating potential to screen these conditions early, which is crucial for a more favorable prognosis. However, additional studies are needed to validate the use of AI models in practical scenarios.

title: #1373 The role of uremic toxins and inflammation in eryptosis and renal anemia among dialysis patients
authors: Andrea N Moreno-Amaral; Erika Dias; Gabriela Bohnen; Julia Monte Alegre; Beatriz Akemi Kondo Van Spitzenbergen; João Vitor Ibrahim; Rebecca Kempis; Fernanda Kussi; Lia Nakao; Nadja Grobe; Peter Kotanko; Thyago Moraes
abstract:
Background and Aims
Elevated levels of uremic toxins (UT) and inflammatory cytokines have been implicated in increased eryptosis, a form of premature erythrocyte death, potentially contributing to renal anemia. This study explores the interplay between UT, eryptosis, inflammation, and cytokines with anemia in dialysis patients.
Method
In this observational cross-sectional study, with approval from the institutional ethics committee, we analyzed blood samples from 41 chronic dialysis patients. Anemia was defined as hemoglobin (Hb) levels below 12 g/dL. Eryptosis was assessed in erythrocytes using Annexin-V to detect phosphatidylserine (PS) exposure. ELISA measured serum cytokine levels (IL-6, IL-1β, IFN-g), and HPLC quantified UT p-cresyl sulfate (pCS) and indole-3-acetic acid (IAA). Correlations were evaluated using Spearman's test, and simple linear regression determined slopes and intercepts.
Results
No significant results were observed in correlation with IS. However, Hb levels were inversely correlated with pCS (Fig. 1A). Increased PS exposure was positively correlated with pCS levels (Fig. 1B). Furthermore, pCS levels directly correlated with the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and IFN-g (Fig. 1C and D), while IAA positively correlated with IL-1β levels (Fig. 1E).
Conclusion
These findings highlight that UT, particularly pCS and IAA, contribute to renal anemia by driving eryptosis and inflammation. Correlations between elevated UT, eryptosis markers, and pro-inflammatory cytokines indicate a mechanism linking uremic toxicity to eryptosis and lower Hb levels. Targeting UT, specifically pCS and IAA and inflammation, may offer a therapeutic approach to mitigate renal anemia in dialysis patients.

title: #284 Gender disparities in CKD before and after referral to nephrology
authors: Frida Welander; Marie Evans
abstract:
Background and Aims
More women than men in the world have chronic kidney disease (CKD)(1). Despite this, observations from several countries and regions show that women in primary health care are less likely to receive a CKD diagnosis, be referred to a nephrologist and receive RAAS inhibitors (RAASi)(2, 3). Less is known to what extent CKD management also differs between men and women in specialized nephrology care, implying gender bias rather than inequalities in access to care. To investigate the impact of gender on CKD management in patients under nephrology care, we conducted a study including data from a nationwide register of nephrology-referred CKD patients, the Swedish Renal Registry Chronic Kidney Disease (SRR-CKD).
Method
All patients registered in the SRR-CKD between 2010–2020 were included. Index date were the first registered visit. Logistic regression models were used to investigate the odds for women versus men (95% confidence interval) of having any CKD diagnosis (according to ICD-10) prior to index date, early referral (defined as eGFR > 30ml/min/1.73 m2), blood pressure (BP) <140/90 mmHg, urinary-albumin/creatinine ratio (ACR) <30 mg/mmol, treatment with renin-angiotensin-aldosterone inhibitors (RAASi), lipid lowering agents (if age>50), or oral anticoagulants if atrial fibrillation (AF) and CHA2DS2-VASc >2 at index. We then used multivariable logistic regression models to investigate the management of CKD in women versus men during the first year of follow-up (a registered follow-up visit, a primary kidney disease diagnosis based on a kidney biopsy, new treatment with RAASi, lipid lowering agents, oral anticoagulants, or BP <140/90 and ACR<30 mg/mmol if not already achieved at index).
Results
In total, there were 31 535 patients included (median age 73 years, 36% were female). Women had lower eGFR (25 vs 27ml/min/1.73m2) and ACR (17 vs 34 mg/mmol) at index. Men more often had a history of diabetes, hypertension and heart disease while women more often had COPD/asthma and psychiatric disease.
Differences between men and women before index date
Women were less likely to have a CKD diagnosis before index (adjusted OR 0.78 (95%CI 0.74–0.82)) and being referred early (OR 0.74 (0.71–0.78)) (Fig. 1). Women were also less likely to be treated with a RAASi (OR 0.92 (0.88–0.97)), and lipid lowering agents (OR 0.90 (0.86–0.96)), but had a higher odds of having ACR<30mg/mmol (OR 1.64 (1.54–1.76)). There was no difference in the odds of anticoagulant treatment in patients with AF or achieving a BP <140/90 mmHg.
CKD management during the first year of follow-up
Women and men were equally likely to have a follow-up visit within the first year (Fig. 2). There were no significant gender disparities in the odds of having a primary kidney diagnosis based on a kidney biopsy (OR 0.97 (0.90–1.04)), achieving a BP <140/90 mmHg (OR 1.03 (0.96–1.11)), receiving treatment with oral anticoagulation if AF (OR 1.09 (0.87–1.36)). There was also no difference in initiating treatment with a lipid lowering agent during follow up (OR 1.04 (0.95–1.14)), although 80% of eligible patients were left untreated. Among patients not already on a RAASi, less women (21%) compared to men (28%) started treatment during the first year (OR 0.77 (0.70–0.84)). More women than men with albuminuria A3 at index achieved an ACR <30 mg/mmol during follow up (OR 1.31 (1.12–1.54)).
Conclusion
Women with CKD are underdiagnosed, undertreated with guideline recommended therapy and referred later than men to nephrology care. After referral, our results suggest that some gender disparities are attenuated. However, women still are undertreated with RAASi, irrespective of comorbidity and ACR while men have consistently higher levels of albuminuria. Both women and men are undertreated with lipid lowering agents. Nephrologists need to consider the risk of gender bias and actively strive for health equity.

title: #2558 Dysregulation in Slc20a1/Slc20a2 associated with myocardial-bone axis in mild chronic kidney disease—mineral and bone disorder: experimental study
authors: Evdokia Bogdanova; Airat Sadykov; Galina Ivanova; Natalia Semenova; Vladimir Sharoyko; Anton Kutikhin; Vladimir Dobronravov
abstract:
Background and Aims
As we have previously shown, inorganic phosphate (Pi) retention and reduced bone formation occur concurrently with myocardial remodeling in a mild CKD-MBD model. This prompts further investigation into the molecular basis of the identified bone and cardiac abnormalities in mild CKD.
Pi has been found to have a number of tissue-specific effects. The perception of Pi by cells suggested to be maintained by receptors or “sensors”, particularly Pi transporters. Pi transporters PiT1/PiT2 widely represented in tissues, both have been detected in bone and cardiomyocytes. Extracellular Pi may alter their expression and the activity of the downstream ERK pathway in vitro. In bone cells, Pi transporters and ERK pathway are involved to matrix mineralization and cell fate. There is a lack of data on PiT1/2 in cardiac pathology. And to our knowledge, the physiological significance of these mechanisms in vivo, have not been studied until recently.
Method
We induced mild CKD-MBD by 3/4 nephrectomy (Nx) in adult male SHRs with a four-month exposure. Sham operated Wistar rats and SHRs (SO) were controls. Animals were fed standard chow, containing 0.6% Pi. We measured creatinine clearance, proteinuria, renal interstitial fibrosis area, systolic blood pressure, myocardial mass index, serum levels of Pi (sPi), calciprotein particles (CPPs), intact PTH and FGF23. Phosphorus concentration (per dry tissue weight) in bone, myocardium and kidney were measured using inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES). Histomorphometry studies were used to address bone static parameters (Toluidine Blue & Fast Green, TRAP, Masson's, H&E) and myocardial remodeling (Masson's, H&E, von Kossa stain). Expressions of PiT1 (Slc20a1), PiT2 (Slc20a2), phospho-ERK1/2 (Mapk1, Mapk3) were evaluated by PCR-RT, WB, IHC with quantitative morphometry, IF with confocal microscopy (Zeiss LSM 710).
Results
Having chronic kidney injury comparable to human CKD G2, Nx rats exhibited features of lower bone turnover: reduced osteoblast and osteocytes numbers (P = 0.009, P = 0.044), eroded perimeter (P = 0.008) (Fig. 1). Serum Pi, CPPs and P content in the myocardium were higher in the Nx group vs SO (P = 0.001, P = 0.023, P = 0.041), without significant differences in Pi excretion, P content in the kidney and bone (P > 0.11), serum PTH and FGF23 levels (P > 0.48). In CKD-MBD, relative expression of Slc20a1 and Mapk1 were lower (P < 0.021) concurrently with a reduction in PiT1 and phospho-ERK1/2 IHC staining in bone morrow and endosteal cells of trabecular bone (Fig. 1). Myocardial P accumulation and obvious histological lesions (cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, interstitial and perivascular fibrosis) in CKD-MBD, were associated with higher myocardial expressions of Slc20a2 and Mapk3 genes (P = 0.013, P = 0.046), PiT2 protein (WB: P = 0.041; IF and IHC: P < 0.009) and phosphorylated ERK1/2 (WB: P = 0.033; IF and IHC: P < 0.011; Fig. 1). The levels of myocardial Slc20a2 and PiT2, Mapk3 and phospho-ERK1/2 were directly related to Pi retention parameters (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
Myocardial remodeling in mild CKD-MBD is associated with phosphorus accumulation and up-regulation of Pit2/ERK signaling, likely as a consequence of lower bone turnover and bone Pi uptake (Fig. 1).

title: #1518 Promising anemia related inhibitors of vascular calcification in chronic kidney disease. Data from systematic review
authors: Annika Adoberg; Liisi Leis; Merike Luman; Fredrik Uhlin; Ivo Fridolin; Jana Holmar
abstract:
Background and Aims
Vascular calcification (VC) demonstrates an accelerated aging process in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. Renal anemia is one of the most challenging complications because constant hypoxic state is associated with high burden of adverse outcomes, including cardiovascular risk. Hypoxia induces transdifferentation of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) into osteo-/chondrogenic cells. This systematic review aimed to demonstrate VC inhibitors and present their serum levels. 8 anemia-related substances was found to be protective against VC and remains with high clinical interest despite current low evidence.
Method
The systematic review was conducted in accordance of PRISMA and registered in PROSPERO August 30th, 2023 (CRD42023459169), advanced search in PubMed and Web of Science was performed, updated December 8th, 2024. The following terms were used for the systematic literature search: vascular calcification AND inhibitor OR inhibition OR enhancer OR promoter OR inducer OR biomarker OR modulator. The search was restricted to kidney disease mentioned in the title or abstract. Reviews and meta-analyses were not searched. All articles found were written in English. 339 papers were included in the extensive analysis, and 192 were eligible for the final review.
Results
Renal anemia, emphasized by disbalance in calcium and phosphate metabolism, oxidative stress, and uremic toxins, creates the environment for VC. VSMCs demonstrate differentiation into osteoblast-like cells in blood vessel media. Hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF), seems to be associated with the presence of VC in vitro. Relevant role for the induction of heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1)/ferritin system to maintain homeostasis of vascular prevents Pi triggered calcification and osteoblastic differentiation of human VSMCs mainly via the ferroxidase activity of ferritin. Hypoxia fortifies VSMCs calcification and osteochondrogenic trans-differentiation and involves HIF-1 activation. The systematic review presents anemia treatment that has shown effect on inhibiting VC. Possible inhibitors are presented in Table 1.
Conclusion
The systematic review is among the first to demonstrate serum levels of VC inhibitors. However the link between anemia and calcification of media of vessels presents promising treatment options for both, although remains to be further researched. Current treatment options that affect metabolic pathways regulating anemia, oxidative stress, uremic toxins should be evaluated carefully for their protective or promoting effect.

title: #3414 Capturing service users’ experience of the integrated community conservative palliative renal care services
authors: Khaled Jallad; Abdalrahman Mohammed; Nicole Mayisva; Waseem Khamboo; Lucia Birch; Sheena Norgaard; Huda Mahmoud
abstract:
Background and Aims
The community-based conservative-palliative kidney care service is currently established in the Black Country, United Kingdom. We have previously presented the entirely community- based service model and the baseline Integrated Palliative Outcome Score (IPOS) survey results for those on supportive care management.
This is a follow-up study, assessing the patient-reported experience measure (PREM), comparing baseline and follow-up symptom burden and assessing the symptom burden in new service users.
Method
Community, nephrology, and palliative care teams devised a service for those individuals identified for conservative kidney care or individuals with renal disease requiring palliative care management.
The service consists of weekly telephone clinics, home visits (HV) by the community nephrology specialist nurse and/or jointly with the palliative care team, and a bi-weekly palliative-renal multidisciplinary team (MDT) meeting.
Symptoms were assessed using the (IPOS)-renal survey, which asks individuals to rate symptom burden from: not at all, slightly, moderately, severely, to overwhelmingly. Home visits were offered to symptomatic patients. This was performed at baseline to service and repeated 12 months later.
A modified Kidney-PREM survey (needling and transport were excluded) was utilized to assess service users’ reflections, as not all themes were appropriate for the Community-Based Conservative-Palliative Kidney Care Service.
Results
Since January 2022 to date, 101 individuals have been managed using these services. These data reflect the 60 current service users. Forty-one original service users have subsequently passed away. Age: 86.79 ± 7.75 years, 55% female (n = 33), current eGFR: 21.8 ± 11.71 ml/min/1.73m².
Patients reported the top-scoring symptoms (severely or overwhelmingly) were poor mobility (20.8%), difficulty sleeping (20.8%), itching (16.7%), followed by poor appetite (12.5%), and weakness/lack of energy (12.5%) in the three days prior to taking the IPOS renal survey. Interestingly, poor mobility and weakness/lack of energy scored highly at baseline and follow-up. As a cohort, itching and poor appetite as priority symptoms varied. This may relate to symptom management.
Sixty-five percent of patients felt that the community approach did not waste time waiting for appointments/treatments. The Modified Kidney PREM survey revealed that service users identified the availability of the kidney team as the most favorable aspect of their care. However, 21% of the cohort rated three factors unfavorably: access to their GP, availability of dietary advice, and communication between kidney team members (Fig. 1).
The median admission rate pre-introduction to the service was 1 (IQR: 0, 3.5), and after introduction to the service, 0.5 (IQR: 0, 2.50), P = 0.2. Ninety-seven-point-five percent had documented end-stage renal failure counselling. Ninety-three percent had documented escalation of care discussions. Only 6% of the service users did not die in their chosen place of death.
Conclusion
The cooperative multi-specialty approach has led to favorable patient satisfaction with the service and reduced the time wasted attending healthcare appointments. There remains developmental work on providing service users with dietary advice. However, the service has successfully resulted in the reduction of hospital admissions, face-to-face hospital outpatient appointments, and with the majority of service users, escalation plans are documented and achieved.

title: #1453 Changes in nutritional intakes over time and subsequent risk of CKD progression—the CKD-REIN cohort study
authors: Anais Doré; Sophie Girerd; Laetitia Koppe; Céline Lange; Maurice Laville; Luc Frimat; Christian Combe; Denis Fouque; Ziad Massy; Benedicte Stengel; Natalia Alencar de Pinho; Sandra Wagner
abstract:
Background and Aims
Adequate nutrition is crucial for delaying the progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD). The understanding of adherence to nutritional guidelines in non-dialysis-dependent CKD (NDD-CKD) patients is limited, primarily focusing on a few nutrients without longitudinal data. This study evaluates nutrient intakes in NDD-CKD patients, adherence to guidelines, changes over time, and the relationship between nutrient intakes change and CKD progression.
Methods
The study involved 910 NDD-CKD patients under nephrology care from 3033 included in the CKD-REIN cohort study, France. Study participants completed a validated food frequency questionnaire twice, in 2017 and 2020. Nutrient intakes were compared with statements from the Kidney Disease Outcomes Quality Initiative (KDOQI) 2020 guidelines. Multinomial logistic regression was used to assess the relationship between changes in nutrient intake over time and CKD progression.
Results
At baseline, the median age was 70 years and eGFR, 32 mL/min/1.73 m². Seventy percent of participants were men, and 36% had diabetes. The median dietary energy intake (DEI) was 21.6 kcal/kg/day, below the KDOQI target of 25–35 kcal/kg/day. Median dietary protein intake (DPI) was 0.83 g/kg/day, with 27% of patients with diabetes meeting the recommended DPI target (0.6–0.8 g/kg/day), compared to only 7% of non-diabetic patients (0.55–0.6 g/kg/day). At the second survey, DEI decreased to 20.9 kcal/kg/day and DPI, to 0.78 g/kg/day. A ≥0.14 g/kg/day increase in DPI in 3 years (OR 1.81, 95% CI 1.39–2.37) as well as a ≥460 kcal/day reduction in DEI (OR 1.99, 95% CI 1.48–2.69) were significantly associated with rapid CKD progression (eGFR decline ≥5 mL/min/1.73 m²/year) compared to slow progression (eGFR decline <2 mL/min/1.73 m²/year).
Conclusion
Nutrient intake in NDD-CKD patients is still far from guideline targets. Despite suboptimal adherence, a mild reduction in DPI was associated with slower eGFR decline. Conversely, significant reductions in DEI were linked to more rapid CKD progression and may be the result of uremic-related anorexia and digestive disorders. Nutritional interventions are critical for encouraging adherence to guidelines, and should be intensified proportionally as patients transition to more advanced CKD stages.

title: #2325 Do lifestyle interventions including exercise using digital apps and medical services reduce CKD progression?—a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Naohiko Fujii; Kanako Oka; Takuya Ohata; Shungo Fukuda; Shun Manabe; Junichi Hoshino; Yoshitaka Isaka
abstract:
Background and Aims
CKD management has increasingly incorporated exercise therapy, particularly for patients in non-dialysis-dependent (NDD-) CKD stages. While some studies suggest that exercise may help maintain GFR in the short term, the current evidence remains insufficient to establish its long-term effects. Underlying factors include decreased adherence to exercise interventions, highlighting the need for strategies to sustain behavioral changes. Recent advancements in digital apps and healthcare services are anticipated to enhance adherence, yet studies specifically evaluating their effectiveness in CKD exercise interventions are limited.
Method
To address this gap, a systematic review was conducted to assess the impact of digital apps and healthcare services on kidney outcomes in CKD patients. The review utilized a search strategy based on the guidelines of the Japanese Society of Renal Rehabilitation published in 2018, covering studies from January 1, 1990, to December 31, 2023. Potential articles matched to the keyword list were extracted from the PubMed database. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts to identify candidates for full-text analysis and data extraction. Meta-analyses were performed if there were a sufficient number of eligible studies (basically three or more). All statistical analyses were performed using Stata 17.0 (StataCorp LLC, TX, USA).
Results
A total of 395 articles were screened, resulting in nine studies that evaluated clinical outcomes such as GFR, proteinuria, and albuminuria. Among the nine studies, eight assessed changes in GFR, primarily focusing on CKD stages G3 to G4. The interventions varied, including monitoring through pedometers, traditional communication methods (e.g., phone calls, emails), and modern digital devices (e.g., smartphones, tablets). Most studies faced challenges in blinding and had high risks of bias, with few employing intention-to-treat analyses. The GFR evaluation relied on serum creatinine-based estimation formulas, excluding cystatin C analyses. Ultimately, seven studies were included in a meta-analysis, revealing no significant changes in GFR from the interventions (+1.40 [95% confidence interval (CI): −1.87, +4.67] mL/min/1.73 m²), with short-term interventions showing a non-significant increase of +2.79 [95% CI: −1.22, +6.80] mL/min/1.73 m².
Additionally, only three studies evaluated proteinuria and albuminuria, with mixed results. One study reported a significant reduction in albuminuria through individualized management using digital tools, while another found no improvement despite a year-long intervention. The inconsistency in outcomes suggests that while healthcare services and digital devices may offer some benefits, their effects on proteinuria and albuminuria remain uncertain.
Conclusion
In conclusion, the evidence supporting exercise interventions using digital apps and healthcare services in NDD-CKD patients is still inadequate, making it premature to draw definitive conclusions. Although small-scale randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have reported potential benefits in maintaining GFR, there is no evidence of deterioration, suggesting a low risk of clinical harm associated with these interventions. However, the psychological stress and discomfort that such new treatment modalities may impose on patients have not been thoroughly investigated. Therefore, the overall recommendation remains "no recommendation," emphasizing the need for comprehensive evaluations, including patient-reported outcomes, in future research. As digital devices become increasingly integrated into daily life, the anticipated surge in clinical trials utilizing these technologies may significantly enhance the evidence base in the coming years.

title: #3252 Anti-fibrotic profile of a next-generation AT2 receptor agonist in human fibrotic kidney tissue
authors: Johanna Gräns; Jimmie Hofman; Johan Raud
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a significant global health burden, underscoring the urgent need for novel and more effective therapies. The angiotensin II type 2 receptor (AT2R) is expressed in renal tissues, and its activation has been shown to elicit anti-inflammatory, anti-fibrotic, and vasodilatory effects—properties that could be beneficial in halting CKD progression. Previous studies with AT2R agonists, such as buloxibutid (also referred to as C21), have demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models of CKD by reducing fibrosis, inflammation, and improving renal function. This study aimed to investigate the therapeutic potential of a new highly potent and selective AT2R agonist, referred to as C112, using ex vivo human fibrotic kidney slices to assess its anti-fibrotic and fibrolytic properties.
Method
Human precision-cut kidney slices (PCKS) were prepared from explanted kidney tissue with early fibrotic changes and incubated for up to 96 hours with either vehicle, the reference AT2R agonist buloxibutid (IC50: 5.7 nM), or escalating concentrations of the novel AT2R agonist C112 (IC50: 0.41 nM). Key profibrotic markers collagen type I alpha-1 (COL1A1) and transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1) levels were quantified using immunoassays. The protein levels of matrix metalloproteinase-1 (MMP-1), a fibrolytic collagenase, were also measured to determine the fibrolytic potential of each treatment. PCKS viability was assessed by immunoassay-based measurement of kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1) levels in the culture supernatants.
Results
Treatment with the buloxibutid and C112 dose-dependently reduced COL1A1 and TGF-β1 levels, with C112 being more potent than buloxibutid. In parallel, both compounds markedly increased MMP-1 levels, potentially reflecting enhanced collagen breakdown. The full effects of buloxibutid and C112 on MMP-1 were seen already at the lowest concentrations tested (0.01 and 0.001 nM, respectively). These findings suggest that C112 exerts a stronger overall anti-fibrotic effect than buloxibutid in this ex vivo model of human renal fibrosis. KIM-1 was relatively stable over the first 48 hours with a subsequent slow increase over the course of the experiment, in keeping with the responses of an aged kidney. No significant increase of KIM-1 was detected in response to any of the treatments used in this study.
Conclusion
The superior anti-fibrotic profile of the novel highly potent and selective AT2R agonist C112 in human fibrotic kidney slices highlights the potential for AT2R-targeted interventions in CKD. By reducing profibrotic mediators (COL1A1 and TGF-β1) and increasing the fibrolytic protease MMP-1, AT2R agonists may offer a valuable new therapeutic approach for CKD management. Studies of C112 in vivo are ongoing to confirm these promising translational ex vivo findings.

title: #1660 Monitoring of renal impairment in rheumatoid arthritis patients with different levels of disease activity the role of cystatin C
authors: Aihua Du
abstract:
Background and Aims
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) disease itself and the medications taken may lead to visceral involvement. Cystatin C (CysC) has been shown to be a predictor of renal function and methotrexate-related toxicity in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA). However, the relationship between CysC levels and renal function and RA disease activity remains to be determined. We aimed to investigate the correlation of CysC and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) based on CysC measurements with disease activity in RA patients.
Method
We retrieved a total of 80 patients with newly diagnosed RA (symptom duration less than 12 months at diagnosis) and RA patients not receiving conventional medication from June 2024 to December 2024. Disease activity score (DAS 28) was calculated based on patients' erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), 28 swollen joints, 28 painful joints, and patients' visual analog scores (VAS, 0–100 mm scale). RA patients were categorized into three groups based on DAS28 score (DAS28<3.2 for remission and low activity; 3.2<DAS28<5.1 for moderate activity; DAS28>5.1 for high activity). Rheumatoid factor (RF) levels and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels have been commonly used in the past to measure disease activity in RA, while creatinine (Scr) and cystatin C (CysC) levels are indicators of renal function. We compared the differences in clinical parameters among the three groups of patients. Correlations were assessed by Spearman's bivariate analysis.
Results
Of the 80 patients, there were 20 in the remission and low activity group (Group-L), 34 in the moderate grade activity group (Group-M), and 26 in the high disease activity group (Group-H) (Table 1). As the disease activity increased, there was a gradual increase in ESR and CRP values. In addition to these findings, we found that RF levels, Cys C, and GFR were significantly higher in Groups H and M than in Group L. Intriguingly, there was no statistically significant difference in Scr levels between the three groups. Subsequently, the intricate correlations between serologic markers and GFP were studied in depth to assess their relationship with DAS28 (Fig. 1). The results showed a strong positive correlation between DAS28 score and several factors: ESR (R = 0.871, P < 0.001), CRP (R = 0.780, P < 0.001), RF (R = 0.504, P < 0.001), CysC (R = 0.328, P = 0.003) and GFR (R = 0.336, P = 0.002). 0.002). There was also a correlation between serologic indicators. Statistical results showed a significant positive correlation between ESR and CRP (R = 0.770, P < 0.001) and RF levels (R = 0.397, P < 0.001), while CRP was positively correlated with RF levels (R = 0.443, P < 0.001).
Conclusion
As disease activity increased in RA patients, CysC and GFR also showed a rising trend, suggesting that patients may be accompanied by impaired renal function.

title: #2778 An novel lectin-mediated sorting protocol for renal tubules as an innovative multi-purpose tool advancing kidney research
authors: Stefan Rudloff; Rahel Bodenmann; Jessica Roskosch; Murielle Spahr; Anne-Christine Uldry; Stefan Jürg Müller; Maurizio Gullo; Uyen Huynh-Do
abstract:
Background and Aims
With an economic burden exceeding $140 billion annually, innovative and affordable diagnostic tools and therapeutic strategies are urgently needed to preserve kidney function and reduce societal costs. These tools should enable large-scale screening, address sex-specific treatment challenges, advance precision medicine, promote regenerative kidney research, and adhere to 3R principles to minimize animal use in preclinical studies. Traditional in vitro models, such as cell cultures and kidney organoids, are constrained by time, cost, and limited physiological complexity. Here, we present a cost-effective, time-efficient, and high-yield lectin-mediated flow sorting technique for isolating glomeruli and four distinct, morphologically and functionally intact nephron tubule segments from a single kidney. title: #2333 Fetuin-A supplementation as a key treatment strategy to mitigate acute kidney injury and prevent its progression to chronic disease
authors: Stefan Rudloff; Miguel Carvalho Ravasco Milhano Correia; Nathan Brinkman; Björn Hegemann; Adrian Zuercher; Uyen Huynh-Do
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with acute kidney injury (AKI), characterized by a sudden loss of kidney function involving structural damage and functional impairment, are particularly prone to developing chronic kidney disease (CKD). Ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI), a major cause of AKI, induces oxidative stress, inflammation, and necrosis. The excessive release of calcium phosphate-enriched debris from necrotic cells exacerbates inflammation by triggering cytokine production and promoting further cell death. Fetuin-A (FA), a liver-derived glycoprotein abundant in extracellular fluids, protects tissues by sequestering these cytotoxic minerals. However, severely ill patients often exhibit reduced FA levels, which correlate with increased morbidity and mortality. This study evaluates the therapeutic potential of human plasma-derived FA (hpdFA) to mitigate renal damage, inflammation, and fibrosis during AKI in mice. Additional objectives include investigating sex-specific differences and pharmacokinetics to assess FA as a potential biomarker for AKI.
Method
Unilateral IRI was induced in young adult wildtype or FA KO mice of both sexes by clamping the renal vessels of the left kidney for 22.5 minutes at 37°C. Two doses of hpdFA or PBS (vehicle control) were administered prophylactically (before surgery) or therapeutically (after surgery). Urine, blood, and kidney tissue samples were collected at 6 or 24 hours post-surgery and analyzed for renal injury, inflammation, and FA levels using immunofluorescence, RT-qPCR, Western blot, and ELISA. Renal fibrosis was assessed histologically three weeks after surgery. Additional in vitro and in vivo characterization of hpdFA included toxicity, calcification propensity, and half-life evaluations. In humans, serum samples from cardiovascular surgery patients were analyzed to assess endogenous FA dynamics during acute inflammation.
Results
Baseline serum levels of endogenous FA were significantly higher in female mice compared to males, a sex difference not observed in human samples. Acute tissue injury—whether IRI in mice (including sham surgery) or cardiovascular surgery in human patients—caused a rapid decline in circulating FA. In mice, this decline was associated with FA accumulation at injury sites (e.g., renal tissue or muscle). Following IRI, FA depletion correlated with greater renal damage and inflammation in male mice compared to females. In FA KO mice, neutrophil infiltration was significantly increased six hours post-IRI compared to wildtype animals. Prophylactic administration of hpdFA reduced tissue injury markers (e.g., Kim1, Lcn2) and inflammatory mediators (e.g., Ccl2, Ccl5, Tnf) in both sexes 24 hours post-IRI. In contrast, therapeutic hpdFA administration after IRI improved outcomes only in males. Three weeks post-IRI, hpdFA treatment attenuated the expression of fibrotic markers (e.g., Tgfb1, Acta2, Col1a1) and reduced fibrotic remodeling, as assessed by picrosirius red staining.
Conclusion
Acute inflammation at surgical wounds depletes systemic FA, creating a mismatch between its availability and increased demand in vulnerable tissues like the kidney, exacerbating local damage. FA supplementation addresses this imbalance by disrupting calcium phosphate-driven inflammation, promoting tissue recovery, and preventing progression from AKI to CKD. Higher baseline FA levels, as seen in female mice, partially protect against IRI, while prophylactic FA administration benefits both sexes by increasing systemic and local FA availability before the onset of injury. Post-surgical administration is especially effective in individuals with lower baseline FA levels, such as male mice. Our findings address the critical unmet need for interventions to prevent chronic disease progression and establish FA as both a promising biomarker and therapeutic option for AKI and related conditions.

title: #740 Blockade of translocator protein ameliorates intrarenal lipid accumulation and kidney injury in obesity-induced chronic kidney disease
authors: Yuchen Feng; Wai Han Yiu; Kong Lam; Jingyuan MA; Kar Neng Lai; Sydney Tang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Dysregulation of lipid metabolism has been implicated in the progression of obesity-induced chronic kidney disease (CKD). Reduction in mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation (FAO) is one of the key pathogenic factors for intrarenal lipid accumulation, leading to kidney fibrosis in CKD. The mitochondrial translocator protein (TSPO) is associated with cholesterol transport into mitochondria and mitochondrial metabolism. However, the role of TSPO in obesity-induced CKD remains unknown.
Method
7-week-old C57BL/6J mice were fed with normal diet (ND) or high-fat diet (HFD) in total for 16 weeks. TSPO antagonist PK11195 or vehicle was administered intraperitoneally daily for 4 weeks to mice from 12 weeks after commencing ND/HFD. Serum and urine samples were collected for biochemical assessment. Kidneys were examined for histological and inflammatory changes and subjected to untargeted lipidomic analysis.
Results
PK11195 treatment significantly reduced urine albumin-creatinine ratio (uACR) and obesity-induced tubular damage in HFD-mice. Induction of TNF-α and CCL-2 mRNA was reduced in kidneys from PK11195-treated HFD-mice compared to vehicle control. The protective role of PK11195 against lipid accumulation was demonstrated with a reduction of lipid droplets in kidney tubules by oil red O staining, along with less triglyceride and cholesterol contents in the kidneys. Furthermore, untargeted lipidomic analysis identified an association between TSPO and sphingolipid metabolism in obesity-induced CKD. PK11195 treatment in HFD-mice reversed the dysregulation of sphingolipid metabolism which plays a critical role in mitochondrial dysfunction in CKD. Electron microscopy demonstrated an increase in mitochondrial number, improvement in mitochondrial ultrastructure and expression of mitochondrial FAO-related markers (PGC1α, PPARα, CPT1α, ACOX1) after PK11195 treatment.
Conclusion
Blockade of TSPO activity alleviated kidney dysfunction, inflammation and lipid accumulation in obesity-induced CKD model. TSPO may play an important role in the progression of CKD through regulating intrarenal mitochondrial FAO pathway and lipid dysmetabolism.

title: #2550 Targeted plasma proteomics links inflammation with progression of chronic kindey disease in a multi-national pediatric cohort
authors: Johannes Benjamin Holle; Rosa Reitmeir; Jonas Hofstetter; Felix Behrens; Uwe Querfeld; Max Liebau; Marietta Kirchner; Nicola Wilck; Marcus Weitz; Alma Zernecke-Madsen; Franz Schaefer; Hendrik Bartolomaeus
abstract:
Background and Aims
The prevention of progression of CKD is of outstanding importance, especially in children where treatments such as SGLT2 inhibitors are not yet available. Inflammation has emerged as a key player in the pathogenesis and progression of CKD, as persistent low-grade inflammation contributes to kidney damage by promoting fibrosis, oxidative stress, and vascular injury. We aim for a better understanding of the role of inflammation in CKD progression in children to finally identify potential therapeutic targets and improve patient outcomes.
Method
We analyzed clinical data longitudinally from the prospective, multicenter cardiovascular comorbidity in children with CKD (4C) Study. At study entry, systemic inflammation was assessed using a targeted serum proteomics approach (OLINK Target 96 Inflammation). After standard QC, we retained 77 plasma proteins for further analysis. For these proteins, at least 70% of the samples reported values above the limit of detection (LOD). Values below LOD were imputed using the log-transformed square root of the exponentiated maximum LOD. First, we performed a cross-sectional analysis to identify associations of inflammatory markers with kidney function and patient demographics. Second, we used a composite endpoint for progression of CKD (eGFR loss >50% or start kidney replacement therapy) or eGFR decline as a continuous variable to associate inflammatory profiles with kidney outcome.
Results
We included 683 children to this analysis (mean age 12.1 ± 3.3 years; 35% females) with a mean eGFR of 28.8 ± 11.4 ml/min*1.73 m2. CAKUT was the most common underlying disease in 68.8% of patients.
First, we employed a step-wise approach of LASSO regression for each category of metadata for each protein. Our results indicate that CKD-related data (eGFR, albuminuria, CKD stage) explained the highest amount of variance for the vast amount of detected proteins. This was similarly reflected in the prinicipal component analysis (PCA), in which both PC1 (27% variance) and PC2 (11%) correlated with eGFR. Using linear modeling, we demonstrate that 46 out of 77 proteins associate negatively with eGFR, of which 44 remained significant after adjustment for age, sex, BMI, country of origin and diagnosis. Plasma CD40, CD137, PD-L1, CXCL1, IL-15RA and VEGFA were the proteins with the strongest associations. Contrast analysis for underlying disease revealed that glomerulonephritis diagnosis was independently associated with higher inflammation.
To investigate whether inflammatory profile at baseline visit associate with kidney disease outcome independent of known risk factors, we performed a confounder-aware analysis (metadeconfoundR). A subset of 10 proteins (including for example CD40, PD-L1, M-CSF, LIFR), was positively associated with the composite kidney endpoint at 12, 24, and 36 months follow-up without being confounded by other parameters. Using a random forest classifier with an 80/20 training/test data-split, we can show that adding either all proteins (AUC = 0.87) or the subset of 10 proteins (AUC = 0.87) slightly improves the predictive power of standard clinical data (eGFR, albuminuria, age, sex, AUC = 0.83) for reaching the combined endpoint after 36 months.
Conclusion
Taken together, our data shows a clear CKD stage-dependent inflammatory signature in pediatric patients that is independent of patient demographics, underlying kidney disease and country of origin. Of note, pediatric patients have the unique advantage of studying CKD signatures irrespective of additional comorbidities such as hypertension or diabetes. Furthermore, we describe a subset of inflammatory serum proteins independently related to kidney outcomes in a representative pediatric cohort. Our analysis suggests that these proteins might be of use as predictive biomarkers.

title: #1213 Interferon regulatory factor 5 in myeloid cells promotes obstructive nephropathy-induced renal fibrosis in vivo
authors: Jia Wei; Gengyu Du; Zixia Li; Xiang Yan; Zihao Xu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Obstructive nephropathy is one of the main causes of chronic kidney disease, which may progress to end stage renal disease, leading to heavy medical burden. The main pathological characteristics of obstructive nephropathy is fibrosis. The source of myofibroblasts in the glomerulus is not completely understood, and it is thought that multiple cells may be involved. Notably, recent studies have shown that the major cells infiltrating the kidney during CKD are mononuclear/macrophages. Interferon regulatory factor 5 (IRF5) is predominantly expressed in myeloid cells and is regarded as a key regulator of macrophage activation. Previous findings suggest the potential involvement of IRF5 in the fibrotic process. However, the role and mechanism of IRF5 in obstructive renal interstitial fibrosis remain unexplored. In this study, we explained the mechanism of IRF5 in macrophages promoting renal fibrosis in obstructive nephropathy.
Method
Renal biopsy specimens were obtained from patients diagnosed with obstructive nephropathy. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) and immunofluorescence (IF) were employed to evaluate the expression of fibrosis markers along with IRF5. Unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO) was performed in WT mice, Irf5 knockout (Irf5−/−) mice, and Irf5fl/fl mice and Irf5 myeloid specific knockout (Irf5fl/flLyz2Cre) mice. Renal tissue was harvested for IHC, RT-qPCR and western blot (WB) to evaluate the expression of target markers. Bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) isolated from Irf5fl/fl mice and Irf5fl/flLyz2Cre mice were cultured and stimulated with TNF-α for subsequent IF, RT-qPCR, and WB. UUO model was established in WT mice, with the treatment group receiving intraperitoneal injections of an IRF5 inhibitor and the control group receiving an equivalent volume of saline. Renal tissue was collected for further analysis to investigate the role of IRF5 in renal fibrosis.
Results
The expression of IRF5 was increased in renal tissue of patients with obstructive nephropathy and there was a positive correlation between the number of IRF5+ cells and the fibrotic area. IF showed that IRF5 was co-localized in macrophages.
In the renal tissues of UUO mice, the fibrosis markers and IRF5 saw a notably increase. Moreover, IRF5 staining was localized to CD68+ macrophages. The results showed a total decrease in collagen deposition and fibrosis marker in the obstructive renal tissue of Irf5−/−mice compared with WT. Besides, RT-qPCR and WB demonstrated the similar outcomes. Renal fibrosis degree and the number of macrophages were markedly reduced in renal tissues of Irf5fl/flLyz2Cre UUO mice. The decreased expression of α-SMA and VIM in renal tissues of Irf5fl/flLyz2Cre UUO mice was verified by RT-qPCR and WB. The RNA-Seq analysis further revealed that the most members of the Matrix Metalloproteinase (MMP) family, especially Mmp9, were positively correlated with Irf5. The finding was demonstrated by IF. Consistently, the protein and mRNA levels of MMP9 were lower in the obstructed renal tissues of Irf5fl/flLyz2Cre mice compared to the Irf5fl/fl mice. IF results indicated that IRF5 and MMP9 co-localized with macrophage.
BMDMs isolated from Irf5fl/fl mice and Irf5fl/flLyz2Cre mice were cultured and stimulated with TNF-α. A significant increase of IRF5 and MMP9 with co-localization within macrophages were observed. TNF-α upregulated Mmp9 mRNA and MMP9 protein expression in BMDMs, and the increase was markedly less in Irf5fl/flLyz2Cre BMDMs. The similar reduces in pro-inflammatory factors were proved by RT-qPCR.
Finally, we established UUO model in WT mice, with the treatment group receiving intraperitoneal injections of IRF5 inhibitor and the control group receiving saline. The fibrotic degree and the expression of α-SMA and VIM in the obstructed kidneys from the treatment group were lower compared to the controls. Evidence from WB showed that MMP9 and α-SMA were higher in the obstructed kidneys from the control group.
Conclusion
IRF5 promotes renal fibrosis in obstructive nephropathy by regulating MMP9 expression and facilitating immune cell infiltration.

title: #1005 Cardio-renal outcomes over time following immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy: a single centre retrospective analysis
authors: Benjamin Elyan; Rob Jones; Ninian Lang; Patrick Mark; Jennifer Lees
abstract:
Background and Aims
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have revolutionised cancer treatment, but their use is associated with cardio-renal side effects. This study evaluated cardio-renal outcomes following ICI initiation.
Method
We linked routine healthcare databases in the West of Scotland (2010–2020, population 1.2 million) to identify adults who received ICI. Integrated data linkage information included clinical, prescribing, laboratory, diagnostic and mortality data. Date of ICI initiation was defined as the index date for each individual. The annual estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) slope was modelled from the index date using linear mixed-effects, limited to two years following ICI therapy initiation and adjusting for age. Cox proportional hazards (censored at whichever came sooner of death or last available creatinine value) and Fine and Gray subdistribution hazards (accounting for competing risk of death) were used to analyse factors associated with a ≥40% decline in eGFR, development of eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m2, major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE, defined as death from cardiovascular disease, de novo heart failure, myocardial infarction or stroke). Multivariable models were adjusted for age, sex, history of ischaemic heart disease, diabetes, baseline eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 and mono/dual ICI therapy.
Results
Among 1036 adults (53.9% male; median age 64.0 years, IQI 57.0–72.0) with a median survival of 0.93 years (IQI: 0.32–2.21), a small but significant overall increase in eGFR was observed (+2.0 mL/min/1.73 m²/year, 95% CI: 0.3–3.7). Patients with baseline eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² (12.0% of cohort) had a rise in eGFR (+11.1 mL/min/1.73 m²/year, 95% CI: +6.3 to +16.0). A ≥40% eGFR decline occurred in 236 individuals and eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m2 in 31 individuals during follow-up. In Cox proportional hazards models, history of ischaemic heart disease was associated with increased hazards of ≥40% eGFR decline (aHR 1.49, 95%CI: 1.01–2.22, P = 0.049) and eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m² (aHR 7.66, 95% CI: 1.91–30.69, P = 0.004). Dual ICI therapy (aHR 6.07, 95% CI: 1.53–24.15, P = 0.01) was associated with increased hazards of eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m². None of these associations held after accounting for competing risk of death. MACE occurred in 65 people, with heart failure and stroke being the predominant events. A history of ischaemic heart disease was associated with increased hazards of MACE (aHR 2.46, 95% CI: 1.31–4.64, P = 0.005): this association remained present after accounting for competing risk of death.
Conclusion
In patients treated with ICI and despite relatively short duration of follow-up, significant cardio-renal events occur in nearly a quarter of patients, and appeared more common among people with pre-existing ischaemic heart disease and those treated with dual ICI. The incongruous average rise in eGFR, particularly among individuals with eGFR <60 at baseline, likely reflects non-GFR determinants of creatinine. The findings underscore the importance of cardio-renal assessment and risk stratification in this group.

title: #3071 The association of dephosphorylated, uncarboxylated Matrix Gla Protein with vascular calcification and oxidative stress in chronic kindey disease patients
authors: Ioannis Neofytou; Aikaterini Stamou; Ioannis Kontogiorgos; Ariti Tsinari; Garyfallia Varouktsi; Eirini Leptokaridou Mourtzila; Athanasios Roumeliotis; Konstantinos Leivaditis; Stefanos Roumeliotis; Leon Schurgers; Vassilios Liakopoulos
abstract:

Matrix Gla Protein (MGP), a vitamin K dependent protein needs vitamin K to undergo carboxylation and phosphorylation in order to be active and act as an inhibitor of vascular calcification. Dephosphorylated, uncarboxylated Matrix Gla Protein (dp-ucMGP), the fully inactive form of MGP reflects vitamin K deficiency and has been identified as a marker of vascular calcification and stiffness and an independent cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factor in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. In this study we aimed to investigate the association of vitamin K deficiency with traditional and non-traditional cardiovascular risk factors in a large cohort of CKD patients.
Method
We recruited 482 CKD patients of all stages (35 stage I, 29 stage II, 79 stage III, 55 stage 4 and 289 end-stage kidney disease, 126 Peritoneal Dialysis-PD and 163 Hemodialysis-HD) and measured plasma levels of dp-ucMGP (CARIM Institute, Maastricht, Netherlands). In these patients we determined arterial stiffness parameters (pulse wave velocity-PWV) by the Mobil-O-Graph device (IEM, Stolberg, Germany), carotid intima- media thickness (cIMT) as a marker of arterial calcification with a B-mode ultrasound and the presence of plaque in the carotid arteries. We also measured serum malondialdehyde (MDA) a marker of lipid peroxidation in the Department of Biochemistry, Medical School of Nis, Serbia, by ELISA.
Results
The mean age of all patients was 65.9 ± 15.4 years and 34% were female. Dp-ucMGP was correlated with central systolic and diastolic blood pressure (r = 0.006, P = 0.023 and r = 0.17, P = 0.014), gfr (r = −0.69, P < 0.0001), age (r = 0.18, P < 0.0001), duration of hypertension, diabetes mellitus and CVD (r = 0.18, P < 0.0001, r = 0.11, P = 0.024 and r = 0.19 P < 0.0001 respectively), hemoglobin (r = −0.51, P = 0.001), sodium (r = −0.023, P < 0.0001), phosphate (r = 0.44, P = 0.005), parathormone (r = 0.43 P < 0.0001), albuminuria (r = −0.5 P = 0.05), serum albumin (r = −0.28, P = 0.044), total cholesterol (r = −0.12, P = 0.02), triglycerides (r = 0.18, P < 0.001), high (r = −0.26, P < 0.0001) and low density lipoprotein cholesterol (r = −0.13, P = 0.011), cIMT (r = −0.14, P = 0.04) and serum MDA (r = −0.16, P = 0.001), Spearman's rho test. Moreover, plasma dp-ucMGP levels increased progressively with CKD stages (P < 0.0001)
