title: #1395 Exploratory study on bone microarchitecture in post-mortem specimens of various skeletal sites from dialysis-dependent patients
authors: Matthias Fuchs; Johannes Werzowa; Marija Bojic; Barbara Misof; Stéphane Blouin; Marlis Huber; Alexander Nader; Markus Hartmann; Jochen Zwerina
abstract:
Background and Aims
Bone fragility is high in dialysis patients. Clinical practice guidelines recommend transiliac bone biopsies in patients with severe chronic kidney disease (CKD), which might provide important information about the type of renal osteodystrophy and for treatment decision, however, its diagnostic power for bone properties of other, more fragile skeletal sites is unknown. We compared bone microarchitecture among various skeletal sites.
Method
The trabecular and cortical bone microarchitecture of iliac crest, femur and lumbar vertebrae was analyzed in 21 patients with dialysis-dependent CKD (aged 79 [69; 81.50] years, median [IQR]) using micro-computed tomography (SCANCO µCT50). Iliac crest outcomes were compared to data from a healthy reference group (REF, aged 79.5 [66.25; 84.75] years). Additionally, within the CKD cohort, cortical and trabecular bone microarchitecture of the iliac crest were compared pairwise and correlated to that of the femur and vertebrae, respectively.
Results
Compared to REF, the CKD group exhibited significantly lower iliac crest bone volume (BV/TV −44%, P < 0.001) and trabecular thickness (Tb.Th −43%, P < 0.001), while trabecular number (Tb.N) or separation (Tb.Sp) were not different. Cortical porosity (Ct.Po.V/TV +298%) and pore number (Ct.Po.N +86%) were elevated, while separation thereof (Ct.Po.Sp −15%) was reduced (all P < 0.001) compared to REF. Within CKD patients, trabecular outcomes of iliac crest and vertebrae were not different, and Tb.Th of these sites was positively correlated (R = 0.67, P < 0.001). Ct.Po.V/TV (+230%, P < 0.001) and pore diameter (Ct.Po.Dm +27%, P < 0.05) were found larger, and Ct.Po.Sp (−12%, P < 0.05) lower in the iliac crest than in the femur.
Conclusion
Our findings indicate that dialysis-dependent patients exhibit compromised bone microarchitecture at the iliac crest. While trabecular microarchitecture of the iliac crest appears predictive for that of the vertebrae, differences in cortical microarchitecture might limit iliac crest bone as a potential marker for fracture risk assessment at cortical bone dominated sites such as the femur.

title: #1810 Prediction of chronic kidney disease using multidimensional data and foundation model
authors: Lin Pei; Chunyang Li; Xiaoxi Zeng
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease is typically a progressive condition. Due to its incurable nature, precise identification of high-risk populations and the prediction of disease onset risk are crucial for timely prevention and intervention. We aimed to develop and validate a machine learning (ML) model based on multidimensional data to predict the risk of CKD.
Method
In this prospective cohort study based on the UK Biobank, individuals who did not have prevalent CKD at baseline and had complete information for model development were enrolled. We randomly divided these participants into a training dataset and a validation dataset at the ratio of 4:1. Using training dataset, a baseline random survival forest (RSF) model (uin-RSF) based on clinical characteristics, and an RSF model (multi-RSF) additionally incorporating optical coherence tomography (OCT) images of the fundus were developed. The OCT image features were extracted using a foundation model based on deep learning. Model performance was evaluated using Harrel's c-index and time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) in the validation dataset. The DeLong test was used to compare the AUCs of the two models at each time points.
Results
Of the 6522 participants, 47.64% were male, with a mean age of 57.80 (±7.64) years. At baseline, the prevalence of hypertension and diabetes was 27.06% and 4.93%, respectively. Over a mean observation period of 12.6 years, 187 individuals in the training dataset and 47 in the validation dataset developed CKD. The uni-RSF model, which incorporated clinical data, achieved a C-index of 0.801 and a mean area under the curve (AUC) of 0.750 for predicting CKD in the validation dataset. The multi-RSF model, which integrated features extracted from fundus images in addition to clinical data, showed an improvement in performance, with a C-index of 0.832 and a mean AUC of 0.792. Specifically, the AUC of the multi-RSF model was 0.706 for the sixth year, 0.783 for the eighth year, and 0.799 for the tenth year after baseline, respectively. All these values were significantly higher than the corresponding performances of the uni-RSF model, as demonstrated by the DeLong test.
Conclusion
The multimodal RSF model, which incorporates both clinical data and retinal fundus OCT images could improve the predictive performance for the incidence of CKD. This model have the potential develop more accurate and tailored prognostic prediction systems that outperform traditional models.

title: #2693 The association of malondiadehyde, catalase and superoxide dismutase with kidney function and vitamin K status in chronic kidney disease

Oxidative stress (OS), defined as the imbalance between pro-oxidants and antioxidants is highly prevalent in end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) and might contribute to the increased cardiovascular (CV) risk that these patients have. In this study we aimed to investigate the associations of markers of OS with various traditional and novel CV risk factors in a large cohort of CKD patients.

The mean age of all patients was 65.9 ± 15.4 years and 34% were female. title: #3742 Ketogenic diet as a therapeutic approach in ADPKD
authors: Sadrija Cukoski; Adrian Kühn; Christoph Heinrich Lindemann; Sita Arjune; Philipp Antczak; Franziska Grundmann; Roman-Ulrich Mueller
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common genetic cause of kidney failure with very limited therapeutic options. title: #358 Improving and personalizing nephrology care with the use of outcome data: examples of national and regional initiatives in the Netherlands
authors: Carlijn Voorend; Marc Ten Dam; Nelly van Uden; Tiny Hoekstra; Hetty Prinsen; Marc Hemmelder; Willem Jan W Bos
abstract:
Background and Aims
Dutch nephrology care aims for a more sustainable way of using outcome data. The national Dutch nephrology quality system includes guideline development, the Nefrodata registry (since 1986), outcome data benchmarking, and periodic peer audits for quality assessment of institutions providing (pre)dialysis care (since 1998). In the Santeon “Better Together” program multiple hospitals collect and share outcome data in a learning network for continuous improvement and personalization of care. We aimed to describe these two initiatives, to analyze their impact on clinical care and outcomes, and share lessons learned.
Method
We applied a mixed-method approach. Quantitative trends in clinical outcomes were analyzed from Nefrodata. In interviews, key players in the quality system were asked for successes, enablers and barriers. We included outcomes from recent programs by the Cooperating Registries and Dutch Kidney Patient Association [1, 2]. For Santeon, the use of outcome data in developing of the Kidney Failure Decision Aid, the CKD Dashboard, and quality improvement cycles were qualitatively analyzed for their success factors.
Results
Over the past two decades, the quality system has made significant progress. Registry checks and audits increased quality awareness, while benchmark reports enriched the local Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle. A nationwide survey showed that 93% of the dialysis centers discuss the benchmark report on a regular basis which led to improvement initiatives in 77% of the dialysis centers. Confidence within kidney care to discuss outcomes is high [1].
Remarkable improvements in trends in clinical outcomes are observed: dialysis initiation halved in older patients (≥65 years) in the past decade, dialysis mortality fell from 20% in 2000 to 10% in 2020, the number of kidney transplants increased since 2000 (see Fig. 1), and median dialysis time before transplantation decreased from 4 to 2.5 years (since 2011). Improvement techniques, shifts in dialysis population due to an increased choice for conservative treatment, and the quality system likely contributed to these changes.
Enablers for the successes included collaboration with various professional and interest groups to ensure broad support, an open culture, and patient participation. Although, variation between centers in the use of outcome data in quality improvement remains. Also, the use of Registry outcomes in scientific publications and guideline development is still limited.
The ’Better Together’ program improved shared decision-making, reduced decisional regret among patients, and slightly shifted choices between kidney transplantation and conservative care. Improvement cycles focused on vascular access care, residual diuresis preservation, and reduction of central venous catheter infections.
The lessons learned for sustainable use of outcomes are summarized in eight general recommendations: (1) Start with establishing a quality framework, (2) Promote collaboration and support, (3) Involve patient representation and/or experienced individuals, (4) Establish a management process for the registration dataset, (5) Identify practice variation with benchmark reports, (6) Apply peer audits for quality assessment, (7) Apply transparency in a learning network, (8) Use outcome information for personalized care.
To promote outcome data use in Dutch nephrology quality system for continuous learning and improvement, recommendations include fostering a quality mindset, expanding registries, aligning guidelines with registry and visitation outcomes, and scaling up the Kidney Failure Decision Aid and CKD Dashboard nationally.
Conclusion
Outcome data use in quality systems and learning hospital networks likely improves and personalizes CKD care. Dutch nephrology care managed to have a stable prevalence and decreased incidence of patients on dialysis, despite the aging of the population and prolonged survival on dialysis.

title: #3531 The microbiome and its metabolites promote cardiac remodeling in chronic kidney disease via the AhR-IL17A Axis
authors: Wibke Anders; Alex Yarritu; Arne Thiele; Istvan Andras Szijarto; Ariana Rauch; Victoria McParland; Sakshi Kamboj; Katja Dettmer; Wolfram Gronwald; Peter Oefner; Hendrik Bartolomaeus; Nicola Wilck
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a major cardiovascular (CV) risk factor, leading to a disproportionately high mortality from CV disease (CVD). Alterations of the gut microbiome composition and function are evident in CKD, leading to an increased production and accumulation of metabolites of bacterial origin. Tryptophan (Trp) metabolites are of particular interest and are known to act as ligands of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), which integrates various environmental signals and has been described as a mediator of immune responses.
We hypothesize that CKD-associated bacterial metabolites from the intestinal microbiome influence AhR-dependent inflammation and cardiac remodeling, thereby promoting the development of CVD.
Method
Experimental CKD was induced in 129/Sv mice by subtotal nephrectomy (STNx), followed by either microbiome depletion using oral antibiotics (Abx) or pharmacological AhR-inhibition (AhRi) with a small molecule AhR inhibitor (BAY 2416964). Phenotyping was conducted by echocardiography, radiotelemetry blood pressure measurements, assessment of vascular reactivity, histology, qPCR and cardiac bulk RNA sequencing, immune phenotyping by multicolor flow cytometry, plasma metabolomics, and in vitro assays for AhR activity and T helper 17 cell (TH17) polarization.
Results
Sequencing (16S) of the fecal microbiome confirmed the suppression of the intestinal microbial load by Abx, along with significant differences in the abundance of Trp metabolites in plasma. AhR reporter assay showed a lower serum AhR activation under Abx treatment. The STNx-induced increase in the heart weight/tibia length was reduced by Abx (10.1 ± 0.5 g/m vs. 7.0 ± 0.2 g/m; P < 0.001). Hearts of STNx + Abx displayed significantly less remodeling than STNx despite similar blood pressure levels. Histological analyses of the left ventricle with Picrosirius Red staining revealed STNx-induced cardiac fibrosis that was ameliorated by Abx (PSR-positive area 12.0 ± 1.5% vs. 5.8 ± 1.8%; P = 0.008) and AhRi (13.64 ± 3.1% vs. 6.9 ± 2.4%; P = 0.060). Differential expression analysis of bulk RNA sequencing identified 2,833 genes significantly upregulated in STNx hearts, of which 1,179 were also among the 1,342 genes downregulated in STNx+Abx. Vascular function, as assessed by wire myography of mesenteric arteries, indicated an impaired endothelium-dependent relaxation in STNx, which improved in STNx+Abx. Both STNx+Abx and STNx+AhRi exhibited reduced systemic inflammation, with significantly lower plasma C-reactive protein levels (0.08 ± 0.005 vs. 0.05 ± 0.01 mg/l; P = 0.034 and 0.09 ± 0.005 vs. 0.07 ± 0.004 mg/l; P = 0.040). Ex vivo flow cytometry analysis revealed a STNx-induced TH17 signature that was attenuated in both treatments. In vitro assays confirmed the effects of BAY 2416964 in reducing uremia-induced TH17 polarization. Gene ontology (GO) term enrichment analysis of the cardiac bulk RNA-Seq data displayed an elevated expression of different TH17-pathways in STNx that were attenuated by Abx and AhRi. Correlation analysis revealed a significant positive association with extracellular matrix gene sets (r = 0.6, P = 0.002), suggesting an effect of TH17 cells in the development of cardiac fibrosis.
Conclusion
Our findings demonstrate that both the Abx-induced reduction of microbial metabolite production in the intestine as well as inhibition of the AhR significantly protect against STNx-induced immune activation, inflammation, and cardiac fibrosis. The reduced IL17A-signature in both Abx and AhRi-treated groups indicates a potential mechanistic link between microbiota-driven AhR activation, TH17 cells, and adverse cardiac remodeling in CKD.

title: #2009 Impact of systemic glucocorticoids on Gd-IgA1 levels in Immunoglobulin A Nephropathy: insights from the TESTING trial
authors: Jincan Zan; Muh Geot Wong; Dana Kim; Sufang Shi; Helen Monaghan; Vlado Perkovic; Jicheng Lv; Hong Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Galactose-deficient IgA1 (Gd-IgA1) is a key player in the pathogenesis of Immunoglobulin A Nephropathy (IgAN), driving immune complex formation and subsequent kidney damage. The Therapeutic Effects of Steroids in IgA Nephropathy Global (TESTING) trial demonstrated that glucocorticoid therapy significantly reduced proteinuria and improved kidney outcomes in patients with IgAN. However, the effect of glucocorticoid therapy on pathogenic IgA levels remains poorly understood. This study aims to assess the impact of systemic glucocorticoids on Gd-IgA1 and total IgA levels in patients with IgAN in the TESTING trial.
Method
Participants with IgAN were randomised to 6–9 months of full-dose (0.6 to 0.8 mg/kg/day) or reduced-dose (0.4 mg/kg/day) oral methylprednisolone versus placebo. Serum samples from 137 participants in the China Cohort were collected at baseline, 6 months, and 12 months. Gd-IgA1 levels were quantified using the KM55 ELISA kit. A linear mixed model was used to compare the changes in Gd-IgA1 and total IgA across each treatment arm from baseline at 6 and 12 months.
Results
In total, 137 participants were included in this study, with 40 in the full-dose methylprednisolone group, 26 in the reduced-dose methylprednisolone group, and 71 in the placebo group. There were no statistically significant differences in baseline total IgA and Gd-IgA1 levels among the three groups. At 6 months, the reduced-dose group exhibited a significant reduction in total IgA by 27.2% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 16.4% to 36.6%) and in Gd-IgA1 by 21.2% (10.6% to 30.6%) from baseline compared to the placebo group. In the full-dose group, total IgA decreased by 34.0% (25.7% to 41.4%) and Gd-IgA1 by 42.7% (36.1% to 48.6%). By 12 months, Gd-IgA1 levels began to rise as treatment was discontinued. Gd-IgA1 levels in the reduced-dose group was marginally lower compared to placebo by 4.6% (−8.3% to 15.9%, P = 0.06), while the full-dose group maintained a significant reduction of 25.4% (16.8% to 33.1%, P < 0.001). There was no significant difference in the ratio of Gd-IgA1 to total IgA across all three groups.
Conclusion
Systemic glucocorticoid therapy effectively reduces total IgA and Gd-IgA1 levels in patients with IgAN compared to placebo, however the treatment effects may diminish over time.

title: #2434 Impact of synbiotics on chronic kidney disease patients: a randomized, placebo-controlled study
authors: Zoi Alexakou; Elpiniki Stathopoulou; Margarita Bora; Panagiota Giannou; Aglaia Chalkia; Nikolaos Tsiamperas; Spyros I Siakavellas; Dimitrios Petras; Spilios Manolakopoulos
abstract:
Background and Aims
The association between microbiota dysbiosis and chronic kidney disease (CKD) is well established. CKD leads to gut dysbiosis by causing changes in the microbiota's composition, biochemical environment, and metabolic functions. On the other hand, gut dysbiosis has significant effects on the human organism, causing renal disease progression and increasing the risk of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality through multiple mechanisms. Little is known about the effects of synbiotics on kidney function and CKD. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effects of synbiotic supplement administration on CKD progression.
Method
We conducted a randomized, placebo-controlled trial in 60 CKD (stages IlIa to V, eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m², CKD-EPI calculation) non-dialysis patients. The participants were randomly divided into two groups to receive either a synbiotic supplement (1 sachet containing 6 x× 105 probiotic bacteria, including Lactobacillus rhamnosus, Lactobacillus acidophilus, Bifidobacterium longum, 640 mg fructooligosaccharides, and 640 mg Psyllium Husk) or a placebo (1 sachet) for 24 weeks. The data were analyzed using SPSS and GraphPad prism. Comparisons were performed using the Mann-Whitney and Tukey test (for non-normally and normally distributed data, respectively).
Blood and urine parameters, as well as kidney function, were evaluated prior to the initiation and after 24 weeks of administration of either the synbiotic or placebo. Patients eligible for entering the study were adults (≥18 years). Exclusion criteria included: diabetes mellitus, gastrointestinal (GI) malignancy or other malignancies affecting the patients' overall status, GI diseases (including inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, enterectomy), recent GI hemorrhage, alcohol consumption ≥40 gr/day over the past 12 months, NSAIDS use in the past 4 weeks, and participants on corticosteroids or immunosuppressant medications.
Results
A total of 60 patients were enrolled and completed the study, with 47/60 male and 13/60 female participants, and a mean age of 66 ± 12. Eighty-seven percent (87%) suffered from arterial hypertension. There was no significant difference in the clinical and epidemiological baseline characteristics and the proportions of patients treated with RAAS inhibitors (RAASi) and SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) between the synbiotic and placebo groups. There was no significant difference in baseline kidney function parameters between the synbiotic group and the placebo group (median eGFR: 38.30 ml/min/1.74 m² vs. 34.92 ml/min/1.74 m², ps = not significant [ns]; creatinine: 1.984 mg/dl vs. 2.332 mg/dl, P = ns; urea: 68 mg/dl vs. 91 mg/dl, ps = ns). A kidney biopsy was performed in 37% of the patients, and no significant difference was noted regarding the cause of CKD, when known, between the two groups. The only significant difference in baseline values was urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR) (synbiotic group: 321 mg/g vs. placebo group: 661 mg/g, P = 0.02).
Over 24 weeks, there were no significant changes in serum urea and creatinine levels, eGFR or ACR in the synbiotic group (urea:68 mg/dl vs. 73 mg/dl, creatinine:1.984 mg/dl vs. 1.933 mg/dl, median eGFR: 38.30 ml/min/1.74 m² vs. 41.53 ml/min/1.74 m², P = ns). In contrast, the placebo group showed a significant increase in creatinine levels (2.332 mg/dl vs. 2.688 mg/dl, P = 0.0004) and a decrease of 3 ml/min/1.73 m2 in eGFR (34.92 ml/min/1.73 m² vs. 31.96, P = 0.0024).
At week 24, there was a significant difference between the synbiotic and placebo groups regarding creatinine levels (1.933 mg/dl vs. 2.688 mg/dl, P = 0.0128) and eGFR (41.53 ml/min/1.73 m² vs. 31.96 ml/min/1.73 m², P = 0.0371).
No adverse events were reported in synbiotic group.
Conclusion
Our data show that a 24-week administration of synbiotics in CKD stages III–V, non-dialysis patients is associated with a trend toward eGFR improvement, although this was not statistically significant whereas patients receiving the placebo showed a significant increase in creatinine levels and a decrease in eGFR.

title: #3139 The association between dexa-measured visceral fat and age-related iohexol-clearance decline -a population-based cohort study-
authors: Karl Brobak; Toralf Melsom; Jon Viljar Norvik; Inger Enoksen; Ludvig Balteskard Rinde; Bjørn Eriksen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Obesity is linked to the development of diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease (CVD), and chronic kidney disease (CKD). However, whether obesity is an independent risk factor for CKD remains debated, partly due to limitations in traditional glomerular filtration rate (GFR) estimation methods. Also, conventional obesity metrics such as body mass index (BMI) and waist-hip-ratio (WHR), do not adequately reflect visceral adipose tissue mass (VAT). This study hypothesizes that increased visceral fat, measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA), is a significant risk factor for GFR decline in non-diabetic individuals.
Method

title: #2769 Impact of body mass index (BMI) on renal function decline in high-risk renal cell carcinoma: implications for first-line systemic therapy eligibility
authors: Pietro Scilipoti; Giuseppe Rosiello; Lucia Salerno; Mattia Longoni; Francesco Trevisani; Arianna Bettiga; Federico Belladelli; Alberto Briganti; Andrea Salonia; Francesco Montorsi; Alessandro Larcher; Umberto Capitanio
abstract:
Background and Aims
For patients at high risk of systemic progression following surgery for renal cancer, several systemic therapies are available. However, an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) below 30 mL/min/1.73 m² often serves as an exclusion criterion for these treatments. Additionally, a high body mass index (BMI) is a well-established risk factor for developing chronic kidney disease (CKD) after surgery, potentially further limiting eligibility for such therapies. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of BMI on renal function in surgically treated patients at high risk of recurrence.
Method
From a prospectively maintained database, we selected renal cell carcinoma (RCC) patients classified as intermediate or high risk based on the Leibovich 2018 score. The estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was calculated using the CKD-EPI formula, and CKD upstage was defined as an eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m². To assess the risk of CKD upstage, a multivariable Fine-Gray competing risk regression model was used, adjusting for baseline eGFR and patient comorbidities, with BMI treated as a continuous variable. The probability of CKD upstage after surgery was graphically represented against BMI using a LOESS function.
Results
A total of 1,059 patients were included in the study. The median age at the time of surgery was 62 years (IQR: 52–71), and 23% (n = 239) of patients had a Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) >2. The median BMI was 26 kg/m² (IQR: 24–28). After a median follow-up of 48 months (IQR: 27–109), 31% (n = 332) of patients experienced disease progression, with a median time to progression of 45 months (IQR: 25–107). Multivariable regression analysis demonstrated that higher BMI was consistently associated with CKD upstage, with a hazard ratio (HR) of 1.06 per 5 kg/m² increase (P = 0.035). Additionally, a marked increase in CKD probability was observed in patients with a BMI >25 kg/m² (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
In patients at high risk of recurrence after surgery for RCC, BMI is a significant risk factor for eGFR decline and CKD upstage. These results indicate that a high BMI may limit eligibility for first-line systemic therapies in this population. To enhance treatment options and prevent progression to severe CKD, a tailored, multidisciplinary approach is recommended.

title: #3176 Measured GFR in oncological solitary kidney: a critical parameter for precision management in onconephrology
authors: Francesco Trevisani; Matteo Paccagnella; Arianna Bettiga; Massimo Locatelli; Eleonora Sabetta; Giorgio Pizzagalli; Matteo Floris; Giuseppe Rosiello; Umberto Capitanio; Andrea Salonia; Alberto Briganti; Francesco Montorsi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) and acute kidney injury (AKI) are among the most significant long-term complications following radical nephrectomy (RN) for renal masses. In clinical practice, precise renal function assessment is crucial to minimize these risks, particularly for patients with an oncological solitary kidney (SK), where management largely depends on glomerular filtration rate (GFR) values. While estimated GFR (eGFR) is the most commonly used method to assess renal function, it carries a notable margin of error compared to the gold standard, measured GFR (mGFR). This study aimed to quantify the discrepancy between eGFR most used formulas and mGFR in a cohort of patients with oncological solitary kidneys to enhance accuracy in clinical decision-making and postoperative care.
Method
We retrospectively analyzed a cohort of 170 patients with a solitary kidney (SK), of whom 79.4% (n = 135) had an oncological SK. Renal function was assessed using measured GFR (mGFR) via Iohexol clearance, considered the gold standard, and compared with estimated GFR (eGFR) calculated using multiple formulas.
To evaluate the agreement between mGFR and eGFR methods, we computed the Concordance Correlation Coefficient (CCC), Total Deviation Index (TDI), and Coverage Probability (CP). Histograms were generated to visualize the distribution of absolute differences between Iohexol clearance and eGFR, while scatter plots were used to compare individual eGFR methods against mGFR.
All statistical analyses and visualizations were performed using R (version 4.4.2). The following packages were used: ggplot2 for scatter plots, epiR for CCC, TDI, and CP calculations, and dplyr/tidyr for data preprocessing.
Results
Descriptive analysis is shown in Table 1. Agreement between mGFR and eGFR varied across formulas (Tables 2, 3). EKFC showed the highest concordance, while CKD-EPI 2012 (cystatin C) and Cockcroft-Gault performed worst (Fig. 1). Histograms (Fig. 2) and scatter plots confirmed these discrepancies.
Conclusion
In daily clinical practice, a tailored nephrological follow-up based on measured GFR (mGFR) is essential for radical nephrectomy (RN) patients with a solitary kidney. Reliance on estimated GFR (eGFR) alone can lead to significant clinical errors, either underestimating or overestimating actual renal function, potentially resulting in critical medical consequences.

title: #3447 Precision medicine in onco-nephrology: unveiling the gap between measured and estimated GFR
authors: Francesco Trevisani; Matteo Paccagnella; Arianna Bettiga; Massimo Locatelli; Eleonora Sabetta; Giorgio Pizzagalli; Matteo Floris; Giuseppe Rosiello; Umberto Capitanio; Andrea Salonia; Alberto Briganti; Francesco Montorsi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Onco-nephrology patients require careful attention in personalized medicine, as acute and chronic kidney injuries are common and significant complications. Whether undergoing surgical treatments that impact renal excretory function, systemic therapies for progressive disease, or receiving contrast agents, antibiotics, or anticoagulant therapies, accurate assessment of renal function is essential. This study aimed to quantify the error margin of commonly used eGFR formulas compared to measured GFR (mGFR) in onco-nephrology patients.
Method
We retrospectively analyzed 615 patients, including 311 (50.6%) with oncological disease. Renal function was assessed using measured GFR (mGFR) via Iohexol clearance, considered the gold standard, and compared with multiple estimated GFR (eGFR) formulas.
To evaluate agreement between mGFR and eGFR, we calculated the Concordance Correlation Coefficient (CCC), Total Deviation Index (TDI), and Coverage Probability (CP) Histograms visualized the distribution of absolute differences, while scatter plots compared individual formulas against mGFR.
All statistical analyses were conducted using R (version 4.4.2) with the ggplot2, epiR, dplyr, and tidyr packages.
Results
Descriptive analysis is shown in Table 1. Agreement between mGFR and eGFR varied across formulas (Tables 2–3). EKFC demonstrated the highest concordance, while CKD-EPI 2012 (cystatin C) and Cockcroft-Gault showed the lowest agreement (Fig. 1). Histograms (Fig. 2) confirmed significant variability in estimation accuracy across methods.
Conclusion
eGFR formulas demonstrated a significant margin of error across all CKD stage classifications when compared to mGFR. In the context of onco-nephrology, the use of mGFR should be considered essential to ensure tailored and precise patient management.

title: #1091 Progression of cardiac remodelling and dysfunction is accompanied by altered metabolic profile in chronic kidney disease
authors: Juliana Boukhaled; Irene Cortijo; Jonas Laget; Rafael Stroggilos; Flore Duranton; Manousos Makridakis; Antonia Vlahou; Agnieszka Latosinska; Anne Dominique Lajoix; Angel Argiles Ciscart; Nathalie Gayrard; Fabrice Raynaud
abstract:
Background and Aims
The heart and kidneys are vital organs that influence each other's function. Dysfunction in one inevitably leads to dysfunction in the other and is known as cardiorenal syndrome (CRS). CRS type 4 is defined by chronic kidney disease (CKD) causing impaired cardiac function, primarily through diastolic dysfunction and structural remodelling, including fibrosis and hypertrophy. This is accompanied by metabolic alterations, characterized by disrupted energy substrate utilization and a metabolic shift towards glycolysis instead of beta-oxidation. The progression of CRS IV occurs dynamically and gradually thus identifying key changes could prove beneficial for treatment and prediction of outcome for the patients. The present study assessed heart remodelling and function after 12 and 24 weeks of chronic kidney disease in rats undergoing subtotal nephrectomy (respectively SNx12 and SNx24).
Method
At 12 weeks, male Sprague Dawley rats underwent 5/6 nephrectomy (SNx) or Sham operation and were sacrificed after 12 or 24 weeks. Serum creatinine was measured with the epoc® Blood Analysis System. Before sacrifice, a carotid artery catheter was inserted to measure systolic arterial pressure (SAP). Left ventricular function was assessed by echocardiography (VisualSonics/Fujifilm) under isoflurane anaesthesia. Fibrosis (Sirius Red staining) in both kidney and heart, and cardiomyocyte size (H&E staining) were quantified. Vevolab 3.1.0 software was used to evaluate left ventricle posterior wall thickness during systole (LVPW_S), diastolic dysfunction by measurement of isovolumic relaxation time (IVRT), early diastolic strain rate (E/SRE) and Doppler mitral inflow velocities of the peak early (E) ‘/ Tissue doppler parameter e′ (E/e’). To further assess molecular alterations in the left ventricle, proteomics analysis was performed using LC-MS/MS method (n = 5 animals from each of Sham and SNx groups). Samples were prepared according to FASP protocol. Gene Set Variation Analysis (GSVA) was conducted using pathway terms from the Molecular Signatures Database and results were analysed using the limma method. Statistical analysis and GSVA was performed using GraphPad Prism 8 and R Studio, two-way ANOVA, non-parametric tests, with log transformation when applicable.
Results
Plasma creatinine levels were increased in both SNx12 and SNx24 animals (Table 1). Fibrosis in the kidney increased between SNx12 and SNx24 versus their corresponding Sham (Table 1). SNx24 rats exhibited increased heart fibrosis, cardiomyocyte size, and SAP in comparison to the respective Sham (Table 1). Cardiac remodelling between SNx12 and SNx24 was observed through the increase in the left ventricle wall thickness (Fig. 1A). In SNx24 diastolic dysfunction was observed through measurement of E/SRE, IVRT and E/e’ (Fig. 1B, Table 1). To better understand the molecular changes that correspond to pronounced hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction, LC-MS/MS analysis was performed with a focus on the group SNx24. A heatmap was generated to illustrate top 20 up- and top 20 down-regulated proteins of SNx24 versus Sham 24 (Fig. 1C). When compared to Sham24, GSVA results indicated that SNX24 samples were associated with disrupted mitochondrial processes, downregulation of fatty acid oxidation, but also with overactivation of extracellular pathways including infiltration of immune cells, wound healing and cell-ECM interactions (Fig. 1D).
Conclusion
These results indicate that the SNx model captures key events in CRS development, cardiac remodelling and dysfunction, and suggest that the observed mitochondrial changes play a supportive role in these processes. This preclinical model also provides an opportunity to evaluate novel anti-fibrotic treatments and assess their impact on mitochondrial function, paving the way for potential therapeutic advancements.

title: #2894 Effect of CKD and hemodialysis on the epigenetic clock: implications for the reverse epidemiology
authors: Renzo Tesser; Pietro Iulianiello; Ilenia Gravina; Davide Viggiano
abstract:
Background and Aims
DNA methylation patterns in peripheral cells can predict chronological and biological age through the “epigenetic clock,” which remains understudied in chronic kidney disease (CKD) and hemodialysis populations. We investigated accelerated biological aging across CKD severity and hemodialysis (HD) patients, examining whether kidney transplantation mitigates these effects. Additionally, we explored whether accelerated aging explains the “reverse epidemiology” phenomenon in HD patients, where overweight individuals show lower mortality rates, hypothesizing that HD accelerates biological aging and shifts the BMI-mortality curve toward higher BMI values.
Method
We analyzed epigenetic clock measurements using the Phenoage algorithm in CKD patients (n = 50), HD patients (n = 30), and kidney transplant recipients (n = 50). Groups were matched for age, blood pressure, gender, and comorbidities. Advanced CKD was defined as eGFR <30 mL/min. Proteinuria and leukocyte counts were evaluated as potential explanatory variables. We conducted a meta-analysis comparing BMI-mortality versus age curves between healthy adults and HD patients to verify the aging process's effect on reverse epidemiology.
Results
Early-stage CKD (eGFR >30 mL/min) showed no significant impact on biological age, while advanced CKD accelerated aging by approximately 10 years. Kidney transplantation partially reversed this effect, reducing biological age by about 9 years, though not reaching early CKD levels. This improvement disappeared when transplanted kidneys developed advanced CKD, resulting in 15-year acceleration beyond chronological age. HD patients showed the most severe acceleration, advancing approximately 20 years beyond chronological age. Early CKD demonstrated significant correlations between accelerated aging and both proteinuria levels and eosinophil counts (P < 0.01), while proteinuria's influence became negligible in advanced CKD.
The BMI-mortality relationship revealed age-dependent patterns. In the general population under 65 years, optimal survival corresponded to BMI 18–25 kg/m², shifting to 25–30 kg/m² above age 65. HD patients showed higher mortality rates across all BMI levels, with younger patients showing optimal survival at BMI 25–30 kg/m² and older patients at 30–35 kg/m². This pattern paralleled that of significantly older individuals in the general population.
Conclusion
Advanced CKD significantly accelerates biological aging, with HD and non-functional kidney transplants showing the strongest effects. While successful transplantation partially reverses this acceleration, CKD's metabolic imprint prevents complete restoration. This accelerated aging provides a novel explanation for reverse epidemiology in HD patients, as their BMI-mortality relationship mirrors that of individuals approximately 10 years older in the general population. The age-dependent shift explains why optimal survival occurs at higher BMI values in HD patients, suggesting accelerated biological aging as the underlying mechanism for the obesity paradox in this population.

authors: Bethany Lucas; Ashveer Randhay; Kelly White; Nicholas Selby; Maarten Taal
abstract:
Background and Aims

Moreover, there is debate as to the optimal BP target for patients with CKD and whether stricter BP targets are achievable and safe for this complex patient group. Method
SMaRT BP CKD is a single centre randomised feasibility trial. The self-management intervention was home BP monitoring (Microlife WatchBP) and an agreed medication plan. Of the 390 participants eligible from 1464 screened, 58 were recruited between July 2023 and May 2024. The lower target of 120 mmHg systolic is difficult to reach even with more intensive BP management.

title: #214 Responsiveness to roxadustat in non-dialysis chronic kidney disease patients with anemia by baseline iron status: a secondary analysis of the ROXSTAR registry
authors: Jianghua Chen; Zunsong Wang; Yuchen Zhang; Shuting Pan; Yiqing Wu
abstract:
Background and Aims
The ROXSTAR Registry (ChiCTR2100046322) is a phase 4, multicenter study conducted in China to evaluate the long-term safety and effectiveness of a 52-week roxadustat treatment in both dialysis and non-dialysis (ND) chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients with anemia. This study enrolled 2021 patients with various comorbidities, including iron deficiency (ID), reflecting real-world clinical practice. This secondary analysis aimed to assess anemia correction and hemoglobin (Hb) target achievement in ND-CKD patients stratified by baseline iron status.
Method
This secondary analysis utilized data from the ROXSTAR Registry, including ND-CKD patients who received roxadustat and had at least one post-baseline Hb measurement. Oral supplemental iron could be administered at any time according to clinical practice. Intravenous iron was administered if clinically indicated per investigator's judgement. Outcomes included the proportion of patients achieving mean Hb levels within 100–130 g/L, changes from baseline (CFB) in Hb over weeks 24–52, CFB in iron metabolism parameters (serum ferritin [SF], transferrin saturation [TSAT], serum iron, total iron binding capacity [TIBC], transferrin), and weekly roxadustat dosage, stratified into three baseline iron subgroups: iron repletion (SF≥100 µg/L and TSAT≥20%), absolute ID (SF<100 µg/L and TSAT <20%), and non-absolute ID (SF≥100 µg/L and TSAT<20% or SF <100 µg/L and TSAT≥20%).
Results
A total of 490 ND-CKD patients were analyzed (iron repletion: 186 [38.0%]; absolute ID: 99 [20.2%]; non-absolute ID: 205 [41.8%]). The absolute ID group had a higher proportion of females (78.8%). Overall baseline mean Hb was 95.3±12.2 g/L (iron repletion: 97.1±11.5 g/L; absolute ID: 91.3±11.9 g/L; non-absolute ID: 95.7±12.7 g/L). The proportion of patients with elevated C-reactive protein was higher in the absolute ID (18.2%) and non-absolute ID (17.6%) groups, compared to the iron repletion group (10.2%) (Table 1).
Patients with absolute ID showed the greatest Hb improvement and the highest proportion achieving target Hb levels over weeks 24–52 (20.7 [95% CI: 17.5, 23.8] g/L; 88.5% [95% CI: 81.4%, 95.7%]), compared to the iron repletion 13.8 [95% CI: 11.8, 15.7] g/L; 83.5% [95% CI: 77.4%, 89.5%] and the non-absolute ID group (15.5 [95% CI: 13.5, 17.4] g/L; 83.9% [95% CI: 77.9%, 89.8%]).
During treatment, 54.7% of patients received iron therapy (iron repletion: 52.2%; absolute ID: 59.6%; non-absolute ID: 54.6%). SF & TSAT increased in the absolute ID groups (CFB: 14.9 µg/L & 7.8% at week 24, 24.4 µg/L & 8.1% at week 52), contrasting with trends in the other groups. Serum iron, TIBC and transferrin level increased across all groups (Table 2).
Roxadustat mean weekly dose was lower in the iron repletion group (195.9 ± 87.0 mg), compared to the absolute ID (237.7 ± 92.1 mg) and non-absolute ID (211.5 ± 80.8 mg) groups. In the iron repletion group, roxadustat weekly dose started at 239.9 ± 71.7 mg, gradually decreased to 168.0 ± 97.1 mg by weeks 24, then increased to 200.0 ± 106.6 mg by week 52. In contrast, the absolute ID group started at 242.3 ± 68.6 mg, increased to 273.0 ± 91.8 mg by week 12, then slightly decreased to 217.4 ± 111.5 mg by week 52.
Conclusion
Roxadustat effectively corrected anemia and maintained target Hb levels in ND-CKD patients across all baseline iron statuses, demonstrating its utility in real-world settings. Notably, even in patients with absolute ID, roxadustat improved Hb level and iron utilization when combined with oral supplemental iron.

title: #1885 Magnetic resonance imaging assessment of kidney morphometry in chronic kidney disease: baseline data from the AFiRM study
authors: Susan Francis; Charlotte Buchanan; Martin Craig; Mark Gilthorpe; Philip A Kalra; Iosif Mendichovszky; Steven Sourbron; Maarten Taal; Nicholas Selby
abstract:
Background and Aims
Standard ultrasound is the only imaging performed in most patients undergoing work-up for chronic kidney disease (CKD), but provides only coarse estimates of kidney volume, shape or appearance. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) provides detailed anatomical images that allow measurement of total kidney volume (TKV) and can be further analysed for quantitative radiomics features such as kidney shape, texture and heterogeneity. The relationship of these MRI features to CKD aetiology and kidney function is not well described.
Method
We analysed baseline data from the AFiRM study, a UK multi-centre prospective study of renal MRI in people with CKD, to describe TKV and shape features across a range of eGFR and CKD aetiologies. All participants underwent a comprehensive renal multiparametric MRI protocol, which included a T2-weighted anatomical image (Fig. 1a). Each kidney was segmented using a machine learning U-Net, followed by visual assessment and manual correction if required. Normalised kidney volumes and radiomics shape descriptors were computed (14 3D features for each kidney and kidney asymmetry (left-right)) along with summed volume, surface area and surface area/volume, resulting in 45 shape features.
Clinical and biochemical data were collected at time of MRI, and primary renal diagnoses were categorised into: diabetic kidney disease (DKD), non-DKD glomerular disease, tubular disease, ischaemic nephropathy, CKD of unknown cause, and other. Those with ADPKD or with single kidneys were not eligible for this study. Descriptive statistics were used to compare radiomics features between diagnostic categories. The relationship of eGFR with MRI metrics were explored using linear and quadratic terms including BSA as a covariable, with the quadratic term retained where the model fit significantly improved at the 10% level.
Results
From a cohort of 420 participants, 411 participants had complete data and were included in this analysis. Mean age was 55.1 years (standard deviation (sd) = 12.8 years) with 63.7% male. Mean eGFR was 42.7 (sd = 18.7) ml/min/1.73m2 and most (86.2%) were in CKD stages G3-4. The most common diagnostic category was glomerular disease (42.0%), followed by CKD of unknown cause (19.2%), DKD (13.6%), tubular disease (12.2%), ischaemic nephropathy (4.9%) and other (8.0%). A total of 218 (53%) had primary renal diagnosis based on kidney biopsy.
A number of MRI shape and volume features differed across diagnostic categories, with differences in the number and strength of associations between MRI variables and eGFR, as shown in Table 1. For instance, DKD had highest kidney volumes and other features relating to kidney size, including surface area, long and short axis, equivalent diameter, moment of inertia (Fig. 1b and c).
Conclusion
We show that there are clear associations between quantitative MRI measures of kidney volume and shape with eGFR, as well as differences between CKD aetiology categories. This demonstrates substantial potential for these MRI measures to be used in prediction modelling to further explore the interplay among these measures to determine potential mechanistic (i.e., causal) understanding relevant to CKD progression. These analyses will be augmented with the addition of T2-weighted radiomics measures of texture and heterogeneity and quantitative T1 and T2 metrics.

title: #412 Reduced arterial stiffness in children with CKD under long-term growth hormone treatment
authors: Stella Stabouli; Maren Leifheit-Nestler; Aysun Karabay Bayazit; Anke Doyon; Łukasz Obrycki; Bruno Ranchin; Jun Oh; Jerome Harambat; Otto Mehls; Uwe Querfeld; Franz Schaefer; Dieter Haffner
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is characterized by low levels of the anti-aging protein α-Klotho and accelerated cardiovascular (CV) morbidity. Reduced levels of sKlotho are associated with premature aging and CV disease. Short-term treatment with growth hormone (GH) was shown to enhance soluble Klotho (sKlotho), the circulating form of α-Klotho, and endothelial function in patients with CKD. We hypothesized that long-term GH treatment in pediatric patients with CKD improves sKlotho levels and arterial stiffness.
Method
We performed a case-cohort study within the Cardiovascular Comorbidity in Children with Chronic kidney disease (4C) study including 101 children with CKD stages 3–5 treated with and without GH treatment. Patients were assessed for serum sKlotho, intact fibroblast growth factor 23 (iFGF23), somatomedin insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) and pulse wave velocity (PWV) at two time points 12 months apart (E1 and E2). Age and sex adjusted z scores were calculated for height, BMI, systolic and diastolic blood pressure (BP), IGF1, sKlotho, and iFGF23 and PWV.
Results
Mean age of the study population was 12.1 ± 2.8 years, and median duration of GH treatment in the GH group was 21.5 months (IQR, 7.0–56.7 months). At the time of first observation (E1), GH-treated and untreated patients did not significantly differ with respect to anthropometric parameters, median eGFR, BP values, hemoglobin, serum phosphate, iPTH, and lipids values. The median change in eGFR during the observation period was −2.21 ml/min/1.73 m2 (IQR, −5.07 to 0.32, P < 0.001) and similar between groups (P = 0.5). During the observation period, serum IGF1 levels and height z-scores significantly increased in GH treated patients, but not in controls.
GH treated patients showed higher sKlotho (Δ1.2 SD) and IGF1 (Δ1.5 SD) z-scores, and lower PWV z-scores (Δ−0.9 SD) compared to controls (each P < 0.01), both at baseline and after 12 months of follow up. PWV z-score was inversely associated with IGF1 z-score (E1: R2 = 0.130, P < 0.001; E2: R2 = 0.095, P = 0.003), and sKlotho z-score (E1: R2 = 0.086, P = 0.004), and positively associated with systolic BP z-score (E1: R2 = 0.134, P < 0.001; E2: R2 = 0.157, P < 0.001), diastolic BP z-scores (E1: R2 = 0.206, P < 0.001; E2: R2 = 0.304, P < 0.001) and iPTH levels (E2: R2 = 0.084, P < 0.01). PWV z-scores were associated with GH treatment in multivariable analysis GEE model adjusted for the above continuous variables, age and sex (P < 0.05). Further explanatory mediation analysis showed that the effect of GH treatment on PWV z-score is mediated by sKlotho and IGF1 z-score with significant indirect effects coefficients 0.28, SE 0.14, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.04–0.59 and 0.29, SE 0.17, 95%CI 0.007–0.71, respectively (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
Long-term GH treatment is associated with reduced PWV in children with CKD, which is at least partly related to GH/IGF1-induced upregulation of sKlotho. Thus, GH treatment could affect intermediate cardiovascular outcomes beyond growth, i.e. through increased IGF1/Klotho synthesis leading to reduced arterial stiffness and therefore, has a potential role in the prevention of accelerated cardiovascular morbidity in pediatric CKD patients.

title: #413 Effects of long-term GH treatment on FGF23/Klotho axis in pediatric patients with CKD
authors: Stella Stabouli; Maren Leifheit-Nestler; Michael Föller; Martina Feger; Jun Oh; Dusan Paripovic; Germana Longo; Jerome Harambat; Anette Melk; Uwe Querfeld; Franz Schaefer; Dieter Haffner
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is characterized by low levels of the anti-aging protein α-Klotho. Growth hormone (GH) is thought to stimulate calcitriol production and the phosphaturic and vascular actions of FGF23 by upregulation of FGF23/Klotho axis. This is based on the observation that short-term GH treatment and endogenous GH excess enhances serum sKlotho concentrations in health subjects, patients with CKD stage 3 and acromegalic patients. The current study investigated the effects of long-term GH treatment on FGF23/Klotho axis in pediatric patients with CKD.
Method
We performed a case-cohort study within the Cardiovascular Comorbidity in Children with chronic kidney disease (4C) study including 101 children with CKD stages 3-5 treated with and without GH treatment. Patients were assessed for somatomedin insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) and mineral bone metabolism parameters including intact parathormone (iPTH,) 1,25(OH)2D3, serum sKlotho, and intact fibroblast growth factor 23 (iFGF23) at two time points 12 months apart (E1 and E2). Age and sex adjusted z scores were calculated for height, IGF1, sKlotho and iFGF23.
Results
Mean age of the study population was 12.1 ± 2.8 years, and median duration of GH treatment in the GH group amounted to 21.5 months (IQR, 7.0–56.7 months). At the time of first observation (E1), GH-treated and untreated patients did not significantly differ with respect to anthropometric parameters, median eGFR, BP values, hemoglobin, serum phosphate, iPTH, 1,25(OH)2D3, and lipids values. IGF1 z-scores were significantly higher in the GH group compared to controls (P < 0.001). sKlotho z-scores were also significantly higher in GH treated patients (P < 0.001), while iFGF23 z-scores did not differ between groups.
The median change in eGFR during the observation period did not differ between the groups (GH group: −1.08 ml/min/1.73 m2 (IQR, −4.5 to 0.69); controls: −2.26 ml/min/1.73 m2 (IQR, −5.09 to −0.09), P = 0.5). During the observation period, serum IGF1 levels and height z-score significantly increased in GH treated patients, but not in controls. sKlotho z-score, iFGF23 z-score, and 1,25(OH)2D3 concentrations did not significantly change within patient groups, while iPTH levels increased in controls only (P = 0.006).
sKlotho z-score at the final observation (E2) was positively associated with eGFR (R2 = 0.051, P < 0.05), IGF1 z-score (R2 = 0.153 P < 0.001), 1,25(OH)2D3 (R2 = 0.038, P = 0.05) levels, and negatively associated with iFGF23 z-score (R2 = 0.093, P = 0.002), and total cholesterol levels (R2 = 0.058, P < 0.05). The slope of the regression line between sKlotho and eGFR at E2 was significant only in controls (β = 1.035, 95%CI 1.01–1.06, P = 0.005, for interaction between control group and final eGFR) (Fig. 1).
In GEE multivariable model, sKlotho z-sores during the observation period were significantly associated with GH treatment, IGF1 z-score, iFGF23 z-score, and total cholesterol levels, while iFGF23 z-scores were associated with eGFR, male sex, calcium and sKlotho z-score.
Conclusion
In this case-cohort study, children with CKD stages 3-5 on long-term GH treatment showed improved levels of sKlotho compared to controls and the difference remained significant during the observation period. GH treatment may attenuate the adverse effect of decreasing eGFR on renal α-Klotho synthesis and thus, sKlotho levels, likely mediated by IGF1, and independently of FGF23.

Growth hormone (GH) is thought to stimulate calcitriol production and the phosphaturic and vascular actions of FGF23 by upregulation of FGF23/Klotho axis. This is based on the observation that short-term GH treatment and endogenous GH excess enhances serum sKlotho concentrations in health subjects, patients with CKD stage 3 and acromegalic patients. The current study investigated the effects of long-term GH treatment on FGF23/Klotho axis in pediatric patients with CKD.

We performed a case-cohort study within the Cardiovascular Comorbidity in Children with chronic kidney disease (4C) study including 101 children with CKD stages 3-5 treated with and without GH treatment. Mean age of the study population was 12.1 ± 2.8 years, and median duration of GH treatment in the GH group amounted to 21.5 months (IQR, 7.0–56.7 months). title: #651 The effects of empagliflozin on fluid and eletrolyte balance
authors: Steffen Flindt Nielsen; Camilla Duus; Niels Henrik Buus; Jesper Bech; Frank Mose
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) exert cardiovascular and renal benefits in type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM2) and chronic kidney disease (CKD), potentially mediated in part by natriuresis and changes in fluid balance. However, the exact mechanisms are not fully clear. We examined the effects of empagliflozin on fluid and electrolyte balance in a cohort of patients with DM2 and preserved kidney function (estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) >60 ml/min/1.73 m2), DM2 and concomitant CKD and non-diabetic CKD (both eGFR 20–60 ml/min/1.73 m2), respectively.
Method
A randomized double blind, placebo controlled cross-over trial. Participants were randomized to 4 weeks of empagliflozin 10 mg/day or matching placebo and crossed over to 4 weeks of the opposite treatment after a wash out. We measured body composition by bio-impedance using a Fresenius Body Composition Monitor, 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure (BP) using a Mobil-O-Graph, urinary sodium, potassium and glucose excretion, free water clearance, plasma levels of renin, aldosterone and copeptin and urinary excretion of epithelial sodium channels (ENaC), aquaporin-2 (AQP2) and sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCC).
Results
49 participants completed the trial, 16 with DM2 and preserved renal function, 17 with DM2 and CKD and 16 with non-diabetic CKD. Mean age was 68, 8 ± 7.5 years, median eGFR was 42.2 ml/min/1.73 m2 (interquartile range: 34.5–73.5). 73% were male, 92% had concomitant arterial hypertension and 20% had ischemic heart disease. Empagliflozin reduced extracellular body water by 0.29 L (95% CI: −0.54; −0.03 L, P = 0.03) and tended towards reducing overhydration (mean difference: −0.23L, 95% CI: −0.51; 0.05L, P = 0.10). Systolic BP decreased by 6 mmHg and diastolic BP decreased by 3 mmHg during empagliflozin treatment compared to placebo (P < 0.001). Change in overhydration was correlated to changes in systolic BP (R = 0.38, P = 0.008). Sodium excretion and urine volume did not change, but empagliflozin increased glucose excretion (P < 0.0001) and fractional potassium excretion (P = 0.046). Furthermore, copeptin levels increased by 30% (P < 0.0001), urinary AQP2 excretion increased by 8% (P = 0.04) and free water clearance decreased (P = 0.0001). Renin levels also increased (P = 0.02) and there were borderline significant rises in aldosterone (P = 0.05) and urinary ENaC excretion (P = 0.08). Urinary excretion of NCC did not change (P = 0.63)
Conclusion
Our results indicate that SGLT2i exert a diuretic effect which, although compensated by increased activity of the renin-angiotensin system and antidiuretic hormone, leads to changes in fluid balance. Furthermore, the BP lowering effect of SGLT2i may be related to changes in fluid balance.

title: #2896 CKD Stage 3 patient monitoring: evaluating current practices in general practice
authors: Amal Qaisar
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) Stage 3, characterised by moderate decline in kidney function, affects a significant proportion of the population and poses a major risk for progression to end-stage renal disease. Early intervention through regular monitoring can slow disease progression and improve patient outcomes. General practitioners (GPs) play a key role in CKD management, primarily through regular monitoring of eGFR, ACR, and initiating medications such as SGLT2 inhibitors and ACE inhibitors. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend testing of eGFR, ACR, and full blood count (FBC) to monitor CKD progression. Despite these recommendations, it remains unclear whether these practices are consistently followed in primary care. This audit evaluates adherence to these guidelines among CKD Stage 3 patients in a general practice setting.
Method
This audit reviewed the medical records of 265 patients diagnosed with CKD Stage 3 who were active members of the GP practice in Shropshire and had not passed away. The study focused on whether these patients received recommended tests for monitoring kidney function (eGFR, ACR, FBC). The frequency of eGFR and ACR testing over the past year was analysed, as well as the timing of their most recent FBC. The data was compared to the monitoring recommendations outlined in NICE guidelines. The study design was retrospective, analysing data from the past year to assess current practices within the general practice.
Results
Among the 265 patients reviewed, 49 (18.5%) had not had their eGFR tested in the past year. Additionally, 66 patients (24.9%) had not undergone an ACR test since 2014, and 29 patients (10.9%) had never had an ACR test. For those who had eGFR tests, 34 patients (12.8%) had results above 60, indicating adequate kidney function. In contrast, 6 patients (2.3%) had an eGFR of less than 29, suggesting the need for further evaluation. Furthermore, 101 patients (38.1%) had a full blood count test within the year. Many of the eGFR tests were conducted as part of investigations for acute illness rather than planned monitoring, meaning some patients missed proper and timely monitoring. The audit also revealed issues with misclassification and miscoding of patients, such as those diagnosed with CKD following an acute kidney injury without waiting for a repeat kidney function test, which can lead to an over or underestimation of their risk.
Conclusion
This audit reveals significant gaps in CKD Stage 3 monitoring, particularly regarding ACR testing and inconsistent eGFR tracking. These gaps pose a risk for missed opportunities to identify CKD progression and intervene in a timely manner. The findings highlight the need for improved coding of CKD stages and better recognition of CKD progression to prevent patients from advancing to Stage 4 without intervention. The decline in urine ACR testing after the removal of funding through the Quality and Outcomes Framework (QoF) in 2014 has led to underestimation of CKD progression and end-organ damage risk.
GPs are crucial in addressing these gaps by improving CKD monitoring and ensuring timely interventions, such as prescribing medications to slow progression. However, primary care is under increasing pressure due to rising CKD prevalence and co-morbidities. The use of AI to support CKD management, alerting GPs and patients about tests and treatments, could help. Timely referrals to secondary care are also vital, particularly as more patients progress without adequate monitoring.
For the future, more GPs need to be involved in CKD management to ensure consistent, timely care. By increasing GP participation in monitoring and improving collaboration with secondary care, we can achieve earlier detection, better disease management, and improved outcomes. Strengthening GPs' role and exploring AI-driven solutions can alleviate the burden on primary care while enhancing proactive, personalised care.

title: #2530 Hyperkalaemia prevalence and risk factors in chronic kidney disease and heart failure: insights from iCaReMe registry middle east and Africa cohort
authors: Sola Aoun; Mustafa Arici; Hussein Bagha; Mohamed Zaki; Ifeoma Ulasi; Elliot Tannor; Haroon Mia; Yüksel Çavuşoğlu; Hiba Barghouthi; Sonia Juarez; Hardik Vasnawala; Ahmed Hadaoui
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyperkalaemia (HK; serum potassium [K+] level >5.0 mmol/L) is common in people with chronic kidney disease (CKD) or heart failure (HF), often due to renal impairment and the use of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors (RAASi), which slow disease progression and improve outcomes. The prevalence and impact of HK in the Middle East and Africa (MEA) are poorly understood, complicating management due to high rates of CKD and HF driven by diabetes, hypertension (HTN), and cardiovascular disease. Our study utilizes data from iCaReMe Global Registry (NCT03549754) to address this gap by assessing HK prevalence and risk factors in patients with CKD and HF in the MEA region.
Method
This cross-sectional observational study included adult subjects with CKD or HF enrolled in the iCaReMe Registry from 11 MEA countries (Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, Iraq, Jordan, Kenya, Lebanon, Nigeria, South Africa, Türkiye, United Arab Emirates). Demographic and clinical characteristics, HK prevalence, and treatment patterns were summarized descriptively. HK risk factors were analysed using stepwise logistic regression.
Results
A total of 5,596 adults (mean age 57.3 ± 14.0 years; 57.3% male) were included, with 3,574 individuals (63.9%) having CKD (mean estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] 35.4 ± 26.4 mL/min/1.73 m2) and 2,797 individuals (50.0%) having HF (mean left ventricular ejection fraction 39.0 ± 13.5%). HTN was present in 78.0% of participants and 50.8% had type 2 diabetes mellitus. Mean serum K+ was 4.5 ± 0.7 mmol/L, with an overall HK prevalence of 17.6% (23.0% in those with CKD and 10.5% in HF patients). Overall, 62.4% of patients were on angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers, or angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors, 38.4% on loop diuretics, 30.5% on sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors, and 25.7% on mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists. Patients with HK (mean K+ = 5.5 ±0.5 mmol/L) exhibited decreased kidney function with more advanced CKD stages (78.3% of subjects with G3b–G5 stage) and lower RAASi use than non-HK patients (mean K+ = 4.3±0.5 mmol/L). Only 10.3% of those with HK were on anti-HK therapies, with 40% receiving potassium binders. Multivariate analysis revealed that RAASi use (odds ratio [OR], 1.5; 95% CI, 1.2–1.9; P = 0.0026) and serum creatinine levels (mg/dL) (OR, 1.1; 95% CI, 1.0− 1.1; P = 0.0217) were positively associated with HK.
Conclusion
This study offers insights into the burden and risk factors of HK in patients with CKD and HF in the MEA region. The findings reveal a substantial prevalence of HK, especially in advanced CKD, along with suboptimal use of RAASi and low utilization of anti-HK therapies. These gaps highlight the need to align real-world practices with guidelines by optimizing RAASi use while managing HK risks. Improving access to novel potassium binders and implementing region-specific strategies could improve outcomes for this high-risk population.

title: #657 Zigakibart-treated patients with IgAN achieved high rates of proteinuria remission and stable eGFR over 76 weeks in a Phase 1/2 study
authors: Laura Kooienga; Eun Young Lee; Hamid Moradi; William Smith; Cong Lin; Jonathan Barratt
abstract:
Background and Aims
Immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) is the leading cause of primary glomerulonephritis with limited treatment options. Zigakibart is an investigational, humanised monoclonal antibody that blocks A PRoliferation-Inducing Ligand (APRIL), a cytokine that promotes pathogenic galactose-deficient IgA1 production, leading to immune complex formation, kidney deposition, inflammation and injury. Herein, we report the percentage of patients achieving reduction in urine protein excretion (UPE) below different thresholds, from baseline to Week 76 in the ongoing Phase 1/2 trial of zigakibart. We also investigated trends in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in patient subgroups defined according to these UPE thresholds.
Method
ADU-CL-19 is an ongoing Phase 1/2 trial (NCT03945318) of zigakibart. Part 3 of the study enrolled patients aged ≥18 years with biopsy-proven IgAN, total urine protein of ≥0.5 g/24 h or a 24 h urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of ≥0.5 g/g, eGFR of ≥30 mL/min per 1.73 m2, and on a stable/optimised dose of renin–angiotensin system inhibitor (RASi) for ≥3 months before screening (or RASi intolerant). Patients received zigakibart 450 mg once every two weeks (Q2W) intravenously (IV), transitioning to 600 mg Q2W subcutaneously (SC) at ≥24 weeks (Cohort 1) or 600 mg Q2W SC (Cohort 2) for up to 124 weeks. Key outcomes of this exploratory analysis are a) the percentage of patients at Week 76 achieving proteinuria remission with UPE thresholds of <300 mg/24 h and <500 mg/24 h, and b) trends in eGFR from baseline to Week 76, stratified by proteinuria remission subgroups (<300 vs. >300 mg/24 h and <500 vs. >500 mg/24 h) determined at Week 52.
Results
In all enrolled patients in the safety set with a non-missing baseline value, mean (standard deviation) UPE at baseline was 1630 (1519) mg/24 h, and mean (standard deviation) eGFR at baseline was 70.7 (26.8) mL/min/1.73 m2. A total of 35 patients were assessed up to Week 52, with 28.6% (10 of 35) and 42.9% (15 of 35) achieving UPE <300 mg/24 h and <500 mg/24 h, respectively. A total of 31 patients were assessed up to Week 76, with 29.0% (9 of 31) and 45.2% (14 of 31) achieving UPE <300 mg/24 h and <500 mg/24 h, respectively. Mean eGFR remained stable from baseline to Week 76 regardless of whether patients achieved UPE reductions of <300 mg/24 h (Fig. 1) or <500 mg/24 h (Fig. 2). At Week 76, mean (standard error [SE]) eGFR change from baseline was 0.00 (2.37) mL/min/1.73 m2 in patients who achieved UPE <300 mg/24 h and −0.17 (2.23) mL/min/1.73 m2 in those who did not. For patients who achieved UPE <500 mg/24 h, mean (SE) eGFR change from baseline to Week 76 was 0.53 (2.91) mL/min/1.73 m2 and −0.67 (2.01) mL/min/1.73 m2 in those who did not achieve this UPE threshold.
Conclusion
Following 76 weeks of zigakibart treatment, 29% and 45% of patients achieved UPE reductions below stringent thresholds of <300 and <500 mg/24 h, demonstrating robust, clinically meaningful proteinuria remission. Sustained eGFR stabilisation was observed independent of the achieved UPE remission thresholds. Taken together, these findings support the disease-modifying effect of zigakibart in IgAN.

title: #435 Sex-specific temporal relationship between common comorbidity patterns and subsequent risk of chronic kidney disease
authors: Chunyang Li; Xiaoxi Zeng; Chao Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD), which affects approximately 10% of the global population, imposes a significant health and economic burden. Identifying comorbidity patterns that precede CKD could facilitate more effective prevention strategies. Our objective was to uncover the temporal relationships and the average time interval between comorbidity patterns and the subsequent onset of CKD in both males and females.
Method
From 502,507 UK Biobank participants 34,740 CKD patients were identified. Sequential pattern mining was performed to identify comorbidity patterns that precede the onset of CKD and to ascertain the average duration from comorbidity to the onset of CKD. Sequential pattern mining is a method employed to find frequent patterns of associated diseases in sequences of ordered events. title: #698 Disease trajectory leading to cause of death among patients with chronic kidney disease
authors: Chunyang Li; Xiaoxi Zeng; Chao Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) has caused approximately 1.5 million deaths. However, comprehensive analysis of the cross-talks with temporary order of disease trajectory leading to cause of death among CKD patients remains unclear.
Method
From 502,507 UK Biobank participants, 5,578 CKD patients without any other pre-existing comorbidities were identified. Trajectories leading to cause of death in CKD patients was constructed in three interrelated steps. Firstly, CKD patients were individually matched with up to 5 participants without CKD by birth year, sex, and Townsend deprivation index (transformed to tertiles). Conditional Cox regression with age as underlying time-scale was performed to evaluate the association between CKD and subsequent risks of 13 causes of death and 468 medical conditions. Mortalities or conditions in at least 250 CKD patients, with a p value < Bonferroni correction threshold and hazard ratio (HR) >1, were considered in the second step of the analysis. Secondly, binomial tests were conducted to explore whether a later diagnosis (Disease 2, D2) following an earlier diagnosis (Disease 1, D1) was dominant (>50%) among CKD patients who had been diagnosed with both D1 and D2 and ultimately died from a specific cause of mortality. D1 and D2 pairs with a temporal order that occurred in at least 50 CKD patients who ultimately died of the specified cause, with a binomial test p value < Bonferroni correction threshold was included in the next step. Thirdly, nested case-control study using conditional logistic regression was performed to evaluate the association between D1 (exposure) and D2 (outcome) pairs identified in the second step among CKD patients who died of the specified cause. At most 2 controls were matched to each case with identical characteristics mentioned above. Disease pairs occurred in at least 10 CKD patients, passing Bonferroni corrected threshold with odds ratio (OR) >1, were considered as significant. The trajectory network was formed by combining disease pairs that share overlapping diseases. For example, the disease pairs D1→D2 and D2→D3, with D2 as the overlapping disease, were combined into the trajectory D1→D2→D3. Medical conditions were retrieved from UK Biobank inpatient records using 3-digit ICD-10 codes, and combined conditions with clinical or biological similarities. Only the first record and corresponding date were maintained for analysis.
Results
CKD significantly increased the risks of mortality from circulatory system disease (HR 2.23, 95% confidence interval (CI) 2.83–5.70, P < 0.001) and neoplastic disease (HR 1.44, 95%CI 1.28–1.62, P < 0.001). For mortality from circulatory system disease, hypertensive disorders occurring after the onset of CKD were associated with a series of downstream conditions, including pneumonia, hypotension, heart failure, sepsis, and anemias, ultimately leading to death from circulatory system diseases. Additionally, hypertensive disorders following CKD were linked to subsequent diseases such as ischemic heart disease and disorders of lipoprotein metabolism and other lipidemia, with progression to acute renal failure and ultimately resulting in death from circulatory system diseases (panel A in the Fig. 1). Furthermore, hypertensive disorders were also important mediators driving downstream conditions such as acute renal failure, pneumonia and anemia, ultimately leading to neoplastic death in patients with CKD (panel B in the Fig. 1).
Conclusion
Individuals with a primary diagnosis of CKD and no prior comorbidities exhibit elevated risks for circulatory and neoplastic disease mortalities. These trajectory networks visualize a series of pathways linking CKD to a broad range of health outcomes, providing potential intervention targets for inhibiting adverse events in CKD patients.

title: #2343 Assessment of safety from a European difelikefalin managed access programme
authors: Jörg Latus; Gert Mayer; Carlos Narváez Mejía; Marius Manu; Sara Jesus; Despina Ruessmann; Lucio Manenti
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease-associated pruritus (CKD-aP) is a debilitating condition with limited treatment options. This ongoing managed access programme (MAP) was initiated in September 2021 to provide early access to the novel antipruritic difelikefalin under controlled conditions to patients with CKD-aP who have no other treatment options or access to other approved or commercially available treatments in their country. The programme will collect real-world data on the safety of difelikefalin to contribute to the overall understanding of its use for CKD-aP treatment. Here, we present the interim safety results obtained up to 31 October 2024.
Method
This interim analysis includes adult patients across 10 European countries in which difelikefalin was not yet commercially available. Patients for whom a healthcare professional had requested difelikefalin are included if they are experiencing moderate-to-severe CKD-aP (assessed as a score of ≥4 on the Worst Itching Intensity Numeric Rating Scale) and impaired quality of life (assessed as B or C on the Self-Assessed Disease Severity scale) and are receiving in-centre haemodialysis (HD) thrice weekly. Difelikefalin (0.5 µg/kg) is administered intravenously at the end of each HD session. All adverse events (AEs) are recorded and assessed in terms of seriousness and causality by the physician and the CSL Vifor Global Drug Safety team. Additionally, comprehensive details on AEs, including outcomes, are systematically recorded.
Results
In total, 438 patients are included in this interim analysis of the MAP data. Patients were provided with an average of 218 days (standard deviation: 197.75 days) of difelikefalin treatment. Among these patients, 167 (38.1%) experienced 458 AEs. A total of 246 serious adverse events (SAEs) were reported by 87 patients (Table). Of these, 10.2% were considered possibly related to difelikefalin. Of the possibly related SAEs for which the outcome is known, 88.0% resolved during the MAP. Of the 246 SAEs, 63 (25.6%) resulted in death; however, none was considered related to difelikefalin. A total of 152 non-serious AEs were reported by 85 patients (Table), of which 97 (63.8%) were deemed related to difelikefalin. Of the related events for which the outcome was known, 86.4% of AEs related to difelikefalin resolved during the MAP. The majority of AEs and SAEs were consistent with conditions typical of patients with chronic kidney disease requiring HD and/or the known safety profile of difelikefalin. Forty-three patients discontinued treatment due to perceived inefficacy of difelikefalin. Of these, time-to-discontinuation data were available for 33 patients, with 16 (48.8%) receiving less than the 12 weeks of difelikefalin treatment used in Phase 3 clinical trials as the time that difelikefalin should be taken prior to concluding that there is a lack of response.
Conclusion
No new safety signals were detected in this interim analysis of MAP data collected over a 3-year period. The overall safety results were consistent with the known safety profile of difelikefalin. These results could influence therapeutic recommendations, as difelikefalin may provide a favourable treatment option for patients with moderate-to-severe CKD-aP receiving HD.
