title: #2711 Geriatric assessment use to frailty prediction in older CKD patients
authors: Ana Farinha; Filipa Trigo; Cátia Simões Lopes Figueiredo; Patrícia Valério; Josefina Santos Lascasas
abstract:
Background and Aims
Frailty is common among chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. The 2024 KDIGO guidelines recommend identifying frailty as a key factor in CKD management. The Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA) is the gold-standard methodology used by geriatricians to define frailty. Our aim was to identify predictors of frailty in CKD patients, using CGA methodology.
Method
We evaluated 204 patients aged ≥65 years in 2024: 111 with CKD stages 3 to 5, 71 on dialysis, and 22 receiving conservative care in a single nephrology unit. A multidisciplinary team, including a nephrologist specialized in geriatrics, conducted the CGA. Data collection included demographics and clinical parameters, as well as assessments of activities of daily living (ADL), cognitive function, nutritional status, mobility, and social support. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS v.29.
Results
Among the 204 patients, the mean age was 79.1 (±7.2) years, 58.2% were male, 32.7% were widowed, and 28% were institutionalized, 52.5% had diabetes, and 27.7% had heart failure. Overall, 25% of patients were classified as frail based on the CGA. Frailty prevalence varied depending on the assessment tool used: 26.5% according to the Fried Index (FI >3), 23.5% according to the Edmonton Frailty Scale (EFS >8), and 58.3% according to the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS >5). Frailty prevalence also differed across CKD stages (Table 1).
Logistic regression identified four significant predictors of frailty: activities of daily livings [(Barthel Index (Exp(B) = 0.191, P < 0.001), Lawton and Brody Scale (Exp(B) = 0.145, P = 0.001)], mobility [Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) (Exp(B) = 0.575, P = 0.001)] and depression (Exp(B) = 21.057, P = 0.013). The model showed an excellent fit (Nagelkerke's R² = 0.835, 92.3% accuracy).
Conclusion
Frailty identification has a significant impact on CKD management. Simple, time-efficient tools should be integrated into routine care to facilitate early detection and intervention. The EFS may be particularly useful due to its shorter administration time while maintaining alignment with CGA results. Identifying frailty syndromes such as impaired mobility (SPPB) and depression could help target modifiable risk factors and improve patient outcomes. Conversely, declines in ADL function, while strong frailty predictors, may indicate a stage too advanced for effective intervention.
To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate frailty across the full CKD continuum, from early to advanced stages, and to identify predictors that may be relevant across all CKD stages.

title: #1011 Management and treatment of chronic kidney disease in the danish Lolland-Falster health study: focus on renoprotection and cardiovascular disease prevention
authors: Ebba Mannheimer; Morten Jørgensen; Kristine Hommel; Anne Lise Kamper; Randi Jepsen; Bo Feldt-Rasmussen; Mads Hornum
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a growing global health challenge and a major contributor to mortality. Even in its early stages, CKD is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. In the Danish population-based Lolland-Falster Health Study (LOFUS), conducted in a rural-provincial area with life expectancy and socioeconomic status below the national average, we recently identified a CKD prevalence of 18%. Importantly, overall disease recognition was only 7.1%, and awareness was as low as 4.4%, revealing a significant gap in CKD identification in the general population which consequently impedes guideline-directed management and treatment of CKD. This study aimed to examine the management of CKD in LOFUS, focusing on renoprotective treatment, including blood pressure control and the use of renin-angiotensin-system inhibitors (RASi), referrals to nephrology units, and the prevalence and prevention of cardiovascular disease, including statin use and lifestyle factors. The findings will help identify gaps in CKD care and guide policy changes to improve public health outcomes.
Method
Cross-sectional study including adult participants with CKD identified in LOFUS (2016-2020), excluding those without eGFR measurements. Data were obtained from biochemical analyses, clinical examinations, and questionnaires, then linked to data in the national medical registers. CKD was defined as albuminuria (urine albumin-creatinine ratio ≥30 mg/g), eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m², or a registered diagnosis. Renoprotective strategies were evaluated by blood pressure levels and use of RASi (redeemed prescription within 12 months) among eligible individuals. Controlled blood pressure was assessed according to the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes guidelines at the time of the study. Cardiovascular disease was defined as either self-reported or recorded in the register. Prevention of cardiovascular disease was assessed by use of statins (redeemed prescription within 12 months), and lifestyle factors (non-smoking and BMI <25 kg/m2). Nephrology referral was defined as outpatient contact within 10 years before the study appointment. Generalized linear mixed-effects models and standard logistic regression models were used to estimate the association between CKD stages and outcomes. The explanatory variables included age, sex, socioeconomic status, and diabetes.
Results
Among 2,881 individuals with CKD, 57.6% were women, and median age was 67.8 years. Most individuals were in CKD stage 1 (32.1%) or stage 2 (39.2%), while less than 30% were in stages 3, 4, or 5. Albuminuria testing was performed in 98.4%. More individuals in stages 1 and 2 had medium or long postsecondary education compared to stages 3–5. Blood pressure control (33.2%) and treatment with RASi (39.2%) were suboptimal overall but more frequent in individuals with diabetes compared with those without. In multivariable analyses, odds ratio for blood pressure control (2.83; 95% CI, 2.30–3.49), and RASi treatment (3.72; 95% CI, 2.59–5.37) were significantly higher in stages 3–5 compared to stage 1; however, odds ratio for blood pressure control was lower in stage 2 than stage 1 (0.77; 95% CI, 0.61–0.96). One-fifth of participants had cardiovascular disease, increasing to 35% in stages 3–5, with ischemic heart disease accounting for over 60% of cases. Less than one-third received statins (32.2%) or had a BMI <25 kg/m2 (32.2%), and >80% self-reported non-smoking. Statin treatment (1.46; 95% CI, 1.00–2.11) was significantly more frequent in stages 3–5 compared to stage 1. Of those meeting nephrology referral criteria (n = 99), one-third had been in contact with a specialized nephrology unit.
Conclusion
This population-based study highlight gaps between guideline-recommended CKD management and practice, particularly in early stages and in non-diabetic individuals, emphasizing the need for early CKD detection and improved guideline adherence.

title: #1092 Serum zinc concentration and long-term mortality in CKD patients: Insights from NHANES (2011–2016)
authors: Lan Ye; Xuan Wang; Xiaoling Zhou
abstract:
Background and Aims
Based on the NHANES database, this study explored the correlation between serum zinc concentration and all-cause mortality and cardiovascular mortality in patients with Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD), aiming to provide data support for improving the prognosis of CKD patients.
Method
The participants in this study were 973 CKD patients from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES 2011-2016). The mortality status and cause of death of the study participants were obtained from the National Death Index (NDI). Participants were divided into four groups based on serum zinc concentrations (µmol/L) quartiles to compare the general clinical data of CKD patients at different serum zinc levels. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis was employed to estimate the cumulative risk of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular mortality across varying zinc concentrations. A restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis combined with a multivariate-adjusted COX regression model was employed to assess the relationship between serum zinc levels and all-cause mortality and cardiovascular mortality in CKD patients.
Results
During the follow-up period, 191 deaths (20%) were recorded, with 68 (35%) attributed to cardiovascular disease. Comparisons across different zinc levels revealed that higher serum zinc concentrations were associated with lower cardiovascular mortality rates. As serum zinc levels increased, total cholesterol, hemoglobin, total protein, albumin, blood calcium, serum iron, and eGFR levels were higher, while the neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio and serum creatinine levels were lower. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis showed that CKD patients with higher serum zinc concentrations had higher survival rates during the follow-up period. The cumulative survival rates for all-cause mortality across different quartiles of zinc concentration (Q1 to Q4) were 57.4%, 68.5%, 72.2%, and 81.8%, respectively (P < 0.05). After multivariable adjustment, COX regression model results indicated that the hazard ratios (HR) for cardiovascular death risk across different quartiles (Q1 to Q4) were 1 (reference), 0.25 (0.10, 0.64), 0.53 (0.26, 1.08), and 0.34 (0.16, 0.74), respectively (P-trend < 0.05).
Conclusion
Higher serum zinc concentration was independently associated with a decreased risk of all-cause and CVD mortality in patients with CKD. These findings suggest that serum zinc levels may be a modifiable risk factor for improving the prognosis of CKD patients, warranting further investigation in prospective studies.

title: #1112 Serum resistin and other predictors of CIMT and cardiovascular events in chronic kidney disease
authors: Rodolfo Almeida; João Cunha; Henrique Borges; José Soares; Roberto Marques; Ana Domingos; Ana Silva
abstract:
Background and Aims
Resistin is a hormone primarily produced by macrophages, and it can act as an inflammatory biomarker. It has been associated with type 2 diabetes, obesity, atherosclerosis, cardiovascular (CV) diseases and is thought to be elevated in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT) is a validated screening tool for CV disease. CKD is already a leading cause of mortality, and CV complications are the primary cause of morbidity and mortality in this population. Thus, the aim of this study was to assess whether resistin and other independent variables could serve as predictive factors for CIMT and CV events in patients with non-dialysis CKD (ndCKD).
Method
We conducted a prospective, observational study that included 1292 patients with ndCKD, followed at a nephrology clinic in a single tertiary center. The population was divided into two groups according to CIMT measured by B-mode ultrasound: G1 (CIMT <0.9 mm) and G2 (CIMT ≥0.9 mm). Comparisons between demography and laboratory findings of the two groups were performed using Student's t-test. Multivariate logistic regression analysis was used to identify predictors of CIMT, while Cox regression was employed to assess predictors of CV events.
Results
Of the 1292 patients, 702 were included in G1 and 590 in G2. The mean age was 56.55 ± 10.96 years in G1 and 67.23 ± 12.16 years in G2. The mean estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was 53.91 ± 23.29 mL/min/1.73 m² in G1 and 33.05 ± 19.62 mL/min/1.73 m² in G2. Significant differences were observed between the two groups in terms of age (P < 0.001), creatinine (P < 0.001), eGFR (P < 0.001), phosphorus (P < 0.001), parathyroid hormone (PTH) (P < 0.001), calcium-phosphate product (P < 0.001), high-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) (P < 0.01), and resistin (P < 0.01) (Table 1). Multivariate logistic regression analysis identified phosphorus ≥ 4.6 mg/dL (OR 1.798, 95% CI 1.278-3.010, P < 0.009), hs-CRP (OR 1.525, 95% CI 1.21-3.745, P < 0.003), serum resistin levels between 3.1–8.5 ng/mL (OR 2.077, 95% CI 1.304–2.982, P < 0.24) and serum resistin ≥ 8.5 ng/mL (OR 3.542, 95% CI 2.267–5.267, P < 0.03) as predictors of CIMT (Table 2). In Cox regression analysis, phosphorus ≥ 4.6 mg/dL (OR 1.254, 95% CI 1.096–3.252, P < 0.005), serum resistin ≥ 8.5 ng/mL (OR 2.004, 95% CI 1.131–6.723, P < 0.005), and CIMT (OR 2.043, 95% CI 1.496–4.187, P < 0.04) were also independent predictors of CV events (Table 3).
Conclusion
Resistin, phosphorus, and hs-CRP were identified as predictors of CIMT. Furthermore, phosphorus ≥ 4.6 mg/dL, serum resistin ≥ 8.5 ng/mL and CIMT itself were found to be predictors of CV events. This study provides valuable insights into potential novel biomarkers for CIMT and CV events in the CKD population, where CV events are increasingly recognized as a leading cause of death. Notably, our findings suggest that resistin and hs-CRP, both inflammatory markers, could play a role in the pathogenesis of CIMT and subsequently in CV events. Further investigation is necessary to validate the clinical utility of these biomarkers.

title: #2259 Serum interleukin-8 concentrations, associated factors, and associated cardiovascular risk in patients with moderate-to-advanced chronic kidney disease
authors: Maxime Pluquet; Said Kamel; Natalia Alencar de Pinho; Luc Frimat; Christian Combe; Ziad Massy; Solene Laville; Sophie Liabeuf
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is associated to increased inflammation and elevated cytokine levels. Interleukins, a group of cytokines, play a crucial role in immune system development and activity, serving as key effectors and signalling molecules. In CKD patients, pro-inflammatory interleukins tend to be elevated. While interleukin 6 (IL-6) has been extensively studied in the context of CKD, other interleukins, such as interleukin 8 (IL-8), deserve further attention. IL-8 is a chemoattractant cytokine primarily involved in neutrophil activation, which is produced by a wide range of cell types, mainly monocytes and macrophages. IL-8 is produced early in the inflammatory response but can persist for prolonged periods, even days or weeks. Despite experimental data suggesting its potential harmful effects, notably in cardiovascular disease, IL-8 has been poorly studied in patients with CKD. Thus, the objectives of the present study were to (i) describe the serum IL-8 concentration in patients at various CKD stages, (ii) assess the correlation between the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and IL-8 concentration, (iii) identify the factors associated with IL-8 levels, and (iv) explore the association between IL-8 levels and the risk of major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE).
Method
CKD-REIN is a French, prospective, nationally representative cohort of 3,033 patients with stage 3 to 5 CKD (eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m²), recruited from 40 nephrology facilities. Participants were neither on maintenance dialysis nor had received a kidney transplant, and were followed-up for 5 years. Baseline IL-8 serum concentrations were measured centrally using an ELISA method. Since IL-8 concentration was not normally distributed in this population, it was log-transformed for analysis. IL-8 levels were compared across CKD stages using analysis of variance. Multivariate linear regression was performed to identify factors associated with serum IL-8 concentrations (log-transformed).
Cox proportional hazards model was used to estimate hazard ratio (HR) for the first major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE, defined as a composite of nonfatal stroke, nonfatal myocardial infarction, hospitalization for heart failure, and cardiovascular death). The models were adjusted for baseline comorbidities, laboratory data and medications.
Results
Among the 2,389 patients included, 66% were men, with a median age of 68 [Q1–Q3: 60–76] years, and a mean (SD) eGFR of 34.8 (13.4) mL/min/1.73 m². The median serum IL-8 concentration was 12.2 [Q1–Q3: 8.0-17.7] pg/mL. IL-8 concentrations were significantly inversely correlated with eGFR (r=−0.21, P < 0.001). IL-8 levels varied across CKD stages, with higher concentrations observed in advanced stages (P < 0.001). Serum IL-8 concentration was independently and positively associated with decreasing eGFR, diabetes, history of cardiovascular disease, anaemia, C-reactive protein (CRP) levels, and proton pump inhibitor use. It was negatively associated with serum albumin. CRP (eβCRP = 1.01), eGFR (eβeGFR = 0.99), albumin (eβalbumin = 0.98), and diabetes (eβdiabetes = 1.16) were the strongest predictors of IL-8 levels.
The risk of MACE increased with higher baseline serum IL-8 concentrations (HR [95% Confidence Interval] for 1-unit change in log(IL-8), 1.30 [1.09; 1.56]), after adjusting for age, sex, smoking status, history of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, anaemia, eGFR, pulse pressure, body mass index, C-reactive protein, serum albumin, serum urea, urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio, and baseline prescriptions for proton pump inhibitors, diuretics, statins, and antithrombotic agents.
Conclusion
Decline of kidney function was associated with an increase in serum IL-8 levels in patients with moderate-to-advanced CKD. Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is associated to increased inflammation and elevated cytokine levels. Interleukins, a group of cytokines, play a crucial role in immune system development and activity, serving as key effectors and signalling molecules. In CKD patients, pro-inflammatory interleukins tend to be elevated. While interleukin 6 (IL-6) has been extensively studied in the context of CKD, other interleukins, such as interleukin 8 (IL-8), deserve further attention. IL-8 is a chemoattractant cytokine primarily involved in neutrophil activation, which is produced by a wide range of cell types, mainly monocytes and macrophages. IL-8 is produced early in the inflammatory response but can persist for prolonged periods, even days or weeks. Despite experimental data suggesting its potential harmful effects, notably in cardiovascular disease, IL-8 has been poorly studied in patients with CKD. Thus, the objectives of the present study were to (i) describe the serum IL-8 concentration in patients at various CKD stages, (ii) assess the correlation between the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and IL-8 concentration, (iii) identify the factors associated with IL-8 levels, and (iv) explore the association between IL-8 levels and the risk of major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE).

title: #2792 Dapagliflozin's effect on kidney oxygenation: analysis of functional MRI data from the randomized GLUTREPRO trial
authors: Elisa Russo; Emilio Venturelli; Francesca Cappadona; Julie Di Vincenzo; Lucia MacCio'; Pasquale Esposito; Giulio Ferrazzi; Rocco Grillo; Beatrice Damasio; Francesca Viazzi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal hypoxia is believed to play a central role in the pathophysiology of both diabetic and non-diabetic chronic kidney disease (CKD). Dapagliflozin has been shown to slow the progression of kidney disease by counteracting several pathogenic mechanisms. The advent of blood oxygenation level-dependent magnetic resonance imaging (BOLD-MRI) has enabled the noninvasive assessment of renal oxygenation in humans. However, it remains uncertain whether dapagliflozin affects changes renal oxygenation as measured by BOLD-MRI.
The aim of the study was to assess whether dapagliflozin modifies kidney oxygenation as a possible mechanism of kidney protection.
Method
The GLUTREPRO study was a randomized controlled trial investigating the effect of dapagliflozin on kidney measures. A secondary end-point of the study was to investigate the changes in global and segmental renal oxygenation estimated by BOLD MRI (changes in R2* value defined as 1/T2*) after randomization to dapagliflozin or placebo. We analyzed data of 360 ROI from 20 patients who underwent BOLD-MRI at baseline and at month 3 after randomization on a 3 Tesla MR scanner.
Results
In BOLD-MRI, the medullary transverse relaxation rate R2* decreased (indicating increased tissue oxygenation) in the dapagliflozin-treated group, while it tended to increase in the placebo group. Accordingly, medullary R2* values at month 3 were significantly lower in the treated group compared to the placebo group (Fig. 1, P = 0.0149). In contrast, cortical kidney oxygenation was not affected by the administration of dapagliflozin.
The effect of dapagliflozin on medullary oxygenation changes appears to be more pronounced in non-diabetic patients (Table 1). Considering all available R2* measurements and dividing the R2* variation into tertiles, we investigated the clinical and laboratory parameters significantly associated with changes in renal medullary oxygenation. The inverse relationship we observed between changes in R2* and changes in eGFR and ACR in the placebo group, was attenuated in patients treated with dapagliflozin. Notably, dapagliflozin was identified as the sole independent determinant of improved medullary renal oxygenation (β −14.4, 95% CI −23.9 / β −4.89, P = 0.003, Table 2).
Conclusion
This prospective sub-study of the GLUTREPRO trial revealed a potentially protective effect of dapagliflozin on renal medullary oxygenation.

title: #1850 The impact of comorbid type 2 diabetes on the prevalence of chronic kidney disease-associated pruritus and its effects on quality of life: data from the CENSUS-EU study
authors: James Burton; Timm Henning Westhoff; Maurizio Gallieni; Stefan Jacobson; Pablo Molina; Amandine Perrin; Despina Ruessmann
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease-associated pruritus (CKD-aP) is common, particularly in patients undergoing haemodialysis, and can impair health-related quality of life (HRQoL). While itch is often observed in patients with diabetes [1–3], the impact of type 2 diabetes (T2D) on CKD-aP prevalence and severity is currently unknown. Here, data from the non-interventional CENSUS-EU study were analysed to determine whether there are differences in CKD-aP prevalence and severity and itch-related HRQoL between patients with and without T2D.
Method
CENSUS-EU was a non-interventional, cross-sectional, multicentre study in Europe that aimed to assess the prevalence of CKD-aP and its impact on HRQoL in adult patients receiving haemodialysis. Patients completed questionnaires on pruritus (including the Worst Itching Intensity Numerical Rating Scale) and HRQoL (including the 5‑D itch scale and the integrated palliative care outcome scale symptom list for end-stage renal disease [IPOS-Renal]). Medical records were used to gather information on comorbidities (including T2D), dialysis, anti-pruritus treatment and healthcare resource use. Data were analysed by pruritus severity (no, mild, moderate, severe) and by the presence or absence of T2D as a comorbidity.
Results
Data from 2963 patients were analysed, of which 2943 included T2D status. Patients living with T2D (n = 1042, 35.4%) were older, had a higher mean body mass index, and were more likely to have comorbidities than those without T2D (Table). CKD-aP prevalence was similar between patients with T2D and those without T2D (54.9% of the T2D subset and 52.6% of the non-T2D subset). CKD-aP distribution by severity subgroup was also similar between patients with and without T2D (Table). HRQoL measures (total 5-D itch score, 5-D itch disability subscale score, IPOS-Renal question 2 [difficulty sleeping] and IPOS-Renal question 5 [feelings of depression]) were similar between the T2D and non-T2D subsets (Fig. 1). In both the T2D and non-T2D subsets, increased itch severity was associated with worse overall impact of itch, worse itch-related disability, more difficulty sleeping and more frequent feelings of depression (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
The data from this non-interventional study indicate no difference between the T2D and non-T2D subsets in terms of prevalence and severity of CKD-aP or its impact on HRQoL. This suggests that screening and treatment of pruritus should be performed on any patient on dialysis, regardless of the presence or absence of diabetes.

title: #1930 Sentinel CKD screening in at-risk patients: six-month follow-up and impact on nephroprotective treatment
authors: Jose Luis Górriz; Elena Giménez-Civera; Francesc Moncho Francés; Camila Solano Rivera; Caterina Rodriguez Velásquez; Adela Pozo Giráldez; Rosa Murria Estal; Maria Jesus Puchades Montesa; María Belén Aguilar-Uriarte Nemiña; Juan F Navarro-González; Enrique Rodriguez Borja
abstract:
Background and Aims
The KDIGO guidelines recommend the implementation of chronic kidney disease (CKD) screening programs in patients with risk factors. However, CKD screening rates in these patients fall significantly short of guideline-recommended targets. Increasing CKD detection in at-risk patients may be associated with improved implementation of nephroprotective treatments. Here, we present the six-month follow-up results of patients included in our sentinel CKD screening project.
Method
Our Health Department serves a population of 341,972 inhabitants through 31 primary care centers. From November 2023 to November 2024, a sentinel CKD screening project was conducted in at-risk patients (hypertension, diabetes mellitus, obesity, and established cardiovascular disease). CKD detection was carried out using a Clinical Decision Support (CDS) Middleware system, a software tool designed to assist in clinical decision-making by integrating electronic health records (EHRs) and laboratory request systems while incorporating an algorithm aligned with CKD referral guidelines.
Changes in treatment were analyzed in patients with at least three months of follow-up. Among 837 patients meeting nephrology referral criteria (eGFR< 30 ml/min/1.73 m2, urine albumin-creatinine ratio [UACR] >300 mg/g or renal progression), results are presented for a subset of 537 patients (64.1%).
Results
A total of 32,618 screenings were performed over 12 months (mean: 141 screenings/day). Among these: 79.1% (n = 25,806) had no CKD, 18.3% (n = 5,975) had CKD but did not meet referral criteria, 2.5% (n = 837) met nephrology referral criteria).
After the online assessment of the 537 analyzed patients who met nephrology referral criteria, 253 (47.9%) were managed remotely without requiring an in-person nephrology consultation, with recommendations provided to primary care physicians, while 284 (52.1%) required a face-to-face nephrology visit and were referred to the outpatient consultation circuit.
The characteristics of these remotely managed patients were: Age: 77 ± 8 years, male: 46%, eGFR: 59 ± 24 mL/min/1.73 m², UACR: 199 ± 186 mg/g. Main reasons for remote resolution in these patients: mild renal impairment (34.4%), mild albuminuria in elderly patients (56.9%), low KFRE score in elderly patients (8.7%).
The characteristics of patients requiring in-person nephrology consultation were:
Age: 77 ± 8 years, male: 60%, eGFR: 52 ± 27 mL/min/1.73 m², UACR: 568 ± 771 mg/g. The reasons for nephrology referral from Primary Care in these latter patients were: eGFR decline (32.5%), proteinuria (38.9%), both (28.6%).
The proportion of nephroprotective treatments implemented at 3 and 6 months of nephrology follow-up is presented in Table 1, with comparisons to baseline values.
Conclusion
The use of sentinel screening systems based on Clinical Decision Support (CDS) is an accessible, effective, and cost-efficient method. Moreover, it efficiently automates CKD identification and provides personalized recommendations to both nephrologists and primary care physicians, optimizing nephroprotective treatments. This system has proven to be highly effective in patients referred to the Nephrology Department, facilitating the optimization of nephroprotective therapies. However, further efforts are needed to develop strategies in collaboration with primary care physicians to improve the implementation of guideline-recommended nephroprotective treatments in patients managed in primary care settings.

title: #1927 Clinical characteristics and healthcare resource utilization, and costs associated in patients with diagnosed and undetected hyperkalemia: IBERIK+ study
authors: Jose Luis Górriz; Roberto Alcazar Arroyo; Patricia De Sequera Ortiz; Enrique Morales Ruiz; Miquel Blasco Pelicano; Marco Montomoli; Miren Sequera Mutiozabal; Ana Roncero Martin; Alberto Ortiz
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyperkalemia (HK) is a common complication of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and heart failure (HF), particularly among patients receiving renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors (RAASi). This study aimed to describe the clinical characteristics and healthcare resource utilization (HCRU) and costs associated in patients with HK, differentiating between diagnosed and undetected HK cases in Spain.
Method
A descriptive, retrospective study conducted using the BIG-PAC database with Python technology in Spain. Patients with relevant diagnosis codes and/or treatments for HK and/or potassium values >5.0 mmol/L recorded in their medical history between January 2013-December 2020, with at least 2 years of follow-up, were included. The inclusion date was defined as the first HK event. HK event was considered undetected when diagnosis and/or treatment were not observed despite potassium >5.0 mmol/L at the index date. Baseline characteristics and HCRUs and cost associated were analyzed by diagnosed HK and undetected HK.
Results
A total of 7,006 patients (mean age: 66.9 ± 15.5 years; 52.0% women; mean BMI: 27.6 ± 4.8 kg/m2; mean eGFR: 38.1 ± 15.1 mL/min/1.73 m²; mean Charlson Comorbidity Index: 1.8 ± 2.0) were analyzed. Among them, only 33.5% were diagnosed with and/or treated for the HK event. Patients with undetected HK (66.5%) (vs diagnosed HK) were younger (66.1 vs 68.5 years), 58.7% had mild HK, 35.8% moderate HK, and 5.4% severe HK (vs 33.3% mild, 41,0% moderate and 25.6% severe) and less frequently experienced comorbid conditions (mean Charlson Comorbidity Index: 1.5 vs 2.5), though 62,4% presented at least one of the following comorbidities: HF (12.3% vs 36.2%), CKD (10.8% vs 42.4%), hypertension (51.0% vs 55.5%) or Type 2 diabetes (27.3% vs 28.5%). During the follow up period, HCRUs and annual costs per patient were higher in diagnosed HK than in initially undetected HK patients (Table 1).
Conclusion
Our data suggest that two-thirds of patients with HK events were undetected, including those with comorbid conditions and moderate-to-severe HK. Although clinical events, HCRU, and costs were higher in detected HK, they were also high among patients with undetected HK.

title: #3410 Guideline adherence in primary and nephrology care for older patients with advanced chronic kidney disease and the association with social and clinical characteristics
authors: Micha Jongejan; Janet Kist; Friedo W Dekker; Marc Groeneveld; Willem Jan W Bos; Marjolijn van Buren; Mattijs Numans
abstract:
Background and Aims
Previous studies indicate that 40% of patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD), a proportion that increases with age, are managed in primary care despite meeting referral criteria. Older patients are more likely to have stable kidney function or may find hospital visits burdensome.
We aimed to describe the proportion of older patients with advanced CKD receiving guideline-adherent care in primary and nephrology care, and describe how clinical characteristics and social determinants of health are associated with guideline adherence. Ultimately, we aim to assess whether primary care can be a suitable setting for managing subgroups of older CKD patients and adequately addressing their needs.
Method
This dynamic, population-based cohort study, used routine health care data of general practitioner (GP) practices and hospitals within the Extramural Leiden University Medical Center Academic Network (ELAN), linked to individual-level registry data from Statistics Netherlands. We included adults aged ≥65 years with incident or prevalent CKD (eGFR ≤30 ml/min/1.73 m2, confirmed by two measurements taken ≥90 days apart) between 2015 and 2023. Follow-up continued until death, kidney replacement therapy initiation, end of study (01-01-2023) or deregistration from a participating GP. Patients were categorized as managed in primary or nephrology care based on diagnosis-treatment combinations. We used descriptive statistics to assess the proportion of patients in each care setting and adherence to CKD guidelines, stratified by clinical characteristics and social determinants of health.
Results
We enrolled 1647 patients, with a median follow-up of 2.25 years; 1194 were managed exclusively in primary care and 453 (part of) follow-up in nephrology care. The mean age was 82 ± 9 years (83 ± 9 in primary care vs 79 ± 8 in nephrology care), with a median eGFR of 26 [22; 28] ml/min/1.73 m2. Of these, 973 patients had at least 15 months of follow-up in primary or nephrology care, allowing for guideline-adherence assessment. Patients with shorter follow-up were more likely to be female (55% vs 46%), older (83 ± 9 vs 81 ± 8 years), and classified as frail (30% vs 21%).
Differences in adherence to quality indicators were observed between the care settings (see Fig. 1), with nephrology care showing higher adherence to kidney function monitoring (≥2 measurements per year: 68% vs 83%), annual testing of albuminuria (45% vs 65%), hemoglobin (74% vs 87%), LDL (49% vs 60%), and HbA1c (50% vs 65%), as well as higher prescription rates of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitor (RAASi) (72% vs 77%). Annual blood pressure measurement and avoidance of NSAIDs were similar across care settings (60% vs 57% and 94% vs 94%, respectively).
In both care settings, we observed lower guideline adherence for women across all indicators and a decrease in adherence with age, except for eGFR monitoring in nephrology care and blood pressure monitoring in both care settings. In primary care, patients with diabetes mellitus were more likely to receive guideline-adherent care compared to those without diabetes, with a similar trend observed for patients with hypertension, albeit to a lesser extent. No differences were found between ethnic and socioeconomic groups, or in relation to eGFR and frailty.
Conclusion
The majority of older patients with advanced CKD are managed in primary care, where guideline adherence is generally acceptable, but less strictly followed than in nephrology care. Among patients with diabetes or hypertension, who are treated in structured care pathways, adherence is higher, suggesting that similar proactive and structured approaches could enhance CKD care. Given the life expectancy and treatment goals of older patients, CKD management should prioritize individual needs and quality of life over strict guideline adherence. Future research should explore whether outcomes, including CKD progression, quality of life and healthcare costs, differ between patients managed in primary and nephrology care.

Differences in adherence to quality indicators were observed between the care settings (see Fig. 1), with nephrology care showing higher adherence to kidney function monitoring (≥2 measurements per year: 68% vs 83%), annual testing of albuminuria (45% vs 65%), hemoglobin (74% vs 87%), LDL (49% vs 60%), and HbA1c (50% vs 65%), as well as higher prescription rates of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitor (RAASi) (72% vs 77%). Annual blood pressure measurement and avoidance of NSAIDs were similar across care settings (60% vs 57% and 94% vs 94%, respectively).
In both care settings, we observed lower guideline adherence for women across all indicators and a decrease in adherence with age, except for eGFR monitoring in nephrology care and blood pressure monitoring in both care settings. In primary care, patients with diabetes mellitus were more likely to receive guideline-adherent care compared to those without diabetes, with a similar trend observed for patients with hypertension, albeit to a lesser extent. No differences were found between ethnic and socioeconomic groups, or in relation to eGFR and frailty.
Conclusion
The majority of older patients with advanced CKD are managed in primary care, where guideline adherence is generally acceptable, but less strictly followed than in nephrology care. Among patients with diabetes or hypertension, who are treated in structured care pathways, adherence is higher, suggesting that similar proactive and structured approaches could enhance CKD care. Given the life expectancy and treatment goals of older patients, CKD management should prioritize individual needs and quality of life over strict guideline adherence. Future research should explore whether outcomes, including CKD progression, quality of life and healthcare costs, differ between patients managed in primary and nephrology care.

title: #1944 Efficacy of β-lactams versus fluoroquinolones for empirical antibiotic treatment of kidney cyst infections in polycystic kidney disease
authors: Yuta Nakano; Shintaro Mandai; Yutaro Mori; Fumiaki Ando; Takayasu Mori; Koichiro Susa; Soichiro Iimori; Shotaro Naito; Eisei Sohara; Kiyohide Fushimi; Shinichi Uchida
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney cyst infections are a frequent and significant complication in patients with polycystic kidney disease. Fluoroquinolones, as lipid-soluble antibiotics, are recommended for empirical therapy due to their superior penetration into cyst fluid. In contrast, water-soluble antibiotics, such as β-lactams, have lower cyst fluid penetration. However, no studies have directly compared the efficacy of these two antibiotic classes, resulting in limited evidence to optimize treatment strategies for kidney cyst infections. Previous studies suggest the potential usefulness of water-soluble antibiotics in clinical practice. This study aimed to clarify the efficacy of β-lactam monotherapy compared with fluoroquinolones using a real-world database.
Method
This observational study analysed 617 patients (median age 67 years; 52.0% women) admitted for the first time with kidney cyst infections who received monotherapy for at least five days from 2010 to 2022. Data were obtained from a nationwide administrative claims database covering over half of all hospital admissions in Japan. Patients were grouped based on the antibiotics they received: β-lactams (sulbactam/ampicillin [SBT/ABPC], n = 45; cefmetazole [CMZ], n = 71; and ceftriaxone [CTRX], n = 265) and fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin [LVFX], n = 127; ciprofloxacin [CPFX], n = 109). The primary composite outcome included in-hospital death, readmission for kidney cyst infections, the need for percutaneous/surgical drainage of kidney cysts, or the requirement for escalation of antibiotics within a 90-day follow-up period. Secondary outcomes—assessed separately—included in-hospital death/readmission, percutaneous/surgical drainage, and antibiotic escalation. Escalation of antibiotics was defined as switching to broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics (e.g. LVFX, CPFX, tazobactam/piperacillin, cefepime, meropenem, or imipenem) after six hospital days. Multiple imputations for missing data were performed using chained equations. Baseline characteristics, including age, sex, body mass index, smoking status, consciousness status, comorbidities, Barthel Index category, ambulance transfer, kidney replacement therapy, hospital volume, and admission year, were balanced using inverse probability of treatment weighting. Risk differences (RDs) were calculated, with a non-inferiority margin set at 15%. P-values below 0.05 were considered statistically significant.
Results
Among the cohort, 6 patients (1.0%) died in-hospital, 33 (5.3%) were readmitted for kidney cyst infections, 10 (1.6%) required nephrectomy, 67 (11.0%) required percutaneous drainage, and 82 required escalation of antibiotics (13.3%). All outcomes of β-lactams were non-inferior to those of fluoroquinolones, as shown by RD for the overall composite outcome: 2.9% (95% confidence interval [CI]: −4.8–10.6; P = 0.457; p for non-inferiority = 0.001), in-hospital death/readmission: 1.2% (95% CI: −3.2–5.7; P = 0.589; p for non-inferiority <0.001), requiring percutaneous/surgical drainage: 1.4% (95% CI: −3.9–6.7; P = 0.603; p for non-inferiority <0.001), and escalation of antibiotics: -0.7% (95% CI: −6.8–5.2; P = 0.798; p for non-inferiority <0.001) (Fig. 1). Among the individual β-lactams, only CTRX showed non-inferior to fluoroquinolones across all outcomes (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
This study demonstrates the non-inferiority of β-lactams to fluoroquinolones in patients with kidney cyst infections. β-lactams, particularly CTRX, may be considered a viable alternative treatment option, potentially reducing the overuse of fluoroquinolones and limiting the emergence of antibiotic resistance.

title: #488 Improving medication safety and prescribing of high-risk medications in individuals with chronic kidney disease: a validation study
authors: Jo-Anne Wilson; Katie Halliday; Natalie Ratajczak; Marisa Battistella; Karthik K Tennankore; Steven Soroka; Penelope Poyah; Keigan More; Cynthia Kendell; Jaclyn Tran; Maneka Sheffield; Heather Naylor
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease affects 10% of the global population. Medications cleared by the kidneys can accumulate and cause harm if not dosed correctly. Community pharmacists are well-positioned to optimize prescribing for this population, but inconsistencies between medication resources can complicate dosing decisions. Validated algorithms for dosing higher-risk medications in kidney disease are lacking in community pharmacy practice. This study aimed to develop evidence and expert-informed medication algorithms for community pharmacists for individuals with an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 30 ml/min/1.73 m² and validate them for content and face validity.
Method
Fifty medication algorithms were developed by team experts and revised using Lynn's 3-step method (domain identification, item generation per domain, and instrument formation). For each algorithm, a 2-part questionnaire was administered to two participant groups: first to team experts, followed by community pharmacists. Each group, consisting of 5-6 participants, rated the content and face validity of each algorithm using Likert scales over at least two rounds. The item-level content validity index (I-CVI) and scale-level content validity index (S-CVI/Average) were computed for each medication algorithm per round. To measure face validity, percentages of those that “agreed” or “strongly agreed” to five statements were calculated for both groups. Virtual interviews were conducted and analyzed using qualitative descriptive analysis. Revisions were made to the algorithms between rounds.
Results
Thirty-eight of the 50 medication algorithms achieved content and face validation by 22 team experts in 2 rounds between August-September 2024. I-CVI and S-CVI/Average ranged from 0.5–1 and 0.83–1 and the overall percentage of participants who agreed or strongly agreed to 5 face validity statements ranged from 50–100%. Thirteen medications were excluded from the community pharmacist's validation. In 2 additional rounds, 23 community pharmacists, with a mean ± standard deviation of 13.74 ± 9.14 years of experience, validated 38 medication algorithms between October-December 2024. I-CVI and S-CVI/Average per medication algorithm ranged from 0.83–1.0 and 0.90–1.0 which met the content validity threshold of 0.83–1.0 (P < 0.05) for at least 5-6 participants per round. Participants overall agreement to face validity statements ranged from 75–100% which was above the prespecified threshold of 70% for face validity consensus.
Conclusion
Thirty-eight medication algorithms achieved high content and face validity. Future research will integrate these algorithms into an electronic drug dosing and decision support kidney (eDoseCKD) tool and assess their effectiveness and safety in community pharmacy practice in people with chronic kidney disease.

title: #1690 Biosensors for measuring cystatin c, creatinine and urea in human sweat
authors: Elena De Gregorio; Giulia Matteoli; Lorena Tedeschi; Sofia Zanotti; Daniel Alejandro Corzo Diaz; Eleni Stamellou; Evangelia Ntounousi; Thomas Herndl; Mario Auer; Marcin Kautsch; Tommaso Lomonaco; Pietro Salvo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects over 10% of the global population, leading to significant morbidity, mortality, and economic burden. The demand for the remote monitoring of patients’ health status has grown during the last decade. In particular, wearable devices may become supporting tools for managing and following up therapies. The levels of CKD biomarkers may be measured unobtrusively and fluids like sweat, saliva or urine can be an alternative to blood for tracking health status over time. A recent project funded by the European Union, Kermit (Kidney Disease Sweat sensor patch for Early diagnosis and Remote MonIToring, www.kermitsense.eu) aims to develop a wearable microfluidic lab-on-chip for measuring in sweat the levels of cystatin c, creatinine and urea. This innovation has the potential to revolutionize CKD management, particularly in remote or underserved areas.
Method
An aptameric nanomaterials-based biosensor was used for measuring the levels of cystatin c whereas two nanomaterial-based sensors for creatinine and urea. The three biosensors were tested using ten volunteers’ sweat, which was stimulated by percutaneous iontophoresis of carbachol. Electrochemical impedance analysis (PalmSens 4, PalmSens, the Netherlands) was used to test the sensors, which were validated by the comparison with the results of liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry. The temperature stability for the cystatin c aptamer was analyzed by simulating its secondary folding between 22 °C and 40 °C. The limit of detection was calculated for cystatin c as 3.3 the standard deviation of intercept divided by the slope of the calibration curve, for creatinine from the standard deviation of the blank, and for urea using the formula for a semilogarithmic curve by Hayashi et al. [1].
Results
Table 1 shows the specifications of the three biosensors. These values are within the parameters of clinical interest although it is worth noting that the levels of cystatin c in sweat were not available in the scientific literature.
Conclusion
The preliminary results of the project KERMIT showed the potential application of cystatin c, creatinine and urea biosensors for monitoring biomarkers of renal diseases in sweat. The biosensor for cystatin c was the first device to perform this analysis in sweat and, with the other two sensors, proved promising for paving the way towards new tools to manage kidney patients. Future work will be to perform a trial on CKD patients to validate the biosensors in clinical settings. This trial will also help to define the levels of clinical interest for the levels of cystatin c in patients’ sweat.

title: #3698 Indicators of vaccination status in patients with chronic kidney disease: importance of healthcare providers’ recommendation
authors: Gizem Kumru; İrem Akdemir; Cengiz Kaan Demir; Sule Sengul
abstract:
Background and Aims
Influenza and pneumococcal vaccination is highly advised for individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD) because of their immunocompromised status. Understanding factors contributing to vaccination status may guide strategies to enhance vaccine uptake in this high-risk patient population.
Method
A cross-sectional study was performed on 307 patients with chronic kidney disease (37.1% on dialysis, 40.4% non-dialysis, 22.5% kidney transplantation), diagnosed for at least one year and presented to our hospital's nephrology outpatient or inpatient clinic from June to August 2024. The individuals' demographic data, clinical conditions, and social factors, including nutritional status, frailty, and health literacy, were assessed. The vaccination statuses for influenza, pneumococcus, and SARS-CoV-2, together with the related variables, have been analyzed.
Results
Participants had chronic kidney disease for a median of 8 years (Table 1). The mean age of the patients was 56.6 ± 15.6 years, with a predominance of males (56.7%). The percentages of individuals unvaccinated against influenza, pneumococcus, and SARS-CoV-2 were 61.9%, 60.9%, and 5.9%, respectively, whereas merely 11 patients (3.9%) received an influenza vaccine annually. Patients consulted a physician a median of 8 times per year; yet, healthcare professionals advised influenza and pneumococcal vaccines to 60.3% and 37.1% of the patients, respectively. No independent correlation was identified between vaccination status and gender, education status, household income, marital status, comorbidities, chronic kidney disease subgroup and stage, or health literacy level. The frequency of regular or infrequent influenza vaccination was independently influenced by healthcare providers’ recommendation (HR, 14.348; 95% CI, 6.842–30.086; P < 0.001), malnutrition or malnutrition risk (HR, 2.722; 95% CI, 1.467–5.050; p: 0.002), and prior pneumococcal vaccination (HR, 2.100; 95% CI, 1.180-3.737; p: 0.012), but frailty diminished vaccination rates (HR, 0.198; 95% CI, 0.083–0.472; P < 0.001). Healthcare providers’ recommendation (HR, 17.804; 95% CI, 9.353–33.892; P < 0.001) and advanced age (HR, 1.024; 95% CI, 1.001–1.046; p: 0.040) were independent factors for pneumococcal vaccination rates.
Conclusion
The recommendation of healthcare professionals is the paramount factor in enhancing immunization rates. The elevated rates of SARS-CoV-2 immunization indicate that vaccination levels can be improved by well-structured national programs. Enhancing immunization rates necessitates the training of healthcare professionals, addressing their hesitation, and developing policies that facilitate effective communication with patients.

title: #794 Phenylacetylglutamine's role in the link between uremic toxins and cognition in chronic kidney disease: a CKD-REIN cohort study
authors: Helene Levassort; Julie Boucquemont; Sophie Liabeuf; Solene Laville; Luc Frimat; Christian Combe; Denis Fouque; Maurice Laville; Christian Jacquelinet; Natalia Alencar de Pinho; Marion Pepin; Ziad Massy
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) leads to the accumulation of uremic toxins (UTs). Many studies have suggested that UTs are associated with cognitive impairment (CI) in CKD patients. It was recently reported that phenylacetylglutamine (PAG) contributes to the association between CKD and CI. To the best of our knowledge, this association has not been investigated in non-dialysis-dependent adults with CKD.
Method
The CKD-REIN cohort study included 3033 patients with CKD stages 2 to 5; the present cross-sectional analysis included those with a serum PAG measurement and a Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score within 3 months of each other. CI was defined as an MMSE score ≤26/30. Logistic regression models were used to assess the association between the serum PAG levels and CI.
Results
Of the 2590 patients included (mean (standard deviation (SD)) age: 67 (13); males: 66%; mean (SD) estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR): 34 (13) mL/min/1.73 m2; median [interquartile range] serum PAG level: 2.1 [1.2–3.6] mg/L), 908 (35%) presented an MMSE score ≤26/30. After adjustment for sociodemographic factors (age, sex, and educational level), cardiovascular risk factors, cerebrovascular disease, eGFR, urinary albumin to creatinine ratio and other UTs known to be associated with CI risk (indoxyl sulfate, p-cresyl sulfate and trimethylamine-N-oxide), a two-fold increase in the serum PAG levels was associated with CI (odds ratio [95% confidence interval]: 1.15 [1.02, 1.29]).
Conclusion
The results of this large study show that elevated serum PAG levels are associated with CI in non-dialysis-dependent adults with CKD and highlight a new physiological pathway underlying this association between UTs and CI. Further studies are needed to confirm the causal nature of this association and to explore strategies for reducing serum PAG levels and thus protecting cognitive function.

title: #118 The new era of glycomics for the identification of prognostic and diagnostic biomarkers of kidney disease: ExoGAG
authors: María Pereira Hernández; Marta Vizoso González; Susana Bravo; Nerea Lago Baameiro; Carmen Vazquez; Candido Diaz Rodriguez; Teresa Cordal Martínez; Maria Pardo Perez; Miguel Garcia Gonzalez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are large polysaccharides formed by repeated sequences of disaccharides that interact through glycosidic bonds with proteins and lipids, forming the extracellular matrix. The glycosylation state is altered as a consequence of different pathologies, such as cancer or kidney disease. GAGs are also present in extracellular vesicles (EVs), nanometric structures bounded by a lipid bilayer that are conservatively released by cells and whose cargo (RNA/miRNA, DNA and proteins) and membrane proteins is a reflection of the cell of origin. Moreover, these molecules play an essential role in intercellular communication.
Our group has developed a method for the isolation of GAGs, glycoproteins and EVs in any type of biological sample, called EXOGAG (marketed by Nasas Biotech), currently already characterised in urine, breast milk and plasma. This method has allowed us to identify new prognostic and diagnostic biomarkers of disease in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), the most prevalent hereditary kidney disease.
Method
urine samples have been collected from patients genetically diagnosed with polycystic kidney disease type I and type II at different stages of the disease. Using ExoGAG, both vesicles and glycated proteins have been isolated and characterised by means of different proteomic techniques (Western Blot, Mass Spectrometry), image characterisation (Electron Microscopy and Immunofluorescence) and vesicle component analysis (ExoView® or Nanoparticle Tracking Analysis®).
Results
ExoGAG is a growing technology that has allowed us to identify a series of biomarkers in urine (in protection) in patients with polycystic kidney disease, which are altered with the progression of the disease, even anticipating currently used markers of loss of function or renal damage. We are currently continuing to explore its potential in other types of liquid biopsies, having optimised the protocols for breast milk and plasma as well.
Conclusion
The development of this new method for isolating the GAG-associated fraction in urine samples has allowed us to identify new prognostic/diagnostic biomarkers of kidney disease, based on the characterisation of the glycoprotein and vesicular profile. This study opens the door to the new era of glycomics in kidney disease.

urine samples have been collected from patients genetically diagnosed with polycystic kidney disease type I and type II at different stages of the disease. title: #3563 Elevated urine albumin-creatinine ratio associates with higher pulse-wave velocity in a population-based cohort
authors: Victor Walendy; Michael Gekle; Alexander Kluttig; Andreas Wienke; Claudia Grossmann; Oliver Thews; Thomas Schmid; Melanie Zinkhan; Matthias Girndt
abstract:
Background and Aims
Moderately elevated albumin excretion in the urine, semiquantified by the urine albumin-creatinine ratio (uACR), has been shown to increase the risk for vascular or renal end-points in patients with diabetes mellitus, arterial hypertension, high cardiovascular risk, or even the general population. The mechanisms behind this relation are still under debate. Pulse wave velocity (PWV) is a marker of arterial stiffness, which includes endothelial function. In patients with renal disease, a relation between uACR and enhanced PWV was described. Until now such relation has not been extensively studied in an average risk, low morbidity cohort.
Method
We cross-sectionally studied individuals participating in a local subcohort of the German National Cohort (NAKO), a large population-based cohort that recruited participants aged 19–74 years. Urinary albumin-creatinine ratio was determined from a spontaneously voided sample and pulse wave velocity was measured using a plethysmographic device (Vascular ExplorerTM) with cuffs at the upper arm and the ankle. The PWV was compared between categories auf uACR (0–<30 mg/g, 30–<300 mg/g and 300+ mg/g) by ANOVA. Further, a multivariate linear model corrected for age, BMI, eGFR, and HbA1c was analyzed.
Results
Complete data sets were available from 4,798 individuals of the local cohort, 51% male, age 50.3 ± 12.9 years, body mass index 26.9 ± 4.9 (mean ± SD). Among these participants, 207 (4.3%) reported a history of cardiac disease, 112 (2.3%) of peripheral artery disease, 353 of diabetes mellitus (7.4%), and 117 (2.4%) of kidney disease, 4.048 (84.3%) reported none of these conditions. The average uACR was 17.6 ± 152.9 mg/g with 341 (7.1%) participants showing a value above 30 mg/g. The average eGFR was 99.0 ± 15.2 ml/min with 65 (1.4%) participants showing eGFR <60 ml/min.
The PWV was slightly higher in participants with uACR >30 mg/g than in those with uACR <30 mg/g (P < 0.001) (Fig. 1). The uACR was predictive for PWV in multivariate analysis correcting for typical vascular risk factors. Sensitivity analysis showed that this relation still held true after excluding individuals who reported a history of vascular, metabolic or renal disease.
Conclusion
Albuminuria is associated with elevated pulse wave velocity in a population-based cohort with low metabolic, vascular, and renal disease load. Further studies should address the role of low-level albuminuria in the absence of overt cardiovascular disease.

title: #3495 How does intradialytic exercise influence emotional well-being and quality of life in renal dialysis patients?
authors: Solmar Rodríguez de Galvís; María Teresa Marín López; Marcos García Olegario; Carmen Peinado; Julia Audije-Gil; Fabiola Dapena; David Hernán Gascueña; Paula Manso
abstract:
Background and Aims
Haemodialysis (HD) is associated with a decline in physical capacity, quality of life (QoL), and the emotional well-being of the patient. Evidence suggests that physical exercise provides benefits to lifestyle, prevents muscle loss, enhances mood, and alleviates symptoms associated with renal disease. Given these benefits, assessing the impact of an intradialytic exercise programme on emotional well-being, health-related QoL, and HD-related symptoms is essential. This study aimed to investigate the effects of such a programme on physical fitness, emotional response, health-related QoL in patients undergoing HD and symptoms associated with renal disease.
Method
Clinical trial with convenience sampling. The patients included in the study participated in an individualised intradialytic exercise programme, which lasted for 5 months with a frequency of 2 days per week, supervised by exercise professionals. Pre- and post-intervention assessments included the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), the 12-Item Short-Form Health Survey (SF-12) for health-related QoL, and the Edmonton Symptom Assessment System (ESAS). IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 29.0.2.0 (Armonk, NY: IBM Corp), was used to analyse the collected data. The significance level was set at P < 0.05.
Results
A total of 71 patients undergoing HD participated in the individualised intradialytic exercise programme. Of these, 37 patients (52.1%) were under 65 years old (mean age 65.6 ± 15.5 years), 43 patients (60.6%) were male, and 25 patients (35.2%) were immigrants. The mean duration of time on HD was 4.9 ± 4.4 years. Regarding the Charlson Comorbidity Index, 40 patients (56.3%) had a score of less than 8, with an overall mean score of 7.1 ± 2.8. The results of the HADS scale showed improvements in anxiety scores pre- and post-intervention (from 4.5 to 4.0; P = 0.013) and also in depression scores (from 8.6 to 7.6; P = 0.006) (HADS, Table 1). The physical and mental components of health-related QoL, as measured by the SF-12, also showed a significant improvement (P < 0.001) (SF-12, Table 1). Regarding the symptoms measured by the ESAS questionnaire, pain, depression, drowsiness, appetite, and sleep improved following participation in the exercise programme (ESAS, Table 1). No significant differences were observed in symptoms related to fatigue, nausea, anxiety, well-being, and shortness of breath.
Conclusion
Participation in intradialytic exercise leads to improvements in both physical symptoms related to renal disease, as well as enhancing mental health and overall health-related QoL. Incorporating intradialytic exercise programmes should be considered an important component of comprehensive care for patients undergoing HD.

title: #3479 Bringing kidney disease prevention into schools: impact of a pilot health education programme to improve kidney health
authors: Julia Audije-Gil; Paula Manso; María Dolores Ojeda Ramírez; Antonio López González; María Concepción Pereira; María Luz Sánchez Tocino; David Hernán Gascueña; Fabiola Dapena; María Dolores Arenas Jiménez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease is a silent condition in which prevention and early diagnosis play an essential role. The Renata Project, a scientific-health education programme on renal health, aims to raise awareness about kidney healthy habits and the prevention of chronic kidney disease (CKD) by educating children in Early Childhood and Primary Education (aged 5 to 10 years). In this project, children learn about renal health by reading the book “Renata, mi nefróloga” and participating in workshops, then share this knowledge with their families, raising awareness. This initiative engages children as health promoters within their family environment. The objective of this study was to analyse the impact of the workshop by assessing knowledge levels before and after the intervention for both students and their families, measuring the effectiveness of information transmission and its impact on increasing awareness about renal health.
Method
A quasi-experimental pre- and post-intervention study with multiple groups was conducted across five Spanish schools, involving children aged between 5 and 11 years. The study consisted of three phases: the first phase involved an initial assessment of knowledge in both children and adults, the second phase was an educational intervention in which only the children participated at school, and the third phase was a post-intervention evaluation to assess changes in knowledge in both children and their families. Knowledge assessment before and after the intervention was carried out using two questionnaires, containing the same questions but specifically adapted to the age of children and adults.
Results
Responses were collected from 591 children's questionnaires (293 pre-, 286 post-intervention) and 126 adults’ (85 pre-, 41 post-intervention). The mean age of the children was 9.9 ± 1.6 years, 50.1% male; the mean age of the adults was 45.4 ± 10.1 years, 28.6% male. The analysis showed significant improvements in the scores (out of 10) of both students and their families. Students' average score increased from 6.5 ± 2.3 to 9.2 ± 1.0 (P < 0.001), while families' score rose from 8.0 ± 1.3 to 8.5 ± 1.4 (P = 0.034) (Fig. 1). No significant gender differences were found in either children or adults.
The least known topics by the students before the intervention (those with less than half of the correct answers) were the name of the kidney specialist (Q1, 46.4% correct), whether kidneys hurt when they are sick (Q2, 45.2%), and the name of the renal function marker (Q3, 34.0%) (Table 1). After the intervention, the percentage of correct answers across all questions ranged from 87.0% to 99.7%, with significant improvement in all questions except for the one about treatment options (Q10; P = 0.063).
In the case of the family members, their initial level of knowledge about kidney-related topics and renal health was higher than that of the children, except for the question about healthy habits (Q8, 68.2% correct vs 85.5% correct in children) and the question about treatment options (28.2% vs 92.9%). After the intervention, the only question in which adults showed significant improvement was Q2 about kidney pain (increasing from 54.1% correct to 80.5%; P = 0.004).
Conclusion
The results of the programme show that the school intervention improved the knowledge levels of both the children who participated and their families. The improvement in the families' scores, despite not being present during the activity, supports the hypothesis that children can act as potential agents of change within their environment, highlighting their ability to transform society by promoting kidney health. They can drive health education in their surroundings and contribute to the prevention of CKD.

title: #718 Intestinal microbiota prevents worsening of sepsis-related outcomes in chronic kidney disease
authors: Qiubo Li; Kailey Flora; Liang Chang; Stefanie Steiger
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is known to be associated with a state of secondary immunodeficiency, referred to as Secondary ImmunoDeficiency related to Kidney Disease (SIDKD). For the majority of those affected, SIDKD represents an acquired form of immunodeficiency. Pathogenic mechanisms underlying the secondary immunodeficiency in kidney disease include immune paralysis, impaired urinary clearance of metabolites, extrinsic immunosuppressors, and a leaky gut and shift in the secretome of the intestinal microbiota [1]. Currently, it is unknown whether intestinal alterations in the gut microbiota contribute to the secondary immunodeficiency in infection in CKD. We hypothesized that depleting the intestinal microbiota with antibiotics further aggravates the innate immune response to infection in mice with CKD.
Method
Alb-creERT2; Glut9lox/lox mice with CKD, and Glut9lox/lox (healthy) control mice were treated with neomycin for 23 days, followed by the induction of sepsis through LPS injection. After 24 hours, systemic inflammation was evaluated by measuring fecal bacterial growth, serum cytokine levels, immune cell activation and recruitment, aging and maturation. Changes of gut permeability was evaluated by everted gut sacs model. Kidney function was determined by measuring the glomerular filtration rate (GFR). In addition, kidney and gut inflammation was determined by measuring the mRNA expression levels of the pro-inflammatory genes.
Results
We found that bacterial sepsis induced systemic inflammation, as evidenced by increased blood neutrophil numbers and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokine levels as compared to the PBS- treated control groups in Glut9lox/lox healthy mice. Interestingly, neomycin-induced depletion of the intestinal microbiota significantly suppressed fecal bacterial growth (Fig. A), increased neutrophil numbers (Fig. B), and endotoxin and IL-6 levels in blood and peritoneal wash with enhanced neutrophil activation, and accompanied by higher gut permeability (Fig. C) in CKD mice with sepsis compared to the control groups. However, no significant differences in kidney function were observed between septic and control mice.
Conclusion
Our findings reveal an unexpected protective role of the intestinal microbiota in modulating the inflammatory response during sepsis in mice with concomitant CKD. In contrast, antibiotic-induced microbiota depletion aggravated disease severity. Therefore, antibiotic therapy may not be a suitable strategy to prevent SIDKD, particularly in the context of sepsis.

title: #1174 Varoglutamstat improves eGFR and offers a new approach to treat diabetic kidney disease (DKD): meta-analysis from two independent phase 2 studies
authors: Frank Weber; Christine Wenzkowski; Michael Schaeffer; Sylvia Schell-Mader; Antje Meyer; Stefan Tasler; Katharina Fuchs; Tanja Wassmann; Howard Feldman; Tobias B Huber; Kevin Carroll
abstract:
Background and Aims
Novel therapies are urgently required for patients with diabetic kidney disease (DKD) because standard of care only slows the decline of kidney function (eGFR) still leading to end-stage kidney disease in many patients.
Varoglutamstat is a first in class glutaminyl cyclase (QPCT/L) inhibitor with potent anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects. Glutaminyl cyclases increase the potency of chemokines like CCL2 and CX3CL1 and thereby amplify inflammation and fibrosis and lead to kidney failure. They also contribute to maturation of certain collagens. QPCT/L inhibitors are therefore specifically promising for kidney disorders driven by chronic inflammation like diabetic kidney disease. A meta-analysis of eGFR from two independent clinical Phase 2 studies in Alzheimer disease (primary endpoint not reached) with a treatment period of 72 and 96 weeks was undertaken to characterize the effects of varoglutamstat on kidney function.
Method
eGFR (MDRD) data from two large independent multi-center, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind phase 2 studies (VIVIAD, NCT04498650 and VIVA-MIND, NCT03919162) in 286 patients with mild AD from Europe and the US were analyzed by a mixed model of repeated measures (MMRM). eGFR was prospectively included as a safety / exploratory parameter in both studies. Only patients receiving 600 mg BID varoglutamstat (N = 112) or placebo (N = 174) were included in the meta-analysis (excluding patients on 300mg BID in VIVIAD not being a fully effective dose). The trial population included older patients with MCI or mild AD. 14% of patients have diabetes as a risk factor for CKD.
Results
A significant and clinically meaningful improvement of eGFR versus placebo was observed in each clinical trial separately and in the meta-analysis: 3.6 mL/min/1.73 m2 in the total trial population (patients receiving 600 mg BID varoglutamstat vs. placebo) and 5.6 mL/min/1.73 m2 in the subpopulation of patients with diabetes.
Fig. 1 shows the results for the total treatment period and by duration of treatment:
No clinically meaningful treatment effects are observed during the first 4 months of treatment including the uptitration phase. A significant increase was observed between 6 months and 1 year of treatment of 4.5 mL/min/1.73 m2 (all patients N = 96/156, varoglutamstat vs. placebo, P = 0.0001) and 7.1 mL/min/1.73 m2 (patients with diabetes N = 16/16, varoglutamstat vs. placebo, P = 0.022) and sustained during the second year 5.3 mL/min/1.73 m2 (all patients N = 77/143, varoglutamstat vs. placebo, P < 0.0001) and 9.0 mL/min/1.73 m2 (patients with diabetes N = 13/14, varoglutamstat vs. placebo, P = 0.015).
These results were consistent between both studies for the total population and the subgroup of patients with diabetes.
Conclusion
Varoglutamstat is a first in class glutaminyl cyclase (QPCT/L) inhibitor which showed a significant and clinically meaningful improvement of eGFR which was prospectively included as safety / exploratory parameter in two independent studies in older patients with and without diabetes. This finding was replicated in both trials independently and provides a strong credibility of the results.
The next step is planned to be a dedicated phase 2b trial in patients with diabetic kidney disease (patients with diabetes and CKD stage 3b/4). The main goal will be to investigate the efficacy on eGFR in this patient population and to obtain additional information on a potential effect on proteinuria and other kidney specific markers.

title: #2658 PROGRAM FOR EARLY DETECTION AND MANAGEMENT OF CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE IN CROATIA – FIRST RESULTS
authors: Mario Laganović; Nataša Ban Toskić; Jadranka Karuza; Jelena Rakić Matić; Ksenija Vučur Šimić; Karla Boras; Tamara Knežević; Bojana Šimunov; Karmela Altabas; Ivan Bubic
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney disease is an increasing global health problem involving about 10% of the global population. Increasing prevalence of diabetes, hypertension and obesity are likely to increase kidney disease prevalence with serious implications for quality of life, survival and health care costs. Early detection is the key strategy to prevent kidney disease. Primary care practitioners (PCP) are crucial in early identification and management of patients with CKD. The aim of this study is to report first results of Early detection program of CKD in Croatia, obtained through new, digital interactive tool “Chronic Kidney Disease Preventive Panel”.
Method
Croatian Society of Nephrology, Dialysis and Transplantation and Association of Croatian Family Physicians launched “Chronic Kidney Disease Preventive Panel”—an interactive, innovative, digital tool for detecting, monitoring and standardizing comprehensive care of patients with CKD on PCP level through interactive interface depending on the degree of renal disfunction according to the latest KDIGO guidelines. The panel has been implemented in electronic health charts of 2300 family medicine practices with intention to facilitate screening of CKD in high risk populations (diabetic, hypertensive and obese population). The CKD Preventive Panel collects anthropometric data, gender, age, medical history, blood pressure values, serum creatinine (sCr), eGFR, albumin/creatinine ratio (ACR) and calculate staging and risk of progression of kidney disease according to KDIGO guidelines for management of CKD.
Results
results are shown for the first 6 months of using the CKD Preventive Panel (May 2024–October 2024). During observed period 10 497 records were obtained, 44% males and 56% women. title: #1444 Persistent effects of territorial and gender inequalities on the care trajectory of dialysis patients: access to transplantation and CKD-related mortality before and after transplantation
authors: Judith Breaud; Sahar Bayat; Marie Agness Bakhoum; Sacha Lavaud; Cécile Couchoud; Juste Goungounga
abstract:
Background and Aims
Different factors influencing chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients’ outcomes have been identified in the literature, such as gender, smoking, socioeconomic status, and various comorbidities (cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease, physical disability and hepatic disease). The outcomes of interest include access to renal transplantation, and mortality related to CKD (excess mortality) for dialyzed patients and for those who received a renal transplant. Yet little information is available on the association between territorial inequalities, and these outcomes. Our work aims to study the association between département of residence and the aforementioned factors with different outcomes of dialyzed patients.
Method
We conducted an observational longitudinal cohort study using national REIN registry, including 29,281 CKD patients aged 18–85 who started dialysis between 2017 and 2019 in France, with follow-up until 31st of December 2022. Among them, 6,329 patients were transplanted. We conducted a complete case analysis using flexible multi-level multi-state relative survival modelling allowing for a frailty term to account for patients clustering by department and to simultaneously examine transplant access, excess mortality in dialysis and excess mortality after transplantation.
Results
Conclusion
We were able to identify persistent effects of territorial and gender inequalities on the outcomes of dialysis patients’ care trajectory. Having identified areas with better and worse outcomes might allow to calibrate the care plans in dialysis patients, and for example plan interventions focused specifically on the areas with lower access to transplant. Similarly, helping CKD-patients stop smoking might be interesting since smoking is associated with a lower access to transplantation and a higher excess mortality in dialysis. For CKD patients with comorbidities, better coordination of care between nephrologists and other specialists could improve patient outcomes.
This study will be extended to the full dataset after imputation process, due to high proportion of missing data.

title: #1657 Dose-response analysis of serum uric acid levels and the risk of developing chronic kidney disease in patients with gout
authors: Liye Xu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Globally, the prevalence of hyperuricemia (HUA) has exceeded 20% and is shifting toward younger age groups. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a common complication of gout, with approximately 24% of gout patients progressing to stage Ⅲ or higher CKD. However, the dose-response relationship between serum uric acid (SUA) levels and CKD development in gout patients remains unexplored. This study, focusing on gout patients in Southwest China, aimed to investigate the relationship and dose-response relationship between SUA levels and CKD risk, providing a scientific basis for CKD prevention and management.
Method
We collected clinical data from 502 gout patients who visited our hospital between February 2023 and February 2024. Gout diagnosis was based on the criteria established by the 2015 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) guidelines. The estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was calculated based on creatinine levels using the CKD Epidemiology Collaboration 2021 (CKD-EPI) equation, with CKD defined as eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m². Patients were divided into two groups based on eGFR: the CKD group (eGFR < 60 ml/min/1.73 m²) and the non-CKD group (eGFR ≥ 60 ml/min/1.73 m²). Multivariate logistic regression was used to assess the association with CKD. A three-node restricted cubic spline (RCS) was employed to model the dose-response relationship between SUA levels and the development of CKD, based on model 2. P-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.
Results
The mean SUA was higher in CKD patients (629.15 μmol/l) compared to non-CKD patients (581.2 μmol/l), (P = 0.006) (Table 1). No significant association was found between CKD and gouty arthritis (χ = 2.332, P = 0.267). However, the presence of CKD was significantly linked to the development of gouty stones (χ = 6.028, P = 0.022). Additionally, three models were developed to adjust for confounders and further examine the relationship between SUA and CKD (Table 2). The results indicated a strong positive correlation between SUA and CKD. In the unadjusted model, the odds ratio (OR) was 1.002, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 1.000 to 1.004 (P = 0.023). This positive association remained statistically significant after adjusting for all confounders in Model 3 (P = 0.034). Using Model 2, the dose-response relationship between CKD and HUA was further explored through RCS analysis. The continuous change in SUA was plotted on the horizontal axis, while the risk of CKD occurrence was plotted on the vertical axis. The results revealed a significant association between SUA levels and CKD incidence risk (P = 0.035). However, the non-linear relationship was not significant, suggesting a more linear association. This implies that the risk of CKD may exhibit a regular upward or downward trend as SUA levels change, rather than a complex curvilinear relationship (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
In gout patients, serum uric acid (SUA) is a significant risk factor for the development of CKD, with the risk of CKD exhibiting a consistent upward or downward trend as SUA levels change. This study offers valuable scientific evidence for the prevention and management of CKD in gout patients, emphasizing that close monitoring of SUA levels and timely intervention could reduce CKD risk and improve clinical outcomes.
