title: #1318 Burden of pruritus in older CKD stage 4-5 patients: 7-year follow-up of the EQUAL study
authors: Enise Çelebi; Esmee Driehuis; Nicholas Chesnaye; Kitty J Jager; Fergus Caskey; Claudia Torino; MacIej Szymczak; Christiane Drechsler; Christoph Wanner; Marie Evans; Friedo W Dekker; Ellen K Hoogeveen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease-associated pruritus (CKD-aP) is ranked within the top 10 most prevalent and burdensome symptoms in patients with kidney failure. CKD-aP is associated with reduced quality of life (QoL), psychological distress, and adverse clinical outcomes such as increased morbidity and mortality. Despite its clinical importance, little is known about the burden of CKD-aP in older CKD stage 4-5 patients. Therefore, our aim is to investigate the prevalence, incidence and burden of CKD-aP in older patients with stage 4-5 CKD.
Method
The European Quality (EQUAL) study is an ongoing, prospective, multicenter study involving patients aged ≥65 years who have experienced an incident drop in eGFR to ≤20 ml/min/1.73 m2. The frequency and burden of CKD-aP was assessed every 3–6 months between March 2012 and May 2022, using the Dialysis Symptom Index. Patients reported the presence of CKD-aP and rated its burden on a five-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 to 5. Burden is categorized into three groups: no burden (score 0 “symptom not present” and score 1 “not at all”), low burden (score 2 “a little bit” and 3 “somewhat”), and high burden (score 4 “quite a bit” and 5 “very much”). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics. We used Kaplan-Meier curve to examine the incidence of CKD-aP and restricted cubic spline analysis to depict the burden over time.
Results
We included 1,380 patients who completed at baseline the question regarding the presence of CKD-aP and followed them for a maximum of 7 years. At baseline, 66% of the participants were men, mean (SD) age was 76 (7) years, eGFR was 17 (5) ml/min/1.73 m2, serum phosphate level was 1.3 (0.3), 41% had diabetes, and 47% had cardiovascular disease. At baseline, 53% of all patients reported having pruritus, and 14% experienced a high burden. About 7% of all patients reported never having pruritus during five years of follow-up, while 10% had persistent pruritus. After five years of follow-up, no patients were identified who either never experienced pruritus or who had persistent pruritus. The average burden of pruritus remained stable with a mean score of 1.5 throughout the 7-years of follow-up. Over 7-years of follow-up, 253 (39%) out of the 655 patients who did not have CKD-aP at baseline developed pruritus.
Conclusion
During 7-years of follow-up, we found a persistently high prevalence of pruritus, exceeding 50%, among older CKD stage 4-5 patients, with more than 10% experiencing a high burden. After five years of follow-up, one in ten patients never experienced pruritus, while another one in ten had persistent pruritus throughout the period. These findings suggest that pruritus is a common and burdensome symptom in this population. It is important to highlight these findings, as pruritus can impair patients’ QoL, yet it often receives insufficient attention in clinical practice. Greater awareness among healthcare providers is needed to ensure early identification and management of pruritus. Treatment of pruritus, ultimately, can improve QoL for patients with advanced CKD.

title: #3575 The copper/zinc balance and anemia in patients with reduced glomerular filtration rate, data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES).
authors: Guido Gembillo; Luca Soraci; Alberto Montesanto; Ersilia Paparazzo; Andrea Corsonello; Vincenzo Calabrese; Luigi Peritore; Domenico Santoro
abstract:
Background and Aims
The balance between copper and zinc plays a crucial role in various physiological processes, including hematopoiesis. This study examines the relationship between the copper-to-zinc (Cu/Zn) ratio and the risk of anemia using data from the 2011–2012 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES).
Method
We conducted a secondary analysis of patients who participated in the NHANES study and for whom data on renal function, serum copper and zinc, and hemoglobin and history of chronic diseases were available. Starting with 5,972 patients, we obtained a final sample of 5,153 patients aged 18 years or older after excluding those aged <18 years. Anemia was defined according to WHO guidelines; eGFR was calculated using the updated version of the CKD-EPI equation (2021). The association between Cu/Zn tertiles and hemoglobin levels was examined cross-sectionally using linear regression; the association with the presence of anemia was examined using logistic regression. All multivariate models were adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity, baseline EGFR, congestive heart failure, coronary heart disease, stroke, cancer, COPD.
Results
634 of 5,153 patients were diagnosed with anemia at baseline (14.4%). A continuous Cu/ZN level was associated with a decreasing hemoglobin level in the entire study population. Increasing Cu/Zn tertiles were associated with increasing risk of anemia; more specifically, compared to the first tertile (Cu/Zn = 0.353–1.22), the second tertile (1.23–1.56) was not significantly associated with anemia (OR, 95% CI: 1.03, 0.99–1.07); the significance of the association was relevant for the third tertile (Cu/Zn = 1.57–5.54) compared to the first (OR, 95%CI: 1.10, 1.07–1.18). There was a stronger association between Cu/Zn ratio and anemia in patients with chronic kidney disease or ACR ≥300 mg/g, with an additive interaction between the last tertile of Cu/Zn ratio and the presence of CKD (P value = 0.01) (Table 1).
Conclusion
Our analysis revealed that a higher Cu/Zn ratio was significantly associated with an increased risk of anemia, suggesting a detrimental role of copper compared to zinc in maintaining healthy hemoglobin levels especially in patients with impaired renal function. In fact, the association between Cu/Zn ratio and anemia was significant in patients with chronic renal failure and marginally significant in patients with normal renal function. These findings highlight the importance of trace metal homeostasis in hematologic health and warrant further investigation to explore the underlying mechanisms and potential clinical implications.

title: #03611 MHR as a biomarker for kidney function decline and cardiovascular disease in a large cohort of geriatric patients
authors: Guido Gembillo; Luca Soraci; Luigi Peritore; Alberto Montesanto; Ersilia Paparazzo; Vincenzo Calabrese; Andrea Corsonello; Domenico Santoro
abstract:
Background and Aims
The Monocyte- to high-High-Density Lipoprotein Ratio (MHR) has emerged as a potential biomarker of inflammation and cardiovascular risk. This study examines the association between MHR, kidney function, mortality, and the incidence of incident cardiac disease over a four-year period using data from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS).
Method
We analyzed 6,453 older adults enrolled in the Health Retirement Study's 2016 Venous Blood Study presenting available data on renal function, history of chronic diseases, and long-term mortality at 4 years. MHR was used either as a continuous variable or categorized into tertiles. Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was calculated using the updated CKD-EPI formula. The cross-sectional association between MHR and eGFR was investigated by using weighted linear regression, while the longitudinal association with mortality and heart disease incidence was examined using weighted Cox regression and Fine Gray models. Study covariates included age, sex, ethnicity, smoking status, history of chronic disease at baseline (hypertension, heart failure, diabetes, lung disease, cancer, stroke/TIA), eGFR at baseline, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, and hemoglobin levels.
Results
The median MHR in the study population was 0.40 (0.31-0.47). Increasing MHR was associated with decreasing eGFR in multivariate linear regression models (β, SE = −1.56, 0.35, p-value < 0.001); patients belonging to the second tertile (MHR 0.30–0.46) and the third tertile (MHR = 0.47–6.45) were characterized by a graded decrease in eGFR values (β, SE −1.40, 0.58, p-value = .036; and −2.89, 0.65, P < 0.001, respectively) compared to patients in the first tertile (MHR = 0.1–0.29). Longitudinal analyzes showed that MHR was strongly associated with all-cause mortality (HR, 95%CI of multivariate models: 1.52, 1.06–2.18) and was associated with age, lung disease, decreasing eGFR, hypertension, stroke, NLR and decreased hemoglobin; analyzes performed in patients without cardiovascular disease at baseline (N = 4.197) showed that MHR was associated with an increased incidence of cardiovascular disease after 4 years (HR, 95% CI: 1.56, 1.54, 1.26–2.24); interestingly, NLR was not associated with an increased incidence of heart disease. There was an additive interaction between the last tertile of MHR and a diagnosis of chronic kidney disease (p-value = 0.001), although the observed associations were only significant in patients with impaired renal function (Table 1).
Conclusion
These results suggest that MHR may be a useful biomarker for identifying individuals at higher risk of renal and cardiovascular complications. Further studies are needed to confirm these associations and explore potential clinical applications.

title: #02095 Sex-specific metabolic dysfunction and reduced lifespan induced by long-term and low-dose dietary phosphorus loading in mice
authors: Ayumi Matsumoto; Isao Matsui; Natsune Tamai; Atsuhiro Imai; Hiroki Okushima; Kazunori Inoue; Yoshitaka Isaka
abstract:
Background and Aims
Modern diets are characterized by high phosphorus content, resulting in chronic phosphorus loading throughout the human lifespan. Previous studies have demonstrated that acute, high-dose (2–3%) phosphorus loading leads to hyperphosphatemia and subsequent organ damage, including renal injury and vascular calcification. title: #2051 Senescence: a translational perspective for uremic cardiomyopathy
authors: Xin-Lu Wang; Bin Wang; Xiaonan Wang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Uremic cardiomyopathy is a major complication in CKD. The mortality from uremic cardiomyopathy is approximately 15 to 30 times higher than that of the general population, accounting for 40% of CKD-related deaths. Previous studies have found that the uremic toxin indoxyl sulfate accumulates in the blood of patients, can bind to and subsequently activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), causing DDR, which leads to the upregulation of cell cycle inhibitors such as p21 and p16INK4a, being associated with uremic cardiomyopathy and senescence and uremic cardiomyopathy is characterized by heart fibrosis. However, the role of cardiomyocyte senescence in heart fibrosis and dysfunction remains poorly understood. We aim to elucidate the mechanism by which cellular senescence leads to CKD-induced cardiomyopathy and decline in cardiac function, providing a promising therapeutic strategy to mitigate the adverse effects of uremic cardiomyopathy - targeting cellular senescence.
Method
CKD was induced in mice via 5/6th nephrectomy. Mice were treated with a senolytic cocktail of dasatinib and quercetin (D&Q) twice weekly for 8 weeks. Markers of senescence, inflammation, oxidative stress, and fibrosis were assessed using immunohistochemistry, immunoblotting, and qPCR. Primary cultured cardiomyocytes were incubated with indoxyl sulfate (IS) to study cellular senescence.
Results
Our study found that, compared with the sham group, the senescence biomarkers in CKD mice were elevated. Specifically, p21 increased by 1.8-fold, p16INK4a increased by 1.7-fold, and both cyclin - dependent kinases CDK1/2 and CDK4 were significantly decreased in the hearts of uremic mice. Fibrotic proteins vimentin, α - SMA, and connective tissue growth factor were significantly upregulated in the uremic hearts. These evidences indicate that experimental CKD leads to cellular senescence in the hearts of CKD mice.
Subsequently, we orally administered D&Q to CKD mice twice a week for 8 weeks. We found that the left ventricular end - diastolic dimension in CKD mice increased and the ratio of heart weight to tibia bone (mg/cm) in CKD mice was significantly higher than that in sham mice (P < 0.01), and these parameters returned to normal after D&Q treatment. The intervention of D&Q prevented the CKD - induced increase in p21 and p16INK4a, and restored the levels of two cyclin - dependent kinases CDK1/2 and CDK4 in the hearts of CKD mice. These results suggest that senolytic treatment alleviated the senescence of the uremic hearts in CKD mice.
In addition, we found that superoxide dismutase (SOD) in the hearts of CKD mice decreased by 51%, and returned to the level of the sham - operated control group after D&Q treatment. D&Q reduced the inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-1β, IL-6) in the uremic hearts. Subsequently, we monitored the effect of D&Q on indoxyl sulfate (IS) in senescence markers. The level of IS in the serum of CKD mice was elevated, which significantly increased the levels of AhR, TGFβ and NF κB, while decreasing PGC - 1α. 1 millimolar (mM) of IS increased p21, p16INK4a and γH2AX in primary cardiomyocytes. However, D&Q reversed the up - regulation of senescence markers and oxidative stress induced by IS.
Our research has revealed that senolytics, such as D&Q, limit senescence by selectively inducing the death of senescent cells, reducing SASP and its damaging effects, and promoting overall tissue health.
Conclusion
Senescent cardiomyocytes contribute to heart fibrosis and dysfunction in CKD through IS-induced AhR activation. Senolytics treatment suppressed AhR activation, reducing oxidative stress and inflammation, which provided therapeutic potential for uremic cardiomyopathy.

title: #1937 Association between the number of parity and the prevalence of chronic kidney disease: a cross-sectional study using KoGES-HEXA data
authors: A Young Cho; Ji Hyun Kim; Ju Hwan Oh; In O Sun; Ha-Eun Lee
abstract:
Background and Aims
Adverse pregnancy outcomes (APOs), such as preeclampsia, gestational diabetes (GDM), and spontaneous abortion, have been reported to increase the risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD) in women. Normal pregnancy induces significant anatomic and physiologic changes in the kidneys. In addition, higher parity has been associated with an increased prevalence of diabetes and hypertension, which are established risk factors for CKD. However, previous studies on the association between parity number and the prevalence of CKD have shown conflicting results. Based on this background, this study investigated the association between the number of parity and the prevalence of CKD. Furthermore, the study analyzed whether the association between parity number and CKD prevalence was present in the absence of APOs.
Method
We analyzed the health examinee data from the Korean Genome and Epidemiology Study (KoGES-HEXA), which comprises participants from Korea between 2004 and 2013. After excluding individuals with histories of pre-existing CKD and participants with incomplete records, 100433 participants were included in this study (Fig. 1). CKD was defined as an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 60 mL/min/1.73 m², calculated using the CKD-EPI (Epidemiology Collaboration) formula or the presence of proteinuria. We compared the prevalence of CKD across four groups, categorized by the number of parity: 0, 1, 2, 3, and ≥4. In addition, we analyzed the association between high parity (≥4) and CKD prevalence based on whether the participants had experienced each APO.
Results
Women in the 3 parity and ≥4 parity groups were older, had more comorbidities, were less likely to smoke or drink, had lower education levels, and had a higher frequency of menopause compared to the 0 or 1 parity groups (Table 1). Since the sample size of the 0 parity group was too small and their lifestyle factors differed significantly from those of parous women, the CKD prevalence was compared among the women with 1, 2, 3, and ≥4 parities. CKD prevalence increased with parity number, being higher in the 3 parity group (4.4%) and ≥4 parity group (7.3%) compared to the 1 parity group (3.1%) (P for trend < 0.001) (Fig. 2). After adjusting for multiple risk factors, parity number ≥4 was significantly associated with the CKD prevalence (odds ratio: 1.182, 95% confidence interval: 1.015–1.375) (Fig. 2). In subgroup analyses, high parity (≥4) was associated with increased CKD prevalence even in the absence of preeclampsia, GDM, or spontaneous abortion events (Fig. 3).
Conclusion
Four or more parity is associated with the increased prevalence of CKD in Korean women. This result was consistently observed in the subgroups without preeclampsia, GDM, or spontaneous abortion events.

title: #01842 The effect of GLP-1 receptor agonists on renal outcomes:a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Takaya Sasaki; Samantha Giang; Jiajia Wu; Martin Gallagher; Rinaldo Bellomo; Amanda Wang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) remains a progressive and incurable condition, contributing significantly to morbidity and mortality rates globally. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP1RAs) are anti-hyperglycaemic agents, with demonstrated cardioprotective effects. However, the renal protective effects of GLP1RAs remain unclear.
This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess the effects of GLP1RAs on renal outcomes in patients with or without diabetes, obesity and chronic kidney disease.
Method
A systematic review and meta-analysis was performed examining all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing the effects of GLP1RAs on renal outcomes. Medline, EMBASE and the Cochrane Register were searched to December 2024. The primary outcome was composite renal outcomes defined as development of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) or dialysis requirement, worsening of renal function (as defined by authors) and changes in proteinuria. Subgroup analysis was performed based on diabetic status. Relative risks (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for individual trials were pooled using random effects models for treatment classes.
Results
The search yielded 19 trials including 90882 patients (Fig. 1). Mean age was 60.77 with male predominance of 57%. Mean follow-up was 25.9 months. Overall, 12 trials primarily assessed diabetic patients, 4 assessed only obese patients, 2 assessed both diabetic and obese patients and 1 assessed the patients with high cardiovascular risk factors. GLP1RAs were associated with a 19% reduction in the occurrence of the composite renal outcomes (10 trials, 33647 participants, RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.73–0.89). Moreover, the risk of declined renal function decreased by 12% (9 trials, 34100 participants, RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.81–0.95) and the risk of increasing eGFR slopes was reduced by 0.45ml/min per year (16 trials, 30538 participants, MD 0.45, 95% CI 0.10–0.81). GLP1Ras also reduced microalbuminuria by 24% (10 trials, 16720 participants, RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.71–0.82), decreased HbA1c by 0.61% (15 trials, 20512 participants, MD –0.61, 95% CI -0.76- -0.49) and achieved an approximate average of 5kg of weight loss (15 trials, 27905 participants, MD -5.24, 95% CI -7.46 - -3.02). Although there were no significant differences in progression to ESKD (6 trials, 28294 participants, RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.71-1.05), GLP1RAs reduced the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) by 15% (15 trials, 46041 participants, RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.81-0.90) and all-cause mortality by 14% (17 trials, 46563 participants, RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.82-0.91). No significant differences were seen in severe adverse events (18 trials, 46611 participants, RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.90-1.01), acute kidney injury or hypoglycaemia. However, there were more gastroenterological side effects. The effect of GLP1RAs on renal outcomes were similar in both diabetics and non-diabetic population. Most trials (17/19) were at low risk of bias.
Conclusion
GLP1 RAs demonstrated cardiovascular and renal benefits in diabetic patients. Further high-quality randomised trials assessing their effects in nondiabetic patients with or without proteinuria are needed.

title: #0907 Genetic screens of imaging-derived kidney volumes identify genes linked to kidney function
authors: Sara Monteiro-Martins; Yong Li; Oleg Borisov; Wilfried Reichardt; Elias Kellner; Martin Büchert; Maximilian Russe; Fabian Bamberg; Peggy Sekula; Marco Reisert; Anna Köttgen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of kidney function typically rely on biochemical biomarkers like serum creatinine or cystatin C to estimate the glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). These biomarkers have limitations, including varying eGFR equations, biological variation, and difficulty distinguishing loci affecting kidney function from those influencing biomarker metabolism. This study explores the genetic architecture of imaging-derived kidney volumes as alternative markers of kidney function.
Method
We utilized the two-point Dixon sequence from abdominal MRIs of 38,816 UK Biobank (UKB) participants of European ancestry. Kidney compartment volumes (total kidney volume (TKV), cortex, medulla, and sinus volumes) were derived from automatically segmented kidney images using Patchwork, which uses a convolutional neural network to train ground truth data established by experienced radiologists. The volumes were normalized to body surface area and an inverse normal transformation of ranks was applied. GWAS was based on imputed UKB genotypes (allele frequency > 1%) and was performed using linear regression as implemented in the regenie software (v3.2.9). Analyses were adjusted for age, age-squared, sex, assessment centre, and the first 10 genetic principal components. We conducted a parallel eGFR GWAS for the same population and calculated genetic effect size correlations between the index SNPs for kidney volumes and eGFR. Causal genes for each locus were prioritized using a developed annotation pipeline incorporating gene proximity, Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor, genetic colocalization with cis-expression and -protein quantitative trait loci (QTL), and linkage disequilibrium. We assessed locus overlap between volumes, marker-based kidney function, and clinical traits using colocalization analyses (genepicoloc package), performed gene enrichment analysis to identify tissue-specific (GTEx v8) and renal cell type-specific (KPMP) gene expression patterns, and Gene Ontology enriched terms. Associations with renal outcomes were evaluated using results from the AstraZeneca PheWAS Portal, a platform that provides phenome-wide association study data derived from UKB exome sequencing.
Results
GWAS identified 34 significant loci for TKV, 24 for medulla, 26 for cortex, and 71 for sinus volumes (P-value < 5e-8). Pairwise colocalization analysis identified nine loci specific to the medulla and 66 to the sinus (probability of colocalization > 0.8). We observed strong correlations between genetic effect sizes of eGFR GWAS and kidney volumes for TKV (r = 0.89), cortex (r = 0.86), and medulla (r = 0.82), but a lower correlation with sinus (r = 0.37).
Enrichment analyses highlighted that genes associated with cortex volume were highly expressed in the kidney cortex, while sinus volume genes were predominantly expressed in adipose and vascular tissues, supported by cell type-specific overrepresentation analyses. Gene Ontology enrichment showed that TKV and cortex genes are involved in renal development, while medulla genes are involved in hypoxia-related processes.
Additionally, colocalization analysis identified 94 shared genetic signals between kidney volumes and traditional kidney function traits, supporting a shared genetic basis. The eGFR-decreasing G allele at rs77924615 (UMOD) was also associated with lower TKV (P-value = 1.5e-21). At the same time, many kidney volume-associated loci established in this study were not previously linked to traditional markers even in large GWAS meta-analyses. Moreover, we found evidence for a shared genetic basis between kidney volumes and hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, diabetes. By mining the AstraZeneca PheWAS Portal we found links between the rare, loss-of-function variants in prioritized genes (e.g., UMOD, SLC22A7) and renal outcomes: chronic kidney disease stages and kidney function markers.
Conclusion
This study reveals novel genetic determinants of kidney structure unreported in previous biomarker-based studies, providing insights into the genetic architecture of kidney structure and its relationship with renal function.

title: #2318 A novel cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome mouse model with inducible HFrEF and atherosclerosis
authors: Arianne van Koppen; Anke Smits; Tri Nguyen; Amélie Dendooven; Ingeborg Bajema; Harry van Goor; Toon van Veen; Willem van Ham; Elsbet Pieterman; Aswin Menke; Hans Princen; Reinout Stoop
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiovascular damage is the major cause of death in chronic kidney disease (CKD). Our institute developed a diet-induced cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome model including obesity, diabetes, hypertension, CKD and HFpEF. To further induce dyslipidemia and CVD, we studied the effects of a recombinant adeno-associated viral vector expressing the gain-of-function mutation of mouse proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (AAV8-D377Y-mPCSK9) on plasma cholesterol, atherosclerosis and cardiac function and pathology.
Method
Male KK-Ay mice, that develop hyperglycemia, hyperinsulinemia, glucose intolerance and obesity at a young age, underwent uninephrectomy (UNx). After recovery, mice received a high fat diet (HFD) with or without the vasoconstrictor L-NNA (50 mg/L) in their drinking water for 13–14 weeks. Half of the mice of either group received an intravenous injection of AAV8-D377Y-mPCSK9 (gain of function mutation mPCSK9) leading to reduced liver LDL receptor levels and high levels of circulating cholesterol, and an increased susceptibility to atherosclerosis development. At week 13, a subset of mice underwent cardiac imaging. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) was measured using a transdermal measurement system. title: #2867 Albuminuria A3 in a central district of Madrid: current situation
authors: Cristina Riaza Ortiz; Clara Garcia Carro; Marina Pujol Pujol; Beatriz Izquierdo Alarcón; Raquel Ramos Corral; Mercedes Martínez-Novillo González; Ana Isabel Sánchez Fructuoso
abstract:
Background and Aims
Albuminuria is a known biomarker of chronic kidney disease progression. Elevated urinary albumin excretion is also associated with increased cardiovascular risk (coronary disease, heart failure, stroke, and peripheral artery disease), as well as increased risk of cancer and all-cause mortality. Diagnosing albuminuria is essential to establish therapeutic strategies aimed at its reduction. However, screening for albuminuria is still low, as does the use of new therapeutic agents for its reduction.
The aim of this study was to determine the incidence of A3 albuminuria (>300 mg/g creatinine) in a cohort of patients from a central district in Madrid who underwent urine analysis requested by Primary Care physicians between January 2024 and October 2024. Additionally, the study aimed to describe the clinical characteristics of these patients, identify the causes of albuminuria, assess referral rates to Nephrology, and evaluate the use of antiproteinuric drugs.
Method
A retrospective single-center study including all patients within the service area of San Carlos Clinical University Hospital (central Madrid, serving 357,000 residents) who underwent urine analysis requested by Primary Care physicians between January and October 2024. Albuminuria was classified according to KDIGO staging criteria.
Results
During the study period, 34.902 patients underwent urine analysis, of whom 450 (1.29%) presented A3 albuminuria. The mean age of the cohort was 73 years, and 58% were male. More than half had diabetes (58.2%), and the majority (81.5%) presented hypertension. Additionally, 6.9% of patients were obese, and 8.2% had a history of cancer. Only 2% had a solitary kidney, 21.8% had hematuria of 5–10 RBC, 23.78% had a urological condition, and 17.5% had suspected urinary tract infections. The mean albuminuria was 643 mg/g and the mean serum creatinine was 1.15 mg/dL.
Remarkably, only 144 patients (32%) were being followed by a Nephrologist, despite Spanish Nephrology and Primary Care guidelines recommending Nephrology referral for patients with albuminuria >300 mg/g. In contrast, 139 patients (31%) were managed by Primary Care and 167 patients (37%) were followed up by other specialties. Patients antiproteinuric treatments are summarized in Fig. 1.
Patients under Nephrology care were younger (69.6 ± 16.5 vs 75.1 ± 14.6 years, P = 0.0004), had lower eGFR (63.2% vs 42.8% eGFR <60 ml/min, P < 0.0001), and exhibited higher levels of albuminuria (43.7% vs 23.2% albuminuria ≥ 1000 mg/g, P < 0.0001) compared with patients not followed by nephrologists. Conversely, patients with albuminuria <500 mg/g were less likely to be referred to Nephrology (P < 0.0001). Baseline characteristics did not differ significantly between groups (Table 1)
Notably, lack of follow-up by Nephrology was associated with a lower prescription rate of antiproteinuric medications. Among patients not managed by Nephrology, 18.6% lacked antiproteinuric therapy vs 8% under Nephrology follow-up (P = 0.0047). There was a significant difference in the use of SGLT2 inhibitors (iSGLT2) and aldosterone receptor modulators (ARM) between specialties: only 38.9% of patients not followed by Nephrology were prescribed iSGLT2 (vs 54.1% in patients followed by nephrologists, P = 0.0023), and only 6% were prescribed ARM compared to 12% among those followed by Nephrology (P = 0.0234).
Conclusion
Albuminuria is a critical cardiovascular risk factor that is often under recognized and undertreated by physicians. Over a 10-month period, we identified 450 patients with A3 albuminuria who underwent urine analysis requested by Primary care physicians. The majority of them were not referred to Nephrology (68%). Additionally, patients managed by Primary Care or other specialties were less likely to receive iSGLT2 and ARMs.
Our findings highlight the need for increased awareness among physicians and the general population regarding the clinical significance of albuminuria. Greater efforts are required to ensure appropriate referral of patients with A3 albuminuria to Nephrology and to emphasize the early use of antiproteinuric therapies to mitigate disease progression and associated risks.

title: #128 Aryl hydrocarbon receptor promotes renal fibrosis via accelerating cell senescence in tubular epithelial cells
authors: Qian Ren; Hui Li; Liang MA; Ping Fu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) has a high prevalence worldwide and tubulointerstitial fibrosis is considered the final convergent pathway of progressive CKD regardless of etiology. However, mechanisms underlying kidney injury-induced fibrosis largely remain unknown. The aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) is a well-known ligand-activated cytoplasmic transcription factor that contributes to cellular responses against environmental toxins and carcinogens. AhR activity is strongly implicated throughout the course of CKD but its certain role and underlying mechanism remains unknown.
Method
AhR expression was examined in the kidney specimens of CKD patients as well as in the kidneys of mouse models with experimental kidney fibrosis (unilateral ureteral obstruction [UUO], adenine nephropathy [Aden], and aristolochic acid-induced nephrotoxicity [AA]). The potential role of AhR in renal fibrosis was further validated by AhR conditional knock out in mice or AhR siRNA in TCMK-1 cells. ATAC-seq combined with RNA-seq was employed to explore the underlying mechanisms.
Results
Increased AhR expression was observed in the kidneys of both CKD patients of various etiology and three mouse models with kidney fibrosis. The elevated AhR expression was mainly located within tubular cells and was associated with the levels of Scr and eGFR in CKD patients. Tubule-specific knock out of AhR in mice alleviated UUO- and Aden-induced renal fibrosis. Mechanistically, in tubular epithelial cells, AhR exerted a profibrotic role via a NF-κB-dependent signaling. AhR promoted the activation of NF-κB by regulating the transcription of IκBα and thus accelerating tubular senescence. Pharmacological inhibition of AhR ameliorated tubular senescence and renal fibrosis in both animal models and TCMK-1 cells.
Conclusion
Tubular AhR plays an important role in kidney fibrosis by suppressing profibrotic NF-κB signaling. Hence, our findings suggest that modulating the activity of tubular AhR may be a new therapeutic option for treating tubulointerstitial fibrosis and subsequent CKD.

title: #1817 An application of urinary peptidomics and in silico methods to guide multifactorial intervention in chronic kidney disease
authors: Agnieszka Latosinska; Felix Keller; Gert Mayer; Peter Rossing; Christian Delles; Joachim Beige; Antonia Vlahou; Karlheinz Peter; Ivan Rychlik; Alberto Ortiz; Harald Rupprecht; Justyna Siwy
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) significantly contributes to global morbidity and mortality. Early, targeted, and personalized interventions offer an ideal strategy for mitigating this burden. Peptidomic changes inform on CKD onset and progression and hold valuable insights for optimized treatment and prevention strategies. We in silico investigated the molecular effects of six different therapeutic interventions in all possible combinations on the urine peptidome, with the aim of identifying the most beneficial treatment strategies for individual patient.
Method
This study assessed the prediction of major adverse kidney events (MAKE), defined as a ≥40% decline in eGFR or kidney failure, using the urinary peptidomic classifier CKD273 in a retrospective cohort of 935 participants. The impact of various treatments on urinary peptidomic profiles, assessed from previous studies for four different drug-based interventions (MRA, SGLT2i, GLP1 receptor agonist and ARB), one dietary intervention (olive oil) or from exercise, was applied. Treatment effects were quantified through fold changes in peptide abundance, calculated by dividing the average peptide abundance after treatment by the average peptide abundance before treatment (representing a result of the intervention), recalibrated to align with outcomes observed in randomized controlled trials. Using an in silico approach, the recalibrated fold changes were applied to patient-specific urinary profiles, allowing simulation of intervention effects and recalculation of CKD273 scores for each individual. For combination treatments, the effects of multiple interventions were integrated multiplicatively to model their cumulative impact on peptide abundances.
Results
Simulated interventions demonstrated a significant reduction in median CKD273 scores when the most beneficial treatment or combination of treatments was applied to each patient. Median CKD273 scores decreased from 0.57 (IQR: 0.19–0.81) before intervention to 0.039 (IQR: -0.192–0.363) after intervention (paired Wilcoxon test, P < 0.0001). A marked shift in score distribution toward negative values was observed, indicating potential improvements in kidney health.
The combination of all available treatments was not the most frequently predicted optimal intervention. Instead, specific combinations, such as MRA + Exercise + GLP1 receptor agonist + SGLT2i + ARB or MRA + Exercise + GLP1 receptor agonist + SGLT2i + ARB + olive oil or MRA + SGLT2i + ARB were much more commonly predicted as optimal interventions compared to single or double interventions. Patients with higher baseline CKD273 scores—indicating greater initial risk—required more complex intervention combinations to achieve the greatest reduction in scores. This finding highlights the importance of individualized treatment strategies in CKD management.
Conclusion
This study demonstrates the utility of in silico proteomic analysis for predicting the effects of therapeutic interventions on CKD progression. By identifying the most beneficial treatment combinations for individual patients, this approach paves the way for precision medicine in CKD care. These findings warrant further validation in prospective clinical trials to confirm the clinical utility of this approach and its ability to guide patient-specific therapeutic strategies.

title: #1792 Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitor utilization and hyperkalemia in patients with chronic kidney disease – results from ZORA China
authors: Sheng Nie; Qing Zou; Shiyu Zhou; Eva Lesén; Lovisa Friberg; Shaosen Zhang; Wenyan Zhao; Yifan Shi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors (RAASi) are a cornerstone of chronic kidney disease (CKD) management, but they can also increase the risk of hyperkalemia (HK). RAASi reduction or discontinuation is common following the occurrence of HK. However, suboptimal use of RAASi is detrimental to renal and cardiovascular outcomes, and recent guidelines recommend using novel potassium binders (PB) to manage HK rather than reducing RAASi. To address the evidence gap in RAASi utilization and HK management in Chinese patients, this study assessed RAASi treatment patterns and the occurrence and management of HK among patients with stage 3–5 CKD in real-world clinical settings.
Method
This observational cohort study utilized real-world medical data between Jan 1, 2018 and Jan 1, 2023 from 24 tertiary hospitals in the China Renal Data System. This analysis included two cohorts: the CKD cohort included adult patients with prevalent stage 3–5 CKD (based on estimated glomerular filtration rate) as of Jan 1, 2022 (the index date for this cohort). The HK cohort included adult patients with prevalent stage 3–5 CKD who experienced HK (indexed at the date of the first HK event). All patients were required to have ≥12 months of available data prior to their respective index dates and were followed for up to 12 months. The primary outcomes were (1) the proportion of patients in the CKD cohort with hospital-issued RAASi prescription(s) within 90 days prior to or at index (baseline), among patients with any recorded prescriptions during the baseline period; (2) the 12-month prevalence of HK (>5.0 mmol/L) during the post-index follow-up in the CKD cohort; and (3) the 12-month cumulative risk of HK recurrence (by Kaplan-Meier analysis) among HK cohort patients with baseline hospital-issued RAASi prescription(s). The secondary endpoint was the proportion of HK events followed by a PB prescription within 10 days, in the HK cohort.
Results
A total of 25,604 eligible patients were included in the CKD cohort. Their mean age was 65.6 years (SD: 16.1) and 57.1% were male. Among the 7,310 patients with any hospital-issued prescription at baseline, 2,605 (35.6%) had ≥1 hospital-issued RAASi prescription. This proportion decreased with increasing CKD severity (stage 3: 39.8%, stage 4: 33.6%, stage 5: 15.9%) (Fig. 1). The most common RAASi class was angiotensin receptor blockers (N = 2,035, 27.8%), followed by mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (N = 753, 10.3%). During the 12-month post-index follow-up, 16.6% (N = 4,260) of the CKD cohort experienced ≥1 HK event; the majority of (83.7%) their first HK events were mild (>5.0–≤5.9 mmol/L), 8.8% were moderate (6.0–≤6.4 mmol/L), and 5.4% were severe (≥6.5 mmol/L). The 12-month prevalence of HK, stratified by CKD stage, was somewhat higher in patients with hospital-issued RAASi prescription(s) at baseline than those without hospital-issued RAASi (stage 3: 12.7% vs. 11.0%, stage 4: 32.6% vs. 27.3%, stage 5: 36.3% vs. 28.2%) (Fig. 2). The HK cohort included 27,481 patients. Their mean age was 67.1 years (SD: 16.2), and 57.1% were male. The index HK event was mild for most patients (84.0%), moderate for 8.7% and severe for 6.8%. Among HK cohort patients with hospital-issued RAASi prescription(s) at baseline, the 12-month cumulative risk of recurrent HK was 48.3% (95% CI 46.8–49.7). This increased with CKD stage (stage 3: 41.5% [39.7–43.3], stage 4: 55.5% [52.5–58.2], stage 5: 62.4% [58.6–65.9]). Of the 82,691 HK events recorded in the HK cohort (including index events and those during the follow-up), 3,272 (4.0%) were followed by a hospital-issued PB prescription within 10 days.
Conclusion
ZORA China investigated the use of RAASi and the occurrence and management of HK among Chinese patients with stage 3–5 CKD in real-world clinical practice. Our results demonstrate that RAASi treatment is often suboptimal, and HK is frequent and with a substantial risk of recurrence, which increases with CKD stage. These findings, together with the low PB prescription rate after HK, signal a need for improved management of CKD and HK in line with current guideline recommendations.

title: #2554 Modulating ER-mitochondrial crosstalk with kunkuibaoshen granules: a novel strategy to combat renal fibrosis in CKD
authors: Weilong Xu; Peipei Zhou; Zihui Liu; Ying Tan; Chuchu Shan; Yu Xu; Xiqiao Zhou; Akinobu Ochi; Jiangyi Yu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a progressive condition marked by renal fibrosis and impaired kidney function. Emerging evidence highlights the critical role of organelle interactions, particularly between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria, in maintaining cellular homeostasis and influencing CKD progression. Disruptions in ER-mitochondrial crosstalk impair calcium signaling, exacerbate oxidative stress, and compromise metabolic processes such as fatty acid oxidation (FAO), all of which drive renal fibrosis.
Kunkuibaoshen Granules (KKG), a traditional herbal formulation composed of Abelmoschus manihot flower, Lobelia chinensis root, Astragalus membranaceus, and processed Cornus officinalis, contains active components such as epicatechin, hyperoside, isoquercitrin, and gossypetin-8-O-glucuronide, etc. These bioactive compounds are hypothesized to modulate ER-mitochondrial interactions, restore cellular homeostasis, and mitigate CKD-associated fibrosis. This study aims to investigate KKG's therapeutic potential in targeting organelle crosstalk to alleviate renal fibrosis in CKD models, offering a novel treatment approach.
Method
A unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO) mouse model was employed to evaluate KKG's effects on lipid metabolism and ER-mitochondria interactions. Mice were treated with KKG at doses of 5, 10, and 20 g/kg/day. Transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses identified potential targets, including ACAT1 and relevant lipid metabolic pathways. Biochemical and histological analyses assessed kidney function and fibrosis. Molecular docking and surface plasmon resonance confirmed interactions between KKG's active components and key metabolic proteins (ACAT1 and SCD1). Organelle interactions were evaluated using mito-DsRed and Sec61β-GFP imaging, super-resolution microscopy, and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). These approaches provided structural and functional insights into KKG's effects on ER-mitochondria coupling.
Results
KKG significantly improved renal outcomes in the UUO model, reducing fibrosis and enhancing mitochondrial function. The active components, including epicatechin, hyperoside, isoquercitrin, and gossypetin-8-O-glucuronide, facilitated increased ER-mitochondrial contact and calcium signaling, restoring FAO and mitochondrial respiration. Biochemical analyses showed decreased fibrotic markers and improved lipid metabolism in kidney tissues. Molecular docking and surface plasmon resonance validated the binding of KKG components to ACAT1 and SCD1. Imaging studies revealed enhanced ER-mitochondria interactions, with TEM confirming improved structural coupling. title: #931 Evaluating the impact of AI-driven interventions on hospital admissions in end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) patients using medicare and EMR data
authors: Sheetal Chaudhuri; Joanna Willetts; Tina Chen; Susan Marsh; Hao Han; Angela Adams; Adriana Lindsey; Greg Garza; Len Usvyat
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) have a high rate of hospitalizations related to fluid overload and infections. AI-powered machine learning models can optimize patient care by predicting hospitalization risk. We implemented a case review intervention for patients at-risk for hospitalization within 7 days, as identified by the imminent hospitalization AI-based prediction algorithm (IHPM). IHPM is a machine learning algorithm with 1424 input variables from the electronic medical record (EMR) system, including treatment data, laboratory values, treatment and clinical notes, hospitalizations, and absences from dialysis appointments. We aimed to assess the effect of the machine-learning-directed case review intervention on odds of hospitalization for patients using the data from EMR and Medicare claims.
Method
We conducted a retrospective, observational, matched cohort study of adult patients with ESKD who were receiving value-based kidney care from one of the 1,786 integrated kidney care clinics across the United States in 2023. A machine learning model calculated risk scores and identified patients with a risk score of >0.64 who were at risk for imminent hospitalization within 7 days related to infection or fluid status abnormalities. To prevent avoidable hospitalizations, case reviews were conducted on patients identified by the model. For comparison, each risk score triggering a case review was matched to five risk scores that did not result in a case review. We linked EMR with Medicare claims data and conducted multivariate logistic regression analyses to examine the impact of machine learning-directed case reviews on the odds of hospitalization in patients with ESKD. An exploratory analysis evaluated odds of hospitalization for patients with risk scores between 0.64 and 0.85, excluding patients with risk scores >0.85.
Results
10,294 patients and 83,928 risk scores were included in the analysis. Machine learning-directed case review was associated with an 8% reduction in odds of hospitalization within 7 days (OR = 0.92, P = 0.025). These case reviews were most effective at reducing hospitalizations for high-risk patients with a risk score between 0.64–0.85 but did not impact hospitalizations for the highest risk patients with scores >0.85 (Table 1). In an exploratory analysis in which the highest risk score population (>0.85) was removed from the analysis set (Table 2), patients with a risk score of >0.64–0.85 who received a case review had a 12% decrease in the odds of being hospitalized (OR = 0.88, P = 0.003) compared to patients with no case review.
Conclusion
AI-directed interventions were associated with a reduction in the odds of hospitalization among patients with ESKD receiving managed kidney care. This reduction was more pronounced when excluding the highest-risk score group, suggesting that case review may be more effective in patients with risk scores between 0.64 and 0.85. These findings underscore AI's potential to assist healthcare providers in targeted risk interventions for patients with ESKD.

title: #3676 Size-selective glomerular filtration is a hallmark of premature kidney ageing
authors: Agne Laucyte-Cibulskiene; Christopher Lars Inge Nilsson; Amra Jujic; Hannes Holm; Anders Christensson
abstract:
Background and Aims
Size-selective glomerular filtration, recently determined as Selective Glomerular Hypofiltration Syndromes (SGHS) and expressed as ratio between cystatin C and creatinine-based glomerular filtration, is less prevalent among younger individuals. The role SGHS plays in natural ageing has not been researched. We hypothesize that SGHS may be a marker of premature kidney ageing, and therefore the interaction between skin autofluorescence acquired advanced end-glycation products (AGEs), endothelial function, and size-selective kidney filtration in a population without pronounced chronic kidney disease and diabetes was analyzed.
Method
3 804 participants of The Malmö Offspring Study (MOS), mean age 42(+/-15) years, 51% women, with data on skin autofluorescence and eGFR measurements based on cystatin C and creatinine (eGFRcys and eGFRcr) were selected. 2 204 of them underwent additional evaluation of reactive hyperemia index (RHI); RHI <1.67 presented endothelial dysfunction (ED) and values > = 1.67 – normal endothelial function. Endothelial pseudodysfunction was also addressed. A sex-disaggregated analysis was performed at all study steps.
Results
A decline in eGFRcys/eGFRcr ratio followed by an increase in AGEs and increase in RHI was observed in both men and women but progressed more rapidly in women (Fig. 1). After adjusting for cardiovascular factors, the lower eGFRcys/eGFRcr ratio was associated with higher AGE levels in men older than 30. A combination of ED and increased AGEs determined that individuals, similar to those with endothelial pseudo-dysfunction and normal values of AGEs, had the highest eGFRcys/eGFRcr ratio.
Conclusion
To conclude, skin autofluorescence indirectly reflects the selective filtration of molecules in the kidneys, even in the absence of diabetes and advanced CKD. Hence, the SGHS might be a pattern of accelerated kidney ageing. The addition of RHI for understanding cardiovascular and kidney interaction is controversial, possibly affected by vascular tone in younger individuals and different timing in cardiovascular and kidney ageing.

title: #2879 Real-world performance of two mortality scores designed for elderly patients with advanced CKD
authors: Aya Moultamis; Paula Ardura; Teresa Ronda Serrat; Kenia Cobo Campuzano; Ivan Corrales Selaya; Juan Abel Iglesias Pascual; Sandra Sanz-Ballesteros; Henar Santana Zapatero; Paula Martín Escuer; Maria Isabel Acosta-Ochoa; Armando Coca Rojo
abstract:
Background and Aims
The choice between renal replacement therapy or conservative management of end-stage renal disease is complex in the elderly, due to the high prevalence of associated comorbidities, frailty, loss of quality of life and high mortality rate. This decision is especially relevant in particularly aged geographic areas. Several scores have been developed to help the decision of dialysis start among elderly patients, although they tend to lack generalizability as they are usually developed in widely different populations. In the present study we aim to compare two different prognostic scores in a sample of CKD stage 4 and 5 elderly patients from our area.
Method
We retrospectively identified all consecutive CKD stage 4 or 5 patients aged ≥70 years, reviewed at our outpatient clinic during a six-month period. Two different prognostic scores (1, 2) were applied at the first visit in which options for renal replacement therapy were discussed with the patient, including conservative management. Need for renal replacement therapy initiation and patient survival during the following 5 years after the visit were recorded.
The scores are summarized in Table 1. Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics 26.
Results
Demographic and clinical characteristics of the study sample are summarized in Table 2. When predicting 6-month mortality, both scores showed an area under the ROC curve of 0.705 (Fig. 1A). The area under the ROC curve decreased for both scores when predicting 5-year mortality (AUC: 0.688 and 0.679 for the Santos J and Wick JP scores, respectively) (Fig. 1B). No survival analysis was performed at the 6-month mark due to the low number of events. Moreover, in Kaplan-Meier analysis, both scores, analyzed as tertiles, were associated with 5-year patient survival (Santos J: Log-Rank: 11.511; P = 0.003; Wick JP: Log-Rank: 11.061; P = 0.004) (Fig. 2C and 2D).
Conclusion
Although a higher result was associated with lower 5-year survival in both scores, they showed poor discrimination of 6-month and 5-year mortality in our study sample to be considered as part of our daily clinical routine. These results highlight the current need to develop predictive models accurate enough to help both patients and physicians in the decision-making progress of when and if to start dialysis.

title: #926 Risk of end-stage kidney disease, death and suicide attempts in men and women with migraine treated with topiramate
authors: Jean Michel Halimi; Valentin Maisons; Jean-Baptiste de Fréminville; Sébastien Roger; Arnaud Bisson; Stéphanie Chadet; Laurent Fauchier
abstract:
Background and Aims
Topiramate is widely used for migraine prevention but has pleiotropic effects, including on renal sodium reabsorption and inflammation. Whether these effects could be associated with lower risk of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) is unknown.
Method
Among 1,745,580 patients with a diagnosis of migraine, the risk of ESKD, death and major outcomes was assessed after propensity matching in patients treated with topiramate vs untreated patients.
Results
Overall, 291,728 patients treated by topiramate were properly matched to 291,728 controls for age (43 years old), sex (women: 86%), body mass index, blood pressure, race, ethnicity, cardiovascular comorbidities, kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, cancer, depression, anxiety and mood disorders, lipids, estimated glomerular filtration rate, albuminuria and baseline medications used. After a median follow-up of 3.5 years, both men and women receiving topiramate had a significant lower risk of ESKD (HR: 0.742 [95% confidence intervals: 0.670–0.824]). They also had a lower risk of death (HR: 0.827 [: 0.799–0.856]), cardiac arrest or ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation (HR: 0.944 [0.898–0.992]) and but a higher risk of ischemic stroke or thromboembolism (HR: 1.366 [1.318–1.416]) than the other patients. In women only, topiramate was associated with a higher risk of suicide attempts (HR: 1.734 [1.541–1.950]).
Conclusion
In men and women with migraine, topiramate was significantly associated with lower risks of ESKD and death, higher risks of ischemic stroke/thromboembolism, and a higher risk of suicide attempts in women.

title: 3608 #BloodyAmazingKidneys - A national awareness campaign to alert the general public about the risks of CKD
authors: Laurie Cuthbert
abstract:
Raising awareness of the risks of Chronic Kidney Disease
Laurie Cuthbert, Kidney Care UK, UK
Background and Aims
1 million people live with chronic kidney disease (CKD) in the UK and don't know they have it. Without action, CKD will be the fifth largest killer worldwide by 2040. By identifying people with CKD earlier, more can be done to prolong kidney health.
Kidney Care UK (KCUK) launched a new #BloodyAmazingKidneys campaign to raise awareness of kidney disease and empower people to manage their kidney health by urging people to check their risk of CKD via the Kidney Health Checker.
Participants were informed of their ‘lower’ or ‘higher’ risk of CKD. Those at lower risk were asked to share the Checker, complete the Checker in 1 year, and discuss their kidney health at their next GP appointment. Those at higher risk were encouraged to see their GP. They could download a results letter for their GP and were offered a CKD guide.
Key objectives:
110,000 completions of the Kidney Health Checker within 12 months
Increased public awareness of kidney health
Increased engagement with KCUK
Earlier diagnosis of CKD and improved support to manage kidney health
Increased understanding of whether awareness campaigns could change behaviour
Method
A 5-week national campaign aimed at those most at risk of CKD
Targeted digital adverts alongside media stories, case studies and social media
Posters in washrooms of selected UK shopping centres and service stations
Message testing with cold target audiences and refined with focus groups
YouGov-commissioned research establishing public awareness of the signs of kidney failure
Campaign assets and Kidney Health Checker developed based on feedback and reviewed by clinical experts
Results
2 million KCUK webpage views, including 300,000 unique visitors to the Checker
>110,000 Checker completions 16 October–15 November 2024
55,518 (∼50%) at higher risk and 55,482 (∼50%) at lower risk
Primary risk factor: high blood pressure; secondary risk factor: NSAID use
60% participants over 60 years of age
2% participants underweight; 32% healthy weight; 36% overweight; 31% obese
1,515 sign-ups for information from KCUK (468 for CKD guide; 1,047 to complete the Checker in 12 months)
130+ pieces of media coverage
Significant engagement with social content (+870k animation views)
1,050 poster scans via QR codes
Conclusion
As the first national awareness campaign run by KCUK, the response exceeded expectations. 110,000 completions of the Kidney Health Checker were received in the first month, compared to a target of 10,000 for that period.
Campaign assets were designed to nudge people to consider their risk and compel to action, but not intimidate. KCUK requested consent to follow-up with participants. Next steps will be to understand if respondents have contacted their GP, are waiting for an appointment, have been tested or are waiting results. A small number have already confirmed they have received a CKD diagnosis. KCUK anticipates an increase in responses in early 2025.
KCUK had not anticipated so many supporters and stakeholders across the NHS would proactively share the campaign through posters in local spaces. Hundreds of medical practices have shared the campaign on social media and with their patients.
The success of the #BloodyAmazingKidneys campaign shows an appetite both within the general population and the NHS to raise awareness of the importance of kidney health.
This campaign was funded as part of a Partnership Framework Agreement with AstraZeneca UK; AstraZeneca had no creative or editorial control over the campaign content, other than a review of medical accuracy. The campaign is owned entirely by Kidney Care UK.

title: #1676 Association between furosemide and serum uremic toxins levels in patients with chronic kidney disease
authors: Margaux Costes-Albrespic; Natalia Alencar de Pinho; Islam Amine Larabi; Solene Laville; Christian Jacquelinet; Christian Combe; Denis Fouque; Maurice Laville; Luc Frimat; Jean-Claude Alvarez; Ziad Massy; Sophie Liabeuf
abstract:
Background and Aims
Furosemide is commonly prescribed to patients with CKD but may impair the kidney's excretion of uraemic toxins (UTs) via the organic anion transporters 1 and 3 (OAT1/OAT3). We evaluated the association between furosemide prescription (status and dose) and free serum levels of OAT1/3-inhibiting UTs in patients with CKD.
Method
We included 2,342 patients with CKD (stages 2–5) from the CKD-REIN cohort and with centralized serum UT assay data at baseline. The UT levels were measured using liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry. Furosemide prescriptions from any medical doctor were collected by clinical research associates based on the anatomical therapeutic chemical (ATC) code (ATC C03CA01), as were patients’ demographic, clinical, and laboratory characteristics. The OAT1/3-inhibiting UTs identified in a literature review included indoxyl sulphate (IS), kynurenine (Kyn), p-cresyl sulphate (PCS), and indole-3-acetic acid (IAA). Multiple linear regression was used to assess fractions of each UT or their sum (ΣUTsfree) as the dependent variable.
Results
Patients prescribed furosemide (n = 799, 34%) were older and had a lower estimated glomerular filtration (eGFR) rate, a higher C-reactive protein level, more comorbidities (cardiovascular (CV) disease, diabetes, acute kidney injury (AKI) history), and more co-prescribed medications than patients not prescribed furosemide. After adjustment for age, sex, the total number of co-prescribed medications, the number of potential OAT1/3 inhibitor drugs, history of AKI and CV disease, serum CRP and albumin levels, diabetes, body mass index, smoking status, urine albumin-creatinine ratio, and eGFR, furosemide prescription was positively associated with ΣUTsfree (+7.0%) and free levels of UTs, Kyn (+5.9%), and PCS (+14.3%). Patients prescribed >120 mg furosemide had significantly higher serum levels of ΣUTsfree (+19.1%), IS (+31.9%), Kyn (+9.3%), PCS (+29.3%) and IAA (+16.9%) than patients not prescribed furosemide.
Conclusion
In patients with CKD, furosemide (particularly at doses >120 mg) is independently associated with higher free serum UT levels. Our findings suggested that drug-UT competition contributes to UT accumulation.
Submission supported by / on behalf of: CKD-REIN study group

title: #3376 The SPIRIT study : A multicenter prospective observational study of patients with CKD to assess therapeutic algorithms,disease management and quality of life in Greece

abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) affects approximately 8-16% of the population worldwide and constitutes an ever-increasing socioeconomic burden. The main purpose of the study is to record the treatment algorithms and disease management of patients presenting for the first time to hospital-based nephrologists with reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and CKD diagnosis, under real-world clinical practice in Greece.
Methods
This is the 6-months interim analysis of an ongoing, multicenter, observational, prospective, national study which included patients with eGFR levels between 15 and 60 ml/min/1,73 m2, presenting for the first time to nephrologists at 15 public hospital units.
Results

Conclusion
The interim analysis results contributed to the collection of real-world data for the therapeutic patterns and the management of CKD in Greece and highlighted the need for wider usage of medications with proven efficacy in this special group of patients (such as SGLT2i), who can mostly profit from their beneficial effects.

title: #3613 Hemostasis abnormalities in patients across different stages of chronic kidney disease, after evaluating a wide spectrum of coagulation parameters
authors: Emelina Stambolliu; Panagiota Giannou; Maria-Panagiota Terzi; Efthimia Pavlou; Elpiniki Stathopoulou; Athanasios Papras; Efrosyni Nomikou; Margarita Bora; Anastasia Politi; Aglaia Chalkia; Dimitrios Petras
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and especially those with end stage renal disease (ESRD) are considered to be prone to both bleeding and thrombosis and a steady state is not easily achieved. The purpose of the present study is to evaluate specific hemostasis parameters and investigate any differentiations in the coagulation process in patients with CKD across different stages.
Method
This is a cross-sectional study that was conducted at the Nephrology Department of a tertiary hospital. Patients over 18 years old with CKD stages 2,3,4,5 (non-dialysis-dependent) and with ESRD on hemodialysis (HD) and peritoneal dialysis (PD) were included in the study. Standard biochemical and coagulation laboratory tests were performed in addition to thromboelastography with platelet mapping tests (TEG-6s), platelet function assay (PFA), proteins of coagulation, fibrinolytic and inhibitory system tests and homocysteine.
Results
120 patients (20 patients in each of 6 different groups) were included in the analysis (mean age 65.6 ± 14.3 years, 75% males). In all coagulation tests performed statistically significant differences were found between groups of CKD stage 2 and 5 (all P < 0.05). Across the different stages, significant differences were found for D-Dimers, FVIII, Protein C, PFA-EPI, PFA-ADP, Antithrombin III, homocysteine, fibrinogen, ristocetin cofactor (RICoF), a PTT, red blood cells (RBC), hemoglobulin (HGB) and TEG parameters (maximal amplitude [MA], R time and K time, Angle, Lysis30) (all P < 0.05). Specifically, FVIII showed very significant differences among the different groups, augmenting with CKD progression. Between groups of CKD stage 2 and 3, significant differences were found in D-Dimers, von Willebrand factor (vWF), RICoF and TEG parameters (MA and K) (all P < 0.05). Moreover, the PD group showed significant differences from CKD stages 2–4 concerning FVIII, RICoF, fibrinogen, homocysteine, aPTT, RBC, HGB (all P < 0.05). Additionally, PD and HD groups had significant differences in FVIII, Antithrombin III, PFA-EPI, PFA-ADP, and TEG parameters (MA, K, Angle) (all P < 0.05). Finally, eGFR was associated (Spearman correlations) with Protein C (ρ = 0.26), vWF (ρ = −0.34), RICoF (ρ = −0.35), INR (ρ = −0.32), aPTT (ρ = −0.4), D-Dimers (ρ = −0.4), homocysteine (ρ = −0.617), FVIII (ρ = −0.575) and TEG parameters [Κ (ρ = 0.48), ADP-MA (ρ = −0.3), AA-MA (ρ = 0.3)] (all P < 0.05).
Conclusion
As depicted, CKD progress affects TEG parameters, platelets assays and most hemostasis examinations, especially FVIII, which creates a prothrombotic profile. Hence, even patients at earlier stages of CKD are in danger of thrombotic complications. Moreover, there are important differences in coagulation parameters between HD and PD patients.

title: #1498 The role of trimethylamine N-oxide in chronic kidney disease progression and mortality: insights from the GCKD study
authors: Arne Thiele; Heike Meiselbach; Markus Schneider; Barbara Bärthlein; Matthias Schmid; Wolfram Gronwald; Peter Oefner; Peggy Sekula; Anna Köttgen; Turgay Saritas; Kai-Uwe Eckardt; Nicola Wilck
abstract:
Background and Aims
Trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) is a gut microbial metabolite derived from dietary phosphatidylcholine and carnitine. Recently, we have shown that TMAO accumulates in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), not only due to impaired kidney clearance, but also due to altered microbial production. Increasing evidence points to TMAO as an emerging contributor to cardiovascular disease. However, the prognostic impact of TMAO on adverse kidney outcomes in patients with established CKD remains unclear. Thus, the aim of this study was to determine the prevalence and prognostic implications of TMAO in patients with CKD.
Method
We analyzed data from 4724 participants of the German Chronic Kidney Disease (GCKD) cohort, a prospective observational cohort of CKD patients with an eGFR of 30-60 mL/min/1.73 m2 or overt proteinuria in the presence of an eGFR>60 mL/min/1.73 m2 at enrollment. TMAO levels were quantified in plasma at baseline using proton nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Creatinine and cystatin C measurements were obtained up to four times during follow-up, enabling the calculation of eGFR trajectories. The primary outcomes were all-cause mortality as well as the incidence of composite kidney endpoint (CKE), defined as eGFR decline >40% from baseline, eGFR <15 ml/min/1.73 m², initiation of kidney replacement therapy (dialysis or transplantation), or renal death, within 6.5 years. Time-to-event analyses were conducted using multivariate proportional hazards regression models.
Results
Median TMAO levels increased with higher CKD GFR and albuminuria categories. Over a median follow-up of 6.5 years, 479 deaths were recorded. Elevated TMAO concentrations at baseline (fourth versus first quartile) were significantly associated with increased all-cause mortality risk. This association remained robust after adjustment for traditional risk factors, history of cardiovascular disease, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, and eGFR as well as albuminuria. Further, higher TMAO levels were consistently associated with increased incidence of CKE and after multivariate analyses independently predicted CKE risk, underscoring its potential as a prognostic kidney biomarker in CKD.
Conclusion
Among patients with CKD, TMAO levels were increased progressively with lower GFR and higher albuminuria. Elevated TMAO levels were independently associated with a greater risk of all-cause mortality and CKE. These findings emphasize the critical role of gut microbiota-derived metabolites in the progression and outcomes of CKD, highlighting TMAO as a potential biomarker for risk stratification and as a potential target for therapeutic intervention.

title: #2688 Developing a risk prediction model for progression events in chronic kidney disease patients
authors: Caterina Tozzi; Philip Ambery; Nils Svangård; Philippa Traill; Claire Donoghue
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a progressive condition characterized by the gradual decline of kidney function, often associated with comorbidities such as diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease. CKD can progress from mild impairment (early stages) to severe kidney damage, ultimately leading to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), which requires dialysis or transplantation. Early identification of patients at high risk of progression is critical to enable timely interventions and improve clinical outcomes. Current methods of identification include urinary albumin testing which can represent a significant barrier to patient screening and leads to underestimation of risk of CKD progression in the general population.
The aim of this study is to develop a non-invasive risk prediction tool without albuminuria testing that identifies CKD patients at high risk of disease progression using routinely available laboratory data and patient characteristics. Implementing such a tool in clinical practice could facilitate earlier interventions, reduce the burden of ESKD, and improve patient quality of life.
Method
A prediction algorithm was developed using a survival model with a boosted tree architecture to estimate the probability of CKD progression. The model utilizes 11 commonly measured laboratory values and patient characteristics to predict the time to a progression event, defined as either a 40% decline in eGFR, ESRD, or other outcomes.
The model was trained and validated using Optum's de-identified Clinformatics® Data Mart Database (CDM), a large real-world dataset. Patients aged 18–95 years with CKD stages 1–4 were included, provided baseline eGFR measurements were available. Patients with prior dialysis dependence or a history of kidney transplant were excluded. After applying these criteria, 534,662 patients were included in the analysis.
The dataset was divided into three subsets: 60% for model training, 10% for hyperparameter tuning, and 30% for validation. Right-censoring was applied for events such as study completion, dropout, or kidney transplant failure.
Results
Diagnoses corresponding to inclusion, progression events, and censoring were identified using ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes. Covariate measurements were aggregated from data available up to 1 month after the date of the first CKD diagnosis.
The prediction model achieved a ROC-AUC around 70% for identifying patients at risk of experiencing a progression event within 1 year, 2 years, 3 years, and 4 years, respectively. While precision and sensitivity varied across intervals, the model demonstrated the ability to achieve precision up to 80% and sensitivity up to 60% over the 3-year prediction period.
Figure 1 illustrates Kaplan-Meier (KM) curves for patients in the CDM test subset population, stratified by risk score severity. Patients with higher risk scores demonstrated significantly increased risk of early disease progression, as reflected in the KM curves.
Conclusion
This study demonstrates the feasibility of identifying CKD patients at high risk of progression using data routinely collected in clinical practice without the need for albuminuria testing. The developed model has the potential to support earlier and more targeted clinical interventions, ensuring timely care for patients at greatest risk. By identifying high-risk individuals earlier, this approach could significantly improve patient outcomes by slowing disease progression, enhancing quality of life, and potentially extending life expectancy.

title: #3291 Evaluating the clinical applicability of KFRE in advanced chronic kidney disease: insights from a spanish cohort
authors: Héctor Bedoya Orozco; Jorge Zamora Carrillo; Juan Carlos Leon Román; Efrain Tatis; Natalia Padron; Susana Valle; Maria José Soler Romeo; Néstor Toapanta Gaibor
abstract:
Background and Aims
Advanced chronic kidney disease (ACKD) poses a significant challenge due to its high risk of progression to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). The Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE) is widely recognized for its predictive accuracy, but its practical integration into clinical decision-making, particularly in the Spanish healthcare context, remains underexplored. This study evaluates the clinical utility of KFRE for early stratification of ACKD patients at risk of requiring renal replacement therapy (RRT) and assesses its performance across specific subgroups, including age and comorbidities.
Method
This retrospective cohort study included 139 ACKD patients monitored at a tertiary nephrology unit in Spain between 2020 and 2022. The 2-year KFRE was assessed using ROC curve analysis, with sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios calculated for various thresholds. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on age (>65 years) and comorbidity profiles. Kaplan-Meier survival analyses were performed to evaluate time-to-RRT based on KFRE risk stratification.
Results
The cohort had a mean age of 72.9 years (71.9% >65 years), with 56.8% males. ROC analysis showed an AUC of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.73–0.91), confirming excellent discriminatory capacity. At a 15% KFRE threshold, sensitivity was 84.1%, specificity ranged from 68%–72%, and the positive likelihood ratio (LR+) was 3.0. Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated a significant difference in time-to-RRT between KFRE-defined risk groups (log-rank: P = 0.006). Subgroup analyses revealed consistent predictive performance, with minor variations in older patients (>65 years) and those with multiple comorbidities.
Conclusion
KFRE demonstrated high predictive accuracy for RRT initiation in Spanish ACKD patients and offers a practical tool for early risk stratification. The integration of KFRE into routine nephrology practice could enhance RRT planning, particularly in healthcare systems prioritizing resource optimization. Further prospective studies are warranted to explore its impact on patient outcomes and healthcare efficiency.

title: #240 Supplemented ketoanalogues (KAs) with plant versus animal based low protein diet (LPD) in non-dialysis CKD
authors: Naveen KumarMedi; Ramphani Jasthi; Naveen Mattewada; Shivanand Nayak
abstract:
Background
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a significant global health challenge, impacting millions of patients worldwide. Nutritional management, particularly protein intake, plays a pivotal role in mitigating disease progression and enhancing patient outcomes. Recent evidence suggests that plant-based protein diets, when combined with KAs of essential amino acids (EAAs), may offer nephroprotective properties, particularly for non-dialysis CKD patients.
Aim
To compare the effects of plant-based versus animal predominant LPD, both supplemented with KAs, on kidney functions and metabolic health in non-dialysis CKD.
Material and Methods
Prospective observational study, from Nov 2021 to Oct 2023 for a period of 2 years, involving 50 non-dialysis CKD patients, stage 3 to 5, divided into 2 groups, of 25 each and followed up for 1 year. After demographic and careful clinical assessment (including anthropometry) basic lab data were recorded. First group received a plant-based LPD, while the other group followed an animal predominant LPD, with both groups supplemented with KAs to ensure adequate nutrition while minimizing nitrogen load in addition to the standard of care. [(LPD: 0.6 gm/kg/day and KAs – 1tab/ 10kg lean body weight (LBW)]. The primary outcomes measured included kidney functional markers (urea, serum creatinine, 24h UP) and nutritional status (serum albumin). Secondary outcomes assessed clinical data, phosphorus and potassium levels, inflammatory markers (hsCRP) and changes in anthropometrical parameters.
Results
Mean age of the patients in the plant based group and second group was 53.16 ± 11.83 years and 57.89 ± 14.49 years respectively, with male predominance (M: F 33: 17 overall) in both the groups. Both dietary interventions when compared with the baseline and at 6 and 12 months, resulted in improved kidney functions with significant reductions in serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen and proteinuria in both the groups. However, the plant LPD group showed a more marked decrease in serum phosphorus and potassium levels and had more stable inflammatory marker hsCRP and blood pressure control when compared to the animal predominant LPD group. There were no statistically significant differences in anthropometric parameters between the groups. Both the LPDs were well tolerated by participants, with no adverse effects.
Conclusion
Plant-based LPD, supplemented with KAs, may offer comparable or even superior benefits over an animal predominant LPD in non-dialysis CKD, in safely postponing KRT to some extent. Plant-based approach not only supports kidney functions, but also contributes to better electrolyte balance, reduced inflammation and oxidative stress. These findings highlight the potential of plant-based protein diets as an effective, kidney-protective dietary strategy in CKD management. Further large-scale studies are needed to validate these results, particularly in diverse patient populations across various stages of the disease.
