abstract:
Background and Aims
The impact of albuminuria as a biomarker of myocardial damage is widely known. In patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D), its presence carries a risk of progression for chronic kidney disease (CKD) and cardiovascular disease (CVD), often accompanied by impaired ventricular remodeling and myocardial fibrosis (MF). Despite scientific progress in the development of new therapeutic options to mitigate these pathogenic pathways, there is still room for further clarification on the relationship between kidney and cardiac damage and the inflammatory-fibrotic mechanisms involved. This study aims to detect the cardiac impact of kidney damage in stage 3 diabetic kidney disease patients by multiparametric cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI), transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and circulating inflammatory-fibrotic biomarkers.
Method
We conducted an observational study in 49 adults with T2D, stage 3 CKD, stratified according to albuminuria, and 20 healthy controls. The degree of cardiac fibrosis and inflammation were assessed by functional CMRI, basic and advanced TTE, as well as the presence of different circulating biomarkers of fibrosis/inflammation (PICP, CITP, MMP1, TIMP-1, MMP10, LCN2 and sST2).
Results
Compared with controls, T2D patients with macroalbuminuria showed higher T1 mapping values and sST2 levels. Additionally, T1 mapping values were directly associated with elevated sST2 levels, particularly in patients with macroalbuminuria (p for interaction less than 0.01). Correspondingly, patients with macroalbuminuria and high sST2 levels (median: 43.9 ng/mL) exhibited increased T1 mapping values 1029 ms (1013 to 10143 ms) vs 1071 ms (1052 to 1087 ms), p-value less than 0.05; and alterations in other cardiac parameters as worsened left ventricle global longitudinal strain assessed by TTE (−18.0% (−18.4% to −16.8%) vs −14.1% (−15.9% to −12.9%), p-value less than 0.05.
Conclusion
Renal damage in T2D, as evidenced by macroalbuminuria, is associated with an increased risk of fibrotic involvement and cardiac dysfunction in relation to higher sST2 levels. These findings highlight the need for an integrative approach between renal and cardiac injury.

title: #2458 Renal multiparametric MRI detects changes in renal blood flow and microstructure related to macroalbuminuria in Stage 3 Diabetic Kidney Disease patients
authors: Saioa Echeverria Andueza; José María Mora-Gutiérrez; Xabier Irazusta Olloquiegui; Loreto Fernandez Lorente; Rebeca Echeverria-Chasco; Susanna Ravassa; Leyre Garcia; Josune Orbe; Francisco Javier Escalada San Martin; Maria A Fernandez-Seara; Nuria García-Fernández
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) affects over half a billion people globally, leading to severe outcomes such as chronic kidney disease (CKD) and cardiovascular events. Current diagnostic tools are imprecise, while renal biopsy is invasive and costly. Multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) offers a non-invasive alternative to assess renal microstructure. Matrix metalloproteinase-10 (MMP-10) and its inhibitor TIMP-1 disbalance has been implicated in DKD. Neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL) serves as a reliable indicator of DKD progression. This study evaluates the utility of mpMRI in the assessment of renal microstructural perfusion, fibrosis and inflammation, and its correlation with circulating serum biomarkers, in patients with DKD. We hypothesise that albuminuria may have an impact on renal microvasculature and fibrosis from the early stages of DKD, and these changes may be quantified by mpMRI.
Method
An observational study was conducted including 47 adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and DKD (CKD Stage 3 of KDIGO classification), categorized according to macroalbuminuria and non-macroalbuminuria. Nineteen healthy controls were included. Participants underwent serum and imaging biomarker assessments, including MMP10, TIMP1, NGAL, and mpMRI (renal blood flow -RBF-, T1 mapping and apparent diffusion coefficient -ADC-). Statistical analyses evaluated the impact of albuminuria on the associations between diverse biomarkers.
Results
Reduced RBF (in cortex and medulla), ADC and T1 cortico-medullary differentiation (CMD) was found in DKD subjects compared to controls. Analyzing patients without (<300 mg/g) and with (≥300 mg/g) macroalbuminuria we noted lower RBF and T1 CMD values in the macroalbuminuric group. An interaction was observed between biomarkers (TIMP, MMP10/TIMP and NGAL) and mpMRI parameters.
Conclusion
Our study suggests that renal mpMRI could be a valuable tool for a more precise evaluation of DKD. Renal mpMRI is able to detect the impact of albuminuria, on renal microperfusion and fibrosis in DKD even among patients with similar grade of CKD.

title: #863 Long-term effect of semaglutide on the glomerular filtration rate slope in high-risk patients with diabetic nephropathy: analysis in real-world clinical practice
authors: Enrique Luna Huerta; Álvaro Álvarez López; Juan Villa Rincón; Jorge Alberto Rodriguez Sabillon; María Victoria Martín Hidalgo Barquero; Noemi Fernández Sánchez; Ana Belén Ruiz Jiménez; Guadalupe García Pino; Coral Martínez del Viejo; Lilia Olivera Azevedo; Rosa Maria Diaz Campillejo; Nicolas Roberto Robles Perez-Monteoliva
abstract:
Background and Aims
The chronic kidney disease associated with type II diabetes mellitus is often linked to a high risk of deterioration in kidney function. In this context, the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RAs) semaglutide has been shown to have a nephroprotective effect which specifically results in reduced proteinuria. Most trials performed to date have failed to show significant effects when applying very robust criteria to evaluate this nephroprotective effect (such as creatinine doubling time or need for dialysis), although very long follow-up times would be required to demonstrate this effect. Of note, the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) slope may help determine the nephroprotective effect without requiring such long follow-ups. However, the effect of on the eGFR slope in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), especially those in stages 3 and 4, has not yet been adequately evaluated.
Method
Our objective was to determine the effect of adding subcutaneous semaglutide to the treatment of 156 type II diabetic patients with CKD, a high risk of progression, and a negative eGFR slope prior to starting the intervention. Of these patients, 72% had stage 3 or 4 CKD and they were followed for an average of 3 years.
Results
The mean eGFR slope was −4.24 mL/min/m2 1.73 m2/year prior to semaglutide but after the start of treatment, and with a mean follow-up of 3 years, an improvement in the slope to −0.34 mL/min/m2 1.73 m2/year (p = 0.005) was observed. The additional use of semaglutide in patients already treated with sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) was especially positive with on eGFR slope (−4.52 vs +0.22 mL/min/1.73 m2/year, p=0.0001). This benefit was also observed in patients with an eGFR of less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2, semaglutide had an even more favourable effect on the slope +1.06 mL/min/1.73 m2/year (p = 0.001). The patients who benefited the most were those with albuminuria of less than 1,000 mg/g creatinine.
Conclusion
In our real-life study in a population at risk for rapid deterioration of renal function, the administration of subcutaneous semaglutide conferred an improvement in the eGFR slope in the medium and long term, with this difference being especially relevant when its treatment was added to patients treated with SGLT2is.

title: #2934 SGLT2 inhibitors awaken the norns: unraveling novel erythropoietic mechanisms in diabetic nephropathy
authors: Davide Viggiano; Ilenia Gravina; Michelangelo Nigro; Pierluigi D'angiò; Marco Guarneri; Carlo Giammaresi; Carola Zummo; Laura Alioto; Simona Laurino; Giuseppe Gigliotti; Angelo Ferrantelli
abstract:
Background and Aims
Interstitial fibroblast-like cells that produce erythropoietin, recently identified as "Norn cells," significantly advance our understanding of renal physiology. Our study examines how sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) influence erythropoiesis in patients with diabetic nephropathy. While SGLT2 inhibitors are established nephroprotective agents, their ability to increase hemoglobin levels remains an underappreciated effect that warrants further investigation. This hemoglobin-raising effect starkly contrasts other nephroprotective agents, particularly renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors (RAASi), which typically reduce hemoglobin levels. Specifically, we analyze changes in hemoglobin levels and explore the mechanistic interactions between SGLT2 inhibition and these specialized interstitial cells in diabetic kidney disease. We aim to elucidate the currently unclear mechanisms underlying this unique therapeutic effect.
Method
In this retrospective, three-center observational study, we analyzed 371 patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). The cohort had a mean age of 65 years and consisted predominantly of male (65%) and Caucasian (98%) individuals. Clinical and laboratory parameters were evaluated at baseline and following 7 months of treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors. Additionally, we performed histological analysis of renal biopsies from 15 SGLT2i-treated patients and 15 matched controls who had not received gliflozins. The control group was matched for age, eGFR, proteinuria and blood pressure to ensure comparable baseline characteristics.
Results
Hemoglobin levels showed a statistically significant median increase of 0.40 g/dL (P-value 2.63 x 10⁻¹¹). Renal biopsy analysis revealed a significant reduction in proximal tubular cell thickness and interstitial cell number, with no changes in endothelial cell count or capillary cross-sectional area. Notably, interstitial cell count correlated with creatinine levels. The observed hemoglobin increase suggests potential interactions with Norn cells, including reduced tubular metabolic stress and restored erythropoietin production.
Conclusion
The study reveals the multifaceted effects of SGLT2 inhibitors on erythropoiesis in patients with chronic kidney disease. Beyond their established glycosuric and nephroprotective properties, these agents can improve hemoglobin levels through mechanisms independent of traditional erythropoietic pathways. Our findings suggest that SGLT2 inhibition may modulate tubular function and potentially enhance the activity of erythropoietin-producing Norn cells in the renal interstitium. However, the precise molecular mechanisms require further investigation. This beneficial effect on hemoglobin levels is particularly noteworthy as it contrasts with the anemic tendencies often observed with other nephroprotective medications.
These observations expand our understanding of SGLT2 inhibitors' pleiotropic effects and suggest new therapeutic possibilities for managing the complex interplay between chronic kidney disease and hematological dysfunction. The ability to simultaneously address renal protection and anemia represents a significant advancement in CKD management, potentially reducing the need for exogenous erythropoiesis-stimulating agents in some patients.

title: #1061 Re-defining carboplatin dosage using eGFR-CR-CYS compared to Cockcroft Gault and impact on platinum-associated adverse events
authors: Si Yuan Khor; Jiaxuan Lyu; Sherley Mejia; Katherine Specht; Tianqi Ouyang; Sachin J Shah; Jennifer Temel; Lesley Inker; Meghan Sise
abstract:
Background and Aims
Carboplatin is first-line chemotherapy for numerous cancers. However, it is primarily really excreted, has a narrow therapeutic index, and high rate of adverse events (AEs), including cytopenias, acute kidney injury (AKI), and gastrointestinal side effects. The Calvert equation for dosing carboplatin was derived using measured GFR, but in clinical practice, it is applied using Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance (CG-CrCl) in many cancer centers. However, CG-CrCl is inaccurate, and overestimates measured GFR in patients with cancer. We aimed to determine how carboplatin dosing would be impacted by replacing CG-CrCl with the CKD-EPI combined equation using creatinine and cystatin C (eGFR-CR-CYS) adjusted for body surface area and expressed in ml/min. We also determined the association between receiving a carboplatin dose >15% higher than the dose indicated using eGFR-CR-CYS and developing platinum-associated AEs, including AKI, cytopenias, hospitalization, and mortality within 90 days.
Method
Prospective study including consecutive adult patients beginning carboplatin for cancer between 2023–2025. Creatinine and cystatin C were measured simultaneously on the morning of the first dose of carboplatin was administered. We compared the dose administered (using CG-CrCl) vs. the dose indicated using eGFR-CR-CYS. We defined “excess carboplatin dose” as receiving a carboplatin dose >15% or higher than the dose predicted by eGFR-CR-CYS and “underdosed” as receiving a carboplatin dose >15% lower than the dose indicated by eGFR-CR-CYS. We fit separate Fine-Gray subdistribution survival models accounting for the competing risk of death to measure the association between “excess carboplatin dose” and the incidence of ≥ grade 2 and 3 AEs (AKI, anemia, thrombocytopenia) and hospitalization for AEs. For the mortality outcome, we fit a Cox model. All models were adjusted for age, sex, Charlson score and cancer stage.
Results
Of 292 included patients, mean age was 66 ± 11.7, 193 (66%) were female. Primary cancer types were thoracic 106 (36%), gynecological 94 (32%), gastrointestinal 35 (12%), breast 31 (11%), and others 26 (10%). Using eGFR-CR-CYS would have led to clinically significant dose adjustments in 76 patients (26% of the cohort); 35 patients (12% of cohort) were given an excess carboplatin dose >15%, 41 (14%) were underdosed by >15%, and 216 (74%) received a dose within 15% of the dose predicted by eGFR-CR-CYS. Receiving an “excess carboplatin dose” was associated with an increased risk of anemia, thrombocytopenia, grade ≥3 AKI, and death within 90 days (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
Using eGFR-CR-CYS to dose carboplatin would lead to significant differences in administered doses of carboplatin in 26% of treated patients. AEs were more common and severe in patients who received an “excess carboplatin dose.” Considering eGFR-CR-CYS may identify patients who are more likely to benefit from a dose reduction to prevent carboplatin toxicity.

title: #3103 Validation of a new simplified method for quick and easy quantification of iohexol as part of precise kidney function measurement
authors: Milen Babic; Henriette Straub; Markus Van der Giet
abstract:
Background and Aims
The exact determination of kidney function (mGFR) in everyday clinical situation is usually very time-consuming, difficult to carry out on a routine basis and hardly available. The estimation formulas used (eGFR) have a variability of 25%. eGFR is not suitable for precise determination of renal function which is necessary in many clinical situations. Kidney function measurement can be carried out precisely using exogenous markers such as iohexol. However, the currently used iohexol methods are complex in preanalytics and analysis, so that they have not yet been able to establish themselves in routine use. Here we tested a new iohexol determination method, which has been available as an CE-approved kit for simple and quick kidney function measurement since May 2022 (Nephrolyx, Berlin)
Method
The method combines a one-step sample preparation using filters and rapid chromatographic separation using a UHPLC-DAD system (Hitachi). The method was checked for the quantification range, as well as precision, variability and accuracy. Renal function was determined in 40 patients using conventional renal function measurement (precipitation-HPLC-UV.
Results
The method was validated with a linear range of 8.6–500 mg/ml iohexol in human serum. The inaccuracy within a day or between different days was ≤0.8% and ≤1.84%. The accuracies within one day and between different days were −1.12% to 1.04% and between 1.24% to 0.1%, respectively. The sample preparation time after receipt of the sample is 20 minutes and the measuring time of the sample is 90 seconds. It usually takes 45–60 minutes from the blood sample to the measured value. When comparing 120 blood samples from 40 patients, the kidney function determination shows a deviation of 1.2%, i.e. 46.2 ml/min (HPLC) vs. 46.8 ml/min (UPLC).
Conclusion
The new simplified method for the iohexol method was successfully validated and shows excellent precision and accuracy. The method is based on a simple sample preparation in a 96-well format, allowing robustness, high sample throughput and automation to be achieved. The new method was able to successfully determine the iohexol concentration in human serum in order to also determine kidney function. The simplicity of the method offers the possibility of easily using it in clinical routine.

title: #3134 Implementation of an iohexol-based GFR-measurement in clinical routine
authors: Milen Babic; Henriette Straub; Markus Van der Giet
abstract:
Background and Aims
The current KDIGO recommendations for the treatment of CKD recommend that every nephrologist should have an option for measuring kidney function (mGFR) with an exogenous substance. Currently, only iohexol or radioactively labeled DTPA are available as exogenous substances for clearance measurements. The iohexol clearance measurement is available in a standardized form and we show the introduction into clinical routine.
Method
A total of 289 patients were evaluated in the nephrology outpatient clinic for a potential kidney function measurement between October 2023 and March 2024. First, a kidney function was carried out by determining creatinine and estimating the GFR using the CKDEpi formula (eGFR). If there were reasons for the implausibility of the creatinine measurement and the associated eGFR, e.g. malnutrition, tumor disease, heart failure, cirrhosis, catabolic diseases or sarcopenic patients, an mGFR was also carried out using iohexol clearance measurement at 3 points in time (after 3, 4 and 5 hours). The iohexol concentration was determined in the central laboratory using a standardized CE-certified laboratory kit (Nephrolyx GmbH, Berlin, Germany) and the kidney function was calculated using a one-compartment model at three measurement timepoints.
Results
289 patients were evaluated. In 56 patients there were reasons why the creatinine value was estimated rather implausible. Typical reasons were rapid weight loss during tumor therapy (n = 12 patients), cardiorenal syndrome (n = 16 patients) and patients with longer intensive care stays (N=8 patients). In 45 patients, kidney function could be determined using iohexol clearance in a technically straightforward manner. The average deviation from eGFR was calculated as the difference expressed in %. title: #2984 Between the rhythm and the function: atrial fibrillation in chronic kidney disease
authors: Ana Rita Almeida; Mafalda Santos Filipe; Beatriz Campos Donato; Adriana Fernandes; Luis Falcao; Isabel Cristina Bettencourt de Simas de Mesquita; Mário Castro Raimundo; Sónia Marina Silva; Edgar A F Fernandes de Almeida
abstract:
Background and Aims
Atrial fibrillation (AF) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) frequently coexist, given their shared pathophysiological mechanisms and overlapping risk factors. Both conditions increase the risk of cardiovascular complications, hospitalization and mortality. While anticoagulation is essential for stroke prevention, its use in advanced CKD is controversial, due to increased bleeding risk and limited evidence. This study aims to evaluate the prevalence of AF in pre-dialysis CKD patients and analyze its impact on clinical outcomes, including mortality, hospitalization rates, cardiovascular events, and renal replacement therapy (RRT) initiation.
Method
Retrospective cohort study including CKD patients across all stages, followed in a Nephrology out-patient clinic in a Portuguese hospital, from February 2012 to October 2019. Clinical data was collected from electronic health records. The presence of AF was accessed by electrocardiogram. Univariate and multivariate cox-regression analysis was employed to determine predictors of the outcomes.
Results
A total of 3008 patients (91.7% caucasians and 54.5% males) with an average age of 68.2 ± 15.9 years were enrolled, out of which 327 (10.9%) presented AF. Two-hundred and one of the latter (61.5%) were treated with oral anticoagulants. Diabetic kidney disease and hypertensive nephropathy were the most frequent CKD etiologies and most patients had CKD stages II and III, with a mean estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 47.6 ± 33.1 ml/min/1.73 m2. The mean follow-up time was 3.2 ± 2.0 years during which 745 patients (24.8%) died and 262 (8.7%) started RRT.
Patients with AF were older (77 ± 11 vs 70 ± 20, P < 0.001), more frequently caucasian (97.2% vs 92.8%, P = 0.010) and had more comorbidities, including hypertension, heart failure, and peripheral arterial disease (P < 0.001 for all). CKD etiology was more frequently hypertensive nephropathy in the AF group (39.85% vs 23.4%), whereas chronic glomerulonephritis (3.1% vs 10.4%) and polycystic kidney disease (0.9% vs 3.3%) were more common in the non-AF group (P < 0.001). The eGFR was significantly lower in the AF group (median 32.6 [IQR 20] vs 43.2 [IQR 39]ml /min/1.73 m2; P < 0.001) with no difference in proteinuria levels. A total of 223 (68.2%) hospitalizations were observed in the AF group, significantly higher than in the non-AF group (n = 1379; 51.5%) (P < 0.001). The incidence of acute kidney injury (11.3% vs 6.2%; P = 0.001) and cardiovascular events (4.9 vs 2.6%; P = 0.034) were also higher in this group. In univariate cox-regression analysis, AF was associated with both all-cause (Hazard ratio [HR] 1.8; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.5–2.2; P < 0.001) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 2.3; 95% CI 1.3–4.3; P = 0.007). However, after adjusting for demographics and comorbidities these associations were no longer present, despite a trend towards higher all-cause mortality in the AF group (HR 1.12; 95% CI 0.99–1.45; P = 0.069). No difference was found regarding RRT initiation.
Among patients with AF, a total of 201 (61.5%) were under anticoagulation therapy. Of these, 149 (74.1%) with VKAs and 52 with DOACs. The group of anticoagulated patients was significantly younger (P < 0.001) without significant differences regarding comorbidities, baseline eGFR or proteinuria. Death of all causes, hospitalizations and cardiovascular events also did not show significant differences across groups.
Conclusion
Despite the limitations of this study (retrospective and unicentric design, limited sample size), a statistically significant correlation was found between AF and several major outcomes. This subgroup of patients has an increased risk of cardiovascular events, hospitalizations, and acute kidney injury, requiring a more intensive and multidisciplinary monitoring. Pre-dialysis CKD patients represent a subgroup of frail individuals and further studies should be encouraged in this population to better understand how to manage their comorbidities and improve long-term outcomes.

title: #1478 Application of estimated glomerular filtration rate equations in patients with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction
authors: Yuanyuan Wei; Yingchun MA; Shuang Li; Dong An; Limin Liao
abstract:
Background and Aims
Neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction (NLUTD), known as “neurogenic bladder”, is one of the important causes of chronic kidney disease (CKD). The estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) equations are the most widely used tool to assess GFR. However, there are currently no recommendation eGFR equations for patients with NLUTD.
This research aimed to evaluate the applicability of the chronic kidney disease epidemiology collaboration (CKD-EPI) eGFR (CKD-EPI eGFR) equations and the eGFR (C-eGFR) equations based on the Chinese chronic kidney disease (CKD) population in patients with NLUTD.
Method
Study design and Participants
This was a prospective study. patients aged ≥18 with NLUTD were enrolled from December 2021 to October 2024. NLUTD was diagnosed according to the Chinese Urological Association (CUA) guidelines.
Measurement and estimation of GFR
GFR was measured using 99mTc-DTPA plasma clearance, which was measured by means of the dual plasma sampling method.
GFR was estimated using the 2021 Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) equation based on serum Cr (CKD-EPI eGFRcr), the 2021 CKD-EPI equation based on serum Cr and Cys C(CKD-EPI eGFRcr-cys), the 2009 CKD-EPI equation based on Cys C (CKD-EPI eGFRcys), the Chinese equation based on serum Cr (C-eGFRcr), the Chinese equation based on serum Cr and cys C (C-eGFRcr-cys) and the Chinese equation based on serum cys C (C-eGFRcys).
Serum creatinine and cystatin C assays
Cr was assayed by the sarcosine oxidase method. Cys C was measured using a particle enhanced immunoturbidimetric method. Both were standardized to the international reference material.
Statistical analysis
Data analysis was conducted using IBM SPSS statistics, version 26.0 and MedCalc for windows, version 22.021. Bias, precision, and accuracy were used to evaluate the performance of each eGFR. Sub-analyses were performed for patients with GFR <60 and ≥60mL/min/1.73 m2. Non parametric tests were used as mGFR and eGFR were not normally distributed.
Results
A total of 142 adult patients with NLUTD were included, with a median age of 29.0 years (range 18–73 years), including 98 males (69%). The median mGFR measured by dual plasma 99mTc DTPA plasma clearance was 60.54 (range 8.32–135.87) mL/min/1.73 m2.
For the overall study population, C-eGFRcr, CKD-EPI eGFRcr, and C-eGFRcr-cys equations overestimated the GFR of adult patients with NLUTD. CKD-EPI eGFRcr-cys, C-eGFRcys, and CKD-EPI eGFRcys equations performed well, and the CKD-EPI eGFRcr-cys equation performed best Among the three equations (Table 1).
For patients with mGFR ≥60mL/min/1.73 m2, the C-eGFRcys and CKD-EPI eGFRcys equations tended to underestimate the GFR of these patients. The CKD-EPI eGFRcr-cys equation performed best Among the three equations (Table 2).
For patients with mGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2, the CKD-EPI eGFRcys equation performed best Among the three equations (Table 3).
Conclusion
Our research results showed that both the C-eGFR and CKD-EPI eGFR equations based on serum Cr overestimated the GFR of NLUTD patients. The CKD-EPI eGFR equation based on serum cys C or a combination of serum Cr and cys C performed better in NLUTD patients.

title: #3716 Change in mGFR following bariatric surgery: A case-crossover study
authors: Patrik Ene; Magnus Sundbom; Kerstin Marttala; Torbjörn Åkerfeldt; Maria K Svensson
abstract:
Background and Aims
Over the last few decades, the prevalence of obesity has increased dramatically. This epidemic is mirrored by an increase in hypertension, diabetes and chronic kidney disease, including a markedly high risk of end-stage kidney disease in individuals with obesity. A main feature of obesity-related kidney disease is glomerular hyperfiltration that in time can lead to kidney damage. One effective and proven method for organ-protecting weight loss is bariatric surgery.
Studies evaluating estimations of GFR in individuals with obesity show that they are severely incorrect regardless of formula used. The simultaneous use of a body surface indexation introduces an additional factor that might potentiate systematic errors, especially in patients undergoing changes in body composition. This study evaluated the impact of a low-calorie diet followed by bariatric surgery, with the associated weight loss, on kidney function. Kidney function was assessed using measured GFR (mGFR) in healthy obese individuals.
Method
The study population comprised of 15 patients between 25–58 years with BMI 35–46 kg/m2. All participants were free from previously diagnosed diabetes, hypertension, or chronic kidney disease and were scheduled to undergo a 4-week low-calorie diet followed by bariatric surgery at Uppsala University Hospital, Sweden. mGFR was assessed using iohexol clearance with four points of measurement: 180, 200, 220 and 240 minutes after injection. The primary outcome for this study was mGFR (without indexation for body surface area) before start of treatment and 6 months after bariatric surgery. Data is presented using box- and spaghetti plots.
Results
At 6 months after surgery, mean BMI had decreased from 38.9 to 30.2, a decrease by 8.7 BMI-units (95% CI 5.72 to 11.69; P = 0.00002). Mean mGFR was reduced by 7.53 ml/min (95% CI −18.24 to 3.17; P = 0.15) compared to baseline (Fig. 1A). When analyzing individual mGFR changes there was a prominent decrease in mGFR in subjects with hyperfiltration (>120 ml/min) and no change or a slight increase in with low or normal GFR at baseline (Fig. 1B). A subgroup analysis in individuals with hyperfiltration at baseline (n = 6) showed a mean mGFR decrease by 26.8 ml/min (95% CI −39.4 to −14.3; P = 0.003) with congruent trajectories in all patients, see Fig. 2A and B.
Conclusion
This study shows a decrease in kidney function (mGFR) in patients undergoing weight loss through low caloric diet and bariatric surgery. Individuals with hyperfiltration at baseline experience a statistically significant GFR reduction, but in individuals with normal or reduced GFR at baseline no change or a slight increase was found. These results illustrate large variations in kidney function and markedly different adaptations to weight loss among seemingly kidney healthy individuals with obesity. This knowledge can inform decisions on individualized treatment strategies in this patient group.

title: #2553 Association between healthy dietary patterns and chronic kidney disease: findings from the Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KNHANES) 2019 – 2021
authors: Minsang Kim; Semin Cho; Sehoon Park; Jin Hyuk Paek; Woo Yeong Park; Kyubok Jin; Seungyeup Han; Dong Ki Kim; Kyungdo Han; Yaerim Kim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Although a healthy dietary pattern is one of the modifiable lifestyle factors that has a preventive effect on CKD, there is a paucity of research investigating the association between a healthy diet and the risk of CKD in diabetic patients in Korea using the Korean Healthy Eating Index (KHEI), a tool designed to assess diet quality in Koreans.
Method
This cross-sectional study included a total of 1,991 diabetic patients from the eighth Korean national health and nutrition examination survey conducted from 2019 to 2021. The KHEI consists of 3 categories and 14 components (eight for adequacy, three for moderation, three for balance), with a higher KHEI indicating healthier eating habits. CKD was defined as an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 or urine albumin-creatinine ratio ≥30 mg/g. The risk of CKD was evaluated according to the median value of the KHEI using logistic regression analysis, adjusted for various clinicodemographic characteristics. The scores for each component of the KHEI were compared between those with CKD and those without using the Student's t-test.
Results
Participants with higher KHEI were older, had lower proportions of men, current smoker, and heavy alcohol drinker. Those with higher KHEI exhibited a significantly lower risk of CKD after adjustment (Adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.73 [0.58–0.93]). Subgroup analysis revealed a stronger association in those without hypertension (aOR 0.57 [0.37–0.87]) and those with at least a high school education (aOR 0.56 [0.38–0.81]). Moreover, diabetic patients with CKD had significantly lower KHEI scores, particularly in the adequacy category components including breakfast consumption, total fruit intake, and dairy product intake.
Conclusion
A healthier dietary pattern, as reflected by higher KHEI scores, is associated with a reduced risk of CKD in diabetic patients in Korea. A dietary intervention, which recommends intakes of fruits and dairy products and having breakfast, may be an effective strategy in CKD prevention among diabetic patients.

title: #1588 Homocitrulline is associated with cardiovascular outcomes in non-dialysis patients with chronic kidney disease
authors: Solene Laville; Stéphane Jaisson; Philippe Gillery; Anais Okwieka; Natalia Alencar de Pinho; Christian Combe; Mansencal Nicolas; Ziad Massy; Sophie Liabeuf
abstract:
Background and Aims
Protein carbamylation contributes to an increase in the cardiovascular risk in certain patient populations (e.g. in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) because of elevated urea concentrations). Homocitrulline (HCit) is a biomarker of overall protein carbamylation. In a study of a large cohort of non-dialysis patients with a confirmed diagnosis of CKD and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <60 mL/min/1.73 m², we sought to determine whether the serum HCit concentration was associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes and all-cause mortality.
Method
CKD-REIN is a prospective cohort of CKD patients with an eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m². The baseline serum HCit concentration was centrally measured, using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. The 2,195 patients included in the analysis were divided into tertiles (Ts) groups as a function of the baseline HCit concentration (T1 <292, T2 = [292–429], and T3 ≥430 µmol/mol lysine). Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) for the first major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE, defined as a composite of nonfatal stroke, nonfatal myocardial infarction, hospitalization for heart failure, and cardiovascular death) and for death before kidney replacement therapy (KRT, defined as the initiation of chronic dialysis or kidney transplantation). The models were adjusted for baseline comorbidities, laboratory data, and medications.
Results
Among the 2,195 included patients, the median [interquartile range (IQR)] age was 68, and the mean eGFR was 34.6 mL/min/1.73 m². The median [IQR] serum HCit was 352 [266–481] µmol/mol lysine.
The serum HCit concentration was correlated with the eGFR and the urea concentrations (r = −0.57 and r = 0.73, respectively). In an adjusted linear regression model, the HCit concentration was independently and positively associated with age, eGFR decrease, urea, anemia, and baseline prescription of diuretics, and negatively associated with male sex and a greatly elevated urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio.
The adjusted HR [95% confidence interval] for MACEs as a function of the baseline serum HCit concentration was 1.32 [0.96; 1.83] for patients in T2 and 1.59 [1.13; 2.24] for patients in T3, relative to patients in T1 (Fig. 1).
The adjusted HR [95% CI] for death before KRT as a function of the baseline serum HCit concentration was 1.42 [0.99; 2.01] for patients in T2 and 2.01 [1.39; 2.91] for patients in T3, relative to patients in T1 (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
Our analysis of a large cohort of patients with CKD demonstrated that the serum HCit concentration was associated with a greater likelihood of a MACE and death. To confirm causality, further studies of therapeutic interventions for preventing or reducing carbamylation are now warranted.

CKD-REIN is a prospective cohort of CKD patients with an eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m². The baseline serum HCit concentration was centrally measured, using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. The 2,195 patients included in the analysis were divided into tertiles (Ts) groups as a function of the baseline HCit concentration (T1 <292, T2 = [292–429], and T3 ≥430 µmol/mol lysine). The models were adjusted for baseline comorbidities, laboratory data, and medications.

title: #1856 Exploring sex-based variations in prescription patterns and adverse drug reactions in chronic kidney disease
authors: Solene Laville; Agathe Mouheb; Natalia Alencar de Pinho; Maurice Laville; Christian Combe; Ziad Massy; Sophie Liabeuf
abstract:
Background and Aims
Pharmacological responses and risks can differ significantly between sexes. In the general population, women are more likely than men to experience adverse drug reactions (ADRs). However, sex-based differences in the therapeutic management of comorbidities among patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) remain poorly described, and the disparity in ADR risk between sexes is largely unknown. This study aims to describe the prevalence and types of drug prescriptions in men and women and to examine sex differences in the risk of ADRs within a cohort of CKD patients.
Method
The French Chronic Kidney Disease-Renal Epidemiology and Information Network (CKD-REIN) is a prospective cohort study including 3,011 nephrology outpatients with confirmed CKD (estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <60 mL/min/1.73 m²) and available data on drug prescriptions. Standard descriptive analyses were conducted to characterize drug prescriptions according to sex at baseline. ADRs were prospectively identified through hospitalization records, medical records, and patient interviews. Expert pharmacologists used validated tools to adjudicate ADRs. Cause-specific Cox proportional hazards model was used to explore the association between sex. The model was adjusted for baseline comorbidities, laboratory data, and medications.
Results
Among the 3,011 included patients, 1,038 were women (W) and 1,973 were men (M).
Compared to men, at baseline, women were younger (median [interquartile range], 67 [58–76] vs 69 [62–77] years, P < 0.001), had lower eGFR (mean ± standard deviation, 33.1 ± 12.9 vs 34.7 ± 13.2 mL/min/1.73 m², P = 0.001), and lower rates of diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, and dyslipidaemia, but higher prevalence of arthrosis and depression. No statistical differences were observed in anaemia prevalence.
Although the number of daily-prescribed medications did not differ by sex (P = 0.13), the types of drugs prescribed varied significantly between men and women. Women were more frequently prescribed drugs for acid related disorders (37% vs 33%), antianemic preparations (23% vs 12%), corticosteroids (9% vs 6%), thyroid therapy (23% vs 6%), analgesics (30% vs 20%), psycholeptics (24% vs 13%), and psychoanaleptics (12% vs 6%). In contrast, they were less frequently prescribed drugs related to cardiovascular health, including antithrombotic agents (41% vs 59%), diuretics (51% vs 57%), calcium channel blockers (44% vs 50%), renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (71% vs 79%) or lipid-modifying agents (57% vs 66%), and oral antidiabetic agents (20% vs 26%). No significant differences were observed for vitamin D supplementation (W, 49%; M, 48%) and beta-blockers (W, 40%; M, 43%).
During a median follow-up of 4.7 [4.6–4.8] years, 964 patients experienced a first ADR (W = 351; M = 613), leading to a global incidence rate of 10.1 [9.5; 10.7] per 100 person-years.
The most common ADRs were renal and urinary disorders (n = 178), followed by gastrointestinal disorders (n = 145) and haemorrhages (n = 107). Among women, the most frequent ADRs were gastrointestinal disorders (n = 59), while renal and urinary disorders were most common in men (n = 134).
The adjusted risk of a first ADR was higher in women than in men (hazard ratio [95% confidence interval], 1.17 [1.02; 1.34]).
Conclusion
In CKD patients, significant sex-based differences were observed in drug prescriptions and ADR risks. Women had distinct prescription patterns, with fewer cardiovascular drugs but more psychoactive and analgesic medications. They also exhibited a higher risk of ADRs, highlighting the need for sex-specific therapeutic strategies.

title: #147 Evidence of impaired myocardial perfusion reserve in asymptomatic non-diabetic patients with advanced CKD
authors: Thomas Anderton; Chin Yit Soo; Bradley Chambers; Raluca Tomoaia; Roshan Patel; Maria Kalaitzoglou; Vinesh Palanimuthu; Andrew Mooney; Sven Plein; Peter Swoboda; Shanmugakumar Chinnappa
abstract:
Background and Aims
Quantitative perfusion (QP) cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) is a validated method to quantify the rest and stress myocardial blood flow (MBF) and the myocardial perfusion reserve (MPR) on a global and segmental level. QP CMR has been shown to improve the diagnostic capability of stress perfusion CMR in settings such as multivessel coronary artery disease and microvascular disease, both commonly seen in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD).
To our knowledge no study has evaluated QP values in patients with advanced CKD (eGFR <30), predominantly due to concerns regarding gadolinium exposure in CKD. This is despite the common occurrence of coronary artery and microvascular disease in these patients. We hypothesised that CKD patients will have altered global myocardial blood flow when quantified with CMR, compared to a healthy cohort.
Method
A cross-sectional study (n = 50) of 33 asymptomatic non-diabetic patients with advanced CKD (eGFR <30) without known heart disease and 17 healthy volunteers. All participants underwent clinical questionnaire, blood serum testing and comprehensive CMR including rest and stress MBF and MPR quantification using automated, in line methods producing both global and segmental myocardial perfusion metrics.
CMR followed a standardised stress protocol with adenosine being infused for 3 minutes to induce hyperaemia, before scanning the left ventricle in an axial 3-slice method with adenosine infusion ongoing and a 0.05ml/kg gadolinium bolus. After a 10-minute washout period rest imaging was then performed with a further 0.05ml/kg gadolinium bolus.
CMR results were interpreted both visually and quantitatively. Quantitative values were produced both segmentally and pixel-wise. Regions with significant infarction on late gadolinium imaging were excluded from analysis.
Continuous, normally distributed variables were compared with independent sample t-test. χ2 tests were used to analyse proportions. Continuous variables are presented as means with standard deviations. P values of <0.05 were considered statistically significant.
Results
CKD patients had a mean age of 57 years (73% men) and the healthy volunteers had a mean age of 48 years (41% men). All patients and volunteers completed CMR, of these 29 (88%) of the CKD patients and 14 (82%) healthy volunteers consented to gadolinium and had acceptable quantitative results after standard post processing checks. The results are presented in Table 1.
Conclusion
In this cohort of asymptomatic patients with non-diabetic advanced CKD, we have shown for the first time abnormal quantitative myocardial perfusion metrics when assessed by CMR, compared to healthy controls.
We have shown CKD patients to have a significantly raised rest MBF, a mildly reduced stress MBF and a significantly reduced myocardial perfusion reserve. There is also evidence of globally reduced endocardial stress perfusion as shown by the significantly reduced stress endocardial/epicardial ratio.
There are not yet definitive diagnostic criteria for coronary microvascular disease from CMR QP. However, a reduced endocardial stress MBF alongside reduced MPR have each been suggested as markers of microvascular dysfunction. Our findings, particularly in the absence of regional perfusion defects suggestive of epicardial coronary disease, may be supportive of global microvascular dysfunction in even asymptomatic patients with advanced CKD.

title: #325 Increased left ventricular mass is caused by extracellular not intracellular expansion in advanced CKD
authors: Thomas Anderton; Chin Yit Soo; Bradley Chambers; Raluca Tomoaia; Roshan Patel; Maria Kalaitzoglou; Vinesh Palanimuthu; Andrew Mooney; Sven Plein; Peter Swoboda; Shanmugakumar Chinnappa
abstract:
Background and Aims
Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) is seen in up to 75% of patients with advanced CKD (eGFR <30). This has been shown to be an adverse prognostic marker compared to patients without LVH and is presumed multifactorial secondary to abnormal preload, afterload and metabolic conditions.
Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) has the unique ability to non-invasively evaluate myocardial tissue characteristics and assess the pathophysiological changes underlying the increase in LV mass seen in advanced CKD. It has previously been utilised to show that the LVH seen in athletic remodelling is caused primarily by an increase in the intracellular but not extracellular volume.
Through the use of advanced CMR techniques we sought to quantify, compared to healthy volunteers, the LVH seen in CKD and to delineate the relative changes in the intra- and extra-cellular compartments.
Method
A cross-sectional study (n = 50) of advanced, non-diabetic CKD patients (eGFR <30) without any known cardiac disease (n = 33) and healthy volunteers (n = 17). The participants underwent comprehensive CMR including left ventricular (LV) volumetric quantification, Native T1 and T2 mapping, extracellular volume (ECV) quantification and late gadolinium enhanced imaging. All patients completed written informed consent.
Left ventricular volumes and mass values were indexed to body surface area (BSA – m2) as is standard in clinical practice. Extra cellular volume calculation – quantified following pre- and post-contrast T1 Mapping techniques – allowed us to quantify the relative proportions that the intracellular and extracellular compartment contributed to any changes in LV mass seen in the CKD group. Late gadolinium enhanced imaging was utilised to report the presence of myocardial infarction or non-ischaemic fibrosis.
Continuous, normally distributed variables were compared with independent sample t-test. χ2 tests were used to analyse proportions. Continuous variables are presented as means with standard deviations. P values of <0.05 were considered statistically significant.
Results
CKD patients had a mean age of 57 years (73% men) and the healthy volunteers had a mean age of 48 years (41% men). Three patients with CKD and 4 healthy volunteers declined gadolinium contrast and did not complete ECV mapping. Therefore, 30 CKD patients and 13 healthy volunteers were used to calculate the relative intra- and extracellular components of the myocardium. The results are presented in Table 1.
Conclusion
As is common, overall LV mass and maximal wall thickness were increased in CKD patients as compared to healthy volunteers. Our results reveal that this hypertrophy is not caused by an increased intracellular compartment but rather by an increase in the extracellular compartment. The quantity of focal fibrosis seen in CKD patients was relatively low, suggesting the increase in LV mass seen in CKD to be primarily driven by global changes such as diffuse collagen deposition or interstitial oedema and not by myocyte cellular hypertrophy.

title: #564 The kynurenine-to-tryptophan ratio in serum is a predictor of cardiovascular mortality in CKD, independent of gut microbiome
authors: Ward Zadora; Mara Lauriola; Sander Dejongh; Pieter Evenepoel; Ricard Farré; Guillaume Fernandes; Björn Meijers
abstract:
Background and Aims
Tryptophan metabolism is altered in chronic kidney disease (CKD), with prior studies focusing on gut microbiome-derived metabolites such as indoxyl sulfate. However, kynurenine, an endogenous tryptophan breakdown product, has been linked to cardiovascular outcomes in CKD [1]. Population studies report significant associations between serum tryptophan metabolite ratios and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), as well as CKD progression [2]. Additionally, Mendelian randomization suggests reduced eGFR causes elevated levels of kynurenine and related metabolites [3]. This study, validated in an animal model, investigates KTR in CKD patients and its association with mortality and cardiovascular events.
Method
Data were derived from the Leuven Mild-to-Moderate CKD study, which enrolled adult CKD patients from the University Hospitals Leuven between 2005 and 2006, with follow-up until 2023 [4]. CKD severity, demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, and outcomes were collected. Serum KTR was measured using LC-MS/MS [5]. Associations between logarithmic KTR and outcomes were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards and Kaplan-Meier analyses, adjusting for demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, and kidney function.
In a validation study, CKD was induced in male Sprague-Dawley rats via 5/6th nephrectomy. Animals were treated with antibiotics to explore the impact of microbiota on KTR. Group differences were assessed using ANOVA/Kruskal-Wallis tests.
Results
KTR levels (both total and serum-free) are increased with CKD progression (P ≤ 2e-16) (Fig. A and B). In the animal model, KTR was elevated in CKD animals, regardless of microbiota depletion (Fig. C). Elevated KTR was significantly associated with increased mortality (Unadjusted HR 6.26 95% CI [4.48–8.74], correction for kidney function 2.48 95% CI [1.49–4.12], demographics 3.77 95% CI [2.5–5.68], all factors 2.77 95% CI [1.45–5.27]) and CV-events (Unadjusted 4.6 95% CI [3.13–6.75], correction for kidney function 2.48 95% CI [1.37–4.48], demographics 2.99 95% CI [1.91–4.69], all factors 2.49 95% CI [1.3–4.79]) in the clinical cohort. (Fig. D)
Conclusion
KTR is a robust predictor of mortality and cardiovascular events in CKD patients after correction for demographics, CV-risk factors, and kidney function. These findings are validated in an animal model and shown to be independent of microbiota. We suggest KTR as a potential clinically relevant biomarker in CKD.

title: #1892 Understanding cardiovascular benefits of finerenone: the role of central arterial stiffness
authors: Nejc Piko; Robert Ekart; Andrijana Koceva; Nika Aleksandra Kravos Tramšek; Aleksandra Kukovič; Luka Varda; Sebastjan Bevc
abstract:
Background and Aims
In recent years, the non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist finerenone has emerged as a game-changing therapy for individuals with DKD and albuminuria. A growing body of research highlights its cardiovascular benefits, including its effectiveness in managing heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Despite its widespread use, the exact ways in which finerenone influences the vascular wall and reduces arterial stiffness remain unknown. This study aimed to explore the effects of finerenone on central arterial stiffness in patients with DKD and albuminuria. Although the research is ongoing and full follow-up data is not yet available, we share intriguing preliminary findings.
Method
We performed a prospective study with 40 patients (70% male) diagnosed with DKD who were prescribed finerenone in our outpatient clinic. At the start of the study, we collected data on their demographics, comorbidities, and laboratory parameters. Arterial stiffness was measured non-invasively using applanation tonometry (SphygmoCor®, AtCor Medical, Sydney, Australia), while volume status was thoroughly evaluated using bioimpedance spectroscopy (BIS) (BCM®, Homburg, Germany) and lung ultrasound in accordance with the LUST study protocol. These assessments were repeated at 6-month and 12-month intervals. Finerenone dose was titrated according to kidney function and potassium level, no modification in other prescribed medications was done during the follow-up visits. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS® version 29.0, with significance defined as a p-value below 0.05.
Results
The mean age of the patients was 66.7 ± 7.4 years. The most prevalent comorbidities included arterial hypertension (n = 40, 100%), hyperlipidemia (n = 36, 90%), pre-existing chronic kidney disease (n = 11, 27.5%), and ischemic heart disease (n = 10, 25%). A majority of patients were on renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system blockers (n = 37, 92.5%) and statins (n = 36, 90%), while 72.5% (n = 29) were receiving sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors, and 40% (n = 16) were on glucagon-like peptid-1 receptor agonists. Laboratory parameters, cfPWV values, and volume assessments are detailed in Table 1. After six months, cfPWV decreased by 9.2% (P = 0.015) compared to baseline, and remained the same at 12 months (p=0.026) (Fig. 1). Serum potassium levels slightly increased following the initiation of finerenone, but the change was not clinically significant. No significant effects on kidney function or blood pressure were noted.
Conclusion
Finerenone substantially decreased central arterial stiffness while preserving kidney function, volume status, and blood pressure. No clinically significant hyperkalemia was observed. Further research is needed to explore the endothelial effects of finerenone, which may provide insights into the observed reduction in central arterial stiffness.

title: #2023 Physical function clusters in an Australian outpatient kidney care clinic
authors: Thái Bình Trần; Jeanette Thom; Shaundeep Sen; Kelly Lambert; Ria Arnold
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is accompanied by impaired physical function and severe symptom burden. Existing data on physical function is biased towards haemodialysis cohorts and few studies have investigated this outcome in other CKD subgroups. Therefore, this study aimed to explore the extent of physical impairment and clusters of physical function across the CKD spectrum.
Method
We collected data from adults (≥18 years old) who completed routine measures of physical function in the kidney outpatient department at an Australian tertiary referral hospital. Additionally, the pain component of the KDQoL evaluated the extent of bodily pain (1: None - 6: Very severe) and the ADL component assessed whether patients’ health limited their capacity to perform daily tasks (10: Limited a lot – 30: Not limited at all).

Data from 455 patients between May-December 2024 was analysed [median age: 74, 41% female]. Most patients (n = 378, 83%) had CKD G3–G5. Our analysis found three distinct physical function clusters in the kidney outpatient setting. Given the association between poor physical function and adverse outcomes, patients with CKD may benefit from early screening for impaired physical function and, if indicated, receive counselling to participate in multidisciplinary rehabilitation with dietetics and exercise physiology input.

title: #1131 Associations between modifiable medical, behavioral and sociopsychological factors with the risk of dementia in chronic kidney disease
authors: Xiaoxi Zeng; Ci Li Nong Bu; Chunyang Li; Ping Fu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD) are at an increased risk of cognitive impairment and dementia, which further exacerbates the disease burden of CKD. Identifying modifiable factors for the prevention of dementia in CKD patients is of great importance. This study aims to evaluate the associations between modifiable medical, behavioral, sociopsychological, and environmental factors and the development of dementia in CKD.
Method
This was a prospective cohort study based on the UK Biobank. We included 10700 Individuals with the diagnosis of CKD or estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 at baseline. We collected information on medical (BMI, hearing loss, diabetes, hypertension, prevalent cardiovascular disease, albuminuria, GFR stages, and depression), behavioral (diet patterns derived by principal component analysis, sedentary lifestyle, physical activity, sleep duration, smoking, alcohol consumption, and playing computer games,), sociopsychological (educational qualification, living alone, friends visiting, and social activity), and environmental (exposure to nitrogen monoxide) factors at recruitment. The outcome was dementia as identified by the inpatient diagnoses during the follow-up. Cox proportional hazard regression models, using age as the time scale, were conducted to evaluate the associations between these potential risk factors with dementia, adjusting for sex, ethnicity, and Townsend deprivation index. The model was additionally adjusted for genetic risk which was estimated by polygenic risk score (PRS) of dementia and by the APOE genotype in 7561 participants with qualified genetic data.
Results
The mean age of this CKD cohort was 63.4 years, and 50.7% were male. Decreased eGFR was present in 64.0% of the participants. During a median follow-up duration of 13.7 years, 488 cases of incident dementia were identified, corresponding to an incidence of 3.3 per 1000 person-years. The results showed that, diabetes (HR 1.51, 95% CI, 1.21 to 1.89, P < 0.001), hearing loss (HR 1.33, 95% CI, 1.11 to 1.59, P = 0.002), prevalent cardiovascular disease (HR 1.52, 95% CI, 1.25 to 1.85, P < 0.001), eGFR less than 30 ml/min/1.73 m2 (HR 1.62, 95% CI, 1.04 to 2.51, P = 0.03), urine albumin/creatinine ratio > 30 mg/mmol (HR 1.67, 95% CI, 1.16 to 2.42, P = 0.006), high wholegrain diet (HR 1.40, 95% CI, 1.08 to 1.82, P = 0.01), and lack of social activity (HR 1.32, 95% CI, 1.09 to 1.59, P = 0.004) was independently associated with increased hazard of newly-onset dementia in CKD (Fig. 1). In 7,561 patients with qualified genetic data, where high genetic risk was associated with a markedly increased risk for dementia (HR 2.06, 95% CI: 1.67–2.58, P < 0.001), depression emerged as an associated risk factor for dementia, while the association between hearing loss and dementia was no longer statistically significant.
Conclusion
Among individuals with CKD, modifiable medical, behavioral, and sociopsychological factors may contribute to the development of dementia. Interventions targeting the improvement of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and social isolation, as well as delaying the progression of CKD, may reduce the risk of dementia in CKD.

title: #1141 Disease burden of chronic kidney disease attributable to modifiable risk factors: findings from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021
authors: Xiaoxi Zeng; Wanyi Yang; Chunyang Li; Ping Fu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD), which affects approximately 10% of the global population, has emerged as a significant public health issue. CKD is often incurable, and the core of its management lies in delaying its progression. Consequently, identifying and controlling modifiable risk factors is of paramount importance. In this study, by utilizing data from the Global Burden Disease 2021 (GBD 2021), we investigated the disease burden of CKD that can be attributed to environmental or occupational, behavioral, and metabolic risk factors. This knowledge can facilitate the formulation of health policy priorities aiming at reducing exposure to risk factors, thus alleviating the overall disease burden of CKD.
Method
Using GBD 2021 data, we calculated the disease burden of CKD that can be attributable to environmental or occupational, behavioral, and metabolic risk factors. Mortality, Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs), and the population attributable fraction (PAF) of DALYs of CKD for 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2021 were explored. These estimates were also analyzed stratified by geographic regions.
Results
From 1990 to 2021, age-standardized DALY and mortality rates of CKD increased with estimated annual percentage change (EAPC) of 0.4% and 0.8%, respectively. This had accumulated to over 44.4 million DALYs and 1.53 million deaths due to CKD globally in 2021, and the upward trend is projected to continue until 2040. As shown in Fig. 1, among level-1 risk factors, the attributable proportion of metabolic risk factors exceeded that of behavioral and environmental or occupational ones. Regarding the level- 2 risk factors, kidney dysfunction was the top contributor to CKD - related DALYs and mortality, followed by high fasting plasma glucose, high systolic blood pressure, high BMI, dietary risks, and non-optimal temperature (Fig. 1). Upon further examination into level-3 factors, we observed the risk factor with the highest increasing rate was high temperature, with EAPCs of 2.6% for CKD-related DALYs and 2.5% for mortality. Other risk factors with significant increasing trends included diets high in sugar-sweetened beverages, red meat, and processed meat (Fig. 1). For the regional variations, metabolic risks consistently rank as the top contributors to CKD-related burden across all regions. High sodium diet was particularly prominent in Central Europe and East Asia, while the impact of cold temperature was more profound in North Africa, the Middle East, and South Latin America.
Conclusion
The substantial and increasing burden of CKD attributable to modifiable risk factors highlights the urgent need for the development and implementation of global and regional public health strategies aimed at controlling these risk factors to effectively reduce the global burden of CKD.

title: #2518 Salvianolic acid C mitigates sepsis-induced kidney injury through promotion of renal gluconeogenesis
authors: Qiming Xu; Pinglan Lin; Jing Hu; Ming Wu
abstract:
Background and Aims
The main pathological progress in sepsis-induced kidney injury is inflammation in the renal interstitium. Renal gluconeogenesis is recently identified as a hallmark of chronic and acute kidney diseases. However, the role of renal gluconeogenesis in septic kidneys is currently unknown. Our recent study showed that Salvianolic acid C (SAC), one of the main polyphenolic components of Salvia miltiorrhiza, displays renal benefits in fibrotic kidneys through promotion of renal gluconeogenesis. We aimed to determine the effect of SAC on septic kidneys and explore its underlying mechanisms.
Method
1. Animal model of sepsis-induced kidney injury (in vivo)
Mice were injected intraperitoneally (i.p.) with 20 mg/kg LPS (l2630, Sigma-Aldrich) to establish an in vivo sepsis-induced AKI model. fifty C57 mice were randomly divided into ten groups, n = 6 per group: (I) Ctr + Vehicle, (II) Ctr + SAC-High, (III) LPS + Vehicle (saline), (IV) LPS + SAC-Low, (V) LPS + SAC-High. (VI) LPS + Ad-Pck1, (VII) LPS + Ad-LacZ (0.5×109 pfu/100 μL), (VIII) Ctr + shRNA-LacZ (0.5×109 pfu/100 μL), (IX) LPS + shRNA-LacZ +SAC, (X) LPS + shRNA-Pck1 +SAC. Adenovirus or shRNA were injected into the left renal artery 3 days before the LPS injection. Mice were treated with saline or 10 mg/kg, 50 mg/kg SAC (i.p.) 1h before LPS injection and sacrificed at 16h after LPS injection, the blood was collected for renal function measurement, and kidneys were harvested for pathological and immunoblotting analysis.
2. Mouse primary murine renal tubule epithelial cells (mRTECs) (in vitro)
mRTECs exposed to 25 μg/mL LPS were treated with SAC. Pck1 was inhibited or deleted by 3-MPA or shRNA, or overexpressed by adenovirus. Protein samples were taken for Western blotting and to evaluate inflammatory and gluconeogenesis. Glucose and lactate were measured in supernatant of culture medium.
Results
1. SAC is protective in LPS induced kidney injury.
In vitro, qPCR analysis showed that SAC dose-dependently reduced the expression of inflammatory factors (IL-1β and MCP-1) (Fig. 1A). Western blotting analysis indicated SAC inhibited the expression of p50 and phosphorylated p65 (pp65) (Fig. 1B) in LPS stimulated mRTECs. In vivo, SAC treatment lowered the level of BUN and Scr of septic kidneys (Fig. 1C). As shown by qPCR or WB analysis, SAC down-regulated the p50 and pp65 and the transcription level of IL-1β and MCP-1 (Fig. 1D–F), indicating that SAC inactivated the pro-inflammatory NF-kB signaling pathway.
2. SAC restored renal gluconeogenesis in the kidney of septic mice
RNA-seq analysis revealed that glycolysis/gluconeogenesis pathway is affected by SAC in septic mouse kidneys (Fig. 2A–C). SAC treatment reversed the gluconeogenic changes in septic kidneys, such as reduced expression of key gluconeogenesis genes (Pck1, Fbp1, G6pc) in mRNA and protein levels (Fig 2D–E), reduced renal lactate concentration and increased glucose concentration (Fig 2F).
3. PCK1 inhibits renal inflammatory in LPS induced sepsis
In vitro, PCK1 inhibitor 3-MPA resulted in increased expression of p50 and pp65, and was associated with increased lactate concentration and decreased glucose concentration in the supernatant (Fig. 3A and B). In contrast, overexpressed Pck1 in LPS stimulated mRTECs lead to a reduction in p50 and pp65 expression (Fig. 3C and D). In vivo, overexpression of the Pck1 gene in mouse kidneys improved the renal function, which were co-related with increased renal lactate concentration and decreased glucose concentration (Fig. 3E and F). Overall, these findings are consistent with an anti-inflammatory effect of the gluconeogenic enzyme Pck1.
4. Inhibition of PCK1-mediated renal gluconeogenesis reversed the anti-inflammatory effect of SAC in septic kidneys
SAC treatment reduced the expression of inflammatory factors, increased glucose concentration and reduced lactate concentration in the supernatant of LPS stimulated mRTECs and 3MPA reversed these changes (Fig. 4A and B). In animals, renal deletion of PCK1 by shRNA reversed the pro-gluconeogenic and decreased renal function of SAC on septic kidneys (Fig. 4C and D).
Conclusion
SAC attenuates sepsis-induced kidney injury through promotion of renal gluconeogenesis.

title: #1706 Treatment patterns of primary Immunoglobulin A Nephropathy (IgAN) in China: evidence from a real-world study using regional electronic health record data
authors: Ziqi Pan; Peng Shen; Zhike Liu; Li Zuo; Siyan Zhan
abstract:
Background and Aims
Advances in clinical trials and guidelines have the potential to improve therapeutic strategies for IgAN. More up-to-date evidence on patient characteristics and treatment patterns, and their association with CKD progression based on multicenter data in China, is needed. This study aimed to evaluate treatment patterns of IgAN in the real-world clinical setting in China, using data from a regional electronic health record database, where healthcare information has been linked across hospitals in this region.
Method
A retrospective observational study of adult patients with biopsy-confirmed primary IgAN from Yinzhou District, Ningbo City, China, was conducted using data from 01/01/2015 to 06/30/2023. Patients with secondary IgAN, history of dialysis or eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m2 at renal biopsy, or a history of kidney transplantation, were excluded. Index date was the date of the initial biopsy which confirmed IgAN. IgAN-related treatment patterns after renal biopsy were described, including initial treatments within 30 days after renal biopsy and initial treatment durations, as well as overall treatments during the entire follow-up.
Results
A total of 978 patients were included (52.0% were women). At renal biopsy, the median age was 43 years, 55.0% had hypertension, 9.1% had diabetes, 40.0% had >1g/day proteinuria, and 70.1% were in CKD stage I or II. Around 85.9% of patients were assigned Grade III-V per Lee's grading system, which is indicative of severe IgAN. During follow-up, 31.8% had time-averaged proteinuria >1 g/day. Of 742 patients with initial treatment records after renal biopsy, 79.5% were treated with RAASi, 15.1% with corticosteroids, 6.1% with immunosuppressants, 3.4% with SGLT2i, and 0.1% with targeted therapies. RAASi combination therapies are most frequently used as first-line therapy (79.5%). Composite renal event (at least one of ESKD, 40% eGFR decline, doubling of serum creatinine or mortality) was experienced by 6.7% of patients with a median time to event of about 31.9 months.
Conclusion
Results suggested that adult patients with IgAN in this Chinese cohort were diagnosed relatively young and were at early CKD stages. While the average proteinuria level was lower than other sites in China, these patients had concomitant high-risk comorbid conditions, and a majority had higher grade (III-V) per Lee's grading indicating risk of progression. Findings indicated adherence to both Chinese and international guidelines for IgAN treatments, where administering RAASi as supportive care has been generally considered. Despite high levels of treatment with RAASi at initial biopsy, a substantial portion of patients have high proteinuria levels at follow-up, indicating an unmet need.

title: #2537 Impact of potassium binders on RASi continuation and outcomes in patients with CKD and heart failure: a swedish national cohort study (DEMONSTRATE)
authors: Hans Furuland; Anders Larsson; Milica Uhde; Thomas Cars; Matilda Almstedt; Maria K Svensson
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyperkalemia is a common complication in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and/or heart failure (HF) treated with renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (RASi). Potassium binders are used to manage hyperkalemia, but their impact on RASi continuation, healthcare utilization and outcomes remains unclear.
Method
We conducted a retrospective cohort study using national data from the DEMONSTRATE database (Sweden), identifying patients with CKD and/or HF who received at least one RASi prescription within 120 days prior to initiation of potassium binder treatment. We further restricted the analysis to only include those potassium binder episodes with at least 180 days of follow-up. We described first and second-generation potassium binders with regard to RASi continuation, comorbid conditions and inpatient care.
Results
Among 10,177 episodes of potassium binder treatment for hyperkalemia, 75.9% had maintained RASi therapy at 180 days. Of those 40.5% also remained on their potassium binder at 180 days, compared to 25.5% of those who discontinued or down-titrated RASi (Table 1). Within the first 180 days of potassium binder treatment, inpatient care was more frequent among those who discontinued or down-titrated RASi than those who maintained RASi (53.4% vs. 35.3%) (Table 1, Fig. 1A). We also observed higher mortality in the former, compared to those who had maintained RASi (Fig. 1B). Notably, the group that discontinued or down-titrated RASi tended to be older (median age 73 vs. 71 years), had higher proportion of HF, and had more inpatient care prior to starting a potassium binder (74.3% vs. 59.3%; Table 1 and Fig. 1A). The most pronounced decline in RASi use post–potassium binder initiation was observed among incident users of first-generation potassium binder. The decline was less pronounced in those with prior use of a first-generation binder or those receiving a second-generation binder regardless of whether they were incident or prior users of potassium binders (Fig. 1C).
Conclusion
Discontinuation or down-titration of RASi therapy was associated with increased inpatient admissions and mortality, although underlying differences in disease severity may have contributed to this finding. Our results also indicate that second-generation potassium binders may help support continued RASi therapy in patients with CKD and/or HF. Further research is required to evaluate the causal relationships between first- and second-generation potassium binder use, RASi continuation, and outcomes in patients with CKD and/or HF.

title: #2660 Implications of integrating the kidney failure risk equation into nephrology referrals from primary care
authors: Mario Román Cabezas; Alba Temprado Collado; María Cristina Sánchez-Pozo; Francisco Javier Toro Prieto; Miguel Ángel Pérez Valdivia
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects more than 10% of the global population, representing a significant burden on healthcare systems. Early identification and effective management of CKD are essential to prevent progression to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). Current KDIGO (kidney disease: Improving Global Outcomes) guidelines (2024) recommend referral to nephrology for patients with severe CKD, defined as albuminuria (urine Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio [uACR] >300 mg/g) or an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <30 mL/min/1.73 m². However, these criteria may lead to over-referral, saturating nephrology services and delaying care for patients at higher risk.
The Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE) is a validated tool that estimates the 5-year risk of kidney failure based on age, sex, eGFR, and uACR. While KDIGO guidelines focus on disease severity, relying on static thresholds for uACR and eGFR, KFRE incorporates a dynamic risk prediction, offering a more individualized and targeted approach. This study evaluates the potential impact of integrating the 5-year KFRE (≥5% risk threshold) into the referral process compared to KDIGO criteria in the province of Seville, Spain, which serves approximately 1.6 million inhabitants.
Method
A retrospective analysis was conducted on referrals from primary care to nephrology at Hospital Universitario Virgen del Rocío during the first semester of 2024. Inclusion criteria were adult patients (≥18 years) with uACR and eGFR (calculated using the 2021 CKD-EPI equation) recorded at least three weeks before referral. Patients were categorized as eligible for referral based on KDIGO guidelines (uACR >300 mg/g and/or eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²) or a KFRE 5-year risk >5%. Statistical analysis was performed using McNemar's test with a 99.5% confidence interval (R version 4.1.2). Results are summarized in Table 1.
Results
Out of 584 referrals, 298 (51%) met the inclusion criteria. The results are shown in Table 1. The application of KFRE criteria reduced referrals by 20.9% overall compared to KDIGO guidelines, particularly in younger patients (aged 18–60), where referrals decreased by 66.7% (P ≤ 0.005). In this age group, KFRE criteria identified one high-risk case not detected by KDIGO guidelines, whereas KDIGO guidelines identified 21 cases not detected by KFRE criteria. For older patients (aged 61–100), KFRE criteria reduced referrals by 9.8% (P = 0.1189) and uniquely identified 19 cases compared to 31 by KDIGO guidelines.
These findings suggest that the 5-year KFRE ≥5% criteria provide a more targeted approach to identify high-risk patients, potentially reducing unnecessary referrals. However, the overlap and divergence between the methods highlight the need for careful consideration of patient characteristics in referral decisions.
Conclusion
The incorporation of 5-year KFRE ≥5% criteria into the referral process could reduce nephrology referrals by over 20%, prioritizing individuals at higher risk of kidney failure. In doing so, KFRE may enhance the efficiency of CKD management, alleviate the burden on nephrology services, and help avoid the psychological stress associated with a severe diagnosis. Future studies should investigate the long-term outcomes of KFRE-guided referrals and its integration into clinical practice across diverse healthcare settings.

title: #1986 Clinical practice gaps in the diagnosis and management of immunoglobulin a nephropathy
authors: Elaine Bell; Rita Moreira Da Silva; Bobby Chacko
abstract:
Background and Aims
Immunoglobulin A Nephropathy (IgAN) is the most common glomerular disease worldwide [1]. Clinical presentation and prognosis for IgAN is heterogenous, therefore effective management requires an individualized approach.
The goal of this activity was for learners to better understand the impact of IgAN on patients' lives, the immunopathogenesis of IgAN, the rationale for novel therapies, the mechanism of action (MOA) and key clinical data for recently approved therapies, and how best to manage patients with IgAN to optimize outcomes.
Method
A 26-question, online, CPD-accredited survey was developed, including knowledge, case-based (competence), and confidence questions. Evidence-based feedback and peer responses highlighted correct responses. The activity launched on 17 May, 2024 and data were collected through 6 September, 2024. We report data for ex US nephrologists who completed all the activity questions.
Results
395 nephrologists completed all questions within the data collection timeframe
Conclusion
This activity uncovered significant gaps in knowledge, competence and confidence related to the impact of IgAN on patients' lives, the immunopathogenesis of IgAN, the rationale for novel therapies and MOA, and key clinical data for recently approved therapies.
As the treatment landscape for IgAN continues to evolve, these results support the need for further education on evolving best practice for the diagnosis, assessment and management of IgAN. This would be beneficial in supporting nephrologists to translate knowledge into clinical practice in order to optimize outcomes for patients.

title: #3416 Development and validation of a prediction model for progression of CKD in European children
authors: Jerome Harambat; Valentine Renaudeau; Xinbei Wan; Elke Wühl; Franz Schaefer; Karen Leffondré
abstract:
Background and Aims
Families and children with chronic kidney disease (CKD) often request prognostic information regarding their child's condition in order to understand its implications and plan for the future. However, prediction of when a child will progress to kidney failure and need kidney replacement therapy (KRT) remains challenging, which complicates planning for dialysis access and transplant. The Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE) has been shown to accurately discriminate risk of progression to kidney failure in children with mild to moderate CKD in the US but has some pitfalls. Our objective was to develop and validate a new easy-to-operate prediction model for progression of CKD in European children.
Method
We used data from the Cardiovascular Comorbidity in Children with CKD (4C) study for model development and from the ESCAPE trial for model validation. A new model (called « 4C equation ») was developed based on clinically relevant variables and variable selection using Random Survival Forest. The primary predictor was the new model which provides estimates of the risk of KRT over a 1-, 2-, 3-, and 4-year horizon. The model is a super landmark Cox model including 8 variables accounting for the last available value of all predictors at each landmark time (0,1,2,3,4 years). Comparisons were made with the KFRE. AUCs were used to compare discrimination of the risk for KRT by the 4C equation, and calibration was assessed by comparing the predicted risk of KRT with the observed KRT rates (calibration plots) and by the Brier score.
Results
622 children with CKD stage 3–4 from the 4C study and 362 children from the ESCAPE trial were included. Median follow-up time was 2.9 years in 4C (IQR 1.3–5.0) and 4.9 years in ESCAPE (IQR 2.8–5.8), respectively. Out of 622 children included in 4C, 291 (47%) reached the event of interest (dialysis n = 132, preemptive transplant n = 156, death n = 3). The 8-variable 4C equation included age, sex, baseline eGFR, albuminuria, cause of CKD, hemoglobin, iPTH and serum albumin. The model strongly discriminated the risk of KRT, with AUC of 0.85, 0.84, and 0.85 in 4C and 0.90, 0.88 and 0.90 in ESCAPE over a 2-, 3- and 4-year horizon, respectively. Regarding calibration, the predicted risk matched the observed KRT rates among children with lower risk of KRT (e.g., earlier stage CKD), but tended to over-predict KRT risk in patients with higher risk of KRT (e.g., more advanced CKD). Brier score remained excellent in the validation cohort. The 4C model showed better predictive performances than the KFRE.
Conclusion
The 4C equation is a simple tool that effectively predicts the risk of KRT in children with CKD in Europe although its performance in more advanced CKD is slightly less robust. A user-friendly App (Shiny on R studio) is under development and will allow clinicians to assess kidney failure risk in their routine practice and inform clinical decision making.
