title: #2620 High urinary TFF3 is a significant risk factor for rapid age-related loss of GFR in the general population
authors: Jon Viljar Norvik; Nikoline Rinde; Bjørn Eriksen; Ludvig Balteskard Rinde; Karl Brobak; Toralf Melsom
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a significant global health challenge, affecting over 800 million individuals worldwide. With prevalence rates projected to rise, there is an urgent need for effective strategies for early detection and management. Trefoil factor 3 (TFF3), a protein expressed by kidney tubular cells, has been proposed as a novel biomarker for glomerular filtration rate (GFR) decline. Previous studies using creatinine-based estimated GFR have shown TFF3 to correlate with the severity and progression of CKD. However, the performance of urinary TFF3 (uTFF3) as a biomarker for measured GFR decline in a general population has not been explored. This study aimed to investigate whether uTFF3 could serve as a biomarker for more rapid age-related loss of measured GFR using iohexol clearance in a general population cohort.
Method
We conducted a prospective cohort study involving 1,316 participants aged 55 to 68 from the second Renal Iohexol Clearance Study (RENIS, 2014–2015). At inclusion in the first RENIS (2007–2008), participants self-reported being free from CKD, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes mellitus. Over a median follow-up period of 5.3 years, participants underwent two to three GFR measurements using iohexol clearance. Urinary TFF3 levels were normalized to creatinine (uTFF3/Cr) and log2 transformed. We utilized linear mixed models to assess the relationship between uTFF3/Cr levels and the rate of GFR decline. Additionally, logistic regression was employed to investigate the association between uTFF3/Cr level tertiles and accelerated GFR decline, defined as the 10% of participants with the steepest decline rates.
Results
The cohort consisted of 50% women, with a median age of 64.1 years. The average GFR was 89.1 ml/min/1.73 m2 and the mean annual GFR decline rate was 1.31 ml/min/1.73 m2. After adjusting for traditional CKD risk factors, including the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR), higher uTFF3/Cr levels were associated with a steeper GFR decline of 0.33 ml/min/1.73 m² for each doubling of uTFF3/Cr (P < 0.001). When participants were divided into tertiles based on uTFF3/Cr levels, those in the highest uTFF3/Cr level tertile had an odds ratio of 2.23 for accelerated GFR decline, compared to those in the lowest tertile, in the fully adjusted model (P = 0.002).
Conclusion
In the general population, elevated uTFF3/Cr levels were a risk factor for steeper GFR decline, independently of ACR and traditional CKD risk factors. These findings suggest that uTFF3/Cr could serve as a tubular biomarker for early GFR loss, addressing a gap in medical practice not filled by conventional CKD biomarkers such as serum creatinine and ACR.

title: #3248 Adjustment of glomerular filtration rate by BSA: an unnecesary error in estimating renal function
authors: Sergio Luis Lima; Patricia Isabel Delgado Mallén; Beatriz Escamilla Cabrera; Sara Estupiñán Torres; Domingo Marrero Miranda; Ana González Rinne; Carlos Alayón; Pablo Jorge Pérez; Coriolano Cruz; Federico Gonzalez Rinne; Laura Díaz Martin; Esteban Porrini
abstract:
Background and Aims
Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the main index of renal function in clinical practice and research. GFR is used to assess renal function at fixed points and to check the evolution of renal disease evolution over time, the response of the kidneys to diverse treatments, to adjust potentially toxic drugs and to establish risk for cardiovascular events and disease progression. Renal function is usually adjusted for body surface area (BSA) by Dubois-Dubois formula, a rudimentary and inexact method to estimate BSA. Also, the indexation of GFR for BSA was based on the hypothesis of the proportionality between metabolic rate and BSA, published at the end of 19th century. This assumption has no scientific basis since metabolic rate is linked to nutritional and maintenance fluid requirements rather that weight or BSA. Later, GFR started to be reported adjusted to a “standard” body surface area of 1.73 m2. Despite these limitations, indexing GFR by the Dubois–Dubois formula is widely used. Additionally, adjusting renal function for BSA has very little impact on GFR in individuals of normal body size, but a large impact by artificially adding or subtracting renal function in patients with extreme body surface areas very different (higher or lower) from 1.73 m2. Furthermore, the adjustment for BSA does not take gender into account, thus ignoring the differences between men and women in this regard. However, the difference between adjusted and unadjusted GFR by gender has been seldom evaluated in a wide cohort. The present study aimed to evaluate the impact of the adjustment of GFR by BSA in our whole cohort of patients with and without CKD.
Method
We evaluated renal function by the plasma clearance of iohexol using dried blood spot technique (iohexol-DBS) at the Renal Function Laboratory of the University of La Laguna in 2389 patients with CKD of diverse aetiologies. We reported measured GFR at Hospital Universitario de Canarias as unadjusted in ml/min. Then, we adjusted the result by applying the formula (GFR unadjusted = GFR adjusted × BSA/1.73). BSA was calculated by DuBois and DuBois formula (BSA = 0.007184 × Weight0.425 × Height0.725). We then analyzed the difference in adjusted GFR compared to the unadjusted GFR by gender. We analyzed the number of cases with a percent difference between both values using a cut-off of 15%. In addition, we analyzed subgroups of men and women with extreme BSAs far from the 1.73 m2 standard: >2.00 and <1.50, to evaluate how adjustment of GFR by BSA affects this subpopulation of patients.
Results
Of the total of 2389 patients, 1561 (65%) were men and 827 (35%) women: 20% had advanced CKD (pre-dialysis), 27% CKD of diverse causes, 19% diabetes, 9% were living kidney donors and 15% kidney transplant recipients and 10% had other causes i.e. non-renal transplantation, cirrhosis, heart failure, etc. In men the mean unadjusted GFR was 61 ± xx ml/min in men, while the BSA-adjusted GFR was 53 ± xx ml/min/1.73 m2. However, in women the adjusted and unadjusted GFR were similar 59 ± xx ml/min or ml/min/1.73 m2. Around half of the men (n = 743, 47%) while only 10% of women (80 of 827) BSA adjustment led to a reduction in GFR with differences < −15% between unadjusted and BSA-adjusted GFR. In men, the average reduction of GFR with BSA adjustment was –24%, distributed as follows: 34% from −15 to −20%; 45% from −20 to −30% and 21% greater than −30%. Only 5 of 1561 male while 53 of 827 women (6%) had an increment > 15%.
Conclusion
The BSA adjustment differentially penalizes male subjects with and without CKD, particularly in those with larger height and/or weight, both variables of the Dobois-Dubois formula used to adjust the GFR, with a false mean reduction of 24% of GFR observed in almost half of the cases. However, this does not occur in women because the latter's body surface area is more similar to the 1.73 m2 standard. Adjustment for renal function should be abandoned because there is no scientific basis for it, and it may overestimate the degree of renal function in almost half of male patients.

title: #3179 Evaluating the association between iron deficiency status and outcomes in patients with non-dialysis dependent chronic kidney disease
authors: Hannah O'keeffe; Firas Altheyaib; Sharmilee Rengarajan; Rajkumar Chinnadurai; Philip A Kalra
abstract:
Background and Aims
Iron deficiency is common in chronic kidney disease (CKD) and may result from either functional or absolute iron deficiency. We postulated that the presence of functional iron deficiency in patients with non-dialysis CKD (NDCKD) is associated with poorer outcomes including increased cardiovascular events and mortality.
Method
CKD patients who received their first dose of an iron infusion in our organisation between January 2017 and December 2019 were included, with follow-up through to December 2023. Demographic, comorbidity, treatment, laboratory, and outcome data were extracted from the organisation's electronic patient record. Of 852 patient records reviewed, 831 had the required data on iron indices and treatments and were included in the study. Patients were categorised into three groups based on iron deficiency status generated by one year time-averaged ferritin and transferrin saturation (TSAT) 12 months before their iron infusion: functional iron deficiency (FID) with transferrin saturation (TSAT) <20% and ferritin >100 µg/ml, absolute iron deficiency (AID) with TSAT <20% and ferritin ≤100 µg /ml, and standard iron parameters (no iron deficiency - NID). Analyses were performed using SPSS software.
Results
Of the 831 patients included, 298 (35.8%) had FID, 321 (38.6%) AID, and 212 (26.0%) NID. Baseline characteristics and outcomes are compared across the groups in Table 1. Patients with FID were older with a median age of 72 (IQR 61–81; P = 0.001) years. 51% of patients with FID, and 45.3% of patients with AID had a history of diabetes mellitus, compared to 36.8% of those with NID (P = 0.024). Median time-averaged ferritin was highest in those with FID (234 µg/ml), and lowest in those with AID (39 µg/ml), (P < 0.001). Median time-averaged TSAT was 13% in those with AID, 15% in those with FID, and 24% in those with NID (P < 0.001). A higher proportion of patients with NID had CKD stages 4 and 5 (FID: 77% vs AID: 64% vs NID: 88%; P < 0.001) as reflected by their lower median baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) (FID: 22 vs AID: 26 vs NID: 17 ml/min/1.73 m2; P < 0.001). Over a median follow-up of 38.5 months, a higher proportion of patients in the FID group died (FID: 62% vs AID: 49.5% vs NID: 46.2%; P = 0.001), and a lower proportion reached renal replacement therapy (FID: 31.9% vs AID: 22.7% vs NID: 45.8; P < 0.001). There were no significant differences between the groups with regard to cardiovascular events, hospitalisations, and erythropoietin stimulating agents or blood transfusion requirements. (Table 1). Multivariate Cox regression models showed factors including a higher age [HR:1.03; CI: 1.02–1.04; P < 0.001], any cardiovascular event history [HR:1.54; CI: 1.11–2.13; P = 0.009], cancer history, lower eGFR at baseline and FID status [HR:1.46; CI: 1.07–2.01; P = 0.017] to have a significant association with all-cause mortality. The Kaplan-Meir chart demonstrates the cumulative survival being significantly lower in patients with FID (Log-rank P < 0.001) (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
Both FID and AID were common in this cohort with NDCKD. No differences in cardiovascular events or hospitalisation episodes were found between the groups. In this cohort, those with NID had more advanced CKD (median eGFR 17 ml/min/1.73 m2) and were more likely to progress to renal replacement therapy. Functional iron deficiency status was found to have strong and independent association with all-cause mortality.

title: #2137 Impact of glomerular hyperfiltration on albuminuria in populations with obesity: an analysis on NHANES (1999-2018)
authors: Kaixin Lei; Ao Chen; Xinqi An; Qinbo Yang; Yupei Li; Baihai Su
abstract:
Background and Aims
Glomerular hyperfiltration (GHF) is the preclinical stage of chronic kidney disease caused by systematic metabolism disorders. However, the relationship between GHF and albuminuria in obese people still remains unclear. This research aims at exploring the association between GHF and albuminuria in U.S. obese adults.
Method
This cross-sectional study included 6363 obese people with complete report on serum creatinine and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UCAR) from 1999-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). According to age and sex-specific estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) percentiles, which was calculated by Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration equations, patients were categorized into 5 cohorts, namely <5th (low filtration), 5th-25th, 25th–75th, 75th–95th, >95th (GHF). Increased albumin excretion/albuminuria was defined as UACR>30mg/g. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression were employed to investigate the correlation between GHF and albuminuria. Additionally, restrictive cubic spline function was further utilized to assess non-linear association of eGFR and albuminuria. Subgroup and interactive analysis were performed to evaluate the underlying effect of covariates.
Results
The final analysis included 2901 male and 3462 female people, of whom 957 (11.7%) were identified as albuminuria. Our research showed that GHF was significantly associated with albuminuria after adjustment of covariates (OR 1.87, 95% CI 1.27–2.77, P = 0.002). Subgroup analysis showed that age may be an influential factor in the association between GHF and albuminuria (P = 0.018). Restrictive cubic spline indicated a U-shape association between eGFR and ORs of albuminuria both in male and female (p for non-linear <0.0001). Sensitivity analysis supported the independent effect between GHF and albuminuria.
Conclusion
GHF was positively correlated to increased risks of albuminuria in obese people, while age< 45 may serve as a susceptible factor. The risk of albuminuria increases accompanying with eGFR growth, indicating a U-shape curve both in male and female.

title: #2380 CT coronary angiography to identify patients at increased risk of developing chronic kidney disease
authors: Gavin Chapman; Peter Gallacher; Eve Miller-Hodges; Dorien Kimenai; Marie de Bakker; Evangelos Tzolos; Edwin van Beek; Marc Dweck; Nicholas Mills; David Newby; Michelle Williams; Neeraj Dhaun
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is common and cardiovascular disease is its commonest complication. Identifying patients at risk of developing CKD is an unmet clinical need. Computed tomography coronary angiography (CTCA) is used to diagnose patients with coronary artery disease but may also provide an opportunity to identify those at risk of developing future CKD.
Method
In a post-hoc analysis of a multicentre randomised controlled trial of CTCA in patients with suspected angina, we analysed routinely collected biochemistry data from time of enrolment. The primary outcome was development of CKD defined by estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) criteria.
Results
Overall, 1,487 patients (58 ± 9 years; 58% male) were eligible for inclusion (baseline eGFR 94 ± 12 mL/min/1.73 m2): 809 patients were randomised to standard of care and 678 were randomised to CTCA plus standard of care. Over a median follow-up of 10.6 years, 247 patients (16.6%) developed CKD irrespective of trial allocation (17.9% versus 15.0%; P = 0.14). Compared to those who retained normal kidney function, those who developed CKD were older (63 ± 7 years versus 57 ± 9 years; P < 0.001), had a higher body mass index (BMI) (31.1 ± 5.9 kg/m2versus 29.3 ± 5.8 kg/m2; P < 0.001), and were more likely to have a history of coronary artery disease (16% versus 11%; P = 0.024), diabetes mellitus (18% versus 10%; P < 0.001), and hypertension (53% versus 33%; P < 0.001). Patients who underwent CTCA and developed CKD had a higher coronary artery calcium score (126 versus 34 AU; P < 0.001), were more likely to have obstructive coronary disease (52% versus 30%; P < 0.001) and aortic valve calcification (18% versus 8%; P = 0.002), and had greater coronary plaque burden (46.9% versus 41.6%; P = 0.002) than patients who underwent CTCA but did not develop CKD. After adjustment for known CKD risk factors (i.e., age, sex, baseline kidney function, BMI, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, smoking status), obstructive coronary artery disease independently associated with the development of CKD (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], 2.66 [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.38–5.11]; P = 0.003). In addition, obstructive coronary artery disease was more strongly associated with the development of CKD than baseline eGFR (aHR per 2.5 mL/min/1.73 m2 lower eGFR: 1.24 [95% CI 1.19–1.30]; P < 0.001) or diabetes mellitus (aHR 2.06 [95% CI 1.23–3.45]; P = 0.006) (Fig. 1). Furthermore, total (aHR per doubling, 1.14 [95% CI 1.02–1.27]; P = 0.020) non-calcified (aHR per doubling, 1.14 [95% CI 1.02–1.27]; P = 0.020), and low-attenuation (aHR per doubling, 1.28 [95% CI 1.06–1.54]; P = 0.009) plaque burden independently associated with incident CKD. The inclusion of obstructive coronary artery disease improved the performance of a multivariable model incorporating known clinical risk factors (i.e., age, sex, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, baseline eGFR) to predict 5-year and 10-year risk of developing CKD.
Conclusion
The presence and extent of coronary artery disease on CTCA independently associates with the development of future CKD therefore potentially identifying those patients most likely to benefit from evidence-based renoprotective therapies.

title: #1742 Impact of cardiorenal unit management on care outcomes: the role of heart failure therapy optimization
authors: Eliecer Soriano Payá; Ana María García Girón; Ismael Arco Adamuz; Francisco José Bermúdez Jiménez; Silvia López Fernández; María José Espigares Huete
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiorenal syndrome (CRS), encompassing heart failure (HF) and chronic kidney disease (CKD), poses significant challenges due to high prevalence and mortality. As CKD progresses, hospitalizations for decompensated HF become increasingly frequent and are linked to higher rates of readmissions, particularly in patients with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 30 mL/min/1.73 m² compared to mild-to-moderate CKD. Although evidence supports cardiorenal protective therapies for HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), advanced CKD often limits therapeutic optimization due to perceived risks, contributing to therapeutic inertia, particularly the reluctance to initiate such treatments in this specific patient population. Cardiorenal units (CRUs) address CRS complexity through multidisciplinary care. This study evaluates the impact of CRU management on outcomes in CRS patients with advanced CKD and explores the role of HF therapy optimization.
Method
A prospective, single-center observational study using an adapted interrupted time series model to compare conventional care with a multidisciplinary approach was designed at the CRU of our center. Patients with HFrEF (< 50%) and eGFR < 30 were included. Patients undergoing renal replacement therapy at baseline were excluded. Recruitment lasted two years, with one-year follow-up per patient. Outcomes included emergency visits and cardiovascular (CV) hospitalizations in the year before and during CRU follow-up. Retrospective data for the prior year were extracted from electronic records. CV events included HF decompensation, coronary artery disease, arrhythmias, cerebrovascular events, peripheral vascular disease, and CV-related renal complications. Baseline and follow-up data at 3-month intervals included demographics, clinical parameters, and therapy. Triple therapy was defined as beta-blockers (BB), renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (RAASi) or angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitors (ARNI), and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRA); adding sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) constituted quadruple therapy.
Results
The cohort (n = 55, mean age 73.9 ± 8.6 years; 78% male) had baseline left ventricular ejection fraction 40.1 ± 9.3% (70.9% ≤ 40%), eGFR 22.3 ± 7.61 mL/min/1.73 m², and potassium 4.52 ± 0.64 mEq/L. Pre-CRU prescription rates were 75.7% (RAASi/ARNI), 51.3% (MRA), 59.5% (SGLT2i), and 94.6% (BB), with triple and quadruple therapy rates of 45.95% and 27.03%, respectively. Significant increase in MRA and SGLT2i prescriptions were observed from the 9th month (P = 0.025) and 3rd month (P = 0.028), respectively. As a result, there was a significant increase in patients receiving both triple (P = 0.049) and quadruple therapy (P = 0.001) (Fig. 1). No significant changes in eGFR or potassium occurred, and no MRA discontinuations due to hyperkalemia were noted. For the stratified analysis by prescribed therapy, patients were divided into two groups based on their treatment during follow-up. Quadruple therapy (n = 29, 52.7%) was associated with reduced emergency visits (P = 0.02) and hospitalizations (P = 0.01), while non-quadruple therapy (47.27%) showed reductions in visits (P = 0.001) but not hospitalizations (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
The findings of this study highlight the effectiveness of a multidisciplinary CRS management program for high-risk patients. Notably, we observed increased prescription rates of triple and quadruple therapies in patients with advanced eGFR impairment, suggesting that a collaborative approach facilitates optimal titration and sustained use of evidence-based treatments. Furthermore, the program led to a significant reduction in emergency department visits and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations, with additional benefits associated with quadruple therapy prescription.

title: #1327 Prognostic value of N-terminal prohormone B-type natriuretic peptide modified by renal function in patients with acute heart failure
authors: Rui Zhu; Yaoyao Wang; Zhanyuan Chen; Yu Wei; Jian-Fang Cai
abstract:
Background and Aims
It remains unclear whether renal function and follow-up duration impact the prognostic value of N-terminal prohormone B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) in patients with heart failure (HF).
Method
A nationwide prospective cohort study was conducted in 4907 adults hospitalized for acute HF, of whom 4766 were eligible for analysis. We used Cox regression to estimate the relative risks and Poisson regression to assess the absolute risks of adverse outcomes associated with NT-proBNP levels at admission. Effect modification by renal function was tested in both Cox and Poisson models.
Results
Over a median follow-up period of 4.6 years, patients with the middle and highest NT-proBNP tertiles had hazard ratios (HRs) (95% CI) of 1.40 (1.24–1.58) and 2.14 (1.88–2.43) for all-cause mortality, 1.59 (1.37–1.84) and 2.34 (2.00–2.74) for cardiovascular mortality, 1.61 (1.35–1.91) and 2.24 (1.87–2.68) for 1-year major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE), and 1.25 (1.09–1.43) and 1.51 (1.30–1.76) for 1-year hospitalization for heart failure (HHF), respectively, compared to those with the lowest NT-proBNP tertile. These associations diminished over time. The associations between NT-proBNP levels and the risks of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, 1-year MACE, and 1-year HHF (P-for-interaction = 0.001, 0.007, 0.005, and 0.008, respectively) were modified by estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) levels, remaining significant yet weaker in HF patients with eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m2. The incidence rates of adverse outcomes at the same NT-proBNP level were higher in HF patients with lower eGFR (P-for-interaction = 0.011, 0.023, 0.031, and 0.065, respectively).
Conclusion
NT-proBNP levels demonstrated graded associations with the risks of adverse outcomes. As eGFR reduced, its excessive relative risks attenuated, while its absolute risks increased. The associations waned over an extended follow-up period. These findings highlight the prognostic significance of NT-proBNP in patients with reduced renal function and underscore the necessity of its dynamic monitoring.

title: #1744 Impact of kidney transplantation on chronic kidney disease-associated pruritus
authors: Vaibhav Tiwari; Vidhi Singla; Manish Malik; Anil Kumar Bhalla; Ashwani Gupta; Vinant Bhargava; Anurag Gupta; Rajdeb Saha
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic Kidney Disease-associated Pruritus (CKD-aP), also referred to as uremic pruritus (UP), is a common complication with a prevalence ranging from 18% to 80%, and approximately 40% of patients reporting severe symptoms. Interleukin-31 (IL-31), often termed the “itch cytokine,” has been implicated in the pathogenesis of pruritus in various dermatological disorders. This study aimed to evaluate changes in pruritus severity and serum IL-31 levels before and after kidney transplantation, and to determine the correlation between these parameters.
Method
A prospective observational study was conducted at Sir Ganga Ram Hospital, New Delhi, involving patients with CKD stage V who were scheduled for renal transplantation. Pruritus was assessed using the 5D Itch Scale, and serum IL-31 levels were measured pre- and post-transplant. A total of 202 patients were screened; 89 of these had pruritus, and 86 were ultimately included in the analysis (after excluding those with primary skin disorders).
Results
Among the 86 patients with pruritus, 75.5% were male. The dialysis vintage ranged from four preemptive transplants to a maximum of 60 months on dialysis. Mean serum IL-31 levels significantly decreased from 145.02 ± 103.27 pg/mL pre-transplant to 89.91 ± 59.51 pg/mL post-transplant (P < 0.001), alongside a significant reduction in mean 5D itch scores from 15.03 ± 4.36 to 7.44 ± 2.11 (P < 0.001). One month post-transplant, 63.9% of patients reported complete resolution of pruritus, 29.1% had mild pruritus, and 6.9% experienced moderate pruritus. Post-transplant itch scores demonstrated a moderate positive correlation with IL-31 levels (r = 0.411, P = 0.001). Changes in itch scores from pre- to post-transplant also positively correlated with changes in serum IL-31 (r = 0.464, P = 0.001).
Conclusion
Kidney transplantation leads to a significant reduction in both pruritus severity and serum IL-31 levels in patients with CKD-aP. These findings highlight the potential role of IL-31 as a biomarker for pruritus and offer insights into targeted therapeutic strategies for CKD-associated pruritus.

title: #502 The potential of share wave elastography in renal imaging
authors: Paolo Albrizio; Annalisa Foschi; Ivo Angelo Antonio Milani; Silvia Muciaccia; Stefano Rindi; Manuela Zucchi; Fabio Milanesi
abstract:
Background and Aims
the ultrasound elastography includes several techniques, qualitative or quantity, static or dynamic, to evaluate tissue stiffness, with a widespread coded use for liver study. Less studied are applications in renal evaluation due to organ depth in abdomen and parenchymal structure complexity with cortical, medulla and high vascularization. Many kind of ultrasound elastographies are available, one of these, the Share Wave Elastography (SWE) is a quantity, static, technique characterized by an induced strain highly localized in tissues with the remotely induced shear waves fully attenuated within a very limited area of tissue in the proximity of the focal point of the focused ultrasound beam. The analysis can be obtained by measuring the shear wave speed (SWS) in m/s and parenchymal stiffness (PS) in kPa with multiple samples of each kidney calculating median (MED) and standard deviation (SD). Harder tissues due to fibrotic changes are associated with higher shear-wave velocities.
Method
we evaluated patients afferent to our ultrasound clinic for evaluation of urinary system between September and November 2024. We excluded patients with renal depth > 5 cm due to abdominal fat, those with unpaired capacity of inspiratory apnoea and those with measurement standard deviation>30%. We selected 53 patients and subjected them to SWE with 5 measurement for each kidney and the software of our ultrasound machine automatically calculated SWS and PS MED and SD in m/s and kPa. For each patient we assessed: age, sex, hypertension or type 2 diabetes comorbidities, glomerular filtration rate (GFR) stage as KDIGO classification. Statistical analysis was done calculating paired t-Test.
Results
we evaluated 35 males and 18 female, medium age 61.6 ± 16.9 years, SWS and PS MED±SD was 3.5 ± 0.8 m/s and 21.1 ± 8.1 kPa. 16 patients were affected by hypertension and 12 by both hypertension and diabetes. 21 patient were GFR stage 1, 16 were GFR stage 2, 10 were GFR stage 3, 6 were GFR stage 4–5.
Evaluating patients by age (<50, between 50–70 and >70 years old) we find out that < 50 years old patients showed a SWS and PS MED±SD significantly lower than 50–70 and >70 years old (respectively 2.9 ± 0.8 vs 3.7 ± 0.7 and 3.6 ± 0.7 m/s; 15.5 ± 7.9 vs 23.6 ± 7.1 and 22.1 ± 8 kPa. P < 0.05). Fig. 1
Evaluating patients by comorbidities (none, hypertension, hypertension + diabetes) we find out that patients affected by diabetes showed significantly higher SWS and PS MED ± SD vs patient without diabetes, regardless of the presence of hypertension (respectively 3.8 ± 0.7 vs 3.3 ± 1 and 3.4 ± 0.7 m/s; 25 ± 7.9 vs 19.7 ± 9.2 and 20.21 ± 7.2 kPa. P < 0.05). Fig. 2
Evaluating patients according KDIGO GFR stage (stage 1≥90 ml/min, stage 2 between 60–89 ml/min, stage 3 between 30–59 ml/min and stage 4–5≤29 ml/min) we find out that patients with GFR stage 4–5 had significantly higher SWS and PS MED ± SD vs patients in GFR stage 1 or 2 (respectively 3.9 ± 0.8 vs 3.3 ± 0.9 and 3.4 ± 0.7 m/s; 26.2 ± 9 vs 19.5 ± 9 and 20.9 ± 7.6 kPa. P < 0,05) and aggregated GFR stages 1–2 shower a significantly lower SWS and PS MED ± SD vs GFR stages 3–5 (respectively 3.4 ± 0.8 vs 3.7 ± 0.7 m/s; 20.1 ± 8.3 vs 23.4 ± 7.5 kPa. P < 0,05). Figs 3 and 4
Conclusion
ultrasound elastography is an unexpensive and relatively simple technique already widespread coded for liver study. Regardless renal parenchymal complexity, our data show how it's possible to use a specific type of elastography, SWE, in selected patients to evaluate parenchymal stiffness and correlate it with comorbidities and kidney function.

title: #2635 Effects of a nutrition education program on quality of life and morphofunctional status in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease: ERCANUT randomized clinical trial
authors: Marina Padial; Ana Rebollo; Tamara Jiménez Salcedo; Verónica López; Carla Maria Avesani; Bengt Lindholm; Gabriel Olveira
abstract:
Background and Aims
Managing diet is essential for patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (ACKD, stages 4–5 non-dialysis), but its complexity often leads to poor adherence, negatively affecting quality of life (QoL) and health outcomes. The ERCANUT trial evaluated the effects of a structured nutrition education program (NEP) using coaching methodology on QoL, psychological well-being, dietary adherence, morphofunctional status, and biochemical parameters in ACKD patients.
Method
This randomized clinical trial included 76 patients with ACKD (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²) attending a nephrology unit at the Regional Hospital of Málaga. Participants were randomized into two groups: NEP group (n = 38), which received a structured nutrition education program (NEP) with an individualized Mediterranean diet (MedDiet), coaching-based workshops, and ongoing support from specialized healthcare professionals (nurse and dietitian); and control group (n = 38), which received general dietary recommendations.
Assessments were made at baseline and 3 months, including QoL (KDQOL-36), anxiety and depression (HADS), self-efficacy (SEMCD), CKD knowledge (KiKS), dietary adherence (PREDIMED), body composition (anthropometry and bioelectrical impedance analysis [BIA]), functional capacity (physical performance [SPPB], handgrip strength, and physical activity [IPAQ]), and biochemical markers.
The NEP featured three interactive workshops on healthy eating, lifestyle modifications, and physical activity, combined with continuous support via phone, text, and digital materials. The NEP group also received a personalized meal plan tailored to energy requirements, preferences, and physical activity.
Results
Of the 76 patients enrolled, 68 completed the study (NEP = 33; control = 35). Mean age: 70.1 years, 68% male, median eGFR: 22.0 mL/min/1.73 m² for both groups. Baseline characteristics showed no significant differences between groups.
The NEP group showed significant improvements across key outcomes:
Conclusion
This randomized clinical trial demonstrated that a NEP using coaching techniques, delivered by specialized healthcare professionals (dietitian and nurse), effectively improved QoL in ACKD patients. The intervention also reduced depression symptoms, increased self-confidence in chronic disease management, boosted CKD knowledge, enhanced diet adherence, and improved morphofunctional status. The control group, receiving non-personalized dietary counseling, showed improvements in body composition, diet adherence, and specific biomarkers.

title: #2242 Iohexol Clearance, but not estimated GFR, reveals a steeper GFR decline in persons with prediabetes—a population-based study
authors: Toralf Melsom; Karl Brobak; Jon Viljar Norvik; Inger Enoksen; Ludvig Balteskard Rinde; Trond Jenssen; Bjørn Eriksen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Prediabetes, an intermediate state between normoglycemia and type 2 diabetes (T2D), affects 750 million individuals worldwide and is associated with hyperfiltration, an early stage of diabetic kidney disease. It remains unclear whether prediabetes is an independent risk factor for long-term kidney function loss, potentially due to the use of imprecise and inaccurate glomerular filtration rate (GFR) estimates in previous studies.
Method
In a prospective longitudinal study of middle-aged Europeans without baseline diabetes, cardiovascular disease, or kidney disease, we measured the GFR (mGFR) using iohexol clearance at baseline (n = 1594) after a median (IQR) of 5.6 (5.2–6.0) years (n = 1299), and 11.0 (10.6 – 11.6) years (n = 1151). A linear mixed model was used to estimate the GFR slope. Accelerated GFR decline was defined as the 10% steepest GFR decline. For comparison, we estimated GFR (eGFR) based creatinine and Cystatin C using the CKDepi equations.
Prediabetes was defined according to the World Health Organization (prediabetesWHO) as fasting glucose (FPG) 6.1–6.9 mmol/l; or according to the American Diabetes Association (prediabetesADA) as FPG 5.6–6.9 mmol/l or HbA1c 5.7%–6.4% (39–46 mmol/mol).
Results
In fully adjusted linear mixed models, people with either prediabetesWHO or prediabetesADA had steeper mean annual mGFR decline rates of 0.30 (95% confidence interval: 0.04 to 0.57) or 0.14 (0.01 to 0.28) mL/min per year. The odds ratios of accelerated GFR decline were 2.6 (95% CI 2.0–5.1) for prediabetesWHO (yes/no) and 2.0 (95% CI 1.3–3.0) for prediabetesADA (yes/no) (Table 1). Prediabetes was not associated with a steeper decline in eGFRcrea or eGFRcys (Table 1). The association between FPG and accelerated mGFR decline is illustrated in Fig. 1.
Conclusion
In a representative sample of Caucasians without diabetes, prediabetes was associated with an accelerated decline in mGFR but not in eGFR decline. Prediabetes may represent a window of opportunity to prevent hyperfiltration and GFR loss before the development of T2D and chronic kidney disease.

title: #2703 The associations of cardiac and stress bio-markers NT-proBNP and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF-15), with incidence and progression of CKD among people, living in war-affected region (Kharkiv, Ukraine). Save kidneys study, granted by Clinical Research Program of the ISN
authors: Olga Chub; Oleksandr Bilchenko; Oleg Chub
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a “silent” pandemia, which affects up to 10% of adults worldwide. Massive disasters, including war, have a devastating impact on the lives of people with CKD and its outcomes are more insidious. CKD with an eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 have a 2-fold higher risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD). However, war-inducible extreme stress, may predispose not only to an accelerated decline of kidney function, but increase the risk of short- and long-term complications, including CVD.
We evaluated the associations of cardiac and stress bio-markers [N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF-15), with incidence and progression of CKD among people, living in war-affected region (Kharkiv, Ukraine). Save Kidneys Study granted by Clinical Research Program of the ISN.
Method
We included 185 adult patients with CKD, who were living in the war-affected region, Kharkiv, Ukraine. Patients are divided onto two groups: diagnosis of CKD before 24 Feb 2022 (group 1), diagnosis of CKD after 24 Feb 2022 (group 2). All biomarkers were measured at entry. Presented results of the study is interim analysis of collected data. The design of the study, assessments and study procedures are specified in Table 1.
Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS 25.0 for Windows. Medians (Me) and interquartile ranges (IQR) were calculated. Associations with quantitative dependent variable were made by using linear regression. We used univariate and multivariate linear regression with simultaneous inclusion of variables and stepwise backward exclusion methods.
The study was approved by the local ethics committee and all participants have provided written informed consent.
Results
Since the first patient was randomized in the study (26 Dec 2023) we have examined 185 patients. The main age was 39.8 yo (IQR 19–80). According to the multivariate analysis the prevalence of CKD has increased from 24 Feb 2022 till know on 30.77% (Fig.1).
The median value of NT-proBNP in group 1 was 90,0 [50,5–163,0] pg/ml, whereas in group 2 was 74,0 [50,0–162,0] pg/ml, p=0.583.
The median values of studied markers depending on the CKD stage and time of CKD onset (Me [IQR)] are presented at Table 2.
Linear association of increase in CKD stage with NT-proBNP, GDF-15, urine albumin (MAU) and uACR levels showed that with progression of CKD stage levels of NT-proBNP also increased by 31,485 (95.0 % CI 16,161–46,810), P < 0.001; GDF-15 levels tended to decrease by −14,891 (95.0 % CI −33,146–3,365), P = 0.108; MAU significantly increased by 50,501 (95.0 % CI 1,667–99,337), P = 0.043; and uACR significantly increased by 12,885 (95.0 % CI 6,758–19,013), P < 0.001 (Fig. 2).
In general sample, eGFRcr significantly negatively correlated with NT-proBNP (P = 0.011), MAU (P = 0.012) and uACR (P = 0.001); positive non-significant correlation was found between eGFR and GDF-15. eGFRcys-c correlated significantly negatively with NT-proBNP (P = 0.010), MAU (P = 0.006) and uACR (P < 0.001); positive non-significant correlation was found between eGFRcys-c and GDF-15 (Fig. 3).
With every increase in eGFR analysis showed significantly decrease of NT-proBNP levels by −1,068 (95.0 % СІ −1,764–0,372), р = 0.003; non-significant increase of GDF-15 levels by 0,390 (95.0 % CI −0,405–1,185), P = 0.331; significant decrease of MAU by −2,274 (95.0 % CI −4,415–−9,134), P = 0.038; and significant decrease of uACR by −0,444 (95.0 % CI −0,719–−0,169), P = 0.002 (Fig. 4).
Conclusion
This is the first results of our study, main aim of which is to investigate the impact of armed conflict on the development and progression of CKD in individuals residing in affected areas. Also we found significant association between NT-proBNP with eGFR, uACR, GDF-15. Increases in NT-proBNP level is associated with decline of kidney function and CKD progression. These biomarkers may inform mechanisms underlying kidney injury.

title: #2529 Nanoparticle-mediated Klotho gene therapy prevents kidney disease progression via PPARα pathway
authors: Hongyu Li; Le Wang; Hanzi Liang; Yufei du; Siweier Luo; Haoran Lv; Yiming Zhou; Qinghua Liu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Klotho is an anti-aging protein produced primarily by tubular epithelial cells (TECs). Down-regulated expression of Klotho in injured TECs plays a key pathogenic role in promoting acute kidney injury (AKI) to chronic kidney disease (CKD) transition, yet therapeutic approaches targeting the restoration of renal Klotho levels remain challenging for clinical application.
Method
Polydopamine-polyethylenimine-l-serine-Klotho plasmid nanoparticles (PPSK NPs) were constructed that can safely and selectively deliver the Klotho gene to the injured TECs through binding kidney injury molecule-1 and maintain the expression of Klotho protein. Two acute kidney injury-chronic kidney disease transition animal models were used to investigate the effect of PPSK NPs in vivo.
Results
In vitro, PPSK NPs effectively reduce the hypoxia-reoxygenation-induced reactive oxygen species production and fibrotic gene expression. In the unilateral ischemia-reperfusion injury- and folic acid-induced AKI-CKD transition mouse models, a single low-dose injection of PPSK NPs is sufficient to preserve the normal kidney architecture and prevent renal fibrosis. Mechanistically, the protective effect of PPSK NPs relies on upregulating a key molecule peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) via the inhibition of p38 and JNK phosphorylation, which in turn improves tubular fatty acid beta-oxidation and reduces renal lipid accumulation, thereby protecting against kidney fibrosis.
Conclusion
In conclusion, our results highlight the translational potential of nanoparticle-based Klotho gene therapy in preventing the AKI-CKD transition.

title: #3001 The effect of prophylactic anticoagulation on major bleeding events in hospitalized chronic kidney disease and lower limb fracture patients. A phase 2, randomized, double blind, control trial
authors: Alejandro Martínez Gallardo-González; Guillermo Navarro Blackaller; Ramón Medina-González; Luz Alcantar-Vallin; Juan Alberto Gomez Fregoso; Gonzalo Rodrígez-García; Gabriela J Abundis-Mora; Jonathan S Chávez-Iñiguez
abstract:
Background and Aims
People with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) have an increased risk of lower limb fractures. During hospitalization with this event the risk of thrombosis increases so prophylactic anticoagulation is recommended. The risk of bleeding may be greater than the benefit of antithrombotic protection in this population. We aimed to assess if enoxaparin (anticoagulation) or placebo (no anticoagulation) are different in the occurrence of major bleeding and thrombosis.
Method
In a phase 2 randomized controlled trial, from March 2019 to October 2024, patients with lower limb fracture and advanced CKD were eligible. We randomly assigned 61 patients to the placebo (n = 30) and anticoagulation groups (enoxaparin 40 mg; n = 31). Primary outcome was the risk of major bleeding. The main secondary objectives were risk of thrombosis, death, number of transfusions, dialysis requirement, hospitalization days, and the adverse events (AEs) related to anticoagulation.
Results
Both groups were similar, mean (SD) age of 65 (19) years; 54% were women, the eGFR of 24 ml/min/1.73 m2. Hip fracture predominate (45.9%), followed by femur and tibia (31.1% and 23%, respectively). The primary outcome major bleeding occurred in 5 (16.1%) in the enoxaparin group and 4 (13.3%) in the placebo group. After adjusted analysis, comparing the enoxaparin with the placebo group, no increase in the risk of bleeding was observed (OR 1.28, CI 0.29–6.06, P = 0.741), nor was stratifying by CKD stages (P = >0.05). The frequency of thrombosis in 2 (6.7%) patients in the placebo and 1 (3.2%) in the enoxaparin group, with no difference between groups (P = 0.61). Hospitalization days were fewer in the placebo group compared to the enoxaparin group (14 vs 19, P = 0.023), reducing the hospital stay by 5.3 days (OR 5.31, 95% CI -10.52- -0.09, P = 0.046). AEs attributed to the intervention, gastrointestinal bleeding occurred in 2 and 1 patient in the placebo and enoxaparin groups, respectively.
Conclusion
In patients with advanced CKD and lower limb fracture, prophylactic anticoagulation with enoxaparin, compared with no anticoagulation, did not promote more major bleeding or prevent DVT, but prolong hospitalization by 5 days.

title: #915 Metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease in advanced chronic kidney disease: impact on patient survival
authors: Yaiza María Rivero Viera; Selene González Nuez; Fátima Batista García; Jesus Gonzalez Martin; Sonia Guinea; Antonio Tugores; Sara Aladro Escribano; Irene Suarez; Rita Guerra Rodríguez; Domingo Jerónimo Hernández Marrero; Mauro Boronat; Cesar García Canton
abstract:
Background and Aims
Metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) is a prevalent liver condition commonly associated with obesity, metabolic syndrome, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. It has also been linked to an increased risk of cardiovascular events and overall mortality. Recent studies have established pathophysiological connections between MAFLD and chronic kidney disease (CKD). This study aimed to determine the prevalence of MAFLD in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (ACKD), identify associated factors, and evaluate its impact on patient survival.
Method
A retrospective longitudinal cohort study was conducted with incident patients diagnosed with stage 4 or 5 CKD, not on dialysis, who initiated care for ACKD between 2011 and 2015. Clinical and laboratory data were collected, and the presence of MAFLD was estimated using the Fatty Liver Index (FLI). To assess the impact of FLI and other variables on survival, Kaplan–Meier univariate analysis and Cox regression multivariate analysis were performed, with follow-up through February 2024.
Results
Among 367 patients, 60.2% had diabetes, and 70.8% had an FLI ≥ 60. Patients with an FLI ≥ 60 were older, had a greater prevalence of diabetes, greater history of cardiovascular events, higher PCR levels and a lower serum albumin level. During follow-up, 149 patients (40.6%) died, 178 (48.5%) initiated RRT, 104 of whom died during the study period, 32 (8.7%) were still in treatment and eight (2.2%) were lost to follow-up. Kaplan–Meier univariate survival analysis showed that the FLI ≥ 60 group had lower survival censoring for RRT initiation and lower overall survival, also taking into account survival time to death after RRT initiation.
In multivariate Cox regression analysis FLI was identified as an independent risk factor for decreased survival in patients with diabetes, after adjusting for other variables (HR, 1.015; 95% CI 1.004–1.027; p = 0.009). However, in non-diabetic patients, FLI was not a significant predictor of lower survival in multivariate Cox regression analysis.
Conclusion
MAFLD is highly prevalent in patients with ACKD, particularly among those with diabetes, for whom it may represent an independent risk factor for reduced survival. This association was not observed in non-diabetic ACKD patients. These results suggest the need to design preventive and treatment strategies for MAFLD in this population.

title: #855 Severe chronic kidney disease increases the risk of appendicular fractures in postmenopausal women
authors: Satu Keronen; Louise Aaltonen; Patrik Finne; Heikki Kröger; Reijo Sund
abstract:
Background and Aims
Mineral and bone disease (MBD) is common in chronic kidney disease (CKD). MBD causes disarrangements in bone turnover, mineralization, volume, and microarchitecture, leading to reduced bone density and quality. In CKD stage 4–5 patients, an increased risk for fractures have been shown in abundant studies, but the effect of CKD stage 3 on bone fragility is more ambiguous. In this observational study we aimed to investigate the effect of renal dysfunction on fragility fractures in postmenopausal women.
Method
We conducted an analysis from the Kuopio Osteoporosis Risk Factor and Prevention (OSTPRE) Study, which is a population-based prospective cohort study. This study, started in 1989, aims to investigate factors associated with bone mineral density, bone loss, falls, and fractures in peri- and postmenopausal women. We identified all patients with at least two measurements of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) being more than 90 days from each other (n = 12 258, that is 93% of individuals with any recorded laboratory measurements and almost 86% of individuals alive at the beginning of 2012 from which point laboratory values were observed), and followed them for repeated eGFR measurements and fracture occurrence from the second measurement date until death or the end of year 2022. Cox regression model for repeated fracture outcome with time-dependent covariate for eGFR-based CKD severity and spline adjusted age was used to evaluate the risk of fractures among patients with severe CKD compared to patients with mild CKD.
Results
Of 12 258 patients with 85 970 person-years (pyrs) of follow-up, we observed 57 540 (67%) pyrs for CKD stage 2, 22 233 (26%) pyrs for CKD stage 3, 1 008 (1.2%) pyrs for CKD stage 4, and 129 (0.15%) pyrs for CKD stage 5. Compared to patients with eGFR 60–90 ml/min/1.73 m2 (CKD stage 2) patients, CKD stage 4–5 (eGFR < 30 ml/min/1.73 m2) was related to an increased risk of incident hip and humerus fracture and eGFR < 15 ml/min/1.73 m2 with ankle fractures. The risk was more pronounced in more severe CKD stage (adjusted HR 2.0 (95% CI 1.2–3.3) for hip fracture CKD stage 4 and 3.2 (95% CI 1.02–10.2) for CKD stage 5, respectively. For humerus fractures, adjusted HR was 2.3 (95% CI 1.2–4.3) for CKD stage 4 and 5.6 (95% CI 2.0–16) for CKD stage 5, respectively. For ankle fractures, adjusted HR was 4.5 (95% CI 1.2–17) for CKD 5. No elevated risk of wrist and vertebral fractures were detected for patients with eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2 compared to patients with 60–90ml/min/1.73 m2.
Conclusion
Compared to CKD stage 2 patients, CKD stage 4 or more advanced renal dysfunction was associated with an increased risk of appendicular, but not with central fractures in postmenopausal women. The risk of fractures increased progressively with loss of GFR. This study did not show association with fracture risk and kidney function in women with CKD stage 3 or above. These results suggest that fracture prevention should be a consideration in postmenopausal women with severe CKD.

title: #1845 Psychosocial factors and risk of chronic kidney disease: a prospective cohort analysis in UK Biobank
authors: Lexi Huang; Ping Fu; Xiaoxi Zeng
abstract:
Background and Aims
Potential impact of psychological distress on the development of chronic kidney disease (CKD) has been implicated in recent research. A thorough investigation of the association between psychosocial factors and the incidence of CKD warrants further. The objective of this study was to evaluate the associations between various psychosocial factors and the risk of CKD.
Method
In this prospective cohort study, we included individuals who were free of CKD at baseline from the UK Biobank. A spectrum of psychosocial factors, encompassing social isolation, loneliness, mental health status, neuroticism, depressive symptoms, traumatic experiences, broad depression, and major depressive disorder, were assessed using validated self-report questionnaires. Cox proportional hazards regression models were conducted to evaluate the associations between these psychosocial factors and the incidence of CKD.
Results
In total, 485,324 participants (mean age: 56.9 ± 8.1 years; 54.5% female) were enrolled in this study. During a median follow-up period of 13.5 years, 20,247 participants (4.17%) were newly diagnosed with CKD. After adjustment for age, sex, and ethnicity, our findings revealed that social isolation (HR 1.14, 95% CI, 1.07–1.20, comparing the most isolated group to the least isolated group), loneliness (HR 1.47, 95% CI, 1.39–1.56) were significantly associated with an increased risk of incident CKD. Participants reporting poorer mental health (HR 1.04, 95% CI, 1.03–1.05), broad depression (HR 1.27, 95% CI, 1.24–1.31), severer depression symptom (HR 2.02, 95% CI, 1.91–2.12) or neuroticism scores ≥5 (HR 1.21, 95% CI, 1.17–1.25) exhibited a heightened risk of developing CKD, when compared to those with better psychological wellbeing. Notably, participants experiencing financial difficulties exhibited higher adjusted HRs (HR 1.51, 95% CI, 1.42–1.60) compared to those without such difficulties. Furthermore, participants who had experienced the death of a close relative (HR 1.41, 95% CI, 1.09–1.55) or a spouse/partner (HR 1.15, 95% CI, 1.02–1.31) displayed elevated HRs compared to those who had not (see Fig. 1).
Conclusion
Psychosocial factors were independently associated with a higher hazard of incident CKD. It is imperative for healthcare professionals within the nephrology domain to possess an awareness of the potential linkage between psychosocial factors and CKD.

title: #1359 Sweat-based protocols for reliable determination of creatine and Cystatin-C in chronic kidney disease
authors: Silvia Ghimenti; Alessio Lenzi; Mariano De Cristofaro; Elena De Gregorio; Daniel Alejandro Corzo Diaz; Eleni Stamellou; Evangelia Ntounousi; Thomas Herndl; Mario Auer; Marcin Kautsch; Pietro Salvo; Tommaso Lomonaco
abstract:
Background and Aims
Creatinine and Cystatin-C are key biomarkers used to estimate eGFR, a critical indicator of kidney function and damage. Current eGFR estimation methods rely on blood or urine analysis, which are invasive and require specialized laboratory equipment. While serum creatinine testing is cost-effective and widely used in clinical practice, Cystatin-C testing presents challenges. Cystatin-C exists in different proteoforms, whose biological significance is not fully understood, although their distribution is largely independent of renal function. Additionally, variability in Cystatin-C assay results can occur due to the limited detection of structural modifications by antibodies in PENIA and PETIA assays, leading to inconsistent results. Cystatin-C testing is also approximately ten times more expensive than serum creatinine testing. To address these challenges, we propose a non-invasive protocol using micro-extraction by packed sorbent (MEPS) coupled with targeted liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) to simultaneously measure creatinine, intact Cystatin-C, and its proteoforms in sweat, offering a reliable tool for kidney function monitoring.
Method
In the EU-funded KERMIT project (www.kermitsense.eu), we prospectively enrolled 50 nominally healthy volunteers (local bioethics committee approval n.18/2024) to test the effectiveness of pilocarpine and carbachol in stimulating sweat via iontophoresis, a commonly used non-invasive technique. Sweat samples were collected passively using filter paper (120 × 80 × 0.13 mm) pretreated with bovine serum albumin (BSA) (0.5 g/L). These samples were used to develop and validate the MEPS-LC-MS/MS platform, following IUPAC guidelines, and to determine the concentration of creatinine and Cystatin-C in the volunteers.
Results
Both pilocarpine and carbachol effectively stimulated sweat production. After 30 minutes, pilocarpine resulted in an average sweat volume of 294 μL (range: 22–815 μL), while carbachol produced a higher average volume of 331 μL (range: 48–1148 μL). Carbachol was generally more effective, providing more sustained sweat production, with significant amounts collected even 3 hours after stimulation. The limit of detection for creatinine was 0.03 mg/dL, and for Cystatin-C was 0.2 μg/L. MS/MS signals showed excellent linearity (R² > 0.995) across tested concentrations. Recovery from filter paper was consistent at approximately 80% for both intra- and inter-day measurements. Precision remained robust, with intra- and inter-day coefficients of variation below 15%. Calibration curves from working solutions and spiked sweat samples showed no significant difference at the 95% confidence level, indicating no measurable matrix effect. Importantly, we found that preconditioning materials in contact with sweat samples using BSA was essential to prevent secondary interactions, ensuring consistent Cystatin-C measurements. Creatinine and native Cystatin-C concentrations in sweat from healthy volunteers ranged from 0.1–1.5 mg/dL and 0.5–2 μg/L, respectively.
Conclusion
For the first time, we have identified the presence of Cystatin-C and its proteoforms in sweat. Our MEPS-LC-MS/MS platform enables the simultaneous measurement of creatinine and intact Cystatin-C in sweat, offering a non-invasive, reliable, and alternative method for monitoring kidney function and disease.

title: #2234 Age and kidney failure etiology: global profiles in Apollo DialDb
authors: Kaitlyn Croft; Melanie Wolf; Yue Jiao; Justin Zimbelman; John Larkin; Stefano Stuard; Adrian Marcos Guinsburg; Milind Nikam; Dinesh Chatoth; Michelle Carver; Franklin Maddux; Len Usvyat
abstract:
Background and Aims
The cause of kidney failure is suggested to differ by age. Understanding age-specific differences in kidney failure etiology is crucial for optimizing care paradigms. This study aims to explore these variations globally, focusing on the youngest (18–44 years) and oldest (75+ years) dialysis patients using global ApolloDialDb™ database.
Method
Apollo DialDb, a global anonymized dialysis database, contains real-world data from patients in 40 countries from January 2018 to March 2021. This analysis assessed kidney failure etiology stratified by four age groups 18–44 (young), 45–64 (middle aged), 65–74 (older adults) and 75+ (elderly) in Asia-Pacific (AP), Europe, Middle East, & Africa (EMEA), Latin America (LA) and Northern America (NA). Subsequently we analyzed the distribution etiology by the 4 major regions, focusing specifically on patients in the young and elderly age groups, to explore age-specific variations across different populations.
Results
The first version of the ApolloDialDb includes data on 543,169 patients, with 4.6% from AP, 13.9% from EMEA, 7.0% from LA, and 74.5% from NA countries. Table 1 shows demographics of the full patient cohort stratified by age group. Sex is steady across all four age groups, while there are differences in kidney failure etiology by age. Diabetes is a less common etiology in the young versus middle-aged, older, and elderly age groups. Young patients more commonly have an etiology of glomerulonephritis, cystic kidney disease and complications from kidney transplants. This finding was consistent across major world regions considering young and elderly age groups (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
We identified differences in kidney failure etiology between age groups. We found consistent signals considering four major world regions. Kidney failure etiology and age may be an important consideration in personalized care paradigms aiming at improving patient care and optimizing treatment strategies. ApolloDialDb offers robust opportunities for investigators to conduct global analytics and advance kidney disease research. An important limitation to note is that combining global data from different health systems, along with the inherent challenges of thorough data anonymization, can impact data quality. Additionally, as this is real-world data, information on comorbidities or etiology may not meet gold-standard accuracy typically seen in controlled clinical studies.

title: #2017 Trend of major cardiovascular events and bleeding in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease: a nationwide study
authors: Anne-Laure Faucon; Stefania Lando; Shunsuke Murata; Morgan Grams; Edouard L Fu; Frida Welander; Karin Modig; Marie Evans; Juan-Jesus Carrero
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with advanced CKD have a high risk of major cardiovascular events and bleeding. However, the recent implementation of standard cardio-nephroprotective drugs and antithrombotic therapies may have resulted in lower cardiovascular risks. We assessed rates and time trends of major cardiovascular events and bleeding in a contemporary nationwide Sweden-representative cohort of patients with advanced CKD.
Method
We included all patients with non-dialysis dependent CKD stage 4 and 5, on hemodialysis (HD) and peritoneal dialysis (PD) from the Swedish Renal Registry, enrolled during 2011–2021. Outcomes included major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), arterial and venous thromboembolic events, and major and minor clinically-relevant bleedings. Patients were followed until event, death or progression to a more severe stage/change of dialysis modality. Poisson models were used to estimate rates and age-sex adjusted rate ratios, along with standardization to matched controls (1:10) from the general population.
Results
We included 25 591 patients with CKD stage G4 (age 74 years, 36% women), 13 968 with CKD stage G5-ND (72 years, 37% women), 10 635 patients on HD (68 years, 34.2% women) and 4511 patients on PD (67 years, 32% women). The rates of all study outcomes increased with more severe stages of CKD, being 1.5 to 4.9 times higher than in the general population. Over time, patients with advanced CKD experienced in general important reductions in the rates of MACE, arterial and venous thromboembolic events (i.e. as much as 39%, 28%, and 57%, respectively) across all CKD stages, with a larger decline than in the general population (Fig. 1). Major bleeding rates also decreased (up to 12% in patients on HD), but minor bleeding events instead increased, particularly in patients with non-dialysis CKD stages 4 (42%) and 5 (69%), and to a larger extent than in the general population. Compared to men, women experienced a lesser reduction in the rate of arterial and venous events and major bleedings, but a greater increase in minor bleeding events.
Conclusion
There have been marked reductions in the rates of arterial, venous thromboembolic events and major bleedings in patients with advanced CKD. Despite such improvements, event rates remained substantially higher than in the general population, evidencing the need for additional strategies to tackle their excess cardiovascular and bleeding risk.

title: #2639 A retrospective, multicenter study on the efficacy and safety of desidustat in chronic kidney disease-induced anemia
authors: Sanjeev Gulati; Dilip Kumar Pahari; Karan Saraf; Rohit Rungta; Vijay Sinha; Prashant Bendre
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) often leads to a relative deficiency of erythropoietin (EpO), resulting in anemia. Exogenous erythropoietin analogs are commonly used to address this deficiency. Desidustat (Oxemia®), a recently approved hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor (HIF-PHI), enhances endogenous EpO production. This study evaluates the multicenter outcomes of Desidustat in treating CKD-induced anemia.
Method
This retrospective analysis included patients with CKD-induced anemia who received Desidustat (Oxemia®). Patients were followed up at 1 month, 2 months, and 6 months post-treatment initiation. Oral or intravenous iron was administered based on iron depletion status. Dosage adjustments, therapy compliance, hemoglobin (Hb) levels, and safety parameters were assessed at each follow-up.
Results
The study included 535 patients with CKD-induced anemia, comprising 39.38% males (211 patients) and 60.61% females (324 patients), with a mean age of 57.86 ± 14.24 years. Comorbid conditions included diabetes mellitus (44.29%, 237 patients) and hypertension (61.31%, 328 patients). The majority of patients (88.18%, 472 patients) received Oxemia 100 mg thrice weekly. Hemoglobin levels increased from a baseline mean of 9.11 ± 1.38 g/dL to 9.83 ± 1.52 g/dL at follow-up 1, 10.10 ± 1.59 g/dL at follow-up 2, and 10.13 ± 1.74 g/dL at follow-up 3 (P < 0.005), reflecting sustained improvements of 9.13% (0.72 g/dL), 12.05% (0.99 g/dL), and 12.39% (1.02 g/dL) from baseline, respectively. Both dialysis-dependent and pre-dialysis patients showed a consistent rise in Hb levels from baseline, with a numerically greater increase observed in the pre-dialysis group, likely due to better residual kidney function. The treatment was generally well-tolerated, with mild adverse events such as constipation and throat pain, which did not require discontinuation of therapy.
Conclusion
Desidustat is a safe and effective oral therapy for CKD-induced anemia, demonstrating consistent Hb increases in both dialysis and pre-dialysis patients. Its oral administration route enhances usability, particularly in tropical conditions.

title: #2802 Integrated proteomic and radiomic signatures to predict ejection fraction improvement in CKD patients listed for kidney transplantation
authors: Gargi Pillai; Chenyu Liu; Ruitao Liu; Anne Huml; Liangliang Zhang; Satish Viswanath; Mirela Dobre
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a major risk factor for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Numerous proteins, including matricellular proteins, growth factor signalling, increased humoral immunity, and angiogenesis proteins are enriched in HFpEF, reflective of its heterogeneity. We aimed to evaluate whether combining untargeted plasma proteomic and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR)-based radiomic features could improve prediction of left ventricle ejection fraction (LVEF) improvement among individuals with advanced chronic kidney disease actively listed for a kidney transplant.
Method
Forty-two patients with CKD stages 5 and 5D actively listed for kidney transplantation were recruited at two clinical sites and underwent proteomic profiling (SomaScan v.4.1) at study baseline. CMR examinations were conducted at baseline and again nine months later, either after kidney transplantation (n = 24) or while remaining on the waitlist (n = 18). The primary outcome was defined as a greater than 5% increase in CMR-derived LVEF at nine-month follow-up. 7,596 baseline plasma proteins were analyzed using DESeq2, and Firth’s bias-reduced logistic regression models adjusted for race, demographics, and clinical covariates. Enrichment analyses were used to explore pathways associated with improved LVEF. After annotating the myocardial wall on CMR T1 maps at baseline and follow-up for each patient, a total of 920 radiomic features were extracted to assess myocardial heterogeneity. Machine learning analysis using Maximum Relevance Minimum Redundancy (MRMR) feature selection identified the most relevant proteomic and radiomic features associated with improvement in EF. These feature sets were evaluated independently and in combination via a Random Forest classifier, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) used as the primary performance metric.
Results
Baseline LVEF (mean ± SD) was 56.17 ± 10.55% and improved significantly to 62.00 ± 6.70% in the transplanted group, compared to a non-significant change of 2.78% in the group who remained waitlisted. Proteomic analysis revealed 72 significant proteins associated with improved LVEF, including inflammatory and oxidative stress-related proteins. Radiomic analysis at study baseline identified texture descriptors, including wave/level patterns, entropy and sum average of gradient co-occurrences associated with improved LVEF. Combining 5 top-ranked baseline proteins and 5 top-ranked baseline radiomic features yielded a cross-validated baseline AUROC of 0.73 ± 0.06 in distinguishing improved LVEF, which was significantly improved compared to using proteomics alone (AUROC 0.70 ± 0.05, P < 0.01) or radiomic features alone (AUROC 0.65 ± 0.08, P < 0.01). Using follow-up radiomic data, the integrated model yielded AUROC 0.71 ± 0.06 which was significantly better than radiomics features alone (0.62 ± 0.08, P < 0.01) and marginally improved over proteins alone (AUROC 0.70 ± 0.05, p = 0.28).
Conclusion
Combining top-ranked proteomic and radiomic features significantly enhanced the prediction of LVEF improvement in patients with advanced CKD compared to using either modality alone. Further research is warranted to validate these findings in larger cohorts and to explore the clinical utility of this multimodal approach for predicting cardiac functional outcomes after kidney transplantation.

title: #3196 Inflammatory cytokine clusters are associated with adverse outcomes in patients with CKD
authors: Alberto Martínez Castelao; Alberto Ortiz; Beatriz Fernandez-Fernandez; Jose Luis Górriz; Juan F Navarro-González; Takehiro Hasegawa; Yuko Saruta; Yun Li Guan
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is one of the fastest growing global causes of death, characterized by a gradual loss of renal function over time leading to kidney failure. Early detection of progression and treatment are key for CKD management. The rate of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) decline can vary substantially among CKD patients, ranging from stable levels to relatively rapid reduction in kidney function. Cross-sectional observational studies demonstrate an association between chronic inflammation, evidenced by elevated levels of circulating inflammatory cytokines, and lower eGFR. Emerging experimental evidence suggests that inflammatory cytokines may directly contribute to glomerular and tubular injury, promote fibrosis, and exacerbate vascular damage, collectively compromising nephron integrity function. Therefore, it is hypothesized that the inflammatory status plays a critical role in the progression of kidney damage. In this study, we examined the relationship between plasma and urinary cytokine levels and the long-term prognosis of progression in CKD.
Method
This study included 165 CKD patients from the original PROGRESER cohort. Plasma and urine cytokine levels were measured at baseline, 18 and 36 months using the Sysmex fully automated immunoassay analysers (HISCL-5000 and HISCL-800). Three-year follow-up clinical parameters were retrieved from the original PROGRESER case report forms, and additional 10-year follow-up data were collected from participating centers. CKD patients were categorized into three groups—non-diabetic (non-DM, N = 100), type 1 diabetes (T1D, N = 5), and type 2 diabetes (T2D, N = 60)—and compared to healthy controls (N = 30). Disease progression was calculated by dividing changes in clinical outcomes by the number of observation days. Cytokines with significant correlations to clinical parameters (eGFR, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio -UACR-, HbA1c) were pre-selected through univariate and multivariate analyses. Multiple logistic regression analysis between KDIGO and other risk categories identified three cytokines for cluster analysis. Descriptive data were reported as medians with interquartile ranges (IQR) due to non-normal distributions. Statistical tests, including Fisher’s exact test, Steel-Dwass test, and Mann–Whitney U test, were conducted using R software (version 4.0.3). Two-tailed p-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.
Results
The median age was 70 years for diabetic CKD patients and 66 years for non-DM CKD patients, UACR 59.7 mg/g and 31.3 mg/g, respectively. All participants had CKD G3–G5. Plasma levels of IL-5, IL-6, IL-8, IL-17, IL-18, PROTEIN-A*, CXCL9, PROTEIN-B, BAFF, and GDF-15 were significantly elevated, whereas IL-10, CCL5, and TWEAK were reduced in non-diabetic and diabetic CKD compared to healthy controls (P < .05). Urinary PROTEIN-A was also significantly elevated (P < .05). Cluster analysis based on IL-8, PROTEIN-B, and GDF-15 identified clusters with distinct inflammatory profiles. Clusters 3 and 4, characterized by higher inflammation, had a greater proportion of patients classified as Very High Risk by KDIGO criteria and a higher prevalence of diabetic kidney disease compared to Cluster 5, which exhibited lower inflammation. Cluster 3 also demonstrated a larger increase in UACR and a higher number of all-cause deaths (P < 0.0001), primarily due to cardiovascular causes.
Conclusion
Inflammatory cytokine clusters are strongly associated with CKD progression and adverse outcomes. Patients in high-inflammation clusters (IL-8, PROTEIN-B, GDF-15) had increased KDIGO Very High-Risk classification, greater UACR progression, and higher mortality, mainly due to cardiovascular causes. These findings highlight the prognostic value of cytokine profiling in CKD management.

title: #3552 Comparative analysis of GFR estimation equations in oncologic patients
authors: Arianna Bettiga; Andrea Angioi; Fabiana Selvaggi; Michela Passera; Francesco Fiorio; Alberto Briganti; Andrea Salonia; Francesco Montorsi; Antonello Pani; Giuseppe Rosiello; Umberto Capitanio; Francesco Trevisani
abstract:
Background and Aims
Precise estimation of glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is crucial for optimizing oncologic patient care. This study evaluates the predictive performance of three CKD-EPI equations—creatinine-based, cystatin C-based, and combined—against measured GFR (mGFR) determined by iohexol plasma clearance, a recognized reference standard.
Method
We retrospectively analyzed 187 oncologic patients who underwent up to six GFR assessments from 2018 to 2024. eGFR values were calculated using the CKD-EPI equations. Statistical analyses included Pearson’s correlation coefficient, Lin’s concordance correlation coefficient, and Bland–Altman plots to assess systematic bias and variability. Predictive accuracy was measured as the percentage of eGFR values within 30% of mGFR (P30). Subgroup analyses evaluated the impact of hydration status, nutritional markers, and body composition on formula performance. Multivariable and linear mixed-effects models adjusted for clinical and demographic confounders.
Results
The creatinine-based equation demonstrated the strongest correlation with mGFR (r = 0.85) and minimal mean bias (+0.07 mL/min/1.73 m²). It achieved the highest P30 accuracy (88.2%) compared to the cystatin C-based (60.4%) and combined formulas (44.9%). Bland–Altman analysis confirmed the superior agreement of the creatinine-based equation, with narrow limits of agreement (−16.84 to +16.99 mL/min/1.73 m²). Performance across CKD stages showed consistent overestimation for cystatin C-based and combined formulas, particularly at mGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m² (Fig. 1). Hydration and nutritional status influenced accuracy; overhydration increased bias for all equations, with the creatinine-based formula maintaining superior predictive stability. Patients with poor phase angle (<5.1) or extreme body composition exhibited reduced accuracy, especially for cystatin C-based and combined formulas.
Conclusion
The creatinine-based CKD-EPI equation provides the most reliable and accurate GFR estimation among oncologic patients, outperforming cystatin C-based and combined approaches in various clinical contexts. These findings emphasize the importance of considering patient-specific factors such as hydration and nutritional status when selecting eGFR formulas, particularly in vulnerable populations.

title: #3230 Clinical frailty scale, surprise question and one-year mortality in older patients approaching kidney failure
authors: Imre Demirhan; Micha Jongejan; Mathijs Van Oevelen; Keanu Kiriwenno; Simon Mooijaart; Marianne Verhaar; Willem Jan W Bos; Hanneke Joosten; Trijntje Tjitske Cnossen; Marjolijn van Buren; Alferso Abrahams

title: #3188 Cerebrovascular changes, cognitive functioning, depressive symptoms and apathy in older adults with advanced CKD
authors: Imre Demirhan; Rochnie Booij; Jeroen de Bresser; Marjolijn van Buren
abstract:
Background and Aims
Older patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) often suffer from various comorbidities, including impaired cognitive (executive) functioning, depressive symptoms and apathy. It is thought that these comorbidities in CKD may have a shared underlying vascular pathophysiology, but the exact association with cerebrovascular changes remains unclear. This study therefore investigates whether cerebrovascular changes on MRI are associated with cognitive functioning, depressive symptoms and apathy in older patients with advanced CKD.
Method
Patients aged ≥65 years with eGFR <20ml/min/1.73 m2 not on dialysis from the Cognitive Decline in Older Patients with ESRD (COPE) study were included. Cerebrovascular changes were assessed on 3T MRI scans, including markers of cerebral large vessel disease (cortical infarcts) and cerebral small vessel disease (lobar and non-lobar microbleeds, subcortical infarcts, white matter hyperintensity volume and global cerebral blood flow). Global cognitive functioning was assessed with the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), the cognitive domain executive functioning using the Trail Making Test (TMT), part B adjusted for A and Stroop card III, and the domain psychomotor speed using the Letter Digit Substitution Test (LDST, correct answers after 60 seconds), TMT-A and Stroop card II. Z-scores were calculated for each cognitive test, composite mean Z-scores were calculated for executive functioning and psychomotor speed. The number of depressive symptoms and presence of apathy were assessed using the GDS-15 and its GDS-3A subscale (≥2 symptoms being indicative of apathy). Cross-sectional associations between cerebrovascular changes and outcomes were assessed using linear and logistic regression analyses, adjusted for age, sex and educational level.
Results
87 patients with advanced CKD were included (mean age 75.4 ± 6.9 years; mean eGFR 15.9 ± 3.8 mL/min/1.73 m2). The presence of cortical infarcts was significantly associated with lower global cognitive functioning (β -1.00, 95% CI -1.60–0.40, p-value 0.001) and lower psychomotor speed (β -0.67, 95% CI −1.19 –0.14, p-value 0.01). White matter hyperintensity volume was significantly associated with lower executive functioning (β -0.03, 95% CI −0.05 to −0.009, p-value 0.003). No significant associations were found between the remaining cerebral small vessel disease markers (microbleeds, subcortical infarcts, global cerebral blood flow) and cognitive functioning (global and executive), nor between any cerebrovascular changes and depressive symptoms or apathy, including both large and small vessel disease markers.
Conclusion
In older patients with advanced CKD, markers of cerebral small vessels disease versus markers of cerebral large vessels disease showed different significant associations with various cognitive functioning domains. These results support an underlying vascular pathophysiology of cognitive impairment in older patients with advanced CKD. In contrast, no were found between cerebrovascular changes (both large and small vessel disease markers) and depressive symptoms and apathy, which might indicate that non-vascular related factors (e.g. uremic or inflammatory factors) may play a role in the occurrence of these comorbidities.
