title: #944 Baseline analysis of the patterns of CKD care in an implementation trial using future health today in primary care
authors: Hannah Wallace; Christopher Preston; Qiumian Wang; Natalie Lumsden; Barbara Hunter; J Oliver Daly; Min Jun; Devaang Kevat; Craig Nelson
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) progression and cardiovascular complications can be attenuated with early recognition and management of CKD. Prior research has found substantial gaps in the early detection and management of CKD. Future Health Today (FHT) is a clinical decision support and quality improvement software that can be used to aid testing, diagnosis and management of CKD, diabetes and cardiovascular disease (CVD). An implementation trial is underway to explore the effectiveness of a program using FHT to improve chronic disease management in primary care. We aim to describe the baseline characteristics of the cohort in relation to CKD testing, diagnosis and management.
Method
The FHT Implementation Trial is a pre-post implementation trial in primary care practices in the Western Health catchment of Victoria, Australia (ACTRN 12623001096640). We assessed the baseline characteristics of adults (≥18 years) who were active patients (defined as 3 visits within 24 months) at one of the 19 participating primary care practices on 1 August 2024. Care quality was assessed across the domains of risk factor documentation, CKD testing in those at risk, and CKD monitoring and management in those with CKD. CKD testing in at risk individuals was defined as a kidney health check, with at least one measure of all of eGFR, UACR and blood pressure, in the last 24 months. The CKD monitoring and management domain included a kidney health check within the last 12 months, and medication prescription within the last 12 months across angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEI) or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB), statins, sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), and in patients with comorbid diabetes glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP1-RA) and non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (nsMRA), each assessed separately.
Results
There were 80,325 active adult patients at the 19 participating primary care practices at baseline. Overall, 57.5% were female, the mean age was 47.4 (SD 17.8), 10.2% had diabetes, 4.8% had CKD and 4.6% had CVD. Risk factor documentation was variable with smoking status being recorded in most patients (87.2%), blood pressure within 2 years in 64.1% and body mass index recorded in 41.2% of patients. Overall, 22.6% of patients at risk of CKD had a kidney health check within the last 24 months, with higher completion in patients with diabetes (55.4%) or hypertension (37.7%) as risk factors (Fig. 1A). In patients with CKD (N = 3,876), 52.3% had a kidney health check in the last 12 months and 52.6% had a coded diagnosis of CKD in the medical record (Fig. 1B). Among those with CKD, 62.6% were prescribed an ACEI/ARB, 57.7% were prescribed a statin and 19.4% were prescribed a SGLT2i. In patients with CKD and diabetes 18.0% received a GLP1-RA and 0.6% an nsMRA.
Conclusion
In this baseline cross-sectional analysis of the FHT Implementation Trial, we found several priority areas for improving early detection and management of CKD including increasing testing in patients with risk factors for CKD and implementation of medications with cardio-renal benefit in patients with CKD.

title: #3096 Is a green nephrology possibile? a lower dialysate flow could not affect therapeutic efficacy in selected patients while saving billions of litres of water
authors: Luca Malatesta; Viviana Finato
abstract:
Background and Aims
Many fields are shifting towards a more sustainable approach. This includes nephrology, with the rise of “Green Nephrology.” Dialysis, a lifesaving therapy for millions of patients, is undeniably one of the medical practices with the most significant environmental impact, due to its production of non-recyclable waste materials and its substantial water consumption. Considering an average reduction in dialysate flow (Qd) of 150 mL/min per patient, each individual undergoing chronic dialysis, would reduce water consumption by approximately 5,200 litres annually. If we multiply this to the estimated 3.5 million patients globally receiving chronic dialysis, this reduction would result in a total savings of approximately 18 billion litres of water per year. Our study aims to investigate the short-term outcomes of Qd reduction on dialysis adequacy, in terms of serum potassium concentration [K+] and Kt/V. This analysis was conducted in both hemodialysis (HD) and hemodiafiltration (HDF).
Method
We conducted a prospective experimental study involving 11 patients (5 male, 6 female; mean age 72.2, range 34–93) who were selected based on their stability in terms of hemodynamic and vascular access and divided into two groups: 6 patients in hemodialysis (HD) and 5 in hemodiafiltration (HDF). The study design alternated between high dialysate flow (Qd) (600 mL/min in HD, 500 mL/min in HDF) and low dialysate flow (Qd) (400 mL/min in both HD and HDF; 1 patient in HDF 300 mL/min) dialysis therapies over 10 consecutive dialysis sessions. Pre- and post-dialysis [K+] and Kt/V were measured; Kt/V was calculated by taking the arithmetic mean of the Kt/V values obtained from the dialysis machine and the Kt/V single pool calculated using the Daugirdas formula. Regarding HDF, the substitution volume was also measured. Throughout the entire evaluation period, all patients were treated using the same dialysis machine, filters and dialysate potassium concentration. Additionally, all patients underwent dialysis sessions of the same duration, maintaining fixed blood flow rates (Qb) (9 out of 10 Qb 300 mL/min, 1 patient Qb 250 mL/min due to vascular access issues).
Results
In Group 1 (HD), the mean Kt/V was 1.5 with high Qd and 1.4 with low Qd (P = 0.33). Pre-dialysis mean [K+] was similar between high and low Qd (5.1 vs 5.2 mEq/L, P = 0.59), and post-dialysis mean [K+] was also comparable (3.7 vs 3.9 mEq/L, P = 0.52). 4 out of 6 patients in Group 1 achieved a Kt/V ≥ 1.2 in both high and low Qd sessions. Only 1 patient (HD) demonstrated, after just four dialysis sessions, mean Kt/V values ≥ 1.2 during sessions with Qd 600 mL/min and mean Kt/V values < 1.2 during sessions with Qd 400 mL/min. Consequently, this patient was excluded from the study to prevent potential long-term issues due to a reduced dialysis adequacy. 1 patient (HD), who received hemodialysis with a Qb of 250 mL/min due to vascular access-related issues, presented mean Kt/V values < 1.2, both during hemodialysis with high Qd (600 mL/min) and low Qd (400 mL/min). In Group 2 (HDF), the mean Kt/V was 1.67 with high Qd and 1.62 with low Qd (P = 0.57). Pre-dialysis mean [K+] was 5.3 mEq/L with high Qd and 5.2 mEq/L with low Qd (P = 0.55), and post-dialysis mean [K+] was also comparable (3.8 mEq/L vs 3.9 mEq/L, P = 0.46). All patients in Group 2 achieved a Kt/V ≥ 1.2 in both high and low Qd sessions. None of the patients analysed experienced death or critical events during the course of the study.
Conclusion
We hypothesize that hemodynamically stable patients with good vascular access often exceed the optimal Kt/V threshold. In these selected individuals, reducing the dialysate flow (Qd) could lead to significant water savings without compromising dialysis adequacy, in terms of Kt/V and serum potassium concentration. However, consistent with the limited studies currently available in the literature, Kt/V fluctuations may occur, which could benefit, albeit minimally, from a higher Qd. A minority of patients may achieve a Kt/V below the threshold considered optimal with low Qd, while achieving a Kt/V within optimal limits with high Qd. Therefore, further analysis of long-term effects, considering additional parameters will be essential.

title: #1806 Green nephrology by low convection volume replacement in post-dilution online hemodiafiltration
authors: Kenji Sakurai; Takeshi Saito; Hiromi Hosoya; Fumi Yamauchi; Yoshitaka Kurihara; Kenichi Kokubo; Daisuke Ishii; Toru Hyodo; Akihiro Yamashita
abstract:
Background and Aims
The number of dialysis patients is increasing worldwide year by year. However, dialysis treatment has a significant negative impact on the global environment, as it requires enormous water consumption, increases greenhouse gas emissions, and leads to large amounts of waste generation. Hemodiafiltration (HDF) has become a mainstream renal replacement therapy. In Japan, at the end of 2023, 59.1% of all dialysis patients (total, 343,508) were receiving HDF, with 68% of these patients receiving online HDF (pre-dilution HDF [pre-HDF]: 93%, post-HDF: only 7%). We have previously reported that post-HDF can provide a high removal efficiency with low volume substitution fluid (10-12 L/session) if a high-performance hemodiafilter is used (1). In this study, from the viewpoint of water resource conservation for protection of the global environment, we examined whether desired removal efficiency (spKt/V for urea [MW:60]: ≥1.5, β2MG [MW:11.8kDa] removal rate: ≥80%, α1MG [MW:33kDa] removal rate: ≥35%) can be obtained by gradually decreasing the total dialysate flow rate (Qd) to 40% in post-HDF. In addition, the effect of reducing the amount of raw water was also examined.
Method
FIX-Seco (ATA membrane, Nipro) and MFX-UWeco (PES membrane, Nipro), both of which have a sieving coefficient (SC) for β2MG of 0.93, 0.88, respectively, and both SCs for albumin of 0.01, were selected as the high-performance hemodiafilters. The study was conducted on a total of 18 patients who were receiving pre-HDF, with FIX used on 9 patients and MFX on 9 patients. The dialysis time was 4 hours/session, with a blood flow rate of 258.9 ± 24.5 mL/min and filter area of 2.1 m2. Since convection volume (CV) is the sum of the substitution fluid volume (Vs) and volume of fluid removal driven by interdialytic weight gain (Vf), CV changes according to the changes according to fluctuation in interdialytic weight gain. To avoid this change, the dialysis conditions for each patient were determined by setting the CV (9-12 L/session) based on their previous laboratory data. Additionally, Qs was calculated each day by subtracting Vf from CV for each session and dividing it by the dialysis time. Vs for pre-HDF was 41.8 ± 4.9 L, and CV for post-HDF was 10.2 ± 0.7 L. We compared the removal efficiency under the following four conditions: pre-HDF, post-HDF using Qd of 400, 350, and 300 mL/min. The reduced volume of raw water was calculated based on the volume of raw water used at a Qd of 300 mL/min (RO recovery rate: 65%), and compared with the volume used at a Qd of 500 mL/min.
Results
The solute removal efficiencies for pre-HDF and post-HDF using a Qd of 400, 350, and 300 mL/min were as follows, spKt/V: 1.64 ± 0.18, 1.75 ± 0.22, 1.73 ± 0.19, and 1.65 ± 0.55, respectively; the β2-MG removal rates (RRs) (%):81.8 ± 3.6, 80.8 ± 4.2, 80.6 ± 3.7, and 80.0 ± 0.55, respectively, and the α1-MG RRs were 35.7 ± 6.9, 38.8 ± 8.2, 37.3 ± 3.7, and 35.8 ± 0.55, respectively. By reducing Qd from 500 to 300 mL/min, a decrease in raw water usage of 39% was obtaind. In post-HDF performed with a high-performance hemodiafilter, a large amount of albumin leakage is likely to occur with s small change in CV. However, by setting the appropriate CV for each patient, we were able to perform stress-free, highly efficient post-HDF with a low vs (7.7 ±1.0 L,7.4 ± 1.0 L, and 7.3 ± 05 L for Qd of 400, 350, 300, respectively), with only slight increase in TMP during dialysis. Moreover, the desired removal efficiency was obtained even when Qd was reduced by 40%.
Conclusion
Post-HDF using an appropriate high-performance hemodiafilter would be an essential dialysis method for the Green Nephrology program, as it enables for an immediate reduction of water consumption while maintaining high removal efficiencies.

title: #2297 Impact of dialysis initiation on drug use patterns in older patients: results from the French national renal replacement therapy registry matched with the national health data system (SNDS)
authors: Lea Faure; Pernelle Noize; Cécile Couchoud; Emilie Hucteau; Jessica Berdougo; Florent Guerville; Christian Combe; Olivier Moranne; Aghiles Hamroun; Jean-Baptiste Beuscart; Karen Leffondré; Mathilde Prezelin-Reydit
abstract:
Background and Aims
Older dialysis patients have complex drug regimen to manage their chronic kidney disease, associated complications, and comorbidities. Our aim was to describe the drug use patterns during the year preceding and following dialysis initiation in patients aged 65 years and older.
Method
All patients initiating chronic dialysis in France at 65 years and older between 2010 and 2019 were identified from the national renal replacement therapy registry (REIN). They were included if they were deterministically matched with the national health data system (SNDS) (85.5%). Drug use prevalence was described by pharmacotherapeutic classes, based on anatomical therapeutic chemical (ATC) codes, and estimated quarterly for patients with at least one drug dispensing within the period. Analysis was stratified according to the dialysis modality: hemodialysis (HD) or peritoneal dialysis (PD), sex, age and calendar year (2010–2019) at dialysis initiation.
Results
Among 55,238 patients included, 76.0% had hyperpolypharmacy (≥10 drugs delivered) at dialysis initiation. Non-dialysis-related drugs, including glucose-lowering, psychotropic, analgesic and non-antihypertensive cardiovascular drugs, showed stable prevalence between the period before and after dialysis initiation, except a transient bound in analgesic use just before dialysis initiation (47.5% to 52.3%) (Fig. 1). Conversely, dialysis-related drugs showed variations in prevalence. Antihypertensive use decreased at dialysis initiation (88.3% to 71.8%), particularly in HD patients, except for diuretics (Fig. 1). Potassium binders (31.1% to 23.6%) and uric acid lowering therapy (35.0% to 24.1%) also declined, while calcium supplementation increased before dialysis initiation and then stabilized thereafter (Fig. 1). Vitamin D supplementation and phosphate binders increased consistently before and after dialysis (Fig. 1). Finally, for management of alimentary tract disorders, proton pump inhibitors use increased before dialysis and then stabilized as laxative use in HD patients. Trends in drug use profiles were generally similar across sex and age groups, with some differences in prevalence observed. Over the study period (2010–2019), psychotropic and calcium supplementation use declined, while analgesic use increased relatively.
Conclusion
In France, dialysis initiation in older patients is associated with changes in the prevalence of dialysis-related drugs, and stable prevalence of non-dialysis-related drug classes. Dialysis initiation is a critical period for drug management, requiring nephrologist oversight and nurse or pharmacist support.

title: #2489 Implementing a clinical governance and performance benchmarking model in dialysis: the DaVita quality index experience in Brazil
authors: Bruno Zawadzki; Ana Vieira; Bruno Vieira; Cristina Pinto; Danilo Cunha; Eric Correa; Fabio Reis; Fernanda Coelho; Marcelo Lopes; Priscila Sampaio; Rogerio Da Hora
abstract:
Background and Aims
The implementation of structured clinical governance and performance management in dialysis is crucial for improving patient outcomes. Recognizing this, DaVita Brazil introduced the DaVita Quality Index (DQI) in 2023 as a benchmarking tool to standardize quality indicators and enhance clinical performance across its network of dialysis clinics. This study aims to evaluate the impact of the DQI on key dialysis-related metrics and compare the observed improvements with national and international benchmarks.
Methods
A longitudinal observational study was conducted across 95 DaVita Brazil dialysis clinics from July 2023 to December 2024. The DQI, with a maximum score of 100 points, was calculated monthly for each clinic based on key performance indicators (KPIs), including the percentage of patients achieving Kt/V ≥ 1.3, hemoglobin control (Hb ≥ 10 and ≥12 g/dL without erythropoietin), phosphorus ≤5.5 mg/dL, interdialytic weight gain (IDWG), and the use of central venous catheters (CVC). Data were extracted from electronic health records, and only patients undergoing hemodialysis (HD) or hemodiafiltration (HDF) for more than 90 days were included. Patients from both the public healthcare system (SUS) and private healthcare providers were analyzed together. Statistical analyses were conducted using paired t-tests and ANOVA to assess significant differences in DQI scores and individual KPIs over time.
Results
A total of 95 clinics participated in the program. The mean DQI score increased from 39.67 in July 2023 to 57.29 in December 2024, reflecting a 44.41% improvement (P < 0.001). Key clinical metrics demonstrated statistically significant improvements, measured as the percentage of patients achieving target values:
Compared to national and international benchmarks, the DQI results demonstrated positive trends, particularly in phosphorus control and dialysis adequacy, where DaVita Brazil outperformed national averages. The implementation of structured clinical governance within DaVita Brazil clinics has facilitated alignment with global standards, including those reported in the Brazilian Society of Nephrology Dialysis Census 2023, ISN Global Kidney Health Atlas 2023, and ERA Registry 2022.
Conclusion
The introduction of the DaVita Quality Index in Brazil has led to significant improvements in dialysis-related clinical indicators, validating the effectiveness of a structured clinical governance model in enhancing dialysis care. These results support the expansion of DQI as a national quality improvement model for dialysis services. Future research should evaluate the program’s impact on hospitalization rates, patient survival, and long-term health outcomes.

title: #2493 The impact of a clinical governance program on mortality and hospitalization rates in dialysis: the DaVita quality index experience in Brazil
authors: Bruno Zawadzki; Ana Vieira; Bruno Vieira; Cristina Pinto; Danilo Cunha; Eric Correa; Fabio Reis; Fernanda Coelho; Marcelo Lopes; Priscila Sampaio; Rogerio Da Hora
abstract:
Background and Aims
The implementation of structured clinical governance is critical in improving patient outcomes in dialysis care. In 2023, DaVita Kidney Care Brazil (DKC Brazil) introduced the DaVita Quality Index (DQI) as a national benchmarking tool, aiming to enhance clinical performance and standardize care across its network of dialysis clinics. The DQI incorporates multiple quality indicators, including dialysis adequacy, anemia control, vascular access, and metabolic parameters, to provide a comprehensive performance score. This study evaluates the impact of DQI implementation on mortality and hospitalization rates over an 18-month period and compares these findings to national and international benchmarks.
Methods
A retrospective observational study was conducted across 95 DaVita Kidney Care Brazil dialysis clinics, covering patients undergoing hemodialysis (HD) and hemodiafiltration (HDF) for more than 90 days. Patients from both public healthcare (SUS) and private healthcare providers were analyzed jointly. The study period was from July 2023 to December 2024. Were analyzed Mortality rate (%) (measured monthly), Hospitalization rate (%) (percentage of patients admitted per month) and DaVita Quality Index (DQI) score (scale 0–100). Data Sources were the Electronic Health Records (EHR) and BI dashboards from DaVita Kidney Care Brazil. Statistical Analysis used Pearson correlation coefficient to assess the association between DQI scores and hospitalization/mortality trends, and paired t-tests were conducted to evaluate significant differences over time. Benchmarking Comparison was data compared with: Brazilian Society of Nephrology (SBN) Dialysis Census 2023, ERA Registry 2022 (European benchmarks) and ISN Global Kidney Health Atlas 2023 (International data).
Results
A total of 20 147 patients were analyzed across 95 clinics. The mean DQI score increased from 30 in July 2023 to 59 in December 2024, reflecting a 96.7% improvement over the study period. The improvement in DQI was associated with significant reductions in mortality and hospitalization rates:
A strong negative correlation was observed between DQI scores and mortality rates (r = −0.82, p<0.001), indicating that clinics with higher DQI scores exhibited lower mortality over time. A similar trend was observed for hospitalization rates (r = −0.76, p=0.004).
Conclusion
The implementation of the DaVita Quality Index (DQI) in DKC Brazil has been positively associated with lower mortality and hospitalization rates, supporting its role as a structured clinical governance tool. Compared to Brazilian national data (SBN 2023) and international benchmarks (ERA Registry 2022, ISN Atlas 2023), DaVita Brazil demonstrated improvements in patient outcomes, particularly in regions with historically lower-quality indicators. The expansion of the DQI program and further refinement of quality improvement initiatives could serve as a model for broader national implementation in dialysis programs, reinforcing the importance of structured governance in renal care.

title: #1164 Efficiency and safety of expanded (HDx) and high-flux hemodialysis in the era of green dialysis
authors: Mauricio Sanabria; Peter Rutherford; Juan Carlos Mario Castillo; Cesar Mauricio Doria; Javier Cely; David Camargo; Viviana Orozco; Daniel Ducuara; Jasmin Vesga; Angela Rivera
abstract:
Background and Aims
Expanded hemodialysis (HDx) enabled by Theranova increases clearance of medium-molecular-weight uremic toxins, improving clinical outcomes such as hospitalization and mortality. The objective of the study was to compare clearance of medium-molecular-weight uremic toxins by HDx versus conventional hemodialysis, with dialysate flow rates of 500 mL/min and a lower rate of 400 mL/min, and to describe their safety.
Method
This is an observational multicenter prospective cohort study. Prevalent patients on dialysis for at least 90 days, older than eighteen, between April 1, 2024, and May 31, 2024, with 12 weeks of follow-up. Two cohorts were assembled, one with HDx and one with high-flux hemodialysis (HF-HD). The sociodemographic and clinical characteristics of all patients were summarized. The Reduction Ratio (RR) was measured for large middle molecules. The frequencies of serious adverse events and hospitalization were also calculated.
Results
A total of 287 patients were included in the analysis (137 in HDx Cohort and 150 in HF-HD); the mean age was 61 years, 42.5% had diabetic kidney disease, the vintage in Kidney Replacement Therapy (KRT) was 5.2 years, the proportion of patients with urine output ≥ 250 ml/day was 16.7 (Table 1). The HDx group achieved greater efficiency in removing β2-microglobulin and free light chains (lambda and kappa); this superiority in removal was statistically significant for both dialysate flows of both 400 ml and 500 ml/min. See Table 2. We found 25.9% fewer serious adverse events in the HDx cohort. None were casually related to the Theranova or HF dialyzers in 11,409 sessions performed. The proportion of hospitalization was 6.7% lower in the HDx cohort compared to HF-HD (6.6% vs 13.3% p-value 0.028) Fig. 1.
Conclusion
Theranova dialyzer-enabled HDx significantly improved the removal of medium-molecular-weight uremic toxins compared to HF-HD at both 500 mL and 400 mL/min dialysate flows. HDx was associated with fewer serious adverse events and fewer hospitalization events.

title: #1368 A practical approach for performing remote monitoring in the care of patients with automated peritoneal dialysis using Share source analytics 1.0
authors: Mauricio Sanabria; Peter Rutherford; Maria Paz Dazzarola; Juan Carlos Mario Castillo; Cesar Mauricio Doria; Jorge Pulido; Fabio Rojas; Javier Cely; Jasmin Vesga; Lady Alba; Angela Rivera
abstract:
Background and Aims
Remote monitoring programs for patients with automated peritoneal dialysis (APD-RMP) have been growing worldwide and lead to improved clinical outcomes. However, a lack of standardization has been observed regarding operating procedures and practical guides on how to use the program in the day-to-day life of PD services. This study aimed to describe the Sharesource Analytics 1.0 platform and generate decision rules for practical implementation in PD programs.
Method
This qualitative research was conducted in six renal clinics with APD-RMP that used the Sharesource Analytics 1.0 platform for three consecutive months between April and July 2024. Expert consensus techniques and focus groups with nephrologists and PD nurses were used to develop the decision rules in response to observations in the Sharesource Analytics 1.0 platform.
Results
Sharesource Analytics 1.0 is an efficient platform for APD-RMP programs. It employs analysis algorithms of key clinical indicators—patient adherence, catheter health, and alarms—presents on a daily basis with 180 day rolling trends (Fig. 1). A total of 27 professionals (20 women and seven men), including nephrologists and nurses, were part of the expert consensus and focus group. Twenty participants were over 40 years old, with a mean of 11.2 years (SD 8.2) of experience in peritoneal dialysis (PD) programs. Figure 2 shows how APD-RMP with Sharesource Analytics 1.0 was used in the clinic. Decision rules regarding adherence and catheter health were created by nephrologists and nurses and are shown in Table 1.
Conclusion
Sharesource Analytics 1.0 is a bidirectional tool that enables clinical teams to securely view patient care data and proactively reduce complications, hospitalizations, and emergency room visits. This study generated decision rules to help its implementation in clinical practice.

title: #1093 Assessment of health-related quality-of-life in hemodialysis patients in Colombia
authors: Mauricio Sanabria; Peter Rutherford; Juan Carlos Mario Castillo; Cesar Mauricio Doria; Javier Cely; David Camargo; Viviana Orozco; Daniel Ducuara; Jasmin Vesga; Angela Rivera
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hemodialysis is a treatment that can significantly impact a patient's quality of life. Due to the high comorbidity and complications of chronic kidney disease, the health-related quality of life (HRQoL) of dialysis patients is often worse than that of the general population of the same age. This study assessed QoL in chronic haemodialysis patients in Colombia.
Method
This is an observational multicenter prospective cohort study. Prevalent patients on dialysis for at least 90 days, >18 years old, between April 1, 2024, and May 31, 2024, with 12 weeks of follow-up, were included. The sociodemographic and clinical characteristics of all patients were summarized. Health states were described using the EQ-5D-5L, which consists of 5 dimensions of health (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression). The EQ VAS records the patient’s self-rated health on a vertical visual analog scale where the endpoints are labeled 'The best health you can imagine' and 'The worst health you can imagine.' As Colombia does not have its data to value set for these calculations, we have calculated the utility measures using the data of a nearby country, such as Uruguay, as recommended by EuroQol.
Results
287 patients were included in the analysis; the mean age was 61 years, 42.5% had diabetic kidney disease, and the proportion of patients with urine output ≥ 250 ml/day was 16.7 (Table 1). Mobility, self-care, and usual activities are the dimensions that have the highest percentages of patients with no problems (49.8%–74.5%). Pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression have a higher rate of patients with mild problems (33.0%–37.6%); see Table 2. The mean utility score was 0.9 SD (0.1); Table 3 shows the most common health conditions reported by patients and their associated utility scores and EQ-VAS scores. The mean EQ VAS score was 69.6 (SD 19.2), reflecting significant variability between patient subgroups, as seen in Fig. 1.
Conclusion
The results highlight that health-related quality of life is mild to moderately compromised in this hemodialysis population; the most affected dimensions are pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression. Using tools such as the EQ-5D-5L allows us to identify critical areas that require intervention to improve the well-being of patients.

title: #2393 Intermediate monocyte and platelet activation within the extracorporeal hemodialysis circuit: novel tools assessing HD-induced thrombo-inflammation
authors: Florine Janssens; Wim Renmans; Eleni Linskens; Freya Van Hulle; Priya Laha; Tom Hauffman; Stefaan Verhulst; Karlien François
abstract:
Background and Aims
During hemodialysis (HD), blood exposure to the extracorporeal circuit (ECC) induces plasma protein adherence to the foreign biomaterials and activation of leukocytes, platelets, coagulation and complement pathways. The spread of prothrombotic and proinflammatory signals to the patient’s circulation contributes to systemic thrombo-inflammation, a major driver of cardiovascular (CV) disease, the leading cause of mortality in HD patients. Yet, the thrombo-inflammatory processes within the ECC—as key drivers of systemic responses—remain poorly understood. This study aims to describe and quantify thrombo-inflammatory cell activation within the ECC.
Method
In this exploratory pilot study, 3 clinically stable patients on maintenance HD using an AV-fistula were included. HD sessions were conducted as per routine care and blood samples were collected pre- and post-HD. After completing a 4-hour HD session and blood retransfusion, the used ECC was rinsed during 20 minutes using a 250 mL PBS-3mM EDTA rinsing solution to retrieve circuit-sequestered cells. Subsequently, an additional 20-minute rinse with a 250 mL proteolytic and collagenolytic enzymes solution (Accutase®) was performed to detach rinsing-resistant cells. Cell counts and flow cytometric analyses were performed on pre- and post-HD blood samples and both rinsing fluids. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of the used dialyzers was used to validate the efficacy of the rinsing procedures. For each patient, SEM analysis of a used non-rinsed and EDTA-only rinsed dialyzer of a consecutive HD session was performed as positive controls.
Results
The rinsing procedures successfully retrieved ECC-sequestered cells. The EDTA rinse fluid yielded a median of 14.1 × 106 leukocytes (range: 10.8–17.8 × 106) and 32.8 × 106 platelets (range: 21.4–46.1 × 106). title: #2994 Chemotherapy administration via arteriovenous fistula in hemodialysed patients: too daring of an option?
authors: Pedro Silva; Noemy Neves; Rita Vicente; Iolanda Santos; Filipa Alves; Cristina Silva; Ricardo Santos; David Fiel; Beatriz Malvar; Manuel Amoedo
abstract:
Background and Aims
An arteriovenous fistula (AVF) is a high-flux vascular access (VA) surgically created for long-term hemodialysis (HD) and is traditionally reserved for this purpose alone. Cancer chemotherapy (CT) is typically administered via central venous catheter (CVC), a VA traditionally associated with higher rates of infectious, mechanic/thrombotic, and hemorrhagic complications. We aim to report cases in which CT was administered via AVF in HD-dependent oncologic patients and to evaluate its safety.
Method
This retrospective, single-centre, case report, includes HD patients who received CT via an AVF for oncologic treatment over the past ten years. Demographic and clinical data were collected from local clinical registries. We analyzed clinical outcomes such as maintenance of dialysis adequacy, adequate AVF arterial blood flow rate and registered any other related complications.
Results
Case 1. A 51-year-old woman with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) initiated chronic HD in 2012 via a radiocephalic AVF. In 2015, she was diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast and underwent tumorectomy and lymph node dissection. Adjuvant chemotherapy was administered until March 2016 (four cycles of epirubicin and cyclophosphamide every three weeks, followed by four weekly cycles of paclitaxel) via AVF puncture using a peripheral catheter. The punctures were performed by dialysis clinic nursing staff, and no complications, such as traumatic or infectious events, were reported. Over a four-year follow-up period, there was no decline in dialysis efficacy (Kt/V: 1.7–2.5) or in AVF arterial blood flow rate (Qa: 660–960 mL/min). Following the completion of CT and radiotherapy, the patient remained in oncological remission.
Case 2. A 76-year-old man with chronic kidney disease (CKD) was diagnosed with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma in 2022 and underwent pancreatectomy with splenectomy, followed by six cycles of adjuvant CT (gemcitabine), achieving disease control. In 2023, he developed ESKD and subsequently required chronic HD. HD initiation was performed via a CVC, but in March 2024, a brachiocephalic AVF was created. Later this same year, following a relapse of his oncologic disease, he was prescribed another cycle of CT (gemcitrabine), which was administered via an AVF puncture using a peripheral catheter. The procedure was performed by dialysis clinic nursing staff without complications. No decline in dialysis efficacy (Kt/V: 1.61–1.80) or AVF arterial blood flow rate (Qa >1000 mL/min) was observed, and no major access-related complications were reported.
Conclusion
The use of AVFs for CT administration has been previously described in patients with central venous access failure (e.g., superior vena cava thrombosis) or a history of thrombotic events limiting the implantation of a chemotherapy port system. Reported complications are generally low and include erythema, thrombophlebitis and skin necrosis. Additionally, in a retrospective observational cohort study of 84 HD patients found that AVF patency rates were similar regardless of the presence of oncologic disease. However, evidence regarding the administration of CT via AVF in CKD patients undergoing HD remains scarce. Our two cases suggest that a pre-existent AVF may serve as a safe VA alternative for CT administration in HD-dependent oncologic patients, provided the puncture is performed by specialized nursing teams. Potential advantages over peripheral access or CVCs are particularly relevant in CKD patients, where vascular preservation is crucial for long-term survival. Given the limitations of this study, which is based on only 2 cases, future multicentre randomized studies are needed to establish patient selection criteria based on a comprehensive risk-benefit assessment, ensuring effectiveness and safety of this approach.

title: #2441 Volume status in haemodialysis patients at extreme body habitus
authors: David Keane; Daniele Trinca; Sebastian Mussnig; Simon Krenn; Manfred Hecking; Daniel Schneditz
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fluid overload and excessive fluid removal are common in haemodialysis and are associated with patient symptoms and clinical outcomes. Measurement of bioimpedance-based volume status and absolute blood volume enable objective assessments to support target weight management in haemodialysis, however uncertainties remain in their application at extreme body habitus. We aimed to assess whether blood volume reflected bioimpedance-based volume status at extreme body habitus and explored normalisation of blood volume in this context.
Method
We defined two volume status phenotypes common in haemodialysis: high body mass index (BMI) with post-dialysis volume depletion by bioimpedance (n = 29); and low lean tissue index (LTI) with post-dialysis volume overload by bioimpedance (n = 29). A third cohort, having residual renal function, interdialytic fluid gains below 0.5 litres, normal volume status and who were haemodynamically stable (n = 20), acted as controls. We compared post-dialysis blood volume measured by dialysate dilution in our high BMI and low LTI cohorts with controls, all at clinical target weight. We explored normalisation of blood volume (n = 98) by body mass, lean tissue mass (LTM) and anthropometric-based blood volume determined by Lemmens’ formula.
Results
Post-dialysis blood volume normalized for body mass (specific blood volume) was lower in the high BMI cohort (57.9 ml/kg; p = 0.02) and higher in the low LTI cohort (84.5 ml/kg; p = 0.001) than in controls (68.0 ml/kg) (Fig. 1). These differences were not present for LTM-normalised or Lemmens’ formula-normalised blood volume. Across all groups, referencing blood volume to body mass results in differences by sex and body mass (Fig. 2). Referencing to Lemmens blood volume, which accounts for fat mass variation, removes the differences between sex and body mass.
Conclusion
These results reiterate the importance of using bioimpedance in combination with clinical assessment and the clear need for personalisation of measurement targets at extreme body habitus. Use of specific blood volume may exacerbate established measurement bias observed with bioimpedance whereas referencing Lemmens’ blood volume can support measurement of blood volume at extreme body habitus.

title: #1245 Assessment of arsenic toxicity in cigarette smokers hemodialysis patients, its correlation with anemia and metabolic bone disease and evaluation of the role of high flux hemodialysis in arsenic clearance
authors: Ezzeldin Shalaby; Amira Elansary; Sarah Khater
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cigarette smoking is widely consumed worldwide. Arsenic is highly detected in cured or processed tobacco leaves at high concentrations. Arsenic poisoning can cause debilitating illness if left untreated, and its management especially in anuric patients by hemodialysis should be evaluated. 1-Assessment of Arsenic toxicity in Cigarette smokers in hemodialysis patients. 2- Assessment of correlation between Arsenic level with anaemia, uric acid and metabolic bone disease in hemodialysis patients. 3- Evaluation of the role of high flux hemodialysis in arsenic clearance.
Method
The study included 20 male patients on regular high flux hemodialysis for 6 months or more from Hemodialysis unit of Souad Kafafi Teaching Hospital- Egypt divided as follows: 1- Group A: 10 patients on regular active cigarette smoking. 2-Group B: 10 male non-smoker patients as control group. After taking a written consent from all participants and approval of ethical committee, the researchers drew venous blood sample (5 ml) by using metal free heparinized tube for Arsenic level pre and post hemodialysis sessions, blood samples for Complete Blood Count (CBC) including MCV, MCHC, RDW %, uric acid, Calcium total and ionized, phosphorus and magnesium. Dialysis Water samples were taken and normal Arsenic level <0.01 mg/L. All lab tests were done in Souad Kafafi central Lab except serum Arsenic level was done in Alborg central lab by Atomic Absorption Spectrometry from Perkin Elmer in Ug/dL.
Results
There was a highly statistically significant mean value of arsenic blood level at pre and post hemodialysis sessions in cigarette smokers group compared to non-cigarette smokers. There was also a highly statistically significant reduction in the mean value of arsenic blood level in the post-hemodialysis session compared to the pre-hemodialysis one. There was a statistically significant positive correlation between arsenic blood level pre hemodialysis session with age, years of smoking, number of cigarettes per day, RDW% and serum uric acid. While, there was a statistically significant negative correlation between arsenic blood level with hemoglobin, serum calcium, ionized calcium and serum magnesium.
Conclusion
Cigarette smoking increases blood arsenic level in hemodialysis patients, high flux hemodialysis is efficient in arsenic clearance, higher arsenic blood level associated with significant anaemia with high RDW%, high uric acid, low calcium and magnesium in hemodialysis patients.

title: #839 The impact of serum uromodulin on aortic arch vascular calcification in hemodialysis patients
authors: Tetsuya Ogawa; Eriko Hirasawa; Youko Nishizawa; Nobuo Nagano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Uromodulin, known as Tamm-Horsfall protein, is the most abundant protein found in urine. We previously reported that uromodulin is present in trace amounts in the blood and serves as a useful biomarker for renal function (Clin Exp Nephrol. 2021). Elevated serum uromodulin levels have been associated with a reduced risk of mortality and cardiovascular diseases in the elderly. Furthermore, in vivo studies have indicated that uromodulin inhibits cytokine-dependent calcification-promoting signals, thereby exhibiting a suppressive effect on vascular calcification. In this study, we examined the influence of uromodulin on vascular calcification in patients undergoing hemodialysis.
Method
We measured the pre-dialysis serum uromodulin levels in 80 maintenance dialysis patients (age 65.2 ± 11.0 years, dialysis history 13.1 ± 9.1 years) using the ELISA method. We compared the aortic arch vascular calcification index on chest X-rays and serum data between two groups based on the second quartile of serum uromodulin levels. The aortic arch vascular calcification index was expressed as the number of calcification segments using a dedicated 16-segment scale for vascular calcification in the aortic arch on chest X-rays.
Results
The overall patient population had an average age of 65.2 ± 11.0 years and a dialysis history of 13.1 ± 9.1 years. The serum uromodulin level was 5.4 ± 7.6 ng/mL, and the aortic arch vascular calcification index was 2.4 ± 2.8. The serum uromodulin levels were 9.84 ± 8.74 ng/mL in the high-value group and 0.87 ± 0.69 ng/mL in the low-value group. The dialysis history was significantly longer in the high-value group, with an average of 15.0 ± 10.7 years, compared to 11.2 ± 6.9 years in the low-value group. Conversely, the aortic arch vascular calcification index was significantly lower in the high-value group, measuring 1.83 ± 2.82, compared to 2.90 ± 2.68 in the low-value group. There were no significant differences in calcium (Ca), phosphorus (P), and intact parathyroid hormone (i-PTH) levels between the two groups.
Discussion
In this study, no significant differences were observed in calcium (Ca), phosphorus (P), and intact parathyroid hormone (i-PTH) levels between the high and low serum uromodulin groups among hemodialysis patients. However, the aortic arch vascular calcification index was significantly lower in the high serum uromodulin group. This suggests that serum uromodulin may be involved in the suppression of vascular calcification in hemodialysis patients.
Conclusion
This study suggests that serum uromodulin may be involved in the suppression of vascular calcification in hemodialysis patients.

title: #960 A single-centre service evaluation of patient-centred twice-weekly dialysis delivery
authors: Hilary Warrens; Arya Falahati; Merlin Peter; Helen Gaffney; Daniel Murphy; Peter Hill; Rishana Shuaib
abstract:
Background and Aims
Many individuals receive twice-weekly haemodialysis with an aim to increase dialysis frequency or as a step towards withdrawing renal replacement therapy. We aim to describe a cohort of individuals who receive long term twice-weekly haemodialysis in a single centre and compare their clinical outcomes, quality of life (QoL) measures and dialysis efficacy with a matched group receiving thrice-weekly dialysis in the same centre.
Method
In this centre with 110 haemodialysis patients, 16.3% receive twice-weekly dialysis. 15 twice-weekly patients were matched by age and sex with 26 patients on thrice-weekly dialysis. Data on biochemical parameters, dialysis adequacy and hospital admissions were retrospectively collected for a 12-month period from electronic patient records and IPOS-Renal QoL questionnaires were collected for service evaluation.
Results
Twice-weekly (n = 15) and thrice-weekly (n = 26) groups were of comparable Charlson Comorbidity index (6.87 vs. 7.04). The Edmonton Frailty Scale was higher in the thrice-weekly group (mean= 7.1 vs. 5.8). Median dialysis vintage in the twice- and thrice-weekly groups were 37 months (Q1–Q3 = 59) and 37 months (Q1–Q3 = 45) respectively. One third of the twice-weekly group had reduced the number of days since commencing dialysis. This subgroup had spent approximately half (54.2%) of their time on dialysis receiving twice-weekly treatment. Thrice-weekly patients received a mean 11.28 (±1.47) hours/week of haemodialysis, compared to 6.91 (±1.26) hours/week in the twice-weekly cohort. Haemoglobin and potassium levels remained within safe parameters in the twice-weekly cohort with a mean Kt/V of 1.46 (±0.31) (Fig. 1). In a single 24-hour urine collection, the twice-weekly patients had greater urinary volumes [0.87 (0.64) vs. 0.37 (0.62) L/24 hrs, median (Q1–Q3)]. The thrice-weekly patients had more than double the number of hospital presentations in the study year (4.54 vs. 2.13, per person-year). The greatest cause for presentation was infection in both groups (44% vs. 43%) (Table 1). More of the thrice-weekly group reported itching, sore or dry mouth and poor appetite. However, fewer of this group reported shortness of breath and drowsiness (Fig. 2). Reporting of psychological symptoms did not appear to differ between the groups. More of the thrice-weekly group reported that practical problems from their illness had not been addressed (50% vs. 20%), and that up to, or more than half of their day is wasted on healthcare appointments (45% vs. 10%).
Conclusion
We observed comparable dialysis safety and adequacy in twice- and thrice-weekly haemodialysis patients matched for age and sex. The twice-weekly population were less frail, had fewer hospital presentations and reported better QoL in some domains. This supports the hypothesis that in carefully selected individuals, long-term twice-weekly haemodialysis schedules may be safe, and potentially beneficial. In a dialysis population that is increasingly old and frail, person-centred care becomes even more paramount. Tailoring haemodialysis prescription to meet shared goals of care may improve QoL of older people treated with haemodialysis. Further work must identify more clearly which patients could be offered twice-weekly dialysis without risk of adverse outcomes.

Thrice-weekly patients received a mean 11.28 (±1.47) hours/week of haemodialysis, compared to 6.91 (±1.26) hours/week in the twice-weekly cohort. In a single 24-hour urine collection, the twice-weekly patients had greater urinary volumes [0.87 (0.64) vs. 0.37 (0.62) L/24 hrs, median (Q1–Q3)]. The thrice-weekly patients had more than double the number of hospital presentations in the study year (4.54 vs. 2.13, per person-year). The greatest cause for presentation was infection in both groups (44% vs. 43%) (Table 1). More of the thrice-weekly group reported itching, sore or dry mouth and poor appetite. The twice-weekly population were less frail, had fewer hospital presentations and reported better QoL in some domains. This supports the hypothesis that in carefully selected individuals, long-term twice-weekly haemodialysis schedules may be safe, and potentially beneficial. In a dialysis population that is increasingly old and frail, person-centred care becomes even more paramount. title: #2382 Effects of a group exercise program supported by audiovisual media on muscle strength of people on maintenance hemodialysis: a pilot study

abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) undergoing hemodialysis (HD) often present muscular complications, reducing functional capacity and increasing mortality. Exercise programs during HD sessions with the aid of technology could help in gaining strength while reducing sedentary behavior in this population.
OBJECTIVES
To assess changes in muscular strength of a group exercise program supported by audiovisual media during HD (GRexID) sessions.
Method
A 4-week randomized experimental study was conducted at the B. Braun Avitum – Massamagrell (Valencia, Spain) Renal Care Center. Participants were HD patients aged ≥18, on HD for ≥3 months, completing 12 hours/week. Patients with lower limb amputations, conditions interfering with test performance, or severe and unstable comorbidities were excluded. Participants were divided into a control group (CG, n = 11) and an exercise group (EG, n = 13). The CG received usual care with no additional intervention, while the EG participated in 12 exercise sessions delivered via television during HD. The exercises were divided into three protocols, lasting approximately 20 minutes each (15 minutes of exercise plus 5 minutes for warm-up/cool-down), targeting upper and lower limbs. The first protocol (lowest intensity), consisted of isolated leg or arm movements, and was applied in the initial 3 sessions the first week. The second protocol included diagonal movements (PNF), while the third protocol involved combined arm and leg movements at a fast pace. During the last 3 weeks of the program the three protocols alternated. Muscle strength was measured pre- and post-intervention. Upper limb strength was assessed with a hydraulic hand dynamometer (Jamar®), while lower limb strength was measured during HD using a handheld dynamometer (MMT Lafayette), focusing on hip flexors and abductors.
Results
Of the 79 patients assessed for eligibility, 29 met the inclusion criteria, but 5 withdrew consent (4 from CG, 1 from EG), leaving 24 participants (EG: 61% male, CG: 54% male). No adverse events such as hypotension or cramps were reported, though one participant discontinued due to persistent fatigue. Right hip flexion strength had a difference of +18.5 N (p = 0.106) in CG and +32.3 N (p = 0.002) in EG, but no differences between groups were achieved (p = 0.511). Left hip flexion strength had a difference of +28.6 N (p = 0.027) in CG and +22.4 N (p = 0.036) in CG, without difference between groups (p = 0.467). Right hip abduction strength had a difference of +12.7 N (p = 0.365) for CG and +22.1 (p = 0.068) for EG. The abduction of the left hip had a difference of +8.2 N (p = 0.379) for the CG and +18.4 (p = 0.025) for the EG, without difference between groups to (p = 0.419).
Conclusion
Despite significant strength gains after an intradialytic group exercise program supported by audiovisual media, difference between groups was not significant, so 12 exercise sessions may not be sufficient to produce clinically effective changes in muscle strength in HD patients. The observed may be due to learning of strength tests.

title: #2655 Feasibility and safety of a group exercise program supported by audiovisual media during hemodialysis (GREXID): an experimental study
authors: Eva Segura-Ortí; Emanuele Poliana Lawall Gravina; Claudia Merino-Ansuategui; Marina Fernández Gámez; Daniel Bellés León; Mariana Díaz Valenzuela; Helena Guillem Cambra; Paula Guzmán Prieto; Carmen Maria Perez-Baylach; Begoña Bonilla Culebras; Daniel Gallego Zurro; María del Mar Ruperto López
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) undergoing hemodialysis (HD) frequently experience muscular complications, which reduce functional capacity and increase mortality. Exercise programs during HD sessions are an effective strategy to mitigate sedentary behavior. Implementing innovative technologies can enhance clinical adoption, benefiting a broader range of patients.
OBJECTIVES
To evaluate the feasibility and safety of an intradialytic group exercise program supported by audiovisual media (GRexID) and participants' opinions about this form of intradialytic exercise.
Method
A 4-week experimental study was conducted at the B. Braun Avitum – Massamagrell (Valencia, Spain) Renal Care Center with patients aged ≥18 years who had been undergoing HD for ≥3 months. Patients with amputations or severe and unstable comorbidities were excluded. A total of 14 participants were included in the study to receive 12 exercise sessions delivered via television during HD. The exercises consisted of three different protocols, lasting approximately 20 minutes each (15 minutes of exercise plus 5 minutes for warm-up/cool-down), targeting Upper (no-fisttula arm) and lower limbs. The protocols were meant to progress from low to high intensity. The first protocol (lowest intensity), consisted of isolated leg or arm movements, and was applied in the initial 3 sessions the first week. The second protocol included diagonal movements (PNF), while the third protocol involved combined arm and leg movements at a fast pace. During the last 3 weeks of the program the three protocols alternated. Feasibility was assessed by adherence rates (number of completed sessions/number of planned sessions × 100) and reasons for non-compliance were computed. Safety was evaluated by monitoring incidents or interruptions during sessions. At the end of the 12 sessions, a questionnaire about GRexID opinions was administered.
Results
At baseline, one patient withdrew consent. The mean age of participants was 77.8 ± 12.6 years, with 61% being male. The average participation rate was 9 out of 12 sessions (75.6% adherence rate). Participants completed an average of 4 sessions of the first protocol and 2 sessions of the second and third protocols. The perceived exertion scores averaged 11.3 for the first protocol, 11.7 for the second, and 11.8 for the third, on a scale of 6 to 20. No adverse events, such as hypotension or cramps, were reported. However, one participant discontinued the program due to persistent fatigue. The primary reason for missed sessions was musculoskeletal pain unrelated to the exercises. Regarding patient feedback, 100% agreed or strongly agreed that the quality of the images and videos was good, that they enjoyed the program, and that it was a pleasant experience following the exercises on television. They also indicated they would recommend the program to others with the same health condition. However, the majority did not agree or disagreed that GRexID could improve their health condition (38.5%) or expressed willingness to continue the program (46.2%). Moreover, most participants preferred alternating between the three protocols during the week (54%) or combining all three protocols in a single session (69%).
Conclusion
An audiovisual-supported exercise program during HD sessions is feasible and safe, with high adherence rates and no severe adverse events. Although participants enjoyed the program and recommended it to others with similar conditions, most were had low motivation since they were not interested in continuing with it.

title: #3022 Association of physical function with chronic pain and sleep quality in patients on hemodialysis
authors: Maycon Moura Reboredo; Fabrício Barros; Gabrielle Gomes Queiroz; Helena Faria Mucci; Letícia Maria Do Carmo Corrêa; Ana Carolina Dumont; Ana Vieira de Souza; Rodrigo Garcia; Heitor Ribeiro; Leda Marília Fonseca Lucinda; Eva Segura-Ortí
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients on hemodialysis have muscle weakness, comorbidities and frailty, which contribute to impaired physical function. Moreover, pain and poor sleep quality are highly prevalent symptoms in these patients, significantly higher than in the general population. Therefore, this study evaluated the association of physical function with chronic pain and sleep quality in patients undergoing hemodialysis.
Method
This cross-section multicenter study included patients aged ≥18 years who were undergoing regular hemodialysis treatment for at least three months. Patients were excluded if they had severe or unstable comorbidities, psychiatric or cognitive disorders, and physical limitations including neurological, musculoskeletal and osteoarticular diseases which prevented the correct execution of the physical function tests. Physical function was assessed using handgrip strength, gait speed over 15 feet and the 5-repetition sit-to-stand (5-STS) test. Chronic pain was classified using the Chronic Pain Grade (CPG) scale, which categorizes pain into five grades, ranging from Grade 0 (no pain) to Grade IV (high disability and severely limiting intensity pain). Sleep quality was evaluated using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), with a score greater than 5 indicating poor sleep quality. The association between each physical function test (dependent variable) and CPG scale grades or sleep quality was analyzed using a univariate linear regression model. If significant associations were found, a multiple linear regression model was constructed, adjusting for potential confounders such as age, sex, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results
This study included 175 patients (59.0 ± 15.7 years, 54.9% male). Based on the CPG scale, 25.1% of patients were categorized as Grade 0, 33.2% as Grade 1, 25.7% as Grade 2, 12.6% as Grade 3, and 3.4% as Grade 4. The majority of patients (62.9%) exhibited poor sleep quality. In the univariate linear regression model, only gait speed showed a weak association with CPG scale grades (R = 0.18; p = 0.023). However, this association did not remain significant in the multiple linear regression model after adjustment for potential confounders. Sleep quality was not associated with handgrip strength, gait speed and the 5-STS test.
Conclusion
Patients on hemodialysis exhibited a high prevalence of chronic pain and poor sleep quality. However, physical function was not associated with chronic pain and sleep quality in these patients.

title: #1597 Oral nutritional support of hemodialysis patients: an intradialytic meal model intake and adherence analysis
authors: Vitor Sá Martins; Jesus Garrido; Leila Aguiar; Bruna Barbosa; Catarina Dias; Rita Figueiredo; Tania Magalhães; Patricia Moreira; Juliana Pereira; Inês Ramião; Carla Santos; Fernando MacÁrio
abstract:
Background and Aims
To ensure optimal maintenance or rehabilitation of nutritional status, nutritional therapy should be complemented with intradialytic nutritional support. This support aims to compensate at least the dialysis-related increase in basal metabolism and protein needs and supports the global nutritional strategy.
We have implemented a simple, feasible and pleasant intradialytic meal model that focus on patient’s autonomy, will (the patient chooses within the models’ available structure and range), literacy, nutritional goals (at least 300 kcal and 7 g of protein/meal/treatment) and clinical targets.
However, this strong emphasis on autonomy may present challenges in achieving optimal intradialytic nutritional intake for patients at higher risk of malnutrition. These individuals often face additional barriers, such as increased catabolic stress, inflammation, and reduced or absent appetite, which may ultimately impact intake profile.
The primary aim of this preliminary analysis was to evaluate the differences in the nutritional intake of intradialytic meal chosen by patients with no significant nutritional risk compared with patients with high nutritional risk. Additionally, the analysis sought to characterize the nutritional intake profiles of both groups.
Method
Cross-sectional nationwide analysis of HD pts from 27 outpatient clinics, examining the intradialytic meal chosen for the mid-week hemodialysis treatment. Nutritional composition data were sourced from manufacturers’ declarations, and when unavailable, the Portuguese Food Composition Table was used. Biochemical data were collected in April, while demographic data were retrieved from patients’ clinical charts.. The malnutrition-inflammation risk was assessed by trained registered nutritionists. Patients were divided into two groups based on their Malnutrition-Inflammation Score (MIS): those with no significant nutritional risk (MIS < 6) and those with significant nutritional risk (MIS ≥ 6) (Sá Martins, 2021). Hospitalized patients and those receiving additional commercial oral nutritional supplements were excluded from the total nutritional intake analysis. Patients who did not consume meals during treatment due to risks such as hypotension were also excluded.
Categorical data were presented as frequencies and percentages, while continuous variables were expressed as medians and interquartile ranges (25th percentile; 75th percentile). Group comparisons were conducted using the Chi-square test for categorical variables and the Mann–Whitney test for continuous variables. All analyses were performed using SPSS 30 (IBM Corp., 2023).
Results
We analyzed 3032 pts and their respective meals, 61.5% males, 38.4% diabetic, 59.5% of patients had MIS≥6, a 66% attained the goal of 300 kcal/7 g of protein. Half of the patients had an intake higher than 358 kcal, 12.7 g of protein, and 4.2 g of fiber. When comparing the 2 groups (Table 1) we observed that gender, sugar, potassium and calcium intake, as well as the clinical parameters were significantly different. No difference was found in diabetes prevalence. Nutritional intake parameters, such as energy, protein, phosphate and sodium were similar between the two groups.
The percentage of daily reference values contribution for fiber, sodium, potassium, calcium and phosphate intake were considered adequate for CKD5d patients (Table 1 and Fig. 1). Sodium contribution was the highest, followed by phosphate contribution.
Conclusion
Despite the limitations observed in patients at high risk of malnutrition, promoting autonomy in choosing the contents of the intra-dialytic meal appears to be safe and suitable for these patients’ needs. Therefore, we believe it should be encouraged and complemented with nutritional education and counseling.

title: #2754 A bleeding concern: incidence of major gastrointestinal bleeding in dialysis
authors: Yue Jiao; John Larkin; Derek Blankenship; Suman Lama; Sheetal Chaudhuri; Anke Winter; Manuela Stauss-Grabo; Len Usvyat; Franklin Maddux; David C Wheeler; Peter Stenvinkel; Jürgen Floege
abstract:
Background and Aims
Gastrointestinal bleeding (GIB) is the most common bleeding event in dialysis,1 yet known incidence rates are based on small studies and the influence of patient characteristics is unknown. We used a nationally representative sample of dialysis patients treated in the United States (US) to characterize the incidence rates of major GIB episodes requiring hospitalization overall and by age, sex, and history of GIB comorbidity.
Method
We used data from a kidney care network from Jan 2018 through Mar 2021. Analysis included data from adult dialysis patients (age ≥ 18 years) who were treated with dialysis for ≥ 30 days. We excluded data from patients who started dialysis on or after Jan 2021 to provide a 3-month minimum follow up for outcomes to occur. GIB hospitalization was identified from international classification of diseases (ICD) diagnosis codes recorded as the primary, secondary, or tertiary discharge reason for hospitalization. ICD clusters defining GIB hospitalization and lesion location were based on the US Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project.2 We calculated the incidence of GIB hospitalization per 1,000 person-years (per 1000 py). Time at risk excluded GIB hospital admission time.
Results
Analysis included 366,839 adults on dialysis (mean age of 62.6 years, 57.7% male, 55.8% white race). A total of 25,057 patients (6.8%) experienced GIB hospitalization, with 18,407 (73.5%) having a single event and 6,650 (26.5%) experiencing recurrent events. The standardized incidence rate of GIB hospitalization was 52.6 per 1000 py (95% CI: 52.1–53.1). Among all GIB episodes, 6,623 were classified as upper GIB, 4,378 as lower GIB, with 2,905 episodes having an upper and lower GIB diagnosed during the same event. A remarkable number of episodes (n = 16,961) did not have a specified lesion location in the ICD code; there were no differences in patient characteristics for those with a known versus unknown lesion location. Assuming missingness at random, the standardized incidence rate of GIB hospitalization was higher for upper GIB (11.4 per 1000 py, 95% CI: 11.2–11.7) versus lower GIB events (7.5 per 1000 py, 95% CI: 7.3–7.7). The incidence rate of GIB hospitalization progressively increased with age, being about three times higher in individuals aged 75 and older versus 18–44 (Table 1). Females had a slight, but statistically significant higher GIB hospitalization incidence rate compared to males. A baseline GIB comorbidity was associated with a four times higher incidence rate of GIB hospitalization.
Conclusion
Major GIB events requiring hospitalization affect about 53 out of every 1000 people on dialysis every year in the US. In the general population, GIB hospitalization affects about 1 of every 1000 people each year. This more than 50-fold higher rate in the standardized incidence of GIB hospitalization reveals a remarkable burden and unmet need in the dialysis population.3 Sixty percent of GIB hospitalizations involved upper GIB, and 40% involved lower. Over 25% of patients had multiple GIB hospitalizations. Rates rose with age and were four times higher with prior GIB. These findings highlight the burden of GIB within this vulnerable population, emphasizing the need for improved strategies for detection, such as data driven prediction algorithms, and treatment before the need for hospitalization. This study’s findings should be interpreted considering certain limitations, including reliance on hospitalization and comorbidity data collected as part of routine dialysis therapy.

Females had a slight, but statistically significant higher GIB hospitalization incidence rate compared to males. Conclusion

title: #1461 Strong-HD-VIE—prevalence of Strongyloides stercoralis infection in hemodialysis patients in Vienna, Austria
authors: Haris Omic; Luzia Veletzky; Yassan Mahdi-Nour-Ali; Simon Hoffmann; Karim Abd El-Ghany; Matthias Lorenz; Marcus Saeemann; Thomas Stulnig; Johannes Werzowa; Ludwig Wagner; Bruno Watschinger; Daniela Gerges
abstract:
Background and Aims
Strongyloides stercoralis (S. stercoralis) infection, a frequently overlooked parasitic disease, is widespread in tropical regions and considered rare in Europe. However, globalization, migration and global warming are contributing to an increase of cases also in Central Europe. Specifically, individuals undergoing high-dose corticosteroid treatment, such as kidney transplant (KTX) recipients, are at risk of the potentially life-threatening hyperinfection syndrome if they harbor latent S. stercoralis infection. This syndrome is characterized by autoinfection with S. stercoralis, leading to a massive worm burden, hyperinflammation, severe sepsis, and possibly death. Hyperinfection syndrome can be prevented by a short course of ivermectin treatment, which has little to no side effects. This raises the question of whether transplant candidates should undergo routine screening for S. stercoralis infection. Thus, we aimed to assess the prevalence of S. stercoralis infection in all patients with end-stage renal disease currently undergoing hemodialysis across the entire metropolitan area of Vienna, Austria.
Method
Blood samples were collected from all consenting hemodialysis patients in the city of Vienna (N = 720) and analyzed for IgG-antibodies using serology testing. A questionnaire was used to determine prior soil exposition, medical history including transplant status, travel history, symptoms indicative of helminthic infection, and immunosuppressive therapy. Positive serologies were reanalyzed by the Austrian reference center for parasitosis to confirm the results, three stool samples were taken for examination for worm eggs/larvae.
Results
Of the 720 patients, 90 (12.5%) had a history of organ transplantation (10 multiple KTX, 2 heart transplants, and 3 liver transplants). IgG-antibodies against S. stercoralis were detected in 69 patients (9.5%), including 9 with prior KTX. Among IgG-positive patients, gastrointestinal symptoms were reported in 14.4% (n = 10), and pruritus in 18.5% (n = 13). Notably, 74.2% (n = 52) had a travel history to endemic areas, 50% (n = 35) were pet owners, and 32.8% (n = 23) reported soil contact. However, there were no statistically significant differences in these variables between IgG-positive and IgG-negative individuals (all P > 0.05).
Conclusion
With globalization, migration, and climate change facilitating the spread of helminth infections, the prevalence of S. stercoralis in Austria is increasing. As one of ten dialysis patients tested positive for S. stercoralis, pre-transplant screening should be considered.

title: #2816 Overhydration and time to recovery after hemodialysis treatment before and after the introduction of a new routine for adjusting target weight (Recova-Recovery)
authors: Maaike Nielen; Maria K Svensson; Hans Furuland; Jenny Stenberg
abstract:
Background and Aims
Recovery time (RT), one aspect of dialysis-related fatigue, and fluid management, are factors significantly impacting the quality of life in patients with advanced kidney failure. A decision aid, Recognition and Correction of Volume Alterations (Recova®) represents a novel approach to improving fluid management in hemodialysis. Recova® integrates clinical assessments with bioimpedance spectroscopy (BIS). A more personalized dialysis prescription can be expected to contribute to shorter RT. The aim of this project was therefore to evaluate whether the use of Recova® is associated with positive changes in overhydration (OH) and RT after dialysis.
Method
In a prospective intervention study Recova® was implemented at 10 dialysis clinics located in five different regions in Sweden, with a stepped wedge cluster randomised design. Patients over 18 years of age with advanced kidney disease, who had been treated with HD for more than three months at one of the participating hemodialysis clinics and had a documented need for ultrafiltration, were screened for eligibility. OH was measured using BIS. Measurement of RT involved asking the question “How long does it take you to recover from dialysis treatment?” Comparisons were made using Wilcoxon’s signed rank test.
Results
At baseline 118 patients reported their self-estimated time to recovery (RT) after dialysis; thirty-one percent (n = 37) had recovered in less than 2 hours, 33.1% (n = 39) needed 2–6 hours, 20.3% (n = 24) needed 6–12 hours and 15.3% (n = 18) needed more than 12 hours to recover. Mean RT decreased from 6.7 hours before the intervention to 5.7 hours after the intervention, but this change did not reach significance, in median RT was 4 (0.75–10) hours at baseline. At follow up the measured OH had decreased from 2.5 ± 1.8 L to 2.3 ± 2.0 L (p = 0.003) and fewer hospitalizations from in mean 1.3 ± 0.5 to 1.2 ± 0.4 (p = 0.024) per six months, were reported. During the 12-week intervention, initially there was a gradual decline in signs and symptoms related to fluid status assessed every second week. However, at the fifth observation (week 10) the volume status score increased again (see Fig. 1).
Conclusion
The Recova® tool demonstrated potential for improving fluid management, as evidenced by a significant reduction in OH and a decline in volume status score. However, the intervention did not have a significant impact on RT. These findings underscore the importance and possibilities of individualized fluid management strategies to enhance quality of life in patients with advanced kidney disease and dialysis treatment.

title: #3543 Impact of intradialytic exercise on cardiopulmonary parameters assessed by cycle ergometer exercise test
authors: Salvador Lopez Gil; Alfredo Fuentes Mercado; Julio Vinicio Pazos Urrieta; Fernanda Garza Romero; Magdalena Madero; Francisco Eugenio Rodríguez Castellanos
abstract:
Background and Aims
Worldwide, the implementation of intradialytic exercise remains low despite the benefits demonstrated in recent studies. Moreover, there is limited published evidence on the appropriate prescription of this type of exercise. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) is considered the gold standard for assessing maximal oxygen consumption (VO2max) and is essential for determining training zones and ventilatory thresholds (VT1 or lactate-aerobic threshold, and VT2 or anaerobic threshold). The objective of this study is to evaluate the impact of intradialytic exercise on CPET parameters, based on a systematic exercise prescription.
Method
An open-label clinical trial with a before and after study was conducted. A baseline CPET was performed to determine VT1, which served as the basis for exercise prescription. Patients performed exercise at this workload for 45 minutes, with weekly increments of 5 minutes until reaching 90 minutes, following international exercise guidelines. After 16 weeks of intervention, a follow-up CPET was conducted.
Results
A total of 21 patients were included (mean age = 38.7 years [SD = 12.9]; 59% women). The pre- and post-intervention results and p-values are shown in Table 1.
Conclusion
A systematic prescription of intradialytic exercise over 16 weeks significantly improved cardiopulmonary efficiency, as evidenced by a significant increase in watts at VT1 (Fig. 1) and in maximal exercise tolerance. Although maximal oxygen consumption improved in all patients, the difference did not reach statistical significance taking to account the sample size, however, the improvement has clinical relevance.

title: #233 Vascular access of incident dialysis patients with polycystic kidney disease. A registry-based study using propensity score matching methodology
authors: Ramon Roca-Tey; Jordi Comas; Amparo Roda Safont; Juan Carlos Gonzalez; Jessica Maria Ugalde Altamirano; Ursula Luz Vadillo Vidal; Verónica Duarte Gallego; Sandy Valeria Pico Ruiz; Jordi Calls; Jaume Tort
abstract:
Background and Aims
Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is the most common hereditary cause of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). There are limited studies about vascular access (VA) of PKD patients (pts) treated by haemodialysis (HD). To analyze the VA profile of incident HD pts with PKD in Catalonia.
Method
Data from the Catalan Renal Registry of 23,243 ESKD pts (1486 with PKD and 21,757 non-PKD) older than 18 years of age starting HD therapy were examined over a 26-year period (1997–2022). Propensity score matching (PSM) was performed to obtain a control group from non-PKD patients (1167 matched pairs were obtained).
Results
Prior to PSM, the first VA used for starting HD in pts with and without PKD was: fistulae AVF (71.2%, n = 994 vs 42.1%, n = 8636; P < 0.001), graft AVG (1.6%, n = 22 vs 1.1%, n = 223; p = 0.092), tunnelled catheter (11.5%, n = 160 vs 23.1%, n = 4734; P < 0.001) and non-tunnelled catheter (15.8%, n = 220 vs 33.8%, n = 6939; P < 0.001). After PSM, the VA distribution was: AVF (70.3%, n = 820 vs 57.4%, n = 670; P < 0.001), AVG (1.9%, n = 22 vs 1.5%, n = 18; p = 0.52), tunnelled catheter (13.3%, n = 155 vs 21.8%, n = 254; P < 0.001) and non-tunnelled catheter (14.6%, n = 170 vs 19.3%, n = 225; p = 0.002).
Regarding gender, the percentage of pts with vs without PKD starting HD by AVF was: 71.0% (n = 538) vs 44.1% (5941) for men and 71.5% (n = 456) vs 38.1% (n = 2695) for women (for both comparisons, P < 0.001). The percentage of men and women starting HD by AVF was: 71.0% (n = 538) vs 71.5% (n = 456) for PKD pts (p = 0.84) and 44.1% (5941) vs 38.1% (n = 2695) for non-PKD pts (P < 0.001).
Probability of starting HD by AVF after adjusting for gender, age, ESKD presentation, cardiovascular disease, body mass index and functional status (multivariate logistic regression analysis) was independently associated with PKD before (odds ratio 2.14 [95% confidence interval CI: 1.87–2.44], p < 0.001) and after (odds ratio 1.66 [95% CI: 1.38–1.99], p < 0.001) PSM.
Through a competing risk model, the hazard ratio (HR) for receiving a kidney graft (KG) within five years from starting HD, depending on the first VA (AVF vs catheter) used, was: 1.65 (95% CI: 1.38–1.97, P < 0.001) for PKD pts and 1.78 (95% CI: 1.68–1.89, P < 0.001) for non-PKD pts before PSM and 1.74 (95% CI: 1.43–2.12, P < 0.001) for PKD pts and 1.62 (95% CI: 1.35–1.93, P < 0.001) for non-PKD pts after PSM. In comparison with non-PKD pts that started HD by AVF, HR of PKD pts for receiving a KG within five years from starting HD by AVF was 2.69 (95% CI: 2.46–2.94, P < 0.001) before PSM and 0.99 (95% CI: 0.87–1.14, p = 0.97) after PSM. In comparison with non-PKD pts that started HD by catheter, HR of PKD pts for receiving a KG within five years from starting HD by catheter was 2.91 (95% CI: 2.47–3.43, P < 0.001) before PSM and 0.96 (95% CI: 0.76–1.19, p = 0.68) after PSM.
The HR of death within five years from starting HD, depending on the first VA (catheter vs AVF) used, was: 1.94 (95% CI: 1.49–2.51, P < 0.001) for PKD pts and 1.56 (95% CI: 1.49–1.63, P < 0.001) for non-PKD pts before PSM and 1.93 (95% CI: 1.45–2.57, P < 0.001) for PKD pts and 1.43 (95% CI: 1.13–1.81, p = 0.003) for non-PKD pts after PSM. In comparison with PKD pts that started HD by catheter, HR of death for non-PKD pts within five years from starting HD by catheter was 2.35 (95% CI: 1.93–2.86, P < 0.001) before PSM and 1.24 (95% CI: 0.95–1.64, p = 0.12) after PSM. In comparison with PKD pts that started HD by AVF, HR of death for non-PKD pts within five years from starting HD by AVF was the 2.98 (95% CI: 2.53–3.51, P < 0.001) before PSM and 1.64 (95% CI: 1.29–2.09, P < 0.001) after PSM.
Conclusion
1) Although AVF was the main type of VA used for starting HD in pts with and without PKD, the percentage of AVF in non-PKD pts was significantly lower than PKD pts at the expense of catheter. 2) There was no difference in the distribution of men and women with PKD starting HD by AVF. 3) PKD was an independent factor associated with a 66% greater probability of starting HD by AVF. 4) In pts both with and without PKD, starting HD through AVF or catheter was associated with the highest or the lowest probability of receiving a KG over time, respectively. 5) Among all pts starting HD through AVF, the presence of PKD confers an added advantage for reducing the risk of mortality over time.
