title: #1299 Association of dialysis shift with morning surge in blood pressure and dipping pattern
authors: Marieta P Theodorakopoulou; Fotini Iatridi; Artemios Karagiannidis; Areti Georgiou; Sofia Manti; Antonios Karpetas; Panagiota Anyfanti; Eleni Gavriilaki; Pantelis Sarafidis
abstract:
Background and Aims
Blood pressure (BP) levels typically present a diurnal variation characterized by a decrease during nighttime and an increase in early morning. Evidence suggests that exaggerated morning surge in BP is associated with higher cardiovascular risk. This is the first study evaluating the association between timing of dialysis and morning BP surge in hemodialysis.
Method
113 patients dialyzed on the morning shift were matched for age and sex in a 1:1 ratio with 113 patients dialyzed on the midday/evening shifts. All patients underwent 48-h ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM); the BP morning surge at the first and second days of the recording was calculated based on three widely used definitions (pre-awakening, sleep-trough and rising morning BP surge).
Results
The two groups were similar in terms of age, BMI, and major comorbidities. Patients dialyzed on morning shift presented higher mean SBP and DBP sleep-through surge (SBP: 18.71 ± 13.11 vs 14.22 ± 10.25 mmHg, p = 0.005; DBP: 12.05 ± 8.04 vs 9.46 ± 8.53mmHg, p = 0.020) and higher mean SBP and DBP pre-awakening surge (SBP: 12.05 ± 8.04 vs 9.46 ± 8.53mmHg, p = 0.020; DBP: 10.16 ± 9.56 vs 6.53 ± 10.78 mmHg, p = 0.008). No significant between-group differences were observed in mean SBP rising surge. During the 1st 24-h period, pre-awakening SBP and DBP surge were significantly higher in individuals dialyzed in the morning shift (SBP: 9.85 ± 11.15 vs 6.22 ± 11.77 mmHg, p = 0.018). During the 2nd 24-h period, SBP/DBP sleep-through surges were higher in participants on morning shift (SBP: 20.02 ± 18.17 vs 12.79 ± 12.91 mmHg, p = 0.001; DBP: 12.49 ± 10.76 vs 9.64 ± 10.53, p = 0.046). No significant between-group differences were observed in dipping patterns.
Conclusion
Patients dialyzed on the morning shift exhibited significantly higher morning BP surge compared to the other two shifts. Future studies should confirm these observations and examine the need for individualizing the choice of dialysis shift for patients with specific circadian BP profiles.

authors: Xixi Zheng; Haiyun Wang; Zijuan Zhou; Peng Xia; Limeng Chen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Peritonitis is the leading cause of technical failure in peritoneal dialysis (PD), often resulting in the cessation of home dialysis. Culture-negative peritonitis poses unique management challenges with limited evidence on optimal strategies.
Method
This retrospective cohort study included consecutive cases of PD-associated peritonitis from 2013 to 2023 in the PD center of Peking Union Medical College Hospital. The clinical data were extracted from electronic health records. The diagnosis, classification, and outcomes of peritonitis were consistent with ISPD guidelines. Depending on the characteristics of the data, comparisons between groups were conducted using t-tests, Mann–Whitney tests, or Fisher’s exact test. Logistic regression was used to analyze the correlation between various factors and outcomes.
Results
Culture-negative (CN) peritonitis accounted for 25.5% (63/247) of all peritonitis. Compared with culture-positive (CP) peritonitis, patients with CN peritonitis were more likely to have smoked (P = 0.031) and had significantly higher rates of antibiotic use before culture collection (47.6% vs. 9.2%, P < 0.0001). Baseline characteristics, including age, diabetes status, BMI, PD modality, and pre-peritonitis bloodwork, were comparable. In multivariate logistic regression, only smoking history (OR = 2.01, 95% CI: [1.024, 3.945], P = 0.042) and the use of antibiotics before culture collection (OR = 58.59, 95% CI: [3.942, 19.54], P < 0.0001) were independently associated with negative culture peritonitis.
The patients initially presented to the emergency room (ER) experienced higher rates of antibiotic use (27.55% vs. 9.85%, P = 0.0007) and delays in effluent culture collection (average 12.7 hours vs. 1.2 hours, P < 0.0001) than those presented to the PD unit. Multivariate logistic regression analysis indicated that CP peritonitis, automated peritoneal dialysis (APD), and non-first episodes of peritonitis independently predicted the poor prognosis of not being medically cured. CN peritonitis generally had better outcomes with higher medically cured rates and fewer refractory cases. However, a subgroup of patients with comorbidities requiring antibiotics (N = 9) use before culture had the worst prognosis: 4 of them died during peritonitis treatment, and the survivors had a catheter removal rate of 60%.
Conclusion
Cultural negativity is influenced by the initial presentation’s location and sample collection delays. CN peritonitis generally has favorable outcomes. Special attention is needed for CN peritonitis patients with comorbid infections, as their prognoses are significantly worse. These findings highlight the importance of tailored management strategies for patients with peritonitis, particularly for those with a history of antibiotic use or recurrent episodes.

title: #3834 A randomized clinical trial on the effect of PEGylated granulocyte-colony stimulating factor on antibody response in hemodialysis patients who had not responded to routine hepatitis B virus vaccine
authors: Jamshid Roozbeh; Fatemeh Masjedi; Sara Rahmanian
abstract:
Background and Aims
Various strategies have been applied to improve the response to hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination in hemodialysis patients. The present study was undertaken to compare the seroconversion rate of hemodialysis patients who had not responded to 3 intramuscular (IM) doses (40 µg each) of HBV vaccine after a fourth IM dose (40 µg) of HBV vaccine that was administered alone or with subcutaneous PEGylated granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (PEG-G-CSF) (6 mg/0.6 mL).
Method
Eighty hemodialysis patients who had not responded to 3 IM injections of HBV vaccine were randomized into two groups: Group 1 received a booster dose of 40 µg HBV vaccine IM, and Group 2 received a booster dose of 40 µg HBV vaccine IM plus 6 mg/0.6 mL subcutaneous PEG-G-CSF. Antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen was measured one month after the booster dose.
Results
The seroconversion rate in group 1 was 33%. There was a trend towards a higher seroconversion rate at 67% in group 2 patients; this was statistically significant (P < 0.01).
Conclusion
This innovative strategy could be suitable for vaccination in hemodialysis patients who had not responded to routine hepatitis B virus vaccine. More prolonged follow-up of the patients is needed to evaluate the duration of protection induced by each method of vaccination.

title: #2862 The ameliorative effects of oral tacrolimus on treatment-resistant pruritus through interleukin 13 signaling pathways in hemodialysis patients: a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial
authors: Fatemeh Masjedi; Jamshid Roozbeh; Zahra Ghayoomi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Uremic pruritus (UP) is one of the major complaints in hemodialysis patients without specific treatment. IL-13 serum level on the other hand may be related to the severity of itch in these patients. Considering the antipruritic effect of Tacrolimus in atopic dermatitis (AD) and similarities in mechanism between pruritus in AD and UP, this randomized clinical trial designed to evaluate the antipruritic effect of Tacrolimus via interleukin 13 signaling pathways on hemodialysis patients with UP.
Method
This multicenter double-blind randomized clinical trial was conducted among the hemodialysis patients with UP. Adult patients were randomly assigned to receive one capsules of Tacrolimus/placebo 1 mg/d for 8 weeks period, followed by a 2-week observational period. Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), % affected Body Surface Area (%BSA) and 12-Pruritus Severity Scale questionnaire (12-PSS) were measured before and after intervention. The serum levels of IL-13 and IL-13 gene expression were measured in chronic hemodialysis and healthy controls using ELISA and qRT-PCR, respectively.
Results
Seventy-five patients under hemodialysis (mean age of 55.62 ± 10.34 years) completed the study. Mean changes in VAS, 12-PSS, and %BSA after the interventions were statistically significant. Tacrolimus was effective in improving UP by reducing IL-13 levels and its receptor expression.
Conclusion
Based on to the preliminary results of this study, Tacrolimus can be introduced as an effective drug for management of pruritus in uremic patients. Tacrolimus exerts its healing effects through interleukin-13 signaling. Optimizing dialysis and targeting this cytokine may provide a potential therapeutic option especially in refractory UP.

title: #3821 Malnutrition is prevalent in dalmatian hemodialysis patients
authors: Josipa Radić; Dragan Klaric; Hana Đogaš; Marijana Vučković; Dora Bučan Nenadić; Borna Cvečić; Mislav Radić
abstract:
Background and Aims
Malnutrition is common in maintenance hemodialysis (HD) patients and is indicator of mortality and morbidity. Malnutrition inflammation score (MIS) is associated with inflammation, nutritional status, quality of life, and 5-year prospective mortality. Also, phase angle (PhA) measured by bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) has been studied as indicator of nutritional status or muscle function in HD patients. Also, lower PhA was associated with a greater risk of malnutrition. The aims of this study are to analyze the prevalence of malnutrition in Dalmatian HD patients using MIS, and to assess the association of MIS and PhA with body mass composition, sociodemographic characteristics, dietary intake, and laboratory parameters.
Method
86 HD patients aged 69 (59.8–76.3) years, 29 women (33.7%) and 57 (33.7%) men with mean HD duration 4.5 (2.6–6.6) years from two Dalmatian HD center were included. For each study participant, data about body composition measured with BIA, laboratory, sociodemographic and clinical parameters were obtained. Also, body mass index (BMI) was calculated, the MIS was used to assess nutritional status, and dietary intake was collected using a 3-day food record.
Results
Using an MIS cut-off point of 6 for malnutrition, 47 (54.7%) HD patients were malnourished. Also, results showed significant positive correlation between MIS, age (r = 0.474, P < 0.001) and C-reactive protein (r = 0,378, P < 0,001). Significant negative correlation between MIS, residual renal function (r = −0.230, p = 0.04), waist circumference (r = −0.300, p = 0.01), serum creatinine (r = 0.418 P < 0.001) and phosphate level (r = −0.234, p = 0.03) was found. There were not significant correlations between any components of dietary intake and MIS. Therefore, significant negative correlation between PhA and age was found (r = −0.248, p = 0.02), while significant positive correlation between PhA and serum creatine level was found (r = 0.353, P < 0.001). Furthermore, significant positive correlations between PhA and biotin intake (r = 0.241, p = 0.03) was found as well as between vitamin B12 intake and muscle mass (%) (r = 0.246, p = 0.03). A multivariate regression analysis showed that age (ß = 0.11, P < 0.001) and fat mass (kg) (ß = −0.08, P = 0.03) were predictive factors for MIS while muscle mass (kg) (ß = 0.71, p = 0.004) and thiamine intake (ß = 1.74, p = 0.001) were predictive factors for PhA.
Conclusion
The prevalence of malnutrition in Dalmatian HD patients was high. These results indicate and highlight the urgent need for individualized and structural nutritional screening (using MIS score and PhA) and nutritional support through advice for proper dietary intake, especially for older HD patients.

title: #2360 Impact of fluid overload changes within the first 6 months of dialysis on hospitalization during a two-year follow-up
authors: Melanie Wolf; Linda Ficociello; Christina Rossi; Meijiao Zhou; Len Usvyat; Stefano Stuard; Franklin Maddux
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fluid overload (FO) is a known risk factor for mortality in dialysis patients; however, less is known about its risk for hospitalization and factors associated with changes in FO. Whole-body bioimpedance spectroscopy (BIS) has been validated for hydration assessment. We used Body Composition Monitor (BCM) data, a whole-body BIS, to evaluate the changes in FO during the first 6 months of hemodialysis (HD) or hemodiafiltration (HDF) in association with hospitalizations.
Method
Data was extracted from the global anonymized dialysis database, ApolloDialDb™, for patients starting dialysis in 2018 and 2019. All patients with 2 BCM measurements separated by ∼6 months, with the first being ≤90 days after HD/HDF start, were included. FO was dichotomized at ≥2.5L overhydration (OH) or at ≥15%/≥13% (for men and women, respectively) OH adjusted for extracellular water (OH/ECW). The patients were categorized into four groups (FO-FO, FO-No overload (NO), NO-FO, and NO-NO) by changes in OH in liters (OH-L) and OH relative to ECW (OH-%) between these two measurements. All cause hospitalization rates were assessed over 2 years following the second BCM measurement, and compared using rate ratios with 95% confidence intervals.
Results
A total of 13,221 adult HD/HDF patients were included. Baseline characteristics and hospitalization rates for OH-L and OH-% are presented in Table 1. Across both definitions, patients improving their fluid status to normally hydrated (FO-NO) or remaining normally hydrated (NONO) had lower hospitalization rates compared to patients staying overhydrated (FOFO) in the first six months of dialysis. Compared to FOFO, there were 19% and 30% fewer hospitalizations in FO-NO and NONO, respectively, for definitions based on OH-L (Fig. 1). Results were similar for OH% definitions (20% and 32% fewer for FO-NO and NONO, respectively).
Conclusion
Hospitalization risk is lowest among patients who maintain or improve fluid status to normal hydration during the first six months of dialysis when compared to fluid-overloaded patients, by either definition. These findings highlight the importance of fluid management in improving patient outcomes. However, the study has some limitations, including reliance on BCM measurements at two time points and the potential impact of unmeasured confounders.

title: #2266 Integrating palliative care into nephrology: a single-center “action-research” process
authors: Marica Mulè; Diana Bertoni; Roberta Zani; Brunella Valzorio; Bernardo Lucca; Marta Tenini; Simona Guerini; Antonella Gandioli; Sara Molgora; Anna Bertoni; Cosimo Chelazzi; Federico Alberici
abstract:
Background and Aims
Recognizing the need to integrate palliative care into nephrology, an “action-research” model was launched in April 2023.
Method
A multidisciplinary pilot group (6 nephrologists, 7 nurses), led by a psychologist, was established and operated through seven focus groups to explore perceived challenges, training needs, and potential strategies for integrating palliative care into clinical practice. The model employed was an “action-research” one, model characterised by a cyclical process of inquiry, action, and reflection, where data is collected, analysed, and used to inform and to promote empowering collaboration to needed change.
The discussions were transcribed and analysed manually (“paper and pencil”). Based on the main themes/topics that emerged, a questionnaire was administered to all nephrologist and nurses of the unit. The questionnaire included four Likert scale questions (1 = not at all, 5 = very much), one multiple-choice question, and one open-ended question, aiming to identify perceived barriers and resources for implementing palliative care. The answers of the open-ended question were analysed using the T-Lab software. The findings informed the creation of a teaching initiative for all the unit staff. Additionally, the number of patients referred to palliative care pathways before and after the initiative was started was recorded to quantify its impact.
Results
The content analysis of the seven focus groups revealed the need to challenge stereotypes about palliative care and to develop tools for timely activation of palliative care pathways. Key findings included characteristics of palliative care patients (psychological suffering [6/10 participants] and physical suffering [4/10 participants]); highly relational tasks (10/10 participants) for nurse-physician roles in order to support patients and families in a flexible decision-making process.
These insights informed the development of a questionnaire distributed to all the unit staff. A total of 114 out of 205 staff members (55%) participated, comprising 77 nurses (68%) and 37 doctors (32%). The findings showed that 66% of respondents considered palliative care “very important”, but 38% felt it was only “fairly” achievable. 62% agreed that palliative care is a “shared treatment pathway”. 31% believed patients were “minimally involved” in decision-making, while 90% felt family members were “quite” or “very involved”.
Thematic analysis identified four key clusters (Fig. 1). Those were classified as “Need for a culture in palliative care” (38% of variance), highlighted primarily by doctors, who cited lack of experience and resources as major barriers. “Patient centered care” (35% of variance), emphasized by nurses. “Necessary approaches” (17% of variance). “Dignified death” (11% of variance).
Following the questionnaire, the pilot group organized for all the unit staff a teaching day on the clinical, psychological and ethical challenges of palliative care, involving palliative care specialists and ethicists. As a measure of the overall initiative impact, patient referrals to palliative care before and after the initiative were compared: in the 390 days before the integration process, 30 patients were referred (26 in the acute settings); in the 390 days following the start of the initiative, 73 patients were referred (61 in the acute settings).
Conclusion
The overall initiative significantly increased awareness of palliative care as an integral treatment option. For the Nephrology Unit, palliative care is viewed as a valuable resource for supporting patients and families at the end of life. However, limitations remain, particularly in terms of experience and resources. From this perspective, a close integration between palliative care specialists and nephrologists is required in order to activate processes for simultaneous care and reduce the number of referrals in the acute setting.

title: #3830 “Radiocephalic fistulas and vascular doppler ultrasound (DUS): beyond conventional limits”
authors: Irati Tapia González; Vicent Esteve Simó; Sara Ibañez Pallares; Fátima Moreno Guzmán; Anna Saurina Solé; Mónica Pou Potau; Patricia Jimenez Costa; Raül Sanchez Marin; Montserrat Yeste Campos; Manel Ramírez de Arellano Serna
abstract:
Background and Aims
Preoperative ultrasound vascular mapping is currently a fundamental tool for the creation of arteriovenous fistulas (AVF). Vascular access clinical guidelines recommend, among other criteria, a radial artery peak systolic velocity (PSV) greater than 50 cm/sec. However, strict adherence to this threshold may exclude patients with optimal arterial and venous diameters for AVF creation.
Objective
To analyze the patency of radiocephalic arteriovenous fistulas (RC-AVF) created exclusively in patients with radial artery PSV below 50 cm/sec, while maintaining other optimal vascular parameters.
Method
A retrospective single-center analysis of RC-AVFs performed over the past seven years was conducted. Two groups were compared: Group 1: RC-AVFs with radial artery PSV < 50 cm/sec but with all other ultrasound parameters within guideline recommendations. Group 2: RC-AVFs with radial artery PSV ≥ 50 cm/sec. Patency rates were assessed at 4 and 12 weeks, along with complications and causes of vascular access failure.
Results
A total of 85 patients were included (82.1% in Group 1, 17.9% in Group 2). Radiocephalic AVF accounted for 59.5% of cases. No significant differences were observed in baseline demographic data. Ultrasonographic parameters were comparable between Groups 1 and 2, with radial artery diameters of 2.6 ± 0.39 mm vs. 2.6 ± 0.41 mm, respectively, and cephalic vein diameters of 2.7 ± 0.43 mm vs. 2.7 ± 0.53 mm. AVF maturation rates were similar between Groups 1 and 2 at both 4 weeks (73.3% vs. 62.3%; p = 0.311) and 12 weeks (66.7% vs. 50.7%; p = 0.503), with no statistically significant differences. No differences in complication rates were observed between groups.
Conclusion
These findings suggest that radial artery PSV below 50 cm/sec may still be compatible with the successful creation of RC-AVFs in patients with adequate arterial and venous diameters. Additional hemodynamic and morphological factors should be considered when planning RC-AVFs. Expanding selection criteria could optimize vascular access planning for hemodialysis patients.

title: #1337 The role of intravenous etelcalcitide in haemodialysis patients with mid-range serum parathyroid hormone levels
authors: Shilpa Vijayasrinivasan; Claire Edwards; Anisha Tanna; Megan Griffith; Zohreh Nazari; Oshini Shivakumar; Neill Duncan
abstract:
Background and Aims
Secondary hyperparathyroidism (sHPT) is a frequent complication in haemodialysis patients and is associated with all-cause mortality, cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, and bone fractures. Clinical trials have demonstrated the efficacy of etelcalcitide in treating sHPT; however, concerns about hypocalcemia remain, underscoring the need for more real-world data to guide clinical practice. This study provides a real-world perspective on the role of etelcalcitide in optimising metabolic outcomes and symptom management in patients with sHPT and mid-range serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels receiving haemodialysis at Northwick Park Hospital dialysis unit in London.
Method
A retrospective review was conducted of adult haemodialysis patients with sHPT receiving etelcalcitide between December 2023 and December 2024. All patients were either unsuitable for or declined parathyroidectomy. Dose and duration of etelcalcitide, changes in laboratory parameters, and adverse events were recorded. The primary outcome was the change in serum PTH levels at the end of data collection compared with baseline pre-treatment levels.
Results
49 patients were included in the study. The median duration on renal replacement therapy was 5.0 years (interquartile range, IQR 3–9), and the median duration on etelcalcitide was 1.0 years (IQR 0.9–2.0). Patients were either calcimimetic naïve (73.5%) or switched from oral cinacalcet (26.5%). 47 patients (95.9%) had pre-treatment serum PTH levels less than 300 pmol/L. The median starting dose of etelcalcitide was 7.5 mg per week and was titrated as required in increments of 2.5–5 mg.
The median percentage reduction in serum PTH from pre-treatment levels to December 2024 was 73.4% (IQR 36.9–85.9), from a median of 130.0 pmol/L (IQR 95.6–180.0) to 38.3 pmol/L (IQR 17.2–77.8). Linear regression analysis revealed no significant difference when stratified by duration on etelcalcitide (p = 0.13), initial etelcalcitide dose (p = 0.90), prior calcimimetic use (p = 0.14), or baseline PTH levels (p = 0.28). Of the 29 patients who had been on etelcalcitide for more than 1 year, 26 achieved greater than 30% reduction in PTH levels from baseline. 14 patients who had been on etelcalcitide for more than 2 years achieved a median reduction of 47.2% (IQR 24.9–68.8) in alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels, from a median ALP of 223.0 IU/L (IQR 152.0–396.0) to 115.0 IU/L (IQR 89.5–148.5).
While 17 patients (34.9%) developed hypocalcemia of less than 2 mmol/L, none were reported as symptomatic. 10 patients (20.4%) had interruptions to etelcalcitide administration due to hypocalcemia or over-suppression of PTH levels.
Conclusion
Etelcalcitide is an effective and safe option to improve biochemical parameters of sHPT in our dialysis population. Although hypocalcemia was common, close monitoring with prompt corrective intervention i.e. increase in calcium supplementation or active vitamin D, or dose reduction and discontinuation of etelcalcitide where necessary, ensured that this did not cause significant morbidity. Our results indicate that etelcalcitide is effective for patients with mid-range PTH levels of less than 300 pmol/L. The improvement in ALP levels suggests a reduction in bone turnover after treatment with etelcalcitide. Further study is needed to evaluate whether this translates to longer-term improvement in mortality, morbidity, and patient-reported outcomes in sHPT.

title: #1328 Novel tidal, steady-concentration sorbent-based PD (viva kompact) reduces glucose exposure and maintains target weight: a comparative pilot study vs. conventional PD
authors: Arsh Jain; Htay Htay; Edwina Anne Brown; Martin Schreiber; Sheena Gow; Jason Lim; Sanjay Singh; Mandar Gori; Marjorie Foo
abstract:
Background and Aims
In conventional PD (CPD), ultrafiltration (UF) will decline over time with diminishing glucose gradient; necessitating fresh dialysate instillation to reestablish the gradient. Viva Kompact (previously AWAK) is a steady concentration sorbent-based peritoneal dialysis (PD) device which tidals 250 mls per cycle, up to 64 cycles, and regenerates new solution at the rate of 2 L/hour after the initial instillation of dextrose solution1. Fig. 1 illustrates a simulated scenario of glucose concentration in the peritoneum over a therapy. In Viva Kompact the rate of glucose infusion can be adjusted between 4 settings (0.4–1.6 ml/cycle of 70% dextrose) based on subject’s need, guided by a nomogram. Therapy time can vary between 7 to 9 hours. This study aims to evaluate the UF patterns and efficiency, with subjects as their own control, while on the Viva Kompact device as compared to CPD.
Method
At Singapore General Hospital between May 2023 to February 2024, 14 subjects were screened and underwent a titration period (up to 21 days), a washout (minimum 2 days), and an at-home treatment period (7 days). Three subjects were offered an optional extension (23 days). During titration a nomogram guide for steady concentration PD was employed to determine cartridge type, therapy duration, initial fill tonicity (Dianeal Low Calcium 1.5%, 2.5% or 4.25%). Overall, as a UF surrogate, dry body weight was used. The aim was to have subjects maintaining their body weight within 5% of target dry weight (average dry weight of Screening and pre-Titration Day 1). CPD (baseline) 24-hour dialysate data was collected at Screening. Daily weight and UF data were collected on all participants when they started the use of Viva Kompact. Fill volumes were kept similar during CPD and Viva Kompact therapy. Dialysate samples were collected on Treatment Day 1 (Cycle 4, 8, 40, 54 and Final drain). Safety bloods were done throughout the study (Day 4, 7, 14, 21 and 30). Calculation of UFEexp / UFEabs (UF generated in 24 hours per gram of glucose monohydrate exposed/absorbed) were derived from these datapoints Descriptive statistics (median, min, max) were used in analysis, with significance testing reported using Wilcoxon signed rank test.
Results
11 out of 14 subjects were enrolled in the study; 2 failed screening and 1 withdrew during the Titration phase. 10 subjects completed the 7-day Treatment period and 3 subjects continued to the 23-day Optional Extension period. 1 subject withdrew on the sixth day of Treatment and was included in the analysis. Table 1 shows the demographic summary of the analysed subjects. Subjects with last fill (n = 6) were continued on Icodextrin 7.5%. All subjects maintained their body weights within 5% of their target body weight (% change in body weight = −0.7% [−4.3–1.3%] during the 7-day Treatment as well as Optional Extension period.
Table 2 compares body weight, glucose exposure, absorption, UFEexp, and UFEabs for CPD vs. Viva Kompact. The UFE (exposed) as significantly better in Viva Kompact as compared to CPD; UFEexp = 5.5[2.9–9.6] mL/g vs 1.8[−0.8 – 5.4] mL/g of glucose exposed, p = 0.0034. Whereas, UFE (absorbed) was similar; Viva Kompact = 8.9[4.8–20.3] mL/g vs CPD = 3.1[−2.1–28.7] mL/g of glucose absorbed, p = 0.1835. Throughout the study, subject serum sodium levels also remained stable; Baseline = 138[134–146] mmol/L vs Viva Kompact = 137[132–141] mmol/L.
Conclusion
This medium-term study demonstrates that steady concentration PD with Viva Kompact is able to maintain patients at their target weight while achieving individually appropriate UF. This approach provides similar UFEabs (UF per gram of glucose absorbed) but significantly improves UFEexp (UF per gram of glucose exposed). The significant reduction in glucose exposure with Viva Kompact may help preserve the peritoneal membrane. Further studies are needed to assess the longer-term impact on technique survival, membrane integrity, and outcomes in PD patients with diabetes.2

title: #969 Critchley-Critchley analysis of DBB-EXA™ vs. Transonic® HD02: accuracy, reproducibility, and clinical implications in vascular access flow measurement
authors: Georgios Kosmadakis; Clemence Deville; Ioana Enache; Aura Necoara; Julien Baudenon; Fatima El Kanouni
abstract:
Background and Aims
Accurate measurement of vascular access (VA) flow rate is crucial for preventing access-related complications in hemodialysis patients. The Transonic® HD02 system, widely regarded as the reference standard, employs ultrasound dilution, while the DBB-EXA™ dialysis machine offers an integrated ultrafiltration-based approach. This study aims to compare the accuracy, reproducibility, and clinical applicability of these methods, incorporating Critchley—Critchley analysis to assess measurement equivalence.
Method
We did a secondary analysis of an observational study with 65 hemodialysis patients (38M/27F, mean age 72 ± 10 years) reanalysing the data with addition of Critchley—Critchley analysis. VA flow rates were measured using both methods during the same dialysis session, with repeat measurements 7–15 days later to assess reproducibility. Bland-Altman plots and Critchley-Critchley analysis were used to evaluate agreement, bias, and precision. Critchley-Critchley analysis enabled a direct estimation of the accuracy of DBB-EXA™ relative to the Transonic® HD02 gold standard.
Results
The Transonic® system recorded a mean VA flow rate of 1413 ± 715 mL/min, while the DBB-EXA™ measured 1297 ± 664 mL/min, indicating a systematic underestimation (Table 1). The mean difference was 159±211 mL/min, with 95% limits of agreement spanning −274 to + 572 mL/min. Reproducibility was assessed by comparing repeated measurements over different dialysis sessions. 80% of Transonic® measurements were within ± 25% of each other, compared to 54% for DBB-EXA™, highlighting greater variability in the latter method. Critchley—Critchley analysis demonstrated that DBB-EXA™ had lower accuracy (45%) compared to Transonic® (15%) and significantly poorer precision (28% vs. 7%). The broader limits of agreement (−23.3% to +59.3%) further emphasize DBB-EXA™’s limited reliability (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
The DBB-EXA™ method provides a simple, dialysis-integrated option for VA flow measurement but underestimates flow rates and lacks reproducibility compared to the Transonic® gold standard. Critchley—Critchley analysis enables the researcher to estimate the accuracy of the method under test, and, by comparing this with the (known) accuracy of the reference method, to directly assess equivalence.

title: #3059 Management of resistant hyperphosphatemia in maintenance hemodialysis (MHD) patients — role of sucroferric oxyhydroxide (SFO): a prospective study
authors: Luvdeep Dogra; Vali Ps; Manisha Sahay
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyperphosphatemia is common in advanced CKD and is associated with increased cardiovascular morbidity, bone mineral abnormalities and mortality. Most patients on MHD require phosphate binders to control hyperphosphatemia. Traditional phosphate binders, such as sevelamer carbonate, are often associated with high pill burdens and limited efficacy in achieving optimal serum phosphorus levels. SFO is a newer calcium-free, polynuclear iron (III) based oral phosphate binder which may offer higher potency with lower pill burden. Our study evaluated the efficacy of SFO in MHD patients who failed to achieve optimum phosphorus control despite maximum tolerated doses of Sevelamer along with usual standard of care (SOC).
Method
This prospective study was conducted in hyperphosphatemic MHD patients. Those patients (n = 32) who failed to achieve optimum Phosphorus control despite maximum tolerated doses of sevelamer carbonate (800 mg, 4–6 tablets daily) for three months were switched to SFO (500 mg chewable tablets). They received either once-daily (n = 12), twice-daily (n = 19), or thrice-daily (n = 1) doses for three months as per phosphorus control. Serum phosphorus levels were measured at initiation and after 3 months of Sevelamer and monthly thereafter for 3 months on SFO. Serum Phosphorus levels at initiation and at 3 months of SFO therapy were analysed for current study. Statistical analysis was performed using a paired t-test.
Results
Thirty-two patients (males = 17 & females = 15) were analysed with a mean age of 61.5 years and a median dialysis vintage of 23 months. The mean serum Phosphorus level significantly reduced from 6.37 mg/dL to 5.07 mg/dL after 3 months of SFO therapy, with a mean change of 1.3 mg/dL (p = 0.03) (Fig. 1).
There was no statistically significant difference in phosphorus level changes between males and females (p = 0.228).
Importantly, the pill burden reduced from average of 3.8 to 2.2 tablets per day (p = 0.02). Sucroferric oxyhydroxide was well-tolerated, with no significant adverse events reported during the study period.
Conclusion
SFO demonstrated superior efficacy in reducing serum phosphorus levels in MHD patients who previously failed to achieve phosphorus control with sevelamer carbonate in tolerated doses.
SFO offered a better phosphorus control (p = 0.03), numerically lower mean daily pill burden (p = 0.02), lower treatment cost and a better treatment adherence than sevelamer carbonate. These findings strongly support the use of SFO as first line hyperphosphatemic patients with advanced CKD to improve phosphorus control, patient longevity and Quality of life.

title: #2043 Comparison of bacterial culture positivity between direct and post-centrifugation inoculation into blood culture bottles for peritoneal dialysis-associated peritonitis
authors: Takehiko Kawaguchi; Moritoshi Kadomura; Azumi Fukuta; Mari Okajima; Yukiko Yasui; Hiroki Omura; Mariko Imai; Keiki Shimada; Mizuho Morooka; Takayuki Yokoi; Toshiyuki Imasawa
abstract:
Background and Aims
The International Society for Peritoneal Dialysis (ISPD) guidelines recommend the use of blood culture bottles (BCBs) to identify causative organisms in peritoneal dialysis (PD)-associated peritonitis. However, evidence regarding optimal culture methods with BCBs remains limited, particularly for reducing culture-negative peritonitis. We compared bacterial culture positivity between direct inoculation and post-centrifugation inoculation into BCBs for PD-associated peritonitis.
Method
This prospective study, conducted at Chiba-Higashi National Hospital in Japan, included cases of PD-associated peritonitis diagnosed between January 2018 and December 2024, based on ISPD criteria. Three bacterial culture methods were assessed using identical PD effluent samples: (A) centrifugation of 50 mL effluent, resuspension in 3 mL normal saline, and inoculation onto solid media; (B) direct inoculation of 10 mL effluent into aerobic and anaerobic BCBs; and (C) centrifugation of 50 mL effluent, resuspension in 20 mL normal saline, and inoculation of 10 mL into aerobic and anaerobic BCBs. Culture positivity rates (CPRs) were compared across methods and analyzed using logistic regression to account for sample clustering. Cases with antibiotic therapy within 30 days prior to diagnosis were excluded from the analysis.
Results
A total of 42 peritonitis episodes were diagnosed during the study period (0.18 episodes per patient-year), with 34 cases meeting the inclusion criteria (median age: 54 years, female: 36%, diabetes: 43%, median PD vintage: 21 months). Among 29 culture-positive cases, 19 involved gram-positive bacteria, 8 gram-negative bacteria, 0 fungi, and 2 multiple pathogens. The most frequently isolated organism was Staphylococcus species (n = 10). The CPRs were 50% for method A, 85% for method B, and 79% for method C. Compared to method B, the odds ratios for CPRs were 0.17 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.07–0.43, P < 0.001) for method A and 0.67 (95% CI: 0.38–1.16, p = 0.15) for method C.
Conclusion
The single-center study found no significant difference in CPRs between direct inoculation and post-centrifugation inoculation of PD effluent into BCBs, although both methods demonstrated markedly higher CPRs than solid media inoculation. These findings may underscore the utility of direct inoculation of PD effluent into BCBs for improving pathogen detection in PD-associated peritonitis.

title: #2747 MOTS-c Levels and sarcopenia risk in patients on chronic peritoneal dialysis: a pilot study
authors: Mariateresa Zicarelli; Michela Musolino; Marta Greco; Stefanos Roumeliotis; Christodoula Kourtidou; Ioannis Alekos; Roberta Misiti; Daniela Foti; Giuseppe Coppolino; Vassilios Liakopoulos; Evangelia Ntounousi; Davide Bolignano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sarcopenia is a common and debilitating condition in patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) undergoing peritoneal dialysis (PD). Its development is influenced by multiple factors, including mitochondrial dysfunction. The mitochondrial open reading frame of 12S rRNA-c (MOTS-c) is a mitochondrial-derived peptide promoting muscle growth which levels are imbalanced in ESKD. Yet, its role in sarcopenia risk in PD patients remains underexplored. This study aimed to assess the balance of MOTS-c in chronic PD patients and investigate its association with sarcopenia risk.
Method
In this observational study, 32 chronic PD patients were assessed for sarcopenia risk using the SARC-F questionnaire (a screening tool used to assess the risk of sarcopenia), physical performance tests such as the 30 seconds chair stand (30SCT) and handgrip tests, and anthropometric measures. Blood, urine and peritoneal fluid samples were collected, and MOTS-c was measured using an ELISA kit. The renal (u/sMOTS-c) and peritoneal (d/s MOTS-c) clearances of this substance were also computed. Correlations between MOTS-c levels and sarcopenia risk indicators were analyzed, and the diagnostic performance was evaluated using ROC analysis.

PD patients at higher risk of sarcopenia (SARC-F≥ 2) exhibited significantly lower serum MOTS-c levels (p = 0.003) and higher dialysate MOTS-c levels (p = 0.04), suggesting increased peritoneal clearance (d/s MOTS-c; p = 0.003) (Fig. 1). sMOTS-c levels correlated directly with physical performance tests and negatively with the SARC-F score while dMOTS-c showed direct correlation with SARC-F score and waist-to-hip ratio and inverse correlation with the 30 SCT. Chronic PD may disrupt MOTS-c balance, potentially contributing to an increased risk of sarcopenia. Our findings suggest that MOTS-c could serve as a non-invasive biomarker for sarcopenia risk assessment in PD patients. Further studies are required to validate its utility in clinical practice and explore its potential therapeutic applications.

title: #3877 Efficacy and safety of an innovative polymethylmethacrylate membrane used for post dilution on-line hemodiafiltration. A crossover randomised controlled study
authors: Pablo Molina; Íñigo Alonso Escudero; Kerlin Vicent Rodriguez; Laura Pérez-Sánchez; Delia Acevedo; Belén Vizcaino Castillo; Mercedes González Moya; Aina Quilis; Manuel Parra; Paula Gandía Ureña; Nuria Estañ; Asunción Sancho-Calabuig
abstract:
Background and Aims
The clearance of protein-bound uremic toxins is minimal with diffusive treatment and limited with convective treatment. A new generation of high-flow polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) membranes has recently been commercialized, which could improve the removal of these uremic toxins and could serve as an alternative to the hemodiafiltration with endogenous reinfusion of ultrafiltrate (HFR-Supra), the reference hemodialysis technique with adsorptive capacity.
The aim of this study was to compare the efficacy and safety of a high-flow PMMA dialyzer (Filtryzer® NF-2.1U) in online postdilution HDF versus HFR-Supra.
Method
A crossover, randomized clinical trial including stable HD patients. Patients received two 4-hour HD sessions with both techniques during two consecutive weeks. The percentage reductions (PR) of urea, creatinine, phosphorus, β2-microglobulin (β2M), free light chains (FLC) kappa (κ) and lambda (λ), indoxyl sulfate (IS), and IL-6 were compared between the two membrane types (primary outcomes). In addition, intradialytic symptoms, postdialysis recovery time, and PR of albumin were analyzed (secondary outcomes).
Results
16 stable hemodialysis patients were included (age: 63 ± 15 years; males: 69%). The PMMA filter, with a mean convective volume of 21.1 ± 2.5 L, achieved a higher percentage reduction in most of the studied toxins (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
OL-HDF with new PMMA membranes could be a good dialysis strategy to add convective transport to the known diffusion and absorption mechanisms previously described with HFR-Supra.

title: #2041 Correlation between protein energy wasting and cognitive impairment in maintenance hemodialysis patients
authors: Jun Liu; Jingfang Wan; Weiwei Zhang; Yani He; Kehong Chen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Maintenance hemodialysis (MHD) patients widely exist malnutrition, which can cause severe cognitive impairment (CI), may relate to protein energy wasting (PEW). Our research aimed at exploring the relationship between PEW and CI.
Method
A total of 160 MHD patients were included and divided into non-CI (nCI) group and CI group. We collected patients’ general information, laboratory data, anthropometric data, diet data, diagnosis and evaluation results of PEW, and montreal cognitive assessment-basic (MoCA-B) score. Independent sample t-test was used to compare clinical characteristics of patients in different groups. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analysis (MLR) were used to screen the influencing factors of CI. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve was used to evaluate the predictive value of the constructed model.
Results
There was significant differences in the detection rate of PEW, prealbumin (PAB), body mass index (BMI), normalized daily protein intake (nDPI), normalized daily energy intake (nDEI), scored patient-generated subjective global assessment (PG-SGA) and malnutrition inflammation score (MIS) score between the nCI and CI groups (P < 0.05). MHD patients merged PEW showed lower scores in MoCA-B total scores, orientation, calculation, abstraction, visual perception and attention compared to MHD patients unmerged PEW (P < 0.05). MLR showed that age, Kt/v, nDPI, MIS score, and PEW were independent influencing factors of CI (P < 0.05). The predictive value of the constructed model based on the aforementioned factors for cognitive impairment was 94.3% (95% CI1, 90.5–98. 1%), the sensitivity and the specificity were 92.4% and 89.7% respectively. The best cut-off for predicting CI was 0.469.
Conclusion
In MHD patients, PEW is an independent risk factor of CI. The model we build showed great specificity and sensitivity for predicting CI, which can improve the prognosis of patients.

title: #2056 Effect of individualized dialysate bicarbonate concentration on patient prognosis: a multicenter retrospective study
authors: Jingfang Wan; Xiao Mei Lu; Lili Fu; Jun Li; Yani He; Kehong Chen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Higher dialysate bicarbonate is associated with an increased risk of mortality in maintenance hemodialysis patients, and the optimal dialysate bicarbonate regimen is unclear. The aim of this study was to investigate whether an individualized dialysate bicarbonate regimen is beneficial for patient prognosis by retrospectively collecting clinical data from multicenter maintenance hemodialysis patients.
Method
Demographic and laboratory data of MHD patients from January 2015 to December 2020 were retrospectively collected from hemodialysis centers in 3 Chinese tertiary hospitals. Inclusion criteria were: dialysis age ≥3 months and age ≥18 years; exclusion criteria: lack of dialysate bicarbonate data, lack of endpoint events, and peritoneal dialysis combined with hemodialysis. The primary end point event was defined as all-cause death, the secondary end point was defined as cardiovascular death, and the individualized dialysate bicarbonate regimen was defined as individualized adjustment of dialysate bicarbonate concentration based on the patient’s monthly pre-dialysis blood bicarbonate concentration. Patients’ dialysate bicarbonate concentrations for the previous 3 months were collected as baseline data. The enrolled patients were divided into an individualized group and a non-individualized group according to whether the center performed an individualized dialysate bicarbonate regimen or not. The survival time of patients in both groups was evaluated using the Kaplan–Meier method. Cox proportional risk regression model was used to assess the association between individualized dialysate bicarbonate concentration and mortality. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results
635 MHD patients were finally enrolled, the mean age of the enrolled patients was 61.23 ± 5.53 years, about 56% were male, the mean dialysate bicarbonate concentration was 31.44 mmol/l, 261 patients in the individualized dialysate bicarbonate group and 374 patients in the non-individualized dialysate bicarbonate group. Patients in the individualized group had higher calcium (2.35 vs. 2.01, P=0.034), iPTH (456.87 vs. 321.56, P = 0.028) and albumin (38.25 vs. 35.43, P = 0.007) concentrations, and there were no significant differences between the two groups with respect to age, sex, diabetes mellitus, age on dialysis, spKT/V, hemoglobin and phosphorus. The mean dialysate bicarbonate concentration of patients in the individualized group was 32.5 mmol/l (range 26–37 mmol/l), and the bicarbonate concentration of patients in the non-individualized group was fixed at 30 mmol/l. The all-cause mortality rate of the two groups of patients in the individualized group and the non-individualized group was 27.59% vs. 32.35%, respectively (P = 0.023), and Fig. 1 shows the Kaplan–Meier survival curve analysis, patients in the individualized dialysate bicarbonate group had a significantly longer survival time compared to patients in the non-individualized group (p = 0.0098, log-rank test). After complete adjustment, the hazard ratio for all-cause mortality was 0.901 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.797–0.987, P = 0.039) in the individualized dialysate bicarbonate group compared to the non-individualized dialysate bicarbonate group.
Conclusion
Individualized dialysate bicarbonate regimens may have a survival benefit in patients with MHD. This provides an evidence-based medicine basis for optimal dialysis prescription in the future.

title: #3875 Optimizing timing for vascular access creation: the role of kidney failure risk equation and eGFR in predicting dialysis initiation
authors: Andreia Dos Santos Henriques; João Venda; Emanuel Eufrásio Ferreira; Nuno Oliveira; Rui Alves
abstract:
Background and Aims
Determining when a patient will start dialysis is a real challenge. Thus, predicting the optimal time for arteriovenous fistula (AVF) creation is often unclear, resulting either on too late referral, leading to HD initiation by central venous catheter (CVC), or too early, exposing patients too unnecessary procedures. In this study, we aimed to evaluate the clinical utility of using a Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE) threshold for vascular access creation and to test if its combination with the traditional eGFR threshold of 15 mL/min/1.73 m2 (eGFR15) for patient referral would result in a more accurate prediction of dialysis.
Method
Observational, single-center cohort study conducted at tertiary center in 2023. Included patients referred for ultrasound vascular mapping, aged ≥ 18 years, regularly followed by a nephrologist (> 3 months), and who had selected HD as their preferred renal replacement therapy modality. The index date was defined as the date of modality selection. The 2-year KFRE at index date were calculated. The proportion of patients initiating HD within 24 months from the index date, the median time from the index date to HD initiation, type of vascular access used, and mortality rates prior to HD initiation were recorded. The predictive performance of eGFR and 2-year KFRE and its combination in forecasting HD initiation within 24 months was evaluated.
Results
A total of 254 patients attended the vascular mapping appointment, with 179 meting the inclusion criteria. 63.7% (n = 114) were males, median age of 73.0 years [IQR: 63.0–81.0]. The median time from index date to HD initiation was 9.0 months [IQR: 5.0–18.0]. Initiated HD within 24 months 58.7% (n = 105) patients, with 39.0% initiated HD using AVF. The mean eGFR at referral for VA construction was 14.2 ± 4.0 mL/min/1.73 m2. The median 2-year KFRE score at the index date was 33.1% [IQR: 18.8–52.7], with patients who initiated HD within 24 months of the index date presented a median 2-year KFRE of 40.3% [IQR: 24.8–61.1].
A calculated eGFR threshold <12.7 mL/min/1.73 m2 (eGFR12.7) at referral was predictive of HD initiation within 24 months (sensitivity: 47.0%, specificity: 76.5%; P ≤ 0.029). However, the establish referral eGFR15 threshold did not significantly differentiate between patients who would from those who would not initiate HD.
Patients who initiated HD within 24 months of the index date had significant higher 2-year KFRE scores, with patients that initiated HD within 24 months presented a 2-Year KFRE thresholds of > 31.0% (sensitivity: 71.4%, specificity: 71.6%; P ≤ 0.001).
When applying the found threshold for 2-year KFRE score and the establish eGFR15 for referral we found sensitivity of 54.5%, and specificity of 79.4% (P = 0.001). Combined eGFR12.7 with a 2-year KFRE > 31.0% increased specificity to 91.2%, but lowered sensitivity to 39.4%.
Conclusion
The eGFR threshold alone is insufficient for timely referral for vascular access creation. When combined with the KFRE at the time of modality choice, the eGFR15 threshold improves sensitivity compared to eGFR alone while maintaining good specificity. This combined approach may enhance timely and appropriate referral for vascular access creation, potentially improving clinical outcomes.

title: #2163 Relationship between antioxidant nutrients intake and oxidative stress in patients treated with hemodialysis
authors: Flaviu Bob; Bodea Alexandra Madalina; Alexandru Sircuta; Iulia Dana Grosu; Adalbert Schiller; Ligia Petrica; Oana-Marina Schiller
abstract:
Background and Aims
Oxidative stress is associated to chronic kidney disease because of chronic inflammation and also because of a depletion of dietary antioxidants. We investigated the relationship between oxidative damage markers, showing oxidation of proteins (glutathione disulfide-GSSG) or of lipids (malondialdehyde- MDA), with the antioxidant nutrients intake. In the studied patients the relationship of the markers of oxidative stress with complications associated to CKD (anemia, CKD–MBD) has also been assessed.
Method
We conducted a single-center cross-sectional study that included 58 CKD G5D patients (mean age 60.39 +/− 11.73 years; 33 male, 25 female; mean hemodialysis vintage of 6.43 +/− 4.89 years). All patients have been assessed regarding dialysis status (medical history), we performed analysis before the dialysis session using standard methods blood biochemistry, complete blood count and using high performance liquid chromatography for GSSG and MDA. In all patients a semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire containing 62 items has been performed and used to estimate the monthly intake of antioxidant nutrients.
Results
In the studied patients mean malondialdehyde was 1.41+/− 0.42 mcmol/l, while mean GSSG was 127.24 U/L +/− 60.711.41 U/l, with no statistically significant correlation between them.
The nutritional status influenced differently the two oxidative stress markers, while GSSG showed a negative statistically significant correlation with BMI (r= −0.28, P = 0.04), patients with a BMI >30 kg/sqm (21 vs. 37 patients) showed a significantly higher level of MDA 1.57+/− 0.51 mcmol/l vs. 1.31 +/− 0.33 mcmol/l, P = 0.02. The level of albumin showed a statistically significant direct correlation with GSSG (r= 0.32, P = 0.02).
Regarding intake of antioxidant nutrients we found a negative statistically significant correlation between Vitamin C intake and MDA level (r = −0.32, P = 0.01), while the intake of Vitamin E alpha (r = −0.32, P = 0.02), Vitamin E beta (r = −0.31, P = 0.02), and carotene alpha (r = −0.28, P = 0.04) showed statistically significant correlations with the GSSG level. We found also a statistically significant negative correlation between coffee quantity intake and MDA level (R = −0.28, P = 0.03).
There were no age or gender differences regarding the two oxidative stress markers, while dialysis vintage seemed to have an influence just on the GSSG level (r = 0.33, P = 0.01). Increased oxidative stress was associated to more severe anemia, proven by negative statistically significant correlation of hemoglobin with GSSG (r = −0.36, P = 0.01), and MDA (r = −0.39, P = 0.002). Regarding inflammatory markers and parameters of CKD-MBD, there were no statistically significant correlations found with oxidative stress markers, with the exception of a correlation between MDA and serum phosphorus (r = −0.29, P = 0.03). We have also found a negative statistically significant correlation between MDA level and serum K (r = −0.29, P = 0.02), patients with predialysis K of higher then 5.5 mEq/l had a statistically significant lower MDA (1.29+/− 0.4 mcmol/l vs. 1.54 +/− 0.4 mcmol/l, P = 0.025).
Conclusion
In our study, we found that the increased intake of some of the antioxidant nutrients is influencing the amount of oxidative stress markers in patients treated with hemodialysis. We have also found that increased oxidative stress (expressed through the MDA and GSSG level) is associated to a more severe anemia.

title: #2872 A multicenter study on two major challenges in late referral patients: outcomes of AVFs and tunneled CVC-related infections
authors: Elettra Lomeo; Roberto Mangiacapra; Francesca Maria D'ascenzo; Fabio Aureli; Domenico Valenti; Reghvinder Gambhir; Giuseppe Grandaliano; Francesco Pesce
abstract:
Background and Aims
Selecting the appropriate dialysis modality for end-stage renal disease (ESRD) patients is a complex decision-making process centered on achieving “the right access, in the right patient, at the right time, for the right reasons.” Early referral of patients with a risk-based threshold >40% or an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <15 ml/min/1.73 m² is associated with improved vascular access patency. Conversely, “late referral” adversely impacts vascular outcomes, quality of life, and overall survival. The organization of healthcare systems and demographic characteristics of a country can influence the preferred vascular access type and the timing of referrals for kidney care. This study compares late referral patients in two high-volume hospitals across different countries, assessing differences in medical management and complications.
Method
We conducted a multicenter retrospective observational study on tunneled central venous catheter (CVC) insertions and arteriovenous fistula (AVF) creations performed between January 2020 and May 2024 at King’s College Hospital, London (N = 249), and Policlinico A. Gemelli Foundation, Rome (n = 214). We analyzed outcomes in patients who received a tunneled CVC and were referred to a nephrologist within 90 days before dialysis initiation.
Results
A total of 463 CVCs were placed in crashlander patients (mean age: 60.4 ± 15.8 years; female: 36.7%, male: 63.3%). Catheter-related bloodstream infection (CRBSI) occurred in 16% of patients, with an earlier onset in the UK cohort compared to the Italian cohort [123 days (IQR 33–222) vs. 228 days (IQR 51–600); P = 0.05] (Table 1). The reinfection rate following CVC removal/replacement was also higher in the UK cohort (19.4% vs. 0%; P = 0.01).
AVF was created after CVC placement in 195 patients (42.1%), with a primary patency rate of 68.7% at two months. Ethnicity (P = 0.01) and age (P = 0.0004) significantly influenced the type of AVF created. In the UK cohort, AVF creation after CVC placement occurred later than in the Italian cohort [140 days (IQR 38–251) vs. 28 days (IQR 1–60); P = 0.001]. Reintervention for AVF was necessary in 32.3% of these patients.
Overall, the mortality rate was 9.9%, significantly lower in AVF patients (P = 0.002), who also had a reduced risk of bacteremia (P = 0.05) compared to non-AVF patients. This finding was consistent across both cohorts [P = 0.0058 (Italy) and P = 0.00051 (UK)] (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
Mortality is significantly lower in crashlander patients with an AVF. Therefore, reducing CVC use, especially in patients eligible for AVF creation, is a key strategy to improve long-term outcomes. National healthcare policies that promote early patient assessment are essential for minimizing the risk of CRBSI and reducing overall mortality.

title: #3443 A safe guidewire-assisted exchange technique for the management of CRBSIs in hemodialysis patients: a single-center study
authors: Elettra Lomeo; Francesca Maria D'ascenzo; Antonio Sturniolo; Roberto Mangiacapra; Fabio Aureli; Francesco Pesce; Giuseppe Grandaliano
abstract:
Background and Aims
The late referral phenomenon and the increasing age of incident dialysis patients have contributed to the widespread and prolonged use of central venous catheters (CVCs) as permanent hemodialysis (HD) access. This trend has been associated with a higher incidence of CVC-related complications, primarily catheter-related bloodstream infections (CRBSIs). Despite their clinical significance, standardized management protocols for infected tunneled CVCs remain inconsistent, leading to variability in clinical practice. We present updated data from our experience with an innovative guidewire-exchange technique for infected tunneled CVCs. The key to this technique is utilizing the inner stylet of the new CVC to prevent direct contact between the old and new catheter, thereby minimizing contamination and preserving the vascular access site, which is crucial for dialysis patients. The primary objectives of this study were to assess infection-free survival (by the same or other pathogen) and catheter function.
Method
We conducted a retrospective single-center observational cohort study on infected tunneled CVC replacement procedures performed at the Nephrology Unit of Policlinico A. Gemelli Foundation in Rome between January 2019 and June 2024. Patients with and without tunnel or exit-site infections were included. Microbiological cultures were obtained from most guidewires used during the procedures. All patients received systemic antibiotic therapy based on susceptibility testing and underwent clinical follow-up ranging from 6 months to 4 years.
Results
During the study period, 99 CVC exchanges were performed (M 48.4%, F 49.4%; median age: 72 years, IQR 62–78.5). The median dialysis duration was 36 months (IQR 5–30), and the median catheter dwell time was 30 months (IQR 25–34).
Among Gram-positive bacteria, the most frequently isolated pathogens were Staphylococcus aureus (73.2%) and coagulase-negative staphylococci (CNST) (19.6%) (Fig. 1).
To validate the safety of this technique, in most cases microbiological cultures of the guidewires were performed, revealing the presence of the same pathogen responsible for the initial CRBSI. Despite positive guidewire cultures, the relapse rate due to the same pathogen was 2%: one case caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa (after three months) and the other by Staphylococcus aureus complex (after eight months) (Fig. 2a). The reinfection rate was 11.1%, with 11 patients experiencing a new CRBSI due to different pathogens after a median of 283 days (IQR 121–642) (Fig. 2b). All CVCs maintained an extracorporeal blood flow ≥ 250 mL/min, ensuring optimal dialysis performance.
Conclusion
Our technique demonstrated excellent infection-free survival, even in cases involving high-risk pathogens such as Staphylococcus aureus. These findings suggest that this method is a safe, effective and reproducible technique for infected tunneled CVC replacement in HD patients.

title: #2448 Peritoneal protein loss: how does it relate to fluid overload, sarcopenia and nutrition on renal disease
authors: Ines Alexandre; Maria Inês Roxo; Ana Rita Calça; Patrícia Matias; Filipa Rodrigues; Raquel Lourenço; Elisabete Costa; Tânia Madeira; Tânia Almeida; Rita Calha; Luísa Santos; Patrícia Branco
abstract:
Background and Aims
Peritoneal protein loss (PPL) through peritoneal effluent is a well-established complication of peritoneal dialysis (PD) and has been linked with malnutrition and mortality. However, the perspective is changing. The association of PPL with malnutrition and sarcopenia has been refuted in recent studies. Moreover, recently, fluid overload and venous congestion have been associated with PPL uncovering the importance of hydrostatic convection in protein transport.
The aim of this study was to explore the relation of PPL with fluid overload, sarcopenia and nutritional markers in prevalent PD patients.
Method
We performed a single-center cross-sectional study that included all PD patients of our unit submitted to a modified peritoneal equilibration test (PET) during the year 2024.
Demographic and clinical data were collected from clinical records. Biochemical data, evaluation of sarcopenia and bioelectrical impedance assessment (BIA) were evaluated at the same time as PET. PPL was measured in a 24h dialysate effluent collection and the PET’s dialysate effluent (4 h). NTproBNP, CA 125 and extracellular water excess in BIA were used as fluid overload markers, and albumin, total proteins, handgrip strength, ultrasound evaluation of rectus femoris and BIA parameters as nutritional and sarcopenia markers.
Statistical analyses were done in SPSS. Univariable analysis were performed with linear regression model and a p value ≤ 0.05 was considered significant.
Results
Our study included 61 patients, 39 (64%) male, with a mean age of 59 ± 13 years, and 20 (33%) were diabetic. Cause of renal failure was diabetes in 15 patients (24.6%), ADPKD in 7 (11.5%), hypertension in 6 (9.8%), IgA nephropathy in 5 (8.2%) and cardiorenal syndrome in 4 (6.5%), other causes were less frequent. Most patients (73%) were on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD).
Median PPL was 0.081g/dL (0.055–0.099) in the 24h dialysate and 0.046 g/dL (0.039–0.063) in the 4 h dialysate. Regarding fluid overload, median NTproBNP was 1260 pg/mL (517–3702), median CA125 was 13 U/mL (9–23) and mean extracellular water excess was 1.5 L ± 1.6. Average handgrip strength was 28 and 26kg, right and left arm, respectively, with a mean rectus femoris muscle thickness of 13.7 mm ± 4.4. Remaining data, including PET parameters, are detailed in Table 1.
Univariable analysis showed a positive association between 4h PPL and NTproBNP (P = 0.001), extracellular water excess (P = 0.018) and lean tissue mass (LTM) (P = 0.006). A negative association was found between 4h PPL and fat mass in BIA (P = 0.015).
Albumin, total proteins, handgrip strength, muscle thickness and other BIA parameters did not correlate with PPL.
Conclusion
Our study coincides with recent data reinforcing an absence of causality and relationship between PPL sarcopenia and malnutrition markers. A positive correlation between LTM and 4 h PPL might be justified by a higher metabolic rate and more significant protein turnover in patients with more lean tissue mass. The same rationale explains a negative association between fat mass and 4 h PPL, as these patients tend to have lower protein turnover. On the other hand, a fluid overload status appears to play a role in PPL as evidenced by a significant relationship between 4 h PPL and NTproBNP and extracellular water excess.

title: #2028 Loop diuretics in anuric hemodialysis patients: an unexplored avenue for removal of protein-bound uremic toxins
authors: Didier Sánchez Ospina; Maria Romero Cote; Maria Isabel Saez Calero; Badawi Hijazi Prieto; Francisco Herrera Gomez; Sandra Delgado Cuesta; Maddalen Mujika Marticorena; Lucia Criado Bellido; Emilio González-Parra; María Jesús Izquierdo Ortiz; Sebastian Mas-Fontao
abstract:
Background and Aims
ESKD is a very difficult kidney problem to have because it can start from many different causes. One of the tough parts about it is how uremic toxins that are bound to protein, like indoxyl sulfate, p-cresyl sulfate, and hippuric acid, keep building up. These substances stick closely to proteins in blood, like albumin, which makes getting them out using standard hemodialysis hard. Sadly, what stays in blood isn’t harmless; it helps link many bad effects including swelling and heart issues.
Loop diuretics are the drugs that come in in the fluid management dance of nephrology. The loop diuretics, mainly represented by furosemide, carry an interesting but largely underutilized potential outside their traditional indications. The very high binding affinity to albumin creates a rather interesting hypothesis: do they possibly displace PBUTs from their protein-binding sites, thus increasing their availability for extraction by dialysis? As attractive as this idea is, it remains speculative because of the absence of solid empirical proof.
Objectives: This study was undertaken to explore the possibility of furosemide in clearing PBUTs. This hypothesized that furosemide might increase the free plasma fraction of these toxins, thus making them more available for hemodialysis.
Method
To validate this assumption, a carefully planned multicenter crossover investigation was carried out at two major Spanish establishments: the University Hospital of Burgos and the Jiménez Díaz Foundation University Hospital in Madrid. The research involved 17 anuric patients who had been receiving hemodialysis treatment for no less than six months. The protocol comprised one week of furosemide treatment and a subsequent week washout. During the weeks designated as treatment, participants were given daily doses of furosemide and blood samples were taken to measure the concentrations of indoxyl sulfate, p-cresyl sulfate, and hippuric acid both before and after dialysis in the second session of the week. All these analytes were quantified by HPLC-MS/MS. Paired t-tests were used to make statistical comparisons of toxin levels before and after dialysis. A value of P < 0.05 was considered significant.
Results
The findings provided compelling evidence for furosemide’s potential role in PBUT clearan The data demonstrated strong evidence for furosemide’s effectiveness in PBUT removal through its influence on Hippuric Acid levels which reduced significantly from 7,865 ± 5,320 μg/L before dialysis to 4,321 ± 1,598 μg/L after dialysis (P < 0.05). P-Cresyl Sulfate: A 40% decrease in P-Cresyl Sulfate concentrations occurred following dialysis as demonstrated by statistical significance (P < 0.05). Indoxyl Sulfate: The concentration of Indoxyl Sulfate declined by 35% following dialysis treatment (P < 0.05).Administration of furosemide showed the unexpected result of increasing blood levels of hippuric acid and indoxyl sulfate before dialysis. The surprising observation implies that furosemide treatment causes PBUTs to move from tissue storage sites into the bloodstream which then improves their removal during dialysis.
Conclusion
The pilot study reveals furosemide as an effective supplementary treatment option for PBUTs in the management of ESKD. Traditional hemodialysis techniques might be improved by furosemide which operates through both toxin displacement from protein-binding sites and toxin mobilization from peripheral reservoirs. These initial results show potential but mark only the start of what requires further research through expanded studies to fully understand their implications.Research confirmation could establish furosemide as a fundamental treatment component for managing PBUT-related issues in ESKD patients.

title: #1045 AVF elective ligation in kidney transplant recipients is not associated with an acceleration of kidney function decline
authors: Francesco La Fergola; Cosma Cortese; Alessandra Pesino; Marco Fiorentino; Loreto Gesualdo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal transplant recipients frequently keep hemodialysis access in case of future allograft failure; however, the persistence of an unused dialysis access may limit vein availability for phlebotomy procedures. A persistent and patent artero-venous fistula (AVF) is associated with some complications such as aneurysm formation, thrombosis, steal syndrome, arm edema and can contribute to left ventricular hypertrophy; in addition, it is still discussed whether AVF ligation after KT is associated with worsening of renal allograft function. This study aims to analyze our single-center experience of the impact of elective AVF ligation on renal function of KTRs.
Method
All patients who underwent elective AVF ligation after KT at the Nephrology Unit at Policlinico-Bari between 2021 and 2023 were retrospectively evaluated and included in this analysis. All the patients included had stable renal function for at least a post-transplant, without any episodes of graft rejection. Baseline patient characteristics and renal function (creatinine clearance, serum creatinine and BUN) and 24-hour proteinuria were evaluated at the time of AVF ligation, at 1-3-6-12-24 months after AVF ligation.
Results
A total of 49 patients were included in this analysis (mean follow-up 18.5 ± 12.1 months). Mean age of the study population was 54.5 ± 12.1 years, with a prevalence of male gender (33/49, 67.3%). Mean serum creatinine and creatinine clearance was 1.5 ± 0.46 mg/dl and 60.4 ± 23.06 ml/min, respectively; no significant protein loss was documented in the study population at the time of AVF ligation, with a median 24-h proteinuria 292 mg/24h (IQR 292–585).
Conclusion
In summary, no acceleration in the decline of eGFR and 24-hour proteinuria are observed within 12 months after the closure of a functioning AVF in kidney transplant recipients (KTRs). The removal of unused AVFs can be safely carried out in renal transplant recipients, especially if symptomatic. Given the potential complications associated with large AVFs, such as high-output cardiac failure, the prevailing approach of preserving asymptomatic hemodialysis access in patients with well-functioning kidney transplants warrants reevaluation.

title: #460 Heparin use on hemodialysis — influencing factors
authors: Martin Pachmann; Hendrik Dannemeyer; Melanie Wolf
abstract:
Background and Aims
Heparin (unfractionated or low molecular weight) is used in the majority of treatments to avoid the activation of coagulation that occurs in all hemodialysis procedures. As there is no laboratory value that can provide reliable information about sufficient anticoagulation for dialysis treatment, the dosage is usually determined pragmatically.
We tried to investigate which patient- and treatment-specific parameters have what influence on the dose of heparin prescribed by nephrologists in Germany.
Method
In our retrospective observational study, all hemodialysis treatments from 14 German dialysis centers that were performed between January 1st, 2021, and October 21st, 2023, and for which data on anticoagulation were available were analyzed.
We collected treatment specific data (dialyzer, dialysis duration, dialysis modality (HD or HDF), blood flow) and patient-specific data (gender, age, weight, diabetes yes/no, platelet count) and the vascular access used (shunt/graft or catheter) for each treatment. In the given time frame, there was a switch from Fx or Fx CorDiax dialyzers to CorAL (all Fresenius Medical Care) in the majority of patients, so the influence of the dialyzer type could be analyzed longitudinal on single-patient-level. The data was analyzed anonymously.
Exclusion criteria were standardized heparin doses of >20,000 IE, dialysis time <180 min and >345 min and patients with only short-term treatments (less than 10 documented dialyses) in the evaluation period.
The study’s main objective was to analyze the influence of treatment- and patient-specific factors on the amount of heparin used for the treatments.
Since the literature indicates a lower dose for low-molecular-weight heparins in dialysis, the comparison of the heparin usage was made on the basis of standardized international units (for both LMWH in use, enoxaparin and tinzaparin, a higher efficacy by a factor of 1.4 was assumed). Doses are therefore given below as units standardized to unfractionated heparin.
Results
The study included 3737 patients. After excluding patients, who did not fulfil the inclusion criteria, data of 2,891 patients and 589,212 dialysis treatments were included in the analysis.
Patient population:
On average, the patients were 69.6 years old, 36.6% were women, the average weight was 77.6 kg, 43.1% of patients had diabetes (one or more ICD-10 code from E11.xx), the average treatment time was 251 minutes. 29.6% of treatments were performed via catheter, HDF was used in 52% of the patients. Low molecular weight heparin was used in 24.3% of patients and unfractionated heparin in 75.7%.
Heparin data:
On average across all centers and patients, 5793.3 IE heparin was used for HD and 5899.9 IE for HDF (nominal difference 106.6 IE, in multivariate analysis −207.0 IE, P < 0.001). In the multivariate analysis we adjusted for vascular access (fistula/graft vs. catheter), treatment modality (HDF vs. HD), blood flow, dialyzer surface, membrane type, dialysis time, age, weight, and patient gender.

title: #534 Pleural effusions among patients on maintenance hemodialysis patients
authors: Keren Cohen Hagai; Naomi Nacasch; Moshe Shashar; Ayelet Grupper; Sydney Benchetrit; Aseel Zidan; Ayal Romem; Ori Wand; Yael Einbinder
abstract:
Background and Aims
Pleural effusions (PE) are frequent among individuals receiving hemodialysis, and may have several etiologies, including volume overload, uremic pleuritis, and comorbidities, such as heart failure and malignancies. Data regarding these cases is mainly derived from studies among hospitalized or otherwise symptomatic patients and from areas endemic for tuberculosis. Thus, data from asymptomatic patients on maintenance hemodialysis (MHD) is needed. The aims were: 1) To measure the prevalence of PE among unselected MHD patients, 2) To assess variables associated with PE, including dialysis adequacy (Kt/V) and interdialytic weight gain (IDWG), 3) To describe etiologies of PE among MHD patients, and 4) To measure if the presence of PE changes immediately following HD sessions and during follow-up.
Method
This prospective study included patients on MHD. They were screened with chest sonography before routine dialysis sessions (Time 1, pre). Sociodemographic, clinical and laboratory data were collected. Chest sonography was repeated immediately after dialysis (Time 1, post) in subjects with PE. Second sonography occurred 4–12 weeks later (Time 2; Figure).
Results
Fifty MHD patients were included. Mean age was 68.6 years, 31 (62%) were male and average dialysis vintage was 3.2 years. Six participants (12%) had bilateral PE at Time 1, with no changes at Time 1-post and Time 2 (Table). No new subjects had developed PE by Time 2. Compared to those without PE, those with PE had lower serum sodium (134.3 ± 3.1 vs. 137.3 ± 3.3 meq/L, p = 0.046) and albumin (3.3 ± 0.6 vs. 3.7 ± 0.3 g/dL, p = 0.005), and higher NT-pro-BNP levels (32,757 ± 5495 vs. 11,661 ± 11,724, P < 0.001). Dialysis adequacy measures and IDWG were comparable between those with/without PE. Etiology for PE was considered to be volume overload plus underdialysis in all cases. Heart failure contributed to 3 PE cases. Three subjects required pleurocentesis, which disclosed transudate in 2 and exudate in 1 (according to Light’s criteria). Dialysis regimen was revised among all PE cases by increasing doses and management of accesses. Pleurocentesis was performed according to clinical judgment. Despite this, all PE remained at Time 2.
Conclusion
PE are common among unselected MHD patients, related to volume overload and underdialysis. Yet, PE were unchanged immediately after HD and during medium-term follow-up. We identified an association between clinical and laboratory parameters and PE but not with Kt/V. The presence of PE may affect MHD management.
