title: #3130 Experiences and health-related quality of life worsen over time in caregivers of dialysis patients, irrespective of home or in-centre dialysis: an observational cohort study
authors: Esmee Driehuis; Anneke Roeterdink; Theodôr Vogels; Namiko Goto; Marjolein Broese van Groenou; Renée de Wildt; Friedo W Dekker; Brigit Van Jaarsveld; Alferso Abrahams
abstract:
Background and Aims
Starting dialysis not only has a major impact on patients themselves, but also on their informal caregivers. To properly inform patients with kidney failure and their caregivers about starting dialysis and the choice of dialysis location (i.e., home or in-centre dialysis), it is important to also discuss what the caregiver may expect. However, available evidence regarding the course of caregivers’ experiences—both positive and negative—and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) after dialysis initiation is limited. Therefore, we aimed to: (1) assess the trajectory of experiences and HRQoL of caregivers of dialysis patients during the first year of dialysis, and (2) assess whether differences in these trajectories exist between caregivers of home dialysis patients and caregivers of in-centre dialysis patients.
Method
We conducted a multicentre, observational cohort study in adult informal caregiver-incident dialysis patient dyads. Measurements were performed at baseline (i.e. dialysis initiation), 6 months and 12 months. Outcomes included: (1) caregivers’ positive experiences measured with the Positive Experiences Scale (where higher scores indicate less positive experiences), (2) caregiver burden measured with the Self-Perceived Pressure from Informal Care questionnaire, (3) depressive symptoms measured with the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale, (4) mental HRQoL measured with the 12-item Short Form (SF-12), (5) physical HRQoL measured with the SF-12, and (6) general HRQoL measured with the EuroQoL-5D-5L. Dialysis location was defined as either home dialysis, consisting of peritoneal dialysis (PD) and home haemodialysis (HHD), or in-centre haemodialysis (ICHD). For the first aim, we assessed the trajectories of all outcomes using linear mixed models with random intercepts. For the second aim, we compared the trajectories of caregivers of home dialysis patients and caregivers of in-centre dialysis patients using linear mixed models with random intercepts and confounder adjustment.
Results
In total, 202 informal caregiver-dialysis patient dyads participated in the study. Caregivers’ mean age was 60.4 ± 14.4, 71.3% was female, and 77.7% cared for a spouse on dialysis. The mean age of patients was 64.8 ± 14.1, 33.2% was female, and 64.4% initiated ICHD. All but one of the caregiver outcomes deteriorated over the first year of dialysis. The change over time (β, 95% CI) was significant for positive experiences (1.31, 0.32; 2.31), caregiver burden (0.82, 0.05; 1.60), depressive symptoms (4.43, 2.11; 6.76), physical HRQoL (−5.48, −9.48; −1.48), and general HRQoL (−0.11, −0.19; −0.04), but not for mental HRQoL (−2.26, −5.84; 1.32). No differences between caregivers of home dialysis patients and caregivers of in-centre dialysis patients were found over time for all outcomes, as shown in Fig. 1.
Conclusion
Our study demonstrates that informal caregivers experience significant challenges during the first year of dialysis treatment, marked by a notable decline in positive experiences, physical HRQoL and general HRQoL, alongside an increase in caregiver burden and depressive symptoms. Importantly, these negative trajectories were consistent regardless of the dialysis location (home versus in-centre). These findings underscore an urgent need for targeted support for informal caregivers in dialysis care.

title: #677 Association between healthcare expenditure per capita and adoption of early home dialysis and kidney transplantation
authors: Jan Dominik Kampmann; Vianda S Stel; Leah Sejrup Christensen; Anneke Kramer; Patrik Finne
abstract:
Background and Aims
By 2030, approximately 5.439 million people will suffer from end-stage kidney disease, leading to increased need for kidney replacement therapy (KRT). Kidney transplantation, followed by home dialysis treatments, offers the best outcomes for mortality, quality of life and costs. However, rates of kidney transplantation and use of home dialysis vary greatly between countries, and the reason for this is not well known. Our aim was to estimate the association between healthcare expenditure per capita and the adoption of early home KRT that is home dialysis and kidney transplantation.
Method
We retrieved data from the ERA Registry Annual Report 2021 on the proportion of patients on home dialysis (peritoneal dialysis or home hemodialysis) or having received a kidney transplant at 91 days from start of KRT. Data on healthcare expenditure per capita were retrieved from the World Bank 2021 database. 31 European countries had all required data and were included. Linear regression was used to estimate the association between healthcare expenditure per capita and home KRT at day 91 from start of KRT.
Results
Healthcare expenditure per capita ranged from 387 USD to 11,207 USD. A higher healthcare expenditure was correlated with an increased proportion of early home dialysis and transplantation. An increase of 1000 USD in healthcare expenditure was associated with a 3.05 (95% CI 1.83–4.25) percentage point increase in the proportion of home dialysis and transplantation. The countries in the lowest quartile (<1000 USD) of healthcare expenditure per capita showed a low average proportion of home KRT of 4%, whereas in the countries in the highest quartile (>6000 USD) the proportion was 30%.
Conclusion
Adoption of early home dialysis and transplantation was higher in countries with greater healthcare expenditure per capita. Further research is needed to find out why countries with lower healthcare expenditure experience lower adoption rates for home dialysis and transplantation.

title: #3043 In vitro evaluation of the antithrombotic properties of a urokinase-coated indwelling hemodialysis catheter
authors: Yohei Shigenaga; Kozue Kobayashi; Kenichi Kokubo; Masaru Kubota
abstract:
Background and Aims
One of the complications associated with indwelling hemodialysis catheters is circulatory failure due to thrombus formation in the catheter. To overcome this issue, a urokinase-coated catheter was developed with the expectation that the fibrinolytic properties of the urokinase immobilized on the inner and outer surfaces of the catheter would confer long-lasting antithrombotic properties on the catheter surface. Previously, we demonstrated in an in vitro experimental circulation system that has been used to evaluate the anti-thrombotic properties of catheters, that the surface coating of hemodialysis catheters with urokinase conferred antithrombogenic effects on the catheter surface lasting for at least 24 hr. In the present study, we conducted a 72-hour long-term circulation experiment using the same in vitro experimental system. We investigated thrombus formation on the inner and outer surfaces of the catheter, with the aim of investigating the long-term usefulness of urokinase-coating of hemodialysis catheters.
Method
Three types of catheters were used: the Blood Access UK catheter (UK), a urokinase coated catheter, manufactured by Nipro Corporation; a catheter with an identical structure to that of the UK catheter, but without any coating (non-UK); and the GamCath catheter (GamCath), manufactured by Baxter Corporation, which is different in structure from both the UK and non-UK catheters. The 72-hour circulation experiment was conducted utilizing fresh porcine blood at a flow rate of 1.5 L/min. The fresh porcine blood was divided into 3 portions so that the same blood could be used for each catheter group. During the experiment mimicking long-term systemic circulation, the circuit was flushed and the circulating fresh porcine blood was replaced every 24 hours. At the start of the systemic circulation and after 68 hours, extracorporeal circulation was performed using an indwelling dialysis catheter to simulate a four-hour dialysis treatment. After 72 hours of circulation, the thrombi that were found adhering to the outer surface of the catheter were categorized by type (no thrombus formation observed: type 0, thrombus formation observed near the withdrawing and returning blood holes: type 1, thrombus formation observed throughout the catheter: type 2). After removal of the large thrombi, the residual blood clots and adherent platelets were extracted, and the hemoglobin (Hb) level and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity in the eluate were measured.
Results
The UK catheters predominantly exhibited type 0 thrombus formation, with only one type 1 thrombus formation. In contrast, more than a half of the catheters from the non-UK and GamCath groups were categorized as showing type 1 and type 2 thrombus formation. The UK catheter group also showed significantly lower residual blood Hb levels as compared with the non-UK and GamCath catheter groups (p = 0.047 vs.non-UK, p = 0.034 vs. GamCath), with no significant difference observed between the latter two catheter groups. The residual blood LDH activity levels were lower in the UK catheter group than in the non-UK and GamCath catheter groups. Based on the visual findings of thrombus formation and results of residual blood evaluation in the 72-hour long-term circulation experiment, we found that urokinase coating of the catheter surface inhibits thrombus formation on the inner and outer surfaces of the catheter, and that the structure of the catheter itself has little effect on the risk of thrombus formation.
Conclusion
This in-vitro experiment demonstrated that surface coating of hemodialysis catheters with urokinase conferred antithrombotic properties of the catheter surface for at least 72 hours of circulation.

title: #2670 Intrapatient relationship between plasma refill and ultrafiltration: is it more linear than we think?
authors: Sabrina Casper; Felix J Meigel; Doris H Fuertinger; Kevin Ho; Hanjie Zhang; Andrea Nandorine Ban; Sheng-Han Yueh; Vincent Filardi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hemodialysis (HD) patients exhibit substantial intra- and interpatient variability in ultrafiltration rate (UFR) and plasma refill rate (PRR). While a strong correlation between UFR and PRR has been well-documented at the population level (see e.g. [1]), it remains unclear if this relationship holds true at the individual patient level. We examined the intrapatient correlation and assessed whether a linear model accurately describes this relationship.
Method
We analyzed 2,202 hemodialysis (HD) patients, with 24 treatments per patient (January 2022–April 2023). For each treatment, the final percentage change in blood volume was obtained from Crit-Line® measurements, while pre-HD blood volume was estimated using the Nadler formula. The total plasma refill volume was then calculated as the difference between the total blood volume change and the removed ultrafiltration volume at the end of treatment. PRR and UFR were standardized to treatment time and post-dialysis weight (ml/kg/hr). Linear regression was performed at both the population and individual patient levels, analyzing UFR against PRR.
Results
Across all sessions, the mean treatment time was 223.0 ± 20.7 minutes, with average UFR and PRR values of 9.36 ± 3.30 ml/kg/hr and 7.80 ± 3.09 ml/kg/hr, respectively. The mean UFR range per patient was 6.74 ± 2.58 ml/kg/hr. At the population level, UFR and PRR exhibited a strong correlation (R² = 0.97, slope = 0.89, intercept = −0.68). Similarly, at the individual patient level, a strong correlation was observed with a median R² of 0.96 (IQR: 0.94–0.98). Patients with wider UFR ranges (≥ 4.5 ml/kg/hr) consistently demonstrated R² values > 0.8. The observed variability in slope (median: 0.82, IQR: 0.77–0.87) and intercept (median: −0.12, IQR: −0.56–0.33) across individual linear regressions are displayed in Fig. 1a. Figure 1b highlights data from three patients with their individual linear regression lines overlaid on the full dataset (UFR vs. PRR).
Conclusion
The intrapatient correlation between PRR and UFR is comparable to the strong relationship seen at the population level, particularly in those patients with greater variability in UFR (≥ 4.5 ml/kg/hr). Further research is needed to determine whether this strong intrapatient relationship reflects an inherent physiological response to treatment or if UF prescriptions are generally well-tailored to the present fluid overload. Supporting the latter, previous studies have identified total body fluid status—specifically interstitial fluid volume or its surrogate, interdialytic weight gain—as a key determinant of PRR alongside UFR [2,3].

Further research is needed to determine whether this strong intrapatient relationship reflects an inherent physiological response to treatment or if UF prescriptions are generally well-tailored to the present fluid overload. Supporting the latter, previous studies have identified total body fluid status—specifically interstitial fluid volume or its surrogate, interdialytic weight gain—as a key determinant of PRR alongside UFR [2,3].

title: #442 Arteriovenous fistula and pulmonary hypertension in patients on hemodialysis
authors: Asalya Abduvakhitova
abstract:
Background
Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a frequent complication in patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) undergoing hemodialysis (HD), particularly in those with arteriovenous (AV) access.
Aim
To determine the relationship between endothelin-1 (ET-1) and nitric oxide (NO) in the development and progression of PH in patients undergoing hemodialysis and AV access.
Method
The study involved 48 patients on maintenance HD at the Republican Scientific and Practical Center for Nephrology and Hemodialysis. Patients were divided into two groups: 22 with PH and 22 without PH. Assessment of PAP was done by Doppler echocardiography, whereas plasma levels of ET-1 and NO metabolites were assessed before and after HD and compared between the groups.
Results
Among the 48 patients studied, 22 (48%) were diagnosed with PH with a mean PAP of 46 ± 2 mmHg (range: 36–82 mmHg), which was significantly higher compared to patients with normal PAP (29 ± 1 mmHg, P < 0.0001). Cardiac output was significantly higher in HD patients with PH than in those without (6.0 ± 1.2 vs. 5.2 ± 0.9 L/min, P < 0.034). Both HD patient groups had higher plasma ET-1 levels than controls (1.6 ± 0.7 and 2.4 ± 0.8 fmol/ml vs. 1.0 ± 0.2 fmol/ml, P < 0.05), while no significant changes were detected after dialysis. Accordingly, following HD, plasma levels of NO increased considerably in both groups. However, this rise was far more significant among those without PH compared with those with PH, that is, 77.1 ± 9.6 μM compared to 24.2 ± 5.2 μM and 39.9 ± 11.4 from 14.3 ± 2.3 μM (P < 0.0001 vs P < 0.0074). The present investigation again illustrates a high prevalence of PH in patients with ESRD during HD with AV fistula. Results also suggest that impaired basal and HD-induced NO production could partly explain the increased pulmonary vascular resistance observed in ESRD patients. title: #3397 Non-conventional nutritional parameters, including adipokines and extracellular water (ECW), in the first three years following renal replacement therapy (RRT): association with long-term mortality in an end stage kidney disease (ESKD) cohort
authors: Ioannis Petrakis; Eleni Drosataki; Dimitra Ligerou; Kleio Dermitzaki; Nikolaos Papadakis; Marinos Mitrakos; Andreas Antonakis; Christos Pleros; Kostas Stylianou; Anastasia Markaki
abstract:
Background and Aims
Malnutrition, inflammation, and altered body composition contribute to high mortality in ESKD. Conventional markers like serum albumin and BMI fail to capture the complex metabolic derangements of ESKD. Given these limitations, we investigated the impact of ECW, serum magnesium, leptin, and adiponectin levels over the first three years post-RRT initiation, on mortality.
Method
From October 2007 to December 2024, 65 ESKD patients on RRT were prospectively studied, with mortality recorded. ECW was measured via BIA (BIA-101, RJL-Akern Systems, USA) 20 minutes post-hemodialysis (HD) or after peritoneal cavity emptying in PD patients. Fasting blood samples were collected for electrolytes, and ELISA assays (R&D Systems, USA) measured serum leptin and adiponectin. Per patient 2 annual measurements for the first three years under RRT were performed. Malnutrition Inflammation Score (MIS) assessed energy wasting, and Cox regression models evaluated mortality risk. Statistical analysis (SPSS 25, IBM, USA) set significance at P < 0.05. Informed consent was obtained from all participants.
Results
Sixty-five ESKD patients (35 male, 43 on HD, 22 on PD, mean age 64) were observed for an average of 43 months. Cardiovascular disease and infection were the primary mortality causes. The average MIS (5.48) suggested no significant energy wasting. In Cox regression analysis, low serum magnesium (<2.23 mg/dL, Wald 6.54, p = 0.038), low leptin (≤12.4 IU/mL, Wald 7.31, p = 0.038), high adiponectin (>25.29 IU/mL, Wald 3.84, p = 0.05), and elevated ECW (>54.1%, Wald 9.7, p = 0.021) were significantly associated with increased mortality (Fig. 1). Conventional nutritional markers were not statistically significant.
Conclusion
This study identifies low magnesium, low leptin, high adiponectin, and elevated ECW as key mortality predictors in ESKD. Paradoxically, high adiponectin (>25.29 IU/mL) was linked to increased mortality (with a marginal statistical significance), highlighting its complex role in malnutrition and inflammation. The findings emphasize the limitations of traditional markers and the need to integrate magnesium, adipokines, and ECW into routine assessments for better risk stratification and personalized care, ultimately improving survival.

title: #1785 Sleep disorders in hemodialysis patients enrolled in a tertiary hospital in davao city
authors: Richelle May Cajoles-Pagarigan; Jennifer Leano; Ritaville Elorde
abstract:
Background and Aims
End stage kidney disease is a chronic condition known to have myriad effects in the different organ systems which directly impact quality of life. One aspect that is commonly affected but, unfortunately, may not be adequately addressed in this population is sleep problems. Various studies have shown that sleep disorders are highly prevalent in the dialysis population. As sleep is one of the inherent reparative mechanisms of the body, screening and identifying sleep problems may greatly translate to an improved quality of life and even over-all health. The aims of this study were to describe the sleep quality of hemodialysis patients in our local setting and ascertain the prevalence of sleep disorders, beginning with assessment of their sleep quality then dwelling more specifically with insomnia and obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSAS). These two sleep disorders are one of the most prevalent in the dialysis population with OSAS specifically related with adverse cardiovascular effects. Ultimately, this study envisioned to educate nurses, primary care physicians, and nephrologists about the importance of screening for sleep disorders in order to make proper referrals or initiate interventions that will improve sleep and well-being of dialysis patients.
Method
This study was a descriptive cross-sectional study conducted at a tertiary government hospital in Davao City, Philippines from July to September 2024. There were 189 adult hemodialysis patients included in the study. Excluded from the study were those below 19 years of age, patients on peritoneal dialysis, patients diagnosed with insomnia or any neurologic disorder that may hinder from understanding the questionnaires used. Sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) Questionnaire. Screening forms used to identify risk for insomnia and OSAS were PSQI and STOP-BANG Questionnaire, respectively.
Results
A total of 189 hemodialysis patients were evaluated for their sleep quality and screened for insomnia and obstructive sleep apnea. Majority of the patients were between the age of 41-60 years, males, and married. The top 3 causes of end stage renal disease were chronic glomerulonephritis, hypertensive kidney disease, and diabetic kidney disease. Common co-morbid illnesses were hypertension, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. Majority were on 3x a week dialysis schedule, in the morning, with a 4-hour dialysis session. Hemodialysis access was mostly via arteriovenous fistula and dialyzers utilized were mostly hi-flux with dialyzer re-use at most for 5 dialysis sessions or below. Mean age was 49.1 years and mean dialysis vintage of 70.2 months. Majority of the patients were anemic with a mean hemoglobin of 106.6 g/L, mean phosphorus level of 5.2 mmol/L, URR reflected adequate hemodialysis with a mean of 69.1%, and mean BMI was 23.2 kg.m2 (overweight based on Asia-Pacific Body Mass Index Classification). The study showed a high prevalence of poor sleep quality and insomnia risk (68.3%) in all age groups of hemodialysis patients using the PSQI Questionnaire. The prevalence rate for OSAS was recorded at 45.0% using the STOP-BANG Questionnaire. None of the demographic and clinical parameters considered were associated with poor sleep quality and risk for insomnia. In contrast, older age, male sex, diabetic kidney disease, presence of co-morbid illness, higher BMI, and larger neck circumference were found to be significantly associated (p-value <.005) with OSAS. Moreover, there was no significant association noted between poor sleep quality and OSAS.
Conclusion
Poor sleep quality, insomnia, and obstructive sleep apnea are common problems in hemodialysis patients. The use of screening questionnaires like PSQI for sleep quality and insomnia and STOP-BANG for OSAS can be very helpful in hemodialysis patients for further evaluation and management.

title: #1513 Evaluating leukocyte test strips for peritonitis diagnosis in peritoneal dialysis patients
authors: Xiaoling Wang; Rasha Hussein; Nadja Grobe; Lisa Watson; Naomi Taylor; Lin-Chun Wang; Kieran Mulroney; Aron Chakera; Peter Kotanko
abstract:
Background and Aims
Peritonitis is a severe complication in patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis (PD). Early diagnosis is crucial for prompt intervention to prevent PD failure, hospitalization, and mortality. Standard diagnostic methods rely on clinical symptoms, white blood cell (WBC) counts in PD effluent, and microbiological cultures. However, the laboratory tests can be time-consuming, costly, and require specialized facilities, potentially delaying treatment of peritonitis.
Leukocyte test strips are commonly used as inexpensive point-of-care diagnostics to detect urinary tract infections. They rapidly react with leukocyte esterase, an enzyme released by neutrophils, producing a color change visible within seconds to minutes. In this study, we evaluated the effectiveness of leukocyte strips in detecting peritonitis in a laboratory setting.
Method
Spent PD effluent samples were collected under two IRB approved research protocols, RRI-19-002 and WA34201 between 2020 and 2024. RRI-19-002 involved the collection of 154 spent PD effluent samples from 30 patients in US, while WA34201 collected 218 PD effluent samples from 218 patients in Australia. All samples were stored at 4°C for varying durations before being frozen at −80°C until analysis.
A buffer containing 1% dextrose in PBS was used as the negative control (NC) for the test. In addition, WBCs were purified from a healthy donor, diluted to 100 cells/µL, aliquoted and stored at −80°C. These were thawed on the day of analysis and used as the positive control (PC).
For the test, a PC, an NC, and six thawed samples (250 µL each) in tubes were aligned in a row and thoroughly mixed by pipetting prior to the test. Eight urinary test strips (LotFancy, 11J-2136-D.1) were simultaneously dipped into samples for two seconds (Fig. 1A), then laid flat while a video was recorded to capture the color changes over 10 minutes (Fig. 1B). Note that only the leukocyte pads were immersed in the solution and subsequently analyzed. Still images were extracted from videos at specific time points. The mean 8-bit grayscale pixel intensity of each leukocyte pad was measured using ImageJ (https://imagej.net/ij/).
Results
We compared the strip results of fresh WBCs at various concentrations, ranging from 25 to 1600/µL, alongside the PC (100 WBC/µL, freeze-thawed once) (Fig. 2A). The results showed that intensity increased with higher cell concentrations and longer elapsed times. As expected, lower WBC concentrations exhibited a more linear signal increase over time, while higher concentrations reached saturation more quickly. Notably, the intensity from freeze-thawed WBCs at 100/µL was consistently higher than that of fresh WBCs (Fig. 2A, blue dotted line vs. blue solid line).
Among the 372 samples, 15 had dwell time under 2 hours, 2 were follow-ups from peritonitis episodes, and 5 clotted before WBC testing. These samples were excluded, resulting in a final dataset of 350 samples. Of the 132 peritonitis samples, 104 exhibited intensities higher than the PC, yielding a test sensitivity of 79%. Of the 218 non-peritonitis samples, 4 showed intensities above the PC, achieving a test specificity of 98%.
We also conducted a literature review and identified four studies exploring similar topics, which included a total of 126 peritonitis and 361 non-peritonitis PD effluent samples. These studies reported a sensitivity of 99% and specificity of 96% for leukocyte strips in testing PD effluent (Table 1).
Conclusion
Our findings suggest that leukocyte test strips can serve as a rapid, easily accessible, and inexpensive screening (less than ten Euro cents) tool for detecting peritonitis in PD patients. The relatively lower sensitivity in our study may be due to cell aggregation at 4°C in peritonitis samples before freezing, potentially reducing the number of detectable cells in aliquots. Additionally, our study highlights the potential of mobile devices (e.g., cell phones) for reading and semi-quantifying results, which could facilitate patient interpretation. Further studies using fresh samples are needed to optimize the threshold of detection and validate their clinical applicability.

title: #1309 Tryptophan metabolites clearance by hemodialysis and hemodiafiltration: an influence of comorbidities
authors: Izabela Zakrocka; Radosław Mlak; Natalia Jaszek; Sylwia Boczkowska; Tomasz Kocki; Ewa Urbańska; Wojciech Tomasz Załuska; Andreas Kronbichler
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with end stage kidney disease (ESKD) are at high risk of premature death, mainly due to cardiovascular diseases. Hemodialysis (HD) and hemodiafiltration (HDF) procedures, although performed to minimize ESKD related organ damage, have limited efficacy regarding removal of selected uremic toxins and improving patients’ outcomes. Products of tryptophan (Trp) degradation, synthesized through the kynurenine (KYN) pathway, represent one of the least studied substances in patients with kidney diseases. In animal models, a direct effect of KYN on hypertension and kidney function decline has been proposed. Interestingly, kynurenic acid (KYNA), which is formed from KYN, was reported to induce natriuresis and lower heart rate in hypertensive rats. However, in multiple studies in humans, serum level of KYN, KYNA, and another Trp metabolite 3-hydroxykynurenine (3-OHKYN) was shown to correlate with kidney function impairment and its complications. The aim of this study was to investigate the removal of Trp and its metabolites: KYN, KYNA and 3-OHKYN in patients treated by HD or HDF, as well as the influence of patients’ medical conditions on KYN pathway product clearance.
Method
The study was conducted in 50 patients with ESKD (median age 65 years, 44% of participants were male, the median dialysis vintage was 29.5 months), receiving HD (70% patients) or HDF (30% of patients) procedures. Dialysis parameters, related with patient (type of vascular access, body mass gain, blood flow) and procedure (dialysate flow, ultrafiltration volume, substitution volume, type and surface of dialyzer), together with patients’ clinical data and medical history have been investigated. Serum level of Trp, KYN, KYNA and 3-OHKYN were measured before and after a dialysis session through high performance liquid chromatography.
Results
The serum concentration of Trp (predialysis 6.2 μM vs postdialysis 7.1 μM, p = 0.133) and 3-OHKYN (53.9 nM vs 30.9 nM, p = 0.0981) remained unchanged, whereas the concentration of KYN (1.6 μM vs 0.7 μM, p = 0.0002), KYNA (418.4 nM vs 245.9 nM, P < 0.0001) and KYN/Trp ratio (0.4 vs 0.1, p = 0.0002) significantly decreased after dialysis procedures. Hypertension was associated with improved KYN clearance (2.4 μM vs 0.8 μM, p = 0.0005) and KYN/Trp ratio (0.4 vs 0.1, p = 0.0007), but not KYNA, although in patients without hypertension higher predialysis KYNA concentration was observed (584.6 nM vs 367.4 nM, p = 0.0044). On the other hand, in patients with heart failure or atherosclerosis lower predialysis serum KYN concentration and higher KYNA levels were found, however both comorbidities did not correlate with the clearance of these substances. Serum KYN removal was higher in HD than in HDF treated patients (2.4 μM vs 0.7 μM, p = 0.0005), but the clearance of other Trp metabolites did not differ between both dialysis modalities.
Conclusion
Our study found incomplete removal of Trp metabolites in ESKD patients treated by HD and HDF procedures. Targeted strategies to lower selected KYN pathway metabolites concentration may be beneficial in patients with ESKD.

Conclusion
Our study found incomplete removal of Trp metabolites in ESKD patients treated by HD and HDF procedures. Targeted strategies to lower selected KYN pathway metabolites concentration may be beneficial in patients with ESKD.

title: #2911 Projections of infection-related cost savings associated with treating CKD associated pruritus (CKD-aP) with difelikefalin in five European countries through the combination of clinical trial data and real-world evidence
authors: Annabel Rayner; James Fotheringham; Praveen Thokala; Marco Soro; Juan-Jesus Carrero; Anne-Laure Faucon
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease-associated pruritus (CKD-aP) is associated with adverse health outcomes, which translates into increased healthcare resource use and consequently increased healthcare costs. Amongst others, infections are common complications associated with CKD-aP. With new evidence-based therapies, there is an imperative to demonstrate potential cost-savings with CKD-aP treatment. Combining high quality evidence in the form of randomized clinical trial (RCT) clinical efficacy data with real-world healthcare resource use achieves this goal.
Method
From all patients free from CKD-aP receiving maintenance hemodialysis in Stockholm, Sweden, between 2006 and 2021, incident CKD-aP was identified by clinical diagnoses, pruritus medication or use of UV-therapy. Event rates were calculated per 100-person years (PY) and compared between pruritus-free and pruritus-affected periods for infection-related hospitalization outcomes including catheter infection, endocarditis, skin infection and sepsis due to Staphylococcus. Patients were followed until death or administrative censoring (December 2021).
These event rates were applied to the proportions of people with moderate or worse CKD-aP recruited into the KALM RCTs comparing difelikefalin to placebo, who had persistent (moderate or worse) or resolved (mild or none) CKD-aP for each 4-week period of the 64-week follow-up. Total national cost savings through treatment with difelikefalin were estimated combining country specific data on costs, hemodialysis prevalence from European Renal Association Registry, and established CKD-aP prevalences for the geographies of Italy, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and the United Kingdom.
Results
Among the 2329 Swedish patients on maintenance hemodialysis free from CKD-aP, 411 (17.6%) developed CKD-aP during follow-up. Compared to patients free from pruritus, patients with incident CKD-aP had a similar age (66 vs 65 years), were more likely female (39% vs 34%), but tended to have a higher prevalence of cardiovascular disease (e.g. 30% vs 24% ischemic heart disease) and longer time on dialysis (4.3 vs 2.5 years). The rate of infection-related hospitalization was 1.5-fold higher in patients with CKD-aP (17.0 [14.9–19.3] per 100-PY) than in patients free from CKD-aP (11.6 [10.7–12.6] per 100-PY, P < 0.001), mainly driven by sepsis due to Staphyloccocus (11.9 vs 7.7 per 100-PY, P < 0.001), followed by skin infection-related hospitalization (4.1 vs 3.2 per 100-PY), although the latter was not statistically significant.
Over the 64 weeks modelled using data from the KALM trials, those treated with difelikefalin had 38.4 weeks free of CKD-aP, compared to 23.9 weeks in those treated with placebo. Estimated cost savings using difelikefalin in people with CKD-aP for national hemodialysis populations were 2.22 million Euros in Italy, 2.11 million Euros in Spain, 6.40 million SEK in Sweden, 0.40 million CHF in Switzerland and 0.55 million GBP in the United Kingdom.
Conclusion
CKD-aP is associated with significant infective hospitalization complications which translate into substantial costs. When modelling these estimates with the clinical effectiveness data of difelikefalin trials, national cost savings projections strongly advocate for the treatment of CKD-aP.

title: #3750 Evaluation of regional citrate anticoagulation in 230 intermittent dialysis, 165 plasma exchange treatments and 95 liver replacement procedures
authors: Sebastian Koball; Stine Koball; Michael Hinz; Jan Stange
abstract:
Background and Aims
Extracorporeal kidney replacement therapies and plasma treatments often require anticoagulation to prevent clot formation within the extracorporeal tubing and filters. Inadequate or absent anticoagulation can lead to clotting, frequently resulting in treatment interruption and the need for a new treatment kit. This not only increases material and personnel demands but may also pose a risk to patient safety. The most commonly used anticoagulation strategy is heparin administration, which, however, carries an increased risk of bleeding complications.
While regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) has been widely established for continuous kidney replacement therapy, its application in intermittent dialysis, plasma exchange, and liver support therapies remains insufficiently studied. This study aims to evaluate the feasibility, efficacy, and safety of RCA in these intermittent extracorporeal treatment modalities.
Method
We report our experience with regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) following an institution-specific protocol in 230 intermittent dialysis sessions, 165 plasma exchange treatments, and 95 liver support procedures. Anticoagulation was achieved through the infusion of ACDA solution. For intermittent dialysis, a calcium-free dialysate was used, and calcium was substituted before returning the blood to the patient.
Results
The treatments were successfully completed as planned in 99% of cases. In 1% of cases, clot formation occurred despite regional anticoagulation, exclusively during plasma exchange treatments. Continuous monitoring of systemic ionized calcium levels and post-filter ionized calcium levels was performed throughout the procedures. No patient-related complications were observed, including clinically symptomatic hypocalcemia, hypotension, or cardiac arrhythmias.
Conclusion
Regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) is a safe and effective anticoagulation strategy for intermittent dialysis, plasma exchange, and liver support therapies when combined with close clinical and laboratory monitoring.

title: #1559 Symptoms burden in dialysis patients: determinants and impact on mortality
authors: Sabrina Mezzatesta; Vincenzo Antonio Panuccio; Federico D'antoni; Giacomo Fiumara; Pietro Salvo; Antonio Vilasi; Claudia Torino
abstract:
Background and Aims
Symptom burden in CKD patients, measured by the KDQoL questionnaire, has a negative impact on functional status and quality of life [Kidney International, 2003; 64(1), 339–349]. Despite the high prevalence in haemodialysis (HD), symptoms are often underestimated and inadequately treated in these patients [Journal of Pain and Symptom Management 2024; 67(1), e34–e57]. With this background in mind, we investigated the determinants of symptoms and their impact on mortality in a large cohort of HD patients.
Method
We included in this analysis 1839 HD patients, enrolled in the HEMO trial, with at least one measurement of symptoms available. Symptoms score ranged from 0 to 100, with higher scores reflecting better health. Machine learning (ML)-based techniques (Select-k-best, Extra Tree Regressor, and Pearson’s correlation coefficient) and linear mixed models (LMM) were used to identify longitudinal variables associated with symptoms. Univariate and multivariate Cox regression analysis was used to investigate the association between symptoms and mortality. The additional prognostic value of symptoms over and above a base model, including the same clinical variables of the Cox model, was explored by using C-statistics. In ML classification analyses, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Support Vector Machines (SVM) with linear kernel, Adaptive Boosting (AdaBoost) and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) were used to assess the predictive value of symptoms for mortality. In this case, two different datasets, containing respectively the 30 or the 10 most associated variables with the outcome, were used.
Results
Among 1839 patients, 798 were males (44%). Mean age was 57 ± 14 years, 96% were hypertensive and 45% diabetics; the mean symptoms score at baseline was 75 ± 14. In Table 1 the top ranked longitudinal determinants of symptoms, selected by ML algorithms, are listed. Among the variables in common between the three methods, four items of the Appetite Assessment Form (Appetite ranking, β = −0.04, 95% CI −0.04/−0.03, P < 0.001; Sick in last 7 days, β = −0.09, 95% CI −0.10/−0.07, P < 0.001; Change in appetite, β = −0.06, 95% CI −0.07/−0.05, P < 0.001; Difficulty following diet, β = −0.06, 95% CI −0.07/−0.05, P < 0.001) were inversely associated to symptoms score also in LMM models. During a median follow-up of 2.2 years (interquartile range: 1.1–3.9 years), 849 patients died. At univariate analysis, symptoms were significantly associated to all-cause death, with a risk reduction of 9% for each 10 unit increase of the score (HR: 0.91, 95% CI 0.87–0.96, P < 0.001). These associations remained unchanged after adjustment for the full set of traditional, inflammation, nutritional status and ESKD-related risk factors (HRfor 10-unit increase: 0.91, 95% CI 0.87–0.96, P < 0.001). The explained variation (R2) in mortality for symptoms alone was 1.1%. The scarce prognostic ability of this measure was evident by adding symptoms to a base model, including the full set of traditional, inflammation, nutritional status and ESKD-related risk factors. In this case, the improvement in R2 was less than 1%. Similarly, the gain in discrimination power (measured by the Harrell’s C index) was null. No improvement in reclassification capability (IDI and NRI) were observed. Similar results were obtained adding symptoms to a parsimonious model, including only age, gender, previous CV comorbidities, current smoking and diabetes. Classification analyses performed by machine learning showed a superimposable performance of the various algorithms, with SVM slightly outperforming other models across datasets, particularly in maintaining high accuracy and F1 Scores. Even in this case, the addition of symptoms score did not significantly improve any of the tested models (Tables 2A and 2B).
Conclusion
In conclusion, our results suggest that considering dietary habits in managing symptoms in dialysis patients may improve symptoms burden and enhance patients’ quality of life. Although a higher symptoms score was associated to a reduction in mortality, the added prognostic power was limited in our cohort. Further studies are needed to confirm our results in different populations.

title: #2523 Clinical events and patient-reported outcome measures in peritoneal dialysis
authors: Aruni Malaweera; Louis Huang; Lawrie McMahon
abstract:
Background and Aims
Tradition markers of dialysis adequacy in peritoneal dialysis (PD) correlate poorly with both patient symptoms and outcomes, and residual kidney function remains the better determinant of each. Largely in response to these findings, guidelines now recommend focusing on patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) where they have been shown to predict mortality, technique survival and hospitalisations. We aim to assess whether PROMs correlated with traditional markers of dialysis adequacy and predicted future patient outcomes.
Method
This was a retrospective study on adult PD patients who underwent a Palliative care Outcome Scale Symptom (POS-S)-renal questionnaire within 2-weeks of their routine Peritoneal Equilibrium Test (PET)-Adequest test. We assessed for the association between POS-S renal scores with adequacy measures (Kt/V and creatinine clearance or CCr) and whether POS-S renal scores predicted future outcomes (remaining on PD, transition to haemodialysis, kidney transplantation or death on PD).
Results
There were 107 patients with at least one paired PET-Adequest and POS-S questionnaire. There was no correlation between markers of dialysis adequacy (CCr and Kt/V) and symptom burden measured by POS-S renal questionnaire. Higher symptom burden predicted less favourable outcomes including technique failure, hospitalisations and death (P < 0.05). There was also an association between a higher symptom burden and a lower serum albumin level (P < 0.001).
Conclusion
There was no association between dialysis adequacy markers and PROMs, but PROMs were able to predict technique failure, hospitalisations and death compared to markers of dialysis adequacy. The measurement of PROMs may provide a beneficial addition to dialysis assessment in routine PD care.

title: #1013 Dialysis with a permanent catheter is associated with higher levels of IL-6 and myostin compared to dialysis fistula
authors: Olczyk Piotr; Miroslaw Banasik; Krzysztof Letachowicz
abstract:
Background and Aims
The global prevalence of treated end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) has risen. Hemodialysis is the most widely used form of kidney replacement therapy. The condition for conducting hemodialysis is obtaining vascular access. The optimal type of vascular access is an arteriovenous fistula (AVF) from the patient’s own vessels. The aim of the study was to compare the concentrations of selected markers in the group of patients dialyzed using a permanent catheter and a dialysis fistula.
Method
The study included 80 patients on chronic dialysis. The patients were divided into 2 groups: patients dialyzed using a permanent catheter (31 people) and a dialysis fistula (49 people). Clinical data were collected for each patient and 5 markers associated with the inflammatory state and oxidative stress were determined (GDF-8 Myostatin, TNF-a, ST2/IL-33 R, IL-6, FGF 23). The characteristics of the group are presented in Table 1.
Results
The study showed a significantly higher concentration of myostatin in patients dialyzed using a dialysis catheter compared to patients with a dialysis fistula (3204 vs 2379 pg/ml, p = 0.017). The IL-6 concentration was also significantly higher in the group of patients with permanent catheters (9.879 vs 7.362 pg/mL, p = 0.02). Detailed data are included in Table 2. Additionally, the study groups were divided according to the occurrence of heart failure. It was shown that both in the group of patients dialyzed with the use of a permanent catheter (13,28 vs 8,01 pg/mL. p = 0,007) and a dialysis fistula(9,49 vs 5,89 pg/mL, p = 0,002), patients with heart failure showed higher concentrations of IL-6 (Table 3).
Conclusion
Patients dialyzed with a permanent catheter show higher cardiovascular risk expressed by IL-6 levels. Additionally, IL-6 levels correlate with the occurrence of heart failure in patients. Additionally, this group of patients also showed higher myostatin levels, which, according to previously published studies, may correlate with the risk of hospitalization and mortality.

title: #3388 Clinical impact of teledialysis in automated peritoneal dialysis vs. hemodialysis: a retrospective comparison
authors: Paolo Luca Maria Lentini; Giorgio Laudadio; Claudia Benedetti; Valeria Fuso; Ilenia Filippi; Federica Vienna; Brenda Menegazzo; Antonino Previti
abstract:
Background and Aims
The application of telemedicine in automated peritoneal dialysis (APD) through teledialysis (TD) programs has shown promising benefits in improving patient outcomes, reducing hospitalizations, and optimizing healthcare resources. This study aims to evaluate the impact of TD on clinical effectiveness, resource utilization, and patient survival, comparing APD patients managed via telehealth with those undergoing conventional in-center hemodialysis (HD).
Method
A retrospective analysis was conducted on incident dialysis patients over a 3-year period. A total of 44 APD patients enrolled in a teledialysis program were compared with 73 incident HD patients managed through standard care. TD was performed by the combination of two systems:
Results
APD patients in the teledialysis program had significantly fewer hospitalizations per patient (0.77 vs. 2.81 in HD, P < 0.05) and showed a lower absolute mortality rate compared to HD (27.6 vs. 52.5 deaths, respectively), possibly reflecting differences in baseline patient characteristics. [Table 1]

title: #3703 Novel biomarkers for cardiac evaluation in obese and non-obese hemodialysis patients
authors: Lazar Chisavu; Flavia Chisavu; Adelina Mihaescu; Nicu Olariu; Luciana Marc; Adalbert Schiller
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hemodialysis-treated patients present high cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Many known traditional factors that increase mortality and morbidity in the general population present reversed epidemiology in HD-treated ones (body mass index, blood pressure, etc.). In addition, new biomarkers prove their utility in evaluating the cardiac implications in both general and specific populations. Identifying the action mechanisms of these biomarkers could lead to specific therapeutic interventions, which, in turn, could increase survival and quality of life.
Method
To address this issue, we performed a prospective observational cohort study on 77 patients over 2 years (October 2021–October 2023). At admission, we measured serum plasma levels of interleukin 1-beta (IL1-B), galectin 3, human suppression of tumorigenicity factor 2 (ST2), bone morphogenetic protein 2 (BMP2), and fibroblastic growth factor 23 (FGF23). We evaluated the correlations of these biomarkers with cardiac function and structure (evaluated by echocardiography), and stratified the patients by their body mass index (obese with BMI > 30 kg/m2, non-obese at BMI < 30 kg/m2).
Results
The median age was 62 (IQR=53-69) years, with 45 (56.2%) males and with a dialysis vintage of 4.95 (2.4–7.8) years. Overall mortality was 22%. Patient with obesity presented similar age, dialysis vintage sex distribution and albumin levels. Obese patients presented a higher inflammation degree with elevated C reactive protein (0.84 mg/dl IQR = 0.31–178 vs 0.36 IQR = 0.21–0.94, p = 0.021) and lower ejection fraction (48 IQR = 41–52.25 vs 52 IQR = 48–56, p = 0.028). There were no statistical differences regarding IL1-B, ST2, BMP2, galectin 3 or FGF23 levels. None of the biomarkers influenced mortality. Regarding valvular alterations, it seems that the presence of obesity increased the risk of mitral valve calcification by 5.95 times (95% CI= 1.25–28.33, p = 0.025) and reduced with 69% the risk of mitral valve fibrosis (OR = 0.31, 95% CI=0.1–0.95, p = 0.041). Only in non-obese patients, an increase with 1 nanogram/ml of ST2, reduced the risk of mitral valve calcification with 2% (OR = 0.98, IQR = 0.97–0.99, p = 0.025, the logistic regression presented a p value of 0.016 with a Nagelkerke R square of 0.15) and of aortic valve fibrosis with 2% (OR = 0.98, IQR = 0.97–0.99, p = 0.024, the logistic regression presented a p value of 0.017 with a Nagelkerke R square of 0.16).
Conclusion
Patients on maintenance hemodialysis with a BMI higher than 30 gk/m2 present higher inflammation degree, lower ejection fraction, higher incidence of mitral valve calcification but lower incidence of mitral valve fibrosis. In non-obese patients, it seems that ST2 levels are negatively correlated with both mitral valve calcification and aortic valve fibrosis. Some of these novel biomarkers could be used to better assess cardiovascular disease in patients on maintenance hemodialysis.

In addition, new biomarkers prove their utility in evaluating the cardiac implications in both general and specific populations. Identifying the action mechanisms of these biomarkers could lead to specific therapeutic interventions, which, in turn, could increase survival and quality of life.
Method
To address this issue, we performed a prospective observational cohort study on 77 patients over 2 years (October 2021–October 2023). At admission, we measured serum plasma levels of interleukin 1-beta (IL1-B), galectin 3, human suppression of tumorigenicity factor 2 (ST2), bone morphogenetic protein 2 (BMP2), and fibroblastic growth factor 23 (FGF23). We evaluated the correlations of these biomarkers with cardiac function and structure (evaluated by echocardiography), and stratified the patients by their body mass index (obese with BMI > 30 kg/m2, non-obese at BMI < 30 kg/m2).
Results
The median age was 62 (IQR=53-69) years, with 45 (56.2%) males and with a dialysis vintage of 4.95 (2.4–7.8) years. Overall mortality was 22%. Patient with obesity presented similar age, dialysis vintage sex distribution and albumin levels. Obese patients presented a higher inflammation degree with elevated C reactive protein (0.84 mg/dl IQR = 0.31–178 vs 0.36 IQR = 0.21–0.94, p = 0.021) and lower ejection fraction (48 IQR = 41–52.25 vs 52 IQR = 48–56, p = 0.028). There were no statistical differences regarding IL1-B, ST2, BMP2, galectin 3 or FGF23 levels. None of the biomarkers influenced mortality. Regarding valvular alterations, it seems that the presence of obesity increased the risk of mitral valve calcification by 5.95 times (95% CI= 1.25–28.33, p = 0.025) and reduced with 69% the risk of mitral valve fibrosis (OR = 0.31, 95% CI=0.1–0.95, p = 0.041). Only in non-obese patients, an increase with 1 nanogram/ml of ST2, reduced the risk of mitral valve calcification with 2% (OR = 0.98, IQR = 0.97–0.99, p = 0.025, the logistic regression presented a p value of 0.016 with a Nagelkerke R square of 0.15) and of aortic valve fibrosis with 2% (OR = 0.98, IQR = 0.97–0.99, p = 0.024, the logistic regression presented a p value of 0.017 with a Nagelkerke R square of 0.16).
Conclusion
Patients on maintenance hemodialysis with a BMI higher than 30 gk/m2 present higher inflammation degree, lower ejection fraction, higher incidence of mitral valve calcification but lower incidence of mitral valve fibrosis. In non-obese patients, it seems that ST2 levels are negatively correlated with both mitral valve calcification and aortic valve fibrosis. Some of these novel biomarkers could be used to better assess cardiovascular disease in patients on maintenance hemodialysis.

title: #580 Vascular access-associated excess mortality
authors: Amun Hofmann; Maria-Elisabeth Leinweber; Suman Lama; Len Usvyat; Jochen Raimann
abstract:
Background and Aims
Central venous catheters (CVC) are one of three vascular access types used for hemodialysis. While they are suitable as the primary options for select patient groups, they are generally considered inferior to arteriovenous access based on associations with impaired outcomes. However, it is not conclusively understood whether such associations are confounded by overall state of health and if so, by what extent.
Method
Patient data was extracted from electronic health records of a large US-based dialysis organization. In total, 160,753 patients initiating hemodialysis between 2016 and 2019 were included in the study population. Kaplan–Meier survival analyses were conducted stratifying for type of vascular access. Propensity score matching was further applied to mitigate the potential confounding of health status at time of initialization using demographic, clinical, and laboratory variables.
Results
In summary, 115,204 (78.4%) patients started on a CVC, 26,478 (18.0%) on an arteriovenous fistula (AVF), and 5,258 (3.6%) on an AV graft (AVG). CVC patients had higher rates of ischemic heart disease, heart failure, and history of myocardial infarction at baseline than controls. Patients who initiated hemodialysis on a catheter also had a shorter median survival than controls (1,106 vs. 1,290 days). Later conversion from a catheter to a fistula or graft increased the survival penalty compared to controls. Propensity score matching reduced survival differences, indicating confounding by baseline health. Receiving hemodialysis exclusively via AVF/AVG was not associated with a survival advantage compared to intermittent CVC use. (all Table 1) Cause-specific mortality was higher in CVC patients for both infections and cardiovascular causes. However, the proportion of infection-associated deaths in CVC patients is comparable to controls. CVC patients also showed signs of chronic inflammation in blood samples but had similar serum potassium, phosphorus, and calcium levels compared to AVF/AVG users.
Conclusion
While limitations in the present analysis such as selection bias should be taken into consideration, the survival disadvantage historically associated with CVCs in hemodialysis patients might not be based on a causal relationship. There is an increasing body of evidence suggesting that differences in vascular access-associated mortality are confounded by overall patient health in general and cardiovascular health in specific.

title: #410 Trying to reduce unnecessary carbon in haemodialysis (TRUNC-HD) — a regional sustainability quality improvement project
authors: Stephanie Choo; Leeanne Lockley; John Stoves; Laura Chase; Shilpa Kaki; V R Latha Gullapudi; Veena Reddy; Mark Wright
abstract:
Background and Aims
Healthcare contributes 4–5% of global carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) emissions. Haemodialysis (HD) contributes disproportionately to this due to its resource-intensive nature. Dialysis services in Yorkshire launched Trying to Reduce UnNecessary Carbon in Haemodialysis (TRUNC-HD), a regional quality improvement (QI) initiative to reduce the environmental impact of HD, building on established renal sustainability programmes within the region.
Method
A sustainability fellow and a regional QI manager engaged and collaborated with stakeholders across participating dialysis services. Local teams attended four face-to-face workshops using modified sustainability-focused (susQI) tools to design and implement interventions. Regional meetings, held thrice annually, facilitated progress sharing and collaboration. Baseline and progress data were gathered to assess environmental and financial impacts. The greenhouse gas (GHG) savings was quantified in carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) and calculated using hybrid carbon footprinting methodology. Data sources to calculate the GHG savings including direct measurements where available, the Department for Energy Security & Net Zero and Department for Environment Food & Rural Affairs 2024 greenhouse gas conversion factors, published carbon footprint estimates of medical equipment and expert opinion.
Results
Between January and December 2024, interventions included using 1:44 instead of 1:34 dialysate acid concentrate, reducing machine heat disinfection cycles, reducing dialysate flow rates, encouraging patients to bring personal blankets instead of unit-provided blankets that must be laundered after every single use and waste reduction. Waste management strategies included reducing food waste, recycling empty acid concentrate canisters, switching from single use to reusable domestic items and streamlining fistula cannulation packs. Combined, these interventions are estimated to achieve annual savings of 45 tonnes of CO2e and £70397 (Table 1).
Patient experiences and outcomes were monitored during the intervention period. Patient-centred initiatives, such as encouraging personal blanket use, improved patient experience and comfort. Two centres observed that optimising machine heat disinfection cycles reduced the wait time for machines to be ready for dialysis, thus improving patient flow and satisfaction. A preliminary 2-month review of dialysis adequacy after reducing the dialysate flow rates from 800 to 500 ml/min in a single unit showed no adverse impact on dialysis adequacy. Feedback from the workshops and regional meetings highlighted the value of collaboration which fostered teamwork, leadership and QI skills within multidisciplinary teams.
Conclusion
In summary, the TRUNC-HD initiative demonstrates the impact of a regional, collaborative approach to addressing climate change, delivering environmental and financial savings, professional development, and service improvements. Scaling up current interventions regionally could achieve annual savings of approximately 120 tonnes of CO2e and nearly £200,000 per year.

title: #1917 Peritoneal dialysis modality and outcomes in the peritoneal dialysis outcomes and practice patterns study
authors: Thyago Proença de Moraes; Charlotte Tu; Brian Bieber; Ron Pisoni; Talerngsak Kanjanabuch; Tadashi Tomo; Fiona Brown; Simon Davies; Jeffrey Perl; Yong-Lim Kim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Automated peritoneal dialysis (APD) is the most common peritoneal dialysis (PD) modality in many high-income countries, with increasing adoption in low/middle-income countries. Whether or not differences exist in outcomes between PD modality (APD vs. continuous ambulatory PD [CAPD]) remains controversial. A better understanding of this relationship could inform further APD uptake globally. We evaluated patient survival, permanent hemodialysis transfer (HDT), and peritonitis by PD modality in a contemporary cohort of patients across facilities and countries with significant variation in APD use.
Method
Using the Peritoneal Dialysis Outcomes and Practice Patterns Study (PDOPPS), we identified patients prescribed either CAPD vs. APD with a dialysis vintage of 4 months or longer at study entry in Australia, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, United Kingdom, and the United States. Thailand was excluded due to very low APD use. Cox models estimated the association between PD modality and outcomes, including patient survival, HDT, and time to first peritonitis, adjusting for case mix and facility-level factors. Subgroup analyses were prespecified. Additional analyses explored APD as the proportion APD use at the facility level with outcomes, to reduce treatment by indication bias.
Results
Among 17,591 included patients, 14,343 (82%) were on APD. APD use ranged from 37% in South Korea to 90% in the United States (Fig. 1A). APD patients had similar comorbidity profile but were younger, had lower urine volume, were more likely to use hypertonic glucose, and less likely to use icodextrin compared to CAPD patients. The hazard ratio (HR) for patient survival for APD vs. CAPD was 0.93 (95% CI 0.81–1.06) overall (Fig. 1B). Country-specific mortality results varied, with HR 1.08 (95% CI 0.89–1.28) in the US and HR 0.55 (95% CI 0.34–1.03) in Japan. In a subgroup analysis, APD was associated with better survival in patients with icodextrin use (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.61–1.00). Risk of HDT was marginally higher among APD patients (HR 1.07, 95% CI 0.97–1.18), despite a lower risk of peritonitis (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78–0.98). In Japan and South Korea where APD use was less common, approximately one quarter of facilities reported use in fewer than 20% of patients), lower facility proportion APD use was associated with higher mortality.
Conclusion
Patients on APD had lower rates of peritonitis. Patient survival did not differ significantly by PD modality in the PDOPPS. However, APD patients had a marginally higher risk of HDT, possibly reflecting its use as a “rescue therapy.” Greater icodextrin use in APD patients may improve survival. Further prospective evaluations are required to explore patient reported outcome differences across PD modalities, to identify specific patients who could benefit from initial APD use or switch from CAPD to APD and to explore the impact of increasing APD use on clinical outcomes across low- and middle-income countries.

title: #3333 Green dialysis? identifying carbon footprint hotspots in a hemodialysis center in Poland
authors: Zuzanna Jakubowska; Małgorzata Kępska-Dzilińska; Jolanta Małyszko
abstract:
Background and Aims
Life cycle assessment (LCA) is a crucial methodology for evaluating the environmental impact of medical procedures, particularly in energy-intensive treatments like hemodialysis (HD). This study aims to assess the carbon footprint of key HD procedures at a dialysis center in Poland, identifying major sustainability hotspots to guide mitigation strategies.
Method
This LCA was conducted to analyze the environmental impact of various HD-related activities, including vascular access creation, routine HD sessions, hybrid and isolated dialysis sessions, and the management of complications. Products used in these procedures were systematically weighed and evaluated for their associated CO₂ emissions based on standardized emission factors. Surveys were conducted among patients and medical staff to determine their means of transportation to the dialysis center, allowing for an accurate assessment of CO₂ emissions related to commuting. Water and electricity usage data were collected and analyzed to quantify their contribution to the overall carbon footprint. Waste management practices were reviewed, focusing on incineration as the primary method and minimal recycling practices. CO₂ emissions were calculated using standard emission factors for energy consumption, transportation, and waste processing. The findings aimed to identify the most significant environmental burdens associated with HD procedures.
Results
The total CO₂ emissions from the dialysis center were estimated at 81,060.04 kg CO₂ annually. Transportation emerged as the largest contributor, accounting for 54,525 kg CO₂/year. Routine HD sessions contributed 17,409.6 kg CO₂/year, while sterilization and machine preparation added 7,020 kg CO₂/year. Vascular access procedures, though infrequent, contributed 207.9 kg CO₂ over a patient’s lifetime. Waste management practices, particularly incineration, significantly impacted the center’s overall carbon footprint.
Conclusion
Transportation and routine HD sessions are the primary sustainability hotspots at the dialysis center. To mitigate the environmental impact, the center should explore sustainable transportation options, such as electric buses, and consider implementing energy-efficient HD machines or transitioning to renewable energy sources. Improving waste management strategies, particularly by reducing reliance on incineration and increasing recycling efforts, could further contribute to lowering overall CO₂ emissions. This study highlights the importance of integrating sustainability considerations into dialysis care to reduce its environmental footprint.

title: #29 Clinical impact of catheter insertion method: a single-center retrospective study using propensity score analysis
authors: Yuji Hidaka; Jien Saito; Masahiro Nakagaki; Fumiko Kuwahara; Kenji Harada; Hidetoshi Kanai; Tetsuro Takeda
abstract:
Background and Aims
There are two main approaches for establishing peritoneal dialysis (PD) access: the SMAP method (embedding the catheter before PD initiation), proposed by Moncrief and Popovich, and the direct method (placing the catheter at PD initiation). Several retrospective studies have examined the SMAP method, but none have adjusted for confounding factors. Therefore, we retrospectively investigated whether the SMAP method offers better outcomes by evaluating PD duration and survival, adjusting for confounders in patients who underwent PD at a single center.
Method
In this single-center study, 691 patients who underwent PD catheter insertion between January 2011 and December 2020 were divided into two groups: Direct Method (D group, n = 318) and SMAP Method (S group, n = 373). Primary outcomes were the first two year PD continuation, total PD duration, and overall survival after PD initiation. Secondary outcomes included emergency hemodialysis (HD), peritonitis, tunnel infections, exit-site revisions, and reasons for PD withdrawal (PD-related problems, mental/physical issues, kidney transplantation, death). Confounding factors (age, sex, serum creatinine, hypertension, diabetes, ischemic heart disease, cardiovascular disease, peripheral artery disease, cancer, history of abdominal surgery, liver disease, COPD, dementia, depression) were balanced by inverse probability weighting (IPW). The first two year PD continuation and the total PD duration were analyzed using the Fine Gray test, and the overall survival period was plotted using the Kaplan-Meier survival curve. Cox proportional hazards models and logistic regression were analysed for multivariable analyses.
Results
Median age was 69 years in both groups. Median PD duration (IQR) was 25.0 (9.4–50.3) months in D and 35.8 (18.9–57.5) in S. Median overall survival was 47.5 (20.4–81.2) months in D vs. 56.4 (33.2–82.8) in S. Median catheter embedding time in S was 4.4 (2.23–8.24) months. PD-related withdrawal occurred in 108 (34%) D patients vs. 142 (38%) S; mental/physical issues in 21 (6.6%) D vs. 26 (7.0%) S; transplant in 15 (4.7%) D vs. 11 (2.9%) S; death in 141 (44%) D vs. 138 (37%) S.
Emergency hemodialysis was required in 117 (37%) D vs. 37 (9.9%) S; peritonitis in 153 (48%) D vs. 182 (49%) S; tunnel infections in 21 (6.6%) D vs. 49 (13%) S; exit-site revisions in 17 (5.4%) D vs. 30 (8.0%) S. Fine-Gray analysis for PD continuation within two years indicated a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.67 (95% CI: 0.45–1.00). For total PD duration, HR was 0.88 (95% CI: 0.67–1.17). Kaplan–Meier curves showed no significant survival difference (log-rank P = 0.55). Cox proportional hazards models revealed HRs of 0.86 (95% CI: 0.72–1.03) for total PD duration and 0.88 (95% CI: 0.68–1.12) for overall survival in S vs. D. Logistic regression indicated that SMAP significantly lowered the risk of leaks lasting over two weeks (HR: 0.18, 95% CI: 0.04–0.78) and emergency hemodialysis (HR: 0.19, 95% CI: 0.14–0.26).
Conclusion
This propensity score-adjusted analysis suggests the SMAP method may reduce early PD withdrawal, emergency hemodialysis, and leaks compared to the direct method, supporting its utility in clinical practice.

title: #2646 Incremental hemodialysis: a single center experience from Singapore
authors: Mahesh Ekanayaka; Mayank Chawla; Boon Cheok Lai; M D Akramul Hoque
abstract:
Background and Aims
Incremental hemodialysis (iHD) is the practice of initiation of hemodialysis (HD) with fewer than 3 sessions per week or shortened duration. Such patients need close monitoring of their residual renal function, control of blood pressure, and fluid status, with the aim of smooth transition to conventional hemodialysis.
Method
A retrospective analysis was conducted on 142 incident End stage kidney disease (ESKD) patients initiated on hemodialysis at our center between June 2020 and April 2022. Outcomes for conventional HD (3 sessions per week, n = 121) were compared with incremental HD (2 sessions per week, n = 21).
Results
The average iHD duration was 13 months, offering financial and quality of life benefits without increased mortality (p = 0.103).
iHD saved 1096 sessions and S $274,000 for the 21 patients. However, iHD patients exhibited increased hospitalizations for fluid overload or acute pulmonary edema with in the first 6 months (p = 0.034). The Conventional HD group had a longer survival (37.2 vs 33.5 months, p = 0.046), but no significant difference in total six-month admissions (p = 0.336).
Conclusion
While iHD patients benefitted from reduced costs and fewer sessions, they had higher early hospitalizations for fluid related issues. Nephrologists should carefully select and monitor suitable patients, focusing on their residual kidney function and fluid status, to facilitate a timely transition to conventional dialysis. Tools like urea and creatinine clearance, bioimpedance spectroscopy, can be used to assess residual renal function and fluid status respectively in routine dialysis clinics. In conjunction with astute patient selection, such measures would potentially reduce the number and severity of complications in iHD patients.

While iHD patients benefitted from reduced costs and fewer sessions, they had higher early hospitalizations for fluid related issues. title: #721 Removal of middle molecules with hemoadsorption plus hemodiafiltration in kidney failure patients
authors: Thiago Reis; Maria Gabriela Guimaraes; Roberto Pecoits-Filho; Jessica Andrade; Sibele Braga; Gisele Guimaraes MacIel; Miguel Goes; Koody Kitawara; Gonzalo Ramírez-Guerrero; Francisco Neves; Claudio Ronco; Irene L Noronha
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hemodiafiltration (HDF) promotes a higher clearance of middle molecules than hemodialysis. Whether the association of hemoadsorption plus HDF (HAHDF) using cartridges with styrene-divinylbenzene further enhances the removal of middle molecules is yet to be defined. We prospectively analyzed the removal of middle molecules in four patients undergoing HAHDF and compared it with HDF.
Method
Patients underwent 3-hour sessions of HAHDF with post-filter replacement or the HDF with same parameters. We measured the reduction ratio (RR) [i.e., 1 – (pre-session/post-session)] of four middle molecules in all sessions.
Results
Four patients performed 29 sessions of HAHDF and 17 sessions of HDF. The main characteristics of the 46 sessions were blood flow of 400 mL/min (IQR 350–400 mL/min), convective post-filter flow of 115 mL/min (IQR 105–115), and dialysate flow of 500 mL/min (IQR 500–800 mL/min). The RR of ß2-microglobulin (12 kDa), myoglobin (17 kDa), and prolactin (23 kDa), were higher with HAHDF. The RR of parathormone (9.4 kDa) was equivalent.
Conclusion
3-hour HAHDF sessions provide a superior reduction ratio of three middle molecules compared to HDF.

title: #2267 Relationship between changes in bone responsiveness to parathyroid hormone and bone mineral density in patients on chronic haemodialysis
authors: Shu Ushimaru; Hirofumi Sumi; Naoto Tominaga
abstract:
Background and Aims
Parathyroid hormone (PTH) has a stimulatory effect on bone resorption, particularly in cortical bone, leading to femoral neck (FN) fractures. In patients undergoing haemodialysis (HD), the bone responsiveness to PTH varies widely among individuals, and the tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase-5b (TRACP-5b) level, a bone resorption marker derived from osteoclasts, varies relative to the intact PTH (iPTH) concentration (TRACP-5b/iPTH ratio). This study examined the relationship between the changes in both the TRACP-5b/iPTH ratio and bone mineral density (BMD) over 5 years in patients undergoing chronic HD.
Method
A 5-year retrospective observational study was performed. Patients on chronic HD at Kawasaki Municipal Tama Hospital (Kanagawa, Japan) from December 2018 to December 2023 were analyzed. Exclusion criteria included patients receiving peritoneal dialysis or those with cancerous bone metastases. We utilized the means of data every 3 months over a 5-year period for albumin, calcium (Ca), phosphorus (P), 25(OH)D, 1,25(OH)2D3, and β2-microglobulin concentrations, and utilized the data in December 2018 and December 2023 for TRACP-5b and iPTH concentrations, and BMD. All blood tests were performed prior to HD, in the first HD session of the week. Patient exposure to clinical independent variables of interest was defined by data on age, sex, body mass index, chronic HD vintage, presence of diabetes, or 5-year continuous medication prescription [i.e., Ca-sensing receptor agonist, vitamin D receptor activator, P binder (Ca containing, Ca non-containing, both), or anti-resorptive medication], or steroid use history. The median TRACP-5b/iPTH ratio in December 2018 was 4.8. Patients with a ratio greater or equal to 4.8 were defined as high bone responsiveness, and those with a ratio below 4.8 as low bone responsiveness. The changes between December 2018 and December 2023 in BMD at the left FN (FN-BMD), which is rich in cortical bone, were retrospectively examined as a dependent variable. Patients were placed in one of three groups based on changes over 5 years in the TRACP-5b/iPTH ratio as follows: 1) from the high to low bone responsiveness to iPTH, 2) no change, and 3) from low to high bone responsiveness to iPTH. In each analysis, statistical significance was set at P < 0.05.
Results
Twenty-two patients were included in this analysis. As of December 2018, the TRACP-5b/iPTH ratios and FN-BMD showed an inverse correlation trend (P = 0.055). The mean over 5 years in P concentration (P = 0.017) and the mean over 5 years in β2-microglobin concentration (P = 0.034) were statistically significantly different between the three groups. In the simple linear regression analysis, female sex (P = 0.027), the mean over 5 years in 1,25(OH)2D3 concentration (P = 0.015), and the 5-year continuous use of anti-resorptive medication (P = 0.003) showed a statistically significant correlation with a higher change in FN-BMD, whereas body mass index (P = 0.040), presence of diabetes (P = 0.035), and change of the TRACP-5b/iPTH ratio group from low to high (P = 0.042) showed a statistically significant correlation with a lower change in FN-BMD. The limitations of this study include the small number of patients undergoing chronic HD who could be followed up for bone metabolic markers and BMD over 5 years, making it difficult to perform multiple regression analysis.
Conclusion
An elevated level of bone responsiveness to PTH, defined as the TRACP-5b/iPTH ratio, may be associated with a decline in FN-BMD in patients undergoing chronic HD. Inhibition of the transition from low to high bone responsiveness to PTH could be considered to prevent FN fractures.

title: #3502 Predicting mortality in unplanned hemodialysis
authors: Camillo Tancredi Strizzi; Ilaria Mariani; Elettra Lomeo; Maria Elena Bracaccia; Valentina Vaiarello; Francesco Pesce; Giuseppe Grandaliano; Nicola Panocchia
abstract:
Background and Aims
The unplanned initiation of hemodialysis is a pivotal event often associated with a heightened risk of in-hospital and short-term mortality. Identifying modifiable predictors of such outcomes is essential to refine clinical decision-making and reduce the burden of futile treatments. This study aims to explore the prognostic factors influencing mortality in this context, tailoring interventions and improving patient-centered outcomes.
Method
This retrospective observational study analyzed a cohort of 139 patients who underwent unplanned hemodialysis during hospitalization between January 2023 and August 2024 at the Policlinico Universitario A. Gemelli IRCCS and Ospedale Isola Tiberina - Gemelli Isola. Demographic, clinical and laboratory characteristics, including hemoglobin, albumin, and total cholesterol levels at admission, were assessed. Functional and prognostic scores, such as the Karnofsky Performance Status (KPSS), Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), and Couchoud Score (CS), were also evaluated. Primary outcomes included in-hospital mortality, post-discharge mortality, functional recovery, and the need for dialysis continuation. A multivariate logistic regression model was employed to identify independent predictors of mortality, with odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) reported. Model performance was evaluated through a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve, with smoothing splines applied to explore non-linear associations between continuous predictors (e.g., KPSS and albumin) and mortality.
Results
The cohort had a mean age of 68.1 ± 14.4 years, with females representing 40.3% of the population. The average duration of hospitalization was 24 ± 20 days, with an overall mortality rate of 33.8% (n = 47), comprising 25.9% (n = 30) in-hospital deaths and 12.2% (n = 17) deaths post-discharge. Functional recovery was observed in 21.6% (n = 30), and the mean number of hemodialysis sessions during hospitalization was 8 ± 7. Multivariate logistic regression (Table 1) identified Karnofsky Performance Status (KPSS) (OR: 0.92, 95% CI: 0.86–0.98, p = 0.001) and serum albumin (OR: 0.82, 95% CI: 0.72–0.94, p = 0.004) as significant independent predictors of mortality. Higher KPSS and albumin levels were strongly associated with reduced mortality risk. In contrast, Cognitive Deficit and Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) did not reach statistical significance in the model. The logistic regression model demonstrated excellent discriminative ability, with an AUC of 0.87, indicating high accuracy in mortality risk stratification (Fig. 2A). Smoothing splines revealed non-linear effects: mortality risk increased markedly for KPSS scores below 70 and albumin levels below 30 g/L, underscoring the pivotal role of functional and nutritional status in determining outcomes (Fig. 2B).
Conclusion
This study highlights the substantial short-term mortality risk associated with unplanned hemodialysis initiation. Incorporating Karnofsky Performance Status and serum albumin levels into the decision-making process offers a robust, evidence-based framework for improving patient risk stratification. By leveraging these predictive factors, clinicians can refine therapeutic strategies, reduce the burden of disproportionate treatments, and enhance the quality of care for patients requiring urgent dialysis.
