title: #971 Dialysis less frequently in the elderly: the D-LITE pilot trial
authors: Christine A White; Hasitha Welihinda; Andrew Day; Rachel Holden
abstract:
Background and Aims
The elderly represent the most rapidly growing end stage kidney disease age group world-wide. The hemodialysis (HD) prescription that provides the best outcomes for this distinct population with reduced life expectancy is unknown. Observational data suggest that quality of life (QOL) could be improved with less frequent HD without increasing mortality in this unique population.
The primary aim of the D-LITE pilot trial was to determine the feasibility and safety of conducting a trial designed to determine whether twice versus thrice weekly HD improves QOL in incident elderly HD patients.
Method
We conducted a pilot randomized open controlled single centre trial in Kingston, Canada. Eligible subjects were incident HD patients ≥ 70 years of age 3 months post HD initiation planning to continue in-centre HD. Forty subjects were randomized to twice weekly versus thrice weekly HD stratified by residual kidney function and were followed for 9 months. The primary outcomes were those of feasibility and safety. Secondary outcomes included patient-reported QOL assessments, hyperkalemic events, mortality and requirement for emergency dialysis.
Results
Figure 1 shows patient flow. Consent rate of eligible subjects was high (77%), adherence approached 100%, and 78% of randomized patients completed study. Subjects randomized to the twice weekly arm had similar pre-HD normokalemia rates (90%) to the thrice weekly arm and fewer than 10% of HD post weights exceeded prescribed target weight by 1.0 kg. Urgent HD treatments for hypervolemia and hyperkalemia was infrequent and similar between arms as were hospitalizations and death.
Conclusion
The results of this pilot randomized controlled study of twice and thrice weekly HD in an elderly incident HD population reveal that the study was both feasible and safe. These results will inform the design of a multi-center RCT with QOL and safety endpoints.

title: #3207 Development of depression and anxiety symptoms in chronic hemodialysis patients during “Ssward of Iron” war
authors: Nomy Levin Iaina; Majd Obid; Yehonatan Marziano
abstract:
Background and Aims
On October 7, 2023, following the attack by Hamas, the “Iron Swords” war broke out in Israel. Since the onset of the war approximately half of the dialysis units in various regions and at different times have been under threat of rocket attacks. This unpredictable attacks may have negative psychological effects on the general population and, in particular, on dialysis patients. Depression and anxiety among dialysis patients may negatively impact their mental health. Prolonged mental stress can worsen existing conditions, affect the effectiveness of dialysis treatments, reduce adherence and persistence in treatments, and shorten dialysis sessions. To the best of our knowledge, no studies have been published examining the impact of war and terrorist attacks on the development of depression and anxiety symptoms among patients undergoing chronic hemodialysis. The current study aimed to assess the impact of the “Iron Swords” war on the development and persistence of symptoms of depression and anxiety among chronic hemodialysis patients in the Nephrology and Hypertension Department at Barzilai University Medical Center in Ashkelon, located less than 20 kilometers from Gaza, with more than 1000 rocket attacks during the first few weeks of the war. The study also sought to evaluate factors that may contribute to the development of these symptoms and to examine their impact on dialysis quality.
Method
This is a prospective, descriptive, and quantitative study that included 30 adult patients, who have been on chronic hemodialysis for at least six months. After signing informed consent, participants completed PHQ9 and GAD7 questionnaires to assess the presence of symptoms of depression and anxiety upon entering the study, during the “Iron Swords” war, and four months later for follow-up. Demographic, socioeconomic, educational, and marital status data were collected, as well as information on comorbidities, including psychiatric disorders and regular medication use. Additionally, dialysis data and routine laboratory tests taken at the start of the study and four months later were gathered, including assessments of dialysis adequacy and quality.
Results
Depression symptoms developed in 43.3% of the patients in the study, and anxiety symptoms developed in 23.3% of participants at the beginning of the study, with the onset of the “Iron Swords” war. Depression and anxiety symptoms significantly improved in most patients, and after 4 months, decreased to 21% and 12.5%, respectively. More women developed symptoms of depression. Depression and anxiety symptoms were more common among patients who were unmarried, secular, and had higher education levels. 53% of the patients lacked a secure room in their homes, and about 23% temporarily moved to other dialysis units. Depression symptoms did not affect dialysis dose and adequacy or lab indicators, except for significantly lower albumin levels at the beginning of the study and a significant decrease in dry weight during the study. Depression and anxiety symptoms resolved or significantly improved in most patients by the end of the study. The development of depression and anxiety symptoms did not affect the number of hospitalization days or mortality rates.
Conclusion
The development of depression and anxiety symptoms was common among chronic hemodialysis patients during the “Iron Swords” war, without affecting the dosage or adequacy of dialysis, but impacting patients’ nutritional status. These symptoms were short-lived and improved significantly without intervention. Given the findings of the study and the high prevalence of depression and anxiety symptoms among dialysis patients during wartime, especially considering the prolonged, indefinite duration of the war, there is an urgent need to establish a psychological and social support infrastructure for dialysis patients, with an emphasis on emergency situations.

title: #786 Large language models for algorithm-based management of bone mineral disorders in patients with hemodialysis
authors: Karin Bergling; Emel Hamilton; Len Usvyat; Peter Kotanko; Hanjie Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Large language models (LLMs) are gaining increased attention in medicine. Their integration into user-friendly interfaces, such as ChatGPT, has led to various exploratory applications. Here, we evaluate ChatGPT’s performance as a clinical decision-support tool by integrating it with a nine page clinically validated paper algorithm. This algorithm seeks to optimize management of hyperphosphatemia, calcium imbalance, and secondary hyperparathyroidism in patients treated with hemodialysis. Based on values of iPTH, calcium, phosphorus and prescribed medications, the algorithm ordered by the attending physicians, guides nurses and dietitians in initiating and titrating calcitriol and cinacalcet, as well as scheduling follow-up tests to achieve target biochemical parameters.
Method
The performance of ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-o1 in providing recommendations according to the algorithm was tested using 25 fictitious patient scenarios. Each scenario included various combinations of laboratory values and prescribed medications; however, designed to resemble real-life cases, with some data fields being imperfect or missing. The LLMs were independently tasked with identifying missing laboratory input and informing the clinician. The LLMs were also responsible for recommending appropriate medication initiation, dose adjustments, physician consultations, and proposing laboratory follow-up schedules aligned with the algorithm’s guidance. The generated recommendations were compared against an expert clinician’s application of the paper algorithm and deemed correct only if all the recommendations precisely aligned with the algorithm’s instructions.
Results
ChatGPT-4o correctly recommended all applicable actions according to the algorithm in 36% of the scenarios, while ChatGPT-o1 achieved accuracy in 48% of the scenarios as demonstrated in Fig. 1. LLM generated instructions were user-friendly, concise, and aligned well with wording used in the algorithm. Both models exhibited issues with interpreting certain laboratory threshold values. For instance, a phosphate level of exactly 5.5 mg/dL was repeatedly interpreted as exceeding the hyperphosphatemia threshold of >5.5 mg/dL, leading to inappropriate recommendations. Other recurring errors, particularly frequent in ChatGPT-4o output, included missed recommendations for initiating calcitriol or cinacalcet, and inaccuracies in laboratory follow-up scheduling after cinacalcet adjustment, which deviated from standard algorithm guidelines.
Conclusion
We observe promising glimpses of the performance and future feasibility of LLMs as clinical support tools for implementing complex algorithms. ChatGPT-o1 slightly outperformed ChatGPT-4o, likely due to its capability of longer reasoning chains yielding more accurate results and fewer hallucinations. However, notable limitations persist for both LLMs, emphasizing the need for refinement. Algorithms designed and formatted for human interpretation may not be fully compatible with the computational logic and interpretative frameworks of LLMs. To enhance accuracy and stability of algorithm interpretation in clinical practice, two factors require additional attention. First, refining algorithms to ensure rigorous decision logic is essential to improve their applicability and adaptation when converted to computerized versions. Second, optimizing prompts for LLMs is crucial to influence the quality and relevance of the outputs generated. By addressing these areas, we expect significant strides in advancement of clinical decision making through the use of LLMs, meaningfully augment the clinicians’ work, and help improve patient outcomes.
Acknowledgement
We wish to thank Tammy Bickimer, RN, for valuable contributions to this work.

title: #396 Oral health care among dialysis patients in France and impact on survival
authors: Linda Jordane Dondjio Jemele; Marie Buzzi; Cécile Couchoud
abstract:
Background and Aims
Oral diseases have been shown to be risk factors of progression in patients with chronic kidney disease and may also be associated with poorer survival. The aim of this study was to describe the use of oral care by dialysis patients in France and to assess its impact on their survival.
Method
We conducted a retrospective cohort study including all patients on dialysis in France between 2015 and 2020. Data were collected from the French REIN registry and matched with the National Health Data System. Factors associated with the probability of having oral care were explored using a logistic regression model. The survival of incident dialysis patients was modelled using a Cox model weighted by the inverse probability of benefiting from oral care and adjusted on age and comorbidities, with the date of first dental treatment and the date of registration on the transplant waiting list introduced as time-dependent variables.
Results
Among the 101,942 prevalent patients included in our sample, 32.5% used oral care at least during the 6 years. Average annual use was 18.7% (versus 43% in general French population) with regional variations. Male gender, HCV status and being on the transplant waiting list were associated with higher use of oral care, while younger and elder age and most comorbidities were associated with lower use. The use of dental care was associated with a lower risk of death (weighted HR 0.53 [95% CI 0.51–0.55], adjusted HR 0.50 [0.48–0.52]).
Conclusion
Dialysis patients in France have a low level of oral care use. Patients’ characteristics and regional practices appear to influence this use. Oral care seems to have a positive impact on the survival of dialysis patients, justifying prevention strategies.

title: #828 Development of a support system for patients on dialysis: examining the implementation and continuation of exercise therapy
authors: Tokuo Umeda; Akiko Okawa; Natsumi Yamamoto; Masahiro Itou
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients on hemodialysis are required to manage vital signs, dialysis information, and dietary intake on a daily basis. However, this self-management often becomes a significant burden and is difficult to maintain.
We are developing a safe and secure support system that connects dialysis patients and medical institutions without relying on internal systems of healthcare providers. To date, we have built a comprehensive regional dialysis patient support system to enable the sharing of vital data, dialysis records, and dietary logs between patients and medical institutions (Fig. 1).
In this study, we focused on supporting exercise therapy for dialysis patients by adding a new exercise support function using an ergometer (dietary therapy support is described in “Development of a Support System for Dialysis Patients: Functionality for Assisting Dietary Therapy”). Furthermore, we developed an ergometer charger equipped with a reward system based on exercise effort and enabled the integration of exercise data with dialysis records. This function allows patients to exercise at home on both dialysis and non-dialysis days and earn rewards for their exercise efforts.
Method
An ergometer was used as the exercise device for dialysis patients with a hub dynamo to convert rotational motion into electrical power (Fig. 2). The rotation of the ergometer is transferred to the hub dynamo via a belt, enabling power generation. Using a newly designed device, the generated power is converted to USB voltage, which is displayed with an easy-to-read USB voltage/current checker. This setup allows exercise effort to be visualized as electrical power, and the generated power can be stored in a USB charger.
The exercise data recorded by the ergometer is output in CSV format and saved to a tablet device. The CSV data can then be transmitted to the existing support system, where it is integrated with dialysis records and dietary data, enabling comprehensive management and visualization of exercise information. A new function was added to integrate daily exercise data into the existing support system.
Results
The developed ergometer power generation device successfully converted exercise into measurable electrical power. Patients were able to confirm their exercise effort visually, and the ability to store the generated power allowed them to exercise on both dialysis and non-dialysis days. The visualization of exercise progress increased patient motivation and promoted participation in regular exercise.
Moreover, the generated power could be used to charge devices, such as smartphones, transforming exercise from a requirement into an enjoyable activity, thus contributing to the establishment of an exercise habit. Healthcare providers observed that patients began exercising voluntarily, and the integration of exercise data with dialysis records enabled better monitoring and assessment of patient conditions.
Conclusion
We successfully added an exercise therapy support function to a dialysis patient support system, creating an environment to facilitate exercise among dialysis patients. This feature not only enables the sharing of dialysis records but also integrates exercise data with medical institutions, allowing healthcare providers to better understand patients’ physical condition. Patients can now continue exercising on both dialysis and non-dialysis days, and their exercise data can be shared with medical staff for more effective management. In addition, the reward system, where exercise efforts contribute to charging devices, increased patient motivation and established exercise habits. Patients themselves have become more proactive in participating in regular exercise.
This research was supported by the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research (JP20H03982).

title: #3214 The thiolomic profile of peritoneal membrane fibrosis: a hypothesis-driven research
authors: Diogo Sequeira; Luísa Santos; Rita Rita Ribeiro Calça; Sofia Anão; Filipa Rodrigues; Raquel Lourenço; Emília Monteiro; Patrícia Matias; Patrícia Branco; Sofia Azeredo Pereira
abstract:
Background and Aims
Our research group is actively searching for novel pharmacological strategies to protect the peritoneal membrane from fibrosis, a major challenge in maintaining the long-term effectiveness of peritoneal dialysis (PD) [1, 2]. While some protective agents for the peritoneal membrane are available, their clinical application remains limited by the lack of reliable indicators to stratify membrane vulnerability before fibrosis becomes irreversible. Oxidative stress is an early event in fibrosis, but most studies have primarily focused on reactive radical species. Alternatively, we hypothesize that oxidized thiol groups, such as oxidized cysteine and related thiols, represent small, non-radical pro-oxidant molecules that play a crucial yet underexplored upstream role in membrane injury. This work aimed to compare the thiol profile (cysteine, cysteinylglycine, glutathione), a profile that we named as “thiolome” [3], in the peritoneal effluent between individuals with or without fibrotic peritoneal membranes.
Method
A cross-sectional, single-center study was conducted in adult patients initiating PD at Unidade Local de Saúde de Lisboa Ocidental (Ethical approval: NMS 50/2019; ULSLO 2024-63). Patients were enrolled consecutively, and histological data from peritoneal membrane biopsies were collected during Tenckhoff catheter placement. Submesothelial compact zone thickness (STM) measurements were analyzed. Serum α-Klotho levels were quantified by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, with values below the established cutoff of 742 pg/mL also used as an indicator of peritoneal fibrosis [2]. Thiol concentrations—Cys (GSH precursor), glutathione (GSH), and cysteinylglycine (CysGly, GSH degradation product)—were quantified in peritoneal dialysate using high-performance liquid chromatography with fluorescence detection [3]. Each thiol was measured in three forms: reduced (SSH), free oxidized (SSX), and protein-bound (SSP), with total thiols calculated as the sum of these fractions, and free total as the sum of oxidized and reduced forms. The interindividual variability of thiol fractions and correlations with STM were assessed through univariate statistical methods and principal component analysis (PCA) was conducted to determine whether the thiol profile could distinguish between patients with and without peritoneal membrane fibrosis.
Results
A total of 41 incident patients on PD were included, aged 55 ± 2 years, 30% female. Peritoneal fibrosis was identified in 16 (39%) patients. Fractions with variability exceeding 50% included total GSH, GSSX, and the protein-bound forms of Cys, GSH and CysGly. PCA of the thiolome did not differentiate between the presence or absence of fibrosis and showed no association with STM. title: #1581 Control of vascular risk factors among patients with stage 5D chronic kidney disease in Spain. Preliminary results of the “objetivo en el punto de mira” (opm) study
authors: Javier Nieto; José Abellán-Alemán; Gloria Anton-Perez; Jorge Valdés-Sotomayor; Carlos Jesús Cabezas Reina; Inés Rodríguez Pastore; Jesús Masiá; María Dolores Martínez-Esteban; María Victoria Guijarro; Emilsi Trinidad-Pérez; Esperanza Moral Berrio; Silvia Montoro
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) are the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with chronic kidney disease on dialysis (CKD-5D). These patients are at a very high vascular risk (VR) and yet do not always achieve optimal control of cardiovascular risk factors (CVRFs). Our goal is to assess, in a large sample of CKD-5D patients in Spain, the degree of control over CVRFs (hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia) and the factors involved.
Method
A multicenter, interventional, prospective study conducted under routine clinical practice conditions. Patients undergoing hemodialysis were randomly selected from 20 dialysis centers across Spain. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee. According to international guideline criteria, control targets were defined as follows: for hypertension (HTN), blood pressure (BP) <140/80 mmHg for patients >65 years and <130/80 mmHg for those <65 years; for dyslipidemia, LDL-c targets of <70 mg/dL for high VR and <55 mg/dL for very high VR; and for diabetes, HbA1c <7% or <8% in patients ≥80 years.
Results
A total of 504 patients were included (347 men, 157 women); among them, 471 (93.4%) were hypertensive, 238 (47.2%) diabetic, and 397 (78.7%) dyslipidemic. A total of 207 patients (41%) were simultaneously hypertensive, dyslipidemic, and diabetic. The percentage of CVRF control was as follows: hypertension, 218 patients (43.2%); diabetes, 155 patients (65.1%); and dyslipidemia, 198 patients (49.8%). Only 38 patients (7.5%) achieved control of all three CVRFs simultaneously. In 5.4% (27 patients), none of the factors (HTN, diabetes, or dyslipidemia) were controlled. Among diabetic patients, 16% had all three factors controlled, while 11.3% had all CVRFs uncontrolled.
Conclusion
Among the population of CKD-5D patients treated in Spain, the control of cardiovascular risk factors is remarkably low. A total of 92.5% of patients are not meeting control targets as defined by international vascular risk guidelines, and only 7.5% achieve these objectives. Active pharmacological intervention by clinicians aimed at managing these factors could improve the prognosis for these patients.

title: #660 Prediction of fistula maturation using central venous oxygen saturation and upper body blood flow
authors: Andrea Nandorine Ban; Laura Rosales Merlo; Xiaoling (Janice) Ye; Peter Kotanko; Frank Van Der Sande; Jeroen Kooman; Len Usvyat; Hanjie Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Arteriovenous fistula (AVF) maturation is a critical factor in ensuring effective and long-term vascular access for hemodialysis (HD) patients. Clinical studies have demonstrated that cardiac output and upper body blood flow (UBBF) increase following AVF creation. This enhanced upper body perfusion is expected to increase central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO₂). A previous multicenter quality improvement project demonstrated that the clinical use of ScvO₂ and estimated UBBF (eUBBF) as indicators of AVF maturation is associated with a significant reduction of central venous catheter residence time after AVF creation [1, 2]. This study aims to evaluate the ability of ScvO₂ and eUBBF to predict if AVF maturation is progressing as expected at 6 weeks after AVF creation.
Method
This multi-center study included thirty-eight maintenance HD patients with newly created AVFs. The Crit-Line monitor (FMC North America, Waltham, MA) is an FDA approved device to measure in the extracorporeal dialysis circuit hematocrit and oxygen saturation (i.e., ScvO2 in patients with central venous catheter as vascular access). Together with anthropometric data ScvO2 and hematocrit were used to calculate eUBBF [2]. To avoid the impact of ultrafiltration on hematocrit, we only considered data collected between 5 and 20 minutes into dialysis. Patient- and population-level ScvO₂ and eUBBF were collected during the month preceding AVF creation (i.e., baseline) and throughout the 6 weeks post-surgery. AVF maturation at week 6 was considered successful based on the clinical judgment of the vascular access surgeon, and if no interventions were required.
The percentage change in ScvO₂ and eUBBF from baseline to 6 weeks post-creation was computed for every patient. Areas under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUC) were computed to assess the predictive value of the relative change of ScvO₂ and eUBBF.
Results
In patients with failed AVF maturation (n = 16), the median relative increases from baseline to six weeks post-AVF creation were 5.4% for ScvO₂ and 20.4% for eUBBF. In contrast, in patients with successful AVF maturation, the median relative increases were 15.5% for ScvO₂ and 47.9% for eUBBF (Fig. 1).
Both ScvO₂ and eUBBF were predictive of AVF maturation outcomes at six weeks. The AUC for ScvO₂ was 0.74 and 0.79 for eUBBF (Fig. 2). The AUCs did not differ statistically significantly.
Conclusion
Both ScvO₂ and eUBBF demonstrate potential as non-invasive indicators for predicting AVF maturation outcomes six weeks post-AVF creation. These parameters may serve as additional tools in clinical practice to identify HD patients at risk for AVF maturation failure, allowing for earlier interventions and improved patient outcomes. Studies in larger cohorts are warranted to further define the clinical utility of ScvO2 and eUBBF.

title: #2022 Turning the tide in heart failure management: the role of peritoneal ultrafiltration
authors: Filipa Rodrigues; Maria Inês Gil Martins Roxo; Ines Alexandre; Ana Rita Pereirinha Ramos; Raquel Lourenço; Tânia Almeida; Tânia Madeira; Gonçalo Rodrigues de Ávila; Patricia Moreira Matias; Sofia Azeredo Pereira; Patrícia Branco; Rita Rita Ribeiro Calça
abstract:
Background and Aims
Loop diuretics are essential for managing fluid overload; however, their reduced effectiveness is a common issue that can negatively impact the patient’s clinical progression and potentially increase hospitalization rates. Peritoneal ultrafiltration has been used to address refractory congestion. This study aimed to investigate the effectiveness of peritoneal ultrafiltration in patients with cardiorenal syndrome.
Method
A retrospective, single-center study was conducted between 2014 and 2023. It involved patients with New York Heart Association (NYHA) classes III-IV heart failure who were resistant to diuretics despite optimal medical treatment and did not qualify for other PD initiation criteria. Clinical and laboratory parameters were collected before and after the technique’s initiation.
Results
Fifteen patients were included, with a mean age of 65.55 ± 11.53 years, and 80% were male. Seven patients (n = 4) had diabetes. Most patients (80%) had reduced left-ventricular ejection fraction, and three patients had congestive right-side heart failure. The most common heart failure etiology was ischemic (n = 4), followed by valvular (20%) and infiltrative (13%) due to amyloid deposition. At the beginning of the technique, the mean estimated glomerular filtration rate was 20 ± 9 mL/min/1.73 m². The median follow-up period was 52 months (IQR 7– 63).
The median hospitalization days due to fluid overload in the 12 months before starting PD was 19 days (IQR 0–37), which significantly decreased to 5 days (IQR 0–7) in the 12 months after beginning PD (P = 0.03). The median level of N-terminal prohormone of brain natriuretic peptide (NT-pro-BNP) in the 12 months before starting PD was 16.723 pg/mL (IQR 6.124–35.000), which declined to 10.506 pg/mL (IQR 3.452–12.560) in the 12 months after (P = 0.02).
Clinical stability allowed for the initiation of prognosis-modifying therapy: 67% were on SGLT2 inhibitors, the same percentage on RAAS inhibitors (including ACE/ARA inhibitors or ARNI), 60% on beta-blockers, and 54% on mineralocorticoid antagonists. Complications included 7 episodes of peritonitis. Eight patients discontinued PD after a median of 75 months (IQR 7–179). The survival rates were 80% at 12 months, 73% at 24 months, and 60% at five years.
Conclusion
The study’s small sample size and gender bias limit generalizability, while occurrences of peritonitis highlight the need for careful complication management and longer-term, multi-center studies for comprehensive insights. Nonetheless, these findings underscore the potential of peritoneal ultrafiltration as a valuable therapeutic approach in managing heart failure and associated complications.

title: #1880 Novel ai-based recipe recommendation system for dialysis patients using retrieval-augmented generation
authors: Sheng-Han Yueh; Karin Bergling; Len Usvyat; Peter Kotanko; Hanjie Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Dietary planning for dialysis patients often relies on time-consuming manual processes. We explore the use of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combined with models from OpenAI to enhance recipe recommendations. RAG is an efficient approach to enhance background knowledge of a base language model without retraining, thereby saving time and cost. By integrating a curated database of kidney-friendly recipes into a RAG pipeline, the system retrieves relevant recipes and provides personalized recommendations tailored to user queries. This approach harnesses RAG and OpenAI’s generative AI capabilities to deliver accurate, scalable, and user-friendly dietary management tools.
Method
We collected 322 kidney-friendly recipes sourced from the website of a large dialysis organization (https://www.freseniuskidneycare.com/recipes-and-nutrition/recipes). Each recipe was formatted into a structured text representation, including fields such as recipe name, description, ingredients, directions, nutrition information, serving size, time for preparation, and reference URL. These structured texts were embedded using a pre-trained model from OpenAI and stored in a vector database (Fig 1). For each query, the Facebook AI Similarity Search (FAISS) method retrieves the 10 most relevant recipes by identifying those with the smallest Euclidean distance to the query vector. These retrieved recipes are then incorporated into the prompt, enabling the response generation to be highly specific and evidence based.
Results
We tested multiple queries, such as: “Provide three chicken-based dinner recipes under 500 calories, with less than 250 mg of sodium per serving, and high in protein. As you know, I am allergic to paprika”. All 10 retrieved documents align with the requirement of chicken-based recipes (Table 1). The retrieved documents were integrated into the prompt for the GPT-4o model, which then generated a response tailored to the query. The response (Fig. 2) provided key details such as nutrients, ingredients, and serving sizes, while highlighting deviations and suggesting ingredient adjustments for better alignment with the criteria.
However, during retrieval phase, several recipes, including “Braised Paprika Chicken” (similarity score: 0.7317) and “Paprika Chicken Thighs with Brussels Sprouts” (0.7166), include paprika, directly contradicting the specified exclusion due to an allergy. This highlights the challenges of accurately interpreting and applying negative constraints. During the generation phase, the GPT-4o model re-evaluate the “Query + Retrieval recipes”, strictly enforcing the exclusion of paprika, ensuring adherence to the hard constraint specified in the query, the final output recipes did not contain paprika.
Conclusion
The results demonstrate the combined strengths of RAG and GPT-4o in providing a more flexible and adaptive solution for recipe recommendations. RAG efficiently retrieves relevant recipes, while GPT-4o enhances the process by addressing nutrient restrictions and allergy constraints. Despite some challenges in enforcing negative constraints during retrieval, such as excluding paprika-containing recipes, GPT-4o successfully refines the output by highlighting discrepancies, suggesting modifications, and adhering to strict requirements. This integration showcases a versatile approach to personalized recipe design, accommodating dietary needs and preferences effectively.

title: #1873 Advanced analysis of high-frequency intradialytic data using artificial intelligence
authors: Sheng-Han Yueh; Vincent Filardi; Len Usvyat; Peter Kotanko; Hanjie Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hemodialysis (HD) generates a vast amount of patient and machine data. These dynamic HD treatment data contain valuable information that can be used e.g., for the near-real-time prediction of intradialytic hypotension (IDH) (Zhang et al. NDT, 2023). To further accelerate data analysis, we explored the use of an autoencoder model, an unsupervised AI deep learning technique primarily used for extracting salient data features and to reduce data dimensionality. This technique is particularly effective (a) because it learns a representation that highlights the underlying patterns in the data while ignoring noise or irrelevant details, and (b) it compresses input data into a lower-dimensional latent space via an encoder and reconstructs it using a decoder, learning essential patterns by minimizing reconstruction loss. The lower-dimensional latent vector then could be used as input to other models, e.g., an IDH prediction model.
Method
We analyzed time series of intradialytic relative blood volume (RBV), arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2), and ultrafiltration volume (UFV). These data are recorded every 10 seconds by the HD machine and the integrated Crit-Line monitor (FME, Waltham, MA). We included treatments lasting at least 3 hours and comprising over 900 SaO2 recordings. The final dataset included 45,804 HD treatments from 22,218 patients, spanning Jan 30 to Feb 5, 2023. The dataset was divided into training (27,482 treatments, 60%), validation (9,161 treatments, 20%), and testing (9,161 treatments, 20%) subsets. The trajectories of RBV, SaO2, and UFV were normalized to a range of −1 to +1 using min-max normalization. An autoencoder (Fig 1), was developed. The encoder compresses intradialytic measurements of the three variables into a latent vector represented by a list of 25 numbers. The decoder then reconstructs data from the latent vector back to its original form. During the training process, the model minimizes the reconstruction loss, defined by mean squared error (MSE). Model performance is evaluated using mean absolute error (MAE) and normalized mean absolute error (NMAE) between the reconstructed and original data.
Results
Each of the three data channels (i.e., RBV, SaO2, UFV) contained 1,513 time steps. Per HD session, the encoder compressed the 3 × 1,513 = 4,539 elements into 25 elements. The three trajectories were then reconstructed from the latent vector through the decoder. The results (Fig 2) demonstrated a high similarity between the original trajectory (Ground Truth, blue) and the reconstructed trajectory (orange), indicating that the latent vector effectively preserves information of the original data and that the decoder successfully learns to reconstruct the trajectory, particularly for RBV and UFV. MAE and NMAE statistics are shown in Table 1.
Conclusion
The encoder-decoder model effectively compresses and reconstructs clinically relevant high-frequency hemodialysis time series trajectories, showcasing its potential as a robust tool for feature extraction. However, this method is unable to faithfully represent the high-frequency SaO2 oscillations. If and to what extent the use of the extracted features in models e.g., to predict IDH enables more accurate and efficient predictions warrants further exploration.

abstract:
Background and Aims
An adequate diet is critical for dialysis patients to manage nutrients like protein, potassium, phosphorus, and sodium. To support this, an efficient method to identify the types of food consumed in patients' daily lives is essential for accurately translating food intake into nutrient levels. The aim of this study is to evaluate the use of ChatGPT for image recognition and its ability to correctly identify ingredients from food images. This approach could provide a valuable tool for assisting in dietary assessment and management for dialysis patients, as current methods rely heavily on self-reporting and manual review, which are labor-intensive and difficult to scale for real-time and large-scale applications.
Method
This study integrated GPT-4o, an optimized version of OpenAI's model with enhanced capabilities for analyzing and responding to a combination of data types, into the process of ingredient recognition from photos of prepared dishes. The model was applied to a diverse range of cuisines, including Mexican, Western, and Chinese. By incorporating various culinary styles, the study aimed to evaluate the model’s performance across dishes with different ingredient combinations and presentation styles. Photos from nine distinct dishes were provided to GPT-4o, with each image analyzed individually. The model was tasked with identifying all ingredients in each dish. To ensure accuracy and relevance, only ingredients confirmed to be present in the images were included in the evaluation (e.g., broccoli would be included whereas salt will be excluded). A matching score was computed for each dish to quantify the model’s performance. This score was defined as the ratio of correctly identified ingredients to the total number of ingredients present in photo.
Results
Among the nine dishes analyzed, each contained at least five visible ingredients, with GPT-4o successfully recognizing all ingredients in six of them (Table 1). Three instances of false recognition are illustrated in Fig. 1. The photos demonstrating suboptimal performance in ingredient recognition are presented to highlight specific challenges encountered during the analysis. Overall, the average matching score across all dishes was 94.97%.
Conclusion
This study investigated the ability of GPT-4o to recognize ingredients from photos of prepared dishes representing a variety of cuisines such as Chinese, Mexican, and Western. The results demonstrate that this approach can accurately identify ingredients, achieving an average matching score of 94.97%. However, challenges remain with certain scenarios, such as overlapping ingredients, misclassification of visually similar items, and the recognition of boiled or blended components. These findings highlight GPT-4o's potential as a tool for ingredient recognition, thus improving patients’ ability to better understand nutritional content of their meals.

title: #2938 Nutritional issues among hemodialysis patients—deficiency and excess body mass
authors: Sylwia Małgorzewicz; Małgorzata Kaczkan; Sylwia Czaja-Stolc; Przemysław Rutkowski; Alicja Dębska-Ślizień
abstract:
Background and Aims
With the growing obesity epidemic, there is an increasing number of patients with excess body weight in the group of hemodialysis patients. At the same time, research indicates the occurrence of protein-energy wasting (PEW) in this group of patients. The aim of the study was to evaluate the prevalence of overweight and obesity and diagnosis of PEW in a cohort of stable HD patients.
Method
Nutritional status was examined by ISRNM criteria, GLIM criteria, s-albumin, nPNA and anthropometry. Body composition was assessed by bioimpedence analysis (BCM). Inflammatory markers (hsCRP, IL-6) and routine laboratory parameters were measured in serum.
Results
165 HD patients with a mean age of 52.3 years were included to the study. In the studied population 37.5% of HD patients presented overweight and 12.5% obesity. 50% of the HD population had a high BMI - above 25 and at the same time presented signs of PEW according ISRNM criteria. The GLIM assessment correlated with the ISRNM criteria. PEW was diagnosed in 23.4% of patients independently to BMI. Also, patients with PEW presented lower nPNA, s-albumin and lean tissue index (LTI) compared to well-nourished (P < 0.05). In multiple regression analysis, the age, low LTI and hsCRP proved to be a predictor of the PEW.
Conclusion
A high BMI does not exclude malnutrition; in the group of hemodialysis patients, a particular problem is the loss of muscle mass (sarcopenia), chronic inflammation and incorrect protein intake.

title: #987 A randomized prospective crossover study on the effects of medium cut-off membranes on FGF-23 and inflammatory mediators in patients receiving regular haemodialysis
authors: Saif Al-Chalabi; Smeeta Sinha; Philip A Kalra; Dawn Evans; Darren Green; Leon Schurgers; Dimitrios Poulikakos
abstract:
Background and Aims
High-flux dialysis (HFD) membranes effectively remove small molecules during haemodialysis but have limited capacity in clearing middle molecules that may contribute to the uraemic milieu. Medium cut-off membranes (MCO) have the potential of removing a wide range of middle molecules. Our study aimed to compare the clearance rate (CR) of Fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF-23) and other selected inflammatory cytokines between medium MCO and HFD membranes and investigate the intrasubject stability of these biomarkers.
Method
This prospective randomised case-crossover study recruited adult patients receiving regular haemodialysis. Twenty patients were randomised into two groups: Group A: to start with 1 week of thrice-weekly dialysis using HFD membrane followed by a 3-weeks washout period and then 1 week of dialysis with an MCO membrane; Group B, to start with 1 week of thrice-weekly dialysis using MCO membrane followed by a 3-weeks washout period then 1 week of dialysis with HFD membrane. Blood samples were taken before and after each dialysis session for analysis of the assessed biomarkers (FGF-23, interlukin-6 [IL-6], interlukin-18 [IL-18], high-sensitivity C-reactive protein [hsCRP] and dephosphorylated uncarboxylated matrix Gla protein [dp-ucMGP]). Average values over the 3 sessions in each arm were used for comparison between the membranes using Wilcoxon signed rank test and paired-t test depending on the distribution of the data. One-way repeated measures ANOVA or Friedman Repeated Measures Analysis of Variance tests were used for the intrasubject stability of the biomarkers depending on the distribution of the data.
Results
There was no significant difference in the CR when using MCO and HFD membranes for the assessed biomarkers: FGF-23 (0.31 vs 0.23], P = 0.242), IL-6 (0.19 vs 0.12, P = 0.215), IL-18 (−0.05 vs − 0.03, P = 0.704), dp-ucMGP (0.33 vs 0.33, P = 0.903) and hsCRP (−0.05 vs −0.08, P = 0.107). There was no significant intrasubject variability for all assessed biomarkers except in pre-dialysis high hsCRP levels when using HFD membrane.
Conclusion
The use of MCO membranes for a short period did not substantially reduce FGF-23 levels or other selected inflammatory cytokines. There was no significant intrasubject variability for all assessed biomarkers apart from hsCRP.

title: #977 Efficacy of vitamin C supplementation in patients undergoing hemodiafiltration: a comparison between oral and intravenous administration
authors: Lilian Cuppari; Carolina S Wagner; Gabriela Foelkel; Gabriela Paula; Christiane Kojima; Cynthia Borges; Andrea Magalhães
abstract:
Background and Aims
Vitamin C deficiency is common among patients on dialysis. While supplementation is recommended to restore serum vitamin C levels, the optimal administration route and its effects on serum oxalate levels remain unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of oral versus intravenous (IV) vitamin C supplementation in hemodiafiltration (HDF) patients with low serum vitamin C levels.
Method
Patients with serum vitamin C levels <0.4 mg/dL, who had not received supplementation for at least three months, were randomized to receive 500 mg of oral (n = 39) or IV (n = 37) vitamin C twice weekly after HDF sessions for 12 weeks. Blood samples were collected in the first dialysis session. Serum vitamin C was measured using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC, reference range: 0.4–1.5 mg/dL), and serum oxalate levels were assessed via spectrophotometry (reference value: <26.6 µmol/L).
Results
A total of 76 patients (54% male, 56.7 ± 17.1 years, 29% with diabetes, dialysis vintage: 44.5 months [19.3–71.3]; mean ± SD or median and interquartile range) were analyzed. Vitamin C levels increased in both groups, with no significant difference between routes (oral: 0.39 mg/dL [0.14–0.74] vs. IV: 0.26 mg/dL [0.08–0.70], P = 0.26). However, serum levels remained <0.4 mg/dL in 43.6% of oral and 53.1% of IV patients (P = 0.36). Serum oxalate levels increased similarly in both groups (oral: 4.79 µmol/L [0.76–12.3] vs. IV: 4.75 µmol/L [−3.0 to 11.1], P = 0.43). Changes in vitamin C positively correlated with changes in serum oxalate (r = 0.37, P = 0.001), hemoglobin (r = 0.30, P = 0.01), and inversely with C-reactive protein (r = −0.33, P = 0.005). Serum ferritin increased post-supplementation (P = 0.004). Among patients who failed to restore vitamin C levels, 60.5% underwent dialysis more than four times weekly compared to 35.1% on three times weekly (P = 0.03).
Conclusion
Both oral and IV vitamin C supplementation increased serum levels without significant differences between administration routes. However, the current dose and /or frequency may not be sufficient to normalize levels in all patients, particularly those with more frequent dialysis sessions.

title: #712 Long-term impact of peritoneal dialysis ultrafiltration on cardiorenal patients
authors: Sara Núñez Delgado; Maria Azancot Rivero; Ana Méndez; Juan Carlos Leon Román; Natàlia Ramos Terrades; Néstor Toapanta Gaibor; Ana Sánchez Escuredo; Jordi Comas; Maria Jose Soler Romeo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Heart failure (HF) prevalence is increasing, and its prognosis worsens in the presence of other comorbidities. Up to 70% of patients develop cardio-renal syndrome (CRS), which is associated with diuretic resistance or kidney deterioration over time. Peritoneal dialysis (PD) for ultrafiltration (PD-UF) could be a potential therapeutic option in CRS, although its long-term outcomes have not been described.
Method
Retrospective registry study of the Catalan Renal Registry on patients with PD-UF indication between 2013 and 2022. Baseline clinical characteristics and follow-up until December/2022 were studied.
Results
Of the 1874 incident patients on PD, 198 (10.6%) were PD-UF, 73.2% of the patients were male and the mean age was 70.7 ± 9.3 years. Median eGFR at start was 22.6 [IQR 14.8–32.8] ml/min·1.73 m2 and 75.0% have an eGFR above 15 ml/min·1.73 m2. Previous history of ischemic heart disease, arrhythmia or cardiac surgery was recorded, 57.6% of patients had ≥2 of these pathologies. The most common HF etiology was ischemic heart disease in 21.7% of patients.
Median overall patient survival was 21 months [IQR 17.3–24.3]. and technique survival at one year was 94.8%. During follow-up, 27 patients (13.6%) were transferred to another RRT (23 to HD, 4 to KT). Patients transferred to HD were mostly because complications associated with comorbidities (70.6%), secondly due to PD complications (23.5%) and 27 patients were transferred to other renal replacement therapy (hemodialysis or kidney transplantation).
Log-rank analysis of categorized variables showed differences on survival by age (≤75 years-old vs. >75 years-old, P < 0.001), BMI (<20 kg/m2 vs. ≥20 to ≤25 kg/m2 vs. >25 kg/m2, P = 0.014), functional status (not frailty vs. mild frailty vs. severe frailty, P = <0.001) and previous history of heart conduction disorders prior the start of PD-UF (P = 0.020) (Fig. 1). In the cox multivariate analysis, age >75 years (HR 1.76 [95% CI 1.20–2.59]), mild frailty (HR 2.18 [95% CI 1.17–2.59]), severe frailty (HR 17.62 [95% CI 1.20–55.48]) and the burden of cardiac disease (2 categories HR 2.17 [95% CI 1.05–4.47]; 3 categories HR 2.26 [95% CI 1.05–4.89]) were associated with poor overall survival. Technique survival was associated with eGFR (<30 ml/min·1.73 m2 HR 5.64 [95% CI 1.32–24.18]) and BMI (<20 kg/m2 HR 6.53 [95% CI 1.06–40.12]) at baseline (Table 1).
Conclusion
PD-HF is a feasible option in patients with advanced HF and CRS. The complexity of this population increases with older age, frailty and higher cardiac burden.

title: #2732 Expanded hemodialysis vs. online hemodiafiltration: comparison of mom control, anemia, and molecular clearance over 4 years of follow-up. Are there differences?
authors: Antonio Luis García Herrera; Carolina Lancho Novillo; Fernando Vallejo Carrión; Sumaya Ed Daoudy Chagouani; Miguel Ángel Bayo Nevado
abstract:
Background and Aims
Online hemodiafiltration (HDFOL) is currently the hemodialysis technique that achieves the highest clearance of middle-molecular-weight solutes, along with better control of inflammation and, consequently, improved anemia response and mineral bone metabolism. These molecules are involved in harmful inflammatory mechanisms for our patients. HDFOL is superior to conventional techniques, but its main drawback lies in the high cost it imposes on hemodialysis units, as well as the requirement for ultrapure water standards. With the advent of expanded hemodialysis (HDX), there is now the possibility of achieving clearance of larger molecules without albumin loss and without increasing the cost of the technique.
Method
We compared the clearance of various molecules with different molecular weights (urea, creatinine, phosphorus, PTH, CRP, Nt-proBNP, free kappa and lambda chains, and albumin) in 20 patients, both pre- and post-dialysis, using HDFOL and HDX with Theranova. Additionally, we evaluated the degree of anemia control, EPO requirements, and mineral bone metabolism status by comparing both techniques after four years of treatment. The cost per session of both techniques was also assessed.
Results
Significant differences were found with respect to a greater clearance of larger molecules using HDx compared to HDFOL, in particular there was a greater clearance of Kappa and Lamda chains and alpha 1 antitrypsin. No significant loss of albumin was detected in HDx compared to HDFOL.
No differences were found with respect to anaemia control, MOM and dialysis dose.
Conclusion
HDX, based on the analyzed biochemical and clinical data, demonstrates effectiveness comparable to HDFOL and is not inferior to it in terms of molecular clearance, anemia control, or mineral bone metabolism. In fact, there was better clearance of large molecules using HDx versus HDFOL. Furthermore, HDX represents a lower cost compared to HDFOL.

title: #2228 Data-driven clustering of secretory bone markers to risk-stratify hemodialysis patients: Insights from a multicentric, prospective observational study
authors: Simon Aberger; Emanuel Zitt; Daniel Cejka; Marco Kaspar; Thomas Bernd Dschietzig; Franz Paul Armbruster; Hildegard Hafner-Gießauf; Maximilian Waller; Corinna Schabhuettl; Alexander H Kirsch; Alexander Rosenkranz; Kathrin Eller
abstract:
Background and Aims
Annual mortality still exceeds 15% in patients receiving maintenance hemodialysis, mainly driven by cardiovascular disease (CVD) burden. Therapies targeting calcium, phosphate and bone metabolism are still lacking evidence for consistent benefits, warranting new approaches to guide treatment decisions.
Method
A prospective, observational study was conducted across three Austrian hemodialysis centers including stable maintenance hemodialysis patients. Blood samples were collected at study entry. Biochemical markers of bone metabolism (iPTH, noxPTH®, betacrosslaps, osteoprotegerin, sRANKL), antioxidative capacity (ImAnOx®) and oxidative stress (PerOx®) were measured with standardized assays provided by Immundiagnostik AG. Unsupervised K-means machine learning algorithm was employed to cluster the dataset based on these biochemical variables. The 1-year mortality rates, treatment-related data and CVD burden were then compared between clusters.
Results
A total of n = 363 patients were included. Basic demographic data include a median age of 72 years, median hemodialysis vintage of 27.5 months and a male preponderance of 63%. Four distinct clusters were identified (Fig. 1A and B). Cluster 0 was defined by low noxPTH® (median 139 pg/mL), low sRANKL levels and high oxidative stress with the highest 1-year mortality rate (24.9%). In contrast, higher antioxidative capacity and beta-crosslap levels distinguished Clusters 1 and 2 with lower mortality rates (13.2% and 0% respectively). Cluster 3 was defined by high noxPTH levels (median 441 pg/mL) and showed an intermediate 1-year mortality rate (17.8%), yet the highest CVD burden (81%). Calcimimetic treatment was highest in Cluster 3 (57.8%), however, over 23% of patients in the low-noxPTH® Cluster 0 were inadequately treated with calcimimetics.
Conclusion
Unsupervised cluster analysis allowed risk-stratification of hemodialysis patients by biochemical profiles, reflecting low-turnover bone disease and oxidative stress as features with unfavourable outcome. This strategy could improve treatment categorization in future trials.

authors: Lin-Chun Wang; Sheng-Han Yueh; Andrea Nandorine Ban; Jeroen Kooman; Peter Kotanko; Len Usvyat; Hanjie Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
While evidence indicate that prolonged intradialytic hypoxemia is associated with increased morbidity and mortality in HD patients (Meyring–Wösten et al., CJASN 2016.), research into arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) patterns during hemodialysis (HD) is scarce. Here we aim to describe the intradialytic dynamics of SaO2 in a large and diverse cohort of HD patients with arteriovenous vascular access. Understanding the SaO2 dynamics may open new avenues to identify HD patients at high risk for adverse clinical outcomes.
Method
SaO2 levels during HD were measured using the Crit-Line monitor (CLM; Fresenius Medical Care, Waltham, MA). CLM measurements were recorded at 10-second intervals and transmitted into Amazon Web Services (AWS) via Apache KAFKA, a real time streaming software. We extracted CLM data between January 2021 and July 2023. A sample data collected on January 2, 2023, was analyzed. During data cleaning, recordings with SaO2 ≤0 or ≥99.9% and hematocrit <15% or >60% were deemed implausible and hence excluded. We then excluded sessions with an SaO2 standard deviation of <0.1%, an SaO2 interquartile range of zero, and less than a total of 60 minutes of recordings. Also, sessions with less than 5 minutes of measurements either at the start or at the end of the session were filtered. Mean SaO2 was calculated for each time point (every 10 seconds) and a plot using locally estimated scatterplot smoothing (LOESS) regression with shaded 95% confidence intervals was generated to analyze the trend of SaO2 during treatments.
Results
The per-10-second average and the LOESS function of SaO2 from 6,068 HD sessions from 6,068 patients are shown in Fig. 1. Right after HD started, SaO2 declined and reached its nadir around 60 minutes into the treatment. Thereafter, SaO2 increased and finally reached levels close to starting values.
Conclusion
Our results of a biphasic intradialytic SaO2 dynamic corroborate an earlier report (Campos et al. Blood Purif 2016). The decline of SaO2 in the first hour on dialysis is notable. We consider two potential explanations. First, the flux of bicarbonate from the dialysate may increase blood pH and reduce the ventilatory drive. Second, the early nadir in SaO2 may be associated with transient, subclinical bio-incompatibility of components in the extracorporeal dialysis circuit that may result in leukostasis in small pulmonary vessels and reduced gas exchange. We think that the subsequent increase in SaO2 may be attributed to ultrafiltration, which alleviates pulmonary congestion and improves oxygen exchange. Whether and to what extent these observations correlate with adverse clinical outcomes warrants further investigation. Real time analysis of continuously measured physiological parameters may provide valuable insights into dialysis pathophysiology.

title: #2910 Changes in quality of life and caregiver burden after starting peritoneal dialysis: first results from the SKIP-SH cohort study
authors: Christopher Göing; Sarah-Yasmin Thomsen; Anneke Dubbeldam; Friedrich von Samson-Himmelstjerna; Jakob Voran; Roland Schmitt; Kevin Schulte; Benedikt Kolbrink
abstract:
Background and Aims
Peritoneal dialysis (PD) is a safe, resource-saving and cost-effective dialysis procedure that offers many patients a better quality of life than hemodialysis (HD). The technical ease with which the procedure can be carried out at home is particularly advantageous. Nevertheless, psychosocial factors and the burden of the therapy are among the most common factors for dropout from PD. It can be assumed that the burden on family caregivers also plays a role here. However, there is no data on the burden on family caregivers after the start of a relative’s PD. Here, we report on the quality of life of new PD patients and the burden on their family caregivers after the onset of PD.
Method
We present here first results from the Intersectoral Coordination Unit for the Sustainable Intensification of Peritoneal Dialysis in Schleswig–Holstein (SKIP-SH) cohort study (study protocol published earlier, PMID: 38429741). In brief, the SKIP-SH cohort study is a prospective cohort study that enrolls people with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) and their relatives and follows them after the initiation of dialysis to generate data to strengthen the use of PD in Germany. Collected data includes demographic information and quality-of-life assessments of CKD patients and their caregivers, as well as medical history, clinical course and laboratory data of the CKD patients. To assess quality of life in CKD patients, we used the Kidney Disease Quality of Life Instrument (KDQOL)-36 survey. Caregiver Burden was assessed with the Burden Scale for Family Caregivers (BSFC). In the analyses presented here, we included all CKD patients and their caregivers who started PD during follow-up so far (either new or as a switch from HD). Available time points for follow up so far were baseline (“PD start”) and 3 and 6 months thereafter. Results are given as absolute numbers (%) and mean (±standard deviation).
Results
The analyses included 30 CKD patients starting PD at baseline, 14 of which (46.67%) were female with a mean age of 65.1 (+−12.5) years. Of these 30 patients, 17 (56.6%) initiated PD as first dialysis therapy and 13 switched to PD from HD. During 6 months of follow-up, 3 (10%) of the new PD patients died and 5 (16.7%) had to transfer to HD. The mean KDQOL-36 scores of the CKD patients starting PD for the scale “symptoms/problems” at baseline, 3, and 6 months were 74.9 (±19.5), 77.8 (±12.3) and 72.9 (±17.6), respectively. For the scale “effects of kidney disease”, the mean score was 62.3 (±20) at baseline, 66.0 (±14.5) after 3 months and 63.2 (±15.4) after 6 months. For the scale “burden of kidney disease”, the mean score at baseline was 48.0 (±26.1) at baseline, 51.7 (±18.6) after 3 months, and 47.7 (±21.9) after 6 months. For the scale “physical health”, the mean score at baseline was 37.3 (±11.3), 39.3 (±10.2) after 3 months, and 38.6 (±11.4) after 6 months. For the scale “mental health”, the mean score at baseline was 48.2 (±10.4), 48.2 (±10.3) after 3 months, and 47.8 (±9.5) after 6 months. In addition to the CKD patients, 13 of their family caregivers participated in the study, 7 (53.8%) of which were female with a mean age of 61.8 (±11.1) years. At baseline, the BSCF score had a mean of 32.8 (±13.9), 29.4 (±11.4) after 3 months, and 28.0 (±16.6) after 6 months.
Conclusion
After starting PD, the quality of life of patients improved in our cohort after 3 months as measured by an improvement in all scales in the KDQOL-36, but returned below baseline after 6 months. Contra intuitively, the burden for family caregivers was rather low and even decreased after their relatives started PD. It will be interesting to see whether a correlation between the burden for family caregivers and PD treatment duration and patient outcomes can be shown in the further follow-up.

title: #1037 Intradialytic exercise modulates vascular biomarkers in CKD: implications for cardiovascular health in hemodiafiltration patients
authors: Maria Fernanda Garza Romero; Rashidi Springall del Villar; Claudia Lerma; Alfredo Fuentes Mercado; Erika Elizabeth Jaime Borja; Julieta Lara Díaz; Freddy Correa-Estrada; Salvador Lopez Gil
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiovascular outcomes are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in patients undergoing kidney replacement therapy. Vascular biomarkers such as Endothelin-1 (ET-1), Angiotensin II (Ang II), and Angiotensin 1–7 (Ang 1–7) are closely linked to the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and endothelial function, both of which are affected by fluid overload, fluid removal, and exercise. This study aimed to analyze the impact of intradialytic exercise on the levels and behavior of ET-1, Ang II, and Ang 1–7 in patients undergoing hemodiafiltration (HDF).
Method
This experimental study included 20 patients on HDF across three phases: a baseline phase (no controlled physical activity), a 4-month non-exercise phase, and a 3-month controlled aerobic exercise phase (90 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise during dialysis). Biomarkers (ET-1, Ang II, Ang 1–7) were measured at 0, 60, 120, and 180 minutes of each session. Linear mixed models were applied to evaluate each biomarker’s response across phases and times, adjusting for covariates and incorporating random intercepts to account for inter-patient variability. Trends over time within each phase were assessed, and interaction terms were included to evaluate differential responses across phases and times.
Results
ET-1 levels significantly decreased following exercise (β =−3.04, 95% CI [−3.93, −2.15], P < 0.001) and showed a smaller reduction in the non-exercise phase (β = −1.23, 95% CI [−2.12, −0.34], P = 0.008). Predicted trends of ET-1 across phases and times are shown in Fig. 1, illustrating the consistent reduction during exercise sessions. For Ang II, exercise reduced levels (β = −184.19, 95% CI [−256.49, −111.89], P < 0.001), with a similar effect in the non-exercise phase (β = −173.32, 95% CI [−245.89, −100.74], P < 0.001). Ang 1−7 levels increased following exercise (β = 32.70, 95% CI [7.39, 58.01], P = 0.012), while ultrafiltration rates were negatively associated (β = −0.015, 95% CI [−0.025, −0.006], P = 0.002). Notably, biomarker trends differed significantly across sessions (P < 0.001), with a linear stabilization of Ang II levels during post-exercise sessions. These predicted trends for Ang II and Ang 1−7 are shown in Fig. 2.
Conclusion
Intradialytic exercise significantly reduces ET-1 and Ang II while increasing Ang 1−7 in HDF patients, also stabilizing Ang II levels and mitigating fluctuations seen in non-exercise phases. Ultrafiltration independently affects Ang II and Ang 1−7 dynamics, reinforcing the need for precise fluid management. The observed biomarker reductions in both exercise and non-exercise phases suggest potential systemic adaptations to chronic HDF, warranting further investigation.

title: #2381 Modifiable factors associated with permanent transfers from peritoneal dialysis: a retrospective study
authors: Carolina Lentisco; Yeilyn Sotolongo; Sara El Fellah; Santiago Cedeño; Maria Sanchez; Milagros Ortiz Librero; Carmen Mon Mon; Mariano Acuña; Irene Galindo Marín; Juan Carlos Herrero
abstract:
Background and Aims
Improving the long-term survival of peritoneal dialysis (PD) remains a significant challenge. This study aims to identify modifiable causes and risk factors associated with permanent transfers from PD, focusing on technique-related and unrelated factors to understand preventable complications and improve outcomes.
Method
This retrospective observational study included permanent PD transfers between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2023. Data included epidemiological factors (age, sex, comorbidities, Charlson comorbidity index), clinical factors (renal replacement duration, advanced chronic kidney disease [ACKD] follow-up), and hospitalizations. Technique-related variables included peritonitis episodes, tunnel infections, ultrafiltration failure (UFF), abdominal complications (leaks, hernias), peritoneal breaks, time to transfer, and transfer reasons. Analytical parameters (albumin, hemoglobin, C-reactive protein [CRP], ferritin), glucose load, adequacy parameters, BMI, and residual diuresis at transfer were analyzed. Post-transfer mortality and causes of death were recorded. Patients from 2010–2016 and 2017–2023 were compared.
Results
We analyzed 89 cases (67.4% male, 8% with ADPKD, 8% with peripheral arterial disease, 6.7% ischemic heart disease, 12.4% with heart failure). Median Charlson index was 4 (IQR 2.5–6), and median PD duration to transfervwas 16 months (IQR 7–31.5). Technique-related hospitalizations occurred in 22% of patients, while non-technique-related hospitalizations occurred in 37%. At transfer, 31% were on CAPD, 12% on NIPD, 29% on CCPD, and 20% on OCPD, with a mean glucose load of 23 ± 12 grams. Mean age was 56 ± 16 years, and 26% had a BMI ≥30. 19% were anuric, and 27% had residual diuresis >1000 mL.
Causes of transfer included transplantation (40%), technique-related issues (46%), death (4%), and unrelated factors (7%). Technique-related causes were peritonitis (27%), inadequate clearance (24%), UFF (22%), abdominal complications (14%), and catheter malfunction (3%). Unrelated causes included patient fatigue (43%), ischemic events (28%), acute infections (14%), and renal function recovery (14%).
Post-transfer mortality was in 24 patients, with a median survival of 34 months (IQR 3–48) and 8% dying within the first year. Peritoneal breaks were associated with transfer in 13 of 19 cases (P = 0.03). Leaks or hernias led to transfer in 14 of 21 patients (P = 0.05). Among patients with BMI ≥30, 18 of 23 were transferred due to inadequate clearance (P = 0.05). ADPKD patients showed higher leak/hernia rates (71%) versus those without ADPKD (20%, P = 0.01). In the UFF subgroup, 66.7% retained residual diuresis >1000 mL. Patients from 2017–2023 were older at transfer (61 ± 16 vs. 51 ± 16, P = 0.01), had higher Charlson indices (P > 0.05), longer ACKD follow-up (40 vs. 20 months, P = 0.01), more frequent abdominal wall complications (34% vs. 10%, P = 0.01), and more frequent peritoneal breaks (32% vs. 8%, P = 0.01).
Conclusion
Approximately 10% of PD transfers were due to reversible causes like abdominal complications and catheter malfunctions. Transfer due to inadequate clearance was associated with BMI ≥30 but not anuria. In UFF cases, 66.7% retained residual diuresis >1000 mL. Peritoneal breaks were significantly linked to PD transfer. Identifying and addressing modifiable factors may improve PD outcomes and reduce transfer rates.

title: #2579 Impact of haemodialysis timing before kidney transplant surgery on early postoperative outcomes
authors: Guillaume Fernandes; Christophe De Terwangne; Nada Kanaan; Tom Darius; Antoine Buémi; Eric Jean Goffin; Michel Jadoul; Laura Labriola; Arnaud Devresse
abstract:
Background and Aims
Mortality in patients with kidney failure on maintenance haemodialysis (HD) is higher after the long inter-dialytic interval, probably from fluid overload and electrolyte disturbances. In HD patients, the optimal timing of a HD session before surgery is unknown. Surgery induces cardiovascular stress and may trigger cardiac events in fluid overloaded or hyperkalemic patients if the interval between the last HD and the intervention is too long. However, a shorter interval might on the contrary increase bleeding risk due to recent anticoagulation. Whether a shorter or longer interval between the last HD session and surgery impacts early post-transplant outcomes has not been investigated yet. In this study, we evaluate the effect of the timing of the last HD session on the occurrence of delayed graft function and the need for early surgical revision in chronic haemodialysis patients receiving a kidney allograft.
Method
In this retrospective monocentric study, we included all adult patients on maintenance HD who received a deceased donor kidney transplant in our centre between 01/01/2015 and 31/12/2022. Patients with no retrievable information regarding the last HD session and multiorgan transplants were excluded. Baseline characteristics (Table 1), data regarding the last dialysis session before transplant surgery (anticoagulation regimen, ultrafiltration volume, haemodialysis modality, dry weight) and transplantation data (date of transplantation, ischemia time, induction therapy) were collected. The timing between the last dialysis and transplantation was defined as the time between the start of the last HD session and anaesthetic induction for kidney transplant. Patients were divided into a “short” (<24h) and “long" (≥24h) interval based on this delay. The primary outcome was a composite of the occurrence of delayed graft function (as defined by the need for dialysis within the first 7 days after kidney transplantation) or surgical revision within the same hospital stay.
Results
202 patients were included, 87 in the “short” and 115 in the “long” group. Baseline characteristics were similar with a median age at transplantation of 55 y. Data regarding transplantation (cold ischemia time (11.4 vs 12.5 hours), donor type (DBD = 71 vs 72%), induction regimen (including plasmapheresis = 21% in both groups), mean peak historic virtual PRA, cardiovascular (25% vs 31%) and diabetes history (20 vs 22%) were similar between the two groups. The median time between the last HD session and transplant surgery was 9 and 35 hours in the “short” and “long” group respectively. In the “short” group, anticoagulation regimen consisted mainly of unfractionated heparin (57%) while some patients did not receive any anticoagulant (13%). Low molecular weight heparin was used in the majority of patients in the “long” group (87%). There was no primary non function in both groups. The primary outcome occurred in 38% of patients in the “short" versus 23% in the “long” group (p-value = 0.02). This was mainly driven by the need for surgical revision (18% vs 8%; p-value = 0.03). The difference in DGF between the two groups was not significant (28% vs 20%; p-value = 0.18) (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
In maintenance HD patients, the timing between the last HD session and transplant surgery may impact postoperative outcomes. Patients dialyzed within the last 24 hours were at an increased risk of surgical revision compared to those dialyzed ≥24h before surgery, despite similar characteristics and the use of unfractionated heparin.

The primary outcome occurred in 38% of patients in the “short" versus 23% in the “long” group (p-value = 0.02). This was mainly driven by the need for surgical revision (18% vs 8%; p-value = 0.03). The difference in DGF between the two groups was not significant (28% vs 20%; p-value = 0.18) (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
In maintenance HD patients, the timing between the last HD session and transplant surgery may impact postoperative outcomes. Patients dialyzed within the last 24 hours were at an increased risk of surgical revision compared to those dialyzed ≥24h before surgery, despite similar characteristics and the use of unfractionated heparin.

title: #3295 Antibacterial and anticoagulant strategies on catheter surfaces for preventing catheter-related bloodstream infection and catheter thrombosis during hemodialysis
authors: Peiyun Li; Ling Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Catheter-related bloodstream infection (CRBSI) and catheter thrombosis are the most critical issues that need to be addressed in patients undergoing hemodialysis. Currently, we have developed a coating that can formulate nano-copper and heparin into an effective antimicrobial and anticoagulant agent.
Method
This method employs a one-pot synthesis using dopamine, which is simple and convenient. The nano-copper coating is prepared through dopamine reduction and further stabilized by polyethylenimine (PEI) to enhance the coating’s stability, antibacterial properties, and grafting amount of heparin (Fig. 1).
Results
The characterization of the PDA@Cu@PEI@Heparin coating (Scanning Electron Microscopy Image, Atomic Force Microscopy, Surface Zeta Potential) is shown in Fig. 2. In this material, the presence of monovalent copper (Cu⁺) plays a strong antibacterial role (Fig. 3). Compared with the previously prepared PDA@Cu@Heparin coating, it shows significant improvements in stability, antibacterial properties, and anticoagulant effects (Figs 4, 5, 6). The PDA@Cu@PEI@Heparin coating also demonstrates good blood compatibility (Fig. 7).
Conclusion
This coating holds great promise for preventing CRBSI and catheter thrombosis in hemodialysis.

title: #2893 The Emboless® venous chamber extensively reduce air contamination passing into HD patients blood
authors: Ulf Forsberg; Per Jonsson; Bernd Stegmayr
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hemodialysis (HD) is a life sustaining treatment for patients with end-stage renal failure, and ongoing efforts aim to enhance both its efficiency and safety. In terms of safety, the precautionary principle has been applied. The quality of the water used in dialysis and the biocompatibility of dialysis filters has been significantly improved, while prevention of air contamination of the bloodline lacks behind. Dialysis machines are equipped with air detectors that shall trigger alarms if larger amounts of air enter the venous side. However, air bubbles larger than 500 µm diameter can bypass these detectors without activating alarms. Air is foreign to the bloodstream and contains inert gases, which can cause severe complications such as emboli and tissue damage, confirmed by case reports and autopsy studies. No data exist of the air volumes contaminating the blood during regular HD and difference in air elimination.
The objective of this interventional clinical study was to ascertain whether the elimination of air entering the patients can be more efficacious.
Method
Twenty chronic HD patients participated in a randomized cross-over study comparing the Emboless® and F5008 venous chambers. Each patient underwent four dialysis sessions divided into two paired series, resulting in 80 analysed sessions. The same dialyzers, blood pump speeds, HD settings, and ultrafiltration parameters were used within each pair.
The cumulative volumes of air bubbles (>20 µm in diameter) were measured at the inlet and outlet line of each venous chamber using an adapted ultrasound device (BCC200, GAMPT). The measurement duration was 30 minutes, extended if fewer than 1000 detections were recorded at the Inlet. The percentage of air volume passing through the venous chamber and reaching the patient was calculated (Mann–Whitney U-test).
Results
The median air Inlet volume of 80 dialyses was 20.5 µL (IQR 12.2–38.4 µL), with no significant difference in air inflow between the two venous chambers. The median proportion of volumes of air leakage passing to the patient was lower with the Emboless® (8.7%) compared to the F5008 chamber (25.9%) (P < 0.001, Fig. 1).
Conclusion
The Emboless® venous chamber is the preferred choice for minimizing potentially harmful air contamination during hemodialysis. Air leakage to patients was reduced to one-third when using the Emboless® compared to the F5008 venous chamber, making it a safer option for clinical use.

title: #3577 Peritoneal infusion of microplastics induces over-expression of GDF-15 in kidney and heart in mice
authors: Edoardo La Porta; Daniela Verzola; Pasquale Esposito; Francesca Viazzi; Paolo Cravedi; Enrico Eugenio Verrina
abstract:
Background and Aims
There is growing concern regarding the potential impact of microplastics (MPs) on human health. Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) undergoing peritoneal dialysis may be particularly vulnerable to exposure to these particles. Recent findings have demonstrated the presence of microplastics in human urine and kidney tissue, highlighting the potential toxicity of these substances. In light of these concerns, we aimed to investigate the effects of microplastics on kidney and heart tissues, with a particular focus on the expression of GDF-15.
GDF-15 (growth differentiation factor 15) is a cytokine involved in various biological processes, including the inhibition of apoptosis and the modulation of inflammation under several pathological conditions. As a member of the TGF-beta family, GDF-15 is expressed in numerous tissues and plays a key role in oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Elevated levels of GDF-15 have been associated with an increased risk of mortality, the onset of CKD, and its progression in individuals with renal impairment. In a recent proteomic study (data not yet published), we identified GDF-15 as a potential biomarker for microplastic exposure in kidney tubular cells.
Method
Eight-week-old male BL/6 mice were housed in standard cages with ad libitum access to chow and water. Green Fluorescent Polymer Microspheres (FMG, maximum excitation wavelength 515 nm), with a diameter range of 1–5 μm, were purchased from Cospheric LLC (Santa Barbara, USA).
The mice were administered 0.25 mg of FMG, diluted in deionized water (total volume of 150 μl), via intraperitoneal injection. This treatment was repeated three times a week for a duration of four weeks. No acute adverse effects were observed following the administrations. Urine samples were collected at various time points until sacrifice. Mice that received FMG treatment, along with one untreated control mouse, were sacrificed 30 days after the first dose to collect blood serum, and kidney, heart, liver, and spleen tissues. Immunohistochemical staining for GDF-15 was performed on kidney and heart tissue sections.
Results
Our analysis revealed the deposition of microplastics in both kidney and heart tissues following peritoneal administration. GDF-15 expression was significantly increased in the heart (P = 0.02) and kidney (P < 0.0001) tissues (Figs 1 and 2).
Conclusion
Our findings demonstrate that microplastics, when administered via the peritoneal route, are detectable in target organs such as the kidney and heart. Furthermore, exposure to microplastics leads to a significant overexpression of GDF-15, a cytokine that may serve as a potential biomarker for inflammation in these tissues. This study provides valuable insights into the toxicological effects of microplastic exposure on organ systems and underscores the need for further investigation into the role of GDF-15 as a potential marker of exposure-related inflammation.
