title: #1951 Prediction of BK Polyomavirus associated nephropathy by the NEPHROVIR method in kidney transplant recipients with BK Polyomavirus-DNAemia
authors: Manon Dekeyser; Marie-Ghislaine de Goër de Herve; Houria Hendel-Chavez; Karen Bargiel; Florence Herr; Yassine Taoufik; Antoine Durrbach
abstract:
Background and Aims
BK Polyomavirus (BKPyV) remains a significant complication after kidney transplantation. Due to BKPyV intra-graft replication, biopsy-proven BKPyV-associated nephropathy (BKPyVAN) affects nearly 10% of patients and causes graft loss in more than 50% of cases. Impaired BKPyV-specific T cell response plays a crucial role in the BKPyVAN pathophysiology. Several teams, including ours, have demonstrated a profound impairment of BKPyV-specific T cells during BKPyVAN. Immunovirological monitoring allows an individual assessment of viral reactivation risk based on the anti-viral immune response.
Method
To assess the risk of BKPyVAN occurrence, our group has developed the NEPHROVIR method. This non-invasive biological method is based on the innovative combination of biomarkers, including BKPyV load, BKPyV-specific T cell response, and histocompatibility between donor and kidney graft recipient.
Results
In our proof-of-concept, the NEPHROVIR method allows the identification of 3 BKPyVAN risk levels: low, intermediate, and high. Based on the assessment of 27 kidney transplant recipients (KTRs) with sustained BKPyV-DNAemia, KTRs with a weak combination of immuno-virological and immuno-genetic parameters (n = 9, 33%) were all patients with biopsy-proven BKPyVAN (lower left-hand quadrant). Conversely, KTRs with a potent combination of immuno-virological and immuno-genetic parameters (n = 7, 26%) had sustained BKPyV-DNAemia without biopsy-proven BKPyVAN (upper right-hand quadrant). The figure below shows the BKPyVAN risk stratification index obtained from the NEPHROVIR method, with associated test performance.
Conclusion
The NEPHROVIR method is an innovative immunovirological surveillance method for predicting the risk of biopsy-proven BKPyVAN occurrence. Characterizing individual BKPyVAN risk levels could help in the individualized follow-up and management of immunosuppression in KTRs. The long-term objective would be to diagnose very early, or even anticipate, the occurrence of BKPyV-DNAemia and to allow early readjustment of the immunosuppressive treatment.

title: #2080 Living kidney donation practices in Europe: a survey of DESCaRTES and EKITA transplantation working groups
authors: Marco van Londen; François Gaillard; Gianluigi Zaza; Gabriel Oniscu; Ilaria Gandolfini; Lucrezia Furian; Jelena Stojanovic; David Cucchiari; Luuk Hilbrands; Geir Mjøen; Christophe Mariat
abstract:
Background and Aims
Thorough evaluation of potential kidney donors (LKDs) ensures safety and graft quality, but European data on LKD-practices are lacking.
Method
An online survey was conducted to assess LKD practices across Europe, focusing on kidney function measurement, risk assessment and follow-up. Responses were received from 125 transplant practitioners in 16 countries, collectively performing ∼3700 LKD transplantations annually.
Results
For kidney function assessment, 56% of centers use eGFRCKD-EPI, 34% use 24-hour creatinine clearance and 70% use measured GFR. Sixty-four percent use age-dependent GFR-thresholds. Sixty-three percent of centers do not impose upper age limits, 91% exclude LKD candidates with hypertension with end-organ damage, and 78% candidates on ≥2 antihypertensives. BMI cut-offs of 30 kg/m2 (39%) and 35 kg/m2 (42%) are common. Candidates are often excluded for a HbA1c ≥53 mmol/mol (46%), fasting glucose ≥7 mmol/L (57%) or glucose after glucose-tolerance test ≥11.1 mmol/L (59%). ApoL1-testing is not routine in 73% of centers, and 38% perform a kidney biopsy if albuminuria/hematuria is present. Albuminuria testing includes both spot and 24-hour urine tests in 38%. Persistent microscopic hematuria is accepted when urological evaluation (15%), kidney biopsy (16%) or both (57%) are normal. Low-risk stones often do not preclude donation. Written informed consent is obtained by 95% of centers, with 65% asking consent for data usage. Lifetime follow-up is offered by 83% of centers.
Conclusion
This first study on practices in the evaluation, selection and follow-up of LDKs in Europe, shows significant variation between centers, suggesting a need for harmonization of donor practices.

title: #1473 Single vs. repeated measurements of 24-hour urinary potassium excretion and long-term outcomes after kidney transplantation
authors: Caspar van Lieshout; Liffert Vogt; Stephan J L Bakker; Martin H de Borst
abstract:
Background and Aims
Low potassium intake is common in kidney transplantation recipients (KTRs). Previous cohort studies suggested that low potassium intake is associated with an increased risk of death-censored graft failure (DCGF) and all-cause mortality. However, these studies estimated potassium intake using single 24-hour urinary potassium excretion (UKV) measurements. Because potassium excretion is highly variable over time, baseline UKV may inaccurately represent long-term potassium intake. Therefore, we aimed to investigate whether using single baseline vs. repeated UKV measurements to estimate potassium intake impacts the association between estimated potassium intake and outcomes after kidney transplantation.
Method
We performed a retrospective analysis of a single-center cohort, consisting of KTRs with available outpatient clinic 24 h UKV measurements collected between 1980 and 2016. To control for potential urine collection errors, we removed the 5% of measurements with the largest difference between expected and collected 24 h urine volumes. Baseline potassium intake was estimated from each participant's first available outpatient clinic UKV measurement after transplantation. Long-term potassium intake was estimated using a time-weighted average of all available UKV measurements. Co-primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and death-censored graft failure. Statistical analysis consisted of Cox regression analyses adjusted for sex, age, BMI, smoking, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, number of antihypertensives, eGFR, proteinuria, and urinary sodium and urea excretion. Models with time-weighted potassium intake also included time-weighted averages of urinary sodium excretion.
Results
The cohort consisted of 1478 KTRs (mean age 44.7 ± 13.6 yr, 44.6% male) with a total of 10,418 twenty-four-hour urine samples (median 3 [IQR 2–8] samples per person. In the study population, mean potassium intake was similar when using baseline (3.47 ± 1.34 g/d) and time-averaged UKV (3.53 ± 1.30 g/d; Fig. 1). During a median follow-up of 13.8 [IQR 7.7–20.8] yr, 732 (49.5%) patients died and 395 (26.7%) developed DCGF. After adjustment for potential confounders, a higher time-averaged potassium-intake was associated with a significantly lower risk of graft failure (HR 0.76 [95% CI 0.64–0.90], P = 0.0015; Table 1), while a single baseline UKV was not (HR 0.90 [0.77–1.05], P = 0.17). Similarly, a higher time-averaged potassium intake was associated with a significantly lower risk of all-cause mortality (HR 0.83 [0.74–0.93], P = 0.0019), while a single baseline UKV was not (HR 0.91 [0.81–1.02], P = 0.11).
Conclusion
Higher long-term potassium intake after transplantation was associated with a reduced risk of graft failure and all-cause mortality. Conversely, a single estimation of potassium intake was not associated with outcomes. These results stress that preferably, repeated 24 h urine collections should be used to adequately assess the relationship between potassium intake and clinical outcomes.

title: #2741 Predicting graft outcomes in kidney transplantation: the strength of standard statistics compared to machine learning techniques
authors: Carolina Salgado; Francisca Gonzalez-Cohens; Felipe Vera Cid; Fernando Gonzalez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Over the last decade, the use of machine learning (ML) techniques in problem modeling and solving has increased significantly, including in kidney transplantation. Numerous studies have used ML to predict outcomes such as delayed graft function (DGF). This study compares various ML models with logistic regression (LR) in predicting DGF, focusing on donor characteristics.
Method
We analyzed 831 deceased donor kidney transplants performed between 1989 and 2020 across three transplant centers. The dataset included 14 donor, 7 transplant, and 60 recipient features. Four problem types were defined based on variable combinations: donor-only (D), donor + transplant (DT), donor + recipient (DR), and donor + transplant + recipient (DTR).
The dataset comprised 44.7% DGF-positive and 55.3% DGF-negative patients, split into 80% for training and 20% for validation/testing. Six ML models—Support Vector Machine (SVM), Decision Trees (DET), Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boost (GB), Extreme Gradient Boost (XGB), and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)—were compared with LR. Hyperparameters were optimized using Random Search and 10-fold Cross Validation. Accuracy was the primary performance metric.
Results
The best-performing model for each problem type achieved accuracies of 55% (SVM), 58% (XGB), 58% (RF), and 64% (XGB) respectively for D, DT, DR, and DTR. LR results were 47%, 62%, 55% and 60%. Across most models, significant predictors included donor creatinine and age, cold and warm ischemia times (transplant variables), and recipient calcium levels.
Conclusion
While most ML models outperformed LR, the differences were not substantial. This may be attributed to the small dataset size, which likely contributed to the overall poor performance. We recommend using these complex models with high-quality datasets that include a sufficient number of variables and observations to fully leverage their potential. The key question for future research is determining the dataset size required for ML to become the primary analytic tool for predicting kidney transplant outcomes.

title: #3526 Identifying risk factors for sedentarism in kidney transplatation
authors: Blanca Serrano Muñoz; Marta Alonso Mozo; Florentino Villanego; José Manuel Amaro; Arshdeep Singh; Ana Maria Gomez Romero; Luis Alberto Vigara; Cristhian David Orellana Chávez; Teresa María García Álvarez; Auxiliadora Mazuecos
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is linked to increased sedentary behavior, with dialysis patients being particularly vulnerable. Although physical activity generally improves following kidney transplantation (KT), it does not reach the levels seen in the general population, which may negatively affect patient outcomes and graft survival. The study aimed to identify factors contributing to low physical activity in KT recipients.
Method
A cross-sectional descriptive study was conducted with KT patients at our center, sampled during follow-up consultations between November 2023 and December 2024. Participants who agreed to complete the "Human Activity Profile (HAP)" questionnaire, which assesses the level of physical activity, were included. Exclusion criteria included severe physical limitations or comorbidities that contraindicated physical exercise. Based on their Adjusted Activity Score (AAS), patients were classified as sedentary (<53 points), moderately active (54–73 points), or active (>74 points). Clinical and demographic data were collected, and comparisons between groups were made. Multinomial logistic regression was used to identify risk factors for low physical activity.
Results
Ninety-two KT recipients were included, with a mean age of 61 ± 12 years and a median of 18 months post-KT. Hypertension was present in 95.7% of them, and diabetes mellitus in 41.3%. The most common primary cause of CKD was glomerular (31.5%). Active patients had a shorter cold ischemia time than sedentary or moderately active patients (P = 0.025). Sedentary patients had a higher number of HLA incompatibilities (P = 0.030) and prior hospitalizations (P = 0.045). In terms of demographics, sedentary patients were significantly older than the other groups (66.9 years vs. 62.45 and 53.32 years, respectively; P < 0.001). No significant differences were found regarding estimated glomerular filtration rate, body mass index, left ventricular ejection fraction, hemoglobin, or the presence of diabetes as a cause of CKD. The multinomial logistic regression revealed that age and the number of prior hospitalizations were significant risk factors for sedentary behavior (HR: 1.12; P = 0.001 and HR: 1.99; P = 0.016), while a longer post-transplant time was a protective factor (HR: 0.966; P = 0.025).
Conclusion
This study highlights that KT patients in the earlier post-transplant period, older age, and a higher number of hospitalizations are more likely to exhibit sedentary behavior. Targeting these factors with early interventions and incorporating patients into physical rehabilitation programs could improve quality of life and optimize KT outcomes.

title: #3395 Plasma cadmium, whole-blood cadmium and late graft failure in kidney transplant recipients
authors: Pien Rawee; Martin H de Borst; Daan J Touw; Stephan J L Bakker; Michele F Eisenga
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cadmium is a nephrotoxic heavy metal associated with adverse kidney outcomes, including graft failure in kidney transplant recipients (KTRs)[1]. Whole-blood cadmium levels are commonly used for biomonitoring, but plasma cadmium may more accurately reflect the kidney cadmium burden, as it better represents the portion filtered by the kidneys. This study aims to investigate the difference between cadmium levels in KTRs compared to healthy donors and examine the associations of plasma and whole-blood cadmium with graft failure in KTRs.
Method
Data were used from the ongoing Transplantlines Biobank and Cohort study, which includes KTRs from the University Medical Center Groningen. Cadmium levels were measured at 6 months, 1 year, and 2 years post-transplantation in KTRs and at screening in donors. Plasma and whole-blood cadmium were quantified using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. Spearman's correlation was used to assess the relationship between plasma and whole-blood cadmium separately at different time points. Mixed models were used to compare cadmium levels between KTRs and donors to account for repeated measures in KTRs. Cox regression with time-varying covariates assessed associations of log-transformed and standardized cadmium levels with death-censored graft failure (DCGF), adjusting for sex, age, body mass index, smoking, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), proteinuria, systolic blood pressure, hemoglobin, and donor type.
Results
The study included 444 KTRs (mean age 56 ± 14 years, 64% males and mean eGFR 50 ± 22 ml/min/1.73 m2 at 6 months after transplantation) with in total 688 plasma and whole-blood cadmium measurements available and 483 donors with cadmium measurement at screening (mean age 57 ± 11 years, 45% males, mean eGFR 89 ± 20 ml/min/1.73 m2). Median plasma cadmium levels were higher in KTRs (0.037 µg/L [IQR: 0.021–0.051]) than in donors (0.009 µg/L [IQR: 0.005–0.013], P < 0.001). Whole-blood cadmium was also higher in KTRs (0.56 µg/L [IQR: 0.37–0.84]) than in donors (0.27 µg/L [IQR: 0.18–0.46], P < 0.001). Plasma cadmium was strongly correlated with whole-blood cadmium in KTRs (6 months: r = 0.83; 1 year: r = 0.66; 2 years: r = 0.62) and donors (r = 0.78). During a median follow-up of 6.3 [IQR: 5.1–7.7] years, 87 KTRs developed DCGF. Plasma cadmium (HR = 1.45 [95% CI 1.11–1.90], P = 0.006) and whole-blood cadmium (HR = 1.41 [95% CI 1.08–1.84], P = 0.01) were both associated with DCGF independent of sex, age, body mass index, smoking, eGFR, proteinuria, systolic blood pressure, hemoglobin, and donor type.
Conclusion
KTRs have significantly higher cadmium levels compared to healthy donors. Plasma and whole-blood cadmium levels are both independently associated with graft failure. These findings highlight the clinical relevance of kidney cadmium burden in KTRs.

title: #2731 Legacy effect of pretransplant immunosuppression in kidney transplant recipients with crescentic glomerulonephritis
authors: Jasper Callemeyn; Annemarie Weissenbacher; Andreas Kronbichler
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney transplant recipients with crescentic glomerulonephritis, including ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV-GN) and anti-glomerular basement disease (GBM-GN), have often received an important burden of immunosuppression before transplantation. It is unclear what effect this pretransplant immunosuppression has on immunological outcomes, such as rejection or relapse, and the risk of infection or malignancy.
Method
In a single-center cohort study of 2978 transplantations that were performed between 2000 and 2023, post-transplant outcomes of transplant recipients with underlying AAV-GN or GBM-GN were compared with a matched control group, adjusting for recipient age and gender, transplant year, previous kidney transplantation and dialysis vintage.
Results
During the study period, 21 recipients with AAV-GN and 25 recipients with GBM-GN received a kidney transplant. Compared to the matched control group (n = 92), no differences were found in the incidence of graft loss (hazard ratio for graft loss 1.6, 95% CI 0.80–3.25) or rejection. Relapse after transplantation occurred in 3/21 patients with AAV-GN and none of the patients with GBM-GN. Severe infections requiring hospitalization occurred more frequently in the AAV-GN and GBM-GN group (HR 1.98 compared to the control group, 95% CI 1.18–3.30, Fig. 1). Similarly, an increased risk for malignancy was found (HR 2.17, 95% CI 1.04–4.55, Fig. 1).
Conclusion
Kidney transplant recipients with underlying crescentic glomerulonephritis are at an increased risk for infection and malignancy. These data suggest that pretransplant immunosuppression exerts an important legacy effect after transplantation, highlighting the need for immunosurveillance and personalized treatment in these patients.

title: #2157 Post-transplant metabolomics: early prediction of renal function and possible therapeutic target discovery
authors: Iris Viejo-Boyano; María Peris-Fernández; Marta Isabel Roca-Marugán; Angel Balaguer-Timor; Julian Luis Amengual-Roig; Pablo González-Calero; Anna Ferri Cortes; Manel Gavila Chornet; Mar Mompó-Ramos; Francisco Marqués Ortega; Isabel Beneyto; Julio Hernandez Jaras
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney transplantation (KT) is the therapy of choice for patients with advanced chronic kidney disease; however, predicting graft outcomes and improving clinical results remain challenging.
Early identification of reliable biomarkers could improve clinical care, which can be achieved through metabolomic analysis. This study employed a semi-targeted metabolomic approach, combining the advantages of targeted and untargeted strategies to identify specific metabolites and discover novel compounds. This study aimed to identify metabolomic biomarkers within the first week after KT that could predict renal function at six months and explore potential therapeutic targets.
Method
We conducted a prospective, observational, single-center study including 50 adult patients who received a deceased donor kidney transplant. Plasma samples were collected one week post-transplant and analyzed using Ultra-Performance Liquid Chromatography (UPLC) coupled to a Q-Exactive Plus mass spectrometer, following a semi-targeted metabolomic approach. Metabolomic data from 48 patients were statistically analyzed using Partial Least Squares-Discriminant Analysis (PLS-DA) to identify metabolic profiles associated with renal function at six months. Patients were categorized into two groups based on serum creatinine levels: ≥1.5 mg/dL and <1.5 mg/dL. Model performance was assessed using Variable Importance in Projection (VIP) scores, with the optimal number of latent variables determined through Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV). Additionally, permutation testing (1000 iterations) was performed.
Results
The study population had a mean age of 53.98 years, predominantly male (70%) and Caucasian (94%). Hypertension (82%), dyslipidemia (70%), and obesity (28%) were the most prevalent comorbidities. The majority of donors were from donation after brain death (DBD) (58%), while 42% were from donation after circulatory death (DCD), with a mean cold ischemia time of 17.30 hours.
The semi-targeted metabolomic analysis identified 226 polar metabolites in plasma samples collected one week post-transplant. A PLS-DA model, optimized using VIP scores >1.5 demonstrated strong predictive performance (AUC: 0.958, accuracy: 87.5%, sensitivity: 86.4%, specificity: 88.5%). Twelve metabolites contributed the most to the differentiation between patients with serum creatinine levels ≥1.5 mg/dL and <1.5 mg/dL at six months post-transplant.
Metabolites associated with better graft function (serum creatinine <1.5 mg/dL) included 3-methylindole (skatole), guaiacol, histidine, 3-indolepropionic acid, and α-lipoic acid. These compounds are known for their antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and gut microbiota-modulating properties. Conversely, metabolites associated with impaired graft function (serum creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL), suggesting a potential link to poorer outcomes, were homocarnosine, 5-methylcytosine, xanthosine, choline, phenylalanine, kynurenic acid, and L-kynurenine. Notably, xanthosine, kynurenic acid, L-kynurenine, and choline have been previously identified as prognostic markers for chronic kidney disease progression in several studies, further supporting their relevance in post-transplant renal dysfunction. Several metabolites from the tryptophan metabolic pathway were identified, underscoring the critical role of tryptophan metabolism in post-transplant renal function and its potential as a therapeutic target.
Conclusion
Early metabolomic profiling following kidney transplantation appears to be a valuable tool for predicting renal function. The identification of metabolites with potential protective antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, alongside others associated with poorer outcomes that could serve as therapeutic targets, highlights their clinical relevance. The observed association of several metabolites with the tryptophan metabolic pathway emphasizes the need for further investigation into its role in post-transplant outcomes. These biomarkers hold promise for improving patient monitoring and optimizing long-term graft survival.

title: #3551 Posttransplant malignancies in kidney transplant recipients—a single center experience
authors: George Kurian; Rajesh R Nair; Anil Mathew; Zachariah Paul; Anjana Gopal
abstract:
Background and Aims
Post-transplant malignancy amongst kidney transplant recipients: a single centre 20-year experience and literature review.
Method
We analysed our data retrospectively which included 794 patients who underwent renal transplantation at our centre between January 2001 to February 2022. Patient's native kidney disease, donor details, duration on hemodialysis, immunosuppression details and duration till diagnosis of malignancies were collected. All details regarding the nature of the malignancy with detailed histopathology, staging, and treatment were also collected. We also did subgroup analysis of multiorgan, liver and hand transplant recipients.
Results
Of the total 816 cases of renal transplant recipients, 17 recipient (2.08%) were diagnosed with malignancy. Nine out of the 17 patients were males (52%). The mean age at diagnosis was 41 ± 10 years and mean duration of occurrence of malignancy following post transplant was 38 months. Nine patients (52%) developed solid organ tumour and 8 (47%) developed post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease. Of the nine cases of solid organ tumors, 4 had squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue followed by one case each of adenocarcinoma of the pancreas, squamous cell carcinoma of the lung and vulva. 2 patients had carcinoma of the colon, out of which one was post combined liver and kidney transplant. Seven out of 17 patients succumbed to their malignancy, a mortality rate of 41%. Of the eight cases of PTLD, 6 had expired (75%), making PTLD the most fatal post-transplant malignancy in our setting. Of the 794 post-kidney transplant cases reviewed in this single center retrospective study, the incidence of malignancy was 1.8 per 100 population. At our centre, there was a prevalence of PTLD as the major type of post-transplant malignancy, as compared to studies from other centers. PTLD being of poor prognosis, is responsible for a higher post-transplant mortality rate in our population. The most aggressive histopathological variant of PTLD (monomorphous variant) was common in our cohort. This may represent either an ethnic predisposition to this disease or some environmental or immunological risk factors contributing to it occurrence.
Conclusion
This study points out the need for meticulous surveillance of all post-transplant cases for malignancy considering the associated high rate of mortality.

title: #3336 Prolonged functional warm ischaemia is associated with metabolic and protease dysregulation in DCD kidneys
authors: Rebecca Vaughan; Sarah Fawaz; Rutger Ploeg; Philip Charles; Maria Kaisar
abstract:
Background and Aims
Functional warm ischaemia (fWIT)—the period after the donors’ blood pressure drops below 50 mmHg following withdrawal of life support until organ cold perfusion—is an inherent part of the donation after circulatory death (DCD) pathway. Causing organ hypoperfusion and cellular energy depletion, fWIT triggers a cascade of ischaemic injury, which is associated with increased incidence of delayed graft function following DCD kidney transplant. Ischaemia causes metabolic dysregulation and disruption to cellular homeostasis, which induces morphological changes and protease dysregulation, contributing to kidney injury. However, the mechanisms of injury associated with fWIT are yet to be described.
To address this gap, this study used specialised proteomic techniques coupled with bioinformatics to investigate changes in endogenous peptide abundance and protease activity associated with prolonged fWIT.
Method
DCD kidney biopsies (n = 42) with short (<25 minutes) and long fWIT (30–107 minutes), obtained from the QUality in Organ Donation (QUOD) biobank were analysed using High-efficiency Undecanal-based N-Termini EnRichment (HUNTER) methods combined with bioinformatic methods. Degradation profiles and changes in protease abundance were further quantified using Western blotting, in both kidney tissue and immortalised podocytes and proximal tubule epithelial cells (PTECs) cultured under hypoxic and varying glucose conditions.
Results
Mass spectrometry analysis identified 2,563 endogenous peptides which were mapped to 1,022 distinct proteins. Of these, seven endogenous peptides—associated with proximal tubule injury, metabolic pathways, and the cytoskeleton—showed increased abundance as fWIT was prolonged (Fig. 1A). Pathway analysis of the mapped proteins revealed significant dysregulation in metabolic processes, particularly affecting glucose, lipid and vitamin metabolism.
Notably, the rate-limiting gluconeogenesis enzyme, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBP1), exhibited significant degradation with prolonged fWIT (Fragment 1 and Fragment 2; P = 0.0004, FDR 5%). Western blot analysis confirmed this result, showing marked increased in FBP1 degradation as fWIT increased (P = 0.0003) (Fig. 1B).
Protease activity was also significantly dysregulated as fWIT was prolonged (Fig. 1C). Legumain activity increased (P = 0.00000009, FDR 5%) with fWIT, yet the activity of Cathepsin B—a substrate of Legumain—decreased (P = 0.004, FDR 5%). Interestingly, Legumain abundance, measured by western blot, did not change with fWIT, yet was significantly reduced in glucose-starved PTECs (but not podocytes), indicating a cell-type-specific metabolic disruption associated with glucose availability and hypoxia. Cathepsin B abundance decreased in kidney biopsies as fWIT increased (P = 0.03). In hypoxic PTECs and podocytes, Cathepsin B abundance decreased after 6 h and 24 h, although this change did not reach statistical significance.
Conclusion
Prolonged fWIT induces metabolic and protease dysregulation in DCD kidneys, which may impair posttransplant function. As ischemia time increases, disruption of glucose metabolism likely drives changes in protease activity and subsequent protein degradation. Legumain is a high specificity protease that along with its regulatory components emerge as promising therapeutic targets to mitigate injury in DCD kidneys and potentially improve transplant outcomes.

title: #3588 Comparative analysis of glomerular filtration rate obtained by different methods in kidney transplanted patients
authors: Zhaklina Shterjova-Markovska; Irena Rambabova-Bushljetik; Galina Severova-Andreevska; Igor Nikolov; Lada Trajceska; Nikola Gjorgjievski; Julijana Usprcov; Tanja Makazlieva; Aleksandra Peshevska; Dragan Cibrev; Goce Spasovski
abstract:
Background and Aims
Since kidney transplanted patients (KTP) experience fluctuating kidney function, having a reliable way to monitor glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is crucial for detecting complications like graft rejection and adjusting immunosuppressive therapies (IT). KTP often face with unique challenges in assessing GFR due to multiple factors. The key focus of this study was to explore correlation between measured (mGFR) and estimated (eGFR) in KTP, specifically comparing mGFR obtained by nuclear method (NM) of slope/intercept by tree plasma sample method (TPSM) and eGFR determined by Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) 2021 and Modification of Diet in Renal Disease (MDRD).
Method
Fifty KTP, from the first to the third year after kidney transplantation, 36 (70%) male, participated in the study. A correlation and comparative analysis were made between the values of mGFR obtained by using the NM with TPSM, after i.v application of [99mTc]Tc-DTPA, as a reference method and eGFR calculated by mathematical equations: CKD epi 2021 and MDRD.
Results
Our study findings showed in the first group with mGFR 0-–60 ml/min/1.73 m2 , that for r = 0.69 (P < 0.05) between TPSM and CKD epi, and for r = 0.71 (P < 0.05) between TPSM and MDRD a strong significant correlation was determined. Second group with mGFR ≥ 61–105ml/min/1.73 m2, showed a very strong significant correlation for r = 0.88 (P < 0.01) between TPSM and CKD epi, and also r = 0.77 (P < 0.05) between TPSM and MDRD. In the first group TPSM showed consistently lower values compared to CKD epi i.e. a clear negative bias (−7.8), simultaneously, TPSM showed a slightly lower values compared to MDRD in the same group, but the bias was much more balanced (−1.3). In the second group compared values of TPSM vs CKD epi showed far more negative bias (−8.5), and TPSM vs MDRD, was more balanced (3.3).
The correlation and Bland Altman plots for both groups are shown in Fig. 1.
Conclusion
GFR obtained by MDRD correlates strongly with GFR values obtained by the reference method and shows less bias, when compared with CKD epi. In general, the bias of the estimate is less in measurements where the estimate for the GFR is higher. Our results confirm the better performance of the MDRD over CKD-epi method for estimation of the GFR in kidney-transplanted patients, particularly when reference method is unavailable. It provides a quick and reliable estimate that can be utilized routinely in the monitoring of this particular group of patients.

title: #3202 Biopsy-based transcript diagnostics improves prognostication along the AMR continuum
authors: Elena Rho; Lukas Weidmann; Kai Castrezana Lopez; Dusan Harmacek; Britta George; Thomas Schachtner; Seraina Von Moos
abstract:
Background and Aims
Clinical utility of biopsy-based transcript diagnostics with respect to risk stratification and prognostication for graft outcome used in addition to histology along the AMR continuum of Banff 2022 has not been investigated.
Method
We examined 297 kidney allograft biopsies by histology and the Molecular Microscope Diagnostic System (MMDx) from 2021 to 2023. Histologic findings were grouped into probable AMR (n = 52), DSA-negative C4d-negative MVI (n = 42), AMR (n = 71), and no AMR (n = 132). Groups were further divided into those with (n = 86) and without molecular signs of AMR (n = 211). Outcome was assessed using a combined endpoint of allograft loss, eGFR < 15 ml/min and eGFR decline of >30%.
Results
We followed kidney allograft biopsy cases for a median of 27 months (IQR 18; 38). Molecular AMR was found in 56% of AMR, 69% of DSA-negative MVI, 13% of probable AMR, and 6% with no AMR. At 1, 3, and 5 years after biopsy, molecular AMR cases had higher rates of the combined endpoint than no molecular AMR (25% vs. 4%, 28% vs. 8%, 54% vs. 11%; P = 0.0003). This difference was reproducible in all histologic groups. Rejection archetype R3 (P < 0.0001), R5 (P = 0.048) and R6 (P < 0.0001) showed significantly higher rates of combined endpoint than no molecular AMR. Creatinine (P = 0.003), proteinuria (P = 0.019), R3 (P = 0.001) and R6 archetype score (P = 0.005) and IFTA classifier score (P = 0.052) remained independent predictors of outcome in a multivariate analysis.
Conclusion
Molecular AMR is associated with higher rates of kidney allograft loss and eGFR decline along the AMR continuum defined by Banff 2022.

title: #2749 Association of stigmatizing language with kidney transplant waitlisting
authors: Joanna Yang; YangDai; Lili Chan
abstract:
Background and Aims
Stigmatizing language assigns negative labels and stereotypes to certain groups of people. Prior research demonstrates that stigmatizing language is more common in patients who are Black and is associated with changes in provider behavior. Patients undergoing kidney transplant (KTx) evaluation must complete an extensive evaluation for suitability. The presence of stigmatizing language within clinical documentation may contribute to inequitable access to kidney transplantation by biasing providers to patients prior to their evaluation. Our aim was to determine whether race/ethnicity is associated with the presence of stigmatizing language in the EHR of patients undergoing KTx and to assess whether the presence of such language is associated with transplant listing status.
Method
We identified a cohort of 7,209 patients from Mount Sinai Hospital who were evaluated for KTx between 2014 and 2023. These patients were all potential candidates for kidney transplantation, have estimated glomerular filtrate rate (eGFR) below 20, and were 18 years or older at time of measurement. We collected the cohort's clinical documentation that spanned five years prior to the transplant evaluation, for a total of 651,333 notes.
We used a pre-trained model, clinical BERT trained on MIMIC-IV, that detects stigmatizing language of three categories: Credibility & Obstinacy, Compliance, and Descriptors. We then had two reviewers conduct manual review of notes to identify examples of stigmatizing language which was used to fine tune the model on Mount Sinai data. We used a negative binomial model to evaluate the association of stigmatizing language with race/ethnicity while controlling for the number of notes. Lastly, we performed logistic regression to investigate associations between stigmatizing language and transplant listing outcomes. We considered only Status 1 listing to mean active on the KTx waitlist.
Results
The distribution of the categories is presented in Fig. 1. Model performance for the fine-tuned model was assessed using F1 scores: 0.88 for Credibility & Obstinacy, 0.92 for Compliance, and 0.95 for Descriptors (Fig. 2). Black and Hispanic individuals had a higher incidence of negative compliance language (IRR of 1.32 and 1.33, respectively) and overall negative stigmatizing language (IRR of 1.26 for both groups). The presence of stigmatizing language was associated with lower odds of KTx waitlisting (Table 1).
Conclusion
Our findings suggest that Black and Hispanic patients are more likely to encounter stigmatizing language in clinical documentation, which may contribute to disparities in kidney transplantation access. Furthermore, the presence of stigmatizing language is associated with lower odds of KTx waitlisting. These findings highlight the need to address potential biases in clinical documentation and their potential impact on KTx.

title: #2257 SGLT2 inhbitors reduce the eGFR slope in diabetic and non-diabetic renal transplant recipients
authors: Diana Rodríguez Espinosa; Jonay Manuel García García; Blerina Mataj; Ricardo Parra; Nuria Esforzado; Ángela González; José Vicente Torregrosa Prats; David Cucchiari; Ignacio Revuelta; Pedro Ventura Aguiar; Jose Jesus Broseta Monzo; Fritz Diekmann
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal graft function decline is an inevitable outcome in renal transplant recipients (RTR). Non-immunological and immunological damage lead to glomerular loss, hyperfiltration, interstitial fibrosis, and tubular atrophy. Despite clinical-trial evidence proves that SGLT2i delay dialysis onset in diabetic and non-diabetic patients with CKD, and observational data show safety in diabetic RTR, there is currently no data in non-diabetic RTR.
Method
In this single-cohort study including all RTR from Hospital Clínic Barcelona under SGLT2i, blood and urine tests at 12, 6 and 3 months before and after the initiation of an SGLT2i were collected. Demographic and clinical variables were obtained from medical health records. Estimated glomerular filtration rate, urine protein to creatinine ratio (UPCR), urinary tract infections (UTI) and treatment abandonment causes were recorded.
Results
From 2021 until 2023, 305 RTR were prescribed an SGLT2i, 33 patients lost follow-up. 190 patients (62%) were male, 153 (50.2%) had diabetes [post-transplant diabetes in 61], 79 (26%) had a history of rejection. 59 (22%) were also receiving a GLP1 agonist. Eleven patients started treatment within 90 days of transplantation. The annual eGFR slope reduced from 1.58 before SGLT2i to 0.32 after, a decline of 1.2 ml/min/1.73 m2 (P = 0.049). UPCR significantly improved 6 months after treatment, going from an increase of 162 mg/g to a reduction of 64 mg/g (P = 0.022). These results were independent from diabetes status. A total of 48 patients abandoned medication due to graft loss (16), UTI (4), erythrocytosis (2), diarrhoea (3), renal function decline (3), unknown (4), struvite kidney stone (1), or died (15). 63 (21%) patients were admitted due to a UTI, 40 (13%) of them only once.
Conclusion
SGLT2 inhibitors slow renal function decline in diabetic and non-diabetic RTR. The observed improvements support their potential as an effective therapeutic option to preserve graft function.

title: #322 Association of HLA system alleles with the occurrence of IgA nephropathy and its recurrence after kidney transplantation
authors: Ivana Dedinska; Karol Graňák; Matej Vnučák; Patricia Kleinova; Tímea Blichová; Andrej Kollár
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is the leading cause of primary glomerulopathy globally, presenting a high lifetime risk of kidney failure, with up to 50% of patients requiring kidney function replacement by age 51. Kidney transplantation (KT) is the preferred treatment method. The recurrence of IgAN post-transplantation is a significant factor leading to graft failure, occurring in 9%–61% of cases based on various studies. Younger age and aggressive disease are associated with higher recurrence risk. The predisposition to IgAN may be linked to specific HLA-DR and -DQ alleles. This analysis sought to identify risk and protective HLA alleles.
Method
This retrospective monocentric analysis included patients with biopsy-verified IgAN who underwent KT at the Transplant-Nephrology Department of the University Hospital Martin. Patients were monitored for IgAN recurrence through histological confirmation in graft biopsies. HLA typing was conducted before placing patients on the KT waiting list. The analysis included a comparison to a control group of 10,000 healthy donors from the Eurotransplant registry, capturing demographic and clinical characteristics of the patients.
Results
Out of 470 patients screened post-KT, 7.2% (n = 48) were found to have biopsy-verified IgAN, primarily affecting men (77%). The allele DRB111 was found in 47.92% of IgAN patients, indicating a significant risk for IgAN (OR 2.09), while DRB103 appeared in 4.17% and was protective against IgAN (OR 0.2). Recurrence of IgAN post-KT was confirmed histologically in 10% of patients (n = 5), all of whom were men, with an average time of 51.4 months to recurrence. All patients with confirmed recurrence had the risky allele DRB111, and 80% also had DRB103. Notably, one patient exhibited early recurrence after a secondary KT and carried both risk alleles.
Conclusion
The study found a 7.2% incidence of biopsy-confirmed IgAN and a 10% recurrence rate in grafts following KT. The allele DRB111 was identified as a risk factor, while DRB103 was protective against the development of IgAN and recurrent disease post-transplantation.

title: #1006 Basiliximab induction alone vs. a dual ATG-basiliximab approach in first living non-sensitized renal transplant recipients with reduced HLA matching
authors: Tamar Hod; Ronen Ghinea; Eytan Mor
abstract:
Background and Aims
Individualizing induction therapy based on immunological risk is crucial for optimizing outcomes in kidney transplantation. Due to the prevalent utilization of living unrelated donor (LURD) transplants in Israel , a substantial proportion of non-sensitized recipients have a reduced level of HLA matching (5–6 HLA mismatch). Our observations revealed a heightened acute rejection rate in this particular population when employing basiliximab induction. In response to this, we have modified our induction protocol, opting for a combination of single ATG dose and basiliximab. The primary objective was to diminish the incidence of acute rejection, and notably, we have significantly decreased the ATG dosage to mitigate the potential adverse effects associated with higher doses of ATG. In this study, we compare the 6-month outcomes between basiliximab induction alone and a dual ATG-basiliximab approach in this population.
Method
A retrospective analysis included 157 first living non-sensitized renal transplant recipients (RTRs). Within this cohort, 96 individuals exhibited low HLA matching (5–6 HLA mismatches). The low HLA match subgroup was categorized into 52 RTRs receiving basiliximab alone and 44 recipients treated with a combined single ATG dose of 1.5 mg/kg and basiliximab. The primary endpoint was early acute cellular rejection (ACR) within 6 months post-transplant while secondary outcomes encompassed infection rates, renal allograft function, length of stay (LOS), and overall admissions.
Results
Transitioning from basiliximab to combined ATG-basiliximab reduced early ACR (from 23.1% to 9.1%, P = 0.067). Age was a predictor for rejection, and subgroup analysis showed consistent rejection reduction across age groups. No significant differences were observed in admission for transplant LOS or in peri-operative complications, nor in infections rate including BK and CMV viremia, allograft function and number of admissions up to 6 months post-transplant.
Conclusion
In non-sensitized first living RTRs with reduced HLA matching, a dual single ATG-basiliximab induction approach significantly reduced early ACR without compromising safety.

title: #26 Monkeypox infection in kidney transplant recipients: a systematic review
authors: Henry Wu; Ola Suliman; Mohammad Joomye; Rajkumar Chinnadurai
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney transplant recipients are vulnerable to viral infections due to immunosuppressive therapy. Whilst there is recognition on the increased risk of Monkeypox (Mpox) infection in kidney transplant recipients, there remain limited discussion detailing disease progression, the effectiveness of current management strategies, and how immunosuppression influences disease course in kidney transplant recipients diagnosed with Mpox infection. As Mpox infection could potentially be severe and fatal, with case incidence continuing to rise globally, there is a need to develop tailored guidance to manage kidney transplant recipients with Mpox infection. To this end, we conducted a systematic review of current publications which described Mpox infection in kidney transplant recipients.
Method
This study is registered with PROSPERO (CRD42024611601). A systematic literature search was performed for full-text articles published in English between Aug 2014 and Aug 2024 through the PRISMA guideline. The inclusion criteria encompassed publications which examined the prevalence, incidence and/or impact of Mpox infection in kidney transplant recipients, and publications reporting on clinical outcomes such as graft failure, mortality or adverse events in kidney transplant recipients with Mpox infection. Publications which did not report data on Mpox infection in kidney transplant recipients and inaccessible full-text publications were excluded. Literature search was conducted by three independent authors (H.H.L.W., O.S. and M.J.). Databases used included PubMed, EMBASE, MEDLINE, Cochrane Library and Scopus. Combination keywords used included: “Monkeypox” AND “Kidney Transplant” AND “Immunosuppression”; “Mpox” AND “Kidney transplant” AND “Immunosuppression”; “Monkeypox” AND “Renal Transplant” AND “Immunosuppression”; “Mpox” AND “Renal Transplant” AND “Immunosuppression”; “Monkeypox” AND “Kidney Transplant”; “Mpox” AND “Kidney Transplant”; “Monkeypox” AND “Renal Transplant”; “Mpox” AND “Renal Transplant”; “Monkeypox” AND “Immunosuppression”; “Mpox” AND “Immunosuppression”; “Monkeypox” AND “Kidney Transplant” AND “Infection Management”; “Mpox” AND “Kidney Transplant” AND “Infection Management”; “Monkeypox” AND “Renal Transplant” AND “Infection Management”; “Mpox” AND “Renal Transplant” AND “Infection Management”. Publications identified in the databases were imported into Mendeley, where duplicates were removed. H.H.L.W., O.S. and M.J. then independently reviewed the remaining publications.
Results
A total of 12,429 articles were initially screened through our search strategy. After evaluation for relevance and applying our defined inclusion and exclusion criteria, 16 publications were included in the final review (Fig. 1). Table 1 provides a summary of included publications. Severity of Mpox can manifest in disseminated forms, including multi-organ involvement such as skin, lung, and pleural complications. Acute kidney injury and aggravation of kidney function was not uncommonly observed. Clinical outcomes were poor and fatalities were high in kidney transplant recipients with other immunocompromised conditions such as HIV. Prompt diagnosis of Mpox infection in kidney transplant recipients to facilitate timely initiation of antiviral treatment may be critical to improving outcomes. In particular, Tecovirimat was reported as an effective treatment option to mitigate the severity of Mpox infection in kidney transplant recipients and aid patient recovery. Modifying or temporarily discontinuing immunosuppression with close monitoring for signs of graft rejection is also considered a key measure to improving outcomes.
Conclusion
This systematic review underscores the heightened risk of severe Mpox infections in kidney transplant recipients due to their immunocompromised status. Current publications revealed a range of clinical presentations from disseminated infections to severe systemic involvement, emphasizing the need for vigilant monitoring and timely intervention with antiviral therapies if indicated.

title: #36 Assessing urinary exfoliated proximal tubule cell multispectral autofluorescence to differentiate between causes of post-transplant graft dysfunction
authors: Henry Wu; Yandong Lang; Shannon Handley; Aline Knab; Adnan Agha; Yuan Tian; Ewa M Goldys; Carol Pollock; Sonia Saad
abstract:
Background and Aims
Complications relating to delayed or deteriorating graft function following kidney transplantation are common. There is no validated method apart from transplant kidney biopsy which can accurately identify between the histopathological causes of graft dysfunction. Proximal tubule cell (PTC) exfoliation into urine is an active process which may generate significant information regarding an individual's kidney status, with PTCs forming majority of the kidney mass. Multispectral assessment of native cell autofluorescence has been specifically shown to be sensitive to metabolic changes and oxidative stress. Considering an unmet critical need for non-invasive diagnostic approaches to reliably identify kidney transplant complications, our group propose a novel methodology based on assessment of multispectral autofluorescence features of extracted urinary exfoliated PTCs from kidney transplant recipients.
Method
Kidney transplant recipients aged 18–75 years were recruited. Urine samples prior to transplant biopsy were collected and stored at −80°C. Exfoliated PTCs were extracted using a validated specific immunomagnetic separation method based on anti-CD13 and anti-SGLT2 antibodies. Multispectral autofluorescence imaging was performed using a standard Olympus iX83™ fluorescence microscope and multispectral excitation lamp from Quantitative™, AU. Images were captured by a Nüvü™ EMCCD camera HNü 1024 cooled to −65°C in our laboratory to reduce sensor-induced noise. For the 34 image channels taken per sample, image acquisition times of up to 5 seconds per channel with multiple averaging (3 times) were applied to optimize image quality. Acquired cellular images underwent preprocessing and segmentation in preparation for quantitative analysis. Single-cell level features were generated. Discriminative analysis between the spectral profiles of imaged PTCs was completed through binary classification of cells, where binary classification was initiated based on the defined group comparisons across three different histopathological diagnoses (i.e. acute tubular necrosis (ATN), graft rejection or non-rejection associated interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy (IFTA)) as concluded from transplant biopsy: 1st comparison—ATN vs graft rejection, 2nd comparison—ATN vs IFTA, and 3rd comparison—graft rejection vs IFTA. Binary classification of cells was carried out by a random forest classifier and the AutoGluon machine learning software. The data generated from this process were assessed using receiver operating characteristic curves and area under the curve (AUC) values (with error bars representing 95% confidence intervals). Results were validated by 5-fold cross validation.
Results
30 kidney transplant recipients who received a clinically indicated post-transplant biopsy took part in this study. There were 10 individuals with ATN, 10 with graft rejection and 10 with IFTA. No statistically significant differences in demographic and clinical characteristics between the groups other than age (55.0 (ATN) vs 39.2 (graft rejection) vs 54.1 years (IFTA), P = 0.028) were observed. Multispectral autofluorescence imaging was completed for 161 PTCs in total (51 PTCs in the ATN group; 60 PTCs in the graft rejection group; 50 PTCs in the IFTA group). Applying our novel methodology, binary classification of urinary exfoliated PTCs based on multispectral autofluorescence between study participants with ATN vs graft rejection, between study participants with ATN vs IFTA, and between study participants with graft rejection vs IFTA displayed AUC values of 0.95 ± 0.05, 0.92 ± 0.08 and 0.91 ± 0.09, respectively (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
Our results provide a proof of concept that urinary exfoliated PTC multispectral autofluorescence could be utilized to differentiate between ATN vs graft rejection, ATN vs IFTA, and graft rejection vs IFTA in kidney transplant recipients with an excellent degree of accuracy. Further studies are anticipated to develop this novel non-invasive methodology as a potential tool to guide clinical decision-making in post-transplant settings.

Further studies are anticipated to develop this novel non-invasive methodology as a potential tool to guide clinical decision-making in post-transplant settings.

title: #1666 Who Says No? Profiles of participants and nonparticipants in an exercise and physical activity intervention study after kidney transplantation
authors: Jasmine De Beir; Marieke Vandecruys; Marie Renier; Stefan De Smet; Amaryllis Van Craenenbroeck; Diethard Monbaliu; Sabina de Geest; Francis Verbeke; Evi Nagler; Wim Van Biesen; Karsten Vanden Wyngaert; Patrick Calders
abstract:
Background and Aims
Exercise therapy has the potential to enhance physical function and quality of life in kidney transplant recipients (KTRs); however, robust evidence on effectiveness is limited due to small trials, narrow eligibility criteria, and short follow-up periods, reducing generalizability. While factors such as health perceptions, self-efficacy, and practical barriers influence participation in exercise studies, barriers to participation in exercise intervention studies among KTRs remain unexplored. This study aimed to profile participants and nonparticipants in an exercise and physical activity intervention study after kidney transplantation, quantify participation rates and explore reasons for nonparticipation.
Method
The PHOENIX-kidney study (NCT06260579) is a multicenter RCT evaluating the effectiveness of a home-based exercise and physical activity intervention following kidney transplantation. All de novo KTRs at University Hospitals of Leuven and Ghent were screened for eligibility. This cross-sectional analysis included adult KTRs transplanted between November 2022 and November 2024. Eligible individuals were informed about the study during hospital admission and asked about participation six weeks post-transplant. Reasons for ineligibility were documented. Those who consented enrolled in ICF-A. Eligible nonparticipants were invited to join ICF-B, which involved a single assessment of baseline characteristics. At three months post-transplant, both ICF-A and ICF-B participants completed questionnaires assessing sociodemographic and medical characteristics, self-reported physical activity levels (PAVS), and perceived barriers and motivators for physical activity (MBQ). Nonparticipation reasons were documented. Group differences and factors associated with nonparticipation were analyzed using chi-square tests, t-tests, and logistic regression.
Results
Of 310 KTRs screened, 59% (n = 184) were eligible. Major reported exclusions included medical contraindications to exercise (25%), language barriers (24%), and multi-organ transplantation (20%). Among eligible individuals, 46% participated in the ICF-A study (n = 69; mean age = 53.8 ± 12.5), and 35% joined the ICF-B study (n = 65; mean age = 56.3 ± 12.2). The most frequently reported reasons for nonparticipation in the ICF-B group included the intervention format (32%), lack of time (25%), and already being sufficiently active (22%). The ICF-B group had more comorbidities (mean = 4.2 ± 2.2 vs. 3.2 ± 2.1 in ICF-A; P = 0.007) and higher self-reported physical activity levels (median total minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity per week [IQR] = 210 [120–360] vs. 113 [11–240] in ICF-A; P = 0.003). The ICF-A group scored higher across motivator domains for physical activity, including psychological outcomes (1.36 ± 1.15 vs. 0.94 ± 0.94; P = 0.021), group activities and financial resources (1.44 ± 0.87 vs. 1.00 ± 0.91; P = 0.005), external influences (1.73 ± 0.81 vs. 1.31 ± 0.82; P = 0.003), and health and physical outcomes (2.45 ± 0.52 vs. 2.06 ± 0.67; P < 0.001), when compared to the ICF-B group. Logistic regression identified factors associated with nonparticipation, including being female (OR = 3.41, 95% CI: 1.39–8.38, P = 0.008), having more comorbidities (OR = 1.35, 95% CI: 1.09–1.59, P = 0.003), reporting higher physical activity levels (OR = 1.005, 95% CI: 1.002–1.008, P < 0.001), and lower health-driven motivation (OR = 0.19, 95% CI: 0.09–0.42, P < 0.001).
Conclusion
Understanding the characteristics of nonparticipants provides valuable insights for future studies. Targeting individuals with low to medium activity levels—who are more likely to participate and benefit—could improve the applicability and cost-effectiveness of exercise programs for KTRs. Additionally, addressing barriers to participation, such as the intervention format and health concerns, through flexible, person-centered approaches may reduce participation bias in future research.

title: #2179 Factors affecting senescent and regulatory T-cell numbers within the first year following kidney transplantation
authors: Stamatia Stai; Georgios Lioulios; Eleni Moysidou; Michalis Christodoulou; Christodoulos Keskinis; Fani Makrovasili; Eleni Iliopoulou; Xaralampos Vagiotas; Georgios Tsoulfas; Asimina Fylaktou; Maria Stangou
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney transplantation (KTx) does not completely reinstate the uremia-mediated immune system changes observed among end-stage renal disease (ESRD) patients. Moreover, it can be responsible for additional alterations in its dynamics, including induction of accelerated immunosenescence, as well as a transient increase of regulatory T-cells (Tregs). The aim of the present study was to explore the potential impact of several parameters on the immunosenescence and immune tolerance processes, by assessing their effect on CD28-null T-lymphocyte and Treg numbers.
Method
Our research was a prospective observational study, with our sample consisting of 113 adult kidney transplant recipients (KTRs). We defined senescent T-cells as either CD4+CD28− or CD8+CD28− and Tregs as CD4+CD25+FOXP3+ and used flow cytometry in order to measure their concentrations at predefined time points: T0: 24 hours following KTx, T3: 3 months after KTx, T6: 6 months after KTx, T12: 12 months after KTx. We then examined the impact of recipient and donor age, anti-cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgG titers, cold ischemia time (CIT), donor type, induction treatment, patient pre-transplantation dialysis status and recipient-donor common human leucocyte antigen (HLA) number on the composition of the previously mentioned cellular subpopulations. We additionally attempted to assess the combined effect of donor and recipient age, using 60 years as cut-off value and subsequently segregating KTRs into the following groups: a) young donor–young recipient (n = 74), b) old donor–young recipient (n = 27), c) old donor–old recipient (n = 12).
Results
There was a negative correlation between recipient age and all recorded Treg concentrations [r(111)= −0.234, p: 0.014 (T0), r(111)= −0.275, p: 0.006 (T3), r(111)= −0.286, p: 0.004 (T6), r(111)= −0.308, p: 0.001 (T12)], while donor age was negatively associated with Treg counts at T12 [r(111)=−0.214, p: 0.028]. Interestingly, with regards to the patient groups, Treg numbers and proportions tended to be more elevated, while CD4+CD28− and CD8+CD28− T-lymphocyte percentages were found to be lower among young recipients, regardless of the donor age (Table 1).
Higher anti-CMV IgG titers at almost any time point were connected to more elevated CD28-null T-lymphocyte counts [for CD4+: r(111) = 0.374, P < 0.001 (T3), r(111) = 0.459, P < 0.001 (T6), r(111) = 0.257, p: 0.015 (T12), for CD8+: r(111) = 0.424, P < 0.001 (T3), r(111) = 0.561, P < 0.001 (T6), r(111) = 0.371, P < 0.001]. Longer CIT was associated with lower Treg concentrations [r(111) = −0.422, P < 0.001 (Τ0), r(111) = −0.365, P < 0.001 (T3)].
We observed higher Treg levels in KTRs who had been subjected to live-donor or preemptive kidney transplantation (PKT), as well as among those who had not received anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG) as induction therapy. Recipients who had either one common HLA-C or one or two common HLA-DR antigens with their donor, also presented more elevated Treg concentrations compared to those who had two common HLA-C or no common HLA-DR antigens. The use of basiliximab as induction regimen was linked to lower CD4+CD28− T-lymphocyte numbers, while patients who had been under peritoneal dialysis (PD) prior to transplantation displayed increased CD8+CD28− T-cell counts as opposed to those with PKT (Table 2).
Conclusion
Within the first year following transplantation, a greater degree of T-cell senescence was observed among KTRs of older age, with higher anti-CMV IgG titers, who had previously been on PD and had not been treated with Basiliximab. Treg levels were negatively associated mostly with recipient, but also with donor age, longer CIT, cadaveric transplantation and prior PD status and ATG administration. Common HLA number between donor and recipient was also found to affect Treg counts.

title: #2483 Identifying risk factors for bone fractures in kidney trasplant recipients: a clinical data perspective
authors: Avinash Chandu Nanwani; José Vicente Torregrosa Prats; Juan Daniel Diaz Garcia
abstract:
Background and Aims
Bone fractures are a significant complication in kidney transplant recipients, contributing to increased morbidity and reduced quality of life. The risk of fractures in this population is influenced by a variety of factors such as advanced age, female sex, history of fractures, diabetes mellitus, and high doses of glucocorticoids. Additionally, the type of dialysis prior to transplantation and the specific immunosuppressive regimen used can also impact fracture risk. Understanding these risk factors is crucial for developing targeted preventive strategies to mitigate the risk of fractures in transplant patients. The primary goal of this study is to characterize the risk factors associated with bone fractures among kidney transplant recipients.
Method
Retrospective cohort study included 999 kidney transplant recipients. Each patient had at least one year post-transplant follow-up. Data were obtained from clinical records and included age, sex, time post-transplant, tobacco use, alcohol use, creatinine levels, calcium and phosphorus levels, diabetes mellitus status, bone mineral density, type of immunosuppressant, number of transplants, combined immunosuppressant and steroid use and presence of osteoporotic fractures. All statistical analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC). The PROC MEANS and PROC FREQ procedures were used for descriptive statistics, PROC LIFETEST was used for Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, and PROC PHREG was used for Cox proportional hazards modeling.
Results
999 kidney transplant recipients with a mean age of 54.85 years (SD = 13.16) were studied. Males accounted for 64% (640 patients) of the population. Smoking was reported by 13.5% (135 patients), and 7% (70 patients) reported alcohol consumption. Diabetes mellitus was present in 18.4% (184 patients) of the cohort. 20.4% (204 patients) were treated with steroids, and 73.2% (732 patients) were treated with ciclosporin. Tacrolimus was used by 76.9% (769 patients), and rapamycin (RAPA) by 20.6% (206 patients). Out of the 999 patients, 117 (11.7%) experienced osteoporotic fractures ( or fracture events) during the follow-up period, highlighting the significant burden of bone fractures in this population. Among the fracture group, males accounted for a higher proportion of cases, with 61 males (9.52% of all males) experiencing fractures compared to 56 females (15.83% of all females). Additionally, a higher incidence of fractures was observed among smokers (15.6%) compared to non-smokers (11%). A log-rank test confirmed a significant difference in survival times between the fracture and non-fracture groups (P < 0.001), suggesting that factors related to time post-transplantation, in conjunction with other covariates, contribute significantly to fracture risk. Patients on glucocorticoid therapy had a higher incidence of fractures compared to those on calcineurin inhibitors (HR = 1.58, P = 0.12), although this difference did not reach statistical significance.
Conclusion
This study has provided critical insights into the multifactorial risk factors associated with bone fractures in solid organ transplant recipients. Through a comprehensive analysis of demographic, lifestyle, and biochemical factors, the research confirms that age, female gender, smoking, and elevated serum phosphorus levels are significant predictors of fracture risk in this population. These findings are consistent with existing literature, further emphasizing the importance of targeted interventions to mitigate fracture risk.
The results highlight the adverse impact of long-term glucocorticoid use on bone health. Glucocorticoids, a mainstay of post-transplant immunosuppressive therapy, were shown to significantly increase fracture risk by reducing bone mineral density (BMD) and altering bone remodeling processes. Consequently, there is a clear need for alternative immunosuppressive strategies that minimize the use of glucocorticoids, particularly in high-risk populations.

title: #2460 CMV infection in CMV-seropositive kidney transplant recipients: does pretransplant CMV IgG titer matter?
authors: Andreia Curto; Miguel Bigotte Vieira; João Figueiredo Martins; Ana Rita Pereirinha Ramos; Fernando Caeiro; Ines Aires; Manuel Anibal A Ferreira; Cristina Rego de Freitas Mendes Jorge
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is the primary infectious complication in kidney transplantation (KT), and it contributes to morbidity and mortality rates. CMV-seropositive solid organ transplant recipients have a relatively lower risk of CMV infection when compared to CMV-seronegative recipients who receive allograft from CMV-seropositive donors. Nonetheless, some patients remain at risk. Our aim was to assess the association between the anti-CMV IgG titer and the risk of post-transplant CMV infection among CMV-seropositive KT recipients.
Method
We conducted a retrospective single-center study on adult CMV-seropositive KT recipients between January 2018 and June 2023. Clinical characteristics, risk factors, and outcomes were extracted from patient medical records. Patients who received anti-thymocyte globulin as induction therapy were given valganciclovir prophylaxis for 6 months post-transplant. The cumulative incidence of CMV infection was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method (defined as detection of CMV DNA in plasma regardless of symptoms). We analyzed CMV-IgG as a predictor of CMV infection using Cox proportional hazards model (SPSS). The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board.
Results
The medical records of a total of 263 KT patients were retrieved, and a total of 27 were CMV-seronegative. A total of 236 CMV-seropositive KT recipients were included, being 66.1% male. Their mean ± SD age was 52.5 ± 11.9 years. Among these, 94% received deceased-donor allograft, of which 8.1% were after circulatory death donors (DCD), and 50.7% were expanded criteria donors. The median [IQR] mismatch was 4 [3.0, 5.0]. Regarding induction therapy, 62.7% of KT recipients received anti-thymocyte globulin. During a mean follow-up of 19.9 months, the cumulative incidence of CMV infection was 61.6% (Fig. 1). Lower titers of pretransplant CMV-IgG were associated with CMV infection (P = 0.031).
Conclusion
We observed that a lower pretransplant anti-CMV IgG titer is associated with an increased risk of post-transplant CMV infection among CMV-seropositive KT recipients. The universally available test for anti-CMV IgG titer could potentially stratify individuals at risk and target them to receive a more specific preventive strategy.

title: #3889 The impact of first year eGFR and subsequent eGFR decline on kidney transplant outcomes—a single centre experience
authors: Andreia Dos Santos Henriques; João Venda; Sofia Ventura; Clara Pardinhas; Rita Gomes Carlos Leal; Maria João Teixeira Guedes Marques; Luís Rodrigues; Emanuel Eufrásio Ferreira; Lídia Santos; Catarina Romãozinho; Arnaldo Figueiredo; Rui Alves
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney graft survival is influenced by multiple factors. The estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) at one year post-transplant is commonly used as a predictor of graft survival. However, the decline in eGFR over time is often overlooked. This study aimed to compare the impact of eGFR at one year (eGFR1) and eGFR decline over the subsequent 5 years to assess their relative influence on long-term graft survival.
Method
We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study using data from the Transplantation Network database of a kidney transplant center. We included adult recipients (≥18 years old) undergoing their first kidney transplant (KT) from a deceased donor aged >10 years between 2012 and 2019. Recipients who experienced graft loss within the first year were excluded. We analysed the impact of eGFR1 and eGFR decline from years 1 to 5 post-transplant (categorized as reductions >10, >20, and >30 mL/min/1.73 m²) on death-censored graft survival and recipient survival.
Results
A total of 753 kidney transplant recipients were included. The median donor and recipient ages were 54.0 years [IQR: 47.0–62.5] and 53.0 years [IQR: 44.0–61.0], respectively. The median donor eGFR was 101.3 mL/min/1.73 m² [IQR: 84.3–110.6]. The median eGFR1 was 57.6 mL/min/1.73 m² [IQR: 44.6–76.6], and the median eGFR at year 5 (eGFR5) was 60.3 mL/min/1.73 m² [IQR: 46.2–78.2].
The mean recipient survival was 11.5 ± 0.1 years, with a mortality rate of 13.9% (n = 105). The mean death-censored graft survival was 11.9 ± 0.1 years, with a death-censored graft loss of 9.8% (n = 65).

title: #2638 Recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV) confers persistent immune responses with no safety concerns 4 to 8 years after vaccination of adults with renal transplant
authors: Melinda Hutton; Adrienne Kuxhausen; Fatine Atig; Manyee Tsang; Ana Isabel Sánchez Fructuoso; Tom Robberechts; Rafael A Pérez Carillo; Jae Berm Park; Fernanda Ortiz; Deepali Kumar; Yang-Jen Chiang; Agnes Mwakingwe-Omari
abstract:
Background and Aims
In immunocompromised populations, vaccination remains an important tool for the prevention of herpes zoster (HZ). RZV is immunogenic and is approved for vaccination of adults 18 years and older who are at increased risk of HZ including those who are immunocompromised due to their underlying diseases or therapy. To understand the durability of protection, long-term data is necessary. We evaluated the persistence of immunogenicity of 2 doses of RZV 4–8 years after vaccination, as well as long-term safety in renal transplant recipients.
Method
This open-label, long-term extension study (NCT04176939) enrolled renal transplant recipients on chronic immunosuppressants who received 2 doses of RZV in the primary study (NCT02058589)1. Immunogenicity persistence was evaluated for 2 years: at enrolment day (D) 1 which started 4–6 years after RZV vaccination in the primary study, month (M) 12, and M24. Results were also analysed by year post-dose 2. Immunogenicity was assessed by humoral immune (HI) response (anti-glycoprotein E [anti-gE] antibody geometric mean concentration [GMC]) and cell-mediated immune (CMI) response (frequencies of gE-specific CD4+ T-cells expressing ≥2 markers among IFN-γ, IL-2, TNF-α, CD40L). Long-term safety after RZV vaccination was also assessed up to M24. Suspected HZ was defined as a new HZ rash clinically diagnosed as per standard of care with no alternative diagnosis. Confirmed HZ cases were evaluated per study algorithm.
Results
A total of 68 participants who received the 2-dose RZV vaccination series were enrolled. The mean geometric increase in anti-gE antibody concentration was 2.93, 2.75, and 2.44 over pre-vaccination levels at D1, M12, and M24, respectively. Yearly assessments collectively with data from the primary study showed HI responses (anti-gE antibody GMC) peak at 1M post-dose 2, which declined by 12M post-dose 2, then remained at a lower, stable plateau from 4 to at least 8 years post-dose 2 and remained above pre-vaccination levels at all time points. At D1, M12, and M24, CMI median frequency remained above pre-vaccination levels, showing the same pattern as HI responses (Table 1). Three (4.4%) participants had suspected HZ episodes from the last visit in the primary study to D1. From D1 to M24, 3 (4.4%) participants had confirmed HZ episodes. There were 2 (2.9%) cases of rejection: 1 acute antibody-mediated rejection and 1 acute T-cell mediated rejection. Both incidents began more than 2000 days post-dose 2 and were deemed unrelated to RZV vaccination. Both participants recovered with treatment, and graft function was preserved. Fatal outcomes due to unrelated serious adverse events (SAEs) were reported for 6 participants. No related SAEs were reported since the last visit in the primary study up to M24.
Conclusion
RZV induced a persistent long-term immune response in renal transplant recipients on chronic immunosuppression. At 4–8 years after RZV vaccination, HI and CMI responses remained at stable levels above pre-vaccination. No safety signals were identified during the long-term follow-up after RZV vaccination.

title: #2733 Elevated soluble ST2 at Day 7 as a prognostic biomarker for adverse outcomes in kidney transplant recipients
authors: Thomas Beaudrey; Thomas Goria; Mirjana Radosavljevic; Sophie Ohlmann; Nans Florens
abstract:
Background and Aims
Soluble ST2 (sST2), a member of the IL-33 receptor family, has been associated with inflammation and adverse outcomes in various clinical contexts. In kidney transplant recipients (KTRs), we aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of sST2 levels in predicting major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), death, and graft loss.
Method
We conducted a monocentric prospective analysis in 444 KTRs, measuring sST2 levels at Day 0 (D0, n = 231) and Day 7 (D7, n = 444) post-transplantation using the Bio-Techne Ella SimplePlex technology. The cohort had a mean age of 53 years, included 169 women, and had a mean dialysis vintage of 1372 months. Delayed graft function (DGF) occurred in 115 patients. Events were censored at 3 years of follow-up as well as for events occurring before D7. Survival analysis was performed using the log-rank test, and a multivariate Cox proportional hazards model adjusted for clinical factors such as age, sex, transplantation rank, donor type, dialysis vintage, and cardiovascular history.
Results
sST2 levels were significantly higher at D7 compared to D0 (27,817 pg/mL vs. 78,644 pg/mL; P < 0.0001). Patients in the highest sST2 quartile at D7 exhibited worse outcomes (MACE, death, and graft loss; log-rank P = 0.0191, Fig. 1). In the multivariate Cox model, each 10,000 pg/mL increase in sST2 at D7 was associated with a higher risk of MACKE (HR 1.024, 95% CI 0.9983–1.046; P = 0.0465). Subgroup analyses confirmed similar associations for death and graft loss (HR 1.036, 95% CI 0.9992–1.067) and MACE alone (HR 1.025, 95% CI 0.9998–1.035). Patients with DGF had significantly higher sST2 levels at D7 compared to those without DGF (72,816 pg/mL vs. 94,570 pg/mL; P = 0.0084).
Conclusion
sST2 levels at D7 post-transplantation are significantly associated with poor outcomes, including MACE, death, and graft loss. Elevated sST2 levels in DGF patients highlight its potential as a biomarker to guide post-transplant surveillance and individualize patient management strategies.

title: #2739 Incidence, risk factors, and impact of coronary artery disease events after kidney transplantation
authors: Thomas Beaudrey; Dimitri Bedo; Sophie Ohlmann; Nans Florens
abstract:
Background and Aims
Coronary artery disease is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality among kidney transplant recipients. The epidemiology and impact of coronary events after transplantation remain poorly understood in France. We investigated these aspects using data from 17 French centers, sourced from the Astre and Divat cohorts.
Method
We included adult kidney allograft recipients transplanted between 2008 and 2022, with follow-up until 03/31/2023. The primary outcome was the incidence of coronary events post-transplantation, defined as the need for coronary angiography with percutaneous transluminal angioplasty. We also studied risk factors and the impact of early events on patient and graft survival (<1 month post-transplantation) using univariate and then multivariate Cox models.
Results
Among the 19,837 kidney transplant recipients included, 764 experienced a coronary event (3.9%), with a cumulative incidence of 1.03% at 1 month post-transplantation, 1.86% at 1 year, 3.77% at 5 years and 6.60% at 10 years. The majority of these events (n = 505, 66.1%) occurred in patients without known coronary artery disease. In multivariate analysis, risk factors for post-transplant coronary artery disease included age, male sex, cardiovascular history, diabetes, smoking, depleting induction therapy, dialysis duration, and delayed graft function. Early coronary events were associated with all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.77, 95% Confidence Interval 1.34–2.33) and graft loss (hazard ratio 1.51, 95% Confidence Interval 1.01–2.25).
Conclusion
Post-transplant coronary artery disease events are frequent, particularly in the first month, and can occur in patients without history of coronary artery disease. They are a significant cause of morbidity and mortality and are associated with an early decline in graft function.
