title: #2717 Glomerulitis and interstitial fibrosis in first year kidney transplant biopsies are associated with cardiovascular risk
authors: Thomas Beaudrey; Jérôme Olagne; Dimitri Bedo; Sophie Ohlmann; Nans Florens
abstract:
Background and Aims
Graft rejection has been linked to cardiovascular risk in epidemiological studies in kidney transplantation, which may result from the pathophysiological link between renal inflammation and cardiovascular events. However, data on the association between histological lesions observed in graft biopsies and cardiovascular risk are lacking.
Method
We included kidney transplant recipients who underwent kidney allograft biopsy between 1 and 12 months post-transplant, from 2008 to 2022, using data from the ASTRE database and the local database of Strasbourg University Hospital. Our objective was to describe, using a Cox model, the association of renal histological lesions according to the 2022 Banff classification with the occurrence of major cardiovascular events (MACE).
Results
We included 3,153 patients who underwent kidney allograft biopsy within the first year post-transplant, of whom 9.1% (n = 287) experienced a MACE, with a median occurrence of 1 year. In univariate analysis, interstitial infiltrates (i), tubulitis (t), glomerulitis (g), interstitial fibrosis (ci), and chronic vascular lesions (cv) were associated with the occurrence of cardiovascular events. In multivariate analysis, after adjusting for recipient age, donor type, renal function at the time of biopsy, cardiovascular history and risk factors, and pre-transplant dialysis duration, three histological lesions were associated with MACE: g (Hazard ratio 1.59, 95% Confidence Interval 1.26–2.00), ci (HR 1.63, CI 1.18–2.24) and cv (HR 1.19, CI 1.00–1.42). Univariate analysis of the Strasbourg cohort (n = 479) showed that microcirculation inflammation without DSA (HR 2.33, 95% CI 1.15–4.71) and BK virus nephropathy (HR 2.57, 95% CI 1.30–5.08) were the most strongly associated with MACE.
Conclusion
Glomerulitis, interstitial fibrosis, and chronic vascular lesions are independently associated with an increased cardiovascular risk when identified in kidney graft biopsies during the first year post-transplantation. This raises the question of a potential relationship within the framework of cardiorenal interactions. However, certain confounding factors must be considered, including long-term decline in renal function and adjustments to immunosuppressive therapy.

title: #1546 Temporal trends in the risk of fractures in adult kidney transplant recipients
authors: Ina Ystrøm; Christian Fynbo Christiansen; Ditte Hansen; Per Ivarsen; Hanne Skou Jørgensen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Despite significant progress in modern immunosuppression, kidney transplant recipients remain at high risk of adverse outcomes including fractures. The reported fracture risk after kidney transplantation vary, with most studies focusing on major osteoporotic fractures (MOF). This study investigated the risk of any fracture in contemporary kidney transplant recipients, with trends over the past 20 years.
Method
This was a retrospective cohort study utilizing national health registries. The study population was defined using the Danish Renal Registry and included all adult patients receiving a first single kidney transplant in Denmark between 2000–2022. Hospital diagnoses derived from the Danish National Patient Registry were used to identify all fracture events after kidney transplantation. Fractures and comorbidity before the time of transplantation was based on diagnosis in the registry up to 10 years prior to transplantation. MOF was defined as spine, hip, proximal humerus or forearm fracture. The incidence rate was computed as the number of events divided by people at risk during follow-up. To examine temporal trends the follow-up was restricted to five years and incidence rates were estimated for separate time periods as crude and as age- and sex-standardized to the earliest calendar period. Cumulative incidence (risk) of any fracture or MOF was computed treating death as a competing risk.
Results
A total of 3997 first kidney transplantations were identified. Median age at transplant was 50 yr, 37% were female, and 22% had diabetes mellitus. A fracture prior to transplantation was noted for 17% of patients, with 4% having had a MOF. During a median follow-up of 5.9 years (IQR 2.6–10.8), 909 patients (23%) sustained any post-transplant fracture. Of all first fracture events, 87% occurred in patients who still had kidney graft function.
The crude incidence rate was 31.8/1000 person years (95% CI 29.8–33.9) for any fracture and 9.2/1000 person years (95% CI 8.2–10.3) for a MOF. The 5-year risk for any fracture was 15% (95% CI 14–16%) and the 10-year risk was 25% (95% CI 23–26%). The annual risk was highest during the first five years after which it declined. During the study period crude incidence rates of any fracture remained stable and this did not change after standardization (Fig. 1).
Patients who sustained a fracture were more likely to be female, have diabetes and a history of previous fracture, and a longer dialysis vintage. Post-transplant fractures were primarily located at the distal skeleton, with fractures of the foot, hand, lower leg and forearm comprising 59% of all first fractures, while MOF comprised 35% (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
Contemporary kidney transplant recipients have high fracture rates, and despite improvements in post-transplant care, fracture rates are unchanged over the past 20 years. The majority of fractures are located at the distal skeleton and the definition of MOF captures only 1/3 of post-transplant fractures. Further efforts are needed to characterize fracture risk factors post-transplant, particularly related to transplant-specific factors such as mineral metabolism disturbances.

title: #2470 Graph neural networks in the nephropathological diagnosis of antibody-mediated rejection (AMR)
authors: Israel Mateos-Aparicio-Ruiz; Anibal Pedraza; Jean-Baptiste Gibier; Alessandro Del Gobbo; Cigdem Gunduz-Demir; Francesco Pesce; Dilek Ertoy Baydar; Caner Süsal; Vitoantonio Bevilacqua; Nicola Altini; Gloria Bueno; Jan Ulrich Becker
abstract:
Background and Aims
Antibody-mediated rejection (AMR) remains a significant cause of late allograft failure. However, considerable variability exists in its diagnosis, even among experts. Weakly supervised machine learning applied to renal biopsy whole slide images (WSIs) could offer cost-efficient and accurate diagnostics with perfect reproducibility.
In this study, we build on our previous work developing diagnostic models for AMR using a multi-institutional dataset including adversarial samples such as accommodation, transmitted, recurrent, and de novo diseases.
Method
A dataset of 1,183 periodic acid-Schiff WSIs from 348 patients from four different institutions was automatically segmented into tissue compartment crops. Graph neural networks (GNNs) were employed to classify AMR and non-AMR (including adversarial samples like accommodation, transmitted and de novo glomerulopathy). The WSIs were represented as fully connected graphs, with glomerular crops as nodes, capturing global spatial relationships. Feature vectors for individual glomerular crops were computed using both supervised (Swin Transformer) and self-supervised (MAE and SimCLR) architectures. Classification was performed using Graph-Transformer and three novel models: SimpleGCN, DenseGCN, and SimpleGAT. These WSI-level classifiers were compared to state-of-the-art patch-level classification methods (Swin and ConvNeXt). Performance was determined in 5-fold internal cross-validation experiments.
Results
The GNN-based methods outperformed baseline patch-level classification models. The best- performing model, SimpleGCN with Swin-extracted features, achieved an accuracy of 71.00% and an AUC of 0.7858, significantly better than the Swin model (accuracy of 65.66% and an AUC of 0.7265).
Conclusion

Background and Aims
Antibody-mediated rejection (AMR) remains a significant cause of late allograft failure. However, considerable variability exists in its diagnosis, even among experts. Weakly supervised machine learning applied to renal biopsy whole slide images (WSIs) could offer cost-efficient and accurate diagnostics with perfect reproducibility.
In this study, we build on our previous work developing diagnostic models for AMR using a multi-institutional dataset including adversarial samples such as accommodation, transmitted, recurrent, and de novo diseases.
Method
A dataset of 1,183 periodic acid-Schiff WSIs from 348 patients from four different institutions was automatically segmented into tissue compartment crops. Graph neural networks (GNNs) were employed to classify AMR and non-AMR (including adversarial samples like accommodation, transmitted and de novo glomerulopathy). Our approach permits easy upscaling of training cohorts for cost-efficient and even more accurate diagnostic support systems. title: #156 Exercise and prediabetes after renal transplantation: EXPRED-II
authors: Raúl Morales Febles; Olav Rivero Martín; Domingo Marrero Miranda; Ana González Rinne; Alejandra Maxorata Álvarez González; Noa Diaz Novo; Ingrid Auyanet Saavedra; Raquel Santana Estupiñan; Adonay Santana Quintana; Antonio Manuel Rivero Gonzalez; Coriolano Cruz; Esteban Porrini
abstract:
Background and Aims
post-transplant diabetes mellitus (PTDM) is frequent after renal transplantation. The cases of PTDM observed beyond 12 months after transplantation develop mainly in subjects with prediabetes. Thus, treating patients with prediabetes after transplantation might prevent PTDM. In the general population, exercise prevents the evolution from prediabetes to diabetes. We showed that exercise reverted prediabetes in 60% of the cases in the Exercise and Prediabetes after Renal Transplantation (EXPRED-I) [1]. This study was non-randomized and exploratory. However, evidence from randomized clinical trials is lacking. We design the EXPRED-II, a clinical trial to evaluate the feasibility of exercise in the reversibility of prediabetes after transplantation, as a first step to prevent PTDM.
Method
a total of 50 patients with prediabetes beyond 12 months after transplantation with capacity to perform exercise will be randomized to standard life-style recommendations as per clinical practice (control group, n = 25) or to a stepped ad-hoc designed training intervention (exercise group, n = 25). Prediabetes will be diagnosed based on fasting glucose levels and an Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT). Patients randomized to exercise will start with aerobic exercise training 5 times/week, 30 min/day for 12 months which may be gradually increased to 60 min/day and combined with strength exercise, prescribed by a physiotherapist. Aerobic exercise consisted of walking, swimming, or cycling. Resistance exercises involved the use of external weights or one's own body weight to perform movements. An adherence plan was implemented in the exercise group, including weekly calls, visits and an activity tracker to collect objective data. The reversibility/persistence/relapse of prediabetes was measured with fasting glucose and OGTT every 3 months to the end of the study, 12 months. Hereby, we present the preliminary data of patients who completed 6 months of follow-up.
Preliminary results
Nineteen patients reached 6 months of follow-up (exercise group: n = 8; control group: n = 11). In the exercise group, 5 patients (63%) reverted to normal glucose levels both at fasting (<100 mg/dL) and after an OGTT (<140 mg/dL) compared to 2 patients (18%) of the control group (P = 0.048). The exercise group also showed a significant reduction in weight (from 75 ± 15 kg to 70 ± 15 kg, P = 0.012) and triglycerides levels (from 131 ± 62 mg/dL to 101 ± 34 mg/dL, P = 0.028). The control group showed no changes in weight, triglycerides, etc. The mean adherence to exercise was 76 ± 13% of completed sessions. No adverse events have been observed in either group.
Conclusion
these preliminary results suggest that exercise is effective and safe for improving glucose metabolism and reverting prediabetes in renal transplant patients at risk of PTDM.

title: #3873 Beyond DSAs: unraveling the complexities of antibody-mediated rejection in kidney transplants
authors: Ana Sofia Domingos; João Figueiredo Martins; João Venda; Rita Gomes Carlos Leal; Helena Viana; Mário Ventura Góis; Cristina Rego de Freitas Mendes Jorge; Fernando Caeiro
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney transplantation is the gold standard treatment for end-stage renal disease, significantly improving survival and quality of life compared to dialysis. However, long-term graft survival remains a challenge due to factors like antibody-mediated rejection (AMR). AMR is characterized by the presence of donor-specific antibodies (DSAs), which are integral to both the pathogenesis and diagnosis of rejection. However, not all patients with AMR show detectable DSAs, leading to questions about the role of DSAs in graft loss and patient survival. This study aims to assess the impact of AMR histological changes in patients with and without DSAs.
Method
This retrospective study included adult kidney transplant patients from two Portuguese centers, focusing on those who exhibited AMR histology. Data on demographics, clinical history, and laboratory results were collected. DSAs and non-donor-specific antibodies (NDSAs) were assessed through Luminex® assays, while histological analysis followed Banff 2019 criteria, focusing on features such as glomerulitis, peritubular capillaritis, and C4d deposition. Statistical tests included the Chi-squared test for categorical variables, the Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables, and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis for graft and patient survival, with a significance threshold of P < 0.05.
Results
A total of 27 kidney transplant recipients were included, with a median age of 48.3 years. The cohort consisted of 11 (40.7%) female and 16 (59.3%) male patients. The majority were Caucasian (85.2%), and 22.2% had prior kidney transplants. HLA mismatch analysis showed 51.9% of patients had 2 mismatches for HLA-A, -B, and -DR, and 40.7% had 4 mismatches, as indicated in Fig. 1. Donors were mostly male (51.9%), with 33.3% being expanded criteria donors. Seven patients (25.9%) had preformed DSAs. Induction therapy included basiliximab (51.9%) and thymoglobulin (37%), while 96.3% of patients received tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone for maintenance.
Of the patients, 74.1% were DSA-positive, 22.2% had NDSAs, and 3.7% had neither. Graft loss occurred in 7 DSA-positive patients (35%) compared to 1 (16.7%) in the NDSA group, and mortality was observed in 2 DSA-positive patients (10%) but in none of the NDSA group. However, these differences were not statistically significant (graft loss P = 0.554, mortality P = 0.685). Figure 2 summarizes baseline characteristics by DSA status. Histological analysis showed acute AMR in 70.4%, with no significant differences in AMR between the DSA-positive and -negative groups (P = 0.277).
Regarding rejection treatment, patients treated with MPD + IVIG had a significantly higher mortality rate (P = 0.014). Graft loss was significantly associated with male donors (P = 0.016) and Class I DSAs (P = 0.038). At the time of rejection, the median serum creatinine was 3.4 mg/dL, decreasing to 2.075 mg/dL at 6 months and 2.160 mg/dL by the end of follow-up. DSA-positive patients had a significantly lower creatinine at rejection (2.705 mg/dL vs 4.800 mg/dL, P = 0.048), but no significant differences were observed after 6 months (P = 0.377) or at the end of follow-up (P = 0.311).
Conclusion
This study highlights the complexity of AMR in kidney transplantation, showing that DSA presence alone may not predict graft loss or mortality. Microvascular inflammation and other histopathological changes, as well as donor characteristics, also play a significant role in long-term outcomes. Further research is needed to identify additional biomarkers and refine therapeutic strategies, particularly for DSA-negative patients, to improve graft survival and reduce rejection risk. Enhanced monitoring and individualized treatment regimens based on a patient's immunological and histopathological profile are essential for optimizing AMR management.

title: #3852 Basiliximab versus anti-thymocyte immunoglobulin: renal and infectious outcomes in kidney transplant recipients
authors: João Figueiredo Martins; Ana Rita Pereirinha Ramos; Andreia Curto; Joana Monteiro Dias; Fernando Caeiro; Ines Aires; Manuel Anibal A Ferreira; Cristina Rego de Freitas Mendes Jorge
abstract:
Background and Aims
Immunosuppressive induction therapy for kidney transplantation typically includes basiliximab or anti-thymocyte immunoglobulin, depending on the recipient's immunological risk. Basiliximab is usually used in patients with lower rejection risk and may be associated with decreased infectious complications. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of chosen induction immunosuppression on rejection, graft function, and infectious events.
Method
We designed a retrospective study including all patients submitted to kidney transplantation between September 2022 and June 2024 at a reference transplant center, with a minimum follow-up of 6 months. All patients were submitted to a per-protocol graft biopsy in the first two weeks following transplantation. Double-organ recipients and those with graft loss due to vascular events were excluded. Clinical, laboratory and histological data were assessed. Data analysis included descriptive statistics, Student t-test, Mann-Whitney U-test and Pearson chi-square, as appropriate.
Results
We included 99 kidney transplant recipients (median age at transplantation 54 years), who received kidneys from live (11.1%), brain-dead (64.7%) and circulatory arrest donors (24.2%). Median follow-up was 512 days.
Biopsy-proven rejection occurred in 32.0% of patients (6.5% borderline, 61.3% T-cell-mediated, 29.0% antibody-mediated, 3.2% mixed).
Bacterial infections were observed in 37.4% of patients, CMV infection in 28.3% and BKV infection in 17.2%. No cases of CMV invasive disease were reported.
Graft loss was noted in 2.0% of patients, and death in 3.0%. All graft losses were due to rejection and all deaths had an infectious cause.
The basiliximab group experienced more rejections (χ2 = 4.510, p = 0.034) but did not show a higher incidence of graft loss (χ2 = 0.846, p = 0.358) or death (χ2 = 0.024, p = 0.876). Graft function did not differ significantly at 3 (p = 0.346), 6 (p = 0.407) or 12 months (p = 0.376) between groups. No association was found between rejection and pre-formed DSA, PRA-CDC or HLA mismatches.
Bacterial infection rates were similar between groups (χ2 = 0.704, p = 0.401). The basiliximab group had fewer BKV infections (χ2 = 5.431, p = 0.020) but more CMV infections (χ2 = 8.083, p = 0.004). CMV donor and recipient status was similar but prophylaxis prescription varied between groups (all anti-thymocyte immunoglobulin patients had received valganciclovir but only CMV IgG negative basiliximab patients had done so).
Conclusion
Kidney transplant recipients undergoing immunosuppression with basiliximab seem to have higher risk of rejection but with no difference in short-term graft function, graft loss or death. Protocol biopsies enabled early diagnosis and treatment of rejection, likely mitigating its impact on graft function. Classical immunological high risk factors were not associated with rejection, presumably due to their influence on the initial immunosuppression choice.
Remarkably, there was no difference in bacterial infection occurrence between both groups. The benefit of basiliximab induction seemed to be less BKV infection.
Longer follow-up is needed to evaluate if these comparable renal outcomes remain the same in the long-term.

title: #2594 Complement system evaluation in blood group incompatible living donor kidney transplantation
authors: Marina Moncada; Julia Martínez; Patricia Molina; Anna Manonelles; Elena Guillén Olmos; Diana Rodríguez Espinosa; Carlos Couceiro; Josep Maria Cruzado Garrit; Marta Palomo; Ignacio Revuelta; Maribel Díaz-Ricart; Miquel Blasco Pelicano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Blood group incompatible living donor kidney transplantation (ABO-iLKT) may allow expanding the living donor pool up to 10%–30%, although a high-risk rejection exists due to anti-blood group antibodies (isoagglutinins) presence and infection rates. Complement dysregulation and endothelial damage are key factors in regulating the immune-mediated injury. The aims are studying complement system and endothelium involvement as potential main elements and to explore in vitro the effect of a complement inhibitory drug (eculizumab) and an endothelial protective agent (defibrotide) as potential therapeutic strategies in ABOi_LKT.
Method
Terminal complement dysregulation was studied through the analysis of C5b-9 deposition on endothelial cells culture in ABO-iLKT patients (n = 10) classified by isoagglutinin levels (high (escriure dilució que hem agafat en cada interval), intermediate and low). Plasma samples were collected at pre-transplantation (T1) and 48h post-transplantation (T2). T2 condition was also incubated in vitro with eculizumab or defibrotide. Area percentage of C5b-9 deposition was expressed in fold increase with respect to T1 of each group of patients.
Results
The group with high isoagglutinin levels showed a significant increase of C5b-9 deposition at T2 and it was significantly reduced in presence of eculizumab and defibrotide (fold increase: 1.6, 0.2 and 0.7, P < 0.05, respectively). In the group of intermediate isoagglutinin levels, a slight increment in T2 was observed (fold increase: 1.1), and T2 incubated with both drugs showed a significant reduction (fold increase: 0.4 and 0.4, P < 0.05, respectively). The group of low isoagglutinin levels exhibited less C5b-9 deposition in T2 and in presence of eculizumab and defibrotide (fold increase: 0.6, 0.2, P < 0.05, and 0.6, respectively).
Conclusion
An increment of C5b-9 deposition after transplantation in ABO-iLKT patients with elevated isoagglutinin levels indicates an overactivation of terminal complement system. This overactivation could be related with higher risk of rejection when isoagglutinin levels are increased. The role of terminal complement blockers and defibrotide can be considered as therapeutic targets in ABO-iLKT context.

title: #2415 Association of early post-donation weight gain with kidney function in obese living kidney donors
authors: Ekamol Tantisattamo; Nicha Wareesawetsuwan; Kanita Mankan; Weerinth Puyati; Nopavit Mohpichai; Urairat Chuenchaem; Wanprapit Noree; Thutpharritchn Phoonakh; Varissara Sinkajarern; Voramol Rochanaroon; Possawat Vutthikraivit; Napat Wongmat; Richelle May Cajoles-Pagarigan
abstract:
Background and Aims
Pre-donation obesity is associated with poor kidney function post-donation. The impact and magnitude of early weight gain post-donation on kidney function is unclear.
Method
A retrospective cohort study using data from OPTN/SRTR included living kidney donors (LKD) undergoing kidney donation between 6/1972 and 9/2022 and generally had follow-up ≥3 visits at 6, 12, and 24 months post-donation. The patients were categorized into 2 groups based on early post-donation weight change (weight gain vs. no weight gain). The association between early post-donation weight gain defined by increased BMI within 2 months post-transplant compared to pre-donation BMI and time-to-event of worsening post-donation kidney function ≥35% from the baseline pre-donation kidney function was examined by multiple Cox proportional hazards regression analysis.
Results
Of 174,311 adult living kidney donors (LKD), 30,422 patients had pre-donation obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m2). Mean age was 41.57 ± 11.05 years and 59.30% were female. The majority were Whites (66.04%) followed by Hispanic (16.15%), Black (14.86%), Asian (1.45%), American Indian/Alaska Native (0.67%), multiracial (0.56%), and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (0.26%). Mean pre- and early post-donation weights were 93.37 ± 13.33 and 91.99 ± 13.68 kg, respectively (meandiff -1.39 ± 8.28; 95%CI −1.50, −1.27; P < 0.0001) (Fig. 1A and B). The incidence rate of worsening post-donation kidney function was 0.08 person-months during the median follow-up time of 6.73 months. Compared to patients without post-donation weight gain, those with weight gain were 24% greater risk of developing the event (HR 1.24; 95% CI 1.18, 1.30; P < 0.0001; Fig. 2A). After adjusting for age, gender, U.S. citizenship, level of education, pre-donation body mass index, hypertension, diabetes, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), proteinuria, and the interaction term between post-donation weight change and race (Black vs. non-Black), the association remained with greater magnitude of the association (HR 1.34, 95%CI 1.09, 1.65; P = 0.006; Fig. 2B). Race was an effect-measured modifier with a decreased risk of the decline in eGFR ≥35% observed in Black LKD (HRinteraction 0.51; 95% CI 0.28, 0.94; P = 0.031).
Conclusion
In addition to pre-donation obesity, early weight gain within 2 months post-donation worsens post-donation kidney function, particularly among non-Blacks. While Blacks are at risk for kidney disease, their risk for the decline in kidney function post-donation is not higher. Therefore, living kidney donation should not be excluded based on race.

title: #2719 Molecular profiling of renal function after liver transplantation
authors: Nadja Grobe; Xiaoling Wang; Barbara Franchin; Josh Levitsky; Paolo Cravedi; Peter Kotanko
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal dysfunction is a common and serious complication in patients with end-stage liver diseases (ESLD). While some patients recover renal function after liver transplantation (LT), others do not. Moreover, patients with normal kidney function (NKF) before LT may develop post-transplant renal dysfunction. Early identification of patients at risk for impaired kidney function (IKF) post-LT is critical to improving outcomes. In this study, we employed integrated metabolomic and proteomic analyses to characterize molecular profiles distinguishing NKF from IKF post-LT. Additionally, we examined a patient demonstrating recovered renal function following LT.
Method
This study included ten ESLD patients from the multicenter clinical study (NCT01672164), all of whom underwent LT. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) was estimated using the CKD-EPI creatinine-based formula. Of these patients, 5 patients (No.1 to 5) with an eGFR greater than 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 both before and 2 weeks after LT were classified into the NKF group. Four patients (No. 7 to 10) with eGFR less than 45 ml/min/1.73 m2 both before and 2 weeks after LT were assigned to IKF group. The baseline characteristics of patients at the time of LT were comparable between the two groups, and no significant differences in liver function were observed two weeks post-LT. The remaining patient (No. 6), with an eGFR of 23 mL/min/1.73 m2 before LT, showed an increase in eGFR to 76 mL/min/1.73 m2 14 days post-LT and to 102 mL/min/1.73 m2 35 days post-LT. This patient was designated as a recovered case.
Serum samples were collected from each patient at 2 weeks (mean 17 ± 4 days; range 13–24 days) and 5 weeks (mean 36 ± 15 days, range 20–66 days) post-transplantation. All samples were stored at −80°C until analysis. Metabolomic and proteomic profiles were assessed by untargeted liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry using Agilent Q-TOF 6546.
Results
Metabolomic analysis identified 108 non-drug metabolites, with 29 significantly altered between NKF and IKF (fold change >2, P < 0.05). Among these, 9 were enriched in NKF, and 20 were enriched in IKF, including creatinine. Principal component analysis (PCA) showed a clear separation between NKF and IKF (Fig. 1A). Samples from the recovered patient (No. 6) on day 14 and day 35 were positioned near the NKF group, with the day-35 sample trending even closer (Fig. 1A). Using the average signal from two samples of the same patients, hierarchical clustering similarly grouped the recovered patient with the NKF group, consistent with the PCA results (Fig. 1B).
Proteomic analysis identified 174 proteins, with 45 proteins differentially expressed between NKF and IKF (fold change >1.25, P < 0.05). Of these, 43 proteins exhibited higher expression in the NKF group, while only 2 proteins showed higher expression in the IKF group: beta-2-microglobin and protein AMBP (alpha-1-microglobulin/bikunin precursor). PCA revealed a separation between NKF and IKF (Fig. 1C), although this separation was less distinct than what was observed for metabolites. Interestingly, for the recovered patient (No. 6), both samples clustered closely with the IKF group, with the day 35 sample trending towards the NKF group (Fig. 1C). In hierarchical clustering, this patient was grouped with the IKF group, contrasting with the results from metabolomic profiling (Fig. 1D).
Conclusion
This study revealed distinct metabolomic and proteomic signatures associated with renal function post-LT. Proteomic profiles indicated a delayed recovery compared to metabolomic profiles, suggesting a dynamic and multi-layered renal recovery process. These findings highlight the limitations of relying solely on serum creatinine measurements to assess kidney recovery or ongoing dysfunction in LT recipients. Incorporating additional monitoring strategies could offer a more comprehensive evaluation of kidney health and facilitate timely interventions. Further research is warranted to elucidate the functional implications of the differential proteins and metabolites for improved monitoring and therapeutic strategies.

title: #905 Immunosuppressive treatment with two drugs (tacrolimus and prednisone) in older adult kidney transplant recipients
authors: Ariadna González García; María José Pérez-Saéz; Anna Buxeda; Betty Odette Chamoun Huacon; Carla Burballa; Aida Martinez; Yolanda Castillo; Michelle Andrea Linárez Brea; Marta Crespo; Dolores Redondo-Pachón
abstract:
Background and Aims
The immunosuppressive regimen in kidney transplant (KT) that has shown the greatest efficacy consists of triple therapy with tacrolimus + mycophenolate + prednisone or tacrolimus + everolimus + prednisone, with no major changes made to adapt to the new profile of kidney transplant recipients (KTR). Often, it is necessary to suspend the third immunosuppressive drug, either due to intolerance or infectious/neoplastic events. Our objective was to analyze KTR on dual therapy and compare their baseline characteristics and posttransplant outcomes with those on triple therapy.
Method
A retrospective study analyzing 552 KTRs (January 2017–March 2022). Data were collected on donor, recipient, and post-transplant outcomes. The median follow-up was 49.5 [32–66] months.
Results
The mean recipient age was 59 years, 41.9% female. 41.9% were on dual therapy with tacrolimus + prednisone at 11 (IQR 3–35) months post-transplant (56.3% initially started with tacrolimus + mycophenolate; 43.7% with tacrolimus + everolimus). The reason for the suspension was infectious events in 64.3%. Analyzing by age, 19.3% of KTRs <65 years suspended the third drug at 14 months post-transplant compared to 54.7% of those ≥65 years who did so at 7.5 months. Only 21.6% had the third drug reintroduced. Patients requiring suspension of the third drug were older, had grafts from older donors, and had worse renal function outcomes. Additionally, patients on dual therapy had more infectious and neoplastic events, with no increase in acute rejection or development of DSA. Multivariate analysis showed that age ≥65 years (OR 2.01 [1.2–3.2]) and having been readmitted ≥3 times for post-transplant infection (OR 3.2 [1.8–5.6]) were factors associated with suspension of an immunosuppressive drug post- transplant.
Conclusion
The suspension of the third immunosuppressive drug is a common phenomenon, especially in older adults KTRs, and usually occurs after infectious/neoplastic events. Anticipating these events and designing more individualized immunosuppression schemes should be a focus of our efforts in the upcoming years.

title: #724 Kidney transplant outcomes in highly sensitized patients with preformed donor-specific antibodies using a DELISTING strategy
authors: Alba Arrebola Montes; Florentino Villanego; María José Torres Sánchez; Inés de la Cueva Flores; Carolina Polo Criado; Antonio Rodríguez; Antonio Nieto; Cristina Gutiérrez de la Fuente; Auxiliadora Mazuecos; Verónica López
abstract:
Background and Aims
Highly sensitized patients represent a significant challenge in kidney transplantation (KT) due to the limited availability of compatible donors and the high risk of antibody-mediated rejection. In this context, the delisting of forbidden HLA antigens emerges as a key strategy to expand transplantation opportunities for this population.
Method
This observational, multicenter, descriptive, and retrospective study included highly sensitized patients (cPRA ≥ 98%) who underwent delisting strategies prior to KT between December 2018 and June 2024.
The delisting process was carried out gradually, initially allowing KT in the presence of low-intensity anti-HLA antibodies (MFI < 4000). In cases where cPRA levels did not decrease, a more aggressive delisting approach was adopted, permitting antibodies with an MFI of up to 10,000. Complement-binding antibodies detected by C1q assays and antibodies targeting antigens from previous transplants were excluded.
The primary objective of the study was to analyze the outcomes of KT following the delisting of forbidden HLA antigens, aiming to reduce cPRA to <98%.
Results
The study included 17 KT patients from three hospitals in Andalusia, all with preformed donor-specific antibodies (DSA) after applying delisting strategies. All patients had a negative complement-dependent cytotoxicity cross-match. The average age was 50 ± 10 years, with 65% female patients and a median dialysis duration of 59 [39–127] months . The time from delisting to transplantation was 16 [4–23] months. Sixty-five percent had undergone a prior transplant. The mean cPRA before delisting was 99.5 ± 0.6, which decreased to 88 ± 14 after delisting. The mean number of mismatches was 5.2 ± 1.3. The number of DSAs at the time of KT was 2 [1.5–3]. Post-transplant desensitization was performed in 82% of patients following the routine clinical practice of each center, and all received induction therapy with Thymoglobulin. Six patients developed acute rejection (five humoral, one mixed) within 12 [9–35] days post-transplant. Among post-transplant complications, 47% experienced infections, including 23% with CMV. Ninety-three percent of grafts were functional at 7 [4–50] months post-transplant, with renal function at 6 and 12 months post-transplant of 48 [27–61] ml/min and 54 [40–66] ml/min, respectively. Patient survival was 100%.
Conclusion
The implementation of delisting strategies optimizes the chances of KT in highly sensitized patients with preformed donor-specific antibodies. Despite a high incidence of acute rejection and infections, the majority of grafts remain functional with acceptable renal function. These findings highlight the effectiveness of delisting in improving access to transplantation in this complex population.

title: #3498 Uremic burden as a predictor of preemptive kidney transplant outcome: insight from a decision tree analysis in France
authors: Orsolya Cseprekal; Emilie Savoye; Nasser Al Hawajri; Camille Legeai; Benedicte Stengel; Ziad Massy; Christian Jacquelinet
abstract:
Background and Aims
Timing of preemptive kidney transplantation (PKT) and the role of eGFR change in outcome prediction remain a subject of debate. This study aims to assess potential factors, with special attention to uremic burden, which may be associated with 5-year outcomes. In our retrospective observational cohort study, first PKT adults registered in CRISTAL between 2013–2019 were analyzed to elucidate the role of eGFR and other associating factors with death and graftloss.
Method
Recipient, donor and transplantation related features were analyzed by using multivariable logistic regression analysis. Conditional inference tree was applied for risk stratification.
Results
2327 first PKT (52.8 (IQR 43–64) years; 38% females) were included. Mean percentage of PKT over time was 14%. Primary kidney disease (congenital anomalies, glomerulonephritis and other causes versus ADPKD), donor age and number of DR mismatches associated with combined 5-year outcomes (OR 2.64 (CI 95% 1.42–4.93); 1.94 (1.1–4.93); 1.76 (1.06–2.92); 1.03 (1.02–1.05); 1.67 (1.1–2.53) P < 0.05), whereas donor type was not associated with the outcomes. By supervised decision-tree analysis, more than 30% risk of failure in PKT was attributed to high recipient risk, higher donor age, uremic burden index (UBI)—a novel parameter defined by the product of eGFR change and the logarithmic time on waiting list—and 2 DR mismatches.
Conclusion
In conclusion, eGFR and donor type were not associated with death or graft failure in PKT. UBI can potentially be a novel parameter of uremic burden and contribute to predict 5-year risk of failure. Clinical decision based on objective risk estimations might be crucial to approach the “PKT in due course” concept.

title: #3671 Longitudinal analysis of the urinary Dickkopf-related protein 3 and its association with kidney function following kidney transplantation
authors: Firas Farisi Alkaff; Daan Kremer; Tim J Knobbe; Rima Destya Triatin; Jiasi Hao; Danilo Fliser; Franz Paul Armbruster; Transplantlines Investigators; Stefan P Berger; Jacob van den Born; Stephan J L Bakker
abstract:
Background and Aims
Previously, urinary Dickkopf-related protein 3 (uDKK3), a stress-induced tubular cell-derived profibrotic glycoprotein, was shown to be associated with tubulointerstitial fibrosis and loss of kidney function in patients with chronic kidney disease. However, its value in kidney transplant recipients (KTR) is debated, potentially because of a disturbing influence of uDKK3 that is also excreted by native kidneys. We aimed to investigate changes of uDKK3 over time and to evaluate its association with changes of kidney function in KTR without urine production prior to transplantation.
Method
Data of KTR enrolled in the TransplantLines Biobank and Cohort Study were used. To eliminate the influence of uDKK3 from the recipients’ kidneys, we only selected KTR that underwent dialysis and were anuric prior to transplantation. uDKK3 was measured using a commercially available ELISA kit in the 24-hour urine samples that were taken at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months after transplantation. The estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was calculated using the 2009 CKD-EPI creatinine-based equation. Changes in uDKK3 over time and its association with eGFR were analyzed using a linear mixed model. The fitted model was checked for homogeneity of variance and normality of residuals to ensure that the model assumption was not violated. uDKK3 were log2-transformed when assessing the changes in uDKK3 over time and scaled when assessing the association with eGFR, as it gives the best model fit based on the Akaike Information Criterion values. Missing observations in covariates were multiply imputed using Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations.
Results
We included 78 KTR (67% male, 63% received a kidney from a deceased donor, 29% with delayed graft function) in the analyses. At baseline (3 months after transplantation), mean (SD) age was 56 (15) years, mean (SD) eGFR was 46 (17) ml/min/1.73 m², median [Q1–Q3] 24 h urinary protein excretion was 0.19 [0.12–0.24] g/24 h, and median [Q1–Q3] 24 h uDKK3 excretion was 1827 [485–5496] ng/24 h. The median [Q1–Q3] intra-individual variation of 24 h uDKK3 excretion over the observed period was 6.8 [5.6–12.4] %. The effect of time on 24 h uDKK3 excretion was not significant (P = 0.3), indicating that the level of 24 h uDKK3 excretion did not significantly change over the observation period (Fig. 1). For the association of 24 h uDKK3 excretion and eGFR, our analysis showed that eGFR decreases by approximately 2.05 mL/min/1.73 m2 per 1 SD increase in 24 h uDKK3 excretion (Table 1). There was no interaction between 24 h uDKK3 excretion and time (pinteraction = 0.2), indicating that the association between 24 h uDKK3 excretion and eGFR did not change over time. Furthermore, there was also no interaction between 24 h uDKK3 excretion and 24 h urinary protein excretion (pinteraction = 0.4).
Conclusion
Our findings showed that uDKK3 is a stable biomarker. Furthermore, it is independently associated with loss of eGFR, regardless of the time measurement. This showed that uDKK3 is a potential non-invasive biomarker for monitoring the outcome of KTR.

title: #2425 Prevalence and correlates of hepatic steatosis and fibrosis in chronic kidney disease patients prior of kidney transplantation: a retrospective cohort study
authors: Carlo Alfieri; Rosa Lombardi; Anna Regalia; Simona Verdesca; Paolo Molinari; Anna Pisacreta; Margherita Di Naro; Giuseppe Castellano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Metabolic dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), is closely linked to CKD and increases the risk of hepatic fibrosis and cardiovascular damage. MASLD is common in the general population but data on dialysis patients is limited. We aim to assess the prevalence of MASLD and related factors in kidney transplant patients at the time of list admission.
Method
We studied 531 kidney transplant patients (age 49 ± 13, 59% male) from 2010–2020. We noted their data at admission. Hepatic steatosis (HS) was gauged by hepatic steatosis index (HSI), with >36 as pathological (HSI+). Advanced fibrosis (>F3) was assessed by Fibrosis-4 index (FIB4), with >1.3 and >2.66 as borderline and pathological (FIB4+), and the NAFLD Fibrosis Score (NFS), with >−1.455 and >0.676 as borderline and pathological (NFS+).
Results
In our study, 67.2% of patients had hemodialysis. At evaluation, 8.8% had diabetes, 15% were obese, and 37.5% had steroid treatment history. Glomerulonephritis and polycystic kidney disease caused nephropathy in 20% and 18% of cases, respectively. HSI, FIB4, and NFS averages were 32.9 ± 6.01, 1.25 ± 1.07, and −1.75 ± 1.5. FIB-4 and NFS correlated strongly (r = 0.65, P < 0.0001). HS by HSI+ was in 27.5% of patients, while hepatic fibrosis by FIB4+ and NFS+ was in 32.8% and 39.3% of patients. HSI+ patients were older with higher BMI, glucose, and urea levels. FIB4+ and NFS+ patients were older with higher glucose and CRP levels. NFS+ patients had higher BMI. These results confirm the concordance between the two fibrosis markers.
In multivariate analysis, BMI and urea were independent risk factors for hepatic steatosis by HSI, while age and CRP were independent risk factors for hepatic fibrosis by both FIB4+ and NFS+.
Conclusion
Our data reveals a high occurrence of MASLD in patients awaiting kidney transplants, particularly in older, overweight individuals. Inflammatory parameters independently predicted hepatic fibrosis, suggesting their potential role. FIB4 and NFS showed a strong correlation, validating their use as fibrosis markers. Future research could shed light on the causes, risk factors, and impacts of HS and fibrosis on kidney transplant outcomes.

Background and Aims
Metabolic dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), is closely linked to CKD and increases the risk of hepatic fibrosis and cardiovascular damage. MASLD is common in the general population but data on dialysis patients is limited. We aim to assess the prevalence of MASLD and related factors in kidney transplant patients at the time of list admission.
Method
We studied 531 kidney transplant patients (age 49 ± 13, 59% male) from 2010–2020. We noted their data at admission. Hepatic steatosis (HS) was gauged by hepatic steatosis index (HSI), with >36 as pathological (HSI+). Advanced fibrosis (>F3) was assessed by Fibrosis-4 index (FIB4), with >1.3 and >2.66 as borderline and pathological (FIB4+), and the NAFLD Fibrosis Score (NFS), with >−1.455 and >0.676 as borderline and pathological (NFS+).
Results
In our study, 67.2% of patients had hemodialysis. At evaluation, 8.8% had diabetes, 15% were obese, and 37.5% had steroid treatment history. Glomerulonephritis and polycystic kidney disease caused nephropathy in 20% and 18% of cases, respectively. HSI, FIB4, and NFS averages were 32.9 ± 6.01, 1.25 ± 1.07, and −1.75 ± 1.5. FIB-4 and NFS correlated strongly (r = 0.65, P < 0.0001). HS by HSI+ was in 27.5% of patients, while hepatic fibrosis by FIB4+ and NFS+ was in 32.8% and 39.3% of patients. HSI+ patients were older with higher BMI, glucose, and urea levels. FIB4+ and NFS+ patients were older with higher glucose and CRP levels. NFS+ patients had higher BMI. These results confirm the concordance between the two fibrosis markers.
In multivariate analysis, BMI and urea were independent risk factors for hepatic steatosis by HSI, while age and CRP were independent risk factors for hepatic fibrosis by both FIB4+ and NFS+.
Conclusion
Our data reveals a high occurrence of MASLD in patients awaiting kidney transplants, particularly in older, overweight individuals. Inflammatory parameters independently predicted hepatic fibrosis, suggesting their potential role. FIB4 and NFS showed a strong correlation, validating their use as fibrosis markers. Future research could shed light on the causes, risk factors, and impacts of HS and fibrosis on kidney transplant outcomes.

title: #1972 Impact of proton pump inhibitor use on renal function in kidney transplant recipients: a longitudinal cohort study
authors: Wiam Dakdouk; Hiba Azar; Maissa Safieddine; Serge Finianos; Dania Nehme Chelala
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney transplantation is considered the optimal treatment for chronic kidney disease. However, recipients often require lifelong immunosuppressive medications and management of comorbidities, leading to polypharmacy. This can raise concerns about potential drug interactions and adverse effects on graft function. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are among the most commonly prescribed medications. Yet, the long-term effects of PPIs on graft survival remain uncertain. The aim of this study is to investigate the impact of PPI use on kidney function in transplant recipients.
Method
This retrospective, single-center cohort study included adult patients who underwent kidney transplantation at Hotel Dieu de France University Hospital between 2015 and 2022. Only patients with relatively stable kidney function were included, excluding recipients with a history of for cause biopsy. Two groups were created based on PPI use. Clinical and demographic data were collected, and graft function was assessed using the CKD-EPI formula at 6 months and end of follow-up. The primary outcome was the difference in relative kidney function decline between 6 months and the end of follow-up, while secondary outcomes included the incidence of gastrointestinal bleeding and new-onset post-transplant diabetes (NODAT). Descriptive statistics were performed on clinical characteristics, and multivariate linear regression analysis was conducted to evaluate the association between PPI and outcomes.
Results
A total of 129 patients were included, 62 were in the PPI-negative group and 65 in the PPI-positive group. The mean follow-up duration was 5.25 ± 2.14 years. At baseline, PPI users were significantly older than non-users (47 ± 15.2 vs. 39 ± 13.9, P = 0.004). Dyslipidaemia (63.1% vs. 35.5%, P = 0.003) and body mass index (BMI) were significantly higher in the PPI-positive group at both 6 months (25.6 ± 4.17 vs. 23.76 ± 4.33 kg/m², P = 0.016) and at the end of follow-up (28.16 ± 4.49 vs. 25.97 ± 4.15 kg/m², P = 0.005). The prevalence of diabetes was also higher in the PPI-positive group (44.6% vs. 24.2%, P = 0.026). However, there was no significant difference between the groups in the incidence of new-onset diabetes (NODAT) (24.6% vs. 14.5%, P = 0.227), or gastrointestinal bleeding (P = 1.0).
Regarding renal function, the primary analysis showed a significant decrease in mean eGFR in the PPI-positive group (−5.86 ± 4.16 mL/min/1.73 m²), compared to an improvement or stability in the PPI-negative group (1.52 ± 4.53 mL/min/1.73 m², P < 0.001). In the multivariate analysis, after adjusting for potential confounders, PPI use remained independently associated with a significant eGFR decline (P < 0.001), with a 10% greater reduction in eGFR compared to the PPI-negative group.
Conclusion
Kidney transplant recipients who use PPIs for an extended period experience a greater loss of graft function compared to non-users. The incidence of gastrointestinal bleeding is rare and does not differ significantly between PPI and non-PPI users. These findings are in concordance with previous studies incriminating PPI use with kidney function decline and question their systematic use in kidney transplant recipients.

title: #1603 Factors associated with early mortality in kidney transplant recipients ≥70 years old
authors: Onia Franquet; Betty Odette Chamoun Huacon; Dolores Redondo-Pachón; Cristina Amoros; Aida Martinez; Carla Burballa; Almudena Juez; Marta Crespo; María José Pérez-Saéz; Anna Buxeda
abstract:
Background and Aims
Older adult kidney transplant recipients (KTRs) face an increased risk of mortality during the first year post-transplant, with a 12-month post-transplant survival rate below 90%. Little is known about early mortality after returning to dialysis. This study aimed to identify factors associated with early mortality to improve outcomes in this vulnerable population.
Method
We conducted a retrospective single-center study of 210 KTRs aged ≥70 years who received deceased donor grafts between 2012 and 2020. Median follow-up until death or April 2024 was 29.24 [8.34–46.88] months, regardless of graft functionality. Early mortality was defined as death occurring within 18 months post-transplant.
Results
The mean recipient age was 74.3 ± 4 years, and 32.8% were women. During follow-up, 31 (14.8%) KTRs died early after transplantation. Patients in the early mortality group were older and had a higher prevalence of cerebrovascular disease (CVD) [Table 1]. No differences were observed in donor characteristics between groups. Recipients in the early mortality group had a higher incidence of non-functioning grafts (PNF, 25.81% vs. 11.17%), delayed graft function (DGF, 54.17% vs. 33.33%), and longer initial hospital stays (25 vs. 14 days). Additionally, they achieved poorer renal function: nadir creatinine (2.09 vs. 1.53 mg/dL) and eGFR at 3 months post-transplant (24 mL/min vs. 36.66 mL/min). Multivariate analysis confirmed pre-transplant CVD (HR 4.8 [1.8–13.1], P = 0.002), PNF (HR 15.4 [1.7–141.1], P = 0.016), and eGFR at 3 months post-transplantation (HR 0.93 [0.87–0.99], P = 0.029) as independent predictors of early mortality. No differences in mortality causes were observed between groups.
Conclusion
Early mortality occurred in 14.8% of KTRs aged ≥70. PNF, poor renal function, and pre-transplant CVD were identified as significant risk factors for early mortality in this age group. Targeted interventions to optimize renal function in these patients could also enhance their survival.

title: #2665 Maternal kidney disease and offspring neurodevelopmental outcomes: a nationwide population-based study
authors: Jeongin Song
abstract:
Background and Aims
Maternal immune activation, triggered by both acute and systemic chronic inflammation, is considered a predisposing factor for offspring neurodevelopmental conditions. However, there is no data about the effect of mothers’ chronic kidney disease on their offspring's neurodevelopmental diseases.
Method
We extracted the data on pregnant women from the National Health Information Database from 2008 to 2017 in South Korea. Subjects were categorized into 4 groups: no CKD, CKD, ESKD (end-stage kidney disease), and kidney transplantation (KT) group according to their pre-pregnancy kidney function. The outcomes are defined as offspring's neurodevelopmental diseases, including motor and cognitive developmental delay, autism spectrum disorders, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, tics, stereotypic behavior, and seizures based on ICD-10-CM codes.
Results
A total of 3,794,031 children were born to 2,680,092 mothers during the study period. We included 487,477 mothers without kidney diseases, 47,099 mothers with CKD, 51 mothers with ESKD, 200 mothers with KT, and 3,637,903 children after the exclusion of multiple pregnancies. Mothers with CKD, ESKD, and KT had older ages and more co-morbidities than those without. They suffered from more adverse pregnancy outcomes, such as preeclampsia, preterm birth, and placenta previa/abruption. Their offspring's neurodevelopmental disease occurred in 13.4%, 15.6%, 36.2%, and 21.5% of the no CKD, CKD, KRT, and KT groups, respectively. Mothers with CKD (adjusted HR [95% CI]: 1.09 [1.07–1.11], P < 0.001), KT (1.24 [0.94–1.65], and ESKD (1.98 [1.33–2.93], P < 0.001) showed a higher risk of offspring's neurodevelopmental diseases even after adjusting for maternal age, parity, underlying hypertension, diabetes, gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, neonatal sex, preterm birth, place of residence, and income level.
Conclusion
In this nationwide cohort study, we first found that maternal pre-pregnancy kidney function was associated with offspring's adverse neurodevelopmental diseases in dose-responsive manners.

title: #2974 Human leukocyte antigen alleles associated with acute antibody-mediated rejection in kidney transplantation in a Mexican population
authors: Carolina Gonzalez-Fuentes; Horacio Cano; Monica Escamilla Tilch; Pamela Michelle Prado Lozano; Mayra Matias Carmona; Citlali Fernández; Rigina Hernandez Canade; Martin Benjamin Yama Estrella; Víctor Ulloa-Galvan
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute antibody mediated rejection (AMR) affects 25% of transplant patients. Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) genetic variation is associated with the immune response. The main objective was to determine the association between human leukocyte antigen alleles and susceptibility to acute rejection in kidney transplantation.
Method
Cross-sectional study. HLA typing was performed in Mexican kidney transplant patients with living or cadaveric donors at least one year after surgery, and the frequencies of allelic and haplotypic blocks were compared between the group with antibody-mediated rejection and the group without rejection. Ancestral, demographic, and clinical information was obtained from patients and medical records.
Results
106 patients were included. 61% were male with a median age of 35 years. 59% of the patients had experienced sensitization events prior to transplantation, mainly with blood transfusions, but the median panel reactive antibody (PRA) was 0. 59% of the patients had a standard immunologic risk at the time of transplantation. The aetiology of kidney disease was unknown in 60% of patients, followed by glomerulopathies in 26%. Kidney donors were female (58%) and 30% of transplants were from cadaveric donors. 53% of patients had induction immunosuppression with basiliximab, 87% were on triple-drug maintenance immunosuppression with prednisone, tacrolimus and mycophenolate; median tacrolimus level was 8.7 ng/dl. The highest gene frequencies in the population for class I alleles were A*02 and A*24, B*39 and B*40, C*07 and C*04. Within class II, the highest gene frequencies were DR*04, DR*08, DQA1*03 and DQA1*05, DQB1*03 and DQB1*05, DPA1*01 and DPA1*02, and DPB1*04 and DPB1*02. HLA-C, HLA-DQ and HLA-DP alleles have not been previously reported in the Mexican kidney transplant population. Fifty-seven patients were diagnosed with AMR; at the time of AMR, PRA class I had a median of 3 and class II had a median of 7. 53% of patients with AMR developed donor-specific antibodies. The alleles found to confer susceptibility risk for AMR were B*39 (OR 2.4), C*07 (OR 3.2), DQB1*05 (OR 2.9), and DPB1*04 (OR 3); however, the alleles B*35 (OR 0.29) and C*04 (OR 0.25) were found to be protective. The haplotype block B*39-DR*08 (OR 2.95) was associated with increased risk and the haplotype blocks B*35-C*04 (OR 0.14) and DR*13-DQA1*01-DQB1*06 (0.15) were protective. A subgroup analysis was performed on HLA-C*07 risk alleles, where demographic and clinical variables in patients carrying the C*07 allele were evaluated univariately between the group with AMR and without diagnosis of rejection, in which it was found that male donors donating to patients with C*07 allele are more associated with AMR (P = 0.007), although there was no difference between immunologic risk (P = 0.49) or induction therapy (P = 0.8). For the subgroup with the HLA-DQB1*05 allele, univariate analysis showed that patients in this subgroup had a high immunologic risk at the time of transplantation (P = 0.04), although there was no statistically significant difference in sensitizing events (P = 0.14).
Conclusion
In the Mexican population, B*39, C*07, DQB1*05 and DPB1*04 alleles confer an increased risk of developing antibody-mediated rejection, so early identification and close monitoring of immunosuppression in these patients is essential to avoid immunological complications of kidney transplantation.

title: #612 Clinical experience with extracorporeal photopheresis in BK Virus-associated nephropathy
authors: Víctor Joaquín Escudero Saiz; Marc Xipell Font; Ángela González; Maria Iraola; Rodrigo Zolezzi Ramirez; Paola Charry; Gaston Piñeiro; Marta Bodro; Joan Cid; Federico Oppenheimer; Miquel Lozano; Fritz Diekmann
abstract:
Background and Aims
BK virus-associated nephropathy (BKVAN) remains a major risk factor for kidney graft loss, particularly in transplant recipients under strong immunosuppression. While reducing immunosuppressive therapy is the cornerstone of BKVAN management, it increases the risk of graft rejection, especially in high-risk patients. Adjuvant therapies, such as intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), leflunomide, and mTOR inhibitors, have been employed with varying success but lack robust evidence. Extracorporeal photopheresis (ECP), an immunomodulatory therapy, has shown promise in conditions involving T-cell-mediated immunity, such as graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) and solid organ rejection in lung, heart and liver transplants. Limited data also suggest its potential immunogenic effects against infections. This study describes the outcomes of ECP in 13 kidney transplant recipients with refractory BKVAN after failure of standard therapies.
Method
A retrospective analysis was conducted at Hospital Clínic from Barcelona between 2018 and 2024. Patients had histologically confirmed BKVAN and underwent ECP after unsuccessful management with immunosuppressant reduction and adjunctive therapies. The cohort had a median age of 51 years [IQR: 42–59], with 46% considered low immunological risk (cPRA 0%) and 54% high risk (cPRA >50%). The median time from transplantation to BKVAN diagnosis was 38.4 weeks [34–58.8]. Prior treatments included tacrolimus reduction (100%), IVIG (77%, median 7.1 weeks after diagnosis), mTOR inhibitors (77%), and leflunomide (15%). ECP was initiated a median of 21.3 weeks [5.9–49.1] after BKVAN diagnosis, with patients receiving a median of 11 sessions [10–20]. Each session processed one total blood volume, employing citrate anticoagulation and UVA irradiation.
Results
BKV viremia peaked at ECP initiation (3.66M cp/mL [847K–7.71M]) and subsequently declined by 55.3%, 95.9%, 99.7%, and 99.9% at 3, 6, 12, and 18 months, respectively (Fig. 1). Despite these reductions, renal function progressively declined, with eGFR decreasing from 40 mL/min/1.73 m² at ECP initiation to 22.5 mL/min/1.73 m² at 18 months. Chronicity indices in baseline biopsies, including interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy (IFTA = 2), interstitial inflammation (ci = 2), and tubular atrophy (ct = 2), likely contributed to irreversible graft damage. Additionally, delayed ECP initiation post-diagnosis may have limited its efficacy. Histologic follow-up demonstrated improvements in three patients, with reductions in BK virus load and negative SV40 immunohistochemistry. Stabilization of graft function was observed in 80% of patients, with only two cases of graft loss due to BKVAN progression (15%). One patient experienced chronic-active antibody-mediated rejection, while another died of non-ECP-related cardiopulmonary arrest, both without graft loss. Importantly, no complications were reported during ECP sessions, and no significant increase in infectious events was observed.
Conclusion
ECP appears to be a safe and effective adjunct in treating refractory BKVAN. While it is not a standalone therapy, ECP may complement existing treatments particularly in sensitized kidney transplant recipients. It contributes to substantial reductions in BKV viremia while minimizing the risk of rejection. However, early initiation may optimize outcomes, as delayed intervention can lead to irreversible graft damage. Further large-scale, multicenter studies are necessary to validate these findings and establish standardized protocols for ECP in BKVAN management.

title: #803 Impact of diabetes and low age- and sex-specific eGFR on post-transplant kidney function recovery in living kidney donors
authors: Shunsuke Goto; Nanako Terada; Yoji Hyodo; Hideaki Miyake; Hideki Fujii
abstract:
Background and Aims
In living kidney transplantation, assessing the potential risks and anticipated benefits for donation is essential to determine the suitability of donor candidates. However, methods for evaluating these risks are not yet fully established, despite age, pre-transplant kidney function, obesity, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus being suggested as potential risk factors. Recently, with the increasing number of elderly donors, individuals with various risk factors have been donating their kidneys. Furthermore, donors with diabetes mellitus, who were previously considered contraindicated, are now being evaluated as potential donor candidates. title: #1081 Higher daily protein intake can reduce the risk of infections in kidney transplant recipients during the early post-transplant period
authors: Bin-Qi Yang; Yuan Liu; Ye Tao; Yun-Ying Shi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney transplantation (KT) is considered the most effective treatment for end-stage renal disease (ESRD), and it significantly contributes to enhancing the quality of life and extending the survival of patients with ESRD. After kidney transplantation, the early and heavy use of immunosuppressants and glucocorticoids can affect the recipients' immune status to varying degrees, increasing the risk of postoperative infections caused by a wide range of pathogens. Thus, the prevention and management of infectious diseases are major factors contributing to improved outcomes in kidney transplantation. Protein-energy wasting (PEW) is commonly observed in uremic patients, and it may persist even after they have undergone kidney transplantation (KT). And PEW is a significant factor in the progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD). Providing appropriate dietary guidance and intervention is essential for enhancing the immune status of recipients, promoting a positive nitrogen balance in the body, minimizing infections, and safeguarding graft function. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between daily protein intake (DPI) and postoperative infections at 3 months post-transplant, which may establish a foundation for the early postoperative protein intake regimen, reducing the incidence of postoperative infections, and improving the early prognosis of kidney transplantation.
Method
This is a retrospective observational study. 176 kidney transplant recipients (KTRs) who underwent kidney transplant in West China Hospital from December 2021 to June 2022 were included and followed up regularly. 24-hour urine urea data were collected at months 1 and 3 post-transplant to calculate their DPI. These KTRs were further divided into two groups according to the recommended DPI for KTRs by the 2021 Practice Guidelines for the Nutritional Management of Chronic Kidney Disease, namely high intake group (Group 1, with DPI ≥ 1.4g/kg·d, n = 66) and low intake group (Group 2, with DPI < 1.4g/kg·d, n = 110). Occurrence of hospitalization and postoperative infections within 3 months were recorded. Multiple logistic regression was utilized to analyze the association between DPI and early postoperative infections at 3 months post-transplant.
Results
Mean DPI levels at month 1 post-transplant were 1.58 ± 0.22 g/kg·d in Group 1 and 1.02 ± 0.31 g/kg·d in Group 2, respectively (P < 0.05), this huge difference in DPI between the two groups continued to month 3. There was no significant difference in age, gender, pre-transplant body mass index (BMI), dialysis type and time, donor type, or the ratio of delayed graft function (DGF) between the two groups. There was a statistically significant difference in the percentage of hospitalization between the two groups during the postoperative period of 3 months (P = 0.027). Pneumonia was the most common reason of hospitalization after transplantation, followed by urinary tract infection. The results of multiple logistic regression analysis showed that higher DPI in the early post-transplant period was a protective factor for infection after kidney transplantation.
Conclusion
In the early post-transplant period, consuming higher levels of dietary protein may reduce the risk of infections and complications, and help preserve the function of the transplanted kidney.

title: #3371 Hypothermic oxygenated perfusion of marginal kidneys with extracellular vesicles from mesenchymal stromal cells: a proteomic analysis
authors: Marilena Gregorini; Maria Antonietta Grignano; Maurizio Bruschi; Simona Granata; Gianluigi Zaza; Stefania Bruno; Emma Diletta Stea; Eleonora Francesca Pattonieri; Elisabetta Margiotta; Giuliana Germinario; Matteo Ravaioli; Teresa Rampino
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hypothermic oxygenated perfusion (HOPE) is a technique for preserving organs by circulating oxygenated solution at 4°C throughout the renal vasculature to deliver oxygen and nutrients. We have previously found that extracellular vesicles (EVs) secreted by heterologous mesenchymal stromal cells significantly reduce ischemia/ reperfusion (I/R) injury and improve energy metabolism in kidneys from older donors. However, the underlying mechanisms are still unclear.
Method
In this study, we used mass spectrometry to analyze the proteomic profile of 5 pairs of marginal kidneys that were considered ineligible for transplantation based on histological scores >6. These kidneys were conditioned for 4 hours at 4°C with HOPE (right kidney) and HOPE+EVs (left kidney). Biopsies were taken at baseline (T0) and after 180 and 240 minutes of perfusion (T180-T240). Renal expression of the principal marker of aging and senescence, P16 antigen, was studied by immunohistochemistry in formalin fixed tissue in 10 non-overlapping high-power fields of each section.
Results
Of the 2467 proteins identified, 710 were dysregulated; 91 showed no differences between groups or over time. In HOPE, 229 protein concentrations increased, 156 decreased and 325 remained unchanged over time. In HOPE+EV, 199 protein concentrations increased, 238 decreased and 273 remained unchanged over time. Compared to HOPE, HOPE+EV showed a greater increase in proteins involved in the maintenance of histoarchitecture, cell cycle regulation/proliferation, protection against oxidative stress and apoptosis (EZR, PEA15, HEXA, CUL4-A, RAB22A, GLRX and TTN) and a greater decrease in proteins involved in senescence and catabolism (CAV1, PSMB6, RAB88B and SCRN1).
According to these results, we found that the widespread expression of P16 protein in HOPE kidneys was almost completely abrogated in HOPE+EV kidneys.
These results are consistent with our previous studies showing that marginal organs perfused with HOPE+EV had less histological damage, were better protected from I/R injury and had higher viability.
Conclusion
This study sheds light on the mechanisms underlying the effect of EVs and provides the basis for developing a new perfusion strategy aimed at improving the quality and survival of organs ultimately increasing the pool of donors in the future.

title: #3520 Gene expression profiles of PBMCs in kidney vs. lung recipients prior to extracorporeal photopheresis: similarities and differences
authors: Marilena Gregorini; Maria Antonietta Grignano; Mario Urtis; Eloisa Arbustini; Emma Diletta Stea; Federica Meloni; Domenica Federica Briganti; Sara Bozzini; Tefik Islami; Cesare Perotti; Claudia Del Fante; Teresa Rampino
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic allograft rejection of the kidney (CKR) and lung transplant (CLAD) represent major causes of mortality and graft loss, with limited therapeutic options currently available. Several centers are now adopting extracorporeal photopheresis (ECP) as a salvage therapy for both conditions. In this study we aimed to identify dysregulated signalling pathways in these diseases that might be targeted by ECP. We compared the gene expression profile (GEP) of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) collected from 5 CKR and 5 CLAD patients before the first session of ECP treatment to investigate differences and similarities.
Method
We used the nCounter® Human Organ Transplant Panel, which assesses the expression of 760 genes involved in 37 signalling pathways of immune response, tissue damage and mechanisms of action of immunosuppressive drugs. The data were analysed using the ROSALIND software according to the instructions provided (nCounter Analysis System).
Results
Differentially expressed genes
The correlation matrix and dendrograms showed different gene expression profile (GEP) in CKR vs. CLAD, with strong correlations within each group (correlation indices: RCR 1–0.95; RCP 1–0.90), categorising the samples into two distinct groups. A total of 38 genes were differentially expressed between the two cohorts. A notable difference in gene expression between CKR and CKR was observed in the Toll-like Receptor Signalling Pathway. Five genes related to the activation of the MAPK-mediated inflammatory pathway (JUN, CXCL8, IL1B, TNF, FOS) were overexpressed in CKR. Conversely, six genes related to the NFKB-mediated inflammatory pathway (CHUK, CASP8, TLR5, IKBKB, IKBKG, TBK1) were overexpressed in CLAD.
Similarly expressed genes.
Both CKR and CLAD showed overexpression of genes involved in important signalling pathways, such as immune/inflammatory response to infection, inflammation and stress; MHC-I and MHC-II complex; regulation of protein synthesis.
Conclusion
The PBMC GEP highlighted distinct differences and similarities between CLAD and CKR patients. Specifically, CLAD showed overexpression the NFKB-mediated inflammatory pathway, while CKR exhibited overexpression in the MAPK-mediated inflammatory pathway. Additionally, both conditions shared overexpression of genes involved in immune and inflammatory response to infections, inflammation and stress. Further investigations on GEP after 6 months of ECP are underway and will help to better understand the effects of ECP on CKR and CLAD.

title: #3491 Engineered ATP-loaded extracellular vesicles derived from mesenchymal stem cells: a novel strategy to counteract cell ATP depletion in an in vitro model
authors: Maria Antonietta Grignano; Marilena Gregorini; Silvia Pisani; Giorgia Rainaudo; Maria Antonietta Avanzini; Stefania Croce; Chiara Valsecchi; Emma Diletta Stea; Giuseppe La Notte; Alessandro Tragni; Bice Conti; Teresa Rampino
abstract:
Background and Aims
The use of ATP-loaded liposomes has shown promise in mitigating ischemic damage in various tissues. However, kidney tubular cells pose a challenge for liposome penetration due to their anatomical and physiological features.
In this study, we present a novel drug delivery system utilizing extracellular vesicles (EVs) engineered with ATP cargo, derived from mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs). EVs offer superior advantages as vectors compared to liposomes. They exhibit greater permeability and stability due to their negatively charged surfaces and possess enhanced targeting properties thanks to their surface molecules.
Method
Extracellular vesicles (EVs) were isolated from porcine MSC, and liposomes were prepared using a microfluidic technique. EVs and liposomes were characterized for size, number, and z-potential using nanoparticle tracking (NTA) and dynamic light scattering (DLS). ATP was encapsulated in liposomes and EVs using microfluidic methods. ATP content and release in PBS at 37°C (4 h) of both EVs and liposomes were tested using an ATP Elisa assay.
To assess the ATP delivery efficiency, a proximal tubular epithelial cell line (HK2), were subjected to ATP depletion injury using 2-deoxy-glucose (inhibiting glycolysis) and antimycin A (mitochondrial respiratory chain inhibitor), for 2 h in PBS. After the chemical ischemia, HK2 cells were treated for 4 h at 37°C in: serum free low glucose DMEM (lgDMEM) (dATP) or in lgDMEM + naïve EVs (EV)/ ATP loaded EV (EV-ATP) (3 × 107 vesicles/mL) or in lgDMEM + empty liposomes (lp)/ ATP loaded liposomes (3 × 107 liposomes/mL) or in lgDMEM with free ATP (0.05 nmol/ml).
Not ATP depleted HK2 cells in complete medium served as the positive control (CTRL+), while in lgDMEM were used as the negative control (CTRL−).
Each condition was tested in quadruplicate, after which cell viability was assessed using trypan blue exclusion, and cell ATP levels were measured with an ATP assay. Expression of the apoptotic genes (Bcl2-Bax) was analyzed using Real Time PCR (RT-PCR).
Results
Naive EVs exhibited a baseline intravesicular ATP concentration of 26.22 ± 3.45 nm/mL. Microfluidic loading doubling it to 54.88 ± 16.23 nm/mL (P < 0.01). Direct encapsulation of ATP within liposomes achieved comparable levels to those in microfluidically-loaded EVs, whereas indirect encapsulation resulted in a lower concentration of ATP (direct vs indirect method, P < 0.05). Due to its comparable loading efficiency to EVs, the direct liposomal encapsulation method was selected for subsequent ATP loading experiments.
DLS confirmed that cargo engineering process maintained EV integrity while achieving comparable efficiency, charge, and size characteristics to direct ATP loading into liposomes.
ATP was released identically by liposomes and EVs within the first hour, but after that, they showed a distinct difference in the rates of release.
While liposomes released all encapsulated ATP starting from the second hour, EVs demonstrated an opposite release profile, with a release rate that decreased over time (P < 0.00001). dATP cells showed significantly reduced ATP levels compared to CTRL+ (P < 0.01). EV and EV-ATP effectively counteracted the prior ATP depletion, but EV-ATP treatment demonstrated the most significant recovery (P < 0.05). On the contrary, Lp-ATP did not enhance intracellular ATP levels, which remained similar to dATP, empty liposomes (placebo), and free ATP treatments. Compared to CTRL+, all conditioning treatments except for EV-ATP resulted in reduced HK2 cell viability (P < 0.05) maintaining the cell viability comparable to both CTRL+ and CTRL−. RT-PCR confirmed an increased expression of BCL2-BAX mRNA in dATP cells after 4 hours of incubation in lgDMEM vs. CTRL+ (P < 0.01).
This upregulation was mitigated only in EV-ATP cells that exhibited a mRNA expression reduction of about 40% (P < 0.05). The other conditioning treatments did not significantly affect BCL2-BAX gene expression.
Conclusion
Our results demonstrate that ATP loaded EV released sufficient levels of ATP to protect cells from ischemic damage. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of using vesicles to directly deliver ATP into tubular renal cells.

title: #2350 PCSK9 inhibitors protect kidney from ischemia-reperfusion injury reducing oxidative stress and enhancing tissue resistance: a metabolomics analysis
authors: Maria Antonietta Grignano; Marilena Gregorini; Maria Chiara Mimmi; Giorgia Rainaudo; Chiara Barisione; Caterina Ivaldo; Daniela Verzola; Emma Diletta Stea; Daniela Picciotto; Francesca Viazzi; Pasquale Esposito; Teresa Rampino
abstract:
Background and Aims
The shortage of kidneys and the growing number of patients requiring a transplant pose a major challenge. Research efforts are focused on developing new therapies to improve both the quantity and quality of transplantable organs. Hypothermic mechanical perfusion (HMP) has enabled the harvesting of organs from marginal donors, such as post-circulatory death donors (DCD). However, these organs are more prone to early post-transplant complications due to their heightened susceptibility to ischemia-reperfusion injury.
In a previous study using a DCD model in rats, we demonstrated that the combined use of HMP and the PCSK9 inhibitor (PEP 2-8) could be a promising strategy for renal conditioning prior to transplantation. Specifically, kidneys perfused with PEP 2-8 exhibited a lower rate of ischemic tubular damage, a higher tubular proliferation index, and elevated ATP levels compared to organs perfused with HMP alone. We aim to understand how PCSK9 inhibitors exert their protective effect via metabolomics pathways.
Method
A total of 15 rats were used as models for Donation after Circulatory Death. The experimental regimen included 30 minutes of warm ischemia followed by 6 hours of cold (4°C) perfusion using either Perf-Gene solution alone for the control group (C) or Perf-Gene solution supplemented with 10 µg of PEP 2-8 for the treatment group (PEP). Each rat's kidney was assigned to either the control or PEP group. Tissue samples from each kidney were embedded in an optimal cutting temperature (OCT) cryogenic well and frozen on dry ice before being stored at –80°C. After extracting the polar metabolites by centrifugation, one-dimensional NMR spectra were acquired using a Bruker Avance NEO 700 MHz spectrometer equipped with a TCI CryoProbe (Bruker BioSpin, Germany).
