title: #3489 The role of protocol biopsies in kidney transplantation: clinical impact and prognostic value of banff criteria
authors: Ana Rita Pereirinha Ramos; Andreia Gaspar Carnevale; José Soares; Madalena Borges; Mário Ventura Góis; Helena Sousa; Fernando Caeiro; Ines Aires; Manuel Anibal A Ferreira; Cristina Rego de Freitas Mendes Jorge
abstract:
Background and Aims
Protocol biopsies are performed in kidney transplant recipients without clinical dysfunction to identify subclinical rejection and early histological changes. Despite their prognostic value, they are neither completely accepted nor universally implemented. This study aims to assess the clinical impact of protocol biopsies and the prognostic significance of Banff criteria in short- and long-term renal outcomes.
Method
A retrospective analysis was conducted on isolated kidney transplants at a single referral center between January 2020 and December 2022. Only protocol biopsies performed within the first 15 days post-transplant were included. Patients with severe surgical or infectious complications requiring prolonged intensive care unit stay, those undergoing repeated transplantation, and recipients of living donor kidneys were excluded. Demographic and clinical data from donors and recipients were collected, including renal function and donor-specific antibodies (DSA). Histological analysis was performed according to Banff criteria. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS (Version 29).
Results
Of 150 kidney transplants, 110 met the inclusion criteria. Recipients were 40.4% female, 64.4% Caucasian, with a mean age of 52.1 ± 11.7 years. Donors were 86.9% brain-dead, with a mean age of 53.9 ± 14.0 years; 38% met expanded criteria, and their mean serum creatinine was 0.90 ± 0.28 mg/dL. The cold ischemia time was 700.9 ± 299.2 minutes. Most recipients had four HLA mismatches (28.4%), and 27.3% had donor-specific antibodies (DSA). Induction therapy consisted primarily of Thymoglobulin (50.5%), followed by Basiliximab (41.4%) and a combination of Thymoglobulin with intravenous immunoglobulin (8.1%).
Rejection was detected in 20.2% of protocol biopsies, predominantly cell mediated (85.0%), with 47.4% classified as Banff grade IA/IB, 36.8% as grade IIA/IIB, 10.5% as grade III, and 1.0% as borderline. Treatment included methylprednisolone and thymoglobulin in 85.0% of cases. Procedural complications occurred in 5.0%, consisting of self-limited macroscopic hematuria. Rejection rates varied significantly by induction regimen (P < 0.001), occurring in 46.2% of basiliximab-treated patients compared to 5.3% with thymoglobulin, representing 94.7% and 5.3% of all rejection cases, respectively.
No significant difference in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was observed between patients with and without rejection in 2 years of follow up (P = 0.933). However, patients with rejection experienced a greater improvement in eGFR after treatment (11.07 ± 14.08 vs. 1.29 ± 9.03 mL/min, P < 0.001). Interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy correlated negatively with eGFR at 2 years (P < 0.05), while vasculitis showed a weak positive correlation (P = 0.032).
Cold ischemia time correlated negatively with interstitial inflammation and tubulitis (P ≤ 0.008). Vasculitis was negatively associated with cold ischemia time (P = 0.046) and donor age (P = 0.041). Chronic vascular lesions correlated positively with donor and recipient age (p ≤ 0.015).
Conclusion
This study highlights the importance of protocol biopsies in detecting early rejection, particularly in basiliximab-treated patients. Despite being an invasive procedure, its safety was confirmed, with no major complications observed. Early detection of rejection allowed for effective interventions, resulting in long-term improvements in renal function comparable to patients without rejection.

title: #2142 Dialysis after graft failure: clinical patterns and one-year outcomes
authors: Filipa Trigo; Beatriz Gil Braga; Sofia Sousa; António Silva Inácio; João Borges; José Silvano; Catarina Ribeiro; Manuela Manuela Barbosa de Almeida; Sofia Pedroso; Maria La Salete Soares Martins Da Silva
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney transplant (KT) remains the best treatment for patients with end-stage kidney disease, offering the greatest increase in life expectancy. Despite a reduction in acute rejection rates, long-term outcomes remain suboptimal. Therefore, late graft failure (GF) poses significant clinical challenges, with complex decisions regarding treatment options and initiation. This study analyzes the characteristics of KT recipients returning to dialysis, focusing on causes, timing, dialysis modalities, and one-year mortality indicators.
Method
A retrospective observational study was conducted, including patients with GF between January 2013 and December 2023. Demographic and clinical data, dialysis modality, timing of initiation, and vascular access type were analyzed, alongside first-year hospitalization and mortality rates. Statistical analyses were preformed using IBM® SPSS® Statistics Version 25.
Results
Among 315 patients returning to dialysis after KT failure, the median age at GF was 51 years (IQR: 42–62), and 58.4% were male. 13% (n = 41) were lost to follow-up. The median time between KT and GF was 12.3 years (IQR: 5.8–18.5). Chronic rejection was the predominant cause of GF (72.3%), while acute rejection accounted for 1.3%.
At dialysis initiation, median creatinine was 5.62 mg/dL (IQR: 3.98–7.10), urea was 208.48 mg/dL (IQR: 171.5–241.0), and hemoglobin was 10.5 g/dL (IQR: 9.3–11.5). Kruskal-Wallis tests showed no significant differences in these parameters across dialysis modalities (P = 0.260, P = 0.803, and P = 0.459, respectively) or vascular access types (P = 0.354, P = 0.157, and P = 0.571, respectively).
Most patients (89.8%) resumed hemodialysis (HD), with 63.9% using arteriovenous fistula (AVF). Peritoneal dialysis (PD) was chosen by 8.1%, and preemptive transplantation occurred in 2%. Dialysis modality was significantly associated with one-year mortality (χ²(2) = 8.989, P = 0.011), with the highest in the PD group (30%), followed by HD (5.7%), and none in the preemptive transplant group. No significant association was observed between dialysis modality and one-year hospitalization rates (P = 0.12). Vascular access type was also significantly associated with one-year mortality (χ²(2) = 12.758, P = 0.002), highest in central venous catheter (CVC, 50%), compared to Tenckhoff catheter (25%) and AVF (2.8%).
Age at GF was positively associated with one-year mortality (B = 0.052, P = 0.027, Exp(B) = 1.054), with each additional year increasing the odds of mortality by 5.4%.
Conclusion
Analytical parameters (creatinine, urea, and hemoglobin) at dialysis initiation did not differ significantly across modalities or vascular access types, aligning with the that emphasizes clinical context and patient-specific factors.
Chronic rejection remains the main cause of graft failure, and mortality is influenced by dialysis modality and vascular access. While higher mortality in PD was statistically significant, this finding contrasts with the literature and is likely influenced by the small number of patients in this group. High mortality associated with CVC highlights the need for careful planning, particularly in older patients, where age increases the risk of mortality. Individualized post-GF management strategies are crucial, including early planning for vascular access and modality selection, as well as intensified monitoring of high-risk groups. Further research is needed to optimize outcomes and quality of life for this growing patient population.

abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney transplantation (KT) is considered the best replacement therapy for chronic kidney disease (CKD), offering superior survival and quality of life compared to dialysis. International guidelines recommend pre-emptive KT from living donors, as prolonged dialysis can lead to comorbidities. This study aimed to compare patient outcomes between recipients with pre-emptive KT and non-preemptive kidney transplant.
Method
We retrospectively reviewed 384 patients receiving kidney transplant in our center between 1st of January of 2000 and 31st of December of 2020 and statistical analysis was conducted. They were divided in two groups: pre-emptive (Group 1) and non-preemptive (Group 2). We used propensity score matching (PSM) based on age, sex, hypertension and diabetes status.
Results
After PSM, we obtained a total of 162 patients, 81 in each group. Baseline characteristics were similar between the groups regarding age, sex distribution, BMI, diabetes, hypertension and active smoking (Table 1). Regarding group 2, a median dialysis time of 17 months (IQR: 36) was observed. The etiology of chronic kidney disease showed significant differences between groups (P = 0.006), with Group 1 presenting a higher proportion of cystic diseases (14.8% vs. 9.9%) and chronic interstitial nephritis (24.7% vs. 8.6%), while Group 2 had a higher prevalence of hereditary diseases (1.2% vs. 8.6%) and unknown causes (7.4% vs. 18.5%).
Regarding transplantation-related variables, no significant differences were observed in HLA mismatches. However, induction therapy differed significantly, with Group 1 receiving more basiliximab (74.1% vs. 43.2%) and less antithymocyte globulin (2.5% vs. 13.6%) compared to Group 2. This difference aligns with the expectation that preemptive transplants are typically performed as first kidney transplants.
Post-transplant outcomes revealed key differences. Primary non-function (<30 days) occurred only in Group 1. Delayed graft function or loss within 30 days was more common in Group 1 but not statistically significant (8.6% vs. 2.5%, P = 0.167). Rejection within the first year was significantly lower in Group 1 (6.2% vs. 16.0%, P = 0.046). Other outcomes, such as infectious complications (58.0% vs. 51.9%, P = 0.430) and overall graft failure (19.8% vs. 16.0%, P = 0.539), showed no significant differences between the groups.
All graft losses in the preemptive group within 30 days were due to vascular complications, and no recipient deaths were observed during this period. The years of follow-up analysis excluded individuals who experienced graft loss within the first 30 days.
Conclusion
Pre-emptive kidney transplantation (Group 1) showed favorable outcomes in terms of rejection rates in the first year post-transplant compared to non-preemptive transplantation (Group 2), suggesting that pre-emptive KT may reduce early immune-mediated complications. However, Group 1 exhibited a higher rate of primary non-function within 30 days, which warrants further investigation into donor and surgical procedures. Baseline characteristics and long-term graft failure rates were comparable between the groups, reinforcing the feasibility of pre-emptive KT as an optimal strategy. Future studies are necessary to explore the mechanisms underlying these differences to improve clinical outcomes.

title: #887 The multi-omic analysis identified CHI3L1 as a potential mediator of immune system deregulation in kidney transplant patients with chronic antibody-mediated rejection
authors: Simona Granata; Francesca Leone; Maurizio Bruschi; Laura Barberio; Paola Pontrelli; Giovanni Candiano; Michele Provenzano; Loreto Gesualdo; Giuseppe Grandaliano; Gianluigi Zaza
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic antibody-mediated rejection (CAMR) is the leading cause of functional loss in kidney transplantation and, in many cases, despite appropriate treatment, does not respond to current therapies. Therefore, there is a need to identify new biological factors to improve early diagnosis or potential therapeutic targets. To achieve these goals, molecular biology and multi-omics methodologies can prove to be very useful tools.
Methods
We compared mass spectrometry-based proteomic profiling of serum samples from 19 patients with CAMR and 26 kidney transplant recipients with normal graft function and histology (CTR) and the transcriptomic analysis of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from an independent cohort of 10 CAMR and 8 CTR patients. Data analysis was conducted using unsupervised hierarchical clustering (multidimensional scaling with k-means) and Spearman's correlation test. Partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) with k-means and variable importance in projection (VIP) score identified key proteins differentiating CAMR from CTR. ELISA was used to validate omics results.
Results
The bioinformatics analysis combined with functional analysis (Gene Ontology), demonstrated that 18 proteins significantly differentiated CAMR from CTR (P < 0.01): five were more abundant (CHI3L1, LYZ, PRSS2, CPQ, IGLV3-32), while 13 were less abundant (SERPINA5, SERPING1, KNG1, CAMP, VNN1, BTD, WDR1, PON3, AHNAK2, MELTF, CA1, CD44, CUL1). Transcriptomic profiling revealed 6 downregulated and 33 upregulated genes in CAMR versus CTR (P < 0.01).
The overlapping analysis identified chitinase-3-like protein 1 (CHI3L1), a protein previously associated with the severity of tissue damage in kidney diseases, as the most significant biological factor simultaneously overexpressed in CAMR patients in both transcriptomics and proteomics. ELISA validated the omics data and CHI3L1 reached good discrimination power for CAMR identification (AUC of ROC curve of 0.81).
Conclusions
The results of the multi-omics analysis confirmed the deregulation of immune system in CAMR patients and identified CHI3L1 as a new potential biomarker and therapeutic target for this significant clinical complication.

title: #253 Frequency, risk factors and long-term outcomes of erythrocytosis in kidney transplant patients
authors: Onur Direk; Harun Coban; Dilek Barutcu Atas; Murat Tugcu; Izzet Hakki Arikan; Ebru Asicioglu; Z Serhan Tuglular; Arzu Velioglu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Posttransplant erythrocytosis (PTE) is defined as prolonged high hemoglobin or hematocrit levels after kidney transplantation. The rate of development of PTE is 8-15%. Erythrocytosis may lead to thromboembolic events by increasing plasma viscosity. The aim of our study was to determine the frequency and risk factors of PTE in kidney transplant patients followed in our center and to examine its effects on adverse events (graft loss, mortality and thromboembolic events).
Method
Our study included 295 kidney transplant patients aged ≥18 years with a follow-up period of at least 1 year in our center between 1999 and 2023. Demographic, clinical, laboratory data and adverse events were obtained from patient files. PTE was considered to have developed in patients with a hemoglobin level above 17 g/dl or a hematocrit level above 51% after kidney transplantation and who remained above these levels for at least 6 months. Demographic and clinical characteristics of patients with and without PTE were compared.
Results
PTE developed in 39 patients (13.2%). The proportion of males was significantly higher in patients with PTE (74.4% vs. 54.3%, P = 0.018). The rate of smoking was higher in those who developed PTE (41% vs. 17.2%, P = 0.001). Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) was present in 20.5% of those who developed PTE compared to 5.5% of those who did not (P = 0.001). The proportion of patients on dialysis before transplantation was 89.7% in those with PTE and 73% in those without PTE (P = 0.024). The mean age of donors was 40.4 ± 11.4 years in patients with PTE and 44.3 ± 11.8 years in patients without PTE (P = 0.045). There was no significant difference between the two groups in male-to-male, female-to-male and male-to-female transplants. However, PTE was not observed in female-to-female transplants (P = 0.001). In multivariate analysis, male gender (P = 0.032), smoking history (P = 0.026), PKD (P = 0.008) and BK viremia (P < 0.001) were considered risk factors for PTE; donor age and pre-transplant dialysis status lost significance. There was no association between PTE and adverse events.
Conclusion
The absence of PTE in female-to-female kidney transplants is the most important finding of our study, which has not been previously reported in the literature. The association with previous BK viremia is another important and novel finding. The rarity of thromboembolic complications in our study may be explained by the effective application of PTE treatment methods.

title: #758 Deep phenotyping of urinary cells with cytometry by time of flight reveals CD8+CD38+ T cells as biomarker to detect T cell-mediated rejection
authors: Nina Görlich; Christopher Skopnik; Diana Metzke; Emil Grothgar; Leonie Wagner; Mira Choi; Pouneh Mirkheshti; Klemens Budde; Kerstin Amann; Jan Klocke; Sabine Baumgart; Philipp Enghard
abstract:
Background and Aims
Non-invasive monitoring and early detection of rejection are of high priority in kidney transplantation. In our previous work, we established urine flow cytometry (FC) as tool for non-invasive kidney transplant monitoring and rejection detection. We hypothesized that an even deeper phenotyping of urinary cells improves the diagnostic yield of urinary T cells. Therefore, we established Cytometry by time of flight (CyTOF) analysis of urine cells to derive an improved biomarker for the detection of rejection. Our findings were subsequently confirmed in a FC-based validation cohort.
Method
A total of 157 urine samples from kidney transplant recipients (KTR) were collected from patients undergoing indication transplant biopsy. Of these samples, 57 were analyzed in the discovery CyTOF cohort. CD8+CD38+ T cells were identified as a potential biomarker for T cell-mediated rejection (TCMR), which was confirmed in a validation cohort (n = 100) using FC. Additionally, we analyzed a publicly available scSeq dataset of KTR biopsies and urine to investigate our biomarker and its expression in TCMR with an additional method.
Results
By utilizing high-dimensional mass cytometry, we identified CD8+CD38+ T cells as a potential biomarker for TCMR. Reassessment of publicly available scSeq datasets demonstrated that CD38 expression in CD8+ T cells in kidney transplant tissue corresponds to CD38 expression in urinary CD8+ T cells. We translated our finding to FC and validated urinary CD8+CD38+ T cells in a validation cohort. CD8+CD38+ T cells showed an AUC of 0.956 to diagnose TCMR and exceeded prior published biomarkers.
Conclusion
Urinary CD8+CD38+ T cells are a new biomarker for TCMR, validated by 3 independent methods in 3 patient cohorts.

title: #3002 Impact of HLA-sensitization on patient and graft outcomes in ABO-incompatible living donor kidney transplants: single decade experience from North India
authors: Narayan Prasad; Jeyakumar Meyyappan; Peeyush Kumar Mishra; Anupma Kaul; Manas Ranjan Behera; Ravi Sankar Kushwaha; Manas Ranjan Patel; Monika Yachha
abstract:
Background and Aims
ABO-incompatible (ABOi) kidney transplantation has expanded the donor pool, providing an option for patients with long waiting times. However, ABOi transplants are associated with higher early mortality and graft loss. Japan's experience with over 2,000 ABOi transplants demonstrated long-term outcomes comparable to ABO-compatible transplants. While India shows promising results, region-specific protocols are evolving. A major challenge in ABOi transplantation is HLA sensitization, which may contribute to early graft rejection. Unlike HLA-incompatible transplants, ABOi transplants involve naturally occurring antibodies against carbohydrate antigens. This study aims to assess the effect of HLA sensitization on graft and patient survival in ABOi kidney transplantation at a high-volume center in North India.
Method
This single-center, retrospective study analyzed data from ABOi kidney transplants performed between January 2014 and December 2023 at a tertiary care center in North India. Patients aged 12 and older were included, with exclusions for those lost to follow-up. Data were collected from electronic records and patient interviews, focusing on immunological risk factors, desensitization protocols, immunosuppression, biopsy-proven acute rejection (BPAR), and infection outcomes. Desensitization included rituximab, plasmapheresis, and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) to achieve anti-ABO titers ≤1:8. Induction therapy consisted of basiliximab or antithymocyte globulin (ATG) based on immunological risk. Immunosuppression included tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), and steroids. Primary outcomes were BPAR at 1 month, 1–12 months, and beyond 1 year. Secondary outcomes included patient and graft survival at 1, 3, 5, and 10 years and serious infections requiring hospitalization (SIRH).
Results
The study included 184 ABOi kidney transplants, with 110 in the non-HLA-sensitized group and 74 in the HLA-sensitized group. Sensitized patients had higher rates of repeat transplants (13.5% vs. 0.9%, P < 0.001) and donor-specific antibody (DSA) positivity (Class I: 27% vs. 5.5%, Class II: 82.4% vs. 10%, both P < 0.001). ATG induction was more frequent in sensitized patients (28.4% vs. 11.8%, P = 0.005). Biopsy-proven acute rejection rates and immediate graft function were comparable between groups. Infections requiring hospitalization were slightly lower in sensitized patients in the first year (31.1% vs. 43.6%, P = 0.080). Patient and graft survival at 5 and 10 years were similar between groups (88.6% vs. 83%, P = 0.396; 85.7% vs. 80%, P = 0.234).
Conclusion
This study is the first to evaluate the impact of HLA sensitization in ABOi kidney transplantation, finding no significant differences in graft survival, patient survival, or biopsy-proven acute rejection between sensitized and non-sensitized recipients. Sensitizing events such as repeat transplants and pregnancy were common. Graft survival at 10 years was 84.9%, similar to other large cohort studies. Despite immunological challenges, effective desensitization protocols, immunosuppressive strategies, and infection prophylaxis contributed to favorable outcomes. The study supports the feasibility and safety of ABOi kidney transplantation in sensitized individuals, expanding access to transplantation and improving outcomes.

title: #1743 Long-term outcomes of renal transplantation from expanded criteria living donors
authors: Roger Alabau Perich; Emma Arcos; Jordi Comas; Leonor Fayos de Arizón; Jaume Tort; Ignacio Revuelta; Anna Manonelles; Marta Crespo; Francesc Josep Moreso; Anna Vila Santandreu; Carme Facundo Molas; Lluis Guirado Perich
abstract:
Background and Aims
In the last decades, we have witnessed a steady increase in the use of donors with expanded criteria in Spain, initially from deceased donors and later from living donors. All of this aims to decrease the waiting time to be transplanted for our recipients. There is considerable concern regarding the long-term outcomes associated with expanded criteria living donors, particularly when faced with the decision between a preemptive transplant using a living donor with expanded criteria or a standard deceased donor after an extended period on the waiting list.
Method
Using the Catalan Registry of Kidney Patients, we analyze and compare the long-term results obtained using standard living donors (<70 years old and >70 ml/min CKD-EPI), standard deceased donors (45–60 years old, CKD-EPI > 70 ml/min, no diabetes), expanded living donors (>70 years old or CKD-EPI < 70 ml/min) and expanded criteria deceased donors (>70 years old or CKD-EPI < 70 ml/min) during the period 2000–2023.
Results
We have obtained the best results in terms of patient survival, death-censored graft survival, and graft survival (including death) when using living donors, regardless of whether they are standard living donors or expanded living donors. Expanded criteria deceased donors offer the worst outcomes. When comparing Expanded Living Donors to Standard Deceased Donors, we obtained 10-year patient survival rates of 81.54% and 72.8%, respectively, 10-year death-censored graft survival rates of 79.3% versus 73.6% and 10-year graft survival rates of 63.9% versus 57.2%. The following table shows the results obtained with these different categories of donors.
Conclusion
Our data confirm that living donors provide better long-term patient and graft survival rates in the kidney transplant population. Notably, the results are superior when using a living donor with expanded criteria compared to a standard deceased donor. When comparing outcomes between expanded criteria living and deceased donors, the differences are significantly in favour of living donors.

title: #1567 Increase in the use of expanded criteria living donors to facilitate preemptive kidney transplantation for our patients
authors: Roger Alabau Perich; Emma Arcos; Jordi Comas; Nuria Serra Cabanas; Jaume Tort; Ignacio Revuelta; Anna Manonelles; Marta Crespo; Francesc Josep Moreso; Anna Vila Santandreu; Carme Facundo Molas; Lluis Guirado Perich
abstract:
Background and Aims
Spain currently has the highest percentage of deceased donors per million population worldwide (50 pmp 2023). Despite this, the median dialysis time on the transplant list was 20.6 months in 2023. Young patients and blood group O recipients have this time increased. The living donor is the best solution to offer them a preemptive kidney transplant. In recent years, the number of living donors with expanded criteria has been growing significantly in our area to facilitate this objective.
Method
Using the Catalan Registry of Kidney Patients, we describe the characteristics of 2.510 living donor kidney transplants performed in Catalonia between the years 2000 and 2023 in order to observe the changes in the acceptance criteria of these donors.
Results
The following table shows the increase in the number of expanded criteria living donors according to different characteristics: donors older than 70 years old, CKD EPI <70 ml/min, proteinuria >150 mg/day, hypertension, diabetes mellitus type 2, lithiasis or obesity. Some of the donors shared different expanded criteria. We found statistical significance in the increase of donors older than 70 years old, CKD EPI <70 ml/min, hypertension, diabetes mellitus type 2 and lithiasis. There is also a parallel growth in the preemptive transplants performed with these donors.
Conclusion
The progressive introduction of living donors with expanded criteria has allowed the constant increase in anticipated kidney transplantation in our patients. The excellent long-term outcome of these grafts in the recipients (10-year patient survival 86.4%, death censored graft survival 82.9% and graft survival 72.2%), as well as the preservation and stability of the donor's kidney function in follow-up over the years allows us to increasingly consider them as a first option for renal replacement treatment that prevents our patients from starting dialysis.

The following table shows the increase in the number of expanded criteria living donors according to different characteristics: donors older than 70 years old, CKD EPI <70 ml/min, proteinuria >150 mg/day, hypertension, diabetes mellitus type 2, lithiasis or obesity. Some of the donors shared different expanded criteria. title: #3324 Are there gender differences in access to kidney transplantation in the Basque country?
authors: Inigo Moina Eguren; Jose Ignacio Minguela; Ainhoa Basterretxea; María Teresa Rodrigo de Tomás; Adriana Aymat; Gorka García Erauzkin; Sofia Zarraga Larrondo; María Isabel Jimeno Martín; Ainhoa Hernando; Olga Castaneda; Guillermo Alcalde Bezhold; Esther Corral
abstract:
Background and Aims
Previous studies have suggested that gender-based discrimination exists in access to kidney transplant waiting list and kidney transplantation, with women reportedly having a lower probability of receiving a transplant. This study aimed to analyse whether gender-based disparities exist in access to kidney transplantation in our country and whether these disparities have changed over time, as societal attitudes toward gender equality have progressed.
Method
This retrospective study utilised data from the regional renal patient registry (UNIPAR–Basque Country). We included all incident patients who initiated renal replacement therapy (RRT) in our country between 1990 and 2023. We analysed differences between males and females in inclusion on the kidney transplant waiting list and in transplantation rates, both overall and across three time periods (1990–2000, 2001–2010, 2011–2023). Non-parametric tests were used for statistical analysis due to the non-normal distribution of the data. Results are presented as median (interquartile range, IQR).
Results
A total of 7889 patients who started RRT were included (67.5% men and 32.5% women), with a median age of 65.7 years (IQR: 53.7–74.0). Women started RRT at a younger age than men (64.9 vs 66.0 years, Welch's t-test, P = 0.0002). The initial modality of RRT was hemodialysis in 5790 patients (73.4%), peritoneal dialysis in 1918 (24.3%) and preemptive transplant in 182 (2.3%), with no significant gender differences (χ2, P = 0.511).
The percentage of patients included on the kidney transplant waiting list was similar between genders (46.3% men vs 49.8% women, χ2, P = 0.089). However, the percentage of patients who received a kidney transplant was slightly higher among women (39.5% men vs 43.8% women, χ2, P = 0.021). There were no significant differences in the time from RRT initiation to waiting list inclusion (W, P = 0.021) or to the first kidney transplant (W, P = 0.729). Subgroup analyses by time period yielded consistent results, with no significant differences observed.
Conclusion
Our findings indicate no evidence of gender-based discrimination in access to the kidney transplant waiting list or kidney transplantation in our country. These results suggest that access to kidney transplantation has been equitable for both men and women throughout the study period.

title: #1177 Glomerular morphometric feature machine learning-driven analysis of deceased donor procurement biopsies: the ComPrePS assessment tool
authors: Beatriz Pedro Fernandes; Alexandra Esteves; Luís Rodrigues; Paul Anindya; Magdy Haitham; Gupta Akshita; Vítor Sousa; Arnaldo Figueiredo; Rui Alves; Avi Rosenberg; Kuang Yu Jen; Pinaki Sarder
abstract:
Background and Aims
Morphometric analysis of kidney biopsies has proven valuable in assessing chronicity and predicting outcomes such as kidney failure and declining renal function. However, its clinical utility is limited by its manual, time-consuming nature. Artificial Intelligence (AI) may enhance clinical efficiency by automating annotations, performing morphometric calculations, and improving diagnostics and workflow.
We developed an open-source cloud-based platform designed for AI/ML-driven analysis, visualization, data management, and annotation of whole-slide digital pathology images. The aim was to investigate the glomerular morphometric features of kidney tissue samples from donors accepted and discarded for transplantation, utilizing the ComPRePS (Computational Renal Pathology Suite) platform. Additionally, we evaluated the correlation between these features and donor clinical data.
Method
We analyzed core needle biopsies from deceased donors who were evaluated for potential kidney transplantation, with some kidneys being allocated and others discarded after evaluation. Tissue samples were processed using a rapid Formalin-Fixed Paraffin- Embedded method, with tissue sections prepared at a thickness of 2–3 µm and stained with Periodic Acid–Schiff. The slides were then digitized using a brightfield microscopy whole-slide scanner at 40× magnification. Our computational pipeline automatically segments glomeruli followed by the calculation of 15 clinically interpretable glomerular morphometric features. These included: glomerular density count, average and standard glomerular area, average and standard glomerular radius, cortical glomerular density area, glomerular/cortex/tubules ratio, glomerulosclerosis density count, standard and average sclerotic glomerular area and radius, percentage of sclerotic glomeruli, mesangial area and fraction. Extensive clinical and laboratory variables from donors were collected, including those needed for the Kidney Donor Profile Index (KDPI) calculation.
Results
Our final sample consisted of 213 renal biopsies from 152 deceased donors, of whom 94 (61.8%) were male with a mean age of 64 ± 12.9 years. Stroke was the leading cause of death (n = 113, 74.3%). A history of diabetes was present in 17 donors (11.0%), and hypertension was noted in 104 donors (68.4%). Donor KDPI was 74 ± 21.8 and most organs (n = 139, 91.4%) were allocated for transplantation. From computational analysis, the average glomerular area was 363,100.9 ± 76,791.1 µm² in the allocated group and 399,288.1 ± 103,586.3 µm² in the discarded group. The mesangial fraction was higher in allocated kidneys, with a mean of 0.353 compared to 0.297 in discarded kidneys. The discarded kidneys exhibited significantly higher glomerulosclerosis density counts and percentages compared to the allocated kidneys: glomerulosclerosis percentage was 13.1% in the discarded group and 6.4% in the allocated group (P = 0.001). The average glomerular area was significantly larger in discarded kidneys (P = 0.004), with a mean difference of 36.187 µm².
Pearson's correlation between morphometric variables and donor KDPI revealed statistically significant positive correlations for standard glomerular area (P = 0.013), glomerular radius (P = 0.081), glomerulosclerosis percentage (P = 0.001), and glomerulosclerosis density count (p< 0.001). A significant negative correlation was observed for mesangial fraction (P = 0.023). Further investigation of donor clinical variables showed weight to be a significant determinant of glomerular (r = 0.182, P = 0.009) and mesangial area (r = 0.208, P = 0.003).
Conclusion
This study highlights the potential of AI-driven morphometric analysis to provide detailed insights into glomerular structural differences in deceased donor kidneys evaluated for transplantation. We hypothesize that a hyperfiltration status primarily accounts for the morphometric distinctions observed in the discarded kidney cohort. Further investigation is warranted to determine whether these variations in the measured variables correlate with poorer graft outcomes.

title: #3402 Glomerular morphometry as a predictor of renal graft function
authors: Ana Carolina Pimenta; Beatriz Pedro Fernandes; Luís Rodrigues; Vítor Sousa; Rui Alves
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney transplantation is currently the best renal replacement therapy; however, the scarcity of available organs requires the use of suboptimal donors. Pre-implantation renal biopsy (PIRB) is a valuable tool in the allocation process, employing non-consensual histopathological scoring systems for prognostic assessment of the renal graft. While glomerulosclerosis negatively correlates with recipient renal function, the relationship between glomerular volumetry and post-transplant outcomes remains uncertain.
Objective
To evaluate the predictive capacity of simple and calculated glomerular morphometric variables concerning graft function at one-year post-transplant.
Methods
We conducted a retrospective study including PIRBs digitized via whole slide imaging and assessed by two experienced observers for histopathological parameters, emphasizing glomerular morphometry (major axis, area, and volume, the latter calculated using the Weibel-Gomez formula). Only representative PIRBs were considered, selecting the five largest glomeruli by visual estimation. Additionally, clinical data from donors (including calculation of the Kidney Donor Profile Index—KDPI) and recipients were collected, including estimated glomerular filtration rate at 12 months (eGFR12).
Results
A total of 133 renal biopsies from 102 deceased donors were analyzed, most of whom were male (n = 65, 63.7%), classified as expanded criteria donors (n = 84, 82.4%), and with KDPI > 85 (n = 55, 53.9%). The leading cause of death was a cerebrovascular accident (n = 69, 67.7%). The mean cold ischemia time was 18.4 hours. Recipients had a mean age of 57.8 years, with 88 patients (66.2%) being male. Five recipients (3.8%) had undergone a previous renal transplant.
Among donor characteristics, male donors exhibited a larger mean glomerular diameter; however, the difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.067). Nevertheless, taller donors (P = 0.037), those with diabetes mellitus (P = 0.001), and those with a higher body mass index (P = 0.023) had larger glomeruli, with their recipients achieving a significantly higher eGFR at one-year post-transplant (P = 0.001; P = 0.012; P = 0.039, respectively).
Conclusion
Based on current knowledge, the association of glomerulomegaly with improved graft function at one-year post-transplant remains controversial, raising questions about the predictive accuracy of mean visual estimation in pre-implantation histopathological assessment. Automated PIRB analysis methods, supported by artificial intelligence, may hold promise for optimizing renal morphometry as a decisive factor in the allocation process.

title: #1970 Dapaglifozin in kidney transplant recipients with diabetes mellitus and urine metabolomics analysis
authors: Giulia Bartoli; Andrea Dello Strologo; Maria Arena; Maria Jose Ceravolo; Anna Paola Mitterhofer; Jacopo Gervasoni; Jacopo Romagnoli; Francesco Pesce; Giuseppe Grandaliano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) are a novel class of antidiabetic drugs recently approved for use in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and/or heart failure (HF) due to their cardiovascular (CV) and renal protective effects, both in patients with and without type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM). SGLT2i inhibit sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) in the proximal tubule, reducing renal glucose reabsorption. This mechanism induces glucosuria and natriuresis, leading to weight loss, improved glucose and systolic blood pressure control, and reduced glomerular hyperfiltration and podocyte injury. The ability of SGLT2i to slow kidney disease progression and reduce CV events may represent a significant therapeutic advance for kidney transplant (KT) recipients. However, their use is currently limited by potential adverse effects, including genital infections, urinary tract infections (UTIs), hypoglycemia, and acute kidney injury (AKI). KT recipients are particularly susceptible to infections due to immunosuppressive therapy. This study aimed to investigate the safety of dapagliflozin in diabetic KT recipients and its impact on urine metabolomics.
Method
This observational, retrospective, single-center study included 17 diabetic KT patients treated with dapagliflozin over a 12-month follow-up period. Recipients with contraindications to dapagliflozin or recurrent UTIs were excluded. Demographic, clinical, and laboratory data were collected at baseline, 1, 6, and 12 months. Complications related to SGLT2i use were monitored. Urine samples were collected from 9 patients at baseline and after dapagliflozin treatment. These samples were analyzed using a mass spectrometry-based targeted metabolite approach, covering 1019 metabolites across 39 metabolite classes. Data analysis was performed using MetaboAnalyst 6.0.
Results
Table 1 summarizes patient demographics, baseline characteristics, and drug-related adverse events. Dapagliflozin was well tolerated during the follow-up period. In our cohort, two patients (11.76%) developed UTIs requiring antibiotic therapy without complications, and two patients (11.76%) developed asymptomatic bacteriuria (ABU). One case of AKI, treated with intravenous hydration and requiring hospitalization, was reported. Urine metabolomics analysis revealed changes in metabolite levels after dapagliflozin treatment. Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (PLS-DA) (Fig. 1) demonstrated a shift in metabolite patterns between pre- and post-treatment groups. Fold-change (FC) analysis and Volcano Plot identified 26 significantly altered metabolites (listed in Fig. 1). Pathway analysis revealed involvement of nine metabolic pathways: glycerophospholipid, linoleic acid, alpha-linolenic acid, glyoxylate and dicarboxylate, histidine, sphingolipid, beta-alanine, arachidonic acid metabolism, and the citrate cycle. The altered metabolites were primarily associated with lipid and energy metabolism, such as triacylglycerols (TG), acylcarnitines (C4:1, C10), phosphatidylcholines (PC O-38:6), and diacylglycerol (DG 16:1_18:2), as well as oxidative stress markers like ascorbic acid. It is known that histidine exhibits important anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects. Linoleic acid, a fatty acid, has been associated with metabolic diseases and influences energy metabolism. Sphingolipid and arachidonic acid (AA) pathways are involved in various cellular processes, including maintaining cellular membrane integrity, and may be altered in CKD and diabetic nephropathy.
Conclusion
Our retrospective study suggests that dapagliflozin use in diabetic KT recipients is not associated with major adverse events, supporting its potential for broader use in selected KT patients to optimize the risk-benefit ratio. The beneficial effects of SGLT2i may stem from their influence on various metabolic pathways. Metabolomics analysis indicates that SGLT2 inhibitors impact lipid and energy metabolism and oxidative stress in KT recipients, potentially improving graft and overall patient survival.

title: #3109 Pre-transplant anti-HLA IgM antibodies and kidney transplant outcomes
authors: Egidio Galeandro; Elvira Poggi; Andrea Dello Strologo; Giulia Bartoli; Maria Arena; Maria Paola Salerno; Patrizia Silvestri; Jacopo Romagnoli; Mariano Feccia; Giuseppe Grandaliano; Francesco Pesce
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgM antibodies are not typically detected using traditional crossmatch techniques, and the literature on pre-transplant anti-HLA IgM antibodies remains limited. Consequently, their role in post-transplant outcomes is not yet fully understood. However, existing studies suggest a lower incidence of acute graft rejection in patients with IgM-positive crossmatches. This effect may be partially explained by studies proposing a potential immunoregulatory role of IgM immunoglobulins. The objective of our study was to evaluate post-transplant outcomes based on the presence of anti-HLA IgM antibodies detected during pre-transplant screening.
Method
This retrospective, single-center study analyzed living-donor kidney transplants performed at Gemelli Hospital in Rome, Italy, over a 5-year period (January 2019–December 2023). The objective was to evaluate post-transplant outcomes based on the presence of anti-HLA IgM antibodies detected during pre-transplant screening. Patients were divided into three groups: (1) anti-HLA IgM-negative, (2) non-donor-specific (DSA) anti-HLA IgM antibodies, and (3) DSA anti-HLA IgM-positive.
The primary endpoint was one year graft function, assessed by the eGFR slope and the presence of proteinuria. Secondary endpoints included incidence of rejection, delayed graft function (DGF), infections and tumor during follow-up (until December 2024). Statistical analyses included Shapiro-Wilk, ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis, and Chi-square tests.
Results
A total of 116 transplants were performed, 80 patients anti-HLA IgM-negative, 14 with non-DSA anti-HLA IgM, and 22 with DSA anti-HLA IgM. There were no differences in the use of induction and maintenance immunosuppression in the 3 study groups. There were six cases of DGF in group 1 and none in group 2 and 3 (P = 0.04). Group 3 patients had higher eGFR values throughout 1 year follow-up compared to group 1 and 2, although the differences were not statistically significant. Group 2 patients were characterized by a higher incidence of anti-HLA IgG DSA after transplantation (P = 0.0002). Notably, in 54.5% of group 3 patients IgM anti-HLA DSA disappeared during follow-up, whereas only 4.5% developed IgG anti-HLA DSA corresponding to pre-transplant IgM.
We observed 4 acute antibody-mediated or cell-mediated acute rejection in group 1, 2 mixed rejections in group 2 and no rejections in group 3 (P = 0.01). Incidence of nephropathy recurrence was similar in the three groups. Finally, group 3 patients exhibited a higher incidence of CMV (P = 0.04) and BK virus (P = 0.023) infections. However, the incidence of other infections and post-transplant neoplasia was similar across groups.
Conclusion
Our findings suggest a protective role of donor-specific IgM antibodies in reducing acute rejection incidence and other transplant complications, ultimately supporting improved graft survival during follow-up.

title: #154 Time trends in European paediatric kidney transplantation: an ESPN/ERA Registry study
authors: Iris R Montez de Sousa; Kitty J Jager; Vianda S Stel; Marjolein Bonthuis
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney transplantation is the optimal treatment modality for most patients with kidney failure particularly in childhood due to survival advantages and improved physical and psychosocial development. While most children initiate kidney replacement therapy (KRT) on dialysis, they are expected to receive a kidney transplant during childhood. title: #3881 Automated segmentation and quantification of arterial intimal fibrosis for Remuzzi score calculation in kidney transplant process
authors: Tatke Anish; Paul Anindya; Luís Rodrigues; Pinaki Sarder
abstract:
Background and Aims
The field of Kidney transplantation requires a significant amount of manual effort and technical knowledge of on-call pathologists for selection of the kidney for transplantation. Moreover, there are many problems like the supply and demand disparity, multiple non-standardized methods for donor quality inspection and variations in biopsy findings and clinical outcomes of evaluations resulting in inconsistent results and incorrect decision making. A reformed evaluation score is the Remuzzi lesion score, which scores four critical histological compartments for evaluating the specimen. The arterial intimal fibrosis is one of these compartments, which is difficult to score on PAS stained procurement biopsy images as it requires quantitative measurement of fibro intimal thickening. We have developed an end-to-end pipeline which uses ML models, computer vision techniques and computational methods to calculate the fibro intimal thickening of WSI biopsy images, making the process of donor kidney evaluation easier for the pathologists.
Method
We aim to calculate the mean thickness, intimal area and the stenosis ratio of the intimal layer. For this we develop a model for segmenting the intimal layer from any given Whole Slide Image (WSI). For training the model, we used 246 cropped artery images derived from several WSIs combined from two different sources, namely University of Coimbra and University of California, Davis. This dataset had a diverse degree of intimal thickening with variety in degree of staining. We used 85% of this data for training and validating of the model. We measured this performance by using standardized metrics like Loss, Accuracy and Average Dice Score. We finally arrived at a validation accuracy of 97.71% and a test set accuracy of 92.1%. The next crucial step of the pipeline is the inference on model, which is part of the ComPRePS Intimal Segmentation. The reviewer pathologist manually selects the most severely affected artery WSI. The best performing intimal segmentation model is then used on cropped version of artery image to generate a predicted intimal mask. Finally feature quantification is performed on this intimal mask for calculating various parameters. Various computer vision techniques like distance transform and morphological skeletonization are performed to calculate the mean thickness and intimal area. Further, we use a formula for calculating the stenosis ratio, which is the ratio of intimal area to the sum of the intimal and luminal areas. Stenosis Ratio (%) = Intimal Area / (Intimal Area + Luminal Area) x 100.
Results
Figure 1 shows the cropped artery image, fibrointimal prediction mask and fibrointimal prediction overlay on top of arterial image. Three different arteries have been selected to showcase the model efficacy on several types of arterial cut and thickening. Top row: transversal cut artery with predicted stenosis ratio = 23.33%, middle row: longitudinal cut artery with predicted stenosis ratio =48.5%, and bottom row: transversal cut artery with predicted stenosis ratio = 94%.
Conclusion
These methods and results highlight the importance of arterial intimal fibrosis as an important histological component for calculation of the Remuzzi score. Moreover, this is the only calculation that measures the arterial thickening. In literature, this thickness highly correlates with the post transplant EGFR. The inter pathologist variability in determining this thickness is high, so the developed computation pipeline gives reliability and efficiency.

title: #2912 Sex differences in transplant outcomes and survival for children on kidney replacement therapy: data from the ESPN/ERA Registry
authors: Lucy Plumb; Vianda S Stel; Sevcan A Bakkaloglu; Julien Hogan; Marjolein Bonthuis
abstract:
Background and Aims
Observational studies among children with kidney failure have demonstrated that there are sex differences in timing of presentation and access to kidney transplantation, with disadvantages for female patients. To date, no study has examined the effect of sex on kidney transplant or overall patient survival for European children and young people treated for kidney failure. The aim of this study therefore was to evaluate differences in graft and patient survival by sex among children with kidney failure. We also investigated whether being transplanted mediated the effect of sex on patient survival, and whether pre-emptive transplantation mediated the effect of sex on graft survival.
Method
The study cohort comprised children <20 years old who commenced long-term kidney replacement therapy (KRT) between January 1, 2000 and December 31, 2019 included in the ESPN/ERA Registry. Patients were followed up until recovery, death or end of study period, whichever occurred first. The exposure of interest was sex. Kaplan Meier and Cox Proportional Hazard modelling were used to examine the unadjusted and adjusted effect estimates of sex on patient (from KRT start) and first graft survival (from transplantation), respectively. Mediation analyses using G-formula simulations were conducted to examine the effect of transplantation on overall survival and pre-emptive transplantation on graft survival, respectively.
Results
Over the study period, 17,422 children (58% males) initiated long-term KRT. The median time since KRT start was 4.2 (interquartile range, IQR, 1.9, 7.1) years, with a median time of 3.6 (IQR 1.4, 6.5) years since first kidney transplantation. There were 1,110 graft failures and 1,053 deaths (486 female deaths) recorded. Overall, mortality on KRT was lower for males in unadjusted analyses (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.73, 0.93); incorporation of a transplant-time interaction variable revealed this was due to a lower risk of death for males in the first year on KRT (adjusted HR (aHR) 0.77, 95% CI 0.64, 0.92), while in other timeframes, mortality risk was similar across the sexes. Being transplanted mediated the effect of sex on overall survival (42%) (Table 1).
A lower hazard of graft loss in the first 5-years post-transplant was also noted for males compared to females (aHR 0.86, 95% CI 0.74, 0.99), followed by a higher hazard in the subsequent 5–10 years (aHR 1.64, 95% CI 1.23, 2.20) (Table 1). For graft survival, we found no evidence of mediation through pre-emptive transplantation.
Conclusion
Overall lower male mortality is observed among European children receiving KRT, which appears to be driven by sex differences in the first year after KRT start. Patient survival is partly mediated through kidney transplantation, but this does not explain all of the association observed. For graft survival, a bidirectional association with sex is seen, with males being less likely to experience graft failure in the first 5-years post-transplant, but more likely in the subsequent 5 years. It is not clear what factors are at play but suggest a tailored approach to kidney transplant management taking into account sex and time post-transplant is required.

title: #3503 Fluid overload in perioperative kidney transplantation: more common than meets the eye
authors: Gregorio Romero-González; Javier Paul-Martinez; Inés Perezpayá; Fernando Parra-Londoño; Carles Cañameras Fugasot; Jordi Soler-Majoral; Pau Satorra-Herbera; Néstor Yesid Rodríguez Chitiva; Maria Molina Gomez; Jordi Bover Sanjuan; Jordi Ara; Anna Vila Santandreu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fluid overload is associated with poor outcomes in various settings, including critically ill patients, acute kidney injury, and the perioperative period of abdominal surgery. In 2024, a total of 4,047 kidney transplants were performed in Spain, with transplantation currently considered the best form of kidney replacement therapy. However, evidence regarding the prevalence and effects of fluid overload in these patients remains limited. Traditional metrics used to assess fluid overload are often insensitive and lack accuracy. The aim of this study was to analyze the prevalence of fluid overload in the perioperative period of kidney transplantation using point-of-care ultrasonography.
Method
This prospective study was conducted in a tertiary hospital over an eighteen-month period. Adult patients (≥18 years) undergoing single-kidney transplantation were included. Exclusion criteria were the requirement for vasopressor or inotropic support in the immediate post-transplant period, the need for surgical reintervention, multi-organ transplantation, and cases where ultrasound imaging was inadequate. Ultrasound examinations included lung ultrasound, assessment of the inferior vena cava (IVC) diameter and collapsibility, and measurement of the portal vein pulsatility index using power Doppler. Examinations were performed at four time points: before surgery (D0), the day after surgery (D1), seven days post-surgery (D7), and thirty days post-surgery (D30).
Results
A total of 164 kidney transplants were performed during the study period. Of these, 115 patients met the exclusion criteria, leaving 45 patients for analysis. Among the included patients, 38.3% were women, with a mean age of 57.7 years (±15.50). Hypertension was present in 84.8% of patients, 65.2% were on pre-transplant hemodialysis, 15.2% on peritoneal dialysis, and 19.6% underwent preemptive kidney transplantation. Only 2.2% had heart failure with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF). Additionally, 34.8% of transplants were from donors after brain death, 43.5% from donors after circulatory death, and 21.7% from living donors. Regarding the prevalence of congestion, 26.7% of patients had ultrasound evidence of congestion before surgery (D0). This prevalence increased to 41.9% on the first postoperative day (D1) and remained similar at D7 (39.5%). By D30, congestion persisted in 15.2% of patients (Fig. 1). Further analysis of congestion phenotypes showed that on D0, 15.6% of patients had tissue congestion, which increased to 31% on D1 before progressively decreasing to 26.3% at D7 and 9.1% at D30. Regarding venous congestion, 20% of patients had evidence on D0, followed by 26.2% on D1, 26.3% on D7, and 12.1% on D30. A mixed phenotype of congestion was observed in 8.9% of patients on D0, increasing to 14.3% on D1 and 13.2% on D7 before decreasing to 6.1% on D30.
Conclusion
Fluid overload is a frequent but often underrecognized complication in the perioperative period of kidney transplantation. Our findings highlight that over a quarter of patients already present with ultrasound evidence of congestion before surgery, with a significant increase immediately post-transplant. Although congestion gradually resolves over time, a notable proportion of patients remain affected even at D30. Future studies should explore the impact of targeted fluid management approaches on post-transplant outcomes.

title: #2346 Prognosis of the kidney transplant patient: the role of "traditional" risk
authors: Michele Provenzano; Roberto Minutolo; Luca De Nicola; Lilio Hu; Giuseppe Grandaliano; Carlo Garofalo; Roberta Arena; Rosita Greco; Gianluigi Zaza
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney transplant is the therapeutic option of choice in patients with kidney failure.
Currently, the number of kidney transplants performed per year is constantly growing in Italy. However, the risk stratification of transplant patients remains an important research question because renal prognosis (risk of graft failure, GF) is still suboptimal, particularly in those who have been transplanted for many years. Furthermore, while the prognostic role of immunological risk factors is well defined, that of the traditional risk factors of chronic kidney disease (CKD) i.e. anemia, hypertension, proteinuria, mineral-bone disease, hyperkalemia, previous cardiovascular event (CVD) and smoking is still little studied.
Method
We designed an observational cohort study, enrolling patients undergoing kidney transplant, followed in 6 Nephrology Centers in Italy.
The baseline visit of the patients was collected 12 (±2) months after the intervention, i.e. after achieving a stable clinical and biohumoral picture.
Demographic and clinical information was collected at the baseline visit. Follow-up continued until the onset of GF. The risk categories were created according to the KDIGO-2024 guidelines.
GF incidence rates were calculated by the Poisson method. The adjusted risk of GF was calculated by Cox regression.
Results
Overall we studied 757 transplant patients, with an average age of 45.9 ± 11.3 years and 66.5% male. Stage distribution was: 54.5% G1-2, 21% G3a, 18.6% G3b, 5.8% G4. The incidence rate of GF, in a mean follow-up of 6.4 ± 3.6 years, was significantly higher in the presence of anemia (risk ratio, rr 1.9, P = 0.0002), hypertension (rr 1.8 P = 0.0018), proteinuria (rr 1.7, P = 0.006), hyperphosphatemia (rr 2.0 P = 0.048), smoking (rr 2.0, P = 0.034). Cox multivariate analysis showed that, proteinuria (HR 1.42, 95% CI 1.14–1.78), anemia (HR 1.46, 95% CI 1.0–2.12), CVD (HR 1.66 95% CI 1.10–2.50) and smoking (HR 2.26, 95% CI 1.16–4.41) were significantly associated with GF.
Conclusion
Risk factors for CKD progression also play a significant role in kidney transplant patients. Such evidence is essential for the management of the transplanted patient during nephrological follow-up.

title: #2455 Impact of low dose thymoglobulin-basiliximab induction therapy on acute rejection and post-transplant neoplasia in kidney transplant recipients
authors: Andrea Dello Strologo; Giulia Bartoli; Maria Paola Salerno; Maria Arena; Patrizia Silvestri; Giovanni Stallone; Jacopo Romagnoli; Francesco Pesce; Giuseppe Grandaliano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney transplantation is the optimal treatment for End-Stage Kidney Disease, yet it carries risks of complications, including rejection, infection, and neoplasia, which threaten graft and patient survival. Optimizing immunosuppressive strategies is critical, particularly for induction therapy post-transplant. This study evaluates an innovative induction protocol using low-dose thymoglobulin (ATG) combined with Basiliximab, comparing it to standard ATG dosing or Basiliximab alone, aiming to balance graft protection efficacy while minimizing adverse effects.
Method
In this observational, retrospective cohort study, 959 kidney transplant recipients at the Gemelli Kidney Transplant Center (2001–2022) were analyzed. Patients were grouped based on induction therapy: standard ATG, Basiliximab, or low-dose ATG and Basiliximab (ATG-Bas). Outcomes assessed included biopsy-proven acute rejection, CMV infections, post-transplant neoplasia within the first year, and graft and patient survival over one and five years.
Results
The study included 155 patients in the ATG group, 494 in the ATG-Bas group, and 310 in the Basiliximab group. title: #2252 Shall we go for a walk? A comparative study of the six-minute walk test and cardiopulmonary exercise test in De Novo kidney transplant recipients
authors: Marieke Vandecruys; Jasmine De Beir; Marie Renier; Karsten Vanden Wyngaert; Francis Verbeke; Evi Nagler; Patrick Calders; Stefan De Smet; Kaatje Goetschalckx; Diethard Monbaliu; Véronique Cornelissen; Amaryllis Van Craenenbroeck
abstract:
Background and Aims
Reduced cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF), characterized by impaired muscular oxygen utilization delivered by the circulatory and respiratory systems during physical activity, is a major contributor to adverse outcomes in kidney transplant recipients (KTRs). The gold standard for assessing CRF is a cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) measuring peak oxygen uptake (VO₂peak). While CPET provides valuable insights, its resource-intensive nature limits its routine use. In contrast, the six-minute walk test (6MWT) is a simpler, cost-effective alternative commonly used to assess functional capacity in chronic disease patients. Previous studies have shown moderate to high agreement between the 6MWT and VO₂peak in heart failure and haemodialysis patients, however, the level of agreement in KTRs remains unclear.
Method
Baseline data from the first 80 participants recruited in the ongoing PHOENIX-Kidney trial (NCT06260579) were analysed. PHOENIX-Kidney includes de novo KTRs from two Belgian hospitals: University Hospitals Leuven and Ghent University Hospital. Eligible participants were adults who had received a kidney transplant within the past three months, with testing conducted at three months post-transplant. All procedures were conducted by trained investigators according to prespecified standard operating procedures. Following a breakfast and maintenance medical therapy, participants performed the 6MWT in a 30-meter corridor, walking up and down as far as possible in six minutes. Heart rate, oxygen saturation, and perceived exertion were recorded during the test, and predicted walking distances were calculated using Duncan's equation. Approximately 20 minutes after the 6MWT, CPET was performed on a cycle ergometer with an incremental ramp protocol until exhaustion. VO₂peak was defined as the highest 30-second average oxygen consumption (ml/min) and adjusted for body weight, with predicted values calculated using Gläser's equation. Pearson's correlation coefficient was used to assess the relationship between 6MWT distance and VO₂peak. Agreement between the assessments was evaluated using Bland-Altman analysis, which calculates mean bias, standard deviation of the differences, and limits of agreement.
Results
Eighty participants were included (31% female). The mean age was 54.3 ± 12.1 years, mean body mass index was 24.7 ± 4.5 kg/m2, and mean eGFR 52.1 ± 19.8 mL/min/1.73 m². CPET results showed a mean VO₂peak of 19.3 ± 6.0 ml/min/kg, corresponding to a predicted VO₂peak of 69.2 ± 15.8%. The mean power achieved during CPET was 116 ± 46 Watts, and the peak heart rate averaged 137 ± 28 bpm (82.7 ± 14.4% of predicted). All patients reached a respiratory exchange ratio of > 1.10, with Borg scores indicating significant exertion (mean ± SD: 8 ± 1). For the 6MWT, the mean distance walked was 511 ± 108 meters, corresponding to 76.5 ± 13.7% of the predicted value. Peak heart rate during the 6MWT was lower (115 ± 21 bpm, 58.8 ± 33.3% of predicted) compared to CPET. Borg scores indicated moderate exertion (leg fatigue: 4 ± 2, dyspnoea: 4 ± 2).
A moderate correlation (r = 0.54, P < 0.001) was found between 6MWT distance and VO₂peak. Bland-Altman analysis revealed rather poor agreement between the percentage predicted 6MWT and percentage predicted VO₂peak, with an overestimation of CRF by the 6MWT (mean bias = 7.7%). The limits of agreement ranged from −26.2% to +41.6%, demonstrating high variability between the tests. Consequently, the 6MWT may not consistently reflect VO₂peak accurately.
Conclusion
Despite the moderate correlation observed between the 6MWT and VO2peak in recently transplanted KTRs, the 6MWT tends to overestimate CRF, and the wide limits of agreement indicate that the 6MWT can either underestimate or overestimate CRF by as much as 26.2% and 41.6%, respectively. These findings suggest that although the 6MWT provides valuable information, it is not interchangeable with VO₂peak in the clinical post-transplant setting.

title: #1749 Exploring psychological distress and quality of life in kidney transplant patients: a study of gender differences
authors: Silvia Bellardinelli; Giulia Bartoli; Eleonora Maggio; Antonio Maria D'onofrio; Rosaria Calia; Giuseppe Grandaliano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney transplantation (KT) is a key therapeutic strategy for patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), often leading to an improvement in quality of life (QoL). However, the transplant eligibility process and the transplant itself impose a significant psychological burden on patients, potentially contributing to the development or worsening of anxiety, depression, and stress, which may influence transplant survival. The aim of this study is to investigate the psychological vulnerabilities in kidney transplant recipients at least one year post-transplant and explore potential relationships between quality of life, clinical variables, and psychological factors.
Method
This is a monocentric observational study conducted on patients who underwent kidney transplantation at least one year ago (n = 105). Exclusion criteria included age over 85, dementia, psychotic, or dissociative disorders. Participants completed self-report questionnaires, including the DASS-21 (for anxiety, depression, and stress), SF-12 (quality of life), and SCL-90 (general symptomatology), along with a clinical history and laboratory data collection. Statistical analyses included descriptive statistics, frequency analysis, t-tests, and linear regression for psychological variables, considering gender differences.
Results
Sixty-one percent of the patients were male (n = 64), with a mean age of 54 years. Analysis of the DASS-21 results revealed that 12.6% of patients experienced general distress, 26.9% reported clinically significant anxiety, 10.7% depression, and 7.8% stress (Fig. 1). Additionally, quality of life (SF-12) was positively correlated with hemoglobin levels (r = 0.264; P < 0.05) and negatively correlated with the number of pills taken per day (r = −0.237; P < 0.05) (Fig. 2). Regarding gender differences, female patients exhibited significantly higher scores in distress, depression, anxiety, and stress compared to male patients, with a negative correlation between quality of life and anxiety and depression in females (P < 0.01); in males, quality of life was negatively correlated with depression and the number of medications taken (P < 0.05) (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
The results confirm previously reported findings regarding the incidence of anxiety and distress in kidney transplant recipients. A significant correlation between pharmacological therapy, quality of life, and psychological symptoms was also found. Notably, gender differences emerged, with females reporting greater emotional difficulties, while males were more affected by pharmacological therapy. These findings highlight the importance of personalized psychological follow-up, focusing on the specific needs of each patient: monitoring pharmacological therapy in males and addressing anxiety and depression in females, to improve adherence to post-transplant care.

title: #3800 Safety and efficacy of SGLT2i in non-diabetic kidney transplant recipients
authors: Cristina Amorós Robles; Aina Quilis; Pilar Fraile Gómez; Verónica López; Luis Alberto Vigara; Pablo González-Calero Borrás; María José Torres-Sánchez; Cristina Canal; Ainhoa Inza San Salvador del Valle; Hernando Trujillo Cuellar; Ana Isabel Sánchez Fructuoso; Anna Buxeda
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) are key therapeutic agents in cardiovascular and renal care. While widely used in kidney transplant recipients (KTRs) with diabetes, evidence on their safety and efficacy in non-diabetic KTRs remains limited. This study aims to evaluate the clinical outcomes of SGLT2i therapy in a cohort exclusively composed of non-diabetic KTRs.
Method
We conducted a multicenter retrospective study of 176 non-diabetic KTRs who initiated SGLT2i therapy. Clinical and analytical data were collected at baseline and after 6 months of treatment.
Results
The mean recipient age was 47.6 ± 13.5 years, with 32.4% being women. SGLT2i therapy was initiated at a median of 6.1 years [IQR 1.9–14.9] post-KT, predominantly with dapagliflozin (85.8%). The primary indication was non-nephrotic proteinuria (75%). Interestingly, 17% of patients were not receiving any concomitant antiproteinuric therapy. After 6 months of treatment, there was a significant reduction in protein/creatinine ratio (607.3 mg/g [IQR 217.8–1390] vs. 400 mg/g [IQR 129–1000], P < 0.001) and albumin/creatinine ratio (545 mg/g [IQR 221–1154] vs. 295.6 mg/g [IQR 106–753.2], P < 0.001) [Fig. 1A]. Adverse effects occurred in 22.7% of patients [Fig. 1B], with 8 (4.5%) requiring hospitalization due to probable SGLT2i-related complications (7 urinary tract infections [UTIs] and 1 case of acute kidney injury [AKI]). Temporary discontinuation occurred in 13.2% of patients, with a median time of therapy reinitiation of 6 months [IQR 4–10]. Additionally, 23.8% of patients permanently stopped therapy due to UTIs (30%), AKI (25%) or unspecified causes (35%).
Conclusion
SGLT2i therapy in non-diabetic KTRs shows an acceptable safety profile with a low rate of severe adverse events. The significant reduction in proteinuria and albuminuria observed at 6 months supports its potential renoprotective effects in this population. However, risks such as UTIs and AKI warrant careful monitoring. Further studies are needed to confirm long-term safety and efficacy.

title: #3890 Physician communication and the patient-provider relationship as factors for non-adherence in kidney transplant recipients
authors: Nathan Andreas Pohl; Aylin Akifova; Bilgin Osmanodja; Bianca Zukunft; Marcel Naik; Fabian Halleck; Friederike Bachmann; Klemens Budde; Wiebke Duettmann
abstract:
Background and Aims
In the care of kidney transplant recipients (KTR), there is an established relationship between non-adherence (NA) to immunosuppressive medications (IM) and rejection (acute and chronic), graft loss and death. NA is influenced by a variety of risk factors that can be categorized as disease-related, socio-economic, patient-related, provider-related and treatment-related.
In this study we analyzed the relationship between NA, barriers to adherence and satisfaction with physician communication skills and the patient-provider relationship. While inadequate doctor communication and doctor-patient relationship are identified as risk factors for NA, no study has investigated those determinants in non-adherence assessment in KTR.
Method
We conducted a monocentric, prospective cross-sectional study using self-report questionnaires for patients assess barriers to adherence in Adherence Barriers Questionnaire (ABQ), NA to IM in Basel Assessment of Adherence to immunosuppressive medications scale (BAASIS) and satisfaction with communication and quality of care in Zufriedenheit mit ambulanter Versorgung (ZAP) post transplant.
For this interim analysis, we included 403 adult KTR recruited since 2020, patients during routine outpatient visits following KTX. Only adult KTR with sufficient German language skills and the ability to consent were eligible to participate.
The ABQ measures barriers to adherence (e.g. forgetfulness, being critical about taking medication, financial constraints etc.). The BAASIS measures NA in 3 different scales; this analysis will focus on the subscale implementation problems, i.e. consistency of IM intake. This analysis is focusing on 2 categories of the ZAP measuring patient satisfaction with doctor information sharing/communication and the doctor-patient interaction/relationship.
Recipients characteristics evaluated include age, sex, time since last kidney transplantation (KTX) and number of KTX.
Results
Demographics
The mean age of the 403 KTR was 54.2 years (+/−13,2), 146 (36.2%) are female, mean time since last KTX is 9.1 years (+/-7.7). 361 (89.6%) KTR received 1 KTX, 34 (8.4%) received 2, 6 (1.5%) received 3 and 2 (0.5%) received 4.
Adherence
In total, 167 (41.4%) reported some form of NA to IM in the last 4 weeks in BAASIS, i.e. they missed a dose completely 58 (14.4%) or/and missed a dose by >2h 147 (36.5%). More specifically, in terms of those self-reported NA events in the last 4 weeks, 65 KTR (16.1%) reported 1 event, 56 (13.9%) 2 events, 23 (5.7%) 3 events and 24 (6.0%) >3 events.
Adherence Barriers
The barriers to adherence in the ABQ are measured in a range 16–64 as shown in the table. On average, the barriers are relatively low (24.8), but they show a considerable range (16–48).
Satisfaction
Satisfaction in the ZAP is measured on a scale of 0–100. Therefore, both satisfaction with communication by the healthcare provider (82.8), as well as with doctor-patient relationship (87.3) show high values in the mean, but a considerable measured range of 0–100 and 4.2–100 respectively.
Correlation Effects (Fig. 1)
Both satisfaction subscales correlate significantly negatively with the BAASIS number of NA events and the ABQ adherence barriers. The correlation effect between satisfaction with communication and NA is ρ = −0.21 (P < 0.001) and ρ = −0.33 (P < 0.001) respectively, higher than between satisfaction with doctor-patient relationship and NA and adherence barriers ρ = −0.14 (P = 0.0051), ρ = −0.28 (P < 0.001) respectively. Noticeable, the effects between satisfaction and adherence barriers are higher than between satisfaction and NA.
Conclusion
As shown, there is a relationship between satisfaction with communication, doctor-patient relationship and IM NA as well as barriers to adherence. In general, the effects are very small, too small, but highly significant.
Therefore, communication and the doctor-patient relationship should be considered as modifiable risk factors of NA in the care for KTR.

title: #1685 Multimodal spatial profiling of microvascular inflammation in kidney allografts
authors: Valentin Goutaudier; Erwan Morgand; Marta Sablik; Fariza Mezine; Thibaut Thalamas; Anaïs Certain; Gillian Divard; Olivier Aubert; Jean-Sébastien Hulot; Carmen Lefaucheur; Aurélie Sannier; Alexandre Loupy
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney allograft microvascular inflammation (MVI) DSA-negative C4d-negative is a new entity recognized by the Banff 2022 classification, but the mechanisms driving this inflammation remain poorly understood. In this context, we aimed to decipher its immuno-molecular landscape.
Method
MVI cases were identified in a multicentric cohort of kidney transplant patients and compared to MVI-negative control cases (total n = 309). Biopsies were graded according to the Banff 2022 classification and sequenced using the Banff Human Organ Transplant panel. Whole-transcriptome digital spatial profiling and cellular deconvolution were performed on each phenotype of interest using the NanoString GeoMx® platform. Finally, microvascular infiltration was characterized using a multiplex immunofluorescence panel staining CD34, CD68, CD3, NKp46, CD15 and CD20.
Results
Three MVI phenotypes were analyzed: 1) MVI DSA− C4d− (n = 49, 15.9%), 2) MVI DSA+ C4d− (n = 45, 14.6%), 3) MVI DSA+ C4d+ (n = 46, 14.9%), as well as a control group of non-MVI cases (n = 169, 54.6%). When compared to controls, all MVI cases shared a common molecular signature, characterized by an upregulation of genes associated with antibody-mediated injury, interferon-gamma response, and activation of macrophages, NK cells, and T cells. This common signature was less intense in MVI DSA− C4d− cases, particularly regarding the interferon-gamma response. Spatial profiling analysis revealed that this molecular signal was more prominent in peritubular capillaries than in the glomeruli. Cellular deconvolution further demonstrated that MVI DSA− C4d− cases were particularly associated with NK cells and conventional dendritic cells. Automated quantification of immunofluorescence staining revealed that microvascular infiltration was predominantly composed of CD68+ macrophages, CD3+ T cells, and NKp46+ NK cells (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
We demonstrate that the immuno-molecular signature in kidney allograft MVI DSA− C4d− is moderate in intensity compared to MVI DSA+ C4d− and MVI DSA+ C4d+, and is predominantly characterized by the presence of NK cells and conventional dendritic cells in the peritubular capillaries. Our findings open avenues for more mechanistically driven therapeutic approaches for MVI.
