title: #2115 Is preemptive kidney transplantation beneficial in elderly kidney recipients?: A comparative, multicentre national study
authors: Hamad Dheir; Erol Demir; Ulkem Cakir; Huseyin Kocak; Aygul Celtik; Ayse Sinangil; Gizem Kumru; Tuba Elif Ozler; Feyza Bayrakdar Caglayan; Tolga Yildirim; Bahar Gurlek Demirci; Ergun Parmaksiz; Halil Yİldİz; Vural Taner Yilmaz; Yağmur Tahıllıoğlu; Mevlut Tamer Dincer; Arzu Velioglu; Ramazan Danis; Ebru Sevinç Ok; Mehmet Emin Demir; Ozgur Akin Oto; Şebnem Karakan; Zeynep Akcalİ; Abdulmecit Yildiz; İbrahim Berber; Adem Uslu; Gulay Asci; Alaattin Yildiz; Siren Sezer; Kenan Keven; Huseyin Toz; Aydin Turkmen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Preemptive kidney transplantation is known to be associated with longer allograft and patient survival. However, there is limited data in the literature regarding the outcomes of preemptive kidney transplantation in elderly kidney transplant recipients. In this study, we aimed to investigate the effects of preemptive kidney transplantation on patient and graft survival in elderly kidney transplant recipients.
Method
Our study is based on a retrospective analysis of data from 17 centers that performed kidney transplantation in patients aged 50 years and older between 2015 and 2020. Patients were divided into two groups: preemptive and non-preemptive groups. The endpoints of the study were graft loss, functional graft death and all-cause mortality.
Results
A total of 1305 kidney recipients, 366 preemptive and 939 non-preemptive, were included in the study. The median age of the patients was 56 years and 39.4% were female. The median follow-up period was 63 (6–115) months and 65 (6–114) months, respectively (P = 0.640). Body mass index, living donor transplantation rate and presence of hypertension were significantly higher in the preemptive group (P < 0.001 for each). In addition, the use of anti-lymphocyte globulin (ATLG) as induction therapy, duration and dose of treatment, and delayed graft function were significantly lower in the preemptive group than in the non-preemptive group (P = 0.028, P = 0.003, P < 0.001, P < 0.001, respectively). The rates of graft loss, death with a functioning graft and all-cause mortality were significantly lower in the preemptive group compared to the non-preemptive group (P = 0.012, P = 0.006, P = 0.002, respectively). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed that patient and graft survival in the preemptive group was better than in the non-preemptive group (P = 0.018 and P = 0.024, respectively). Furthermore, Cox regression analysis showed that only preemptive kidney transplantation reduced all-cause mortality by 40% (HR:0.62, CI 95%: 0.42–0.93; P = 0.02).
Conclusion
In elderly kidney transplant recipients, preemptive kidney transplantation provides longer patient, and graft survival compared to non-preemptive approach. These findings suggest that preemptive kidney transplantation should be preferred in elderly end-stage renal failure patients.

title: #3708 SGLT2 inhibitors in kidney transplant recipients: renal, cardiovascular and safety outcomes: a narrative review
authors: Reima Almarshoodi; Hemant Sharma
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) are novel anti-diabetic medications that have emerged in the last decade. It has been shown to be both effective and safe for patients with diabetes. Recent studies have demonstrated the benefits of these medications for diabetic patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and heart failure, showing significant cardiovascular and renal protective effects. While it benefits both diabetic and non-diabetic patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), studies have not yet evaluated its advantages for kidney transplant recipients. To address the existing knowledge gap, a systematic review was conducted to evaluate the safety and efficacy of SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) in renal transplant patients, regardless of their diabetes status. The review also examined the emerging cardiovascular and renal benefits of SGLT2i in the kidney transplant population. The findings from this review offer valuable insights into the cardiovascular and renal advantages of SGLT2i, along with their safety profile in this specific patient group.
Method
This review examines the efficacy and safety of SGLT2 inhibitors in kidney transplant recipients, regardless of their diabetes status, and evaluates whether these medications improve renal and cardiovascular outcomes in this population. The research question was: Are SGLT2 inhibitors effective, safe, and improve renal and cardiovascular outcomes in kidney transplant recipients? The search strategy included reviewing English literature from five medical databases: PubMed, MEDLINE, SCOPUS, Cochrane, and Google Scholar, covering the period from inception through August 2024. A total of 418 studies were extracted from these databases, and seventeen eligible studies were selected for analysis. This study offers a qualitative synthesis of findings regarding the efficacy, safety, and cardiovascular and kidney outcomes of SGLT-2 inhibitors in kidney transplant recipients.
Results
SGLT2 inhibitors have demonstrated effectiveness in reducing HbA1c levels and promoting weight loss among renal transplant recipients with diabetes. It demonstrated a favorable safety profile in renal transplant recipients with diabetes, with urinary tract infections being the most commonly reported side effect. Few studies indicate that SGLT2 inhibitors have a renal protective effect and improve the survival of allografts in renal transplant recipients. This is consistent with evidence available in patients with diabetes and chronic kidney disease who have not had kidney transplants in large randomised trials (CREDENCE, DAPA-CKD and EMPA-KIDNEY). Additionally, SGLT2 inhibitors demonstrated a reduction in all-cause and cardiac mortality among patients with kidney transplants and diabetes. The results align with findings from other studies in the general population with diabetes that investigated the cardiovascular benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors. Major randomized controlled trials, including EMPA-REG OUTCOME, DECLARE-TIMI 58, and CANVAS, have consistently shown these SGLT2 inhibitors' positive effects on cardiovascular outcomes in diabetic patients.
Conclusion
SGLT2 inhibitors may offer similar efficacy and cardiovascular, renal, and all-cause mortality benefits in kidney transplant recipients with diabetes as in patients with diabetes mellitus. It can be safely used in diabetic renal transplant recipients. However, precautions should be taken to monitor for urinary tract infections, particularly in high-risk populations. The limited available evidence on using SGLT2 inhibitors in non-diabetic renal transplant patients makes it challenging to determine the potential benefits and risks regarding cardiovascular and renal protection in this population. Further studies are needed to determine the long-term cardiovascular and renal benefits of these inhibitors, especially in renal transplant recipients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) or heart failure who do not have diabetes.

title: #2647 Effect of reducing dialysate sodium concentration on blood pressure variability in hemodialysis patients: a randomized controlled trial
authors: Hoda Mahmoud Mohammad Abdulaziz; Hadeer Gomaa; Ghada Elsaid
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hypertension is recognized as an important modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease among hemodialysis patients. Apart from blood pressure levels, blood pressure variability (BPV) has been described as an independent risk factor that is linearly associated with all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in hemodialysis patients. Sodium load is associated with thirst, fluid retention, interdialytic weight gain, and hypertension. This study aimed to investigate the effect of lowering dialysate sodium concentration on visit-to-visit (interdialytic) BPV in hemodialysis patients.
Method
This was a single-center, prospective, single-blind, randomized controlled study. One-hundred and ten hemodialysis patients were assessed for eligibility and 89 were randomized to receive hemodialysis either with standard sodium dialysate (143 mmol/L) or reduced sodium dialysate (140 mmol/L) for 3 months. Eighty-three patients completed the study. Predialysis blood pressure readings were recorded with an automated device during the two weeks before and after the intervention. The interdialytic BPV was quantified by 3 metrics: the standard deviation of the blood pressure, the coefficient of variation, and the average real variability. Differences between both groups regarding the three metrics of BPV were tested using the analysis of covariance test after adjustment of baseline BPV values. The study was approved by the local ethical committee (MS.21.06.1547) and registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05169125). All patients provided valid informed written consent and were managed according to the Declaration of Helsinki.
Results
The mean age of the studied patients was 51.2 (±14.5) years. Fifty-four patients (62.8%) were males. The mean baseline systolic and diastolic blood pressures of the included patients were 140.9 ± 11.3 mmHg and 85.2 ± 4.4 mmHg, respectively. At the end of the study, the adjusted standard deviation, coefficient of variation, and average real variability of systolic blood pressure were significantly lower in the low-sodium dialysate group (9.72 mmHg vs, 11.29 mmHg, P = .020; 7.2% vs. 8.2%, P = .034; 11.28 mmHg vs. 12.93 mmHg, P = <.001, respectively). No significant difference was observed between both groups in terms of diastolic BPV measures. Furthermore, interdialytic weight gain was significantly lower in the low-sodium dialysate group after 3 months (2.5 ± 0.73 kg vs. 2.9 ± 0.86 kg, P = 0.02). Intradialytic adverse events were comparable for both groups.
Conclusion
Lowering dialysate sodium could potentially be a therapeutic intervention to lower interdialytic BPV and thus improve cardiovascular outcomes. Further studies are needed with more reduction of dialysate sodium and longer follow-up periods to confirm postulated cardiovascular benefits.

title: #3795 Childhood Takayasu arteritis: a multicentre retrospective cohort study
authors: Katrina Evers; Despina Eleftheriou; Paul Brogan; Matko Marlais; Kjell Tullus
abstract:
Background and Aims
Takayasu arteritis (TA) is a rare, large vessel vasculitis affecting mainly the aorta and its major branches. The diagnosis is often difficult to make due to nonspecific constitutional symptoms including fever, fatigue and weight loss and no recognised pediatric diagnostic criteria. We explored how many children diagnosed with TA fulfilled existing classification criteria or adult diagnostic criteria; and which criteria for TA were used by clinicians when considering the diagnosis of pediatric TA.
Method
We conducted an international multicentre retrospective cohort study of children diagnosed with TA from 37 centres in 20 countries. Epidemiological and clinical data were collected from patients' charts. Information was also sought on which, if any, classification or diagnostic criteria were used, and we retrospectively reviewed how many of the diagnosed children fulfilled the main criteria currently in use, including the only pediatric classification criteria from EULAR/PRINTO/PRES.
Results
198 patients were included (76% female). The median age of disease onset was 12 years. In 96 (48.5%) children the treating centre reported that they had used the classification criteria proposed by EULAR/PRINTO/PRES; 31 (15.7%) used the 1990 ACR criteria for adults; and 9 (4.5%) the diagnostic criteria from Ishikawa, 1988. Eleven (5.6%) centres used other criteria such as the Indian Takayasu clinical activity score, modified Ishikawa criteria from 1996 or simply diagnosed the patient based on clinical findings highly suspicious for TA.
We found that 197 (99.5%) patients fulfilled the mandatory EULAR/PRINTO/PRES classification criterion, angiographic abnormality; of the non-mandatory criteria 22 (14%) had claudication, 95 (65%) had a difference of ≥10 mmHg between any two limbs, 87 (50%) had decreased pulses, 35 (46%) had absent pulses, and 39 children (26%) had a bruit detected over the aorta or subclavian artery. Two (1%) children had the mandatory angiographic finding, but none of the further listed criteria. Thus, a total of 195 (98%) children fulfilled the classification criteria suggested by EULAR/PRINTO/PRES; and 197 (99.5%) the ACR classification criteria. Regarding diagnostic criteria, only 150 (75.8%) patients fulfilled the modified Ishikawa criteria from 1996.
Conclusion
Our study represents the largest pediatric cohort of children diagnosed with TA. Most patients fulfilled the pediatric classification criteria suggested by EULAR/PRINTO/PRES; as well as the ACR criteria. In contrast, only three-quarters of cases fulfilled the modified Ishikawa diagnostic criteria suggesting that these cannot be used with confidence for the diagnosis of pediatric TA. Our findings support the ongoing use of the pediatric EULAR/PRINTO/PRES criteria to classify TA from other forms of vasculitis; and emphasise that these are particularly useful to make sure that a homogeneous or consistent population is selected for trials and research. These criteria should not be misused as diagnostic criteria, however, because they were not tested against important disease mimics such as non-inflammatory genetic vasculopathies.
Thus, clinicians should be minded that classification criteria are not the same as diagnostic criteria, and these should not be misused for diagnostic purposes.

title: #3065 Effect of dapagliflozin and empagliflozin on phosphate-FGF23 homeostasis in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Hande Altunkaynak; Carsten Wagner
abstract:
Background and Aims
Emerging clinical evidence suggest that SGLT2 inhibitors could modulate serum phosphate levels. However, the impact of these drugs on fibroblast growth factor-23 (FGF23) levels remains unclear. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the impact of SGLT2 inhibitors on phosphate-FGF23 homeostasis in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).
Method
PubMed and Web of Science databases were searched using key words: “SGLT2 inhibitor”, and “FGF23” up to January 2025. A random effects model was used, with the outcome expressed as standardised mean difference (SMDs) with 95% confidence interval [CI]. Heterogeneity was quantified by I2 values. Subgroup analysis was also performed according to duration of treatment (≤ 6-, >6–24 weeks). P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results
In total, four active- or placebo-controlled clinical studies involving patients with T2DM met our inclusion criteria. Among the studies included, dapagliflozin and empagliflozin were the SGLT2 inhibitors administered at a dose of 10 mg/day and the follow-up durations ranged from 3-days to 24 weeks. Overall, dapagliflozin and empagliflozin significantly increased serum phosphate levels in T2DM patients (SMD = 0.64 [0.20, 1.09], P = 0.005), consistent across duration of treatment (≤ 6-, >6–24 weeks). The meta-analysis also showed that use of SGLT2 inhibitor presented a non-significant increase in serum levels of FGF23 in T2DM patients (P = 0.54). However, discrepancies in reported FGF23 assays (intact-, c-terminal FGF23 or both) among these studies were observed.
Conclusion
This meta-analysis suggest that dapagliflozin and empagliflozin induce increments in serum phosphate levels in patients with T2DM. Nonetheless, the observed between-study heterogeneity due to variations among limited number of studies, and different assays for FGF23 measurement in these studies complicates the understanding of the phosphate-FGF23 homeostasis in T2DM patients. To clarify the impact of these drugs on FGF23 levels, further research is needed with additional efforts elucidating the measurement of intact FGF23 and c-terminal FGF23 in patients with T2DM and extend studies also to individuals without T2DM.

title: #1561 Atypical chemokine receptor 4 is involved in blood pressure regulation and ameliorates experimental glomerulonephritis
authors: Daniel Leitinger; Stefan Russo; Corinna Schabhuettl; Elin Hub; Julia Gutjahr; Maryna Samus; Alexander H Kirsch; Philipp Eller; Alexander Rosenkranz; Kathrin Eller; Katharina Artinger; Antal Rot
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hypertension is a multifactorial disease that affects nearly 50% of all adults and represents the second most prevalent cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD).
Atypical chemokine receptors are homologous to other G-protein coupled chemokine receptors, however, no G-protein mediated intracellular signaling is triggered by chemokine ligation. Instead, ACKRs modulate chemokine availability in defined microenvironments and modify chemokine-induced leukocyte migration. ACKR4 ligates chemokines involved in adaptive immune responses and accordingly its expression and function are well characterized in primary and secondary lymphatic organs. Conversely, the role of ACKR4 in parenchymal organs, such as the kidney remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the expression of ACKR4 in the murine kidney and its contribution to the pathogenesis of experimental nephrotoxic serum nephritis (NTSN) and the ensuing changes in blood pressure.
Method
Expression of ACKR4 and renin in the murine kidney was assessed using confocal laser scanning microscopy of multicolor immunofluorescence stainings in ACKR4+/eGFPKI reporter mice. NTSN was induced in ACKR4+/+ (wild type), ACKR4 eGFPKI/eGFPKI (ACKR4-deficient) and ACKR4+/eGFPKI (heterozygous) reporter mice, and the renal disease phenotype, blood pressure, serum renin, and aldosterone as well as urinary sodium levels were evaluated on days 0, 14, and 28 after the induction of NTSN.
Results
Confocal imaging revealed that ACKR4 expression in the kidneys was restricted to few glomerular parietal epithelial cells (PECs) localizing at the glomerular vascular pole adjacent to the renin-producing cells. Notably, this spatial association with the vascular pole was exclusively observed by ACKR4-positive PECs beginning at postnatal day 28, suggesting that these cells undergo positional refinement within the glomerulus during earlier stages of development. After induction of NTSN, ACKR4 expression was reduced, particularly in severely sclerotic glomeruli. The ACKR4-deficient mice showed aggravated parameters of NTSN, including albuminuria and histopathology as compared to WT controls. Moreover, serum renin was significantly increased in nephritic ACKR4-deficient mice, whereas aldosterone levels and urinary sodium showed no significant differences. Surprisingly, ACKR4-deficient mice exhibited significantly higher systolic (139.3 ± 15.55 mmHg vs. 118.3 ± 9.87 mmHg, P = 0.039) and diastolic (111.4 ± 14.02 mmHg vs. 87.08 ± 10.60 mmHg, P = 0.016) blood pressure as compared to ACKR4 WT mice in norm as well as 14 and 28 days after induction of NTSN.
Conclusion
ACKR4 is expressed in glomeruli by PECs close to the glomerular vascular pole. The aggravated NTSN phenotype in ACKR4-deficient mice suggests a new regulatory role of ACKR4 in the kidney, limiting the development of nephritis. The close spatial association of ACKR4-expressing cells with the juxtaglomerular apparatus, together with the observed increase in serum renin levels and elevated blood pressure in ACKR4−/− mice suggests a potential role of ACKR4 in regulating blood pressure, potentially impacting the renin-angiotensin system.

Background and Aims
Hypertension is a multifactorial disease that affects nearly 50% of all adults and represents the second most prevalent cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD).
Atypical chemokine receptors are homologous to other G-protein coupled chemokine receptors, however, no G-protein mediated intracellular signaling is triggered by chemokine ligation. Instead, ACKRs modulate chemokine availability in defined microenvironments and modify chemokine-induced leukocyte migration. ACKR4 ligates chemokines involved in adaptive immune responses and accordingly its expression and function are well characterized in primary and secondary lymphatic organs. Conversely, the role of ACKR4 in parenchymal organs, such as the kidney remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the expression of ACKR4 in the murine kidney and its contribution to the pathogenesis of experimental nephrotoxic serum nephritis (NTSN) and the ensuing changes in blood pressure.
Method
Expression of ACKR4 and renin in the murine kidney was assessed using confocal laser scanning microscopy of multicolor immunofluorescence stainings in ACKR4+/eGFPKI reporter mice. NTSN was induced in ACKR4+/+ (wild type), ACKR4 eGFPKI/eGFPKI (ACKR4-deficient) and ACKR4+/eGFPKI (heterozygous) reporter mice, and the renal disease phenotype, blood pressure, serum renin, and aldosterone as well as urinary sodium levels were evaluated on days 0, 14, and 28 after the induction of NTSN.
Results
Confocal imaging revealed that ACKR4 expression in the kidneys was restricted to few glomerular parietal epithelial cells (PECs) localizing at the glomerular vascular pole adjacent to the renin-producing cells. Notably, this spatial association with the vascular pole was exclusively observed by ACKR4-positive PECs beginning at postnatal day 28, suggesting that these cells undergo positional refinement within the glomerulus during earlier stages of development. After induction of NTSN, ACKR4 expression was reduced, particularly in severely sclerotic glomeruli. The ACKR4-deficient mice showed aggravated parameters of NTSN, including albuminuria and histopathology as compared to WT controls. Moreover, serum renin was significantly increased in nephritic ACKR4-deficient mice, whereas aldosterone levels and urinary sodium showed no significant differences. Surprisingly, ACKR4-deficient mice exhibited significantly higher systolic (139.3 ± 15.55 mmHg vs. 118.3 ± 9.87 mmHg, P = 0.039) and diastolic (111.4 ± 14.02 mmHg vs. 87.08 ± 10.60 mmHg, P = 0.016) blood pressure as compared to ACKR4 WT mice in norm as well as 14 and 28 days after induction of NTSN.
Conclusion
ACKR4 is expressed in glomeruli by PECs close to the glomerular vascular pole. The aggravated NTSN phenotype in ACKR4-deficient mice suggests a new regulatory role of ACKR4 in the kidney, limiting the development of nephritis. The close spatial association of ACKR4-expressing cells with the juxtaglomerular apparatus, together with the observed increase in serum renin levels and elevated blood pressure in ACKR4−/− mice suggests a potential role of ACKR4 in regulating blood pressure, potentially impacting the renin-angiotensin system.

title: #908 Predicting the risk of and days without albuminuria in patients with diabetes mellitus: a development and validation study
authors: Roemer Janse; Chava Ramspek; Marretje Oomen; Friedo W Dekker; Juan-Jesus Carrero; Merel Van Diepen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) are at high risk of kidney disease, which may be ameliorated by early detection of albuminuria. Clinical prediction models (CPMs) can tailor guideline-indicated screening to the individual patient, but no adequate CPMs are currently available. Modern methods allow us to predict more than just a single risk at a single point in time. We aimed to predict 3-year albuminuria risk to show how risk progresses over time, albuminuria-free time in days as a more intuitive outcome, and the risk of different outcomes over 3 years, at the moment of a first normoalbuminuric test.
Method
We used data from the Stockholm Creatinine Measurements cohort. We selected patients with T2DM, a normoalbuminuric test, and no prior albuminuria between 2007–2021 from all Stockholm residents. Subsequently, we created a development (2007–2013) and temporal validation (2014–2021) cohort. Predictors were selected based on clinical expertise, literature, and previous CPMs. Albuminuria was defined as urine albumin-creatinine ratio (uACR) ≥30 mg/g. We predicted an individual's risk of albuminuria using a Fine-Gray CPM taking into account the competing risk of death and showing risk progression over time. Additionally, we predicted the albuminuria-free time using an accelerated failure time (AFT) CPM. Lastly, we simultaneously predicted the risks of microalbuminuria (uACR ≥30 mg/g & <300 mg/g), macroalbuminuria (uACR ≥300 mg/g), and death using a multistate CPM. Model discrimination and calibration were assessed in the development and temporal validation cohort.
Results
The development cohort contained 38,649 individuals with 6,904 events and the validation cohort contained 45,009 individuals with 6,499 events. The Fine-Gray CPM had adequate discrimination internally (C-statistic, 95% CI; 0.64, 0.64–0.65) and temporally (0.66, 0.66–0.67). Calibration was good. The Fine-Gray model was also able to accurately show individual albuminuria risk progression over 3 years. The AFT CPM had adequate discrimination (internally: 0.63, 0.62–0.63; temporally: 0.65, 0.64–0.65), but poor calibration. The multistate CPM allowed individual predictions for each state over 3 years. An example of an individual's predictions is shown in the Fig. 1.
Conclusion
Predicting albuminuria in T2DM patients allows tailoring albuminuria screening to the individual. We developed multiple CPMs that accurately provide the probability of developing different stages of albuminuria over time. The Fine-Gray model and multistate model give the patient and healthcare provider insight in how the risk of albuminuria develops over time. Additionally, the multistate CPM allows shared decision-making taking into account not only the main outcome of interest, but also other events that may occur (e.g. death). These models can serve to improve albuminuria screening and ameliorate the risk of kidney damage in patients with T2DM, partially through novel presentation of prognostic information.

title: #3269 The effects of self-performed dietary sodium reduction on blood pressure and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
authors: Camilla Lundgreen Duus; Steffen Flindt Nielsen; Bodil Hornstrup; Frank Mose; Jesper Bech
abstract:
Background and Aims
Lifestyle factors as contributors to cardiovascular disease has been the focus of attention in recent years. Dietary sodium intake is a known risk factor to high blood pressure (BP) and thus cardiovascular disease. Several studies have shown a blood pressure decreasing effect of reducing dietary sodium however only few of these studies examined self-performed sodium reduction. Instead, they used hand-out low-sodium diets and results from these are therefore sparsely transferable to a real-life setting. Additionally, knowledge on the underlying physiology of the BP response is still lacking.
This study aimed to test the effects of a self-performed dietary sodium reduction on BP in patients with essential hypertension and examine the effects on the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
Method
A randomised, non-blinded clinical trial including 72 patients with hypertension was conducted. Participants were randomized 2:1 to either self-performed sodium reduction or a control group for a study period of four weeks. Both oral and written advice on lowering sodium intake was provided to the intervention group. Blood samples, 24-hour urine collection and 24-hour ambulatory BP measurements were performed before and after the intervention.
Results
Urinary 24-hour sodium excretion decreased 66 mmol (95% CI −96; −37 mmol) in the intervention group compared to the control group, which attained no significant change (5 mmol, 95% CI −12; 21 mmol). Systolic 24-hour BP decreased 9 mmHg after low-sodium diet compared to the control group (95% CI −13; −4 mmHg). Similarly, the difference in reduction in diastolic BP between the groups was 5 mmHg (95% CI −8; −1 mmHg)
Plasma levels of renin increased significantly in the intervention group compared to the control group (median change 6.8 pg/ml vs. 0.0 pg/ml, P < 0.0005). Likewise, did we find an increase in plasma aldosterone in the intervention group with a mean difference of 37.68 pg/ml compared to the control group (95% CI 17.34; 58.01, P = 0.0004) An association between change in aldosterone levels and change in BP was found (P = 0.005), however we did not find this association for renin and BP. Neither changes in renin nor aldosterone were associated to the reduction in sodium excretion.
Conclusion
A self-performed dietary sodium reduction of 66 mmol/day led to a decrease in 24-hour BP of 9/5 mmHg compared to a control group. Plasma renin and plasma aldosterone levels increased significantly compared to a control group, likely as a compensatory mechanism. The change in BP was related to the change in plasma aldosterone.
Advice on how to lower sodium intake as part of treatment of patients with essential hypertension could lead to better blood pressure control and thus lower risk of cardiovascular disease.

title: #1277 Sex differences in ambulatory central blood pressure and arterial stiffness in hemodialysis patients
authors: Artemios Karagiannidis; Marieta P Theodorakopoulou; Fotini Iatridi; Antonios Karpetas; Areti Georgiou; Sofia Manti; Panagiota Anyfanti; Eleni Gavriilaki; George Giannakoulas; Pantelis Sarafidis
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sex differences have a significant role on epidemiology of cardiovascular complications in chronic kidney disease. Among hemodialysis patients, central blood pressure (BP) levels and increased arterial stiffness parameters are independent predictors of cardiovascular and all-cause- mortality. This is the first study examining differences in ambulatory central BP and arterial stiffness parameters between male and female hemodialysis patients.
Method
A total of 129 male and 91 female hemodialysis patients were included in this analysis. All participants underwent 48-h ambulatory BP monitoring with Mobil-O-Graph-NG; indices of central hemodynamics (SBP, DBP and pulse pressure), wave reflection (augmentation pressure (AP) and augmentation index (AIx)) and pulse wave velocity (PWV) were estimated.
Results
Age, dialysis vintage and history of major comorbidities did not differ between men and women. Male patients had higher 48-h cSBP (124.7 ± 15.7 vs 119.8 ± 16.7 mmHg, P = 0.027) and 48-h DBP (83.7 ± 12.2 vs 77.5 ± 11.9 mmHg, P < 0.001) compared to female patients; relevant differences were also evident during the 44-h (excluding hemodialysis), 1st 24-h and 2nd 24-h periods and the corresponding daytime and nighttime periods of the recording. Central pulse pressure did not differ between groups. Regarding wave reflection parameters, AP, AIx, and AIx(75) were significantly lower in males versus females during the 48-h (AIx, 25.6 ± 8.2 vs 32.3 ± 8.6 mmHg, P < 0.001), 44-h, 1st and 2nd 24-h and also during respective daytime and nighttime periods. The two groups displayed similar PWV during all studied intervals (48-h PWV, 9.6 ± 1.9 vs 9.7 ± 2.1 m/s, P = 0.612).
Conclusion
Male hemodialysis patients present with higher levels of ambulatory central BP but significantly lower levels of AP, AIx and Aix(75) than females. PWV does not differ between sexes.

title: #2567 The association between oxidative balance score and its combination with advanced lung cancer inflammation index and risks of chronic kidney disease in hypertension: NHANES 1999–2018
authors: Xuejing Chen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Oxidative stress and inflammation are both correlated with chronic kidney disease (CKD) in hypertension. A common tool for evaluating dietary and lifestyle exposures to oxidative stress is the oxidative balance score (OBS), with higher OBS suggesting more substantial antioxidant exposures. And advanced lung cancer inflammation index (ALI) is used for evaluating inflammation and is calculated as follows: ALI = BMI × Alb/NLR, where BMI = weight in kilograms/(height in meters)2, Alb = serum albumin in grams per deciliter, and NLR was derived using the = absolute neutrophil count/absolute lymphocyte count. Investigating the association between OBS and its combination with ALI and risks of CKD in hypertension was the purpose of this study.
Method
This cross-sectional study included 13637 adults from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 1999–2018. Multivariate linear regression models and restricted cubic spline (RCS) were used to assess associations of ALI, OBS and risks of CKD in hypertension. To assess the joint effects between ALI and various OBS on CKD, pairwise combinations were performed and induced four subgroups. Mediation analysis explored the mediating role of ALI in the above relationships. Multiplicative interaction tests were carried out to analyze whether there was an interaction between sex and aforementioned different combinations of ALI and various OBS. All statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.2.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) and statistical significance was ascertained by a two-sided P value < 0.05.
Results
Among the 13637 study subjects, the prevalence of CKD in hypertension was 22.0% (3004). There was a significant negative linear relationship between OBS, dietary OBS, lifestyle OBS and CKD (all p for trend <0.001), but a negative nonlinear relationship between ALI and CKD (p for trend <0.0001, p for nonlinear <0.0001). In joint analysis, compared to the reference subgroup(low ALI + low OBS/dietary OBS/lifestyle OBS), lower risks of CKD were shown in other three groups, especially in the high ALI+ high OBS/dietary OBS/lifestyle OBS group (all p for trend <0.0001). After adjustment of poverty impact ratio (PIR), marital status, educational level, diabetes and cardiovascular disease, the relationship persisted. In mediation analysis, ALI mediated 5.71%, 3.62% and 2.43% of dietary OBS-/lifestyle OBS- and OBS-CKD associations, respectively. In stratified analysis, paired combinations of ALI and OBS/dietary OBS/lifestyle OBS were associated with lower risks of CKD across sex groups compared to the reference subgroup (P = 0.017, P = 0.014, P = 0.027, respectively), and the ORs were smaller in the female group than in the male group.
Conclusion
Diet and lifestyle might influence risks of CKD in hypertension by modulating inflammation. Antioxidant diets and lifestyles were important in reducing risks of CKD especially in females.

title: #2685 Research kidney biopsies in type 2 diabetes: clinical and laboratory parameters alone are not enough to identify candidates for kidney biopsy
authors: Signe Kjærgaard Jakobsen; Marie Møller; Rikke Borg; Iain Bressendorf; Karina Haar Jensen; Eva Gravesen; Peter Rossing; Frederik Persson; Ditte Hansen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Type 2 diabetes is present in approximately one-third of patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), making it crucial to ensure correct diagnosis and treatment of the underlying kidney disease. Most individuals with CKD and type 2 diabetes do not undergo a kidney biopsy and are directed to standard diabetic-CKD-management, risking misdiagnosis and wrong treatment if non-diabetic kidney disease is present. Identifying clinical characteristic that help predict when a biopsy will alter management could help optimize patient selection for diagnostic kidney biopsy.
The aim of this study was to evaluate clinical and laboratory parameters in patients with type 2 diabetes and severe albuminuria undergoing research kidney biopsies, comparing patients whose biopsy results led to changes in clinical management with those who continued conventional diabetes-CKD treatment.
Method
We have established an ongoing national prospective cohort, PRIMETIME 2, where we aim to conduct research kidney biopsies in 300 adult patients with type 2 diabetes and severe albuminuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) >700 mg/g) and simultaneously collect a broad range of clinical data and biological samples.
In this preliminary analysis of the first 95 patients, we categorized renal pathology diagnoses into two groups based on clinical implications: (1) a “no change”-group requiring conventional diabetes-CKD-management (including diabetic nephropathy, hypertensive nephropathy, and/or non-nephrotic FSGS), and (2) an “altered management”-group with diagnoses leading to altered clinical management (including IgA nephropathy, membranous nephropathy, minimal change disease, and amyloidosis). We compared clinical and laboratory parameters between groups with adjustment for multiple comparisons.
Results
Of 95 participants, 84 patients (88%) were categorized in the “no change”-group and 11 patients (12%) had diagnoses leading to altered management (Table 1). The groups were comparable regarding age, diabetes duration, diabetic complications, number of comorbidities, estimated GFR, HbA1c and microscopic hematuria. The significant differences between groups were mainly related to protein excretion, with the “altered management”-group showing higher UACR and lower P-albumin, but with considerable overlap of ranges between the two groups.
Conclusion
Clinical and laboratory parameters alone cannot reliably differentiate between patients with diabetes and severe albuminuria whose kidney biopsy findings will or will not change clinical management. Although p-albumin and UACR showed significant differences between the two groups, the extensive overlap in their ranges limits their use as reliable predictors. New tools, such as biomarkers, are necessary to better direct kidney biopsies in patients with diabetes and severely elevated albuminuria to diagnose and rightfully treat non-diabetic kidney disease.

title: #2037 Renal perfusion assessment by magnetic resonance imaging in patients with diabetic cardiac autonomic neuropathy
authors: Kywe Kywe Soe; Joao Periquito; Steven Sourbron; Dinesh Selvarajah
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiac autonomic neuropathy (CAN) is an independent risk factor for the incidence and progression of diabetic kidney disease (DKD), but the exact mechanism is unclear. One hypothesis is the reduction in renal perfusion caused by over-activation of the sympathetic nervous system and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). In this study, we test this hypothesis by using magnetic resonance imaging (dynamic contrast enhanced-MRI) to measure renal perfusion in patients with CAN and diabetes (type 1 and type 2).
Method
Participants were recruited from the iBEAt study, which included participants with type 1 and type 2 diabetes, aged between 18–80 years and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) greater than 30 ml/min/1.73 m². Exclusion criteria included those receiving renal replacement therapy, renal transplant, acute kidney injury, obstructive uropathy, active cancer or liver disease, claustrophobia or contraindications for MRI. Diagnosis of CAN was established using Ewing's cardiovascular autonomic reflex tests (CARTs).
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data were acquired in free-breathing using a 2D Turbo-FLASH sequence on a general electric (GE) MRI scanner. The contrast agent Dotarem (Gd-DOTA) was injected intravenously to enhance the visualisation of the kidneys, providing high-resolution images and quantifiable data on renal blood flow.
Participants were stratified into two groups based on the presence or absence of CAN. Correlation analysis was conducted using Spearman's rank and Chi-square tests to compare renal perfusion between the CAN and no-CAN groups. Renal perfusion differences between the groups were compared and analysed by Mann-Whitney U test or Kruskal Wallis test. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS (version 29), and results were considered statistically significant if the p-value was less than 0.05.
Results
Table 1 summarises the participants characteristics, comparing the ‘no CAN’ (n = 27) and ‘CAN’ groups (n = 54). Participants with CAN had lower body weight (P = 0.03), lower systolic blood pressure (P = 0.023) and higher UACR (P = 0.04). No differences were found in renal perfusion (no CAN vs CAN; 297 vs 286 ml/100 ml/min, P = 0.645) and cortical perfusion (310 vs 315 ml/100 ml/min, P = 0.711) (Fig. 1). This indifference in renal perfusion parameters remains consistent even when compared in different CAN stages (350 vs 280 vs 286 ml/100 ml/min in no CAN, early CAN and confirmed CAN, P = 0.266) and different eGFR grades (G1 no CAN vs CAN; 347 vs 385 ml/100 ml/min, P = 0.445, G2 no CAN vs CAN; 289 vs 251 ml/100 ml/min, P = 0.132). Further analysis of renal perfusion in type 1 (no CAN vs CAN; 291 vs 369 ml/100 ml/min, P = 0.123) and type 2 diabetes (295 vs 224 ml/100 ml/min, P = 0.146) separately also did not show any significant difference.
Conclusion
This study investigated the impact of CAN on renal perfusion in individuals with type 1 and type 2 diabetes using DCE-MRI. title: #1849 Wide-proteome analysis on renal tissue samples reveals new intriguing outcomes on NA-Milan hypertensive rat strain phenotype
authors: Luciano D'apolito; Antonio Miele; Yoko Suzumoto; Anna Iervolino; Alessandra Altomare; Lara Davani; Giovanna Baron; Chiara Livia Lanzani; Luca Rampoldi; Paolo Manunta; Giovambattista Capasso; Francesco Trepiccione
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hypertension (HT) is a complex and heterogeneous pathological condition: the interaction between genetic and environmental factors leads to an increase in blood pressure (BP). HT represents a risk factor for cardiovascular disease and the major cause of mortality in industrialized countries, affecting 20% of the adult population. One of the environmental factors that plays an important role in the development of HT is sodium intake. The regulation of renal sodium and chloride are fundamental for the management of BP levels. Sodium sensitivity is a crucial factor that determines a more complex patient phenotype. The link between BP regulation, HT, sodium sensitivity, and HT-mediated organ damage has not yet been fully explored and is currently an unmet clinical need.
To date, the change of molecular signature in the kidney from normal to hypertensive state is not entirely clear. It is possible to investigate this endpoint by having a rat model which spontaneously develops HT. Hypertensive rats called NA are congenic and carry a missense mutation in the alpha-Adducin 1 (ADD1) gene associated with HT. These rats developed HT in the form of early increase of systolic blood pressure (SBP) and proteinuria however without changes in GFR.
To deepen our knowledge on the multi-omic field the following study aims to compare these outcomes integrating the data with profiling of renal tissue proteome in normal and hypertensive state of rats.
Method
Rats of MN and NA strains, starting from 4 up to 16 weeks of life, were enrolled to the study. The MN rat strain is the normotensive one, representing the non-pathological control of NA rats.
Phenotyping was conducted on male rats over the time in terms of SBP, controlled with tail cuff method, evaluations of kidney physiology (transdermal monitoring of GFR in awake rodents with MediBeacon device), oximetry, blood gas analysis and urinary excretion of proteins and electrolytes.
A label-free quantitative proteomic analysis was performed on renal cortex samples, carefully collected and stored to ensure optimal downstream processing, using nano-LC–HRMS (nano liquid chromatography–high-resolution mass spectrometry), with a Dionex Ultimate 3000 nano-LC coupled to an Orbitrap Fusion Tribrid mass spectrometer. Data were processed with MaxQuant v.1.6.0, while Perseus v.1.6.1.43 facilitated statistical analysis. Differentially regulated proteins were analyzed to identify modulated pathways across experimental groups, with functional insights obtained using STRING v.1.7.0 and Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA).
Results
Physiological evaluations conducted on rats revealed an SBP increase starting from 12 weeks in NA rats compared to MN relative controls. At 16 weeks of age SBP reached in hypertensive strain a mean value around 160 mmHg (P = 0.039) (Fig. 1a). The parameter of urinary ratio of total proteins to creatinine was higher in NA rats starting from 12 weeks and a significative variation was visible at 16 weeks (P = 0.014) (Fig. 1b). The same trend has been observed for urinary total protein excretion after 24 hours with a significative variation between the two strains starting from 12 weeks (P = 0.0029) (Fig. 1c).
Proteomic analysis revealed a clear modulation of pathways associated with inflammation, heme-toxicity, ferroptosis and fatty acid metabolism. In NA rats, starting from week 8, distinct markers of oxidative phosphorylation dysfunction emerged, indicating mitochondrial alteration and a consequent oxidative stress state. Furthermore, amino acid metabolism pathways were profoundly dysregulated, along with sodium transport mechanisms, as shown in Fig. 2.
Conclusion
Our pre-clinical study developed in vivo confirmed the hypertensive phenotype of NA rats in terms of early increase of SBP and proteinuria. The intriguing outcomes from proteome analysis suggest early kidney damage secondary to hypertension and sodium retention which exacerbates the energetic metabolism. Further studies are ongoing to better investigate the role of HT-associated biomarkers of prognostic/diagnostic value integrating the obtained data with single cell RNA-sequencing profile.

title: #1529 Impact of SGLT2 and dual SGLT1/2 inhibition on salt-sensitive hypertension progression in Dahl SS rats
authors: Olha Kravtsova; Vladislav Levchenko; Ruslan Bohovyk; Ganesh Halade; Timo Rieg; Alexander Staruschenko
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sodium-glucose co-transporter inhibitors (SGLT2i) have emerged as a cornerstone therapy for diabetes mellitus and, more recently, for cardiovascular diseases. Large clinical trials have demonstrated the remarkable benefits of SGLT2i on renal and cardiovascular outcomes. Recently, the dual SGLT1/2 inhibitor sotagliflozin received FDA approval for the treatment of heart failure regardless of ejection fraction, highlighting its potential broad applicability. Despite these promising findings, the molecular mechanisms mediating the effects of SGLT inhibitors, particularly in the context of salt-sensitive hypertension, remain underexplored. The primary objective of this study was to investigate the effects of SGLT inhibition on the development of salt-induced hypertension and to elucidate the underlying mechanisms contributing to these effects.
Method
Dahl salt-sensitive (SS) rats, a well-established model of salt-induced hypertension, were used to evaluate the effects of SGLT2 and dual SGLT1/2 inhibitors, dapagliflozin (Dapa) and sotagliflozin (Sota), respectively. Eight-week-old male SS rats were treated with or without Dapa (2 mg/kg/day in drinking water) or Sota (30 mg/kg/day in food) for 3 weeks. To investigate potential molecular mechanisms underlying the beneficial effects of SGLT2 inhibition, additional analyses were performed on tissues collected from SS rats fed a high-salt (HS) diet and treated with either vehicle or Dapa. The effects of Dapa on renal sodium channels and transporters were assessed using RT-PCR, Western blot analysis, and patch clamp techniques. Transcriptomic analyses and lipid mediator profiling were conducted in the kidney cortex of male SS rats on a 3-week HS diet with or without Dapa treatment to further explore the metabolic impacts of SGLT2 inhibition.
Results
Administration of dapagliflozin (Dapa) mitigated the development of salt-induced hypertension in both male and female Dahl SS rats, as demonstrated by lower blood pressure and a leftward shift in the pressure-natriuresis curve (Kravtsova et al., AJP: Renal, 2022; Kravtsova et al., Sci Rep, 2023). However, neither mRNA nor protein expression levels of key renal transporters, such as SGLT2, NHE3, NKCC2, NCC, and α-, β-, and γ-ENaC subunits, showed significant differences between groups. Additionally, electrophysiological experiments indicated no significant effects of Dapa on the conductance or activity of ENaC. Dual SGLT1/2 inhibition with Sota effectively prevented the development of salt-sensitive hypertension in both male and female Dahl SS rats without affecting heart rate. By the 21st day of the HS challenge, mean arterial pressure was reduced by more than 30 mmHg in Sota-treated groups compared to vehicle controls. Sota treatment significantly increased diuresis, glucose excretion, and sodium excretion in both sexes. Despite these effects, no changes in kidney weight or glomerular filtration rate and creatinine clearance were detected. However, Sota treatment reduced the heart-to-body weight ratio, attenuated kidney fibrosis, decreased protein cast formation, and lowered albuminuria.
Conclusion
This study demonstrates that SGLT2 and SGLT1/2 inhibition in a nondiabetic model of salt-sensitive hypertension attenuates the development and severity of salt-induced hypertension. Chronic SGLT2 inhibition enhances glucose and sodium excretion without impacting the expression or function of other sodium transporters and channels along the nephron or altering hormone levels in the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Transcriptomic analyses of the kidney cortex identified lipid and amino acid metabolism, molecular transport, and cell function as the top biological pathways influenced by SGLT2 inhibition. Furthermore, dual SGLT1/2 inhibition provided even higher protection against salt-sensitive hypertension and associated kidney damage compared to SGLT2 inhibition alone.

title: #2045 Antagonistic DcR2 peptides ameliorate renal fibrosis by inhibiting renal tubular cells senescence in diabetic nephropathy
authors: Xin Yang; Yani He; Kehong Chen; Jia Chen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diabetic nephrology (DN) is one of the most common and devastating complications of diabetic mellitus, making the leading cause of end stage renal disease (ESRD) all over the world. And there is no satisfactory therapy to delay DN progression in clinic. Renal tubular epithelial cell (RTEC) senescence is an important biological event in the progression of DN. Decoy receptor 2 (DcR2), a transmembrane receptor for TRAIL, is specifically highly expressed in the membrane and cytoplasm of senescent RTECs, and promotes renal fibrosis in DN. This study is aim to design DcR2 antagonistic peptide, and confirm its role and mechanism in alleviating renal fibrosis in DN.
Method
A phage display peptide library was employed to screen candidate DcR2 antagonistic peptides after three rounds of elution and neutralization through 12 peptide libraries, based on DcR2 protein. The best DcR2 antagonistic peptide was selected according to mass spectrometry, HPLC detection and affinity test by bio-layer interferometry (BLI). This study was conducted by setting high glucose (HG) models based on primary RTECs in vitro. Firstly, CCK8 was applied to measure the effect of DcR2 antagonistic peptide on cell viability. Immunofluorescence staining was used to confirm the colocalization relationship between DcR2 and its antagonistic peptide. SA-β-gal staining showed the influence of DcR2 antagonistic peptide on RTEC senescence. Then we assessed senescent biomarkers like p21, p16 and DcR2 by quantitative PCR (qPCR). Western blot (WB) was used to evaluate the effect of DcR2 antagonistic peptide on cellular senescence and renal fibrosis by senescent biomarker p21, p16, DcR2, γ-H2AX, LaminB1, etc and fibrotic marker like CollagenⅠ.Finally, Immunofluorescence staining of α-SMA, a fibrotic marker, also measured its impact on renal fibrosis.
Results
Ten candidate DcR2 antagonistic peptides were screened by a phage display peptide library. And the best DcR2 antagonistic peptide, namely RF8 was selected with purity of 91.59% and dissociation constant of 9.76E−05 M. CCK8 showed that RF8 enhanced cell viability in a concentration-dependent manner. The colocalization assay exhibited favorable combination of DcR2 and RF8 in vitro. SA-β-gal staining demonstrated RF8 largely reduced the expression of senescent RTECs in HG group. After administration of RF8, the mRNA levels of p16 and p21 were significantly inhibited. WB indicated RF8 reduced the expression of senescent and fibrotic markers induced by HG. Similarly, immunofluorescence staining demonstrated that HG-induced increase of α-SMA was negated by RF8, which indicated well inhibition of RF8 on RTEC senescence and renal fibrosis in vitro.
Conclusion
This study reveals that RF8 is a potent therapeutic remedy that mitigate RTEC senescence and renal fibrosis, which could relieve the progression of DN by targeted antagonism of DcR2, providing hope for the treatment of DN.

title: #2050 Single-cell transcription combined with spatial transcriptome reveals the role of senescent proximal tubules in the progression of diabetic nephropathy
authors: Zhiyao He; Kehong Chen; Jia Chen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is one of the leading causes of end-stage renal disease around the world. However, there is currently a lack of effective treatment methods and intervention targets. Renal tubular cell senescence is one of the important mechanisms of DN progression, but the characteristic biomarkers and molecular mechanisms are still unclear.
Method
We selected renal tissue of biopsy-proven early DN (n = 3), progressive DN (n = 3), and normal control (n = 3) to construct the single-cell atlas and unsupervised cluster, which was based on the single-cell expression profile and marker genes. The senescent cell atlas was drawn according to 26 senescence marker genes such as P16, P21. Then top senescent genes were analyzed by heat map, and functional signaling pathways were analyzed by KEGG. The spatially anchored atlas of senescence was constructed by combining spatial transcriptome and the single-cell transcriptome data. The expression of top senescence genes was evaluated by Quantitative PCR in STZ-induced DN mouse models and the high glucose-induced HK-2 cell model. At the organizational level, it was evaluated by Immunohistochemistry.
Results
In the single-cell atlas, renal cells could be divided into 14 cell groups, of which the proximal tubular (PT) cell group was the major cell type. PT cells, monocytes and podocytes were the most susceptible cells to senescence in DN. Among them, PT cells showed the highest abundance of senescence genes and the highest score of senescence gene set, indicating that PT cells were the major cell senescence population in DN. The Top senescence genes were CXCL8, CXCL6, MMP7 and TM4SF1, which were senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Senescent PT was mainly enriched in fibrin formation, Rap1 signaling pathway, PI3K/Akt signaling pathway, which were mainly related to inflammation and fibrosis. Spatially anchored atlas revealed senescent PT was mainly more enriched in progressive DA than early DN. Compared with normal control and early DN, the expression of the CXCL8, CXCL6, MMP7 and TM4SF1 was significantly up-regulated in progressive DA.
Conclusion
This study identified CXCL8, MMP7 and TM4SF1 as markers of senescent PT in DN. It may be a potential therapeutic approach to delay the progression of DN by interfering with the senescent PT cells through targeting these markers.

title: #238 SGLT2 and HIF-PH inhibitors restore podocyte abnormalities in diabetes
authors: Chuanlei Li; Kit-Chung Ng; Cheuk Chun Szeto
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase (HIF-PH) inhibitors have pleiotropic properties beyond blood glucose-lowering and erythropoietin-increasing effects. We studied the effects of SGLT2i and HIF-PH inhibitor on podocyte protection in diabetic kidney disease (DKD).
Method
We studied cultured human podocytes treated with high glucose, dapagliflozin or roxadustat. Podocyte-associated molecules expression and morphology changes were assessed. We then studied 5 DKD patients who were started on 3-month SGLT2i treatment and 5 patients who were not treated (control group). The histological patterns of podocyte-associated molecules were assessed in renal biopsies in DKD patients with and without SGLT2i treatment.
Results
Cultured podocytes exposed to hyperglycemia had reduced mRNA expression of nephrin, podocalyxin and synaptopodin, while treatment with dapagliflozin, roxadustat, or both restore their mRNA expression. Their intracellular protein levels were similarly reduced when treated with hyperglycemia; dapagliflozin, roxadustat, or both restore their intracellular levels. Under hyperglycemia, podocyte cell bodies were shrunken, and the expression of nephrin and podocin on the cell surface were reduced and became granular. Dapagliflozin, roxadustat, or their combination restored the distribution of nephrin and podocin in podocytes. Under hyperglycemia, podocalyxin at apical cell membrane appeared disorganized, and the expression of synaptopodin was reduced, especially at the cell processes, and the punctate appearance was disrupted. Treatment with dapagliflozin, but not roxadustat, partly restored the normal distribution of podocalyxin and synaptopodin. In human DKD, kidney biopsy showed disruption of nephrin, podocin, podocalyxin, and synaptopodin distribution. In the SGLT2i treated patient, their immunofluorescence staining pattern returned to a linear and continuous distribution.
Conclusion
SGLT2i and HIF-PH inhibitor have significant effects on restoring the podocyte morphology, cytoskeleton architecture, and intracellular levels of podocyte-associated molecule in a diabetic milieu.

title: #239 The Effect of SGLT2 inhibitor therapy on urinary podocyte markers in diabetic kidney disease
authors: Chuanlei Li; Kit-Chung Ng; Cheuk Chun Szeto
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) is a standard treatment for kidney and cardiovascular protection in diabetic kidney disease (DKD). Previous studies suggested that urinary level of podocyte-associated molecules may predict the progression of DKD. We determined the effect of SGLT2i on the urinary podocyte-associated molecules levels in patients with DKD.
Method
We studied 24 DKD patients who were started on SGLT2i treatment and 25 patients who were not treated (control group). Urinary levels of podocyte-associated molecules, their corresponding mRNA levels in urinary sediment, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), and urine albumin-creatinine ratio (UACR) were measured at baseline and then again at 3 months.
Results
Urinary levels of podocin, podocalyxin, nephrin and synaptopodin did not change from baseline to 3 months in the SGLT2i treatment group. However, in the control group, urinary podocin, podocalyxin, and synaptopodin levels increased from (4.63 ± 4.84 to 18.49 ± 22.22 ng/μmol-Cr, 489.75 ± 480.62 to 1399.53 ± 1265.27 ng/mmol-Cr, and 38.61 ± 42.56 to 78.50 ± 85.61 ng/μmol-Cr; P = 0.0006, 0.0002, and 0.03, respetively) over 3 months, while unriary nephrin level did not change significantly. Urinary sediment podocin, podocalyxin, nephrin and synaptopodin mRNA levels did not change from baseline to 3 months in control and SGLT2i treatment groups. There were no significant correlations between urinary podocyte-associated marker levels and eGFR and UACR at baseline, and there was no significant correlation between urinary sediment mRNA levels of nephrin, podocin, podocalyxin, synaptopodin and eGFR or UACR at baseline. After 3-month treatment, podocalyxin mRNA level had a significant inverse correlation with eGFR (r = −0.392, P = 0.009) but not UACR. In the control group, the change in podocalyxin (r = −0.389, P = 0.017) and nephrin (r = −0.471, P = 0.010) mRNA level had significant inverse correlations with the change in eGFR and UACR, respectively.
Conclusion
SGLT2i has a small but significant effect on preventing the progressive rise in urinary podocyte-associated molecule levels but not sediment mRNA level. Our result suggests that SGLT2i therapy may affect podocyte function in DKD.

title: #2087 Urinary and serum aminoacids may be associated to podocyte, proximal Tubule, and renal endothelial injury in early diabetic kidney disease in type 2 diabetes mellitus patients
authors: Maria Mogos; Carmen Socaciu; Andreea Socaciu; Ligia Petrica; Adrian Vlad; Sorin Ursoniu; Oana Milas; Anca Suteanu-Simulescu; Lavinia Balint; Mihaela Glavan; Silvia Ienciu; Iuliana Alioani
abstract:
Background and Aims
The pathogenesis of diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is complex and multifactorial. Because of its complications reduced number of diagnostic biomarkers, it is important to explore new biomarkers with possible role in the early diagnosis of DKD. Our study aims to investigate the pattern of previously identified metabolites and their association with biomarkers of endothelial dysfunction, proximal tubule (PT) dysfunction, and podocyte injury. A total of 110 participants, comprising 20 healthy individuals and 90 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus divided in 3 groups were enrolled in the study: normoalbuminuria, microalbuminuria, and macroalbuminuria.
Method
Untargeted and targeted, univariate and multivariate metabolomic methods were employed to assess urinary and serum biomarkers, as well as indicators of endothelial dysfuntion, podocyte damage, and PT dysfunction through ELISA techniques.
Results
Our research has identified metabolites that could act as promising biomarkers for the early detection of DKD. Specifically, certain metabolites are capable of distinguishing between patient subgroups. For instance, glycine is effective in differentiating between group C and the normoalbuminuric cohort, as well as between groups P1 and P2–P3. Additionally, glycine displays a significant correlation with endothelial markers, particularly VCAM, with a statistically significant result (P < 0.001). Kynurenic acid shows a gradual decrease from group C to group P3, and this biomarker also reveals an inverse relationship with p-selectin and VCAM, with significant p-values (P < 0.001 for p-selectin and P < 0.05 for VCAM). Tryptophan levels also decline progressively from group C to P3, exhibiting a negative correlation with p-selectin and VCAM. Furthermore, urinary tiglylglycine differentiates among various patient groups, with lower concentrations observed as the disease advances, and it shows a strong positive correlation with numerous markers related to podocytes and proximal tubules, including nephrin, podocalyxin, KIM1, and NAG.
Conclusion
In this study, we utilized LC-UHPLC techniques to analyze the trend of serum and urine metabolites, aiming to identify the distinctions between control groups and various patient subgroups with diabetic kidney disease, with a specific focus on the normoalbuminuric subgroup. Our findings indicated several metabolites that may serve as putative biomarkers for early DKD, including glycine, kynurenic acid, tryptophan and tiglylglycine.

title: #2589 Association of glomerular hyperfiltration with mortality in stroke: an analysis using pooled individual patient data from the MICON multi-centre collaboration
authors: Philip Nash; Gareth Ambler; Rob Simister; David C Wheeler; David Werring; Tae-Jin Song
abstract:
Background and Aims
Associations of glomerular hyperfiltration with vascular events and death have been reported, particularly in community populations, but have scarcely been investigated in patients with stroke.
Method
Centres from the Microbleed International Collaborative Network (MICON) contributed data on estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), recurrent stroke events and death. Using Cox proportional hazards regression modelling, we investigated associations of glomerular hyperfiltration with recurrent ischaemic stroke (IS), symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (ICrH), death and vascular death. Hyperfiltration was defined as eGFR greater than the age and gender-adjusted 95th percentile. Hypofiltration was defined as eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2.
Results
11,175 patients (mean age 70.7, 42% female) were included, 554 with hyperfiltration and 2815 with eGFR<60. Compared to normofiltration, the hyperfiltration group had similar event rates for recurrent IS (37 vs. 35 events per 1000 patient-years) and ICrH (8 vs. 7 events). The rates of death (147 vs. 61) and vascular death (27 vs. 11) were significantly higher in the hyperfiltration group. In multivariable Cox regression models there was no significant association of hyperfiltration with IS (aHR 0.91, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.38) or ICrH (aHR 0.91, 95% CI 0.37 to 2.27). Compared to normofiltration, hyperfiltration was independently associated with the risk of death from any cause (aHR 1.53, 95% CI 1.22 to 1.93) and the risk of vascular death (aHR 1.83, 95% CI 1.09 to 3.08).
Conclusion
In this large international stroke population, glomerular hyperfiltration was independently associated with 53% increased risk of death, and 83% increased risk of vascular death. Nephrology advisory bodies could recommend screening for hyperfiltration to detect increased vascular risk earlier and in younger age groups.

title: #998 The association between analogue compared to human insulin, prescribed dialysate glucose load, body mass index and mortality in people with kidney failure and type 2 diabetes on peritoneal dialysis
authors: James Fotheringham; Jennifer Williams; Shailesh Agarwal; Thomas Ebert; Martin Wilkie; Brian Bieber; Mark Lambie; Simon Davies
abstract:
Background and Aims
Type II diabetes is highly prevalent in people with kidney failure on peritoneal dialysis, with a proportion requiring insulin therapy. Compared to human insulin, analogue (genetically altered) insulin has been associated with superior survival in hemodialysis. Inferior glycemic stability can increase thirst, reduce ultrafiltrate, therefore require higher daily dialysate glucose load (DDGL) which have been associated with worse outcomes in peritoneal dialysis. How analogue insulin associates with prescribed dialysate glucose, body mass index (BMI) and patient survival is unknown.
Method
People with kidney failure and type 2 diabetes receiving peritoneal dialysis and recruited into PDOPPS (2014–2022) who received insulin treatment at the start or during follow-up were identified from seven countries. Cox proportional hazards models with inverse probability weighting adjustment for country, study phase and patient characteristics including BMI and HBA1c estimated the hazard for mortality by insulin type over two years. The relationship between insulin type and the variables of BMI and DDGL, estimated using dialysate prescribed glucose strength and volume, was assessed longitudinally using mixed effects linear regression.
Results
13,146 people with type 2 diabetes receiving peritoneal dialysis were identified, of whom 3,387 (26%) received a purely analogue or human insulin, either before recruitment into the study (2,789) or during follow-up (628). 355 received analogue and 3,032 received human insulin. The proportion of type 2 diabetics receiving an insulin, and the proportion on insulin who received a human insulin varied by country but patient characteristics by insulin type were similar.
Crude survival at two years in those receiving analogue insulin was 77% compared with 68% in human insulin users (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.94), and in adjusted models was 77% and 65% respectively (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.92). Similar effect sizes were obtained when stratifying by incident or prevalent peritoneal dialysis use.
While in incident cohorts DDGL did not vary over time or by insulin type, in prevalent cohorts mixed effects models estimated that DDGL increased by 1.0 g/month of peritoneal dialysis in the human insulin group. This increase with time was significantly slower in the analogue insulin group (difference −0.9 g/month, 95% CI −1.2 to −0.5) but DDGL was 23 g higher in the analogue insulin group at baseline. In prevalent cohorts BMI did not statistically change with time (0.1/month, −0.2 to 0.4) in human insulin group and in analogue users was not higher at baseline (1.4, 95% CI −1.6 to 4.4) or increase more quickly (−0.1/month, 95% CI −0.4 to 0.2).
Conclusion
Analogue insulin was associated with superior patient survival in people with kidney failure and type 2 diabetes receiving peritoneal dialysis. DDGL was statistically higher in analogue insulin at baseline, however the absence of insulin-specific changes in DDGL over time or in BMI measures generally suggest the metabolic impact of analogue insulin is limited. Although residual confounding may be present, this is reassuring given recent announcements from insulin manufacturers regarding halting human insulin production.

title: #2268 How to screen for diabetes mellitus before kidney transplantation?—the Norwegian experience
authors: Espen Nordheim; Anders Åsberg; Trond Jenssen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diabetes mellitus is a common disease among kidney transplant candidates with impact on transplant outcome. As part of a national program, all transplant candidates in Norway without known diabetes mellitus are screened both with HbA1c and an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) as part of the kidney transplant work-up.
Method
This study analysed on a national basis the number of patients with new-diagnosed diabetes mellitus found through our screening program between 2007–2022. We analysed the distribution of patients fulfilling different diagnostic criteria for diabetes defined by the American Diabetes Association (ref): HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol or plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L or 2-hour plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L.
Results
Screening of 2261 patients without known diabetes revealed 166 patients fulfilling the diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus (7.3%) prior to wait listing. Out of these 166 patients, 123 fulfilled the 2-hour plasma glucose criterion, 24 patients fulfilled the fasting plasma glucose criterion and 48 patients the HbA1c criterion. If the 2-hour plasma glucose information were not available in this screening, 90 patients who fulfilled the diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus would have been missed (54%).
Conclusion
Without the use of an oral glucose tolerance test in the screening program for kidney transplantation, about 50% of the cases with pre-transplant diabetes mellitus will be missed. This may negatively influence kidney transplantation outcome.

title: #3655 Eosinophilic infiltration in biopsies of patients with diabetic nephropathy
authors: Jorge Torres Ortiz; David Arroyo Rueda; Javier Carrillo Checa; Andrea Hernández García; Gema Sanchez; Miguel Villa-Valdés; Miguel Angel Encalada; Javier Carbayo; Francisco Diaz Crespo; Marian Goicoechea
abstract:
Background and Aims
Eosinophilic infiltration has been studied as a potential prognostic factor for renal survival in patients with diabetic nephropathy. The aim of this study is to describe the clinical and histological characteristics of diabetic patients based on the presence of eosinophils.
Method
Retrospective observational study including patients with diabetes who underwent a kidney biopsy between April 2017 and July 2022. Clinical, analytical, and histological variables were collected. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS version 25.
Results
Twenty-three patients were included, with 18 men (78.3%) and a mean age of 60.0±10.0 years. Most patients had type 2 diabetes (22, 95.7%), with a median time since diagnosis of 2.7 years (IQR 1.4–16.0). The majority (16, 69.6%) were receiving insulin. The median glycated hemoglobin was 6.6% (IQR 5.9–8.3). Four patients (17.4%) had started renal replacement therapy at the time of the renal biopsy.
The main indications for biopsy were worsening of renal function (12, 52.2%), nephrotic range proteinuria (6, 26.1%) and complete nephrotic syndrome (5, 21.7%). The Tervaert class of diabetic nephropathy was: class I, 1 (4.3%); IIa, 3 (13.0%); IIb, 2 (8.7%); III, 10 (43.5%); and IV, 7 (30.4%). Nine patients (39.1%) had an additional histological diagnosis to diabetes, being the most frequent one immunoallergic interstitial nephritis (3, 13.0%), followed by focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (2, 8.7%), IgA nephropathy (1, 4.3%) endocapillary glomerulonephritis (1, 4.3%), extracapillary glomerulonephritis (1, 4.3%), and thrombotic microangiopathy (1, 4.3%). In 9 biopsies (39.13%) eosinophils were found, with a median of 0.3 (IQR 0.2–0.4) eosinophils/mm2. Eosinophilic interstitial infiltration was associated with the number of sclerosed glomeruli (r = 0.590, P < 0.05), tubular atrophy (r = 0.500, P < 0.05), and interstitial inflammation (r = 0.563, P < 0.05).
Patients with eosinophils in the biopsy were younger (56.0 vs. 62.0 years), had a longer time since diabetes diagnosis (16.0 vs. 11.0 years) and a lower glomerular filtration rate (36.4 ± 15.0 vs. 43.4 ± 19.0 mL/min), although these differences did not reach statistical significance.
The presence of eosinophils was not predictive of renal function loss or mortality. The sample size may be a limitation for the interpretation of these results.
Conclusion
Eosinophilic infiltration in renal biopsies of patients with diabetic kidney disease correlates with the number of sclerosed glomeruli and with greater inflammation and tubular atrophy, possibly related to more chronic damage. The prognostic clinical implication of this finding is still unclear and further studies are needed.

title: #1705 Prevalence of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and predictors of adverse outcomes: 5-year retrospective review in a tertiary referral center
authors: Vincent Anthony Tang; Abigail Marie Quiza; Lynn Gomez; Raymond Oliva
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) are a leading cause of maternal morbidity and mortality globally. Renal impairment often complicates the clinical course of patients with HDP and has been linked to long-term progression towards chronic kidney disease (CKD). However, epidemiologic data on the burden of HDP and the role of renal impairment in mediating its associated adverse outcomes is sparse across developing countries. Hence, we determined the prevalence of HDP among pregnancy-related admissions and identified risk factors for adverse renal and maternal outcomes.
Method
We conducted a single-center, cross-sectional study covering the period of January 2019 to December 2024. A review of medical records of adult pregnant patients diagnosed with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy admitted at the University of the Philippines – Philippine General Hospital was done. Eligible patients included pregnant patients at least 18 years of age and diagnosed with hypertension. Sociodemographic, clinical, and laboratory data were collected solely from each patient's medical record. Statistical analyses were done using SPSS version 29. Categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages. Continuous variables were reported as measures of central tendency. Bivariate and multiple logistic regression analyses were done to identify factors associated with adverse outcomes [a 95% confidence interval (CI) with p-value <0.05 was considered significant].
Results
HDP complicated 17% (803 of 4,729) of pregnancy-related admissions, with 13 maternal deaths, and 21 fetal deaths reported throughout the study period. Among those with HDP, 16% had chronic hypertension, 41% had gestational hypertension, 29% had pre-eclampsia, and 14% had chronic hypertension with superimposed pre-eclampsia. The prevalence of HDP was highest among those with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of <30%. Among those with renal impairment, the most common adverse maternal outcomes were liver dysfunction (12.1%), HELLP syndrome (5.1%), eclampsia (3.7%), and pulmonary edema (2.2%). Acute kidney injury (AKI) stage III (OR 4.87; 95% CI 4.53–5.02; p-value = 0.013), preexisting CKD (OR 3.94; 95% CI 3.46–4.23; p-value = 0.019), pre-eclampsia (OR 1.84; 95% CI 1.23–2.35.; p-value = 0.044), and chronic hypertension with superimposed pre-eclampsia (OR 2.02; 95% CI 1.79–2.45; p-value = 0.038) were significantly associated with dialysis-dependence on discharge. Nephrotic-range proteinuria (OR 2.71; 95% CI 2.25–3.14; p-value = 0.048), pre-eclampsia (OR 4.15; 95% CI 3.64–4.86; p-value = 0.032), and chronic hypertension with superimposed pre-eclampsia (OR 3.73; 95% CI 3.15–4.11; p-value = 0.021) were significantly associated with non-resolution of AKI on discharge.
Conclusion
HDP remains to be a significant source of maternal morbidity and mortality, especially at lower eGFRs. Those with both HDP and renal impairment represent a subset of high-risk patients that require early identification and close monitoring on admission. Patients with pre-existing CKD, those who develop AKI Stage III during admission, or those who have nephrotic-range proteinuria are at higher risk for dialysis dependence and non-resolution of AKI at time of discharge, thus requiring closer long-term monitoring and follow-up. Future research can look into defining specific management strategies aimed at mitigating the aforementioned adverse outcomes.

Background and Aims
Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) are a leading cause of maternal morbidity and mortality globally. Renal impairment often complicates the clinical course of patients with HDP and has been linked to long-term progression towards chronic kidney disease (CKD).
