title: #2328 Exploring the role of KDM6A as a regulator of proximal tubular epithelial cell dysmetabolism in diabetic kidney disease
authors: Maya Bozzo-Rey; Yue Tian; Katarina Zorcic; Felix Liu; Rogelio Cruz Gonzalez; Ria Patel; Caiden Hong; Ali Rizwan; Sergi Clotet Freixas
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease and progresses faster in males. In DKD, proximal tubular epithelial cells (PTECs) increase the breakdown of glucose (via glycolysis) and glutamine for utilization in the TCA cycle, the major energy-producing mechanism. This shift leads to the accumulation of pathogenic products, such as lactate, thus promoting DKD.
Epigenetics partly mediates metabolic alterations in DKD. KDM6A is a histone demethylase that erases the repressive mark H3K27me3 at DNA promoters, resulting in upregulation of many target genes. These include metabolic and inflammation genes increased in DKD. High levels of KDM6A were found in mouse and human diabetic kidneys, and in PTECs exposed to high glucose. Loss of KDM6A in podocytes attenuated glomerular lesions in mice with DKD, however, the effect of targeting this enzyme in PTECs in DKD remains unknown.
We aim to determine, in a sex-specific fashion, the role of KDM6A in mediating PTEC dysmetabolism under high glucose.
Method
Human PTECs of a male or a female donor were subjected to siRNA-mediated KDM6A inhibition for 48 h, then treated them with normal glucose (5.5 mM), high glucose (25 mM), or osmotic control (5.5 mM glucose + 19.5 mM mannitol) for 24 h.
Results
Male-derived PTECs displayed significantly higher levels of extracellular lactate than female PTECs (P < 0.05). High glucose treatment significantly increased lactate secretion in male PTECs, an effect that was only modest in female PTECs. Silencing of KDM6A reduced lactate secretion in both sexes, regardless of the glucose concentration. At the gene level, high glucose significantly increased the expression of LDHA and MDH2 (enzymes involved in glycolysis and the TCA cycle, respectively) in male, but not female PTECs, and this effect was prevented by KDM6A inhibition.
Conclusion
Our findings suggest that KDM6A mediates alterations in glucose and glutamine metabolism induced by high glucose in male PTECs. This work has the potential to establish KDM6A as a novel clinical target in DKD.

title: #3217 Incremental hemodialysis with tight control of overhydration as an option for pregnant woman in RRT
authors: Rita Santarsiere; Caterina Vitagliano; Alessandro Cerrone; Daniela Terracciano; Laura Sarno; Giovambattista Capasso; Alessandra Perna; Giorgina Piccoli; Francesco Trepiccione
abstract:
Background and Aims
Pregnancy in patients with CKD with or without RRT is uncommon and carries a high risk of pregnancy interruption. The management of pregnant women in RRT is challenging in order to achieve adequate purification and optimal body water control. Intensive dialysis prescription is considered fundamental to manage these cases.
We present here the case of a 28 y/o woman with CKD due to PAX2 associated glomerulopathy. She was at her fourth pregnancy with a progressively fast worsening of kidney function. She started hemodialysis at 13th week of gestation with a progressive dose-incremental scheme. In order to prevent overhydration and/or fetal ischemia, we designed an innovative approach to evaluate the body water content based on the use of both body composition measurement and placental markers of stress, namely PlGF and sFlt.1.
Method
For our case, we used a dose-incremental HD scheme from 7.5 h to 24 h per week, adjusting the dose by achieving a pre-dialysis BUN level <48 mg/dl and preserving residual diuresis (Fig. 1).
The blood flow (Qb) also increased from 250 ml/min to 300 ml/min, while dialysate flow (Qd) was constantly 500 ml/min. We develop an algorithm to estimate the dry weight by integrating multifrequency bioimpedance data with ultrasound-evaluated fetal weight. This method helped us to minimize the occurrence of intradialytic and peridialytic hypotensive events and maintain optimal blood volume, thereby reducing the risk of placental hypoperfusion. In order to monitor the placental stress, we measured pre and post dialysis value of PIGF and sFlt1. As nutritional therapy the patient was on 1800 Kcal/day with a protein intake 1.2 g/kg/day in a mostly vegetarian diet supplemented with keto-analogs.
Results
With this approach our patient gave birth at week 34th of gestation without complications. Residual diuresis was around 1000 mL/day at the end of the pregnancy. We experienced only one complication as the infection of the CVC that was managed with proper antibiotic therapy. About placental factors, our findings indicated that during the hemodialysis session, the values never reached levels associated with pre-eclamptic risk or placental distress, as reported previously.
Conclusion
In conclusion we propose here that incremental HD is possible in selected patients. Optimal control of total water content by our method helps in avoid complication as preclampsia. We have confirmed the predictive role of placental growth factors and BUN variation. Moreover, an intensive approach is not always necessary, and residual kidney function could be preserved.

title: #1041 The impact of metformin on CKD progression and mortality in diabetic patients using SGLT2 inhibitors—a real world cohort study
authors: Timna Agur; Benaya Rozen Zvi; Tali Steinmetz; Boris Zingerman; Shira Goldman; Eshcar Meisel; Ittai Fattal
abstract:
Background and Aims
Selecting the optimal first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes is crucial for glycemic control and providing cardiovascular and renal protection, though the combined benefits of metformin with SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), remain uncertain. This study aimed to compare outcomes in adults with type 2 diabetes treated with SGLT2i alone versus in combination with metformin.
Method
This retrospective cohort study analysed data from Clalit Health Services (2016–2021). Propensity score matching was applied to balance baseline characteristics between groups. Primary outcomes were a composite kidney outcome (40% decline in eGFR, or progression to ESRD), and all-cause mortality. Safety outcomes included hospitalizations and metabolic acidosis.
Results
The study included 45,545 patients, with 6774 patients in each group following propensity score matching. The median follow-up time was 1166 days. Combination therapy with metformin and SGLT2i was associated with significantly reduced risk of all-cause mortality (aHR 0.74, 95% CI 0.64–0.84), and composite kidney outcomes (aHR 0.65; 95% CI 0.48–0.87) even after accounting for mortality as a competing risk (aHR 0.67; 95% CI 0.5–0.9). Furthermore, combination therapy reduced the risks of hospitalization (aHR 0.93; 95% CI 0.87–0.99) and metabolic acidosis (aHR 0.58; 95% CI 0.4–0.83), compared with SGLT2i alone.
Conclusion
Patients receiving combination therapy with metformin and SGLT2i showed significantly reduced risks of CKD progression and mortality compared to those treated with SGLT2i alone. These findings support the use of metformin with SGLT2i as a first-line treatment for type 2 diabetes irrespective of glycemic control or cardio-renal risk factors.

title: #3724 Pregnancy, primary aldosteronism and renal tubular disorders: a systematic review of the utility of amiloride in pregnancy
authors: Kaitlyn Cinnamond; David Yerushalmy; Stanly Varghese; Liam Casserly
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diagnosis of secondary causes of hypertension, such as primary hyperaldosteronism and renal tubulopathies, during pregnancy is underreported [1]. Pregnancy has been described as a valuable but frequently missed opportunity for serious disease identification and often affords the first opportunity for diagnosis of kidney or cardiovascular disease in women. Amiloride is arguably suitable for use in these disorders during pregnancy due to its reversible binding to the epithelial sodium channels of principal cells [‘ENaC’].
Method
A systematic review of the literature regarding the use of amiloride during pregnancy was conducted, utilising PRISMA on PubMed and EMBASE databases. 442 papers were screened, broadly searching [“amiloride” AND “pregnancy”], with duplicates/non-english/animal studies/amiloride not utilised/outcomes not documented were excluded, with a total 27 papers, incorporating 30 cases, included for review.
Results
The use of amiloride in pregnancy has been documented in thirty cases, outlined in Fig. 1. Most of these cases (28 of 30) had favourable outcomes. The adverse complications in two cases could likely be related to uncontrolled hypertension. Notably, amiloride was discontinued in both cases. Amiloride has been used without adverse effects in pregnancies complicated by Liddle's syndrome (cases 1–2), Bartter syndrome (cases 13–15), Geller syndrome (cases 11–12), Gitelman's syndrome (3–10), among various others such as nephrotic syndrome, hypokalaemic gain of function mutations and a case of spontaneous decapsulation of a transplant kidney (cases 26–28). It has been suggested that the use of amiloride should be given early consideration in complex cases with risk of hypokalaemic paralysis [2], a cautionary case with both maternal and foetal demise due to difficulty treating Gitelman's syndrome. Awadalla et al. [3)] report that there has been a hesitancy to use diuretics in pregnancy due to the risks of volume depletion and uteroplacental hypoperfusion. Amiloride reduces the mechanism of hypertension through reversal of excessive sodium reabsorption and volume expansion, acting on the luminal membrane of the distal convoluted tubule and collecting ducts, reversibly binding to the ENaC of principal cells. This leads to a limited capacity for the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct to reabsorb sodium, causing hyperpolarisation of the luminal membrane, which under normal circumstances would facilitate normal cation secretion thereby inhibiting the excessive secretion of same. In renal tubular disorders (such as Liddle syndrome), mutations in the ENaC result in hyperactivity leading to problematic hypertension. As such, amiloride offers many benefits in pregnancy complicated by potassium wasting disorders and further research on its use is warranted.
Conclusion
Pregnancy often presents the first opportunity to diagnose serious disease in women. Hypertension is frequently attributed as being pathognomonic of preeclampsia when associated with intrauterine growth retardation, leading to a failure to consider secondary testing. While there may be a negative reporting bias for side effects of amiloride during pregnancy, it has been used successfully and appears to be low risk base on the reported cases. It is particularly suitable in pregnancy complicated by renal tubular disorders with hypokalaemia. Prompt recognition and treatment of these conditions in pregnancy is vital both for short-term foetal and maternal outcomes as well as long-term chronic disease management for the mother. Our review suggests that amiloride is a safe option during pregnancy.

title: #3319 Sex related disparities in the management of diabetic kidney disease: a retrospective analysis in a health region
authors: Israel Fernández Espinosa; Angela Molina; MacArena Saez; Saioa Sanchez; Guillermo Alcalde Bezhold; Sarai Camino; Raquel Berzal; Oriana Carmona; Andrea Bedia Raba; Maria del Carmen Robledo; Pierre Phillippe Neyra; Óscar García Uriarte
abstract:
Background and Aims
The aim of this study is to assess adherence to international guidelines for the screening and management of diabetic kidney disease (DKD) in a health region serving a population of approximately 300,000. Specifically, we aim to evaluate the annual screening rates for albuminuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), as well as the use of SGLT2 inhibitors (iSGLT2) in the treatment of DKD, as recommended by the KDIGO guidelines.
Method
This observational, retrospective study utilized an anonymized database extracted from electronic health records. The study included prevalent patients with T2DM during 2021, excluding those with type 1 diabetes, gestational diabetes, non-residents in the Health Region, patients under 18 years old, and those who died in 2021. A total of 21,199 patients with T2DM were included, comprising 11,584 men (54.6%) and 9,615 women (45.4%).
DKD was defined as the presence of T2DM with either an eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² or albuminuria ≥30 mg/g in a spot urine sample or 24-hour urine collection. The study assessed the proportion of patients who underwent annual screening for albuminuria and eGFR, as well as the proportion of patients with DKD who were treated with iSGLT2 inhibitors.
Results
Of the 21,199 patients with T2DM, 19,480 (91.9%) had at least one plasma creatinine measurement in 2021, but only 12,200 (57.5%) had at least one albuminuria test, indicating suboptimal adherence to the recommended annual screening for DKD.
Among the 21,199 patients, 6,175 (29.1%) met the criteria for DKD. Of these, 1,146 had both reduced eGFR and albuminuria, 2,226 had albuminuria with normal eGFR, and 2,503 had reduced eGFR without albuminuria. Among the 6,012 patients with DKD and eGFR ≥20 mL/min/1.73 m², only 1,238 (20.6%) were treated with iSGLT2 inhibitors. The treatment rate was higher in patients with albuminuria (24.9%) compared to those without albuminuria (14.4%); OR 1.96 (95% CI: 1.71–2.24).
Further analysis revealed gender disparities in the screening and treatment of DKD. Among the 6,175 patients with DKD, 55.47% were men and 44.3% were women. Men were less likely to have albuminuria testing (63.4%) compared to women (51.9%), with an odds ratio (OR) of 0.62 (95% CI: 0.589–0.658). Additionally, women with DKD were less likely to receive treatment with iSGLT2 inhibitors (14.6%) compared to men (25.4%), with an OR of 0.50 (95% CI: 0.439–0.573).
Conclusion
The study highlights significant gaps in the screening and management of DKD in patients with T2DM. Despite international guidelines recommending annual screening for albuminuria and eGFR, only 58% of patients underwent both tests. Furthermore, the use of SGLT2 inhibitors, which are recommended as first-line treatment for DKD, was suboptimal, with only 20.6% of eligible patients receiving this therapy (consistent with previous reports). The treatment rates with iSGLT2 inhibitors were particularly low in DKD patients without albuminuria, especially in women, indicating potential gender disparities in the management of DKD that cannot be justified by fear of urinary tract infections.
These findings underscore the need for improved adherence to clinical guidelines, particularly in early detection and treatment of DKD. Enhanced screening protocols and greater awareness of the benefits of iSGLT2 inhibitors, especially in women, could lead to better outcomes for patients with DKD.

title: #2295 Characterization and standard of care efficacy testing in a translational mouse model of cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome
authors: Arianne van Koppen; Anke Smits; Tri Nguyen; Amélie Dendooven; Ingeborg Bajema; Harry van Goor; Toon van Veen; Willem van Ham; Elsbet Pieterman; Aswin Menke; Reinout Stoop
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome is a multifactorial disease involving the interconnection of cardiovascular and kidney disease, obesity and type 2 diabetes which can exacerbate one another. To study the dynamics of the physiological interactions and efficacy of novel therapies, a translational mouse model is key. We developed and characterized a diet-induced hypertension-accelerated mouse model in which obesity, type 2 diabetes, progressive kidney disease and cardiovascular damage are present, and which can be modulated by standard-of-care therapy.
Method
Male KK-Ay mice underwent uninephrectomy (UNx). After recovery mice received high fat diet (HFD, 45% LARD) and 50 mg/L L-NNA in drinking water (wk 0) until termination (wk 16). Body weight, blood glucose, food and water intake and albuminuria were determined regularly. GFR was measured regularly transdermally by FITC-sinistrin clearance. Cardiac imaging was performed at wk 12. Renal and cardiac histology was scored. Non-induced and induced non-treated mice were used as controls. In the treatment group, at week 4, lisinopril (2.5 mg/kg/day in drinking water) and at week 8 dapagliflozin (5 and 20 mg/kg/day in diet) were started.
Results
Male KK-Ay mice developed obesity, type 2 diabetes, renal insufficiency (initial hyperfiltration followed by a continuous decline of GFR resulting in CKD), increased plasma cholesterol and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Pathological scoring showed glomerulosclerosis, tubulo-interstitial fibrosis and cardiac fibrosis. Dapagliflozin lowered blood glucose. The combination therapy of lisinopril and dapagliflozin rescued GFR decline and resulted in a higher number of healthy glomeruli and reduced interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy. Combination therapy reduced lung wet weight, significantly reduced heart weight and significantly decreased cardiac fibrosis.
Conclusion
Male KK-Ay mice on a HFD and L-NNA develop obesity, type 2 diabetes, kidney failure and cardiovascular damage thereby resembling CKM. title: #1009 Impact of glycemic variability on mortality risk in patients with diabetes and end-stage kidney disease undergoing maintenance dialysis
authors: Hanri Afghahi; Salmir Nasic; Björn Peters; Anna Wãrme; Helena Rydell; Maria K Svensson
abstract:
Background and Aims
Glycemic variability, defined as fluctuations in blood glucose levels throughout the day or over longer periods, may contribute to diabetic complications and increased mortality risk beyond persistent hyperglycemia. This study aimed to evaluate glycemic variability, as measured by HbA1c variability, and its association with mortality in patients with diabetes and end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) undergoing maintenance hemodialysis (HD) or peritoneal dialysis (PD).
Method
Data were extracted from the Swedish Renal Register (SRR). The long-term glycemic variability was quantified as the coefficient of variation (CV) calculated as the ratio of the standard deviation (SD) of individual HbA1c measurements (SD) and the mean value of individual HbA1c measurements i.e. [SD(HbA1c)/mean (HbA1c)] × 100. After exploring the HbA1c-variability patients were categorized into three groups based on CV ≤4, CV 5–15 and CV ≥15. Associations between HbA1c variability and mortality were assessed using Cox regression models to estimate hazard ratios (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI), with adjustments for demographic factors, laboratory findings, and comorbidities. Patients with CV≤4 served as the reference group.
Results
A total of 1,685 patients with diabetes and ESKD on maintenance dialysis, including 1,360 on HD and 325 on PD, were analyzed. The mean age was 65 ± 13.1 years, and 67% were men. The mean follow-up duration was 3.2 ± 2.4 years, during which 850 deaths (50.4%) were recorded 50% (n = 678) in HD patients and 52% (n = 167) in PD patients. The mean CV HbA1c was higher in HD patients compared to PD patients (13 vs. 11, P < 0.001). A CV HbA1c ≥15 was observed in 30% (n = 402) of HD patients and 18% (n = 60) of PD patients (P < 0.001). In an adjusted multivariate model, high glycemic variability (CV HbA1c ≥15) was significantly associated with increased mortality risk in both HD (HR = 1.43, 95% CI: 1.12–1.83, P = 0.005) and PD patients (HR = 1.89, 95% CI: 1.13–3.16, P = 0.015).
Conclusion
Elevated glycemic variability is associated with a higher risk of mortality in patients with diabetes and ESKD undergoing maintenance dialysis. Glycemic variability was significantly greater in HD patients compared to PD patients, with a larger proportion experiencing very high variability. Future research should explore the influence of dialysis modality on glycemic variability and its clinical implications.

title: #1608 Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and the risk of emergency department visits and hospitalization in patients across the spectrum of kidney disease
authors: Kevin Yau; David Cherney; Ron Wald
abstract:
Background and Aims
Glucagon-like-peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP1RA) have emerged as a therapy that promotes weight loss and confers cardiorenal protection. While recent trials have suggested benefit on heart failure hospitalizations; their effects on all-cause emergency department (ED) visits and hospitalizations have not been well characterized. In this population-based study we examined the effect of initiating a GLP1RA versus a dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitor (DPP4i) on ED visits and all-cause hospitalization in patients across the spectrum of chronic kidney disease (CKD).
Method
This retrospective cohort study was conducted in Ontario, Canada, using administrative databases housed at ICES. We included a cohort of patients aged ≥18 years with eGFR <90 ml/min/1.73 m2 who received a first prescription of a GLP1RA or DPP4i through the Ontario Drug Benefit between September 30, 2019 to December 31, 2021. Follow-up extended until June 30, 2022. We used inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) based on a propensity score conditioned on 72 covariates to address confounding. We evaluated the effect of GLP1RA initiation on all cause ED visits and hospitalization using time-to-recurrent-event approaches with the Prentice-Williams-Peterson (PWP) gap time model which assumes an event-specific hazard for each ED encounter or hospitalization. In an additional analysis, we evaluated recurrent ED visits and/or hospitalizations using the Andersen-Gill extension of the Cox proportional hazards model and robust sandwich estimators to obtain the 95% confidence intervals.
Results
The study cohort included 24,576 patients who were new users of a GLP1RA, and 23,600 who were new users of a DPP-4i eGFR <90 ml/min/1.73 m2. Baseline characteristics were balanced between groups (mean age of 69 years, 50% female, 92% with type 2 diabetes mellitus, 3.5% had heart failure, and 41% had CKD stages 3–5). Semaglutide represented 98.4% of GLP1RA prescriptions. Across the cohort, 9.6% had more than one hospitalization while 25.8% had more than one emergency department encounter. Using the PWP gap time model, new use of GLP1RA was associated with a lower risk of all-cause ED encounters or hospitalizations: HR 0.90 (95% CI, 0.87 to 0.94; P < 0.0001). This finding was consistent when we used the calendar time model (HR 0.90; 95% CI, 0.87 to 0.94) or the Andersen-Gill extension of the Cox proportional hazards model (HR 0.87; 95% CI, 0.82 to 0.92) (Table 1).
Conclusion
In this large population-based study, GLP1RA initiation was associated with a reduction in all-cause ED visits and/or hospitalizations when compared to DPP-4 inhibitor initiation. This finding has potentially substantial implications on health care delivery and resource utilization.

title: #2047 Trends in the global, regional, and national burden of diabetic kidney disease from 1990 to 2021: a systematic analysis of the global burden of disease study 2021
authors: Sixiu Liu; Ying Liu; Jing Liu; Qingyan Zhang; Qiuyuan Shao; Chun-Ming Jiang
abstract:
Background and Aims
This research depicted the global, regional, and national burden of diabetic kidney disease (DKD) from 1990–2021 to assess its epidemiological patterns and trends, which was vital for healthcare interventions.
Method
To study DKD epidemiological patterns, a comparative analysis of type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), DKD induced by type 1 diabetes (DKD (T1DM)), and DKD induced by type 2 diabetes (DKD (T2DM)) was done. Using 2021 GBD data, incidences, prevalences, mortality rates, and DALYs from 1990–2021 were calculated across 204 regions. Burdens by age, gender, and SDI were evaluated. Risk factors were explored, and projections for 2022–2031 were made.
Results
The age-standardized incidence rate (ASIR), age-standardized prevalence rate (ASPR), age-standardized death rate (ASDR), and age-standardized disability-adjusted life-years rate (ASDAR) of T1DM, T2DM, DKD (T1DM), and DKD (T2DM) exhibited diverse variations across different regions globally. The ASIR and ASPR of T1DM, T2DM, DKD (T1DM), and DKD (T2DM) globally showed a positive correlation with the sociodemographic Index (SDI) score, while the ASDR and ASDAR demonstrated a negative correlation with the SDI score. We selected the risk factors including high fasting plasma glucose, kidney dysfunction, high systolic blood pressure, diet low in fruits, low physical activity, and low temperature, and analyzed the effects of these risk factors on the ASDR and ASDAR of diseases in different regions. Predictions for the next decade (2022– 2031) indicated that, except for a reduction in the mortality burden of T1DM, the disease burdens of T2DM, DKD (T1DM), and DKD (T2DM) would show a gently upward trend.
Conclusion
DKD burden varied across regions, SDI levels, and countries. It had been increasing since 1990. Large-scale screening was essential for DKD control and prevention.

title: #1700 Heterogeneity in characteristics of target population and definitions of renal outcome on evaluating the renoprotective effect of GLP-1RA in patients with diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies versus randomized controlled trials
authors: Xiaoyu Wu; Zhaohui Bai; Yue Zhang; Dongze Ji; Na He; Yang Xu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Growing research suggests that glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) might exert potential renoprotective effects in patients with diabetes. However, existing evidence from observational studies and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was inconsistent, which may be attributed to differences in characteristics of population and definitions of renal outcomes. Therefore, this study systematically summarized the characteristics of target population and definitions of renal outcomes, and evaluated the heterogeneity between RCTs and observational studies in these aspects.
Method
A systematic search was conducted in PubMed and Embase databases, RCTs and observational studies investigating the renal effects of GLP-1RA in patients with diabetes were included. Characteristics of study design, baseline characteristics of target population, the definitions of renal outcomes, and the corresponding findings were extracted. Baseline characteristics of target population were compared between RCTs and observational studies using random effects meta-analyses with Knapp-Hartung adjustment. The effects of GLP-1RA on renal outcomes were estimated using random effects model based on the different definitions of renal outcomes. Data were pooled using hazard ratios (HRs) or odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Meta-regression was performed to explore whether the differences in study designs, types of controls, and characteristics of target population could explain the heterogeneity of renal outcomes.
Results
Overall, 42 studies were included in analysis, comprising 10 RCTs and 32 observational studies. In the main analysis of observational studies, propensity score matching was used in 23 studies, average treatment effects for the treated and average treatment effects for the control were estimated in 17 and 6 studies, respectively. Inverse probability of treatment weighting was applied in 7 studies to estimate average treatment effects, and overlap weighting was employed in one study to estimate the average treatment effects for the overlap population. Additionally, propensity score regression adjustment was used in one study and the conditional average treatment effects were estimated. Compared to patients enrolled in observational studies, those in RCTs were on average 3.9 years older (P = 0.004), had a 3.5-years longer duration of diabetes (P = 0.03), and presented with worse renal function: the proportion of patients with albuminuria was 23.4% higher, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was 14.7 ml/min/1.73 m2 lower among RCT participants (albuminuria: P = 0.019; eGFR: P = 0.067). For renal outcomes, the meta-analysis suggested that GLP-1RA significantly reduced the risk of composite renal outcomes compared with placebo (HR 0.75 [95% CI 0.70–0.80], P < 0.0001), and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor (DPP-4i) (HR 0.78 [95% CI 0.74, 0.82], P < 0.0001). While, GLP-1RA were associated with a significantly higher risk than sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) (HR 1.29 [95% CI 1.08, 1.53], P = 0.005). Regarding other renal outcomes, including the development of macroalbuminuria, decline in eGFR, progression to end-stage renal disease, acute kidney injury, and renal related death, the effects of GLP-1RA on renal outcomes in patients with diabetes varied.
Conclusion
Substantial systematic differences were observed in the characteristics of target population and definitions of renal outcomes between RCTs and observational studies for patients with diabetes. Therefore, the efficacy seen in RCTs may not reflect real-world effectiveness.

title: #2014 Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) use in people with diabetes (PwD) on dialysis: a retrospective, cross-sectional, observational Study
authors: Chi Peng Chan; Gauri Jagadesh; Srikanth Bellary; Jyoti Baharani
abstract:
Background and Aims
There is limited evidence surrounding the long-term glycaemic benefits from continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in people with diabetes (PwD) on dialysis. The aim of this study was to establish the potential benefits of CGM use on glycaemic control, guiding insulin therapy regimen, and improving clinical outcomes in PwD on dialysis.
Method
A retrospective, cross-sectional study was conducted across all dialysis units within University Hospitals Birmingham (UHB) NHS Foundation Trust, United Kingdom. Patients aged >18 years, with known diagnosis of diabetes receiving regular dialysis—including haemodialysis (HD), peritoneal dialysis (PD), and home haemodialysis (HHD)—who used CGM (FreeStyle Libre or Dexcom) for more than 3 months were included. Patients not sharing CGM data were excluded. Data was extracted by accessing electronic patient records and CGM (LibreView or Dexcom Clarity) Portals. The demographic characteristics, insulin treatment, and CGM metrics (time in range [TIR], time above range [TAR], time below range [TBR], glucose variability [GV], HbA1C levels and number of hypoglycaemia events) were recorded.
Results
A total of 55 adult patients were included. 76.4% (n = 42/55) of patients were on HD; 21.8% (n = 12/55) on PD; and 1.8% (n = 1/55) on HHD. The median number of months on CGM was 26 (IQR = 19.31). All patients were on insulin therapy. 29.1% (n = 16/55) patients had their insulin therapy regimen changed following CGM use. 63.6% (n = 35/55) patients were on basal-bolus regimen. 4.65% (n = 2/43) of HD and HHD patients had required different insulin doses between their dialysis and non-dialysis days. There was no difference between measured baseline and latest HbA1C following CGM introduction (68.22 ± 21.86 vs 63.38 ± 17.96 [mmol/mol], P = 0.757). Furthermore, there was also no difference between the mean glucose on CGM over the last 14-days and 90-days period (11.94 ± 3.31 vs 12.08 ± 3.26 [mmol/L], P = 0.586). The latest median TIR for our patients remained suboptimal at 38.0%. The hyperglycaemic burden was excessive, with a median TAR-very high of 26.0% and TAR-high of 28.0%. Of the 48 patients who were on FreeStyle Libre, 77.1% (n = 37/48) had at least one prolonged hypoglycaemia event of >15 minutes over the last-90-days. 29.7% (n = 11/37) did not have any further hypoglycaemia event over the last 14-days (P < 0.001).
Conclusion
While significant improvements in overall glycaemic control were not observed, our findings underscore the complexity of glycaemic management in this population and the need for tailored interventions. We strongly advocate for large-scale randomised controlled trials to explore how CGM technology can be further optimised to achieve meaningful improvements in glycaemic and clinical outcomes for this challenging patient group.

title: #3133 The association between hemoglobin A1c and complications among individuals with diabetes and severe chronic kidney disease
authors: Dea Kofod; Nicholas Carlson; Thomas Peter Almdal; Tobias Bomholt; Christian Torp; Kirsten Nørgaard; Jesper Svendsen; Bo Feldt-Rasmussen; Mads Hornum
abstract:
Background and Aims
The predictive value of hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) in severe chronic kidney disease (CKD) remains uncertain. We examined the association between HbA1c and complications in individuals with diabetes and severe CKD.
Method
In a Danish nationwide registry-based cohort study, we included individuals ≥18 years with diabetes and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <30 mL/min/1.73 m2 (not on dialysis) between 2010 and 2022. Each individual with severe CKD was age- and sex-matched with three individuals with diabetes and no/mild CKD (eGFR ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m2) and three individuals with diabetes and moderate CKD (eGFR 30–59 mL/min/1.73 m2), respectively. Multiple Cox regressions were used to estimate the standardized 1-year risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), microvascular complications, and hospitalization due to hypoglycemia across strata of HbA1c levels.
Results
We included 27,113 individuals with severe CKD. The standardized 1-year risks of outcomes across strata of HbA1c levels for the three cohorts are presented in Fig. 1. For the individuals with severe CKD, the risk of MACE increased significantly at HbA1c levels <40 mmol/mol (5.8%) and ≥55 mmol/mol (7.2%), compared with an HbA1c level of 45–49 mmol/mol (6.3–6.6%). The risk of microvascular complications increased significantly at HbA1c levels ≥55 mmol/mol (7.2%), whereas there was no statistically significant difference between HbA1c levels of 30–54 mmol/mol (4.9–6.7%). Lastly, the risk of hospitalization due to hypoglycemia was lowest for those with an HbA1c level of 40–44 mmol/mol (5.8–6.2%), while the risk increased significantly with increasing levels of HbA1c ≥45 mmol/mol (6.3%). The patterns of association between HbA1c and outcomes were similar in the severe CKD cohort compared to the matched cohorts with no/mild CKD (n = 80,797) and moderate CKD (n = 80,131).
Conclusion
HbA1c remained an important predictor of complications in severe CKD. Our data suggest an HbA1c range of 50–54 mmol/mol (6.7–7.1%) to be most favorable with regards to long-term complications in this high-risk population.

The predictive value of hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) in severe chronic kidney disease (CKD) remains uncertain. We examined the association between HbA1c and complications in individuals with diabetes and severe CKD.

title: #1999 Mechanisms of GPCR19-mediated protection in diabetic kidney disease: regulation of mitochondrial homeostasis and therapeutic potential
authors: Lijun Zhao; Fang Liu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is a leading cause of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). Diabetic tubulopathy plays a central role in the progression of DKD, particularly through tubular fibrosis. Mitochondrial dysfunction in renal tubular cells under high glucose is a key contributor to DKD. G protein-coupled receptor 19 (GPCR19) is highly expressed in renal tubules and involved in various pathophysiological processes. This study investigates the role of GPCR19 in maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis in renal tubular epithelial cells and its potential as a therapeutic target for DKD.
Method
Renal biopsy samples from DKD patients and db/db diabetic mice were analyzed for GPCR19 expression via immunohistochemistry. In vivo, CRISPR/Cas9 technology was used to construct C57BL/6J background mice (TEC-GPCR19OV) with specific overexpression of GPCR19 in proximal renal tubular epithelial cells. Intraperitoneal injection of streptozotocin combined with high-fat and high-glucose feeding was used to establish a type 2 diabetes model. Renal function, histopathology, apoptosis, and mitochondrial dynamics were assessed. In vitro, human renal tubular cells (HK-2) were treated with the GPCR19-specific agonist INT-777 under high glucose conditions. Cellular apoptosis, mitochondrial function, and mitophagy were measured using flow cytometry, Western blot, and immunofluorescence.
Results
GPCR19 expression was significantly reduced in the renal tubules of DKD patients and db/db mice. Overexpression of GPCR19 in transgenic mice alleviated DKD-related renal damage (Fig. 1), reduced apoptosis, and improved mitochondrial function, including enhanced mitochondrial fusion and mitophagy (Fig. 2). INT-777 treatment in HK-2 cells under high glucose promoted mitochondrial fusion, inhibited ROS production (Fig. 3), and improved mitochondrial membrane potential, while reducing apoptosis. Additionally, the PKA/CREB signaling pathway was involved in GPCR19-mediated protection, with CREB regulating BNIP3 expression in mitophagy (Fig. 4).
Conclusion
GPCR19 is downregulated in DKD, and its overexpression in renal tubular cells protects against tubulopathy by maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis. INT-777, a GPCR19 agonist, improves mitochondrial function and reduces apoptosis in high glucose conditions, suggesting its potential as a therapeutic agent in DKD. The PKA/CREB pathway, through regulation of BNIP3, is a key mechanism in GPCR19-mediated protection in diabetic nephropathy.

title: #1924 The overlooked players: immunomodulatory endothelial cells in diabetic kidney disease
authors: Baharak Hosseinkhani; Eleonora Lama; Mieke Dewerchin; Anwar Khan; Dries Deleersnijder; Diether Lambrechts; Peter Carmeliet; Amaryllis Van Craenenbroeck
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) has become the leading cause of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) worldwide. DKD is a microvascular disease characterized by renal endothelial cell (EC) dysfunction. Studies by the Carmeliet lab and others using scRNA-seq highlighted EC heterogeneity in different pathophysiological contexts, including kidney disease. Further, these studies identified similar patterns of gene expression in EC subsets as in immune cells (ICs) raising the question if these immunomodulatory ECs (coined “IMECs”) participate in immune responses, such as during vascular inflammation and associated EC dysfunction. However, while inflammation, oxidative stress and fibrosis are considered to contribute to EC dysfunction in DKD, a comprehensive unbiased understanding of signatures in renal ECs at single cell resolution is lacking. We are characterizing the (patho)-biological role of ECs in dkd by using single nuclei/cell multi-omics. We identified several unexplored genes (lacking functional annotation and publications) with a predicted IMEC function using in-house generated AI-based tools. Their functional role in the context of DKD will be further investigated.
Method
Droplet-based snRNA-seq (10X Genomics Chromium) was performed on cryopreserved kidney biopsy cores from 6 patients with severe DKD (6 patients (3 females; 3 males), median age 65 yrs; median eGFR: 15 ml/min/1.73 m2; median albuminuria: 1 g/g creatinine) and 6 sex/age-matched healthy controls. Healthy control samples were pre-perfusion biopsies from patients undergoing living kidney donation. EC subclusters were annotated based on the expression of canonical EC marker genes. Differential gene expression analysis for patient samples vs. controls included all ECs and differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were filtered for log2FC > 0.25 or < −0.25 and adjusted p-value of <0.05. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) on the identified DEGs was performed with Enrich, using GO terms. Leveraging generated snRNA-seq data and a curated set of training genes with documented immunomodulatory functions, we used in-house generated AI-based gene discovery and prioritization tools to select the most promising IMEC unexplored candidate drivers of EC dysfunction in DKD. In vitro, the RNA expression levels in HUVECs were analyzed using qRT-PCR after 72 hours of culture under three conditions: control (5.5 mM glucose), hyperglycemic (33 mM glucose), or inflammatory (10 ng/ml TNF-α).
Results
Cell type annotation showed the presence of ca 6,000 ECs in the snRNA-seq dataset (Fig. 1A). Initial differential gene expression analysis of the EC population in the patient vs control samples identified several potential immunostimulatory genes. Using the in-house AI-based prioritization tools, we identified three potential unexplored IMEC genes, coded KIMEC1, KIMEC2, and KIMEC3 (the identity of the genes cannot be disclosed due to IP reasons). These genes were among the top upregulated, with log2FC values of 0.57, 0.34, and 0.522 (adjusted p-value of <0.05), respectively. Of note, all 3 genes are predicted to be involved in oxidative stress. In addition, they tend to be also upregulated in ECs in vivo in various inflammatory conditions (Fig. 1B.; shown for KIMEC3) and in vitro in hyperglycemic and/or pro-inflammatory culture conditions (shown for KIMEC3 in Fig. 1C–D).
Conclusion
We identified previously unexplored IMEC genes expressed in renal EC in DKD. Their potential role in mediating vascular inflammation and endothelial cell dysfunction in DKD will be further investigated.

title: #814 Angiotensin dysregulation in patients with arterial aneurysms
authors: Maria-Elisabeth Leinweber; Corinna Walter; Afshin Assadian; Chantal Kopecky; Oliver Domenig; Johannes J Kovarik; Amun Georg Hofmann
abstract:
Background and Aims
Besides playing a critical role in maintaining cardiovascular homeostasis, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAS) has been strongly implicated in AAA pathogenesis. This study aims to investigate systemic and local levels of angiotensin (Ang) and its metabolites in patients with arterial aneurysms, predominantly abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA), using advanced biochemical profiling techniques to provide new insights into the involvement of RAS in aneurysm genesis.
Method
A prospective, single-centre study was conducted between October 2023 and July 2024.
Serum samples and aortic tissue were collected from patients undergoing surgery or having received invasive aneurysm treatment. Serum Ang metabolite levels were measured using RAS Fingerprint technology. Aortic tissue samples were analysed for local RAS activity, including Ang levels and enzyme activity. Additionally, pre-, and postoperative serum samples were obtained in a select group of patients.
Results
In total, 37 aneurysm patients and 56 controls were included. Aneurysm patients exhibited higher systemic levels of nearly all Ang metabolites compared to controls, with notable differences in Ang I (P = .002), Ang II (P = .047), Ang 1–5 (P = .004), and Ang IV (P = .095) as well as Renin (P = .014) in patients without pharmacological RAS interference. Aneurysm patients receiving ACE inhibitors showed a significant reduction in ACE2 activity (P = .042) and increased Ang IV levels (P = .049) compared to controls. Postoperative changes indicated declining angiotensin metabolite levels in patients treated with ACE inhibitors, whereas those without ACE inhibitors showed increased levels post-surgery.
Conclusion
This study provides the first comprehensive characterization of RAS profiles in aneurysm patients. These findings add to the body of evidence regarding associations between of RAS and the pathogenesis of arterial aneurysms.

title: #798 Real-life study of finerenone, efficacy and safety assessment
authors: Paola Donoso Naranjo; Luis Luque Caraballo; Ana Massé Palomo; Francisco Orti Cuerva; Clarencio Cebrián Andrada; Manuel López Mendoza; Miguel Ángel Pérez Valdivia; David León Jiménez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Finerenone is a novel synthetic nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) that specifically targets the mineralocorticoid receptor in renal tissues. It has been shown to exert nephroprotective effects, particularly in patients with diabetic kidney disease (DKD), which is characterized by progressive renal dysfunction and often leads to end-stage renal disease. Unlike traditional MRAs, finerenone offers a more selective mechanism of action, which mitigates the risk of adverse effects, particularly hyperkalemia, a common concern associated with mineralocorticoid receptor blockade. The recent approval of finerenone for clinical use represents a significant advancement in the management of DKD, enhancing the therapeutic options available to clinicians.
This study aims to assess the impact of initiating finerenone one month after treatment onset on estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR), and potassium (K+) levels in patients with DKD treated with the maximum tolerated and stable doses of renin angiotensin system inhibitors (RASi) and sodium-glucose cotransporter type 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) for the previous six months.
Method
Retrospective analysis of patients with diabetic kidney disease (DKD) initiating finerenone 10 mg/day. Demographic, clinical, and laboratory parameters were collected at baseline and one month post-treatment, including glucose, creatinine, eGFR (CKD-EPI), ACR, urea, potassium, and baseline HbA1c. Statistical analysis using SPSS v29 included descriptive statistics and comparison of pre/post-treatment values using paired t-tests or Wilcoxon test as appropriate (significance P < 0.05).
Results
Fifteen patients (53.33% male, mean age 71.8 ± 10.5 years) were analyzed. At one month (n = 15), ACR showed a significant median reduction of 58 mg/g (IQR: 19.9–492.5; P = 0.034). Potassium levels showed non-significant increases of 0.12 mEq/L. eGFR remained stable throughout the study period. Treatment discontinuation occurred in two patients (13.3%): one due to hyperkalemia and another due to treatment inefficacy.
Conclusions
Finerenone demonstrated a favorable safety profile with minimal treatment discontinuation (2/15 patients) and no significant increases in potassium levels in a real-world elderly population with advanced CKD.
• A 29.11% reduction in microalbuminuria was observed after one month of treatment, although not reaching statistical significance
(P = 0.161), in patients with diabetic kidney disease receiving standard therapy.
• Further research with larger sample sizes and extended follow-up periods is warranted to establish long-term efficacy and safety
in real-world settings.

title: #555 Stromal cell-derived factor-1, P-selectin, and advanced oxidation protein products may be associated with cerebral vessels in normoalbuminuric diabetic kidney disease
authors: Ligia Petrica; Florica Gadalean; Adrian Vlad; Livia Oana Milas; Flaviu Bob; Anca Suteanu - Simulescu; Mihaela Glavan; Lavinia Balint-Marcu; Lavinia Iancu; Silvia Ienciu; Maria Mogos-Stefan; Catalin Jianu
abstract:
Background and Aims
The kidney and the brain share similarities in terms of structure and function, and are coordinated by common pathogenic mechanisms, such as inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction. The aim of our study was to evaluate the interrelation of these pathogenic pathways with proximal tubule (PT) dysfunction, podocyte damage, and cerebral vessels remodeling in normoalbuminuric DKD in type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM) patients.
Method
A cohort of 223 patients (64 patients with normoalbuminuria, 59 patients with microalbuminuria, and 61 patients with macroalbuminuria) and 39 age- and gender-matched healthy controls were enrolled in this case series study. All patients were assessed concerning urinary albumin/creatinine ratio (UACR), biomarkers of podocyte damage (synaptopodin, podocalyxin) and of proximal tubule dysfunction (kidney injury molecule-1-KIM-1, N-acetyl-β-(D)-glucosaminidase-NAG), serum and urinary stromal cell-derived factor-1 (SDF-1), P-selectin, advanced oxidation protein products (AOPPs).
MtDNA-CN and nuclear DNA (nDNA) were quantified in peripheral blood and urine by qRT-PCR (ABI 7900-HT–Applied BioSystem). TaqMan assays were utilized for the assessment of cytochrome b (CYTB) gene, subunit 2 of NADH dehydrogenase (ND2), and of beta 2 microglobulin nuclear gene (B2M). mtDNA-CN was defined as the ratio of the number of mtDNA/nDNA copies, through analysis of the CYTB/B2M and ND2/B2M ratio.
The cerebrovascular hemodynamic indices were evaluated by an ultrasound equipment with high resolution (MYLAB 8-ESAOTE Italy) equipped with a colour ultrasound system. Subclinical atherosclerosis and arteriosclerosis were assessed by intima-media thickness (IMT) in the common carotid arteries (CCAs), the pulsatility index (PI) and the resistivity index (RI) in the internal carotid arteries (ICAs) and middle cerebral arteries (MCAs), bilaterally. Cerebrovascular reactivity (CVR), which represents the vasodilatory reactivity of cerebral vessels in response to a vasodilatory stimulus, was assessed by the breath-holding test and the breath-holding index (BHI).
Results
In multivariable regression analysis, serum mtDNA correlated directly with eGFR and negatively with serum P-selectin and serum SDF-1 (R2 = 0.6564; P < 0.0001). Urinary mtDNA correlated directly with podocalyxin, urinary P-selectin, and urinary SDF-1 (R2 = 0.6280; P < 0.0001). IMT-CCAs correlated negatively with eGFR and directly with UACR, synaptopodin, serum P-selectin, and serum AOPPs (P < 0.0001; R2 = 0.7020). PI-ICAs correlated indirectly with eGFR and directly with serum P-selectin and serum SDF-1 (P < 0.0001; R2 = 0.5113). PI-MCAs had a negative correlation with eGFR and direct correlations serum P-selectin and serum SDF-1(P < 0.0001; R2 = 0.5886). RI-ICAs was included in a complex model which displayed an indirect correlation with eGFR and direct correlations with NAG, serum P-selectin, serum SDF-1, and UACR (P < 0.0001; R2 = 0.7629). RI-MCAs were included in a model which showed a negative correlation with eGFR and direct correlations with NAG, KIM-1, synaptopodin, podocalyxin, serum P-selectin and serum SDF-1 (P < 0.0001; R2 = 0.8482). The CVR the BHI correlated negatively with eGFR and directly with podocalyxin, serum P-selectin, and serum SDF-1 (P < 0.0001; R2 = 0.7897).
Conclusion
The study demonstrates a concurrent association of SDF-1, P-selectin, AOPPs, and mitochondrial dysfunction with early DKD and significant cerebrovascular modifications in neurologically asymptomatic patients with type 2 DM and normoalbuminuric DKD.

title: #3569 Early clinical experience of finerenone in patient with chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes in real Life. Comparison with FIDELITY pooled
authors: Sara Aladro; Fátima Baptista García; Ivan Chamorro; Noemí Esparza Martín; Selene González Nuez; Saulo Jesús Fernández Granados; José María Medina Gil; Yaiza María Rivero Viera; Ksenia Zhvakina Gavrilova; Ester Domenech; Mario Galvan; César García Cantón
abstract:
Background and Aims
Finerenone is a novel non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) that has been shown to improve renal outcomes in patients with diabetic kidney disease (DKD), as demonstrated in FIGARO and FIDELIO-DKD trials. Our purpose is to describe finerenone used, compare with FIDELITY pooled patients (FIGARO + FIDELIO-DKD), and analyze the impact of finerenone in a short follow-up.
Method
A descriptive, observational, prospective study including patients with DKD who initiated finerenone between May 2024 and January 2025. Demographic data, clinical characteristics, laboratory parameters, echocardiographic findings, and treatment history were analyzed. A subanalysis was conducted to evaluate the impact of finerenone in patients with at least four months of follow-up.
Results

title: #1415 Role of ACE2 in the prediction of preeclampsia
authors: Cristina Amorós Robles; Onia Franquet; Isabel Galcerán; Marta Crespo; Marta Riera; Anna Oliveras; Susana Vazquez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Preeclampsia is a multisystemic disorder of pregnancy or postpartum and is the leading cause of maternal-perinatal morbidity and mortality. Various potential predictive factors for the development of preeclampsia have been widely investigated. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) may play a pathophysiological role that has been underexplored. The aim of this study is to evaluate different components of the RAAS, including angiotensin-converting enzyme-2 (ACE2), as predictors of preeclampsia during the first trimester of pregnancy.
Method
This was a prospective observational study involving 144 pregnant women evaluated during the first trimester of pregnancy at Hospital del Mar (Barcelona). Two cohorts were identified: cohort I—normotensive pregnant women (n = 124, 86.1%) and cohort II—pregnant women with chronic hypertension (n = 20, 13.9%).
The occurrence of preeclampsia was observed. RAAS parameters were assessed throughout pregnancy, including circulating enzymatic activity of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) and ACE2.
Results
The incidence of preeclampsia in cohorts I and II was 6.4% and 55%, respectively. Pregnant women in cohort I who developed preeclampsia showed higher ACE2 activity compared to those with a normal pregnancy (mean [95% CI]: 18.3 RFU/µL/h [6.5–27.1] vs. 11.3 RFU/µL/h [4.55–29.6]; P = 0.015). In cohort II, ACE2 activity levels (preeclampsia vs. no preeclampsia) were 13.2 RFU/µL/h [6.8–27] vs. 12.3 RFU/µL/h [9.3–21.4], respectively; P = 0.884. Other RAAS components, including plasma aldosterone, plasma renin activity (PRA), and ACE, showed no statistically significant differences between those who developed preeclampsia and those who did not in either cohort.
Regarding ACE2 in cohort I, its predictive ability for preeclampsia was assessed, yielding a cutoff point of 14.28 RFU/µL/h (area under the ROC curve of 0.76 [95% CI: 0.59–0.92]).
Conclusion
ACE2 enzymatic activity measured during the first trimester in normotensive pregnant women is a good early predictor of preeclampsia, allowing for the implementation of appropriate preventive measures.

title: #2562 Oxidative status in chronic kidney disease. Effect of dialysis and kidney transplantation
authors: Gemma Valera Arévalo; Maria del Mar Rodriguez San Pedro; Maria Gabriela Ortiz-Diaz; Andrea Figuer Rubio; Celia Aranda-Cuervo; Natalia Guerra-Pérez; Paula Jara Caro Espada; Claudia Yuste; Manuel Ramírez Chamond; Matilde Alique; Enrique Morales Ruiz; Julia María Carracedo Añón
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is associated with a REDOX imbalance, with increased reactive oxygen species (ROS), increased prooxidant enzyme activity and decreased antioxidant enzyme activity due to a state of chronic inflammation, the accumulation of uremic toxins or the effect of renal replacement techniques (haemodialysis (HD) and peritoneal dialysis (PD)). The treatment of choice for CKD is renal transplantation (TX). Oxidative stress has been proposed as one of the precursors to the increased incidence of cardiovascular disease in CKD. The aim of the study is to analyze the REDOX status in different stages and treatments of CKD.
Method
Cross-sectional study of 156 patients (40 chronic kidney disease (ACKD), 40 HD, 36 PD and 40 TX) and 18 healthy subjects (CT). Levels of prooxidant parameters (xanthine oxidase (XO), lipid peroxidation products (malondialdehyde (MDA)/lipid peroxidation reactive substances (TBARS)) and oxidised glutathione (GSSG) were analyzed by colorimetry. Levels of antioxidant parameters (glutathione peroxidase (GPx), superoxide dismutase (SOD) and reduced glutathione (GSH)) were analyzed by colorimetry. Prooxidant and antioxidant parameters were analyzed in plasma isolated from peripheral blood, and mononuclear leukocytes (MN) and polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMN) isolated by Ficoll gradient. The oxidative stress level of each participant was determined using an individualized OXY-SCORE. Statistical analyses were performed with SPSS 21.0.
Results
In plasma XO levels are higher in PD and TX (P = 0.000). TBARS levels are higher in ACKD, HD, PD and TX related to CT (P = 0.0144, P = 0.0079, P = 0.000 and P = 0.000). SOD levels are higher in TX related to CT, ACKD, HD and PD (P = 0.000), while GPx levels are lower in ACKD and HD with respect to CT (P = 0.0164 and P = 0.0122) as well as higher in TX (P = 0.000). GSH levels are lower in HD and PD with respect to CT (P = 0.000). In MN XO levels are lower in HD (P = 0.000). MDA levels are higher in TX (P = 0.000). SOD levels are lower in ACKD and PD with respect to CT (P = 0.03 and P = 0.004) and are higher in TX with respect to ACKD and PD (P = 0.000). GPx levels are elevated in TX (P = 0.000). GSSG levels are higher in HD, PD and TX compared to CT and ACKD (P = 0.000), while GSH levels are lower in ACKD compared to CT (P = 0.0128) and are higher in TX compared to the rest of the groups (P = 0.000). In PMN there is a higher amount of XO in ACKD (P = 0.000). SOD levels are higher in TX (P = 0.0134 vs CT, P = 0.0027 vs ACKD and P = 0.0003 vs PD). GPx levels are higher in TX compared to CT and HD (P = 0.000). GSSG levels are higher in ACKD and HD compared to CT (P = 0.000 and P = 0.003). GSSG levels are also higher in TX compared to CT, ACKD, HD and PD (P = 0.000). GSH levels are elevated in HD with respect to CT and ACKD (P = 0.003 and P = 0.000). The GSSG/GSH ratio is higher in ACKD with respect to the other groups (P = 0.000 vs CT, P = 0.0018 vs HD and P = 0.032 vs PD). When evaluating the REDOX status of patients based on the OXYSCORE, ACKD and HD subjects had a higher OXYSCORE compared to CT (P = 0.000 and P = 0.000), showing PD and TX patients a similar OXYSCORE to CT (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
ACKD and HD subjects have a high OXYSCORE, which is evidence of increased oxidative stress. In PD and TX subjects, although they have elevated levels of pro-oxidant parameters, OXYSCORE levels are similar to those of CT, which could indicate a greater REDOX balance. The study of REDOX status in CKD patients can provide information on the cardiovascular risk of each subject.

title: #1582 Clinical performance of the new plasma filter PX2 in therapeutic plasma exchange: an interventional multicenter study
authors: Jana Schmitt; Christine Gillen; Ansgar Erlenkötter; Lena Rauber; Anja Derlet-Savoia; Manuela Stauss-Grabo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) is a procedure within the field of therapeutic apheresis, and as such, it follows the recommendations set forth by the American Society for Apheresis (ASFA) (Connelly Smith et al., 2023). TPE is an extracorporeal blood purification technique designed to remove high molecular weight substances, such as immunoglobulins and pro-inflammatory factors. It is primarily indicated for diseases associated with increased concentrations of plasma components and where a rapid depletion of these molecules mitigates or halts a pathogenic process. Additionally, the use of fresh frozen plasma as plasma substitute allows for the replacement of large amounts of deficient plasma components (e.g. ADAMTS 13 in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)). To achieve the desired clinical outcome, the ASFA Guidelines recommends an exchange equivalent to 1.0 to 1.5 times the plasma volume (PV) for the majority of diseases. It is assumed that this corresponds to a removal of 63%–72% of the initial plasma constituents.
The study (NCT06382675) is an interventional, single-arm study aimed at evaluating the clinical performance and safety of the new plasma filter PX2 (developed by Fresenius Medical Care in Bad Homburg, Germany) for use in extracorporeal blood purification during plasmapheresis therapy. Preclinical studies have already demonstrated the filter's excellent hemocompatibility.
Method
In total, 230 therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) treatments, will be conducted, with a targeted plasma volume exchange ranging from 0.7 to 2.0, according to clinical routine practice. The evaluation will focus on several key aspects, such as the actual delivered treatment dose, the sieving coefficients of various plasma constituents (e.g. albumin, IgG, IgM, LDL-C) and the occurrence of potential complications, including hemolysis, clotting, or clogging of the filter. Blood and filtrate samples will be collected at multiple time points—before, after every 0.5 PV processed, and at the end of the treatment.
The performance benchmark—defined as achieved absolute plasma separation volume in comparison to planned plasma separation volume—will be used to analyze if the new filter will be able to deliver the treatment dose. This benchmark will be used to analyze whether the new filter can effectively deliver the required treatment dose and thus the expected clinical outcome.
The sample size was calculated to achieve sufficient power to demonstrate that the mean success rate (completion of prescribed PV per treatment) using the new plasma filter PX2 is at least 75%. Key assumptions included a mean success rate of 85%, an alpha level of 2.5%, and a power of 90%. An exact binomial test was used, assuming independent and binomially distributed data, resulting in a required sample size of 172. However, assuming that each TPE treatment is independent of the others is a strong assumption. Therefore, in addition to the primary endpoint, the data will be analyzed using a generalized mixed model with repeated measurements and patients as a random effect. To account for potential discrepancies, as well as treatment discontinuations unrelated to the filter, the sample size will be increased by 15% and 10%, respectively.
Results
The study is designed to clinically evaluate the PX2 plasma filter under in vivo condition in respect to sieving coefficients and safety. Additionally, the impact of patient-related factors on the success of TPE treatment (in terms of delivered treatment dose) will be evaluated through subgroup analyses. The findings from these subgroup analyses will be presented using descriptive statistics.
Conclusion
The study aims to assess the clinical performance and safety of a newly developed plasma filter. Moreover, the study intends to broaden the knowledge about patient factors influencing the treatment success.

title: #3375 The alternative pathway of the renin angiotensin aldosterone system is overactivated in severe COVID-19 at baseline
authors: Irene Martínez Díaz; Jordi Vilardell; Sara Núñez-Delgado; Pablo García de Frutos; José Tomas Ortiz; Antonio Cano Cámara; Carmen Llorens Cebrià; Albert Morales; Conxita Jacobs Cachá; Maria José Soler Romeo
abstract:
Background and Aims
The angiotensin converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) is a key factor for maintaining the balance in the renin-angiotensin system (RAAS). In addition, it is the main cell entry receptor for SARS-CoV-2 virus. For this reason, we hypothesize that increased soluble ACE2 (sACE2), due to the viral entry, could be related to a dysregulation of the RAAS in COVID-19 patients. This dysregulation could have an impact on COVID-19 severity or in the associated complications like pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE). Our study, aims to evaluate if COVID-19 produces a RAAS dysregulation and, if so, whether it could be related to the disease severity.
Method
During 2020 we collected serum samples of a cohort (n = 2100) of COVID-19 patients at admission that we classified according to disease severity considering severe patients those who required intensive care unit (ICU) admission during hospitalization or died because of COVID-19. We analyzed the circulating ACE2 activity using a fluorescent enzymatic assay. To study the RAAS state, we selected a subgroup of patients to perform a RAAS fingerprint by analyzing the levels of Ang I, II, III, IV, 1–5 and 1–7 in serum by mass spectrometry. The groups selected for this substudy were: (I) patients who did not require ICU admission (n = 20); (II) patients who required ICU admission (n = 18), and (III) patients who required ICU admission and presented a PTE event during hospitalization (n = 23). A propensity score matching was performed to match the patients considering sex, age, comorbidities and RAAS blockers treatment.
Results
Circulating ACE2 activity was significantly increased at admission in severe COVID-19 patients as compared to non-severe patients [0.94 ± 0.99 (0.00, 6.73); 0.58 ± 0.51 (−0.02, 7.27), P < 0.001, respectively]. Patients who required ICU admission (independently to PTE presence) had decreased levels of Angiotensin I, II, III and IV compared to those who had better COVID-19 progression suggesting an increased consumption of angiotensinogen in severe COVID-19 patients (Fig. 1). No differences were found in the case of angiotensin 1–5, and 1–7 peptides. Additionally, surrogate markers of ACE activity (ACE-S), ACE2 activity (ALT-S: Ang 1–5 + Ang 1–7)/(Ang II + Ang 1–7 + Ang I + Ang III + Ang IV) and renin activity (PRA-S: Ang I + Ang II) were calculated. In this case, we found that ALT-S was increased in the patients that required ICU (group II and III) as compared to non-severe patients (group I). Contrarily, renin activity surrogate (PRA-S) was decreased in groups II and III as compared to group I. We did not find differences in the case of ACE-S. These results indicate that severe patients had more activation of the RAAS alternative pathway in the first moments of the infection. These results support our previous conclusions that circulating ACE2 activity is involved in COVID-19 severity. Finally, we also measured the aldosterone levels and the aldosterone/angiotensin II (AA2) ratio to investigate the adrenal response. Patients who developed a PTE had increased levels of aldosterone and AA2 ratio, probably related to an increased adrenal response that would promote thromboembolic events.
Conclusion
The RAAS alternative pathway at baseline was increased in patients who developed severe COVID-19. This dysregulation seems not to be related to further complications during COVID-19 progression as it was similar in all ICU patients independently to the presence of PTE. Aldosterone and increased AA2 ratio was basally increased in those patients that required ICU and developed PTE as compared to the other 2 groups possibly due to a basal increased adrenal response.

title: #1595 Global trends and adverse events of SGLT2 inhibitor use in acute kidney disease
authors: Chih-Ning Chen; Jui-Yi Chen; Vin-Cent Wu
abstract:
Background and Aims
The 2024 KDIGO guidelines advocate the prescription of sodium-glucose cotransporter inhibitor (SGLT2i) in individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD), given their benefits in alleviating CKD progression and extensive cardiovascular outcomes. Nevertheless, current evidence for the administration of SGLT2i in patients with acute kidney disease (AKD) remains unsettled. Following acute kidney injury (AKI), AKD is a critical period marked by heightened vulnerability to further renal and cardiovascular events. Given the potential of SGLT2i to ameliorate chronic kidney damage, their application in AKD has generated significant interest. However, the safety and prescription patterns of SGLT2i in patients recovering from AKI are less well understood. This study aims to address this gap by examining global trends in SGLT2i prescriptions among AKD patients, evaluating both short- and long-term adverse events.
Method
This study was conducted using the TriNetX Research Network. A total of 128,867,568 individuals were screened between January 1, 2013, and December 31, 2023. AKD was defined as the cessation of previously acute dialysis within 3 months after hospital discharge. In this intention-to-treat analysis, SGLT2i users were identified based on prescriptions issued during the AKD period. The primary outcome focused on the prescription trend of SGLT2i within 3 months after discharge in patients with AKD throughout the years. Secondary outcomes pivot on factors associated with SGLT2i prescription in this population. Regarding potential adverse events of SGLT2i administration, we looked into the incidence rates of urinary tract infection, volume depletion, hypotension, AKI, diabetic ketoacidosis, hypoglycemia and foot ulcers within 3 to 6 months after prescription as well as femur or hip fracture and amputation of lower limbs within 6 months to 2 years after prescription.
Results
A total of 1,252,126 patients diagnosed with AKD between 2013 and 2023 were included in which 1.99% of patients (n = 24,934) were recognized as SGLT2i users. Sixty-three percent of those were male with a mean age of 67 years (standard deviation [SD], 13.3). Comorbidity rates of essential hypertension (90% vs 70%), heart failure (74% vs 28%), hyperlipidemia (82% vs 49%) and ischemic heart disease (73% vs 37%) were significantly higher in SGLT2i users than non-users.
The prescription rate of SGLT2i from 2013 to 2023 increased consistently in patients with AKD (0.09% to 4.04%). This trend was particularly pronounced in those with diabetes, especially type 2 (0.39% to 12.69%). The rates of prescription for patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus increased sharply after 2016, while that for type 1 diabetes mellitus also saw a steady rise, though to a lesser extent. In contrast, the prescription rates for AKD patients without diabetes had a more dramatic increase after 2020 (0.01% to 2.00%).
Multivariable logistic regression showed patients with heart failure (odds ratio [OR] 3.96, p-value <0.001), ischemic heart disease (OR 1.53, p-value <0.001) and hyperlipidemia (OR 1.51, p-value <0.001) were more likely to receive SGLT2i prescription during the AKD period.
With respect to the adverse events, incidence rates of urinary tract infection (p-value = 0.014), hypotension (p-value = 0.009), hypoglycemia (p-value = 0.01) and AKI (p-value = 0.023) significantly decreased in SGLT2i users over the study period. Comparing patients with type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus prescribed with an SGLT2i, a significant reduction in the incidence rate of diabetic ketoacidosis (p-value = 0.009) was observed in the former, while a significant reduction in that of hypoglycemia (p-value = 0.008) was reported in the latter.
Conclusion
From 2013 to 2023, the prescription rate of SGLT2i in patients with AKD had significantly risen, regardless of diabetes mellitus status. Patients with concurrent cardiovascular diseases were more likely to be prescribed with an SGLT2i during the AKD period. Incidence rates of previously worrisome short- and long-term adverse events after SGLT2i administration decreased through the years.

title: #2950 Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) in critically ill patients: a nationwide analysis from DaVita Brazil
authors: Bruno Zawadzki; Fernanda Coelho; Marcelo Lopes; Rogerio Da Hora; Alline Alves; Bruno Tokuda; Elber Barbosa; Elicivaldo Juvencio; Florisvaldo Lira; Guilherme Santa Catharina; Luis Pinto
abstract:
Background and Aims
Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) plays a crucial role in the management of acute kidney injury (AKI) in critically ill patients, particularly in intensive care units (ICUs). Variability in access, catheter management, and anticoagulation strategies impacts treatment efficacy and patient outcomes. DaVita Brazil provides CRRT services in more than 300 hospitals across the country, supporting both public (SUS) and private sector patients. This study aims to analyze the operational, clinical, and regional characteristics of CRRT patients between 2023 and 2024, comparing trends with international benchmarks when available.
Methods
A retrospective observational study was conducted using data from the DaVita Brazil hospital dialysis network from January 2023 to December 2024. The study included all patients undergoing CRRT during hospitalization. Key variables analyzed included: CRRT utilization (total number of sessions, treatment duration, and downtime rates), filter patency (percentage of sessions achieving ≥60h filter lifespan), catheter utilization (type of vascular access, reasons for catheter replacement, and site of insertion), anticoagulation strategy (use of citrate anticoagulation and absence of dialysate manipulation), clinical outcomes (mortality rates, early discontinuation (<24h), and treatment interruptions) and regional variability (differences in CRRT access and outcomes across hospital networks). When applicable, comparisons were made with global data sources, including the ERA Registry 2022 and the ISN Global Kidney Health Atlas 2023.
Results
A total of 3,744 patients underwent CRRT across 2023 and 2024, with the following findings:
1. CRRT Utilization and Filter Patency
• 22,411 sessions were conducted.
• More than 90% of sessions achieved a filter lifespan ≥60h, ensuring sustained therapy efficiency.
• 100% of therapies used regional citrate anticoagulation, without manipulation of dialysate composition.
2. Catheter Utilization and Management
• 1,614 vascular catheters were implanted for CRRT initiation by DaVita nephrologists.
• Reasons for catheter replacement were low blood flow (30.5%), mechanical obstruction (24.6%), medical decision (21.8%), signs of
infection (12.9%) and bleeding (1.3%)
• Site of catheter insertion were right internal jugular vein (39.4%), right femoral vein (22.9%), internal left jugular vein (16.4%) and
subclavian and other sites (1.9%).
3. Clinical Outcomes
• Early discontinuation (<24h) occurred in 11.7% of cases, primarily due to rapid hemodynamic deterioration.
• Overall CRRT mortality was 34.8%, consistent with international benchmarks for critically ill patients requiring continuous dialysis.
• Early mortality (<24h post-initiation) was 23.4%, highlighting the severity of underlying conditions.
• ICU mortality with CRRT remained within global standards (∼35-40%, as reported in the ERA Registry 2022).
4. Regional Variability
• Highest CRRT utilization: Southeast (31.2%) and Northeast (28.4%) regions.
• Lowest CRRT access: North region (1.8%), reflecting disparities in advanced nephrology services.
Conclusion
DaVita Brazil's CRRT program demonstrates high adherence to international best practices, particularly in catheter management, filter patency, and anticoagulation strategy. The exclusive use of citrate anticoagulation and high filter lifespan (≥60h in over 90% of cases) align with global standards, contributing to stable treatment delivery. However, regional disparities persist, with limited access to CRRT in the North and Midwest regions. Expanding CRRT availability in underserved areas and optimizing catheter management protocols remain key priorities. Further studies are needed to evaluate long-term renal recovery and ICU survival trends among CRRT patients in Brazil.

title: #2940 Demographic and clinical profile of hospitalized patients requiring dialysis: insights from the DaVita Brazil Hospital service 2023–2024
authors: Bruno Zawadzki; Fernanda Coelho; Marcelo Lopes; Rogerio Da Hora; Elicivaldo Juvencio; Guilherme Santa Catharina; Luis Pinto; Florisvaldo Lira; Alline Alves; Elber Barbosa; Bruno Tokuda
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) are leading causes of hospitalization, often requiring renal replacement therapy (RRT). DaVita Brazil provides hospital-based dialysis services across more than 300 hospitals, serving both public (SUS) and private-sector patients. This study examines the demographic and clinical characteristics of hospitalized dialysis patients, evaluates trends from 2023 to 2024, and benchmarks findings against international data.
Methods
A retrospective observational study analyzed DaVita Brazil's hospital dialysis network data from January 2023 to December 2024, focusing on: Patients undergoing hemodialysis (HD), hemodiafiltration (HDF), continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), or peritoneal dialysis (PD) during hospitalization. Variables analyzed were: age, gender, regional distribution, dialysis modality use (HD, HDF, CRRT, PD), trends between 2023 and 2024 and regional differences in hospital dialysis access. Patients categorized by primary renal diagnosis: AKI (IRA—new-onset acute kidney injury requiring dialysis), CKD 5D (DRC 5D – pre-existing dialysis patients requiring hospitalization), CKD-A (DRC A – CKD patients experiencing acute worsening), CKD Stable (IRC—hospitalized CKD patients requiring dialysis without acute deterioration). Comparisons were made with international benchmarks (ERA Registry 2022, ISN Global Kidney Health Atlas 2023) when applicable.
Results
A total of 55,766 hospitalized dialysis patients were analyzed over two years.
1. Demographics:
• Gender: 52.3% male, 47.7% female.
• Age distribution: <18 years: 1.8%, 18–30 years: 2.8%, 30–45 years: 8.6%, 45–60 years: 19.4%, 60–80 years: 46.5%, >80 years: 20.2%. The mean age: 63.4 years (SD ± 11.5).
2. Clinical Diagnosis:
• AKI (IRA): 43.8% (most frequent cause of hospital dialysis).
• CKD 5D (DRC 5D): 26.2% (pre-existing dialysis patients).
• CKD-A (DRC A): 20.3% (CKD patients with acute deterioration).
• CKD Stable (IRC): 14.2% (hospitalized CKD patients requiring dialysis but without acute worsening).
3. Dialysis Modality Use:
• HD dominated hospital dialysis (85.2%).
• CRRT use was 5.5%, below global ICU standards (∼10%).
• PD was rarely used (0.6%).
• These findings are consistent with global trends, as the ERA Registry 2022 reports similar AKI prevalence (∼40%–45%) in hospitalized dialysis patients.
4. Regional Disparities:
• Northeast Brazil had the highest hospital dialysis volume (34.9%), followed by São Paulo (29.4%) and the Southeast (21.7%). The North had the lowest case volume (1.8%), reflecting nephrology care access limitations. Public health system (SUS) patients represented 48.8%, while private-sector patients accounted for 51.2%.
5. Trends from 2023 to 2024 were hospital dialysis cases rose by 8.1%, AKI (IRA) cases increased from 42.5% to 45.1%, reinforcing the rising burden of acute kidney injury, CRRT use expanded from 4.8% to 5.7%, indicating better ICU nephrology care. The North and Midwest continued to show the lowest dialysis service availability.
Conclusion
The DaVita Brazil hospital dialysis program provides key insights into the epidemiology of hospitalized dialysis patients. AKI remains the primary driver of hospital dialysis needs, aligning with global data. 26.2% of patients were already on chronic dialysis (CKD 5D) before admission. HD dominates as the primary dialysis modality, while CRRT use remains lower than global ICU standards. Significant regional disparities exist, with the Northeast and São Paulo hosting the highest dialysis volumes, while the North faces the greatest access limitations. This study underscores the need for improved access to nephrology services in underserved regions and better integration of hospital-based dialysis with outpatient CKD management.
Future research should focus on patient outcomes, mortality trends, and healthcare strategies to optimize hospital-based dialysis care in Brazil.
