title: #2507 SALL1 is essential for histone H3K27 methyltransferase EZH2 to regulates apoptotic responses in renal ischemia/reperfusion injury
authors: Shuqin Mei; Cheng Xue; Zhiguo Mao
abstract:
Background and Aims
The role of histone methylation modifications in renal disease, particularly in ischemia/reperfusion-induced acute kidney injury (AKI), remains unclear. This study aims to investigate the potential involvement of the histone methyltransferase zeste homolog 2 (EZH2) in ischemia/reperfusion-induced AKI and its impact on apoptosis.
Method
We first examined the expression of EZH2 in the kidney of ischemia/reperfusion-induced AKI mice and hypoxia-stimulated tubular epithelial cells. We next constructed the EZH2 knockout mice to further confirm the effects of EZH2 on apoptosis response in AKI. Subsequently, we constructed the EZH2 knocked-down cells again and performed Chromatin Immunoprecipitation sequencing to screen out the target genes regulated by EZH2 and the enrichment pathway. Then we confirmed the EZH2 target gene and its regulatory pathway in vivo and in vitro experiments.
Results
The study found that EZH2 was upregulated in ischemia/reperfusion-induced AKI and that silencing EZH2 could reduce renal tubular injury by decreasing apoptosis response of tubular epithelial cells. Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing and polymerase chain reaction identified SALL1 as a target of EZH2. EZH2 was found to be enriched on the promoter of SALL1. Silencing EZH2 resulted in a significant increase in the transcriptional level of SALL1 and activation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. The study further reversed the effects of EZH2 silencing by silencing SALL1 or administering the Wnt/β-catenin inhibitor icg001. It was also found that SALL1 positively regulated the expression of Wnt/β-catenin pathway-related genes. Finally, the study showed that the EZH2 inhibitor GSK-126 significantly alleviated ischemia/reperfusion-induced AKI.
Conclusion
Our results indicate that silencing EZH2 can protect renal function by relieving transcriptional inhibition of SALL1, activating the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, and attenuating tubular epithelial apoptosis response. These results highlight the potential therapeutic value of targeting EZH2 in ischemia/reperfusion-induced AKI.

title: #1769 Neutrophils protect against Staphylococcus aureus -induced kidney injury in part through the release of neutrophil extracellular traps
authors: Caroline Martens; Jered Myslinski; Mathias Stroobants; Anne Long; Marleen Lox; Carrie Philips; Farooq Syed; Thomas Vanassche; Peter Verhamme; Takashi Hato; Pierre Dagher; Kimberly Martinod
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sepsis is the most frequent cause of acute kidney injury (AKI) in the intensive care unit. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) sepsis is particularly nefarious, with the kidney frequently affected leading to AKI or chronic complications. Whereas sepsis-associated AKI is often attributed to hemodynamic changes and toxic insults, small cohort studies show increased infiltration of neutrophils and macrophages in post-mortem kidney tissue from sepsis patients. Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are extracellular DNA strands released from activated neutrophils. Their formation is mediated through the activity of the protein citrullinating enzyme peptidylarginine deiminase 4 (PAD4). NETs have been shown to contribute to antibacterial defense in the kidney, but may also propagate thrombosis and vascular dysfunction in the renal microvasculature. We aimed to gain mechanistic insights into the roles of neutrophils and NET release in MRSA-induced kidney injury.
Method
Wild-type (WT), LysM-GFP (myelomonocytic reporter mice), MRP8Cre+PAD4fl/fl (NET-defective), or PAD4fl/fl (NET-proficient) mice were injected with MRSA (laboratory strain USA300). Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) was used to induce neutrophilia and prime for NET release prior to MRSA injection. Blood samples were collected to measure creatinine. Kidneys were harvested to visualize structural abnormalities (hematoxylin and eosin stain), bacterial invasion (Gram stain), collagen content (Masson's Trichrome stain), myelomonocytic cells (LysM-GFP), and Padi4 gene expression (RNAscope). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was used to assess glomerular structure. Local RNA levels of KIM-1 (kidney injury molecule 1) and NGAL (neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin) were measured using quantitative reverse transcription PCR analyses. Detailed cellular profiling was performed using isolated nuclei from snap-frozen kidneys to perform single-nucleus RNA sequencing and single-cell suspensions for deep immunophenotyping in both kidneys and spleens using spectral flow cytometry.
Results
MRSA induced abscess and tubular cast formation in kidneys from WT mice, resulting in profound renal fibrosis. Whereas local levels of KIM-1 and NGAL were elevated in MRSA-infected mice as compared with controls (P < 0.001 for both), creatinine levels were not significantly different (P = 0.073). SEM revealed a normal glomerular structure. Myelomonocytic reporter mice showed predominant infiltration of neutrophils and macrophages inside abscesses. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing revealed a heterogeneous set of neutrophils with only a small subset expressing Padi4. RNAscope showed that these Padi4 expressing cells were located at the outer region of abscesses. In the spleen, MRSA induced extramedullary hematopoiesis. Interestingly, G-CSF administration prior to MRSA infection protected against disease severity and mortality. Compared with vehicle-injected controls, G-CSF-treated WT mice showed increased neutrophil numbers prior to sepsis induction and more pronounced neutrophilia following MRSA infection. G-CSF-treated WT mice showed lower levels of creatinine as compared with vehicle-injected controls (P = 0.017), less infiltration of MRSA through the kidney, better bacterial containment in the renal papilla and lack of abscess formation along with an increase in CCR2+ macrophages in the kidney. Interestingly, G-CSF-treated NET-defective mice showed higher levels of creatinine following MRSA infection than similarly treated NET-proficient controls (P = 0.010). NET-defective neutrophils did not entirely constrain bacteria in the renal papilla, thus impacting the dissemination of MRSA throughout the kidney. Recruitment of CD11b+ myeloid cells was impaired in kidneys from NET-defective mice.
Conclusion
Administration of G-CSF protects against MRSA-induced AKI in mice, which is partially mediated through NET release impacting bacterial containment and immune cell recruitment to the kidney. These data may inform future clinical applications targeting neutrophils to protect the kidney.

Wild-type (WT), LysM-GFP (myelomonocytic reporter mice), MRP8Cre+PAD4fl/fl (NET-defective), or PAD4fl/fl (NET-proficient) mice were injected with MRSA (laboratory strain USA300). Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) was used to induce neutrophilia and prime for NET release prior to MRSA injection. Blood samples were collected to measure creatinine. Kidneys were harvested to visualize structural abnormalities (hematoxylin and eosin stain), bacterial invasion (Gram stain), collagen content (Masson's Trichrome stain), myelomonocytic cells (LysM-GFP), and Padi4 gene expression (RNAscope). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was used to assess glomerular structure. Local RNA levels of KIM-1 (kidney injury molecule 1) and NGAL (neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin) were measured using quantitative reverse transcription PCR analyses. Detailed cellular profiling was performed using isolated nuclei from snap-frozen kidneys to perform single-nucleus RNA sequencing and single-cell suspensions for deep immunophenotyping in both kidneys and spleens using spectral flow cytometry.
Results
MRSA induced abscess and tubular cast formation in kidneys from WT mice, resulting in profound renal fibrosis. Whereas local levels of KIM-1 and NGAL were elevated in MRSA-infected mice as compared with controls (P < 0.001 for both), creatinine levels were not significantly different (P = 0.073). SEM revealed a normal glomerular structure. Myelomonocytic reporter mice showed predominant infiltration of neutrophils and macrophages inside abscesses. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing revealed a heterogeneous set of neutrophils with only a small subset expressing Padi4. RNAscope showed that these Padi4 expressing cells were located at the outer region of abscesses. In the spleen, MRSA induced extramedullary hematopoiesis. Interestingly, G-CSF administration prior to MRSA infection protected against disease severity and mortality. Compared with vehicle-injected controls, G-CSF-treated WT mice showed increased neutrophil numbers prior to sepsis induction and more pronounced neutrophilia following MRSA infection. Interestingly, G-CSF-treated NET-defective mice showed higher levels of creatinine following MRSA infection than similarly treated NET-proficient controls (P = 0.010). NET-defective neutrophils did not entirely constrain bacteria in the renal papilla, thus impacting the dissemination of MRSA throughout the kidney. Recruitment of CD11b+ myeloid cells was impaired in kidneys from NET-defective mice.
Conclusion
Administration of G-CSF protects against MRSA-induced AKI in mice, which is partially mediated through NET release impacting bacterial containment and immune cell recruitment to the kidney. These data may inform future clinical applications targeting neutrophils to protect the kidney.

title: #2880 Results of the COVID-19 patients treated with the Seraph® 100 Microbind® Affinity filter (COSA) registry
authors: Julius J Schmidt; Jan T Kielstein
abstract:
Background and Aims
The COVID-19 pandemic has had serious health and economic consequences worldwide. Several extracorporeal treatments have been evaluated for their potential to improve the clinical course and outcome of critically ill patients with COVID-19. The Seraph® 100 Microbind® Affinity Adsorber (Exthera Medical, CA, USA) has been introduced for the removal of various pathogens from the blood and has been granted emergency approval by the FDA for patients with COVID-19. Bacteria, viruses (including the SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein), fungi and toxins have been shown to bind to the immobilized heparin on the ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene beads of the device in a manner similar to the interaction with heparan sulphate on the cell surface and are thus removed from the bloodstream. Because of these properties, the Seraph® 100 was used in COVID-19 patients. Here we report the results of the COVID-19 patients treated with the Seraph® 100 Microbind® Affinity Filter (COSA) registry. The aim of the registry was to collect data on the safety and feasibility of the Seraph® 100 in the treatment of COVID-19 patients.
Method
Participating sites were encouraged to enter patient data of COVID-19 patients treated with the Seraph® 100 during their hospital stay into the COSA registry (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04361500) without reimbursement. Patient characteristics and outcome parameters were documented in a web-based platform.
Results
117 patients with 142 treatment sessions from 13 different hospitals were reported to the registry (Table 1). The overall mortality rate was 44% and the time from ICU admission to treatment with the Seraph 100 was significantly longer in patients who did not survive (2 vs. 4.5 days, P = 0.0083). Most patients were treated in the ICU (88%) and invasive ventilation was required in 67.5% of enrolled patients. The most commonly used anticoagulation strategy was heparin-based. (72.5%), but the device was also used with regional citrate anticoagulation (Fig. 1). The median treatment time with the adsorber was 6 hours and most patients (85.2%) were treated with a single (reported) treatment session. Adverse events were reported in 12 treatments (mostly minor) and 11 coagulation events were reported.
Conclusion
This multi-centre registry provides insight into the treatment experience with a novel pathogen adsorber. The reported uses of the Seraph® 100 showed a variety of treatment modalities (haemoperfusion as well as in conjunction with renal replacement therapy), which were generally well tolerated. Many reported treatments lasted longer than 4 hours, which was the treatment duration in the CE mark study of the device. However, in vitro data suggest a prolonged pathogen adsorption capacity of the Seraph® 100.
Reported patients surviving 30 days after treatment were treated earlier in their ICU course. SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA was frequently detected in the blood of critically ill COVID-19 patients early in their ICU course and correlated with disease severity. In vitro data show that the Seraph® 100 can bind to the viral spike protein and that pro-inflammatory cytokines can be reduced by the device. Therefore, the use of the Seraph® 100 in critically ill patients shortly after ICU admission may be useful. However, these uncontrolled registry data cannot provide conclusive evidence of treatment efficacy. Prospective clinical data are needed to describe the potential benefits of the Seraph® 100 in the treatment of critically ill COVID-19 patients.

title: #2560 Acute kidney injury associated with immune-checkpoint inhibitors in cancer patients: a single centre retrospective study
authors: Jyothirmaye Kuppa; Nitesh Rao; Rajiv Juneja; Caroline Milton
abstract:
Background and Aims
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are a novel class of immunotherapy that has become widely prescribed in recent years, significantly improving cancer prognosis. However, these benefits are sometimes accompanied by immune-related adverse effects (IRAEs), including acute kidney injury (AKI). The purpose of this retrospective observational study is to examine and summarise the rates of AKI related to ICI (ICI-AKI) and their outcomes, at Flinders Medical Centre, South Australia.
Method
Patients who received anti-PD-1/PDL1/CTLA4 antibody therapy at Flinders Medical Centre between January 2020 and January 2023 were enrolled. Patients were excluded if they were on dialysis, had a renal transplant, or did not have bloods post ICI therapy. Basic demographic data including patient characteristics, immunotherapy agent, number of cycles, and renal function were collected from patient records, and the incidence of AKI was determined. AKI was defined as an increase in serum creatinine ≥2× from baseline or requirement of renal replacement therapy; or an increase in serum creatinine ≥1.5× from baseline and at least one of the following: acute tubulointerstitial nephritis on renal biopsy; ICI therapy held for at least 1 cycle or delayed due to concern for ICI-AKI; or treatment with corticosteroids due to suspected ICI-AKI, within 12 months post last cycle of ICI. The AKI cohort were divided into AKI attributed to ICI (ICI-AKI), and AKI due to other/unclear causes, based on examining patient records. ICI-AKI was determined based on evidence in patient records of delayed or discontinued ICI due to suspicion of ICI-AKI, renal biopsy suggestive of tubulointerstitial nephritis, or treatment with corticosteroids due to concern for ICI-AKI. Further data was collected from the ICI-AKI population including concomitant chemotherapy, serial laboratory values up to 12 months, renal biopsy, treatment with steroids, ICI rechallenge and AKI recurrence. Renal recovery was assessed and defined as return of serum creatinine to within 25% of baseline levels.
Results
A total of 578 patients were included. Among them, 73 cases (12.6%) developed an AKI, with only 14 episodes (2.4%) attributed to ICI-AKI, involving 11 patients. The remaining cases were due to pre-renal, obstructive, or unknown causes, with no clear evidence of ICI contributing to the AKI. The mean age of ICI-AKI cohort was 70 years, with 6 males and 5 females. The mean baseline creatinine was 101.6 µmol/L (eGFR 62.4 ml/min/1.73 m2) while the mean creatinine at AKI onset was 257 µmol/L (eGFR 29.2 ml/min/1.73 m2). 3 patients had dual immunotherapy with PDL1/CTLA4, 7 PDL1 alone and 1 CTLA4 alone. The time to AKI onset after the last ICI cycle ranged between 1–12 cycles, with a mean of 4.3 cycles. 45% of patients had concomitant chemotherapy, all of which included a platinum agent. 3 patients had concomitant PPI use. 8 out of 11 patients were treated with corticosteroids, and only 2 had pulse methylprednisolone. Renal biopsy was performed in 4 patients, and pathology confirmed tubulointerstitial nephritis in all. 4 patients were rechallenged with immunotherapy following the initial diagnosis, out of which only 1 patient had recurrence in AKI. Only 1 patient needed renal replacement therapy. Only 3 patients had renal recovery.
Conclusion
In our cohort, AKI occurred at a notable frequency in patients treated with ICIs. However, reassuringly, the rates of AKI attributed to ICI requiring discontinuation were lower than those reported in previous studies.

title: #561 Acute kidney injury in acute heart failure patients undergoing aggressive diuresis and its impact on short term outcome
authors: Anil Jhajhria; Manisha Dassi; Neeru Agarwal; Saurabh Gupta; Shipra Choudhary
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute heart failure (AHF) patients treated with diuretics often develop worsening of renal functions with resultant acute kidney injury (AKI) during hospitalization. This AKI could be a result of either renal tubular injury or simply indicate a hemodynamic or functional change in glomerular filtration.
Method
100 AHF patients who underwent aggressive diuresis were included (excluding patients requiring inotropic support or haemodialysis). Urine NGAL was measured on the day of admission and after 72 hours. Serum creatinine levels were measured on day of admission, at 48 hours and at 72 hours post admission. AKI was defined as per KDIGO clinical practice guidelines as increase in serum creatinine by 0.3 mg/dL or more within 48 hours or urine output less than 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours. All patients were contacted at 30 days from the day of admission and reviewed regarding requirement of readmission/mortality. All patients who developed AKI during the study by day 3 got their creatinine checked again at day 30 from the day of admission.
Results
Mean eGFR of patients was 48.1 ml/min/m2. Mean NT-proBNP was 11000 pg/ml. Mean LVEF was 43.65%, with 38% patients having HFrEF and 62% patients had HFpEF (LVEF >40%). Of total 100 patients, 37 (37%) developed AKI. Rise in NGAL from day 0 to day 3 was noted in 34 (34%) cases. There was no correlation found between rising creatinine levels and rising NGAL levels (including patients with AKI). Mean NT-proBNP was higher in patients with AKI as compared to those without AKI (p-value = 0.048). Of 37 AKI patients, 10 (27%) patients had creatinine value at day 30 higher than at day 3, while 27 (73%) patients had creatinine value at day 30 lower than at day 3. 30 patients required readmission within 30 days after discharge; 5 patients expired by day 30 (from start of study). Occurrence of AKI did not show association with readmission within 30 days or with mortality at 30 days.
Conclusion
AKI occurred in 37% patients with AHF undergoing aggressive diuresis in our study (Table 20, Fig. 18). This AKI had no correlation with serial NGAL levels (tubular injury biomarker) but was associated with an elevated baseline NT-proBNP levels (Table 21, Fig. 19). Furthermore, 73% AKI patients showed improvement in creatinine levels by day 30 post discharge (Table 25, Fig. 23) & occurrence of AKI did not affect short term morbidity (readmission at 30 days) and mortality at 30 days (Table 26, Fig. 24). This implies that AKI in the setting of AHF & aggressive diuresis is mild, mainly functional/hemodynamic and should not affect decisions with decongestive therapy.

title: #070 The impact of an acute kidney injury service on patient outcomes at a large district general hospital in the United Kingdom
authors: Shelagh Bickerton; Emilia Sobczyk; Katie Harris; Lauren Catchpole; Chantal Owens; Manivarma Kamalnathan; Shashidhar Cherukuri
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is one of the major complications of the acutely unwell, which carries a significant risk of mortality and morbidity, and is associated with long hospital stays and substantial healthcare costs.
Local and national audit data in 2019 showed that our 950-bedded district general hospital was an outlier for AKI mortality and length of stay (LOS) and highlighted severe follow-up deficits, despite the existence of an on-call renal consultant. In response a structured approach was taken to provide AKI leadership with an ambition to improve safety and outcomes for this vulnerable group of patients. In September 2020, an AKI consultant, Lead Nurse for AKI and a team of AKI clinical nurse specialists were appointed, creating a service which covers seven days a week. The goals we identified for AKI care delivery were prompt AKI recognition and expert intervention, simultaneously providing support and education to patients and across the clinical specialties, in order to prevent further deterioration and to foster early recovery. We have put a large focus on post discharge follow-up so that care extends beyond the hospital walls into the community. We have created a monthly cardiorenal meeting to discuss this challenging sub-group of patients, working closely with our heart failure colleagues to ensure collaborative input. Finally, we have also developed an AKI ‘hot-clinic’ which serves to see community-acquired AKI patients, negating the need for admission if clinically well whist being able to investigate and treat in a timely and appropriate manner.
Our aim is to assess the impact our AKI service has had on patient outcomes, as detailed below.
Method
A retrospective study, data was gathered on all patients who presented to the hospital with AKI stages 2 and 3 over a twelve-month period 2023–2024 and outcome data such as LOS, need for renal replacement therapy, mortality associated with AKI and readmission rates were determined and compared with pre-AKI service data, where available, or the national average.
Results
There were 2039 patients with AKI stages 2 and 3 during the period under review. Median LOS was 8.9 days, which is a 19.1% improvement from 2021 figure of 11 days, and is 25.8% below the current national median LOS of 12 days (UK Renal Registry, 2022). Inpatient mortality associated with AKI was 31%, perhaps reflecting a local population with a high chronic disease burden and was largely in line with national figures.
6% of patients required renal replacement therapy during their admission with only 3% still being dialysis-dependent at 90 days. When examining the impact of AKI on long term kidney health it showed that 27.5% of patients developed/had progression of CKD, compared to 30% shown in research data.
All-cause readmission rate at 30 days post discharge following AKI was 19%, similar to that highlighted in UKRR data, 2022. Cardiac re-admission rate at 90 days was only 0.8% whilst 90-day readmission rates with any-cause AKI was only 10% compared to a 25% readmission rate recorded in UKKR data, demonstrating the effectiveness of our comprehensive AKI follow-up service. Indeed, 100% of all suitable patients received AKI follow-up, a significant improvement from 50% in our pre-AKI service era.
Conclusion
There is little published data on AKI outcomes either nationally or internationally making comparison a challenge. Our data collection tool is, we believe, one of the most comprehensive and detailed tools to date, which we hope can be used to benchmark against and be used to tailor improvements.
The introduction of a dedicated AKI service has led to improvement in patient outcomes, especially in LOS and readmission rates. Not only does this indicate significant cost savings in a cash-strapped national health service, but it helps to free up potential bed capacity in the midst of unending pressure on acute hospital beds. Patients are robustly safety-netted and healthcare staff are supported and educated to deliver the best outcomes for this patient cohort. Expansion of the service is now needed to provide community outreach support with a focus of AKI prevention.

title: #1688 Reducing the incidence and severity of acute kidney injury in people with ileostomies—a nurse-led trifecta approach in a district general hospital in the United Kingdom
authors: Shelagh Bickerton; Lauren Catchpole; Katie Harris; Emilia Sobczyk; Chantal Owens; Joanna Ryder; Rajbinder Khunkun
abstract:
Background and Aims
Having an ileostomy is an independent risk factor for the development of acute kidney injury (AKI) due to an increased risk of dehydration. 30%–50% of people with ileostomies will develop high output at some point, 20% of which require hospital admission due to severe dehydration. 25% will develop chronic kidney disease within two years of stoma formation. Having a stoma can cause significant body images issues and, with high output, can affect self confidence and cause social isolation.
Colorectal clinical nurse specialists (CNSs) are often the first port of call for patients with stoma issues so it was vital that the approach to reducing incidence and severity of high output/AKI was a collaborative one between the Colorectal and AKI CNSs.
Method
This abstract outlines work being done to try to address this issue, using a three-pronged approach:
(1) Development of assessment tool for Colorectal CNSs to triage patients for intervention in the event of a high output ileostomy (HOI).
(2) Improving in-patient care for patients presenting with HOI by extending current national guidelines to include renal-protective measures.
(3) Development of a patient information leaflet to improve knowledge and self-management of stoma output and strategies to maintain kidney health.
Results
The HOI assessment tool is now being used at five acute NHS trusts across the UK as well as one community stoma nurse group. Feedback has been excellent with users stating that it gives them confidence and a framework to formally assess patients and safety net and escalate patients where indicated. Preliminary data of own-trust use indicates the tool has reliability but more formal validity testing is required which we hope to undertake in the near future. It has been used for 12 months in Wolverhampton.
Improving in-patient care for patients with HOI has been extended from current national guidelines to include renal protective measures. This consists of a bundle of care which addresses care in the first 24 hours, then on-going care as an in-patient with high output, and then finally post discharge follow-up. The guideline is based on best evidence/national guidelines from renal, acute medical and surgical fields, in order to provide a holistic and comprehensive approach to this specific patient cohort. Data has been collected on incidence and outcomes; 56 patients admitted with AKI stages 2 or 3 were caused or complicated by a HOI in a 12-month period resulting in 849 bed days. Only 53.6% of patients were back to their baseline renal function at 90 days demonstrating the long-term impact of high output on kidney health. It illustrates the need for prevention of high output, and this has been the focus of the patient information leaflet.
This leaflet has been developed in association with the Ileostomy Association (IA) and has engaged with service users to ensure it is clear and practical. It has been endorsed by UK Kidney Association and Association of Nephrology Nurses UK and is used widely nationally by both renal/AKI teams as well as colorectal services to support this patient group. Patient feedback through the IA has been very positive with recipients reporting an increase in understanding and confidence in self-management and knowing when and how to seek help.
Conclusion
Having an ileostomy increases the risk of developing AKI and therefore chronic kidney disease and its associated complications. A comprehensive approach has been taken to prevent renal disease through patient/carer education and support, as well as a close partnership between the colorectal and AKI CNSs to ensure a holistic approach. In-patient care has been enhanced by extending current guidelines which look at management through a renal lens. All of these measures have increased clinician confidence and ensures a robust safety net for this patient group. Promotion of self-care and management of stoma output will foster patient independence and confidence and help to allay some of the psychological issues related to having a stoma.

Background and Aims
Having an ileostomy is an independent risk factor for the development of acute kidney injury (AKI) due to an increased risk of dehydration. 30%–50% of people with ileostomies will develop high output at some point, 20% of which require hospital admission due to severe dehydration. 25% will develop chronic kidney disease within two years of stoma formation. Colorectal clinical nurse specialists (CNSs) are often the first port of call for patients with stoma issues so it was vital that the approach to reducing incidence and severity of high output/AKI was a collaborative one between the Colorectal and AKI CNSs.

This abstract outlines work being done to try to address this issue, using a three-pronged approach:

The HOI assessment tool is now being used at five acute NHS trusts across the UK as well as one community stoma nurse group. title: #1592 Impact of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors on outcomes in patients with type 1 diabetes with acute kidney disease
authors: Chung-An Wang; Jui-Yi Chen; Vincent Wu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT-2is) have shown significant benefits in improving cardiovascular and kidney outcomes, primarily in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and acute kidney disease (AKD). This study evaluated the association between SGLT-2 is use and cardiorenal outcomes in type 1 diabetes (T1D) patients with AKD.
Method
We included patients aged 18 years or older with T1D who could wean from acute dialysis and were discharged from hospitals between January 1, 2012, and April 1, 2024 from TriNetX network. SGLT-2i users were compared to non-users following one-to-one propensity score matching (PSM). Primary outcomes included all-cause mortality, major adverse kidney events (MAKEs), and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs).
Results
A total of 614 patients (3.74%) with T1D (mean [SD] age: 61.1 [13.6] years, 275 [44.8%] male) were SGLT-2i users during the AKD period, matched with their counterparts (mean [SD] age: 61.5 [15.6] years, 294 [47.9%] male). After a mean follow-up of 1.7 years, SGLT-2i users were associated with a lower risk of all-cause mortality (6.4% vs. 15.6%; adjusted hazard ratio [aHR]: 0.49, P < 0.001) and MAKEs (4.9% vs. 10.8%; aHR: 0.53 P = 0.003) compared with non-users. The E-value for mortality (3.54) and MAKEs (3.19) showed limited unmeasured bias. However, no significant reduction was observed for MACEs. The risk of genital infections and volume depletion were higher among SGLT-2i users, but no differences were found in the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis, urinary tract infections, or hypoglycemia.
Conclusion
In this study, SGLT-2i users was associated with improved kidney outcomes and reduced all-cause mortality in patients with T1D and AKD. These findings underscore the potential of SGLT-2is as adjunctive treatment to enhance renal recovery and survival in T1D population, although the pronounced cardiovascular benefits or complication were less evident.

title: #452 Plasma extracellular cold-inducible RNA-binding protein (eCIRP) is associated with acute kidney injury in patients after cardiac arrest
authors: Astrid Ruyant; Sandrine Lemoine; Delphine Baetz; Fitsum Guebre-Egziabher; Guillaume Monneret; Fabienne Venet; Thomas Bochaton; Laurent Argaud; Martin Cour; Maxime Schleef
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a predictor of mortality after a resuscitated cardiac arrest (CA). We aimed to evaluate plasma extracellular cold-induced RNA-binding protein (eCIRP), a pro-inflammatory alarmin released in metabolic stress situations, in predicting AKI after CA.
Method
We retrospectively analyzed data of patients prospectively followed-up after their admission to a tertiary hospital following CA. eCIRP levels were assessed using ELISA on frozen plasma samples from admission to day 3. We considered the maximum eCIRP value within the first 24 h (eCIRPmax) for subsequent statistical analyses.
Results
We included 153 patients with a median age of 64 years and 91 (59%) were male. The mortality rate was 77%, and AKI occurred in 47% of the patients. Plasma eCIRP was higher in patients who developed AKI (diagnosed after day 1) than in those who did not, regardless of the timing of measurement from admission to day 3, or when using eCIRPmax (Fig. 1A). Plasma eCIRPmax was higher in patients who died than in survivors (Fig. 1B). The AUC of the ROC curve for eCIRPmax in diagnosing AKI was 0.745 (95% CI 0.651–0.840; Fig. 1C). In multiple regression analyses, plasma eCIRPmax remained associated with AKI when accounting for covariates related to patient demographics (Model 1; P < 0.001), admission severity (Model 2; P = 0.018), CA characteristics (Model 3; P < 0.001), or all of them (Model 1 + 2 + 3; P = 0.006).
Conclusion
Plasma eCIRP measured in the first 24 h after CA is an independent predictor of AKI and has promising value as a biomarker.

title: #2253 Urinary CXCL9 and renal outcome in acute kidney injury
authors: Ashok Kumar Yadav; Jaskiran Kaur; Vivek Kumar
abstract:
Background and Aims
C-X-C motif ligand 9 (CXCL9) is a chemokine that primarily attracts activated T lymphocyte and regulates immune response. Levels of CXCL-9 were 5.5 times higher in patients with acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) compared to other acute kidney injury causes suggesting a promising biomarker to identify AIN in patients with AKI. However, CXCL-9 has been studied as diagnostic marker for AIN, its role in predicting renal outcome after the hospital discharge remains unclear. We aimed to identify the association between urine CXCL-9 at the time of discharge and renal outcome in patients with AKI.
Method
In this prospective observational study, stable patients of either sex, aged between 18-70 years, and diagnosed with community acquired AKI were enrolled at the time of hospital discharge. Patients with underlying CKD, obstructive uropathy, Glomerulonephritis, decompensated chronic liver failure, malignancy or heart failure were excluded. The patients were followed at 4th months after hospital discharge to assess the outcome (recovery and non-recovery). Renal non-recovery was defined as eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2. Levels of urinary CXCL9 was analysed by commercially available ELISA kit. We analysed the association of urine CXCL-9/creatinine with renal non-recovery using logistics regression analysis with adjustment for age, sex, hospitalization duration, requirement of dialysis during admission, discharge creatinine and uPCR. Non-normally distributed continuous variables includes urine CXCL-9/creatinine (ng/g) and urine protein creatinine ratio (uPCR) (mg/g) and discharge creatinine were standardized log transformed for logistics regression analysis.
Results
A total 291 patients were enrolled. Out of 291 patients, 218 (75%) patients had complete renal recovery from CA-AKI whereas 73 (25%) patients had not recovered completely with persistent eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2. Mean age of study participants was 37 ± 15 years and 53% were male. The levels of serum creatinine and uPCR were significantly higher in renal non-recovery group at the time of discharge (5.04 ± 2.17 mg/dL versus 3.4 ± 2.5 mg/dL, P < 0.001 and 1318 (649, 5187) mg/g versus 305 (134, 786) mg/g, P < 0.001) as compared to renal recovery group. At 4th month follow up, eGFR was significantly low in renal non-recovery group (26.4 (14.2, 41.0) mL/min/1.73 m2 versus 101.8 (82.0, 118.7) mL/min/1.73 m2, P < 0.001) when compared with renal recovery group. Urine CXCL-9/creatinine was significantly higher in patients who did not recover from AKI [7301 (1971, 20800) ng/g versus 1305 (471, 3956) ng/g, P < 0.0001] (Fig. 1). Urine CXCL-9/creatinine were significantly associated with renal non recovery in univariate (OR 1.69, 95% CI: 1.42–2.05, P < 0.001) as well as multivariate analysis (OR:1.42, 95% CI:1.15–1.76, P < 0.001) adjusted with age, hospitalization duration, dialysis requirement during admission, discharge creatinine and uPCR. The multivariable logistic model incorporating selected parameters demonstrated a ROC-AUC of 0.88 (95% CI 0.78–0.89), significantly outperforming individual predictors: urine CXCL-9/creatinine (AUC 0.73, 95% CI 0.66–0.80), discharge serum creatinine (AUC 0.71, 95% CI 0.65–0.77), and discharge uPCR (AUC 0.78, 95% CI 0.73–0.84) (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
Urine levels of CXCL-6 at the time of hospital discharge may serve a prognosis biomarker for renal non recovery and progression to CKD either alone or in multivariable model.

title: #2800 Demographic variations in acute kidney injury risk during hot weather: a nationwide case-crossover analysis of a million AKI alerts
authors: Nithin Bodapati; Shakoor Hajat; Anna Casula; Retha Steenkamp; Tom Gray; Zoe Plummer; Dorothea Nitsch
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a critical global health issue, with an estimated incidence of 21% in adults and 33% in children during hospital episodes. In England, AKI incidence is rising, with approximately 13,000 cases per million population annually with mortality reaching 35% for AKI stage 3. Seasonal variations in AKI are well-documented, with heat related dehydration playing a key role, particularly in the elderly and frail populations. In the UK, the prevalence of kidney disease is varied and influenced by a range of demographic factors. However, research on ethnic differences in heat-related AKI remains limited. This study investigates the impact of rising temperatures on AKI incidence, emphasizing ethnic variability and the risks among hospitalized patients. As weather extremes become frequent due to climate change, identifying vulnerable groups is essential to inform public health interventions.
Method
AKI episodes during the warm months (April–September) in England from 2017 to 2021 were identified using the AKI alerts (severity graded as per the KDIGO criteria) reported to the UK renal registry. Each AKI episode, defined as one or more alerts within a 30-day period was linked to localised daily maximum temperatures using the HadUK-Grid dataset from the Met office and hospital admissions using the HES (Hospital Episode Statistics) data. A bidirectional, time-stratified case-crossover design was used to assess acute associations between temperature and AKI episodes occurring throughout the warm months. With the case-crossover design, each case is represented by temperatures on and around the day of the AKI episode, and controls by temperatures on nearby day implicitly controlling for the confounding factors. Distributed lag non-linear models were used to evaluate non-linear and delayed effects of temperature on AKI. Odds ratios were calculated for temperatures above the minimum morbidity temperature, and the attributable fraction of AKI episodes due to high temperatures was estimated.
Results
A total of 947,342 AKI episodes were analysed, of which 66% were community-acquired AKI. With each 1°C rise above 25°C, the overall Odds ratio (OR) of an AKI episode was 1.038 (95% CI 1.036–1.040). The odds of AKI stage 3 are higher with OR of 1.047 (95% CI 1.039–1.055) compared to AKI stages 1 and 2.
As shown in Fig. 1, patients admitted to the hospital with delirium had the highest risk with an OR of 1.061 (95% CI 1.029–1.094), followed by respiratory diseases, OR of 1.044 (95% CI 1.037–1.052). Surprisingly, cancer related admission had the lowest OR 1.018 (95% CI 1.009–1.027) followed by OR of 1.020 (95% CI 1.001–1.040) in those with diabetes mellitus. Cardiovascular patients had an intermediate odds ratio of 1.035 (95% CI 1.029–1.042) in the subsets analysed.
Males had a significantly higher risk of AKI with OR of 1.041 (95% CI 1.037–1.044) compared to females. In people of White ethnicity, those in lower socioeconomic deciles had higher risk of AKI compared to the higher deciles.
Table 1 shows that Chinese ethnicity was the most sensitive with an odds ratio of 1.054 increased risk of AKI (95% CI 1.012–1.098) per 1°C rise compared to OR of 1.041 (95% CI 1.038–1.043) in White population. Other ethnicities were comparatively less affected, with Indians having an increased OR of 1.033 (95% CI 1.019–1.047) and Pakistani/Bangladeshi individuals having an OR of 1.027 (95% CI 1.011–1.044). African and Caribbean people had the lowest OR of 1.001 (95% CI 0.98–1.021) and 1.024 (95% CI 1.005–1.042) respectively. This trend was consistent across all age groups although less pronounced in people above 65 years.
Conclusion
This study highlights the complex relationship between weather, ethnicity and AKI risk and identifies the various demographic factors and comorbidities that could lead to AKI. Policymakers should consider measures such as weather alerts, sick-day drug guidance, public awareness on hydration during hot spells to reduce AKI incidence. Global efforts to improve climate resilience are necessary in addressing both the immediate and long-term impacts of climate change on kidney health.

title: #656 Epidemiology and mortality risk factors for cirrhosis—associated—acute kidney injury
authors: Carmen Bogeanu; Daniela Radulescu; Ileana Adela Vacaroiu; Elena Stepan; Flavia Liliana Turcu; Elena Cuiban; Larisa Florina Serban Feier; Cristiana David; Daiana Brehui-Bertea
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with liver cirrhosis (LC) have increased risk for acute kidney injury (AKI) that, in turn, is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Recognizing the common causes of AKI in cirrhosis and prompt diagnosis and treatment are important for improving outcomes. The aims of our study were to analyze the epidemiology of non-hepatorenal syndrome-AKI in patients with cirrhosis and to describe the factors associated with risk of in-hospital death.
Method
Adult patients admitted in the hospital during the year 2024 and discharged with concomitant AKI and cirrhosis diagnosis were included in the study. Both AKI and acute-on-chronic kidney disease cases were considered eligible. Patients discharged with hepatorenal syndrome were excluded. Also, maintenance dialysis patients with LC, patients with LC and stable chronic kidney disease (CKD) and postrenal AKI cases were excluded.
Factors related to the patients, cirrhosis and AKI and also to evolution during hospitalization were collected, analyzed and compared between survivors and deceased patients. In statistic analysis, P < 0.05 was considered significant.
Results
75 patients were included in this 1-year study. Characteristics of study group are presented in Table 1. Male gender and alcohol-associated cirrhosis prevailed and Child-Pugh class C cirrhosis was the most frequent present. AKI and acute-on-chronic kidney disease had similar incidence. Classification of AKI into prerenal and intrinsic was done according to the most severe etiology. Hypovolemia—secondary to fluid loss or to gastrointestinal bleeding—was the main cause of AKI (58 cases), followed by drug-related direct toxicity or allergy (20 cases) and by sepsis (17 cases). In 36 patients, AKI had multifactorial etiology. There was no relation between KDIGO stage of AKI and Child-Pugh cirrhosis class and neither between type of AKI (prerenal versus intrinsic) and Child-Pugh cirrhosis class (chi-square-test, P > 0.05). Recovery of renal function in survivors was complete in 34.09%, but only partial in 61.36% of cases.
31 patients (41.33%) died during hospitalization. Deceased patients were significantly younger, the majority had advanced cirrhosis and had significantly more often history of chronic heart failure (P < 0.05; Table 2). There was a higher prevalence of previous CKD in survivors (P = 0.0381); no differences were found regarding the other comorbidities. Among laboratory data at admission, lower serum albumin, lower sodium and higher C-reactive protein were associated with increased risk of death (Table 2); other parameters were not significantly different between deceased patients and survivors. Regarding AKI-related factors, we observed that intrinsic AKI and higher KDIGO-AKI stage were significantly more present in deceased patients compared with survivors (Table 2). Occurrence of MODS (multiple organ dysfunction syndrome) and ICU (intensive care unit) admission were noted almost exclusively in patients who died during hospitalization.
Conclusion
AKI superimposed on cirrhosis is frequently associated with incomplete renal recovery and increased risk of death. Lower serum albumin, lower sodium and higher C-reactive protein at hospital admission are associated with increased in-hospital mortality. Hypovolemia and medications are the most common causes of AKI in patients with cirrhosis and they are potentially reversible, therefore close monitoring of the patients must become a routine in clinical practice.

In 36 patients, AKI had multifactorial etiology. There was no relation between KDIGO stage of AKI and Child-Pugh cirrhosis class and neither between type of AKI (prerenal versus intrinsic) and Child-Pugh cirrhosis class (chi-square-test, P > 0.05). Recovery of renal function in survivors was complete in 34.09%, but only partial in 61.36% of cases.
31 patients (41.33%) died during hospitalization. Deceased patients were significantly younger, the majority had advanced cirrhosis and had significantly more often history of chronic heart failure (P < 0.05; Table 2). There was a higher prevalence of previous CKD in survivors (P = 0.0381); no differences were found regarding the other comorbidities. Among laboratory data at admission, lower serum albumin, lower sodium and higher C-reactive protein were associated with increased risk of death (Table 2); other parameters were not significantly different between deceased patients and survivors. Regarding AKI-related factors, we observed that intrinsic AKI and higher KDIGO-AKI stage were significantly more present in deceased patients compared with survivors (Table 2). Occurrence of MODS (multiple organ dysfunction syndrome) and ICU (intensive care unit) admission were noted almost exclusively in patients who died during hospitalization.
Conclusion
AKI superimposed on cirrhosis is frequently associated with incomplete renal recovery and increased risk of death. Lower serum albumin, lower sodium and higher C-reactive protein at hospital admission are associated with increased in-hospital mortality. Hypovolemia and medications are the most common causes of AKI in patients with cirrhosis and they are potentially reversible, therefore close monitoring of the patients must become a routine in clinical practice.

title: #2099 Teneligliptin alleviates acute kidney injury by exerting anti-ferroptotic effects on renal tubules
authors: Chiemi Ema; Takamasa Iwakura; Kuuya Okazaki; Hideo Yasuda
abstract:
Background and Aims
Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors have been shown to mitigate various types of acute kidney injury (AKI) in animal models [1–3]. Additionally, our previous research suggests that DPP-4 inhibitors may reduce cisplatin-induced AKI in humans [4]. However, the precise mechanisms underlying their renoprotective effects remain unclear. Recent studies have indicated that DPP-4 inhibition can prevent ferroptosis—an iron-dependent form of cell death—in experimental colon cancer cell lines [5]. Given that AKI primarily results from tubular cell death, we hypothesized that DPP-4 inhibitors may alleviate AKI by preventing tubular ferroptosis.”
Method
We investigated the renoprotective effects of DPP-4 inhibitors by orally administering teneligliptin (TG), a DPP-4 inhibitor, to mice and inducing AKI using folic acid and glycerol, which are established models where ferroptosis has been reported to play a role [6, 7]. In vitro experiments were conducted using human tubular epithelial cells (HK-2). Cell death was induced using erastin, a known ferroptosis inducer, as well as folic acid and myoglobin, to correspond with the animal experiments. To determine whether folic acid- and myoglobin-induced cell death is ferroptosis-dependent, we employed a ferroptosis inhibitor (Fer-1), an apoptosis inhibitor (z-VAD), and a necroptosis inhibitor (Nec-1s). Cell viability was assessed using the MTT assay and calcein/PI staining.
Results
In animal studies, TG attenuated both folic acid-induced [Fig. 1A and B] and rhabdomyolysis-induced [Fig. 1C and D] AKI. In vitro, TG reduced folic acid- and myoglobin-induced cell death in HK-2 cells. The ferroptosis inhibitor Fer-1 effectively inhibited folic acid- and myoglobin-induced cell death [Fig. 2A and B], whereas the apoptosis inhibitor z-VAD and the necroptosis inhibitor Nec-1s had no significant effect. Furthermore, TG inhibited erastin-induced cell death [Fig. 2C], indicating that its renoprotective effects are likely mediated through an anti-ferroptotic mechanism in tubular cells.
Conclusion
Our study demonstrates that the DPP-4 inhibitor TG provides renoprotective effects against folic acid- and rhabdomyolysis-induced AKI by inhibiting ferroptosis in renal tubular cells. The findings suggest that TG reduces tubular cell death by specifically targeting ferroptotic pathways, as evidenced by its effectiveness in suppressing erastin-induced cell death and the lack of effect from apoptosis and necroptosis inhibitors. These results highlight the potential of TG as a therapeutic option for AKI by modulating ferroptosis-related mechanisms.

title: #1727 Kidney function associated with mortality in hantavirus infection: a cohort study in BRAZIL
authors: Jeff Murilo Silva de Castro; Da Silva Raoni de Oliveira Domingues; Renan Gomes Mendes Diniz; Mota Ramalho Janaína de Almeida; Taina Veras de Sandes Freitas; Geraldo Bezerra Da Silva; Elizabeth De Francesco Daher
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hantavirus infection is a severe zoonotic disease characterized by high mortality, especially when complicated by cardiopulmonary syndrome. Despite its clinical significance, the role of kidney injury in prognosis and its association with mortality remains poorly understood. This study aimed to investigate the impact of kidney function and other risk factors on mortality in hantavirus infection.
Method
This was a retrospective cohort study that included adult patients with a confirmed diagnosis of hantavirus infection recorded between 2012 and 2023 in Brazil, where hantavirus is endemic. Sociodemographic and clinical data were obtained in January 2025 from DataSUS, the public health database of the Brazilian healthcare public system (SUS). Patients with unconfirmed diagnoses or incomplete records were excluded. Kidney injury was considered if creatinine exceeded the reference value according to age and sex. Patients were divided into groups based on kidney function: normal function (NF, n = 361) and altered function (AF, n = 311). The primary outcome evaluated was mortality.
Results
The cohort was predominantly male (77.5%) and caucasian (67.7%), with the AF group being older (38.5 ± 15.1 vs. 35.0 ± 13.3 years, P = 0.003). AF group presented with more thrombocytopenia (64.0% vs. 47.5%, P < 0.001), lymphocytic atypia (32.4% vs. 17.8%, P < 0.001) and hematocrit greater than 45% (73.4% vs. 54.1%, P < 0.001). Treatment was also more intensive among those in the AF group, requiring more respiratory support (66.3% vs. 37.1%, P < 0.001), corticoid use (44.6% vs. 36.1%, P = 0.029), vasoactive drugs (57.6% vs. 28.4%, P = 0.001) and antibiotics (87.0% vs. 75.9%, P < 0.001). The most severe form of the infection, cardiopulmonary syndrome, was also more prevalent in group AF (75.2% vs. 62.3%, P < 0.001) as well as mortality (55.9% vs. 30.7%, P < 0.001). In multivariate analysis, altered kidney function (HR = 1.34, 95% CI 1.04–1.72, P = 0.024) and hematocrit <45% (HR = 0.62, 95% CI 0.46–0.83, P = 0.001) were independently associated with mortality.
Conclusion
Altered kidney function and increased hematocrit were associated with mortality among patients with hantavirus infection. These findings underscore the importance of early recognition and management of kidney dysfunction to improve patient outcomes in this high-risk population.

title: #3343 Acute kidney injury in critical care patients in BRAZIL: a prospective cohort study
authors: Renan Gomes Mendes Diniz; Tacyano Tavares Leite; Alefe Islleyker Aguiar Santiago; Domingues Da Silva Raoni de Oliveira; Mota Ramalho Janaína de Almeida; Geraldo Bezerra Da Silva; Elizabeth De Francesco Daher
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is frequent in patients admitted to intensive care units (ICUs), being associated with prolonged hospitalization, high healthcare costs and elevated mortality rates. Among the main causes related to AKI in low/middle income countries are shock, sepsis, nephrotoxicity including contrast-induced AKI and tropical diseases. Most epidemiological studies on AKI have been conducted in low/middle income countries. In comparison, the outcomes observed in these settings differ from those in high-income countries. In Brazil, a low-middle income country, studies on the topic are limited and often retrospective, most of them with no comparison with a control group. The aim of this study was to investigate predictors of poor prognosis in critically ill patients with AKI in an ICU of a tertiary hospital in Brazil.
Method
This was a prospective cohort study, conducted in a public tertiary hospital in Brazil, with data collection from ICU-admitted patients. Patients were stratified into Group A (patients admitted with AKI or developing AKI during hospital stay) and Group B (patients without AKI). Parameters such as clinical and laboratory findings, need of advanced life support, length of stay in ICU and mortality were evaluated and compared between the groups.
Results
A total of 69 patients were analyzed, with a mean age of 52 ± 10 years, of whom 70% were female. AKI was identified in 58% of them. Concerning KDIGO stratification, 44% were classified as KDIGO 1; 30% as KDIGO 2 and 26% as KDIGO 3. Group A patients remained in the ICU for a longer period (8 [5, 8] vs. 4 [5, 18] days, P < 0.001). Sepsis was more frequent in the AKI group (68% vs. 31%; P = 0.003), as well as the need for mechanical ventilation (58% vs. 21%; P = 0.003) and emergency surgery (38% vs. 14%; P = 0.025). Group A also presented with an increased RDW (13.15% [11.90, 15.15] vs. 12.15% [11.43, 12.68], P = 0.041). Progression to death was also higher in group A (18% vs. 0%; P = 0.017).
Conclusion
AKI is still a frequently observed complication in critically ill patients and may be present at admission or develop during hospitalization. It is also associated with an increased need for advanced life support and mortality rates, prolonged hospital stays, and increased healthcare costs. Considering that AKI is an important leading cause of morbidity and mortality in ICUs, there is an urgent need for additional studies, preferably controlled and randomized, to establish more effective protocols for the prevention and management of this condition.

title: #3816 Acute kidney injury and associated factors in people living with HIV/AIDS hospitalized for disseminated histoplasmosis in a referral hospital in Brazil
authors: Matheus Alves de Lima Mota; Geraldo Bezerra Da Silva; Gdayllon Meneses; Jacó Ricarte Lima de Mesquita; Marcos MacIel Sousa; João Victor Monteiro Souza; Renan Gomes Mendes Diniz; Mota Ramalho Janaína de Almeida; Paulo Germano de Carvalho; Jéssica Maria de Sousa Oliveira; Júlia Lemos Lima Verde; Elizabeth De Francesco Daher
abstract:
Background and Aims
Disseminated histoplasmosis (DH) is a common opportunistic infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum in people living with HIV/AIDS (PLWHA) in endemic areas, causing 5%–15% of AIDS-related deaths. HIV infection is associated with acute kidney injury (AKI) due to drug nephrotoxicity, HIV-associated nephropathy, and deposition of immune complexes. Black race, family history of nephropathy, low CD4+ T lymphocyte (CD4) count, high viral load (VL), Hepatitis B and C, advanced age, and smoking increase this risk. Common causes of AKI in PLWHA are prerenal causes, acute tubular necrosis, and drug nephrotoxicity. São José Hospital for Infectious Diseases (HSJ) is a reference hospital in Fortaleza, the capital of the state of Ceará, in northeastern Brazil, an endemic region of DH. This study aims to describe the prevalence of AKI and associated factors in PLWHA with DH.
Method
This retrospective observational study evaluated clinical, epidemiological, and laboratory aspects in PLWHA with DH at HSJ from March 2023 to May 2024. Inclusion criteria were PLWHA aged 18 years or older with DH, excluding those with chronic kidney disease (CKD). AKI and CKD definitions followed Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guidelines. Categorical variables were presented as counts and relative frequencies in percentages. Chi-square tests were used to assess the association between categorical variables. Continuous variables were first evaluated for normality using the Shapiro-Wilk test and by analyzing Q-Q plots, histograms, and dispersion measures. Variables considered normally distributed were presented as mean ± standard deviation, while non-normally distributed variables were reported as median and interquartile range. Student's t-test was used for normally distributed data, and the Mann-Whitney test for non-normally distributed data, with a significance level of P < 0.05. The analysis was conducted using R software (v4.3.1; R Core Team, 2021). The study was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee of HSJ (Process Number 60380022.0.0000.5044).
Results
Sixty-one patients were initially included in the study, but three with pre-existing CKD were excluded. Among the 58 remaining patients, the average age was 40.4 + 11.3 yrs, with 79.3% being men. During hospitalization, 89.7% progressed to AKI, categorized as follows: 19.0% to Stage 1, 29.3% to Stage 2, and 41.4% to Stage 3. No statistically significant differences were found in demographics or comorbidities between the non-AKI group (NAG) and the AKI group (AG). However, patients in the NAG used antiretroviral therapy more frequently (P = 0.003). Patients in the AG had higher HIV VL (P = 0.018), while there was no difference in CD4 count between the two groups. The AG presented with more respiratory symptoms (P = 0.009) and hepatomegaly (P = 0.04) and had higher rates of diagnoses via direct microscopy in the buffy coat (BC) (P = 0.029) and peripheral blood (P = 0.016), and BC culture (P = 0.006), indicating a likely higher fungal load. Additionally, the AG exhibited more thrombocytopenia (P = 0.04), uremia (P = 0.01), elevated alanine aminotransferase (P = 0.007) and aspartate aminotransferase (P < 0.001), hypertriglyceridemia (P = 0.028), hyperbilirubinemia (P = 0.012) and increased lactate dehydrogenase (P < 0.001). They received more days of amphotericin B (AmB) lipid complex treatment (P = 0.007). Among the patients, 25.1% died, all from the AG, with 5.9% in stage 2 and 54.2% in stage 3.
Conclusion
The high prevalence of AKI in PLWHA with DH is concerning. It is crucial to identify laboratory abnormalities indicating tissue damage and their association with AKI progression. The elevated mortality in the Stage 3 subgroup underscores the need for early diagnosis, avoidance of nephrotoxic drugs, and treatment with lipid formulations of AmB, which can improve outcomes.

title: #2397 Ravulizumab in atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome: analysis of quality of life outcomes in adult and paediatric phase 3 trials
authors: David Kavanagh; Yoshitaka Miyakawa; Katherine Garlo; Masayo Ogawa; Larry A Greenbaum
abstract:
Background and Aims
Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) is a rare thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) caused by complement dysregulation. Patients with aHUS often present with acute kidney failure and have an impaired quality of life (QoL) from the symptoms they experience, and challenges associated with medical care [1, 2]. Ravulizumab is a complement C5 inhibitor approved for the treatment of aHUS and has demonstrated immediate, complete, and sustained terminal complement inhibition in clinical trials. The aim of this analysis was to assess the effect of ravulizumab on QoL in patients with aHUS.
Method
This analysis reports data from complement C5 inhibitor naive patients with aHUS in two completed phase 3, single-arm clinical trials of adult (NCT02949128) and paediatric patients (NCT03131219). Intravenous ravulizumab was administered every 4–8 weeks, depending on body weight. The two main QoL assessments were the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Fatigue (FACIT-Fatigue scale; for adult and paediatric patients) and 5-dimension 3-level EuroQol questionnaire (EQ-5D-3L; for adult patients) [3, 4]. The FACIT-Fatigue score ranges from 0 to 52 and the mean score in the general population is 44 [3]; a ≥ 3-point improvement from baseline is considered clinically meaningful (FACIT-Fatigue version 4 [patients ≥18 years]; Pediatric FACIT-Fatigue [patients <18 years]). The EQ-5D-3L is a participant-reported questionnaire that scores five dimensions: mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression, and index scores generally range from 0 to 1. Normal EQ-5D-3L population values range from 0.8 to 1.0, depending on age and country [4]. QoL measures were summarized at baseline and each post-baseline time point using descriptive statistics for continuous variables for the observed value as well as the change from baseline; an increase in either score indicates an improvement in QoL. Data were collected through the extension period of each trial, which was up to 4.5 years or at product approval/registration (whichever occurred first).
Results
Overall, 56 adults and 20 paediatric patients were included in the full analysis set. At baseline, the mean adult FACIT-Fatigue score was 24 (n = 51) and the paediatric score was 31 (n = 9). Across Days 8–71, mean FACIT-Fatigue scores generally improved; at Day 71 scores were 42 (adults; n = 50) and 48 (paediatric; n = 9). Scores were generally stable over the extension period (Fig. 1). Among adult patients, by Day 8, 63.3% (31/49) of patients had a ≥ 3-point improvement in FACIT-Fatigue score, which increased to 77.1% (n = 37/48) at Day 29, and 79.4% (n = 27/34) at Day 743. Among paediatric patients, by Day 8, 33.3% (n = 3/9) of patients had a ≥ 3-point improvement in FACIT-Fatigue score, which increased to 100% (n = 9/9) at Day 71 and then remained constant through Day 911 (7–8 patients reporting on Days 575, 743, and 911). At baseline, adult patients with available data (n = 53) had a mean EQ-5D-3L score of 0.56. From Day 29 through the extension period, mean EQ-5D-3L scores ranged between 0.8 and 0.9 (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
This analysis demonstrated that ravulizumab treatment was associated with rapid clinically meaningful improvement in QoL measures. Scores improved following ravulizumab treatment and were sustained at or near normal ranges throughout the extension period.

title: #680 Kidney injury post Covid-19—a nationwide Swedish register study
authors: Hanna Jerndal; Angele Ahelba; Sebastian Kalucza; Ioannis Katsoularis; Bernd Stegmayr; Marie Eriksson; Osvaldo Fonseca Rodriguez; Anne-Marie Fors Connolly
abstract:
Background and Aims
Covid-19 is a multiorgan disease affecting the kidney. However, the risk of kidney injury after infection remains unknown. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the risk and time of first ever diagnosed kidney injury following Covid-19, and determine the impact of Covid-19 disease severity on this risk.
Research Questions
Is the risk of a first ever kidney injury increased following Covid-19 in a nationwide Swedish whole population setting?
If so, which patients are at higher risk?
Method
The total Swedish adult population were included in the study from January 1, 2020, to July 26, 2022. Nationwide multi-registry data was used and cross-linked with Personal Identification Numbers. Data was retrieved from the Swedish Inpatient, Outpatient, Covid-19 (SmiNet), Vaccination, Intensive Care, Cancer and Cause of Death Registries. Covid-19 date (exposure) was defined as the first SARS-CoV-2 related date registered in SmiNet based on the date of symptom onset, sample date, diagnosis date or date of report. All ICD-codes (IDC9 and ICD10) used for kidney injury registered since 1987 and 2000 respectively were identified to exclude patients with previous kidney injury. Outcome was defined as all first-time events of kidney injury diagnosis (acute, non-specified and chronic) reported with ICD10 codes post Covid-19 date, during the study period. We used the Self-Controlled Case Series (SCCS) method to determine the incidence rate ratio (IRR) of kidney injury during risk periods up to 6 months after infection. In the SCCS analysis, all individuals with reported Covid-19 (exposure) and first time diagnosed kidney injury (outcome) were included. The adjusted SCCS model was used, which considers deaths in the model.
Results
Among the total 2 426 423 Covid-19 cases, there were 10 351 first kidney injury events diagnosed. In a preliminary analysis, the risk of developing kidney injury after Covid-19 was increased up to 90 days post infection with the highest IRR during the first week (day 1–7) of Covid-19 onset being 56.1 (95% CI 52.5–60). The highest risk was day 0 with nearly 200-fold increased risk, however, due to risk of selection bias (Fonseca-Rodriguez O., 2021) when including day 0, this data is excluded from the first week and should be considered with caution. The IRR was elevated for a longer time for men than for women. For women, the IRR was elevated up until 60 days post infection, compared to 90 days for men. Stratified by age groups, the IRRs were highest in the group aged 51–74 years, compared with those ≤50 years and >74 years. Individuals with higher Covid-19 disease severity were also at higher risk than those with mild infection.
Conclusion
Covid-19 is associated with an increased risk of kidney injury according to this nationwide preliminary analysis, including more than two million Covid-19 cases in Sweden. The risk of a first ever diagnosed kidney injury is elevated up to 90 days after Covid-19, which is later than previously shown. The risk was higher for men than for women and was highest for age group 51–74 years. These results highlight the importance of vaccination to prevent severe Covid-19, and if diseased by Covid-19, follow up to detect kidney injury post Covid-19.

title: #3604 Evaluating middle cut-off membranes in renal support—potential for enhanced cytokine removal
authors: Stine Koball; Adrian Dominik; Sebastian Koball; Jan Stange
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute and chronic liver failure are often associated with systemic inflammation and the accumulation of both water-soluble and albumin-bound toxins, contributing to multi-organ dysfunction, including acute kidney injury (AKI). Elevated levels of inflammatory mediators, such as IL-6 and TNF-α, have been implicated in worsening kidney function due to their role in endothelial dysfunction and hemodynamic instability.
Extracorporeal albumin dialysis employs asymmetric semipermeable membranes and ultrapure, albumin-enriched dialysate recycled through adsorbents to optimize toxin clearance. The efficiency of these systems in reducing cytokines may contribute to improved renal outcomes.
Using an established in-vitro two-compartment model for liver support techniques, this study aimed to compare the membrane performance of the FX CorDiax 1000 dialyzer (Fresenius Medical Care, Bad Homburg, Germany) and the middle-cut-off (MCO) Theranova 500 dialyzer (Gambro, Baxter International, Hechingen, Germany). The technological platform utilized was the OPAL system (Albutec GmbH, Rostock, Germany).
Method
Samples were collected over six hours and analyzed via photometric assays using a Cobas Mira Plus analyzer and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Key analytes included water-soluble toxins, cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α), albumin, and albumin-bound toxins such as toxic bile acids. Additionally, dansylsarcosine titration was performed to evaluate a potential effect on binding capacity at albumin's binding side Sudlow II.
Results
Bile Acid Removal: Both filters exhibited comparable bile acid clearance. The smaller surface area of the Theranova 500 filter appeared to be offset by its enhanced performance, making both filters equally effective.
Bilirubin Removal: Both filters effectively reduced bilirubin concentrations despite continuous addition throughout the experiment, with no significant difference between them.
IL-6 Clearance: Both filters demonstrated decreasing IL-6 levels over time, with the Theranova 500 showing a slight advantage.
TNF-α Removal: The Theranova 500 was more effective in removing TNF-α than the FX CorDiax 1000, as indicated by sieving coefficients over time.
Sudlow II binding site marker titration: The Dansylsarcosine titration showed no significant change in maximum available binding sites (Bmax) or changes in binding affinity (Kd) between membranes, however overall Bmax was increased for both membranes.
Conclusion
The middle-cut-off (MCO) membrane demonstrated specific advantages in removing inflammatory mediators. The superior performance of the Theranova 500 in reducing IL-6 and TNF-α levels suggests potential benefits for treating renal conditions with an inflammatory component, as it effectively clears larger molecules that conventional high-flux membranes retain. By lowering inflammatory cytokine levels, this membrane could improve hemodynamic stability and reduce inflammatory responses, potentially supporting patient recovery.
Additionally, the results suggest that detoxification by albumin dialysis might be indicated for renal patients with an inflammatory component. Pfensig et al. (Artif Organs., 2016) demonstrated that the simple addition of albumin to the dialysate leads to an increase in cytokine removal, by putative protein-cytokine interactions.
Both used membranes could lead to an increased number of available albumin binding sites, thereby significantly enhancing the detoxification of blood and tissue, directly reducing the burden on the kidneys and supporting overall organ recovery in critically ill patients.
However, further clinical studies are necessary to validate these in-vitro findings in patient populations.

title: #2347 Regional citrate anticoagulation is a safe and effective strategy for treating critically ill patients undergoing kidney replacement therapy for metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA): definitive documentation through serum citrate measurements
authors: Maria Chiara Pacchiarini; Giuseppe Regolisti; Benedetta Mordà; Paolo Greco; Caterina MacCari; Tommaso Di Motta; Chiara Italiano; Teresa Coccini; Elisa Roda; Umberto Maggiore; Enrico Fiaccadori; Francesca Di Mario
abstract:
Background and Aims
Metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA) is an infrequent but potentially fatal complication of metformin therapy, mainly reported in patients with acute kidney injury (AKI). Due to its pharmacokinetic characteristics, metformin can be effectively removed via kidney replacement therapy (KRT), which is the cornerstone of management in cases of acute intoxication. Sustained low-efficiency dialysis (SLED) has emerged as a valid hybrid technique combining the advantages of enhanced hemodynamic stability of Continuous KRT with elevated clearance efficiency typical of conventional intermittent hemodialysis.
Regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) is widely recognized as the preferred anticoagulation strategy for prolonged KRT, owing to its ability to maintain extracorporeal circuit patency while minimizing bleeding risk. However, its application in the context of metformin toxicity poses specific challenges. The impairment of aerobic oxidative cellular metabolism associated with metformin intoxication might increase the risk of citrate accumulation, potentially leading to significant electrolyte imbalances and disturbances in acid-base homeostasis.
This study seeks to evaluate the efficacy and safety of SLED with RCA in critically ill patients with MALA. For the first time, the investigation incorporates both direct measurements of serum metformin and citrate concentrations, to definitely exclude citrate accumulation.
Methods
We conducted a prospective observational study involving a cohort of critically ill patients with severe AKI and highly suspected MALA, who underwent a 16-hr SLED session with RCA. The study was performed at the Renal Intensive Care Unit (r-ICU) of Parma University Hospital (Italy) between March 2022 and August 2024. All participants received supportive care in conjunction with treatments of coexisting medical conditions. Within 2 hrs of Emergency Department admission, a 16-hrs SLED session with RCA was scheduled with Surdial X Nipro machines and a polysulfone hemofilter (surface: 2.1 m²; KUf 27 mL/h/mmHg; Elisio 21M, Japan) or 5008 CorDiax Fresenius with polysulfone hemofilter (surface 2.2 m2; KUf 68 mL/h/mmHg, FX100, Italy), depending on availability. Demographic and clinical data, as well as complete laboratory workup were collected. Additionally, during and up to 8 hrs after the SLED end, serum samples were collected to measure metformin (via high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry) and citrate concentrations (via enzymatic spectrophotometric analysis).
Results
The study analysed 23 critically ill patients, all of whom exhibited serum metformin concentrations exceeding the therapeutic range (median 29.1 mg/L; 13–39.1) (Table 1). The overall ICU mortality rate was 22% (n = 5), with two patients dying during dialysis and three within 72 hrs following the completion of SLED session. Hemodynamic and acid-base parameters improved progressively in all but two patients during SLED, with a significant reduction of lactate levels. Serum metformin concentrations decreased substantially during the SLED session, achieving a mean value of 3.95 mg/L (±0.5) at KRT end, and minimal post-treatment rebound (Table 2, Fig. 1A). Of the 23 SLED sessions evaluated, 4 (17%) were prematurely interrupted, with circuit clotting being the cause in only one instance. Importantly, no patient exhibited clinical or biochemical manifestations indicative of citrate accumulation. This finding was further confirmed by persistently low serum citrate concentrations during SLED, with mean levels consistently below 0.5 mmol/L (Table 2, Fig. 1B).
Conclusions
The results of this study demonstrate the safety of citrate as anticoagulant for the extracorporeal circuit in critically ill patients undergoing prolonged KRT for MALA. This safety was, for the first time, confirmed through direct serum citrate measurements, which definitively excluded the possibility of citrate accumulation. Furthermore, the use of RCA ensured an adequate filter lifespan, thereby facilitating rapid drug clearance, restoration of acid-base status, and resolution of clinical symptoms.

title: #1455 Plasma free Hemoglobin, Haptoglobin, and risk of CSA-AKI. A translational systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Nathalia Gonzalez- Jaramillo; Moritz Saxenhofer; Anna Schnell; Alexander Schaub; Thomas Gentinetta; Daniel Couto; Giorgia Jurisic Snijder; Monika Edler
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients undergoing cardiac surgery (CS) are at high risk of developing cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB)-induced hemolysis and acute kidney injury (AKI). The associations of free Hemoglobin (fHb) and its scavenger protein Haptoglobin (Hp) with the incidence of cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury (CSA-AKI) remain unclear. Understanding the role of fHb and Hp in the development of AKI among patients undergoing CS could help identify individuals at higher risk of kidney injury, suggest future research and clinical interventions, and eventually improve preventive care bundles. Therefore, we aimed to systematically assess the longitudinal changes in fHb and Hp during cardiac surgery and their pooled associations with the incidence of CSA-AKI.
Method
We conducted a Systematic review and Meta-analysis. PubMed, Embase, and COCHRANE databases were systematically searched through December 31, 2024. Additionally, the first 200 hits of a Google Scholar search were screened. We selected observational and interventional studies analyzing the associations of changes in Hp and fHb with CSA-AKI. Additionally, studies were selected if they reported fHb and Hp measurements from at least two different time points. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed data quality. Published incidence of AKI and mean concentrations of fHb and Hp with their 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random effects models. We used ‘metafor’ package in R (version 4.0.0) to synthesize and display findings from included studies.
Results
200 studies were screened for title and abstract and 13 for full text. Seven studies from four countries and a total of 547 patients were included and meta-analyzed. In studies among children, the mean age ranged between 1.3 and 2.5 years. In adults, the mean age ranged between 61 and 72 years. The overall pooled incidence of AKI was 31% [95% CI 21–42]. Mean fHb values increased progressively during CPB, reaching maximum concentrations at the end of CPB. The pooled maximum mean concentration of fHb was 55 µmol/L heme equivalents [95% CI 29–103]. Mean Hp values decreased progressively during CPB, reaching minimum concentrations several hours after CPB. The pooled minimum mean concentration of Hp was 28 mg/dl [95% CI 23–35]. Both maximum fHb and minimum Hp concentrations after CPB were significantly associated with the incidence of AKI. fHb maximum value after CPB was associated with a 1.1 times fold increase in the incidence of CSA-AKI (OR 1.1 [95% CI 1.02–1.21]). Hp depletion was associated with a 2.5 times fold increase in the incidence of CSA-AKI (OR 2.5 [95% CI 1.2–5]). The overall risk of bias was moderate.
Conclusion
This meta-analysis of seven studies, encompassing 547 patients, revealed that one-third of the patients developed CSA-AKI. The findings underscore hemolysis and Hp depletion as significant mechanisms contributing to the incidence of AKI post-CS. Given the stronger association of Hp with CSA-AKI, future clinical trials should focus on monitoring Hp levels and evaluating the preventive use of Hp to reduce the incidence of CSA-AKI.
