title: #1447 Pre-operative CKD stages IIIb–IV in renal cancer surgery: are AKI and ESRD inevitable? Insights from real-life experience
authors: Francesco Trevisani; Federico Belladelli; Andrea Angioi; Chiara Re; Giuseppe Rosiello; Matteo Floris; Alessandro Larcher; Umberto Capitanio; Andrea Salonia; Francesco Montorsi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a global health challenge, especially in renal surgery, where preserving kidney function while ensuring oncological safety is crucial. Partial nephrectomy (PN) is preferred over radical nephrectomy (RN) for localized renal masses, but the impact of preoperative CKD severity, acute kidney injury (AKI), and progression to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) remains unclear, especially in pre-operative CKD stage III and IV patients.
Our study investigates patients with localized renal tumors (cT1-2cN0cM0) and preoperative CKD undergoing surgery, focusing on AKI and ESRD rates in CKD stage IIIb and IV.
Method
This study analyzed patients with localized renal masses (cT1-2cN0cM0) and preoperative CKD (eGFR <60 mL/min), identified from a prospective database after IRB approval (Protocol Rene-2007). CKD stages were classified using the CKD-EPI equation and KDIGO guidelines, with AKI defined as a serum creatinine increase of 0.3 mg/dL and ESRD as eGFR <15 mL/min. Patients were stratified by CKD severity and evaluated for postoperative AKI and ESRD rates, with data on comorbidities (Charlson Comorbidity Index) and BMI collected. Statistical analyses, including locally weighted polynomial smoothing and significance tests (P < 0.05), were performed using R software (version 4.3.2).
Results
Descriptive analysis is shown in Table 1. About 54% of patients with preoperative eGFR below 45 mL/min were surprisingly subjected to RN, a highly invasive procedure that could potentially halve the overall renal reserve. However, only 28% of these patients developed AKI and 9% ESRD post-operatively. (Fig. 1)
Conclusion
The rate of AKI and ESRD in RN for renal cancer in pre-operative CKD stage 3b-4 is surprisingly not high, with less than 10% of patients who developed ESRD requiring chronic haemodialysis.

title: #2354 Endotoxin and cytokines removal with new microporous (CA) sorbent prototypes
authors: Anna Lorenzin; Natascha Perin; Massimo de Cal; Monica Zanella; Claudio Ronco
abstract:
Background and Aims
Endotoxin, also referred to as lipopolysaccharide (LPS), is a major stimulus of the inflammatory response capable of leading to sepsis and septic shock. Extracorporeal blood purification therapies are increasingly employed in the treatment of sepsis. Timely and thorough removal of endotoxin and cytokines can help to mitigate the inflammatory cascade during septic shock. Hemoadsorption (HA) is a promising approach to achieve this goal. title: #2337 Extracorporeal hemoadsorption therapy in the treatment of sepsis induced by Gram-negative bacteria: in vitro assessment of two new sorbent cartridges
authors: Natascha Perin; Anna Lorenzin; Massimo de Cal; Monica Zanella; Claudio Ronco
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sepsis is one of the major causes of hospital mortality, characterized by a dysregulated immune response to infection that can lead to multiorgan failure and death. Gram-negative bacteria have emerged as primary contributors to sepsis and septic shock. Patients with sepsis induced by Gram-negative bacteria exhibit high endotoxin activity. Endotoxin, or lipopolysaccharide (LPS), is a component of the Gram-negative bacterial membrane and a potent stimulator of the inflammatory cascade. Therefore, effective strategies for LPS removal are crucial in sepsis treatment. Extracorporeal blood purification therapies, particularly hemoadsorption, have been extensively studied for their potential to modulate the immune response in septic patients. This in vitro study aimed to assess the endotoxin and cytokines removal capacity of two new cartridges.
Method
We studied a downscaled module of the CA and pHA cartridges (Jafron Biomedical, Zhuhai City, China) in an in vitro closed-loop hemoadsorption configuration (Fig. 1). The characteristics of the two cartridges are summarized in Fig. 2. A total of 1,300 mL of blood were inoculated with 25 mg of LPS, and each cartridge was perfused with a batch of 500 mL of blood. Two additional batches of 150 mL of blood was maintained as negative (CTR−) and positive control (CTR+). Blood was maintained at 37° and continuously stirred throughout the experiment. Circulation was performed using the GALILEO testing platform with a blood flow rate of 100 mL/min and lasted 2 hours. Solution samples were collected from the experimental batches at different time-points. Adsorption capacity towards endotoxin and inflammation factors was assessed by measuring Endotoxin Activity Assay (EAA) and the Removal Ratio (RR) of LPS, Interleukin-6 (IL-6) and Interleukin-1β (IL-1β).
Results
The cartridges exhibited distinct trends in removing target molecules, both effectively adsorbed endotoxin and cytokines. EAA values showed a significant decay over time: pHA and CA achieved a notable reduction of endotoxin activity, reduced by 51.2% and 65.9%, respectively (Fig. 3).
CA cartridge showed a progressive and constant decrease in LPS concentration, whereas the pHA displayed a more variable pattern (Fig. 4), both cartridges achieved a similar LPS concentration, with LPS removal of about 30% at the end of the experiments.
Promising results of CA cartridge were confirmed by its cytokines removal capacity. IL-6 concentration decreased exponentially with CA, reaching a RR of 49.2% within 10 minutes and 83.9% at 120 minutes. pHA instead, showed a more gradual reduction, reaching a RR of 43.5% at the end of the experiment (Fig. 5). Similarly, IL-1β decreased exponentially with CA, reaching very low levels within 30 minutes of circulation. RR obtained with pHA followed a linear trend, reaching a value of 63.9% at the end of the experiment, compared to 92.6% with CA (Fig. 6).
Conclusion
The reduction in endotoxin activity and concentration of LPS and cytokines represents an initial evidence of the efficacy of the two cartridges examined. This study demonstrated that both cartridges, CA and pHA, are capable of adsorbing endotoxin as well as pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines. These results provide a foundation for further studies aimed at more comprehensive characterization of these devices. In particular, their application in vivo will be essential to confirm the immunomodulation capacity in septic patients.

title: #2515 Intravital ATP imaging reveals unexpected associations between proximal tubular ATP levels and ischemia reperfusion injury severities in aged mice
authors: Masahiro Takahashi; Shigenori Yamamoto; Shinya Yamamoto; Motoko Yanagita
abstract:
Background and Aims
The incidence of acute kidney injury (AKI) is increasing globally. Among AKI patients, elderly patients have a higher risk for disease progression. Although impaired ATP metabolism and increased oxidative stress have been proposed as parts of characteristic features of kidney aging, analyzing ATP levels in aged kidneys has been technically challenging. By using an intravital ATP imaging technique, we previously showed the association between ATP recovery in proximal tubules (PTs) after ischemia reperfusion injury (IRI) and kidney prognosis in mice (Yamamoto S et al., J Am Soc Nephrol 2020). We therefore analyzed ATP kinetics in aged murine kidneys utilizing this technique to seek age-related changes in ATP and their influence on prognosis after IRI.
Method
In vivo ATP imaging in the kidneys of young (8–12 weeks old) and aged (>24 months old) mice systemically expressing FRET-based ATP biosensor (GO-ATeam2 mice) were performed using multiphoton microscopy before and during IRI. Ex-vivo ATP imaging using kidney slices of GO-ATeam mice was also performed to assess ATP producing pathways in aged and young proximal tubules (PTs). Pathological changes in the kidneys after IRI were assessed using PAS staining, immunostaining, and electron microscopy. Relationships between ATP levels in PTs and the IRI severities were assessed.
Results
We first analyzed ATP levels in young and aged kidneys under normal condition. Unexpectedly, aged mice showed significantly higher ATP levels in PTs and distal tubules than young mice (Fig. 1A and B, P < 0.0001 and P = 0.0002, respectively). ATP levels in interstitial cells, including fibroblasts, macrophages, and endothelial cells were comparable between young and aged kidneys. Electron microscopy showed mitochondrial fragmentation in aged PTs (P = 0.011), suggesting impaired mitochondrial homeostasis. Aged PTs also showed a tendency to have lower mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) than young PTs. Higher ATP levels in aged PTs was also confirmed in ex-vivo ATP imaging (P = 0.018), suggesting that ATP elevation in aged PTs is independent of systemic regulation, such as blood components and blood pressure. The administration of ATP synthesis inhibitors during ex-vivo ATP imaging revealed comparable ATP decrease in young and aged PTs after inhibition of mitochondrial ATP synthesis, and no significant ATP decrease after glycolytic inhibition either in young or aged PTs. These results showed similar ATP production pathways both in young and aged mice, and suggest the possibility that decreased ATP consumption, not increased ATP production, could result in ATP elevation in aged PTs. To examine relationships between ATP levels and IRI severities, unilateral 30-min IRI was induced to kidneys of aged and young GO-ATeam2 mice. Unexpectedly again, ATP decline after ischemia induction and ATP recovery after reperfusion in PTs were comparable between young and aged mice. On the contrary, tubular injury 24 hours after IRI was severer in aged kidneys, although not statistically significant. Reduced expression of Hmox1 (heme oxygenase-1) in aged kidneys after IRI possibly suggest vulnerability of aged kidneys to oxidative stress after IRI. Interestingly, ATP levels in PTs before IRI were strongly associated with the expression of Havcr1 (coding PT injury marker KIM1) 24 hours after IRI (Fig. 1C, P = 0.006, R2 = 0.634).
Conclusion
Despite signs of impaired mitochondrial homeostasis, proximal tubular ATP levels are higher in aged kidneys. In addition, higher ATP levels in aged PTs before injury predict severer tubular injury after IRI in aged kidneys.

title: #2005 Association between admission serum phosphate level and in-hospital acute kidney injury
authors: Youjun Xu; Hua Zheng; Guoqing Zhang; Hanshu Liu; Kaiyue Wang; Xiangyang Ye; Peng Xia; Qun Luo; Limeng Chen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a severe complication with poor prognosis in in-hospital patients. The study aimed to evaluate the correlation between admission serum phosphate level and AKI.
Method and Results
This retrospective study included 42,692 in-hospital adult patients with 16.6% of AKI (defined by KDIGO) from 2014 to 2021 at Peking Union Medical College Hospital. Patients with end-stage renal disease, renal transplantation, admission eGFR <15 ml/min/1.73 m2, length of hospital stay <2 days or >365 days, without or delayed serum phosphate measurement were excluded. Overall, patients with AKI had a higher proportion of comorbidities, took more medication, and experienced longer in-hospital days. The percentages of AKI were 27.2 and 43.5% in patients with phosphate <0.81 and ≥1.78 mmol/L, respectively. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) curves demonstrated the nonlinear correlation between serum phosphate levels and AKI (Fig. 1). After adjusting for comorbidities, laboratory indicators, and treatment medications, both serum phosphate levels <0.97 mmol/L (OR = 1.121, 95% CI = [1.003, 1.252], P = 0.045) and ≥1.45 mmol/L (OR = 1.157, 95% CI = [1.034,1.294], P = 0.011) were associated with the AKI. Hypophosphatemia was a risk factor for AKI, but hyperphosphatemia was only predicted AKI in patients with the admission eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2 subgroup.
Conclusion
We identified serum phosphate levels predicted AKI in the large in-hospital cohort, which shed light on the potential proximal tubule disorder as a new pathophysiological mechanism.

title: #2192 The contribution of epigenetic factors to CRS3 development induced by AKI: role of methyltransferase SET7
authors: Lara Mei Honda; Guilherme Lunardon; Raquel Silva Neres Dos Santos; Fernanda Fogaça-Ruiz; Gabriela Placoná Diniz; Marcela Carneiro-Ramos
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiorenal syndrome type 3 (CRS3) is a condition in which acute kidney injury (AKI) triggers cardiac alterations, such as cardiac hypertrophy and arrhythmias. AKI is a multifactorial syndrome characterized by the loss of glomerular filtration over short periods, ranging from hours to days, with ischemia being one of the most common causes. In this context, different research approaches have been employed to understand the development of this condition, identify potential therapeutic targets, and discover potential biomarkers. Epigenetics, the field of study that investigates how external stimuli can induce changes in gene expression without modifying the DNA sequence, has made significant contributions to the study of renal and cardiac diseases. Among the various epigenetic mechanisms, the modification of histone and non-histone proteins mediated by the methyltransferase enzyme SET7 plays a relevant role in several pathologies. In light of this, the study focuses on investigating the role of SET7 in CRS3 induced by AKI. Thus, the work aims to evaluate functional and inflammatory markers in the kidneys and heart following AKI induced by ischemia and reperfusion (I/R).
Method
Male C57BL/6 mice, including wild-type (WT) and SET7 knockout (KO) strains, aged 6–8 weeks, weighing 22–26 g, were utilized to investigate the role of SET7 in I/R induced injury. The animals were anesthetized using an intraperitoneal injection of xylazine (10 mg/kg) and ketamine (80 mg/kg). Mice in the I/R group underwent unilateral left renal pedicle occlusion using a microvascular clamp for 60 minutes to induce ischemia, followed by clamp removal to allow reperfusion. Sham-operated mice underwent identical surgical procedures without renal pedicle occlusion. After 15 days of reperfusion, the animals were euthanized by a single dose of xylazine (20 mg/kg) and ketamine (160 mg/kg) intraperitoneally. Blood samples are collected through puncture of the inferior vena cava, and organs including the heart, kidneys, and tibia were carefully harvested and preserved for later analysis. The kidneys will be weighed for morphometric analysis (weight of the kidneys/length of the tibia). Gene expression analysis of kidney injury and inflammatory markers was conducted using RT-qPCR. Target genes included KIM-1, NGAL, vimentin, IL-6, and IL-1β. Total RNA was extracted from kidney and heart tissues, followed by cDNA synthesis and RT-qPCR using specific primers for each gene. Statistical analysis was performed using one-way ANOVA in GraphPad Prism, with significance set at P < 0.05 and n = 4 per group. Protocol approved by the CEUA ICB/USP nº 9344271022.
Results
Morphometric analysis revealed a statistically significant reduction in the size of the left kidney in the I/R group compared to the Sham group in WT mice (41.19 ± 8.52 vs. 76.08 ± 5.86). Similarly, in KO mice, the I/R procedure also resulted in a notable decrease in left kidney size when compared to the Sham group (45.49 ± 9.37 vs. 84.42 ± 11.73). Conversely, the contralateral right kidney exhibited a significant compensatory hypertrophy in the WT-I/R group compared to the Sham group (104.30 ± 7.80 vs. 80.64 ± 7.28, P < 0.05). However, no significant changes in right kidney size were observed in KO mice between the I/R and Sham groups (92.12 ± 8.93 vs. 88.08 ± 13.37). Regarding the molecular markers of kidney injury, no significant changes were detected in the expression levels of KIM-1, NGAL, and vimentin in the right kidney, nor for the inflammation markers IL-6 and IL-1β, in both experimental groups. In contrast, the left kidney exhibited a substantial upregulation of injury-associated biomarkers following I/R injury. Specifically, KIM-1 and NGAL expression levels increased approximately one hundredfold compared to Sham, while vimentin expression showed a twenty fold increase, indicating a robust injury response. Notably, these changes were not mitigated in KO mice.
Conclusion
AKI induced by I/R causes structural and functional damage to the left kidney, and SET7 knockout does not improve renal structure or inflammatory marker expression.

title: #3304 Acute kidney injury and renal replecement therapy after heart transplantation: epidemiology and short-term outcomes
authors: Marco Fiorentino; Giuseppe Fischetti; Elisabetta Sturdà; Francesco La Fergola; Lorenzo Giovannico; Domenico Parigino; Luca Savino; Tomaso Bottio; Loreto Gesualdo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Heart transplantation (HT) is the treatment of choice for patients with end-stage heart failure. The main benefit of HT is to increase survival, exercise capacity, and quality of life, compared to medical treatment. Considering the shortage of organ availability, an increased number of marginal donors has been considered in the last years, with increased risk of short- and long-term complications. Acute kidney injury (AKI) requiring renal-replacement therapy (RRT) after HT is common and severely affects clinical outcomes. The aim of this study was to evaluate the epidemiology and outcomes of HT-associated AKI requiring RRT.
Methods
We conducted a single-centre retrospective analysis including adult patients who underwent HT at Cardiac Surgery Unit at the University Hospital Policlinico, Bari, Italy between March 2022 and August 2024. We classified patients in two groups based on the need of RRT after HT (no-RRT group and RRT group). The primary outcome was to assess the incidence of AKI requiring RRT and related 30-day mortality. Differences in baseline HT characteristics between groups were tested with t tests or Mann–Whitney U tests for continuous data, as appropriate, and chi-square test for categorical data. Multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to assess risk factors for post-transplant RRT and 30-day mortality.
Results
137 HT recipients were included in the study; 60 patients developed AKI requiring RRT (43.7%), while the remaining 77 were classified as no-RRT group (56.3%). Mean recipient age was 58 years with a predominance of male gender (81%), without significant differences between groups. Days on waiting list for HT were higher in the no-RRT group, as most of patients received HT in election. title: #722 Acute kidney injury in the very elderly: evolving times, evolving epidemiology in an aging society
authors: Francesca Cappadona; Stefania Prenna; Marita Marengo; Marco Fiorentino; Paolo Fabbrini; Erika Naso; Francesco Garzotto; Elisa Russo; Francesca Viazzi; Giuseppe Castellano; Vincenzo Cantaluppi; Pasquale Esposito
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a complex entity associated with an increased risk of complications and mortality. Its occurrence and outcome are influenced by several patient and organizational-related factors.
Among these, age plays a pivotal role, as aging is linked to multiple biological and social changes that significantly impact the risk, development, and outcomes of AKI,
In recent years, the general population—particularly in Western countries—has experienced a marked increase in life expectancy, resulting in a growing population of very elderly individuals.
However, the impact of this demographic shift on AKI epidemiology and outcomes remains poorly understood. This retrospective study aimed to evaluate the epidemiology, severity, and outcomes of AKI in a large cohort of hospitalized patients aged ≥75 years,
Method
We analyzed clinical data from adult patients admitted to two large university hospitals in Italy between 2016 and 2019. Collected data included serum creatinine (sCr) levels, comorbidities, discharge outcomes, length of hospital stay (LOS), and mortality. Patients with stage 5 chronic kidney disease (CKD) reported on administrative documentation were excluded.
From the general cohort, we focused exclusively on very elderly patients (≥75 years), categorizing them into three age groups: middle-old (MO, 75–84 years), old-old (OO, 85–99 years), and centenarians (C, ≥100 years).
AKI was defined and staged according to KDIGO criteria, using the peak sCr level during hospitalization compared to the lowest recorded sCr, assuming the latter represented baseline kidney function.
Results
A total of 87,087 patients (mean age 69.2 ± 17.7 years; 49.9% male, 50.1% female) were analyzed. Of these, 41,102 patients (47.2%) were aged ≥75 years and were classified as follows: MO (n = 23.644, 57.7%), OO (n = 17.312, 42%), and C (n = 126, 0.3%) (Table 1). The prevalence of female patients increased with age, peaking at 83% among centenarians.
Baseline comorbidities varied across age groups: diabetes was more prevalent in the MO group, while heart failure (HF) was more common in the OO group. Admission through the emergency department was more frequent among the older age groups. Mean admission sCr levels exceeded the laboratory reference limit (1.1 mg/dL) in all groups.
Overall, 10,818 patients (26.3%) developed AKI, with a higher proportional incidence observed in the oldest groups (Table 2). However, centenarians experienced less severe forms of AKI, with a higher incidence of AKI stage 1. Among centenarians with AKI, a higher prevalence of pre-existing CKD and HF was observed, while sepsis was less frequent during hospitalization.
Outcomes analysis revealed higher mortality rates in the OO and C groups with AKI, while their LOS was shorter compared to MO patients. Notably, none of the centenarian patients with AKI were admitted to the ICU. SCr levels remained elevated at discharge across all groups.
30-day Kaplan-Meier survival analysis demonstrated that AKI was associated with increased mortality in the MO group. Conversely, there was no significant association between AKI development and mortality in the OO and C groups (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
This study highlights significant differences in AKI epidemiology, severity, and outcomes among very elderly hospitalized patients. While AKI was more prevalent in older age groups, centenarians experienced less severe forms of AKI, potentially due to unique biological or care-related factors. Despite this, mortality remained highest among the oldest patients, underscoring their vulnerability. The lack of a clear association between AKI and mortality in the OO and C groups suggests that non-AKI factors may play a more critical role in determining outcomes in these populations. These findings emphasize the need for age-specific prevention and management strategies to address the growing population of very elderly individuals at risk for AKI.

title: #2353 The role of Foxp2 in kidney ischemia-reperfusion injury
authors: Yixin Zou; Wai Han Yiu; Jingyuan MA; Yuchen Feng; Kar Neng Lai; Rongguo Fu; Sydney Tang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Our recent study found that the transcription factor of Forkhead box P2(Foxp2) was upregulated in renal tubules from human and mouse models of chronic kidney diseases (CKD) and is involved in the progression of cell cycle arrest and renal fibrosis [1]. However, the role of Foxp2 on kidney injury and the associated mechanisms remain largely unknown.
Method
Foxp2 expression was detected by immunohistochemical staining on renal biopsies from patients with acute tubular injury. Tubule-specific Foxp2 knockout mice (Foxp2fl/fl,Cre) and the corresponding control (Foxp2fl/fl) were subjected to unilateral ischemia-reperfusion injury (UIRI) for 30 mins, followed by contralateral nephrectomy at one day before sacrifice. Mice were sacrificed at 7-day post-surgery for examination of renal injury and apoptosis.
Results
Foxp2 expression was increased in nucleus of injured renal tubules. Tubular injury marker kidney injury molecule 1 (Kim1) was significantly decreased in Foxp2 knockout mice compared to that in control mice at 7-day post-surgery. Increased expression levels of Bcl2 associated x (Bax) and p53 were attenuated with the absence of tubular Foxp2 at both mRNA and protein levels.
Conclusion
Foxp2 plays a pathogenetic role in kidney ischemia-reperfusion injury. Suppression of tubular Foxp2 alleviates apoptotic effects in kidney injury.

title: #1414 Acute kidney injury in critically ill cancer patients: risk factors and impact on survival
authors: Patrícia Valério; Joana Masumi; João Pereira
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common complication in critically ill cancer patients, influencing morbidity and mortality. This study aims to evaluate AKI incidence, risk factors, and outcomes in cancer patients admitted to a intensive care unit (ICU).
Method
We conducted a retrospective analysis of 4861 ICU admissions of cancer patients from a tertiary hospital. Patients were classified according to KDIGO criteria for AKI. Multivariate Cox proportional hazards models and survival analysis (Kaplan-Meier curves, Log-Rank test) were used to assess risk factors and mortality.
Results
Our population presented a median age of 69 years-old and 56,9% were male. The most common comorbidities included hypertension (37.3%), diabetes (32.9%), obesity (19.9%), and heart failure (19.1%). Around 10% of patients had chronic kidney disease. AKI was observed in 87.1% of patients (n = 4234), of which 7.7% (n = 325) had KDIGO stage 1, 20.4% (n = 865) had stage 2, and 71,9% (n = 3044) had stage 3. A total of 19.9% (n = 844) of AKI patients required kidney replacement therapy (KRT). A total of 783 patients (16.1%) had neoplastic disease. Regarding cancer distribution, 87.4% (n = 684) had solid tumors, 37.0% (n = 290) had metastatic disease, and 15.5% (n = 121) had hematological malignancies. Compared to non-cancer patients, cancer patients had a significantly higher incidence of AKI (P < 0.001), a greater need for KRT (P = 0.003) and increased mortality (Log Rank P < 0.001). The main risk factors associated with severe AKI included age (HR 1.02, 95% CI 1.01–1.02, P < 0.001), higher SAPSII score (HR 1.02, 95% CI 1.01–1.02, P < 0.001), sepsis (HR 1.47, 95% CI 1.28–1.70, P < 0.001), chronic hepatic disease (HR 1.70, 95% CI 1.30–2.22, P < 0.001), obesity (HR 1.26, 95% CI 1.07–1.48, P = 0.005), and invasive mechanical ventilation (HR 1.28, 95% CI 1.10–1.50, P = 0.001). Hematological malignancies had a stronger association with AKI compared to solid tumors. Though metastatic disease did not independently predict AKI severity. Mortality at one and two years was significantly higher in patients with severe AKI (Log-Rank test P < 0.001).
Conclusion
AKI is highly prevalent in ICU cancer patients and significantly impacts short- and long-term survival. Identifying modifiable risk factors may aid in early intervention strategies. Hematological malignancies appear more susceptible to AKI than solid tumors.

title: #520 Is acute hemodialysis precluded in the oldest-old patients?
authors: Maria Isabel Acosta-Ochoa; Jimmy Reinaldo Sanchez Gil; Francisco Mateo de Castro; Arturo Lorenzo Chapatte; Carmen Calderón González; Karina Ampuero Anachuri; Esther Hernández García; Victoria Oviedo Gómez; Rubén Velasco Pilar; Armando Coca Rojo
abstract:
Background and Aims
AKI is a global public health problem, occurring in 6%–10% of hospitalized individuals. In the last decades the worldwide phenomenon of aging is leading to the growing need to serve aged individuals. These circumstances lead to a clinical scenario in which nephrologists must care more frequently for elderly patients and decide to initiate or not hemodialysis (HD) in the acute setting. Few studies compare hard outcomes between the old and the oldest old individuals, when suffering from AKI, with emphasis on the need for acute HD.
Method
Real world, retrospective, observational study from 2 hospitals (1 located inland and 1 located in an island territory). We studied individuals hospitalized in nephrology wards or that underwent in-hospital nephrological consultation from other units during hospitalization, for a 5-year period. Individuals were divided into 2 groups: ≥65 to ≤79 years (old) and ≥80 years (oldest old). Patients that met AKI criteria by KDIGO-2012 classification were finally included. We compared clinical variables and hard renal and clinical outcomes between groups.
Results
We included 2115 AKI episodes that occurred in 1359 individuals. 869 (41%) occurred in the ≥80y group. Mean age in the old group was 73 ± 4, oldest old group 85 ± 4. Patients in the ≥65–≤79y group suffered more DM and coronary artery disease (CAD), and less hypertension (HTN), chronic heart failure (CHF), dementia and CKD. The oldest individuals were classified more frequently into KDIGO stage 2 and less into Stage 1, with no statistically significant differences in Stage 3 between groups. Oldest old individuals were admitted more frequently in medical (MD) wards and less in the ICU, and had a significantly higher Charlson's index (ChaI) (see Table 1A: Features). Analyzing hard outcomes, there were no differences in time to nephrology consultation, hospital length of stay was shorter in the oldest group, they received acute HD less frequently, were less dialysis dependent at discharge, and showed a higher mortality rate (see Table 1B: Results). Association of age and mortality in patients ≥ 80y was: OR 2.02 (95% CI: 1.62–2.52, P < 0.001); mortality associated with acute HD in the eldest group was: OR 1.92 (95% CI: 1.01–3.42, P = 0.022). In the oldest old the proportion of females rose from 25% to 41%. When comparing the baseline characteristics and outcomes between hospitals, we didn't find statistically significant differences in the studied outcomes.
Conclusion
We found that in our institutions HD in the oldest old individuals was not precluded by age in the acute setting: 53 (6%) underwent acute HD and 19 (2%) were HD dependent at discharge. We observed that individuals ≥80y received acute HD less frequently (consequently their rate of HD dependence at discharge was smaller) and exhibited a significantly higher mortality. We found significant differences in baseline clinical characteristics and morbidities between groups, e.g. dementia and CKD were more prevalent in the oldest old group. The proportion of oldest old individuals in our cohort is noteworthy (41%) and we underline that these figures may grow in the near future. The rise in the proportion of females in the oldest old group could be explained by the fact that globally women live longer than men and we should study how sex differences affect health outcomes in the elderly population. In the future we will collect more data to gain statistical power to compare the outcomes in the current and probably more regions. We consider that the decision of initiating HD in this context should carefully evaluate baseline characteristics and prognosis, not only age. We didn't analyze AKI etiologies, nor frailty or cognitive tests, but we should consider the use of morbidity, mental and nutritional scores in the holistic evaluation of oldest old individuals to add information that could aid in this hard-decision-making process. It is also important to take into account patients and families expectations, and engage them in the process. These findings should be addressed as a public health issue too, because of the economic and social burden that the initiation of renal replacement therapy means for national health systems.

title: #271 Tubular epithelial cells are the primary source of Flt3L in acute kidney injury, independent of immune cells
authors: Na Li; Stefanie Steiger; Zhihua Zheng; Yun Chen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Dendritic cells (DCs) play a key role in the recovery following acute kidney injury (AKI). Fms-like tyrosine kinase receptor 3 ligand (Flt3L) is essential for the generation and maintenance of DCs. However, the cellular source of Flt3L during AKI remain unclear.
Method
The expression of FLT3LG (FLT3L) was analyzed using SP (Visium and CosMx) datasets. Specimens were collected from AKI patients, with or without acute myocardial infarction (AMI), to assess FLT3L expression. The distribution of FLT3L in humans was confirmed in kidney sections. In mice, wild-type (WT) and T cell-deficient (TcraKO) mice were subjected to unilateral ischemia-reperfusion (IR) to induce AKI. Flt3L expression was evaluated in serum, urine, and kidney tissues. Additionally, in vitro experiments were performed using the HK-2 cell line, the Jurkat T cell line, the THP-1 monocyte cell line, and cDC1 cells to validate the secretion of Flt3L.
Results
Most cells expressing FLT3L were proximal tubular epithelial cells in the injured kidney samples. Clinically, serum and urinary FLT3L levels were significantly elevated in patients with AKI (as shown in Fig. 1), and this elevation correlated with the degree of kidney dysfunction observed in these patients. In human kidneys, FLT3L expression was primarily localized to proximal tubular cells, while its expression in blood immune cells was independent of AKI severity. Interestingly, FLT3L was also produced by human Jurkat T cells under necrotic stimuli, while T cell-deficient mice showed no changes in circulating FLT3L levels during AKI. Finally, FLT3L secretion was observed in HK-2 cells under hypoxic, necrotic, and H2O2-induced stimuli. The secreted factors led to the activation of FLT3-related signaling pathways, including phosphorylation, in cDC1 cells.
Conclusion
FLT3L is upregulated in both humans and mice during IRI-induced AKI and is produced by tubular epithelial cells. These findings suggest that FLT3L could serve as a promising biomarker for AKI, and its associated signaling pathways may represent potential therapeutic targets for AKI.

title: #2570 Time trends and predictors of acute kidney injury in the complete region of Stockholm, Sweden
authors: Jim Alkas; Carl-Gustaf Elinder; Franz Peter Barany; Arvid Sjölander; Juan-Jesus Carrero
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a serious medical condition. Much of the existing literature on the burden of AKI derives from hospitalized patient cohorts for a particular cause, such as hospitalizations for cardiac/vascular surgery or sepsis requiring intensive care. Population-based studies on AKI burden are limited as well as its trends over time. Method

title: #2520 Rechallenge of immune checkpoint inhibitors in cancer patients with biopsy-confirmed renal injury: a case series
authors: Stavros Fokas; Alexander Gerakis; Ioannis Giatras; Christine Kaitantzoglou; Harikleia Gakiopoulou
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a possible immune related adverse event (IRAE) of immunotherapy on cancer patients. Rechallenging with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) after acute kidney injury is a complex clinical decision with potential risks and benefits. Current data on the timing and the outcomes of rechallenge following AKI are sparse, but the potential benefits of continued ICI therapy may outweigh the risks of rechallenge, especially if there are limited alternative treatment options.
Method
We assessed the records of all patients from January 2020 to February 2024 that were treated with ICIs, developed biopsy proven kidney injury associated with immunotherapy and then after the resolution of kidney injury they were rechallenged with ICI.
Results
We included 7 patients, 5 males and 2 females, with mean age at the time of kidney biopsy 66 years, and median follow up time 13 months. The most common primary malignancy was non-small cell lung carcinoma (n = 6) and there was one case of renal cell carcinoma (n = 1). Most patients (n = 6) were treated with the PD-1 inhibitor pembrolizumab, and one patient received a combination of two checkpoint inhibitors ipilimumab and nivolumab. Four patients were also treated with chemotherapy apart from ICI, and one also received targeted therapy (axitinib). Six patients were presented with AKI [AKI stage 2 KDIGO (n = 4), AKI stage 3 (n = 2)] and one patient with severe nephrotic syndrome. The median time to developing kidney injury from immunotherapy initiation was 13 months. Five patients also developed extrarenal immune related adverse events (IRAEs) during the follow-up time. Dermatitis (n = 3) and pneumonitis (n = 2) were the most common followed by hepatitis (n = 1) and colitis (n = 1). Renal biopsy showed acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) in 2 patients, acute tubular injury (ATI) in 2 patients, mixed ATI/AIN in one patient, ATI with diabetic nephropathy in one patient and membranous nephropathy (MN) with a lupus-like pattern in immunofluorescence in the patient with nephrotic syndrome. All patients received corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg) empirically. Prednisone was withdrawn in patients with ATI and DN/ATI. Immunotherapy was temporarily withheld. All patients experienced recovery of kidney function 2 months after the initiation of prednisone (among them the patient with DN/ATI who required renal replacement therapy at the time of biopsy) and the patient with nephrotic syndrome experienced partial remission of proteinuria. After rechallenging, five patients continued ICI treatment without recurrence of kidney injury until the end of follow-up time. The patient with DN/ATI developed severe pneumonitis one month after rechallenging that required reinitiation of corticosteroids and the patient with MN experienced proteinuria relapse, so immunotherapy was withdrawn in both patients.
Conclusion
Reintroducing immunotherapy after AKI is feasible in selected cases after timely diagnosis and therapy of renal injury, especially when there is lack of alternative oncological treatment options and it requires close collaboration among nephrologists and oncologists to continue ICI therapy while safeguarding renal health.

title: #229 Health inequalities and outcomes following acute kidney injury: a systematic review & meta-analyses of observational studies
authors: Christopher Grant; Anita Dahiya; Taylor Palechuk; Emilie Lambourg; Beatrix Tan; Ravindra Mehta; Neesh Pannu; Samira Bell
abstract:
Background and Aims
Inequalities in health describe the uneven distribution of health outcomes that result from genetic or environmental factors. The social determinants of health (SDOH) represent the socioeconomic context within which people are born, grow, work, live and age. Inequalities have been described in relation to AKI incidence and aetiology, including by sex/gender and race/ethnicity, but the extent to which inequalities and the SDOH impact on AKI outcomes is uncertain. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to determine the impact of health inequalities on AKI outcomes.
Method
This review has been registered on PROSPERO (CRD42023422307). We included observational studies of adults who experienced at least one episode of AKI that reported outcomes with stratification or subgroup comparison by sex/gender, race/ethnicity, socioeconomic status, income, education, employment, housing, smoking, mental health conditions, geography or insurance status. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality at any time post-AKI. Secondary outcomes were: progression to acute kidney disease; incident chronic kidney disease (CKD); progressive CKD; AKI recovery; cardiovascular events; hospitalisations; intensive care unit admission and hospital length of stay. The search was conducted in MEDLINE, Embase and Web of Science from inception to 10th January 2024. Study selection, extraction and risk of bias via the Newcastle-Ottawa scale were performed independently and studies meta-analysed where possible.
Results
7,312 titles/abstracts were screened, and 36 studies included (n = 2,038,441 patients with AKI). Most studies were from high-income countries (n = 31) based on the World Bank classification. No studies contained data from low-income settings and few included data from lower-middle income countries (n = 3) (Fig. 1). Evidence predominantly related to sex/gender (n = 25), race/ethnicity (n = 14) and socioeconomic status (n = 11). Table 1 summarises the results for the primary outcome. In random-effects meta-analyses of relevant studies, no sex/gender differences in all-cause mortality (OR 1.02 [95% CI 0.83–1.25], I2 99%, n = 14) or AKI recovery (OR 0.88 [95% CI 0.69–1.11], I2 67%, n = 7) were seen. Of twelve studies reporting mortality by race/ethnicity, six found no variation by racial/ethnic group. Nine studies reported mortality by socioeconomic status, six of which showed an increase in all-cause mortality among the most deprived sub-populations compared to the most affluent with relative effect sizes varying from minimal (i.e. HR 0.999 least vs most deprived) to modest (i.e. HR 1.20 most vs least deprived). Few studies assessed the impact of mental health (n = 3), insurance (n = 1), housing (n = 2), geography (n = 1) or smoking status (n = 3) and no reports quantified the impact of income, education, employment or substance use. Heterogeneity and level of evidence were not formally assessed.
Conclusion
This systematic review highlights a paucity of evidence related to health inequalities and AKI, specifically from low-income settings and pertaining to the impact of mental health conditions, substance use, income, education, employment, insurance access, housing and geography. No sex/gender differences in AKI mortality or recovery were identified. Our results support the need for increased resource allocation for patients with AKI who live in socioeconomic deprivation due to increased mortality. There is a need for further evidence to inform policy and target interventions to achieve equitable kidney care.

title: #684 Prognostic value of changes in the serum indoxyl sulfate concentration in septic-shock-associated AKI: the Tox-AKI cohort study
authors: Dimitri Titeca-Beauport; Sandra Bodeau; Clement Brault; Momar Diouf; Touria Mernissi; Alexis Lambour; Yoann Zerbib; Loay Kontar; Michel Slama; Youssef Bennis; Gabriel Choukroun; Julien Maizel
abstract:
Background and Aims
Indoxyl sulfate (IxS) is a gut-derived toxin that accumulates with kidney function loss and presents endothelial toxicity. Elevated serum concentrations of IxS are associated with adverse outcomes in chronic kidney disease. We sought to determine whether changes over time in the serum IxS concentration predict 90-day mortality in patients with septic-shock-associated acute kidney injury (AKI).
Method
We performed a prospective study in a 16-bed intensive care unit at a university medical center. We included 114 patients with septic shock and AKI within a median [IQR] time of 6.0 [2.0–12.0] hours after norepinephrine initiation. We measured the serum IxS concentration and six other uremic toxins on inclusion and every 24 hours thereafter until day six (seven time points). The aim of this study was to analyze the relationship between changes in serum IxS concentration over the first six days and mortality within 90 days following inclusion using joint modelling for longitudinal and survival data.
Results
On inclusion, the median serum IxS concentration was significantly higher in stage 3 AKI (3.03 [1.37–5.74] µg/ml, n = 46) than in stage 2 AKI (1.50 [0.66–2.20] µg/ml, n = 34) or stage 1 AKI (0.80 [0.38–1.79] µg/ml, n = 34) (P < 0.001). In the longitudinal analysis, IxS showed significant variation over time (estimate (standard error) −0.160 (0.026) P < 0.0001) and as a function of the AKI stage on each day (0.292 (0.030) P < 0.0001). Fifty-three patients (46.1%) died within 90 days of inclusion. After adjusting for explanatory variables, changes in serum IxS concentration over time were not associated with 90-day mortality (hazard ratio (HR) [95% confidence interval (CI)]: 0.98 [0.92–1.04]). With the exception of hippuric acid and trimethylamine N-oxide (which accumulated to a moderate extent in patients with stage 3 AKI only), we did not observe any significant accumulations of the other assayed uremic toxins in the study participants.
Conclusion
The change in serum IxS concentration over time correlated with the severity and trajectory of AKI during septic shock but was not associated with 90-day mortality.

title: #3076 Engineering primed extracellular vesicles with enhanced anti-inflammatory properties and ROS-responsive drug delivery for AKI treatment
authors: Chuyue Zhang; Liang MA; Ping Fu; Xiangmei Chen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) pathogenesis is characterized by the interplay between inflammation and oxidative stress, presenting a significant therapeutic challenge.
Method
Here, we report a novel nanomedicine platform combining inflammation-educated extracellular vesicles (pEVs) with ROS-responsive drug delivery capabilities for targeted AKI therapy. Through strategic exposure to inflammatory cytokines, mesenchymal stem cells were educated to generate pEVs with enhanced targeting capabilities and anti-inflammatory properties. These pEVs were further engineered by conjugating the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant SS31 via ROS-responsive thioketal linkers, creating pEV-TK-SS31.
Results
Comprehensive characterization revealed that inflammatory education altered the membrane proteins of engineered EVs endowing them with inflammation-targeting capabilities, and simultaneously upregulated anti-inflammatory cargo levels to enhance immunomodulatory effects. Furthermore, pEV-TK-SS31 exhibited precise stepwise targeted delivery: pEVs specifically accumulated in injured kidneys through inflammation-targeting capabilities, followed by ROS-triggered SS31 release, effectively disrupting the inflammation-oxidative stress cycle. The engineered pEV-TK-SS31 demonstrated superior therapeutic efficacy in both ischemia/reperfusion and lipopolysaccharide-induced AKI models, significantly improving renal function and attenuating tissue damage.
Conclusion
This smart system, adaptable for combining customized cargoes and therapeutic agents, holds promise for treating AKI and broad implications for treating various inflammation and oxidative stress-related disorders.

title: #617 Exploring the physiopathological role of labile iron in acute kidney injury: a model of porcine polymicrobial septic shock
authors: Aymeric Couturier; Matthias Haenggi; David Berger; Christos E Chadjichristos; Coralie Grange; David Buob; Souhila Ouchelouche; Axel Aigle; Thomas Brichart; Saber Barbar; Bernard Allaouchiche; Olivier Tillement
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sepsis-induced acute kidney injury (AKI) remains a leading cause of mortality, with no effective treatments. Recent studies implicate ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death, in tubular injury during sepsis-AKI. This study aimed to establish a reproducible porcine model of sepsis-AKI and evaluate iron chelation therapy during dialysis.
Method
Sepsis was induced in three pigs using autologous fecal slurry, followed by hemodynamic stabilization and 24-hour dialysis sessions with a novel iron-chelating polymer (MEXCD1) in the dialysate. Clinical, biochemical, and histological analyses were performed to assess AKI and iron-related pathology.
Results
All pigs developed AKI, evidenced by reduced urine output and tubular necrosis, with 100% survival at 48 hours. Oxidative stress and iron overload were observed in tubular epithelium. Dialysis with MEXCD1 extracted 158–712 µg of iron and reduced transferrin saturation, while other trace metals remained within safe ranges.
Conclusion
The porcine sepsis-AKI model is reproducible, providing insights into ferroptosis. Iron chelation therapy shows promise as a targeted intervention, warranting further studies to refine treatment protocols.

title: #2696 Contrast-induced nephropathy: a prospective comparative study using capillary blood sampling with point of care creatinine measurement
authors: Tae Won Lee; Sehyun Jung; Se-Ho Chang; Dong Jun Park
abstract:
Background and Aims
Contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) is one of the common causes of acute kidney injury (AKI), often presenting with a favorable prognosis, which makes it easily overlooked during diagnosis. Due to limited awareness among healthcare professionals, reluctance to perform blood sampling, and concerns about time and cost, renal function evaluation after contrast media exposure is frequently neglected. This study aimed to measure creatinine levels using capillary blood sampling and compare the results with laboratory data to investigate the occurrence of CIN.
Method
This study was conducted as a single-center, prospective, observational study and targeted patients hospitalized at Geongsang National University Changwon hospital from July 2024 to December 2024. The study included adults aged 18 years or older with chronic kidney disease (CKD) who were exposed to contrast media through procedures such as computed tomography (CT) or coronary angiography (CAG). Exclusion criteria were pediatric patients, patients undergoing hemodialysis, those with AKI within the past three months, and individuals who did not consent to participation. Creatinine levels were measured using capillary blood sampling with the StatSensor device (Nova Biomedical) at three time points: pre-exposure (P0), within 24 hours post-exposure (P1), and within 48 hours post-exposure (P2). These measurements were compared to venous blood samples taken pre-exposure (V0) and within 24–96 hours post-exposure (V2). CIN was defined as an increase in creatinine by ≥0.5 mg/dL or by ≥25% from baseline after contrast media exposure.
Results
A total of 182 participants were enrolled in the study, with a mean age of 73.25 ± 12.8 years; 56% were male. CIN based on venous blood creatinine criteria was identified in 33 patients (18.1%). Among these, 23 patients (12.6%) had CKD stage 3, and 5 patients (2.7%) each had CKD stages 4 and 5. CIN based on capillary blood creatinine criteria was identified in 37 patients (20.3%), with 29 patients (15.9%) in CKD stage 3 and 4 patients (2.2%) each in CKD stages 4 and 5. CIN occurrence was significantly higher in patients using angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) (53.7% vs. 72.7%, P = 0.046) and inotropic agents (4.7% vs. 18.2%, P = 0.007) in both capillary and venous blood sampling groups. title: #1157 Quality of life after acute kidney injury, not just an acute problem
authors: Rebecca Noble; Nicholas Selby
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients who suffer acute kidney injury (AKI) are at increased risk of long-term health consequences including Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD), but relatively little is known about how patients feel after an episode of AKI. We aimed to evaluate quality of life (QOL) 90 days after an episode of AKI, and compare QOL between those with and without recovery of kidney function.
Method
QOL was assessed in a prospective observational cohort of hospitalised patients recruited at the time of AKI and then followed-up at serial timepoints until day 90. We also compared QOL scores between those who did and did not meet the kidney components of Major Adverse Kidney Events at day 90 (MAKE90), either GFR drop of >25% from baseline or new renal replacement therapy. Two QOL questionnaires were assessed at day 90, EQ-5D-5L, and Modified Brief Fatigue Inventory (MBFI), a validated assessment tool of 9 items relating to how well a person is able to function and assessment of symptoms of fatigue. A mean score of more than 2.38 is classified as higher than normal fatigue. Scores for QOL measures were compared between those with and without MAKE90 outcomes.
Results
From a cohort of 92 surviving participants, 73 (79%) completed the questionnaires in full. The mean age of these participants was 65 ± 11years. Comorbidities included ischaemic heart disease (n = 25, 34%), heart failure (n = 16, 22%), and diabetes (n = 32, 44%). Median baseline GFR was 67 ml/min/1.73 m2 (IQR 45–89 ml/min/1.73 m2). Participants had AKI of all stages; stage 1 (n = 12, 16%), stage 2 (n = 18, 25%), and stage 3 (n = 43, 59%). Overall, mean EQ-5D-5L was 9.8 ± 3.9, where no or mild symptoms would be a score of less than 5. The domains with highest reported symptoms were ‘ability to perform usual activities’, ‘reduced mobility’ and ‘anxiety/depression’. MBFI showed higher than normal fatigue with a mean average score of 3.4 ± 1.7, and 68% (n = 50) had a higher than normal fatigue score.
Of the 73 participants, 53 (73%) did not have a MAKE90 kidney outcome, whilst 20 did (27%). Across each domain of EQ-5D-5L, participants had higher scores (i.e. were more dependent/symptomatic) when they had a MAKE90 outcome compared with those who didn't. This was most pronounced in ‘self-care’ (mean 1.25 +/- 0.62 vs 1.80 ± 0.95, P = 0.005), ‘usual activities’ (mean 2.04 ± 1.13 vs 2.90 ±1.33, P = 0.007) and ‘anxiety/depression’ (1.77 ± 0.97 vs 2.50 ± 1.15, P = 0.009). Mean total EQ-5D-5L score was 8.98 ± 3.61 in those without MAKE90 vs 11.8 ± 4.03 those with MAKE90 (P = 0.005). MBFI score was 3.07 ± 1.6 for those without MAKE90 compared with 4.36 ± 1.43 for those with MAKE90 (P = 0.002) indicating higher levels of fatigue in the latter.
Conclusion
Recovery from AKI is associated with significant reductions in QOL and increased fatigue. Symptoms were worse in those who had a significant decline in kidney function, which supports the relevance of MAKE90 as a patient-centred outcome. Post-discharge AKI care should incorporate holistic assessment of these symptoms as a first step towards development of targeted interventions.

title: #1159 Insulin-like growth factor-binding protein is upregulated after acute kidney injury in those with major adverse kidney events at day 90
authors: Rebecca Noble; Vic Sun; Nicholas Selby
abstract:
Background and Aims
Development of chronic kidney disease (CKD) after acute kidney injury (AKI) is well-recognised. It remains unclear how to best identify patients at risk of CKD, including at earlier timepoints (before day 90). If we were able to understand which patients with AKI were at most risk of CKD those patients could be selected for more intense follow up. Insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 6 (IGFBP6) is a protein involved in several cellular processes, including cell migration and fibrogenesis. As such, this novel biomarker may provide relevant information in the AKI to CKD transition, and we aimed to study the levels of IGFBP6 in a prospective cohort of AKI patients at serial time points.
Method
A total of 102 participants were recruited to a prospective cohort study with bloods taken at time of AKI, day 30, 60 and 90. Major adverse kidney events at day 90 (MAKE90) were recorded, a composite of a GFR drop of >25% from baseline, new kidney replacement therapy and death. Serum was collected simultaneously, centrifuged and stored at −80°C. Stored serum samples were then analysed using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Samples were run in duplicate with average concentrations of IGFBP6 reported in pg/ml. Data are presented using descriptive statistics of serial measures as well as a comparison between those with and without MAKE90.
Results
Of 102 participants, 90 (88%) were alive at day 90 whilst 12 (12%) had died. Participants had a mean age of 65.1 ± 12.9 years old with co-morbidities including ischaemic heart disease (n = 37, 28.9%), heart failure (n = 26, 20.3%), and diabetes (n = 44, 34.4%). Median baseline GFR was 69 ml/min/1.73 m2 (IQR 51 – 89 ml/min/1.73 m2). Participants had AKI of all stages; stage 1 (n = 18, 17.65%), stage 2 (n = 24, 23.53%), and stage 3 (n = 60, 58.82%). The most common cause of AKI was dehydration (n = 46, 35.9%). Peak serum creatinine at the time of AKI for the whole cohort was 254 μmol/l (IQR 146–430 μmol/l) falling to 112 μmol/l (IQR 83–162μmol/l), 99 μmol/l (IQR 80–148μmol/l), and 103 μmol/l (IQR 49–143 μmol/l) at day 30, 60 and 90 respectively. IGFBP6 also peaked for the cohort overall at time of AKI (median 1997 pg/ml (IQR 1284–3285 pg/ml), but did not follow the same decreasing trend of creatinine, remaining elevated at day 30 (median 1681 pg/ml (IQR 1101–2819 pg/ml) and at day 60 (median 1878 pg/ml (IQR 1166–2980 pg/ml) before falling at day 90 (1553 pg/ml (IQR 1115–2952 pg/ml). MAKE90 outcomes were observed in 41 (40.2%) of the cohort. Figure 1 shows the comparison of creatinine and IGFBP6 over time for those with and without MAKE90 outcomes, and IGFBP6 levels were significantly higher in those with MAKE90 as compared to those without (at day 30 P = 0.002), at day 60 P = <0.001).
Conclusion
IGFBP6, a protein with several biological functions and implicated in fibrogenesis, remains elevated after an episode of AKI, and does not follow the same trajectory of serum creatinine recovery. IGFBP6 was also significantly elevated in those who experienced MAKE90, and may be a promising biomarker of the AKI to CKD transition.

title: #2076 Concomitant use of renin-angiotensin system inhibitors and bortezomib were associated with a higher incidence of hyponatremia
authors: Yuki Miyaguchi; Miho Murashima; Kodai Suzuki; Takahisa Kasugai; Tatsuya Tomonari; Masashi Mizuno; Takayuki Hamano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyponatremia is highly prevalent and associated with worse outcomes among patients with malignancy. We previously demonstrated that bortezomib and cisplatin were associated with hyponatremia among antineoplastic agents (Clin Kidney J. 2023). We aimed to identify modifiable risk factors by increasing the number of patients enrolled. We chose renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (RASi) as potential candidates as they were reported to cause hyponatremia in some settings.
Method
This is a retrospective cohort study among patients with malignancy at our University Hospital from 2018 to 2023. We utilized mixed-effects logistic regression analyses to examine the association of bortezomib and cisplatin with hyponatremia (Na ≤130 mmol/L) and an effect modification by RASi. We further analyzed the association between RASi and hyponatremia among bortezomib and cisplatin users on antihypertensives.
Results
We enrolled 5506 patients. Median age was 68 (57–75) years and median eGFR was 70.2 (57.5–82.9) mL/min/1.73 m2. Of these, 1313 (23.9%) developed hyponatremia at least once during the study period. Bortezomib and cisplatin were associated with hyponatremia {odds ratio [OR] 1.93 [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.35–2.76] and OR 1.40 [95% CI 1.13–1.74], respectively}. The incidence of hyponatremia was particularly high with simultaneous use of RASi and bortezomib [OR 11.8 (95% CI 3.42–40.80) for RASi users and OR 1.54 (95% CI 1.02–2.32) for non-users, p for interaction = 0.14]. On the other hand, cisplatin was not associated with hyponatremia among RASi users [OR 0.85 (95% CI 0.42–1.73)]. Among those who received bortezomib (n = 172) and cisplatin (n = 923), 90 (52.3%) and 318 (34.5%) respectively were taking antihypertensive medications. In a subset analysis limited to patients receiving antihypertensive medications, the concomitant use of RASi was significantly associated with hyponatremia compared to the use of other antihypertensive medications among bortezomib users [OR 4.27 (95% CI 1.24–14.72), P = 0.02] but not among cisplatin users [OR 1.16 (95% CI 0.60–2.25), P = 0.66].
Conclusion
The association between bortezomib and hyponatremia was stronger among RASi users. Bortezomib is known to suppress CYP11B2 expression and secretion of aldosterone. The excessive suppression of RAS by the concomitant use of RASi might explain the observed increased incidence of hyponatremia among patients receiving bortezomib. Conversely, in patients receiving cisplatin, tubular sodium wasting, and resultant volume contraction activate the RAS, which might partially counteract the effects of RASi. Prescribing any antihypertensives other than RASi might reduce the incidence of hyponatremia in patients receiving bortezomib.

title: #1616 Clinicopathological features and outcomes of acute kidney injury in patients undergoing diagnostic native kidney biopsy
authors: Emilio Venturelli; Francesca Costigliolo; Lucia MacCio'; Elisa Russo; Francesca Viazzi; Pasquale Esposito
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) is a common syndrome associated with significant morbidity and mortality and is recognized as a risk factor for progression to chronic kidney disease (CKD). However, AKI encompasses a broad spectrum of underlying etiologies, making accurate differential diagnosis essential for guiding targeted treatment and follow-up strategies. Despite the established utility of kidney biopsy in evaluating renal pathology, its role in AKI remains underutilized. This study aims to describe the clinico-pathological characteristics, histological diagnoses, outcomes, and procedure-related complications in patients presenting with AKI who underwent native kidney biopsy.
Method
We conducted a retrospective review of 253 native kidney biopsies performed at our center between 2017 and 2018. At the biopsy, patients were classified according to KDIGO AKI stages based on serum creatinine and urine output criteria. Clinical and laboratory data, histological findings, and follow-up outcomes were collected.
Results
Among the 253 biopsies, 96 patients (38%) presented with AKI whose baseline characteristics are reported in Table 1. The cohort had a mean age of 60.2 years, with a slight male predominance (55%). The mean serum creatinine at presentation was 4.85 ± 3.36 mg/dL. The distribution of AKI severity was: 44.8% Stage 1, 26% Stage 2, 18.7% Stage 3, and 10.4% Stage 3D (requiring renal replacement therapy, RRT).
The most frequent histological diagnoses (reported in Fig. 1) included crescentic glomerulonephritis (17.7%), monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance (MGRS), and cast nephropathy (12.5% each), followed by acute interstitial nephritis (AIN, 12.5%). Diagnostic yield was high, with only 2% of biopsies being insufficient for evaluation. Procedural complications were rare (2% requiring transfusion), and no biopsy-related deaths occurred.
Based on clinical presentations, AKI patients were classified into three subgroups: AKI with urinary abnormalities (AKI-U; 49%), AKI with nephrotic syndrome (AKI-NS; 38%), and isolated AKI (AKI-I; 13%). The histological diagnoses according to the clinical presentation are reported in Fig. 2. In the AKI-U subgroup, crescentic glomerulonephritis (36%) and IgA nephropathy (13%) were the most prevalent diagnoses. In AKI-NS, MGRS, minimal change disease, and diabetic nephropathy were equally represented (16.3% each). In AKI-I, AIN was the predominant diagnosis (60%).
Patients in the AKI-U group tended to have a more prevalent ANCA positivity (p: 0.013), while at biopsy indication, mean serum creatinine was higher in the AKI-I group (p: 0.0159).
Following biopsy, 78 patients (81%) received a biopsy-directed immunosuppressive treatment.
At 90-day follow-up, 60% of patients developed CKD, 10% achieved complete renal recovery, 5% died, and 15% required RRT.
Finally, of the 10 patients requiring dialysis at presentation 4 patients (40%), all of whom were treated, were not dialysis-dependent at the last available follow-up.
Conclusion
AKI presents with heterogeneous renal lesions, many of which are treatable but underrecognized without biopsy. Kidney biopsy has a high diagnostic yield and can guide treatment, particularly in severe or dialysis-dependent AKI. Expanding biopsy indications and standardizing diagnostic approaches may improve the identification of treatable conditions, ultimately enhancing patient outcomes.

title: #3026 An ultrasmall ruthenium-based nanoparticle to protect acute kidney injury and promote renal repair
authors: Zhuyun Zhang; Jiameng Li; Qinbo Yang; Shanshan Chen; Baihai Su
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is common, with high morbidity and mortality. However, treatment options are limited. Many studies have shown a strong link between AKI and the development of chronic kidney disease (CKD), with AKI greatly increasing the risks of CKD and end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Recently, nanotechnology-based antioxidative therapy has emerged as a promising approach to alleviating oxidative stress caused by excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS). This study reports an ultrasmall ruthenium-based nanoparticle as a ROS scavenger to mitigate AKI and promote renal repair in C57 mice.
Method
The ultrasmall ruthenium-based nanoparticles, designated as Ru@TiO2, were synthesized by a facile one-pot solvothermal method. First, 10 ml of N, N'-dimethylformamide and 30 ml of isopropyl alcohol were mixed as the organic solvent. Subsequently, tetrabutyl orthotitanate and RuCl3 were added. We analyzed the morphology and chemical structure using transmission electron microscopy (TEM). We also assessed its enzyme-mimicking abilities in vitro, biocompatibility of Ru@TiO2, and the toxicity of Ru@TiO2 on HK2 cells and C57 mice. For AKI experiment, AKI was induced by intramuscular injection of 50% glycerin (8 ml/kg) into both hind thighs. Mice in the treatment group received Ru@TiO2 via intravenous injection into the tail following AKI induction. 24 hours later, the mice were sacrificed. For post-AKI experiment, AKI mice were treated with Ru@TiO2 every three days. 14 days later, the mice were sacrificed, and serum and renal tissue were collected for analysis.
Results
Characterizations of Ru@TiO2 nanozyme
The low-magnification TEM images of Ru@TiO2 confirm the morphology of the nanoparticles, with a specific size of approximately 50 nm (Fig. 1c–d). High-resolution TEM (HR-TEM) of the surface region showed Ru clusters measuring approximately 1.7 nm (Fig. 1d). Figure 2a–g confirmed that Ru@TiO2 had excellent antioxidant property, SOD-like and CAT-like capabilities.
Biocompatibility of Ru@TiO2 nanozyme
As shown in Fig. 3a, the hemolysis rate of Ru@TiO2 was under 5% even at a high dose of 200 µg/mL, meeting the ASTM standard. It has negligible effect on routine blood tests, coagulation, or liver and kidney function (Fig. 2b–e), and did not alter the histopathology of major organs in normal mice (Fig. 2f). title: #535 Audit of the clinical implementation of urinary NGAL in the diagnostic work-up of acute kidney injury at an Irish Hospital
authors: Michael Strader; Ellen Saghie; Bernadine Louis; Candice Fraser; Sharjeel Imran; Vladamir Stoyanov; Abdullah Tariq; Patrick Twomey; Jean Maxime Cote; Patrick Murray
abstract:
Background and Aims
Differentiating functional acute kidney injury (AKI) from structural tubular injury AKI remains challenging with existing clinical tools. urinary NGAL (uNGAL) has shown promise in distinguishing functional AKI, such as “Pre-Renal” AKI, from tubular injury (“Intra-Renal”) AKI. We evaluated the implementation of uNGAL in the clinical nephrology consult service over 3-year period in a heterogenous medical AKI population at a single center in Ireland.
Method
A retrospective audit investigating the clinical utility of uNGAL in an adult population at an Irish hospital was conducted from 2020–2023. Standard clinical data, such as clinical history, examination findings, radiology reports, serial serum creatinine and urea levels, proteinuria, FENa, and infection status around the time of AKI and uNGAL request were recorded. Blinded adjudication of the standard clinical data was performed between two expert Nephrologists. Responses were limited to: “Pre-Renal”, “Intra-Renal”, “Post-Renal”, “No-AKI”, or “Not Enough Information”. uNGAL accuracy in differentiating Intrinsic AKI from Functional AKI (Pre-renal & Post-renal) was assessed, and box plots visualized uNGAL and FENa levels across groups.
Results
A total of 320 uNGAL tests were performed between 2020 and 2023, which 292 were adjudicated to their AKI case. Adjudicated intra-renal AKI patients (n = 120) demonstrated significantly higher raw uNGAL levels (median: 1052 ng/ml [IQR: 302.4–1314.4]) compared to functional (median: 228.2 ng/ml [IQR: 69.7–895.1; P = 2.00 × 10-9) (Table 1). Similarly, cr-corrected uNGAL levels were significantly higher (P = 8.20 × 10⁻¹¹) in the intrinsic group (median: 1288.7 ng/mg [IQR: 438.2–2317.2]) compared to the functional group (median: 323.7 ng/mg [IQR: 86.9–1083.7]). These differences remained significant after adjusting for UTI status (Raw uNGAL: P = 1.34 × 10⁻¹²).; cr-corrected uNGAL: P = 5.66 × 10⁻¹²). The diagnostic accuracy of raw uNGAL at the manufacturer-recommended threshold of 150 ng/ml for adjudicated intrinsic AKI was moderate, with an AUC of 0.71 (95% CI: 0.64–0.77). At a lower threshold of 125 ng/ml, a similar diagnostic performance was observed. Cr-corrected uNGAL demonstrated slightly better performance, with an AUC of 0.73 (95% CI: 0.67–0.79) at a threshold of 150 ng/mg. FENa, in comparison, showed moderate diagnostic accuracy at a threshold of 2% (AUC: 0.67 [95% CI: 0.67–0.75]), with higher specificity (0.73) but lower sensitivity (0.47). After controlling for UTI status, the diagnostic accuracy of both raw and cr-corrected uNGAL improved. The AUC for raw uNGAL increased to 0.77 (95% CI: 0.71–0.84), while cr-corrected uNGAL improved to 0.76 (95% CI: 0.70–0.83). Sensitivity remained high for both raw uNGAL (0.87 to 0.86) and cr-corrected uNGAL (0.92 to 0.90), with NPV remaining stable (0.82 to 0.82 for raw uNGAL; 0.87 to 0.85 for cr-corrected uNGAL).
Conclusion
The use of uNGAL, raw or cr-corrected, improved the accuracy of differential diagnosis of AKI in clinical practice by differentiating intrinsic AKI from functional. Specificity was lower at the recommended manufacturer (150 ng/ml) and pediatric (125 ng/ml), but the sensitivity and NPV was high therefore supporting the use to rule-out an intrinsic injury clinically. The presence of UTI does not consistently result in an increase in uNGAL levels.

title: #3385 The short and long-term accuracy of urinary C-C motif Chemokine-14 in an ICU population
authors: Michael Strader; Stephen Duff; Lynn Redahan; Patrick Murray
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) is a life-threatening syndrome associated with significant short- and long-term negative outcomes. Current AKI clinical biomarkers, such as serum creatinine and urine output, are limited. The DAMAGE study, which included an ICU population, previously reported on the clinical accuracy of novel biomarkers (BMs) on short-term outcomes. However, other novel BMs, such as CCL14, have demonstrated success in identifying patients at risk for persistent-severe AKI (PS-AKI), but little is known about their long-term prognostic abilities for major adverse kidney events (MAKE) in comparison to other BMs.
Method
A post-hoc analysis of the DAMAGE dataset was conducted. Sixteen urinary biomarkers were measured from samples collected on the day of AKI diagnosis. The primary endpoint was the diagnostic accuracy for PS-AKI (stage 2/3 KDIGO AKI lasting ≥48 hours). Secondary endpoints included MAKE at 7 days, 30 days, 3 months, and 12 months, defined as death, dialysis, or a ≥25 mL/min/1.73 m² reduction in eGFR (≥3 months).
Results
186 ICU patients diagnosed with AKI and followed for 12 months, 79 developed PS-AKI. Of the BMs, albumin (AUC 0.82 (95% CI: 0.75–0.88) and CCL14 (AUC 0.81 [95% CI: 0.74–0.87]) demonstrated the highest accuracy for PS-AKI. IL-18 (aOR 3.20 [95% CI: 2.0–5.45]) and CCL14 (aOR 2.26 [95% CI: 1.49–3.54], P < 0.001) had the highest adjusted odds ratio for PS-AKI and all subsequent timepoints compared to other biomarkers. 85, 108, 83, and 103 patients experienced MAKE at 7D, 30D, 3M, and 12M, respectively. CCL14 showed good discrimination for MAKE at 7D (AUC 0.78 [95% CI: 0.71–0.85]) and 30D (AUC 0.8 [95% CI: 0.73–0.87]), though accuracy declined beyond 30 days aOR remained significant for CCL14 at all timepoints.
Conclusion
CCL14 in critically AKI patients enriches the short-term prognosis of these patients and has some prognostication potential at long-term from 3-month to 12 months. Among the biomarker panel, CCL14 demonstrated high accuracy and prognostic value for PS-AKI up to 30 days. While prognostic accuracy declined over time, elevated CCL14 at AKI diagnosis remained a strong predictor of adverse long-term outcomes. These findings highlight its potential for short-term prognosis and long-term risk stratification in AKI patients.

title: #889 Malaria is the leading cause of acute kidney injury in paediatric patients in Nigeria. Evidence from a point-of-care creatinine study in a Nigerian Primary Health Care Centre
authors: Dimitrios Poulikakos; Yetunde Ikuru; Vivean Laurent-Ordu; Dorathy Emem Model; Oluo Doris Chiemela; Siyeofori Dede; Kinikawo Green; Adaeze Oreh; Pedro Emem-Chioma; David Lewis; Ibi Erekosima
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is associated with poor health outcomes in low and middle-income countries due to delayed diagnosis and limited access to renal replacement therapy. However, its true burden remains poorly understood due to lack of timely biochemical testing. We previously evaluated the accuracy of point of care creatinine (POC Cr) technology [1] and its implementation using a clinical algorithm to identify patients at risk of AKI in the Hospital Emergency Department in Port Harcourt in Nigeria. In this phase of the project POC Cr was introduced in a large primary care health centre in Nigeria.
Method
The study took place at Ozuoba Model Comprehensive Primary Health Care Centre in Nigeria. Historically, decision making is based largely on clinical judgement and renal function tests when requested from external laboratories are reported in >48 hours. During this project POC Cr was performed for high-risk adult patients, using the clinical algorithm developed in the previous stage. Paediatric patients were tested with POC Cr based on diminished urine output or severity of clinical presentation as judged by the attending clinician. POC Cr was adjusted based on the evaluation phase as follows: POC Cr adjusted (a) = POC Cr −27.2 [1]. AKI stages were calculated based on KDIGO criteria using as baseline creatinine the upper limit of normal range (100 umol/L) in adults and based on upper limit of normal range according to age category for paediatric patients as proposed by the Paediatric Laboratory Medicine Network [2].
Results
A total of 424 patients (299 adult and 125 paediatric patients), underwent POC Cr testing. The median age was 31 (range 0.1 to 97) years. Amongst these patients, malaria was the most common presenting diagnosis (293 patients 61.1%), followed by gastroenteritis (25 patients (5.8%) with gastroenteritis, upper respiratory tract infection (24 patients, 5.8%) , urinary tract infection ( 20 patients, 4.7%), and acute appendicitis (4 patients, 3%) . Median POC Cr(a) (for the total population was 72.8 umol/L, Interquartile Range (IQR) 310).
In the 299 adult patients, median POC Cr(a) was 72.8 umol/L (IQR 310). Two cases of AKI (0.6%) were detected (one stage 1 and one stage 2), both associated with malaria.
Amongst the 125 paediatric patients 70 (56%) cases of AKI were detected (AKI stage 1 was 20%, AKI stage 2 was 20.8% and AKI stage 3 was 15.2%) with 49 (70 % of AKI cases) with associated with malaria diagnosis. Out of the 125 paediatric patients assessed in the centre 88 (70.4%) were diagnosed with malaria and amongst those 49 (56%) had AKI (AKI stage 1:18%, AKI stage 2: 20.4% and AKI stage 3: 17%) (Fig. 1).
The highest rates of AKI rate were observed in younger children declining to zero after the age of 12 (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
AKI was identified in over half of paediatric patients diagnosed with severe malaria based on clinical assessment in our study highlighting AKI as common complication of malaria in young children. These findings emphasise the need to revise WHO malaria guidance [3] with incorporation of the KDIGO definition of AKI to support early detection and treatment.

title: #1330 Glomerular filtration rate and albuminuria predicts outcomes in patients with acute kidney disease
authors: Szu-Yu Pan; Tao-Min Huang; Chih-Hsiang Chang; Vincent Wu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney disease (AKD) represents the transitional period between acute kidney injury (AKI) and chronic kidney disease (CKD). AKD patients are highly heterogeneous, and outcome prediction is challenging. The ADQI 16 Workgroup proposed an AKD staging system based on a serum creatinine ratio similar to the AKI staging system. In contrast, a KDIGO consensus conference proposed an AKD staging system similar to the CKD staging system, based on the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and albuminuria. We aim to investigate the ability of recently proposed AKD staging systems to predict outcomes in patients with AKD.
Method
We performed a post-hoc analysis of a clinical trial that tested the effects of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone blockade and multidisciplinary health education in patients with AKD not under dialysis (201811079MINC). The data of serum creatinine were extracted for calculation of AKD ratio and eGFR. The AKD ratio was defined as the ratio of serum creatine level during AKD period to the baseline period. Urine samples were used for albuminuria tests. The area under the curve (AUC) of the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC), logistic regression models, and Cox models were generated to test the association between patient outcomes and different AKD staging systems. To fit the model, AKD ratio, eGFR, and albuminuria were used to represent AKDsCr stages, AKDeGFR stages, and AKDUACR stages, respectively. The primary endpoint was dialysis or death within 6 months.
Results
A total of 130 AKD patients were included in the analysis. The patients had an average age of 64 ± 15 years, baseline eGFR of 54 ± 33 mL/min/1.73 m², and a Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score of 6.3 ± 2.8. Among the patients, 47% had comorbid diabetes mellitus, and 56% had K-DIGO stage 3 AKI including dialysis-requiring AKI. During the 6-month follow-up period, thirteen (10%) patients reached the outcome. In the univariable logistic regression models, the outcome was significantly associated with eGFR and albuminuria, but not significantly associated with AKD ratio. The AUC was the highest for eGFR (eGFR 0.764, albuminuria 0.722, AKD ratio 0.721). Furthermore, a multivariable logistic regression model incorporating eGFR, albuminuria, and nine other covariates had a better fit than a model integrating the AKD ratio and the same nine covariates (Fig. 1). The results of survival analyses with Cox models were similar.
Conclusion
Glomerular filtration rate and albuminuria measured during the AKD period are associated with the risk of dialysis or death in patients with AKD. These results should be validated in independent cohorts.
