title: #2630 Adult stem cell-derived kidney organoids (tubuloids) to model renal ciliopathies
authors: Aurelius Roskothen; Tess Beekink; Ruben van Esch; Kate Liang; Carola Ammerlaan; Carla Pou Casellas; Iris Lekkerkerker; Marc Lilien; Laura Claus; Albertien M Van Eerde; Marianne Verhaar; Gisela Slaats
abstract:
Background and Aims
Ciliopathies are genetic disorders in which cilia or cilia-associated signaling are impaired. The kidney is among the organs most commonly affected in ciliopathies. Advanced in vitro models for renal ciliopathies are essential for disease modeling and therapy development. Tubuloids are adult stem cell-derived kidney organoids that can be generated from urine (non-invasively) or from kidney tissue (e.g. biopsy) material. Tubuloids represent the tubular epithelium and display primary cilia at the apical site of the 3D cell structures. We aim to create a deeper understanding of the pathomechanism of renal ciliopathies and to develop therapeutic strategies.
Method
To generate tubuloids, a straightforward and reproducible protocol was established. This method enables disease modeling directly from patient material (tissue or urine) without the need for gene editing. We enabled tubuloid biobanking via two local biobank infrastructures Kidneybank and GeNepher.
Results
In addition to non-cilia related inherited kidney diseases or drug-induced tubulopathies, we have biobanked tubuloids of renal ciliopathy patients and successfully utilized them to model autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)-associated heterozygous NEK8/NPHP9 variants. The same methods used in standard cell culture are applied to characterize for example ciliation and polarization of tubuloids. Furthermore, DNA damage-associated phenotypes could be confirmed in renal ciliopathy nephronophthisis-related studies. As an advancement over primary urine cell cultures in 2D, 3D tubuloid cultures offer a patient-specific cell culture model with increased complexity, representing progenitors of tubular nephron segments of human origin.
Conclusion
Tubuloids represent a valuable model for fundamental and pre-clinical/translational research which aims to study disease mechanisms as well as therapeutic strategies. Eventually, tubuloids can be used to assess the efficacy and safety of small molecules and gene therapies for renal ciliopathies.

title: #3842 Significant association between B lymphocytes and their subpopulations with peripheral T follicular cells is evident in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) at remission
authors: Eleni Moysidou; Michalis Christodoulou; Georgios Lioulios; Christodoulos Keskinis; Stamatia Stai; Theodoros Dimitroulas; Eleni Frangou; Asimina Fylaktou; Maria Stangou
abstract:
Background and Aims
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), as a multifaceted autoimmune disease, is characterized by significant alterations in adaptive immunity. T follicular helper (TFH) cells are specialized to select high-affinity B cells in germinal centers. As their role in peripheral circulation is still unknown, we aimed to investigate the interaction between peripheral B and TFH cells in patients with SLE
Method
In this cross-sectional study, flow cytometry was performed estimate B lymphocytes and their subpopulations, IgD+CD27−, IgD+CD27+, IgD−CD27+, IgD−CD27−, in 63 patients with SLE and 48 healthy controls (HC), and results were correlated with peripheral TF cells, and their subtypes, TFH1, TFH2, TFH17, TF regulatory (TFR) and TF cells expressing ICOS (TFICOS). SLE patients were classified as active and non-active disease based on systemic lupus erythematosus disease activity index 2000 (SLEDAI-2K).
Results
Patients with SLE (Male/Female 5/58, Age = 39 ± 13.5 yrs, 50/63 with lupus nephritis) compared to healthy Controls (HC), had significantly increased levels of neutrophils, 4728 (3200) vs. 3400 (1100)/μL, P < 0.001 and neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio 3.08 (3.7) vs. 1.9 (1.2), P < 0.001, reduced Lymphocytes 1537 (871) vs. 2000 (1000)/μL, P < 0.001, CD19 78.5 (144) vs. 186 (100) P < 0.001 and their subtypes IgD+CD27−, IgD+CD27+, IgD−CD27+, IgD−CD27− [39 (101) vs. 107 (76) P = <0.001, 4.3 (9.1) vs. 17 (27) <0.001, 15.7 (18) vs. 26 (44) <0.001, 10.7 (20) vs. 19 (23) 0.003 respectively). TFH1 and TFICOS proportion predominated in SLE patients (P = 0.005, P = 0.02) as well as the ratio of TFH1/TFH2 (P = 0.008).
There were no significant differences in B lymphocytes between patients with active (n = 32) and non-active (n = 31) disease, although a substantial redistribution of B cell subpopulations included increase in IgD−-CD27− cells. In non-active SLE patients (SLEDAI-2K ≤4) strong correlations were evident between TF with CD19, IgD+CD27−, IgD+CD27+, IgD−CD27+ and IgD−CD27− (r = 0.6, P = 0.04; r = 0.6, P = 0.04; r = 0.6, P = 0.02; r = 0.7, P = 0.003, respectively). Moreover, IgD−CD27+ cells also correlated with TFH1, TFH2, TFH17 (r = 0.7, P = 0.01; r = 0.7, P = 0.01; r = 0.6, P = 0.02, respectively). No such correlations were evident in the active SLE group (SLEDAI-2K >4).
Conclusion
Immune alterations still exist in non-active SLE, including redistribution of B lymphocyte subtypes and their significant cross talk with peripheral TF cells, which may act as a memory reservoir to sustain B lymphocytes activation.

title: #3515 Diabetes insipidus induced by eosinophilic granuloma from pulmonary paragonimiasis: a case report
authors: Maribel Alquizar; Reina Lynn Antonio; Myrna Ngo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diabetes insipidus (DI) typically causes hypernatremia, but in rare cases like Paragonimiasis, which can lead to eosinophilic granulomatosis and result in syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, hyponatremia can occur even in the presence of DI.
Method
We present a case of a 37-year-old cachectic Filipino female with a history of possible resistant tuberculosis (TB). Despite extensive treatment, her condition did not improve, leading to admission due to severe pulmonary distress. During her hospital course, she experienced chronic polyuria, and her serum sodium levels remained low-normal, with episodes of hyponatremia. Due to inadequate clinical response to treatment, further investigation ultimately confirmed Paragonimiasis as the underlying etiology.
Results
Upon admission, a complete blood count revealed leukocytosis with a predominance of neutrophils and a significantly elevated eosinophil count. A high-resolution chest CT scan was subsequently performed, revealing multiple small non-calcified and calcified nodules scattered throughout both lungs. title: #824 PKD1 gene mutations as a key determinant of early onset and accelerated progression in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
authors: Tsielestina Poulli; Maria Konsta; Maria Varveri; Leandros Lazaros; Eirini Evangelou; Dimitra Gkalitsiou; Angeliki Poula; Niki Markou; Eleni Frangou; George Tsirpanlis
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is a genetically heterogeneous disorder primarily attributed to mutations in the PKD1 and PKD2 genes, leading to the formation of renal cysts and eventual progression to end-stage renal disease (ESRD). This study aims to investigate the clinical and demographic correlations in ADPKD patients with different genetic mutations, with a focus on understanding how these genetic variations influence disease onset, progression, and severity.
Method
In this study, demographic, clinical, laboratory, imaging, and genetic data were collected and analyzed from a cohort of 135 patients attending the ADPKD outpatient clinic at our hospital. All participants underwent genetic testing (including targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) of over 600 phenotypically relevant genes, Sanger sequencing, and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA)). Based on the genetic findings, patients were classified into five groups: (1) those with mutations in PKD1, (2) mutations in PKD2, (3) mutations in other genes (GANAB, IFT140, DNAJB11, etc.), (4) mutations in PKD1 combined with mutations in other genes (PKD1+PKHD1 heterozygosis, PKD1+COL4A4, etc.), and (5) patients with no detectable genetic mutations.
Results
Patients with PKD1 mutations had an earlier median age of diagnosis (20.5 years, IQR: 12–31) compared to PKD2 (27.5 years, IQR: 21–36) and other groups (P = 0.002). Early onset diagnosis (before 15 years of age) was predominantly seen in PKD1 patients (24 out of 27 cases). First degree relatives of PKD1 patients developed ESRD earlier (median 51 years, IQR: 45–58) than those in other groups (PKD2 median 60.5 years, IQR: 54–75; other mutations median 57.5 years, IQR: 50–65) (P = 0.02). Hypertension was more common and developed earlier in PKD1 patients (mean age 30.3 years, SD ± 10.3) compared to PKD2 (mean age 40 years, SD ±9.4) and other groups (P = 0.0005). Additionally, PKD1 patients exhibited significantly higher total kidney volume (TKV) (median 1005.6 mL) and height-adjusted TKV (median 584 mL) compared to PKD2 patients (median TKV 920 mL, height-adjusted TKV 502 mL) (P = 0.04 and P = 0.02, respectively). The Mayo Clinic Imaging categories (A–E) demonstrated significant variation, with 44% of PKD1 patients classified as D and E, in contrast to only 11% of PKD2 patients. The PROPKD score, reflecting disease severity, was notably higher in PKD1 patients (mean 5.8, SD ±1.8) and PKD1 combined with other mutations (mean 6 ± 0) compared to PKD2 (mean 2.3 ± 1.6), with a highly significant p-value (<0.0001). No statistically significant differences in the aforementioned parameters were observed between patients with PKD1 truncating and non-truncating variants, except, as is expected in PROPKD score (6.3 ± 1.6 vs 4.3 ± 1.4, P = 0.0001). Finally patients with frameshift PKD1 variants tend to have higher height-adjusted TKV compared to patients with other variant types (median 958 vs 428, 838, 656 and 409 ml/min in nonsense, splicing, CNV—large deletions, missense and non-frameshift, P = 0.08).
Conclusion
The findings emphasize the pivotal role of PKD1 gene mutations in driving early disease onset and accelerated progression in ADPKD, as evidenced by earlier age at diagnosis, earlier hypertension onset, increased total kidney volume (TKV), and elevated PROPKD scores among patients with PKD1 mutations. These results highlight the importance of genetic profiling to better understand the clinical heterogeneity of ADPKD and to improve guidance in patient management.

title: #1795 Next-generation sequencing in chronic kidney disease of unknown etiology: a step toward precision medicine
authors: Vaibhav Tiwari; Tarun Kumar; Anil Kumar Bhalla; Vinant Bhargava; Anurag Gupta; Ashwani Gupta; Manish Malik; Rajdeb Saha; Devinder Singh Rana
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects over 850 million people globally and is a significant contributor to mortality and morbidity. Approximately 10% of adult CKD cases are hereditary, predominantly involving autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) and other ciliopathies, glomerular diseases, and tubulopathies. CKD of unknown etiology (CKD-U) poses diagnostic and management challenges, particularly in advanced stages where renal biopsy is uninformative.
Method
A cross-sectional observational study was conducted at Sir Ganga Ram Hospital, New Delhi. Patients with CKD-U were recruited and underwent clinical evaluation, laboratory investigations, and genetic testing via next-generation sequencing (NGS). The analysis included genetic variant classification and assessment of pathogenicity based on American College of Medical Genetics guidelines. Patients were categorized into subgroups based on disease phenotype, and diagnostic yield was analyzed for each subgroup. The study also evaluated the implications of genetic findings on patient management, including treatment changes, donor selection, and genetic counseling.
Results
Genetic testing was performed on 100 patients, revealing pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 26% of cases. Variants of uncertain significance (VUS) were identified in 35% of patients. The highest diagnostic yield was observed in tubulopathies (100%), cystic renal diseases (57.14%), and glomerular diseases (37.5%). Alport syndrome and ADPKD were the most common genetic diagnoses. Among patients with genetic diagnoses, 23.07% had revised clinical diagnoses, 30.07% had their diagnoses confirmed, and 61.5% experienced management changes. These management changes included treatment modification (19.23%), donor selection (23.07%), and family planning guidance (19.23%). Patients with pathogenic variants were younger at disease onset compared to those without genetic diagnoses. Notably, reverse phenotyping based on genetic findings led to better disease characterization and informed management in several cases.
Conclusion
NGS provided valuable insights into the genetic basis of CKD-U, enabling more precise diagnoses and personalized management strategies. These findings emphasize the utility of genetic testing in CKD-U, particularly in cases with complex phenotypes or late presentations. Broader adoption of genetic testing in CKD-U has the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, guide therapeutic decisions, and support at-risk families through genetic counseling and informed donor selection.

title: #1155 Family planning in patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease—results from the DIPAK consortium
authors: Willemijn Vrijlandt; Thomas Bais; Lisa Margot Vijn-Villalever; Stefan P Berger; Esther Meijer; Ronald Gansevoort; Margriet De Jong
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) can impact family planning, as it can result in reduced fertility, increased risks of adverse pregnancy outcomes, and a 50% chance of disease transmission to their offspring. This study explored the considerations of patients with ADPKD regarding family planning.
Method
This prospective cohort study included patients from the developing intervention strategies to halt progression of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (DIPAK) Observational study. We analysed patient demographics, disease characteristics, and reproductive outcomes. Patients with children were grouped by whether they reported that ADPKD had influenced their family size, with a specific focus on females. Non-single, childless patients aged >27 years were categorized as voluntarily or involuntarily childless. Univariable and multivariable regression analyses were conducted to identify socio-demographic and disease-related characteristics associated with dissatisfaction with family size. Satisfaction with family size and birthrates in the DIPAK-cohort were compared to data from the general Dutch population.
Results
We included 696 patients with the majority having children (n = 462, 66.3%) and being female (n = 416, 59.8%). Among them, 35 (12.4%) reported ADPKD had influenced their family size. Of the childless individuals, 16 (22.5%) were involuntarily childless. Those reporting influence of ADPKD on family size more often were female (p < 0.001), had hypertensive pregnancy complications (p = 0.026), and a Mayo imaging classification class D/E (p = 0.042). Involuntarily childless patients were more likely to report reduced fertility (p < 0.001), to be older (p = 0.034), and to have a family member with kidney failure (p = 0.013) (Fig. 1). We found no differences in the age-adjusted birth rates when we compared our cohort to the general population, but we did find slightly higher dissatisfaction rates with family size, primarily driven by by concerns about disease transmission and declining health.
Conclusion
Women with ADPKD were more likely than men to report negative influence of their disease on family size, which was linked to disease severity and pregnancy complications. Despite comparable birthrates to the general population, patients with ADPKD showed higher dissatisfaction with family size. These findings highlight the need for physicians to consider factors affecting family planning and to provide comprehensive counselling on reproductive health and genetic testing options.

title: #2531 Improvement of the diagnostic delay of primary hyperoxaluria
authors: Lara Cabezas; Cécile Acquaviva; Aurelie De Mul; Laurence Derain Dubourg; Justine Bacchetta; Sandrine Lemoine
abstract:
Background and Aims
Primary hyperoxaluria (PH) is a rare recessive autosomal genetic disease leading to abnormalities in the hepatic glyoxylate metabolism. The prognosis of the disease depends, among other factors, on patients’ age, diagnosis delay and time to initiate treatment. A diagnostic delay significantly shorter in children compared with adults (1.2 (0.1–3.0) versus 30 (17–36) years) was reported in a French cohort of PH patients diagnosed between 2015 and 2019. Since then, the development of new treatments, such as lumasiran (an RNA interference therapy), has increased awareness of the disease within the nephrology community. We aimed to evaluate whether education within the nephrology community, following the introduction of this new treatment, has contributed to reducing the diagnostic delay of PH.
Method
We report on a nationwide retrospective study including all patients that had receive a positive genetic test of PH, from our reference laboratory in Lyon between January 2020 and December 2024. Diagnosis delay was defined by the time between the first symptoms and the genetic test.
Results
A total of 54 patients were included, 31 (57%) patients were children, 25 (46%) patients were women. Forty-two (78%) patients had PH type 1, 5 (9%) had PH type 2 and 7 (13%) patients had PH type 3. Only two patients were not managed in a University Hospital. The practitioners who requested the genetic analysis were either nephrologists (23, 43%) or pediatricians (31, 57%). The diagnostic delay was still significantly shorter in children as compared to adults (0.5 (0–1.3) versus 14 (0–30) years, P < 0.05). In the pediatric population, two patients were diagnosed antenatally, one was diagnosed post-mortem and five were diagnosed during a family screening without symptoms. In the adult population, one genetic test was done to confirm the diagnosis already made and five were diagnosed during a family screening without symptoms.
Conclusion
The diagnostic delay for PH has been reduced by half over the past five years, driven by advancements in treatment and improved knowledge and awareness of the disease. This may facilitate earlier management and limit complications with appropriate therapies.

title: #689 First report of kidney failure in PEX6-related peroxisomal disorder
authors: Guillaume Buia; Xavier Zanlonghi; Marie-Pierre Audrezet; Nikola Zagorec; Elisabet Ars; Claire-Marie Dhaenens; Sylvie Odent; Emilie Cornec-Le Gall
abstract:
Background and Aims
Peroxisomes are semiautonomous subcellular organelles involved in key metabolic pathways. Biallelic pathogenic variants in any of the 14 currently known PEX proteins are responsible for a genetically heterogeneous group of multi-organ disorders named as peroxisome biogenesis disorders (PBDs). Main symptoms of PBDs spectrum include retinopathy, sensorineural hearing loss, enamel hypoplasia, liver dysfunction and neurologic disorders and prognosis ranges from relatively mild form to lethal outcome regarding to involved genes and/or pathogenic variant. PEX1 and PEX6 biallelic variants together account for up to 70% of Zellweger syndrome disorder (ZSD), a subset of PBDs. We present here for the first time evidence of renal involvement in the clinical spectrum of ZSD, previously confined to anecdotal observations of isolated kidney cysts.
Method
We conducted a detailed clinical, genetic, and biochemical evaluation of a 60-year-old female proband referred for kidney failure (KF) of unknown origin, as well as her extended family with similar clinical histories.
Results
The proband presented with a history of progressive sensorineural hearing loss from age 2, retinopathy from age 20, amelogenesis imperfecta requiring full dental extraction by age 28, proteinuric chronic kidney disease (CKD) diagnosed at 17 years (eGFR 67 mL/min/1.73 m²) and bland urinary sediment. No kidney biopsy was performed. She reached KF by age 50 and received a kidney transplant at age 51. There were no cardiac or liver disorder. Previously, two next-generation sequencing (NGS) panels targeting Usher syndrome-associated genes were inconclusive, as was a panel analyzing over 300 kidney disease-associated genes. Ultimately, an NGS retinal dystrophy panel covering 230 genes identified a biallelic missense variant in PEX6 (c.659G>T, p.Gly220Val). The variant was unanimously predicted to be pathogenic by in silico tools (Phred CADD score 26, Alpha Missense likely pathogenic). Clinical and biochemical findings, such as elevated pipecolic acid and a slight increase in very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFA), confirmed the suspected diagnosis and supported its classification as ACMG class IV. The familial history was notable. Her sister, who died young from an unknown cause, had a history of albuminuria, sensorineural hearing loss and pigmentary retinopathy. Two paternal ninth degree male cousins presented with proteinuria at age 2 and 23, progressing to CKD reaching KF at age 25 and 40, respectively. Both exhibited severe childhood-onset sensorineural hearing loss, pigmentary retinopathy, and amelogenesis imperfecta. A kidney biopsy in the first cousin at age 20 showed nonspecific glomerulosclerosis and interstitial fibrosis. He died by suicide at age 58. Segregation genetic analysis in the second cousin revealed the same biallelic variant PEX6 c.659G>T. Browsing the Genomics England 100KG database revealed no additional cases of PBD associated with kidney failure.
Conclusion
This study provides the first evidence of kidney involvement with progression to KF within the spectrum of PBDs. The phenotypic consistency among distantly related individuals and the absence of alternative pathogenic variants support a direct link between the PEX6 variant and the renal phenotype. This case highlights the importance of regular re-evaluation of KF of unknown cause, including after kidney transplantation, and underscores the critical role of comprehensive genetic analysis in uncovering previously unrecognized disease associations.

The potential pathogenicity and clinical relevance of D313Y variation in patients with FD remains debated. D313Y patients do not show clear signs of alpha-galactosidase A deficiency and Gb3 accumulation at an early stage. For this reason, other molecular biomarkers are required for patient risk stratification. The development and application of epigenetic predictors, for healthcare research has grown dramatically over the last decade. These markers also known as epigenetic clocks, can aid FD risk stratification as they resulted to be very accurate for estimating biological age in different diseases. However, data on the epigenetic clock in Fabry disease are still lacking. Our working hypothesis is that the application of epigenetic clocks to quantify the biological age of Fabry patients could provide independent prognostic information for disease risk stratification in patients harboring the D313Y mutation.
Therefore, we developed a mathematical model for biological age prediction in healthy individuals and applied it to blood samples from FD patients with the D313Y mutation to identify patterns of accelerated aging.
Method
The epigenetic clock was developed in a healthy cohort of 201 healthy subjects. FD sample was represented by a cohort including 25 untreated FD patients harboring the D313Y mutation. Genomic DNA from whole blood was extracted using a standard commercial kit. The clock includes five DNAm biomarkers strongly correlated with chronological age (ELOVL2, C1orf132, FHL2, KLF14 and TRIM59). Methylation levels were measured by using a SNaPshot assay and then through the Illumina Methylation EPICv2 Array technology.

We found a strong correlation between the epigenetic clock and chronological age in DNA samples from healthy subjects (r = 0.97) (Fig. 1).

title: #2199 Fibroblast-macrophage dynamics and midkine signaling in ischemic induced renal fibrosis
authors: Sunhwa Lee; Hyunjeong Cho; Kyu Hong Kim; Jaewoo Park; Seongmin Lee; Eunjin Bae; Yong Chul Kim; Dong Ki Kim; Kyuho Kang; Yon Su Kim; Seung Hee Yang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Understanding the process of fibrotic deposition by resident renal fibroblasts provides crucial insights into the mechanisms underlying renal fibrosis. Utilizing a unilateral ischemia-reperfusion injury (uIRI) mouse model, we aimed to identify the specific cell populations involved in fibrosis, assess how these cells are influenced by various signaling factors secreted through intercellular interactions, and characterize changes in gene expression associated with this process.
Method
To establish an acute kidney injury (AKI) to chronic kidney disease (CKD) transition model, the left kidney of mice was subjected to 30 minutes of ischemia followed by reperfusion. Kidneys were harvested on days 10 and 20 post-surgery. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was performed on whole kidney samples at each time point. Cell clustering and differential gene expression (DEG) analyses were conducted, along with analyses of incoming and outgoing interaction strengths to elucidate cell-to-cell communication dynamics.
Results
Fibroblasts and macrophages exhibited the highest incoming and outgoing interaction strengths at both days 10 and 20, highlighting their central roles in the reperfusion injury environment. These cell populations were identified as key upstream regulators in the pathophysiological progression of fibrosis. A more detailed analysis of macrophage subtypes revealed a significant increase in the proportion of IL-10-positive macrophages on day 20. Additionally, in the group analyzed 20 days post-uIRI, increased gene expression related to the midkine signaling pathway was observed, coinciding with enhanced fibroblast-macrophage interaction strength.
Conclusion
In summary, IL-10, macrophages, and fibroblasts play pivotal roles in the transition from AKI to CKD in the ischemia-reperfusion injury model. These processes appear to be regulated, at least in part, by midkine signaling, providing new insights into the molecular and cellular mechanisms of renal fibrosis.

title: #2446 Collagen IV diseases—genetic testing yield of a single-center cohort
authors: Telma Pais; Ana Patrícia Jesus; Márcia Rodrigues; José de Almeida Agapito Fonseca; Yuri Chiodo; Catarina Silveira; Sara Gonçalves; José António Lopes; Sofia Jorge
abstract:
Background and Aims
Type IV collagen is a key structural component of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM). Variants in COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5 genes disrupt GBM integrity, leading to genetic kidney diseases (KD) such as Alport syndrome and thin basement membrane nephropathy. These variants impair collagen assembly, leading to hematuria, proteinuria, and progressive kidney dysfunction. Recently, an expanded spectrum of clinical phenotypes has been attributed to type IV collagen variants, namely proteinuria, focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis and cystic KD.
Advances in molecular genetics are improving understanding of the genetic and phenotypic spectrum of type IV collagen-related nephropathies.
Method
Genetic and phenotypic characterization of the COL4 renal disease cohort of patients in the adult Nephrogenetics’ Clinic of a tertiary-level care hospital, between 2014 and 2024. Genetic testing was performed through next generation sequencing gene panels based on whole exome sequencing.
Results
Of the 332 screened patients, 41 patients (27 families) presented variants in the type IV collagen gene. Variants were reported in COL4A3 (n = 14), COL4A5 (n = 14), COL4A4 (n = 11), COL4A1 (n = 3) and COL4A6 (n = 1). Two patients had more than one identified mutation.
According to American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics criteria, variants were classified as follows: 7 pathogenic (P); 23 likely pathogenic (LP); 11 variants of uncertain significance (VUS) and 2 as likely benign.
A total of 30 patients had P/LP variants: 10 in COL4A5 (heterozygous), 1 COL4A5 heterozygous deletion, 11 in COL4A3 (10 heterozygous, 1 homozygous), 8 in COL4A4 (heterozygous).
The majority of patients were female (n = 24), and mean age at diagnosis was 48.7 ± 15.8 years. Most (n = 27) had positive family history for CKD. The most common renal presentations included chronic kidney disease (n = 23) and hematuria and/or proteinuria in the remaining patients. Six patients had kidney cysts. Hypoacusia was reported in 6 patients, and one had reduced visual acuity.
Of note, we highlight co-existing variants in other genes, in addition to P/LP COL4 variants: heterozygous CFHR3/CFHR1 deletion (2 patients); NADSYN1 LP variant (1 patient), CC2D2A LP variant (1 patient), MYH9 VUS (1 patient), KIAA0586 LP variant (1 patient).
Conclusion
Genetic testing for mutations in type IV collagen is crucial for early diagnosis, accurate classification, and prognostic assessment of hereditary kidney diseases. Genetic diagnosis also enables personalized Nephrology care in the era of precision medicine, namely for actionable genes as COL4.

title: #3572 Developing a model for nephrotoxicity testing from human proximal tubular epithelial cells derived from kidney biopsy
authors: Tadej Petreski; Luka Varda; Lidija Gradišnik; Uroš Maver; Robert Ekart; Radovan Hojs; Sebastjan Bevc
abstract:
Background and Aims
Given the rising prevalence of kidney diseases and polypharmacy in ageing populations, advanced methods for studying drug interactions and nephrotoxicity are critical. Our research aimed to develop a functional nephrotoxicity model using human cells derived from kidney biopsy to enable systematic in vitro testing of drug-induced kidney injuries, especially such caused by drug-drug interactions (DDIs) related to tubular drug secretion. Unlike existing models based on immortalised cells, these testing platforms will better replicate native renal functions, improving the relevance of results to human physiology.
Method
Isolation and cultivation of primary human adult renal proximal tubular epithelial cells (PTECs) obtained from kidney biopsy during the regular diagnostic procedure were performed and presented previously (named MFUM-RPTEC-1). For the nephrotoxicity model, solutions of cyclosporin A (CsA), omeprazole, or their combination were prepared to a final concentration of 1 µg/mL in PBS. MFUM-RPTEC-1 were seeded at 10,000 cells/well on a P96 plate, incubated overnight, and treated with serial dilutions of the solutions (1 µg/mL to 0.0625 µg/mL). After 24 hours, an MTT assay was performed to assess cell viability. Absorbance for the violet formazan was measured at 570 nm using a Varioskan spectrophotometer.
Results
Our results demonstrated that MFUM-RPTEC-1 maintained stable viability when exposed to therapeutic concentrations of CsA and omeprazole, confirming the applicability of the developed model for further testing toward mechanistic nephrotoxicity studies. Results even showed an enhanced proliferation when a combination of CsA and omeprazole was used. Possible explanations for these phenomena might include drug interactions at multiple levels, including transporters like OCT-2, which reduce the uptake of nephrotoxic agents and exhibit nephroprotective effects.
Conclusion
Our model validates the safety of clinically relevant concentrations of CsA and omeprazole. Additionally, preliminary findings suggest potential pharmacokinetic interactions between these drugs, warranting further investigation. By offering mechanistic insights into DDIs at the level of tubular secretion, the model indicates the possibility of detecting nephrotoxicity and nephroprotective effects occurring through a reduced uptake and accumulation in PTECs.

title: #1375 Correlating symptom burden with polycystic liver volume progression in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
authors: Carolin Brigl; Julia Münster; Constantin Aaron Wolff; Robin Schmidt; Thula Walter-Rittel; Kai-Uwe Eckardt; Joost Ph Drenth; Ria Anne-Rose Schönauer; Jan Halbritter
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is one of the most common genetic kidney diseases leading to kidney failure and is usually due to pathogenic variants in either PKD1 or PKD2. The most common extrarenal manifestation is Polycystic Liver Disease (PLD) which can result in a high symptom burden, even requiring liver transplantation in rare cases. The polycystic liver disease questionnaire (PLD-Q) was developed to better quantify these PLD related symptoms [1]. The score ranges from 1–100 points with 32 being the threshold for treatment [2]. Recently, our group proposed three progression groups (PG) to better predict PLD progression based on age-adjusted normalized Total Liver Volume (nTLV) [3]. The groups range from 1 to 3 and each show an increasing risk of patients experiencing a PLD-related hospitalization. The PGs were validated in both patients with ADPKD and isolated ADPLD, however, validation with regards to a patient reported outcome measure (PROM), such as the PLD-Q, is still needed.
Method
In a tertiary care center, ADPKD patients were selected based on the following criteria: confirmed genetic diagnosis of typical ADPKD (PKD1 or PKD2 genes), Magnetic Resonance Imaging or Computer Tomography performed and consent given. Patients who had received a liver transplant or were pregnant were excluded. Subsequently, the patients who had completed a PLD-Q in routine care were identified and underwent semi-automated liver segmentation of available imaging. Additionally, Total Kidney Volumes were obtained through the ellipsoid formula.
Results
Currently, 155 patients have been included in the study. Preliminary analysis shows the cohort includes almost twice as many females as males (101:54) with a mean age of 47.5 years (±1.0 SEM). The PLD-Q scores show a normal distribution with a mean of 32.3 (±1.5 SEM). [Fig. 1a] Almost half of the patients (n = 75) scored above the 32-point threshold. Females had a significantly higher mean score of 36.8 (±1.9 SEM) compared to 23.9 (±2.1 SEM) for males (Welch's t test P < 0.0001). Thus far, 78 patients (50.3%) have received semi-automated liver segmentation. When grouping patients into the three PGs, the mean PLD-Q score rose in each successive group: 27.8 (±3.7 SEM) in PG1, 33.2 (±3.4 SEM) in PG2 and 39.8 (±5.3 SEM) in PG3. [Fig. 1b] However, the differences in this early cohort were not statistically significant (Games-Howell‘s multiple comparisons test PG1-PG2 P = 0.533, PG2-PG3 P = 0.556 and PG3-PG1 P = 0.169). Finally, PLD-Q scores were compared for genetic subgroups: the mean score for ADPKD-PKD2 patients (34.9 ± 3.0 SEM) was slightly higher than that of ADPKD-PKD1 (31.4 ± 1.8 SEM), without reaching statistical significance (Welch's t test P = 0.315) [Fig. 1c].
Conclusion
Preliminary analysis of the study cohort confirmed the long-standing observations of a more severe course of PLD in females. While renal outcomes are known to be worse in ADPKD-PKD1 as compared to ADPKD-PKD2, our data suggests that liver outcomes are not milder in ADPKD-PKD2. A final statistical analysis and inclusion of an independent validation cohort will fully contextualize these findings. In summary, nTLV-based progression groups appear to correlate with symptom burden and hold promise for guiding treatment for this prevalent manifestation of ADPKD.

title: #2225 The effect of fluconazole on polyuria and urine concentration ability in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
authors: Line Aas Mortensen; Claus Bistrup; Boye L Jensen; Jens Michael Hertz; Kai Schmidt-Ott; Enno Klussman; Christian Hinze; Gitte Rye Hinrichs
abstract:
Background and Aims
Congenital nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (NDI) is a rare disease with severe polyuria, often >10L/day, polydipsia and risk of life threatening dehydration upon water deprivation. It is primarily caused by loss-of function mutations of the vasopressin-2 receptor gene, causing inability to insert otherwise functional aquaporin 2 (AQP2) in the apical membrane of the principal cells in the renal collecting ducts. No causal treatment exists. Administration of fluconazole, an antimycotic drug, increased plasma membrane localization of AQP2 and reduced urinary output in the absence of vasopressin in tolvaptan treated mice. We aimed to test if fluconazole reduces diuresis and improves urinary concentration ability in patients with NDI. We present the interim analysis of the first four patients to complete the study as defined in the protocol.
Method
The study is an ongoing Danish-German, open-label, non-randomized intervention study. The aim is to include 10 male patients with X-linked NDI due to a verified mutation in AVPR2. The patients were treated with fluconazole 400 mg per day for two weeks. This was extended to three weeks if there were indications of a beneficial effect. 24-hour urine samples, blood samples, body weight and body composition monitoring (BCM) were performed weekly during the intervention. A water deprivation test was performed before and after two weeks of treatment. During the water deprivation test, blood and urine samples were obtained hourly along with body weight and BCM measurements. Plasma sodium concentration above 150 mmol/L or a weight loss of 3% body weight from baseline during the water deprivation test were defined as stop criteria.
The primary outcomes were 24-hour urinary volume and the urinary concentration ability evaluated urine osmolality and time to reach the stop criteria in the water deprivation test. Secondary outcomes were urine- and plasma osmolality, plasma vasopressin, co-peptin and electrolyte concentrations, micturition frequency and the abundance of AQP2 in urinary exosomes.
Results
Four patients have completed the study. Median age was 39 years (range 32 to 57). One patient terminated the treatment after two weeks (ID2) due to increasing diuresis after initiating fluconazole, whereas the remaining patients completed three weeks of treatment. Baseline 24-hour diuresis ranged from 4846 mL/day to 13270 mL/day. Fluconazole did not decrease diuresis in any of the four participants (Fig. 1A) nor impact 24-hour urinary osmolality (Fig. 1B). Two patients completed 8 hours of water deprivation without fulfilling the stop criteria at baseline and their maximal urine osmolality during water deprivation did not increase after two weeks of fluconazole. Of the remaining two participants, one increased his urinary concentration ability to a maximum of 179 mOsm/L after fluconazole compared to 101 mOsm/L at baseline (ID4, Fig. 1C and D) and completed 7 hours of water deprivation before fulfilling the stop criteria compared to 4 hours at baseline. The other participant (ID1) did not increase his maximal urinary osmolality nor the tolerated water deprivation time. Fluconazole was well tolerated in all participants with no reported side effects. Analyses of plasma osmolality, vasopressin, co-peptin and urinary AQP2 are pending.
Conclusion
Fluconazole for two to three weeks did not reduce polyuria in four patients with NDI. Two participants had a weak phenotype allowing 8 hours of water deprivation without severe dehydration or hypernatremia despite genetically proven mutations in the AVPR2 gene. One patient had a clinically meaningful improvement of his urine concentration ability albeit still far from normal level. Based on the results of this interim analysis, a beneficial effect of fluconazole in selected patients cannot be ruled out. It is primarily caused by loss-of function mutations of the vasopressin-2 receptor gene, causing inability to insert otherwise functional aquaporin 2 (AQP2) in the apical membrane of the principal cells in the renal collecting ducts. No causal treatment exists. Administration of fluconazole, an antimycotic drug, increased plasma membrane localization of AQP2 and reduced urinary output in the absence of vasopressin in tolvaptan treated mice. title: #2585 Life-threatening hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis after positively charged amino acid infusion for renal protection during Peptide receptor radionuclide therapy for metastatic neuroendocrine tumor: a case report and proposed mechanisms
authors: Gil Bar; Doron Schwartz; Yuval Horowich; Inna Ospovat; Ayelet Grupper; Orit Kliuk Ben-Bassat
abstract:
Background and Aims
Peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) is a systemic radiotherapy with targeted radioligands used for the treatment of metastatic neuroendocrine tumors (NETs). Tubular uptake of the radioligands exposes kidney cells to radiation, with a potential risk for nephrotoxicity. Co-administration of positively charged amino acid (AA) solutions is a standard renoprotective regimen for patients at high risk of kidney injury.
Method:
Results
We report a case of a 69-year-old man with a medical history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and CKD3b, admitted for administration of PRRT for metastatic NET. The patient received a renoprotective regimen with positively charged AA lysine and arginine solution at a dose three times higher than the recommended protocol, administered at a rapid infusion rate.
Three hours after therapy completion, the patient developed cardiogenic shock secondary to extreme hyperkalemia (9 mmol/L), severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.07, HCO3⁻ 9.1 mmHg, lactate 7 mmol/L, with an anion gap of 4), and anuric acute kidney injury (AKI) on CKD. Possible mechanisms for hyperkalemia included movement of potassium from cells into extracellular fluid due to cationic AA (lysine and arginine) entering muscle cells in exchange for potassium, hyperosmolarity of the AA solution causing water to diffuse out of cells (carrying potassium as “solvent drag”), and metabolic acidosis resulting from H⁺ shifts out of cells in exchange for cationic AA, AA metabolism in the liver generating H⁺, and rapid NaCl infusion. The low and unexpected anion gap was attributed to increased concentrations of unmeasured cations (cationic AA, hyperkalemia, hypercalcemia).
Additional contributing factors included the sequence of events leading to decreased distal tubule fluid delivery and tissue hypoperfusion, secondary to cardiogenic shock, as well as the patient's baseline characteristics, including type 4 renal tubular acidosis, CKD, and medications such as ACE inhibitors.
Due to hemodynamic instability, and despite extreme hyperkalemia, the patient was initially treated with continuous venovenous hemodialysis (CVVHD) for 12 hours, resulting in significant improvement in hyperkalemia and hemodynamic stability. Inotropic support was no longer needed, and urine output improved.
Conclusion
This case emphasizes the importance of careful dosing and administration rates of positively charged AA solutions as renal protection during PRRT, particularly in patients with risk factors such as CKD, diabetes, and predisposing medications. Awareness of the potential for life-threatening complications, early recognition of symptoms, laboratory monitoring, and prompt intervention are essential for optimal management and patient safety.

title: #2978 Genetic testing outcomes: insights from a decade of experience at a single center
authors: Telma Pais; Ana Patrícia Jesus; Márcia Rodrigues; Yuri Chiodo; Catarina Silveira; José de Almeida; Agapito Fonseca; Sara Gonçalves; José António Lopes; Sofia Jorge
abstract:
Background and Aims
Continuous advances in molecular genetics have enabled the diagnosis of an increasing number of genetic kidney diseases in recent years. Establishing a Nephrogenetics' Clinic aims to contribute to better renal care, especially in the era of precision medicine. We present our experience over the past 15 years.
Method
We conducted a retrospective analysis of genetic testing performed in adult patients since 2010. Since 2015, all patients have been studied with targeted panels based on whole exome sequencing, progressively amplified according to the state of the art.
MUC1 was analyzed using Snapshot since 2014 and PKD1 with PCR long range (since 2020). Pre and post genetic counselling were performed by nephrologists and geneticists. Variants of uncertain significance (VUS) were evaluated by geneticists for segregation studies and periodically reclassified. Negative results were reviewed regularly and reanalyzed when relevant.
Results
A total of 369 index patients were studied, 173 (47%) females, mean age 51.5 years. Until mid-2023, genetic panels with ≤ 85 genes were used. Among 220 patients tested, 15.4% (n = 34) were found to have pathogenic (P) or likely pathogenic (LP) variants. The remaining patients either had VUS or a single pathogenic variant in a gene with autosomal recessive inheritance (n = 85), or their results were negative (n = 101). All reported VUS were reinterpreted, with 17 being reclassified: 8 patients had their VUS upgraded to LP, while 9 were downgraded to benign.
In 2023, broader genetic panels, including copy number variation (CNV) analysis, were implemented. Since then, 29.6% (n = 24) of the 81 index cases tested with these broader panels revealed LP/P variants. We identified both a deletion and a microduplication that would have been missed without CNV analysis. Additionally, reanalysis of 24 negative samples using broader panels resulted in positive findings in four of them (17%).
Phenotypes at presentation were: 38% glomerular disease, 29% uncharacterized chronic kidney disease (CKD), 18% tubulo-interstitial, 11% cystic and 4% others.
Positive results (P and LP variants) in 69 index patients, of which we highlight: 30 COL4; 5 MUC; 1 biallelic REN; 4 UMOD; 2 INF2, 3 PAX2, 4 PKD1, 5 HNF1β; 15 high-risk APOL1 genotypes. Additionally, 1 family (4 patients) was studied for the MUC1 variant by PacBio with positive results.
Conclusion
Of note, COL4 variants were the most frequent genetic cause of monogenic CKD. ADPKD is probably under-represented in our cohort due to selective testing of atypical cases. The use of broader gene panels and the systematic re-evaluation of variant classifications are pivotal in nephropathy genetic testing. These approaches enable accurate initial diagnoses, facilitating effective patient treatment, family screening, and counseling.

title: #3516 Genetic insights into persistent hypouricemia in adults: novel findings from a nephrogenetic clinic
authors: Ahmet Burak Dirim; Seda Safak; Yağmur Tahıllıoğlu; Mirioglu Safak; Ayse Serra Artan; Ozgur Akin Oto; Savas Ozturk; Tugba Kalayci; Leyli Senturk; İlknur Suer; Sukru Ozturk; Halil Yazici
abstract:
Background and Aims
Persistent hypouricemia (HU) (serum uric acid <2.5 mg/dL) is a rare condition. HU due to rare genetic causes, without full-blown Fanconi syndrome (FS) (characterized by glucosuria and hyperuricosuria alongside aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, and renal tubular acidosis), is typically associated with familial renal HU due to SLC12A22 and SLC2A9 variants, as well as xanthinuria linked to XDH and MOCOS variants.
Method
Nine patients were included. Malnutrition and full-blown FS were excluded. Clinical Exome Sequencing was performed, and pathogenicity of variants were evaluated with 1-SIFT, Polyphen2, and Mutation Taster prediction tools.
Results
8 of 9 patients had at least one rare variant as a possible cause of HU. 5 patients had isolated HU, while 3 had both glucosuria and HU without other signs of FS. One patient with recurrent acute kidney injury had a homozygous variant in SLC2A9. Two patients with nephrolithiasis (NL) were diagnosed with xanthinuria type 1 and type 2. The patient with xanthinuria type 2 also had concurrent glucosuria due to additional heterozygous SLC5A2 variant. Homozygous and heterozygous SLC22A12 variants were detected in 2 patients with persistent HU. One patient with glucosuria and HU due to hyperuricosuria had no variants related to HU, but compound heterozygous SLC5A2 variants. The last case had a rare heterozygous FTL (Ferritin-light-chain) variant. This patient had hyperuricosuria. Transcriptomic and single-cell RNA databases showed that FTL has high expression in the proximal tubule, suggesting it may be a candidate gene.
Conclusion
Genetic HU is rare but often overlooked entity. This study demonstrates, for the first time, the co-occurrence of renal glucosuria and familial renal HU, as well as the coexistence of xanthinuria type 2 and renal glucosuria in two patients. Rare FTL variants have not been previously reported in the literature as a possible cause of renal HU. Our study expands the spectrum of genetic findings of HU. Based on our findings, genetic studies have high diagnostic accuracy and should be used in patients with HU. Additionally, they may identify new candidate genes.

title: #422 Evolutionary roots of renal tubulopathies: integrating Homer Smith's hypothesis with novel phylogenomic methodologies
authors: Camillo Tancredi Strizzi; Tony Chen; Barbara Natterson-Horowitz
abstract:
Background and Aims
In his landmark 1953 publication, From Fish to Philosopher, physiologist Homer Smith presented the evolutionary history of renal function as a source of insights for medicine. Seven decades later, it is increasingly clear that the evolutionary story underlying the emergence of renal physiology can provide novel insights into the causes of and potential treatments for renal pathologies. Why are humans vulnerable to renal tubulopathies (RT)? Shouldn't natural selection have favored phenotypes resistant to illness? The evolutionary story of this susceptibility can provide novel insights with salience for research and clinical practice. Importantly, not all traits are adaptive. While natural selection produces adaptive phenotypes, evolutionary trade-offs may lead to both non-adaptive and adaptive characteristics. Emerging phylogenomic methods can help identify potential selective pressures shaping the evolutionary emergence of specific disease vulnerabilities. Here, a novel methodology is used to uncover the origins of RT vulnerability from the dawn of cellular life to modern human kidney.
Method
This methodology analyses RT gene sets to identify the biologically beneficial processes underlying vulnerability to disease. Gene curation from DisGeNET (v7.0) and MalaCards (v1.14) identified genes for seven RT chosen for their well-characterized genetic bases and relevance to human renal physiology: Fanconi, Bartter, Gitelman, Liddle, Gordon, Distal Renal Tubular Acidosis, and Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus. Phylostratigraphic analysis (PhyloFastStrat, v0.2.2) was performed to map the genes’ emergence and adaptations, tracing their origins from cellular life (∼3.6 billion years ago) to Homo sapiens. Gene enrichment analysis (GOEnrichr v3.0) was performed on each set of genes to elucidate their biological, molecular, and cellular roles in renal physiology.
Results
While analyses encompassed seven RT, evolutionary histories underlying only two, Fanconi and Gitelman, are featured in this abstract. Fanconi syndrome (63 genes) exhibits a distinctive evolutionary trajectory, with early emergence during the cellular organism stage, highlighting the foundational role in solute transport, metabolic homeostasis and waste excretion. As life transitioned to multicellularity, additional genes emerged, particularly during the metazoan stage (∼770 MYA), enabling tissue-specific solute transport. A notable peak in Mammalia (∼220 MYA) reflects functional diversification to terrestrial life adaptations, followed by core gene conservation (Fig. 1). Gitelman syndrome (34 genes) also shows ancient origins, with high initial genes emergence at the cellular organism stage. Key innovations occurred in jawed vertebrates (∼420 MYA), with the development of complex ion transport systems, land-dwelling tetrapods (∼370 MYA), refining mechanisms for electrolyte and water conservation on dry land, and mammals (∼125 MYA), specializing the distal nephron to meet metabolic demands of warm-blooded physiology. A minor uptick in Homo sapiens suggests slight genetic fine-tuning in renal electrolyte handling, potentially reflecting unique human dietary or environmental adaptations (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
This study highlights the evolutionary trajectory of genes implicated in RT suggesting that vulnerability emerged as an evolutionary trade-off for positive selection for biological processes critical to tubular function. RT vulnerability was linked to several evolutionary milestones including the emergence of ion transport systems, terrestrial adaptations, and tubule refinement. The ancient origins of tubular pathology offer a novel framework for a strengthened understanding of the triggers and natural history of these often enigmatic disorders. This finding is aligned with the prescient premise of Homer Smith's 1953 publication.

title: #1165 HNF1B genotype-phenotype correlation in renal patients from Galicia
authors: Eloísa Sánchez Cazorla; Pedro Fortes González; Adela Urisarri Ruiz de Cortázar; Maria Garcia Murias; Ana Maria Barcia de la Iglesia; Laura Núñez González; Candido Diaz Rodriguez; Noa Carrera Cachaza; Miguel Garcia Gonzalez
abstract:
Background and Aims
The HNF1B gene encodes a transcription factor that regulates gene expression in various tissues, including pancreatic beta-cells, kidneys, liver, intestines, and neurons, playing crucial roles during embryonic and postnatal development. Genes regulated by Hnf1b are involved in key processes such as nephrogenesis, ion transport, cellular polarity, tight junctions, primary cilia development, and renal metabolism. Consequently, pathogenic alterations in HNF1B disrupt its molecular functions, leading to a broad spectrum of renal and extrarenal manifestations. Patients with HNF1B alterations are categorized into three groups based on the type of genetic alteration: (1) 17q12 microdeletion carriers; (2) truncating point mutation carriers; and (3) missense point mutation carriers. Our group has established a large cohort of renal patients with suspected hereditary kidney disease, predominantly from Galicia (approximately 76%), a region in western Europe characterized by unique geographical, ethnic, and consanguinity patterns. These factors enhance the genetic value of this population for genotype-phenotype correlation studies. This study aims to establish genotype-phenotype correlations for HNF1B variants in a Galician cohort.
Method
This retrospective, observational, multicenter study analyzed a large cohort of patients with suspected hereditary kidney diseases enriched in the Galician population. Genetic studies were performed using Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) and/or Sanger sequencing. Patients carrying HNF1B alterations were selected from this cohort. A total of 31 subjects (27 probands and 4 relatives) were included, and detailed clinical data were collected and analyzed.
Results
Among probands, 55.55% carried the 17q12 microdeletion, 18.52% carried truncating alterations, and 25.93% exhibited missense alterations. Over 60% of probands presented with hyperechogenicity, renal cysts, and/or hypomagnesemia. Additional observed manifestations included hyperuricemia, Congenital Anomalies of the Kidney and Urinary Tract (CAKUT), diabetes/ Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY), hypertransaminasemia, as well as pancreatic, hepatic and psychiatric/neurological anomalies. Distinct trends were observed across the three alteration groups for clinical features such as renal cysts, initial clinical suspicion, hyperuricemia, and hypomagnesemia.
Conclusion
This study highlights the broad and variable multi-systemic manifestations associated with HNF1B alterations and provides valuable insights into genotype-phenotype correlations. Proving that accurate genetic diagnosis is essential for providing personalized genetic counseling and implementing appropriate follow-up care based on the specific mutation type.

title: #1593 Cystine-binding drugs are poorly available for the treatment of cystinuria
authors: Rik Olde Engberink; Roos Marsman; Giovanna Capolongo; Marie Courbebaisse; Bertrand Knebelmann; Francesco Trepiccione; Francesco Emma; Aude Servais; Elena Levtchenko
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive disease characterized by defective transepithelial transport of cystine, lysine, arginine, and ornithine in the renal proximal tubule. The high urine cystine concentrations put cystinuria patients at great risk for the development of cystine stones. The treatment consists of lifestyle advices, hyperhydration and alkalizing supplements, whereas in refractory cases cystine-binding drugs, such as tiopronin or D-penicillamine, are used to lower the risk for renal stone disease and subsequent chronic kidney disease. Because of limited number of manufacturers and high costs, the availability of cystine-binding drugs is highly variable.
Method
An online questionnaire was distributed to members of the European Reference Network for Rare Kidney Diseases (ERKNet) on behalf of the Metabolic Nephropathy Workgroup to assess the availability of cystine-binding drugs for patients with cystinuria. Additional questions about the local availability of tiopronin and/or D-penicillamine were asked when physicians prescribed these drugs in the last two years. We excluded participants who completed less than 95% of the questionnaire. The collected data were analyzed using descriptive statistics.
Results
We included 40 physicians from 15 countries (Fig. 1A), including pediatric nephrologists (55%), adult nephrologists (40%) and adult urologists (5%). title: #2194 Effect of genotype on renal outcome among the patients with inherited cystic kidney disease
authors: Hayne Cho Park; Dha Woon Im; Yong Chul Kim; Curie Ahn; Yaerim Kim; Hee Gyung Kang; Jungmin Choi; Yun Kyu Oh
abstract:
Background and Aims
Inherited cystic kidney disease is a constellation of heterogenous genetic diseases that commonly share renal cystic phenotype. We have analyzed renal outcome (annual change of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and total kidney volume (TKV)) among Korean genetic cohort of inherited cystic kidney disease.
Method
Primary genetic analysis was conducted using a targeted gene panel including 89 ciliopathy-associated genes. A total of 1319 patients were included in the cross-sectional analysis. A total of 502 patients with longitudinal data without history of Tolvaptan treatment were included in the renal outcome analysis. Genotypes were classified into PKD1, PKD2, or minor genotypes.
Results
PKD1 group showed younger age at diagnosis of cystic kidney disease and hypertension, and higher proportion of rapid progressor. Interestingly, the patients with minor genotypes showed a significantly higher rate of diabetes (11.6%) and proteinuria (3.6 ± 25.4 g/g) compared to other genotypes. In addition, the minor genotype group showed smaller kidneys (858 ± 913 mL) with atypical cystic phenotype (Mayo class 2). In longitudinal analysis, PKD1 genotype showed faster eGFR decline (−2.44 ± 6.1 mL/min/1.73 m2/yr) compared to PKD2 (−1.09 ± 8.5 mL/min/1.73 m2/yr) and minor genotypes (−0.5 ± 5.4 mL/min/1.73 m2/yr, P = 0.037). PKD1 group showed faster growth of kidneys (40.2 ± 188.2 mL per year) while PKD2 (9.6 ± 315.2 mL per year) and minor genotype group (13.4 ± 55.7 mL per year) demonstrated minimal TKV growth during study period (P = 0.635).
Conclusion
PKD1 genotype demonstrated poorer renal outcome compared to other genotypes. Minor genotypes showed favorable renal outcome with minimal growth of TKV.

title: #3206 An in vivo study of novel genetic modifiers in autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD)
authors: Soniya Malik; Paraskevi Goggolidou
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) is a rare genetic disorder that manifests with bilaterally enlarged, cystic kidneys, hepatic fibrosis and pulmonary hypoplasia, with death reported in around 30%–50% of affected neonates. Mutations in PKHD1 and DZIP1L have been identified as causative genes for ARPKD with both genes localising to the primary cilium. Ciliary signalling pathways, such as Wnt signalling, have been investigated to dissect potential molecular mechanisms of ARPKD, however, these remain unclear. To overcome this, researchers have tried to develop rodent models that replicate human ARPKD and thus far, this has proven challenging.
Method
Using our current understanding regarding pathogenic variants in ARPKD patients, we have developed the novel Pkhd1T36M/T36M mouse model that carries the most common and severe truncating mutation in human ARPKD. For this study, we aimed to characterise this model by performing experiments in the kidney, liver and lung, across different developmental stages, as presented in human ARPKD.
Results
From our data, we found that the kidney phenotype in Pkhd1T36M/T36Mmice was overall mild, presenting as tubular dilation from around P2, and cytoskeletal defects in aged mice. Furthermore, novel Pkhd1 targets, including Muc1, Tacstd2 and Epor, were identified via RNA-sequencing analysis with metabolic pathways such as oxidative phosphorylation appearing dysregulated. In the liver, Pkhd1T36M/T36M mice presented progressive liver fibrosis and increased canonical Wnt signalling. Excitingly, for the first time, we provide evidence that the lung may be a primary characteristic of ARPKD, rather than a secondary consequence, with mutations in Pkhd1 resulting in changes in the gross morphological structure of Pkhd1T36M/T36M mouse lungs and aberrant expression of key PKD and Wnt signalling genes, including Pkd1, Atmin and Vangl2. Interestingly, RNA-sequencing analysis also identified Aqp2, Foxf1 and Igfbp2 as novel Pkhd1 targets in the lung, as well as dysregulation of STAT3 signalling in Pkhd1T36M/T36M mice.
Conclusion
Together, this data further highlights potential mechanisms of action for the lung phenotype and sets the ground for future investigations to dissect these relationships. Overall, our study shows that the Pkhd1T36M/T36M mouse exhibits an ARPKD-like phenotype and could be a useful tool to advance our understanding of ARPKD and the potential molecular mechanisms involved.

title: #3313 A novel identification of anti-hypertensive drug spironolactone as an inhibitor of paraoxonase 2 lactonase and anti-ROS activities
authors: Yoko Suzumoto; Eros Antonio Lampitella; Maria Marone; Giovambattista Capasso; Giuseppe Manco; Francesco Trepiccione
abstract:
Background and Aims
Paraoxonase 2 (PON2) is a membrane-associated antioxidant protein also showing hydrolytic activity against 3-oxo-C12 homoserine lactone (HSL), a signaling molecule produced by gram-negative bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa [1]. Previous reports demonstrated that PON2 is expressed in the principal cells of distal nephron where PON2 may play a regulatory role on epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) [2, 3]. Recently, we have discovered that PON2 expression in rat renal cortex is associated with ENaC channel function. These regulations might be dependent on aldosterone, since treatment with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist spironolactone reversed PON2 expression profile (Suzumoto et al., unpublished data). Because spironolactone contains a lactone residue, we hypothesized there might be a direct interaction between spironolactone and PON2, which may affect ENaC function and ROS levels in distal nephron. Therefore, in the current study we aimed at investigating the physical interaction between spironolactone and PON2 which could modulate PON2 lactonase activity and anti-ROS function in distal nephron.
Method
Human recombinant PON2 (rPON2) was overexpressed in HEK293T cells, and antimycin A-induced superoxide generation was evaluated using dihydroethidium with and without pre-treatment with spironolactone. For the lactonase activity assay, rPON2 was expressed in E. coli and purified from inclusion bodies. PON2 kinetic parameters were measured using 3-oxo-C12 HSL as substrate in the presence of spironolactone as a putative inhibitor. In order to integrate with kinetic data, molecular dockings using PON2 model with spironolactone as well as 3-oxo-C12 HSL were performed.
Results
PON2-overexpressed HEK293T cells showed lower superoxide generation induced by antimycin A treatment with respect to mock-transfected cells. However, this effect was abolished by pre-treatment with spironolactone. Furthermore, kinetic measurements utilizing purified rPON2 revealed spironolactone inhibits lactonase activity of PON2, suggesting the direct interaction between PON2 and spironolactone. In particular, we observed a correlation between Vmax and spironolactone concentrations. These kinetic results indicate a mixed type enzyme inhibition of rPON2 activity by spironolactone, with different binding of spironolactone to free PON2 with respect to PON2-substrate complex. The molecular docking analyses demonstrated that binding sites for spironolactone (inhibitor) and 3-oxo-C12 HSL (substrate) are partially overlapping in the proximity of PON2 active site, which indicates a competition between spironolactone and PON2 substrate binding.
Conclusion
Our study demonstrated that anti-hypertensive drug spironolactone inhibits both PON2 lactonase and antioxidant activities presumably through binding near the active site of PON2. Further study is required to confirm the type of inhibition and unveil the role of PON2 serving as a potential ROS scavenger mechanism protecting the kidneys from aldosterone-promoted renal pathologies, such as hypertension, inflammation and fibrosis.

title: #3599 ADTKD diagnosis: an evolving challenge
authors: Telma Pais; Márcia Rodrigues; José de Almeida Agapito Fonseca; Ana Patrícia Jesus; Yuri Chiodo; Catarina Silveira; Sara Gonçalves; José António Lopes; Sofia Jorge
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (ADTKD) encompasses a group of hereditary kidney disorders characterized by tubulointerstitial fibrosis. These conditions typically follow an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern and are subclassified based on their genetic cause when identified. Pathogenic variants in UMOD, MUC1, REN, HNF1B, and SEC61A1 have been implicated in ADTKD pathogenesis. Advances in molecular diagnostics have improved genetic identification, though the true prevalence is likely underestimated. We present a cohort of ADTKD patients identified in the Nephrogenetics’ Clinic of our department between 2010 and 2024.
Method
Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) of unknown cause and undefined phenotype, or those exhibiting a renal phenotype suggestive of chronic interstitial nephritis, particularly with a family history of similar CKD, were referred to the Nephrogenetics’ Clinic for ADTKD investigation.
Genetic testing methods evolved over time: Before 2015, Sanger sequencing was used. Since 2015, a stepwise genetic approach was used: (1) next-generation sequencing (NGS) for UMOD, REN, HNF1B, and SEC61A1; (2) if negative, targeted analysis for the insertion of a single cytosine in the variable-number tandem repeat (VNTR) sequence of MUC1; (3) if still negative, multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) was performed to detect HNF1B deletions (P241-D2 kit, MRC-Holland).
For patients with CKD and undefined phenotype, broader NGS panels for CKD were applied. Negative results underwent periodic re-evaluation, including deeper phenotyping when possible, and re-analysis using expanded gene panels, whole-exome sequencing (WES), or additional methods in reference laboratories.
Pre-test genetic counseling was conducted by a nephrologist, while post-test counseling was performed jointly by a nephrologist and a geneticist, particularly for family screening and segregation studies.
Results
Among 35 families studied, a confirmed genetic diagnosis was obtained in 15 (43%), identifying 42 patients with ADTKD. The implicated variants were: MUC1: 5 families (18 patients); UMOD: 4 families (11 patients, all diagnosed via Sanger sequencing); HNF1B: 5 families (12 patients); REN: 1 patient with biallelic REN mutations (heterozygous).
Four families presented with an undefined phenotype: two families underwent CKD panel testing due to young age at onset; two families had a cystic kidney phenotype and were tested using a cystic kidney disease panel.
Notably, all these families harbored pathogenic or likely pathogenic HNF1B variants. One family underwent additional PacBio sequencing for MUC1 at a reference laboratory, leading to the identification of the dup60A variant in MUC1.
Re-analysis of negative results led to the identification of pathogenic variants in two additional families: COL4A3 (heterozygous) in 1 family (2 patients); SDCCAG8 (homozygous) in 1 family (2 patients). Likely pathogenic variants were identified in: PAX2 in 1 family (3 patients); PKD1 in 1 family (3 patients); COL4A5 in 1 family (3 patients).
Studies are ongoing in two families, while the remaining negative cases will undergo re-evaluation. Additionally, segregation studies are in progress for three families to assess the pathogenicity of variants in: UMOD (1 family, at least 2 patients); HNF1B (1 family, 2 patients); a family with CKD (3 patients) where the index patient carries VUS in both HNF1B and UMOD.
Conclusion
A genetic diagnosis of ADTKD was established in 43% of the families studied, and genetic CKD was confirmed in 57% of the families. MUC1 and UMOD were the most prevalent genes associated with ADTKD, though a significant number of cases involved HNF1B (mostly CNVs). Re-analysis of initially negative results increased the diagnostic yield for ADTKD and genetic CKD with an ADTKD-like phenotype. These findings suggest that broader gene panels as a first-line approach may enhance diagnostic accuracy. Additionally, the limitations of NGS and WES in detecting MUC1 and HNF1B variants underscore the importance of collaboration with specialized reference laboratories for ADTKD diagnosis.

title: #3718 The role of kidney biopsy in genetic evaluation: analysis of a hereditary renal diseases consultation
authors: Andreia Gaspar Carnevale; Ana Rita Pereirinha Ramos; José Soares; Madalena Borges; Mário Ventura Góis; Helena Viana; Joaquim F Tomaz Rodrigues Moita Calado; Rui Furtado Dias Barata; Cristina Rego de Freitas Mendes Jorge
abstract:
Background and Aims
Genetic kidney disease accounts for over 10% of chronic kidney disease causes. In this context genetic testing may be used to reach a diagnosis in selected cases and can potentially exclude the need for a kidney biopsy. However, in reality many genetic evaluations are conducted after a biopsy, when either the histomorphology or clinical findings suggest a possible genetic cause. The hereditary disease referral can also be important in the evaluation of a patient for future transplantation by estimating the risk of either disease recurrence (such as in the case of FSGS) or family kidney disease progression in case of kidney donation (if a hereditary familiar disease is not previously detected), further improving our treatment of these patients.
This study attempts to analyze the correlation between the kidney biopsy findings and genetic testing results and their importance in achieving a diagnosis.
Method
An observational retrospective study was conducted with patients followed in a Hereditary Renal Diseases consultation between January 1st of 2013 to 31st of December 2024. Those that had been subjected to both a renal biopsy and genetic testing were selected. Clinical and demographic data was collected, including the genetic test results and kidney biopsy findings.
Results
From the 499 patients that were followed in a Hereditary Renal Diseases a total of 22 patients were selected, of which 59% (n = 13) were male, with an average age of 43 ± 17.2 years. The main reasons for conducting a kidney biopsy were proteinuria (n = 10, 45.5%), worsening renal function (n = 5, 22.7%), microhematuria (n = 4, 18.2%), nephritic syndrome (n = 2, 9.0%) and chronic kidney disease of unknown cause (n = 1, 4.5%). The findings included focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS; n = 11, 50.0%), thrombotic microangiopathy (n = 5, 22.7%), proliferative glomerulonephritis, normal histology (both n = 2, 9.0%), uromodulin nephropathy and chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (both n = 1, 4.5%). Only 3 (13.6%) biopsies were conducted after a previous hereditary renal diseases consultation.
The genetic testing was conducted primarily to confirm a genetic cause of FSGS (n = 9, 40.9%), alternative complement disfunction (n = 6, 27.3%), tubulointerstitial kidney disease (n = 3, 13.6%), Alport syndrome (n = 3, 13.6%) or APOL1 risk alleles (n = 1, 4.5%). The genetic testing was requested to assess disease recurrence or hereditary disease compromising family kidney donation in the context of future kidney transplantation in 7 patients (31.8%). In another 7 patients (31.8%) a confirmed or possibly pathological variant was found, and the kidney biopsy findings were concordant with the diagnosis in six of them (85.6%).
Conclusion
Genetic testing can be conducted to avoid the need for kidney biopsy but in many cases the reported findings and their association with other clinical and familiar data are what guides our genetic testing, allowing us to potentially reach a diagnosis. In our cohort almost a third of the patients had a positive genetic test after the kidney biopsy, as the morphologic findings were mostly consistent with the suspected genetic disease, which illustrates that carefully selected patients can benefit from this approach.

title: #667 Investigate the effect of retinoid X receptor in renal tubular cell senescence
authors: Wu Meng-Hsuan; Shuei-Liong Lin
abstract:
Background and Aims
The increasing human lifespan has led to a projected rise in the elderly population worldwide. Aging is frequently accompanied by the accumulation of age-related diseases. Studies have shown that approximately 37% of Taiwanese individuals aged 65 and over have chronic kidney disease (CKD). Moreover, elderly individuals suffering from acute kidney injury (AKI) face a significantly higher risk of mortality compared to younger individuals. Even those who survive AKI are at an elevated risk of developing CKD. Recent research has indicated that the nuclear receptor retinoid X receptor (RXR) is closely linked to cellular senescence in human lung fibroblasts. We are intrigued by the potential role of RXR in renal aging. Therefore, this study aims to elucidate the impact of RXR regulation on the growth and senescence of renal tubular epithelial cells.
Method
Primary tubular epithelial cells (PTECs) were utilized for in vitro studies. Bexarotene and HX531 were used as an RXR agonist and antagonist to regulate RXR pathway activation and inhibition in PTECs. Population doubling assay was conducted to assess the proliferative capacity of PTECs, and flow cytometry was performed for cell cycle analysis.
Results
Population doubling assay revealed that PTECs maintained a continuously rising growth curve under the recommended culture conditions. Treatment with RXR agonist bexarotene significantly upregulated the expression of RXR downstream genes compared to the control group (P < 0.01). Bexarotene treatment also caused a gradual plateau in the growth curve, indicating reduced proliferation and growth arrest. Flow cytometry analysis demonstrated that bexarotene induced the accumulation of PTECs in the G0/G1 and G2/M phases of the cell cycle. In contrast, treatment with the RXR antagonist HX531 promoted PTECs growth, resulting in a faster growth rate than the control group. Furthermore, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels in the culture medium remained unchanged following bexarotene and HX531 treatments compared to controls, indicating no significant cytotoxicity under the experimental conditions.
Conclusion
This study confirmed that RXR activation influences the growth and senescence of renal tubular epithelial cells. RXR activation by bexarotene reduced cell proliferation and promoted growth arrest, while inhibition of RXR using HX531 may mitigate the senescent process of renal tubular cells.
