title: #1793 Renal protective effect of SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with Fabry disease
authors: Hayaki Okamoto; Shunsuke Goto; Mika Fujita; Hideki Fujii
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fabry disease is a rare X-linked congenital metabolic disorder caused by mutations in the alpha-galactosidase A (GLA) gene. These mutations lead to the accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3), a substrate of α-galactosidase A, within various tissues, including the kidneys. Renal involvement is a major complication in patients with Fabry disease (FD). Although enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) and chaperone therapy can slow the progression of kidney dysfunction, some patients eventually develop end-stage kidney disease. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, initially developed as therapeutic agents for diabetes mellitus, have recently been explored for their potential in treating non-diabetic chronic kidney diseases (CKD). While several studies have demonstrated the renal protective effects of SGLT2 inhibitors in various CKD, their efficacy in FD remains unclear. The present study aims to evaluate the renal protective effects of SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with Fabry disease by analyzing data from our institutional database.
Method
As of December 2024, the database included 34 patients. Patients who had not received SGLT2 inhibitors were excluded, resulting leaving 10 patients for analysis. To assess the renal protective effects of SGLT2 inhibitors, we analyzed the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) slopes over two periods: one year before and one year after initiating SGLT2 inhibitor therapy. The eGFR slopes were calculated using two methods: an ordinary least-squares linear regression and a linear mixed-effects model. The eGFR slopes derived from the ordinary least-squares linear regression model were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. For the linear mixed-effects model, covariates were adjusted across three models: Model 1: included age and sex; Model 2: included the variables in Model 1 plus ERT and chaperone therapy; Model 3: further adjusted for the use of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers, and angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors.
Results
Of the patients included in the analysis, 70.0% (n = 7) were men. At baseline, the mean age was 40.6 ± 17.6 years, and the mean eGFR was 87.9 ± 33.5 mL/min/1.73 m2, 70.0% (n = 7) received renin-angiotensin system inhibitors, and 90% (n = 9) received ERT (agalsidase-alpha, n = 6; agalsidase-beta, n = 3). No patient received chaperone therapy. Using the ordinary least-squares linear regression model, the eGFR slope significantly improved following SGLT2 inhibitor therapy, changing from -4.4 (interquartile range [IQR]: −10.6, 0.6) to 1.3 (IQR: −4.2, 9.7) mL/min/1.73 m²/year, P = 0.037). Similarly, the linear mixed-effects model showed significant improvement, with eGFR slope changing from −6.6 (95% confidence interval [CI]: -11.5, −1.7) to 1.0 (95% CI: −4.0, 6.0) mL/min/1.73 m²/year (P = 0.013). The improvement in eGFR slope remained statistically significant after adjusting for covariates (Model 1, from −3.9 (95% CI: −9.0, 1.2) to 4.1 (95% CI: −1.0, 9.3), P = 0.010; Model 2, from −4.8 (95% CI: −10.0, 0.4) to 2.4 (95% CI: −2.9, 7.8), P = 0.023; Model 3, from −2.5 (95% CI: −8.3, 3.2) to 6.0 (95% CI: 0.1, 12.0), P = 0.022).
Conclusion
SGLT2 inhibitors may mitigate kidney function decline in patients with FD, highlighting their potential as a novel therapeutic strategy for managing kidney disease in this population.

title: #2878 Theranostics in organ cross-talk: the impact of serum albumin in blood extracellular vesicles characterization by AFM-IR
authors: Jéssica Verônica Da Silva; Otávio Berenguel; Raquel Silva Neres Dos Santos; Herculano Da Silva Martinho; Marcela Carneiro-Ramos
abstract:
Background and Aims
Extracellular vesicles (EVs) contain cell-type specific signatures and have been proposed as biomarkers in various diseases, including in heart-kidney cross-talking. However, due to their small dimensions, quantification, and size distribution, the biophysical characterization of these particles is challenging and still controversial. In the same way, due to light diffraction limits, imaging EVs samples in the “fingerprint” range of wavelengths of biomolecules makes mid-IR spectroscopy impossible to capture images and spectra at the nanoscale (nm) by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). Objective: Therefore, we aimed to use the nanospectroscopy (AFM-IR) technique to elucidate the molecular signature of EVs isolated from blood (serum and plasma) and the direct correlation of their topography and biochemical signature concerning the isolation method and context
Method
For this, three isolation methods have been tested using serum or plasma from C57BL/6 male mice and evaluated, where we have carried out the standardization of drying of the isolated vesicle sample and its analysis by micro-reflectance in FTIR followed by AFM-IR analysis. The first isolation method used was carried out according to the total exosome isolation reagent (TEIR) from the serum kit protocol using blood serum; the second isolation method was the isolation from plasma samples by ultracentrifugation at 100,000g for 90 min of the plasma isolated; resuspending the pellet in 500 µL of PBS 1× exosome free; and the third and last one method was by size exclusion chromatography (SEC) and resuspending the pellet in 500 µL of PBS 1× exosome free.
Results
The results largely corroborate the schematic spectrum proposed by the literature on infrared signatures from studies dedicated to characterizing extracellular vesicles from blood. However, the spectra also overlap with albumin signature, except for bands associated with membrane-bound oligosaccharide, lipids, and nucleic acid signatures, where a spectra red-shift was observed according to the isolation method.
Conclusion
In this way, knowing the potential use of nanospectroscopy in the study of EVs and the lack of information about the spectral composition of blood-based EVs in acute kidney injury (AKI) and its uremic context, our next step consists of characterizing these EVs in ischemic-reperfusion injury mice model combined with potential heart damage uremic toxins: indoxyl sulfate and p-cresyl sulfate, comparing these results with proteomic analysis.

Renal hypouricemia (RHUC) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by impaired renal tubular uric reabsorption. Although the majority of patients with RHUC have been reported in east Asian population including that of Japan. RHUC has also been reported in Jewish and Roma populations. title: #1909 Characteristics of patients with a diagnosis of de novo polycystic kidney disease
authors: Judith Martins Muñoz; Belén Gil Fournier; Soraya Ramiro León; Jessy Korina Peña-Esparragoza; Alberto de Lorenzo Álvarez; Laura Espinel; María Teresa Naya; Alfonso Cubas
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common hereditary kidney disease. Its prevalence ranges from one in every 500 people to one in every 2,000. Its primary mode of transmission is autosomal dominant, but 10%–20% of cases are estimated to be de novo, with no positive family history, which presents an additional diagnostic challenge for polycystic kidney disease.
Method
This is a descriptive, retrospective observational study of cases seen in our clinic with suspected polycystic kidney disease and no known family history. Genetic studies were requested for all cases following an established protocol with the Genetics Service: (1) Sanger sequencing of the PKD1 and PKD2 genes, (2) MLPA of PKD1 and PKD2, (3) whole exome sequencing with a panel for cystic diseases.
Results
A total of 70 cases referred to our clinic since 2017 were analyzed for various reasons: radiological imaging of cysts (72.8%), renal function deterioration (15.7%), cyst complications (5.7%), urinary sediment abnormalities (4.28%), and arterial hypertension (1.4%). All had radiological imaging showing multiple cysts and no known family history. Most patients were male (56.3%) with an average age of 57.3 ± 13.2 years. Of all the cases analyzed, pathogenic mutations were detected in 18 cases (25.7%), variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in 9 cases (12.8%), and benign variants (BV) in 6 cases (8.5%). No mutation was detected in 27 cases (38.5%), and in 10 cases (14.2%) the study was not completed.
The identified pathogenic mutations were: 6 in PKD1, 4 in PKD2, 2 in GANAB, 2 in ALG8, 1 in COL4A3, 1 in HNF1B, 1 in WDR19, and 1 case of Joubert syndrome. Patients with pathogenic mutations, compared to those with BV or VUS, had a higher average total renal volume (2261.8 cc ± 234 cc) versus (1210 ± 143 cc), lower initial glomerular filtration rates, and greater comorbidity (hypertension: 55% vs 43%, diabetes mellitus: 22.8% vs 16%). The percentage of liver involvement was higher in the group with pathogenic mutations (61% vs 46%), as was the percentage of cystic complications (15.7% vs 12.8%).
Conclusion
A comprehensive genetic study should be performed in all patients with renal cystic involvement and no known family history. Given the significant impact it can have, including renal function deterioration, hypertension, and cystic complications, patients should be referred to a nephrology clinic as early as possible.

title: #2449 Treatment of chronic hypomagnesemia with SGLT2-inhibitor in a patient with Gitelman syndrome—a case report
authors: Nóra Ledó
abstract:
Background and Aims
Gitelman syndrome is an inherited distal tubulopathy with low potassium and magnesium levels. The magnesium supplementation has great limitations in the patients because of its side effects.
The inhibitors of the sodium-glucose-cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) can help magnesium-sparing, independently from the distal tubules. Therefore, SGLT2-inhibitors may also increase magnesium levels in patients with Gitelman syndrome. This hypothesis was examined in a patient with Gitelman syndrome (proven with genetic test), who had symptomatic hypomagnesemia with the highest dose of tolerable supplementation. The patient had no other indications for the use of SGLT2-inhibitors.
Method
After the informed consent of the 38-year-old female patient, a request for medication use beyond its indication was sent to the National Center for Public Health and Pharmacy. After the approval, the patient started on empagliflozin 10 mg therapy with the same salt-supplementation. Laboratory tests were conducted before the initiation of the treatment and after two weeks.
Results
Serum creatinine levels rose (56 vs. 65 umol/L) but kidney function remained stable (creatinine clearance 129 vs. 127 ml/min) after initiation of the therapy. Proteinuria became lower (240 vs. 216 mg/day, urinary albumin/creatinine ratio 1.2 vs. 0.9 mg/mmol). The urinary excretion of sodium was more (261 vs. 325 mmol/day) but the serum sodium level was stable (137 vs. 137 mmol/L). The rise of the chloride excretion (350 vs. 479 mmol/day) did not affect the serum chloride levels (101 vs. 101 mmol/L). The increased potassium excretion (193 vs. 262 mmol/day) resulted in lower potassium levels (3.6 vs. 3.1 mmol/L). The serum magnesium level increased (0.56 vs. 0.71 mmol/L). There were no side effects of the treatment.
Conclusion
The use of SGLT2-inhibitors may help the treatment of hypomagnesaemia in patients with Gitelman syndrome. Clinical trials are needed to evaluate their efficacy and safety in this patient group.

title: #2980 Association between body mass index and nephrolithiasis markers in the Mexican population
authors: Monica Perez Escobar; Ximena Atilano Carsi; Paola Miranda-Alatriste
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney Stone Disease is a common condition with a prevalence ranging from 10% to 15% in the population of industrialized countries in the Americas. The incidence of nephrolithiasis has been directly associated with factors such as metabolic syndrome and a Western lifestyle, characterized by the consumption of ultra-processed foods and low physical activity. In this context, body mass index (BMI) has been identified as a potential risk factor for Kidney Stone formation due to its role in metabolic alterations that affect urinary composition. This study aimed to analyze the association between BMI and nephrolithiasis markers such as pH, oxaluria and calciuria in Mexican patients diagnosed with kidney stones.
Method
This retrospective study included a sample of Mexican participants diagnosed with nephrolithiasis between the years 2013–2014, from whom a review of medical records was conducted. BMI was calculated based on patients’ height and weight, while nephrolithiasis markers were assessed through a 24-hour urine sample. Pearson correlation and multivariate regression analyses were performed to examine the association between BMI and nephrolithiasis markers, adjusting for potential confounding variables such as sex and age.
Results
A total of 585 patients with nephrolithiasis were included, of whom 59.1% were women. The mean age and BMI of the population were 53.2 ± 13.5 years and 27.9 ± 5.04 kg/m², respectively. The urinary profile of the patients was within normal parameters: pH 6.0 ± 0.9, calcium 161.4 ± 98.8 mg/day, sodium 158.6 ± 70.4 mEq/day, potassium 59.6 ± 36.9 mEq/day, phosphorus 650.7 ± 319 mg/day, oxalates 28.0 ± 18.2 mg/day, and citrates 407.9 ± 248.9 mg/day.
Significant correlations were found between body weight and the following urinary parameters: pH (r = −1.88, P = 0.0001), calcium (r = 0.188, P = 0.0001), sodium (r = 0.34, P = 0.0001), oxalates (r = 0.282, P = 0.001), and phosphorus (r = 0.308, P = 0.0001). BMI showed significant correlations with fewer urinary parameters: pH (r = −1.51, P = 0.0001), sodium (r = 0.24, P = 0.0001), oxalates (r = 0.203, P = 0.023), and phosphorus (r = 0.144, P = 0.001).
In the linear regression analysis, BMI was not a strong predictor of urinary parameters. However, body weight was found to be a significant predictor of urinary pH, calcium, sodium, potassium, phosphate, and citrates (Table 1). For each kilogram of body weight, urinary pH decreased by 0.11, while urinary calcium increased by 2.15 mg. Despite being a predictor of urinary parameters, the β values were low, and the R² of the models explained only a small proportion of the variability in the patients' urinary profiles. These findings suggest that weight gain in patients with nephrolithiasis may alter urinary composition, increasing the risk of crystallization and the formation of new kidney stones.
Conclusion
This study reveals that BMI is not a predictor of the urinary profile in patients with nephrolithiasis. Body weight was identified as a predictor of urinary pH, calcium, sodium, potassium, phosphate, and citrates. Although body weight explains only a small proportion of the variations in these parameters, maintaining an adequate body weight in patients with nephrolithiasis is essential to reduce the risk of recurrent kidney stone formation.

BMI showed significant correlations with fewer urinary parameters: pH (r = −1.51, P = 0.0001), sodium (r = 0.24, P = 0.0001), oxalates (r = 0.203, P = 0.023), and phosphorus (r = 0.144, P = 0.001).

Conclusion
This study reveals that BMI is not a predictor of the urinary profile in patients with nephrolithiasis. Although body weight explains only a small proportion of the variations in these parameters, maintaining an adequate body weight in patients with nephrolithiasis is essential to reduce the risk of recurrent kidney stone formation.

title: #3423 Efficacy and safety of ravulizumab for the maintenance of aHUS remission after kidney transplant
authors: Adrian Domagalski; Karolina Skalec; Marta Kepinska; Patryk Jerzak; Andrzej Konieczny; Magdalena Kuriata-Kordek; Miroslaw Banasik
abstract:
Background and Aims
Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) is a rare thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) triggered by complement dysregulation. Ravulizumab, a next generation complement inhibitor provides immediate and sustained complement C5 inhibition. The aim of this study was to assess clinical efficacy, safety and tolerability of ravulizumab in aHUS patients.
Method
Patients with a clinical diagnosis of aHUS treated with eculizumab for at least three months were switched to ravulizumab. The first ravulizumab infusion was administered at least two weeks after the last eculizumab dose, followed by a second infusion two weeks later and subsequent doses every eight weeks.
Results
Four patients with end-stage renal disease due to aHUS had previously undergone kidney transplant. At the time of switching to ravulizumab, none required dialysis, and no new dialysis events occurred during treatment. Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), platelet count, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), creatinine, haptoglobin and hemoglobin levels remained stable throughout the study. No clinical signs of TMA or adverse event (AE) relapses were reported. Genetic testing confirmed at least one aHUS associated variant in the complement system in all patients. No meningococcal infections were reported during the study.
Conclusion
Long-term treatment with ravulizumab proved to be well tolerated and associated with sustained hematologic and renal parameters, and improved quality of life. Furthermore, the close attention to vaccinations status and preventive antibiotic therapy ensured no meningococcal infections during the treatment. Decision which patients required lifelong treatment involved consideration of a wide range of factors. Our study provides compelling evidence on the complexity of safety aspects of ravulizumab treatment.

title: #1632 Blood cellular indices in relation with D-dimer and thrombin levels in patients with end stage renal disease
authors: Vinod Bansal; Hamzah Hussain; Jawed Fareed; Fakiha Siddiqui; Debra Hoppensteadt; Pamela Abulencia; Kavitha Vellanki
abstract:
Background and Aims
End-stage renal disease (ESRD) is often associated with thromboinflammatory complications. Besides the biomarkers of thrombin generation such as D-dimer (DD) and peak thrombin (PT) levels, cellular indices (CI's) have been reported to change with the severity of ESRD. Such CI's as neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet to lymphocyte ratio (PLR), systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), lymphocyte to monocyte ratio (LMR), neutrophil to monocyte ratio (NMR) and their relevance with biomarkers such as DD and PT were profiled in ESRD patients.
Method
Citrated plasma samples from patients with confirmed ESRD were collected in the Hemodialysis Clinic at Loyola University Medical Center. 50 healthy plasma samples served as control. Commercially available sandwich ELISA methods were used for DD levels, and PT was quantified by using a fluorogenic method. Blood CI's were extracted from complete blood counts. Applicable statistical methods were performed and P < 0.05 were considered significant.
Results
The ESRD group comprised 56.9% males and 43.1% females, with a median age of 66 years. Comparing controls to ESRD cohort, DD increased significantly from 7.1 to 905.8 ng/mL (P < 0.05) while PT levels decreased from 138.4 to 109.9nM (P < 0.05). NLR increased from 1.6 to 3.4, SII increased from 444.5 to 583.2, and LMR decreased from 4.1 to 2.4 (P < 0.05). PLR and NMR showed no significant difference. Table 1 represents the composite results. There was no correlation between DD and PT. There were varying degrees of correlation between cellular indices.
Conclusion
These studies suggest that beside thromboinflammatory biomarkers, CI's may provide additional prognostic parameters in the risk stratification of ESRD. All of the CI's included in this study are increased except for LMR. CI's represent an emerging tool to risk stratify ESRD patients.

title: #1959 The role of molecular genetics in the etiological diagnosis of microscopic hematuria
authors: Cristina Daniela Cana Ruiu; Daniela Puscasoiu; Romeo Popa; Fota Naomi Corina; DanielaTeodora Maria
abstract:
Background and Aims
Microscopic hematuria, whether hereditary or non-hereditary, is a common finding in the general population. Genetic testing frequently aids in diagnosing patients, even when a histopathological diagnosis has been obtained through renal biopsy. In light of this, we conducted a study to analyze the role of genetic testing in diagnosing these patients.
Method
Sixteen patients, consisting of eight women and eight men, who presented with microscopic hematuria, were included in the study. This group included both hospitalized patients and outpatients from the nephrology department of our hospital. The average age of the patients was 47.75 years for women and 43.87 years for men. In six patients, a renal biopsy was performed to aid in diagnosis and obtain histopathological findings.
The study included patients at various stages of renal dysfunction, ranging from those with preserved renal function to those with renal damage progressing to the dialysis stage. Genetic tests related to renal pathology were conducted for all patients.
Results
Out of the 16 patients with microscopic hematuria included in the study, a genetic anomaly was identified in 10 patients. Three patients were diagnosed with hyperoxaluria type I and had the AGXT mutation (NM_000030.3): c.508G>A. One patient had hyperoxaluria type II with a mutation in the GRHPR gene (NM_012202.2): c.701T>C. Additionally, three patients were found to have Alport syndrome, with mutations in the COL4A3 gene (NM_000091.5): c.145-2A>G, and in the COL4A4 gene (NM_000092.5): c.1820C>T. One patient had an autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease with a PKD1 gene mutation (NM_001009944.3): c.1987C>T. Furthermore, two patients exhibited other genetic abnormalities, classified as variants of uncertain significance. One patient had a GANAB gene mutation (NM_198334.3): c.340C>T, while another patient had a double mutation involving two variants of uncertain significance: a TTC21B gene mutation (NM_024753.5): c.14A>C and a TSC2 gene mutation (NM_000548.5): c.670G>C.
Conclusion
Utilizing molecular genetic tests to diagnose patients with microscopic hematuria is crucial for accurate diagnosis, patient outcomes, and subsequent treatment decisions. Without a genetic diagnosis for microscopic hematuria, both the prognosis for these patients and their family members may be unfavorable.

title: #713 Extrarenal manifestations-clinical marker for early onset of renal replacement therapy in COL4 nephropathy
authors: Nikola Gjorgjievski; Vlatko Karanfilovski; Ana Stojanoska; Zhaklina Shterjova- Markovska; Julija Gjorgievska; Todor Arsov; Julia Hoefele; Velibor Tasic; Nora Abazi; Igor Nikolov
abstract:
Background and Aims
Type IV collagen nephropathy (COL4) encompasses a spectrum of hereditary disorders caused by mutation in genes COL4A3, COL4A4 or COL4A5. The phenotypes of this disorder range from isolated hematuria to end-stage renal disease requiring renal replacement therapy (RRT). The age of initiating RRT is a crucial clinical marker closely associated with extrarenal manifestations, such as hearing loss and ocular abnormalities
Method
We performed a retrospective analysis of the clinical and genetic features of 91 participants, evaluated by Next Generation Sequencing (NGS), in which 48 (52,8%) were male. Mutation in COL4A5 was confirmed in 61 (67%), mutation in COL4A4 was confirmed in 24 (26,5%), and mutation in COL4A3 was confirmed in only 6 (6.5%) participants. The primary aim of our study was to analyze the association between age of initiating RRT with hearing loss and ocular abnormalities.
Results
The mean age of participants was 29.9 ± 17.6 years. Twenty patients (22%) receive RRT at a mean age of 43.7 ± 15.8 years, while seventy-one patients (78%) who do not require RRT at a mean age of 25.2 ± 15.9. Our analysis did not show a statistically significant association between the type of mutation in COL4 and the initiation of RRT (P = 0.336). Ocular abnormalities and hearing loss were observed in 20 patients (22%) and were significantly associated with earlier initiation of RRT (P < 0.05), compared to patients without extrarenal manifestations. Additionally, gender and other demographic characteristics did not show a significant association with the early onset of RRT.
Conclusion
Our study highlights the important link between extrarenal manifestations and early onset of RRT in COL4 nephropathy, emphasizing their potential as clinical marker of renal progression. Identifying this association is crucial for improving patient stratification, guide clinical monitoring and facilitating timely interventions to mitigate and delay the progression of kidney failure and the need of RRT.

title: #3631 Renal biopsy: a key tool for diagnosing hyperoxaluria
authors: Meriam Hajji; Ilhem Ben Othman; Erij Ben Kmicha; Imen Gorsane; Harzallah Amel; Hayet Kaaroud; Fethi Ben Hmida; Ezzedine Abderrahim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyperoxaluria arises from either genetic defect in glyoxylate metabolism (primary) or increased intestinal oxalate absorption (secondary). It can cause calcium oxalate supersaturation, leading to urolithiasis and oxalate nephropathy. This is characterized by tubulointerstitial oxalate deposits along with an interstitial inflammatory reaction.
Method
This study aimed to assess the epidemiological and clinical characteristics of hyperoxaluria diagnosed through renal biopsy. We conducted a retrospective study of cases diagnosed via renal biopsy between January 2004 and December 2024.
Results
A total of 31 cases of hyperoxaluria were identified, including 12 children and 19 adults, with a male-to-female ratio of 0.7. The mean age at diagnosis was 21.5 ± 6.4 years. Parental consanguinity was noted in 20 cases (64.5%), a family history of chronic kidney disease in 15 patients (48.3%), and a personal history of urinary lithiasis in 11 cases (35.4%). Hypertension was present in 5 patients, Hematuria in 10 cases while Proteinuria (range: 1.2–1.9 g/24 h) was noted in 14 patients. Renal biopsy confirmed the diagnosis in all cases. The main indication for biopsy was renal failure with a mean serum creatinine level of 648.3 ± 106.5 μmol/L. In two patients, hyperoxaluria was diagnosed following early recurrence in a kidney graft. Primary hyperoxaluria was identified in 28 cases, while three cases were secondary: two of our patients have short bowel syndrome as a result of ileocolic resection following an operation for a complication of their inflammatory bowel disease, and another patient has been diagnosed with exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.
Conclusion
Diagnosing hyperoxaluria in patients with renal failure is a difficult task. When clinical and radiological findings are inconclusive, renal biopsy remains a crucial tool for reaching a definitive diagnosis.

title: #1167 The impact of pregnancy on renal function in women with ADPKD: a retrospective analysis
authors: Lucas Aboud; Daniel Rocha; Géssika Gomes; Maria Vaisbich; Ana Cristina Matos; Ita Pfeferman Heilberg
abstract:
Background and Aims
Women with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) presenting three or more pregnancies have been considered at risk for progression of the disease. However, the relationship between pregnancy and long-term maternal renal prognoses in ADPKD remains controversial. The aim of the present study was to evaluate the impact of pregnancy on the progression of ADPKD.
Method
This was a retrospective cross-sectional analysis on data collected from the medical records of women with ADPKD who were followed up as outpatients, for at least three years. Baseline clinical and laboratory data were analysed, and imaging results comprising Mayo imaging classification (MIC) were retrieved. The slope of the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was used for evaluating disease progression comparing nulligest women (G0) with those who had had one or more pregnancies (G1). Patients with stage 5 chronic kidney disease were excluded.
Results
Ninety-four (94) patients were included as G0 (n = 28) or G1 (n = 66). As shown in the Table 1 below, the median follow-up period was not different between groups. G1 women were older, more obese and hypertensive and exhibited lower baseline eGFR. There has been no statistical difference regarding distribution of MIC between groups. A multivariate analysis to assess the factors determining eGFR slope (data not shown in the Table 1), including all aforementioned parameters, showed no independent association.
Conclusion
These preliminary data suggest that ADPKD women with one or more past pregnancies did not present a worse renal outcome than the nulligest, despite other risk factors such as age, arterial hypertension, obesity and lower baseline eGFR. The similar distribution of rapid progressors in both groups might have contributed to the lack of difference between them. A larger number of patients and a longer follow-up period are still warranted to confirm the present findings.

title: #2534 Oral acid load for distal tubular acidosis diagnosis: are urinary ratio useful?
authors: Lara Cabezas; Charlotte Monneuse; Aurelie De Mul; Laurence Derain Dubourg; Sandrine Lemoine
abstract:
Background and Aims
The acid-base balance plays a fundamental role in the homeostasis of the human body, regulated in part by the kidneys. Any disturbance in renal function will lead to an imbalance in the acid-base homeostasis leading to renal tubular acidosis. Distal renal tubular acidosis (RTA type 1) is defined by a decrease in proton excretion into the urine via the H+ ATPase transporter. Several tests are available to diagnose RTA like the oral acid load charge. Traditionally, ammoniuria and titratable acidity standards are expressed in mol/min/1.73 m². The aim of our research is to propose the urinary standards ratio to improve RTA diagnosis.
Method
We report a single-centre retrospective study. All patients who underwent an oral acid loads performed in the renal functional exploration department of the Edouard Herriot Hospital, HCL, France from May 2010 to December 2024 were included. Patients were admitted for a pre-test blood work-up, including blood and urine tests (at baseline and 1-hour after). The acid loading test was performed using oral ammonium chloride capsules at a dose of 1 mg/kg over 3 to 5 days before returning for post-test analyses. Good adaptation to the test is defined by a minimum urine pH (pH min) <5.5 and ammoniuria >39 µmol/min/1.73 m². The aim of the study was to establish mean urinary NH4/creatinine and urinary AT/creatinine ratios in patients with and without urinary acidification disorders.
Results
Fifty-three patients were included in our study; 30 patients were considered with an adapted response to acid load and 23 patients were considered with a non-adapted response. The classification of our patients between the adapted and non-adapted group seems correct with a higher ammoniuria in the adapted group after the test (before 31.92 ± 24.74 µmol/min/1.73 m², after in the adapted group 75.82 ± 36.20 µmol/min/1.73 m² and after in the non-adapted group 49.74 ± 38.90 µmol/min/1.73 m², p-value <0.05) and a higher AT in the adapted group after the test (before 32.23 ± 32.10 µmol/min/1.73 m², after in the adapted group 23.23 ± 10.09 µmol/min/1.73 m² and after in the non-adapted group 18.32 ± 7.51 µmol/min/1.73 m², p-value <0.05). There were no significant differences of AT/creatinine and NH4/creatinine ratio between the adapted and the non-adapted group after the oral acid load test for UT (first urinary sample) and U1 (second urinary sample one hour after the first one) except for the NH4/creatinine U1 ratio (6.43 ± 2.21 in the adapted group versus 4.86 ± 3.74 in the non-adapted group, p-value = 0.021).
Conclusion
Our study did not show any contribution of AT/creatinine and NH4/creatinine ratio in the interpretation of the acid load test. Renal acidification problems are still rare in France, making them difficult to study. The idea of ratio standards should continue to be explored with a larger population in order to gain statistical power.

title: #2595 Comparison study of human resourced ellipsoid method vs kidney volumetry using artificial intelligence in polycystic kidney disease
authors: Jihyun Yang; Young Rae Lee; Young Youl Hyun; Hyun Jung Kim; Tae Young Shin; Kyu-Beck Lee
abstract:
Background and Aims
As the Mayo imaging classification (MIC) for polycystic kidney disease (PKD) has established itself as a crucial basis for clinical treatment decisions, volumetric assessment for its evaluation has been a tedious and inaccurate process that required labor. While the ellipsoid method measuring total kidney volume (TKV) in PKD patients provides a practical TKV estimation using MRI or CT, its limitations highlight the need for improved, accessible techniques in real world clinics. Accurate TKV assessment is essential for guiding PKD therapy, predicting progression, and optimizing PKD outcomes.
Method
This study evaluates the agreement between manual ellipsoid methods and AI-based kidney volumetry methods for measuring total kidney volume (TKV) in patients with PKD. Total 32 PKD patients in tertiary single hospital were evaluated. Manual ellipsoid volumetry by two ADPKD specialists were compared to a cloud-based AI platform. Bland-Altman analysis and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) were used to evaluate agreement and reliability.
Results
Median age was 56 years old, average TKV was 1200.24 ml. We included all five MIC 1A to 1E. Most of the patients allocated to MIC 1B to 1C by ellipsoid method which was similar by AI volumetry. AI volumetry outperformed with highly correlated score (AI vs. nephrology professor ICC: r = 0.99, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.9780 to 0.9948, P < 0.01), AI vs. trained clinician ICC: r = 0.98, 95% CI 0.9608 to 0.9907, P < 0.01). The Bland-Altman plot also showed the mean differences between professors and AI volumetry were statistically insignificant (mean difference 159.5 ml, 95% CI −11.8368 to 330.7817, P = 0.07).
Conclusion
AI-based kidney volumetry demonstrates strong agreement with expert manual measurements and offers a reliable, labor-efficient alternative for TKV assessment in clinical practice. Its consistent performance across imaging modalities makes it a valuable tool for managing PKD and optimizing therapeutic outcomes. Serial volumetry evaluation may improve accuracy and expand its utility.

title: #2834 When Fabry was not the one to blame
authors: Catarina Oliveira Silva; Johanna Viana; Cláudia Coelho; Luis Falcao; Carlos Soares
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fabry Disease (FD) and Alport syndrome (AS) are genetic kidney diseases that account for 0.2 to 1% of patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD), respectively. AS is caused by pathogenic variants in COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5 genes, including autosomal, X-linked, or digenic inheritance. It encompasses a spectrum of nephropathy, from microscopic hematuria to progressive renal disease and ESRD. FD is an X-linked disorder caused by the hereditary deficiency of the enzyme α-galactosidase A (α-Gal A), potentially causing disease in the kidneys, heart, and peripheral and central nervous systems. Diagnosing these entities can be challenging and usually integrates family history, kidney biopsy and genetic testing.
Method
We present a case of X-linked AS in a patient with familial microscopic hematuria and a previous family diagnosis of FD.
Results
A 30-year-old male patient was referred to the nephrology department at the age of 18 for microhematuria and proteinuria 1 g/24 hours. He had family history of microhematuria in his 14-year-old brother, 13-year-old sister, and two male paternal first-degree cousins of 19 and 30 years old. His kidney biopsy showed mesangial hypercellularity, podocyte cytoplasm vacuolization, and interstitial foamy macrophages on light microscopy (LM), immunofluorescence exhibited IgM(+)/IgA(−)/IgG(−)/C3c(+)/C1q(−) and electron microscopy (EM) revealed diffuse podocyte foot process effacement and mesangial and glomerular basement membrane (GBM) sclerosis, without myeloid bodies. Genetic analysis was negative for COL4 gene variants but revealed a hemizygous GLA variant c.427G>A; p.(Ala143Thr). He had no skin lesions, acral paresthesias or pain, gastrointestinal distress, or heat intolerance. His electrocardiogram, echocardiography, brain magnetic resonance, and ophthalmologic and ear/nose/throat evaluations were unremarkable. α-Gal A leukocyte and plasma activity were below the normal range but above 30 percent of the mean normal, and plasma lysoGb3 and urinary Gb3 were normal. Targeted genetic testing evidenced the same variant in both siblings, his mother, his paternal male cousins, and in one of their sisters, who later developed hematuria, and their mother. None had clinical features or enzymatic study compatible with FD, except for limb paresthesia in one cousin. The patient's brother eventually developed proteinuria of 1 g/g and underwent a KB at 18 years old, with similar histologic features on LM and EM. Over the years, the patient's kidney function remained unaltered, and proteinuria ranged from 0.9 to 2.2 g/g on a renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitor. Due to worsening proteinuria and an uncertain etiology, he underwent a second kidney biopsy after eight years. LM showed focal mesangial hypercellularity, and EM revealed irregular GBM with variable thick and thin segments, without myeloid bodies. Repeated genetic testing showed a probable pathogenic variant in COL4A5 gene c.3791G>T p.(Gly1264Val). A diagnosis of X-linked AS was thus established. The same variant has already been identified in his brother and cousin.
Conclusion
We present a case of familial hematuria associated with a pathogenic variant in COL4A5 and a variant of uncertain significance in GLA. To this date, we could not establish how two variants in the X chromosome were inherited in patients whose familiar connection is through their fathers. Their respective mothers have hematuria and are from the same region in northern Portugal, so we hypothesized that they could be related. The absence of FD clinical and biochemical phenotypes in this family supports previous observations of the non-pathogenicity of this GLA variant and reflects the challenges surrounding the interpretation of genetic variants in clinical practice. Surrogate biomarkers and tissue biopsy provided insight into its clinical relevance and prevented unnecessary treatment. Finally, a re-take genetic testing almost ten years apart led to the identification of a previously unknown COL4A5 variant, highlighting the importance of re-evaluating genetic testing in cases of uncertain etiology and clinical suspicion of a genetic disease.

title: #3157 Renal involvement and functional impact in the pediatric age of a cohort of patients with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) and contiguous gene syndrome (CGS)
authors: Pedro Arango Sancho; Yolanda Calzada Baños; Ana Cristina Aguilar Rodríguez; Víctor Alfonso López Báez; Yarima López Espinoza; Emma Fortes Marín; Oreste Ferra Neto; Romina Escalante; Federico Ramos; Héctor Salvador Hernández; Álvaro Madrid Aris
abstract:
Background and Aims
TSC is a rare multisystem genetic disorder (1:6,000), autosomal dominant, due to mutations in TSC1(Cr9)/TSC2(Cr16), predisposing to tumor development by deregulation of the mTOR pathway. Premature deterioration of glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in adults (40%, without hemorrhages due to angiomyolipomas-AML-/interventions), suggesting the presence of intrinsic kidney disease. Cysts, associated or not with SGC (joint TSC2/PKD1 genes deletion), AML, arterial hypertension or the risk of nephrolithiasis (ketogenic diet or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors) are the other parameters to control. Our aim is to determine renal involvement and GFR affectation in a pediatric cohort of TSC and/or CGS followed in our service in the last decade (2013–2023).
Method
Retrospective observational study of 116 patients (66 males, 50 females) diagnosed and/or in follow-up for TSC (111 patients/95.68%) or CGS (5 patients/4.32%) between 2013-2023. Patients with known renal damage unrelated to TSC/CGS were excluded. Data were collected on diagnosis/disease progression, ultrasound, abdominal MRI, serum and urinary tests, mTORi or other treatment and their responses after a variable follow-up period.
Results
Mean age 13.39 years (SD 6.228). Kidney involvement 54.9% (67): AML 41.8% (mean 10.33 mm/SD 14.64), cysts 29.5% (mean 12.39 mm/SD 17.23. Patterns: multicystic 11.5%, polycystic 3.3%, cortical cystic 4.1%, cortical microcystic 9.8% and focal cystic 0.8%), 3 tumors of other type (1 hamartoma, 1 PEComa and 1 exophytic renal mass). HBP 4.1% (80% grade I/20% high BP), proteinuria 4.1% (median Pr/Cr 0.63mg/mg [0.28–59.32]. Median Alb/Cr 32.9 mg/mmol [6.1–75.1]. Only 2 CGS presented elevated B2 microglobulin) and 2 patients, both. Those who presented HBP and/or proteinuria were treated with ARB/ACE inhibitors and 2 of them with amlodipine. Only 1 patient with CGS presented CKD (stage IV) with the rest of the cohort having normal eGFR. 3 patients presented prelithiasis (1 hypocitraturia/microlithiasis ultrasound and 2 lithogenic risks: hypercalciuria/hypocitraturia and hypercalciuria/hyperuricosuria) in the context of ketogenic diet or topiramate use. 64% were taking mTORi (3 for renal indication/AML >30mm). 1 patient presented hemorrhage treated with embolization. There was a statistically significant correlation (P = 0.02) of renal implications with GCS, as well as between mTORi and control of AML/cyst size (P = 0.03).
Conclusion
GFR impairment was exceptional, only in one patient with GCS, and LMA and renal cysts were the predominant conditions (41.8%/29.5%). early recognition (by MRI) and management of renal impairment, avoiding surgery and promoting the use of mTORi if indicated, are the fundamental factors for preserving renal function in these patients.

title: #274 Genotype of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease in Greek patients
authors: Tsielestina Poulli; Maria Konsta; Maria Varveri; Danai Palaiologou; Eirini Evangelou; Angeliki Poula; Niki Markou; Andreas Kourkounakis; Eleni Frangou; George Tsirpanlis
abstract:
Background and Aims
Genetic testing in patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) provides critical information about the disease, enhances prognostic evaluation, and plays a vital role in patient management. This study aims to investigate the genetic etiology of ADPKD in a cohort of Greek patients.
Method
A total of 135 ADPKD patients (62 females, 73 males; median age at diagnosis: 24 years, IQR: 17–34) were included in this study, with 27 patients diagnosed before the age of 15. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed in 104 patients, revealing more than 10 renal cysts. Children with a positive family history (FH) displayed at least one cyst in echography, while two without FH had multiple renal cysts. All patients underwent genetic testing, including targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) of over 600 clinically relevant genes, Sanger sequencing, and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA).
Results
Genetic analysis confirmed a diagnosis in 126 of 135 patients (93.3%). Variants in the PKD1 gene were detected in 90 patients (66.6%), with 66 (75.9%) resulting in truncated protein production. Variants in the PKD2 gene were identified in 20 patients (14.8%). The variant types of PKD1 and PKD2 genes are illustrated in Fig. 1. Genetic variants in genes other than PKD1 and PKD2 were identified in 12 patients (8.9%), including GANAB (3 cases), IFT140 (2 cases), and SEC61B gene (2 cases, a father and son, with high hepatic cyst charge), the later classified as variant of uncertain significance (VUS) according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) guidelines. In two other cases involving a father 73 and a daughter 35 years old (who had 3 other family members with chronic renal failure of unknown etiology), two variants were identified in PKHD1 and COL4A3 genes, both classified as VUS. Finally, three cases with multiple kidney cysts showed variants in DNAJB11, SEC63, and SLC3A1 genes, which were classified as frameshift, splicing and missense, respectively. Simultaneous variants in PKD1 and other genes were observed in four patients. In three related patients (a father, son, and grandson with typical polycystic kidneys), variants in PKD1 and PKHD1 were identified, both classified as VUS. In another case (categorized as Mayo Imaging Class 1C), a pathogenic frameshift mutation in PKD1 and a pathogenic missense mutation in COL4A4 were detected. Overall, 42.9% of identified variants were classified as pathogenic, 50% as likely pathogenic, and 7.1% (9 cases) as VUS, according to ACMG guidelines.
Conclusion
This study highlights the genetic diversity of ADPKD in Greek patients. The predominance of the variants identified in PKD1 and PKD2 genes, particularly those leading to truncated Polycystin-1 production, underscores their critical role in ADPKD pathogenesis. The identification of variants in other genes such as GANAB, IFT14O etc. reveals the genetic heterogeneity of the disease. The findings also reveal the complexity of genetic counselling, as double mutations and VUS are frequently observed, in patients with typical and atypical phenotypes, emphasizing the importance of comprehensive genetic testing in the diagnosis and management of ADPKD.

title: #1925 Genetically unresolved kidney cystic patients: the neglected population
authors: Floriana Secondulfo; Giovambattista Capasso; Alessandra Perna; Miriam Zacchia
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most prevalent genetic kidney disorder, characterized by age-dependent bilateral cysts formation and progressive decline of renal function.
About 80% of cases are explained by PKD1 mutations, 15% by PKD2 mutations. The remaining 5%–10% may harbor mutations in other genes, but often no pathogenic mutations are detected.
In the setting of positive family history, ADPKD diagnosis mainly relies on kidney ultrasonography in adult individuals. Considering that 10%–20% of ADPKD patients are sporadic, requiring identification of a genetic mutation for diagnosis, negative genetic analysis is a significant burden. Most ADPKD molecular diagnoses rely on short-reads next generation sequencing (NGS), accurate for missense and indels, but with intrinsic limitations for more complex variants.
The aim of this study is to provide a critical characterization of kidney cystic individuals with no pathogenic PKD1-PKD2 variants, to select candidates for further analyses and to providing clues toward precision medicine.
Method
84 patients (48 males, 36 females) referring to our Nephrology Unit between 2018 and 2023 with a clinical suspicion of ADPKD underwent NGS analysis. Patients without pathogenic PKD1-PKD2 mutations were retrospectively evaluated and compared with genotyped ADPKD patients. The estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), kidney volume and Mayo class were assessed. The eGFR decline rate was observed over years, with a mean period of observation of 4.25 years. Fast-progressors were defined as patients with an eGFR slope ≥3 ml/min/year.
Results
Fifty -seven and 4 patients showed PKD1 and PKD2 mutations, respectively; 23 patients (27% of the entire cohort) showed no PKD1-2 variants. Among these patients, 1 presented a SEC63 mutation. Eleven PKD1-2 negative patients (48%) were lost at follow-up after genetic analysis; 2 of them started dialysis in the following years.
Mean annual eGFR slope was 2.92 ± 2.49 ml/min/1.73 m2, indicating a less severe disease than patients with PKD1 truncating mutations (6.03 ± 3.44) and more severe than patients with missense PKD1 variants (2.32 ± 2.67). High standard deviation indicated high heterogeneity. Seven of them (58%) were fast progressors; 5 (42%) had a milder disease.
Among negative patients, common risks factors were equally distributed between fast and slow progressors (diabetes, hypercholesterolemia and hypertriglyceridemia, P > 0.999; hypertension P = 0.523, Fisher exact test).
Basal eGFR, with a great intra-group variability, was also similar (slightly greater for fast progressors, with no statistical significance: 78.86 ± 36.22 vs 69.60 ± 27.26, P = 0.642, Student's t-test). However, basal height adjusted total kidney volume was greater in rapid progressors (1137.70 ± 528.19 vs 415.20 ± 366.98), a not statistically significant difference (P = 0.1981, Student's t-test), probably because of little patients numerosity. Mayo class, when appliable, was 1D (75%) or 1C (25%) for fast progressors.
Conclusion
kidney cystic patients with no PKD1-PKD2 mutations are believed to have a milder disease and a better prognosis. Unfortunately, in a real-life experience this paradigm is not universally respected.
Many negative patients may have a rapid progression to the end stage renal disease.
Among the possible causes, apart from unknown genes, there are mutations not detectable with short-reads NGS, as deletions and duplications. In the era of specific treatment for fast progressor ADPKD patients, genetic confirmation should be considered a starting point for personalized patient care.

title: #3773 Exploring prognostic markers in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
authors: Ana Merino-Ribas; Andrea Fumagalli; Jose Manuel Fernandez-Real; Sonia Valenti; Anna Vallmajo; Jehimy Jean Alvarez Saltos; Leyre García Cantalejo; Nadia Martín Alemany; Gabriel Manuel González Suárez; Claudia Marcela Castillo; Yanel Acosta; Jordi Calabia Martínez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common hereditary kidney disease and one of the most common causes of end-stage kidney disease (ESRD). The major ADPKD genes are PKD1 and PKD2, accounting for >90% of diagnosed families. The causal gene (PKD1>PKD2 or minor genes), type of PKD1 mutation, sex (male>female), environmental factors (obesity, salt intake), and total kidney volume (TKV), among others, are associated with severity and risk of progression to ESRD in ADPKD. TKV may be associated with intrarenal vascular involvement by kidney cysts. The best way to estimate TKV is by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Mutational analysis and MRI are expensive techniques, require expertise, and they are not always available in all centers. An increase in renal resistive index (RRI) assessed by ultrasonography (US) reflects intrarenal vascular involvement and has been related to a decrease in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in other nephropathies. Gut microbiome has not been explored in ADPKD patients, but it has been demonstrated its relevance in other kidney diseases.
Therefore, our aim was to explore the gut microbiome, and the RRI in ADPKD patients and to investigate their link with prognostic markers, such as causal gene, sex, obesity, and TKV.
Method
A cross-sectional observational study was performed including patients diagnosed with ADPKD. Relevant clinical, demographic, and analytical information were gathered for each participant. Mutational analysis was performed. TKV was measured by MRI. RRI was assessed by US. Gut microbiome profile was obtained by Shotgun.
Results
This study included 50 ADPKD patients with a median age of 44.5 years old (IR: 34.8–57.5). Men presented higher TKV compared to women (1786.8 vs 943, P = 0.007). TKV was positively correlated with RRI, and body mass index (BMI) and inversely correlated with GFR, and 1.25 dihydroxyvitamin D. BMI was positively correlated with hemoglobin and inversely correlated with 1.25 dihydroxyvitamin, and GFR. In the multivariate analysis, TKV, GFR, and sex were independent predictors of RRI, with statistical significance.
The gut microbiome was compared between ADPKD patients according to GFR, using ANCOM-BC methodology adjusted by age, sex, and BMI. A statistically significant higher prevalence of species from the phylum Actinomycetota was observed in ADPKD patients with GFR≥60ml/min/1.73 m2, and a higher prevalence of species from the phylum Bacteroidota and Bacillota was found in ADPKD patients with GFR <60ml/min/1.73 m2.
The taxonomic profiles when comparing between ADPKD patients with RRI <0.65 to ADPKD patients with RRI≥0.65 were distinct at species level, observing a predominance of Streptococcus genus in the group RRI ≥0.65. Analyzing RRI as a continuous variable, an increase in Streptococcus genus was confirmed while RRI rises. Moreover, higher RRI levels were associated to an increase in Pseudomonadota and Thermodesulfobacteriota and lower RRI levels were associated to an increase in Bacteroidota.
Comparing taxonomic profiles in ADPKD patients according to the presence of PKD1 or PKD2 mutations, an increase in Actinomycetota, and Bacteroidota at phylum level, and Bacilalles, and Veionella at order level was observed in PKD1 group.
Conclusion
TKV, GFR, and sex are independent predictors of RRI in ADPKD, which implies a link between these factors and renal macro and microvascular involvement. Regarding the gut microbiome in our ADPKD patients, some specific taxa have been shown to be associated to well-stablished prognostic markers. Future studies may explore the role of these bacterial groups as potential biomarkers in ADPKD.

title: #495 Genetic Insights into renal diseases in Armenian children
authors: Sofi Sarinyan; Milena Voskanyan; Mariam Kalajyan; Helen Nazaryan; Diana Voskanyan; Sergey Babloyan; Tanya Aramyan; Nane Aleksanyan; Carsten Bergmann; Valeska Frank; Ashot Sarkissian
abstract:
Background and Aims
Advances in genetics have significantly enhanced our understanding of kidney diseases, enabling earlier diagnoses and more targeted interventions. This study aims to evaluate the diagnostic utility of genetic testing, conducted for the first time in Armenia, in children with kidney diseases.
Method
Since 2022, 25 patients aged 2–18 years (57.7% male) were included in this study. Genomic DNA was analyzed using next-generation sequencing (NGS). Target regions, including coding exons and corresponding exon-intron boundaries, were enriched with Twist Bioscience technology.
Results
The clinical presentations included isolated proteinuria (in 11), isolated hematuria (in 6), a combination of both (in 4), and steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (in 3). Additional findings were hearing deficits (in 4), thrombocytopenia (in 1), and behavioral issues (in 1). A positive family history of renal disease was noted in 9 patients. Kidney biopsies performed in 9 patients revealed minimal changes (in 2), FSGS (in 2), thinning of the basement membrane (in 3), and Alport syndrome (in 2).
Genetic testing identified pathogenic variants in 18 patients (60%). Detected mutations included COL4A5 (in 6), COL4A3 (in 2), COL4A4 (in 1), COL4A3/A4 (in 1), AMN (in 1), CUBN (in 2), CLCN5 (in 1), OCRL (in 1), MYH9 (in 1), CFB (in 1), and monosomy X (n = 1).
Final diagnoses comprised Alport syndrome (in 4; dominant in 3, X-linked in 1), Dent disease type 1 (in 1) and type 2 (in 1), Epstein syndrome (EPTS, in 1), Imerslund-Gräsbeck syndrome (IGS, in 3), atypical HUS (in 1), and Turner syndrome (in 1).
Conclusion
Genetic testing has proven instrumental in diagnosing kidney diseases in children, reducing the need for invasive procedures like kidney biopsy in many cases and expanding the spectrum of identified disorders. Importantly, some conditions (EPTS, IGS) were diagnosed for the first time in Armenia. Genetic findings facilitated personalized management and family counseling, underscoring the significance of this diagnostic approach.

title: #902 Are metabolic kidney stone clinics clinically effective?
authors: Federico Maffei Faccioli; Mario Gennaro Cozzolino; Shabbir Moochhala
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney stone disease (KSD) is a prevalent condition with significant clinical and economic impact. This study evaluates patients attending the Royal Free Hospital's metabolic stone clinic between January 2018 and December 2023, focusing on demographics, comorbidities, suspected and final clinical underlying diagnosis and clinical outcomes.
Method
Data from 444 patients were reviewed. Patients with inadequate 24-hour urine analyses or non-attendance after performing biochemical tests (n = 106, 23.9%) were excluded, leaving 338 patients (76.1%) for analysis of age, gender, ethnicity, eGFR, comorbidities and suspected clinical diagnosis at their initial visit. A subgroup of 68 patients, composed of patients who had their initial visit in the year 2018, allowed evaluation of stone recurrence rate and clinical outcomes up to a five-year period.
Results
The median age of patients was 45.5 years, with 58% male prevalence. Ethnicity data was available for 51% of patients and reflected London's diverse population, with a slight prevalence of Europeans (51%). Other notable findings included:
-Prevalence of comorbidities at first visit:
◯ Chronic kidney disease at a stage ≥2 (eGFR <90) was present in 27% of patients.
◯ Diabetes mellitus was present in 14% of patients.
◯ Obesity, defined by a BMI >30, was present in 17% of patients.
◯ Osteopenia or osteoporosis was confirmed in only 9% of patients. However, 84% of patients lacked bone health data.
◯ Prevalence of known cardiovascular abnormalities (5%) or a history of bowel surgery was low (4%).
-Referrals & diagnostic evaluation at first visit:
Most referrals originated from urology and GPs (mostly at urologist's request) but with 19.2% of referrals coming from other nephrologists or paediatricians. 19% of patients were referred with an established diagnosis at presentation, with cystinuria being the most common. Of the remainder, the commonest suspected diagnosis was “lifestyle factors” (defined as poor water intake and lithogenic diet).
-Diagnoses and outcomes:
29% of patients were discharged after their first visit. Of the remainder 42% required follow-up for 1 year only, while 23% were monitored long term (for five years) and 12% did not attend their planned follow-up visit.
The initial suspected diagnosis was subsequently confirmed in 54% of previously undiagnosed patients, with “lifestyle factors” being the most common diagnosis. The remainder (n = 19 patients) had an alternative diagnosis, the commonest of which was primary hyperparathyroidism, followed by infective causes and then other rarer diagnoses. 8 others were lost to follow-up.
Rates of stone recurrence across all patients, defined as either clear evidence of new stones on imaging, the spontaneous expulsion of a stone or the surgical removal of a stone, were stable across follow-up periods (23%, 17%, and 21% for years 1, 2, and 3–5, respectively). Most patients (81%) did not require surgical intervention over their period of follow-up.
Conclusion
Although based on prevalence data only, this study highlights the role of this specialised metabolic stone clinic in diagnosing 54% of kidney stone formers without a previously known cause. In these patients, specific treatment options were available in 27% of all diagnosed kidney stone formers under follow up, while 44% of patients had disorders which could be managed by targeting their personal risk factors. Therefore, a total of 71% of referred patients benefitted from either a drug or personalised lifestyle intervention which is predicted to reduce their future stone recurrence.

title: #3541 Twelve years of genetic studies in polycystic kidney disease: a descriptive review in a tertiary center
authors: Cristina García Parejo; María Verónica Torres; Nathalie Martínez Tejeda; José Antonio Garrote Adrados; Blanca Martín Álvarez; Fernando Martín Caballero; Ángela Eraso Nájera; Luisa Gemma Sánchez García; Margarita Delgado Cerón; Sara Álvarez Tundidor; Danay Areli Ticona Espinoza; Belén Gómez Giralda
abstract:
Background and Aims
Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is a hereditary nephropathy characterized by progressive renal cyst formation, often leading to end-stage renal disease. It is classified into two main forms: autosomal dominant PKD (ADPKD), primarily caused by mutations in PKD1 and PKD2, and the rarer autosomal recessive PKD (ARPKD), linked to PKHD1 mutations. Other less frequent genes involved are GANAB and DNAJB11.
ADPKD is among the most prevalent monogenic disorders worldwide, yet its genetic and phenotypic variability complicates diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment. Advances in molecular diagnostics have expanded our understanding of PKD genetics, highlighting gaps in genotype-phenotype correlations and potential therapeutic targets.
Method
A retrospective observational study was conducted on patients treated at the Nephrology outpatient clinic of a tertiary center between 2012 and 2024.
Patients with suspected PKD, defined by suggestive findings on imaging studies or a family history of the disease, who had undergone genetic testing as part of the diagnostic process, were included in the study.
Demographic and clinical data were collected. The genetic study performed and the results obtained were recorded, classifying the identified variants based on the affected gene and their pathogenicity according to the criteria established by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG).
Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Categorical variables were expressed as frequencies and percentages, while continuous variables were presented as median and interquartile range.
Confidentiality was ensured by anonymizing patient data, in compliance with data protection regulations and ethical principles for clinical research.
Results
A total of 80 patients were analyzed, with a median age of 51 years [15−82], 57.5% were men. 70% of the patients had at least one cardiovascular risk (hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, obesity, ischemic heart disease, smoking, hyperuricemia).
Hypertension was the most common risk factor (65%), followed by diabetes (10%). No other cases of renal pathology or obstructive disease were identified in the studied cohort.
66.3% of the genetic studies tested positive, 32.5% negative and 1.3% the result is pending. Among the positive cases, genetic alterations were distributed as follows: 31.3% had mutations in the PKD1 gene, 22.5% in the PKD2 gene, 7.5% showed alterations in other genes associated with ADPKD and 2.5% had alterations in genes unrelated to ADPKD. Among patients with PKD1 mutations, 59.26% had a truncating mutation.
All patients included in the analysis underwent an abdominal ultrasound, with the following findings: 1.3% showed no abnormalities, 36.3% had renal involvement only, 58.8% had both renal and hepatic involvement, 3.8% had hepatic involvement only.
Additionally, 18 patients underwent abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to calculate total kidney volume, with a median value of 1096.4 mL [422.1−5068.6]; based on this measurement, the ADPKD classification was determined (1A: 5.26%, 1B: 21.05%, 1C: 31.58%, 1D: 36.84%, 1E: 5.26%).
Additionally, patients with a positive genetic study were classified according to the PROPKD Score (0: 28.85%, 1: 28.85%, 2: 3.85%, 3: 7.69%, 4: 13.46%, 5: 15.38%, 6: 1.92%).
Conclusion
These data show that more than half of the analyzed patients had a positive genetic variant, highlighting the importance of genetic testing in the diagnosis of PKD. The proportion of negative results is also significant, suggesting the possible influence of unidentified genes or limitations in the detection capacity of certain variants.
These findings confirm that PKD1 and PKD2 are the most frequently altered genes, consistent with existing literature on ADPKD. However, the detection of variants in other genes underscores the need for further studies to evaluate their clinical impact and potential role in disease progression.

title: #1088 Leveraging AI for early detection of chronic kidney and hereditary kidney diseases: a focus on Alport syndrome
authors: Elizabeth Romelia Viera Ramírez; Gabriel de Maeztu; Leonor Fayos de Arizón; Melissa Pilco Teran; Roser Torra
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a significant public health concern, with hereditary kidney diseases (HKDs), which can represent 10%–30% of CKD [1], often are underdiagnosed. Early identification is critical to improve outcomes and facilitate timely interventions. Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) is a standardized vocabulary that describes phenotypic abnormalities and clinical features, making it easier to identify the signs and symptoms that may indicate a condition. By systematically organizing these phenotypes, a HPO-based approach can help pinpointing specific trait combinations that might otherwise be overlooked, aiding in earlier detection of potential HKD cases. This project aims to identify potential HKD patients using natural language processing (NLP) and other artificial intelligence (AI) techniques applied to electronic medical records (EMRs) to find the HPO clinical features from existing clinical records. The study specifically focuses on validating the clinical utility of automated HPO feature extraction and evaluating potential patients that fulfill the HKD HPO phenotypes, starting with Alport syndrome, as this syndrome has a well established phenotype that has already been validated by experts.
Method
This multicentric initiative started with the standardization of the EMR data into the OMOP Common Data Model (CDM), a widely-used data standard in healthcare research that harmonizes diverse data sources. This enabled consistent analysis across different institutions, facilitates interoperability, ensuring data comparability and quality. NLP tools were employed to extract HPO terms associated with HKD, focusing on Alport syndrome as a case study, that were integrated back to the OMOP CDM.
Then a systematic search was performed in the OMOP CDM, that yield 267 patients diagnosed with an already confirmed Alport syndrome and 45,382 patients without a diagnosis but with one or more HPO terms compatible with the diagnosis. Of the 45,382 patients with HPO terms compatible, our target cohort, various techniques, including vector similarity, clustering algorithms, dimensionality reduction, and graph-based approaches, were used to further identify phenotypic patterns and undiagnosed cases. The patients with an already confirmed diagnosis, help to enhance the definition of phenotypic patterns, and 50 potential candidates were yielded for a further evaluation. These patients are being followed up in a nephro-urological monographic center to confirm the diagnosis with genetic testing. In parallel a verification and validation assessment of the AI tool was independently performed, both for the on the HPO term extraction process and the identification of the subject.
Results
The NLP model achieved an accuracy of 78.3% and an F1 score of 83.3% in extraction of the HPO terms, underscoring its robustness in identifying meaningful patterns. Validation results confirmed that non-significant outliers did not compromise overall data quality, enhancing confidence in the findings. The phenotypic clustering revealed potential undiagnosed cases, which are at the moment going through a genetic testing for a confirmation on the result.
Conclusion
The study demonstrates the potential of NLP-driven approaches for identifying undiagnosed HPO terms in the existing clinical records. However, challenges such as data completeness and variability were observed, emphasizing the necessity for broader, more diverse datasets to strengthen future analyses and applications. While potentially effective for the identification of patients with a potential Alport syndrome, the methodology requires further optimization and expansion to other HKD types.

title: #3831 Clinical course of autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease in adults
authors: Irene Vázquez Raso; Isabel Galan Carrillo; Amir Shabaka; Víctor Martínez Jiménez; Juan Piñero; Diego Morante Martinez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) is a rare genetic disease with a wide phenotypic variability, that usually manifests in the peri-neonatal period and is characterized by the formation of renal and/or hepatic cysts with or without congenital hepatic fibrosis and/or pulmonary hypoplasia. The mortality rate in the neonatal period is high, and in those who survive the incidence of developing renal insufficiency requiring renal replacement therapy during infancy is around 50%. There is a scarce knowledge of the clinical course of ARPKD in patients who reach adulthood without end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). The aim of our study was to describe the kidney outcomes in adult patients with ARPKD.
Method
We performed a retrospective observational study of patients diagnosed with ARPKD in infancy who transitioned to the adult nephrology outpatient clinic without developing ESKD during infancy, and those who were diagnosed of ARPKD during adulthood. We recorded demographic data, gestational information, gene mutation findings, comorbidities and the clinical course of kidney disease during follow-up. Kidney disease progression was evaluated by the rate of decline of estimated glomerular filtration rate calculated by the CKD-EPI formula.
Results
Seven patients from 7 different families were included in the study. The median age at diagnosis was 11.6 years (IQR 6 months–40 years). From diagnosis, median follow-up was 13 years (IQR 7–23 years). Only 1 patient had presented oligohydramnios, and 2 patients presented a preterm birth. During the neonatal period, none of the patients had presented pulmonary hypoplasia, and before the age of 18 years 2 patients presented hypertension and 3 patients presented signs of portal hypertension. Beyond the age of 18 years, only 1 additional patient developed hypertension (onset at 39 years) and no additional patients developed hepatic manifestations. At the onset of follow-up in the adult Nephrology clinic, median estimated glomerular filtration rate was 51 ml/min (IQR 17-130 ml/min). After a median of 8 years of follow-up, 3 patients remained with a normal kidney function, 2 patients remained with a stable stage 3a CKD without progression during adulthood, and 2 patients progressed to ESKD.
Conclusion
This study underlines the broad clinical spectrum of adult patients diagnosed with ARPKD. The majority of patients who reach adulthood without renal insufficiency remained with a normal/stable kidney function, while a subset of patients progress to end-stage kidney disease.

title: #1100 “Unraveling the genetic complexity of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease: insights from gene conversion events”
authors: Paola Donoso Naranjo; Raquel Fernández García; Natalia Santos Collado; José Antonio Cidoncha Murillo; Manuel López Mendoza; José Luis Rocha Castilla
abstract:
Background
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is a genetic disorder characterized by the progressive development of renal cysts, which can ultimately result in end-stage renal failure. This condition is linked to pathogenic variants occurring in a heterozygous state in the PKD1 (located on chromosomal region 16p13.3) and PKD2 (located on 4q21–23) genes. One significant molecular event is the phenomenon of gene conversion, which occurs between PKD1 and one of its pseudogenes. This process involves the transfer of DNA sequences from the pseudogene to the functional PKD1 gene, potentially leading to mutations that cause a loss of PKD1 protein function and the subsequent manifestation of the disease.
Case Report
We present the case of a 38-year-old male patient with a family history of polycystic kidney disease (PKD). His father required renal replacement therapy (RRT) at the age of 44 and is presently a kidney transplant recipient. The patient was diagnosed with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (PKDAD) in 2012, based on his clinical history and compatible renal ultrasound findings. Follow-up evaluations began in 2018, showing normal renal function with a creatinine level of 0.94 mg/dL and a calculated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 107.6 mL/min/1.73 m². In May 2019, a genetic study utilizing massive sequencing was conducted, but it did not identify specific variants clearly associated with polycystic kidney disease. A subsequent analysis for copy number variations (CNVs) also revealed no alterations in the studied genes. Consequently, the patient was informed that pre-implantation genetic diagnosis could not be considered for any future offspring.
In April 2024, the Pediatric Nephrology department recommended a genetic study for the patient's 2-year-old daughter, as renal ultrasounds indicated the presence of cysts. The analysis of point variants in genes associated with cystic kidney disease revealed a PKD1 allele with three missense mutations (c.8279T>C; c.8282G>C; c.8291T>C), all in heterozygous form. While each substitution is considered a variant of uncertain clinical significance on its own, the combination of all three has been described as probably pathogenic. This particular combination has been reported as a result of gene conversion between PKD1 and its pseudogene PKD1P3. In light of these findings, a genetic study was repeated for the patient, and the same PKD1 alteration was identified.
Conclusion
Gene conversion occurs when DNA sequences are exchanged between highly similar genes due to unequal crossing over during meiosis. This process can lead to mutations if the exchanged sequence affects the gene's coding region or contains pre-existing mutations. In the context of PKDAD, gene conversion complicates molecular diagnosis because it makes the precise identification of pathogenic mutations challenging. As a result, advanced sequencing techniques are often necessary for accurate genetic evaluation. The findings emphasize the importance of periodically re-evaluating cases that previously returned negative genetic results, especially with the availability of new methodologies, databases, and updated research publications.

title: #1699 ChatGPT performance in solving medical residency questions in nephrology: a pilot study in Brazil
authors: Helvécio Neves Feitosa Filho; João Filipe Cavalcante Uchoa Furtado; Pedro Vianna Caldas Ribeiro; Eduardo Correia Eulálio; Lucas MacÊdo Aurélio Paiva; Isabela Diógenes Feitosa; Elizabeth De Francesco Daher; Geraldo Bezerra Da Silva Junior
abstract:
Background and Aims
Large-scale language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, have significantly influenced advances in artificial intelligence (AI). Although they demonstrate competence in general medical examinations, the effectiveness of GPT in answering specific questions in Nephrology is still poorly investigated. This study aimed to evaluate the performance of ChatGPT 4 and 3.5 in answering Nephrology questions from medical residency tests in Brazil.
Method
This is an experimental study comparing the performance of ChatGPT 4 and 3.5, analyzing 411 Nephrology questions extracted from 310 medical residency tests applied between 2010 and 2024 in Brazil. Multiple-choice questions were selected, with and without images, excluding open-ended or binary questions. For questions with images, only GPT 4 was applied. The questions were organized into 4 main themes: chronic kidney disease (CKD), hydroelectrolyte/acid-base disorders (DHAB), tubulointerstitial diseases (TID) and glomerular diseases (GD). The results and possible potential machine errors were cataloged in a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet and the statistical analysis was conducted through the SPSS software, using the chi-square test.
Results
Among the 411 questions selected, 389 without images and 22 with images; GPT 4 presented an overall accuracy of 79.80% (328) and GPT 3.5 56.29% (219) with P < 0.001; OR: 3.086; CI: 2.256–4.220. In the main themes, DHAB GPT 4 achieved 79.11% (125) vs 55.17% (80) of 3.5 (P < 0.001; OR: 3.078; CI: 1.859–5.096), TID 4 had an accuracy of 88.23% (60) vs 52.63% (35) of 3.5 (P < 0.001; OR: 6.857 and CI: 2.845 - 16.528), CKD 4 with 75.51% (74) vs 61.95% (57) (P < 0.001; OR: 1.893 and CI: 1.015–3.533) and GD 4 obtained 79.31% (69) vs 54.65% (47) of 3.5 (P < 0.001; OR: 3.099 and CI: 1.582–6.070). When comparing the performance of GPT 4 in questions without and with image, the machine presents an accuracy of 81.49% (317) vs 54.54% (12) with an accuracy of 60% (6) in electrocardiogram analysis. Regarding the errors, there were 36 in common, 19 in DHAB where 68.42% (13) were in acid-base calculation; 12 in GD where 58.33% (7) in conduct, TID 3 and CKD 2.
Conclusion
The widely used open source GPT 3.5 Chat has low reasoning capacity in solving nephrology questions compared to GPT-4, illustrating knowledge gaps. Other themes in nephrology still need to be explored by this AI tool.

title: #1803 Therapeutic potential of propylparaben in modulating pathophysiological features of Fabry nephropathy
authors: Eun Sil Koh; Mina Son; So Young Lee; Yong Kyun Kim; Sungjin Chung
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fabry disease is a rare X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutation in the GLA gene, resulting in deficient α-galactosidase A enzyme activity, leading to progressive multi-organ damage, including kidney failure. Despite the widespread use of enzyme replacement therapy (ERT), some patients experience disease progression. This study evaluated the therapeutic potential of propylparaben (PP) in a Fabry disease model, focusing on renal fibrosis, oxidative stress, inflammation, and urine albumin excretion.
Method
Histological changes, inflammatory markers, oxidative stress markers, and lipid peroxidation in the kidneys were assessed in wild-type control mice, untreated Fabry disease mice, and Fabry disease mice treated with PP.
Results
Fabry disease mice exhibited increased renal interstitial fibrosis compared to wild-type controls, as evidenced by trichrome and Sirius red staining, but PP treatment significantly reduced fibrosis in Fabry disease mice. Elevated renal mRNA levels of pro-inflammatory markers such as IL-1β and IL-6 in Fabry disease were downregulated by PP treatment. In PP-treated Fabry disease mice, renal HO-1 protein levels were significantly increased and 4-HNE expression was reduced. Additionally, Fabry disease mice showed elevated albuminuria levels, which were significantly reduced following PP treatment.
Conclusion
This study demonstrates that PP mitigates renal inflammation, fibrosis, oxidative stress, and albuminuria in a Fabry disease model. These findings suggest that PP holds promise as a potential therapeutic option, warranting further investigation in clinical settings.
