title: #1967 Why is the genetic test for the ADTKD subtype MUC1 so complex and what alternative diagnostic procedures are available?
authors: Christian Scheidler; Bernt Popp
abstract:
Background and Aims
The European patient organization for Autosomal Dominant Tubulointerstitial Kidney Disease (ADTKD) raises awareness and funds cure research (www.adTKD.de/en-gb). At least five disease genes (UMOD, MUC1, REN, HNF1B, and SEC61A1) have causative mutations, with more expected [1]. Due to its non-specific clinical presentation, only a genetic test can diagnose it.
The variable number tandem repeat (VNTR) region in ADTKD-MUC1, the second most common subtype, makes detection difficult. Therefore, many patients are misdiagnosed or undiagnosed [2]. Due to the Broad Institute in the US and the University of Erlangen in Germany testing potentially effective ADTKD compounds, this unsatisfactory diagnostic situation is growing [4]. Moreover, a European initiative is registering ADTKD patients in the ERKNet database, paving the way for clinical drug trials. We aim to highlight the complexity of ADTKD-MUC1 genetic testing and examine recently published diagnostic solutions that could make testing more common in clinical practice.
Method
We conducted a comprehensive review of the latest literature on ADTKD-MUC1, focusing on the challenges of the VNTR region and evaluating existing and newly developed testing strategies. We compared these methods based on feasibility, accuracy, cost, invasiveness, and usability in clinical laboratories.
Results
The gold standard for MUC1 gene testing, SNaPShot, targets the VNTR region (up to 130 repeats of 60 base pairs with high GC content) but is only offered by a small number of European laboratories. This method is labor-intensive and does not reveal the exact location of the pathogenic variant. In countries such as Germany, reimbursement remains problematic, further limiting its routine use [2]. Our survey revealed that some European countries (e.g., the Netherlands, Ireland, and the United Kingdom) still lack in-country options for MUC1 genetic testing, making cross-border collaborations essential [2].
Recent advances allow detection of MUC1 variants in short-read next-generation sequencing (NGS) data, but the VNTR region's repetitive and GC-rich nature complicates straightforward bioinformatic analysis. Newly developed approaches, such as VNtyper [3], provide alignment-free genotyping from NGS data, detecting whether a pathogenic insertion is present (Fig. 2). VNtyper has now been updated to version 2.0, featuring improved variant-calling algorithms, a more user-friendly pipeline, and a web server (vntyper.org) offering free, online access. Version 2.0 can integrate additional modules for improved filtering (SHARK) and alternative genotyping (code-adVNTR), expanding its utility for various sequencing setups.
Immunohistochemistry can identify mutated MUC1 in kidney tissue, confirming ADTKD-MUC1 status non-genetically. This method requires a kidney biopsy and does not pinpoint the mutation's location.
Long-read sequencing platforms (e.g., Oxford Nanopore and PacBio) can overcome the limitations of short-read methods by avoiding reliance on PCR amplification in the repetitive VNTR region. Although still under development for clinical application, they have the potential to pinpoint the exact location of the MUC1 variant.
Conclusion
The diagnostic complexity of ADTKD-MUC1 arises primarily from the VNTR region's repetitive, GC-rich structure. Although SNaPShot remains the diagnostic gold standard, new NGS-based methods, such as the updated VNtyper 2.0 pipeline, will allow for broad screening, while long-read sequencing approaches will provide promising alternatives for more detailed diagnostics. With clinical trials for new ADTKD treatments looming [4], improving and standardizing MUC1 testing is critical. The widespread adoption of accessible, reliable genetic testing methods in Europe and beyond will be critical for identifying patients early, guiding therapeutic interventions, and accelerating drug development for ADTKD-MUC1.

title: #3187 Computational modelling to predict genotype–phenotype relationships in autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease
authors: Taylor Richards; Paraskevi Goggolidou
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) is a rare inherited disease that affects 1:20,000 children globally. The disease is characterised by progressive cystic kidney disease and liver fibrosis, with variable presentation even between related individuals.
ARPKD is most commonly caused by mutations in polycystic kidney and hepatic disease 1 (PKHD1), with only a few familial cases being linked to other genes. Although most cases of ARPKD will feature mutations in PKHD1, there is considerable clinical variability in the presentation of the disease. Many patients will present with severe kidney and liver disease. Some patients will present with severe disease in one of the two organs or mild disease in both. Efforts to address relationships between genotype and phenotype have so far only highlighted a relationship between patients with dual stop gain variants and severe presentations of ARPKD, linked to perinatal/neonatal death. A complication of linking mutations to disease severity in ARPKD is that, outside of a few founder and hotspot mutations, most families have a unique combination of PKHD1 mutations.
To elucidate relationships between genotype and phenotype, this project has sought to use machine learning to highlight relationships between variant position and disease presentation. It aims to predict disease outcomes in ARPKD patients, allowing for the prioritisation of high-risk candidates for limited resources, such as organ transplants.
Method
A database of patient variant combinations (genotype) and disease outcomes (phenotype) was created from existing literature on PKHD1 mutations using available resources and data from journals published in the period 2003 – 2022. Machine learning was applied to the disease outcomes to identify relationships between genotype and phenotype. Data from published resources (2010 – 2020) and the AregPKD database was used as test data.
The program AlphaFold, developed by Google's DeepMind, was used to estimate the 3D structure of the PKHD1 protein Fibrocystin (FPC) using the UseGalaxy.eu servers. Domain predictions were performed using the FoldSeek webserver. Variant combinations from the genotype—phenotype database was compared to the 3D structure to highlight relationships between protein structure and disease outcomes.
Results
AlphaFold predicted the complete 4,074 amino acid protein Fibrocystin. Regions linked to the homology predicted structures (IPT, PA14, PBH and G8 domains) with high (pLDDT >70) confidence. The region encompassing the most prolific ARPKD mutation (T36M) and the intracellular tail were predicted with low confidence (pLDDT <50).
Comparing the 3D structure to known protein structures suggests similarities to human Fibrillin-2 (E-value = 0.00e+0), Laminin subunit alpha-1 (E = 0.00e+0) and Nesprin-2 (E = 3.72e−76), two of which are proteins involved in either migration, cell organisation or the actin cytoskeleton. Other structural similarity involved the human TMEM2 ectodomains (E-value = 2.97e−21), calmodulin-binding transcription activator 1 (E = 2.79e−2) and mouse Plexin A1 extracellular domains (E = 5.27e−9).
Conclusion
AlphaFold has been useful in predicting the tertiary structure of FPC confirming the structural domains previously highlighted by homologous modelling. Additionally, AlphaFold has been useful in highlighting potential functional activities of FPC by comparing it to the tertiary structure of other known proteins. Future work will involve mapping previously reported disease-causing variants in PKHD1 to highlight a relationship between the tertiary structure of FPC and disease outcomes. Additionally, a categorical model will be trained on previously reported mutation combinations to further define genotype–phenotype relationships.

title: #3783 Beyond clinical limits: genetic testing as a key tool to correctly identify the cause of microscopic hematuria
authors: Carolina Ciavaglia; Andrea Latessa; Samantha Innocenti; Luigi Cirillo; Viviana Palazzo; Samuela Landini; Valentina Raglianti; Benedetta Mazzinghi; Marco Allinovi; Paola Romagnani; Francesca Becherucci
abstract:
Background and Aims
Collagenopathies primarily manifest as isolated microscopic hematuria, usually followed by proteinuria and progressive kidney function loss. Currently available guidelines recommend genetic testing for COL4A3–COL4A5 genes in patients with persistent hematuria (>6 months) without any obvious cause. The aim of this study was to identify clinical and laboratory features that predict a conclusive genetic diagnosis of collagenopathies long-term kidney outcomes in patients with persistent microhematuria.
Method
In this monocentric, retrospective study, we enrolled all patients with persistent microhematuria who underwent genetic analysis with whole exome sequencing (WES) at our Center. For each patient, we collected demographic, clinical and laboratory data at onset and during follow-up. Patients were classified in two groups (genetic and non-genetic) according to the results of genetic testing. Between groups differences were evaluated through Student's t test, Mann-Whitney U test and Chi-square test with Yates correction, as appropriate. Kaplan–Meier estimates were used to generate an overall survival curve for the development of CKD in genetic and non-genetic group. Differences among groups were assessed by log-rank test. Logistic regression models were used to estimate the risk of CKD (eGFR at last available follow up <90 mL/min/1.73 m2) according to baseline demographic and clinical parameters. Results were reported as crude odds ratios (ORs), with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs). A P value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. According to Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcome Guideline (KDIGO), we defined CKD as estimated GFR (eGFR) <90 ml/min/1.73 m2 present for at least 3 months. We estimated the glomerular filtration rate by the formula CKiD U25 for the pediatric patients and with CKD-EPI for the adults.
Results
We enrolled 112 patients with persistent microscopic hematuria (Table 1). The median level of hematuria at onset was 96 red blood cells per high power field (RBC/HPF; IQR 20–3402 RBC/HPF). Proteinuria was present in 45% of cases at onset. The median length of follow-up was 6.5 years (IQR 3–51 years). Kidney biopsy had been performed prior to referral in 35/112 (31%) patients. WES combined with reverse phenotyping led to a conclusive genetic diagnosis of Collagenopathies in 83/112 (75%) cases. In the remaining 29 cases, genetic testing was uninformative. By comparing data at onset and referral in two subgroups, we did not identify any distinctive features suggesting a genetic diagnosis of Collagenopathies. The median length of follow-up was 4 years (IQR 2–5 years) in the genetic group and 3 years (IQR 1–10 years) in non-genetic one. We observed CKD in 16/64 (25.1%) of patients classified as genetic and in 13/29 (44.9%) of non-genetics (P = 0.095). The two populations did not differ in terms of proteinuria at last follow-up (P = 0.73). Kaplan Meier kidney-survival analysis showed that non-genetics had a significantly worse kidney survival rate in comparison to patient with collagenopathies (P = 0.019). At univariate analysis, birth weight, birth age, proteinuria, hypertension at onset were not found to increase the risk of CKD at last follow-up, whereas the presence of eGFR <90 and <60 ml/min/1.73 m2 at onset (OR 5.3455 (IC 95%: 1.4197–20.1273; OR 6.92 IC 95%: 1.13–42.13) were significant predictors for development of CKD at last follow-up (P = 0.03).
Conclusion
The results of this study highlight the need for genetic testing to provide patients with microscopic hematuria a conclusive diagnosis. Indeed, clinical and laboratory features at onset do not allow clinicians to reliably identify patients affected by collagenopathies, who may benefit from early nephroprotective therapies.

title: #2256 Rate of HMGCR gene methylation in diabetic patients on hemodialysis
authors: Magdalena Mokrejsova; Sylvie Dusilova Sulkova; Jaroslav Kalous
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with chronic kidney disease, especially those on hemodialysis (HD), exhibit a pronounced risk for cardiovascular mortality. Unfortunately and conversely to general population, cholesterol-lowering medication, such as inhibitors of HMGCR-statins, does not reduce this CV risk.
The incidence and severity of CV complications in CKD patients correlates with changed epigenetic mechanisms. The most studied epigenetic phenomenon is DNA methylation, i.e. methyl group bound at the cytosine of DNA. Methylated parts of DNA are not readily accessible to the transcriptional machinery. Therefore final gene expression is suppressed.
The aim of this study was to elucidate the methylation status of HMGCR gene in diabetic patients during hemodialysis procedure and its interplay with statins medication and LDL cholesterol plasma levels.
Method
Cell-free DNA was isolated in pre- and post-HD plasma samples of 45 HD patients (26 diabetics and 19 non-diabetics; 17 of them on statin medication). LDL cholesterol plasma levels were measured in these patients.
Bisulfite conversion was carried out to distinguish methylated and unmethylated form of the DNA. The primers of HMGCR genes promotors were designed, after that methylation specific PCR and sequential analysis of PCR products were performed.
Percentage of methylated cytosines in HMGCR gene promoter amplicons was subsequently assessed.
Results
The lower methylation rate of HMGCR gene was found in diabetic compared withnondiabetic patients before dialysis session (68.39% versus 78.24%, P < 0.005).
Additionally HD procedure itself led to the increase of methylation status just in diabetics (68.39% versus 74.94%, P < 0.005) (Fig. 1).
A significantly higher rate of HMGCR gene methylation before HD was associated with statin therapy (79.82% versus 68.95%, P < 0.05). After dialysis there was no statistically significant difference (Fig. 2).
Methylation of HMGCR gene was not associated with LDL cholesterol concentration.
Conclusion
This pilot study showed that HMGCR gene before dialysis was hypomethylated just in diabetic patients. Only in this group the methylation rose during the dialysis session.
We confirmed higher methylation status of HMGCR gene in patients treated using HMGCR inhibitors.

title: #3763 Usage of genetic testing, awareness levels, and barriers in nephrology practice in turkey: a national survey study
authors: Zeynep Ural
abstract:
Background and Aims
Genetic testing is gaining prominence in the diagnosis and management of chronic kidney disease (CKD), with an increasing number of adult kidney diseases being linked to genetic causes. However, its adoption in clinical practice remains limited due to knowledge gaps and systemic barriers.
This study investigates the awareness, knowledge, and implementation of genetic testing among nephrologists in Turkey. We aim to identify key barriers such as cost, accessibility, and interpretation issues while assessing the impact of demographic and professional factors. Furthermore, we explore potential policy recommendations to integrate genetic testing into routine nephrology practice.
Method
A nationwide survey was conducted from June 25 to July 25, 2024, involving adult and pediatric nephrologists, including fellows, through national associations and online platforms. Data were collected using an online questionnaire. Descriptive statistics and chi-square tests were used for data analysis.
Results
A total of 158 nephrologists participated. The participants represented various healthcare institutions, including university hospitals (44.9%), research and training hospitals (36.1%), and private clinics (7.6%), covering 48 cities across Turkey.
Several barriers were identified as obstacles to genetic test implementation. The most frequently cited issue was the lack of available genetic testing at their centers (46.8%), followed by insufficient knowledge about genetic testing (42.4%) and high costs (36.1%). Other barriers included delays in obtaining test results due to long processing times (31.6%) and the perception that genetic tests are not essential for clinical outcomes (22.8%). Regarding knowledge levels, only 25.3% of nephrologists considered themselves adequately informed, while 55.7% felt they had partial knowledge. Furthermore, 44.3% emphasized the requirement of filling out detailed genetic test request forms, which they believed significantly impacted the interpretability of results. Only 20.3% of the participants expressed confidence in interpreting genetic test results independently, indicating a reliance on multidisciplinary collaboration.
Conclusion
To enhance the integration of genetic testing into nephrology practice, several key policy recommendations must be implemented. First, improving genetic literacy among nephrologists through structured education programs and accessible resources is essential. Collaborative efforts should be strengthened by establishing multidisciplinary councils that bring together nephrologists, geneticists, and other specialists to streamline diagnosis and management. Developing national clinical guidelines for the use of genetic testing will provide standardized protocols and improve consistency in practice. Additionally, addressing financial and logistical barriers by reducing costs and improving test accessibility is critical.
Our findings align with a previous survey conducted among 149 adult nephrologists in the United States, which identified similar barriers such as high costs (46%), limited accessibility, and insufficient knowledge on genetic testing applications. This demonstrates the global nature of challenges surrounding genetic testing in nephrology. However, unlike previous studies, our survey represents the most comprehensive assessment of its kind in Turkey, covering a broad spectrum of both adult and pediatric nephrologists across multiple institutions and regions. As the first national-scale study in Turkey, it provides critical insights into the gaps and opportunities for integrating genetic testing. By adopting a personalized and multidisciplinary approach and building on international collaborations, these findings can serve as a foundation for future improvements and innovations in genetic nephrology practices globally.

title: #72 Procalcitonin levels at hospital admission are increased in cyst infection in patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
authors: Jihad Abdelmalki; Laurence Seidel; Frédéric Frippiat; Pierre Lovinfosse; François Jouret
abstract:
Background and Aims
The diagnosis of cyst infection in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) remains difficult due to nonspecific symptoms overlapping with other cystic and non-cystic complications. [18F]FDG PET/CT imaging is helpful but not definitive, and early diagnosis remains challenging. Procalcitonin (PCT), a serum biomarker for bacterial infections, has not been evaluated in ADPKD-related cyst infections. This study aims to assess PCT's diagnostic value in ADPKD patients with suspected cyst infections.
Method
A retrospective review (between 2009–2023) identified all ADPKD patients who were (i) hospitalized (ii) with serum PCT measurements. Cyst infection diagnosis was conventionally based on the concomitant parameters: (i) fever; (ii) abdominal pain; (iii) high plasma C-reactive protein (CRP, ≥70 mg/L); (iv) absence of alternative inflammatory causes; and (v) pathological uptake of [18F]FDG above the physiological hepatic background. Statistical analyses, including univariate and multivariate logistic regressions, assessed the association between clinical/biological parameters and cyst infection risk. PCT association with [18F]FDG uptake was analyzed using ordinal logistic regression.
Results
The cohort included 104 patients (mean age of 65.5 ± 14.9 years; 49% post-kidney transplantation; 16.3% on chronic dialysis). Cyst infections occurred in 24 cases. The hospitalization motives of the remaining cases were infections or inflammation in the lungs (n = 19), the urinary tract (n = 9), or the digestive tract (n = 12). COVID-19 was evidenced in 13 cases, while inflammation remained of unknown origin in 18 cases. Cyst hemorrhage was suspected in 9 cases. [18F]FDG PET/CT was performed in 47 patients, detecting cyst infections in 17 cases and non-cystic inflammation in 11. In the whole cohort, CRP levels at admission were elevated at 97.3 [42.8; 164] mg/L, while white blood cell counts averaged 8.52 [6.3; 12.1] 10³/mm³. Serum PCT level was measured within 72 hours post admission in 83/104 (79%) cases, and the median value reached 0.47 [0.18–2.04] µg/L. PCT >0.59 µg/L significantly predicted cyst infections (OR = 6.30, P = 0.0047). Higher PCT was associated with cyst [18F]FDG uptake above the pathological threshold (OR = 2.01, P = 0.0028).
Conclusion
PCT >0.59 µg/L within 72 hours post-admission is a significant marker for cyst infection in ADPKD patients, being associated with [18F]FDG PET/CT findings.

title: #777 Genetic testing for kidney disease—single centre experience
authors: Svetlana Jovicic Pavlovic; Jelena Nikolic; Kristina Petrovic; Milorad Stojadinovic; Anita Skakic; Sonja Pavlovic; Milan Radovic
abstract:
Background and Aims
Advances in gene sequencing techniques have made them available in clinical practice, which has changed the approach in the diagnosis of kidney diseases and revealed the etiology of many previously unrecognized conditions and diseases. Recent studies have shown that about 9% of patients with chronic kidney disease have a genetic cause. The aim of our study was to determine the usefulness of genetic analyzes in the diagnosis of kidney diseases.
Method
At the Clinic for Nephrology of the University Clinical Center of Serbia, in cooperation with the Institute for Molecular Genetics and Genetic Engineering (IMGGI) University in Belgrade, since February 2023, gene analyzes in the diagnosis of kidney diseases have been carried out. In the period until June 2024, 30 patients with suspected hereditary kidney diseases (certain phenotypes, positive family history) were analyzed. Clinical diagnoses before testing were: suspected hereditary glomerulonephritis, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, suspected Gitelman syndrome, atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, and chronic renal failure that occurred at a young age with a family history. At IMGGI, the coding exons of clinically relevant genes were sequenced using the TruSight One (Illumina) panel and compared with the sequence of the reference human genome.
Results
18 patients had a positive test result. The following were diagnosed: X-linked inherited Alport syndrome (1 patient and 2 female patients carrying the mutation), PKD 1 mutation for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (1), INF 2 mutation in focal segmental glomerulosclerosis with familial occurrence (2), SLC12A3 mutation for Gitelman syndrome (1), SLC3A1 mutation for cystinuria (1), mutations in complement factor I genes in two families (5), PLEC mutation in a family of a patient with unknown cause of chronic renal failure (4) and heterozygous mutation MTMR2 for Charcot Marie Tooth in a potential kidney donor (1). There were negative findings in 12 patients, namely in genes for complement factors (6), Alport syndrome (4), panel for focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (2).
Conclusion
The application of genetic analyzes made it possible to establish a precise diagnosis, determine the therapy and prognosis of the disease in 60% of the analyzed patients. Determining the mode of disease inheritance is important for assessing the risk of disease in family members, for family planning and prenatal screening. The negative findings of the genetic analyzes in remaining patients were used to rule out hereditary forms of the disease.

title: #817 Genetic testing in adults with nephrocalcinosis enables precision diagnosis
authors: Elena Emanuela Rusu; Gabriel-Robert Pandele; Andreea Blaga; Diana Zilisteanu; Sonia Balanica; Gener Ismail
abstract:
Background and Aims
Nephrocalcinosis (NC) refers to the parenchymal form of nephrolithiasis (NL), and could be detected by ultrasonography or computer tomography (CT), isolated or in association with NL. The etiology of NC and NL is multifactorial and includes both environmental components and genetic components. Molecular analysis in patients with NC allows an appropriate evaluation. Genetic testing for known pathogenic mutations has become more accessible due to technologic advances and decreasing of the cost.
Method
We report a retrospective observational study that included adults with diagnosis of nephrocalcinosis diagnosed by renal ultrasound or CT scan, on whom we performed a genetic test using nephrolithiasis panel, from two commercial genetic laboratories. The study was conducted between September 2020–December 2024 in the nephrology department, Fundeni Clinical Institute. Demographics, personal and family history, clinical and biological data were recorded at the time of genetic test performance. The estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was calculated using CKD-EPI equation, and CKD stage was classified according to the KDIGO guideline.
Results
The study included 13 adult patients, 6 males and 7 females. The mean age at the time of genetic testing was 33.0 ± 10.3 years, but the mean age of the NC diagnosis was 20.1 ± 10.9 years. All patients presented medullary NC; in nine patients (69.2%) had NC associated with NL, and four patients (30.8%) had isolated NC. Family history was positive for NL and/or NC in 8 patients (61.5%). Also, 7 patients (53.8%) presented pediatric onset of the disease.
We found a Mendelian disease in 10 patients: inherited distal renal tubular acidosis (dRTA) (SLC4A1; n = 3), Dent disease (CLCN5; n = 2), infantile hypercalcemia type 1 (CYP24A1; n = 2), familial hypomagnesaemia with hypercalciuria and NC (CLDN16; n = 1), primary hyperoxaluria (PH) type 1 (AGXT; n = 1), Bartter syndrome type 2 (KCNJ1; n = 1). One patient had a monoallelic pathogenic variant in SLC34A3 gene, another patient had a monoallelic variant of uncertain significance of SLC3A1 gene, and in one patient the genetic test was negative. Analyzing the inheritance type of the Mendelian diseases we noticed that 5 patients had an autosomal recessive genetic disease, 3 had an autosomal dominant genetic type of inheritance, and 2 patients had an X-linked disease.
Considering the chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage, 6 patients had CKD G1-G2, 4 patients had CKD G3, 2 patients had CKD G4, and 1 patient had a kidney transplant. Other specific manifestations in those 12 patients with positive genetic test included, distal renal tubular acidosis (n = 4), hypercalciuria (n = 3), low intact parathormone (n = 2).
Although the clinical diagnosis was concordant with the molecular diagnosis in 5 patients with Mendelian disease, another 5 patients remained clinically undiagnosed due to the association with other genetic disease (mutation of GANAB gene, n = 1), the presence of advanced kidney disease that altered the clinical phenotype, and the variability of the phenotype.
Knowing the molecular diagnosis, we implemented a personalized management that included: initiating the specific treatment such as the newly introduced small interfering RNA treatment for the PH type 1 patient, avoiding vitamin D for patients with infantile hypercalcemia type 1, correction of acidosis, hypokalemia for inherited dRTA patients.
Conclusion
In our study, 12/13 patients tested for genetic causes of NC presented mutations of different genes, and 10/13 patients had a Mendelian disease. Our results confirm that NC is a manifestation which is frequently associated with a genetic disease. Thus, genetic testing should be considered in all patients with nephrocalcinosis. Genetic testing enables accurate diagnoses, changes in disease management, and precision medicine, that could significantly influence the long-term outcomes.

Demographics, personal and family history, clinical and biological data were recorded at the time of genetic test performance. The estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was calculated using CKD-EPI equation, and CKD stage was classified according to the KDIGO guideline.
Results
The study included 13 adult patients, 6 males and 7 females. The mean age at the time of genetic testing was 33.0 ± 10.3 years, but the mean age of the NC diagnosis was 20.1 ± 10.9 years. All patients presented medullary NC; in nine patients (69.2%) had NC associated with NL, and four patients (30.8%) had isolated NC. Family history was positive for NL and/or NC in 8 patients (61.5%). Also, 7 patients (53.8%) presented pediatric onset of the disease.
We found a Mendelian disease in 10 patients: inherited distal renal tubular acidosis (dRTA) (SLC4A1; n = 3), Dent disease (CLCN5; n = 2), infantile hypercalcemia type 1 (CYP24A1; n = 2), familial hypomagnesaemia with hypercalciuria and NC (CLDN16; n = 1), primary hyperoxaluria (PH) type 1 (AGXT; n = 1), Bartter syndrome type 2 (KCNJ1; n = 1). One patient had a monoallelic pathogenic variant in SLC34A3 gene, another patient had a monoallelic variant of uncertain significance of SLC3A1 gene, and in one patient the genetic test was negative. Analyzing the inheritance type of the Mendelian diseases we noticed that 5 patients had an autosomal recessive genetic disease, 3 had an autosomal dominant genetic type of inheritance, and 2 patients had an X-linked disease.
Considering the chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage, 6 patients had CKD G1-G2, 4 patients had CKD G3, 2 patients had CKD G4, and 1 patient had a kidney transplant. Other specific manifestations in those 12 patients with positive genetic test included, distal renal tubular acidosis (n = 4), hypercalciuria (n = 3), low intact parathormone (n = 2).
Although the clinical diagnosis was concordant with the molecular diagnosis in 5 patients with Mendelian disease, another 5 patients remained clinically undiagnosed due to the association with other genetic disease (mutation of GANAB gene, n = 1), the presence of advanced kidney disease that altered the clinical phenotype, and the variability of the phenotype.
Knowing the molecular diagnosis, we implemented a personalized management that included: initiating the specific treatment such as the newly introduced small interfering RNA treatment for the PH type 1 patient, avoiding vitamin D for patients with infantile hypercalcemia type 1, correction of acidosis, hypokalemia for inherited dRTA patients.
Conclusion
In our study, 12/13 patients tested for genetic causes of NC presented mutations of different genes, and 10/13 patients had a Mendelian disease. Our results confirm that NC is a manifestation which is frequently associated with a genetic disease. Thus, genetic testing should be considered in all patients with nephrocalcinosis. Genetic testing enables accurate diagnoses, changes in disease management, and precision medicine, that could significantly influence the long-term outcomes.

title: #1496 Evaluation of the diagnostic and therapeutic management of hyponatremia in a tertiary hospital: are we doing it right?
authors: Sara Aldana Barceló; Irene Vázquez Raso; Maria Soriano Guillén; Maria Maldonado-Martin; Javier Azores Moreno; Gema Maria Fernandez Juarez; Cristina Vega-Cabrera; Begoña Rivas
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyponatremia is a highly prevalent condition among hospitalized patients, associated with increased mortality, prolonged hospital stays and higher healthcare costs. Due to its occurrence in the context of multiple pathologies, a significant number of specialists are involved in its identification and management.
Method
A retrospective review was conducted of hospitalized patients at La Paz University Hospital in Madrid between January 2021 and November 2022. The review included patients for whom a consultation with the nephrology department was requested to evaluate hyponatremia during their clinical course. Data collected included variables related to the diagnosis of hyponatremia (e.g., serum and urinary osmolality, urinary electrolytes, volume status, medications), as well as its management at presentation, during follow-up by Nephrology, and over the course of one year.
Results
A total of 90 episodes were analyzed. Of the patients included, 55.6% were males and the mean age was 71.33 years. Half of the patients were taking one or more medications predisposing to hyponatremia, and 50% had recent oncological history. Upon arrival at the emergency department, 54.4% presented with hyponatremia, with a mean sodium (Na) level of 126.22 mmol/L. At the time of diagnosis, only 33.7% had both plasma osmolarity and urinary electrolytes/osmolality measured, although this percentage increased to 80% in patients with Na <120 mmol/L. Immediate treatment was initiated in 61%, with the most common being 0.9% saline solution (37.8%). Among patients with Na <120 mmol/L, 30% did not receive any correctional treatment. Sodium levels were monitored within 24 hours of presentation in the majority of patients (81%).
The average waiting time for a Nephrology consultation was 7.64 days (median 3 days), with a mean Na of 125.58 mmol/L. A moderate-to-strong positive correlation was observed between the time until consultation and the time to achieve normonatremia. The most frequent etiology of hyponatremia was SIADH (40%), followed by hypovolemic/diuretic induced (33.3%). Of the 31% of patients who did not achieve normonatremia at discharge, 46.4% died within the first year of follow-up. However, no statistically significant association was found between sodium correction and one-year mortality.
Conclusion
Establishing an adequate etiological diagnosis of hyponatremia is essential to optimize treatment and improve both the clinical course and hospital outcomes. In our study, the involvement of the Nephrology Department was associated with a timely achievement of normonatremia, highlighting the importance of specialized evaluation in the management of hyponatremia.

title: #2877 The use of demoralization scale in patients with Fabry disease: preliminary data
authors: Federica Caccia; Luigi Zerbinati; Federica Baciga; Nicola Vitturi; Giacomo Marchi; Gianni Carraro; Yuri Battaglia
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fabry disease (FD) is a genetic X-linked, multisystemic, progressive lysosomal storage leading to a range of debilitating symptoms and psychiatric complications. Due to the stressful nature of diagnosis, psychosocial challenges, and adjustment needs, FD patients may face an increased risk of demoralization (DEM). DEM is a syndrome distinct from depression, characterized by a loss of meaning and purpose, with feelings of hopelessness and helplessness. It is considered a maladaptive coping response, often arising in chronic medical illness and stressful situations, such as the suffering associated with a diagnosis. Currently, no studies are available on demoralization within the FD population. Our study aimed to investigate the prevalence of demoralization in FD patients and, secondly, to explore its association with other psychological and physical symptoms.
Method
Adult patients (age >18 yrs) diagnosed with Fabry disease were enrolled. The exclusion criterion was the absence of cognitive disorders (mini-mental state examination ≥ 24). Each patient filled in four self-report instruments: Demoralization scale (DS-IT), Edmonton Symptom Assessment System (ESAS), generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), and experience in close relationships (ECR-S) (Table 1). Statistical analysis was performed using the SPSS-30 package. Continuous variables were reported as mean ± standard deviation. Categorical variables were shown as frequencies (%).
Results
Eight patients (12.5% male) were included with a mean age of 49.2 ± 15.8. Six patients had a classical FD phenotype. Of the participants, 50.0%, 37.5%, and 12.5% reported high, moderate, and low DEM levels, respectively. The average anxious attachment scores were highest in the high-DEM group (25.0 ± 10.9) compared to moderate/low-DEM group (16.0 ± 4.0). Similarly, the high-DEM group reported higher average physical (ESAS-PHYS:16.5 ± 15.8) and psychological (ESAS-PSY:9.5 ± 9.1) distress sub-scores higher than moderate/low-DEM group (ESAS-PHYS 6.75 ± 8.84 and ESAS-PSY, 2.5 ± 2.6). Notably, higher fatigue (4.0 ± 4.1) and depression (4.5 ± 3.7) ESAS sub-scores were found in the high-DEM group. No differences were found in the GAD-7 scores and avoidance attachment scores across the three DEM groups.
Conclusion
This preliminary data suggests that 50% of FD patients experienced high levels of demoralization, which appears to be associated with increased symptom burden (both psychological and physical) and an anxious attachment style.

title: #3161 Monogenic causes of nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis in children and adults—a single center experience
authors: Margareta Fistrek Prlic; Lovro Lamot; Ivana Vukovic Brinar; Sanda Huljev Frkovic; Ivanka Kos; Ivana Vojtušek; Zivka Dika; Ema Ivandic; Vesna Furić Čunko; Bojan Jelaković; Bodo B Beck
abstract:
Background and Aims
Nephrocalcinosis (NC) is strongly related to nephrolithiasis (NL). Patients with NL and NC have an elevated risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD). The causes of NL and NC are environmental and genetic. Although monogenic causes of NL/NC are uncommon, they represent a considerable disease burden. This study aimed to determine the diagnostic yield of genetic analysis in children and adults with NL/NC and the clinical characteristics of the patients with a positive result.
Method
A retrospective chart review of children and adults with NL/NC was conducted. Inclusion criteria were the presence of NL/NC on diagnostic imaging and performed genetic analysis between 2020 and 2023. Use of the genetic analysis, i.e. NL/NC panel was based on clinical background and suspicion for genetic disease.
Results
22 participants were included in the study, 14 adults (ADL), and 8 children (CHL). The most common clinical feature in both groups was hypercalciuria as well as hypocitraturia. CKD was present in 50% of patients in the ADL group and 37% in the CHL group. Low serum bicarbonate was found in 29% of participants in the ADL group and 25% in the CHL group. There was no significant difference in analyzed clinical features between the groups (all P > 0.05). Overall, in 9 (41%) of participants, the result of genetic analysis was positive. The most common cause of the NL/NC in the ADL group was primary distal renal tubular acidosis. Familial hypomagnesemia with hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis was the most common cause of NL/NC in the CHL group. Infantile hypercalcemia 1 is the second most common cause of NL/NC in the ADL group. In the CHL group, one case of infantile hypercalcemia 1 was identified as a cause of NL/NC, as well as one case of Bartter syndrome. One case of Dent disease was recognized as a cause of NL/NC in the ADL group.
Conclusion
This study shows that up to 50% of patients may have a positive result of genetic analysis regarding NL/NC causes. Finding the possible explanatory genetic variant in these patients is of great importance for the management of the NL/NC patient. Therefore, targeted genetic testing is a promising aid regardless of the patient's age.

title: #1347 Urinary uromodulin levels in febrile children: a prospective study
authors: Evgenia Gurevich; Mays Ali; Yael Segev; Eden Arazi; Daniel Landau
abstract:
Background and Aims
Uromodulin (UMOD) is the most abundant urinary protein, expressed exclusively in the kidney and excreted into both urine and blood. UMOD plays a role in urinary tract infection, blood pressure and stone formation prevention, in addition to local and systemic immunomodulatory functions. Normal serum UMOD levels in children and adults, as well as males vs females were found to be comparable. However, normal pediatric urinary UMOD (U-UMOD) values have not been established yet. In a preliminary study, we showed a decreased U-UMOD excretion (contrary to albumin) in children with transient febrile proteinuria. This study aimed to further investigate the trends in U-UMOD levels during inflammatory states such as febrile infectious diseases in children, compared to non-febrile healthy controls.
Method
This prospective study included children (age 0–16 years) admitted to our medical center with febrile disease of non-renal source and non-febrile children were controls. U-UMOD was analyzed using the Biovender Human UMOD ELISA kit. The study protocol was approved by Local Ethical Committee.
Results
Thirty-six febrile patients and 35 controls were recruited. Febrile patients were younger than controls (60 ± 52 vs 107 ± 53 months, P < 0.001). Maximal fever was 39 ± 0.780C, its length was 46 ± 30 hours, blood WBC was 12 ± 5.5 *103/uL, and median (IQR) CRP levels were 24.6 (10–59) mg/L. There was no difference in U-UMOD/creatinine levels between febrile vs control groups [median (IQR): 1011 (455–1678) vs 336.5 (108.5–802) pg/mg, P = 0.12]. No correlation between U-UMOD/creatinine to age, sex, length of fever or blood WBC was found in both groups. In the febrile group U-UMOD/creatinine was inversely correlated to CRP (R = 0.46) and was lower in patients with CRP >50 mg/L (n = 9) compared to others [425 (158–528) vs 868 (403–1518) pg/mg, P = 0.01].
Conclusion
U-UMOD levels are inversely correlated with CRP in febrile patients with no kidney disease, suggesting a concurrent increase in UMOD secretion to circulation as a renal response to the systemic inflammation. Further simultaneous evaluation of urine and blood UMOD levels in febrile disease is warranted.

title: #2128 Stone analysis and 24-hour urine characteristics of kidney stone patients in Thailand
authors: Suramath Isaranuwatchai; Petchdee Oranrigsupak; Sarawoot Cherthong; Taweedate Muenkhamsee; Phanupong Phutrakool; Wonngarm Kittanamongkolchai; Kriang Tungsanga; Kearkiat Praditpornsilpa
abstract:
Background and Aims
Nephrolithiasis is one of the leading causes of chronic kidney disease in Thailand. Previous studies showed that, in northern and northeastern part of the country, kidney stones occurred in 15%–17% of the population with a recurrent rate of 50% in 5 years. Moreover, the patients had a strong family history of kidney stone disease (KSD) in Thailand. Hence, we conducted a prospective study to compare biochemical data between these patients in the endemic area of KSD who had and had not a family history of KSD.
Method
We recruited patients with KSD treated at Nan hospital in Nan, one of the northern provinces in Thailand. The enrollment was made from February 2024 to January 2025. Inclusion criteria were age 18–60 years with evidence of kidney stone. Exclusion criteria were patients with estimated glomerular filtration rate of less than 30 ml/min/1.72 m2, received renal replacement therapy or kidney transplantation, had advanced-stage diseases or with pregnancy. We collected demographic data, biochemical data including 24-hour urine and blood chemistry. Stone analysis was done with infrared spectroscopy if the stones were available.
Results
We enrolled 354 patients into our study. The median age was 57.47 years, and only 29.5% of patients were female. Family history of kidney diseases was presented in 41.5%, which 93.7% of patients reported that their family member also had a KSD. Stone analyses were available in 53 patients. Calcium oxalate stone was the most common major stone composition (62.2%), followed by uric acid stone (18.9%), and calcium apatite stone (18.9%). There was no difference between the composition of stone in patients with and without family history of renal stone disease. There was also no difference between patients with and without family history with respect to 24-hour urine volume, urine sodium, urine potassium, urine calcium, urine phosphate, urine magnesium, urine citrate, urine uric, urine oxalate, and urine protein (Table 1).
Conclusion
There was no difference in stone composition and biochemical data between patients with KSD with or without family history. However, since more than 40% of patient had family history of renal stone, genetic testing might reveal genetic contribution in this group of patients.

title: #2587 Is the generic treatment as effective as the original drug? A comparative study of the treatment with tolvaptan in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease at the Virgen Macarena University Hospital
authors: María Ramírez Peña; Alfonso Lara Ruiz; Águeda López de la Torre Molina; Melissa Cintra; Mercedes Salguiera Lazo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common hereditary kidney disease in the population. So far, Tolvaptan is the only drug approved for its treatment. Recently, the generic version of the drug has been marketed, although a post-marketing study of the original drug has not yet been published. The objective of our study is to compare the available outcomes in patients treated with the original drug versus the generic one in our healthcare area.
Method
A total of 44 patients treated with Tolvaptan for at least one year were selected:
− 27 treated with the original drug (Group 1)
− 17 treated with the generic drug (Group 2).
The dose adjustment was similar in all cases: during the first month, the dose was 45/15, in the second month 60/30, and from the third month onwards, 90/30. This last dose was maintained for at least six months. After six months, the treatment regimen/drug used was modified according to the patients' outcomes. Those who did not achieve urinary osmolarity (Uosm) targets were switched to the original drug
Sociodemographic variables (sex, age), total renal volume adjusted to body surface area (TRV), and analytical parameters (eGFR, sodium, Uosm, and uric acid levels (UA)) were collected at the start of treatment, after one month, at six months, and one year after treatment initiation.
The groups were compared using Student's t-test or the Mann-Whitney U test, depending on whether the variable showed a normal distribution or not.
Results
Global data: Mean age: 43.8 ± 8 years. 29 (67%) women.
TRV (Total Renal Volume): 1117.65 ± 686.79 cc. Mayo classification: Stage B: 2 (5%), Stage C: 11 (28%), Stage D: 17 (44%), Stage E: 9 (23%).
At baseline: eGFR (estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate): 62.7 ± 29.66 ml/min, serum sodium 140.85 ± 2.23 mEq/L, Uosm (urinary osmolarity) 565.8 ± 161.7 mOsm/kg, uric acid (UA) 5.86 ± 1.48 mg/dl.
The comparison between the two groups is provided in the attached table.
Conclusion
The decline in GFR at one year was greater in the group treated with the generic drug, although no significant differences were found.
The urinary osmolarity (Uosm) in the group treated with the generic drug remained >300 mOsm/kg until the sixth month, above the recommended values. After the sixth month, the strategy of switching patients who did not achieve the desired Uosm to the original drug was implemented, resulting in appropriate figures by the end of the year.
In conclusion, given the limitations of our study due to the sample size, the results show that the generic group did not achieve the desired beneficial effects, with the same side effects observed.

title: #1772 Pilot results from evaluation of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease diagnosis impact on the patients’ quality of life
authors: Niloufar Ebrahimi; Zohreh Gholizadeh Ghozloujeh; Amir Abdipour; Sayna Norouzi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Deterioration of quality of Life (QoL) in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is closely linked to physical and mental health, with pain playing a significant role. Many patients with ADPKD also endure depression, fatigue, sleep disturbances, and anxiety during their disease progression. Moreover, the hereditary nature of ADPKD frequently leads to genetic guilt feeling, which might intensify anxiety. To evaluate the impact of ADPKD diagnosis on patients’ QoL, we utilized the PROMIS-29+2 Profile v2.1 (PROPr) questionnaire, a validated tool designed to evaluate multiple health domains.
Method
This ongoing study was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) at Loma Linda University. To date, we have recruited 15 adult participants aged 18 years or older with a confirmed diagnosis of ADPKD through genetic testing. Participants completed the PROMIS-29+2 Profile v2.1 (PROPr) questionnaire, which evaluates multiple health domains, including physical function, anxiety, depression, fatigue, sleep disturbance, ability to participate in social roles and activities, pain interference, cognitive function, and pain intensity. For each domain, the respective scores were calculated and analyzed to evaluate the overall and domain-specific impact of ADPKD on patients’ QoL.
Results
The pilot results included 15 patients with ADPKD. The mean age of participants was 45 years (SD = 17), ranging from 21 to 76 years, predominantly consisted of females (11, 73.3%) compared to males (4, 26.7%). The racial distribution showed that White/Caucasian patients comprised 60.0% (9) of the sample, while 40.0% (6) were classified as Other, among which one was Filipino, and one was Black/African American. According to genetic analysis, PKD1 mutations were most common (9, 60.0%), followed by negative/variant of uncertain significance (VUS) results (4, 26.7%) and PKD2 mutations (2, 13.3%). Regarding treatment, only four patients (26.7%) received tolvaptan, while the majority (11, 73.3%) were not on this medication. Based on the participants' responses, physical function was slightly below average at 48 (SD = 9), indicating mild restrictions in physical activity. Anxiety levels were significantly higher at 58 (SD = 12), reflecting more anxiety symptoms than the reference population. Depression was graded near average (52; SD = 10), suggesting normal depressive symptoms. Fatigue was elevated with a mean score of 59 (SD = 13), indicating greater levels of exhaustion relative to the general population. Sleep disturbance and the ability to participate in social roles and activities were consistent with the population at a mean average of 51 (SD = 11). Pain interference was nearly average at 49 (SD = 9), indicating that pain has a usual impact on daily activities. Cognitive function abilities were assessed at the population mean of 50 (SD = 10). Multiple linear regression analysis revealed several significant predictors across PROMIS-29+2 domains. For anxiety, being male (B = −13.763, P = .021) and having PKD2 mutation (B = −17.257, P = .035) were associated with significantly lower anxiety scores. Depression scores were significantly lower in males (B = −17.988, P = .015). Fatigue scores were significantly higher in White participants (B = 13.001, P = .027) and those with Negative/VUS mutations (B = 11.972, P = .047). Pain interference was significantly higher in those with Negative/VUS mutations (B = 14.735, P = .033). Cognitive function scores were significantly better in males (B = 17.783, P = .028) (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
The pilot results highlight notable gender and mutation based disparities in the QoL among patients with ADPKD. Males and individuals with PKD2 gene mutations exhibited lower anxiety and depression scores, while fatigue and pain interference were more pronounced in the white race and those with Negative/VUS mutations.

title: #3554 Genetic insights into tubulopathies: a retrospective study of unexplained renal disorders
authors: Cristina García Parejo; Blanca Martín Álvarez; Fernando Martín Caballero; María Verónica Torres; Ángela Eraso Nájera; Nathalie Martínez Tejeda; Danay Areli Ticona Espinoza; Luisa Gemma Sánchez García; María Begoña Alaguero del Pozo; María de la Flor Rodríguez Martín; Belén Gómez Giralda
abstract:
Background and Aims
Recent advances in genetic molecular techniques have significantly enhanced our understanding of tubular disorders of genetic origin.
Renal ion transport occurs through transcellular and paracellular pathways. The paracellular route is governed by specialized proteins, such as occludins and claudins, which regulate ion permeability.
Michaelis–Manz syndrome (MMS) is a rare autosomal recessive tubulopathy of unknown prevalence, caused by mutations in the CLDN16 and CLDN19 genes, encoding claudin-16 and claudin-19, respectively. These proteins are primarily expressed in the loop of Henle and distal convoluted tubule, where they play a key role in paracellular calcium and magnesium reabsorption. Defects in this process result in excessive urinary excretion of these ions, leading to hypomagnesemia, hypercalciuria, and progressive renal dysfunction due to calcium deposition in the kidneys.
Additionally, claudin-19 is present in the retinal pigment epithelium, which can result in ophthalmologic abnormalities.
This case series aims to highlight the role of genetic mutations in the development of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and to underscore the need for further research to improve diagnostic precision and therapeutic interventions.
Method
A retrospective single-center analysis was conducted on patients who underwent genetic testing for suspected tubulopathies of unknown etiology.
Within this cohort, patients with clinical suspicion of MMS were identified, yielding two cases.
The Custom Constitutional Panel 17Mb sequencing panel was used for genetic analysis, and variants of interest were identified relative to the hg19 reference genome.
Results
A 49-year-old male with a history of CKD of unknown origin, who had undergone kidney transplantation, partial nephrectomy due to calcium lithiasis, and had bilateral coloboma, was analyzed.
Genetic testing revealed a homozygous mutation in CLDN19, confirming the diagnosis of MMS.
This case suggests that MMS should be considered as a potential cause of CKD, although the incidence and recurrence of the disease in renal transplant recipients remain unknown.
The second patient was the father of the previous one, an 80-year-old male on hemodialysis due to CKD of unknown origin, with suspected tubulointerstitial nephropathy of mixed etiology (nephrocalcinosis and obstructive uropathy). His medical history included encrusting pyelitis due to Corynebacterium urealyticum and calcium lithiasis requiring lithotripsy, but no ophthalmologic abnormalities.
Laboratory findings showed severe hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia, though urinary calcium and magnesium levels were not available.
Genetic testing identified a heterozygous missense variant in CLDN19. However, as MMS typically requires a homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation, this did not confirm a definitive diagnosis. Despite this, the clinical and family history strongly suggested a probable diagnosis of MMS, reinforcing the need for further studies to elucidate the phenotypic variability and expressivity of genetic alterations in MMS.
Conclusion
A significant proportion of CKD cases of unknown etiology may be attributed to underdiagnosed genetic mutations. In this context, the GENSEN project, led by the Spanish Society of Nephrology, aims to identify the genetic causes of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) of unknown origin, which accounts for 18% of CKD cases.
The rapid evolution of genetic research is expected to revolutionize nephrology, providing new diagnostic tools and targeted therapeutic strategies. However, many genetic mutations identified to date do not fully explain the clinical manifestations of CKD, underscoring the need for further research.
Advancing genetic insights into kidney disease holds great potential to improve patient prognosis, develop personalized therapies, and ultimately enhance both quality of life and life expectancy for affected individuals.

title: #3442 Case report in Heart Center Kazakhstan: successful application of hemadsorption techniques using Jafron HA 280
authors: Dariga Koichubayeva; Ainamkoz Amanzholova; Bolat Bekishev; Gulsharat Metchenova; Altynshash Toktassyn
abstract:
Background and Aims
This article presents a case of a patient admitted to the Cardiac surgery center who had previously undergone multiple cardiac surgical interventions. A comprehensive approach involving hemoadsorption improved the outcomes
The aim of this case report is to contribute to the existing scientific literature by highlighting the potential benefits and challenges of this approach in neurology, cardiac surgery. A literature search for studies investigating the use of HA-280 Jafron for this cohort of patients in myasthenic crisis revealed limited studies on the combined application of HA-280 Jafron in patients. Hemoadsorption has the potential to become a valuable adjunct in the treatment of this patient cohort by optimising therapeutic outcomes and improving the quality of care.
We report a case of patient with Myasthenia Gravis with predominant involvement of bulbar, facial, axial, respiratory and skeletal muscles. The myasthenic crisis did not respond adequately to methylprednisolone therapy but showed improvement with immunoadsorption therapy using HA-280.
The HA-280 immunoadsorption column is widely used worldwide for the treatment of immune-related rheumatic diseases. However, its suitability for myasthenic crisis remains unclear. This case suggests that the HA-280 column has a potential therapeutic effect in Myasthenia Gravis and myasthenic crisis and may serve as an alternative adjunctive treatment. This topic warrants further research and the results may provide new insights into the treatment of this patient cohort.
Method
The patient was transported by an emergency medical team to the emergency department. She was unable to report complaints independently. She was hospitalized in the cardiology department with the following diagnosis: Ischemic heart disease. Myocardial infarction without ST-segment elevation. Comorbidities: Acute kidney injury, prerenal form. Chronic heart failure with moderately reduced ejection fraction. Severe Myasthenia Gravis (predominantly affecting bulbar, facial, axial, respiratory, and skeletal muscles, MGFA Class III B, seropositive form). Myasthenic crisis.
Given the myasthenic crisis, weakness of respiratory muscles, the patient's general condition is severe due to respiratory failure. Breathing through the endotracheal tube, shallow breathing due to respiratory muscle weakness, respiratory rate 25–30 breaths per min. Oxygen saturation (SpO₂): 99%. Heart rate (HR): 90 beats per minute. Blood pressure (BP): 110/70 mmHg. Urination via urinary catheter, diuresis is adequate. Meningeal signs are negative. No signs of cerebral syndrome. Cranial nerves: Pupils OD = OS, photoreaction preserved. Face symmetric, hypomimic. Pharyngeal reflexes are reduced. Muscle tone is reduced. There is weakness in axial, masseter and scapula muscles. Muscular strength of the upper and lower extremities is reduced. Tendon reflexes are reduced bilaterally. There is no sensory disturbance.
CT signs of ischemic stroke (subacute stage) in the medulla oblongata.
Results
Hemoadsorption parameters: HA 280 (Jafron Biomedical Co., Ltd. China) cartridge on a Jafron machine was used with the following destination parameters: Flow rate 180–200 ml/min; Anticoagulation: no heparinization; Adsorber priming: Heparin 5000 IU in 1L of 0.9% NaCl. Procedure duration: 4 hours per session for 3 days. Vascular access: Right internal jugular vein, dual-lumen catheter. Hemodynamic parameters before and after the procedure stable, BP 125/62 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, SpO₂:98%.
Post-hemoadsorption treatment: Pyridostigmine (Kalymin 60N): 1 tablet every 4 hours. Intravenous immunoglobulin G for 5 days. Plasmapheresis 5 sessions. Pulse therapy: Intravenous prednisolone and methylprednisolone for a total of 5 sessions.
Conclusion
In dynamics the patient's condition has improved, with independent spontaneous breathing and SpO₂ at 99% without oxygen support. There are no signs of cerebral syndrome, and pharyngeal reflexes have been restored. Muscle tone remains reduced, but improvement is noted in axial and masticatory muscles. Laboratory tests show a decrease in IgG antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor.

title: #3037 Longitudinal factors to consider when modelling home blood pressure as an endpoint in clinical trials of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)
authors: James Elhindi; Priyanka Sagar; Gopi Rangan
abstract:
Background and Aims
Home blood pressure (HBP) measurement has an established role in clinical practice but is not commonly utilised as an endpoint in clinical trials. Previously we found that beetroot juice (nitrate-replete and nitrate-depleted) lowered both office and HBP in hypertensive adults with ADPKD (Sagar et al. Kidney Int Rep 2024;9:3045). The aim of this study was to determine the kinetics and factors affecting the decline in HBP.
Method
Functional principal analysis (Wang et al. Annu Rev Stat Appl 2016;3:257) was performed using daily HBP measurements (2nd and 3rd readings analysed) which were performed on 30 consecutive days in 60 patients randomised to either beetroot juice with or without nitrate.
Results
Three eigenfunctions explained at least 80% of the functional variance in both systolic and diastolic HBP measurements. The first eigenfunction was large (69% to 77% functional variance explained) and the second and third eigenfunctions were smaller (4% to 7% functional variance explained each). Respectively, we observed three factors contributing to longitudinal variation in HBP: (i) subject-specific baseline HBP; (ii) piecewise linear variation with the steepest decline between days 0 to 14; and (iii) periodic variation that oscillated approximately every 10 days. Age, gender, eGFR, hypertension vintage, and beetroot juice group did not explain the piecewise linear or periodic variation. A model accounting for the sources of longitudinal variation concurred with the original study result that observed no difference in HBP change between beetroot juice groups.
Conclusion
HBP correlated with office BP and provided a valid secondary endpoint that is convenient for study participants. These results suggest that future clinical trials utilising HBP measurement should be at least 2 weeks in duration given the piecewise linear variation. Statistical modelling of HBP should consider including: random effects for the subject-specific; fixed and random effects for the piecewise-linear variation, and possibly fixed and random effects for the periodic variation.

title: #2949 Colocalization of complement C3 and IgA in glomerular immune-complex deposits of patients with IgA nephropathy correlates with the Oxford classification MEST-C scores
authors: Lea Novak; Stacy Hall; Graham Gurganus; Dana Rizk; Bruce A Julian; Mark Haas; Jan Novak
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is a common primary glomerulonephritis, often leading to kidney failure. Pathogenesis of IgAN is associated with immune complexes formed in the circulation from aberrantly glycosylated IgA1 that is bound by IgG autoantibodies. Additional serum components, such as complement C3 (C3), are also associated with these immune complexes. Some of these circulating immune complexes deposit in the glomeruli and induce kidney injury with varying manifestations of glomerulonephritis. IgAN is diagnosed by evaluation of kidney biopsy specimens. Routine immunofluorescence microscopy reveals glomerular immune-complex deposits containing (co)dominant IgA with variable presence of IgG and/or IgM and usually C3. Light microscopy features describe the degree of kidney injury based on the Oxford classification MEST-C scores: Mesangial hypercellularity (M0 or M1), endocapillary hypercellularity (E0 or E1), segmental glomerulosclerosis (S0 or S1), interstitial fibrosis/tubular atrophy (T0, T1, or T2), and cellular/fibrocellular crescents (C0, C1, or C2). In this study, we used high-resolution confocal microscopy and multi-fluorochrome staining to assess colocalization of C3-IgA, C3-IgG, and IgA-IgG in glomerular immune-complex deposits of kidney-biopsy specimens from patients with IgAN and correlated the data with the Oxford classification MEST-C scores.
Method
Frozen-tissue sections (4 μm) of remnant kidney-biopsy specimens from 17 IgAN patients were fixed, blocked, and stained with fluorochrome-labeled reagents specific for human C3 (polyclonal goat IgG), IgA (polyclonal goat IgG), and IgG (Fc-specific nanobody). DAPI was used to stain nuclei. Using a high-resolution confocal microscope (Nikon A1R/SIM), z-stacks of glomerular images with four fluorochromes from multiple optical planes were acquired (objective 60×). For each slide, 60 regions of interest (ROIs) were selected in multiple optical planes of glomeruli in areas with C3 staining. Pearson's correlation coefficient (PCC) colocalization data were collected for C3-IgA, C3-IgG, and IgA-IgG pairwise comparisons in 60 ROIs. Mean values of PCC for each pairwise comparison were calculated. To correlate the results with Oxford MEST-C scores, patients were divided in paired groups based on the absence or presence of each Oxford MEST-C score variable: M0 vs. M1, E0 vs. E1, S0 vs. S1, T0 vs. T1+T2, C0 vs. C1+C2. Differences in PCC in C3-IgA, C3-IgG, and IgA-IgG for each paired group were evaluated. Furthermore, proteins from the glomerular immune-complex deposits of additional pooled remnant kidney-biopsy specimens were extracted and analyzed by SDS-PAGE immunoblotting with C3-specific antibody.
Results
All 17 samples showed staining for C3, IgA, and IgG, including those that had been reported negative for IgG (n = 14) or C3 (n = 1) by routine immunofluorescence microscopy. Immunoblotting confirmed the presence of C3 in the immune-complex deposits, revealing α chain and β chain of C3. Pairwise comparison of Pearson correlation coefficient values showed greater colocalization of C3-IgA than that of C3-IgG (P < 0.0001) and IgA-IgG (P < 0.0001), whereas colocalizations for C3-IgG and IgA-IgG were similar (P = 0.063). Only colocalization of C3-IgA correlated with MEST-C scores. Specifically, colocalization of C3-IgA was higher in IgAN patients with M1 (P = 0.0185), E1 (P = 0.0042), and C1+C2 (P = 0.0043) scores compared to IgAN patients with M0, E0, and C0 scores, respectively. C3-IgA colocalization for S0 vs. S1 and T0 vs. T1+T2 did not differ.
Conclusion
Our results support the role of C3-IgA-IgG immune complexes in the pathogenesis of IgAN. Greater C3-IgA colocalization was associated with mesangial hypercellularity, endocapillary hypercellularity, and cellular/fibrocellular crescents, underscoring a role of complement for inducing acute kidney damage in IgAN.

Some of these circulating immune complexes deposit in the glomeruli and induce kidney injury with varying manifestations of glomerulonephritis. IgAN is diagnosed by evaluation of kidney biopsy specimens. Routine immunofluorescence microscopy reveals glomerular immune-complex deposits containing (co)dominant IgA with variable presence of IgG and/or IgM and usually C3. Light microscopy features describe the degree of kidney injury based on the Oxford classification MEST-C scores: Mesangial hypercellularity (M0 or M1), endocapillary hypercellularity (E0 or E1), segmental glomerulosclerosis (S0 or S1), interstitial fibrosis/tubular atrophy (T0, T1, or T2), and cellular/fibrocellular crescents (C0, C1, or C2). In this study, we used high-resolution confocal microscopy and multi-fluorochrome staining to assess colocalization of C3-IgA, C3-IgG, and IgA-IgG in glomerular immune-complex deposits of kidney-biopsy specimens from patients with IgAN and correlated the data with the Oxford classification MEST-C scores.
Method
Frozen-tissue sections (4 μm) of remnant kidney-biopsy specimens from 17 IgAN patients were fixed, blocked, and stained with fluorochrome-labeled reagents specific for human C3 (polyclonal goat IgG), IgA (polyclonal goat IgG), and IgG (Fc-specific nanobody). DAPI was used to stain nuclei. Using a high-resolution confocal microscope (Nikon A1R/SIM), z-stacks of glomerular images with four fluorochromes from multiple optical planes were acquired (objective 60×). For each slide, 60 regions of interest (ROIs) were selected in multiple optical planes of glomeruli in areas with C3 staining. Pearson's correlation coefficient (PCC) colocalization data were collected for C3-IgA, C3-IgG, and IgA-IgG pairwise comparisons in 60 ROIs. Mean values of PCC for each pairwise comparison were calculated. To correlate the results with Oxford MEST-C scores, patients were divided in paired groups based on the absence or presence of each Oxford MEST-C score variable: M0 vs. M1, E0 vs. E1, S0 vs. S1, T0 vs. T1+T2, C0 vs. C1+C2. Differences in PCC in C3-IgA, C3-IgG, and IgA-IgG for each paired group were evaluated. Furthermore, proteins from the glomerular immune-complex deposits of additional pooled remnant kidney-biopsy specimens were extracted and analyzed by SDS-PAGE immunoblotting with C3-specific antibody.
Results
All 17 samples showed staining for C3, IgA, and IgG, including those that had been reported negative for IgG (n = 14) or C3 (n = 1) by routine immunofluorescence microscopy. Immunoblotting confirmed the presence of C3 in the immune-complex deposits, revealing α chain and β chain of C3. Pairwise comparison of Pearson correlation coefficient values showed greater colocalization of C3-IgA than that of C3-IgG (P < 0.0001) and IgA-IgG (P < 0.0001), whereas colocalizations for C3-IgG and IgA-IgG were similar (P = 0.063). C3-IgA colocalization for S0 vs. S1 and T0 vs. T1+T2 did not differ.

title: #2447 Prognostic value of urinary periostin in the frequent primary glomerulopathies of the adult
authors: Nicolae Pana; Ana-Maria Mehedinti; Gabriel Stefan; Bogdan Obrisca; Vasile Nastase; Alin Stochita; Gener Ismail; Gabriel Mircescu; Cristina Capusa
abstract:
Background and Aims
Primary glomerulopathies (GPs) represent a major cause of end stage renal disease and are potentially amenable to disease modifying treatment, but the treatment decisions still rely on invasive histological parameters and on classic serum and urine biomarkers that do not accurately reflect the disease processes. Periostin (POSTN) has recently emerged and a biomarker of inflammation and fibrosis in various settings, including kidney diseases. We aimed to investigate the utility of urinary POSTN as a non-invasive biomarker of fibrosis and its prognostic value in the most frequent primary GP of the adult—IgA nephropathy (IgAN) and membranous nephropathy (MN).
Method
This prospective, dual-center, observational study enrolled adults with biopsy-proven IgAN and MN between December 2018–April 2023, who were followed for 12 months. Exclusion criteria were: prior immunosuppressive treatment or renal replacement therapy initiation, diseases with over-expression of POSTN (asthma, infections, neoplasms), kidney graft or a repeated biopsy, and insufficient tissue sample. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, histological and treatment data were collected at baseline and at the end of the follow-up period. Urinary POSTN was measured by ELISA and was expressed as ratio to urinary creatinin. Spearman correlation rank, linear regression and logistic regression models (with logarithmic transformed values for non-parametric variables) were used to analyse data.
Results
A total of 46 subjects were enrolled, 34 with IgaN and 12 with MN. IgAN patients were younger, had a smaller burden of comorbidities (lower Charlson comorbidity index), lower levels of proteinuria and a higher renal histopathological prognostic score, but no significant differences in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and urinary POSTN, as compared to MN group. At baseline, urinary POSTN was strongly and directly correlated with proteinuria and albuminuria in both study groups (rs = 0.63 and 0.68 in the IgAN group, P = 0.001 and rs = 0.7 and 0.64 in the MN group, P = 0.01, respectively). Similar correlations were documented in the MN group in relation to histological parameters—the renal histopathological prognostic score (rs = 0.58, P = 0.04), global (rs = 0.63, P = 0.02) and segmental glomerulosclerosis (rs = 0.63, P = 0.03). In both groups, inverse correlations of urinary periostin with the changes over 12 months in proteinuria and albuminuria were found, but not with changes in eGFR. Moreover, in multivariate analyses (adjusted for comorbidities, therapeutic regimens and histological findings), higher urinary POSTN along with age were the independent predictors of a lower reduction in proteinuria and albuminuria.
Conclusion
These findings suggest that the urinary POSTN could be an early indicator of fibrotic lesions in adults with MN and mildly decreased kidney function, as supported by the correlations with glomerulosclerosis. More important, urinary POSTN seems to be an independent predictor of the therapeutic response in adults with IgAN and MN.

title: #3061 Collagen type IV alpha-1 (CO4A1) is necessary for glomerular regeneration through PAX2 regulation
authors: Joanna Cunanan; Daniel Zhang; Vanessa De Gregorio; Samantha Ricardo; Bilge Caparali; Ana Konvalinka; Moumita Barua
abstract:
Background and Aims
Podocyte loss in glomerular diseases is irreversible due to the terminally differentiated state of these cells. Glomerular parietal epithelial cells (PECs) express stem cell and developmental markers such as the transcription factor PAX2. Our previous work showed mice with a Pax2 mutation (Pax2-MUT) displayed impaired podocyte regeneration (Fig. 1A), but mechanisms underlying PEC-mediated glomerular regeneration are largely unknown. The aim of this present study is to characterize the molecular mechanisms of impaired podocyte regeneration in Pax2-MUT mice.
Methods
Glomeruli from Pax2-MUT and wildtype mice at baseline and after Adriamycin-induced podocyte injury were isolated using Dynabeads and were subjected to mass spectrometry proteomics.
Results
We analyzed the proteomic profile of Pax2-MUT and wildtype glomeruli at 14 and 28 days after Adriamycin-induced podocyte injury. A total of 2648 glomerular proteins were identified by mass spectrometry; among these, 16 were differentially regulated and statistically significant by ANOVA and Tukey's post hoc test (P < 0.01) at day 14. Of these 16 differentially regulated proteins, 8 are upregulated and 8 are downregulated in Pax2-MUT glomeruli compared to wildtype at day 14 after injury (Fig. 1B). To prioritize targets in our proteomics data, proteins of interest were identified using bioinformatically predicted ligand-receptor pairs and PAX2 gene targets. Our analysis revealed that among the 1400+ differentially expressed proteins in our proteomics dataset, only CO4A1 (Collagen type IV alpha-1) is a predicted PAX2 transcriptional target that is also one of the top ligands/receptors critical for glomerular repair. None of the other identified proteins met both criteria for further investigation.
First, using a publicly available glomerular single-cell RNA-sequencing data set of Adriamycin-injured wildtype mice, a ranking of top 40 ligand-receptor pairs was generated. Of these, CO4A1 was the only ligand differentially expressed in Pax2-MUT compared to wildtype glomeruli after podocyte injury in our proteomics dataset (Fig. 1B and C). While glomerular CO4A1 was unchanged in wildtype, CO4A1 was reduced in Pax2-MUT mice at 14 days after injury (Fig. 1B). The Col4a1 gene is also a predicted PAX2 target for expression, determined through bioinformatics-based predictions of known transcription factor binding site motifs. In contrast, a Cd2ap knockout mouse model of podocyte injury showed increased CO4A1 expression (Fig. 1D), suggesting that reduced CO4A1 is specific to Pax2-MUT mice post-injury.
Studies show that CO4A1 provides a “flexible” matrix during embryonic development and organogenesis to support the dynamic demands of tissue growth and morphogenesis, and this mechanism can be harnessed in glomerular repair. Therefore, decreased CO4A1 levels in Adriamycin-injured Pax2-MUT mice could result in a lack of this flexible matrix and impair normal reparative processes. Consistent with this, gene ontology and pathway analysis of Pax2-MUT glomeruli revealed processes indicative of dysregulated repair at day 28 after Adriamycin injury, including nuclear abnormalities, persistent cell proliferation, motility and migration associated with abnormal Rho-GTPase signalling, abnormal protein turnover, and decreased metabolism.
Conclusion
Our novel findings suggest that impaired glomerular regeneration in Pax2-MUT mice is due to decreased regulation of CO4A1 by PECs expressing mutant PAX2 (Fig. 1E). This is also an interesting, novel finding since to our knowledge, PAX2-CO4A1 signalling has never been implicated in the context of glomerular repair and regeneration and can therefore serve as novel therapeutic targets for glomerular diseases which are primarily caused by podocyte injury and loss.
