title: #2575 The importance of the Japanese classification system for predicting renal prognosis in Chinese patients with histologically confirmed diabetic kidney disease
authors: Ying Shi; Suyan Duan; Chengning Zhang; Bo Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is a major cause of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), significantly impacting patient outcomes. As the number of patients diagnosed with DKD continues to rise, the significance of accurate pathological diagnosis and prognosis evaluation has become increasingly apparent. Traditional pathological classifications, such as the Renal Pathology Society (RPS) classification, primarily focus on glomerular changes, limiting their prognostic utility in predicting disease progression. To address this limitation, the Japanese Renal Pathology Society (JRPS) proposed a comprehensive classification system in 2018, incorporating glomerular, tubulointerstitial, and vascular lesions in the kidney. This study comparatively evaluated the clinical significance of the JRPS classification grade in predicting DKD progression in Chinese patients.
Method
This retrospective cohort study included 124 patients diagnosed with DKD from 2014 and 2020. Patients were classified into four JRPS grades based on the J-score . Kaplan-Meier analysis and the log-rank test were performed to assess renal survival differences. And the time dependent receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were used to characterize the predictive accuracy. Cox proportional hazards regression models were applied to estimate the association between JRPS grade and renal outcomes, adjusting for potential confounding factors.
Results
Over a median follow-up of 40.58 months, 76.6% of patients experienced renal outcomes, including 40.3% progressing to ESKD (Fig. 1). Higher JRPS grades correlated with worse renal outcomes, characterized by elevated serum creatinine, severe proteinuria, and advanced pathological changes. Cox regression confirmed JRPS grade as an independent predictor of renal prognosis. However, further time-dependent receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves revealed that the J-score (area under the curve AUC = 0.784) had lower clinical significance than the traditional RPS classification system (area under the curve AUC = 0.892).
Conclusion
The JRPS classification grade, particularly the J-score holds significant potential to enhance prognostic assessments in diabetic nephropathy and guide clinical treatment decisions.

title: #2614 A thematic analysis of healthcare provider perspectives on the care pathway and unmet needs in C3G and primary IC-MPGN in the US and Europe
authors: Carly Rich; Elizabeth Holdsworth; Sarah Clayton; Mona Amet; Laura Mirams; Ryan Naylor; Mingyi Huang; Katie Gordon; Lucia Quintana Gallardo
abstract:
Background and Aims
C3 glomerulopathy (C3G) and primary (idiopathic) immune complex membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (IC-MPGN) are rare chronic kidney diseases estimated to affect approximately 5000 people in the US and 8000 in Europe. Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) have published clinical practice guidelines for the management of these two glomerular diseases, however there are currently no approved treatments that target the underlying cause of disease. Achieving diagnosis is complex due to the heterogeneous nature of the disease and the need for biopsy. Patients with milder symptom presentation may progress silently to kidney failure without being adequately treated. The aim of this study was to understand HCP perceptions of the care pathway and unmet needs in patients with C3G and primary IC-MPGN in the US and Europe.
Method
We performed a cross-sectional qualitative study, which included 1-hour semi-structured interviews with healthcare providers (HCPs) who were nephrologists and specialist treaters of patients with C3G/IC-MPGN. 20 HCPs were included (n = 8 US; n = 2 France; n = 3 Germany; n = 2 Italy; n = 3 Spain, n = 2 UK). Interview transcripts were reviewed by the study team and inductively coded using ATLAS.ti software. During multiple discussion sessions, researchers searched for themes amongst the data. Themes were reviewed and refined until consensus was reached.
Results
Receiving a timely diagnosis was perceived as a key unmet need by most HCPs. Patients with “milder” or asymptomatic disease when first presenting to primary care were felt to be at greatest risk for misdiagnosis and/or delays in onward referral to specialist care, resulting in delayed diagnosis and treatment initiation. This was attributed to a failure to recognise and thoroughly investigate non-specific symptoms (e.g. proteinuria) at primary care levels as potential indicators of a rare disease. Conversely, those who initially presented with acute symptoms were often rapidly referred to specialist nephrology services, an aspect of the care pathway that was considered effective ("It can be a smouldering burn, but it's not a bonfire. Those people who have a bonfire going on in those kidneys, they get picked up. It's the burn, the smouldering disease, that is slowly eating away the kidneys, those people get missed... They don't have symptoms, and they don't get their urine test done because it's not being suspected. It's a rare disease." Nephrologist, US).
Biopsy, stated by HCPs as providing a definitive diagnosis, could be challenging to obtain due to systemic factors and/or patient preference. (“The organisational related factors will be the case of arranging a bed because the NHS is under a huge pressure from other problems, so to find a bed for an elective procedure, such as the biopsy, it sometimes takes a bit of a long time.” Nephrologist, UK; “Once the patient is in our system, the biopsy could be the most time-consuming, either because the patient does not want to perform it urgently for personal reasons or because, at a specific moment, there is something else overloading.” Nephrologist, ES)
When discussing post-diagnostic care for patients with C3G/IC-MPGN, HCPs perceived a lack of effective treatment options as a key unmet need (“I don't have any drugs that are really approved for it and provide the performance I want.” Nephrologist, DE). HCPs were, however, excited and hopeful for the future of treatment options, especially treatments that target the complement cascade (“I think the most interesting thing at the moment for C3G is the inhibition of C3…the dream a little bit is being able to sort of characterize specifically where we have to impact the complement cascade” Nephrologist, ES).
Conclusion
Timely diagnosis can be improved by raising awareness of this rare disease as a potential consideration when patients present with “milder” or non-specific symptoms in primary care. Furthermore, once diagnosed, patients have limited access to effective treatments that specifically target the underlying pathological mechanism—C3 dysregulation—underscoring the urgent need for innovative and effective therapies.

Receiving a timely diagnosis was perceived as a key unmet need by most HCPs. Conversely, those who initially presented with acute symptoms were often rapidly referred to specialist nephrology services, an aspect of the care pathway that was considered effective ("It can be a smouldering burn, but it's not a bonfire. Those people who have a bonfire going on in those kidneys, they get picked up. It's the burn, the smouldering disease, that is slowly eating away the kidneys, those people get missed... Timely diagnosis can be improved by raising awareness of this rare disease as a potential consideration when patients present with “milder” or non-specific symptoms in primary care. title: #2935 Real-world treatment patterns of patients with immunoglobulin a nephropathy (IgAN) in the United States
authors: Helen Trenz; Briana Ndife; Anran Shao; Elizabeth Nagelhout; Danielle Sienko; Titte Srinivas; Ruth Haile-Meskale; Margaret Helmuth; Laura Mariani
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgAN is a highly heterogenous autoimmune disease and the most common primary glomerulonephritis globally, with a therapeutic landscape that has been evolving rapidly in recent years. The aim of this analysis was to evaluate real-world treatment patterns in US patients with IgAN.
Method
This retrospective cohort study enrolled adults (≥18 years of age) with biopsy-confirmed IgAN, diagnosed between July 1, 2016, and November 5, 2023, who had linked pharmacy and medical claims data in the Komodo Healthcare Map™ database and renal biopsy data in the Diaceutics proprietary DXRX database. The index date was that of diagnostic renal biopsy. Patients had ≥6 months of pre-index (baseline period) and ≥12 months of post-index (follow-up period) continuous enrollment in medical and pharmacy claims, and those with a history of renal transplant were excluded. Outcomes included the proportion of patients receiving IgAN therapies approved during the identification period, including renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system inhibitors (RAASi), immunosuppressants (IS), sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), targeted-release budesonide (TRB), and sparsentan (SPAR); the proportion of patients discontinuing treatment; and treatment duration. Treatment duration was measured from the date of the first record of a drug to the earliest of discontinuation or disenrollment. Treatment discontinuation was defined as the absence of a subsequent medication claim for ≥60 days.
Results
In total, 918 patients were included, with a mean ± standard deviation (SD) age of 52.9 ± 16.2 years, and 42.7% were female. During baseline or at the index date, the median (Q1, Q3) estimated glomerular filtration rate was 50.8 (37.5, 84.8) mL/min/1.73 m2, and histopathology findings scored via Oxford MEST-C classification system (mesangial [M] and endocapillary [E] hypercellularity, segmental glomerulosclerosis [S], interstitial fibrosis/tubular atrophy [T], and cellular crescents [C]) showed 50.2% of patients had M1, 49.5% had E1, 71.0% had S1, 22.5%/7.4% had T1/T2, and 41.2%/5.2% had C1/C2. The mean ± SD follow-up time (index date to end of enrollment in closed claims) was 34.9 ± 19.5 months. During follow-up, 653 (71.1%) patients had ≥1 IgAN treatment pharmacy fill. Among those patients, 93.7% received RAASi, 12.4% received IS, and 22.4% received SGLT2i. Of the recently approved IgAN therapies, 6.9% of patients received TRB and 1.4% received SPAR. Among first treatment regimens, most treated patients (89.3%) received RAASi (median [Q1, Q3] number of fills 7.0 [3.0, 12.0]), 6.4% received IS (1.0 [1.0, 3.0]), 8.1% received SGLT2i (6.0 [2.0, 10.0]), 2.8% received TRB (4.5 [2.0, 13.0]), and 1 patient received SPAR (4.0 fills). First regimens were discontinued by 80.2% of treated patients after a mean ± SD of 15.5 ± 15.1 months. A total of 322 (49.3%) patients received second treatment regimens (any change from first treatment regimen [additional agent or treatment switch]), which were discontinued by 85.7% of these patients after a mean ± SD of 10.7 ± 11.4 months. Third treatment regimens were received by 124 (38.5%) patients; 88.7% of these discontinued after a mean ± SD of 7.7 ± 6.3 months. The most common treatment sequence was RAASi without subsequent therapy (41.0%). Median (Q1, Q3) treatment duration for all regimens was 18.1 (9.8, 28.6) months for RAASi, 1.8 (0.9, 4.7) months for IS, 8.8 (3.1, 16.2) months for SGLT2i, 6.9 (2.5, 9.6) months for TRB, and 1.9 (1.0, 4.7) months for SPAR.
Conclusion
These real-world data show that approximately two-thirds of patients with IgAN received treatment for their disease. Almost all treated patients received RAASi, and for almost half of this population, it was the only treatment received during follow-up. Use of the newer IgAN-specific therapies was low in this study population, though their approval timings relative to the study period must be considered. Given the heterogenous nature of IgAN, these findings highlight a need for expanded use of all available IgAN therapies.

title: #3290 Renal thrombotic microangiopathy in lupus nephritis: a case-control study
authors: Soumaya Chargui; Soumaya Mekki; Nada Sellami; Tasnim Ben Ayed; Amel Harzallah; Meriam Hajji; Ezzeddine Abderrahim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) seems to be associated with poor renal outcomes in lupus nephritis (LN). In this study, we aimed to evaluate the impact of these features on renal presentation and prognosis.
Method
We conducted a case-control study in our department between 1998 and 2020. As case group, we included patients whose kidney biopsies showed LN and TMA. Controls were patients with LN, matched two to one by age and gender. Patients with antiphospholipid syndrome were excluded.
Results
Fifty patients with renal TMA and 102 controls were included. Mean age was 35 ± 11.7 years in case group (P = 0.66), and gender ratio was nine females for one male in both groups. There was no difference in the disease activity score. Kidney disease was more severe in the case group, with higher level of proteinuria (P = 0.03), and serum creatinine (P = 0.00001). As for histological feature, there were no significant differences in LN classes between the groups. However, endocapillary proliferation was more frequent (P = 0.04) and interstitial inflammation was more important (P = 0.03) in TMA group. Chronicity markers were more intense in cases of TMA with more frequent tubular atrophy lesions (P = 0.01) and more extensive interstitial fibrosis (P = 0.000002). The complete remission rate was lower in case group (P = 0.008). The annual rate of renal failure was 10.7% (95% CI: 5.6–15.8) in case group and 2.4% (95% CI: 1.13–3.6) in controls (P < 0.05). Renal TMA was associated with increased risk of renal failure (OR = 2.8; 95% CI: 1.3–5.8; P = 0.006). In multivariate analysis, kidney injury at the time of biopsy (OR = 2.6; 95% CI: 1.6–6.7; P = 0.01), renal TMA (OR = 1.4; 95% CI: 1.06–3.5; P = 0.04) and non-response to treatment (OR = 2.9; 95% CI: 1.15–7.4; P = 0.01) were independent risk factors for the progression to end stage renal disease.
Conclusion
Patients with LN and renal TMA have more chronic kidney injury at presentation and worse renal outcomes under classical therapy.

title: #3436 Representation of women and sex-disaggregated outcomes of trials in ANCA-associated vasculitis
authors: Vanja Ivkovic; Annette Bruchfeld; Lauren Floyd; Andreas Kronbichler; Jennifer Lees; Karl Emil Nelveg-Kristensen; Jae Il Shin; Maria Weiner; Kate Stevens
abstract:
Background and Aims
Women are generally underrepresented in randomized controlled trials (RCTs). No data exists on potential differential outcomes in ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) between women and men. Thus we sought to evaluate representation of women and reporting of sex-disaggregated outcomes in RCTs of AAV.
Method
A PubMed search was carried out for RCTs published from beginning of indexation to May 2024 on granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. RCT quality was assessed using modified Jadad 8-point scale (mJS) Representation of women was expressed as participation-to-prevalence ratio (PPR) calculated as the ratio between enrollment of women and prevalence of AAV in women (data on prevalence was obtained from a recently published FAIRVASC study). A PPR of less than 0.8 indicates underrepresentation and 1.2 or higher indicates overrepresentation.
Results
A total of 572 publications were identified, of which 56 original (main) RCTs were included. Of 5,336 enrolled patients 2,415 were women (45.3 ± 10.7%; min-max: 21.9% to 69.8%, with a PPR of 0.94 (min-max: 0.46 to 1.45). Even after exclusion of RCTs in EGPA (n = 12), there were no changes to percentage of women enrolled or PPR (44.1% and 0.92, respectively). Women were underrepresented (PPR < 0.8) in 13 (25%) and overrepresented (PPR ≥ 1.2) in 7 (13%) RCTs. There was a geographical imbalance with women more frequently recruited in RCTs based in Australasia (61.2%) compared to Europe (41.8%) and globally (defined as RCT which enrolled patients from two or more continents) (47.7%) (P < 0.001) (Fig. 1A). Enrollment of women increased over time (Beta = 0.003, P = 0.05) (Fig. 1B), and was not associated with RCT size or study quality. Most studies reported sex of participants (96%), but none compared baseline characteristics between women and men. Only three studies (5%) reported sex-disaggregated outcomes: two for the primary efficacy outcome and one for the primary safety outcome and of these just one RCT reported sex-disaggregated outcomes in the main text.
Conclusion
Women are generally not underrepresented in AAV RCTs. However, trials almost never report sex-disaggregated outcomes or discuss on any differences between women and men.

title: #703 Three years of avacopan treatment in patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis
authors: Jolijn van Leeuwen; Ben Sprangers; Luca Quartuccio; Iva Gunnarsson; Y K Onno Teng
abstract:
Background and Aims
Avacopan has been approved for the treatment of ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) and recent, European guidelines recommend to use avacopan as steroid-sparing agent for the management of severe AAV. However, there is a pivotal lack of evidence for avacopan treatment beyond one year, prompting guidelines to recommend no more than 12 months treatment. This highlights the urgent unmet need to address the gap of knowledge on prolonged avacopan treatment. Therefore, we aimed to assess characteristics and outcomes in patients who continued avacopan treatment beyond the recommended one-year duration.
Method
The AVAC-EUR study is a multicenter, European retrospective, observational study to investigate avacopan use since its early access availability from 2020 onwards. In order to investigate prolonged avacopan treatment, we selected all patients with >1.5 years of follow-up since the start of avacopan (regardless of treatment duration). We compared patients treated with <1 year avacopan treatment versus prolonged avacopan treatment (defined as >1 year). We described patient characteristics, treatment characteristics and three important clinical outcomes (relapses, hospitalizations and infections).
Results
We identified 13/32 patients in the AVAC-EUR database had a follow-up time of >1.5 years. Seven patients had prolonged avacopan treatment with a median [IQR] avacopan treatment of 3.1 [2.8–3.2] years and a total follow-up time of 3.1 [3.1–3.6] years. Six patients had <1 year avacopan treatment with a median avacopan treatment of 1.0 [0.5–1.0] years and a total follow-up time of 2.4 [1.6–4.4] years. Baseline characteristics are shown in Table 1. All patients achieved remission (BVAS =0) within 6 months.
3/7 patients with prolonged avacopan treatment stopped avacopan during follow-up, because of side effects (n = 1), infection (n = 1) or achieving sustained remission (n = 1). In patients with <1 year avacopan treatment reasons to discontinue avacopan were side-effects (n = 1), pregnancy wish (n = 1), major flare (n = 1), achieving sustained remission (n = 2) and non-adherence (n = 1).
During the first year of follow-up, 6/7 patients with prolonged treatment received a steroid-taper and 3/7 (43%) patients received rituximab maintenance treatment. The median prednisone dosage was 15 [10–30] mg/day at baseline, 2.5 [0–5.6] mg/day after 6 months and 0 [0–3.8] mg/day after 12 months. Of the 6 patients with <1 year avacopan treatment, 5/6 patients received a steroid-taper and 4/6 (67%) received rituximab maintenance in the first year of follow-up. The median prednisone dosage was 23 [16–29] mg/day at baseline, 3.8 [0.6–6.9] mg/day after 6 months and 2.5 [0–5] mg/day after 12 months. In this first year, the relapse rate was 0.29 per patients year (PPY) (1 major and 1 minor relapse) for patient with prolonged treatment and 0.17 PPY (1 major relapse) for patients with <1 year avacopan treatment. Hospitalization rates and infections rates were lower in patients with prolonged treatment (0.14 an 0.43 PPY respectively) than in patients with <1 year treatment (0.83 and 0.67 PPY respectively).
After the first year of follow-up, 3/7 patients with prolonged avacopan treatment continued steroids and 4/7 patients received RTX maintenance treatment. In patients were avacopan was discontinued 3/6 patients continued steroids, 3/6 received RTX maintenance treatment and 1/6 received azathioprine treatment. After the first year, the relapse rate was 0.13 PPY (2 minor relapses) in patients with prolonged avacopan treatment and 0.09 (1 major relapse) in patients with <1 year avacopan treatment. Hospitalization rates and infections rates remained lower in patients with prolonged treatment (0.20 and 0.33 respectively) than in patients with <1 year avacopan treatment (0.34 and 0.43 PPY respectively).
Conclusion
Our study is the first descriptive analysis of three years avacopan treatment in severe AAV patients in which we observed lower hospitalization and infection rates when compared to stopping avacopan treatment <1 year. These data warrant further confirmation in larger, observational studies including the currently recruiting AVAC-EUR study.

title: #3791 Efficacy and safety of biologic therapies for the treatment of lupus nephritis/lupus erythematosus: experience of our hospital
authors: Cristhian David Orellana Chávez; Florentino Villanego; Jose Manuel Amaro Martin; Juan Manuel Cazorla Lopez; Luis Alberto Vigara; Javier Naranjo Muñoz; María Auxiliadora Mazuecos Blanca
abstract:
Background and Aims
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a disease with complex immunopathogenesis. Lupus nephritis (LN) affects up to 60% of patients with SLE, increasing their morbidity and mortality. Better knowledge of the disease has allowed advances in the therapeutic approach. Biologic agents are approved for the treatment of SLE and LN with the aim of controlling the disease, avoiding new outbreaks and preventing chronic damage. Aims: describe the effectiveness of biologic agents in preventing new outbreaks and reducing the dose of immunosuppressive treatment. Describe the safety of biological agents. In patients with LN subanalysis to observe if there is a relationship between the histological class, the activity/chronicity indices and their evolution towards end-stage chronic kidney disease.
Method
Observational and retrospective study of our series of patients (n:60) treated with biologic agents for LN and SLE at the Puerta del Mar University Hospital in Cádiz, Spain (Nephrology, Internal Medicine and Rheumatology). We analyzed clinical, analytical and histopathological variables to assess response to treatment, safety of biological agents, reduction in doses of usual immunosuppressive treatment and evolution of the disease.
Results
Biologic agents prevented new SLE outbreaks in 86.7%, achieving a complete response in 66.7%. No side effects in 85%. In patients with LN, a statistically significant difference is observed between the different pre- and post-treatment variables (creatinine, glomerular filtration rate, proteinuria, complement, Anti-DNA. Renal biopsies in 22 patients, class IV was the most frequent 36.4%. The activity and chronicity index show a statistically significant relationship with creatinine and proteinuria after treatment. Renal survival at 10 years is 86.1%.
Conclusion
In our study, biologic agents for the treatment of SLE and LN have proven to be safe and effective, achieving a lower number of flares, achieving a complete response in 66% of patients without complications after treatment. They have made it possible to reduce immunosuppressive treatment in up to 75% of patients.

Background and Aims
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a disease with complex immunopathogenesis. Lupus nephritis (LN) affects up to 60% of patients with SLE, increasing their morbidity and mortality. Better knowledge of the disease has allowed advances in the therapeutic approach. Biologic agents are approved for the treatment of SLE and LN with the aim of controlling the disease, avoiding new outbreaks and preventing chronic damage. Aims: describe the effectiveness of biologic agents in preventing new outbreaks and reducing the dose of immunosuppressive treatment. Describe the safety of biological agents. In patients with LN subanalysis to observe if there is a relationship between the histological class, the activity/chronicity indices and their evolution towards end-stage chronic kidney disease.
Method
Observational and retrospective study of our series of patients (n:60) treated with biologic agents for LN and SLE at the Puerta del Mar University Hospital in Cádiz, Spain (Nephrology, Internal Medicine and Rheumatology). We analyzed clinical, analytical and histopathological variables to assess response to treatment, safety of biological agents, reduction in doses of usual immunosuppressive treatment and evolution of the disease.
Results
Biologic agents prevented new SLE outbreaks in 86.7%, achieving a complete response in 66.7%. No side effects in 85%. In patients with LN, a statistically significant difference is observed between the different pre- and post-treatment variables (creatinine, glomerular filtration rate, proteinuria, complement, Anti-DNA. Renal biopsies in 22 patients, class IV was the most frequent 36.4%. The activity and chronicity index show a statistically significant relationship with creatinine and proteinuria after treatment. Renal survival at 10 years is 86.1%.
Conclusion
In our study, biologic agents for the treatment of SLE and LN have proven to be safe and effective, achieving a lower number of flares, achieving a complete response in 66% of patients without complications after treatment. They have made it possible to reduce immunosuppressive treatment in up to 75% of patients.

title: #3807 Cardiac involvement in monoclonal gammopathies: a single center experience
authors: Manel Zakhama; Sirine Bchir; Mouna Hamouda; Meriem Ben Salam; Nouha Ben Mahmoud; Manel Ben Salah; Ahmed Letaief; Habib Skhiri
abstract:
Background and Aims
Monoclonal gammopathies can be associated with systemic complications, including cardiac involvement, which is responsible for significant morbidity and mortality.
The objective of this study is to describe the clinical, biological, and radiological characteristics of cardiac involvement associated with monoclonal gammopathies.
Method
We included all patients with monoclonal gammopathies and cardiac involevement identified between 2020 and 2024 in our department.
Results
Out of a total of 100 patients with monoclonal gammopathies and renal involvement, 15 (15%) had documented cardiac involvement. The mean age of these patients was 64.9 ± 16.17 years. Among them, 46.7% had no medical history, while 13.3% had a history of cardiac conditions such as atrial fibrillation (AF) or pacemaker implantation, and 53% were hypertensive. Additionally, none of the patients had heart failure prior to the diagnosis of monoclonal gammopathy.
Regarding the types of gammopathies: 9 patients (60%) had multiple myeloma, 2 patients (13%) presented with MGRS (Monoclonal Gammopathy of Renal Significance), and 3 patients (20%) had AL amyloidosis without multiple myeloma. In the entire cohort, 80% of patients presented with a glomerular renal profile. Furthermore, among the patients with multiple myeloma (MM), 88% (8 cases) presented with a glomerular renal profile. Based on kidney biopsies, 3 cases were identified as AL amyloidosis, 2 cases as Randall's disease, and for 3 patients, no kidney biopsy was performed. The mean free light chain ratio was 62 ± 125.
About cardiac manifestations, the most frequent clinical manifestation was dyspnea (80%) then hypotension (33%). In addition, five patients (33%) had electrical abnormalities. Echocardiography was practiced to all patients. We found 40% of LVH, also 40% showed interventricular septal hypertrophy with a hyperechoic appearance, then 1 case of restrictive cardiomyopathy, and 2 cases of reduced strain. LVEF was above 50% in 73% of patients. Global hypokinesia was observed in 3 cases (20%). In Biological findings, Elevated NT-proBNP levels (≥3500 pg/mL) were noted in 86.7% of cases, with an average troponin level of 105 ± 86 ng/mL.
Conclusion
Cardiac involvement associated with monoclonal gammopathies is common. Early identification based on clinical, biological, and echocardiographic characteristics is essential to improve patient outcomes.

title: #3882 Prognostic factors for cardiovascular events in pauci-immune glomerulonephritis: a retrospective cohort study
authors: Stathis Tsiakas; Emmanuel Kalaitzakis; Chrysanthi Skalioti; Eleni Kapsia; George Liapis; Ioannis Boletis; Smaragdi Marinaki
abstract:
Background and Aims
Pauci-immune glomerulonephritis is a severe form of renal vasculitis, often associated with ANCA positivity and multisystem involvement. Small-vessel vasculitis is an increasingly recognized risk factor for cardiovascular disease. Our study aimed to identify potential prognostic factors associated with cardiovascular events at the time of diagnosis.
Method
We conducted a retrospective cohort study including data of all patients with biopsy-proven PIGN who were followed at our center between 1999 and 2024, with a minimum follow-up period of six months. Cardiovascular events were defined as myocardial ischemia, stroke, congestive heart failure (CHF), atrial fibrillation (AF), and pericarditis. Univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses were used to assess the relationship between potential risk factors at diagnosis and adverse cardiovascular outcomes.
Results
A total of 88 patients (male 53.4%) with a median age of 63 years (IQR 53 –70) at renal diagnosis were included in the study. Among traditional risk factors examined at presentation, hypertension, diabetes mellitus (DM), and previous history of cardiovascular disease (CVD) were present in 44.3%, 15.9% and 10.2% of the participants, respectively. Twenty patients (22.7%) were dialysis-dependent at the time of kidney biopsy. MPO-ANCA were the most prevalent type (54.5%). Crescentic and sclerotic classes were observed in 24.7% and 10.4% of the individuals, respectively. The median Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score (BVAS) was 15 (IQR 12–19). Cyclophosphamide was administered to 81.8%, rituximab to 69.3% and therapeutic plasma exchange to 34.1% of the patients.
Over a median follow-up period of 62 months (IQR 29–133), 26 patients (29.5%) developed cardiovascular events. Nine of those events (36%) were observed during the first 12 months from diagnosis. Acute myocardial ischemia occurred in 15.4%, stroke in 3.8%, CHF in 34.6 %, AF in 38.4% and pericarditis in 7.7% of them. Univariate Cox regression analysis identified age, hypertension and BVAS at diagnosis as prognostic factors for cardiovascular events in our cohort. In multivariate Cox regression model adjusted for age, sex, hypertension, DM, CVD, hemodialysis at diagnosis, ANCA type and BVAS, the presence of hypertension (HR: 4.38, 95% CI: 1.40–13.69, p-value: 0.011) and higher BVAS at presentation (HR: 1.15, 95%CI: 1.00–1.32, p-value: 0.046) were recognized as risk factors for cardiovascular events.
Conclusion
Cardiovascular events were common in patients with pauci-immune glomerulonephritis in our cohort, with a considerable proportion of them occurring within the first year of diagnosis. Hypertension and higher disease activity at presentation were identified as independent predictors of adverse cardiovascular outcomes.

title: #395 Diabetic nephropathy evaluation in an non-genotypic animal model of type 2 diabetes
authors: Silvia Teixidó-Trujillo; Maria Fernanda Toniolo; Esteban Porrini; Sergio Luis-Lima; Laura Díaz Martin; Rosa Rodríguez-Rodríguez; Luis Manuel Menéndez-Quintanal; Armando Torres Ramírez; Cecilia Fumero; Ana Elena Rodríguez-Rodríguez
abstract:
Background and Aims
The pathogenesis of diabetic nephropathy (DN) is not completely known. This could be related with a lack of pre-clinical models. Current animal models, mostly genotypic and monogenic, do not fully reflect diabetic organ damage. In previous studies of our group we observed that Tacrolimus (TAC) induce a beta-cell toxicity in the context of obesity that resembles the pathogenesis of diabetes [1–3]. We proposed a new non-genotypic animal model of type 2 diabetes in which evaluate the DN.
Method
26 Sprague Dawley male rats were fed with high fat diet to induce obesity and metabolic syndrome (MS) during 30 days. Then, animals were randomized to TAC or placebo during 6–9 months. The first 15 days animals were treated daily with a dose of 0.5 mg/kg. The next 30 days, animals were treated 3 times/week with 0.5 mg/kg of TAC. Then, until month 6 animals were treated 2 times/week with 0.5 mg/kg. At months 6 to 9, the dose used was 0.5 mg/kg 1 times/week. Animals continued with HFD until the end. Weight control was performed weekly. Blood levels of TAC were measured every month. Hyperglycemia and insulin resistance were analyzed regularly with fasting glucose, intraperitoneal glucose tolerance test (IPGTT) and insulin tolerance test (ITT). Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) was measured by iohexol-DBS plasma clearance. Urine at 24 hours was collected to analyze albuminuria and proteinuria. At the endpoint, renal morphology histology was analyzed (Fig 1A).
Results
HFD induced obesity and MS in all animals. Then, animals on TAC, compared with those in vehicle, developed diabetes at baseline and after glucose load since day 15 to 9 months. In the pancreas, diabetic animals on TAC showed characteristics similar to those observed in diabetic patients (e.g. decrease in islet number and area, fibrosis, disbalance in alpha/beta cells number) (data not shown). Blood levels of TAC at 24 h were 7.5 ± 2.4 ng/mL the first 15 days, 5.1 ± 1.8 ng/mL on month 1, 4.3 ± 1.4 ng/mL on month 3, 4 ± 1.6 ng/mL on month 6 and 0.9 ± 0.2 ng/mL on month 9. Animals increased the GFR after 30 days of HFD. Then, GFR continue to increase up to 6 months. From 6 months on, GFR started to decline. Animals on TAC showed higher GFR than control. In the kidney, diabetic animals on TAC showed increased glomerular area (TAC: 5260.6 ± 1922.8 pixel/µm vs. Control: 1910.6 ± 1051,7 pixel/µm, P ≤ 0.0001), mesangial expansion (P ≤ 0.0001) and fibrosis intraglomerular (TAC: 17.9 ± 16.5 % vs. Control: 8.8 ± 6 %, P ≤ 0.0002) and a higher proportion of glomeruli with nodular sclerosis (TAC: 34.8 ± 9.1 glomeruli (14%) vs. Control: 22.6 ± 4.3 glomeruli (6%), P ≤ 0.0043). Proteinuria was increased in diabetic animals (3932,8 ± 2872 mg/dL vs. 1257,7 ± 569,4 mg/dL, n.s.) (Fig. 1B).
Conclusion
in an animal model of chronic diabetes induced by Tacrolimus in a context of obesity and metabolic syndrome we observed markers of diabetic kidney disease: hyperfiltration and GFR decline, proteinuria, increased mesangial expansion and nodular sclerosis. This model can be used for studying the pathogenesis of DKD and as a platform for testing new drugs.

title: #813 Clinical and laboratory manifestations of kidney damage in various types of ANCA-associated vasculitis
authors: Maria Yefremova; Konstantin Chyzh; Maria Smaliakova; Aliaksei Narbin
abstract:
Background and Aims
The kidneys are one of the most vulnerable organs in antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis. Kidney damage can significantly worsen the prognosis and quality of life of patients. Clinical and laboratory manifestations of renal dysfunction vary depending on the subtype of disease and the degree of vascular damage.
The aim of this study is to analyze the clinical and laboratory manifestations of renal pathology in patients with various types of ANCA-associated vasculitis.
Method
The study included 45 patients diagnosed with ANCA-associated vasculitis (60.0% (n = 27) women and 40.0% (n = 18) men), who were observed at the Minsk Scientific and Practical Center for Surgery, Transplantology and Hematology from 2017 to 2024. The average age was 59.1 ± 12.3 years. 57.8% (n = 26) patients had granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), 24.4% (n = 11)—microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), 17.8% (n=8)—eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA).
We analyzed blood creatinine levels, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), hematuria, leukocyturia, cylindruria and daily proteinuria at the time of disease onset to assess the type and severity of renal damage. In addition to clinical and laboratory examination, the diagnosis of ANCA-associated vasculitis and secondary glomerulonephritis was confirmed by the results of immunological tests (ANCA, antibodies to myeloperoxidase and proteinase-3) and nephrobiopsies.
Results
A higher level of serum creatinine (237 (103; 463) μmol/l) and low eGFR (18.1 (12.3; 76.2) mL/min/1.73 m²) were diagnosed in the group of patients with MPA compared with the GPA and EGPA groups (P < 0.005). Proteinuria was diagnosed in 75.6% (n = 34), most often—in patients with MPA (90.9%). The level of proteinuria ranged from mild to nephrotic. It exceeded 1 g/day in 66.7% (n = 30). Nephrotic syndrome was found in 8.9% (n = 4) patients and was not observed in EGPA group.
In 9 cases (20.0%) isolated urinary syndrome was diagnosed, but without significant decrease in renal function and arterial hypertension. In 42.2% (n = 19) cases kidney damage was accompanied by arterial hypertension, its highest frequency was recorded in the MPA group: 7 out of 11 patients (63.6%).
eGFR <90 ml/min/1.73 m² was found in 82.2% (n = 37) patients, 20.0% (n = 9) showed the most pronounced decrease (eGFR <15 ml/min/1.73 m²), mainly in MPA group (n = 7), P < 0.05. The clinical picture of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis developed in 63.6% (n = 11) of patients with MPA, while in the GPA and EGPA groups this figure was 23.1% (n = 6) and 12.5% (n = 1), P < 0.05, respectively.
Conclusion
Variants of ANCA-associated vasculitis exhibit a wide range of clinical and laboratory manifestations, with the most severe forms of renal damage reported in patients with MPA. Proteinuria is detected in a significant number of patients, especially with MPA. Nephrotic syndrome developed in 8.9% of patients and was absent in the EGPA group. Kidney damage is often accompanied by arterial hypertension, which is most pronounced among patients with MPA. The incidence of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis supports the fatal role of renal damage in ANCA-associated vasculitis.

title: #1046 The impact of remission occurrence on long-term renal survival in IgA nephropathy
authors: Bogdan Obrisca; Roxana Jurubita; Stefan Lujinschi; Teodora Craciun; Valentin Mocanu; George-Alexandru Dimofte; Bogdan Sorohan; Andreea Ioana Berechet; Andreea Gabriella Andronesi; Nicu Caceaune; Gabriela Lupusoru; Gener Ismail
abstract:
Background and Aims
We sought to evaluate the impact of remission occurrence on long-term renal survival in IgA Nephropathy (IgAN).
Method
We conducted a retrospective study that enrolled 230 patients with biopsy-proven IgAN and at least 6 months of follow-up. Complete remission was defined as achievement of 24-h proteinuria reduction to less than 0.3 g/day at any time point during follow-up. Partial remission was defined as at least 50% reduction in 24-h proteinuria from baseline values and less than 1 g/day. The primary composite endpoint was the occurrence of an eGFR decline by at least 50%, progression to ESRD or death, whichever came first.
Results
The study cohort had a median age at biopsy of 41 years (IQR: 33–51), 67% being males. The median eGFR and 24-h proteinuria were 52 ml/min (IQR: 29–77) and 1.5 g/day (IQR: 0.8–3.2), respectively. During a median follow-up time of 44 months (IQR: 17–88.3), 3.91% of patients showed an eGFR decline by at least 50%, 27.8% progressed to ESRD, 1.74% died without CKD progression and 1.3% died after progressing to ESRD. In terms of remission occurrence, 35.2% and 23.1% of patients achieved either a complete or partial remission at any time during the follow-up period, respectively. Patients that achieved a complete remission had a better renal function at biopsy [eGFR, 74 ml/min (IQR: 53–95.5)], a lower proteinuria [0.82 g/day (IQR: 0.34–2)] and a lower prevalence of T1-2 score (21%) compared to those that achieved a partial remission [eGFR, 59 ml/min (IQR: 37–85); 24-h proteinuria, 1.5 g/day (IQR: 0.8–3.3); T1-2 score, 43.4%] or no remission [eGFR, 30.5 ml/min (IQR: 19.2–48); 24-h proteinuria, 2.2 g/day (IQR: 1.2–3.99); T1-2 score, 64.6%], respectively (P < 0.001 for all comparisons). By multivariate logistic regression analysis, a better renal function at biopsy (OR, 1.02 for 1 ml/min; 95% CI, 1.007–1.03) and absence of T2 score (T2 vs. T0 score: HR, 0.19; 95% CI, 0.04–0.92) were identified as independent predictors of complete remission occurrence. When evaluating the predictors of renal outcome, by multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression analysis, baseline eGFR (HR, 0.94 for 1 ml/min; 95%, 0.92–0.96), C2 score (HR, 3.22; 95% CI, 0.96–10.7) were independent predictors of the primary composite endpoint. In addition, the achievement of a complete remission during follow-up independently determined a 94% reduction in the risk of the primary composite endpoint (HR, 0.06; 95%CI, 0.01-0.25), while occurrence of a partial remission independently determined a 57% reduction in the risk of disease progression (HR, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.21–0.88). The time to an event was significantly longer for patients with complete remission [median, 138 months (IQR: 131–138)] compared to patients with partial remission [median, 102.4 months (IQR: 57.1–129.2)] or no remission [median, 29 months (IQR: 8.3–70.8)] (P < 0.001).
Conclusion
Our study confirmed that achievement of a complete or a partial remission significantly improved the long-term renal outcome of patients with IgAN.

Our study confirmed that achievement of a complete or a partial remission significantly improved the long-term renal outcome of patients with IgAN.

title: #2212 Atopic dermatitis-like chronic inflammation may be associated with kidney inflammation
authors: Arisa Ikeda; Ge Peng; Wanchen Zhao; Alafate Abudouwanli; Shigaku Ikeda; François Niyonsaba; Yusuke Suzuki
abstract:
Background and Aims
Some studies recently indicated the association between renal abnormalities and atopic dermatitis (AD). AD causes not only skin lesions, but also the dysregulation of a wide range of cytokines. However, the underlying mechanism for a potential link between AD and chronic kidney diseases remains unknown.
Method
To evaluate the status of kidney functions of patients with AD, the serum and urine samples of US adults from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) were analyzed.
Additionally, a chronic AD-like mouse model was induced by applying 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene. The renal function was evaluated by urine and serum examinations, histological staining and electron microscopy imaging of kidneys. The expression of glomerular filtration barrier proteins was evaluated by immunoblotting and immunofluorescence staining. Furthermore, real-time PCR and ELISA assays were performed to analyze kidney inflammation.
Results
Analysis of NHANES data confirmed the upregulation of urine protein creatinine ratio and downregulation of estimate GFR in patients with AD.
In addition, AD-like mice showed higher albuminuria and serum creatinine than control mice. Moreover, AD mice had an increase in glomerular cell infiltration, and foot process effacement of podocytes, indicating dysfunction of glomerular filtration by AD-like inflammation. Kidneys from AD mice showed downregulated expression of glomerular filtration barrier proteins. Concurrently, S100A8 and S100A9, which are the Ca2+ binding proteins derived from neutrophils and macrophages, were found to be elevated in the serum and renal cortex of these AD mice.
Conclusion
Our findings suggest that dysfunctional glomerular filtration and reduced kidney function in AD-like mice might be correlated with the increased levels of S100A8 and A100A9.

title: #2276 Serotonin receptor HTR2A drives parietal epithelial cell activation in glomerular disease downstream of platelet activation
authors: Eleni Stamellou; Caroline Haas; Claudia van Roeyen; Ina Verena Martin; Bart Smeets; Ute Raffetseder; Yingying Gao; Luc Maroteaux; Jürgen Floege; Pierre-Louis Tharaux; Gerald Braun; Tammo Ostendorf
abstract:
Background and Aims
The mechanisms driving the development of extracapillary lesions in crescentic glomerulonephritis (CGN) and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) remain poorly understood. This study investigates the role of serotonin (5-HT) and its receptors, specifically HTR2A and HTR2B, in murine models of these diseases.
Method
This study employed a combination of genetic, pharmacological, and in vitro approaches to elucidate the role of serotonin receptors in CGN and FSGS.
Results
We found that both receptors were upregulated in glomerular parietal epithelial cells in both human and murine CGN. We found that both genetic deletion and pharmacological inhibition of the 5-HT2A receptor effectively reduced glomerular crescents and sclerosis, while the compensatory upregulation of 5-HT2A receptors in response to 5-HT2B receptor deficiency or antagonism underscores a complex interplay between these receptor subtypes. Bone marrow-specific deletion and repletion of HTR2A-competent cells did not alter the course of experimental CGN, suggesting that the 2A signals driving CGN originate from the kidney. The Alport model, which is primarily degenerative, also benefitted in a similar way from 2A deletion, further corroborating the role of kidney resident 2A signaling in these diseases. Additionally, platelets were identified as a source of 5-HT and a crucial upstream factor in promoting PEC activation and exacerbating the disease, with their depletion leading to significant mitigation of disease severity. Finally, in vitro studies using murine PECs indicated the pivotal role of 5-HT signaling in PEC activation.
Conclusion
Our findings highlight a critical role of 5-HTR2A in PEC activation, proposing it as a new potential target for the treatment of glomerular kidney diseases.

title: #2580 Renal thrombotic microangiopathies: etiological spectrum and prognostic factors
authors: Meriam Hajji; Ilhem Ben Othman; Imen Gorsane; Hayet Kaaroud; Fethi Ben Hmida; Ezzedine Abderrahim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) is a histopathological lesion that can arise in multiple pathological conditions. This study aimed to assess the clinical, biological, histological, prognostic, and therapeutic aspects of patients diagnosed with renal TMA while identifying distinguishing features across different etiological contexts.
Method
We conducted a retrospective descriptive and analytical study (2010–2024), reviewing cases of patients over the age of 16 years old who had biopsy-confirmed TMA on renal biopsy.
Results
A total of 160 cases of renal TMA were analyzed. The mean patient age at the time of the renal biopsy was 44.2 ± 15.3 years. Hypertension was the most common presentation, affecting 133 patients (83%). Laboratory findings revealed acute kidney injury in all patients at the time of renal biopsy. The majority of patients (n = 128) exhibited biological markers of TMA (80%): hemolytic anemia in 151 cases (94.3%), thrombocytopenia in 142 cases (88.7%). Renal histopathological examination identified arteriolar involvement in all cases and glomerular TMA in 48 patients (30%). The primary underlying conditions associated with TMA included lupus nephritis (54 cases), non-lupus glomerulopathies (53 cases), malignant HTN (36 cases), and post kidney transplantation (14 cases). Threes cases were attributed to atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (1.8%). Disease progression to stage 5 chronic kidney disease (CKD) was observed in 145 patients (90%).
Age <20 years (P = 0.003), Male sex (P = 0.04), thrombocytopenia at initial presentation (P = 0.03) were identified as independent risk factors for progression to stage 5 CKD in patients with non-lupus glomerulopathy.
Conclusion
The overall prognosis remains poor, especially in terms of renal function. There is no particular histological parameter that is indicative of an irreversible decline in renal function.

title: #3172 Regulation of mRNA, miRNAs, and alternative splicing events in an FSGS-like zebrafish injury model
authors: Francescapaola Mattias; Felix Kliewe; Tim Lange; Anna Iervolino; Olga Tsoy; Alexander Gress; Chit Tong Lio; Stefan Simm; Olga V Kalinina; Jan Baumbach; Giovambattista Capasso; Nicole Endlich
abstract:
Background and Aims
Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is a renal disease characterized by podocyte cytoskeletal damage, resulting in impaired podocyte foot process morphology and kidney function. Despite significant advancements in our understanding of FSGS, the molecular mechanisms underlying glomerular damage and disease progression remain largely elusive. MiRNAs and alternative splicing (AS) of pre-mRNAs are predicted to play a substantial role in the physiology and pathology of kidney diseases.
The present study aims to identify changes in miRNAs and pre-mRNA splicing events that may be responsible for the pathogenesis of FSGS.
Method
The present study used an established FSGS study model based on transgenic zebrafish larvae expressing bacterial nitroreductase and the fluorophore mCherry at podocyte levels. The addition of the prodrug Nifurpirinol to zebrafish larvae at 4 days post-fertilization (dpf) led to its enzymatic conversion into a toxin, causing glomerular damage that models FSGS pathology. Glomeruli and whole larvae were collected for RNA sequencing at 5 and 6 dpf, followed by gene set enrichment analysis based on biological processes.
To identify AS events, RNA-Seq data were analyzed using different bioinformatic tools such as rMATS, leafcutter, Whippet, and IsoformSwitchAnalyzeR.
Results
Zebrafish larvae exposed to Nifurpirinol developed periorbital and abdominal edema, along with fluorescence accumulation in proximal tubules, indicating podocyte loss. These effects were more pronounced 48 hours post-treatment.
Transcriptome analysis revealed a marked increase in differentially expressed genes in whole larvae and isolated glomeruli.
Podocyte-specific genes, including nephrin, podocin, podocalyxin, and wt1, were significantly downregulated, confirming the injury model. Gene ontology analysis showed enrichment in glomerular development, rRNA processing, catabolic processes, extracellular matrix, and cytoskeleton organization. MiRNAs dre-mir-21-2 and dre-mir-193, previously associated with CKD and FSGS, were found to be upregulated.
AS analysis detected ∼7,000 events in isolated glomeruli, with exon skipping as the most frequent event (∼80%).
Differential splicing was notable in the serine/arginine-rich splicing factors (SRSF) family. Across methods (rMATS, Leafcutter, Whippet), 612 and 136 alternatively spliced genes were identified in Nifurpirinol-treated glomeruli at 6 and 5 dpf, respectively. Two candidates, epb41l5 and fgfr1a, showed significant isoform changes and were selected for further studies. Novel splicing variants, including altered epb41l5 isoforms critical for podocyte adhesion and fgfr1a isoforms linked to fibroblast growth signaling, may contribute to podocyte dysfunction.
Conclusion
The present study identified alterations in pre-mRNAs expression, including epb41l5 and fgfr1a, using a zebrafish model mimicking FSGS. Additionally, up-regulation of specific miRNAs were identified, suggesting a crucial role in the development and progression of FSGS. These findings offer new insights into the pathogenesis of FSGS, supporting the discovery of disease biomarkers and the development of targeted therapeutic strategies.

title: #3249 Minimal changes disease in patients over 60 years of age
authors: Juraj Maris; Zuzana Zilinska; Martin Chrastina; Michaela Javorkova; Marcela Cvoligova; Martina Hivková; Jana Otavkova; Katarína Štefančíková; Andrea Bystricanova
abstract:
Background and Aims
Minimal glomerular changes (MCD) is a disease characterized by increased permeability of glomerular capillary vascular wall for proteins, without the presence of immune deposits in glomeruli. It is the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, less so in adults (10%–15%). Most cases of MCD are idiopathic and manifest mainly by sudden onset of nephrotic syndrome. Secondary MCD may be related to medicaments, tumors, infections, allergies or autoimmune diseases. Approximately 30% of patients have reduced renal function at the time of diagnosis, usually responding well to glucocorticoids. In contrast to children, the cause of MCD in adults is more often secondary. In the elderly, renal impairment and hypertension is more common at the time of diagnosis. Remission occurs later than in children, relapses are less frequent and the time interval between them is longer.
Method
We present a cohort of adult patients with MCD who underwent renal biopsy at our institution renal biopsy between 1/2021 and 10/2024. From the total number of 116 biopsies, MCD was found in 18 patients (17%). Of these, 10 (56%) were men and 8 (44%) women. There were 9 (50%) seniors >60 years of age. Mean proteinuria was 10.3 g/24 h in younger patients and 9,04 in older patients. Renal dysfunction was more frequent in elderly patients (mean s-creat.: 353.7 μmol/l) than in younger patients (115,8 μmol/l). Normal renal function had 4 younger patients (45%), but no one >60 years of age.
Results
Older patients had a higher incidence of tubulointerstitial fibrosis (44%) and arteriolo/arteriosclerosis (44%) versus 2% and 33%. Comorbidities were present in 100% of seniors, while only in 44% of the younger ones. The most common were arterial hypertension and diabetes mellitus. Intravenous boluses of 6-methylprednisolon were given to 43% of younger patients, but only 25% of older patients due to more frequent occurrence of comorbidities. Most elderly patients were treated with prednisone at an initial dose of 1 mg/kg/day (max. 80 mg/day) with rapid up-titration to a maintenance dose. In the elderly group we observed complete remission in 67% and partial remission in 33%. Treatment with corticosteroids led to complete remission in 66% and to partial remission in none of the younger patients. Equally 17% of the younger patients were corticodependent and corticoresistant.
Conclusion
In our cohort, we found higher proteinuria in younger patients, whereas in older patients were more likely to have reduced renal function corresponding with a higher incidence of chronic changes in histological findings. Older patients had a higher incidence of comorbidities. Complete remission was more often achieved in younger patients, while in older patients was more common partial remission.

title: #3287 Immunomediated tubulo-interstitial nephritis. Acumulated experience in Infanta Sofía Hosptial (Madrid)
authors: Verónica Ruth Mercado Valdivia; Raquel Diaz Mancebo; Gabriel Ledesma Sánchez; Yesika María Amezquita Orjuela; Sílvia Caldés Ruisánchez; Yolanda Hernández Hernández; Ángel Gallegos Villalobos; Rocío Echarri Carrillo; Gilda Carreño Cornejo; María Covadonga Hevia Ojanguren; Antonio Cirugeda García
abstract:
Background and Aims
Immunotherapy has revolutionized the treatment of various neoplasms, although it is not without adverse events. Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis (ATIN) is the most common histopathological finding in kidney biopsies of patients with acute renal failure (ARF) and the use of Checkpoint Inhibitors (CPI).
Our goal is to describe the clinical, analytical, and histological characteristics of tubulointerstitial nephritis attributed to the use of CPIs (CITN).
Method
A retrospective, descriptive observational study of patients diagnosed with CPI-related tubulointerstitial nephritis (CITN) from January 2018 to February 2023 in the Nephrology Department of the Infanta Sofía University Hospital. The statistical analysis was performed using the SPSS® platform.
Results
We describe a total of 9 patients, 8 received anti-PD1 and 1 received anti-PDL1. Regarding the cancer diagnoses, 4 were urological (all treated with nivolumab), 4 were lung cancer (one treated with nivolumab, another with nivolumab and pemetrexed, and 2 with pembrolizumab), and 1 was infiltrating breast cancer (treated with atezolizumab). At the time of diagnosis, 4 patients had locally advanced neoplasia, and 5 had metastases.
In relation to concomitant treatment, 6 patients were on proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), 3 were using NSAIDs, and 1 was on antibiotics. One patient was on a triple combination therapy. Forty-four percent experienced other immune-mediated side effects. The average latency period from the initiation of CPI to acute renal failure (ARF) was 6 months. The median maximum creatinine level was 1.98 mg/dl. Forty-four percent of cases presented with eosinophilia, hematuria, and leukocyturia. The median albuminuria was 310 mg/g. A kidney biopsy was performed in 55% of cases. Severe interstitial infiltration was found in 56% of cases, with eosinophils and plasma cells present in 82% and 75% of cases, respectively.
Treatment was carried out with corticosteroids, with an average cumulative dose of 1831 mg. More pulses were administered, but with lower doses (125 × 3). The average recovery time was 42 days, with no differences when comparing corticosteroid doses used.
Seventy-eight percent of patients showed favorable outcomes with a 62% reduction in creatinine levels. At the end of follow-up, the median creatinine was 1.24 mg/dl with albuminuria of 150 mg/g. Twenty-two percent of patients did not recover renal function.
Conclusions
In our cohort, unlike what is described in the literature, the presence of eosinophilia is more frequently observed in the clinical presentation, and there is a higher percentage of eosinophils and plasma cells in the kidney biopsy. The latency period is similar to the data described in various reviews. In our study, there seems to be a trend toward using lower shock doses of corticosteroids (125 × 3), likely due to a shift in the management of interstitial nephritis currently.

title: #3512 Pregnancy-associated aHUS: triggers, diagnosis, and outcomes
authors: Lucrezia Dimartino; Daniela Palazzetti; Gianfilippo Di Liberato; Francesca Bruno; Rocco Baccaro; Giuseppe Grandaliano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) is a rare condition caused by dysregulated activation of the alternative complement pathway. In 60% of cases, mutations in genes encoding complement factors and co-factors have been identified. AHUS accounts for 20% of thrombotic microangiopathies (TMA) occurring in women of reproductive age, and approximately 7% of diagnoses occur during pregnancy, with onset during gestation, at delivery, or in the postpartum period. Maternal exposure to fetal-placental material can trigger complement activation, which worsens during pregnancy and peaks at delivery. Differential diagnosis typically involves HELLP syndrome and other thrombotic microangiopathies, often leading to delayed treatment and placing both mother and fetus at risk. Untreated aHUS is associated with a 78% risk of progression to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) within 24 months postpartum.
Method
We collected data on pregnancy-associated aHUS cases at our center between May 2020 and January 2025.
Results
During this period, 9 pregnant women developed aHUS in the peripartum period. The primary triggers included placental abruption and intrauterine fetal death, which occurred in 4 patients. Genetic testing was performed on all patients: one patient showed a missense mutation in CD46, a gene encoding a cofactor of a regulatory protein in the alternative complement pathway, while another patient had a mutation in PCH2.
Diagnosis was made between 1 and 16 days (mean: 4.9 days) from the onset of clinical symptoms, with Eculizumab therapy initiated within an average of 26.1 hours from diagnosis. Only two patients required dialysis, and two others underwent plasmapheresis before starting Eculizumab treatment. The vast majority of patients gradually recovered normal renal function and experienced no further complications. (Fig. 1).
Scatter plots (Figs 2 and 3) show the correlation between the time to diagnosis and the start of therapy with key safety parameters of the disease. These findings highlight the critical importance of early diagnosis, identified as the primary determinant, and prompt therapeutic intervention, both of which have a significant prognostic impact.
Conclusion
This case series demonstrates that pregnancy-associated HUS, triggered by pregnancy and/or childbirth, does not necessarily require a significant genetic background, and underscores the critical need for early diagnosis. Background and Aims
Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) is a rare condition caused by dysregulated activation of the alternative complement pathway. In 60% of cases, mutations in genes encoding complement factors and co-factors have been identified. AHUS accounts for 20% of thrombotic microangiopathies (TMA) occurring in women of reproductive age, and approximately 7% of diagnoses occur during pregnancy, with onset during gestation, at delivery, or in the postpartum period. Maternal exposure to fetal-placental material can trigger complement activation, which worsens during pregnancy and peaks at delivery. Differential diagnosis typically involves HELLP syndrome and other thrombotic microangiopathies, often leading to delayed treatment and placing both mother and fetus at risk. Untreated aHUS is associated with a 78% risk of progression to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) within 24 months postpartum.
Method
We collected data on pregnancy-associated aHUS cases at our center between May 2020 and January 2025.

During this period, 9 pregnant women developed aHUS in the peripartum period. The primary triggers included placental abruption and intrauterine fetal death, which occurred in 4 patients. title: #3779 CD4 cells and peripheral T follicular cells may play a protective role in the development of cardiomyopathy in patients with SLE and LN
authors: Eleni Moysidou; Michalis Christodoulou; Georgios Lioulios; Konstantinos Kambas; Charilaos Spyropoulos; Christodoulos Keskinis; Asimina Fylaktou; Theodoros Karamitsos; Eleni Frangou; Maria Stangou
abstract:

Cardiomyopathy is a significant complication of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). While its pathogenesis is still under investigation, traditional cardiovascular risk factors do not fully account for its increased incidence in SLE patients. Emerging evidence suggests that disruptions in the innate and adaptive immune systems may play a critical role, potentially linking immune dysregulation with myocardial and kidney involvement. In the present study, we evaluated the correlation of peripheral T follicular cells (TF), as a memory T lymphocyte reservoir, with myocardial abnormalities in SLE.
Method
The incidence of myocardial involvement was investigated in patients with SLE, using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) to quantify biventricular volumes, myocardial mass, and ejection fraction. The same day of MRI, flow cytometry was performed to measure CD4 and peripheral T Follicullar (TF) cells, and their subtypes, TFH1, TFH2, TFH17, TF regulatory (TFR) and TF cells expressing ICOS (TFICOS).
Results
Thirty two patients with SLE (Male/Female 28/4, Age 36 ± 10.8 yrs, 25 with lupus nephritis, LN) demonstrated increased Left and Right Ventricular End-Diastolic Volumes/Body surface area (LV-EDV/BSA, RV-EDV/BSA) 89 ± 21 and 95 ± 17 ml/m2 (normal values 78 ± 8.7 and 78 ± 9 ml/m2, respectively) and LV-end systolic volume (LV-ESV), 35 ± 11 ml/m2 (normal values 26 ± 4.7 ml/m2).
Patients with LN compared to non-LN, had impaired LV volumes, increased LV-EDV/BSA 80.6 ± 18 vs. 59 ± 21 ml/m2, LV-EDV 151 ± 50 vs. 106 ± 27 ml/m2, P = 0.05, LV-ESV/BSA 31 ± 8 vs. 23 ± 8 ml/m2, and LV mass 95 ± 36 vs. 74 ± 13 ml/m2, P = NS.
Lymphocyte counts and CD4 cells were reduced in SLE compared to Healthy Controls (HC) 1660 (724) vs. 1183 (1002)/μl, P < 0.001, and 745 (515) vs. 511 (530)/μl, P = NS, respectively, while, proportion of TFH1, 40.3 (41.8) vs. 4 (3.7)%, P = 0.005, TFICOS, 0.2 (0.5) vs. 0.1 (0.3)%, P = 0.03, and the ratio of TFH1/TFHR 20.3 (120) vs. 4.5 (4.8) P = 0.02, and TFH1/TFH2 1 (0.8) vs. 1 (0.2), P = 0.008), were increased in SLE compared HC.
Concentration of CD4 had a significantly negative correlation with LV-EDV, LV-ESV/BSA, LV-ESV, r = −0.7, P = 0.005; r = −0.7, P = 0.005, r = −0.6, P = 0.03 respectively, and LV mass, r = −0.6, P = 0.04. MRI findings of cardiomyopathy are common within SLE patients, and more prominent in LN patients. CD4 and various peripheral T follicular cell subtypes seem to have a protective role in the development of cardiomyopathy.

title: #424 Long-term efficacy and safety of successful pregnancy in a patient with IgA nephropathy treated with telitacicept
authors: Xuehong Lu; Jia Lv; Lihua Liu; Manyu Luo
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is the most common cause of primary glomerulonephritis, with complex pathogenic mechanisms involving abnormal B-cell activation. Women with IgAN are at a higher risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes such as preeclampsia and miscarriage, especially those with uncontrolled massive proteinuria and advanced chronic kidney disease. Therefore, IgAN disease control before and during pregnancy is essential. Telitacicept inhibits both B-lymphocyte stimulating factor and a proliferation-inducing ligand. It also inhibits both B cells and plasma cells and the production of galactose-deficient IgA1 (Gd-IgA1) and its autoantibodies, thus exerting an immunosuppressive effect. We report the case of a woman with IgAN who had a successful pregnancy with significant improvement and long-term remission after treatment with telitacicept.
Method
Based on clinical manifestations, laboratory analysis and pathological results, the patient was diagnosed as IgAN.We mainly used telitacicept during her treatment,and conducted long-term follow-up.
Results
A 32-year-old female was found to have 3+ urinary protein levels in 2016 but did not receive any specific treatment. A follow-up examination in 2019 revealed a 3+ urinary protein level, 3+ urinary blood level, and serum creatinine level of 90 µmol/L. The outpatient physician prescribed the maximum tolerated dose of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibitor valsartan (150 mg orally once daily). In September 2021, the patient was hospitalized due to proteinuria and hematuria, and a renal biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of IgAN (Lee classification, grade 3; Oxford classification, M1E1S1T0). The patient was prescribed oral prednisone acetate (50 mg/day). In October 2021, the patient's creatinine, urinary protein, urinary erythrocytes, and leukocytes in the blood increased significantly, with a possible urinary tract infection, likely related to long-term administration of steroid therapy. The patient expressed a desire to avoid the side effects of high-dose steroids use, as well as a strong desire to conceive and, therefore, hoped that the disease could be controlled as quickly as possible. After 1 week of admission for infection control, we treated her with steroid therapy combined with telitacicept. After 1 week of telitacicept treatment, the patient's proteinuria, hematuria, and creatinine level decreased significantly. Since then, her 24-h proteinuria had remained stable at less than 0.5 g. We adjusted the dosage of steroids and telitacicept according to the patient's condition. Following the successful reduction of the dose of prednisone acetate to 10 mg, the dosage was slowly tapered to 0 mg. The treatment course is presented in Fig. 1. She received her last dose of telitacicept on June 17, 2022; at the same time, the prednisone acetate was also discontinued. However, the patient became pregnant 3 months after stopping the medication. After a comprehensive evaluation by the obstetrician and nephrologist and after explaining the potential risks to the patient, the patient requested to continue the pregnancy. The patient's 24 h proteinuria remained consistently below 0.5 g during pregnancy, her blood creatinine was stable at 70–95 µmol/L, her urine erythrocytes were stable at 5–18/µL, and her blood pressure was within the normal range, weight gain during pregnancy 15 kg. On June 5, 2023 (39 week and 3 days of pregnancy), she delivered a boy, weighing 2750 g and measuring 41 cm, with an Apgar score of 9 at 1 min and 10 at 5 min. Considering the patient's need for breastfeeding, we administered hydroxychloroquine 200 mg/dose twice daily oral maintenance therapy. Thereafter, the patient's condition stabilized. From the start of telitacicept treatment until the last follow-up at our hospital on on September 23, 2024, she had no recurrence of the disease, and her condition was significantly controlled (Table 1).
Conclusion
This report describes the efficacy of telitacicept in patients with IgAN and explores its value in women of childbearing age, suggesting effective and safe treatment options for women who wish to conceive.

title: #1083 A Systemic scoping review on interventions for cardiovascular risk management in glomerulonephritis
authors: Kar Min; Claire Chan; Jia Dong James Wang; Wei Yu Chua; Cynthia Lim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Individuals with glomerulonephritis and renal vasculitis have higher risk of cardiovascular disease compared to the general population. This elevated risk may be driven by disease-specific inflammatory processes and immunosuppressive treatment, in addition to traditional risk factors. There is thus a need for cardiovascular risk management and optimization among individuals with glomerulonephritis. We performed a systematic scoping review on the utilization, types and effectiveness of cardiovascular risk management strategies among individuals with glomerulonephritis.
Method
A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, EMBASE, and Cochrane Library for studies from inception to 24th September 2024, according to our pre-registered protocol (osf.io/anrjd) The search terms were related to glomerulonephritis, vasculitis, and cardiovascular risk. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction and synthesis. We included studies of chronic kidney disease populations that encompassed glomerulonephritis but excluded studies that specified non-glomerulonephritis conditions such as diabetic kidney disease.
Results
Figure 1 shows the PRISMA flow chart. Among 3162 studies screened, 48 studies were included. A third were systematic reviews of studies in chronic kidney disease that included some people with glomerulonephritis (15 studies). There were only 4 randomized controlled trials (3 studies in glomerulonephritis and 1 study in patients with CKD that included glomerulonephritis).
There were diverse approaches to cardiovascular risk management in glomerulonephritis and CKD. These included identifying risk factors with or without developing risk prediction models (7 studies), screening for cardiovascular risk factors (2 studies), use of risk-modifying pharmacotherapy such as renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors (14 studies), sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i; 3 studies); and/or modified immunosuppressive regimens such as glucocorticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors and biologics (19 studies).
However, few studies focused on glomerulonephritis, e.g. many cardiovascular risk prediction models were not validated in glomerulonephritis. In CKD, RAS inhibitors emerged as cornerstone therapies due to their dual benefits of reducing proteinuria and controlling hypertension. Emerging therapies, including SGLT2i, demonstrated potential in reducing cardiovascular events and improving renal outcomes.
Conclusion
Cardiovascular risk management in GN requires tailored strategies that account for the unique pathophysiology of the disease. While existing therapies offer significant benefits in CKD, gaps in GN-specific evidence highlight the need for further research. Future efforts should prioritize the validation of predictive models, optimization of combination therapies, and exploration of novel interventions in glomerulonephritis to improve patients’ cardiovascular outcomes.

title: #1104 Clinicopathological characteristics and predictors of survival and renal function in pulmonary-renal syndrome: a single-center experience
authors: Selim Benhadda; Kaoutar Darbal; Loubna Benamar; Naima Ouzeddoun; Tarik Bouattar
abstract:
Background and Aims
Pulmonary-Renal Syndrome (PRS) is a severe and life-threatening condition characterized by simultaneous pulmonary and renal involvement, commonly associated with ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) and anti-GBM disease. Despite advances in immunosuppressive therapies, PRS continues to pose significant challenges due to high mortality rates and progression to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). This study aims to evaluate the survival rates and prognostic factors associated with renal outcomes in patients with PRS.
Methods
A retrospective study was conducted on 33 patients diagnosed with PRS at the Nephrology Department of Ibn Sina University Hospital between January 2019 and January 2024. Patients were included based on defined pulmonary and renal impairment criteria, serological positivity for ANCA, anti-GBM, or other autoantibodies, and histopathological evidence of crescentic glomerulonephritis. Clinical, laboratory, and histopathological parameters were analyzed, and treatment responses were assessed over a one-year follow-up period. Statistical analysis was performed to identify predictors of ESKD and mortality.
Results
The mean age of the cohort was 49.6 years, with a male predominance (51.5%). Common clinical manifestations included hemoptysis (45.5%), hypertension (57.6%), and anuria (57.6%). MPO-ANCA positivity was observed in 39.4% of patients, while PR3-ANCA and anti-GBM positivity were present in 6.1% and 9.1%, respectively. Renal biopsy revealed crescentic glomerulonephritis in 69.8% of cases, with Type III (pauci-immune) being the most frequent.
Patients who progressed to ESKD had significantly higher baseline creatinine levels (143 vs. 75 mg/L, P = 0.011) and a higher incidence of anuria (90% vs. 50%, P = 0.004). The overall mortality rate was 39.4%, with non-survivors showing trends toward lower hemoglobin, higher CRP, and hypoalbuminemia, although these differences were not statistically significant.
Conclusion
PRS remains a highly fatal condition with a substantial risk of ESKD despite aggressive immunosuppressive therapy. Elevated baseline creatinine and anuria were strong predictors of poor renal outcomes. Early recognition and individualized treatment strategies may improve survival and renal prognosis. Future research should focus on optimizing therapeutic approaches to reduce morbidity and mortality in PRS patients.

title: #2287 Efficacy of Rituximab-based regimen in the treatment of obese patients with membranous nephropathy
authors: Chenhao Yang; Yanan Liu; Haozhang Yu; Jie MA; Cai Yue; Wenling Ye; Ke Zheng; Gang Chen; Chao Li; Hang Li; Peng Xia; Yan Qin
abstract:
Background and Aims
Rituximab (RTX) is a first-line treatment for Idiopathic Membranous Nephropathy (IMN). Previous studies have demonstrated that obesity may exacerbate proteinuria levels in IMN patients. The objective of this study is to investigate the impact of obesity on IMN patients treated with RTX.
Method
This single-center retrospective cohort study enrolled patients with IMN who received at least 1 dose of RTX treatment at Peking Union Medical College Hospital between Dec. 2017 and Dec. 2023. The diagnosis of IMN was confirmed by renal biopsy or the presence of serum anti-PLA2R antibodies. Other inclusion criteria included: (i) nephrotic range proteinuria (urinary protein ≥3.5 g/day); (ii) Patients with Body Mass Index (BMI) ≥28 kg/m2. Non-obese IMN patients treated with RTX-based regimen were selected as control group. The demographic data, lab results, medications and treatment responses were collected. Treatment responses were defined as complete remission (CR, urinary protein < 0.3 g/day and normal serum albumin level), partial remission (PR, urinary protein decreased by 50% or more and serum albumin was at least 30 g/L), and non-remission (NR, failure to meet the criteria for CR or PR). The effect of obesity and covariates was analyzed by logistic regression analysis.
Results
A total of 283 cases were enrolled in this study, and 89 of them were obese (mean BMI = 31.40 ± 1.67kg/m2). In terms of baseline data, the obese were younger (mean age was 45.9 ± 14.2 years vs. 55.6 ± 13.4 years, P < 0.001), with higher baseline proteinuria level (10.11 ± 5.58 g/d vs. 7.48 ± 3.49 g/d, P < 0.001) , higher baseline CD19(+) B-cell counts (256.0 (IQR 158.0, 382.0)/μL vs.198.0 (IQR 106.3, 345.8)/μL, P = 0.016), and less of them received sole RTX treatment (22 (24.72%) vs. 77 (39.69%), P = 0.014, χ² = 6.01), while they were comparable in gender ratio (male 69.66% vs. 67.01%, χ² = 0.20, P = 0.657), serum albumin levels (26.19 ± 7.78 g/L vs. 25.42 ± 5.02 g/L, P = 0.317) , anti-PLA2R antibody levels (84.70 (IQR 37.85, 224.5) U/L vs. 94.00(IQR 35.35, 243.25) U/L, P = 0.890; 36 patients (12.72%) with negative anti-PLA2R antibody), and serum creatinine levels (96.77 ± 46.72μmol/L vs. 97.26 ± 49.74 μmol/L, P = 0.938). During the follow-up, 54 of 283 patients were lost, of whom 15 (27.78%) were obese. In the remaining patients, cumulative dose of RTX (1.92 ± 0.88 g vs 1.86 ± 0.73 g, P = 0.668) and the negative conversion rate of anti-PLA2R (65.8% vs. 58.8%, P = 0.606) were comparable between the two. Ten obese patients (13.51%) vs. 31 non-obese patients (20.81%) achieved CR, and 44 (59.46%) vs. 73 (48.99%) achieved PR. It was comparable in the CR rate (P = 0.186, χ² = 1.75) and overall remission rate (CR and PR) (P = 0.623, χ² = 0.24) and time to achieve CR (8.2 ± 3.8 vs. 8.5 ± 3.1 months, P = 0.83) or PR(6.8 ± 3.2 vs. 6.5 ± 3.4 months, P = 0.675. Univariate logistic regression analysis revealed that the female (P = 0.003, OR = 0.35 [0.18–0.69]), lower baseline proteinuria level (P = 0.033, OR = 0.89 [0.81–0.99] and higher CD19(+) B-cell counts (P = 0.004, OR = 1.01 [1.01–1.01]) were significantly associated with achieving CR. Obesity was not significantly associated with the overall remission rate (P = 0.623) nor CR (P = 0.189).
Conclusion
Obese patients with IMN exhibited a higher baseline proteinuria level. After RTX-based therapy, about 70% of patients achieved remission. Obesity was not significantly associated with remission.

Non-obese IMN patients treated with RTX-based regimen were selected as control group. The demographic data, lab results, medications and treatment responses were collected.
