Obese patients with IMN exhibited a higher baseline proteinuria level. After RTX-based therapy, about 70% of patients achieved remission. Obesity was not significantly associated with remission.

title: #2808 A mechanistic biopsy study of the effect of iptacopan on immunopathology in patients with IgA nephropathy (IgAN)
authors: Dana Rizk; Bart Maes; Hong Zhang; Matthias Kretzler; Frank Eitner; Clint Abner; Marie-Anne Valentin; Vipin N; Maria Fernanda Di Tata; Jonathan Barratt
abstract:
Background and Aims
Overactivation of the complement system via the alternative pathway (AP) is a key driver of immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) pathophysiology. This mechanistic study aims to evaluate the effects of iptacopan, a selective oral complement factor B inhibitor, on the underlying immunopathology in patients with IgAN.
Method
This Phase IIa multicenter, single-arm, open-label, repeat-biopsy study will enroll up to 20 adult patients with biopsy-proven IgAN, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m2, proteinuria ≥0.8 g/g or 1 g/day, and receiving a maximally tolerated and/or stable dose of supportive care treatment (angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker and sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors) for ≥90 days before baseline (Fig. 1). Patients will receive iptacopan 200 mg bid for 9 months, with kidney biopsies at baseline and study end. The primary objective is to quantify changes in mesangial complement 3c (C3c) and its C3c-containing fragment deposition from baseline to 9 months. The secondary objectives are to describe the histopathological changes after iptacopan treatment, changes in CD68+ cells and immunoglobulins from baseline at 9 months. The exploratory objectives include evaluating the histopathological changes in complement biomarkers after iptacopan treatment, changes in the MEST-C scores from baseline at 9 months; describing changes in urine protein–creatinine ratio (UPCR; log-transformed ratio to baseline of UPCR), hematuria (change from baseline in dipstick and red blood cell per high power field [RBC/HPF] at 9 months), and eGFR (change from baseline at 9 months); and exploring the correlation of histopathological changes with UPCR and eGFR changes.
Results
Conclusion
This study will explore the impact of iptacopan on IgAN immunopathology by assessing glomerular complement activation together with renal histopathology, kidney function, and key biomarkers. The findings will enhance understanding of iptacopan's mechanistic effects on IgAN and potential kidney protective benefits.

title: #2873 Correlation of GBP2 expression with histopathological and clinical findings in prevalent glomerulopathies
authors: Zeynep Nur Karaca; Ganime Coban; Ömer Celal Elçioğlu; Meltem Gursu; Rumeyza Kazancioglu
abstract:
Background and Aims
The most commonly observed glomerulopathy types include IgA Nephropathy (IGAN), Membranous Glomerulonephritis (MGN), Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), and Diabetic Nephropathy (DN). Diabetes and glomerulonephrities are among the primary reasons for the need for renal replacement therapies. Although the pathogenesis of glomerulopathies is known to be related to the immune system, it has not yet been fully elucidated. Research has shown that in the pathogenesis of Diabetic Nephropathy, the protein Guanylate Binding Protein 2 (GBP2), released from M1 macrophages accumulating in the glomerular and tubulointerstitial areas, inhibits the NOTCH-1 signaling pathway, leading to macrophage accumulation in the kidneys. In Lupus Nephritis, it has been demonstrated that GBP2 protein secretion in the glomeruli and tubulointerstitial areas is increased compared to normal kidneys, and GBP2 plays a role in the interferon signaling pathway. The aim of this study is to understand the effect of GBP2 expression on the histopathological and clinical prognosis of patients with the most common glomerulopathies, whose pathogenesisis still not fully understood.
Method
The study included 150 kidney biopsy cases (71 males, 81 females) diagnosed with IGAN (46), MGN (34), FSGS (42), and DN (30) at Bezmialem Vakıf University Hospital (2014–2023). Sections of 4 microns in thickness were obtained from paraffin-embedded blocks fixed in 10% buffered formaldehyde, containing sufficient tissue for hematoxylin eosin staining. The appropriate titer (1:25) for the GBP2 antibody was determined, and a 3,3-diaminobenzidine (DAB) detection kit was used to cover the tissues with a ready film. Immune cells stained with GBP2 were counted in three high-power fields with the most intense staining. H score was calculated by using chronicity (%) x intensity (1–3) (Fig. 1). Data were analyzed for correlations between GBP2 expression and histopathological markers (glomerulosclerosis, tubular atrophy, fibrosis, immune complex deposition), clinical parameters (proteinuria response, hematuria, creatinine doubling time, GFR, blood pressure), comorbidities (Hypertension, Congestive Heart Failure, Type II Diabetes, Ischemic Heart Disease), demographics (sex, age, BMI, smoking). Statistical analyses utilized Pearson Correlation and Kruskal-Wallis tests.
Results
Over a mean follow-up of 26.1 months, the mean immune cell count was 4 in DN, 2 in IGAN, and 1 in MGN and FSGS, with an overall mean of 1.717. The mean H score was highest in DN (8.9), followed by IGAN (6.4), MGN (3.9), and FSGS (3.1), with an overall mean of 5. The number of immune cells and H score were found to be significantly different among the four groups (P = 0.0017; P = 0.0026) (Graphic 1). The correlation between H Score and systolic blood pressure is found positively correlated (r = 0.226, P = 0.006). H Score and global sclerosis showed a significant positive correlation (r = 0.191, P = 0.019). A negative correlation is found between H Score, immune cell count and follow-up duration (r = −0.175, P = 0.033; r = −0.168, P = 0.040). Positive correlation was found between immune cell count and hematuria (r = 0.188, P = 0.021). In patients with DN group, H Score and creatinine doubling time exhibited a strong negative correlation (r = −0.745, P = 0.034). Among MGN group, immune cell count and hypertension showed a significant positive correlation (r = 0.428, P = 0.012). Immune cells count or H score showed no significant difference among the proteinuria response (P = 0.9).
Conclusion
GBP2 expression varies across glomerulopathies. GBP2 expression was found to be positively correlated with hematuria, systolic blood pressure, and global sclerosis. Additionally, GBP2 expression showed a negative correlation with follow-up duration. In Diabetic Nephropathy, GBP2 expression may have a shortening effect on the creatinine doubling time. GBP2 expression is found not significantly influencer on proteinuria response. Further studies are needed to elucidate GBP2's role in glomerulopathy pathogenesis and prognosis.

title: #1500 Clinical, histological characteristics, and evolution of fibrillary glomerulonephritis in a Spanish Cohort
authors: Candela Moliz Cordon; Lara Perea-Ortega; Pedro Ruiz-Esteban; Remedios Toledo Rojas; Myriam León; Verónica López
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fibrillary glomerulopathy is a rare glomerulonephritis defined by the presence of medium-sized fibrils (15–20 nm), randomly arranged and usually Congo red negative. Its diagnosis requires the use of electron microscopy. It has been associated with multiple secondary causes, although in most cases, no association with another disease is found. To date, several series have shown the characteristics and progression of this disease. Our purpose is, following the work of other research groups, to describe the clinical and histological characteristics, as well as the progression of fibrillary glomerulopathy in a cohort of patients in Spain.
Method
A retrospective, single-center study describing the clinical, histological characteristics, progression, and response to treatment of fibrillary glomerulopathy in the province of Málaga between 2007 and 2023.
Results
21 patients were diagnosed with fibrillary glomerulopathy through electron microscopy. Table 1 summarizes the baseline characteristics. The most common presentation was nephrotic syndrome (14, 66%). 10 (47%) patients had microhematuria at the time of diagnosis. Table 2 shows the values for serum creatinine, glomerular filtration rate, and protein/creatinine ratio at diagnosis and at the end of follow-up. No differences were found when comparing these parameters. In 4 patients, coexisting causes were identified (1 monoclonal gammopathy, 1 hepatitis C virus, 1 HIV, and 1 Sjögren's syndrome). 3 patients tested positive for DNAJB9 in the renal biopsy. Regarding histological characteristics, the most observed histological pattern was mesangial expansion (11, 55%), followed by the membranoproliferative pattern (6, 30%). 18 (94%) patients had low C3 levels in the biopsy, and the most identified light chain was lambda.
14 (66%) patients received only antiproteinuric (supportive) treatment, and 6 (28%) patients additionally received immunosuppressive (IS) treatment. All but one in the group that received IS treatment progressed to end-stage renal disease (ESRD), compared to 9 in the supportive group, without showing statistically significant differences (P = 0.3). The median time to the need for renal replacement therapy was 2 ± 3.75 years. After 5 years of follow-up, almost 70% had lost renal function. 8 (38%) patients underwent kidney transplantation. Any of them have showed recurrence of the disease.
Conclusion
In our court the use of immunosuppression is comparable to supportive treatment in terms of renal response. Transplanted patients have not shown recurrence of the disease.

title: #1933 Clinico-pathologic classification of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis to inform on treatment and prognosis
authors: Jennifer Horwitz; Ayub Akbari; David Massicotte-Azarniouch
abstract:
Background and Aims
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is classified into primary (idiopathic, immune-mediated), secondary (maladaptive, medication-induced or viral-associated), and genetic forms, each differing in disease progression and treatment responses. Despite advancements, misclassification of subtypes remains common due to limited access to genetic testing and lack of definitive biomarkers for primary FSGS. We aimed to determine whether serum albumin, degree of proteinuria, and podocyte foot process effacement (FPE) could be used to improve subtype classification and predict response to immunosuppressive treatments.
Method
This retrospective, observational cohort study included adult patients with biopsy-proven FSGS at The Ottawa Hospital between 2010 and 2023. Participants were classified into 3 subtypes of FSGS based on clinical and histologic criteria: presumed primary FSGS (serum albumin <35 g/L and proteinuria >3.5 g/day at time of biopsy, and diffuse FPE [>80%] on electron microscopy (EM)), presumed secondary FSGS (serum albumin ≥35 g/L and no diffuse FPE on EM, regardless of the level of proteinuria), and uncategorized FSGS (cases not meeting either criterion). Outcomes included achievement of complete remission (CR) (proteinuria <0.3 g/day), partial remission (PR) (proteinuria <3.5 g/day and > 50% reduction from baseline), progression to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) (requiring dialysis for ≥12 weeks or initiation of kidney transplant evaluation), death, and change in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Logistic regression was performed to examine the association of FSGS category with outcomes, using the presumed secondary FSGS subtype as the reference group, and adjusting for age, sex, and baseline serum creatinine at the time of biopsy. Linear mixed models were performed to examine eGFR throughout follow-up, by FSGS category.
Results
187 patients were included with a mean age of 53.8 ± 15.6 years, mean serum creatinine of 167.9 ± 124 μmol/L, and mean urine albumin to creatinine ratio (ACR) of 370.9 ± 431 mg/g at time of kidney biopsy. 54 patients were categorized as having presumed primary FSGS, 72 as presumed secondary, and 61 patients were uncategorized. In the presumed primary FSGS group, 29.6% (aOR = 2.67, reference group Presumed Secondary FSGS; 95% CI: 1.07, 6.63) of patients achieved CR, compared to 15.3% and 9.8% in the presumed secondary and uncategorized FGSG groups, respectively. PR was achieved by 40.7% in the presumed primary FSGS group (aOR = 0.52, reference group Presumed Secondary FSGS; 95% CI: 0.24, 1.10), 58.3% in the presumed secondary and 60.7% in the uncategorized FSGS groups. Those in the presumed primary group more frequently received immunosuppressive treatment in the first 6 months post-biopsy (42.6%, compared to 1.4% in presumed secondary and 16.4% in the uncategorized groups) and had an early improvement in mean eGFR relative to the other groups based on a linear mixed model adjusted for baseline age and eGFR (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
In patients with biopsy-proven FSGS, disease subtype classification based on serum albumin, level of proteinuria, and degree of FPE at the time of diagnosis may help identify patients with an underlying immune-mediated disease who could respond to immunosuppressive therapy, in terms of achieving remission and potentially improving kidney function. These simple, readily available biomarkers may be useful when deciding on the optimal therapeutic approach for patients.

title: #2799 Predicting outcomes in lupus nephritis: the role of histological and immunocytochemical findings
authors: Elena Gutierrez; Isabel Hernandez; Julio Colina; Marina Alonso; María Galindo; Enrique Morales
abstract:
Background and Aims
Lupus nephritis (LN) is one of the most frequent and severe manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), affecting 40-65% of SLE patients and resulting in end-stage renal disease (ESRD) in 10%–20% of them. Clinical and histological prognostic factors such as race, chronicity index or tubulointerstitial damage have already been described, but little is still known about the prognostic value of immunocytochemical (ICC) data from renal biopsies.
Objectives
To identify demographic, clinical, histological and immunocytochemical factors which can help to predict the prognosis of LN patients. To build a predictive model based on these factors for estimating disease outcome in a cohort of LN patients.
Method
Retrospective study including patients diagnosed of LN in a tertiary clinic between January 2014 and May 2024, confirmed by renal biopsy. Data was recorded regarding clinical and laboratory variables as well as information from renal biopsies that included histology, indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) and immunohistochemistry (IHC).
A univariate logistic regression analysis was first carried out to preselect possible predictive variables, selecting those which were considered clinically relevant or had a determination of p-value <0.30. These were included in a multivariate logistic regression analysis to build different prognostic models, a first model with clinical variables and a second one with data from renal biopsies. The best predictive model was chosen based on criteria such as goodness-of-fit tests and its discriminatory power. A local Ethics Committee approved the execution of this project.
Results
From an initial sample of 55 patients, 38 fulfilled criteria to be included in our study. 84.2% were female with a mean age of 39.5 ± 14.4 years at onset of LN and a mean of 4.57 ± 2.81 years of follow-up during the study. 94.7% of patients had extrarenal SLE manifestations, being articular involvement the most frequent (79.0%), while the most common types of renal disease were proliferative forms (81.6%) with mean baseline values of proteinuria of 2.6 ± 3.3 g/24 h. Complete renal response was achieved by 47.4% of patients.
The multivariate analysis allowed us to select the best predictive models for poor outcome in our cohort. The clinical model included as statistically significant variables age at onset, baseline eGFR and quantification of hematuria, while the model based on information from renal biopsies related the presence of interstitial inflammation and CD68+ macrophages with worse outcomes (Table 1). Both of these models presented adequate discriminatory power with values of AUC >0.8 as well as correct classification rates over 80%.
Conclusion
This study has aimed to develop a prognostic index based on clinical variables and data obtained from renal biopsies of LN patients, which could be useful in clinical practice to help predict which patients will have a worse disease outcome and to adjust therapeutic regimens and management accordingly. Other than clinical and histological variables, the inclusion of ICC characteristics from renal biopsies, such as CD68+ macrophage infiltration, could play a role in predicting renal prognosis in LN.

This study has aimed to develop a prognostic index based on clinical variables and data obtained from renal biopsies of LN patients, which could be useful in clinical practice to help predict which patients will have a worse disease outcome and to adjust therapeutic regimens and management accordingly. title: #3092 Are the hematological parameters of inflammation predictors of IgA nephropathy in adults with chronic nephritic syndrome?

abstract:

title: #3288 Building CRESCENDO—a global registry of crescentic glomerulonephritis
authors: Vanja Ivkovic; Andreas Kronbichler; Annette Bruchfeld
abstract:
Background and Aims
Crescent formation is a non-specific reaction to severe glomerular injury, derived from parietal epithelial cells of the Bowman's capsule. Patients with cellular crescents on kidney histology, especially over 50%, often present with rapidly-progressive glomerulonephritis (GN) and have high risk of progression to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). There is significant variability in clinical characteristics, histology and outcomes between different forms of crescentic GN and a paucity of evidence on optimal therapy. The aim of CRESCENDO is to establish a global registry of crescentic GN integrating data on clinical characteristics, histology and outcomes, eventually evaluating treatment modalities to manage crescentic GN. Furthermore, we plan to study patients with a lower proportion of crescents and different crescent types (cellular, fibrocellular and fibrous) and the impact thereof on kidney prognosis.
Method
CRESCENDO is a project of the European Renal Association Immunonephrology Working Group (ERA-IWG). We plan to enroll 2 000 patients with GN and crescents on histology. Both prospective and retrospective patients with at least 5 years of follow-up will be enrolled. Patients with 5% or more crescents will be included. Exclusion criteria include kidney transplant recipients, patients with missing data or having less than 8 glomeruli on histology, cancer at the time of diagnosis, those already undergoing kidney replacement therapy for ESKD at diagnosis (except for acute kidney injury) and pregnant women will be excluded. We will leverage REDCap, a secure web application for managing databases, and carefully constructed electronic case report forms (eCRF) to obtain high-quality, highly granular data from participating centers. Data on demographic, socio-economic and anthropometric data, clinical characteristics including medical history and data on diagnosis of GN, blood biochemistry and serology, urinalysis, kidney histology, complications and outcomes will be collected. Kidney histology will be systematically assessed using a comprehensive Glomerulonephritis Scoring Form. This will allow systematic collection of histopathology, grading lesion on a scale ranging from 0 to 4, including crescents, fibrosis, glomerulosclerosis, inflammation, necrosis, vascular lesions, etc. Centers will have an option to contribute high-resolution images of histology which will be processed using machine learning approaches. Detailed data on therapy (immunosuppressive and non-immunosuppressive), including on dose and therapy change, will be collected as the registry will be used to design studies based on a target trial emulation approach which will test the efficacy of different therapies across the spectrum of crescentic GN. Studied outcomes will include death from any cause, cardiovascular mortality, progression to ESKD, recovery from dialysis, severe infections and malignancy.
Results
We are currently recruiting interested high-volume excellence centers and hope to have first preliminary results in 2027.
Conclusion
CRESCENDO is the first registry to systematically study the impact of crescents on the prognosis in the full spectrum of crescentic GN and beyond. Leveraging highly granular data, artificial intelligence and a target trial emulation approach we hope to improve diagnostic steps and prognosis of crescentic GN.

title: #3549 Importance of renal biopsy for the early diagnosis and treatment of primary amyloidosis
authors: Gilda Carreño Cornejo; Gabriel Ledesma Sánchez; Verónica Ruth Mercado Valdivia; Raquel Diaz Mancebo; Yesika María Amezquita Orjuela; Sílvia Caldés Ruisánchez; Yolanda Hernández Hernández; Ángel Gallegos Villalobos; Rocío Echarri Carrillo; Antonio Cirugeda García
abstract:
Background and Aims
Primary amyloidosis (AL) is a rare disease. It is caused by the incorrect folding and extracellular deposition of circulating proteins, resulting in dysfunction of the organs where they are deposited. Renal involvement in AL occurs in approximately 70% of cases.
Objectives
To demonstrate the importance of renal biopsy in the early diagnosis and treatment of amyloidosis with renal involvement, in comparison to other diagnostic procedures.
Method
The medical records of all patients who underwent renal biopsy due to nephrotic syndrome at Infanta Sofía Hospital, from May 2008 to March 31, 2024, were reviewed. The study included those patients who were diagnosed with amyloidosis through this intervention. Data was collected on the date of the renal biopsy, as well as other diagnostic methods such as bone marrow biopsy and subcutaneous fat biopsy, along with the results of these procedures.
Results
The sample consisted of 11 patients with renal amyloidosis. Five (45.4%) had secondary amyloidosis, and six (56.5%) had primary amyloidosis. The average age of the patients was 64 years, with 5 men and 6 women. Five (83.3%) of the patients with AL had Bence Jones proteinuria due to Lambda light chains. Amyloidosis AL was diagnosed in the bone marrow biopsy of only one patient, and no deposits were observed in the subcutaneous fat biopsy. In 4 (66%) of the patients, the renal biopsy was performed before other diagnostic tests. No patient experienced complications related to the renal biopsy, and all biopsies were diagnostic.
Conclusion
The results of our study are consistent with previous reports, showing that renal biopsy provides good diagnostic performance, even better than bone marrow and subcutaneous fat biopsies. Demonstrating AL deposition in renal tissue guided the treatment of patients who had been labeled with monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance.
Directly managing renal biopsies without having to go through a referral process allows patients to be diagnosed in a timely manner, even before undergoing bone marrow biopsy and other complementary tests (subcutaneous fat biopsy, body CT scan).

title: #3625 Navigating a diagnostic quandary of ANCA-associated vasculitis and Sweet's syndrome a case report
authors: Ajith Kurien; Hafiz Jilane; Ahmed Elshahawy; Milton Das; Fateh Chattah
abstract:
Introduction
Sweet syndrome (SS), known as Acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis is an uncommon condition. These dermatoses are often associated with systemic inflammatory disease and generally have a predilection in middle-aged women; however, the elderly may also be affected. It is characterised by an abrupt onset of painful skin lesions associated with variable systemic symptoms such as fever and elevated inflammatory markers. These skin lesions can persist for days and have a wide range of appearances, ranging from blisters or papules to ulcers. Specific treatment generally results in rapid improvement of symptoms within a few days, commonly without scarring.
We describe a diagnostic dilemma in a patient with MPO-positive ANCA-associated vasculitis, presenting with clinical signs that closely mirrored Sweet's Syndrome.
History
A 71-year-old man who was recently diagnosed with MPO+Ve AAV with renal involvement for 3 months, presented to ED with fever and new skin lesions for 5–6 days. He was already on immunosuppression with Mycophenolate mofetil and a tapering dose of steroids. His baseline renal function was reasonable with an eGFR 45. He has an extensive past medical history that includes OSA, T2DM and Prostate cancer that was cured.
On examination, there were discrete tender blisters across his upper chest, back and sides along with a few pockets of papulopustular lesions on his upper thighs and right lower leg.
Day 1
Lab results revealed leucocytosis 14.8 × 103/ul with 77% neutrophils, CRP 68 mg/L and ESR 65 mm/H. The MPO-ANCA titres were downtrending at 17 IU/ml (70 IU at diagnosis). Procalcitonin levels were low (0.10 ng/ml) and ruled out bacterial infection. At certain areas, few lesions formed larger confluent ones. Dermatology team conducted 3 punch biopsies from 3 different sites for analysis.
Meanwhile, the MMF was stopped at admission as it was suspected to be drug induced/active infection(pending lab confirmation) and steroids were resumed at a higher dose. Skin antibodies were negative for Bullous pemphigoid and Pemphigus vulgaris. The skin biopsy results revealed focal epidermal degeneration, with subepidermal vesiculation. A mixed subcorneal inflammatory infiltrate composed of neutrophils and other polymorphonuclear cells along with a tightly cuffed superficial and deep perivascular inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis were seen. Immunofluorescence studies showed subtle accentuation of the basement membrane zone, but was otherwise unremarkable. In conclusion, a report compatible with vasculitis was suggested based on clinical context, although histology was not typically suggestive
The skin lesions began to improve significantly with the steroids and a diagnosis of atypical SS was considered. Towards the end of the admission, there was secondary skin infection that needed a short course of antibiotics.
Discussion
There are different histological types of SS described in literature : subcutaneous, eosinophilic, histocytoid and lymphocytic.
The Von den Driesch criteria helps in the diagnosis of SS. The major crteria include abrupt onset of painful skin lesions along with histologic evidence of dense neutrophilic infiltrates without evidence of vasculitis. The minor criteria include fever, raised inflammatory markers (ESR,CRP) with neutrophilic leucocytosis along with an excellent response to treatment with systemic corticosteroids or potassium iodide. The criteria mandates 2/2 major criteria and 2/4 minor criteria to qualify for the SS diagnosis.
Historically, the presence of vasculitis exclude classical SS. However, several newer reports have challenged this. There are emerging reports of AAVs associated with SS in small but promising numbers. Distinctive presentations, with several meeting the clinical criteria for SS have at times had evidence of vasculitis in biopsy samples. Certain common pathophysiological mechanisms such as neutrophil dysregulation could explain a possible overlap. Further clinical research and likely a revision of the criteria may be required to delineate between these two conditions.

title: #2011 Data from the single largest native kidney biopsy center in Croatia (1996–2023)
authors: Ivica Horvatić; Danica Galešić Ljubanović; Petar Šenjug; Dino Kasumović; Nikola Zagorec; Ivana Matešić Abramović; Patricia Kacinari; Matija Crnogorac; Antonela Šarac; Luka Toric; Miroslav Tisljar; Kresimir Galesic
abstract:
Background and Aims
Epidemiologic data on biopsy-proven renal disease are of utmost importance for determining true incidence and prevalence of those relatively rare diseases. Our hospital native kidney biopsy database contains data on adult patients who had biopsy performed in our center from the year 1996 and is the largest in Croatia. The aim of this report was to review patients’ clinical and histological data from 1996 till the end of 2023.
Method
Demographic (age, gender) and clinical/laboratory (hypertension, eGFR according to CKD-EPI 2009 equation, urine sediment, 24-hours proteinuria) data were analyzed as well as indications for kidney biopsy and histological diagnoses. The indications were classified into: asymptomatic proteinuria and/or hematuria, nephrotic syndrome, acute or rapidly progressive nephritic syndrome and chronic nephritic syndrome (defined by KDIGO guidelines). Indications that didn't fit the criteria for these syndromes were classified as other. Every kidney biopsy was analyzed by light and immunofluorescent microscopy, while electron microscopy was performed in the majority of the patients.
Results
After exclusion of 119 patients with repeated kidney biopsy (4.94%), there were 2287 patients for analysis. Median age at biopsy was 50 years (interquartile range, IQR 38–63), the majority of patients were men (57.8%), and had hypertension (69.8%). Median eGFR was 54.7 ml/min/1.73 m2 (IQR 25.9–85.2), and median 24-hours proteinuria was 2.3 g (IQR 0.7–6.0). The most common indication for biopsy was nephrotic syndrome (34.7%), followed by asymptomatic proteinuria and/or hematuria (30.5%). The most common diagnoses overall were: IgA nephropathy (IgAN, 19.2%), followed by focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS, 14.9%) and membranous nephropathy (MN, 8.4%). The diagnostic category of FSGS included primary forms as well as secondary forms where it was the only histological finding. The most common secondary forms of kidney diseases were: diabetic nephropathy (5.7% overall), lupus nephritis (5.6%) and kidney diseases related to monoclonal gammopathies (4.1%). Compared to women, men had more often hypertension (73.5 vs. 64.7%, P < 0.001), higher 24-hour proteinuria (median 2.8 vs. 1.8 g, P < 0.001), and lower eGFR (median 49.94 vs. 60.85 ml/min/1.73 m2, P < 0.001). The most common indication for biopsy in men was nephrotic syndrome (36.3%), while in women it was asymptomatic proteinuria and/or hematuria (38.1%). The most common diagnoses in men were: IgAN, FSGS and MN (24.5, 14.9 and 9.2% respectively), and in women: FSGS, Alport spectrum disorders (including thin basement membrane nephropathy and Alport syndrome) and IgAN (13.9, 12.6 and 11.9% respectively). The most common diagnosis among patients with asymptomatic proteinuria and/or hematuria were IgAN and Alport spectrum disorders (26.1 and 20.8% respectively), among patients with acute/rapidly progressive nephritic syndrome the most common were ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis (GN) and IgAN (38.4 and 20.1% respectively) and among patients with nephrotic syndrome, MN and FSGS (21.0, 18.1% respectively). There were 468 older patients (age ≥ 65 years) in the database. They had more often hypertension (81.0 vs. 66.9%, P < 0.001), lower EGFR (median 27.52 vs. 62.63 ml/min/1.73 m2, P < 0.001) and higher 24-h proteinuria (median 3.68 vs. 2.06 g, P < 0.001). The most common indication for biopsy in this group was nephrotic syndrome, and the most common diagnoses were: ANCA-associated GN and MN (12.8 and 12.0% respectively).
Conclusion
The presented data should serve as a source for nephrologists and health care providers to stimulate new analysis and investigations and to improve prevention and treatment of biopsy-proven kidney diseases in Croatia and Europe through comparison with data from other registers. The data from the year 2019 onwards are also included into the Croatian national register of native kidney biopsies.

authors: Eva Baier; Alexander Lukasiewicz; Samy Hakroush; Ingmar Kluge; Björn Tampe
abstract:
Background and Aims
Steroid-sparing regimen are key to improved management of the potentially life-threatening autoimmune conditions ANCA-associated renal vasculitides (AArV). However, treatment reality is hallmarked by undeniable steroid dependency necessitating indulgent weighting of steroid dosing and tapering due to steroid's toxicities and sequelae. Though outcome guidance heavily depends on renal histopathology, to date, impacting factors predicting steroid demand remain elusive.
Therefore, we aimed to identify histopathological denominators of an increased steroid demand during the initial hospitalization phase in patients with AArV.
Method
A retrospective single-center study enrolling all cases of biopsy-affirmed AArV within the observational period of 2015 until 2021 was performed. After ethics approval, medical records were utilized to assess patient characteristics (age, sex, comorbidities, medication), date of admission and discharge from hospital, laboratory serum parameters at baseline (creatinine, eGFR, BUN, potassium, white blood cells, platelets, C-reactive protein, C3/C4 levels), and conducted treatment measures to induce remission (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, plasma exchange). Cumulative prednisolone demand (CPD) and ICU scores were calculated (APACHE II, SAPS II, SAPS III). Blinded histopathological analysis was independently performed by two nephropathologists evaluating the extent of tubulointerstitial immune cell infiltration, especially plasma cell (PC) richness (PC+) vs. PC scarcity (PC-). ROC curve analysis and maximized Youden index (MYI) calculation was conducted. Survival curve analyses were performed by means of Kaplan-Meier method and log rank testing. The event was defined as achieving a CPD level above the total cohort median of 2395 mg, exitus was censored.
Results
The total cohort (TC) contained n = 50 patients (22/50 being female) with a median age of 63 y (53–74), an in-hospital stay of 14 d (7–26) and a mean CPD of 2582 ± 1683 mg. CPD independently correlated with APACHE II score (β = 0.51, P < 0.001) implying the state of critical illness to be crucial for CPD elevation. We then identified the cut-off of 15.5 points (APACHE II) by means of MYI calculation in line with ROC curve analysis (AUC: 0.8, 95% CI: 0.7–0.9, P = 0.0003) (Fig. 1A), which enabled cohort subgrouping (ICU vs. non-ICU). Subgroup baseline characteristics were compared: sig. increase of CPD levels (4.5 g ± 1.1 g vs. 2.1 g ± 1.4 g, P < 0.0001) and sig. elevation of serum creatinine levels, 5.6 (4.4–7.2) mg/dL vs. 2.0 (1.1–3.6) mg/dL, characterized the ICU subgroup. CPD levels independently correlated with serum creatinine elevation (TC: β = ß.53, P = 0.019; ICU: β = 0.65, P < 0.029) (Fig. 1B) and PC infiltration (TC: β = 0.328, P = 0.03; ICU: β = 0.71, P = 0.033) (Fig. 1B), which was not observable in the non-ICU group. Finally, we performed a survival curve analysis applying the ICU-subgroup median of PC infiltration (0.3%) as a cut-off defining two groups: PC+ vs. PC−. PC infiltration of >0.3% sig. predicted increased CPD levels (logrank: P = 0.0036, HR 2.8, 95% CI 1.1–6.7) (Fig. 1C).
Conclusion
We here show that prognosis-affecting steroid demand during short-term management is determinable depending on distinct histopathological lesions and the state of critical illness, which might be implemented in future models enabling individualized outcome prediction for patients with ANCA-associated renal vasculitides.

title: #272 Sparsentan reduces glomerular dysfunction and proteinuria in a rat model of serum-factor-induced nephrotic syndrome
authors: Michael Crompton; Holly Stowell-Connolly; Jack Mills; Viktoriia Vasylchenko; Celia P Jenkinson; Bruce Hendry; Radko Komers; Hiroshi Kawachi; Matthew Butler; Gavin Welsh; Rebecca Foster; Simon Satchell
abstract:
Background and Aims
Glomerular function is dependent on the three-layer structure of the glomerular filtration barrier (GFB): glomerular endothelial cells and their surface glycocalyx, the glomerular basement membrane and podocytes. Proteinuric kidney diseases are associated with glomerular dysfunction and loss of barrier integrity. Sparsentan is a single-molecule dual endothelin type-A and angiotensin II type 1 receptor antagonist (DEARA) that has received approval in the United States and European Union for the reduction of proteinuria in adults with IgA nephropathy and is under clinical development for FSGS. Using a model of targeted podocyte injury to induce proteinuria, we sought to determine whether sparsentan could prevent the development of proteinuria, by maintaining the GFB.
Method
Female Lewis rats were given vehicle or sparsentan daily (60 mg/kg or 120 mg/kg, p.o.) from day 0, until sacrifice at day 8. At day 1, mAb 5-1-6 (rat anti-nephrin antibody) was injected (33 mg/kg, i.v.) to induce proteinuria. Ringer perfused kidneys were processed for immunofluorescence and glomeruli were isolated to directly measure albumin permeability (Ps’alb) within individually trapped glomeruli using our validated assay [1]. Urine was collected to analyse urinary albumin: creatinine ratios (uACR). Blood pressure was measured using a tail cuff method.
Results
In mAb 5-1-6 treated rats, uACR and Ps’alb (expressed as means (±SEM)) were significantly increased compared to control rats (uACR: control, 20 ± 3 mg/mmol; vehicle + mAb 5-1-6, 5,304 ± 986 mg/mmol, P < 0.0001; Ps’alb: control, 6.2 x 10−7 ± 0.2 x 10−7 cm/s; vehicle + mAb 5-1-6, 10.1 x 10−7 ± 0.4 x 10−7 cm/s, P < 0.0001). Sparsentan-treatment of mAb 5-1-6 rats resulted in a significant dose-dependent reduction in uACR and Ps’alb (uACR: sparsentan (60mg/kg) + mAb 5-1-6, 1,410 ± 424 mg/mmol, P < 0.0001; sparsentan (120 mg/kg) + mAb 5-1-6, 1,028 ± 269 mg/mmol, P < 0.0001; Ps’alb: sparsentan (60 mg/kg) + mAb 5-1-6, 8.2 x 10−7 ± 0.3 x 10−7 cm/s, P = 0.0026; sparsentan (120 mg/kg) + mAb 5-1-6, 7.7 x 10−7 ± 0.3 x 10−7 cm/s, P = 0.0002). Nephrin staining in mAb 5-1-6 rats changed from a typical linear pattern to a punctate pattern, and staining intensity was decreased—this change was prevented with sparsentan treatment. These observations were independent of changes in blood pressure and body weight.
Conclusion
We have shown that the DEARA sparsentan, reduces glomerular permeability and proteinuria in a rat model of serum factor-induced podocytopathy. These findings suggest that the action of sparsentan on the GFB could help maintain barrier integrity in podocytopathic proteinuric kidney diseases.
This work was funded by Travere Therapeutics, Inc.

title: #2317 Prospective validation of multiple deep learning model assisted diagnostic program for glomerular diseases using immunofluorescence images
authors: Peng Xia; Shilu Cao; Yu-Bing Wen; Xueyuan Zhang; Xuesong Zhao; Hao-Yuan Cui; Baolin Du; Fei Ren; Limeng Chen
abstract:
Background and Aims
The immunofluorescence (IF) tests for renal tissues are crucial in glomerular disease diagnosis. We optimized and prospectively validated our multiple deep learning model-assisted diagnostic program for glomerular diseases previously developed.
Method
In 2022, we developed an artificial intelligent-assisted immunofluorescence image diagnosis system based on a convolutional neural network (CNN), consisting of glomeruli identification (YOLOv5 algorithm), IF intensity, deposition appearance, location classifier (Swin Transformer model), and decision adjustment trained with more than 5000 slides. With the continuous algorithm optimization, it could output IgA nephropathy (IgAN), idiopathic membranous nephropathy (IMN), anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody disease (anti-GBM), membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN), post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), C3 nephritis, and manual review reminder (Fig. 1) by putting the positive IF images. In the prospective validation experiment, patients in Peking Union Medical College Hospital (PUMCH, n = 1286) included IgAN, IMN, lupus nephritis (LN), anti-GBM disease, and other glomerular diseases classified as unidentified diseases requiring further manual review, such as diabetic nephropathy, secondary MN.
Results
The accuracy of this program for diagnosing IgAN, IMN, LN, and anti-GBM was 93.2%, 94.6%, 93.9%, and 99.7%, with sensitivity of 88%, 89.6%, 72.8%, 85.7%, and specificity of 98.6%, 96.2%, 99.1%, 99.8%, respectively. The corresponding F1 scores were 0.99, 0.88, 0.95, and 0.75. For those unidentified diseases requiring manual review, the accuracy and specificity of this program were 85.1% and 87.2%, which is better than the Junior pathologists.
Conclusion
The assisted diagnostic program based on multiple deep learning networks performs well in diagnosing glomerular diseases, shedding light on the future application perspective.

title: #2810 Characterization of membranous glomerulonephritis in adults presenting with nephrotic syndrome: a 13-year observational study
authors: Joana Andrade Lopes; Rafael Figueiredo; Bernardo Faria; Ricardo Neto; João Frazão; Luís Mendonça
abstract:
Background and Aims
Membranous glomerulonephritis (MGN) is a major cause of nephrotic syndrome (NS) and nephrotic-range proteinuria. To better understand the population presenting with NS due to MGN, we analyzed our NS cohort over a 13-year period.
Method
We conducted a retrospective observational study from 2010 to 2022, including patients with inaugural nephrotic syndrome and first biopsy-confirmed MGN. Data were collected anonymously from electronic health records, covering patient demographics, comorbidities, laboratory findings at diagnosis (serum albumin, serum creatinine, 24-h proteinuria, and hematuria), pathological features, and clinical outcomes (mortality, dialysis requirement three years post-diagnosis, immunosuppressive treatments, remission/relapse rates, and yearly eGFR progression). The primary goal was to characterize adult population presenting with inaugural NS caused by MGN. Data analysis was conducted using SPSS® v28.0.1.0.
Results
48 adults with inaugural presenting nephrotic syndrome and first biopsy-proven MGN diagnosis were retrieved from the primary analysis. Thirty-two (66.7%) were classified as primary—17 (35.4%) PLA2Rab positive, 12 (25%) PLA2Rab status unknown and 3 (6.3%) PLA2Rab negative. Autoimmune disease was the most common cause of secondary MGN (14.6%), followed by neoplasia (8.3%), infection (6.3%) and drugs (4.2%). Thirty-three (68.8%) patients were males, 47 (97.1%) were Caucasian, and the median age at diagnosis was 56 years. Seven (14.6%) patients had previous CKD, 7 (14.6%) were diabetic, and 3 (6.3%) had previous neoplasia of which 1 (2.1%) was active. Median serum creatinine, serum albumin, and 24 h-proteinuria at diagnosis were 0.96 mg/dL, 23.7 g/L and 7.78 g, respectively. (Micro)hematuria was observed in 22 (45.8%) patients. The most common pathological findings were GBM thickening (median 99.8% of glomeruli), tubular necrosis (75% of biopsies), and interstitial inflammatory infiltrate (35.4% of biopsies). Regarding first line immunosuppression used, the modified Ponticelli regimen was the most common (31.3% of patients)- mainly driven by the first years of analysis, followed by the rituximab-based regimen (10.4%), corticosteroid only (10.4%) and calcineurin inhibitors (8.3%). Fifteen (31.3%) patients underwent partial remission, and 22 (45.8%) complete remission—achieved with a median of 18 months. Fifteen (31.3%) patients relapsed, with a median of 1 relapse. The rituximab- based regimen was the most frequent second-line immunosuppressant (22.9%). Three years post-diagnosis, 6 (12.5%) patients were chronically hemodialyzed, 4 died (8.3%) and, for the remaining, the median eGFR was 66 ml/min/1.73m2.
Conclusion
In our MGN-NS population, most patients were male, presented with severe hypoalbuminemia and without renal dysfunction. The overall prognosis was good. The modified Ponticelli regimen was the most common first-line induction immunosuppressive scheme, surpassed by Rituximab-based regimens in the latter years.

title: #3659 Belimumab use in patients with systemic erythematous lupus and lupus nephritis—cohort of a tertiary center
authors: José Oliveira Da Costa; Natália Marchão; Iolanda Godinho; Marta Sofia Henriques Pereira; Cristina Resina; José António Lopes; Estela Nogueira
abstract:
Background and Aims
Belimumab is a monoclonal antibody that targets and neutralizes soluble B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS—also known as BAFF), that induces B-cell proliferation and maintains survival. It has been used successfully to treat systemic erythematosus lupus (SLE) manifestation and is now currently approved to treat lupus nephritis (LN).
Method
The authors retrospectively analyzed all SLE patients with lupus nephritis that were treated with belimumab either as add-on therapy to LN standard of care or to treat extra-renal manifestations in patients with LN. We evaluated indications for belimumab treatment, improvement of extra-renal manifestations, as well as renal outcomes.
Results
We evaluated 19 patients, 84% female, 3 black African and 16 Caucasian.
Patients that started belimumab had histologically class III (n7), IV (n11) and V (n1).
All patients reported had SLE and LN, but the indication to start belimumab as add-on treatment for LN occurred in 10 patients (53%). In these patients, belimumab was added to standard of care induction LN therapy for different reasons: frequent LN relapses and risk of CKD, need of glucocorticoid (GC) sparing due to GC adverse events, extra-renal manifestations poorly controlled with standard of care therapy (arthritis, rash and fatigue, polyserositis) and persistent serological activity. The other patients also had LN but started belimumab to control extra-renal manifestation, either close to LN diagnosis, or during follow-up.
Mean and SD Scr and proteinuria at the initiation of belimumab was 0.88 ± 0.3 mg/dL [0.5–1.8] and 350 ± 500.84 mg/day [9–1525].
At 1 and 2 years of belimumab mean and SD of Scr was 0.79 ± 0.39 mg/dL vs 0.85 ± 0.5 mg/dL and proteinuria 88.9 ± 161 mg/day vs 44.2 ± 58.3 mg/day.
Regarding patients treated with belimumab for active LN, 8 and 4 patients reached one and two years of follow-up and 7/8, 3/4 achieved complete renal remission at both time end points. Additionally, there was an improvement in complement and DsDNA levels.
Extra-renal manifestations also improved in all patients except for one patient that stopped belimumab due to sinusitis and respiratory infection which was related to the need of prolonged high-dose GC for uncontrolled arthritis. Belimumab was well tolerated in all patients, except for one patient who discontinued therapy due to psychiatric secondary effects.
Conclusion
As reported in this cohort, belimumab can be used in patients with SLE and LN as add-on treatment to increase the probability of renal remission and decrease the progression to CKD, but also as an adjunctive treatment to better control extra-renal manifestations, namely arthritis, rash, serositis and fatigue, that in some patients are not well treated with standard of care therapy. Importantly, the need to reduce GC adverse related events in patients already suffering from GC complications was also an indication to use belimumab, in order to achieve faster GC discontinuation. In our cohort belimumab was well tolerated and clinical and renal response were favorable, although the number of patients and their follow-up is still short to draw significant conclusions.

title: #2400 Combination cyclophosphamide and rituximab with early glucocorticoid withdrawal for the treatment of ANCA-associated vasculitis
authors: Tania Salehi; Gavin Chapman; Tariq Farrah; Fiona Chapman; Dan Pugh; Robert Hunter; Neeraj Dhaun
abstract:
Background and Aims
Anti-neutrophil cytoplasm antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV) is a multisystem, autoimmune disorder with variable presentation and organ involvement. Glucocorticoids are the mainstay of treatment for AAV, but their use is associated with significant morbidity. Recent trials have evaluated glucocorticoid-sparing regimens for AAV, however minimal glucocorticoid dose and optimal duration of therapy remain unclear. A few data suggest that induction treatment with a combination of cyclophosphamide and rituximab in patients with AAV and kidney involvement may allow a rapid glucocorticoid taper. Here, we present long-term follow-up of a large cohort of patients with AAV who received combination cyclophosphamide and rituximab induction treatment with a rapidly reducing and withdrawing oral glucocorticoid taper.
Methods
In a tertiary referral centre with a dedicated Vasculitis Service, we identified patients with AAV treated with combination intravenous (i.v.) cyclophosphamide and i.v. rituximab induction therapy. We analysed biochemical, histological, and outcome data, including time to remission, relapse rate, and renal recovery. A secondary analysis evaluated whether outcomes differed based on cumulative glucocorticoid dose.
Results
Overall, 112 patients (67 [IQR 56–76] years; 57% male) received combination i.v. cyclophosphamide (median dose 1g) and i.v. rituximab (median dose 2g). 85% (95/112) had kidney involvement (baseline eGFR 24 [13–52] mL/min/1.73 m2; urine protein: creatinine ratio 101 [36–199] mg/mmol).
107 patients (96%) achieved treatment-induced disease remission (median time to remission 77 [64–92] days). The remaining five patients (5%) died with active vasculitis within four months of diagnosis. In those with kidney involvement, the greatest improvement in kidney function (eGFR at diagnosis versus at 12 months: 24 [13–52] mL/min/1.73 m2versus 45 [31–69] mL/min/1.73 m2, P < 0.001) was seen in those with more severe kidney disease at diagnosis (Fig. 1). 75 patients had a kidney biopsy at diagnosis, of which 19 (25%) had an interval kidney biopsy at a median time interval of 143 (117–186) days. title: #3478 Lenvatinib-associated hyaline occlusive glomerular microangiopathy
authors: Amir Daher; Danny Zorbavel; Marina Tchirkov; Yael Kenig Kozlovsky; Ofer Ben Itzhak; Suheir Assady
abstract:
Background and Aims
Immunotherapies and small molecules have transformed therapeutic protocols in modern oncology, resulting in improved quality of life and patient outcome. However, severe adverse events (SAE) may compromise the duration of administration of such treatments. Lenvatinib is an oral receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor that targets multiple proangiogenic and oncogenic pathways related to vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and fibroblast growth factor receptors, among others. Although not studied directly with lenvatinib, it is postulated that the reported SAE of proteinuria, hypertension, and rarely thrombotic microangiopathy could be related to the inhibition of VEGF/VEGF receptors signaling pathways in podocytes and/or vascular endothelial cells. Herein, we described a distinct histopathological glomerular pattern of injury, previously reported in few patients treated with bevacizumab or anti VEGFR2 antibodies, but not with lenvatinib.
Method
Case report.
Results
We present a 56-year-old male patient with a medical history of hypertension, dyslipidemia, and metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma, who was referred to our nephrology department because of uncontrolled hypertension (194/121 mmHg), acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.8 mg/dL), and nephrotic syndrome, with lower limb swelling, pulmonary edema, hypoalbuminemia (1.67 g/dL), protein to creatinine ratio 3.99 g/g and microscopic hematuria. Twenty-seven months prior to the current presentation, the patient was started on lenvatinib 18 mg/d. During oncology clinic follow-up, his blood pressure was stable on Valsartan, his serum creatinine levels were 0.8–0.9 mg/dL, and serum albumin levels remained normal until 9 months prior to current presentation. 24-h urine collections contained 151 mg, 240 mg, and 980 mg of protein prior to, 7, and 13 months after the initiation of lenvatinib, respectively. When admitted to our department, lenvatinib was stopped. Comprehensive clinical and laboratory evaluation were performed. Of note, full immunologic panel and viral serology were negative. Complement factors (C) 3 and 4, electrolytes, liver function test, c-reactive protein, and complete blood count were within normal limits.
A kidney biopsy revealed a) thickened eosinophilic glomerular basement membranes (GBM) with double-contour areas, b) glomerular capillary hyaline globuli (pseudothrombi) and subendothelial hemicrescents, which were positive for IgM (+2 to +3), C1q (+2 to +3), lambda and kappa (+2), C4d (strong +3), IgA (+2), IgG (+1 to +2 ), and fibrinogen (+1 to +2) immunostaining, and negative for C3 and CD61, c) the eosinophilic bright hemicrescents were PAS-positive, silver-negative, and red in Masson's trichrome staining, d) electron microscopy showed multilayered GBM with subendothelial fine granular electron-dense material in the dilated glomerular capillaries, with intact podocyte foot processes in one glomerulus and widespread effacement in another, e) tubular injury, and f) one artery showed myxoid intimal proliferation with narrowed lumen. These findings were summarized as hyaline occlusive glomerular microangiopathy.
Following the discontinuation of lenvatinib and adjustment of blood pressure medications, kidney function and blood pressure significantly improved, and proteinuria normalized within two months.
Conclusion
Our case exemplifies the importance of kidney needle biopsy in elucidating putative mechanisms of drug-related nephrotoxicity and proteinuria in cancer patients. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first documented case of hyaline occlusive glomerular microangiopathy associated with lenvatinib therapy. We suggest that this rare entity is reversible and could be linked to the inhibition of the VEGF-VEGFR2 pathway and endothelial injury.

title: #3615 Prediction of response to intensified immunosuppression in childhood steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome by multimodal machine learning
authors: Jan Ulrich Becker; Huy Quoc; Charlotte Gimpel; Sengül Boral; William Morello; Moin Saleem; Nicola Altini; Chandra Mohan; Hien V Nguyen; Franz Schaefer
abstract:
Background and Aims
There are no established models to predict the varied response to intensified immunosuppression in steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome. Multimodal machine learning, integrating clinical and genetic data with nephropathology imaging, holds great promise to deliver such classifiers with perfect reproducibility. Here, we present such a theranostic classifier based on a multi-centric dataset.
Method
The PodoNet cohort with n = 201 biopsies was collected from 14 European centres with large domain shifts in whole slide images. The clinical input data contained 19 parameters including mutation (yes/no) and eGFR at biopsy; the ground truth theranostic endpoint was treatment response as no remission (n = 114), partial (n = 42) and complete (n = 45), defined by serum albumin and proteinuria. We trained our proprietary multimodal MorphSet++ architecture in a weakly supervised fashion. MorphSet++ integrates the clinical data vector from a shallow network at various stages with the transformer-based deep network analysing the nephropathology imaging data. Results are given as mean after 5-fold internal cross-validation.
Results
Mean AUC was .80 for complete, .77 for partial and .81 and xx for no remission.
Mean positive predictive value was 89.72, 89.83, 89.27,
mean negative predictive value was 94.83, 93.43 and 97.59;
mean sensitivity was 84.21, 67.09, 98.47;
mean specificity was 96.77, 98.40, 83.94; mean F1 Score was 86.88, 76.81, 93.65; mean accuracy was 84.21, 67.09, 98.47; mean balanced accuracy was 90.49, 82.75, 91.21 for no, partial and complete remission, respectively.
Performance was best with both clinical data and histology as input.
Conclusion
Our MorphSet++ architecture shows promising results as a theranostic tool, predicting response to immunosuppression in SRNS. MorphSet++ allows for rapid up-scaling with additional, larger datasets for even better and more robust performance. This might lead to a re-appraisal of nephropathology in the clinical management of SRNS.

title: #1263 Cardiovascular risk in systemic lupus erythematosus with and without lupus nephritis: a cross-sectional comparative study
authors: Miguel Martínez-Belotto; Cristina Corrales-Selaya; Leyre Riancho-Zarrabeitia; Juan Carlos Ruiz; Ricardo Blanco; Gema Fernández Fresnedo; Alfonso Corrales; Luis Martin Penagos
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) have an increased cardiovascular risk (CVR) compared to the general population. Some studies have observed that a history of lupus nephritis (LN), even with preserved renal function, further increases CVR. Our objective is to compare and analyse whether there are differences in CVR in our sample of patients with SLE with and without a history of LN.
Method
A cross-sectional comparative study was conducted on 206 patients with SLE from our centre, in whom CVR was assessed using the SCORE2 and QRISK3 scores and carotid ultrasound for detecting atheromatous plaque. Patients were divided into two groups based on a history of LN, and differences were analysed using binary logistic regression with SPSS software.
Results
The main characteristics of the sample are presented in Table 1, along with results from univariate analysis and those adjusted for sex, disease duration, and renal function. No differences were found in univariate analysis for CV events or in the CVR assessment tools used. Differences were observed in hypertension (OR 2.043 [1.069–3.904], P = 0.031) and uricemia (OR 1.300 [1.044–1.617], P = 0.019) in the univariate model, with a trend toward significance in dyslipidaemia (with a protective OR for HDL 0.976 [0.954–0.997], P = 0.028); all of which were corrected after adjustment. C3 hypocomplementemia, high values of high-sensitivity CRP and ESR showed OR >1 in univariate analysis but were corrected after adjustment. Only native anti-DNA antibodies, positive at the time of the study, were significantly more frequent in patients with LN after adjustment (OR 2.463 [1.053–5.759], P = 0.038).
Conclusion
No significant differences were found in the regression model after adjusting for factors, scores, and CV risk assessment tests between SLE patients with and without a history of LN. In our sample, patients with LN were 2.4 times more likely to have positive anti-DNA antibodies.

title: #1993 Recommendations on management of adult-onset IgA vasculitis proposed by the European IgA vasculitis study group
authors: Alexandra Audemard-Verger; Giorgio Trivioli; Antoine Hankard; Jürgen Floege; Evangeline Pillebout; Noemie Jourde-Chiche; Seza Ozen; Carmela Errichiello; Alojzija Hocevar; Marija Jelusic Drazic; Louise Oni; Jonathan Barrat; Annette Bruchfeld; Miguel A González-Gay; Alfred Mahr; Thomas Neumann; Valentin Maisons; Marie Jachiet; Lisa Willcocks; Alexandre Karras; Ahmet Gul; Haner Direskeneli; Rosanna Coppo; Karuna Keat; Anette Bygum; Maxime Battistella; Sara Brolin; Allyson C Egan; Jessica Ryan; Janak de Zoysa; Cord Suenderkoetter; Ingeborg Bajema; Santos Castaneda; Benjamin Terrier; David R W Jayne; Maria Cid; Augusto Vaglio
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA vasculitis (IgAV) is a small-vessel vasculitis with predominant IgA deposits that involves the skin, the joints, the gastrointestinal tract and the kidneys, causing glomerulonephritis pathologically indistinguishable from IgA nephropathy [1]. Adults are less frequently affected than children but more often experience a relapsing/refractory course with severe kidney involvement [2]. As the treatment of this condition remains controversial, especially for adults, we have been working on developing recommendations for the management of adult-onset IgAV. Here, we report on the progress of this initiative with a focus on kidney involvement.
Method
The European IgA Vasculitis Study Group (EUGAVAS) is a multidisciplinary group of experts in the field of IgAV established in 2023. Members were initially asked to vote on key questions using a Delphi approach and questions that achieved a level of agreement ≥70% drove a systematic literature review (SLR) on Medline/Pubmed, Cochrane and Embase databases. Small working groups of 4–5 members drafted recommendation statements based on the SLR results and, where required, expert opinion. The preliminary statements were then discussed and amended by the whole group and are currently being voted on in the second Delphi round. The initiative was endorsed by the European Vasculitis Society (EUVAS).
Results
EUGAVAS consists of 38 experts, including 11 nephrologists, 10 internists/rheumatologists, four dermatologists, four pediatricians, four fellows, two pathologists, one representative IgAV patient, one vasculitis nurse, and one methodologist. Following the first Delphi round, 14 out of 16 key questions were retained. The SLR identified 335 relevant publications out of 3,784 abstracts reviewed (1,058 excluded as duplicates). The group agreed that the level of evidence available in the literature was insufficient to establish guidelines and drafted recommendation statements.
Of the 14 preliminary statements, three focus on diagnosis and classification, three on disease staging, six on treatment, including general and organ-specific principles, and two on disease assessment and patient follow-up. Four statements are specifically dedicated to kidney involvement and discuss: 1) definition of kidney involvement and role of baseline prognostic factors; 2) indications to kidney biopsy and histological classification; 3) goals of treatment and options according to severity of kidney involvement; 4) role of nephroprotective measures. Kidney involvement is also discussed in other statements on definition of response and remission, use of biologic therapies, such as rituximab, and frequency and modality of patient follow-up.
Conclusion
A set of recommendations on management of adult-onset IgAV has been developed following a standardized approach and will soon be available for communication. The result of this initiative may help clinicians, especially nephrologists, manage patients with this condition and improve their prognosis.

title: #2243 Incidence of infection and its relationship with Ig G level and B cell subset post rituximab infusion in Sussex Kidney Unit in Royal Sussex and County Hospital in Brighton
authors: Chin Lin Ng; Farid Ghalli
abstract:
Background
Rituximab, a monoclonal antibody targeting CD20 antigen on B lymphocytes leading to B cell depletion. It showed good therapeutic outcome in remission induction and maintenance of glomerular diseases. Despite its beneficial therapeutic effect, its immunosuppressive effect raised a significant concern about the increased susceptibility to infection. Rituximab cause depletion of B cell subset and disruption of immunoglobulins production. Hence understanding the relation between B cell depletion, hypogammaglobulinemia and incidence of infection is important to patient care.
Aim
To evaluate the incidence of infection in patients who received Rituximab according to current protocol adopted by Sussex Kidney Unit (SKU) and compared it with the recommendation with EULAR guidelines. At the same time to understand the relation between B cell subset, Ig G level and infection.
Method
It is a retrospective study, included patients who received rituximab from 1 January 2020 to 31 December 2023 at SKU for the management of vasculitis and glomerular diseases. Data gathered from electronic renal patient database—CV5, and electronic patient system—Panda and GP records.
Results
Total number was 99 patients, 55 male (56%) and 44 female (44%). Majority of the patient were from age group >50 years old. Total dose of rituximab delivered was 273 doses which equals 273 g. The mean dose of rituximab delivered were 2.75 g. The mean of Ig G level pre 1st dose of rituximab was 7.6 g/l. The mean of B cell subset (in %) pre 1st dose of rituximab was 12.75. Among the 273 doses rituximab given 29 doses were associated with infection (10.6%). The commonest infection was Covid-19 infection. There were 5 infections required hospital admission, other infection episodes were treated as outpatient, and no death related to those infection. The mean of Ig G level pre infection was 7.3 g/l. The mean of B cell subset (in %) pre infection was 1.17%. There were 22 patients who received rituximab infusion with pre 1st dose Ig G level <5 g/l, 3 only of them had infection.
Conclusion
Rituximab is getting popular in the treatment of various glomerular diseases. The local guidelines in SKU for rituximab infusion, had lower threshold of giving rituximab according to Ig G level (>3 g/l) compared to EULAR recommendation for rituximab use in rheumatoid arthritis, which is not recommending giving rituximab if Ig G <5 g/l, due to infection risk. From our results, we found that only 3 patients among 22 patient who had pre rituximab Ig G <5 g/l were associated with infection. Those infections were covid-19 infection and gastroenteritis. The mean Ig G level before infection for all other infection cases was 7.3 g/l. The mean B cell subset before infection for all infection related cases was 1.17%.
From our results the infection risk seemed most likely related to B cell subset level, rather than pre- infusion Ig G level. It was safe to give rituximab for patient who had pre-dose Ig G level >3g/l. Further larger study is needed to confirm the findings.

title: #2457 The clinico-pathologic characteristics of fibrillary glomerulonephritis: a Portuguese cohort
authors: Andreia Curto; Filipa Rodrigues; Carla Ferreira Nicolau; Ana Rita Pereirinha Ramos; Isabel Cristina Bettencourt de Simas de Mesquita; Afonso Valadas Da Costa Sepúlveda Santos; Rita Theias Manso; Helena Viana; Mário Ventura Góis; Cristina Rego de Freitas Mendes Jorge
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fibrillary glomerulonephritis (FGN) is a rare glomerular disease with poor renal prognosis and lacking evidence to guide therapy. The aim of this work was the characterization of the clinical-pathologic spectrum and associated outcomes of our cohort of patients diagnosed with FGN.
Method
We identified patients with FGN from two Kidney Biopsy centers, aggregating cases from 5 hospitals between January 2011 and December 2024. The biopsies were reviewed by an experienced physician in kidney pathology. The staining for DnaJ heat shock protein family member B9 (DNAJB9) was not available in both centers. Retrospective chart review was performed to obtain demographic and clinical characteristics. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of both centers.
Results
A total of 13 Caucasian patients, 46% male, with a median follow-up period of 28.2 months (IQR: 10–60) were included in the study. The median age at diagnosis was 59 years (IQR: 46–64). Eleven patients had hypertension (84.6%), and 53,8% (n = 4) had diabetes. Work up for secondary associations revealed the presence of monoclonal protein (7.6%, n = 1), autoimmune conditions (38.5%, n = 5), and solid tumor malignancy (7.6%, n = 1, colon cancer). One patient had treated hepatitis C infection (sustained negative viral load).
At presentation, the median proteinuria and creatinine levels were 4.7 g/day (IQR: 2.5–8.6) and 1.6 mg/dL (IQR: 1.27–2.8), respectively. Nephrotic-range proteinuria was observed in 54% of patients, but only 4 presented with nephrotic syndrome. All patients presented some degree of hematuria.
Regarding pathology, light microscopy showed pure mesangial (46%) followed by endocapillary hypercellularity (30.7%) as the most common patterns of injury. Two patients (15.3%) had crescents, and ten patients (77%) had positive immunofluorescence staining for IgG/C3/Kappa/Lambda. Electron microscopy showed fibrillary deposits in the mesangium, in most patients. The fibrils were randomly oriented with diameters ranging between 3 and 24 nm.

Conclusion
FGN is a rare disease with poor outcome. In our cohort, up to 38% of patients died during the follow-up. Autoimmune diseases were exceedingly common in our cohort (38.5%), when compared to other published series. Treatment strategies vary. Prospective, multicenter studies are necessary to better understand the disease pathogenesis and identify appropriate therapy.

title: #2890 Echocardiographic and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging abnormalities in patients with sustained remission of ANCA-associated vasculitis
authors: Louis Nygaard; Nils Lundgren; Ása Wraae Olsen; Signe Juul Riddersholm; Michael Bang; Per Ivarsen; Jens Brøndum Frøkjær; Tomas Zaremba; Christoffer Polcwiartek; Salome Kristensen; My Svensson; Jon Waarst Gregersen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in contemporary cohorts of patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV). During the last decade, the application of comprehensive cardiovascular screening through echocardiograms and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) has been proposed to identify patients at high risk and to potentially mitigate cardiovascular disease risk. However, the clinical application among cardiovascular asymptomatic patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) and microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) in long-term disease remission is limited and no clear directions are provided in clinical guidelines. The aim of this study was to examine if asymptomatic patients with AAV in long-term disease remission have a higher prevalence of echocardiographic and CMR abnormalities compared to age- and sex-matched controls.
Method
Using a cross-sectional study design, asymptomatic patients with GPA or MPA in long-term disease remission (Birmingham vasculitis activity score of 0) without former cardiovascular disease were included. Patients were matched 1:1 with controls on age and sex. Cardiac assessment included echocardiograms performed on a Vivid™ E95 Ultrasound System and CMR performed on a 3 Tesla GE scanner. Statistical differences between patients with AAV and matched controls were assessed using χ-square or Mann-Whitney U tests.
Results
A total of 50 AAV patients (median age 62.5 years, 56% male) and 50 matched controls (median age 64.5 years, 56% male) were included. The median AAV disease duration was 8.5 (IQR 5.1–13.4) years, and the median time in disease remission was 2.9 (IQR 2.02–7.01) years. The majority of AAV patients were Pr3 positive (80%), with 20% positive for MPO. On echocardiograms patients with AAV had a higher prevalence of diastolic dysfunction (64% vs. 32%, P = 0.01), with lower E/A ratios (0.85 vs. 1.01, P = 0.044) and lateral e’ velocities (9.0 cm/s vs. 10.0 cm/s, P = 0.040) compared to matched controls. AAV patients similarly had slight reductions in right ventricular systolic function as measured by tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) (22 mm vs. 24 mm, P = 0.002). However, no significant difference was found when categorized as a normal or reduced TAPSE (8% vs. 4%, P = 0.67). For left ventricular systolic function, patients with AAV had a normal ejection fraction (58% vs 55.5%, P = 0.61). However, early signs of subclinical left ventricular systolic dysfunction were measured through an impaired global longitudinal strain (GLS) among patients with AAV compared to matched controls (−16.4% vs. −18%, P < 0.001). On CMR, patients with AAV similarly had an impaired GLS (−14.8% vs −16.8%, P = 0.001), in addition to higher native T1 values (1190 ms vs 1164 ms, P = 0.005), suggesting increased myocardial fibrosis among patients with AAV. On both echocardiograms and CMR, patients with AAV also had a trend towards lower atrial and ventricular volumes compared to controls.
Conclusion
Patients with AAV in long-term remission exhibited several echocardiographic and CMR abnormalities compared to age- and sex-matched controls. However, these abnormalities were considered minimal and do not necessitate additional pharmacological treatment in the absence of symptoms. Although these findings do not support the routine use of in-depth screening with echocardiograms and CMR for asymptomatic patients, their association with long-term outcomes warrants further investigation.

title: #3051 Atypical familial Mediterranean fever presenting AA amyloidosis
authors: Shoko Ochiai; Masao Kikuchi; Shouichi Fujimoto; Koichi Kaikita
abstract:
Case presentation
A 72-year-old Japanese woman presented with lower leg edema, proteinuria and renal dysfunction. On admission, she exhibited nephrotic syndrome (protein/creatinine ratio: 7.0 g/gCr, serum albumin: 2.2 g/dL), elevated SCr (1.26 mg/dL) and an increased C-reactive protein (CRP)level of 3.74 mg/dL. There was no marked decrease in complement levels, and test results for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, anti-GBM antibodies, T-SPOT, viral hepatitis were negative. Renal biopsy revealed segmental mesangial AA amyloid deposits in glomeruli, interstitium, and vessels wall. The serum amyloid A protein level was 970 μg/mL. No inflammation or malignancy was noted on PET-CT, and blood and urine cultures were negative. The etiology of AA amyloidosis was unknown, and we interviewed her in detail regarding her symptoms and observed her vital signs in the hospital. These revealed that she recurrent experienced episodes of fever (37.0°C to 37.6°C) with no symptom such as chest or abdominal pain. Genetic analysis identified an R202Q heterozygous mutation in the MEFV gene. We therefore diagnosed the patient with an atypical FMF (FMF type 2), and we concluded that her AA amyloidosis is due to FMF. Colchicine was discontinued due to side effects, and treatment with canakinumab resulted in improved renal function (serum creatinine: 2.0 mg/dL), normalized CRP, and increased serum albumin to 3.5 g/dL. The serum amyloid A protein level improved to 58.2 μg/mL.
Discussion
FMF is most prevalent among individuals living around the Mediterranean basin, such as those of Turkish, Armenian, and Middle Eastern descent. In contrast, its prevalence in Japan is significantly lower compared to these ethnic groups. However, recently, in Japan there has been increase in the number of FMF cases and it reveal "atypical" FMF is major than typical FMF. Atypical FMF differs from typical FMF in the severity of fever, which may not exceed 38°C. This case shows the diagnostic challenges posed by atypical FMF, particularly in elderly patients with nephrotic syndrome and no systemic symptoms. Early recognition and intervention are crucial to prevent progression to AA amyloidosis. Genetic testing plays a pivotal role in diagnosing atypical FMF when clinical features are subtle.
Conclusion
Nephrologists should consider rare autoinflammatory diseases like FMF in patients with unexplained proteinuria and chronic inflammation. In recent study, genetic analysis of patients with CKD who initiated RRT without a definitive cause revealed that 11.1% carried pathogenic variants in CKD-related genes. As our case, genetic testing can provide valuable diagnostic clues and guide appropriate treatment strategies.

title: #3141 Kidney biopsy in patients with lupus nephritis, what it can add to diagnosis and therapy?
authors: Barbara Bullo-Piontecka; Agnieszka Perkowska-Ptasińska; Michal Komorniczak; Ewa Krol; Alicja Dębska-Ślizień; Anna Masiak
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney involvement is one of the severe complications in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and has been associated with higher mortality in these patients.
Method
We analyzed 158 renal biopsy results performed at the Department of Nephrology, Transplantology, and Internal Medicine, Medical University of Gdańsk, from 2008 to 2024.
All patients were diagnosed with SLE according to ACR/EULAR criteria.
The examined group included 120 women and 38 men, with a mean age of 38.9 ± 13.7 years (range 18–76).
Proteinuria >0.5 g/24 h and/or erythrocyturia >5 cells per high-power field were indications for performing a kidney biopsy. In the examined group, the indications for kidney biopsy were: initial diagnosis of nephropathy—113 patients, lupus nephritis (LN) flare—34 patients, and treatment nonresponse—11 patients. Nephrotic syndrome was observed in most patients (96; 61%).
Kidney biopsies were examined by an experienced kidney pathologist (Medical University of Warsaw) and classified according to the International Society of Nephrology (ISN)/Renal Pathology Society (RPS) scheme.
Results
Lupus nephritis was confirmed in 145 (91.8%) patients, while in 13 (8.2%) biopsies, other pathological changes were found.
The most common presentation of lupus nephritis was class IV—64/145 (40.5%). Class III was noted in 17 (10.8%), class V in 16 biopsies (10.1%), class IV+V in 13 (8.2%), and class III+V in 19 (12%). Other classes were less frequent: class II—11 (7%) and class VI—only 5 (3.2%) of the examined patients.
In 13 biopsies (8.2%) not fulfilling the ISN/RPS criteria for lupus nephritis, other diagnoses were established: podocytopathy—6 patients, IgA nephropathy—4 patients, diabetic kidney disease—2 patients, and anti-GBM disease—1 patient (rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis).
Furthermore, in one patient with a diagnosis of LN, coexisting light chain disease was observed. After electron microscopy, in one patient with LN class II, collagen type IV disease was suspected, and genetic testing ultimately confirmed Alport's syndrome.
Conclusion
Kidney biopsy in SLE patients not only confirms lupus nephritis but also reveals other nephropathies that may either coexist with LN or occur independently.
Our findings highlight that renal biopsy remains essential for the accurate diagnosis of lupus nephritis and the identification of coexisting renal pathologies, which may significantly impact patient management and therapeutic decisions.
