title: #3481 FSGS and nephrotic syndrome in mantle cell lymphoma: an exception or an underrecognized entity?
authors: Catarina Veiga; Joaquim Milheiro; Raquel Pinto; Adriana Dias; Carolina Ferreira; Andre Ferreira; Ines Sá; Carla Lima; Sergio Lemos
abstract:
Background and Aims
FSGS is rarely reported as a paraneoplastic glomerulopathy and has only been reported in three other patients with mantle cell lymphoma prior to this case report.
Case Description
We describe the case of a 69-year-old male with a three-month history of lower limb and edema and foamy urine. Laboratory evaluation revealed acute kidney injury (creatinine 5.99 mg/dL), dyslipidemia, hypoalbuminemia (2.5 g/dL) and nephrotic-range proteinuria (6g/24 h). Renal ultrasound was unremarkable. Serum protein electrophoresis revealed a gamma-region spike, later identified as monoclonal IgM lambda. Urinary protein immunofixation was normal. Autoimmune workup (ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM, anti-PLA2R and anti-THSD7A antibodies) was negative, as were serologies for HIV, HBV and HCV. The patient was immune to parvovirus, CMV, and EBV. Bone marrow biopsy revealed an increased number of B lymphocytes (negative for CD5, CD23, Cyclin D1, and CD43), suggesting lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma/Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Renal biopsy (14 glomeruli) exhibited segmental sclerosis and extensive tubular necrosis, with no chain restriction or amyloid deposits. Immunohistochemical analysis identified a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate positive for CD20, CD22, and CD5, and negative for CD10. Based on these findings, secondary FSGS was assumed, likely due to an underlying yet-to-be-fully-characterized lymphoproliferative disorder. Due to progressive renal failure (maximum creatinine of 9 mg/dL) the patient started hemodialysis. Evaluation using PET revealed hypermetabolic infradiaphragmatic lymph nodes and involvement of the esophagogastric junction. Gastric biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of blastoid-variant MCL (positive CD20, CD5 e Cyclin D1). Corticosteroid (prednisone 60mg/day) were initiated for tumor debulking, with a reduction of proteinuria from 3.70 to 1.7g/day and normalization of serum albumin within ten days. The patient then started VR-CAP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and prednisone with bortezomib) with a marked analytical improvement: resolution of nephrotic syndrome, reduction in proteinuria (760 mg/day) and partial renal function recovery.
Discussion
FSGS is a histopathological pattern of glomerular injury classified as primary or secondary. Secondary FSGS is a consequence of adaptive glomerular response, exposure to drugs, toxins or viral infections. While lymphoproliferative diseases are a known cause of glomerulopathies, their association with FSGS is rare. The temporal relationship between the onset of renal disease and the diagnosis of hematologic malignancy, as well as clinical and laboratory improvement following lymphoma-directed therapy, strongly supports the classification of this case as secondary FSGS in the context of a lymphoproliferative disorder. Notably, the occurrence of nephrotic syndrome is more commonly associated with primary FSGS rather than secondary forms. The pathophysiological mechanism linking FSGS to MCL, however, remains unclear. One plausible hypothesis is the presence of a plasma-soluble factor secreted by the malignant clone, leading to podocyte injury. This is supported by a previous case in the literature where nephrotic syndrome associated with MCL resolved after plasmapheresis, suggesting a role for a circulating factor in podocyte dysfunction, resembling the pathophysiology of primary FSGS.
Conclusion
This case highlights FSGS as a rare paraneoplastic renal manifestation of MCL. Although the exact pathophysiological mechanism remains unclear, the observed renal response to lymphoma-directed therapy reinforces the importance of early recognition and timely treatment to optimize renal recovery and patient outcomes.

title: #398 Fibrillary glomerulonephritis: analysis of cases diagnosed over 14 years
authors: Amparo Roda Safont; Ramon Roca-Tey; Juan Carlos González Oliva; Jessica Maria Ugalde Altamirano; Ursula Luz Vadillo Vidal; Verónica Duarte Gallego; Sandy Valeria Pico Ruiz; Jordi Calls
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fibrillary glomerulonephritis (FGN) is a rare disease observed in 0.5%–1% of native kidney biopsies. To analyse cases of FGN from June 2011 to June 2024 in our centre.
Method
Data of patients (pts) older than 18 years of age with a histological diagnosis of FGN (deposition of IgG, usually IgG4, and C3 in mesangium and/or capillary walls of glomerulus; Congo red negative) through both light and electron microscopy and immunohistochemistry techniques (DNAJB9) was analysed. Baseline demographics, clinical variables, laboratory findings, treatment performed, and follow-up of included pts were recorded.
Results
Out of 250 consecutive native kidney biopsies, five patients were diagnosed with FGN, yielding a frequency of 2% and incidence of 0.35 cases/year. Mean age at diagnosis was 61.6 ± 11.84 years (range 47–79) and 60% were women (ratio 1.5:1). Mean age for women and men was 54.3 ± 6.3 years and 72.5 ± 9.2 years, respectively (P = 0.16).
Four pts were hypertensive, and one of these was diabetic. Haematuria and proteinuria were present in all pts at baseline; one of them had nephrotic syndrome, and two had nephrotic proteinuria. title: #2492 Real-world study on the effectiveness and safety of telitacicept in treating IgA nephropathy
authors: Chengning Zhang; Suyan Duan; Bo Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA nephropathy (IgAN) represents the most prevalent form of primary glomerular disease globally. Telitacicept is a humanized fusion protein that combines a transmembrane activator and calcium-modulating cyclophilin ligand interactor receptor with human IgG. The purpose of this study is to examine the effectiveness and safety of telitacicept in individuals diagnosed with IgAN.
Method
Eight patients with IgAN who were treated with telitacicept at the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University between January 2023 and Sep 2024 were included in this retrospective study. All patients had proteinuria ≥0.5 g/d despite optimal supportive therapy and received subcutaneous telitacicept 160 mg weekly for more than 3 months. Clinical and laboratory parameters were evaluated before and after telitacicept treatment.
Results
Among the patients, there were 4 men and 4 women. The table displays the baseline demographic characteristics and follow-up data for these patients. Prior to administering telitacicept, the mean serum creatinine level was 143.71 ± 32.73 µmol/L, and the median protein excretion was 1.79 (IQR, 1.16–2.78) g/d. Following a median follow-up period of 107 days (IQR, 84–161) post-telitacicept therapy, the mean proteinuria level was 1.00 (IQR, 0.64–1.66) g/d. The estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) remained stable over time. No adverse events were observed during the follow-up period.
Conclusion
Preliminary data indicate that short-course telitacicept therapy significantly reduced proteinuria levels in individuals with IgAN, a finding of clinical relevance. However, validation through multicenter, prospective trials with extended follow-up periods is imperative to establish therapeutic efficacy and safety.

title: #317 Autophagy related Protein 5 is a promising autophagy marker in lupus nephritis with good predictive value of response to treatment
authors: Howayda El Shinnawy; Sahar Shawky; Manal Salman; Marwa Abdelsamea; Ahmed Shamseldeen; Shaimaa Zaki Abdelmegied
abstract:
Background and Aims
Conventional biomarkers may not be useful enough to monitor response to treatment in lupus nephritis (LN). Increasing evidence implicates autophagy in the pathogenesis of LN. This study assessed serum autophagy related protein 5 (ATG5) and its staining in renal biopsies in LN and its relation to the diagnosis of autophagy and treatment response.
Method
A pilot, prospective study included 31 active LN patients and 9 healthy subjects. ATG5 was assessed in LN renal biopsies before starting treatment and in the serum of all subjects. Serum ATG5 was followed at 3 and 6 months after treatment.
Results
Serum ATG5 was significantly low in LN at cut-off ≤312.3 ng/l with AUC 0.943. The prevalence of ATG5 staining in renal biopsies with summation score >3 was 87.1% (27 patients) and multiplication score >8 was 58.1% (18 patients). There was a significant recovery of serum autophagy marker ATG5 in response to treatment (baseline versus 3 and 6 months after treatment) p-value <0.001. Complete and partial responders had lower summation and multiplication scores in biopsies also, they showed better recovery of serum ATG5 at 3 and 6 months versus non-responder p-values of 0.004, and 0.009 <0.001, 0.001 respectively. Summation score of ATG5 ≤6 in biopsies can predict response to treatment by AUC 0.88, sensitivity 69.57%, specificity 100%, PPV 100%, and NPV 53.3%. Patients who received MMF had better responses than Cyclophosphamide (P-value 0.042). Serum ATG5 at 3 and 6 months was negatively correlated with serum creatinine and protein/creatinine ratio while positively correlated with e-GFR (p-value <0.05). ATG5 Summation and multiplication scores were negatively correlated with serum ATG5 after 6 months (p-value 0.026, 0.018).
Conclusion
ATG5 is a promising autophagy marker in LN with good predictive value for treatment response. A lower autophagy biopsy score is linked to a positive response to treatment especially with MMF.

title: #556 Cardiometabolic risk, evaluation and control in Southeast Asians with lupus nephritis: a cross sectional study
authors: Dawn Lim; Felicia Loo; Hui Zhuan Tan; Tung Lin Lee; Irene Mok; Jason Choo; Lydia Lim; Cynthia Lim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Lupus nephritis (LN) predicts a nine-fold higher risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease compared to lupus patients without nephritis. Early recognition of cardiometabolic risk in patients with LN can allow risk optimization, such as achieving blood pressure, lipid and diabetes control with lifestyle changes and disease-modifying medications to reduce cardiovascular disease.
To identify potential gaps in cardiometabolic risk management, we aimed to evaluate the prevalence of cardiometabolic risk, evaluation and control in LN in real-world practice.
Method
We performed a cross-sectional study of all patients with biopsy-confirmed LN at the Singapore General Hospital between 2011 and 2022. Demographics, laboratory investigations and medications were obtained from electronic medical records.
The prevalence of cardiometabolic risks (age, sex, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, ischemic heart disease [IHD], reduced kidney function [estimated glomerular filtration rate, eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio [UPCR] >0.15 g/g, glucocorticoid use), evaluation (office blood pressure [BP], fasting glucose and lipid and HbA1c) and control at the time of diagnosis in three time periods (2011–2014, 2015–2018 and 2019–2022) were compared.
Results
Among 326 patients with LN, the median age at diagnosis was 42.0 years (interquartile range: 30.9, 52.7) and 81.6% were female. When categorized by eGFR and UPCR, a quarter (25.8%) were at the highest risk categories for cardiovascular disease (Fig. 1).
Table 1 showed that across the three time periods, the prevalence of IHD and traditional cardiometabolic risk factors such as age, male gender, diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidemia were not significantly changed while hypertension reduced in 2019–2022.
Systolic BP <120 mmHg was achieved in 20.9% in 2011–2014, 32.7% in 2015–2018 and 25.1% in 2019–2022; while BP <130/80 mmHg was achieved in 31.3%, 42.7% and 40.4%, respectively. The use of BP-lowering therapies and renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors were lowest in 2019-2022, even among patients with hypertension or BP >130/80 mmHg, and among those with G1–G4 and A2–A3 proteinuria.
Lipid evaluation was performed in 75.8%; only 32.0% achieved LDL-cholesterol <2.6 mmol/L. There was no significant change in the prevalence of lipid evaluation or LDL- and HDL-cholesterol levels across the three time periods.
Glycemic evaluation was significantly less frequent in 2019–2022 (78.7%) compared to the earlier time periods. Fasting glucose was not significantly different in the three time periods, but HbA1c was lowest in 2019–2022.
Conclusion
Use of RAS inhibitors was suboptimal despite indications for their use (hypertension or BP >130/80 mmHg and in the presence of G1–G4 and A2–A3 proteinuria), while glycemic evaluation and achievement of BP target (SBP < 120 mmHg) were lower in 2019–2022 compared to 2015–2018. These are areas for improvement in cardiometabolic risk management for patients with LN.

title: #1249 Impact of HALP score on renal prognosis in IgA nephropathy
authors: Beyza Benlioğlu; Gizem Korkut; Meltem Sezis Demirci; Ege Girtine; Sait Şen; Banu Sarsık Kumbaracı
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is the most common type of primary glomerulonephritis, and 15%–40% of patients develop end-stage renal disease (ESRD) within 10–20 years. New biomarkers are needed to predict the prognosis of IgAN. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of the HALP score (hemoglobin, albumin, lymphocyte, and platelet) on disease prognosis and renal survival in patients with IgAN.
Method
A total of 204 patients diagnosed with IgAN through kidney biopsy between 2012 and 2023, registered in the nephrology database of Ege University Hospital, were retrospectively analyzed. Patients were categorized into three groups based on their HALP scores:
Group 1: HALP <36.6 Group 2: HALP 36.6–51.4 Group 3: HALP >51.4 Numerical variables were presented as median with interquartile range (IQR), and a p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results
Among 204 patients, 67.2% were male, and the median age at diagnosis was 42 years.
Patients with a high HALP score had significantly longer mean renal survival compared to those with a low HALP score (P < 0.01) (Fig. 1).
ROC analysis was performed to determine the predictive value of HALP, showing that the cutoff value for IgAN patients was 42.4 with 72.7% sensitivity and 55% specificity (Fig. 2).
After adjusting for age, gender, hypertension (HT), diabetes mellitus (DM), number of red blood cells in urine, 24-hour proteinuria, use of renin-angiotensin system (RAS) blockers, and number of globally sclerotic glomeruli in biopsy, Cox regression analysis showed that patients with high HALP scores had an 87% lower risk of developing ESRD compared to those with low HALP scores (P < 0.001, HR: 0.13).
Conclusion
The HALP score is considered a strong predictor of renal prognosis in patients with IgAN. Patients with high HALP scores exhibited better renal survival and a lower risk of ESRD. The HALP score can be used as a prognostic tool in the management of IgAN and may play a significant role in guiding treatment strategies. The results of this study should be validated with larger patient populations.

title: #1291 Rosuvastatin induced acute kidney injury—a case report
authors: Gordan Dorčić; Maja Mačković; Marijana Coric; Stela Bulimbasic; Jelenko Lazić
abstract:
Background and Aims
Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is a significant cause of acute kidney injury. According to the literature, AIN is most commonly induced by antibiotics or anti-inflammatory drugs. Secondary minimal change disease (MCD) can also have iatrogenic trigger, although very rare. In this case report, we present a 67-year-old female patient with biopsy-proven combined AIN and MCD induced by rosuvastatin.
Case report
This patient, with previously normal renal function and no significant comorbidities or chronic therapy, presented to the emergency department with acute onset of eyelid and extremities edema lasting for 10 days, along with decreased urination. She had no skin changes such as rash or pruritus but had a persistent cough and pain in the calves and heels.
The workup revealed acute kidney injury (Urea: 26.3 mmol/L; Creatinine: 465 µmol/L; eGFR: 8 ml/min/1.73 m²) accompanied by hyperkalemia (5.5 mmol/L), hypocalcemia (2.05 mmol/L), hyperphosphatemia (2.23 mmol/L), hypoalbuminemia (27 g/L), and an elevated sedimentation rate (68 mm/3.6 s). The blood count, coagulogram, hepatogram, and ferrogram were unremarkable, and inflammatory parameters were stable. On examination, the patient was hypertensive (175/105 mmHg), oliguric and had anasarca. Urinalysis showed proteinuria (3+) and erythrocyturia (3+).
The patient was admitted to the department for further treatment, and non-selective proteinuria of nephrotic range was confirmed in 24-hour urine collection (protein: 10,200 mg/dU; albumin: 5,500 mg/dU). Additional history revealed that she had been taking rosuvastatin, prescribed for mixed hyperlipidemia, for the past two months.
Conservative supportive therapy was initiated to manage proteinuria, control blood pressure, and reduce peripheral edema. An ACE inhibitor was introduced at the maximum dose, and diuresis was stimulated with parenteral human albumin combined with diuretics. An ultrasound examination revealed bilateral kidneys of normal size (100 mm) with normal parenchyma. On the fifth day after admission a kidney biopsy was performed and sent for analysis by immunofluorescence, light, and electron microscopy. The findings from light and immunofluorescence microscopy were consistent with acute tubulointerstitial nephritis with eosinophilia and minimal change disease with extensive loss of podocyte foot processes on 85% of the examined surface.
The histopathological and clinical findings were indicative of combined acute kidney injury caused by presumably rosuvastatin. Upon admission rosuvastatin was discontinued and renal function recovery was already underway, with a decrease in creatinine levels. Oral prednisone therapy (1 mg/kg of body weight daily for 14 days) was initiated, followed by tapering over four weeks.
The patient was discharged with additional therapy consisting of perindopril, indapamide, amlodipine, and moxonidine. At the four-week follow-up after initiating corticosteroid therapy, the patient achieved complete recovery of renal function (Urea: 6.9 mmol/L; Creatinine: 86 µmol/L; eGFR: 61 ml/min/1.73 m²), correction of electrolyte imbalances (K: 4.0 mmol/L; Na: 140 mmol/L; Ca: 2.14 mmol/L; P: 1.7 mmol/L), and regular diuresis with proteinuria <60 mg/dU and albuminuria <10 mg/dU. Prednisone therapy was successfully tapered, with the recommendation to avoid statins.
Conclusion
To our knowledge and based on a review of the literature, this is so far the only case of combined AIN and secondary MCD induced by rosuvastatin use. In our patient, who had no other potential cause of acute kidney failure, eight weeks of rosuvastatin therapy led to acute renal injury with nephrotic syndrome. Kidney biopsy findings showed interstitial infiltrates predominantly composed of eosinophils and extensive podocyte foot processes effacement. Withdrawal of the culprit drug, combined with prednisone treatment (1 mg/kg/day), resulted in complete recovery of renal function.

Conclusion
To our knowledge and based on a review of the literature, this is so far the only case of combined AIN and secondary MCD induced by rosuvastatin use. Withdrawal of the culprit drug, combined with prednisone treatment (1 mg/kg/day), resulted in complete recovery of renal function.

title: #3657 Unveiling the role of peroxiredoxins 1–5 as markers in early diagnosis and monitoring of IgA nephropathy, membranous nephropathy and lupus nephritis
authors: Natalia Krata; Barbara Moszczuk; Emilia Knioła; Julia Tanska; Bartosz Foroncewicz; Leszek Paczek; Krzysztof Mucha
abstract:
Background and Aims
The early diagnosis of glomerulonephritis (GN) continue to present significant challenges in nephrology. Oxidative stress (OS) and its associated markers, particularly the peroxiredoxins (PRDXs), have been implicated in the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying several renal disorders. This study aimed to assess the clinical relevance of PRDXs 1–5 as diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers in patients with IgA nephropathy (IgAN), membranous nephropathy (MN) and lupus nephritis (LN) over a 7-year longitudinal follow-up.
Method
A cohort of 108 GN patients initially tested for abnormalities in serum concentrations of peroxiredoxins 1–5, was followed longitudinally over a 7-year period (2017–2024). The regular evaluations of renal function, including measurements of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and timed proteinuria (TUP) at each in-person visit, were further analysed regarding to the change of PRDX concentration. The biomarker levels were re-evaluated in total of 25 patients (IgAN—14, LN—8, and MN—3). Statistical analysis was performed using the Wilcoxon, Mann Whitney-U or Kruskal-Wallis test, and Pearson's correlation coefficient, with significance level of P < 0.05.
Results
Serum levels of PRDXs 2–4 exhibited significant variability between measurements (2017 vs. 2023), whereas PRDX 1 and 5 remain on the similar level. However, upon analysing the relationship between PRDX levels and eGFR, significant differences were observed, specifically for PRDX 1 and 4 (P = 0.015 and P = 0.008) in relation to eGFR deterioration. TUP revealed the association (P = 0.01) with PRDX 1 only.
The mean eGFR and proteinuria at the time of 2nd PRDX evaluation were: 67.12 ml/min/m2 and 1.17 g respectively. The deterioration of eGFR was predominantly observed in IgAN patients, although a doubling of serum creatinine was noted in only 4 of these patients.
Conclusion
This study highlights the clinical significance of PRDXs in the diagnostic and prognostic evaluation of glomerular diseases. We assume, that incorporating PRDX measurement (especially 1 and 4) into standard diagnostic protocols, could improve early detection of disease progression and facilitate personalized management of GN.

title: #2538 Remission and relapses in lupus nephritis among multi-racial Southeast Asians: a single center retrospective study
authors: Julia G Andres; Hui Zhuan Tan; Dawn Lim; Hanyang Du; Harini Manivannan; Tung Lin Lee; Irene Mok; Jason Choo; Cynthia Lim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Lupus nephritis occurs in up to 60% of all patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and has a relapsing/remitting course that can progress to kidney failure. This study aims to assess the treatment outcomes in adult patients treated for lupus nephritis and factors associated with remission among multi-racial Southeast Asians.
Method
This was a single-center, retrospective cohort study of adults with biopsy-proven lupus nephritis diagnosed between 2018 and 2020 at the Singapore General Hospital. Clinical, laboratory and pharmacotherapy data were collected from electronic health records every 6 months (“visits”) for three years from diagnosis. We excluded visits with incomplete follow-up data for immunosuppressive therapy and remission status.
The outcomes were remission and relapses during follow-up. To account for variability across patients and repeated measures over time, mixed effects logistic regression analyses were used to examine factors associated with remission. The mixed effects model included random intercepts for patients and repeated measures for 6-monthly time points, and fixed effects for (1) follow-up time point alone; and (2) follow-up time point, age at diagnosis; gender; presence of diabetes and hypertension at diagnosis; laboratory results at diagnosis for estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, urine red blood cell number, serum complement C3 and C4 levels, presence of FSGS on kidney histology; and treatment with hydroxychloroquine, mycophenolate and multitarget therapy within 6 months before the follow-up visit. The base model included these factors that were determined a priori. The sensitivity analysis added factors that were significantly associated with remission after adjustment for follow-up duration.
Results
We included 73 patients with 301 visits. Figure 1 shows that remission and complete remission occurred in 63.0% and 39.7% respectively at Month 6. The remission rate increased to 82.9% at Month 24 but were lower during the third year of follow-up. The complete remission rate increased to 75.0% at Month 30 and was lower at Month 36.
Nephritic relapses occurred in 1.4% at Month 6, increased to 5%–7% at Month 12–24, and increased to 11% in the third year of follow-up.
Table 1 shows the clinical and histological characteristics of the cohort and in the groups with and without remission at follow-up. After adjusting for the follow-up duration, known SLE at kidney biopsy, hyperlipidemia, and acute kidney disease at presentation were associated with reduced likelihood of remission, while higher eGFR was associated with higher likelihood of remission.
The mixed effects logistic regression found that follow-up at Month 18 and 24 (OR 3.478 [95% CI: 1.015–11.912] and 8.620 [95% CI: 2.008–36.995] respectively, compared to Month 6), higher eGFR (OR 1.032 [95% CI: 1.012–1.053]), and higher C4 (OR 1.662 [95% CI: 1.011–2.732]) levels were independently associated with remission during follow-up. Higher C3 (OR 0.043 [95% CI: 0.005–0.364]) levels at kidney biopsy and use of multitarget therapy within 6 months before follow-up (OR 0.172 [95% CI: 0.035–0.838]) were inversely associated with remission. The sensitivity analysis (addition of SLE and hyperlipidemia) found that SLE was inversely associated with remission (OR 0.127 [95% CI: 0.037–0.435]); this model had lower correct classification and poorer model fit than the base model.
Conclusion
This study highlighted that despite increased remission rates, especially during the first two years, approximately 5%–10% may relapse in the 2nd and 3rd year. Factors independently associated with remission were follow-up time point, higher eGFR, higher C4, lower C3 and absence of multi-target therapy. Future studies should aim to further elucidate the relationship between different induction regimens including multitarget therapy and clinical outcomes.

title: #2897 Kidney disease spectrum in patients with haematological malignancies
authors: Thomas Zimmermann; Juliane Schneider; Robert Erdelkamp; Christoph Walz; Michael Fischereder; Ulf Schoenermarck; Anke von Bergwelt-Baildon
abstract:
Background and Aims
Haematological malignancies can present with kidney manifestations of various types. At first presentation kidney biopsy can help to diagnose the malignancy, whereas during follow-up a biopsy can differentiate between malignancy-related and unrelated findings. The aim of our study was to investigate the spectrum of kidney diseases associated with haematological malignancies.
Method
In this single-center retrospective study we analyzed patients with native kidney biopsies and a diagnosis of a haematological malignancies over a 10-year period (2015–2024) at our University hospital.
Results
We identified 79 patients (male n = 41, female = 38) with 82 native kidney biopsies. The diagnosis of the haematological malignancy (other than MGUS) was known in 50% at time of biopsy, mean age of the patients was 63 years. 11 patients presented after bone marrow transplantation. Impaired kidney function (65/82 with creatinine >1.2 mg/dl) and proteinuria were the main biopsy indications. Proteinuria >3g/g were present in one third (28/82 patients).
The spectrum of kidney disease included AL-amyloidosis (n = 21), cast nephropathy (n = 10), lymphoma infiltration (n = 11), glomerulonephritis (n = 8) including cryoglobulinemia (n = 5), interstitial nephritis (n = 8), thrombotic microangiopathy (n = 11) and others manifestations (including podocytopathies) (Table 1). Lymphoma infiltration occurred in different malignancy types (DLBC, B-ALL, marginal zone lymphoma, immunocytoma, CLL, CMML, multiple myeloma). In biopsies after bone marrow transplantation thrombotic microangiopathy (n = 8) and interstitial nephritis (n = 2) were the main findings. Among the 41 patients with the diagnosis of a haematological malignancy based on kidney biopsy the main findings were AL-amyloidosis (32%), cast nephropathy (20%), cryoglobulinemia (12%), lymphoma infiltration (12%) and others.
Conclusion
Our study confirms the broad spectrum of kidney lesions with haematological malignancies. While kidney biopsy can reveal the diagnosis of haematological malignancy in so far undiagnosed patients, it is helpful in differentiation of unrelated kidney disease versus kidney involvement in patients with known haematological disease.

title: #2922 The relative and absolute quantity of qualitative research in nephrology compared to other specialities: a scoping review covering over two decades
authors: Matt Gittus; Anthea Sutton; Lukasz Lagojda; Alicia O'cathain; James Fotheringham
abstract:
Background and Aims
Qualitative research provides invaluable insights into patient experiences, clinical perspectives and the complexities of care processes. It has the potential to transform clinical practice, enhance patient-centred care, and improve health outcomes. Yet, the speed and scale of adoption in nephrology compared to other medicine clinical specialities remains undefined.
Method
Three databases were systematically searched using speciality-specific terms for 12 medical specialities, including nephrology, to estimate absolute and relative numbers of qualitative studies between 01/01/2000 and 31/12/2024. The speciality-specific impact of COVID-19 on the results necessitated the exclusion of COVID-19 studies. A follow-up search was conducted to explore the number of qualitative studies in 10 nephrology subspecialities. Quality assessment was conducted on 100 randomly selected nephrology qualitative studies using the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Tool for Qualitative Research.
Results
Between Jan 2000 and Dec 2024, 1,608,917 studies were retrieved, of which 17,533 were qualitative. Each of the other medical specialities had a higher number of qualitative studies, ranging from 35,787 in haematology to 135,909 in neurology. There was statistically significant variation between the speciality and the proportion of qualitative studies (P < 0.001). The proportion of studies that were qualitative across all specialties was 1.62% (95% CI: 1.61%–1.63%), with nephrology significantly lower at 1.09% (95% CI: 1.07%–1.11%). In comparison, the proportion of qualitative studies in other specialities ranged from 1.08% in haematology (95% CI: 1.07%–1.09%) to 4.56% in infectious diseases (95% CI: 4.53%–4.60%). The proportion of qualitative studies in nephrology increased from 0.49% in 2000 to 1.78% in 2024 (1.29% absolute increase). This increase was below the rise in proportion of qualitative results across all the specialities, which grew from 0.87% in 2000 to 2.49% in 2024 (1.62% absolute difference).
Nephrology subspeciality was identified for 15,942 studies (91%). Chronic kidney disease had the highest number of qualitative results at 6,092 compared to acid-base imbalances at 440. The overall proportion of studies that were qualitative across nephrology subspecialities was 1.17%, ranging from 0.57% in acute kidney injury (95% CI: 0.53%–0.61%) to 1.98% in peritoneal dialysis (95% CI: 1.84%–2.11%).
While quality assessments demonstrated a strong alignment between research methodology and objectives in nephrology qualitative studies, key elements such as reflexivity (self-examination of researcher influence) and transparency (explicit documentation of research processes) were often lacking.
Conclusion
Despite evidence that patient experience and care processes are crucial for achieving positive patient outcomes in nephrology, the low absolute and relative number of qualitative results is concerning. This paucity hinders the nephrology community's efforts to fully understand and respond effectively to the complex challenges faced by patients. Although some nephrology subspecialities have shown greater adoption of qualitative methodologies, greater uptake in larger subspecialities such as acute kidney injury may be needed for nephrology to compete with other specialities.

title: #3326 Differences in the clinical and histological presentation of interstitial nephritis acute in relation to the use of drugs and inhibitors of the check point in the nephrology unit of our center between the years 2008–2023
authors: Verónica Ruth Mercado Valdivia; Raquel Diaz Mancebo; Yesika María Amezquita Orjuela; Gabriel Ledesma Sánchez; Gilda Carreño Cornejo; Yolanda Hernández Hernández; Sílvia Caldés Ruisánchez; Ángel Gallegos Villalobos; Rocío Echarri Carrillo; Antonio Cirugeda García
abstract:
Background and Aims
The incidence of acute tubulo-interstitial nephritis in renal biopsies ranges between 5%–27%. The pharmacological cause is responsible for 60%–70%. The CheckPoint inhibitors represent up to 2.2%–5%. So far the histological data seem to be similar between both entities.
Method
Retrospective and descriptive study of patients with acute tubulointerstitial nephritis biopsied secondary to the use of drugs (ATIN) or Checkpoint Inhibitors (IMN) in our center from February 2008 to February 2023.
Results
We describe a total of 25 patients with a diagnosis of AITN (clinical characteristics in Fig. 1). We biopsied 100% of the patients with AITN and only 55.5% of those patients with IMN. Greater interstitial infiltrate and more presence of eosinophils and plasma cells in the IMN, without being statistically significant. The acute kidney failure is more common in the AITN group. We found a greater presence of eosinophilia, hematuria, leukocyturia and proteinuria in the IMN group. We found no statistical differences significant between recovery time or between dose of steroids received. There seems to be a tendency to use higher doses in the AITN group, probably due to having a more severe acute kidney failure. There are no differences in the development of advanced chronic kidney disease and in starting dialysis.
Conclusion

title: #60 Mortality profile of patients with anca-associated vasculitis
authors: Amparo Roda Safont; Ramon Roca-Tey; Juan Carlos Gonzalez; Alejandra Fernández Luque; Elisabet Garcia Casares; Jessica Maria Ugalde Altamirano; Ursula Luz Vadillo Vidal; Verónica Duarte Gallego; Sandy Valeria Pico Ruiz; Jordi Calls
abstract:
Background and Aims
ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) is a group of autoimmune diseases that affect multiple orgysubtype (MPA, GPA, EGPA), organ involvement (kidney and lung) and ANCA type (MPO or PR3) that may influence the mortality risk of patients (pts).
The clinicopathological variants of AAV are categorized based on clinical, laboratory and pathologic findings: microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA).
Aim: To analyze the relationships between orgysubtype, organ involvement and ANCA type of AAV pts who died during follow-up.
Method
Retrospective observational study including consecutive pts older than 18 years of age with a diagnosis AAV over a 12-year period (2012–2024). All pts met the American College of Rheumatology criteria for EGPA and GPA and the criteria of the last Chapell Hill Consensus Conference in 2012 for these vasculitides and MPA. Demographic variables, follow-up time, and mortality were analyzed.
Results
Thirty-four pts were included in this study. Mean follow-up of 55.8 ± 45.84 months. Mean age at baseline was 67.21 ± 14.78 years (range, 33–92 years). Female to male ratio was 16:18. Eight pts (23.5%) met the criteria for GPA, three pts (8.8%) for EGPA and twenty-three (67.6%) for MPA. Kidney involvement (KI) was the most frequently manifestation, present in almost all MPA and in most GPA compared to EGPA (95.6%, 75%, 33.3% respectively, P = 0.011). Lung involvement (LI) was more frequent in GPA and EGPA (87.5%, 66.6%, respectively), and it occurred in one third of MPA cases (34.8%) (P = 0.031).
Nine pts died (26.5%), 55.6% were male. The mean age of survivors and those who died was 65.4 ± 14.7 years and 73.3 ± 12 years, respectively (P = 0.13). Classification of deceased pts according to subtypes: 4 were affected by MPA (17.4%), 4 by GPA (50%) and 1 by EGPA (33.3%) (P = 0.19). The mean follow-up time was 32.5 ± 14.8 months. KI was the most prominent clinical finding (87.5% of cases) and LI was present in 75% of pts. Mean creatinine and proteinuria were 7.1 ± 2.8 mg/dl and 1.4 ± 1.1 g/day, respectively. MPO antibody was more prevalent than PR3 (66.7% vs 33.3%, P = 0.068), hazard ratio = 0.188 (95% confidence interval CI): 0.037–0.968, P = 0.078).
Conclusion
1) The average age of deceased pts was higher than survivors. 2) Although the wide confidence interval suggesting variability, the risk of mortality was lower for MPO-positive pts compared to PR3-positive pts. 3) Advanced age, decreased kidney function (eGFR) and higher proteinuria levels were significant risk factors for mortality. On the contrary, higher hemoglobin levels and a diagnosis of MAP were associated with a better prognosis. These results underscore the importance of monitoring specific clinical markers in the management of this pts.

title: #319 Coagulation changes in the coagulation system in nephrotic syndrome: a clinical multicenter study
authors: Sarah Kelddal; Erik Lerkevang Grove; Camilla Duus; Louis Nygaard; Tilde Kristensen; Frank Mose; Jon Waarst Gregersen; Anne-Mette Hvas; Henrik Birn
abstract:
Background and Aims
Nephrotic syndrome is accompanied by a disruption of haemostasis shifting towards a prothrombotic state. Despite advances in anticoagulation treatment, venous thromboembolism remains a significant and unresolved challenge in nephrotic syndrome. Studies on the underlying mechanisms have primarily focused on selected components of the coagulation system, leaving critical gaps in the understanding and potentially mitigating the increased thrombosis risk. We aimed to characterize changes in the coagulation system in nephrotic syndrome to identify abnormalities that may provide targets for prevention.
Method
A Danish multicentre, cross-sectional, clinical study including adult patients from four nephrology departments between April 2021 and May 2024. Inclusion criteria were plasma albumin <30 g/L, urine albumin-creatinine ratio >2200 mg/g, and well-managed or no diabetes. Exclusion criteria were estimated glomerular filtration rate <30 mL/min/1.73 m2, anticoagulant treatment, thrombophilia, prior thrombosis, current infection, malignancy, or pregnancy.
Patients with nephrotic syndrome and healthy individuals were compared using either unpaired t-tests or Mann-Whitney U-test.
Results
We included 47 nephrotic patients with mean plasma albumin level of 22 g/L and urine albumin-creatinine ratio at 5,161 mg/g (Table 1). Thrombin generation markers were significantly elevated, particularly prothrombin fragment 1+2 (nephrotic: mean 509 pmol/L, 95% confidence interval (CI) 426–592; healthy: 183 pmol/L, 95% CI 171–196; P < 0.0001), and thrombin-antithrombin complex (nephrotic: mean 3.5 µg/L, 95% CI 3.2–3.8; healthy: 2.5 µg/L, 95% CI 2.3–2.7; P < 0.0001) (Fig. 1A and B). Fibrinolysis was impaired, with 50% clot lysis time significantly prolonged (nephrotic: mean 1281 s, 95% CI 1101–1462; healthy: mean: 964 s, 95% CI 843–1085; P = 0.004) (Fig. 1D). Platelet count and platelet aggregation were within normal ranges and did not differ between groups (Table 1).
Conclusion
Patients with nephrotic syndrome exhibit a prothrombotic pattern, characterised by normal platelet aggregation but elevated thrombin generation and impaired fibrinolysis. Thus, antithrombotic strategies to reduce the risk of thrombosis should target secondary haemostasis.

title: #391 Clinical utility of international IgA nephropathy prediction tool in Japanese patients
authors: Sayumi Kawamura; Yukihiro Wada; Keiichi Matsuzaki; Tomomi Motohashi; Tetsuya Abe; Akizumi Tsutsumi; Yasuo Takeuchi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Clinical course of IgA nephropathy (IgAN) varies by patients. Treatment strategy based on accurate prediction of renal prognosis is critical to prevent the disease progression. Compared to European countries and the United States, early pathological diagnosis for IgAN is possible in Japan as results of the health check-up system and differences in renal biopsy practice patterns. Additionally, tonsillectomy and corticosteroid pulse therapy (TSP) is commonly performed. Recently, International IgA Nephropathy Prediction Tool (IPT) has been reported. However, the utility of IPT is still unelucidated, especially it remains elusive whether IPT is useful compared to the grading system based on the combination of the clinical and histological severity from Japanese patients (J Nephrol 2013, Clin Exp Nephrol 2019). We attempted to validate the value of IPT in Japanese patients with IgAN.
Method
We retrospectively reviewed 145 patients (male 51.0%) with biopsy-proven IgAN in our hospital from 2014 to 2019. We collected the clinical indicators, pathological findings, and treatment options during the observation period (mean 36.9 ± 29.5 months). According to IPT score, patients were divided into quartiles from prognostic score (PS), group I to IV. The study outcomes were end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) 30% reduction. Clinicopathological findings and study outcomes were compared among the study groups. Moreover, compatibility between IPT score and risk stratification for dialysis proposed from JSN, (JSN classification consisted of low, middle, high, and super high risk), was assessed.
Results
At baseline, mean proteinuria and eGFR were 1.5 g/gCr and 60.0 ml/min/1.73 m2, respectively. The proportion of patients receiving corticosteroid was 40.0%, and TSP was 36.6%, respectively. Base level of proteinuria and eGFR reduction were remarkable as IPT-score increased (Proteinuria: PS I/II/III/IV, 0.5/1.1/1.6/3.0 g/gCr, P = 0.0001; eGFR: PS I/II/III/IV, 81.7/63.9/55.1/38.6 ml/min/1.73 m2, Kruskal-Wallis test, P = 0.0001). Degree of M1, E1, S1, and C1-2 lesions in the Oxford classification were comparable among the study groups, whereas the ratios of tubulointerstitial (T1-2) lesions were significantly increased in PS-III or PS-IV compared to PS-I or PS-II groups. Rates of patients receiving steroid therapy or TSP were comparable between those study groups. The proportion of patients who were treated with renin-angiotensin system inhibitor is significantly higher in PS-III or IV group than in PS-I or II group. During a follow-up period, 5.6% and 15.9% of the 145 enrolled patients progressed to the ESKD and eGFR 30% reduction. Incidence of high and super high risk for dialysis in JSN classification was significantly higher in PS-III or IV group compared to PS-I or II group (PS-I/II/III/IV, 2.7/33.3/61.0/83.2%, Fisher exact test, P = 0.000001) (Fig. 1). On Kaplan-Meier analysis, the cumulative probabilities of ESKD and eGFR 30% reduction were significantly higher in group PS-IV than in group PS-I to III (ESKD: Log-rank test, P = 0.0036; eGFR 30% reduction: Log-rank test, P = 0.0011) (Fig. 2). However, there was no significant difference in the cumulative probabilities of ESKD and eGFR 30% reduction among groups of PS I to III. Similarly, in JSN classification, cumulative probabilities of ESKD and eGFR 30% reduction were significantly higher in super high-risk group than other groups (ESKD: P = 0.0003; eGFR 30% reduction: P = 0.0033). No significant difference was detected in the cumulative probabilities of such renal outcomes between low-risk to high-risk groups.
Conclusion
Although Japanese IgAN patients tend to receive early diagnosis and intensive treatments, IPT is useful to assess disease severity and predict renal prognosis as well as JSN classification. Especially, IPT might be helpful to evaluate mild stage or advanced stage of Japanese patients with IgAN.

title: #511 A case of MPO-ANCA positive dense deposit disease (DDD) with normal C3 levels presenting with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) at admission
authors: Keum Hwa Lee; Cheol Ho Park; Beom Jin Lim; Jae Il Shin; Hyung Woo Kim; Ji Hong Kim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Dense Deposit Disease (DDD) is a type of C3 glomerulopathy, a rare form of glomerulonephritis caused by abnormal regulation of the alternative complement pathway. It is primarily diagnosed in children aged between 5 and 15 years and is typically characterized by hypocomplementemia, specifically reduced serum C3 levels, although cases with normal C3 levels comprise only about 10% of all patients. Additionally, the presence of myeloperoxidase anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (MPO-ANCA) in DDD patients is extremely uncommon. We present a case of a DDD patient with normal C3 levels and positive MPO-ANCA, a combination that, to the best of our knowledge, has not been previously reported in either adults or children.
Case
We report the case of a 14-year-old girl who was admitted with severe renal failure requiring hemodialysis. In June 2024, the patient visited a local clinic with bilateral leg edema as the chief complaint, where blood tests revealed elevated BUN and serum creatinine levels of 59.0 mg/dL and 3.1 mg/dL, leading to her referral to our pediatric nephrology outpatient clinic in July 2024. She stated that she had never been informed of any urine abnormalities during previous school health screenings and that this was her first time undergoing a blood test. Laboratory tests performed at our institution revealed elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of 73.3 mg/dL, serum creatinine of 4.84 mg/dL, potassium of 6.0 mmol/L, and hemoglobin of 8.5 g/dL, along with high blood pressure measuring 130/89 mmHg. Initial immunological tests performed after admission revealed normal complement levels, including C3 and C4, but positive MPO-ANCA, raising suspicion for ANCA-associated vasculitis or thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA). However, there were no other organ findings suggestive of ANCA vasculitis, and no hemolytic signs indicated TMA, so hemodialysis was initiated, and a kidney biopsy was performed. The biopsy results confirmed a rare condition known as DDD, characterized by dominant C3 deposits and dark transformation of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM). She was later confirmed to have end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and has been continuing hemodialysis since then. Subsequent follow-up immunologic testing revealed persistent MPO-ANCA positivity, and she is being monitored in collaboration with the pediatric immunology.
Conclusion
This case highlights a rare instance of DDD, where initial C3 levels were normal and MPO-ANCA was positive. In cases of acute renal failure with unknown causes, a kidney biopsy may be necessary for definitive diagnosis. Additionally, the persistence of positive MPO-ANCA raises concerns about the potential for poor renal prognosis and rapid progression, warranting further consideration. On the other hand, it also underscores the necessity of ongoing monitoring, including the potential development of symptoms associated with ANCA vasculitis.

title: #597 Beneficial effects of voclosporin on reducing proteinuria in lupus nephritis and extrarenal effects in SLE: insights form a small cohort with limited follow-up
authors: Marc Patricio Liébana; Josefina Cortés Hernández; Maria José Soler Romeo; María Alejandra Gabaldón; Marina López Martínez; Sheila Bermejo Garcia; Jorge Zamora Carrillo; Héctor Bedoya Orozco; Sara Núñez-Delgado; Oriol Bestard Matamoros; Irene Agraz Pamplona
abstract:
Background and Aims
Voclosporin, an oral calcineurin inhibitor, is a recently approved drug for treating lupus nephritis (LN), one of the severe manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). This medication has been demonstrated to improve renal remission rates, reduce proteinuria, and preserve renal function in patients with active LN, offering an alternative therapeutic approach, especially in patients with predominant proteinuric LN and without having to report CNI plasmatic levels with fewer secondary effects. We aim to present the most relevant data from a single-centre cohort of our patients who have recently started voclosporin and analyse our real-life experience.
Method
We performed a retrospective observational study that included patients diagnosed with LN at our centre who initiated voclosporin between June and September 2024. LN diagnosis was confirmed using a combination of clinical, histological, and serological findings, paying attention to dsDNA antibodies. Patients with both newly diagnosed and relapsing were included.
Data collected included demographic variables (age, sex, comorbidities) and disease characteristics (LN ISN class and clinical severity). Laboratory markers analysed included serum creatinine, hematuria, leukocyturia, and proteinuria. Treatments, including corticosteroids, rituximab, and cyclophosphamide, were recorded. Safety outcomes included infections, hospitalisations, and mortality during follow-up.
Results
We included four patients (2 men and 2 women) with a mean age 51 years. 2 had arterial hypertension, none had diabetes. SLE and LN were diagnosed at a mean age of 45 years. Mean baseline creatinine was 0.6 mg/dL, and mean sCr at diagnosis 0.78 mg/dL, with peak value 1.1 mg/dL during flares; follow-up since voclosporin initiation was 6 months. All patients presented with microscopic hematuria and leukocyturia; mean albuminuria was 2.5 g/24 h. Three of them had extrarenal activity. Induction therapy included methylprednisolone 3g in one patient, rituximab in two patients and cyclophosphamide in other two patients. None of the patients required plasma exchange or renal replacement therapy. Three of the patients presented a class V LN with or without an overlapping proliferative class and one patient presented a IV class alone.
During follow-up, we observed proteinuria showed rapid improvement, reflecting the mechanisms of voclosporin both as antiproteinuric and disease-controlling agent. One patient presented gingival hyperplasia remembering some patients under cyclosporine which has been controlled with mouth hygiene without voclosporin withdrawal and other patient presented a rash in the hip region which voclosporin collaborated in its improvement. There was no need of withdrawal of the drug due to renal function decline during the 6 months of follow-up. Complement C3 and C4 factors also remained stable and antidsDNA titers diminished steadily. There were not infections or death of any patient during follow-up.
Conclusion
Our preliminary findings suggest that voclosporin is effective, safe and valuable and provides a prompt improvement in proteinuria and serologic profile with extrarenal benefits in some cases, especially valuable in refractory patients. Further large-scale studies are needed to determine the long-term efficacy and safety and identify subgroups of patients who may benefit the most from it. Even further, despite its posology, patients maintained good compliance with voclosporin.

title: #1815 A new GN on the block? Case of unknown glomerular disease with organized deposits in a 76 year old Filipino male
authors: Kiara Marie Padua; Beryl Anne Louise Tan; Eladio Miguel Peñaranda; Sonia Chicano
abstract:
Background/Aims
Glomerulonephritis (GN) with organized deposits is a rare cause of nephrotic syndrome due to deposition of immune complexes, fibrils, or organized material within the glomeruli leading to inflammation and renal dysfunction. It presents a histopathological challenge, requiring renal biopsy for accurate diagnosis.
Method
This is a case report on a 76 year old Filipino hypertensive male presented with two-month history of progressive bilateral leg edema. The baseline creatinine was 1.16 mg/dL and a 24-hour urine protein of 10.8 g. Ultrasound showed normal sized kidneys, ascites, and pleural effusion. Cardiac function was normal with small pericardial effusion. Liver panel was normal except for albumin at 2.3, dyslipidemia, and previous Hepatitis A infection. The patient has a slightly elevated CEA, but colonoscopy results were unremarkable. ESR was high, but the rest of the metabolic, immunologic, hematologic, and oncologic workup were unremarkable. Kidney biopsy showed collapsing FSGS (equivocal for Congo red stain); diffuse trace segmental mesangial staining for IgM, C1q, and 1+ focal granular vascular staining for C3; and banded fibrils with frayed ends with a mean periodicity of 32 nm. Empiric rituximab at 1 g IV every two weeks for two doses resulted in a reduction of the 24-hour urine protein to 2.4 g. Patient was then started on tacrolimus.
Results
Based on the results of the histopathology and laboratories, the equivocal Congo stain points to a non-amyloid disease in which immunofluorescence stain showed negative anti-IgG, IgA, fibrinogen, C3, but trace anti-IgM, C1q, which suggests a possible non-immunoglobulin derived GN. Despite extensive investigation, the diagnostic findings do not match any established diagnostic criteria for known disease entities such as fibrillary, immunotactoid, collagenofibrotic, cryoglobulinemic GNs, and MGRS. Additionally, local diagnostic limitations, like enzyme digestion on paraffin tissue to unmask possible immunoglobulins, complicated reaching a definitive diagnosis. From the differential diagnoses, there is still no specific therapy due to its rarity. The response to rituximab, targeting CD20 antigen on B cells, suggests it neutralized an unknown antibody in our patient or hints at a B cell-related pathology despite no primary hematologic disorder identified.
Conclusion
This case challenges our current understanding of GN underscoring the complexity and variability inherent in renal pathology, urging open-mindedness towards atypical presentations for further exploration.

title: #1996 Adherence to ANCA-associated vasculitis guidelines in clinical practice: a survey investigating facilitators and barriers to implementation
authors: Valentina Querin; Tamara Popov; Irmi Neumann; David R W Jayne; Augusto Vaglio; Ingeborg Bajema
abstract:
Background and Aims
Clinical guidelines for ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) have been developed by various scientific societies, such as European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatologists (EULAR), Kidney Disease Improving Clinical Outcomes (KDIGO), and American College of Rheumatology (ACR), through an evidence-based approach that synthesizes the published literature into useful recommendations for clinical practice. However, the level of adherence to these guidelines remains uncertain, and it is unclear what factors may influence a successful implementation strategy. This survey aimed to explore the perceptions and experiences of medical specialists regarding the use of AAV guidelines and to identify the main barriers and facilitators to their implementation in clinical practice.
Method
A cross-sectional survey was conducted among the active members of the European Vasculitis Society (EUVAS) between January 13th and January 24th, 2025, by using an online survey platform. title: #2058 Clinical manifestation and prognosis of membranous nephropathy in aged patients with primary Sjögren syndrome
authors: Fangxing Hou; Linfeng Zou; Xiaoxiao Shi; Peng Xia; Yu-Bing Wen; Yan Qin; Limeng Chen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Primary Sjögren syndrome (pSS) in aged patients complicated with glomerular disease was rare, with only a few reported cases. We tried to analyze the clinicopathological features and prognosis in elderly pSS patients complicated with membranous nephropathy (pSS-MN).
Method
Twenty-one patients (>65 years) admitted to Peking Union Medical College Hospital from January 1993 to September 2022 diagnosed with pSS and MN confirmed by pathology were retrospectively enrolled. The clinicopathological results and prognosis were collected and analysed.
Results
The aged pSS-MN patients were predominantly female (71.4%), with a median age of 69 years, eGFR was lower (70.8 ± 22.7 vs. 96.4 ± 22.5, P = 0.001), ESR (67.7 ± 29.7 vs. 50.0 ± 30.6, P = 0.029) and serum IgA (3.8 (0.9–10.3) vs. 2.7 (0.8–7.4), P = 0.002) were higher in aged patients than 75 non-aged patients and without significant difference in hematologic involvements, 24 h proteinuria, and serum albumin level. The positive serum anti-PLA2R antibody and positive tissue PLA2R antigen were in 37.5% and 100% of patients. Fourteen cases of elderly pSS-MN patients companied with mesangial hyperplasia and interstitial lymphocytic infiltration. All patients were treated with a combination of glucocorticoids, immunosuppressants (cyclophosphamide, calcineurin inhibitors), and/or rituximab with a mean 22-month follow-up, with an overall response rate of 90.5%. The complete response rate was only 15.8%, with a mean response time of 12 (1–12) months.
Conclusion
Elderly patients over 65 years in pSS-MN have poorer renal function and lower complete response rate than non-elderly patients, but there is no difference in partial and overall response rate, and eGFR can be maintained stable with immunosuppressive treatment.

title: #2127 HIV-associated nephropathy in a patient with undetectable viral load: a case report
authors: Mariana Dias Pais; Maria Rita Da Silva Gonçalves Dias; Filipa Rodrigues; Diogo Borges; Ana Messias; Fernando Godinho Pereira; Rita Gouveia; Cristina Vilela
abstract:
Background and Aims
Managing nephropathy in human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infected patients present unique challenges due to the interplay of various contributing factors. These include antiretroviral therapy (ART), prophylactic medication, comorbidities, concurrent infections, and other immune or non-immune associated nephropathies. HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN) incidence significantly decreased following the introduction of ART. Nevertheless, it remains a notable cause of kidney disease, particularly in patients who are undiagnosed or inadequately treated. Genetic predispositions also play a role, as shown by higher prevalence in African ancestry and APOL1 polymorphisms. While high viral loads are a recognized risk factor for HIVAN, it is uncertain whether it is a necessary condition. There are limited case reports documenting the occurrence of HIVAN in patients with low or undetectable HIV viral loads.
Method
This report details an atypical case of HIVAN in an HIV patient with an undetectable viral load.
Results
We present the case of a 52-year-old man of African descent with a history of HIV 1 infection and intermittent periods of nonadherence to ART. He was on a regimen of bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir Alafenamide and had additional comorbidities, including chronic lung disease and active smoking. He had a basal serum creatinine (sCreat) of 1.2 mg/dL and urinalysis two months before admission showed de novo proteinuria ++. The patient presented to the emergency department with a 4-day history of fever, dyspnea and diarrhea. He was diagnosed with influenza A pneumonia and was hospitalized due to hypoxemia, initiating oseltamivir treatment. Other respiratory viruses, such as SARS-CoV-2, were negative. Initial laboratory tests revealed kidney function similar to his basal function, HIV 1 RNA <20 copies/mL, and CD4+ T-cell count of 116 cells/µL. Two days after admission, the patient developed bacterial pneumonia, and piperacillin-tazobactam was initiated. Although the patient showed clinical improvement after 7 days of treatment, he developed worsening renal function (sCreat 9.1 mg/dL, urea 152 mg/dL), reduced diuresis and metabolic acidosis. Urinalysis showed hematuria and nephrotic range proteinuria, with a protein-creatinine ratio of 30.7 g/g and an albumin-creatinine ratio of 13.9 g/g. Serum albumin was 2.5 mg/dL, cholesterol and triglycerides were in the reference range. ART was subsequently changed to ritonavir/darunavir and dolutegravir. Immunologic studies were negative. Complement C3 and C4 levels were normal. Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation ruled out monoclonal gammopathy, and serologies for hepatitis B and C were negative. Renal ultrasound revealed a right kidney measuring 12 cm and a left kidney measuring 14 cm, with increased echogenicity and reduced parenchymal-sinus differentiation. Doppler studies excluded renovascular lesions. Kidney biopsy was performed and showed a collapsing form of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, confirming HIVAN, and 40% tubulointerstitial fibrosis. The patient required hemodialysis due to fluid overload. HIV 1 RNA testing was repeated two weeks after the initial test, revealing 23 copies/mL and CD4+ T-cell count of 338 cells/µL. At one year follow-up, the patient remained without renal recovery, maintained good adherence to ART with controlled viral load. APOL1 genotyping was not performed.
Conclusion
Nephropathy in HIV patients presents a multifactorial challenge. This case highlights the complexity of diagnosing HIVAN, emphasizing the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion even in patients with undetectable or low HIV RNA levels, particularly in the presence of a history of nonadherence to ART and CD4+ T-cell counts below 200 cells/µL. We may hypothesize if the respiratory infection was the trigger for developing the disease, although the patient had prior de novo proteinuria. Renal biopsy remains the gold standard for confirming the diagnosis.

title: #2334 Rituximab based regimen is safe and effective for primary membranous nephropathy patients presented with nephrotic syndrome and advanced renal dysfunction
authors: Yanan Liu; Peng Xia; Yan Qin
abstract:
Background and Aims
The immunosuppressive therapy is often limited for the idiopathic membranous nephropathy (IMN) patients with advanced renal dysfunction due to potential increased risks. This study compared the efficacy and safety of the rituximab-based regimen (RTX) and corticosteroid plus cyclophosphamide (ST-CP) regimen in IMN patients with nephrotic syndrome (NS) and advanced renal dysfunction.
Method
This is a single-center retrospective cohort study. IMN patients with NS and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <45 mL/min/1.73 m2 who received RTX therapy were included. Patients matched with baseline proteinuria, serum albumin and eGFR levels who received the ST-CP regimen were included as a control group. Baseline data and follow-up data were collected.
Results
A total of 64 patients were included, 32 in the RTX group and 32 in the ST-CP group. The baseline median eGFR was 37.34 (IQR 29.01, 40.50) vs 37.45 (IQR 29.76, 42.48) mL/min/1.73 m2 in RTX and ST-CP group, respectively (P = 0.444). At the 12th month, partial and complete remission was achieved in 20 (62.55%) patients in the RTX group, compared to 24 (75%) in the ST-CP group (P = 0.281). Both groups showed stabilization or improvement of eGFR in most patients. In the RTX group, there were 3 fatal events and 5 serious adverse events. While in the ST-CP group, 5 fatal events and 11 serious adverse effects occurred.
Conclusion
Rituximab-based therapy is effective in IMN patients with nephrotic syndrome and advanced renal dysfunction. Compared with the ST-CP regimen, the rituximab-based regimen had a similar efficacy but fewer side effects.

title: #2464 Case report of a granulomatous interstitial nephritis in chronic lymphocytic leukemia
authors: Aurélie Huber; Lena Berchtold; Sophie de Seigneux
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is known for involving extranodal sites, but its manifestation as direct kidney infiltration leading to significant renal dysfunction and granulomatous interstitial nephritis (GIN) remains a rarity. This report underscores the diagnostic challenges and highlights the necessity of considering CLL as an etiology in patients with renal dysfunction and a history of CLL, providing insights into a unique clinical scenario of CLL-related GIN.
Method
We present a detailed case study of a patient.
Results
A 70-year-old patient with a history of Parkinson's disease, untreated B-cell CLL, and stage 4 chronic kidney disease was admitted due to worsening renal function. At admission, creatinine levels had risen sharply to 4.76 mg/dL from 2.95 mg/dL three months prior, with a glomerular filtration rate of 13 mL/min/1.73 m² and urea levels at 31 mmol/L. Urinalysis showed non-glomerular proteinuria (0.8 g/24 h) with severe albuminuria (albumin-creatinine ratio of 62 mg/mmol). Viral serologies were negative, and no significant paraproteinemia or autoantibodies (anti-nuclear, anti-ANCA) were detected; complement levels were normal. Renal imaging techniques such as scintigraphy and echography indicated bilateral renal dysfunction without structural abnormalities, and PET-CT scans suggested indolent lymphoma. A renal biopsy revealed chronic, granulomatous tubulointerstitial nephritis without necrosis. Differential diagnoses such as sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, and drug-induced nephritis were systematically excluded, implicating CLL as the underlying cause. The diagnosis was confirmed by typical immunostaining (CD20+, CD5+, CD23+, Cycline D1−). Remarkably, post-corticotherapy, the patient's renal function returned to baseline levels.
Conclusion
This case report enhances the understanding of CLL's potential to cause GIN and subsequent renal failure, emphasizing the importance of considering CLL in the differential diagnosis of unexplained renal dysfunction in patients with a known history of CLL. It also illustrates the efficacy of corticotherapy in reversing renal decline in such contexts.

title: #2532 Patient characteristics and treatment patterns in ANCA-associated vasculitis: an observational study based on the DEMONSTRATE database, Uppsala, Sweden
authors: Klytaimnistra Voudouri; Ann Knight; Johanna Dahlqvist; Milica Uhde; Maarit Korkeila Liden; Thomas Cars; Matilda Almstedt; Maria K Svensson
abstract:
Background and Aims
ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) are rare but severe autoimmune conditions characterized by inflammation and damage to small- and medium-sized blood vessels. Any organ can be affected by inflammation, including the kidneys, lungs, and upper respiratory tract. Using an extensive observational data source (DEMONSTRATE), this study aimed to explore the management of AAV in clinical practice by evaluating patient characteristics and treatment trends.
Method
This observational study, utilizing the DEMONSTRATE database, identified all patients aged 18 years or older in Region Uppsala, Sweden, with at least two recorded diagnoses of AAV between January 1, 2007, and December 31, 2022. Diagnoses were based on ICD codes M31.3 (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, GPA) and M31.7 (microscopic polyangiitis, MPA). The study population was restricted to patients diagnosed within the specialties of Nephrology, Rheumatology, Ear-Nose-Throat, Pulmonary Medicine, and Internal Medicine. Descriptive statistics were applied to analyze patient characteristics and treatment patterns for AAV, focusing on two distinct time periods, 2016–2018 and 2019–2022, to evaluate potential changes in treatment approaches over time.
Results
A total of 150 patients were identified: 83 (55%) with GPA and 67 (45%) with MPA. Patients diagnosed with GPA were generally younger, with a median age of 63.9 years (IQR 55.6–73.1), compared to a median age of 71.9 years (IQR 64.4–77.7) for patients with MPA (Table 1). GPA was predominantly diagnosed in Rheumatology department, while MPA was primarily diagnosed in Nephrology department (Table 1). Patients with MPA had a higher comorbidity burden compared to those with GPA, with higher rates of heart failure (20.9% vs. 3.6%), hypertension (67.2% vs. 37.3%), and diabetes (26.9% vs. 15.7%). At the time of diagnosis, MPA patients also had substantially lower median eGFR levels (25.8, IQR 19.1–44.9) compared to GPA patients (67.9, IQR 43.6–84.4), reflecting more severe kidney involvement at diagnosis. Around the time of diagnosis, there was an increase in the use of intravenous corticosteroids from 2016–2018 (45.2% of patients) to 2019–2022 (73.5% of patients). Similarly, rituximab use increased from 16.1% (2016–2018) to 49.0% (2019–2022), while cyclophosphamide use showed a slight decrease from 38.7% (2016–2018) to 34.7% (2019–2022) (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
These findings suggest a shift in treatment for AAV patients in region Uppsala, with more use of intravenous corticosteroids and rituximab in recent years. The study also highlights differences in patient characteristics and comorbidity profiles between patients with GPA and MPA, which may influence treatment decisions and outcomes.

title: #2592 Evaluating the safety and impact of kidney biopsy in elderly patients
authors: Juliana Francisca Da Costa e Silva Barbosa Damas; Filipa Trigo; Ana Pereira Piedade; Mário Góis; Helena Viana; Cristina Rego de Freitas Mendes Jorge
abstract:
Background and Aims
The prevalence of chronic kidney disease (CKD) continues to rise alongside the aging population and its associated comorbidities. Kidney biopsy (KB) remains an essential diagnostic procedure for identifying the cause of renal disease, guiding prognosis, and informing therapeutic decisions. However, in patients older than 80 years, KB is often avoided due to potential complications, despite its value in optimizing targeted treatment strategies. This study evaluates the risks, histopathological findings, and therapeutic outcomes associated with KB in a Portuguese cohort aged >80 years.
Method
A multicenter retrospective observational study was conducted, including patients aged ≥80 years who underwent KB between January 2015 and March 2024. Demographic, clinical, and histopathological data were analyzed, alongside immediate complications, dialysis initiation timing, and therapeutic changes. Statistical analysis was performed using IBM® SPSS® Statistics.
Results
A total of 71 patients (52.1% female) with a median age of 83 years (range: 80–92) were included. The most common indications for KB were rapidly progressive renal insufficiency (21.1%) and nephrotic syndrome (22.5%). Histopathological findings identified ANCA-associated vasculitis (15.5%) as the most frequent diagnosis, followed by IgA nephropathy (9.9%) and diabetic nephropathy (7.0%). Immediate complications occurred in 23.9% of patients, predominantly hematomas (14.1%), with no major adverse outcomes.
KB findings directly influenced therapeutic decisions in 23 patients (32.4%), leading to specific interventions, including targeted immunosuppression. Six patients (8.5%) initiated renal replacement therapy (RRT) within six months after the procedure, including one patient who required RRT initiation after 12 months. Among patients who started RRT, 2 out of 6 (33.3%) successfully discontinued therapy, indicating transient renal dysfunction. Mortality at one-year post-KB was recorded in 23 patients (32.4%), with most deaths attributed to the progression of renal or systemic disease rather than procedural or therapeutical complications.
Conclusion
Despite the inherent risks, KB in patients aged >80 years provides significant diagnostic and prognostic value, guiding tailored therapeutic strategies. Complication rates were consistent with those reported in younger cohorts, emphasizing the feasibility of the procedure when risks are carefully weighed against potential benefits. These findings highlight the critical role of KB in this age group, allowing for more accurate diagnoses and enabling personalized therapeutic and immunosuppressive strategies.

Background and Aims
The prevalence of chronic kidney disease (CKD) continues to rise alongside the aging population and its associated comorbidities. Kidney biopsy (KB) remains an essential diagnostic procedure for identifying the cause of renal disease, guiding prognosis, and informing therapeutic decisions. However, in patients older than 80 years, KB is often avoided due to potential complications, despite its value in optimizing targeted treatment strategies. This study evaluates the risks, histopathological findings, and therapeutic outcomes associated with KB in a Portuguese cohort aged >80 years.
Method
A multicenter retrospective observational study was conducted, including patients aged ≥80 years who underwent KB between January 2015 and March 2024. Demographic, clinical, and histopathological data were analyzed, alongside immediate complications, dialysis initiation timing, and therapeutic changes. Statistical analysis was performed using IBM® SPSS® Statistics.
Results
A total of 71 patients (52.1% female) with a median age of 83 years (range: 80–92) were included. The most common indications for KB were rapidly progressive renal insufficiency (21.1%) and nephrotic syndrome (22.5%). Histopathological findings identified ANCA-associated vasculitis (15.5%) as the most frequent diagnosis, followed by IgA nephropathy (9.9%) and diabetic nephropathy (7.0%). Immediate complications occurred in 23.9% of patients, predominantly hematomas (14.1%), with no major adverse outcomes.
KB findings directly influenced therapeutic decisions in 23 patients (32.4%), leading to specific interventions, including targeted immunosuppression. Six patients (8.5%) initiated renal replacement therapy (RRT) within six months after the procedure, including one patient who required RRT initiation after 12 months. Among patients who started RRT, 2 out of 6 (33.3%) successfully discontinued therapy, indicating transient renal dysfunction. Mortality at one-year post-KB was recorded in 23 patients (32.4%), with most deaths attributed to the progression of renal or systemic disease rather than procedural or therapeutical complications.
Conclusion
Despite the inherent risks, KB in patients aged >80 years provides significant diagnostic and prognostic value, guiding tailored therapeutic strategies. Complication rates were consistent with those reported in younger cohorts, emphasizing the feasibility of the procedure when risks are carefully weighed against potential benefits. These findings highlight the critical role of KB in this age group, allowing for more accurate diagnoses and enabling personalized therapeutic and immunosuppressive strategies.

title: #2604 A delayed diagnosis of pauci-immune glomerulonephritis and vasculitis is associated with increased severity of disease presentation and higher probability of death
authors: Sophia Lionaki; Chrysanthi Skalioti; Evaggelia Pantzopoulou; Christodoula Kourtidou; Luiza Gkika-Zervou; Maria Koukoulaki; Synodi Zermpala; Evangelos Papachristou; George Moustakas; Ioannis Petrakis; Stylianos Panagoutsos; Smaragdi Marinaki
abstract:
Background and Aims
It has been repeatedly suggested that significant delays in diagnosing pauci-immune glomerulonephritis (PIGN) and vasculitis are common and have a negative effect in the long term of patients. This study aimed to investigate the impact, if any of the delay in diagnosing PIGN and vasculitis in disease presentation and outcome.
Method
Included patients should be older than 16 years, with biopsy-proven PIGN, who were followed for a minimum of 12 months or until end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) or death, and received the standard immunosuppressive therapy. We recorded demographics, disease related characteristics and short and long-term outcomes including response to therapy, treatment resistance, remission, ESKD, and death from any cause. The observation period started when the patients entered the medical system until ESKD i.e. initiation of chronic dialysis, or death or the last visit to the nephrology clinic. All patients were tested for ANCA by immunofluorescence or ELISA or both. Clinical phenotypes were assigned according to the Chapel Hill vasculitides nomenclature consensus conference. Disease activity was estimated using the BVAS score. Patients were categorized with respect to the management following the 1st medical assessment in “delayed” (non-associated with the disease management) and “non-delayed” diagnosis (subsequent workup led to prompt diagnosis or direct nephrology referral).
Results
148 patients with a mean age of 61.8 (±13.9) years were included, of whom 85 (57.4%) were males and 147 (99.3%) were Caucasians. Overall, 141 (95.8%) were positive for ANCA and 88 (62.4%) had P/MPO-ANCA. 43 patients were categorized as “delayed” diagnosis and 102 as “non-delayed”. The proportion of patients with renal limited disease was 16,3% for the “delayed” group vs. 26.3% for the “non-delayed” group (P = 0.19). The time to the diagnostic kidney biopsy from the 1st medical assessment was 105.5 (±21.6) days for the “delayed” diagnosis group and 20.1 (±8.5) days for the “non-delayed” (P < 0.0001). Serum creatinine at 1st medical assessment was similar between patients with “delayed” and “non-delayed” diagnosis [2.4 (±2.6) mg/dl vs. 2.7 (±1.8) mg/dl] but measurement at diagnosis revealed a significant increase for patients with “delayed” diagnosis when compared with their value at 1st assessment [3.8 (±2.8) mg/dl, P = 0.03], while this was not observed for patients with “non-delayed” diagnosis of PIGN. Also, BVAS at diagnosis was shown significantly increased in the “delayed” diagnosis group when compared with the corresponding estimate of the same group at the 1st assessment [12.7 (±6.9) vs. 19.2 (±6.6), P = 0.0001], while this increase was not observed in the “non-delayed” diagnosis group. The probability of response to therapy was not shown different between groups but the death rate was significantly higher in the “delayed” diagnosis patients compared to the non-delayed group (12.2 vs. 2.2, P = 0.0125).
Conclusion
According to our findings patients with PIGN who experience significant diagnostic delays are more likely to start treatment with advanced disease severity and face higher probability of death.
