title: #2018 Real-world effectiveness and safety of voclosporin in the treatment of lupus nephritis with poor prognostic clinical and histological factors
authors: Marc Xipell Font; Cecilia Garbarino; Raul Jordà; Elena Guillén Olmos; Maria Iraola; Maria Argudo; Miquel Blasco Pelicano; Jose A Gómez-Puerta; Ricard Cervera; Gerard Espinosa; Luis Fernando Quintana Porras
abstract:
Background and Aims
Lupus nephritis (LN), a serious complication of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), impacts patients' quality of life and survival. Voclosporin (VCS), a novel calcineurin inhibitor, has demonstrated efficacy in clinical trials for LN classes III, IV, and V. However, its real-world effectiveness, safety, and adherence require further study. This study aims to describe the outcomes of LN patients who received VCS due to inadequate renal remission or poor prognostic histological criteria. Additionally, it evaluates the adverse event profile during VCS treatment.
Method
A retrospective and descriptive analysis was conducted on a series of patients followed up in the Systemic Autoimmune Diseases and Nephrology Unit of Hospital Clínic, who were affected by LN and received treatment with VCS due to refractoriness to treatment or poor histological prognostic criteria. Demographic, clinical, and analytical data were collected at the start of treatment with VCS and during follow-up. Data are presented as mean ± SD or median [IQR].
Results
Five patients were identified (80% women, mean age 32.2 ± 9.1 years). All had joint involvement, three had skin involvement, and two had serositis and hematological involvement. VCS was used after treatment failure in three patients, while two received it as first-line therapy due to poor prognostic histological factors.
The median time on VCS treatment was 7 [4–8] months with a median of 20 (5.5–52.5) months from the last LN flare diagnosis to VCS initiation. LN classifications included two class IV, one class IV+V, one class III with podocyte lesions in electron microscopy, and one class I with lupus podocytopathy. Excluding the class I patient, median renal biopsy activity and chronicity indices were 7 [3.5–11] and 0.5 [0–2], respectively. One patient had incident LN, while the others had recurrent LN.
For the treatment of the current LN episode, before starting VCS, one patient had been treated with a combination of mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) and tacrolimus; another had received cyclophosphamide, MMF, tacrolimus, belimumab, and rituximab; a third had received MMF, tacrolimus, and rituximab; while the remaining two patients started VCS immediately after cyclophosphamide (ELNT schedule) as first-line therapy due to poor prognostic histological criteria. At the time of VCS initiation, all patients were on hydroxychloroquine, and three were receiving prednisone (median: 5 mg/day); three patients were switched from MMF and tacrolimus to MMF and VCS, while the remaining two started VCS immediately after cyclophosphamide as first-line therapy. Four patients were on ACE inhibitors and SGLT-2 inhibitors, while one patient was receiving angiotensin receptor blockers, all at the maximum needed and tolerated dose. In fact, nephroprotective treatment was reduced in two patients given the good response. One patient was on semaglutide.
After starting VCS, all patients showed a reduction in proteinuria (UPCR) (Fig. 1). Median proteinuria at the start of VCS was 1793 [1697–5240] mg/g. The median reduction in UPCR from the start of VCS to the last analytical control was -1033 mg/g [357.5–4376]. Renal function (eGFR) remained stable in all patients. The median C3 levels increased from 0.73 [0.61–0.98] g/L at the time of starting VCS to 0.85 [0.74–1.16] g/L, at last visit. No extrarenal lupus flares were observed, and the safety profile of VCS was favorable, with no adverse events or treatment discontinuation. Adherence to treatment was 98.1% [74.1–99.68], assessed by the Department of Pharmacy based on the count of medication dispensed and consumed. These data will be updated during the ongoing patient follow-up at the time of the results presentation.
Conclusion
VCS was effective, in the short term, for optimizing treatment in LN patients with incomplete renal remission despite treatment or with poor prognostic histological factors, in real-world settings and with a good safety and adherence profile. Further studies are needed to evaluate its impact in real-world clinical scenarios. Moreover, to our knowledge, this cohort include the first report of a patient with lupus podocytopathy treated with VCS.

title: #2159 The rare within the uncommon; highlighting the broad spectrum of clinical presentations of podocytopathies
authors: Teresa Ronda Serrat; Paula Ardura; Aya Moultamis; Ana Luisa Martins Da Silva; Kenia Cobo Campuzano; Carlos Merizalde; Raquel Julia Gordillo Martín; Jennypher Margaret Navas Alfonzo; Astrid Rodriguez Gomez; Armando Coca Rojo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Podocytopathies are caused by direct or indirect injury to podocytes and can be categorized into four main types: diffuse mesangial sclerosis, minimal changes, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and collapsing glomerulopathy. Genetic variants, infections, immune diseases, exposure to toxics, as well as obesity, or a combination of any of them, can induce podocytopathies. Podocyte injury translates into proteinuria and, in many cases, nephrotic syndrome. As such, proteinuria and its associated symptoms are usually the main or even only symptom of these diseases. Here we present a patient with an uncommon clinical presentation of a podocytopathy with low-grade proteinuria.
Results
A 15-year-old male without past medical history, family history of renal disease or pre-episode renal tests presented with three days of fever and odynophagia. His primary care physician performed a basic lab test which showed serum creatinine (SCr): 1.53 mg/dL and hypertransaminasemia. The patient was taken to the hospital, were he tested positive for Epstein-Barr viral capsid antigen IgG and IgM. Subsequent testing included urinary albumin to creatinine ratio (UACR) of 505 mg/g and abdominal ultrasound with hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, as well 9.6 cm kidneys with loss of corticomedullary differentiation. The patient received oral prednisone for three weeks, with rapid improvement of symptoms and hypertransaminasemia but, due to lack of renal recovery, he was referred to nephrology for further study.
SCr remained steady between 1.4–1.6 mg/dL, with UACR of 250–350 mg/g, non-dysmorphic hematuria of up to 1–3 erythrocytes per field and a 24 h urinary protein excretion of 660 mg.
Follow-up tests revealed normal thyroid function, HbA1c levels, serum and urinary proteinograms, viral serologic testing and negative ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM and complement tests. Genetic testing was performed; the patient was found to be an heterozygous carrier of the NM_000092.4:c.193G>A, NP_000083.3:p.G65S variant in the COL4A4 gene, classified as possibly pathogenic in relation to the development of Alport syndrome and/or benign familial hematuria. A renal biopsy was performed; the highlighted results included notable glomerular hypertrophy and focal mesangial proliferative nephropathy without any image of glomerular sclerosis. No deposits of any kind were observed in immunofluorescence. Diffuse foot process effacement (>80%), consistent with podocytopathy with mesangial hyperplasia was observed in electron microscopy. A monozygotic twin brother of the patient was screened for renal dysfunction, with negative results.
The patient was started on antiproteinuric therapy with dapagliflozin and cardiovascular risk factor management. No RASi was initiated due to low blood pressure. SCr and UACR remained stable at 1.4–1.5 mg/dL and 200 mg/g respectively during the following 12 months. The patient has remained asymptomatic during this period.
Conclusion
Podocytopathy-related histologic patterns describe unspecific lesions that do not define a precise diagnosis. Our case presented with histologic findings that could be described as an early-onset diffuse mesangial sclerosis, one of the more uncommon variants of podocytopathies, with an also uncommon presentation, including significant renal impairment, low-grade proteinuria, no associated symptoms an unremarkable genetic testing. Repeat biopsies could provide additional information on the nature and evolution of these rare diseases, as well as inform about the patterns of response to treatment strategies.

Background and Aims
Podocytopathies are caused by direct or indirect injury to podocytes and can be categorized into four main types: diffuse mesangial sclerosis, minimal changes, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and collapsing glomerulopathy. Genetic variants, infections, immune diseases, exposure to toxics, as well as obesity, or a combination of any of them, can induce podocytopathies. Podocyte injury translates into proteinuria and, in many cases, nephrotic syndrome. As such, proteinuria and its associated symptoms are usually the main or even only symptom of these diseases. Here we present a patient with an uncommon clinical presentation of a podocytopathy with low-grade proteinuria.
Results
A 15-year-old male without past medical history, family history of renal disease or pre-episode renal tests presented with three days of fever and odynophagia. His primary care physician performed a basic lab test which showed serum creatinine (SCr): 1.53 mg/dL and hypertransaminasemia. The patient was taken to the hospital, were he tested positive for Epstein-Barr viral capsid antigen IgG and IgM. Subsequent testing included urinary albumin to creatinine ratio (UACR) of 505 mg/g and abdominal ultrasound with hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, as well 9.6 cm kidneys with loss of corticomedullary differentiation. The patient received oral prednisone for three weeks, with rapid improvement of symptoms and hypertransaminasemia but, due to lack of renal recovery, he was referred to nephrology for further study.
SCr remained steady between 1.4–1.6 mg/dL, with UACR of 250–350 mg/g, non-dysmorphic hematuria of up to 1–3 erythrocytes per field and a 24 h urinary protein excretion of 660 mg.
Follow-up tests revealed normal thyroid function, HbA1c levels, serum and urinary proteinograms, viral serologic testing and negative ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM and complement tests. Genetic testing was performed; the patient was found to be an heterozygous carrier of the NM_000092.4:c.193G>A, NP_000083.3:p.G65S variant in the COL4A4 gene, classified as possibly pathogenic in relation to the development of Alport syndrome and/or benign familial hematuria. A renal biopsy was performed; the highlighted results included notable glomerular hypertrophy and focal mesangial proliferative nephropathy without any image of glomerular sclerosis. No deposits of any kind were observed in immunofluorescence. Diffuse foot process effacement (>80%), consistent with podocytopathy with mesangial hyperplasia was observed in electron microscopy. A monozygotic twin brother of the patient was screened for renal dysfunction, with negative results.
The patient was started on antiproteinuric therapy with dapagliflozin and cardiovascular risk factor management. No RASi was initiated due to low blood pressure. SCr and UACR remained stable at 1.4–1.5 mg/dL and 200 mg/g respectively during the following 12 months. The patient has remained asymptomatic during this period.
Conclusion
Podocytopathy-related histologic patterns describe unspecific lesions that do not define a precise diagnosis. Our case presented with histologic findings that could be described as an early-onset diffuse mesangial sclerosis, one of the more uncommon variants of podocytopathies, with an also uncommon presentation, including significant renal impairment, low-grade proteinuria, no associated symptoms an unremarkable genetic testing. Repeat biopsies could provide additional information on the nature and evolution of these rare diseases, as well as inform about the patterns of response to treatment strategies.

title: #2246 Renal biopsy and clinical frailty in elderly renal disease patients
authors: Fumika Taki; Takuya Fujimaru; Yugo Ito; Masahiko Nagahama; Michiko Suzuki
abstract:
Background and Aims
With the aging of the population, the number of elderly patients with renal disease are increasing. The safety of renal biopsy in these patients and its impact on treatment strategy is still little known. Also, the frailty should also be taken into consideration for the elderly management. The aim of this study is to evaluate the impact of renal biopsy for the elderly.
Method
Patients aged 60 years or older who underwent renal biopsy at St. Luke's International Hospital, Tokyo, Japan, between January 2013 and December 2023 were studied. Patients' age, gender, comorbidities, laboratory data, and clinical conditions were extracted from medical records. For the analysis, patients were stratified in 10-year age increments, and the following data were examined; complication rate, concordance rate between clinical and pathological diagnosis, and renal and life prognosis. Also, we assessed the frailty of these patients, by Cardiovascular Health Study Frailty Index. From the indexes we classified the patients as robust (score = 0), prefrail (score = 1–2), and frail (score = 3–5).
Results
From January 2013 to December 2023, 144 elderly patients underwent renal biopsy in our hospital. Of these, 69 (47%) were in their 60s, 62 (40%) in their 70s, and 19 (13%) in their 80s or older, Ninety six (67%) were male, 82 (57%) had nephrotic proteinuria, and their baseline eGFR was 36.8 ± 5.9 mg/dl/min, Complication after biopsy occurred in 2 patients (1.3%), there are no complication in over 80s patients. Concordance rate between clinical and pathological diagnosis was 109 (76%). Average of Frailty Index score was 3.8 ± 1.2 in overall, and this scale score decreases, as age increases; 60 s, 3.9 ± 1.1, 70 s, 3.5 ± 0.9, 80 s, 2.3 ± 1.2. Twenty-three patients initiated dialysis and 15 patients died within a year, after the biopsy.
Conclusion
The results suggest that renal biopsy can be performed safely and contributes to select appropriate treatment in elderly patients. Those who are older and able to perform renal biopsies are less frail, only relatively healthy older adults may be undergoing renal biopsy. More large population study is in need.

title: #3695 Contemporary epidemiological analysis of adult inaugural nephrotic syndrome: thirteen-year experience of a tertiary center
authors: Rafael Henriques de Figueiredo; Joana Andrade Lopes; Bernardo Faria; Ricardo Neto; Joao M Frazao; Luís Carlos Ferreira Mendonça
abstract:
Background and Aims
Nephrotic syndromes (NS) are defined by nephrotic range proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and edema. According to classical epidemiological studies, membranous glomerulonephritis (MGN) is the leading cause of NS, followed by other etiologies. To understand local epidemiology, we studied our NS population based on 13 years of experience.
Method
We conducted an observational and retrospective study at Hospital São João, between 2010 and 2022. Adult patients with inaugural presenting and first biopsy nephrotic syndrome were included. Patient data was collected anonymously from their electronic health record namely patient-related characteristics (demographic variables and comorbidities), analytical values at diagnosis (serum albumin, serum creatinine, 24 h-proteinuria at diagnosis and the presence of hematuria), and the number of patients that died or required dialysis at diagnosis. The primary objective was to perform an epidemiological characterization the adult patient presenting with inaugural nephrotic syndrome. We further stratified the analysis by the main pathological entities and analyzed temporal tendencies. Analysis was performed using SPSS® software v28.0.1.0.
Results
Two hundred and fifty-four adults with inaugural presentation and first biopsy nephrotic syndrome were included, corresponding to a median 2.1 biopsies per 100.000 habitants. One hundred and forty-three (56.3%) patients were males, 250 (98.4%) were Caucasian, and the median age was 55.5 years. Sixty-eight (26.8%) patients had previous CKD, 58 (22.8%) were diabetic, and 24 (9.4%) had neoplasia of which 13 (5.1%) were active. Median serum creatinine, serum albumin, and proteinuria at diagnosis were 1.49 mg/dL, 25.2 g/L and 6.66 g, respectively. (Micro)hematuria was observed in 143 (56.3%) patients. Forty patients (15.7%) required dialysis and 2 (0.8%) died at diagnosis. Focal Segmental Glomerular Sclerosis (FSGS)/Minimal Change Disease (MCD) was the most represented etiology with 54 (21.3%) patients, followed by membranous glomerulonephritis (MGN) (18.9%), lupus nephritis (9.8%), amyloidosis (9.8%), IgA nephropathy (8.7%) and vasculitis (7.5%). Stratifying by age, FSGS/MCD and MGN were the two most frequent etiologies both before and after 55 years, followed by lupus nephritis [before 55 years] and amyloidosis [after 55]. Stratifying by biopsy representation and temporal trends, FSGS/MCD and MGN were also the most represented with a median of 20% and 17.6% biopsies per year.
Conclusion
Despite some literature pointing MGN as the most frequent cause of adult NS, in our center FSGS/MCD were the dominant cause of NS, both in younger (≤55 years) and older (>55 years) patients.

title: #3733 Predictors of disease progression in primary membranous nephropathy
authors: Beatriz Silva; Beatriz de Barros; Sandra Pereira; Ana Cunha; Pedro Pereira; Sofia Correia; Andreia Campos; Josefina Santos
abstract:
Background and Aims
Primary membranous nephropathy (PMN) is a common etiology of nephrotic syndrome in adults and can have a highly variable disease course. Several clinical and histopathological markers have been proposed as potential predictors of long-term outcomes. Understanding how these factors impact disease prognosis may facilitate the implementation of personalized treatment strategies. This study aims to identify predictors of adverse outcomes in PMN.
Method
We conducted a retrospective analysis of 35 patients diagnosed with PMN between 2007 and 2022 at a tertiary center. Clinical and biochemical characteristics, along with kidney biopsy results, were assessed at baseline. Patients were divided into favorable and unfavorable outcome groups based on estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), proteinuria, progression to end-stage renal disease or death at two years of follow-up. In addition to this classification, patients were categorized according to proteinuria levels higher or lower than 1 g/g at two years of follow-up.
Results
Patients with adverse disease progression experienced significantly more thromboembolic events (29% vs. 0%, P = 0.019), and had a higher frequency of PLA2R positivity (90% vs. 42%, P = 0.033) at diagnosis. Univariate analysis revealed that both higher creatinine levels (OR = 3.854, 95% CI: 1.039–14.303, P = 0.044) and PLA2R positivity (OR = 12.0, 95% CI: 1.178–122.274, P = 0.036) at diagnosis were significantly associated with unfavorable disease progression. In the multivariate logistic regression model, only PLA2R positivity remained significantly associated with adverse outcomes (OR = 11.31, 95% CI: 1.039–123.286, P = 0.016). Analysis of proteinuria at two years revealed that PLA2R levels at diagnosis were significantly higher in patients with proteinuria >1 g/g (U = 28, P = 0.038), and were associated with proteinuria >1 g/g at two years in the univariate analysis (OR = 1.010, 95% CI: 1.000–1.019, P = 0.040). Notably, histopathological characteristics had no impact on the results at two years.
Conclusion
PLA2R positivity is a predictor of disease progression, with higher PLA2R levels correlating with the development of significant proteinuria at two years of follow-up. This finding suggests that immune-mediated mechanisms, particularly those involving PLA2R, modulate the clinical response, potentially influencing disease course and therapeutic outcomes. In contrast, histopathological features, although useful for diagnosis, have limited prognostic value in predicting long-term outcomes.

title: #3765 Hereditary minimal change disease (MCD): about three cases reports
authors: Manel Zakhama; Sirine Bchir; Meriem Ben Salem; Mouna Hamouda; Nouha Ben Mahmoud; Manel Ben Salah; Ahmed Letaief; Habib Skhiri
abstract:
Background and Aims
Minimal change disease (MCD) is a frequent cause of nephrotic syndrome. Although often idiopathic, secondary cases or rare hereditary forms may be observed. Only rare cases of familial forms of MCD have been reported and most of them only in one generation.
Method
We describe three siblings in three different family presenting with nephrotic syndrome with minimal change disease (MCD).
Results
Case 1: An 18-year-old girl followed since the age of 6 for an impur nephrotic syndrome with hypertension. The initial presentation was a severe nephrotic syndrome, which was initially corticosteroid-dependent and later became corticosteroid-resistant. The diagnosis of MCD was confirmed with Renal Biopsy. She was treated with cyclophosphamide for 1 year, but she showed resistance, leading to a switch to MMF. Frequent relapses occurred, prompting a switch to cyclosporine. Frequent relapses with worsening renal function led to a second renal biopsy, which revealed focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). In addition, Her brother has been followed since the age of 6 years also for a impur nephrotic syndrome with hypertension and corticosteroid resistance. The diagnosis of MCD was confirmed also with Renal Biopsy and he was treated with MMF, then cyclosporine.
Case 2: A 26-year-old woman followed since 2002 for pure nephrotic syndrome with corticosteroid dependence and frequent relapses. The First Renal Biopsy has proven MCD. Lost to follow-up since 2008, she was hospitalized in 2023 for a relapse of pure nephrotic syndrome and the diagnosis of MCD was confirmed with a second renal biopsy. Her brother, 18 years old, has been followed since the age of 4 for corticosteroid-dependent pure nephrotic syndrome and the MCD was proven also with renal biopsy.
Case 3: A 22-year-old woman followed since the age of 4 for severe corticosteroid-dependent pure nephrotic syndrome, cyclosporine-dependent, and MMF-dependent. After five relapse she was treated with rituximab (RTX). Her brother, 11 years old, has been followed since the age of 4 for corticosteroid-dependent and cyclosporine-dependent pure nephrotic syndrome. The diagnosis of MCD was confirmed with Renal Biopsy with this sibling.
Conclusion
Familial form of MCD is extremely rare. Genetic testing is important to confirm the diagnosis guide therapeutic decisions, and provide a better understanding of the mode of transmission; but no genetic defect has been identified yet. Although, in recent study, anti-nephrin autoantibodies are increasingly implicated with nephrotic syndrome and especially MCD. In addition to the genetic testing, a relation with this new markers of disease activity must be explored.

title: #3794 Distress tolerance in lupus nephritis: the relationship between psychological resilience and disease severity
authors: Zohreh Gholizadeh Ghozloujeh; Amir Abdipour; Sayna Norouzi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is known to significantly impact patients’ stress levels and coping mechanisms, particularly in its severe manifestation as lupus nephritis (LN). While psychosocial factors like perceived stress and coping strategies influence disease activity and quality of life, their specific contributions remain unclear. Distress tolerance; the capacity to endure negative emotional states; may be a key determinant of resilience in LN patients, yet it remains underexplored despite its potential clinical relevance.
This study evaluates distress tolerance in LN patients using the Distress Tolerance Scale (DTS) , examining its associations with demographic, clinical, and disease activity factors to enhance understanding of psychosocial influences on disease burden.
Method
This cross-sectional study was conducted at Loma Linda University Medical Center and included 20 adult patients aged ≥18 years with biopsy-confirmed LN. Data collected during routine clinic visits included demographic (age, sex, employment status), clinical (SLE Disease Activity Index, SLEDAI), and psychosocial variables assessed using the Distress Tolerance Scale (adjusted 1–5 scale; higher scores indicate greater distress sensitivity and lower coping ability). Descriptive statistics summarized patient characteristics, and normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Group differences were analyzed using t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables and chi-square tests for categorical variables. Correlations between DTS and SLEDAI were examined, and multiple linear regression evaluated predictors of distress sensitivity.
Results
This interim analysis included 20 LN patients, with a mean age of 41.2 years (SD = 13.7). The cohort was predominantly female (75%, n = 15). Patients were stratified by disease activity using the SLEDAI, with 45% (n = 9) classified as mild, 40% (n = 8) as moderate, and 15% (n = 3) as severe. Female patients exhibited significantly higher SLEDAI scores compared to males (mean: 8.6 ± 4.8 vs. 2.4 ± 3.5, P = 0.012). However, distress sensitivity scores (DTS) did not differ significantly by sex (mean: 2.4 ± 0.5 in females vs. 2.8 ± 1.2 in males, P > 0.05).
Median DTS scores across SLEDAI severity groups were 2.45 (IQR: 1.83–2.95) in mild disease, 2.60 (IQR: 1.60–3.30) in moderate disease, and 2.20 (IQR: 1.80–2.98) in severe disease, with no statistically significant differences observed (P > 0.05). Patients who were unemployed (55%, n = 11) had higher median SLEDAI scores (8.0, IQR: 5.0–9.0) compared to employed patients (4.0, IQR: 0.0–11.75), though this difference was not significant (P > 0.05). Similarly, DTS scores were comparable between unemployed (median: 2.5, IQR: 1.8–2.6) and employed patients (median: 2.9, IQR: 1.75–3.15, P > 0.05).
A multiple linear regression model assessing predictors of DTS, including sex, employment status, SLEDAI, and age, identified no significant predictors. Higher SLEDAI scores showed a non-significant positive association with distress sensitivity (B = 0.029, P = 0.455), while age (B = −0.005, P = 0.728), female sex (B = −0.602, P = 0.259), and employment status (B = 0.116, P = 0.793) also did not significantly influence DTS. The results suggest that distress sensitivity in LN patients was not significantly associated with demographic or clinical variables; however, the limited sample size may have reduced statistical power, and larger studies are needed to further elucidate these relationships.
Conclusion
Demographic features, socioeconomic status, employment status, sex, and disease severity were not significant predictors of distress sensitivity. However, this result may have been influenced by the small sample size, and larger studies are needed to better define the role of distress tolerance in LN and its impact on disease management.

title: #1217 Sex differences in glomerular diseases and their long-term outcomes
authors: Emelina Stambolliu; Aglaia Chalkia; Elpiniki Stathopoulou; Athanasios Papras; Margarita Bora; Anastasia Politi; Martha Mitropoulou; Panagiota Giannou; Dimitrios Petras
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sex differences in kidney diseases have received limited attention. Research in this area is crucial for developing targeted prevention and intervention strategies that address the unique needs and risk factors of diverse populations.
Method
Retrospective, single-centre study at a reference centre for glomerular diseases. We evaluated the prevalence of glomerular diseases among males and females in terms of clinical characteristics and long-term outcomes. Logistic regression analysis and time-to-event analyses were employed.
Results
232 patients were included; 63% male and 37% female. The most common glomerular disease in males was IgA nephropathy (29%), while females most frequently presented with ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis (19%) and FSGS (19%). Notably, IgG4-related nephritis and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis were observed only in males. At diagnosis, hypertension was more prevalent in males (71% vs 56%, P = 0.035). There were no significant differences in the severity of kidney disease between sexes with the total cohort having a median (interquartile range) eGFR of 51 (25–85) ml/min/1.73 m2 and proteinuria 3 (1–6) g/24 h]. During the first year, females had a higher likelihood of infections compared to males (adjusted odds ratio OR 3.0 [95% CI 1.31–7.3], P = 0.01), after adjusting for the type of immunosuppressive treatment. title: #2933 The use of patient reported outcomes in lupus nephritis clinical trials: a narrative review
authors: Cliona Cowhig; Wan-Fai Ng; Grainne Murphy; Sarah Moran
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patient-reported outcomes (PRO) were identified as a core systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) outcome in 1999. A PRO is any report of a patient's health condition that comes directly from the patient without interpretation by a clinician or anyone else. PRO measures (PROMs) are tools that are employed to quantify PROs, most commonly through the means of self-reported questionnaire. Medication regulatory bodies are accepting PROMs as endpoints in clinical trials. Initiatives to identify meaningful research outcomes for patients, such as Standardized Outcomes in Nephrology–Glomerular Disease (SONG-GD), have highlighted areas including fatigue, depression and ability to work as important outcomes. These outcomes can only be captured through patient reporting. Given the increasing prominence of PROs we embarked on a review of PROMs in the lupus nephritis literature.
Method
Literature was identified by searching 3 trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov, ISRCTN registry, WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform). Inclusion criteria were Phase 2 and 3 interventional clinical trials in SLE, in patients aged over 18. Exclusion criteria were trials still ongoing and those without results. Titles and study overviews were reviewed for duplicates and inclusion/exclusion criteria. Study protocols and results published on trial platforms were reviewed for outcome measures as were publications where available. Data was analyzed using Microsoft Excel and R Studio 2024.04.2+764.
Results
Review of the trials registries occurred in October 2024 and 389 trials were identified. Duplicates and those not adhering to inclusion criteria were excluded resulting in 141 unique studies. The study protocols for each of these were reviewed to assess for the inclusion of PROMs. 64 of the 141 studies (45.39%) included PROMs in their stated study outcomes. 11 (17.19%) of the 64 studies including PROMs were for lupus nephritis specifically. Of the trials not including PROMs as outcome measures there were 22 (28.57%), seven (9.09%), and 48 (62.37%) for lupus nephritis, cutaneous lupus, and systemic lupus respectively. The odds ratio of a PROM being included as an outcome in a lupus nephritis trial versus a generalized SLE trial was 0.4615 ( 95% CI 0.2026 to 1.0513, P = 0.0657).
The SF-36 questionnaire or subsets of this questionnaire were the most used PROMs in the identified lupus nephritis trials, nine of 11 studies employed this PROM. The Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy–Fatigue (FACIT-F) and LupusPRO were utilized in two trials each, with a fatigue VAS and the fatigue severity scale included in one trial each. The highest number of PROMs in a lupus nephritis study was three (one trial). As detailed in Fig. 1 the inclusion of PROMs in lupus nephritis trials peaked in trials registered 2006–2008, however in the past 10 years few trials meeting inclusion criteria have included PROMs as an outcome measure.
Conclusion
There is increasing recognition of the utility of PROMs and both patients and regulatory bodies advocate their widespread use. This review highlights the limited use of PROMS in studies relating to lupus nephritis. It may be considered that there is a lack of PROMs specific to and/or validated in glomerular disease specifically. Furthermore, there may be limitations to a single instrument capturing the complexity of a multisystem inflammatory condition in conjunction with independent complications of renal disease such as nephrotic syndrome or end stage renal disease. A limitation of this review is limiting trials to those with results, given the lag time from inception to completion of large scale clinical trials. This review highlights the need for increased research in the field of PROMs in intrinsic renal disease and the need for more widespread use of PROMs in the nephrology literature.

title: #184 A case report of Bartonella henselae endocarditits presenting as a PR-3 positive, immune-complex, necrotising glomerulonephritis
authors: Sharafuddin Shah Bin Rhasbudin Shah; Jayana Devathasan
abstract:
Background and Aims
Infective endocarditis is a known cause of necrotising glomerulonephritis however invasive Bartonella henselae infection in humans is considered rare in New Zealand. We report a case of Bartonella henselae glomerulonephritis in a young Maori female, initially presenting a diagnostic and therapeutic conundrum.
Results
We report the case of a clinically well 17 year old Maori female who presents with severe anaemia and acute kidney injury with active urinary sediment in the context of known rheumatic heart disease and aortic and mitral metallic valves.
Serology and renal histology were consistent with a necrotising, crescentic PR-3 ANCA positive, full-house immune complex mediated non-exudative glomerulonephritis. A thorough search for an underlying cause including serial blood cultures, serial transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiograms did not identify any suggestion of infection. Our patient therefore received immunosuppression with good initial response however relapsed within the same month. On discussion with glomerulonephritis experts worldwide, Bartonella henselae serology was sent which returned highly positive. Subsequent to this, our patient underwent a PET-CT scan which identified subtle signs of aortic valve endocarditis. Her immunosuppression was discontinued and she was commenced on Doxycycline and Rifampicin with excellent response.
Conclusion
This case highlights the importance of a thorough investigation for infection in patients who present with ANCA positivity and necrotising glomerulonephritis. This case also highlights the vast manifestations of endocarditis in terms of renal serological and histological markers.

title: #2672 Real-life analysis of a monocentric cohort of IgA nephropathy patients
authors: Alessandro Barruscotti; Chiara Livia Lanzani; Giuseppe Vezzoli; Paolo Manunta; Giorgio Slaviero
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA nephropathy (IgAN) exhibits a great clinical variability in terms of onset, disease progression, and response to treatment. Data from clinical studies, due to the homogeneous characteristics of the patients analyzed, may provide literature values that differ from in clinical practice.
To describe and analyse the main characteristics of IgAN, observe any factors influencing the annual decline of eGFR and the consequent progression toward chronic kidney disease (CKD), as well as analyse the factors contributing to the reduction of proteinuria.
Method
A monocentric study conducted at the Nephrology and Dialysis Department of San Raffaele Hospital in Milan, involving 34 patients with a histological diagnosis of IgAN. Patients were monitored through renal function analysis, proteinuria, and blood pressure measurements from the first nephrological visit (T0), at the time of renal biopsy (T1), and at the end of follow-up (T2). MEST-C score was calculated according to histological data.
Results
In our cohort, IgAN was more common in males, with a mean age of 34 years. A delay in nephrological diagnosis and renal biopsy was observed from symptom onset (35 month). This diagnostic delay can be attributed to an initial conservative approach in treating patients with proteinuria and/or microhematuria, reserving renal biopsy for patients showing renal function deterioration or persistent proteinuria despite maximal tolerated antiproteinuric therapy. Analysis of comorbidities in the 34 patients revealed hypertension as the most common (58.8% of patients). These data confirm a significant incidence of uncontrolled hypertension at disease onset, with notable improvement in blood pressure control during follow-up (Patients whit uncontrolled hypertension: 26.5% at T0 vs 9,5% at T2) due to a more targeted therapeutic approach using ACE inhibitors/ARBs, which may help slow the progression of IgAN and have positive effects on renal function. Most patients (91%) had persistent or intermittent microhematuria on standard urine testing during follow-up. Microhematuria is one of the most common clinical signs of IgA nephropathy, and its persistence over time is aspect of disease management and prognosis. In our cohort, the average eGFR value at T0 was 78.43 ml/min/1.73 m² (using the CKD-EPI formula). The average annual eGFR decline in our cohort was 5.08 ml/min/1.73 m², with 41% of patients showing an annual eGFR decline >3.16% of patients started hemodialysis, with 3% undergoing renal transplantation.
The average proteinuria value in our cohort at T0 was 2.21 g/24 h. At the end of follow-up, the average proteinuria value was 0.74 g/24 h, which is particularly significant as proteinuria values <1 g/24 h are generally associated with a lower risk of disease progression. Proteinuria values significantly correlate (P < 0.05) with the annual eGFR decline, with a 2.8 ml/min/1.73 m² decline in patients with proteinuria <0.5 g/24 h, while in patients with higher proteinuria values (1–3.5 g/24 h), the annual eGFR decline was 8.276.
Conclusion
In our cohort IgAN proves to be a heterogeneous condition that can progress rapidly to end-stage kidney disease in a portion of patients. Therefore, it is essential to raise awareness for the referral of patients to nephrology for earlier histological diagnosis, enabling timely therapeutic intervention. Control of proteinuria and blood pressure is crucial for slowing disease progression, and consistent monitoring along with a targeted therapeutic approach are key to improving long-term prognosis.

title: #2977 Urinary red blood cells correlation with histopathology of lupus nephritis—single tertiary center
authors: Natália Marchão; José Oliveira Da Costa; Estela Nogueira; Marta Sofia Henriques Pereira; Cristina Resina; José António Lopes; Iolanda Godinho
abstract:
Background and Aims
Urine sediment is extremely valuable for nephrologists. Several groups suggest urinary sediment examinations can correlate with the histopathology of lupus nephritis (LN), with a lesser role in predicting outcomes.
Method
The authors retrospectively analyzed all systemic lupus erythematous (SLE) patients that presented with LN followed at a tertiary center. We compared renal histopathology in patients with and without urinary red blood cells (uRBCs) and evaluated renal prognosis in both groups. From our sample of 138 patients followed at our nephrology clinic for the last 30 years, we've selected 85 patients with complete information on urinary sediment and renal histopathology at presentation.
Results
From the 85 patients, a minority (12; 14%) had no uRBCs at presentation. We analyzed differences between both groups. Demographic distribution for both groups (with and without uRBCs at presentation) is presented in Table 1. Despite tendency for Black African ethnicity in the negative uRBCs group, the relation between ethnicity and uRBCs did not reach statistical significance (P = 0.066).
In the negative uRBCs group, patients presented with asymptomatic proteinuria (5; 42%), nephrotic syndrome (5; 42%), AKI (1; 8%) and CKD (1; 8%). In the uRBCs group, patients presented with hematoproteinuria (35; 48%) asymptomatic proteinuria (9; 12%), nephrotic syndrome (17; 23%), AKI/RPGN (11; 13%) and CKD (1, 1%). Patients presentation was statistically different between negative and positive uRBCs group (P = 0.008). As expected all patients with hematoproteinuria and RPGN were in the uRBCs group with a bigger proportion of patients with asymptomatic proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome in the negative uRBCs.
LN classes distribution in the negative uRBCs group was: class I (1; 8%), class II (3; 25%), class IV-A (4; 33%), class V (4; 33%). The three cases of LN class II represented three patients with lupus podocytopathy. LN classes distribution in the positive uRBCs group was: class I (2; 3%), class II (8; 11%), class III A/AC/C (15; 21%), class III-A+V (2; 3%), class IV A/AC/C (38; 52%) and class V (8; 11%). LN classes distribution was statistically different between negative and positive uRBCs group (P = 0.046).
In the negative uRBCs group, mean and SD proteinuria and serum creatinine (sCr) at presentation were 2.90 ± 1.72 g/d [0.19–5.18], 1.16 ± 0.65 mg/dL, respectively. In the uRBCs group, mean and SD proteinuria and sCr at presentation were 2.45 ± 2.27 g/day, 1.32 ± 1.67 mg/dL, respectively. Proteinuria and sCr at presentation were not statistically different (P = 0.80 and P = 0.71, respectively).
In the negative uRBCs and positive uRBCs group, mean follow-up was 10 years [5–25] and 9.2 years [0.3–30], respectively.
In the negative uRBCs and positive uRBCs group, mean SCr and proteinuria at last follow-up was 0.88 ± 0.44 mg/dL vs. 0.99 ± 0.93 mg/dL and 190 ± 140 mg/d vs. 330 ± 514 mg/g/d, respectively. In the negative uRBCs and positive uRBCs group, at 5, 10 years and at the last follow-up, SCr was 0.93 vs. 0.85/0.79 vs. 0.80/0.88 vs. 0.99 mg/dL, respectively. In the negative uRBCs and positive uRBCs group, progression to ESKD occurred in 0% of the patients in both groups. 51 patients completed 5 years of follow-up, 8 in the negative and 43 in the uRBCs group, and of them 12.5% (1/8) and 16% (7/43) reached CKD stage 3–5, respectively (all stage CKD stage 3a or 3b). Progression to CKD 3–5 was not statistically significant between the two groups (P = 0.787).
Conclusion
In our cohort, uRBCs absence at presentation was infrequent and correlated less frequently to proliferative classes on renal histology and more frequently with class V and lupus podocytopathy. Noteworthily, there were also some cases of class IV-A in the negative uRBCs group. Renal outcomes in this small sample were satisfying and similar in both groups.

title: #2013 Real-world experience of Iptacopan in C3 glomerulopathy
authors: Ana Huerta; Esther Rubio González; Alba Maroto; Lucía Martin Testillano; Javier Martin; Marina Alonso Riaño; Maria Luisa Serrano Salazar; Maria De San Miguel Marques Vidas; Paula Sanchez Briales; Maria De Valdenebro Recio; Jose Maria Portolés; Santiago Rodriguez de Cordoba
abstract:
Background and Aims
C3 Glomerulopathy (C3G) is a rare glomerular disease characterized by dysregulation of the alternative pathway of the complement system. It was relatively recently described, and there remains a need to expand our understanding of its progression and therapeutic management. Currently, with the available treatment options, the prognosis for patients with C3G is poor, with approximately 50% of patients requiring renal replacement therapy within 10 years of diagnosis.
Iptacopan is an oral first in class inhibitor of Factor B, a key serine protease in the alternative pathway of the complement cascade. Clinical trials of this drug in C3G have shown promising results, but it is not yet commercially available, and thus real-world experience with its use is limited.
Method
We present a real-world case of a 59-year-old woman with C3G in a native kidney, treated with Iptacopan, through compassionate use program of Novartis after signing informed consent. She was diagnosed with C3 glomerulonephritis via kidney biopsy in November 2023. Immunological studies were largely unremarkable, except for a low serum C3 level (60–70 mg/dL). Monoclonal gammopathy was excluded, and functional and genetic testing of the complement system were unremarkable.
By February 2024, the patient exhibited proteinuria was 3.5 g/day, despite treatment with angiotensin II receptor antagonists (ARAII) and SGLT2 inhibitors (iSGLT2). Serum creatinine was 1.2 mg/dL, with and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 50 ml/min/1.73 m2, and she had concomitant microhematuria (40 RBCs/high power field). A treatment regimen including prednisone at 0.5 mg/kg/day and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) was initially planned. However, due to gastrointestinal intolerance to MMF (she received only 3 doses), treatment with Iptacopan was initiated at a dose of 200 mg every 12 hours, via compassionate use.
Results
The renal response to Iptacopan was remarkable, with progressive improvement in proteinuria, reaching a proteinuria-to-creatinine ratio of 0.2 mg/dL after one year of treatment. Additionally, urinary sediment became negative, and renal function improved (latest serum creatinine: 1 mg/dL, eGFR 62 ml/min/1.73 m2). Furthermore, serum C3 levels normalized.
Conclusion
As of today, real-world evidence is available only for patients with post-renal transplant recurrence. This represents the first real-world clinical case of a patient with C3G in a native kidney treated with Iptacopan. Iptacopan appears to be a promising therapeutic alternative for patients with C3G, with the potential to significantly impact disease prognosis, as demonstrated by this case.

title: #2135 Infectious complications in glomerular disease: experience from a tertiary care centre in Eastern India
authors: Paromita Das; Priti Meena; Anish Garg; Badari Mylliengap; Prity Rai; Suvendu Pukait; Sandip Panda
abstract:
Background and Aims
Infections are the Achilles heel in glomerular disease. They can complicate the course of glomerular diseases, adding to both morbidity and mortality.
Method
We conducted a retrospective, observational study among adult patients with biopsy proven glomerular disease with estimated GFR (eGFR) >15 ml/min/1.73 m2 . Patients who underwent a kidney biopsy and were diagnosed with glomerular disease and subsequently treated in department of Nephrology between March 2022–December 2024 were included in the study. We evaluated the demographic characteristics, type of immunosuppression and other treatment, type of infection, infectious agent, infection related hospitalization and mortality in our study.
Results
We evaluated 279 patients (146 females, 133 males) with a median follow up of 14.4 months. Mean age of the patients was 39 ± 21 years. The histopathological diagnosis was podocytopathy in 28.3% patients, lupus nephritis in 25.8%, IgA nephropathy in 22.9%, membranous nephropathy in 22.2%, idiopathic MPGN in 7.1% of the patients.
Majority of patients had received one or more immunosuppression (89%). Among patients treated with immunosuppression, 89.6% received steroids, 53.7% received cyclophosphamide, 22% received mycophenolate mofetil, 12% received rituximab, 6.2% received tacrolimus. 40.8 % patients received antimicrobial prophylaxis.
Infectious complications were seen in 28.7% patients receiving immunosuppression. Among those with infections, most common site of infection was upper respiratory tract (43.3%), skin and soft tissue (31.3%), lower respiratory tract (14.4%), gastrointestinal tract (4.8%), genitourinary tract (4.8%) and bone and joints (1.2%). Bacterial infections were the most common, 6.4%and 4.3% of patients receiving immunosuppressive treatment had fungal (most commonly dermatophytosis) and viral infections respectively (most commonly herpes zoster), while 1.7% had parasitic infection. Among those with infection 20 patients (28.1%) required hospitalisation. 11 (3.7%) patients died during the course of their treatment, majority of them (72.7%) were attributed to infection.
Conclusion
Almost one-third of patients requiring immunosuppressive treatment developed infections during the course of their illness, morbidity associated with infection was also higher. Patient education regarding infection prevention measures and close monitoring are of paramount importance in patients on immunosuppressive therapy.

title: #3644 Type II cryoglobulinemic vasculitis with renal involvement in a patient with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma: a rare case report
authors: Ana Catarina Oliveira; Bernardo Fernandes; Pedro Lisboa; Nuria Paulo; Bernardo Faria; Luís Mendonça; Ricardo Neto; João Frazão
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cryoglobulins (CGs) are immune complexes that precipitate at low temperatures, potentially leading to cryoglobulinemic vasculitis (CryoVas). CryoVas has been associated with lymphoproliferative disorders, infections, and autoimmune diseases. Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (LPL) is a rare B-cell lymphoma that primarily affects the bone marrow, with occasional involvement of the spleen and lymph nodes. LPL does not always produce monoclonal immunoglobulins and its progression is usually indolent. We present an unusual case of CryoVas with renal involvement in a patient with LPL, where no circulating monoclonal immunoglobulin was detected.
Case description
A 71-year-old woman diagnosed with systemic sclerosis (SSc), followed in rheumatology consultation since 2013, medicated with prednisolone 5 mg/day and mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice a day, myasthenia gravis treated with pyridostigmine three times a day, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma under surveillance in hematology consultation, and bimalleolar cutaneous ulcers under dressing treatment for several months, presented to our hospital's emergency department with symptoms of dyspnea, orthopnea, and lower limb edema with a two-week evolution.
She was hospitalized for further evaluation with suspected nephritic syndrome, presenting with anasarca, hypertension (BP 160/80 mmHg), and new-onset non-oliguric acute kidney injury KDIGO 1 (serum creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, previously 1 mg/dL), with urinalysis showing leukocytes (+++) and erythrocytes (+++), and urinary sediment evaluation revealing dysmorphic erythrocyturia.
Renal ultrasound and transthoracic echocardiogram did not reveal any significant findings. Laboratory tests revealed mild normocytic normochromic anemia (8.6 g/dL), normal haptoglobin, peripheral blood smear without schistocytes, and negative Coombs test. Proteinuria of 3g/24 h and albuminuria of 2300 mg/24 h were present, with normal serum albumin level. There were elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, at 86 mm/1st hour and 39 g/dL, respectively. Serological tests were negative for Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV. The immunological study revealed negative results for rheumatoid factor, anti-Ds DNA, ANCA, anti-glomerular basement membrane, with ANA titers of 1/640 with a speckled pattern, low C4 (<1 mg/dL), normal C3 levels, and the presence of positive cryoglobulins, which were later characterized as type 2 (immunoglobulins of IgA, IgG, and IgM types with polyclonal characteristics but including one monoclonal IgM/Kappa fraction with slight rheumatoid factor activity).
Serum protein electrophoresis, serum immunofixation electrophoresis, urinary protein electrophoretic/immunofixation analysis were negative. Serum free light chain kappa and lambda were 1.64 mg/dL and 2.37 mg/L, respectively, with a FLC ratio of 1.45, which is normal.
CT scan and PET showed no findings. Subsequently, she underwent a renal biopsy, which showed a membranoproliferative pattern on optical microscopy, with mesangial and endocapillary proliferation, without evidence of intraluminal thrombi. Immunofluorescence showed restriction of IgM chains ++ (mesangial and membranous) and kappa light chains ++ (mesangial and membranous). Electron microscopy revealed the presence of dense mesangial, subendothelial, and mesangiocapillary deposits, focal fusion of podocyte foot processes, and absence of organized structures.
In the presence of glomerulonephritis secondary to type 2 CryoVas, with no evidence of progression of the hematological disease, and no infectious or immunological cause identified, it was decided to treat with rituximab 1g separated by 15 days along with the initiation of corticosteroid therapy with prednisolone at a dose of 0.5 mg/kg/day.
Conclusion
We present a rare case of type 2 CryoVas with negative rheumatoid factor and renal involvement in a patient with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, a condition that typically follows an indolent course. To the best of our knowledge, this is only the second such case reported in the literature.

title: #600 The efficacy and safety of ripertamab in inducing remission of primary membranous nephropathy: a retrospective study
authors: Liangxiang Xiao; Mengjiao Lin
abstract:
Background and Aims
Ripertamab composed of 70% human IgG1 constant region Fc fragments targeting CD20. Compared to rituximab, ripertamab minimize the immunogenicity of the drug while preserving its therapeutic efficacy. This study aims to investigate the efficacy and safety of ripertamab in inducing remission of PMN in adults.
Method
This retrospective study included 13 patients diagnosed with PMN via renal biopsy or positive serum PLA2R antibodies between February 1, 2023 and November 31, 2023. Patients were classified into PLA2R-positive (n = 9) and PLA2R-negative(n = 4) groups. All patients received ripertamab (375 mg/m² weekly for 4 doses or 1 g biweekly for 2 doses) with a follow-up period of 6 months. Primary outcomes included remission rates, changes in renal function, anti-PLA2R antibody levels, and B-cell depletion. Complete remission (CR) was defined as 24-hour proteinuria <0.3 g, serum albumin >35 g/L, and stable renal function. Partial remission (PR) was defined as a ≥ 50% reduction in proteinuria with serum albumin >30 g/L. Kaplan-Meier were used to compare differences in prognosis.
Results
After 6 months, 69.23% patients achieved remission (CR: 38.46%, PR: 30.77%). PLA2R-negative patients exhibited a higher rate of composite remission (100%) compared to PLA2R-positive patients (55.56%). Among the PLA2R-positive group, 7 of 9 showed reductions in anti-PLA2R antibody levels, with 5 achieving seroconversion. All patients demonstrated significant improvements in renal function, with B-cell depletion was achieved. No adverse events were observed during the study.
Conclusion
This study suggests that ripertamab could be an effective and safe treatment for PMN.

title: #2982 Immune complex made by immunoglobulin A and Cnm protein expressing in Streptococcus mutans might induce IgA nephropathy like kidney lesion
authors: Yasuyuki Nagasawa; Shuhei Naka; Taro Misaki; Seigo Ito; Kensaku Shojima; Yuto Suehiro; Kana Suehara; Daisuke Matsuoka; Ken Shinmura; Ryota Nomura; Michiyo Nakano; Kazuhiko Nakano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Streptococcus mutans is known to be a major pathogen of dental caries. Approximately 10%–15% of S. mutans strains isolated from the oral cavity are shown to possess collagen-binding properties due to the presence of 120-kDa collagen-binding protein (cnm) encoded by the cnm gene. Cnm−(+) S. mutans strains have the ability to bind to the extracellular matrix, which has been demonstrated to be associated with several diseases, such as infective endocarditis, aggravated cerebral hemorrhaging, inflammatory bowel disease and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. In addition, recent studies revealed that cnm−(+) S. mutans strains are also associated with the virulence of IgAN (Misaki-T et al., CEN, 2015)(Misaki-T et al., Sci Report). Our group revealed that in animal models, intravenous administration of Cnm−(+) S. mutans and severe dental caries induced by Cnm−(+) S. mutans could cause IgAN like kidney lesions (Naka-S et al., CEN, 2020) (Naka-S et al., Sci Report, 2021). In this study, the binding ability between Cnm protein and IgA were evaluated, and also the co-localization between Cnm protein and IgA in the glomerulus in the rat IgA nephropathy model induced by intravenous Cnm−(+) S. mutans treatment.
Method
Binding abilities between recombinant Cnm protein and human IgA1, IgA2, IgG were evaluated by ELIZA methods. And also, binding abilities between IgA1 and several bacterial cell surface proteins, such as recombinant Cnm protein, recombinant GTFB (glucan transfer enzyme B), recombinant GbpC (glucan binding protein C) were evaluated by ELIZA methods. Moreover, in rat IgA model induced by intravenous recombinant biotin-labeled Cnm protein treatment, the localizations of Cnm and IgA were confirmed by immune-fluorescence staining.
Results
The binding ability between IgA1 and recombinant Cnm was higher than that between IgA1 and any other surface protein (P < 0.05 see Fig. 1, Left). The binding ability between recombinant Cnm and IgA1 was higher than that between recombinant Cnm and any other globulins (P < 0.01 see Fig. 1, Right). In rat IgA nephropathy model kidney, recombinant Cnm and IgA were colocalized in mesangial areas in glomeruli.
Conclusion
After Cnm protein invaded into blood stream, Cnm protein might bind to IgA1, and the immune complex of Cnm protein and IgA1 would deposit in mesangial area in glomerulus, possibly resulting in incidence of IgA nephropathy.

title: #3647 Clinical characteristics and outcomes of adults with IgA nephropathy: a retrospective study
authors: Marta Margarido; Ana Rita Pereirinha Ramos; Filipa Trigo; Inês Clemente Duarte; Paulo Santos
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is the most common type of primary glomerulonephritis. Clinical presentation is highly variable, including asymptomatic hematuria and/or proteinuria detected on routine screening. IgAN is an important cause of kidney failure, so it is crucial to identify patients with the disease and those at the highest risk of progression.
The primary objective of this study was to characterize the population diagnosed with IgAN in the Nephrology Department of Médio Tejo Local Health Unit (ULS-MT) over the past 15 years, aiming to better understand disease progression and evolution over time, pharmacological treatments and kidney outcomes.
Method
This was a descriptive and retrospective study encompassing all patients from the Nephrology Department of the ULS-MT with a diagnosis of IgAN who underwent renal biopsy from 2010 to the present.
Results
A total of 53 patients were diagnosed with IgAN. Thirty-five patients were male (66%), with a mean age of 47 ± 15 years (range 18–75 years). Seventy percent (n = 37) had hypertension, 25% (n = 13) were obese, 25% (n = 13) had a history of smoking, and 8% (n = 4) had diabetes mellitus.
The mean follow-up time until biopsy was 1.06 ± 1.99 years. At the time of biopsy, the mean serum creatinine level was 1.54 ± 0.80 mg/dL and the mean proteinuria was 2.47 ± 2.06 g/24 h. The indications for biopsy were hematuria with sub-nephrotic proteinuria (n = 32, 80%), sub-nephrotic proteinuria without hematuria (n = 9, 17%), hematuria with nephrotic proteinuria (n = 8, 15%) and nephrotic proteinuria without hematuria (n = 4, 8%). On average, 3.53 cases of IgAN were diagnosed per year, with a minimum of one annual case (2010 and 2011) and a maximum of seven cases (2018).
Considering the Oxford classification: 38 (72%) patients presented mesangial hypercellularity in >50% of glomeruli, 16 (30%) had endocapillary hypercellularity, segmental glomerulosclerosis was observed in 34 (64%) cases, tubular atrophy involving >25% of tubules was noted in 25 (47%) patients and crescents were detected in 4 (8%) biopsies.
Regarding therapy, 49 patients (92%) were treated with ACE inhibitors (ACEi) or angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARB), 36 (68%) received SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and 18 (34%) underwent corticosteroid therapy. Among those treated with corticosteroids, 72% (n = 13) had complications, the most frequent being weight gain (n = 12, 92%), infections (n = 4, 31%), insomnia/depression (n = 4, 31%) or acne (n = 3, 23%).
The mean follow-up time after diagnosis was 6.23 ± 3.89 years. Forty-four patients (83%) remained under follow-up, presenting a mean serum creatinine level of 2.06 ± 1.77 mg/dL and mean proteinuria of 1.23 ± 1.73 g/24 h. Nine patients (17%) experienced worsening renal function and required renal replacement therapy. Of these, 7 (78%) had previously been treated with ACEi/ARB, 2 (22%) received SGLT2i and 3 (33%) underwent corticosteroid therapy. These patients were already in an advanced stage of the disease when diagnosed and started dialysis, on average, four years after diagnosis.
Conclusion
The treatment patterns used in our center demonstrated a reduction in proteinuria by >50% and those who started dialysis had been diagnosed at an advanced stage of chronic kidney disease (CKD), reinforcing the importance of early identification. This study demonstrated that the characteristics of patients with IgAN in the ULS-MT align with those observed in the European population as do long-term outcomes following diagnosis. Characterizing these patient clusters provides deeper insight into the disease and its progression over time, enabling the prediction and potential modification of outcomes in our patients with CKD. Thus, early diagnosis can delay the progression of the disease.

title: #3836 Nodular glomerulosclerosis complicating MIDD: report of 2 cases in young patients
authors: Manel Zakhama; Sirine Bchir; Mouna Hamouda; Meriem Ben Salem; Nouha Ben Mahmoud; Manel Ben Salah; Ahmed Letaief; Habib Skhiri
abstract:
Background and Aims
Monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease (MIDD) is a malignant hematologic disorder that primarily occurs in older adults and is associated with multisystemic complications.
Method
We report two cases of MIDD associated to multiple myeloma complicated by nodular glomerulosclerosis in two young patients, highlighting the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges posed by this malignant hematologic condition.
Results
The two patients were young females: The first patient, aged 44, had no significant medical history and was hospitalized for acute renal failure (creatinine level of 330 µmol/l) in the context of polyarthralgia, fatigue, and dyspnea. title: #2182 Acute kidney injury in multiple myeloma patients: experience of the Nephrology Department of Monastir
authors: Maissa Ben Rhouma; Nouha Ben Mahmoud; Meriem Ben Salem; Manel Ben Salah; Sirine Bchir; Ahmed Letaief; Mouna Hamouda; Habib Skhiri
abstract:
Background and Aims
Multiple myeloma (MM) is a hematologic malignancy involving plasma cell proliferation, accounting for 1%–2% of all cancers. In North Africa, MM prevalence and mortality are notably higher compared to regions like Kuwait and the UAE. Kidney impairment, often an early complication, occurs in nearly half of MM patients, driven by both monoclonal immunoglobulin-related and unrelated factors. This study examines the presentation, diagnosis, treatment, and outcomes of MM patients with acute kidney injury (AKI).
Method
This is a single center retrospective, cross-sectional study carried out in the Nephrology Department of Fattouma Bourguiba's university hospital in Monastir between March 2020 and March 2024, focusing on MM patients presenting with AKI. Clinical, biological, and evolutionary data were recorded.
Results
The study included 31 patients with a median age of 64 ±12.47 years. A slight male predominance was noted with sex ratio of 1.06. The most frequent clinical signs were asthenia (16 patients) and dehydration (10 patients). Most patients presented an AKI with previously normal kidney function (17 patients) and the median creatinine level was 373 µmol/L. Proteinuria was present is most of cases (20 patients) and its median level was 2 g/d. Anemia was the most common laboratory findings (29 patients; 93.5%).MM was diagnosed in 21 patients at the moment of hospitalization for AKI. Kidney biopsy was only performed in 7 patients, and it showed features of light chain cast nephropathy in 4 patients, MIDD in 1 patient, fibrosis in one patient and was inconclusive in one patient. Most patients received intravenous hydration (22 patients; 71%) and corticosteroids (25 patients; 83.3%). Hemodialysis was performed in 9 patients (29%). Most of patients exhibited partial renal recovery (14 patients; 45.6%) while absence of recovery was noted in 3 patients.
Conclusion
In the setting of multiple myeloma, AKI is mainly due to light chain deposition in the tubules and kidney biopsy is not always mandatory when the presentation is typical. Hemodialysis is required in one-third of cases and fluid management all along with chemotherapy remain the cornerstone of treatment.

title: #2793 Th17.1 cells in glomerulonephritis. Potential differences between primary and secondary glomerulonephritis
authors: Miguel Giovanni Uriol Rivera; Elena Seren Couso; Aina Obrador Mulet; Vanessa Daza; Maria Rosa Julia Benique
abstract:
Background and Aims
T-helper (Th) cells play a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of glomerulonephritis (GN). The Th17.1 subset, characterized by the expression of chemokine receptors CCR6 and CXCR3, has been implicated in systemic lupus erythematosus and associated with inflammation and models of renal fibrosis. Notably, Th17.1 cells express multidrug resistance protein 1 (MDR-1) and P-glycoprotein, which have been linked to corticosteroid resistance. Our prior research highlighted the potential involvement of Th17.1 cells in IgA nephropathy (IgAN). However, their role in other primary forms of GN remains poorly understood. Additionally, we aimed to evaluate differences between primary and secondary GN and their relationship with proteinuria.
Method
This retrospective, cross-sectional study analyzed peripheral blood levels of Th1, Th2, Th17, Th17.1, Treg, and CD19+ cells. Th subpopulations were identified using anti-CXCR3-FITC and anti-CCR6-PCy7 antibodies (BioLegend, USA). Additional antibodies, including anti-CD45-FITC, anti-CD4-PE, anti-CD8-ECD, anti-CD3-PCy5, anti-CD56-PCy5, anti-CD3-PCy7, anti-CD19-ECD, anti-CD127-FITC, anti-CD25-PCy5, and anti-CD4-PCy7 (Coulter Immunotech, France), were used to evaluate T, B, and Treg cells. Multicolor flow cytometry was conducted using a Navios cytometer, and data analysis was performed with Kaluza software (Beckman Coulter, USA). Th17.1 cells (CXCR3+CCR6+) were quantified as a percentage of CD4+ lymphocytes.
Results
The study included 50 patients (mean age: 49 ± 18 years; 70% male). Secondary GN cases comprised lupus nephritis (n = 7) and ANCA-associated vasculitis (n = 8), while primary GN cases included IgAN (n = 30) and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) (n = 5). A positive correlation was observed between Th17 and 24-hour proteinuria (r = 0.30, P = 0.03), which remained significant in primary GN (r = 0.33, P = 0.04). A significant positive correlation was also identified between Th17.1 and proteinuria (r = 0.27, P = 0.04). An inverse relationship was noted between Th1 and Th2 cells with Th17, particularly Th17.1. Th2 cells showed a strong inverse correlation with Th17.1. No significant differences in age, sex, duration of diagnosis, eGFR, or proteinuria were observed between primary and secondary GN, although proteinuria tended to be higher in primary GN (1,342 mg vs. 787 mg, P = 0.18). Primary GN displayed significant differences compared to secondary GN in terms of Th2 (18%, 95% CI: 15–21 vs. 24%, 95% CI: 19–28, P = 0.03), Th17.1 (27%, 95% CI: 23–30 vs. 21%, 95% CI: 16–25, P = 0.04), and ratios of Th2/CD19 (3, 95% CI: 0.3–5 vs. 11, 95% CI: 7–15, P = 0.002), Th1/Th17.1 (1.4, 95% CI: 1.0–1.7 vs. 2.1, 95% CI: 1.6–2.6, P = 0.018), Th2/Th17 (0.8, 95% CI: 0.6–1 vs. 1.2, 95% CI: 0.9–1.5, P = 0.028), and Th2/Th17.1 (0.7, 95% CI: 0.3–1.2 vs. 1.8, 95% CI: 1.1–2.4, P = 0.011). ANCA vasculitis exhibited the lowest Th17.1 levels (15.7%), whereas FSGS showed the highest levels (34.8%).
Conclusion
A predominance of Th17.1 cells was observed in primary GN, underscoring their significant role in inflammation, with the highest levels detected in FSGS. Conversely, lower Th2 cell levels in primary GN suggest reduced anti-inflammatory capacity. An inverse relationship between Th2 and Th17.1 cells was consistently observed across all GN subtypes. Secondary GN demonstrated a more autoimmune-driven profile, as evidenced by a higher Th2/CD19 ratio. These findings underscore distinct inflammatory and immunoregulatory mechanisms underlying primary and secondary GN and highlight the potential of Th17.1 cells as therapeutic targets in primary GN.

title: #3226 A case report of a concurrent axonal neuropathy and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis treated with ocrelizumab and plasma exchange
authors: Megan Telford; Stephen May; Malcolm Green; James Hughes
abstract:
Background and Aims
There are documented cases of concurrent focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) or minimal change disease (MCD) with inflammatory polyneuropathies, such as chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) and Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) [1, 2]. However, the pathogenesis linking the two is unclear. Previous cases have been treated with immunosuppression and plasma exchange (PLEX) [1, 2]. Both neurological and renal improvement with immunosuppression and PLEX suggests a common autoimmune pathogenesis.
Method
We describe a case of a patient with FSGS and an axonal neuropathy, both of which responded to PLEX and immune agents including B-cell depleting therapies. Given multiple previous drug reactions, ocrelizumab, a humanized anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody usually reserved for multiple sclerosis (MS), was used as a novel therapy in this case with reasonable efficacy in our patient when they suffered a relapse.
Results
A 54-year-old female presented with renal failure requiring dialysis with a creatinine of 616 μmol/L and urine protein:creatinine ratio of 3076 mg/mmol. Biopsy revealed resolving acute tubular injury, MCD, FSGS and thin membrane disease with negative immunofluorescence. She was initially treated with steroids. Repeat biopsy at 3 months was most consistent with MCD and FSGS. Given ongoing dialysis dependence she was treated with PLEX and rituximab with an improvement in renal function to a creatinine of 129 μmol/L but ongoing proteinuria. She was weaned off dialysis but required maintenance PLEX. She was started on tacrolimus but transitioned to ciclosporin due to side effects. A third biopsy was performed showing FSGS. PLEX was eventually weaned after 2 years. She remained off kidney replacement therapy for nearly 3 years.
3 years post her initial presentation, she re-presented with renal failure requiring dialysis and a progressive mixed motor and sensory lower limb neuropathy. Nerve conduction studies were most consistent with GBS and nerve biopsy showed an axonal neuropathy. Repeat renal biopsy showed FSGS with mild interstitial inflammation. Vasculitis screen was negative apart from a positive ENA and anti-SSA. A genetic nephrotic panel was unremarkable. The patient recommenced PLEX and received IVIG and rituximab. Unfortunately, she had a severe reaction to rituximab requiring steroids, however her neuropathy and renal injury improved. She was maintained on PLEX ongoing.
She had two further neuropathy flares over the following 18 months, both treated with more intense PLEX regimens. During the second flare she was unable to be weaned from three times a week PLEX. Given previous reactions to tacrolimus, rituximab and IVIG she was trialled on ocrelizumab. Subsequently PLEX was weaned to fortnightly to good effect. The patient's renal function is stable with a creatinine of 200 μmol/L and an albumin:creatinine ratio of 225 mg/mmol. She remains off dialysis.
Conclusion
The mechanism linking FSGS and inflammatory neuropathies is unclear. However, the response to PLEX and B-cell depleting therapies suggest an autoimmune component with perhaps a common circulating antibody or factor yet to be identified. Further research into a unifying pathophysiology is needed.
Additionally, to our knowledge ocrelizumab has not been used for FSGS prior to our case. We found one case report where ocrelizumab was used in membranous nephropathy with concurrent MS [3]. Our case illustrates the potential role for other antiCD20 agents other than rituximab, such as ocrelizumab, for patients with concurrent FSGS/MCD and inflammatory neuropathies.

title: #3734 Predictors of kidney outcomes in ANCA-associated vasculitis: a retrospective cohort study
authors: Beatriz de Barros; Beatriz Silva; Ana Cunha; Sofia Correia; Andreia Campos; Pedro Pereira; Josefina Santos
abstract:
Background and Aims
ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) is characterized by small vessel inflammation with kidney involvement being a major determinant of outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate clinical and serological parameters at diagnosis and their association with kidney outcomes at 6 and 24 months of follow-up.
Method
This retrospective cohort study included adult patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis who were followed at a tertiary center between 2000 and 2018. Demographic, clinical, and laboratory data were collected at diagnosis and at 6 and 24 months. Patients were excluded if they lacked baseline positive ANCA serology or if records of follow-up proteinuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) were missing. Patients were divided according to proteinuria (higher or lower 0.5 g/G) and kidney function (eGFR higher or lower than 45 mL/min/1.73 m²).
Results
Twenty-six patients were included in the study. Comorbidities included hypertension (38.5%), dyslipidemia (42.3%), and chronic kidney disease (26.9%). At the time of diagnosis, median GFR was 19.0 mL/min/1.73 m² (IQR 20.00), serum creatinine 2.87 mg/dL (IQR 2.60), proteinuria 0.70 g/G (IQR 1.16) and microscopic hematuria was present in 88.5% of patients. Clinical manifestations included ear-nose-throat (ENT) involvement (38.5%) and alveolar hemorrhage (23.1%). MPO-ANCA were present in 84.6% of patients, while 15.4% had PR3-ANCA. During follow-up, 83.3% became ANCA-negative and 24.0% showed recurrent positivity. After treatment, most patients (n = 18, 69.2%) did not require kidney replacement therapy (KRT). Five patients (19.2%) died.
Patients with higher proteinuria at 6 months showed significantly higher baseline creatinine (P = 0.0012), PR3 levels (P = 0.029), and lower GFR (P = 0.016). At 24 months, only baseline creatinine remained significantly higher in the proteinuria ≥0.5 g/d group. Binary logistic regression identified lower GFR at diagnosis was associated with higher proteinuria at 6 months (Or = 0.923; P < 0.05), while higher creatinine at 6 months was associated with higher odds of proteinuria at 24 months (Or = 2.388; P < 0.05).
MPO levels at diagnosis were significantly higher in patients with eGFR ≤45 mL/min/1.73 m² at both 6 months and 24 months. This tendency was also observed at 6 months with MPO levels associating with lower eGFR at 24 months.
Conclusion
Our study demonstrates that in ANCA-associated vasculitis, baseline kidney function significantly impacts long-term outcomes, particularly regarding the levels of proteinuria and eGFR. The identification of baseline eGFR and 6-month creatinine as independent predictors of persistent proteinuria highlights the importance of early kidney function in determining disease trajectory. Despite significant kidney involvement at presentation, the majority of patients avoided KRT, suggesting effective response to standard therapeutic approaches.

title: #658 Georeferencing of patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis and renal involvement in Bogotá, Colombia, between 2012 and 2023
authors: Daniel Augusto Martin Arsanios; Kateir Contreras; Yeimmy Vanessa Galvis Galindo; Maria Alejandra Gomez Galan; Hernán David Torres; Diana Carolina Vargas Angel; Camilo Alberto González González; Paola Garcia; Paula Violeta Rodriguez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis is a systemic autoimmune condition characterized by significant morbidity and mortality, particularly with renal involvement. Environmental and geographic factors may play a role in its distribution. This study aims to describe the geospatial distribution of ANCA-associated vasculitis cases with renal involvement in Bogotá, D.C., and identify potential spatial patterns.
Method
This cross-sectional, observational study utilized retrospective data from medical records of patients diagnosed with ANCA-associated vasculitis in Bogotá from 2012 to 2023. Data included clinical, sociodemographic, and environmental variables. Geospatial analysis was conducted using specialized software (R), and regression models were applied to identify spatial patterns and risk factors associated with the disease.
Results
2431 medical records from three tertiary and quaternary hospitals in Bogotá were analyzed, identifying 151 cases of ANCA-associated vasculitis with renal involvement confirmed by renal biopsy. Among these patients, 84 were women (55.6%), and 73 (48.3%) were aged between 50 and 69 years. Socioeconomic analysis revealed that 77 patients (50.99%) were from the middle strata, 62 (41.05%) from the low strata, and 12 (7.9%) from the high strata. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis was the most frequent nephrological syndrome at presentation, affecting 98 patients (64.9%), with no significant differences among socioeconomic strata (P = 0.59).
The localities of Engativá and La Candelaria recorded the highest number of cases, followed by Puente Aranda, Bosa, and Teusaquillo. Analysis of official city records indicated that the most affected areas experienced accumulated precipitation exceeding 600 mm during the study period. Prior to 2018, these areas had average ozone levels of 15–18 ppb, which increased to 22–28 ppb after 2018. PM2.5 levels ranged between 14 and 18 µg/m³, while PM10 levels were more variable, fluctuating between 42 and 64 µg/m³ across the two most affected localities. Before 2015, the average temperature ranged from 13 to 13.5°C, rising to 13.5–14.5°C citywide after that year.
Conclusion
This study highlights the geospatial clustering of ANCA-associated vasculitis with renal involvement in specific localities of Bogotá, suggesting the potential influence of environmental and climatic factors on disease distribution. The findings underscore the importance of integrating geographic and environmental data into the epidemiological analysis of autoimmune diseases. Further research is needed to explore causal relationships and inform public health interventions aimed at mitigating environmental risks associated with the disease.

This cross-sectional, observational study utilized retrospective data from medical records of patients diagnosed with ANCA-associated vasculitis in Bogotá from 2012 to 2023. Data included clinical, sociodemographic, and environmental variables. Geospatial analysis was conducted using specialized software (R), and regression models were applied to identify spatial patterns and risk factors associated with the disease.
Results
2431 medical records from three tertiary and quaternary hospitals in Bogotá were analyzed, identifying 151 cases of ANCA-associated vasculitis with renal involvement confirmed by renal biopsy.
