Socioeconomic analysis revealed that 77 patients (50.99%) were from the middle strata, 62 (41.05%) from the low strata, and 12 (7.9%) from the high strata. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis was the most frequent nephrological syndrome at presentation, affecting 98 patients (64.9%), with no significant differences among socioeconomic strata (P = 0.59).
The localities of Engativá and La Candelaria recorded the highest number of cases, followed by Puente Aranda, Bosa, and Teusaquillo. Prior to 2018, these areas had average ozone levels of 15–18 ppb, which increased to 22–28 ppb after 2018. PM2.5 levels ranged between 14 and 18 µg/m³, while PM10 levels were more variable, fluctuating between 42 and 64 µg/m³ across the two most affected localities. Before 2015, the average temperature ranged from 13 to 13.5°C, rising to 13.5–14.5°C citywide after that year.
Conclusion
This study highlights the geospatial clustering of ANCA-associated vasculitis with renal involvement in specific localities of Bogotá, suggesting the potential influence of environmental and climatic factors on disease distribution. The findings underscore the importance of integrating geographic and environmental data into the epidemiological analysis of autoimmune diseases. Further research is needed to explore causal relationships and inform public health interventions aimed at mitigating environmental risks associated with the disease.

title: #929 Successful treatment of steroid-dependent mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis with telitacicept: a case report
authors: Hanwei Huang; Yuehua He; Ling Huang; Qiongjing Yuan; Zhangzhe Peng
abstract:
Background and Aims
To evaluate the efficacy of telitacicept combined with corticosteroid therapy for mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN).
Method
We report a case of a 46-year-old male presenting with nephrotic syndrome. In January 2021, his urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) was 5.49 g/g and serum albumin was 26.3 g/L. Renal biopsy confirmed MPGN with diffuse mesangial electron-dense deposits and 35% foot process fusion. Sequential immunosuppressive therapies including rituximab (cumulative dose 3.2 g), tacrolimus, cyclophosphamide (CTX) (cumulative dose 6.0 g) and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) showed limited efficacy. Full-dose methylprednisolone reduced proteinuria (the lowest UPCR 0.88 g/g) but tapering steroids resulted in proteinuria rebound (UPCR 1.25 g/g), indicating steroid dependence. Additionally, prolonged steroid use led to steroid-induce diabetes. Innovative combination therapy with telitacicept 80 mg weekly and methylprednisolone 20 mg daily was initiated in July 2024. Serial monitoring of proteinuria, serological markers, immunological profiles, and adverse events was performed.
Results
After eight weeks of treatment, the patient's UPCR dropped to 0.08 g/g. Although IgG levels decreased at the initial treatment, they remained within the relatively safe range after dose adjustment. Currently, glucocorticoid was successfully discontinued and the telitacicept dose is subsequently reduced to 80 mg every 4 weeks. The combined therapy achieved to a rapid and sustained remission, with UPCR remaining at a low level. Importantly, no serious infections or disease relapses occurred during glucocorticoid tapering.
Conclusion
This is the first report of telitacicept combined with glucocorticoid treatment for steroid-dependent MPGN, effectively alleviating clinical symptoms , reducing proteinuria and enabling a rapid glucocorticoid taper with minimal adverse effects. These results highlight telitacicept as a promising treatment option for steroid-dependent MPGN, warranting further randomized trials.

title: #1360 Mortality and kidney failure among adults with primary podocytopathies
authors: Ruzita Ghani; Hui Zhuan Tan; Cynthia Lim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Primary podocytopathies such as minimal change disease (MCD) and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) with nephrotic syndrome are at risk of adverse outcomes. We aimed to describe the long-term kidney and patient outcomes in our center.
Method
This was a single-center, retrospective cohort study of all adults ≥21 years old diagnosed between 2016 and 2020 with MCD and FSGS and had nephrotic-range proteinuria (urine protein:creatinine ratio [UPCR] >3 g/g) and hypoalbuminemia (serum albumin <30 g/L). We excluded patients with membranous nephropathy and secondary glomerulonephritides (lupus nephritis, ANCA-associated vasculitis, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, and diabetic nephropathy). Sociodemographic, comorbidity, laboratory and pharmacotherapy data were retrieved from the electronic medical records.
The outcome was the incidence of death or kidney failure (estimated glomerular filtration function [eGFR]<15 ml/min/1.73 m2 or required kidney replacement therapy).
Results
We included 60 adults (80% Chinese, 10% Malay, 5% Indian, 5% other races) with MCD (37 patients) and FSGS (23 patients). The morphological lesions in FSGS included cellular (2 patients), tip (2 patients), perihilar (7 patients), collapsing (3 patients) and not otherwise specified (17 patients). The median age was 53.8 (interquartile range 35.7, 71.2) years. Ischemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disease and liver cirrhosis were present in 8.3%, 5.0% and 1.7%, respectively.
Table 1 shows that compared with the MCD group, patients with FSGS had significantly older age and poorer baseline kidney function. The FSGS group had higher levels of serum creatinine, hematuria and global glomerulosclerosis at presentation; but lower total and LDL-cholesterol, than the MCD group.
Twelve patients (20.0%) died or had kidney failure during the median follow-up of 26.3 (8.9, 50.3) months. Fig. 1 showed that the death or kidney failure rate was highest in the first 9 months after diagnosis. Five (8.3%) had kidney failure at 2.8 (1.1, 11.9) months after diagnosis and 7 (11.7%) died at median 6.4 (4.1, 32.6) months after diagnosis. The causes of death were attributed to kidney failure (1 patient), cardiovascular disease (1 patient), infection (3 patients); and unknown (2 patients).
Among the group with FSGS, 11 patients (47.8%) died or had kidney failure during median follow-up of 11.1 (3.8, 44.0) months. Among the group with MCD, 1 patient (2.7%), died or had kidney failure during median follow-up of 33.4 (13.9, 52.6) months. The Kaplan-Meier survival curve for death or kidney failure (Fig. 2) showed that patients with MCD had better patient and kidney outcomes than those with FSGS (log rank P < 0.001). Cox regression analysis (adjusted for age) found that FSGS was significantly associated with death or kidney failure (adjusted hazard ratio 18.17, 95% confidence interval 2.28–145.07, P = 0.006), compared with MCD.
Conclusion
Adults with severe primary podocytopathy due to FSGS had worse patient and kidney outcomes than MCD.

title: #1428 Laboratory markers of nephrolithiasis
authors: Shamansurova Elmira; Makhkamova Gulnoza; Abdurazakova Shirin; Yorkin Rasulev
abstract:
Background
Urolithiasis (urolithiasis (NL)) is a widespread pathology throughout the world, occurring on all continents and climatic zones, in every race and nationality, in every country with any level of economic development. About 2% of the world's population have experienced the symptoms of this pathology at least once, often at the age of 20–30 years, a widespread disease throughout the world. The incidence of NL fluctuates between 0.5–5.5% annually, and in certain endemic areas for this pathology - within 13–20%.
Aims
To study the most common indicators of general and biochemical blood tests, as well as coagulograms in children with urolithiasis.
Method
Children under 7 years of age with a diagnosis of urolithiasis with damage to the left kidney - 22 children, the right - 18 children, both - 17 children were examined. The gender ratio of the patients studied was 1.1:1 in favor of boys. A control group (CG) of 30 practically healthy patients was formed.
Results
There were 1.3 times more children with left kidney LD than children with right and both kidneys, their number was almost identical. In 75.44% of patients' stones, the average concentration of whewellite was 42.79 ± 2.25% and this was the highest concentration of oxalate salts in the group, weddellite was found in 84.21% with an average concentration of 39.67 ± 2.34%, thus, oxalates prevailed in our study in children. Reliable laboratory markers of nephrolithiasis were: mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (337.5 g/dl, P < 0.01), platelet distribution width (11.9 ± 0.4%, P < 0.001), large platelet coefficient (17.5 ± 0.8%, P < 0.001), hypomagnesemia, hypernatremia, and increased thrombin time (32.7 ± 1.2 sec, P < 0.001). According to the composition of stones, biurate/ammonium hydrourates (46.7%), wevelites (42.8%), wedelites (39.7%), and triglyceride (16.7%) were most often recorded.
Conclusion
Thus, the reliable differences we obtained in the above indicators between the studied groups of patients allow us to recommend them as markers for early diagnosis of the risk of developing urolithiasis in children.

title: #1524 Report of the Croatian registry of native kidney biopsies 2019–2023
authors: Mario Laganović; Kresimir Galesic; Danica Galešić Ljubanović; Ivana Vukovic Brinar; Stela Bulimbasic; Tina Đogaš; Merica Glavina Durdov; Karmela Altabas; Tihana Šimundić; Dario Nakic; Ivan Bubic; Ivica Horvatić
abstract:
Background and Aims
This report describes data collected by the Croatian Registry of Renal Biopsies (CRRB) for the period of 5 years. The aim of this study is to report the relative frequency of nephropathies according to gender, age, clinical presentation, and renal function at the time of renal biopsy based on the histologic diagnosis.
Method
Ten centers (90%) provided the data for 1732 native kidney biopsies during the period 2019-2023. We assessed the anthropometric data, data on kidney function(eGFR), 24-hour proteinuria, hematuria, serum albumin level, arterial hypertension, histological diagnosis, and complications after renal biopsy.
Results
Examined group consisted of 58% males, median age 55 y (18–93 y) and 42% women, median age 56 y (18–87 y). Biopsy rate of 86, 6 p.m.p./year was relatively constant through the 5-year period except for pandemic years 2020 and 2021 when it was reduced by half. Males had a more impaired renal function at the time of renal biopsy (eGFR 53.1 vs 60 ml/min/1.73 m2P < 0.001), nephrotic syndrome (24-hour proteinuria 4.9 vs 3.8 g/dU P < 0.001), and hypertension (139/83 vs 133/81 mmHg P < 0.001). The most prevalent clinical presentations were urinary abnormalities e.g. asymptomatic proteinuria and hematuria (32.9%) and nephrotic syndrome (28.3%) Among all biopsy cases, primary glomerular diseases were the most prevalent histology group (45.2%); IgA nephropathy (IgAN) being most frequent (39.5.1%), followed by focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) (27.6%) and membranous nephropathy (MN) (19.1%). Secondary glomerular diseases were diagnosed in 33.1% of cases. Within secondary glomerular diseases, pauci-immune glomerulonephritis (PIGN) was most often found (28.8%), followed by lupus nephritis 19.3% and diabetic nephropathy 16.3%. During the observed period IgAN was the most prevalent disease 16.5% except for the year 2020. when PIGN was most prevalent reflecting the indications for biopsy during COVID pandemic. Incidence of IgAN decreased from 2.5 to 2.2/per 100 000 population during the 5 year period while FSGS increased 1.4–2.1/per 100 000 population. Among secondary causes we observe increase in incidence of diabetic nephropathy by 25% and decrease of vascular causes by 22%. The most common disease in patients presented with nephrotic proteinuria was minimal change disease (MCD) (78%) and membranous nephropathy 75% in those presented with urinary abnormalities thin membrane disease (55%) and lupus nephritis (53%) and in nephritic syndrome acute tubulointerstitial nephritis (25%) and acute tubular injury (23%). Patients with DN had the highest blood pressure levels (147/82 mmHg) at the time of kidney biopsy. Patients older than 65 years had higher sCr (263 vs 183 μmol/l) and proteinuria (4.79 vs 4.29 g/dU). Most prevalent diagnosis in older group was PIGN. There were no significant differences in any parameters between continental and Mediterranean part of Croatia. The frequency of severe complications ( symptomatic hematoma, blood transfusion or gross hematuria) was 6%.
Conclusion
CRRB provides representative data of the epidemiology of biopsy proven renal disease in Croatia. Availability of these data will be a valuable source to nephrologists to stimulate further research and comparison with other national registries.

title: #1913 Fifteen-year follow-up of outcomes of patients treated for membranous nephropathy
authors: Marko Baralic; Selena Gajic; Ana Bontic; Jelena Pavlovic; Voin Brkovic; Milorad Stojadinovic; Kristina Filić; Ivana Mrdja; Lara Hadzi-Tanovic; Kristina Petrovic; Aleksandra Kezic; Milan Radovic
abstract:
Background and Aims
Membranous nephropathy (MN) is a glomerular disease that can occur at all ages but is more frequently encountered in adults than children. In White adults, it is the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome. In ∼80% of patients, there is no underlying cause of MN (primary MN), and the remaining cases are associated with medications or other diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus, hepatitis virus infection, or malignancies. MN is characterized by the deposition of immune complexes leading to diffuse thickening of glomerular basement membranes. Disease outcomes are difficult to predict; around one-third of patients will undergo spontaneous remission. In those at high risk of progression, immunosuppressive therapy with cyclophosphamide plus corticosteroids has substantially reduced the need for kidney replacement therapy. Nevertheless, up to 30% of patients fail to respond to standard therapy. This study aims to study long-term outcomes in MN patients, identifying risk factors for developing chronic kidney disease (CKD) and end-stage kidney disease (ESKD).
Method
The retrospective cohort study included 94 patients with kidney biopsy diagnosed MN between 2008 and 2023. Demographic, clinical, and laboratory data were obtained from medical histories and data on applied therapeutic protocols. All patients with proteinuria (PRT) were treated with angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors (ACEi) or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and patients with nephrotic range proteinuria were treated with a modified Ponticelli regimen. We monitored patients for clinical signs of remission and developing CKD and ESKD. Logistic regression was used to identify risk factors for developing CKD and ESKD. Definition: remission: reduction of PRT to <0.5 g/day and with creatinine clearance (Ccr) of >60 ml/min/1.73 m2. CKD: (Ccr) of <60 ml/min/1.73 m2 and/or PRT ≥0.5 g/day. ESKD <15 ml/min/1.73 m2. A p-value of <0.05 was considered significant.
Results
The study included 94 patients. At the time of diagnosis, the mean age was 45.83 ± 16.40 years, with 54.3% being men. The mean PRT, serum creatinine (sCr), serum uric acid (sUA), and (Ccr) was 9.05 ± 6.23 g/day, 114.71 ± 89.38 μmol/L, 378.34 ± 107.05 μmol/L and 95.91 ± 44.36 ml/min/1.73 m2, respectively. On histology, 27.7% of patients had immunoglobulin (Ig) G deposits, 10.6% IgM deposits, 2.1% IgA deposits, 38.3% mix deposits, and 21.3% were with no deposits. The median follow-up was 24 months. Statistical significance of lower baseline sCr and higher Ccr was observed in the remission group than in the CKD and ESKD group of patients (P < 0.001). Significantly higher baseline sUA was observed in the CKD (P = 0.009) and ESKD (P = 0.034) groups than in the remission group of patients. A statistically significant difference was observed in outcomes according to the histology stage of MN; 22% of patients with stage I and stage II developed ESKD and 55.6% of patients with stage III (P = 0.046). Significant predictors for outcome were Ccr (χ2 = 12.74, P = 0.002) and sUA (χ2 = 12.20, P = 0.002). Furthermore, the type of Ig deposits also contributed significantly (χ2 = 23.96, P = 0.002) to differentiating outcome categories, although its individual parameter estimates were not statistically significant. Examination of parameter estimates showed that Ccr was negatively associated with being in the CKD group relative to the remission group (Exp (B) = −0.038, P = 0.003). In contrast, sUA was positively associated with both CKD (Exp (B) = 0.012, P = 0.010) and ESKD (Exp (B) = 0.025, P = 0.019), suggesting that higher sUA levels increased the odds of more severe outcomes. Other variables did not reach statistical significance.
Conclusion
These analyses indicate that lower Ccr and higher sUA levels at the time of diagnosis are risk factors for developing CKD and ESKD in MN.

authors: Jorge Zamora Carrillo; Marina López Martínez; Natàlia Ramos Terrades; Marc Patricio; Sheila Bermejo Garcia; Jorge Alexander Sánchez Olaya; Juan Carlos Leon Román; Irene Agraz Pamplona; Maria José Soler Romeo
abstract:
Background and Aims
In recent years, new humanized anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies have been developed to optimize B-cell depletion. Several clinical trials are currently underway to evaluate their effectiveness in immune-mediated glomerular diseases. The objective is to describe the experience at our center with the use of new anti-CD20 drugs in glomerular diseases.
Method
We included patients from our center treated with second-generation anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies for glomerular diseases between January 2017 and January 2024. Patients were followed for one year after the initiation of treatment.
Results
Six patients were included, 2 (33%) men, with a mean age of 59.5 (49–75) years. Diagnoses included 2 (33%) minimal change disease (MCD); 1 (16.7%) mixed cryoglobulinemia type-II; 1 (16.7%) membranous nephropathy (MN); 1 (16.7%) fibrillary glomerulonephritis (FGN); and 1 (16.7%) focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). All patients had previously been treated with rituximab (Rtx). The indications for the new anti-CD20 therapy were: 4 (66%) for refractory disease, 1 (16.7%) for recurrent flares, and 1 (16.7%) due to an anaphylactic reaction to rituximab. The new anti-CD20 therapies used were: obinutuzumab in 4 (66%) patients and ofatumumab in 2 (33%). Before the start of the treatment median serum albumin was 2.7 g/dL [2.5–3.9 g/dL] and urine protein-creatinine ratio (UPCR) 5.75 g/g [2.38–4.85 g/g]. All patients treated with a new anti-CD20 antibody showed CD19 depletion one month after treatment. Whereas with Rtx only the patient with FGN and one of the patients with MCD had achieved CD19+ B cell depletion. A total of 5 (83%) patients achieved partial/complete remission within the first 6 months of follow-up. By month twelve of the follow-up 4 (66.67%) patients remain with partial/complete remission and 2 (33.33%) with complete CD19+ B cell depletion. Serum albumin at month twelve had a median of 3.8 g/dL [3.4–4.35 g/dL] and UPCR 1.75 g/g [0.63–4.2 g/g]. As for side effects, none of the patients had serious side effects, two patients developed severe hypogammaglobulinemia (<300 mg/dL); two had lymphopenia (<1200 × 10⁹/L), and two experienced mild adverse events during administration, which resolved after reducing the infusion rate. No infectious complications were observed during the follow-up period.
Conclusion
The use of new anti-CD20 therapies for the treatment of immune-mediated glomerular diseases appears to be more effective than Rtx in inducing remission of glomerulopathy in refractory cases. New anti-CD120 achieved CD19 depletion in all cases and with an adequate safety profile. Further research and clinical trials should be conducted to confirm these positive results.

title: #2510 Biomarkers for predicting the efficacy of immunosuppressive therapy in IgA nephropathy: the role of serum MCP-1 and TGF-ß
authors: Junseok Jeon; Youngmin Yoon; Kyungho Lee; Jung Eun Lee; Wooseong Huh; Hye Ryoun Jang
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is the most common glomerulonephritis, with many patients progressing to end-stage kidney disease. Accurately predicting patient prognosis and treatment response is crucial for effective management. This study aims to identify key clinical factors and biomarkers that can predict immunosuppressive therapy outcomes in patients with IgAN.
Method
We conducted a retrospective study of adult patients with biopsy-proven IgAN diagnosed between 2010 and 2020. The study evaluated clinical and pathological variables, including serum and urine biomarkers (MCP-1, RANTES, TGF-beta, VEGF) and tissue CD45+ cell count. The outcome was Good prognosis defined as: urine protein to creatinine ratio (uPCR) ≥ 50% reduction or < 0.5 mg/mg, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 or decrease < 5 mL/min/1.73 m2 at one-year post-biopsy.
Results
Mean age was 44.3 ± 12.7 versus 42.0 ± 13.3 years, eGFR 56.9 ± 29.4 versus 68.6 ± 30.7 mL/min/1.73 m2, and uPCR 2.1 ± 1.6 versus 1.6 ± 1.6 mg/mg in the control and Good prognosis groups, respectively. Good prognosis at one year was a reliable indicator of long-term renal prognosis. Predictors of Good prognosis included: high body mass index, absence of hypertension, high eGFR, low uPCR, low histologic grade, and immunosuppressive therapy. After adjusting for clinical and pathological variables, lower serum MCP-1 and higher serum TGF-β were associated with Good prognosis in patients receiving immunosuppressive therapy, but not in those with conservative treatment. CD4+ cell proportion did not correlate with Good prognosis in immunosuppressive therapy patients.
Conclusion
Immunosuppressive therapy was associated with good prognosis in patients with IgAN with serum MCP-1 and TGF-β potentially serving as biomarkers for treatment response. Further research is required to validate these preliminary results.

title: #2516 Adult Henoch-Schönlein purpura nephritis presenting as RPGN: staggered symptoms and management dilemmas
authors: Vi Dang; Thao Huynh; Vien Duong Duc
abstract:
Background and Aims
Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP), primarily a pediatric vasculitis, can present with atypical manifestations in adults. We present a case initially misdiagnosed as inflammatory bowel disease that progressed to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, highlighting the variable presentation sequence, importance of early renal biopsy, and management challenges in resource-limited settings.
Method
Case report
Results
A 49-year-old male presented with edema and purpura. His symptoms began three weeks earlier with periumbilical pain and bloody diarrhea following alcohol consumption. Initial treatment led to improvement, but symptoms recurred two weeks before admission. Evaluation at that time showed normal stool examination and lipase levels. Endoscopic evaluation demonstrated severe erosive antral gastritis (CLO test was negative) and ileocolonic ulcerations with active bleeding. Pathology excluded malignancy and tuberculosis. The patient was diagnosed with IBD and discharged on mesalazine 2000 mg twice daily with a serum creatinine of 0.84 mg/dL.
Four days after discharge, the patient was readmitted with bilateral lower extremity edema and purpura. Laboratory finding showed in Table 1. Autoimmune workup (ANA, anti-dsDNA, ANCA) was negative, complement levels were normal. Protein electrophoresis, and fixed immunoelectrophoresis were negative. Hemoglobin electrophoresis revealed HbE disease. Echocardiography was performed to exclude endocarditis. Treatment was modified from mesalazine to methylprednisolone, with concurrent albumin infusion and intravenous furosemide for acute kidney injury management. Despite maintaining adequate urine output (approximately 2000 mL daily), renal function did not improve, with creatinine levels persistently elevated (2.1–2.3 mg/dL) for a week. Subsequently, a kidney biopsy was performed.
Given the clinical evidence of nephritis, pulse methylprednisolone therapy (250 mg daily) was initiated for five days. However, creatinine levels continued to rise, reaching 3.6 mg/dL. Preliminary biopsy results revealed cellular crescents in 7 of 18 glomeruli, with immunofluorescence results pending. Due to rapidly worsening renal function, therapeutic plasma exchange was initiated but discontinued after two sessions due to resource limitations. The treatment strategy was then modified to include three sessions of hemoperfusion using an HA 280 cartridge, combined with mycophenolate mofetil (1000 mg twice daily) and methylprednisolone (24 mg daily).
The diagnosis of IgA vasculitis nephritis was established based on gastrointestinal symptoms, purpura, and biopsy findings (Figs 1 and 2). One week after hemoperfusion, the patient showed marked improvement with decreased creatinine (1.66 mg/dL), resolved edema, and no new purpuric lesions.
Conclusion
This case illustrates the diagnostic challenges of adult-onset HSP, particularly when gastrointestinal manifestations precede other symptoms. While our patient showed improvement with a combination of immunosuppression and hemoperfusion when standard plasma exchange was not available, this represents a single case experience. The case reinforces the importance of considering HSP in the differential diagnosis of adults presenting with gastrointestinal symptoms followed by renal involvement, and the value of early renal biopsy in guiding diagnosis and therapy.

title: #2644 Alpost syndrome in genes, or Alpost syndrome on biopsy. That is the question
authors: Nihal Bashir; Ahmad Chaaban; Suhail Abdalla
abstract:
Background and Aims
Alport syndrome with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis on biopsy is rare but reported. Alport syndrome can be complicated by segmental glomerular scarring, which can mimic primary FSGS. At the same time, familial FSGS can result from mutations in the collagen IV network of the glomerular basement membrane. The association of FSGS with pathogenic COL4A3–COL4A5 variants has been confirmed with massively parallel sequencing.
Method
A 36-year-old female with hypertension, a mother of two started following up with nephrology service for proteinuria and hematuria during her pregnancy in 2012. She had her first kidney biopsy 2 years later which was consistent with minimal change disease with normal thickness of the basement membrane and absence of immune complex deposits on electron microscopy, she was started on steroids and calcineurin inhibitors with on-and-off relapses of her nephrotic syndrome. The second biopsy was done 5 years later, following a rise in her proteinuria to 4.46 g/g, consisting of a cellular variant of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). Sher autoimmune work up was unremarkable. She continued steroids and tacrolimus; she had no edema with normal albumin level but persistent proteinuria. A third biopsy was done due to persistent proteinuria in 2024 and was consistent with focal segmental proteinuria.
Results
The patient had a genetic test that showed heterozygosity in COL4A3. The patient suffered a recent sensory neural deafness in one year and her son tested positive for the same mutation with haematuria and her daughter was negative. She is currently on empagliflozin and losartan. She had a normal ocular examination.
Conclusion
Diagnosing Alport syndrome can be tricky and difficult, especially given the normal glomerular basement membrane on kidney biopsy. In this patient, a family member's presentation with haematuria and genetic test came 10 years after her initial presentation with nephrotic syndrome.

title: #2967 Real-world outcomes of belimumab in systemic lupus erythematosus and lupus nephritis
authors: Celia Rodríguez Tudero; Cristina Hidalgo Calleja; Alberto Martin Arribas; Daniel Martín Hidalgo; Angelo Roberto Falconi Sarmiento; Elena Villanueva Sánchez; Daniel Ruddy Quispe; Jose Luis Lerma Marquez; Anunciacion Fernanadez De La Fuente; Belen Miguel Ibañez; Susana Gomez De Castro; María del Pilar Fraile
abstract:
Background and Aims
Belimumab is a human monoclonal antibody (Ab) indicated for the treatment of patients with active systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with serological activity (hypocomplementemia and/or anti-DNA) in addition to the standard treatment. Additionally, it has been indicated for patients with lupus nephritis (LN) for four years now.
Method
Observational, cross-sectional, retrospective and descriptive study of patients with SLE who received treatment with belimumab (n = 17), recruited from 2015 to the present date and treated by a multidisciplinary team (Rheumatology and Nephrology). The study includes the clinical and demographic variables of the patients, the time of evolution of the disease, concurrent treatment and, additionally, data on the effectiveness and safety in patients with LN (n = 10).
Statistical Analysis: To evaluate changes in laboratory parameters (creatinine, proteinuria, and anti-dsDNA) at baseline, 6 months, and 12 months, statistical tests were applied based on the characteristics of the data: The Shapiro-Wilk test was used to assess normality. The Levene test evaluated the homogeneity of variances. For normally distributed data with homogeneous variances, a one-way ANOVA was applied to compare means across the three time points. For data that did not meet normality assumptions, the Friedman test was used as a non-parametric alternative. Results were considered statistically significant with a p-value < 0.05. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 24.
Results
The mean age of the 10 patients is 36 years (21–57). The mean time with belimumab was 16,9 ± 10,69 months. 5 patients are still receiving treatment, and the reasons for the interruption are varied. In one patient, the treatment was interrupted due to lupus psychosis. The criteria to start treatment with belimumab was serological activity associated with musculoskeletal and/or skin symptoms, and it was administered to 7 patients due to LN.
Table 1 shows the characteristics of LN patients. 5 patients with LN showed complete renal response after 1 year. The mean evolution of creatinine (initial, after 6 and 12 months) was (0.713 mg/dl ± 0.166 mg/dL, 0.763 mg/dL ± 0.189 mg/dL, 0.783 mg/dL ± 0.116 mg/dL (P = 0.748). The mean evolution of proteinuria (initial, after 6 and 12 months) was (0.822 g/24h ± 0.567 g/24h, 1.027 g/24h ± 0.824 g/24h, 0.796 g/24h ± 0.557 g/24h (P = 0.725). The mean evolution of dsDNA antibodies were (initial, after 6 and 12 months) (162.5 U/mL±160.37 U/mL, 74.33 U/mL ± 65.34 U/mL, 72.00 U/mL ± 54.80 U/mL) (P = 0,093). There was a decrease in proteinuria and serological activity, and only 1 patient required salvage treatment with rituximab due to persistence of proteinuria. In one patient, belimumab had to be interrupted and salvage therapy with anifrolumab was administered, because in spite of the renal and biological response (decrease in proteinuria, negative results for ds-DNA and normal levels of complement), she presented several highly aggressive skin symptoms. One patient is being treated with tacrolimus as a corticosteroid sparing agent in addition to belimumab.
Conclusion
Belimumab, together with the standard immunosuppressive treatment, was seen to be effective against the renal and systemic involvement in the patients in our series, in spite of the limitations caused by the low number of patients.

title: #3035 Nephrotic syndrome that changed the course of chronic myeloid leukemia treatment
authors: Matija Martinic; Nadira Durakovic; Danica Galesic Ljubanovic; Mario Laganović; Bojana Maksimovic
abstract:
Background and Aims
An unusual instance of membranous nephropathy (MN) that developed concurrently with tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) treatment for chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is reported in this case. Hematologic malignancy and glomerular pathology management together posed a special treatment challenge that called for a creative multidisciplinary strategy.
Method and Results
After being diagnosed with CML, a 45-year-old woman was started on imatinib and achieved complete hematologic remission. However, two months after initiating TKI therapy, she developed nephrotic syndrome (NS). Kidney biopsy revealed MN. Serum anti-PLA2R were negative. Given the severity of her condition, a combined immunosuppressive regimen of systemic corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide was initiated.
Recognizing the association between TKI therapy and NS, second-generation TKIs (bosutinib, followed by dasatinib) were trialed sequentially, but both resulted in recurrent NS. Complete remission of MN was achieved only after discontinuing TKI therapy while continuing immunosuppressive treatment. Due to contraindications for further TKI use, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (alloHSCT) was performed, with interferon-alpha used as an interim cytoreductive therapy.
Long-term follow-up post-transplant revealed sustained molecular remission of CML and no recurrence of MN. The patient remains in complete remission of both conditions without requiring maintenance medication, and no signs of MN relapse or graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) have been observed.
Conclusion
This case of MN associated with CML raises important questions regarding the pathophysiological link between TKI therapy and glomerular injury. The favorable clinical outcome, marked by sustained remission of both CML and MN, without GVHD or maintenance therapy, suggest that TKI were probable culprit in this case. This case underscores the importance of strategic therapeutic planning and coordinated multidisciplinary care in managing complex hematologic conditions with significant renal complications.

title: #3165 Molecular phenotype shifts in podocytes of primary FSGS: insights into WT-1, Podocin, and Mesenchymal Markers
authors: Evdokia Bogdanova; Natalia Semenova; Irina Karabak; Zinaida Kochoyan; Anastasiia Anpilova; Vassili Sipovski; Vladimir Dobronravov
abstract:
Background and Aims
Podocyte injury is a central feature of proteinuric glomerular diseases, including primary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (pFSGS), leading to podocyte loss and progressive kidney dysfunction. We previously demonstrated that podocytes in pFSGS undergo significant molecular changes, including reduced expression of Wilms' tumor suppressor protein (WT-1), a key transcription factor for podocyte integrity. This study explores the molecular phenotype of podocytes in immune glomerulopathies, with a focus on WT-1 and markers of epithelial (podocin) and mesenchymal (desmin, vimentin, nestin) phenotypes in pFSGS.
Method
We conducted a quantitative immunomorphological analysis and confocal microscopy to assess glomerular expression of WT-1, podocin, desmin, vimentin, and nestin in kidney samples from patients with morphologically confirmed pFSGS (n = 14), IgA nephropathy (IgAN, n = 14) with CKD G1-3, and negative controls (NC, n = 12). NC samples were obtained from unaffected renal cortex during nephrectomy for malignant neoplasms (Fig. 1a).
Results
Patients with pFSGS exhibited nephrotic syndrome and typical glomerular alterations on light and electron microscopy (Fig. 1b, c), while IgAN showed milder proteinuria (Fig. 1d). Compared to controls, pFSGS demonstrated significantly lower glomerular expression of WT-1 and podocin, alongside elevated desmin and nestin levels (Fig. 2a). In the combined pFSGS and IgAN group, WT-1 and podocin expression correlated positively (r = 0.51, P < 0.013) and both markers inversely associated with proteinuria (WT-1: r = −0.49, P < 0.05; podocin: r = −0.52, P < 0.05). title: #3364 Epidémiologie des cas d'IgAN en France : évaluation à partir des bases de données médico-administratives hospitalières en France (PMSI)
authors: Khalil El Karoui; Aurélie Schmidt; Thomas Spoljar; Jennifer Courias; Nicolas Maillard
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is the most common primary glomerulopathy, with incidence varying from country to country. In France, epidemiological data are available, but only at the level of individual centers or regions. In addition to these clinical data, medico-administrative databases are a relevant source of data on a national scale. The aim of this study was to develop an algorithm to identify cases of IgAN from French hospital medico-administrative databases (PMSI).
Method
All patients hospitalised with at least one ICD-10 code related to IgA-deposited nephropathy between January 1, 2015 and December 31, 2022 were included from the PMSI database. IgAN diagnosis being confirmed by a renal biopsy, the related codes were searched for in a 2-year retrospective period before the appearance of the first IgAN code. Finally, a set of criteria was applied to identify and exclude patients with biopsies related to other pathologies (renal tumour, as well as to differentiate secondary IgAN (vasculitis, cirrhosis, connective tissue diseases, inflammatory bowel disease, spondyloarthropathy)).
Results
Between 2015 and 2022, 8,467 patients were identified with a diagnosis code related to IgA deposits. Of these patients, 3,213 (37.9%) had undergone a renal biopsy in the previous 2 years. Patients had an average age of 47 ± 2 years and 71.5% were male. A total of 1,653 patients (19.5%) had a biopsy procedure associated with another pathology, the main cause of secondary IgAN being IgA vasculitis (10% of patients).
Conclusion
This preliminary study has made it possible to develop an algorithm for identifying IgAN cases using PMSI data. In order to assess the performance of the algorithm, a validation study of the identification of cases will have to be carried out using clinical and/or histological data to confirm the identification of these patients.

title: #3468 Relapse of ANCA-associated vasculitis in patients undergoing renal replacement therapy: a rare but severe complication. Case Series
authors: Júlia Ollé; Marta Martínez Chillarón; Gaston Piñeiro; Alicia Molina-Andujar; Marc Xipell Font; Lida Rodas; David Cucchiari; Luis Fernando Quintana Porras; Miquel Blasco Pelicano; Elena Guillén Olmos
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal involvement is one of the most severe and common manifestations in patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV), progressing to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD, stage G5T) in 20–25% of cases. Due to its recurrent nature, immunosuppressive treatment must be maintained for at least two years, which can increase morbidity and mortality due to its potential adverse effects. Although the risk of relapse after initiating renal replacement therapy (RRT) is lower, relapses can present with extrarenal manifestations, leading to potentially severe complications.
Method
Here, we describe our experience with four patients who developed an AAV relapse after initiating RRT between 2020 and 2024.
Results
The results are summarized in Table 1. All patients had MPO-ANCA positivity. Two patients were undergoing hemodialysis, one was on peritoneal dialysis, and one experienced relapse within the first few weeks post-kidney transplantation. Of the four patients, only one was receiving maintenance therapy after initiating RRT. The time on RRT at the moment of relapse varied widely; however, all patients had elevated ANCA titers at the time of relapse. In three cases, alveolar hemorrhage was the predominant clinical manifestation. All cases were treated with plasma exchange, corticosteroids, and rituximab ± cyclophosphamide, with favorable clinical outcomes.
Conclusion
Our experience highlights that, although uncommon, AAV relapses can occur in patients undergoing RRT and may be potentially severe. The management of this condition poses the challenge of balancing the risks and benefits of long-term immunosuppression. Although there is no established consensus on the follow-up of these patients, maintaining regular laboratory monitoring and a high clinical suspicion for warning symptoms is crucial to enable early and effective treatment of relapse.

title: #3508 A case of membranous nephropathy that reached remission with SGLT2 inhibitor alone
authors: Masao Kikuchi; Koichi Kaikita; Shouichi Fujimoto
abstract:
Case Presentation
A 70-year-old woman was presented with proteinuria and lower leg edema. She was being treated for diabetes, dyslipidemia and coronary spastic angina, and her HbA1c was in the 6% range, indicating good blood glucose control. There were no abnormalities in the urinalysis, but proteinuria had been noted for three months prior to admission, and she was also presenting with hypoalbuminemia (serum albumin: 3.3 g/dL), so she was admitted to hospital. The urine occult blood test was negative, and the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio was 4.45 g/g·Cre. Renal function was normal, with an eGFR of 83 mL/min/1.73 m2. A renal biopsy was performed, and the patient was diagnosed with membranous nephropathy (MN). Anti-PLA2R antibodies and anti-THSD7A antibody are absent. A chest and abdominal CT scan did not reveal any malignancies as the cause. Her systolic blood pressure was in the 90 mmHg range, and she was unable to tolerate treatment with Renin-angiotensin system (RAS) blockers. After starting treatment with dapagliflozin, her urine protein became negative after 2 months of treatment, and she has been able to maintain remission for over 2 years.
Discussion
MN is the most common cause of adult-onset nephrotic syndrome; even though up to one-third of the patients may reach spontaneous remission at any time during the course of follow-up, one-third may persist with nephrotic syndrome, half of which may finally develop end-stage kidney disease. According to the KDIGO guidelines, all patients with MN should receive supportive management with antiproteinuric measures including RAS blockers, optimal blood pressure control, dietary sodium restriction, and diuretic therapy as needed. RAS blockers are a cornerstone of supportive treatment in the management of MN, but they cannot be used if they are not tolerated. In recent years, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors have emerged as a promising adjunctive therapy to RAS blockers in managing MN, and in this case, a good outcome was obtained with SGLT2 inhibitors alone.
Conclusion
Patients with primary MN should receive optimal supportive therapy centered on RAS inhibitors, but in cases where RAS inhibitors are not tolerated, SGLT2 inhibitors can be used as an alternative. Furthermore, we believe that they are also beneficial in terms of blood pressure and fluid management, and salt restriction.

title: #678 Assessing safety and efficacy of kidney biopsy by nephrologists in patients with severely impaired glomerular filtration rate
authors: Priti Meena; Sandip Panda; Paromita Das; Anish Garg; Badari Mylliemngap; Prity Rai; Suvendu Pukait; Krishna Yadav
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing kidney disease but carries a higher risk of complications, particularly in patients with significantly reduced glomerular filtration rate (GFR).
Method
We conducted a prospective observational study involving adult patients with an estimated GFR (eGFR) <30 ml/min/1.73 m² who underwent kidney biopsy at our nephrology department. Patients with solitary or transplanted kidneys were excluded. No prophylactic desmopressin was administered. Automated biopsy devices with 18G needles were utilized, and patients were hospitalized for the procedure. Post-biopsy monitoring included ≥8 hours of bed rest, close observation of vital signs, urine output, and urine color. Hemoglobin levels and ultrasound scans for hematomas were repeated 12–18 hours post-biopsy. Bleeding complications, including hemoglobin reduction, transfusion requirement, hematoma presence, symptomatic hematoma, urgent radiological intervention, and hypotension, were analyzed.
Results
A total of 304 patients were included, with 70% being male and 30% having diabetes. The median eGFR was 10.5 ml/min/1.73 m². Acute kidney injury accounted for 55% of cases, while the remainder had chronic kidney disease. Hemodialysis was performed in 25% of patients prior to biopsy. Major complications necessitating angioembolization occurred in 1.6% (n = 6), while perirenal hematomas >4 cm were identified in 15%. Blood transfusions were required in 10 cases (3.3%), and macroscopic hematuria was observed in 20% of cases. eGFR <10 ml/min/1.73 m² and kidney size <8.5 cm were independently associated with a higher risk of complications.
Conclusion
Kidney biopsy is relatively safe in patients with advanced kidney disease, but careful consideration of the risk-benefit balance is essential when eGFR is <15 ml/min/1.73 m². The routine use of desmopressin for bleeding prevention is unnecessary.

title: #1399 The prognostic significance of the Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score on the outcome of ANCA- associated vasculitis
authors: Saimir Seferi; Suela Mumajesi; Merita Selmani; Merita Rroji; Erjola Likaj; Elena Gjecka; Ariana Strakosha
abstract:
Background and Aims
Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) -associated vasculitis (AAV) is related to substantial morbidity and mortality, even with the latest treatments. Renal involvement is common in AAV and the most important mortality predictor. The Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score (BVAS) has emerged as an essential tool in assessing disease activity and predicting long-term prognosis. The study evaluated the association between BVAS and outcomes in renal vasculitis patients.
Method
A retrospective study was carried out from 2021 to 2024. Twenty patients (13 women and 7 men) with systemic vasculitis were included in the study. Clinical and laboratory data were collected. The BVAS was evaluated for all the patients. Patients were divided into three groups according to their outcomes: remission, renal replacement therapy (RRT), and nonsurvivors.
Results
Eight patients had the presence of PR3- ANCA and twelve patients were positive for MPO-ANCA. All patients were presented with impaired renal function. Nine patients made renal remission, three patients needed RRT, and eight patients did not survive. The BVAS ranged from 6 to 22 (mean 13.2 ± 3.6). The mean BVAS in the remission group was 10.89 ± 2.89, in the RRT group 13.00 ± 1.73, and in the nonsurvivors 15.88 ± 3.18. Independent Kruskal- Walli's test showed a significant relationship between groups χ²(2) = 8.724, P = 0.013, but without specifying among which groups. After the Bonferroni adjustment, a significant difference between BVAS in the remission group and nonsurvivors was found, χ²(2) = 8.444, P = 0.009, and no difference between remission and RRT groups, and RRT and nonsurvivors was found.
Conclusion
These findings indicate that BVAS might be a prognostic indicator of ANCA-associated vasculitis. Moreover, BVAS can contribute to the early identification of high-risk patients requiring more aggressive therapeutic interventions. However, further investigation would be necessary to confirm this hypothesis.

title: #1798 Plasma metabolomics analysis of renal dysfunction in patients undergoing immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment
authors: Yuqun Zeng; Chenyue Li; Qiang He; Jiyu Tang; Juan Jin; Chu Chu; Bin Zhu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have demonstrated remarkable efficacy in cancer treatment. However, their associated immune-related adverse events, particularly renal dysfunction remain a significant concern. The pathophysiology of ICI-associated renal impairment is still not fully understood, and there is a lack of specific, non-invasive biomarkers for diagnosing this condition. This study aims to analyze blood samples from patients with ICI-related renal dysfunction using metabolomics, with the goal of identifying metabolic biomarkers that could aid in diagnosis and provide new insights for clinical management.
Method
The study collected plasma samples from 38 patients with pan-cancer who had received ICI treatment, yielding a total of 76 samples. Patients were divided into two groups based on changes in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) following two consecutive ICIs treatments: the Yang group (n = 18, 36 samples) and the Yin group (n = 20, 40 samples). Plasma metabolomics analysis was performed using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Differential metabolites were identified using T-tests, analysis of variance (ANOVA), principal component analysis (PCA), and orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA). These metabolites were then structurally characterized by mass spectrometry and compared with the KEGG pathway database for further analysis.
Results
Twenty metabolites were identified as differentially expressed metabolites (DEMs) during the onset and progression of ICIs-associated renal impairment. Amino acids, fatty acids, and their analogues were the most prominently regulated metabolites, with dysregulation in amino acid and fatty acid metabolism playing a key role in ICIs-associated renal damage. Data analysis revealed a progressive increase in glutamine, citrulline, valine, histidine, and linoleic acid, while glutamic acid, docosahexaenoic acid, and cis-5-tetradecenoylcarnitine progressively decreased as renal function declined.
Conclusion
The metabolism of amino acids and fatty acids in vivo is altered with the decline in renal function, serving as relative metabolic biomarkers.

title: #2442 Ten years of C3 glomerulopathy: a nationwide cohort study
authors: Rick Overwijk; Fiona Kolbinger; Mark Eijgelsheim; Olaf Dekkers; Andreas Kronbichler; Ingeborg Bajema
abstract:
Background and Aims
C3 glomerulopathy (C3G) is a rare but potentially devastating disease affecting both children and adults. It frequently leads to kidney failure within ten years after diagnosis and currently no specific treatment exists. C3G is used as a collective term for dense deposit disease (DDD) and C3 glomerulonephritis (C3GN) and is thought to sometimes occur in post-infectious settings (C3-PIGN). The diagnosis is made by combining clinical data with light microscopy (LM), immunofluorescence (IF) and electron microscopy (EM) findings. Currently, little is known about the incidence and subtype distribution throughout the population. We constructed a large cohort of C3G patients in the Netherlands of the past ten years. With this cohort we were able to identify incidence and potential variances between subtypes across different regions of the country. We also correlated disease subtypes with certain histopathological findings and analyzed these histopathological findings throughout the years.
Method
A search in the national Dutch pathology database (PALGA) was performed. Patients diagnosed with C3G from January 2014 until December 2023 were identified by two independent observers. Cross tabulations were used to assess the correlation of disease subtypes and glomerular patterns, and the geographical distribution of C3G subtypes and histological disease patterns. Non-parametric analysis was used to evaluate the age distribution at diagnosis.
Results
The selection resulted in a cohort of 280 patients, consisting of: C3GN (n = 101), DDD (n = 39), unspecified C3G (i.e. either DDD or C3GN, n = 106), C3-PIGN (n = 29) and 5 others. The median age of biopsy at the time of diagnosis was 19 for DDD (range 4 to 75) and 58 for C3GN (range 2 to 86), showing that age distribution depends on C3G subtype (P < 0.001). C3G subtypes were associated with specific glomerulonephritis patterns (P < 0.001), namely that DDD and C3GN were associated with membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, and C3-PIGN was associated with endocapillary or exudative pattern. There were no statistically significant variations found in C3G subtype distribution between different provinces or province clusters (P = 0.142).
Conclusion
We present the largest C3G cohort known today, consisting of biopsy proven C3G patients in the Netherlands over a ten year period. We investigated the incidence of C3G in different regions and its disease presentation in kidney biopsies. Results show that C3G incidence is evenly distributed across different regions of The Netherlands. The variability in histological presentation was substantial, therefore we conclude that diagnosing and subtyping C3G cannot be done confidently based on histological pattern alone. This emphasizes the need for optimal and well-defined IF and EM evaluation. This cohort will be an important tool for testing subsequent hypotheses, and inspire future research.

title: #2777 Telemedicine impact in glomerular diseases
authors: Miguel Giovanni Uriol Rivera; Elena Seren Couso; Aina Obrador Mulet
abstract:
Background and Aims
Telemedicine enables substantial time savings and resource optimization while providing instant accessibility to clinical care teams, potentially improving clinical outcomes. Glomerular diseases, characterized by their rarity, significant impact on younger patients, reliance on off-label medications, and the need for highly specialized care, often necessitate frequent clinical visits. This study retrospectively evaluates the impact of telemedicine during two periods: 2016–2020 (pre-telemedicine) and 2020–2024 (post-telemedicine). Furthermore, it projects trends and outcomes for 2030. We analyzed patient numbers, visit frequencies, and time requirements within a hybrid healthcare model (combining in-person and telehealth visits), quantifying efficiency gains attributable to telemedicine. Additionally, we identified key determinants influencing telemedicine utilization. Since 2023, the proportion of in-person versus telemedicine consultations has been guided by patient demand.
Method
Data from 2016 to 2024 were retrospectively analyzed to model trends in patient numbers, annual visits per patient, and time utilization. Predictive models for 2030 were developed using linear regression to forecast patient numbers and visits per patient. Time requirements were estimated assuming 30 minutes per in-person visit and 20 minutes per telemedicine visit. Key metrics included total annual visits, total hours required without telemedicine, total hours required with telemedicine, and time saved. Telehealth was implemented via a smartphone using WhatsApp, which was exclusively utilized for logistical or administrative communications.
Results
The number of patients progressively increased from 244 in 2016 to 340 in 2024 (R² = 0.89, P = 0.001), with an average annual growth rate of 4.92%. Annual visits per patient increased from 3.73 to 4.95 (R² = 0.68, P = 0.006). Total patients evaluated during the pre-telemedicine (2016–2020) and post-telemedicine (2020–2024) periods were 1,106 and 1,636, respectively. The mean annual difference in patient numbers was −51 (95% CI: −24 to −77, P = 0.003), while the mean difference in visits per patient/year was −0.55 (95% CI: −1.19 to 0.07, P = 0.077). Telemedicine accounted for an average of 35% of consultations, reflecting patient demand during 2023 and 2024. Between 2020 and 2024, the hybrid model saved a total of 458 hours, equivalent to 61 full workdays (12 days annually). Predictive modeling suggests that by 2030, patient numbers will increase to 421, with an estimated 2,216 visits annually and 5.68 visits per patient/year.
Stratified analysis of telemedicine utilization from 2020 to 2023 identified key reasons: COVID-19-related (9.9%), medication queries (17%), clinical symptoms (14%), consultation management (34%), and other reasons (25%). Consultation management, defined as adapting medical appointments to the needs and conditions of patients or the clinical care team, emerged as the most frequent reason for telemedicine use, with a 21% annual growth rate (R2: 0.95, P = 0.025).
Conclusion
In the context of glomerular diseases, healthcare resource demands are progressively increasing. Telemedicine has demonstrated its transformative potential to optimize time and resources, benefiting both patients and clinical care teams. Immediate accessibility to clinical support via telemedicine may drive significant advancements in care delivery. Notably, enhanced consultation management has emerged as a critical unmet need, highlighting the potential for telemedicine to address evolving demands in this patient population.

title: #3243 Remission rates of immunotherapy with anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody (rituximab) in patients with membranous nephropathy
authors: Maria Styliani Trivyza; Adamantia Bratsiakou; Argyro Siapika; Marios Papasotiriou; Theodoros Ntrinias; Theodoros Mpimpis; Konstantinos Tsiotsios; Evangelos Papachristou; Dimitrios Goumenos
abstract:
Background and Aims
Long-term remission of albuminuria in patients with membranous nephropathy is the main therapeutic goal, contributing to the preservation of renal function. The aim of the present study was to investigate the efficacy and safety of monoclonal anti CD20 antibody administration in patients with membranous nephropathy, depending on serum anti-PLA2R titer at diagnosis.
Method
The effect of treatment with monoclonal anti CD20 antibody (rituximab) in two doses of 1 g at 2 weeks interval was studied retrospectively in patients with histologically documented membranous nephropathy. Serum anti-PLA2R titer was measured at diagnosis. Rituximab was given either as treatment after relapse of nephrotic syndrome, or upon failure of the first immunosuppressive regimen (failure to achieve remission), or as first-line therapy. All patients were followed up for at least one year after administration.
Results
A total of 21 patients (19 men) with a mean age of 58.3 ± 10.7 years were studied. Thirteen participants (62%) had positive serum anti-PLA2R titer at diagnosis, while 8 patients (38%) had negative titer. Patients who received Rituximab maintained their kidney function with a mean eGFR from 81.2 ± 27.9 to 80 ± 24.8 ml/min/1.73 m² at the end of one year follow up, while proteinuria decreased from 7.5 ± 5.7 to 3.0 ± 2.9 gr/24h regardless of anti-PLA2R titer. Eight patients (5 anti-PLA2R positive) had complete remission, 6 patients (3 anti-PLA2R positive) had partial remission, while 7 patients (5 anti-PLA2R positive) did not respond to treatment. Further analysis according to serum anti-PLA2R titer showed that patients with negative anti-PLA2R titer (n = 8) had a greater reduction in albuminuria at 12 months compared to patients with positive anti-PLA2R titer (n = 13) (from 9.4 ± 8.8 to 2.4 ± 2.5 gr/24 h and from 6.3 ± 2.1 to 3.1 ± 3.2 gr/24 h, respectively), although the difference in proteinuria reduction at 12 months between the two groups was not significant (P = 0.176).
Conclusion
Treatment with Rituximab in patients with membranous nephropathy achieves preservation of renal function during the follow-up period and partial or complete remission of proteinura regardless of serum anti-PLA2R titer.

title: #3476 Recurrent hypokalemia and nephrotic syndrome in a patient with renal amyloidosis: a case report
authors: Suni Grace Castillo-Babaran
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal involvement in amyloidosis common, however, the occurrence of nephrotic syndrome and tubulopathies are rarely reported in literature.
Method
We report a case of renal amyloidosis presenting as nephrotic syndrome with concurrent tubulopathy.
Results
A 62-year old Filipino female was admitted in our institution for a two-month history of worsening anasarca, exertional dyspnea, intermittent abdominal pain, frothy urine, with occasional loose stools, and generalized body weakness. Initial work-up revealed +3 albuminuria, +3 glucosuria, and spot urine protein-creatinine of 57.9 g/day. She also had hypercholesterolemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypoalbuminemia. Ultrasound revealed normal-sized kidneys with preserved cortical thickness. She had recurrent hypokalemia, which on work-up revealed a urine potassium-creatinine ratio of 29.7, combined high- and normal-gap metabolic acidosis on arterial blood gas, and urine pH 6.0 which were all consistent with proximal renal tubular acidosis. Renal amyloidosis was eventually confirmed through kidney biopsy revealing diffuse Congo red-positive, apple-green birefringent, acellular mesangial and glomerular capillary loop deposits. She received empiric chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone, as well as diuretics and electrolyte replacement, with eventual improvement in her symptoms.
Conclusion
Deposition of amyloid protein fibrils in the glomerulus can lead to increased capillary permeability, massive proteinuria, and nephrotic syndrome. On the other hand, deposition in the tubules can lead to tubulopathies such as Fanconi syndrome. This case underscores the importance of including amyloidosis in the differential diagnoses for patients presenting with nephrotic syndrome. High clinical suspicion can direct the diagnostic evaluation so that prompt treatment can be instituted and progression to end-stage kidney disease be prevented.

title: #748 Use of avacopan-based therapy among adults with severe active ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV): a cross-sectional survey of physicians in Germany and the UK
authors: Wolfram Jabs; Udo Schneider; Paul Warner; Tamara Popov
abstract:
Background and Aims
Avacopan, a selective C5aR1 inhibitor, has demonstrated efficacy and safety in its development program in patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) (specifically granulomatosis with polyangiitis [GPA] and microscopic polyangiitis [MPA]) and has been approved in combination with rituximab or cyclophosphamide for the treatment of adults with severe active GPA/MPA. Here, we describe results from a physician survey assessing avacopan usage patterns in adults with severe active GPA/MPA in daily clinical practice.
Method
A quantitative online survey was completed by physicians in Germany and the UK from April 17 to May 20, 2024. Respondents were required to be qualified in their primary specialty (nephrology, rheumatology, internal medicine with a secondary qualification in rheumatology or nephrology [Germany only], pulmonology, or ear, nose and throat [ENT] medicine) for 2 to 40 years, spend ≥60% of their time in direct patient care, be responsible for making treatment choices for adults with GPA/MPA, and have personally managed ≥5 patients with AAV in the last 12 months, including ≥2 with severe active GPA/MPA. Each respondent completed patient record forms for 2–3 GPA/MPA patients (≥18 years) with severe active disease (new-onset or relapsed) as of the most recent induction therapy, currently receiving induction therapy, or previously severe active now on maintenance therapy. Statistical significance testing was conducted with a type 1 error rate (alpha) of 5% using independent t-tests for means testing and independent p-tests for proportion testing. The survey included additional attitudinal/perceptual questions on GPA/MPA patient categorisation, ‘active’ definition, guidelines followed, and treatment attitudes, responses to which will be presented elsewhere.
Results
Survey response rate was 51% (63% in Germany; 43% in the UK). A total of 206 patient record forms were completed by 81 respondents (40 in Germany; 41 in the UK), including 26 nephrologists, 39 rheumatologists, 9 pulmonologists and 7 ENT specialists. At their most recent induction, 93/206 patients (45.2%) were receiving avacopan-based therapy. Of these, 5 (5.4%) were continuing previous avacopan treatment and 88 (94.6%) were newly initiated. Significantly more patients in the avacopan group (vs. the non-avacopan group) had depression (25% vs 11%, P = 0.008) or BMI >35 kg/m2 (17% vs 7%, P = 0.026) at their initial AAV diagnosis (Table 1). The proportion of patients with other pre-selected comorbidities at the time of AAV diagnosis, including hypertension, dyslipidemia, Type 2 diabetes, and anxiety, was similar between treatment groups. Significantly more patients in the avacopan vs. the non-avacopan group had multiple (5+) organ involvement (25% vs 9%; P = 0.004), lung involvement (58% vs 43%, P = 0.04), skin involvement (43% vs 13%, P = 0.001), and/or presented with ‘general’ (65% vs. 44%, P = 0.004) or skin (34% vs 15%, P = 0.002) symptoms at the start of their most recent induction (Table 2). Patients receiving avacopan-based therapy also had significantly higher CRP values (30 mg/dL vs 24.8 mg/dL, P = 0.035) and showed a trend towards lower eGFR values (50 ml/min vs 55 ml/min, P = 0.094) than those treated without avacopan. Results were consistent in Germany and the UK.
Conclusion
Survey results (patient record forms) suggest broad use of avacopan as part of induction therapy in adults with severe active (new-onset or relapsed) GPA/MPA in Germany and the UK. A significantly higher proportion of patients receiving avacopan- (as opposed to non-avacopan-) based therapy had depression or were overweight at their initial AAV diagnosis. Additionally, a significantly greater proportion of these patients had multiple organ involvement, lung or skin involvement, presented with ‘general’ or skin symptoms, and/or had higher CRP values at their most recent induction. Limitations of this research include potential bias of the respondents, small sample size and incompleteness of the data in certain fields on patient record forms.

title: #3487 Recurrent admissions with life threatening hypokalaemia due to acquired distal renal tubular acidosis
authors: Hsu Pheen Chong; Andra Caracostea
abstract:
Background and Aims
Distal renal tubular acidosis (dRTA) is an uncommon diagnosis, especially in adults, with most cases being secondary to autoimmune conditions. Generally, this is a transient phenomenon, and patients seemed to have maintained adequate potassium levels on discharge. This case report presents a patient with recurrent admissions due to dRTA.
Method
41-year-old male presented initially in August 2024 to the emergency department with overuse of ibuprofen due to recurrent pain. On the day of admission he took 64 tablets (without suicidal ideation) due to severe tooth pain. He had been vomiting since February 7–8 times per day. Initial blood tests revealed a microcytic anaemia, a mild kidney injury (baseline Creatinine 73 µmol/L, admission creatinine 108 µmol/L), potassium level of 2.7 mmol/L, anion gap of 10.4, chloride level of 114 mmol/L and bicarbonate level of 14 mmol/L. An OGD was performed showing multiple ulcers and he was started on omeprazole and referred for psychological therapy. He was diagnosed with distal renal tubular acidosis secondary to overuse of NSAIDs and was started on potassium citrate therapy for 6 weeks and discharged home.
Readmission in October 2024, the patient returned with vomiting (unable to keep food or fluids down) following 4 days of ibuprofen use for tooth pain. His potassium level was 1.8 mmol/L initially, with significant muscle weakness and a normal ECG. Immediate treatment with 1 liter of sodium chloride 0.9% with 40 mmol of KCl was initiated. Despite 3 liters of the potassium replacement over the night his repeated K was 1.7 mmol/L, 1.8 mmol/L and respectively 2.0 mmol/L. He required ITU admission for high concentrate K replacement. His acidosis resolved, bicarbonate climbed to 22.0 mmol/L and potassium stabilised at 3.9–4.1 mmol/L so he was discharged home on potassium citrate 3 g in 10 mL oral liquid for maintenance after 7 days of admission.
The patient had in total three admissions in the space of 8 weeks with similar presentations (vomiting, muscle cramps, generalised weakness, dizziness). Each time he had severe hypokalaemia, acidosis, with low bicarbonate and a mild kidney injury. He received each time sodium chloride with 40 mmol of K and bicarbonate replacement.
Results
He was given potassium citrate 3 g in 10 mls oral liquid on discharge. It was underlined to patient the importance of discontinuation of ibuprofen and sick day rule. If he is unable to orally tolerate the K citrate then he will need to present to hospital for IV replacement.
Conclusion
In conclusion, this case highlights the critical impact of ibuprofen overuse, leading to significant complications such as distal renal tubular acidosis. Ibuprofen is widely available over the counter with common side effects well known. We highlight this case of life threatening acquired distal tubular acidosis which persisted despite medication cessation.

title: #3550 Complement mediated thrombotic microangiopathy (C-TMA) clinical presentation and outcomes—single centre experience
authors: Ivana Vukovic Brinar; Klara Profeta; Margareta Fistrek Prlic; Ana Boban; Ema Ivandic; Marijana Medic; Ana Vujaklija Brajkovic; Ivana Stanusic; Nadira Durakovic; Marijana Coric; Marija Bakula; Bojan Jelaković
abstract:
Background and Aims
Complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy (C-TMA) is a life- and organ-threatening disease characterized by endothelial injury and microvascular thrombosis due to complement overactivation. Genetic susceptibility is often triggered and exacerbated by predisposing factors. The concept C-TMA, rather than the traditional classification into primary and secondary TMA, is gaining increasing attention. In line with this perspective, we present our single-center experience with complement-mediated TMA over a two-year period.
Method
All adult patients diagnosed with C-TMA at the University Hospital Centre Zagreb between March 2022 and August 2024 were included in this study. Data are presented as median (M) and quartiles (25th–75th percentiles) or as numbers and percentages unless otherwise stated.
Results
Eleven patients (7 female, 63.5%) with a median age of 34 years (range: 21–50) presented with new-onset hypertension (M 170/90 mmHg). Gastrointestinal symptoms were observed in 4 patients (36.4%), while 2 patients (18.2%) exhibited neurological symptoms. All patients had some degree of acute kidney injury (creatinine 193 µmol/L [135–335]; eGFR 31 ml/min/1.73m² [16–43]); 2 patients (18.2%) were anuric, and 4 patients (36.4%) required renal replacement therapy (RRT). Active urine sediment was present, with 7 patients (63.6%) exhibiting erythrocyturia and 10 patients (90.9%) presenting with proteinuria in the absence of urinary infection. Additionally, 4 patients (36.4%) developed respiratory failure and required mechanical ventilation.
Extensive microbiological testing was negative in all cases except for one patient with concomitant COVID-19 infection. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) was excluded (ADAMTS13 = 0.44 [0.30–0.75]). Identified triggering conditions for complement overactivation and C-TMA included pregnancy (n = 3; 27.3%), allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT, n = 3; 27.3%), viral infection (n = 2; 18.2%), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE, n = 1; 9.1%), and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH, n = 1; 9.1%).
Elevated C5b-9 levels were found in 10 patients (90.9%) (M 653 ng/ml [276–815]). Three patients (27.3%) had low complement factor H (CFH) levels, 2 patients (18.2%) had low complement factor I (CFI) levels, and 1 patient (9.1%) had elevated complement factor B (CFB) levels. Kidney biopsies were performed in 4 patients, all of whom showed evidence of TMA in kidney tissue.
Seven patients (63.6%) initially received plasmapheresis, followed by eculizumab therapy. The median duration of anti-complement therapy was 3 months (range: 2–5). Genetic analysis revealed pathogenic mutations in MCP in 2 patients (18.2%) and variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in 3 patients (27.3%). Genetic analysis was not performed in 3 patients who had undergone HSCT.
During follow-up, 2 patients (both with uncontrolled hematological disease) died. The remaining 9 patients experienced resolution of TMA and improvement in kidney function (creatinine 113 µmol/L [74–206]; eGFR 56 ml/min/1.73m² [30–111]). Two patients continued anti-complement therapy, while the others were weaned off treatment and are being regularly monitored for signs of TMA recurrence and organ involvement.
Conclusion

Background and Aims
Complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy (C-TMA) is a life- and organ-threatening disease characterized by endothelial injury and microvascular thrombosis due to complement overactivation. Genetic susceptibility is often triggered and exacerbated by predisposing factors. The concept C-TMA, rather than the traditional classification into primary and secondary TMA, is gaining increasing attention. In line with this perspective, we present our single-center experience with complement-mediated TMA over a two-year period.
Method
All adult patients diagnosed with C-TMA at the University Hospital Centre Zagreb between March 2022 and August 2024 were included in this study. Data are presented as median (M) and quartiles (25th–75th percentiles) or as numbers and percentages unless otherwise stated.

Eleven patients (7 female, 63.5%) with a median age of 34 years (range: 21–50) presented with new-onset hypertension (M 170/90 mmHg). Active urine sediment was present, with 7 patients (63.6%) exhibiting erythrocyturia and 10 patients (90.9%) presenting with proteinuria in the absence of urinary infection. title: #3822 Experience in a single center with standard treatment of lupus nephritis
authors: María Ramírez Peña; Melissa Cintra; Francisco José De la Prada; Fabiola Alonso Garcia; Mercedes Salguiera Lazo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Lupus nephritis (LN) is one of the most frequent manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus, affecting 40% of patients and representing an important risk factor for morbidity and mortality. Standard of care treatment achieves complete remission rates between 20–30%, with 20–35% of recurrences between three to five years, in clinical trials [1, 2].
We review patients with biopsied lupus nephritis, monitoring our unit, their treatment and response to it.
Method
Retrospective study of 56 patients, 48 women (85.71%) and 8 men (14.28%), with biopsied lupus nephritis. 78.6% (44 patients) had extrarenal involvement at presentation. All had positive anti-DNA and 19.64% (11 patients) had positive antiphospholipid antibodies.
Results
The type of LN was: Type 1: 2 patients (3.57%), Type II: 6 patients (10.71%), Type III: 12 patients (21.42%), Type IV: 26 patients (46.43% ) and Type V: 9 patients (16.2%). One patient presented a type C3 membrano-proliferative pattern.
Creatinine at debut was 0.95 +/− 1.13 mg/dl, with a protein/creatinine ratio of 1798 +/− 2106 mg/gr. The anti-DNA level was 178 +/− 195 IU/mL, with C3/C4 levels of 64.7 +/− 19.9/7.9 +/- 6 mg/dL.
In 42 patients (75%) the standard treatment was boluses of Methylprednisolone, Hydroxychloroquine and Mycophenolate Mofetil. Belimumab was added in 5 patients (8.9%), and intravenous Cyclophosphamide was added in 10 patients (17.85%). 2 patients (3.57%) were treated with Calcineurin Antibodies and another 4 (7.14%) required anti-CD20 Antibodies.
Relapses were observed in 8 patients (14.28%).
In the last review of the patients, the mean Creatinine was 0.95 +/− 0.94 mg/dl (but 11 patients (19.64%) had Creatinine >1.2 mg/dl (CKD 3–4)), with a protein/creatinine ratio of 103.3 +/− 948 mg/gr (but 9 patients (16%) had a protein/creatinine ratio >0.5 mg/g). The anti-DNA level was 11.79 +/− 63.4 IU/mL, with C3/C4 levels of 90.88 +/-26.62 / 14.54 +/- 7.52 mg/dL.
Prednisone administration was maintained in 29 patients (51.78%) with a mean dose of 2.13 +/- 2.21 mg/day.
4 patients (7.14%) required renal replacement treatment and death occurred in 1 patient (1.78%).
Conclusion
In routine clinical practice, the results, in terms of remission, of the treatment of Lupus Nephritis could be better than those reported in clinical trials. However, in our experience, a non-negligible percentage of patients presented with chronic kidney disease and Proteinuria, and in addition, prednisone could not be discontinued in 50% of the patients. Perhaps a more intensive initial treatment will improve these results.

title: #1763 The incidence of biopsy-proven glomerulonephritis in the Republic of North Macedonia: a five-year follow-up
authors: Vlatko Karanfilovski; Nikola Gjorgjievski; Ana Stojanoska; Adrijana Spasovska Vasilova; Sabir Suleyman; Lada Trajceska; Galina Severova- Andreevska; Pavlina Dzekova-Vidimliski; Igor Nikolov; Gordana Petrushevska; Vesna Ristovska; Gjulsen Selim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Glomerular diseases are a prevalent cause of end-stage renal disease; however, there is a scarcity of population-based epidemiological data concerning glomerulonephritis. This study aims to analyze the epidemiological patterns and clinical presentations of biopsy-proven primary and secondary glomerular diseases sourced from a tertiary nephrology unit, which serves as a reference center for the diagnosis and treatment of glomerular diseases in the Republic of North Macedonia, a country with a population of 1.8 million.
Method
This investigation is a single-center, retrospective study encompassing 228 adult patients (aged over 14 years) diagnosed with biopsy-proven primary or secondary glomerular disease. The study was conducted at the University Hospital of Nephrology in Skopje, North Macedonia, over a five-year period (2020–2024). Excluded from the analysis were the biopsies of kidney transplant patients and those with incomplete data.
Results
A total of 228 native renal biopsies were evaluated via light microscopy, with 62 patients (27.2%) undergoing immunofluorescence analysis and 127 patients (55.7%) undergoing electron microscopy. The majority of the patients were male (143 patients; 62.72%), with a mean age at the time of renal biopsy of 47.45 ± 15.92 years; 37 patients (16.23%) were aged over 65 years. The average serum creatinine level at the time of biopsy was 182 ± 150.66 µmol/l, the mean glomerular filtration rate was 58.9 ± 36.77 ml/min/1.73 m², and the mean proteinuria was 3.04 ± 3.0 g/l. Geographically, 92 patients (40.35%) resided in the Skopje Region, followed by the Eastern Region (11.84%), and the Pelagonia and Southwestern Regions (each with 10.08%) within North Macedonia. The most frequently diagnosed glomerulonephritis in our cohort was membranous nephropathy, identified in 33 patients (14.47%), followed by focal segmental glomerulosclerosis in 27 patients (11.84%), and IgA nephropathy in 25 patients (10.96%). Other diagnoses included amyloidosis and various fibrillary glomerulopathies in 23 patients (10.08%), minimal change disease in 22 patients (9.65%), membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis in 20 patients (8.77%), extracapillary glomerulonephritis in 19 patients (8.33%), diabetic nephropathy and/or nephroangiosclerosis in 15 patients (6.57%), mesangial glomerulonephritis without IgA in 15 patients (6.57%), lupus nephritis in 12 patients (5.26%), global glomerulosclerosis in 7 patients (3.07%), acute kidney injury in 3 patients (1.31%), and other diagnoses in 7 patients (3.07%). Re-biopsy procedures were performed in only a small minority of the patients.
Conclusion
The data presented herein provide valuable insights into the incidence of glomerular diseases in North Macedonia and could serve as a foundational resource for the establishment of a National Registry for Glomerular Diseases. Such a registry would facilitate the assessment of the burden that these diseases impose on the healthcare system and budget, as well as enable comparisons with data from registries in other countries across Europe and globally.
