title: #1778 A rare case of Kallmann syndrome combined with primary membranous nephropathy
authors: Hou Shihui; Jie Yang; Fang Yu; Jia Chen; Kehong Chen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kallmann Syndrome (KS) is a rare genetic disorder characterized by hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia, resulting from defective migration of GnRH neurons and olfactory bulb development. Primary Membranous Nephropathy (PMN) is a common cause of nephrotic syndrome, characterized by thickening of the glomerular basement membrane and proteinuria. The co-occurrence of these two conditions has not been previously reported in the literature. This case report presents a rare instance of KS combined with PMN, and their potential pathophysiological relationship remains unclear, the AMER1 gene mutation may be a mutation point related to KS.
Method
A 37-year-old male presented with bilateral lower extremity edema for 1 year, which aggravated in the past 1 week. He was diagnosed with KS in our hospital 5 years ago and without any treatment currently. Comprehensive evaluations were performed, including:
Clinical assessment: Detailed history, physical examination, and evaluation of KS-related features (anosmia, hypogonadism).
Laboratory tests: Urinalysis, 24-hour urine protein quantification, blood routine, liver function, blood lipid, serum albumin, and sex hormone levels, and Anti-phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) antibody assay.
Imaging studies: Electrocardiogram, renal and cardiac ultrasound, chest CT, and brain MRI;
Renal biopsy: Histopathological, immunofluorescence and electric mirror examination.
Others: Genetic testing.
Results
The patient exhibited symptoms of nephrotic syndrome, including edema of both lower limbs, proteinuria (19 g/24 h), hypoalbuminemia (27.8 g/L), and hyperlipidemia; The renal biopsy pathological results (Fig. 1) and increased PLA2R (Table 1) clearly indicated that the patient was diagnosed with primary membranous nephropathy. After hormone and tacrolimus treatment, the patient achieved partial remission of nephrotic syndrome (Table 1).
The patient had concurrent symptoms of KS. He had lost his sense of smell since childhood and had slower development than his peers with no development of secondary sexual characteristics at the age of 14. Small penis and testicles were investigated in our patient. Relevant hormone tests showed significantly reduced testosterone (0.32 ng/ml) and luteinizing hormone (0.29 mIU/ml), while the levels of other hormones such as estrogen, growth hormone were normal. And abdominal ultrasound indicated the absence of the left kidney, and the Cardiac ultrasound showed dextrocardia (Fig. 2). The diagnosis of KS in this patient is clear.
To further investigate the cause of the patient's KS and whether there is an association between KS and PMN, we performed whole-exon sequencing on the patient and his parents. The patient did not see any of mutations in KS reported so far,but the patient was found to have a missense variant mutation in the AMER1 gene with 100% mutation abundance in whole-exon sequencing (Table 2). AMER1 is located on the X chromosome and it plays an important role in the middle stage of embryonic development. There is no reported indication that the AMER1 gene is related to KS, but the gene is specifically expressed in the nervous system and nasal epithelium, and is also widely expressed in the gonads and kidneys, which are highly overlapping with the target organs of KS, and the association with KS needs to be further investigated. Unfortunately, no similar mutations were found in his parents. Whether this patient is the precursor of KS caused by AMER1 gene mutation and the mechanism of its occurrence cannot be clarified at present, and it needs to be verified by the offspring or other cases or animal experiments.
Conclusion
In conclusion, this case is the first reported case of KS combined with primary membranous nephropathy, and the missense base mutation of AMER1 is expected to be a novel mutation site in KS patients, which needs to be verified in subsequent cases.

title: #2033 First small steps…a pilot study on changes in Immunoglobulin G N-glycome during immunosuppressive treatment of ANCA-associated vasculitis
authors: Matija Crnogorac; Anđelo Beletić; Lovorka Djerek; Ana Strizić; Maja Hanić; Ivica Horvatić; Gordan Lauc
abstract:
Background and Aims
ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) activity during and after the treatment lacks adequate biomarkers. Immunoglobuline G (IgG) N-glycome is an enzymatically attached oligosaccharides network crucial for IgG functional “phenotype”. Glicosylation is necessary in inflammatory reactions in which changes occur to glycosylation of numerous plasma proteins including IgG. Recently published paper by Wojcik I et al. pointed to specific IgG glycosylation differences preceding relapse in PR3-AAV patients both with and without ANCA titre rise. By presenting the pilot results of our GlycANVasc (Glycans in ANCA-associated vasculitis) study, evaluating IgG N-glycome changes during the immunosuppressive treatment, we wish to invite collaborators to join in.
Method
The pilot cases were two female patients, aged 63 (MPO-AAV) and 67 (PR3-AAV), both with lung and renal involvement. Serum was collected at four-time points: The first and second points (both patients) were the at the induction treatment (cyclophosphamide + methylprednisolone) and remission achievement. The third point (only the first patient) was maintenance treatment Rituximab (RTX) administration (three months later), and the fourth point (only the first patient) was one month after RTX. N-glycans were enzymatically released from isolated IgG, fluorophore-labeled, separated using capillary gel electrophoresis, and the glycan traits were calculated using the individual glycans' relative abundances.
Results
During induction treatment in the “MPO-AAV” patient, the relevant relative changes were the increase in digalactosylated glycans (12.2%) and the decrease in agalactosylated (8.5%) and afucosylated (12.3%). An analogous pattern was present between the second and third samples. Still, the changes were lower: digalactosylated glycans went up by 3.8%, with a reduction of 4.4% in agalactosylated and 2.0% in afucosylated traits. A month after the RTX administration, the relative decreases in the disialylated (8.8%) and monosialylated (3.8%) glycans appeared, while the abundance of (a)galactosylated and afucosylated glycans remained stationary. The “PR3-AAV” during the induction treatment, showed a relative increase in digalactosylated glycans (79.7%) and bisecting GlcNAc of (43.5%), accompanied by a relative decrease in agalactosylated glycans (45.4%).
Conclusion
The pilot cases evidenced IgG N-glycome changes during immunosuppressive treatment administered in both AAV subtypes. The increase in the galactosylated glycans during remission achievement could indicate a transition towards anti-inflammatory IgG “phenotype” both in MPO and PR3 AAV. The interpretation might be similar for the increase in bisecting GlcNAc in PR3 AAV, while for afucosylation and sialylation, straightforward assumptions would be challenging. These pilot data justify further “mining” of IgG N-glycome changes in the search for AAV activity biomarker candidates.

title: #3286 Safety and efficacy of SGLT2 inhibitors in the elderly with CKD
authors: Vjollca Godanci-Kelmendi; Mimoza Ramadani Piraj; Fatime Imeri; Shega Konjufca
abstract:
Background and Aims
SGLT2 (Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2) inhibitors have attracted the attention of clinicians in the fields of nephrology, endocrinology, cardiology, etc.
These drugs have demonstrated not only high effectiveness in the treatment of DN, but also in other chronic kidney diseases with proteinuria, regardless of the cause.
The use of SGLT2i in the elderly with chronic kidney disease (CKD) was met with initial skepticism due to fears of side effects such as dehydration, urinary tract infections, worsening of diabetic angiopathy, risk of amputation, hypotension, risk of fractures or falls.
Method
Descriptive and comparative cohort study. 125 outpatients, who were divided into groups. 50 patients—DT2 and ND of different stages and 25 patients have primary glomerular disease with CKD with SGLT2i, and a control group of 50 diabetic patients who were treated with conventional therapy.
50 T2D patients with ND treated with empagliflozin, compared with a control group of 50 diabetic patients with ND treated with ACE/ARB and other glucose-lowering agents. 25 non-diabetic patients treated with SGLT2i for glomerular disease were also included in this study.
In the group of 68 patients over the age of 65 treated with SGLT2i, specific changes and results were observed (Table 4). In addition, the frequency of dehydration, hydro and electrolytic disorders, as well as cases of falls, fractures and amputations were monitored to evaluate the safety of treatment in the elderly population.
Results
Age - 68 patients with SGLT2i > 65 years, this group was specifically analyzed for side effects such as hyponatremia, dehydration, polyuria, low blood pressure, urinary tract infections (UTIs), falls, fractures and amputations.
Inclusion criteria: Patients with albuminuria and T2D for the first group and the control group. Patients with albuminuria and CKD due to glomerular disease in the other group.
Exclusion criteria: Patients with eGFR below 20. Patients were followed for an average of 18 months.
The results of our study showed a significant improvement in the group of patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D) treated with SGLT2i. (see tables 1, 2, 3 and 4)
Conclusion
Our results suggest that SGLT2i treatment is a safe and effective modality for DN and CKD diseases with proteinuria, regardless of cause.
In patients over 65 years of age the benefits of treatment were evident, SGLT2i were well tolerated and proved safe for the elderly, with special care for the most frail subjects.

title: #3745 Assay validation and quantification of new urinary kidney safety biomarker candidates for the detection of glomerular injury
authors: Wael Naboulsi; Amelie Vogt; Robin Kretz; Sophia Samodelov; Santosh Sutradhar; Erina Paul; Yi-Zhong Gu; Shashi Ramaiah; Lila Ramaiah; Manish Ponda; Oliver Poetz; Harald Seeger
abstract:
Background and Aims
Urine biomarkers for tubular kidney damage have been studied comprehensively and qualified for non-clinical safety assessments. Their use in cohort-level applications during Phase 1 trials with healthy volunteers is well-established, particularly when nephrotoxicity is a concern. Yet, there is a paucity of data on biomarkers for drug-induced glomerular damage, especially for identifying subclinical injury occuring before changes in GFR and/or albuminuria. The Translational Safety Biomarker Pipeline (TransBioLine) project is exploring a range of urinary protein biomarkers to detect drug-induced glomerular damage. Its goal is to address this gap by evaluating candidate glomerular injury biomarkers in at-risk patients. The project focuses on how a panel of biomarkers for both glomerular and tubular damage can provide insights into the mechanisms of drug-induced kidney injury. Here, we present findings from the learning phase studies, which were used to select protein biomarkers to be included in confirmatory phase studies aimed at supporting biomarker qualification.
Method
We present the results for glomerular protein biomarkers—nephrin (NPHS1), podocin (NPHS2), and podocalyxin (PODXL)—alongside tubular injury biomarkers KIM 1 and NGAL, as well as two vascular component markers, vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM1) and matrix metalloproteinase 3 (MMP3). Using IA-LC-MS/MS assays, we quantified these urinary glomerular, tubular, and vascular protein biomarkers in urine samples from patients with confirmed glomerular injury (n = 48) and healthy volunteers (n = 50) as part of an ongoing biomarker qualification initiative.
Results
Geometric mean ratios (GMRs) calculated for each biomarker in diseased versus healthy cohorts were 3.83 for NGAL (2.17–6.76, P < 0.0001)), 1.43 for PODXL (1.08–1.89, P = 0.0128), 2.9 for MMP3 (1.93–4.38, P < 0.0001), and 6.04 for VCAM1 (4.16–8.78, P < 0.0001), while NPHS1 and NPHS2 showed no significance (p-values = 0.2034 and 0.7515, respectively). In cases with glomerular damage where eGFR was preserved (≥60 ml/min, n = 24), NPHS1, NPHS2, and PODXL displayed GMRs of 1.41, 1.74, and 2.16, respectively, compared to normal healthy volunteers. With respect to overall biomarker performance, VCAM1 and PODXL demonstrated the best discrimination between disease cases and controls with areas under the curve of 0.92 and 0.83, respectively.
Conclusion
Our findings highlight the potential of biomarkers like PODXL, VCAM1, and MMP3 for detecting glomerular damage in clinical urine samples. NPHS1, NPHS2, and PODXL may offer predictive value, particularly in cases with normal eGFR. To better understand the dynamics of these candidate biomarkers, longitudinal sample analysis is crucial, especially in the context of drug- or disease-related kidney damage. This will help clarify how these biomarkers compare to traditional metrics like eGFR and albuminuria and support their integration as valuable tools in drug development.

title: #248 Effects of obinutuzumab on urinary renal biomarkers in lupus nephritis: a post hoc exploratory analysis of the phase II nobility study
authors: Juan Manuel Mejía Vilet; Holly J Clarke; Ben Lanza; Veronica Anania; William F Pendergraft; Theodore A Omachi; Ioannis Parodis; Rachel B Jones; Liz Lightstone; Brad Rovin; Harini Raghu
abstract:
Background and Aims
B cells are central to lupus nephritis (LN) pathogenesis. Formation of T- and B-cell complexes and production/deposition of immune complexes within the kidney lead to inflammation and tissue damage in patients with LN. Positive results from the Phase II NOBILITY (NCT02550652) and Phase III REGENCY (NCT04221477) studies demonstrated the efficacy of B-cell depletion with obinutuzumab (OBI), a humanised type II anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, in LN. Although a standard measure of kidney involvement, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) provides limited information on underlying kidney pathology. Urine biomarkers such as CD163 (monocyte/macrophage marker), CCL2/MCP1 (monocyte chemoattractant), epidermal growth factor (EGF, marker of renal repair and tubule health/function) and kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM1, proximal tubular injury marker) have been shown to correlate with histological activity and treatment response in LN, offering potential insights into disease activity and treatment responses. This exploratory post hoc analysis investigated the impact of OBI on urine biomarker samples from the NOBILITY study.
Method
Patients with active LN received standard therapy (mycophenolate mofetil and glucocorticoids) plus OBI 1000 mg or standard therapy plus placebo (PBO) on Weeks 0, 2, 24 and 26. The study's primary endpoint was complete renal response (CRR) at Week 52: a composite measure requiring UPCR <0.5, normal renal function (serum creatinine ≤ upper limit of normal) without worsening of baseline serum creatinine by >15% and inactive urinary sediment (<10 red blood cells [RBCs]/HPF without RBC casts). Urine samples were analysed using ELLA immunoassays. Urine biomarker concentrations were normalised to urine creatinine (reported as “pg/mg uCr”) and were analysed using mixed models for repeated measures. Models included baseline biomarker value for each patient, visit, treatment received, baseline UPCR category (≥ vs <3), study randomisation stratification factors and the interaction between treatment and visit or interaction between CRR status and visit, as covariates. An α = 0.2 significance level was used (80% CIs) for these analyses.
Results
Following treatment with OBI, significantly greater reductions in urine CCL2, KIM1 and sCD163 and increases in urine EGF were observed compared with the PBO group over the course of the treatment (Fig. 1). Rapid and significantly greater decline in urine CCL2 and KIM1 levels were observed as early as Week 12 and Week 24, respectively, in the OBI group compared with the PBO group (Fig. 1A–B). Significantly greater increases in urine EGF levels were observed in the OBI group by Week 24, while levels in the PBO group did not increase (Fig. 1C). Urine sCD163 levels decreased in both groups through Week 24; however, levels in the OBI group continued to decline and were significantly lower than the PBO group by Week 52 (Fig. 1D).
In patients achieving CRR at Week 52, compared with non-responders, significantly greater decreases in urine CCL2, KIM1 and sCD163 and increases in urine EGF were observed at Week 12, persisting through Week 76 (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
Exploratory analyses from the Phase II NOBILITY study showed that OBI may induce early beneficial effects on kidney inflammation and damage markers in LN, as evidenced by reduced urine CCL2, KIM1 and sCD163 and increased urine EGF. Importantly, these urinary changes occurred within 24 weeks of OBI initiation (later for sCD163), preceding improvements in UPCR observed at Week 52 [1]. These findings suggest (i) a mechanistic hypothesis whereby OBI modulates the kidney inflammatory microenvironment to promote repair and protect the parenchyma and long term function, reinforcing its potential as a promising therapy for patients with LN; and (ii) urine biomarkers may offer early insights into treatment responses and warrant further investigation in larger studies for potential use in therapeutic response monitoring.

title: #590 Inhibition of Histone deacetylase 6 restores kidney fibrosis in a mouse model of unilateral ureteral obstruction
authors: Ting-Yu Wu; Hong-Mou Shih; Shuei-Liong Lin
abstract:
Background and Aims
Due to the critical role of histone acetylation in kidney development and pathology, numerous preclinical and clinical studies have explored the therapeutic potential of histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors in managing kidney diseases. However, most available HDAC inhibitors are pan-HDAC inhibitors, which lack specificity and are associated with notable side effects, highlighting the need for selective HDAC inhibitors. Among the various HDACs, we are particularly interested in HDAC6. In our previous study, we synthesized selective HDAC6 inhibitors (HDAC6i) #60, featuring a quinazolinone-based structure and a difluoromethyl oxadiazole zinc-binding group, designed to reduce side effects. We conducted in vitro and in vivo experiments to investigate the role of HDAC6 in chronic kidney disease (CKD), and to analyze the impact of HDAC6 inhibition on renal fibrosis.
Method
We analyzed the gene expression of HDAC isoforms in the kidneys and used immunostaining with Collagen I (α)1-GFP+ transgenic mice to localize HDAC6 expression. Subsequently, we employed Slc34a1CreERT2/+; Rosa26fsEGFP-L10a/+ mice to study mRNA expression in slc34a1-expressing proximal tubular epithelial cells (PTECs) through translating ribosomal affinity purification (TRAP). Additionally, we used C57BL/6 mice to perform qPCR, western blotting and picrosirius red staining to assess fibrosis marker and acetylation levels. We used HDAC6i #60 to conduct both in vitro and in vivo tests.
Results
First, we performed unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO) surgery to induce pericyte-myofibroblast transition and progressive renal fibrosis in mice. Protein levels of α-SMA and HDAC6 in the UUO kidney increased over time. Acetyl-H3 levels initially decreased but later normalized during the later stages, suggesting that HDAC6 suppresses acetyl-H3 during the early stages of fibrosis. Through immunostaining, we also observed an upregulation of HDAC6 expression following UUO, particularly in tubular epithelial cells. We further confirmed the localization of HDAC6 by TRAP of mRNA populations in Slc34a1-expressing PTECs. Next, we treated PTECs with the HDAC6i #60 and found that, although the protein levels of HDAC6 were not reduced by HDAC6i treatment, the acetylation levels of H3 and α-tubulin were increased. This indicates that HDAC6i effectively restores acetylation in tubular cells. Finally, after 10 days of oral gavage with HDAC6i #60 following UUO surgery, qPCR and western blot analysis revealed a significant decrease in Acta2 and Pdgfrβ expression, along with a downward trend in Col1a1, Col3a1, and Tgfβ1 levels. Quantification of picrosirius red staining further confirmed reduced fibrosis following HDAC6i treatment.
Conclusion
Our study demonstrates the critical role of HDAC6 in the early stages of UUO-induced renal fibrosis. The selective HDAC6i #60 effectively attenuates fibrosis, underscoring its potential as a therapeutic strategy for CKD.

title: #2379 Predicting long-term benefits of improvements in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) with iptacopan on delaying kidney failure in complement 3 glomerulopathy (C3G)
authors: Novartis Renal Council; Raisa Sidhu; Serge Smeets; Clare Proudfoot; Briana Ndife; Fionn Woodcock
abstract:
Background and Aims
Complement 3 glomerulopathy (C3G) is an ultra-rare glomerulonephritis that leads to progressive loss of renal function. Progression to kidney failure occurs in up to 50% of adults within 10 years of diagnosis. Current treatments do not address the pathophysiology of C3G (overactivation of the alternative pathway) and have limited effectiveness. Thus, there remains a strong unmet need for treatments that delay time to dialysis/transplant.
Iptacopan is an oral, first-in-class complement inhibitor that specifically targets Factor B, inhibiting the alternative pathway of the complement system. The efficacy and safety of iptacopan were assessed in a Phase 2, single-arm study, and are currently being investigated in the ongoing Phase 3 trial, APPEAR-C3G, and a roll-over extension study. APPEAR-C3G is a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study investigating iptacopan 200 mg twice daily compared with placebo, in addition to supportive care and background therapy (based on blood pressure management and immunosuppression, respectively), in patients with C3G. Treatment with iptacopan led to a statistically significant reduction versus placebo in 24-hour urine protein creatinine ratio (UPCR), a numeric improvement in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) at 6 months, and stabilization of eGFR trajectory at 12 months compared with historical data. This model-based analysis aimed to estimate the long-term benefits of improvements in eGFR with iptacopan treatment on delaying the time to kidney failure (TTKF) and reducing the requirement for dialysis and kidney transplant.
Method
The analysis modelled the progression of kidney disease using the following health states: chronic kidney disease (CKD) Stages 1–4, kidney failure (including dialysis and post-transplant), and death. eGFR slope data were used to model progression through CKD stages for patients treated with iptacopan or SoC over the patient's lifetime. Once patients reached kidney failure (eGFR <15 ml/min/1.73 m2), they received either chronic dialysis or a kidney transplant.
In the base case, pooled data from APPEAR-C3G, the Phase 2 study, and the roll-over extension study informed the treatment effect on eGFR slope observed with iptacopan. The historic, pre-iptacopan eGFR slope was compared with the eGFR slope following initiation of iptacopan treatment. The analysis included data from 90 patients, with up to 4.7 years of iptacopan exposure. A scenario analysis used data from APPEAR-C3G, with 74 patients providing eGFR slope data based on up to 2 years of iptacopan treatment. Discontinuation of iptacopan was modelled at the rate observed in the pooled data.
Inputs used to model outcomes following kidney failure were obtained primarily from an analysis of the UK National Registry of Rare Kidney Diseases (RaDaR). This included rates of kidney transplant and graft failure for patients with C3G. Outputs of this analysis included change in median TTKF and additional kidney replacement therapy-free life-years (KRTFLY) with iptacopan, due to modelled delays in TTKF.
Results
The model shows a median TTKF between 9.5 and 10.75 years with current SoC (depending on the modelled eGFR slope), with mean KRTFLYs between 10.58 and 12.08 years. With iptacopan, the median TTKF increases to between 21.0 and 23.75 years, with mean KRTFLYs between 21.29 and 23.93 years (Table 1). Sensitivity analyses show that this is sensitive to the rate of discontinuation, with lower rates of discontinuation leading to larger gains on KRTFLYs (Fig. 1), as well as the mean eGFR at baseline, with greater gains observed in patients in CKD Stage 1 at baseline.
Conclusion
C3G is a rare disease that often affects children and young adults and can lead to kidney failure, with approximately 50% of patients requiring dialysis or transplantation within 10 years of diagnosis. This analysis shows that treatment with iptacopan may extend KRTFLYs by at least 10 years, enabling patients to live a normal, active life for longer. Additionally, both dialysis and kidney transplant are associated with large costs to the healthcare system, which may be alleviated if patients are treated with iptacopan.

title: #2086 Dickkopf-3 (DKK3) and the progression of diabetic kidney disease in primary health care
authors: Felix Keller; Stefan Schunk; Sara Denicolo; Stefanie Thöni; Susanne Eder; Johannes Leierer; Hiddo J L Heerspink; Patrick Mark; Laszlo Rosivall; Andrzej Jan Wiecek; Gert Mayer; Danilo Fliser
abstract:
Background and Aims
In type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), progressive CKD is a global public health problem and associated with significant co-morbidity and reduced life expectancy [1–3]. However, it is challenging to predict the individual course of diabetic kidney disease as patterns of progression in patients with T2DM include linear and nonlinear trajectories of eGFR decline. Moreover, in a substantial portion of patients with T2DM, loss of kidney function occurs in the absence of gross albuminuria [4]. Thus, novel biomarkers are needed to improve the detection of incipient kidney injury and the prediction of the individual course of CKD in patients with diabetes. Dickkopf-3 (DKK3) is a tubular protein which is released under stress conditions and promotes the development of kidney fibrosis via the Wnt/β-catenin signalling pathway [5]. Urinary DKK3 (uDKK3) is a promising biomarker for detecting early kidney injury and predicting the progression of CKD [5]. We explored the clinical utility of uDKK3 as a biomarker of kidney function decline and adverse cardiovascular outcomes in patients with T2DM in a primary healthcare setting.
Method
We analysed 3232 patients from the PROVALID study, a prospective study of patients with T2DM followed at the primary care level. The primary endpoint was a kidney composite outcome, including a sustained eGFR decline of ≥40%, a sustained increase in the urine albumin-creatinine ratio (UACR) of ≥30% (with a transition in albuminuria class), progression to end-stage kidney disease, or death due to kidney failure. The secondary endpoint encompassed a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke. Additionally, we evaluated all-cause mortality.
Results
The median age was 64 (58–70) years and 43% of participants were female. 20% of the participants had an eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m², 20% had an UACR >30 mg/g creatinine, and 34% met the diagnostic criteria of CKD according to KDIGO. The median follow-up time was 4.26 (2.91–5.56) years. When adjusted for age, gender, eGFR and UACR, uDKK3 values >200 pg/g creatinine were associated with a significantly higher risk of reaching the composite kidney endpoint (HR 1.52 [95% CI 1.13–2.04, p-value = 0.006]). title: #1864 Time in target range of systolic blood pressure and cardiovascular disease in patients with chronic kidney disease: a Korean nationwide cohort study
authors: Soo-Young Yoon; Jeong-Yeun Lee; Yoosun Joo; Yang Gyun Kim; Ju-Young Moon; Sang-Ho Lee; Jin Sug Kim; Hyeon Seok Hwang; Kyunghwan Jeong
abstract:
Background and Aims
Time in target range of systolic blood pressure (SBP-TTR) is the percentage of time that the SBP remains within 110–130 mmHg. The association between the SBP-TTR and clinical outcomes in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) remains unclear. We evaluated the risks of cardiovascular disease (CVD), all-cause mortality, and renal events across the SBP-TTR groups.
Method
Overall, 193,289 patients with CKD who underwent at least two health checkups between 2012 and 2015 were selected from the Korean National Health Insurance Database. The patients were categorized into three categories based on their SBP-TTR levels: 76%–100%, 26%–75%, and 0%–25%. The primary outcome was CVD risk and the secondary outcomes were all-cause mortality and progression to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) according to SBP-TTR using Cox regression analysis.
Results
Compared with patients with SBP-TTR of 76%–100%, the adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) for CVD were 1.07 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.03–1.10) and 1.09 (95% CI, 1.06–1.13) for patients with SBP-TTR of 26%–75%, and 0%–25%, respectively. The adjusted HR for all-cause mortality was 1.04 (95% CI, 1.003–1.07) and 1.37 (95% CI, 1.28–1.46) for patients with SBP-TTR of 26%–75% and 0%–25%, respectively. The adjusted HRs for ESKD progression increased gradually: 1.14-fold (95% CI, 1.07–1.21) for the SBP-TTR 26%–75% group and 1.37-fold (95% CI, 1.28–1.46) for the SBP-TTR 0%–25% group. For patients not taking antihypertensive medications, a lower SBP-TTR was associated with a higher risk of CVD events and ESKD progression than in those taking antihypertensive medications.
Conclusion
Among patients with CKD, those with a lower SBP-TTR had a higher risk of cardiovascular events, mortality, and progression to ESKD.

title: #994 Chronic kidney disease specific astrocyte is related with cognitive function
authors: Samel Park; Dong-Jin Lee; Nam-Jun Cho; Eun Young Lee; Jong-Seok Moon; Hyo-Wook Gil
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is increasingly recognized as a major global health burden, with neurological manifestations such as cognitive impairment and depression significantly contributing to patient disability. Despite the rising prevalence of cognitive decline in CKD, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study aims to elucidate the mechanisms associated with cognitive impairment in CKD by utilizing single nucleus RNA sequencing of CKD-brain, providing novel insights into potential pathways and therapeutic targets.
Method
A rat model of chronic kidney disease (CKD) was established through 5/6 nephrectomy, followed by a 10-week observation period. Behavioral analyses were performed to assess cognitive function prior to brain tissue collection. The frontal lobe of the brain was then harvested for single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq), conducted using the 10× Chromium Single Cell 3’ v3.1 protocol (10× Genomics, document no. CG000315), to investigate transcriptional changes linked to cognitive impairment.
Results
The study identified eight cell type clusters, with astrocytes, excitatory neurons, and inhibitory neurons showing significant transcriptional changes in CKD. Total cell counts were higher in controls, but cell type proportions were comparable between groups. Astrocytes exhibited the most differentially expressed genes (DEGs), including upregulated Kcnj3 and Nmnat2 and downregulated Zmiz2. These findings, supported by pseudobulk analysis, highlight astrocytes’ key role in cognitive impairment in CKD. The results align with their involvement in other brain diseases, such as Alzheimer's and inflammatory conditions. Sub-clustering and trajectory analysis identified six astrocyte sub-clusters, with clusters 2, 3, and 5 showing increased proportions in CKD rats, indicating their role in CKD-related cognitive impairment. Cluster 4, with no proportional change, was linked to reactive astrocytes and inflammatory pathways. In contrast, cluster 5, unique to CKD, was associated with synaptic signaling, neurotransmitter receptors, and ion channel dysfunction. Pathway analysis revealed metabolic derangement in cluster 2, similar to Alzheimer's disease, and ferroptosis in cluster 3, a novel cell death mechanism. Collectively, CKD astrocytes exhibited distinct mechanisms of cognitive impairment, including metabolic disruption, ferroptosis, and synaptic dysfunction.
Conclusion
Astrocytes, especially CKD-specific sub-clusters, were identified as one of the most affected cells by snRNA-seq analysis. Our study demonstrated for the first time the heterogeneity of reactive astrocytes in response to the CKD environment. The presence of the CKD-specific astrocyte population suggested that the heterogeneity of reactive astrocytes could be a crucial target for future research. In addition, our findings would provide valuable insights into the pathogenesis of cognitive impairment in patients with CKD.

title: #3379 Prognostic value of triglyceride glucose (TyG) index in population with chronic kidney disease
authors: Jeong-Yeun Lee; Jin Sug Kim; Kyunghwan Jeong; Hyeon Seok Hwang; Soo-Young Yoon; Dae Kyu Kim
abstract:
Background and Aims
The triglyceride glucose (TyG) index has been proposed as a reliable marker of insulin resistance and an independent predictor of cardiovascular (CV) event. However, its prognostic value in chronic kidney disease (CKD) remains unclear. This study aims to assess predictive value of the TyG index for clinical outcomes in CKD population.
Method
This study was conducted using the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. A total of 123,249 individuals with CKD who underwent a national health examination between 2012 and 2015 were enrolled and divided into four groups based on TyG index quartiles. The primary outcome was a CV event, including myocardial infarction and stroke, and the secondary outcomes were progression to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) and all-cause mortality.
Results
During a median follow-up time of 58.6 months, CV event, progression to ESKD, and all-cause mortality occurred in 15,400 (12.5%), 5,668 (4.5%) and 10,245 (8.3%) cases, respectively. The cumulative event rate of cardiovascular events, progression to ESKD, and all-cause mortality was the highest among population with TyG quartile 4 (all P < 0.001). In multivariate Cox-regression analysis, a higher TyG index was associated with an increased risk of CV event. Compared with participants in the lowest quartile of TyG index, hazard ratios (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for CV event were 1.05 (1.00–1.10), 1.09 (1.04–1.15), 1.29 (1.23–1.36) for those in second, third, and fourth quartile of TyG index. The risk of progression to ESKD was also increased as TyG quartile increased [adjusted HR (95% CI) 1.15 (1.05–1.26), 1.22 (1.10–1.35), and 1.75 (1.60–1.91)] for population with TyG quartile 2, 3, and 4, respectively. The risk of all-cause mortality was significantly elevated in individuals with TyG index quartile 4.
Conclusion
The TyG index serves as a valuable predictor of CV event, progression to ESKD and all-cause mortality in CKD population.

title: #2241 The urinary proteome as a window to the transition from AKI to CKD after repeated acute kidney injuries
authors: Joana del Valle Mercado Hernández; Andriy Kovalchuk; Sandra M Sancho Martinez; Isabel Fuentes-Calvo; David Martin-Calvo; Francisco J Lopez-Hernandez; Carlos Martinez Salgado
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) episodes frequently lead to chronic kidney disease (CKD) when recovery is inadequate or incomplete, with the risk of progression escalating alongside the frequency and severity of these episodes. In this context, traditional diagnostic tools, such as plasma creatinine (pCr) levels, fail to detect early renal damage, as pCr levels may remain within non-pathological ranges. This study develops a novel in vivo model replicating the AKI-to-CKD transition, mimicking the apparent normalization of renal filtration, and identifies early urinary biomarkers underlying this progression.
Method
We developed an AKI-to-CKD transition model using 2-month-old Wistar rats divided into two groups: cisplatin-ischemia (cP-I) and control groups (C). The cP-I group received an initial dose of 5 mg/kg cisplatin (nephrotoxic AKI) followed after recovery by ischemia-reperfusion of the left kidney (second AKI episode). Renal function and histological evolution were monitored for 90 days, assessing pCr, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine clearance, and excretion fractions of sodium and glucose. Progression of tissue damage was evaluated using haematoxylin-eosin and Masson's trichrome staining on days 56 and 90. Differential urinary proteomics analysis was conducted on day 56 to identify protein fingerprints associated with the AKI-to-CKD transition.
Results
Despite apparent normalization of pCr levels,(cP-I group show a progressive decline in renal filtration (subtle increases in pCr and blood urea nitrogen and decreases in creatinine clearance) and tubular reabsorption (elevated sodium and glucose excretion fractions). Histological analysis revealed progressive tissue damage, with increasing inflammation, and advancing fibrosis over the 90-day period. Urinary proteomics identified a total of 129 proteins whose excretion was significantly elevated (log2 [abundance ratio (cP-I/C)] ≥ 1 and Bonferroni adjusted p-value < 0.05) in the cisplatin-ischemia group, of which 57 were human orthologues. These proteins were associated with wound repair, immune response, complement system activation, coagulation, and iron transport.
Conclusion
This AKI-to-CKD transition model highlights subtle renal dysfunction and progressive histopathological changes that are not detectable by conventional biomarkers like pCr. The identified proteomic fingerprint provides novel insights into pathophysiological mechanisms and potential biomarkers, paving the way for developing targeted preventive and therapeutic strategies to mitigate CKD progression.

title: #2491 Exploring the association between non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and chronic kidney disease: insights from NHANES 1999–2016
authors: Yaerim Kim; Jin Hyuk Paek; Kyubok Jin; Woo Yeong Park; Seungyeup Han
abstract:
Background and Aims
Although non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) increases the risk of kidney dysfunction genetically, the clinical association in different conditions has not been evaluated yet. Herein, we aimed to evaluate the association between NAFLD and chronic kidney disease (CKD) using a fatty liver index (FLI), a useful non-invasive method for assessing the status of NAFLD.
Method
This study utilized data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 1999–2016. The participants were categorized into FLI quartiles, with the 1st quartile serving as the reference group. CKD was defined based on the estimated glomerular filtration rates (eGFR) <60 mL/min/1.73 m2. To evaluate the risk of CKD, we performed multivariate logistic regression model adjusted with age, sex, ethnicity, education, alcohol consumption, smoking status, comorbidities, laboratory parameters, and total calorie intake.
Results
Among 51,688 participants, 9.4% (n = 4,843) were defined with CKD. The 4th quartile of FLI significantly increased the risk of CKD with 1.81 times than 1st quartile, and it was maintained after adjustment with such variables (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.35, 95% CI 1.18–1.55). In the subgroup analysis, the significance of FLI was prominent in age ≥60 (aOR 1.38, 95% CI 1.19–1.61). The impact of the highest quartile of FLI was maintained irrespective of sex. In comparing the participants according to the presence of comorbidities, the significance of 4th quartile of FLI was maintained in participants without hypertension (aOR 1.47, 95% CI 1.15–1.87), without diabetes (aOR 1.42, 95% CI 1.21–1.66), or without dyslipidemia (aOR 1.50, 95% CI 1.24–1.82).
Conclusion
NAFLD representing with higher FLI is significantly associated with the risk of incident CKD. The association between FLI and CKD was more prominent in elderly population and without comorbidities such as hypertension, diabetes, or dyslipidemia. FLI could be applied in specific populations as a good predictor of CKD.

title: #299 Can creatinine muscle index be a biomarker for diagnosing sarcopenia and predicting renal prognosis in CKD patients?
authors: Natsuki Yamakawa; Yukari Mae; Tomoaki Takata; Hajime Isomoto
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sarcopenia is an important health concern for patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and is associated with renal dysfunction and poor prognosis. Many coexisting conditions in CKD such as uremic toxin accumulation, loss of appetite, metabolic acidosis accelerate sarcopenia. Protein restriction often recommended for CKD patients can also increase the risk of sarcopenia. Therefore, it is necessary to assess the presence of sarcopenia in CKD patients. Sarcopenia is assessed by skeletal muscle mass and muscle quality. Several modalities such as computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), and dual-energy X-ray, are usually used for such purpose. However, these modalities have limitations in terms of time and cost, and cannot be always applied to CKD patients. This necessitates novel diagnostic indices to assess sarcopenia. Creatinine muscle index (CMI) is recently recognized as a simple marker to evaluate muscle mass. However, its usefulness to diagnose sarcopenia in CKD patients remains unknown. The aim of this study was to evaluate the feasibility of CMI for the assessment of sarcopenia and renal prognosis.
Method
A prospective, observational study was conducted on 93 patients with CKD who underwent blood tests and BIA at Tottori University hospital from April 2021 to October 2022. Serum creatinine (Cr) and cystatin C were measured, and estimated glomerular filtration rate was determined from both Cr (eGFRcr) and cystatin C (eGFRcys) using equations from the Japanese Society of Nephrology. CMI was calculated as serum Cr × eGFRcys as previously reported. Muscle mass was assessed by the appendicular skeletal muscle mass (ASM) and skeletal muscle mass index (SMI) calculated from ASM divided by height. Muscle quality, which reflects myofiber density and myocyte condition, was assessed by phase angle (PhA), using MC-780A-N (TANITA, Tokyo, Japan). Sarcopenia was determined by grip strength (HGS) and SMI based on the EWGSOP2 algorithm. The respective cutoff values were determined according to the AWGS 2019 sarcopenia diagnostic criteria. Correlations of CMI to age, eGFRcre, BMI, HGS, ASM, and PhA were analyzed using Pearson's correlation coefficient. Influencing factor for CMI was determined by multiple linear regression analysis, which includes age, sex, eGFRcre, HGS, ASM, and PhA as explanatory variables. In addition, CMI cutoff values to diagnose sarcopenia were determined. Patients were further classified into high and low CMI groups, and renal prognoses were compared using the Kaplan-Meier analysis. The surrogate endpoint of renal function was defined as a 30% decrease in eGFR or induction of dialysis. Renal survival analysis was performed by the Cox proportional hazards model.
Results
The patient's characteristics were 60.2% male, 62.8 ± 16.9 years old, and eGFRcre 47.81 ± 22.2 mL/min/1.73 m2, and the CKD stages were G1-2 23.7%, G3a 24.7%, G3b 28.0%, G4 23.7%, respectively. CMI correlated with age, HGS, ASM, and PhA (age; r = −0.501 and P < 0.001, eGFR; r = 0.294 and P = 0.013, BMI; r = −0.005 and P = 0.965, HGS; r = 0.560 and P < 0.001, ASM; r = 0.463 and P < 0.001, and PhA; r = 0.583 and P < 0.001). Multiple linear regression analysis showed that PhA was the only influencing factor for CMI (Stdβ = 0.301 and P = 0.033). The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of CMI for sarcopenia showed an area under the curve of 0.915. The cut-off value of CMI was determined at 44.1 with a sensitivity of 88.7% and a specificity of 100% (Fig. 1). The renal survival rate was significantly lower in patients with low CMI (P = 0.016) (median follow-up 581 days) (Fig. 2). Multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression analysis adjusted for age, sex, BMI and eGFRcre revealed that low CMI was the independent predictor of CKD progression (Hr = 6.18, 95% CI = 1.26–30.29, P = 0.025).
Conclusion
CMI was independently associated with muscle quality assessed by PhA. CMI is a novel marker to diagnose sarcopenia and predict renal prognosis in CKD patients.

Background and Aims
Sarcopenia is an important health concern for patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and is associated with renal dysfunction and poor prognosis. Many coexisting conditions in CKD such as uremic toxin accumulation, loss of appetite, metabolic acidosis accelerate sarcopenia. Protein restriction often recommended for CKD patients can also increase the risk of sarcopenia. Therefore, it is necessary to assess the presence of sarcopenia in CKD patients. Sarcopenia is assessed by skeletal muscle mass and muscle quality. Several modalities such as computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), and dual-energy X-ray, are usually used for such purpose. However, these modalities have limitations in terms of time and cost, and cannot be always applied to CKD patients. This necessitates novel diagnostic indices to assess sarcopenia. Creatinine muscle index (CMI) is recently recognized as a simple marker to evaluate muscle mass. However, its usefulness to diagnose sarcopenia in CKD patients remains unknown. The aim of this study was to evaluate the feasibility of CMI for the assessment of sarcopenia and renal prognosis.
Method
A prospective, observational study was conducted on 93 patients with CKD who underwent blood tests and BIA at Tottori University hospital from April 2021 to October 2022. Serum creatinine (Cr) and cystatin C were measured, and estimated glomerular filtration rate was determined from both Cr (eGFRcr) and cystatin C (eGFRcys) using equations from the Japanese Society of Nephrology. CMI was calculated as serum Cr × eGFRcys as previously reported. Muscle mass was assessed by the appendicular skeletal muscle mass (ASM) and skeletal muscle mass index (SMI) calculated from ASM divided by height. Muscle quality, which reflects myofiber density and myocyte condition, was assessed by phase angle (PhA), using MC-780A-N (TANITA, Tokyo, Japan). Sarcopenia was determined by grip strength (HGS) and SMI based on the EWGSOP2 algorithm. The respective cutoff values were determined according to the AWGS 2019 sarcopenia diagnostic criteria. Correlations of CMI to age, eGFRcre, BMI, HGS, ASM, and PhA were analyzed using Pearson's correlation coefficient. Influencing factor for CMI was determined by multiple linear regression analysis, which includes age, sex, eGFRcre, HGS, ASM, and PhA as explanatory variables. In addition, CMI cutoff values to diagnose sarcopenia were determined. Patients were further classified into high and low CMI groups, and renal prognoses were compared using the Kaplan-Meier analysis. The surrogate endpoint of renal function was defined as a 30% decrease in eGFR or induction of dialysis. Renal survival analysis was performed by the Cox proportional hazards model.
Results
The patient's characteristics were 60.2% male, 62.8 ± 16.9 years old, and eGFRcre 47.81 ± 22.2 mL/min/1.73 m2, and the CKD stages were G1-2 23.7%, G3a 24.7%, G3b 28.0%, G4 23.7%, respectively. CMI correlated with age, HGS, ASM, and PhA (age; r = −0.501 and P < 0.001, eGFR; r = 0.294 and P = 0.013, BMI; r = −0.005 and P = 0.965, HGS; r = 0.560 and P < 0.001, ASM; r = 0.463 and P < 0.001, and PhA; r = 0.583 and P < 0.001). Multiple linear regression analysis showed that PhA was the only influencing factor for CMI (Stdβ = 0.301 and P = 0.033). The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of CMI for sarcopenia showed an area under the curve of 0.915. The cut-off value of CMI was determined at 44.1 with a sensitivity of 88.7% and a specificity of 100% (Fig. 1). The renal survival rate was significantly lower in patients with low CMI (P = 0.016) (median follow-up 581 days) (Fig. 2). Multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression analysis adjusted for age, sex, BMI and eGFRcre revealed that low CMI was the independent predictor of CKD progression (Hr = 6.18, 95% CI = 1.26–30.29, P = 0.025).
Conclusion
CMI was independently associated with muscle quality assessed by PhA. CMI is a novel marker to diagnose sarcopenia and predict renal prognosis in CKD patients.

title: #805 Effects of healthcare quality on renal outcomes in early-stage chronic kidney disease patients: a nationwide cohort study
authors: Hon-Yen Wu; Le-Yin Hsu; Kuo-Liong Chien
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a major global health concern due to the rising prevalence of risk factors such as diabetes and hypertension. Early intervention in CKD patients may reduce the risk of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), emphasizing the importance of early multidisciplinary care (MDC). In Taiwan, early-stage CKD patients are less frequently enrolled in MDC programs compared with those in advanced stages. Furthermore, existing quality indicators (QIs) primarily target ESKD or advanced CKD populations. This study aimed to investigate the association between care quality and major renal outcomes in stage 1–3A CKD patients without diabetes.
Method
We analyzed National Health Insurance claims data and death registries from the Health and Welfare Data Science Center in Taiwan. We included nondiabetic adults with stage 1–3A CKD who enrolled in early-stage CKD MDC program during 2016–2019 and received care at facilities managing ≥10 CKD patients. Three QIs were assessed: prescription of renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors, testing for proteinuria, and avoidance of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Primary outcomes included ESKD, all-cause mortality, acute kidney injury (AKI), and hyperkalemia through 2020. Cox proportional hazards models and two-stage residual inclusion models with an instrumental variable approach were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for associations between QI scores and outcomes.
Results
The study cohort comprised 130,372 patients (mean age 64.9 years, 47.2% female, mean Charlson Comorbidity Index score: 4.2)(Fig. 1). Of these, 37% received CKD care in physician clinics, 27.4% in metropolitan hospitals, 21.2% in academic medical centers, and 14.4% in local community hospitals. Overall, 14.3% achieved the maximum QI score of 3, 40.9% scored 2, and 35.6% scored 1. Individually, 53.3% received RAS inhibitors, 47.9% underwent proteinuria testing, and 59.2% avoided NSAIDs. Higher overall QI scores were associated with lower risks of all-cause mortality (HR 0.677, 95% CI 0.510–0.898) and AKI (HR 0.788, 95% CI 0.683–0.910) (Table). Although higher QI scores showed a trend toward reduced risks of ESKD and hyperkalemia, these findings were not statistically significant. Each individual QI independently correlated with reduced risks of all-cause mortality and AKI.
Conclusion
In this nationwide cohort study of stage 1–3A CKD patients without diabetes, better adherence to QIs in early CKD care correlated with improved patient outcomes, notably reduced risks of mortality and AKI. These results highlight the value of implementing quality metrics in early CKD care and suggest that adherence to evidence-based QIs may improve patient outcomes, although further research is needed to clarify their impact on ESKD. This study underscores the importance of continued efforts to optimize early CKD management and promote quality improvement in this patient population.

title: #2151 Prevention of renal fibrosis with allogeneic perinatal stem cells—a long-term preclinical model of kidney injury
authors: Agne Gryguc; Justinas MacIulaitis; Lukas Mickevicius; Arvydas Laurinavicius; Neringa Sutkeviciene; Ramune Grigaleviciute; Vilma Zigmantaite; Inga Bumblyte; Romaldas MacIulaitis
abstract:
Background and Aims
Recurrent episodes of acute kidney injury (AKI) progress to chronic kidney disease (CKD) in 15% of patients. Allogeneic type human placental mesenchymal stromal cells (hpMSCs) have been shown to have short-to-medium term beneficial effect in preventing the progression of CKD; however, long-term efficacy and immunogenicity remains unknown. We aimed to assess the preventive effect of hpMSCs on renal fibrosis after preclinical ischaemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) and to prevent the development of CKD.
Method
HpMSCs was isolated using Good manufacturing practice (GMP) grade materials, cultivated and characterised by yield, viability, flow cytometry and in vitro potency for immunosuppression.
Rats underwent preclinical IRI - both kidney roots were clamped with atraumatic microvascular clamps and were removed after 60 minutes of occlusion. After removal of the clamps, the IRI-hpMSC treated group (cells group) received 3×10⁵ hpMSCs into the corticomedullary region of each kidney. IRI-PBS control group (PBS group) received phosphate buffer solution (PBS); untreated group with only induced IRI (IRI group); healthy control group without IRI. Survival analysis was carried out till day 56. Blood and kidney tissue samples collected on the days 0, 3, 7, 21–28, and 56. At least 3 rats per end point (a total of 57 rats). Serum creatinine was analysed in surviving animals.
Kidney histology. Acute tubular necrosis (ATN), dilatation (TD), casts, loss of brush border (LBB), tubulitis, leukostasis, interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy (IFTA) were scored in 10 fields of each section. The degree of renal injury was assessed by assessing the percentage of affected tubules - renal injury score (RIS).
Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS Statistics version 17.0 and GraphPad Prism 7.04 software. Non-parametric data were analyzed using the median test and Kruskal-Wallis Test (statistical significance p-value < 0.05). Survival - the curve comparison test.
Results
hpMSCs had a consistent yield, viability, MSC expression markers and suppressed proliferation of T cells in a dose-dependent fashion.
Rats survived 100 percent in cells group while only 68 percent in PBS (P = 0.010) and 72 percent in IRI group (P = 0.021), at the end of the study.
hpMSCs significantly improved kidney function by decreasing median creatinine level in serum and on day 7 compared to the surviving rats in comparison to the death-censored control groups (Cells vs IRI P = 0.014; Cells vs PBS P = 0.034).
The histological findings indicated that hpMSCs mitigated the injury to renal morphology in both the early and especially at the late phases. The cells group exhibited significantly lower median level of ATN on day 3 compared to the IRI (P = 0.047) and PBS (P = 0.028) groups. Comparatively, the cells group had a distinct tendency toward a smaller casts formation (Cells vs IRI P = 0.014; PBS P = 0.034), with ATN devoid of focal coagulative necrosis visible as early as day 7. On days 21–28, significant RIS differences were observed between cells group and both IRI (P = 0.048) and PBS (P = 0.029) groups. TB (Cells vs IRI P = 0.019; PBS P = 0.017), LBB (Cells vs IRI P = 0.048; PBS P = 0.017), casts formation (Cells vs IRI P = 0.048), and IFTA (Cells vs IRI P = 0.048; PBS P = 0.029) were significantly lower in the cells group than in the IRI and PBS groups on days 21–28. IFTA was significantly lower in the cells group than in the IRI (P = 0.018) and PBS (P = 0.049) groups on day 56.
Serum creatinine normalized on day 28 and 56, but fibrosis persisted only in controls.
Conclusion
Perinatal stem cells have the potential to prevent acute kidney damage and consequential fibrosis cascade. The results of the histological study demonstrated that perinatal stem cells provided long-lasting (56 days) protection against fibrotic kidney injury. A superior 100% survival rate of treated animal group exhibits the potential of characterised hpMSCs to be used in a larger scale preclinical tumorigenicity and toxicity studies and subsequent clinical studies.

title: #710 Impact of nutritional and inflammatory conditions on kidney outcomes and mortality in individuals with diabetes
authors: Maki Murakoshi; Nozomu Kamei; Marenao Tanaka; Tatsuya Sato; Masato Furuhashi; Shinji Hagiwara; Yusuke Suzuki; Tomohito Gohda
abstract:
Background and Aims
Malnutrition and chronic inflammation are not only common complications of chronic kidney disease (CKD) but also significant risk factors for the development and progression of CKD as well as mortality. Furthermore, malnutrition and inflammation are interrelated through a bidirectional association. The prognostic nutritional index (PNI), a composite marker integrating nutritional and inflammatory conditions, has emerged as a useful tool. However, the role of PNI in predicting CKD progression and mortality, while accounting for inflammatory markers, remains underexplored in individuals with diabetes. This study aimed to evaluate whether PNI predicts adverse outcomes independently of tumor necrosis factor receptor 2 (TNFR2), a well-established predictor of kidney outcomes, in individuals with diabetes.
Method
This study included 640 Japanese individuals with diabetes, stratified into two groups based on PNI levels: quartile 1 and quartiles 2–4. Serum TNFR2 levels were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Nutritional status was assessed using three markers: PNI, the geriatric nutritional risk index (GNRI), and the controlling nutritional status (CONUT) score. Spearman's correlation coefficients were calculated to assess relationships among the three nutritional markers and their associations with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and TNFR2. Cox proportional hazards models, adjusted for age, sex, glycated hemoglobin, albuminuria, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), and TNFR2, were used to examine associations between the nutritional markers and adverse outcomes, including a kidney outcome (≥30% decline in eGFR), mortality, and their composite outcomes.
Results
The mean age of participants was 65 years, and 53.9% were male. During a median follow-up of 5.4 years, 75 individuals (11.7%) experienced a kidney event, 44 (6.9%) died, and 112 (17.5%) reached composite outcomes. PNI showed moderate correlations with GNRI (r = 0.57) and CONUT (r = −0.59) and weak correlations with eGFR (r = 0.23) and TNFR2 (r = −0.35). In multivariate Cox proportional hazards models, all three nutritional markers were significantly associated with kidney outcomes (PNI [Q1 (ref.) vs. Q2–4]: HR, 1.84; 95% CI [1.13, 3.02]; GNRI [Q1 (ref.) vs. Q2–4]: HR, 1.81; 95% CI [1.10, 2.98]; CONUT (per 1 increase): HR, 1.23; 95% CI [1.03, 1.47]) and composite outcomes (PNI: HR, 1.94; 95% CI [1.30, 2.89]; GNRI: HR, 2.23; 95% CI [1.51, 3.30]; CONUT: HR, 1.18; 95% CI [1.02, 1.37]) even after adjusting for clinical confounders, including TNFR2. Furthermore, GNRI was the only marker that independently predicted mortality (HR, 2.90; 95% CI [1.56, 5.37]).
Conclusion
PNI, GNRI, and CONUT are strongly associated with kidney and composite outcomes in individuals with diabetes, highlighting the critical role of nutritional evaluation and management as integral components of care for people with diabetes. These findings emphasize the need for further research to develop targeted nutritional interventions aimed at improving long-term outcomes in this population.

title: #1672 Cost-effectiveness analysis of voclosporin vs mycophenolate or belimumab in the treatment of patients with lupus nephritis from the Spanish National Healthcare System perspective
authors: Nuria Paladio Duran; Laura Salinas-Ortega; Alberto de la Cuadra-Grande; Itziar Oyagüez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Voclosporin (VCS) is an oral immunosuppressant agent for active lupus nephritis (LN) class III, IV and V (also included mixed classes III/V and IV/V). This study aims to estimate the cost-effectiveness of VCS in combination with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) vs MMF alone or vs belimumab (BEL) in combination with MMF or cyclophosphamide (CYC), for Spanish patients with LN III-V (and mixed classes) from the perspective of the Spanish National Health System (NHS).
Method
A Markov model with health states according to the specific stages of chronic kidney disease (CKD) (CKD1-3a [active disease, partial response, complete response], CKD3b-4, CKD5 [including dialysis and transplantation] and death) (Fig. 1) was used to estimate, in 6-months cycles, the lifetime costs and health benefits for oral VCS (combined with MMF), MMF alone and BEL (combined with MMF or CYC).
Baseline characteristics for the cohort assessed (mean age: 33.2 [SD: 11.0 years] years, 87% female, weight: 65 [SD: 16.6] kg and body surface area [BSA]: 1.71 m2) reflected an average Spanish patient with LN class III-V.
Clinical efficacy and safety data were derived from pivotal phase III clinical trials (AURORA-1 [ClinicalTrial.gov ID: NCT03021499] and AURORA-2 [ClinicalTrial.gov ID: NCT03597464]) comparing VCS in combination with MMF, hereafter VCS vs MMF, and a network meta-analysis that compared VCS vs BEL in combination with MMF or CYC, hereafter BEL, using BLISS-LN trial [ClinicalTrial.gov ID: NCT01639339]. Utilities and mortality rates were extracted from the literature.
Total costs (€, 2024) included pharmaceutical (public ex-factory prices), administration (intravenous [€233.81] and subcutaneous [€20.62]), CKD-management, end-of-life and treatment-emergent adverse events costs (only grade III adverse events were considered). All costs were derived from published sources specific to the Spanish setting.
The authorized posology of 47.4mg/day for VCS; as well as 10 mg/kg on days 0, 14, 28 and every 4 weeks for BEL; and 2,000 mg/day for MMF, were used. Available BEL formulations (95% intravenous-IV, 5% subcutaneous-SC) were considered.
An annual discount rate (3%) and half-cycle correction were applied. Clinical experts validated the parameters and assumptions.
The effect of future price reduction following BEL biosimilars availability, joined to alternative proportions of BEL formulations usage, were tested through linear regression analyses.
Results
In the case of VCS vs MMF alone, VCS resulted in additional life years (LYs) vs MMF (20.95 vs 19.66) and additional quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) (16.47 vs 15.25) and provided an incremental total cost of €17,762 per patient. VCS was a cost-effective option (€14,543 per QALY) for a €20,000/QALY threshold. When comparing VCS vs BEL, VCS was a dominant option, yielding LYs vs BEL (20.95 vs 20.89) and additional QALYs (16.47 vs 16.41) and reducing total costs by €−42,398 per average patient.
In all regression models, VCS vs. BEL remained a cost-saving option, even for BEL price reductions above 50% when equivalent use is assessed for IV and SC BEL (50% of patients using each administration route).
Conclusion
In the current situation, the use of VCS could provide more health benefits and cost-savings for the Spanish NHS. Even if BEL price was heavily reduced, VCS would still be a cost-effective intervention for treatment of patients with LN III-IV (and mixed classes).

title: #2921 Resistin: a potential predictor of adverse outcomes in chronic kidney disease?
authors: João Cunha; Rodolfo Almeida; José Soares; Henrique Borges; Filipa Brito Mendes; Ana Silva
abstract:
Background and Aims
Resistin is an adipocytokine, mainly secreted by mononuclear and bone marrow cells, with multiple proinflammatory effects—it's capable of inducing several intracellular pathways leading to transcription of proinflammatory cytokines, adhesion molecules and growth factors. While firstly discovered as a link between obesity and diabetes, and being named by its ability to interfere with insulin action, it has now been associated with cardiovascular disease, including atherosclerosis. Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), were found to have higher resistin levels, and this molecule can have modulating effects on renal function. In this study, we evaluated serum resistin levels in a population with CKD not requiring kidney replacement therapy, comparing them to several variables related to complications of this disease, such as anemia, CKD-mineral bone disorder (MBD), malnutrition and cardiovascular risk. Our aim is to measure the potential impact of resistin in the development of adverse outcomes in CKD.
Method
This is an observational and retrospective study, that englobed 1292 patients with CKD stages G1–G5 (not on dialysis) followed at a nephrology clinic in a tertiary hospital. According to serum resistin levels, patients were divided into 3 groups: <3.1 ng/mL (G1), 3.1–8.5 ng/mL (G2) and >8.5 ng/mL (G3). In each patient, different variables of interest were measured, which included serum hemoglobin (Hb), calcium (Ca), phosphorus (P), parathyroid hormone (PTH), fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF 23), albumin (Alb), left ventricular mass index (LVMI) and pulse pressure (PP). SPSS was used to make the statistical analysis. Kolmogorov-Smirnov test confirmed the normal distribution of the variables, and Levene statistic didn't reject the equality of variances. ANOVA and Scheffé test were used to assess the differences on the previously mentioned variables, between the three resistin serum levels groups.
Results
The mean age of the sample was 61 years old, with 37% of females (n = 478), and a mean estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 44.39 ml/min/1.73 m2. The number of patients in each group defined by serum resistin levels was similar: 405 with <3.1 ng/mL, 415 with 3.1–8.5 ng/mL and 472 with >8.5 ng/mL. A significant difference (p-value 0.000 on Scheffé test) was observed between the G1 (<3.1 ng/mL) and the other two groups, concerning Hb values, with higher mean value in the first group: 13.11, versus 12.44 and 12.52 g/dL, respectively. In the variables that contribute to CKD-MBD, differences in calcium levels weren't statistically significant. On the other hand, levels of phosphorus, PTH and FGF-23, had significant differences between the three groups (p-value 0.000 on Scheffé test), with the >8.5 ng/mL group (G3) showing the higher mean values, and the <3.1 ng/mL group (G1) the lower mean values, of these variables. Albumin mean values were significantly lower in the G3 (3.91 g/dL), compared with the two other groups (4.32 g/dL in G1, and 4.25 g/dL in G2), with a p-value of 0.000 on Scheffé test, but no statistically significant differences were found between G1 and G2. LMVI and PP were the cardiovascular measures analyzed, and increased mean values of both variables were seen in G2 compared to G1, and in G3 compared to G2 and G1, with statistically significant differences (p-value of 0.000).
Conclusion
In this study, higher serum resistin levels was found to be associated with several parameters related to unfavourable outcomes in CKD, such as variables related to cardiovascular risk or molecules with a direct impact on CKD-MBD. In respect to Hb and albumin levels, statistically significant differences were only observed in one group comparing to the other two. Thus, it is possible to think that resistin could be an important biomarker to measures in patients with CKD, aiming to predict worst outcomes in this group. Further research needs to be done, to reinforce the results shown in our work.

title: #264 Kidney function and the metabolome in the general population
authors: Johan Ljunggren; Lars Lind; Maria K Svensson
abstract:
Background and Aims
A reduction in kidney function cause metabolites that normally are cleared by the kidney to accumulate. These metabolites could potentially link kidney function to an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. To assess the relationships between creatinine-based estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and the metabolome (791 endogenous metabolites) in the general population, with particular focus on the cortisol to cortisone ratio.
Method
Three population-based cohorts, Epihealth, PIVUS and POEM (total n = 3444), were used with a discovery/validation approach. Metabolomics was measured by mass spectroscopy. eGFR was calculated using the 2021 CKD-EPI creatinine-based equation. Multivariate linear regression was used to assess the correlations between each metabolite concentration and eGFR adjusting for sex, % fat mass, cardiovascular risk factors and medications. A pathway enrichment analysis was performed using MetaboAnalyst 6.0.
Results
In the fully adjusted regression model, 227 metabolites were significantly related to eGFR. Six of these were positively while the remaining were inversely correlated. Creatinine was the strongest negatively and cortisone the strongest positively correlated metabolite. The cortisol/cortisone ratio was significantly negatively related with eGFR (FDr = 0.021). Pathway enrichment analysis found 11 significantly enriched pathways (see table 1). The majority of these involved amino acid metabolism.
Conclusion
In this study of kidney function vs metabolome in a general population with only mild to moderately reduced kidney function, several metabolites, including the cortisol to cortisone ratio, related also to risk of cardiovascular disease were associated with kidney function.

title: #1786 Urinary microcholesterol and progression of chronic kidney disease
authors: Hirotaka Furuta; Ryosuke Umeda; Shun Minatoguchi; Masato Hoshi; Hiroki Hayashi; Shigehisa Koide; Hiroyuki Naruse; Midori Hasegawa; Naotake Tsuboi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Recent advancements in treatment options for chronic kidney disease (CKD) have led to an urgent need for a diagnostic tool that can identify patients at a high risk of CKD progression. The primary route of cholesterol excretion is believed to be via the bile in the feces (0.2-0.6 g/day), although trace amounts of cholesterol are also detected in the urine. A preliminary study in our age-adjusted cohort indicated that patients with CKD exhibited elevated levels of urinary microcholesterol (mCHO) compared with healthy individuals (1.42 [0.92, 2.54] mg/gCr [median (IQR)] vs. 0.54 [0.37, 0.86] mg/gCr, P < 0.001). This study aimed to elucidate the association between urinary mCHO level and CKD progression.
Method
A prospective observational study was conducted on outpatients with CKD who visited the Department of Nephrology at Fujita Health University between April and July 2022. Urinary mCHO levels were evaluated, along with a series of presumed progression factors. The primary outcome was defined as the time to major adverse kidney events, which was measured as the composite of a decline in eGFR ≥50% from baseline, dependence on kidney replacement therapy, and kidney-related death during the follow-up period until October 2024.Patients were stratified by baseline urinary cholesterol levels, and associations with outcomes were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier survival curve analysis and Cox proportional hazards models.
Results
Out of 1,798 cases, 39 cases were excluded due to ineligibility, and 1,759 cases were included in the analysis. The participants' mean age was 65.0 ± 16.8 years, 43.7% were female, and the mean BMI was 23.6 ± 4.19. The baseline characteristics included a urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) of 1.13 ± 1.94 g/gCr, eGFR of 43.2 ± 25.8 mL/min/1.73 m², and total cholesterol of 184.2 ± 39.9 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol (LDL-cho) of 97.7 ± 31.1 mg/dL, HDL cholesterol of 53.2 ± 17.1 mg/dL, and triglycerides of 142.5 ± 88 mg/dL. The urinary mCHO value was 1.56 [0.96, 3.03] mg/gCr (Fig. 1). Urinary mCHO levels demonstrated a moderate positive correlation with UPCR (r = 0.69), as shown in the scatter plot (top right). However, no relationship was observed between urinary mCHO levels and age, eGFR, or total cholesterol levels. In the survival curve analysis, patients were categorized into four groups based on urinary mCHO quartiles. The higher quartile groups showed significantly higher event rates for the primary outcome (log-rank test, P < 0.005) (Fig. 2). A subsequent analysis using a Cox proportional hazards model, adjusted for age, sex, UPCR, eGFR, and LDL-cho, revealed that male sex (hazard ratio [HR] 1.56, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.14–2.12), UPCR (HR 1.21, 95% CI 1.12–1.30), eGFR (per 10 mL/min/1.73 m², HR 0.26, 95% CI 0.22–0.33), and log urinary mCHO (HR 2.11, 95% CI 1.31–3.40) were significantly associated with the primary outcome ( model concordance, 0.93).
Conclusion
In patients with CKD, urinary mCHO is significantly associated with major adverse kidney events, suggesting that urinary mCHO may serve as a promising biomarker for predicting CKD progression.

title: #2208 Causal association between constipation and chronic kidney disease: a two-sample mendelian randomization analysis
authors: Kipyo Kim; Joon Ho Song
abstract:
Background and Aims
Previous epidemiological studies have suggested a potential association between constipation and chronic kidney disease (CKD). The high prevalence of constipation among CKD patients and the longitudinal relationship between constipation and incident CKD support this association. However, the causal relationship between these two conditions remains unclear. To investigate this, we performed a two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis using genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from large biobank datasets.
Method
GWAS summary data on constipation and CKD were obtained from the FinnGen (DF12) and CKDGen consortium, comprising sample sizes of 500,348 and 480,698, respectively. Constipation was defined using ICD-10 codes and laxative medication purchases, while CKD was defined as a creatinine-based estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m². Genetic instruments for CKD and constipation were selected to evaluate the bidirectional relationship between the two conditions. Independent instrumental variables were identified based on significant associations with the exposure (P < 5 × 10⁻⁸, clumping window of 10,000 kb, and r² < 0.001). Due to the limited number of SNPs associated with constipation, a more relaxed threshold (P < 5 × 10⁻⁶) was applied for instrument selection.
Results
A total of 19 and 21 independent instrumental variables were selected for constipation and CKD, respectively. The MR analysis did not reveal a significant association between genetically predicted constipation and CKD (inverse-variance weighted [IVW] Or = 1.033, 95% CI: 0.898–1.190). However, reverse MR analysis indicated that genetically predicted CKD was causally associated with an increased risk of constipation (IVW Or = 1.052, 95% CI: 1.003–1.104). No evidence of horizontal pleiotropy was observed.
Conclusion
Our findings suggest that constipation is not causally associated with CKD; rather, CKD may have a causal impact on the development of constipation.

title: #3075 Comparison of β-blocker with other anti-hypertensive drugs in patients with chronic kidney disease in Korea: a national health insurance data
authors: Seung Hyun Han; Mina Kim; Sang Youb Han
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is strongly associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular events. While β-blockers are widely used for managing heart failure and arrhythmia, their effectiveness in CKD patients without these conditions remains unclear. This study evaluates the clinical outcomes of β-blocker use in CKD patients without heart failure or arrhythmia, utilizing data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service (NHIS).
Method
This study included patients with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 60 mL/min/1.73 m². Patients with a history of dialysis, kidney transplantation, arrhythmia, congestive heart failure, malignancies, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (based on relevant ICD-10 codes) were excluded.
Control individuals were matched 1:2 by age, sex, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, body mass index, albuminuria, and antihypertensive medication class. The primary outcomes included all-cause mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; 4-point), ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, and heart failure.
Results
Among 325,584 individuals with CKD, 94,495 met the inclusion criteria. After matching, 26,376 patients (9,149 in the β-blocker group and 17,227 in the non-β-blocker group) were analyzed.
After adjusting for covariates, β-blocker users exhibited a significantly higher risk for adverse outcomes:
All-cause mortality: Adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) 1.178 (95% CI, 1.074–1.293; P < 0.0005)
4-point MACE: aHR 1.345 (95% CI, 1.252–1.445; P < 0.0001)
Non-fatal myocardial infarction: aHR 1.391 (95% CI, 1.182–1.637; P < 0.0001)
Heart failure: aHR 1.653 (95% CI, 1.476–1.850; P < 0.0001)
Arrhythmia: aHR 1.552 (95% CI, 1.436–1.677; P < 0.0001)
Notably, despite β-blockers being known to provide benefits in heart failure and arrhythmia, their use in CKD patients was associated with significantly worse outcomes in these conditions. In addition to an increased risk of mortality and MACE, β-blocker users exhibited a higher incidence of heart failure and arrhythmia, raising concerns about their safety in this population.
Conclusion
Our findings suggest that β-blockers may not offer the expected benefits in CKD patients without heart failure or arrhythmia. Instead, their use is associated with a significantly higher risk of mortality and cardiovascular complications, including worsened outcomes in heart failure and arrhythmia. These results challenge the conventional role of β-blockers in this patient population and highlight the need for a more tailored approach to antihypertensive therapy in CKD.
