title: #1250 Latent tuberculosis in advanced chronic kidney disease- single centre experience in the UK
authors: Anu Jayanti; Mohammedelnour Ishag; Seema Brij; Mohamed Elewa
abstract:
Background and Aims
As of 2022, England remained a low tuberculosis (TB) incidence country with a TB notification rate of 7.75 per 100,000 population, below the World Health Organization (WHO) threshold (10 per 100,000 population). Over a lifetime, a healthy individual with latent TB has a 10–15% chance of developing active TB infection. Patients receiving hemodialysis are at increased risk of latent TB reactivation with estimations as great as 25 times that of an otherwise healthy individual. The WHO recommends testing for all patients receiving dialysis. In a published report from Birmingham in 2018, the overall incidence of active TB within the 8767 strong renal cohort over a decade, was 126/100,000 patient-years ranging from 92/100,000 in those with CKD 1 or 2 to 257/100,000 patient-years in those receiving dialysis (Journal of Infection, 77, 2018). Most TB cases reported in the NW England in 2021, were born outside the UK (72.9%). Of these, 16.4% were diagnosed within one year of entry and 39.5% were diagnosed 11 or more years after entry (gov.uk/regional reports).
Informed by the increased incidence of patients presenting with advanced chronic kidney disease, born outside the UK, we launched a new testing program for latent and active tuberculosis in patients attending the renal center in Manchester, UK.
Method
This is a single centre report of incidence of TB specifically in patients with Advanced CKD- eGFR < 30 mls/min, including those on dialysis. Electronic records were used for data capture over a three-year period. 4672 patients had advanced CKD and therefore deemed to be the ‘at-risk’ group. Gamma Interferon Assay was employed as the test for latent TB detection. Of the at-risk group, 707 patients were tested prior to commencement of immunosuppression (either transplant or autoimmunity related). Clinical and treatment variables were also obtained. Descriptive analysis has been carried out.
Results
Over the three-year period, 76 patients were found to have either confirmed or indeterminate reports on Gamma Interferon assay. Median age of patients was 60.5 years and 68% were male. 27.6% of patients belonged in the White British category. Patients of Pakistani origin dominated the proportion of patients in the ethnic minority group (23%). 26% of patients also had diabetes and 35.5% were on dialysis therapy. 26.3% of patients were actively immunosuppressed and 38.2% were on steroid therapy. 35% of these cases were detected when screening was undertaken as part of transplantation work-up. Inadequate information was available on historic BCG vaccination. 13.2% of patients also had past treatment for tuberculosis. 24% of GIFN positive patients had histological/microbiological evidence of tuberculosis and 7.8% had extrapulmonary TB. 44.7% of patients went on to receive treatment with anti-tuberculosis therapy. The reasons for others not receiving treatment include non-referral/ refused therapy or did not attend clinics. Mean duration of treatment was 3.7 months. A third of the patients on treatment experienced treatment-related side effects. Within the scope of the somewhat limited uptake of GIFN testing amongst practitioners during this period, the incidence rate of active tuberculosis in this cohort is 92.7/100,000 patient-years. The incidence rate of GIFN positive patients in this at-risk group is 392.4/100,000 patient-years.
Conclusion
The incidence of latent tuberculosis in advanced CKD population is significantly high in our unit. Active case finding in this at-risk group is essential, as part of routine preventative care.

Conclusion
The incidence of latent tuberculosis in advanced CKD population is significantly high in our unit. Active case finding in this at-risk group is essential, as part of routine preventative care.

title: #898 Comparative performance of the new-generation large language model o1 pro and the established model GPT-4 on japanese nephrology board renewal questions
authors: Chiaki Yuasa; Ryunosuke Noda; Fumiya Kitano; Daisuke Ichikawa; Yugo Shibagaki
abstract:
Background and Aims
Large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-4 have demonstrated strong performance on medical exams, but their capacities to handle specialized domains like nephrology remain under investigation. Recently, a next-generation LLM called o1 pro was released, claiming superior reasoning abilities and fewer hallucinations. This study evaluated whether o1 pro could outperform GPT-4 on a rigorous set of Japanese nephrology board renewal questions. By comparing their accuracy and consistency across various subdomains and question types, we aimed to clarify the potential of these models as clinical and educational tools in nephrology.
Method
We used the Self-Assessment Questions for Nephrology Board Renewal, a set of annually administered, Japanese-language multiple-choice questions. These 209 questions (covering 2014–2023) encompass fundamental concepts, clinical management, and image interpretation in nephrology. Each question was categorized by cognitive level (recall, interpretation, and problem-solving), question type (general vs. clinical), the presence or absence of images, and nephrology subspecialty. Both o1 pro and GPT-4 were tested through separate chat sessions for each item, with accuracy determined by official answers from the Japanese Society of Nephrology. Statistical comparisons of correct-answer proportions were made using chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered significant.
Results
Overall, o1 pro achieved a proportion of correct answers of 81.3% (170/209), significantly exceeding GPT-4’s 51.2% (107/209; P < 0.001). When analyzed by examination year, o1 pro consistently surpassed the 60% pass threshold and exhibited strong annual performance (70%–95% accuracy). In contrast, GPT-4 displayed notable variability and passed the 60% mark in only two of the ten examination years. By cognitive level, o1 pro showed superior accuracy for recall (83.3% vs. 49.1%), interpretation (75.0% vs. 50.0%), and problem-solving (84.4% vs. 57.8%) questions (P < 0.001, 0.011, 0.011, respectively). Similar trends were seen for general versus clinical question types: o1 pro achieved 83.8% and 78.6%, whereas GPT-4 attained 49.5% and 53.1% (P < 0.001, < 0.001, respectively). Additionally, o1 pro displayed marked advantages on image-based questions (77.5% vs. 42.5%; P = 0.003), suggesting enhanced capacities in multimodal information processing. Subspecialty analyses confirmed that o1 pro outperformed GPT-4 in critical areas like chronic kidney disease/end-stage kidney disease.
Conclusion
This study demonstrated that o1 pro significantly outperformed GPT-4 in multiple facets of nephrology board renewal questions, spanning basic recall, complex clinical reasoning, and image-based interpretation. These findings underscore the rapidly evolving capabilities of LLMs and their potential as educational and clinical support tools in nephrology. As further refinements in LLM architecture, training data, and multimodal integration continue, o1 pro and similarly advanced models may play an increasingly vital role in enhancing nephrology education and decision-making. However, real-world validation and assessments across diverse medical settings are necessary before fully integrating next-generation LLMs into routine clinical practice.

title: #2680 Differences in chronic kidney disease management based on identification and diagnosis in a population-based observational study
authors: Michael Olszewski; Karl Bjurström; Markus Lingman; Dan Henrohn; Poyan Shojaiyan; Magnus Garell; Björn Agvall
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD), affecting 6–10% of adults, often progresses silently until advanced stages, resulting in frequent underdiagnosis and inadequate management. To compare diagnosed, proxy-diagnosed, and undiagnosed CKD patients in terms of prevalence, assessment, nephroprotective treatment, healthcare utilization, and mortality.
Method
A retrospective observational study using Region Halland's healthcare data included adults meeting the confirmed CKD criteria defined by Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) from January–December 2019. Participants were classified into three groups: ICD-coded CKD (diagnosed CKD), CKD-related diagnoses (proxy-diagnosed CKD), and those meeting CKD criteria without an ICD diagnosis (undiagnosed CKD).
Results
Among 20488 CKD patients, 21% had an ICD-documented diagnosed CKD, 18% had a proxy-diagnosed CKD, and 61% were undiagnosed CKD. The mean ages were 76.4 years for diagnosed CKD, 62.4 years for proxy-diagnosed CKD, and 81.8 years for undiagnosed CKD (P < 0.001). Blood pressure follow-up rates were 88% for diagnosed, 67% for proxy-diagnosed, and 80% for undiagnosed, while glucose testing rates were 83%, 69%, and 76%, respectively. eGFR testing rates were 73%, 53%, and 66%. Urine albumin-creatinine ratio (UACR) testing rates were 25% in the overall population, 45% among individuals with diagnosed CKD, and 19% in both the undiagnosed CKD and proxy-diagnosed CKD groups. Renin-angiotensin system inhibitors were used in 45% of the cohort: 51% in diagnosed CKD, 28% in proxy-diagnosed CKD, and 47% in undiagnosed CKD. The relative risk of hospitalization, adjusted for age and comorbidities, was 2.71 (CI: 2.59–2.84) for patients with diagnosed CKD and 1.38 (CI: 1.31–1.46) for those with proxy-diagnosed CKD. The adjusted all-cause mortality hazard ratios were 2.22 (CI: 1.95–2.52) for CKD-diagnosed patients and 1.31 (CI: 1.08–1.60) for those with a proxy-diagnosed CKD.
Conclusion
The study highlights gaps in CKD diagnosis and management, with many patients remaining undiagnosed despite meeting CKD criteria. Diagnosed CKD patients received better follow-up but faced higher risks of hospitalization and mortality due to more complex comorbidities and more advanced CKD. Proxy-diagnosed CKD were common and associated with suboptimal management. These findings emphasize the need for consistent and accurate CKD identification to improve outcomes and optimize care.

title: #3932 Desidustat in chronic kidney disease anaemia: real-world experience and outcomes
authors: Syeda Hurmath; Srushti S Hiremath; Arvind Conjeevaram; Sanjeev Kumar Hiremath
abstract:
Background and Aims
Anaemia is a common and debilitating complication in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), contributing to a range of adverse outcomes, including fatigue, reduced quality of life, and cardiovascular health. Current management strategies are oral or IV iron and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs). Desidustat, a novel oral hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor(HIF-PHI)offers a new mechanism of action by stimulating erythropoiesis through the body's natural hypoxic response, providing an alternative to ESA therapy. This retrospective analysis aims to evaluate the real-world effectiveness and safety of Desidustat in managing anaemia in CKD patients.
Method
This retrospective observational study included patients with stage 3-5 CKD who had been prescribed Desidustat along with oral iron, with a mean duration of 6 months. Patient data were extracted from electronic health records from various nephrology centres. The primary endpoint was the change in Hb levels from baseline to the end of treatment. Secondary endpoints included the proportion of patients achieving a Hb ≥10 g/dL, the incidence of adverse events (AEs), and overall treatment tolerability.
Results
Of the 99 patients included in the analysis, the mean age was 60 years. The mean baseline Hb level was 9.3 g/dL. After 6 months of Desidustat treatment, the mean Hb increase was 1.63 g/dL, with 73% of patients reaching a Hb level ≥10 g/dL by the end of the study. The response to treatment was consistent across both stages 3 and 4–5 CKD, with similar increases in Hb regardless of baseline renal function. Notably, Desidustat treatment was well tolerated, only 10% of patients reported mild gastrointestinal symptoms (such as nausea, abdominal pain and diarrhoea ), which resolved with continued therapy. The overall rate of adverse events was low, and there were no cases of treatment discontinuation due to side effects.
Conclusion
Desidustat significantly improved haemoglobin levels in the majority of patients, with a response profile that was consistent across various stages of CKD without causing severe adverse drug reactions.
The treatment was associated with minimal side effects suggesting that Desidustat may offer a safer alternative to traditional ESA therapy, particularly for patients at risk for cardiovascular events or those who prefer oral medication over injections. Further randomised controlled trials are warranted to validate these findings and assess the long-term benefits of Desidustat in CKD-related anaemia.

title: #654 The active ingredient in the Nuphar lutea plant, 6,6′-dihydroxythiobinupharidine (DTBN) ameliorates inflammation and anaemia in a mouse model of CKD
authors: Daniel Landau; Eden Arazi; Jannat Khalilia; Jacob Gopas; Yael Segev
abstract:
Background and Aims
EPO resistance and iron deficiency in CKD-related anemia are associated with an increase in inflammatory cytokines associated with the innate immune response, such as IL-6, IL-1, and TNF-α. Recently (Bandach et al, Sci Reports 2021) we reported that kidney fibrosis and anemia of CKD can be worsened or relieved when IL1 effects are enhanced or inhibited respectively.
The water lily Nuphar lutea plant has been widely used as a traditional remedy for the treatment of rheumatism, scars, pain, and more. Gopas et al (Cancer Biology Therapy 2009) extracted an active ingredient from the family of nupharidines, 6,6′-Dihydroxythiobinupharidine (DTBN), which showed anti-inflammatory properties, mainly through the inhibition of NF-κB. The purpose of this study was to test the effects of DTBN in a mouse model of CKD-associated anemia.
Methods
8 weeks old male C57BL/6 mice were divided into 3 groups: Control, CKD (induced by adenine diet) and CKD-DTBN. Animals were injected with saline-DMSO or 30 μg DTBN, every two days and sacrificed after 3 weeks from dietary intervention.
Results
Serum urea and kidney TGFβ mRNA were significantly decreased in CKD-DTBN Vs CKD. Macrophage infiltration and renal fibrosis were ameliorated in CKD-DTBN Vs CKD. A significant improvement in systemic inflammation indices (blood lymphocytes, liver IL-6 and CRP), as well as kidney pSTAT3/STAT3 protein ratio, immunostainable NF-κB and F4\80, which were increased in CKD, were all decreased in CKD-DTBN. CKD anemia indices (hemoglobin, hematocrit and RBC count) significantly improved in CKD-DTBN Vs CKD. Kidney HIF-2α and EPO mRNA were significantly decreased in both uremic groups, but was unchanged in CKD- DTBN Vs CKD. However, serum iron and transferrin saturation were significantly increased in CKD-DTBN Vs CKD. Liver hepcidin was elevated in both uremic groups.
Conclusion
Uremic mice treated with DTBN showed improvement in kidney fibrosis, inflammation and anemia indices, in association with improved iron availability. Thus, DTBN may be a novel therapeutic alternative for CKD and its complications.

title: #1325 Real-world use of HIF-PH inhibitors and ESAs in non-dialysis-dependent CKD with anemia: insights from a Japanese database study
authors: Takahiro Kuragano; Kiichiro Ueta; Manabu Ishii; Kenichi Nishimura; Kenji Arakawa; Toshio Hashimoto; Akira Oku
abstract:
Background and Aims
In addition to erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs), which has been the standard treatment for renal anemia in chronic kidney disease (CKD), hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase (HIF-PH) inhibitors were introduced in Japan in 2020; however, data on their actual use in clinical practice were lacking. The purpose of this study was to investigate the real-world use of HIF-PH inhibitors versus ESAs in Japanese patients with anemia and non-dialysis-dependent CKD.
Method
This retrospective cohort study made use of data from the Medical Data Vision database (April 2008–March 2024). Two patient cohorts were studied: Cohort 1 included those starting renal anemia treatment (HIF-PH inhibitors or ESAs) between 2021 and 2024, and Cohort 2 included patients who had received ESA in 2020. Data from Sub-cohorts 1 and 2 with known iron repletion status were also examined. The study examined treatment initiation, switching rates, and hemoglobin (Hb) trends
Results
Cohort 1 included 9,253 patients. ESAs remained the primary initial treatment; however, the proportion of patients starting HIF-PH inhibitors increased annually, from 15.1% in 2021 to 54.8% in the first quarter of 2024. In Sub-cohort 1, prescriptions of HIF-PH inhibitors also annually increased. In all of these cohorts, initiation with HIF-PH inhibitors showed trends to maintain higher Hb levels than ESAs groups. This trend was particularly notable in patients with functional iron deficiency (ferritin>100 ng/mL and TSAT<20%), the proportion of patients with severe anemia (Hb<10 g/dL) was lower in the HIF inhibitor group (3%) than in the ESA group (32%) after 12 month (Fig. 1). In the Cohort 2 (n = 1,998) there was no change in Hb levels in the ESA continuation group, on the other hand, after switch from ESA to HIF-PH inhibitor, Hb level increased and the proportion of patients with severe anemia (Hb<10g/dL) was decreased from 42% to 15%) (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
Real-world data indicates that the proportion of patients with HIF-PH inhibitor initiation in non-dialysis CKD anemia increased to match ESA levels by 2024. HIF-PH inhibitors reduced the proportion of patients with severe anemia more than ESAs, and this tendency was more pronounced in patients with functional iron deficiency. Furthermore, switching from ESAs to HIF-PH inhibitors may be effective even in patients in whom ESAs do not sufficiently improve anemia.

title: #1242 Depressive mood and cognitive dysfunction to predict renal outcome and mortality in elderly patients
authors: Bo Keung Peun; Heeseung Choi; Ki Young Na; Ho Jun Chin
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cognitive impairment and depressive mood significantly affect the elderly population and patients with chronic kidney disease. However, their contribution to the outcomes such as mortality and renal dysfunction remains unclear. This study evaluated the role of cognitive function and depressive mood in predicting renal replacement therapy (RRT) and mortality in elderly patients.
Method
This retrospective cohort study included 5,191 individuals aged ≥ 65 years who underwent geriatric assessment including the Korean Mini-Mental Status Examination (MMSE) and Korean Short Geriatric Depression Scale (SGDS) at a university hospital in Korea between January 2016 and December 2020. Participants with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of more than 15 ml/min/1.73 m² and at least three months of follow-up were included. Cognitive function and depressive mood were assessed by MMSE and SGDS, respectively.
Results
There were 2388 (46.0 %) male participants aged 77.7 ± 5.6 years. During around 45 months of mean follow-up period, there were 1,512 mortalities (29.1 %) and 68 (1.3%) incident end stage renal diseases. AUCs by ROC analysis showed significant inverse relationship (P < 0.01) between MMSE and outcomes and positive relationship (p<0.001) between SGDS and outcomes. AUCs to predict incident RRT were not different between MMSE and SGDS (P = 0.686), however, AUC by MMSE to predict mortality was higher than AUC by SGDS (P = 0.018). Using Cox's hazard proportional model, depressive mood (SGDS ≥ 5) was associated with a higher risk of RRT (HR 1.849, 95% CI 1.092–3.131, P = 0.022) and mortality (HR 1.394, 95% CI 1.244–1.562, P < 0.001). Severe depressive mood (SGDS ≥ 10) increased the risk of RRT (HR 2.072, 95% CI 1.006–4.269, P = 0.048) and mortality (HR 1.472, 95% CI 1.256–1.723, P < 0.001), more. Cognitive dysfunction (MMSE ≤ 23) was associated with a higher risk of mortality (HR 1.319, 95% CI 1.170–1.486, P < 0.001). However, it was not associated with RRT risk (P = 0.467). Severe cognitive decline (MMSE ≤ 19) was significantly associated with increased mortality (HR 1.332, 95% CI 1.151–1.542, P < 0.001). C-indexes by Cox's models including MMSE or SGDS were not different in predicting outcomes. For participants aged <75 years, both abnormal MMSE (≤ 23) and SGDS (≥ 5) were significantly associated with increased RRT risk (MMSE: HR 3.489, P = 0.013; SGDS: HR 3.014, P = 0.029). In participants aged ≥75 years, only SGDS (≥5) was significantly associated with RRT risk (HR 1.904, P = 0.021), while abnormal MMSE (≤23) showed no significant association (HR 1.638, P = 0.079). Depressive mood (SGDS ≥ 5) was a risk factor for incident RRT in participants with higher eGFR (> 75 ml/min/1.73 m2) (P = 0.036) as well as in participants with lower eGFR (P = 0.026), but cognitive dysfunction (MMSE ≤ 23) was a risk factor for incident RRT in participants with higher eGFR (> 75 ml/min/1.73 m2)(P = 0.027), but not in participants with lower eGFR (P = 0.091). Abnormal MMSE and SGDS scores were associated with an elevated risk of mortality in participants aged < 75 years (all p-values <0.001), as well as in participants aged > 75 years (all p-values <0.001). Abnormal MMSE and SGDS scores were also associated with an elevated risk of mortality in participants with a higher eGFR (all p-values <0.001), as well as in participants with a lower eGFR (all p-values <0.001).
Conclusion
Depressive mood is a more powerful predictor of RRT than cognitive dysfunction, and both depression and cognitive dysfunction are risk factors of mortality in elderly patients.

Abnormal MMSE and SGDS scores were also associated with an elevated risk of mortality in participants with a higher eGFR (all p-values <0.001), as well as in participants with a lower eGFR (all p-values <0.001).
Conclusion
Depressive mood is a more powerful predictor of RRT than cognitive dysfunction, and both depression and cognitive dysfunction are risk factors of mortality in elderly patients.

title: #2495 The impact of adolescent smoking initiation on the risk of end-stage kidney disease: a nationwide cohort study
authors: Seong Geun Kim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a growing global health challenge, with smoking identified as a significant risk factor. This study investigates the long-term impact of adolescent smoking initiation on the development of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD).
Method
A retrospective cohort study was conducted using data from the Korean NHIS claims database. The cohort included 201,678 CKD patients aged 40 and above with a documented smoking history. Patients were stratified by age at smoking initiation (<20 years vs. ≥20 years) and cumulative smoking exposure (pack-years, PY). The primary outcome was the incidence of ESKD, defined as the initiation of kidney replacement therapy. Cox proportional hazards models assessed the relationship between smoking initiation age, smoking burden, and ESKD risk.
Results
Those with higher PYs were older and had more comorbidities, such as hypertension and diabetes. Patients who began smoking before age 20 and accumulated ≥20 PYs had a significantly higher risk of ESKD (HR, 1.26 [1.16–1.38]) compared to those with the same exposure but later smoking initiation. Increased cumulative smoking exposure further elevated the risk. When PYs were divided according to initiation age, a higher ratio was associated with an increased risk of ESKD.
Conclusion
Early smoking initiation during adolescence was associated with a significantly higher risk of progression to ESKD in patients with CKD, especially in those with higher cumulative smoking exposure. Public health interventions focusing on preventing adolescent smoking can mitigate the long-term burden of CKD progression.

title: #3788 Estimated glomerular filtration rate in pediatric neurogenic bladder patients using cystatin C and creatinine based CKiD and EKFC equations – usefulness of cystatin C
authors: Teresa Tavares; Rosa Amorim; Maria Do Sameiro Faria; Teresa Costa
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with neurogenic bladder (NB) can develop progressive chronic kidney disease (CKD), so early detection of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) reduction is essential to prevent morbimortality. Due to decreased muscle mass in children with NB, there may be significant inaccuracy when using creatinine-based eGFR formulas. This study aims to analyse eGFR calculated by different equations using serum creatinine (Cr) and/or cystatin C (CysC) and compare between patients with and without motor neurological injury.
Method
A retrospective study was conducted on pediatric patients with NB and CKD with stable renal function (stages 1 and 2), based on Chronic Kidney Disease in Children (CKiD) Under25 (U25)-Cr formula, from a Pediatric Nephrology Unit of a tertiary hospital. The eGFR was calculated using CKiD U25-Cr, CKiD U25-CysC, European Kidney Function Consortium (EKFC)-Cr and EKFC-CysC equations.
Results
Forty-four patients were included in the analysis, with a median age (IQR) of 14.2 years (9.1–17), 50% (n = 22) were male, 63.6% (n = 28) had lipo/myelomeningocele and 72.7% (n = 32) were classified as stage 1 CKD.
The median (IQR) eGFR (ml/min/1.73 m2) calculated by different formulas was: CKiD U25-Cr 101.0 (79.6–130.7); CKiD U25-CysC 73.6 (61.9–93.5); EKFC-Cr 110.4 (86.9–123.6) and EKFC-CysC 84.6 (70.7–97.9). When compared to CKiD U25-Cr, the CKiD U25-CysC and EKFC-CysC formulas showed significantly lower values of eGFR (p < 0.001), while EKFC-Cr was similar (P = 0.076).
When CKiD U25-CysC and EKFC-CysC equations were used, 40.9% and 44.2% of the patients respectively, moved to a more advanced CKD stage.
In patients on wheelchair or orthosis, with more muscle atrophy (52.3%, n = 23), the median eGFR calculated using the CKiD U25-Cr and EKFC-Cr equations was significantly higher (P = 0.04 and P = 0.011, respectively) when compared to those with autonomous gait. However, there were no differences between the two groups when using CKiD U25-CysC and EKFC-CysC-based equations (P = 0.698 and P = 0.525, respectively).
Conclusion
In pediatric patients with NB and muscle mass depletion Cr-based formulas can overestimate eGFR and delay the diagnosis and correct staging of CKD. CysC seems to be a more reliable and earlier marker of kidney dysfunction, especially in those with greater muscular atrophy, thus being a valuable tool for identification of pediatric patients with NB who may benefit from early Pediatric Nephrology referral.

title: #1123 Inhibition of histone 3 lysine 9 trimethylation improves kidney fibrosis in a mouse model of unilateral ureteral obstruction
authors: Chia Chi Wu; Hong Mou Shih; Shuei-Liong Lin
abstract:
Background and Aims
Following kidney injury, the transition of pericytes into myofibroblasts, the primary collagen-producing cells in kidney fibrosis, is accompanied by increased alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) expression. Acta2 repressors, such as Rasal1, Pura, Tead1, Ybx1, and Ybx2, decrease during this process, leading to elevated α-SMA levels in myofibroblasts. SUV39H2, a lysine methyltransferase, induces trimethylation of histone 3 lysine 9 (H3K9me3), repressing gene transcription. We hypothesized that increased H3K9me3 from SUV39H2 downregulates Acta2 repressors, promoting α-SMA expression. This study investigates whether chaetocin, an H3K9me3 inhibitor, can reverse these epigenetic changes and mitigate kidney fibrosis.
Method
A kidney fibrosis model was developed using C57BL/6 mice subjected to unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO) surgery. Gene expression was assessed at sham, 7, 10, and 14 days post-UUO. Mice were treated with vehicle or chaetocin. Real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) was used to evaluate fibrosis-related genes, histone methyltransferases, and Acta2 repressors. Western blotting analyzed key fibrosis-related proteins, and picrosirius red staining quantified fibrosis. In vitro, C3H10T1/2 cells were treated with TGF-β1 (5 ng/mL) or TGF-β1 with chaetocin (10 nM). Gene expression related to fibrosis and Acta2 repressors was analyzed to elucidate chaetocin's molecular mechanisms.
Results
As the duration of UUO increased, the expression levels of pro-fibrotic markers, including Acta2, Col1a1, and Col3a1, showed a progressive upregulation. Similarly, the expression of Suv39h2, a H3K9me3 methyltransferase, was significantly elevated in the UUO kidney, whereas the expression of Suv39h1, another H3K9me3 methyltransferase, remained unchanged. In contrast, Acta2 repressors such as Ybx2 were progressively downregulated over time.
In vitro, when C3H10T1/2 cells were stimulated with TGF-β1, they exhibited a more pro-fibrotic phenotype characterized by the upregulation of Acta2, Col1a1, and Tgfb1. This stimulation also induced the expression of Suv39h2 but had no effect on Suv39h1. Notably, treatment with chaetocin reversed the expression of Acta2 and Col1a1, indicating its anti-fibrotic potential. However, Suv39h2 expression remained unaffected by chaetocin, suggesting that the drug's effects are mediated primarily through functional activity rather than transcriptional regulation. Furthermore, expression of Ybx2, an Acta2 repressor, was inhibited by TGF-β1, but the addition of chaetocin restored its expression, counteracting TGF-β1's inhibitory effects.
To investigate whether chaetocin's inhibition of H3K9me3 can attenuate fibrosis in vivo, we conducted experiments using the UUO kidney fibrosis model. Intraperitoneal injection of chaetocin significantly reversed the upregulation of fibrotic gene expression observed in vehicle-treated UUO mice.
In Western blot analyses, the expression of collagen α1 type I precursor (pro-Col1a1) and α-SMA was markedly elevated in UUO mice on day 10 compared with the contralateral kidney. Chaetocin treatment significantly reduced the expression of pro-Col1a1 and α-SMA, indicating its anti-fibrotic effects. Similarly, the expression of Ybx2, which was significantly decreased in the UUO kidney on day 10, was restored in the Chaetocin-treated group.
Histological evaluation using picrosirius red staining revealed a notable increase in fibrosis in UUO kidneys on day 10. However, Chaetocin treatment effectively mitigated fibrosis formation. These findings demonstrate that Chaetocin reduces fibrosis by modulating key pro-fibrotic genes and reversing epigenetic changes associated with the progression of kidney fibrosis.
Conclusion
Chaetocin effectively attenuates kidney fibrosis by modulating pro-fibrotic genes and reversing epigenetic changes associated with fibrosis progression. Its ability to restore Acta2 repressors and inhibit TGF-β1-induced pericyte-to-myofibroblast transition highlights its potential as a therapeutic agent for epigenetically mediated fibrosis.

title: #1329 Association of time-updated body mass index with the initiation of kidney replacement therapy in patients with chronic kidney disease: results from the KNOW-CKD study
authors: Jayoun Kim; Minsang Kim; Kook-Hwan Oh
abstract:
Background and Aims
The association between body mass index (BMI) and the risk of kidney replacement therapy (KRT) initiation in patients with non-dialysis-dependent chronic kidney disease (NDD-CKD) remains uncertain. Given the controversies around using baseline BMI as the only exposure in analysis, we aimed to investigate the association between time-updated BMI and the risk of KRT initiation in NDD-CKD patients, employing a marginal structural Cox model (Cox-MSM).
Method
A total of 2136 patients enrolled in the KoreaN Cohort Study for Outcome in Patients With CKD were included in this study. The exposure was baseline and time-updated BMI. The outcome was the initiation of KRT including dialysis or kidney transplantation during the follow-up period. A multivariable Cox proportional hazards (Cox-PH) model, a time-dependent Cox-PH model without inverse probability weights, and a Cox-MSM were fitted, adjusting for both time-fixed covariates, including age, sex, smoking, and comorbidities, and time-varying covariates including systolic blood pressure, creatinine, and hemoglobin.
Results
During the median follow-up of 8.3 years, the KRT initiation occurred in 723 patients (34%). In patients with a BMI higher than 25 kg/m2, a higher time-updated BMI was significantly associated with a lower risk of KRT initiation compared to the reference group with BMI 23–25 kg/m2 and a gradual decrease in the risk of KRT initiation with increasing BMI was observed. The BMI 25–27.5 kg/m2 group (hazard ratio [HR], 0.80; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.64–1.00), BMI 27.5–30 kg/m2 group (HR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.59–0.98), and BMI ≥30 kg/m2 group (HR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.58–0.97) exhibited a significantly lower risk of KRT initiation compared to the reference group.
Conclusion
A higher time-updated BMI has a lower risk of KRT initiation in obese patients with NDD-CKD in Korea. Therefore, clinicians should carefully monitor the weight fluctuations and maintain appropriate weight range through regular weight measurements.

title: #104 Online patient education improves understanding of IgAN
authors: Amy Larkin; Meghan Wilson
abstract:
Background and Aims
This study assessed the impact of online patient education on knowledge, confidence and intent to act regarding IgAN.
Method
The educational intervention consisted of 2 activities comprised of text, integrated visuals, and video commentary published on WebMD Education in July and August 2024. Demographic questions were asked prior to each activity. Knowledge questions were asked both before and after to assess learning gains. Intent to change and confidence questions were asked at the end of each activity. Absolute improvements were calculated for pre/post questions.
Results
Activity 1: What is Immunoglobulin A Nephropathy?
11,243 learners; 1,570 completers of all questions
Age: 53% >60 years old, 32% 46–59 years old
Geographic Location: 30% Midwest, 28% Southeast, 24% Northeast, 9% Southwest, 8% West
Highest Grade Level Completed: 24% some college but no degree; 22% high school/GED; 20% 2-year degree; 18% 4-year degree; 15% more than 4-year degree; 1% some high school
On post-test, 75% understood how kidney failure can happen when your kidneys don't filter blood well enough. Additionally, 40% are confident talking to healthcare team about risk for IgAN and 38% will work with healthcare team about IgAN.
Activity 2: Things to Know About Immunoglobulin A Nephropathy
12,041 learners; 1.662 completers of all questions
Age: 48% >60 years old, 35% 46–59 years old
Race/Ethnicity: 77% White or Caucasian/non-Hispanic, 2% Black or African-American, 4% Hispanic or Latino
Gender: 74% female, 16% male, 10% prefer not to answer, <1% non-binary
After the education, 13% increase in knowledge regarding the impact of IgAN on your kidney health (45% pre to 58% post). Additionally, 59% are confident talking to healthcare team about risk for IgAN and 50% will work with healthcare team about IgAN.
Conclusion
The metrics and outcomes gathered in this assessment are a strong indicator that online patient activities on WebMD Education improved knowledge and confidence and prompted intent to act related to IgAN.

title: #247 The effect of pravastatin on insulin resistance in patients with CKD stage 1-3. A randomized, placebo-controlled cross over trial
authors: Mai-Britt Skadborg; Henrik Birn; Niels Moeller; Niels Jessen; Lara Aygen Ozbay
abstract:
Background and Aims
Insulin resistance is highly prevalent in patients with impaired kidney function, which increases the risk of Diabetes Mellitus Type 2 and cardiovascular morbidity.
Statins are recommended as primary prophylaxis in most patients with non-dialysis-dependent CKD (chronic kidney disease); however, they have been associated with insulin resistance and diabetes mellitus.
This diabetogenic effect appears to be dose dependent, yet some statins may have neutral or beneficial effects on glucose metabolism. Pravastatin is consistently reported as the least diabetogenic statin, however this has not been established in patients with CKD using a hyperinsulinaemic euglaemic glucose clamp. We aimed to test if pravastatin improves insulin sensitivity compared to placebo in non-diabetic patients with CKD stage 1–3.
Method
We conducted a randomized, placebo controlled, double blinded cross-over trial of 12 weeks of pravastatin treatment (40 mg/day) in 13 non-diabetic CKD patients.
Botnia clamps (Intra Venous Glucose Tolerance Test (IVGTT) followed by hyperinsulinaemic euglycaemic glucose clamp) were performed after each treatment period (12 weeks of pravastatin and 12 weeks of placebo). IVGTT was performed with 50% glucose 0.3 g/kg total body weight/2 min., and the hyperinsulinaemic clamp with insulin 1.0 mUnits/kg total body weight/min. The primary endpoint was the difference in insulin sensitivity measured as glucose infusion rate/M value during each clamp. Secondary endpoints included first phase insulin secretion during intravenous glucose tolerance test and 2-hour plasma glucose after an oral glucose tolerance test.
Results
There was no significant difference in insulin sensitivity following pravastatin treatment when compared to placebo, with a mean difference in M-value of 0.11 mg/kg/min. (95% CI −1.09 to 1.31, P = 0.84). Mean M-value was 7.66 mg/kg/min (SEM ±0.50, 95% CI 6.57 to 8.75) after treatment with Pravastatin and 7.69 mg/kg/min (SEM ±0.77, 95% CI 6.01 to 9.36) after placebo treatment.
Mean fasting P-glucose was 5.6 mmol/l (SEM ±0.1) and 5.5 mmol/l (SEM ±0.1) following treatment with Pravastatin and placebo, respectively, with a non-significant difference of −0.1 mmol/l (95% CI −0.3 to 0.1, P = 0.39)
Mean HbA1c was 35.0 mmol/mol (SEM ±0.83) and 35.5 mmol/mol (SEM ±1.21) following treatment with Pravastatin and placebo, respectively, with a non-significant difference between treatments of 0.75 mmol/mol (SE ±0.60, 95% CI −0.56 to 2.06, P = 0.23). Mean 2-h P-glucose following an OGTT was 7.0 mmol/l (SEM ±0.9) and 5.4 mmol/l (SEM ±0.3) following treatment with Pravastatin and placebo, respectively, with a non-significant difference between treatments of −0.6 mmol/l (SE ±0.3, 95% CI −1.3 to 0.1, P = 0.10).
Conclusion
Twelve weeks of treatment with Pravastatin is not associated with any significant changes in insulin sensitivity in patients with CKD stage 1–3. The results are generalizable to a wide range of patients with chronic kidney disease, since we have results from a group of non-immunosuppressed CKD stage 1–3 patients. In patients with CKD and a high risk of developing both diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease, we now have a good option for cardiovascular risk reduction that does not concurrently increase the risk of diabetes mellitus.

This diabetogenic effect appears to be dose dependent, yet some statins may have neutral or beneficial effects on glucose metabolism. Pravastatin is consistently reported as the least diabetogenic statin, however this has not been established in patients with CKD using a hyperinsulinaemic euglaemic glucose clamp. We aimed to test if pravastatin improves insulin sensitivity compared to placebo in non-diabetic patients with CKD stage 1–3.

We conducted a randomized, placebo controlled, double blinded cross-over trial of 12 weeks of pravastatin treatment (40 mg/day) in 13 non-diabetic CKD patients.
Botnia clamps (Intra Venous Glucose Tolerance Test (IVGTT) followed by hyperinsulinaemic euglycaemic glucose clamp) were performed after each treatment period (12 weeks of pravastatin and 12 weeks of placebo). IVGTT was performed with 50% glucose 0.3 g/kg total body weight/2 min., and the hyperinsulinaemic clamp with insulin 1.0 mUnits/kg total body weight/min. The primary endpoint was the difference in insulin sensitivity measured as glucose infusion rate/M value during each clamp. Secondary endpoints included first phase insulin secretion during intravenous glucose tolerance test and 2-hour plasma glucose after an oral glucose tolerance test.
Results
There was no significant difference in insulin sensitivity following pravastatin treatment when compared to placebo, with a mean difference in M-value of 0.11 mg/kg/min. (95% CI −1.09 to 1.31, P = 0.84). Mean M-value was 7.66 mg/kg/min (SEM ±0.50, 95% CI 6.57 to 8.75) after treatment with Pravastatin and 7.69 mg/kg/min (SEM ±0.77, 95% CI 6.01 to 9.36) after placebo treatment.
Mean fasting P-glucose was 5.6 mmol/l (SEM ±0.1) and 5.5 mmol/l (SEM ±0.1) following treatment with Pravastatin and placebo, respectively, with a non-significant difference of −0.1 mmol/l (95% CI −0.3 to 0.1, P = 0.39)
Mean HbA1c was 35.0 mmol/mol (SEM ±0.83) and 35.5 mmol/mol (SEM ±1.21) following treatment with Pravastatin and placebo, respectively, with a non-significant difference between treatments of 0.75 mmol/mol (SE ±0.60, 95% CI −0.56 to 2.06, P = 0.23). Mean 2-h P-glucose following an OGTT was 7.0 mmol/l (SEM ±0.9) and 5.4 mmol/l (SEM ±0.3) following treatment with Pravastatin and placebo, respectively, with a non-significant difference between treatments of −0.6 mmol/l (SE ±0.3, 95% CI −1.3 to 0.1, P = 0.10).
Conclusion
Twelve weeks of treatment with Pravastatin is not associated with any significant changes in insulin sensitivity in patients with CKD stage 1–3. The results are generalizable to a wide range of patients with chronic kidney disease, since we have results from a group of non-immunosuppressed CKD stage 1–3 patients. title: #2040 Revisiting frequent premature atrial contractions and cerebrovascular events in non-dialysis CKD patients
authors: Mei-Chuan Kuo; Yun-Ping Chen; Lu-Heng Lu; Yi-Ting Lin; Yi-Wen Chiu; Ping-Hsun Wu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiac arrhythmias are common in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) now considers frequent premature atrial contractions (PACs) as associated with an increased risk of ischemic stroke rather than being benign. This study aims to evaluate the cerebrovascular and mortality risk of frequent PACs in non-dialysis-dependent CKD patients.
Method
The CKD patients who joined the pre-end-stage renal disease program and examined 24-hour Holter monitor were recruited in the Kaohsiung Medical University Hospital healthcare system from April 2009 to December 2021. The total PAC counts were calculated, and the frequent PACs were defined with a cut off value of 218 beats per day. The relationship between frequent PACs and cerebrovascular events (acute ischemic stroke [AIS] and transient ischemic attack [TIA]) and mortality were analysed using survival analysis and the Cox regression model.
Results
After excluding 195 individuals with a history of atrial fibrillation (AF) and 239 individuals with newly detected AF, 1,743 patients were included in the final analysis. Frequent PACs were associated with a higher risk of cerebrovascular events in survival analysis (log-rank P < 0.01 in AIS and log-rank P < 0.01 in TIA) and multivariable-adjusted Cox regression model (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], 1.26; 95% Confidence interval [CI], 1.12–1.42; P < 0.001 in AIS and aHR, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.14–1.43; P < 0.001 in TIA).The Kaplan-Meier curve indicated that individuals with PACs greater than 218 beats per day were linked to an increased risk of all-cause mortality compared to those with lower PACs frequency. In a multivariable-adjusted Cox regression model, frequent PACs were associated with an increased risk of all-cause mortality (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.36; 95% Confidence interval, 1.13–1.63; p-value = 0.001).
Conclusion
Our study demonstrated that non-AF CKD patients with frequent PACs were associated with a higher risk of cerebrovascular events. Further studies are required to establish the threshold for frequent PACs and the cerebrovascular prevention strategy for frequent PACs CKD subjects.

title: #2150 Impact of dapagliflozin on the kidney failure risk equation (KFRE) in patients with stage G4 chronic kidney disease
authors: Francisco Javier Toro Prieto; Paola Donoso Naranjo; Natalia Santos Collado; Lola María Bueno Mena-Bernal; Mercedes Acevedo Ribo
abstract:
Background and Aims
The new KDIGO 2024 guidelines emphasize the use of the Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE) to estimate the need for initiating renal replacement therapy (RRT). The importance of monitoring patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (ACKD) has been widely recognized, as it can help slow disease progression and delay the need for RRT. Additionally, the introduction of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) in recent years has garnered significant interest due to their proven effectiveness. However, there is currently no evidence in the literature regarding the impact of SGLT2 inhibitors on the KFRE equation. Our objective was to compare the probability of starting renal replacement therapy at two years (KFRE 2) in patients attending ACKD consultations, specifically those with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) calculated using the CKD-EPI formula between 25 and 30 ml/min/1.73 m². This comparison focuses on patients who initiate treatment with Dapagliflozin 10 mg/day versus those who do not.
Method
A retrospective observational case-control study was conducted to analyze patients with stage G4 CKD who initiated treatment with Dapagliflozin compared to those who did not over a period of 24 months. The KFRE was utilized to assess the risk of starting RRT at the two-year mark for each patient, 12 months before the start of CKD consultations and 12 months after the initiation of follow-up. In addition to this, other demographic and analytical variables were examined. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 28.0 and Jamovi version 2.3.28.
Results
We analyzed 160 patients, and their demographic and analytical characteristics are presented in Table 1. When comparing the medians between the two groups based on the KFRE equation, we found that patients who initiated ACKD consultation and started dapagliflozin had a 10.9% reduced risk of requiring RRT within 12 months, compared to those who did not start dapagliflozin, who had a 6.8% risk (P = 0.032). Furthermore, although both groups showed an upward trend in means, the rate of increase was lower in the patients who initiated iSGLT-2 treatment.
Conclusion
The addition of Dapagliflozin for patients with stage G4 chronic kidney disease who begin advanced chronic kidney disease consultations may be linked to a lower risk of starting RRT. These findings suggest that Dapagliflozin therapy could have a beneficial effect on the progression of chronic kidney disease. However, further studies are necessary to confirm these results and to assess the impact of SGLT2 inhibitors on the Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE).

title: #2196 Trajectories of serum total carbon dioxide and the risk of cardio-renal outcomes in chronic kidney disease: results from the KNOW-CKD study
authors: Ji Yong Jung; Yun Jung Oh; Kook-Hwan Oh; Wookyung Chung
abstract:
Background and Aims
Serum bicarbonate levels fluctuate over time in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), which may indicate a higher risk for adverse clinical outcomes. However, most studies struggle to analyze the association between baseline levels and outcomes, even with repeated measurements during the observation period.
Method
This study aimed to perform a time-updated longitudinal analysis to evaluate the association between serum total carbon dioxide (TCO2) levels and long-term clinical outcomes. A total of 1,809 patients from the Korean Cohort Study for Outcome in Patients With Chronic Kidney Disease (KNOW-CKD) were included in the analysis. The median duration of follow-up was 7.9 years. Group-based trajectory modeling (GBTM) was used to classify patients based on their TCO2 levels over time, and Cox regression models were employed to examine the relationship between the trajectory groups and clinical outcomes.
Results
GBTM identified six distinct TCO2 trajectories, which were subsequently consolidated into three trajectories based on clinical pattern similarities (high, n = 559; intermediate, n = 781; low, n = 469). After adjusting for confounders, patients in the low TCO2 trajectory group had a significantly higher risk of renal outcomes (HR 1.606; 95% CI 1.228–2.101; P < 0.001), while those in the high TCO2 trajectory group showed a reduced risk (HR 0.453; 95% CI 0.305–0.672; P < 0.001). The intermediate TCO2 trajectory group was not associated with renal outcomes, and no significant association was observed between TCO2 trajectories and cardiovascular events.
Conclusion
This study demonstrated that patients in the low TCO2 trajectory group experienced worse renal outcomes, whereas those in the high TCO2 trajectory group showed improvements in renal outcomes alone, supporting the potential clinical utility of bicarbonate supplementation in patients with CKD.

title: #2261 2-y crovalimab paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) data for fatigue, a relevant symptom in atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (aHUS) and PNH
authors: Hannah Staunton; Jennifer Stefani; Patty Leon
abstract:
Background and Aims
aHUS is a rare, life-threatening, complement-mediated disease characterised by thrombotic microangiopathies. Established C5 inhibitors (C5is), such as eculizumab and ravulizumab, are effective for aHUS management but can be burdensome, typically requiring regular intravenous infusions every 2 weeks (eculizumab) or every 8 weeks (ravulizumab). Crovalimab is a novel C5i with low-volume, subcutaneous dosing every 4 weeks, with the possibility for self-administration. Crovalimab is currently being evaluated in two ongoing global, Phase III, single-arm trials in aHUS: COMMUTE-a (NCT04861259) and COMMUTE-p (NCT04958265). Crovalimab has also been evaluated in patients (pts) with PNH, another complement-mediated rare blood disorder, in the global, randomised, Phase III COMMODORE 2 (NCT04434092) and COMMODORE 1 (NCT04432584) trials (Röth AJH 2024; Scheinberg AJH 2024). Fatigue is a debilitating symptom that occurs in both aHUS and PNH. It is among the three most reported symptoms in aHUS (Greenbaum Kidney Int Rep 2020) and is the most common symptom in PNH (Cella J Patient Rep Outcomes 2023). Here, we report Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy (FACIT)-Fatigue (Smith PM R 2010) data, a widely used pt-reported outcome (PRO) measure in aHUS and PNH, with a median 2-y follow-up from COMMODORE 2 and 1.
Method
COMMODORE 2 enrolled C5i-naive pts and COMMODORE 1 enrolled C5i-experienced pts with PNH, respectively. Pts in COMMODORE 2 and 1 were randomised 2:1 and 1:1, respectively, to receive crovalimab (Arm A) or eculizumab (Arm B) during the primary treatment period (baseline to Week 25). After the primary treatment period, pts assigned to the crovalimab arm continued crovalimab (Arm A) and pts assigned to the eculizumab arm (Arm B) switched to crovalimab (Arm B switch) if continuing in the extension period (>Week 25). Fatigue was assessed at scheduled visits from baseline throughout the extension period to Week 97 using FACIT-Fatigue, a 13-item PRO instrument designed to assess fatigue-related symptoms and impacts on daily functioning, with a total score ranging from 0 to 52 (higher scores indicate less fatigue). A ≥5-point increase in FACIT-Fatigue score is considered a clinically meaningful improvement (Cella J Patient Rep Outcomes 2023), and the normative population mean score is 43.5–46.6 (Cella J Pain Symptom Manag 2002; Butt J Pain Symptom Manag 2010; Montan Value Health 2018). Mean FACIT-Fatigue scores are reported. The clinical cutoff date (CCOD) was 12 March 2024.
Results
In COMMODORE 2, 129 of the 135 pts randomised to crovalimab in Arm A continued crovalimab, and 68 of the 69 pts randomised to eculizumab in Arm B switched to crovalimab (Arm B switch), in the extension period. At the CCOD, 116 pts in Arm A and 59 pts in Arm B switch were receiving ongoing crovalimab treatment. At Week 25, Arm A pts had achieved fatigue levels similar to healthy people without PNH. Mean absolute FACIT-Fatigue scores were maintained from >Week 25 to Week 97 and ranged from 41.9–44.3 in Arm A and 40.3–42.2 in Arm B switch (Fig. 1). In COMMODORE 1, all 44 pts randomised to crovalimab in Arm A continued crovalimab and 40 of the 42 pts randomised to eculizumab in Arm B switched to crovalimab (Arm B switch), in the extension period. At the CCOD, 42 pts in Arm A and 32 pts in Arm B switch were receiving ongoing crovalimab treatment. Mean absolute FACIT-Fatigue scores remained stable from >Week 25 to Week 97 and ranged from 40.8–42.9 in Arm A and 38.2–40.8 in Arm B switch (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
In COMMODORE 2, the improvements in pt-reported fatigue levels observed with crovalimab in the primary treatment period were maintained over a 2-y median follow-up. Accordingly, in COMMODORE 1, fatigue levels remained stable over this same time frame. Overall, these results indicate the long-term benefit that can be achieved with crovalimab. The COMMUTE-a and COMMUTE-p trials evaluating crovalimab in aHUS are ongoing, including assessment of fatigue using the FACIT-Fatigue PRO measure, given its importance in this population.

title: #3044 Cognitive functions in elderly and senile patients with arterial hypertension, depending on the presence of concomitant chronic kidney disease stage 3A and 3B
authors: Olga Ostroumova; Kantemir Dzamikhov; Aleksey Kochetkov; Svetlana Litvinova; Tatyana Ostroumova; Elizaveta Ebzeeva
abstract:
Background
the frequent comorbidity of arterial hypertension (AH) and chronic kidney disease (CKD), each of which is a risk factor for cognitive impairment, determines the need to diagnose cognitive deficits in these multimorbid patients.
Aims
to assess the impact of concomitant CKD on cognitive functions (CF) in elderly and senile patients with AH.
Materials and methods
330 patients ≥60 years old with АH were included and divided into 2 groups: (1)—without CKD (n = 110, mean age 76 [69.8; 82.3] years, 45.5% women), (2) —patients with CKD G3a/G3b (n = 220, mean age 81 [73;85] years, 53.6% women). All the patients underwent cognitive assessment including the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), Mini-Mental Status Examination (MMSЕ), Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale–Cognitive Subscale (ADAS-cog), Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST), Verbal fluency test.
Results
patients with CKD G3a/G3b, compared to patients without CKD, had significantly lower MoCA (23 [21; 25] versus 24 [22; 26] points, respectively, P = 0.005) and MMSE (27 [25; 29] versus 28 [25.8; 29] points, respectively, P = 0.002) scores and significantly higher ADAS-cog score (14 [11; 18] versus 11 [9; 15] points, P < 0.001), worse letter fluency (11 [10; 13] versus 12 [11; 13] words, respectively, P < 0.001), and worse DSST score (20 [17; 23] versus 21.5 [19; 25], respectively, P < 0.001). Patients with CKD G3b compared G3a and without CKD had worse MoCА, MMSE, and ADAS-cog results. In the single-factor logistic regression analysis, there was significant association between decreased MMSE scores (≤23 points) and stage G3a and G3b CKD: (odds ratio [OR] 3.25, P = 0.048; and OR 5.53, P = 0.003, respectively). There was also an association between decreased MoCA scores (≤25 points) and CKD G3a and G3b: OR 1.97, P = 0.040 and OR 2.24, P = 0.016, respectively.
Conclusion
our results indicate an unfavorable effect of concomitant CKD stage G3a/G3b on the CF of elderly and senile patients with AH and a worsening of CF as the severity of CKD increases.

title: #1583 Urinary exosome miRNAs as biomarkers associated with proteinuria and eGFR in lupus nephritis
authors: Denis Delic; Helmut Schumacher; Martina Uzzo; Patrick Baum; David R W Jayne; Ingeborg Bajema; Jürgen Steffgen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Lupus nephritis (LN) is a life-threatening disorder characterized by a relapsing-remitting disease course necessitating immunosuppression to control disease activity. Urinary exosome microRNAs (miRNAs) were previously tested as biomarkers for fibrosis and inflammatory pathways in different kidney diseases, including LN.
Method
Small RNA sequencing was conducted on urinary exosome miRNAs in 93 patients with ISN/RPS class III/IV ± V LN from a trial with the anti-CD40 mAB BI655064*. Univariable and multivariable regression models were used to identify associations between miRNAs and spot urine protein/urine creatinine ratio (UP/UC, log-transformed), and eGFR, at time of randomization into the study.
Results
MiRNAs with high correlation (P < 0.01) in the univariable analysis are listed in Table 1 for UP/UC and in Table 2 for eGFR.
A multivariable model selection procedure, taking also into account the correlation between individual miRNAs, revealed an association between miR-143-3p, miR-510-5p, miR-429, miR-509-5p, miR-10b-5p, miR-9-3p, miR-509-3p, miR-411-5p, miR-574-5p, and miR-3182 and UP/UC (model R2 = 0.613). Likewise, miR-17-5p, miR-101-3p, miR-146b-5p, miR-3173-3p, miR-545-3p, miR-6790-3p were associated with eGFR (model R2 = 0.453). title: #1973 The effect of endogenous serotonin on vitamin K metabolism and vitamin K-dependent bone mineralization in an experimental model of chronic kidney disease in rats
authors: Krystyna Pawlak; Magdalena Kopanko; Beata Sieklucka; Magdalena Zabludowska; Katarzyna Sokolowska; Dariusz Pawlak
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is associated with the development of mineral bone disorder (CKD-MBD), leading to abnormalities in bone metabolism and impaired bone mineralization. In the regulation of the mineralization process in CKD, many factors play a key role, such as parathormone (PTH), vitamin D, and vitamin K (VK), which can occur in two forms - K1 (phylloquinone) and K2 (menaquinones; MKs). Serotonin (5-HT), a neurotransmitter that regulates a wide range of physiological processes, plays also an important role in the regulation of bone mass and metabolism. The present study aimed to determine whether endogenous 5-HT can affect VK metabolism and whether the above effect will translate into the bone mineralization process in rats with CKD.
Method
Seventy-one male, 4-week-old Wistar rats were randomly divided into two groups: 5/6 nephrectomy (CKD, n = 61) and controls (n = 10). Three months later, the CKD group was randomized into 4 subgroups (n =14–16 in each): untreated (CKD); administered with vehicle (VEH); treated with a small-molecule inhibitor of tryptophan hydroxylase-1 - LP533401 at a dose of 30 mg/kg (LP 30), and 100 mg/kg (LP 100). After 8 weeks of experiment, the animals were sacrificed, and blood samples and tibial bones were collected. The components of the serotonergic system were determined by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), whereas VK1, MK4, and MK7 concentrations were measured by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry/mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) method in the Laboratory of Perlan Technologies, Polska. The mineral status of the tibia was determined by densitometry. The expression of key genes involved in the VK cycle was performed by RT-PCR.
Results
The treatment with LP533401 significantly reduced 5-HT turnover. The most visible effect was observed in the LP100 group, where serum 5-HT levels were decreased compared to other CKD groups (all P < 0.05). The expression of enzymes of VK cycle: UbiA prenyltransferase containing 1 (UBIAD1), γ-glutamyl carboxylase (GGCX), and vitamin K epoxide reductase complex subunit 1 (VKORC1) in bone tissue was increased in CKD and particularly in VEH group compared to other groups. As a result, in all groups with CKD, the accelerated conversion of VK1 to the form of menaquinones has been observed. However, in the CKD and VEH groups, VK1 was mainly metabolized towards MK4. In the LP 30 group, the highest concentrations of both MK4 and MK7 were observed, whereas in the LP 100 group, VK1 metabolism towards MK7 predominated. There was no direct relationship between serum 5-HT levels and VK metabolism in animals treated with LP533401; however, the inverse association existed between the advantage of 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25OHD) over 5-HT, reflected by the 25OHD/5-HT ratio and MK4 (r = −0.372, P = 0.043) and MK7 levels (r = −0.481, P = 0.007). In contrast to this, the PTH/5-HT ratio positively correlated with MK7 (r = 0.429, P = 0.018). Rats with CKD had significantly decreased densitometric parameters of tibia: bone mineral content (BMC) and bone mineral density (BMD) compared with controls. The treatment with LP533401 improved these parameters; the strongest effect was observed in the LP30 group. The positive association was between MK7 and BMC, BMD values in animals treated with LP533401. VEH administration also partially normalized BMC and BMD, but in this group, there was no correlation between VK7 levels and densitometric parameters.
Conclusion
The results of the present study showed that rats with CKD have the accelerated conversion of VK1 to the form of menaquinones. LP533401 treatment resulted in a shift of VK1 to MK7 metabolism, which was particularly evident in the LP100 group. The intensified MK7 production was associated with the improvement in BMC and BMD values in CKD rats treated with LP533401. Although serum 5-HT was not directly related to VK metabolism, changes in the interrelationships between calciotropic hormones and 5-HT, resulting from LP533401 administration, appear to have a significant effect on VK metabolism.

title: #2195 Persistent higher trajectories of waist-to-hip ratio are associated with greater risk of cardio-renal outcomes: results from the KNOW-CKD study
authors: Yun Jung Oh; Kook-Hwan Oh; Wookyung Chung; Ji Yong Jung
abstract:
Background and Aims
The obesity paradox, where high body mass index (BMI) is associated with better survival has been observed in chronic kidney disease (CKD), while waist-to-hip ratio (WHR) representing central obesity has been found to be directly associated with cardiovascular risk in these patients. However, the impact of long-term WHR changes on cardiovascular and renal outcomes in patient with CKD has been rarely studied.
Method
We investigated the longitudinal association between WHR trajectories and risk of cardiovascular event and renal outcome. A total of 2,076 patients from the Korean Cohort Study for Outcome in Patients With Chronic Kidney Disease (KNOW-CKD) were included in the analysis. Group-based trajectory modeling (GBTM) was used to identify the distinct trajectory groups for repeated measurements of WHR over time. The relationship between the WHR trajectory groups and clinical outcomes was investigated using Cox regression models.
Results
Five distinct WHR trajectories were identified: group 1 (n = 274, 13.2%), group 2 (n = 546, 26.3%), group 3 (n = 269, 13.0%), group 4 (n = 503, 24.2%), and group 5 (n = 485, 23.4%), from group 1 to group 5, the WHR gradually increase. Crude hazard ratio (HR) of cardiovascular outcome was significantly increased in trajectory group 2–5 compared with those in trajectory group 1. After adjustment for potential confounders, there was still significant increased cardiovascular risk in the highest trajectory group 5 compared with those in the lowest trajectory group 1 (HR, 2.248; 95% CI, 1.060–4.766). Crude HR of renal outcome was also significantly increased in trajectory group 2–5 compared with those in trajectory group 1. Adjusted HR of renal outcome was significantly increased the highest trajectory group 5 compared with those in the lowest trajectory group 1 (HR, 1,390; 95% CI, 1.050–1.842).
Conclusion
The majority of patients with CKD remained their degree of WHR level showing stable and slightly upward or downward WHR trajectory over the long time. This study found that higher WHR trajectory was associated with greater risk of cardiovascular and renal outcomes in patients with CKD. Our findings highlight the prognostic significance of central obesity on clinical outcomes in those patients.

title: #2272 HNF4a drives metabolic reprogramming in podocytes through ChREBP/SREBP-mediated pathway and promotes cell cycle progression
authors: Hyun Ji Lim; Youngyoon Moon; Yoosun Joo; Hana Choi; Tae Hoon Lee; Su Woong Jung; Sang Ho Lee; Ju-Young Moon
abstract:
Background and Aims
Metabolic adaptation of podocytes plays an important role in diabetic kidney disease (DKD) progression. Recent studies have highlighted the importance of metabolic regulation in maintaining podocyte function under diabetic stress conditions. While hepatocyte nuclear factor 4 alpha (HNF4α) expression is elevated in diabetic podocytes and is known to regulate cellular metabolism in other tissues, its specific role and downstream metabolic effects in podocyte metabolism remain unclear. Understanding this mechanism is important, as podocytes require precise metabolic control to maintain their specialized functions.
Method
To investigate the metabolic regulatory role of HNF4α, we generated stable HNF4α-overexpressing mouse podocytes using lentiviral vectors. Metabolic changes were evaluated by measuring oxygen consumption rate (OCR), while the underlying mechanisms were assessed through Western blot analysis of metabolic enzymes and transcription factors. To determine the effect on cell growth, we performed cell cycle analysis using flow cytometry and proliferation assays.
Results
We found increased HNF4α expression in podocytes from db/db mice and DKD patients. To investigate the functional implications of this increased expression, we established HNF4α-overexpressing mouse podocytes. Western blot analysis showed upregulation of metabolic transcription factors, particularly ChREBP and SREBP, compared to control cells, along with increased protein levels of glycolytic enzymes, including PKM and HK2. Seahorse analysis demonstrated enhanced mitochondrial function in these cells, with increased basal OCR and maximal respiratory capacity compared to controls. Flow cytometry analysis revealed enhanced cell cycle progression in HNF4α-overexpressing podocytes, as evidenced by increased S phase population.
Conclusion
Our findings suggest that HNF4α influences podocyte metabolic pathways, potentially involving ChREBP/SREBP signaling, and affects cell cycle progression. These results provide insights into the role of HNF4α in podocyte metabolism, which may contribute to our understanding of podocyte regulation in DKD.

title: #373 Explaining the gap between guidelines and practice in myocardial infarction care for people with chronic kidney disease
authors: Jemima Scott; Lucy E Selman; Matthew Graham-Brown; Fergus Caskey; Tom Johnson; Yoav Ben-Shlomo; Pippa Bailey
abstract:
Background and Aims
The gap between guidelines and practice regarding care for myocardial infarction is greater amongst individuals with chronic kidney disease than those without. Identifying why variation exists enables determination of its clinical significance and facilitates the development of effective interventions to reduce disparities in care, where appropriate. The aim of this study was to understand the process of treatment decision-making for myocardial infarction amongst patients with kidney disease and their clinicians.
Method
Semi-structured qualitative interviews were conducted with patients and clinicians from four National Health Service hospital centers in the United Kingdom from February 2022 to July 2024. All centers offered cardiology and acute medical services; some offered nephrology in addition. Participants were purposively sampled, aiming for diversity in gender, ethnicity, specialty (clinicians only) and/or use of kidney replacement therapy (patient participants). Clinicians were senior doctors-in-training or consultants in cardiology, nephrology, acute or emergency care or cardiac surgery. Patient participants had chronic kidney disease, defined as an estimated glomerular filtration rate of less than 60 ml/min/1.73 m2, or receipt of kidney replacement therapy, in addition to a recent hospital admission for myocardial infarction. Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis was used to analyze interview data and generate themes associated with myocardial infarction treatment decision-making for, and by, patients with chronic kidney disease.
Results
Participants included 32 clinicians (12 cardiologists, 9 nephrologists, 8 acute and emergency clinicians and 3 cardiac surgeons) and 14 patients with chronic kidney disease. Seven main themes were identified:(1) Limited patient involvement in treatment decisions, (2) Inter-clinician communication supports high-risk decision-making, (3) Variation in use of written guides to decision-making, (4) The safety net of associated health services support intervention, (5) The value assigned to experience over evidence, (6) Individual perception of risk and benefit, (7) Harm from action perceived as worse than inaction. Despite holding strong health preferences, patients had minimal involvement in inpatient treatment decisions regarding myocardial infarction. Clinicians’ decision-making was driven by the fear of causing harm by active intervention. Fear and self-blame for negative outcomes were some of the most influential factors biasing clinicians towards making conservative treatment decisions for patients with chronic kidney disease (Figs 1 and 2a). This was despite evidence and guidelines recommending more aggressive treatment. Collaborative decision-making between trusted colleagues and the existence of a clinical safety-net for managing treatment complications were however reported by clinicians to counter this bias and enable them to make what they perceived to be appropriately aggressive treatment decisions (Fig. 2b).
Conclusion
Interventions to foster teamworking between specialists and ensure adequately resourced clinical service safety-nets may improve access to perceived “higher-risk” treatments for myocardial infarction amongst people with chronic kidney disease. Intervention development and evaluation should follow to determine if quality of care and outcomes for people with chronic kidney disease and myocardial infarction can be improved by these means.

title: #704 Protective effects of TRIM33 via inflammasome suppression on ischemia-reperfusion injury-induced kidney fibrosis in mice
authors: Hyejin Jeon; Jin Hyun Kim; Sehyun Jung; Seunghye Lee; Hani Jang; Se-Ho Chang; Hyun-Jung Kim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) is a major contributor to acute kidney injury (AKI), making the development of effective therapeutic interventions imperative. AKI is also a significant risk factor for chronic kidney disease (CKD). Tripartite motif-containing 33 (TRIM33), a member of the TRIM family with E3 ubiquitin protein ligase activity, is involved in various biological pathways, including the transforming growth factor (TGF)-β signaling pathway and the Wnt/β-catenin pathway. However, its role in IRI-induced kidney injury remains unclear.
Method
Mice were divided into three groups: a sham group, an IRI-only group, and a TRIM33-treated IRI group. The TRIM33 plasmid was administered once after reperfusion and then once a week for a total of four doses. All mice were sacrificed 21 days after IRI, and renal tissue, serum, and urine samples were collected. Histological evaluations and biochemical analyses were performed to assess renal injury.
Results
TRIM33 plasmid administration significantly attenuated renal dysfunction, as indicated by improvements in the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and reduced tissue injury. Inflammatory cell infiltration, including macrophages and Th17 cells, was also significantly reduced in TRIM33-treated mice, as reflected by decreased mRNA levels of CX3CR1, CX3CL1, ROR-γt, and IL-17RA. Furthermore, TRIM33 treatment significantly downregulated inflammasome-related factors, including NLRP3, cleaved caspase-1, IL-1β, and IL-18. Finally, TRIM33-treated IRI mice exhibited only moderate injury, minimal fibrosis, and substantial reductions in the expression of epithelial-mesenchymal transition-related genes, including α-SMA, pSmad2/3, Twist, and Snail.
Conclusion
This is the first study to demonstrate that TRIM33 protects against IRI-induced CKD in a mouse model by inhibiting the NLRP3 inflammasome and preventing kidney fibrosis. These findings suggest that TRIM33 could be a potential therapeutic option for CKD associated with IRI.

title: #3617 Valuing overhydration in stable, non-dialysis stage 4 and 5 kidney disease patients
authors: Ana Cristina Rodenas Galvez; Isabel Galan Carrillo; Maria Aurora García Alcaraz; Sergio Aleman Belando; Miguel Martin Cascón; Carmen Lourdes Zarate Riscal; Javier Meseguer Guerrero; Cristina Jimeno Griño; Serena Gatius; Alberto Andreu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Subclinical overhydration has been linked to renal and overall survival in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. It is a diagnostic challenge in stable stage 4 and 5 CKD patients who are not on dialysis. BIS (bioimpedance spectroscopy) is a worldwide tool for evaluating overhydration in hemodialysis patients. VEXUS (Venous Excess Ultrasound Grading System) and LUS (Lung ultrasonography) are new and revolutionary tools for measuring overhydration in heart failure (HF) and dialysis patients. Jugular vein diameter ratio (JVD ratio) is used to assess the risk of HF. Aim: To test these tools in CKD stage 4–5 stable patients.
Method
We examined stable outpatients with stage 4 and 5 non-dialysis CKD, with clinical exam and lab tests. Then we measured VEXUS, BIS, LUS, and JVD ratio (Valsalva/basal diameters). We conducted a descriptive cross-sectional study. It is the start of a long-term survival study.
Results
61 patients. 36 males (59%), mean eGFR 17 ± 5 ml/min, hypertension (95.1%), diabetes (57.4%). More frequent CKD causes were renal diabetic disease (31.1%) and nephroangiosclerosis (29%). 47 (77%) had no diagnosis of HF, 7 preserved HF, and 7 reduced HF. No one had HF in the last 3 months.
Measured by BIS, median OH/ECW was 6.6 ± 7.9. Patients with OH/ECW > 10% were 17 (27.9%). They had higher NT-ProBNP levels (P = 0.030), and no differences in eGFR or Ca125. This group's membership had no link to hypertension, DM, HF history, or ischemic heart disease. It was correlated with having VEXUS > stage 1, but wasn't with LUS.
46 patients (75.4%) had no overhydration by VEXUS (VEXUS 0), 3 patients (4.9%) had overload fluid VEXUS stage 1, 2 patients (3.3%) VEXUS-2, and 10 patients (16.4%) VEXUS-3. VEXUS-3 patients had higher OH/ECW by BIS (5.4 ± 7.0 vs 15.9 ± 9.2, P < 0.001), and higher NT-proBNP levels (5308,401199,95 pg/ml vs 671,6791,61 pg/ml, P = 0.02). Among clinical tests, only edema and orthopnea showed differences between these groups (P < 0.001). Others did not (dyspnea, crackles, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea). There were no differences on hypertension or DM, but they had more history of HF (P = 0.028).
12 patients (19.7%) had pathological LUS. These results were not related to pathological clinical examination, higher nt-proBNP or Ca125, nor overhydration by BIS or VEXUS.
We divided the JVD ratio into tertiles. There were no differences in BIS, VEXUS or Ca125 levels. NT-ProBNP was higher in the lower tertile (603 ± 622 pg/ml vs 2129 ± 3110 pg/ml, P = 0.022). Being in this tertile was also significantly correlated with dyspnea (P = 0.029) and edema (P = 0.008).
Conclusion
Measuring overhydration in stable CKD 4-5 patients is challenging. Nt-proBNP could help but, in our experience, measuring ca125 levels or the history of heart disease don't give any clue. Thus, ultrasound and BIS may be useful to assess fluid overload in patients with no clinical alarms (subclinical overhydration). We need studies with long-term follow-up to help us find which parameters link best to events and when to test them. That's why our group is conducting this long-term study to try to figure it out.
