Background and Aims
Subclinical overhydration has been linked to renal and overall survival in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. It is a diagnostic challenge in stable stage 4 and 5 CKD patients who are not on dialysis. BIS (bioimpedance spectroscopy) is a worldwide tool for evaluating overhydration in hemodialysis patients. VEXUS (Venous Excess Ultrasound Grading System) and LUS (Lung ultrasonography) are new and revolutionary tools for measuring overhydration in heart failure (HF) and dialysis patients. Jugular vein diameter ratio (JVD ratio) is used to assess the risk of HF. Aim: To test these tools in CKD stage 4–5 stable patients.
Method
We examined stable outpatients with stage 4 and 5 non-dialysis CKD, with clinical exam and lab tests. Then we measured VEXUS, BIS, LUS, and JVD ratio (Valsalva/basal diameters). We conducted a descriptive cross-sectional study. It is the start of a long-term survival study.
Results
61 patients. 36 males (59%), mean eGFR 17 ± 5 ml/min, hypertension (95.1%), diabetes (57.4%). More frequent CKD causes were renal diabetic disease (31.1%) and nephroangiosclerosis (29%). 47 (77%) had no diagnosis of HF, 7 preserved HF, and 7 reduced HF. No one had HF in the last 3 months.
Measured by BIS, median OH/ECW was 6.6 ± 7.9. Patients with OH/ECW > 10% were 17 (27.9%). They had higher NT-ProBNP levels (P = 0.030), and no differences in eGFR or Ca125. This group's membership had no link to hypertension, DM, HF history, or ischemic heart disease. It was correlated with having VEXUS > stage 1, but wasn't with LUS.
46 patients (75.4%) had no overhydration by VEXUS (VEXUS 0), 3 patients (4.9%) had overload fluid VEXUS stage 1, 2 patients (3.3%) VEXUS-2, and 10 patients (16.4%) VEXUS-3. VEXUS-3 patients had higher OH/ECW by BIS (5.4 ± 7.0 vs 15.9 ± 9.2, P < 0.001), and higher NT-proBNP levels (5308,401199,95 pg/ml vs 671,6791,61 pg/ml, P = 0.02). Among clinical tests, only edema and orthopnea showed differences between these groups (P < 0.001). Others did not (dyspnea, crackles, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea). There were no differences on hypertension or DM, but they had more history of HF (P = 0.028).
12 patients (19.7%) had pathological LUS. These results were not related to pathological clinical examination, higher nt-proBNP or Ca125, nor overhydration by BIS or VEXUS.
We divided the JVD ratio into tertiles. There were no differences in BIS, VEXUS or Ca125 levels. NT-ProBNP was higher in the lower tertile (603 ± 622 pg/ml vs 2129 ± 3110 pg/ml, P = 0.022). Being in this tertile was also significantly correlated with dyspnea (P = 0.029) and edema (P = 0.008).
Conclusion
Measuring overhydration in stable CKD 4-5 patients is challenging. Nt-proBNP could help but, in our experience, measuring ca125 levels or the history of heart disease don't give any clue. Thus, ultrasound and BIS may be useful to assess fluid overload in patients with no clinical alarms (subclinical overhydration). We need studies with long-term follow-up to help us find which parameters link best to events and when to test them. That's why our group is conducting this long-term study to try to figure it out.

title: #134 The evolution of consultation practices with general practitioners and nephrologists for patients with CKD before and after the COVID-19 pandemic in France
authors: Juliette Piveteau; Sahar Bayat; Cécile Vigneau; Cécile Couchoud; Latame Komla Adoli; Hoang Giang Pham; Maxime Raffray
abstract:
Background and Aims
The COVID-19 pandemic led to concerns about disruptions in the care of chronic diseases, including chronic kidney disease (CKD). The aim of this study was to assess the immediate and short-term consequence of the COVID-19 pandemic on consultation practices for patients with CKD who did not have kidney replacement therapy in France.
Method
We used the French National Health Data System (SNDS) that contains healthcare data of the whole French population. A validated algorithm was applied within the SNDS to identify two cohorts of patients: i) a 2019 cohort including individuals exposed to the COVID-19 pandemic and ii) a 2017 cohort including individuals unexposed to the pandemic. We followed these cohorts for 2 years and divided the follow-up in eight periods according to the lockdown periods in France during the pandemic. The percentage of patients who had at least one GP and nephrologist consultations in each period was compared between cohorts. For each period, the sum of person-time alive was calculated and used as denominator in order to neutralize the effect of death.
Results
We identified 4,866,096 and 5,089,706 individuals with CKD in 2017 and 2019, respectively. The characteristics of individuals were similar (mean age = 62 years in the 2017 cohort and 63 years in the 2019 cohort). In the 2019 cohort, 94 % had at least one consultation (in-person or teleconsultation) with a GP and 6.3 % had at least one consultation with a nephrologist during the first year of follow-up (vs 95.2% and 6.4% in the 2017 cohort). Teleconsultations did compensate a deficit of in-person GP and nephrologist consultations throughout the acute periods of the pandemic in 2020 and 2021 (40.5% of patients in the 2019 cohort had at least one GP consultation in-person and 52.5% an in-person or tele-consultation during the period of the first lockdown). The analyses stratified by age and sex did not show differences in GP or nephrologist consultation rates between cohorts.
Conclusion
In France, outpatient healthcare use remained stable for individuals with CKD during the 2 years following the COVID-19 pandemic, with minimal changes in consultation rates with GPs and nephrologists. Indeed, thanks to teleconsultations, the yearly proportion of patients with at least one consultation with a GP or nephrologist did not change much between cohorts.

title: #2290 ALOX5 regulates renal fibrosis through modulation of matrix remodeling and inflammatory responses
authors: Youngyoon Moon; Hyun Ji Lim; Yoosun Joo; Hana Choi; Tae Hoon Lee; Su Woong Jung; Sang-Ho Lee; Ju-Young Moon
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal fibrosis, a common pathological feature of Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD), exhibits excessive extracellular matrix accumulation and inflammatory cell infiltration. 5-lipoxygenase (ALOX5), a key enzyme in leukotriene B4 (LTB4) biosynthesis, plays crucial roles in inflammatory cell recruitment and inflammatory responses. While ALOX5-mediated LTB4 production is known to regulate inflammatory cascade activation and immune cell recruitment, its specific contribution to collagen deposition and matrix remodeling in renal fibrosis remains unclear.
Method
We investigated the role of ALOX5 in renal fibrosis using TGFβ-stimulated HKC8 cells (human proximal tubular cell line) with pharmacological ALOX5 inhibition. We analyzed the expression of fibrotic markers and pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α) using Western blot and qPCR. We further examined matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) expression and collagen turnover through molecular and biochemical analyses. To evaluate immune cell recruitment, we established co-culture systems with immune cells.
Results
ALOX5 inhibition effectively suppressed TGFβ-induced increases in alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) and kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1) expression in HKC8 cells. Notably, ALOX5 pathway modulation significantly affected collagen composition and turnover, as evidenced by normalization of the TGFβ-induced elevation in collagen I to III ratio. Mechanistically, ALOX5 inhibition restored the TGFβ-suppressed expression of key collagenases (MMP1, MMP3, and MMP8) and their enzymatic activities, thereby maintaining appropriate collagen turnover. Furthermore, ALOX5 pathway blockade reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α levels and decreased immune cell infiltration in co-culture experiments, demonstrating its regulatory role in both matrix remodeling and inflammatory responses.
Conclusion
Our findings reveal that ALOX5 serves as a critical mediator in renal fibrosis by regulating both collagen deposition and inflammatory responses. ALOX5 pathway modulation affects multiple aspects of fibrotic progression: regulation of collagen turnover, inflammatory cytokine production, and immune cell recruitment. These results establish ALOX5 as a potential therapeutic target in renal fibrosis, particularly through its novel role in matrix remodeling.

title: #3850 Central obesity: a key concern in chronic kidney disease patients
authors: Aljoša Kuzmanovski; Bojan Knap; Jelka Lindič
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is associated with various nutritional disorders, including both malnutrition and obesity, which have a detrimental effect on patient health, disease progression, and outcomes. Central obesity, in particular, is known to be harmful to health, contributing to increased risk of cardiovascular disease and other comorbidities. This study aimed to assess the prevalence of malnutrition and obesity in outpatient CKD patients, specifically examining the proportion of patients with central obesity. Additionally, we evaluated their nutritional status, dietary habits, and physical performance.
Method
The study included CKD stage 1–5 patients monitored at the nephrology outpatient clinic of the University Clinical Centre Ljubljana, Slovenia. Participants completed a food frequency questionnaire and provided information on physical activity, body weight, height, and waist circumference. Obesity was defined as a body mass index (BMI) > 29.9 kg/m², while central obesity was defined as an increased waist circumference (> 80 cm in women and > 94 cm in men). Body composition was measured using a 4-frequency bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), and muscle strength was assessed using handgrip strength. Malnutrition was determined according to the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition (GLIM) criteria.
Results
A total of 199 CKD patients (stages 1–2: 95 patients; stages 3–5: 104 patients) participated, of whom 50.8% (n = 101) were male, and 41.2% (n = 82) were older than 64 years. Normal body weight and waist circumference were observed in 16.1% of patients (n = 32). Obesity based on BMI was found in 26% (n = 53) of patients, while 80.3% (n = 159) had an increased waist circumference. All obese patients also had an increased waist circumference. BIA revealed an elevated fat mass in 58.3% (n = 116) of patients, 96.6% (n = 112) of whom also had an increased waist circumference (P = 0.001), and 92.5% were classified as obese by BMI (P = 0.001). Based on GLIM criteria, 22 patients (11 %) were classified as moderately malnourished. Sarcopenia was diagnosed in 2 patients (1.0%) (CKD stages 3 and 4), with 1 patient (0.5%) (CKD stage 4) having sarcopenic obesity. Reduced muscle mass (myopenia) was present in 10.6% (n = 21) of patients, more frequently in women (15.3%) than in men (5.9%) (P = 0.06). Simultaneous myopenia and elevated fat mass were identified in 6% (n = 12) of patients. No significant differences were observed in dietary habits between obese patients with central obesity (26%, n = 52) and those with normal body weight and waist circumference (16%, n = 32). Both groups reported similar and excessive intake of sugar, sweets, and refined flour products, alongside insufficient consumption of legumes and leafy green vegetables. The only notable difference was in physical activity: obese patients with central obesity were less likely to engage in ≥150 minutes of weekly physical activity than other patients (P = 0.003).
Conclusion
Central obesity is the most prevalent nutritional disorder in outpatient CKD stage 1–5 patients, affecting 80% of them. Malnutrition, as determined by the GLIM criteria, is present in a moderate proportion of patients, further highlighting the need for early intervention. Myopenia is present in one-tenth of patients, more frequently in women, while sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity are less common. Elevated fat mass, as measured by BIA, can be reliably identified using waist circumference rather than BMI, making waist circumference an essential part of clinical assessments. Most patients exhibit suboptimal dietary patterns; however, those who are more physically active tend to have better body composition. The scope of intervention required to address the identified nutritional disorders, including malnutrition, is extensive. Early identification of nutritional issues calls for intensified multidisciplinary management by nephrology educators, clinical dietitians, and kinesiologists.

title: #793 Factors influencing rapid eGFR decline in outpatients: a retrospective cohort study
authors: Pattharawin Pattharanitima; Suthiya Anumas
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a significant contributor to high morbidity and mortality. However, the rate of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) decline varies among individuals. While numerous studies have identified risk factors for CKD progression, there is limited clinical data distinguishing rapid progressors from non-rapid progressors. Such information is essential for prioritizing individuals who may benefit from early targeted interventions to mitigate disease progression and associated risks. Therefore, our study aims to investigate the risk factors associated with rapid progression in CKD.
Method
We conducted a retrospective analysis of data from outpatients aged >18 years who were followed from 2018 to 2022. Laboratory data were obtained from electronic health records (EHR), and comorbidities were identified using ICD-10 codes. Rapid progressors were defined as individuals with an eGFR decline >5 mL/min/1.73 m²/year, in accordance with KDIGO guidelines. Logistic regression was used to analyze risk associations.
Results
Among 19,435 outpatients with a mean age of 61.2 years and median follow-up time of 3.4 (2.2–4.1) years, 3,260 patients (16.8%) were identified as rapid progressors. Median eGFR decline of rapid progressor and non-rapid progressor was −7.9 (−11.3 to −6.2) and −0.6 (−2.1 to 1.2) mL/min/1.73 m²/year, respectively. Multivariable analysis revealed that age >60 years (OR 0.79, P = 0.002), female sex (OR 0.82, P = 0.005), BMI ≥25 Kg/m2 (OR 0.85, P = 0.04), and statin use (OR 0.82, P = 0.008) were associated with a reduced risk of being a rapid progressor. Conversely, low BMI (OR 1.65, P = 0.002), systolic blood pressure (SBP) >120 mmHg (OR 1.19, P = 0.045), LDL cholesterol >100 mg/dL (OR 1.23, P = 0.006), triglyceride >150 mg/dL (OR 1.21, P = 0.01), serum albumin <3.5 g/dL (OR 1.45, P < 0.001), hemoglobin <10 g/dL (OR 1.34, P = 0.02), diabetes mellitus (OR 1.81, P < 0.001), and diuretic use (OR 2.09, p <0.001) were associated with an increased risk of rapid progression.
Conclusion
The risk factors for rapid progression include younger age, male sex, diabetes mellitus, low BMI, uncontrolled SBP, high LDL cholesterol, high triglyceride, low serum albumin, low hemoglobin, and the use of diuretics or non-statin medications. Patients with these risk factors require closer follow-up and more intensive treatment to slow the progressive decline in eGFR and prolong the dialysis-free period.

title: #1662 Asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA) and citrulline are risk factors for cardiovascular disease independently of both estimated and measured GFR
authors: Nikoline Balteskard Rinde; Toralf Melsom; Ole-Martin Fuskevag; Bjørn Eriksen; Jon Viljar Norvik
abstract:
Background and Aims
Nitric oxide (NO) plays a crucial role in endothelial dysfunction, and deficiency has been linked to cardiovascular disease (CVD) and impaired kidney function. While previous research has explored NO-metabolism in individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD), diabetes mellitus (DM), or CVD, the relationship in healthy individuals remains unclear. These studies have used estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) to adjust for kidney function. This may have resulted in non-GFR-related factors confounding the association between NO-metabolism and CVD. We investigated the association between NO-related biomarkers and incident CVD in a healthy population, comparing adjustments using estimated GFR (eGFR) and measured GFR (mGFR).
Method
In a 14-year longitudinal study, we evaluated 1,564 middle-aged participants without preexisting DM, CVD, or kidney disease in the Renal Iohexol Clearance Survey (RENIS). Cox regression models assessed the effects of asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA), symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA), arginine, citrulline, and ornithine serum levels on the incidence of CVD and all-cause mortality. Analyses were adjusted for GFR utilizing mGFR by iohexol clearance, eGFR based on serum creatinine (eGFRCrea), or cystatin C (eGFRCys), and the results were compared.
Results
Elevated ADMA levels were associated with incident CVD across all GFR adjustment methods, with a hazard ratio (HR) of 1.21 (95% CI, 1.06–1.38) for mGFR. SDMA was associated with CVD only when adjusting for eGFRCrea (HR 1.19; 95% CI, 1.03–1.38), not with mGFR or eGFRCys. Higher citrulline levels were consistently associated with CVD independently of the GFR assessment method (HR, 1.17; 95% CI, 1.03–1.33 for mGFR). No biomarkers were associated with all-cause mortality.
Conclusion
In a population without preexisting kidney disease, DM, or CVD, ADMA and citrulline were associated with incident CVD, regardless of the GFR adjustment method. However, the association between SDMA and CVD depended on the GFR adjustment method.

title: #1771 The association of sodium-glucose transporter 2 inhibitor prescription and incident chronic kidney disease in a multi-ethnic Asian population: a retrospective cohort study using Singhealth Diabetes Registry
authors: Yi Lin Ong; Zhong Hong Liew; Gek Hsiang Lim; Jason Choo; Yong Mong Bee; Jia Liang Kwek
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sodium-glucose transporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) are well-established for slowing chronic kidney disease (CKD) progression. However, their role in preventing incident CKD in diabetic individuals without CKD remains unclear. This study evaluates the association of SGLT2i use with incident CKD in a multi-ethnic Asian population with type 2 diabetes (T2D).
Method
This retrospective cohort study analysed patients with T2D from 2016 to 2020 using the SingHealth Diabetes Registry. Inclusion criteria were baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) ≥60 ml/min/1.73 m2 and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR) <30 mg/g. The exclusion criteria included age <21 years, baseline eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2, uACR ≥ 30 mg/g, history of renal transplant or maintenance dialysis. The primary outcome was incident CKD, defined as sustained eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m² or uACR >30 mg/g with consecutive readings of >90 days apart. Secondary outcomes included eGFR change over time. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed on SGLT2i users and non-users, matched on age, gender, housing type, body mass index, HbA1c, baseline eGFR, renin-angiotensin-system inhibitors (RASi), metformin, and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist. We used conditional logistic regression to estimate the odds ratio (OR) of incident CKD and mixed-effects linear regression to assess eGFR change over time.
Sensitivity analysis using Cox regression was used to examine the effect of association between SGLT-2i and CKD. Patients were followed up from the date of first prescription to date of incident CKD or up to 1 January 2021.
Results
Of 39,734 patients in the database during the study period, 15,938 met inclusion criteria. After propensity score matching, 1,662 patients (831 in each group) were analysed. Median baseline eGFR and uACR were 104.67 ml/min/1.73 m² and 12.14 in cases; and 103.65 ml/min/1.73 m² and 10.61 in controls. SGLT2i users had lower CKD incidence (OR: 0.39, 95% CI: 0.32–0.49; P < 0.001) compared to non-users. No significant interactions were observed between SGLT2i and age, HbA1c, baseline uACR, RASi, or metformin use. Longitudinal analysis revealed no significant difference in eGFR decline between groups over four years [difference: 0.83 (95% CI: −0.59, 2.25); P = 0.25]. title: #3254 Effect of dapagliflozin on arterial stiffness and cognitive impairment in patients with chronic kidney disease
authors: Anastasia Vagkopoulou; Ioannis Ventoulis; Ioannis Tsimoulas; Iraklis Ioannidis; Eftixia Polizogopoulou; Evaggelia Papadopoulou; Dimitrios Makridis; Rigas Kalaitzidis; Evangelia Ntounousi; Despoina Karasavvidou
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors are a new class of antidiabetic agents that inhibit reabsorption of glucose and sodium in the proximal convoluted tubule. Many clinical studies have demonstrated their cardioprotective and nephroprotective effects in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). However, data regarding their effects on arterial stiffness and cognitive function remain rather limited.
Method
We studied 24 consecutive patients with CKD (stages 1–4), in whom dapagliflozin, 10mg once daily, was added to their therapeutic regimen. Their blood pressure was controlled by using perindopril and amlodipine, with appropriate dose adjustments when necessary. The patients were followed for a period of 3 months. Arterial stiffness was measured by means of pulse wave velocity (PWV) with the use of SphygmoCor Cardiovascular Management System (CVMS; AtCor Medical Pty Ltd, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia). Meanwhile, central arterial pressure waveforms were recorded. Concurrently, the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) test was administered to evaluate the patients' cognitive function both at baseline and after 3 months of treatment with dapagliflozin. Baseline patient characteristics are presented in Table 1.
Results
At 3-month follow-up, there was a significant reduction in peripheral systolic blood pressure (pSBP) compared to baseline (129.83 vs 140.91 mmHg respectively, P < 0.001), in peripheral diastolic blood pressure (pDBP) (69.87 vs 77.58 mmHg, P < 0.001), in central systolic blood pressure (cSBP) (146.20 vs 156.25 mmHg, P < 0.001), and in central diastolic blood pressure (cDBP) (82.04 vs 89.58 mmHg, P = 0.007) (Table 2). Dapagliflozin administration also resulted in a statistically significant decrease in PWV by 1.457 (P < 0.001). Additionally, it was observed that increased values of arterial stiffness were associated with worse patient performance on the MoCA test (P = 000). After 3 months of dapagliflozin treatment, a statistically significant improvement by 1.33 was evident in the MoCA test performance (MOCA at baseline 1.54, at 3 months 1.13. (P < 0.001).
Conclusion
In our small cohor of patients with stage 1-4 CKD, the addition of 10 mg of dapagliflozin seems to cause reductions in both arterial stiffness and blood pressure over a period of 3-month treatment. During the same time interval, dapagliflozin seems to improve cognitive function, as evidenced by improvement in the MoCA test performance. Further studies of longer duration and of larger sample sizes are warranted in order to validate these initial promising observations.

title: #3519 Baseline characteristics and decision-making in the management of incident and recurrent hyperkalaemia in Spain: Interim results from the prospective TRACK study
authors: Jordi Bover Sanjuan; Pilar Fraile Gómez; Aleix Fort Pal; Marta Cobo; María José Espigares Huete; Domingo Pascual Figal; Meredith Bishop; Anna-Karin Sundin; Ana Roncero Martin; Miren Sequera Mutiozabal; Gabriel Ledesma Sánchez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyperkalaemia (HK) is a frequent complication in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and heart failure (HF), notably among those taking renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors (RAASi). Prospective data on healthcare professionals' (HCP) decision-making and patient management regarding HK remain limited. The aim is to describe the HCPs decision-making and management of incident and recurrent HK patients within the Spanish cohort of the TRACK multinational study.
Method
Multinational, observational and prospective study conducted in US, UK, Germany, Italy and Spain. The TRACK study enrolled adults with serum K+ >5.0 mmol/L and recorded HCP management decisions for 12 months. Baseline characteristics as well as initial treatment, treatment objectives and planned treatment duration by incident and recurrent HK patients were analyzed descriptively for Spanish cohort.
Results
A cohort of 259 patients (mean age 69.2 ± 11.4 years; 67.6% male; BMI 28.2 ± 5.6 kg/m²; eGFR 32.0 ± 22.2 ml/min/1.73 m²) was enrolled across 17 Spanish sites, with 43.8% experiencing incident HK and 56.2% recurrent HK; 1 patient with this specific missing information. At baseline, most patients had CKD (91.2% in incident HK vs. 89.0% in recurrent HK); 45.2% had HF (52.2% in incident HK vs. 40.0% in recurrent HK) with HFrEF predominating in both groups, and the coexistence of CKD and HF was more frequent in incident HK (45.1% vs. 31.0%). Most recurrent HK patients (72.1%) were in CKD stages IV–V, while incident HK patients were mainly in stages III–IV (74.7%). Initially, 70.7% patients were treated with ACEi/ARB/ARNi (80.5% in incident HK vs 62.8% in recurrent HK) and 26.3% with MRA (31.9% in incident HK vs 22.1% in recurrent HK).
Incident and recurrent HK management at baseline was presented in Table 1. Key strategies in HK included RAASi therapy continuation (73.5% vs. 60.7%), low-potassium diets (63.7% vs. 55.2%), and potassium binders (26.5% vs. 42.8%). The primary treatment goal was patient safety (43.5% vs. 52.6%), with potassium-lowering as the main expectation (80.2% vs. 90.3%). Recurrent HK patients were mostly treated until potassium levels normalized (61.8%), while incident HK patients mainly followed a defined therapy period (43.6%), often indefinite, or treatment until normalization (37.3%).
Conclusion
More than half of the patients had recurrent HK, and potassium levels were not monitored in nearly 50% of them. Preliminary results highlight slightly different approaches between incident and recurrent HK, but an overall conservative management approach was observed, with low-potassium diets being more common than potassium binders, despite guideline recommendations.
These results highlight a need for optimizing management strategies, including earlier interventions and adherence to guidelines.
TRACK study final results will provide further insights to optimize HK management.

title: #3521 Hypophosphatemia following intravenous iron in chronic kidney disease
authors: Fabio Procaccini; Juan Antonio Martín Navarro; Veronica Rubio Menendez; Amir Shabaka; Ángela Rey Cárdenas; Laura Medina Zahonero; Miryam Elena Polo Cánovas; Roberto Alcazar Arroyo; Patricia De Sequera Ortiz
abstract:
Background and Aims
Intravenous iron therapy is a cornerstone in the management of iron deficiency anemia in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. Among available formulations, ferric carboxymaltose (FC) has been shown to induce a more profound and sustained decrease in serum phosphate compared to other formulations such as ferric derisomaltose and iron sucrose. Recent trials link this effect to the elevation of fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), which increases renal phosphate excretion and suppresses vitamin D synthesis. This disruption in calcium-phosphate homeostasis can lead to clinical manifestations such as muscle weakness, bone pain, and osteomalacia.
Although hypophosphatemia has been described in the general population receiving IV iron, most studies have focused on patients without renal impairment. The role of CKD as a potential modulator of this effect remains unclear. CKD patients exhibit an inherently altered phosphate metabolism, with progressive elevations in FGF23 levels due to inadequate renal phosphate excretion. It has been hypothesized that the effects of IV iron on phosphate metabolism may be attenuated in this population.
Our study aims to evaluate the incidence and severity of hypophosphatemia in CKD patients receiving IV iron therapy. We sought to quantify the magnitude of phosphate depletion across different CKD stages and assess whether cumulative iron doses influence this effect. Understanding the extent and clinical significance of IV iron-induced hypophosphatemia in CKD is essential for optimizing treatment strategies and minimizing potential risks in this vulnerable patient population.
Method
A retrospective study was conducted at two nephrology outpatient clinics in Madrid. Patients ≥18 years with CKD who received IVIT over a 12-month period were included. Those undergoing dialysis or without phosphate measurements were excluded. Serum phosphate levels were evaluated before and after iron administration, with follow-up intervals of up to 3 months. The available intravenous iron formulations were Ferinject 50 mg/mL (FC) and Venofer 20 mg/mL (IS). Doses and intervals were determined by usual physician, without research team interference. Definition of hypophosphatemia was serum phosphate <2.5 mg/dL. Statistical analyses were conducted using Stata v18 (StataCorp) and included paired t-tests and two-way linear prediction.
Results
A total of 191 IVIT administrations were analyzed. The cohort had a mean age of 77.0 ± 13.6 years, with 52.9% male. The most common CKD etiologies were nephroangiosclerosis (27.2%) and diabetic nephropathy (18.5%). Of the patients, 95.2% received FC, while 4.7% received IS.
The mean FC dose was 897.3 ± 465.8 mg (range 500–3500 mg), and the mean IS dose was 257.1 ± 181.3 mg (range 100–600 mg). The median time between IVIT administration and follow-up laboratory testing was 28 days (IQR 7–68).
Post-IVIT hypophosphatemia was observed in 22.5% (43/191) of patients, with 7.8% (15/191) exhibiting severe hypophosphatemia (<2 mg/dL) and 1.05% (2/191) with levels <1 mg/dL. Mean serum phosphate decreased from 3.60 ± 0.84 mg/dL to 3.26 ± 0.96 mg/dL (P = 0.000).
Phosphate decline was significant across CKD stages until eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m² (Fig. 1), with a statistically significant reduction observed in: Stage 1 (n = 22): P = 0.01Stage 2 (n = 43): P = 0.02Stage 3 (n = 55): P < 0.001 The reduction was not statistically significant in: Stage 4 (n = 45): P = 0.33Stage 5 (n = 26): P = 0.18 Hypophosphatemia severity increased with cumulative doses (Fig. 2). No significant differences were found in vitamin D levels (P = 0.77) or calcium levels (P = 0.03). Parathyroid hormone levels showed a non-significant increase (199 vs. 204 pg/mL, P = 0.87).
Conclusions
Our study confirms that intravenous iron administration is associated with a measurable decline in serum phosphate levels, even in CKD patients. This effect is more pronounced until stage 3 and with higher cumulative iron doses, independently of baseline vitamin D and calcium levels. Given its potential clinical implications, routine phosphate monitoring should be considered, especially in patients receiving prolonged or high-dose IVIT.

title: #3609 Cognitive functions in multymorbidity patients with atrial fibrillation depending on the presence of concomitant chronic kidney disease stages 3A, 3B and 4
authors: Svetlana Litvinova; Kantemir Dzamikhov; Aleksey Kochetkov; Sofya Eremina; Elizaveta Ebzeeva; Olga Ostroumova
abstract:
Background
сognitive impairment (CI) is one of the significant public health problems. Multimorbidity patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) are at higher risk of developing CI, which can lead to deterioration in quality of life, difficulties in adherence to medication regimens and a higher incidence of adverse drug reactions, which determines the need to diagnose cognitive deficit in these multimorbid patients.
Aims
to assess the impact the stage of concomitant CKD on cognitive functions (CF) in patients with AF.
Materials and methods
we included 142 patients of both sexes ≥18 years old with AF in combination with CKD stages C3 and C4; 47 (33.1%) men and 95 (66.9%) women, aged 58 to 99 years (median age 84 [76; 90] years). Patients were divided into 3 groups: (i) with CKD C3a (n = 50), (ii) with CKD C3b (n = 50), (iii) with CKD C4 (n = 42). All patients underwent cognitive assessment including the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Trial Making Test (parts A, B), Category Fluency, Word-List Recall and Stroop color-word conflict.
Results
patients with CKD C4 had a statistically significantly lower number of points on the MMSЕ, compared with patients with CKD C3a (27 [24;28] vs. 28 [26;29] points, respectively, P = 0.048). Among patients with CKD C4, there were statistically significantly fewer patients who scored ≥29 points on the MMSЕ, compared with patients with CKD C3a (8 (19%) vs. 19 (38%) patients, respectively, P = 0.047). Patients with CKD C4 reproduced a statistically significantly smaller number of words an hour after memorization than patients with CKD C3a (2 [0;3] vs. 3 [0;4] words, respectively, P = 0.017). To complete the TMT part A test, patients with CKD C4 required a statistically significantly longer time than patients with CKD C3a (89 [61;117] vs. 71 [58;91.5] seconds, respectively, P = 0.047).
Conclusion
the results obtained in this study indicate an adverse effect of concomitant CKD C4 on CF in patients with AF and a deterioration in CF with increasing severity of CKD.

title: #5 The adjustment of GFR by body surface area: a misleading procedure in trials focused on weight reduction and GFR changes
authors: Elia Reseghetti; Olav Rivero Martín; Raúl Morales Febles; Patricia Isabel Delgado Mallén; Rosa Miquel; Sara Estupiñan Torres; Maria Angeles Cobo Caso; Sergio Luis Lima; Coriolano Cruz; Laura Díaz Martin; Domingo J Hernández Marrero; Esteban Porrini
abstract:
Background and Aims
controversies exist on the benefits of estimated GFR (eGFR) by formulas (more uncertain) of gold standards (more accurate). Another problem is the adjustment of GFR for body surface area (BSA). The scientific background of the adjustment is weak and mostly relies on the fact that GFR always changes in parallel with weight. This is not true for all patients, and the changes of GFR according to weight are highly variable and unpredictable. Also, the need to adjust a value of GFR remains obscure. Finally, the adjustment to a “standard” BSA of 1.73 m2, which is the average BSA of US subjects of the east cost of 1920, seems difficult to justify today. In brief, the adjustment for BSA “artificially” reduces GFR in obese subjects and increases GFR in small and lean subjects. Also, the adjustment for BSA limits the observation of changes in GFR associated with weight loss due to pharmacological treatments, diets, or exercise.
We evaluated the impact of the adjustment of BSA in the analysis of GFR changes in 30 patients with chronic kidney disease, obesity, and metabolic syndrome who underwent a 6-month therapy with exercise (EXRED study, abstract n°119). We investigated whether mGFR adjusted for BSA (mGFR-BSA) or eGFR would adequately reflect GFR changes after weight loss, compared to mGFR.
Method
we included 30 patients from the EXRED study. mGFR with plasma clearance of iohexol was performed at months 0, 3, and 6. On the same day, samples were collected for analytes, including serum creatinine for eGFR (CKD-EPI 2021). BSA was calculated through DuBois-DuBois formula. Changes in mGFR, mGFR-BSA, and eGFR were assessed using the non-parametric statistics. We performed the analysis as follows:
Overall—we considered the 30 patients as a whole (Fig. 1A). Subgroups—in the EXRED study, mGFR changes were heterogeneous: over six months, half of the patients (n = 15) showed a significant reduction (>8%) in mGFR (“mGFR-decliners”), whereas the other half (n = 15), with similar weight loss and baseline characteristics, did not (“mGFR-stable”) (Fig. 1B). We compared the original mGFR with the GFR-BSA or eGFR values.
Results
after 6 months
OVERALL (Fig. 1A)—mGFR significantly reduced from 59.3 ± 20.4 to 54.1 ± 19.4 ml/min (p 0.006). mGFR-BSA showed only a modest reduction from 49.7 ± 17.3 to 47.7 ± 17 ml/min/1.73 m2 (p 0.001), lower than with mGFR, P < 0.001. eGFR had a slight significative increase. SUBGROUPS—in “mGFR decliners” (n = 15), mGFR reduced from 62.9 ± 22.2 to 50.5 ± 18.3 ml/min (P < 0.001) (Fig. 1B). According to mGFR-BSA, the same 15 patients still had a significative, although less marked, GFR decline (53.3 ± 19 to 45.5 ± 16.8 ml/min/1.73 m2, P < 0.001) (Fig. 1C). eGFR did not change at all (Fig. 1D). mGFR values were significantly higher than mGFR-BSA and eGFR throughout the study.
Conclusion
GFR changes following weight loss were not adequately detected by mGFR-BSA or eGFR. The correction for BSA artificially reduces GFR in obese subjects and artificially increases GFR after they lose weight. This is particularly true for the patients who experience a significant GFR decline.
In studies where GFR decline is the main outcome and weight loss is the therapeutic approach, the use of gold standard methods such as mGFR unadjusted for BSA is crucial for a correct interpretation of results. Furthermore, the consequences of the heterogeneous GFR response to weight loss need to be better investigated with long-term studies and larger numbers of patients.

Background and Aims
controversies exist on the benefits of estimated GFR (eGFR) by formulas (more uncertain) of gold standards (more accurate). Another problem is the adjustment of GFR for body surface area (BSA). The scientific background of the adjustment is weak and mostly relies on the fact that GFR always changes in parallel with weight. This is not true for all patients, and the changes of GFR according to weight are highly variable and unpredictable. Also, the need to adjust a value of GFR remains obscure. Finally, the adjustment to a “standard” BSA of 1.73 m2, which is the average BSA of US subjects of the east cost of 1920, seems difficult to justify today. In brief, the adjustment for BSA “artificially” reduces GFR in obese subjects and increases GFR in small and lean subjects. Also, the adjustment for BSA limits the observation of changes in GFR associated with weight loss due to pharmacological treatments, diets, or exercise.
We evaluated the impact of the adjustment of BSA in the analysis of GFR changes in 30 patients with chronic kidney disease, obesity, and metabolic syndrome who underwent a 6-month therapy with exercise (EXRED study, abstract n°119). We investigated whether mGFR adjusted for BSA (mGFR-BSA) or eGFR would adequately reflect GFR changes after weight loss, compared to mGFR.
Method
we included 30 patients from the EXRED study. mGFR with plasma clearance of iohexol was performed at months 0, 3, and 6. On the same day, samples were collected for analytes, including serum creatinine for eGFR (CKD-EPI 2021). BSA was calculated through DuBois-DuBois formula. Changes in mGFR, mGFR-BSA, and eGFR were assessed using the non-parametric statistics. We performed the analysis as follows:
Overall—we considered the 30 patients as a whole (Fig. 1A). Subgroups—in the EXRED study, mGFR changes were heterogeneous: over six months, half of the patients (n = 15) showed a significant reduction (>8%) in mGFR (“mGFR-decliners”), whereas the other half (n = 15), with similar weight loss and baseline characteristics, did not (“mGFR-stable”) (Fig. 1B). We compared the original mGFR with the GFR-BSA or eGFR values.
Results
after 6 months
OVERALL (Fig. 1A)—mGFR significantly reduced from 59.3 ± 20.4 to 54.1 ± 19.4 ml/min (p 0.006). mGFR-BSA showed only a modest reduction from 49.7 ± 17.3 to 47.7 ± 17 ml/min/1.73 m2 (p 0.001), lower than with mGFR, P < 0.001. eGFR had a slight significative increase. SUBGROUPS—in “mGFR decliners” (n = 15), mGFR reduced from 62.9 ± 22.2 to 50.5 ± 18.3 ml/min (P < 0.001) (Fig. 1B). According to mGFR-BSA, the same 15 patients still had a significative, although less marked, GFR decline (53.3 ± 19 to 45.5 ± 16.8 ml/min/1.73 m2, P < 0.001) (Fig. 1C). eGFR did not change at all (Fig. 1D). mGFR values were significantly higher than mGFR-BSA and eGFR throughout the study.
Conclusion
GFR changes following weight loss were not adequately detected by mGFR-BSA or eGFR. The correction for BSA artificially reduces GFR in obese subjects and artificially increases GFR after they lose weight. This is particularly true for the patients who experience a significant GFR decline.
In studies where GFR decline is the main outcome and weight loss is the therapeutic approach, the use of gold standard methods such as mGFR unadjusted for BSA is crucial for a correct interpretation of results. Furthermore, the consequences of the heterogeneous GFR response to weight loss need to be better investigated with long-term studies and larger numbers of patients.

title: #117 Patients’ perspectives on the use of the kidney failure risk equation and shared decision making in multimorbidity and frailty: a qualitative interview study
authors: Heather Walker; Michael Sullivan; Bhautesh Jani; Patrick Mark; Katie Gallacher
abstract:
Background and Aims
Clinical guidance recommends the use of the Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE) to guide referral and management of individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD) to secondary kidney care services. People living with CKD frequently experience multiple long-term conditions (multimorbidity) and/or frailty. This may impact individuals’ perceptions of kidney failure in the context of other health problems and associated risks and emphasises the need for shared decision-making. This study aims to investigate patients’ perspectives on the use of KFRE in individuals with CKD and multimorbidity and/or frailty, communication of kidney failure risk from health professionals, and experiences of shared decision-making.
Method
In person semi-structured interviews with patients with a diagnosis of CKD and multimorbidity and/or frailty from primary and secondary care settings in the United Kingdom were conducted between March–December 2024. Interviews used open-ended questioning, supported by a topic guide that was developed based on the research questions, the Ottawa Decision Support Framework and the Ottawa Personal Decision Guide. Long-term conditions were self-reported and clinical frailty status assessed with support from the interviewer. Interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim. Data were analysed by framework analysis, underpinned by Normalisation Process Theory, to explore the patient experience of the processes involved in the communication of kidney failure risk and shared decision making about CKD management. A second researcher check coded a subset of interviews to enhance rigour. We explored data that fell outside of the coding frame to determine any findings undetected using the predefined theoretical framework. Nvivo 14 was used for data analysis.
Results
Nineteen participants from primary care settings and twelve from a secondary care setting were interviewed. Participants were aged between 46–94 years old, reported living with 3–10 long-term health conditions and had a clinical frailty scale of 1–7. Five factors were found that influence the experience of communication of risk and shared decision making: (i) Individuals knowledge and understanding CKD and kidney failure as part of multimorbidity and/or frailty; (ii) The work required to understand and be involved in the shared decision making processes for CKD together with other health conditions and risk of kidney failure; (iii) Relationships and interactions with healthcare professionals, the healthcare system and their support networks; (iv) An individual's context and priorities and (v) Uncertainty of health conditions/functional status and consideration of death.
Conclusion
We found many individuals were unaware of having a diagnosis of CKD and described a desire to understand this and their risk of kidney failure alongside other chronic health problems. The relationships and interactions between individuals, healthcare professionals, the healthcare system and their support networks are complex and vary by individual context and priorities. This study aids our understanding of how individuals understand CKD and kidney failure risk alongside multimorbidity and/or frailty. Additionally, it describes how kidney failure risk prediction and the use of KFRE can be embedded in the care of and impact individuals with multimorbidity or frailty and shared decision making in this context. The findings will help promote a more holistic and comprehensive approach to shared decision making around kidney failure risk for this sub-group of patients.

title: #258 To sleep or not to sleep: that is the (renal) question
authors: Giulia Talarico; Anteo Di Napoli; Alessandro Domenici; Paolo Mene'; Fulvio Marrocco
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sleep disturbances are common in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), with a prevalence around 45%–80%. Poor sleep quality is related to the onset or progression of cognitive and mood disorders, cardiovascular and respiratory diseases and a worsening of the quality of life. The reason for the closed link between these seemingly distant pathologies finds its origins in the pathophysiology of CKD and its complications.
Our aim is to analyze the quality of sleep in patients with CKD, observing whether there are differences between patients in end-stage renal disease (ESRD) in conservative therapy and patients on replacement therapy (RT): hemodialysis (HD), peritoneal dialysis (PD), kidney transplantation (TPX).
Method
We conducted a retrospective cohort study on 155 nephropathic patients undergoing conservative therapy or RT (HD/DP/TPX) for at least 2 months belonging to the “Sant’ Andrea” University Hospital and the Local Health Unit “ASL Roma 4.” The outcome variable analyzed was sleep quality, measured by administering the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality index (PSQI), whose overall score was dichotomized into good (≤5) and poor (>5) quality. A multivariate logistic regression model was applied, corrected for age, comorbidities (cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity, hypertension, respiratory disease) and blood nitrogen, sodium, potassium, calcium, phosphorus, parathormone, hemoglobin.
Results
The mean (SD) age of patients was 63.7 (14.6) years. The females were 31.8%. The 60.5% of patients obtained a global score greater than 5. We didn't observe significant differences in the items and in the global score between the various modalities. The lowest median global score, so the best one, was found in ESRD patients (Fig. 1). HD patients were found to have shorter sleep duration, longer sleep onset latency and a higher percentage of PSQI >5. PD patients had a higher subjective sleep quality, lower prevalence of sleep disturbances and a better PSQI compared to hemodialysis (Fig. 2). Sleep disturbances were found to be more frequent in females (68% vs 57%), with a worse daytime fitness state (P = 0.004). Lower hemoglobin values, especially if associated with comorbidities such as respiratory system diseases, can compromise not only the daytime fitness state reported by the patient (P = 0.0176), but also the global quality of sleep (P = 0.064). All patients tested was positives for sleep disorders, but only 20 (12.9%) of them were taking sleep-inducing drugs.
Conclusion
The results of the study show that although ESRD patients often have many symptoms related to pre-dialysis uremia, they still have a better quality of sleep than patients on RT. Therefore RT have an impact on sleep quality that should not be underestimated. Contrary to what one might think, PD does not have a worse impact on sleep than HD, even though it is a modality that is often performed at night. It will be interesting to expand the study by correlating these data with the execution of polysomnography to describe the sleep disorders detected both from a qualitative and quantitative point of view. For a first screening we could also benefit from the use of smart devices (smart watches or rings).
Furthermore the extremely limited use of sleep-inducing drugs, even in presence of very poor sleep quality, may suggests that nephrologists have not yet developed care to the issue. Higher attention to this aspect can improve patient's quality of life and reduce the risks associated with sleep disorders.

title: #826 Assessing performance of creatinine and cystatin-c based estimating glomerular filtration rate equations in South Asian populations: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Ayush Sinha; Alexander Sarnowski; Kathryn Dalrymple; Pierre Delanaye; Kate Bramham; Rouvick Gama
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) prevalence continues to rise and is predicted to be the 5th leading cause of mortality worldwide by 2040. It is common in people from South Asian backgrounds and may be associated with rapidly progressive disease. Accurate measurement of kidney function is essential to diagnose, manage and classify CKD.
Widely used creatinine-based estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) equations had minimal South Asian representation in their development cohorts and subsequent studies in South Asians and diaspora have demonstrated reduced accuracy related to non-GFR determinants, such as muscle mass and vegetarian diets.
We aimed to compare performance of creatinine (Cr)-based, cystatin C (CysC)-based and combined (Cr and CysC) eGFR equations with measured GFR (mGFR) in South Asians and diaspora.
Method
Systematic review was undertaken according to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines and included the following database searches from 1946 to 30th November 2024: PubMed/Medline, Embase (Ovid), Scopus, Web of Science and Cochrane Library for Systematic Reviews and Clinical Trials.
Inclusion criteria: studies which included eGFR compared to mGFR and/or measures of accuracy (bias and 30% accuracy) in South Asian populations. Sample size, demographic and renal characteristics (endogenous and exogenous filtration markers, with assay methods, eGFR, mGFR, bias and 30% accuracy) were extracted. Aggregate data, for each study and by eGFR equation were reported as weighted (by sample size) mean ± standard deviation, 95% confidence intervals or standard error and illustrated using forest plot. Heterogeneity was calculated using Cochran's Q and I2 statistic. Data were analysed using Software R 4.2.2.
Results
37 studies including 35 independent cohorts (n = 4725) and 16 eGFR equations (Cr = 9, CysC = 4, combined = 3) were included. Weighted mean age was 46.8 ± 14.6 years, BMI was 25.6 ± 5.3 kg/m2 and 48.4% were male (n = 2289). Half the cohort were of Indian heritage (n = 2389; 50.6%) and the majority were prospective kidney donors or healthy volunteers (n = 2569; 54.4%). Fewer had CKD (n = 1523; 32.2%). Weighted mean mGFR was 65.8 ± 35.0 mL/min/1.73 m2. Study characteristics are summarised in Table 1.
Cr-based and combined eGFR estimates frequently overestimated mGFR. MDRD 4-variable was most commonly used with weighted mean bias 3.56 [95% CI 2.80 to 4.32] mL/min/1.73 m2 and P30 65.3% (15 cohorts). The most commonly used combined equation was CKD-EPI 2012 (5 cohorts), with weighted mean bias of −2.26 [95% CI −2.51 to −2.01] mL/min/1.73 m2 and P30 74.8%. CysC equations underestimated mGFR 44.4% of the time and had the lower reported aggregate bias. The CysC CKD-EPI 2012 equation was most commonly used (6 cohorts) with bias of -1.44 [95% CI −1.60 to −1.28] mL/min/1.73 m2 and P30 68.2%. The most accurate equation was the CysC EKFC with mean bias of 0.30 [95% CI −0.13–0.73] mL/min/1.73 m2 and P30 of 60% reported in one cohort (n = 412). Weighted mean bias with heterogeneity is illustrated in Fig. 1.
Conclusion
To our knowledge this is the largest meta-analysis of South Asian participants. CysC-based eGFR equations are more closely correlated with mGFR compared to Cr-based or combined eGFR equations. Cr-based equations tended to overestimate mGFR with greater variability, however accuracy (weighted mean P30 = 60.4 ± 0.4%) was lower than studies in European or US cohorts.
Heterogeneity was high (100%), which is likely related to variability in the cohorts, biomarkers, assays and methodologies used. Other limitations include missing covariate data in studies (e.g. BMI), small sample sizes in cohorts outside of South Asia and few participants with CKD.
Overestimation of kidney function may lead to delays in diagnosis or inappropriate administration of renally excreted medication, thus negatively impacting outcomes for high-risk groups. Use of cystatin-C eGFR equations should be considered when evaluating kidney function in South Asian populations, particularly if non-GFR creatinine-based determinants are present.

title: #1619 Protein intake and the risk of age-related kidney function decline in the general population—the Renal Iohexol Clearance Survey
authors: Ludvig Balteskard Rinde; Laila Hopstock; Nikoline Balteskard Rinde; Marit Dahl Solbu; Marie Lundblad; Karl Brobak; Inger Enoksen; Jon Viljar Norvik; Monica Carlsen; Juan-Jesus Carrero; Bjørn Eriksen; Toralf Melsom
abstract:
Background and Aims
In experimental studies, a high-protein diet (>1.3 g/kg/day) has been shown to cause hyperfiltration, which may lead to an accelerated decline in the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) with and without preexisting kidney disease. However, evidence is inconsistent regarding the impact of higher protein intake on GFR decline in individuals with normal kidney function. This inconsistency may stem from imprecise creatinine-based GFR estimates (eGFR), which can be biased by protein intake and muscle mass variations. We aim to use GFR measured as iohexol clearance (mGFR) to address the knowledge gap regarding protein intake and the risk of GFR decline.
Method
We analyzed data from the second Renal Iohexol Clearance Survey, RENIS, involving 1,066 participants without self-reported diabetes and cardiovascular disease, where mGFR was measured at baseline and after a median follow-up of 5.3 years. Protein intake (g/kg/d) was assessed using a validated food frequency questionnaire specifically designed to capture comprehensive dietary information based on Norwegian dietary habits and food items. We excluded participants with extreme total energy and/or protein intakes, defined as participants in the 1st and 100th percentiles of energy intake (<3417 kJ/d and >19666 kJ/d) and protein intake (<37.6 g/d and >200.9 g/d) to exclude unrealistic energy intakes (n = 35). We used linear mixed models and logistic regression to examine the association between estimated protein intake and the mean GFR decline rate and the odds ratio of accelerated GFR decline (top 10% steepest annual GFR reduction), adjusted for potential confounders.
Results
The mean baseline age of the participants was 63.7 years (52% women). The mean GFR was 88.8 ml/min/1.73 m2, and 4% had diabetes. The mean protein intake was 1.2 ± 0.4 g/kg/day. The lowest quartile of protein intake ranged from 0.4 to 0.9 g/kg/day, while the highest quartile ranged from 1.4 to 3.7 g/kg/day. Mean baseline mGFR was higher in groups with higher protein intake: 86.1, 88.5, 88.9, and 91.9 mL/min/1.73 m² from lowest to highest quartile, respectively.
No association was found between estimated protein intake and mGFR decline, with a yearly change of −0.03 (95% CI: −0.08 to 0.02) per 0.1 g/kg/d increase. No differences were observed across protein intake quartiles. Increased protein intake was not associated with accelerated GFR decline. Results were consistent in sensitivity analyses using absolute GFR without body surface area adjustment.
Conclusion
The amount of protein consumed in the diet did not correlate with the rate of GFR decline in healthy individuals with normal kidney function. These findings suggest that restricting dietary protein intake does not prevent CKD.

title: #2167 Dapagliflozin improves metabolic profile in non-diabetic chronic kidney disease: a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial
authors: Mohamed Elshayeb; Mostafa Gamal; Ahmed Elsaeed; Amr El-Husseini; Samir Sally; Wael I Mortada; Kareem A Nabieh; Mohamed A Sobh
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) have revolutionized the management of type 2 diabetes, largely due to their glucose-lowering effects. However, emerging evidence suggests that their therapeutic potential extends beyond glycaemic control, particularly in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). The pleiotropic effects of SGLT2is, including improvements in hemodynamic parameters and metabolic profiles, have drawn significant interest, prompting investigations into their application in non-diabetic CKD. This trial studied the metabolic effects of SGLT2is in non-diabetic patients with CKD.
Method
This randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 100 non-diabetic adults with CKD with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 25–75 ml/min/1.73 m2. Participants were randomized 1:1 to receive either dapagliflozin 10 mg or placebo daily for 12 months and stratified by age and eGFR. Body weight, body mass index (BMI), blood pressure, serum creatinine, eGFR, uric acid and lipid profile were measured at baseline and after 12 months.
Results
Participants had a mean age of 53.5 ± 11.1 years, with no significant baseline differences between groups. Patients treated with dapagliflozin exhibit significant decrease in BMI compared to placebo (P = 0.005), without a significant effect on eGFR. Lipid profile analyses revealed a significant decrease in low density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels in the dapagliflozin group compared to the placebo group (P = 0.003). There was a notable but non-significant decrease in the serum uric acid level in dapagliflozin group. There were no significant changes in mean systolic or diastolic blood pressure between the two groups at one year. Within-group analysis of baseline versus follow up also showed a significant decrease in body weight in dapagliflozin group (P = 0.001) and a significant increase in serum LDL cholesterol level in the placebo group (P = 0.008).
Conclusion

title: #2247 Trandolapril attenuates renal fibrosis in rats with a dual-injury model of kidney disease progression
authors: Andriy Kovalchuk; Joana del Valle Mercado Hernández; Nuria Martín-Fernández; Isabel Fuentes-Calvo; Sandra M Sancho Martinez; Francisco J Lopez-Hernandez; Carlos Martinez Salgado
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a progressive and currently irreversible disease affecting almost 10% of the global population. Its burden on patients and healthcare systems becomes increasingly significant every year. The lack of preventive and therapeutic strategies is evidenced by the rising mortality and underlying risk to suffer kidney failure and cardiovascular disease. This study aimed to evaluate the renoprotective effects of the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor trandolapril in a rat model of CKD progression.
Method
We developed a transition model from acute kidney injury (AKI) to CKD, where the acute phase of the disease is induced through the administration of a nephrotoxic single dose of cisplatin (5 mg/kg). Following recovery of kidney function, a subsequent kidney injury induced through unilateral renal ischemia-reperfusion surgery initiated the transition to CKD. During this transition, impaired renal repair mechanisms facilitate the development of a pronounced fibrotic and inflammatory response within the kidney. Treatment with 0.7 mg/kg trandolapril in drinking water is administered for 3 months during the aforementioned transition phase to evaluate whether it is effective in preventing the development of interstitial fibrosis and focal inflammation infiltrates.
Results
We observed a distinct fibrogenic pattern in the kidney, where individual nephron failure and death lead to scarring of isolated regions of tissue, surrounded by interstitial fibrosis, tubular atrophy, and accumulation of inflammatory cells. The administration of trandolapril was effective in reducing the accumulation of extracellular matrix as a consequence of the fibrotic process. This was assessed and quantified through collagen specific histology stains and immunohistochemistry staining for fibrosis and inflammation markers. The mechanism through which trandolapril prevents AKI to CKD transition is not yet elucidated. However, we did not observe a decline in blood pressure in the treatment groups, possible due to the dose employed being lower than the therapeutic range for hypertensive patients. Although the treatment did improve the kidney morphology, we did not observe significant changes in kidney function in the treatment group, evidenced through biochemical analyses used in daily clinical practice.
Conclusion
Our study provides evidence that trandolapril can mitigate the development of renal fibrosis in a rat model transitioning from AKI to CKD. This beneficial effect, observed despite the absence of hemodynamic and kidney function changes, highlights the potential of ACE inhibitors to prevent long-term structural damage and may have important implications for the management of patients at risk for CKD progression after AKI episodes.

title: #2691 A safety and survival analysis of sequential systemic anticancer treatment in patients with end-stage kidney disease and metastatic renal cell carcinoma
authors: Tomaž Milanez; Vinay Srinivasan; Bostjan Seruga; Miha Arnol; Janja Ocvirk; Edgar Jaimes
abstract:
Background and Aims
Systemic anticancer treatment (SACT) prolongs overall survival (OS) in patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC) but is associated with various adverse events (AEs). Many mRCC patients develop chronic kidney disease, that can progress to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), requiring chronic hemodialysis (HD). Unfortunately, pivotal randomized trials usually exclude cancer patients with ESKD, resulting in a lack of high-quality data on the efficacy and safety of SACT in this population. The incidence of serious AEs, particularly bleeding and infection, and the primary outcome in terms of OS in mRCC patients with ESKD receiving SACT, remains unclear.
Method
We retrospectively identified all patients with mRCC and ESKD who received SACT with VEGFR inhibitors, immune check point inhibitors (ICI), or mTOR inhibitors, alone or in combinations, at the Institute of Oncology Ljubljana in Slovenia between December 2009 and January 2025. Data on the frequency and severity of bleeding and infections were collected from electronic health records. OS was defined as the duration of time from the initiation of SACT to death. Mean and median OS were calculated across all risk groups according to the International Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma Database Consortium (IMDC).
Results
We identified 38 patients with mRCC and ESKD treated with SACT. Their median age at SACT initiation of was 70.5 (64.3–75) years, with 30 patients (79%) being men. According to IMDC criteria, 12 patients had a good prognosis, while 26 (68.4%) had intermediate or poor prognosis. Eighteen patients (47%) experienced a least one cycle of ICI. Before SACT, 25 patients (65.8%) were already on HD and 16 patients (34.2%) later developed ESKD. Three patients (7.9%) had an eGFR of ≤15 ml/min/1.73 m2, and six (15.8%) had an eGFR of 15–29 ml/min/1.73 m2 at SACT start. Eight patients (21%) experienced bleeding episodes before SACT initiation, including three with gastrointestinal bleeding (GIB). Grade 4 epistaxis occurred in three patients, with one patient who developed hemorrhagic shock during first-line treatment with sunitinib. Two patients experienced grade 4 anal hemorrhage, one related to hemorrhoids during sunitinib therapy. Two patients required urgent nephrectomy during pazopanib or sunitinib treatment. One patient required urgent local treatment for massive upper GIB during corticosteroids therapy due to immune-related AEs. Overall, seven patients (18.4%) experienced grade 4 GIB during or after SACT. The cumulative incidence of grade 3/4 bleeding was 0.53 (20 events/38 patients), and all-grade bleeding was 1.24 (47 events/38 patients). Twenty eight patients (73.7%) experienced grade 4 infections during SACT, with seven developing sepsis, and one, experiencing septic shock while on HD and receiving first-line treatment with sunitinib. Across all prognostic groups, the median OS was 32 months (95% CI: 15.7–48.3) and the mean OS was 38 months (95% CI: 25.8–51). All censored patients were alive at the end of the study.
Conclusion
Serious bleeding and infections are common complications in mRCC and ESKD patients treated with sequential SACT. Clinicians should consider these potentially life-threatening complications when selecting the type and duration of SACT. Given the significant management challenges, treatment should occur in dedicated onco-nephrology services.
The IMDC risk model and the primary outcomes for mRCC and ESKD patients warrant further evaluation in prospective trials to enhance treatment strategies and improve outcome.

title: #2197 Prevalence and trends of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) Syndrome among Korean Adults, 2013–2022
authors: Hyun Kyu Kim; Soo-Young Yoon; Jeong-Yeun Lee; Youngyoon Moon; Yoosun Joo; Yang Gyun Kim; Ju-Young Moon; Sang-Ho Lee; Jin Sug Kim; Hyeon Seok Hwang; Kyunghwan Jeong
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) syndrome, a term coined by the American Heart Association, emphasizes the interconnectedness of these diseases and the need for multidisciplinary prevention and treatment approaches. This study aimed to investigate the long-term trends in the prevalence of CKM syndrome in the South Korean population.
Method
We used data from the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KNHANES), including Korean adults from 2007 to 2022, drawn from a representative longitudinal cohort. The CKM syndrome stages were defined as: stage 0 (no CKM health risk factors), stage 1 (excess adiposity or prediabetes), stage 2 (metabolic risk factors or chronic kidney disease), stage 3 (very high risk of chronic kidney disease or a highly predicted 10-year cardiovascular disease risk), and stage 4 (diagnosed cardiovascular disease, with or without kidney failure). Trend analysis for each stage was assessed using linear regression. Additionally, the prevalence of CKM stages was compared among subgroups by age, sex, residential area, education level, household income, smoking, drinking, and physical activity.
Results
A total of 79,391 adults from 2007 to 2022 were analyzed. The prevalence was 18.97% for stage 0, 28.19% for stage 1, 44.66% for stage 2, and 8.19% for stages 3 and 4. The prevalence of each stage showed an upward trend over time (P for trend <0.05 for each stage). In the interaction analysis, CKM stage 2 showed a statistically significant increase over time compared to the other stages (P for interaction <0.05). Adults over the age of 65 tended to show increases in advanced stages and decreases in stages 0–2. Populations with higher household income were more likely to have stages 0–2, while the prevalence of stages 3 and 4 decreased in this group.
Conclusion
This study is the first large-scale investigation into the longitudinal prevalence of CKM syndrome from 2007 to 2022. Further research is needed to fully understand the changes in prevalence and temporal trends and to incorporate these findings into national healthcare policies.

title: #3126 Combined use of SRAA blockers and SGLT2 inhibitors for reduction of proteinuria in paediatric patients with chronic kidney disease
authors: Víctor Alfonso López Báez; Yolanda Calzada Baños; Yarima López Espinoza; Ana Cristina Aguilar Rodríguez; Emma Fortes Marín; Romina Escalante; Oreste Ferra Neto; Pedro Arango Sancho; Álvaro Madrid Aris
abstract:
Background and Aims
To assess the reduction of proteinuria and tolerability of iSGLT2 in paediatric patients with CKD
Method
Retrospective observational study, patients aged 8-21 years with CKD grade 2–3 and proteinuria >0.5 mg/mg. Excluded patients with uncontrolled baseline disease, UTI in the last 3 months and orthostatic proteinuria. Dapagliflozin was administered, single daily dose of 5 mg for patients ≤30 kg and 10 mg for patients >30 kg. Statistical analysis was performed using T-student, assessing the reduction in proteinuria and its effect on glomerular filtration rate, potassium, haematocrit, changes in weight or adverse effects at 6 months.
Results
Six patients were studied, of whom one patient was excluded after 3 months due to comorbidities that worsened the progression of CKD. Mean age was 14.8 years, four of six were female. All with RAAS blockage, none diabetic. The most frequent diagnosis was nephrotic syndrome (50%). Mean proteinuria reduction was 42.8% (initial proteinuria 2.8 mg/mg and 1.6 mg/mg at 6 months). Mean eGFR at baseline was 72.4 ml/min/1.73 m2 and at 6 months was 112.6 ml/min/1.73 m2. Mean potassium at baseline was 4.53 mg/dL and at 6 months 4.13 mg/dL. Mean haematocrit at baseline and 6 months was 35.6% and 39% respectively. Mean weight at baseline was 46.3 kg and at 6 months 44.6 kg (3.6% reduction). No patients reported adverse effects (urinary symptoms, digestive symptoms, dyslipidaemia).
Conclusion
iSGLT2 is considered one of the gold standard treatments for CKD in adults. In combination with RAAS blockade, they have been shown to be effective in reducing proteinuria regardless of the underlying renal disease mechanism. In our cohort, with the combined use of RAAS blockade and iSGLT2, an added reduction in proteinuria was observed. No deterioration of renal function was observed, as described in the literature. In addition, an increase in haematocrit was observed, which may be of added value in the management of anaemia in paediatric patients with CKD, and must be monitored to avoid hyperviscosity phenomena. No adverse effects were reported with the use of iSGLT2, as demonstrated by Paige, G. and Robert, B. in 2022 in a paediatric diabetic population. Therefore, the combined use of these drugs appears to be well tolerated and effective. It is important to mention that due to the number of participants it is not appropriate to draw conclusions. Undoubtedly, this study can be a starting point for future research. We consider necessary and urgent to conduct multicentre studies.

title: #558 Population pharmacokinetic modelling of canagliflozin in advanced chronic kidney disease
authors: Elias Elenjickal; Thomas Mavrakanas; Ari Gritsas; Rita Suri; Amélie Marsot
abstract:
Background and Aims
Canagliflozin is an orally active, selective, reversible sodium-glucose cotransport-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor used in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) to prevent cardiovascular (CV) and renal outcomes [1–3]. Its initiation is currently not recommended in advanced CKD (eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m²), end-stage kidney disease, or in those on kidney replacement therapies due to insufficient clinical and safety data [4]. This study aimed to develop a population pharmacokinetic (popPK) model using data from patients with advanced CKD, including those on maintenance hemodialysis (HD), to characterize the steady-state pharmacokinetics (PK) of canagliflozin at 100 mg and 300 mg doses, and to assess the impact of significant covariates on its PK.
Method
PK data were obtained from a single-center, prospective, single-arm, open-label interventional study conducted in two cohorts. The first cohort involved detailed PK sampling in 10 patients receiving intermittent HD, while the second included sparse PK sampling in 13 patients with CKD stage 4 or 5 not yet on dialysis [5]. A total of 332 PK observations from 23 patients were analyzed. Canagliflozin PK parameters were modeled using nonlinear mixed-effects modeling (NONMEM® version 7.5) with the first-order conditional estimation method with interaction. Model performance was evaluated using goodness of fit plot, bootstrap (n = 1000) and normalized prediction distribution error (NPDE).
Results
A two-compartment popPK model of canagliflozin with lag-time, sequential zero- and first-order absorption, and first-order elimination was developed. Age was a significant covariate of the absorption rate constant (Ka), which increased with age. Sex was a significant covariate for the apparent volume of distribution (V/F), which was lower in females (80.7 L in males and 49.1 L in females). The steady-state area under the curve (AUC) was higher in older patients and females, especially at the 300 mg dose. No difference in steady-state exposures was observed between patients with advanced CKD and those undergoing hemodialysis.
Conclusion
The developed model effectively characterizes the pharmacokinetics of canagliflozin in patients with advanced CKD, including those undergoing hemodialysis. The study demonstrates that steady state canagliflozin exposure is higher in older patients and females, particularly at the 300 mg dose, while renal function was not a significant determinant of exposure in advanced CKD patients.

title: #872 An overview of 67 national-level factors potentially related to the incidence of kidney replacement therapy across European countries
authors: Eva Pella; Rianne Boenink; Anneke Kramer; Kitty J Jager; Alberto Ortiz; Vianda S Stel
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney replacement therapy (KRT) incidence varies considerably across European countries. We aimed to provide a comprehensive and up-to-date overview of national-level factors potentially related to KRT incidence for all individual European countries and across low, middle and high KRT incidence countries. Secondly, we aimed to describe the relationship between these factors and KRT incidence.
Method
We obtained unadjusted KRT incidence rates from the European Renal Association (ERA) Registry annual reports and studies. Countries were divided into low [0–100 per million population (pmp)], middle (100–200 pmp) and high (>200 pmp) KRT incidence countries. Online sources were searched for information on factors potentially related to KRT incidence, including geographic, socioeconomic, sociocultural and health-related factors and factors related to chronic kidney disease (CKD) and national capacity for CKD prevention. Linear or polynomial regression was used to model linear or curvilinear univariate relationships using data from all individual countries, with the R coefficient as metric of correlation strength. As secondary analysis, we evaluated the univariate relationship between each significant factor from the main analysis and the KRT incidence separately for the wealthy (gross domestic product (GDP) per capita >$40,000) and less affluent (GDP per capita <$40,000) countries.
Results
38 European countries were included in this study, and divided into 12 low, 21 middle, and 5 high KRT incidence countries. Among the 67 factors evaluated, the number of practicing physicians (R = 0.374, P = 0.023), the population density (R = 0.508, P = 0.001), the median age at KRT initiation (R = 0.549, P = 0.001), the percentages of CKD-attributed deaths (R = 0.418, P = 0.038) and disability-adjusted-life-years (R = 0.420, P = 0.010) and the physical inactivity prevalence (R = 0.569, P < 0.001) were statistically significantly positively correlated with KRT incidence. According to our secondary analysis these findings were consistent among less affluent countries, while only the median age at KRT initiation remained significant among wealthy countries. After multiple test correction, median age at KRT initiation, physical inactivity prevalence and population density remained statistically significantly positively correlated with KRT incidence (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
We visualized the distribution of 67 national-level factors potentially related to KRT incidence across 38 European countries. We did not aim to prove causality and inevitably some of the factors studied may be both the cause and the consequence of differences in the KRT incidence. We found that the median age at KRT initiation, physical inactivity prevalence and population density were the most important factors significantly correlated with KRT incidence. These findings may be a first important step for policy makers, stakeholders and nephrologists to optimize healthcare (planning) regarding KRT initiation and minimize disparities in KRT incidence.

Online sources were searched for information on factors potentially related to KRT incidence, including geographic, socioeconomic, sociocultural and health-related factors and factors related to chronic kidney disease (CKD) and national capacity for CKD prevention. Linear or polynomial regression was used to model linear or curvilinear univariate relationships using data from all individual countries, with the R coefficient as metric of correlation strength. As secondary analysis, we evaluated the univariate relationship between each significant factor from the main analysis and the KRT incidence separately for the wealthy (gross domestic product (GDP) per capita >$40,000) and less affluent (GDP per capita <$40,000) countries.

38 European countries were included in this study, and divided into 12 low, 21 middle, and 5 high KRT incidence countries. According to our secondary analysis these findings were consistent among less affluent countries, while only the median age at KRT initiation remained significant among wealthy countries.
