Conclusion
We visualized the distribution of 67 national-level factors potentially related to KRT incidence across 38 European countries. We did not aim to prove causality and inevitably some of the factors studied may be both the cause and the consequence of differences in the KRT incidence. We found that the median age at KRT initiation, physical inactivity prevalence and population density were the most important factors significantly correlated with KRT incidence. These findings may be a first important step for policy makers, stakeholders and nephrologists to optimize healthcare (planning) regarding KRT initiation and minimize disparities in KRT incidence.

title: #1816 Effectiveness of chronic kidney disease education in patients with advanced stages: a retrospective study
authors: Soo Jeong Choi; Seon Min Kim; Yoon Won Choi; Geo Neul Park; Byeong Chul Yu; Mooyong Park; Jin Kuk Kim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) education has demonstrated benefits, including preservation of kidney function, an increased proportion of patients starting hemodialysis with permanent access, greater preference for home dialysis, and improved survival rates. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of CKD education in patients with advanced stages of CKD.
Method
A retrospective study was conducted on CKD patients who visited the nephrology department between January 2001 and March 2024. Patients with at least six months of follow-up and a decline in eGFR were included, while those who initiated renal replacement therapy were excluded. The progression to the next CKD stage was compared between patients who received CKD education and those who did not. Propensity score matching (PSM) analysis was performed to adjust for confounding factors.
Results
A total of 1,526 patients (mean age 60.4 ± 14.9 years, 662 female) were included in the study. The mean follow-up period was 1,015.1 ± 827.3 days. Among 859 stage 3b patients, 815 (94.9%) progressed to the next stage, while 644 (96.5%) of 667 stage 4 patients progressed. Of these, 76 (8.8%) and 146 (21.9%) patients had received CKD education, respectively. Patients who received CKD education were generally younger and had more severe proteinuria and cerebrovascular disease compared to those who did not. Although the CKD education group (particularly stage 4 patients) progressed faster to the next stage, no significant difference was observed after PSM analysis.
Conclusion
Only 4.4% of patients with advanced CKD stages maintained their current stage. CKD education was received by 21% of stage 4 patients, but it did not appear to delay disease progression.

title: #1828 Albuminuria and coronary artery calcium in a general Japanese population
authors: Koji Takahashi; Daisuke Morita; Yori Inoue; Kazuhiro Tada; Sho Shimamoto; Kenji Ito; Tetsuhiko Yasuno; Shintaro Ishida; Toshiki Maeda; Hisatomi Arima; Kosuke Masutani
abstract:
Background and Aims
Both albuminuria and coronary artery calcium (CAC) are well-established cardiovascular risk factors. However, the relationship between albuminuria and CAC remains controversial. This study aimed to investigate their association in a general Japanese population.
Method
This was a population-based, cross-sectional observational study utilizing annual health check data collected between 2019 and 2022 in Nakagawa City and Fukuoka City, Japan. A total of 599 individuals aged 30 years or older who underwent both urine testing and CAC scanning were included in the analysis. Albuminuria was assessed using the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR). Participants were categorized into three groups based on UACR tertiles: tertile 1 (<28.6 mg/g), tertile 2 (28.6–58.3 mg/g), and tertile 3 (>58.3 mg/g). CAC was measured using multi-detector computed tomography, and CAC scores were calculated according to the Agatston method. The presence of CAC was defined as a CAC score >0. Logistic regression analysis was conducted to estimate odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for CAC in relation to albuminuria.
Results
Among 599 participants (mean age: 65.4 ± 8.3 years), 295 (49.3%) were women and 327 (54.6%) had detectable CAC. The prevalence of CAC increased across albuminuria tertiles (p for trend = 0.014). After adjusting for traditional cardiovascular risk factors, the ORs for CAC were 1.09 (95% CI, 0.69‒1.70) for tertile 2 and 1.77 (95% CI, 1.10‒2.84) for tertile 3 compared with tertile 1. A significant dose-response relationship was observed between albuminuria and CAC (p for trend = 0.019).
Conclusion
Albuminuria was significantly associated with an increased risk of CAC in a general Japanese population.

title: #2108 High-sensitivity C-reactive protein levels and mortality, cardiovascular events, and adverse kidney outcomes in non-dialysis-dependent CKD patients
authors: Shigeru Tanaka; Hiromasa Kitamura; Kazuhiko Tsuruya; Toshiaki Nakano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Systemic inflammation is a recognized factor in adverse outcomes, yet few studies have explored its impact in patients with non-dialysis-dependent chronic kidney disease (CKD). This study aimed to investigate the association between high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) levels and all-cause mortality, cardiovascular events, and kidney outcomes.
Method
We prospectively followed 4219 patients with stage G1–G5 CKD who underwent hs-CRP measurements between 2013 and 2017. Determinants of hs-CRP ≥2 mg/L were evaluated using logistic regression. Cox regression models assessed the association between hs-CRP categories and adverse outcomes, including all-cause mortality, major cardiovascular events, and end-stage kidney failure.
Results
The median hs-CRP level was 0.53 mg/L, with 19% of participants having hs-CRP ≥2 mg/L. Cross-sectional analyses showed that hs-CRP ≥2 mg/L was negatively correlated with urine albumin, total cholesterol, serum albumin, and statin use, and positively correlated with systolic blood pressure and beta-blocker use. During a median follow-up of 4.5 years, 413 participants died, 365 experienced cardiovascular events, and 830 progressed to end-stage kidney failure. The cumulative incidence of these outcomes increased linearly with higher hs-CRP levels (log-rank P < 0.05). Compared to participants with hs-CRP <1.0 mg/L, those with hs-CRP ≥3.0 mg/L had significantly higher risks of all-cause mortality (hazard ratio [HR] 2.00, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.57–2.54) and major cardiovascular events (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.23–2.14). No significant association was observed between hs-CRP levels and kidney outcomes.
Conclusion
Approximately 20% of non-dialysis-dependent CKD patients exhibited systemic inflammation, as indicated by elevated hs-CRP levels. Higher hs-CRP levels were associated with increased risks of mortality and cardiovascular events but not with adverse kidney outcomes.

title: #2303 PDE5 inhibitor LW1646 improves kidney fibrosis by alleviating ER stress and mitochondrial calcium overload
authors: Minghui Wang; Long Xu; Xiaoduo Zhao; Deyan Wu; Qinghua Liu; Chunling Li; Hai-Bin Luo; Weidong Wang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal fibrosis is the terminal pathological manifestation of most chronic kidney diseases (CKDs). Inhibitors targeting phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE5) have been used to treat erectile dysfunction and pulmonary arterial hypertension by increasing cGMP levels and activating the cGMP/PKG signaling pathway. Studies have shown that PDE5 inhibitors can attenuate the progression of CKD, although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. LW1646 is a newly identified inhibitor with higher specificity and potency against PDE5. This study aims to investigate the therapeutic effects of LW1646 on renal fibrosis and its underlying mechanisms.
Method
In vitro, pro-fibrotic response in HK2 cells was induced by TGF-β1 and intervened with LW1646. In vivo, renal interstitial fibrosis model was established by unilateral ureteral obstruction for 7 days (7UUO) in Pde5a-/- mice. mRNA expression level of Pde5a was analyzed by qPCR. Western blot was used to assess changes in fibrosis markers, endoplasmic reticulum stress indicators, mitochondrial homeostasis metrics, and components of mitochondrial-associated membranes (MAM). Mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) and reactive oxygen species were evaluated using flow cytometry, fluorescent imaging was employed to visualize mitochondrial networks, accumulation of mitochondrial calcium (mtCa2+) and formation of MAM. Histological assessments of renal fibrosis were performed using H&E staining and Masson's trichrome staining. Morphology of mitochondria and ER and mitochondria-ER contact in kidney cortex were investigated by transmission electron microscope (TEM).
Results
mRNA expression level of Pde5a was elevated in renal cortex in 7UUO-induced kidney fibrosis mice. Expression of fibrosis markers and endoplasmic reticulum stress indicators were markedly upregulated both in vitro and in vivo. Meanwhile, mitochondrial biogenesis was inhibited, which was accompanied by increased oxidative stress, decreased MMP and augmented mitochondrial fission. MAMs formation and mtCa2+ level were enhanced. LW1646 significantly prevented development of fibrosis in mice with 7UUO and exhibited a more pronounced effect than sildenafil. Pde5a knockout was associated with alleviated fibrosis in mice. LW1646 or Pde5a knockout attenuated ER stress and altered mitochondrial homeostasis in fibrotic kidneys and HK2 cells exhibiting pro-fibrotic responses.
Conclusion
Our data demonstrated that LW1646 ameliorated renal fibrosis likely through inhibiting ER stress and maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis. Mechanistically, activation of cGPM/PKG pathway by LW1646 or Pde5a knockout conferred mitochondrial protection by inhibiting the formation of MAMs, thereby reducing mtCa2+ overload and alleviating renal fibrosis.

title: #3197 Cardio-renal butterfly effect: myocardial infarction with coronary reperfusion triggers kidney disease and induces interstitial fibrosis
authors: Dimitri Bedo; Thomas Beaudrey; Jérôme Olagne; Sophie Ohlmann; Philippe Boucher; Nans Florens
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic cardiovascular and kidney disorder (CCKD) remains a challenge in healthcare, characterized by the intricate interplay between cardiac and renal diseases. Acute cardio-renal aggressions are frequent and have significant long-term prognostic implications. Moreover, growing evidence supports the concept of the cardio-renal butterfly effect, whereby an acute cardiorenal event initiates a vicious cycle of organ crosstalk, impacting both the affected and distant organs. While the remote cardiac repercussions of acute renal failure are well-documented, the reverse relationship remains to be explored. The aim of this study was to describe the histological, biochemical, and molecular-scale renal dysfunctions following a coronary ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI).
Method
We used a coronary IRI model in wild-type mice (C57B6) consisting with a reversible ligation of the left anterior descending artery of 1-hour. Sham operated mice underwent a thoracotomy without IRI. Histological, biochemistry and transcriptomics (RNAseq) were performed on kidney tissue from mice at day 1, 7 or 28 after IRI.
Results
Using Masson's trichrome staining, a significant increase in renal interstitial fibrosis was observed in mice following IRI (2% for IRI versus 1%, P = 0.028, Fig. 1). Plasma measurements exhibited a significant elevation of urea in IRI mice (median urea 6.97 mmol/L for sham versus 8.44 mmol/L, P = 0.018 for IRI). At D28, Western blot analysis on kidney tissue indicated a trend towards increased KIM-1 expression, while NGAL levels remained unchanged after IRI.
At D7, renal transcriptome analysis revealed a deregulation of genes involved in kidney disease, as well as in heart failure and myocardial infarction. Interestingly, genes associated with metabolic syndrome, obesity, and diabetes were also affected. Notably, qPCR showed a significantly lower expression of PPARα and PPARγ genes in IRI mice at D7.
At D28, renal transcriptome analysis further demonstrated a deregulation of genes linked to chronic kidney disease and heart failure, along with genes involved in mitochondrial function. For instance, Western blot analysis at D28 revealed a decreased expression of PGC1α and SOD2 proteins, confirming persistent mitochondrial dysfunction in the kidneys of IRI mice.
Conclusion
In a murine model, myocardial infarction with coronary reperfusion triggers kidney disease, induces interstitial fibrosis associated with probable mitochondrial dysfunction. Further research is needed to understand the pathophysiology.

title: #3532 Bariatric surgery reverses ORG and exhibits a distinct transcriptomic profile compared to weight loss through a low-fat diet
authors: Marina López Martínez; Maria Pilar Armengol; Irina Pey; Xavi Farré; Paula Rodríguez-Rodríguez; Mireia Ferrer; Esteban Porrini; Sergio Luis Lima; Ana Elena Rodríguez-Rodríguez; Coriolano Cruz-Perera; Marta Alcalde; Maruja Navarro-Díaz
abstract:
Background and Aims
The therapeutic option of obesity comorbidities has always been weight loss. Clinically relevant weight loss improves clinical parameters of kidney damage, such as proteinuria. However, the histological kidney effects and the gene expression changes after low fat diet (LFD) or bariatric surgery (BS) have never been evaluated. In this project we aim to assess the impact of low fat diet versus bariatric surgery in obesity and obesity related glomerulopathy (ORG).
Method
28 rats were randomized into three main groups and fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 10 weeks when they became obese. Subsequently, 8 obese rats were sacrificed (HFD-group), 8 animals were fed a LFD (LFD-group) during 10 weeks and 12 underwent BS through sleeve gastrectomy (CB-group) and fed a standard diet until the end of the study. Parameters like body weight, measured glomerular filtration rate (mGFR), albuminuria, kidney histological lesions and transcriptomic expression between groups were assessed.
Results
The LFD-group reduced their weight a 1.58% until 476.16 ± 26.06 gr and the BS-group reached a 13.2% of weight loss 435.61 ± 36.85 gr. The rate of weight loss of the CIR-group was of 2.1 times higher than that of the LFD group. Albuminuria in HFD-group reached 10384.04 ± 1167.96 ng/mL, while in LFD and CIR groups the albuminuria decreased substantially to 7228.04 ± 514.22 (P = 0.008) and 6241.50 ± 418.33 (P = 0.006), respectively. Albuminuria correlated with weight loss (coef R² = 0,78203). Glomerular area was significantly smaller in both LFD (9109.76 ± 1185.51 µm²; P = 0.019) and BS (8218.31 ± 916.72 µm²; P < 0.001) groups compared with HFD-group (10640.92 ± 1220.62 µm²). All the rats of the HFD-group developed ORG, LFD-group also some of the characteristic histologic lesions of ORG (mesangial matrix increase, mesangial cell proliferation, podocyte hypertrophy), while none of the BS-group showed any visible glomerular lesions. Direct comparison of BS and LFD revealed a substantial number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with a notable cluster of up-regulated genes. Moreover, there was a differential pattern of small RNAs in both kidney tissue and urine, depending on whether the rats were from the BS or LFD group. While LFD induced transcriptional changes, these were less extensive that after BS, supporting a unique transcriptomic response associated with the surgical intervention. Gene ontology and reactome pathway analyses revealed that both interventions modulate specific pathways related to cellular metabolism (particularly mitochondrial processes), amino acid metabolism, and other biological processes within the kidney.
Conclusion
Bariatric surgery is much more effective for drastic weight loss than low fat diet in obese rats. Albuminuria in both LFD and BS-groups was significantly reduced and albuminuria correlated with weight loss. Strikingly, this project confirmed for the first time in scientific literature that bariatric surgery reverses all the histological lesions of obesity-related glomerulopathy. Finally, bariatric surgery has a profound impact on renal gene expression. There is a differential pattern of gene expression in kidney tissue, as well as of small RNA in both kidney tissue and urine. Specific pathways such as mitochondrial processes and amino acid metabolism are specifically modulated. These results offer new insights into potential therapeutic strategies for obesity-related kidney disease.

title: #3702 Creatinine and cystatin C: refining stratification risk of adverse outcomes in a high cardiovascular risk population
authors: Cristina García Majado; Cristina Baldeón Conde; Emilio Rodrigo; María José Ortega Fernández Reyes; José Enrique Pasache; Miguel Martínez-Belotto; Juan Carlos Ruiz San Millán; José Luis Hernández Hernández
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal function is strongly related to cardiovascular risk. Although both creatinine and cystatin C are reliable markers of renal function at the population level, it has been described that cystatin C stratifies more accurately cardiovascular risk. The aim of this study was to assess the predictive capacity of both biomarkers in stratifying the risk of cardiovascular and renal events in a high cardiovascular risk population.
Method
We conducted a retrospective observational study of patients admitted to the Cardiac Intensive Care Unit between 2012 and 2022 with a diagnosis of acute coronary syndrome, who had concomitant analytical measurements of both creatinine and cystatin C. We used the cystatin C/creatinine ratio (Cys/Cr) as well as the absolute difference between eGFR based on cystatin C and on creatinine (eGFRdiff = eGFRcys–eGFRcr), establishing three categories: difference less than −15 ml/min/1.73 m² (eGFRcys < eGFRcr), difference between −15 ml/min/1.73 m² and 15 ml/min/1.73 m² (eGFRcys ≈ eGFRcr) and difference over 15 ml/min/1.73 m² (eGFRcys>eGFRcr). We investigated associations with risks of all-cause mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), and kidney function decline, expressed as a 50% increase in baseline creatinine (ΔCr).
Results
A total of 804 patients were included in the study, with a mean age of 61.5 ± 12.7 years; 80.1% were male. The mean follow-up time was 7.4 ± 2.5 years. Mean values for creatinine and cystatin C were 0.90 ± 0.30 mg/dL and 0.86 ± 0.30 mg/L, respectively. title: #177 Association of SLC13A2 genotypes with the risk of kidney function decline in patients with nephrolithiasis in Ukraine
authors: Liliia Fishchuk; Yaroslav Dubovyi; Natalia Stepanova; Nataliia Gorovenko; Andriy Sahalevych; Taisa Dovbynchuk; Ganna Tolstanova
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney stone disease (KSD) is a common urological condition that can progress to chronic kidney disease (CKD). However, not all individuals with KSD develop CKD, despite the presence of established risk factors. The sodium dicarboxylate cotransporter-1 (NaDC1), encoded by the SLC13A2 gene, is essential for regulating urinary citrate levels, intestinal oxalate absorption, and stone formation. We hypothesize that specific SLC13A2 genotypes are associated with a greater risk of kidney function decline in patients with KSD and may serve as genetic markers for identifying high-risk individuals. Therefore, the present study aimed to investigate the association between the rs11567842 variant of the SLC13A2 gene and kidney function in patients with calcium-oxalate KSD.
Method
This cross-sectional study included 80 patients with KSD admitted to the urology department in Kyiv, Ukraine. The determination of the rs11567842 variant of the SLC13A2 gene was performed using the PCR-RFLP method. Clinical and laboratory data were collected, and the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was calculated using the CKD-EPI formula. Statistical analyses, including chi-square tests, Kruskal-Wallis tests, and logistic regression (univariate and multivariate), were performed to evaluate the association between SLC13A2 genotypes (AA, AG, GG) and kidney function decline (eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m²).
Results
The cohort comprised 50 males (62.5%) and 30 females (37.5%) with a mean age of 54.2 ± 16.2 years and a median disease duration of 12 (1–120) months. Among the patients, 39 (48.7%) had a history of recurrent KSD, 9 (11.3%) had diabetes, and 47 (58.7%) had arterial hypertension. The median eGFR level was 61 (49–72.5) mL/min/1.73 m², with 35 patients (43.7%) having an eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m².
Genotype frequencies for the rs11567842 variant of the SLC13A2 gene were as follows: AA 45% (n = 36), AG 43.7% (n = 35), and GG 11.3% (n = 9). There were no significant differences in KSD duration (P = 0.15) and eGFR levels (P = 0.52) between genotypes. However, the G allele was associated with an increased risk of kidney function decline, with the GG genotype exhibiting the highest frequency of eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² compared to the AA and AG genotypes (χ² = 10.2, P = 0.006).
Univariate logistic regression showed that the GG genotype of the SLC13A2 gene was significantly associated with kidney function decline (OR = 12.2, 95% CI: 2.2–27.8, P = 0.002). This association was further confirmed by multivariate logistic regression adjusted for key confounders, including sex, age, diabetes, hypertension, KSD duration, and recurrence (OR = 8.7, 95% CI: 1.2–16.9, P = 0.02) (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
This study suggests that genetic variations in SLC13A2 may significantly impact the risk of kidney function decline in Ukrainian patients with KSD. The GG genotype of the rs11567842 variant of the SLC13A2 gene is strongly associated with a higher risk of kidney function decline, even after adjusting for clinical factors, while the AA genotype seems to offer a protective effect. However, larger-scale prospective studies are needed to confirm these preliminary findings.

title: #522 Acute-on chronic kidney disease. Factors associated to CKD progression
authors: Maria Isabel Acosta-Ochoa; Arturo Lorenzo Chapatte; Francisco Mateo de Castro; Carmen Calderón González; Karina Ampuero Anachuri; Esther Hernández García; Victoria Oviedo Gómez; Rubén Velasco Pilar; Armando Coca Rojo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Many studies show that individuals with baseline chronic kidney disease (CKD) that experience several consecutive episodes of acute kidney injury (AKI) are at higher risk of CKD progression need for acute in-hospital hemodialysis (HD) and HD dependence at discharge; this unique clinical entity is called Acute-on-CKD (AoCKD). In daily practice we observe that some patients do progress and some remain steady. We aimed to analyze factors for CKD progression when suffering from serial AKI episodes.
Method
We conducted a real world, retrospective, observational study of individuals from two hospitals. We evaluated all nephrology admissions and in-hospital consultations during a 3-year period. We included patients with documented CKD (i.e. GFR 15–60 ml/min calculated by CKD-EPI 2021 formula, during for at least 3 months), that met AKI KDIGO-2012 criteria and suffered minimum 3 consecutive AoCKD events. Cohort was divided into two groups: progress and steady. We defined progression as worst baseline CKD stage in the next AKI episode, high Charlson's Index (ChaI) as ≥5 points, and anemia as Hb ≤11 gr/L in women, ≤12 gr/L in men. We included acute HD and HD dependence at discharge as progression criteria; in-hospital mortality was not considered a criterion. We compared baseline characteristics and hard outcomes between groups, and studied factors that led to CKD progression or non-progression.
Results
We included 247 patients that suffered 921 AoCKD episodes (range 3–9, median 4). 170 individuals that suffered 226 (25%) events progressed, 76 (34) needed acute HD and 33 (15%) were HD dependent at discharge. We found no statistically significant differences between groups in sex distribution (∼70% males), age, hypertension (HTN), hospitalization in surgical wards or hospital acquired AKI. Progressors had a higher Charlson's I (ChaI), more DM and coronary artery disease (CAD), were more frequently admitted in the ICU and classified in AKI Stage 3 (Table 1A; Features). We found no statistically significant differences in time to nephrology consultation and mortality, and patients that progressed had a higher length of hospital stay (Table 1B; Results). OR analysis of factors associated with progression: KDIGO stage 1, 2 were protective; KDIGO Stage-3 3.50 (95% CI: 2.56–4.78, P < 0,001), ICU admission 1.74 (95% CI: 1.18–2.57, P = 0.005), ChaI ≥5 2.38 (95% CI: 1.52–3.71, P < 0.001), DM 1.35 (95% CI: 1.08–1.62, P = 0.04) and anemia associated with maximum creatinine (MaxCr) 1.78 (95% CI: 1.45–2.11, P = 0.04) (Table 1C; Factors).
Conclusion
We found that not every AoCKD episode leads to CKD progression (in fact only 25%), and observed that some characteristics of a singular event could lead to worsen CKD stage. In our study, variables associated with progression were the magnitude of AKI episode (in a dose dependent manner), admission to ICU, a higher ChaI, DM and anemia MaxCr (the only modifiable factor). We couldn't explain the absence of differences in the mortality rate. We will need well designed, prospective studies to determine if controlling anemia throughout the hospitalization period can curb CKD progression during an AKI episode. AKI affects CKD progression depending on the magnitude of the event, and since it has no approved treatment, we should pursue new and creative prevention measures. Once AKI is established we should try to limit its severity in order to avoid its deleterious consequences.

title: #523 Erythropoiesis-stimulating agent hyporesponsiveness and malignancy development in non-dialysis-dependent CKD patients: a prospective cohort study
authors: Nobuhiro Hashimoto; Terumasa Hayashi; Tatsuo Kagimura
abstract:
Background and Aims
Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESA) are widely used to treat anemia in chronic kidney disease (CKD), but their hyporesponsiveness may be linked to malignancy. Although this relationship is highlighted in clinical guidelines, there are limited studies directly examining this association in CKD patients.
Therefore, this study aimed to examine whether ESA hyporesponsiveness are linked to the development of malignancies in patients with non-dialysis-dependent CKD.
Method
This study used data from the BRIGHTEN, a prospective observational study in non-dialysis-dependent CKD patients with anemia. Initial ESA responsiveness was assessed using the erythropoietin resistance index (ERI-1B), calculated as the ratio of darbepoetin-alfa dose (µg) to hemoglobin concentration (g/dL) at 12 weeks after darbepoetin alfa initiation. ESA responsiveness trends after 12 weeks were analyzed using a joint latent class model (JLCM). The associations of both initial ESA responsiveness and ESA responsiveness trends after 12 weeks with malignancy development were analyzed using a Cox proportional hazards model.
Results
Of the 1,641 patients analyzed, 44 developed new malignancies, with colorectal cancer being the most frequent. Patients with poor ESA response at 12 weeks (ERI-1B > 3.8 µg/g/dL) had a higher incidence of malignancy compared to those with better ESA response (adjusted hazard ratio [HR]: 2.06; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.07–3.99). Furthermore, based on JLCM, patients in the poor response group, characterized by a faster decline in ESA responsiveness after 12 weeks, had a higher risk of malignancy compared to the good response group (adjusted HR: 1.90; 95% CI: 1.02–3.54).
Conclusion
This study demonstrated that both initial ESA hyporesponsiveness and subsequent declines in responsiveness were significantly associated with the development of malignancy in patients with non-dialysis-dependent CKD. Monitoring ESA responsiveness could provide valuable insights for identifying patients at potential risk for malignancy.

title: #1296 Comparison of urinary biomarkers in different diabetic kidney disease phenotypes
authors: Yunus Kaygusuz; Deniz Aral Ozbek; Arda Erdut; Rukiye Abanoz; Melek Korkut; Oğuz Uyaroğlu; Füsun Özmen; Tolga Yildirim; Şeref Rahmi Yilmaz; Mustafa Arici; Yunus Erdem; Bulent Altun
abstract:
Background and Aims
It has been shown that 20%–40% of diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is non-albuminuric; however, the pathophysiologic differences between albuminuric (A-DKD) and non-albuminuric (NA-DKD) phenotypes have not been elucidated. Our study aimed to clarify the clinical and pathological features in DKD phenotypes by comparative analysis of nephrin, epidermal growth factor (EGF), vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1), and interleukin 18 (IL-18) as markers of glomerular, tubular, vascular, and inflammatory damage respectively, and Rac Family Small GTPase-1 (Rac-1) as a marker of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) independent mineralocorticoid receptor activator.
Method
Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) diagnosis for at least 5 years were included and divided into four groups according to glomerular filtration rate (GFR) estimated by CKD-EPI and urine albumin to creatinine ratio (UACR) values. Non-albuminuria was determined by no UACR value ≥30 mg/g at a mean 10-year retrospective screening. Group 1 patients were defined as GFR ≥60 ml/min/1.73 m2-UACR <30 mg/g as a control group, group 2 as GFR ≥60 ml/min/1.73 m2-UACR ≥30 mg/g, group 3 as GFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2-UACR <30 mg/g and group 4 as GFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2-UACR ≥30 mg/g. Patients with GFR ≤15 ml/min/1.73 m2 and documented kidney diseases with other causes were excluded. Spot urine samples were obtained, and biomarkers were measured using the ELISA method.
Results
A total of 211 diabetic patients were included. The mean age was 64.7 years, and 105 patients were female (49.7%). The mean duration of diabetes was 14 years. Fifty-four of the patients were classified as group 1 (GFR ≥60 ml/min-UACR <30 mg/g), 57 as group 2 (GFR ≥60 ml/min-UACR ≥30 mg/g), 48 as group 3 (GFR <60 ml/min-UACR <30 mg/g), and 52 as group 4 (GFR <60 ml/min-UACR ≥30 mg/g). NA-DKD patients were older than A-DKD, were more likely to be female, had lower hbA1c, and had the prevalence of cardiovascular diseases and hypertension was higher. There was no difference in lipid levels, duration of diabetes, RAAS blocker use, and retinopathy. VCAM-1 was significantly higher in patients with UACR ≥30 mg/g (both in groups 2–4) compared to those with UACR <30 mg/g (both in groups 1–3) (P < 0.001), also group 1 had lower than group 3 (P = 0.02), and there is no difference between groups 2–4 (P = 0.58). EGF was significantly lower in patients with GFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2 (both in groups 3–4) compared to those with GFR ≥60 ml/min1.73 m2 (P < 0.001), also group 4 had lower than group 3 (P = 0.005), and there is no difference between groups 1–2 (P = 0.56). No significant difference was observed between the groups in nephrin, IL-18, and Rac-1. Rac-1 was lower in those using RAAS and SGLT2 inhibitors (P = 0.008 and 0.001). A positive correlation was found between EGF and GFR (P < 0.001, r = 0.6), VCAM-1 and UACR (P < 0.001, r = 0.41), and Rac-1 and IL-18 (P = 0.002, r = 0.24) (Fig. 1). Multivariate logistic regression analysis revealed that VCAM-1 predicted patients with UACR ≥30 mg/g (P < 0.001, OR = 1.7), and EGF predicted patients with GFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2 (P = 0.001, OR = 0.91). ROC analysis showed that EGF had diagnostic value in predicting GFR (P < 0.001, AUC: 0.818) and VCAM-1 in predicting albuminuria (P < 0.001, AUC: 0.713) (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
EGF and VCAM-1 were found to be powerful in predicting GFR decline and albuminuria development, respectively, in the entire cohort. Higher EGF levels involved in tubular regenerative response to injury and lower VCAM-1 levels related to vascular inflammation in NA-DKD than A-DKD may point to distinct underlying pathophysiological pathways specific to these two phenotypes.

title: #1446 Beyond the scalpel: how postoperative AKI and comorbidities shape CKD progression after partial nephrectomy
authors: Francesco Trevisani; Pietro Scilipoti; Francesco Cei; Giacomo Musso; Arianna Bettiga; Roberto Bertini; Alberto Briganti; Andrea Salonia; Francesco Montorsi; Alessandro Larcher; Giuseppe Rosiello; Umberto Capitanio
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) following partial nephrectomy (PN) is known to negatively impact long-term renal function. However, a tailored nephrological follow-up is rarely conducted for PN patients, as the procedure is considered less invasive compared to radical nephrectomy, and the risk of CKD progression over time is often deemed negligible. Nonetheless, it remains uncertain whether pre-existing comorbidities in PN patients may increase the risk of AKI and amplify its adverse effects on long-term renal outcomes.
Method
We retrospectively identified 552 patients treated with PN for cT1 renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and complete functional follow-up data at a tertiary-referral center from 2000 to 2023. AKI was defined using K-DIGO guidelines, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was calculated with the CKD-EPI formula 2021. Multivariable logistic regression models predicted AKI, assigning a comorbidity score to each patient (hypertension, smoking, gender, age, body mass index), and adjusting for clinically relevant characteristics. The odds ratio-based scores stratified patients into low, intermediate, and high-risk groups according to the Q1/Q3 score distribution. Chronic kidney disease (CKD)-upstage ≥IIIB was defined as an eGFR<45 ml/min/1.73 m2 at last follow-up for patients with a baseline eGFR ≥45 ml/min/1.73 m2. Cumulative incidence curves assessed the risk of CKD-upstage ≥IIIB, considering any-cause death as a competing risk, based on the occurrence of AKI and risk group classification. Cox regression models separately evaluated the association of previous AKI occurrence and comorbidity-based risk groups with CKD-upstage.
Results
Median follow-up was 60 months, median age was 60 years. Median tumor size was 3.2 cm (IQR 2.5–4.30). Based on weighted score assignments, 236 (43%), 149 (27%), and 167 (30%) patients were classified as low, intermediate, and high-risk, respectively. The 10-year cumulative risk of CKD-upstage ≥IIIB was significantly higher in patients who experienced AKI post-surgery (36% vs. 12%, HR 2.75, 95% CI, 1.55–4.89, P < 0.001). Similarly, patients in the intermediate (15%, HR 1.64, 95% CI, 0.81–3.33, P = 0.2) and high-risk groups (28%, HR 2.42, 95% CI, 1.26–4.66, P = 0.008) had a higher risk of CKD-upstage ≥ IIIB compared to those in the low-risk group (9.4%) (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
Patients with significant preoperative comorbidities who develop AKI after PN should undergo a rigorous nephrological follow-up able to prevent or mitigate the risk of severe CKD onset.

title: #1680 Epidemiology of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease among patients incident on kidney replacement therapy between 1990–2022, in Northwest Portugal
authors: Alexandra Silva; Pedro Lisboa Gonçalves; Isabel Tavares; Susana Fernandes; João Paulo Oliveira
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) is the most common monogenic kidney disease, being the cause of the kidney failure (KF) in 5%–10% of incident patients in kidney replacement therapy (KRT). ADPKD is genetically heterogenous, but pathogenic variants in the genes encoding polycystin-1 (PKD1) and polycystin-2 (PKD2) explain most cases (respectively ∼78% and ∼15%).
Clinical experience at a major academic hospital in Northwest Portugal (ULSSJ-Porto) suggests that the relative prevalence of ADPKD-PKD2 is significantly higher than reported, mainly due to a founder polycystin-2 nonsense mutation—PKD2 p.(Gln61*); many patients carrying this variant survive to the 9th decade of life without reaching KF.
The purpose of this study was to describe the epidemiology of ADPKD among patients starting KRT at ULSSJ, and to compare ADPKD-PKD1 to ADPKD-PKD2.
Method
Medical reports for KRT initiation issued at the ULSSJ between 01/01/1990–31/12/2022 were systematically reviewed to identify patients diagnosed with ADPKD. Genotyping data were obtained from the Genetics Laboratory of the Faculty of Medicine, University of Porto. For patients who have not been directly tested, the genotype was inferred from genealogical analysis. Data from non-ADPKD patients starting KRT between 2010–2022 were collected for selected comparisons with the general KRT population.
Results
Out of 6615 medical reports reviewed, 408 ADPKD patients were identified; of the latter, 139 (34.1%) had genotyping information available, which was imputed in 85 (59.0%). Among genotyped patients, prevalences of ADPKD-PKD1 and ADPKD-PKD2 were, respectively, 67.3% and 29.2%. Mean age at KRT initiation was 54.1 years for ADPKD-PKD1 patients and 67.6 years for ADPKD-PKD2. Heterozygosity for the PKD2 p.Gln61* allele was identified in 33 patients (78.6%). Between 2010–2022, prevalence of ADPKD was 7.33% at ULSSJ and 4.90% nationwide (P < .0001).
Conclusion
Prevalence of ADPKD among incident patients on KRT at ULSSJ was significantly higher than nationwide. This is explained by the higher prevalence of ADPKD-PKD2, particularly associated with the PKD2 p.(61Gln*) variant, in the local population. As expected, ADPKD-PKD1 was associated with KF significantly earlier than ADPKD-PKD2. The prevalence of ADPKD-PKD2 in the local population is higher than estimated in this study, given the lower risk of KF in patients with ADPKD-PKD2.

title: #1969 Association between estimated glomerular filtration rate and mortality in elder population
authors: Ohchul Kwon; Su-Ryeong Go; Ho Jun Chin
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal hyperfiltration (RHF) has been associated with mortality in several studies from various cohort groups which is estimated by the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) based on CKD-EPI equation. However, definition of RHF is not established and researchers have used various criterion for RHF. Furthermore, the association between higher eGFR and mortality is remained to be confirmed in elderly population, especially in population aged more than 75 years. We searched the significance of higher eGFR on all-cause mortality in patients aged 65 to 74 years (elderly group) and in population aged ≥ 75 years (elderly elder group).
Method
This retrospective cohort study included 6,118 individuals aged ≥65 years having serum creatinine test who underwent comprehensive geriatric assessment at a university hospital in Korea between January 2016 and December 2020. Participants with eGFR of more than 15 ml/min/1.73 m² estimated by CKD-EPI equation and at least three months of follow-up were included. We grouped participants by eGFR as follows; G1; eGFR ≥ 90, G2; 75–89, G3; 60–74, G4; 45–59, and G5; <45 ml/min/1.73 m2.
Results
There were 2750 (44.9%) male participants. Mean age was 78.7 ± 6.0 (range: 65.0–104.8) years and mean eGFR was 75.8 ± 19.4 ml/min/1.73 m2. During 43.1 ± 21.4 months of mean follow-up period, there were 2,117 mortalities (34.6%). Mortality rates were 33.6% (460/1370) in G1, 29.8% (721/2421) in G2, 32.0% (353/1103) in G3, 42.5% (290/682) in G4, and 54.1% (293/542) in G5 (P < 0.001). AUC by ROC analysis showed increased risk of mortality with decrease of eGFR (AUC = 0.556, 95% CI: 0.540–0.574, P < 0.001).
In whole participants, hazard ratio (HR) was 0.974 (95% CI: 0.952–0.998, P = 0.032) to estimate mortality by increase of eGFR 10 ml/min/1.73 m² calculated with Cox's hazard proportional model adjusted by related factors to mortality. The group of eGFR was also a significant risk factor to mortality (P = 0.007). Risk of mortality was increased in G3 (HR 1.155, P = 0.040), G4 (HR 1.233, P = 0.006), and G5 (HR 1.277, P = 0.002) subgroups compared to G2 subgroup. Risk of mortality in G1 subgroup was not higher compared to that of subgroup G2 in whole participants (P = 0.055).
However, in elderly elder participants, HR for mortality were 1.176 (95% CI; 1.013–1.364, P = 0.033) in G1 subgroup compared to G2 subgroup (Fig. 1). Risk of mortality was increased in G4 subgroup (HR 1.222, P = 0.014) and G5 subgroup (HR 1.288, P = 0.002), not in G3 subgroup (P = 0.057), compared to G2 subgroup.
The finding that patients with higher eGFR had higher risk of mortality compared to patients with eGFR 75-89 ml/min/1.73 m2 was also evident in males, patients without diabetes mellitus, normotensive patients whereas, and patients with lesser comorbidities defined as Charlson's Comorbidity index (CCI). It was not observed in females, patients with diabetes mellitus, hypertensive patients, and patients with CCI ≥ 3.
Conclusion
Mortality risk was increased in patients with eGFR <75 ml/min/1.73 m2 in elder population compared to that of patients with eGFR 75–89 ml/min/1.73 m2. Furthermore, elderly elder patients with eGFR ≥90 ml/min/1.73 m2 had higher risk of mortality compared to patients with eGFR 75–89 ml/min/1.73 m2, that was not evident in elder patients with age between 65–74 years.

title: #2166 Efficacy and safety of Dapagliflozin in patients with stage G4 chronic kidney disease
authors: Francisco Javier Toro Prieto; Paola Donoso Naranjo; Lola María Bueno Mena-Bernal; Natalia Santos Collado; Alba Temprado Collado; Mercedes Acevedo Ribo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sodium-glucose cotransporter type 2 (iSGLT2) inhibitors have become a cornerstone treatment for both diabetic and non-diabetic chronic kidney disease (CKD) due to their ability to slow the decline in glomerular filtration rate and reduce the risk of death from renal and cardiovascular causes. The benefits of iSGLT2 inhibitors seem to be independent of their blood sugar-lowering effects and may be due to their natriuretic effect, which leads to decreased intraglomerular pressure. However, there is limited data on their real-life effects, safety, and efficacy in patients with stage G4 CKD, as well as in managing other complications of renal impairment, such as anemia, hyperuricemia, and electrolyte disturbances. Our objective was evaluate the efficacy and safety of initiating Dapagliflozin treatment in patients with CKD G4, focusing on renal function, electrolyte alterations, uric acid levels, urine albumin-creatinine ratio (ACR), and hemoglobin at a one-year follow-up.
Method
This retrospective descriptive study followed patients who began treatment with Dapagliflozin 10 mg/day during ACKD consultations, with an eGFR of 25–30 ml/min according to the CKD-EPI formula. Over one year, we analyzed demographic data, home treatments (ISRRA and diuretics), episodes of acute kidney injury (AKI), genital infections, and serum levels of sodium (Na), potassium (K), uric acid (Au), hemoglobin (Hb), hematocrit (Hct), and albumin-creatinine ratio (ACR) at baseline, 6 months, and 12 months post-treatment. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 28.0 and Jamovi 2.3.28.
Results
A total of 75 patients were analyzed, revealing a statistically significant (P = 0.08) decrease in ACR (albumin-to-creatinine ratio), serum potassium, and an increase in hematocrit levels. Patients undergoing treatments that could directly influence the outcomes were excluded from the analysis for a more accurate comparison. No significant differences were found regarding renal function, uric acid levels, or serum sodium. There were no withdrawals by the end of the study, and no instances of acute kidney damage or genital infections were reported.
Conclusion
The use of Dapagliflozin seems to be safe for patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). While there was a slight decrease in renal function, this change cannot be fully evaluated without a control group. A reduction in the rate of progression of CKD was observed, particularly in patients with CKD stage G4. Dapagliflozin appears to have a protective effect against hyperkalemia and anemia. However, a larger sample size would be necessary to confirm these findings.

title: #2339 Application of contrast enhanced ultrasound assessments of renal perfusion in younger and older age groups, and in those with and without CKD
authors: Kerry Horne; Jonathan Bowley; Praise Tokode; Eleanor F Cox; Susan Francis; Bethan Phillips; Maarten Taal; Nicholas Selby
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal perfusion, the delivery of oxygenated blood to kidney tissues, is important in the pathophysiology of acute and chronic kidney diseases. Despite this, accessible methods do not exist in clinical practice to measure renal perfusion or monitor the response to interventions in real time. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) is an emerging technique which uses a microbubble contrast agent which allows for continuous imaging of the vasculature and blood flow. The expected values for perfusion parameters of CEUS in healthy individuals and chronic kidney disease are not currently known.
Method
We conducted a prospective, observational study that recruited three groups of participants. Group 1 was comprised of healthy volunteers ≤40 years old, group 2 were healthy volunteers aged ≥70 years, and group 3 were people with CKD (eGFR 15–45 ml/min/1.73 m2). CEUS was performed using a Philips EPIQ ELITE ultrasound machine and an intravenous infusion of SonoVue® (Bracco) contrast. After achieving systemic steady-state of contrast, five destruction-reperfusion sequences were recorded for each participant, and videoclips were analysed using VueBox software. A time-intensity curve was generated from which mean transit time (mTT), the time taken to reach 50% maximal intensity, was derived. The median mTT across destruction-reperfusion sequences was used to generate a single mTT value per participant that were compared between the three groups using one-way ANOVA.
Results
For this analysis, 37 participants (10 healthy volunteers ≤40 years, 10 healthy volunteers ≥70 years and 7 patients with CKD) were included. Mean age was 30.5 ± 4.8 years in young healthy volunteers, 75.7 ± 3.0 years in older healthy volunteers, and 70.7 ± 4.2 years in the CKD group. Median eGFR was 110.0 [IQR 85.5–118.8] ml/min/1.73 m2 in the young volunteers, 85.5 [IQR 75.5–89.3] ml/min/1.73 m2 in the older volunteers, and 31.0 [IQR 26.0–38.0] ml/min/1.73 m2 in the CKD cohort. Cause of CKD was diabetic nephropathy in 3 participants, IgA nephropathy in 3 participants and tubulointerstitial nephritis in 1 participant.
Mean mTT was significantly slower in individuals with CKD (3.6 ± 1.4 seconds) compared to both older (2.3 ± 0.6 seconds, P = 0.01) and young (1.8 ± 0.3 seconds, P < 0.001) healthy volunteers (Fig. 1). The difference between young and older volunteers was not significant (P = 0.4). The CKD group also displayed much greater dispersion of the mTT values (range: 2.1–4.7 seconds), compared with older (2.0–2.5) and younger (1.6–2.0) volunteers.
Conclusion
CEUS is able to detect a difference in kidney cortical perfusion between healthy kidneys and those with CKD. These changes are distinct from age-related changes in perfusion. The higher degree of variability in the CKD cohort suggests greater heterogeneity between patients in the degree to which reductions in perfusion are associated with lower kidney function.

title: #2929 Early versus delayed anticoagulation in acute ischaemic stroke in those with chronic kidney disease: a pre-specified subgroup analysis of the OPTIMAS randomised controlled trial
authors: Philip Nash; Hakim-Moulay Dehbi; Jonathan Best; Hannah Cohen; Martin James; Gregory Lip; Bo Norrving; Nikola Sprigg; Nick Freemantle; David C Wheeler; David Werring
abstract:
Background and Aims
The OPTIMAS trial showed that early initiation of direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) after acute ischaemic stroke (IS) related to atrial fibrillation is non-inferior to delayed initiation. Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) are at increased risk of IS and intracerebral haemorrhage, so the safety and efficacy of early DOAC in those with CKD is of interest.
Method
OPTIMAS was a randomised, parallel-group, open-label trial with blinded outcome assessment. title: #2939 Exploring roxadustat effect on oxidative stress: a pilot study in patients with CKD
authors: Martina Cacciapuoti; Ilaria Caputo; Giulia Driussi; Pulcherie Ghislaine Makoudjou; Anna Basso; Calò Lorenzo; Federico Nalesso
abstract:
Background and Aims
Oxidative stress (OxSt) occurs early in Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) and is associated with inflammation and poor prognosis. OxSt in CKD is a major contributing factor to the pathogenesis of anemia and also promotes atherosclerosis. Roxadustat is a HIF-PHIs, a novel therapy for anemia treatment in CKD that has multiple pleiotropic effects on iron and lipid metabolism and seems to reduce inflammation. Pre-clinical studies conducted on mice models revealed that pre-treatment with roxadustat reduced the level of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in cardiomyocytes after induction of LPS-mediated-septic shock, via activation of HIF-1α that up-regulates two anti-oxidant enzymes: endogenous antioxidant superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) and Heme Oxygenase 1 (HO-1) in a dose-dependent manner, improving mice survival. Moreover, in mice models with induced ischemia-reperfusion AKI, roxadustat decreased renal fibrosis and progression to CKD also via the anti-oxidant effect of SOD-2. Finally, in Ang-II induced hypertensive mice, roxadustat led to AT1R down- and AT2R up-regulation thus preventing Ang-II-induced OxSt and ameliorating hypertension and organ injury.
The aim of this study is to evaluate in CKD patients the effect of 3 months- treatment with roxadustat on OxSt.
Method
in this prospective pilot study 5 patients with CKD G4-5 starting anemia treatment with roxadustat were included. The expression of OxSt related proteins p22phox, subunit of NADPH oxidase and the phosphorylation state of MYPT-1 (p-MYPT-1/MYPT-1), as a marker of activity of RhoA/RhoKinase (ROCK) pathway, were quantified with Western Blots analysis and values at baseline (T0) and after 3 months (T1) treatment with roxadustat were compared. Continuous variables were expressed as mean and SD or median and IQR depending on the distribution. T-student test and Wilcoxon paired test were performed for comparisons. Statistical significance was reached with P < 0.05.
Results
The mean baseline hemoglobin level was 8.8 ± 0.64 g/dL and the mean hemoglobin level at T1 was 11.08 g/dL, with a mean increase of 2.28 g/dL, that was statistically significant (P = 0.038, Fig. 1). A reduction in both the expression of p22phox from baseline (T0 = 0.498 d.u., IQR 0.0914 d.u.) to T1 (0.344 d.u., IQR 0.1497 d.u.) and the rate of phosphorylation of MYPT-1 (pMYPT-1/MYPT-1) (T0 = 0.281 d.u., IQR 0.4794 d.u.; T1 = 0.119 d.u., IQR 0.07276 d.u.) were observed although not reaching statistical significance (P = 0.1875 for p22phox; P = 0.1250 for pMYPT-1/MYPT-1). (Fig. 2)
Conclusion
To our knowledge, this is the first study in patients with CKD evaluating the effect of roxadustat on OxSt. Although not reaching statistical significance and with the limitation of a very small sample size, our results indicate a reduction of OxSt after only 3 months of roxadustat treatment and support a study on a larger cohort of patients and for a longer duration of time. If confirmed, these results might reveal new positive clinical implications of roxadustat on CKD progression and risk of cardiovascular disease of these patients.

title: #3322 Insights into patients’ sexual-related symptom burden and (un)met information and support needs in routine nephrology care
authors: Anouk I Haine; Eline Schade van Westrum; Friedo W Dekker; Yvette Meuleman
abstract:
Background and Aims
Symptoms in chronic kidney disease (CKD) are common and are increasingly being measured and discussed in routine nephrology care. However, this increase does not seem to apply to sexual symptoms, which remain un(der)discussed due to barriers such as taboos and insufficient education of healthcare providers. As a result, patients' informational and support needs may go unmet. This is especially concerning given the high prevalence of sexual symptoms across different stages of CKD. To facilitate the discussion about sexual symptoms, it is essential to understand patients’ (i) experienced burden of sexual symptoms and its impact on daily life; (ii) experiences with discussing sexual symptoms with their healthcare providers; and (iii) support and informational needs to cope with sexual symptoms.
Method
A Dutch nationwide cross-sectional survey study was conducted in collaboration with the Dutch Kidney Patients Association, who distributed the web-based survey which was completed by patients between 8 February 2024 and 31 May 2024. The survey consisted of 22 close-ended and 4 open-ended questions, including demographics, symptom duration and burden, impact on daily life, experiences with discussing sexual symptoms with healthcare providers, as well as (social) support and informational needs. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the results, also stratified by gender and age (<40, between 40–65 and 65+).
Results
In total, 232 patients (mean age 56 ± 14 years, 53% female) from different CKD populations (134 kidney transplantation, 32 dialysis and 66 without kidney replacement therapy) completed the survey. Most patients (83%) were in a relationship, of which 69% married. In the total group, 122 patients (53%) experienced sexual symptoms, predominantly: decreased interest in sex (65%), difficulty becoming sexually aroused (44%) erectile problems (in males 68%, of which 53% older males 65+). Females more often experienced less enjoyment of sex (49% in females vs 15% in males). Most patients (82%) experienced sexual symptoms regularly or always, for longer than 6 months (92%), and as a very burdensome symptom (58%). Males more often considered sexual symptoms in their top 3 of most burdensome symptoms than females (59% vs 48%). Sexual symptoms had a negatively impact on patients daily lives (61%) which was more pronounced in patients aged 40-65 (69%) than in younger (58%) or older patients (46%). Patients mainly experienced a lack of intimacy ((emotional and physical closeness) 35%).
Females and patients below 40 less often discussed sexual symptoms with their healthcare providers (32% female vs 66% males; 26% younger vs 53% older patients). Only 32% (n = 17) of the patients who did discuss sexual symptoms, received treatment. The most important reasons for not discussing sexual symptoms included: patients felt ashamed or considered it private information, patients did not expect the healthcare provider to be able to help, and healthcare providers did not initiate a discussion on these symptoms or provided a private space. Only 5 patients (7%) expressed that they did not want to discuss these symptoms with their healthcare providers. The majority of the patients (65%), regardless of their gender and age, sometimes or always experienced insufficient social support. Patients shared that they would like to receive more information about the relationship between CKD and sexual symptoms (n = 81, 66%), treatment for sexual symptoms (n = 58, 48%) and, especially females, how to cope with sexual symptoms (n = 57, 47%; 59% females vs 34% males).
Conclusion
Patients with CKD of all ages and gender often experience a high burden of sexual symptoms, which is persistent over time and negatively impacts their daily lives. Despite this, most patients never discuss sexual symptoms and those who do, often do not receive treatment. Furthermore, many patients express a need for more information about sexual symptoms in CKD. To address these unmet needs, it is important that healthcare providers initiate discussion on sexual symptoms more regularly with their patients.

title: #3490 Serum acrolein as a potential biomarker of aortic stiffness in patients with non-dialysis chronic kidney disease stage 3 to 5
authors: Chiu Huang Kuo; Bang-Gee Hsu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acrolein, a reactive aldehyde found in environmental pollutants and generated endogenously, has been associated with increased cardiovascular disease risk. Aortic stiffness predicts cardiovascular disease and is associated with aging-associated vascular diseases. The study aimed to investigate the correlation between serum acrolein level and aortic stiffness measured by cfPWV values in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 3 to 5.
Method
Fasting blood samples and baseline characteristics were obtained from 204 CKD stage 3 to 5 patients. Commercially available enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays determined serum acrolein levels. cfPWV was measured using the SphygmoCor system. Patients with carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (cfPWV) >10 m/s were defined as the aortic stiffness group.
Results
Among 204 CKD patients, 69 (33.8%) were in the aortic stiffness group. When compared to those in the control group, the aortic stiffness group had a high prevalence of diabetes mellitus (DM, P = 0.002), hypertension (P = 0.001), older age (P = 0.018), higher systolic blood pressure (SBP, P < 0.001), diastolic blood pressure (DBP, P < 0.001), serum fasting glucose (P = 0.001), triglyceride (P = 0.012), blood urea nitrogen (BUN, P = 0.013), creatinine (P = 0.011), acrolein level (P < 0.001), urine protein–creatinine ratio (UPCR, P < 0.001), while lower in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR, P = 0.013). Multivariate logistic regression analysis of the factors significantly associated with aortic stiffness revealed that serum acrolein levels (odds ratio (OR): 1.013, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.000–1.026, P = 0.048) were the independent predictors of aortic stiffness in CKD patients. By Spearman correlation analysis, logarithmically transformed acrolein (log-acrolein) levels were significantly positively correlated with age (P = 0.048), SBP (P < 0.001), DBP (P < 0.001), cfPWV (P < 0.001), log-BUN (P < 0.001), log-creatinine (P < 0.001), and log-UPCR levels (P = 0.004) and negatively correlated with eGFR (P < 0.001) and hemoglobin (P = 0.007). The area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve for serum acrolein was 0.719 (95% CI: 0.641–0.798, P < 0.001) to predict the development of aortic stiffness in patients with CKD stage 3 to 5.
Conclusion
Serum acrolein level is an independent marker of aortic stiffness and is positively associated with cfPWV values in patients with CKD stage 3 to 5.

title: #3504 Shear wave elastography: a non-invasive tool for assessing chronicity and predicting recovery of kidney function
authors: Manas Ranjan Behera; Anupma Kaul; Pallavi Prasad; Raghunandan Prasad; Narayan Prasad; Ankita Singh; Hira Lal; Vinita Agrawal; Manas Ranjan Patel; Monika Yachha; Ravi Sankar Kushwaha; Jeyakumar Meyyappan
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney fibrosis is a critical prognostic factor in assessing response to therapy and predicting progression to end-stage kidney disease. It also serves as an indicator of chronicity, helping identify the potential for reversal of kidney dysfunction. Traditional methods of quantitatively assessing kidney fibrosis by histology and histomorphometry are invasive, represent only localized areas, and are subject to sampling biases. In contrast, shear wave elastography (SWE) is a non-invasive technique primarily used to assess liver fibrosis, though its application in kidney patients is less studied. This study aimed to establish the diagnostic value of SWE in evaluating kidney fibrosis and predicting recovery of kidney function.
Method
This prospective study included patients who underwent kidney biopsy due to kidney dysfunction between September 2019 and September 2021. Participants were categorized into two groups: acute kidney injury (AKI) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) based on recovery of kidney function. Patents showing partial to complete recovery were categorized as AKI. Exclusion criteria included patients with a BMI ≥23 kg/m², a kidney depth greater than 6 cm from the skin, or those unable to hold their breath during the SWE procedure. SWE was performed prior to the kidney biopsy, and kidney stiffness was expressed as kPa. After the biopsy, the extent of kidney fibrosis was assessed by a pathologist and was described as a “histopathological chronicity score.” The kidney stiffness was correlated with histopathological chronicity score and recovery of kidney function.
Results
A total of 145 patients were included in the study, with 65% male and 35% female. AKI and CKD were diagnosed in 38.62% (n = 56) and 61.38% (n = 89) of patients, respectively. The mean histopathological chronicity scores were 2.20 ± 1.61 for AKI and 7.06 ± 1.71 for CKD (P < 0.001). The mean kidney stiffness (kPa) was 17.95 ± 4.46 for AKI and 30.31 ± 7.12 for CKD (P < 0.001). A positive correlation was found between histopathological chronicity scores and kidney stiffness (r = 0.697; n = 145; P < 0.001). The histopathological chronicity score has AUC 0.982 ((95% CI: 0.964–1.000, P < 0.001) with a best cutoff value of 4.5 (sensitivity 97.8%; specificity 92.9%) for predicting nonrecovery of kidney function. Similarly, the kidney stiffness has AUC 0.933 (95% CI: 0.896–0.970, P < 0.001) with a best cutoff value of 23.51 (sensitivity 82%; specificity 83.9%) for predicting nonrecovery of kidney function.
Conclusion
The kidney stiffness measured by SWE, though inferior to the “histopathological chronicity score,” still effectively predicts the extent of kidney fibrosis and may serve as a valuable noninvasive tool for predicting the potential recovery of kidney function. It is beneficial in critical care settings or situations where kidney biopsy is challenging to perform.

title: #3511 Is higher resting heart rate only explanation to an increased risk for cardiovascular events and mortality in patients with predialysis chronic kidney disease?
authors: Ingrid Prkačin; Valentina Ćorić-Martinović; Domagoj Marković; Tomislav Bulum; Ivo Vučko
abstract:
Background and Aims
An elevated resting heart rate is an independent risk factor for cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality in the general population. However, the correlation between heart rate and mortality in patients with chronic kidney disease is unclear. We aimed to investigate the association between resting heart rate and adverse clinical outcomes from Registar for predialysis chronic kidney disease patients in Clinical Hospital Merkur, Zagreb.
Method
Date between the January of 2020 to the January of 2024 were included for data investigation. We enrolled 1052 patients with predialysis chronic kidney disease (median age, 69 years; 48.7% men). To exclude measurement variability we measured heart rate using an electrocardiograph, and an automated device. Variables such as underlying health conditions (include diabetes, heart disease, obesity and cancer with kidney disease) and lifestyle factors (smoking, depression, chronic stress, excess weight, physical inactivity, trouble sleeping, smoking and substance use) were measured. The primary outcome was cardiovascular events (including myocardial infarction, angina pectoris and heart failure) and secondary all-cause mortality.
Results
We analyzed the longitudinal data of patients. Cohort was stratified into four groups on the basis of resting heart rates: <70, 70–79, 80–89, and ≥90 beats/min. The median estimated glomerular filtration rate (stage G3-G4) was on start G3a and at the end of study G3b (51.2–39.5 mL/min/1.73 m2), with median heart rate of 76 beats/min on start and 79 on the end (min 56, max 114). During the median observation period of 4 years, 28% (293) developed cardiovascular events (heart failure 75% (210), angina pectoris 17% (52) and myocardial infarction 8% (31)) and 15% (143) died. Our analysis showed that the risks of cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality were significantly different amongst the four groups (χ2 test, P < 0.001), The risk for cardiovascular events was higher in patients with a heart rate of 80–89 beats/min than in those with a heart rate <70 beats/min (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.70). Patients with a resting heart rate of 80–89 and ≥90 beats/min had an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.72 and 2.60 for all-cause mortality, compared with patients with a resting heart rate <70 beats/min. In proportion of patients with measured albuminuria (40%) higher resting heart rate was linked to albuminuria A2, independent of other conditions. We did not analyze impact of Covid infection, drugs for hypertension, drugs for diabetes or drugs like painkiller on chronic kidney disease progression and heart rate, because of lack of informations.
Conclusion
The observational nature of this study precluded the relationships between heart rate and outcomes in predialysis chronic kidney disease patients. This study supported the idea that reducing heart rate might be effective for predialysis chronic kidney disease patients with a heart rate ≥70/min, since the lowest risk of mortality was seen in patients with heart rate <70/min.

title: #3897 Retinal vascular analysis, a systematic review
authors: Claire van der Pluijm; Jan Van Eigen; Bert Demeulenaere; Ingeborg Stalmans; Amaryllis Van Craenenbroeck
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a growing global health burden, with cardiovascular (CV) complications as the leading cause of morbidity and mortality. Despite advances in risk stratification models, traditional markers fail to explain the increased CV risk in CKD patients fully. Microvascular dysfunction plays a key role in CKD progression and associated CV events. Given the anatomical and functional parallels between retinal and renal microvasculature, retinal imaging offers a promising non-invasive tool for systemic microvascular health assessment. This review aims to systematically summarize the current literature on structural and functional retinal imaging in CKD, focusing on its value in early detection, risk stratification, and disease monitoring.
Method
A systematic review was conducted following the PRISMA guidelines. Databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library, were searched for studies published between January 1, 2012, and January 1, 2024, investigating retinal vascular changes in CKD. Eligibility was determined based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Two independent reviewers extracted and analyzed data on study design, population characteristics, imaging modalities, and primary outcomes.
Results
A total of 189 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and 40 were included in this review. The studies used different structural (static vessel analysis, speckle flowmetry, optical coherence tomography (OCT), optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA)) and functional (dynamic vessel analysis (DVA), color doppler imaging, laser speckle flowgraphy) imaging techniques. Of these, DVA, OCT, and OCTA demonstrated the most potential for evaluating microvascular changes in CKD. DVA offers a functional assessment of endothelial health, with impaired flicker-induced arteriolar dilation associated with accelerated declines in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and increased CV risk. Similarly, impaired venular dilation independently predicted all-cause and infection-related mortality in hemodialysis patients. OCT detects structural retinal changes, particularly macular and choroidal thinning, which correlated with CKD progression. Choroidal thickness was also associated with histological indexes of renal injury and systemic inflammatory markers, a likely driver of endothelial dysfunction and cardiovascular risk in CKD. In one article, living kidney donors experienced choroidal thinning over 12 months, despite maintaining normal eGFR, suggesting potential long-term risks of kidney donation in developing CKD and CV disease. OCTA enhances OCT evaluation by quantifying retinal and choroidal vessel density. A decrease in superficial vessel density (SVD) was associated with CKD progression and inversely associated with the superficial vascular plexus (SVP) flow void area showed. The systolic blood pressure specifically associated with the SVP flow area, but not with SVD. This finding suggests that the SVP flow void area may reflect the cumulative burden of hypertension on the microvasculature and could serve as an early indicator of microvascular injury in CKD patients.
Conclusion
Retinal vascular analysis provides an accessible and non-invasive approach to understanding microvascular dysfunction in CKD. Although no retinal imaging tool fully captures renal health independently, combining structural (OCT, OCTA) and functional (DVA) imaging techniques seems to better reflect systemic microvascular health. This integrated strategy shows promise for early disease detection, CV risk stratification, and disease progression monitoring. Further validation is warranted before implementation on a large scale can be expected.

title: #13 Variability and severity of HIF-PHIs’ adverse events in CKD population
authors: Sara Maria Majernikova
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl-hydroxylase inhibitors (HIF-PHIs) offer significant options in CKD anaemia therapy. However, there are unmapped areas regarding adverse events (AEs) related to HIF-PHIs. This systematic review aims to find EAs related to HIF-PHIs and analyse their variability, severity, preventability, and outcomes in individual CKD patients reported as case reports.
Method
A literature search of published case reports was conducted from January 2018 to May 2024 across electronic sources such as CenterWatch, Clarivate/Web of Science, Embase, PubMed/Medline, Reaxys, Science.gov, and SciFinder. Of the total identified studies (n = 2123), only 8 case reports (13 patients) were included after applying inclusion and exclusion criteria.
Results
AEs to HIF-PHIs included retinal haemorrhage (7.7%), hypertension (15.4%), stroke (23.1%), hypothyroidism (7.7%), rhabdomyolysis (7.7%), and elevation of serum copper (38.4%). The mean ADR time-to-onset was 6.5 months. Specific causality and non-preventability of AEs to HIF-PHIs were confirmed in one report (12.5%), and definite probability and severity in two reports (25%) due to HIF-PHIs ADRs.
Conclusion
This review suggests HIF-PHIs could be safe for patients to treat CKD anaemia. Thanks to personalised dosages that maintain the recommended haemoglobin value and sufficient management of comorbidities, the probability and severity of ADRs could be decreased.

title: #400 Treatment optimization and standard of care adherence in CKD primary care: the TOSCA-CKD project
authors: Francesco Pesce; Domenico Pasculli; Giuseppe Castellano; Luca De Nicola; Giovanni Gambaro; Vincenzo Panichi; Domenico Santoro; Francesca Viazzi; Monica Zanella; Loreto Gesualdo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Effective collaboration between general practitioners (GPs) and nephrologists is crucial for optimizing the management of chronic kidney disease (CKD). Early detection, prompt referral, and collaborative management are essential for slowing CKD progression. The TOSCA-CKD project (treatment optimization and standard of care adherence in CKD primary care) aimed to evaluate the implementation of clinical guidelines and the use of nephroprotective therapies, including RAAS inhibitors and SGLT2 inhibitors, in primary care settings, optimizing CKD management to improve patients’ outcomes.
Method
Clinical data, comprising estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR), and pharmacological treatments, were collected from the medical records of general practitioners across 12 Italian regions. The data were analyzed at baseline (T0) and after 6 months (T6) of GPs collaboration with Nephrologists. During this observational period, GPs were involved in remote education programs, which included expert-led webinars and clinical case-based learning.
Results
A total of 76 GPs and 9 Nephrologists were involved in the project, evaluating a cohort of 124,759 patients. There was an increase of 23.3% in the uACR test from T0 to T6 (19.6% vs. 20.4%; P < 0.001). Similarly, there was an increase of 15.2% in the use of eGFR from T0 to T6 (29.7% vs. 34.2%; P < 0.001). The rate of CKD diagnosis increased by 17.5% among patients with eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m² (from 4% to 4.7%) and by 40% among patients with ACR > 30 mg/g (from 0.5% to 0.7%) (Fig. 1). The use of ACEi/ARBs remained stable at approximately 50%, while the treatment with SGLT2i, the new standard of care according to the current CKD guidelines, increased by 29.8% (from 4.7% to 6.1%). Dapagliflozin (the only SGLT2i reimbursed per CKD in Italy in that observational period) accounted for more than half of all prescribed SGLT2i, with its use rising from 2.6% at T0 to 3.5% at T6 (relative increase of 34.6%) (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
The TOSCA-CKD project demonstrated that GPs’ remote educational program and a structured co-management approach significantly enhanced the early identification and improved the management of CKD in primary care.

title: #821 Avascular necrosis and risk factors in kidney transplant recipients: a single-center experience
authors: Omer Faruk Akcay; Asil Demirezen; Veysel Tomar; Özant Helvacı; Galip Guz
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal osteodystrophy, osteoporosis, bone fractures, and avascular necrosis (AVN) are prevalent complications observed in the post-transplant period among kidney transplant recipients (KTRs). Despite advances in the transplantation area, AVN remains an important complication after kidney transplantation (KT).
Method
The study included all patients who underwent KT at Gazi University's Nephrology, Dialysis, and Transplantation Unit and had at least one year of routine follow-up (n = 343). Cases of symptomatic AVN were diagnosed by X-ray, radioisotope bone scan, or magnetic resonance imaging. Univariate and multivariate analysis was performed to identify independent risk factors for AVN. Only variables with a p-value < 0.1 were considered for multivariate analysis.
Results
The frequency of AVN in our KTRs was 7.9% during the follow-up period, with a median diagnosis time of 15.2 (10.2–34.9) months. In KTRs with AVN, the leading cause of end-stage renal disease was glomerulonephritis (GN) (52% vs. 20%, P < 0.001), and more rejection episodes occurred at long-term follow-up (33% vs. 15%, P = 0.01). Other demographic characteristics of the study population were similar between groups (Table 1). In univariate analysis, GN [Odds ratio (OR):4.325, 95% Confidence interval (CI), 1.936–9.661], cumulative steroid dosage at post-transplant first year (OR: 1.001, 95% CI, 1.000–1.002) and rejection episodes (OR: 2.792, 95% CI, 1.185–6.578) detected as possible risk factors for AVN. Upon multivariate analysis, GN was identified as an independent risk factor for the development of AVN (OR: 4.373, 95% CI, 1.935–9.880; P < 0.001) (Table 2).
Conclusion
Although limited by a small sample size, our study found GN to be associated with an increased risk of AVN. A higher incidence of AVN may attributed to long-term pre-transplant steroid therapy in this group. In KTRs with a history of GN, early discontinuation of steroids may be considered.

title: #1301 Structural and functional capillary integrity in CKD patients with and without nocturnal hypertension
authors: Marieta P Theodorakopoulou; Fotini Iatridi; Konstantinos Stavropoulos; Artemios Karagiannidis; Maria Schoina; Sofia Manti; Nasra Haddad; Theodoros Dimitroulas; Michael Doumas; Pantelis Sarafidis
abstract:
Background and Aims
Nocturnal hypertension is associated with increased risk for renal and cardiovascular events in patients with chronic-kidney-disease(CKD). Endothelial dysfunction and microvascular damage are highly prevalent in CKD and related to CKD progression and adverse cardiovascular outcomes. The aim of this analysis was to compare for first time microcirculatory function parameters in CKD patients with and without nocturnal hypertension.
Method
96 pre-dialysis CKD patients underwent 24-h ABPM (Mobil-O-Graph-NG device) and nailfold video-capillaroscopy, during which capillary density was measured at baseline, after 4-min arterial occlusion (postocclusive reactive hyperemia) and following 2-min venous occlusion (congestion phase).
Results
The two groups (with and without nocturnal hypertension) were similar in terms of age, eGFR, BMI and major comorbidities. Patients with nocturnal hypertension presented significantly lower capillary density at baseline (30.6 ± 3.6 vs 33.1 ± 3.2 capillaries/mm2; P = 0.003), during post-occlusive reactive hyperemia (36.6 ± 4 vs. 39.5 ± 3.9 capillaries/mm2; P = 0.003), and during venous congestion (38.1 ± 4.2 vs. 41 ± 3.5 capillaries/mm2; P = 0.003) compared to those without nocturnal hypertension. Pulse wave velocity (PWV) was nonsignificantly higher in patients with nocturnal hypertension. Participants with nocturnal hypertension had significantly higher aortic BP and numerically, but nonsignificantly higher PWV; no differences were found in the other parameters of arterial stiffness. The above observations were more prominent in patients with diabetes.
Conclusion
Capillary density during postocclusive hyperemia and after venous congestion is lower in patients with nocturnal hypertension compared to those with normotension, suggesting that nocturnal hypertension is a factor superimposed on the microvascular changes characterizing CKD to further impair capillary recruitment.
