title: #1825 Monitoring of atrial indicators in patients with chronic kidney disease and atrial fibrillation after radio-frequency ablation
authors: Ranokhon Igamberdieva; Sherzod Abdullaev; Muzaffar Asomov
abstract:
Background and Aims
Left atrial (LA) strain is a predictor of the effectiveness of radio-frequency ablation (RFA). This treatment of atrial fibrillation (AF) in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients leads to the development of the LA post ablation dysfunction with inhibition of all components of the deformation, which may cause the development of paroxysms of atrial tachyarrhythmia and thrombus formation in the early postoperative period. The aim is to evaluate atrial dynamic changes in patients with CKD stage III and AF after RFA.
Method
The study involved 114 CKD stage 3 patients with AF, who were divided according to the form of AF into the following groups: group with paroxysmal form AF (n = 80) and group with persistent form AF (n = 34). All patients underwent RFA. All patients underwent transthoracic echocardiography (before RFA, after 72 hours, after 3 months, after a year) against the background of sinus rhythm. During the study, the LA reservoir function, the LA conduit function, the LA emptying fraction, the peak right atrium longitudinal strain was evaluated.
Results
At the beginning of the study, patient performance in the groups with paroxysmal form AF and persistent form AF was statistically consistent: LA reservoir function 27.0 ± 4.6% and 21.1 ± 4.9% (р = 0.047); LA conduit function 17.2 ± 5.5% and 16.2 ± 4.7% (р = 0.58); LA emptying fraction 9.9 ± 4.1% and 7.6 ± 2.7% (р = 0.056); the peak right atrium longitudinal strain 28.2 ± 5.6% and 27.8 ± 6.9% (р = 0.82). In the group with paroxysmal form AF and CKD 3 after RFA, LA functions statistically significantly decreased after 3 days: LA reservoir function 20.7 ± 3.9% (р < 0.001), LA conduit function 11.9 ± 3.1% (р < 0.001), LA emptying fraction 7.83 ± 3.4 (р < 0.001) and increased the peak right atrium longitudinal strain 31.1±6.5% (р = 0.021). After 3 months, there was a statistically significant increase in LA reservoir function 26.6 ± 4.3% (р < 0.001), LA conduit function 16.7 ± 4.3% (р < 0.001), LA emptying fraction 9.9 ± 4.1% (р = 0.004). After a year, LA reservoir function was 26.2 ± 5.7% (P < 0.001), LA conduit function 16.8 ± 5.0% (P < 0.001), LA emptying fraction 9.5 ± 3.6% (P = 0.003), which was statistically significantly higher than in the early postoperative period. The peak right atrium longitudinal strain after a year was statistically significantly higher than before RFA 33.6 ± 6.3% (P < 0.001). In patients with persistent form AF and CKD 3 after RFA, LA functions were statistically significantly depressed: LA reservoir function 19.0 ± 4.3% (р < 0.001), LA conduit function 14.0 ± 3.9% (р < 0.001), LA emptying fraction 5.3 ± 2.6% (р = 0.001). After 3 months, the LA reservoir function increased statistically significantly 23.8 ± 4.1% (р < 0.001), LA conduit function 16.5 ± 3.2% (р < 0.001), LA emptying fraction 7.2 ± 2.2% (р = 0.003). After a year, LA reservoir function was 25.1 ± 3.7% (P < 0.001), LA conduit function 16.5 ± 3.2% (P = 0.001), LA emptying fraction 8.6 ± 2.7% (P = 0.008), which was statistically significantly higher than in the early postoperative period. The peak right atrium longitudinal strain after a year was 31.7 ± 6.2% (P = 0.03), which was statistically significantly higher than before RFA.
Conclusion
In the early postoperative period after RFA in patients with CKD stage III and AF, inhibition of the LA reservoir function, conduit function and emptying fraction is observed, while the peak right atrium longitudinal strain increases. Recovery of LA deformation is noted 3 months after RFA and also persists for a year. The peak right atrium longitudinal strain after a year is statistically significantly higher compared to the preoperative and 3-month stages.

title: #1841 Lipoprotein(a) and chronic kidney disease: a descriptive study in a Spanish cohort
authors: Rodrigo García Marina; David Arroyo Rueda; Gema Sánchez Sánchez; Ursula Verdalles; Andrea J Hernández; Luis Sanchez Camara; Jorge Torres Ortiz; Javier Carbayo; Miguel Angel Encalada; Emina Pervan; Marian Goicoechea
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients have an increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD). Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined risk factor for CVD in general population. Studies suggest that the kidney has a role in Lp(a) catabolism, and Lp(a) levels are increased in kidney disease.
This study aims to describe Lp(a) concentrations and to identify related clinical factors in non-dialysis CKD patients.
Method
Cross-sectional descriptive study. Inclusion criteria were adult patients (18 years or older) visited in the Nephrology Clinic between September 2024 and January 2025 that had a Lp(a) value. Clinical and laboratory data were collected from medical records. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS version 15.
Results
Eighty-six adults were included, 32 (62.8%) males with a mean age of 69.2 ± 17.5 years. The prevalence of comorbidities included 74 patients (85.9%) with dyslipidemia, 63 (73.3%) with hypertension, 32 (37.2%) with diabetes and 9 (10.5%) with fatty liver disease. Twenty-eight patients (32.6%) had a history of cardiovascular events. The most frequent etiologies of CKD were vascular (21, 24.4%) and diabetic (19, 22.1%).
Mean creatinine-based estimated GFR (eGFR) was 49.3 ± 22.8 mL/min, and mean cystatin C-based eGFR was 38.4 ± 22.9 mL/min. Most frequently prescribed antidiabetic drugs included SGLT2 inhibitors (48, 55.8%) and metformin (17, 19.8%), while 10 patients (11.8%) were also on insulin.
Mean Lp(a) levels were 47.3 ± 60.5 mg/dL, with a median of 20.5 mg/dL (IQR 10–57.8). Mean values for the lipid panel were (in mg/dL): LDL-cholesterol, 84.7 ± 43.0; HDL-cholesterol, 53.4 ± 17.4; and triglycerides, 134.9 ± 72.9. Regarding lipid-lowering therapies, 66 patients (76.7%) were on statins, 31 (36.0%) on ezetimibe, 4 (4.7%) on bempedoic acid, 4 (4.7%) on fibrates and 2 (2.3%) on PCKS9 inhibitors.

Patients with Lp(a) levels above the median had a higher urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (22 mg/g, IQR 3–287.5 vs. 20 mg/g IQR 3–164.0, P = 0.041), and an increased prevalence of atrial fibrillation (23.8 vs. 14.7%, P = 0.011).
Conclusion
Lp(a) is an important predictor of cardiovascular events. Some studies have established a relationship between Lp(a) levels and chronic kidney disease. In our cohort, serum Lp(a) levels showed a correlation with a worse kidney function and higher albuminuria. Further implications of these associations need to be investigated in larger cohorts.

title: #1898 Investigating the skeletal muscle and kidney function crosstalk in survivors of critical illness
authors: Heitor Ribeiro; Dário Mondini; Guilherme Santa-Catharina; Lia Marçal; Leila Antonangelo; Luis Yu; Dirce Zanetta; Linamara Battistella; Geraldo Busatto; Carlos Carvalho; Emmanuel Burdmann
abstract:
Background and Aims
The skeletal muscles and kidneys are frequently affected during critical illness, yet their crosstalk remains poorly explored in the long-term. We investigated the crosstalk between skeletal muscle and kidney function in survivors of COVID-19.
Methods
A cross-sectional analysis of a prospective cohort study with survivors of moderate to severe COVID-19 hospitalization in São Paulo, Brazil. Skeletal muscle assessments included handgrip strength, calf circumference, ultrasound-measured quadriceps thickness, and gait speed. Probable and confirmed sarcopenia were assessed by modified European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People (EWGSOP2). Kidney function was assessed by estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR), and urine sediment. Abnormal kidney function was defined as an eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2, albuminuria (≥30 mg/g), and leukocyturia and/or hematuria.
Results
743 survivors (46% female, 43% ≥60 years, 35% with diabetes) were assessed 7 ± 2 months post-hospital discharge. Positive significant associations with eGFR were observed for calf circumference (β = 0.42 ml/min/1.73 m2, 95% CI: 0.06 to 0.78) and thicknesses (mm) of rectus femoris (β = 0.47, 95% CI: 0.01 to 0.94) and vastus intermedius (β = 0.55, 95% CI: 0.14 to 0.96). None of the skeletal muscle parameters were associated with UACR (mg/g). Survivors with sarcopenia (35% probable + 6% confirmed) had lower eGFR (‒9.9 ml/min/1.73 m2, 95% CI: ‒14.4 to ‒5.5) and a higher prevalence of low eGFR (26% vs. 15%; P < 0.001) as compared to those without sarcopenia, but similar frequencies of albuminuria and abnormal urine sediment. Sarcopenia was associated with a higher odd for low eGFR (adjusted odds ratio = 1.83, 95% CI: 1.25 to 2.70), but not with albuminuria nor abnormal urine sediment.
Conclusion
In survivors of moderate to severe COVID-19 hospitalization, muscle mass parameters were associated with eGFR, and those with sarcopenia exhibited lower eGFR, suggestive of chronic kidney disease. These findings suggest the existence of a muscle-kidney crosstalk in this population; moreover, sarcopenia should be considered a significant factor for chronic kidney disease.

title: #2864 Increasing role of digital education—MARKUS@HOMe and the NDT collaboration
authors: Carolin Schneppe; Marlies Antlanger; Insa Elena Emrich; Sara Helena Ksiazek; Marcus Säemann; Andreas Kronbichler; Hans-Joachim Anders; Gunnar Henrik Heine
abstract:
Background and Aims
Continuing medical education (CME) has seen substantial changes in recent years, and nephrologists are increasingly turning to digital content. While traditional media—including textbooks and journals—shall remain the flagship of nephrology education, the increasing role of virtual platforms requires scientific analysis of their visibility and acceptance.
Nephrology Dialysis Transplantation (NDT), one of the official journals of the European Renal Association, and the trinational independent non-profit educational YouTube channel MARKUS at HOMe launched an academic collaboration in September 2023. Together with the NDT's Editor-in-Chief, two nephrology editors from MARKUS at HOMe select one NDT paper each month and invite its corresponding author(s) to participate in a webinar, which is shared on YouTube after recording and editing (Fig. 1).
Method
We compared views (“click rates”) of all NDT/MARKUS at HOMe webinars streamed between September 2023 and December 2024 with access rates of educational content streamed by international nephrology societies (ERA, ASN, ISN) via YouTube, which had a similar number of subscribers compared to MARKUS at HOMe (as of January 2025: 5100 [MARKUS at HOMe], 3860 [ERA], 3710 [ASN] and 3710 [ISN]).
Results
Between 2023 and 2024, authors of 21 articles were invited to an NDT/MARKUS at HOMe webinar. 17 authors (groups) accepted the invitation.
As of 23th January 2025, 13 NDT/MARKUS at HOMe webinars were streamed on YouTube. Their average length was 52:41 minutes, while the average viewing time was only 7:03 minutes. The number of views was on average 691 [463–803].
NDT/MARKUS at HOMe webinars are longer than webinars streamed by leading international nephrological societies (average duration: ERA: 28:00 min, ASN: 25:29 min, ISN: 06:40 min) and median views were higher (ERA: 206 [84–443], ASN: 92 [53–152], ISN: 43 [24–104] Fig. 2).
Conclusion
The cooperation of a leading international journal with an independent educational platform allowed substantial visibility of online CME content. Despite their substantial length, NDT/MARKUS at HOMe videos reach a notable number of views. Of notice, mean viewing time is substantially shorter than the length of the webinars.

title: #2990 The effect of DAPAGLIFLOZIN on biomarkers of CKD progression in patients with β-thalassemia and/or sickle-cell disease
authors: Konstantinos Tsiotsios; Sotirios-Spyridon Vamvakas; Adamantia Bratsiakou; Dimitra Kalavrizioti; Vasiliki Labropoulou; Dimitrios Goumenos; Evangelos Papachristou; Marios Papasotiriou
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with β-thalassemia are at increased risk of developing chronic kidney disease (CKD) due to chronic anemia, iron overload and the administration of iron chelating agents. Accordingly, patients with sickle-cell syndromes, which include sickle-cell anemia and sickle-cell trait, present with typical kidney functional and structural alterations, resulting in urinary concentrating defects, distal nephron dysfunction and albuminuria. Sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT-2i) have been shown to slow the progression of CKD, which may be reflected in decreased albuminuria. The aim of this prospective, non-randomized, open-label study is to investigate the effect of Dapagliflozin at a dose of 10 mg daily on biomarkers of CKD progression in patients with β-thalassemia and/or sickle-cell disease undergoing regular blood transfusions.
Method
In this study, we included adult patients with β-thalassemia and/or sickle cell disease undergoing regular blood transfusions, with a baseline albuminuria of ACR>30 mg/grCr (assessed with a spot urine sample) who received treatment with Dapagliflozin and a second group of patients without albuminuria who did not receive such treatment. In all patients biomarkers of kidney inflammation (MCP-1) and degradation of extracellular matrix (MMP-9) were assessed in urine samples (normalized for urine creatinine) with commercial ELISA kits at baseline and at six months.
Results
We included 16 patients (7 males) with β-thalassemia and/or sickle-cell disease with ACR > 30 mg/grCr and 35 patients (17 males) with β-thalassemia and/or sickle-cell disease without albuminuria. Patients that received Dapagliflozin showed a significant reduction in MCP-1 urine levels (from 40 ± 29 to 23 ± 18 pg/grCr, P = 0.013), whereas there was no difference in MMP-9 levels at six months [from 0.15 (0.02–0.41) to 0.27 (0.01–3.54) ng/grCr, P = 0.160]. Patients that did not receive Dapagliflozin showed an increase in both biomarkers which was though not statistically significant [MCP-1: from 8.91 (5.34–23.3) to 21.92 (9.98–34.75) pg/grCr, P = 0.073; MMP-9: from 0.07 (0.02–0.4) to 0.08 (0.02–0.35) ng/grCr, P = 0.173].
Conclusion
Treatment with Dapagliflozin could be a therapeutic option in patients with β-thalassemia and/or sickle-cell disease and albuminuria, as it could reduce glomerular and interstitial inflammation with favorable impact on CKD progression.

title: #3040 The association of cognitive dysfunction with markers of oxidative stress and vitamin K deficiency in Chronic Kidney Disease patients
authors: Garyfallia Varouktsi; Aikaterini Stamou; Ariti Tsinari; Ioannis Neofytou; Eirini Leptokaridou Mourtzila; Athanasios Roumeliotis; Konstantinos Leivaditis; Stefanos Roumeliotis; Leon Schurgers; Vassilios Liakopoulos
abstract:
Background and Aims
During recent years, it became evident that cognitive impairment is highly prevalent in End-Stage Kidney Disease (ESKD), which was mainly attributed to advanced age and vascular calcification (VC). However, the actual prevalence and incidence of cognitive impairment in Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) are probably underreported. In this study we aimed to investigate the prevalence of cognitive impairment and the possible associations of cognitive function with various traditional and novel VC risk factors in a large cohort of CKD patients.
Method
We recruited 482 CKD patients of all stages (35 stage I, 29 stage II, 79 stage III, 55 stage 4 and 289 end-stage kidney disease-126 Peritoneal Dialysis-PD and 163 Hemodialysis-HD) and measured plasma levels of the inactive vitamin-K dependent Matrix Gla Protein (dp-ucMGP) (CARIM Institute, Maastricht, Netherlands). In these patients we determined arterial stiffness parameters (pulse wave velocity-PWV) by the Mobil-O-Graph device (IEM, Stolberg, Germany), carotid intime media thickness (cIMT) as a marker of arterial calcification with a B-mode ultrasonography and the presence of plaque in the carotid arteries. We also measured serum malondialdehyde (MDA) a marker of lipid peroxidation in the Department of Biochemistry, Medical School of Nis, Serbia, by ELISA.
In our population, we used the MoCA (Montreal Cognitive Assessment) test, a 30-point screening test to detect cognitive impairment in 8 different areas (memory, language, attention and concentration, conceptual thinking, orientation, calculations, executive functions and visuoconstructional skills).
Results
The mean age of all patients was 65.9 ± 15.4 years and 34% were female. Moca score was correlated with central systolic and diastolic blood pressure (r = 0.15, P = 0.02 and r = 0.28, P < 0.0001), cardiac rhythm (r = 0.12 P = 0.04) creatinine (r = 0.35, P = 0.03), age (r = −0.53, P < 0.0001), duration of hypertension, diabetes mellitus and CVD (r = −0.18, P = 0.001, r = −0.32, P < 0.0001 and r = −0.28 P < 0.0001 respectively), glycated hemoglobin (r = −0.35, P = 0.03), high density lipoprotein cholesterol (r = 0.12, P = 0.003), serum MDA (r = 0.12, P = 0.023) and plasma dp-ucMGP (r = −0.22, P < 0.0001), Spearman's rho test. Kruskal-Wallis analysis showed that Moca score was significantly increased in patients with previous history of CVD (P < 0.0001) and those having a plaque in the carotid artery (P < 0.0001). Moreover, MoCA score decreased progressively with CKD stages (P < 0.0001)

Conclusion
Cognitive dysfunction starts early in CKD, is progressively increased with deterioration of kidney function and might be associated with vascular calcification, vitamin K deficiency and increased oxidative stress that are common in this population.

title: #3403 The effect of an integrated community nephrology multi-disciplinary clinic on patients with chronic kidney disease
authors: Erica Zhang; Abdur-Rahman Mirza; Benjamin Dimbleby; Sohaib Feroz; Abu-Bakr Ahmed; Jigyasa Narang; Abdul-Rahman Othman; Nicole Mayisva; Sheena Norgaard; Majeed Khan; Huda Mahmoud
abstract:
Background and Aims
The community-nephrology multidisciplinary team (MDT) service aims to manage individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD) without patients needing to attend hospital appointments.
This analysis aimed to assess the effect of MDT intervention on key markers of renal function.
Method
The virtual community nephrology MDT is conducted weekly. Members include an MDT coordinator, pharmacist, specialist nurse, advanced care practitioner (ACP), and nephrologist. Patients are selected from nephrology outpatient, inpatient and community cohorts, with suitability for inclusion determined by:
Immobility due to age or disability Kidney risk failure equation (KRFE) >5%, medications optimised, and requirement for continued monitoring in outpatient setting Data was collected from service users at a centre in the United Kingdom. Vitals (blood pressure, weight) and biochemical tests (bloods, urine ACR) were collected in the community. MDT interventions included optimising CKD management by initiating therapies such as RAAS blockade, SGLT2 inhibitors, sodium bicarbonate, calcium supplementation, erythropoietin and roxadustat, as well as initiating advanced care planning.
Data was collected at three timepoints: prior to MDT intervention, initiation of first MDT, and most recent follow-up.
Results
A total of 460 service-users from April 2023 to date were recorded. Current active users numbered 135 at the time of data collection, with 106 referred within the last 11 months. Within the last 12 months, 98 individuals have died and a further 121 have been discharged from the service.
114 participants had complete eGFR data for all timepoints. Median delta eGFR from baseline to time of MDT was −5 (IQR −12, 1) ml/min/1.732. Post-MDT median delta GFR was 1 (IQR −4, 9) ml/min/1.732 (P < 0.001).
128 participants were included in BP analysis. Median systolic BP prior to MDT was 132.5 (IQR 120, 146.6) mmHg; post-MDT median systolic BP was 130 (IQR 120, 139) mmHg (P = 0.0491).
Median diastolic BP was 74 (IQR 66, 81) mmHg prior to MDT and 72 (IQR 67, 79.5) mmHg post-MDT (P = 0.17).
Post-MDT, there was a significant improvement in the proportion of patients who had a measured bicarbonate level, with 29.6% of patients having a measured bicarbonate pre-MDT compared to 76.3% post-MDT. 34 patients had bicarbonate measurements both at the time of MDT (median bicarbonate 24.1; IQR 21.8, 29.6 mmol/L) and post-MDT (median bicarbonate 22.8; IQR 19.8, 25.4)) (P < 0.001).
The sub-group that were discharged from the MDT had a median kidney-risk-failure-equation of 1.7 (IQR 0.5, 2.55)%, versus 6.2 (IQR 1.95, 11.4)%, (P < 0.001) in those that remained.
Cost analysis demonstrated a saving of £99.20 per patient to the NHS, comparing MDT virtual follow-ups to single-specialty consultant outpatient appointment at £125 (see Fig. 1).
Conclusion
In this data, a virtual MDT approach resulted in a reduced rate of eGFR decline, reduction of systolic blood pressure, and improved proportion of bicarbonate measurement. This analysis demonstrates that the virtual MDT approach can facilitate improved management of renal health in patients with CKD.

This analysis aimed to assess the effect of MDT intervention on key markers of renal function.
Method
The virtual community nephrology MDT is conducted weekly. Members include an MDT coordinator, pharmacist, specialist nurse, advanced care practitioner (ACP), and nephrologist. Patients are selected from nephrology outpatient, inpatient and community cohorts, with suitability for inclusion determined by:
Immobility due to age or disability Kidney risk failure equation (KRFE) >5%, medications optimised, and requirement for continued monitoring in outpatient setting Data was collected from service users at a centre in the United Kingdom. Vitals (blood pressure, weight) and biochemical tests (bloods, urine ACR) were collected in the community. MDT interventions included optimising CKD management by initiating therapies such as RAAS blockade, SGLT2 inhibitors, sodium bicarbonate, calcium supplementation, erythropoietin and roxadustat, as well as initiating advanced care planning.
Data was collected at three timepoints: prior to MDT intervention, initiation of first MDT, and most recent follow-up.
Results
A total of 460 service-users from April 2023 to date were recorded. Current active users numbered 135 at the time of data collection, with 106 referred within the last 11 months. Within the last 12 months, 98 individuals have died and a further 121 have been discharged from the service.
114 participants had complete eGFR data for all timepoints. Median delta eGFR from baseline to time of MDT was −5 (IQR −12, 1) ml/min/1.732. Post-MDT median delta GFR was 1 (IQR −4, 9) ml/min/1.732 (P < 0.001).
128 participants were included in BP analysis. Median systolic BP prior to MDT was 132.5 (IQR 120, 146.6) mmHg; post-MDT median systolic BP was 130 (IQR 120, 139) mmHg (P = 0.0491).
Median diastolic BP was 74 (IQR 66, 81) mmHg prior to MDT and 72 (IQR 67, 79.5) mmHg post-MDT (P = 0.17).
Post-MDT, there was a significant improvement in the proportion of patients who had a measured bicarbonate level, with 29.6% of patients having a measured bicarbonate pre-MDT compared to 76.3% post-MDT. 34 patients had bicarbonate measurements both at the time of MDT (median bicarbonate 24.1; IQR 21.8, 29.6 mmol/L) and post-MDT (median bicarbonate 22.8; IQR 19.8, 25.4)) (P < 0.001).
The sub-group that were discharged from the MDT had a median kidney-risk-failure-equation of 1.7 (IQR 0.5, 2.55)%, versus 6.2 (IQR 1.95, 11.4)%, (P < 0.001) in those that remained.
Cost analysis demonstrated a saving of £99.20 per patient to the NHS, comparing MDT virtual follow-ups to single-specialty consultant outpatient appointment at £125 (see Fig. 1).
Conclusion
In this data, a virtual MDT approach resulted in a reduced rate of eGFR decline, reduction of systolic blood pressure, and improved proportion of bicarbonate measurement. This analysis demonstrates that the virtual MDT approach can facilitate improved management of renal health in patients with CKD.

title: #3558 Echographic evaluation over time of cardiovascular disorders related to chronic kidney disease in a rat model
authors: Quentin De Berny; Gérémy Blot; Loic Louvet; Gabriel Choukroun; Denis Chatelain; Said Kamel; Lucie Hénaut; Youssef Bennis
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is associated with cardiovascular (CV) disorders, including CV calcifications that contribute to the development of cardiac dysfunction. This study aimed to assess functional cardiovascular impairments due to CKD-related CV calcifications over time using cardiac echography.
Method
CKD associated with cardiovascular calcifications was induced in a rat model using a diet enriched with adenine and phosphate. Twelve male Sprague-Dawley rats (8 weeks old) were divided into two groups: the control group (CT) and the adenine-phosphate (AP) group, which received a diet enriched with 0.3% adenine and 1.2% phosphate for 9 weeks. Cardiac echography was performed at baseline, week 5, and week 9 before euthanasia, followed by histological analysis of the heart and aorta.
Results
AP rats exhibited progressive kidney function impairment, elevated serum phosphorus levels, and CV calcifications. Echographic imaging revealed a progressive decline in cardiac output in AP rats compared to CT rats (Week 0: 87.3 [81.3–95.2] vs. 68.0 [63.8–84.3] mL/min, P = 0.43; Week 5: 38.8 [31.2–40.4] vs. 79.2 [57.5–94.4] mL/min, P = 0.01; Week 9: 33.9 [30.1–35.9] vs. 78.2 [62.4–94.8] mL/min, P = 0.029). No differences were observed in contractility parameters. However, by week 5, isovolumetric relaxation time was significantly prolonged in AP rats (31.5 [27.1–32.7] vs. 24.9 [24.6–25.1] ms, P = 0.009) compared to CT rats, suggesting diastolic dysfunction. This dysfunction occurred without left ventricular hypertrophy. Linear regression analysis revealed a relationship between systolic aortic expansion and kidney function (P = 0.002) as well as the phosphocalcic product (P < 0.001), suggesting aortic stiffness resulting from kidney function impairment and CV calcifications.
Conclusion
Our CKD rat model was associated with cardiovascular calcifications, aortic stiffness and exhibited diastolic dysfunction over time. Further studies are needed to confirm these findings and elucidate the underlying mechanisms.

title: #3601 Challenges in treatment approaches in calciphylaxis: insights from two case studies
authors: Sandra Clementina Salgado Pereira; João Pedro Peixoto de Bessa e Silva; Sofia Leitão e Sousa; Beatriz Silva; Beatriz de Barros; Andreia Campos; Josefina Santos
abstract:
Background
Calciphylaxis is a rare and severe medical condition primarily affecting people with advanced kidney disease, especially those on dialysis. In addition to the time on dialysis, risk factors include uncontrolled hyperparathyroidism, the use of certain medications such as vitamin K antagonist and corticosteroids, female gender, obesity, and diabetes. Calciphylaxis is associated with high morbidity and mortality and there are no specific treatments approved. Sodium thiosulfate is an off-label therapy that reduces tissue calcification. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy has also emerged as a complementary therapeutic option to improve tissue oxygenation and promote wound healing.
Case report
We present two cases of calciphylaxis with similar approaches but different outcomes. The first case is about a 76-year-old woman with over 30 years of hemodialysis, uncontrolled secondary hyperparathyroidism and taking warfarin, who presented with painful skin lesions on her lower limbs that progressed over time. Biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of calciphylaxis. Dialysis strategy was optimized and warfarin was discontinued. Additionally, treatment with sodium thiosulfate and vitamin K agonist was initiated. The patient also started hyperbaric oxygen therapy. She continued to be followed by dermatology for wound care and pain management by anesthesiologists. Despite all treatments, the lesions progressed, leading to lower limb ischemia and amputation. The patient died 132 days after admission. The second case involved a 20-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease due to IgM nephropathy, on hemodialysis for about 3 years following a kidney transplant, and still on corticosteroid therapy and tacrolimus. She also had uncontrolled secondary hyperparathyroidism and her hemodialysis sessions were often shorter than the prescribed 4 hours. She presented with painful ulcers on her lower limbs, and biopsy confirmed calciphylaxis, similar to the first case. Dialysis was optimized and she also started sodium thiosulfate and hyperbaric oxygen therapy. The patient also maintained wound care according to dermatology recommendations and pain management adjustments from the anesthesia team. The patient showed progressive improvement in lesions. The patient completed a total of 22 hyperbaric oxygen therapy sessions and was discharged after 60 days of hospitalization.
Conclusion
The disparate outcomes of the two patients are likely related to the more severe vascular disease in the first patient, due to age and longer duration on dialysis. Optimized wound care and pain management should be prioritized, requiring a multidisciplinary approach to enhance patient care. Sodium thiosulfate and hyperbaric oxygen therapy are off-label treatments that can be complementary and effective therapies and it should be considered on a case-by-case basis.

title: #3630 Cardioprotective effect of a low-protein diet in patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease stages 3-4
authors: Marcela Avila Diaz; Mariana Mora; Daniela Martínez; Edoardo Bermúdez Mercado; M A del Carmen Prado; Ramon Paniagua
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiorenal syndrome is highly prevalent in patients with Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) and significantly increases the risk of cardiovascular mortality. It is currently unknown if the low protein diet might be useful as a nonpharmacologic treatment to prevent cardiovascular events in patients with type 2 diabetes. We aim to know the effect of the low protein diet supplemented with ketoanalogues (KA) on NT-proBNP in patients with chronic kidney disease stages 3–4 and type 2 diabetes.
Method
In a Secondary Analysis of a multicenter randomized clinical trial, which included 161 patients with type 2 diabetes and Chronic Kidney Disease stages 3–4 from 10 hospitals of the Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social. The patients were randomly assigned to Group 1 (with ketoanalogues) or Group 2 (without ketoanalogues). At baseline, patients had a protein intake of 0.8 ± 0.2 g/kg/day. Thereafter, patients were prescribed a diet of 0.6 protein gr/kg/day. We registered clinical and biochemical data from 161 patients at baseline, 136 in the sixth month, and 125 at the twelfth month. We measured NT-proBNP levels with an ELISA assay. Data was analyzed with repeated measures ANOVA and multivariate analysis.
Results
The mean age was 67.5 ± 7.5 years, with a BMI of 28.8 ± 4.5 kg/m² and an eGFR of 23 ± 9 mL/min; 59% were men. At baseline, clinical and biochemical variables were the same in both groups. They showed a decrease in NT-proBNP levels at 6 and 12 months: 1832 (1459–2263), 1606 (1266–1953), 1545 (1249–1703) P < 0.001 vs 1746 (1356–2040), 1572 (1191–1923), 1513 (1185–1822) pg/mL, P < 0.003 in Group 2. However, there were no differences between groups over time. Renal function did not decline during this period, and patients did not transition to dialysis.
Conclusion
In patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease stages 3–4, a low-protein diet, with or without ketoanalogues, had a cardioprotective effect. This approach can help prevent cardiorenal complications and delay the initiation of dialysis, thereby improving the patient's quality of life and reducing costs for healthcare institutions.

title: #3638 Correction of functional iron deficiency & iron sequestration in patients with chronic kidney disease with desidustat: a retrospective study
authors: Anil Jhajhria; Saurabh Gupta; Manisha Dassi; Shipra Choudhary
abstract:
Background and Aims
Functional iron deficiency is a common complication in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. It is mainly due to chronic inflammation causing hepcidin upregulation, which inhibits gut absorption of iron as well as inhibits release of iron from its stored pool in reticuloendothelial system and macrophages.
Current approach for managing functional iron deficiency is to bypass gastro- intestinal (GI) absorption by Intravenous (I/V) dosing of freely available iron with targeting higher levels of ferritin in comparison to absolute iron deficiency, but does not address iron sequestration.
Ill effects of functional Iron deficiency and iron sequestration increase the oxidative stress, cardiovascular risk, contribute to cognitive decline, malnutrition, impaired wound healing, and increased risk of infection.
Desidustat is a Hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor (HIF-PHI), which by stabilizing HIF increases endogenous erythropoietin secretion & suppresses hepcidin. In this study, we have used a novel agent (Desidustat) and compared it with standard of care in correcting iron sequestration and functional iron deficiency.
Method
This was a multi-center retrospective cohort study. Data was collected for period of May 2023 to August 2024. This study included adults, (age > 18 years) who were diagnosed as CKD stage 5 on maintenance haemodialysis (CKD5-D) with anemia and were on maintenance dialysis with dialysis vintage of >3 months and have follow up data for at least 6 months. Patients with other etiology of anemia were excluded (GI bleed etc.). Patients with at least 80% of clinical and laboratory data were included.
Patients were divided into 2 groups. First group was Desidustat group (group size—59). Second group was current standard practice i.e. erythropoietin (EPO) (group size—154). Both groups received I/V iron therapy in proactive based fashion till ferritin >700, Transferrin Saturation >40%. Patients were also on Vit B12 & folate supplement and other standard of care.
Dosing of erythropoietin was as per KDIGO guidelines. Desidustat was started at a dose of 100 mg thrice per week and titrated as per hemoglobin. Patients were on monthly monitoring of Hemoglobin. Ferritin & Transferrin saturation were done at baseline and 3 monthly. Other laboratory tests as per standard of care. Groups were compared using Mann-Whitney U test for difference in hemoglobin & iron status (baseline, 6 months, and change from baseline).
Results
The baseline characteristics were comparable between the two group. There was no significant difference in the hemoglobin, ferritin and Transferrin saturation at baseline. There was no significant difference the rise of hemoglobin between the two groups (Desidustat—3 gram over 6 months vs 2.8 gram in EPO group). There was significant difference in ferritin levels at 6 months in the both groups (Ferritin 380 µg/L in Desidustat group with 58 µg/L decreases from baseline vs 558 µg/L in EPO group, with 110 µg/L rises from baseline). Transferrin saturation level was comparable (Transferrin saturation 30% in Desidustat group, 6% rise from baseline vs 33% in EPO group, 7% rise from baseline).
Conclusion
This retrospective cohort study demonstrate that Desidustat achieves desired hemoglobin levels with significantly less iron sequestration in comparison to EPO group in patients of CKD 5-D with anemia. Patient receiving Desidustat may be switched to I/V iron given in a reactive fashion as it will be more cost effective as well as avoid long term oxidative stress of iron sequestration while also avoiding the ill effects of supraphysiological exogenous erythropoietin.

title: #111 Characteristics of patients with chronic kidney disease and inadequately controlled hypertension: insights from the EnligHTN study
authors: Joachim Weil; Naomi Ben Dor; Terry McCormack; Carmen Suarez Fernandez; Tom Norris; Clement Erhard; Samuel Adamsson Eryd; Vivek Bhalla
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hypertension (HTN) and in particular, uncontrolled and resistant hypertension, is common in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), yet large-scale data on the characteristics of patients with CKD and inadequately controlled HTN are sparse. This study aims to analyze and compare the clinical profiles of patients with CKD who exhibit inadequately controlled blood pressure (BP) while on treatment with at least two antihypertensive medications, against those whose BP is well-controlled under similar treatment conditions.
Method
The EnligHTN study is an observational database study using data from claims and health registries to assess the burden of inadequately controlled HTN. This analysis included data from IQVIA Ambulatory EMR linked with IQVIA PharMetrics® Plus in US (data from other countries will be added later). A total of 8,397 patients diagnosed with CKD and HTN and treated with ≥2 antihypertensive drugs between 2018–2023 were included. CKD was defined as either ≥2 eGFR measures ≥90 days apart, both <60 mL/min/1.73 m2, or a recorded diagnosis of: CKD; end-stage renal disease; hypertensive CKD; diabetic CKD; glomerular diseases; or renal tubulo-interstitial diseases. Patients were considered inadequately controlled if their first office BP (oBP) measurement was above BP target (130/80 mmHg) while being treated with ≥2 antihypertensive drugs for at least 30 days (index). Patient characteristics at index were summarized by oBP control status.
Results
Among patients with CKD treated with ≥2 antihypertensive drugs, 65% had inadequately controlled HTN. Patients with inadequately controlled HTN had a mean oBP of 139/82 mmHg, mean age of 60 (standard deviation (SD): 11) years and 56% were male. Patients with controlled HTN had a mean oBP of 116/69 mmHg, mean age of 62 (SD: 11) years and 54% were male.
The average number of antihypertensive drugs was similar in both groups (2.4 vs. 2.5).
The most prevalent comorbidities in patients with inadequately controlled and controlled HTN were dyslipidemia (63% and 66%, respectively), obesity (62% and 54%, respectively) and type 2 diabetes (44% and 49%, respectively).
A higher proportion of patients whose HTN was controlled were taking sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (8% vs 5%) and statin (52% vs 45%) medications at index, compared to CKD patients with inadequately controlled HTN.
Conclusion
Two thirds of the patients with CKD who were treated with at least 2 antihypertensive drugs had inadequately controlled BP. Comorbidities were commonly present in both those with and without BP at target level. This indicates a significant burden of uncontrolled BP in patients with CKD and comorbid HTN.

title: #719 Urinary collagen-derived peptides as a potential read-out of kidney fibrosis in UUO mouse model
authors: Teresa Frattini; Breuil Benjamin; Marie Buleon; Guylene Feuillet; Mickaël Chabbert; Eléonore Delecroix; Babacar Sylla; Harald Mischak; Igor Golovko; Agnieszka Latosinska; Jean Sébastien Saulnier Blache; Joost Schanstra
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney fibrosis is defined by excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition, primarily collagens, and arises from an imbalance between collagen synthesis and degradation. While collagen synthesis has been extensively investigated, the mechanisms underlying collagen degradation are underexplored. Collagen degradation involves the activity of proteases, including both endo- and exo-peptidases, which generate collagen-derived peptides (CDPs). Based on the assumption that collagen degradation is impaired in fibrosis, the product of collagen degradation, CDPs, are presumed to have an inverse relationship with the progression of fibrosis. CDPs are highly abundant in urine, however, their association with kidney fibrosis remains unclear. The unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO) model is a well-established preclinical approach for inducing kidney fibrosis in rodents, typically within days. Fibrosis only occurs in the obstructed kidney and progresses with time. The UUO model therefore would allow to study the changes in CDPs during the progression of fibrosis. Urinary CDPs collected from the renal pelvis urine would mainly reflect kidney-specific collagen degradation, while bladder urine would predominantly represent adaptations of the non-obstructed, non-fibrotic, contralateral kidney.
Method
To verify the hypothesis whether fibrosis progression could be driven by reduced collagen degradation, we used urinary CDPs as a readout of collagen degradation in the UUO model. 8 weeks old C57Bl6 male mice underwent either UUO or sham surgery and were sacrificed 3- or 7-days later. Kidney fibrosis was evaluated histologically and urinary CDPs present in pelvis and bladder were identified and quantified using mass spectrometry (MS). UUO-pelvis and UUO-bladder urine were both compared to sham-urine. Differences in peptide abundances were considered significant when an FDR-corrected p-value <0.05 was obtained.
Results
Fibrosis was minimally detectable after 3 days and became clearly visible after 7 days in the obstructed kidney following UUO. After 3 days, UUO-pelvic urine contained more than 320 significant and differentially abundant CDPs compared to sham bladder urine, with 70% of them being down-regulated. Similar data were obtained at 7 days. This supports the hypothesis that protease activity against collagen, and consequently collagen degradation, is attenuated in the fibrotic kidney. These data also suggest that impaired collagen degradation is an early event in the development of fibrosis. Additionally, CDPs abundance displayed contrasting trends in the renal pelvis and bladder: CDPs were notably downregulated in the renal pelvis of the fibrotic kidney, but markedly upregulated in bladder urine derived from the contralateral kidney compared to sham animals. This suggest increased protease activity against collagen that might be associated to the compensatory hypertrophy typically observed in the contralateral kidney.
Conclusion
These findings demonstrated that, unlike its effect on bladder urine, UUO induced a rapid alteration in the CDPs content of pelvic urine prior to the onset of detectable fibrosis. Background and Aims
Kidney fibrosis is defined by excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition, primarily collagens, and arises from an imbalance between collagen synthesis and degradation. While collagen synthesis has been extensively investigated, the mechanisms underlying collagen degradation are underexplored. Collagen degradation involves the activity of proteases, including both endo- and exo-peptidases, which generate collagen-derived peptides (CDPs). Based on the assumption that collagen degradation is impaired in fibrosis, the product of collagen degradation, CDPs, are presumed to have an inverse relationship with the progression of fibrosis. CDPs are highly abundant in urine, however, their association with kidney fibrosis remains unclear. The unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO) model is a well-established preclinical approach for inducing kidney fibrosis in rodents, typically within days. Fibrosis only occurs in the obstructed kidney and progresses with time. The UUO model therefore would allow to study the changes in CDPs during the progression of fibrosis. Urinary CDPs collected from the renal pelvis urine would mainly reflect kidney-specific collagen degradation, while bladder urine would predominantly represent adaptations of the non-obstructed, non-fibrotic, contralateral kidney.

title: #1392 Effective interventions to manage the impact of climate change on cardio-renal health: a systematic literature review
authors: Li Li; José Vicente Sánchez Polo; Lucas Hofmeister; Daniel Sierra Lara- Martínez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Climate change is associated with more frequent and extreme weather events that impact human health. The impacts of climate change on cardio-renal health are becoming more apparent. High temperatures can lead to elevated core temperatures, dehydration, and blood hyperosmolality, which in turn result in acute kidney disease, heat-induced inflammatory injury to the kidney, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and kidney stones. Recurrent heat and dehydration are thought to have a role in the growing epidemics of CKD in hot regions of the world where workers are exposed to extreme heat. Increased PM2.5 exposure has been shown to be associated with greater risks of cardiovascular and kidney events in patients with CKD and type II diabetes. There is undoubtedly a growing need for interventions to protect the health of patients, detect and prevent cardiovascular and renal complications opportunely, as well as mitigate climate change. Healthcare professionals are well placed to help their patients alleviate and adapt to the impacts of climate change on health. Therefore, we performed a systematic literature review to research effective interventions that can be implemented by healthcare professionals to manage the impacts of climate change on their patients’ cardio-renal health.
Method
PubMed and Embase were searched for all publications reporting climate change and cardio-renal health-related interventions up to June 2024, using the terms community, individual, healthcare professional, intervention, climate change, and cardio-renal. Studies reporting preventive measures and/or adaptive strategies, observational studies, real-world studies, clinical studies, and case series with ≥10 cases were included.
Results
The searches identified 16,912 eligible records in total. After removing duplicate records, the titles/abstracts of 12,239 records were screened. Of these, the full text of 128 records were reviewed, and the results of nine articles relevant to renal health were summarised (Fig. 1).
The interventions that are directly related to renal health primarily focused on rest-shade-hydration and included: minimising heat exposure through mandatory breaks and provision of shade; hydration before and during exposure, the volume of which matters more than the sugar content (more than 6 L for a 10-hour shift); acclimatisation to hot weather conditions before exertion; inclusion of electrolytes in hydrating liquid; wearing light clothing to allow sweating; and promptly dealing with heat-related illness.
Measures that indirectly impact renal health by promoting cardiovascular health included: use of air conditioning and electric fans, increasing fluid intake, accessible public cooling facilities, improved kitchen ventilation, use of face masks, portable air-filtration units, ‘eco-wellness’ through mindfulness (e.g. encouraging plant-based eating), and heat warning systems during heatwaves for the general population.
Conclusion
The widespread impact of climate change, combined with the increase of an older proportion of the population might lead to a deterioration of cardio-renal health patient outcomes. While there are effective measures to protect patient health, there is an urgent need for research on evidence based strategies to reduce the cardio-renal complications related to climate change. We encourage healthcare professionals to continue to grow their knowledge and develop interventions in this rapidly growing field for patient and planetary health benefits.

title: #1860 Alterations in physical performance and body composition are already present in patients with chronic kidney disease stage G3
authors: Elife Ozturk; Jessica Noelmans; Monique Mullens; Jeroen Kooman; Marc Hemmelder
abstract:
Background and Aims
The prevalence of physical frailty and sarcopenia is high in patients with end stage kidney failure. However, it is not well known how and to which extent abnormalities in physical performance, muscle strength and body composition are developing in patients with earlier stages of chronic kidney disease (CKD). In the present study we compared parameters related to these domains in patients with CKD stage 3–5ND to control subjects.
Method
In a cross-sectional study, 131 patients with CKD (41.2% stage 3, 58.8% stage 4–5ND) and 72 control subjects were included. Physical performance was assessed by the 6 minute walk test, 4 meter walk test and, muscle strength by handgrip strength, body composition measurement and ultrasound of the quadriceps muscle. Data are provided as mean ± standard deviation.
Results
Patients with CKD were 68 ± 9 years, 69% was male and had an eGFR of 28.7 ± 12,5 ml/min/1.73 m; controls patients were 66 ± 10 years; 75% were male and had an eGFR of 77.3 ± 10.2 ml/min/1.73 m. There was no significant difference in age (P = .07) and sex (P = .3) between the two groups. Performance on the 6 minute walk test (control subjects 662 ± 72 meters vs patients with CKD 469 ± 146 meter, P < 0.001), 4 meter walk test (control subjects 2.4 ± 0.4 seconds vs patients with CKD 3.1 ± 1.0, P < 0.001), as well as handgrip strength (control subjects 37 ± 9 kg vs patients with CKD 32 ± 11 kg, P < 0.001) were significantly lower in CKD patients as compared to control subjects. We found the same differences in the subgroup of patients with CKD G3 (6 minute walk test 490 ± 141 meters, 4-meter walk test 3.0 ± 1.0 seconds, handgrip strength 34 ± 12 kg, all P < 0.01 compared to control subjects). Fat tissue index was significant different between CKD patients and controls (t (187) = −5.63, P < 0.001), the diameter of the quadriceps muscle was significantly reduced in CKD patients (t (198) = 2.9, P < 0.01]. Lean tissue index was not significant different between patients with CKD and controls [t(188) = .69,P = .49].
Conclusion
Physical performance and muscle strength were significantly lower in CKD patients compared to control subjects and already apparent in patients with CKD stage G3. Quadriceps ultrasound appears to be a more sensitive tool than bioimpedance to detect changes in muscle mass. Both observations may have direct relevance for timing and focus of intervention programs in earlier stages of CKD.

title: #3204 Uremic toxicity impairs the endothelial barrier through phosphorylation of tyrosine 658 on VE-cadherin
authors: Regiane Da Cunha; Carolina Amaral Bueno Azevedo; Guilherme Miniskiskosky; Maria Vitória Guimarães del Amo; Paulo Cézar Gregorio; Roberta Kelly Lemos de Souza; Fellype Barreto; Andréa E M Stinghen
abstract:
Background and Aims
p-Cresyl sulfate (PCS) and indoxyl sulfate (IS) are protein-bound uremic toxins that are closely linked to endothelial dysfunction in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). The structure of the endothelium is compromised in CKD, especially due to the disruption of cell-cell junctions. One of the affected proteins is VE-cadherin, the main component of the endothelium's adherens junctions and crucial for maintaining vascular integrity. Post-translational regulation of VE-cadherin is crucial for its function and stability, with phosphorylation at the Tyr658 site playing a key role in weakening cell junctions and increasing endothelial permeability. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying the disruption of cell-cell junctions are not yet fully understood in the uremic environment. This study aims to evaluate the effects of PCS and IS on VE-cadherin expression and its Tyr658 phosphorylation site, a crucial regulator of endothelial intercellular junctions.
Method
Human endothelial cells (EA.hy926, ATCC CRL-2922) were exposed to PCS (23 mg/L) and IS (37.07 mg/L) at uremic concentrations for 24 hours. Cell viability was assessed by the MTT assay. The protein levels of total VE-cadherin and its Tyr658 phosphorylated fraction were evaluated by western blotting and immunofluorescence assay.
Results
IS significantly reduced (ANOVA and Dunn's multiple comparisons test: P < 0.0001) the cell viability of endothelial cells compared to the control (untreated cells). No significant changes in total VE-cadherin protein levels were observed across the different treatments. However, our data demonstrated a significant increase (Kruskal-Wallis test: P = 0.0029; Dunn's multiple comparisons test: P = 0.0014) in the fraction of phospho-VE-cadherin at the Tyr658 site in endothelial cells exposed to IS compared to the control (Fig. 1A). The immunofluorescence assay also showed greater immunolabeling of phospho-VE-cadherin in cells treated with IS (Fig. 1B).
Conclusion
Our data demonstrated that IS induced the phosphorylation of VE-cadherin at the Tyr658 site, a signaling event closely associated with a reduction in barrier function by the endothelium. These alterations may lead to increased endothelial permeability and, ultimately, to the development of atherosclerotic lesions and other cardiovascular diseases.

title: #3238 Longitudinal study in a population with CAKUT and risk factors
authors: Rosita Greco; Teresa Papalia; Michele Provenzano; Agata Mollica; Gianluigi Zaza
abstract:
Background and Aims
Congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT) are a group of disorders responsible for the majority of pediatric end-stage renal disease cases. CAKUT is phenotypically variable and can affect the kidney(s) alone and/or the lower urinary tract. The spectrum includes more common anomalies such as vesicoureteral reflux and, rarely, more severe malformations such as bilateral renal agenesis. The aim of the study was to assess the risk factors for the onset of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and the progression to kidney failure (KF, i.e. the need of dialysis or kidney transplantation) in a cohort of patients with CAKUT.
Method
We conducted a retrospective, observational study at the Nephrology, Dialysis and Transplantation Units of Annunziata Hospital of Cosenza. We enrolled consecutive patients with CAKUT from 2005 to 2020 Risk factors of CKD and KF were assessed via Logistic Regression. Stepwise selection method (p value of 0.100) was used the most related risk factors for each endpoint.
Results
We studied 51 patients with CAKUT, 17 females and 34 males. The most frequent causes of CAKUT were renal agenesis (13.7%), renal dysplasia (17.6%), vesicoureteral reflux (31.4%). Cystic diseases, renal hypoplasia, and more rare causes such as Prune-Belly syndrome or Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome were also reported. When testing the risk factors for CKD we found that irregular growth (odds ratio, OR 97.4, P = <0.001) and arterial hypertension (OR 73.2, P = 0.001) were independently associated with CKD. Risk factors for KF were arterial hypertension (OR 10.9, P = 0.022), proteinuria (OR 6.5, P = 0.040), and body weight at birth (OR 0.1, P = 0.005). Body weight at birth was significantly lower in patients who developed KF (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
The long follow-up in these children with CAKUT allowed us to find traditional and non-traditional predictive risk factors for CKD and progression of kidney damage to ESRD. Early and appropriate treatment of these risk factors could improve the prognosis of renal disease. In addition, the correlation between low birth weight and renal failure may be explained by lower functional renal activity at birth. Indeed, the number of nephrons correlates with birth weight.

title: #3514 Outcomes of young adults in an advanced kidney care service in the United Kingdom
authors: Hannah O'keeffe; Rosemary Donne; Philip A Kalra; Constantina Chyrsochou; Ibrahim Ali
abstract:
Background and Aims
Information provided to patients in advanced kidney care services (AKCS) is often focused on overall outcomes with an emphasis on quality versus quantity of life, including consideration of conservative care. This is usually not appropriate for younger patients, with a gap identified by young adults and clinicians in our service regarding the requirement for more bespoke education materials. Working towards this, we have considered outcomes of younger adults in a longitudinal cohort in AKCS.
Method
Patients between 18 and 30 years old who first attended AKCS in our organisation between September 2011 and September 2018 were included. Patients are routinely referred to AKCS once their estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) falls below 20 ml/min/1.73 m2. Patients had a minimum of five years follow-up to September 2023. Patients with a prior transplant, and those who recovered renal function and were discharged from AKCS were excluded, leaving 53 aged 18 to 30 years at first attendance. Analyses were conducted using SPSS.
Results
Of the 53 patients, 25 (47.2%) were female and 28 (52.8%) male. At first AKCS attendance median age was 26.4 years (IQR 23.3–28.0) with median eGFR 13.0 ml/min/1.73 m2 (IQR 10.5–17.5). Median follow-up was 9.1 years (IQR 7.2–10.6). 73.6% (n = 39) were of white ethnicity, 18.9% (n = 10) Asian, 1.9% (n = 1) black, 3.8% (n = 2) mixed and 1.9% (n = 1) other or not stated. A wide variety of CKD aetiologies was observed, the most common being IgA nephropathy in 17.0% (n = 9), an obstructive cause in 15.1% (n = 8), and diabetes in 9.4% (n = 5).
The median time from first AKCS visit to renal replacement therapy (RRT) commencement was 24.8 months (IQR 13.2–36.0). The first RRT modality was haemodialysis in 32.1% (n = 17), peritoneal dialysis in 28.3% (n = 15), and a pre-emptive transplant in 30.2% (n = 16). The remaining 5 patients (9.4%) had not reached RRT by the end of follow-up. The majority of patients (71.7%, n = 38) were transplanted by the end of follow-up, with median time to transplantation of 24.4 months (IQR 7.7–37.8). Of those transplanted, 55.3% (21/38) received a deceased donor transplant, 42.1% (16/38) a living donor transplant, 2.6% (1/38) a simultaneous pancreas and kidney transplant, and 42.1% (16/38) of the transplants were pre-emptive. Unfortunately, there were 3 deaths in the cohort during follow-up. The 95% 5-year survival of this younger cohort contrasts to the 5-year survival of 50% for the overall AKCS cohort (median age 66.1 years) for the same period.
Conclusion
Approximately a third of patients started RRT on each of haemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, or with a pre-emptive transplant, with a significant proportion (71.7%) transplanted during follow-up. First visit to AKCS was at a median eGFR of 13 ml/min/1.73 m2, and earlier review would be expected to further increase pre-emptive transplantation rates by enabling greater time for evaluation and listing. A patient-identified gap in our young adult service is the requirement for targeted and age-appropriate education materials which should be co-designed with patients to reflect the information they require. These results can help to improve information shared with these patients, by providing an improved understanding of the outcomes of young adults with advanced kidney disease.

title: #3571 ATTR V30M amyloidosis and kidney-heart axis: how DPD-scan cover a misleading interpretation
authors: José Pedro Escaleira; João Bessa; Andreia Campos; Ana Cunha; Patrícia Rodrigues; Lúcia Costa; Josefina Santos; Luísa Correia Lopes Lobato
abstract:
Background and Aims
ATTR V30M amyloidosis is a rare hereditary disease characterized by the deposition of transthyretin (TTR), commonly leading to chronic kidney disease (CKD) and heart failure. Technetium-99m-3,3-diphosphono-1,2-propanodicarboxylic acid (DPD) scintigraphy is crucial for non-invasive cardiac amyloidosis (CA) diagnosis. However, amyloid fibril composition appears to influence its sensitivity. This study aims to clarify possible shadowed kidney-heart interfaces, unravelling future therapeutic approaches.
Method
We retrospectively analyzed ATTRV30M patients followed by nephrologists at a single centre from 2014 to 2025; 111 cases who underwent DPD scintigraphy and echocardiography were included; DPD images were reviewed based on visual scoring Perugini method. Diagnostic criteria for CA: interventricular septal thickening ≥12 mm (without other cause) or a Perugini score ≥2 (positive DPD), besides no plasma cell disease. The cardiorenal assessment was established on the National Amyloidosis Centre (NAC) staging system, based on N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR): stage 1, NT-proBNP ≤3000 ng/L and eGFR ≥45 ml/min; stage 3, NT-proBNP >3000 ng/L and eGFR <45 ml/min; stage 2, remainder. eGFR was calculated using the CKD-EPI creatinine-cystatin equation (2021).
Results
49 (44%) patients had no evidence of CA, the majority women (71%) having developed the first symptoms of the disease, mainly neuropathy, at 34 yo, median. Non-CA cases showed low NAC scores (77%), however males accounted for half of NAC stages 2 or 3, mainly due to higher rates (29%) of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), compared to women (6%). title: #215 Responsiveness to roxadustat in non-dialysis chronic kidney disease patients with anemia by baseline hemoglobin: a secondary analysis of the ROXSTAR Registry
authors: Jianghua Chen; Weiming He; Shirui Tang; Cuihua Huang; Qionghua Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Clinical practice guidelines recommend initiating anemia treatment in non-dialysis (ND) chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients when hemoglobin (Hb) levels fall below 100 g/L. However, in real-world clinical practice, treatment is often delayed until Hb levels drop below 90 g/L. This secondary analysis of the ROXSTAR Registry (ChiCTR2100046322) aimed to evaluate Hb target achievement with 52-week roxadustat use in ND-CKD patients, stratified by baseline Hb levels.
Method
This secondary analysis utilized data from the ROXSTAR Registry. ND-CKD patients who received roxadustat and had at least one post-baseline Hb measurement were included. Oral supplemental iron could be administered at any time according to clinical practice, while intravenous iron was administered if clinically indicated per investigator's judgement. Outcomes included the proportion of patients achieving mean Hb within 100–130 g/L and changes from baseline (CFB) in Hb averaged over weeks 24–52, stratified by baseline Hb subgroups (<90 g/L, ≥90 g/L); CFB in iron metabolism parameters (serum ferritin [SF], transferrin saturation [TSAT], serum iron, total iron binding capacity [TIBC], transferrin) and roxadustat weekly dose by visit were also evaluated by subgroup.
Results
Overall, 490 ND-CKD patients (baseline Hb <90 g/L: 146; baseline Hb ≥90 g/L: 344) were included (196 male [40.0%]), with a mean ± standard deviation age of 55.0 ± 14.0 years. The overall mean baseline Hb was 95.3 ± 12.2 g/L (baseline Hb < 90 g/L: 80.5 ± 8.0 g/L; baseline Hb ≥ 90 g/L: 101.6 ± 7.3 g/L). Patients with baseline Hb <90 had lower SF (median: 109.7 µg/L vs. 119.1 µg/L), lower TSAT (21.8% vs. 26.3%), and a higher proportion of elevated C-reactive protein (19.2% vs. 13.1%), compared to those with baseline Hb ≥90 g/L (Table 1).
Overall, 84.8% (95% CI: 81.1%, 88.6%) of patients achieved mean Hb levels within 100–130 g/L, with higher achieving Hb target rates in the baseline Hb ≥90 g/L group (88.3% [95% CI: 84.4%, 92.3%] vs. 76.6% [95% CI: 68.6%, 84.6%]). Patients with Hb<90 g/L demonstrated greater Hb CFB (27.0 [95% CI: 24.6, 29.3] g/L vs. 11.2 [95% CI: 10.0, 12.5] g/L). During treatment, 54.7% of patients received iron therapy, with higher utilization in the baseline Hb <90 g/L group (64.4% vs. 50.6%) (Table 1).
Patients with baseline Hb<90 g/L experienced larger declines in SF (CFB: −63.6 µg/L vs. −35.6 µg/L at week 24; −46.3 µg/L vs. −35.6 µg/L at week 52), and greater increases in TSAT (CFB: 3.4% vs. 0.1% at week 24; 6.5% vs. 0.0% at week 52), similar increased trend was observed for serum iron, TIBC and transferrin (Table 2).
Roxadustat mean weekly dose was higher for patients with baseline Hb <90 g/L (250.9 ± 82.7 mg vs. 193.9 ± 82.8 mg): it started at 261.8 ± 63.0 mg, slightly decreased to 239.7 ± 104.9 mg at week 24, and then slightly increased to 245.8 ± 101.3 mg at week 52; while for patients with baseline Hb ≥90 g/L, it started at 227.4 ± 69.2 mg, decreased to 180.3 ± 98.2 mg at weeks 24, then increased to 192.5 ± 102.8 mg at week 52.
Conclusion
Roxadustat effectively corrected anemia, maintained target Hb levels, and improved iron utilization in ND-CKD patients in real-world settings, irrespective of baseline Hb levels. However, fewer patients with baseline Hb <90 g/L achieved target Hb levels despite higher roxadustat doses and iron use, highlighting the potential benefits of earlier anemia treatment initiation when Hb levels are ≥90 g/L.

title: #348 Deletion of hypoxia-inducible factors in erythroid progenitor cells does not significantly impair erythropoiesis
authors: Pei-Zhen Tsai; Szu-Yu Pan; Shuei-Liong Lin
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor (HIF-PHI) has been shown to promote erythropoiesis through the activation of erythropoietin production and iron mobilization. However, the effects of HIFs in the erythroid lineage are not clear. We aimed to study the effects of erythroid lineage-specific deletion of HIFs on erythropoiesis using preclinical models.
Method
EporGFP-Cre/+;Hif1aF/F;Hif2aF/F mice were used to achieve erythroid lineage-specific deletion of HIFs. Surface expressions of TER-119, CD44, and forward scatter (FSC) were used to define erythroblast, reticulocyte, and red blood cell in the bone marrow. Propidium iodide and surface annexin V expressions were used to define apoptosis. The adenine nephropathy model was used to mimic chronic kidney disease in humans.
Results
Compared with littermate Hif1aF/F;Hif2aF/F mice, EporGFP-Cre/+;Hif1aF/F;Hif2aF/F mice had similar hematocrit and a similar percentage of TER-119+ cells in the bone marrow. The differentiation and apoptosis of erythroblasts, reticulocytes, and mature red blood cells were not affected. When mice were challenged with adenine nephropathy model to mimic chronic kidney disease, the hematocrit and differentiation of erythroid lineages also remained similar between EporGFP-Cre/+;Hif1aF/F;Hif2aF/F mice and littermate Hif1aF/F;Hif2aF/F mice.
Conclusion
Inactivation of HIF in murine erythroid progenitor cells does not significantly impair erythropoiesis. Factors other than HIFs, such as erythropoietin, may play a more significant role in erythroid lineage survival and differentiation during erythropoiesis.

title: #714 Disease trajectory among patients with chronic kidney disease
authors: Chunyang Li; Xiaoxi Zeng; Chao Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD), imposes a significant burden on both health and the economy. However, comprehensive analysis of the cross-talks with temporary order of disease trajectory following CKD diagnosis remains unclear.
Method
From 502,507 UK Biobank participants, 5,578 CKD patients without any other comorbidity preceding CKD diagnosis were identified. Disease trajectory after CKD was constructed with three interrelated steps. Firstly, CKD patients were individually matched with up to 5 participants without CKD by birth year, sex, and Townsend deprivation index (transformed to tertiles). Phenome-wide association analysis (PheWAS) using conditional Cox regression with age as underlying time-scale was performed to evaluate the association between CKD and subsequent risks of 468 medical conditions. Conditions occurred in at least 250 CKD patients, with a p value less than the Bonferroni correction threshold and hazard ratio (HR) >1, were considered in the second step of the analysis. Secondly, we conducted binomial tests to explore whether a later diagnosis (Disease 2, D2) occurring after another previous diagnosis (Disease 1, D1) was dominant (>50%) among CKD patients with both D1 and D2 diagnoses. All possible D1 and D2 pairs with a temporal order that occurred in at least 125 CKD patients, with binomial test p value <Bonferroni correction threshold was included in the next step. Thirdly, nested case-control study using conditional logistic regression was performed to evaluate the association between D1 (exposure) and D2 (outcome) pairs identified in the second step. At most 2 controls were matched to each case with identical characteristics as mentioned above. Disease pairs occurred in at least 50 CKD patients, passing Bonferroni corrected threshold with odds ratio (OR) >1, were considered as significant. The trajectory network was formed by combining disease pairs that share overlapping diseases. For example, the disease pairs D1→D2 and D2→D3, with D2 as the overlapping disease, were combined into the trajectory D1→D2→D3. Medical conditions were retrieved from UK Biobank inpatient records using 3-digit ICD-10 codes, and combined conditions with clinical or biological similarities. Only the first record and corresponding date were maintained for analysis.
Results
CKD significantly increased the risks of 43 subsequent medical conditions, including infectious disease, metabolic, circulatory, respiratory and musculoskeletal system diseases. There were two main clusters of affected diseases following CKD: circulatory and metabolic system diseases. Hypertensive disorder and diabetes served as important mediators linking a series of downstream health outcomes originating from CKD. For example, hypertensive disorder after CKD led to downstream sepsis, iron deficiency anemia, diabetes, obesity, hypothyroid conditions, heart failure, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, inflammatory arthritis, as well as acute renal failure from ischemic heart disease (Fig. 1A). CKD preceding diabetes was associated with a range of downstream trajectories, including progression from anemia to disorders of fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance, as well as from disorders of lipoprotein metabolism and other lipid abnormalities to heart failure and hypotension (Fig. 1B). Furthermore, CKD was also associated with a subsequent trajectory leading from acute renal failure to pneumonia (Fig. 1C).
Conclusion
Individuals with a primary diagnosis of CKD and no prior comorbidities exhibit increased risks of a variety of subsequent medical outcomes, which offer potential intervention targets for inhibiting adverse events in CKD patients.

title: #1438 Population-based analysis of metabolic-associated steatotic liver disease as a risk factor for end-stage kidney disease in chronic kidney disease patients
authors: Sehoon Park; Dong Ki Kim; Kwon Wook Joo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Metabolic-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a newly introduced terminology for liver disease associated with metabolic dysfunction. The clinical significance of MASLD requires further investigation, particularly in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD).
Method
We utilized the claims database of South Korea, which includes comprehensive health screening examination results, to identify MASLD and evaluate kidney function. A total of 190,025 CKD patients without a prior history of end-stage kidney disease were included in the analysis. We assessed the incidence of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), defined as the initiation of dialysis or receipt of a kidney transplant. Multivariable Cox regression analysis was performed, adjusting for factors including age, sex, income, smoking status, physical activity, baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) or albuminuria, body mass index (BMI), total cholesterol, and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels.
Results
The mean age of the study population was 63.3 years. Among the participants, 63,833 patients had MASLD, while 93,348 had no evidence of steatotic liver disease (SLD). Additionally, 3,600 patients had metabolic-associated liver disease (MetALD), and 6,926 had alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD). In terms of ESKD risk, the MASLD group showed a significantly higher risk (HR 1.15, 95% CI 1.08–1.22). Conversely, the risk was not elevated in the MetALD group (HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.83–1.15) or the ALD group (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.99–1.22). Subgroup analyses revealed that the increased risk was more pronounced in females (HR 1.61, 95% CI 1.49–1.73) than in males (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.90–1.02), with a significant interaction term (P < 0.001).
Conclusion
MASLD is a significant risk factor for ESKD in CKD patients, particularly among females. Clinicians should be aware of this elevated risk when managing CKD patients with MASLD.

title: #1441 Diet-by-polygenic score interaction effects on kidney function
authors: Giulia Barbieri; Michele Filosi; Ryosuke Fujii; Giovanni Malerba; Dariush Ghasemi-Semeskandeh; Martin Gögele; Pramstaller Peter; Cristian Pattaro; Essi Marjatta Hantikainen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects 10% of the worldwide population. While diet plays a key role in CKD prevention and management, interaction between diet and CKD genetic predisposition is largely unexplored. We investigated the interplay between a polygenic score (PGS) and dietary patterns in determining the CKD-defining trait, the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), in the Cooperative Health Research In South Tyrol (CHRIS) study.
Method
We derived eGFR for 5,717 individuals without CKD and related morbidities (median age: 40 years; 53% females; median eGFR: 101.7 ml/min/1.73 m2). Using data from the GA2LEN food frequency questionnaire, we estimated the CKD-relevant nutrients protein, potassium, and phosphorus, and the overall diet quality as the Dietary Approach to Stop Hypertension (DASH) index. We derived the eGFR PGS using 131 high-quality imputed variants, with effect sizes derived from a large genome-wide association study meta-analysis (n = 1,046,070), and where variants were selected for kidney function relevance and identified using an additive genetic model. We fitted multiply adjusted generalized additive models incorporating tensor product smooths and diet-PGS interaction terms to model non-linear associations with eGFR.
Results
The PGS explained 1.5% of the eGFR variance. Among dietary exposures, the DASH score explained the largest proportion (2.2%), followed by potassium (1.9%), proteins (1.8%), and phosphorus (0.2%). In all models, the PGS was linearly associated with eGFR (P < 0.0001), regardless of dietary exposures. All nutrients showed statistically significant linear associations with eGFR, while the association with the DASH score was not significant. Proteins and phosphorus showed significant non-linear interactions with the PGS (protein:PGS P = 0.0298; phosphorus:PGS P = 0.0283), indicating that higher intake of these nutrients was associated with lower eGFR levels in individuals with a high PGS but not in those with a low PGS.
Conclusion
The PGS explained a modest proportion of eGFR variance and interacted significantly with dietary proteins and phosphorus. These findings suggest genetic predisposition to potentially modify the association between protein and phosphorus intake, and kidney function.

title: #1538 Sleep habits, sleep quality, and fatigue among people with chronic kidney disease
authors: Ginger Chu; Andrea Viecelli; Shilpanjali Jesudason; Sarah Russo; Vasif Abdullatheef; Ben Lazarus; Lisa Matricciani; Cassandra Foster; Catherine Blackmore; Richard Leleu; Ritin Fernandez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Healthy sleep habits are highly recommended for individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD) to improve quality of life and reduce kidney function decline. However, there is limited research on sleep habits of people with CKD and their impact on sleep quality and fatigue. This study aims to describe sleep habits among the CKD population and identify its correlation with sleep quality and fatigue.
Method
A cross-sectional survey was conducted in four nephrology units across three Australian states between 1 August 2024 and 31 December 2024. Data were collected from adults with CKD anonymously using both paper-based questionnaires and online surveys. title: #2277 Trends and associations between decreased estimated glomerular filtration rate, metabolic syndrome, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease in children and adolescents: a 15-Year data analysis
authors: Keum Hwa Lee; Kyungchul Song; Jae Il Shin; Hyun Wook Chae
abstract:
Background and Aims
Metabolic syndrome and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) are well-known risk factors for decreased estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in adults. However, studies on their association and prevalence trends in children and adolescents are limited. This study aims to investigate the trends and associations between decreased eGFR, metabolic syndrome, and NAFLD in Korean children and adolescents aged 10–18 years from 2007 to 2021.
Method
This cross-sectional study analyzed data from 8,971 youths aged 10–18 years with an eGFR of less than 90 mL/min/1.73 m2 using data from the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KNHANES). The study examined the association between low eGFR and various factors, including age, sex, height, weight, body mass index (BMI), waist circumference, fasting glucose, triglycerides, blood pressure, alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and nutritional intake (calories, carbohydrates, protein, and fat).
Results
The prevalence of low eGFR showed a decreasing pattern, with a 24.5% reduction from 2008–2010 compared to the previous year and a 6.1% reduction from 2013–2021 (P = 0.037, 0.018). In contrast, NAFLD showed an increasing trend since 2010 with a 7.5% increase (P < 0.0001), although no significant change was observed from 2008–2010 (P = 0.281). This pattern was more pronounced in children aged 10–12 years, with no significant findings in other age groups.
Carbohydrate intake showed an increasing trend until 2011, followed by a decline until 2021 (P = 0.0118, 0.0354). Protein intake increased (P < 0.0053), while fat intake also increased (P = 0.0017). Correlation analysis revealed that an increase in fat intake was associated with a decrease in low eGFR (P < 0.001), while greater carbohydrate intake was linked to a reduced prevalence of NAFLD (P = 0.0081).
Conclusion
Although a positive correlation between low GFR and NAFLD is generally reported, this study observed an inverse correlation in adolescents aged 10–12 years. In contrast to adult chronic kidney disease (CKD) where protein and fat intake are restricted, the trends in this study suggest that protein and fat intake do not directly influence the prevalence of low GFR in children. However, increased fat intake may be associated with NAFLD. These findings indicate that children with low eGFR may adopt different dietary patterns compared to the general population, possibly due to cautious dietary habits.
