title: #2705 Trends of congestive heart failure in patients with non-dialysis and dialysis-dependent chronic kidney disease: a nationwide study
authors: Roosa Lankinen; Juan-Jesus Carrero; Marie Evans; Anne-Laure Faucon
abstract:
Background and Aims
In patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), impairment in sodium and water excretion often results in fluid overload and an increased risk of congestive heart failure, conditions associated with unfavorable outcomes. Whether temporal trends of heart failure hospitalization have changed compared to the general population is not fully investigated, particularly since the implementation of current standard cardio-nephroprotective drugs. Here, we assess rates and temporal trends of hospitalization for congestive heart failure in patients with advanced CKD.
Method
Using data from the Swedish Renal Registry, we conducted an observational study including patients with non-dialysis dependent CKD stages G4 and G5, and patients on hemodialysis (HD) and peritoneal dialysis (PD) from 2011 to 2021. Patients were followed until occurrence of hospitalization for heart failure, death or progression to a more severe stage of CKD or change in dialysis modality. Poisson models were used to estimate rates and age-sex adjusted rate ratios, along with standardization in proportion 1:10 to an age- and sex-matched general population. The consumption of diuretic medications including loop diuretics, thiazides and thiazide-like diuretics, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists was also described.
Results
We included 25 591 patients with CKD stage 4 (age 74 years, 36% women), 13 968 with CKD stage 5-ND (72 years, 37% women), 10 635 patients on HD (68 years, 34.2% women) and 4511 patients on PD (67 years, 32% women). Prevalence of heart failure was relatively similar across patient groups (approximately 25% in patients with CKD G4, G5-ND and PD, and 32% in HD), whereas diuretic use increased with more severe CKD (65% in patients with CKD G4, 71% in CKD G5, 73% in HD, and 86% in PD).
Overall, the rates of hospitalization for congestive heart failure increased with more severe stages of CKD, being 3.5 to 7.6 times higher than in the general population. During 2011–2021, use of diuretic medications decreased in patients with non-dialysis dependent CKD (8.7% and 5.1% decrease in CKD G4 and G5, Fig. 1 A). This was paralleled by an increase in the rates of heart failure (51% and 36% increase in patients with CKD G4 and G5, Fig. 1B–C). Increasing trends in standardized rates (Fig. 1D) suggest the increased HF rate to be higher than that observed in the general population.
In contrast, while use of diuretic medications increased both in patients on maintenance HD and PD (24.3% in HD, 8.3% in PD), the rate of heart failure increased substantially in HD (30%), but remained relatively stable in patients on PD (1%).
Conclusion
During 2011–2021, this nationwide study shows that patients with non-dialysis dependent CKD stages 4–5 and on HD experienced increasing rates of hospitalization for congestive heart failure. Although it is possible that a lower use of diuretic medications explains, in part, this trend in non-dialysis patients, there is an urgent need for optimized cardiorenal protection with appropriate dosing and improved management of fluid overload in this high risk population.

title: #2917 Efficacy and safety of low protein diet on top of SGLT2i regarding glycemic control in patients with CKD and type 2 DM
authors: Elena Cuiban; Ileana Adela Vacaroiu; Daniela Radulescu; Flavia Liliana Turcu; Elena Stepan; Ovidiu Ionut Mihailescu; Liliana Garneata
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sodium-glucose-transporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and low protein diet are guideline-recommended interventions for the management of chronic kidney disease (CKD). Data supports that both interventions express synergistic kidney-protective effects, delaying the progression of CKD by decreasing glomerular hyperfiltration and proteinuria. In patients with diabetes mellitus treated with SGLT2i, the long-term benefits and safety of low protein diets are debated, especially because of the high carbohydrate intake, with a potential negative impact on the glycemic control secondary to decreased protein intake.
Method
We are reporting a multicenter two-arms randomized controlled trial (ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT06281899) aiming to evaluate the effectiveness and the safety of low protein regimens on top of SGLT2i in reducing the progression of CKD in patients with type 2 Diabetes Mellitus with eGFR 60 to 25 ml/min/1.73 m2 and/or proteinuria >500 mg/g urinary creatinine. A total number of 200 patients have to be enrolled, with a follow-up duration of 12 months. Patients in the intervention arm are prescribed a plant-based low protein diet (LPD) (0.6 g proteins/kg weight per day) associated with dapagliflozin 10 mg per day, patients in the control group are prescribe normal protein diet (NPD) (0.8 g proteins/kg weight per day) associated with dapagliflozin 10 mg per day. The primary composite outcome is time to the first occurrence of any of the components of the composite: ≥30% sustained decline in eGFR or reaching end stage kidney disease or cardiovascular death or renal death, but several non-renal secondary outcomes, including change in HbA1C and serum albumin levels are included.
Results
We present the preliminary results on 86 enrolled patients who reached the end of the follow-up period (see Fig. 1 for general characteristics). However, we have not achieved the statistical significance for the primary composite outcomes, preliminary results suggested a positive impact of low protein regimen over SGLT2i on glycemic control in study population. In control (NPD) group patients the HbA1c decreased, but not significantly at 3 months (7.42 ± 1.63 vs 7.11 ± 1.05, P = 0.111) and 12 months (7.42 ± 1.63 vs 7.22 ± 1.35, P = 0.944). In the intervention (LPD) group, HbA1c lowered significantly at 3 months (6.17 ± 0.86 vs. 6.68 ± 1.11, mean difference = −0.5 ± 0.36, P = 0.035) and at 12 months (6.17 ± 0.86 vs. 6.88 ± 1, mean difference = −0.57 ± 0.09, P < 0.001). The decrease in HbA1c at 3 months was not significantly different between the analyzed groups (P = 0.690), however, at 12 months, the decrease of HbA1c was consistent at 12 months only in the intervention group (median = −0.6, IQR = −0.61 to −0.5) compared to NPD (control) group (median = 0, IQR = −0.45–0.5) (P = 0.027) (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
Low protein diet on top of SGLT2i is safe and effective in terms of glycemic control in patients with CKD and type 2 diabetes mellitus.

title: #2986 Patient reported outcome measures and individualized strategies using electronic feedback (PROMISE): implementation outcomes
authors: Zhihua Huang; Fiona Yeo; Li Choo Ng; Jason Choo; Cynthia Lim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Health literacy is defined by the ability to access, understand, evaluate and apply healthcare-related information and services to make informed health decisions. Low health literacy may limit self-management and cause poorer health outcomes. We designed, implemented and evaluated a digital intervention utilizing patient-reported measures to support patient health literacy and self-management.
Method
We performed a single-center prospective single-arm pilot study with a post-design on the implementation outcomes and utility of telephone text message-based self-administered surveys on (i) symptom self-monitoring (swelling in the ankles, legs or face and worsening frothy urine); (ii) health-related quality of life (HrQOL assessed by the EQ5D5L general health status score and domains of mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain or discomfort, and anxiety or depression); (iii) self-management resources, and (iv) self-efficacy (assessed using the SES6C survey).
The Patient Reported Outcome Measures and Individualized Strategies using Electronic Feedback (PROMISE) program was offered to patients with active glomerulonephritis receiving immunosuppressants on follow up at the Glomerulonephritis Disease Management Clinic, Singapore General Hospital. Patients who gave verbal consent were sent a telephone message with a link to a survey to confirm their consent and preferred language (English, Chinese, Bahasa Malay and Tamil). Subsequent text messages with links to surveys for patient-reported measures were sent every month for the first 6 months then 3-monthly for the next 6 months then 6-monthly for the next 12 months (“milestones”).
We evaluated the patients who were enrolled between December 2023 and November 2024 during the first 12 months of the program, with data collection until 31st December 2024. The implementation outcomes were adoption (number of patients enrolled and number of responses), fidelity (proportion of eligible patients who completed the surveys at each milestone) and feasibility (patient self-management and the clinical team's follow-up to patients’ responses).
Results
Twenty-six patients with active glomerulonephritis receiving immunosuppressants were enrolled from the Glomerulonephritis Disease Management Clinic between November 2023 and December 2024. Figure 1 shows that the response rate was 50% for the first survey and subsequently fluctuated between 28%–50% at each milestone. There were 84, 57, 42 and 56 responses for the symptom self-monitoring survey, EQ5D5L survey, self-management resources survey and self-management ability survey, respectively. The median health status was 82 (67, 98). The patients with “abnormal” responses in the symptom self-monitoring or EQ5D5L surveys (moderate or severe problems in mobility [n = 2], usual rogramo v [n = 1], pain or discomfort [m = 4], and anxiety or depression [n = 2]) were followed up by the clinical team via telephone call within a week. One patient was scheduled for an early clinic review where she was found to have a relapse that required augmented immunosuppression. One patient was advised to be hospitalized for evaluation for fever and lethargy. The other patients received advice over the telephone and declined further intervention.
Resposes requesting for information related to glomerulonephritis (n = 27), chronic kidney disease (n = 25), immunosuppressant medications (n = 21) were directed to online resources hosted by our institution. There were fewer responses requesting consultations with the renal coordinator (n = 8), pharmacist (n = 2), dietician (n = 5), physiotherapist (n = 3), occupational therapist (n = 2), and medical social worker (n = 1).
Figure 2 shows the self-efficacy scores in all responses. The mean scores in all domains remained consistently high during the first 12 months of the program.
Conclusion
A digital intervention utilizing telephone text message-based self-administered surveys can support patient self-management during immunosuppressive therapy for active glomerulonephritis.

title: #3441 Nephrology and primary care: integrated care program for chronic kidney disease
authors: Patricia Fernández de la Llama; Nadia Ayasreh Fierro; Mª Antonia Llauger; M A Victoria Feijoo; Elisabet Coll Piera; Silvia Benito; Elizabeth Romelia Viera Ramírez; Lluis Guirado Perich; Francesca Calero
abstract:
Background and Aims
Over the past 26 years, we have developed a strategic program for the management of chronic kidney disease (CKD) in collaboration with primary care (PC) to enhance renal health and improve the quality of care for CKD patients.
Method
This program has involved implementing various initiatives, including clinical actions, training sessions, coordination efforts, and activities with patients. title: #764 Association of plasma trace element levels and Mini Mental State Examination scores in HD, PD and CKD patients
authors: Esin Oğuz Kozan; Cagla İpek Sayın; Baris Sariakcali; Suleyman Koz
abstract:
Background and Aims
Association between trace elements and cognitive functions is a growing area of interest in the general population. Cognitive impairment is prevalent among dialysis patients. Plasma boron (B) chromium (Cr), manganese (Mn) copper (Cu), nickel (Ni), zinc (Zn) selenium (Se), strontium (Sr) and molybdenum (Mo) body stores and plasma levels may change with decreasing glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and dialysis. Here, we aimed to analyse the relationship between the elements mentioned above and some aspects of cognitive functions.
Method
This cohort was derived from a larger cohort. The data we present here are from subjects in the main cohort who agreed to and were able to complete the Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE).
Trace element data from the main cohort were previously published (https://academic.oup.com/ndt/article/38/Supplement_1/gfad063d_2947/7196120, accessed on 2 January 2025). Of the 172 participants in the main study, 136 were able to perform the MMSE.
Hemodialysis (HD), peritoneal dialysis (PD) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients with decreased GFR and a control group (CG) with GFR >90 ml/min were included in this study (n = 136). Plasma samples from participants were analyzed for trace elements by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) (Thermo Scientific™ iCAP Q ICP-MS, USA) for the trace element assays. Sensitivity was in the range of ppb (µg/L). A validated MMSE was used to assess cognitive function, with a score higher than 23 suggesting intact cognitive functions, and scores lower than 23 indicating impaired cognitive functions (Ethical permission no: 2020-01/38).
Results
In total, 55 participants (40.4%) had an MMSE score below 23, while 81 participants (59.6%) scored 23 or higher. Univariate analysis conducted on all participants (n = 136) show that Cr53 and Se are significantly associated with MMSE. The data are presented in the Tables 1 and 2.
Conclusion
The present data suggest significant associations between cognitive function and some trace elements. However, no further conclusions can be drawn at this moment.

title: #993 Clinical implications of diabetic retinopathy as a predictor of the severity of diabetic kidney injury and systemic inflammation in patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus: focusing on a histologically confirmed diabetic nephropathy
authors: Eun Young Seong; Sang Heon Song; Da Woon Kim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) has been the most common causative disease of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) and commonly combined with diabetic retinopathy (DR). However, some DKD patients do not present with DR. This study aimed to investigate clinical implications of DR in histologically confirmed DKD, and to highlight the importance and give new meaning to DR testing in DKD.
Method
A total of 250 patients who underwent kidney biopsy were enrolled, patients with missing data or combined glomerulonephritis were excluded. In the final analysis, a total of 108 patients were analyzed (DKD with DR, n = 71 vs. DKD without DR, n = 37). Histologically confirmed-DKDs were classified as class I through IV according to Renal Pathology Society Classification. We used Red blood cell distribution width (RDW)/Albumin ratio (RAR), C-reactive protein for comparative analysis of systemic inflammation.
Results
Patients in DR (+) group were younger and had higher systolic blood pressure compared to those in DR (−) group. The DR (+) group had lower estimated glomerular filtration rate and serum albumin levels than the DR (−) group (eGFR; 36.7 vs. 59.9 mL/min/1.73 m2, P = 0.001 / albumin; 3.4 vs. 3.9 g/dL, P = 0.001). There was no difference in CRP levels between the two groups, but RAR was higher in the DR (+) group compared to the DR (−) group (3.935 vs 3.407, P = 0.003). Histologically, the degree of kidney injury was significantly more severe, and linear deposition of IgG and kappa positivity in IF staining was more common in the DR (+) group compared to the DR (−) group (class III; 54.9% vs. 37.8% / class IV; 35.2% vs. 18.9% / IgG; 66.2% vs. 43.2% / kappa; 53.5% vs. 29.7%).
Conclusion
The presence of DR in histologically confirmed DKD patients may indicate the presence of severe kidney injury and higher systemic inflammatory condition associated with diabetes. Therefore, screening for diabetic retinopathy should be performed to provide important clinical clues for appropriate and effective management of diabetes-related kidney damage and systemic inflammation.

title: #1315 Circulating extracellular vesicles: a mediator of renal tubular oxidative stress, mitochondrial Ca2+ overload and SIRT1/PGCα axis suppression in obesity
authors: Xiaqing Li; Lianghong Yin; Zibo Xiong; Meng Yu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Obesity is associated with an increased risk for kidney disease. Oxidative stress has been involved in the pathogenesis of kidney diseases. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) act as endocrine factors and mediate metabolic organ crosstalk. However, their roles in renal tubular damage in obesity main unknown. We intend to investigate the related mechanisms of circulating EVs in obesity-induced oxidative stress, mitochondrial Ca2+ overload and damage of renal tubular epithelial cells (RTECs).
Method
To construct obesity models, 4-week-old C57BL/6J male mice were treated with a high-fat diet for 18 weeks. Aiming to explore the function of EVs, plasma EVs were isolated from lean subjects (Lean-EVs) and patients with obesity (Obese-EVs). 8-week-old HFD mice received an intraperitoneal injection of GW4869 (a blockade of EVs) and RTECs were co-cultured with EVs. The generation of intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) was assessed by confocal microscopy using DCFH-DA staining. Mitochondrial Ca2+ content in RTECs was assessed by Fura-2 AM staining using a microplate reader. The levels of renal tubular markers KIM-1 and NGAL were assessed by qRT-PCR, Western blog(WB) analysis and immunohistochemistry. Levels of serum creatinine (sCr), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and urinary ACR(UACR) were detected. In addition, bioinformatics analysis were also executed to pinpoint the function of SIRT1/PGC-1α in obese-related renal tubular injury, which was also confirmed by WB in vitro experiments.
Results
We showed that HFD mice had significantly increased sCr, BUN, UACR, and renal tubular injury markers KIM-1 and NGAL. Obese-EVs significantly increased tubular ROS generation and mitochondrial Ca2+in vitro. Moreover, the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis was downregulated in RTECs co-cultured with Obese-EVs. The blockade of Obese-EVs effectively alleviated renal tubular injury.
Conclusion
Obese EVs-mediated promoted oxidative stress by ROS overgeneration, mitochondrial Ca2+ overload and SIRT1/PGC-1α axis downregulation, thus exacerbating the progression of obesity-related renal tubular injury, which can emerge as a promising therapeutic avenue to treating obesity-related renal afflictions.

title: #1652 Clinical characteristics and healthcare resource utilization associated with mild, moderate and severe Hyperkalemia in Spain: IBERIK+ Study
authors: Marco Montomoli; Enrique Morales Ruiz; Patricia De Sequera Ortiz; Roberto Alcazar Arroyo; Miquel Blasco Pelicano; Miren Sequera Mutiozabal; Ana Roncero Martin; Alberto Ortiz; Jose Luis Górriz
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyperkalemia (HK) is a frequent complication in patient with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and heart failure (HF), especially among those treated with renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors (RAASi). This study aims to explore the clinical characteristics of these patients and analyze their healthcare resource utilization (HCRU), comparing groups that developed mild, moderate, and severe HK in Spain.
Method
A descriptive, retrospective study conducted using the BIG-PAC database with Python technology in Spain. Patients with relevant diagnosis codes and/or treatments for HK and/or potassium values >5.0 mmol/L recorded in their medical history between January 2013-December 2020, with at least 2 years of follow-up, were included. The inclusion date was defined as the first HK event. Baseline characteristics and HCRUs were analyzed by HK severity: mild (5.0–5.4 mmol/L), moderate (5.5–5.9 mmol/L), and severe (≥6.0 mmol/L).
Results
A total of 7,006 patients (mean age: 66.9 ± 14.5 years; 52.0% women; mean BMI: 27.6 ± 4.8 kg/m2; mean eGFR: 68.1 ± 26.9 mL/min/1.73 m²; mean Charlson Comorbidity Index: 1.8 ± 2.0) were analyzed. Among them, 50.3%, 37.5%, and 12.2% had mild, moderate, and severe HK, respectively. The proportion of patients with a diagnostic code and/or treatment for HK increased with severity (mild: 22.3%, moderate: 36.6%, severe: 70.5%). Patients included with severe HK were older (mean age: 75.7 years vs 69.4 years moderate, 62.9 years mild), had a higher prevalence of comorbidities, including at least one of the following: CKD, Type 2 diabetes, hypertension and HF (81.8% vs. 79.5% moderate, 47.5% mild) and higher use of medications, particularly cardiovascular drugs (88.6% vs. 79.9% moderate, 60.1% mild) (Table 1). During the follow up period, patients included with severe HK had higher HCRUs (Table 2), including more primary care visits (14.6 vs. 13.4 moderate, 12.5 mild), specialist visits (4.8 vs. 3.2 moderate, 2.1 mild), emergency room visits (3.6 vs. 3.0 moderate, 2.1 mild) and higher hospitalization rates (34.6% vs. 25.3% moderate, 15.4% mild).
Conclusion
Our data highlight those patients with severe HK face greater clinical complexity and worse outcomes, as well as increased HCRU. These findings could underscore the critical importance of early detection to slow disease progression and improve HK management. This is particularly significant given that most patients experiencing mild to moderate HK episodes remain largely underdiagnosed and undertreated, representing a critical gap in care.

title: #2795 Dimethylaminoparthenolide as a new inhibitor of renal fibrosis in rat
authors: Jonas Laget; Juliana Boukhaled; Irene Cortijo; Joost Schanstra; Jean Sébastien Saulnier Blache; Anne Dominique Lajoix; Bernard Jover; Flore Duranton; Angel Argiles Ciscart; Fabrice Raynaud; Nathalie Gayrard
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is predicted to become the 5th leading cause of death by 2040. Current treatment of CKD mostly relies on non-specific therapies targeting hypertension (RASi, inhibitors of the renin angiotensin system) or blood glucose elimination (SGLT2i, inhibitors of SGLT2) that positively affect intrarenal hemodynamic. CKD progression is associated with kidney fibrosis. Successfully preventing and reversing renal fibrosis should be complementary to currently available therapies. Dimethylaminoparthenolide (DMAPT, a water-soluble form of parthenolide) is a sesquiterpene lactone with anti-inflammatory and anti-tumour activity. It has previously been shown to protect from diabetic kidney disease in mice [1]. We tested the hypothesis that DMAPT could prevent kidney fibrosis in a rat model of surgically induced CKD and aimed to compare DMAPT with the currently used therapies, Ramipril (RASi) and Dapagliflozine (SGLT2i).
Method
Eight-week-old Sprague-Dawley rats underwent subtotal nephrectomy (SNx, n = 34) or Sham surgery (Sham group, n = 8). After 1 week of recovery, SNx rats where treated with placebo (SNx group, n = 12), DMAPT at 10 mg/kg/day (DMAPT group, n = 12) or Ramipril at 10 mg/kg/day and Dapagliflozine at 1 mg/kg/day (RD group, n = 10) in the food for 7 weeks. At the end of the protocol, transdermal glomerular filtration rate (GFR, Medibeacon device) and arterial blood pressure were measured before blood, urine and organs (kidney, heart) sampling. Plasma creatinine and urea (Epoc instrument), albuminuria (ELISA kit), Sirius Red, Periodic Acid Schiff (PAS) and Collagen I immunohistochemistry (IHC) stainings in kidney, were determined, as well as mRNA expression of pro-inflammatory (Mcp1, Il1β) and kidney injury markers (Kim-1, Lcn2). Data were analysed with one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc tests comparing groups two by two.
Results
GFR was reduced whereas plasma creatinine and urea concentrations were increased in SNx group versus Sham (P < 0.001) and treatments with DMAPT or Ramipril + Dapagliflozine did not improve these parameters versus SNx (Table 1). Urine albumin-creatinine ratio was increased in SNx (versus Sham, P = 0.0038) and reduced by Ramipril + Dapagliflozine (RD vs Sham, P = 0.0099). Higher systolic arterial pressure (P = 0.0572) and left ventricle weight (indexed to tibia length, P = 0.0336) were seen in SNx (vs Sham), and the values were normalised after treatment with Ramipril + Dapagliflozine (P = 0.0358 and 0.0021, respectively) (Table 1). Treatment with DMAPT decreased Sirius Red (P = 0.0020), PAS (P = 0.009) and Collagen I IHC (P = 0.0012) stainings in kidney, versus SNx (Fig. 1a–d). Similar tendencies were observed in RD group but with lower statistical significance (P = 0.0213, P = 0.0657 and P = 0.0793 for Sirius Red, PAS and Collagen I, respectively). Finally, DMAPT reduced the mRNA expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines Mcp1 (P = 0.0091) and Il-1β (P = 0.0551) whereas Ramipril + Dapagliflozine decreased expression Il-1β (P = 0.0543) and of kidney injury markers such as Kim-1 (P = 0.0050) and Lcn2 (P = 0.0340) (Fig. 1e).
Conclusion
Arterial pressure increase and left ventricle hypertrophy, typically observed in the SNx rat model, were normalised by Ramipril + Dapagliflozine treatment but unchanged by DMAPT treatment. Interestingly, in presence of hypertension, DMAPT treatment reduced kidney fibrosis (Sirius Red and Collagen I IHC stainings), glomerulosclerosis (PAS staining) and expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Mcp1, Il-1β). DMAPT is a promising anti-fibrotic compound for the treatment of CKD, complementary to existing therapies.

title: #3005 Asiaticoside alleviates renal fibrosis by regulating Th17/Treg cell homeostasis through binding to STAT3
authors: Li-Jun Xie; Bin Wang; Bicheng Liu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal fibrosis (RF) is a significant pathological change in chronic kidney disease (CKD) that leads to kidney function loss and ultimately results in end-stage kidney disease (ESRD). CD4+ T cells play a role in RF development. Th17 cells promote RF, whereas Treg cells help alleviate it. Centella asiatica was a traditional herb with a variety of pharmacological activities, which was used in traditional Chinese medicine for anti-inflammation and anti-scar formation. Asiaticoside (AS), the primary active ingredient in Centella asiatica, is known for its therapeutic properties. It has been reported in many animal experiments that AS could alleviate renal fibrosis, but its mechanism have not been well defined. Thus, we employed network pharmacological analysis and mouse renal tissue transcriptome sequencing to systematically elucidate how AS alleviates RF.
Method
We used network pharmacological analysis to predict the potential targets and signaling pathways of RF treatment by AS. To verify and evaluate these mechanisms, we constructed a UUO (10 d) mouse model, which was divided into normal control group, UUO model group, and AS drug group (divided into 3 dose groups, 100 mg/ (kg*d), 50 mg/ (kg*d), and 10 mg/ (kg*d), with 10 mice in each group. DdH2O was used to dissolve AS to the appropriate concentration. title: #109 Managing PASC in CKD patients: implications for long-term care and health outcomes
authors: Rumen Filev; Mila Tsankova; Boris Bogov; Krasimir Kalinov; Lionel Rostaing
abstract:
Background and Aims
The COVID-19 pandemic has had profound implications for individuals with Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD), a population already at risk for severe health outcomes. Post-Acute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 Infection (PASC), or long COVID, has emerged as a significant challenge, particularly for CKD patients. This study examines the long-term impact of PASC on CKD patients over a three-year period, highlighting the effects on renal function and overall health.
Method
This single-center, prospective observational study followed 120 COVID-19-positive patients, including 70 with pre-existing CKD, for three years. Patients underwent regular clinical assessments focusing on renal function (serum creatinine, eGFR) and the presence and severity of PASC symptoms such as fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and chest pain. The study also evaluated the role of ARB/ACEi therapy in managing PASC symptoms in CKD patients. Statistical analyses, including ANCOVA and logistic regression, were performed to identify significant differences between groups.
Results
CKD patients exhibited slower recovery of renal function post-COVID-19 compared to non-CKD patients, although no permanent deterioration in renal function was observed. The study revealed that CKD patients exhibited a slower recovery from COVID-19, also in terms of the persistence of PASC symptoms. At the 12-month mark, 60% of CKD patients continued to report significant fatigue, compared to 50% of non-CKD patients. By 18 months, cognitive dysfunction persisted in 45% of CKD patients, while only 35% of non-CKD patients reported the same. Chest pain was reported by 25% of CKD patients at 18 months, compared to 20% of non-CKD patients. All these changes can be seen on Fig. 1.
Notably, no significant association was found between ARB/ACEi therapy and the severity or duration of PASC symptoms, suggesting that these medications do not exacerbate long COVID in CKD patients.
Conclusion
The study highlights the vulnerability of CKD patients to prolonged PASC symptoms, which can significantly impact their quality of life and recovery trajectory. While no permanent renal impairment was observed, the extended duration of PASC symptoms underscores the need for ongoing monitoring and comprehensive care strategies tailored to this population. ARB/ACEi therapy remains a safe and viable option for managing CKD in the post-COVID-19 context, without exacerbating PASC symptoms.

title: #606 Relationship between vascular biomarkers, NT-proBNP and renal function in chronic kidney disease, IgA nephropathy
authors: Balázs Sági; Tibor Vas; Csenge Gál; Zoltán Horváth-Szalai; Tamás Kőszegi; Judit Nagy; Botond Szabolcs Csiky; Tibor Kovács
abstract:
Background and Aims
IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is the most common primary glomerular disease. Endothelin-1 (ET-1) is one of the strongest vasoconstrictor material in the blood. N-terminal prohormone of brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) is associated with renal function and poor outcomes in chronic kidney disease (CKD). Serum endocan is a biomarker associated with proinflammatory cytokines and the increase of serum level plays a critical role in inflammatory, proliferative, and neovascularisation processes associated with poor cardiovascular outcomes in patients with CKD too. Identifying high-risk patients using biomarkers could help to optimise their treatment.
Method
Ninety patients with biopsy-confirmed IgAN were included in the study (50 males/40 females, mean age: 54.9 ± 14.4 years). Serum endocan, ET-1 and NT-proBNP were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay kits. Echocardiography was performed and carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (cfPWV) was measured by SphygmoCor in this cross-sectional study.
Results
Patients were divided into two groups based on serum endocan median level (cut-off: 44 µg/l). There was significantly higher aorta systolic blood pressure (SBPao) (P = 0.013), NT-proBNP (P = 0.028), albumin/creatinine ratio (P = 0.036) and uric acid (P = 0.045) in case of the higher endocan group compared to the lower. There was also significantly higher SBPao (P = 0.037) and NT-proBNP (P = 0.038) in the case of higher endothelin-1 (ET-1) levels compared to the lower (cut-off: 231 pg/ml) group by two-sample t-test. Then we divided the patients into two groups based on the eGFR (CKD 1–2 vs. CKD 3–5). The serum endocan, NT-proBNP, cfPWV, SBPao, left ventricular mass index (LVMI), uric acid and albuminuria were significantly higher in the CKD 3–5 group compared to the CKD 1–2 group. The serum endocan and NT-proBNP levels were significantly higher in the diastolic dysfunction group (P = 0.047, P = 0.015). There was a significant increase in serum endocan levels (CKD 1 vs. CKD 5; P = 0.008) with decreasing renal function.
Conclusion
In IgAN, vascular biomarkers (endocan, ET-1) may play a role in endothelial dysfunction through vascular damage and elevation of SBPao. Serum endocan, ET-1 and NT-proBNP biomarkers may help to identify IgAN patients at high risk.

title: #1003 Co-exposure of environmental DEHP and melamine increases adverse kidney outcomes in patients with early chronic kidney disease—a prospective cohort study
authors: Yi-Chun Tsai; Hui-Ju Tsai
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a global public health problem. The impact of environmental change on CKD onset or progression was gradually attracted. This study aimed to explore the interaction of environmental phthalates, particularly di-(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) and melamine in adverse kidney outcomes in early CKD cohort.
Method
We conducted this prospective cohort study to enroll patients with CKD stages 1–3 in 2006–2010. Urinary corrected ten phthalate metabolites and melamine levels (ratio of urinary melamine/urinary creatinine) were measured by LC-MS/MS at enrollment. Kidney outcomes included doubling of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) decline >5 ml/min/1.73 m2 per year, doubling of serum creatinine levels, and progression to end stage kidney disease (ESKD). Subjects were followed till targeted renal outcomes, cancer, death, last contact, or the end of observation in December 2020.
Results
A total of 396 subjects, the median urinary corrected MEHP and melamine levels were 2.4 μg/g and 0.7 μg/mmol. Over a median follow-up period of 7.6 years, 56 subjects (15.2%) had decline of eGFR >5 ml/min/1.73 m2 per year and 113 reached doubling of serum creatinine levels or ESKD (30.6%). Subjects in the highest quartile of urinary corrected MEHP had a 4.01 (95% CI: 1.72–9.35) hazard risk for eGFR decline >5 ml/min/1.73 m2 per year compared to those in the lowest tertile. Similar significant dose-response results were found in doubling of serum creatinine levels or ESKD. Furthermore, subjects with both urinary corrected MEHP and melamine above the median value had the fastest eGFR decline.
Conclusion
Urinary MEHP level can predict adverse kidney outcomes in early stage CKD patients. Synergistic effect between MEHP and melamine exposure on rapid decline in kidney function is further noticed in our environment.

title: #1564 Is testosterone a risk factor for age-related loss of kidney function in men? the renal iohexol study
authors: Vetle Saastad; Toralf Melsom; Ludvig Balteskard Rinde; Bjørn Eriksen; Inger Enoksen; Guri Grimnes
abstract:
Background and Aims
The reasons for sex differences in chronic kidney disease (CKD) prevalence are not well understood but may involve sex differences in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) decline rates. Healthy women in their 50s have lower measured GFR (mGFR) than men, yet men experience a steeper age-related decline. These differences are not explained by comorbidities or traditional CKD risk factors.
Testosterone is hypothesized to be a risk factor for GFR decline in men through its effects on renal tubular cells and the renin-angiotensin system. We investigated the association of serum levels of total testosterone, free testosterone, and sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) with age-related mGFR decline and new-onset CKD.
Method
The Renal Clearance Survey in Tromsø6 (RENIS-T6) is a prospective cohort study conducted from 2007 to 2009 as part of the population-based sixth Tromsø study. A representative sample of 800 men aged 50–62 years old from the general population without cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or kidney disease was investigated with iohexol clearance in RENIS-T6. Participants were followed with repeated mGFRs in RENIS-FU (2013–2014, n = 656) and RENIS-3 (2018–2020, n = 578) with a median follow-up time of 11 years.
The association of free-and total testosterone and SHGB on mGFR decline, new incident CKD, and accelerated mGFR decline, defined as 10% with steepest GFR slope (>1.7 ml/min per 1.73 m2 per year), were analyzed using linear mixed models, interval-censored Cox regression, and logistic regression.
Results
Total testosterone (per unit increase; 0.27 ml/min per 1.73 m2, 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.10 to 0.45; P < 0.01) and SHBG (per unit increase; 0.83 ml/min per 1.73 m2, 95% CI, 0.23 to 1.0; P < 0.01) were associated with a higher mGFR at baseline in the multivariable-adjusted linear mixed model analyses. Neither free testosterone, total testosterone, nor SHGB was associated with mGFR decline (Table 1). ((Per 1 unit increase in free testosterone: GFR change of 0.004 ml/min per 1.73 m2 per year, 95% CI, −0.11 to 0.12; P = 0.95), per 1 unit increase in total testosterone: GFR change of −0.02 ml/min per 1.73 m2 per year, 95% CI, −0.04 to 0.01; P = 0.17) and per 10 unit increase in SHBG (−0.06 ml/min per 1.73 m2 per year, 95% CI, −0.15 to 0.03; P = 0.18)).
The odds ratio (OR) of accelerated GFR decline decreased by 10% (OR, 0.90; 95% CI, 0.84–0.96) per unit higher total testosterone level and 27% (OR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.61–0.89) per 10 unit higher SHBG level adjusted for only age. These results were not statistically significant after adjusting for BMI (P > 0.05).
Conclusion
Total testosterone and SHBG were associated with a higher mGFR at baseline in a healthy male population aged 50 to 75 years. The sex hormones were not independently associated with mGFR decline or incident CKD during 11 years of follow-up.

title: #1794 Association between simple renal cyst and renal function: a retrospective cohort study
authors: Mikhail Olalo; Trisha Michelle Manalaysay
abstract:
Background and Aims
Simple renal cysts are prevalent, benign kidney lesions often found incidentally in older adults, requiring no intervention unless symptomatic or causing mass effect. They are considered harmless; yet their association with renal function as an indicator of kidney disease remains unclear. This study aims to identify the association of simple renal cyst and renal function in terms of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), proteinuria and hematuria.
Method
The research was conducted in the out-patient department of a tertiary government hospital in Davao City, Philippines utilizing a retrospective cohort design. The patients enrolled in the study were those with simple renal cysts from January 2015 to December 2023. The eGFR, proteinuria, and hematuria, together with the characteristics of simple renal cysts in terms of cyst count and maximum cyst diameter, were analyzed for correlation with interval data after at least one year. Chi-square test was used to determine the association of the variables in terms of renal decline. Patients with ultrasound findings suspicious for polycystic kidney disease, solitary kidney and incomplete data were excluded.
Results
This study included a total of 523 patients. The results showed that simple renal cysts were predominantly solitary (51.1%) and frequently observed in males (66.3%), primarily in those over 60 years of age (70.7%) with chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 2 (43%) at baseline. After a year, the frequency of multiple cysts significantly increased (58.1%), with a higher incidence in CKD stages 3–5. The average diameter of the cysts was mostly 11–20mm in both baseline and interval measures, with an estimated mean annual diameter increase of 1.34 mm or 6.14%. The Chi-square test showed that the increase in the number of simple renal cysts from both baseline and interval groups is associated with a significant decline in eGFR (p-value <0.01) and the progression of proteinuria (p-value =0.02), but not with hematuria. Meanwhile, both the baseline and interval groups showed a significant association between the size of simple renal cysts and the reduction in eGFR (p-value <0.01); however, no association was found with proteinuria nor hematuria.
Conclusion
Despite being regarded as benign lesions, this study advocates for close follow-up and renal function monitoring in patients with simple renal cysts, owing to their correlation with a significant elevation in serum creatinine and proteinuria, which may serve as an early indicator for progression of kidney disease.

title: #2107 Dietary fiber intake and frailty in patients with and without chronic kidney disease: a nationally representative analysis
authors: Lingshan Shen; Changyuan Yang; Bengt Lindholm; Xusheng Liu; Guobin Su
abstract:
Background and Aims
Higher dietary fiber intake (DFI) is linked to lower risk of frailty in older population. However, people with chronic kidney disease (CKD) often eat less fiber due to concerns about fiber and potassium-rich foods causing hyperkalemia. It remains unclear if the link between DFI and frailty applies to people with and without CKD.
Method
This cross-sectional study analysed data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES 2003–2018). DFI was calculated based on average of two days dietary recall. Frailty was evaluated by the 36-item frailty index. CKD was defined as estimated glomerular filtration rate < 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 and/or urinary albumin creatinine ratio ≥30 mg/g. The association of DFI with frailty were analysed using weighted multivariate logistic regression and restricted cubic splines (RCS).
Results
A total of 15304 adults (median age 63 years, 55% female) were included in this analysis. The prevalence of frailty was 30% in 4037 CKD patients and 9.5% in 11267 non-CKD population. Each SD (3.95 g/1000 kcal/day) increase of DFI was associated with 41% reduced odds of frailty in whole population {adjusted odds ratio (aOR) 0.59 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.46–0.76]} and 44% in non-CKD population (aOR: 0.56, 95% CI: 0.41–0.77), but not in the CKD population (aOR: 0.67, 95% CI: 0.44–1.03). title: #2140 Association between bone mineral density and C-reactive protein in patients with kidney failure
authors: Dieter Smout; Pieter Evenepoel
abstract:
Background and Aims
Mounting evidence suggests that inflammation contributes to bone mineral density (BMD) loss, not only in patients with chronic autoimmune conditions but also in postmenopausal women. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is also a state of low-grade systemic inflammation. A plethora of endogenous and exogenous mediators seems to be involved, with metabolic endotoxemia gaining much interest in recent years. This study explores the association between metabolic endotoxemia, inflammation and bone mass in patients with kidney failure.
Method
This cross-sectional observational study included patients with kidney failure eligible for kidney transplantation. Data on demographics, comorbidities, parameters of mineral and bone disorder, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP, as a marker of inflammation), lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP, as a marker of metabolic endotoxemia), plasma bone turnover markers (BALP, iPINP and TRAP5b by IDS-iSYS) and bone mineral density (BMD), assessed by Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) at lumbar spine (LS), total hip (TH), femoral neck (FN), 1/3 distal radius and ultradistal radius, were collected. Univariate and multivariate analyses were conducted to investigate the determinants of bone loss and inflammation.
Results
The cohort included 649 patients (age 57 ± 12 years, 63% male). Median CRP was 3 (IQR 1, 7) mg/L and median LBP (subset only, n = 190) was 19 (14, 23) . Higher BMI and elevated LBP were associated with increased CRP (P < 0.01), independently of age and sex. High CRP was a risk factor for low BMD at all skeletal sites, after adjustment for traditional risk factors (age, BMI, sex) and PTH, remaining significant at all sites except LS after additional adjusting for any of the bone turnover markers BALP, iPINP or TRAP5b. Interestingly, the inverse association between CRP and BMD was only revealed after adjusting for BMI (Table 1 ).
Conclusion
CRP emerged as a significant risk factor for low bone mass in patients with kidney failure, particularly when adjusting for BMI. While obesity is linked to higher BMD, through estrogen production from adipocytes and increased skeletal loading, obesity is also associated with chronic low-grade inflammation, underscoring the complex relationship between inflammation, BMI, and bone mass (Fig. 1 ). Present findings call for additional studies exploring the link between metabolic endotoxemia and bone health.

title: #2903 Effect of denosumab on bone mineral density and microarchitecture assessed by HRpQCT in dialysis patients: a longitudinal study
authors: Benjamin Batteux; Pablo Antonio Urena Torres; Agnes Ostertag; Martine Cohen-Solal
abstract:
Background and Aims
Dialysis patients have higher risk of fragility fracture. Denosumab (Dmab) had been shown to increase bone mineral density (BMD) in short term open trials. The effect of Dmab on trabecular and cortical bone microarchitecture assessed by high-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography (HRpQCT) in dialysis patients has not been reported over a long-term period.
Method
32 consecutive dialysis patients managed at a single center between 2014 and 2024 and having performed at least one HRpQCT were included. Patients with recent fractures and BMD lower than −2.5 SD at the total hip were treated with Dmab 60 mg every 6 months. The study protocol included a HRpQCT at the right distal tibia and radius at baseline and every year, and a dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) at the lumbar spine, total hip, femoral neck, one-third and ultradistal radius at baseline and annually during the follow-up. HRpQCT data were not analyzed if performed (i) one year after a kidney transplantation or a parathyroidectomy and (ii) in the Dmab group, 6 months after the last administration in cases of treatment withdrawal. We applied linear mixed models for repeated measures (MMRMs) to assess the effect of Dmab on (i) HRpQCT parameters studied: ratio of bone volume to total volume (BV/TV), trabecular volumetric mineral density (Dtrab), cortical volumetric mineral density (Dcomp), cortical thickness (CtTh), and cortical perimeter (CtPm) and (ii) bone mineral density (BMD) obtained by DXA at each measurement site.
Results
During a median [interquartile range (IQR)] follow-up period of 1.8 [1.2–2.5] years, 19 dialysis patients had repeated HRpQCT over time, including nine patients treated with Dmab. The median [IQR] age of the whole population was 68.9 [62.1–76.6] years, 23 (71.9%) were female (including 21 menopausal women). The only baseline characteristic significantly associated with the use of Dmab was a previous fracture (92.9% in the Dmab group vs 50% in the no-Dmab group, P = 0.027). The mean (standard deviation (SD)) trabecular BV/TV changes between baseline and the last HRpQCT measurement (regardless of the time between the two HRpQCTs) was a gain of +2.2% ± 4.5% in the Dmab group vs a loss of −15.9% ± 11.7% in the no-Dmab group at the distal tibia, and a gain of +3.5% ± 7.4% in the Dmab group vs a loss of −14.8% ± 12.4% in the no-Dmab group at the distal radius. These Tb BV/TV changes in the Dmab group (vs no-Dmab group) were significant in MMRM analyses at the distal tibia (P = 0.006), and at the distal radius (P = 0.002). The mean (SD) Dtrab changes was +2.2% ± 4.5% in the Dmab group vs −15.9% ± 11.7% in the no-Dmab group at the distal tibia, and +3.3% ± 7.7% in the Dmab group vs −14.6% ± 12.6% in the no-Dmab group at the distal radius. The Dtrab changes in the Dmab group vs no-Dmab group were significant in MMRM analyses at the distal tibia (P = 0.006), and at the distal radius (P = 0.002). Changes over time in cortical parameters (Dcomp, CtTh and CtPm) were not statistically significant between groups in MMRM analyses. The mean (SD) BMD changes between the first and the last DXA (regardless of the time between the two DXA) at the lumbar spine, total hip, femoral neck, one-third and ultradistal radius were +9.3% ± 11.5%, +4.9% ± 6.2%, +13.6% ± 17.9%, +7.2% ± 12.4% and +6.4% ± 8.8% in the Dmab group, respectively, and −4.0% ± 11.8%, −8.5% ± 9.4%, −10.2% ± 4.6%, +0.9% ± 3.4% and −4.5% ± 13.1% in the no-Dmab group, respectively. These changes between groups were significant at total hip site in MMRM analyses (P = 0.008).
Conclusion
Dmab treatment improves trabecular bone volume parameters over time in dialysis patients with low BMD, thus preventing the persistent and progressive trabecular bone loss observed in the absence of treatment.

title: #3380 The association between estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and disability worsening in patients with multiple sclerosis
authors: Florica Gadalean; Parv Florina; Irina Lata; Mihaela Simu; Anca Suteanu-Simulescu; Milas Oana; Lavinia Balint; Mihaela Glavan; Cristina Gluhovschi; Silvia Ienciu; Flaviu Bob; Ligia Petrica
abstract:
Background and Aims
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune neurological disease characterized by focal demyelinated lesions of the central nervous system, leading to heterogenous neurological impairments. In recent years, emerging evidence suggests a complex interrelation between MS and kidney disease. While renal abnormalities are common in individuals with MS, there are no data concerning the impact of kidney function on MS disability progression. Therefore, the aim of the study was to investigate the association between the baseline level of kidney function and disability worsening in patients with MS.
Method
This prospective observational study enrolled 373 MS patients (mean age: 44.2 ± 11.4 years; 242 (64.89%) females). Confirmed disability worsening (CDW) was defined as an increase in the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score by at least 1 point from baseline, sustained between 2 follow-up visits separated in time by no less than 6 months (or by 1.5 points if the EDSS score at baseline was 0, or by 0.5 points if the baseline EDSS score was ≥5.5). Kidney function was assessed by estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) calculated by the CKD-EPI equation. Socio-demographic, clinical and biological data were analyzed with logistic uni- and multivariable regression methods to investigate their association with CDW. A two-tailed value <0.05 was considered significant.
Results
During a median follow-up period of 10 years, a total of 109 patients (29.22%) developed CDW. Individuals with CDW presented an older age at MS onset (median age of onset 37 years vs. 26 years, P = 0.0002), lower baseline median eGFR (89.8 ml/min/1.73 m2 vs. 116 ml/min/1.73 m2, P < 0.001), higher baseline median EDSS score (3.5 vs. 1, P = 0.001), and a higher prevalence of secondary-progressive MS (SPMS) phenotype (3.67% vs. 0.38%, P = 0.027), as compared to non-CDW patients. In univariate regression analysis, the CDW was associated with age of MS at onset (OR = 1.04; 95% CI: 1.02 to 1.06, P = 0.001), baseline EDSS score (OR = 1.16; 95% CI: 1.04 to 1.03, P = 0.009), baseline eGFR (OR = 0.97, 95% CI: 0.96 to 0.98, P < 0.001), and the SPMS phenotype (OR = 9.98; 95% CI:1.1 to 90.34, P = 0.041). In multivariate analysis, baseline eGFR remains an independent predictor for the risk of CDW (OR = 0.97, 95% CI: 0.95 to 0.98, P < 0.0001, Nagelkerke R2 = 0.110).
Conclusion
This study showed that a lower baseline eGFR contributed to disability worsening in MS patients. The relationship between kidney function and disability risk in MS should be further investigated to improve disease prognosis and quality of life for MS patients.

title: #3433 Burden of disease and management of hyperkalemia in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease managed at Spanish endocrinology services
authors: José Ignacio Martínez Montoro; Belen Pimentel; Ana Roncero Martin; Miren Sequera Mutiozabal; Mónica Juarez Campo; José Carlos Fernández García
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a global public health problem with a high impact on morbidity and mortality. Diabetes is the one of the leading causes of CKD, and up to 40% of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) have CKD. Despite patients with metabolic diseases are mainly managed by Endocrinology units, there are currently no studies describing the burden associated to the loss of kidney function and the risk of developing hyperkalemia in these patients. The ENDO_CKD study aimed to describe and characterize the prevalence, associated burden and management of hyperkalemia in patients with T2D and CKD managed by Endocrinologists in Spain.
Method
This was a retrospective observational study using data from the TELOTRON database in Spain. Adult patients with T2D (diagnosis code or at least one HbA1c value ≥6.5% or prescription of any antidiabetic drug) and CKD (diagnosis code or lab criteria for CKD diagnosis (one eGFR value < 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 and/or one UACR value ≥30 mg/g)) with at least one visit to the endocrinology services between January 2013–November 2023 were included. Hyperkalemia was defined as per diagnosis code and/or with potassium laboratory values >5 mmol/L. Baseline characteristics, treatments, and hyperkalemia management were analyzed.
Results
A total of 8,017 patients were identified, mean age 70.7 (SD 11.8) years, 45.2% female, mean BMI 31.8 (SD 6.5) kg/m², mean eGFR 61.9 (SD 24.6) mL/min/1.73 m², median UACR 53.5 (IQ 25.0–146.2) mg/g, and median Charlson index 4.0 (IQ 2.0–5.0). These patients were highly comorbid (81.6% hypertension; 77.8% hyperlipidemia; 45.6% obesity; 21.4% heart failure) and had a high use of drugs (96.1% glucose-lowering; 83.5% lipid-lowering; 80.6% RAASi; 63.7% SGLTi2; 43.1% beta-blocker).
Among them, 26.4% (2116) had an event of hyperkalemia, yet only 29.7% (628) were formally diagnosed and 12.6% (267) received treatment with potassium binders (Table 1).
Conclusion
Hyperkalemia is a prevalent condition but remains underdiagnosed and undertreated in patients with CKD and T2D managed in Spanish endocrinology services, despite guideline recommendations to achieve optimal cardio-renal-metabolic therapy. Over 70% of hyperkalemia cases are not formally identified, and more than 85% of patients do not receive appropriate treatment. Our findings underscore the need for early detection and management of hyperkalemia in these high-risk patients.

title: #3453 The role of centre characteristics and type of water treatment plant in the environmental impact of hemodialysis
authors: Julia Audije-Gil; Rodrigo Martínez Cadenas; Natalia Martín Vaquero; Miquel Gomez; Jesús Portillo; Gerard Pereda; Brett Duane; Marta Sanjuan; José Luis Fernandez-Martin; Alberto Ortiz; Marta Arias Guillen; María Dolores Arenas Jiménez
abstract:
Background and Aims
In-centre haemodialysis (HD) represents approximately 70% of all kidney replacement therapy. This technique requires a large amount of resources such as water and electricity. In a previous study by our research group, it was observed that the factors influencing water and energy consumption include: the size of the facility (lower consumption per HD session in larger centres), operating schedules (lower consumption in centres that operate daily), choice of the water treatment plant, and seasonality (water usage tends to be higher during summer, whereas energy consumption is higher during the winter months).
Optimising building infrastructure and management systems requires a deeper understanding of each factor's combined impact on consumption levels. The aim of this study was to determine the weight of each factor influencing water and energy consumption within the environmental model, in order to understand how centre characteristics and the type of water treatment plant jointly influence a centre's water and energy usage.
Method
This study examined data from a 5-year multicentre follow-up of 20 HD centres across various geographic regions, focusing on water (L/HD session) and energy (kWh/HD session) consumption. The analysis considered several operational characteristics that were significantly influential in the univariate model of our previous study: centre size (<10,000 sessions per year for small facilities, and >10,000 HD for larger ones), operating schedule (thrice-weekly or daily), type of commercial provider plant (anonymized as Type 1, 2 and 3), and water treatment plant disinfection methods (chemical disinfection or a combination of thermal and chemical disinfection). Seasonality was excluded from the analysis as it is not a modifiable factor.
Multivariate analyses were performed to develop an environmental impact model based on contributing factors. The collected data were analysed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 29.0.2.0 (Armonk, NY: IBM Corp). The significance level was set at P < 0.05.
Results
A total of 919,059 HD sessions were performed over 5 years at 20 geographically diverse HD centres. Over this duration, the combined water usage was 311,027.2 m3, and energy consumption amounted to 7,155.8 MWh. The relationship between water and energy consumption and the organizational factors were evaluated in a linear regression analysis. The operating hours coefficient had a significant independent effect on water and energy consumption per HD session (P = 0.007 and P = 0.010, respectively), while the size of the facility only independently influenced water consumption per HD session (P = 0.025 and P = 0.759, respectively) (Table 1).
Adding water treatment plant type to the model resulted in Type 1 (β = 230.6; standardized β = 0.51; P < 0.001) and Type 3 (β = −131.9; standardized β = −0.34; P = 0.001) independently influencing water consumption per HD session, while Type 2 was not a predictor of the model (P = 0.171). Plant Type 2 (β = 6.3; standardized β = 0.40; P < 0.001) and Type 3 (β = −4.1; standardized β = −0.31; P = 0.005) were independently associated with energy consumption per HD session, while Type 1 was not an independent predictor of the model (P = 0.970).
Conclusion
Centre size and operating days were found to be significant factors influencing water consumption, whereas the primary factor affecting energy consumption was the number of operating days. Additionally, the type of water treatment plant is a key factor in both water and energy consumption, meaning that the selection of the most sustainable commercial providers can optimise efficiency and reduce the environmental impact of HD.
This study highlights the importance of HD centres assessing their environmental impact and establishing tailored benchmarks to guide sustainability efforts. Since it is not feasible to eliminate water and energy consumption in HD entirely, implementing targeted measures presents a promising approach to mitigating its environmental burden.

In a previous study by our research group, it was observed that the factors influencing water and energy consumption include: the size of the facility (lower consumption per HD session in larger centres), operating schedules (lower consumption in centres that operate daily), choice of the water treatment plant, and seasonality (water usage tends to be higher during summer, whereas energy consumption is higher during the winter months).
Optimising building infrastructure and management systems requires a deeper understanding of each factor's combined impact on consumption levels. The aim of this study was to determine the weight of each factor influencing water and energy consumption within the environmental model, in order to understand how centre characteristics and the type of water treatment plant jointly influence a centre's water and energy usage.
Method
This study examined data from a 5-year multicentre follow-up of 20 HD centres across various geographic regions, focusing on water (L/HD session) and energy (kWh/HD session) consumption. The analysis considered several operational characteristics that were significantly influential in the univariate model of our previous study: centre size (<10,000 sessions per year for small facilities, and >10,000 HD for larger ones), operating schedule (thrice-weekly or daily), type of commercial provider plant (anonymized as Type 1, 2 and 3), and water treatment plant disinfection methods (chemical disinfection or a combination of thermal and chemical disinfection). Seasonality was excluded from the analysis as it is not a modifiable factor.
Multivariate analyses were performed to develop an environmental impact model based on contributing factors. The collected data were analysed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 29.0.2.0 (Armonk, NY: IBM Corp). The significance level was set at P < 0.05.
Results
A total of 919,059 HD sessions were performed over 5 years at 20 geographically diverse HD centres. Over this duration, the combined water usage was 311,027.2 m3, and energy consumption amounted to 7,155.8 MWh. The relationship between water and energy consumption and the organizational factors were evaluated in a linear regression analysis. The operating hours coefficient had a significant independent effect on water and energy consumption per HD session (P = 0.007 and P = 0.010, respectively), while the size of the facility only independently influenced water consumption per HD session (P = 0.025 and P = 0.759, respectively) (Table 1).
Adding water treatment plant type to the model resulted in Type 1 (β = 230.6; standardized β = 0.51; P < 0.001) and Type 3 (β = −131.9; standardized β = −0.34; P = 0.001) independently influencing water consumption per HD session, while Type 2 was not a predictor of the model (P = 0.171). Plant Type 2 (β = 6.3; standardized β = 0.40; P < 0.001) and Type 3 (β = −4.1; standardized β = −0.31; P = 0.005) were independently associated with energy consumption per HD session, while Type 1 was not an independent predictor of the model (P = 0.970).
Conclusion
Centre size and operating days were found to be significant factors influencing water consumption, whereas the primary factor affecting energy consumption was the number of operating days. Additionally, the type of water treatment plant is a key factor in both water and energy consumption, meaning that the selection of the most sustainable commercial providers can optimise efficiency and reduce the environmental impact of HD.
This study highlights the importance of HD centres assessing their environmental impact and establishing tailored benchmarks to guide sustainability efforts. Since it is not feasible to eliminate water and energy consumption in HD entirely, implementing targeted measures presents a promising approach to mitigating its environmental burden.

title: #418 Nutritional status and outcomes after one year in older patients with advanced CKD
authors: Imre Demirhan; Lotte Veltman; Simon Mooijaart; Willem Jan W Bos; Wesley Visser; Marjolijn van Buren; Alferso Abrahams
abstract:
Background and Aims
Malnutrition is common in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) in various stages, especially among older patients with advanced CKD. Whether malnutrition in this older population is associated with one year mortality, eGFR decline, and progression to kidney replacement therapy (KRT), is not well known. Exploring this may help identify older patients at higher risk of deterioration. This study therefore investigates whether the nutritional status in older patients with advanced CKD is associated with one year mortality, eGFR decline below 10 mL/min/1.73 m2 within one year and progression to KRT within one year.
Method
Patients ≥65 years with eGFR 20–10 mL/min/1.73 m2 were included from the ongoing prospective observational cohort study DIALOGICA. Nutritional status was assessed at baseline as part of nephrology-tailored geriatric assessments by using the Mini Nutritional Assessment Short-Form (MNA-SF), which yields scores ranging between 0 and 14. Patients were classified as ‘malnourished, or at risk’ with a MNA-SF score ≤11 and as ‘well-nourished’ with a MNA-SF score ≥12. The outcomes ‘one year mortality’, ‘eGFR decline below 10 mL/min/1.73 m2 within one year’ and ‘progression to KRT within one year’ were defined as death occurring within one year, eGFR dropping below 10 mL/min/1.73 m2 within one year of follow up, and dialysis initiation or kidney transplantation occurring within one year after inclusion, respectively. Associations between nutritional status at baseline and the aforementioned outcomes were explored using Kaplan-Meier curves, log-rank tests and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models.
Results
610 patients were included with mean age 76.6 years (SD 5.8) and mean eGFR 14.8 mL/min/1.73 m2 (SD 3.1). In total, 160 patients (26.2%) had the nutritional status ‘malnourished, or at risk’. Of the entire cohort during one year of follow up, 55 patients (9.0%) died, 114 patients (18.7%) had eGFR declining below 10 mL/min/1.73 m2 and 68 patients (11.1%) progressed to KRT. Of the 68 patients who progressed to KRT, 66 had initiated dialysis and 2 received a kidney transplant. Poor nutritional status was associated with higher risk of mortality occurring within one year (adjusted-HR 1.88, 95% CI 1.08; 3.25), but not with eGFR declining within one year (adjusted-HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.70; 2.15) or progression to KRT (adjusted-HR 1.25, 95% CI 0.72; 2.15).
Conclusion
In older patients with advanced CKD, poor nutritional status is associated with a higher early mortality risk, but not with early eGFR decline nor early progression to KRT. These findings may help identify vulnerable patients who are at high risk of early mortality, which may have consequences for shared decision-making (SDM) for kidney replacement therapy. Future research should investigate whether dietary interventions can lower mortality risk in this vulnerable population.

title: #1160 Insights from native kidney biopsies: a step towards establishing a renal biopsies database in Latvia
authors: Līga Pūsepa; Zane Ķiece; Kristīne Locika; Gaisma Gurska; Marija Škuļtecka; Inese Folkmane; Veronika Mesecko; Aivars Petersons; Anna Popova; Kārlis Rācenis; Ieva Ziedina; Viktorija Kuzema
abstract:
Background and Aims
Percutaneous kidney biopsy is a cornerstone diagnostic procedure for the identification and characterization of kidney diseases, particularly glomerulonephritis, and for understanding their underlying pathophysiological mechanisms. However, the absence of comprehensive data on kidney disease patterns in Latvia hampers progress in disease management and population-level trend monitoring. This study presents an analysis of native kidney biopsy findings collected at Pauls Stradiņš Clinical University Hospital (PSCUH) from 2013 to 2024, in collaboration with the National Centre of Pathology in Vilnius.
Method
A retrospective analysis was conducted on 1752 patients undergoing percutaneous kidney biopsy, excluding transplant recipients and donors, leaving a cohort of 1002 patients. 34 biopsies were excluded due to insufficient biopsy material, 968 native kidney biopsies diagnosis were analyzed. Patients were categorized into four age groups: 18–44 years, 45–64 years, 65–74 years, and >74 years. The total number of case biopsies from 2013 through 2024 was used to calculate incidence rates, expressed as biopsies per million individuals per year (p.m.p./year). Since our center performs about 85% of all adult kidney biopsies nationwide, the official population counts at the beginning of each year were reduced by 15% in the denominator, ensuring the calculated rates accurately reflect the coverage of our kidney biopsies database.
Analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 29.
Results
The incidence rate of Latvian adults undergoing first kidney biopsy was 58.3 p.m.p./year. The cohort's median age was 52 years, with 53.5% of biopsies on males and 46.5% on females. Yearly distribution of kidney biopsies ranged from 3.4% in 2013 to 14.1% in 2023 and 12.3% in 2024. Most biopsies were performed on patients aged 18–44 years (37.5%) and 45–64 years (37.9%), followed by 15.9% in those aged 65–74 years and 8.7% in individuals older than 74 years.
IgA nephropathy (IgAN) was the most common (23.3%), followed by rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) (15.0%), membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) (7.6%), focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) (7.2%), lupus nephritis (5.9%), amyloidosis (6.5%), minimal change disease (MCD) (4.8%), and acute tubulointerstitial necrosis/acute tubular necrosis (ATIN/ATN) (7.5%). Other diagnoses included thrombotic microangiopathy/hemolytic uremic syndrome (TMA/HUS) (3.4%), diabetic nephropathy (DN) (3.4%), multiple myeloma (MM) (1.5%), hereditary interstitial nephritis (HIN) (1.0%), Alport syndrome (Alp)/Primary basement membrane syndrome (PBMS) (2.4%), and non-IgA mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis (non-IgA MPGN) (1.7%).
A higher male predominance was noted for IgAN (9:5) and membranous GN (3:2), while female predominance was seen in lupus nephritis (1:10), Alp/PBMS (1:5), and MM (3:5) (Fig. 1).
Regarding age, IgAN prevailed in younger adults aged 18–44 (37.0%), while RPGN dominated in older adults aged ≥65 (21.6%), particularly those over 74 years (26.5%). Amyloidosis and ATIN/ATN showed a progressive increase in frequency with age, rising from 2.7% in the 18–44 age group to 13.3% for ATIN/ATN and 14.5% for amyloidosis in the >74 age group (Table 1).
Conclusion
This single-center study offers the most extensive biopsy-confirmed overview of kidney disease patterns at PSCUH to date, demonstrating a pronounced prevalence of IgAN overall and highlighting notable gender and age-related trends. The data also reveal rising rates of RPGN in older cohorts. These findings emphasize the need for a comprehensive, nationwide renal biopsies database in Latvia to advance epidemiological insights, optimize clinical management, and unify future research efforts.

title: #1532 Effectiveness & cost-effectiveness of post-discharge transitional care programmes for fluid overload readmissions amongst chronic kidney disease patients in Singapore
authors: Soon Nan Wee; Cynthia Lim; Zhihua Huang; Ee Won Leong; Lourdes Ducusin Galang; Jamie Lim; Wei Yi Tay; De Zhi Chin; Wan Jin Sia; Hairil Rizal Bin Abdullah; Chieh Suai Tan; Nicholas Graves
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hospitalizations for fluid overload are common in chronic kidney disease (CKD) and are expected to increase healthcare utilization. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of transitional care programs (TCPs) in reducing readmissions for fluid overload and their cost-effectiveness in Singapore.
Method
We performed a retrospective cohort study that utilized electronic medical records between 2022–2024 for data related to hospitalizations, comorbidities, laboratory and pharmacotherapy, and billing data from the Inappropriate Nephrotoxic Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drug in Diabetes, Elderly and Renal Impairment (INSIDER) study (2015–2017). We included patients with CKD stage G3 to G5 without dialysis or kidney transplant with an index fluid overload-related hospitalization. The outcomes were 30- and 90-day fluid overload-related readmissions.
To evaluate the TCPs’ effectiveness, we used Fine-Gray competing risk models with death as a competing event to compare patients who received TCP between 2022 and 2024 and a propensity score-matched control group that received standard care during the same period.
For cost-effectiveness, we constructed Markov models with and without TCPs (Fig. 1). Micros-simulation of 1000 samples over 10,000 patients were used to evaluate uncertainty intervals. Utility was estimated empirically for TCPs and extracted from literature for hospitalization and community. Costs for fluid overload-related hospitalizations were estimated by cluster analysis using billing data from 2015–2017 and predicting clusters in the 2022–2024 study cohort with internal validation. Costs for standard care and TCPs were extracted from literature. All costs were adjusted for inflation to 2024. Sensitivity analysis for estimated costs, utilities and transition probabilities were conducted by varying these parameters. Net Monetary Benefit was calculated to estimate the probability of TCPs being cost-effective.
Results
We included 3,986 fluid overload-related hospitalizations in 2022–2024, among whom 178 received TCPs. Table 1 shows that compared to patients who did not receive TCPs, patients who received TCPs were significantly more likely to have CKD Stage 3B, peripheral vascular disease, SGLT-2 inhibitors and high-dose intravenous furosemide during their hospitalization.
The 30-day (6.18% vs 5.14%, P = 0.11) and 90-day (7.30% vs 9.14%, P = 0.44) were not different in the TCP and standard care groups, respectively. However, competing risk models accounting for death showed a trend towards reduced 90-day readmissions in the TCP group compared to the standard care group (7.25% vs 12.9%, P = 0.08).
Markov simulations for the base case show a cost saving of Singapore Dollars (SGD) $622 over 90 days (Uncertainty Intervals: S$609–S$626) and an improvement in QALY of 0.0414 over 90 days (Uncertainty Intervals: 0.0412–0.415) and a net monetary benefit of SGD$2,485 (Uncertainty Intervals: S$2,471–S$2,490). Sensitivity analyses showed that cost savings and utility improvements were observed throughout all scenarios tested, even when estimated hospitalization costs were halved. Cost-effectiveness acceptance plots of net monetary benefits show that TCPs are 100% cost-effective at the S$45,000 willingness-to-pay threshold.
Conclusion
Post-discharge TCPs may reduce 90-day readmissions for fluid overload and can be a cost-effective strategy to reduce healthcare resource utilization and costs.

title: #1774 Therapeutic potential of omentum dECM in promoting angiogenesis and reducing fibrosis for renal tissue regeneration and failure repair
authors: Boyun Kim
abstract:
Background and Aims
The utilization of decellularized extracellular matrix (dECM) has emerged as a pivotal strategy in tissue engineering, offering a natural scaffold for regenerative applications and potential as a bioartificial organ for transplantation. This study highlights the efficacy of omentum dECM and presents a novel approach to artificial tissue by alleviating renal failure through the transplantation of dECM in an implantable patch under the kidney capsule layer.
Method
The omentum was decellularized using vascular perfusion and detergent agitation. Protein composition was analyzed using the ELISA array. The dECM was fabricated into a patch for cell culture and animal studies. For animal experiments, the omentum dECM tissue was processed into a film-like patch using a bioadhesive and implanted under the kidney capsule layer of a renal failure mouse model. Apoptosis was measured by RT-PCR, and fibrosis by IHC staining.
Results
In this study, we applied two approaches to evaluate the effects of omentum dECM: cell culture and animal experiments. Prior to these experiments, we analyzed the composition of omentum dECM. ELISA array revealed high levels of angiogenesis-related factors (FGFR1, NRP1, TGFBR3) in omentum dECM compared to adipose tissue. In cell experiments, endothelial cells, as key vascular components, exhibited enhanced proliferation when cultured with dECM. In the renal failure mouse model, the dECM patch significantly promoted angiogenesis and reduced fibrosis.
Conclusion
Omentum dECM promoted angiogenesis, which played a crucial role in inhibiting renal fibrosis. These findings highlight the potential of omentum dECM as a low-immunogenic scaffold for artificial tissue in regenerative medicine and transplantation.

title: #1957 Factors associated with hyperkalemia and hyperphosphatemia in non-dialysis dependent CKD: the role of dietary knowledge, attitude, and behaviour
authors: Calvin Mulyadi; Elizabeth Yasmine Wardoyo; Anggraini Sari; Aryan Djojo; Johanes Sarwono; Fidkya Alisha; Herlinda Lizamona; Akromah Sofyan
abstract:
Background and Aims
Electrolyte derangements, particularly hyperkalemia and hyperphosphatemia, pose significant challenges in managing non-dialysis dependent chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. In many middle- to low-income countries, limited data on contributing factors often leaves clinicians with few insights to identify the high-risk individuals. This study investigates the association between clinical factors and patients’ perspectives on low-phosphate and low-potassium diets in the development of hyperkalemia and hyperphosphatemia among CKD patients.
Methods
This cross-sectional, single-center study was conducted in Jakarta, Indonesia. A validated 24-item questionnaire was used to assess patients' knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors regarding low-phosphate and low-potassium diets. Demographic and clinical data were collected through direct interviews during outpatient visits. Bioimpedance spectroscopy (BIS) measurement was performed to assess nutritional status. Daily energy, protein, potassium, and phosphate intake were evaluated by using a food frequency questionnaire administered by trained nutritionists.
Results
The study included 103 participants (mean age 63.3 ± 12.3 years; 54.4% male). Most participants were identified as CKD stages 4–5 (42.7% and 31.1%, respectively), of 70.9% had a high school education or lower. Among the subjects, 46 (44.7%) were identified as having the episodes of either hyperkalemia and/or hyperphosphatemia during the visit. Significant differences were observed in age, serum urea, and creatinine levels between hyperphosphatemic and normophosphatemic groups (P = 0.046, P = 0.001, P = 0.002, respectively), and in overhydration status between hyperkalemic and normokalemic groups (P = 0.044). Majority of participants obtained scored below the cut-off value for the knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors domain and the overall score toward low-phosphate and low-potassium diets (56.3%, 54.4%, 55.3%, and 45.6%, respectively). Low formal education was significantly associated with lower knowledge and overall scores (P = 0.032 and P = 0.039). The hyperphosphatemic group showed slightly higher attitude scores compared to the normophosphatemic group (P = 0.045).
Conclusion
The study population demonstrated generally low levels of knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors related to low-phosphate and low-potassium diets. The development of electrolyte derangements in CKD is influenced by a complex interplay of many factors, underscoring the need for comprehensive, multifactorial management strategies.
