title: #2059 Disease progression and its association with proteinuria among patients with primary immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN): results from a real-world study in China
authors: Youxia Liu; Yue Xing; Hongfen Li; Yan Qi; Sasikiran Nunna; Zhaoxin Chen; Yuelin Zhuang; Yilong Zhang; Wentian Lu; Jiaqi Kou; Li Zuo; Tiekun Yan
abstract:
Background and Aims
Current literature indicates that up to 40% of patients in China with IgAN progressed to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) within 20 years of diagnosis. Proteinuria has been identified as a predictor of kidney failure in IgAN. In China, real-world evidence on the differences in disease progression across various levels of proteinuria is limited. This study aimed to assess the association of proteinuria with disease progression of IgAN in China.
Method
A retrospective observational study of adult patients with biopsy-confirmed primary IgAN from Tianjin City, China was conducted using data between 01/01/2015 to 06/30/2023. Patients with secondary IgAN, history of dialysis or eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m2 at renal biopsy, or a history of kidney transplantation, were excluded. Index date was the date of the initial biopsy which confirmed IgAN. Patients were followed from index biopsy until clinical outcomes (ESKD, doubling of serum creatinine, 40% decline in eGFR or mortality) and censored for disenrollment, or end of study. Time-to-event analysis was performed for these outcomes. Associations of time-averaged proteinuria with composite renal event were estimated using Cox proportional hazard regression.
Results
A total of 1,674 patients were included, with 50.4% being female. At renal biopsy, 55.0% of patients were aged <40 years, 60.3% had hypertension, 6.6% had diabetes and 67.3% were in CKD stage I or II. RAAS inhibitors (62.1%), corticosteroids (59.6%) and immunosuppressants (30.3%) were the most frequently used treatments during the follow-up, with a high proportion of concomitant use of traditional Chinese medicine (86.8%). Of 1,357 patients with time-averaged proteinuria during the follow-up, 26.9% had <0.5 g/day, 27.4% had 0.5–<1 g/day, and 45.7% had ≥1 g/day. Over a median (mean) follow-up period of 1.7 (2.2) years, 9.2% of patients experienced composite renal event (6.5% progressed to ESKD, 5.0% experienced 40% decline in eGFR, 3.6% experienced doubling of serum creatinine, 1.3% had mortality). Unadjusted hazard ratios (HRs) of composite renal event occurrence were higher in patients with time-averaged proteinuria ≥0.5 g/day than those with proteinuria <0.5 g/day (HR [95% confidence interval]: 1.5 [0.7, 3.1] for 0.5–<1 g/day, 2.7 [1.4, 5.3] for 1–<2 g/day, 4.8 [2.3, 10.0] for 2–<3 g/day, and 13.7 [7.4, 25.3] for ≥3g/day).
Conclusion
Results showed that IgAN patients in this Chinese cohort had relatively preserved kidney function but high-risk comorbid conditions. Sustained proteinuria over 1 g/day during the follow-up is a strong predictor of CKD progression. Patients with 0.5–1 g/day proteinuria had an elevated risk of CKD progression; however this was not statistically significant and should be contextualized with other risk factors for rapid progression. Findings support the goal of lowering proteinuria to <0.5 g/day to reduce the risk of renal failure among IgAN patients in China.

title: #2071 Cardiovascular risk surveillance and management among older patients with glomerulonephritis treated with immunosuppressive therapy
authors: Jovan Sim; Dawn Lim; Felicia Loo; Felice Leong; Jason Choo; Cynthia Lim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Glomerulonephritis and its treatment may be associated with cardiovascular disease. We aimed to describe the real-world practices in glycemic and lipid surveillance and control among older adult patients with glomerulonephritis receiving immunosuppressive therapy.
Method
This was a single-center, retrospective cohort study of all individuals ≥40 years old on follow-up for active glomerulonephritis and receiving immunosuppressants, before their enrolment in the ConFIRM (cardiovascular, infection and frailty risk in older adults with immune-mediated renal disease treated with immunosuppressant: recognition, intervention and self-management) program.
Data for demographic, clinical and laboratory results performed during follow-up visits were retrieved from the electronic medical records at 6-monthly intervals. The outcomes were the prevalence of glycemic and lipid evaluation and control (HbA1c ≤7%, fasting glucose <6.1 mmol/L and LDL-cholesterol <2.6 mmol/L). To understand real-world practices in cardiovascular risk surveillance, we compared the prevalences during visits in the first, second, third, fourth, fifth and subsequent follow-up years.
Results
We included 815 follow-up visits between 1997 and 2024 among 155 adults diagnosed with glomerulonephritis between 1989 and 2023. Table 2 shows the patient characteristics during the follow-up visits. The median age was 57 (48, 68) years and follow-up duration was 60 (24, 108) months.
Table 2 shows that glycemic evaluation was performed in 53.8% of the visits. The prevalence was higher during the first year (68.5%), compared to subsequent follow-up years (50.7% beyond the sixth year, P = 0.007). Fasting glucose was assessed in 29.6%, with 63.8% achieving levels <6.1 mmol/L. Fasting glucose was assessed most frequently during the first year (44.9%) compared to subsequent years. Similarly, HbA1c was performed most frequently during the first year (52.8%). HbA1c ≤ 7% was achieved in 79.1% among those tested in the first year, with a trend towards better glycemic control in the subsequent years.
Lipid evaluation was performed in 40.3% of visits, with no significant difference across follow-up years. Among those evaluated, 47.9% achieved LDL-cholesterol levels <2.6 mmol/L. Statin use increased significantly across the follow-up years.
Conclusion
Glycemic and lipid surveillance and control may be suboptimal among older patients with glomerulonephritis receiving immunosuppressive therapy and at risk for cardiovascular disease. Future research should focus on identifying barriers to regular surveillance and exploring interventions to sustainably assess cardiovascular risk factors for better clinical care.

title: #2122 Impact of albuminuria screening in primary care on the detection and management of chronic kidney disease: evidence from the ONDAAS study
authors: Didier Sánchez Ospina; Sebastian Mas-Fontao; Maria Martin Palencia; Badawi Hijazi Prieto; Cristina Gomez Sánchez; Silvia Paredes Carcedo; Jesus Egido; Alberto Ortiz; Emilio Gonzalez Parra; María Jesús Izquierdo Ortiz
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a global health challenge, affecting over 850 million individuals. Its rising prevalence underscores the need for effective early detection and management strategies. Despite the availability of diagnostic tools, many individuals with CKD remain undiagnosed, delaying interventions that could slow disease progression and improve outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate the utility of systematic urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR) screening in primary care settings to enhance early CKD detection, improve risk stratification, and optimize therapeutic decisions.
Method
This cross-sectional, multicenter epidemiological study was conducted across primary care centers in the province of Burgos, Spain, between February and May 2024. Adults undergoing routine clinical testing were included, with uACR measured in 9,890 participants. CKD classification adhered to KDIGO 2024 guidelines, combining uACR and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Descriptive and inferential statistics were employed to analyze the data, with significance set at P < 0.05.
Results
CKD diagnostic thresholds were met by 22.29% of the participants. Albuminuria (uACR > 30 mg/g, KDIGO categories A2–A3) was present in 14.1%, and 10.88% of those with preserved eGFR (>60 ml/min/1.73 m²) exhibited pathological albuminuria, underscoring its role in early CKD identification. Importantly, albuminuria reclassified 35.6% of patients into higher KDIGO risk categories, influencing therapeutic recommendations. For example, the study identified 14.6% of participants as candidates for renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (RASi) and 10.89% for sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors. Among participants younger than 50 years, 18.3% displayed mildly reduced eGFR (60–90 ml/min/1.73 m²), signaling early renal impairment despite not meeting traditional CKD diagnostic criteria.
Conclusion
Systematic uACR screening in primary care settings enhances early CKD detection, particularly in individuals with preserved eGFR. This approach identified 14.1% of participants with undiagnosed CKD and reclassified 35.6% into higher-risk categories, highlighting its critical role in guiding therapeutic interventions. These findings advocate for the integration of albuminuria testing into routine primary care diagnostics to improve early detection, optimize treatment strategies, and ultimately reduce the burden of CKD.

title: #3024 Retrospective single center analysis of Desidustat in CKD anemia
authors: Ashwinikumar Khandekar
abstract:
Background and Aims
Relative deficiency of erythropoietin in chronic kidney disease (CKD) necessitates erythropoietin therapy for patients. Recently approved hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor, Desidustat (Oxemia®), stimulates endogenous erythropoietin production and is used for CKD-related anemia. This study focuses on the clinical utilization of Desidustat in managing CKD anemia.
Method
Patients with CKD-related anemia treated with Desidustat were enrolled in the study. They were regularly followed up to monitor efficacy and dose adjustments. Hemoglobin and serum potassium levels were measured at baseline and at each follow-up point (FU1 to FU5).
Results
A total of 116 patients were enrolled in the study, including 66.38% (77) pre-dialysis CKD patients, 28.45% (33) dialysis-dependent patients, 5.17% (6) post-transplant anemia patients, 59.48% (69) de novo patients initiated on Oxemia®, and 40.52% (47) patients switched over from ESA. From baseline (9.65 g/dL) to the latest follow-up (11.13 g/dL), there was a significant rise of 1.47 g/dL in hemoglobin levels (P < 0.05) (Fig. 1). Pre-dialysis patients showed a significant increase in hemoglobin levels after starting Desidustat therapy, with an absolute change of 1.14 g/dL from baseline (P < 0.05). In contrast, dialysis-dependent patients showed a delayed response, with significant improvements observed in later follow-ups (Fig. 2). Both de novo patients treated for CKD anemia with Desidustat and patients switched over from ESA therapy showed similar responses to Desidustat treatment, with no significant difference between the groups (P > 0.05) (Fig. 3). Throughout the study duration, serum potassium levels remained stable, indicating the safety of Desidustat therapy in maintaining electrolyte balance (Fig. 4). Adverse events were observed in 11 patients (9.48%), including AV fistula failures in 4 patients (3.45%), left ventricular failure (LVF) in 2 patients (1.72%), arterial thrombosis in 1 patient (0.86%), deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in 2 patients (1.72%), acute pancreatitis in 1 patient (0.86%), haemorrhagic stroke in 1 patient (0.86%), and transaminitis in 1 patient (0.86%).
Conclusion
The study demonstrates significant improvements in hemoglobin levels across all patient groups, with the most notable increases observed in pre-dialysis patients. Serum potassium levels remained stable throughout the follow-up period. These findings suggest that Desidustat therapy is effective in managing anemia in CKD patients, providing a viable alternative to traditional erythropoietin therapy.

title: #3305 Progression of renal disease and mortality in patients with CKD who do or do not receive loop diuretics
authors: Htet Htet Ei Khin; Jocelyn Friday; Luis Loureiro Harrison; John Cleland; Pierpaolo Pellicori; Sokratis Stoumpos
abstract:
Background and Aims
Loop diuretics (LD) are often prescribed in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) with or without a diagnosis of heart failure, to treat hypertension or symptoms and signs of congestion. The prognostic association of the LD use with change in kidney function and other important clinical outcomes has rarely been evaluated.
Method
Electronic medical records for adults from the Greater Glasgow region (covering a population of approximately 1.5 million people) who had at least two serum creatinine measurements between 1 January 2012 and 31 December 2014 were analysed. Patients already receiving renal replacement therapy (RRT) were excluded. Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was calculated using the CKD-EPI (2009) formula, without adjusting for ethnicity. Patients were stratified according to the last eGFR measured prior to 01/01/2015. LD prescribing immediately prior to 2015 and its association with the eGFR slope, the need for renal replacement therapy, and mortality over the following three years was assessed.
Results
The cohort comprised 94,006 patients, including 2,152 with eGFR <30, 8,062 with eGFR 30–44, 19,192 with eGFR 45–59, and 64,600 with eGFR >60 mL/min/1/73 m2. LD were prescribed to 12,252 (13%) patients at baseline, with higher rates in patients with lower eGFR (11%, 14%, 21%, and 33.5% for patients with eGFR >60, 45–59, 30–44, and <30 mL/min/1.73 m2, respectively). Amongst those prescribed LD, the prevalence of heart failure was nearly 10 times higher compared to those not receiving LD across all eGFR groups (1.3% vs. 16% in those with eGFR >60 and 3.3% vs. 21.5% in those with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2) but only a minority of patients treated with LD had a formal diagnostic record of heart failure (∼21% overall). Using a mixed-effects model with individual-level random effects over 3 years, eGFR declined by 2.5 mL/min/1.73 m2/year for the entire cohort. Within 3 years, 474 (0.5%) patients in the entire cohort required RRT. Patients prescribed LD were more likely to receive RRT than those who were not (1.1% versus 0.4%). Mortality at 3 years was considerably higher for those prescribed LD (30%) compared to those who were not (14%), across the spectrum of eGFR (see Table 1).
Conclusion
Patients with a lower eGFR are more often prescribed LD and have a higher prevalence of heart failure. Prescribing LD is associated with a substantially higher mortality rate even in the absence of a diagnosis of heart failure. This may reflect under-diagnosis of heart failure in this population, an adverse effect of LD on prognosis, or the use of LD may be a pharmaco-epidemiological surrogate marker of undiagnosed heart failure, accelerate cardiovascular disease progression or multi-morbidity.

title: #3622 Empiric antibiotic treatment deviates from antibiogram suggested treatment in chronic kidney disease: a single center study
authors: Andreas Antonakis; Kostas Stylianou; Eleni Drosataki; Kleio Dermitzaki; Dimitra Ligerou; Ariadni Androvitsanea; Ioanna Stayrakaki; Sevasti Alexandra Maragkou; Myrto Konidaki; Christos Pleros; Ioannis Petrakis
abstract:
Background and Aims
Infectious diseases are a major cause of morbidity and mortality. The effectiveness of treatment depends on empiric antimicrobial therapy, however, discrepancies between antibiotic resistance patterns and the intended treatment regimen can lead to treatment failure and increased mortality. This study retrospectively examines the rates of such discrepancies in the nephrology department of a tertiary hospital in Greece, intending to optimize individualized treatment strategies.
Method
Electronic medical records were assessed for microbiological, clinical and laboratory data. R programming language (version 4.2.0) was used for statistical analysis and especially the AMR package (University of Gröningen, Netherlands—version 2.1.1) for antibiogram resistance pattern detection. Non-parametric statistical tests were used such as Chi-squared test and Fisher´s exact test. Statistical significance was set at 0.05.
Results
We retrospectively collected data for the years 2023 and 2024. Nine hundred eighty four patients (222 hemodialysis patients-HD, 38 kidney transplanted patients-NTx, 73 patients with Acute Kidney Disease-AKD, 17 peritoneal dialysis patients-PD, and 500 chronic kidney disease patients-CKD) were admitted during that period. Over 10,000 microbiological samples were acquired.
Suspicion of infection during admission was raised in 310 out of 984 patients, who were clustered according to the suspected infection site. Cases lacking clinical and laboratory findings consistent with infection upon admission, comprised 68.5% of the total; however, the majority showed signs of infection during hospitalization needing antimicrobial treatment.
Antibiotic prescription rates were studied; glycopeptides/linezolid were the most frequently used antibiotics (23.0%), followed by cephalosporins (22.3%) and aminopenicillins (9.8%). Catheter-related infections (15.2%) were mainly treated with glycopeptides/linezolid (35.5%) and cephalosporins (24.3%). Significantly high prescription rates were exhibited in quinolones (13.2%) and cephalosporins (17.2%)—especially in renal transplant recipients.
Conversely, the prevalence of antimicrobial resistance patterns, is evidenced by the elevated resistance rates in fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin: 66.8% in hemodialysis), cephalosporins (ceftriaxone: 67.2% in hemodialysis, 69.7% in transplant patients), carbapenems (imipenem: 51.2%), and colistin (28.3%). Some of these antibiotics are commonly used as empirical antimicrobial therapy across all patient classes (Chi-squared = 469.83, df = 16, p-value <10–4).
Conclusion
The observation that most cases without initial infection suspicion showed microbiological evidence of infection during hospitalization, highlights the necessity for improved antimicrobial surveillance and early detection protocols to enhance patient outcomes in renal care.
High prescription rates of advanced antimicrobials in CKD and transplant patients and the fact that numerous widely used antibiotics (fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins, carbapenems) exhibit some of the highest resistance rates, underscore the significance of targeted antimicrobial stewardship programs in optimizing treatment strategies and counteracting resistance development, particularly among patients suffering from renal disease.

Significantly high prescription rates were exhibited in quinolones (13.2%) and cephalosporins (17.2%)—especially in renal transplant recipients.
Conversely, the prevalence of antimicrobial resistance patterns, is evidenced by the elevated resistance rates in fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin: 66.8% in hemodialysis), cephalosporins (ceftriaxone: 67.2% in hemodialysis, 69.7% in transplant patients), carbapenems (imipenem: 51.2%), and colistin (28.3%). Conclusion
The observation that most cases without initial infection suspicion showed microbiological evidence of infection during hospitalization, highlights the necessity for improved antimicrobial surveillance and early detection protocols to enhance patient outcomes in renal care.

title: #572 Multimarkers based response to SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with chronic kidney disease
authors: Giuliana Papalia; Irene Capelli; Daniele Vetrano; Giuseppe Cianciolo; Gaetano La Manna; Gianluigi Zaza; Michele Provenzano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a group of disorders defined by the presence of abnormalities of kidney structure or function for a minimum of 3 months with implications for health. The sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) are a new therapeutic option with a proven cardio and nephroprotective efficacy in patients with or without type 2-diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and preserved or reduced kidney function.
Method
We conducted a retrospective, observational study at the Nephrology, Dialysis and Transplantation Units of Sant'Orsola Hospital of Bologna and Santissima Annunziata Hospital of Cosenza. We enrolled 118 patients since 2020 affected by CKD, with or without T2DM. We aimed at investigating the efficacy of current SGLT2i through the analysis of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), uric acid, hemoglobin, serum potassium and systolic pressure from baseline to month 6 visit.
Results
After 6 months of therapy, a significant correlation between variation of proteinuria and eGFR was found. Proteinuria significantly decreased from baseline (953 mg/die IQR 450–2600) to 6-month visit (621 mg/die IQR 289–1900) (P = 0.0001) with the greatest reduction of proteinuria observed in patients who also experienced a reduction of the eGFR. Estimated GFR (P = 0.898), serum potassium (P = 0.689) and blood pressure (P = 0.829) did not significantly change. Hb increased at visit 2, as for treatment effect moving from 13.8 ± 1.7 g/dL to 14.2 ± 1.8 g/dL (P = 0.0008). Uric acid significantly decreased from 6.1 ± 1.4 mg/dL at baseline to 5.4 ± 1.3 mg/dL at follow-up visit (P = 0.0004) and a positive correlation between uric acid reduction and eGFR increase from baseline to follow-up visit was found (P = 0.037) (Fig. 1). No significant correlations between proteinuria and the other parameters analysed were observed.
Conclusion
In our real-life experience a 30% reduction of proteinuria and a stabilization of eGFR were observed after the initiation of SGLT2i therapy. Concomitantly we observed a change of other parameters that was mainly independent from change in proteinuria. Change in eGFR was associated with change in uric acid concentration. We suggest to monitor multiple parameters before taking decision to continue or withdraw SGLT2 inhibitors, in clinical practice.

title: #1172 Association between blood pressure and chronic kidney disease progression in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease: findings from CRIC and KNOW-CKD study
authors: Cheol Ho Park; Hyung Woo Kim; Jung Tak Park; Tae-Hyun Yoo; Amanda Anderson; Wei Yang; Jordana Cohen; Mahboob Rahman; Shin-Wook Kang; Seung Hyeok Han
abstract:
Background and Aims
Blood pressure (BP) control is important in the management of chronic kidney disease (CKD). However, in patients with advanced CKD, the benefits of BP control in delaying the progression of CKD remains uncertain. We aimed to explore the association of BP levels with kidney outcomes in patients with advanced CKD.
Method
We analyzed 2,939 participants with chronic kidney disease (CKD) G3b to G5 (estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] <45 ml/min/1.73 m2) without kidney replacement therapy (KRT) from the Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC) study and the KoreaN Cohort Study for Outcome in Patients With Chronic Kidney Disease (KNOW-CKD). The main predictors were baseline and time-updated systolic BP (SBP) and diastolic BP (DBP). The primary outcome was a composite kidney outcome of ≥50% decline in eGFR from baseline measurement or the initiation of KRT. In the analyses, multivariate cause-specific hazards models and marginal structural models were fitted for baseline and time-updated BPs, respectively.
Results
During 17755 person-years of follow-up (median, 4.7 years), the composite outcome occurred 1,627 (55.4%) participants. Compared with baseline SBP <120 mmHg, the hazard ratios (HRs) (95% CIs) for 120–129, 130–139, and ≥140 mmHg were 1.33 (1.15–1.54), 1.48 (1.27–1.72), and 1.82 (1.58–2.10), respectively. This association was more evident in analysis with time-updated SBP, where the corresponding HRs (95% CIs) were 1.29 (1.09–1.54), 1.75 (1.46–2.10), and 2.79 (2.36–3.29), respectively. Furthermore, the slopes of eGFR decline were −1.20 (−1.36 to −1.04), −1.77 (−1.97 to −1.57), −2.11 (−2.35 to −1.88), and −2.48 (−2.70 to −2.27) for respective SBP categories. Additional analyses with DBP also showed similar results.
Conclusion
In patients with advanced CKD, higher BP levels were associated with an increased risk of CKD progression.

title: #1303 Short-term effect of finerenone on albuminuria and potassium levels in patients with diabetic kidney disease: analysis in real clinical practice
authors: Álvaro Álvarez López; Juan Villa Rincón; Enrique Luna Huerta; Jorge Alberto Rodriguez Sabillon; Andrea Guerrero Fernández; Teresa de Jesús; Giraldo Rua; Beatriz Gómez Gallego; Lucia Martin Jiménez; Nicolas Roberto Robles Perez-Monteoliva
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease associated with type 2 diabetes mellitus is often linked to a high risk of renal function deterioration. The presence of pathological albuminuria has been described in relation to the decline in glomerular filtration rate. Since mid-2024, we have had the option to prescribe finerenone. This new medication is a highly selective, non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, which, unlike non-selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs), could directly reduce inflammation and fibrosis, providing added value in the management of these patients. Clinical trials have shown a reduction in albuminuria, as well as slowing of the progression of chronic kidney disease, with a lower rate of hyperkalemia compared to non-selective MRAs.
Our aim was to assess the effect of adding oral finerenone to the treatment of 167 type 2 diabetic patients with albuminuria and varying degrees of eGFR. We also aimed to evaluate a subgroup of patients who switched from non-selective MRAs to finerenone due to previous hyperkalemia events.
Method
A follow-up was conducted between 1 and 6 months, monitoring estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) using the CKD-EPI formula, serum potassium (K) levels, albuminuria (measured in a 24-hour urine sample or by albumin/creatinine ratio). Serum C-reactive protein (CRP), GGT, hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), and plasma sodium levels were also measured. In addition, other concomitant medications aimed at treating kidney disease were recorded, including whether or not patients had previously been taking non-selective MRAs.
Results
In our study, data from a total of 167 patients were collected. After one month, data was available for 54 patients, in whom an initial drop in eGFR of 14.37% was observed, which then recovered to baseline levels by the third month and remained stable (n = 30 at the third month and n = 21 at the sixth month). Regarding serum potassium levels, a slight increase was observed after one month (n = 58), with an increase of +0.066 mg/dl, remaining stable in the following months. Only 5.2% of patients experienced an adverse event of hyperkalemia after starting finerenone. Regarding the subgroup of patients previously treated with non-selective MRAs, it was observed that they initially had higher serum potassium levels (4.59 vs. 5.10). After switching to finerenone, there was a significant decrease in potassium levels. As for albuminuria control, we observed that those previously treated with non-selective MRAs showed a rebound in albuminuria one month after starting treatment. Other parameters evaluated, such as serum CRP, GGT, hemoglobin A1c, and plasma sodium, showed no significant differences.
Conclusion
In our real-world study of a population of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and albuminuria with varying degrees of eGFR, the administration of finerenone was safe and well-tolerated. As described in clinical trials, the initiation of the drug led to a slight increase in serum potassium, a decrease in albuminuria, and stability of eGFR during the 6-month follow-up. In the subgroup of patients previously treated with non-selective MRAs, a decrease in serum potassium levels was observed, but there was poorer control of albuminuria. This may be due to the drug being started at a dose of 10 mg every 24 hours due to concerns about hyperkalemia, and as the follow-up period increases and the dose is optimized, the anti-albuminuric effect can be further evaluated. Real-world studies are needed to confirm the results of clinical trials.

title: #1748 Single-dose pharmacokinetics of extended-release calcifediol in healthy Japanese and non-Japanese volunteers
authors: Charles Bishop; Akhtar Ashfaq
abstract:
Background and Aims
ERC is currently approved in the United States and certain European countries at a daily dose of 30 mcg, escalating as needed to 60 mcg, for the treatment of secondary hyperparathyroidism (SHPT) in patients with non-dialysis chronic kidney disease (CKD). This study examined, for the first time, racial differences in fasting and fed pharmacokinetic (PK) profiles of serum calcifediol and its primary metabolites after oral administration of extended-release calcifediol (ERC).
Method
This single-dose, open-label study was conducted at one United States Phase 1 unit to evaluate the PK profiles of serum vitamin D metabolites after oral ERC in 67 healthy male and female Japanese and non-Japanese volunteers having ages of 18 to 55 years. A total of 35 Japanese and 32 non-Japanese participants were randomized with gender balance (at least 8 per group) to ERC doses of 450, 900 and 1,800 mcg (all fasting) and 900 mcg (fed). Participants were housed for 2 days prior to randomization and through the first 48 hours post dose, received standardized and timed meals while in the unit, and provided blood samples at pre-dose baseline, 2-hour intervals through 24 hours, and decreasing frequencies through 28 days. Collected samples were analyzed for serum calcifediol, 24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (24,25D3), total 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25D), corrected calcium (Ca) and phosphorus (P).
Results
Maximum serum concentrations (Cmax) of calcifediol were achieved between 9 and 28 hours (both medians) under fasted conditions, and 9 hours (median) under fed conditions. Dose-related increases were observed in baseline-adjusted Cmax and area under the curve (AUC) in both Japanese and non-Japanese participants in the fasting condition. Cmax was approximately 5-fold higher, and AUC was 3-fold higher under fed conditions. The geometric mean ratios for AUC in Japanese and non-Japanese participants were close to unity after adjustment for body weight. Baseline-adjusted serum Cmax and AUC were not dose-proportional for either nominal dose or dose normalized for body weight. In general, male participants had higher baseline-adjusted AUC and slightly lower clearance compared with female participants of both races. Mean terminal elimination half-life (t1/2) ranged from 10.0 to 16.7 days. Serum 1,25D reached maximum levels on Day 3 then decreased to near baseline levels by Day 7 for both races, and the increases were greater under fed compared to fasting conditions. Serum 24,25D3 concentrations were elevated between Day 1 and Day 28, and were comparable under fasting and fed conditions for both races. Serum Ca and P remained constant after all doses and treatment-emergent adverse events were all mild and unrelated to treatment.
Conclusion
No racial differences in PK profiles of serum calcifediol and its primary vitamin D metabolites (24,25D3 and 1,25D) were observed between Japanese and non-Japanese participants after single doses of oral ERC in fasting and fed conditions.

title: #2193 Dietary management strategies for Koreans with chronic kidney disease: a nutrient intake analysis based on Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KNHANES)
authors: Jung-Hyun Kim; Min-Sook Kyung; Sehoon Park; Dong Ki Kim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Since the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KNHANES) began, sodium intake among Koreans aged 19 and older has decreased from 4975.0 mg to 3178.9 mg by 2022. However, this level still exceeds the Korean Dietary Reference Intakes (KDRIs), which recommend an adequate intake (AI) of 1500 mg and a maximum of 2300 mg to reduce the risk of chronic diseases. This study aims to develop a dietary management program targeting individuals aged 30–64 who are at risk of kidney health issues or have chronic kidney disease (CKD) by addressing dietary risk factors.
Method
We utilized raw data from the first year of the 8th KNHNES(2019) to analyze associations among blood pressure, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), serum creatinine levels, and the intake of major nutrients, focusing on sodium intake. The analysis was conducted with 3223 Koreans aged 20 years and older. Regression analysis was utilized to assess differences in nutrient intake associated with physician-diagnosed hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, and CKD. We excluded individuals with energy intake levels below 500 kcal or above 500 kcal. Statistical analyses were performed using SAS 9.4 software, and the findings were used to develop a community-based low-sodium dietary management strategy for the prevention and management of CKD.
Results
Our regression analysis indicated that individuals diagnosed with hypertension showed significantly lower fat and sodium intake in both genders, while those with CKD exhibited significantly lower energy and dietary fiber intake (P = 0.0384, P = 0.0345). Notably, protein, calcium, and water intake were significantly lower in males (P = 0.0001), whereas fat intake was significantly lower in females exclusively (P = 0.0031). Potassium intake was significantly lower in both genders (P = 0.0030, P = 0.0065). However, sodium intake exhibited no significant differences (N.S.). Furthermore, regression analysis revealed a positive correlation among systolic and diastolic blood pressure, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), serum creatinine levels, and nutrient intake for every 100 mg increase in sodium intake (P = 0.0045, P < 0.0001, P = 0.0065, P < 0.0001). Thus, we developed a dietary management program for individuals with CKD risk group and CKD patients within community settings, considering gender-specific nutritional intake patterns. The program emphasized the improvement of cooking methods rather than ingredient selection, and proposed practical sodium reduction guidelines. The guidelines suggest to control soup and broth intake, encouraging fresh vegetables over pickled foods, such as kimchi, reducing takeout meals, using low-sodium soy sauce, fostering the habit of checking nutritional labels, and utilizing umami flavors as an alternative to salt for seasoning.
Conclusion
In conclusion, the community-based dietary management program for the prevention and management of CKD in Koreans, incorporating gender-specific guidelines, is essential to empower the individuals in adopting and maintaining healthier dietary practice. Further studies are needed to verify its effectiveness in the near future.

title: #2591 The anticholinergic burden in patients with chronic kidney disease: patterns, risk factors, and the link with cognitive impairment
authors: Agathe Mouheb; Hélène Levassort; Ziad Massy; Natalia Alencar de Pinho; Marion Pepin; Solene Laville; Sophie Liabeuf
abstract:
Background and Aims
People with chronic kidney disease (CKD) have an elevated risk of cognitive impairment (CI). Medications with anticholinergic activity are recognized for their adverse reactions on central nervous system. The putative association between the anticholinergic burden and CI has not previously been evaluated in patients with CKD. The study aimed to (i) describe prescriptions of medications with anticholinergic activity, (ii) analyze factors associated with these prescriptions, and (iii) evaluate the anticholinergic burden's association with cognitive performance.
Method
CKD-REIN, a prospective cohort study, enrolled nephrology outpatients with a confirmed diagnosis of CKD (eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m2). Drug prescriptions were recorded prospectively during the 5-year follow-up. Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE) was assessed at baseline and CI was defined as an MMSE score <24/30. For each patient, the anticholinergic burden was determined by summing the Anticholinergic Cognitive Burden (ACB) scores of all prescription drugs at baseline. Multinomial logistic regression was used to analyze factors associated with the ACB score. Logistic regression was used to evaluate the association between the cognitive impairment and the anticholinergic burden at baseline.
Results
At baseline, 3007 patients (median age [IQR], 69[60–76]; 65% men) had MMSE data and were included. 1549 (52%) of these patients were taking at least one drug with anticholinergic properties. Most (1092; 70%) had a low anticholinergic burden, 294 (19%) had a moderate anticholinergic burden, and 163 (11%) had a high anticholinergic burden. A history of neurological/psychiatric disorders and a higher number of daily drugs were associated with a greater probability of having a high anticholinergic burden (odds ratio (OR) [95% confidence interval (95% CI)] = 1.88 [1.29; 2.74] and 1.53 [1.45; 1.61], respectively). Patients with a high anticholinergic burden had a significantly higher probability of presenting cognitive impairment, compared with patients without an anticholinergic burden (OR [95% CI] = 1.76 [1.12; 2.75]) after adjustment for sociodemographic factors, comorbidities, laboratory data, and the number of medications taken daily. Anxiolytic agents (hydroxyzine) and antidepressants (amitriptyline) were the most used drug classes with a high anticholinergic score.
Conclusion
The results of our study emphasize the need for caution in the prescription of drugs with anticholinergic properties to patients with CKD.

For each patient, the anticholinergic burden was determined by summing the Anticholinergic Cognitive Burden (ACB) scores of all prescription drugs at baseline. Anxiolytic agents (hydroxyzine) and antidepressants (amitriptyline) were the most used drug classes with a high anticholinergic score.
Conclusion
The results of our study emphasize the need for caution in the prescription of drugs with anticholinergic properties to patients with CKD.

title: #3032 Frailty and kidney replacement therapy choice, a single centre, observational study
authors: Kelly Chenlei Li; Kylie Turner; Xiaobing MA
abstract:
Background and Aims
Frailty is a syndrome of reduced physiological reserve and is highly prevalent in the kidney failure population. It is associated with adverse health outcomes such as death and healthcare utilisation, particularly in those receiving dialysis. However, whether frailty impacts decisions about kidney replacement therapy (KRT) in predialysis patients is not clear. The primary objective of this observational study is to describe the association between frailty status and KRT choice in a predialysis cohort. Secondary objectives are to describe the association between frailty and symptom burden, malnutrition risk, and referral for transplant assessment.
Method
Patients were sequentially recruited from their first visit to the Kidney Disease Education Clinic (KDEC) at a tertiary metropolitan centre in Sydney, Australia March 2021–August 2024. KDEC provides predialysis education to assist KRT-suitable patients to make an informed choice about KRT modality, and facilitates dialysis access creation and dialysis initiation. KRT modalities were grouped as 1) supported haemodialysis, 2) home dialysis, 3) pre-emptive transplant, and 4) non-KRT.
Frailty was assessed objectively using fried frailty assessment, incorporating 5 domains of weight loss, weakness, exhaustion, slowness and low physical activity. A score of 0–2 was non-frail, and 3–5 was frail. Symptoms are assessed by the iPOS Renal, and nutritional by Malnutrition Screening Tool (MST). Transplant assessment can occur for both pre-emptive and for deceased donor waitlist.
Results
148 out of 157 patients attending KDEC completed frailty assessment. 40 (27%) were frail and 108 non-frail. Both groups had a median age of 65 and median eGFR of 15 ml/min, with no differences observed in gender, ethnicity, and co-morbidities. Compared with non-frail patients, frail patients were more likely to choose supported haemodialysis (40% vs 25%), and less likely to choose home dialysis (25% vs 50%) or receive pre-emptive transplant (2% vs 8%), P < 0.01 (Fig. 1A). Frail patients had a higher prevalence of physical symptoms (nutritional and non-nutritional) (Fig. 1B), and higher malnutrition risk on MST P < 0.01 (Fig. 1C). There were no differences in transplant referral (33% vs 50% P = 0.065).
Conclusion
Frail predialysis patients were less likely to choose home dialysis and had a higher burden of physical symptoms.

title: #634 The role of pain in reducing quality of life in patients with stage 5 CKD: a systematic review
authors: Yorkin Rasulev; Botir Daminov; Aziz Tursunbayaev; Javokhir Khalmukhamedov; Rakhmankulova Zukhra
abstract:
Background and Aims
Pain is a common but often undertreated symptom in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), with a much higher prevalence than in the general population. In the general population, the prevalence of pain in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) is reported to be 40 to 60% for patients receiving renal replacement therapy (RRT), 60 to 70% for patients with pre-terminal kidney disease (PTKD), and up to 100% for hospitalized patients with CKD. Musculoskeletal pain predominates at 60%–70% in both the general and CKD populations [1]. The aim of this systematic review is to obtain up-to-date population-based estimates of the prevalence of different types of pain in different subgroups of the CKD patient population (CKD without dialysis, dialysis, kidney transplant recipients, palliative care), and the impact of chronic pain on the quality of life of patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD).
Method
a retro and prospective analysis of 1767 medical records of patients aged 20 to 75 years hospitalized in various departments of the State Institution "Republican Specialized Scientific and Practical Medical Center for Nephrology and Kidney Transplantation" for 2021–2023 was carried out. The study to assess QOL was carried out using the Russian-language version of the SF36 questionnaire (short form medical outcomes study), which is most often used abroad (USA, European countries) and in domestic studies on clinical medicine, and allows for a quantitative description of the physical, psychological and social components of QOL. Statistical processing was performed in Microsoft Office Excel 2023.
Results
the main causes of chronic kidney disease are: diabetic nephropathy—23.76% (420), hypertensive nephrosclerosis—18.9% (334), chronic glomerulonephritis—32.48% (574), tubulointerstitial nephritis—7.38% (13), cystic kidney disease—18.05 (319) and others—5.94% (105).
In the survey results, such a factor as the use of tobacco products: 51.49% (910) have never used, 16.41% (290) currently smoke, 31.91% (564) of patients previously smoked.
The severity of pain syndrome according to the pain intensity scale in patients with CKD stage 5 was: average values 83.42 ± 21.12 points, in men 86.58 ± 19.15 and 78.48 ± 22.7, in women, there was a statistically significant difference in the intensity of pain syndrome between males and females (P < 0.001). There was no statistically significant correlation between the VAS indicators and the etiology of CKD (Pearson coefficient—0.06). This confirms the postulate that the etiology of CKD is not related to the severity of pain. The pain intensity scale (bodily pain—BP) indicates the impact of pain on the ability to perform daily activities, including work at home and outside the home. Low scores indicate that pain significantly limits the patient's activity, for example: 0–10 points—unbearable pain (absolute disorders); 10–30 points—severe pain (severe disorders); 40–60 points—moderate pain (moderate disorders); 60–80 points—moderate pain (moderate disorders); 80–90 points—mild pain (mild disorders); 100 points—no disorders.
According to the questionnaire results, unbearable pain was noted in 10 patients, severe pain in 72 patients, moderate pain in 1447 patients, mild pain in 238 patients and 79 patients did not experience pain syndrome.
Conclusions
The results of the assessment of the quality of life of patients with terminal CKD, corrected by PG, allow us to identify the features of the holistic, both physical and mental, response of the patient's body to the pathological process and tolerability of treatment, which must be taken into account when prescribing planned and emergency treatment measures.
Pain has a significant negative impact on quality of life in patients with CRF undergoing PG. Subgroups with higher risk included older patients, women, patients with higher BMI, individuals without higher education, unemployed, individuals with low monthly income, smokers, individuals with multiple comorbidities, and patients with longer dialysis experience.

title: #870 Estimation of allergy frequency with tryptase in hemodialysis patients
authors: Turker Emre; Nazife Nur Özer Şensoy
abstract:
Background and Aims
In patients undergoing hemodialysis, pruritus has both uremic and non-uremic causes , its treatments differ significantly, Additionally, some allergies are life-threatening and require immediate treatment.
The increase in serum levels of tryptase, released from mast cells following contact with an allergen, indicates that the event is an allergic reaction.
Based on this, we designed this study to investigate the occurrence of allergies during dialysis, determine their prevalence, and identify the factors contributing to this process.
Method
104 patients enrolled in a chronic hemodialysis program, blood samples were taken at three time points: before the initiation of hemodialysis (hour 0), and at the 1st and 4th hours after dialysis began.
Analyses were primarily conducted for tryptase, eosinophilic cationic protein, total IgE, anti-latex IgE, magnesium (Mg), zinc (Zn), and vitamin D.
Results
Data from 86 out of 104 hemodialysis patients were analyzed. Of these, 45 were male (mean age: 58.6 years, min–max: 24–79);and 41 were female (mean age: 57.8 years, min–max: 25–84).
Among the 86 patients, 39 (45%) demonstrated elevated tryptase levels at the 1st hour compared to baseline. Subsequently, the mean serum tryptase levels at 0, 1, and 4 hours for these 39 patients were analyzed and compared using the Wilcoxon test, producing the following results:
When the mean serum tryptase levels at 0 and 1 hour were compared, the levels at the 1st hour were found to be significantly higher (P < 0.000) (Table 1).
When the mean serum tryptase levels at 0 and 4 hours were compared, the levels at the 4th hour were found to be significantly lower (P < 0.000) (Table 2).
Specific Latex IgE positivity was detected in 8 out of 100 patients (8%). Among these 8 patients, only 1 showed an increase in tryptase levels at the 1st hour.
Based on this, with 39 patients showing elevated serum tryptase levels and 7 patients with elevated serum latex IgE levels, it is estimated that 46 out of 86 patients (53%) had allergies.
Correlation analysis of test parameters revealed significant relationships, particularly between Zinc (Zn) and Tryptase, Magnesium (Mg), Phosphorus (P), Total IgE, and Eosinophilic Cationic Protein (EoKP) (Table 3).
A linear relationship was identified between dialysis duration (in months) and both eosinophil count and eosinophilic cationic protein (EoKP) levels in the patients (r = 0.394, P = 0.013; and r = 0.422, P = 0.007, respectively).
The mean vitamin D level was found to be significantly lower in the allergic group.
(P = 0.024).
Conclusion
In this study, 53% (46/86) of patients were found to have elevated allergic parameters, indicating that allergies are more common than expected in hemodialysis patients.
The increase in eosinophil count and eosinophilic cationic protein levels, as dialysis duration increases, suggests that the patients may become sensitized during the dialysis process.
According to this study, this condition is not only related to factors such as toxins and allergens but also to the patient's immune defense, which may be affected by deficiencies in substances like zinc and vitamin D that are associated with the immune system.

title: #1275 Physical activity in patients with chronic kidney disease: the effects of caregivers and residential factors
authors: Marieta P Theodorakopoulou; Fotini Iatridi; Io Giannopoulou; Eleni Karkamani; Artemios Karagiannidis; Nasra Haddad; Erasmia Sampani; Konstantina Dipla; Pantelis Sarafidis; Afroditi Boutou
abstract:
Background and Aims
Physical inactivity is common in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients; several patient- and disease-related factors are linked to a sedentary lifestyle, but social and environmental influences remain unexplored. This study evaluates the level of physical activity in patients with CKD and investigates the associations with caregivers' physical activity levels, characteristics of the residential environment, and objective measures of exercise capacity.
Method
Eighty CKD patients (20 per CKD stage 2–4) were included; patients and their carers filled out the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ), questionnaires about residential environment and past exercise habits. The CKD patients also performed a 30-sec sit-to-stand-test (30-STS) as a measure of exercise capacity.
Results
According to the IPAQ-score, CKD patients were largely inactive (only 10% reported health-enhancing activity levels); no differences were found between CKD stages. The 30-STS was also impaired, and the number of repetitions significantly decreased with advancing CKD stages (14.2 ± 2.9 vs. 12.6 ± 5.4 vs. 10.4 ± 3.3 vs. 10.5 ± 3.5; P = 0.008). Carers were also highly inactive but still had higher physical activity compared to patients (moderate intensity metabolic equivalents (METS) P = 0.03, vigorous intensity METS P = 0.053); no correlation between carers' and patients' physical activity was noted (P = 0.702). Patients' physical activity was associated with residential factors: living in a detached house compared to an apartment (P = 0.013 for moderate intensity and P = 0.017 for vigorous METS), having a garden (P = 0.019 for moderate intensity and P = 0.022 for vigorous METS) and accessing house by stairs (P = 0.037 for vigorous METS), were associated with higher physical activity.
Conclusion
Physical activity was significantly reduced in CKD patients, irrespectively disease stage. Carers were also highly inactive, but no association was found between the patients' and carers' daily activities. Residential characteristics were the only factors found to be associated to patients' physical activity levels. Personalized, supportive interventions are required, taking into account the patients' social support and microenvironment, in order to increase the physical activity level in this population.

title: #1409 Potential inhibitors of vascular calcification of plant origin—data from systematic review
authors: Annika Adoberg; Liisi Leis; Merike Luman; Fredrik Uhlin; Ivo Fridolin; Jana Holmar
abstract:
Background and Aims
Vascular calcification of chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients remains challenging in effective treatment options. The risk of cardiovascular death is the highest among these patients [1]. The aim of the systematic review was to find possible inhibitors and their serum levels, the knowledge that could be correlated with the removal of uremic toxins, neutralizing oxidative stress, and modifying renal replacement therapy. However several substances of plant origin were demonstrated and as this topic of interest is often discussed with outpatient clinics as well as in-patient wards, the current abstract presents the results from the search of the systematic review.
Method
The systematic review was conducted in accordance of PRISMA and registered in PROSPERO on August 30th, 2023 (CRD42023459169), advanced search in PubMed and Web of Science was performed, and the latest update was December 8th, 2024. The following terms were used for the systematic literature search: vascular calcification AND inhibitor OR inhibition OR enhancer OR promoter OR inducer OR biomarker OR modulator. The search included kidney disease mentioned in the title or abstract. Reviews and meta-analyses were not searched. All articles found were written in English. Of 463 papers, 339 were included in the extensive analysis, and 192 were eligible for the final review.
Results
Although evidence of all the possible inhibitors of plant origin originates from rodent studies and therefore remains low, five possible inhibitors of plant origin were found to give the base for further studies. These five substances that show mechanisms of action that might prevent vascular calcification in CKD patients are presented in Table 1.
Conclusion
Possible inhibitors of vascular calcification, Table 1, remain in scope for research, current studies about substances of plant origin provide a good starting point for discussion and further studies to confirm these novel findings.

title: #2004 Artificial intelligence in optimizing nephrology outpatient managment: result of a pilot study
authors: Rosita Greco; Teresa Papalia; Michele Provenzano; Fiorella Iorio; Chiara Summaria; Antonella Guzzo; Gianluigi Zaza
abstract:
Background and Aims
Process mining (PM) has been defined “a new research frontier for process reorganization in health care”. It is an approach of Artificial intelligence (AI) comprising a wide range of methods and techniques for analyzing processes from data collected during routine activity. This is the first application of PM to the clinical management of outpatients, although there are experiments in the literature in administrative processes or emergency room admissions. We evaluated the effectiveness of these AI methods for monitoring and improving outpatient processes in our Nephrology Department and highlighting their potential and critical issues.
Method
The experimentation included two phases. Phase1: Identification, collection, preprocessing of clinical data and construction of the dataset in the XES standard (Fig. 1). Adherence to the standard will make it possible to be “compliant” with all PM tools and to implement different types of analysis. In addition, observation flows and variables, particularly demographic and clinical variables (age, sex, BP, BMI, CKD stage, age of transplantation, major comorbidities), reception/end visit times, and detection of exams are defined. Phase2: Analysis of the dataset with different PM models: Process Map for process/flow extraction from the data (gap analysis), Process Key Performance Indicator for time and load analysis, Process Simulator for dynamic flow simulation and bottleneck detection, Process Conformance for compliance analysis and deviations from process standards.
Results
In phase 1 we collected a dataset of 46 outpatients. In phase2 PM tools analysis provided time and load values related to the correct execution process (Fig. 2). Critical issues emerged such as noncompliance with the expected procedure: about 60 percent of patients bypassed admission, and in some the clinical assessments expected in a proper outpatient visit were not detected (e.g., BP was not detected in 9% and BMI in 20%). The simulation also revealed bottlenecks at several points in the process and timing anomalies. The results analysis enabled the identification of action points on which to act to improve management. On the same time, the analysis brought out some situations that the method flagged as abnormal. For instance, some patients diverged from the ideal flow (indicated by AI) and the divergence was related to specific clinical conditions that the model could not identify.
Conclusion
This pilot study highlights the enormous benefits of AI techniques such as PM to monitor and optimize outpatient management and performance. However, the success of AI is related to the synergy between technology and physician, which helps in the interpretation of analysis data.

authors: Yaerim Kim; Ping-Hsun Wu; Soie Kwon; Jeonghwan Lee; Ming-Yen Lin; Yi Wen Chiu; Dong Ki Kim; Seungyeup Han; Chun Soo Lim; Shang-Jyh Hwang; Jung Pyo Lee
abstract:
Background and Aims
Elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels are linked to higher mortality. However, the significance of ALP level variability on patient outcomes, particularly in chronic kidney disease (CKD), has not been well explored. This study aimed to investigate the impact of ALP variability on all-cause mortality in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD).
Method
This multi-ethnic, multi-center retrospective cohort study analyzed data from Taiwan and Korea from January 2001 to December 2021. Patients aged ≥18 years with CKD, defined by an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <60 mL/min/1.73 m2, were included. ALP variability was measured using standard deviation (SD), coefficient of variance (CoV), and variance, and categorized into quartiles for analysis, with the first quartile as the reference group. A Cox-proportional hazard model, adjusted for demographic factors, comorbidities, and laboratory variables, was used to assess the impact of ALP variability on mortality.
Results
A total of 13,451 patients with CKD were included; the mean age was 63.6 ± 13.6 years; 62.2% were male. Comorbidities included hypertension (54.1%), diabetes (44.5%), and cardiovascular disease (17.0%). The mean eGFR was 36.6 ± 13.9 mL/min/1.73 m2, with 23.4% of patients in CKD stage 4 and 8.4% in stage 5. Higher ALP variability, as indicated by the top quartile in SD, CoV, and variance, was significantly associated with increased all-cause mortality (SD, aHR 1.81, 95% CI 1.61–2.04; CoV, aHR 1.49, 95% CI 1.33–1.67; Variance, aHR 1.81, 95% CI 1.61–2.04). Subgroup analysis based on comorbidities such as hypertension, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease showed that the hazard impact was consistently maintained. The impact of ALP was prominent in patients with eGFR 30–60 (aHR 2.03, 95% CI 1.76–2.34).
Conclusion
Variability in ALP levels is a significant predictor of all-cause mortality in patients with CKD, highlighting the need to monitor ALP fluctuations as part of the comprehensive risk assessment in individuals with CKD.

title: #2907 “Use a machine learning model that estimates survival curves to identify patients at high risk of rapid progression of chronic kidney disease.”
authors: Slawomir Zmonarski; Wojciech Rafajłowicz; Ewaryst Rafajłowicz; Ewa Skubalska-Rafajłowicz; Magda Skoczeń; Szczepan Barnaś; Magdalena Krajewska; Michał Zmonarski; Miroslaw Banasik; Magdalena Kuriata-Kordek
abstract:
Background and Aims
The appropriate modification of care for patients with chronic kidney disease provides an opportunity to slow its progression. Aims: To test a machine learning strategy aimed at selecting patients at high risk of rapid progression of chronic kidney disease and to attempt a medical assessment of the validity of the results of the proposed machine learning model.
Method
We propose a machine learning-based computational system that extends Cox survival function estimation by clustering into similar groups based on readily available raw laboratory results from patients admitted to a hospital ward for treatment. The system requires a laptop to run already trained classifiers, e.g., neural networks and stored survival curves for patient subgroups. Our learning/testing data consisted of 13 laboratory results including: urine specific gravity, serum and urine protein concentrations, and serum creatinine concentration for 520 patients each. Data from patients (320 persons) whose creatinine concentration increased were clustered into two groups by applying the spectral method. Each cluster was then split into four subgroups according to age and sex.
Results
Different spectra of impairment affecting the rate of endpoint achievement were correctly identified. Also, the system correctly indicated that the group with the highest risk of renal disease progression was the population of older men with an initial mild degree of renal impairment, clustered in cluster two.
Conclusion
The machine learning-based system that estimates survival curves can be a reliable tool for accurately identifying patients at high risk of progression of chronic kidney disease. The system operates in accordance with current medical knowledge, therefore it can be a tool for quick preliminary analysis for nephrologists, as well as support for doctors with specialties other than nephrology, thus contributing to reducing the burden of routine nephrology consultations.

title: #3751 The comparison of cognitive function in chronic kidney disease patients on renal replacement therapy in Albania
authors: Vilma Cadri; Ariana Strakosha; Elvana Rista; Nevi Pasko; Elida Luri; Sabina Tahsimi; Elizana Petrela; Anita Pilika; Brikena Allkoja
abstract:
Background and Aims
Change in cognitive function (CF) is one of the known consequences of end stage renal disease (ESRD). Cognitive impairment (CI) is likely to become an increasingly important public health issue in the ESRD population, but little is known about the influence of different therapy modalities on cognitive function. The aim of this study was to determine the frequency of CI in patients on hemodialysis (HD) and to compare them with patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis (PD), renal transplantation (Tx) and a control group.
Method
We assessed various cognitive abilities in 62 patients on renal replacement therapy (RRT) and compared the effect of renal treatment on cognitive abilities with a control group of 57 individuals. Throughout this analysis, we used age and education level as criteria to define the sample and control groups. CF was estimated using the MOCA test. Paired t-test and ANOVA test were used to obtain the results.
Results
Individuals involved in the analyses are in the age group of 25–50 years, with a mean of 34.5 years for the control group and 37.16 years for the sample patients. ANOVA test confirms that there is no difference between the age and educational level of individuals involved in the analyses with kidney disease (sample) vs. those with no kidney disease (control groups).
The prevalence of normal cognition is 47.4% in the control group and 27.4% in the observed patients. Mild cognitive impairment is 52.6% for the control group and 64.5% for the patients, while moderate/severe cognition with a prevalence of 8.1% is observed only in patients with chronic kidney disease (see Fig. 1). Severe CI is observed only among patients with HD. Moderate CI has a prevalence of 13% among HD patients while lowering to 8% for PD patients and just 1% among TX. Among chronic kidney disease patients on renal replacement therapy, we found an improvement in cognitive performance in transplanted patients (see Fig. 2).
The overall MOCA score for the control group was 25.57, while the mean MOCA score for the patient sample was 22.61. The paired t-test shows that this difference is statistically different. We analyzed all the components of the CI assessment and tested the statistical differences between the control and observed patients. The paired t-test for the mean difference shows that attention and cognitive skills that help people perform actions are statistically lower for observed patients if compared to a control group.
To further analyze how cognitive abilities differ among patients with kidney disease and the control group, we used ANOVA (analysis of variance), which corrects for any bias in testing if non-constant variance). We found evidence that there is a statistical difference in cognitive ability between control and observed patients that affects their ability to name things and recall events from the past. Patients with kidney disease manifest as well a lower ability to use language. Abstraction skills do not appear to manifest differences between control and observed patients (see ANOVA results).
Conclusion
CI is an important problem in chronic kidney disease and RRT, regardless of the modality used, even in non-elderly patients. We found that renal transplantation as a treatment modality in ESRD patients is superior to HD and PD in terms of cognitive performance improvement. We also found that cognitive problems may occur earlier and more frequently in PD patients than in the general population, but with a lower incidence than in HD patients. These considerations are important to communicate to patients when choosing between the different replacement modalities.

title: #3919 Klotho protein associated with worse cognitive function in chronic kidney disease patients
authors: Anaiara Lucena Queiroz; Elizabeth De Francesco Daher; Geraldo Bezerra Da Silva Junior; Raoni de Oliveira; Domingues Da Silva; Laura Pinheiro Correia; Maria Fernanda Lucena Karbage; Gdayllon Meneses; Alice Maria Costa Martins; Alissandra Lima Barbosa de Oliveira; Danielle MacÊdo Gaspar
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cognitive decline is a major concern among patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), significantly impacting quality of life and increasing mortality. Despite the relevance, its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Klotho, a protein with neuroprotective properties primarily produced by the kidneys, is known to have reduced levels in individuals with CKD. This study explores the association between Klotho levels and cognitive performance in CKD patients.
Method
Cross-sectional study including adults with CKD assessed at a medical center in Northeast Brazil. Clinical and laboratory data were obtained, including Klotho, FGF23, VCAM-1, ANG1, and ANG2 biomarkers. Cognitive function was assessed through the application of the following neuropsychological tests: Rey's Auditory-Verbal Learning Test (RAVLT), Five Digit Test (FDT), Corsi's Cube Task (CCT), Stroop Test, Trial Making Test (TMT) and Phonemic and Semantic fluency tasks. Patients were classified according to their eGFR into 3 groups: control group, with no CKD; mild CKD (group A), eGFR ≥ 45 mL/min/ 1.73 m2; moderate/severe CKD (group B), eGFR < 45 mL/min/1,73 m2.
Results
A total of 52 patients were included in the study, mostly female (59.6%), with a mean age of 53.3 ± 15.4 years. Group A had 29 (55.7%) patients, group B had 11 (21.1%), and the control group had 12 (23.0%). When compared to control, groups A and B had significantly lower Klotho levels (0.2 [0.17–1.46] and 0.38 [0.17–3.18] vs. 1.61 [0.28–2.03] ng/mL, P = 0.01), higher FGF23 (0.7 [0–2.3] and 4 [0.5–11.6] vs. 0.2 [0–4] ng/mL, P = 0.05) and VCAM-1 levels (726 ± 275 and 920 ± 162 vs. 604 ± 180 ng/mL, P = 0.01). Klotho levels were associated with a deficit in RAVLT's learning (0.19 [0.15–0.88] vs. 1.54 [0.2–2.22], P = 0.02) and retention index (0.2 [0.18–0.43] vs. 0.33 [0.17–1.79], P = 0.52); and FDT's time to count (0.19 [0.15–0.43] vs. 1.74 [0.2–2.27], P = 0.01), to choose (0.21 [0.15–1.53] vs. 1.59 [0.19–2.22], P < 0.01), to shift (0.2 [0.15–1.49] vs. 1.78 [ 0.21–3.18], P < 0.01), and inhibition time (0.19 [ 0.13–1.46] vs. 1.09 [0.19–2.23], P < 0.01].
Conclusion
Lower Klotho levels were associated with more advanced CKD and worse cognitive performance in patients without prior cerebrovascular diseases. These findings highlight the potential use of Klotho as an early biomarker of cognitive deficit among CKD patients.

title: #738 Low serum Na-Cl difference level before alkali therapy is an independent predictor of rapid renal deterioration in CKDG3b-G5 patients with hyperkalemic metabolic acidosis
authors: Shuzo Kaneko; Ririko Murata; Ainori Hoshimoto; Rina Hisada; Makiko Harano; Emi Anno; So Hagiwara; Eri Imai
abstract:
Background and Aims
Advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) is often complicated by serum potassium[K]-elevated metabolic acidosis (high K-MA) and MA can be a cause of CKD progression. High K-MA can occur with decreased mineralocorticoid action (e.g., use of RAAS inhibitors (RAASi), hyporeninemic states such as diabetes and volume expansion) or, in advanced CKD, with decreased nephron mass exceeding compensatory excretion of H+ (NH4+) and K+ in the renal tubules. Metabolic acid-base status is usually assessed by serum HCO3−/total-CO2 concentrations, but respiratory status, especially respiratory compensatory changes in severe metabolic acid-base imbalance, also affect these values. On the other hand, the serum Na-Cl difference ([Na-Cl]) is a simplified strong ion difference and is useful as an indicator of the dominant metabolic component independent of respiratory status. In patients with advanced CKD, especially those with high K-MA requiring alkalizing therapeutic intervention, it is unclear whether pre-intervention [Na-Cl] determines renal prognosis and incidence of cardiovascular events.
Method
In this single-center retrospective observational study, CKDG3b-G5 outpatients with ([HCO3−] <22 mM) and elevated K (serum [K] ≥5.0 mEq/L) at our center and who had started alkali therapy for high K-MA were included. Total of 59 patients were selected, excluding those who had already been prepared for renal replacement therapy at the start of alkali therapy.
Background factors such as age, sex, cause of CKD, and parameters immediately prior to the initiation of alkali therapy (i.e., estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), CKD stage, urinary protein (g/gCr), serum [K]/[HCO3−]/[Na-Cl]/albumin/phosphate, hemoglobin levels, and use of RAASi/K binders/diuretics) were investigated. The endpoints were the incidence of renal events (>30% reduction in eGFR or renal replacement therapy) and cardiovascular events within 2 years of starting alkali therapy.
Results
In all 59 subjects, the mean age was 72.0 ± 11.7 years, 81% were male, mean eGFR was 19.6 ± 7.2 mL/min/1.73 m2, CKDG4/5 account for 92% (G4 60%/G5 32%), primary disease was diabetic nephropathy 30%, nephrosclerosis 43%, RAASi use 68%, mean [K] 5.5 ± 0.4 mEq/L, mean [HCO3−] 18.1 ± 2.2 mM and mean [Na-Cl] 28 ± 3.2 mEq/L. In a multivariate analysis among potential determinants for metabolic acid-base status (i.e., [Na-Cl], albumin, phosphate, hemoglobin), lower[Na-Cl] (P = 0.002) and lower hemoglobin level (P = 0.005) were significantly associated with poor cumulative renal survival. In a multivariate analysis performed among factors drawn from background factors that were significant in univariate analysis, lower eGFR (P = 0.004), lower [Na-Cl] (P = 0.006), no RAASi use (P = 0.006), and lower hemoglobin level (P = 0.051) were associated with poor renal outcome. Neither [HCO3−] (used instead of [Na-Cl]) nor [K] was significant (P = 0.252 and P = 0.199). In tertile classification of [Na-Cl], the lowest ([Na-Cl] ≤ 26) group had significantly poorer cumulative renal survival (P = 0.001) (Figure). In Cox regression analysis, adjusted hazard ratios for [Na-Cl] ≤ 26 (reference [Na-Cl] ≥ 30) were 4.47–6.84 (P < 0.001- P = 0.022), adjusted for many factors including age, sex, cause of CKD, eGFR, affecting metabolic acid-base status, and type of alkalizing treatment (Table). There were only a few cardiovascular events during the study period, and the relationship between [Na-Cl] and these events was not evident.
Conclusion
In advanced CKD (G3b-G5) patients complicated by metabolic acidosis with elevated serum potassium requiring alkalizing therapeutic intervention, a low serum Na-Cl difference level can be an independent determinant of rapid renal deterioration.

title: #1322 Artificial intelligence in the identification of key metabolites associated with diabetic kidney disease
authors: Inha Jung; Sungjin Park; Soon Hyo Kwon; Ji A Seo; Hyeong Kyu Park; Nan Hee Kim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Despite the increasing prevalence of DKD, reliable biomarkers for its early detection remain scarce. This study aimed to identify urine and serum metabolites that differentiate between DKD stages through bioinformatics analysis.
Method
We analyzed 92 participants, categorizing them by eGFR and ACR combinations to identify criteria that best distinguish metabolites. Using these criteria, we trained and validated separate AI models. The criterion with the highest accuracy was selected for further investigation of metabolites that varied under this criterion. To understand the relationships and functions of these metabolites, we conducted a metabolic network analysis.
Results
The classification based on ACR achieved the highest prediction accuracy. We identified nine urine and thirteen serum metabolites common among the top 20 from each group. Four metabolites—Adenosine and 5-MTA in urine, and m2,2G and cis-Aconitic acid in serum—demonstrated significant differences across ACR groups (Fig. 1). Metabolic network analysis revealed hub proteins and networks linking these metabolites, with significant mRNA expression differences in hub proteins between healthy controls and those with DKD in both urine and serum networks (Fig. 2). Notably, IL4I1 mRNA was identified in both urine and serum.
Conclusion
The ACR-based classification demonstrated the highest accuracy. Urinary adenosine and 5-MTA, and serum m2,2G and cis-aconitic acid showed distinct patterns across ACR groups, highlighting their potential as biomarkers. Metabolic network analysis revealed hub proteins, including IL4I1, and networks connecting these differentially expressed metabolites. Further investigation into IL4I1's involvement in DKD is recommended.

title: #1984 Online education improved nephrologists’ knowledge of the immunopathogenesis of immunoglobulin A nephropathy and rationale for novel therapies
authors: Elaine Bell; Rita Moreira Da Silva; Jonathan Barratt
abstract:
Background and Aims
Globally, immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) is the most common form of glomerulonephritis, and the primary cause of chronic kidney disease and renal failure. IgAN has a heterogenous clinical presentation and prognosis and has a complex immunopathogenesis. Current management strategies focus on supportive care and the use of off label hypertensive drugs, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and systemic glucocorticoids. As the treatment landscape evolves, there is a clear need for education on the immunopathogenesis of IgAN and the rationale for development of novel therapies.
The goal of this activity was for learners to better understand the immunopathogenesis of IgAN and the mechanism of action (MOA) of emerging therapies.
Method
This online video activity was a 30-minute discussion between 2 expert faculty, with accompanying slides [1]. Responses to 3 pre- and post-assessment multiple-choice, knowledge questions and 1 self-efficacy, 5-point Likert scale confidence question were analyzed. Educational effect was assessed using a repeated-pair design, pre-/post-assessment. A paired samples t-test was conducted for significance testing on overall average number of correct responses and for confidence rating. A series of McNemar's tests were conducted at the question level (5% significance level, P < .05). Cohen's d with correction for paired samples estimated the effect size of the education on number of correct responses (<.20 modest, .20–.49 small, .59–.79 moderate, ≥.80 large). The activity launched on 27 June 2024 with data collection through 5 September 2024.
Results
Of 1,427 nephrologists who viewed the education within this time period, 84 completed all pre- and post-assessment questions. The average percentage of correct responses increased significantly from 60% at baseline to 71% post-activity (P < .001), and there was a moderate educational impact (Cohen's d = 0.60). The proportion of nephrologists answering all 3 questions correctly rose from 23% at baseline to 37% post-activity.
Nephrologists significantly improved their knowledge of the immunopathogenesis of IgAN (58% correct responses at baseline rising to 74% post-activity; P < .001), and the MOA of the emerging IgAN therapy iptacopan acting via the alternative complement pathways (73% vs 85% post-activity; P < .01). There was a numerical improvement in knowledge of the MOA of the APRIL (proliferation-inducing ligand) inhibitor sibeprenlimab acting via reduction of circulating levels of galactose-deficient IgA1 (Gd-IgA1) and associated immune complexes (48% vs 56% post-activity; P = .070).
After completing the activity, 44% of nephrologists reported improved confidence in understanding of the mechanism of action of emerging treatments for IgAN, resulting in a notable confidence shift of 61%.
Conclusion
This online activity significantly improved nephrologists’ knowledge of the immunopathogenesis of IgAN and the rationale and MOA of some emerging therapies for IgAN. Given the rapidly evolving treatment landscape for IgAN, nephrologists would benefit from additional education to improve their knowledge of emerging therapies and translate this knowledge into clinical practice and improved patient outcomes.

title: #2172 Evaluation of the impact of COVID-19 vaccines on renal function in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients
authors: Fatos Mete Altun; Turker Emre
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients are at higher risk for severe complications from COVID-19. This study aimed to assess the effects of three COVID-19 vaccines (Sinovac, Biontech, Turkovac) on renal function. The primary focus was to analyze changes in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and creatinine levels, specifically examining the average monthly rates of change before vaccination, during the vaccination period, and after vaccination.
Method
This retrospective observational study included 140 CKD patients aged 20–80 years with a mean age of 63.1 years. Inclusion criteria required baseline GFR values between 30–90 ml/min/1.73 m². Creatinine levels and GFR values were collected at three time points: two years prior to vaccination (pre-vaccination), during the vaccination period, and two years post-vaccination. Average monthly changes in creatinine and GFR were calculated for each period to compare trends. Statistical analyses included Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Tests to assess median differences and Kruskal-Wallis Tests to compare vaccine groups.
Results
The Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Tests revealed that the average monthly creatinine changes had a median of −0.0025 with a p-value of 0.015. This indicates a significant reduction in the rate of creatinine progression, suggesting that the vaccines did not adversely affect renal function decline. Monthly GFR changes had a median of 0.0004 with a p-value of 0.995, showing no significant changes in GFR values. Kruskal-Wallis Tests comparing vaccine groups showed significant differences in creatinine monthly changes for the Biontech group with a p-value of 0.029. However, there were no significant differences for Sinovac (P = 0.196) and Turkovac (P = 0.265). No significant differences were observed in GFR monthly changes across vaccine groups. Biontech demonstrated distinct creatinine trends compared to other vaccines, while Sinovac and Turkovac showed no significant renal function alterations.
Conclusion
The comparison of trends suggests that COVID-19 vaccines, particularly Biontech, did not adversely affect renal function. This highlights the safety of vaccination for CKD patients, but continued monitoring of renal health remains critical, especially with aging populations.
