title: #2410 Albuminuria as a marker of kidney damage in individuals with previously undiagnosed chronic kidney disease based on data of AURA registry
authors: Mikhail Batyushin; Ekaterina Tarlovskaya; Gregory Arutyunov; Alexander Arutyunov; Dmitry Polyakov; Marina Trubnikova; Tatiana Batluk; Roman Bashkinov; Elizaveta Gordeychuk; Evgenii Melnikov; Anastasiia Ermilova
abstract:
Background and Aims
Albuminuria (AU) is a marker of kidney damage and is included in the diagnostic criteria for chronic kidney disease (CKD) according to KDIGO guidelines. However in real-world clinical practice the use of this indicator is less widespread compared to the calculation of the glomerular filtration rate (GFR).
To determine the phenotype of patients with previously undiagnosed CKD who are more likely to have diagnostically significant AU.
Method
AURA (NCT05690009) is a real-world clinical practice registry encompassing 34 regions of the Russian Federation. It included 4,531 patients aged >40 years without previously confirmed chronic kidney disease (CKD) or type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus. The level of albuminuria (AU) was determined once using test strips during patient enrollment into the registry. A threshold value of AU was set at 20 mg/L. For comparative analysis, all included patients were divided into two groups based on their test results.
Results
AU < 20 mg/L was observed in 1,592 patients (35.1%), while AU ≥20 mg/L was identified in 2,939 patients (64.9%). AU was more frequently detected among smokers (19.1% vs. 15.7%, P = 0.006), males (44.2% vs. 38.6%, P < 0.001), and older individuals (mean age 61 vs. 59 years, P < 0.001). Among registered chronic conditions, patients with “AU+” more commonly had cardiovascular diseases, prediabetes, metabolic syndrome, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) (Fig. 1).
It should be noted that the detection of albuminuria (AU) did not influence the severity of arterial hypertension (AH), but it was more prevalent among patients with functional class 3–4 chronic heart failure (CHF) (29.8% vs. 52.1%, P = 0.049) compared to functional class 1–2 (70.2% vs. 74.9%, P = 0.049), as well as among those with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <50% (15.2% vs. 10%, P = 0.007) compared to >50% (84.8% vs. 90%, P = 0.007).
Conclusion
Among patients with cardiovascular diseases, metabolic syndrome, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), diagnostically significant albuminuria was significantly more frequent. Thus, patients in these groups represent a high-risk population for chronic kidney disease (CKD), requiring early diagnosis, including the use of test strips, dynamic monitoring for confirming the diagnosis, as well as timely nephroprotective measures.

title: #709 Limitations of urine dipstick testing in early diagnosis of diabetic kidney disease (DKD) and the necessity of measuring urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR)
authors: Taro Kamimura; Kana Ota; Haruka Sumi; Yuichiro Hara; Shunta Kimura; Ryoji Hashimoto; Shohei Nakamura; Eriko Okinaga; Mika Kibune; Oka Hideaki
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diabetic Kidney Disease (DKD), the leading cause of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) worldwide, must be diagnosed early to allow for timely intervention and prevention of severe progression. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) can be easily diagnosed and its severity determined by estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and urine protein-creatinine ratio (UPCR) or urine albumin-creatinine ratio (UACR). However, recent studies suggest that efforts to achieve early diagnosis of CKD have been insufficient. We evaluated the accuracy of urine dipstick testing in the early diagnosis of DKD and confirmed the importance of UACR measurement.
Method
Data were used from 1,323 diabetes education inpatients at our hospital. Results from simultaneous urine dipstick testing and UACR measurement upon admission were analyzed. Results of urine dipstick testing were classified into five levels (−, ±, 1+, 2+, 3+), and results of UACR were categorized into three groups: normoalbuminuria (UACR < 30 mg/gCr), microalbuminuria (30 ≤ UACR < 300 mg/gCr), and macroalbuminuria (UACR ≥ 300 mg/gCr). Urine dipstick testing was considered positive with a result of 1+ or higher, and microalbuminuria or greater was defined as DKD. The accuracy of urine dipstick testing in diagnosing DKD was then evaluated.
Results
Of the 1,323 cases, there were 202 true positives, 262 false negatives, 13 false positives, and 846 true negatives (Table 1). When diagnosing DKD with urine dipstick testing 1+ or higher, the prevalence was 35.1%, the positive and negative rate was 16.3% and 83.7%, the accuracy was 79.2%, the sensitivity was 43.5%, the specificity was 98.5%, the positive and negative predictive value was 93.9% and 76.3% (Table 1).
In addition, when the cut-off for a positive result in urine dipstick testing was set to ± or higher, there were 314 true positives, 150 false negatives, 108 false positives, and 751 true negatives. The prevalence was 35.1%, the positive and negative rate was 31.9% and 68.1%, the accuracy was 80.5%, the sensitivity was 67.7%, the specificity was 87.4%, the positive and negative predictive value was 74.4% and 83.4% (Table 2).
Conclusion
Urine dipstick testing demonstrated low sensitivity (43.5%) for early DKD diagnosis, with a high risk of misdiagnosing 66.5% of patients with microalbuminuria or higher as normoalbuminuria. Even with a cutoff value adjusted to ± to improve sensitivity, the sensitivity was limited to 67.7%, leaving 32.3% of early cases undetected. These findings highlight the limitations of dipstick testing for early detection of DKD. Regular UACR measurements are essential, as emphasized in the 2024 clinical practice guidebook for the diagnosis and treatment of CKD published by the Japanese Society of Nephrology, to enable early detection and timely intervention in DKD.

title: #820 Association of POCUS and biomarkers of congestion in cardiorenal syndrome in a monographic nephrology consultation
authors: Zoila Stany Albines Fiestas; Axenia Babara; Jerson Andrés Alvarado Zelaya; Amelia Campos Sáenz de Santamaría; Laura Karla Esterellas Sánchez; Concepción Álamo Caballero; María Victoria Rubio Rubio; Nieves López Ibort; Ana Belén Hernández Ruiz; Jorge Rubio Gracia; Ignacio Giménez López; Pablo Iñigo Gil
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiorenal syndrome is a complex entity, in which up to 49% of patients with heart failure show some degree of renal dysfunction, significantly increasing morbidity and mortality. Certain biomarkers such as natriuretic peptides and Ca-125 together with the use of ultrasound could help in a more accurate diagnosis of volume overload in these patients. Point-of-Care Ultrasonography (POCUS) is a approach where the treating physician directly performs ultrasonography at the bedside, and has emerged to assess volume in cardiorenal syndrome patients.
In this study, we explored the association of ultrasound congestion with biomarkers of patients evaluated in a cardiorenal pathology monographic consultation.
Methods
A retrospective unicentric observational study was conducted on a database of patients evaluated in the cardiorenal pathology monographic consultation between June 2023 and June 2024 in a tertiary hospital.
Clinical data were extracted from electronic patient records. ProBNP, Ca-125 and the presence or absence of ultrasound congestion were evaluated in all patients.
In POCUS, tissue congestion was assessed by lung ultrasound (LUS) using the 8-zone method; and venous congestion was assessed using Venous Excess Ultrasound (VexUS), evaluating the inferior caval vein and the anomalies on hepatic, portal and intrarenal venous Doppler. Mixed congestion was considered to be the simultaneous presence of tissue and venous congestion.
The correlation between biomarkers and ultrasound congestion was evaluated using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient for bivariate analysis, conducted with IBM SPSS®.
Results
74 patients were evaluated. Most were male (68%). The mean age of the patients evaluated was 77.89 ± 8.27 years. The mean glomerular filtration rate estimated by CKD-EPI was 32.47 ml/min ± 10.65. The mean albumin creatinine ratio in urine was 78.90 ± 114.62 mg/g. Within the etiology of cardiac pathology, 41.89% were ischemic followed by valvular in 31.08% (Fig. 1); and 69% presented atrial fibrillation (Fig. 2). 54% had preserved left ventricular ejection fraction and 58% had NYHA functional class II.
In the analysis of proBNP levels and ultrasound congestion, 12 patients with tissue congestion, 10 with venous congestion, and 25 with mixed congestion had proBNP levels >1800 ng/L. A statistically significant correlation was found between proBNP levels and the presence of congestion by ultrasound (Table 1).
In the analysis of Ca-125 levels and ultrasound congestion, 9 patients with tissue congestion and 21 with mixed congestion had Ca-125 levels >35 U/mL. A statistically significant correlation was found between Ca-125 levels and the presence of congestion by ultrasound (Table 2).
Conclusion
We found a significant assessment between the biomarkers analyzed (ProBNP, Ca-125) and tissue/venous congestion in patients assessed in the cardiorenal pathology monographic nephrology consultation. These tools contribute to an adequate multiparametric assessment of congestion. Likewise, the POCUS performed by the treating physician helps to resolve the doubts that arise in the consultation in real time, which will allow us to optimize treatment.

title: #1025 Observational study of the clinical use of roxadustat for treatment of chronic kidney disease-related anaemia in Sweden: the MOROCCO study
authors: Aurora Caldinelli; Juan-Jesus Carrero; Anne-Laure Faucon; Elinor Cockburn; Kirsten Leyland; Marie Evans
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors, such as roxadustat, are oral treatments for chronic kidney disease (CKD)-related anaemia that stimulate endogenous erythropoietin production. Roxadustat was granted marketing authorisation for the treatment of CKD-related anaemia in adults in the European Union in 2021, with reimbursement granted in Sweden from 2022. However, real-world data on the use of roxadustat in this patient population in Sweden are lacking. MOROCCO is an ongoing, observational cohort study to evaluate clinical use of roxadustat for the treatment of CKD-related anaemia in Sweden; here we report an interim analysis.
Method
Data were collected from the Swedish Renal Registry, a continuously updated online register of patient data from ≥96% of nephrology clinics in Sweden. Patients aged ≥18 years with CKD stages 3–5 and CKD-related anaemia, and who were newly prescribed roxadustat between September 2022 and August 2024, were included in the analysis. The primary objective was to describe clinical characteristics and comorbidities of patients at the date of first roxadustat prescription (index date), stratified by dialysis status (non-dialysis dependent [NDD] or dialysis dependent [DD]).
Results
Overall, 111 patients were included in the analysis (median [interquartile range (IQR)] age: 75.2 [60.0–82.3] years; 30.6% female), of whom 69.4% were NDD and 30.6% were DD (Table 1). Of DD patients, 58.8% were receiving haemodialysis and 41.2% were receiving peritoneal dialysis. NDD patients were older (median [IQR] age: 78.1 [67.7–84.0] years) than DD patients (median [IQR] age: 60.8 [49.7–76.0] years), and a lower proportion of NDD patients were female (NDD: 27.3%; DD: 38.2%). The majority of NDD patients had CKD stages 4–5 (80.5%), 10.4% had CKD stage 3, and 9.1% had received a kidney transplant. Median (IQR) estimated glomerular filtration rate for NDD patients was 17.7 (10.2–26.3) mL/min/1.73 m2. The prevalence of multiple comorbidities at index date was higher in NDD patients than DD patients, especially for cerebrovascular diseases.
Median (IQR) haemoglobin levels at roxadustat initiation were 9.5 (9.1–10.0) g/dL for NDD and 9.3 (8.5–9.9) g/dL for DD patients. Median (IQR) C-reactive protein (CRP) and ferritin values were higher for DD (CRP: 9.5 [3.3–35.5] mg/L; ferritin: 406.0 [302.5–632.5] µg/L) than NDD patients (CRP: 4.5 [3.0–15.5] mg/L; ferritin: 247.0 [150.5–445.8] µg/L).
Before initiating roxadustat, the majority (64.9%) of NDD patients were erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA) naïve, compared with only 11.8% of DD patients. For patients converting from ESA, the prior median (IQR) weekly ESA dose was 12,000 (6,000–22,000) iU and 14,000 (10,000–20,000) iU for NDD and DD patients, respectively. At index date, over half of DD patients had been treated with either intravenous (55.9%) or oral iron (2.9%), compared with 39.0% and 11.7% of NDD patients respectively; 15.6% and 20.6% of NDD and DD patients, respectively, had received a blood transfusion. The most common reason for prescribing roxadustat for NDD patients was preference for an oral treatment (76.6%), while for DD patients, the main indication was ESA resistance (70.6%).
Conclusion
In Sweden, the characteristics of patients with CKD-related anaemia treated with roxadustat, and reasons for its prescription, differed by dialysis status. NDD patients were older than DD patients, had a higher prevalence of cerebrovascular diseases and lower CRP and ferritin values, and were more likely to be ESA-naïve at roxadustat initiation.

title: #1223 Inflammatory states affect composition of peripheral blood immune cell compartment in stage 5 CKD patients
authors: Ivan Zahradka; Filip Tichanek; Lucia Majercikova; Jana Duskova; Mathias Streitz; Stephan Schlickeiser; Klara Osickova; Vojtěch Petr; Petra Hruba; Petra Reinke; Ondrej Viklicky
abstract:
Background and Aims
Stage 5 chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients are at higher risk of various infections and malignancies due to uremia-associated alterations of the immune system. Little is known about other factors affecting peripheral blood immune cell compartment (PBICC) composition in this patient population.
Method
This cross-sectional study included 107 kidney transplantation candidates (CKD5 patients) and 29 healthy controls. B cell, T cell, and dendritic cell populations were measured using a standardized and validated flow cytometry panel of The ONE study.
Results
CKD patients exhibited B and T cell lymphopenia with an immunosenescent phenotype predominantly in the CD4+ compartment and significantly higher counts of APCs. Multivariable PERMANOVAs identified smoking (R2 = 0.041, P < 0.001), CMV seropositivity (R2 = 0.05, P < 0001), age (R2 = 0.02, P = 0.03), past dialysis treatment (R = 0.035, P = 0.019), and presence of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (R2 = 0.02, P = 0.03) as factors associated with the changes in PBICC composition. Poisson regression models revealed that smoking was associated mainly with increase in switched memory B cells (RR = 2,4, adj.P = 0.18), CMV seropositivity with increase in CD4+ (RR = 5.8, adj.P < 0.001) and CD8+ (RR = 3, adj.P < 0.001) TEMRA cells, age with decrease in naive CD8+ T-cells (RR = 0.34, adj.P < 0.001), and dialysis with increase in marginal-zone B cells (RR = 2.3, adj.P = 0.007).
Conclusion
Factors associated with systemic inflammatory response significantly modify the composition of PBICC in patients with stage 5 CKD. Whether such alterations of immune compartments represent a risk for adverse outcomes needs to be explored further.

title: #1243 Functional impairment as a predictor of renal outcomes and mortality in elderly patients
authors: Bo Keung Peun; Su-Ryeong Go; Ho Jun Chin; Ki Young Na
abstract:
Background and Aims
Functional impairment in daily activities is prevalent among elderly patients and population with chronic kidney disease and it may influence on their prognosis. This study investigated the association between activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL) scores with incident renal replacement therapy (RRT) and mortality.
Method
This retrospective cohort study included 6,087 individuals aged ≥65 years (2,737 men and 3,350 women) who underwent geriatric assessments including ADL and IADL at a Korean university hospital between January 2016 and December 2020. Participants exhibited an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) >15 ml/min/1.73 m² and were followed for more than three months. ADL and IADL were evaluated using the Barthel Index and Lawton-Brody Index, respectively. The analyses were conducted separately for males and females due to gender-specific differences in IADL scale scores.
Results
Participants aged 78.7 ± 6.0 years had eGFR 75.8 ± 19.4 ml/min/1.73 m² at the point of test. Over a median follow-up period of 42 months, 2,108 participants (34.6%) died and 103 (1.7%) required RRT. The AUCs by ROC analysis showed reverse relationship between ADL or IADL and possibility of incident RRT or mortality in each gender (all p-values for estimating RRT in both gender <0.01, all p-values for estimating mortality in both gender <0.001). In men, abnormal IADL scores (<5) significantly increased the risk of RRT (HR 2.097, P = 0.024), whereas abnormal ADL scores (<100) were not related to the risk (HR 1.612, P = 0.145). Abnormal IADL was associated with a 68.9% increased risk of mortality (HR 1.689, P < 0.001) and abnormal ADL increased the mortality risk by 41.5% (HR 1.415, P < 0.001). In the analysis grouped by age and eGFR, younger men (<75 years) exhibited a significantly higher risk of RRT with abnormal ADL and IADL (ADL: HR, 13.931; IADL: HR, 14.237; both P < 0.001) than older men (≥75 years) (ADL: HR 2.894, P < 0.001; IADL: HR 3.445, P < 0.001). Abnormal ADL and IADL were also associated with an increased risk of RRT in men with both higher (eGFR ≥ 75 ml/min/1.73 m2) (ADL: HR 4.164, P = 0.004; IADL: HR 5.302, P < 0.001) and lower renal function (eGFR < 75 ml/min/1.73 m2) (ADL: HR 4.133, P < 0.001; IADL: HR 4.220, P < 0.001). Furthermore, abnormal ADL and IADL were significantly related with increased mortality risk in both younger and older men (P < 0.001). Participants grouped by eGFR, the correlations between ADL and IADL and outcomes remained significant (P < 0.001). In women, abnormal IADL scores (<8) were not associated with an increased risk of RRT (HR 1.634, P = 0.231) and impaired ADL scores (<100) showed borderline significance for an increased risk of RRT (HR 2.078, P = 0.065). However, abnormal IADL was associated with an increased risk of mortality (HR 2.016, P < 0.001) and abnormal ADL was also related to the mortality risk (HR 2.158, P < 0.001). In subgroup analysis, abnormal ADL and IADL scores were significantly correlated with mortality risk in both younger (P < 0.001) or older women (P < 0.001) and, in women with higher eGFR (≥75 ml/min/1.73 m2) (P < 0.001) or lower eGFR (<75 ml/min/1.73 m2) (P < 0.001).
Conclusion
ADL and IADL are critical predictors of RRT, especially in elderly men, and mortality in elderly patients. Association between mortality and functional impairment were more evident in younger elder persons (aged between 65 and 74 years).

title: #2152 Prospective observational cohort study on the treatment of anemia and iron deficiency with hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor in patients with CKD
authors: Federico Bari; Gianluca Samele; Mauro Martello; Xhensila Grabocka; Valentina Nastasi; Osmy Paci Della Costanza; Sara Belcastro; Laura Diotallevi; Hrissanthi Kulurianu; Assunta Cardillo; Francesca Pizzolante; Marina Di Luca
abstract:
Background and Aims
Anemia is a common and debilitating complication in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), significantly affecting their quality of life and contributing to increased morbidity and mortality. The pathophysiology of CKD-related anemia is multifactorial, arising from inadequate erythropoiesis due to diminished erythropoietin production, functional iron deficiency, and inflammatory processes. Traditional treatment modalities, including erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) and iron supplementation, are effective but have limitations such as the necessity for injections, cardiovascular risks, and suboptimal responses in certain patients.
Roxadustat, an oral hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor (HIF-PHI), presents a novel therapeutic approach for managing anemia in CKD, particularly in patients not on dialysis. By mimicking hypoxic conditions, roxadustat stimulates endogenous erythropoietin production, lowers hepcidin levels, and enhances iron bioavailability offering a potential alternative to traditional ESAs, especially for ESA-naïve patients. This study aimed to evaluate the clinical outcomes of roxadustat in ESA-naïve CKD patients receiving conservative treatment. The primary objectives were to assess the efficacy of roxadustat in improving hemoglobin levels, iron metabolism, and overall patient health over a 90-day period. Secondary objectives included evaluating the safety profile of roxadustat, the incidence of adverse events, and the need for iron supplementation during treatment.
Method
A prospective observational cohort study was conducted at the UOC Nephrology AST1 Pesaro-Fano to investigate the efficacy and safety of roxadustat in ESA-naïve CKD patients with anemia. A total of 13 patients, aged 18 years and older, diagnosed with CKD and hemoglobin levels <10.0 g/dL, were enrolled. Inclusion criteria mandated that patients be ESA-naïve and not receiving iron supplementation. Exclusion criteria included active malignancy, recent blood transfusions, or contraindications to roxadustat. Dosing of roxadustat was individualized based on baseline hemoglobin levels and renal function, with adjustments made during follow-up according to hemoglobin values, as outlined in the technical data sheet. The primary outcomes were changes in hemoglobin levels (g/dL) from baseline to 90 days (T4) and alterations in iron parameters, including ferritin and transferrin saturation (TSAT). Renal function was assessed using the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR).
Results
The cohort comprised 13 patients, with a mean age of 73.8 years (8 males, 5 females). The etiologies of CKD included glomerulonephritis (n = 5), diabetic nephropathy (n = 4), nephroangiosclerosis (n = 3), and a genetic disorder (n = 1). Patients were evaluated at baseline and at follow-up intervals of 15 (T1), 30 (T2), 60 (T3), and 90 (T4) days.
At baseline, the mean hemoglobin level was 9.8 g/dL, eGFR was 24.5 mL/min, ferritin was 185.3 ng/mL, and TSAT was 37%. Treatment with Roxadustat resulted in a significant increase in hemoglobin levels, rising from 9.8 g/dL at baseline to 12.0 g/dL at T4 (P < 0.001). Ferritin levels decreased to 154.6 ng/mL and TSAT dropped to 27.2% at T4, indicating improved iron utilization. The mean roxadustat doses were reduced from 56.2 mg at baseline to 45.7 mg at T4, reflecting effective dose optimization.
Conclusion
Roxadustat demonstrated significant efficacy in increasing hemoglobin levels and improving iron metabolism in ESA-naïve CKD patients over a 90-day treatment period. Hemoglobin levels rose significantly (P < 0.001), and iron parameters, including ferritin and TSAT, exhibited positive trends, highlighting enhanced erythropoiesis and reduced iron stores. These findings underscore the potential of roxadustat as a safe and effective treatment option for managing anemia in non-dialysis CKD patients.

title: #2409 Association of sunlight on multiple sclerosis prevalence in patients with kidney disease
authors: Sheetal Chaudhuri; Joanna Willetts; Ingrid Adelsberger; Greg Garza; Richard Weller; John MacMahon; Len Usvyat
abstract:
Background and Aims
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by inflammation and demyelination in the central nervous system (CNS). It is known to exhibit a geographical variation, with lower prevalence in areas closer to the equator where the sunlight exposure is higher. This phenomenon is attributed primarily to the immune-regulating effects of ultraviolet (UV) radiation and its role in autoimmunity. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) and end stage kidney disease (ESKD) patients often face multiple comorbidities and compromised immunity, which are further exacerbated by the presence of MS. They often have seasonal responses to inflammation, which may influence their mortality for those with autoimmune disorders like MS. In this abstract, we explore the potential impact of sunlight on the MS prevalence in patients with kidney disease.
Method
We evaluated active CKD patients from a large CKD registry and active ESKD patients dialyzing at a large dialysis organization in the United States as of September 30, 2024. We mapped the zip code for the patients into 9 geographic zip code groups and the zip code groups were categorized into 3 levels based on the average total daily sunshine hours per year: least sunny, moderately sunny and the sunniest. We calculated the percentage of active CKD and ESKD patients in each of the 3 categories of sunshine and reported p-value from a z-score comparing the category of sunniness to the overall population.
Results
As of September 30, 2024, there were 253,668 active CKD patients in the registry and 207,768 active ESKD patients dialyzed at a large dialysis organization. Of the CKD patients, there were 254 patients diagnosed with MS (0.10%) Similarly, of the ESKD patients, there were 226 patients diagnosed with MS (0.11%) Overall, as shown in Fig. 1, there were 0.13% (P = 0.0006) of patients living in the least sunny states, 0.11% (P = 0.265) of patients living in moderately sunny states and 0.07% (P = 0.0025) patients living in the sunniest states.
Conclusion
The relationship between UV and the presence of MS is evident in patients with CKD and ESKD. A better understanding of this relationship could pave the way for tailored interventions, including phototherapy and lifestyle modifications, to improve patient outcomes. Further research is essential to confirm these findings and their implications for clinical practice.

title: #2546 Hyperkalaemia prevalence and risk factors in chronic kidney disease and heart failure: insights from iCaReMe Registry Latin America Cohort
authors: Magdalena Madero; Luiz Aparecido Bortolotto; Jessica Ivonne Bravo Zuñiga; Chih H Chen Ku; Dario Xavier Jimenez Acosta; Gregorio Obrador; Ricardo Reinaldo Bergo; Abdias Nicanor Hurtado Arestegui; Jorge Endara; Sonia Juarez; Hardik Vasnawala; Ahmed Hadaoui
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyperkalaemia (HK) is a common and serious electrolyte imbalance characterized by serum potassium >5.0 mmol/L, frequently observed in chronic kidney disease (CKD) and heart failure (HF). It poses a major therapeutic challenge, as its occurrence is closely linked to the use of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors (RAASi), essential treatments for slowing CKD progression and improving HF outcomes. In Latin America (LATAM), increasing rates of CKD and HF highlight an urgent need to better understand HK and its management. However, data on HK prevalence and associated factors in this region remain scarce. Using iCaReMe Global Registry (NCT03549754) data, our study examines the prevalence, risk factors, and clinical context of HK in CKD and HF patients across LATAM, aiming to address key gaps for evidence-based care.
Method
Adult CKD and HF people from 6 LATAM countries (Argentina, Brazil, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Mexico, Peru) were included in this cross-sectional analysis. The study examined HK prevalence, patient demographics, clinical features, and treatment patterns (reported as frequencies and percentages). Risk factors for HK were identified using stepwise logistic regression.
Results
A total of 1,721 subjects (mean age, 61.6 ± 14.4 years; 52.5% male) were analysed. CKD was present in 61.0% of participants (mean estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR], 33.3 ± 23.1 mL/min/1.73 m²), HF in 47.0% (mean left ventricular ejection fraction, 43.8 ± 15.8%), type 2 diabetes mellitus in 53.2% and 73.0% had HTN. The mean serum potassium (K⁺) was 4.6 ± 0.7 mmol/L with an overall HK prevalence of 24.2% including 18.5% in HF and 27.5% in CKD. Medications included angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin II receptor blockers/angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (80.7%), sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors (39.1%), loop diuretics (27.1%) and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRA; 26.7%). Individuals with HK (mean K⁺: 5.5 ± 0.5 mmol/L) showed lower kidney function, more severe CKD stages (G3b-G5, 88.4% vs 68.5%), and reduced MRA use (25.8% vs 33.4%) compared to those without HK (mean K⁺: 4.4 ± 0.4 mmol/L). Only 8.9% of patients with HK received anti-HK therapies, among them, potassium binders were used in 15% of patients. Multivariate analysis identified a significant association between HK and MRA use (odds ratio, 2.1; 95% CI, 1.09–4.19; P < 0.0276).
Conclusion
Our findings highlight the substantial prevalence of HK in patients with HF and CKD in the LATAM region, particularly in advanced CKD. The association of HK with MRA use underscores the challenge of optimising guideline-based therapies while managing HK risks. Despite the need for effective HK management, anti-HK therapies, including potassium binders, remain low. Region-specific strategies to improve HK management and ensure optimal RAASi use are essential to improve patients’ outcomes in this high-risk population.

A total of 1,721 subjects (mean age, 61.6 ± 14.4 years; 52.5% male) were analysed. title: #3182 Chronic kidney disease (CKD) in patients with obesity who underwent bariatric surgery
authors: Maya Sanchez-Baya; Angel Jose Rosales Rojas; Karla Marcela Mariaca Riveros; Federico Vázquez; Iara Da Silva; Elisabeth Massó Jiménez; Paula Anton-Pampols; Monica Bolufer; Jordi Ara; Jordi Bover Sanjuan; Ana Silvia Pellitero Rodriguez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Obesity is associated with an increased risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD), CKD progression, and end-stage renal disease. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and obesity-related glomerulopathy, both of which are linked to proteinuria, have been described in patients with severe obesity. Obesity-related glomerulopathy may be reversible with weight loss and data suggest that bariatric surgery leads to significant improvements in markers of obesity-related nephropathy and CKD.
The aim of this study was to evaluate the prevalence of CKD in patients with obesity who underwent bariatric surgery, as well as the evolution of kidney function post-surgery.
Method
We included patients with obesity who underwent bariatric surgery between 2022 and 2024 at Germans Trias i Pujol Hospital. Data on creatinine levels and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) were assessed prior to surgery and at the end of 2024.
Results
Between 2022 and 2024, 253 bariatric surgeries were performed. Of these, 76% (n = 192) of the patients were women, and the average age was 50 ± 10 years.
Prior to bariatric surgery, 15% (n = 37) of patients had a diagnosis of CKD, defined as an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <60 ml/min/1.73 m² and/or a UACR >30 mg/g. Among these, 78% (n = 29) had albuminuria, and after bariatric surgery, 66% (n = 19) experienced remission of albuminuria. In 29% (n = 8), albuminuria did not remit but the ratio decreased.
During follow-up, 14% (n = 5) of CKD patients required renal replacement therapy; four patients underwent hemodialysis (those with the worst prognosis and greatest complications), and one patient received a kidney transplant.
After bariatric surgery (by the end of 2024), only 20 patients remained diagnosed with CKD, indicating a remission of the disease in 46% of the CKD cases.
Conclusion
In our patient cohort, bariatric surgery leads to improvements in CKD markers, with a significant percentage of CKD remission.

title: #3408 Desidustat in CKD anemia: a single center experience
authors: Prakash Khetan; Seema Khetan
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) induced anemia is multifactorial. Traditionally, erythropoietin analogues and iron therapy are used to maintain hemoglobin (Hb) levels between 10–12 gm/dl. Desidustat, a newer oral agent, stimulates endogenous erythropoietin production and improves anemia. This study focuses on the outcomes of using desidustat in CKD anemia.
Method
This retrospective, single-center, observational study enrolled patients with CKD anemia treated with Desidustat (Oxemia®). Patients were regularly followed up for treatment response, dose changes, safety analysis, and treatment outcomes.
Results
A total of 171 patients were included in the study, comprising 98 males (57.31%) and 73 females (42.69%). The distribution of CKD stages among the patients was as follows: Stage II: 1 patient (0.58%), Stage III: 29 patients (16.96%), Stage IV: 35 patients (20.47%), and Stage V: 106 patients (61.99%). The treatment groups included 116 pre-dialysis patients (67.84%), 50 dialysis-dependent patients (29.24%), and 5 post-kidney transplant patients (2.92%). The dosages of desidustat administered were 50 mg in 39 patients (22.81%), 75 mg in 2 patients (1.17%), 100 mg in 114 patients (66.67%), and 150 mg in 16 patients (9.36%). There were 18 cases where dose changes were necessary: 7 cases (4.09%) required a dose decrease due to hemoglobin levels rising above 12 gm/dl, and 11 cases (6.43%) required a dose increase due to low hemoglobin levels. Specifically, 9 cases (5.26%) had their dose increased from 50 mg to 100 mg thrice weekly, and 2 cases (1.17%) had their dose increased from 100 mg to 150 mg thrice weekly. In current study we observed significant rise in Hb from baseline 7.87 gm/dl to 10.97 gm/dl with absolute change in Hb of 3.1 gm/d (P < 0.001) (Fig. 1). With desidustat therapy patients maintained renal function and stable serum Potassium levels. With desidustat therapy patients maintained good compliance, there were self-limiting adverse events observed.
Conclusion
This study demonstrates that desidustat is an effective and safe alternative to traditional erythropoietin analogues for treating CKD-induced anemia. The significant increase in hemoglobin levels, along with stable renal function and serum potassium levels, highlights its efficacy and safety. Patients showed good compliance with the therapy, and adverse events were self-limiting. Overall, desidustat offers a promising and convenient option for managing anemia in CKD patients.

title: #3420 Application of ChatGPT 4o to implement local registries in low-resourced countries. A proof of concept for the Jamaican Registry Initiative
authors: Lori-Ann Fisher; Ana Catalina Alvarez-Elías; Katherine Yan; Neisha Ross; Len Usvyat; Hanjie Zhang; Peter Kotanko
abstract:
Background and Aims
Middle-income and low-income countries face substantial challenges to build local registries for chronic and end-stage kidney disease (CKD/ESKD) patients that allow to characterize disease and build evidence to inform policy makers. The primary challenges stem from limited access to technology and inefficient communication systems. As a result, the use of printed forms to collect data via handwritten registries remains a more feasible option in healthcare settings that lack advanced technological infrastructure. Conversely, mobile and cellphone technologies are increasingly being leveraged to address communication gaps and facilitate clinical research in healthcare settings. In a proof-of-concept study, we aimed to use ChatGPT to extract patient information from pre-designed hand-written medical record forms and to transfer the data to a database.
Method
We used a pre-designed patient information form from the Nephrology Department at Grenada General Hospital in Grenada and the University of West Indies Mona in Jamaica. The form was created to establish a local, national, and international CKD Caribbean registry. Each form comprised 28 data fields, such as name, address, diagnosis, etc. We distributed the form to healthy volunteers and requested them to fill out the form in English with hand-written sham data. Photographs of the filled-out forms were then imported into ChatGPT, version 4o, and a request for data extraction was prompted. The ChatGPT generated data extracts were then exported into an Excel spreadsheet. To assess the accuracy of the process, the extracted data were then compared with the original hand-written data. We assessed the global discrepancy rate between original form and Excel data base entry. In addition, we categorized discrepancies by four groups: a) Letters, b) Numbers, c) Special characters/symbols, and d) Checkbox discrepancies. Descriptive analyses were done with SAS On Demand for Academics 3.1.0.
Results
Twenty-two forms with a total of 616 entries (= 22 x 28 data fields) were evaluated. Discrepancies between original and abstracted data occurred in 48 (8%) instances (Fig. 1). The median discrepancy count per form was 2 (interquartile range: 2). Most frequent discrepancies occurred with numbers (54% of all discrepancies), followed by checkbox discrepancies (23%; Fig. 2).
Conclusion
The extraction of hand-written medical data from pre-defined medical record forms using ChatGPT showed a satisfactory performance in English language with a median error rate of 8%. Human error research indicates spreadsheet cell entry error rates between 1% and 5%. However, these studies did not consider handwritten source data but entry of printed data into spreadsheets (see panko.com for extensive literature and discussion). Additionally, performance may vary according to language and alphabet used. Efforts to improve the writing of numbers by hand and attention to detail when checking boxes are important steps to improve accuracy. Adapting the available resources for the establishment of local registries in low-resourced countries is key for collecting evidence on kidney disease in disadvantaged areas.

title: #3786 Dose-dependent effects of tolvaptan on serum uric acid levels in ADPKD patients
authors: Ali Osman Polat; Şeyda Gül Özcan; Mevlut Tamer Dincer; Sinan Trabulus; Nurhan Seyahi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Tolvaptan, a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist, is widely used in the autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). However, the relationship between tolvaptan dosing and serum uric acid levels has not been fully explored. We aimed to examine whether the effects of tolvaptan on uric acid metabolism were dose dependent and to gain insights into any possible determinants of this relationship.
Method
We included 40 ADPKD patients undergoing tolvaptan therapy in this study We collected serum uric acid levels at baseline and after administering tolvaptan at 60 mg, 90 mg, and 120 mg daily doses. We performed dependent t-tests and repeated sample ANOVA analysis to assess changes in uric acid levels. Additionally, we evaluated effects of thiazide diuretic use on uric acid levels.
Results
Demographic and clinical data are shown in Table 1. More than half of the patients were male (65%), and mean age was 42.10 ± 8.05 years. Uric acid levels showed a significant increase with tolvaptan dose escalation (baseline: 5.87 ± 1.69 mg/dL; 60 mg: 6.33 ± 1.50 mg/dL; 90 mg: 6.43 ± 1.60 mg/dL; 120 mg: 6.74 ± 1.74 mg/dL; p = 0.0111). Thiazide diuretic use did not significantly affect uric acid levels at any dose (p > 0.05).
Conclusion
Tolvaptan therapy is associated with a dose-dependent increase in serum uric acid levels. There is no significant effect with concomitant use of thiazide diuretics. Uric acid levels should be carefully monitored in patients receiving high-dose tolvaptan particularly if they had preexisting hyperuricemia. Future studies are needed to define the molecular basis of these interactions.

title: #1345 The implication of zinc deficiency on renal and overall survival in patients with chronic kidney disease
authors: Mariana León Póo; Deborah Roldan; Eva López Melero; Clara Maria Cases Corona; Enrique Gruss; Amir Shabaka
abstract:
Background and Aims
Zinc (Zn) deficiency is associated with the development and progression of cardiovascular disease. Recently, it has also been observed that Zn supplementation can reduce albuminuria in patients with diabetic kidney disease. The aim of this study was to analyze the prevalence of Zn deficiency in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and evaluate its implications for their renal and overall prognosis.
Method
A retrospective observational study was conducted, including patients with CKD who were evaluated at our hospital between January 2019 and May 2022, and who had a baseline serum Zn measurement and follow-up of >1 year. The cohort was stratified according to baseline Zn levels into three groups: severe deficiency (<60 µg/dl), mild deficiency (60–80 µg/dl), and normal (≥80 µg/dl). Demographic, analytical, and comorbidity variables were collected. The composite outcome was defined as doubling of serum creatinine, progression to end-stage CKD, and/or death.
Results
A total of 78 patients were included, with a mean age of 61.4 ± 17.3 years; 67.9% were men, with a mean glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 43.9 ± 27.9 ml/min and median proteinuria of 3 g/24 h (IQR 1.17–5.29 g/24 h) at baseline. Baseline serum Zn levels were 74.9 ± 15.2 µg/dl. Of the patients included, 28 (35.9%) had mild deficiency, and 15 (19.2%) had severe deficiency. A direct correlation was found between baseline Zn levels and serum albumin (r = 0.68, P < 0.001) and calcium (r = 0.23, P = 0.047), while an inverse correlation was found with proteinuria (r = −0.33, P = 0.02) and serum phosphate levels (r = −0.33, P = 0.003). No correlation with age or GFR was found.
After a median follow-up of 25 months, 13 patients (16.7%) progressed to end-stage CKD, and 14 patients (17.9%) died. A total of 30 patients (38.5%) reached the composite outcome. Severe Zn deficiency was associated with higher mortality (40% vs. 12.7%, P = 0.013). In survival analysis for the composite outcome, the group of patients with severe Zn deficiency exhibited the worst survival (Log-rank χ² 6.5, P = 0.039). The Cox proportional hazards model, adjusted for age, GFR, proteinuria, and baseline calcium, showed a higher risk of reaching the composite outcome in the severe Zn deficiency group (HR 5.31, 95% CI 1.14–24.77).
Conclusion
Zn deficiency in CKD is common and may represent a risk factor for CKD progression and mortality. Monitoring Zn levels and supplementation in patients with Zn deficiency should be considered. Prospective studies are needed to assess the effect of Zn supplementation.

title: #1385 Low urinary marinobufagenin (uMBG) levels as a prognostic marker for accelerated progression in non-advanced CKD
authors: Mariateresa Zicarelli; Marta Greco; Loredana Tripodi; Mario D'agostino; Paola Cianfrone; Roberta Misiti; Sara Pugliese; Michela Musolino; Daniela Foti; Michele Andreucci; Giuseppe Coppolino; Davide Bolignano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) has now reached pandemic proportions but risk prediction towards end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) remains challenging. Kidney fibrosis is a key determinant in the transition from CKD to ESKD. In this prospective study, we investigated the prognostic significance of urinary Marinobufagenin (uMBG), a cardiotonic steroid with acknowledged pro-fibrotic activity, for stratifying the risk of CKD progression in individuals with non-advanced renal disease.
Method
After baseline uMBG measurements, 108 CKD patients (eGFR 40.54 ± 17 mL/min/1.73 m²) were prospectively followed up to 24 months. The study (renal) endpoint was a composite of serum creatinine doubling, eGFR decline >25% from baseline values, or ESKD requiring chronic renal replacement therapy.
Results
During follow-up (mean 21 months), 32.4% of patients had progressive CKD. These individuals displayed almost halved baseline uMBG excretion as compared to others (P < 0.0001). At ROC analysis uMBG showed a remarkable diagnostic capacity on CKD progression (AUC 0.898) and patients with uMBG ≤310 pmol/L (Best ROC-derived cut-off) had a significantly faster progression to the endpoint (Log-rank 57.9; P < 0.0001). Restricted cubic splines fitting Cox-regression analyses (Fig. 1) revealed that the risk association between uMBG and CKD progression was best described by a curvilinear, inverse J-shaped trend, the highest risk associated with very low uMBG levels. This trend remained unaffected by adjustment for age, baseline eGFR, and 24 h-proteinuria.
Conclusion
Low urinary excretion of MBG is an independent prognostic factor for CKD progression in patients with non-advanced CKD. These findings suggest that uMBG may serve as a valuable biomarker for early risk stratification in CKD. Further validation in larger cohorts is needed to confirm its role in clinical practice.

title: #1768 Decline of kidney function is associated with lower sweat weight in patients with chronic kidney disease
authors: Tarik Shoumariyeh; Florian Logar; Oliver Helk; Johannes Hofer; Klaus Schmetterer; Brigitte Mersi; Saskia Gruber; Marcus Säemann; Christopher Kaltenecker; Johannes J Kovarik
abstract:
Background and Aims
Excretion of sodium and water through the skin as sweat represents a regulatory mechanism of electrolyte- and fluid balance. Since patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) exhibit increased skin sodium content, we investigated the feasibility of sweat testing as a novel experimental tool to provide a more complete assessment of fluid- and sodium status.
Method
In this cross-sectional feasibility study, we applied pilocarpine iontophoresis to induce sweat testing in 58 patients across various stages of CKD including kidney transplant recipients and a healthy control cohort (n = 6) to investigate possible effects of CKD and transplantation status on sweat weight and sodium concentration. Due to non-linear relationships, we modeled our data using polynomial regression.
Results
Decline of kidney function showed a significant association with lower sweat weight: adj R²= 0.2278, F(2, 61) = 10.29, P = 0.0001. Sweat sodium concentrations were increased in moderate CKD, however, this effect was lost in end-stage kidney disease: adj R² = 0.3701, F(4, 59) = 10.26, P = 2.261e-06.
Conclusion
Diagnostic sweat analysis represents an innovative, non-invasive option for a more thorough investigation of sodium- and fluid homeostasis in CKD. Lower sweat weight and higher sweat sodium concentrations represent a unique feature of CKD patients with potential therapeutic implications.

title: #1814 Transcriptional intermediary factor 1γ ameliorates kidney fibrosis by enhancing irisin levels in skeletal muscle of db/db mice
authors: Hyun-Jung Kim; Jin Hyun Kim; Sehyun Jung; Seunghye Lee; Hyejin Jeon; Hani Jang; Se-Ho Chang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Transcriptional intermediary factor 1γ (TIF1γ) is a negative regulator of TGF-β1 signaling and has been correlated with the survival of patients with renal cell carcinoma. However, its role in diabetic nephropathy (DN), the most common cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD), remains unknown. This study aimed to investigate the role of TIF1γ in treating multiple diabetic complications.
Method
Mice were assigned to four groups: db/m+, db/db, and db/db mice treated with CMV- or TGF-TIF1γ plasmids (40 μg/mouse; intraperitoneally, weekly for 16 weeks). Kidney injury, fibrosis, and function were assessed. Changes in the expression of fibrosis- and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-related genes in the kidneys, as well as atrophy- and regeneration-related genes and myokines in skeletal muscles, were measured along with exercise capacity. C2C12 cells were exposed to palmitate in the presence or absence of TIF1γ transfection, and irisin expression and secretion were analyzed. To assess muscle-kidney crosstalk mediated by TIF1γ, palmitate-treated human kidney (HK) cells were incubated in conditioned media from both non-transfected and TIF1γ-transfected C2C12 cells, and EMT markers in HK cells were evaluated. To further confirm irisin-mediated kidney effects of TIF1γ, palmitate-treated HK cells were incubated in conditioned media from FNDC5-knockdown C2C12 cells, and EMT marker expression was analyzed.
Results
TIF1γ-treated mice exhibited reduced renal tubulointerstitial fibrosis, attenuated glomerular and tubular injury, improved kidney function, and decreased levels of EMT-related factors (P < 0.05, respectively). The administered TIF1γ plasmids were more abundant in muscle than in the kidney. TIF1γ expression was significantly increased in the skeletal muscle of db/db mice treated with either plasmid. Mice in both plasmid-treated groups exhibited reduced pathological muscle morphology and atrophy-related gene expression, increased muscle regeneration-related gene expression, improved muscle function, and increased irisin expression in skeletal muscles and serum (P < 0.05, respectively). In TIF1γ-transfected C2C12 cells, irisin secretion was significantly increased (P < 0.05). Conditioned medium from TIF1γ-transfected C2C12 cells reduced EMT in palmitate-treated HK cells compared to that from non-transfected C2C12 cells. Additionally, FNDC5 knockdown in C2C12 cells accelerated EMT in palmitate-treated HK cells, as indicated by decreased BMP-7 and increased α-SMA and pSmad2/3 expression compared to palmitate alone and siRNA controls.
Conclusion
This study identifies TIF1γ as a potential mediator of muscle-kidney crosstalk that improves muscle and kidney function while attenuating fibrosis in diabetic conditions.

title: #1847 Breaking barriers in nephroprotection for advanced chronic kidney disease: SGLT2 inhibitors in the treatment of CKD Stage 4–5
authors: Lida Rodas; Sergi Aragó Sorrosal
abstract:
Background
In recent years, SGLT2 inhibitors have been primarily studied in patients with an eGFR greater than 25 ml/min/1.73 m², with caution advised in advanced CKD due to potential fluid-electrolyte imbalance and acidosis risks. However, their well-documented nephroprotective and cardioprotective effects, achieved by reducing intraglomerular pressure and regulating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, have reassured us about their safety. The initial concern about the reduction in eGFR in patients with advanced CKD and eGFR <25 ml/min has been addressed, as it is now known that eGFR declines only by 10%–20% and tends to stabilize over time.
Aims
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the impact of implementing SGLT2 inhibitors as a nephroprotective treatment for advanced CKD patients at the Hospital Clínic of Barcelona on disease progression over one year.
Method
This is a retrospective, observational cohort study. Patients from the Advanced CKD Clinic with an eGFR of 18–24 ml/min who initiated SGLT2 inhibitors between November 2023 and December 2024 were included. Changes in creatinine, eGFR, and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) were assessed at 6 and 12 months. The data was collected and analyzed using standard statistical methods to evaluate the impact of SGLT2 inhibitors on disease progression over one year.
Results
Data were collected from 66 patients (60.6% male, mean age 75.3 years ± 8.6 SD), with 89% having hypertension, 83% type 2 diabetes mellitus, and 15% having a history of cardiovascular disease. All patients received antiproteinuric therapy (ACEIs and/or ARBs) at baseline, and 100% were treated with dapagliflozin.
Baseline characteristics: blood pressure (BP) 135 mmHg [131–144 IQR], HbA1c 7.6% (±1.3 SD), mean eGFR 21.5 ml/min (±5.7 SD), creatinine 2.28 mg/dL (±1.2 SD), UACR 484.32 mg/g (range 288.3–642.9, ±168.7 SD). At 6 and 12 months, eGFR values were 19.41 (±3.5 SD) and 20.1 (±1.9 SD), respectively. UACR was reduced to 381.6 (±183.3 SD) and 316.7 (±158.7 SD) at 6 and 12 months, respectively. This reduction in UACR, although not statistically significant, suggests a potential improvement in kidney function and a reduction in the risk of CKD progression. Adverse events included treatment discontinuation in 4 patients due to abdominal pain, with no severe adverse events reported.
Conclusion
The initial concerns about early renal function deterioration with SGLT2 inhibitors were not observed during follow-up. Overall, the treatment was deemed safe for patients with advanced CKD stages 4–5. While the reduction in UACR showed only a trend, this trend is a promising sign of the potential benefits of these medications. Their well-established long-term nephroprotective and cardioprotective effects are considered fundamental, and this positive trend in UACR reduction adds to our optimism about their potential benefits.

In all situations, patients were diagnosed, treated, and monitored according to prospective protocols.

title: #3539 Identifying risk factors for chronic kidney disease progression in sickle cell disease
authors: Irene Vázquez Raso; Amir Shabaka; Ruth Martínez Galindo; Marta Morado Arias; Maria Soriano Guillén; Javier Azores Moreno; Sara Aldana Barceló; Gema Maria Fernandez Juarez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with sickle cell disease (SCD) are at high risk of developing renal involvement due to various mechanisms, including chronic microvascular damage from repeated vaso-occlusive events. This damage may lead to progressive chronic kidney disease (CKD). The aim of this study was to evaluate the natural history of kidney disease in SCD patients and identify risk factors for its progression.
Method
We conducted a retrospective observational study that included all patients diagnosed with homozygous (HbSS) or heterozygous (HbSC) sickle cell disease who were followed in the Hematology clinic at our center between May 2011 and March 2024. We analyzed demographic data, comorbidities, treatments, complications (e.g., vaso-occlusive crises, transfusion requirements, development of hemoglobinuria), and kidney function tests throughout the follow-up period. Glomerular hyperfiltration was defined as an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) >130 ml/min, as measured by CKD-EPI. The annual rate of eGFR loss was calculated, with rapid progression defined as a loss of >3 ml/min/year. Renal outcome was defined as progression to eGFR <90 ml/min with a decline of >25% from baseline and/or the need for renal replacement therapy.
Results
The study included 30 patients, with a mean age at the start of follow-up of 26.5 ± 12 years; 60% of whom were women. Of the patients, 23 (76.7%) had HbSS, and 7 (23.3%) had HbSC, with one patient also having alpha-thalassemia. At the start of follow-up, 14 patients (46.7%) exhibited glomerular hyperfiltration, and 5 patients (16.7%) had albuminuria. During follow-up, most patients (86.7%) experienced vaso-occlusive crises, and 7 patients (23.3%) developed hemoglobinuria. Sixteen patients (53.3%) were treated with hydroxyurea, and 4 patients (13%) participated in clinical trials (etavopirat, crizanlizumab). Six patients (20%) received renin-angiotensin system blockade. After a median follow-up of 45 months (IQR 12–113 months), the mean annual eGFR loss was −2.5 ml/min/year (±5.5), with 14 patients (46.7%) showing rapid progression. Three patients (10%) reached the renal outcome: 2 with progression to eGFR <90 ml/min and 1 with progression to end-stage renal disease. The annual rate of eGFR loss was significantly higher in men (−5 ± 4.8 vs. −0.6 ± 5.5 ml/min/year, P = 0.048). Only homozygous patients and those with vaso-occlusive crises developed albuminuria at the end of follow-up (33.3% and 28.6%, respectively) and reached the renal outcome (13% and 11.5%, respectively).
Conclusion
A significant proportion of patients with sickle cell disease present with glomerular hyperfiltration, and a notable number experience rapid renal function decline, particularly among men, homozygous patients, and those with vaso-occlusive crises. These findings underline the need for prospective studies to analyze the potential benefits of nephroprotective therapies that could improve the natural course of renal disease associated with sickle cell disease.

title: #3668 Adiposopathy, inflammation and perirenal fat
authors: Luis Gerardo D Marco Gascon; Owahabanun-Joshua Okojie; Nelia Steib; Pilar Salvador; Pablo Gonzalez-Calero; Ana Checa-Ros
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) show high cardiovascular complication rates. There are classical cardiovascular risk factors, such as obesity, dyslipidemia, and diabetes affecting general and renal disease populations. Moreover, non-classical factors of risk such as meta-inflammation (chronic low-grade inflammation) are also present in renal-affected patients. In this sick scenario, visceral adiposity has been shown as another threat to the general and CKD population. Although it has not been widely evaluated, the adipose tissue surrounding the kidneys (perirenal fat [PRF]) could provide additional information of interest in the CKD population. The present study aims to assess the relationship between biomarkers of adiposopathy, inflammation, and PRF in patients with mild CKD stages.
Method
An observational and cross-sectional study was designed. Patients were evaluated at the outpatient clinic in Vithas Consuelo Hospital in Valencia Spain (January–November 2024).
Forty-eight patients with different stages of CKD (G1A1 to G3A3) were included. All the patient's data from electronic medical and analytical records were entered into a protocol sheet. The patients that met the inclusion criteria (eGFR ≤90 or >30 ml/min/1.73 m2; age ≥18 years at the time of signing informed consent, and a life expectancy higher than 1 year) were eligible to participate in the study. As exclusion criteria, patients with active inflammatory processes such as infection, active cancer, or other inflammatory states were excluded beyond those mentioned in inclusion. Patients with an AKI, ADPKD, or CKD requiring RRT were also excluded.
Patients were discriminated according to the levels of serum leptin (higher or lower than the mean). The thickness of the PRF was measured in centimeters (cm) through a B-mode ultrasound with a 3.5-MHz convex transductor (Alpinion®E-CUBE9; Alpinion Medical Systems, Seoul, Korea). Patients underwent a bilateral renal ultrasound, and the kidneys were measured anteroposteriorly, transversally, and longitudinally. PRF was measured in the distal third between the cortex and the hepatic border and/or spleen.
Results
The mean age of the patients was 61.7 ± 16 years and the weight and BMI mean were 77.7 Kg and 27.6 Kg/m2, respectively. Patients with higher leptin levels (mean 25.8 ng/ml) showed a correlation with higher levels of triglycerides (146.7 vs 90.3 mg/dl), TNF-α (9.1 vs 8.5 pg/mL), IL-6 (4.3 vs 3.8 pg/mL), and PCR (5.6 vs 4.2 mg/L) than those patients with low levels. The mean PRF thickness of the right and the left kidney was 1.65 and 1.29 cm (SD ± 0.30) respectively (general PRF mean 1.47 cm). Of note, those patients with higher leptin levels show greater accumulation of PRF (1.7 vs 1.1 cm; p 0.005). There was no association between other adiposopathy and kidney function biomarkers (TFGe, creatinine and/or albuminuria. However, as expected, we found a positive correlation between CKD stages and inflammatory markers. Thus, stage G1: TNF-α 6.6 pg/mL and IL-6 3.0 pg/mL; stage G2: TNF-α 8.0 pg/mL and IL-6 3.9 pg/mL; stage G3: TNF-α 10.2 pg/mL, IL-6 5.4 pg/mL.
Conclusion
These preliminary results show a positive relationship between adiposopathy biomarkers and the inflammatory load in CKD patients. Besides, we found a link between higher levels of leptin and the thickness of PRF. Finally, achieving a decrease in the latter could reduce visceral adipose tissue, thus reducing the cardiovascular risk in CKD-affected patients. Further research with larger sample sizes and longitudinal designs is warranted to validate these findings and explore the underlying mechanisms.

title: #3774 The role of social media in nephrology training and continuous education: a survey-based analysis
authors: Elia Reseghetti; Gianmarco Sabiu; Matteo Abinti; Luca Della Volpe; Giulia Frontini; Chiara Ghilardini; Alessia Guarino; Sara Khemara; Manuel A Podesta'; Carlo Maria Alfieri; Maurizio Gallieni
abstract:
Background and Aims
The number of nephrology-related educational channels on social media (SoMe) has increased in recent years. Since 2020, the School of Nephrology at Università degli Studi di Milano (UNIMI) has built a community of over 1,600 nephrologists participating in online events. However, little is known about the role of SoMe in the professional development of Italian nephrologists.
Method
A multiple-choice questionnaire comprising 23 questions was administered to our followers – including residents and attending physicians, nephrologists and other specialists—through our channels. Each question utilized a five-point Likert scale (strongly agree, agree, neutral, disagree, strongly disagree).
First, a descriptive analysis of responses was performed. Participants were then divided into subgroups (male/female; under/over 35 years old; residents/attending physicians), and a contingency table analysis was conducted using the Chi-square test for independence. Since some statistically significant differences emerged from minor variations between adjacent responses (e.g., strongly agree vs. agree), responses were reclassified into three categories: agree (including strongly agree and agree), neutral, and disagree (including disagree and strongly disagree). Statistical tests were repeated accordingly.
Results
We collected responses from 100 consecutive participants. 72% were female, 55% were under-35 years old, 85% were nephrologists (15% other disciplines), and 53% were residents.
Social Media and Scientific Dissemination: 91% of participants found scientific dissemination via SoMe useful (Fig. 1A), and 75% regularly read scientific articles found through SoMe (Fig. 1B).
Participation in Journal Clubs and Online Events organized from their own hospitals or faculties: 71% regularly attended internal journal clubs, with a higher frequency among those under-35 years old (75% vs. 66% of over-35, p 0.004) (Fig. 2A). Additionally, 76% regularly attended online events, particularly those over-35 years old (89% vs. 65% of under-35, p 0.027) (Fig. 2B). Participants did not perceive online events as lower quality than in-person ones.
Impact on Research and Clinical Practice: among those who attended at least three events of our Nephrology School, 69% reported reading more scientific articles than before, and 64% stated that participation impacted their clinical practice. Surprisingly, this effect was stronger in the over-35 group (78% vs. 58% of under-35, p 0.038). Furthermore, 67% reported increased interest in research (Fig. 1C).
Conclusion
Social media represents a valuable tool for continuous medical education and specialist training, fostering engagement with nephrology research, particularly among younger physicians.
The School of Nephrology at the Università degli Studi di Milano (UNIMI) has demonstrated that high-quality content can be created and effectively disseminated through SoMe. This approach should be encouraged by all Nephrology Schools and Scientific Societies.
Further studies with larger sample sizes should be conducted to provide a more comprehensive overview. Additionally, repeating the survey on the same participants could help assess the evolving role of SoMe in education, training, and clinical practice.

title: #3893 Supply of probiotics with L. rhamnosus and B. longum evaluation of the improvement of uremic gastrointestinal symptoms in patients aged 30–70 years, with hemodialysis treatment at the SENETO clinic, for 1–120 days

abstract:

A prospective longitudinal study was conducted with 44 male and female patients undergoing hemodialysis treatment at the Specialized Nephrology Services Clinic. title: #1661 HK-QIP study design: a prospective, multicenter, single-arm study to evaluate the impact on the implementation of standardized hyperkalemia management in CKD patients
authors: Yeqing Xie; Yang Li; Mingjie Zhang; Xiaoqiang Ding
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyperkalemia (HK, defined as sK+> 5.0 mmol/L), a common electrolyte disturbance, occurs frequently among patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), exhibiting an escalating prevalence as CKD progresses, especially for CKD patients undertaking Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System Inhibitors (RAASi). Despite well-established guidelines and consensus for HK management, gaps remain between clinical practice and guideline recommendations. These gaps primarily manifest in suboptimal monitoring frequencies of sK+ levels, underuse of RAASi (early discontinuation or down-titration of RAASi before potassium binder use), and lack of HK treatment adherence. Moreover, there is currently insufficient data on the cardio-renal benefits of RAASi optimization with long-term standardized management of HK in patients with CKD. The HK-QIP study aims to generate evidence of quality improvement interventions can enhance the care processes and clinical outcomes of patients with CKD and HK through driving guideline adoption. Furthermore, this study will emphasize value of guideline adoption and drive clinical practice change of HK management.
Method
Participants and centers—This multi-center, prospective, single-arm, 96-week study will enroll 1000 adult Chinese patients with non-dialysis-dependent CKD and HK from 50 centers across 30 provinces in mainland of China (Fig. 1).
Description of intervention
The interventions include HK disease management and quality audits for health care professionals (HCPs) and patients (Fig. 1). The main contents of HK disease management in CKD include a standardized clinical pathway based on guideline adoption and medical trainings to educate HCPs and patients. The clinical pathway encompasses HK diagnostic criteria, HK long-term management strategies, the target dose of RAASi, RAASi dose adjustment strategy when HK occurs, and standardized sK+ monitoring protocols. Medical education includes at least five guideline adoption trainings (before the first patient is enrolled and at week 4, 16, 28, 40) for HCPs, and six trainings about HK disease knowledge with self-management for patients (week 12, 24, 36, 48, 72, and 96). The quality audits will be conducted at week 12, 24, 36, 48, 60 and 96, during which the perception (through questionnaire) and actions (through sK+ test arrangement, medication records, etc) of HCPs on standardized HK management and patient adherence to medication and sK+ monitoring (through patient daily checklist and sK+ records) will be tracked. The additional intensive training will be offered to HCPs if their HK management doesn't follow clinical pathway.
Results
This study will examine the impact of the effectiveness of standardized management in patients with CKD and HK for achievement of sK+ control target (3.5 ≤sK+ ≤ 5.0 mmol/L) and RAASi optimization (including newly initialization, up titration and dosage maintenance). The primary endpoint is the proportion of patients achieving RAASi therapy optimization with normal sK+ level after 48 weeks intervention. Key secondary outcomes will describe the achievement of sK+ control target (3.5 ≤ sK+ ≤ 5.0 mmol/L) and RAASi optimization, HK medication possession ratio, time to first HK recurrence, severe HK incidence, long-term HK treatment status and changes, UACR improvement and cardiorenal benefits (including sustained eGFR decline ≥50%, ESRD, renal death, eGFR slope, HF worsening hospitalization & ER visit, and CV death). Adverse events will be included as safety endpoints. Enrollment of the first subject is anticipated to commence in May 2025.
Conclusion
The HK-QIP study is the first trial to generate evidence for clinical outcomes and cardio-renal benefits after intervention of HK guideline adoption management in CKD patients. It will bridge the gaps between guideline recommendation and clinical practice to improve quality of care for HK in CKD.

title: #3585 A postbiotic-based approach to reduce the risk of developing cardiovascular complications seen in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD)
authors: Natalia Pietrzkowska
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic low-grade inflammation is a hallmark of CKD. In recent years, an important role of gut dysbiosis has been pointed out in the development of inflammation observed in the course of CKD. Inflammation plays not only a key role in the progression of CKD, but also in the complications associated with it, incl.: cardiovascular disease (CVD) which is the leading cause of death in patients with CKD. Due to the above, the use of microbiome modulating therapies has become an attractive strategy for the treatment of CKD. Despite numerous studies confirming the clinical effectiveness of probiotics in the treatment of various diseases (including CKD), there are reports questioning their safety. For these reasons, more and more attention is being paid to postbiotics, i.e. preparations derived from non-living microorganisms and/or their ingredients that have a beneficial effect on the body. The undoubted advantage of using postbiotics is the lack of risk of translocation of live microorganisms from the intestinal lumen to the bloodstream, which is particularly dangerous for people with a leaky intestinal barrier, among others. Unlike probiotics, in the case of postbiotics there is no risk of transmitting antibiotic resistance genes or producing harmful metabolites. In addition, postbiotics are easier to store and have a longer shelf life, which may be particularly important when using these preparations in areas where maintaining appropriate storage conditions is still limited. Therefore, the aim of this study was to summarize the current knowledge about postbiotics and their potential use as agents to reduce the risk of developing cardiovascular complications seen in patients with CKD.
Method
PubMed and Google Scholar databases were searched for literature. The keywords used were the combination between gut dysbiosis, probiotic, postbiotics, SCFA, butyrate, cell-free supernatant, blood pressure, cholesterol, hypertension, CVD, inflammation, CKD, uremic toxins, PBUTs, IS, atherosclerosis, heart failure, endothelium, and LPS. Literature search and data collection were conducted between January 1 and January 15, 2025.
Results
The effect of postbiotics or ingredients that may be included in a postbiotic preparation is multidirectional. Postbiotics may show among others: antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial properties. They also have the ability to modulate the immune response. Postbiotics can act not only locally (in the gut), reducing gut dysbiosis and improving the integrity of the intestinal barrier, but also in distant organs (e.g. the heart and kidneys), inhibiting their fibrosis. Moreover, the results of preclinical studies indicate that some of them lower blood pressure and exhibit lipolytic effects, which may be helpful in reducing serum lipid levels.
Conclusion
Due to their pleiotropic effect, postbiotics may be an attractive method of reducing the risk of developing CVD, however, further research is needed on their mechanism of action and effectiveness. Future research should include the selection of an appropriate bacterial strain and the determination of the mechanisms responsible for their beneficial effects. In addition, studies should be performed to identify the appropriate fraction of microorganisms (e.g. cell-free supernatant). Moreover, it will be necessary to select appropriate concentrations and duration of use of such preparations. The implications of this research go beyond the management of CKD and may be helpful in the development of a wide range of innovative products also for patients without renal dysfunction.

title: #3091 What do patients with kidney disease want? A survey of patient preferences in decision-making in Sri Lanka
authors: Desha Fernando; Chathumi Dassanayake; Sathilka Dissanayake; Mythili Aravinthan; Santhushi Amarasuriya; Dilushi Wijayaratne
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autonomy is one of the fundamental ethical principles of clinical practice. The concept of autonomy, as applied to medical care, has been largely shaped by Western culture and ideals, favouring patient-led decision-making. However, attitudes towards patient involvement in clinical decision-making may vary between socio-culturally different populations. The aim of this study was to describe patient preferences in decision-making in a cohort of patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) in Sri Lanka.
Method
A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted at the University renal clinic of National Hospital of Sri Lanka, a state-funded hospital, during May and June 2024. Patients with CKD defined as eGFR < 60 ml/min or albuminuria > 30 mg/g for at least 3 months were invited to participate. A data collection tool comprising 14 questions scored on a 5-point Likert scale was developed by modification of an existing questionnaire (the Ideals of Patient Autonomy scale) followed by cultural and contextual validation by an 8-person expert panel. Responses were presented as proportions on the Likert-scale. The questions broadly aligned with 3 aspects of decision-making. 1) Right to information 2) Right to non-participation 3) Patient- vs doctor-lead clinical decision-making. Within each of these categories scores of the Likert-scale was summed up with the strongly agree and agree and strongly disagree and disagree being considered as agreeing and disagreeing with the statement, respectively. For three statements, scoring was reversed to maintain alignment with the direction of preference within that category. Additional data on socio-demographics and medical history were collected and the association between these and responses was assessed using the Chi square test. A p-value of <0.05% was considered to be significant.
Results
A total of 248 patients participated in the study. Mean age was 52.6 years (±14.8), and 52.0% were male. Majority identified as Buddhist (77.8%), followed by Christian (14.5%), Hindu (4.4%), and Islamic (3.2%). Most were married (82.3%), 13.3% were single and 3.6% were widowed. In terms of income, 62.1% reported a monthly income of less than LKR 50,000 (160 Euros), 31.0% between LKR 50,000 and LKR 100,000 (160–320 Euros) and 6.8% > LKR 100,000 (>320 Euros). There were 57.0% in CKD 1–3, 11.1% in CKD 4, 12.7% in CKD 5 non-dialysis, 9.8% in CKD 5 on dialysis, and 9.4% who were post-kidney transplant. The results of the 14-point scale are presented in Table 1. Almost all the patients (96.8%) agreed with statement corresponding to right to information, while 44.4% agreed, 51.6% disagreed, and 4.0% were neutral with right to non-participation, and 14.9% agreed, 56.8% disagreed, and 28.2% were neutral with patient-lead clinical decision-making. Age, sex, religion, income category did not appear to affect any of the three aspects of decision-making. However, patient- lead clinical decision-making was preferred among those with only primary education compared to those educated beyond primary level (P = 0.005).
Conclusion
In this cohort representing patients with CKD receiving treatment in a state hospital in Sri Lanka, most expressed a desire for all relevant information regarding options and risks of treatments and did not agree with right to non-participation in decision-making. However, most patients demonstrated strong reliance on their doctor for final decision-making related to health care.

title: #307 Parathyroid hormone levels, rather than calcium or phosphate, as independent predictor of ischemic heart disease in CKD stages 3–5 non-dialysis patients: a retrospective cohort study
authors: Suthiya Anumas; Pichaya Tantiyavarong; Pattharawin Pattharanitima
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease–mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD) significantly contributes to various complications in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), including ischemic heart disease (IHD), which is associated with increased mortality. While the minimum parathyroid hormone (PTH) threshold is well-established for dialysis-dependent patients, such a threshold remains undefined for non-dialysis-dependent individuals. This study aims to identify the minimum PTH level required to mitigate the risk of IHD in patients with CKD stages 3–5 non-dialysis (ND) and to examine other factors associated with an elevated risk of IHD.
Method
We retrospectively analyzed data from CKD stage 3–5 ND patients aged over 18 years, followed from 2018 to 2022. IHD was identified using ICD-10 codes. Four adjusted Cox regression model and joint modeling analysis were used to assess the association between risk factors and IHD outcomes.
Results
Among the 1,210 CKD stage 3–5 ND patients included in the analysis, the median follow-up duration was 513.5 days (IQR 189–979).The incidence of IHD was 7.5%. In the unadjusted analysis, baseline PTH levels ≥166 ng/L was significantly associated with an increased risk of IHD (HR 1.87, 95% CI 1.11–3.13, p = 0.02). In the final adjusted model, elevated PTH levels (≥166 ng/L) (HR 1.87, 95% CI 1.05–3.35, p = 0.03) and age ≥65 years (HR 1.68, 95% CI 1.00–2.81, p = 0.04) were significantly associated with an increased risk of IHD. Conversely, statin use was associated with a reduced risk of IHD (HR 0.44, 95% CI 0.27–0.73, p = 0.002). In a joint modeling analysis that incorporated longitudinal PTH data and a survival submodel, the longitudinal submodel demonstrated that PTH levels significantly changed over time (coefficient: 0.15, 95% CI: 0.12–0.18, p < 0.001). The survival submodel, which accounted for time-varying PTH, calcium, phosphorus, age ≥65 years, sex, diabetes mellitus (DM), hypertension, and medication use, identified time-varying PTH as significantly associated with an increased risk of IHD (coefficient: 0.001, 95% CI: 0.0001–0.002, p = 0.022). Age ≥65 years and DM were also significant risk factors, while ARB and statin use were associated with a reduced risk. Calcium and phosphate levels did not demonstrate significant associations with IHD risk.
Conclusion
Baseline PTH levels (≥166 ng/L) and time-varying PTH were independently and significantly associated with an increased risk of IHD. In contrast, calcium and phosphate levels showed no significant association with IHD risk.

Among the 1,210 CKD stage 3–5 ND patients included in the analysis, the median follow-up duration was 513.5 days (IQR 189–979).The incidence of IHD was 7.5%.
