title: #287 Effective muscle index based on muscle mass and quality to diagnose sarcopenia and predict renal survival in CKD patients
authors: Yukari Mae; Tomoaki Takata; Natsuki Yamakawa; Yudai Fujino; Kana Kageyama; Sosuke Taniguchi; Takuji Iyama; Katsuya Hikita; Hajime Isomoto
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sarcopenia is highly prevalent in CKD patients due to specific pathophysiologies such as chronic inflammation and uremic toxin accumulation, and is strongly associated with renal dysfunction and poor prognosis. Muscle quality, which reflects myofiber density and myocyte condition, has been recently recognized as an important factor to assess sarcopenia as well as muscle mass. Worsened muscle quality is associated with poor physical performance and renal prognosis. Therefore, it is desired to diagnose sarcopenia based on both muscle mass and quality. However, no definite criterion, which include muscle quality, has been proposed to assess sarcopenia. We recently developed effective muscle index (EMI), an index that reflects both muscle mass and muscle quality, to accurately assess sarcopenia. The aim of this study is to evaluate the feasibility of EMI to assess sarcopenia and renal prognosis.
Method
We conducted a single-center, prospective study. This study included 116 patients with CKD who underwent blood tests and bioelectrical impedance analysis between April 2021 and October 2022. Muscle mass was assessed by appendicular skeletal muscle mass (ASM) and skeletal muscle mass index (SMI), calculated from ASM divided by height. Muscle quality was assessed by phase angle (PhA) using MC-780A-N (TANITA, Tokyo, Japan). Sarcopenia was determined by grip strength (HGS) and SMI based on the EWGSOP2 algorithm. The respective cutoff values were set according to the AWGS 2019 sarcopenia diagnostic criteria. EMI was calculated as ASM × PhA. Correlations of HGS to age, eGFR, body mass index (BMI), SMI, ASM, PhA, and EMI were analyzed using Pearson's correlation coefficient. Influencing factors for HGS were determined using multiple linear regression analysis that include age, sex, eGFR, BMI, SMI, and EMI as explanatory variables. In addition, a cutoff value of EMI to diagnose sarcopenia was determined. Patients were further classified into high and low EMI groups, and renal prognoses were compared. The surrogate endpoint of renal function was defined as a 30% decrease in eGFR or initiation of dialysis. Renal survival was assessed by the Kaplan-Meier analysis and the Cox proportional hazards model.
Results
Included patients were 57.8% male, 64.2 ± 16.9 years old, and eGFR 39.69 ± 27.7 mL/min/1.73 m2. CKD stages of the subjects were G1–2 19.0%, G3a 19.8%, G3b 22.4%, G4 19.0%, G5 19.8%, respectively. HGS correlated with age, eGFR, BMI, SMI, ASM, PhA, and EMI (age; r = 0.501 and P < 0.001, eGFR; r = 0.331 and P < 0.001, BMI; r = 0.361 and P < 0.001, SMI; r = 0.777 and P < 0.001, ASM; r = 0.843 and P < 0.001, PhA; r = 0.679 and P < 0.001, and EMI; r = 0.856 and P < 0.001). Multiple linear regression analysis showed that EMI independently affected HGS (age; Stdβ = −0.059 and P = 0.398, sex; Stdβ = 0.196 and P = 0.004, eGFR; Stdβ = 0.056 and P = 0.378, BMI; Stdβ = −0.174 and P = 0.799, SMI; Stdβ = 0.160 and P = 0.252, and EMI; Stdβ = 0.554 and P < 0.001). The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of EMI for sarcopenia diagnosis showed an area under the curve of 0.976/0.975 (male/female, respectively). The cut-off value of EMI was determined at 87.7/47.5 with a sensitivity of 89.8/91.9% and a specificity of 100/100% (male/female, respectively) (Fig. 1). The renal survival rate was significantly lower in patients with low EMI (P < 0.001) (median follow-up 545 days) (Fig. 2). Multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression analysis adjusted for age, sex, BMI and eGFR revealed that low EMI was an independent predictor of CKD progression (Hr = 3.54, 95% CI = 1.06–11.83, and P < 0.001).
Conclusion
This study demonstrated the following: (1) EMI is the novel diagnostic marker for sarcopenia that reflects muscle mass and quality. (2) Sarcopenia can be simply assessed by EMI without measuring muscle strength. (3) EMI is a prognostic factor for renal progression in CKD patients.

title: #1574 Effect of hydration status on fat mass assessment in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease
authors: Gloria Anton-Perez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Obesity is defined as “an excessive accumulation of energy in the form of fat” (>33% in women; >25% in men), being a significant risk factor in chronic kidney disease (CKD). One of the most common methods to determine fat mass (FM) is bioimpedance analysis (BIA). In CKD, overhydration can occur, affecting the measurement; therefore the need to use more complex methods (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry—DXA, air displacement plethysmography—ADP) for accurate assessment.
To evaluate the influence of hydration status on fat mass determination by bioimpedance in advanced CKD patients.
Method
A prospective study was conducted on 30 patients (age: 65 ± 11 years, 19 men, BMI: 27.5 ± 3.7 kg/m², 50% diabetics) diagnosed with CKD stages 4–5 (glomerular filtration rate [GFR]: 18.9 ± 6.1 ml/min). Clinical data were collected, and body composition was evaluated using BIA and DXA.
Results
Patients were classified into two groups according to hydration status: normohydrated (NH, n = 16) and overhydrated (OH, n = 14), based on the ratio of extracellular water (ECW) to total body water (TBW), with a cutoff of 0.390. FM determined by BIA was significantly higher in the OH group (36.8 ± 7.5% vs. 30.2 ± 5.2%, P < 0.01) compared to the NH group. However, FM measured by DXA did not show significant differences between groups (NH: 33.5 ± 7.8%, OH: 34.1 ± 6.4%, P = NS).
Conclusion
Hydration status significantly affects the measurement of fat mass by bioimpedance analysis in patients with advanced CKD. Overhydration leads to an overestimation of fat mass. DXA provides a more reliable assessment of fat mass in these patients, independent of hydration status. Further studies are required to validate these findings in larger populations.

title: #1670 Gut-lung-kidney axis: gut microbiota and kidney disfunction in patients with COPD
authors: Durdona Saipova; Dano Egamberdieva; Iroda Ruzmetova
abstract:
Background and Aims
Emerging research highlights the critical role of the gut-lung-kidney axis in the pathophysiology of COPD, with gut microbiota acting as a central modulator. Aim of the study to study gut microbiome in patients with kidney disfunction and COPD.
Method
This study analyzed the gut microbiome, systemic inflammation, and lung function in 180 patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). title: #1737 The role of oxalate in end-stage kidney disease
authors: Viola D'ambrosio; Keith Siew; Alessandra Grillo; Robert Moss; Robert Speller; Ben Cheung; Amandine Maréchal; Candice Roufosse; Reza Motallebzadeh; Ammar Almidani; Stephen Walsh; Pietro Manuel Ferraro
abstract:
Background and Aims
Oxalate is an end-product of metabolism and in human biology, it derives from endogenous and exogenous sources, and it is almost completely excreted by the kidney. We owe our knowledge of oxalate metabolism to a condition called primary hyperoxaluria (PH). PH is a rare, autosomal recessive, progressive disease caused by excessive hepatic production and elevated oxaluria. This condition leads to recurrent nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis and eventually, kidney failure. As GFR declines oxalate accumulates leading to systemic oxalosis, characterized by extra renal deposit of calcium oxalate that is not only extremely debilitating, but also resistant to treatment. High plasma oxalate, however, is not only present in patients with PH, but can also affect patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), especially those requiring hemodialysis (HD) or peritoneal dialysis (PD). Moreover, recent evidence suggests the role of oxalate as a uremic toxin involved in inflammation and atherogenesis, two well-known cardiovascular risk factors, even in the absence of PH. Our aim was to investigate the presence of calcium oxalate crystals in peripheral arteries of patients with ESKD.
Method
We included 14 adult patients affected by ESKD and scheduled to receive a living donor kidney transplant at Royal Free Hospital in London. We investigated iliac artery patch biopsies, discarded tissue that is normally the site for the transplant anastomosis. The presence of microcalcifications in the samples was investigated with microCT, whereas biochemical composition (specifically the presence of calcium oxalate monohydrate (COM) and brushite crystals) was examined using FTIR spectroscopy. Specifically, FTIR qualitative analysis was performed by recording spectra of every ESKD and control sample and comparing them to the spectral signatures of COM and brushite powders. Quantitative analysis was performed by manually calculating the contribution of COM and brushite in the samples, from the amplitude of characteristic absorption peaks at 1317 cm−1 and 879 cm−1, respectively. Lastly, the presence of calcium oxalate crystals was investigated with light microscopy (polarized light) on sectioned tissues with Von Kossa and H&E stainings. The study had ethics committee approval.
Results
Patients’ baseline characteristics are shown in Table 1 . 7 patients received a pre-emptive kidney transplant, 3 patients were undergoing HD and 4 patients were undergoing PD at transplantation. Four samples presented calcifications at microCT. One sample was heavily calcified (Fig. 1a), the other three presented spot calcifications (Fig. 1b–d). From the FTIR spectra's qualitative analysis, no major differences could be seen between the pre-emptive, PD and HD group, even after grouping the samples according to the presence of microcalcifications at microCT (Fig. 1e). Interestingly, the amplitude of the signal at 879 cm−1, that we attributed to brushite, was higher in the controls, followed by the non-calcified and the calcified group. The amplitude of the signal at 1317 cm−1, that we identified as the COM signature, did not differ significantly among the three groups (Fig. 1e). From the FTIR spectra's quantitative analysis, no differences could be seen between the manually calculated amplitude for the COM and brushite peaks between the pre-emptive, HD, PD and control groups (Fig. 1f–g). At the Von Kossa staining, calcifications either in the media or adventitia could be seen in 6 samples out of 14. No intimal calcification was observed. No calcium oxalate crystals were detected under polarized light (Fig. 1h–o).
Conclusion
Starting from the hypothesis that even transient hyperoxalemia in ESKD patients may favor the ectopic deposition of calcium oxalate crystals and therefore increase the cardiovascular morbidity and mortality of ESKD patients, we investigated arterial tissue for the presence of COM crystals. Although we couldn't find any calcium oxalate crystals, we cannot exclude that a high level of oxalate within tissue causes a direct or an indirect detrimental effect on endothelial cells and worsens these patients’ cardiovascular outcomes.

title: #2697 Predictors of complications in percutaneous kidney biopsy: a single-center experience
authors: Bruno Pepe; Maria Inês Gil Martins Roxo; Leonor Gomes; Rita Veríssimo; Tiago Carvalho; Artur Mendes
abstract:
Background and Aims
Percutaneous kidney biopsy (PKB) is an invaluable procedure in Nephrology. It is routinely performed guided by real-time ultrasonography (US), and, as an invasive procedure, its benefits must be weighed against its risks, despite being mostly safe. Bleeding is its main complication, usually resulting in hematuria, hematoma and/or pain, according to the affected renal compartment—collector system, perirenal/retroperitoneal or subcapsular space, respectively. Infrequently, arteriovenous fistulas (AVF) can form. In rare cases, major bleeding may occur and warrant percutaneous embolectomy or nephrectomy.
Our study aims to evaluate potential risk factors associated with PKB complications.
Methods
A single center retrospective study was conducted in our Nephrology department, where PKB is performed by nephrologists. Our protocol warrants antiplatelet therapy (APT) and anticoagulation (ACO) suspension prior to PKB. Post PKB, a 24 h-period of strict bed rest is required. In this period, complete blood count is collected at 6 and 24 h, and kidney US is performed at 24 h, with subsequent discharge in the absence of complications.
We collected demographic, laboratory, clinical and procedure-related data, including complications and histopathology results (diagnosis and chronicity score, as defined by Sethi et al., 2017) from all patients undergoing native kidney (N-PKB) and renal allograft (G-PKB) from 1 January 2018 to 31 December 2024.
Major complications were defined as clinically significant hematoma or hematuria requiring prolongation of hospital stay, blood transfusion and/or radiological or surgical intervention.
We used SPSS® software for statistical analysis, performing Chi-squared test for categorical data and Mann-Whitney test for continuous data, and statistical significance was assumed if P < 0.05, with a confidence interval of 95%.
Results and Discussion
A total of 475 patients were submitted to PKB, of which 60.8% were N-PKB and 39.2% were G-PKB. The mean age of the patients was 52 ± 16 years and 57.9% were male.
We observed a 10.1% rate of major complications (n = 48). 4 patients required blood transfusion. 10 developed an AVF, 2 requiring percutaneous embolization.
No patient needed surgery or died as a result of the procedure.
We observed a statistically significant difference in the number of complications between N-PKB and G-PKB (P = 0.006), with a rate of 13.1% and 5.4%, respectively. The higher rate of complications in N-PKB may be explained by the increased complexity of the procedure when compared to G-PKB.
We performed further analysis to look for additional risk factors for complications. Patients submitted to N-PKB had significantly more proteinuria (P = 0.005) and hematuria (P = 0.035), but there were no differences between N-PKB and G-PKB regarding sex, age, serum creatinine [sCr], glomerular filtration rate [GFR], and hypertension or diabetes diagnosis.
We further evaluated the subgroup of patients submitted to N-PKB and found a significant negative correlation between complications and sCr (P = 0.019) and GFR (P = 0.023), but not with the number of needle passes (P = 0.300). We found no association with chronicity score in the obtained native kidney tissue samples (P = 0.104). No correlations with previous APT or ACO were found.
Conclusion
Our results highlight that N-PKB are technically more complex than G-PKB and, therefore, associated with a higher rate of clinically relevant complications. Among these, the degree of kidney impairment also seems to contribute to an increased risk of complications, a finding probably attributable to uremia-associated bleeding diathesis. This suggests that these patients might benefit from dialysis or desmopressin administration prior to PKB.
Interestingly, the severity of the pathological chronicity score in N-PKB samples was not associated with increased risk of procedure complications, suggesting that the degree of uremia (which can be due to acute kidney injury) is more relevant, in this regard, than the chronicity of the kidney disease.
The absence of association between complications and the use of APT or ACO suggests that the timing for suspension is appropriate.

title: #383 Survey on nurse practices in the care pathway within the CKD stage 4 and 5 multidisciplinary package
authors: Georgios Kosmadakis; Helene Pages; Marie Antunes
abstract:
Background and Aims
The chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage IV–V package aims to reduce the incidence of dialysis, including a consultation with a coordinating nurse (IDE) for educational guidance. This survey analyzes the areas covered in this consultation.
Method
An online survey was sent to all establishments to evaluate practices.
Results
We received 24 responses from university hospitals (CHU) (5/24), peripheral hospitals (4/24), and associations (2/24). All nurses had over five years of experience with CKD. Their structures collectively follow 11,376 patients with CKD stage IV-V (mean ± SD: 452 ± 257). Fifteen nurses use specific frameworks for the consultation, covering dialysis techniques (22/24), conservative care (18/24), and kidney transplantation (20/24). All nurses discuss vascular access for dialysis and explain dialysis techniques (21/24) as well as indications and contraindications (13/24). They address the pre-transplant work-up and key elements of kidney transplantation, and the reversibility of patient choices for conservative treatment. They cover renal anemia, mineral bone disorders, CKD symptoms, and biological aspects. Quality of life and patient perception of the disease are often discussed. Consultations are tailored to patient needs, with specific materials provided.
Conclusion
There is noted homogeneity and relative exhaustiveness of the topics covered. Specific recommendations could facilitate these indispensable consultations within the care pathway.

title: #565 I will present the results of a novel automated method for screening chronic kidney disease (CKD) in primary care, leveraging artificial intelligence and adherence to established clinical guidelines
authors: María Salinas; Alberto Ortiz; Maite Lopez-Garrigós; Alvaro Blasco; Ruth Torreblanca; Rosa Carbonell; Irene Gutierrez; Estanislao Puig; Emilio Flores
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a significant global health concern due to its high prevalence and associated complications. Often undiagnosed until advanced stages, early detection is crucial for effective management. The KDIGO and National Scientific Societies guidelines provide evidence on which patients should be screened. Primary Care Centers (PCCs) can play a vital role in identifying undiagnosed CKD, but they require tools to assist in this process.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming clinical laboratories, and one of its applications is Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS). These digital solutions are designed to assist healthcare professionals in making clinical decisions and can be instrumental in opportunistic screening to facilitate early CKD detection and management.
The objectives were to explore a new method to screening for CKD in PCC patients using a CDSS, and to present the results of a pilot study.
Method
A cross-sectional intervention study was conducted from August 1st, 2023, to December 31, 2024, in patients visiting PCCs for any reason and requiring laboratory tests. The study was approved by the Hospital Ethics Research Committee.
The pilot study was carried out at the San Juan PCC, serving a population of 26,129 inhabitants (52% female, 19% aged over 65 years). The PCC employs 15 doctors and 24 nurses and handles 199,816 primary care consultations annually.
Our laboratory has implemented a CDSS as a rule engine (AlinIQ CDS v8.2; Abbott, Chicago, IL) to manage pathways and actions. The CDSS allows identification of requests including a specific test in current and recent previous requests. In addition, the CDSS integrates with clinical databases, such as electronic medical record, to get information on all current and previous patient diagnoses. If certain conditions are detected in its rules engine, CDSS is capable of generating alerts or adding tests.
Figure 1 illustrates the implemented workflow. The CDSS identified patients eligible for potential CKD screening based on inclusion criteria that implemented a Spanish National Scientific Societies consensus document: patients from the local health catchment area and aged ≥60 years or having specific comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes, or coronary heart disease). Exclusion criteria included age <18 years, previous CKD diagnosis, pregnancy, or prior screening within one year.
The CDSS offered clinicians, via real-time pop-ups, the option to assess CKD risk and add urine albumin:creatinine ratio (UACR) and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) tests. Laboratory reports provided CKD risk assessments and management recommendations aligned with KDIGO guidelines.
The reagent costs for UACR were 0.26€ for strip analysis and 0.62€ for quantification. Costs were divided by the number of patients classified as KDIGO low and high risk and further divided by high-risk patients to evaluate two key performance indicators: cost per patient screened and cost per patient identified as high CKD risk.
Results
During the study period, 18,377 requests were analyzed, and 1,515 patients were flagged for CKD screening. This represented 8.2% of requests and 5.8% of the population. A total of 1,318 patients (87.0%) accepted and provided samples (mean age 62.4 ± 11.7 years; 53.0% female). The CDSS classified 1,222 patients (92,7%) as low CKD risk. Ninety-six patients (7.3%) were identified as moderate risk. Of these, eleven patients were directly classified as CKD, while 85 required confirmation of values, with 43 ultimately confirmed. Overall, fifty-four patients (4.1%) were identified with CKD (47 were recommended for managed in PCC, while 7 follow-up in nephrology).
The cost analysis showed an expense of 0.51€ per screened patient. The total reagent expenditure was 671.28€. The cost per identified CKD patient was 12.4€.
Conclusion
Opportunistic CKD screening is feasible, cost-effective, and well-received. The acceptance rates and significant identification of high-risk patients support CKD detection and management. Future research should expand this approach and evaluate long-term impacts.

title: #850 Tumor-like calcification in patients undergoing haemodyalisis
authors: Omaima Taie
abstract:
Background and Aims
Tumor-like calcinosis is a condition where calcium phosphate crystals accumulate in the tissues around joints, forming large, calcified masses. Although the exact mechanisms are not fully understood, it is believed that an elevated calcium-phosphate product and severe hyperparathyroidism play key roles in its development. While surgery is commonly suggested for treatment, there remains ongoing debate regarding the best approach.
Method
We describe a 63-year-old diabetic patient on long-term hemodialysis who presented with a six-month history of worsening left hip pain and limited mobility. A CT scan was performed, revealing a calcified mass in the posterior thigh. Laboratory tests were conducted, which showed elevated calcium-phosphate levels and hyperparathyroidism, supporting the diagnosis of tumor-like calcinosis. The patient's condition was evaluated, and due to the mass's close proximity to vascular and nerve structures, surgical removal was considered unfeasible. A conservative management approach was adopted, which included angioplasty to improve blood flow and alleviate symptoms.
Results
The CT scan findings suggested the calcified mass was causing sharp, electric-shock-like pain and compressing the superficial femoral artery, leading to critical limb ischemia. Angioplasty temporarily improved blood flow and provided symptom relief, but the patient continued to experience persistent pain and functional limitations. The rarity of tumor-like calcinosis in hemodialysis patients, combined with the calcified masses, posed significant challenges in both diagnosis and treatment.
Conclusion
This case highlights the diagnostic and treatment challenges of tumor-like calcinosis in chronic hemodialysis patients. Despite conservative management, the patient experienced persistent pain and functional impairment. Endovascular intervention, including double dilation with stenting, temporarily restored blood flow and relieved symptoms. However, this approach is not curative and carries a risk of rethrombosis. The complexity of managing calcinosis-related vascular complications in hemodialysis patients calls for further investigation into optimal treatment strategies for such rare cases.

This case highlights the diagnostic and treatment challenges of tumor-like calcinosis in chronic hemodialysis patients. title: #1629 Use of Cystatin C to estimate glomerular filtration rate based on nutritional status in older adults
authors: David Connellan; Sadhbh McLoughlin; Colm Cronin; Sorcha Murray; Nisshata Subramaniam; Ruth Cullen; Catherine McGorrian; Dermot Power; Paula O'shea; Graham Lee; Denise Sadlier
abstract:
Background and Aims
Serum creatinine (sCr) often inaccurately estimates eGFR due to non-GFR determinants such as malnutrition. The 2024 KDIGO Guidelines recommend greater use of Cystatin C (CysC) for confirmatory eGFR testing and CKD staging. This study aimed to audit the utilization of CysC in confirmatory eGFR testing among older patients and examine the relationship between eGFR measurements and nutritional status, as assessed by the controlling nutritional status (CONUT) score.
Method
This retrospective cross-sectional study included hospitalized patients aged 65 years or older who underwent routine renal function testing. The frequency of prior Cystatin C (CysC) testing was recorded, and CysC measurements were taken to calculate combined CysC–serum creatinine (sCr) eGFR in all patients.
Nutritional status was evaluated using the CONUT score, derived from serum albumin, total cholesterol, and lymphocyte count (Table 1). Differences in CKD staging between sCr-based eGFR and combined CysC–sCr eGFR were analysed using the chi-square test to determine any association with nutritional status.
Results
The study included 100 patients (median age: 81 years) with significant co-morbidities, including congestive cardiac failure (28%), diabetes mellitus (26%), and respiratory disease (23%). Biochemical nutritional deficits were prevalent, with 75% of patients showing intermediate or high CONUT scores.
None of the patients had prior CysC testing for confirmatory eGFR assessment. Application of the combined CysC–sCr equation reclassified 55% of patients to a lower CKD stage, while only 2% were reclassified to a higher CKD stage. This re-classification of CKD stage is displayed in Graph 1. The relationship between CONUT score and differences in CKD staging was not statistically significant (P = 0.78).
Conclusion
This study highlights the underutilization of Cystatin C in the assessment of renal function in older adults, despite its ability to significantly alter CKD staging. The CONUT score was not a reliable predictor for identifying patients requiring confirmatory eGFR testing, underscoring the need for comprehensive nutritional assessments. Integrating CysC into renal function evaluation may improve diagnostic accuracy in this population.

title: #1796 The impact of metabolic syndrome components on renal function in patients with heart failure
authors: Muzaffar Asomov; Gulchehra Atakhodjayeva; Olimkhon Sharapov; Ilkhomjon Kasimov
abstract:
Background and Aims
According to numerous prospective studies, even a slight decrease in renal function is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular diseases and cardiovascular outcomes, regardless of other risk factors. It has been shown that the prevalence of CVD in the population of patients with reduced renal function is 64% higher than in individuals with normal function. Aim was to determine the frequency and degree of renal function impairment (glomerular filtration rate, creatinine, microalbuminuria) in patients with chronic heart failure (CHF) with mid-range ejection fraction (HFmrEF) depending on the presence and severity of metabolic syndrome (MS) components.
Method
197 men with ischemic CHF of functional class II–III (NYHA) aged 40–60 years who had a myocardial infarction (6 months–5 years ago) were examined. The EF level was determined using echocardiography (ESC 2016). The HFmrEF group included patients with an EF of 40%–49%. MS was verified according to the IDF criteria (2009): abdominal obesity (AO), hypertriglyceridemia (TG >1.7 mmol/l), decreased HDL-C (<1.03 mmol/l), arterial hypertension (>130/85 mm Hg), hyperglycemia, or the presence of type 2 diabetes. Patients with HFmrEF were divided into three groups: 28 HFmrEF patients without MS; 28 HFmrEF patients with MS (without type 2 diabetes); 32 HFmrEF patients with MS (+DM2).
Results
The frequency of microalbuminuria (MAU) increased as the metabolic background became more complex: from 35.7% in the group without MS to 53.6% in the presence of MS and up to 85.7% in the combination of MS and DM2. A progressive decrease in eGFR and an increase in creatinine levels were noted (by 11.3% and 12.7% in group II, by 23.0% and 21.8% in group III relative to patients without MS). As MS worsened, the proportion of patients with stage III chronic kidney disease (CKD) increased: from 0%–7% in the group without MS to 21.4% and 43.7% with MS and MS+DM2, respectively.
Conclusion
(1) In patients with HFmrEF, metabolic syndrome (especially in combination with type 2 diabetes mellitus) significantly worsens the functional state of the kidneys, which is manifested by an increase in the frequency of MAU and a decrease in eGFR. (2) Correction of risk factors (obesity, hypertriglyceridemia, arterial hypertension, hyperglycemia) seems to be an important direction in slowing the progression of renal dysfunction and preventing cardiovascular complications.

title: #2305 Association between proteinuria and clinically meaningful endpoints in patients with C3G/IC-MPGN: a Delphi consensus of European experts
authors: Fernando Caravaca Fontan; Matthew C Pickering; Edwin Wong; Fadi Fakhouri; Christoph Licht; Franz Schaefer
abstract:
Background and Aims
C3 glomerulopathy (C3G) and primary (idiopathic) immune complex-mediated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (IC-MPGN) are rare, progressive kidney diseases caused by dysregulation of the complement system, leading to excessive breakdown and glomerular deposition of the C3 protein. Accumulation of glomerular C3 is followed by inflammation and kidney damage. The most common symptoms of these diseases include hematuria, proteinuria and hypertension. Both diseases are associated with a poor prognosis.
Since kidney failure occurs late in the natural history of the disease, and repeat biopsy is not commonly practiced due to its invasive nature, it is necessary to measure other surrogate endpoints to assess outcomes in clinical trials and clinical practice. While surrogate markers are limited, eGFR is the most commonly used; however, it can be affected by non-disease factors such as comorbidities and medications, making it a limited, less reliable endpoint.
Although proteinuria is used as a primary endpoint in C3G and IC-MPGN clinical studies due to a growing body of real-world evidence demonstrating its association with long-term kidney outcomes, uncertainty remains on what constitutes a clinically meaningful change. This Delphi consensus aims to contribute to the evidence base and gather expert opinions on defining clinically meaningful changes. It focuses on validated statements regarding the use of proteinuria, alongside other markers, as appropriate endpoints for assessing treatment efficacy in patients with C3G/primary IC-MPGN.
Method
This European study used a modified Delphi technique involving two rounds of survey. A literature review was conducted to identify existing evidence and knowledge gaps, and facilitate setting an agenda for discussion. We recruited a steering group of 7 nephrologist experts in C3G and IC-MPGN, who attended a virtual meeting to discuss three main themes to inform the basis of consensus statement generation:
The meeting was used to generate 26 statements related to the above themes, which were used to develop an online survey for testing with a wider panel of nephrologists and kidney pathologists, recruited anonymously via a third-party agency, M3 Global. Survey respondents (n = 51) shared their level of agreement using a 4-point Likert scale on each statement. Statements that did not reach the predefined consensus threshold of 75%, or required further clarification (e.g., testing different cut-off points), were selected by the group for an additional survey round.
Results
Overall, 51 survey responses were received from 26 nephrologists and 25 kidney pathologists in the first round of testing. Respondents were from different European countries including France (n = 9), Germany (n = 11), Spain (n = 11), Italy (n = 10) and the United Kingdom (n = 10).
Respondent nephrology experience varied [≤5 years (n = 12), 6-10 years (n = 12), 11-20 years (n = 17), >20 years (n = 10)]. At the end of the first round, 24/26 (92%) statements achieved consensus.
The steering group agreed to test a further 12 statements in Round 2, with 50 additional survey responses received from 25 nephrologists and 25 kidney pathologists. 11/12 (92%) of these statements achieved consensus.
Over the two rounds of survey, 35 statements achieved consensus in total: 3 on the importance of endpoints, 11 on commonly used endpoints, and 21 on proteinuria as a clinically meaningful endpoint.
Conclusion
A modified Delphi consensus methodology was used to develop expert-informed statements regarding the use of proteinuria as a clinically meaningful endpoint in C3G and IC-MPGN.
These statements aim to guide clinical trial design and treatment practices by providing a framework to determine disease progression and treatment response, and validating the use of proteinuria as a surrogate marker in C3G and IC-MPGN clinical trials. The final results and statements will be presented at the meeting.

title: #2320 Multimorbidity, frailty and body composition in chronic kidney disease
authors: Ashveer Randhay; Nicholas Selby; Maarten Taal; Tarek Eldehni
abstract:
Background and Aims
Body composition has major impact on health, clinical outcomes, survival and functionality in the general population. High fat mass and high muscle mass have opposing associations with survival, where high fat mass leads to higher mortality and higher muscle mass is associated with better survival. Visceral adiposity in particular is implicated in developing cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, breast cancer, colorectal cancer and dementia. It is well recognised that patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) have high levels of multimorbidity and frailty. The Multimorbidity and Sarcopenia Study in CKD (MaSS-CKD) aims to study body composition in patients with at different stages of CKD and examine their association with frailty and multimorbidity.
Methods
People with CKD stage 3, 4 and 5 were recruited with age and gender matched control group (no history of kidney disease, with eGFR >60 ml/min) from a single centre. People who were pregnant, had neuromuscular conditions, or had cardiac implantable electronic devices were excluded. Bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) was utilised to measure body composition parameters. Frailty was assessed with Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) and multimorbidity was quantified with Cambridge Multimorbidity Score (CMS). T tests and ANOVA tests were used to assess the difference in means between different groups. Ordinal and linear regression analysis was used to assess significant determinants of frailty and multimorbidity in this cohort respectively.
Results
83 participants were recruited to MaSS-CKD. The median age of the cohort was 71 years, with 21 participants with eGFR >60 ml/min, 19 with CKD 3, 26 with CKD 4 and 17 with CKD 5. There were 42 male and 41 female participants. Multimorbidity and frailty score were higher in patients with CKD compared to controls (CFS 3 vs 1 P < 0.001, CMS 4 vs 1, P < 0.001). Higher multimorbidity index scores correlated with higher clinical frailty scores (r = 0.561, P < 0.001).
Mean BMI in the CKD group was 29.29 kg/m2, and in controls (eGFR >60 ml/min) 24.67 kg/m2, the difference in means was significant (P = 0.004). When comparing body composition measurements between the groups, mean body fat mass was higher in the CKD group (P = 0.014) as was visceral fat area (P = 0.008). There was no significant difference in skeletal muscle mass between the groups (P = 0.405).
In a univariate linear regression analysis visceral fat area was associated with higher CMS (β = 0.239, P = 0.029). A multivariate ordinal regression analysis identified visceral fat area, age and eGFR to be independently associated with frailty scores, Table 1.
Conclusion
Multimorbidity is predominant in patients with CKD and is associated with higher levels of frailty. Body composition in particular visceral adiposity seems to correlate with higher levels of multimorbidity and frailty in this population. Visceral adiposity has been previously linked to metabolic syndrome, CKD progression and a significant risk factor for cardiovascular events and mortality. This is a potentially modifiable risk factor, and novel therapies and public health policies may improve multimorbidity and frailty burden in people with CKD.

title: #1867 Spanish renal health cohort: Mulagua study
authors: Sergio Luis Lima; Raúl Morales Febles; Laura Díaz Martin; Talía Cury; Patricia Isabel Delgado Mallén; Juana Reyes Padrón Morales; Alejandra González Delgado; Angel Hernández; Rocío Morales Perdomo; María del Pilar Correa Martín; María José Rodriguez Plaza; Esteban Porrini
abstract:
Background
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a serious Health problem. It is the eighth leading cause of death worldwide, is going to be the fifth in 2040, and the second in 2100. CKD is a first-order disease, carrying a high burden to the health system: approximately 5% of the health budget is used to cover renal replacement therapy. In Spain, the "estimated prevalence" of CKD is 10% and I supposed to increase to 18% in 2040 and 24% in 2100. However, the "real prevalence" of CKD in Spain is unknown since the few population studies available have discrepant data, making impossible to devise strategies for early prevention. This is probably due to the silent nature of CKD, which symptoms go unnoticed for years, until progress to more advanced stages. Also, the unreliability of classic markers of kidney dysfunction, such as serum creatinine and the estimation by formulas, which present a mean error of ±30% with respect to the measured renal function, adds another factor of uncertainty. The population studies available rely on the estimation of renal function which makes them not fully reliable.
We aimed to develop a population-based study in the region of Mulagua, in the towns of Agulo and Hermigua, Canary Islands, Spain. We will analyze a large group of adults subjects who will undergo the plasma clearance of iohexol with dried blood spots (iohexol-DBS) to measure GFR.
Specific aims: To evaluate (1) the real prevalence of CKD and its stages using measured GFR; (2) the prevalence of occult renal disease (ORD) i.e. GFR <60 ml/min + serum creatinine in the normal range and estimated GFR >60 ml/min with or without albuminuria; (3) the error of formulas in estimating CKD and its stages; (4) the association of classic risk factors with CKD (hypertension, overweight-obesity, diabetes, dyslipidemia); (5) the prevalence of CKD by age ranges; (6) gender differences in the prevalence of CKD; (7) establish a baseline group for prospective studies.
Method
Cross-sectional study. Inclusion criteria: 1. Age over 18 years; 2. Ambulatory status; 3. Clinical stability. Exclusion criteria: 1. allergy to iodinated contrasts; 2. Inability to understand the protocol; 3. Pregnancy; 4. Active cancer. Measured GFR: All patients will undergo plasma clearance of iohexol by dried blood spot analysis (iohexol-DBS). Estimated GFR by formulas in the baseline serum sample, creatinine and cystatin-C based formulas. Clinical variables: biochemistry analysis, albumin/creatinine ratio, demographic data (date of birth, sex, race), anthropometric data (weight, height, abdominal circumference, BMI, blood pressure), tobacco and alcohol consumption, underlying disease (if any), treatments received (if any) Surveys: dietary adherence, exercise and sedentary lifestyle and socio-economic. Serum/plasma/urine/DNA banks: the study presented in this project is cross-sectional and will be the basis for different prospective studies creating nested cohorts in which the association between variables in different subgroups will be studied.
Sample size and calculation
The main objective of our study at this early stage is to assess the prevalence of CKD in a representative population of the Spanish population using a precise and accurate method (iohexol-DBS). To do this, we have calculated the sample size as follows: Spanish population (47,435,537), with a confidence level (1-alpha) of 95%, a precision of 1.6%, an expected proportion of CKD (10%), the sample size should be 1352, but considering losses of 15%, the total sample to observe 10% of CKD with this level of precision would be 1576. If losses of 10% are considered, the total sample would be 1501. In principle, this is our study population (n = 1576). Ad-interim studies will be carried out to analyse partial prevalence of CKD and to see the need to increase the sample size. The population of the two towns is sufficient to cover these figures. The sample size is in line with the Renal Iohexol Clearance Survey in Tromsø 6 (RENIS-T6) study where the authors studied kidney function in 1621 inhabitants, a representative sample of middle-aged people from the general Norwegian population.

title: #2459 Risk score for onset of kidney failure in patients with chronic kidney disease
authors: Michele Provenzano; Lilio Hu; Roberta Arena; Rosita Greco; Roberto Minutolo; Giulia Capitoli; Tye Sok Cin; Tamas Szili-Torok; Chiara Ruotolo; Martin H de Borst; Gianluigi Zaza; Luca De Nicola
abstract:
Background and Aims
Nephrology is the reference of care for patients with overt chronic kidney disease (CKD). Optimization of stratification of the risk of kidney failure (KF) is therefore essential for proper management of CKD in renal clinics.
Method
We analyzed data from a prospective observational study involving 3957 non-dialysis-dependent CKD (ND-CKD) patients followed in renal clinics for at least six months. A stepwise selection of predictors was conducted to develop a risk prediction model.
Results
Patients who developed KF were younger (61.3 vs. 68 years, P < 0.001), had higher systolic blood pressure (142 vs. 139 mmHg, P = 0.001), higher proteinuria (1.2 vs. 0.3 g/24 h, P < 0.001), lower eGFR (21.3 vs. 35.5 mL/min, P < 0.001), and less frequent use of RAAS inhibitors (68.2% vs. 73.3%, P = 0.003). The 3-year KF risk prediction model included 10 key variables: age, gender, systolic blood pressure, eGFR, 24-hour urine protein, hemoglobin, serum calcium and phosphate, cardiovascular disease (CVD), and RAAS inhibitor use at baseline. The model demonstrated good discrimination, with a C-index of 0.85 (95% CI 0.83–0.87).

title: #2535 Osteoactivin levels are correlated with eGFR and proteinuria in diabetic kidney disease
authors: Won Kim; Hyeongwan Kim
abstract:
Background and Aims
The molecular mechanisms underlying chronic kidney disease (CKD) are gradually being discovered, and several biomarkers that can be used clinically are being developed. However, few studies have reported a correlation between osteoactivin levels and kidney function changes in patients with diabetic CKD. This study investigated the changes in the serum and urine concentrations of osteoactivin according to the stage of diabetic CKD and investigated their potential use as biomarkers.
Method
Thirty-three patients with diabetic CKD and seven control patients were included in this observational study. Patients with CKD were divided based on CKD stage (stages 3–4 and stage 5). The serum and urine osteoactivin levels and clinical parameters such as eGFR and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of each group were evaluated. The relationships between these factors and other biomarkers including urine placental growth factor (PlGF), serum platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF)-C and urine PDGF-C, serum fatty acid-binding protein (FABP)4, and urine FABP4 in diabetic CKD were determined.
Results
Serum and urine osteoactivin levels were negatively correlated with estimated glomerular filtration rate (P < .001, r = −.827; P < .001, r = −.576, respectively) and positively correlated with serum creatinine. The serum and urinary osteoactivin concentration was higher in patients with stage 3–4 CKD (P = .012) and patients with stage 5 CKD (P < .001) than in control patients. Serum and urine osteoactivin levels were positively correlated with the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (P = .009, r = .430; P < .001, r = .579, respectively). Serum and urine osteoactivin levels are positively correlated. The area under the curve (AUC) for serum and urine osteoactivin was 1.00 and .896 (95% confidence interval: 1.00–1.00, P < .001; 95% confidence interval: .775–1.017; P < .001, respectively). Serum osteoactivin levels are correlated with urine PlGF, serum PDGF-C and urine PDGF-C, serum FABP4, and urine FABP4 levels. title: #2740 Metabolomic shifts in advanced CKD patients starting hemodialysis
authors: Maria Peris-Fernandez; Marta Isabel Roca-Marugán; Iris Viejo-Boyano; Amparo Soldevila-Orient; Ramon Devesa Such; Pilar Sánchez-Pérez; Julio Hernandez Jaras
abstract:
Background and Aims
Uremia, caused by reduced kidney function, leads to metabolic waste accumulation, contributing to symptoms like fatigue and nausea and increasing mortality in advanced CKD. Despite advances in dialysis and therapies such as high-dose hemodiafiltration, mortality remains high due to insufficient removal of uremic toxins. These toxins are inadequately cleared by dialysis compared to native kidney function, partly due to limited solute distribution volume and reabsorption mechanisms in healthy kidneys. Recent metabolomics studies have identified metabolic changes linked to dialysis outcomes, but gaps remain in understanding these shifts during dialysis initiation. This study employs semi-targeted metabolomics to quantify metabolomic changes over one year in patients initiating hemodialysis, providing insights for personalized treatment.
Method
This longitudinal observational study enrolled stage 5 CKD patients starting hemodialysis at Hospital La Fe. Blood samples were collected at baseline (pre-first session) and one year later (pre- and post-dialysis). Samples underwent protein precipitation and semi-targeted analysis using UPLC-QToF-MS. Data were processed with MAVEN software, normalized, and analyzed via univariate and multivariate approaches, including PCA and pathway enrichment analysis. Quality control ensured reproducibility. Metabolite changes were identified based on statistical significance (P < 0.01) and clinical relevance.
Results
The metabolomic analysis revealed significant changes in polar metabolites across different stages of hemodialysis. Between baseline and post-dialysis samples, 78 metabolites were significantly altered, with 75 showing decreased levels post-dialysis. Notable reductions included linoleic acid (VIP: 7.73), and 3-indoxyl sulfate (VIP: 3.53) (Fig. 1) At the one-year mark, pre- and post-dialysis comparisons identified 85 significantly altered metabolites, with all showing decreased levels post-dialysis. Key metabolites included glucose (VIP: 1.92), lactate (VIP: 2.46), and pyruvate (VIP: 3.10).
Multivariate analysis validated these findings, with OPLS-DA models confirming distinct metabolic profiles between baseline and post-dialysis, as well as pre- and post-dialysis groups. Pathway enrichment analysis highlighted alterations in amino acid metabolism, energy production, and uremic toxin pathways for baseline vs. post-dialysis samples, with most pathways showing reduced activity post-dialysis. Significant pathways included glutathione metabolism (impact: 0.32) and alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolism (impact: 0.24).
For pre- vs. post-dialysis comparisons, affected pathways included fatty acid metabolism, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, and branched-chain amino acid metabolism, reflecting a decrease in energy-related metabolites.
Conclusion
Our findings reveal significant metabolomic changes in advanced CKD patients after initiating hemodiafiltration. Metabolites such as linoleic acid and 3-indoxyl sulfate showed marked differences between baseline and post-dialysis sessions, highlighting key alterations in metabolic pathways. Pathway enrichment analyses identified biologically significant disruptions, including lipid metabolism and amino acid pathways, which are implicated in uremia-related complications. These results underscore the potential of semi-targeted metabolomics to enhance our understanding of metabolic shifts during dialysis.

title: #3838 Hungry bone syndrome (HBS) as an outcome of parathyroidectomy as a treatment of hyperparathyroidism in a third level hospital in a medium-income country
authors: Nicte Alaide Ramos García; Carolina Gonzalez-Fuentes; Kren Hopf Estandia; Mario Eduardo Alamilla Sanchez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyperparathyroidism is a common disorder of mineral metabolism that is due to excessive secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) from one or more of the four parathyroid glands. It can be classified as primary, secondary and tertiary. In end stage renal disease (ESRD) the definitive treatment in severe disease is parathyroidectomy. Hungry bone syndrome (HBS) is one complication after the surgery, some risk factors to develop this condition are the levels of PTH, alkaline phosphate (AP), hypocalcemia and remove of all glands.
Method
Retrospective cohort study with information (January 2023 and January 2024) in a third level hospital “Centro Médico Nacional 20 de Noviembre”. The objective was to describe and analyze the incidence of HBS on patients with hyperparathyroidism primary, secondary and tertiary treated with parathyroidectomy. We made a Principal Component Analysis (PCA), to observe the factors that made more impact on HBS.
Results
51 cases were included. There were 16 patients with primary, 29 patients with secondary and 5 with tertiary hyperparathyroidism. Patients with ESRD with secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism were mainly in hemodialysis (71%) as Kidney Replacement Therapy (n = 25). The mean value of PTH before surgery was 728 pg/ml among all patients. 80% patients (n = 41) have AP >100 mg/dl as a parameter of high bone replacement and the mean value was 242 U/L. 30% patients (n = 15) develop hungry bone syndrome. 86% of patients (n = 13) that developed HBS have 3½ surgery. We made a PCA we observed that the principal components that predict to developed HBS in our population were the levels of AP and PTH and the surgery 3½ and patients have more risk if they have the three of them together.
Conclusion
In our population 30% of patients develop HBS. The principal components observed that predict the developed HBS in our population were AP, PTH and the surgery 3½ and patients have more risk to develop HBS if they have the three of them together. The PCA could be a tool that will allow us in the future to generate a risk scale for HBS.

title: #3879 The role of a Mediterranean-like controlled protein diet (MCPD) in the conservative management of kidney disease in uro-oncological patients
authors: Arianna Bettiga; Andrea Angioi; Fabiana Selvaggi; Michela Passera; Francesco Fiorio; Alberto Briganti; Andrea Salonia; Francesco Montorsi; Antonello Pani; Giuseppe Rosiello; Umberto Capitanio; Francesco Trevisani
abstract:
Background and Aims
The incidence of chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 3 and beyond in patients with cancer is present between 12 and 25%, depending on the type of cancer or chemotherapy administered to the patient. While well-defined guidelines with varying levels of supporting evidence exist for patients with CKD and for patients with cancer without CKD, there is no precise nutritional management when considering patients with both CKD and cancer and, consequently, no shared clinical strategy is currently applied in clinical practice. This study aimed to confirm our previously published data (doi: 10.3390/nu14235193) regarding the safety and efficacy of a MCPD in a consecutive cohort of onconephrological patients evaluated over a longer (3 years) and intensive follow-up.
Method
We retrospectively identified 186 patients, enrolled at our tertiary-care institution from 2019 and 2024, with a history of urological malignancies in conservative management for CKD followed by multidisciplinary team including a nephrologist and nutritionist, among others. Exclusion criteria: age (<18 years old), malnutritional screening tool (MST ≥3), urological cancer aggressiveness (metastatic process), informed consent (not signed). All patients underwent an initial nutritional evaluation and received a MCPD with a defined protein (0.7–1.0 g/kg/die), phosphorus (<1 g/die) and salt (<5 g/die) content, tailored on the presence or not of metabolic alterations (hyperazotemia, metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia…) and on the specific stage of CKD. The resting energy expenditure was determined using Mifflin-St Jeor for obese patients and the Harris-Benedict equation for all the others. A correction coefficient of 1.4–1.6 was used for adult patients performing light physical activity. CKD stages were defined using estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) with CKD-EPI formula (2021). In order to assess the patients’ nutritional status, anthropometric measurements (weight, height, waist and hip circumference) and bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) were performed. The following data on patients’ body composition were collected: phase angle (PA), body cellular mass (BCM %), extracellular water (ECW)/intracellular water (ICW) ratio, total body water (TBW%), fat mass (FM%), free fat mass (FFM%) and skeletal muscle index (SMI, kg/m²). Statistical analysis: Wilcoxon signed-rank test and the paired t-test. Data analysis: JMP®, Version 17 Pro. In all tests, a P < 0.05 was regarded as significant.
Results
Table 1 shows the baseline characteristics of the cohort studied. Table 2 shows anthropometric indices and parameters collected at pre- and post-dietary intervention for 108 patients who completed the nutritional follow-up. Our data showed that 60.7% of patients was overweight (with 1/3 of them being obese) at baseline; at the follow-up visits, a substantial improvement was observed in terms of BMI, of surrogate measurement of abdominal obesity (waist circumference) and FM%. Analysing the BIA parameters correlating with nutritional status of patients, we observed an overall improvement not only in PA and BCM% but also in SMI, which indicates advancement in the nutritional status of the patients. In terms of fluid balance, we observed an increase in TBW% and a decrease in ECW/ICW ratio, indicating an improvement in body fluids distribution between the intracellular and extracellular compartments, consisting of muscle cell mass and plasma and interstitial fluids respectively. Compared to anthropometric parameters, the nephrological scenario is more complex and characterized by an improvement of uremia, stable Cystatin C values and a non-statistically significant worsening of creatinine values and eGFR.
Conclusion
No significant negative changes have been noticed in any of the anthropometric parameters measured in the cohort of patients studied compared to baseline, suggesting that the application of a MCPD in uro-oncological patients affected by different grades of CKD is safe and could be relevant to ameliorate non only the nephrological scenario but above all the nutritional status resulting in a better quality of life.

title: #132 Exploring the Interactions between drugs and metabolic disturbances in CKD: an example with oral anticoagulants
authors: Touria Mernissi; Stéphane Jaisson; Pierre Spicher; Said Kamel; Anais Okwieka; Julien Demagny; Gabriel Choukroun; Solene Laville; Sandra Bodeau; Sophie Liabeuf
abstract:
Background and Aims
The metabolic disturbances associated with chronic kidney disease might alter drug distribution, decrease albumin drug binding, and thus increase the free (unbound) drug concentrations. Along with direct toxic effects on tissues, uremic toxins can affect the pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic activity of certain drugs. Vitamin K antagonists (VKA) are interesting candidates for the evaluation of potential interactions between uremic toxins and drugs. The primary objective of the present study was to investigate the association between free VKA concentrations and the decline in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Furthermore, we sought to determine whether this relationship was mediated by protein carbamylation (measured by homocitrulline levels) and/or the accumulation of protein-bound uremic toxins (PBUTs).
Method
In this prospective cross-sectional study, 389 adult patients treated with VKA were included between May 2021 and June 2023. For each patient, levels of free VKAs, total VKAs, homocitrulline and PBUTs were assayed using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. We used a linear regression model to explore the association between kidney function and free VKA levels and used conventional mediation analyses to determine whether the association between kidney function and free VKA levels was mediated (at least partly) by PBUTs and/or protein carbamylation.
Results
Of the 389 patients included, the median age [IQR] was 75 [66–83]. Patients with an eGFR <40 mL/min/1.73 m² or those on chronic hemodialysis had lower total VKA levels, higher free VKA levels and thus a higher of free/total VKA ratio than those with an eGFR ≥40 mL/min/1.73 m². Kidney function was independently associated with free VKA levels (β1 = 0.31 [0.19; 0.43], P < 0.001). Twenty percent [95% CI, 0.7%–34%] of the association between kidney function and free VKA levels was mediated by homocitrulline. This association was not mediated by PBUTs.
Conclusion
Our results showed that a decline in kidney function was associated with an elevation in the free drug fraction (taking VKAs as an example). This association was independent of blood albumin levels and appeared to be partly mediated by protein carbamylation.

title: #163 Tangential ultrasound-guided renal biopsy of native kidneys (KB): an innovative technique
authors: R Haridian Sosa Barrios; Cristina Riaza Ortiz; María Pilar Morán Magro; Víctor Miguel Burguera Vion; Irene Mínguez Toral; Milagros Fernandez Lucas; Maite Rivera
abstract:
Background and Aims
KB is the gold standard to diagnose renal diseases, but it has complications. In the conventional approach (CA) the needle approaches at 60-90º. The tangential approach (TA) is proposed as an alternative since it minimizes crossing the renal sinus (angle<60º) and vessels of larger caliber (Fig. 1).
Objective: demonstrate the non-inferiority of TA in native KB vs CA regarding diagnostic yield and complications.
Method
Retrospective single center study (May 2022-March 2024). Demographic data, KB and complications comparing CA vs TA were collected. The physician performing the KB chose one approach or the other according to the patient's anatomical characteristics and personal preferences.
Results
A total of 102 patients were biopsied, 65 (63.7%) male, mean age 54.18 ± 17.3 years, 51% hypertensive. Twenty-two patients were anticoagulated/anti-aggregated and 24 required intravenous desmopressin preKB.
Lower pole was biopsied in all cases, 86.3% left kidneys and only in one case both were biopsied. The mean number of passes was 2.5 (N.S.), obtaining a mean of 2 cylinders.
Cost-effectiveness of BR: Both diagnostic sample and cortical percentage obtained was statistically superior for AT, not so for the mean number of glomeruli obtained 18 ± 11 vs 19 ± 9 (P = 0.647).
Complications
There were no statistically significant differences regarding major or minor complications.
- Major: One patient required embolization and transfusion of blood products (CA).
- Minor: We found statistically significant difference in the rate of asymptomatic arterio-venous fistulae (P = 0.003), but not in minor hematoma or hematuria.
Conclusion
Native KB by TA is a novel technique. In our experience, TA showed higher diagnostic yield without increasing complications, probably because large vessels are avoided during the procedure. We propose this alternative approach in selected cases, but larger prospective studies are needed.

title: #361 A southeast London primary care allied health professional led point-of-care kidney clinic to pharmacologically optimise people with chronic kidney disease (protect kidney)
authors: Rouvick Gama; Kathryn Griffiths; Nathan Beencke; Kathryn Dalrymple; Stephanie Mitchell; Prema Ravi; Joseph Mayhew; Sharlene Greenwood; Kate Bramham
abstract:
Background and Aims
A new generation of treatments for chronic kidney disease (CKD) have potential to significantly improve cardiovascular and renal outcomes. However, barriers to implementation include renal function monitoring after renin-angiotensin-aldosterone-system inhibitors (RAASi) initiation and dose changes as well as lack of resources in primary care.
This study aims to co-develop and evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of a pilot protocolled point-of-care (POC) kidney clinic, for RAASi and sodium-glucose-cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) optimisation in primary care.
Method
This quality improvement project (QIP), was conducted in three South London GP practices, co-developed with patient and public involvement and Clinical Effectiveness Southeast London.
A red-amber-green (RAG) protocol guiding rapid RAASi up-titration was developed based on local and national guidelines. POC potassium and creatinine RAG thresholds were validated against the reference laboratory.
Inclusion criteria: (1) adults; (2) eGFR 30–75 mL/min/1.73 m2 ; (3) urine albumin:creatinine ratio (uACR) ≥3 (if diabetic) or ≥22.6 mg/mmol (non-diabetic).
Exclusion criteria: (1) RAASi/SGLT2i contra-indication; (2) baseline potassium >5.0 mmol/L; (3) taking insulin (4) eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2; (5) patients under nephrology services.
Blood pressure and blood (capillary or venous) tests were performed in each clinic visit and analysed using the POC Epoc Blood Analysis System (Siemens Healthineers). Medication adjustments were based on RAG protocol outcomes.
Primary outcome was recruitment number. Secondary outcomes were patients who were pharmacologically optimised (maximum tolerated RAASi with SGLT2i), completed the pathway and numbers who did not attend (DNA); POC test success rates, adverse events, medication dose changes and change over time in blood pressure, creatinine, eGFR and potassium were also recorded. Patient acceptability was assessed using the Likert Scale for an adapted validated questionnaire (PSQ-18).
Results
After exclusions, 25/48 (52.1%) suitably identified patients agreed to participate (Fig. 1). Mean age was 64.5 ± 9.3 years and 17 were male (68%). Baseline characteristics are summarised in Table 1. There were 8 (14.8%) DNA's from 54 clinic appointments; mean duration between appointments were 25 ± 19 days; 23/25 (92%) patients completed the pathway; 20/25 (80%) were optimised. Thirty-nine (85%) protocol outcomes were green, 7 (15%) amber and none red, resulting in 40 medication changes (RAASi = 20; SGLT2i = 20). Following RAASi uptitration, there were small increases in renal biochemistry between visits (eGFR 2.82 ± 11.16 mL/min/1.73 m2; potassium 0.04 ± 0.29 mmol/L).
The majority of the samples were capillary (43/44; 97.7%). POC tests were successful from 44/57 (77.2%) attempts. One patient developed visible haematuria after starting SGLT2i. There were no major adverse events.
Overall, 92% (12/13) questionnaire respondents were ‘very satisfied’ with their clinic experience and 77% (10/13) were ‘very comfortable’ with finger-prick testing. The majority indicated they would prefer an advanced nurse practitioner (n = 10) or pharmacist (n = 9) for future pathways.
Conclusion
Patient recruitment numbers were modest, suggesting larger scale (e.g. primary care network) or wider screening of unidentified CKD would be required. The POC testing was successful (77.2%) with most patients becoming optimised and reporting a positive experience.
Scale up of the clinic (across Southeast London) with a health economic evaluation is underway to assess cost effectiveness and long-term sustainability.

title: #937 Goals of frail older people living with chronic kidney disease
authors: Benignus Logan; Kristiana Ludlow; Elaine M Pascoe; Andrea Viecelli; David W Johnson; Carmel Hawley; Laura E Hickey; Charani Kiriwandeniya; Misa Matsuyama; Allison Jaure; Ruth E Hubbard
abstract:
Background and Aims
Frail older adults with chronic kidney disease (CKD) have complex care needs, and their priorities may differ from those assumed by healthcare providers. Understanding their goals is crucial to delivering person-centred care. This study aimed to identify and categorise the goals of this population, and determine any association with participant's frailty status, quality of life, and CKD stage.
Method
We report the goals of frail older people living with moderate to severe CKD enrolled as participants in the GOAL trial, a cluster-randomised controlled trial assessing the effectiveness of comprehensive geriatric assessment. This study employs a mixed-methods approach, utilising triangulation design and a data transformation model. Participants set goals by Goal Attainment Scaling. Deductive content analysis was undertaken, aided by a pre-specified matrix (physical health; psychological health; function; planning; social engagement). Descriptive statistics assessed relationships between goals and participant characteristics.
Results
The 224 participants (mean age 77 [±6.7]; 56% male; 84% white/European; median FI 0.39 [IQR: 0.33–0.47]) set 408 goals in the categories of function; physical health; social engagement and leisure; psychological health; and future readiness. Most participants set one or two goals (n = 183, 82%). They were most frequently set in the function (n = 172, 42%), physical health (n = 86, 21%), and social engagement and leisure (n = 79, 19%) domains. The number and nature of set goals were similar across participant frailty status, quality of life (EQ-5D-5L) scores or CKD stage.
Conclusion
Frail older adults with CKD most frequently focus their goals on function, physical health, and social engagement and leisure. These goals did not vary by participants’ frailty status or CKD stage. This study's findings can guide healthcare professionals in ensuring management plans consider these identified priorities. Geriatricians may have a role in managing this population given the commonality of these goals with those of older people more generally.

title: #1033 A Study of hidden germs and superbugs in CKD patients
authors: Hardik Shah; Kriya Shah; Bahaar Athavale
abstract:
Background and Aims
Emergence of newer pathogens with multi drug resistance causing infections needing hospitalisation and causing deaths has wreaked havoc in CKD patients. Ubiquitous presence of these organisms in disinfectant solutions, surfaces and water in hospital settings can pose a hidden danger that is often overlooked. This prospective observational study attempts to identify few such pathogens, their clinical manifestations and the antimicrobial resistance pattern.
Method
A prospective analysis of positive body fluid cultures of CKD patients hospitalised from Jan 2023 to Dec 2024 for infection related ailments was done.
Results
66/329 (20%) positive body fluid cultures (blood: 49, BAL: 7, sputum: 4, urine: 4, pleural fluid: 1, wound swab: 1) showed uncommon organisms.
Of these, 15/66 had negative blood culture from outside lab prior to hospitalization.45/66 had dialysis access infections (Tunnelled catheter: 38, non-tunnelled catheter: 5, CAPD catheter: 2). 85% organisms showed resistance to higher antibiotics including third generation cephalosporins and carbapenems.
Conclusion
Active surveillance and high index of clinical suspicion for identification of these hidden germs who have already become superbugs is the need of the hour. Effective preventive strategies and strict implementation of infection control policies is essential in reducing morbidity and mortality in CKD patients.

title: #1287 Changes in non-invasive bone specific biomarkers after 12 months of self-administered exercise in patients with chronic kidney disease: sub study of RENEXC—a randomized controlled trial
authors: Vaida Petrauskiene; Matthias Hellberg; Philippa Svensson; Yunan Zhou; Naomi Clyne
abstract:
Background and Aims
Osteoporosis and fractures are common in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Exercise is recommended in the general population to decrease bone loss. Bone specific biomarkers have been increasingly used in clinical management of osteoporosis. However, research is scarce on the effects of exercise training on bone quality and bone specific biomarkers, reflecting bone remodulation in patients with CKD.
Bone turnover markers released during the bone remodelling cycle reflecting bone remodelling rate need to be selected with care due to decreased renal excretion in CKD.
Monomeric fragments of PINP is a reference marker of bone formation, but as it accumulates in CKD it is necessary to use specific assays for the intact, trimeric form.
Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase isoform 5b is released from osteoclasts and considered a highly specific marker of bone resorption.
The aim of the study was to evaluate the effects of 12 months of self-administered exercise on non-invasive bone specific biomarkers reflecting both bone formation and bone resorption in patients with chronic kidney disease stages 3–5 not on kidney replacement therapy.
Method
In this single centre, randomized controlled trial 151 patients were allotted to 60 minutes of endurance training in combination with 90 minutes of either balance or strength training. The exercise was prescribed and monitored by a physiotherapist and performed at home or at a gym.
A marker of bone formation: trimeric procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide (intact PINP; assay range 2–4600 µg/L) and a marker of bone resorption: tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase isoform 5b (TRAP5b; assay range 0.9–56 U/L) were measured at the beginning of the study (T0) and after 12 months of exercise (T12) with the ImmunoDiagnostic Systems iSYS instrument.
Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS for Windows 24. Statistical significance was assessed using Mann–Whitney or Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank tests. Values are given as median [min-max]. A p-value <0.05 was accepted as the level of significance.
Results
112 patients completed the study and blood samples were obtained from 101 (73 men, 28 women; age 71 [23–87] years, measured GFR 20 [10–48] ml/min per 1.73 m2), 11 blood samples were missing. The strength group comprised 49 patients (37 men, 12 women) and the balance group 52 (36 men, 16 women).
The strength group showed a tendency to increase intact PINP (T0: 71.8 [21.8–169.5] and T12:79.7 [26.8–174.2], P = 0.20) and decrease TRAP5b (T0: 2.2 [0.9–7.1] and T12: 1.9 [0.9–4.7], P = 0.26). The balance group showed a non-significant decrease in intact PINP value (T0: 80.8 [23.8–413.6] and T12: 63.8 [19.1–256.9], P = 0.15) and no change in TRAP5b (T0: 1.60 [0.9–9.4] and T12: 1.7 [0.9–7.4], P = 0.16).
Analyses according to sex showed no significant changes of either bone specific biomarker in the strength group. In the balance group women showed unchanged intact PINP and a significant decrease in TRAP5b (T0: 2.2 [0.9–9.4] to T12: 1.5 [0.9–2.8], P = 0.03).
Conclusion
Bone specific biomarkers of bone formation and bone resorption were unchanged in both the strength and balance groups, respectively, after 12 months of self-administered exercise. Considering that bone resorption is progressive in patients with CKD 3–5, a stabilising of biomarkers for bone formation and bone resorption could infer a positive effect of exercise.
Interestingly, women in the balance group showed a significant decrease of TRAP5b, a marker of bone resorption, after 12 months of self-administered exercise, indicating that balance training in combination with endurance training could have a positive effect on moderating bone resorption in women with CKD 3 to 5. Further research is needed to ascertain whether changes in bone specific biomarkers due to exercise can be associated with positive changes in bone remodelling in patients with CKD.

title: #1979 The treatment with β-blockers reduced IL-6 and MMP-2/TIMP-2 system in patients with chronic kidney disease on conservative treatment
authors: Dariusz Pawlak; Marta Zieminska; Anna Krupa; Magdalena Kopanko; Magdalena Zabludowska; Beata Sieklucka; Katarzyna Sokolowska; Krystyna Pawlak
abstract:
Background and Aims
The prevalence of hypertension is high among patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), with approximately 60% of the population requiring treatment with three or more antihypertensive drugs. Early diagnosis and appropriate treatment of hypertension play a central role in CKD management, as achieving optimal blood pressure (BP) is associated with reduced renal and cardiovascular risk in this population. Although β-adrenoceptor antagonists (β-blockers) are not recommended as first-line therapy for hypertension in CKD, they may be beneficial for patients with specific indications. Beyond their antihypertensive effects, treatment with certain β-blockers has been associated with reduced systemic inflammation and enhanced antioxidative effects, which could explain their therapeutic benefits in the cardiovascular system. This study aimed to determine whether the use of β-blockers affects metalloproteinase 2 (MMP-2) and its tissue inhibitor (TIMP-2) in patients with CKD undergoing conservative treatment.
Method
Circulating levels of the MMP-2/TIMP-2 system, proinflammatory cytokines (tumor necrosis factor-alpha [TNF-α] and interleukin-6 [IL-6]), and the oxidative stress marker Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase (Cu/Zn SOD) were measured using ELISA with commercially available standard kits. The study included 23 CKD patients treated with β-blockers [β-blockers (+)], 27 CKD patients not receiving β-blockers [β-blockers (−)], and 12 healthy volunteers matched for gender and age with the CKD patients (controls). Statistical analyses were performed using Statistica v. 13 software (StatSoft, Tulsa, Oklahoma, United States), and graphical representations of the results were prepared using GraphPad Prism 6 (GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, USA).
Results
The β-blockers (+) and β-blockers (−) groups were comparable in terms of age, gender, BP values, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), and CKD stage. There were no significant differences in hematological and biochemical parameters or CKD etiology between the two patient groups. Other classes of antihypertensive drugs were prescribed with similar frequency in both groups. Median levels of MMP-2 and TIMP-2 in the entire CKD group were similar to those observed in the controls. However, the use of β-blockers was significantly associated with lower MMP-2 (P < 0.01) and TIMP-2 (P < 0.05) concentrations in CKD patients. No relationship was observed between the MMP-2/TIMP-2 system and the use of other antihypertensive drug classes. The levels of MMP-2 (P < 0.01), TIMP-2 (P < 0.05), and IL-6 (P < 0.05) were significantly lower in the β-blockers (+) group compared to the β-blockers (−) group, while TNF-α and Cu/Zn SOD concentrations were not affected by β-blocker use. A strong, independent association between MMP-2 and TIMP-2 was observed in both patient groups (P < 0.001 for both). The MMP-2/TIMP-2 ratio, reflecting an imbalance between MMP-2 and its endogenous inhibitor, was increased in both β-blockers (+) and β-blockers (−) groups compared to controls (P < 0.05 and P < 0.001, respectively). This parameter was higher in the β-blockers (−) group than in the β-blockers (+) group (P < 0.05). In the β-blockers (+) group, MMP-2 levels were independently associated with inflammatory markers, whereas in the β-blockers (−) group, alterations in the MMP-2/TIMP-2 system were independently associated with oxidative stress markers and CKD etiology.
Conclusion
This study demonstrates that the use of β-blockers is associated with a reduction in IL-6 and the MMP-2/TIMP-2 system in CKD patients. Given that the MMP-2/TIMP-2 system contributes to the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis, cardiovascular disease, and CKD progression, our findings suggest a pharmacological rationale for using β-blockers in clinical practice to reduce inflammation and abnormal vascular remodeling, thereby potentially lowering the risk of cardiovascular events in CKD patients.

title: #2189 Assessment and analysis of knowledge on hemodialysis in patients with stage 5 chronic kidney disease
authors: Khadija Harmak
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a major public health issue due to its severity, silent progression, associated constraints, and high cost. In its terminal stage, kidney function becomes irreversibly impaired, necessitating renal replacement therapy such as dialysis or kidney transplantation. Some CKD patients develop particular perceptions of hemodialysis, often associating it with a sense of inevitability. However, hemodialysis remains one of the essential treatments for end-stage renal failure, enabling many patients to survive this potentially fatal condition. To evaluate the general knowledge of patients with stage 5 CKD regarding hemodialysis, as well as their psychological perceptions, particularly their emotional response to the treatment. The goal is to develop an awareness program aimed at improving understanding and adherence to renal replacement therapy.
Method
We conducted a cross-sectional descriptive study using a questionnaire administered to patients being followed for CKD at the Ibn Rochd University Hospital Center (CHU) in Casablanca. The study was carried out over one year, from November 2023 to October 2024. The surveys were conducted in the consultation pavilion 28 and the nephrology department of CHU Ibn Rochd. We included patients diagnosed with stage 5 CKD. Participation in the study was voluntary and anonymous, with informed consent obtained from participants after they were fully briefed on the study's objectives.
Results
Over the one-year period, 102 patients with stage 5 CKD participated in the study by completing the questionnaire, which was developed in collaboration with a psychiatrist, following informed consent. The patients' ages ranged from 18 to 81 years, with a mean age of 47 ± 15 years and a median age of 48 years. A slight female predominance was observed, with a male-to-female ratio of 0.76. Of the participants, 80 lived in urban areas. The educational levels varied: 22 patients had never attended school, while 21 had higher education. The majority of patients were unemployed, representing 57 individuals. In terms of marital status, 47 patients were married, 30 were single, and 25 were divorced. The underlying nephropathy responsible for CKD remained undetermined in 44 patients, was glomerular in 36 patients, and vascular in 22 patients.
