title: #1314 Nutritional status: the silent risk of falls in hemodialysis patients
authors: Helena Salem; Myriam Dabily; Maria Jose Demirdjian; Marianne Moussallem; Najat Joubran; Valerie Hage
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hemodialysis patients are at an increased risk of falls, a significant health concern that can lead to serious injuries and reduced quality of life. Several factors contribute to this elevated risk including impaired balance, muscle weakness, and cognitive dysfunction. Nutritional status is increasingly being recognized as a critical factor influencing fall risk in this population. Malnutrition, protein-energy wasting, and micronutrient deficiencies are prevalent in haemodialysis population and can exacerbate their existing fall risk factors. This study will assess the complex interplay between nutritional status and fall risk in the hemodialysis population, exploring the possible underlying mechanisms. It will also investigate other potential risk factors of fall in this population.
Method
This is a prospective, single centre study, of patients on dialysis for at least 3 months, aged over 18. The study included a total of 68 patients. The patients were followed up for a period of 2 years and were tracked for the occurrence of fall either at home or at our institution. The nutritional status was assessed biannually by the clinical dieticians of the centre. Protein–energy wasting (PEW) was evaluated with anthropometric measurements, including Body Mass Index (BMI) and weight changes over 3 and 6 months. Functional muscle assessment included handgrip strength. It was also supported by a Nutrition Focused Physical Exam (NFPE) to evaluate the muscle loss severity. Malnutrition was diagnosed using the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition (GLIM) criteria; incorporating weight loss, dietary intake, and muscle mass. Serum albumin levels were recorded at each evaluation. We also collected data from the patient's files that included baseline characteristics, demographic parameters, biochemical markers, hemodialysis parameters, presence of orthostatic hypotension or vision problems and anti-hypertensive medications. We also recorded the ambulatory status of the patient and their mean of transportation to the centre (alone/accompanied). Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics software, version 22.0. Student's t-test, the Mann-Whitney U test, and chi-square tests were used at the bivariate level, and logistic regressions were done for multivariate analysis.
Results
The studied population consisted of 68 patients. The mean age (±SD) was 66.5 ± 13.3 years. The mean BMI was 26 ± 5.65 kg/m2. A total of 48.5 % of the patients were female. 38.2% of the patients experienced fall, and of these 46% had fallen once, 46% had fallen twice and 8% had fallen three times.
In the bivariate analysis the risk of fall was significantly associated with the age of the patients (P = 0.003), the age at onset of dialysis (P = 0.009), serum albumin levels (P < 0.001) and potassium levels (P = 0.001), muscle loss severity (NFPE) (P = 0.057), the mode of transportation (P = 0.019), the ambulation status (P = 0.001) and the presence of orthostatic hypotension (P = 0.008).
Logistic regression analyses’ results showed that muscle loss severity (NFPE) (P = 0.020), albumin levels (P = 0.015), potassium levels (P = 0.53), ambulation status (P = 0.001) and orthostatic hypotension (P = 0.035) were significantly associated with an increased risk of fall.
Conclusion
Our study revealed a significant contribution of nutritional compromise to fall risks in hemodialysis patients. It showed that the severity of muscle loss along with lower levels of serum albumin and potassium are strongly associated with falls. Additionally, assisted/dependent ambulation and orthostatic hypotension were independently associated with a higher incidence of falls. These findings provide insight into the risk factors associated with falls enabling the development of targeted fall prevention strategies. Further interventional studies are warranted to investigate the effect of nutritional interventions in reducing fall risk in this patient group. title: #1903 The dialysis quality parameters as predictors of symptom burden in cluster analysis
authors: Konstantin Vishnevskii; Karim Al-Barbari; Alexander Zemchenkov; Aleksander Rumyantsev
abstract:
Background and Aims
Achieving better outcomes from dialysis treatment is hampered by limited monitoring of important parameters and a lack of consensus on minimum and optimal standards for safety, the quality of dialysis, and its organization. This hinders comparative analysis of interventions. Researchers have exhausted opportunities to improve outcomes through enhanced diffusion and convective transfer as well as correction of anemia. They are now turning to evaluating patient-reported outcomes and methods for improving them.
Method
Symptoms were assessed using the Dialysis Symptom Index (DSI). There were 30 symptoms, each with a score ranging from 1 to 5 (“not bothering at all” to “very bothering”). The dialysis program included routine monitoring every month or quarter for indicators of uremic syndrome correction, bioimpedance assessment, degree of protein energy deficiency, and sarcopenia.
Results
The study included 137 patients aged 55 ± 15 years from one center, 41% of whom were women. The most frequent primary kidney diseases were: glomerulonephritis (27%), diabetes (18%), hypertension and vascular nephropathy (14%), interstitial diseases (13%), and polycystic disease (10%). The dialysis schedule was 4–4.5 hours trice a week. The average symptom score was 50 ± 15 (Me; Q1–Q3: 50, 37–60, ranging from 30 [no symptoms] to 109). A direct relationship was found between the severity and prevalence of symptoms (R² = 0.815). The most common symptoms were Feeling tired (66%), Trouble falling asleep (56%), Trouble staying asleep (52%), Restress legs (50%), Numbness (50%) Worrying (50%), whereas gastrointestinal symptoms were reported in less than 30% of cases (Vomiting (9%], Constipation (16%], Nausea (20%), Diarrhea (26%] and decreased appetite [29%]).
Some symptoms were associated with a number of patient characteristics and dialysis parameters. Some other symptoms showed almost no association. For example, KRT duration (+1 year) was directly related to severity of feeling tired (+0.49 out of 5 points of full range) and dry skin (+0.05), and inversely—with a feeling of irritable (−0.06). Men have less pronounced manifestations of trouble staying asleep (−0.91), muscle soreness (−0.62), feelings of irritable (−0.61), and feelings sad (−0.54), dry skin (−0. 59), worrying (−0.67) is also less common in men. higher hemoglobin (+1 g/dl) was associated with lower severity of RLS (−0.13), headache (−0.12), decreased interest in sex (−0.14), and difficulty becoming sexually aroused (−0.16), and feeling anxious (−0.16). The higher the UF per session (+1 liter), the more pronounced Feeling tired (+0.22), RLS (+0.18), Dry skin (+0.22) and Chest pain (+0.13).
The overall DSI score in the multiple regression analysis was directly related to the severity of protein-energy wasting (+3.8 points/PEW-degree, (95% CI 0.5–7.0; P = 0.022), phosphate levels (+0.17 points/0.1 mM/L; (0.03–0.30; P = 0.017), and inversely—with hemoglobin level (−0.26 points per 1 g/dL; −0.49–(−0.03); P = 0.024), albumin (−0.18 points per 0.1 g/dL; −0.36–(−0.001); P = 0.047), grip strength (−0.17 points per 10 kg; −0.49–(−0.03); P = 0.024)
The overall assessment of symptoms was used to create clusters with a factor load >0.50. Four clusters of symptoms were identified, designated as mental health (Cronbach's α 0.65), bodily health (α = 0.69), sex (α = 0.89), gastrointestinal symptoms (α = 0.78), each of which was independently associated with 5–9 parameters characterizing patients and dialysis.
Table 1 shows the association of four symptom clusters with patient`s and dialysis treatment feature in multiple regression models. Dialysis adequacy parameters (targets: eKt/V > 1.44; ultrafiltration rate <12 ml/hour/kg), anemia correction (10< Hb <12 g/dl), MBD-CKD (phosphate <1.9 mmol/l, PTH <585 pg/ml), presumed depression (Beck Depression Inventory >6) as well as age and gender were included in initial models.
Conclusion
The study results provide directions for a potentially more effective cluster approach to the correction of symptoms, responding to recommendations for more patient-centered approach.

title: #2600 Dialysate leaks in peritoneal dialysis patients—a retrospective review
authors: Anandkumar Pari; Zain Ul Abideen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Peritoneal Dialysis (PD) is a cost-effective form of renal replacement therapy. Recent GIRFT suggests that at least 20% of patients should be on home renal replacement therapies. Home renal replacement therapies allow patients a better quality of life by allowing them to spend more time at home.
Infection-related complications, such as peritonitis and exit site infection, are common in PD patients. Non-infection-related complications, such as dialysate leaks, including pleuroperitoneal leaks and peri catheter leaks, are relatively uncommon but significantly impact technique survival. Dialysate leaks are a consequence of loss of peritoneal membrane integrity. Early leaks are classified as those occurring within 30 days of catheter insertion, and late leaks arise thereafter. The incidence of dialysate leaks in Peritoneal dialysis patients is somewhat more than 5% [1].
Method
We performed a retrospective review to determine the incidence of dialysate leaks in our PD patient population. Given the low incidence of the condition, we looked at several years of data. We analysed the data of patients who underwent PD catheter insertion in our hospital between 1 January 2019 and 31 October 2024. Out of 320 patients, 19 (5.9%) developed dialysate leaks.
Results
Of these 19 patients, 9 were male and 10 were female. Seven patients had pleural leaks, 8 had abdominal (inguinal-scrotal) leaks, and 4 had peri catheter leaks. All pleural and abdominal leaks were right-sided. Five patients had BMIs between 18.5 and 25, 9 between 25 to 30, and 5 had BMIs more than 30.Seven patients developed leaks within 1 month, 7 between 1 and 3 months, and five any time after 3 months. Of the seven dialysate leaks within 1 month of insertion, 5 were abdominal leaks, one was pleural, and 1 peri catheter leak. Of those who developed dialysate leaks nine patients had medical insertions, 4 had radiological insertions, and 6 had surgical insertions.
Conclusion
We did not find any statistically significant associations between dialysate leaks and BMI, previous abdominal surgery, type of PD catheter insertion, peritonitis or exit site infections, age, gender, or aetiology of kidney disease. 74% of the leaks happened within 3 months of starting dialysis. Retrospective studies looking at dialysate leaks are relatively scarce, given the uncommon occurrence of these complications in PD. title: #3587 Beyond the kidney: unconventional roles of indoxyl sulfate in modulating purinergic receptors, transporters, and cytokines in mouse aorta
authors: Jeferson Stabile; Isabela Hernandes; Raquel Dos Santos; Marcela Carneiro-Ramos; Cristina Furstenau
abstract:
Background and Aims
Indoxyl sulfate (IS) is a uremic toxin present in kidney diseases. It has hypertrophic effects on the heart, fibrotic effects on the kidney, and impairs the functioning of blood vessels through inflammatory processes. Purinergic signaling plays a role in the control of vascular tone and inflammatory processes. Chronic activation of purinergic receptors in the mouse aorta accelerates inflammation, which synergizes with the deleterious effects of IS. We evaluated the effects of IS on inflammatory and renal injury markers, P1 and P2 receptors, and ectonucleotidases.
Method
Fifty male C57BL/6 mice, 6 to 8 weeks old, weighing between 20 g and 28 g, were treated with saline solution (Control group-C, 21 days) and IS (intraperitoneal, 100 mg/kg/day) for 7 d, 14 d and 21 days. Total RNA was extracted from the aorta for cDNA synthesis and real-time PCR (qPCR). Serum samples were collected for renal marker analysis. Tibia was collected for morphometric analysis. Statistical analyses were performed using analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey's post hoc test. Data presented as mean ± standard error of the mean.
Results
No significant variations were found in body weight, morphometric parameters, serum urea, or genes related to the transport of IS and ROS production. Creatinine levels were decreased at 14 and 21 days (respectively for C, 14 d, 21 d: 0.74 mg/dL, 0.59 mg/dL, 0.44 mg/dL). There was a decrease in the expression of cytokine transcripts. For IL-6-C, 7 d, 14 d, 21 d: 1 ± 0.25, 0.15 ± 0.04, 0.13 ± 0.02, 0.28 ± 0.6; IL-1β-7 d, 21 d: 1 ± 0.23, 0.15 ± 0.03, 0.26 ± 0.05; TNF-α-C, 7 d, 14 d, 21 d: 1 ± 0.14, 0.55 ± 0.11, 0.23 ± 0.02, 0.50 ± 0.08; TGF-β-7 d, 21 d: 1.28 ± 0.16, 0.38 ± 0.15; IL-13-C, 7 d, 14 d: 1 ± 0.27, 0.10 ± 0.016, 0.17 ± 0.04, IL-10-C, 7 d, 14 d, 21 d: 1 ± 0.28, 0.08 ± 0.01, 0.05 ± 0.01, 0.11 ± 0.03. The P2 and the P1 receptors had their transcript levels decreased in the aorta of IS-treated animals. For P2X4-C, 7 d, 14 d, 21 d: 1 ± 0.10, 0.17 ± 0.02, 0.63 ± 0.04, 0.61 ± 0.07; P2Y6-C, 7 d, 14 d: 1 ± 0.11, 0.61 ± 0.07, 0.66 ± 0.04; A1-C, 7 d, 14 d, 21 d: 1 ± 0.3, 0.28 ± 0.06, 0.31 ± 0.03, 0.23 ± 0.04; A2a-C, 21 d: 1 ± 0.27, 0.34 ± 0.06; A3-C, 7 d: 1 ± 0.36, 0.21 ± 0.07. title: #3614 Is hyponatremia at the beginning of peritoneal dialysis relevant?
authors: Jara Caro; Ana Cordoba Fajardo; Lizbeth Karolina Vivanco; Claudia Yuste; Begoña Aguado Navarro; Inmaculada Tapia Herrera; Andrea Cifuentes; Jose Enrique Ruiz Caballero; Lucía Rodríguez-Gayo; Soledad Pizarro Sanchez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyponatremia is a common electrolyte disorder in patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis (PD). Hyponatremia has been identified as a poor prognostic factor and an independent mortality predictor, associated with fluid overload and weight gain. We aimed to analyze the impact of hyponatremia on mortality among PD patients.
Methods
A single-center retrospective study of incident PD patients treated at tertiary hospital between August 2015 to December 2024. We analyzed the demographic and epidemiologic data, along with baseline plasma sodium (Na) levels, adequacy and the results of the baseline peritoneal equilibration test (PET).
Results
We studied 154 incident PD patients (mean age 55.9 ± 14.7 years, 60.4% male, 93.5% with hypertension, and 26% with diabetes) mainly on automatized PD (79.2%) followed during a mean of 24.4 ± 18.5 months.
Patients were divided according to plasma Na levels as normonatremic (Na >135 mEq/L) and hyponatremic (≤135 mEq/L). Hyponatremia was found in 20 patients (13%) with a mean plasma Na of 131 ± 4.5 mEq/L, while normonatremic patients presented a mean Na of 141.1 ± 2.6 mEq/L.
Hyponatremic patients were older (63.2 ± 15.9 vs 54.86 ± 14.3 years, p 0.017), were also more frequently anuric at baseline (25% vs 8.2% p 0.022), and associated more comorbidities (Charlson index 6.8 ± 2.4 vs 5.6 ± 2.3, p 0.04) compared with normonatremic.
Patients with hyponatremia underwent more frequently to continuous ambulatory (40% vs 17%, p 0.027) and assisted PD (25 vs 6%, p 0.004).
Although total y renal KTV were similar in both groups, total baseline peritoneal KTV was significantly higher in hyponatremic patients (1.5 ± 1.8 vs 1.03 ± 0.4; p 0.01).
Hyponatremic patients presented higher baseline peritoneal transport (41% vs 14, p 0.001), as well as higher sodium sieving (12.2 ± 7.7 vs 8.67 ± 6 mEq/L, p 0.04) and lower total ultrafiltration (428 ± 282 vs 667.3 ± 249 6 ml, <0.001) compared with normonatremic.
The mortality rate in patients with hyponatremia was higher (n = 6, 30%) compared to normonatremic patients (n = 11, 8.2%) (p 0.004). No significant differences were found between those who discontinued the PD technique due to transfer to hemodialysis or kidney transplant, nor in the rate of peritonitis.
Conclusions
Baseline hyponatremia in patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis appear to be an early marker of poor prognosis. Patients with hyponatremia were older and more frail, which can explain its association with higher mortality. Hyponatremic patients presented higher baseline peritoneal transport, higher sodium sieving and lower total ultrafiltration compared with normonatremic patients. Further studies should explore the effectiveness of an early approach in PD patients with baseline hyponatremia.

title: #2906 Ultrafiltration pattern in automated peritoneal dialysis
authors: Hayriye Sayarlioglu; Ercan Turkmen; Ibrahim Dogan; Ersin Cinar; Emel Ucar
abstract:
Background and Aims
Prescriptions that can correct hypervolemia in automated peritoneal dialysis (APD) reduce patient complications. Using the Sharesource remote patient monitoring programme, it has been observed that some APD patients have no or low UF, especially in the early cycles. However, in continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis, ultrafiltration is higher when the patient is first connected to dialysis and during the first few hours when the patient is more hypervolemic. Determining which has the most UF from these cycles will show us the best UF time in the patient's treatment and help to reduce hypervolemia. In our study, we aimed to evaluate the UF amounts of the patients during the nocturnal cycles.
Method
The study included 32 patients (13 women, 19 men) who had been on APD for at least 3 months. The mean age of the patients was 58.4 ± 17.3 years (26–87). Patients were euvolemic and non-infection. Drainage volumes of each night cycle of the last month were averaged. The UF volume was calculated for each cycle. Patient UF profiles were calculated using descriptive analysis. UF profiles were compared between tidal therapy and standard therapy. In addition, both groups were evaluated for PET KTV.
Results
When all patients were evaluated, 1 patient had 4 cycles, 17 patients had 5 cycles, 11 patients had 6 cycles and 3 patients had 7 cycles. UF averages were calculated for each cycle in the patients. The mean UF levels of the patients are shown in the graphs (Figs 1 and 2). While 20 of the patients received conventional APD treatment, 11 received tidal treatment. When both treatment groups were evaluated, it was seen that the amount of UF decreased until the third filling in tidal treatment, that is, until complete drainage was achieved, and increased in subsequent cycle. In the standard treatment, it was seen that ultrafiltration gradually increased with each drainage. There was no difference in total UF between the two treatment methods. In 20 patients receiving standard treatment, positive UF was 67.9% in the first cycle, 85.7% in the second cycle, 90.5% in the third cycle, 95.2% in the fourth cycle, and 85.7% in the fifth cycle. The number of cases was low in the 6th and 7th cycles, but there were positive UF. When the patients receiving tidal and standard treatment were evaluated together, negative UF was also obtained in the 4th cycle due to the tidal treatment application procedure. There was no difference between PET and KTV between the two groups (P = 0.25, P = 0.62 respectively).
Conclusion
A pattern of increasing UF with increasing number of cycles has been observed with standard therapy. This may help to guide treatment options in APD. The pattern of increasing UF, usually in the first few hours with the expected first fill in CAPD, was found to be more pronounced with subsequent cycles in APD. This may represent a different kinetic pattern. The nightly sleeping position and the increase in peritoneal interstitial glucose may contribute to this situation. In addition, endogenous hormones (such as ADH, catecholamines, prolactin) whose levels change during the night may also play a role, but further studies are needed.

title: #3513 A multicenter retrospective study of erythropoietin combined with low-dose roxadustat in the treatment of renal anemia in hemodialysis patients
authors: Song Wang; Kai Wang; Yulan She; Yue Wang
abstract:
Background and Aims
To explore the efficacy of erythropoietin (EPO) combined with low-dose roxadustat in the treatment of hemodialysis patients with renal anemia whose hemoglobin (Hb) levels did not reach the guideline-recommended targets with EPO alone.
Method
This retrospective study included patients undergoing hemodialysis from January 2020 to December 2023 at three general hospitals in Beijing. Patients included were those whose Hb levels could not be maintained within the guideline-recommended range with EPO alone, for whom increasing EPO doses posed risks, or who had already reached the maximum EPO dose per the drug label, and those who could not afford full conversion to roxadustat. Changes in Hb levels and influencing factors before and after combination therapy were analyzed.
Results
A total of 125 patients were included (74 males, 50 females, mean age 61 ± 14 years, range 29–89 years). The median dialysis vintage was 55 ± 67 months (range 5–370 months). Primary diseases included diabetic nephropathy (48 cases), glomerulonephritis (42 cases), hypertensive nephropathy (10 cases), ADPKD (9 cases), tubulointerstitial nephropathy (3 cases), and unknown etiology (13 cases). Hb levels were persistently <110 g/L for 3 months before adding roxadustat. At the start of combination therapy, Hb was 96.66 ± 15.86 g/L, which increased to 102.64 ± 20.48 g/L (P = 0.001) at 1 month and 110.70 ± 16.07 g/L (P < 0.001) at 3 months. The average roxadustat dose was 197 ± 92 mg/week, approximately two-thirds of the recommended dose per the label. No significant changes were observed in EPO dose (P > 0.05), intravenous iron dose, transferrin saturation (TSAT), ferritin (SF), dialysis parameters, adequacy (KT/V), us-CRP, or iPTH levels (all P > 0.05). No significant adverse events were reported.
Conclusion
Low-dose roxadustat combined with EPO is safe and effective for hemodialysis patients with renal anemia whose Hb levels cannot be maintained within target ranges with EPO alone.

title: #531 Exploring differences in cognitive and behavioral outcomes of home-based self-care retraining in peritoneal dialysis patients
authors: Woan-Jean Lin; Ching-I Cheng; Yi-Ting Chen; Adonis Chih-Kang Chiang
abstract:
Background and Aims
The self-care ability of peritoneal dialysis patients has a great impact on their quality of life and survival rate. If a patient encounters a problem during home dialysis, he or she will call the on-duty consultation hotline. This study integrated the problem categories of patients' dialing events and designed problem-oriented guidance and treatment to provide patients with re-education, and to explore the cognitive and behavioral differences in their self-care abilities.
Method
This research tool analyzes the consultation call events from July to December 2019 and divides the consultation call events into five categories, including APD (Automated peritoneal dialysis) machine operation-related issues accounting, other non-emergency-related events accounting, Peritoneal dialysis-related emergencies accounted, CAPD (Continuous Ambulatory Peritoneal Dialysis)Continuous ambulatory procedure-related problems accounted, and peritoneal dialysis catheter-related events accounted. The self-designed questionnaire content is designed in a problem-oriented manner for non-emergency events to measure common problems in home self-care. The questionnaire in this study adopted expert validity and was reviewed by three experts with more than 7 years of senior peritoneal dialysis practice experience. After the patient agrees, a pre-test cognitive questionnaire is collected. The nurse will explain to the patient or primary caregiver one-on-one, provide explanations on the conditions that peritoneal dialysis patients will face during dialysis, and explain and publicize self-care at home. The post-test questionnaire was conducted 1–3 months after the pre-test questionnaire was collected.
Results
Totally 302 questionnaires were collected for this study. After t-test analysis, 18 cognitive assessment items and the number of non-emergency consultation calls reached statistical significance (see Table 1). The accuracy rate of the cognitive questionnaire before and after the test increased from 85.08% to 97.47%. The number of non-emergency consultation calls decreased from 78 (29.2%) to 46 (20.6%), which was also significant difference (P < 0.007).
Conclusion
Peritoneal dialysis is a home dialysis with self-care as the core. The patient's self-care ability directly affects the dialysis efficacy and quality of life. Continuous health education and regular skill retraining can promote patients' problem-solving skills and improve the quality of dialysis care.
Keywords: Peritoneal dialysis, education, self-care ability, cognition

title: #1199 Revolutionizing dialysis care for the elderly: lessons from the AHHD program
authors: Mostafa Fottoh Elshirbeny; Mohamed Yahya Abdelhai; Abdullah Hamad; Mossab Filali; Ahmed Adel Abd El Wahed; Teha Almohanadi; Hoda Tolba; Hala Frahna; Shajahan Joseph; Mohamad Alkadi; Hassan Almalki
abstract:
Background and Aims
The number of elderly dialysis patients in Qatar is rising, with 58% over the age of 60. Many face mobility challenges, often needing ambulance transport for treatment. To address this, the assisted home hemodialysis (AHHD) program was introduced, providing at-home dialysis to improve their quality of life. We highlight the challenges faced during its implementation and the solutions adopted.
Method
We documented all challenges encountered during the implementation of the AHHD program from its inception in June 2021 through December 2024. Additionally, we recorded the solutions applied to overcome these obstacles to ensure the program's success and sustainability.

title: #1340 Transfer of patients from cinacalcet to etelcalcetide: a retrospective cohort study in real world practice
authors: Ekaterina Parshina; Roman Gerasimchuk; Alexander Zemchenkov; Aleksei Zulkarnaev
abstract:
Background and Aims
The prevalence of secondary hyperparathyroidism (SHPT) depends on the control strategy, primarily on achieving the target level of parathyroid hormone (PTH). According to materials from the KDIGO Controversies Conference (2023) on Chronic Kidney Disease-Mineral and Bone Disorder (CKD-MBD), there is currently insufficient data to make a strictly justified choice of goals and strategies for SHPT correction.
A retrospective, multicenter, cohort study was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of ethelcalcetide in real-world practice. The aim of the study was to determine whether ethelcalcetide could effectively reduce PTH levels after 6 months of treatment in hemodialysis patients. The study also sought to identify baseline characteristics of CKD-MBD patients that predict whether they would achieve the desired therapeutic goal.
Method
The study included 302 hemodialysis patients who were treated with ethelcalcetide at 20 dialysis units in large city.
The primary endpoint was the percentage of patients who achieved the target range of parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels six months after starting treatment (300–599 pg/mL) after unintended one-month washout period after cinacalcet use. The secondary endpoint was a decrease in absolute and relative PTH levels. The results were analyzed in subgroups based on baseline PTH levels (<600, 600–1000, and >1000 pg/mL) as well as in patients with and without evidence of autonomous parathyroid adenoma (a gland volume exceeding 500 mm³ or a maximum linear dimension greater than 10 mm, in combination with qualitative assessment of blood flow through the gland).
Results
Among the 302 patients included in the study, aged 56 ± 12 years (61% men), with a median dialysis duration of 36 months (Q1–Q3: 23–55 months), ranging from 6 to 132 months, and a baseline PTH level of 729 pg/mL (548–957 pg/mL), ranging from 287 to 1,473 pg/mL, and baseline calcium and phosphate levels of 2.35 mmol/L (0.25 mmol/L) and 1.97 mmol/L (0.47 mmol/L), respectively, the proportion of patients who achieved the target PTH range by the end of the follow-up period was 49.7%.
The odds of achieving the target PTH value were higher for patients with a baseline PTH between 600 and 1,000 pg/mL compared to those with a PTH level above 1,000 pg/mL. Specifically, 79.3% of patients with baseline PTH levels between 600–1000 achieved the target level, compared to only 36.4% of those with PTH levels above 1000 (P < 0.001).
Among patients with parathyroid adenomas, the frequency of achieving the target range was 48% for those with baseline PTH 600–1,000, compared to 85.6% for those without adenomas (P < 0.001). For patients with baseline PTH over 1000 pg/mL, the corresponding figures were 25% and 57.9%, respectively (P = 0.016). The presence of parathyroid adenoma (n = 63) was the most significant independent predictor of likelihood of achieving the target PTH level (OR = 0.3 [95%])
Conclusion
Etelcalcetide treatment resulted in a decrease in PTH levels in most hemodialysis patients. No new side effects or drug intolerance were observed when transferring patients from cinacalcet to etelcalcetide. In patients with moderate SHPT (PTH 600–1000 pg/mL), it is possible to achieve the target PTH in most cases, but in those with higher baseline PTH levels, the outcome was worse. Signs of autonomous parathyroid adenoma better predict the lack of response to ethelcalcetide than high baseline PTH.

title: #1374 Time and motion study in a peritoneal dialysis program using Sharesource Analytics 1.0 remote patient management
authors: Mauricio Sanabria; Peter Rutherford; Maria Paz Dazzarola; Juan Carlos Mario Castillo; Cesar Mauricio Doria; Jorge Pulido; Fabio Rojas; Javier Cely; Jasmin Vesga; Lady Alba; Angela Rivera
abstract:
Background and Aims
Peritoneal dialysis (PD) programs worldwide are challenged by a shortage of trained personnel, high workloads, and multiple tasks, some of which are performed in the patient's home. Remote patient management (RPM) of PD patients may improve outcomes but adds to workload concerns. The objective of this study was to estimate the time spent by nephrologists and nurses in PD programs using Sharesource Analytics 1.0 RPM in Colombia.
Method
An external consultant used continuous time measurements to perform the time and motion methodology and measure the takt time defined as the period of time or cadence in which a task must be performed, in this case specialized peritoneal dialysis consultation. Three hundred thirty-six hours were measured for nurses and 196 hours for nephrologists. The study was conducted in four dialysis clinics of Renal Care Services in Colombia. Time was measured for nurses and nephrologists regarding all the APD program activities, including the time spent in Sharesource Analytics 1.0 for daily remote monitoring and the review performed during the monthly comprehensive peritoneal dialysis program consultation.
Results
13 nurses and 7 nephrologists participated in this study. The ratio between PD patients and nurses was 45:1, and between dialysis patients (PD and HD) and nephrologists was 140:1. The nurse's time spent on daily RPM follow-up and during the monthly comprehensive consultation averaged 2 minutes per patient, and similar results were observed in the nephrologists' review of Sharesource Analytics 1.0 in that consultation. The takt time for nephrology was 35 minutes; 16 minutes were spent directly evaluating the patient. Nurses see a new patient every 34 minutes and spend 24 minutes directly assessing the patient (Fig. 1). We found that remote monitoring consumes only 1% of the time spent by nephrologists and 3% of nurses each day (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
RPM support for PD patients can improve clinical outcomes. The time invested in RPM with Sharesource Analytics 1.0 does not exceed 5% of the daily task time for the PD team demonstrating its overall efficiency.

title: #1633 Increased levels of tissue factor is associated with upregulation of d-dimer and decreased levels of thrombin generation in end stage renal disease
authors: Vinod Bansal; Hamzah Hussain; Jawed Fareed; Fakiha Siddiqui; Debra Hoppensteadt; Kavitha Vellanki
abstract:
Background and Aims
End-stage renal disease (ESRD) is often associated with vascular complications. Tissue factor (TF) plays a very important role in triggering the thrombogenesis and biomarkers associated with thrombin generation (TG) such as D-Dimer (DD). TF levels in chronic kidney disease are known to be upregulated, however such a study in ESRD patients is not reported. In this study, we sought to measure TF antigen and activity levels, and their association with DD and TG potential.
Method
72 patients plasma with confirmed ESRD was collected in the Hemodialysis Clinic at Loyola University Medical Center (LUMC). 50 plasma samples from a commercial source and 12 plasma samples from LUMC served as a control. Commercially available sandwich ELISA methods were used for TF antigen and DD levels, while a chromogenic substrate method was used to measure TF activity. TG was quantified by using a fluorogenic method. Applicable statistical methods were performed and p<0.05 were considered significant.
Results
ESRD patients showed marked increase in TF and DD levels compared to the control. DD increased from 121.1 to 905.8 ng/mL (7.5-fold, P < 0.05) and TF concentration increased from 107.5 to 283.6 pg/mL (2.6-fold, P < 0.05). Peak thrombin levels reduced in the patient cohort from 138.4 to 109.9 nM (−1.26-fold, P < 0.05), while lag time increased from 1.7 to 2 minutes (1.2-fold, P < 0.05). TF activity and ETP showed no significant difference. Table 1 represents the composite results in the patient cohort and controls.
Conclusion
These studies demonstrate that while TF activity is undetectable, TF antigen is quantifiable in ESRD patients. Simultaneously, the peak thrombin level decreased and DD levels increased. These results suggest that coagulation system is activated where thrombin is consumed leading to DD formation. Thus, TF upregulation plays a central role in the pathogenesis of ESRD and its measurement may be helpful in prognostic management.

title: #1730 Investigation of the correlation between the Hemodialysis Vascular Sound Index and conventional vascular access surveillance indexes
authors: Toshihide Naganuma; Kentaro Shin; Risa Nakanishi; Tamoaki Iwai; Yoshiaki Takemoto; Junji Uchida
abstract:
Background and Aims
Auscultation as vascular access (VA) monitoring is performed frequently at each hemodialysis session, but it is largely dependent on the subjective judgment and experience of the staff, and there are some difficulties in sharing information with other staff. The electronic stethoscope “HVSI (Hemodialysis Vascular Sound Index) Monitor” (manufactured by Air Water Medical) was launched in May 2024 (Fig. 1). In addition to its use as a stethoscope, it can also quantify vascular sounds, and these are measured as HVSI values. On the other hand, the Access Blood Flow (Qa) obtained using the ultrasound dilution method, the Qa (DU) obtained using the ultrasound Doppler method, and the Resistance Index (RI) are well-known as indicators for VA surveillance. In this study, we measured the HVSI and compared it with the conventional VA surveillance index.
Method
We conducted a cross-sectional study of the correlation between the HVSI value measured by the HVSI monitor and conventional surveillance indicators, using 104 hemodialysis patients with arterio-venous fistula (AVF) who underwent hemodialysis at our hospital between May 2024 and December 2024. The measurement items HVSI, Qa, Qa (DU), and RI were measured at the start of dialysis at approximately the same time. Qa (DU) and RI were measured using the HS2 manufactured by KONICA MINOLTA, and the measurements were taken in the brachial artery. The NIPRO HD03 dialysis monitor was used to measure Qa. HVSI measurements were taken directly above the AVF anastomosis. The measurement values were expressed as median (IQR), and Spearman's rank correlation was used to examine the correlation. In addition, ROC analysis was used to examine the threshold values for detecting Qa, Qa (DU) 350 ml/min or less, and RI 0.6 or more. This study protocol was conducted in accordance with the Principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The ethics review boards of Osaka Metropolitan University approved the study (No. 2021-243). Opt-out consent was obtained instead of written informed consent; i.e. we provided patients with information explaining the proposed project (purpose, required individual data, and duration of the study) by means of an information sheet or hospital website and gave them the opportunity to opt out.
Results
The measured values were HVSI: 196 (113, 400), Qa: 780 (510, 1010) ml/min, Qa (DU): 657 (454, 894) ml/min, and RI: 0.52 (0.46, 0.57). HVSI was significantly positively correlated with Qa and Qa (DU), and significantly negatively correlated with RI (ρ = 0.47, P < 0.001, ρ = 0.55, P < 0.001, ρ = −0.31, P < 0.001). The threshold values for the HVSI values that detect Qa/Qa (DU) 350 or less were 96/178, and the AUCs were 0.75/0.82, respectively. HVSI was not a useful indicator for RI.
Conclusion
The HVSI value, which is a monitoring indicator, was found to have a positive correlation with Qa and Qa (DU), which are established as surveillance indicators, and a weak negative correlation with RI. In addition, it was shown that it is possible to set a certain threshold for reduced blood flow. In the past, monitoring using a stethoscope was influenced by the subjective factors of the staff, but by using the HVSI Monitor, an electronic stethoscope, it is now possible to treat it as an objective indicator called the HVSI value. In addition, HVSI monitors are relatively inexpensive, and the method for measuring HVSI values is simple and the measurement time is short, so it was thought that they could be a game changer for the daily management of VA.

title: #1857 The efficacy and safety of using various combinations of antithrombotic therapy in patients with AF and ESKD undergoing program hemodialysis
authors: Ranokhon Igamberdieva; Sherzod Abdullaev
abstract:
Background and Aims
The problem of tactics of management of patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) and end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) undergoing program hemodialysis is one of the most poorly studied and unresolved. One of the main problems still remains the choice of correct antithrombotic therapy. The aim is to study the efficacy and safety of using various combinations of antithrombotic therapy in patients with AF and ESKD on hemodialysis.
Method
Participants in study were 86 patients with AF and ESKD, requiring hemodialysis: group 1 patients received combination therapy (warfarin and aspirin (75 mg), n = 38)) and group 2 received warfarin monotherapy (n = 48). The warfarin dose was adjusted according to international normalised ratio data and maintained in the target therapeutic range of 2.0–3.0.
Results
In terms of prevention of thromboembolic complications, therapy in both groups of patients demonstrated statistically insignificant results. In the combination therapy group, the hazard ratio (HR) for ischemic stroke was 0.75 (95% CI: 0.08–1.66), and for myocardial infarction, the HR was 0.79 (95% CI: 0.70–1.31). Among patients receiving monotherapy, these indicators were HR 0.80 (95% CI: 0.44–1.70) and HR 0.84 (95% CI: 0.55–0.92). However, during the observation period, bleeding was more often recorded in the combination therapy group (21% of cases) compared to the monotherapy group (8% of cases, P = 0.02). In the combination therapy group, major and clinically significant bleeding occurred twice as often (HR 2.59 (95% CI: 1.46–4.69) and HR 2.37 (95% CI: 1.49–6.16)) than in the warfarin monotherapy group (HR 1.17 (95% CI: 0.95–3.15) and HR 1.34 (95% CI: 1.14–2.84)). The number of minor bleeding events was almost the same in both groups.
Conclusion
Antithrombotic therapy in the form of warfarin and warfarin+aspirin combination did not show the expected results in preventing thromboembolic and hemorrhagic complications in patients with AF and ESKD, who received hemodialysis. In particular, combination therapy dramatically increased the incidence of life-threatening bleeding.

title: #2010 Association between blood flow (Qa) monitored over time by ultrasound and the risk of thrombosis in autologous and prosthetic AV accesses
authors: Mariia Romanova; Lorenza Magagnoli; Mario Gennaro Cozzolino
abstract:
Background and Aims
The use of arteriovenous (AV) access for hemodialysis is hampered by the risk of thrombosis. This study aims to investigate the association between repeated ultrasound measurement of blood flow (Qa) and its percentage variation with thrombosis risk, in distal and proximal autologous AV fistulae (dAVF and pAVF) and AV grafts (AVG).
Method
This retrospective cohort study included all AV accesses created through the multidisciplinary AV access team in our centers in Milan (IT), between 2013 and 2024. Accesses with a post-operative Qa measurement within 30 days from creation were included and followed up until the first thrombosis, study end, or patient death. Qa was measured as the product of the cross-sectional area and the time-averaged mean velocity in the brachial artery. The associations of interest were studied by time-dependent Cox models, adjusted for patient's age, sex, and comorbidities, using splines for non-linear effects.
Results
A total of 224 AV accesses (88 dAVF, 88 pAVF, and 48 AVG) were created in 197 patients. At first post-operative visit, median Qa was 935, 1260, and 1665 ml/min, respectively for dAVF, pAVF, and AVG. Thereafter, Qa increased in all access types in the first 3–6 months, and then kept on slowly increasing only in pAVF. During a median follow up of 1.05 [0.24, 2.34] years, 70 AV access thrombosis occurred. In dAVF, we found a significant L-shaped association between longitudinal Qa and thrombosis risk. title: #2239 Association between chronic pain, quality of life and perceived social support among patients on maintenance hemodialysis
authors: Jasna Trbojević-Stanković; Natalija Damnjanović; Edvin Hadzibulic; Selma Hadžibulić; Zoran Bukumiric
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic pain is a common health problem among maintenance hemodialysis (HD) patients. Its multifactorial origin may be related to underlying renal disease, comorbidities, or dialysis treatment itself. Nevertheless, there is a lack of consistent data quantifying the burden of chronic pain in this population and its association with quality of life (QoL). This study aimed to examine the prevalence and characteristics of chronic pain in patients treated with chronic HD, and assess its relationship with QoL and perceived social support.
Method
This cross-sectional study involved 120 maintenance HD patients. General demographic, clinical and laboratory data were collected from the patient's medical records. The Brief Pain Inventory was used to evaluate determinants of chronic pain: prevalence, pain severity and pain interference with daily activities. Pain chronicity was specified by persisting or recurring pain for at least 3 months. Quality of life (QoL) was assessed with a 36-item Short-Form Health Survey (SF36), yielding two summary measures: the Physical Component Summary (PCS), defined by dimensions of physical functioning, physical role, bodily pain and general health; and the Mental Component Summary (MCS), which includes dimensions of vitality, social functioning, role emotional and mental health. Higher scores indicated better QoL. The Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support (MPSS) was used to measure individual perception of support. Results were analyzed with adequate descriptive statistics, T-test for parametric data and Hi-square or Fisher's exact test for frequencies.
Results
The study population included 71 (59%) males, mean age 62.9 ± 11.01 years, dialysis vintage 4–283 months (Med 54), body mass index 24.6 ± 4.5. Diabetes, secondary hyperparathyroidism and hypertension were present in 37%, 23.3% and 87.5% of cases respectively. Charlson's Comorbidity Index was 6.13 ± 2.23. Only 12.5% of patients lived alone, whereas others resided with spouses, children, or both (31.7%, 21.7% and 34.2% respectively). Two-thirds of patients (80; 66.7%) suffered from chronic pain. Pain severity was reported as mild, moderate or severe by 57.5%, 27.5% and 15.0% of subjects respectively. The patients rated pain interference with daily activity as none, mild, moderate and strong in 17.5%, 15.0%, 36.3% and 31.3% of cases respectively. The majority reported one (41.3%) or two (25.0%) areas affected with pain, most commonly the knees (26.%) and lumbosacral region (19%). Half of the patients (50.5%) used pain medications, while 74.4% practised alternative methods for pain relief. Only 8.9% reported successful pain management. The majority of patients perceived high social support (85.8%)
Patients with chronic pain had significantly lower PCS (41.0 ± 19.7 vs 60.0 ± 19.4; P < 0.001), MCS (54.4 ± 22.9 vs 68.0 ± 22.5; P = 0.003), and total SF36 score (47.7 ± 19.8 vs 64.0 ± 19.4; P < 0.001), indicating significantly worse QoL compared to patients without pain. Patients with perceived lower social support also had significantly lower PCS (37.5 ± 20.1 vs 49.0 ± 21.4; P = 0.04), MCS (43.1 ± 19.3 vs 61.5 ± 23.3; P = 0.003), and total SF36 score (40.3 ± 19.0 vs 55.3 ± 20.7; P = 0.06). There was no significant difference in pain severity (4.9 ± 2.9 vs 3.8 ± 1.9, P = 0.095) and pain interference (4.3 ± 2.8 vs 4.0 ± 2.8, P = 0.688) between patients with moderate and high social support respectively. Patients with moderate support reported significantly less painful spots (2.5 ± 2.2 vs 4.0 ± 3.7, P = 0.048).
Conclusion
Maintenance HD patients are commonly affected by chronic pain which significantly impacts their QoL. Patients mostly perceived high social support, which was associated with better QoL. Pain is generally undermanaged in HD population and strategies are needed to address this matter systematically.

title: #2260 Should dialysate sodium be routinely prescribed to patients with chronic haemodialysis?
authors: Ferah Taran; Hayriye Sayarlioglu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic hemodialysis patients often experience fluid and electrolyte imbalances, including hyponatremia, which can has been linked to increased mortality, morbidity, and poor quality of life. Since patients' individual hypothalamic sodium (Na) set point is variable, the dialysate Na concentration also contribute to above mentioned outcomes a large extent. Dialyzing patients with standard dialysate solutions can lead to Na transfer in individuals with low Na set points. This study aims to investigate the relationship between serum Na (sNa) level, interdialytic weight gain (IDWG), and predialysis arterial pressure in chronic hemodialysis patients.
Method
This was a retroprospective cohort study conducted at 6 hemodialysis units. We included adult patients who had been on maintenance hemodialysis for at least 3 months. Patients with active infection, current malignancy, adrenal insufficiency, untreated hypothyroidism and uncontrolled diabetes, advanced congestive heart failure, advanced chronic liver disease, or use of centrally acting drugs associated with hyponatremia were excluded. Demographic and clinical data, as well as, laboratory values were collected from electronic medical records, including predialysis sNa levels corrected due to glucose, as an average value of the last 3 months. Patients were categorized into two groups based on their mean predialysis sNa levels: those with lower (≤137 mEq/L) and those with higher (>137 mEq/L) Na. Comparisons were made between the groups using one-way ANOVA and chi-square tests as appropriate. These patients were then observed for 1 year for incremental dialysis need and mortality outcomes. Patients who died within 1 year were compared to those who survived in terms of their predialysis Na levels, IDWG, and predialysis blood pressure. Correlation analysis were performed to determine the associations between independent variables.
Results
A total of 176 patients were included, with a mean age of 58.1 ± 15.2 years and 50% were male. The mean predialysis sNa level was 138.8 ± 2.6 mEq/L (Table 1). Patients in the lower Na group (n = 49) had higher IDWG compared to the higher Na group (n = 127), but did not reach statistical significance (4.92 vs 4.46 kg, P = 0.565). Predialysis systolic blood pressure was significantly higher in the lower Na group compared to the higher group (130.8 vs 138.9 mmHg, P = 0.032). A negative correlation was found between predialysis systolic blood pressure and sNa level (r = −0.213, P = 0.005), while a positive correlation was found between the number of antihypertensive medications used (r = 0.207, P = 0.006). Positive and significant correlations were found between IDWG and hemodialysis vintage (r = 0.210, P = 0.005), as well as, between IDWG and the need for increased dialysis (130.8 vs 138.9 mmHg, P = 0.032). The one-year mortality rate did not show any significant differences between the groups due to sNa levels.
Conclusion
The study reveals that lower sNa levels in chronic hemodialysis patients are associated with higher predialysis systolic blood pressure. Therefore, closely monitoring sNa levels and customizing dialysate Na concentrations may help optimize hemodynamic stability and reduce complications in this patient population.

title: #2461 A rare cause of orbital apex syndrome
authors: Aarthi Muthukumaran; Onn Kon
abstract:
Background and Aims
Orbital apex syndrome is a symptom complex of ophthalmoplegia and optic neuropathy due to multiple cranial nerve pathology resulting from involvement of the bony orbital apex. The causes of this rare neurological condition can be infectious, inflammatory, neoplastic or traumatic. A multi-systemic approach is required to identify the underlying etiology and provide appropriate treatment, as the visual prognosis is dependent on accurate diagnosis and timely management. We describe a rare cause of this neurological syndrome in a patient on hemodialysis.
Method
A 35 yr old lady on hemodialysis for 5 years, awaiting a deceased donor renal transplant, presented acutely with proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, pain and visual loss in right eye. She was clinically diagnosed with orbital apex syndrome involving 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 6th cranial nerve palsies. MRI of orbit confirmed a right orbital apex process causing optic perineuritis and multiple orbital neuropathies. She underwent systemic evaluation to rule out infection, inflammatory etiologies and malignancy.
Results
Her autoimmune screen including ANA and ANCA were negative. Anti-acetyl choline receptor and anti-MUSK antibodies—negative. MRI of cervicothoracic spine was normal. The cerebrospinal fluid was negative for oligoclonal band, aquaporin 4 antibody and anti-MOG antibody. ACE level—normal. Plasma IgG4 level—normal. No paraprotein in serum protein electrophoresis. Syphilis serology—negative. The initial contrast enhanced CT imaging of her chest and abdomen showed evidence of nodal calcification but no evidence of active granulomatous disease or significant lymphadenopathy. The PET-CT revealed small FDG avid nodes in the supraclavicular fossae, metabolically active mediastinal and ileocolic nodes and intense tracer uptake in the proximal half of the stomach. Small calcified nodes as well as minor left apical lung scarring and calcified granulomata. She underwent left supraclavicular lymph node biopsy that showed granulomatous reaction with multi nucleated giant cells and necrosis and negative for AFB stain and TB PCR. She had no previous history or family history of tuberculosis or leprosy. Interestingly, her original kidney biopsy done 5 years ago had shown tubulointerstitial nephritis, before she ended up in end stage kidney disease. An endobronchial ultrasound guided mediastinal lymph node biopsy was done that showed granulomatous inflammation with positive AFB culture for mycobacterium tuberculosis that was resistant to isoniazid. In the meantime, her ocular symptoms worsened and a repeat MRI orbit showed non-specific inflammatory process of the right orbital apex, with subsequent crowding and mass effect on structures passing through it (CN II, III, IV, VI and superior opthalmic vein).
Conclusion
She was initiated on anti-tuberculous treatment with rifampicin, pyrazinamide and moxifloxacin. But she developed QT prolongation with the fluoroquinolone, hence given an extended treatment for 12 months with rifampicin and pyrazinamide, with which her ocular symptoms fully subsided and she regained normal vision. This case is reported to highlight the need for prompt recognition and treatment of this rare but sight-threatening manifestation of tuberculosis in immunosuppressed and vulnerable patients on haemodialysis.

title: #2526 Anemia as a predictor of peritoneal dialysis withdrawal in stable peritoneal dialysis patients
authors: Kenta Torigoe; Emiko Otsuka; Kiyokazu Tsuji; Ayuko Yamashita; Mineaki Kitamura; Kumiko Muta; Tomoya Nishino
abstract:
Background and Aims
Anemia is recognized as a risk factor for early withdrawal of peritoneal dialysis (PD). However, its impact on patients with stable PD has not yet been fully elucidated. This study aimed to explore the association between anemia and PD withdrawal in patients with stable PD.
Method
A total of 43 patients who underwent PD for at least 6 months were included in this study. Patients were categorized into two groups based on hemoglobin (Hb) levels: those with Hb ≥11 g/dL (22 patients) and those with Hb <11 g/dL (21 patients). The subsequent PD withdrawal rates were compared between the groups. Additionally, the relationship between Hb levels and subsequent annual decline in urinary volume was examined.
Results
The median PD duration was 14 months, and 37 patients transitioned from PD during a mean follow-up of 37.5 months. The PD withdrawal rate was significantly higher in the Hb level <11 g/dL group (log-rank test, P = 0.02). Moreover, in a Cox proportional hazards model adjusted for patient background, Hb level remained a significant predictor of PD withdrawal (hazard ratio [HR], 0.73; 95% CI: 0.54–0.99, P = 0.04). Furthermore, Hb levels were inversely correlated with the subsequent annual rate of urinary volume decline (r = −0.34, P = 0.02). Multivariable analysis also showed that Hb levels were independently correlated with the subsequent annual rate of urinary volume decline (standard β = −0.35, P = 0.03).
Conclusion
These findings suggest that anemia is a risk factor for PD withdrawal in stable PD patients, potentially due to its association with a decline in residual renal function.

title: #2782 Clinician usage and perception of an AI-based model predicting peritoneal dialysis dropouts
authors: Caitlin Monaghan; Susan Lewis; Paul Smith; Beverly Wesley; Len Usvyat
abstract:
Background and Aims
A machine learning (ML) model was developed to identify patients likely to leave peritoneal dialysis (PD). Weekly reports containing model predictions and relevant information were provided to care teams for clinical decision support. Prior to piloting an updated model in a subset of clinics receiving the report, a survey was conducted to gather feedback on current usage and perceptions of the original model and report. The primary goal of the survey was to collect a baseline for tracking changes in usage after switching to the new model and dashboard.
Method
177 clinics were identified to pilot the new model, which would be delivered via a dashboard instead of the weekly emailed report. Home therapy clinic managers (HTCMs) overseeing pilot clinics completed a survey and reviewed training materials with their Interdisciplinary Team (IDT).
We received 102 responses covering 96 unique clinics (54% of clinics). After excluding duplicate responses, we were left with valid responses reflecting report use in 91 clinics.
Questions covered frequency of use, roles reviewing report, how the report is used, report printing, and agreement with each of five statements assessing the ease of accessibility of the report, understandability of the report, usefulness of the information provided, provision of better patient care, and report satisfaction.
Results
Of the 91 valid responses, 49.5% used the report 1–3 times per month, 44% used it weekly, and 5.5% used it multiple times per week. In all clinics reporting usage (n = 90), a nurse and/or HTCM reviewed reports at a minimum. Social workers reviewed the report in 42.2% (n = 38) of the clinics, dieticians in 43.3% (n = 39), patient care technicians in 13.3% (n = 12), kidney care advocates in 2.2% (n = 2), physicians in 35.6% (n = 32), area team leads in 13.3% (n = 12), directors of operations in 10% (n = 9), patients in 12.2% (n = 11), and other roles indicated in 3.3% (n = 3). Reports were reviewed during IDT meetings, Quality meetings to review programs at a high level, and physician rounds in 32.2% of clinics (n = 29) each.
In clinics reporting usage (n = 90), agreement with statements was endorsed most of the time for all items (Fig. 1). Agreement was endorsed by 76.7% of clinics (n = 69) for ease of access, 82.2% (n = 74) for ease of understanding, 82.2% (n = 74) for the provision of useful information, 72.2% (n = 65) for bettering patient care, and 73.3% (n = 66) for satisfaction with the report. The statement with the most disagreement was regarding the ease of report access; 15.6% (n=14) strongly disagreed or disagreed and 7.8% (n = 7) were neutral.
Within clinics using the report 1 or more times per week (49.5%, n = 45), only 4.4% (n = 2) reported disagreement with the statement that the report was easy to access. Clinics reporting less frequent usage of 1-3 times per month (49.5%, n = 45) were much more likely to endorse disagreement regarding ease of access (26.7%, n = 12) (Fig. 2).
In clinics that reviewed the report with patients (12.1%, n = 11), reports were also reviewed by physicians, and none of the clinics endorsed disagreement with any of the five statements (Fig. 3).
Conclusion
Clinician survey responses assessing use and perceptions of a report displaying ML predictions and related information surrounding patients leaving PD were overwhelmingly positive. A relationship was found between frequency of usage and reported ease of access of this weekly emailed report, where those expressing dissatisfaction with the ease of access used the report less frequently. This emphasizes the critical role of workflow integration and ease of use in driving adoption of AI tools.
Additionally, clinics reviewing the reports with patients directly also always endorsed reviewing with physicians; these clinics did not express disagreement with any of the statements. This likely reflects the level of buy-in and understanding of the report needed to bring to patients directly.

Social workers reviewed the report in 42.2% (n = 38) of the clinics, dieticians in 43.3% (n = 39), patient care technicians in 13.3% (n = 12), kidney care advocates in 2.2% (n = 2), physicians in 35.6% (n = 32), area team leads in 13.3% (n = 12), directors of operations in 10% (n = 9), patients in 12.2% (n = 11), and other roles indicated in 3.3% (n = 3). Reports were reviewed during IDT meetings, Quality meetings to review programs at a high level, and physician rounds in 32.2% of clinics (n = 29) each.
In clinics reporting usage (n = 90), agreement with statements was endorsed most of the time for all items (Fig. 1). Agreement was endorsed by 76.7% of clinics (n = 69) for ease of access, 82.2% (n = 74) for ease of understanding, 82.2% (n = 74) for the provision of useful information, 72.2% (n = 65) for bettering patient care, and 73.3% (n = 66) for satisfaction with the report. The statement with the most disagreement was regarding the ease of report access; 15.6% (n=14) strongly disagreed or disagreed and 7.8% (n = 7) were neutral.
Within clinics using the report 1 or more times per week (49.5%, n = 45), only 4.4% (n = 2) reported disagreement with the statement that the report was easy to access. Clinics reporting less frequent usage of 1-3 times per month (49.5%, n = 45) were much more likely to endorse disagreement regarding ease of access (26.7%, n = 12) (Fig. 2).
In clinics that reviewed the report with patients (12.1%, n = 11), reports were also reviewed by physicians, and none of the clinics endorsed disagreement with any of the five statements (Fig. 3).
Conclusion
Clinician survey responses assessing use and perceptions of a report displaying ML predictions and related information surrounding patients leaving PD were overwhelmingly positive. A relationship was found between frequency of usage and reported ease of access of this weekly emailed report, where those expressing dissatisfaction with the ease of access used the report less frequently. This emphasizes the critical role of workflow integration and ease of use in driving adoption of AI tools.
Additionally, clinics reviewing the reports with patients directly also always endorsed reviewing with physicians; these clinics did not express disagreement with any of the statements. This likely reflects the level of buy-in and understanding of the report needed to bring to patients directly.

title: #2992 Modifiable factors involved in sudden death risk in a large population on chronic hemodialysis
authors: Carla Santos Araújo; Domingos MacHado; Eliana Silva; Carlos Lucas; Fernando MacÁrio
abstract:
Background and Aims
End-stage renal disease patients receiving hemodialysis (HD) have an exceedingly high risk of cardiac sudden death, that may occur between treatments (extra dialytic sudden death, SD) or during the dialysis session (intradialytic SD). Even considering that these two entities may represent different clinical situations, the identification of potentially modifiable risk factors for SD in HD patients seems fundamental for the implementation of strategies to reduce the incidence of such events. Some HD registry-based observational studies have suggested some factors eventually implicated in SD risk, but the results are conflicting and further clarification is needed. The aim of our study was to evaluate the variables associated with the risk of SD in a large population of HD patients.
Method
We performed a retrospective cohort study using data from an international HD provider database. All patients in maintenance HD during 2024 were included. Deaths occurring during the year were gathered and divided in two groups: Group 1) non-sudden deaths; Group 2) sudden deaths, defined as unexpected, natural deaths occurring within 1 hour of symptom onset if witnessed or, if unwitnessed, within 24 hours of having been last seen alive and symptom-free. The last demographic, clinical and analytical data available before the event were collected and the two groups compared using ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis test for continuous variables and Chi-square (X²) test for categorical variables. We used Cox regression analyses to evaluate survival, adjusted for age, gender, time on dialysis, diabetic status, Charlson comorbidity index (CI), type of vascular access, body mass index (BMI), dialysis adequacy (eKt/V), interdialytic fluid gain, intradialytic blood flow, hemoglobin, albumin, calcium and phosphorus. Results were presented as hazard ratios (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) and a p-value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results
A total of 4,820 occurred during the period, 28% of which meeting the criteria for sudden death. Of all the sudden deaths, 34.1% were attributed to a cardiac event and 65.9% to unknown causes. The sudden death occurred more significantly in patients of male gender, longer time on dialysis, diabetic, higher BMI, higher fluid gain between HD treatments, higher blood flow during the treatment, use of central venous catheter as dialysis access and higher levels of hemoglobin, albumin and phosphorus. No differences between groups were found in age, CI and eKt/V. In the survival analysis, diabetics status, presence of a tunneled catheter and higher values of plasmatic phosphorus were independently associated with higher HR of sudden death (Table 1).
Conclusion
Sudden death is a common phenomenon in HD patients, being responsible for more than a quarter of all deaths. In our population, diabetes, the presence of a tunneled central venous catheter and higher phosphate levels were independently associated with a higher risk of SD. Our findings may provide preliminary evidence on some modifiable factors related to SD in HD patients and create the basis for the implementation of multidimensional interventions aiming at reducing the occurrence of sudden fatal events in this population.

title: #3105 Hyperglycaemia impact on the accuracy of plasma sodium levels estimated by the 6008 CAREsystem hemodialysis monitor
authors: Marta Bermejo Mata; Paula Jara Caro Espada; Stephanía de Fátima; Velandres Tabarné; Maria Jose Gutierrez; Irene Martín Capón; Maria Fernandez Vidal; Andrea Cifuentes-Talavera; Soledad Pizarro Sanchez; Claudia Yuste Lozano
abstract:
Background and Aims
The Sodium Management sensor integrated into the hemodialysis (HD) 6008 CAREsystem monitors can estimate plasma sodium (Na) levels, allowing to achieve “zero Na balance” by diffusion. However, the impact of the predialysis plasma glucose (Glu) levels and the correction of hyperglycaemia by diffusion during HD session can interfere the “zero Na balance.”
Method
We conducted an observational study on a poorly controlled diabetes patient on chronic HD with treated with the 6008 CAREsystem monitor. We have studied the intradialysis kinetics of plasma Na, Glu and bicarbonate (Bic) levels (at 0, 30, 60, 120 and 240 minutes respectively). The Na was: (i) measured in the biochemistry laboratory using indirect potentiometry in mEq/l, (ii) estimated by the Sodium Management sensor into the 6008 CAREsystem monitors, and (iii) corrected by glucose. We have also measured the Na, Glu and bicarbonate in the dialysate. The dialysis prescription was consistent across the 4 sessions studied: 240 min conventional HD session with a high cut off membrane (Theranova®) with fixed Qb 420 ml/min. The dialysate contained potassium 2 mmol/L, Calcium at 1.75 mmol/L, magnesium at 0.5 mmol/L and a prescribed bicarbonate at 28 mmol/L.
Results
A total of 4 dialysis sessions were studied (total ultrafiltration 138.5 [136.2–140]) ml, final Na elimination 392.5 [202–460]) mmol, final diffusive Na balance 43 [1.75–95.5]), and an estimated conductivity of 138 [136.5–140]), at the beginning and 138.5 [136.5–145.5] at the end of the HD session.
A total 20 plasma Na and Glu levels measurements and estimations were examined (Fig. 1).
Although the “zero Na balance” was set, there was an increase between laboratory plasma Na levels measured at 0 min (131 [126.5–133.5]) and 240 min (133 [131.5–134.5]), not seen in the estimated Na levels at 0 min (137 [133.9–137]) and 240 min (137.5 [137–138]).
On the contrary, a reduction on laboratory plasma Na levels corrected by glucose were observed between 0 min and 240 min (136 [134.15–137.7] and 133.9 [132.05–134.95], respectively), with an slight increase during the first hour HD session (60 min 136.8 [134.8–138.95]). Similarly, a reduction on estimated Na levels corrected by glucose was observed between 0 min and 240 min (142.8 [136.9–142.8] and 137.9 [137.5–138.6], respectively).
The correction in the plasmatic glucose levels occurred progressively during the HD session (Fig. 1).
Finally, the levels of Na, Glu and bicarbonate in the dialysate estimated by the 6008 were accurate compared with the levels measured in the laboratory.
Conclusion
The Sodium Management sensor integrated into the HD 6008 CAREsystem monitor is unable to accurately estimate plasma sodium levels in case of hyperglycaemia. The correction of hyperglycaemia by diffusion occurred slowly during the HD session. The “zero Na balance” guided by the sodium management sensor does not guarantee an actual zero Na diffusive balance in case of hyperglycaemia. Further studies should verify the external validity of these studies.

title: #3111 SphygmoCor parameters in hemodialysis (HD) patients with or without advanced non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)
authors: Nina Vodošek Hojs; Robert Ekart; Sebastjan Bevc; Pavel Skok; Radovan Hojs; Nejc Piko; Tadej Petreski; Vanja Kalacun
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiovascular diseases are important comorbidities in chronic kidney disease and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFDL). SphygmoCor is the gold standard to noninvasively measure central blood pressure and arterial stiffness, which are critical indicators of cardiovascular health and disease risk. Therefore, our research aimed to study all these parameters in hemodialysis (HD) patients with or without advanced NAFLD.
Method
HD patients were included and divided according to abdominal ultrasound and two-dimensional shear wave elastography (2D-SWE) measurements into two groups: (1) no NAFLD or no advanced NAFLD (2D-SWE <9 kPa) and (2) advanced NAFLD (2D-SWE ≥9 kPa). Medical history data were collected. SphygmoCor diagnostic was performed by two experienced doctors on a non-dialysis day during the short interdialytic interval. We measured carotid to femoral pulse wave velocity (cfPWV) and performed pulse wave analysis of the peripheral radial artery on the non-AVF arm.
Results
Seventy-seven HD patients were included (65.14 ± 12.34 years, 59.2% male). Data of our patients are presented in Table 1. The advanced NAFLD group had significantly lower aortic systolic pressure (P = 0.018), augmentation index (AIx; P = 0.008) and AIx normalized for heart rate 75/min (Aix@75; P = 0.018). The groups did not differ in cfPWV, aortic diastolic pressure, ejection duration (ED) and subendocardial viability ratio (SEVR).
Conclusion
Our results are unexpected compared to SphygmoCor results in non-HD NAFLD patients. Since till now, no such research has been done in HD patients with NAFLD, further studies are needed to confirm and understand our results.

title: #3323 Arteriovenous dialysis access use and haemodiafiltration are associated with lower frequency and severity of intradialytic symptoms in a Singapore cohort
authors: Yan Yi Cheung; Yuk Yi Chan; Sugandha Saxena; Berit Goethel-Paal; Andrea Gualdoni; Nandakumar Mooppil; Suzie Buford; Aileen Rubas; Luca Neri; Benjamin Hippen; Franklin Maddux; Milind Nikam
abstract:
Background and Aims
End-stage kidney disease (ESKD) patients receiving dialysis often experience a diminished health-related quality of life (QoL) [1], making the collection of patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) essential for identifying key to enhance dialysis effectiveness and patients’ experiences. Our study aims to explore the association between haemodialysis (HD) treatment related factors and PROMs.
Method
In this cross-sectional study, we analysed electronic-PROM survey results, targeting 1,485 patients at Fresenius Medical Care (FMC) Singapore clinics from August to December 2024. The study was approved by the local Institutional Review Board. Patients enrolled for ≥90 days, provided consent, and completed the survey were included in the analysis.
The survey comprised 3 questionnaires: Kidney Disease (KD) QoL-36 [2], Itch-5D, and intradialytic symptom questionnaire. We also analysed hospitalisation outcomes in this cohort. The KDQoL-36 includes 36 multiple-choice questions that assess five domains, generating scores (0 to 100), with higher scores indicating better QoL. Only patients who reported they were ‘very much bothered’ by itching on the KDQoL were asked to fill in the Itch-5D questionnaire (score: 5—mild impact to 22—severe impact) and only those patients who experienced symptoms during the previous dialysis were asked to rate the severity (1—not at all to 5—severe) of the 12 common intradialytic symptoms. Patients who received haemodiafiltration (HDF) for ≥75% of all treatments were classified as HDF group. We used linear and logistic regression models for numerical and binary outcomes, respectively and Poisson regression for hospitalisation. We analysed the results using R (version 4.1.1) and considered a two-sided p-value of <0.05 as significant.
Results
In total, 1,023 patients agreed to participate in the ePROM survey, yielding a response rate of 69%. Of the 681 patients who completed the survey and met the inclusion criteria, 122 used central venous catheter (CVC), 555 used arteriovenous fistulas (AVF) or grafts (AVG) (non-CVC), and VA was not reported for 4 patients. Three hundred and two patients (44%) were in the HDF group and 56% in the conventional HD group. The characteristics of patients by VA type and dialysis modality are presented in Tables 1 and 2, respectively. Ninety-seven patients (14%) reported experiencing intradialytic symptoms during the last dialysis session, with the most common being tiredness (13%) and muscle cramping (10%).
The CVC group had significantly higher odds of experiencing intradialytic symptoms, including dizziness [OR: 2.10, (95% C.I.: 1.06, 4.03)], tiredness [OR: 1.97, (95% C.I.: 1.14, 3.40)], and shivering [OR: 2.50, (95% C.I.: 1.29, 4.76)] compared to the non-CVC group (Table 3). Furthermore, CVC group reported more severe vomiting, dizziness, tiredness, and shivering (P < 0.05) albeit with small effect size. Tiredness and shivering are common symptoms of catheter infection, and we observed that CVC use was associated with higher risk of infection-related hospitalisation [Incidence rate ratio: 3.16 (95% C.I.: 1.46, 6.70)] in our cohort.
The HDF group was significantly associated with lower occurrence of muscle cramps [OR: 0.57, (95% C.I.: 0.32, 0.98)], headache [OR: 0.51, (95% C.I.: 0.25, 0.98)], and tummy pain [OR: 0.31, (95% C.I.: 0.09, 0.87)] (Table 3). Headache was also reported to be less severe in the HDF group (P < 0.05) albeit with a small effect size. We observed no significant relationships between CVC use and HDF and the five KDQoL domain scores, Itch-5D score, or recovery time.
Conclusion
Our results demonstrate that the use of AVF or AVG as VA and HDF modality are associated with fewer and less severe patient-reported intradialytic symptoms in our stable prevalent HD cohort.

title: #3808 Bone density and vascular calcification association in patients on hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis
authors: Dimitra Bacharaki; Kyriaki Stamatelou; Eftyhia Gourdoupari; Evaggelia Pantzopoulou; Ourania Tsotsorou; Petros Nikolopoulos; Sophia Lionaki
abstract:
Background and Aims
Maintenance hemodialysis (HD) and peritoneal dialysis (PD) patients have higher incidence of bone fractures and cardiovascular morbidity and mortality compared to the general population. We aimed to investigate the association between bone density and vascular calcification in HD and PD patients.
Method
In a pilot observational cohort study we included 56 patients (39 HD, 17 PD), 34 men with mean age 60 (±13) years and dialysis vintage 41 months (15–74 range). Vascular calcification was recorded as abdominal aortic calcification (AAC) by Leena Kauppila (LK) score (range 0–24) in a lateral lumbar spine x-ray. It was categorized as low score if AAC ≤4 or increased if >4. Bone density was recorded based on DEXA scan of right femoral bone as normal (NBD), osteopenia or osteoporosis. Laboratory parameters of Chronic kidney disease- Mineral Bone Disorders were recorded plus drug use and the presence or no of cardiac valve calcification.
Results
The prevalence of increased AAC in the three bone density groups (normal 29%, osteopenia 46%, osteoporosis 25%) was respectively 31, 46 and 50% (P = 0.050). Serum levels of Parathormone, calcium and calcium phosphate product were statistically increased in osteoporosis group compared to NBD and osteopenia. The same was found for use of calcimimetics, vitamin D agonists, aspirin and heparin (see Table 1). In patients with osteopenia and osteoporosis (n = 40) higher serum magnesium was associated with lower risk of AAC >4 [OR = 0.05 (95%CI: 0.0–0.067)]. On the other hand heparin use between hemodialysis sessions [OR = 13.48 (95%CI: 1.53–119.13)], arterial hypertension [OR=16.77 (95% CI: 1.27–221.27)], cardiac valve calcification [OR = 12.54 (95% CI: 1.48–106.58)], were associated with higher risk of AAC >4. Increase of LK score by 1 was associated with almost 5 times higher risk of coronary artery disease [OR = 5.40 (95% CI: 1.18–64.25)]. In patients with NBD, male sex, pulse pressure and aspirin use were positive predictive factors of AAC >4.
Conclusion
In this pilot observational study, abnormal bone density and increased vascular calcification (AAC > 4) are highly prevalent in hemodialysis patients (71% and 43%). Maybe their investigation by simple tools as DEXA and LK score could help in identifying patients with high risk of cardiovascular disease.

title: #827 Effect of tenapanor on serum phosphorus (Pi), creatinine (Cre), and body weight (BW) gain in hemodialysis patients
authors: Shu Iwasawa; Takeshi Nakanishi; Takahiro Morino; Shinichi Nariyama; Tetsuya Noguchi; Takahiro Kuragano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyperphosphatemia occurs in most patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) and is associated with several adverse clinical outcomes. Intestinal inhibition of sodium/hydrogen exchanger isoform 3 (NHE3) by Tenapanor (TENAP) has been shown to reduce Pi absorption alongside sodium absorption inhibition, although the mechanism is not entirely elucidated. TENAP was originally developed for the treatment of constipation and not specifically as an intestinal Pi absorption inhibitor, leaving many unknown aspects from a clinical perspective. This study investigates the relationship between the serum Pi-lowering effect of TENAP and the increase in body weight between hemodialysis (HD) sessions, and other parameters.
Method
In 44 patients on maintenance HD who were able to take TENAP for at least three months and whose drug effects had stabilized, we studied the effects on weight gain and electrolyte changes. Weight gain during the two-day interdialysis period in patients receiving HD three times per week was observed. The effects of TENAP administration on serum Pi, creatinine (Cre), and body weight gain (ΔBW) were measured twice a month. Mean levels of Pi, Cre and ΔBW during the three-month period were compared between the three months before and after TENAP administration. We also evaluated the relationship between the changes in the mean values of the difference before and after treatment for each parameter (ΔPi, ΔCre, ΔBW).
Results
Most patients took 5 mg of TENAP twice daily before breakfast and dinner to alleviate constipation. In the analysis of the three months before and after TENAP administration, Pi levels significantly decreased in 26 patients, with no significant increase observed. In some patients, the administration of phosphate binders was reduced. After TENAP administration, Cre decreased significantly in 12 patients, and ΔBW decreased significantly in 13 patients.
