In HD patients, TENAP administration has been confirmed to stably lower serum Pi for a relatively long period. The decrease in Pi and the change in BW by TENAP administration have been suggested to be related to the inhibition of Na absorption by NHE3 in the gastrointestinal tract. It is also suggested that a decrease in Cre may occur in conjunction with a decrease in Pi, although the cause remains unknown.

title: #1476 Utility of multi-segmental bioimpedance for the diagnosis of sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity in dialysis
authors: Paula Gandía Ureña; Kerlin Vicent Rodriguez; Manuel Parra; Aina Quilis Pellicer; Elena Galván Barrilero; Laura Porcar Saura; Íñigo Alonso Escudero; Alba Durbà; MacArena Arancibia García; Belén Vizcaino Castillo; Asunción Sancho-Calabuig; Pablo Molina
abstract:
Background and Aims
Due to the overestimation of muscle mass (MM) caused by hyperhydration when using conventional bioimpedance monitors, it has historically been recommended to perform bioimpedance measurements 30 minutes after completing hemodialysis (HD). However, this complicates its applicability in routine clinical practice and the diagnosis of sarcopenia. A new bioimpedance device (InBody S10®) has recently emerged, with very limited experience in HD patients. It is unknown whether this device is less affected by hydration status.
Objective
To compare the prevalence of sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity using InBody measurements taken before and after a dialysis session (primary objective) and to assess changes in body composition before and after dialysis (secondary objectives).
Method
This observational study included stable HD patients whose prevalence of sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity was estimated using segmental multifrequency bioimpedance (InBody S10®) before and after an HD session. Sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity were diagnosed based on the EWGSOP2 2019 and ESPEN-EASO 2024 criteria, respectively. Muscle strength was assessed using handgrip dynamometry.
Results
A total of 35 HD patients were included [mean age: 68.9 ± 13.3 years; women: 37% (n = 13)], of whom 17 (49%) showed reduced handgrip strength. According to ESPEN-EASO criteria, the prevalence of hyperadiposity, sarcopenia, and sarcopenic obesity before the HD session was 40%, 31%, and 23%, respectively. The prevalence of all three parameters remained similar after dialysis (Fig. 1), despite an average ultrafiltration of 1921 mL (95% CI: 1606–2235). According to EWGSOP2 criteria, the prevalence of sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity tended to decrease from 29% to 20% post-HD, but this was not statistically significant (P = 0.13).
Significant differences were found in pre- and post-dialysis analyses for the following body composition variables: total skeletal muscle mass (P < 0.05), bone mineral mass, and phase angle (P < 0.01).
Conclusion
The prevalence of sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity estimated using the InBody S10 bioimpedance device does not appear to be significantly affected by the dialysis session, which may facilitate its implementation in routine clinical practice. However, variables such as phase angle and bone mineralization seem to be influenced by the hydration status of HD patients, suggesting the need to explore new tools to better understand how dialysis and overhydration affect body composition.

title: #1522 Impact of hemodialysis treatment start time on intradialytic sleep apnea patterns
authors: Andrea Nandorine Ban; Lin-Chun Wang; Peter Kotanko; Len Usvyat; Hanjie Zhang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Intradialytic hypoxemia is a common but often overlooked condition in patients undergoing maintenance hemodialysis (HD), potentially contributing to adverse clinical outcomes. Sleep apnea, a condition marked by intermittent "saw-tooth patterns" (STP) in arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2), may underlie some cases of intradialytic hypoxemia. Identifying these patterns during HD could provide critical insights into the prevalence of intradialytic sleep apnea and its clinical implications. This study aimed to estimate the distribution of SaO2 STPs based on the start time of HD treatments.
Method
We analyzed intradialytic SaO2 data from a large cohort of HD patients across the United States. SaO2 was continuously monitored during HD sessions using the Crit-Line Monitor (CLM; Fresenius Medical Care North America), an FDA-approved device for measuring oxygen saturation and hematocrit in the extracorporeal dialysis circuit. SaO2 data were recorded at 10-second intervals and transmitted to a secure cloud-based platform for analysis. Data was collected between January 14, 2021, and July 30, 2023.
SaO2 levels were tracked continuously during the HD sessions. To construct the one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D CNN), a random sample of HD sessions was chosen. The time series data from these sessions were segmented into consecutive 5-minute intervals, and each segment was independently reviewed by a physician and a researcher who categorized them as either containing a saw-tooth pattern or not. The trained 1D CNN was then applied to the entire dataset to classify each segment as exhibiting an STP or not. Figure 1 provides a visual example of SaO2 measurements during a single HD session, highlighting segments classified as STP by the 1D CNN.
The timing of these segments was categorized based on the hour during which the HD treatment began. For example, all 5-minute segments from treatments starting between 6:00 and 6:59 were assigned to the 6 hours. The STP rate was then calculated for each hourly category.
Results
Following rigorous data cleaning, the dataset included more than 3 million HD sessions from over 49,000 patients treated at 714 clinics. Analysis revealed that 11% of the 5-minute segments were classified as STP, while 89% were non-STP. The proportion of 5-minute segments exhibiting STP exceeded 15% in treatments starting between 4:00 and 4:59 local time. Conversely, the lowest STP rates were observed in treatments beginning between 14:00 and 15:59. These findings were further detailed in Fig. 2A, which shows the total number of 5-minute segments analyzed alongside the number of STPs for each hourly category, and Fig. 2B, which illustrates the hourly STP rates. Night, defined as a start time between 20:00 and 5:00, was associated with a higher prevalence of STP at 13.36%, compared to 10.77% during the daytime. Patients who initiated HD at night exhibited a significantly greater occurrence of STP (P < 0.00001).
Conclusion
Our results indicate a high rate of STP in patients who have started HD during the nighttime. Since patients may be more likely to sleep during night and since STP of SaO2 are a hallmark of sleep apnea, we hypothesize that sleep apnea is a likely condition in these patients. As a next step, patients with a high rate of SaO2 STP should undergo formal testing for sleep apnea and, if confirmed, receive adequate treatment.

title: #2258 Cognitive impairment and associated factors in patients undergoing hemodialysis
authors: Ana Alonso Fuente; Korina Peña Esparragoza; Rocio Gimena Muñoz; Mohammad Manouchehri; Cristina María Rodríguez Poza; Diego Rodríguez-Puyol; Patricia Martínez Miguel
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cognitive impairment is highly prevalent among patients undergoing hemodialysis, and its origin appears to be multifactorial. The aim of this study is to evaluate the prevalence of cognitive impairment in patients from our Hemodialysis Unit and identify the factors associated with it.
Method
A cross-sectional study was conducted on patients undergoing hemodialysis, excluding those with a confirmed diagnosis of dementia. Cognitive impairment was assessed using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA) test. Clinical history data were collected, the meaning of various laboratory parameters over the past year was determined, and the presence of sarcopenia was evaluated by analyzing muscle mass through bioimpedance and strength through dynamometry. Statistical analysis was performed using parametric tests, with statistical significance set at P < 0.05.
Results
A total of 52 patients were included in the study, with a cognitive impairment prevalence of 63.5%. The most relevant results are shown in the Table 1. Age (r = −0.480; P < 0.001) and months on hemodialysis (r = −0.402; P = 0.004) were negatively correlated with the MOCA test, indicating an increase in cognitive impairment with advancing age and longer duration on hemodialysis.
Conclusion
Cognitive impairment is highly prevalent among patients undergoing hemodialysis. In our study, sarcopenia was not associated with cognitive impairment. However, patients with cognitive impairment exhibited lower phosphorus levels. Additionally, their weight tended to be lower, which may suggest that nutritional and metabolic factors could influence this condition. Clearly, age, duration of hemodialysis, and a history of cardiovascular disease were associated with cognitive impairment. Interventions aimed at improving dialysis techniques and preventing vascular disease could be beneficial in mitigating this condition.

title: #3455 Why are ultrasound parameters not sufficiently informative to predict the risk of primary AVF dysfunction?
authors: Ekaterina Parshina; Aleksei Zulkarnaev; Vadim Stepanov; Bylov Konstantin; Natalia Fominykh
abstract:
Background and Aims
Doppler ultrasound (DUS) parameters can be used to predict primary dysfunction of native AVF. In practice, this is often simplified to identifying binary thresholds of parameters that allow to classify patients as having a high or low risk of primary dysfunction. However, this approach often works poorly and does not provide sufficient power. Aim: to model the association of the most common DUS parameters with the risk of various variants of primary AVF dysfunction.
Method
A retrospective case-control study included 40 adult patients with normal AVF maturation (successful puncture 3 months after creation), 37 patients with AVF thrombosis before first use within three months after creation, and 32 patients with immaturation: AVF functioning but not available for puncture three in months after creation.
The threshold of normal maturation at 3 months was defined due to local criteria.
All patients received a native AVF in the lower third of the forearm of the non-dominant upper limb. To reduce the influence of other factors, we did not include patients with coagulopathy, hypotension, vasculitis, history of drug abuse, etc.
DUS is routinely performed on all patients. The diameter of the cephalic vein (V_d) with compression at the shoulder, the length of its segment with a depth less than 6 mm from the skin (V_length), the diameter of the radial artery (A_d), the volume blood flow (VBF) and the resistive index in the reactive hyperemia test (RH_RI) [1] were evaluated.
Modelling was performed using multinomial logistic regression with three outcomes of interest: maturation, immaturation and thrombosis.
Results
The model fitted the observed data well: Nagelkerke R² 0.75 (full vs. null model), AUC 0.93 [95%CI 0.87; 0.99] for normal maturation, AUC 0.89 [95%CI 0.82; 0.96] for thrombosis and AUC 0.88 [95%CI 0.81; 0.96] for immaturation.
Within relatively favourable conditions (fixed V_d = 4 mm, V_length = 70 mm, A_d = 3 mm, VBF = 30 ml/min and RH_RI = 0.5), the reduction in vein and artery diameter is mainly associated with the risk of thrombosis, the risk of primary dysfunction is almost independent of vein extension with a depth of less than 6 mm. An increase in the resistive index greater than 0.7–0.8 significantly increases the risk of primary dysfunction, mainly by increasing the risk of immaturation—Fig. 1.
In other conditions, as illustrated in Fig. 2 (V_d = 2.5 mm, V_length = 60 mm, A_d = 2 mm, VBF = 20 ml/min and RH_RI = 0.5), DUS indices are differently associated with the risk of primary dysfunction.
The Figs 1 and 2 show that within different conditions, various DUS parameters have different optimal cut-offs for classifying a patient as being at high risk of primary dysfunction.
Conclusion
Individual DUS parameters allow poor prediction of the risk of primary dysfunction (and its variants), because each parameter has different informativeness at different values of other parameters. The risk of dysfunction cannot be assessed on the basis of a single DUS parameter. Probably the decision tree based on a set of DUS parameters may be a solution.

title: #15 Efficacy of ginger on lipid profile and fasting blood glucose in diabetic patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis: a systematic review & meta-analysis
authors: Zeyad Elariny; Marwan Farhan; Abdelrahman Ali; Seif Sayed
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death among peritoneal dialysis (PD) patients, driven by lipid abnormalities, elevated serum glucose, and systemic and vascular inflammation. These factors not only accelerate disease progression but also severely affect the quality of life for these patients. With increasing interest in natural therapies, ginger (Zingiber officinale), a safe and widely used spice, has shown potential to improve fasting glucose, glycemic control, lipid profiles, and overall nutritional health. In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we aim to evaluate its efficacy in diabetic PD patients.
Method
Following the PRISMA guidelines, we searched databases to identify relevant RCTs. Using RevMan 5.4 software, we analyzed outcomes, including serum concentrations of triglycerides, total cholesterol, LDL-C, and fasting blood glucose. Pooled mean difference (MD) and their 95% confidence interval (CI) were calculated using the inverse variance method.
Results
We included four RCTs with a total of 154 patients. Compared to the placebo group (control), patients who received ginger (Zingiber officinale) showed significant improvement in serum concentrations of triglycerides, total cholesterol, and fasting blood glucose (MD = −31.6, 95% CI [−36.9 to −26.4], P = 0.00001), (MD = −6.9, 95% CI [−12.89 to −0.93], P = 0.02), and (MD = −45.4, 95% CI [−54 to −36.9], P = 0.00001), respectively. There was no significant difference in LDL-C between the two groups (MD = −3.38, 95% CI [−8.11 to 1.36], P = 0.19).
Conclusion
Ginger (Zingiber officinale) is significantly efficacious in improving lipid profiles and fasting blood glucose in diabetic patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis. Further RCTs on more diverse populations still need to be conducted.

title: #149 Evolution of clinical performance metrics in chronic dialysis patients: a comparative analysis of DaVita Kidney Care Brazil and global standards
authors: Bruno Zawadzki; Rogerio Da Hora; Fernanda Coelho; Ana Vieira; Bruno Vieira; Cristina Pinto; Danilo Cunha; Eric Correa; Fabio Reis; Marcelo Lopes; Priscila Sampaio
abstract:
Background and Aims
The quality of dialysis care is assessed by key clinical indicators, including dialysis adequacy (Kt/V), vascular access type (fistula vs. catheter), and anemia management. Achieving optimal levels in these areas is critical to improving patient outcomes and reducing complications. While global nephrology guidelines emphasize Kt/V ≥1.2, DaVita Kidney Care (DKC) Brazil has adopted a more ambitious threshold of Kt/V ≥1.3 to drive further improvements in dialysis adequacy. This study evaluates the evolution of these clinical performance metrics at DKC Brazil, comparing them to global and national benchmarks using data from the SBN Census 2023, ISN Atlas 2023, Lancet Report 2024, and the ERA-EDTA 2022 Registry.
To analyze the evolution of clinical performance indicators at DKC Brazil (December 2024), particularly Kt/V achievement, vascular access rates (AVF vs. CVC), and anemia management, and compare these outcomes with national and international data.
Methods
We retrospectively analyzed data from DKC Brazil's BI dashboard (December 2024), assessing trends in dialysis adequacy (Kt/V), vascular access, and anemia management from January of 2023 to December 2024. These were compared with national data from the SBN Census 2023 and global benchmarks from the ERA-EDTA Registry 2022, ISN Atlas 2023, and recent literature (Lancet 2024). Key metrics included:
- Kt/V ≥1.3 (as per DKC Brazil's internal KPI) vs. the benchmark of Kt/V ≥1.2 - Percentage of patients with arteriovenous fistula (AVF) vs. central venous catheter (CVC) - Anemia management (Hb levels, iron and ESA therapy usage)
Results
Dialysis Adequacy (Kt/V Achievement) At DKC Brazil (December 2024), 78% of patients achieved Kt/V ≥1.3, reflecting a continuous improvement in dialysis adequacy.This is significant when compared to early 2023, where only 75% met Kt/V ≥1.2, demonstrating a consistent upward trend despite adopting a stricter KPI.The ERA-EDTA Registry 2022 reported a median Kt/V of ∼1.2, indicating that DKC Brazil's performance is aligned with or surpasses international standards. Vascular Access (AVF vs. CVC Usage) The use of arteriovenous fistula (AVF) at DKC Brazil increased to 78.5% in Dec 2024, surpassing the SBN Census 2023 national average of 74%.This trend aligns with global best practices, as the ERA-EDTA Registry reports an AVF prevalence of ∼80% across European countries.Conversely, CVC usage at DKC Brazil decreased to 21.5%, approaching international benchmarks for catheter reduction. Anemia Management 83% of patients at DKC Brazil maintained Hb between 10-12 g/dL, within the KDIGO-recommended range.ESA (erythropoiesis-stimulating agents) use was optimized, with targeted therapy adjustments based on ferritin and transferrin saturation (TSAT) levels.The prevalence of Hb <10 g/dL decreased by 10% compared to early 2023, indicating improved anemia control.
Conclusion

title: #297 Subcutaneous lignocaine for CKDaP in a haemodialysis patient—time to revisit an old remedy
authors: Kelly Chenlei Li; Elizabeth Josland; Skye Xu; Frank Brennan
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease associated pruritus (CKDaP) affects around 60% of dialysis patients and can significantly impair sleep, mood, and quality of life. The pathophysiology of CKDaP is complex and incompletely understood, and is thought to involve non-histamine dependent pruritic pathways. Treatment options are limited.
Method
Case: A 65 year old woman with kidney failure from single kidney and diabetic kidney disease has been on haemodialysis (HD) for 4 years. Her long history of severe itch started 6 months prior to dialysis initiation, and the diagnosis of CKDaP was supported by dermatology assessment including skin biopsy. Biochemistry, apart from a short period of acute illness, has been consistently within target, with Ca <2.6 mmol/L, PO4 <2 mmol/L, and PTH <30 pmol/L during the 4 years.
In addition to skin emollients, treatments sequentially included pregabalin up to a daily dose of 75 mg, Evening Primrose Oil oral capsules up to 2 daily, dialysis initiation with extended hours nocturnal HD to optimise clearance (>6 hours, Kt/V >2), oral cetirizine 10 mg daily, and topical compound ointment (menthol 5%, lignocaine 7%, and capsaicin 0.025%). Treatments had, at best, partial responses, and subsequent reescalation of symptoms occurred within weeks to months. Difelikefalin at 0.5 mcg/kg 3 times weekly post dialysis did result in dramatic improvement in itch, but 18 months later, itch had surged. Difelikefalin was increased to 1 mcg/kg, with a further 5 months of good symptom control.
Results
Thereafter, the patient developed an acute exacerbation of itch affecting her entire body, associated with severe sleep disturbance, ferocious scratching (Fig. 1), and emotional distress, despite continuing her existing treatments of emollients, pregabalin, difelikefalin 1 mcg/kg, and an empirical course of ivermectin (follow up of skin scraping for scabies were negative). Dermatology assessment confirmed CKDaP. She commenced continuous subcutaneous infusion (CSCI) of lignocaine at 200 mg over 24 hours, with up-titration to 600 mg CSCI over 24 hours. Itch had almost completely resolved by day 4, but rapid cessation of lignocaine at day 5 led to an acute surge in itch at day 9, and lignocaine was recommenced, with good result 48 hours later. At day 14, lignocaine was weaned and transitioned to ongoing oral mexiletine 150 mg twice daily. 4 months later, itch continued to be mild.
Conclusion
Case Discussion: CKDaP is a challenging condition to manage and severe cases can be extremely distressing for patients. Lignocaine blocks sodium channels in neuronal cell membranes and is widely and safely administered by CSCI in palliative care settings for pain relief. Its use is also described for intractable itch in T cell lymphoma, another condition associated with non-histamine-dependent pruritic pathways. Parenteral Iignocaine on haemodialysis has been tested and found efficacious as early as 1977 [1] but not routinely used, presumably due to monitoring, logistical, or safety concerns. The use of lignocaine as CSCI, and ongoing treatment with mexiletine, an oral medication with the same mechanism of action, may provide a therapeutic option for intractable CKDaP.

title: #462 Intimal hyperplasia rate as a predictor of hemodialysis arteriovenous fistula on the primary patency after percutaneous transluminal angioplasty
authors: Xuyang Luo; Wei Yang; Yuwei Kang; Shijie MA; Yi Fan; Jiaojiao Du; Huan Luo; Xudong Wang; Fei Deng
abstract:
Background and Aims
Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA) is an important method for evaluating hemodialysis dysfunction. We investigated factors associated with post-PTA primary patency rate in patients with arteriovenous fistula (AVF), including the intimal hyperplasia rate and previously reported factors. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of intimal hyperplasia rate on the outcomes of PTA for de novo dysfunctional AVF lesions.
Method
The medical records at Sichuan Provincial People’ s Hospital were collected to retrospectively identify and analyze general information, clinical characteristics, and hemodialysis-related factors for post-PTA primary patency in a cohort of 66 patients with AVF who underwent PTA after vascular access construction between January 2019 and December 2023. They were followed up for 12 months. When the patients needed to treat with PTA or AVF reconstruction due to re-occlusion, follow-up was terminated. The morphological assessment of stenotic lesion in dysfunctional AVF using ultrasound. Morphological assessment of stenotic lesion at the minimum lumen area site was conducted using ultrasound imaging to determine the intimal hyperplasia rate. The inner and outer diameters at the stenotic site were measured, and the intimal hyperplasia rate was calculated using the following formula: Intimal hyperplasia rate (%) = (outer diameter − inner diameter)/outer diameter.
Results
Multivariate analysis with the Cox proportional hazard model showed that post-PTA primary patency in patients with AVF is significantly associated with the intimal hyperplasia rate (hazard ratio 3785.345, 95% confidence interval 83.537 ∼ 171526.979, P < 0.001). ROC curve analysis showed that the intimal hyperplasia rate difference was statistically significant (AUC = 0.748, 95% confidence interval 0.630–0.866; P < 0.001) and had predictive value; the cut-off value of the intimal hyperplasia rate was 0.556. When the intimal hyperplasia rate was stratified into two categories, the risk of outcome events defining the end of post-PTA primary patency was significantly greater for >0.556 (hazard ratio 0.124, 95% confidence interval 0.029–0.527) than for <0.556 (P < 0.001).
Conclusion
The intimal hyperplasia rate is an important predictive factor for post-PTA primary patency in patients with AVF.
Keywords Hemodialysis, patency, intimal hyperplasia rate, percutaneous transluminal angioplasty, arteriovenous fistula

title: #575 Mapping national variation in haemodialysis central venous catheter management: a UK-wide survey
authors: Yimeng Zhang; Saeed Ahmed; Tamasin Stevenson; Jyoti Baharani
abstract:
Background and Aims
Both the UK Kidney Association (UKKA) and Kidney Disease Outcomes Quality Initiative (KDOQI) have limited guidance on the insertion and removal of HD central venous catheter (CVC) lines. Anecdotally the practice across the UK is not consistent with variations in clinical practice. While some Trusts maintain local guidelines, standardized national protocols are lacking. We aimed to evaluate current practices related to HD CVC insertion and removal within UK renal units to identify variations and highlight potential best practices.
Method
An online questionnaire on the local protocol and practice surrounding temporary and tunnelled HD line insertions and removals was used. Information surveyed included individual renal centre's procedural protocols such as operator, assistant, location, personal protective equipment (PPE) and infection prevention practices. The online survey was finalized in December 2023 and disseminated nationally. A list of the 72 main rental units were obtained from the UK Kidney Association (UKKA). The number of responses per centre was not limited.
Results
120 responses were obtained over the nine-month data collection period. 4 responses were excluded as they were from centres not considered as a ‘main renal unit’ by UKKA. Two units have since merged, and hence data from 71 renal units were utilized. Duplicated responses from the same renal centre were removed and responses from senior nephrologists prioritized.
42 (59%) of the centres analysed stated to have an interventional nephrology service. In 70 (99%) and 55 (77%) of centres, renal registrar and consultants insert temporary dialysis lines respectively. Temporary dialysis lines are most often removed by the ward nurses (69%) and the dialysis nurse (42%). Renal staff commonly insert both inpatient and outpatient right internal jugular and femoral tunnelled dialysis lines. The remainder of the lines are most frequently done by the interventional radiology team.
Among the centres, the median number of days which temporary femoral dialysis lines should remain in place is 7, and14 days for temporary internal jugular dialysis lines.
The majority of centres do not use heparin during the first dialysis following a temporary (59%) or tunnelled line (61%) insertion.
Most centres use a BiopatchTM or similar dressing over the exit sites of temporary (62%) and tunnelled lines (72%). 21 (30%) and 10 (14%) units do not routinely use any MSSA/ MRSA decolonization following temporary and tunnelled line insertions respectively. In units which use decolonization treatment, the most common treatments are mupirocin nasal ointment, octensian skin lotion and chlorhexidine wash.
Conclusion
Our results indicate substantial variability in the practices of inserting and removing of both temporary and tunnelled haemodialysis lines nationally. These findings underscore the need for nationally standardized, evidence-based guidelines to improve patient safety, reduce complications, and enhance overall care quality. Sharing these results within the renal community may inform future consensus building and policy development.

title: #838 Development of a support system for patients on dialysis: functionality for assisting dietary therapy
authors: Akiko Okawa; Tokuo Umeda; Natsumi Yamamoto; Masahiro Itou
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients on hemodialysis are required to self-manage aspects of daily life, such as vital signs, dialysis information, and dietary intake. However, the burden of such self-management often results in nonadherence. Recent studies have emphasized the need for comprehensive kidney rehabilitation (“kidney rehab”) to mitigate the physical and psychological impacts of kidney disease, improve symptoms, and enhance life expectancy. This long-term program includes exercise therapy, dietary and fluid management, medication management, education, and psychological support, with dietary therapy serving as a core component. Dietary therapy has been shown to significantly improve the quality of life (QOL) of patients on dialysis. Despite its importance, the long-term nature of kidney rehab poses challenges to consistent adherence. Previously, we developed a regional support system for patients on dialysis that promotes the implementation and continuation of exercise therapy (see “Development of a Support System for Patients on Dialysis: Examining the Implementation and Continuation of Exercise Therapy”). Building on this system, we have now added functionality to support dietary therapy, a key element of kidney rehab.
Method
Figure 1 shows an example of the patient-side system display. The support system allows patients to record key dialysis-related data:
Daily record: start time of dialysis, dialysate/plasma ratio, drainage volume, infusion volume, water removal volume, drainage time, drainage volume, blood pressure, and blood glucose. Drainage color check: patients can upload photos of their drainage packs. Vital signs: a button is provided for inputting daily vital signs data. Data entry is facilitated through automated input or dropdown menus to reduce errors. A Notifications section allows patients and healthcare providers to send and receive messages, ensuring efficient communication. In addition, the system integrates dietary information, enabling patients to input their meals as text or upload photos of their meals. The system automatically registers timestamps for all records.
Results
A trial of the enhanced support system featuring dietary therapy functionality was conducted with simulated patients on dialysis. Figure 2 shows an example of the institution-side display. Daily record: patients could log dialysis details using a dropdown menu or by selecting file uploads to avoid input errors. Input fields allowed for dialysis-related data and photos of dialysis sites to be recorded. Automated timestamps were implemented.
Dietary records: patients could document their meals via text or by uploading photos. These entries were timestamped automatically, ensuring chronological accuracy.
Healthcare provider access: as shown in Fig. 2, healthcare providers could review patient data, including dietary records, by selecting individual patients within the system. Notifications: The notifications section facilitated bidirectional messaging between patients and providers. New notifications were highlighted using banners for visibility.
Conclusion
The developed support system, designed to assist patients on dialysis, now includes functionality to support dietary therapy based on the principles of kidney rehab. This enhancement enables the sharing of dietary and dialysis records between patients and healthcare providers, aiding in better monitoring of patients’ conditions. Consequently, patients can share their dietary data consistently, regardless of dialysis days. Healthcare providers can provide timely advice on dietary habits through the Notifications feature, improving adherence to dietary therapy. This system offers a promising solution for overcoming the challenges of long-term dietary therapy adherence.
This research was supported in part by Gakushin Kaken (JP20H03982).

title: #885 Urodynamic finding and urinary symptoms in patienmts undergoing hemodialysis
authors: Giovanni Palleschi; Valeria Rossi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) affect patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) undergoing hemodialysis (HD). These symptoms reduce the quality of life and can be responsible for severe complications. Furthermore, patients on waiting list for kidney transplantation that are not adequately treated risk to develop functional damages to the graft in case of transplant. We investigated LUTS in patients attending our HD center and explored their urodynamic (UD) outcomes.
Method
From January 2022 to July 2024, clinical, laboratory, and UD outcomes have been extracted from two electronic database systems of our HD center. The following symptoms were assessed: urinary urgency and frequency, nocturia, urinary incontinence, urinary burning, poor voiding flow, haematuria, bladder pain. Prevalence of symptoms in the population was assessed, and correlation with UD findings was explored. Demographic data were evaluated by the Student T test; Chi-Square test was applied for nominal data. Correlation between type of symptoms, patients’ age, dialytic age, were calculated using the Spearman correlation test.
Results
A total number of 199 patients (101 males, 98 females) has attended our HD center during the time interval of this investigation. Patients were caucasian, mean age was 71,4 (range 20–86) years. Mean dialytic time of the cohort resulted 51.4 months (range 4–78). Dialytic age and mean age did not significantly differ between sexes. Anuric individuals were 45% of the cohort diaries. The following symptoms were reported (as number of events): urinary burning (122), urinary frequency (108), urinary urgency (102), nocturia (67), poor voiding flow (52), hematuria (39), urinary incontinence (22), pelvic pain (11). The total number of events caused by LUTS was 523 and represented the third reason for seeking medical assistance by these patients in the time interval of this study, if compared with cardiovascular symptoms (923 records), respiratory symptoms (788 records), abdominal symptoms (478 records), other minor symptoms (460 records). Patients with shorter dialytic age and residual renal function had more nocturia than subjects with longer dialytic age and anuric (coefficient −0.22, P < 0,01). Urinary urgency and urinary frequency were symptoms significantly associated with the diagnosis of diabetes either in men and in women (coefficient 1,16, P > 0.01) and to blood hypertension in men (coefficient 1,13 P > 0.01). Sixty-one patients of the cohort (40 males, 21 females) underwent UD due to persistent urinary urgency and urinary frequency, recurrent bacterial urinary tract infections, urinary burning, bladder pain, stress urinary incontinence. UD findings were represented by detrusor overactivity, bladder outlet obstruction, detrusor underactivity, reduced bladder compliance, sphincteric striated urethral deficiency.
Conclusion
LUTS can be considered a prevalent condition in our population, being urinary burning associated with urinary tract infection the most represented. Nocturia resulted associated with diabetes and dialytic age. Concerning UD findings, bladder functional alterations in patients undergoing HD are often the consequence of progressive reduction of bladder filling and emptying cycle that is associated with bladder atrophy. In subjects waiting for kidney transplant, UD may contribute to prevent that functional alteration of lower urinary tract put on risk the transplanted kidney.

title: #933 How to increase PD based on cost-effectivenes analysis in Polish heathcare system
authors: Jacek Zawierucha; Cezary Pruszko; Karolina Dziadek; Magdalena Stefańska-Dzik; Wojciech Marcinkowski; Jacek Lange; Jolanta Malyszko
abstract:
Background and Aims
Peritoneal dialysis (PD) is one of well-established renal replacement therapy method and its usefulness is unquestionable. Despite this fact the number of patients treated with PD in Poland remains on the level about 4% of all patients treated with dialysis. There are several reasons of such low patients ratio e.g. late referral to dialysis, limited access to PD services as well as procedure description and public Payer requirements.
The aim of analysis was peritoneal dialysis cost-effectiveness assessment compared with hemodialysis in patients starting chronic dialysis treatment and detailed comparison of both methods in terms of their cost-effectiveness for healthcare system.
This study also assessed the impact of increasing the prevalence of peritoneal dialysis compared to hemodialysis on the Polish healthcare system.
Method
Assessment of cost-effectiveness of peritoneal dialysis versus hemodialysis was performed on cost-utility analysis basis, which result is incremental cost-utility ratio (ICUR) where the measure of health effect is quality-adjusted life years (QUALY). Health effect assessment was made on systematic review basis (studies comparing directly hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis have been taken into consideration).
Additionally one way sensitivity analysis was perform to check additional factors which may influence on ICUR.
In budget impact analysis three scenarios have been taken into consideration – current status as base scenario and two additional scenarios with PD patients population growth in 5 years horizon (where the PD patient population will grow to 10% patients on dialysis in the fifth year)
All calculations were performed according Polish Health Technology Assessment (HTA) regulations.
Results
The analysis showed that peritoneal dialysis is cost-effective compared to hemodialysis. The costs of an additional quality-adjusted life year obtained using PD instead of HD are lower than the applicable cost-effectiveness threshold (set, according to Polish HTA recommendation, at PLN 217,641).
Peritoneal dialysis generates additional savings for the payer in selected cost categories like hospitalizations, costs of creating renal replacement access and costs related to deaths.
Also peritoneal dialysis instead of hemodialysis is a treatment option with superior health benefits in terms of quality-adjusted survival.
Results of one-way sensitivity analysis, conducted for the results of cost-utility and cost-consequence analysis indicate the possibility to get even better results (lower ICUR rate) than in the basic analysis. The main factor improving the results is PD patients better quality of life arising from possibility of home treatment and higher independence, less visits in hospital/dialysis center, lower dietary and fluid restrictions, possibility of professional of social activity at an unchanged level.
Budget impact analysis shows that PD patients ratio increase (from 4% to 10% of dialyzed patients population) won't significantly influence on total healthcare system spendings for dialysis. In 5 years horizon this change will generate 0.7% growth of overall spending for dialysis.
Conclusion
According to analysis performed, peritoneal dialysis appears as cost effective treatment option from healthcare system perspective. The origin of low PD patient number lies in other limitations like regulatory barriers (procedure description and public payer requirements), low awareness of possible treatment option (low quality or lack of predialysis education) and late referral to dialysis. To increase PD patients population in Poland systemic changes are needed—incentive for the centers achieving specified PD ratio, obligation for predialysis education for all patients referred to renal replacement therapy, access facilitation for the patients unable to self-treatment (assisted PD with nurse or medical assistant).

title: #1105 PAn-european Registry Addressing Difelikefalin in Goal-oriented Medical treatment for chronic kidney disease-associated pruritus (PARADIGM): study design and research goals
authors: Angelo Karaboyas; Sammantha Fuller; Michelle Maxim; Despina Ruessmann; Roberto Pecoits-Filho
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease-associated pruritus (CKD-aP) affects 40%–60% of patients with kidney failure undergoing hemodialysis (HD). This debilitating condition significantly impacts health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and is associated with poor sleep, depression, hospitalization, and increased mortality. Despite its high prevalence, CKD-aP remains under-recognized and inadequately treated, with limited therapeutic options. Difelikefalin (DFK), a selective kappa-opioid receptor agonist, was approved by the FDA 2021 and EMA in 2022 for CKD-aP treatment. Clinical trials have shown DFK reduces pruritus, improves HRQoL, and alleviates symptoms like sleep disturbances in dialysis patients. However, real-world data on DFK's effectiveness, safety, and healthcare resource utilization (HCRU) are limited, necessitating further investigation. The Pan-European Registry Addressing Difelikefalin in Goal-oriented Medical treatment for chronic kidney disease-associated pruritus (PARADIGM) study aims to fill this gap by collecting real-world data on the use of DFK in patients undergoing HD. PARADIGM aims to (i) characterize patients initiating DFK, (ii) examine treatment patterns, (iii) assess effectiveness, (iv) evaluate safety and tolerability, and (v) assess HCRU among HD patients taking DFK.
Method
PARADIGM is an investigator-initiated, observational treatment registry led by Arbor Research Collaborative for Health, an organization serving as the coordinating center for the Dialysis Outcomes and Practice Patterns Study (DOPPS). PARADIGM will collect data from at least 400 DFK initiators across HD facilities in France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and the United Kingdom. Adult patients initiating DFK for CKD-aP while receiving in-center HD are eligible. Data will be collected via medical records, patient-reported outcome (PRO) questionnaires, and facility questionnaires, using ArborLink, a web-based electronic data collection system.
At baseline (prior to DFK initiation), and at months 1, 3, 6, and 12 after DFK initiation, data on DFK prescription, medications, dialysis characteristics, lab measurements, and hospitalizations will be collected via medical record review. At each of the aforementioned timepoints, patients will complete PRO questionnaires, which include validated instruments, to assess itch severity, sleep quality, fatigue, depression, life participation, fall risk, dialysis recovery, side effects/symptoms, and HCRU. In patients who continue DFK treatment beyond 12 months, data collection will continue in 6 months intervals. If DFK is discontinued, providers will report reasons for discontinuation, and patients will complete follow-up PRO questionnaires 2 weeks, 2 months, and 6 months after their last treatment. Annual facility questionnaires will track DFK uptake and prescribing practices at participating facilities.
Results
Results from PARADIGM are not yet available, as patient recruitment is expected to begin in Q2 2025. PRO questionnaires will assess changes in itch severity, sleep quality, fatigue, depression, and life participation. Safety and tolerability will be evaluated through adverse events (e.g. dizziness, somnolence) monitoring, while HCRU analysis will focus on hospitalizations, emergency department visits, missed dialysis sessions, and healthcare referrals.
Conclusion
The PARADIGM study will advance the clinical understanding of CKD-aP treatment and provide essential real-world data on the use of DFK in the management of this condition in HD patients. By evaluating treatment patterns, effectiveness, safety, and HCRU, the study will help optimize DFK's role in CKD-aP management. The findings will inform clinical practice guideline development, future clinical trials, regulatory decisions, and healthcare policy, ultimately improving patient outcomes and enhancing the quality of life for CKD-aP patients undergoing hemodialysis.

title: #1458 Prevalence of smoking and smoking effect on the CKD-related mortality of French dialysis patients
authors: Sacha Lavaud; Judith Breaud; Cécile Couchoud; Sahar Bayat; Juste Goungounga
abstract:
Background and Aims
Smoking has been described in the literature as a factor associated with kidney failure, an increased risk of cancer in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and lower access to transplantation. However, few studies have investigated its role in the mortality associated with CKD in France. This study aims to investigate the factors associated with smoking prevalence and its role on the CKD-related mortality among French dialysis patients.
Method
Thanks to the French Epidemiologic and Information Network in Nephrology (REIN) 29,281 patients aged between 18 and 85 years old who started dialysis between 2017 and 2019 were included in the study and followed until the end of 2022. Patient's characteristics and neighbourhood social deprivation level (the European deprivation index (EDI)) were extracted. A joint modelling imputation was performed due the presence of missing data in smoking and EDI. A multinomial logistic regression with a random effect of department was used to assess the factors associated with smoking prevalence. Survival analysis was conducted, using the excess hazard modelling framework with a random effect to account for the presence of territorial inequalities between French departments in terms of mortality.
Results
Among the 29,281 included patients, 11,425 (39.02 %) died during the follow-up time. Regarding the smoking status, 5,375 patients had missing data (18.3 %). Of the remaining 23,906 complete data, 3,619 (15.1 %) patients were current smokers, 7,966 (33.3 %) were former smokers and 12,321 (51.5 %) were non-smokers. The odds of being a former smoker and current smoker compared to non-smoker were lower for female, respectively, (OR: 0.34 [0.32, 0.37]) and (OR: 0.2 [0.18, 0.21]). The odds of being current smoker was not associated with social deprivation and decreased with age. The CKD-related mortality increased for former smokers (EHR 1.24 [1.15, 1.32]) and for current smokers (EHR 1.51 [1.38, 1.64]). The standard error of random effects was significant, indicating heterogeneity in CKD-related mortality between departments.
Conclusion
To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first to quantify the smoking effect on the CKD-related mortality of dialyzed patients. Further analysis will be conducted to distinguish heterogeneity in excess mortality from expected mortality aiming to better understand territorial inequalities in the mortality of dialyzed patients.

title: #1462 Dialysis symptoms relation with medication beliefs and medication compliance in dialysis patients
authors: Fatma Elİf Erİşen; Murat Tugcu; Izzet Hakki Arikan; Ebru Asicioglu; Arzu Velioglu; Dilek Barutcu Atas; Z Serhan Tuglular; Mehmet Koc
abstract:
Background and Aims
Non-compliance with drug therapy is an important problem in patients receiving dialysis treatment and can cause an increase in healthcare costs, morbidity and mortality, and may make it difficult to improve symptoms in patients. Many studies have been conducted to evaluate medication compliance and thoughts about medication in hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis patients, but we have not encountered many examples in the literature that evaluate these two groups mutually. The aim of our study is to determine medication compliance and medication confidence in dialysis patients and its relationship with dialysis symptoms.
Method
A total of 460 patients, 379 receiving hemodialysis and 81 peritoneal dialysis treatments from 5 different centers, were included in the study. It is a cross-sectional study. BMQ (Medication Beliefs Scale), MARS-5 (Medication Compliance Report Scale) and DSI (Dialysis Symptom Index) questionnaires were administered to the participants face to face and the data were recorded. Other demographic and clinical data were obtained from patient files and recorded. Patient data were analyzed in R (version 4.2.2).
Results
55% (n:255) of the patients included in the study were male. The total MARS-5 score of HD patients was 23.7 (SD = 2.44), and the total MARS-5 score of PD patients was 23.64 (SD = 2.4) (P = 0.35). Most of all patients (71% n:329) had good medication compliance (MARS-5 total score > 23), while a minority of patients (29% n:131) had poor medication compliance (MARS-5 total score ≤ 23) (P = 0.001). In the BMQ survey, the majority of all patients (95% n:438) had positive thoughts about drugs (BMQ1-BMQ2 score > 0), and a very small number (5% n:22) had negative thoughts about drugs (BMQ1-BMQ2 score ≤ 0) (P = 0.001). The mean BMQ1-BMQ2 score of patients with good medication compliance was found to be higher at 17.1 (SD = 5.7) (P = 0.001). The mean MARS-5 total score was found to be higher in patients with positive thoughts about medications, at 23.8 (SD = 2.3) (P = 0.001). The most common symptom was fatigue (78% n:361). Other most common symptoms are muscle cramps (69% n:316), feeling sad (62% n:286), itching (59% n:271), sleep problems (54% n:249), constipation (52% n:238), nausea (43% n:238). Nausea (P = 0.001) and involuntary movements in the legs (P = 0.002) were less common in the group with good medication compliance. Itching (P = 0.002) and leg swelling (P = 0.007) were less common in the group with positive thoughts about the drug.
Conclusion
While medication compliance was evaluated as good in the majority of patients in our study, it is noteworthy that patients with good medication compliance had more positive thoughts about medications. In addition, the fact that some symptoms are less common in those with better medication compliance confirms the effectiveness of medication compliance in treatment. There is no significant difference between hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis patients in terms of medication compliance, medication-related beliefs and symptom burden.
Keywords: dialysis, medication compliance, beliefs about medication

title: #1525 Sex-specific arterial remodeling in AVF maturation: implications for personalized vascular access management in ESKD in young women
authors: Stella Bedogni; Claudia Morganti; Vincenzo Oliva; Umberto Maggiore; Enrico Fiaccadori; Tommaso Di Motta; Sara Alibrandi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Arteriovenous fistula (AVF) is the preferred vascular access for hemodialysis (HD) in end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) due to its superior long-term patency and lower complication rates. The maturation process of an AVF involves complex vascular remodeling of both the inflow artery and outflow vein, mediated by hemodynamic and inflammatory pathways over a 4–6-week period. A sex difference in AVF outcome is in debate, with studies documenting women experiencing lower patency rates, delayed maturation and an increased risk of complications and reinterventions, while others have reported no significant sex-based differences. This discrepancy has intensified research interest in elucidating the potential sex-specific factors influencing vascular remodeling during AVF maturation. Despite this growing focus, the arterial adaptations occurring during AVF development remain inadequately characterized, highlighting a critical knowledge gap in the field. This study aims to address this limitation by investigating the sex-specific arterial changes during AVF maturation, potentially informing more personalized approaches to vascular access management in ESKD patients.
Method
We conducted a single-center retrospective study from December 2021 to March 2024, involving 55 ESKD patients (37 males, 18 females) undergoing native AVF creation, preceded by pre-operative vascular mapping. Post-operative Doppler ultrasound assessments were performed at 2-, 10-, and 30-days, measuring arterial and vein diameter and arterial flow. Brachial artery wall shear stress was estimated using a modified Hagen-Poiseuille equation (τ= 4ηQ / πRi³). AVF maturation was evaluated at 30 days and functionally assessed by successful two-needle cannulation of AVF for 4 consecutive HD sessions with HD blood flow ≥300 ml/min, followed by a one-year clinical monitoring.
Results
AVF maturation was achieved in 85% of patients (34.0% of females, 66.0% of males, p-value 0.215). Matured AVFs showed significant increases in arterial diameter, flow, and wall shear stress in both sexes (Fig. 1A–E), with more pronounced effects in females. Males had larger initial brachial artery diameters and higher flow rates, while females exhibited greater relative increases, especially at 2 days post-surgery (Fig. 1A and B). Brachial shear stress was initially higher in females but decreased significantly by day 10, while remaining stable and lower in males (Fig. 1C). Radial artery growth was more pronounced in females, eventually matching male diameters (Fig. 1D and E). Age-specific differences were observed: males under 70 had higher brachial flow and greater shear stress reduction (Fig. 2A–F), while females under 70 showed the most significant vascular remodeling, particularly in radial arteries (Fig. 2 G and H). Females over 70 exhibited lower shear stress and minimal changes (Fig. 2F). Despite these differences, functional outcomes and intervention-free periods were similar across sexes (free from intervention 64.3% male and 60% female, p value 0.47).
Conclusion
While sex-based differences in arterial remodeling exist, they may not translate to significant disparities in functional outcomes. The more pronounced vascular adaptations in females, especially those under 70, suggest a potential compensatory mechanism to overcome initial anatomical disadvantages. These findings emphasize the need for personalized approaches to AVF creation and management. Further research into hormonal and physiological factors is essential to optimize outcomes and refine treatment strategies for ESKD patients requiring hemodialysis access.

title: #2001 Evaluating serum alkaline phosphatase trajectories for fracture risk prediction in hemodialysis patients
authors: Chin Wen Hsieh; Liping Hsu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Guidelines recommend measuring serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) or bone-specific alkaline phosphatase (bALP) to diagnose bone disease in chronic kidney disease–mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD). However, the distinct roles of these biomarkers require further clarification. Since ALP is secreted by osteoblasts, it may serve as a better indicator of bone disease. Due to the limited availability of bALP testing, total ALP is widely used for its accessibility and practicality. CKD-MBD guidelines recommend measuring ALP annually. Nevertheless, long-term ALP variations beyond one year remain uncertain. Additionally, while elevated ALP is associated with cardiovascular (CV) disease and mortality, its link to fractures is not yet well established. This study aims to evaluate ALP trajectory patterns during the first two years of hemodialysis (HD) and assess its predictive value for fractures and CV outcomes.
Method
This longitudinal cohort included patients who initiated HD between Jan. 2005 and Dec. 2012. title: #2306 Determinants of quality of life at twelve months in a multinational population on dialysis
authors: Carla Santos Araújo; Eliana Silva; Suzanne Pearce; Israel Silva; Carlos Lucas; Fernando MacÁrio
abstract:
Background and Aims
Quality of life (QoL) is increasingly recognized as an important patient-centered outcome when assessing hemodialysis’ (HD) impact on people undergoing such treatment. Despite the evidence gathered so far, the evolution of QoL through time on dialysis and factors potentially involved on those changes remain to be clarified. Our primary objective was to evaluate the predictors of QoL at twelve months in a sample of patients with chronic kidney disease in maintenance HD, using the Quality of Life Short Form Health Survey (KDQOL SF-36). Additionally, we intended to (i) characterize the people with CKD in maintenance HD, (ii) identify the variables associated with KDQOL SF-36 score at baseline, and (iii) evaluate if the KDQOL SF-36’s PCS and the MCS progress similarly at 12 months.
Method
We performed a retrospective cohort study using data from an international HD provider database. All patients 18 years or older that voluntarily responded to the Kidney Disease Quality of Life 36-item short form health survey (KDQOL SF-36) in 2021 and 2022 were included. The test was preferably self-administered, but patients could be assisted by a health professional during dialysis session when needed. At baseline, demographic, clinical, physical and analytical data from these patients were collected. The physical (PCS) and mental (MCS) component summary scores of 2021 and 2022 were analyzed and related to the different covariates using multiple linear regression and the results presented as coefficients and 95% confidence intervals.
Results
A total of 19,756 persons (53% of the eligible individuals) answered to both KDQOL SF-36 questionnaires in 2021 and 2022 and were included in the study. We have documented low baseline QoL in our sample particularly in physical domains, with a slight, but significant, increase after twelve months. PCS was significantly and consistently lower than MCS, a finding observable in all age groups, in both genders, regardless of dialysis vintage, the presence of diabetes and comorbidity index. Significant differences in PCS and MCS scores were observed in the different regions of the sample studied. Living in Iberia or Eurasia was associated with higher PCS, whereas being an inhabitant in Western Europe was associated with a significant decrease in MCS. Both at baseline and after 12 months, male gender, albumin levels higher than 35 g/L and be included in the waiting list for kidney transplantation (KT) were independently associated with higher values of PCS and MCS scores. Blood flow on dialysis, haemoglobin levels above 10 g/dL and normal weight/overweight were also independently associated with higher PCS levels. Presence of diabetes was independently associated with lower PCS and MCS scores at baseline and after twelve months, while using a central venous catheter for dialysis and longer time on dialysis were predictors of lower scores only at second assessment timepoint. Older age and higher Charlson comorbidity index were also predictors of low PCS at both timepoints.
Conclusion
Despite the slight, but significant, increase in QoL after twelve months, in our sample we have documented low baseline QoL, particularly in physical domains. A more significant impact on the PCS, when compared to the MCS, was observed, independently of the demographic and clinical characteristics of the sample. Male individuals, with higher albumin levels and included in the waiting list for KT presented higher physical and mental domain scores of QoL. On the other hand, having diabetes, a central venous catheter and being longer time on dialysis were the main predictors for lower PCS and MCS in our sample indicating that these group of people should receive targeted interventions to promote both QoL components. Our findings provide evidence on the main factors related to a low QoL in HD and support the need for timely implementation of multidimensional interventions aiming at the promotion of QoL in persons treated with chronic HD.

title: #2937 The prevalence and disease burden of CKD associated pruritus in Danish dialysis patients and current treatment practices
authors: Gustav Østerlund Larsen; Krista Dybtved Kjærgaard; Christian Fynbo Christiansen; Ida Nørager Tietze; Bodil Hornstrup; Ylian Serina Liem; Marie Bangstrup; Jesper Moesgaard Rantanen; Milica Uhde; Christian Daugaard Peters
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease associated pruritus (CKD-aP) is rarely assessed by health care providers and potentially under-reported by patients despite the potential negative impact on health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Our aim was to investigate the prevalence of CKD-aP in a large cohort of Danish dialysis patients based on validated patient-reported outcome (PRO) instruments. A secondary aim was to investigate CKD-aP awareness among renal physicians including current treatment practices.
Method
The study was designed as a non-interventional, cross-sectional multicentre study. Chronic dialysis patients from four different regions in Denmark were invited to participate. CKD-aP was assessed with a one-page questionnaire containing Danish versions of two validated PRO instruments. The worst itch numeric rating scale (WI-NRS) was used for itch severity within the previous 24 hours (ranging from 0 to 10 with CKD-aP defined as WI-NRS score >4). The 5-D itch scale was used as a multidimensional measure of itching and HRQoL. The five dimensions of the 5-D itch scale (degree, duration, direction, disability, and distribution) were summed together to obtain total score ranging from 5 (no pruritus) to 25 (most severe). CKD-aP awareness and treatment practices among doctors from participating hospitals were investigated with a simple self-developed questionnaire.
Results
We recruited 642 chronic dialysis patients of which 83% were treated with haemodialysis (HD), 13% with peritoneal dialysis (PD) and 4% with home HD (HHD). Median age (min-max) was 68 (18–93) years and 66% were males. CKD-aP prevalence (based on WI-NRS score >4) was 21% (all patients regardless of dialysis modality) and tended to be higher among PD patients (28%) in comparison with HD (20%) and HHD (17%) as shown in Fig. 1. No pruritus (WI-NRS score = 0) was found in 59% of patients and 21% had mild pruritus (WI-NRS score ≤4).
Median 5-D itch score (IQR) was 5 (5–10) (all patients regardless of dialysis modality). Itch intensity over the past 2 weeks was rated moderate to unbearable by 23% and not present in 52% of patients. Itch duration was less than 6 hours in 89% of patients and 30% of patients had no change in itching over the past 2 weeks. Overall, the impact of CKD-aP on daily activities (leisure/social, housework/errands and work/school) was minimal in most patients but sleep disability (score >1) was found in 20%. Sleep disability correlated with higher WI-NRS score (P < 0.001 X2-test).
Perceived CKD-aP prevalence was 41%–60% by most physicians (41%) with uraemia as the most probable cause (64%) based on 75 questionnaires from 46 trained nephrologists, 25 residents and 4 medical students (Fig. 2). Dialysis was the preferred treatment (42/11% as first/second option) followed by topical therapy with fatty cream (34/20% as first/second option) and treatment of hyperphosphataemia (21/24% as first/second option). Gabapentinoids (gabapentin and pregabalin) were rated third choice by most, but nephrologist prescribed pregabalin more than residents as their first or second treatment choice (P = 0.03 X2-test). Difelikefalin was not chosen (90%) or rated as fourth choice by 4% of nephrologists in our survey.
Conclusion
Roughly one out of five patients on chronic dialysis treatment suffers from CKD-aP. HRQoL is negatively affected by CKD-aP primarily manifested as sleep disturbance. Most physicians tend to overestimate CKD-aP prevalence and use dialysis and fatty cream as their preferred treatment.

title: #3389 Ultrasound evaluation of fluid overload in hemodialysis patients: comparison between VExUS score and lung ultrasound in a cross-sectional study
authors: Luigi Peritore; Guido Gembillo; Vincenzo Calabrese; Claudia Spinella; Chiara Casuscelli; Veronica Maressa; Federica Ricca; Fiorenza Rauseo; Flavia Sudano; Simona Di Piazza; Domenico Santoro
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fluid overload is defined as an increase in total body water or a relative increase in extracellular water. Clinically, it is defined by the presence of edema, weight gain or positive balance and can affect various organs such as the kidneys, intestines, lungs, brain and liver [1]. In hemodialysis patients, chronic hyperhydration was associated with frequent cardiovascular complications and an increased risk of death [2]. Unfortunately, both physical examination and laboratory tests have proven to be less specific and sensitive in detecting fluid overload. Therefore, there is growing evidence to support the use of ultrasound testing in ICU patients, including inferior vena cava diameter and collapsibility, lung ultrasound and, more recently, the VExUS score, a new diagnostic tool that combines hepatic, portal and renal veins [3]. Accordingly, further research is needed to determine which of these ultrasound applications is the best solution for fluid overload in hemodialysis patients.
Method
Thirty-three (33) patients undergoing maintenance hemodialysis were examined immediately before the start of ultrafiltration. All patients underwent ultrasonography of the inferior vena cava, hepatic vein, portal vein, renal interlobular vein and lungs. The results of this examination were compared with a previously empirically determined increase in dry weight. The ultrasound examination of the lungs was performed according to the protocol described by Zoccali et al. [4]. The VExUS score was scored 0 if the inferior vena cava was smaller than 20 mm, 1 if it was larger than 20 mm and there was a normal or mildly abnormal hepatic or portal vein pattern, 2 if at least one pattern was severe, and 3 if both the hepatic and portal veins were severely affected.
Because renal vascularization testing is of limited use in uremic patients, interlobar vein tracing was not evaluated.
Results
The absolute weight gain compared to the previously estimated dry weight was 2,5 ± 1.1 kg, while the relative gain was 3.2% ± 1.2%. The mean albumin value was 3.7 ± 0.16 g/dL. B-lines were detected with a median of 2 [0–9] and a maximum value of 18. 47% of patients had more than 4 B-lines, 31% more than 8 and 22% more than 12. An inferior vena cava of more than 20 mm was found in 22%, a VExUS score of 1 was found in 22% of patients, while a score of 2 was found in 15% and a score of 3 in 3% of patients. The correlation index is shown in Table 1. The VExUS score is associated with both absolute and relative weight gain, while the B-line score is only significantly associated with relative obesity.
The use of dichotomized values for weight gain (more or less than 2.5 kg or more and less than 3%) leads to the following values for sensitivity and specificity:
Conclusion
To our knowledge, this is the first cross-sectional study of multiple hemodialysis patients in which the VExUS score and lung ultrasound were coupled. Although limited by the small population, our work demonstrates how the VExUS score can also play a role in hemodialysis and confirms the utility of lung ultrasound in this patient cohort.

title: #3811 Adiposity in haemodialysis patients: measuring obesity beyond body mass index
authors: Ascensión Lupiañez-Barbero; Shaira Martínez-Vaquera; Alicia Rivas; Sonia Caparrós; Neus Sala; Sol Otero; Mouhssen el Manouar
abstract:
Background and Aims
Obesity is a complex chronic multifactorial pathology characterised by an accumulation of often dysfunctional adipose tissue (AT). Leading scientific societies propose to replace the term ‘obesity’ by ‘Chronic Adipose-Based Disease’ or ‘Chronic Adipose Metabolic Disease’ to reflect the metabolic disturbances due to accumulation and dysfunction of AT. Classical techniques such as Body Mass Index (BMI) or Waist Circumference (WC) may not detect those patients with higher cardiometabolic risk phenotypes. In addition, in the nephrological setting, the assessment of obesity may be hampered by edema and hyperhydration. Aim: To determine the prevalence of obesity in haemodialysis (HD) patients according to gender and using different health indicators.
Method
Retrospective multicentre study of 301 HD patients. Clinical data including gender, height and dry weight (DW) will be collected. Body composition will be assessed by Inbody® S10 segmental multifrequency bioimpedance (BIA-MF) post-dialysis. BMI will be calculated based on BP and height at the time of data collection. Obesity is defined according to BMI ≥30 kg/m2 and body fat percentage (BFp) >25% men and >33% women. Visceral fat will be expressed as visceral fat area (VFA) obtained by BIA-MF considering a risk value ≥100 cm3. Risk CC cut-off point ≥102 cm men and ≥88 cm women. Kolmogorov-Smirnov test to assess normality and parametric statistics to assess difference between groups: Student's t-test and Chi-square for quantitative and categorical variables respectively. Statistical significance P < 0.05.
Results
Of the 301 patients, 189 (62.8%) were male with a mean age 69.3 ± 14.9 years and 112 (37.2%) were female with a mean age 66.7 ± 16.4 years (NS). The prevalence of obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m2) was 13.2% in men and 28.6% in women (P < 0.013). According to the PGC, the obesity rate was 47.6% in men and 48.2% in women (NS). Among patients with a BMI<30 kg/m2, we observed that 34.9% of men and 23.2% of women had a PGC in the obese range (P = 0.033). In relation to the distribution of visceral adipose tissue, 38.9% had a VFA value ≥100 cm3 (29.6% of men and 54.5% of women (P < 0.001)]. 22.6% (68) of patients had elevated CC [6.6% (23) men vs. 31.2% (45) women (P < 0.001)]. We observed that 18% (56) of patients with a CC in the normal range had VFA values ≥100 cm3 [20.1% (38) men vs. 16.1% (18) women (NS)].
Conclusion
In our study, a poor correlation between BMI, PGC and AGV was observed, so we conclude that both the classical indicator of BMI and CC underestimate the ‘real’ obesity rate. We believe that the assessment of HD patients should not only be multidisciplinary, but should also shift from a weight-centred approach to a body composition-based approach. This will allow us to target patients with higher cardiometabolic risk phenotypes and initiate better therapeutic strategies.

title: #3846 Intradialytic hypotension and associated factors in chronic hemodialysis patients: a descriptive study
authors: Dahmane Rihem; Sonia Dziri; Nour Mattoussi; Asma Fradi; Nada Jedidi; Khadija Guellim; Azzabi Awatef; Samira Ben Amor; Feriel Mlika; Latifa Boukhris; Guedri Yosra; Dorsaf Zellama
abstract:
Background and Aims
Intradialytic hypotension (IDH) is a common complication of chronic hemodialysis, significantly impacting session tolerance and dialysis quality. This study aims to identify the factors associated with IDH and assess its influence on the biological and clinical parameters of dialysis patients.
Methods
We conducted a descriptive study of 117 patients on chronic hemodialysis. Sociodemographic, clinical, and biological data were collected, including patient characteristics (age, sex, comorbidities, etc.), dialysis data (vascular access type, session frequency, residual diuresis), and biological parameters (ferritin, PTH, bicarbonates). A statistical analysis was performed to evaluate the correlations between these factors and the occurrence of IDH.
Results
Our sample was mainly composed of men (67.8%) and diabetic patients (32.2%), with a high prevalence of arterial hypertension (64.4%) and degenerative complications of diabetes (60.9%). IDH was observed in 48.3% of patients during the first month of dialysis. We observed a reduction in residual diuresis (from 54% to 17.2%) during follow-up. title: #3898 Quality of life in haemodialysis: are we improving? Comparison 2022–2024
authors: Shaira Martínez-Vaquera; Mª Paz Sorribes; Ascensión Lupiañez-Barbero; Mirco Dalmaso; Teresa Martínez-Sánchez; Ignacio Ponce de León
abstract:
Background and Aims
Studies have shown that poorer quality of life (QoL) is associated with higher mortality and hospitalisation in dialysis patients. Measuring QoL in this patient population is a key indicator for assessing the impact of treatment and the effectiveness of medical interventions. Aim: To analyse the results of the baseline and 2-year survey to identify improvements and areas of opportunity in the care of haemodialysis (HD) patients in outpatient centres.
Method
Observational, retrospective, multi-centre study analysing QoL surveys applied to prevalent eligible patients on HD (>3 months) in 2022 and 2024, using the KDQOL-SF36 instrument, in 49 HD centres. The different areas of the generic and the CKD-specific part were assessed. Descriptive analysis was performed to compare the composite scores in these categories and to determine significant variations between groups and over time. Variables are measured in absolute survey scores.
Results
Of the completed surveys analysed: 3,157 in 2022 and 3,789 in 2024, results show an overall trend of improvement in perceived QoL: Significant improvements in the domains of sexual function (+1.46 points), work status (+1.37 points), pain (+1.17 points) and energy/fatigue (+0.87 points). Perception of the effect of kidney disease increased by 1.07 points. Satisfaction with the dialysis team remained high (100% at the median), with a slight increase in the mean score (+0.41 points). Moderate improvements in disease-associated symptoms (+0.35 points) and in physical and emotional limitations (+0.30 and +0.23 points, respectively).
Conclusion
The results suggest a positive evolution in the quality of life of haemodialysis patients between 2022 and 2024, highlighting improvements in physical well-being, adaptation to the disease and satisfaction with the care received. These results reinforce the importance of continuing to invest in strategies for a holistic approach to the patient and in measurement tools to assess and continuously improve the quality of life of this population and therefore medical outcomes.

title: #2545 Home medication in the US based on the assignment of NDC to ATC codes
authors: Judith Wiegand; Astrid Feuersenger; Yue Jiao; Otto Arkossy; John Larkin; Jan Walter; Hans-Juergen Arens
abstract:
Background and Aims
The analysis of US medication patterns by ATC code in dialysis treatment using a NDC (National Drug Code) to ATC/DDD Index (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical Classification System/Defined Daily Dose) mapping has been rarely conducted so far. This project aims to examine the representation of selected drug classes based on ATC codes. We applied a publicly available NDC to ATC mapping algorithm and verified the mapping from a pharmaceutical perspective. The focus is placed on home medication in the US patient population from the ApolloDialDb™ database.
Method
The presented multi-center, retrospective analysis uses real life data from adult dialysis patients in the US captured in the first version of the ApolloDialDb dataset. It contains anonymized dialysis data (longitudinal observation level data) on more than 540,000 unique dialysis patients in 40 countries from Jan 2018–Mar 2021. The NDC to ATC mapping was applied to US home medication data including number of patients and frequencies per NDC as well as official product information from the FDA. This analysis was focusing on the frequencies of NDC prescriptions regardless of the duration of the prescription. Six ATC codes on a 4–5-digit level (A10A, A10BJ, A10BK, B01AA, C10AA, H05BX) were analyzed. As the NDC to ATC mapping algorithm provides a one-to-multiple matching, only the first three assigned ATC codes per NDC were included in the manual pharmaceutical plausibility checks. Initially, it was checked how many prescriptions occurred for NDCs that have been mapped to the specific ATC code (e.g., A10BJ). As some NDCs have not been assigned to ATC codes, a manual search was performed for substances belonging to the ATC code (e.g., A10BJ: semaglutide). This ensured that the number of prescriptions for NDCs were recorded even though the mapping has not been successful. The numbers for the two procedures have been combined. All identified drug names have been double-checked for pharmaceutical compatibility with the mapped ATC code. Particular attention was paid to active substance combinations and the area of application specified by the ATC classification. Drug combinations were excluded if a separate ATC code exists in the ATC/DDD Index (e.g., A10AE: insulin degludec/liraglutide).
Results
8,931,154 home medication prescriptions in US patients were analyzed. The following results are obtained from the NDC to ATC mapping including manual verification and completion for the ATC codes (outlined in Figure 1). The total numbers and percentages of prescriptions for each ATC code are presented. Thus, the graph illustrates that there are e.g., 320,678 prescriptions for drugs classified in A10A, accounting for 3.59 % of all prescriptions. The totality of prescriptions results from the sum of all NDCs recorded in the dataset. Percentages are calculated by n/8,931,154 × 100.
Conclusion
The mapping provides an initial insight into the use of home medication in the US based on ATC codes. The ATC/DDD Index provides a meaningful combination of drug classes with regard to the area of application. Figure 1 demonstrates the possibility of applying the concept to data based on NDC level. It has been demonstrated that important medications such as insulins, HMG CoA reductase inhibitors and other anti-parathyroid agents are represented with 816,316 prescriptions, i.e. 9.14 % of the total home medication. Using ATC codes, medication in specific therapeutic areas (e.g., cardiac medication) could be highlighted to facilitate a comparison of the use of different active substance classes within one therapeutic area. Analyzing medication patterns while using NDC to ATC mapping will be advantageous for future cross-national analyses based on the clear definition of the ATC/DDD Index to ensure consistency and comparability. In this way, it can be ensured that the same active substances are included for the desired therapeutic area in the appropriate dosage form.

title: #2552 Fragmented physical activity in hemodialysis patients—results from a prospective observational study
authors: Maggie Han; Rakesh Malhotra; Xia Tao; Priscila Preciado Rojas; Lela Tisdale; Ohnmar Thwin; Peter Kotanko
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fragmentation of physical activity may indicate poor physical functioning and potential clinical decline. This study aims to evaluate the degree of physical activity fragmentation in a cohort of in-center hemodialysis patients.
Method
HD patients from 4 New York City clinics were enrolled starting in June 2018 and followed for up to 1 year. Ambulatory patients ≥18 years, on maintenance HD, and owning a mobile device were included. Each patient was provided with and taught how to use a wearable activity tracker (Fitbit Charge 2®), and they were instructed to wear the device continuously. Minute-by-minute activity data over a 7-day period were used to categorize each minute as either active (≥10 steps/minute) or sedentary. Only physical activity data from 05:00 to 23:00 was extracted to exclude sleep periods. We extracted features including activity fragmentation (ratio of active segments to total active minutes*100), and three categories of activity bouts (<5, 5–10, and ≥10 consecutive active minutes).
Results
79 HD patients (54 ± 11 years, 63% Black, 75% male, 34% diabetic were included in our analysis. Mean and median activity fragmentation was 42% (IQR 33%–49%) and 42% ± 13%. The mean percent of time spent in activity bouts of <5 min, 5–10 min, and ≥10 min was 87%, 9%, and 4%, respectively.
Conclusion
HD patients have highly fragmented physical activity patterns. The association between activity fragmentation and outcomes should be further investigated.
