title: #3390 Variability of symptoms and complaints in dialysis patients
authors: Elife Ozturk; Jessica Noelmans; Martijn Spruit; Jeroen Kooman; Marc Hemmelder
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients treated with dialysis [hemodialysis (HD) and peritoneal dialysis (PD)] have a high burden of disease. The amount of and the burden of symptoms and conditions experienced by dialysis patients is often underestimated. Limited data are available regarding the weekly variability of symptoms. We analyzed the variability of symptoms and conditions in a cohort of HD and PD patients.
Method
This prospective study was performed as a single center study. Patients completed baseline questionnaires on quality of life (SF-12), anxiety and depression (HADS), and patient activation measurement (PAM). After installing of a mobile application (Your Research®) on the patients’ smartphone, patients received 8 times a day during 7 consecutive days a questionnaire on 25 different symptom burdens and conditions. In the mobile application symptoms and conditions were scored on a scale from 1 (no symptoms) to 7 (most severe intensity). The results of the baseline questionnaires are given in mean (SD). The variability of frequently occurring symptoms was assessed by measuring the mean (SD) and coefficient of variation (CV, %).
Results
25 patients on dialysis were included (15 on HD and 10 on PD), of which were 52% female, with a mean age of 57.6 years (SD 17.6) and a mean Charlson comorbidity index of 4.3 (SD 1.9). The mean results of the SF-12 physical and mental component score were respectively 37 (SD 10) and 48 (SD 8) which suggests below average health related quality of life. Mean depression or anxiety scores were not significantly elevated since the patients had a mean HADS-anxiety score of 4 (SD 4) and a HADS-depression score of 5 (SD 4). The mean PAM score was 37 (SD 7) which is lower than the Dutch mean PAM score of 61.3. Regarding the results of the mobile application 80% of the symptoms and conditions were prevalent in more than 50% of the patients. The overall variation coefficient (CV) for all the symptoms/complaints was 33% for the total group, 31% for the HD patients and 39% for the PD patients. The symptoms/conditions which were prevalent in more than 80% of the overall group were muscle pain (mean 2.1, SD 0.8, CV 39%), dizziness (mean 3.5, SD 1.0, CV 33%) and loss of smell (mean 2.8, SD 0.7, VC 26%) but also a low feeling of happiness (mean 2.2, SD 0.5, CV 29%). In patients on HD, the 4 most prevalent symptoms and conditions were low feeling of happiness (100%), muscle pain (87%), dizziness and loss of smell (both 93%) in HD patients. For PD patients the 4 most prevalent symptoms and conditions were loss of smell (100%), low feeling of happiness (90%), headache (80%), sore throat (80%) and nausea (80%).
Conclusion
This study showed that there is a high variability of symptoms and conditions in dialysis patients both in patients on HD and PD. Variability of symptoms and conditions in PD and HD patients should be taken into account when analyzing them for clinical or research purposes.

title: #254 Assessing middle-molecular and protein-bound uremic toxins: a six-month study of ATA vs PS membranes in hemodiafiltration
authors: Niccolò Morisi; Marco Ferrarini; Giulia Ligabue; Silvia Giovanella; Nicola Bonato; Fabrice Innocent Fogue Bwopda; Ettore Tempesti; Gaetano Alfano; Lucia Stipo; Fabio Olmeda; Gabriele Donati
abstract:
Background and Aims
Haemodiafiltration (HDF) is highly effective in removing uremic toxins, particularly small molecular weight solutes. However, traditional assessments of dialysis efficiency have focused primarily on small molecules, often overlooking middle molecular weight toxins (MMUTs) and protein-bound uremic toxins (PBUTs), which play a significant role in the progression of chronic kidney disease complications. Filling these gaps is critical to improving patient outcomes and advancing dialysis strategies. The development of innovative dialysis membranes, such as cellulose triacetate (ATA), has paved the way for more personalised therapies and offers alternatives for patients with hypersensitivity to conventional helical polysulfone (PS). The CHORALS study aims to evaluate the performance of the ATA membrane compared to the widely used PS membrane, focusing on its ability to reduce MMUT and PBUT over six months, while confirming its safety by assessing albumin retention.
Method
The CHORALS study is a non-randomised, open-label, prospective, controlled clinical trial funded by the European Union - Next Generation EU. The study enrolled 20 chronic haemodialysis patients who were switched to post-dilution HDF with individualised convective volumes tailored to their body surface area. The control group (10 patients) used a PS filter (Fx 100, 2.2 m², Fresenius), while the experimental group (10 patients) used an ATA membrane (Solacea 21-H, 2.1 m², Nikkiso). Biomarkers included β2-microglobulin (B2M), free light chains κ and λ (κFLC, λFLC) as MMUT markers and total/free p-cresol (PC) and indoxyl sulfate (IS) as PBUT indicators. Albumin (AL) levels were monitored to detect potential loss due to prolonged HDF use. Blood samples were taken monthly for six months during the second week of treatment. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test and longitudinal changes were analysed using paired t-test and linear regression, expressed as R2 and slope.
Results
All HDF sessions were well tolerated with no filter-related adverse events. Concerning MMUT, both membranes reduced κFLC levels over the six-month observation period (PS: P = 0.001; ATA: P = 0.0009), with the ATA membrane achieving a more significative reduction (ATA R2 = 0.146, slope = −6.280, P = 0.0013; PS R2 = 0.0479, slope = −6.285, P = 0.073). A detailed month-by-month analysis showed a significant reduction in κFLC from the fourth month for PS and the fifth month for ATA. In contrast, B2M and λFLC showed gradual decreases, with no significant differences between groups. For PBUTs, the ATA membrane significantly reduced free IS (P = 0.041) and showed a modest reduction in total IS and PC. Conversely, the PS membrane showed no significant changes in IS or PC, with only a slight decrease in total PC. Both membranes maintained AL levels, confirming no protein leakage during the study. Table 1 summarises these findings, while Fig. 1 illustrates the monthly trends in toxins reduction.
Conclusion
This study is the first to compare the ATA membrane with the PS membrane for MMUT and PBUT reduction in HDF. The ATA membrane showed some advantages, particularly in reducing κFLC and IS levels while maintaining albumin levels, ensuring both efficacy and safety. These results suggest that the ATA membrane is a valuable alternative for patients with hypersensitivity to PS, offering comparable dialysis performance without compromising biocompatibility. Although promising, these results should be interpreted with caution due to the short follow-up and small sample size. The planned one-year follow-up data from CHORALS will be essential to confirm these preliminary trends and to establish the non-inferiority of ATA. This study highlights the potential of the ATA membrane and the need for further investigation to fully understand its clinical utility in HDF.

title: #649 Consideration of the amount of serum ferritin required to increase hemoglobin
authors: Chie Ogawa; Ken Tsuchiya; Taku Morito; Kunimi Maeda
abstract:
Background and Aims
Last year, we investigated changes in body iron levels in hemodialysis (HD) patients during low-dose oral iron replacement therapy, utilizing total body iron (TBI), a new index calculated as the sum of red blood cell (RBC) iron and iron stores. Our findings suggested that a mucosal block occurs once iron sufficiency is reached, leading to stabilization of body iron levels. We also reported that iron deficiency inhibits not only hemoglobin (Hb) synthesis but also RBC differentiation and proliferation. Additionally, serum ferritin levels below 60 ng/mL may indicate iron deficiency in HD patients (Ogawa C, et al. Nutrients 2022, 14). Erythropoietin-stimulating agents (ESAs) are commonly used to treat renal anemia in chronic kidney disease patients; however, maintaining adequate iron stores for hematopoiesis is crucial to fully utilize their benefits. The serum ferritin level required to support increased Hb levels remains unclear. Therefore, we aimed to estimate the serum ferritin level necessary for effective hematopoiesis by examining the relationship between changes in Hb and serum ferritin when the body's iron stores stabilize during oral iron replacement therapy.
Method
Data from 105 oral iron therapy sessions in 83 HD patients were analyzed. For patients who underwent multiple courses of iron replacement therapy, their age and duration on HD were recorded at the start of each therapy course when blood samples were taken. Oral iron replacement therapy was administered to patients with serum ferritin <60 ng/mL and Hb <12 g/dL and continued for at least seven months. Hb levels were managed with darbepoetin alfa (DA), a long-acting ESA, to maintain a target range of 10–12 g/dL according to Japanese guidelines. Blood samples were collected twice a month for Hb and once a month for iron-related factors. Transferrin saturation (TSAT) was calculated from serum iron (Fe) and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) using the equation: TSAT = Fe/TIBC × 100. Two consecutive data points (point 1 and point 2) with minimal change in TBI were selected for analysis from each course of oral iron therapy. The relationships between changes in Hb, RBC count, mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH), and serum ferritin were examined. Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient and a generalized linear regression model were used. TBI was calculated using the formula proposed by Cable et al (Transfusion. 2016, 56, 2005).
Results

title: #1887 High-volume plasmapheresis algorithm in patients waiting for OLTx
authors: Małgorzata Kępska-Dzilińska; Jolanta Małyszko
abstract:
Background and Aims
In patients with acute liver injury, in addition to treat the underlying cause and supportive care, liver transplantation is the only definitive treatment option. However, one of the main problems is availability of an organ. Therefore, it is important to develop care for patients waiting for a transplant. Fresh frozen plasma exchange therapy is an established therapy used in many disorders, including patients with advanced liver damage or in the anhepatic phase before transplantation. In our center we performed high-volume plasmapheresis procedures with simultaneous slow low efficiency dialysis (SLED) in patients with acute liver injury waiting for liver transplantation. Due to the specific nature of the center and the growing number of liver transplantations (315 in 2024 in our center), it was necessary to develop a simple algorithm of procedures for nephrologists and anesthesiologists.
Method
Based on case analysis, experience of the center and taking into account organizational difficulties, possible complications and available equipment in 2024, as part of a multidisciplinary team, we have developed a protocol for performing high-volume plasmapheresis with (if it necessary) SLED using Genius mobile Fresenius system (using also intraoperatively during liver transplantation in the operating room and if needed during postoperative period).
Results
In 2024 we performed 206 plasmaphereses including 11 high-volume plasmaphereses as a bridge to orthotropic liver transplantation. In order to optimize the procedure, we have created a simple protocol for performing high-volume plasmapheresis that can be used in intensive care units. As a result, the percentage of procedures performed by anesthesiologists has increased significantly. We did not observe increase of complications or risk for the patient.
Conclusion
Procedure protocols are a method used in many areas to facilitate access to therapy for doctors with less experience. The high-volume plasmapheresis protocol is a helpful tool enabling effective treatment while waiting for OLTx.

title: #1912 High-risk group is avalid predictor of all cause hospitalisation among patients on maintainance hemodialysis
authors: Mohammed Alhomrany; Ayman Fadlallah; Islam Elshazly; Ali Alharbi
abstract:
Background and Aims
This study aims to compare clinical and laboratory parameters between high-risk and low-risk dialysis patients classified based on the individual patient performance score (IPPS) and Charlson comorbidity index (CCI) and to investigate differences in hospitalization rates between these groups. The IPPS, adopted by Diaverum in 2021, comprehensively evaluates dialysis patient outcomes across various domains, including vascular access management, dialysis adequacy, anemia management, CKD-MBD management, fluid management, Hypertension management, nutritional parameters, vaccination status, and kidney transplant eligibility with a total score of 100.
Method
A total of 4667 patients on maintenance hemodialysis in 40 dialysis clinics in Diaverum Saudi Arabia were initially assessed. excluding 436 (9.4%) patients due to age below 18 years (20; 0.4%), dialysis duration of less than 6 months (315; 6.7%), or incomplete data (112; 2.4%), total 4231 (90.6%) patients were included in the study with follow up for 24 months (2023–2024). Patients were classified into high-risk (CCI ≥6 or IPPS <75) and low-risk (CCI <6 and IPPS ≥75) groups. Demographic, clinical, and laboratory data, including age, gender, BMI, dialysis modality, vascular access type, dialysis duration, and key laboratory parameters (serum albumin, hemoglobin, phosphorus, calcium-phosphorus product, hemoglobin A1c), were collected. Hospitalization rates and % of patients Hospitalized during the 12-month follow-up period were also evaluated. Statistical analysis was performed using t-tests for continuous variables and chi-squared tests for categorical variables, with a significance threshold of P < 0.05.
Results
Of the 4231 patients, 2482 (58.7%) were classified as high-risk, while 1749 (41.3%) were classified as low-risk. The high-risk group had a higher mean age (55.4 ± 16.2 vs. 54.1 ± 15.8 years, P = 0.009) and a significantly higher prevalence of diabetes mellitus (52.7% vs. 45.3%, P < 0.001) and hypertension (87.8% vs. 84.2%, P < 0.001). The high-risk group also had a significantly lower IPPS score (75.1 ± 10.1 vs. 92.8 ± 9.1, P < 0.001) and higher comorbidity index score (7.4 ± 2.8 vs. 3.8 ± 1.7, P < 0.001). Regarding dialysis modality, more patients in the high-risk group were on hemodialysis (65.1% vs. 61.3%, P < 0.001), and fewer were on hemodiafiltration (34.9% vs. 38.7%, P < 0.001). The median duration on dialysis was longer in the high-risk group (63 months vs. 55 months, P < 0.001). Hospitalization rates were significantly higher in the high-risk group (22.9% vs. 10.5%, P < 0.001), with 569 (22.9%) hospitalized patients from the high-risk group compared to 229 (10.5%) from the low-risk group. Further analysis of the components of the high-risk group by its primary elements as in Fig. 1 showed that Low-risk patients G1 (CCI < 6 and IPPS ≥ 75) tend to have a relatively stable health status and lower comorbidity burden, leading to lower hospitalization rates. High-risk patients G2 (CCI < 6 and IPPS < 75), and G3 (CCI ≥ 6 and IPPS ≥ 75) show increasing hospitalization rates of 16.7% & 23.6% respectively due to different combinations of IPPS and CCI values. G4 (CCI ≥ 6 and IPPS < 75) with a high comorbidity burden and low IPPS score combination represents the most vulnerable group, with the highest hospitalization rate 31%.
Conclusion
Our results highlight the significance of the high-risk group with a greater burden of comorbidities, lower IPPS scores, had higher hospitalization rates. These findings underscore the predictive value of IPPS and CCI scores in guiding clinical decision-making and the need for targeted interventions to improve outcomes in high-risk dialysis patients.

title: #2557 CKD-associated pruritis and its impact on quality of life in a cohort of Russian patients on hemodialysis
authors: Ekaterina Parshina; Tatiana Nikitina; Alexey Tolkach; Aleksei Zulkarnaev; Alexey Tutin; Olga Lemeshevskaya; Tatiana Ionova
abstract:
Background and Aims
This is the first study to date aimed to assess the prevalence of pruritus and its impact on quality of life in a cohort of Russian hemodialysis patients.
Method
The prospective cohort study included 225 hemodialysis patients from 2 dialysis centers. Validated Russian versions of the WI-NRS, Skindex-16, Itch MOS and 5D Elman scales were used. Pruritis severity was graded using WI-NRS scale as follows: 0—no pruritus; 1–3—mild; 4–6—moderate; 7–8—severe; 9–10—very severe pruritus.
Results
The mean (SD) age of patients was 56.3 (15) years, and 32.8% of them were older than 65 years. The median (IQR) Charlson's score was 5 [3; 7]. The median (IQR) dialysis vintage was 46 [12.5; 88.5] months. Arteriovenous fistula was used for dialysis in 86.7% of patients and central venous catheter in 7.1%. In all patients polysulfone membranes were used. Conventional hemodialysis was used in 96% of patients with good adequacy - mean (SD) eKt/V was 1.4 (0.24).
Prevalence of moderate to very severe pruritis (WI-NRS score ≥4) was 15.6% [95%CI 11.2; 21.1] (Fig. 1). Pruritus was moderate in 11.6%, severe in 3.1% and very severe in 0.9% of patients.
According to 5D Elman scale, the parts of the body most affected by itching were: back (53.2%), head (35%), shins (31.7%) and thighs (25%), forearms (21.7%) and shoulders (20.8%) (Fig. 2).
Patients with moderate-to-severe pruritus (WI-NRS score ≥4) were more likely to experience itch-related problems, such as sleep disturbance, physical symptoms and emotional distress (Fig. 3).
Patients with severe and very severe pruritis demonstrate higher scores across the subscales and overall Skindex-16 score compared to moderate: 70.8 [IQR 50; 91.7] vs 25 [12.5; 41.7], P = 0.000 for symptom subscale; 28.6 [IQR 14.3; 85.7] vs 11.9 [0; 31], p=0.022 for emotional subscale; 34.5 [IQR 21.4; 71.8] vs 12.7 [IQR 5.8; 26.6], P = 0.004 for overall scores, respectively.
Sleep disturbance, as assessed by the Itch MOS questionnaire, was also more pronounced in patients with severe to very severe pruritus: median scores were 42.5 [IQR 26.3; 63.8] vs 22.5 [IQR 0.01; 30.2] in patients with moderate pruritis, P = 0.008. The adequacy of sleep was also less likely in this group: median Itch MOS scores were 10 [IQR 0; 40] vs 50 [IQR 40; 80] in moderate group, P = 0.004 (inverted scale).
Lastly, overall 5D Elman scores were higher in patients with severe to very severe pruritis: 15 [IQR 13; 30] vs 12 [IQR 10; 14] in patients with moderate pruritis, P = 0.008.
Conclusion
The prevalence of CKD-associated pruritis in Russian hemodialysis patients remains high despite good dialysis adequacy. The results confirm the greatest severity of pruritus-related quality of life problems in patients with moderate to severe pruritus. Among them, patients with severe and very severe pruritus have the most itch-related sleep disturbances, lower sleep adequacy, and significantly higher scores on the symptom scale, emotional scale, and total Skindex-16 score, as well as significantly higher total 5-D Elman score.

title: #2815 Prevalence and predictors of sarcopenia in patients on maintenance hemodialysis and its relationship with cathepsin D
authors: Samar Karawya; Eman Nagy; Ahmed Mohammed Abdel Wahab; Rasha Elzehery; Samar Tharwat; Alaa Sabry
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sarcopenia is the progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength, primarily associated with aging. Its prevalence varies widely and is influenced by multiple factors. Cathepsin D, an endoprotease, plays a physiological role by inducing apoptosis through various molecular pathways. This study aimed to determine the prevalence and predictors of sarcopenia in patients undergoing maintenance hemodialysis (MHD) and to investigate the relationship between cathepsin D and sarcopenia.
Method
This cross-sectional study was conducted on patients undergoing maintenance hemodialysis (MHD). Data collected included patient age, sex, duration of hemodialysis (HD), and comorbidities. Nutritional status was evaluated using dry body weight, body mass index (BMI), mid-arm muscle circumference (MAC), triceps skinfold thickness (TSF), and the malnutrition-inflammation score (MIS). Muscle mass was assessed using musculoskeletal ultrasound of the quadriceps muscle, measuring its thickness and cross-sectional area (CSA). The CSA cutoff values indicating skeletal muscle loss were 1.88 cm² for males and 1.43 cm² for females. Muscle strength was assessed using handgrip strength (HGS), with low strength defined as <30 kg for males and <20 kg for females. Sarcopenia was diagnosed based on the presence of low muscle mass and/or low muscle strength. Laboratory data, including white blood cell count, hemoglobin, serum calcium, phosphorus, creatinine, albumin, total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), and intact parathyroid hormone (iPTH), were retrieved from patient records. Cathepsin D levels were measured in all patients using pre-dialysis blood samples via enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) with the Human Cathepsin D ELISA Kit.
Results
The study included 87 patients undergoing MHD, comprising 51 males and 36 females, with a median age of 49 years. Sarcopenia was diagnosed in 50 patients (57.5%). Patients with sarcopenia had significantly BMI, MAC, TSF, and MIS compared to those without sarcopenia (P = 0.047, 0.016, 0.001, and <0.001, respectively). Additionally, serum creatinine, albumin, and TIBC levels were significantly lower in patients with sarcopenia than in those without (P = 0.025, 0.001, and 0.010, respectively). In contrast, Cathepsin D levels did not show significant differences between the two groups (P = 0.941). Binary logistic regression analysis was performed to identify significant predictors of sarcopenia. MIS, followed by TSF and BMI, were identified as significant predictors of sarcopenia, with odds ratios (OR) of 1.331, 0.890, and 0.827, respectively, and corresponding P-values of 0.012, 0.038, and 0.038 (Table 1).
Conclusion
Sarcopenia is prevalent among patients undergoing MHD. MIS, TSF, and BMI were found to be reliable predictors of sarcopenia. However, Cathepsin D appeared to be an unreliable predictor for diagnosing sarcopenia.

title: #113 Body composition as a determinant of erythropoietin resistance in hemodialysis patients: insights from a Serbian single center cohort study
authors: Sonja Golubović; Vladimir Đurović; Vladimir Veselinov; Dejan Ćelić; Gordana Strazmester Majstorovic; Violeta Knežević
abstract:
Background and Aims
Resistance to erythropoietin-stimulating agents (ESA) is a common challenge in treating anemia among hemodialysis patients. This study examines the relationship between body composition parameters and erythropoietin resistance index (ERI) to identify potential predictors of ESA responsiveness.
Methods
This cross-sectional study included 90 chronic hemodialysis patients (60% male; mean age: 60.45 ± 11.58 years) receiving ESA therapy at the Clinic for Nephrology and Clinical Immunology, Clinical Center of Vojvodina. Patients had been on ESA therapy for at least three months, with transferrin saturation >25% and ferritin >800 ng/mL to ensure adequate iron stores. Body composition was assessed using bioimpedance analysis (BCM Monitor, Fresenius), measuring BMI, lean tissue index (LTI), fat tissue index (FTI), relative fat mass (rel FAT), and adipose tissue mass (ATM). ERI was calculated as weekly ESA dose (IU/kg)/hemoglobin (g/dL) and categorized into percentiles for subgroup comparisons.
Results
The median ERI was 4.98 (IQR: 3.13–7.68 UI/kg/week/(g/dL)). title: #585 Preserving dialysis continuity: the efficacy of the Peri-Patch device in catheter salvage
authors: Boon Cheok Lai; Peishan Lee; Md Akramul Hoque; Mahesh Ekanayaka
abstract:
Background and Aims
Peritoneal dialysis (PD) requires the placement and ongoing maintenance of a catheter that traverses the abdominal wall, extending from the external surface into the peritoneal cavity. Exit-site infections (ESIs) significantly increase the risk of peritonitis and catheter failure, necessitating varied management approaches, especially in refractory cases with tunnel tract involvement. This study evaluates the efficacy of a partial PD catheter replacement technique using the Peri-Patch device (Fig. 1) as a salvage strategy to manage persistent ESIs while preserving catheter function.
Method
Mdm KLH, a 70-year-old Chinese female, had been on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) for five years. She had a history of multiple ESIs over the past four years, including infections with Candida parapsilopsis, Achromobacter species, and Staphylococcus lugdunensis, all successfully treated with antibiotics.
She presented with persistent ESI due to Staphylococcus lugdunensis, initially treated at another institution. She was started on empirical oral cefuroxime per center guidelines and later switched to clindamycin based on culture sensitivities. Despite three weeks of treatment, the infection persisted. Fortunately, she remained asymptomatic for peritonitis, and her peritoneal dialysate cell count was unremarkable.
Due to persistent ESI, an ultrasound was performed, confirming tunnel tract involvement up to the external cuff. She was offered the following options:
Catheter removal and reinsertion via a different tract, with interim conversion to hemodialysis.
Catheter salvage using the Peri-Patch device.
Conservative management with extended antibiotic therapy, albeit with a high risk of peritonitis and eventual catheter loss.
External cuff shaving was considered but posed risks of incomplete debridement, recurrent infection, catheter damage necessitating removal, or infection progression into the internal cuff, increasing the likelihood of peritonitis.
Eventually, patient opted for catheter salvage using the Peri-Patch device. A surgical procedure (Fig. 2) was performed to remove the affected portion of the PD catheter, including the external cuff, without breaching the peritoneal cavity. The remaining catheter was connected to a Peri-Patch device, linking it to a new catheter segment with an external cuff. A new subcutaneous tunnel and exit site were created, and the infected catheter portion was excised.
Post-procedure outcomes were monitored, focusing on healing, infection recurrence, and catheter functionality.
Results
The patient experienced complete healing at the new exit site with no recurrence of infection. The catheter remained fully functional, requiring no additional manipulation or intervention. Since the peritoneal cavity was not breached, she was able to resume peritoneal dialysis immediately post-surgery. This approach proved to be a safe and effective alternative to full catheter replacement, reducing downtime and minimizing associated risks.
Conclusion
Partial PD catheter replacement using the Peri-Patch device is a promising strategy for managing persistent ESIs with tunnel tract involvement. This approach reduces the need for invasive interventions, maintains catheter integrity, and lowers the risk of peritonitis. Favourable patient outcomes support its role as an effective catheter salvage solution, ensuring continuity of peritoneal dialysis while minimizing complications.

title: #1775 Outcome of the peritoneal dialysis program in patients with heart failure
authors: Celia Rodríguez Tudero; Karen Rivero García; Angelo Roberto Falconi Sarmiento; Elena Villanueva Sánchez; Daniel Ruddy Quispe; Nestor Leonardo Sampedro Chica; Karla Antonela Pinoargote Cañar; Alberto Martin Arribas; María del Carmen Barnes Caso Bercht; Luis Armando Correa Marcano; Jose Antonio Menacho Miguel; María del Pilar Fraile
abstract:
Background and Aims
Congestive heart failure (CHF) is a clinically complex condition in which managing the volume overload in renal patients is highly difficult. This is a growing problem which leads to an increase in hospitalization, with an elevated sanitary cost and a high risk of mortality. The role of peritoneal dialysis (PD) in renal patients has some clear advantages. The objective of this study is to analyze the effect of peritoneal dialysis on patients with heart failure and to confirm the impact it has on hospitalization
Method
A retrospective and comparative study was conducted with PD patients treated in 2022 and 2023. Patients with CHF were compared with patients without CHF, and the study assessed their demographic data, comorbidities, volume status according to bioimpedance (BCM), EXUS ultrasound (Venous Excess Ultrasound Score), physical examination, history of cardiac disorders, ejection fraction, cardiac functional capacity, and pro-BNP and CA-125 plasma levels. Those data were collected before starting PD and a months 6 and 10 after PD.
Results
The study included 27 patients with an average age of 58 ± 14 years. 85% were men. Table 1 shows that all the patients with signs of congestion in the VEXUS ultrasound present fluid overload in the physical examination (edema, crackles) and their bioimpedance shows an excess volume of +5L ± 1.6, as well as elevated values of Pro-BNP and CA-125. In addition, they showed an average number of hospitalizations of 1.5 ± 0.5/year. After starting PD (10 months), an important decrease is observed in all the congestion parameters and biomarkers, as well as a reduction in the number of hospitalizations (P = 0.016). On the contrary, in the group of patients without CHF, the variables remained stable.
Conclusion
Peritoneal dialysis is clearly beneficial for patients with ESRD. Our study reveals that, in comparison, patients who also have CHF benefit more from it, since it effectively reduces the volume excess and leads to clinical improvement and a decrease in the hospitalization rate.
VEXUS ultrasound, BCM and heart biomarkers (Pro-BNP and CA-125) are useful tools for a comprehensive approach in patients receiving PD who present signs of systemic congestion.

title: #1844 Remote monitoring of peritoneal dialysis via telemedicine: a solution for volume management in refractory heart failure
authors: Paolo Luca Maria Lentini; Giorgio Laudadio; Claudia Benedetti; Ilenia Filippi; Federica Vienna; Brenda Menegazzo; Daniela Cremasco; Valeria Fuso; Sofia Andrighetto; Graziella Berlingò; Antonino Previti
abstract:
Background and Aims
Heart failure (HF) refractory to diuretics presents significant challenges in managing fluid overload, especially in patients with CKD stage IV who are not yet uremic. These patients, often referred to as ``frequent flyers,'' are prone to recurrent hospitalizations, poor prognosis, and substantial healthcare costs due to frequent hospital admissions. The primary objective of peritoneal dialysis (PD) in this population is fluid volume management rather than traditional solute clearance. This study evaluates the role of telemedicine and teledialysis (TD) in enhancing PD, reducing hospitalizations, and optimizing clinical and resource outcomes.
Method
10 patients with CKD stage IV and diuretic-resistant fluid overload were enrolled. The primary indication for PD) was volume removal to manage fluid retention and prevent recurrent hospitalizations. Inclusion criteria included preserved renal function (eGFR >15 mL/min/1.73 m²), New York Heart Association (NYHA) class III–IV symptoms, and frequent hospitalizations due to fluid overload.
TD was performed using a combination of two integrated systems:
Sharesource Web Platform (Baxter®):
This system integrates with an APD device to support remote patient management via secure communication.
It provides detailed insights into the home dialysis treatment and allows clinicians to remotely adjust cycler settings based on patient-specific needs.
Totem eVISUS System (TesiSquare®):
A plug-and-play system with two components:
a) A remote station (Totem) at the patient's home equipped with a high-performance camera, touchscreen monitor, speaker microphone, router, and wireless access point.
b) A control station at the hospital, enabling healthcare personnel to monitor patients in real-time, evaluate catheter status, PD effluent color, and provide remote training or instructions.
Daily monitoring of PD sessions was conducted through Sharesource© (Vantive SRL), while clinical evaluations and training were performed using the eVISUS System® (T4MED,Italy).
Results
Patients were followed for 12 months with the following outcomes:
Hospitalizations: Average of 1.8 per patient, demonstrating reduced healthcare burden.
NYHA Class: Improved by an average of 0.3 classes, reflecting better functional capacity.
NTproBNP Levels: Decreased slightly (−536.2 pg/mL), indicating partial reduction in cardiac stress.
Ejection fraction (EF): Improved by an average of 7.6%, reflecting better cardiac function (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
Telemedicine and TD enhance the management of fluid overload in HF patients with CKD stage IV, prioritizing volume control as the main therapeutic goal. The approach reduced hospitalizations and optimized care delivery, demonstrating its potential for broader application in managing complex, high-risk populations.

title: #2524 Pre-dialysis bile acids level and peritoneal dialysis patient outcome
authors: Siyuan Zhao; Qiong Bai; Wen Tang
abstract:
Background and Aims
The role of bile acids in regulating glucose and lipid metabolism, as well as their influence on the development of gut microbiota, has been well-established. Despite obvious abnormality of glucose metabolism and gut microbiota in PD patients, the relationship between bile acid levels and the risk of all-cause mortality in PD remains poorly understood. Therefore, this study aims to explore how pre-dialysis bile acid levels, in conjunction with various clinical factors and demographic characteristics, may impact the risk of all-cause mortality in PD patients.
Method
A single-center, retrospective cohort study was conducted on patients who underwent PD catheter placement at Peking University Third Hospital between July, 2010 and April 12, 2024, and followed up until September 25, 2024. Pre-dialysis bile acid level just before PD catheter placement were collected. The relationship between pre-dialysis bile acid levels and all-cause mortality risk was analyzed. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality risk.
Results
A total of 532 PD patients were included and the mean pre-dialysis bile acid level was 3.03 µmol/L [IQR: 1.4–3.5]. The RCS-based BAs cutoff value was 2.2 µmol/L. Bile acid levels were negatively correlated with triglycerides (r = −0.0939, P = 0.031), total cholesterol (r = −0.1290, P = 0.003), LDL-c (r = −0.138, P = 0.001), parathyroid hormone (r = −0.0907, P = 0.035), and serum phosphorus (r = −0.120, P = 0.005), while they were positively correlated with direct bilirubin (r = 0.268, P < 0.001), HDL-c (r = 0.144, P < 0.001), and total bilirubin (r = 0.177, P < 0.001). During an average follow-up of 3.65 years (IQR: [1.34, 5.26]), 212 of 532 patients died. Compared with the low bile acid group (<2.2 µmol/L), the high bile acid group had a significantly higher risk of all-cause mortality (HR 1.67, 95% CI 1.288–2.230, P < 0.001) (Fig. 1). The risk of cardiovascular events (HR 1.431, 95% CI 1.099–1.864, P = 0.0075) and cerebrovascular events (HR 1.716, 95% CI 1.083–2.717, P = 0.020)was significantly higher in the high bile acid group compared to the low bile acid group. Cox regression analysis revealed that pre-dialysis bile acid levels (HR 1.045, 95% CI 1.003–1.092, P = 0.035) remain to be independent risk factor for mortality risk by adjudging for age, gender, BMI blood glucose, serum calcium, hemoglobin, serum albumin, serum PTH, total bilirubin, and comorbidities in Cox regression models (HR 1.396, 95% 1.049–1.859, P = 0.022).
Conclusion
In PD patients, elevated pre-dialysis bile acid levels were identified as an independent risk factor for all-cause mortality, as well as for cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events after PD initiation.

title: #3099 Infrared thermography: a novel method to assess hand temperature and its association with ischemic signs and symptoms in dialysis patients
authors: Laura Lehtinen; Sami Rauhia; Jorma Lahtela; Heini Huhtala; Jukka Mustonen; Ilkka Pörsti; Velipekka Suominen; Satu Mäkelä; Jenni Koskela
abstract:
Background and Aims
Arteriovenous (AV) fistula for hemodialysis can lead to significant alterations in circulation, sometimes causing hand ischemia. The diagnosis of ischemia is primarily clinical. This study aimed to evaluate the utility of infrared thermography in assessing vascular access-induced hand ischemia.
Method
Thirty-two dialysis patients underwent hand inspection, symptom evaluation suggestive of hand ischemia, and infrared thermal imaging (Fig. 1). Finger blood pressures were measured in both the AV fistula and non-fistula hands, along with the brachial artery pressure of the non-fistula side to calculate the digit-brachial index (DBI).
Results
Twenty-five patients had a native upper extremity AV fistula. Twelve (48%) of these patients had fistula hand temperature ≥1.0°C colder, while four (16%) had a warmer fistula hand compared to the non-fistula hand. However, finger pressures or DBIs did not differ between hands. None of the seven patients without fistula had a temperature difference ≥1.0°C between hands. Patients with either peripheral or coronary artery disease (n = 8) exhibited a greater temperature difference between the non-fistula and fistula hands compared to patients without cardiovascular disease (−1.64°C vs. −0.18°C, respectively, P = 0.040). Among all participants, 17 (53%) reported ischemic hand symptoms, though only five patients had clinical findings suggestive of ischemia. Symptoms did not correlate with temperature or finger pressure measurements.
Conclusion
Infrared thermography identified significant temperature differences between the AV fistula and non-fistula hands in hemodialysis patients. Ischemic symptoms were common but did not correlate with temperature differences or clinical findings. Patients with either peripheral or coronary artery disease showed statistically significant differences between fistula and non-fistula hand temperatures compared to patients without cardiovascular disease.

title: #3124 Interdialytic weight gain and cardiac geometry in hemodialysis patients
authors: Ilda Isufaj
abstract:
Background and Aims
Interdialytic weight gain is known as a marker of volume overload in hemodialysis patients. Chronic volume overload is associated with cardiovascular changes that may compromise the clinical status of patients and significantly affect their survival. This study aims to find correlations between interdialytic weight gain and changes in cardiac geometry and function in hemodialysis patients.
Method
A cohort of 138 ESKD patients on hemodialysis under treatment from a single hemodialysis center participated in this study. Interdialytic weight gain, laboratory, echocardiographic data were obtained throughout 2023–2024. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analysis, ROC curve analysis were used.
Results
Mean age of patients was 61.9 years ±12.6, 56.5% were male, median time on dialysis was 65.5 months and median IDWG 3.9%. Hypertension was found in 77.5% of cases, Diabetes mellitus in 29%, and ischemic cardiomyopathy in 15.9% of patients. Median dialysis time was 65.5 months which varied from 4–264 months. Significant correlation was found between the mean values ​​of IDWG and tricuspid regurgitation (P = 0.01). A significant and independent predictor factor for tricuspid regurgitation was high IDWG, low renal residual function, high PASP, low ejection fraction; According to ROC curve analysis, the 4.25% cut-off value of IDWG would predict Left Ventricular Hypertrophy with 74.7% sensitivity and 47.2% specificity. Significant and independent predictive factor for left ventricular hypertrophy resulted: old age, Gender (men), high IDWG, hypertension, hyperphosphatemia, hyperparathyroidism.
Conclusion
These findings emphasize the importance of interdialytic weight management through fluid and dietary sodium restriction as well as by careful individualisation of ultrafiltration according to metabolic needs and specifics of volume control (renal residual function, IDWG, hemodynamic variations) in order to improve cardiovascular prognosis in these patients. Moreover it is important to rigorously manage mineral-bone disorder, arterial blood pressure, and preserve renal residual function. Inclusion of PAPS and right heart chambers in studies and as a target therapy would help in the improvement of these outcomes in dialysis patients.

Significant correlation was found between the mean values ​​of IDWG and tricuspid regurgitation (P = 0.01). title: #3641 Bleeding risk detection in chronic hemodialysis patients with non valvular atrial fibrillation on apixaban
authors: Dimitra Bacharaki; Elias Kyriakou; Konstantinos Gkiolas; Petros Nikolopoulos; Georgios Triantafyllis; Athina Drakou; Fotis Makris; Eleni Spanou; Eleni Triantou; Emmanouil Chaviaras; Athanassia Fatourou; Sophia Lionaki
abstract:
Background and Aims
The use of Apixaban (Apx) in hemodialysis patients for non-valvular chronic atrial fibrillation (NVAF) is still controversial. This study seeks to determine whether bleeding risk can be predicted using Rotational Thromboelastometry (ROTEM), a method that evaluates clot formation in whole blood, in hemodialysis patients receiving apixaban (Apx) for NVAF.
Method
This multi-center prospective observational study involved 19 CKD-5D patients with NVAF treated with apixaban (Apx). Patients were divided into four groups based on their dosing regimen: two patients received 2.5 mg once daily on non-dialysis days (Group 1), four patients received 2.5 mg once daily (Group 2), ten patients received 2.5 mg twice daily (Group 3), and three patients received 5 mg twice daily (Group 4). Dosing decisions were primarily guided by stroke and bleeding risk assessment tools, (CHAD2DS2-VASc, HAS-BLED, and ATRIA scores). Standard coagulation tests, along with an extended evaluation of hemostasis using rotational thromboelastometry (EXTEM) and platelet function analysis (PFA), were performed before (pre) and two hours after (post) Apx administration. Patients were subsequently monitored for bleeding events and all-cause mortality.
Results
Over a median follow-up period of 36 months, six patients experienced a bleeding event (Group A), while the remaining 13 patients remained free of bleeding (Group B). Additionally, six deaths were recorded: three due to major bleeding events, one from thrombotic stroke, and two unrelated to coagulopathy—one caused by septic shock and the other by sudden death. EXTEM clot time (CT)-post was the only parameter that significantly differed between Groups A and B (118 seconds (100–144) vs. 87 seconds (77–107 respectively). A multivariate logistic regression analysis, including CT-post and factors closely associated with it (Apx peak levels and PFA), revealed that each 1-second increase in CT-post was linked to an 8% higher likelihood of a bleeding event (OR = 1.08, 95% CI: 1.0–1.17; P = 0.048). A statistically significant progressive increase was observed with both the drug's trough levels (P = 0.020) and peak levels (P = 0.048) across the four dosing regimens. However, no significant relationship was found between CT and Apx dose groups, indicating a lack of a dose-dependent anticoagulation effect. Notably, the two patients who died from fatal bleeding had the lowest drug dose and Apixaban levels, along with the highest CT-post values.
Conclusion
Early detection of bleeding risk in CKD-5D patients with NVAF on Apx can be effectively achieved through frequent monitoring using Rotem (CT), which helps reduce associated morbidity. In contrast, neither Apx levels nor its dosing regimens provide meaningful information about the hemostatic status in patients treated with Apx.

title: #3675 Evaluation of outcomes and challenges in arteriovenous fistulas as hemodialysis access in pediatric patients
authors: Maria Do Sameiro Faria; Teresa Tavares; Teresa Costa
abstract:
Background and Aims
Pediatric patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) often require hemodialysis (HD) when transplantation is not feasible. Arteriovenous fistulas (AVFs) are the preferred vascular access for HD due to their lower rates of infection and thrombosis compared to central venous catheters (CVCs). However, the creation and maintenance of AVFs in children present significant challenges, including smaller vessel size and higher risks of primary failure. This study aims to describe and update our experience in AVF creation and assess its patency in children and adolescents undergoing HD.
Method
We retrospectively analyzed all the AVFs performed in our center in patients under 18 from January 2006 to December 2024. Collected data included demographics, clinical parameters, dialysis history, surgical details, and laboratory results. We reviewed medical records and entered data into a database for analysis using SPSS software.
Results
A total of 46 AVFs were created in 36 pediatric patients. The median age at first AVF construction was 13.0 years (range: 4.8–17.9). Congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract were the most frequent cause of ESRD (n = 21, 58.3%), and most patients (n = 27, 75.0%) were already on kidney replacement therapy. The median follow-up was 11 months (range: 1–98.4), and 61.1% of patients (n = 22) were transplanted during this period. The mortality rate was 5.6% (n = 2).
Radiocephalic AVFs were the initial choice in 47.2% of cases (n = 17), representing 37.0 % of all AVFs. Brachiocephalic AVFs were initially created in 30.6% of patients (n = 11) and comprised 23.9% of all AVFs, including revisions. Brachiobasilic AVFs were the initial choice in 22.2% of cases (n = 8) and accounted for 17.4% of the total. Primary AVF failure occurred in 27.8% of cases (n = 10), with successful re-intervention at the same site in 40.0% of these failures (n = 4). Primary and secondary patency rates at one year were, respectively, 62.2% and 91.1%. No statistically significant relationship was found between the occurrence of primary AVF failure and either the age at first AVF creation and AVF location. Regarding AVF complications: Thrombosis was the most common complication, occurring in 23.9% of AVFs. Stenosis was observed in 17.4%, distal ischemia in 4.3%, and high flow/aneurysmal dilations also in 6.5%. A negative correlation (Pearson coefficient −0.394, significance level 0.018) was seen between the age of patients and the presence and number of complications.
Conclusion
Arteriovenous fistulas (AVFs) are increasingly acknowledged as a reliable and efficacious option for hemodialysis in pediatric patients. Our findings indicate favorable outcomes in this group, with elevated primary and secondary patency rates, irrespective of AVF location.

title: #3723 Implementation of a holistic quality improvement framework is associated with lower mortality in hemodialysis patients across 6 countries
authors: Hansel Palencia; Wisam Albadr; Szymon Brzosko; Leyder Corzo Caro; Joao Frazao; Tan Li Ping; Bruno Zawadzki; Partha Das
abstract:
Background and Aims
Quality of care for patients receiving hemodialysis has historically centred around the analysis of indicators such as small solute clearance or anemia. Whilst important, reliance on such indicators can overlook the importance of patient safety (the detection and management of adverse incidents) and the role of effective nursing care in the provision of effective hemodialysis. Quality assurance in hemodialysis should consider objective measurements of these areas and consider them as important as traditional indicators.
In 2021 a novel quality framework (‘InterStellar’) was introduced across Davita International hemodialysis clinics around the world. The InterStellar framework was designed to assess quality of care provided within clinics using a basket of metrics incorporating patient safety and dialysis nursing care and not limited to traditional ‘medical’ indicators. It was hypothesised that a more holistic quality framework could have a positive impact on high level outcomes such as mortality.
Methods
6 countries (Brazil, Colombia, Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, Poland and Portugal) in the Davita International network were evaluated in an observational study between January 2021 (following introduction of the InterStellar framework) and December 2024.
InterStellar assessed care of in-centre hemodialysis (ICHD) patients using 35 key performance indicators (KPIs) including (but not limited to) numbers of safety incidents reported, blood stream infection rates, incidence of venous needle dislodgements and intradialytic hypotension, and results of infection control and vascular access care audits. Medical KPIs assessed included adequacy, anemia, use of central venous catheters (CVCs) and phosphorus control.
Targets for each KPI were set in advance and performance against target was measured on a quarterly basis. Performance was scored on a sliding scale and aggregated to give a final InterStellar score (0–100).
All-cause mortality was used as the primary outcome. Data was extracted from individual country clinical data repositories. Differences in outcomes were assessed with paired t-tests.
Results
Records from 38,000 ICHD patients across 276 clinics were evaluated. Total InterStellar scores increased by 17% [10%–24%] across all countries over the study period. InterStellar scores stratified by thematic area showed improvement across all countries. Patient safety indicators improved by 20.1% [2%–34%], nursing care audit indicators by 15% [8%–26%] and traditional medical outcomes by 16% [9%–30%].
Patient census also increased by 18% [4%–61%] over the same time due to organic growth of clinic operations.
All-cause annualised mortality improved from 17.8% [7.2%–26%] at the beginning of the InterStellar framework to 13.6% [5.1%–19%]. Performed t-tests showed a statistically significant reduction in annualised mortality in all except one country.
Conclusion
Assuring high quality care across multiple countries with different population demographics, healthcare regulations and cultures of practice, can be challenging. Embedding robust clinical governance, with a focus on patient safety and good nursing care practices, is arguably as important as meeting consensus targets on hemoglobin or Kt/V. The InterStellar framework attempts to combine all of these into a holistic quality improvement system within the in-centre hemodialysis setting. Four years after implementation, InterStellar has been associated with a reduction in all-cause mortality. Further research is required to better characterise confounding and bias as well as identify which specific components within the framework may have contributed to the overall effect observed.

title: #3772 The detrimental effect of proteinuria on residual renal function in hemodialysis patients
authors: Beatriz Sanchez Alamo; Irene Mínguez Toral; Milagros Fernandez Lucas
abstract:
Background and Aims
Residual renal function (RRF) provides several benefits for hemodialysis (HD) patients, including improved survival and enhanced quality of life due to better volume control and more efficient toxin removal. RRF loss is linked to complications such as vascular calcification and poor anemia management, as well as influencing the dialysis prescription, particularly in incremental HD. Factors like intradialytic hypotension and high ultrafiltration rates may accelerate RRF decline. Proteinuria is a well-established risk factor for renal function loss in chronic kidney disease (CKD), but its role in RRF loss in HD patients remains unclear. This study aims to determine if proteinuria influences RRF decline and whether renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors (RAASi) treatment can help preserve it in this population.
Method
This prospective study included 97 incident HD patients who preserved RRF at enrollment, defined by urea clearance (KrU) ≥2.5 mL/min/1.73 m². Patients with anuria (urine output <100 ml/24 h), acute kidney failure, or those starting HD after kidney transplant loss were excluded. Proteinuria was measured in 24-hour urine (g/24 h) and as protein/creatinine ratio in early morning urine sample (mg/g). Patients were grouped based on baseline proteinuria (above or below 3.5 g/24 h or 3000 mg/g in morning urine spot sample). The primary objective was to assess whether proteinuria affects RRF decline, defined as a decrease in KrU to <2.5 mL/min/1.73 m² within the first year of HD.
Results
Of the 97 patients (74.2% male, mean age 64.35 ± 14.95 years), there were no significant differences in age, sex, or comorbidities based on proteinuria levels. Diabetic nephropathy was the most frequent cause of CKD (39%), followed by glomerulonephritis (10%). Baseline urine output, KrU, and KrCr levels did not differ between patients with proteinuria above or below 3.5 g/24 h. Serum albumin, prealbumin, and hemoglobin levels were significantly lower in patients with higher proteinuria. In our cohort, 23% of patients were treated with RAASi and 81.4% with diuretics.
In total, 31.1% of patients met the primary endpoint, with a significant association between proteinuria >3.5 g/24 h and RRF loss (P = 0.02). According to the Kaplan-Meier curves, patients with proteinuria >3.5 g/24 h reached the primary endpoint significantly faster (LR 5.25; P = 0.02). Cox regression models confirmed proteinuria as an independent predictor for the primary endpoint, even after adjusting for diuresis and ACE inhibitor/ARB treatment.
Conclusion
Proteinuria >3.5 g/24 h at the start of HD independently predicted faster RRF decline, regardless of diuresis volume or ACE/ARB treatment. The absence of protective effects from ACE inhibitors/ARBs highlights the need for further research on novel strategies to preserve RRF in HD patients.

title: #3934 Impact of short intradialytic exercises on frailty and nutritional indices in hemodialysis patients: a prospective study in a developing country
authors: Syeda Hurmath; Rajeevalochana Parthasarathy; Sanjeev Kumar Hiremath; Veenaa S Manjari
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients undergoing hemodialysis (HD) often experience impaired exercise tolerance and functional decline, contributing to poor clinical outcomes. Low physical activity, exacerbated by protein-energy wasting, reduced physical function, enforced inactivity during dialysis, and post-dialysis fatigue, is a significant determinant of this decline. Enhancing physical activity through structured exercise may offer a beneficial strategy to improve overall health and quality of life in HD patients. This study aimed to assess the feasibility and impact of intradialytic exercise on functional outcomes, frailty, and key clinical markers in HD patients.
Method
This prospective study enrolled 72 HD patients (mean age 59 years, 71% male) who began an intradialytic exercise program one hour into their dialysis sessions. The exercise regimen included muscle strengthening using Thera-band and free weights, along with endurance training via a bed cycle ergometer. The exercise intensity and type were individualized based on each patient's physical capacity. The effects of the exercise program were evaluated at baseline and after one year. Statistical analysis was performed using paired t-tests to compare pre- and post-intervention outcomes.
Results
Among 72 patients enrolled, mean age was 59 years and 71% were males. Statistical analysis using paired t test revealed significant improvements in frailty score (49% v/s 57% p 0.0189), serum albumin (48% v/s 37% P < 0.0190), muscle cramps (49% v/s 45% p 0.0001) and systolic hypertension (19% v/s 17% p 0.0296). 83% of the patients had an uneventful period during exercise and rest 17% experienced weakness and hypotension.
Conclusion
This study demonstrates that intradialytic exercise is a feasible and effective intervention for improving frailty, reducing muscle cramps, managing systolic hypertension, and enhancing serum albumin levels in HD patients. The results suggest that intradialytic exercise can be safely incorporated into routine care for HD patients to improve functional outcomes and overall health. These findings provide strong support for further integration of exercise programs in dialysis care.

title: #283 Evaluation of sleep disorders in peritoneal dialysis and hemodialysis patients
authors: İnale Behbudlu; Murat Tugcu; Izzet Hakki Arikan; Ebru Asicioglu; Arzu Velioglu; Dilek Barutcu Atas; Z Serhan Tuglular; Mehmet Koc
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sleep problems are common in patients undergoing renal replacement therapy and significantly affect their quality of life. Our study aimed to compare the sleep quality between end-stage renal disease (ESRD) patients receiving hemodialysis (HD) and peritoneal dialysis (PD) treatments and to determine the factors affecting sleep quality.
Method
A total of 483 patients undergoing dialysis, including 403 HD and 80 PD patients from 5 different centers, were included in the study. The sleep quality of the patients was assessed using the Epworth sleepiness scale (ESS) and insomnia severity index (ISI) questionnaires, while symptoms were evaluated using the dialysis symptom index (DSI). Other demographic and clinical data were obtained from patient records. Patient data were analyzed using the R (version 4.2.2) program.
Results
Of the patients included in the study, 45% (n = 217) were female. The mean age was 55 ± 14 years in PD patients and 62 ± 13 years in HD patients (P < 0.001). According to ISI scores, 47% (n = 227) of all patients had insomnia (ISI score >8). Among the patients with insomnia, 88% (n = 199) were receiving HD, and 12% (n = 28) were receiving PD treatment (P = 0.019). According to ESS scores, 13.2% (n = 64) of all patients had excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) (ESS score >10). Of these patients, 86% (n = 55) were receiving HD and 14% (n = 9) were receiving PD treatment (P = 0.56). The proportion of patients with pathological sleepiness (ESS score >16) was 1.9% (n = 9), and this rate was higher in the PD group (P = 0.003). The majority (55%, n = 124) of the patients diagnosed with insomnia were female (P < 0.001). Symptom severity (s-score = 61 ± 13) and symptom burden (s-burden = 17.1 ± 2.8) values calculated using the DSI were higher in patients with insomnia (P < 0.001).
Conclusion
Sleep disorders are significant factors that negatively affect the quality of life in patients undergoing renal replacement therapy. In our study, approximately 47% of patients were found to have insomnia, while 13% had excessive sleepiness. However, only 13% of patients with insomnia were receiving medical treatment for their condition. Therefore, we believe that routine screening using easy-to-administer and low-cost sleep questionnaires could be an effective method for identifying and managing sleep disorders in these patients, potentially reducing sleep-related mortality and morbidity.

title: #1383 The SarQoL score is a novel tool for assessing sarcopenia risk and well-being in chronic peritoneal dialysis patients: a pilot study
authors: Michela Musolino; Federico Ruosi; Stefanos Roumeliotis; Christodoula Kourtidou; Ioannis Alekos; Mariateresa Zicarelli; Giuseppe Coppolino; Vassilios Liakopoulos; Evangelia Ntounousi; Davide Bolignano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sarcopenia, marked by the progressive loss of muscle mass and strength, is an increasing concern among peritoneal dialysis (PD) patients, negatively affecting health, frailty, hospitalization rates, and survival. The SarQoL questionnaire is a validated tool that addresses 55 questions exploring physical function, mobility, fatigue, and the social limitations caused by muscle loss, with higher scores indicating a better quality of life (QoL) and a lower risk of sarcopenia. In geriatric patients, the SarQoL score reflects muscle impairment and mass and physical condition. However, its usefulness in the PD setting has never been investigated. In this pilot study, we tested for the first time the SarQoL questionnaire in a small cohort of chronic PD patients and evaluated the possible relationships between the SarQoL score and common clinical sarcopenia risk factors, such as the more validated SARCF questionnaire, indexes of physical functioning and anthropometric measures.
Method
32 PD patients from two Greek hospitals (University Hospital of Ioannina and AHEPA University Hospital of Thessaloniki) were assessed for sarcopenia risk using the SARC-F questionnaire (a self-reported and widely validated questionnaire for identifying individuals at risk for sarcopenia; the higher the score the higher their risk), anthropometric measures, handgrip strength, and the 30-second chair stand test. Patients also completed the SarQoL questionnaire. Correlations between sarcopenia risk factors, clinical and lab values, and the SarQoL score were investigated.
Results
The average SarQoL score was 70.95 ± 15.96, with APD patients showing higher scores than those on CAPD (P < 0.0001). These values suggested, on average, a mild risk for sarcopenia and a good quality of life. A strong inverse correlation was found between SarQoL and SARC-F scores (r = −0.77, P < 0.0001). SarQoL score also directly correlated with hypoalbuminemia (r = 0.47, P = 0.0064), number of repetitions at the Chair Stand test (r = 0.46, p= 0.02), patient age (r = −0.50, P = 0.0035), and diastolic blood pressure (r = 0.50, P = 0.0039) while inverse correlations were found with fat percentage and history of cardiovascular events (r = −0.34, P = 0.05 ; r = −0.45, P = 0.009, respectively).
Conclusion
The SarQoL questionnaire may give novel insights into sarcopenia risk and the overall well-being of PD patients and may serve as a new screening tool for risk stratification also in this population setting. Further research is needed to confirm its validity and explore its potential as a tool for guiding targeted interventions.

title: #1601 Sleep disorders and sleep quality among hemodialysis patients in a Tertiary Hospital in Valenzuela, Philippines: a one center cross sectional study
authors: Geraldine Jettee Gales-Villar; Albert Lu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sleep disturbances, including sleep-disordered breathing (SDB), insomnia, and poor sleep quality, are highly prevalent among hemodialysis patients. These issues not only impair quality of life but also worsen cardiac comorbidities, increasing morbidity and mortality risks. Despite their impact, sleep disturbances are often underrecognized and undertreated, particularly in resource-limited settings where costly diagnostics like polysomnography are inaccessible. This study aimed to identify risk factors for poor sleep quality and sleep disorders and demonstrate how validated, cost-effective screening questionnaires can identify high risk hemodialysis patients and eventually improve dialysis outcomes in Filipino hemodialysis patients.
Method
A cross-sectional study was conducted involving 51 hemodialysis patients. Data on demographics, dialysis adequacy (Kt/V), body mass index (BMI), and sleep outcomes were collected. Validated tools, including the Berlin q uestionnaire, Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), were used to assess sleep disturbances. Statistical analyses were performed to identify significant associations.
Results
The prevalence of SDB, moderate insomnia, and poor sleep quality was 68.6%, 31.4%, and 72.5%, respectively. Male sex was significantly associated with SDB (77.1% vs. 25%, P = 0.0005), moderate insomnia (81.3% vs. 51.4%), and poor sleep quality (73% vs. 28.6%). Inadequate dialysis adequacy (Kt/V <1.2) was strongly associated with SDB (54.1% vs. 0%), moderate insomnia (75% vs. 22.9%), and poor sleep quality. Overweight and obese patients were also more likely to have SDB (31.4% and 11.4%) and moderate insomnia (50%).
Conclusion
Male sex, poor dialysis adequacy, and elevated BMI are significant risk factors for sleep disturbances in hemodialysis patients. Routine screening using validated questionnaires (Berlin, ISI, PSQI) offers a cost-effective strategy to identify high-risk individuals in resource-limited settings like the Philippines. Early detection allows nephrologists to implement timely interventions that improve dialysis adequacy, address weight management, and reduce complications such as cardiac comorbidities. For high-risk patients, recommending more objective assessments like polysomnography ensures comprehensive care and supports better long-term health outcomes and quality of life.

title: #1644 Evaluation of clinical consequences in diverse forms of fistula elevation procedure
authors: Mitsunori Matsuzaki; Masayoshi Nanami; Yasuyuki Mimura; Akihiro Kuma; Yukiko Hasuike; Takahiro Kuragano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Arteriovenous fistula (AVF) superficialization is a recommended alternative autologous vascular access (VA) in patients for whom conventional AVF creation is not possible because of insufficient forearm vessels. This procedure utilizes a deeply located vein as an outflow conduit in AVF creation and makes the vein accessible for cannulation. Tunnel transposition (TT) is employed in a standard manner as a venous superficialization technique. This is accomplished by tunneling the transected vein through a subcutaneous tunnel. However, TT is frequently associated with stenosis at the area of transposition because the transposed vein is torsed, kinked, or compressed by external tissue. Thus, TT tends to be exclusively applied to the basilic vein in the upper arm considering both the anatomic positional relation and the inherent limitations of this procedure. We recently reported that elevation transposition (ET) can serve as a practical substitute for TT (Contrib Nephrol 2019:198:1–11). ET is a simplified minimally invasive superficialization approach in which the vein is elevated and positioned in a subcutaneous pocket immediately beneath the incision. In AVF superficialization employing ET (i.e., fistula elevation procedure [FEP]), three potential outflow veins are available in the upper arm: the cephalic, basilic, and brachial veins. This study was performed to comprehensively evaluate the clinical consequences of three valid FEP techniques to ascertain whether they are reasonable alternatives to autologous VA and which, if any, have superior performance.
Method
The demographic and outcome data of 111 patients who underwent the FEP from April 2016 to June 2024 were retrospectively collected and analyzed. The outcomes of the three fistula techniques were assessed and compared in terms of patency rates, requirements for VA intervention therapy (VAIVT), and complication rates.
Results
The mean follow-up period was 47.9 ± 29.3 months. The basilic, cephalic, and brachial vein-based FEP was performed in 64.3%, 22.5%, and 13.2% of cases, respectively. The overall cumulative primary and secondary patency rates were 77.4% and 97.6% at 1 year and 69.7% and 96.6% at 2 years, respectively. VAIVT was required in 33.3% of cases, and the patency rates at 1 and 2 years after VAIVT were 62.0% and 56.4%, respectively. There were no significant differences in these patency rates among the three FEP types. Minor complications such as lymphorrhea or epidermolysis occurred in only 3.9% of cases.
Conclusion
Our results suggest that the FEP provides three equivalently reliable options to accommodate the deeply located venous anatomy of the upper arm on individual-patient basis. The diversity of the FEP may contribute to avoiding prosthetic VA and central venous catheter-based dialysis, at least in part, by expanding the applicability of the autologous VA.

title: #1932 Evolution of vascular risk factors control in hemodialysis patients in SPAIN following the intervention of the ``objetivo en el punto de mira'' (OPM) study
authors: Javier Nieto; José Abellán-Alemán; Gloria Anton-Perez; Francisco Javier Ahijado; Laura Blanco-Andrews; Alfonso Pobes Martínez de Salinas; Pablo Rodríguez-Doyagüez; Pilar Segura-Torres; Diego Fabian Sidel; Begona Rincon; Eliana Olazo Gutierrez; Clara Cotón
abstract:
Background and Aims
Control of cardiovascular risk factors (CVRFs) among patients with stage 5 chronic kidney disease on dialysis (CKD-5D) is inadequate despite their elevated vascular risk, resulting in a significant increase in morbidity and mortality. Nonadherence and therapeutic inertia are proposed as the main causes of failure to achieve these targets. Our objective is to assess the effect of a brief intervention aimed at improving the control of CVRFs (hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia) in a population of Spanish patients with CKD-5D as part of the OPM study.
Method
A multicenter, interventional, prospective study was conducted under routine clinical practice conditions in CKD-5D patients randomly selected from 20 dialysis centers across Spain. According to European vascular risk guidelines, control criteria were defined as follows: blood pressure (BP) <140/80 mmHg for patients >65 years and <130/80 mmHg for patients <65 years; controlled dyslipidemia (very high VR LDL-c <55 mg/dL); controlled diabetes (HbA1c <7% or <8% if ≥80 years). Monthly follow-ups were conducted for four months, collecting laboratory parameters at visits 1, 3, and 4, with treatments being freely modified in cases of poor control.
Results
A total of 504 patients (157 women and 347 men) were included. Among them, 471 (93.4%) were hypertensive, 238 (47.2%) diabetic, and 397 (78.7%) dyslipidemic. A total of 207 (41%) were simultaneously hypertensive, dyslipidemic, and diabetic. The control of hypertension improved from 43.2% to 50% (P < 0.01), diabetes from 65.1% to 63.5% (P = ns), and dyslipidemia from 49.8% to 55.2% (P < 0.01). Patients with control of hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia simultaneously increased from 7.5% to 10.2%, while those without control of any of the three factors decreased from 5.4% to 3.2%. Initially, 18.6% were considered nonadherent patients, a figure that dropped to 6.9% by the end of the study.
Conclusion
Among our population of CKD-5D patients in Spain, an improvement in the control of vascular risk factors and adherence was observed following a brief intervention. However, control of all risk factors was achieved in only 10.2% of the analyzed population according to international guidelines. Therapeutic inertia likely remains a barrier to achieving these goals.

title: #2304 Brazilian dialysis survey from 1999 to 2023: trends in demographics, nutritional status, primary disease, and viral serology
authors: Fabiana Nerbass; Helbert Lima; Ricardo Sesso; Jocemir Lugon
abstract:
Background and Aims
Since 1999, the annual Brazilian dialysis survey (BDS) has been a vital source of primary data on the chronic dialysis population in Brazil. This study aimed to report trends in demographic and clinical characteristics, as well as status of viral serology, among chronic dialysis patients from 1999 to 2023.
Methods
This retrospective study assessed trends in sex distribution, age (elderly >65 years), primary causes of chronic kidney disease (CKD), nutritional status, and the prevalence of positive serology for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV. The first year of data collection varied among the variables: 1999 for viral serologies, 2006 for age, 2008 for CKD primary cause, 2009 for sex, and 2014 for nutritional status. The Mann-Kendall test was used to evaluate trends, and the Kendall's Tau (τ) coefficient to quantify their magnitude.
Results
The proportion of men undergoing dialysis therapy increased slightly from 57% to 59%, while the percentage of elderly individuals rose from 24.9% in 2006 to 36.7% in 2023. Significant changes in nutritional status were observed with shifts across all categories. Hypertension remained the most prevalent primary cause of CKD; however, its prevalence declined over time, while diabetes increased, and glomerulonephritis decreased as a primary cause of CKD. The prevalence of positive serology for hepatitis B and C viruses decreased substantially (from 4.3% to 0.6% and 19.9% to 2.1%, respectively). In contrast, the prevalence of HIV increased from 0.3% to 1.2%. Median values of the two half-periods and Mann-Kendall test results are presented in Table 1.
Conclusion
This retrospective analysis highlights the impact of demographic and epidemiological shifts on the chronic dialysis population in Brazil. Over the decades, we observed the effects of an aging population with chronic diseases, along with a marked decline in the serum prevalence of hepatitis B and C virus.

title: #2371 Home dialysis and hypertension: evaluating the role of the dialysate
authors: Anna Ferri Cortes; Amparo Soldevila-Orient; Ramon Devesa Such; Pilar Sánchez-Pérez; Iris Viejo Boyano; Ester Cholbi Vives; Manel Gavilà; Enrique Garrigos-Almerich
abstract:
Background and Aims
Home hemodialysis has gained attention as an effective alternative to in-center dialysis, offering patients more freedom and clinical benefits with lower cost.
Several studies have associated the implementation of low-flow but more frequent hemodialysis protocols with improvements in the cardiovascular profile of our patients, observing a better blood pressure control together with other parameters.
Among the available alternatives for home dialysis in our unit, we can choose between either bicarbonate-based or lactate-based dialysis, depending on the buffer used for the bath. Based on our subjective observation, we have the impression that the patients on a lactate-based dialysis have a better blood pressure control, despite the fact that the final sodium contribution is the same in both baths. However, we wanted to explore whether this empirical perception could be supported by objective data.
The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of the different types of dialysate on blood pressure control after one year in our home hemodialysis program.
Method
We conducted a retrospective, observational, single-center study, including all patients who had been in our home hemodialysis program for at least one year, since 2018 to the present day. A total of 19 patients were included. We recorded the number and dosage of antihypertensive medications at baseline and after one year in the program, and classified them based on whether they had decreased (0), remained the same (1), or increased (2) in number or dosage. We then performed the Mann-Whitney U test to compare whether there were differences in these changes based on the dialysis bath.
Results
The basic characteristics of the analyzed patients are showed in Table 1.
A total of 13 patients had a bicarbonate-based dialysis, among which only 3 were able to reduce the number or dosage of antihypertensive drugs after one year in our home dialysis program. The rest either remained the same (5) or needed a treatment enhance (5). Amid the lactate-based group, also 3 were able to diminish the antihypertensive treatment, 2 did not had a medication change and only 1 required an increase in therapy.
Although there appears to be a trend supporting our hypothesis, the Mann-Whitney U test comparing changes in antihypertensive medications between the two groups (buffered with lactate or bicarbonate) was not statistically significant (U = 26.0, P = 0.227).
Conclusion
In our sample, we observed a trend in which more patients on bicarbonate-based dialysis tend to maintain or increase antihypertensive medications compared to those using lactate. However, these differences were not statistically significant, likely due to the small sample size. Therefore, we consider that it may be worth exploring the pathophysiological mechanisms that may lead to this phenomenon, for which further studies will be necessary.

title: #2528 Prognostic value of Glasgow Prognostic Score and its derived scores in patients undergoing hemodialysis
authors: Kenta Torigoe; Emiko Otsuka; Shinichi Abe; Mineaki Kitamura; Kumiko Muta; Tomoya Nishino
abstract:
Background and Aims
The Glasgow Prognostic Score (GPS), its modified version (mGPS), and the high-sensitivity mGPS (HS-mGPS) are widely recognized as effective tools for predicting outcomes in patients with cancer. However, their prognostic utility in individuals undergoing hemodialysis remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of the GPS, mGPS, and HS-mGPS in predicting the prognosis of patients undergoing hemodialysis.
Method
A retrospective cohort analysis was performed on 339 patients undergoing hemodialysis. GPS, mGPS, and HS-mGPS scores were determined, and their associations with all-cause mortality were examined using Kaplan–Meier survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards models. Additionally, the predictive performance of GPS for all-cause mortality was assessed by calculating the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).
Results
During the median follow-up period of 1558 days, 221 patients (65.2%) died. Survival rates declined with higher GPS scores (0, 1, and 2), whereas in the mGPS and HS-mGPS scores, similar survival rates were observed between scores of 0 and 1. title: #2718 Usefulness of nutritional ultrasound as an indicator of cardiovascular risk. Pilot study
authors: Yanet Parodis López; Angel Nogueira Perez; Francisco Alonso Alman; Sebastian Hillebrand Ortega; Jose Luis Zerpa Belisario; Angela Angel Angulo; Gloria Anton-Perez; Fernando Henriquez
abstract:
Background and Aims
There is a high prevalence of overweight and obesity in patients on hemodialysis (HD). Bioimpedance is a method of studying body composition, widely used to assess the state of hydration.
One of the problems of the technique is that the values of lean mass and fat mass can be altered if the patient is not normohydrated, in addition to not differentiating between subcutaneous and visceral fat, whose cardiovascular impact is different. For this reason, it is important to combine it with other assessment tools that are not influenced by hydration status, such as abdominal ultrasound.
The objective of the pilot study is to determine the usefulness of nutritional ultrasound for the assessment of abdominal fat and to determine whether implantation in the dialysis room is feasible.
Method
A total of 22 patients were evaluated in HD, a nutritional ultrasound was performed where abdominal fat was evaluated, differentiating between superficial fat (SF), deep fat (DF) and pre-peritoneal fat (PPF). Data from the medical history related to cardiovascular health such as cholesterol (COL) or triglycerides (TG) were collected.
Results
17 men, Xage 69.68 ± 12.57 years (Males: 68.35 ± 12.06, vs females: 74.20 ± 14.67 years P = 0.373). We found differences between men and women with respect to SF, and DF, both being greater in men, but not with PPF.
We found greater length of fat tissue in patients over 65 years of age (SF: 0.88 ± 1.07 vs 2.61 ± 1.69, P = 0.008; PF: 3.98 ± 5.46 vs 8.60 ± 5.24, P = 0.064; PPF: 3.35 ± 4.82 vs 4.24 ± 3.88, P = 0.665).
