title: #2768 Multicentric validation of an Italian version of the uremic pruritus in dialysis patients (UP-Dial) questionnaire
authors: Mariateresa Zicarelli; Federico Ruosi; Antonietta Errante; Michela Musolino; Davide Mauro; Irma Figlia; Chiara Ambrosio; Giovanni Mazzitello; Arcangelo Sellaro; Salvatore Chiarella; Davide Bolignano; Giuseppe Coppolino
abstract:
Background and Aims
Uremic pruritus is a prevalent and distressing symptom among patients undergoing haemodialysis (HD). Despite its significant negative impact on patients' quality of life, it remains an often-underestimated issue in clinical practice. Various tools are available to assess pruritus in a general setting. In uremic patients, the only validated instrument for evaluating the severity and clinical impact of pruritus, the uremic pruritus in dialysis patients (UP-Dial) was made available in 2017. To date, it has only been validated in English language and in a Polish version (Świerczyńska K. et al. 2022). The objective of this study was to translate and validate an Italian version of the UP-Dial questionnaire.
Method
The translation process followed international guidelines, involving forward and backward translations to ensure linguistic and conceptual equivalence. The validation study was conducted on a multicentre cohort of 182 haemodialysis patients experiencing uremic pruritus from seven HD units located in different hospitals in the Calabria region (Italy). To assess reliability, respondents completed the questionnaire twice, with a 7-day interval between assessments.
Results
The Italian version of the UP-Dial questionnaire demonstrated excellent internal consistency, with a Cronbach's alpha coefficient of 0.91 for the total score. Test-retest reliability was also high, as indicated by an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) of 0.92. These findings confirm the robustness and reproducibility of the translated instrument, making it a reliable tool for assessing uremic pruritus in Italian-speaking patients (Table 1).
Conclusion
The Italian version of the UP-Dial questionnaire is a valid, reliable, and reproducible instrument for evaluating uremic pruritus. It can be effectively utilized in both research settings and routine clinical practice to better assess and manage pruritus in HD patients.

title: #2956 NT-proBNP and Serum CA-125 in peritoneal dialysis: developing a decision algorithm for fluid overload assessment
authors: Ana Rita Pereirinha Ramos; Filipa Trigo; Rui Duarte; Rita Valerio Alves; Hernâni Ricardo Martins Gonçalves; Paulo Santos
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fluid overload (FO) in peritoneal dialysis (PD) increases cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, but clinical signs often appear late, making early detection challenging. NT-proBNP is an established marker of hypervolemia, while serum CA-125 may reflect extracellular volume. This study proposes a biomarker-based algorithm to enhance FO diagnosis and management in PD.
Method
We conducted a retrospective analysis of peritoneal dialysis (PD) patients assessed between July 2023 and December 2024 at a Portuguese PD center. On the same day, patients underwent adequacy testing, bioimpedance analysis, and biomarker quantification (NT-proBNP and serum CA-125). Fluid overload (FO) was defined as overhydration (OH) ≥5% of total body water (TBW). Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS v29, applying parametric tests when appropriate. To evaluate diagnostic performance, we calculated sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and the area under the curve (AUC) from receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves.
Results
A total of 88 measurements were collected from 46 chronic PD patients: 38.80% (n = 16) were female, with a mean age at PD initiation of 61.5 ± 10.6 years (PD duration 15.00 ± 10.60 months) and automated PD was used by 52.17% (n = 24). Serum CA-125 was 11.85 ± 14.28 U/mL, NT-proBNP 1091.0 ± 3055.0 U/mL, OH 1.76 ± 1.90 L, and %OH 9.55 ± 13.30.
FO (%OH ≥5%) was present in 71.6% (n = 63). Edema was detected in 23.9% of the general population, and 33.9% of FO cases, showing low sensivity (33.0%) and NPV (37.9%).
No significant correlation was found between serum CA-125 and OH (r = 0.154, P = 0.151) while its diagnostic performance for FO detection showed an AUC of 0.597. However, a significant association with FO was observed (χ² = 5.730, P = 0.017; Fisher's exact test P = 0.021).
NT-proBNP (with cutoff 801 pg/mL) showed 84.1% sensitivity, 24.0% specificity and an AUC 0.857. In patients with NT-proBNP ≥801 pg/mL, serum CA-125 (cutoff 15.5 U/mL) had 43.3% sensitivity, but 100% specificity and PPV.
Conclusion
This study underscores the relevance of a biomarker-based algorithm in refining the diagnostic approach to fluid overload in peritoneal dialysis. The combination of NT-proBNP ≥801 pg/mL and serum CA-125 >15.5 U/mL demonstrates high specificity, strongly supporting the diagnosis of fluid overload in this population. While clinical assessment remains fundamental in volume evaluation, this algorithm provides an objective and reproducible tool to support decision-making, particularly in scenarios of diagnostic uncertainty or when direct patient assessment is not possible.

title: #3233 Renal replacement therapy in a patient with severe hemophilia A and ESRD: a case report
authors: Vladimir Veselinov; Sonja Golubović; Siniša Živković; Danilo Medin; Nikola Glogonjac; Dejan Ćelić; Violeta Knežević
abstract:
Background and Aims
Selecting an appropriate renal replacement therapy (RRT) for patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and severe hemophilia A is complex due to the high risk of bleeding and vascular access complications. Peritoneal dialysis (PD) is often preferred to avoid systemic anticoagulation, but it may not always be feasible. Hemodialysis (HD) requires careful hemostatic management, particularly regarding vascular access. This case report highlights the decision-making process and challenges in choosing the optimal RRT modality for a patient with severe hemophilia A and ESRD.
Methods
A 55-year-old male with severe hemophilia A (Factor VIII activity <1%) and insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus developed ESRD requiring RRT. Severe hemophilic arthropathy limited mobility, ruling out PD. Lack of social support further excluded home-assisted PD. AVF creation was not a viable option, as the patient was set to begin chronic hemodialysis at a regional center with limited experience in hemophilia management and, crucially, an unstable supply of recombinant Factor VIII (rFVIII), essential for controlling prolonged bleeding from the AVF. Consequently, a tunneled central venous catheter was placed under prophylactic rFVIII administration. Post-procedure bleeding at the catheter site was successfully managed with additional rFVIII and hemostatic sutures. HD was performed without systemic anticoagulation, using saline flushes to maintain circuit patency.
Results
Over nine months, the patient underwent 111 HD sessions, achieving an average Kt/V of 1.1. No major bleeding or thrombotic complications occurred. Heparin was avoided during HD, and post-dialysis administration of 2000 units of rFVIII minimized bleeding risk. Four episodes of intradialytic hypotension were recorded. The patient was planned for transition to emicizumab to enhance long-term hemostatic stability. Unfortunately, he passed away at home, likely due to sudden cardiac death.
Conclusions
This case underscores the challenges of RRT selection in patients with ESRD and severe hemophilia A. While PD avoids vascular access complications, it requires patient capability and adequate support. AVF use demands rigorous hemostatic control. A tunneled catheter, combined with prophylactic rFVIII, was a viable alternative in this setting. Future advancements, such as emicizumab, may improve long-term hemostatic control and expand RRT options for this complex patient population.

title: #3645 Clinical and echocardiographic profile of patients initiating unplanned haemodialysis due to cardiorenal syndrome
authors: Rafael Henriques de Figueiredo; Ana Catarina Oliveira; Hugo Diniz; Luis Coentrao
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiovascular disease, particularly cardiorenal syndrome (CRS) is a strong determinant of access-related and patient-related outcomes. This study aims to characterize the profile of patients requiring unplanned haemodialysis (uHD) initiation due to CRS and clinical predictors of mortality.
Method
A retrospective analysis of the patients who initiated uHD due to CRS at our center in 2022–2023 was performed. Demographic, echocardiographic and access-related data, and 1-year outcomes were collected from their health records. CRS cases were classified by two independent authors. The primary outcome was to characterize this subset of patients and the secondary aim was to identify clinical predictors of 1-year mortality. Statistical analysis was conducted with SPSS v28.0.1.
Results
Of the 184 patients requiring uHD, 57 were due to CRS, with a majority being male (68.4%). The mean age was 74.8 (±9.7) years and the median (IQR) Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) was 7 (6–8). All patients had a history of heart failure (HF) and chronic kidney disease (CKD).
Regarding HF, the most common etiology was ischemic (47.4%) and the median NYHA score was 1. Thirty-one patients (54.4%) had moderate to severe valvulopathies-particularly tricuspid and mitral regurgitations; 12 (23.5%) had diastolic dysfunction [mitral E/e´ >10]; 17 (29.8%) had reduced left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF <40%]; and 10 (17.5%) right ventricular dysfunction [TAPSE <17mm].
Regarding CKD, the most common etiology was diabetes (40.4%) and the dominant nephrological syndrome was acutely decompensated CKD (71.9%). Forty-six (80.7%) patients had a prior nephrology appointment and 7 (12.3%) had a kidney transplant. At HD initiation, median sCr was 4.91 mg/dL (Δ +1.44 from baseline), BNP was 1272 pg/mL (Δ +571) and Hgb was 9.0 g/dL (Δ −1.3). Two-thirds started HD with a central venous catheter.
Within one year, 16 (28.1%) patients died,—mostly due to MACE (8 patients). This was significantly higher when compared to non-CRS uHD patients (vs 15.0%, P = 0.036). One patient recovered kidney function (1.8%). No access-related variables, comorbidities or echocardiographic features per si were predictors of 1-year mortality.
Conclusion
Patients requiring uHD due to CRS are highly comorbid and face significantly higher mortality compared to non-CRS patients. Our analysis did not find specific clinical or echocardiographic predictors of 1-year mortality.

title: #3691 Successful use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP1-RA) in a patient with obesity and diabetic kidney disease under peritoneal dialysis: a Case Report
authors: Pavlo Yavorskiy; Silvio Borrelli; Luca De Nicola; Chiara Ruotolo; Roberta Germano'; Annarita D'ambra; Martina Vitale; Christian Nardelli; Filomena Gagliardi; Riccardo Palladino; Federica Marzano; Carlo Garofalo
abstract:
Background
Semaglutide is a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP1-RA), which showed a significant effect in slowing renal progression and reducing cardiovascular risk in patients affected by obesity and diabetic kidney disease in the recent FLOW trial. However, there is a scarcity of observations regarding the effects of semaglutide in patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis (PD).
Methods
This is a case report to describe the first use of semaglutide for six months in a diabetic patient under continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) who was ineligible for kidney transplantation due to obesity.
Clinical case
A 59-year-old male patient with type 2 diabetes following intensive insulin therapy, treated in the last two years with CAPD, had been considered ineligible to kidney transplantation due to obesity. The hypocaloric diet had always been ineffective due to low patient compliance. We therefore chose to use semi-injective semaglutide to allow a weight loss sufficient to be listed for kidney transplantation.
Body weight was 97.5 kg (BMI 33.7 Kg/m2) and blood pressure (BP) 150/90 mmHg. The patient was treated with insulin 43 U/day (18 U Aspart and 25 U Degludec), along with furosemide 250 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, eplerenone 50 mg, bisoprolol 2.5 mg/day, clopidogrel/aspirin 70/100 mg, omega−3 fatty acids 3000 mg and atorvastatin 40 mg (Fig. 1). Residual diuresis was 1000 ml/24 h and residual kidney function was 5 ml/min. The CAPD schedule consisted of two 5 h dwells of 2 L of 1.36% glucose and a 14 h dwell of 2 L icodextrin.
On 1st March 2024, the patient began subcutaneous semaglutide with the following schedule: 0.25 mg/week for the first 4 weeks then uptitrated to 0.5 mg/week if tolerated.
After 4 weeks, the patient achieved a weight loss of 2.8 kg. The patient experienced nausea; however, since this adverse effect was well tolerated, the semaglutide dose was increased to 0.5 mg/day.
From week-4 to week-16, a body weight reduction from 94.7 kg to 86.5 kg was observed. The weight loss was associated with a reduction in glycated haemoglobin from 7.6% to 6.1% with a remarkable reduction in daily insulin requirement, from 43 to 15 U/day.
Similarly, the dependent effect on BP control led to the discontinuation of amlodipine and eplerenone and the decrease in daily furosemide dose from 250 to 50 mg. No significant change in residual diuresis and weekly KtV was observed. Therefore, dialysis prescription could remain unmodified.
The BMI goal, that is a BMI value allowing inclusion in the list for KTR, was achieved within 16 weeks. Due to volume depletion episodes related to the high temperature in Naples (Southern Italy) occurring in the July–August period, the semaglutide dose was reduced to 0.25 mg/week to allow a higher intake of nutrients and salt. This adjustment resulted in a slight increase in BW (up to 87.5 kg at 24 weeks) coupled with improvement in gastric symptoms (Fig. 1). The patient was successfully considered suitable for kidney transplantation.
Conclusions
This case report highlights the positive effects of GLP1-RA in an obese patient with diabetic kidney disease undergoing CAPD. After six months of semaglutide therapy, the patient achieved notable weight loss and reduced his daily insulin dosage by 50%. These improvements made him eligible for kidney transplantation listing.
The significance of weight loss in patients receiving PD is further amplified by the fact that these patients cannot undergo bariatric surgery unless they switched to extracorporeal dialysis.
Beyond weight loss, we observed a remarkable amelioration in BP control, likely due to reduced overhydration and insulin resistance, improving his cardiovascular risk.
Regarding side effects, the patient experienced mild gastric symptoms during semaglutide therapy; however, these symptoms were less tolerated during the hot season, prompting a need for dose reduction to prevent volume depletion.
In conclusion, GLP1-RAs may help improve metabolic control in patients with obesity and diabetes treated by PD potentially making kidney transplantation feasible. GLP1-RAs is well tolerated, though a careful monitoring is required.

Body weight was 97.5 kg (BMI 33.7 Kg/m2) and blood pressure (BP) 150/90 mmHg. The patient was treated with insulin 43 U/day (18 U Aspart and 25 U Degludec), along with furosemide 250 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, eplerenone 50 mg, bisoprolol 2.5 mg/day, clopidogrel/aspirin 70/100 mg, omega−3 fatty acids 3000 mg and atorvastatin 40 mg (Fig. 1). Residual diuresis was 1000 ml/24 h and residual kidney function was 5 ml/min. The CAPD schedule consisted of two 5 h dwells of 2 L of 1.36% glucose and a 14 h dwell of 2 L icodextrin.
On 1st March 2024, the patient began subcutaneous semaglutide with the following schedule: 0.25 mg/week for the first 4 weeks then uptitrated to 0.5 mg/week if tolerated.
After 4 weeks, the patient achieved a weight loss of 2.8 kg. The patient experienced nausea; however, since this adverse effect was well tolerated, the semaglutide dose was increased to 0.5 mg/day.
From week-4 to week-16, a body weight reduction from 94.7 kg to 86.5 kg was observed. The weight loss was associated with a reduction in glycated haemoglobin from 7.6% to 6.1% with a remarkable reduction in daily insulin requirement, from 43 to 15 U/day.
Similarly, the dependent effect on BP control led to the discontinuation of amlodipine and eplerenone and the decrease in daily furosemide dose from 250 to 50 mg. No significant change in residual diuresis and weekly KtV was observed. Therefore, dialysis prescription could remain unmodified.
The BMI goal, that is a BMI value allowing inclusion in the list for KTR, was achieved within 16 weeks. Due to volume depletion episodes related to the high temperature in Naples (Southern Italy) occurring in the July–August period, the semaglutide dose was reduced to 0.25 mg/week to allow a higher intake of nutrients and salt. This adjustment resulted in a slight increase in BW (up to 87.5 kg at 24 weeks) coupled with improvement in gastric symptoms (Fig. 1). The patient was successfully considered suitable for kidney transplantation.
Conclusions
This case report highlights the positive effects of GLP1-RA in an obese patient with diabetic kidney disease undergoing CAPD. After six months of semaglutide therapy, the patient achieved notable weight loss and reduced his daily insulin dosage by 50%. These improvements made him eligible for kidney transplantation listing.
The significance of weight loss in patients receiving PD is further amplified by the fact that these patients cannot undergo bariatric surgery unless they switched to extracorporeal dialysis.
Beyond weight loss, we observed a remarkable amelioration in BP control, likely due to reduced overhydration and insulin resistance, improving his cardiovascular risk.
Regarding side effects, the patient experienced mild gastric symptoms during semaglutide therapy; however, these symptoms were less tolerated during the hot season, prompting a need for dose reduction to prevent volume depletion.
In conclusion, GLP1-RAs may help improve metabolic control in patients with obesity and diabetes treated by PD potentially making kidney transplantation feasible. GLP1-RAs is well tolerated, though a careful monitoring is required.

title: #3720 “Measuring for improvement: changes in the perception of care in haemodialysis patients over four years”
authors: Shaira Martínez-Vaquera; Mª Paz Sorribes; Mirco Dalmaso; Lidia Romero; Jonathan Porras; Ignacio Ponce de León; Teresa Martínez-Sánchez; Fernando MacÁrio
abstract:
Background and Aims
Perception of care is a key indicator for assessing the quality of health services, especially in patients with chronic conditions such as those on haemodialysis (HD), who face physical, emotional and social challenges due to their disease burden and prolonged treatment. Assessing this perception through tools such as the Patient Perception of Care (PPC) Survey allows us to understand what is really important to patients and to identify areas of direct impact on their quality of life. This approach generates valuable data to humanise care, optimise resources, guiding strategies towards a holistic and patient-centred approach
Method
A multicentre retrospective observational study was performed in HD patients, by analysing the responses of the annual, voluntary and anonymous PPC Survey. It consists of 39 specific questions organised in 12 domains involving the care of HD patients: “Access”, “Communication”, “Fluid intake and diet”, “Information”, “Needling”, “Privacy and dignity”, “Scheduling and appointment planning”, “Shared decisions about treatment”, “Support about your care”, “Tests and investigations”, “Environment” and “Transport”. Responses were analysed considering two main scales: Global Score (GS), which measures patient perception by domain on a scale of 0 to 7, and Patient Global Experience (PGE), which assesses overall patient experience on a scale of 0 to 10. In addition, Net Promoter Score (NPS) and participation rate were collected and analysed from survey implementation in 2021 to 2024. Trends in overall patient experience were identified and domain-specific conclusions were drawn to highlight improvements and challenges.
Results
Of the 49 outpatient dialysis centers analysed, the average participation rate was 94.45% over the study period. Of the total 16,187 surveys analysed, 3,703 (93%) were completed in 2021, 4,154 (97%) in 2022; 4,201 (98.71%) in 2023 and 4,129 (96.7%) in 2024, reflecting significant patient engagement. The GS showed continued improvement from 6.30 in 2021 to 6.48 in 2024, reflecting overall progress in the perception of quality of care. Meanwhile, the PGE increased from 8.67 in 2021 to 8.81 in 2024, highlighting an overall positive and growing experience. The NPS, a key indicator of satisfaction and loyalty, remained consistently above the threshold of excellence (>50), with an upward trend, reaching 61.98% in 2024, the highest point of the period analysed. In terms of specific domains, notable improvements were observed in key areas such as ‘Communication’ (from 6.26 in 2021 to 6.47 in 2024) and ‘Fluid Intake and Diet’ (from 6.40 in 2021 to 6.53 in 2024), reflecting significant progress in these essential dimensions for patients. Detailed analysis at question level showed steady progress in patients' reported comfort and access to additional assistance, consolidating the positive perception of the care received. However, areas such as ‘Support’ presented opportunities for improvement in some of the periods studied, suggesting the need for a continued focus on strengthening this dimension.
Conclusion
The PPC survey has proven to be an effective tool for monitoring trends in patient experience. The sustained growth of these indicators reaffirms the importance of continuing to apply and refine these measurement instruments, consolidating a patient-centred model of care and promoting a positive impact on both the quality of life of haemodialysis patients and standards of clinical practice.

title: #294 Construction and evaluation of risk prediction model for peritoneal dialysis patients with volume overload
authors: Lina Fu; Yupu Dou; Lu Li; Na Chen; Yaqi MA; Gordon Chun-Kau Chan; Philip K T Li; Na Tian
abstract:
Background and Aims
This study was designed to analyze the risk factors for the occurrence of volume overload in peritoneal dialysis (PD) patients and construct a risk prediction model.
Method
97 peritoneal dialysis patients attending the General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University from January 1 2019 to May 31 2020 were collected and analyzed. The influencing factors of volume overload in PD patients were initially screened, the final independent influencing factors were determined, the risk prediction model was established, and the differentiation degree, true value and predicted value of the prediction model, as well as the effect of the prediction model were evaluated.
Results
The incidence of volume overload in PD patients was 52.58%, with ECW, E/T, and IPTH as independent risk factors for the occurrence of volume overload in PD patients. The AUC of the modeling set was 0.896, 95% CI: 0.8301–0.9627, sensitivity was 0.843, specificity was 0.870 with moderate differentiation, and the model predictive efficacy was favorable.
Conclusion
The risk prediction model established in this study showed that the influencing factors for the occurrence of volume overload in PD patients were ECW, E/T, and IPTH, which can help the clinical staff to recognize the high-risk group and intervene in time.

title: #591 A murine model of peritoneal fibrosis in adenine-induced chronic kidney disease
authors: Yi-Ting Wu; Yi-Ting Chen; Shuei-Liong Lin
abstract:
Background and Aims
Peritoneal fibrosis is a complication in end-stage-renal-disease patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis, leading to peritoneum function failure. However, most studies investigate peritoneal fibrosis using animals with normal renal function. This study establishes a murine model of peritoneal fibrosis in adenine-induced chronic kidney disease.
Method
6-week-old C57BL/6 mice were fed a 0.2% adenine diet for 6 weeks to induce chronic kidney disease. A single intraperitoneal injection of 0.05% Sodium hypochlorite (NaClO) was used to induce peritoneal fibrosis. After 7 days of NaClO injection, mice were sacrificed and plasma was collected to measure renal function. The adhesion score evaluated the intent of peritoneal fibrosis and Masson's trichrome stain quantified the thickness of the peritoneal membrane. The peritoneal equilibration test was performed by injecting 2 mL 2.5% peritoneal dialysis solution for 30 minutes, to assess the changes in the peritoneal solute transport rates and ultrafiltration volume.
Results
In the adenine-CKD group, each mouse consumed an average of 3.14 g of food daily, equivalent to 6.28 mg of adenine per day. Blood urea nitrogen and creatinine levels were significantly elevated in the adenine-CKD group. (Fig. 1)
After NaClO injury, peritoneal adhesion scores were significantly higher in both the normal and adenine groups, especially the adenine group. Peritoneal adhesions in the adenine group were particularly observed in the intestines and omentum. (Fig. 2A) Thickening of the parietal and visceral peritoneal membrane was observed in NaClO-injured mice, with no differences in the two diets. (Fig. 2B) The peritoneal equilibration test showed that NaClO-injured mice absorbed more glucose from the dialysate, resulting in a corresponding decrease in net ultrafiltration. (Fig. 2C and D)
Conclusion
NaCIO-induced peritoneal fibrosis led to thickened, adhesive peritoneal membranes and a loss of the osmotic gradient, resulting in reduced water removal. Although the adenine group exhibited higher adhesion scores, the decline in renal function did not affect membrane thickening, peritoneal solute transport, or ultrafiltration. This model is relevant to human patients with peritoneal fibrosis and impaired renal function.

title: #2024 Innovative tools for peritoneal dialysis catheter insertion: impact on clinical skills and PD adoption
authors: Patrick Jolomba
abstract:
Background and Aims
Peritoneal dialysis (PD) remains underutilized in many healthcare settings, partly due to limited training opportunities for catheter insertion. This study evaluated virtual reality (VR) as an innovative educational tool for PD catheter insertion training and investigated barriers to PD adoption among renal clinicians.
Method
A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining quantitative surveys of 53 renal clinicians from multiple countries, in Europe, Africa and Asia with qualitative interviews of 15 multi-professional stakeholders (nephrologists, educators, and digital creators). The study evaluated clinician perspectives on PD adoption and assessed a VR-based PD catheter insertion training prototype through the lens of Adult Learning Theory and Technology Acceptance Model.
Results
70% of respondents supported implementing innovative learning tools (40% agree, 30% strongly agree). As shown in Fig. 1, while 34% of clinicians were familiar with simulation training, there is significant potential for growth, with 18.9% expressing interest despite being unfamiliar. Key barriers included lack of PD resources (51.9%) and limited guideline awareness (37.7%). Qualitative findings revealed VR's potential for enhancing spatial understanding of anatomy and procedures, with participants emphasizing its value as a complementary training tool rather than a replacement for traditional methods.
Conclusion
The findings demonstrate strong support for innovative training tools among African renal clinicians, despite current limited exposure. VR-based training shows promise as a complementary educational tool, particularly for enhancing procedural understanding and confidence. Implementation strategies should address resource constraints while leveraging high interest levels among clinicians.

title: #2188 Erythropoietin resistance index (ERI) independently predicts mortality in hemodialysis patients. So, what's beneath the surface?
authors: Matteo Abinti; Deborah Mattinzoli; Masami Ikehata; Giulia Porata; Carlo Maria Alfieri; Lara Caldiroli; Giuseppe Castellano; Simone Vettoretti
abstract:
Background and Aims
The management of anemia is a cornerstone of therapy in hemodialysis patients (HDps), but in most cases high doses of erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) are needed for obtaining good Hemoglobin levels, due to a persistent low-grade inflammation and alterations in martial balance (MB) and mineral metabolism (MM).
Recent data would identify the erythropoietin resistance index (ERI) as an indicator of all-cause and cardiovascular (CV) mortality risk in HD-ps. Despite this, its use and validation in clinical practice are lacking, as is the evaluation of its potential relationship with other relevant biochemical markers.
Aims of the present study were to evaluate: (1) the power of ERI to independently predict mortality in a cohort of HD-ps; (2) the influencing factors of ERI at baseline.
Method
An observational-retrospective study was performed on 100 prevalent HD-ps, excluding those with acute or chronic infections (3 months), neoplasia, or immunosuppressive therapy. Also, patients transferred to other Centers or that underwent kidney transplant were excluded from the analyses.
Patients were divided into two groups based on the median ERI level (9.26 IU*dl/kg/g). ERI was calculated as follows: ESA (IU/week)/weight (kg, post-dialysis)/hemoglobin level (g/dL). At baseline, biochemical characteristics and some specific inflammatory markers were assessed as the average of three measurements taken over three consecutive months.
All-cause mortality was considered as primary outcome along a 3-year follow-up (FU), while CV mortality was a secondary outcome.
Results
HD-ps, predominantly males, had advanced mean age, good Hb values and fair biochemical control (Table 1). As comorbidities, 46% were diabetic and 83% hypertense.
After 3 years of FU, 58% of HD-ps died. High ERI levels strongly predicted all-cause mortality (P = 0.008), with a significant difference between groups after every year (Fig. 1). Interestingly, these significances were lost when considering hemoglobin or weight alone. Notably, no significant evidence was found between ERI and CV mortality (P = 0.096).
We noticed that, at baseline, ERI showed significant correlations with some elements related to inflammation, MB and BM, such as c-terminal FGF23 (Table 1). At logistic regression, ERI remained mainly influenced by markers related to MB (Table 2a), including Activin A, a protein previously suggested to have pro-inflammatory effects and to promote anemia in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD).
Despite these relevant associations at baseline, on the long run ERI remained highly significant in predicting all-cause mortality at multivariate analyses, together with age, C-reactive protein and hepcidin (Table 2b).
Conclusion
Our data showed a strong value for ERI in predicting all-cause mortality in a 3-year FU. On the opposite, this was not confirmed for CV mortality, probably because of the low numerosity of the cohort.
Furthermore, ERI was found to be related to several factors, including cFGF23 and Activin A, both known to be implicated in maintaining an inflammatory state and anemia in CKD patients. Also, multivariate Cox regression suggested that many factors related to inflammation (i.e. age, hepcidin and C-reactive protein) are relevant for survival, even without affecting the high significance of ERI.
In fact, our results suggest the possible presence of some pathological mechanisms that act silently on the development of ESAs resistance, with a strong negative impact on patients’ survival. For its simplicity, ERI should be included in clinical practice, to carefully look at patients’ health and ameliorate their management.
Certainly, increased numbers and a prospective design could better clarify the explored relationships in the future.

title: #3055 Efficacy and safety of recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (r-TPA) in assisted home hemodialysis: a retrospective study from Qatar
authors: Mossab Filali; Abdullah Hamad; Mohamed Yahya Abdelhai; Mostafa Fottoh Elshirbeny; Hamza Ilyes Hassaine; Hoda Tolba; Sandhya Chembolu; Mayson Alali; Dalia Ayed; Shajahan Joseph; Mohamad Alkadi; Hassan Almalki
abstract:
Background and Aims
Qatar's national assisted home hemodialysis (AHHD) is an innovative care model developed to address the distinct challenges of elderly hemodialysis patients with limited mobility. This vulnerable patient population exhibits a high prevalence of central catheter utilization as dialysis vascular access, necessitating comprehensive management of associated complications, primarily dysfunction and infection. Many in this population have exhausted other options and required recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (r-TPA) to maintain good catheter function. This study assessed the efficacy and safety of utilizing the high-risk medication, r-TPA, as a tunneled catheter lock solution in a home healthcare setting.
Method
This retrospective descriptive study examines patients undergoing AHHD between January 1, 2023, and December 31, 2024. Clinical data were extracted from medical records, including demographic information, treatment specifics, and key outcomes. The primary efficacy outcomes assessed included dialysis adequacy (measured by KT/V), blood flow rate (BFR), arterial pressure average and the incidence of catheter-related bloodstream infections (CRBSI). Safety outcomes were evaluated based on the occurrence of adverse events during the study period.
Results
A total of 38 patients on r-TPA maintenance catheter lock were included in the study (24.5% of total AHHD patients), with a mean age of 74.5 years, reflecting the elderly population served by the program. In all instances, diluted r-TPA at a concentration of 1 mg/mL was administered, with the dose adjusted based on the catheter lumen size. Dwell times ranged between 24 and 72 hours, and patient follow-up ranged between 1 and 24 months with a mean of 9.13 months.
The r-TPA successfully maintained adequate BFR >250 mL/min in 86.84 % of cases. Dialysis adequacy (measured by KT/V) remained within acceptable ranges in 86.84 % with a mean of 1.45.
CRBSI occurred in 4 patients over the study period (0.19/1000 catheter days). No major adverse events were reported (allergic reaction or bleeding), and minor bleeding occurred in 5.2 % of cases. Overall, catheter replacement was required in 9 cases (23.6 %) (4 for CRBSI and 5 for persistent catheter malfunction).
Conclusion
The use of r-TPA as a tunneled catheter lock solution in the AHHD program demonstrated excellent efficacy and safety. The incidence of CRBSI and serious bleeding was very low, underscoring the safety of this high-risk medication in a home healthcare setting when used properly. Despite These findings, highlight the feasibility and safety of incorporating r-TPA into AHHD programs.

title: #3215 The prevalence of tunnelled line-associated MRSA and MSSA bacteraemias in a Maltese haemodialysis patient cohort between 2017 and 2024
authors: Elena Farrugia; George Sultana; Peththawadu Thihan Daksitha De Silva; Abigail Azzopardi; Athira Lal; Emanuel Farrugia; Michael A Borg; Elizabeth Scicluna; Claire Farrugia; Diana Vassallo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sepsis is the second most common cause of death in haemodialysis patients and patients dialysing through tunnelled dialysis lines have a 2 to 3-fold increased risk of hospitalization for infection and death compared to patients dialysing through an arteriovenous fistula or graft. This is the first audit looking at the prevalence of catheter-related blood stream infections (CRBSI) in patients receiving haemodialysis via a tunnelled line in Malta. Our aims are to benchmark local data to UK renal registry data and to assess clinical outcomes.
Method
CRBSI were defined as per KDOQI Vascular access 2019 definition. Data regarding demographics, tunnelled line insertion and removal dates, microbiology results and clinical outcomes (admission to intensive therapy unit, seeding and mortality) was collected retrospectively using hospital electronic records between 1st January 2017 and censored on 16th October 2024. Data was analysed using SPSS version 24.0 and Microsoft Excel.
Results

title: #220 Effect of cholecalciferol supplementation on anemia in hemodialysis patients with vitamin D deficiency
authors: Micol Manzuoli; Stefano Costantini; Sandro Feriozzi; Carlo Massimetti
abstract:
Background and Aims
Vitamin D [25(OH)D3] deficiency is common in hemodialysis (HD) patients and is considered an often ignored component in the pathogenesis of anaemia. We evaluated the effect of cholecalciferol supplementation on haemoglobin (Hb) levels in HD patients with vitamin D deficiency and anemia.
Method
Retrospectively, 117/256 patients with Hb levels <11 g/dl and vitamin D levels <30 ng/ml treated with cholecalciferol at a weekly dose of 25,000 IU p.o. for at least 12 months were selected. At follow-up (F-U), only 74 patients had taken cholecalciferol (G1); the remaining 43 were considered the control group (G2). PTH, 25(OH)D3 and ferritin were determined every 6 months.
Results
At baseline, there were no significant differences between the two groups; Hb levels were significantly correlated with 25(OH)D3 (r = .367; P < 0.001) and PTH (r = −.110; P < 0.05). At F-U in the G1 group, there was an increase in Hb from 10.2 ± 0.7 to 11.8 ± 1.2 g/dl (P < 0.001) and in 25(OH)D3 from 13.4 ± 6.2 to 35.0 ± 8.4 ng/ml (P < 0.05), PTH levels decreased from 542 ± 427 to 338 ± 280 pg/ml (P < 0.01). At the same time, the average dosages of ESAs remained unchanged. In this group, the patients insufficient for vitamin D (10–29 ng/ml) went from 69% to 39%, those deficient (<10 ng/ml) from 31% to 0%, while those sufficient (≥30 ng/ml) from 0 to 61%. In the G2 to F-U, there were no significant changes in the main parameters examined.
Conclusion
Vitamin deficiency seems to be associated with anemia, so its supplementation would be desirable to improve the parameters of CKD-MBD and anemia. Our results need to be confirmed from studies conducted on a larger population.

title: #438 Evaluation of toxic effect of cola containing beverages on blood calcium, phosphorus and magnesium level in hemodialysis patients
authors: Ezzeldin Shalaby; Mohammed Abd Elkhaleke; Medhat Othman; Sherif Abd El Rahman; Mostafa Kamal
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cola containing beverages are widely consumed worldwide, however, the actual risk and allowed amount of cola containing beverages in haemodialysis patients still not well studied yet, especially it contains phosphoric acid. Our study aim to evaluate the chronic toxic effect of Cola containing beverages on blood calcium, phosphorus and magnesium level in haemodialysis patients.
Method
The study was conducted at haemodialysis centre of Alzawya One Day Surgery Hospital, Egypt including 60 end stage renal disease patients on regular high flux haemodialysis. Patients divided into 3 groups every group 20 patients: Group A: on high intake of Cola containing beverages more than 400 ml/day or more than 2800 ml/week. Group B: on low intake of Cola containing beverages less than 400 ml/day or less than 2800 ml/week, and Group C: not intake Cola containing beverages at all. After full history taking about intake of cola containing beverages, after medical examination, we drew blood sample from all participants to measure calcium, phosphorus and magnesium blood level for comparison between groups regarding its correlation with duration and amount of intake of Cola containing beverages.
Results
Our study shows that there was a statistically significant difference between groups with higher mean value in non-intake of cola group, followed by Cola low intake group and the lowest value in Cola high intake group regarding calcium “mg/dl”. Additionally, there was a highly statistically significant difference between groups with higher mean value in Cola high intake group, followed by Cola low intake group, and the lowest value in Non-intake of cola group, regarding phosphorus “mg/dl”, but there is no statistically significant difference between groups regarding magnesium “mg/dl”.
Conclusion
Our study results show that Cola containing beverages in higher dose more than 400 ml/day or 2800 ml/week raise phosphorus statistically highly significant, lower calcium level statistically significant, and has no effect on magnesium level in haemodialysis patient.

title: #443 Changes in cardiac output and development, progression of pulmonary hypertension in patients on hemodialysis with an existing arteriovenous fistula
authors: Asalya Abduvakhitova
abstract:
Background and Aims
Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a common complication in hemodialysis patients, potentially linked to arteriovenous fistula (AVF) flow. Understanding the relationship between AVF characteristics, fistula flow, and cardiac function is vital for managing these patients effectively.
To examine the association of pulmonary hypertension (PH) with arteriovenous fistula (AVF) formation and to evaluate the relationship between AVF flow and fistula characteristics.
Method
At the Republican Scientific and Practical Center of Nephrology and Hemodialysis, 52 patients undergoing program hemodialysis were examined. Before AVF placement, patients underwent echocardiography to assess systolic pulmonary artery pressure (PAP), cardiac output (CO), and ejection fraction (EF). After 6 months of follow-up, a second echocardiographic evaluation and Doppler sonographic evaluation of the course of the fistula were performed. Complete data were available for 32 patients.
Results
Study data were collected from 32 patients, 26 males and 6 females with a mean age of 52 years ranging from 15–78 yrs. The data showed a statistically significant positive correlation between fistula flow and PAP2 and PAP changes (P < 0.05). Mean fistula flow was 1322 ml/min in patients without PH and 2750 ml/min in patients with PH. This difference (1428 ml/min) was statistically significant (P = 0.03). We found a significant negative correlation between PAP1 and EF1 and PAP2 and EF2 (P < 0.05). In addition, the mean EF2 in patients without PH was 57% in contrast to 46% in patients with PH. Mean fistula flow in radial fistulae (mean = 422 ml/min, range: 370–474 ml/min) was significantly less than brachial fistulae (mean = 1463 ml, range: 270–3300 ml/min) (P = 0.03). Mean systolic PAP2 of 14.8 mmHg in transplanted patients was 5.9 mmHg less than those who were not transplanted (20.7 mmHg). Diabetes was the most common cause of renal failure and diabetics had a significant reduction in their EF (15.5%) compared with non-diabetic patients (1% reduction) (P = 0.016)
Conclusion
Fistula flow, PAP and EF of all patients should be checked at least 6 months after fistula creation. Patients with higher fistula flow rates and patients with diabetes mellitus need to be more closely observed. In addition, elderly patients with significant cardiac and other comorbidities may be more prone to develop symptoms after AVF creation.

title: #1505 Low handgrip strength predicts long term mortality in patients treated with hemodialysis
authors: Dror Ben-Noach; Dina Levy; Orit Kliuk Ben-Bassat
abstract:
Background and Aims
Handgrip strength (HGS) is an objective, validated and inexpensive method for assessing muscle strength and sarcopenia in patients treated with hemodialysis. Low HGS, defined as values below 27 kg for men and 16 kg for women, is relatively common among this population. It is associated with increased mortality risk in this population. We previously reported a significantly higher mortality rate in hemodialysis patients with low compared to normal HGS, during mean follow up time of 7.66 months (OR for mortality 9.32). The aim of the current report is to evaluate long-term mortality risk in this population.
Method
Our cohort included prevalent hemodialysis patients treated in a single dialysis center in a tertiary hospital. Primary outcome was mortality. HGS was measured pre-dialysis, using a Handgrip Dynamometer in the dominant hand. It was defined as a dichotomous parameter (normal/low). Relevant medical history, clinical and biochemical nutritional parameters were documented and included in the statistical analysis. Univariate Kaplan-Maier and multivariate Cox proportional regression was used to identify predictors of mortality.
Results
The cohort included 74 hemodialysis patients, mean age 69.2 ± 14.3, 24 (32.5%) females. Low HGS was measured in 33 patients (44.5%). During mean follow-up time of 27.06 + 1.43 months, 28 (37.8%) patients died. Low HGS significantly predicted mortality on Cox multivariate analysis, HR 2.84 P = 0.039, 95% CI 1.05–7.65.
Kaplan-Meier curves for time to event for the primary outcome differ significantly (P = 0.001 by log-rank test, Fig. 1).
Conclusion
HGS is a simple device used for muscle strength evaluation in patients treated with hemodialysis. Its strong correlation with short and long-term mortality provides an important prognostic tool as part of patient's assessment.

title: #1702 How to facilitate discussion and management of patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) in routine Dutch dialysis care: a qualitative study
authors: Eline Schade van Westrum; Willem Jan W Bos; Marc Hemmelder; Friedo W Dekker; Yvette Meuleman
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) have been implemented in all Dutch dialysis centers and can, among others, improve symptom burden recognition and patient-professional communication. However, guidance is needed on how to respond and act on PROMs-results. This study aimed to acquire in-depth knowledge about stakeholders' experiences with PROMs, and their perspectives on how to facilitate PROMs discussion and management in routine dialysis care.
Method
A qualitative study was conducted using an interpretive description approach. Individual semi-structured interviews were held (July–October 2024) face-to-face or online with a purposively-sampled heterogeneous group of stakeholders in nephrology care. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analyzed inductively using thematic analysis.
Results
Stakeholders (n = 17; 7 nephrologists, 3 medical social workers, 3 nurses, 1 researcher, 2 policymakers) considered PROMs an important tool to ensure sufficient attention is being paid to patients’ quality of life and symptom burden, and to start a conversation about these health aspects. However, several barriers were encountered when discussing and acting on PROMs, and stakeholders shared their perspectives on how to facilitate PROMs discussion and management.
First, sufficient clarity is needed about the different roles that (healthcare) professionals should fulfill across the whole PROMs-healthcare trajectory. For example, who should invite patients to fill in PROMs, take the lead in discussing PROMs, and contribute to the treatment of such broad spectrum of symptoms—both within and outside the multidisciplinary dialysis team. Second, more knowledge in required on how to support patients with lower levels of (health) literacy to ensure they can also fill in (adapted) PROMs.
Third, guidance is needed on how to discuss ‘less medical’ symptoms (e.g. sleep-, mental- and sexual problems, fatigue). Certain levels of uncertainty and discomfort were experienced based on various factors, including it being sensitive topics (some even considered a cultural taboo), prejudices and personal barriers (e.g. gender- or age differences when discussing such topics), and not knowing how to intervene.
Fourth, there is a clear need for a comprehensive and easily accessible guide on how to manage symptoms. It should contain information about evidence-based multidisciplinary symptom management strategies and referral-options outside the multidisciplinary dialysis team (e.g. psychologist, sexologist). Recommendations for symptom management should take, among others, into account differences in patients’ healthcare insurance and preventing excessive healthcare consumption. Healthcare professionals shared a variety of guidelines and information they used as sources for symptom management, both within and outside nephrology.
Finally, stakeholders stressed the need to incorporate patients’ opinion on how to deal with PROMs-results at the individual level, including symptom management strategies.
Conclusion
To ensure optimal PROMs-usage in routine dialysis care, guidance is needed on how to organize, discuss, and act on PROMs-results. Special attention should be paid towards role-clarification across the PROMs-healthcare trajectory, providing multidisciplinary symptom management guidance (including best practices and referral-options outside the multidisciplinary dialysis team), and strategies to make sure support is tailored to the varying needs and (health) literacy levels of individual patients. Further research should identify patients’ experiences and needs regarding discussing and acting on PROMs.

title: #1703 Annual aortic valve velocity as a predictor of systemic calcification and mortality: a novel monitoring approach in dialysis
authors: Ege Erbay; Ayse Colak; Yelda Deligoz Bildaci; Mehmet Asi Oktan; Cihan Heybeli; Caner Cavdar; Ilker Atay; Serpil Muge Deger; Berfu Korucu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Valvular calcification is concordant with vascular calcification and develops faster in end-stage renal disease patients than in the average population. There are contradictory reports about the pathophysiology and the predictive value of valvular calcification regarding mortality in this patient population. Aortic peak wave velocity (Vmax) measurement is a non-invasive and reliable marker for the diagnosis of valve calcification. Our study analyzes the cardiovascular risk prediction effect of increasing levels of Vmax at different time points in dialysis patients.
Method
We conducted a retrospective, single-center study of incident hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis patients under follow-up between January 1990 and December 2024 in our clinic. Demographics, laboratory, and echocardiographic findings were obtained from medical records. Patients without a baseline echocardiography were excluded. ΔVmax is defined as the last Vmax minus baseline Vmax levels. The patients were divided into two subgroups: Vmax-stable and Vmax-increased.
Results
The baseline demographics, laboratory, and clinical characteristics, including daily elemental calcium and calcitriol or paricalcitol usage, were similar between Vmax-stable and Vmax-increased groups. Annual CaXP levels were significantly and longitudinally higher in the Vmax-increased group. The within-subject effect of the groups was insignificant (F [3.65, 86.91] = 0.851, P = 0.49). The between-subjects effects of the groups were significant, with overall higher values in Vmax increased group (F [1, 80] = 6.86, P = 0.01). Cardiovascular mortality was 9.2% in the Vmax-stable group and 23% in the Vmax-increased group within a median of 11 (IQR: 6–18) years of follow-up of the study population (P = 0.02).
Conclusion
During a follow-up of 24 years, increasing Vmax values were associated with longitudinally higher CaxP levels and mortality in dialysis patients. Even if the increase is subclinical, Vmax follow-up is a non-invasive, easily accessible method and might identify the high-risk group regarding cardiovascular mortality in the dialysis population.

title: #2121 The relationship between low serum magnesium levels and frailty among hemodialysis patients in the West Bank: a cross-sectional study
authors: Mohannad Hassan; Ramzi Shawahna; Mohammad Amro; Rama Elawiy; Hadeel Madieh; Rania Muwafi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a progressive decrease in kidney function that needs renal replacement therapy. Hemodialysis is a type of renal replacement therapy that improves and enhances hemostasis. Patients with CKD will face multiple comorbidities, including frailty; it's a physiologic state of increased vulnerability to stressors that results from decreased physiologic reserves or dysregulation of numerous physiologic systems. Magnesium deficiency is a known risk factor for protein energy wasting, which is closely related to frailty among CKD and end-stage renal disease patients.
This study aims to investigate the relationship between low serum magnesium levels (hypomagnesemia) and frailty among hemodialysis patients in the West Bank, where it will specifically examine the association between hypomagnesaemia and the hemodialysis process, as well as the correlation between frailty and hypomagnesemia among hemodialysis patients.
Method
A cross-sectional study was conducted from January 2024 to January 2025 at Najah National University Hospital (NNUH), Nablus, Palestine, a tertiary care center with a dialysis department where 269 individuals undergo hemodialysis treatment; 252 of them participated after implementation of exclusion criteria. title: #2966 Indirect evaluation of bone metabolism in dialysis: do we all have the same bones?
authors: Matteo Righini; Anna Mistretta; Martina Titone; Davide Martelli; Lilio Hu; Olga Baraldi; Andrea Buscaroli
abstract:
Background and Aims
Bone disorders have emerged as a new area of study in the context of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney diseases (ADPKD). The observed bone defect in patients with ADPKD is discernibly different from the presentation observed in individuals with other etiologies of chronic kidney disease (CKD). It is marked by an adynamic bone disorder, which refers to reduced bone turnover and mineralization and it manifests during the initial phase of CKD. Do ADPKD patients on dialysis have the same bone remodelling as non ADPKD patients? Do they differ in mineral bone disorders treatments? Our goal is to indirectly analyze whether patients with ADPKD also exhibit a different bone metabolism compared to non ADPKD patients while on dialysis, by examining the differences in the type of treatment they have undergone.
Method
Our work is a retrospective, single-center cohort study that analyzes patients on HD and PD who were followed by our Unit from 01/01/2017 to 31/12/2024 (632 patients). We analyzed demographic data (date of birth, gender, blood type), comorbidities (diabetes, hypertension), dialysis data (type of dialysis technique, dialytic age), blood tests (calcium, phosphate, parathormone, vitamin D), therapies (magnesium aluminate, calcium carbonate, sevelamer, sucroferric oxyhydroxide, lantanium carbonate, cholecalciferol, calcitriol, paracalcitol, cinacalcet, etelcalcetide) and fractures. Concerning therapies, we calculated the mean dose (weekly or daily) for each treatment. Normality was evaluated with the Shapiro-Wilks test, the proper test of statistical significance depends on the nature of the examined variables. Differences among means in different groups were analyzed using the t-test or the ANOVA. Categorical data were analyzed using contingency tables and χ2. Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation or as median and Interquartile interval (IQR) when appropriated. Statistical analysis was performed with R software. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results
Overall we considered 150 patients (34 ADPKD and 117 non ADPKD). The group of control was created with a matched propensity score to reduce the selection bias. We considered 10 treatments for mineral bone disorders and we observed the mean dose of each treatment for every patient in both groups. Our thought was that there could be differences among patients with different kidney disease even on dialysis. In our analysis we evidenced no differences among treatment in ADPKD patients compared to non ADPKD. Results are expressed in the Table and in lower Box Plots.
Conclusion
In our analysis, we did not find any differences among the treatments for CKD-MBD to which the patients were subjected during the observed period. Our data suggest that, although preclinical studies and early stages of CKD showed that ADPKD patients exhibit distinct bone mineral disorders, no differences in treatment are observed in dialysis patients. Our data even confirm that there is no difference in fracture risk among hemodialysis patients. Many questions remain unanswered regarding the CKD MBD in patients with ADPKD and many studies still need to be conducted.

title: #3309 Impact of medium cut-off dialysis membranes on outcomes in COVID-19 patients with acute kidney injury
authors: Omer Faruk Akcay; Taha Cetin; Saliha Yıldırım; Hasan Hacı Yeter; Ülver Derİcİ
abstract:
Background and Aims
Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has led to significant morbidity and mortality worldwide, with acute kidney injury (AKI) emerging as a significant non-pulmonary complication of COVID-19. The optimal dialysis strategy for COVID-19 patients with AKI remains a subject of ongoing investigation. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of hemodialysis (HD) membrane type—medium cut-off (MCO) versus low-flux (LF)—on the outcomes of COVID-19 patients with AKI requiring dialysis.
Method
A retrospective analysis was conducted on COVID-19 patients with AKI who required HD (n = 82) between April 2020 and January 2022. Patients were categorized based on the type of dialysis membrane used (MCO vs. LF). Demographic data, clinical characteristics, laboratory findings, and hospital outcomes, including 28-day mortality, were analyzed.
Results
The mean age of the study population was 69.7 ± 11.6 years, with 45% being female. The median time to the initiation of HD was 8 (4–17) days and shorter in the LF group compared to the other group [5 days (3–11) vs. 11 days (6–21), P < 0.001]. Although the groups had similar bloodstream infections and ICU admission rates, the 28-day mortality rate was significantly lower in the MCO group (43% vs. 67%, P = 0.03) (Table 1). Multivariate analysis identified ICU admission as an independent risk factor for 28-day mortality (OR: 7.367, 95% CI: 1.369–39.651, P = 0.03), while HD with MCO membrane was associated with a reduced 28-day mortality risk (OR: 0.344, 95% CI: 0.126–0.942, P = 0.03) (Table 2).
Conclusion
The findings suggest that using MCO membranes in HD may improve survival outcomes in COVID-19 patients with AKI. Further prospective studies are needed to validate these results and elucidate the potential anti-inflammatory benefits of MCO membranes in this patient population.

title: #3636 Frailty and sarcopenia in patients on the kidney transplant waiting list
authors: Avinash Chandu Nanwani; Ester Domenech; Raquel Martínez Mifsut; Jonay Manuel García García; Ingrid Auyanet Saavedra; Gloria Anton-Perez; Ángel Nogueira; Elvira Bosch Benítez-Parodi; Ivan Chamorro Bucheli; Rita Guerra Rodríguez; Ernesto Jose Fernandez Tagarro; César García Cantón
abstract:
Background and Aims
The increasing number of kidney transplants in elderly recipients requires consideration of sarcopenia and frailty in addition to comorbidities, as these conditions are highly prevalent in these patients. They are associated with a higher risk of surgical complications, delayed graft function and reduced graft and patient survival. Early diagnosis of these risk factors in the development of chronic kidney disease (CKD), especially before kidney transplantation, is crucial to improve clinical outcomes in these patients. The aim was to evaluate sarcopenia and frailty in patients on renal replacement therapy (RRT) (hemodialysis (HD) and peritoneal dialysis (PD)) on the waiting list for kidney transplantation.
Method
A descriptive, cross-sectional study of 44 patients on HD or PD who were on the waiting list for kidney transplantation. Assessments of sarcopenia and frailty were performed using analytical parameters including haemoglobin, lipid profile, urea, albumin, prealbumin, transferrin, total lymphocytes, vitamin D levels and C-reactive protein (CRP). In addition, body composition analysis was performed using bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) and nutritional ultrasound. The evaluation was completed with validated and recommended scales such as the Malnutrition-Inflammation Score (MIS), the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) and the FREID scale.
Results
43 patients with a mean age of 54 ± 14 years; 63.6% male and a mean BMI of 26.2 ± 4.3 kg/m² (63.6% overweight, 4.5% underweight) with end-stage chronic kidney disease of various etiologies (20.5% polycystic kidney disease; 20.5% glomerular disease; 15.9% unclassified pathology) on renal replacement therapy (75% hemodialysis; 25% peritoneal dialysis) for 39 ± 26 months.
Analytical parameters were analyzed (6% anemic; 27% with absolute lymphopenia; 11.4% hypoalbuminemic and 18% hyperalbuminemia; 27% hypocholesterolemic; 70.5% with low transferrin levels, 38.6% with elevated inflammatory parameters (CRP >1) and 41% with vitamin D deficiency). Additionally, various validated scales were used (MIS with 29.5% of patients malnourished, FREID with 38.6% pre-frail and 15.9% frail, and SPPB with 29.5% pre-frail and 13.6% frail), associated with BIA (34.1% with high fat mass and 4.5% with high skeletal muscle mass). Nutritional ultrasound of the dominant leg's rectus femoris was also performed (75% compatible with sarcopenia).
Conclusion
There is a high prevalence of frail and sarcopenic patients on the kidney transplant waiting list. Therefore, a comprehensive evaluation using various tools is essential to detect this group of patients and establish a prehabilitation program with a multidisciplinary approach.

title: #267 Comparison of simulated dialysis efficacy and actual dialysis efficacy of hemodialysis patients
authors: Tomoyuki Tanaka; Takeshi Shigematsu
abstract:
Background and Aims
In hemodialysis, the choice of the dialyzer and settings, such as blood flow rate, significantly affect the effectiveness of the treatment. It would be helpful to create a computer-programmed simulator that would allow the preliminary verification of the effect of treatment by changing the blood volume, dialysate flow rate, dialysate time, and dialyzer. However, such a simulator has not yet been developed. Therefore, this study created a simulator to validate the efficiency of dialysis according to the treatment conditions.
Methods
A program was developed using Python to calculate the Kt/V values and postdialysis blood urea nitrogen (BUN) concentrations from the published performance ratings of each dialyzer (clearance, blood flow, and dialysate flow) and hemodialysis treatment conditions (choice of the dialyzer, blood flow, dialysate flow, dialysis time, water removal, and body weight). Data on postdialysis BUN concentration were collected from 17 patients on chronic maintenance hemodialysis treatment from the collaborating medical institutions. The actual Kt/V values were calculated using the Shinzato formula (Shinzato Kt/V). The data and simulated values were compared using correlation analysis and Bland-Altman plots.
Results
Data were obtained from 17 patients from the collaborating medical institutions: age, 70 ± 8.5 years; treatment method, hemodialysis; Shinzato Kt/V, 1.4 ± 3.5; dialysis time, 4.4 ± 1.5 h; blood flow, 200 ± 20.5 ml/min; and dialysate flow, 500 ± 10 ml/min. The simulated Kt/V was 1.5 ± 0.5. The correlation coefficient between simulated Kt/V (SimKt/V) and Shinzato Kt/V was 0.7 [mean = 0.5; standard deviation (SD) = 0.17]. The correlation between simulated and actual postdialysis BUN concentrations was 0.8 [mean = −3.9 mg/dl; SD = 2.9 mg/dl].
Conclusion
The simulated Kt/V was higher than the actual Kt/V and the simulated postdialysis BUN concentration was smaller than the actual value due to the fluid volume and clearance being assumed to be ideal during simulation, which may have been overestimated. The errors were not considered to be clinically significant.

title: #806 Serum activin A and bone metabolism in patients undergoing hemodialysis
authors: Yosuke Nakagawa; Hiroo Takahashi; Toru Hyodo; Miho Hida; Takao Suga; Takatoshi Kakuta; Hirotaka Komaba
abstract:
Background and Aims
Activin A, a widely expressed factor involved in cell differentiation, proliferation, and inflammation, is increased with declining kidney function. It promotes osteoclast differentiation in kidney failure, and might be involved in bone metabolism abnormalities in patients with chronic kidney disease. However, few studies have examined the association of activin A between bone metabolism, bone mineral density (BMD), and fracture risk in hemodialysis patients.
Method
We measured serum activin A levels using a sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN, USA) in 35 healthy individuals and 654 hemodialysis patients enrolled in the Tokai Dialysis Prospective Cohort Study. We employed multivariable linear regression to explore the associations of serum activin A levels with bone alkaline phosphatase (BAP), tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase-5b (TRACP-5b), and metacarpal BMD. We also compared activin A levels between patients with and without previous or incident fractures.
Results
The median serum activin A level in hemodialysis patients was 733 pg/mL (interquartile range [IQR], 591–912 pg/mL), which was 2.6-fold higher than that in healthy individuals (277 pg/mL; IQR 216–289 pg/mL; P <0.001). Patients with higher activin A had longer duration of dialysis; were more likely to have polycystic kidney disease; had higher serum alkaline phosphatase and phosphorus. There was no difference in serum calcium or intact parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels across activin A tertiles. In a univariate analysis, higher serum activin A levels were strongly associated with higher TRACP-5b levels. This result was unchanged after adjustment for age, gender, dialysis vintage, diabetes, body mass index, and serum intact PTH. Similar trend was observed for serum BAP levels. However, activin A levels were not associated with metacarpal BMD and previous or incident fractures.
Conclusion
These findings suggest that in patients undergoing hemodialysis, activin A may be involved in high bone turnover, independent of secondary hyperparathyroidism and gender. However, serum activin A levels were not associated with BMD or fracture risk in hemodialysis patients. Additional research is required to determine the role of activin A in bone metabolism in kidney failure.

title: #1280 Hemodialysis session effects on autonomic nervous system function: hemodynamic responses and baroreflex sensitivity
authors: Erasmia Sampani; Artemios Karagiannidis; Marieta P Theodorakopoulou; Fotini Iatridi; Danai Faitatzidou; Aggelos Koutlas; Nasra Haddad; Panagiotis Giamalis; Despoina Sarridou; Konstantina Dipla; Andreas Zafeiridis; Pantelis Sarafidis
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiac arrhythmias are the first cause of death in hemodialysis patients and autonomic dysfunction possesses a predominant role in the arrhythmogenic substrate of these patients. This is the first study comparing baroreflex sensitivity (BRS) and hemodynamic responses at rest and after mental- and physical-stimulation maneuvers at multiple timepoints around and during the dialysis session.
Method
36 hemodialysis patients underwent continuous measurements of beat-to-beat blood pressure (BP) and heart rate (HR) with Finometer-PRO. Recordings at rest and during mental arithmetic, orthostatic, and handgrip exercise tests were used for calculation of BRS and hemodynamic responses in each individual.
Results
BRS did not differ significantly when assessed at different timepoints around hemodialysis and as a response to mental and physical stress tests. Regarding hemodynamic parameters, during mental stress, systolic (SBP, 149.2 ± 29.8 vs 157.2 ± 27.3 mmHg, P = 0.035), diastolic BP (DBP, 70.2 ± 18.3 vs 79.8 ± 13.2 mmHg, P = 0.001), mean arterial pressure and HR were significantly higher at mid-dialysis compared to the non-dialysis day. During the orthostatic test, SBP (137.4 ± 25.7 vs 128.6 ± 32.5 mmHg, P = 0.031), stroke volume and cardiac output were significantly reduced, and HR significantly increased post-dialysis (80.9 ± 13.4 vs 87.5 ± 16.8 bpm, P < 0.001). During the handgrip test, no differences in SBP/DBP levels were evident in pre- versus post-dialysis, while HR was higher in post-dialysis measurements (81.6 ± 13.3 vs 86.7 ± 15.3 bpm, P = 0.002).
Conclusion
Dialysis session per se provokes significant changes in hemodynamic responses after stimulation with multiple physiological test maneuvers but did not affect BRS. This hemodialysis-provoked autonomic dysregulation could in part explain the increased cardiovascular risk of these patients.

During the orthostatic test, SBP (137.4 ± 25.7 vs 128.6 ± 32.5 mmHg, P = 0.031), stroke volume and cardiac output were significantly reduced, and HR significantly increased post-dialysis (80.9 ± 13.4 vs 87.5 ± 16.8 bpm, P < 0.001). title: #1326 Effect of agave inulin on constipation and quality of life in peritoneal dialysis patients
authors: Xunaxi Nahomi García Rodríguez; Paola Azucena Alvarado Pelayo; Ari Cisneros Hernández; Jose Manuel Rodriguez Chagolla
abstract:
Background and Aims
Constipation affects a large part of the population with chronic kidney disease (CKD), in peritoneal dialysis (PD) it is the most prevalent symptom, producing deterioration in the patient's quality of life and is related to cardiovascular outcomes [1–4].
Objective
To compare the impact of agave inulin supplementation versus the use of lactulose on constipation, gastrointestinal symptoms and quality of life in peritoneal dialysis patients.
Method
Randomized controlled clinical trial, two intervention groups both with nutritional therapy, one group with agave inulin supplementation 9 gr/day and the other with lactulose 10 ml c/8 hrs. Subjects with <3 months of PD onset, >18 years old, with constipation (Bristol scale and/or Rome IV criteria) were included, and a gastrointestinal symptoms questionnaire was applied.
Results
38 participants, inulin (n = 20) and lactulose (n = 18); after 3 months of intervention, in the inulin group there was a reduction in the presence of constipation according to the Bristol scale of 65% (P = .001) and the lactulose group of 17% (P = .158) with increase in cases of diarrhea in these group. By Rome IV criteria, constipation and the presence of symptoms were reduced in the inulin group 50% (P = .001) and in 4 symptoms (P = <.05); and in the lactulose group 45% (P = .017) and in 2 symptoms (P = <.05). (Table 1)
Conclusion
Supplementation with agave inulin for the correction of constipation in patients on peritoneal dialysis and nutritional assessment is not inferior to the use of lactulose, improves stool consistency, gastrointestinal symptoms associated with constipation and the number of bowel movements, being this an alternative to treatment without causing diarrhea in patients.
Key words: constipation, peritoneal dialysis, treatment.

title: #1667 SARC-F questionnaire as a screening tool for identifying hemodialysis patients at high risk of falls and fractures
authors: Minoru Ito; Ikuto Masakane
abstract:
Background and Aims
Falls and fractures are common complications in hemodialysis patients, significantly impacting their quality of life and mortality. Hemodialysis patients are prone to sarcopenia and frailty, leading to increased fall risk. The SARC-F (strength, assistance in walking, rise from a chair, climb stairs, and falls) questionnaire is commonly used as a screening tool for sarcopenia. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of the SARC-F questionnaire in assessing fall risk among hemodialysis patients.
Method
This retrospective observational study included 590 hemodialysis patients with dialysis vintage ≥3 months (mean age: 68.2 ± 11.8 years, male: 74%, diabetes: 46%). SARC-F scores, nutritional status, and clinical data were assessed in June 2023. Falls, fractures, and mortality were analyzed as outcomes during the follow-up period until June 2024.
Results
Among 590 patients, 146 (24.7%) experienced falls (including 17 fractures), and 24 (4.0%) died during the study period. Multivariate logistic regression analysis, adjusted for age, dialysis vintage, diabetes, sex, and nutritional status, revealed that SARC-F score ≥4 was independently associated with falls (OR: 2.19, 95% CI: 1.37–3.51, P = 0.0011) and fractures (OR: 4.8, 95% CI: 1.64–14.1, P = 0.0042), but not with mortality (OR: 1.65, 95% CI: 0.65–4.15, P = 0.2979).
Conclusion
Recent studies have highlighted SARC-F's low sensitivity in detecting sarcopenia among hemodialysis patients. However, our findings demonstrate that SARC-F score ≥4 is a significant predictor of falls and fractures in this population. The SARC-F questionnaire, combined with other clinical assessments, can help identify high-risk patients who may benefit from targeted fall prevention interventions.

title: #1886 Can the prediction power of mechanistic models be augmented by using clinically acquired data?
authors: Giustina Casagrande; Andrea Ambrosini; Carlo Jovane; Carla Colturi; Philipp Grosse; Mariagiulia Magatti; Gianvincenzo Melfa; Silvio Pianca; Antonio Bellasi; Reto Martin Venzin; Marialaura Costantino
abstract:
Background and Aims
Dialysis is a lifesaving treatment for end-stage renal disease. Because it impacts the equilibrium of fragile patients, customized treatments are required. To guarantee the patient the highest therapy tolerance, the development of tools to support the clinician in tailoring the patient's prescription is encouraged.
The increased availability of health-related data has pushed the development of many machine learning (ML) studies that bypass the need for causality and focus exclusively on prediction. Mechanistic models are usually developed to answer specific scientific cause-effect questions. A hybrid approach consisting of a synergistic combination of mechanistic and ML models appears as the best compromise.
Here, we want to quantify the improvement obtainable by using clinically acquired data to augment the prediction power of an existing mechanistic model of the exchange of fluids and solutes during dialysis treatment.
Method
The parametric multicompartment kinetic model, developed by Casagrande et al., taken as a reference, is based on mass and fluid balance equations both in the patient and across the dialyzer membrane: two pools (intra- and extra-cellular) are considered to describe the solute mass exchange and three for fluid transfer (plasmatic, interstitial, and intracellular.
A set of parameters has been inserted into the models (ρ [-], k(s) [L/s], η(s). [-], CaBuffer_coeff [mmol]) modulating the exchanges across the main involved membranes. In the basic version of the model, these parameters are set to default values as from the literature. In the data-trained model version, they were estimated in 3 consecutive sessions, exploiting a Constrained Non-Linear Optimization method and allowing the model to appraise the peculiar response to the dialysis for each patient. After the training, the model can predict the patient-specific response of the patient (ID outputs). The normalized Root Mean Squared Error (nRMSE), was used to evaluate the prediction correctness, for each clinically measured solute Sodium, Potassium, Chloride, Calcium, Bicarbonate, Glucose, and Urea.
Results
The identification of the patient-specific parameters based on the data coming from the dialysis session implies a significant improvement in modeling performance from DEFAULT to ID outputs. With an average error reduction of the nRMSE error of 1%–2% point for solutes already well simulated as Potassium and Sodium and achieving a reduction of as much as 9%–10% points for Ca and Mg, for which, leaving the values at default, does not allow a correct description all over the patients. The use of hybrid models also shows improved performances compared to other literature models describing the patient's body fluid and solute shift during dialysis. The possibility to tailor the model to patient characteristics is surely a key factor.
Conclusion
The use of mechanistic models based on data is becoming increasingly widespread precisely because it allows us to exploit the potential of large amounts of data without losing the possibility to study the relationships between causes and effects. In the specific case, the data-informed mechanistic models, coupling patient-specific clinical data with a detailed description of the phenomena involved in the dialysis treatment, allows a better description of the patient's peculiar response without losing the explainability of the involved phenomena. The analysis of a larger population will also give the possibility to infer the relationship between the patient characteristics and their response to the treatment.
