title: #1276 Arteriovenous fistula flow: unlocking the link to cardiac complications in hemodialysis patients
authors: Omaima Taie; Hassan Chtata
abstract:
Background and Aims
The impact of arteriovenous fistulas (AVFs) on cardiac health in long-term hemodialysis patients, particularly their role in heart failure (HF), remains controversial. This study examines the relationship between AVF flow and cardiac function to determine HF prevalence. It identifies an AVF flow threshold predictive of HF risk and evaluates cardiac changes over six months in patients with end-stage kidney disease.
Method
This study prospectively tracked 92 individuals undergoing dialysis from their initial enrollment to subsequent follow-ups at three and six months. Evaluations encompassed clinical assessments, heart imaging via echocardiography, Doppler ultrasound to measure AVF blood flow, and laboratory tests. The severity of heart failure (HF) was classified using the New York Heart Association (NYHA) system.
Results
The average duration of dialysis prior to inclusion was 31.75 ± 16.62 months. Approximately 38% of participants were diagnosed with HF. Patients with HF displayed significantly higher AVF flow rates compared to those without HF (P < 0.001). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis identified an AVF flow threshold of ≥1230 mL/min as a robust indicator of HF risk (AUC: 0.988, CI 95%: 0.93–1.00, P < 0.0001). Over the monitoring period, left ventricular ejection fraction (EF) and shortening fraction (SF) showed slight increases without statistical significance, likely due to a significant rise in hemoglobin levels (P = 0.009) and reductions in blood pressure (P = 0.482 for systolic and P = 0.025 for diastolic). Although cardiac output and AVF flow decreased, no significant relationship was observed between the two. Additionally, the left ventricular mass index (LVMi), an indicator of heart strain, was notably higher in participants with HF compared to those without (P < 0.001).
Conclusion
Effectively managing high blood pressure, anemia, and ventricular hypertrophy is crucial to slowing HF progression in individuals with end-stage kidney disease. An AVF flow rate of ≥1230 mL/min serves as a strong predictor for identifying patients at greater risk of developing HF.

title: #1712 Adrenal insufficiency in hemodialysis patients may be a more frequent problem than we thought
authors: María Teresa Fernandez Quirós; Aurora Polo Moyano; Maria Laura Fuentes Sanchez; Magdalena Palomares Bayo; María José Espigares Huete
abstract:
Background and Aims
Adrenal insufficiency (AI) is a rare endocrine disorder, with a prevalence in Europe of 2.1–4.2/10,000 people. Its diagnosis is challenging due to its nonspecific clinical presentation. In patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) requiring hemodialysis (HD), the diagnosis is even more difficult, as both conditions share similar signs and symptoms. Given its likely underdiagnosis, we conducted a screening for AI among patients with chronic hypotension (CH) in our HD unit.
Method
We selected patients with CH, defined as systolic blood pressure (SBP) below 100 mmHg for at least 3 months. Cortisol, ACTH, aldosterone, and renin levels were measured in the morning.
Results
The detection of patients with chronic hypotension (CH) was conducted in January 2024. The total sample for the screening consisted of 124 hemodialysis (HD) patients. Twelve patients (9.6%) were diagnosed with CH, and two cases of adrenal insufficiency (AI) were identified, representing 16.67% of the CH group and 1.61% of the total HD population.
Among patients with CH, 50% were male and 50% female. The mean time on dialysis for patients with CH was 9.36 years. A significant majority (92%) had a history of hypertension. Additionally, 75% of these patients utilized a central venous catheter (CVC) as their vascular access. The primary causes of CVC use included a history of arteriovenous fistula (AVF) thrombosis, primary AVF dysfunction, vascular access-related steal syndrome, or a situation of exhausted vascular access (33.3% of hypotensive patients). Notably, 50% of the patients diagnosed with chronic hypotension died during 2024, within a one-year follow-up period.
Furthermore, 50% of patients exhibited elevated aldosterone levels, likely as a reactive response to hypotension.
Conclusion
CH in HD patients is associated with high morbidity and mortality, as well as a significant impact on quality of life. AI, a rare disorder in the general population, may have a higher prevalence among HD patients and could be underlying the cause of some of these cases. Its detection is crucial, as appropriate treatment may improve survival and quality of life in these patients.
CH is a clinically significant issue in HD patients. Its presence complicates managing HD patients, for example by hindering the achievement of necessary ultrafiltration and impairing the creation and maintenance of a functioning arteriovenous fistula, leading to a higher prevalence of central venous catheters as vascular access. These patients exhibit higher morbidity and mortality compared to those with normal or elevated blood pressure. AI is likely underdiagnosed and often presents with nonspecific symptoms that can easily be mistaken for those of CKD or HD. In our unit, we identified two cases, which suggests a prevalence rate of 161 per 10,000 HD patients, considerably higher than that in the general population. This may be due to the increased risk factors in CKD patients, including high-dose corticosteroid use, intra-abdominal infections, and hypoalbuminemia.

title: #1858 Optimizing phosphate removal: is an extended dialyzer the answer?
authors: Natasha Eftimovska-Otovikj; Bojana Vrevezoska; Elizabeta Poposka; Evgenija Nikolova; Teodora Krstevska
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyperphosphatemia is a significant factor in hemodialysis-related morbidity and mortality. In addition to dietary phosphate restriction and phosphate binders, phosphate removal via dialysis plays a crucial role. This study aimed to evaluate the influence of dialyzer membrane type and surface area, purified blood volume, serum phosphate levels, and dialysis session length on phosphate elimination.
Method
Eight patients (3 women, 5 men) with serum phosphate levels ≥2.0 mmol/L were included. They underwent midweek bicarbonate hemodialysis using a high-permeability polysulfone membrane (ultrafiltration coefficient: 55 mL/h/mmHg) with surface areas of 1.8 m² and 2.1 m² (4:4 patients, respectively) for an average of 263.12 ± 23.97 minutes, with a dialysate flow of 550 mL/min. In the following midweek session, they received expanded hemodialysis with a medium-permeability polyarylethersulfone membrane (UF coefficient: 59 mL/h/mmHg) with surface areas of 1.8 m² and 2.0 m². Phosphorus clearance (MPO4) was calculated based on treatment time, phosphate concentrations in dialysate and blood, and total depurated phosphorus per session. MPO4 was analyzed in relation to plasma phosphorus levels, dialysis duration, and dialyzer type and surface. All patients had an arteriovenous fistula as vascular access.
Results
Phosphate removal correlated positively with pre-HD serum phosphate levels and purified blood volume (P = 0.001), while dialyzer type (high-flux: 32.67 ± 9.5 mmol/session vs. extended medium-flux: 34.94 ± 10.01 mmol/session), dialyzer surface area, and session length showed no significant impact (P = 0.29; P = 0.67; P = 0.15, respectively). Multivariate regression analysis confirmed that pre-HD serum phosphate levels and purified blood volume are predictive factors for phosphate removal.
Conclusion
Pre-HD serum phosphate levels and purified blood volume are key predictors of phosphate removal during dialysis, with no significant influence from dialyzer type, surface area, or session length.

In addition to dietary phosphate restriction and phosphate binders, phosphate removal via dialysis plays a crucial role. This study aimed to evaluate the influence of dialyzer membrane type and surface area, purified blood volume, serum phosphate levels, and dialysis session length on phosphate elimination.
Method
Eight patients (3 women, 5 men) with serum phosphate levels ≥2.0 mmol/L were included. They underwent midweek bicarbonate hemodialysis using a high-permeability polysulfone membrane (ultrafiltration coefficient: 55 mL/h/mmHg) with surface areas of 1.8 m² and 2.1 m² (4:4 patients, respectively) for an average of 263.12 ± 23.97 minutes, with a dialysate flow of 550 mL/min. In the following midweek session, they received expanded hemodialysis with a medium-permeability polyarylethersulfone membrane (UF coefficient: 59 mL/h/mmHg) with surface areas of 1.8 m² and 2.0 m². Phosphorus clearance (MPO4) was calculated based on treatment time, phosphate concentrations in dialysate and blood, and total depurated phosphorus per session. MPO4 was analyzed in relation to plasma phosphorus levels, dialysis duration, and dialyzer type and surface. All patients had an arteriovenous fistula as vascular access.
Results
Phosphate removal correlated positively with pre-HD serum phosphate levels and purified blood volume (P = 0.001), while dialyzer type (high-flux: 32.67 ± 9.5 mmol/session vs. extended medium-flux: 34.94 ± 10.01 mmol/session), dialyzer surface area, and session length showed no significant impact (P = 0.29; P = 0.67; P = 0.15, respectively). Multivariate regression analysis confirmed that pre-HD serum phosphate levels and purified blood volume are predictive factors for phosphate removal.
Conclusion
Pre-HD serum phosphate levels and purified blood volume are key predictors of phosphate removal during dialysis, with no significant influence from dialyzer type, surface area, or session length.

title: #2341 Analysis of the skeletal muscle index in hemodialysis patients over 80 years old
authors: Kunimi Maeda; Chie Ogawa; Taku Morito
abstract:
Background and Aims
The average age of patients with chronic renal failure treating with hemodialysis therapy has increased by 10 years to 69.8 years in about 25 years, and the age of 70 is imminent. Of the 334653 dialysis patients at the end of 2022, 23.8% were aged over 80 years old. In case of the treatment of elderly dialysis patients, it is very important to measure and evaluate frailty measures. It is important to implement exercise therapy aimed at maintaining muscle mass as part of frailty countermeasures. In our clinic, we have been conducting exercise therapy using exercise bikes and other equipment during dialysis for averagely 20 mintues. Skeletal muscle index based on the BIA method is considered to be an effective method for evaluating muscle mass maintenance by exercise therapy and confirming and evaluating its effects. However, there are few reports that evaluate changes in skeletal muscle index in elderly dialysis patients with continuous exercise therapy. The aim of this study was to evaluate skeletal muscle index by providing continuous exercise therapy during dialysis to outpatient dialysis patients over 80 years and older, and to evaluate skeletal muscle index by performing InBody, and to investigate whether exercise therapy performed during dialysis treatment is effective in maintaining muscle mass in the elderly.
Method
InBody was performed on 17 dialysis patients aged 80 years or older (80 to 98 years old) (9 men, mean age 84.5 years, 8 women, mean age 87.3 years) who went to the outpatient clinic after dialysis was completed, and the skeletal muscle index was calculated using the BIA method. We compared the skeletal muscle index of patients who had been on exercise therapy for some time and those who had not. Patients who did not receive exercise therapy were given exercise therapy for one year, and skeletal muscle index was measured after one year, and changes in skeletal muscle index due to exercise therapy were evaluated.
Results
The mean skeletal muscle index of the 17 subjects was 5.9 kg/m2 for males and 4.5 kg/m2 for females. Only two male patients were identified who met the criteria for skeletal muscle mass loss. Both of the two patients who had cleared the criteria had experience with ergometer exercise therapy while on dialysis. At the same time, daily activities and physical activity were also good. The skeletal muscle index of three patients who had not undergone exercise therapy and who had started exercise therapy while on dialysis was 0.1 kg/m2 and 0.2 kg/ m2, respectively, at the start of exercise therapy and after 1 year.
Conclusion
Exercise therapy during dialysis was thought to have the effect of stopping the decline of skeletal muscle index muscle in elderly dialysis patients and maintaining and improving muscle mass. Maintaining muscle mass through exercise therapy during dialysis is effective in preventing the onset of frailty.

title: #2689 Healthcare team's opinion about an exercise program with audiovisual support during hemodialysis
authors: Eva Segura-Ortí; Emanuele Poliana Lawall Gravina; Claudia Merino-Ansuategui; Daniel Bellés León; Marina Fernández Gámez; Helena Guillem Cambra; Paula Guzmán Prieto; Mariana Díaz Valenzuela; Daniel Gallego Zurro; Carmen Maria Perez-Baylach; Begoña Bonilla Culebras; María del Mar Ruperto López
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) undergoing hemodialysis (HD) experience a significant reduction in muscle mass and strength, which decreases physical and functional capacity increasing morbidity and mortality rates. Although the importance and safety of exercise during maintenance HD are well-documented in the literature, the impact of such programs on the daily workflow of the multidisciplinary healthcare team remains unclear.
Objective
To evaluate the opinion of a hemodialysis center's healthcare team regarding the implementation of an intradialytic exercise program supported by audiovisual resources.
Method
A qualitative study was conducted with the healthcare team at the B. Braun Avitum Renal Care Center in Massamagrell, Valencia, Spain. A 12-question questionnaire was used as part of the feasibility study for an audiovisual-supported intradialytic exercise program (GRexID). In this program, patients performed 12 sessions of upper and lower limb exercises guided by a 20-minute video, shown either individually or in groups during HD sessions. After the intervention period, the healthcare team was invited to complete the questionnaire anonymously and virtually. The questionnaire included questions about the importance of implementing exercise programs during HD, perceived benefits, and potential barriers. Additionally, it assessed the team's interest in engaging in an exercise program during their work hours. The questionnaire included open-ended, multiple-choice, and Likert-scale questions (ranging from 1 “strongly disagree” to 5 “strongly agree”).
Results
A total of 19 professionals (79% women) completed the questionnaire, comprising 21% doctors, 58% nurses, and 21% nursing assistants. The median age of professionals was 38 (18) years and the median time working with CKD patients on HD was 10 (12) years. Regarding program implementation, 89.5% of respondents agreed with its implementation. When asked about the importance of exercise, 42.1% agreed, and 57.9% strongly agreed that patients with CKD on HD should increase their physical activity levels. Additionally, 73.7% agreed that exercise should be performed during HD sessions. The primary benefits identified by the professionals included promoting physical activity (89.4%), maintaining muscle and joint function (84.2%), improving health-related quality of life (78.9%), enhancing cardiovascular function (68.4%), and supporting mental health (63.1%). The main barriers to patient participation in the program were identified as low motivation (78.9%), preexisting health conditions (73.6%), and poor physical conditioning (63.1%). The presence of a physiotherapist (84.2%) and adequate training for both patients (68.4%) and healthcare staff (52.6%) were highlighted as essential resources for the program's success. Regarding the healthcare team, 79% reported experiencing physical pain, particularly lower back pain (68.4%) and neck pain (57.8%), and 57.9% agreed with engaging in an exercise program during working hours to address these health issues.
Conclusion
The healthcare professionals at a hemodialysis clinic expressed strong support for the implementation of an audiovisual-supported intradialytic exercise program.

title: #236 Utilization of peritoneal dialysis (PD) in ESKD with refractory ascites: a case series
authors: Naveen Kumar Medi; Naveen Kumar Mattewada; Shivanand Nayak
abstract:
Background and Aims
Refractory ascites, a complication of end organ damage especially related to liver and heart, poses significant management challenges due to its resistance to diuretic therapy and repeated large-volume paracentesis (LVP). PD has emerged as a primary therapeutic option, particularly in those with concurrent renal dysfunction and are unresponsive to conventional treatments. This case series evaluates the role of PD in the management of refractory ascites in 3 of our patients.
Methodology and Results
We had 1 patient with cirrhosis, hepatitis C related and refractory ascites with ESKD stage V on conservative care and 2 patients with ‘HD related ascites’ with a HD vintage of more than 12 months, who also received conventional therapies, including diuretics and multiple LVP but with no significant improvement. All 3 patients were initiated on PD with a break in time of 2 weeks in all the cases, followed by APD for 10 days (under observation) and then CAPD was continued. (conservative care continued in cirrhotic patient and HD was stopped in the other 2 patients). Patients were closely monitored for clinical parameters like hemodynamics, fluid balance, leaks, renal functions and other lab parameters. Follow-up included assessment of complications and survival outcomes.
All 3 patients demonstrated marked improvements in ascitic fluid removal and overall stable clinical status after initiating PD. The mean volume of ascitic fluid removed was significant and none of the patients required intermittent HD, for renal failure during the follow-up period. Overall patients experienced a substantial reduction in hospital readmissions, while the patient with liver failure required couple of admission's in last 6 months and recovered with medical management. No major adverse events related to PD were recorded, and the overall quality of life with complications risks were very low when compared to HD.
Conclusion
PD appears to be a safe and effective option for managing refractory ascites in cirrhotic patients, particularly in those who do not respond to conventional therapies. This case series provides preliminary evidence supporting PD as a feasible therapeutic management in this category of patients. Larger, prospective studies are warranted to confirm these findings and establish clear guidelines for the use of PD in refractory ascites.

title: #362 Success of online, interactive, case-based CME at improving nephrologists’ competence and confidence related to DD-CKD-anemia diagnosis and management
authors: Amy Larkin; Donald Blatherwick
abstract:
Background and Aims
We sought to determine if online continuing medical education (CME) could improve the competence and confidence of nephrologists related to dialysis dependent-CKD-anemia (DD-CKD-anemia) diagnosis and management.
Method
Educational design included a “test, then teach” approach to elicit cognitive dissonance, with evidence-based feedback provided following each learner response. A repeated pairs pre-/post-assessment study design and a McNemar's test (P < .05 is considered significant) assessed educational effect, with Cohen's d being used to assess educational impact (<0.2 modest effect, 0.2–0.49 small effect, 0.5–0.79 moderate effect and >0.8 extensive effect). The activity launched October 31, 2024 and data were collected through December 3, 2024.
Results
In total, 441 nephrologists participated and 34 answered all pre-/post-assessment questions within the data collection period and were included in the study.
Overall improvements were seen after participation: Overall, 38% of nephrologists improved their competence9% of nephrologists demonstrated improvements in diagnosing DD-CKD (P = .08), for a moderate impact of d = .6824% of nephrologists demonstrated improvements in diagnosing ESA hyporesponsiveness (P < .01)15% of nephrologists demonstrated improvements in managing DD-CKD-anemia (P = NS)38% of nephrologists had a measurable improvement in confidence in using HIF PHIs to treat anemia of DD-CKD (P < .01) Continued educational gaps: 18% of nephrologists need additional education on managing difficult-to-treat patients with anemia of DD-CKD
Conclusion
This study demonstrates the success of online, interactive, case-based CME on improving competence of nephrologists related to diagnosis and management of DD-CKD-anemia, as well as the confidence in using HIF PHIs to treat DD-CKD-anemia. Continued gaps were identified related to management of DD-CKD-anemia that should be addressed in future education, focused on knowledge of newer treatments followed by case-based application, for the most impactful education.

title: #979 Therapeutic plasma exchange: 13-year center experience
authors: Mariana Dias Pais; Diogo Borges; Catarina Cardoso; Filipa Rodrigues; Maria Rita Da Silva Gonçalves Dias; Ana Messias; Cristina Vilela
abstract:
Background and Aims
Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) is an extracorporeal technique in which plasma is removed and replaced with another fluid to correct blood abnormalities. Nephrologists in Portugal are central to its prescription, although in some centers, intensivists are also autonomous in TPE prescription. It is a life-saving technique where prompt initiation is crucial. Generally it is well tolerated, however some serious adverse events must be accounted for. The aim of this study is to evaluate the utilization, indications, and safety profile of TPE in a Portuguese tertiary care hospital.
Methods
We performed a retrospective analysis of 75 patients who underwent TPE at Hospital Garcia da Orta, Almada, Portugal, between January 2011 and December 2024. In our center, TPE is prescribed by Nephrologists. Information on TPE indications, replacement fluids, and adverse events was collected while maintaining patient anonymity.
Results
The study included 50 patients (67%) in medical and surgical wards and 25 in the intensive care unit (ICU), accounting for a total of 597 TPE sessions. All sessions were done with membrane filtration TPE and, when adequate, heparin was used for anticoagulation. Most patients were women (n = 48, 64%) with a mean age of 52.8 years (±17.6 years). Most of the patients had neurologic (n = 25, 33%) or hematologic (n = 25, 33%) indications, although the most frequent indication was thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (n = 21, 28%). In the ICU, patients were slightly younger (average 49.5 years vs 54.3 years in the wards). Hematologic conditions were more prevalent in the ICU (n = 9, 36%), while neurological conditions were more prevalent in the wards (n = 20, 40%). Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) was the most used replacement fluid (n = 387 sessions, 65%). There was a total of 144 reported complications (0.24 per session or 1.92 per patient). Considering the complete duration of the treatment, per patient (n = 75), the most common complication was non-catheter related infection (n = 29, 38%), symptomatic or non-symptomatic hypocalcemia (n = 21, 3.5%), significant platelet count decrease, leading to thrombocytopenia (n = 18, 3%). We did not find a correlation between non-catheter-related infections and the number of sessions (P = 0.232), nor a difference in the prevalence of these infections between albumin or FFP as replacement fluids (P = 0.711). Catheter-related infections were less frequent (n = 4, 4%). Compared to FFP, albumin use was significantly associated with anemia (P = 0.039). Overall, the sessions were very well tolerated. Two anaphylactic reactions occurred in different patients using FFP as replacement fluid, with good response to adrenalin and corticosteroids. There was no mortality directly related to the procedure, however 3 patients died (4%) during the cycle of treatments with septic shock, in the ICU.
Conclusion
Hematologic and neurological conditions continue to be the most prevalent indication for TPE. Nephrology has a pivotal role in prescribing TPE, an extracorporeal technique which may be performed in the ICU, medical and surgical wards. Infections are one of the most relevant complications, and it is essential to maintain a low threshold for identifying and treating them. Insights into a center practice are valuable to be aware of potential complications, to take preventive measures and act promptly to improve TPE practices in different hospital settings.

title: #1036 Does peritoneal dialysis have an actual impact on normal respiratory physiology? Our first experience with nocturnal polygraphy monitoring
authors: Anna Petrosino; Serena Bruno; Silvia Treglia; Matteo Siciliano; Luigi Carroccio; Maria Grazia Porri; Mariarita Andreani; Giuseppe Grandaliano; Francesco Pesce; Silvia D'alonzo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients undergoing nocturnal automated peritoneal dialysis (APD) experience fluctuations in intra-abdominal pressure due to the cyclic loading and unloading of dialysate. These fluctuations may impact diaphragmatic and pulmonary function, supporting the rostral fluid shift hypothesis as a contributing factor to sleep apnea. However, no scientific studies have specifically examined the effects of APD on respiratory physiology during sleep. This study aims to evaluate the impact of peritoneal dialysis on various polysomnographic parameters.
Method
We analyzed data from 18 out of 60 patients (30%) undergoing APD for at least six months at our center, all with a BMI between 25 and 30 kg/m². Seventeen patients were on APD, while one was on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD). We assessed underlying kidney disease, polygraphy results (cardiorespiratory nocturnal monitoring), intra-abdominal pressure measurements, and dialysis treatment settings.
Results
In our cohort, 22.2% of patients had autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD).
Patients had been on APD for an average of 30 ± 36 months, with mean dialysate volumes of 1655 ± 409 mL, an average BMI of 25.6 ± 4.5 kg/m², an intraperitoneal pressure (IPP) of 15 ± 3.7 cm H₂O, and an average Kt/V of 2 ± 0.5.
One patient had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and another presented with an influenza-like illness at the time of polygraphy.
Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) was detected in all patients: 62.5% had moderate sleep apnea (mean apnea-hypopnea index [AHI]: 23.35 ± 3.5 events/hour).25% had severe sleep apnea (mean AHI: 41.7 ± 2 events/hour).The remaining patients had mild sleep apnea (mean AHI: 8.6 ± 4.1 events/hour). In 61% of cases, the supine AHI/non-supine AHI ratio exceeded 2, indicating positional sleep apnea based on AASM criteria.
Conclusion
Our findings indicate that all patients in this study had OSA, highlighting the potential underdiagnosis of sleep apnea in this population. Despite its significant clinical implications, sleep apnea is often overlooked in dialysis patients. Given these findings, we recommend routine screening for sleep apnea in all patients under renal replacement therapy, not only those on APD, even in the absence of overt symptoms.

title: #2204 Recent trends in kidney replacement therapy in Latvia: room for improvement
authors: Anna Proskurina; Kārlis Rācenis; Jana Eke; Aivars Petersons; Maija Motivane; Ieva Muižniece; Anna Popova; Ilze Puide; Baiba Runca; Nadezda Sersnova; Ieva Ziedina; Viktorija Kuzema
abstract:
Background and Aims
Important parameters characterizing a high-quality national kidney replacement therapy (KRT) program include comprehensive predialysis care, timely formation of dialysis access, and planned start of dialysis itself. This retrospective study aimed to assess these key parameters in patients receiving KRT in Latvia.
Method
The Latvian Kidney Patients Database (LKPD) collects demographic and clinical data from 33 KRT centres, covering ∼92% of KRT patients in Latvia. In this study, we analysed LKPD data on all KRT patients from 2022 and 2023. Microsoft Excel was used for data processing and analysis.
Results
There were 1046 and 1142 prevalent KRT patients in 2022 and 2023, respectively. In 2023, KRT modality distribution was as follows: 568 (49.7%) kidney transplant recipients, 470 (41.1%) patients on haemodialysis, and 105 (9.2%) on peritoneal dialysis. There was a consistent male predominance, with 55.8% and 55.4% male patients in 2022 and 2023, respectively. The mean patient age was 56±15 years.
A total of 115 new patients (60% male, 40% female; mean age 59±15 years) started KRT in 2022, increasing to 184 (53.8% male, 46.2% female; mean age 61±15 years) in 2023. The leading cause of end-stage kidney disease was glomerulonephritis in 59 (19.7%) patients, diabetes mellitus in 57 (19%), hypertension/renal vascular disease in 37 (12.3%), autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease in 34 (11.4%), and pyelonephritis in 25 (8.3%) patients, with the remaining cases attributed to other specific or unknown causes.
Among incident patients, 246 (82.3%) started haemodialysis, 48 (16%) started peritoneal dialysis, and five (1.7%) underwent pre-emptive kidney transplantation. Out of all incident patients, only 44.8% had regular nephrology consultations for at least 6-12 months before starting KRT, while 25.4% were in regular nephrology follow-up for less than 6 months. For 29.7% patients, there was no pre-KRT data. Only 53 (21.5%) of incident haemodialysis patients started dialysis using an arteriovenous fistula or arteriovenous graft. Overall, 199 (66.5%) patients started KRT in an acute setting.
Conclusion
This study highlights several significant gaps in pre-dialysis care in Latvia, such as timely nephrology referral, structured pre-dialysis education, and improved dialysis access planning to ensure a more structured and timely transition to KRT. In response, a nationwide project to improve KRT quality was launched in November 2024, aiming to address these challenges and improve patient outcomes.

title: #2609 Complications associated with tunneled hemodialysis catheters: a retrospective study
authors: María Ramírez Peña; Águeda López de la Torre Molina; Marina Almenara Tejederas; María Jesús Moyano Franco; María Ángeles Rodríguez-Perez; Mercedes Salguiera Lazo
abstract:
Background and Aims
The most recommended vascular access for chronic hemodialysis is the arteriovenous fistula (AVF). In some cases, access via a tunneled catheter (TC) is required, which has a higher complication rate. The objective of our study is to analyze the complications related to the TC (bacteremias and mechanical complications) in patients undergoing chronic hemodialysis in our healthcare area.
Method
A retrospective cohort study was conducted, including patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) undergoing hemodialysis (HD) with a TC implanted from 2005 to 2021 at the HUVM. Clinical-demographic variables related to the catheter and complications (catheter-related bacteremias (CRBs) and mechanical complications) were recorded. The patients were followed up from catheter implantation until death, loss to follow-up, or the end of the study (December 31, 2023).
Results
The sociodemographic, clinical characteristics, and TC types are summarized in Table 1.
Complications: 84 patients (22%)
CRB: 65 (19% of total patients with TCs)
Mechanical complications: 25 (7% of total):
10 stenosis (15% of total)
14 thrombosis (22% of total)
1 superior vena cava syndrome (2%)
Bacteremia rate: 0.39/1000 days of TC use. Median time until first bacteremia: 518 days (95% CI: 492–774).
Time until first mechanical complication: 922 days (95% CI: 791-1768).
The most frequently isolated microorganisms:
S. epidermidis (41.1%)
S. aureus (31.6%), of which 83.3% were methicillin-sensitive
S. marcescens (5.3%)
P. aeruginosa (3.5%)
Corynebacterium spp. (3.5%)
A total of 173 (49.1%) TCs were removed. The reasons were:
Use of AVF: 56 (15.9%)
Independence from HD: 52 (14.8%)
TC dysfunction: 24 (6.8%)
Complications (CRB or mechanical): 42 (11.9%). Of these, 32 (9.1%) were specifically due to CRB.
Conclusion
In our sample, the incidence of complications related to TC was low after a long follow-up period, with the bacteremia rate being considerably lower than described in other studies.
The percentage of stenosis and thrombosis was also lower in our series compared to other studies. This is likely to be underreported, as imaging tests would be needed to confirm a mechanical complication in cases of catheter dysfunction.

title: #2942 Feel good and live longer: association of baseline quality of life and changes over one year with mortality in patients on hemodialysis
authors: Carla Santos Araújo; Eliana Silva; Suzanne Pearce; Israel Silva; Carlos Lucas; Fernando MacÁrio
abstract:
Background and Aims
Baseline measurement of quality of life (QoL) and changes over time are widely recommended in most hemodialysis (HD) guidelines. Besides the evaluation of the patients’ well-being, QoL assessment may provide useful information on relevant patient outcomes. The relationship of QoL with mortality in HD patients has been scarcely evaluated previously, almost exclusively in cross-sectional studies involving a small number of patients. The effect of time on HD in QoL scores and the impact of those changes on the mortality of HD patients remains to be defined. The aim of our study was to examine whether the physical (PCS) and mental (MCS) component summary scores of the quality of life short form health survey (KDQOL SF-36) were related to all-cause mortality in a sample of patients in maintenance HD, both at baseline as after one year of follow-up.
Method
We performed a multicentre, observational, prospective cohort study using data from an international HD provider database. All patients 18 years or older that voluntarily responded to the KDQOL SF-36 in 2021 and 2022 were included and followed for one year (from July 2022 until June 2023). The test was preferably self-administered, but patients could be assisted by a health professional during dialysis session when needed. The PCS and MCS scores of 2021 and 2022 were obtained and used to divide the population in two groups using the mean values of both scores. Subsequently, we formed three additional groups based on their composite scores dynamics over one year: one group with an increase of more than 5 points in the scores during that period (“increase”), one group with a decrease of more than 5 points (“decrease”) and a group with the remaining patients (“stable”). We used Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression analyses to evaluate survival, adjusted for age, gender, time on dialysis, diabetic status, Charlson comorbidity index, type of vascular access, dialysis blood flow and treatment time, kidney transplant status, mean arterial pressure, body mass index, hemoglobin, dialysis adequacy (eKt/V), plasmatic albumin, potassium and phosphorus. Results were presented as hazard ratios (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) and a p-value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results
A total of 19,756 persons (53% of the eligible individuals) answered to both KDQOL SF-36 questionnaires in 2021 and 2022 and were selected for the study; of those, 1853 died during the evaluation period. The mean value of PCS was 38.2 ± 9.3 points in 2021 and 38.6 ± 9.6 points in 2022, whereas the mean value of MCS was higher (45.7 ± 10.2 points in 2021 and 46.1 ± 10.3 points in 2022). After one year, 31.1% showed an increase in PCS, 39.9% remained stable and 29.0% decreased the score. For MCS, we have observed an increase in 33.5% of patients, with 35.4% remaining stable and 31.1% decreasing after twelve months. In the survival analysis, a significant increase in mortality odds was observed in patients with composite scores below average, with higher HR being observed for PCS in both years and in the last survey before death for both scores (Fig. 1). Patients showing a significant decrease in PCS had a higher adjusted mortality HR (HR = 1.17; 95% CI, 1.04–1.31) when compared to both “increase” and “stable” patients, with no significant differences being documented in the HR of death between these two last groups (Table 2). Considering the MCS evolution, no difference in the mortality HR was observed between the three groups.
Conclusion
QoL physical and mental composite scores below the average value of the population were associated with a significant increase in mortality risk. After one year, an increase or a stable value of PCS, but not of MCS, correlated with a significant and independent reduction in mortality risk. These findings underscore the potential of QoL as a valuable patient-reported tool for guiding clinical interventions in the HD population to enhance patient survival.

title: #3466 Impact of peritoneal ultrafiltration in cardiorenal syndrome
authors: Henrique Fernando de Gouveia Rodrigues; Ana Francisca Caires Gomes Da Silva Correia; Gil Duarte Freitas Gomes Da Silva
abstract:
Background and Aims
CRS is a frequent problem in clinical practice and causes significant morbidity in nephrology patients, due not only to the symptomatic burden but also to recurrent hospitalizations and increased mortality. Its approach is challenging as many of the main randomized clinical trials in heart failure exclude patients with advanced CKD, and there is a relative scarcity of evidence-based therapy in this group of patients. Thus, CRS treatment strategies have been largely empirical and goal-directed to improve the function of one organ, often at the expense of the other. Peritoneal ultrafiltration or peritoneal dialysis have emerged as a therapeutic alternative for controlling fluid overload in patients with refractory congestive HF, providing slow, daily ultrafiltration on an outpatient basis. In our unit, the criteria for peritoneal ultrafiltration are the need for long cycles of subcutaneous furosemide in an elastomeric pump, with difficult weaning; frequent clinical relapses, requiring at least 3 cycles of subcutaneous furosemide in an elastomeric pump in the last year; dependence on subcutaneous furosemide in an elastomeric pump for clinical stability, with clinical worsening upon weaning; patients with CRS and ascites requiring frequent evacuation paracenteses.
Method
Retrospective analysis of 8 patients presenting symptoms and signs of severe refractory congestive HF despite optimal pharmacological therapy who were treated with peritoneal ultrafiltration. Demographic and clinical characteristics of our patients were collected and analyzed, as well as their laboratory data. P value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results
Our study population was comprised of 1 female and 7 male patients, with an average age of 73.8 ± 12.7 years. The most common cause of heart failure was ischemic cardiomyopathy (50%) and most patients suffered from heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (62.5%), had 3 or more hospital admissions for decompensated heart failure in the past year (75%) and had stage 3 CKD (50%). Prior to starting peritoneal ultrafiltration, 5 (62.5%) patients were classified as NYHA III, regarding their symptoms. 5 patients were prescribed 1 exchange per day with icodextrin, 1 patient was prescribed 2 exchanges per day with icodextrin, and the remaining 2 patients were prescribed 2 exchanges with 1.36% glucose based solution and 1 exchange with icodextrin. All patients presented clinical and analytic improvement after starting peritoneal ultrafiltration, as shown by the reduction in NYHA class (4 [IQR 1] vs 2 [IQR 1]; P = 0.000), in VExUS score (3 [IQR 1] vs 1 [IQR 2]; P = 0.001), in inferior vena cava diameter (29 ± 5 vs 19 [IQR 19]; P = 0.006), and in NTproBNP (34046 [IQR 18470] vs 6350 [IQR 10776]; P = 0.039) and Ca125 (249.8 ± 147.3 vs 151.9 ± 263.5; P = 0.014) levels. No patient was hospitalized in the first 6 months after starting peritoneal ultrafiltration, and only one was admitted in a hospital in the first year, although for reasons unrelated to the ultrafiltration technique or to CRS complications.
Conclusion
Peritoneal ultrafiltration or peritoneal dialysis can allow efficient management of fluid overload, avoiding hospital admissions and ensuring a better quality of life.

title: #3499 The influence of anemia on quality of life of patients on hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis
authors: Gergana Todorova; Aygulya Akisheva; Vasil Todorov
abstract:
Background and Aims
Quality of life (QoL) is a broad concept that includes an assessment of personal well-being formed by various criteria of physical, psychological, emotional and social nature. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) often leads to anemia, due to lack of erythropoietin production. Combination of CKD, renal anemia and dialysis treatment significantly worsens the QoL of patients. The Kidney Disease and Quality of Life SF-36 v 1.3 (KDQOL-SF-36™) is specialized questionnaire for measuring QoL in patients with CKD, using 8 domains like the classic SF-36 and one section with 12 domains measuring the QoL of patients on CKD with or without dialysis treatment. The aim of this study is to evaluate QoL related to CKD and also to establish the renal anemia effect on QoL in CKD patients on dialysis, using the disease specific items of the KDQOL-SF-36.
Method
The study includes 79 patients with CKD and anemia on hemodialysis (HD) and peritoneal dialysis (PD) treatment. Demographic data, comorbidities, haematological parameters, vascular access, duration of dialysis were recorded. Every patient completed the questionnaire after given informed consent.
Results
There were 40 (50.6%) men and 39 (49.4%) women, with average age of 57.9 ± 14.2 years and duration of HD of 79.9 ± 79.4 months and of CAPD—48.0 ± 47.1 months. Haemodialysis are 67, PD—12 patients. The leading causes for CKD are chronic glomerulonephritis (32.9 %), hypertensive nephropathy (29.1%), autosomal dominant polycyclic kidney disease (11.4%).
Patients on HD have haemoglobin—104.8±14.1 g/l, and weekly dosage of erythropoietin 5196.9 ± 2962.43 E. These on PD have better correction of renal anemia, haemoglobin— 112.8 ± 15.2 g/l with lower need of erythropoietin – 4111.1 ± 2800.2 E/weekly.
The group of PD patients have a better score in six domains—physical functioning (FF), role physical (RL), body pain (BP), role emotional (RLE), social function (SF), energy fatigue (VEF), and better in kidney disease specific domains—effects of kidney disease(EFKD), burden of KD (BKD), sleep.
A tendency was registered among the HD group about one domain—General Health perception (GHP)—patients with longer stage of HD treatment—between 3 and 30 years have higher score, than the patients who started HD sooner—in less than 3 years.
Conclusion
Patients with CKD and anemia have changed due to insufficiency of energy levels, fatigue, insomnia, poоr tissues oxidation, etc. Due to multifactorial reasons, the patients on dialysis treatment with anaemia have even lower score of QoL. Patients on PD not only have a more flexibility than HD ones, but also they have better QoL. We prove, that patients adapted to the treatment's regimen and specificity, have better perception of life, than the newly started ones. KDQOL-SF-36™ is a sure and organ specific instrument for measuring QoL in the population of dialysis patients.
This is the first study in Bulgaria evaluating and comparing QoL in patients treated with both dialysis methods—HD and PD.

title: #3584 SINGLE centre experience with daptomicin sealing of Tenckhoff catheter in relapsing and refractory peritonitis
authors: Elena Villanueva Sánchez; Karen Rivero García; Angelo Roberto Falconi Sarmiento; Celia Rodriguez Tudero; Daniel Ruddy Quispe; Karla Antonela Pinoargote Cañar; Nestor Leonardo Sampedro Chica; Alberto Martin Arribas; Gonzalo Delgado; María del Pilar Fraile
abstract:
Background and Aims
Peritonitis is one of the most frequent complications in patients on peritoneal dialysis (PD), it can cause deterioration of the peritoneal membrane and the need to suspend the technique. In addition to intraperitoneal antibiotic therapy, Tenckhoff catheter sealing with daptomycin has been shown to help with the control of relapsing peritonitis. We aim to study the effectiveness of daptomycin sealing as a complementary treatment in refractory and relapsing peritonitis in a series of patients.
Method
We collected data from 4 patients on peritoneal dialysis from the peritoneal dialysis unit of the Clinical Hospital of Salamanca who suffered peritonitis and underwent daptomycin seals over the years 2022–2024. Regarding antibiotic treatment, the intraperitoneal antibiotics were scheduled following the protocol of our hospital (taking into account local antibiotic resistance) starting empirical treatment with intraperitoneal cefazolin and ceftazidime; and oral fluconazole for 21 days. Then, it was followed by antibiogram-guided treatment, which was different in each patient, for 2-3 weeks following ISPD guidelines. The sealing regimen we used was the same for the 4 patients and consisted of weekly catheter sealing with Daptomycin 350 mg (diluted in 7 ml of physiological saline) for 4 weeks. The sealing was applied after the infusion of the longest permanence exchange by trained nursing staff in our ward.
Results
We studied the clinical characteristics and evolution of these 4 patients who presented peritonitis, the clinical information of the patients is shown in Fig. 1. In 3 of the patients the daptomycin sealings were applied due to suspicion of biofilm due to relapsing peritonitis in the second episode, and in the other patient they were applied due to poor clinical evolution with little response to the antibiotic therapy on the first episode.

title: #3635 Intravesical sodium hyaluronate for treatment of radiation-induced hemorrhagic cystitis in hemodialyzed patients: a viable option?
authors: Pedro Silva; Noemy Neves; Miguel Coimbra; Iolanda Santos; Rita Vicente; Filipa Alves; Cristina Silva; Vítor Ramalho; Pedro Pessegueiro; David Fiel; Beatriz Malvar; Manuel Amoedo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Radiation-induced cystitis is a late complication of pelvic radiation therapy, potentially manifesting months to years after treatment. Defects in the glycosaminoglycan (GAG) layer of the bladder mucosa have been implicated as a pathogenic mechanism in this condition, which is commonly associated with irritative voiding symptoms, bladder spasms and macroscopic hematuria (MH). Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) undergoing hemodialysis (HD) are at an increased risk of hemorrhagic events due to multiple factors, including uremia-induced platelet disfunction, the use of extracorporeal circuit anticoagulation during dialysis, endothelial disfunction and vascular calcification. Sodium hyaluronate (SH), a derivative of hyaluronic acid, has been developed to temporarily restore the deficient GAG layer of the bladder and is widely used in the management of interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome. We aim to report cases of radiation-induced hemorrhagic cystitis (RIHC) in CKD patients undergoing HD and to evaluate the efficacy of intravesical SH administration in controlling persistent MH.
Method
This retrospective case series includes HD patients who received intravesical SH for persistent MH secondary to RIHC at our centre over the past four years. Demographic and clinical data were collected from local clinical registries. We analysed resolution of MH following SH treatment and other potential reported complications.
Results
We report the cases of three male patients, aged 69 to 79 years, who had previously undergone pelvic radiotherapy for prostate adenocarcinoma (two cases) and rectal adenocarcinoma (one case). At the time of presentation, one patient was already on chronic HD, while the other two initiated HD during the episode. All three developed MH in the context of RIHC, which was unresponsive to initial management, including continuous bladder irrigation with 0.9% sodium chloride and discontinuation of antiplatelet therapy. For severe anemia (serum hemoglobin < 7.0 g/dL), all cases were submitted to red blood cell transfusion. Two patients were treated with aminocaproic acid, which was contraindicated in the third patient due to a high thrombotic risk; however, hematuria persisted. To address this, we implemented a standardized protocol for SH administration in HD patients, using a 40mg SH solution in a 50ml vial, as follows: (1) Prophylactic antibiotic administration (cephalosporin) immediately after the HD session on the day before the procedure; (2) Bladder catheterization with complete drainage of residual urine; (3) Intravesical instillation the entire SH solution, retained in the bladder for a minimum of 60 minutes; (4) Weekly administration for four weeks, with the option of monthly maintenance treatments until symptom resolution. All patients received four intravesical SH instillations according to the protocol, with complete resolution of MH after one or two treatments. Hemodyalisis was continued throughout the treatment period without anticoagulation. No major complications or MH recurrence were observed during follow-up (12 months in two patients and 6 months in one patient).
Conclusion
Treatment options for RIHC are often limited in efficacy, carry an increased risk of thrombotic complications (e.g., aminocaproic acid), or are contraindicated in HD patients (e.g., alum). A randomised trial demonstrated that SH therapy was at least as effective as hyperbaric oxygen therapy for the treatment of hematuria in RIHC; however, that study did not include CKD patients. Although our study is limited by a small sample size, our findings suggest that intravesical SH instillation may be a safe and effective alternative approach for treating MH secondary to RIHC in HD-dependent patients. Further research is warranted to corroborate our results and optimize treatment protocols for this idiosyncratic population.

title: #3826 Comparison of pre- and post-dialysis vascular access flow measurements: implications for monitoring strategies
authors: Sandra Clementina Salgado Pereira; João Pedro Peixoto de Bessa e Silva; Beatriz Silva; Beatriz de Barros; Paulo Pinheiro; Fernanda Silva; José Da Silva Gonçalves Queirós
abstract:
Background and Aims
Vascular access monitoring is crucial in the management of patients on hemodialysis, and vascular access flow (Qa) plays a key role in monitoring its function. Guidelines recommend that Qa measurement be performed under hemodynamically stable conditions to ensure greater accuracy of the results. Due to variations in blood volume and intravascular pressure during dialysis, the literature frequently suggests that Qa measurement should occur before the start of the hemodialysis session. However, studies directly comparing measurements taken before and after dialysis are insufficient. The objective of our study was to compare the pre- and post-dialysis Qa in patients from a hospital-based hemodialysis program.
Method
Patients from a hemodialysis program at a hospital center were selected, and Qa measurements were taken both before and after hemodialysis. Flow measurements were performed pre and post hemodialysis by the same professional.
Results
A total of 40 patients were included in the study, with a mean age of 63.93 ± 16.10 years. Among them, 21 were male (52.5%). Regarding vascular access, 15 patients had a humerocephalic arteriovenous fistula, 10 had a radiocephalic fistula, 7 had a humerobasilic fistula, 7 had an arteriovenous graft, and 1 had a humerohumeral AVF. The majority (n = 25, 62.5%) were undergoing hemodiafiltration. The most common etiology of kidney disease was glomerular (n = 11, 27.5%), followed by an undetermined cause (n = 9, 22.5%) and diabetic kidney disease (n = 7, 17.5%). Hypertension was highly prevalent (n = 38, 95%), as were diabetes (n = 27, 67.5%) and documented atherosclerotic disease (n = 29, 72.5%). The mean of the three Qa measurements taken before hemodialysis was 1249.04 ± 410.29 mL/min, while the mean after hemodialysis was 1190.00 ± 401.83 mL/min, showing a significant reduction post-hemodialysis, as indicated by the paired t-test (t (39) = 5.837, P < 0.001, 95% CI [34.01, 70.07]).
Conclusion
As supported by existing literature, our study confirms a statistically significant reduction in Qa after hemodialysis. However, from a clinical standpoint, the mean difference before and after hemodialysis is only 59 mL/min, a change that is often not meaningful in vascular access assessment. While variations in intravascular volume and pressure can influence vascular access flow, their clinical relevance remains uncertain despite statistical significance. Larger studies are needed to determine whether post-hemodialysis Qa measurement could serve as a reliable monitoring strategy.

title: #3920 Peritoneal dialysis for heart transplant recipients with end-stage renal disease: a tertiary hospital experience
authors: Antonia Lopez; Daniela Cecilia Cannarile; Luciano Potena; Annalisa Zucchelli; Martina Titone; Juna Brazhda
abstract:
Background and Aims
The management of heart transplant recipients who develop end-stage renal disease (ESRD) requiring dialysis, presents unique challenges in modern nephrology. Calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity and long-term steroid use contribute to progressive renal dysfunction in this population, alongside other well-known risk factors. While hemodialysis has traditionally been the preferred modality, peritoneal dialysis (PD) offers potential advantages, including better hemodynamic stability and preservation of residual cardiac function.
Method and Results
Among the more than 200 heart transplants performed in our hospital in the last five years, we have followed all patients who subsequently developed chronic kidney disease (CKD). Since 2020, among those who progressed to stage 5 CKD, we decided to use as a replacement therapy, peritoneal dialysis too. Our selection of PD was based on considerations of patient survival, cardiovascular stability, and quality of life. Special emphasis was placed on immunosuppression management, infection prevention strategies, and volume status optimization. We treated 7 patients with PD, for 5/7 we have a survival rate between 1 month and 40 months, and 2/7 are still on treatment.
All 7 patients had never had peritonitis. 1 was dropped out for acute abdominal surgery due to appendicites,1 died for calciphylaxis,1 for cancer, 2/7 died for cardiac failure.
Conclusion
As reported in the literature, peritoneal dialysis is a viable option for heart transplant recipients with ESRD, demonstrating survival rates better to those of matched hemodialysis cohorts. The incidence of peritonitis is similar to that observed in non-transplanted PD patients, but we haven't at all. The flexibility of PD schedules facilitated, improved medication adherence and immunosuppression management. However, meticulous attention to volume status and regular monitoring of peritoneal membrane transport characteristics, were crucial for achieving optimal outcomes. Notably, we also observed that right heart function played a significant role in patient prognosis.
Peritoneal dialysis represents the best renal replacement therapy also for heart transplant recipients with ESRD. Successful outcomes depend on careful patient selection, stringent infection prevention protocols, and close monitoring of both cardiac and renal parameters. Further studies are necessary to tailor the cure for this unique population.

title: #3925 Overhydration biomarkers in peritoneal dialysis
authors: Barbara Cancho Castellano; Enrique Matallana Encinas; Beatriz Gómez Gallego; Jaime Hernán Merino; Elena García de Vinuesa; Teresa de Jesús; Giraldo Rua; Lucia Martin Jiménez; Nicolas Roberto Robles Pérez-Monteoliva
abstract:
Background and Aims
The main cause of mortality in chronic kidney disease (CKD) is cardiovascular in origin. In addition, several studies have shown an increased risk of cardiovascular events in patients with CKD, with this clinical condition being considered an independent risk factor. Overhydration in peritoneal dialysis (PD) leads to increased morbidity and mortality in the patient and is a frequent cause of discontinuation of the technique. Ca-125 and NT-proBNP are biomarkers of emerging congestion in PD.
Method
Descriptive observational study with a retrospective cross-sectional design. Patients on Peritoneal Dialysis were included in the period from January to December 2023. Body composition measured by multifrequency bioimpedance, peritoneal kinetics measured by the peritoneal equilibrium test, congestion biomarkers such as NT-proBNP and Ca-125 and other demographic and clinical variables were collected.
Quantitative variables are described by the mean and standard. Qualitative variables are described by the absolute and relative frequency. The Kruskal-Wallis test was performed to compare the means of OH, PA, BMI, abdominal circumference, LTI and FTI in the different categories of peritoneal kinetics obtained in the PET. A non-parametric test was applied because, although the distribution of the variables was normal overall, when making the categories some groups only had one or two members, so normality could not be assumed in these groups. To study the differences between means, Student's t tests and the ANOVA test were used. To study the differences between proportions, the χ2 test and the p for trends were used. The analyses were carried out with SPSS Statistics 17.0.
Results
17 participants were included in the study, within the prevalence of the period from January 1st to December 31st, 2023. Of the individuals included in the study: women (52.9%). The mean age was 55 ± 12.10 years.
The mean time on renal replacement therapy with PD was 12 months, range (2-29). The etiology of the CKD: diabetic nephropathy (5.9%), glomerulopathies (41.2%), tubulopathies (11.8%), hereditary nephropathies (11.8%), unspecified pathology (17.6%) and affiliated pathology (11.8%).
Table 1 reflects the characteristics of the study sample. As can be seen, there are significant differences in weight and FTI, women weigh more and have more fat mass. It is also observed that both the body surface area and the Watson distribution volume, as well as TBW, ECW and ICW, are significantly greater in men. There are not significant differences in OH, OH/ECW, AF or ECW/ICW. There are also no significant differences in age, time on dialysis, eGFR at the start of dialysis or abdominal circumference. Overhydration, only one patient has an OH/ECW >10% (5.9%).
A significant negative correlation was found between NT proBNP and hemoglobin r = −0.652 (P = 0.006). No patients in higher transport categories tend to have a lower phase angle and higher Ca-125. Higher transportation categories tend to have higher FTI and lower LTI.
Conclusion
No significant correlation was found between hydration and Ca-125 or NT proBNP levels in this sample.
Differences that almost reached significance between groups were found depending on peritoneal kinetics. Subjects with a high or high average transport peritoneal membrane had higher concentrations of Ca-125, but without reflection in overhydration.
A good correlation was found between NT-proBNP and anemia, which could be considered as a more useful biomarker in relation to cardiovascular prognosis.

title: #501 Novel intradialytic system of monitoring vascular access. A monocentric experience
authors: Paolo Albrizio; Annalisa Foschi; Ivo Angelo Antonio Milani; Silvia Muciaccia; Stefano Rindi; Manuela Zucchi; Fabio Milanesi
abstract:
Background and Aims
a well performing vascular access is a key condition for a high-quality dialysis. Artero-venous fistula (AVF) is, when practicable, the first choice but it's prevalence in dialysis patients is often limited because of complications which may reduce access survival. The prevention of these complications with a regular ultrasound monitoring is frequently not affordable for organization and resources issues. 6008® dialysis machines integrate the system “Access Flow Monitor®” (AFM) which allow, temporarily reversing lines flow, to calculate the AVF flow by confronting differences in intradialytic clearance. This system, associated with item “Twister®” which allows to reverse flow immediately without any line disconnection, could result in a useful monitoring resource with limited organisational impact.
Method
we selected chronically hemodialysis patients with a native AVF as vascular access, already treated in our Centre with 6008® dialysis machines. We evaluated: type and frequency of treatment, medium dialysis length and medium blood flow rate (Qb) of last six treatments. Then, without changing any parameter, we calculated with AFM+Twister system AVF flow during a dialysis in short interdialytic interval comparing it with medium Qb of last six treatments.
Results
17 patients, 15 with three times a week and 2 with two times a week dialysis; 4 in bicarbonate hemodialysis (HD), 11 in post-dilution hemodiafiltration (HDF post) and 2 in pre-dilution hemodiafiltration (HDF pre) respected the parameters. We excluded the 2 patients treated with HDF pre due to an increased risk of circuit clotting for coagulative issues which contraindicate heparin use. Medium length of dialysis was 220.6 ± 36.6 minutes while medium Qb was 285.6 ± 24.1 ml/min. Among the 15 patients evaluated, 2 had a AVF calculated flow <500 ml/min, 2 between 500–1000 ml/min, 7 between 1000–2000 ml/min and 4 >2000 ml/min (Fig 1). Comparing these date with medium Qb we find out that patients with AVF calculated flow <500 ml/min had a medium Qb of 235 ± 21 ml/min, while those with 500–1000 ml/min of 285 ± 35 ml/min and those >1000 ml/min of 300 ml/min (Fig 2).
Conclusion
the AFM® system integrated on 6008® dialysis machines has been a useful instrument to calculate the AVF flow during hemodialysis treatments. Associating this measure with Twister® item we obtained our results without any line disconnection. AVF calculated flow values correlated with medium Qb of previous treatments: patients with a low AVF flow were also those with lover medium Qb. Those are monocentric data, to obtain more informations will be necessary to: extend measurement also on prosthetic AVF and on patients commonly on different dialysis machines, monitoring AVF flow trend during months and planning ultrasound screening for selected patients with a reduced AVF flow.

title: #584 Single center experience: peritoneal dialysis in acute kidney injury in severe lupus nephritis
authors: Min Tham; Mei Sian Fu; Xue Qi Tan; Wen Jiun Liu; Hoe Jiunn Wong
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is common in lupus nephritis (LN) and it denotes a poorly favorable outcome. A prompt and timely treatment is essential to preserve kidney function in order to reduce morbidity and mortality associated with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Up to present day, hemodialysis (HD) remains the frequent-used modality in AKI. We have been practicing peritoneal dialysis (PD) dates back to year 2000. It was more apparent during the COVID pandemic whereby resources were limited. Hence, this study aims to evaluate effectiveness of PD in LN patients with AKI.
Method
The analysis is based on retrospective data collected via paper and electronic medical records through patient charts and the dialysis unit registries. title: #841 Hemodialysis in focus: patient survival through the lens of time and hazard factors
authors: Stella Kushnirenko; Oksana Lysianska; Liubov Savytska
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hemodialysis (HD) patients are at high mortality risk, especially during the first year of treatment, due to insufficient adaptation (USRDS, 2020). Those undergoing HD for more than five years exhibit better survival rates, but remain vulnerable to chronic complications (ERA-EDTA, 2018). This study aims to evaluate the impact of key hazard factors (hazard ratio - HR) on survival in HD patients.
Method
A prospective cohort study involved 120 HD patients aged 18-68 years over a 12-month period. Patients were divided into three groups according to the HD duration: Group 1—up to 12 months (n = 38), Group 2—13–60 months (n = 55), Group 3—over 60 months (n = 27). The study assessed forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) and forced vital capacity (FVC) of lungs using spirometry. During the HD session, arterial blood pressure (BP), heart rate (HR), and blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂) were monitored using portable automated device and non-invasive pulse oximetry. Statistical analysis was performed using Cox regression, correlation analysis (r), χ²-test, and mean comparison.
Results
Key mortality and complication HRs included: male gender (HR = 1.14; 95% CI: 1.03−1.26; P = 0.009), age over 60 (HR = 1.3; 95% CI: 1.12−1.49; P = 0.00044), and inter-dialytic weight gain (IDWG >3.5 kg) (HR = 1.8; 95% CI: 1.5−2.2; P = 0.0002). Among comorbidities, the highest hazards are associated with diabetes mellitus (DM) (HR = 1.7; 95% CI: 1.3−2.2; P = 0.0005), hypoglycemia episodes (HR = 1.6; 95% CI: 1.2−2.0; P = 0.0017), and prolonged intradialytic hypoxemia (PIH) (HR = 2.07; P < 0.001). For arterial hypertension (AH), the hazard was HR = 1.5 (95% CI: 1.1−2.0; P = 0.0018), while for blood pressure variability (BPV >10 mmHg), HR = 1.3 (95% CI: 1.0−1.6; P = 0.023) (Fig. 1).
Patients in Group 1 had the highest HR = 1.8 (95% CI: 1.3−2.5), P = 0.01; followed by Group 2—HR = 1.3 (95% CI: 1.1−1.5), P = 0.05; while patients in Group 3 showed a trend toward better survival, HR = 1.0 (95% CI: 0.9−1.2), P = 0.1. However, differences between the groups based on HD duration were not statistically significant (P = 0.114) (Fig. 2).
In Groups 1 and 3 patients, a statistically significant relationship was found between actual and predicted FEV1 values: ra = 0.93; pa = 0.002; rp = 0.766; pp = 0.0059 indicating that the pulmonary function is preserved in patients with HD >60 months. At the same time, HD duration strongly correlates with obstructive disorders (r = 0.99; P < 0.001), suggesting progressive obstructive changes over time. HD duration >60 months is associated with worsening dyspnea (r = −0.91; P = 0.032) but negatively correlates with IDWG frequency (r = −0.87; P = 0.002), reflecting better fluid balance control in Group 3 patients.
Group 3 had the lowest proportion of patients with AH compared to Groups 1 and 2 (χ² = 8.44; P = 0.015), but the highest frequency of intradialytic hypotension (P = 0.013), highlighting the need for careful BP monitoring in this category of patients.
The difference in mean HR values across the groups was 10 beats/min (95% CI: 3.52−16.48; P = 0.027). Group 1 patients had a higher HR compared to those with HD duration >60 months (P = 0.035). HD duration had no statistically significant impact on the presence or absence of PIH (P = 0.2776).
Conclusion
Survival in HD patients is determined by multiple hazard factors. Diabetes and hypoglycemia have a significant impact, as do effective IDWG control and BPV levels. Prolonged PIH is associated with increased mortality risk.
Long-term HD therapy also affects the respiratory function: while the lungs adapt with partial preservation of the function, obstructive disorders progress, and dyspnea worsens over time. Longer HD duration improves fluid balance control; however, patients with extended HD duration experience a higher risk of intradialytic hypotension. Patients with HD duration <12 months have the highest mortality risk, while prolonged treatment (>60 months) shows a trend towards improved survival, although differences between groups were not statistically significant.

title: #1089 Outcomes of medical and surgical peritoneal dialysis catheter insertion: a single centre experience
authors: Leanne Stannard; Sharon Lang; Rachael Stannard; Hilary Cramp; Rebecca Herbert
abstract:
Background and Aims
Medical insertion of peritoneal dialysis (PD) catheters has been common practice within the renal unit at University Hospitals Plymouth NHS Trust for over 25 years. Historically, uncomplicated patients with no previous abdominal surgery were suitable for Seldinger insertion whereas more complex patients required peritoneoscope insertion. Patients with a history of major abdominal surgery or those with a hernia were referred for surgical insertion of PD catheter.
Following changes to EU medical device regulations, equipment production for the peritoneoscope ceased, resulting in a reduced ability to provide medical PD catheter insertions. With mounting pressures for surgical waiting times and increasing theatre demands, there has been a need to adapt practice and expand the criteria for medical insertions to maintain the PD service. The national drive to promote and increase access to home dialysis therapies (National Kidney Federation, 2024) has provided an opportunity to benchmark our practice and review our patient criteria for Seldinger insertion to ensure safe and effective practice.
Method
All renal units within the South West were contacted as a benchmarking exercise to establish current practice and identify patient selection for Seldinger insertion of PD catheters. UK Renal Registry data (26th Annual Report) was reviewed to understand the incidence of PD as choice of renal replacement therapy (RRT) in each of the units contacted allowing incidence of PD therapy to be compared to insertion method.
Electronic and paper case notes were retrospectively reviewed for all patients who underwent PD catheter insertion from March 2021 to September 2024 (43 months). Data collected included demographic data, method of PD catheter insertion, complications and outcomes at two months and one year post insertion.
Descriptive statistics were used to analyse the data. Coding of previous surgical history, complications and outcomes enabled themes to be established.
Results
The benchmarking exercise highlighted a limited number of units undertaking medical insertion of PD catheters (2/6). Practices in the units offering medical insertion were aligned, with similar criterion for both types of insertion. There appears to be a correlation between greater incidence of PD uptake in the units with access to medical insertion of PD catheters as opposed to units who solely offer surgical insertion.
The review of patient case notes sampled one hundred patients. There was no difference in baseline demographic data for each technique. Complication rates were similar for each category of abdominal surgery in both medical and surgical techniques. Patients who had a failed medical insertion of PD catheter or those with a history of gastric/bowel surgery were routinely offered surgical insertion.
Primary non-function, need for reposition/replacement, infection or drainage problems were similar between each method of insertion. A slightly higher rate of exit site leak was observed in surgical insertions in comparison to either of the medical insertion techniques. Importantly, there was no mortality associated with the procedure itself for any type of insertion.
A larger number of medically inserted PD catheters were functional at two months than those surgically inserted. At one year, more patients remained on PD following a medically inserted catheter as opposed to those inserted surgically.
Conclusion
Historically, there have been concerns over undertaking Seldinger insertion of PD catheters in patients with previous abdominal surgery. Yet, we have observed similar complication rates amongst each insertion method, along with more patients remaining on PD following a medical insertion. In this cohort, Seldinger insertions appear to be safe and effective in patients with a range of surgical histories. Although this is a single centre review, with a small sample size, this audit supports the broadening of local criteria for medical insertion of PD catheters. This may allow for timelier insertion; increasing ease of access to home therapies and lower waiting times for tube insertion.

title: #2063 Association between CKD–MBD and mortality, cardiovascular events, and fractures in peritoneal dialysis patients
authors: Motoyasu Kurahashi; Fukuoka Kosuke
abstract:
Background and Aims
This observational study aimed to investigate the association between changes in chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD)parameters and clinical outcomes in patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis (PD). It is well-established that abnormalities in CKD–MBD parameters are associated with an increased risk of adverse outcomes, including mortality, in hemodialysis patients. However, there is limited evidence regarding the relationship between CKD–MBD parameters and clinical outcomes such as mortality, cardiovascular events, and fractures in PD patients. This study aims to fill this gap by investigating the association of CKD–MBD parameters with these outcomes in PD patients.
Method
We included 63 patients who started PD at our facility between April 2017 and March 2022. The study examined the mean values of corrected calcium (Ca), phosphate (P), and intact parathyroid hormone (iPTH) during the first year from dialysis initiation, measured every three months. Cox proportional hazards models were employed to analyze the relationship between these CKD-MBD parameters and mortality, cardiovascular risk, and fracture risk.
Results
The study included 63 patients, with a mean age of 71 ± 17 years, and 44 males (69.8%). The mean observation period was 31 ± 15 months. The mean values of corrected Ca, P, and iPTH were 9.1 ± 0.4 mg/dL, 5.1 ± 0.9 mg/dL, and 258 ± 130 pg/mL, respectively. During the follow-up, 25 patients died, 16 experienced cardiovascular events, and 8 had fractures. In the analysis of cardiovascular events, the group with corrected Ca ≥9.5 mg/dL had a higher risk of cardiovascular events compared to the group with 9.0 ≤ corrected Ca < 9.5 mg/dL (hazard ratio 7.51, 95% CI 1.7–32.6, P = 0.007). Additionally, the group with P ≥ 5.5 mg/dL had a higher risk of cardiovascular events compared to the group with 4.5 ≤ P < 5.5 mg/dL (hazard ratio 4.71, 95% CI 1.1–19.8, P = 0.035). No significant associations were found between CKD-MBD parameters and mortality or fracture risk.
Conclusion
In PD patients, higher corrected Ca and P levels were associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular events, but no significant associations were found with mortality or fracture risk. These findings suggest that managing Ca and P levels may be crucial for reducing cardiovascular risk in this population.

title: #2249 Trends in dialysis population in Albania over the last 5 years: rising age and increased mortality among diabetic patients
authors: Fjona Nasto
abstract:
Background and Aims
The dialysis population in Albania has experienced significant changes in recent years, with an aging patient demographic and an increasing prevalence of diabetes among individuals with end-stage renal disease (ESRD). These trends are of concern due to the association between diabetes and higher mortality rates in dialysis patients. This study aims to examine the demographic and clinical shifts within the dialysis population in Albania over the past five years, with a focus on the rising age of patients and the disproportionately higher mortality rate among diabetics.
Method
A retrospective cohort study was conducted using data from five dialysis centers in Albania between 2020 and 2024. We analyzed patient demographics, comorbidities (particularly diabetes), treatment modalities, and mortality rates. The study specifically assessed changes in the average age of dialysis patients and the mortality rates among those with diabetes.
Results
The average age of dialysis patients in Albania has increased over the last five years, with a notable rise in patients aged 65 and above. The mean age of our dialysis population in January 2020 was 59.9 years old and in December 2024 was 63.1 years old.Diabetic patients have shown a particularly significant rise, constituting a growing proportion of the dialysis population, from 23.5% in 2020 in 30.0% in 2024. The mortality rate for diabetic dialysis patients was found to be significantly higher compared to non-diabetic patients, with an observed increase of more than 10% in deaths among diabetics during the study period. Diabetes-related complications, including cardiovascular disease and poor glycemic control, were identified as major contributors to the increased mortality rate in this group.
Conclusion
The dialysis population in Albania has shifted over the past five years, with an increasing average age and a growing proportion of diabetic patients. This trend is associated with a concerning rise in mortality rates, particularly among diabetic individuals, underscoring the need for targeted interventions. Enhanced diabetes management, early identification of comorbid conditions, and individualized care plans are essential to improving survival and quality of life for this high-risk group.
