title: #498 How novel drugs changed clinical practice in hemodialysis patients?
authors: Paolo Albrizio; Annalisa Foschi; Ivo Angelo Antonio Milani; Silvia Muciaccia; Stefano Rindi; Manuela Zucchi; Fabio Milanesi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hemodialysis patients are affected by many complications due to their pathological condition. Anaemia and mineral bone disease are two of the heavier and commonly found. During last years, two novel drugs became routinely used in dialysis centres: ferric carboxymaltose and etelcalcetide. Ferric carboxymaltose is a novel intravenous iron supplement easily injectable at the end of dialysis with high effectiveness and less adverse effects compared to former analogue molecules. Etelcalcetide is the first injectable calcimimetic drug with comparable efficacy to cinacalcet without the inevitable adherence limitations given by oral formulation.
Method
We evaluated efficacy and safety of ferric carboxymaltose and etelcalcetide in chronic hemodialysis patients afferent to our Centre for one year (from July 31th 2022 to August 1st 2023). Each patient was subjected to monthly laboratory blood exams.
Patients were treated with ferric carboxymaltose if they demonstrated a clinically and laboratory significant iron deficiency unresponsive to oral supplements. These patients were compared to those without intravenous iron supplement regarding percentage of dialysis with erythropoietin therapy administration, percentage of haemoglobin between KDIGO recommended levels (10–11.5 g/dl), medium dosage of erythropoietin and adverse events.
For etelcalcetide we evaluated for the same period all chronic patients treated with intravenous calcimimetic regarding medium dosage, number of dosage changes, percentage of PTH between latest KDIGO recommended levels (for our laboratory 130–585 pg/ml), frequency of hypocalcaemia (<8 and <7.5 mg/dl, corrected by serum albumin levels) and adverse events.
Results
65 of 83 patients underwent intravenous therapy with ferric carboxymaltose (47 males and 18 females, medium age 70.3 ± 12.6 years, NS vs not treated). Medium erythropoietin dosage was 3429 IU for ferric carboxymaltose treated patients vs 3576 IU for non-supplemented ones (P = NS). Percentage of dialysis with erythropoietin administration was 16.72 ± 8% for ferric carboxymaltose treated patients vs 31.6 ± 7% for non-supplemented ones (P < 0.05) (Fig. 1). Percentage of haemoglobin samples between KDIGO recommended levels was 89.97% ferric carboxymaltose treated patients vs 87.04% for non-treated ones (P = NS). No events effects were recorded and needed drug discontinuation.
32 patients (19 males and 13 females, medium age 68.06 ± 14.84 years old) were treated with etelcalcetide. Medium dosage was 4.48 ± 1.54 mg. Number of dosage changes was 0.71 ± 1.16 per patient. 93.73% of blood exams demonstrated PTH dosages between KDIGO recommended levels while hypocalcaemia, considered as <8 mg/dl, was reelevated in 17.61% of exams and considered as <7.5 mg/dl in only 5.37% of blood samples (Fig. 2). None of hypocalcaemia cases was clinically significant. No events effects were recorded and needed drug discontinuation.
Conclusion
Ferric carboxymaltose demonstrated great efficacy in maintaining target haemoglobin levels in patients with clinically significant iron deficiency unresponsive to oral supplements significantly reducing the frequency of erythropoietin administration without the necessity of increasing medium dosage compared to other patients without any recorded side effect.
Etelcalcetide demonstrated great efficacy in maintaining target PTH levels with limited drug dosage and minimal necessity of dosage adjustment. Hypocalcaemia was rare and never clinically significant. No other side effects were reported.
Both ferric carboxymaltose and etelcalcetide represent important innovations for the treatment of two of main complication for dialysis patients: anaemia and mineral bone disease and deserve and extensive use in dialysis centres.

title: #2479 A qualitative study to understand cardiovascular disease and coronary revascularization treatment strategies in patients with kidney failure
authors: Silvi Shah; Pragati Basera; Sunshine Barhorst; Sushmitha Patnana; Rachael Nolan
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiovascular disease remain the leading cause of death in patients with kidney failure. Despite two-thirds of patients with kidney failure having prevalent coronary artery disease, the optimal method of coronary revascularization is a matter of debate. We sought to describe the experiences of patients with kidney failure in the decision-making process for coronary revascularization treatment.
Method
We conducted semi-qualitative interviews involving 25 adult patients with kidney failure receiving maintenance dialysis and history of coronary artery disease in the United States, following which thematic saturation was reached. Interview transcripts were analysed thematically.
Results
We identified five key themes: 1) patient perception of dialysis as critical, life-sustaining treatment, 2) limited awareness of the elevated cardiovascular disease risk associated with kidney failure, 3) variable knowledge regarding treatment options for coronary artery disease, and inadequate information on the risks and benefits of coronary revascularization strategies, 4) lack of interdisciplinary care coordination for managing coronary artery disease in patients receiving dialysis, and 5) importance of shared decision-making and decision-making tools for cardiovascular care in patients with kidney failure.
Conclusion
Patients with kidney failure often experience emotional challenges related to cardiovascular health and report insufficient counselling about the risks and benefits of coronary revascularization treatments. Implementing strategies such as effective communication, shared decision-making tool, and interdisciplinary coordination can help enhance the quality of cardiovascular care for patients receiving dialysis.

title: #3461 Association of ACE and IL-1B gene polymorphisms with erythropoietin resistance in dialysis patients with anemia
authors: Pavlina Dzekova-Vidimliski; Natasha Eftimovska-Otovikj; Igor Nikolov; Vlatko Karanfilovski; Nikola Gjorgjievski; Gjulsen Selim; Nadica Matevska-Geshkovska; Aleksandar Dimovski
abstract:
Background and Aims
The polymorphisms of the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) gene and interleukin-1 beta (IL-1B) gene may be associated with resistance to anemia treatment in dialysis patients receiving recombinant human erythropoietin (rHuEPO). The aim of this study was to evaluate the association between ACE and IL-1B gene polymorphisms and the response to rHuEPO therapy in dialysis patients with anemia.
Method
The study investigated 69 dialysis patients with anemia who were treated with rHuEPO for 12 months. Genotyping of ACE and IL-1β polymorphisms was performed in all study participants at the beginning of the study. The patients' demographic characteristics, dialysis vintage, and laboratory parameters were also evaluated as factors associated with rHuEPO resistance. The erythropoietin resistance index (ERI) was calculated as the weekly rHuEPO dose per kg of body weight, divided by the hemoglobin (Hb) concentration in g/dL.
Results
The mean Hb level in all patients was 109.4 ± 11.1 g/L, achieved with an average weekly rHuEPO dose of 6909 IU. The mean transferrin saturation index (TSAI%) was 29.4 ± 7.6%, and the mean ferritin level was 468.8 ± 343.1 µg/L. The mean ERI was 9.6 ± 6.2 IU/kg/week/dL. An ERI ≥ 10 IU/kg/week/g/dL was observed in 27 (39.1%) patients. Patients with ERI ≥ 10 IU/kg/week/g/dL had significantly lower levels of Hb, cholesterol, and iron, and significantly higher levels of ferritin, CRP, and weekly rHuEPO dose compared to patients with ERI < 10 IU/kg/week/g/dL. The ACE gene polymorphisms (ACE I/D, rs1799752) were represented by three genotypes: ACE II, ACE ID, and ACE DD. The ACE ID genotype had the highest frequency (59.4%), detected in 41 patients. There was no significant difference in ERI between the three ACE I/D genotypes. The IL-1B gene polymorphisms (IL-1B-511 C/T, rs1143627) were represented by three genotypes: IL-1B CC, IL-1B CT, and IL-1B TT. The IL-1B CT genotype had the highest frequency (50.7%), detected in 35 patients. There was no significant difference in ERI between the three IL-1B-511 C/T genotypes.
Conclusion
Polymorphisms of the ACE and IL-1B genes were not significantly associated with the response to erythropoietin therapy in dialysis patients with anemia. Iron deficiency, malnutrition, and inflammation were factors associated with anemia and resistance to erythropoietin therapy in dialysis patients.

title: #1397 Hyperphosphatemia in hemodialysis patients may be driven by the consumption of ultraprocessed foods
authors: Andrea Sczip; Jyana Moraes; Adaiane Calegari; Tatiana Kruger; Jorgiane De Oliveira; Natália Scatone; Rafaela G Dos Santos; Fellype Barreto; Fabiana Nerbass
abstract:
Background and Aims
The relationship between diet quality and kidney health has been recently studied, with increasing evidence suggesting that dietary composition plays a significant role in the management of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and in the management of associated complications, such as hyperphosphatemia. We aimed to investigate the role of dietary diversity of natural foods and the intake of ultraprocessed foods (UPFs), along with their respective phosphorus source subgroups, in hyperphosphatemia among chronic hemodialysis (HD) patients.
Method
This cross-sectional multicenter study involved patients from seven dialysis units in Brazil. Two simplified and validated questionnaires were used to assess dietary diversity of natural foods and UPFs intake on both dialysis and non-dialysis days. Scores for total dietary diversity, UPFs, and their phosphorus source subgroups were calculated.
Results
A total of 297 patients participated (age: 52.1 ± 14.1 years; 57.9% men; 42% with hyperphosphatemia). While natural phosphorus sources were more commonly consumed, multivariate analysis revealed that UPFs, particularly those from animal sources, were independently associated with hyperphosphatemia. Each one-point increase in UPFs intake scores corresponded to an increased likelihood of hyperphosphatemia: 25% for total UPFs, 76% for animal-based UPFs, and 24% for other UPFs sources.
Conclusion
Our findings indicate that although phosphorus sources from UPFs were consumed less frequently than from natural sources, UPFs—especially those from animal sources—were independent determinants of hyperphosphatemia in a multicentric hemodialysis population. These results highlight the necessity for dietary interventions that prioritize natural foods in the management of hyperphosphatemia.

Our findings indicate that although phosphorus sources from UPFs were consumed less frequently than from natural sources, UPFs—especially those from animal sources—were independent determinants of hyperphosphatemia in a multicentric hemodialysis population. title: #2206 Phase angle following intradialytic neuromuscular electrical stimulation and oral protein supplementation in patients undergoing chronic hemodialysis
authors: Jungho Shin; Jae Hyeon Park; Jae Yoon Park; Ran-Hui Cha
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sarcopenia is a prevalent condition in patients undergoing chronic hemodialysis. Therefore, a convenient and reliable method of monitoring muscle health is required. This study identified the utility of the phase angle (PhA) to estimate muscle health, and evaluated its changes following intradialytic neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) and oral nutritional supplement interventions in patients undergoing chronic hemodialysis.
Method
This post-hoc analysis was conducted using data obtained from a 12-week multicenter randomized trial that examined the effects of NMES and protein supplementation. The participants were divided into four groups according to intradialytic NMES and protein supplementation. The PhA, muscle mass, muscle strength, and physical performance were measured every 4 weeks.
Results
Overall, 59 participants completed the study. PhA values were linearly associated with muscle mass and muscle strength. Additionally, high PhA levels indicated fast gait speed and shortened timed up-and-go (TUG) results. We further evaluated the association between the PhA slope and muscle health-related parameters. In participants with the PhA slope <0° over 12 weeks, TUG results worsened over time, relative to those with a slope ≥0° over 12 weeks, independent of age, sex, diabetes, and body mass index. NMES did not improve the PhA values over time; however, protein supplementation tended to increase the PhA values.
Conclusion
PhA is a reliable marker for estimating and monitoring muscle health in patients undergoing chronic hemodialysis, and a strong association exists between PhA and TUG results.

title: #3370 Efficacy and safety of paediatric continuous veno-venous hemodialysis (CVVHD) with MultiFiltratePRO: a prospective multicenter study
authors: Ahmed Dellaa; Anja Derlet-Savoia; Ahmad Shahir Nazari; Christine Gillen; Manuela Stauss-Grabo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Continuous kidney replacement therapy (CKRT), specifically continuous veno-venous haemodialysis (CVVHD), is a common clinical intervention in hospitalized children, particularly in paediatric intensive care units (PICU). The novel paediatric mode of the MultiFiltratePRO system offers a tailored approach for paediatric patients with specific needs related to body weight and clinical conditions, features a total blood priming volume of 116 mL, optimized for smaller paediatric patients. This study evaluates the efficacy and safety of the MultiFiltratePRO paediatric mode by analysing its ability to deliver prescribed effluent doses and its impact on clinical parameters, including haemodynamic stability, electrolyte balance, and fluid overload correction. The study aims to provide evidence for the utility of this device in paediatric patients requiring CVVHD.
Method
This prospective, open-label, interventional, multicenter study aims to enroll 42 paediatric patients (aged <18 years, 8–40 kg body weight) for CVVHD indication. Patients will be treated for a maximum of 10 days, based on investigator´s decision, and data will be collected every 24 hours. Statistical analyses will include descriptive statistics and hypothesis testing to evaluate outcomes upon study completion.
Results
This study expects to achieve at least 80% of the prescribed effluent dose at 72 hours, demonstrating the performance of the MultiFiltratePRO paediatric mode. Additional anticipated findings include correction of electrolyte, acid-base imbalances, haemodynamic instability and data on circuit longevity, and solute clearance. These results will collectively validate the efficacy and safety of this system.
Conclusion
The paediatric mode of MultiFiltratePRO is hypothesized to demonstrate efficacy and safety in delivering prescribed CVVHD effluent doses. This study is expected to provide valuable evidence to support its clinical use in paediatric CVVHD indication, with results contributing to future practices.

title: #89 Omentum wrapping of peritoneal dialysis catheter and peritoneal inflammation
authors: Zhifeng Jiang; Aiqiao Feng; Tao Li; Sai Xie
abstract:
Background and Aims
Omental wrapping of peritoneal dialysis catheters is a huge challenge for clinicians and peritoneal dialysis patients, there is a lack of reports on the risk factors associated with peritoneal dialysis omental wrap.
Method
We retrospectively analyzed a total of 313 PD cases in the Department of Nephrology, Xiaogan Central Hospital from 2010 to 2023, including 160 males and 153 females. Statistical significance of omentum wrap in different gender, whether associated with peritoneal dialysis peritonitis, catheter displacement and pelvic inflammatory disease. Multivariate logistic retrospective analysis was used to analyze the correlation between omental wrapping and women, pelvic inflammatory disease, and peritonitis associated with peritoneal dialysis.
Results
Compared with patients without pelvic inflammatory disease, omental wrap is more likely to occur in patients with a history of pelvic inflammatory disease, compared with patients without peritonitis, omental wrap is more likely to occur in patients with peritonitis associated with peritoneal dialysis, and the incidence of omentum wrap is higher in patients with catheter displacement. Multivariate regression analysis showed that omentum wrapping was related to pelvic inflammatory disease and peritonitis associated with peritoneal dialysis.
Conclusion
Omentum wrap is more likely to occur in patients with peritoneal dialysis-associated peritonitis, pelvic inflammatory disease.

title: #717 Assessment of cognitive function in patients receiving dialysis and its association with various parameters: a single-center cross-sectional study
authors: Vasiliki Gkika; Alexia Papalexandrou; Evdokia Efthymiou; Eleni Gkogka; Thomas Nitsotolis; Foteini Alourda; Ioanna Revela
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cognitive impairment is a severe issue for dialysis patients that affects quality of life. In this study we used the mini-mental state examination (MMSE), a screening tool that evaluates multiple cognitive functions such as orientation and memory with a maximum score of 30, in order to standardize cognitive assessment in dialysis individuals and investigate its associations with several discrete factors.
Method
We conducted a cross-sectional study of fifty-nine (59) dialysis patients, thirty-nine (39) males and twenty (20) females, at Frontis Dialysis Center in Keratsini in 2024. With the aim of minimizing confounding factors such as hemodynamic fluctuations, the MMSE was administered prior to dialysis sessions. Demographics, history, and laboratory parameters are presented in Table 1a. Statistical analyses included t-tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and univariate and multivariable linear regression. The Stata/MP 14.0 software was applied to analyse all data.
Results
The median patients’ age was 71 years (IQR:18), and the median dialysis duration was 4 years (IQR:7). The median MMSE score was 26 (IQR:5), with males scoring 27 and females 25.5 (P = 0.09, Table 1a, Graph 1). In the univariate analysis, statistically significant associations were revealed between MMSE scores and age (β = −0.1, P = 0.02), serum albumin (β = 3.7, P = 0.006), hemodiafiltration (HDF, β = 2.7, P = 0.02), and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFreEF, β = −3.7, P = 0.025) (Table 1b). In the multivariable analysis, hemodiafiltration (β = 2.3, P = 0.04) and serum albumin (β = 3, P = 0.013) continued to present significant associations with MMSE scores (Table 1c).
Conclusion
Our study underlines the potential role of hemodiafiltration and albumin on cognitive function in dialysis patients. Higher serum albumin levels were associated with better MMSE scores, highlighting the significance of nutritional status in maintaining cognitive health. In addition, hemodiafiltration appeared to improve mental functioning, possibly as a result of the removal of uremic toxins. To clarify underlying pathways and develop strategies to mitigate cognitive decline, further research and trials are warranted.

title: #2926 Congestion parameters in a peritoneal dialysis program
authors: Jehimy Jean Alvarez Saltos; Gabriel Manuel González Suárez; Claudia Marcela Castillo Devia; Nadia Martín Alemany; Ana Merino Ribas; Cristina Noboa Paez; Leyre García Cantalejo; Yanel Adriana Acosta Baptista; Maria Cufi Vallmajor; Jordi Calabia Martínez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Volume overload is associated with increased mortality in dialysis patients, making it essential to maintain euvolemia. Currently, several methods have been developed to help manage the volume including clinical and paraclinical parameters.
The primary objective of this study is to describe the relationship between parameters associated with hypervolemia in patients enrolled in a peritoneal dialysis (PD) program. The secondary objective is to characterize these patients using point-of-care ultrasound (PoCUS) and composite congestion score (CCS) as methods to complement the assessment of congestion phenotypes.
Method
A cross-sectional observational comparative study was conducted involving PD patients. Patients were divided into two groups based on the results of congestion assessed by bioelectrical impedance: non-congestive (Group 1, n = 15) and congestive by bioelectrical impedance (Group 2, n = 7). Additionally, an ultrasound examination was performed twice (Lung US, inferior vena cava diameter, portal vein pulsatility) during the visit for the peritoneal equilibration test (PET) and afterward.
Results are presented as means ± standard deviation for variables exhibiting a normal distribution and as medians for variables displaying a non-normal distribution. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Group comparisons were conducted using the Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis tests for variables with a non-normal distribution. Relationships between parameters were examined using Spearman's correlation test. Significance was established at P < 0.05. The statistical software used was SPSS version 30.
Results
We found that patients in Group 2 had hypertension, heart failure, and valvulopathies: mitral and aortic regurgitation. Additionally, statistically significant differences were identified in intraperitoneal pressure and interventricular septum thickness, which were greater in this group. However, Group 1 showed higher residual diuresis (Table 1).
A relationship was identified between residual diuresis and the CHARLSON score (P = 0.035) as well as pulmonary artery systolic pressure (P = 0.023). Additionally, BNP values were correlated with Ca-125 (P = 0.05) and the vena cava diameter during PET and post-PET (P = 0.005), but no significant correlations were found with the rest of the variables analyzed. In the group analysis, the Composite Congestion Score showed a significant correlation with age (P = 0.043) and Ca-125 (P = 0.042), as well as hypervolemia determined by bioimpedance and residual diuresis (P = 0.033).
Conclusion
In the Group 2, the CCS did not show a significant correlation with any of the variables analyzed. Additionally, the US assessment before and after PET did not reveal significant variations. Ca-125 and NT-proBNP levels were higher in Group 2, but without statistical significance. Given the complexity of maintaining euvolemia in dialysis patients, analyzing the characteristics of congestive patients is key to adjusting depletive treatment.

title: #3079 Intradialysis physical exercise and quality of life
authors: Aziz Daminov; Olimkhon Sharapov; Maksud Sabirov
abstract:
Background and Aims
The aim of the study was to investigate the effect of intradialytic physical activity on the subjective assessment of the quality of life during hemodialysis.
Method
The present study included 103 patients with CKD5d and 20 healthy volunteers of the corresponding age. All study participants underwent an examination, including a study of quality of life. The data obtained in the group of patients with CKD5d (103 people) were compared with the data obtained in the group of healthy volunteers (CG, 20 people). Quality of life (QOL) was assessed using the SAM (Well-Being, Activity, Mood) questionnaire. In this work, we used the online version of the questionnaire—www.psytets.org/emo/san.html. Intradialytic physical exercise was used as an intervention, the effectiveness of which was studied in the course of the present study. For this purpose, a portable exercise machine was used, designed for pedaling with hands or feet in a sitting or lying position.
Results
During HD with intradialytic FN, a decrease in all SAN scores was noted, while the relative dynamics were comparable with the dynamics during standard HD (on scale C—well-being, the relative dynamics was −3.71%, against −3.18% during standard HD, on scale A—activity—−0.92% and −4.72%, respectively, on scale N—mood—−12.85% and −21.13%), however, by the 3rd day after HD, the SAM score indicators increased significantly above the scores achieved after the standard procedure and pre-dialysis data. Thus, the relative dynamics of C with pre-dialysis data was +31.44% versus −0.57 with standard HD (P < 0.001), A according to the A scale—+51.06% versus −2.56% (P < 0.001), according to the H scale—+24.82% versus −1.19% (P < 0.01).
Conclusion
In CKD patients, compared to healthy individuals, the QOL score according to the SAM system is reduced (8.27 points vs. 17.98 points, P < 0.001). HD contributes to further deterioration of these health aspects, with restoration to the initial level by the beginning of the next session. Intradialytic physical activity helps limit the degree of deterioration in quality of life by the end of the HD procedure and improves QOL in the interdialytic period.

title: #3263 Abdominal wall complications in peritoneal dialysis patient with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
authors: Aygulya Akisheva; Gergana Todorova; Kiril Nedyalkov
abstract:
Background and Aims
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the fourth leading cause of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) in adults worldwide. It is characterized with enlarged kidneys which decrease the effective peritoneal surface area leading to increased intraabdominal pressure, as well as collagen defects. This is why it is often considered to be a relative contraindication for peritoneal dialysis (PD) because patients are at increased risk of “pressure-driven” complications, such as abdominal wall hernias, pericatheter leaks, hydrothorax and gastrointestinal reflux.
Method
The patient is a 67-year-old female patient with ADPKD with liver involvement. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) was diagnosed in 2015. In September 2022 the patient began treatment with continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) due to progression to ESKD. The peritoneal catheter was implanted laparoscopically through infraumbilical access, and the coiled end was positioned in the Douglas cavity.
Results
Two months after catheter insertion and beginning of treatment the patient developed abdominal wall edema which propagated towards the left flank and the back and reduced in supine position. PD prescription was reduced to three exchanges with 1000 ml PD solution daily. There was no negative dynamics in the serum urea and creatinine levels. Exploratory laparoscopy showed a migration of the distal cuff ventrally, dragged parietal peritoneum and PD dialysate leakage. Similar complains returned three months after the defect correction, and a PD catheter malposition was diagnosed on X-ray. During laparoscopy a catheter migration under the transverse mesocolon was found, as well as multiple adhesions. Adhesions were removed laparoscopically and the PD catheter was replaced. Patient continued with low volumes of PD exchanges, which were gradually increased for a month up to 2000 ml. Unfortunately, a new hernia defect appeared in the upper right quadrant of the abdominal wall, where an old scar from a trocar insertion was present. The defect disappeared in supine position. A hernioplasty with polypropylene mesh was performed, PD was resumed with lower volumes of the exchanges.
Conclusion
Although, different studies report higher incidence of abdominal wall hernias in ADPKD-patients on PD, compared to non-ADPKD-patients on PD, there is no difference in PD discontinuation rate between the two groups, which implies that abdominal wall hernias are treatable without the need to transfer to hemodialysis.
Furthermore, the usage of tension-free hernia repair technique using polypropylene mesh allows the patient to continue PD within 24 hours after surgery, thus avoiding the need for temporary hemodialysis. The procedure does not differ from the one in healthy individuals in terms of morbidity and mortality rates.

title: #3813 Comparison between different methods in evaluating haemodialysis adequacy
authors: Julijana Usprcov; Vladimir Pushevski; Zhaklina Shterjova- Markovska; Angela Kabova; Mimoza Milenkova; Stefan Filipovski; Lada Trajceska; Irena Rambabova- Bushljetik; Nikola Gjorgjievski
abstract:
Background and Aims
An increasing number of patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) increased the need for hemodialysis. Inadequate hemodialysis affects morbidity and mortality of hemodialysis patients. KDOQI guidelines recommend that Kt/V should be kept above 1.2 or URR 65% for thrice weekly routine hemodialysis. The aim of this study was to compare the urea reduction ratio (URR), Kt/V estimation by Daugirdas formula with the results measured by an Online Clearance Monitor (OCM).
Method
Cross-sectional study was conducted on 15 patients on hemodiafiltration (HDF) with age 36–79 years, 4-hour hemodiafiltration sessions three times a week and hemodialysis experience ≥ 6 months, using highflux dialyzers. For every patient blood flow rate was ≥ 350 ml/min and dialysis flow rate was 500 ml/min. According to vascular access all had AVF. Kt/V was calculated by the OCM of the Nipro Surdial X machine (the hemodialysis machine automatically calculate the measured sodium ion clearance based on the plasma conductivity).
Results
A total of 80 sessions were assessed with a predominance of males 51% (8). The mean of URR was 78.4 ± 10. Mean Kt/V values obtained with the Daugirdas formula was 1.9 ± 0.19. Mean Kt/V delivered by machine (OCM) was 1.87 ± 0.2. There was no significant difference between age, sex, comorbidities with adequacy of hemodialysis. The study show that there was no significant difference between the URR and Kt/V calculated with the Daugirdas formula and the OCM in the evaluation adequacy of hemodialysis.
Conclusion
Online Clearance Monitor (OCM) can be used as noninvasive guide to the real-time adjustment of the dialysis dose.

A total of 80 sessions were assessed with a predominance of males 51% (8). The mean of URR was 78.4 ± 10. Mean Kt/V values obtained with the Daugirdas formula was 1.9 ± 0.19. Conclusion
Online Clearance Monitor (OCM) can be used as noninvasive guide to the real-time adjustment of the dialysis dose.

title: #1966 Non-invasive detection of calcineurin inhibitor toxicity using urinary mRNA expression in kidney transplant recipients
authors: So-Young Lee; Hey Yun Jeong; Jihyun Baek; Yu Ho Lee
abstract:
Background and Aims
Although immunosuppressive drugs have improved to reduce renal allograft rejection, renal allograft failure has not markedly diminished. Biochemical examination and invasive biopsy have low sensitivity for diagnosis of tacrolimus toxicity and kidney injury in kidney transplantation. Therefore, the development of non-invasive diagnosis for tacrolimus toxicity and acute and chronic kidney injury using expression level of urinary mRNA is required for long-term graft survival in the kidney transplant patients.
Method
110 urine specimens (35 stable, 30 acute rejection (AR), 15 acute calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity (CNI), 10 chronic CNI and 20 acute tubular necrosis (ATN)) were collected after transplantation. RNA extracted from urine pellets was reverse-transcribed and 4 transcripts associated with calcinurin inhibitor toxicity in microarray results published by Maluf et al. were investigated using real-time PCR.
Results
Four transcripts (LTF, NNMT, WFDC2, and HIF1A) were selected in published microarray data for diagnosing tacrolimus toxicity by real-time PCR analysis. The expression levels of LTF, NNMT, and HIF1A were significantly decreased in CNI group while 18S were increased. There was no difference of the expression of WFDC2 mRNA between groups. These transcripts discriminated patients with tacrolimus toxicity from patients with ATN and AR. A combination of mRNAs for 18S, LTF, NNMT, and HIF1A that distinguishes CNI from ATN and AR yielded the area under the curve of 0.94 and 0.87, respectively.
Conclusion
We investigated genetic biomarkers to develop a noninvasive diagnostic assay in urine of kidney transplant patients. These urinary mRNAs may be useful to non-invasively monitor allograft kidney in clinical decisions.

title: #268 Sex differences in the risk of bladder cancer among kidney transplant recipients and patients with kidney failure receiving hemodialysis
authors: Hoon Yu; Chan-Young Jung
abstract:
Background and Aims
Although both patients with kidney failure (KF) receiving hemodialysis (HD) and kidney transplant (KT) recipients (KTRs) have a high risk of bladder cancer, how this risk changes in the transition from dialysis to KT is unknown. In this study, we aimed to investigate the risk of bladder cancer in KTRs and patients on HD.
Method
This was a nationwide longitudinal cohort study of 66,547 participants from the National Health Insurance Service cohort who started HD for KF or received KT from 2002 to 2020. The primary outcome was the diagnosis of bladder cancer, which was defined as the composite of diagnostic codes and either hospitalization or ≥2 outpatient visits for bladder cancer.
Results
During mean follow-ups of 4.2 and 7.9 years in the HD and KT groups, respectively, the incidence rates of bladder cancer were 1.1/1,000 and 0.3/1,000 person-years, respectively. In the time-dependent multivariable Cox models, compared to patients on HD, the adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) for bladder cancer among KTRs was 0.36 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.21–0.60; P < 0.001). Among men, this aHR was 0.29 (95% CI, 0.15–0.55; P < 0.001); however, no statistically significant association between the kidney replacement therapy modality and the risk of bladder cancer was observed among women. Landmark analysis performed to avoid immortal time bias by redefining time zero as a specific landmark time (2 and 5 years after HD initiation or KT) revealed similar results.
Conclusion
The risk of bladder cancer was significantly lower among KTRs than that among patients receiving HD, particularly among men.

title: #1990 Safety of continued belatacept treatment after kidney graft rejection
authors: Matthias von Garrel; Helene Mühle; Jan Hinrich Bräsen; Benedikt Kolbrink; Roland Schmitt; Kevin Schulte; Friedrich von Samson-Himmelstjerna
abstract:
Background and Aims
Transplant rejections are a common complication after kidney transplantation, significantly impacting long-term outcomes. While calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs) remain the gold standard for immunosuppression, belatacept has become increasingly relevant in specific patient groups. Despite its benefits, belatacept-based therapy has been associated with a slightly higher rejection rate. The aim of this study was to investigate the safety of continued belatacept application after a rejection episode.
Method
We analyzed data from a single-center registry of kidney transplant recipients who underwent biopsy due to clinical suspicion of graft injury. Patients were followed for up to three years. The primary endpoint was the composite occurrence of subsequent rejection or graft failure. Secondary endpoints were the individual occurrences of subsequent rejection and graft failure.
Results
We identified 101 patients with biopsy-proven rejection, of whom 54 received CNI-based and 47 belatacept-based immunosuppression following rejection.
The distribution of T cell-mediated rejections (TCMR), antibody-mediated or mixed rejections (AMR ± MR), and borderline lesions did not significantly differ between groups (chi-square test, P = 0.59). Specifically, TCMR occurred in 23 vs. 17 patients, AMR ± MR in 10 vs. 7, and borderline lesions in 21 vs. 23 (CNI vs. belatacept).
At three years, event-free survival for the primary endpoint was 80.6% (95% CI, 69.9–93.1) in the CNI group and 87.3% (95% CI, 77.4–98.6) in the belatacept group (P = 0.57). For the secondary endpoint of graft failure, dialysis-free survival at three years was 87.6% (95% CI, 78.8–97.5) in the CNI group and 97.9% (95% CI, 93.8–100.0) in the belatacept group (P = 0.09). For the secondary endpoint of recurrent rejection, rejection-free survival at three years was 91.6% (95% CI, 84.0–99.9) in the CNI group and 89.2% (95% CI, 79.7–100.0) in the belatacept group (P = 0.86).
Conclusion
We found no evidence of harm in the continued use of belatacept-based immunosuppressive therapy after kidney graft rejection.

title: #405 Assessment of frailty and sarcopenia in kidney transplant patients
authors: Tunahan Isik; Harun Coban; Busra Can; Dilek Barutcu Atas; Murat Tugcu; Izzet Hakki Arikan; Ebru Asicioglu; Z Serhan Tuglular; Arzu Velioglu
abstract:
Background and Aims
In chronic kidney disease (CKD), frailty and sarcopenia may develop due to uremia, metabolic acidosis and inflammation. Frailty and sarcopenia are associated with increased cardiovascular disease and mortality. The main recommended treatment for CKD is kidney transplantation. However, sarcopenia and frailty are also seen in kidney transplant patients. The aim of our study was to determine the prevalence and risk factors for frailty and sarcopenia in renal transplant patients in our center.
Method
Our study included 123 kidney transplant patients followed in our center. Fried frailty criteria and FRAIL scale were used for frailty assessment. European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People 2 (EWGSOP2) criteria were used for the diagnosis of sarcopenia. Threshold values for hand grip strength were used as 32 kg in men and 22 kg in women as determined in our country; threshold values for Appendicular Skeletal Muscle Mass Index (ASMI) were used as 7.0 kg/m2 in men and 5.5 kg/m2 in women as recommended in EWGSOP2.
Results
The mean age of the patients was 49 ± 12 years, 45.5% were female and 54.5% were male. According to Fried criteria, 41.5% (n = 51) were prefrail and 4.1% (n = 5) were frail; according to FRAIL scale, 28.5% (n = 35) were prefrail and 3.3% (n = 4) were frail. According to Fried and FRAIL criteria, frail and prefrail patients had higher phosphorus levels than non-frail patients (OR: 2.432, 95% CI:1.150–5.143, P = 0.02 and OR: 2.018, 95% CI:1.080–3.771, P = 0.028). 32.5% (n = 40) were probable sarcopenic and 4.9% (n = 6) were confirmed sarcopenic. The frequency of cadaveric transplantation was higher in sarcopenics (13 (28.3%) vs. 6 (7.8%), P = 0.004). According to Fried criteria, 69.6% (n = 32) of sarcopenics were prefrail and 8.7% (n = 4) were frail; 24.7% (n = 19) of nonsarcopenics were prefrail and 1.3% (n = 1) were frail. According to the FRAIL scale, 39.1% (n = 18) of sarcopenics were prefrail, 6.5% (n = 3) were frail; 22.1% (n = 17) of nonsarcopenics were prefrail, 1.3% (n = 1) were frail and both criteria were significantly associated with sarcopenia (P < 0.05).
Conclusion
Frailty and sarcopenia should be evaluated together in renal transplant patients. In our study, both Fried and FRAIL scales were associated with high phosphorus levels; phosphorus-lowering approaches can be applied to prevent frailty. Cadaveric kidney transplantation was found to be a risk factor for sarcopenia. This may be explained by longer duration of cold ischemia and higher doses of immunosuppression.

title: #2667 The effect of pravastatin on insulin resistance in kidney transplant recipients. A randomized, placebo-controlled cross over trial
authors: Mai-Britt Skadborg; Henrik Birn; Niels Moeller; Niels Jessen; Lara Aygen Ozbay
abstract:
Background and Aims
Insulin resistance is highly prevalent in renal transplant recipients, which increases the risk of post-transplant diabetes mellitus (PTDM) and cardiovascular morbidity.
Statins are recommended as primary prophylaxis in most transplant recipients; however, they have been associated with insulin resistance and diabetes mellitus.
This diabetogenic effect appears to be dose dependent, yet some statins may have neutral or beneficial effects on glucose metabolism. Pravastatin is consistently reported as the least diabetogenic statin, however this has not been established in kidney transplant recipients using a hyperinsulinaemic euglaemic glucose clamp.
We aimed to test if pravastatin improves insulin sensitivity compared to placebo in non-diabetic kidney transplant recipients.
Method
We conducted a randomized, placebo controlled, double blinded cross-over trial of 12 weeks of pravastatin treatment (40 mg/day) in 11 non-diabetic kidney transplant recipients.
Botnia clamps (Intra Venous Glucose Tolerance Test (IVGTT) followed by hyperinsulinaemic euglycaemic glucose clamp) were performed after each treatment period (12 weeks of 40 mg pravastatin and 12 weeks of placebo). IVGTT was performed with 50% glucose 0.3 g/kg total body weight/2 min, and the hyperinsulinaemic clamp with insulin 1.0 mUnits/kg total body weight/min. The primary endpoint was the difference in insulin sensitivity measured as glucose infusion rate/M value during each clamp. Secondary endpoints included first phase insulin secretion during intravenous glucose tolerance test and 2-hour plasma glucose after an oral glucose tolerance test.
Results
There was no significant difference in insulin sensitivity following pravastatin treatment when compared to placebo, with a mean difference in M-value of -0.403 mg/kg/min (95% CI −1.83 to 1.02, P = 0.54). Mean M-value was 7.34 mg/kg/min. (SEM ± 0.61, 95% CI 5.99–8.69) after treatment with pravastatin and 8.06 mg/kg/min. (SEM ± 1.07, 95% CI 5.74–10.39) after placebo treatment.
Mean fasting P-glucose 5.5 mmol/l (SEM ± 0.14, 95% CI 5.15 to 5.77) after pravastatin treatment and 5.4 (SEM ± 0.17, 95% CI 5.06 to 5.78) after placebo treatment, with no significant difference between the two groups (95% CI −0.33 to 0.33, P = 1.00).
Mean HbA1c was 36.9 mmol/mol (SEM ± 1.4) and 36.3 mmol/mol (SEM ± 1.5) after pravastatin and placebo treatment, respectively, with a non-significant difference of −0.5 mmol/mol (SEM ± 0.8, 95% CI −2.4 to 1.3, P = 0.53). Mean 2-h P-glucose following an OGTT was 7.4 mmol/l (SEM ± 1.0) and 7.0 mmol/l (SEM ± 0.8) following treatment with pravastatin and placebo, respectively, with a non-significant difference between treatments of 0.2 mmol/l (SE ± 0.5, 95% CI −0.9 to 1.2, P = 0.70).
Kidney graft function remained stable throughout the trial for all patients.
Conclusion
Twelve weeks of treatment with pravastatin does not cause any significant changes in insulin sensitivity in non-diabetic kidney transplant recipients. In transplant recipients who are at increased risk of both PTDM and cardiovascular disease pravastatin seems to be a good option for cardiovascular risk reduction without a concurrent increase in risk of PTDM.

title: #487 Post-transplantation management of calcium and parathyroid hormone levels and its association with kidney graft survival and fibrosis
authors: Manabu Okada; Shunji Narumi; Yuki Shimamoto; Tomoki Himeno; Yuki Hasegawa; Kenta Futamura; Takahisa Hiramitsu; Toshihiro Ichimori; Yoshihiko Watarai
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyperparathyroidism (HPT) is a potential risk factor for graft loss after kidney transplantation (KTx). However, the effects of HPT management on graft outcomes remain unclear. This retrospective study aimed to investigate the impact of HPT status and its management on graft outcomes.
Method
Patients who underwent KTx were categorized based on their HPT status and treatment at 1-year post-KTx into four groups: normal (no HPT), normocalcemic HPT, hypercalcemic HPT with no subsequent treatment, or intervention (parathyroidectomy or calcimimetics within 1 year after KTx). Patients treated for HPT beyond the first year post-KTx were excluded. The primary outcome was death-censored graft survival and the secondary outcome was the progression of interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy (IFTA) at 1 year post KTx.
Results
Among 1,248 patients, the 10-year death-censored graft survival rate was lowest in the hypercalcemic HPT group (80.9%), whereas the intervention group had a survival rate of 100.0%. In multivariate Cox regression analysis, untreated hypercalcemic HPT was significantly associated with an increased risk of graft loss (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.28, P = 0.048, compared to the normal group). In contrast, the intervention group did not show an increased risk of graft loss (HR = 0.26, P = 0.209). Additionally, hypercalcemia during the first year after KTx was significantly associated with IFTA progression (odds ratio = 1.98, P = 0.045).
Conclusion
Hypercalcemic HPT was associated with inferior graft survival and IFTA progression. Proactive management of HPT may reduce the risk of graft loss and mitigate IFTA progression.

title: #2288 Survival and care trajectory of kidney graft patients after age 65: Let's look at the cardiovascular comorbidities rather than age
authors: Vabret Elsa; Juliette Piveteau; Mathilde Lassalle; Cécile Couchoud; Cécile Vigneau; Sahar Bayat
abstract:
Background and Aims
The latest French recommendations (HAS 2015) suggest offering renal transplantation as a replacement therapy up to the age of 85, in the hope of improving the survival and quality of life of eligible stage V chronic kidney failure patients. Nevertheless, renal transplantation remains a major procedure, with a significant risk of complication or death for these elderly patients.
Method
The aim of our study is to identify risk factors for one-year mortality after renal transplantation and complications requiring hospitalization by cross-referencing data from the REIN registry and the SNDS (Système National des Données de Santé) in patients starting replacement therapy after the age of 65.
Results
Between 01/01/2017 and 31/12/2018 10642 patients aged 65 to 85 started renal replacement therapy, 807 were transplanted before 31/12/2020 and followed up until 31/12/2021, after a median time on the waiting list of 9.3 month. Among them, 71 patients died during the first year of transplantation. Age was not associated with a higher risk of death as diabetes or donor type. Only the number of cardiovascular comorbidities was significantly associated (HR 3.6 CI 1.4–9.4 p :0.008), i.e. a 3.6-fold higher risk of death when patients had 3 cardiovascular comorbidities vs. none. Age was also not associated with a longer length of hospital stay at the time of transplantation, or with an increased risk of early re-hospitalization within 30 days. Looking more specifically into cardiovascular comorbidities, we found that having been hospitalized for a peripheral vascular condition within the two years prior to being placed on the transplant waiting list was associated with an increased risk of mortality in the year following the transplant, all other factors being equal (HR 2.14 CI 1.08–4.27 p : 0.029).
Conclusion
Mortality in the first year after kidney transplantation in elderly patients seems to be mainly related to pre-transplant cardiovascular comorbidities, especially peripheral vascular condition with need of hospitalization and not to patient age. Nor does age seem to increase the length of hospital stay or the risk of early re-hospitalization, which would impact on these patients' quality of life. The official age is therefore not a reliable marker for not referring patients for transplantation, but enhanced cardiovascular monitoring to detect vascular conditions as early as possible during chronic kidney disease is likely important.

title: #2227 Can ALC be used to optimise ATLG dose inkidney transplant patients?
authors: Akash Gupta; Sanjeev Gulati; Ajit Narula; Ishrat Mir
abstract:
Background and Aims
The present is a prospective study evaluating the use of absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) in determining anti T lymphocyte globulin (ATLG) induction dose in kidney transplant recipients (KTR).
Method
The present is a prospective observational study conducted in kidney transplant department of tertiary care centre. As per protocol, 40 KTR of intermediate risk group were given dynamic ATLG-Grafalon dosing as induction agent along with standard triple immunosuppressive therapy. Patients with high and low immunological risk were excluded. As per dynamic dosing, the KTR received first dose (3 mg/kg) on the day of transplant. Subsequent doses were determined according to ALC. The ATLG was targeted to keep the mean ALC < 500. The patients were followed up for infections and incidences of acute rejection till 3 months. A comparison of graft outcome, rejections and infections between 40 KTR receiving dynamic Grafalon dosing was done with historical data of 27 KTR who received standard Grafalon dosing (8 mg/kg).
Results
In the study, 40 KTR received Grafalon dosing according to ALC. The KTR receiving dynamic Grafalon dosing had mean age of 41.35 ± 13.98 years with male to female ratio of 3.4.The mean Grafalon dosage was 6.33 ± 1.10 mg/kg. The incidence of infection at 7 days, 1 month and 3 months follow up were 6 (15.00%), 4 (10.00%) and 0 (0%),whereas the incidence of acute rejection were 1 (2.5%), 2 (5%) and 0 (0%). The historical data of 27 KTR receiving Grafalon dosage of 8 mg/kg had mean age of 43.67 ± 14.5 years with male to female ratio of 2.85. The incidence of infection at 7 days, 1 month and 3 months was found to be 6 (22.22%), 3 (11.11%) and 0 (0%) whereas the incidence of acute rejection was 3 (11.22%), 2 (7.41%) and 2 (7.41%). On comparing the KTR receiving dynamic Grafalon dosage according to ALC count to historical data of KTR receiving standard Grafalon dosage, there was no statistical difference in the rate of infection and rejection (P value >0.05). The study further showed that KTR with dynamic induction dosage had 20.88% reduction in mean Grafalon dose with reduction in mean cost of Grafalon by 20.91%, compared to historical KTR.
Conclusion
The present study suggests that ALC can be used as a simple bedside tool in optimising the dosage of induction agent in KTR. Reduced dosage of ATLG decreases the risk of infections and also reduces the cost of kidney transplant. Further studies in larger number of patients with longer duration of follow up are needed to evaluate the risk of infections as well rejections in these patients.

title: #2673 Efficacy and safety of SGLT2 inhibitors in kidney transplant recipients with proteinuria, irrespective of diabetes status
authors: Zeng-Jie Wang; Yun-Ying Shi; Bin-Qi Yang; Yuan-Zhen He
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney transplantation is the most effective treatment for end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Previous studies have shown that post-transplant proteinuria is strongly associated with reduced long-term survival and graft function loss. Although SGLT-2 inhibitors have demonstrated efficacy in CKD, their role in KTRs, particularly those without diabetes, remains underexplored due to the complexity of post-transplant physiology and immunosuppressive therapies, which may alter drug efficacy and safety profiles. This study aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of dapagliflozin in proteinuric KTRs, irrespective of diabetes status.
Method
This prospective, real-world study enrolled 103 KTRs treated with dapagliflozin (ChiCTR2400087630). Mixed-effects repeated-measures models were used to assess changes in urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) over 12 months, with subgroup analysis based on diabetes status to assess the efficacy of proteinuria reduction. Secondary efficacy outcomes included changes in routine blood and urine biomarkers, and safety outcomes were also evaluated.
Results
Significant reductions in UACR were observed at all post-baseline time points (P < 0.001, Fig. 1), indicating a decrease in proteinuria over time. Although eGFR showed a slight decline at month 12 (from 63.43 ± 18.58 mL/min/1.73 m² at baseline to 61.28 ± 19.44 mL/min/1.73 m²), this change was not statistically significant (P > 0.05, Fig. 2). Regardless of diabetes status, dapagliflozin was similarly effective in reducing proteinuria among KTRs, with no significant differences observed between the two groups (P > 0.05, Fig. 3). Additionally, there were notable improvements from baseline in red blood cell count (P = 0.01), hemoglobin (P = 0.029), fasting blood glucose (P < 0.001), serum magnesium (P < 0.001), and serum phosphorus (P = 0.007). The use of dapagliflozin did not significantly affect the stability of immunosuppressive drug concentrations, which remained within the therapeutic range throughout the study period. A total of 15 patients (14.6%) reported adverse events. The most common adverse event was urinary tract infection (7.8%), followed by kidney-related adverse events (4.9%). No serious adverse events or deaths were reported during the study.
Conclusion
Dapagliflozin significantly reduced proteinuria in kidney transplant recipients, irrespective of diabetes status, and helped correct hypophosphatemia and hypomagnesemia. The drug demonstrated a favorable safety profile, with no serious adverse events and no significant impact on eGFR or immunosuppressive drug concentrations. These findings provide evidence for the anti-proteinuric efficacy and safety of short-term dapagliflozin in KTRs.

title: #3149 Evaluation of kidney biopsy quality: a single-center comparative analysis of direct core microscopy-controlled and non-microscopically controlled techniques
authors: Gatis Saknitis; Mikus Saul; Aivars Petersons; Viktorija Kuzema; Martins Zvackis; Kārlis Rācenis
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney biopsy serves as an essential diagnostic modality in nephrology, particularly in the assessment of transplant recipients. The diagnostic accuracy and subsequent clinical management are highly dependent on biopsy specimen adequacy. This study provides a comparative analysis of transplant kidney biopsies performed with direct microscopic quality control, predominantly conducted by nephrologists, versus those performed without microscopic control by radiologists. The investigation focuses on key parameters including specimen adequacy, complication rates, and factors influencing biopsy outcomes.
Method
A retrospective, single-center analysis was conducted on 127 transplant kidney biopsies performed between 2023 and 2024. Data on glomeruli count, number of core biopsy samples, biopsy adequacy, complication rates (hematomas, site infections), and patient characteristics (age, gender, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, and time from transplantation to biopsy) were analyzed. An adequate biopsy was defined as one containing more than 10 glomeruli and at least 2 arteries. The Chi-squared test was employed to compare the proportions between groups for categorical variables. To compare means (along with standard deviations) for continuous variables, the Independent Samples t-test was used. Multinomial logistic regression was applied to multivariable analysis. Statistical analysis was conducted using SPSS version 29.0, with the alpha significance level 0.05.
Results
During the study period, a total of 127 kidney biopsies were performed. Among these, nephrologists conducted 38 biopsies, while 89 were performed by radiologists (T1). Nephrologists (microscopically-controlled biopsies) achieved significantly higher glomeruli counts (P = 0.01) and obtained a greater number of core biopsy samples (P < 0.001) compared to radiologists (non-microscopically controlled biopsies). Additionally, a non-significant trend suggested that nephrologists may achieve higher biopsy adequacy (P = 0.07). There were no statistically significant differences in hematoma rates or site infections between the two groups. Additionally, factors such as age, gender, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, and the time from transplantation to biopsy showed no significant differences between the nephrologists and radiologists.
In multivariate analysis after adjusting for other variables in the model (e.g., age, gender, hypertension), nephrologists are 2.48 times more likely to perform a sufficient biopsy than radiologists. However, the results are not statistically significant (P = 0.27). A longer interval between transplantation and biopsy was slightly associated with reduced odds of adequate biopsy (borderline P = 0.05).
Conclusion
Microscopy-controlled biopsies demonstrated superior biopsy adequacy regarding glomeruli count and the number of core samples obtained. However, the results did not achieve statistical significance. Despite the different number of cores obtained, no differences in complication rates were obtained between groups.

title: #3167 Factors associated with allosensitization from kidney allograft failure to retransplantation
authors: Elena Rho; Madeleine Thommen; Kerstin Hübel; Dusan Harmacek; Lukas Weidmann; Kai Castrezana Lopez; Lukas Frischknecht; Seraina Von Moos; Britta George; Thomas Schachtner
abstract:
Background and Aims
Retransplantation is becoming more and more common and is for many patients the best renal replacement therapy after the failure of a first graft. Considering that allosensitization might prolong the time on the waiting list for a retransplantation, preventing it is essential. Which is the best maintenance immunosuppression after graft failure is still matter of debate.
Method
We conducted a retrospective single-centre study including kidney transplanted recipients (KTR) who underwent a kidney retransplantation at the University Hospital of Zurich between 2012 and 2023. We analysed which factors and especially which kind of maintenance immunosuppression after allograft failure could affect allosensitization.
Results
In our cohort 129/1040 KTRs (12%) underwent retransplantation. Of these, 27/129 (20%) were living donations. The median waiting time for deceased-donor transplantation was 3.2 (1.2-3.6) years and 2.7 (0.6–6.2); 3.5 (2.4–4); 4.8 (2.1–5.7) and 6.0 (4.9–17) years for the blood groups A, O, B and AB respectively (P < 0.0001).
Upon univariate analysis previous allograft nephrectomy was performed in 35/129 (27%) and was associated with a higher calculated panel reactive antibody: 90% vs. 29% (P < 0.0001). Interestingly, the use of an antimetabolite at the time of retransplantation was associated with a lower median cPRA (23% for azathioprine, 20% for MPA, and 88% for no antimetabolite; P < 0.0001). The same was true for the use of prednisone (24% vs. 66%, P = 0.02), but it was not true for the use of calcineurin inhibitors (P = 0.2). A higher urine volume was associated with a lower cPRA when compared to anuric KTRs (2% vs. 21% vs. 73% for normal volume, oliguria, and anuria, respectively). Moreover, haemodialysis was associated with a higher cPRA when compared to peritoneal dialysis or no dialysis (62% vs. 33% vs 1%, P = 0.02). First retransplantation was also associated with a lower cPRA if compared to a second or a third one (41% vs. 78% vs. 88%, P = 0.02). Surprisingly, we could not find a correlation between cPRA and time to retransplantation (r < 0.2, P = 0.3).
Conclusion
Our results suggest that many factors may influence allosensitization, some of which are modifiable. Nevertheless, time to retransplantation, in our cohort did not correlate with allosensitisation, suggesting that other factors as blood group might have a bigger influence on waiting time.

title: #3729 Perioperative congestion assessment in kidney transplant recipients: the role of multiparametric evaluation with ultrasound and biomarkers
authors: Jordi Soler-Majoral; Gregorio Romero-González; Javier Paul-Martinez; Inés Perezpayá; Fernando Parra-Londoño; Marina Urrutia-Jou; Maria Molina Gomez; Néstor Yesid Rodríguez Chitiva; Pau Satorra-Herbera; Jordi Bover Sanjuan; Jordi Ara; Anna Vila Santandreu
abstract:
Background
More than 50% of patients with chronic kidney disease on dialysis have heart failure (HF), and approximately 20%–40% may continue to have HF in the post-kidney transplant period, with delayed graft function (DGF) being one of the mechanisms that may perpetuate it. In these patients, congestion is a key pathophysiological mechanism contributing to adverse outcomes. However, there is limited evidence regarding the presence of congestion during the perioperative period in kidney transplant (KT) recipients, who are subjected to the administration of large amounts of fluids to promote renal recovery. Notably, in critically ill patients, liberal fluid strategies have not shown a clear beneficial effect, particularly in those who are fluid intolerant (FI). Currently, the concept of multiparametric congestion assessment is emerging, combining point-of-care ultrasonography with congestion biomarkers such as NT-proBNP and CA125, in addition to physical examination. This approach aims to improve the estimation of left and right ventricular filling pressures and better identify patients who may benefit from fluid administration or fluid tolerant (FT).
The aim of this study was to evaluate the evolution of congestion biomarkers and ultrasound parameters during the perioperative period in patients undergoing KT.
Method
This prospective study was conducted at a tertiary hospital over an 18-month period. Patients aged ≥18 years undergoing KT were included. Exclusion criteria included the need for inotropic or vasopressor support in the immediate post-transplant period, surgical reintervention, multi-organ transplantation, or poor ultrasound image quality. NT-proBNP and CA125 were measured preoperatively (D0), on postoperative day 1 (D1), day 7 (D7), and day 30 (D30). Patients were classified as FI if they had >3 B-lines in two fields on lung ultrasound, inferior vena cava >2 cm with a collapsibility <50%, or a portal vein pulsatility index ≥30%. Those who did not meet these criteria were considered FT.
Results
A total of 164 KT were performed during the study period. Of these, 115 patients met the exclusion criteria, leaving 45 patients for analysis. Among the included patients, 38.3% were women, with a mean age of 57.7 years (±15.50). Hypertension was present in 84.8% of patients; 65.2% were on pre-transplant hemodialysis, 15.2% on peritoneal dialysis, and 19.6% underwent preemptive KT. Additionally, 34.8% of transplants were from donors after brain death, 43.5% from donors after circulatory death, and 21.7% from living donors. NT-proBNP levels were elevated preoperatively D0: 2471.50 pg/mL (1027–5635) and decreased on D1: 2008 pg/mL (796–3818) before peaking again at D7: 2760 pg/mL (418–6257) and stabilizing at lower levels by D30 800 pg/mL (212–1549). Similarly, CA125 levels showed a progressive increase post-transplant, with a median of 17.5 U/mL (9.3–28) at D0, 16.85 U/mL (9–28) at D1, peaking at D7: 39 U/mL (19–70), and declining at D30: 21 U/mL (10.5–42.3). At baseline (D0), 26.7% of patients were FI, while 73.3% were FT. On D1, the proportion of FI patients increased to 41.9%, while FT patients decreased to 58.1%. By D7, FI was observed in 39.5% of patients, with 60.5% remaining FT. At D30, the proportion of FI patients decreased to 15.2%, while FT increased to 84.8%.
DGF was present in 37.8% of patients. Of these, 54.5% met the criteria for FI at D1, compared with 26.3% of FT patients without DGF. At D7, the prevalence of FI increased to 65.7% in patients with DGF, while it remained lower (28.2%) in FT patients without DGF.
Conclusion
FI is common post-transplant, especially in patients with DGF. Multiparametric assessment with ultrasound and biomarkers improves congestion detection, emphasizing the need for personalized fluid management to optimize outcomes. Future studies should explore the impact of targeted fluid management approaches on post-transplant outcomes.

title: #79 Semaglutide enabled waitlisting and transplantation of otherwise unlisted obese renal transplant candidates
authors: Caroline La; Emilie Navaux; Sylvain Dufour; Thomas Caes; Nicolaos Koliakos; Dimitri Mikhalski; Vincent Huberty; Alain Le Moine; Concetta Catalano
abstract:
Background and Aims
Obesity is an increasing health concern among kidney transplant candidates. While transplantation should be encouraged to treat advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD), obesity often hinders access to transplant due to the higher rate of post-operative complications. Pre-transplant bariatric surgery provides significant weight loss but is not free of risk. ‘Glucagon Like Peptide-1’analogues (GLP-1Ras) demonstrated efficacy to treat obesity in the general population but data in renal transplant candidates are poor. This study aims to determine whether treatment with semaglutide enabled waitlisting and transplantation of otherwise unlisted obese renal transplant candidates.
Method
Between 01/01/2021 and 30/10/2023, patients recused from renal transplantation due to obesity received pre-transplant subcutaneous semaglutide up to 1 mg/week.
Results
Of the 23 patients included, initial mean body weight, BMI and waist circumference were 106 Kg, 35.6 and 119 cm respectively. title: #326 Metabolomic profiling of urine in post-kidney transplant patients: insights into allograft function and creatinine clearance
authors: Ivana Dedinska; Eva Baranovičová; Karol Graňák; Matej Vnučák; Patricia Kleinova; Tímea Blichová; Andrej Kollár
abstract:
Background and Aims
End-stage kidney disease is optimally managed through kidney transplantation. However, the suboptimal function of the transplanted kidney can lead to imbalances in processes controlled by the kidneys, necessitating long-term monitoring of the graft's function and viability. Given the kidneys' high metabolic activity, a metabolomics approach is well-suited for tracking systematic changes in post-transplant patients and holds significant potential for monitoring graft function.
Method
In this study, which follows the study on blood plasma, we analyzed morning and 24-hour urine samples from 55 patients who underwent primary kidney transplantation and were uniformly treated with immunosuppressants with a minimal follow-up of 50 months post-surgery. We assessed the relative levels of urinary metabolites detectable by NMR spectroscopy and investigated correlations between these metabolite levels and renal function.
Results
We observed rather unexpected independence of levels of urinary creatinine on serum creatinine as well as on allograft function expressed by eGFR. This observation allowed a very good agreement of outcomes from raw and creatinine-normalized data, consistent for both morning urine samples and 24-hour urine collections. The urinary levels of citrate and acetone were detected to be sensitive to allograft function, and the urinary levels of metabolites in combination showed promising prediction for kidney function, on the level of p-value: for 24 h pooled urine: 4.6 × 10−12 and morning urine: 5.36 × 10−9.
Conclusion
Based on the results, we support the opinion of critical assessment of creatinine clearance when judging the filtration function of the allograft, where surely factors such as alterations in the tubular secretion of creatinine may play a particular role. As the next, urinary metabolomics can serve as an easily available supplement to prediction for allograft function in patients after kidney transplantation.

title: #486 Smartphone addiction as a new behavioral risk factor for medication non-adherence in renal transplantation
authors: Özant Helvacı; Asil Demirezen; Omer Faruk Akcay; Ulver Derici; Muhammed Hakan Aksu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Medication non-adherence (MNA) is a significant contributor to graft rejection, impaired graft function, and mortality in renal transplant recipients. Despite well-documented risk factors such as younger age, depression, and complex regimens, the role of smartphone addiction (SPA) in MNA remains unexplored. SPA, linked to cognitive impairments like poor time management and forgetfulness, may negatively impact adherence to immunosuppressive therapy. This study investigates SPA as a potential behavioral risk factor for MNA in renal transplant recipients.
Method
This cross-sectional study included 140 renal transplant recipients followed at the Gazi University Transplant Outpatient Unit. Smartphone addiction (SPA) was assessed using the Smartphone Addiction Scale-Short Version (SAS-SV) and weekly screen time data objectively recorded from participant devices.
Medication non-adherence (MNA) was evaluated with the Immunosuppressant Therapy Adherence Scale (ITAS). ITAS scores were categorized as perfect adherence (12), acceptable adherence (10–11), and non-adherence (0–9). Statistical analyses were conducted to identify associations between SPA, screen time, and adherence levels.
Results
Patients with poor adherence (ITAS 0–9) reported significantly higher weekly screen times (27 ± 10 hours) compared to those with perfect (20 ± 10 hours) and acceptable adherence (21 ± 11 hours) (P < 0.001). Additionally, 66% of the poor adherence group scored above the SAS-SV threshold (median score: 23) versus 38% and 36% in the perfect and acceptable adherence groups, respectively (P = 0.020). Younger age was significantly associated with poor adherence (P = 0.031). No significant differences were found for gender, transplant duration, donor type, or rejection history across adherence groups.
Conclusion
SPA may represent a novel behavioral risk factor for MNA in renal transplant recipients, with weekly screen time serving as an objective and practical marker for identifying at-risk patients. Screening for SPA and incorporating behavioral interventions to manage excessive smartphone use may improve adherence and transplant outcomes. Longitudinal studies are required to establish causality and evaluate the effectiveness of targeted interventions.

title: #871 Glycemic variability in early post-transplant period and its impact on the development of later metabolic complications
authors: Karol Graňák; Matej Vnučák; Patricia Kleinova; Tímea Blichová; Andrej Kollár; Ivana Dedinska
abstract:
Background and Aims
It is well known that hyperglycaemia occurs very often after kidney transplantation (KT), but previous findings suggest that glycaemic variability (GV) may have a major impact on the development of later complications and patient's outcome. The aim of our study was to identify the impact of GV in the early post-transplant period on the development of metabolic complications using continuous glycaemic monitoring (GCM).
Method
This prospective study was performed in patients after primary KT at the Transplant-nephrology department of University hospital Martin, Slovakia. Adult patients with excluded diabetes and prediabetes were given a Dexcom G6 CGM before KT. This system was paired with a smartphone and continuously recorded blood glucose over a period of 7 days after KT. We recorded all patients' demographic and clinical characteristics on day 0, 5 and on the third and twelfth month, including findings in protocol biopsy, or donor specific antibodies. Oral glucose tolerance test was performed in the third and twelfth month. The total length of follow-up was 12 months, and all patients were set on the same immunosuppression.
Results
Currently, 20 patients (mean age 47.5 ± 14.6; 65% males) have completed the total length of follow up and were therefore included in the data analysis. The study group consisted of a total of 10 patients who were diagnosed with post-transplant diabetes mellitus—PTDM (n = 7) and prediabetes (n = 3). At baseline, we found no significant differences in basic characteristics between the control and the study group. On the 5th day after KT, we found significantly higher glycated haemoglobin—HbA1c (P = 0.0382) and lower insulin 2 hours post load (P = 0.0417) in the study group. In the study group, we identified significantly higher HbA1c (P = 0.0420), homeostatic model assessment index for insulin resistance, HOMA-IR (P = 0.0420) at month 3 and fasting insulin (P = 0.0219), HbA1c (P = 0.0059), HOMA-IR (P = 0.0060) at month 12 compared to the control group. By analysing the 7-day data from the CGM, we found a significantly higher average glucose (P = 0.0208), standard deviation - SD (P = 0.0006), estimated A1c (P = 0.0169), time in hyperglycaemia (TIH)—high (P = 0.0423), TIH—very high (P = 0.0194) and lower time in normal range (P = 0.0365) in the study group. We determined a criterion of >2.1 for SD as a predictor of PTDM/prediabetes occurrence using CGM models based on ROC curve analysis with a sensitivity of 70 and specificity of 80.
Conclusion
The first results of our study demonstrate the impact of GV in the early post-transplant period on the development of glucose metabolism disorders in the third and twelfth months after KT. CGM is an ideal tool for measuring GV in the early period after KT.

title: #1682 Dapagliflozin is a potentially safe and effective antidiabetic in diabetic renal transplant patients. Randomised controlled clinical trial
authors: Magdy Elsharkawy; Heba El Said; Ahmed Tawfik; Omar Haddad; Nahla Teama
abstract:
Background and Aims
Evidence concerning the efficacy and safety of SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) post renal transplantation is limited. This study evaluates the clinical impact of dapagliflozin in diabetic patients following renal transplantation.
Method
This randomized controlled clinical trial was conducted in single centre on 72 stable post-renal transplantation diabetic patients, equally assigned to dapagliflozin and control groups. All patients received standard care medications, with the SGLT2i group receiving an additional 10 mg of dapagliflozin. Baseline characteristics, including age, gender, end stage renal disease (ESRD) aetiology, post renal transplant diabetes, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), were well-balanced. After 6 months of follow-up, primary outcomes included 2-hour post-prandial levels, glycosylated haemoglobin (HbA1c), changes in mean body weight, eGFR, and the number of urinary tract infection episodes or any complications.
Results
Both groups exhibited body weight reduction, with the intervention group experiencing a median weight loss of −4.00 kg, which was statistically significantly greater than the control group, which showed a median change of 0.75 kg (P = 0.00). There was no statistically significant difference in eGFR (P = 0.54) or 2-hour post-prandial levels (P = 0.25) between the two groups, no recorded episodes of major hypoglycaemia. In terms of HbA1c levels, the intervention group initially presented with higher levels compared to the control group (6.50% for the intervention group vs 6.24% for the control group). Throughout the study, there was no statistically significant difference in glycosylated haemoglobin (P = 0.17).
In the context of safety of dapagliflozin in renal transplant patients there was no statistically significant difference regarding attacks of urinary tract infections (P = 0.48), hypoglycaemia, or any drug interaction with immune suppressants as the patients were on triple maintenance therapy of steroids, tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil, no attacks of volume depletion, diabetic ketoacidosis, fractures, any ischemic insults or amputations (Fig. 1).
The use of other oral hypoglycaemic agents decreased substantially in the intervention group, with 64% of patients not needing them, compared to only 25% in the control group (P = 0.00). There was also a significant downward trend in the number of other OHGs needed in the intervention group (P = 0.08) (Fig. 2). The need for basal insulin decreased to 13.9% in the intervention group, compared to 38.9% in the control group (P = 0.002). Additionally, the intervention group showed a lower need for short-acting insulin, at 8.3%, compared to 16.7% in the control group (P = 0.48).
Conclusion
SGLT2 inhibitors may be considered in managing post-transplant diabetes mellitus in renal transplant recipients, as they are anti-diabetic drugs with significant effects on weight reduction and glycemic control. Additionally, they can be used to reduce the number of other oral hypoglycemic drugs and the dosage of short-acting and basal insulin. Monitoring is required, particularly for urinary tract infections and other side effects.
