title: #2307 Obesity and renal transplantation—a scoping review
authors: Asad Ullah; Roham Sadeghimakki
abstract:
Background and Aims
The prevalence of obesity has increased among the general population and individuals with end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Obesity affects the care pathways for kidney transplantation (KT) at pre-, peri-, and post-transplant stages. This scoping review examines the evidence on KT care disparity and outcomes in adults with ESRD and obesity, focusing on: (1) access to the waiting list for KT; (2) post-KT outcomes based on pre-transplant body mass index; and (3) obesity management in transplant recipients.
Method
Following the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) guidelines for scoping reviews, a comprehensive literature search was performed in PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library for relevant English-language publications (January 2010 to August 2024).
Results
The literature search identified 119 publications on waiting-list enrolment for and access to KT, of which seven were included. For post-KT outcomes, 1,147 publications were identified, of which fifty-seven were included. Three hundred and sixty four publications concerning obesity management were identified, and forty-four publications were included, focusing on the pre-, peri-, and post-transplantation management of obesity in transplant recipients. There were disparities in body weight, gender, age, race, and ethnicity for KT waiting-list enrolment and access. In comparison to the recipients without obesity, recipients with obesity had suboptimal post-KT outcomes, including delayed graft function), acute rejection, increased mortality, and higher peri-transplantation complications, i.e., prolonged hospital stay, wound complications, lymphocele, and urinary leaks. However, when compared to remaining on dialysis, they derive survival benefits from renal transplantation. As far as the management is concerned, bariatric surgery, (BS) offers a safe and rapid decline in body weight in renal transplant candidates with morbid obesity. A significant proportion of patients were enlisted and received renal transplantation. BS was also considered safe post renal transplant and resulted in sustainable weight loss. Sleeve gastrectomy was preferred to other forms of BS due to minimal or no impact on immunosuppression kinetics. Lifestyle modifications resulted in modest but unsustainable weight loss. The literature about pharmacotherapies in renal transplant patients is limited.
Conclusion
This review revealed that patients with ESRD and obesity encounter challenges in being referred and gaining access to renal transplantation. Renal transplant recipients with pre-existing obesity also experience suboptimal clinical outcomes compared with normal-weight recipients. Bariatric surgery is the safest and most effective method for achieving appropriate weight for transplantation. Data on improvements in outcomes following weight loss are limited. It is crucial to assess each patient with ESRD and obesity individually and make risk-informed and unbiased decisions on KT access and care.

title: #3484 Torque teno virus loads and leukocyte populations in stable outpatient kidney transplant recipients
authors: Jip Jonker; Sietske Doorenbos; Edmund J Gore; António W Gomes-Neto; Jan-Stephan F Sanders; Jo Linssen; Stefanie Klatte; L Joost van Pelt; Transplantlines Investigators; Coretta van Leer-Buter; Stephan J L Bakker
abstract:
Background and Aims
Plasma concentrations of Torque teno virus (TTV) have been proposed as a biomarker of immune function, which could aid in personalized dosing of immunosuppressive medication after solid organ transplantation. It has been suggested that after replication, TTV enters the circulation through release from leukocytes, particularly granulocytes, or cells within the bone marrow. We hypothesize that leucocyte subpopulations are associated with circulating plasma TTV concentrations in kidney transplant recipients (KTR). We therefore aimed to explore the association of leucocyte subpopulations with plasma TTV concentrations in KTR.
Method
A total of 350 KTR with both detectable TTV load and leukocyte population counts at 1 year post-transplantation were selected from the TransplantLines Biobank and Cohort Study. TTV load was measured by real-time PCR assay (TTV R-GENE®, bioMérieux) and leukocyte populations were counted by a Sysmex XN hematology analyzer. Linear regression analyses were performed to assess associations between leukocyte populations and TTV load.
Results
Mean age of the included KTR was 56.3 ± 14.5 years, and 133 (38.0%) were female. In multivariable regression analysis, after adjusting for age, sex, smoking behavior, alcohol intake, C-reactive protein, tacrolimus and mycophenolic acid trough levels, and other granulocyte subpopulations, we found that immature granulocyte count was positively associated with TTV load (st. β = 0.44, P < 0.001) and neutrophil count was negatively associated with TTV load (st. β = −0.39, P < 0.001).
Conclusion
These results support the theory that TTV replicates in immature granulocytes. The mechanism underlying the negative association between neutrophiles and TTV load remains to be determined. Potential explanations include the suppression of TTV load by antiviral properties of neutrophiles or the possibility that TTV affects the lifespan of neutrophiles. Understanding these relationships might improve the interpretation of TTV load as a marker of immune function in clinical practice.

title: #3562 Bridging the gap: the effect of proximity on transplant care in a remote island community
authors: Jimmy Reinaldo Sanchez Gil; Avinash Chandu Nanwani; Maria Isabel Acosta-Ochoa; Maria Alejandra Rodriguez Garcia; Pablo Jesús Castillo Matos; Jose Luis Velasco González; Diego Silva Seco
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fuerteventura is one of the largest islands in terms of surface area in the Canary Island; however, it is not one of the most populated. Since 2020, the island's population has increased considerably, requiring an expansion of available healthcare services. In 2022, with the aim of improving the quality of life of renal patients, a kidney transplant follow-up clinic was established to operate alternately with the referral hospital. This study evaluates the effectiveness of this clinic and the clinical advantages of having a nephrologist accessible most of the time. The follow-up protocol consists of consultations every 2–3 months at the regional hospital and once a year at the referral hospital.
Method
A cross-sectional study was conducted with 42 kidney transplant recipients, who were followed up jointly between the clinic at Hospital Virgen de la Peña (Fuerteventura) and Hospital Insular Materno Infantile (Gran Canaria). The estimated glomerular filtration rate, the albumin/creatinine ratio, total proteinuria in 24-hour urine, and the number of emergency hospital admissions per patient were compared over two periods: before the establishment of the transplant clinic (2020–2022) and after its implementation (2022–2024). Additionally, population characteristics and comorbidities were evaluated, and the data were analyzed using SPSS v25.
Results
Currently, there are 42 kidney transplant patients on the island, with a mean age of 55.4 ± 13.1 years, of whom 11.9% (N = 5) have undergone a second transplant. The primary cause of kidney disease was, in order of frequency, of unidentified etiology (23.8%) and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (16.7%). Significant differences were found in the reduction of the number of urgent hospital admissions, from 0.83 ± 1.2 admissions between 2020–2022 to 0.40 ± 0.734 admissions between 2022–2024. Differences were also observed in 24-hour proteinuria, with values of 409.85 ± 412 mg/24 h and 356 ± 528 mg/24 h, respectively.
Conclusion
These results highlight the impact of having a kidney transplant clinic closer to patients, improving proteinuria, thereby enhancing the longevity of renal grafts and reducing urgent complications. This, in turn, leads to an improved quality of life for transplant patients. Additionally, the reduction in hospital costs allows for the implementation of new diagnostic and therapeutic techniques.

title: #3880 Outcomes of ABO-incompatible living kidney donor transplantation according to isoagglutinin titers
authors: Michelle Andrea Linárez Brea; Carla Burballa; Eulàlia Solà-Porta; Betty Odette Chamoun Huacon; Anna Buxeda; Ariadna González García; Dolores Redondo-Pachón; María José Pérez-Saéz; Marta Crespo
abstract:
Background and Aims
ABO-incompatible (ABOi) living kidney donor transplantation (LKDT) has been successfully adopted by transplant centres worldwide. A reduction in isoagglutinin titres < 1:8 is (arbitrary) necessary for ABOi-LKDT and elevated titres prior to desensitization or a rebound after the procedure can potentially impact on the LKDT outcomes. The aim of the study was to analyse the ABOi-LKDT short and mid-term outcomes according to the initial, after desensitization and post-LKDT isoagglutinin titres.
Method
We retrospectively reviewed the evolution of kidney function (KF) in 32 patients undergoing ABOi-LDKT in Hospital del Mar between June 2014 and December 2024. KF 7 days, 3, 6, 12, 24 and 36 months after LKDT was evaluated according to maximum baseline, after-desensitization and maximum post-LKDT both IgG and IgM isoagglutinin titers, considering also post-LKDT rebound. Desensitization consisted of rituximab administration and apheresis (plasmapheresis, immunoadsorption, or both). Infection rate, graft and patient survival were also assessed.
Results
We analyzed 32 ABOi-LKDT recipients (28 male) with a mean age of 57.8 ± 13.4 years and a mean follow-up of 36 months [14.8–56.3]. No LKDT recipient had baseline isoagglutinin titres >256 and all of them had ≤8 titres before surgery. A higher number of apheresis sessions was necessary in those cases with higher IgG maximum baseline isoagglutinin titres (<8: 1[1–2]; 64: 3[2.5–4]; 128: 3[2.5–3.5]; 256: 3[3–3]; p< 0.002). Isoagglutinin titres at evaluated time-points or rebound after LKDT had no influence on the ratio of acute rejection (15.6%), infectious complications (cytomegalovirus 18.7%; BK virus 15.6%). We did not observe differences in patient survival or graft survival during follow-up, according to isoagglutinin titres considered or rebound post-LKDT.
Conclusion
Maximum baseline IgG or IgM isoagglutinin titers, after-desensitization and maximum post-LKDT had no influence on graft survival or rejection ratio. Those recipients who needed a higher number of apheresis sessions to achieve pre-LKDT isoagglutinin target, did not have a higher rate of infections.

title: #2275 The importance of anti-AT1R antibodies in patients with diabetic nephropathy
authors: Magdalena Król-Kulikowska; Krzysztof Letachowicz; Andrzej Konieczny; Miroslaw Banasik; Marta Kepinska
abstract:
Background and Aims
The role of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and its components in the pathogenesis of diabetic nephropathy has been the subject of many studies for years. The importance of angiotensin, but also angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) and angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1R) is emphasized. What is more, the occurrence of anti-AT1R antibodies is associated with an increased risk of an immunologic rejection after an organ transplantation. The aim of the study was to determine the concentration of these antibodies in the group of patients with diabetic nephropathy and in the group of patients with diabetic nephropathy and after kidney transplantation.
Method
The study group consisted of 232 patients who were divided into the following subgroups: patients with diabetic nephropathy (N = 85), patients with diabetic nephropathy and after kidney transplantation (N = 97), control group (N = 50). Antibodies against AT1R were determined in the serum of all patients using ELISA. The results >17 U/mL were considered positive. The statistical analysis of the obtained results was performed using the STATISTICA 13.3 package. The Kruskal-Wallis H test was used to determine significant differences between the studied subgroups.
Results
Although differences in anti-AT1R antibodies serum concentrations of the studied subgroups could not be demonstrated, the obtained result was on the borderline of statistical significance (P = 0.068). Interestingly, the median of patients with diabetic nephropathy and after kidney transplantation was lower compared to the median of patients with diabetic nephropathy and patients from the control group (10.40 U/mL vs. 11.24 U/mL; 10.40 U/mL vs. 11.64 U/mL). 15.05% of patients after kidney transplantation were anti-AT1R antibodies-positive. In the group of patients with diabetic nephropathy this percentage was 20.00%, and in the control group 19.57%.
Conclusion
In the group of patients with diabetic nephropathy ad after transplantation the percentage of anti-AT1R antibodies-positive is low and comparable to the control group. The presence of anti-AT1R antibodies is associated with an increased risk of kidney transplant rejection, therefore more attention should be paid to the presence of these antibodies not only in patients after kidney transplantation, but also in patients preparing for it. In order to increase the effectiveness of renal replacement therapy, continuous monitoring of patients who have anti-AT1R antibodies before transplantation is desirable.

title: #3944 Natural killer subpopulations in kidney transplant patients with BK viruria
authors: Jesus Martin Centellas; Maria Belen Vidriales; Pilar Fraile Gómez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Infection in kidney transplant recipients (KTR) is, with cardiovascular disease, an important cause of morbidity and mortality. During last two decades, polyomavirus BK incidence has increased notably, being nowadays the most important virus targeting kidney tissue. As there is no directed treatment proved efficient, reduction in immunosuppression is the standard of care to control BK replication. Owing that this measure suppose a rise in rejection risk, identify patients at risk of BK nephropathy is crucial. Immune response study has raised interest during last years. Although virus-specific T cells plays a main role in elimination of reactivated BK, natural killer (NK) cells also are a central component of innate immune system against virus, so that their response in KTR has been studied in other viral infection as cytomegalovirus and herpesvirus.
Method
In our centre we perform screening for BK viruria by urine PCR in KTR monthly after transplantation until month 6, and afterwards at month 9 and 12 post-transplantation. We conduct a descriptive, observational and transversal study, to assess lymphocyte subpopulations in KTR who present viruria (defined by urine BK PCR >10x106 copies/ml) compared to KTR without viruria. Using flow cytometry we assessed lymphocyte subpopulations in blood at diagnosis of viruria in cases and at reclutation time in controls. In cases, we determined subpopulations for a follow up period of 2 months. Data were analyzed with SPPS 20.0; Chi square, Student-t and Wilcoxon tests are applied.
Results
24 patients were studied, 14 cases and 10 controls. Clinical characteristics are presented in Table 1, with no statistical difference between groups. Number of NK cells in blood is higher in patients with BK viruria at the moment of diagnosis (110 [SD 95.2] vs 66.2 [SD 36.4], p=0.18). Assessing NK subpopulations, number of CD56+ and CD56+CD27- cells are higher in KTR with viruria (99.76 [89.41] vs 59.85 [34.62], p=0.19; 93.68 [85.27] vs. 55.74 [33.8], p=0.19) (Fig. 1). In the follow-up period for BK viruria KTR, we observed decreased number of CD56++ cells (p=0.22), a rise in CD56+ CD27+ cells (p=0.15), and steady number of CD56+ cells and CD56+ CD27- cells (p=0.51, and p=0.47; respectively). The same trend is observed at month 2 (no statistical significance).
Conclusion
NK cells respond early during viral infection, a rapid activation could explain a rised number in patients with viral BK replication detected in urine.
The majority of NK cells in circulating blood are CD56+, and most do not express CD27. NK CD27- contains higher levels of perforin and granzyme, meaning a cytotoxic activity, as expected in patients at earlier stages of viral replication.
Although the results did not reach statistical significance, due in part to small sample, we can elucidate how the assessment of innate immunity can play a role in the evaluation of KTR with BK virus reactivation, and settled basis for further research.

title: #437 Prevalence, risk factors and long-term outcomes of diabetes mellitus after kidney transplantation
authors: Shahla Aghamaliyeva; Harun Coban; Dilek Barutcu Atas; Murat Tugcu; Izzet Hakki Arikan; Ebru Asicioglu; Z Serhan Tuglular; Arzu Velioglu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Posttransplant diabetes mellitus (PTDM) is the development of diabetes after organ transplantation in people without a previous diagnosis of diabetes mellitus (DM). PTDM occurs in 4% to 25% of kidney transplant patients. PTDM is associated with decreased patient/graft survival and increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD). The aim of our study was to investigate the frequency, risk factors, CVD and survival effects of PTDM in kidney transplant patients in our center.
Method
In our study, 220 patients who were followed up in our center between 2007 and 2022, above the age of 18 years, who did not have a diagnosis of DM before kidney transplantation and who were followed up for at least 1 year after transplantation were included. The 2023 American Diabetes Association criteria were used for the diagnosis of PTDM; fasting plasma glucose (FPG) and random plasma glucose (RPG) levels were used on day 45, and FPG, RPG levels and HbA1c values were used in the first year and after. Patients were analyzed in terms of demographic, clinical, laboratory data, patient/graft survival and CVD according to the development of PTDM at day 45 and one year.
Results
PTDM was detected in 47 patients (21.4%) at day 45. In univariate analysis; age (P < 0.001), body mass index (BMI) (P = 0.001), polycystic kidney disease (P = 0.010), cadaveric donor (P = 0.006), insulin use in the first week after transplantation (P < 0.001), APG level in the first week after transplantation (P = 0.001), HLA mismatch number (P = 0.010) were found to be associated with PTDM on day 45 (Table 1). In multivariate analysis, only age (OR:1.055, 95% CI:1.010–1.102, P = 0.017) was found significant (Table 2). The prevalence of PTDM in the first year was 15% (n = 33). Age (P = 0.046) and insulin dose used in the first week after transplantation (P = 0.010) were associated with late PTDM. The incidence of coronary artery disease was higher in the first year PTDM group (P = 0.036), but there was no significant difference in terms of graft loss.
Conclusion
BMI, which was found to be associated with PTDM diagnosis at day 45 in our study, is a modifiable risk factor and those with BMI ≥ 25 kg/m2 should be encouraged to lose weight before transplantation. Those on higher doses of insulin in the first post-transplant week are more likely to have persistent PTDM and should be followed more closely for diabetes regulation and complications.

title: #2435 The impact of resistive index on kidney allograft and transplant recipients’ survival after successful transplant renal artery stenosis stenting
authors: Natalya Belavina; Nataliya Klochkova; Lyudmila Artyukhina; Ekaterina Ivanova; Oxana Manchenko; Svetlana Kondrashkina; Iulia Barkova; Alina Nikitina; Eugene Zeltyn-Abramov; Nadiya Frolova; Oleg Kotenko; Mariana Lysenko
abstract:
Background and Aims
Transplant renal artery stenosis (TRAS) is the most common vascular complication after kidney transplantation (KTx). Duplex ultrasonography (DUS) is a primary noninvasive modality for diagnosing of TRAS. The prompt surgical repair of TRAS leads to significant regression of kidney allograft (KA) dysfunction and stabilization of blood pressure indicators. The objective of this study is to investigate the impact of resistive index (RI) after successful percutaneous transluminal stenting (PTS) on the survival of KA and recipients.
Method
62 patients after successful PTS were included into a single-center retrospective study from June 2018 to June 2024. The diagnosis of TRAS was detected by DUS. 58 patients underwent control DUS in 7–10 days after PTS, 2 patients were lost for follow-up. The peak systolic velocity (Vmax) and the minimal diastolic velocity (Vmin) were determined in the segmental arteries with a convex transducer (Vivid E90, GE, USA). The RI was calculated as [1−(Vmin ÷ Vmax)]. Results of three measurements at three places in the transplant (lower/middle/upper parts) were averaged measured RI. The combined end point was terminal transplant failure requiring the re-institution of dialysis or death from any cause. Statistical analysis was performed using the STATISTICA 13 and Online ROC Curve Calculator (Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine).
Results
A total of 56 recipients were included. In a ROC analysis, we defined a cut-off value of the RI of 0.79 (True Positive Fraction 0.82, False Positive Fraction 0.12, Fitted ROC Area 0.9). Therefore, the observation group was divided into two subgroups: (1 sgr) 45 patients with an RI < 0.79 and (2 sgr) 11 patients with an RI ≥ 0.79. The results of comparative analyses of demographic, clinical and laboratory data are presented in Table.
The study subgroups did not significantly differ in age, gender, donor's age, Diabetes Mellitus, duration of replacement therapy, mean Blood Pressure, Pulse Pressure and Pcr at the time of TRAS diagnosis. Patients with an RI of 0.79 or higher were more likely to suffer from coronary heart disease and chronic occlusive disease of the lower limb arteries. The significant differences in Pcr were detected in subgroups within 7–10 days and a month after PTS, the patients with an RI of 0.79 or higher demonstrated higher Pcr.
3 (27.3 %) patients with an RI of 0.79 or higher have lost graft function (1 patient – KTx, 2 patients – hemodialysis) and 2 patients (18.2 %) died (1 – from sepsis, 1 – from progressive heart failure). All patients with an RI of less than 0.79 are alive with preserved KA function. The results of cumulative survival are presented in the Fig. 1.
Conclusion
RI of 0.79 or higher after successful PTS in patients with TRAS, as compared with a lower RI, is associated with progressive renal dysfunction and adverse outcomes.

title: #3712 Simultaneous liver—kidney transplantation: a single-center experience in Croatia
authors: Bojana Maksimovic; Mladen Knotek; Ksenija Vučur Šimić; Zeljka Jurekovic; Bojana Šimunov; Tajana Filipec Kanizaj; Danko Mikulic; Jadranka Pavicic Saric; Maja Mijic; Stipislav Jadrijevic; Mario Laganović
abstract:
Background and Aims
Simultaneous liver and kidney transplantation (SLKT) has been established as the treatment of choice for patients with concurrent end-stage liver and end-stage kidney diseases. The objective of this study was to analyze the outcomes of SLKT in Croatia.
Method
Databases of the Eurotransplant and Clinical Hospital Merkur from December 2007 to July 2024 were retrospectively reviewed. Patient survival was analysed by the Kaplan Meier method, while multiple logistic regression was used to assess independent association of predictors (donor and recipient age at time of SLK, pretransplant dialysis vintage and liver disease diagnosis) with patient survival.
Results
From 2007–2024, a total of 34 SLKT were performed at our institution. There were 7 female patients and 27 male patients. The median age of the patients at the time of SLKT was 57.9 (interquartile range 51.2;64) years). The indications for liver transplantation were ethylic liver cirrhosis, hyperoxaluria type 1, polycystic liver disease, primary or secondary biliary cirrhosis, hepatitis B and C cirrhosis and criptogenic liver disease. The kidney transplantation indications were end-stage renal disease of various causes, glomerulonephritis, hyperoxaluria type 1, polycystic kidney disease, diabetic nephropathy and chronic kidney disease of unknown etiology The median follow-up duration for SLKT patients was 4.1 (1.4;10.5) years.
The 1-year, 5 -year and 10-year overall patient survival rates were 75.5 %, 65.4 % and 45.3 %, respectively.
In a multivariate analysis only higher donor age was associated with poorer patient survival (OR 1.073 [1.006–1.145] P = 0.0325), while other variables ( recipient age, liver disease and dialysis vintage) were not independently associated with overal patient survival.
Conclusion
Our results are in line with other major publications on SLKT patient survival. SLKT is good treatment option for selected patients with liver and end stage kidney disease.

title: #39 Incidence and outcome of BK virus-associated nephropathy in renal transplant recipients—a single centre experience over fifteen years
authors: Zi Chan; Ka Lok Chan; Wan Ning Cheung; Chi Kwan Lam; Wai Ping Law; Shuk Wa Li; Wai Lun Will Pak; Yick Hei Wong; Sze Ho Sunny Wong
abstract:
Background and Aims
BK virus infection is one of the common clinical problems encountered by transplant physicians. It was estimated that 1–10% of kidney transplant recipients develop BK Virus-Associated Nephropathy (BKVAN). Previous studies were mainly from Europe and the United States. The incidence in the Asian population is less well known. There is no standardised protocol for the treatment of BKVAN. The long-term outcome after diagnosis of BKVAN is also not well defined. This study aimed to look at the incidence and long-term outcome after BKVAN.
Method
The data from the renal unit of a regional hospital in Hong Kong was reviewed. Cases of biopsy-confirmed BKVAN were identified. Adult renal transplant recipients with renal biopsy done between 1/1/2009 and 31/12/2023 were included. Repeated renal biopsy showing BKVAN was excluded. The total number of renal transplant recipients during the specified period was identified from the Organ Registry and Transplant System. Clinical data, including patient demographics, serum creatinine and immunosuppressants used, were analysed. Death-censored graft survival was analysed by Kaplan–Meier curve.
Results
A total of 28 cases of biopsy-proven BKVAN were identified. Six were excluded due to recurrent episodes. There were 512 prevalence renal transplant cases during the study period. The incidence of BKVAN was 4.3%. Their baseline characteristics were shown in Table 1. The median time to diagnosis of BKVAN after transplant was 6.3 (3.4–55.2) months (Fig. 1). The median graft survival after diagnosis of BKVAN was 8.3 (6.7–12.3) years. The overall median graft survival for the BKVAN group and the non-BKVAN group was 11.8 (95% CI 6.1–17.5) years and 22.3 (95% CI 18.6–26.1) years, respectively (P = 0.001). (Fig. 2).
The immunosuppressants immediately before and after diagnosis of BKVAN were recorded in Table 2. All patients were on prednisolone, but with an overall slight decrease in dose after diagnosis of BKVAN (8.0 ± 5.4 mg vs 7.6 ± 5.7 mg). While majority of patients were on three immunosuppressants regimen (one of which being steroid), one patient was on two immunosuppressants regimen before the diagnosis of BKVAN. Three patients were put on two immunosuppressants regimen after the diagnosis. Two patients were given intravenous immunoglobulin.
Conclusion
The incidence of BKVAN was 4.3% among renal transplant recipients in our hospital. In patients with BKVAN, graft survival was significantly shortened compared with those who did not develop BKVAN. The treatment for BKVAN was heterogeneous. Further large-scale studies are needed to determine the optimal immunosuppressant regimen after diagnosis of BKVAN to optimise graft survival.

title: #540 Cancer screening examination can decrease the death with the functioning graft after living donor kidney transplantation
authors: Takahisa Hiramitsu; Tomoki Himeno; Yuki Shimamoto; Yuki Hasegawa; Kenta Futamura; Manabu Okada; Toshihiro Ichimori; Shunji Narumi; Yoshihiko Watarai
abstract:
Background and Aims
The immunosuppressive (IS) medication is essential for the long-term graft survival. However, death with the functioning graft (DWFG) due to cancer after kidney transplantation (KT) can be caused by administration of IS medications and can shorten the graft survival.
Method
The effectiveness of cancer screening examination after living donor KT to decrease DWFG was investigated in this single center retrospective cohort study including 1274 living donor KTs between January 2008 and December 2021. Cancer before graft failure was identified in 141 recipients. The impact of the cancer screening examination on DWFG was investigated in recipients classified into three groups; recipients with cancer detected through screening examinations, with cancer detected incidentally or symptomatically, and without cancer using time dependent Cox regression analysis.
Results

title: #818 Correlation between proteinuria and soluble IL-33 receptor levels in kidney transplant recipients
authors: Reka P Szabo; Boglárka Bujáki; Marianna Pócsi; Béla Nagy; József Balla
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney transplantation is a curative procedure for end-stage kidney disease with improving short-term outcomes over the past two decades. However, long-term outcomes including both graft and patient survival seem to lag behind. Intensive biomarker research is underway to identify additional clinical targets in an attempt to break this conundrum. We investigated the relationship between proteinuria, a known predictor of graft outcomes and several cardiac biomarkers in a subset of kidney transplant patients with congestive heart failure.
Method
The study included 16 kidney transplant patients with congestive heart failure and 37 gender and age-matched controls with kidney transplant and without heart failure. All subjects received post-transplant care between November 2023 and June 2024 in the Division of Nephrology at the University of Debrecen. Exclusion criteria included anti-rejection treatment within 6 months, acute bacterial or viral infection, malignant disease requiring hospitalization, active oncological treatment and pregnancy. Routine laboratory parameters used for correlation analysis included complete blood count, liver and kidney function tests, lipid panel, C-reactive protein, total protein and albumin, Il-6, PCT, ntProBNP, cardiac troponin T, troponin I and soluble IL-33 receptor levels.
Results
A total of 45 male patients and 8 female patients were selected for analysis. In the heart failure group, there was a close correlation between urinary protein excretion (mg/mmol) and soluble Il 33 receptor levels (pg/ml) (Pearson r = 0.666, 95% CI: 0.1112–0.9047, P = 0.0251). A significant correlation was also found between NT-proBNP (ng/L) and soluble Il-33 receptor levels (pg/ml) (Pearson:r = 0.6691, 95% CI:0.1156–0.9055, P = 0.0244). Also in the heart failure group, hemoglobin (g/L) concentration and NT-proBNP (ng/L) showed a significant correlation (P = 0.0360, 95% CI: −0.839 to −0.0479, r = 0.6173).

title: #952 Inference of donor-type proportions among the prevalent kidney-transplant population in the United States
authors: David J Joerg; Benjamin Hippen; Doris H Fuertinger
abstract:
Background and Aims
In the United States, the organ procurement & transplantation network (OPTN) provides publicly reported data on incident kidney-transplant patients, including proportions of patients receiving a living-donor (LD) or deceased-donor (DD) kidney. However, complete, longitudinal information is not available for the prevalent transplant population. Since LD and DD kidney transplantations differ both in frequency and survival prospects, it is unclear how the prevalent LD/DD distribution differs from the incident population. Here, we reconstruct the 2020 prevalent donor-type distribution by biological sex, using extrapolations of historical data on incidence and post-transplantation survival.
Method
Using annual kidney-transplant survival data from the US Renal Data System for the years 1996–2020 [1, 2], we inferred long-term post-transplantation survival curves per donor type (LD and DD) and biological sex via data fits with exponential and Gompertz-type survival functions. Together with reported annual incidence data by donor type, this enables a reconstruction of the 2020 prevalent kidney-transplant population. Post-2020 datasets were excluded because COVID-19-related changes in survival trends prevent the required extrapolation of earlier data. Results were validated by comparing donor type-pooled results to reported total prevalent counts for 2020, showing a deviation of –3.3% (or a total of –8.1k out of 245.5k) (Fig. 1a).
Results
The inferred prevalent counts for 2020 were 63.5k female patients and 90.8k male patients with a deceased-donor (DD) kidney transplant and 32.7k female patients and 50.4k male patients with a living-donor (LD) kidney transplant (Fig. 1b). This corresponds to living/deceased-donor ratios of 34% : 66% among female patients (96.2k in total) and 36% : 64% among male patients (141.2k in total).
Conclusion
Inferred donor-type proportions suggest a 1 : 2 ratio of living- and deceased-donor kidney transplant patients in the United States, largely independent of biological sex, whereas incident LD/DD ratios increased from 1 : 1.8 in 2010 to 1 : 3.5 in 2020 [2] (Fig. 1c). This reflects better graft and patient survival in LD recipients.

title: #1076 Assessing health-related quality of life in non-directed versus directed kidney donors: implications for the promotion of non-directed donation
authors: Assaf Vital; Eytan Mor; Tamar Hod
abstract:
Background and Aims
Living kidney donation has increased significantly, but little is known about the postdonation health-related quality of life (HRQoL) of non-directed donors (NDs) vs. directed donors (DDs).
Method
We thus examined the outcomes of 112 living kidney donors (82 NDs, 30 DDs).
Results
For the primary outcomes – namely, the mean physical component summary (PCS) and mental component summary (MCS) scores of the 12-item Short Form Survey (SF-12) questionnaire – scores were significantly higher for the NDs vs. the DDs (PCS: +2.69, MCS: +4.43). For secondary outcomes, NDs had shorter hospital stays (3.4 vs. 4.4 days), returned to physical activity earlier (45 vs. 60 days), exercised more before and after donation, and continued physical activity post-donation. Regression analyses revealed that donor type and white blood cell count were predictive of the PCS-12 score, and donor type was predictive of the MCS-12 score. Nondirected donation was predictive of a shorter hospital stay (by 0.78 days, p < 0.001) and the odds of having PCS-12 and MCS-12 scores above 50 were almost 10 and 16 times higher for NDs, respectively (p < 0.05).
Conclusion
These findings indicate the safety and potential benefits of promoting nondirected donation. However, careful selection processes must be maintained to prevent harm and exploitation.

title: #1523 Two cases of hyperacute rejection after AB0 incompatible kidney transplantation – unexpected antibodies
authors: Elena Rho; Anne Halpin; Lori West; Kerstin Hübel; Fabian Rössler; Jakob Nilsson; Lukas Frischknecht; Thomas Schachtner
abstract:
Background and Aims
Although ABO-incompatible (ABOi) living donor kidney transplantation is currently performed on a routine basis, it remains a procedure with a high immunologic risk requiring both immunosuppression aimed at diminishing antibody production and removal of circulating antibodies from the recipient's blood.
Method
We describe two cases of kidney transplant recipients (KTR) who experienced hyperacute antibody-mediated rejection after ABOi transplantation and further testing was performed on their sera using a novel bead-based ABO antibody assay to understand the cause of such unfortunate outcomes.
Results
Both patients were ABO-O recipients who received ABO-A grafts; neither had donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies (DSA). Both received rituximab >4 weeks and standard immunosuppression according to the Swiss ABOi protocol, starting 10–25 days before transplantation; basiliximab was used for induction at time of transplant. Immunoadsorption was performed before transplant with a nonselective Therasorb column; immunoadsorption effectiveness was analyzed by measuring the anti-A-IgG titer and anti-A-IgM titer by gel column agglutination technique. Case 1: Transplantation was performed after 17 immunoadsorption runs (prolonged due to postponed date of surgery for non-immunological reasons); post-adsorption anti-A titres were negative IgG and <1:8 IgM. After an initial diuresis, the patient became anuric within 24 hours. Biopsy histology revealed hyperacute rejection. Graft nephrectomy was performed two days post-transplant. Case 2: transplantation was performed after 11 immunoadsorption runs; post-adsorption anti-A titres were negative IgG and 1:1 IgM. After an initial diuresis urine output decreased within hours. Biopsy histology showed hyperacute rejection. Plasmapheresis was started empirically approximately 15 hours after transplant despite negative anti-A titer and no anti-HLA DSA, and treatment with high dose steroids, IVIG and eculizumab was administered. Graft nephrectomy was performed seven days post-transplant.
Analysis of the original sera with a novel single antigen bead assay for anti-A subtype-specific antibodies showed an initial drop in MFIs of IgG and IgM for both patients. However, at time of transplant, despite acceptable anti-A titers with our standard hemagglutination methods, patient 1 and 2 MFI were still 17200 and 9300, respectively for anti-A-IgG isotype antibodies (II, III and IV averaged) and 3300 and 3800 for anti-A-IgM isotype IgM (II, III and IV averaged). Analysis of sera from the days immediately after transplantation showed a rebound for these subtype-specific anti-A antibodies in Case 1, with an MFI up to 26000 (anti-A-IgG) and 5000 (anti-A-IgM). In Case 2 (where samples were drawn after plasmapheresis) the MFIs of the anti-A-II/III/IV further dropped to 2100 (IgG) and 1200 (IgM). Refer to Fig. 1 for antibody data.
Conclusion
Hyperacute AMR in these two ABO-A-incompatible kidney transplant cases was likely due to insufficient removal of anti-A antibodies. Whether this is due to insufficient removal of anti-A antibodies by the nonselective Therasorb column needs to be further investigated. These results suggest that for such an immunological high-risk procedure, a switch from titer-based diagnostics to single bead Luminex diagnostics should be considered. Of further note, transcriptome diagnostics might support the histology, but it is not yet established in ABOi graft biopsies.

title: #1874 Clinical implications of the PREVENT equations among kidney transplant recipients in Korea
authors: Soo-Young Yoon; Jeong-Yeun Lee; Yoosun Joo; Yang Gyun Kim; Ju-Young Moon; Sang-Ho Lee; Jin Sug Kim; Hyeon Seok Hwang; Kyunghwan Jeong
abstract:
Background and Aims
Multivariable equations have recently been recommended by prevention guidelines to monitor the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD). The aim of this study was to evaluate the clinical relevance of the American Heart Association's Predicting Risk of CVD Events (PREVENT) equations in Korean kidney transplant recipients.
Method
This nationwide prospective cohort study enrolled kidney transplant patients between May 2014 and December 2022. Individual CVD and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) scores were calculated for each participant. Associations between the PREVENT equation scores and the risk of mortality, cardiovascular events, and renal allograft loss were assessed using Cox regression analysis.
Results
A total of 1,282 kidney transplant recipients were included in the analysis, with a mean CVD risk score of 7.05 and a mean ASCVD risk score of 3.95. Cox regression analysis showed that the adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for mortality were 1.10 (95% CI: 1.06–1.13) and 1.17 (95% CI: 1.11–1.24) for the CVD and ASCVD risk scores, respectively. For cardiovascular events, the adjusted HRs were 1.07 (95% CI: 1.05–1.10) and 1.14 (95% CI: 1.09–1.19) for the CVD and ASCVD risk scores, respectively. However, no statistically significant associations were found between either risk score and the risk of graft loss.
Conclusion
The PREVENT equation scores were significantly associated with composite clinical outcomes, including mortality and cardiovascular events, but did not predict renal allograft loss in Korean kidney transplant recipients. Further research incorporating transplant-specific factors such as rejection episodes is needed to improve risk prediction in this population.

title: #2748 Using machine learning to develop a kidney DQI for predicting transplant outcomes within the first three months post-procedure
authors: Carolina Salgado; Felipe Vera Cid; Francisca Gonzalez-Cohens; Fernando Gonzalez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Optimizing graft allocation is a major challenge in kidney transplantation, aiming to maximize graft survival, recipient survival, and dialysis-free survival. While Donor Quality Indices (DQIs) are used globally, Chile lacks its own. This study explored whether a DQI could be developed using existing transplant data and predictive models for clinical outcomes.
Method
We analyzed 831 kidney transplants (1989–2020) from three centers. The dataset included 14 donor, 7 transplant, and 60 recipient features. Predictions with Machine Learning (ML) targeted:
Clustering models were used to identify transplant risk groups, and predictions were combined to develop a DQI reviewed by clinical staff for validation using a survey.
Results
DGF and SC predictions aligned with clinical expectations but had lower performance metrics, while APC and MAP predictions were accurate but less interpretable. Clustering analysis identified four risk groups varying in DGF and the APC categorization. A DQI was constructed using a risk classification based on DGF and APC predictions, as preferred by potential users.
Conclusion
Despite data limitations, predictions for APC and MAP were accurate, whereas DGF predictions were less reliable but clinically interpretable. The proposed DQI balances performance and transparency, combining DGF and APC predictions to guide donor evaluation. Further refinement and higher-quality data are essential for improving DGF predictions and advancing DQI implementation to optimize transplant outcomes. ML models certainly can be improved as feeding clinical data allows that.

title: #2774 Management of post-trasplant renal graft artery stenosis and outcomes: a single-center experience
authors: Sara Aldana Barceló; Javier Azores Moreno; Maria Ovidia Lopez Oliva; Elena Gonzalez; Cristina Fuentes Fernández; Ruth Martínez Galindo; Lina León; Carlos Jiménez Martín
abstract:
Background and Aims
Transplant renal artery stenosis (TRAS) is a well-recognized complication post-kidney transplantation that can compromise graft function and patient outcomes. The optimal management approach, particularly the choice between balloon angioplasty and stent placement, remains controversial. We present an analysis of post-transplant renal graft artery stenosis cases managed with endovascular treatment at our center from 2017 to 2024, focusing on procedural outcomes and complications.
Method
A retrospective review was conducted of kidney transplant recipients treated for TRAS in our center between 2017 and 2024. Patient demographics, location of stenosis, procedural complications, re-stenosis rates and clinical outcomes were reviewed.
Results
A total of 21 patients (71.43% male, 28.57% female) underwent 24 angiographic procedures during this period, with a prevalence in our cohort being 5.9%. The median age was 50.49 years. TRAS was predominantly located at the anastomotic site (66.7%). The median time from transplantation to intervention was 175 days, ranging from 46 to 1852 days. Balloon angioplasty was performed in 95.8% of cases (n = 23), with stent placement reserved for one case of anastomotic rupture during the procedure.
Post-procedure, significant clinical and biochemical improvements were observed. The mean reduction in antihypertensive medications was 0.75 (median: 1), with a mean pre-intervention requirement of 2.79 medications (median: 3). This reduction in the need for antihypertensive drugs was statistically significant. Serum creatinine decreased at least by ≥0.3 mg/dL at one month in 67% of cases, with this improvement in renal function also being statistically significant (P < 0.05).
Complications were observed in 20.8% of cases, with 8.3% (n = 2) being minor (one hematoma, one pseudoaneurysm) and 12.5% (n = 3) major. Severe complications included one case of intrarenal dissection resulting in 10% parenchymal hypoperfusion, one arterial laceration necessitating graft nephrectomy, and one anastomotic rupture requiring stent placement.
During follow-up, significant re-stenosis necessitating reintervention occurred in 3 patients (14.28%). These findings are consistent with reported rates in the literature. As of the latest follow-up, 87.5% of grafts remained functional.
Conclusion
Balloon angioplasty without stent placement has been shown to be an effective approach for managing TRAS, leading to significant improvements in hypertension control and graft function. This procedure can be performed in the early post-transplant period and offers the added advantage of avoiding stent placement, thereby eliminating the need for antiplatelet therapy. While effective, the procedure is not without the risk of serious complications. These findings contribute to the ongoing effort to optimize care for transplant recipients with vascular complications.

Background and Aims
Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is a common cause of kidney disease. Its primary form is rare, but recurrence in kidney transplantation (KT) occurs in 30–60%, compromising short-term graft survival. Despite advances in understanding and treatment, KT in this population remains a challenge. Our study aims to describe the characteristics of patients with FSGS recurrence in kidney transplantation.
Method
Retrospective study of KT patients with recurrent FSGS at our centre since 1982. Clinical, analytical, and histological data, as well as transplant characteristics, were collected.
Results
A total of 117 FSGS patients with KT were identified: 20.5% with secondary forms, 6.8% genetic, and 38.5% primary. 40 patients were unclassifiable. Among the primary cases, 11 recurrences (24.4%) were observed, with a mean age at disease onset of 26 ± 18 years, proteinuria of 11 ± 2.7g/day, and albuminemia of 16.6 ± 3.9 g/L. At KT, 73% had nephrotic syndrome. Two patients received living donor KT, and 9 deceased donor KT. The median time to recurrence was 6.2 ± 8 months. 90% presented nephrotic-range proteinuria, 36% with nephrotic syndrome. 3 patients received plasmapheresis, 3 rituximab, and 3 methylprednisolone. All were on ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and calcineurin inhibitor levels were increased.
3 patients achieved complete remission, 2 partial remission and 5 had no response, with graft loss and reinitiation of hemodialysis. 2 patients received a second KT, with one recurrence.
Patients with graft loss had higher pre-transplant proteinuria (9.8 vs 6.2 g/day) and received older grafts (58.2 vs 35.8 years), all from deceased donors. They presented delayed graft function more frequently (60% vs 0%, P = 0.061), earlier recurrence (71 vs 283 days), along with higher proteinuria at diagnosis (9.2 vs 6.6 g/day) and more acute rejection (60% vs 17%). Recurrence within 3 months was associated with earlier disease onset (20 vs 34 years) and more severe hypoalbuminemia (15 vs 20 g/L, P = 0.065).
Conclusion
According to our results, patients with FSGS diagnosed at an earlier age, with more severe hypoalbuminemia, who receive a KT from older donors, with higher proteinuria at the time of transplantation, would benefit from more rigorous post-transplant monitoring to detect and address early recurrence.

title: #3517 “That's just part of having a transplant, that's the price you pay” perceived barriers and facilitators of immunosuppressant medication adherence among transplant recipients: a qualitative study
authors: Lisa Mellon; Cheyenne Downey; Aisling Walsh; Frank Doyle; Peter J Conlon; Conall O'seaghdha
abstract:
Background and Aims
Adherence to immunosuppressant medication is a central part of treatment for individuals living with a solid organ transplant to support the long-term function of their transplant. However, the rate of non-adherence is substantial, estimated as 1 in 5 patients. Reasons for non-adherence are multi-dimensional and can be intentional or non-intentional; multi-component interventions to support good immunosuppressant medication adherence have demonstrated limited effectiveness, and challenges to developing interventions tailored to individual patient need still exist. This study explored patient perceived challenges of adhering to the immunosuppressant regimen. Patients also identified strategies that support good adherence to immunosuppressant medication.
Method
Semi-structured interviews were held with heart, lung, liver and kidney transplant recipients (n = 16) who were taking prescribed immunosuppressant medication for a minimum of 6 months post-transplant. Inductive thematic analysis was conducted with themes and subthemes identified.
Results
Three major themes were identified, with themes consistently occurring across all transplant types: (1) The practicalities of adhering to medication, including in-hospital medication training, implementing a routine, managing domestic responsibilities and social situations, and coping with side effects; (2) the psychological processes that affect medication adherence, including lack of post-transplant psychological support, the importance of peer support from fellow transplant recipients, and reflecting on the health benefits given by transplantation, and (3) recommended strategies and advice for good adherence to immunosuppressant medication for newly transplanted patients, including interactive mobile apps, mobile phone alarms, visual reminders and medication pillboxes.
Conclusion
Patient-reported barriers and facilitators to good medication adherence highlight the complexities of adherence with immunosuppressant medication consistent across all organ transplant types, with a number of factors related to intentional and unintentional non-adherence identified. Findings provide a framework to inform the development of future complex interventions to improve adherence to immunosuppressant medication.

title: #2821 Outcome of simultaneous pancreas-kidney transplant from a tertiary care center in India
authors: George Kurian; Ramachandran N Menon; Sudhindran S; Rajesh R Nair; Anil Mathew; Zachariah Paul; Anjana Gopal
abstract:
Background and Aims
Simultaneous simultaneous pancreas-kidney (SPK) transplantation is one of the treatment options for type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) patients with chronic kidney disease stage 5. The SPKT outcomes are reported to be excellent with a 5 year patient, kidney and pancreas graft survival of 88%, 77% and 69% respectively. Here, we present data regarding outcome of the SPKT done at our institution.
Method
We studied patients who underwent SPKT in our institution. 13 T1DM patients who were CKD-5 underwent SPKT from 2014 to 2022. Their graft function and complications were analysed.
Results
A total of 13 patients were studied. 46 % were males and 54% were females. Mean age at diagnosis was 11 ± 4 years. Mean age at transplantation was 31 ± 6 years. Induction was with Basiliximab in 1 patient, Alemtuzumab in 6 patients and ATG in 6 patients. Maintenance immunosuppression was tacrolimus and mycophenolate in 9 patients; and, tacrolimus, mycophenolate and everolimus in 2 patients. Mean duration of hospital stay was 28 ± 18 days. Mean graft kidney function at 1 month was 1.38 ± 0.48 mg/dl. Mean graft kidney function at 6 months was 1.1 ± 0.47 mg/dl. At 1 year, one patient had severe renal graft dysfunction requiring HD. Among the other 10 patients who completed one year, mean kidney graft function at 1 year was 1.25 ± 0.23 mg/dl. Three (23%) patients had renal allograft loss with need for initiation of HD after 30, 21 and 6 months. Two patients with renal allograft loss required insulin after 19 and 25 months. Three (23%) patients had delayed graft function. Five (41.7%) patients had renal allograft rejection at 1 month. Among the five, three had another episode of rejection at 17, 11 and 4 months. Three (23%) patients had suspected pancreatic graft rejection at POD 13, 13 and 14, which resolved with intravenous steroids. Eight (66.6%) patients had infections in the first year following transplant which included urosepsis, LRTI, tuberculosis, varicella, CMV, cellulitis, periodontal abscess, dental caries and esophagial candidiasis. Seven (58.3%) had surgical complications including pseudo aneurysm of graft pancreas, urinoma, perinephric hematoma, abdominal bleed and DIC, jejujno-jejunal anastomotic site bleed, kinked renal vein requiring re-exploration, graft pancreas fat necrosis with impending GB rupture and peritonitis, and splenic vein thrombosis requiring re-exploration. Other complications noted were incisional hernia, subacute intestinal obstruction, bilateral femoral head avascular necrosis and acute myeloid leukemia.
Conclusion
The graft survival and outcomes in our institution is comparable to that of international standards. Surgical complications were noted to be higher compared to renal transplantation. SPK remains to be treatment of choice in T1DM patients with ESRD.

title: #3050 Post transplant diarrhoea in ABO-incompatible kidney transplant—a nemesis for patient and nephrologist
authors: Abhishek Kumar
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diarrhoea is a frequent complication affecting kidney transplant recipients. The incidence of diarrhea is approximately 11.5 % at 1 year and 22.6 % at 3 years post transplant [1]. This becomes a nemesis for patients because of associated fatigue, weight loss, increased hospitalization and negative impact on quality of life and graft survival [2]. Even for the treating transplant physician the situation is tricky because diarrhea can be due to both—infections and immunosuppressive drugs. Hence establishing an accurate diagnosis is of utmost importance in managing such patients.
Method
We report a case of 44 year old male who underwent live related ABO incompatible kidney transplant (Recipient O-positive , Donor A-positive) in December 2020. He had a good graft function with triple drug immunosuppression until February 2024 when he presented to our out patient department with 6 months history of diarrhoea, generalized weakness and significant weight loss (10 kgs). He had consulted some local physicians but there was no relief.
Patient was admitted and routine investigations were done. Stool was sent for routine microscopy and multiplex Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) (Biofire™ Gastrointestinal Panel). Serum Creatinine was 1.3 mg/dl which was comparable to his previous value of 1.2 mg/dl. Liver functions and complete blood counts were within normal limits. Routine examination of stool showed cyst of giardia lamblia. Cytomegalo Virus (CMV) was ruled out as the DNA PCR was negative.
Results
Patient was managed with Intravenous fluids along with antibiotics and metronidazole. His mycophenolate sodium was reduced to 360 mg once a day from previous dose of 360 mg thrice a day. Tacrolimus was continued at previous dose of 1.5 mg twice a day. Steroid dose was increased to 10 mg daily from previous 5 mg daily. Tablet Nitazoxanide 500 mg twice a day was added. With these adjustments patient's general condition improved and he was symptomatically better. Later his Stool for Biofire report showed presence of Noro Virus , Giardia Lamblia , Entero Pathogenic Escherichia Coli (EPEC) and Entero Aggregative Escherichia Coli (EAEC). (Fig. 1).
This further supported our decision of reducing immunosuppression by cutting down dose of mycophenolate to one-third and starting antibiotics. In his follow-up visit after 15 days patient had gained 5 kg of weight and his symptoms had completely resolved.
Conclusion
This case highlights the need to finely balance the immunosuppression in post transplant patients especially ABO-incompatible kidney transplant recipients where transplant physicians tend to over immunosuppress the patients. This can sometime lead to viral infections like Noro virus , CMV or other serious infections. This case reinforces the well known fact that Noro Virus is a common cause of post transplant diarrhea [3].

title: #3320 Review of vascular access in kidney transplant recipients: an overlooked topic. experience of a non-transplant hospital
authors: Gabriel Ledesma Sánchez; Sílvia Caldés Ruisánchez; María Covadonga Hevia Ojanguren; Gilda Carreño Cornejo; Verónica Ruth Mercado Valdivia; Raquel Diaz Mancebo; Rocío Echarri Carrillo; Ángel Gallegos Villalobos; Yolanda Hernández Hernández; Yesika María Amezquita Orjuela; Antonio Cirugeda García
abstract:
Background and Aims
A significant number of patients undergo kidney transplantation from hemodialysis (HD) with an arteriovenous fistula (AVF). There is evidence of AVF-related cardiotoxicity, particularly in high-flow fistulas, due to increased cardiac mass. However, its impact on cardiovascular events, mortality, or renal graft function remains unclear. There is no consensus on AVF management after transplantation, leading to high variability in clinical practice among centers. Factors such as cardiac status, graft prognosis, and future dialysis and vascular access options are crucial when considering AVF closure. This study aims to review vascular access management in the kidney transplant outpatient clinic at Hospital Infanta Sofía.
Method
We conducted a descriptive cross-sectional observational study including 71 kidney transplant recipients followed in a non-transplant center. The vascular access history was reviewed, and a Doppler ultrasound was performed on functioning AVFs.
Results
Among the 71 patients, 35 came from HD (49%), 29 from peritoneal dialysis (41%), and 7 underwent preemptive transplantation (10%). Of the HD patients, 8 had a tunneled catheter (23%), and 27 had an AVF (77%). At the time of the study, 21 AVFs were non-functioning (78%), and 6 were functioning (22%). Among the non-functioning AVFs, 12 cases (57%) were due to spontaneous thrombosis, while 9 cases (43%) resulted from surgical closure, performed on average 6 years post-transplant, mainly due to aneurysms (6 cases, 67%). Among the functioning AVFs, all were native, with a mean arterial flow (Qa) of 1634 ml/min. In 3 cases (50%), Qa exceeded 1500 ml/min, with one case reaching 3000 ml/min. This patient was the only one who required hospitalization for heart failure (HF) after transplantation. All patients with a functioning AVF had preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), though two exhibited mild left ventricular hypertrophy.
Conclusion
The management of AVFs in kidney transplant recipients is a subject of debate, especially when these fistulas remain functional post-transplant. In this study, a high rate of spontaneous thrombosis (57%) and a significant prevalence of surgical closure due to aneurysms (43%) was observed. These findings are consistent with previous studies suggesting that most AVFs do not remain functional in the long term, but their management remains an area of clinical uncertainty.
The presence of a functional AVF, especially with high arterial flows, can have significant implications for the patient's cardiovascular health. In fact, in our study, the only patient who was hospitalized due to heart failure had an elevated Qa of 3000 ml/min. This is consistent with the literature, which has documented that high-flow AVFs can induce a hemodynamic burden on the cardiovascular system, contributing to the development of heart failure.
It is important to note that the lack of consensus regarding the management of functional AVFs post-kidney transplantation has led to a heterogeneous practice across centers. Some prefer to close AVFs preventively, while others take a more conservative approach, intervening only when signs of heart failure or renal graft dysfunction appear. The decision to close or not close the AVF should consider multiple factors, such as cardiovascular status, graft function, and the potential future need for vascular access for dialysis.

title: #3885 Expanding pre-implantation renal biopsy criteria for expanded criteria donors
authors: José Manuel Amaro; Florentino Villanego; Arshdeep Singh; Luis Alberto Vigara; Marta Alonso Mozo; Blanca Serrano Muñoz; Marina Arnaiz Pérez; Cristhian David Orellana Chávez; Teresa García Álvarez; Auxiliadora Mazuecos
abstract:
Background and Aims
The progressive increase in the number of patients on the kidney transplant (KT) waiting list has led to a growing use of expanded criteria donors (ECD), raising concerns about their quality. Traditionally, pre-implantation biopsy has been performed to adequately assess these donors. However, this approach may sometimes result in discarding potentially viable kidneys due to limitations in interpretation, prompting a reconsideration of biopsy protocols in various centers.
Method
We conducted a retrospective cohort study of KT recipients from ECDs at our center between February 2021 and October 2024, in which pre-implantation biopsies were performed on grafts. The study period was divided into two phases:
Phase 1: ECD biopsy according to the classical definition: age >60 years or age >50 years with at least two of the following characteristics: high blood pressure, serum creatinine (Cr) ≥1.5 mg/dL, and stroke as the cause of death.
Phase 2: ECD biopsy only if the donor was older than 70 years, had diabetes mellitus (DM), or if any condition raised doubts about the organ's viability.
We compared the percentage of grafts discarded due to biopsy results and analyzed clinical and demographic variables of donors and recipients, biopsy scores, and histological compartment scoring. Renal function at three months post-transplant (maximum follow-up time for the last included patient) and graft losses due to surgical complications were evaluated. Pre-implantation biopsies were processed using PrestoChill, excluding biopsies from other centers.
Results
In the first phase, 309 KTs were performed, including 146 pre-transplant biopsies. In the second phase, 60 KTs were performed, with 15 biopsies. The pre-implantation graft discard rate was similar between phases (17.6% vs. 20.5%; P = 0.786).
The mean donor age was slightly higher in the second phase: 66.1 (7.2) years vs. 69.8 (7.6) years; P = 0.063. Additionally, there were more donors with hypertension (73.3% vs. 35.4%; P = 0.012) and diabetes (46.7% vs. 10.4%; P = 0.001) in phase 2. Regarding histological variables, the total biopsy score was significantly higher in the second phase: 3 [3;3.75] points vs. 2 [2;3] points; P = 0.03.
Recipient age was similar between groups: 63 [56.5; 70] years vs. 66 [60; 77] years; P = 0.581. The first group consisted mostly of men (70.5% vs. 33.3%; P = 0.005), and the percentage of re-transplanted patients was similar between phases (20.5% vs. 27.8%; P = 0.686).
Time on renal replacement therapy (RRT) was shorter in the second phase, though not significantly different: 9 [4.5; 24] months vs. 14 [7.5; 24] months; P = 0.321. However, a higher percentage of preemptive transplants was observed in phase 2 (40% vs. 11.4%; P = 0.036). The re-transplantation rate was similar between groups (79.5% vs. 72.2%; P = 0.686).
Graft losses due to surgical complications within the first 30 days post-transplant were rare and slightly higher in the second group, though not significantly different (2.9% vs. 0%; P = 0.507).
Among the remaining grafts, good renal function was observed in the first months post-KT, with no differences between phases at three months. Serum creatinine levels (1.60 [1.29;1.95] mg/dL vs. 1.84 [1.38;2.1] mg/dL) and estimated glomerular filtration rate (41.9 (17.5) mL/min vs. 35.1 (12.5) mL/min) were similar between groups (P = 0.489 and P = 0.150, respectively). There were also no significant differences in albumin/creatinine ratio at three months post-transplant: 81.5 [29.9; 195.6] mg/g vs. 164 [49;236] mg/g (P = 0.553).
Conclusion
Expanding the criteria for performing pre-implantation biopsies on ECD kidney grafts has allowed an increase in the number of effective donors, improving access to KT. Early graft loss due to surgical complications was rare despite the older age and higher comorbidities of the donors. It remains essential to continue using assessment tools and evaluating outcomes in this type of donor population.

Time on renal replacement therapy (RRT) was shorter in the second phase, though not significantly different: 9 [4.5; 24] months vs. 14 [7.5; 24] months; P = 0.321. title: #1475 A Pharmacogenetic and body weight-informed predictive model for tacrolimus dosing in Taiwanese kidney transplant recipients
authors: I-Ru Chen; Ting-Yuan Liu; Fuu-Jen Tsai; Chiu-Ching Huang; Ping-Chin Lai; Huey-Liang Kuo; Chang-Cheng Jiang; Chi-Ping Huang; Yu-Cyuan Hong; Hsing- Fang Lu; Yu-Chia Chen; Hsing-Yu Hsu
abstract:
Background and Aims
Tacrolimus is a key immunosuppressant in kidney transplantation, with a recommended starting dose of 0.1–0.15 mg/kg. Maintaining optimal tacrolimus levels is crucial, as excessive levels increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and infection, while insufficient levels heighten rejection risk. Dose variability is influenced by multiple factors, underscoring the need for personalized precision medicine. In clinical practice, adherence to Western dosing guidelines has led to a high incidence of tacrolimus levels exceeding 10 ng/mL during hospitalization post-transplant. Given ethnic differences in drug metabolism, particularly CYP3A5 polymorphisms, this study aims to establish an appropriate tacrolimus starting dose for Taiwanese kidney transplant recipients.
Method
From August 2018 to December 2023, all kidney transplant recipients at our hospital were included, excluding cases of thrombotic microangiopathy, ABO-incompatible transplants, donation after circulatory death, donor-specific antibody positivity, or Everolimus use within one year. All patients received an initial tacrolimus dose of 0.1–0.15 mg/kg with antithymocyte globulin induction therapy, along with corticosteroids and mycophenolate mofetil as standard immunosuppressive agents. Tacrolimus trough levels were monitored during hospitalization, documenting cases where levels exceeded 10 ng/mL and required dose reduction. The target trough level (6–10 ng/mL) was maintained throughout the first postoperative year, with the annual tacrolimus dose normalized to body weight (mg/kg). Patients were categorized based on CYP3A5 pharmacogenetic polymorphisms into normal, intermediate, and poor metabolizers. The one-year average tacrolimus dose (mg/kg) among pharmacogenetic groups was compared using the Kruskal-Wallis test, with results reported as median [25th, 75th percentiles]. A series of univariate linear regression analyses firstly screened the potential association of patient characteristics, including continuous variables (age, body weight, BMI, dialysis duration) and categorical variables (weight status and pharmacogenetic classification). Since body weight and pharmacogenetic classification were significantly associated with tacrolimus dosing, a multivariable linear regression model was developed to predict the required tacrolimus dose.
Results
A total of 56 kidney transplant recipients were included in the study, among whom 36 patients (64.2%) required tacrolimus dose reduction during hospitalization due to supratherapeutic levels. Pharmacogenetic testing revealed that 7 patients were CYP3A5 normal metabolizers, 20 were intermediate metabolizers, and 29 were poor metabolizers. The one-year average tacrolimus dose (mg/kg) was significantly lower in the poor metabolizers (0.04 [0.03, 0.06] mg/kg) than that in the normal (0.10 [0.09, 0.13] mg/kg) and intermediate metabolizers (0.10 [0.08, 0.11] mg/kg). The multivariable analysis showed that body weight (regression coefficient [B] = −0.0012, 95% CI: −0.0017 to −0.0007) and dichotomous pharmacogenetic classification (B = −0.0444, 95% CI: −0.0603 to −0.0285), with a variance explained by 50.3%. The derived predicted tacrolimus dose (mg/kg) = 0.181–0.0012 × body weight –0.0444 × gene status; where gene status: 1 = poor metabolizer, 0 = normal/intermediate metabolizer.
Conclusion
This study presents the first predictive model for tacrolimus starting dose in Taiwanese kidney transplant recipients, demonstrating that CYP3A5 polymorphisms significantly impact dose requirements, with poor metabolizers requiring lower doses. The proposed dosing formula enables personalized tacrolimus initiation, optimizing immunosuppressive therapy while minimizing toxicity and rejection risks. Despite the limitation of a small sample size, this preliminary study underscores the need for larger-scale validation and serves as a valuable reference for individualized tacrolimus dosing, advancing precision medicine in transplantation.

title: #1971 Cat scratch disease in a kidney transplant recipient: the role of steroids in persistent systemic symptoms
authors: Joelle Yaman; Hiba Azar; Elie Haddad; Toufic Lteif
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cat scratch disease is caused by a bacterial infection due to Bartonella henselae and typically follows a self-limiting course in immunocompetent patients. However, its presentation and progression can be more severe in kidney transplant recipients. We present a case of a 21-year-old patient who experienced a prolonged course of the disease, despite receiving appropriate therapy, with significant improvement only after the initiation of steroid treatment.
Method
This young patient received a kidney transplant from his father at age 15 after being on peritoneal dialysis for two years due to genetically confirmed atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) as the underlying nephropathy. He was given eculizumab prophylaxis for the first six months post-transplant, and his immunosuppressive regimen included mycophenolate mofetil and tacrolimus. The post-transplant course was uneventful, with no significant infectious events, and his baseline creatinine was stable at 1.4 mg/dL. The patient presented to the emergency room with a high-grade fever that had been ongoing for five days, accompanied only by headache and fatigue. His physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests revealed elevated creatinine (2.77 mg/dL), pancytopenia (Hb 9.2 g/dL, WBC 2400/mm³, ANC 1490/mm3, platelets 92,000/mm³), and elevated C-reactive protein (CRP 54 mg/L). Given his history of aHUS, further investigations were conducted to rule out a relapse. The anemia was microcytic, regenerative, and non-hemolytic, with an LDH of 297 U/L, normal haptoglobin (0.9 g/L), and no schistocytes on the peripheral smear. The Coombs test was negative. Extensive workup included multiple blood and urine cultures, bone marrow biopsy for pathology and culture, PCR testing for CMV, BK virus, EBV, SARS-CoV-2, and influenza, as well as Wright, Widal, and parvovirus B19 serologies, all of which yielded negative results. Imaging studies, including a chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound, were unremarkable. Over the next few days, the fever persisted, and inflammatory markers worsened (CRP 199 mg/L), while creatinine levels remained elevated at 2.7 mg/dL. A CT scan revealed no significant findings, except for a lymph node in the right axillary region, measuring 28×19 mm. An axillary lymph node biopsy was performed, revealing significant vascular proliferation consistent with bacillary angiomatosis.
Results
This finding was diagnostic of cat scratch disease. At that point, the patient recalled a minor scratch from his cat, was barely visible on physical exam upon admission. He received a single dose of azithromycin, followed by a 4 day course of gentamicin and continuous treatment with doxycycline. However, one week later, the fever persisted at 40°C, and there was no improvement in the inflammatory markers. Prednisone at a dose of 20 mg was then started. Within 48 hours, the patient became afebrile, with a notable reduction in CRP from 171 to 73 mg/L and a decrease in creatinine from 2.3 to 1.7 mg/dL. The patient was discharged with a continued course of doxycycline and corticosteroids for a total of 4 weeks.
Conclusion
The use of corticosteroids in cat scratch disease is controversial and while used in ocular and neurological involvement, their role in treating systemic symptoms is less clear. In this case, the patient continued to experience fever despite appropriate antibiotic therapy and improved only after the initiation of steroids. Therefore, corticosteroids may have a role in reducing inflammatory reactions following infection and should be considered in the treatment of cat scratch disease with severe systemic manifestations in kidney transplant patients.

title: #2431 Arterial hypertension and markers of cardiovascular complications after kidney transplantation
authors: Michaela Javorkova; Zuzana Žilinská; Martin Chrastina; Juraj Maris; Jana Otavkova; Katarína Štefančíková; Marcela Cvoligova; Martina Hivková
abstract:
Background and Aims
Arterial hypertension (AH) represents the main cause of cardiovascular (CV) morbidity and mortality in the period after kidney transplantation (KT). It is an independent risk factor for atherosclerosis and related CV complications including concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, coronary artery disease and overall CV mortality. Inadequate hypertension control in the grafts leads to glomerulosclerosis, intraglomerular hypertension, proteinuria and it is a non-immunological cause of progressive graft dysfunction. KT recipients exhibit varying blood pressure (BP) measured at home, in the doctor's office and through systematic BP monitoring methods including ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM).
Method
We present prospective study of CV risk factors and ABPM in cohort of patients (n = 50) transplanted from deceased (80%) and living donors (20%) during the period from January 2022 to February 2024. Follow up was 12 months after KT.
Results
Prior to KT 92% of patients were hypertensive, which decreased to 86% within the 1. year post-KT. Positive trends were noted in the prevalence of abnormal AH phenotypes with non-dippers and reverse dippers reduced by 8% and 4%, respectively, and normal dipping pattern restored in 12% of patients by the end of the 1. year. There was a marked decrease (35%) in the number of AH medications required, particularly in patients on triple and more AH regimens. The incidence of acute coronary syndrome within the 1. year post-KT was 8%, including STEMI, NSTEMI and unstable angina pectoris, CV events such as paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (6%), hypertensive emergencies (6%) and strokes (4%) were recorded. Graft loss occurred in 6% of patients, mortality was 6% (COVID-19, stroke, MODS). Additional findings included improvements in eGF (P = 0.022) and proteinuria (P = 0.304) comparing results from 3rd month post-KT and 12th month post-KT, and improvements in anaemia (P = 0.00000001), hyperuricemia (P = 0.024) and hyperparathyroidism (P = 0.00002) comparing results prior to KT and from 12th month post-KT.
Conclusion
KT significantly improves BP control, metabolic profiles and echocardiographic findings in the 1. year. Long-term strategies to minimize CV risk should include maintaining BP ˂140 mmHg, early intervention for dyslipidaemia and glucose metabolism disorders, obesity prevention and individualized immunosuppressive therapy.

title: #2895 Clinical characteristics and outcome of superficial fungal infection in kidney transplant recipients
authors: Wejden Ltaief; Meriem Ben Salem; Yosra Soua; Manel Ben Salah; Nouha Ben Mahmoud; Sirine Bchir; Ahmed Letaief; Mouna Hamouda; Habib Skhiri
abstract:
Background and Aims
Superficial fungal infections (SFIs) frequently affect kidney transplant recipients as a result of immunosuppressive therapy and related risk factors. Although these infections are generally mild, they can significantly impact quality of life and may indicate underlying immune system vulnerabilities. This study aimed to investigate the clinical presentation, treatment approaches and outcomes of SFIs in individuals who have undergone kidney transplantation.
Method
This study prospectively analysed 139 kidney transplant recipients screened for superficial fungal infections at the Fattouma Bourguiba University Hospital between December 2023 and December 2024.
Results
Among 139 kidney transplant recipients analyzed, 23 (16.5%) were diagnosed with superficial fungal infections (SFIs). The most frequent conditions were pityriasis versicolor (7.2%) and onychomycosis (7.2%), collectively affecting 20 patients. These were followed by dermatophytosis (1.4%) and a case of rhinosinus mucormycosis complicated by ethmoiditis and sphenoiditis (0.7%). The infections were primarily caused by dermatophyte species and Malassezia. Commonly affected sites included the skin, nails, and mucosal surfaces, with specific localization to the abdomen, back, neck, toes, nasal cavity, and rhinosinus. The median time from kidney transplantation to the onset of SFI was 82 months. Treatment with topical or systemic antifungal agents achieved a success rate of 91.3% (21/23), with no recurrence. The mucormycosis case required antifungal therapy with amphotericin B and surgical intervention (ethmoidectomy and sphenoidectomy), both of which were successful. No progression to systemic fungal infections was observed.
Conclusion
In kidney transplant recipients, SFI is a significant but treatable complication. Early detection and targeted treatment are crucial to ensure favorable outcomes. Preventive measures, including regular screening and addressing modifiable risk factors, could further reduce the burden of these infections.
