title: #3689 Complication of self-catheterization in a kidney transplant recipient: psoas abscess
authors: Ilhem Ben Othman; Mohamed Mongi Bacha; Hajer Rzig; Zran Najla; Mondher Ounissi; Amine Hermi; Riadh Ben Slama; Hafedh Hedri; Nada Sellami; Ezzedine Abderrahim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Psoas abscesses are rare but serious complications in kidney transplant recipients, potentially developing at any time post-transplant. Their nonspecific symptoms often overlap with other abdominal conditions, leading to delayed diagnosis and treatment.
Method
We report an unusual case of a psoas abscess in a renal transplant recipient associate to recurrent UTIs and frequent self-catheterizations, which increased the risk of traumatic inoculation. Diagnosis was delayed by 15 days before treatment began.
Results
A 20-year-old male underwent a living donor kidney transplant for end-stage renal disease due to posterior urethral valves and bilateral vesico-ureteral reflux. Despite 10 UTI episodes over 15 years, his graft function remained stable. At 18 years post- transplant, he presented with fever, fatigue, right flank pain, and restricted hip mobility lasting two weeks. Clinical examination revealed fever, graft tenderness, and signs of psoitis. Laboratory tests showed anaemia, elevated white blood cells, and increased CRP, with sterile blood and urine cultures. CT and MRI revealed a right psoas abscess (66 × 48 × 42 mm), displacing the graft. A failed CT-guided drainage attempt was followed by six weeks of empirical antibiotic therapy. The abscess showed near-complete resolution on follow-up imaging, and no relapse occurred in the three-month follow-up.
Conclusion
Psoas abscesses in kidney transplant recipients can be linked to gastro-intestinal, genito urinary issues, or catheter infections. In this case, self-catheterization likely contributed to the abscess. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial for favourable outcomes.

title: #55 The role of integrin a3ß1 in the development of morphological changes in renal tissue in patients with diabetic nephropathy
authors: Tatyana S Ryabova; Irina A Rakityanskaya
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is a common microvascular complication and a major cause of renal failure in patients with diabetes mellitus. DKD is a type of kidney disease that harms the glomerular filtration barrier. This barrier is made up of three parts: fenestrated endothelial cells, the glomerular basement membrane, and podocytes. Progression of DKD affects podocyte structure and leads to foot process effacement. Podocyte damage and loss plays a major role in the development and final progression of DKD. Podocytes are terminally differentiated cells, which is why their loss is a key factor contributing to the progression of DKD. The main podocyte receptor involved in attachment to the GBM is the alpha3beta1 integrin. Loss or reduction of α3β1 integrin can lead to detachment of podocytes from the glomerular basement membrane (GBM). In the absence of α3β1, disorganization of the GBM occurs.
The aim of the study is to investigate the role of alpha3beta1 integrin expression in renal tissue in patients with type 2 diabetes with different morphological classes of diabetic nephropathy (DN) and to assess its impact on the development and progression of histological changes in renal tissue.
Method
The study included 50 patients with type 2 diabetes complicated by diabetic nephropathy. The average age was 66.58 ± 3.27 years. There were 35 women and 14 men. The disease duration in patients with diabetes was 17.70 ± 0.35 years. The duration of DN from the detection of microalbuminuria to the morphological examination of the renal tissue and diagnosis was 1.65 ± 0.34 years. According to light microscopy, class IIa was detected in 12 patients, class IIb in 14 patients, class III in 19 patients, and class IV in 5 patients. According to the results of light microscopy, no signs of glomerulonephritis were found in any of the patients. In addition to light microscopy, the expression of integrin alpha3beta1 in the GBM and mesangial cells was determined in all patients.
Results
It was shown that α3β1 expression in the renal tissue of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus is detected in the area of ​​the glomerular basement membrane (1.400 ± 0.364 Me = 1.264 (95% CI: 0.700–2.100)) and mesangial cells (0.851 ± 0.145 Me = 1.042 (95% CI: 0.574–1.148)). The highest levels of α3β1 expression were found in patients with class IIa DN. As the disease progressed to class IV, the levels of α3β1 expression decreased significantly (P = 0.001) (Fig. 1). Correlation analysis showed reliable associations of α3β1 expression in GBM with the development of nodular lesions (R = −0.358 р = 0.014) and segmental sclerosis (R = 0.437 р = 0.002), and expression in mesangial cells - with the expansion of the mesangial matrix (R = 0.303 р = 0.039) and segmental sclerosis of renal tissue (R = 0.614 р = 0.000). Regression analysis showed a relationship between alpha3beta1 expression in mesangial cells and the development of segmental sclerosis (R2 = 0.377 F = 27.21 β = 0.614 P = 0.000).
Conclusion
The expression level of α3β1 in the glomerular basement membrane and mesangial cells plays a role in the mechanism of morphological tissue damage. Therefore, the loss of podocytes in diabetes mellitus acts as a major participant in the glomerulosclerotic process.

The aim of the study is to investigate the role of alpha3beta1 integrin expression in renal tissue in patients with type 2 diabetes with different morphological classes of diabetic nephropathy (DN) and to assess its impact on the development and progression of histological changes in renal tissue.
Method
The study included 50 patients with type 2 diabetes complicated by diabetic nephropathy. The average age was 66.58 ± 3.27 years. There were 35 women and 14 men. The disease duration in patients with diabetes was 17.70 ± 0.35 years. The duration of DN from the detection of microalbuminuria to the morphological examination of the renal tissue and diagnosis was 1.65 ± 0.34 years. According to light microscopy, class IIa was detected in 12 patients, class IIb in 14 patients, class III in 19 patients, and class IV in 5 patients. According to the results of light microscopy, no signs of glomerulonephritis were found in any of the patients. In addition to light microscopy, the expression of integrin alpha3beta1 in the GBM and mesangial cells was determined in all patients.
Results
It was shown that α3β1 expression in the renal tissue of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus is detected in the area of ​​the glomerular basement membrane (1.400 ± 0.364 Me = 1.264 (95% CI: 0.700–2.100)) and mesangial cells (0.851 ± 0.145 Me = 1.042 (95% CI: 0.574–1.148)). The highest levels of α3β1 expression were found in patients with class IIa DN. As the disease progressed to class IV, the levels of α3β1 expression decreased significantly (P = 0.001) (Fig. 1). Correlation analysis showed reliable associations of α3β1 expression in GBM with the development of nodular lesions (R = −0.358 р = 0.014) and segmental sclerosis (R = 0.437 р = 0.002), and expression in mesangial cells - with the expansion of the mesangial matrix (R = 0.303 р = 0.039) and segmental sclerosis of renal tissue (R = 0.614 р = 0.000). Regression analysis showed a relationship between alpha3beta1 expression in mesangial cells and the development of segmental sclerosis (R2 = 0.377 F = 27.21 β = 0.614 P = 0.000).
Conclusion
The expression level of α3β1 in the glomerular basement membrane and mesangial cells plays a role in the mechanism of morphological tissue damage. Therefore, the loss of podocytes in diabetes mellitus acts as a major participant in the glomerulosclerotic process.

title: #101 Klotho supplementation reverses senescence in aldosterone-salt hypertension
authors: Tsuneo Takenaka
abstract:
Background and Aims
We previously reported that aldosterone induced senescence in renal tubular cells. Our preliminary data showed that renal expression of klotho, an anti-aging protein that inhibits IGF and TGFβ signalings, was reduced in aldosterone-salt hypertension (ASH). In the present study, we assessed the effects of klotho supplementation on senescence in ASH.
Method
Using osmotic minipump, aldosterone was dissolved in DMSO, and infused (0.75 µg/hr) into abdominal cavity in Wistar rats. Rats were allowed free access to normal rat chaw and drinking water containing 1% NaCl. Rats were divided into 2 groups: one group was given daily subcutaneous injection of human recombinant klotho (30 µg/kg/day), and the other was received the vehicle only (0.1% saline containing 0.1% BSA, 0.1 ml/day). Control group was implanted osmotic minipump to infuse DMSO, and allowed free access to normal rat chaw and water. Two weeks later, animals were killed with anesthesia overdose to harvest the kidney.
Results
Compared to the control animals, blood pressure, albuminuria, isoprostane excretion, glomerular filtration rate (GFR), the number of mesangial cells in a glomerulus, fibrosis index, PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1) protein, renal expression of p21 and angiotensinogen were elevated in ASH rats. In contrast, renal expression of mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM), superoxide dismutase (SOD) and klotho were reduced in ASH rats, compared to the controls. Of note, beclin staining was unaltered between control and ASH. Klotho supplementation to ASH rats attenuated the increments of blood pressure, albuminuria, oxidative stress, GFR, single glomerular mesangial cells, fibrosis index, PINK1 protein, renal expression of p21 and angiotensinogen. Klotho supplementation also reversed the decrements of renal expression of TFAM, SOD, and klotho in ASH. Of interest, klotho enhanced beclin staining in ASH rats.
Conclusion
The present data indicated that klotho supplementation decreased GFR, blood pressure and albuminuria at least partly via inactivation of renal renin-angiotensin system in ASH rats. Furthermore, our results provided the evidence that klotho protein supplementation inhibited IGF signaling to attenuate mesangial proliferation, to induce SOD that lowered oxidative stress and mitochondrial damage, and to enhance autophagy, thereby attenuating tubular senescence in ASH rats. Finally, the present findings were consistent with the notion that klotho suppressed TGFβ signals to reduce renal fibrosis in ASH rats.

title: #3007 The role of coronary artery calcification in advanced cardio-kidney-metabolic syndrome staging: beyond diabetes and hypertension
authors: Hae-Ryong Yun; Seung Hyeok Han
abstract:
Background and Aims
Chronic kidney disease (CKD), driven by Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and hypertension, increases cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. Within the Cardio-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) Syndrome framework, Coronary Artery Calcification (CAC) is a marker of advanced CKM stage. This study examines whether CAC independently predicts CVD risk in CKD patients, beyond T2DM and HTN, to enhance CKM staging and refine risk stratification.
Method
This multicenter, prospective cohort study included 2,063 CKD patients aged 20–75 years. Participants were stratified by kidney disease etiology [diabetic kidney disease (DKD), hypertensive kidney disease (HKD), non-metabolic cause kidney disease (NMKD)] and CAC status. The primary outcome was 4-point MACEs, and Cox proportional hazards models were used.
Results
Among 2,063 CKD patients, the incidence of MACEs was highest in the DKD group (9.9%), followed by HKD (4.3%) and NMKD (3.1%). CAC significantly increased MACE risk across all groups. Compared to NMKD patients without CAC, NMKD patients with CAC had a 3.53-fold higher risk (95% CI: 1.66–7.53), while DKD patients with CAC had a 6.49-fold higher risk (95% CI: 2.97–14.2). HKD patients with CAC showed an elevated risk (HR 2.48; 95% CI: 1.05–6.07). In the absence of CAC, there was no significant difference in risk between DKD, HKD, and NMKD patients. Sensitivity analysis confirmed CAC as a key independent predictor of MACEs, irrespective of T2DM or HTN history.
Conclusion
CAC independently predicts cardiovascular risk in CKD patients, underscoring its significance in advanced CKM staging and highlighting the need for tailored management strategies beyond diabetes and hypertension.

title: #550 Hyperuricemia induces hypertension and kidney injury via endoplasmic reticulum stress
authors: Gheun-Ho Kim; Sua Kim; Chor Ho Jo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyperuricemia may induce hypertension associated with renal injury, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress was shown in hypertensive animal models. We hypothesized that ER stress may play a role in hyperuricemia-induced hypertension and kidney injury.
Method
In animal experiment 1, Sprague-Dawley rats were randomly divided into four groups for four weeks: normal controls (NC), hyperuricemic controls (HC, induced by adding 2% oxonic acid and 3% uric acid to food), allopurinol-treated rats (HA), and benzbromarone-treated rats (HB). Animal experiment 2 included four groups for two weeks: NC, HC, 4-phenylbutyric acid-treated rats (HP), and tauroursodeoxycholic acid-treated rats (HT).
Results
Compared with NC, plasma urate and systolic blood pressure (SBP) increased in HC in both experiments. In experiment 1, SBP at four weeks was lowered by urate lowering agents in HA and HB compared with HC. Renal expression of glucose-regulated protein 78 (GRP78) increased in HC compared with NC and attenuated in HA and HB. In experiment 2, elevated SBP in hyperuricemia was mitigated by ER stress inhibition. Increased plasma urate and renal expression of GRP78 in HC were attenuated in HP and HT. Upregulation of NADPH oxidases and NLRP3 inflammasome induced by hyperuricemia were also ameliorated by ER stress inhibition. Renal histopathology revealed that remarkable tubulointerstitial injury was induced by hyperuricemia but blocked by ER stress inhibition.
Conclusion
In summary, hyperuricemia-induced hypertension and kidney injury were associated with the upregulation of ER stress markers and reversed by ER stress inhibition. We conclude that hyperuricemia induces hypertension and tubulointerstitial injury via ER stress in the kidney.

title: #1032 Non-proteinuric kidney disease and Type II diabetes: CKM (cardio kidney metabolic) parameters and current recommended treatment modalities
authors: Khalid Ahmed; Omer Hassan Tagelsir Ali; Aisha Ahmed
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients with renal insufficiency but without albuminuria in type II diabetes are often excluded from trials in overt nephropathy, leaving their optimal treatment unclear. Factors like female sex, obesity, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and glomerular hyperfiltration may contribute to GFR decline. This study examines the prevalence and treatment modalities for this under-represented group.
Method
We conducted a cross-sectional study using data from the Diamond database at Imperial College Diabetes Centre, UAE's largest treatment center for type II diabetes. Patients aged ≥18 with a GFR and albumin-creatinine ratio (ACR) measured at least annually per ADA guidelines were included. Non-proteinuric CKD (NP-CKD) was defined as GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² with ACR <30 mg/mmol. Blood pressure, laboratory parameters, and treatment data were analyzed using STATA MP v17.
Results
Among 33,524 T2DM patients, 7% (2594) had GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m², of which 35.5% (921) had NP-CKD. Breakdown by CKD stage: 71.6% G3a, 18.6% G3b, and 1.9% G4. Mean age was 72.62 ± 10.05 years, with 62.6% female. Key parameters: hemoglobin 12.23 ± 1.62 g/dL, systolic BP 126.2 ± 16.97 mmHg, diastolic BP 67.77 ± 8.54 mmHg, and BMI >25 in 74.1%. Treatment rates were 42.6% for SGLT2 inhibitors, 40.5% for RAS inhibitors, 17.8% for GLP-1 receptor agonists, and 4.2% for finerenone.
Conclusion
SGLT2 inhibitors are recommended by the ADA for T2DM patients with cardiovascular risks, yet their uptake is 42.6% in this cohort. RAS inhibitors, despite guidelines against use in normotensive, normoalbuminuric patients, showed similar use to proteinuric CKD (40.5%). Finerenone use (4.2%) aligns with its indication in proteinuria, suggesting quadruple therapy may lead to non-proteinuric status. GLP-1 receptor agonists, with direct nephroprotective and cardiovascular benefits, remain underutilized. Elevated BMI (80%), residual hypertension (50%), and hypercholesterolemia indicate high cardiovascular risks, necessitating comprehensive CKM-targeted therapies. Future studies should explore emerging treatments and refine strategies for this population.

title: #1254 Renal biopsy in diabetic patients—25 years of a single center experience
authors: Adrián Okša; Martin Demes; Andrea Farkašová; Dušan Daniš; Peter Talarčík; Pavol Gomolčák; Oľga Nyitrayová
abstract:
Background and Aims
A significant part of patients with CKD and diabetes mellitus especially of type 2 (DM2T) may have a nephropathy of non-diabetic origin, and renal biopsy (RB) is needed in a differential diagnostics. The aim of this study was to evaluate clinical and laboratory data and the results of RB performed in diabetic patients in our department during a period of 2000–2024.
Method
Diabetic patients with clinical suspicion of a non-diabetic nephropathy were indicated for RB. In all patients, RB was performed by a biopty gun with ultrasonography control. Obtained specimens were analyzed by the light, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy. Results were evaluated by descriptive statistics and unpaired t-test.
Results
From 883 of all patients indicated for RB during a period of 2000–2024, there were 131 diabetics (14.8%) including 112 with DM2T, 16 with DM1T and 3 with secondary diabetes. Among them, 77 men and 54 women were present with a median age (range) 58 (20–74) years, duration of diabetes 9.0 (0–33) years, duration of nephropathy 8 (1–264) months, serum creatinine in time of RB 150 (56–1000) μmol/l, and proteinuria 7.8 (0.5–34) g/24 h. Nephrotic range proteinuria was present in 110 (84.0%), hematuria in 79 (60.3%) and hypertension in 118 (90.1%) diabetics. Histological diagnosis was established in 125 (95.4%) patients and a mean amount of glomeruli in a specimen (for all 3 methods of analysis) was 30 (0–83). In 47 (37.6%) patients, a typical diabetic nephropathy (DN) was diagnosed, while in 78 (62.4%) other nephropathies were present either alone in 59 (47.2%) patients or in combination with DN in 19 patients (15.2%). Among single non-diabetic nephropathies, membrane glomerulonephritis (GN) in 23, systemic lupus or vasculitis associated GN in 10 and IgA nephropathy in 6 patients were the most common. In combination with DN, nephroangiosclerosis in 5, IgA nephropathy in 4 and membrane GN as well as minimal change disease in 3 patients were the most frequent. Patients with typical DN did not differ from others in terms of duration of nephropathy, serum creatinine, proteinuria or hematuria, but were of significantly lower age (53.1 vs 58.5 years, p<0.02), longer diabetes duration (14.3 vs 7.6 years, P < 0.001) and had a diabetic retinopathy more frequently (26 vs 3 patients, P < 0.001). Diabetic retinopathy had a high specificity (96.2%) and positive predictive value (89.3%) as a marker of DN. In one patient with a combination of DN and nephroangiosclerosis of stage G4A3, RB was complicated with a large hematoma and nephrectomy.
Conclusion
Up to 62.4% of diabetic patients indicated for RB had a nephropathy of non-diabetic origin (either alone or combined with DN). Clinical and laboratory data were of no value in differential diagnostics except for age, diabetes duration and diabetic retinopathy. Properly indicated RB is a valuable tool for the assessment of precise diagnosis, prognosis and focused therapy in these patients.

title: #2426 Exploration of cagrilintide's mechanism of action in the kidney
authors: Vera Wulfmeyer; Anja Billing; Sagar Bhayana; Mette Viberg Østergaard; Markus Rinschen
abstract:
Background and Aims
The hormone amylin, co-secreted with insulin from the beta-cells of the pancreas, induces satiety. Previous studies have highlighted a physiological role of amylin in glucose/sodium homeostasis and blood pressure regulation. However, in states of (pre)diabetes, amylin deposits have been described in the kidneys and other organs. Cagrilintide, a long-acting amylin analogue, which binds to both calcitonin and amylin receptors (G-protein-coupled receptors), has demonstrated a dose-dependent and clinically significant effect on weight loss in humans. Despite this, the kidney-specific metabolic pathways affected by amylin agonism remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we investigated cagrilintide's mechanism of action in the kidneys of healthy and diabetic Zucker Diabetic Fatty (ZDF) rats using an ex vivo approach.
Method
For a total of 20 fasted, male ZDF rats, 13 to 15 weeks in age (10 obese/diabetic and 10 lean/healthy), one third of a kidney was reserved for histological evaluation, while the remaining tissue underwent enzymatical digestion into cortical and medullary tubule fractions. Tubules were exposed to a phosphodiesterase inhibitor (IBMX 0.5 mM, 15 minutes) and then treated with vehicle, cagrilintide (1 µM), or salmon calcitonin (1 µM) for 30 minutes. Intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels were quantified using a commercially available detection kit (HTRF cAMP Gi Detection Kit, Revvity). Residual tubular samples were snap-frozen for subsequent phosphoproteomic analyses.
Results
In healthy rat tubules, cagrilintide treatment induced phosphorylation of ion transporters in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle (TAL) and the distal convoluted tubule (e.g., NKCC2 and NCC), while also modifying mTOR regulators. Obese ZDF rats proved to be diabetic with a mean HbA1c of 7.2% (4.0% in healthy rats; P < 0.0001). In addition, diabetic ZDF rats showed evidence of diabetic nephropathy, characterized by glomerular hyperfiltration (as evaluated by plasma creatinine levels) and severely increased albuminuria (mean 18682 µg/mg vs. 52 µg/mg in healthy rats). In these diabetic ZDF rats, cagrilintide significantly increased intracellular cAMP levels in cortical tubules (P = 0.00055; t-test vs. vehicle). In contrast, healthy rats showed no significant cAMP response to cagrilintide. Preliminary findings suggest that the distal nephron in diabetic rats may be more responsive to cagrilintide. Phosphoproteomic measurements are ongoing and expected to reveal downstream signaling alterations modulated by cagrilintide in both cortical and medullary nephron segments.
Conclusion
Our results point to a diabetes-specific mechanism by which cagrilintide elevates cAMP in cortical tubules, providing initial evidence of mode of action in diabetic kidney physiology compared with healthy controls. Ongoing phosphoproteomic analyses will offer deeper insights into the molecular pathways affected, potentially guiding the therapeutic application of cagrilintide in diabetic kidney disease.

title: #3810 Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis associated with the use of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors: a case series
authors: Motaz Obeidat; Aysheh Obeidat; Liyan Bastoni
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a known acute complication of diabetes mellitus (DM). It can lead to serious morbidities, and sometimes to death, if not well recognized and managed. Blood glucose is usually significantly high in patients presenting with DKA. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) are one of the medications used for management of DM. They are also used to slow the progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD) in both diabetics and non-diabetics. In addition, they are used in the management of heart failure patients. Their use is also expanding for other indications. title: #767 Sarcopenia-related markers derived from creatinine and cystatin C, GDF-15 and adverse outcomes in people with diabetes
authors: Tomohito Gohda; Nozomu Kamei; Marenao Tanaka; Tatsuya Sato; Masato Furuhashi; Shinji Hagiwara; Yusuke Suzuki; Maki Murakoshi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Protein catabolism and chronic inflammation are key drivers of sarcopenia and frailty in individuals with diabetes and chronic kidney disease (CKD). The difference between cystatin C-based and creatinine-based estimated glomerular filtration rates (eGFRcys and eGFRcr, respectively), termed eGFRdiff, along with growth differentiation factor-15 (GDF-15), have emerged as promising markers of metabolic and inflammatory dysregulation. Lower eGFRdiff and elevated GDF-15 levels are associated with sarcopenia, frailty, CKD progression and mortality. However, the interplay between eGFRdiff and GDF-15 and their respective impacts on adverse outcomes, such as a kidney event and mortality in diabetes, remains unclear.
Method
A total of 638 Japanese individuals with diabetes were stratified into tertiles based on eGFRdiff. Serum GDF-15 levels were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Spearman's correlation coefficients were used to assess relationships between eGFRdiff, GDF-15 and kidney function markers, including eGFRcr, eGFRcys and the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR). Multivariate ordered logistic regression was used to evaluate the association between eGFRdiff and GDF-15. Cox proportional hazards models with restricted cubic splines, adjusted for confounders, were used to examine associations of eGFRdiff and GDF-15 with adverse outcomes, including a kidney event (≥30% decline in eGFRcr), mortality and composite outcomes.
Results
The mean age of patients was 65 years and 53.9% were male. Over a median follow-up of 5.4 years, 75 patients (11.8%) experienced a kidney event, 44 (6.9%) died and 112 (17.6%) reached composite outcomes. GDF-15 was weakly but significantly negatively correlated with eGFRdiff (r = –0.35). Both markers showed weak-to-moderate correlations with kidney function markers: eGFRcr (GDF-15: r = –0.26; eGFRdiff: r = –0.14), eGFRcys (GDF-15: r = –0.45; eGFRdiff: r = 0.54) and UACR (GDF-15: r = 0.28; eGFRdiff: r = –0.23). Multivariate regression confirmed an independent inverse association between eGFRdiff and GDF-15. Lower eGFRdiff and higher GDF-15 levels independently predicted adverse outcomes after adjustment for clinical variables.
Conclusion
Both eGFRdiff and GDF-15 were independently associated with adverse outcomes in individuals with diabetes. Although eGFRdiff was more strongly linked to a kidney event, GDF-15 showed a stronger association with mortality. These findings underscore the potential utility of these markers in risk stratification for diabetes-related complications.

title: #3686 The effects of dapagliflozin on renal outcomes in diabetes mellitus type II - a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Malcolm Mintoff; Claire Vassallo; Dan Pugh
abstract:
Background and Aims
The class effects of sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors on cardiorenal outcomes have been demonstrated in previous trials. The impact of dapagliflozin on renal outcomes in adult patients with diabetes mellitus type II (DMII) as well as the effects in participants with advanced chronic kidney disease remain unanswered.
Method
A systematic literature search of clinicaltrials.gov, PubMed, Cochrane Central Register Of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) and Embase was performed from inception until 1st March 2021. Randomised controlled trials (RCT) reporting renal outcomes in adult patients with DMII receiving dapagliflozin versus placebo or standard diabetic treatment were included. Outcomes included mean change in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), mean change in serum creatinine, mean change in albuminuria, progression and regression of albuminuria, end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) and renal death. The effect of dapagliflozin on sub-groups of patients according to comorbidities other than DMII was also assessed. Odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) was used for analysis of dichotomous outcomes whilst mean difference or standardised mean difference with 95% CI was used for the analysis of continuous outcomes. Random effects models were incorporated to measure the results of pooled outcomes.
Results
23 papers were included. These consisted of 14 RCTs, 7 exploratory analyses and 2 extension phases of a RCT. Compared to placebo or other hypoglycaemic treatments, dapagliflozin was associated with a significant reduction in albuminuria and trends towards reduction in ESKD and renal death. The use of dapagliflozin over placebo or standard hypoglycaemic treatment was not associated with any meaningful changes in creatinine or eGFR.
Conclusion
Dapagliflozin is associated with beneficial renal effects. Renal safety does not appear jeopardised in patients with DMII and eGFR values of at least 25 ml/min/1.73 m2. Further results from real-world studies and large trials are necessary to confirm the findings from this review.

title: #2177 It is possible to predict the clinical course of chronic kidney disease in patients with type 2 diabetes: the significance of selected biomarkers
authors: Agnieszka Gala-Błądzińska; Małgorzata Rodzoń - Norwicz; Natalia Potocka; Marzena Skrzypa; Izabela Zawlik; Patryk Kogut; Krzysztof Gargasz; Magdalena Sowa - Kućma; Michael Maes
abstract:
Background and Aims
Clinical practice indicates that the course of diabetic kidney disease (DKD) in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and the prognosis of this condition are highly heterogeneous, often difficult to predict, and at the same time crucial for diagnostic and therapeutic decision-making. Therefore, identifying patients at high risk of developing and progressing DKD is of critical importance.
The aim of this retrospective observational study was to evaluate the utility of selected biomarkers correlated with pathophysiology in assessing the progression and phenotype of DKD.
Method
The study recruited 97 (32♂, 49♀) patients with T2DM at an average age of 67 ± 11.5 years from nephrology outpatient clinics and a dialysis center. The patients were assigned by a nephrologist to DKD phenotypic groups based on clinical history, eGFR values (ml/min/1.73 m²), and uACR (mg/g). The groups were defined as follows:
The division into DKD phenotypes is illustrated in Fig. 1.
Analyses of biomarkers associated with DKD pathogenesis were performed using urine and blood samples from these patients.
The Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) method was used to evaluate complex relationships among independent variables (age, sex, biomarkers), mediating variables (angiotensin-converting enzyme concentration - ACE, atherogenic index of plasma - AIP), and the dependent variable – estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Discriminant analysis was performed to differentiate three groups (F1, F2, F3) using four variables (log API, age, serum ACE protein, and uric acid levels), achieving 86.2% correct classifications with statistically significant results (Wilks' Lambda, P < 0.05).
Results
We found that 61.9% of the variance in eGFR was explained by regression on ACE protein levels, age, and the AIP as well as hsa-miR-423-5p (positively correlated).
Figure 2 shows the final PLS model with all significant paths. The model fit accuracy was very good (SRMR = 0.024). All specific indirect effects of age, BMI, via AIP and ACE, male sex and mir-126.3p were significant (P < 0.05). All in all, eGFR was associated (in descending order of importance) with age, ACE, AIP, male sex, mir-126-3p and mir-423-5p.
Discriminant analysis was conducted to differentiate between phenotypic groups. The classification results were visualized in the Fig. 3.
Finally, based on the conducted analysis of clinical and laboratory data, the DKD phenotypes were characterized according to the following statistically significant features:
Conclusion
We identified new modifiable risk factors for the adverse progression of DKD, such as serum ACE, uric acid concentration, AIP, hsa-miR-423-5p and hsa-miR-126-3p. These, when correlated with clinical and epidemiological data, appear to be useful for determining the phenotype of CKD and assessing prognosis in the course of T2DM.

title: #3855 Pregnancy outcomes in chronic hypertensive patients with superimposed preeclampsia: a nephrology outpatient experience
authors: Yesika Amezquita; Yolanda Hernández Hernández; Raquel Diaz Mancebo; Sílvia Caldés Ruisánchez; Gabriel Ledesma Sánchez; Ángel Gallegos Villalobos; Rocío Echarri Carrillo; Gilda Carreño; María Covadonga Hevia Ojanguren; Antonio Cirugeda García
abstract:
Background
Chronic or pregestational hypertension affects 5%–10% of pregnancies and is associated with adverse maternal and neonatal events.
Hypertension in pregnancy is associated with an increased risk of premature birth, low birth weight, and small-for-gestational-age newborns, especially due to a superimposed preeclampsia (PE). Up to 25% of women with chronic hypertension develop PE.
Aims
To evaluate pregnant women with chronic hypertension followed by a nephrology outpatient clinic and describe those who develop superimposed PE.
Method
Observational, descriptive, retrospective cohort study of 45 patients with chronic hypertension followed the nephrology hypertension-pregnancy clinic from 2017 to 2022. We analyzed the association between PE and clinical variables using Chi-square, Student's t-test, and ANOVA or their non-parametric equivalents.
Results
Mean age 36 years +/– 5.8. Caucasian race: 82% (n:37). Comorbidities: smokers (20%, n:9), type 2 Diabetes (8.9%, n:4), chronic hypothyroidism (8.9%, n:4), A family history of hypertension was present in 61.7% (n:21). Obstetric history revealed prior pregnancies in 68.9% (n:31), abortions (48.8%, n:22), and prior PE in 16.1% (n:5). Current pregnancy: first pregnancy (31.11%, n:14), multiple gestation (8.89%, n:4). Assisted reproduction (17.8%, n:8), Gestational diabetes (9.7% n:3).
In the table, we compare patients with added PE versus those without it.
20 patients were previously receiving treatment, the most common therapies were ACE inhibitors (60%, n:12), ARBs (25%, n:5), Diuretics (10%, n:2), and B-Blockers (15%, n:1).
In the third trimester, 20% (n:9) associated a second antihypertensive, the most used being Labetalol 11.1% (n:5) and 4.44% (n:2) received a third antihypertensive.
Conclusion
Maternal age, high BP in the first trimester, and the use of 2 or more antihypertensive drugs from the second trimester onwards are risk factors for superimposed PE in patients with chronic hypertension. Superimposed PE increases the risk of premature birth.

title: #84 Early to mid pregnancy renal parameters and adverse pregnancy outcomes in women with early stage chronic kidney disease
authors: Alessandra Orsillo; Erandi Hewawasam; Shilpanjali Jesudason
abstract:
Background and Aims
Early-stage chronic kidney disease (CKD) contributes to increased risk of adverse maternal and fetal outcomes in pregnancy. The impact of preconception factors is well understood, however few studies investigate links between renal parameters during pregnancy and adverse outcomes. We aimed to investigate whether renal ‘red flags’ in early to mid-pregnancy predict pregnancy complications in women with early-stage CKD.
Method
Retrospective data collection was undertaken from a single tertiary centre in Adelaide, Australia. All women with CKD stages 1–3 who had a pregnancy >20 weeks gestation between January 2018 and April 2023 were included. Maternal medical, infant and delivery data were collected from medical records. ‘Red flag’ markers were evaluated when available including: failure of serum creatinine to fall by 10% between pre-pregnancy and second trimester; protein:creatinine ratio (PCR) >30 mg/mmol in second trimester and lack of physiological drop in blood pressure between pre-pregnancy and second trimester. The primary outcome was a composite adverse pregnancy outcome of gestational age <37 weeks, birth weight <2500 grams and pre-eclampsia. Fisher's exact test was used to assess the relationship between red flag markers and the composite outcome.
Results
Results from 38 mothers and 47 pregnancies were analysed. There were three twin pregnancies and therefore 50 infants. Median maternal age at delivery was 32.5 years (IQR: 30.4–35.3). Stage 1 CKD was most common (n = 34, 72%), followed by stage 2 (n = 8, 17%) and stage 3 (n = 5, 11%). Glomerulonephritis was the most frequent cause of CKD (n = 23, 61%). 16% (n = 6) of mothers had chronic hypertension. Of the pregnancies 38% (n = 18) were complicated by hypertension and 19% (n = 9) by pre-eclampsia. The median birth weight of infants was 2895 grams (IQR: 2460–3170), with 6 (12%) <10th centile for gestational age. The median gestational age was 37.3 weeks (IQR 35.8–38). Red flags occurred in a high proportion of women: serum creatinine did not fall in 27/41 (61%), PCR was elevated in 24/35 (69%), and blood pressure did not fall in 24/33 (73%). The composite outcome occurred in 22/45 (49%). The rate of the composite outcome was not increased in women experiencing adverse renal parameters (creatinine 58%, P = 0.176; blood pressure 52%, P = 1.00; proteinuria 65%, P = 0.066).
Conclusion
Though this cohort of predominately early-stage CKD patients had a high rate of the composite adverse outcome, traditional red flags in mid-pregnancy were not consistently predictive of this. This highlights the need for alternative markers to assess risk throughout pregnancy.

title: #3332 Podometric findings in arterial hypertension and diabetes mellitus type 2
authors: Christopher Paschen; Rainer Oberbauer; Heinz Regele
abstract:
Background and Aims
Arterial hypertension (aHTN) and diabetes mellitus type 2 (DM2) are key drivers of chronic kidney disease (CKD). Both HTN and DM2 lead to hyperfiltration with subsequent glomerulomegaly and podocyte depletion. These structural changes in turn lead to glomerulosclerosis and CKD progression. This retrospective study aimed to assess glomerular and podocyte alterations in patients with aHTN and explore the additive effects of coexisting DM2.
Method
Morphometric analyses on glomerular and podocyte structure were performed on unaffected kidney regions from tumor nephrectomy specimens of 99 patients. The cohort was divided into three groups: aHTN only (n=47), aHTN+DM2 (n=32), and controls without aHTN or DM2 (n=20). Glomerular and podocyte characteristics were compared using analysis of variance. Multivariable linear regression examined the influence of glomerular- and podometrics on renal compensatory capacity, defined as the change in estimated glomerular filtration rate (∆eGFR) from the presurgical baseline to 12 months after nephrectomy.
Results
Proteinuria was observed in 36% of patients with aHTN and 50% of those with aHTN+DM2. There was no difference in glomerular volume between the aHTN+DM2 group and controls (2.7±0.8 vs. 2.3±0.8 ×10⁶ μm³; P=0.16), and to aHTN alone (2.7±0.9 ×10⁶ μm³; P=0.95). Individuals with aHTN+DM2 showed a lower podocyte density compared to controls (217±66 vs. 279±75 per 10⁶ μm³; P=0.02) but no difference to aHTN alone (233±87 per 10⁶ μm³; P=0.67). Subjects with aHTN+DM2 exhibited podocyte nuclear hypertrophy compared to controls (230±28 μm³ vs. 201±32 μm³; P=0.004), and did not differ significantly from the aHTN group (221±33 μm³; P=0.39). Glomerular enlargement (P=0.009) decreased podocyte density (P=0.003), and larger podocyte nuclei (P=0.01) correlated with reduced compensation of eGFR.
Conclusion
Relative podocyte depletion and nuclear hypertrophy were evident in both aHTN and aHTN+DM2. However, the presence of DM2 in individuals with aHTN did not exert additional structural changes beyond those observed with aHTN alone. Morphometric parameters like glomerular volume, podocyte density, and podocyte nuclear volume could be estimated in patients undergoing nephrectomy (either oncologic, traumatic, or living kidney donation) to identify individuals at risk for impaired renal compensation, which require close monitoring of kidney function.

Both HTN and DM2 lead to hyperfiltration with subsequent glomerulomegaly and podocyte depletion. These structural changes in turn lead to glomerulosclerosis and CKD progression. This retrospective study aimed to assess glomerular and podocyte alterations in patients with aHTN and explore the additive effects of coexisting DM2.
Method
Morphometric analyses on glomerular and podocyte structure were performed on unaffected kidney regions from tumor nephrectomy specimens of 99 patients. The cohort was divided into three groups: aHTN only (n=47), aHTN+DM2 (n=32), and controls without aHTN or DM2 (n=20). Glomerular and podocyte characteristics were compared using analysis of variance. Multivariable linear regression examined the influence of glomerular- and podometrics on renal compensatory capacity, defined as the change in estimated glomerular filtration rate (∆eGFR) from the presurgical baseline to 12 months after nephrectomy.
Results
Proteinuria was observed in 36% of patients with aHTN and 50% of those with aHTN+DM2. There was no difference in glomerular volume between the aHTN+DM2 group and controls (2.7±0.8 vs. 2.3±0.8 ×10⁶ μm³; P=0.16), and to aHTN alone (2.7±0.9 ×10⁶ μm³; P=0.95). Individuals with aHTN+DM2 showed a lower podocyte density compared to controls (217±66 vs. 279±75 per 10⁶ μm³; P=0.02) but no difference to aHTN alone (233±87 per 10⁶ μm³; P=0.67). Subjects with aHTN+DM2 exhibited podocyte nuclear hypertrophy compared to controls (230±28 μm³ vs. 201±32 μm³; P=0.004), and did not differ significantly from the aHTN group (221±33 μm³; P=0.39). Glomerular enlargement (P=0.009) decreased podocyte density (P=0.003), and larger podocyte nuclei (P=0.01) correlated with reduced compensation of eGFR.
Conclusion
Relative podocyte depletion and nuclear hypertrophy were evident in both aHTN and aHTN+DM2. However, the presence of DM2 in individuals with aHTN did not exert additional structural changes beyond those observed with aHTN alone. Morphometric parameters like glomerular volume, podocyte density, and podocyte nuclear volume could be estimated in patients undergoing nephrectomy (either oncologic, traumatic, or living kidney donation) to identify individuals at risk for impaired renal compensation, which require close monitoring of kidney function.

title: #3589 Renal AhR controls blood pressure regulation and cysteine metabolism in an in vivo model of Obstructive Sleep Apnea
authors: António Pimpão; Maria João Correia; Nuno Coelho; Elsa Mecha; Antonio Melo Junior; Luísa Santos; Pedro Costa; Teresa Serra; Maria Bronze; Xavier Coumoul; Emília Monteiro; Sofia Azeredo Pereira
abstract:
Background and Aims
Arterial hypertension (HTN) associated with Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA), often drug-resistant, poses a challenge in treatment and needs innovative therapeutic approaches. Chronic intermittent hypoxia (CIH) is the main clinical feature of OSA and is associated with several disease mechanisms, including inflammation and oxidative stress. Our group was pioneer in linking the CIH-induced drug-resistant HTN with the overactivation of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) in the kidney, which was reverted by the treatment with a selective AhR antagonist (CH-223191). Moreover, we identified a new AhR activator (cystine, an oxidized form of cysteine) and a new AhR antagonist (Hydroxytyrosol – OHTyr – a NRF2 agonist) in vitro and in vivo, respectively. As a ligand-activated transcription factor from the Per-Arnt-Sim (PAS) superfamily, the AhR shares its dimerization partner with the hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs). As the role of the AhR in CIH-induced changes is not well characterized, in this work, we aimed at identifying putative genes under the AhR control associated with HTN development, as well as understanding the impact of both CIH, when HTN is already established, and AhR blockade in the AhR-HIF signaling and cysteine metabolism, to better understand the effect of CIH exposure in the kidney, and the role of the AhR in these changes.
Method
Briefly, Male Wistar rats (n ≥ 4) were subjected to CIH (21%–5% O2, 5.6 cycles/h, 10.5 h/day, during the animals’ inactive period) for 21 days, to establish HTN, and from the 22nd day they were treated orally with the AhR antagonist CH-223191 (5 mg/kg/day in vegetable oil, gavage) or hydroxytyrosol (OHTyr, 15 mg/kg/day in vegetable oil, gavage) for 14 days under CIH. Animals under 35 days of normoxia (Nx) or CIH, treated or not with the drug's vehicle, were used as controls. Blood pressure was monitored during active and inactive periods using radiotelemetry. The renal cortex was collected and used for Western Blot quantification of AHR-related signaling (e.g., CYP1A1, PON1, HIFs) and cysteine/H2S metabolic enzymes (e.g., CBS, PDO). The cysteine-related thiols (e.g., GSH, Cys) were quantified by HPLC-FD. Transcriptomics analyses of kidney cortex by RNA-Seq. was performed in CH-223191 and OHTyr-treated animals. The study has the Ethical approval by DGAV and NMS ethic committee.
Results
The blockade of the AhR by both CH-223191 and OHTyr was able to revert the CIH-induced increase in blood pressure, coincident with a normalization of renal protein levels of CYP1A1 (hallmark of AhR activation). CIH exposure altered the expression of AHR-related signaling proteins and cysteine metabolic enzymes, which were at least partially reverted by the AhR blockade. OHTyr treatment was also able to revert the CIH-induced increase in oxidized cysteine levels. In turn, we found that CH-223191 selectively altered 10 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in CIH which are primarily involved in metabolic stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, lipid accumulation, inflammation, and heme metabolism (Alad).
Conclusion
Altogether, our findings show that, in the kidney, CIH affect the AhR-HIF axis and cysteine metabolism, which are normalized upon AhR blockade. Moreover, we identify AHR pharmacological pathways, putatively relevant to OSA-HTN.

title: #1002 Spanish plan for hypertensive disorders in the puerperium: zero vascular and renal risk
authors: Carolina Gracia-Iguacel; M A Dolores Del Pino Y Pino; Marta Arias Guillen; Itziar Castaño; Mercedes Salgueira Lazo; Marco Montomoli; Lara Karlla Dasilva Santos; Maria Dolores Arenas; Claudia Yuste Lozano; Beatriz Fernandez-Fernandez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) are associated with increased postpartum risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) or kidney failure. Given the change in the profile of the current pregnant woman (older age at pregnancy, obesity, diabetes, use of assisted reproductive technologies, chronic hypertension and CKD) an increase in the incidence of HDP is being observed; according to the WHO 2%–10%. However, there is scarce information on current practice regarding follow-up of HDP in diverse healthcare systems in an evolving demographic environment. Spain is one of the western European countries without yet having a national HDP registry. An interdisciplinary Spanish group carries out by Nephrology, Primary Care; Obstetric proposed the need for a vascular and renal protection plan in the postpartum period focus on prevention, health promotion and monitoring in our healthcare system with universal free access.
Aims: Analyze for the first time the incidence, development of HDP in Spain between 2016––2022 and its differences between different regions of Spain.
Method
Data was provided by the Registry of Specialized Care Activity of the Spanish Ministry of Health. HDP events were identified using ninth international classification of disease (ICD) codes from 2016 to 2023: pre-existing hypertension complicating pregnancy, childbirth and the puerperium [010], chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia [O11], gestational [pregnancy-induced] oedema and proteinuria without hypertension [012], gestational hypertension [O13]. Incidence was analyzed with the number of cases divided by the number of births and multiplying by 100. Incidents were compared with the initial year (2016) to assess the evolution. These comparisons were made by calculating the incidence ratio or relative risk (RR), and its 95% confidence interval. Statistically significant was consider when the confidence interval not contain 1. The incidence between 2016 and 2022 was initially analyzed overall in Spain and subsequently was done individually among the different Spanish regions. Poisson regression models were perform to analyze the temporal evolution of different regions of Spain. Statistical significance of this interaction term was assessed using the likelihood ratio test. Additionally, p values ​​were corrected for multiple comparisons by the Benjamini-Hochberg method. If p of the interaction was less than 0.05, means that the temporal evolution was different in the two regions compared.
Results
A significant increased of HDP incidence was observed in 2021 [(1.80 vs 1.84; RR 1.055 (1.033–1.076)] and 2022 [(1.80 vs 1.90; RR 1.063 (1.041–1.084)] compared to 2016; table 1. The Spanish regions with higher incidence rate between 2016–2022 were : Balearic Islands, Canary Islands, Melilla, Aragón, Catalonia and Ceuta, Fig. 1. There was a significant difference in variability between the incidences of the different Spanish regions between the years 2016–2022; Table 2.
Conclusion
This is the first study to analyze the incidence of HDP in Spain and its different regions. A significant incidence increased over time from 2016 to 2022 was observed in Spain. Low overall incidence in Spain (1.8) compared to other European countries (France 2.3, Greece 2.2, Norway 4.0). Most regions in Spain present an incidence below 1, Fig. 1. The significant difference in incidences variability between the different regions in Spain points out the need for a homogeneous follow-up discharge - hospitalization protocol for Primary Care. The low incidence indicates an under diagnosis with a possible loss of follow-up of patients with the possible loss of follow-up of women with HDP and the cardiovascular risk that it entails.

title: #3693 Urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio as a biomarker for predicting coronary artery disease severity
authors: Merita Rroji; Edison Koltraka; Artan Goda; Alban Dibra
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cardiovascular diseases, particularly coronary artery disease (CAD), represent a leading global health burden. Among the markers associated with CAD, the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) has garnered attention for its predictive value. Albuminuria, reflecting endothelial dysfunction and microvascular damage, has been implicated as a strong independent risk factor for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. This study investigates the correlation between UACR levels and the presence and severity of CAD.
Method
A cross-sectional study was conducted over six months (January 2024–June 2024) at two tertiary care centers. A total of 150 patients admitted for suspected or confirmed CAD were enrolled. UACR was measured using early-morning urine samples and classified into categories: normal (<30 mg/g), microalbuminuria (30–300 mg/g), and macroalbuminuria (>300 mg/g). Coronary angiography determined the severity of CAD using Syntax Scores. Statistical analyses included correlation, regression, and subgroup analyses.
Results
Among the 150 participants (65% male, mean age 66.4 years), elevated UACR levels were strongly associated with higher Syntax Scores, indicating more severe CAD. Patients with UACR levels >30 mg/g were significantly more likely to present with multivessel disease, with 68% of those exhibiting macroalbuminuria having severe CAD (Syntax Score >27) Figs 1 and 2. A positive correlation was observed between UACR and the number of affected coronary vessels (Pearson's r = 0.621, P < 0.01). Additionally, elevated UACR levels were linked to markers of systemic inflammation (e.g., CRP) and metabolic disorders such as diabetes and hypertension, further underscoring its role as a comprehensive cardiovascular risk marker.
Conclusion
UACR serves as a robust predictor of CAD severity and a potential biomarker for identifying high-risk patients. Its utility extends beyond kidney function assessment, providing critical insights into cardiovascular health. Incorporating UACR into routine clinical evaluations may enhance risk stratification and guide therapeutic interventions in CAD management.

title: #1819 The role of renal functional reserve in eGFR decline over 2 years in hypertensives and normotensives with preserved renal function
authors: Katerina Damianaki; Emelina Stambolliu; Kyriakos Dimitriadis; Konstantinos Tsioufis; Dimitrios Petras
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal Functional Reserve (RFR) has been considered as a promising tool for the diagnosis of early nephron loss and functional renal mass. We aimed to assess whether RFR plays a role in the change of eGFR over time in normotensive and hypertensive patients with preserved renal function and also to examine any correlation of RFR with hemodynamic load, inotropic response and target organ damage.
Method
In a 24-month prospective study, newly diagnosed essential hypertensives and normotensives with eGFR≥60 ml/min/1.73 m2 were included. The following parameters were measured at baseline: RFR (determined by endogenous creatinine clearance after an acute oral protein load), office blood pressure (BP), 24h ambulatory BP profile, treadmill stress test, and echocardiographic examination. Serum creatinine measurements were also measured at months 12 and 24.
Results
A total of 51 hypertensives and 20 normotensives completed the study (mean age 53.2 ± 12.1 and 54.3 ± 10.0 years, respectively). Non-significant differences were found between these two groups regarding RFR levels (25.1 ± 18.7 vs 27.7 ± 15.7 ml/min, P = 0.6), annual change (Delta(12–0)m) of eGFR (0.04 ± 1.8 vs −0.75±0.9 ml/min/1.73 m2, P = 0.06) and two-year change (Delta(24–0)m) of eGFR (−0.70 ± 2.3 vs −1.1 ± 1.1 ml/min/1.73 m2, P = 0.46).
Hypertensives with RFR≥30ml/min showed a smaller change in the Delta(24–0)m eGFR compared to those with RFR<30ml/min (0.5 ± 2.6 vs −1.4 ± 1.7 ml/min/1.73 m2, P = 0.002). Similarly, the Delta(24-0)m eGFR was significantly lower in normotensives with RFR ≥30ml/min compared to normotensives with RFR <30 ml/min (−0.6 ± 1.3 vs -1.6±0.7 ml/min/1.73 m2, P = 0.02). A dipping pattern of 24 h-SBP was significantly more frequent in hypertensives with high RFR (64.4 vs. 34.4%, P < 0.05). Moreover, patients with lower RFR values showed a blunted heart rate response to exercise during treadmill test (r = 0.29, P < 0.05). None of the echocardiographic parameters differed between the groups of hypertensives.
Conclusion
RFR did not differ between hypertensive and normotensive subjects with preserved renal function. However, normotensives and hypertensives with RFR≥30ml/min showed a less pronounced change in eGFR at 2 years than those with RFR <30ml/min. Finally, in hypertensive patients with preserved GFR, reduced RFR was related to non-dipping BP phenotype as well as to attenuated exercise HR response.

title: #681 Blood pressure modulation through altered epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) expression induced by microbiome exchange between Milan normotensive and hypertensive rat strains
authors: Yoko Suzumoto; Cristoforo Silvestri; Abbas Shams; Luciano D'apolito; Antonio Villanova; Francesco Trepiccione; Vincenzo Di Marzo; Giovambattista Capasso
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hypertension constitutes a major health problem leading to cardiovascular diseases. Recent studies showed gut microbiome changes in hypertension, suggesting kidney-gut axis in hypertension. A congenic strain of Milan hypertensive (NA) rats with a mutation in α-adducin gene develops hypertension at 3 months age. Our preliminary study revealed diverse expression of renal sodium transporters in NA rats compared with normotensive strain (MN) rats, indicating abnormal renal salt handling in NA rats. Present study aimed at investigating a possible connection between gut microbiome and blood pressure phenotype in these two strains. Furthermore, we evaluated whether exchange of faeces between two strains may transfer phenotypes via gut microbiome, and mechanisms underlying altered phenotypes.
Method
NA and MN rats were subjected to ‘homogenization (HOM)’ of the microbiome, consisted of exchanges of bedding with faeces, followed by co-housing in the same cage (MN-HOM and NA-HOM groups). For the baseline (BSL) condition, rats were homogenized within the same strain (MN-BSL and NA-BSL). Systolic blood pressure (SBP) was measured every month. Faeces were collected for microbiota metataxonomic analysis using next generation sequencing of 16S ribosome encoding DNA. Expressions of renal sodium transporters were evaluated by westernblot utilizing kidney samples from those rats.
Results
At 5 months age, MN-HOM showed a significantly enhanced SBP compared to MN-BSL, suggesting that homogenization did have impact on SBP in MN rats. In contrast, there was no difference in the average SBP between NA-BSL and NA-HOM. The SBP of MN-HOM was still significantly lower than both the NA-BSL and NA-HOM groups. Different gut microbiota compositions were observed in the two strains of rats at baseline, and HOM altered both. Westernblot analyses for the screening of the renal sodium transporters possibly associated with the enhanced SBP in MN-HOM revealed the upregulation of a-ENaC in the cortex of MN-HOM with respect to MN-BSL. Putative role of ENaC on enhanced SBP in MN-HOM was further suggested by amiloride challenging on these rats, in which MN-HOM showed a reduction in SBP comparable to MN-BSL after amiloride treatment.
Conclusion
We have demonstrated that the hypertensive phenotype in NA rats was transferred to MN rats through homogenization, indicating that the intestinal microbiota or metabolites derived therefrom could modulate ENaC in the cortex and eventually modulate SBP. Further studies are underway to identify metabolites from gut microbiota which may modulate ENaC and eventually blood pressure.

title: #1809 Targeting N -acetyltransferase 10 with remodelin ameliorates renal oxidative stress in diabetic mice
authors: Eun Sil Koh; Mina Son; So Young Lee; Sungjin Chung
abstract:
Background and Aims
N-terminal (Nt) acetylation is known to be a highly abundant co-translational protein modification, but can also be added post-translationally. Recent advances highlight Nt-acetylation as a key factor in many biological pathways and remodelin, a small molecule inhibitor of N-acetyltransferase 10, can reverse the cancerous conditions such as epithelial to mesenchymal transition and hypoxia. This study examined the potential renoprotective effect of remodelin in type 2 diabetic mice.
Method
Four groups of male C57BLKS/J db/m and db/db mice were used. Diabetic and nondiabetic mice were intraperitoneally injected with 1 mg/kg body weight remodelin weekly for 12 weeks, starting at 8 weeks of age.
Results
The amount of albuminuria was significantly reduced in the remodelin-treated db/db mouse group compared to the control group. title: #3377 Not everything is diabetic nephropathy. Analysis of kidney biopsies in type 2 diabetic patients on a 15-year-old cohort
authors: Verónica Ruth Mercado Valdivia; Gilda Carreño Cornejo; Gabriel Ledesma Sánchez; María De Las Cuevas; Raquel Diaz Mancebo; Carmen Bollain Carbonell; Yolanda Hernández Hernández; Yesika María Amezquita Orjuela; Sílvia Caldés Ruisánchez; Ángel Gallegos Villalobos; Rocío Echarri Carrillo; Antonio Cirugeda García
abstract:
Background and Aims
There are predictive models that guide the performance of renal biopsy in diabetic patients in whom there is no clear relationship between kidney pathology and diabetes mellitus. The García-Martín score assigns a score based on the presence or absence of diabetic retinopathy, chronic ischemia in the lower limbs, overweight, insulin dependence, nephrotic proteinuria and microhematuria. A value less than −0.5 is suggestive of non-diabetic kidney disease (NDKD) and greater than 3 is suggestive of diabetic kidney disease (DKD). We analyze this score in our cohort.
Method
Retrospective descriptive study of the clinical-histological findings in all patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus biopsied between 2008 and 2023 in our hospital.
Results
Of the 427 biopsies, 80 were from type 2 diabetic patients, whose characteristics Demographics and clinical-histological results are shown in Fig. 1.
The entire cohort presented significant renal dysfunction, median creatinine of 1.9 mg/dl (IQR, 0.8–11) in the time of kidney biopsy. Proteinuria measured by protein/creatinine ratio was 2700 mg/g (32–7000) and 50% presented microhematuria. All of patients (n:36) with a score less than 1 point (−4 to 0.5) were NDKD, among which the membranous nephropathy, nephroangiosclerosis and IgA nephropathy.
Of the patients with a score greater than or equal to 1 point (n:44), there was only one patient with NDKD, all of whom the rest DKD (n:43) with a Score range between 1 and 3.5 points. Unlike other studies, in our cohort diabetic retinopathy did not predict the presence of DKD (P > 0.88). The histological lesions had greater glomerular involvement, interstitial and vascular in DKD versus NDKD and a high percentage progressed to advanced kidney disease (15%) or initiation of renal replacement therapy (20%).
Conclusion
In our cohort a score less than 1 point had a high specificity for NDKD with a negative predictive value of 100%. Therefore, it reinforces the indication of a kidney biopsy in this group of patients.

title: #1144 Emphysematous pyelonephritis: experience in a tertiary care hospital of Bangladesh
authors: Abdul Latif; Sharmin Moonmoon; Tabassum Samad; Tufayel Chowdhury; Mehruba Alam Ananna; Mohammad Mehfuz E Khoda; Mostarshid Billah; Muhammad Rahim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Emphysematous pyelonephritis (EPN) is an acute and severe necrotizing infection involving kidney parenchyma, collecting system and surrounding tissues. The diagnosis is characterized by demonstrating gas in these areas. Risk factors for EPN include diabetes mellitus, obstruction in urinary flow by stone or tumors and immunosuppression. Clinical presentation of EPN is like acute pyelonephritis. Being an uncommon diagnosis, cases are managed differently and the outcome has improved in previous years. This study was planned to enlist the demographic, clinical, laboratory and imaging characteristics and in-hospital outcomes of patients with EPN.
Method
This was a cross-sectional study, performed at Bangladesh Institute of Research and Rehabilitation in Diabetes, Endocrine and Metabolic Disorders (BIRDEM) General Hospital, Dhaka, Bangladesh from January 2021 to December 2023. Radiologically confirmed [by computed tomography (CT) scan] EPN cases were included in this study. Patients with recent history of genitourinary intervention and patients having fistula between gut and urinary tract were excluded from the study. Patients’ clinical, laboratory and imaging characteristics and in-hospital outcomes were recorded in case record forms from patients’ clinical notes and/or hospital records, at the time of discharge or death, if were any.
Results
Total numbers of patients were 16 with 10 females. Their age ranged between 29 and 67 (mean 57) years. Risk factors for EPN included diabetes mellitus (16, 100%) and kidney stones (3, 18.8%). Common presenting features were fever (16, 100%), loin pain (11, 68.8%), vomiting (10, 62.5%) and dysuria (10, 62.5%). All (16, 100%) patients had leukocytosis and uncontrolled blood glucose (HbA1c >7%). Seven (43.8%) patients were complicated by acute kidney injury (AKI), five (31.3%) had hyponatremia and three (18.8%) were complicated by bacteremia. Escherichia coli (11, 68.8%) was the most common urinary isolate. Class 2 EPN (11, 68.8%) was the most prevalent CT class followed by class 3B (3, 18.8%), class 3A (1, 6.3%) and class 4 (bilateral disease) (1, 6.3%). Besides medical management, four (25%) patients required surgery (open drainage in three, open drainage with double J stenting in one). None required nephrectomy. Duration of hospital stay was eight (range 6–11) days and there was no death.
Conclusion
Female diabetic patients with poor glycemic status were predominant in this EPN cohort. Their common clinical features were fever, loin pain, vomiting and dysuria. Two-fifths of patients had AKI and one-fourth required surgery. Nobody required nephrectomy and there was no mortality in this series.

title: #3948 Differences between in-office and ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) for cardiovascular risk stratification in a cohort of hypertensive patients
authors: Patricia Torres Martínez; ÁngelaGarcía Zuazola; Shehab Sayed; Julian Segura; Enrique Morales Ruiz
abstract:
Background and Aims
cardiovascular risk (CVR) assessment includes in-office blood pressure (BP) measurements, despite its limitations compared to ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM). The aim of this study is to analyze whether such stratification in patients with uncomplicated hypertension (HT) is modified when using ABPM.
Method
this is a cross-sectional study in patients with uncomplicated hypertension. For the assessment of the CVR, we used the grades of HT according to office BP defined in the guides and established equivalent grades when using 24-hour and nocturnal ABPM. The kappa index was used to analyze the concordance between both techniques.
Results
we included 481 patients with uncomplicated HT, 53.0% had >2 risk factors (RF), 40.7% had 1–2 RF, and 6.3% had none. 46.1% of patients presented the same CVR category (kappa index = 0.311; P < 0.001) by in-office BP vs. 24-hour ABPM. Using nocturnal ABPM, the concordance was 40.7% (kappa index = 0.242; P < 0.001). Patients with white coat HT (82%) showed lower CVR when stratified by ABPM. Patients with masked HT (53%) showed higher CVR according to ABPM.
Conclusion
CVR stratification was specially modified based on the way blood pressure was measured. These changes were more evident when dividing the population into the 4 HT phenotypes, being more significant in patients with white coat HT or masked HT. These results highlight the importance of using advanced measurement techniques as ABPM for BP measurement allowing a more accurate CVR assessment, with the prognostic and therapeutic implications that this entails.

title: #1575 Higher dietary potassium intake and a lower dietary Na/K ratio are associated with a lower incidence of new-onset hypertension
authors: Charlotte Zwager; Anne Myrthe van Vliet; Rik Olde Engberink
abstract:
Background and Aims
A diet high in potassium (K) and low in sodium (Na) has been associated with lower blood pressure in the general population. With the advent of potassium-rich salt substitutes it is of interest to investigate how dietary Na and K intake interact in the setting of hypertension prevention. For this purpose, the 24-hour urine Na/K-ratio could be of added value.
Method
We selected adult outpatients of a Dutch tertiary hospital who collected 24-hour urine with Na and K measurements, as a proxy for dietary intake, between 1998–2023. We excluded subjects with a history of renal replacement therapy or hypertension (clinical diagnosis or an office blood pressure of >140/90 mmHg). We used Cox-regression analyses to explore the association between 24-hour urine Na, K or Na/K-ratio and new-onset hypertension. We adjusted for age, sex, diabetes mellitus, history of cardiovascular events and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR).
Results
We included 2104 patients, of whom 54% were female. The mean age of the patients was 46 ± 15 years, 22% had diabetes mellitus, and 9% a history of CVE. Baseline eGFR was 90 ± 29 ml/min/1.73 m². Mean 24-h urine Na was 155 ± 70 mmol/24 h, K was 69 ± 27 mmol/24h and the Na/K-ratio 2.4 ± 1.2 mmol/mmol.
During a median follow-up duration of 12 (2–20) years, hypertension was diagnosed in 32%. Higher 24-hour urine K was associated with a 22% lower risk (HR 0.78 per standard deviation (SD) change, 95% CI 0.95–0.87, p-value < 0.001) for new-onset hypertension, whereas 24-hour urinary Na was not associated with the composite outcome (HR 0.93 per SD change, 95% CI 0.93–1.07, p-value = 0.37). A higher 24-hour urine Na/K ratio was associated with a 19% (HR 1.19 per SD change, 95% CI 1.12–1.28, p-value < 0.001) for new-onset hypertension.
Conclusion
Higher 24-hour urine K and a lower 24-hour urine Na/K-ratio are associated with a lower incidence of new-onset hypertension. These data support the notion that high potassium intake contributes to the prevention of hypertension in the outpatient setting.

title: #2829 Orthostatic blood pressure reduction is associated with renal organ damage in fit elderly patients with arterial hypertension
authors: Alejandra Ramos-Galí; Alex de la Sierra; Anna Oliveras; Pedro Armario; Nadia Ayasreh Fierro; Piedad Arias; Susana Vazquez; Carme Camps; Pere Castellanos; Francesca Calero; Patricia Fernández de la Llama
abstract:
Background and Aims
Blood pressure (BP) has specific characteristics in older patients. We evaluated the association of positional changes in BP during orthostatism with the presence of hypertension-mediated organ damage (HMOD) in elderly fit hypertensive patients.
Method
This was a multicenter and cross-sectional study of 156 hypertensive patients aged 75 ± 5.9 years (49% women). Office and 24-hour central and peripheral BP were measured with an oscillometric device. BP changes induced by the standing position were reported according to the conventional definition of orthostatic hypotension (OH) and as a continuous variable (supine – orthostatic BP). We classified patients into two groups depending on orthostatic BP changes, below or above the median of the distribution. HMOD was assessed as renal (reduction of glomerular filtration rate and/or increase in albuminuria), cardiac [left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH)], and arterial (increased aortic pulse wave velocity).
Results
OH was present in 33 patients (21.1%), whereas orthostatic BP change presented a wide distribution. A total of 145 patients (92.9%) had HMOD (49.3% kidney disease, 48% LVH, and 81.4% arterial stiffness). All patients with OH had HMOD involvement and significantly higher values of all systolic BP estimates. Although OH and HMOD were not significantly associated, the analysis of orthostatic BP changes showed greater renal damage in the group with BP reduction above the median compared to those with BP reduction below the median, after adjustment for age, gender, the presence of previous cardiovascular event, office BP, and alpha-blocker treatment (P < 0.05).
Conclusion
Orthostatic BP reduction is associated with renal damage in elderly fit hypertensive patients.

title: #2053 FTO-mediated m6A demethylation inhibits the senescence of renal endothelial cells in diabetic nephropathy
authors: Feng Liang; Gui Li; Junling He; Kehong Chen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is one of the common microvascular complications of diabetes mellitus, and has become the leading cause of end-stage renal disease. The stress-induced senescence of Endothelial cell is an important pathological basis for the occurrence and development of DN. FTO is a demethylase that can specifically remove the m6A modification on RNA, thereby affecting mRNA metabolism and regulating non-coding RNA. The role of FTO in DN in regulating endothelial cell senescence through m6A modification has not yet been studied.
Methods
The levels of m6A and m6A methylation-related proteins were assessed by immunohistochemistry in renal tissue samples from DN patients. In the kidney tissues of db/db mouse, m6A methylation related proteins were co-stained with endothelial cell markers by immunofluorescence. Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC) with high glucose and high lipid (HG+PA) stimulation were used to simulate the establishment of an in vitro diabetic model. In this vitro HUVEC model, the senescence level was evaluated by SA-β-gal staining. And the expression of senescence biomarkers such as p21, p16, and lambin1 was evaluated by qRT-PCR and WB. Furthermore, the methylation level of HUVEC cells was detected by dot blot. The expression of m6A methylation related proteins was examinated by qRT-PCR, WB, and immunohistochemistry. Finally, FTO knockdown or FTO overexpression in HUVEC cell lines were constructed in vitro, and the effects of FTO on the senescence of HUVEC cells under HG+PA stimulation were analyzed by qRT-PCR, WB, and immunofluorescence staining.
Results
Immunohistochemical staining of kidney tissue of DN patients showed that m6A methylation level tends to be up-regulated, while the expression of FTO is down-regulated, with no significant changes in the expression of METT3, METTL14. The immunofluorescence staining of kidney tissues in db/db mice showed that FTO was co-located with CD31, a marker of renal vascular endothelial cells, and FTO also was co-located with p16.This finding indicates that the downregulation of FTO expression is related to the senescence of endothelial cells. Under the stimulation of HG+PA, the expression levels of SA-β-gal, p21, and p16 increased, and the expression of lambin1 decreased in HUVEC cells. In addition, dot blot results showed that m6A methylation levels were significantly up-regulated, which suggested that the increase of m6A methylation level is associated with the significant downregulation of FTO. In vitro, both qRT-PCR and WB results showed that FTO knockdown promoted the senescence of HUVEC cells and FTO overexpression significantly reversed induced cell senescence under diabetic condition.
Conclusion
This study showed that the expression of FTO in endothelial cells of DN was inhibited, leading to the upregulation of m6A methylation level, which promoted the senescence of endothelial cells. In vitro experiments showed that overexpression of FTO can inhibit the expression of senescence genes and reduce endothelial cell damage. Therefore, FTO can be used as a marker to inhibit endothelial cell senescence and alleviate DN progression.

title: #1203 Blood pressure variability in CKD patients with and without nocturnal hypertension
authors: Artemios Karagiannidis; Marieta P Theodorakopoulou; Fotini Iatridi; Areti Georgiou; Eleni Karkamani; Maria Schoina; Sofia Manti; Erasmia Sampani; Konstantinos Stavropoulos; Pantelis Sarafidis
abstract:
Background and Aims
Nocturnal hypertension is highly prevalent in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and represents a strong predictor of cardiovascular events. Increased blood pressure variability (BPV) is also independently associated with cardiovascular events in these patients. This study examined differences in short-term BPV indices between CKD patients with and without nocturnal hypertension.
Method
This study included 96 patients (73 with and 23 without nocturnal hypertension) who underwent 24-h ambulatory BP measurement. Standard deviation (SD), weighted SD (wSD), coefficient of variation (CV), and average real variability (ARV) of systolic (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) were calculated using validated formulas for the 24-h and the respective daytime (07:00–23:00) and nighttime (23:00–07:00) periods.
Results
24-h, daytime and nighttime SBP and DBP were higher in patients with nocturnal hypertension. During the 24-h period, wSD and ARV for 24-h SBP (wSD, 14.0 ± 3.8 vs 11.7 ± 3.1 mmHg, P = 0.009; ARV, 10.5 ± 2.7 vs 9.2±1.9 mmHg, P = 0.035) and 24-h DBP were higher in patients with nocturnal hypertension. Regarding the daytime period, patients with nocturnal hypertension presented higher daytime SD and ARV for SBP (SD, 14.8 ± 4.0 vs 13.0 ± 3.6 mmHg, P = 0.008; ARV; 10.5 ± 3.2 vs 9.1 ± 2.0 mmHg, P = 0.016) and DBP, with daytime SBP and DBP CV being numerically but not significantly higher (P = 0.110 and P = 0.08 respectively). During the nighttime period, no significant differences between groups were present for all nighttime BPV indices.
Conclusion
CKD patients with nocturnal hypertension have higher systolic and diastolic BPV indices during the 24-h and daytime periods, but not the nighttime period. These findings signify that increased BPV may be responsible for higher cardiovascular risk in CKD patients compared to those without nocturnal hypertension.

Standard deviation (SD), weighted SD (wSD), coefficient of variation (CV), and average real variability (ARV) of systolic (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) were calculated using validated formulas for the 24-h and the respective daytime (07:00–23:00) and nighttime (23:00–07:00) periods.

24-h, daytime and nighttime SBP and DBP were higher in patients with nocturnal hypertension. CKD patients with nocturnal hypertension have higher systolic and diastolic BPV indices during the 24-h and daytime periods, but not the nighttime period. title: #1569 Estimation of sodium intake can be improved by correcting 24-hour urinary sodium for 24-hour urine volume
authors: Rik Olde Engberink; Anne Myrthe van Vliet; Manfred Rauh; Jens Titze
abstract:
Background and Aims
Long-term sodium balance studies demonstrated that 24-hour urinary sodium excretion does not accurately reflect 24-hour sodium intake, which complicates the use of 24-hour urinary sodium measurements for sodium intake estimation. This discrepancy has been linked to infradian rhythms of aldosterone and cortisol, which are responsible for adaptive responses targeted to (renal) water conservation. We hypothesize that correction for these parameters will improve the accuracy of sodium intake estimates.
Method
This is a post-hoc analysis on data from two sodium balance studies that controlled dietary salt intake for 105 (4 men) and 205 days (6 men) at levels of 6, 9 and 12 g/day. We tested whether correcting 24-hour urinary sodium for 24-hour urine volume, 24-hour urinary potassium, 24-hour urinary urea, 24-hour urinary aldosterone, 24-hour urinary cortisol, 24-hour urinary cortisol/cortisone and/or urinary osmolality, increased the accuracy of 24-hour sodium intake estimates using forward selection linear mixed-effects analysis with a random intercept per participant.
Results
The median difference between 24-hour dietary and urinary sodium was 26 mmol (IQR 13–45 mmol). 24-hour urinary sodium explained only 49% of the variance in 24-hour dietary sodium. In 7 out of 10 subjects, 24-hour urine volume was of most added value to the model, after 24-hour urinary sodium, increasing R2 with 0.08 ± 0.03. Including 24-hour urine volume in the model significantly improved the model fit (P < 0.001, marginal R2 0.55). The addition of urinary urea, urinary aldosterone and urinary osmolality also contributed significantly but the marginal R2 only further increased to 0.56. After correction of 24-hour urinary sodium for 24-hour urine volume, sodium intake could be estimated more accurately: the 50-mmol discrepancy between 24h dietary and urinary sodium was reduced from 18% to 8% and the 25-mmol discrepancy from 52% to 40% (P < 0.001, Fig. 1).
Conclusion
In healthy young males, estimation of sodium intake can be improved by correcting 24-hour urinary sodium for 24-hour urine volume.
