title: #1889 Inflammatory mediators predicting eGFR loss in diabetic kidney disease
authors: Beatriz Fernandez-Fernandez; Takehiro Hasegawa; Yuko Saruta; Yun Li Guan; Jinny Sánchez-Rodríguez; Alberto Ortiz
abstract:
Background and Aims
Inflammation plays a critical role in the development and progression of diabetic complications, particularly diabetic kidney disease (DKD). Elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines are frequently observed in individuals with diabetes and are associated with key markers of renal damage, such as reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and increased urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR). Our hypothesis is that inflammation, as evidenced by elevated cytokine levels, significantly contributes to the progression of renal damage in this population. This study aims to examine the relationship between cytokine levels in plasma and urine and the long-term prognosis of eGFR in DKD patients. Clarifying these associations could provide new insights into the inflammatory mechanisms driving kidney function deterioration and inform strategies to improve patient outcomes.
Method
Cross-sectional biomarker analysis with prospective follow-up on laboratory parameters though electronic health records. Ninety-three adults with DKD and 28 healthy subjects were enrolled in this study.
Plasma and urine cytokines levels were mainly measured using Sysmex fully automatic immune analyzer (HISCL-5000 and 800). Biochemical and hematology parameters were obtained from the medical records, and the eGFR was calculated following MDRD-4 equation. The eGFR slope was calculated by dividing the change in eGFR by the number of observation days (median follow-up 2683 days). Data were described in terms of medians and interquartile ranges (IQR) due to non-normal distribution. Two-tailed P values < 0.05 were considered significant. Fisher's exact test, the Steel–Dwass test, and the Mann–Whitney U test was performed using R version 4.0.3 (r-project).
Results
Median age was 66 years. The median hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) level was 7.4%, UACR 123.8 mg/g, and eGFR was 54.4 mL/min/1.73 m². CKD G3–G5 was present in 56%. Plasma levels of IL-5, IL-6, IL-17, PROTEIN-A, CCL20, CXCL9, CXCL13, GDF15, and PROTEIN-B were significantly elevated, while IL-10, CCL5 and TWEAK levels were decreased compared to healthy controls (P < .05 and q <0.1). In urine, IL-6, PROTEIN-A, CXCL13 and TWEAK levels were elevated (P < .05 and q <0.1).
Plasma PROTEIN-A, CXCL9, PROTEIN-B, GDF-15, and urinary IL-18 levels were significantly associated with eGFR, while plasma PROTEIN-B was significantly associated with eGFR slope (P < .05 and q <0.1). Plasma PROTEIN-A and PROTEIN-B differentiated between patients with stable eGFR and those whose eGFR declined, with respective AUC values of 0.76 (cut-off levels 19.1 pg/mL) and 0.77 (cut-off levels 15.4 pg/mL). Higher plasma levels of PROTEIN-B and PROTEIN-A correlated with greater progression to Very High KDIGO risk in patients initially categorized as lower risk.
Conclusion
This study highlights the potential of PROTEIN-B and PROTEIN-A as biomarkers for predicting renal decline in DKD patients.

title: #332 Investigation of aldosterone breakthrough phenomenon after administration of angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI)
authors: Atsuhiro Ichihara; Yasufumi Seki
abstract:
Background and Aims
Administration of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor antagonists reduced plasma aldosterone levels (PACs), but in 30–50% of cases, long-term administration caused re-elevation of PAC, called “aldosterone breakthrough phenomenon.” Angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs) induce elevations in atrial sodium peptides, and atrial sodium peptides suppress the production of aldosterone in adrenal cells. There is no clinical report on the effect of ARNI on this phenomenon, and this study examined the changes in PAC before and after ARNI administration.
Method
We compared PAC before administration and at least 1 year after administration in 58 patients with essential hypertension who continued to receive ARNI at our center for at least 1 year after September 2021.
Results
The subjects were 63.9 ± 14.6 years old, male-to-female ratio 31 : 27, BMI 25.3 ± 4.9, and eGFR 66.6 mL/min/1.73 m2. Both systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) were significantly reduced after ARNI administration (SBP; 147 ± 22 to 132 ± 19 mmHg, DBP; 83 ± 14 to 77 ± 15 mmHg), PAC was significantly reduced and plasma renin activity (PRA) was significantly increased [PAC; 65.7 (3.7–767.2) to 48.1 (4–437) pg/ml, PRA; 1.3 (0.1–16.3) to 2.5 (0.5–27.9) ng/ml/h], 20 of 58 patients (34.5%) had an elevated PAC after 1 year of administration [3 out of 31 patients (9.7%) in those with 60 or more pg/ml of prior PAC value].
Conclusion
At more than 1 year after administration of ARNI, PAC was significantly reduced compared to before administration, suggesting that ARNI may be less likely to cause aldosterone breakthrough phenomenon.

title: #390 Primary hypertension: first cause of thrombotic microangiopathy in patients with malignant hypertension
authors: Milagros Ortiz Librero; Carmen Mon Mon; Maria Sanchez; Carolina Lentisco Ramirez; Santiago Cedeño; Mariano Acuña; Irene Galindo; Sara Fellah; Yeilyn Alicia Sotolongo Lorenzo; Juan Carlos Herrero
abstract:
Background and Aims
Malignant hypertension (mHTN) is defined as very high BP levels accompanied by acute hypertensive retinopathy (exudates and/or hemorrhages with/without papilledema) and/or acute multiorgan damage at other levels (thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), neurological, cardiac) in relation to acute arteriolar injury. The prevalence of TMA associated with mHTN is variable (14–46%) and its presence is associated with a worse renal outcome.
Method
Retrospectively, we investigated the presence of TMA associated with mHTN in a cohort of 42 patients between Feb/2003 and Mar2024. A comparative analysis was performed between patients with and without TMA. Basal characteristics at diagnosis, aetiology of HTN (primary, secondary) and renal and vital patient outcomes were analyzed. Results expressed as median and interquartile ranges (p25–p75). P < 0.05.
Results
-No genetic mutations in the complement regulatory factors were found in the 5 patients in whom the study was performed (4 with MAT/1 without MAT). In two, risk haplotypes in heterozygosity for CFH (H1, H3) were found (1 with MAT/1 without MAT).
-In all patients, the treatment was BP control. In patients in whom a secondary cause was found, the underlying cause was specifically treated.
Conclusion
-In our series, essential hypertension was the most frequent cause of mHTN with TMA.
-Patients with mHTN and TMA had higher SBP figures and a more severe acute renal failure with a greater need for dialysis at diagnosis.
-40% of patients with mHTN and TMA stopped dialysis and 61.5% of them, recovered renal function during the follow-up.
-Treatment was based, in all patients, in blood pressure control. In patients in whom a secondary cause was found, the underlying cause was specifically treated.
-We found no differences in the progression of renal failure or the need for dialysis during follow-up. Renal survival at 5 years was similar in both groups.

title: #1550 Evaluation of the effect of mirabegron on blood pressure and kidney function tests in oak vale medical center patients-LIVERPOOL-UK
authors: Ahmed Omer Elalfy; Ezzeldin Shalaby
abstract:
Background and Aims
Mirabegron is a beta 3-receptor agonist used to treat overactive bladder symptoms including Urinary frequency, urgency, and urge incontinence. The medication is contraindicated in severe hypertension, as most of the patients who use it are old and need long-term uses for this drug, its effect on blood pressure, and kidney function tests should be evaluated. Aim: Assessment of the impact of Mirabegron on systolic and diastolic blood pressure and kidney function tests over 1 year post initiation of the drug.
Method
The study included randomly selected 20 patients divided into 11 females and 9 males who started Mirabegron from 2020–2023 in Oak Vale Medical Centre-Liverpool –UK, after obtaining consent from all participants .Blood pressure and kidney function test including urea, creatinine and GFR were monitored before starting drug use, after 6 months and one year of drug initiation.
Result
Regarding study population, age ranged from 43 to 88 years with mean ± SD of 75.95 ± 11.86. With female predominance with a percentage of 55%. There was a statistically significant positive correlation between age “years” with Systolic BP and blood urea at baseline before the start of Mirabegron and after start. There is no statistically significant difference between males and females according to Systolic BP, Diastolic BP, Serum Creatinine, Blood urea and eGFR. In all patients Regarding Systolic and Diastolic BP there was a highly statistically significant highest mean value of blood pressure at 6 months and one year after Mirabegron compared to baseline before Mirabegron initiation. Regarding Serum creatinine and blood urea there was a statistically significant highest mean value at 6 months and one year after Mirabegron compared to baseline before Mirabegron. Regarding eGFR: there is no statistically significant difference between before and after Mirabegron intake.
Conclusion
Blood pressure and kidney function tests should be monitored before starting treatment with Mirabegron and regularly during treatment, especially in patients with pre-existing hypertension or renal impairment. In addition, Mirabegron should be avoided if systolic BP is above 180 and better not to be given until control Bp.

title: #2003 Fine with finerenone in Croatia—advancing renal care for our diabetic chronic kidney disease patients
authors: Matija Crnogorac; Luka Toric; Ana Strizić; Ivan Durlen; Patricia Kacinari; Ivana Matešić Abramović; Dino Kasumović; Ivica Horvatić
abstract:
Background and Aims
Finerenon has only recently been available in Croatia and it is not reimbursed by the state insurance. We managed to introduce it to therapy to limited number of patients by using approved hospital funds. Up until recently, the tools to fight proteinuric kidney disease in diabetic patients were limited. We aimed to present data on effectiveness of finerenone in treatment of proteinuria in diabetic patients with or without CKD in our center.
Method
We enrolled 26 diabetic patients (20 males) with proteinuria, median age 64,7 years (IQR 37–79). All of the patients but one (who had type 1 diabetes) had type 2 diabetes while all the patients had arterial hypertension and cardiovascular comorbidities. Follow up point was at month 3 after the start of treatment. Most of the patient had finereone for only 3 months in therapy. Also based on the data of FIDELIO-DKD trial, first measured effects of finerenone on UACR were at 4 months of treatment. All of the patients were receiving RAAS inhibitor (either ACE-i or ARBs), 23 patients had prior SGLT2 inhibitor in the treatment and 8 had GLP1 agonist. All of the patients had CKD on the basis of diabetes and hypertension. Non parametric continuous variables were compared using paired t-test.
Results
The median eGFR at the start of treatment was 51.6 ml/min/1.73 m2 (IQR 29.8-103), with initial UACR of 123.62 mg/mmol (IQR 5.2–500), albuminuria of 817.96 mg/l (IQR 9–5040) and potassium levels at the introduction of finerenone of 4.2 mmol/l (IQR 3.5–4.8). During the 3 month follow up point all the patients were alive and there were no cardiovascular events. At the 3 months control point median eGFR was 46 ml/min/1.73 m2 (IQR 17.9–94), median UACR was significantly lower 73.96 mg/mmol (IQR 1.03–398.6; P = 0.007) as well as albuminuria was 296.72 mg/l (IQR 11–1096; P = 0.007). Median potassium levels at the control point were 4.4 mmol/l (IQR 3.1–5.5). There were no reported side effects of the treatment including hyperkaliaemia that would require either stopping treatment or reducing finerenone dosing. Though median values showed significant reduction in albuminuria levels there were two patients that didn't reach the adequate albuminuria reduction. These patients were shown to have unregulated glycemia as well as significantly increased BMI (>35 kg/m2) so these factors are quite possibly influencing finerenone effectiveness.
Conclusion
Finerenone is effective in improving both treatment of CKD and proteinuria reduction in diabetic patients thus potentially reducing the proteinuria driven progression of CKD. The significant effects on albuminuria reduction seen as early as 3 months after the start of finerenone. In our cohort it is worth noting most likely add on effect of finereone to the one of SGLT2i and in some patients of GLP1 agonists. This, as well as the reduction in albuminuria, show that the proactive treatment of diabetic kidney disease is possible. We hope to bring finerenone to more of our patients.

title: #2473 Long-term effects of renal denervation in arterial hypertension: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Federico Napoli; Ifunanya Nnajiofor; Clara Campoverde; Alanís Yael Szyferman; Henrique Neves; Paula Dibo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal denervation (RDN) is a relatively novel therapeutic procedure for reducing blood pressure in patients with resistant hypertension. However, its long-term efficacy and safety in patients with uncontrolled hypertension remains unknown. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the long-term effects of RDN compared to a sham procedure in patients with uncontrolled hypertension.
Method
PubMed, Scopus and Cochrane database were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared RDN with sham procedures in patients with uncontrolled hypertension with a minimum follow up of 1 year and reported the outcomes of (1) defined daily dose (DDD) of antihypertensive medications; (2) in-office and ambulatory 24-hour systolic (SBP) and diastolic blood pressures (DBP); (3) day-time and night-time SBP and DBP; (4) all-cause mortality; (5) major vascular complications; (6) hypertensive crisis; and (7) changes in glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Heterogeneity was assessed using I2 statistics. A random-effects model was used for outcomes with high heterogeneity.
Results
We included 5 RCTs with 1155 patients, of whom 511 (51.5%) underwent RDN. Mean follow-up ranged from 1 to 3 years. RDN resulted in a significant reduction in office SBP (MD −6.35 mmHg; 95% CI −12.58 to −0.13; P = 0.05; Fig. 1A) and DBP (MD −4.16 mmHg; 95% CI −7.26 to −1.05; P = 0 .009; Fig. 1B) compared to sham procedure. However, no differences were observed between the groups in ambulatory 24-hour, day-time, and night-time SBP and DBP. Patients undergoing RDN demonstrated a significantly decreased medication burden, as indicated by a lower DDD (MD −0.74; 95% CI −1.13 to −0.35; P = 0.0002; Fig. 1C). title: #2083 Age-specific relationship between Insulin Resistance and Obesity : a machine learning-based interpretation machine learning-based interpretation
authors: Se Won Oh; Youngro Lee; Kyungjin Kim; Jongmo Seo; Tai Yeon Koo; Myung-Gyu Kim; Sang-Kyung Jo
abstract:
Background and Aims
There has been a threefold surge in the global prevalence of obesity over the last four decades. Obesity is related to the increased risk of cardiovascular and kidney disease. Obesity in the elderly exhibits distinct features, such as sarcopenia and an increased visceral fat mass. We investigate the risk factors for obesity according to age by developing machine learning (ML) model.
Method
We performed ML analysis on 3768 individuals whose age was over 18 from the 2021 Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey dataset. ML predicted individual body mass index (BMI) values, and the predictive values were labeled into normal (BMI<25 kg/m2) and obese (BMI>25 kg/m2). Through 5-fold cross-validation, the performance and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values, representing the feature importance in each sample, were calculated in the test set of every fold and collected.
Results
The Light Gradient Boosting Machine demonstrated reliable prediction, yielding an area under ROC curve of 0.813 (higher than other ML algorithms) and an error of 2.199 ± 1.654. SHAP analysis revealed high importance for Homeostatic Model Assessment for Insulin Resistance (HOMA-IR) and fasting insulin, displaying an increasing trend with higher BMI (Fig. 1a). Important indicators were followed by, systolic blood pressure, alanine-transaminase, uric acid, HDL-cholesterol, hypertension, age and occupation. Age showed the highest interaction with the impact of HOMA-IR. A dependence plot (Fig 1b) illustrated that the impact of high HOMA-IR on BMI was higher in younger adults compared to older adults. Table 1 underscored a significant disparity in obesity ratio between HOMA-IR>5 and HOMA-IR<5, particularly pronounced in individuals under 65 years.
Conclusion
While HOMA-IR is recognized for its significance in BMI and diabetic diseases, this study highlights its prominence over other known BMI-related features. The analysis showed that younger ages with high insulin resistance is more vulnerable to obesity compared to older adults.

title: #3557 Gut derived metabolites as biomarkers of inflammation in incipient diabetic kidney disease
authors: Lavinia Balint-Marcu; Carmen Socaciu; Andreea Socaciu; Adrian Vlad; Florica Gadalean; Livia Oana Milas; Anca Suteanu-Simulescu; Mihaela Glavan; Silvia Ienciu; Maria Mogos; Lavinia Iancu; Ligia Petrica
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is a microvascular complication of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and a major contributor to end-stage renal disease, with detrimental effects on patient quality of life and overall mortality. The hyperglycemic milieu triggers the activation of hemodynamic, metabolic and inflammatory pathways which inevitably lead to the occurrence of DKD. Moreover, in an inflammatory state, gut microbiota releases various toxic compounds that may have an impact on renal structures and functionality. Since albuminuria is not a reliable early disease indicator, the prompt diagnosis of DKD is still an ongoing challenge. This work intends to identify gut-derived metabolites, as potential biomarkers of early DKD, using metabolomic techniques and highlight their relationship with markers of renal inflammation in T2DM individuals.
Method
The metabolomic analysis was performed on blood and urine specimens from 90 T2DM patients, categorized into normal to mildly, moderately, and severely elevated albuminuria, and 20 individuals in good health. The samples were evaluated using untargeted and targeted ultra-high performance liquid chromatography coupled with electrospray-ionization quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UHPLC-QTOF-ESI+-MS) to acquire the metabolites that are specific for the normal to mildly increased albuminuria subgroup. Inflammation was assessed via ELISA technique and consisted of the quantification of various markers from serum and urine such as: interleukin (IL)-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-12, IL-17, IL-18, tumor necrosis factor- α (TNF- α), tumor growth factor-β (TGF- β). The association between gut derived metabolites and markers of inflammation was studied through univariable and multivariable linear regression analyses.
Results
For the normal to mildly elevated albuminuria subgroup, a subset of metabolites expressing biomarker features were identified using UHPLC-QTOF-ESI+-MS targeted analysis and further analytical assessments. Subsequent to univariable analysis, the relevant serum metabolites were found to be the following: arginine (sArg), hippuric acid (sHA), indoxyl sulfate (sIS), butenoylcarnitine (sBCA), sorbitol (sSorb). In parallel, the urine univariable analysis revealed arginine (uArg), butenoylcarnitine (uBCA), indoxyl sulfate (uIS) and p-cresyl sulfate (uPCS), as putative biomarkers. In this study, the following particular associations between serum metabolites and inflammatory indicators were shown by the multivariable linear regression analysis: a high correlation was found between sArg and sTNF- α, sTGF-β, sIL-8 (R2 = 0.4321); sHA has shown a strong association with sTNF- α, sTGF-β, sIL-17, and eGFR (R2 = 0.629); sSorb was correlated with sTNF- α, sIL-17 (R2 = 0.336); sBCA was strongly associated with sTNF- α, and sTGF-β. The following were identified by analysis data as possible urine biomarkers of inflammation in DKD: uArg was linked with uTNF-α, uTGF-β, uIL-8, urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR) (R2 = 0.3676); uHA was associated with uTNF-α, uTGF-β, uIL-10, uACR; uIS has shown strong correlations with uTNF-α, uTGF-β, uIL-6, and uIL-18 (R2 = 0.5330); uBCA was associated with uTNF-α, uTGF-β, uIL-6, and uIL-8 (R2 = 0.5283); uPCS was linked with uTNF-α, uTGF-β (R2 = 0.5416).
Conclusion
This study identified a group of metabolites from serum and urine such as: sArg, sHA, sSorb, sBCA, uArg, uHA, sBCA uIS, uPCS, produced by the intestinal microbiota which could serve as biomarkers of early activation of the inflammatory pathway in T2DM patients suffering from DKD.

title: #2991 Arterial stiffness in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus and excess weight. A cross-sectional study
authors: Eirini Kostopoulou; Marios Papasotiriou; Themistoklis Paraskevas; Evangelos Papachristou; Dimitrios Goumenos; Dionysios Chrysis
abstract:
Background and Aims
The relationship between pediatric obesity or Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) and cardiovascular disease in adulthood is well established, with pathogenesis being already present in childhood. Arterial stiffness is a strong, independent predictor of cardiovascular disease in adulthood. However, data on arterial stiffness in young age and in relation to certain comorbidities are scarce. In this study, we evaluated arterial stiffness indices in children and adolescents with T1DM or excess weight, in order to detect subclinical vascular alterations at a very early stage.
Method
In this cross-sectional study, a total of 199 children and adolescents aged 2–18 years were included. Ninety six participants were diagnosed with T1DM, 49 with overweight or obesity, and 54 were used as healthy controls. Arterial stiffness indices such as pulse wave velocity (PWV), central (aortic) systolic (cSBP) and diastolic (cDBP) blood pressure were measured using the automated oscillometric device Mobil-O-Graph during regular outpatient visits.
Results
Baseline demographic data, except weight, did not differ among groups. Peripheral systolic blood pressure (pSBP) and central SBP (cSBP) were significantly increased in both patients with overweight/obesity and those with T1DM compared to controls. Furthermore, overweight/obesity patients had higher SBP, cSBP and cDBP compared to patients with T1DM, whereas DBP was significantly increased only in overweight/obesity patients compared to controls. Pulse wave velocity values were also significantly increased in both overweight/obesity patients and those with T1DM compared to controls, while overweight/obesity patients had significantly higher PWV when compared to patients with T1DM (Table 1).
Conclusion
Impaired arterial elasticity, expressed as increased cBP, and PWV, was found in children and adolescents with T1DM and overweight/obesity, particularly in the latter. PWV could potentially serve as a screening and diagnostic tool for impaired vascular health and, perhaps, as a prognostic tool for future cardiovascular disease in children and adolescents with T1DM or overweight/obesity.

title: #631 Hyperaldosteronemia and increased interleukin-6 as a cardiovascular risk factors in hemodialysis patients and kidney transplant recipients
authors: Maria Smaliakova; Aleh Kalachyk; Kirill Komissarov
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal replacement therapy prolongs life in patients with Stage 5 Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD). Сardiovascular diseases are the main cause of death in this group of patients. Identification and correction of cardiovascular risk factors improve the quality and increase the life expectancy of patients receiving renal replacement therapy.
The aim of the study was assessment the blood levels of aldosterone and interleukin-6 in patients receiving renal replacement therapy and their association with adverse cardiovascular events.
Method
The study included 52 dialysis patients with Stage 5 CKD. 46.2% (n = 24) of them were men, the average age was 54.6 ± 5.2 years. 50.0% (n = 26) patients underwent donor kidney transplantation, others continued hemodialysis treatment 12 hours a week. The study groups were comparable by gender, age and traditional cardiovascular risk factors (smoking, family history, obesity, hypertension, hyperglycemia, hypercholesterolemia).
Results
For three years of observation 44.2% (n = 23) study patients had adverse cardiovascular events such as acute coronary syndrome, acute heart failure and life-threatening rhythm disturbance. These cardiovascular complications were more common in patients on hemodialysis (57.7% (n = 15)) than in kidney transplant recipients (30.8% (n = 8)), P < 0.05.
Dialysis patients with adverse cardiovascular events more often had episodes of hypotension (40.0% (n = 6) versus 9.1% (n = 1)), increased blood levels of aldosterone (73.3% (n = 11) versus 36.6% (n = 4)) and interleukin-6 (26.7% (n = 4) versus 0.0), P < 0.05, at the time of inclusion in the study than dialysis patients without adverse cardiovascular events.
Kidney transplant recipients did not have such differences. Moreover, six months after kidney transplantation the aldosterone blood level in recipients was 122 (73–240) pg/ml. It was lower than in the preoperative period – 465 (197–1000) pg/ml, P < 0.05. The incidence of hyperaldosteronemia also decreased from 65.4% (n = 17) to 15.4% (n = 4), P < 0.05. An elevated interleukin-6 level was diagnosed in 7.8% (n = 2) patients in the preoperative period and in 3.8% (n = 1) – six months after transplantation, P > 0.05.
Conclusion
Based on the study it was found that the incidence of adverse cardiovascular events in patients receiving renal replacement therapy is high. Patients with adverse cardiovascular events on hemodialysis have a higher preceding incidence of hypotension and elevated blood levels of aldosterone and interleukin-6 than patients without these complications. Kidney transplantation has a positive effect on eliminating these risk factors.

title: #1755 Association between glycated hemoglobin and elevated urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio: a cross-sectional analysis
authors: Vangjelka Kovacheska Shavreska; Jetmir Ziba; Natasha Taleska-Matovska; Olga Caposka; Gjulsen Selim; Tatjana Stojanoska; Aleksandar Poposki; Osman Murtezai; Selami Zhaku; Mervin Zabzun; Sami Mena; Shkelqim Muharremi
abstract:
Background and Aims
Diabetic kidney disease remains a significant global health concern, with microalbuminuria serving as an early marker of kidney damage. The relationship between glycemic control, as measured by glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) is crucial for understanding disease progression and optimizing patient care. This study aimed to investigate the correlation between HbA1c levels and elevated UACR (>30 mg/g) in a cohort of patients, while also examining the distribution of albuminuria severity and its relationship with glycemic control.
Method
A cross-sectional study was conducted on Total patients in study: 78. Elevated albuminuria was defined as UACR >30 mg/g, and diabetes was defined as HbA1c ≥6.5%. UACR values were stratified into three categories: moderately increased (30–300 mg/g), severely increased (300–1000 mg/g), and nephrotic range (>1000 mg/g). Pearson correlation analysis was performed to assess the relationship between HbA1c and UACR in patients with elevated albuminuria. Descriptive statistics were calculated for both parameters, and the distribution of UACR severity was analyzed.
Results
Among the study population, Patients with UACR > 30 mg/g: 56 (71.8%) demonstrated elevated UACR (>30 mg/g). Notably, Patients with elevated UACR and HbA1c ≥ 6.5%: 51 (91.1%) indicating a high prevalence of diabetes in patients with elevated albuminuria. A significant positive correlation was observed between HbA1c and UACR levels in patients with elevated albuminuria (Correlation coefficient: 0.291 P-value: 0.0295 ). The mean UACR in the elevated group was Mean ± SD: 940.5 ± 1806.9 with a median of Median: 234.0. HbA1c levels in this group showed Mean ± SD: 7.7 ± 1.3% with a median of Median: 7.5%. The severity distribution analysis revealed that among patients with elevated UACR, 32 had moderately increased albuminuria (30–300 mg/g), 13 had severely increased albuminuria (300–1000 mg/g), and 11 presented with nephrotic-range proteinuria (>1000 mg/g).
Conclusion
This study demonstrates a significant positive correlation between HbA1c levels and elevated UACR, suggesting that poor glycemic control is associated with higher degrees of albuminuria. The high prevalence of diabetes (91.1%) among patients with elevated UACR emphasizes the substantial overlap between these conditions. The distribution of UACR severity highlights that while most patients present with moderate albuminuria, a considerable proportion (42.9%) exhibit severe or nephrotic-range proteinuria, indicating advanced kidney damage. These findings underscore the importance of regular screening for albuminuria in diabetic patients and suggest that optimal glycemic control might play a crucial role in preventing or slowing the progression of kidney damage. Further longitudinal studies are warranted to establish causality and evaluate the impact of glycemic control interventions on UACR progression.

title: #1068 Establishment of urine-derived tubuloid system from pediatric leukemia patients on methotrexate treatment
authors: Hyeyoun Kim; John Hoon Rim
abstract:
Background and Aims
While nephrotoxicity has been reported across a wide range of medication classes, anticancer drugs are among the most common contributors to acute kidney injury (AKI). Many anticancer drugs exhibit a high rate of renal excretion, making it critical to adjust drug concentrations based on individual renal function to optimize treatment outcomes. Methotrexate, a cornerstone of first-line chemotherapy for pediatric leukemia patients, requires precise dosing to mitigate the risk of drug-induced AKI.
Method
In this study, we established kidney tubular epithelial organoids, also known as tubuloids, derived from the urine of pediatric leukemia patients undergoing methotrexate treatment. Clean mid-voided urine samples were collected from three patients to culture tubuloids and build a biobank of pediatric tubuloid models. Despite variability in methotrexate induction doses, all pediatric tubuloids displayed cystic epithelial structures, distinct from patient-derived tubuloids used as controls.
Results
Ex vivo methotrexate treatment of tubuloids demonstrated dose-dependent increases in renal injury markers, including NGAL, which correlated with clinical outcomes. Additionally, cytotoxicity assays revealed significant inter-individual variability in response to anticancer drugs, considerating the need for careful dosing strategies.
Conclusion
In conclusion, tubuloids derived pediatric leukemia patients effectively mimic anticancer drug-induced renal injury, demonstrating their potential as a platform for integrating clinical and in vitro based data to screen patients at risk of AKI. This newly developed tubuloid-based system offers a promising approach for tailoring chemotherapy dosing to optimize therapeutic efficacy and minimize nephrotoxicity.

Results
Ex vivo methotrexate treatment of tubuloids demonstrated dose-dependent increases in renal injury markers, including NGAL, which correlated with clinical outcomes. Additionally, cytotoxicity assays revealed significant inter-individual variability in response to anticancer drugs, considerating the need for careful dosing strategies.
Conclusion
In conclusion, tubuloids derived pediatric leukemia patients effectively mimic anticancer drug-induced renal injury, demonstrating their potential as a platform for integrating clinical and in vitro based data to screen patients at risk of AKI. This newly developed tubuloid-based system offers a promising approach for tailoring chemotherapy dosing to optimize therapeutic efficacy and minimize nephrotoxicity.

title: #1116 Pericytes mediate renal recovery after acute kidney injury through CXCL12
authors: Yu-Han Shao; Yu-Hsiang Chou; Shuei-Liong Lin
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) causes various complications, including the need for kidney replacement therapy (KRT), progression to chronic kidney disease (CKD), and increased risk of death. Pericytes, mesenchyme-derived perivascular cells, are thought to play a protective role following AKI. Our previous studies demonstrated that pericytes become activated and differentiate into myofibroblasts in animal models of unilateral ureteral obstruction and ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI). Furthermore, we found that inhibiting pericytes during IRI-induced AKI resulted in decreased expression of the C-X-C motif chemokine 12 (CXCL12) gene. CXCL12 has been shown to play a critical role in the recovery from organ injury. However, the role of CXCL12 and its underlying mechanisms in AKI remain poorly understood.
Method
In human study, we measured the plasma levels of CXCL12 of critical ill patients with AKI. In animal study, we used Gli1CreERT2/+;iDTR mice to ablate pericytes. Additionally, we utilized Gli1CreERT2/+; Cxcl12F/F and Tg(UBC-CreERT2); Cxcl12F/F mice to conditionally knock out CXCL12/SDF-1 specifically in pericytes or globally prior to IRI. In vitro, we treated a mouse tubular cell line with recombinant CXCL12 protein.
Results
In the human study, we found that plasma levels of CXCL12 were elevated in critically ill patients with AKI. In the animal study, we demonstrated that CXCL12 was primarily secreted by pericytes, while its receptors, CXCR4 and CXCR7, were expressed on tubular cells during IRI, as shown by in situ hybridization. Furthermore, we discovered that pericyte ablation during IRI-induced AKI worsened tubular cell proliferation, leading to poorer recovery of renal function. Both pericyte-specific and global knockout of CXCL12/SDF-1 impaired renal function recovery after IRI-AKI through mechanisms including renal microvascular rarefaction, reduced proliferation, and increased apoptosis in renal tubular cells. In vitro, CXCL12 was found to stimulate proximal tubular cell proliferation and growth factor production via activation of the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway in both proximal and distal tubular cells.
Conclusion
CXCL12 levels increased after AKI and were primarily expressed in renal pericytes, which contribute to renal repair following IRI. CXCL12 activated the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway, stimulating proliferation and growth factor production in renal tubular cells during IRI-AKI.

title: #276 Shifts in acute kidney injury trends post-alert system implementation: a comprehensive analysis
authors: Jiwon Ryu; Jinyeong Yi; Sejoong Kim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is now recognized as a complex syndrome affecting 10–15% of hospitalized patients and over 50% in ICUs, leading to significant morbidity and mortality. While various early detection methods exist, their clinical implementation has been challenging, leading our team to develop an electronic AKI alert system in 2014 that showed promising initial results in improving AKI detection and outcomes. After a decade, we aim to evaluate the system's continued effectiveness in early detection, prevention of progression, and recovery outcomes.
Method
We conducted a retrospective cohort study at a Korean tertiary care center (2013–2023), analyzing three periods: pre-alert (2013–2014), alert introduction (2014–2019), and continuation phases (2020–2023, COVID period). The study included adult inpatients with serum creatinine (sCr) measurements, excluding those on renal replacement therapy, with end-stage renal disease, in nephrology, who died on AKI onset, or were previously enrolled. The AKI alert system screens for creatinine increases (≥0.3 mg/dl or ≥1.5 times baseline) and notifies physicians via electronic medical record pop-up alerts. We evaluated whether its beneficial effects on overlooked AKI (cases without subsequent sCr measurements after AKI diagnosis), severity progression, and recovery (sCr ≤1.2 times baseline) were sustained over the decade.
Results
During the study periods, 2,915, 6,702, and 3,684 patients were included in the pre-alert, alert introduction, and alert continuation (COVID) periods, respectively. The incidence of AKI showed 9.7% in the pre-alert period, 5.3% in the introduction period and 4.4% in the continuation period. Baseline serum creatinine levels were higher in the post-alert periods (0.9–1.0 mg/dl) compared to the pre-alert period (0.6 mg/dl). Over the decade following system implementation, early nephrology consultation rates increased substantially from 6.1% in the pre-alert period to 19.4% and 17.2% in the introduction and continuation periods respectively (representing a 2.65–3.32 fold increase). The proportion of overlooked AKI cases decreased significantly from 22.2% to 7.4%–8.9% (a 52%–58% reduction). While the progression to severe AKI showed a modest but non-significant decrease in both the introduction and continuation periods compared to the pre-alert period (OR 0.92 and 0.94 respectively), the AKI recovery rates at day 7 showed marked improvement, increasing from 42.9% to 70.2% (representing a 2.04–2.35 fold increase).
Conclusion
The electronic AKI alert system demonstrated sustained effectiveness over a decade, significantly increasing nephrology consultations and reducing overlooked AKI cases. While the system's impact on AKI progression remained modest, it consistently improved recovery outcomes, suggesting its long-term value in enhancing AKI care despite evolving healthcare challenges including the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: #1251 Risk factors and long-term outcomes in a prospective acute kidney injury cohort in Korea
authors: Naye Choi; Ji Hyun Kim; Hee Gyung Kang; Sang Hun Song; Hyun Kyung Lee; Yo Han Ahn
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common complication in severely ill patients, significantly worsening patient outcomes. Its occurrence leads to longer hospital stays and higher mortality rates. Moreover, AKI is a well-recognized risk factor for the development of hypertension, cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease (CKD) later in life. Despite the significance of AKI, there is a lack of longitudinal studies examining kidney outcomes following AKI in children in Korea.
Method
This study included children under 18 who were diagnosed with AKI at Seoul National University Children's Hospital from February 2016 to July 2021. Of the 781 patients, 763 patients were analyzed. The diagnosis of AKI was defined according to the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes guidelines. Participants were followed up at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months post-AKI development, with annual assessments thereafter. During these follow-ups, we measured estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) to evaluate kidney function and overall health. Long-term major adverse kidney events (MAKE-LT) was defined as the occurrence of at least one of the following: all-cause mortality, long-term kidney replacement therapy (KRT, including transplantation or dialysis), or chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 2–5.
Results
Among 763 patients with AKI (442 males [57.9%]; median [IQR] age, 5.8 [0.0–18.9] years), MAKE-LT occurred in 377 patients (49.4%). On multivariable analysis, prematurity (adjusted hazard ratio (aHR), 2.0; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.3 to 3.1, P = 0.002) and chronic kidney disease or kidney disease (aHR, 1.8; 95% CI, 1.1 to 2.7, P = 0.011) were associated with MAKE-LT.
Conclusion
This study provides an in-depth characterization of a prospective AKI cohort in Korea, including baseline demographics, disease etiology, and long-term outcomes. Prematurity and chronic kidney disease were significant predictors of MAKE-LT, highlighting the need for targeted interventions in these high-risk populations.

title: #1113 Monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio changes and mortality in AKI patients on CRRT
authors: Sehyun Jung; Seunghye Lee; Hani Jang; Hyejin Jeon; Jin Hyun Kim; Tae Won Lee; Eunjin Bae; Dong Jun Park; Hyun-Jung Kim; Se-Ho Chang
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a prevalent and life-threatening complication in intensive care units (ICUs), often requiring renal replacement therapy (RRT), with continuous RRT (CRRT) being the preferred modality. The monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio (MLR) serves as a marker of systemic inflammation and immune response and has shown prognostic value in various diseases. This study aimed to evaluate the association between MLR changes over the first three days of CRRT and mortality outcomes in CRRT patients.
Method
We conducted a retrospective study of adult patients diagnosed with AKI who underwent CRRT at our hospital between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2016. Of 920 patients, we excluded those under 18 years of age, with end-stage renal disease, insufficient records, or who died within three days of CRRT. A total of 494 patients were included in the final analysis. Laboratory data were collected, and logistic regression calculated odds ratios for mortality outcomes.
Results
Among 494 AKI patients treated with CRRT, 187 were in the survival group and 307 in the non-survival group. The non-survival group was older (65.7 ± 14.0 vs. 61.8 ± 16.5, P = 0.008) and had higher rates of inotropes use [99.0% vs. 94.1%, P = 0.004] and mechanical ventilation [78.1% vs. 89.9%, P < 0.001]. Logistic regression analysis showed that a higher MLR change was associated with a lower mortality odds ratio of 0.72 (P = 0.03), with consistent results across multivariate models (Table 1).
Conclusion
Changes in the MLR during the first three days of CRRT are associated with mortality outcomes in AKI patients. A greater MLR change indicates improved survival, highlighting its potential as a prognostic marker in critically ill patients. Further studies are needed to confirm these findings.

title: #1175 Regulatory T cells: a promising therapeutic strategy for AKI
authors: Federica Petrillo; Mark Richards; Jack Tuffin; Hernán González-King Garibotti; Matthew Dearman; Aurelie Thomas; Asha Seth; Julie Williams; Pernille B L Hansen; Kevin Woollard
abstract:
Background and Aims
Inflammation plays a crucial role in the injury and repair process following acute kidney injury (AKI). This involves complex interactions between myeloid and lymphoid immune cell subpopulations, and kidney parenchymal cells. However, severe, or persistent AKI can lead to incomplete or maladaptive repair, characterized by prolonged inflammation and continuous tissue damage resulting in CKD or kidney failure. Further research in this field is essential to understand the interplay between pro- and anti-inflammatory actions of immune cell populations in the pathogenesis and progression of kidney diseases. In the current study we aim to assess the therapeutic potential of regulatory T cells (Tregs), a specialized CD4+ lymphoid subpopulation with anti-inflammatory capacity, in acute kidney disease.
Method
C57BL/6J male mice 9 weeks old were intraperitoneally (i.p.) injected with 12.5 mg/kg cisplatin to induce AKI and treated after 24 hours with a single intravenous injection (i.v.) of 3 × 106 murine regulatory T cells (CD4+ CD25+), expanded ex vivo. Plasma Creatinine, Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN) and Kidney Injury markers, KIM-1 and NGAL were analysed. Further work with qPCR and MSD analysis, were used to characterise kidney immune cell subpopulations and cytokine profiles.
Results
Cisplatin-induced AKI mice, treated with Tregs 24 hours after AKI induction showed a significant reduction in plasma Creatinine and BUN levels compared to control mice, as well as decreased excretion of urinary kidney injury markers KIM1 and NGAL. Interestingly, we saw an increase of FOXP3 and CD4 gene expression in kidney tissue, but no effect on IL-6, IL-1b, TNF-α, CCL2 pro-inflammatory cytokines, in plasma, urine and kidney, after Treg transfer, despite potent benefit on kidney function. Further analyses are ongoing to characterize the kidney immune cell and full cytokine landscape.
Conclusion
This data indicates the potential therapeutic efficacy of enhanced anti-inflammatory actions of regulatory T cells in an acute kidney injury mouse model. This data suggests that targeting or the use of Tregs as a promising therapeutic intervention strategy for AKI.

title: #1240 Tamoxifen induces antioxidants to attenuate ischemia-reperfusion renal injury
authors: Yu-Hsiang Chou; Yu-Han Shao; Shuei-Liong Lin
abstract:
Background and Aims
The incidence of acute kidney injury (AKI) is increasing, posing a significant burden on global morbidity and mortality rates. Additionally, AKI serves as a critical risk factor for the development of chronic kidney disease (CKD), with both conditions contributing to substantial healthcare costs worldwide. Despite these pressing challenges, there are currently no effective therapeutic agents available in clinical practice to prevent AKI, lessen its severity, or promote renal recovery. Notably, our research has demonstrated that tamoxifen (TAM), a well-established and widely utilized selective estrogen receptor modulator for breast cancer, exhibits significant protective effects in reducing the severity of AKI.
Method
The ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) model was used to study AKI. In the in vivo experiments, TAM was administered prior to AKI induction. Renal function was assessed, and the proliferation and apoptosis of tubular cells were analyzed. To gain deeper insights, we used the Translating Ribosome Affinity Purification (TRAP) method in conjunction with Pax8 rtTA;LC-1;EGFP-L10a triple-transgenic mice to isolate and sequence mRNA from tubular cells. Single-cell RNA sequencing was also conducted on mice with and without TAM treatment. Furthermore, the oxidative stress resistance capacity was evaluated in mouse renal proximal tubular epithelial cells (MRPTEpiC) treated with TAM.
Results
In the animal model of IRI-AKI, mice treated with TAM exhibited lower plasma levels of blood urea nitrogen and creatinine compared to the non-TAM group. TAM treatment also led to fewer apoptotic tubular cells and an increase in proliferative tubular cells. TRAP and single-cell RNA sequencing analyses revealed elevated gene expression of both oxidase-related and antioxidant factors in tubular cells following tamoxifen administration. Furthermore, in vitro experiments showed that TAM-treated MRPTEpiC cells had an enhanced oxygen radical absorbance capacity.
Conclusion
TAM shows promise in alleviating the severity of IRI-AKI by reducing tubular cell apoptosis. Preconditioning with TAM boosts antioxidative capacity in mice, significantly reducing the severity of subsequent IRI-AKI. These results highlight TAM's potential as a therapeutic agent for AKI prevention.

title: #3354 Temporal trends in acute kidney injury-related mortality across 43 countries, 1996–2021, with projections up to 2050: a global time series analysis and modelling study
authors: Hyeon Seok Hwang; Soeun Kim; Hayeon Lee; Soo-Young Yoon; Dong Keon Yon
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a major global public health concern. However, a major challenge in addressing the AKI burden is the lack of global data on AKI-related mortality and its predictions, leaving significant limitations in understanding its trends over time. Therefore, we aimed to estimate AKI-related mortality rate trends and forecast future deaths.
Method
We evaluated the temporal trends in age-standardized AKI-related mortality from 1996 to 2021 across 43 countries using the World Health Organization Mortality Database, with future projections through 2050. Temporal trends were assessed using locally weighted scatter plot smoother curves based on age-standardized mortality rates, and future projections up to 2050 were calculated using a predictive model that considered attributable risk factors from the Global Burden of Disease Study. This analysis aimed to identify specific patterns of variation in AKI-related mortality rates across different age groups, sexes, income levels (categorized according to the World Bank country classification), and levels of human development (classified according to the United Nations Human Development Index [HDI]). Furthermore, a decomposition analysis was conducted to assess the contributions of population growth, aging, and epidemiological changes to the variations in AKI-related deaths over time.
Results
Age-standardized AKI-related mortality rate per 1,000,000 people remained stable from 1996 to 2021 (10.47 [95% confidence interval, 8.84–12.11] to 9.94 [8.32–11.57]). The overall mortality rate is lower in high-income countries (HICs) than in low-to-middle income countries (LMICs). However, HICs revealed an upward trend in mortality (5.83 [4.21–7.46] to 7.3 [5.66–8.95]), while LMICs demonstrated a decline (19.66 [16.78–22.53] to 15.33 [12.37–18.29]). Similar trends were observed when countries were compared based on the HDI. Increasing trends in age-standardized AKI-related mortality rates among older populations were found in females, HICs, and countries with very high HDI, whereas rates declined in the young population. Future age-standardized AKI-related mortality was predicted to increase gradually (9.94 per 1,000,000 people [8.32–11.57] in 2021 to 11.36 [10.65–12.07] in 2050), and the primary contributor was population aging.
Conclusion
This global time-series and modelling study found that countries with higher socioeconomic status and older populations have increasing trends in age-standardized AKI-related mortality, a trend projected to continue through 2050. This study provides valuable information for developing strategies to reduce the global burden of AKI-related mortality.

authors: Maria Rosa Melero; Andrea Hernández García; Javier Castrodeza; Arturo Bascuñana Colomina; María Rodríguez Benítez; Marian Goicoechea
abstract:
Background and Aims
Long-term mechanical circulatory assist devices are a therapeutic alternative in patients with end-stage heart failure (ESHF).
The HeartMate 3 is a third-generation assist device approved for the treatment of left ventricular dysfunction refractory to inotropic therapy with preserved right ventricular function. This type of device supplements ventricular function, being a valid alternative as destination therapy in patients who are not candidates for cardiac transplantation.
In type II Cardiorenal Syndrome (CRS), chronic cardiac dysfunction leads to chronic progressive deterioration of renal function.
HeartMate 3 may favor the maintenance of renal function in patients with CRS II.
Method
We present a retrospective observational study of patients with ICCT treated with HeartMate 3 as destination therapy, between 2015 and 2023.
We evaluated baseline characteristics, post-implantation complications, survival, acute renal dysfunction during the postoperative period and evolution of renal function, at 3 and 12 months post-implantation of the device.
Results
We recruited 9 patients, mean age 70.1 ± 2.6 years, 55.6% were female, 100% hypertensive, 44.4% had hyperuricemia, baseline renal function with mean cr 1.46 ± 0.55 mg/dl, Fg CKD-EPI 52.15 ± 17.70 ml/min/1.73 m2. 77.8% were receiving chronic inotropic treatment with Levosimendan. 100% had severe left ventricular dysfunction with LVEF<30%, Nt-proBNP 4618 (1958–20000) pg/ml and right ventricular function measured by TAPSE 16 ± 4.95mm, with preimplantation Intermacs Score of 2.2 ± 0.83.

77.8% had some degree of acute renal dysfunction, 33.3% AKI I, 22.2% AKI II and 22.2% AKI III, 1 patient required RRT in the AKI III group, with complete recovery of renal function at 12 months.
Renal function improved significantly at 3 months post-implantation with cr 1.46 ± 0.55 vs 1.10 ± 0.35 P = 0.01 and Fg CKD -EPI 52.16 ± 17.71 vs 67.21 ± 16.19 ml/min 71.73 m2P = 0.02, with no significant change at 12 months cr 1.46 ± 0.55 vs 1.36 ± 0.62, FG CKD EPI 49.32 ± 16.61 vs 46.52 ± 28.36 ml/min/1.73 m2.
The 44.4% presented ICTUS, hemorrhage with analytical repercussion 77.8% and 66.7% had chronic infection of the driveline device, without finding a relationship with renal function.

Conclusion
The HeartMate 3 device, as a target therapy for heart failure, allows stability in renal function to be maintained at 12 months, and may have an impact on the favorable renal evolution of patients with CRS II.

title: #3299 Percutaneous native kidney biopsy performed by nephrologists: safety, desmopressin use and complications
authors: Eva López Melero; Mariana León Póo; Ángel Méndez Abreu; Amir Shabaka; Clara Maria Cases Corona; Deborah Roldan; Enrique Gruss
abstract:
Background and Aims
Percutaneous renal biopsy (PRB) is a reliable and safe procedure for diagnosing kidney disease, providing quick diagnostic capability with a low complication rate.
Haemorrhage is the main complication, with consequences ranging from silent hematomas to severe complications such as embolization and nephrectomy. The incidence of these complications varies widely across studies due to differences in biopsy techniques and post-procedure monitoring protocols.
It has been reported that the presence of renal insufficiency, female sex, cortical thinning, and conditions such as vasculitis or rapidly progressive diseases are associated with a higher risk of complications. Several studies recommend desmopressin in these patients before the biopsy, as it reduces bleeding time and uremic bleeding. However, data on its safety and clinical use are limited.
This study aimed to evaluate PRB complications at our center and the effect of pre-procedure desmopressin administration.
Method
A retrospective observational study was conducted, including 248 patients who underwent renal biopsy at Hospital Fundación Alcorcón between January 2019 and December 2023. Desmopressin was administered to patients with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) below 30 mL/min or an altered primary hemostasis time, at a dose of 0.3 mcg/kg body weight.
Post-biopsy renal ultrasound was performed to assess immediate complications, and all patients remained hospitalized for 24 hours. Before discharge, a blood count was performed, along with a renal ultrasound that was always conducted by the same nephrologist.
Major complications were defined as the need for blood transfusion, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, nephrectomy, embolization, or patient death. Minor complications were defined as a hemoglobin drop of more than two points without transfusion, macroscopic hematuria, arteriovenous fistula, or asymptomatic hematoma.
Results
The mean age of the study population was 60.6 ± 18 years, with 22.6% of patients being over 75 years old. Males accounted for 62.5% of the cohort. The left kidney was biopsied in 95.6% of cases, and two biopsy passes were performed in 57.3% of patients. Desmopressin was administered to 49.2% of the patients. The overall incidence of complications was 22.6% for minor complications and 4.4% for major complications. No cases of nephrectomy or death occurred; three patients required embolization, seven required blood transfusion, and one was admitted to the ICU.
An exploratory analysis of complications was performed, revealing a significant increase in total complications in patients with platelet counts <100,000/µL(P = 0.032) in the multivariate analysis. No significant association was found with antiplatelet therapy, pre-biopsy hemoglobin levels, age, renal function, altered primary hemostasis time, or desmopressin use.
A univariate analysis of major complications showed a significantly higher frequency in anticoagulated patients (P < 0.01) and those with platelet counts <100,000/µL (P < 0.01). In the group of patients who received desmopressin, after adjusting for renal function, no increase in major complications was observed.
Conclusion
PRB performed by nephrologists is a safe procedure with a low incidence of major complications. However, caution should be exercised in high-risk patients, such as those on anticoagulation therapy or with thrombocytopenia. In our study, the incidence of minor complications was high, mainly due to asymptomatic hematomas, which were diagnosed through a routine ultrasound 24 hours after the procedure but had no clinical significance.
Desmopressin use is common in our center and was not associated with an increased risk of complications, despite being administered to patients considered to be at higher risk.

title: #3590 Investigating AKI in ICU trauma patients: incidence, risk rofiles, and outcome implications
authors: Marsida Kasa; Merita Rroji; Nereida Spahia (Zeneli); Alfred Ibrahimi; Silvana Leka; Xhesiana Caushi; Saimir Kuci; Hektor Sula
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a critical complication in trauma patients admitted to intensive care units (ICUs), significantly increasing morbidity and mortality. This study aimed to determine the incidence of AKI, identify associated risk factors, and evaluate its clinical impact in trauma patients admitted to the ICU in the only tertiary Trauma Center ICU of our country.
Method
A prospective observational study was conducted over 9 months, involving 120 trauma patients admitted to a university-affiliated ICU. AKI was diagnosed and staged according to the kidney disease: improving global outcomes (KDIGO) criteria inclusion criteria were age ≥18 years, baseline glomerular filtration rate (GFR) >90 mL/min (to exclude pre-existing chronic kidney disease), and survival beyond the first 3 days of ICU admission. Patients with direct renal trauma were excluded. Descriptive statistics characterized the patient cohort, and comparisons between AKI and non-AKI groups were conducted to assess differences in demographic, clinical, and laboratory variables. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify potential risk factors, while correlations were analyzed between AKI and biochemical markers, antibiotic use, and nephrotoxic drugs.
Results
The cohort had a mean age of 54.5 years (±19.5 SD), with most patients being male (84.7%). Hypertension and obesity were observed in 34.5% of patients each, while diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease were present in 29.5% and 10.6%, respectively. Surgical interventions were performed in 13.9%, while critical care interventions included intubation (70.8%), inotropic drugs (19.4%), and nephrotoxic agents (9.7%).
AKI occurred in 40.28% (60 patients) of patients, classified as KDIGO Stage I (23/60, 37.93 %), Stage II (25/60, 41.38 %), and Stage III (12/60, 20.69 %). Elevated white blood cell counts (>15×10³) and mean arterial pressure (>89 mmHg) within the first 24 hours were associated with an increased risk of AKI. Patients with AKI exhibited higher lactate levels (>2.2) and lower bicarbonate levels (<22 mmol/L) than those without AKI (P < 0.05). ICU stays were significantly prolonged in patients with AKI, with a median survival time of 14 days for AKI Stage I–III compared to 79 days for non-AKI patients. Logistic regression indicated that nephrotoxic agent use (OR: 2.8, 95% CI: 1.1–7.1), lactate levels (OR: 3.2, 95% CI: 1.3–8.4), and bicarbonate levels (OR: 2.1, 95% CI: 1.1–5) were potential predictors of AKI, although the limited sample size reduced statistical significance (P > 0.05). Combining a PLT/Albumin ratio at day 2 with a cutoff of 77.42 and lactate > 2.2 mmol/L in the first 24 hours showed excellent predictive performance for AKI occurrence after day 3, with an AUC of 0.87, sensitivity of 90%, and specificity of 85.7%, highlighting their potential as early biomarkers for AKI in critically ill trauma patients. Additionally, vancomycin and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use showed positive correlations with AKI (P < 0.05).
Conclusion
AKI was a common and severe complication in ICU trauma patients, with significant impacts on resource utilization and patient outcomes. Early identification of risk factors—such as elevated lactate levels, high white blood cell counts, and exposure to nephrotoxic medications—may enable timely interventions to mitigate AKI risk. Additionally, the PLT/Albumin ratio on day 2, combined with lactate levels >2.2 mmol/L within the first 24 hours, demonstrates strong predictive potential for AKI occurrence beyond day 3, with excellent diagnostic accuracy. Larger cohort studies are needed to confirm these findings and improve predictive models for clinical management.

title: #779 From hospital acute kidney failure to chronic renal replacement therapy: a complex patient journey in a public health system
authors: Ana Muñoz Sánchez; Jose Portoles; Leyre Martin Rodriguez; Maria De Valdenebro Recio; Paula López Sánchez; Maria Luisa Serrano Salazar; Maria De San Miguel Marques Vidas
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) occurs frequently and carries adverse outcomes. Our principal aim was to analyze the impact of hospital and community-acquired AKI on renal replacement therapy (RRT) requirement five years post-discharged.
Method
We conducted a retrospective study that includes all patients admitted between 2013–2014 in 8 reference hospitals in a regional health system attending almost 7 million people. We linked the admission data base with a follow-up from the Madrid Registry of Renal Patients (REMER) over the subsequent 5 years. The data were analyzed prior to COVID-19 pandemic to avoid the bias of COVID-19 on acute renal failure.
Admissions were grouped into 3 categories: AKI as the primary diagnosis (community acquired-AKI (CA-AKI)), AKI as an additional diagnosis to another primary diagnosis (hospital-acquired AKI (HA-AKI)) in those admitted by other causes, and admissions without AKI (Non-AKI). Patients aged under 18, previous RRT or women to give birth were excluded. The study was approved by the ethics committee.
Results
Our study includes 277,996 patients, of which 6.7% had pre-admission chronic kidney disease (CKD) and 34.6% had previous comorbidities but without CKD.
CA-AKI accounted for 0.6% of all admissions. We found that it prolonged average stay, increased mortality, and after a mean follow-up time of 459 days, 7.2% of those patients, were admitted to chronic RRT.
HA-AKI group represented 6.1% of all admissions, associating the highest mortality (22.9% vs. 14.4% in the CA-AKI group) and the longest average stay (12.6 days vs. 7.1 days in no AKI). Only 2% of patients initiated chronic RRT after a mean follow-up time of 594 days.
After discharge, 61 patients remained in dialysis program, and after a 5-year follow-up, 434 patients initiated RRT.
In a multivariate model, RRT onset within a 5-year period follow-up was more likely in patients with prior CKD (HR 164.5 [136.6–198.0] CI 95%) or in those without prior CKD who had relevant risk factors such as diabetes or previous cardiovascular events (HR 4.2 [3.3–5.2] CI 95%).
Conclusion
AKI remains a common issue in clinical practice, negatively influencing patients´ morbidity and mortality. It is associated with longer hospital stays, higher mortality, and increases the risk of starting renal replacement therapy in the medium-long term.
We propose areas for improvement in this care pathway, including post-discharge Nephrological follow-up, the inclusion of acute kidney disease (AKD) history in patient records, and a comprehensive analysis of the AKD-CKD-RRT process. Only through these efforts we can define specific protocols and interventions to reduce the long-term AKI impact.

title: #2298 Modeling ischemia-reperfusion injury in kidney organoids
authors: Anna Radajewska; Alina Rak-Pasikowska; Helena Moreira; Aleksandra Piotrowska; Piotr Dzięgiel; Iwona Bil-Lula
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kidney ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) is one of the causes of acute kidney injury (AKI) and kidney transplant injury and complications after replacement therapy. Increased oxidative stress and metabolic alterations lead to cell death and trigger the inflammatory process. Kidney organoids were previously developed to study toxic kidney injury and genetic disorders of a kidney. Here we propose a kidney organoid model of ischemia-reperfusion injury. The aim of this study was to develop a kidney organoid-based model to investigate cell death, specifically focusing on the pro-inflammatory pathway involving caspase 1.
Method
Kidney organoids derived from human induced pluripotent stem cell were used for this study. Kidney organoids were subjected to low oxygen condition (1% O2, 5% CO2, 94% N2, 37°C) and cultured for 5, 24 or 48 hours subsequently moved to standard oxygen condition (21% O2, 5% CO2, 74% N2, 37°C) for another 2 hours to mimic reperfusion phase of ischemia-reperfusion injury. Corresponding control groups were cultured for 5+2, 24 + 2 and 48 + 2 hours in normoxic condition. Later, kidney organoids were harvested for further experiments. Supernatant was collected and frozen both after hypoxia time and after reoxygenation. Pyroptosis-related proteins: caspase 1 was evaluated. LDH activity was measured to assess cell injury along with carbonylated protein content as indicator of oxidative stress. qPCR was performed to determine the expression of KIM-1, Bax, Bcl-1 and p53 gene expression. Apoptosis and necrosis were determined by flow cytometry.
Results
We detected significantly higher activity of LDH in culture medium supernatant after 24 hours and 48 hours of hypoxia plus 2 hours of normoxia (P = 0.0006; P = 0.0173) compared to control groups and enhanced caspase 1 protein content (P = 0.0159; 0.0289). Increased oxidative stress expressed by protein carbonyl concentration was indicated only in the group subjected to hypoxia for 48 hours followed by reoxygenation compared to corresponding control (P = 0.0480). qPCR proved increased KIM-1, p53 and Bcl-1 gene expression in the 48H plus 2N group (0.0286; P = 0.0022; P = 0.0022). However, flow cytometry did not showed significant changes in a percentage of apoptotic and necrotic cells.
Conclusion
We have proven that 48 hours of hypoxia and 2 hours of reoxygenation are the optimal condition to study ischemia-reperfusion injury on kidney organoid model. The selected group showed elevated injury markers and oxidative stress markers. We detected enhanced expression of apoptosis related genes and marker of proximal tubule cells injury.
This work was supported by the National Science Centre, Poland [2021/41/N/NZ3/01692].

title: #2657 Urinary excretion of TNF-a and IL-9 in patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors. Potential application in the subclinical renal damage diagnosis
authors: Javier Tascón; Alfredo G Casanova; Laura Vicente-Vicente; Elena Villanueva Sánchez; Pilar Fraile Gómez; Moisés Pescador; Marta Prieto Vicente; Ana Isabel Morales Martín
abstract:
Background and Aims
Previous studies from our laboratory have shown that treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in monotherapy and in combination with chemotherapy induces subclinical kidney damage evidenced by the excretion of biomarkers such as kidney injury molecule 1 (KIM-1) and albumin, among others. Based on the immune-mediated pathophysiological mechanism of ICIs, the aim of this work was to study the association between the urinary excretion of two urinary biomarkers of inflammatory origin (TNF-α and IL-9) and kidney damage.
Method
This study was carried out following a previously published protocol [1]. Patients treated with ICIs or with the combination of ICIs and chemotherapy were recruited in two Medical Oncology Services. The inflammatory biomarkers interleukin-9 (IL-9) and tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) were analysed in urine samples taken before treatment, before (PRE-3) and after (POST-3) the administration of the third cycle. Patients were classified into: Control group (patients without renal damage) and Cases group (patients with renal damage evidenced by an increase in plasma creatinine concentration, a decrease in glomerular filtration rate or electrolyte alterations compatible with treatment with ICIs) evaluating the first twelve treatment cycles. In addition, correlation analyses were carried out between biomarkers of kidney damage, albumin and NGAL and the inflammation biomarkers, TNF-α and IL-9
Results
The biomarkers TNF-α and IL-9 showed a higher excretion after receiving the third cycle in the Cases group compared to the Control group. ROC curve analysis confirmed the ability of IL-9 to predict kidney damage over the study period. The correlation analysis showed the association of TNF-α with albumin and NGAL at the POST-3 sampling time.
Conclusion
This study highlights the relationship between inflammation and the risk of suffering kidney damage in the field of ICI-based therapy. In this sense, the biomarkers IL-9 and TNF-α could be possible candidates to predict kidney damage associated with these drugs.

title: #3477 Effect of increasing age on pre-renal AKI incidence and severity in dehydrated and normohydrated rats
authors: Giada Carniglia; Noelia Diaz-Morales; Eva M Baranda-Alonso; Annette Düwel; Nuria Martín-Fernández; Joana del Valle Mercado Hernández; Isabel Fuentes-Calvo; Sandra M Sancho Martinez; Carlos Martinez Salgado; Francisco J Lopez-Hernandez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) is a clinical condition that can be exacerbated by factors such as hemodynamic frailty and the combined use of potentially nephrotoxic drugs. A dehydration state associated to a concomitant use of Renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (ACEIs/ARBs), diuretics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)—a combination also known as the Triple Whammy (TW) significantly increases the risk of acute kidney injury (AKI). This study explores the effect of age on the development of AKI incidence and severity in male Wistar rats subjected to dehydration and the TW.
Method
Two- and thirteen-month-old male Wistar rats were divided into three experimental groups:
TW group: with free access to water during the whole experiment receiving TW therapy for two days (oral doses of 0.7 mg/kg/day trandolapril, i.p. doses of 60 mg/kg/day ibuprofen, and of 20 mg/kg/day furosemide).
P48 h + TW group: subjected to acute dehydration by total water deprivation during the 48 h before the administration of TW therapy. This group had ad libitum access to water during TW treatment.
P48 h + TW + R50% group: subjected to 48 h water deprivation followed by 60% water restriction during the two days of TW treatment.
Blood and 24-hour urine samples were collected at basal state (B), after 48 h of water deprivation (D0), and two days after TW therapy (D2). Parameters including body weight, water balance hematocrit, plasma osmolality, creatinine (Jaffe reaction), urea (Jung method) urinary flow, specific gravity, osmolality and creatinine clearance were measured.
Results
After 48 hours of water deprivation, both groups show increased plasma osmolality, reduced urinary flow and concentrated urine with higher specific gravity and osmolality. Two-month-old rats lose 3.2% of total body water, compared to 1.6% in thirteen-month-old rats. These changes are reflected in hematocrit values, which increase significantly in younger rats but remain stable in older ones. No changes in kidney function are observed.
Prolonged, partial dehydration exacerbates the effects of TW causing AKI in some animals, as indicated by elevated plasma creatinine and urea levels. AKI development is confirmed by plasma creatinine values 1.5–1.9 times the base line, per KDIGO criteria. AKI occurs in 87.5% of younger rats in specific groups, while older rats show AKI in 100% of cases in some groups.
Conclusion
These results suggest that age increases the susceptibility to AKI under dehydration and TW use, and that younger rats show variability in renal homeostasis efficiency across individuals.

title: #2210 Extracellular vesicles derived from ITGAM + innate immune cells augmented renal inflammation via activating CD8+ T cells in acute kidney injury
authors: Yuqi Fu; Anran Shen; Yan Bao; Tao-Tao Tang; Bicheng Liu; Linli Lv
abstract:
Background and Aims
Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as critical mediators of immune processes. However, the involvement of immunocytes derived EVs in the pathogenesis of acute kidney injury (AKI) remains largely unclear. This study aims to profile EV subpopulations constituting the renal microenvironment via single EV analysis to delineate the role of critical immunocytes derived EVs in AKI.
Method
Single-vesicle proteomic analysis using a proximity barcoding assay (PBA) was applied to characterize renal EVs in a murine ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) model (35 minutes of unilateral ischemia, sacrifice after 1 day). Surface proteomics of individual EV were captured using DNA-labeled antibody conjugates, converting protein expression into unique DNA barcodes (Fig. 1). Differential proteomic and enrichment analyses revealed distinct EV subpopulations with specialized functions, validated through Western blotting, nanoparticle flow cytometry, and immunohistochemistry. Functional characterization of the most prominent EV subset was performed via immunomagnetic isolation, co-culture assays, flow cytometry, ELISA, and a reporter mouse model, which enabled in vivo EV tracking and elucidated their roles in AKI.
Results
Using cell-specific markers, we traced the origins of EVs in the IRI microenvironment and identified increasing immunocytes derived EVs, predominantly from M1 macrophages, followed by dendritic cells, neutrophils, T cells, and B cells. Tubular epithelial and endothelial cells were the primary sources of EVs among renal parenchymal cells. Matrix analysis revealed eight major EV subpopulations, with ITGAM/HAVCR1-dominant EVs being the most abundant (33.63%). Proteomic analysis uncovered 14 upregulated proteins, with ITGAM emerging as the key protein which linked to T cell cytotoxicity, leukocyte-mediated cytotoxicity, antigen presentation, and positive regulation of immune responses. These findings highlight the potential role of EV subset derived from ITGAM+ innaute immune cells.
ITGAM+ EVs was then purified with immunomagnetic bead isolation which was consequently characterized with nanoscale flow cytometry, identifying macrophages (F4/80+, 60.82%), neutrophils (Ly6G+, 55.64%), and dendritic cells (CD11c+, 34.24%) as primary sources from innate immunocytes. Functional assays demonstrated that IRI kidney-derived ITGAM+ EVs enhanced CD8+ T cell proliferation, with increasing TNF-α and IFN-γ secretion and reduction of IL-10.
Proteomic analysis revealed S100A9 as remarkably upregulated in IRI-derived ITGAM+ EVs, with immunoelectron microscopy confirming its surface localization. Blockade of S100A9 suppressed TNF-α and IFN-γ cytokine secretion. Interestingly, stimulation with ITGAM+EVs induced a significant upregulation of IFN-γ expression in CD8+ T cells compared to recombinant S100A9 protein. Using an IRI model with ITGAM-CD63-PA-GFP transgenic mice, we observed increased secretion of ITGAM+ PA-GFP+EVs colocalized with CD8+ T cells in renal lymphatic vessels, with augmented renal inflammation and CD8+ T cell activation after AKI.
Conclusion
This study profiled immune microenvironment constituted with immunocytes derived EV via single EV analysis in AKI. ITGAM+ EVs derived from immunocytes promoted CD8T cell activation through the membrane protein S100A9, providing new insights into the immune process of AKI.
