title: #2471 Clinical, laboratory, and genetic risk factors of acute kidney injury after on-pump cardiac surgery in adult Caucasians—analysis of the INFLACOR prospective cohort study
authors: Izabella Kuźmiuk-Glembin; MacIej Michał Kowalik; MacIej Brzeziński; Bartosz Słomiński; Krzysztof Pastuszak; Krzysztof Lewandowski; Andrzej Łoś; Romuald Lango; Alicja Dębska-Ślizień
abstract:
Background and Aims
Early postoperative complications following cardiac surgery are critical determinants of long-term outcomes, increasing postoperative mortality, prolonging ICU and hospital stays, and raising healthcare costs. Notably, acute kidney injury (AKI) after cardiac surgery is a major concern due to its association with reduced survival rates and increased risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD). The incidence of post-operative AKI varies widely (5%–42%) and depends on various patient-specific factors as well as specific surgical interventions.
This study aimed to develop a comprehensive risk assessment model for postoperative AKI/MAKE (major adverse kidney events), integrating clinical, laboratory, and genetic predictors. Specifically, the study explored whether single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in BBS9 rs10262995 and GRM7 rs13317787are associated with AKI following cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) in adult Caucasians.
Method
A prospective, observational cohort study: INFLACOR (INFL-ammation, A-fter, C-ardiac, O-pe-R-ation) was conducted. It enrolled adult patients scheduled for planned open-heart surgery with CPB. Patients with off-pump procedures, reoperations, or emergency surgeries were excluded. Clinical data was collected preoperatively, intraoperatively, and postoperatively. Blood samples for biomarkers analysis were collected before and after 18 hours after surgery. The primary endpoint was the occurrence of AKI within first post-surgery day, defined by the KDIGO criteria. The secondary endpoint (MAKE) combined severe kidney function impairment, RRT necessity, and death. The statistical logistic regression models adjusted for potential confounders were created. Out of 561 patients screened, 503 were included in the final analysis. The mean age was 64.6 ± 11.6 years , and 55.9% were male.
Results
The postoperative AKI (stage 1 to 3) occurred in 61 patients (12.1%). Severe AKI (stage 3 according to KDIGO 2012) requiring renal replacement therapy manifested in 13 patients (2.6%). The composite outcome of MAKE was observed in 14.7% of the patients. Preoperative risk factors for AKI included older age (69 vs 65 years, P = 0.02), higher baseline serum creatinine levels (AKI and non-AKI group: 1.06 mg/dL vs. 0.89 mg/dL, respectively; P < 0.001), preexisting CKD (P < 0.001, OR 18, 95% CI 5.4–62.6), and comorbidities such as atrial fibrillation and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (P < 0.05, OR 1.8 and 4.5 respectively). Intraoperative risk factors involved longer surgery duration (5 hours vs. 4.2 hours; P < 0.001), intraoperative transfusions, epinephrine and dopamine use and elevated lactate levels (>2 mmol/l) (Fig. 1). Postoperatively the correlation with AKI/MAKE was found for the increased white blood cell counts, high-sensitivity troponin I/CK-MB levels and higher APACHE III scores (AKI group 43 points vs non-AKI 32 points, P < 0.001). Furthermore longer time of mechanical ventilation or intra-aortic balloon pump were also identified to correlate with AKI/MAKE incidence. Genetic analyses of BBS9 and GRM7 SNPs revealed no significant associations with AKI or MAKE.
Conclusion
This study identifies multiple preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative risk factors for AKI in patients undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass. Despite the exploration of genetic markers, no significant association was found between BBS9 and GRM7 SNPs and postoperative kidney injury. The findings highlight the importance of preoperative screening for kidney function, comorbidities, and the careful management of surgical and postoperative factors to reduce the risk of AKI. Despite the lack of genetic markers predicting AKI, the study provides valuable insights into modifiable clinical factors that could guide the development of a risk model for early intervention in high-risk patients.

title: #3080 Obstructive AKI: post nephrostomy mortality, dialysis, and short-term renal function
authors: Claudia Strazza; Gianfilippo Di Liberato; Camillo Tancredi Strizzi; Gabriele Morettoni; Roberto Iezzi; Giuseppe Grandaliano; Nicola Panocchia; Francesco Pesce
abstract:
Background and Aims
Obstructive Acute Kidney Injury (O-AKI) accounts for 5–10% of all AKI cases but affects up to 20% of elderly individuals, particularly those with cancer. Although O-AKI generally has a more favorable clinical course than other forms of AKI, it is associated with prolonged hospitalization, impaired renal recovery, and increased mortality risk.
This study aimed to identify factors associated with the following in-hospital outcomes in O-AKI patients undergoing nephrostomy: in-hospital mortality, dialysis dependence, and persistent renal damage at discharge.
Method
We conducted a single-center retrospective study of 163 O-AKI patients who underwent percutaneous nephrostomy at Policlinico A. Gemelli, Rome between January 1 and August 31, 2024.
Data on demographics, comorbidities, causes and extent of urinary tract dilation were collected from medical and interventional radiology records. Kidney function was assessed at admission and discharge. Significant variables from univariate analyses were included in multivariate logistic regression models, with separate models for each outcome. Results were expressed as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and statistical significance was set at p < 0.05
Results
Table 1 presents the patient characteristics. Mortality was significantly associated with lower autonomy scores (p = 0.0037), higher BUN levels (p = 0.0013), and lower hemoglobin levels (p = 0.0417). In multivariate analysis, elevated BUN levels at discharge were the strongest predictor of mortality (p = 0.001, OR = 1.05), while autonomy and hemoglobin levels were not independently associated after adjustment.
Persistent renal damage was associated to older age (p = 0.0180), lower autonomy (p = 0.0060), and higher creatinine levels at admission (p = 0.0002). Multivariate analysis identified male sex as a strong predictor of persistent renal damage (p = 0.001, OR = 3.36), while autonomy and creatinine levels showed trends toward significance (p = 0.061 and p = 0.098, respectively).
Dialysis dependence was independently associated with higher creatinine levels at admission (p = 0.02, OR = 1.28). Comparison between patients achieving functional recovery and those requiring dialysis showed significantly higher creatinine levels at admission in the dialysis-dependent group (p = 0.039, Fig. 1).
Conclusion
Despite its treatable causes, O-AKI remains associated with high mortality and morbidity. While nephrostomy resolved obstruction, several clinical factors strongly influenced patient outcomes. Elevated BUN levels at the time of death were an independent predictor of mortality, and lower hemoglobin levels were observed in deceased patients. Male sex was identified as an independent risk factor for persistent renal damage. Additionally, older age, lower autonomy, and higher creatinine levels at admission were associated with an increased risk of persistent kidney injury. The causes of O-AKI, particularly cancer-related cases, did not significantly impact patient outcomes.
Our findings emphasize that O-AKI should not be considered as mere structural interruption of urine flow. Instead, patient-related risk factors—such as age, autonomy, and baseline renal function—must be carefully evaluated when assessing the risk of long-term complications. title: #3528 Contrast media in hospitalized patients with acute kidney injury- renal and clinical outcomes
authors: Alon Bnaya; Razan Said; Linda Shavit
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common condition among hospitalized patients, associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Although intravenous contrast media is frequently used in diagnostic imaging, there is a lack of data in the literature regarding its impact on renal function in patients with established AKI. This study aimed to evaluate renal and clinical outcomes in hospitalized patients with AKI undergoing computed tomography (CT) scans with intravenous contrast media.
Method
This is prospective study included hospitalized patients with AKI who underwent CT scans with or without contrast media (contrast and non-contrast groups, respectively). The primary outcome was defined as renal recovery within 7 days of the CT scan. Secondary outcomes included improvement in kidney function within 72 hours post-CT, length of hospital stay, the need for renal replacement therapy and in-hospital mortality. The primary analysis used inverse probability weighting (IPW) to account for baseline differences. Subgroup analyses were conducted for age, diabetes, congestive heart failure, CKD stage, and AKI etiology. Predictors of recovery were assessed using logistic regression.
Results
A total of 505 patients were included in the study, with 483 analyzed using inverse probability weighting (IPW) (296 in the non-contrast group and 187 in the contrast group). The median age was 76 years (IQR 65–84), 58.6% were male, and 26.1% had a history of chronic kidney disease. On the day of the CT scan, AKI stages were distributed as follows: stage I in 49.5% of patients, stage II in 26.7%, and stage III in 23.8%. The etiology of AKI was primarily classified as pre-renal (43.8%) and acute tubular injury (33.9%). In the IPW-adjusted analysis, renal recovery at seven days was observed in 154 patients (52.1%) in the non-contrast group and 120 patients (64.4%) in the contrast group (P = 0.055). Renal improvement within 72 hours was observed in 67.1% of the non-contrast group compared to 62.2% of the contrast group (P = 0.475), length of hospital stay (median 8 days [IQR 4–17.7] vs. 9 days [IQR 5–22], P = 0.097), dialysis requirement (4 patients vs. 2, P = 0.564), and in-hospital mortality (18.1% vs. 19.3%, P = 0.784) showed no significant differences between the groups. Subgroup analyses revealed no significant interaction between contrast exposure and recovery across age groups, diabetes status, or CKD stages. Non-recovery of renal function within seven days was associated with a higher AKI stage and acute tubular injury as the underlying etiology.
Conclusion
Intravenous contrast administration in hospitalized patients with AKI was not associated with worse renal or clinical outcomes and may be considered safe in appropriate clinical context.

Conclusion
Intravenous contrast administration in hospitalized patients with AKI was not associated with worse renal or clinical outcomes and may be considered safe in appropriate clinical context.

title: #1675 Are ICD-10 codes for acute kidney injury suitable for use in research? Evaluating sensitivity and positive predictive value in Denmark
authors: Sidse Høyer; Uffe Heide-Jørgensen; Simon Kok Jensen; Anton Pottegaard; Christian Fynbo Christiansen
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common and serious syndrome associated with increased morbidity and mortality but may be under recorded in health registers. This study examined the sensitivity and positive predictive value (PPV) of a diagnosis of AKI, compared with laboratory-identified AKI.
Method
In this observational study, we analyzed data from the Danish National Patient Register and Danish laboratory databases from 2007 through 2023. Diagnoses of AKI according to the International Classification of Disease, 10th Revision (ICD-10) were compared with laboratory-identified AKI episodes defined by the kidney disease: improving global outcomes (KDIGO) creatinine criteria. Sensitivity was defined as the proportion of laboratory-identified AKI episodes captured by ICD-10 codes within 30 days before or after the episode's index date, and PPV was defined as the proportion of ICD-10-coded AKI episodes confirmed by the KDIGO criteria within a ±30-day window. Analyses were stratified by sex, age, AKI stage, setting, and comorbidity.
Results
A total of 947,209 laboratory-identified AKI episodes and 80,649 ICD-10-coded AKI episodes were included. The overall sensitivity of ICD-10 coding for AKI was 7.5% (95% CI: 7.4–7.5%), varying by stage (4.0% for stage 1 vs. 21.7% for stage 3) and setting (6.0% for hospital-acquired vs. 8.6% for community-acquired). The overall PPV was 90.6% (95% CI: 90.4–90.9%), with little variation across subgroups. The sensitivity increased from 3% in 2007 to 10% in 2023, while the PPV remained stable (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
ICD-10 codes of AKI demonstrate a high PPV, ensuring accuracy in identifying true AKI cases. However, the low sensitivity implies a substantial risk of underestimating AKI occurrence. Therefore, laboratory test results should be prioritized for AKI identification when available. These results underscore the importance of evaluating the potential biases induced when relying on ICD-10 codes for AKI identification.

title: #1878 Amikacin dosing in pediatrics: virtual population insights into avoiding nephrotoxicity
authors: Felix J Meigel; Ana Catalina Alvarez-Elías; Rasha Hussein; Doris H Fuertinger
abstract:
Background and Aims
Aminoglycosides, such as Amikacin, are the cornerstone to treat severe infections in pediatric patients. Amikacin dosing requires achieving high peak concentrations to ensure efficacy against bacterial strains (up to > 60 mg/L depending on the strain) while maintaining trough levels < 2.5 mg/L to minimize nephrotoxic risks [1]. The minimum effective dose and frequency has been a debate due to the challenges of predicting ontogeny physiological changes. Current dosing schemes often miss peak and trough target levels in pediatric populations [1]. We present an age-stratified in-silico study to evaluate Amikacin dosing strategies in pediatric patients aged 2 to 24 months, focusing on optimizing peak and trough levels within a 24-hour dosing interval.
Method
An in-silico pharmacokinetic (PK) model based on [2] was validated against the clinical study results in [1]. Age-stratified virtual pediatric populations (2–24 months) were generated to account for maturational changes in GFR, weight, and height age-dependence based on growth charts and GFR data derived from (51)Cr-EDTA clearance measurements using a single blood sample method [3, 4]. Virtual populations were created for 2-, 6-, 12-, and 24-month-old cohorts (Table 1). The body surface area was computed using Mosteller's formula. Simulations in Python were conducted to evaluate Amikacin dosing strategies with 24-hour dosing intervals over 5 days of treatment.
Results
Using the standard maximal dosing scheme of 30 mg/kg once daily [1], the simulation shows that the fraction of patients with trough levels > 2.5 mg/L after 24 hours was 61.3%, 19.7%, 4.7% and 1.1% for the 2-, 6-, 12-, and 24-month age cohorts, respectively. Simulations using an optimized 24-hours dosing scheme, designed to maximize peak levels while maintaining trough levels below 2.5 mg/L, revealed a marked age-dependent difference in peak concentrations (Fig. 1). Median peak concentrations after initial administration were 42.5 mg/L, 48.9 mg/L, 50.9 mg/L, and 52.0 mg/L for the 2-, 6-, 12-, and 24-month age cohorts, respectively. A fraction of 6.2% of 2-month-olds and 18.8% of 24-month-olds reached peak levels >60 mg/L after the initial administration. Peak concentrations declined progressively across all age groups over the treatment days. The median peak concentration decreased by 56.4% for the 2-month-olds and 13.8% for the 24-month-olds by day 5 of treatment. Moreover, by day 5, none of the 2-month-olds and 11.4% of the 24-month-olds reached peak concentrations >60 mg/L.
Conclusion
Further dosage stratification of Amikacin by age is necessary in infants due to physiological kidney maturation and other developmental changes. High inter-patient variability emphasizes the need for therapeutic drug monitoring and dose adjustments during the treatment to optimize efficacy while minimizing the risk of nephrotoxicity.

title: #2155 Abiraterone- related renal events: description, risk factors and association with mortality in a Spanish cohort of patients with advanced prostate cancer
authors: Cristina Riaza Ortiz; Marina Pujol Pujol; Marta Rivero Martínez; Javier Puente Vazquez; Natalia Vidal Cassinello; Marta Álvarez Nadal; Marta Calvo Arévalo; Antolina Rodriguez-Moreno; Mercedes Lucía Velo Plaza; Ana I Sánchez-Fructuoso; Clara Garcia Carro
abstract:
Background and Aims
Abiraterone is a hormonal antagonist that inhibits CYP17 used in advanced prostate cancer. Due to its mechanism of action, it diverts steroidogenesis toward aldosterone synthesis, causing secondary hyperaldosteronism (hypertension, hypokalemia, hypernatremia and volume overload). The aim of this study is to determine the incidence of renal events (RE), associated risk factors for RE, and the association of RE with mortality in a series of patients with advanced prostate cancer treated with abiraterone.
Method
A single-center retrospective study including patients with advanced prostate cancer who initiated abiraterone from 1/1/2013 to 31/7/2024, follow-up until 31/12/2024. Renal event defined by: new-onset or worsening hypertension (HTN), acute kidney injury (AKI), electrolyte imbalance (hypokalemia or hypernatremia) and/or volume overload (defined by clinical criteria or initiation/increased diuretic treatment).
Results
79 patients, mean age 76.05 ± 9.50 years; 70.90% had castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) and 89.87% had metastatic disease (M). At baseline, 21.5% presented known CKD (estimated glomerular filtration rate <60 ml/min/1.73 m²), 21.52% had an AKI prior to abiraterone initiation, 55.7% had HTN and 22.78% were on diuretics. Mean follow-up: 17 months (11.25–27.25 months).
At the end of follow-up, 63.29% presented RE (30.38% AKI, 25.52% de novo HTN, 36.71% electrolyte imbalance and 16.45% volume overload). In 4% of cases, RE led to abiraterone discontinuation. Patients who presented RE showed no significant difference in age, baseline CKD, HTN, diabetes or sodium/potassium values compared to those without RE. However, M and prior AKI were significantly more common in patient with RE (M: 98% vs 75.86%, P = 0.0017; previous AKI: 30% vs 6.89%, P = 0.0110). Multivariate analysis showed that HTN and M were a risk factor for RE (HTN: 3.33; 95% CI 1.091–10.206, P = 0.0347; M: 13.3, 95% CI 1.418–124.444, P = 0.0235).
Among patients with AKI (24/79), 33.3% presented KDIGO-AKI stage 2 and 25% stage 3, at a mean time of 18 months (7.25–43 months) after starting abiraterone. No patients required dialysis. Following AKI episode, 50% developed CKD. Patients with AKI had an increased bCr (1 mg/dl vs 0.8 mg/dl, P = 0.027) and presented more frequently HTN (75% vs 43.64%, P = 0.0230). Multivariate analysis showed that HTN was a risk factor for AKI during the abiraterone treatment (OR 3.946; 95% CI 1.127–13.818, P = 0.0318).
Electrolyte imbalance occurred in 36.71% patients at a mean of 10.5 months (4–27 months) after starting abiraterone. Hypokalemia (31.65%) was more common than hypernatremia (11.39%), with mild cases predominating. The mean potassium and sodium levels were 3.2 mmol/L (3.00–3.3 mmol/L) and 145.5 mmol/L (145–148 mmol/L), respectively.
New-onset or worsening HTN appeared in 25.52% patients at a mean of 10 months (2–32.5months) after starting abiraterone. 16.45% patients had volume overload at a mean of 16 months (4.5–37 months) after starting abiraterone; all required diuretic adjustment, but no cases of acute pulmonary edema were reported.
At the end of follow-up, 18.99% of patients died at a mean of 13 months (9–29 months) after starting abiraterone. CRPC and AKI were associated with mortality (CRPC: 93.3% vs 64.1%, P = 0.0310; AKI 60% vs 23.44%, P = 0.041). Multivariant analysis including age, CRPC, M, AKI and RE showed that AKI was a risk of factor for mortality (OR 6.35; 95% CI 1.152–34.957, P = 0.0338).
Conclusion
In a cohort of patients with advanced prostate cancer treated with abiraterone, 63.29% had RE. HTN and metastatic cancer were risk factor for RE. AKI episode occurred in 30.38% patients during treatment and HTN was a risk factor for presenting it. Electrolyte imbalance was usually mild and occurred in 36.71% patients. HTN occurred in 25.52% patients, and volume overload in 16.45% patients. 18.99% abiraterone-treated patients died at the end of follow-up; developing AKI during the treatment increased the risk of death by 6.3 times. Thus, these data highlight the importance of monitoring renal function, electrolytes and blood pressure during the follow-up in patients treated with abiraterone.

title: #3231 Trends of occurrence and mortality in dialysis requiring acute kidney injury
authors: Anne Grethe Tuisk; Mai Ots-Rosenberg; Anne Kuudeberg
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) remains a major global health challenge with high prevalence and significant mortality. However, trends in its prevalence and associated mortality over time are not well known. In 2013, the International Society of Nephrology (ISN) launched the 0 by 25 initiative to eliminate preventable deaths from AKI by 2025. This study aimed to evaluate trends in the occurrence and inpatient mortality of dialysis-requiring AKI patients at a university hospital across two distinct time periods.
Method
This retrospective cohort study analysed patients with dialysis-requiring AKI admitted during two periods: 2009–2011 (Period 1) and 2019–2023 (Period 2). Patient demographics, occurrence rates, and outcomes were compared. Data were extracted from hospital records, and the cases were identified using standardized diagnostic codes.
Results
In total, 318 patients (65.1% men) with dialysis-requiring AKI were identified in Period 1, with a mean age of 61.3 ± 15.7 years for men and 62.7 ± 16.5 years for women. In Period 2, 1493 patients (57.1% men) were identified, with a mean age of 60.6 ± 15.5 years for men and 62.3 ± 16.0 years for women. While the mean age remained stable, the proportion of women increased over time. The annual number of patients with dialysis-requiring AKI rose from 106 per year in Period 1 to 299 per year in Period 2. The proportion of intensive care unit (ICU) dialysis decreased from 67.6% to 42.3%, while the nephrology unit dialysis increased from 19.8% to 50.7%. Inpatient mortality decreased significantly from 33.4% (106 deaths) in Period 1 to 20.7% (309 deaths) in Period 2.
Conclusion
In our centre the occurrence of dialysis-requiring AKI has increased over the past decade, potentially reflecting a higher burden of multimorbidity. Despite this, inpatient mortality has decreased, likely due to improved recognition, management, and treatment strategies of AKI. These findings highlight progress in AKI care while underscoring the ongoing need for continued efforts to reduce its incidence and improve outcomes.

title: #2336 Treatment of acute kidney injury with renal replacement therapy and CytoSorb in critically ill hospitalised patients
authors: Robert Ekart; Maša Knehtl; Eva Jakopin; Tadej Zorman; Tina Stropnik Galuf; Benjamin Dvorsak; Nina Vodošek Hojs; Nejc Piko; Sebastjan Bevc; Radovan Hojs
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common complication in critically ill patients, often caused by sepsis, shock and multiple organ failure. Hemoadsorption with CytoSorb is used in AKI to reduce the high inflammatory burden. CytoSorb is often combined with renal replacement therapies (RRT), such as continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) or intermittent haemodialysis (IHD). The aim of our study was to evaluate the 30-day survival of patients with AKI, all of whom were treated in the intensive care unit (ICU) with RRT and CytoSorb.
Method
This is a retrospective observational study of patients admitted to the medical and surgical ICU between 2015 and 2019. A total of 78 patients were treated with RRT in combination with CytoSorb. Inflammatory and biochemical markers at ICU admission, length of ICU stay, characteristics of RRT and mortality on day 30 after ICU admission were analysed.
Results
The mean age of patients was 56 ± 14.3 years, 57 (73.1%) were men. Forty-eight (61.5%) patients were treated in the medical ICU and 30 (38.5%) in the surgical ICU. The main reasons for ICU admission were septic shock (26.9%), acute respiratory failure (19.2%), cardiopulmonary resuscitation (14.1%), post-operative complications (12.8%), cardiogenic shock (6.4%) and post-operative haemorrhagic shock (5.1%). The most common concomitant diseases were hypertension (46.2%) and diabetes (17.9%). Seventy-four (94.9%) patients required mechanical ventilation. During hemoadsorption with CytoSorb, all patients were treated with CRRT. In most patients (74.4%) only one CytoSorb cartridge was used, in 21.8% of patients two cartridges were used, one patient was treated with three cartridges, one with four cartridges and one patient with 12 CytoSorb cartridges.
Sixty-three (80.8%) patients were treated with CRRT only, the others (19.2%) were also treated with IHD. The mean ICU length of stay was 18.4 ± 18.9 days, and forty-nine (62.8%) patients died during the observation period 30 days after ICU admission. Using an independent-samples T-test, we compared the two groups of patients in terms of survival (Table 1). The patients who survived were younger (50.8 vs. 59.1 years; P < 0.012) and had a longer time of RRT treatment (P = 0.008). We found no statistically significant difference between the two groups in terms of total duration of treatment with CytoSorb (P = 0.348).
Conclusion
ICU patients with AKI treated with RRT and CytoSorb who died during the observation period were older, had lower systolic blood pressure on admission, a shorter duration of treatment with RRT, less ultrafiltration and a shorter ICU stay compared to surviving patients.

title: #94 A data driven digital health approach to improve CRRT delivery in the ICU
authors: Ruben Martinez Raposo; Javier Neyra; Ashita Tolwani; Jin Chen; Sarah Roberts
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a frequent complication in the intensive care unit (ICU). About 15% of critically ill patients with AKI require renal replacement therapy, commonly in the form of continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). This project aimed to develop a data pipeline to feed scalable smart dashboards of patient- and CRRT-relevant data to monitor key performance CRRT indicators and patient outcomes.
Method
We utilized EHR and CRRT device data from UAB from 1/2022 to 2/2024.
Extracted CRRT device data (n = 42 devices). Loaded data from CRRT cards to a secure storage location for data processing. Created an ETL (extract, process, and load) data process in a virtual server environment using Python code to clean and normalize the data. Connected the Python data pipeline to feed the visualization layer via the Tableau cloud server and refresh automatically. Designed specific interactive dashboards with Tableau that exhibit key performance. CRRT indicators that are sustainably trackable on a weekly or monthly basis.
Results
We developed smart dashboards and AI-powered data analytics to support providers in exploring data for multiple use cases including quality assurance, process or clinical outcome predictions and CRRT data to augment support clinical decision-making.
Conclusion
The development of digital health solutions that integrate multimodal data from EHR and CRRT devices is feasible. While this is a key milestone to enable AI-powered CRRT delivery, the impact of these digital health solutions on processes and clinical outcomes needs to be tested with contemporary implementation science tools.

title: #1900 Artificial diuresis, a miniaturized device for ultrafiltration: comparison between animal study and mathematical model to assess ultrafiltration
authors: Anna Lorenzin; Natascha Perin; Massimo de Cal; Alessandra Brendolan; Claudio Ronco; Monica Zanella
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fluid overload is associated with adverse outcome both in heart failure patients and critically ill patient admitted to intensive care. Extracorporeal ultrafiltration represents a solution to avoid acute kidney injury due to fluid overload; for this purpose, an ultrafiltration miniaturized device, named AD-1, has been developed. The reduced priming volume, the low pressures and flow regimes at which it operates makes this device safer and smaller than the conventional machine for renal replace therapy. The device has been already tested in vitro and animal studies have been conducted, no adverse events has been reported.
The aim of this study was to develop an ultrafiltration mathematical formulation capable to mimic the ultrafiltration behaviour of the device. Data collected from the previous animal study were used to validate this model.
Method
The device, named AD-1 (Medica S.p.a, Medolla, Italy), is equipped with a single peristaltic pump that regulates the blood flow and a polysulfone mini-filter MediSulfone (Fig. 1). The transmembrane pressure, the driving force of ultrafiltration, is modulated by blood flow setting (Qb) and the height at which is hanging of the collection bag below the device. The collection bag position is important because this generate a negative pressure inside the ultrafiltration compartment of the filter: higher is the gap between the device and the bag, greater is the negative pressure, increasing transmembrane pressure and thus ultrafiltration rate.
In animal study, three healthy male pigs were prepared and anesthetized. Jugular vein was cannulated with a double lumen catheter (Temporary set double-lumen catheter 11.5 Fr, ref. HD9120105, Bioengineering Laboratories S.r.l.). Six hours ultrafiltration sessions were scheduled for all the animals with a blood flow of 30 ml/min and the collection bag was 20 cm below the device (Fig. 2). Data regarding clinical parameters and the extracorporeal treatments have been collected during the circulation.
The ultrafiltration mathematical formulation is based on hydrostatics and hydrodynamics laws. The parameters considered are blood flow, height of the collection bag, haematocrit, and the geometrical dimensions of the vascular catheter.
Ultrafiltration experimental data were compared with the formulation.
Results
In the animal sessions the ultrafiltration (UF) was in a range of 3–5 ml/min. Average data relating to target UF, observed UF during the animal study and the corresponding estimation derived from the model are reported in Fig. 3.
In all treatments the target value of ultrafiltration was obtained in the absence of major clinical or technical problems with a maximum deviation from the target ultrafiltration rate lower than 10%. Formulation reported a maximum error compared to the experimental data less than 10%.
Conclusion
The model reported data comparable with the results observed in the animal study. The selected parameters and the implementation adequately estimate the UF in the animal model. Data derived from clinical trials will be necessary to further assess and improve the model.

title: #1090 Incidence and adverse outcomes of acute kidney disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Changyuan Yang; Marcello Tonelli; Matthew James; Zhi Tan; Wisanne Bakker; Ronald Gansevoort; Priya Vart
abstract:
Background and Aims
The estimated incidence of acute kidney disease (AKD) and its association with adverse outcomes are heterogeneous, which in part may be due to between-study differences in the definition of AKD. This study aims to summarize these estimates by definitions of AKD and to identify other study-level characteristics that may explain the observed heterogeneity.
Method
We searched MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane and references from eligible studies from inception until February 1, 2024 without language restriction for observational studies that assessed the incidence of AKD and its association with adverse outcomes including all-cause mortality, incident chronic kidney disease (CKD), and kidney failure. AKD definitions were classified as: 1) ADQI/ADQI-equivalent and 2) KDIGO/KDIGO-equivalent. We used random effects meta-analysis to calculate pooled estimates of incidence and outcomes, presented as incidence and odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
Results
Of 1,883 identified reports, 59 studies involving nearly 6 million participants met inclusion criteria. Most studies were classified as having good quality per New-Castle Ottawa scale (n = 44). The pooled incidence of AKD was higher when defined with ADQI/ADQI-equivalent compared with KDIGO/KDIGO-equivalent criteria {27.1% (95% CI: 20.6–35.7%) and 11.2% (95% CI: 7.8–16.1%), respectively (p for difference <0.001)} (Fig. 1). The pooled odds ratio of all-cause mortality associated with AKD was similar whether defined with KDIGO/KDIGO equivalent or ADQI/ADQI-equivalent criteria {3.9 (95% CI: 2.2–6.8) vs. 2.9 (95%CI: 2.0–4.2), p for difference = 0.4} (Fig. 2). After accounting for the baseline AKI status in study populations, both incidence and odds risk of all-cause mortality were similar for the two definitions. For instance, the incidence of AKD was 13.7% and 11.2% and odds ratio of all-cause mortality was 4.2 and 3.9 per ADQI/ADQI-equivalent and KDIGO/KDIGO-equivalent definition, respectively, in cohorts that did not restrict study populations to patients with AKI. Similar results were observed for CKD and kidney failure, except that the association between AKD and kidney failure was stronger for studies using the KDIGO-equivalent definition.
Conclusion
Estimates for AKD incidence and AKD associated risk for clinical outcomes vary by the AKD definition. The application of standardized and harmonized definitions of AKD especially regarding a distinction between study population with and without baseline AKI is essential for establishing AKD burden and informing preventive and management approaches.

title: #2315 TES-AKI-01 preserves renal function in a rat model of ischemia-reperfusion injury
authors: Nicola Giacche'; Francesca De Franco; Cristina Geroni; Paride Liscio; Emiliano Rosatelli; Carolina Colliva; Marco Cipolloni; Gianmario Ciaccioli; Janet Robertson; Roberto Pellicciari
abstract:
Background and Aims
α-Amino-β-Carboxymuconic-ε-Semialdehyde Decarboxylase (ACMSD) is predominantly expressed in the kidney and liver and serves as a branch point in the de novo NAD+ biosynthesis pathway. Prior research has demonstrated that selective inhibition of ACMSD stimulates NAD+ biosynthesis and sirtuin-1 activation and confers protective effects in preclinical mouse models of acute kidney injury (AKI) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH).
This study aims to elucidate the protective effect of intravenous (IV) administration of TES-AKI-01 in a rat model of renal ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) induced AKI.
Method
Male Sprague-Dawley rats were anesthetized and maintained on a heating pad during surgical procedures. Bilateral renal I/R was induced by clamping the renal artery and vein for 35 minutes per kidney, with the kidneys being temporarily returned to the abdominal cavity to prevent desiccation. TES-AKI-01 was administered IV at a dosage a 50 mg/kg one day before I/R, 1 hour before I/R and continuing the treatment at 24h, 48h and 72h after I/R. Blood samples were collected at 24h, 48h and 72h, to quantify plasma creatinine (pCr) and urea nitrogen (pUN) levels. Additionally, cumulative urine volume samples were collected, from 24h to 48h, in metabolic cages for creatinine clearance (CrCl) evaluation.
Results
The I/R injury induced significant elevations of pCr and pUN in the vehicle-treated pathological group, compared to the sham-operated group. The IV administration of TES-AKI-01 at 50 mg/kg significantly reduced the increases in pCr and pUN levels. Furthermore. TES-AKI-01 treatment markedly improved CrCl values, suggesting protected renal function compared to the pathological group.
Conclusion
The pharmacological inhibition of ACMSD with TES-AKI-01 significantly protects from AKI-induced I/R injury. These findings underscore the potential of TES-AKI-01 as a therapeutic candidate for the treatment of AKI.

title: #3651 Extracellular vesicles from the in vitro AKI model promote cardiac cells stress
authors: Raquel Silva Neres Dos Santos; Dylan Burger; Marcela Carneiro-Ramos
abstract:
Background and Aims
Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are blebs released by all cell types, exerting intercellular communication function due to their cargo. EVs have been reported to play a role in the pathophysiology of several diseases, such as cancer, cardiovascular, and renal diseases. However, whether EVs contribute to the pathological crosstalk between the kidney and the heart is unknown. We aimed to characterize EVs from in vivo and in vitro acute kidney disease models and to assess whether they would impact cardiac cellular viability.
Method
C57Bl/6 male mice (uOttawa Animal Facility Protocol: OHRIe3961-A1 and UFABC animal facility commenting number: 9019180122) left kidney were submitted to 60 minutes of warm ischemia and 1 and 8 days of reperfusion (IR1 and IR8). The sham animals (control) only had the left flank opened. HK-2 cells were exposed to hypoxia for 24 hours, followed by 3 hours of reperfusion (HR). The normoxia cells were kept under 21% O2 throughout the HR period. The AKI in vivo model was validated by histological analysis stained with PAS, BUN, and qPCR for KIM-1, and the HR in vitro models were validated by western blot to HIF-1α. EVs were isolated by ultracentrifugation from the plasma and conditioned medium, and characterized by NTA. H9C2 cells were treated with 6000 EVs/ cell from both biofluids for 48 hours, followed by MTT assays. The results were expressed as mean ± standard deviation and analyzed by t-test and ANOVA, in which p-values < 0.005 were considered statistically significant.
Results
The IR results indicated that in 24 hours of reperfusion, there was a high acute tubular necrosis in the left kidney (0% vs 60%) followed by tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis in 8 days (0% vs 73.66%), KIM-1 was upregulated in the left kidney of both 1 and 8 days of reperfusion groups (Sham: 1 ± 1.22 vs IR1: 434.80 ± 192.55, and IR8d: 162.22 ± 84.74), and there was an impairment of the kidney function in 8 days of reperfusion (Sham: 1.66 ± 0.22 vs IR8d: 2.15 ± 0.15). HK-2 submitted to HR expressed 2-fold more HIF-1α than normoxia cells (Normoxia: 1.00 ± 0.11 vs Hypoxia: 1.93 ± 0.81). Regarding EVs characterization, the IR protocol did not induce changes in the total particles/mL (IR1: 2.54 ± 0.52 and IR8: 2.03 ± 0.51 vs Sham: 2.43 ± 0.54) but promoted the particle size (nm) decrease (IR1: 126.33 ± 2.37 and IR8: 128.90 ± 0.86 vs Sham:154.90 ± 4.80). HR-induced HK-2 cells release 2-fold more EVs with bigger sizes (nm) than the control group (Hypoxia: 14.52 ± 7.47 vs Normoxia: 5.30 ± 1.34 particles/mL) (Hypoxia: 183.92 ± 3.90 nm vs Normoxia: 159.55 ± 10.20 nm). Plasma EVs did not affect the cellular viability of H9C2 cells (Sham: 0.94 ± 0.07, IR1: 1.04 ± 0.10 and IR8: 0.98 ± 0.98 vs Untreated: 1.00 ± 0.09), nevertheless, both normoxic and hypoxic EVs induced the reduction of the cellular viability (Normoxia: 0.85 ± 0.02 and Hypoxia: 0.90 ± 0.04 vs Untreated: 1.00 ± 0.04).
Conclusion
The present results indicated the accomplishment of the IR model as well as HR. The characterization results suggested that hypoxia stimulates EVs biogenesis, release in renal epithelial cells, and also modification in the size. The MTT results indicated that EVs caused stress in cardiac cells affecting their viability.

title: #1578 Structured post-AKI follow-up: a nurse-led kidney health check model for improved pharmacological interventions and secondary prevention
authors: Leah Torr; Claire McGuire; Elita Phiri; Riccardo Piscia; Nitin Kolhe; Nicholas Selby
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) is associated with significant long-term risks, including chronic kidney disease (CKD), cardiovascular events, readmissions and increased mortality. However, it remains unclear how best to provide post-discharge hospital care for the large number of patients who have been affected by AKI. A lack of clear guidelines for post AKI care contributes to significant variation in practice, with post AKI clinics differing widely in structure, location, scope and the type of healthcare professional overseeing them. We have developed a model for a nurse-led post-AKI clinic that incorporates standardised assessments linked to management algorithms (together, termed the Kidney Health Check). After testing and refining, we implemented this within a secondary-care nurse-led post-AKI clinic and studied its impact on processes of care.
Method
Between November 2023 and April 2024, 127 patients discharged following an AKI episode attended the nurse-led clinic and underwent the Kidney Health Check (KHC) protocol that included evaluation of kidney recovery, CKD progression, cardiovascular risk factors, and physical functioning. A KHC clinic visit was implemented either at recovery of AKI or at a 90 day time point post AKI. Clinical data was collected from the KHC template including information on AKI episode, blood and urine tests from clinic (estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and urine albumin-creatinine ratio (uACR)), blood pressure, and frailty metrics. The number of pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions that were made as a result of the KHC assessment were recorded.
Results
The mean age of the cohort was 70.8 ± 13 years, 60% were male, and 89.8% had severe AKI (Stage 2/3). The most common causes of AKI were sepsis and volume depletion. At the time of the clinic visit eGFR was significantly lower than pre-AKI levels (61.0 ± 19.8 mL/min/1.73 m² versus 69.8 ± 21.9 mL/min/1.73 m², P < 0.001) and only 59 (46.5%) had recovered to within 10% of baseline serum creatinine by day 90 post AKI. A2/A3 albuminuria was present in 76 (62.8%).
Prior to the clinic and at the time of hospital discharge 48% of patients were prescribed ACEi/ARB therapy, 52.8% were prescribed statins, and 8.7% were on SGLT2i. Following the KHC assessments, ACEi/ARB prescriptions increased to 69.3%, statin prescriptions to 76.4%, and SGLT2i prescriptions to 40.2%. A total of 22 (17.9%) had frailty and over 80% of patients had abnormally low sit-to-stand values. At least one recommendation to care was made in 87 (68.5%) of patients.
Conclusion
These findings highlight the significant burden of long-term health consequences following an AKI episode in an older population, predominantly male, with a high prevalence of severe AKI (Stage 2/3). The decline in eGFR and limited recovery of baseline kidney function underscore the need for ongoing renal monitoring. The nurse-led post-AKI clinic plays a critical role in identifying unmet care needs, implementing evidence-based therapies, and enhancing the overall management of patients recovering from AKI. These findings emphasize the importance of structured follow-up to mitigate long-term complications and improve patient outcomes. As shown here, there are frequently opportunities to improve care. By implementing a structured assessment linked to proactive management algorithms we have shown that a nurse led AKI clinic is effective in improving processes of care and rates of prescribing.

title: #2761 Role of urinary biomarkers in the diagnosis of kidney damage due to immune checkpoint inhibitors
authors: Javier Tascón; Alfredo G Casanova; Laura Vicente-Vicente; Elena Villanueva Sánchez; Pilar Fraile Gómez; Moisés Pescador; Marta Prieto Vicente; Ana Isabel Morales Martín
abstract:
Background and Aims
Nephrotoxicity associated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), although less common than other complications, worsens the patient's prognosis. On the other hand, the diagnosis based on plasma creatinine has limitations. The aim of this study was to investigate the role of urinary biomarkers in the diagnosis of ICI-induced kidney damage.
Method

title: #2927 The predictive ability of β2 microglobulin for survival in ICU patients requiring continuous renal replacement therapy
authors: Gordana Strazmester Majstorovic; Vladimir Đurović; Tijana Azasevac; Sonja Golubović; Nikola Glogonjac; Violeta Knežević
abstract:
Background and Aims
β2 microglobulin (β2M) is a polypeptide found in all nucleated cells and plays an important role in adaptive immunity. It is continuously released into circulation, freely filtered and completely reabsorbed by the kidneys. β2M is associated with various clinical conditions, including malignancies, and chronic inflammatory diseases. Additionally, it predicts adverse outcomes in pulmonary and cardiovascular diseases, as well as in patients (pts) on dialysis.
The aim of study was to evaluate the ability of β2M to predict short-term mortality in pts in Intensive Care Units (ICU) who require continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT).
Method
The research was conducted as an observational, retrospective study on pts requiring CRRT in ICU of the University Clinical Centre of Vojvodina. β2M levels were measured at the beginning of 230 CRRT procedures during the period 2022–2025. Demographic, clinical, survival data, and information regarding kidney function recovery, were collected from medical records. Blood samples for laboratory testing were taken at baseline. Using appropriate statistical tests, we compared β2M levels with various parameters. Based on pts survival at 1 and 3 months after CRRT, we divided pts into groups and compared them. Using the multivariate logistic regression, we assessed the potential of β2M to predict survival.
Results
Patients` median age was 59.5 years (IQR 47–71), with 66.96% men, and 33.04% women. The median β2M level was 12.975 mg/L (IQR 8.92–17.05). Pts who survived 1 month (N = 89) had significantly lower β2M (10.73 mg/L), compared to those who deceased (N = 141) (14.15 mg/L) (P < 0.001). Pts who survived 3 months (N = 75) also had significantly lower β2M (10.38 mg/L), compared to those who deceased (N = 155) (14.15 mg/L) (P < 0.001). When dialysis-dependent pts before the current disease were excluded, those who recovered renal function (N = 87) had significantly lower β2M (10.59 mg/L), compared to those without renal function recovery (N = 143) (13.54 mg/L) (P < 0.001). Pts with malignant diseases (N = 33) had significantly lower β2M (10.6 mg/L), compared to others (N = 197) (13.54 mg/L) (P = 0.018). Pts who had surgery prior to needing CRRT (N = 110) had lower β2M (12.72 mg/L), compared to those without surgery (N = 120) (13.54 mg/L), with the difference being borderline significant (P = 0.050). There was no significant difference between the groups of pts with and without sepsis (12.93 mg/L vs. 13.49 mg/L; P= 0.804), autoimmune disease (10.99 mg/L vs. 13.08 mg/L; P = 0.082), diabetes (13.64 mg/L vs. 12.78 mg/L; P = 0.141), or hemodynamically stabile and unstable pts (13.24 mg/L vs. 12.87 mg/L; P = 0.138). β2M was positively correlated with creatinine (P < 0.001, r 0.367), urea (P < 0.001, r 0.219) and pts` age (P = 0.012, r 0.166). No significant correlation was found with CRP (P = 0.223). PCT (P = 0.464), leucocyte count (P = 0.264), lymphocyte count (P = 0.252), albumin (P = 0.705), erythrocyte count (P = 0.431), hematocrit (P = 0.295), or body weight (P = 0.454).
In the multivariate logistic regression, β2M emerged as a significant predictor for survival at 1 month OR 1.112 (95%, P < 0.001), survival at 3 months OR 1.173 (95%, P < 0.001), and renal function recovery OR 0.898 (95%, P = 0.001), along with the parameters shown in Table 1. ROC curve analysis for overall models demonstrated good predictive ability for survival at 1 month (AUC = 0.846), survival at 3 months (AUC = 0.860) and renal function recovery (AUC = 0.788) (Graph 1). When examining β2M individually, it showed AUC = 0.642, cut-off 12.23 mg/L for survival at 1 month, AUC = 0.687, cut-off 12.23 mg/L for survival at 3 months, and AUC = 0.681, cut-off 14.11 mg/L for renal function recovery.
Conclusion
The median value of β2M for pts in ICU, requiring CRRT was 12.975 mg/L. β2M was lower in pts who survived the first month, as well as pts who survived the first 3 months, compared to non-survivals. Pts who recovered renal function had lower β2M compared with those without renal function recovery. β2M was positively correlated with creatinine, urea, and pts` age. The models including β2M showed good ability for predicting survival at 1 month, survival at 3 months, and renal function recovery.

title: #3780 Outcomes of acute kidney injury in pediatric patients with severe malaria: observations in Khartoum, Sudan
authors: Rasha Hussein; Nahla Allam; Mohamed Yousif; Lin-Chun Wang; Jochen Raimann; Peter Kotanko
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a frequent and significant complication of severe malaria, contributing to its high morbidity and mortality rates, especially in resource-limited settings like Sudan. Despite its high prevalence, there is limited information on the clinical outcomes of malaria-associated AKI. Our study aims to evaluate the outcomes of AKI in Sudanese children hospitalized with malaria-associated AKI with a focus on correlates and predictors of successful clinical recovery.
Method
We conducted a chart review of patients with malaria-associated AKI, treated in a tertiary referral center, the Soba University Hospital (SUH) in Khartoum, Sudan from 2014 to 2023. Descriptive statistics include age, sex, and laboratory parameters at hospital admission (blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, hemoglobin, potassium, sodium, and total white blood cells (TWBCs). Recovery was defined as the normalization of kidney function at discharge. Non-recovery was defined as the development of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and death. We constructed logistic regression models with recovery as binary outcomes and demographic and laboratory variables as predictors.
Results
We included 70 patients in this analysis. Their mean (SD) age was 67.2 (55.5) months, 54.3% were males. Plasmodium falciparum was the leading cause of malaria (90%), mixed infection with plasmodium falciparum and vivax accounted for 10%. Dialysis was initiated in 25 patients (14 hemodialysis, 11 peritoneal dialysis), the remainder received conservative care. Patients who did not recover (N = 20) were older, and at admission had significantly higher levels of creatinine and BUN levels, and lower levels of hemoglobin (Table 1). Multiple logistic regression identified age (odds ratio (OR) 0.98, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.96 to 0.99), hemoglobin (OR 1.81, 95% CI 1.16 to 2.82), and serum creatinine (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.00) as significant predictors of clinical recovery. Recovery was independent of the dialysis modality.
Conclusion
In our study, patient age, along with hemoglobin and serum creatinine levels at hospital admission, were significant predictors of outcomes. Early identification, preferably at the time of admission—of patients with malaria-associated AKI who are at high risk for adverse outcomes, is crucial. Timely recognition allows for the prompt initiation of therapeutic interventions, helping to reduce the severity of AKI, prevent long-term complications, and ultimately decrease mortality rates.

title: #3854 The impact of immunotherapy on renal function in metastatic cancer patients: an unseen challenge in onco-nephrology
authors: Francesco Trevisani; Andrea Angioi; Davide Izzo; Matteo Floris; Arianna Bettiga; Ornella Garrone; Michele Ghidini
abstract:
Background and Aims
Immunotherapy has revolutionized cancer care, improving survival in metastatic renal, bladder, lung, and skin cancers. However, its renal impact, particularly Acute Kidney Disease (AKD)—a potential precursor to CKD—remains underrecognized. Unlike AKI, AKD involves renal dysfunction lasting 7 days to <3 months. This study examines the incidence, persistence, and impact of AKD in patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors.
Method
A retrospective analysis of 165 metastatic cancer patients treated with ICIs assessed kidney function using eGFR trends (CKD-EPI 2021). AKD (KDIGO 2023) was defined as an sCr increase ≥0.3 mg/dL or ≥1.5× baseline for 7 days to <3 months, with persistent AKD exceeding 3 months. Patient data, treatment regimens, and kidney outcomes were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Fisher's exact test.
Results
Descriptive statistics are in Tables 1 and 2. Mean eGFR decline was −5.24 mL/min/1.73 m². AKD occurred in 16.2% of patients. AKD patients had a greater eGFR decline (−15.06 mL/min/1.73 m²) vs. non-AKD (P = 0.001, Fig. 1). AKD was significantly associated with age (P = 0.012). During follow-up, 48% of AKD patients had CKD progression vs. non-AKD (P = 0.0001, Fig. 4). eGFR trends showed greater decline and variability in AKD patients (Figs 2–3). AKD moderately correlated with CKD progression (Pearson R = 0.324, Spearman ρ = 0.324, both P = 0.000).
Conclusion
This study highlights AKD as a common yet underrecognized complication of immunotherapy, with implications for renal and overall patient outcomes. Integrating onco-nephrology into the care continuum may offer critical benefits in managing these challenges.

title: #263 Diet-induced kidney protection—a translational research approach
authors: Luisa Knieps; Sadrija Cukoski; Francisco Lopes; Martin R Späth; Franziska Grundmann; Andreas Beyer; Guenter Schwarz; Dirk Stippel; Christine Kurschat; Volker Burst; Roman-Ulrich Mueller; Felix Köhler
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common complication among hospitalized patients and is associated with significant mortality and morbidity. Although being a frequent and substantial threat, therapeutic and preventive strategies for AKI are still lacking. Importantly, a reduction of cellular stress resistance contributes to the development of AKI in rodents. Protective dietary strategies activate evolutionarily conserved metabolic pathways leading to an increase in cellular stress resistance and may prevent from AKI. However, the successful transfer to the clinic is still lagging behind since the optimal diet for humans and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unknown.
Method
Five established dietary preconditioning protocols—caloric restriction (CR), a fasting-mimicking diet (FMD), a ketogenic diet (KD) and the dietary restriction of either branched-chained amino acids (BCAA) or sulfur-containing amino acids (SAA) - were systematically examined in a. rodent model of renal ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) to quantify diet-induced kidney protection. Based on this effort, the most beneficial dietary interventions were determined and are now examined in a prospective, randomized pilot trial (NCT05709600, DILKID trial) during living kidney donation in humans to elucidate feasibility and safety in humans. In addition, this trial allows to obtain human tissue and biofluids in the context of the beneficial dietary interventions. An integrative multi-layered omics approach including single nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNAseq) is used to delineate the underlying mechanisms of diet-induced kidney protection in rodents and man.
Results
FMD, a low-SAA diet and CR efficiently protect from IRI-induced kidney failure as quantified by survival rates, kidney function and tissue damage in mice. Of note, these beneficial dietary interventions show overlapping changes in cysteine catabolism as a potential underlying mechanism of diet-induced kidney protection. Preconditioning with KD leads to moderate benefits after IRI, whereas BCAA fails to protect from ischemic kidney damage. With regard to humans, more than 50% of participants have been enrolled in the DILKID-Trial to date without any indication towards relevant safety issues. This points towards an overall good feasibility and tolerability of the diets at hand.
Conclusion
Dietary preconditioning with FMD, CR, KD and low-SAA diets effectively protect against renal IRI in rodents. As these diets are feasible in humans, our findings provide an important outlook towards novel protective strategies in the clinic. Based on the identification of an underlying mechanism mediating diet-induced organ protection, our molecular analyses will provide additional information on potential future pharmacological approaches to protect from organ injury in the kidney and beyond.

title: #644 A phase 2b dose finding study to assess the efficacy of RMC-035 on renal function in participants at high risk for kidney injury following open-chest cardiac surgery (POINTER)
authors: Alexander Zarbock; Tobias L Agervald; Michael Reusch; Maxime Laflamme; Andrej Myjavec; C David Mazer; Benoit de Varennes; Johannes Böhm
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common and serious complication of cardiac surgery, potentially leading to the onset or progression of CKD. There are no approved pharmacotherapies for the prevention of AKI or the subsequent development or progression of CKD. RMC-035, a therapeutic variant of the endogenous protein alpha-1-microglobulin, demonstrates nephroprotective effects in numerous preclinical disease models1. Results from the Phase 2a AKITA trial2 indicate that RMC-035 improves long-term kidney outcomes after cardiac surgery. The Phase 2b POINTER trial aims to confirm the findings from AKITA and identify the optimal RMC-035 dose prior to initiating a pivotal Phase 3 study.
Method
POINTER (NCT06475274) is an international, multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial. A total of approximately 160 high-risk patients scheduled for open-chest cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) will be recruited in Europe and Canada. Two RMC-035 dose levels (30 and 60 mg) will be compared with placebo. Study drug will be administered by IV infusion 10 min before CPB, and at 6- and 24-h post-surgery. Patients will be followed daily until day 4, and on days 7, 60, and 90. The primary endpoint is the change in eGFR at day 90 compared to baseline. A key secondary endpoint is major adverse kidney events on day 90 (MAKE90). Other secondary endpoints include the occurrence of AKI, and plasma concentrations of RMC-035. Safety will be assessed by treatment-emergent adverse events, vital signs, electrocardiogram and routine blood biochemistry and hematology parameters.
Results
Not applicable.
Conclusion
In the completed AKITA trial, RMC-035 improved eGFR by day 90 vs placebo, and fewer patients treated with RMC-035 met the secondary MAKE90 endpoint. The eGFR benefit was more pronounced in the predefined subgroup of patients with lower preoperative eGFR (<60 mL/min/1.73 m²). Herein, we present the design of the Phase 2b POINTER trial, aimed at determining the optimal dosing regimen of RMC-035 and confirming its nephroprotective properties prior to a Phase 3 trial. The results are expected to advance our understanding of novel therapeutic strategies for the prevention of AKI and permanent loss of renal function in patients at high risk for AKI following cardiac surgery.

title: #1078 High volume haemodiafiltration outcomes in obese Covid 19 patients with acute kidney injury and respiratory failure
authors: Kunigal Shivakumar; Prasad Rajendran; David Stanley; Darshan Pandit
abstract:
Background and Aims
SARS-CoV-2 Pandemic had a very high mortality in patients with Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) and respiratory failure especially if obese. We present here an outcome data of our patients admitted with stage 3 AKI and respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support treated with intense daily High Volume Haemodiafiltration (HV-HDF).
Method
Patients positive for Covid 19 by RT-PCR during the pandemic in 2020/21, with stage 3 AKI and high BMI (Body Mass Index > 30) admitted to a Teaching Hospital trust in the West Midlands United Kingdom, with respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support were managed with either intensive daily HV-HDF using Fresenius 5008s machine or conventional methods such as Intermittent HD, HDF or CVVHF.
The intensive group had 4 to 5 hours of daily HV-HDF sessions with minimum of 30 liters (aiming > 23L/1.73 m2) substitution fluid; CorDiax, FX1000 and 120 dialyzers were used. Patients with pneumonitis had volume control ventilation with targeted tidal volumes of 4 to 6 ml/kg of ideal body weight. If this modality failed Proportional assist ventilation (PAV) was attempted with proning as required.

title: #2957 Immune checkpoint inhibitors associated acute kidney injury: a case series
authors: Adrien Lengelé; Florian Collard; Tess Van Meerhaeghe
abstract:
Background and Aims
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have become a cornerstone in cancer treatment, improving overall survival in many patients. However, their use is associated with immune-related adverse events (irAEs), including rare but significant renal complications. Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated acute kidney injury (ICI-AKI) can affect kidney function, complicate cancer outcomes, and interfere with ongoing cancer treatment. This study aims to describe our experience in managing ICI-AKI and evaluate long-term outcomes.
Method
This case series includes patients diagnosed with ICI-AKI (defined according to KDIGO criteria), between 2017 and 2025, as confirmed by clinical symptoms or biopsy, excluding kidney transplant recipients. Baseline demographic data, clinical course, management strategies, and outcomes are presented. Kidney function recovery was defined as serum creatinine ≤ 1.5 times baseline creatinine before AKI at 90 days.
Results
We identified 22 patients with ICI-AKI, 54.5% of whom were male, with a mean age of 70.1 ± 9.5 years. The mean interval between the initiation of ICI therapy and AKI onset was 106.5 days (IQR 55–251). The mean interval between the last injection of ICI and AKI onset was 70.5 days. Pre-ICI chronic kidney disease (eGFR < 60 ml/min) was present in 18.2% of patients and the mean of creatinine was 0.98 +/– 0.28 mg/dL. Proton pump inhibitors (PPI) were used in 63.6% of patients, while only a few were on NSAIDs (9.1%) or antibiotics (13.6%) prior to or during ICI therapy. Other irAEs were observed in 54.5% of the cohort. The mean peak plasma creatinine level was 3.2 ± 1.7 mg/dL, and the mean estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) at the time of AKI was 21.5 ± 10.2 ml/min. ICI therapy was withheld in 17 patients, and 18 patients received corticosteroid treatment for a median duration of 74 days (IQR 25–105). Only 2 patients required additional immunosuppression: one with Infliximab for severe Fanconi syndrome, and another with Rituximab for membranous nephropathy. Kidney function fully recovered in 12 patients, partially recovered in 6, and did not recover in 4. Rechallenge with ICI therapy was attempted in 2 patients. In terms of cancer response, 15 patients (68.1%) had an overall response (complete or partial), while 3 (13.6%) had stable disease and 4 (18.2%) had progressive disease. The median survival in our cohort was 3.03 years, with a median time to death of 377 days (IQR 233–781) following ICI initiation. (Fig. 1).
Conclusion
ICI-AKI, although rare, presents as a late-onset complication and is associated with poor renal outcomes and high corticosteroid use. Despite this, the cancer response rate in our cohort was favorable, with an overall response rate of 68.1%. Future studies are needed to optimize the management of ICI-AKI and its impact on long-term patient outcomes.

title: #3494 Incidence and frequency of immune-related nephropathy in patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors: a FAERS analysis (2020–2024)
authors: Aydan Mütiş Alan; Ozkan Alan
abstract:
Background and Aims
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are widely used in cancer immunotherapy, but their use is associated with immune-related adverse events, including immune-related nephropathy. This study aims to evaluate the incidence and frequency of immune-related nephropathy among patients treated with different ICIs, as reported in the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) between 2020 and 2024.
Method
We conducted a comprehensive analysis of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-associated renal adverse reactions using data from the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS). Our study covers the period from January 1, 2020, to December 31, 2024, focusing on ICIs, including anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 agents.
Results
A total of 137,286 adverse events were reported in the FAERS database between 2020 and 2024. Immune-related nephropathy was identified as an adverse event in 6,482 (4.7%) patients. This was most commonly reported in male patients and those aged 65–85 years (57.6% and 50.9%, respectively). Among the immune checkpoint inhibitors, Pembrolizumab was associated with 2,761 cases (5.1%), Nivolumab with 2,424 cases (5.3%), Durvalumab with 257 cases (2.2%), Atezolizumab with 928 cases (3.7%), and Avelumab with 112 cases (4.7%). A statistically significant difference was observed between the immune checkpoint inhibitors (P < 0.01). When grouped by PD-1 and PD-L1 inhibitors, a significant difference in the frequency of adverse events was noted (5.2% vs 3.4%, P < 0.01). No significant difference was found among the PD-1 inhibitors, but a statistically significant difference was observed among the PD-L1 inhibitors [ Avelumab vs Durvalumab, Avelumab vs Atezolizumab and Durvalumab vs Atezolizımab ( p value; < 0.01, 0.01 and < 0.01, respectively)]. Adverse event findings are outlined in Table 1.
Conclusion
Our study demonstrates significant differences in the incidence of immune-related nephropathy among ICIs, with higher rates observed in PD-1 inhibitors and notable variability among PD-L1 inhibitors, highlighting the need for careful renal monitoring in patients receiving ICI therapy.

title: #1617 Risk factors and long-term outcomes of acute kidney disease in hematopoietic stem cell transplant—cohort study
authors: Manuel Lopes Da Silva; Gonçalo Sousa; Carolina Branco; Cláudia Costa; Filipe Cordeiro Marques; Pedro Vasconcelos; Carlos Martins; José António Lopes; Natacha Rodrigues
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney disease (AKD) is a recent definition reflecting ongoing pathophysiological processes following acute kidney injury (AKI). Hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) represents a potentially curative treatment for various types of hematologic cancers, which have seen higher diagnostic rates in recent years. While AKI has been widely studied in the context of HSCT, information on AKD following HSCT remains scarce. This study aimed to determine the cumulative incidence of AKD within the first 100 days after HSCT, identify risk factors for AKD in HSCT, and assess the impact of AKD on 3-year overall survival and relapse-free survival in HSCT patients.
Method
A retrospective cohort study was conducted, considering AKD when AKI was observed and the patient remained in KDIGO stage 1 or higher for ≥7 days, based on creatinine or urinary output criteria. Survival analysis methods considering competing risks were used to identify risk factors and disease-free survival, Cox proportional hazards regression for overall survival, and stepwise regression for multivariable models.
Results
Among the 422 patients included in the study, the cumulative incidence of AKD within the first 100 days after HSCT was 22.9% (95% CI: 19.2%–27.4%). Higher body mass index (HR: 1.05, 95% CI 1.01–1.10; P = 0.034), HCT-Comorbidity Index (HCT-CI) score ≥2 (HR:1.83, 95% CI 1.11–3.13; P = 0.027), allogeneic transplantation (HR: 2.03, 95% CI 1.26–3.33; P = 0.004)), elevated C-reactive protein (HR: 1.01, 95% CI 1.01–1.02; P < 0.001), and exposure to nephrotoxic drugs (HR: 4.81, 95% CI 1.54–4.95; p00.038) were independently associated with AKD. Furthermore, AKD was found to significantly impact 3-year overall survival, conferring a 1.75-fold higher risk of death compared to patients without AKD (HR: 1.75; 95% CI 1.27–2.39; P = 0.001).
Conclusion
This study highlights the significant impact of AKD on 3-year overall survival in patients after HSCT and identifies key risk factors for its occurrence. Therefore, it is crucial to implement preventive measures and establish early interventions for AKI to prevent progression to AKD and its detrimental effects on survival.

title: #3624 Proteinuria-creatinuria index as an early prognostic marker in patients with acute kidney injury
authors: Jorge David Salazar Hurtado; Víctor Ulloa-Galvan; Jose Torres-Cuevas; Mario Eduardo Alamilla Sanchez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is described as the sudden loss of renal function, reflected as an increase in serum creatinine levels and/or a decrease in urine output. AKI is a complication associated with higher mortality in hospitalized patients. Beyond creatinine, a widely used surrogate for glomerular filtration assessment, another marker of glomerular integrity is the proteinuria-creatininuria index (PCI), which has been less studied in the context of AKI.
This study analyzes the proteinuria-creatininuria index in patients with acute kidney injury and its association with early renal outcomes at seven days.
Method
A descriptive, prospective cohort study. Adults ≥18 years with AKI were included. Frequencies, central tendency, and dispersion measures were analyzed for clinical history, sociodemographic variables, and biochemical values. Logistic regression analysis was performed to evaluate the correlation between the proteinuria-creatininuria index and renal outcomes of interest at 7 days of AKI (renal recovery, acute kidney disease, need for renal replacement therapy, and mortality), with a confidence interval (CI) of 95%.
Results
A total of 56 patients were included, with a mean age of 63.3 (±11.59) years; 35 were men (62.5%), 44 had a history of systemic arterial hypertension (78.6%), 24 had diabetes (42.9%), and 9 had chronic kidney disease (16.1%). A PCI > 0.3 mg/mg was documented in 29 patients (51.78%). The median PCI in patients with renal recovery at 7 days was 0.24 mg/mg (0.11–0.59) vs. 1.33 mg/mg (0.50–2.26) in patients without renal recovery. An odds ratio (OR) of 5.66 (95% CI: 1.51–21.24) was documented for renal recovery at 7 days in patients with PCI < 0.3 mg/mg.
Conclusion
In this study, we found that a proteinuria-creatininuria index lower than 0.3 mg/mg is associated with a higher probability of renal recovery at 7 days. This may be explained by a greater ability to restore tubular reabsorption capacity, which has significant implications for the nephrological recovery process.

title: #1541 Development of new method for continuous kidney replacement therapy weaning
authors: Won Min Hwang; Ji Won Lee; Yohan Park; Sung-Ro Yun; Se-Hee Yoon; Sua Lee
abstract:
Background and Aims
The discontinuation of continuous kidney replacement therapy (CKRT) lacks a well-established protocol. Creatinine and cystatin C (CysC) are well-known markers of kidney function, with molecular weights of 113 Da and 13.3 kDa, respectively. This study aimed to develop a novel CKRT discontinuation protocol by predicting kidney function using changes in serum cystatin C (CysC) levels after switching the CKRT mode to continuous veno-venous hemodialysis (CVVHD), which has a lower clearance rate for middle molecular weight solutes.
Method
We hypothesized that CysC would be affected by the change from continuous veno-venous hemodia-filtration (CVVHDF) mode to CVVHD mode, given that CVVHD has lower clearance of middle molecular weight solutes compared to CVVHDF, unlike crea-tinine. Therefore, we aimed to assess kidney function recovery by monitoring periodic changes in serum CysC levels after switching from CVVHDF mode to CVVHD mode (Fig. 1). This study included 17 patients undergoing CKRT. Patients who maintained stable vital signs without vasopressor support were switched from CVVHDF to CVVHD. Serum creatinine and CysC levels were measured at 6, 12, and 24 hours after switching to CVVHD mode, along with daily urine output. Kidney replacement therapy (KRT) reinitiation was defined as the resumption of KRT within 7 days after discontinuing CKRT.
Results
Out of 17 patients, 7 experienced KRT reinitiation. Following the switch to CVVHD mode, serum creatinine levels remained stable or decreased in all patients, whereas an increase in serum CysC was observed in the KRT reinitiated group. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was conducted to predict KRT reinitiation. The 12hr CysC to baseline CysC ratio had the highest area under the ROC curve (AUROC) value of 0.857, with a cutoff value of 0.97. The AUROC value for daily urine output was 0.871, with a cutoff value of 214 mL. A multivariate model incorporating both the 12hr CysC to baseline CysC ratio and daily urine output demonstrated an AUROC value of 0.986, showing exceptional predictive performance for KRT reinitiation (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
The multivariate model using the 12 hr CysC change and daily urine output after switching to CVVHD mode proved to be an excellent predictor of KRT reinitiation. Based on this pilot study, a CKRT discontinuation protocol could be developed, and if validated in larger studies, may lead to a paradigm shift in CKRT discontinuation practices.

title: #2640 Predictive value of the ATRIA score for contrast-induced nephropathy in patients undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention for non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
authors: Sumeyra Koyuncu; Yasemin Dogan
abstract:
Background and Aims
Contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) is a complication that causes significant morbidity and mortality in patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS), even after successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Early identification of high-risk patients is crucial for prognosis. In this study, we aimed to investigate the predictive value of the Anticoagulation and Risk Factors in Atrial Fibrillation (ATRIA) score, an alternative thromboembolism risk scoring model, in the development of CIN in patients with non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) undergoing PCI, independent of atrial fibrillation.
Method
This retrospective study included patients hospitalized in the coronary intensive care unit between 2017 and 2023 with a diagnosis of NSTEMI and treated with PCI. Patients were divided into two groups based on the development of CIN, and their clinical, demographic, and laboratory findings were statistically compared. The ATRIA and CHA2DS2-VASc scores of the patients were calculated.
Results
A total of 550 patients who underwent PCI due to NSTEMI were included in the study. CIN was observed in 78 patients (14.1%) following PCI. While no difference was found between the groups in terms of gender, the mean age of patients who developed CIN was significantly higher at 67.1 ± 10.8 years compared to those without CIN (P < 0.001). The rates of diabetes, heart failure, and prior stroke were higher in the CIN group. The ejection fraction assessed via transthoracic echocardiography was significantly lower in the CIN group (43.4 ± 12.5%) compared to the non-CIN group (52.2 ± 10.6%) (P < 0.001). The volume of contrast media used during PCI was similar between the groups (P = 0.538). CHA2DS2-VASc and ATRIA scores were significantly higher in patients who developed CIN compared to those who did not (4.31 ± 1.52 vs. 2.23 ± 1.34, P < 0.001; 4.25 ± 2.55 vs. 3.26 ± 2.68, P < 0.001).
Conclusion
We demonstrated that a high ATRIA score has predictive value for the development of CIN in NSTEMI patients undergoing PCI. Additionally, the CHA2DS2-VASc score, previously shown to be associated with CIN in ACS patients, was also found to provide supplementary information for predicting the incidence of CIN in our study.
