title: #3342 Venous excess ultrasound score and acute kidney injury in patients with decompensated heart failure
authors: Christina Danai Skondra; Theodora Oikonomaki; Stamatios Georgopoulos; Maria Samara; Alexandros Nikolaos Liatsos; Eleytheria Panousi; Athanasios Trikas; Maria Darema
abstract:
Background and Aims
Systemic venous congestion is associated with an increased risk of acute kidney injury (AKI) in critically ill patients with cardiorenal syndrome. Venous excess ultrasound score (VExUS) has been proposed as a non-invasive tool to assess systemic venous congestion. This study aimed to evaluate the association between VExUS score, acute kidney injury (AKI) defined by KDIGO criteria, and renal outcome in patients with decompensated heart failure.
Method
This is a prospective, single-center study including 22 patients with a mean age of 78,18 ± 9,3 years, with chronic kidney disease (2 patients with stage 3a, 8 with stage 3b and 12 with stage 4). Patients were admitted to our hospital with decompensated heart failure and acute kidney injury, between April and September 2024 for 14,06 ± 9,5 days of hospital stay. VExUS and Focus Cardiac Ultrasound (FoCUS) regarding IVC ultrasound and right ventricular pathology were performed at the bedside during the first 24 hours of hospitalization and on discharge. Patients on renal replacement therapy, patients with portal hypertension, and transplant patients were excluded from the study. We recorded patient demographics, daily clinical characteristics, biochemistry blood test and urine analysis, hemodynamic factors, fluid balance, and diuretics during hospitalization. Echocardiographic variables including left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT), and atrial and ventricular dimensions were also recorded.
Results
Seven patients had a VExUS Score of 0, three patients had a Score of 1, six patients had a Score of 2 and six patients had a Score of 3. Ten patients with a VExUS Score < 2 were classified as non-congested and 12 patients with a VExUS Score ≥ 2 as congested. Dyspnea was the main indication for hospitalization in 75% of patients in the VExUS ≥ 2 group. Congested patients had higher BMI, IVC and diuresis on the first day compared to non-congested. There was no significant correlation between the VExUS score at admission and the total dose of diuretics administered. Lower Tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) was significantly associated with higher diuretic doses during the initial 24-hour period (P = 0.048). However, there was no correlation between TAPSE and AKI levels. Patients with VExUS Score >=2 at admission had a lower eGFR (26.7 ± 11.6) ml/min/1.73 m² compared to the VExUS Score <2 (35 ± 7.5) ml/min/1.73 m², a statistically significant difference (0.021). Patients with a VExUS score of 3 demonstrated higher serum creatinine levels at admission. Moreover, patients with a VExUS score exceeding 2, exhibited significantly elevated serum creatinine levels throughout their hospitalization and upon discharge, possibly due to the need for higher doses of diuretics or prolonged hospital stay, compared to those with a VExUS score of <2. All patients experienced a reduction in VExUS score by the time of discharge. There was no correlation between VExUS score and readmission at 3 months.
Conclusion
VExUS Score is a promising tool for the evaluation of systemic venous congestion. Further studies are needed to clarify the role of VExUS Score for treatment guidance and prediction of renal outcomes in the complex management of patients with chronic kidney disease and decompensated heart failure.

title: #1691 Assessment of oXiris membrane adsorption towards Linezolid: implications for optimizing antibiotic therapy in critically ill patients
authors: Natascha Perin; Anna Lorenzin; Massimo de Cal; Silvia De Rosa; Claudio Ronco; Monica Zanella
abstract:
Background and Aims
Sepsis in critically ill patients triggers dysregulated inflammation, leading to organs dysfunction. Antibiotic therapy is crucial in treatment, but faces challenges in optimal delivery due to potential loss in the effluent or adsorption on the sorbents surface. Linezolid (LZD), a common anti Gram-positive antimicrobial, with high volume of distribution, low protein binding (31%), may experience subtherapeutic levels during renal replacement therapies (RRT). This study aimed to evaluate LZD in vitro interaction with the membrane which the oXiris fibers are made of and its pharmacokinetic implications.
Method
The filter oXiris (Baxter, Deerfield, USA) features a membrane of polyacrylonitrile methalysulfonate coated with polyethyleneimine and unfractioned heparin used in septic patients.
In order to test LZD removal via adsorption, the dialysate inlet and outlet were clamped. A customized circuit was assembled to circulate the tested solution inside the fibers and applied to the GALILEO testing platform, specifically developed for in vitro extracorporeal circulation (Fig. 1).
600 mL of tested solution (300 mL of saline solution and 600 mg/300 mL of LZD solution) were circulated through the filter at 120 mL/min for 120 minutes in a closed-loop configuration. Samples were collected at 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 60, 90 and 120 minutes from the reservoir. LZD concentrations were measured through ARK Linezolid Assay using ILab 650 (Werfen) instrument. LZD removal ratio (RR) and mass adsorption were assessed.
Results
In vitro circulation highlighted a mild affinity of oXiris to bind LZD. The membrane showed a rapid adsorption only in the first minutes of the test. LZD concentration in the reservoir significantly dropped within 5 minutes of circulation, from 0.92 mg/mL to 0.59 mg/mL. Indeed, the RR reached 36% and settled around that value for the remaining time (Fig. 2). Throughout the experiment, LZD mass adsorbed resulted 305.6mg (from 554.4 to 248.9mg).
Conclusion
This in vitro study underscores the potential risk of LZD subtherapeutic levels during RRT with oXiris, stressing the importance of optimizing antibiotic therapy in critically ill patients undergoing extracorporeal treatments. The implementation of therapeutic drug monitoring is essential to ensure sufficient antimicrobial dosing and enhance patient outcomes.

title: #1085 Acute kidney injury in Iraqi cancer patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors. (project ICI-AKI Iraq) interim analysis
authors: Ala Ali; Zainab Nouri
abstract:
Background and Aims
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have revolutionized cancer treatment and are now the backbone of therapy for several malignancies. However, the trade-off is the occurrence of Immune-Related Adverse Events (irAEs). ICIs can cause a spectrum of renal irAEs, including acute kidney injury (AKI), most commonly manifesting as acute interstitial nephritis (AIN). In a recent meta-analysis of eighteen studies, ICI-AKI incidence was 16%. Here, we present a six-month interim analysis of a one-year project (ICI-AKI Iraq). The objective is to define the incidence of AKI in Iraqi cancer patients treated with ICIs and any related risk factors.
Method
The study employs a cross-sectional design with a prospective analytical component. From June 1, 2024, patients were recruited and followed up for six months at the Oncology Hospital and the Nephrology and Renal Transplantation Centre in Baghdad. Patients with ESKD or transplant recipients or those who were unwilling to participate were excluded. Patients who commenced therapy six months before the study were also evaluated under a retrospective arm, but any patient who previously had a diagnosis of ICI-AKI was excluded. All the medical, oncology, and pharmaceutical data were recorded and analyzed. The study's outcome is to define the incidence of AKI according to the KDIGO criteria. The project was conducted according to the National Research Ethics Code, and the patient consented to the study before enrollment. The project completion will be in June 2025.
Results
A total of 185 cancer patients have been recruited for the study till now. The mean age of the study group is 55.5 + 15 years, with 108 males (58%). Among these patients, 35 individuals (19%) were diagnosed with chronic kidney disease (CKD) in Stages II, III, and IV. At baseline, the mean serum creatinine level of the study group was 1 + 0.37 mg/dl. AKI was confirmed in 26 patients (14%). Four patients were in KDIGO-AKI stage II, while the other 22 patients were in KDIGO-AKI stage I. The mean time for occurrence of AKI is 119 + 80 days. At six months, two patients had a persistent low eGFR, CKD stage III. At all time points (C1 to C6), the creatinine was statistically significantly higher for the AKI groups than the non-AKI group (p-value <0.05). The correlation between AKI risk and age, sex, cancer diagnosis, or baseline chemotherapy didn't reach statistical significance.
Conclusion
With this six-month interim analysis, the incidence of AKI in Iraqi cancer patients treated with ICIs is 14%. Further evaluation will elucidate the one-year incidence and related risk factors. Patients who start immunotherapy with ICIs merit close monitoring of kidney function and vigilance to detect AKI.

title: #1379 Direct medical cost of hospital care for leptospirosis among adult filipinos in the Philippine General Hospital
authors: Adrian Santos; Eloina Faye Gampoy; Kevin Elissandro Gumabon
abstract:
Background and Aims
Leptospirosis is an acute febrile illness caused by pathogenic Leptospira species widely distributed geographically. The Philippines experiences an average of 680 cases and 40 leptospirosis-related deaths annually, but the trend has been increasing over the past years. Antibiotic therapy remains to be the cornerstone of treating leptospirosis, however, severe manifestations of the disease require specialized interventions such as renal replacement therapy and respiratory ventilation. The treatment of leptospirosis has an economic impact that extends beyond direct medical costs to include indirect costs such as lost productivity and income, thus highlighting the importance of understanding the relationship between treatment and economic burden. There is limited information on the economic burden of leptospirosis in the Philippines. Costing studies guide policymakers to formulate evidence-based health interventions, allocate resources efficiently, and prioritize preventive measures. This study represents the latest research endeavor on the direct medical expenses incurred by healthcare providers for managing leptospirosis patients in hospitals.
Method
A cross sectional descriptive study design was used, with data taken from Filipino adults admitted for leptospirosis in the Philippine General Hospital from March 2020 to December 2023.
Results
There were 200 included patients with a mean age of 39.9 ± 13.1 years, in which 92% were males and 71.5% had no comorbidity. Majority of the patients (61.5%) presented with Weil's syndrome and 62% received hemodialysis. The mean length of stay was 6.9 ± 3.8 days. 70.5% were discharged while 26.5% died from complications of leptospirosis. The average cost per patient was 100,781.83 PHP (1,654.53 EUR) in 2020; 63,345.48 PHP (1,039.94 EUR) in 2021; 59,464.59 PHP (976.23 EUR) in 2022; and 71,053.71 PHP (1,166.49 EUR) in 2023. The highest cost was from diagnostics, followed by medications (including antibiotics), and then logistical costs.
Conclusion
The cost of hospital admission and treatment for leptospirosis is financially debilitating for minimum wage Filipino workers because it can cost up to 20% of their annual income.

title: #2825 Comprehensive hemodynamic multi-organ ultrasound evaluation in AKI
authors: Míriam Montero Estopiñá; Gregorio Romero-González; Desirée Catalán García; Eduardo Cortés; Valentina Manuela Blanco Fernández; Jordi Soler-Majoral; Néstor Yesid Rodríguez Chitiva; Javier Paúl; Fredzzia Amada Graterol Torres; Jordi Bover Sanjuan; Jordi Ara del Rey
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is common in patients with hematological malignancies, especially multiple myeloma (MM). The primary cause of kidney damage in MM is light-chain cast nephropathy (LCCN). Patients with MM and blood light chain (LC) levels >500 mg/L are at high risk of developing LCCN, which commonly manifests as severe AKI. MM is also associated with cardiovascular complications, including high-output heart failure (HOHF), which, although rare, is clinically significant due to its poor prognosis. HOHF is characterized by systemic congestion in the presence of elevated cardiac output (CO), often exceeding 8 L/min, cardiac index >3.9 L/min/m² ² or LVOT VTI >23cm. This condition arises from reduced peripheral vascular resistance and widespread vasodilatation, leading to compensatory increases in CO.
By performing an echocardiography, we can assess the LVOT VTI (left ventricular outflow tract velocity-time integral), which is a surrogate marker of systolic volume, and if multiplied by the heart rate, the CO is obtained. The aim of this case-report is to describe the use of FoCUS for the nephrologist.
Method
The case report describes the use of point-of-care ultrasound (PoCUS), including venous excess ultrasound (VExUS), lung ultrasound (LUS), and focus cardiac ultrasound (FoCUS) in evaluating a patient with AKI in the context of MM.
Results
A 45-year-old woman with no cardiovascular risk factors was diagnosed with plasma cell leukemia and stage 3 AKI (creatinine: 2.73 mg/dL, baseline: 0.68 mg/dL) in May 2024. Proteinuria (Bence Jones) of 2984 mg/24 h was observed. At diagnosis, the patient's serum LC levels were 2.9 mg/L for κ LC and 4150 mg/L for λ LC. Bone marrow biopsy revealed 60% plasma cells, with 27% showing an aberrant phenotype. A kidney biopsy was not performed due to severe thrombocytopenia. Treatment with bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone improved serum creatinine to 2.09 mg/dL at discharge. However, in June 2024, the patient was readmitted with worsening AKI (creatinine: 3.75 mg/dL), edema, hypotension, tachycardia, jugular venous distention, and lower limb edema. PoCUS revealed tissular congestion (B-lines on LUS), venous congestion (dilated inferior vena cava), an elevated portal flow pulsatility index (58%) and biphasic intrarenal vein flow. FoCUS showed hyperdynamic circulation with a LVOT VTI of 26.43 cm, an estimated CO of 10.8 L/min, and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin: 6.5 g/dL, NT-ProBNP: 1224 pg/mL, and proteinuria: 3298 mg/24 h.
The patient was diagnosed with AKI due to LC cast nephropathy, congestive nephropathy, and HOHF. Retreatment included a negative furosemide stress test, transfusions, and MM therapy with isatuximab, carfilzomib, and dexamethasone. Hemodialysis with a polymethylmethacrylate dialyzer improved congestion and reduced λ LC by 75%, but the patient remained dialysis-dependent with high cardiac output and increasing LC levels. The patient passed away four months later.
Conclusion
MM frequently leads to LCCN, a common cause of AKI. Patients with LC levels >500 mg/L are at increased risk of LCCN. In this case, the patient's λ LC peaked at 8890 mg/L, correlating with AKI progression and dialysis initiation. About 8% of hematological malignancy patients develop HOHF, which has a poor prognosis and high mortality. HOHF in MM involves complex mechanisms, including arteriovenous shunts, angiogenesis, and alterations in blood viscosity, which reduce systemic resistance and increase circulatory demands. Clinical manifestations of HOHF include dyspnea, congestion, and tachycardia. PoCUS played a key role in diagnosing and monitoring this patient's condition, helping to assess congestive nephropathy and HOHF. By integrating imaging, clinical and laboratory findings, PoCUS provides real-time insights that enhance multiorgan ultrasound assessment (Fig. 1) and guide therapy in nephrology.

title: #3221 The challenge of using continuous renal replacement therapy anticoagulated with citrate in cirrhotic patients
authors: Maria Iraola; Albert Baronet; Esteban Poch; Gaston Piñeiro; Marina Moncada; Rodrigo Zolezzi Ramirez; Alicia Molina-Andujar
abstract:
Background and Aims
The purpose of this study is to determine the feasibility of using regional anticoagulation with citrate (RAC) in Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy (CRRT) in cirrhotic patients.
Method
Observational descriptive study, including 10 cirrhotic patients admitted to the hepatic ICU at Hospital Clínic de Barcelona between 03/2023 and 03/2024 who required CRRT. Patient characteristics were compared between those without and with citrate anticoagulation using Mann-Whitney U tests for quantitative variables and Chi-square tests for qualitative variables.
Results
Of the 10 patients, 4 used the technique without citrate and 6 with RAC. The patients receiving RAC had a median age of 57 years (47–63.25), 66.6% were male. Only one patient started the technique with citrate as the first option, and the reason for switching to citrate in 4 patients was early clotting, and in 2 patients after TOH (therapeutic hemodialysis), with median flow rates of Qb 120 mL/min, Qd 1200 mL/h, and Qr 500 mL/h. 50% switched to RAC within the first 48 hours, two of them due to elevated tCa/iCa ratio, and one as a precaution in an unstable patient. There were no differences between the two groups in age, ACLF (acute-on-chronic liver failure), or liver parameters; however, comorbidity was more prevalent in the non-citrate group (P = 0.083). Overall mortality was 80% (P = 0.747).
Conclusion
The use of regional anticoagulation with citrate in cirrhotic patients is feasible and safe if the technique is closely monitored, with potential benefits regarding filter lifespan and the consequent increase in the effective dose of therapy.

title: #894 Baseline data of the multiECCO2R study: a safety and efficiency study to evaluate CO2 removal in combination with continuous veno-venous hemodialysis/hemodiafiltration therapy
authors: Anna Wammi; Stefan Kluge; Dominik Jarczak; Carsten Willam; Karl Bihlmaier; Matthias Lubnow; Stefan Blaas; Bertram Ottillinger; Jennifer Braun; Natalia Korolev; Manuela Stauss-Grabo
abstract:
Background and Aims
Extracorporeal carbon dioxide removal (ECCO2R) therapy was proposed to reduce the level of blood CO2 and the risk of ventilator-induced lung injury in patients with combined renal failure and hypercapnia due to acute lung failure. The utilization of CO2 removal gas exchangers enables non-invasive ventilation techniques or protective invasive mechanical ventilation, thereby minimizing pulmonary stress. The multiECCO2R blood gas exchanger featuring a surface of 1.35 m2 can be integrated into a CRRT platform downstream of the dialyzer, facilitating the simultaneous treatment of adult patients with ARDS and acute kidney injury.
Method
The open, interventional post-market clinical follow-up study has progressed through an interim analysis and is now in the final analysis phase. 28 patients with combined renal failure and hypercapnia due to acute lung failure in COVID-19 and other forms of respiratory insufficiency (e.g. ARDS) have been recruited and treated on the multiFiltrate (MFT)/MFT PRO with the multiECCO2R gas exchanger (EUROSETS) for up to 72 hours.
Results
17 patients (12 males) have been included in the interim analysis with a mean age of 66.8 ± 11.3 years and a baseline paCO2 value of 59.2 ± 8.3 mmHg treated with best possible protective ventilation setting. The leading cause for renal disease was sepsis (42.1%), and the leading cause for lung disease was pneumonia (50%). All included patients were treated in a CVVHD setting, with a mean blood flow of 186.5 ± 75.3 ml/h and anticoagulation with heparin (47.1%) or citrate (52.9%).
Conclusion
The multiECCO2R study evaluates safety and efficiency of CO2 removal in combination with CRRT treatment. The recruitment phase has been completed by the end of 2024. Trial results are planned to be reported in second quarter of 2025.

title: #1570 Multicentric study of clinical characteristics and risk factors of acute renal failure in oncological patients under treatment with checkpoint inhibitors
authors: Elena Villanueva Sánchez; Javier Tascón; Marta Prieto Vicente; Alfredo G Casanova; Laura Vicente-Vicente; Pilar Fraile Gómez; Ana Isabel Morales Martín
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute renal failure (AKI) is a common complication in oncology patients, it limits therapeutic options and can obscure the prognosis. Drugs such as checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are being used increasingly in clinical practice, and are not exempt from adverse effects due to their own mechanism of action, as they produce overstimulation of the defense cells, which can cause immune-mediated toxicities. These inflammatory side effects can affect multiple organs, if they affect the kidney, they can cause acute kidney failure. The most common type of clinical-pathological pattern is acute tubulointerstitial nephritis (ATIN). We aim to study the risk factors of AKI in patients receiving ICI treatment. Being able to identify patients with a higher risk of renal failure during treatment may allow us to implement protective measures and carry out a closer surveillance.
Method
We carried out a multicenter retrospective cohort study including 84 patients participating in the ICITOX study [1], recruited between 2022 and 2024, in the Oncology and Nephrology services of the Clinical Hospital of Salamanca and Clinical Hospital of Valladolid. We defined acute kidney injury according to the guidelines published in 2012. The follow-up time was from the inclusion of the patients by the Oncologist which was the time of prescription of the first cycle of ICI treatment, until 3 months after finishing treatment. The demographic and analytical data of the patients were collected using a spreadsheet computer program and the data were analyzed by statistical study with SPSS program.
Results
The clinical characteristics of patients with and without AKI are shown in Fig. 1. Compared to controls, the cases had a higher incidence of nephrourological history, with a higher average baseline creatinine in the case group, and the predictive ability of this parameter is shown in Fig. 2. Twenty-eight patients had extrarenal autoimmunity related to ICI administration and it was more prevalent within the AKI patients. Most of the patients included had different types of lung cancer and were being treated with Pembrolizumab. Patients with urinary tract cancer, such as renal carcinoma and urothelial carcinoma, were at higher risk of AKI. The patients in both groups had received approximately the same number of ICI cycles at the time of inclusion in the study. Fourteen patients had already died, the drug was discontinued in 31 patients due to progression, 19 had it stopped due to side effects (12 of them due to AKI suspected to be nephritis secondary to ICIs), 4 patients completed the total number of cycles scheduled by Oncology, and 16 patients were still under treatment. In the cases, AKI occurred on average in cycle 8,7, that is, on average, 17,5 weeks after starting ICI treatment. The patients who developed AKI had received a higher number of drugs that could promote the development of ATIN, including proton pump inhibitors, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, antibiotics, diuretics, allopurinol, statins, metamizole, ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Electrolyte imbalances were also studied, finding hypomagnesemia in 29 patients, which was associated with the development of AKI, the predictive ability of this parameter for AKI is shown in Fig. 2.
Conclusion
In this cohort study, we identified some of the risk factors that predispose patients undergoing treatment with ICI to develop AKI. The main factors involved are baseline creatinine, nephrourological history, type of neoplasia, the use of other drugs that promote ATIN, and hypomagnesemia. Taking these clinical and analytical risk factors into account helps us to be more attentive to certain patients to whom it is advisable to closely monitor renal function, allowing for early detection of AKI. This could help initiate treatment early, minimizing the harmful effects on renal function in patients, which could be crucial for their survival.

title: #1868 “Pink cocaine” (tusi): a new cause of acute kidney injury?
authors: Jessy Korina Peña-Esparragoza; Ángela Fernández; Alberto de Lorenzo Álvarez; Laura Espinel; María Teresa Naya; Alfonso Cubas; Judith Martins Muñoz
abstract:
Background and Aims
Recently, a new drug called Tusi, a phonetic translation of 2C or 2C-B, has emerged in Latin America and Europe. It is composed of a low proportion of various substances such as ketamine, 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA), methamphetamines, and opioids. It is also known as pink cocaine, as it is usually found in pink powder form, though it rarely contains actualcocaine.
Its primary effect is hallucinogenic and is mediated by its activity on serotonin receptors. The effects appear within 1–3 hours and can last up to 8 hours. It may cause fever, hypertension, tachycardia, nausea, rhabdomyolysis, seizures, and behavioral effects. Its metabolism occurs in the liver, and it is excreted through the kidneys, remaining detectable in urine for up to 3–4 days after consumption.
Case 1
A 22-year-old male from Colombia presented to the emergency department after a street fight following alcohol consumption. He was discharged with a normal physical examination. 48 hours later, he returned with abdominal pain, vomiting, and decreased urine output. Laboratory tests revealed a creatinine level of 4.06 mg/dL and creatine kinase (CK) of 1778 U/L. An abdominal CT scan ruled out obstructive uropathy and bleeding. Urine toxicology was positive for cannabis, benzodiazepines, and methylenedioxymethamphetamine. He was admitted to the Nephrology department and started on intravenous fluids, showing improvement in renal function and a decrease in CK levels (peaking at 4593 U/L). Upon further questioning, he confirmed using Tusi on the same day as the altercation. He was discharged with a creatinine level of 1 mg/dL.
Case 2
A 42-year-old male from Ecuador was brought to the emergency department with muscle weakness that prevented him from moving. He mentioned being at a bar where people nearby were snorting Tusi. Ten hours later, he developed vomiting and decreased urine output. Upon arrival at the emergency department, a loss of strength in the lower limbs was confirmed.
Laboratory results revealed a creatinine level of 4.17 mg/dL and CK of 55,000 U/L. Urine toxicology was negative. After receiving intravenous fluids, he remained oliguric and was admitted to the ICU. Forty-eight hours later, his CK reached 179,500 U/L and his creatinine increased to 9.6 mg/dL. Blood ethanol level was 0.2 g/L.
Upon discharge from the ICU, he was transferred to the Nephrology department with ongoing renal dysfunction and oliguria, with a peak creatinine of 11.6 mg/dL, at which point he began hemodialysis. After 7 days, he showed improvement in urine output and a decrease in creatinine, reaching 1.9 mg/dL at discharge.
Samples were sent to the National Institute of Toxicology and Forensic Sciences in Madrid. In Case 1, the sample was obtained on the 4th day after consumption, testing positive only for cannabis. In Case 2, the sample was collected on the 5th day after consumption, and it was negative for drugs.
MDMA has been associated with acute renal failure (ARF), primarily attributed to non-traumatic rhabdomyolysis and the direct toxic effect of the drug on myocytes. Dehydration worsens the nephrotoxicity of myoglobinuria. In the case of methamphetamines, rhabdomyolysis is common, and dehydration and alcohol consumption contribute to renal damage.
Conclusion
Tusi is a growing drug combination in Spain that can cause ARF secondary to rhabdomyolysis, and its effects are exacerbated by simultaneous alcohol consumption. The detection of this drug is complex: the mixtures vary in their compounds and concentrations, which limits its detection. There is a delay in obtaining toxicology samples due to the lack of awareness of this drug's existence.

title: #2414 Evaluation of the frequency of contrast-induced nephropathy and associated factors following fundus fluorescein angiography
authors: Nur Sena Çoban; Meral Gulay Kocak
abstract:
Background and Aims
Fluorescein is a non-iodine-based contrast agent used during fluorescein fundus angiography (FFA) to detect retinal pathologies. In the literature, data on the frequency of development of contrast nephropathy (CN) after FFA and the risk factors affecting its development are limited. In this study, we aimed to investigate the incidence of CIN and the risk factors associated with its development in patients undergoing FFA at the retina outpatient clinic of our hospital.
Method
A total of 216 patients who underwent FFA at the Retina outpatient Clinic of Prof. Dr. Cemil Taşçıoğlu City Hospital between February and July 2024 were prospectively evaluated. Patients who had been exposed to nephrotoxic drugs or contrast agents within the past two weeks, those on hemodialysis due to end-stage renal failure, or those with an eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m² were excluded from the study. The laboratory data, chronic diseases, and medication history of the included patients were recorded prior to FFA. Blood urea and creatinine levels were analysed on the day of the procedure and 48–72 hours post-procedure. CIN was assessed separately according to the KDIGO and AKIN criteria.
Results
Among the 216 patients evaluated, 22.2% (n = 48) had stage 1, 35.6% (n = 77) had stage 2, 32.4% (n = 70) had stage 3, and 9.7% (n = 21) had stage 4 chronic kidney disease (CKD). According to KDIGO criteria, 5.6% (n = 12) of patients developed CIN, while 2.3% (n = 5) developed CIN according to AKIN criteria. When both KDIGO and AKIN criteria were combined, 6% (n = 12) developed CIN. The frequency of CIN increased from stage 2 to stage 4 according to AKIN criteria, while the incidence across CKD stages was similar when assessed with KDIGO criteria. No statistically significant differences were found between the group with and without CIN regarding age, gender, diabetes, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, heart failure, COPD, and chronic kidney disease (P > 0.05). However, when patients with CIN were evaluated according to both KDIGO and AKIN criteria, elevated serum uric acid levels were identified as an independent risk factor for the development of CIN.
Conclusion
The development of CIN following FFA is a pathological event for which we still have limited knowledge. It is not associated with well-established risk factors for iodine-based contrast-induced nephropathy, such as underlying kidney dysfunction. Further studies on the pathophysiology of CIN following FFA are needed. Considering the increased incidence according to KDIGO criteria, we believe that the diagnostic criteria for CIN should be reevaluated.

title: #3480 Dehydration and hypertension differently prime intrinsic and pre-renal AKI
authors: Noelia Diaz-Morales; Eva M Baranda-Alonso; Giada Carniglia; Annette Düwel; Nuria Martín-Fernández; Isabel Fuentes-Calvo; Sandra M Sancho Martinez; Carlos Martinez Salgado; Francisco J Lopez-Hernandez
abstract:
Background and Aims
Knowledge of factors predisposing to different types of acute kidney injury (AKI) is essential for the design of prophylactic strategies. AKI may develop mainly from tubular damage (as in intrinsic AKI) or by alterations in renal haemodynamics (as in prerenal AKI). Although dehydration and hypertension are recognized “risk factors” for AKI, the potentially distinct contribution of these comorbidities, individually and in combination, to the development, evolution and pathophysiology of intrinsic and haemodynamic AKI is not well defined. For this reason, the aim of our work was to study the role of dehydration and hypertension in two experimental models of intrinsic and pre-renal AKI.
Method
AKI was induced in 2–3 months-old male Wistar and spontaneously hypertensive (SHR) rats:
Three experimental hydration states were studied in each model:
Blood and 24-hour urine samples were collected at basal state (B), two days after water deprivation (D0, i.e., when the triggering insult was administered), and in the day of AKI development (four days after cisplatin administration [D4] or two days after TW therapy [D2]).
Concentration of creatinine (Jaffe reaction), urea (Jung method) and sodium (ion selective electrode) were determined in plasma. Urinary flow was recorded, and sodium concentration was measured in urine samples.
Results
Renal function was conserved after 48 h water deprivation. Cisplatin induced a slight loss of renal function (i.e., intrinsic AKI) in normohydrated Wistar rats. Water deprivation followed or not by water restriction did not modify the severity of AKI induced by cisplatin. On the contrary, the renal function of hypertensive rats seems to be protected from the same level of exposure to cisplatin; but in this case, previous dehydration did turn it susceptible to this drug. TW treatment did not impaired renal function under control conditions, whereas normotensive rats previously deprived of water showed alterations of the renal function (i.e., pre-renal AKI) that worsened when dehydration was partially sustained during the TW therapy. Interestingly, under hypertensive conditions, renal function was only altered after TW treatment in the group of rats with water deprivation followed by water restriction.
Conclusion
Dehydration differently primes intrinsic and pre-renal AKI under normotension and hypertension. Thus, in normotensive animals, dehydration constitutes an important risk factor for pre-renal AKI induced by TW but not for intrinsic AKI induced by cisplatin, where loss of hydration status did not aggravate renal dysfunction observed after cisplatin treatment. However, in hypertensive animals, whereas dehydration sensitize them to intrinsic AKI caused by cisplatin, it does not constitute a risk factor for TW-induced pre-renal AKI unless sustained over the time.

Giada Carniglia is recipient of a Carlos III Health Institute predoctoral contract (FI22/00208) funded by European Union-NextGenerationEU.

title: #3859 Prolonged renal ischemia: time is ticking
authors: André Silva; Gonçalo Avila; Ana Rita Calça; Ana Martins; Celia Nascimento; Rita Birne; Maria Boquinhas
abstract:
Background and Aims
Renal ischemia can be a potentially reversible cause of kidney failure. Early intervention (within hours to a couple of days) offers the best chance for kidney recovery after ischemic injury. The kidneys' ability to recover diminishes significantly with prolonged ischemia, as ischemic injury can progress to irreversible kidney damage, such as acute tubular necrosis (ATN), fibrosis, and nephron loss. However, there are some reports of successful kidney revascularization after prolonged kidney ischemia, sometimes leading to partial or limited functional recovery. This recovery is highly dependent on the degree of ischemic injury and the viability of the kidney tissue.
Method
The patient's medical records were reviewed and summarized.
Results
We report the case of a 70-year-old male patient with a history of hypertension and valvular and ischemic cardiopathy, who was admitted for aortic conduit and aortic valve replacement revision following the detection of an ascending aorta aneurysm. The procedure was complicated by a complex aortic dissection extending to the abdominal aorta, encompassing the emergence of both renal arteries. The patient became hemodynamically unstable and anuric and was admitted to the intensive care unit for monitoring.
CT angiography revealed that the right renal artery was emerging from the false lumen, and the left renal artery was stenotic due to the dissection extending to the proximal part of this artery. The renogram showed delayed enhancement of the renal parenchyma, and renal Doppler ultrasound revealed no flow in the right renal artery and severely reduced flow in the left renal artery.
Due to infectious and neurological complications, renal artery intervention was not feasible, and the patient remained anuric, dependent on continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration for 19 days. Once the patient became stable enough, renal angiography was performed, demonstrating partial patency of the left renal artery and virtually complete occlusion of the right renal artery. An endoprosthesis was placed in the right renal artery, restoring patency after the procedure. The patient became independent of renal replacement therapy 5 days later and continued to regain kidney function, reaching a minimum serum creatinine level of 1.3 mg/dL.
Conclusion
Although the chances of recovery from kidney failure sharply decrease after a few hours, there may still be a role for intervention, even in cases of prolonged ischemia. These patients should be carefully selected, preferably in the case of incomplete occlusions without clear imaging evidence of irreversible damage. We still lack the tools to accurately assess the extent and reversibility of kidney damage; therefore, more precise functional studies are needed, as there is often a mismatch between imaging findings, the actual patency of the renal arteries, and the cellular response to ischemia. Cases like these, although anecdotal, cast doubt on our current ability to predict the renal outcome of acute vascular kidney injury and our reluctance to intervene.

However, there are some reports of successful kidney revascularization after prolonged kidney ischemia, sometimes leading to partial or limited functional recovery. This recovery is highly dependent on the degree of ischemic injury and the viability of the kidney tissue.
Method
The patient's medical records were reviewed and summarized.
Results
We report the case of a 70-year-old male patient with a history of hypertension and valvular and ischemic cardiopathy, who was admitted for aortic conduit and aortic valve replacement revision following the detection of an ascending aorta aneurysm. The procedure was complicated by a complex aortic dissection extending to the abdominal aorta, encompassing the emergence of both renal arteries. The patient became hemodynamically unstable and anuric and was admitted to the intensive care unit for monitoring.
CT angiography revealed that the right renal artery was emerging from the false lumen, and the left renal artery was stenotic due to the dissection extending to the proximal part of this artery. The renogram showed delayed enhancement of the renal parenchyma, and renal Doppler ultrasound revealed no flow in the right renal artery and severely reduced flow in the left renal artery.
Due to infectious and neurological complications, renal artery intervention was not feasible, and the patient remained anuric, dependent on continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration for 19 days. Once the patient became stable enough, renal angiography was performed, demonstrating partial patency of the left renal artery and virtually complete occlusion of the right renal artery. An endoprosthesis was placed in the right renal artery, restoring patency after the procedure. The patient became independent of renal replacement therapy 5 days later and continued to regain kidney function, reaching a minimum serum creatinine level of 1.3 mg/dL.
Conclusion
Although the chances of recovery from kidney failure sharply decrease after a few hours, there may still be a role for intervention, even in cases of prolonged ischemia. These patients should be carefully selected, preferably in the case of incomplete occlusions without clear imaging evidence of irreversible damage. We still lack the tools to accurately assess the extent and reversibility of kidney damage; therefore, more precise functional studies are needed, as there is often a mismatch between imaging findings, the actual patency of the renal arteries, and the cellular response to ischemia. Cases like these, although anecdotal, cast doubt on our current ability to predict the renal outcome of acute vascular kidney injury and our reluctance to intervene.

title: #3860 Predicting ICU outcomes in trauma patients: the prognostic value of SOFA score and AKI severity
authors: Merita Rroji; Marsida Kasa; Nereida Spahia (Zeneli); Aldo Shpuza; Alfred Ibrahimi; Saimir Seferi; Saimir Kuci; Xhesiana Caushi; Hektor Sula
abstract:
Background and Aims
Critically ill trauma patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) experience significant morbidity and mortality, often driven by multi-organ dysfunction and acute kidney injury (AKI). AKI is a common and severe complication that contributes to poor outcomes, yet its prognostic significance in trauma-related ICU mortality remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between organ dysfunction, AKI severity, and ICU mortality in a tertiary trauma center to improve risk stratification and clinical management strategies.
Method
This prospective observational study was conducted over nine months, enrolling 120 trauma patients admitted to the ICU. Organ dysfunction was assessed using daily Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) scores, while AKI was classified according to Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria. The association between SOFA scores, AKI severity, and hemodynamic parameters with ICU mortality was analyzed using logistic regression, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, and Youden's J statistic.
Results
The cohort had a mean age of 54.5 years (±19.5 SD), with most patients being male (84.7%). Surgical interventions were performed in 13.9%, while critical care interventions included intubation (70.8%), inotropic drugs (19.4%), and nephrotoxic agents (9.7%). AKI occurred in 40.28% (60 patients) of patients, classified as KDIGO Stage I (23/60, 37.93 %), Stage II (25/60, 41.38 %), and Stage III (12/60, 20.69 %).
Among the 120 patients, 70 (58.33%) died during ICU admission, with 80.95% (57/70) of deceased patients having AKI at the time of death, highlighting a strong association between renal dysfunction and mortality. After adjusting for age, SOFA score, injury severity score (ISS), and mean arterial pressure (MAP), AKI emerged as an independent predictor of mortality, with affected patients showing a 2.31-fold increased risk of death (RR: 2.31) and 5.25 times higher odds of mortality (OR: 5.25, P = 0.006) compared to non-AKI patients.
Organ dysfunction severity, as measured by the maximum daily SOFA score, was a strong predictor of ICU mortality (AUC = 0.84, 95% CI: 0.75–0.93). A SOFA score of ≥8 was identified as the optimal cutoff, significantly increasing mortality risk (Fig. 1). Furthermore, higher SOFA scores were strongly associated with severe AKI (KDIGO Stage II-III), with each 1-point increase in SOFA score raising the odds of severe AKI by 27.5% (OR: 1.28, 95% CI: 1.08–1.50, P = 0.004) (Fig. 2). Additionally, MAP was marginally associated with AKI duration (P = 0.054), suggesting that lower MAP values may contribute to prolonged renal impairment, emphasizing the role of hemodynamic stability in ICU outcomes.
Conclusion
This study demonstrates that SOFA scores strongly predict ICU mortality and AKI severity, with a SOFA threshold of 8 serving as an effective mortality cutoff. The high prevalence of AKI among deceased patients underscores its critical role in ICU outcomes, necessitating early identification and intervention. Hemodynamic monitoring and AKI risk assessment should be integrated into ICU protocols to mitigate mortality and renal dysfunction in critically ill trauma patients. These findings highlight the urgent need for multidisciplinary strategies focused on organ dysfunction management and renal protection to improve survival in ICU trauma populations.

title: #131 Predictors and prevalence of hypomagnesemia in critically ill non oliguric acute kidney injury patients
authors: Nimish Gupta; Kshitij Pandey; Jyoti Goyal
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hypomagnesemia is common in critically ill patient and magnesium levels play pivotal role in homeostasis. Fraction excretion of magnesium which is a surrogate of magnesium wasting in critical care patients. Data regarding association and prevalence of hypomagnesemia in non oliguric AKI patients is scarce.
Current study aims to study prevalence of hypomagnesemia and associated risk factors in non-oliguric AKI patients.
Method
It is a prospective observational single center non-randomized trial. Total of 52 non oliguric AKI (KDIGO Stage 2 and stage 3) patients admitted in Intensive care were studied over the duration of 2 years. Serum magnesium and fraction excretion of magnesium were monitored on day 1, day 3 and day 7 of hospital admission. Various risk factors that may be associated with hypomagnesemia were also studied.
Results
Out of 52 admitted patients in ICU, 3 patients required ventilatory support. 38 out of 52 (73.1%) had hypomagnesemia within 7 days of admission. FeMg (Fraction excretion of magnesium) was high in all non-oliguric AKI patients. Mean FeMg was 6.83% + 2.26 on Day 1 which rose to 8.19% + 2.77 on day 3 and decreased slightly to 6.77% + 2.52 on Day 7. None of the predictors, including ICU stay duration, age, sex, ventilatory support, history of diabetes or hypertension, alcoholism, urine output, vasopressor need and neuromuscular changes show statistically significant associations with hypomagnesemia (P > .05).
Conclusion
Magnesiuria and hypomagnesemia is common in non-oliguric AKI patients in critical care settings. Early monitoring is required which may prevent morbidity. More studies are required to assess risk factors and to address mitigation strategies.

title: #1882 Unseen Hazards: Rhabdomyolysis in CKD patients due to ticagrelor and colchicine
authors: Tefik Islami; Marilena Gregorini; Grazia Soccio; Emma Diletta Stea; Francesca Castoldi; Alessandro Marchi; Chiara Martinelli; Nicoletta Serpieri; Giuseppe La Notte; Alessandro Tragni; Maria Antonietta Grignano; Teresa Rampino
abstract:
Background and Aims
Rhabdomyolysis (RM) is a medical condition characterized by the release of intracellular elements into the bloodstream following muscle injury. It manifests with symtoms as muscle pain (MP), weakness (W), and dark urine, which are associated with elevated levels of creatine kinase (CK) in the blood. Among the various forms of RM, drug-induced RM (DIR) is particulary notable due to its idiosyncratic nature, making it challenging to study and predict. However, this risk of DIR may be significantly higher when given the widespread use of both exclusive and combined drug therapies.
Method
Description of a case series involving four patients diagnosed with drug-induced rhabdomyolysis (DIR) at our center from July 2020 to November 2024. Data were collected from electronic medical records (Tables 1 and 2).
Case 1
An 86-year-old female (F) presented to the hospital (H) with general malaise, asthenia (A), and MP. Blood tests (BT) confirmed rhabdomyolysis (RM), hepatic injury (HI), and acute kidney injury (AKI) with preserved urine output (UO). Six weeks earlier, she was hospitalized for non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with stent placement (SP). Ticagrelor (T) and rosuvastatin (R) was initiated. Following the RM diagnosis, T and R were discontinued, and conservative treatment was given, with resolution of RM and HI, but only partial renal function (RF) recovery.
Case 2
An 87-yo (F) was electively admitted for coronary angiography due to angina pectoris and underwent Percutaneous CI with SP. T was added to her chronic medication, which included R. After 10 days, she developed severe MP and A. BT showed elevated CK, AST and ALT, as well as AKI. Hemodialysis (HD) was initiated but poorly tolerated, leading to bradycardia and cardiac arrest, ultimately resulting in her death.
Case 3
A 64 yo man with end stage renal disease (CKD) on peritoneal dialysis (PD) started colchicine (Co) therapy for acute pericarditis. Two months later, he was admitted to the H for lower limb W, and exercise-MP. BT indicated RM with associated HI and initial thrombocytopenia. Atorvastatin (A) was discontinued, and PD continued with limited benefits. An MRI showed myositis, with negative autoimmune investigations. Co therapy was discontinued, and HD initiated due to reduced UO. His condition was further complicated by severe pneumonia and melena, leading to hemodynamic and respiratory instability, culminating in the patient's death.
Case 4
A 56 yo F with Stage III CKD due to previous preeclampsia, presented to the H with marked W and MP after excessive sweating from work conditions. BT indicated RM, AKI and HI. The patient was on chronic Co therapy for gout, not adjusted for RF. After other causes of RM were ruled out, the condition was attributed to Co, and the medication was discontinued. This led to a gradual decrease in CK levels and resolution of HI. However, renal dysfunction persisted, necessitating the initiation of HD.
Results
In all cases, muscle toxicity was caused drugs. In the A and B cases, this was due to the combination of R and T, which share some metabolic pathways. In C case the combined use of A and Co resulted in severe muscle damage. Lastly, in the D case, severe dehydration led to AKI and in additional drug accumulation. In our case series, the renal outcome was unfavorable, with progression of known CKD in B,C and D cases: two required HD, and one resulted in the loss of residual UO. In terms of survival, two patients died due to complications related to their H stay, rather than directly from the drugs or RM.
Conclusion
RM is a rare but severe condition commonly associated with statin use, but less well-known in relation to T and Co. Patients with CKD are at higher risk due to the partial renal metabolism of these drugs. Despite adjusting drug dosages based on RF, reduced cytochrome functionality is a hidden danger that must be considered to identify patients at risk of RM. Additionally, worsening of RF in CKD patients increases toxicity risks, as drug dosages are not always properly adjusted.

title: #2349 Increased baseline circulating ACE2 activity and Gas6 levels predict COVID-19 severity
authors: Irene Martínez Díaz; Sara Núñez-Delgado; José Tomas Ortiz; Pablo García de Frutos; Jordi Vilardell; Antonio Cano Cámara; Carmen Llorens Cebrià; Albert Morales; Conxita Jacobs Cachá; Maria José Soler Romeo
abstract:
Background and Aims
The angiotensin converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) is the main cell entry receptor for SARS-CoV-2. SARS-CoV-2 participates in ACE2 shedding from cell membrane, increasing soluble ACE2. On the other hand, the receptor AXL also cooperates in the entry of SARS-CoV-2. The present study aims to evaluate if the initial serum levels of circulating ACE2 activity, sAXL and its ligand, the vitamin-K dependent protein Gas6, are related with the disease prognosis.
Method
Serum samples were collected from 2123 COVID-19 diagnosed patients, at two referent centers from Spain, on their first emergency between 2020 and 2021. Age, sex, previous comorbidities and clinical and analytical variables were recorded. Patients were categorized depending on their disease progression during hospitalization considering severe patients those who required intensive care unit (ICU) admission or died because of COVID-19. ACE2 activity was measured by a fluorescence enzymatic activity assay. Serum Gas6 and sAXL levels were measured by ELISA. Data was analyzed using RStudio.
Results
Patients with severe COVID-19 were older and with a major number of comorbidities. We used the cohort from one hospital (n = 1655)to perform multivariate cox regression model adjusted by age, sex, previous conditions and different analytical parameters (IL6, PCR, DD, lymphocytes count), and we found that elevated circulating ACE2 activity and higher levels of Gas6 were associated with a worse prognosis (HR: 1.23, 95% CI:1.02–1.48, p-value = 0.027; HR: 1.03, 95% CI: 1.01–1.04, p-value>0.001, respectively). In addition, we followed-up the patients for 30 days during hospitalization and carried out a Kaplan Meier Survival test that revealed that higher circulating ACE2 activity and levels of Gas6 were associated to worse survival (Log-rank = 0.0014 and Long-rank <0.001, respectively) (Fig. 1A). On the contrary, sAXL levels did not associate to a worse outcome of the disease. Finally, to analyze the predictive power of our model, we performed a time dependent ROC curve analysis obtaining an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.80 (Fig. 1B). To validate the results, the same study was also performed in the external cohort from the second hospital (n = 468) where the AUC was 0.79 providing a sensitivity of 84% and a specificity 66%.
Conclusion
Our results indicate that elevated circulating ACE2 activity and higher levels of Gas6 at admission are risk factors for severe COVID-19 disease. In addition, according to our multivariate cox model circulating ACE2 activity and higher levels of Gas6 at admission could be useful tool to predict COVID-19 severity.

title: #3387 Hepatitis, acute kidney injury and myositis due to atorvastatin
authors: Adrien Bocquillon; Serge Treille de Grandsaigne; Anne Lemy; Nathan Neveux; Aline Pourcelet; Ahmed Benahmed; Benoit Guillaume; Ishak Beklevic
abstract:
Background and Aims
A 77 year old male patient consulted the emergency department due to a new onset of jaundice without other clinical symptoms besides asthenia. Patient had a medical history of high blood pressure, dyslipidemia, type 2 diabetes and alcohol use disorder. He had no medical history of chronic liver disease or chronic kidney disease. Two months prior to the admission, the patient had been hospitalized in cardiology 2 months prior for an aortic valve replacement and quadruple CABG, with introduction of statins. During current hospitalisation, patient developed acute kidney injury, followed by acute myositis.
Method
An exhaustive work-up including full viral and bacterial screening and auto-immune testing was performed. Hepatic iconography (MRCP), kidney ultrasound and quadriceps MRI were also realised. Liver and kidney biopsies were performed.
Results
Initial blood tests showed cytolysis (AST > 35x ULN and ALT > 30x ULN) and hyperbilirubinemia (8.42 mg/dL). Two days after admission, he developed an acute kidney injury (Plasmatic Creatinine up to 8.43 mg/dL) complicated by hypervolemia and metabolic acidosis, which required hemodialysis. Surprisingly, six days after admission, he developed an elevation of Creatinine Phosphokinase up to 40855 U/L.
We quickly stopped nephrotoxic therapy and excluded urinary tract obstruction, but despite that, the renal function kept getting worse. Auto-immune screening was negative, with immunoglobins and complement were within normal limits. Also, leptospirosis and hantavirus research were negative on 2 times. Urinary sediment showed no leucocyturia or hematuria, while urinary chemistry showed tubular proteinuria (P/C 1912 mg/g creat, ACR 841 mg/g creat), with negative Bence-Jones. Kidney biopsy showed rhabdomyolysis.
Extended hepatic viral work-up was negative. MRCP showed no signs of hepatic parenchym or bile duct pathology. Liver biopsy showed sign of acute hepatitis, with toxic/pharmacologic as first hypothesis.
As previously said, patient had negative auto-immune screening, including anti-HMGCOA antibodies were negative. Muscle MRI showed acute sign of quadriceps myositis. It is important to note that EKG and transthoracic ultrasound showed no sign of myocardial infarction.
After discontinuation of Atorvastatin, liver test and Creatinine Kinase returned to normal levels. Patient still required hemodialysis after discharge from the hospital, a potential normalization of renal function is expected within 6 to 8 weeks.
Conclusion
Our patient showed a rare case of hepatitis, myositis and acute kidney injury after introduction of atorvastatin. As we know, this is the first case of acute kidney injury caused by statins with a delay of elevation of creatinine kinase. It shows the necessity to monitor the patients after introduction of statins to prevent the occurrence of side effect, although generally minor, but in some cases lead to major medical conditions.

title: #1716 Polymethylmethacrylate membranes: a cost-effective and viable strategy for renal recovery in multiple myeloma
authors: María Teresa Fernandez Quirós; Elena Delgado Sánchez de Murga; Aurora Polo Moyano; Magdalena Palomares Bayo; María José Espigares Huete
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) due to cast nephropathy is a complication in multiple myeloma (MM), 20–50% at diagnosis. Current therapeutic, such as high-cut-off (HCO) hemodialysis, its reduces serum free light chains (FLCs) but associated with high costs and albumin loss. Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) membranes have emerged as a cost-effective alternative, with comparable efficacy in FLC reduction and renal recovery. We evaluate the outcomes of intensive hemodialysis with PMMA membranes in MM patients with severe AKI-3.
Method
A single-center, prospective observational study included 13 patients with MM and AKI-3 between June 2019-December 2023, followed at least one year. All patients underwent intensive high-flow hemodialysis with PMMA and standard chemotherapy. title: #554 Severe hyponatraemia: a retrospective cohort study of clinical characteristics, management strategies, and outcomes
authors: David Connellan; Emma Kate Lally; Damien Kelly; Louise Dervan; Victoria Cooper; Blathnaid Keyes; Brendan Byrne; Denise Sadlier
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyponatraemia is a common electrolyte abnormality among hospital inpatients, with severe cases (serum sodium ≤120 mmol/L) carrying a high risk of morbidity and mortality. This retrospective cohort study examined demographic characteristics, diagnostic investigations, clinical management, and outcomes of patients admitted with severe hyponatraemia over an 18-month period. The primary aim was to compare management strategies and correction rates, evaluating their impact on long-term outcomes.
Method
Data from 202 inpatients admitted with severe hyponatraemia (serum sodium ≤120 mmol/L) between February 1, 2022, and July 31, 2023, were retrospectively analysed. Duplicate entries were removed, but re-admission events were documented. Outpatient cases and spurious sodium readings were excluded. Demographic data, diagnostic evaluations, therapeutic interventions, and sodium correction rates were reviewed. Long-term outcomes, including re-admission and 18-month mortality rates, were recorded. Subgroup analyses focused on specific management strategies (e.g., hypertonic saline use), rapid correction (>8 mmol/L in 24 hours), and extreme hyponatraemia (serum sodium ≤110 mmol/L).
Results
Cohort Characteristics
The median age was 68 years (range 16–95), with a balanced sex distribution (50.5% male). Common aetiologies included hypovolaemia (22.3%), syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH, 21.8%), and hypervolaemia (17.3%). Alcohol-related hyponatraemia accounted for 12.4% of cases, while 6.4% (n = 13) had extreme hyponatraemia (serum sodium ≤110 mmol/L).
True hyponatraemia (serum osmolality <285 mmol/kg) was observed in 78.2%, while pseudohyponatraemia was rare (3.4%, n = 7). Diagnostic work-up revealed high urine osmolality (>300 mmol/kg) in almost 50%, while low urine osmolality (<100 mmol/kg) and low urine sodium (<20 mmol/L) were noted in 5% and 41.1%, respectively. Urine sodium was >40 mmol/L in 25.7%. Thyroid dysfunction and adrenal insufficiency were uncommon contributors.
Management
Hypertonic saline (HS) was administered to 25.2% of patients, primarily in critical care settings (92.2%). HS recipients had lower baseline sodium levels (median 116 mmol/L vs. 119 mmol/L in non-recipients). Rapid sodium correction (>8 mmol/L/24 hours) occurred in 31.4% of HS patients versus 27.2% of non-HS patients, while safe correction rates (≤8 mmol/L/24 hours) were higher (39.2% vs. 34.4%). Sodium correction rates by HS use are displayed in Table 1.
Rapid correction of sodium in any 24-hour period in the first 72 hours of diagnosis was observed in 28.2%, with clinical characteristics detailed in Table 2.
Patients with extreme hyponatraemia (serum sodium ≤110 mmol/L) were more likely to have alcohol-related causes (23.1%), require critical care management (92.3%), and receive hypertonic saline (84.6%).
Outcomes
The overall 18-month mortality was 40.1% (n = 81). Mortality was highest (50%) among patients with no correction at 24 hours, followed by those with slow correction (45.5%) and rapid correction (26.3%). Re-admission within 6 months was common (31.2%), with recurrent hyponatraemia in 60.3% of these cases. Long-term care requirements arose in 8.4% of patients, reflecting the chronic impact of severe hyponatraemia.
Hypertonic saline use was associated with lower mortality (27.5% vs. 45.7%) and re-admission rates (25.5% vs. 33.1%) compared to non-HS management. One case of osmotic demyelination syndrome occurred in association with rapid correction, emphasizing the need for vigilant monitoring during treatment. Mortality was lower in the extreme hyponatraemia group at 23.1% compared 41.3% in the Na 111–120 mmol/L group, but these patients were more likely to have hyponatraemia on re-admission (80% vs. 58.6%).
Conclusion
Severe hyponatraemia management requires a balance between timely correction and avoidance of complications like osmotic demyelination. Hypertonic saline appears beneficial when judiciously applied, with lower mortality and re-admission rates. Further research is warranted to refine correction protocols and improve long-term outcomes.

title: #3382 Machine learning approach using ct-based morphological features for evaluating acute kidney injury severity
authors: Kipyo Kim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is associated with severe complications and poor outcomes, and its rapidly increasing incidence has placed a significant burden on healthcare systems. The diagnosis of AKI relies on baseline serum creatinine, and underlying chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a crucial risk factor for AKI. Pure AKI and AKI superimposed on CKD present different clinical scenarios and require distinct treatment strategies. In this study, we aimed to develop a machine learning (ML) model to accurately assess baseline creatinine and AKI severity using CT images obtained in acute settings.
Method
We initially screened individuals aged ≥18 years who underwent non-contrast abdominal CT scans at Inha University Hospital (n = 458) for training and internal validation, and at Keimyung University Hospital (n = 118) for external testing. Patients were included if they had at least two serum creatinine measured at a steady state within three months before the CT scan and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of <60 mL/min/1.73 m² at the time of imaging. Baseline creatinine was determined as the lowest stable serum creatinine value measured within three months before the CT scan. Kidney segmentation was performed using a semi-automated tool, and all images were resampled to isotropic voxels (1 mm × 1 mm × 1 mm). Various morphological features were then extracted from the kidney masks.
Results
Using clinical variables (sex, age, laboratory findings, and comorbidities) along with 12 selected morphological features—including kidney volume, surface-to-volume ratio, and parenchymal thickness—we developed a predictive model for baseline creatinine using various ML algorithms (logistic regression, support vector machine, random forest, LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost). The best-performing model was the LightGBM model (RMSE: 0.258 in the internal test set, 0.278 in the external test set). Additionally, we developed an ensemble ML model, which achieved improved predictive performance (RMSE: 0.257 in the internal test set, 0.265 in the external test set). Based on the predicted baseline creatinine, AKI staging was determined more accurately compared to the conventional method, which assumes an eGFR of 75 mL/min/1.73 m².
Conclusion
Our study suggests that an ML model for estimating baseline creatinine in patients with AKI could enhance the evaluation of AKI severity and facilitate appropriate clinical management.

title: #3451 Elderly patients with acute kidney injury: what predicts mortality ?
authors: Ilhem Ben Othman; Harzallah Amel; Sahar Agerbi; Meriam Hajji; Hayet Kaaroud; Fethi Ben Hmida; Soumaya Chargui; Ezzedine Abderrahim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common and severe condition within elderly patients, often associated with high mortality rates due to their vulnerability and frequent comorbidities. This study aimed to identify mortality risk factors in a cohort of elderly patients hospitalized for AKI.
Method
A retrospective study including patients aged 65 years or older admitted for AKI in a nephrology department between 2012 and 2023. Demographic, clinical, and laboratory data were collected. Mortality at one year was the primary outcome. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were conducted to identify independent risk factors of mortality.
Results
Study included 75 patients aged meanly 72.9 ± 5.7 years, with a predominance of females (62.7%). Most patients (65%) presented with stage 3 AKI according to KDIGO classification. The one-year mortality rate was 25.3%.
Univariate analysis identified low systolic blood pressure (P = 0.031), dehydration (P = 0.049), low hemoglobin levels (p=0.049), high potassium levels (P = 0.032), hypoalbuminemia (P = 0.002) and high creatinine at discharge (P = 0.043) as significant predictors of mortality.
Multivariate analysis confirmed dehydration (Odds Ratio [OR]=1.12; 95% Confidence Interval [CI]: 1.02–1.80; P = 0.029), low hemoglobin (OR = 1.49; 95% CI: 1.30–1.81; P = 0.006), hyperkalemia (OR = 2.00; 95% CI: 1.06–3.58; P = 0.032), and hypoalbuminemia (OR = 1.83; 95% CI: 1.71–1.96; P = 0.013) as independent risk factors for mortality.
Conclusion
This study highlights the significant impact of dehydration, anemia, electrolyte imbalances, and nutritional status on the survival of elderly patients hospitalized for AKI. Early recognition and management of these modifiable risk factors may improve outcomes in this high-risk population.
Further prospective studies are necessary to validate these findings and guide clinical interventions.

title: #3931 Risk factors for hospitalization for a major acute cardiovascular event after acute kidney injury with full recovery: a single center experience
authors: Nouha Ben Mahmoud; Mouna Hamouda; Meriem Ben Salem; Manel Ben Salah; Sirine Bchir; Ahmed Letaief; Habib Skhiri
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute kidney injury (AKI) was found to be associated with an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in the general population. We aim to evaluate the risk factors of patients having had an episode of AKI with full recovery exposing them to the risk of MACE.
Method
We conducted a retrospective single center study including all patients hospitalized in the nephrology ward since 2002 to 2015, which experienced an AKI episode with full recovery. AKI was defined according to KDIGO criteria. Our primary outcome was to identify risk factors in our population exposing them to MACE after AKI.
Results
Our study included 107 men and 107 women with median age was 61 years. KDIGO stage 3 was the major stage (115 patients), 31 of whom required hemodialysis. Hypertension was found to be the major co morbidities in our population with 37.4% of patients followed by diabetes (32.2%). Median creatinine was 3.79 mg/l (1.26–34.57 mg/l). Most patients had anemia (65.4%).
Among 176 patients for whom we have followed up, in the short, medium and long term: 19, 20 and 2 patients had respectively developed a MACE. The characteristics of patients according to the occurrence of MACE or not are illustrated by the Table 1. The risk factors found in our population were presence of co morbidities, vascular disease and anemia in univariate analysis and only anemia in multivariate analysis (Table 2). Patients with anemia and vascular disease had 2.4 times more the risk ti develop MACE after AKI with full recovery than patients without anemia and no past history of vascular disease.
Conclusion
Patients with anemia, past history of vascular disease are at risk of MACE after AKI with full recovery and those patients should be better monitored in the short, medium and long term. Our aim is to detect the MACE earlier so we decrease the cardiovascular mortality.

title: #3138 Risk factors associated with acute kidney injury in cancer patients
authors: Mücahid Kulaksız; Arzu Velioglu; Bülent Demirelli; Dilek Barutcu Atas; Ebru Asicioglu; Izzet Hakki Arikan; Mehmet Koc; Murat Tugcu; Sultan Temiz; Z Serhan Tuglular
abstract:
Background and Aims
Cancer and renal disorders are interconnected. Patients with malignancy are susceptible to renal complications due to cancer and its treatment, leading to acute kidney injury (AKI). AKI itself can cause increased mortality in individuals with malignancy. The aim of this study was to determine the incidence and risk factors for AKI and the impact of AKI on mortality in patients with solid organ malignancies.
Method
We conducted a single-center retrospective study on patients with an incident cancer diagnosis between January 2017 and December 2017 and ensured a minimum follow-up period of six months. We recorded comorbidities, cancer stage, oncological treatments, renal complications during follow-up such as proteinuria and electrolyte imbalance, demographic parameters, performance status, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR, CKD-EPI) adjusted for body surface area, and serum albumin levels. We aimed to determine the risk factors of cancer patients for the development of AKI and mortality.
Results
Six-hundred-sixty-nine patients with solid organ malignancies were included in the study. One hundred thirty-one patients (19.6%) developed AKI during the follow-up period. The association between the development of AKI and mortality was statistically significant (P < 0.001). Multivariate analysis revealed that the following parameters were positively correlated with the onset of AKI: male sex (P < 0.001, HR:2.850), diabetes mellitus (p:0.04, HR:1.550), stage 3–4 disease (p:0.012, HR:1.725), ECOG performance status ≥2 (p:0.006, HR:2.230), cisplatin administration (p:0.007, HR:1.752), and anti-VEGF therapy (p:0.016, HR:1.792). A better initial eGFR (p:0.002, HR:0.985) and higher initial serum albumin levels (p:0.001, HR:0.605) were negatively correlated with AKI occurrence.
Conclusion
Our study shows that the risk factors for the development of AKI are advanced-stage cancer, male gender, poor ECOG performance score, diabetes mellitus, cisplatin treatment, anti-VEGF therapy, decreased eGFR, and low serum albumin levels. We also observed an association between the development of AKI and mortality. Therefore, managing modifiable risk factors and acknowledging non-modifiable factors may decrease the incidence of nephropathy and mortality in cancer patients. Further research in this field will provide improved identification of these risk factors, providing an accurate evaluation of the effects of their management on the incidence of AKI and death.

title: #2820 Plasmapheresis as a life-saving intervention in amiodarone-induced thyroid storm
authors: Joana Andrade Lopes; Ana Catarina Oliveira; Odete Pereira; Ana Varela; Patrícia Martins
abstract:
Background and Aims
Amiodarone-induced thyroid storm (AITS) is a rare but life-threatening endocrine emergency caused by excessive thyroid hormone levels. When standard medical therapies fail to achieve stabilization, plasmapheresis can serve as a life-saving intervention to reduce circulating thyroid hormones and bridge patients to total thyroidectomy. We present a successful case report demonstrating the effectiveness of plasmapheresis in managing AITS.
Case Report
A 49-year-old male with a history of difficult-to-control cardiac arrhythmias was started on amiodarone in 2022. In April 2024, the patient was diagnosed with mixed type amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT). Amiodarone was discontinued, thiamazole and prednisolone were started.
However, in July 2024, he was admitted to hospital care with acute limb ischemia and required the reinstatement of amiodarone for cardiac rhythm stabilization. Subsequently, he developed a fulminant thyroid storm with undetectable TSH, free T4 levels exceeding 5.0 ng/dL, and a peak T3 of 3.91 ng/mL. Despite aggressive medical therapy with beta-blockers, corticosteroids, and antithyroid drugs, the patient's condition remained refractory, with persistent hemodynamic instability and severe thyrotoxicosis.
Urgent plasmapheresis was initiated as a salvage therapy in the intensive care unit (ICU). The patient underwent three consecutive sessions of plasmapheresis, each involving the exchange of 1.5 plasma volumes. Albumin was used as the primary replacement fluid, with the addition of two units of fresh frozen plasma (FFP) at the end of each session. This approach resulted in progressive stabilization of cardiovascular parameters, as illustrated by the evolution of T3 and free T4 levels (Fig. 1).
Following stabilization, the patient underwent a total thyroidectomy, resolving the hyperthyroid state. Postoperatively, the patient recovered without complications and was transitioned to lifelong levothyroxine therapy.
Conclusion
This case highlights the efficacy of plasmapheresis in managing refractory AIT, particularly in patients with critically thyrotoxicosis and severe clinical instability. Plasmapheresis offers rapid hormonal control by removing protein-bound thyroid hormones, bridging the gap between medical therapy and surgical intervention. Early recognition and initiation of plasmapheresis in high-risk patients, especially when standard therapies fail to control symptoms, could improve outcomes and reduce morbidity associated with AITS. Additionally, this case underscores that plasmapheresis is a safe and effective procedure, even in the intensive care unit setting, enabling timely stabilization and facilitating definitive treatment.
