Background and Aims
Amiodarone-induced thyroid storm (AITS) is a rare but life-threatening endocrine emergency caused by excessive thyroid hormone levels. When standard medical therapies fail to achieve stabilization, plasmapheresis can serve as a life-saving intervention to reduce circulating thyroid hormones and bridge patients to total thyroidectomy. We present a successful case report demonstrating the effectiveness of plasmapheresis in managing AITS.
Case Report
A 49-year-old male with a history of difficult-to-control cardiac arrhythmias was started on amiodarone in 2022. In April 2024, the patient was diagnosed with mixed type amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT). Amiodarone was discontinued, thiamazole and prednisolone were started.
However, in July 2024, he was admitted to hospital care with acute limb ischemia and required the reinstatement of amiodarone for cardiac rhythm stabilization. Subsequently, he developed a fulminant thyroid storm with undetectable TSH, free T4 levels exceeding 5.0 ng/dL, and a peak T3 of 3.91 ng/mL. Despite aggressive medical therapy with beta-blockers, corticosteroids, and antithyroid drugs, the patient's condition remained refractory, with persistent hemodynamic instability and severe thyrotoxicosis.
Urgent plasmapheresis was initiated as a salvage therapy in the intensive care unit (ICU). The patient underwent three consecutive sessions of plasmapheresis, each involving the exchange of 1.5 plasma volumes. Albumin was used as the primary replacement fluid, with the addition of two units of fresh frozen plasma (FFP) at the end of each session. This approach resulted in progressive stabilization of cardiovascular parameters, as illustrated by the evolution of T3 and free T4 levels (Fig. 1).
Following stabilization, the patient underwent a total thyroidectomy, resolving the hyperthyroid state. Postoperatively, the patient recovered without complications and was transitioned to lifelong levothyroxine therapy.
Conclusion
This case highlights the efficacy of plasmapheresis in managing refractory AIT, particularly in patients with critically thyrotoxicosis and severe clinical instability. Plasmapheresis offers rapid hormonal control by removing protein-bound thyroid hormones, bridging the gap between medical therapy and surgical intervention. Early recognition and initiation of plasmapheresis in high-risk patients, especially when standard therapies fail to control symptoms, could improve outcomes and reduce morbidity associated with AITS. Additionally, this case underscores that plasmapheresis is a safe and effective procedure, even in the intensive care unit setting, enabling timely stabilization and facilitating definitive treatment.

title: #158 Citrate accumulation during therapeutic plasma exchange in acute on chronic liver failure
authors: Swee Ping Teh; Mayank Chawla; Shashidhar Baikunje
abstract:
Background and Aims
Citrate accumulation is an uncommon complication of therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE). Apart from the citrate use as an anticoagulant for the extra-corporeal circuit, citrate can be found in blood product, particularly higher concentration in fresh frozen plasma (FFP). Patients with liver failure may have difficulty in the metabolism of citrate which result in citrate accumulation. We describe a case of citrate accumulation in a patient with acute on chronic liver failure (ACLF) during TPE.
Method
We describe a case of an 83-year-old Chinese lady with the background history of cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis B on Tenofovir Alafenamide (TAF), presented to our ED with nausea, giddiness, loss of appetite and jaundice for 2 weeks. She had received Co-amoxiclav as empirical treatment of urinary tract infection for a week prior to presentation. She had missed taking TAF for the past 2-3 weeks as she had run out of medications.
Results
She had elevated transaminases (ALT 1400 U/L, AST 2540 U/L), hyperbilirubinaemia (total bilirubin 241 µmol/L), elevated INR (INR 2.25) with normal renal function. She was treated as decompensated liver cirrhosis from drug induced liver injury and possible flare of hepatitis B.
During her admission, her liver function progressively worsened, and she developed acute kidney injury (KDIGO stage 3). Clinically, she developed grade II hepatic encephalopathy. A referral was made to the nephrology team for consideration of therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) in the light of ACLF (CLIF-C ACLF score: 62 points).
She received 2 sessions of non-anticoagulated membrane filtration TPE with 4.5 L of plasma exchanged (1.5 times plasma volume) during each session replaced with FFP. She developed hypoxia, slurred speech, and cramping sensation in the upper limbs towards the end of the first session which resolved spontaneously. She had anion-gap metabolic acidosis (anion gap: 32.2) with normotensive hyperlactataemia (serum lactate of 11.1 mmol/L). Her total calcium was noted to be 2.49 mmol/L immediately post TPE. Twenty-four hours later, she underwent the second TPE session. Two hours into the session, she developed slurred speech, bilateral carpopedal spasm and hypoxia again, accompanied by recurrent anion gap metabolic acidosis (anion gap: 29.4). Her ionized calcium was noted to be 0.51 mmol/L. Her symptoms resolved after calcium replacement. Subsequent metabolism of the accumulated citrate resulted in metabolic alkalosis (serum bicarbonate: 33.5 mmol/L) and hypokalaemia (serum potassium 2.9 mmol/L). Investigations done across TPE were recorded in Table 1.
Further TPE sessions were withheld due to deterioration in her overall condition. She subsequently demised after a few days.
Conclusion
Citrate accumulation may occur during TPE in a patient with liver impairment especially when FFP is used as the replacement fluid used. Close monitoring with repeated check of ionized calcium or prophylactic calcium infusion may avoid the occurrence of life threatening hypokalaemia during TPE in patient with liver impairment.

title: #1934 NSAIDs: painkillers or kidney killers? The ICU perspective
authors: Carolina Gomes; Maria Inês Pereira; Patrícia Valério; João Pereira
abstract:
Background and Aims
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAID) are widely used in Intensive Care Units (ICU) for pain management. However, their nephrotoxic potential raises concerns. The relationship between NSAID use and acute kidney injury (AKI) in critically ill patients remains controversial. Identifying risk factors for AKI in this population is essential to improve outcomes, particularly given the heterogeneity of patient profiles and admission types. This retrospective cohort study investigates the association between NSAID use and AKI in critically ill patients.
Method
We included 1157 ICU patients admitted between 2015 and 2023 at Vila Franca de Xira Hospital. NSAID exposure was defined as administration for ≥24 consecutive hours. AKI was diagnosed and staged according to KDIGO criteria (stages 1–3). Patients with pre-existing advanced chronic kidney disease (defined as CKD-EPI ≤ 20 mL/min/1.73 m2), early death (within 24 hours), and early AKI (within 48 hours of admission) were excluded. Patients were stratified by admission type (medical, elective surgery, and urgent surgery) and NSAID use. Multivariate logistic regression was performed to identify independent risk factors for AKI, while Cox proportional hazards models evaluated long-term survival.
Results
The total cohort included 1157 patients, of which 851 medical admissions (73.6%) and 306 surgical admissions (26.4%) [166 elective (54.2%) and 140 urgent (45.8%)]. NSAID use was more common in surgical patients (62.1% in urgent surgery, 61.4% in elective surgery) compared to medical patients (23.5%, P < 0.001). AKI was more prevalent in medical admissions (P < 0.001), but severe AKI was more frequent in urgent surgery admissions (P = 0.003). NSAID use was associated with a higher incidence of AKI (67.2% vs. 51.2%, P = 0.009) and severe AKI (34.4% vs. 26.7%, P = 0.008). Surgical patients on NSAIDs had increased rates of AKI compared to those not exposed (43.4% vs. 26.5%, P = 0.003). Independent risk factors for severe AKI included NSAID use (OR 1.978, 95% CI 1.429–2.738, P < 0.001), diabetes Mellitus (OR 2.616, 95% CI 1.758–3.893, P < 0.001), chronic hepatic disease (OR 1.666, 95% CI 1.212–2.291, P = 0.002), SAPSII score (OR 1.025, 95% CI 1.008–1.041, P = 0.003), invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) (OR 2.056, 95% CI 1.259–3.357, P = 0.004), and sepsis (OR 2.070, 95% CI 1.125–3.811, P = 0.019). Among NSAID-exposed patients, independent risk factors for severe AKI included SAPSII (OR 1.025, 95% CI 1.008–1.041, P = 0.003), and IMV (OR 2.056, 95% CI 1.259–3.357, P = 0.004, and sepsis (OR 2.070, 95% CI 1.125–3.811, P = 0.019). Survival was worse for medical admissions (log-rank 0.004) (Fig. 1). Over two years, survival was significantly lower in patients with severe AKI (log-rank <0.001) (Fig. 2).
Conclusion
NSAID use significantly increases the risk of AKI, particularly in surgical patients. Severe AKI independently worsens long-term survival, irrespective of the underlying cause. Identifying high-risk patients, ensuring hemodynamic stability, and considering alternative analgesic strategies may help reduce the incidence and severity of AKI in critically ill patients.

title: #2846 Comparison of three different amikacin guidelines for pediatric patients: virtual population insight
authors: Rasha Hussein; Felix J Meigel; Ana Catalina Alvarez-Elías; Doris H Fuertinger
abstract:
Background and Aims
Amikacin, a key aminoglycoside for treating severe pediatric infections, requires precise dosing to achieve therapeutic efficacy while minimizing nephrotoxic risks. Effective treatment depends on achieving high peak concentrations (20–80 mg/L) to ensure bacterial eradication and maintaining low trough levels (2.5–5 mg/L) to prevent toxicity. However, dosing guidelines differ across centers and countries, leading to variations in achieving these targets across pediatric populations. We present an in-silico study to compare Amikacin peak and trough levels based on different dosing guidelines. We selected guidelines from France, the United States, and the United Kingdom, representing a diverse range of dosing strategies, with many low- and middle-income countries adopting practices that fall within these ranges.
Method
An in-silico pharmacokinetic (PK) model, adapted from [1] and validated against clinical data from [2], was used to simulate Amikacin dosing. A virtual pediatric population (N = 1000), accounting for maturational changes in GFR, weight, and height, was generated to match the study population in [5] (median [range] age: 6 months [0.8–89], weight: 6.6 kg [2.8–22], eGFR: 116 mL/min/1.73 m² [48–290]), where eGFR was determined based on serum creatinine using the Schwartz formula. The body surface area was calculated using Mosteller's formula. Simulations in Python evaluated 24-hour dosing regimens over 7 days, following national guidelines from France [3] (dose: 30 mg/kg, peak levels >60 mg/L, and trough levels <2.5 mg/L), Stanford's Lucile Packard Children's Hospital (US) [4] (dose: 15–30 mg/kg, peak levels >20 mg/L, and trough levels <2.5 mg/L), and Sheffield Children's NHS Foundation Trust (UK) [5] (dose: 20 mg/kg, trough levels <5 mg/L). Amikacin dosing was not held when trough levels were not met in simulations.
Results
Amikacin peak and trough concentrations varied across dosing guidelines (Fig. 1). Median peak levels for 30 mg/kg (French guideline) ranged from 61 to 74 mg/L over the treatment days, while 15 mg/kg (UK and US) produced lower peaks of 24–29 mg/L. The 20 mg/kg dose resulted in intermediate peaks of 42–51 mg/L. Trough levels showed distinct patterns of compliance with the defined thresholds (Table 1). For the stricter <2.5 mg/L threshold, compliance decreased over the 7-day period: 99.5% to 56.6% for 15 mg/kg, 93.5% to 34.8% for 20 mg/kg, and 71.9% to 9.6% for 30 mg/kg. For the UK's less stringent <5 mg/L threshold, compliance remained higher, with 96.3% at Day 7 for 15 mg/kg, 85.6% for 20 mg/kg, and 56.6% for 30 mg/kg. By Day 7, median trough levels for 30 mg/kg exceeded 2.5 mg/L in 90.4% of the population, while 43.4% exceeded 5 mg/L. For 15 mg/kg, 43.4% of the population exceeded 2.5 mg/L, but only 3.7% exceeded 5 mg/L.
Conclusion
The differences in dosing guidelines result in varying treatment efficacy and nephrotoxic risks, with substantial fractions of the pediatric population not meeting trough targets across all guidelines. Moreover, without adapting the dosing during treatment, trough levels progressively increase. This highlights the need for an improved understanding of Amikacin's nephrotoxic effects in pediatric patients and the development of optimized and harmonized dosing strategies.

title: #3121 “Acute kidney injury in patients with kyasanur forest disease”
authors: Bhagyalaxmi Paramshetti; Ravindra Attur Prabhu; Shankar Prasad Nagaraju; Dharshan Rangaswamy; Indu Ramachandra Rao; Srinivas Vinayak Shenoy; Mohan V Bhojaraja; Nisha Abdul Khader; Nitin Gupta; Chiranjay Mukhopadhyay
abstract:
Background and Aims
Kyasanur Forest Disease (KFD) is a viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the KFD virus (KFDV), transmitted to humans through tick bites. It has been endemic to the Western Ghats of India for over 60 years but is now emerging as a tropical disease with changes in its epidemiological pattern.
The clinical presentation is biphasic and includes fever, hemorrhagic manifestations early, and neurological symptoms later. Hemorrhagic complications contribute to a case fatality rate of 2 to 10%. Post-mortem findings show focal liver necrosis, tubular kidney damage and spleen involvement.
KFD could lead to AKI, either through immune-mediated responses or direct viral damage. We studied the prevalence and outcomes of AKI in KFD.
Aim is to assess acute kidney injury (AKI) in patients with microbiologically diagnosed Kyasanur Forest disease (KFD) and its outcomes in a tertiary care facility.
Method
After institutional ethics committee approval we did a retrospective case record based study of all consecutive adult patients with confirmed KFD admitted between January 2024 to December 2024. Demography, clinical and laboratory parameters were recorded. Development of AKI was diagnosed based on KDIGO serum creatinine criteria. Outcomes assessed were mortality, number of days of hospitalization, ICU stay and requirement of mechanical ventilation. Statistical analysis was done on the SPSS 22 version.
Results
Of 63 patients, 24 (38%) developed acute kidney injury (AKI), stage 1 were 20(83.3%), stage 3 were 4(16.7%) none in stage 2. Median age was 63 years (IQR 40, 60) , the number of males was 39 (61.9%). Factors predicting AKI were male sex (48.7% vs. 20.8%, P = 0.02), presence of dyspnoea at admission (100% vs. 0 %, P < 0.001). All patients had raised Creatine phosphokinase levels (CPK) and these were significantly higher in those with AKI median 1462(IQR 976, 5036) versus 844(IQR 459, 2048) in those with normal kidney function (P = 0.04).
AKI patients had a significantly higher need for ICU care (29.1% vs. 5.1% P = 0.021) and mechanical ventilation (25% v/s 0, P < 0.01). Hemodialysis was required in 3/24(12.5%) of AKI. Mortality was 6/63(9.5%) all in AKI patients.
Conclusion
In KFD, Acute kidney injury (AKI) is seen in 38%. Male sex, presence of dyspnoea at admission are predictors of AKI. Significantly higher CPK may indicate muscle injury as a possible cause of AKI. AKI patients have higher mortality, need for ICU care and mechanical ventilation.

title: #639 Prognostic value of the red blood cell distribution width-to-albumin ratio in scrub typhus-associated acute kidney injury
authors: A Young Cho; In O Sun; Ju Hwan Oh; Ha-Eun Lee
abstract:
Background and Aims
This study aimed to investigate the clinical significance of the ratio of red blood cell distribution width (RDW) to albumin ratio (RAR) in patients with scrub typhus complicated by acute kidney injury (AKI).
Method
From 2009 to 2023, 650 patients were diagnosed with scrub typhus. Of these, we enrolled 636 patients who were followed up until renal recovery or for at least 3 months. We divided the patients into two groups (Non-AKI vs. AKI) based on the RIFLE criteria and compared clinical characteristics between the two groups.
Results
Of 636 patients, 147 patients had scrub typhus-associated AKI. The overall incidence of AKI was 23.1%; of which, 15.1%, 7.0%, and 1.0% of cases were classified as Risk, Injury, and Failure, respectively. Compared to patients in the Non-AKI group, patients in the AKI group were older (71 ± 11 vs. 62 ± 14 years, P < 0.001), and had comorbidities such as hypertension (63.3% vs 29.0% P < 0.001), diabetes (29.9% vs 13.7% P < 0.001) and chronic kidney disease (10.9% vs 1.0% P < 0.001). The AKI group had a significantly longer hospital stay (8.4 ± 5.6 vs 6.1 ± 2.8 days, P < 0.001) and received intensive care unit admission (19.0% vs. 0.2%, P < 0.001) more frequently. The patients in the AKI group had poorer renal function (40 ± 17 vs. 78 ± 20 mL/min/1.73 m2, P < 0.001) on admission and had a higher total leukocyte count (9.43 × 103/ mL vs. 6.51 × 103/mL, P < 0.001). The AKI group had a higher RAR (4.24 ± 0.87 vs 3.58 ± 0.63, P < 0.001). Furthermore, the RAR correlated with AKI severity (4.02 ± 0.79 vs 4.56 ± 0.84 vs 5.27 ± 0.75, P < 0.05). In a multivariate logistic regression analysis for predicting AKI, age, presence of co-morbidities, leukocytosis, and RAR were significant predictors for AKI.
Conclusion
The RAR is helpful to predict the development of scrub typhus-associated AKI.

title: #1400 The platelet-to-white blood cell ratio is potentially the most predictive indicator of mortality among inflammatory markers based on complete blood counts in patients with acute kidney injury
authors: Jan Nicikowski; Robert Kozłowski; Katarzyna Nowak; Marta Kołodziej; Maria Żuchowska; Ireneusz Habura; Bartosz Kudliński; Marcin Zaniew
abstract:
Background and Aims
Complete blood count (CBC) is a routine, low-cost, readily available test and is increasingly becoming a systemic biomarker of inflammation in patients. The present study aimed to investigate the correlation between different inflammatory markers derived from complete blood count (CBC) on hospital admission, such as neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), derived NLR (dNLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio (MLR), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte × platelet ratio (NLPR), platelet-to-white blood cell ratio (PWR), aggregate index of systemic inflammation (AISI), systemic inflammatory response index (SIRI) and systemic inflammatory index (SII), up to 30-day mortality after hospital admission of patients with acute kidney injury (AKI).
Method
We performed a single-center retrospective cross-sectional study, we examined the records of 409 patients hospitalized due to AKI, according to AKIN classification at the Clinical University Hospital of Zielona Góra, between March 2024 and July 2015. The data was initially cleaned, after which we employed a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC) for our analysis. The cut-off of the highest AUC parameter according to the Youden Index was applied to divide into two groups for the survival curve analyses. The correlations of mortality with PWR were evaluated by Cox proportional-hazards regression.
Results
Following data cleansing, the dataset encompassed a total of 289 patients, with a mean age of 72 ± 15.35 (18–111) years. 52.2% (151) were female and a length of stay in hospital was 12.29 ± 16.42 days. 45.7% (132) of patients were included in dialysis treatment. Sixty-one (21.1%) of the patients died during the 30-day follow-up period after hospital admission. The median PWR of the patients was 18.44 (range 0.65–88.22) respectively. The results of the ROC test obtained are shown in Table 1. The highest AUC from inflammatory markers was obtained in PWR (AUC = 0.719, P < 0.0001), with a cut-off of ≤16.28, 70.49% sensitivity, 68.86% specificity. In the univariate Cox regression analysis model (Fig. 1), the only significant correlated factor was PWR, HR = 0.961, 95% CI 0.902–0.968 (P = 0.0002).
Conclusion
CBC-derived inflammation indexes were associated with the survival outcome of confirmed AKI patients. In our study we suggest that PWR was a dominant sensitive biomarker to predict 30-day mortality patients with AKI.

title: #3351 A case report on Wunderlich syndrome in a 32-year-old male: diagnostic and clinical challenges
authors: Genelyn Uy; Mark Raymund Rodriguez
abstract:
Background and Aims
In patients presenting with flank pain, when the most common causes like urinary tract infection, nephrolithiasis, gallbladder disease among many others do not coincide with the clinical picture, spontaneous renal hemorrhage or Wunderlich syndrome must be sought. This is a life-threatening condition, much rarer than hemorrhage secondary to drug-induced and traumatic conditions. Given the rarity and the severity of this condition, it is essential to identify this at the shortest time possible.
Wunderlich syndrome is a severe and rare condition manifested by an acute onset of spontaneous renal hemorrhage into the pararenal, perirenal or subcapsular spaces in the absence of inciting trauma. Classic symptoms of flank mass, flank pain and hypovolemic shock makes up for the Lenk triad seen in less than a quarter of patients. Given acute flank pain as the universal presenting symptom, the most appropriate to be performed in the emergency department is an abdominal CT scan. Most cases are attributed to renal neoplasms (60–65%), renal vascular diseases (20–30%) and renal infections among many others. Wunderlich syndrome has been described more than a century ago with only 165 cases reported worldwide from 1985 to 1999, reduced to 102 cases between 2000 and 2016, and eventually to 41 cases between 2016 and 2022, reflecting its rarity. In the Philippines, only one (1) has been documented.
Although rare, a high index of suspicion for spontaneous renal hemorrhage is vital as this presents with insignificant symptomatology but should be managed critically. Once established, conservative measures must be done to stabilize the patient. Identification of cause should be sought to decide whether to pursue surgical intervention. At times, renal arterial embolization can be an option if urgent nephrectomy is not required. In this study, a case of Wunderlich syndrome in a young adult presenting with sudden right flank pain, declining blood pressure with findings of right renal hematoma and active bleeding of the right inferior polar artery is described. After prompt management, clinicians successfully prevented hemodynamic instability resulting to favourable outcome. This report highlights the diagnosis, optimal management and further elaborate the disease entity.
Method
Case Report
Results
After renal angiogram and embolization, angiogram showed occlusion of the branches of the right inferior polar artery. The patient's systolic BP was stable at 120–130mmHg. His hemoglobin level was steady at 12.3 g/dL with normal renal function (eGFR of 91 mL/min/1.73 m2) and complete resolution of hematuria.
One week after discharge, CBC showed no further decline in hemoglobin and abdominal ultrasound showed right perinephric hematoma measuring 11.3 cm x 9.5 cm x 4.1 cm with an estimated volume of 231.51 mL. One month after discharge, repeat ultrasound revealed a significant decrease in size of the previously noted hematoma, now measuring 6.2 x 2.9 x 6.6cm with an estimated volume of 64 mL. Overall, well-being has improved.
Conclusion
Among the plethora of causes responsible for left flank pain, Wunderlich Syndrome, needs due consideration while ruling out the common differentials. The timing and choice of diagnostic imaging is important, as it helps guide treatment by identifying the cause of the disease. However, if the patient has life-threatening symptoms, imaging may be delayed until the patient's condition has stabilized. Conservative management with follow-up imaging is a good approach to avoid unnecessary surgery. By delving into this rare occurrence and its characteristics and outcomes, the goal is to shed insights on the complexities of a dreaded complication, a relatively benign condition that can rise.

title: #3770 Next generation extracorporeal albumin detoxification/dialysis (ECAD) but not MARS reverses leucocyte dysfunction caused by severe cholestasis
authors: Sebastian Koball; Michael Hinz; Jan Stange; Julia Leonhardt; Andreas Kortgen; Michael Bauer
abstract:
Background and Aims
In liver failure, albumin bound toxins (ABT) are associated with hepatic encephalopathy, renal failure, hemodynamic instability, coagulation disorders, pulmonary dysfunction, hepatotoxicity and pruritus. On top of providing renal support therapy, one goal of extracorporeal liver support is to remove ABT to accelerate resolution of secondary organ failures, which are frequently perpetuated by inflammation, most frequently induced by infection. Recent research has revealed that elevated levels of certain bile acids due to cholestasis cause leucocyte dysfunction. The aim of this study was to compare the effect of extracorporeal Albumin Dialysis (ECAD) using MARS and OPAL (“Open Albumin Dialysis”), an ECAD method using enhanced efficacy charcoal for dialysate albumin recycling, on patient's plasma toxicity towards human leucocytes.
Method
In a prospective randomized controlled study (NCT99287235), subjects with progressive jaundice and/or HE and/or RF and/or PR were treated first with one ECAD (MARS or OPAL) and afterwards crossed over to the other. Subjects were not made aware of which ECAD they had been treated with. The machine platforms were identical. Pre-and post-values of markers for ABT, Safety and other clinical parameters were compared. Pre- and post-treatment plasma samples were tested for efficacy of ABT removal by Albumin Binding Functions (ABF) using two different methods (dansylsarcosine binding and Electron Spin Resonance-ESR-Spectroscopy), concentrations of Bile Acids and suppressive effects on leucocyte function.
Results
After incubation in plasma samples from patients the percentage of phagocytotic granulocytes remained unchanged when samples before and after MARS were compared while it increased significantly when samples pre-OPAL were compared to samples post OPAL. Total Bile Acids were reduced significantly by MARS and OPAL, the change from baseline (CFBL) during OPAL was significantly higher than for MARS. In parallel, patient`s Albumin Binding Function increased significantly during OPAL treatments, but not during MARS. Analysis of the pattern of individual bile acids revealed elevation of inhibitors of monocyte function (via TGR5) which was reduced during OPAL and MARS. After definition of a pathological level of TGR5 induction, this was restored in more individuals after OPAL when compared to MARS.
Conclusion
Since ECAD appears to have an efficacy dependent effect on reversing leucocyte dysfunction related to accumulation of albumin bound toxins, further clinical studies should investigate if these laboratory findings translate into patient centered benefits such as reduction of infection rates, improvement of antibiotic response in subjects with liver failure on extracorporeal support.

title: #992 Altered mental status in patients undergoing 5-fluorouracil based chemotherapy: think of the zebras
authors: Alyssa Simmons; Kalathil Sureshkumar
abstract:
Background and Aims
Altered mental status is cancer patients could arise for a multitude of reasons. Prompt diagnosis and early interventions could be lifesaving in some such situations. 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) is a commonly used antineoplastic agent in gastrointestinal malignancies. Its mechanism of action involves the generation of double-stranded DNA breaks via inhibition of production of deoxythymidine monophosphate (dTMP), an enzyme necessary for DNA repair and replication. The most common side effects in 5-FU administration include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Much more rarely, however, systemic administration of 5-FU has been linked to hyperammonemic encephalopathy in the absence of hepatic impairment. Here we report a case of a patient who, less than 36 hours after starting chemotherapy with 5-FU, experienced profound mental status changes that was found to be related to hyperammonemia and underwent successful treatment with dialysis.
Method
The patient in question is a 77 year-old African American male with a past medical history of squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus and recently diagnosed non-small cell lung cancer. The day prior to presentation he had been initiated on a chemotherapy regimen of 5-FU (via continuous pump), as well as pembrolizumab, leucovorin, and oxaliplatin. Shortly after arriving home the patient began to experience severe nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, which progressed over the course of the day to include altered mental status characterized by slurred speech and increased somnolence. He was found unresponsive on the floor by his wife that evening, and EMS was called. On arrival to the emergency department, the patient was found to have a GCS of 7, and was emergently intubated for airway protection.
Results
The chest X-ray was clear. CT of the head did not show any acute intracranial abnormality and MRI brain showed only small vessel ischemic disease. Serum electrolytes and calcium were normal, with serum creatinine of 1.8 mg/dL (baseline 1.4–1.6 mg/dL). Serum lactic acid was high at 9 mmol/L, and ammonia level was 603 mcmol/L (normal range 16–60 mcmol/L). Confirmatory lab testing indicated increasing ammonia levels, with next value of 731 mcmol/L. Liver function tests were normal. Due to severe hyperammonemia and metabolic encephalopathy, pt was initiated on CVVHDF with an effluent dose of 40 mL/kg/hr. In addition, 5-FU pump was removed and lactulose, rifaximin, and uridine triacetate (a specific antidote for 5-FU toxicity) were initiated. With the above treatment, the patient's ammonia levels rapidly decreased (Fig. 1). Patient's altered sensorium resolved. He was extubated 72 hours after admission. He has since been discharged to follow up with Oncology as an outpatient for ongoing therapy of his malignancy.
Conclusion
Severe hyperammonemia is a rare but potentially life-threatening adverse effect of 5-FU therapy. Our case illustrates the importance of high index of suspicion to facilitate early diagnosis and intervention with dialysis to improve outcomes. It is postulated that fluoroacetate, a catabolite of 5-FU suppresses Kreb's cycle causing dysfunction of ATP-dependent urea cycle, thus preventing conversion of ammonia into urea resulting in hyperammonemia. Disruption of Kreb's cycle also causes lactic acidosis as in our case due to the body's reliance on anaerobic metabolism to compensate for the lack of ATP.

title: #1692 Renal replacement therapy is not associated with increased mortality in patients with sepsis and acute kidney injury in the intensive care unit
authors: Jessy Korina Peña-Esparragoza; Judith Martins Muñoz; Ángela Fernández; Alberto de Lorenzo Álvarez; Laura Espinel; María Teresa Naya; Alfonso Cubas; José A Lorente
abstract:
Background and Aims
Critically ill patients with acute kidney injury (AKI) have a high mortality rate, with septic shock being the most frequent cause. In cases of AKI, delays in nephrology consultation and follow-up are associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Despite medical advances, there remains significant controversy regarding prevention strategies, specific treatments, and a lack of conclusive studies to establish solid recommendations.
Aims
A) To evaluate the prevalence of renal replacement therapy (RRT) in patients with sepsis and AKI in the intensive care unit (ICU).
B) To analyze the relationship between RRT and mortality.
Method
A retrospective study of 46 patients admitted to the ICU for sepsis with stage 2–3 AKI according to the KDIGO classification, during the period 2021–2022. Analytical parameters, RRT requirement, and mortality were analyzed. A p-value <0.05 was considered significant.
Results
The majority of patients were male (73.9%), had hypertension (58.7%), and had normal renal function prior to admission (57.8%). The average ICU stay was 22 days ± 41.5, and the most common cause of sepsis was abdominal-origin sepsis (52.2%). RRT was required in 25 patients (54.3%), with continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration being the most commonly used technique (92%). During the ICU stay, 27 patients died (58.7%), of whom 14 (56%) had received RRT. See table for further details.
Conclusion
More than half of the patients with sepsis and AKI admitted to the ICU required RRT. However, RRT was not associated with increased mortality in our sample, although the interpretation of these findings is limited by the small sample size. Given the prevalence of sepsis and AKI in the ICU, active involvement of the nephrology team and a multidisciplinary approach are recommended, which could lead to a reduction in morbidity and mortality in this patient group.

title: #97 Respiratory acidosis as risk factor for mortality in older patients with acute kidney injury that require dialysis
authors: Lillana Pacchiano Alemán; Gustavo Alejandro Casas Aparicio; Marcos García Nava; Adrián Esteban Caballero Islas; Arnulfo Mendoza Quintero; Jose Antonio León Ortiz
abstract:
Background and Aims
Patients older than 65 years old with chronic kidney disease (CKD) particularly those who require renal replacement (RRT) are a growing population and some tools have been developed to help clinician and patients to make decisions regarding.
However, information about patients with acute kidney injury on dialysis (AKI-D) is scarce. In this study we describe a group of 65 years and older patients admitted due to respiratory diseases that developed AKI and required RRT. We aim to identify risk factors associated with mortality in this population.
Method
This study is a retrospective analysis that included 118 patients admitted to our hospital between May 2022 and April 2024. We performed descriptive statistics with means and standard deviations for normally distributed continuous variables, medians and interquartile ranges for non-parametric distributions, and proportions for categorical variables. Patients were stratified according to their initial arterial partial pressure of CO2 (pCO2) values at the start of haemodialysis. The comparison between survivors and non-survivors was conducted using Fisher's exact test for categorical variables and the Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables. A logistic regression analysis was used to identify the association between the pCO2 range tertiles and mortality. All statistical tests were two-tailed, and a p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis was performed to assess the time to death, comparing the pCO2 tertiles. SPSS version 27 was used.
Results
The patients were classified in two groups: survivors and not survivors. Overall, the mean age was 75.91 years, 55.93% of the patients were male; mean BMI was 27.94 kg/m2. As comorbidities 48.31% had diabetes, hypertension was found in 63.56% of patients. In the multivariate analysis, adjusted for gender and age (CI 95%) having a determination of CO2p >45 mmHg at the beginning of dialysis had an OR 4.066 (1.517–10.899, p 0.005) for mortality.
Conclusion
This study suggests that elevated pCO2 levels in the early stages of respiratory distress may indicate a more severe underlying condition, which could negatively impact short-term prognosis and recovery outcomes. Further research is needed to fully understand the underlying mechanisms of this phenomenon, this find could help clinicians, patients and their families to make better informed decisions.

title: #475 Relation of serum creatinine twitches and outcomes among myocardial infarction patients
authors: Yacov Shacham; Shmuel Banai; Shir Frydman
abstract:
Background and Aims
From a wide array of in-hospital compilations, acute kidney injury (AKI) is notoriously associated with adverse outcomes and mortality in many acute conditions and in acute coronary syndrome patients in particular. However, using the general cutoff of 0.3 mg/dL increase from baseline for AKI definition and neglecting smaller changes could result in late diagnosis and impaired prognostication. Therefore, early reports evaluated the use of minor creatinine changes, that do not meet formal criteria, as a marker for adverse outcomes. We aimed to assess the prognostic utility of minor creatinine changes (“twitches”) in a large cohort of STEMI patients and identify a more specific cutoff for future use.
Method
This retrospective analysis of a prospective database included 2933 consecutive patients admitted with STEMI between 2008–2022 to the cardiac intensive care unit. Renal function was assessed upon admission and at-least once daily thereafter. title: #552 A machine learning approach to predict acute kidney injury in hospitalised heart failure patients
authors: Jun Ming Julian Tan; Jia Qi Low; Soo Ying Yew; Alexander Loch; Che Ruhana Yusof; Soo Kun Lim
abstract:
Background and Aims
Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) is a critical complication of heart failure. Manifesting within the complex frameworks of cardiorenal syndrome, AKI often progresses to Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) and other severe diseases, thus warranting early detection and intervention. In this study, AKI is defined by an increase in serum Creatinine (SCr) by more than 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours or by 1.5 times baseline SCr during hospitalisation according to the kidney disease: improving global outcomes (KDIGO) criteria. This study sought to develop a predictive model to predict whether heart failure patients would develop acute kidney injury within a hospitalised setting.
Method
Demographic data, past medical history, drug history, laboratory test results and vital signs were recorded for 221 heart failure patients across 498 hospitalisations at the University Malaya Medical Centre (UMMC) in Malaysia from January 2020 to June 2024 . Characteristics between the AKI and non-AKI group were compared using the Student's t test; non-normally distributed data were analysed using Mann-Whitney U test; categorical data were analysed using Chi-squared test. Logistic Regression, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Random Forest and K-Nearest Neighbour (KNN) models were built to predict the development into AKI. Established machine learning (ML) models were assessed based on their Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUROC) Curve, precision, recall and F1 score.
Results
27.3% of the hospitalized patients developed AKI during hospitalization. Hypertension, CKD, length of stay in hospital, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, mean arterial pressure, respiratory rate, hypotensive episodes during hospitalization, cumulative dose of furosemide during hospitalisation, haemoglobin level, white blood cell count, albumin level and C-reactive protein level were identified as significant predictors of AKI, thus were included within the ML models. Random Forest achieved the best performance with an accuracy of 74.3%, AUROC of 76.5% and an F1 score of 31.6%, balancing precision (54.5%) with recall (22.2%). XGBoost showed comparable AUROC (75%), but lower recall (11.1%). KNN demonstrated moderate performance, however with a higher recall (25.9%) and F1 score (34.1%). Logistic Regression underperformed across all metrics.
Conclusion
The Random Forest Model performed the best in predicting AKI in hospitalised heart failure patients. However, a low F1 score across all 4 models suggests the ineffectiveness of detecting positive AKI cases, possibly due to the positive AKI class being underrepresented in this study. Further studies should focus on addressing class imbalance through various techniques to improve the detection of AKI.

title: #903 Continuous renal replacement therapy in octogenarian and nonagenarian AKI patients: short- and long-term outcomes by age group
authors: Yusuke Watanabe; Koji Tomori; Tsutomu Inoue; Hirokazu Okada
abstract:
Background and Aims
With the increasing prevalence of acute kidney injury (AKI) among elderly populations worldwide, continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) has become a critical intervention. However, data on the short- and long-term outcomes of patients aged ≥80 years undergoing CRRT remain scarce. This study aimed to evaluate these outcomes and identify key prognostic factors to guide clinical decision-making.
Method
We conducted a single-center, retrospective observational study at Saitama Medical University International Medical Center, a Japanese university hospital specializing in Heart disease, cancer, and emergency medicine. The study included patients aged ≥80 years who underwent CRRT for AKI between April 1, 2007, and June 30, 2024. Short- and long-term survival outcomes were analyzed.
Results
A total of 210 patients (64.8 % male) were included, with a median age of 83 years (IQR 81–86; maximum age 96).
The primary causes of AKI requiring CRRT were:
• Cardiac surgery: 49 cases.
• Non-surgical heart disease: 82 cases.
• Sepsis: 40 cases.
• Acute exacerbation of chronic kidney disease or hyperkalemia: 16 cases.
• Other causes: 23 cases.
The median CRRT duration was 6 days (IQR 3–14). Overall in-hospital mortality was 80.0%, with dialysis dependence at discharge observed in 33.3 % of survivors (14/42 cases).
Mortality rates by cause of AKI were:
• Cardiac surgery: 65.3 % (32/49).
• Non-surgical heart disease: 89.0 % (73/82).
• Sepsis: 95.0 % (38/40).
• CKD exacerbation/hyperkalemia: 31.3 % (5/16).
• Other causes: 88.0 % (20/23).
• A significant difference in mortality was observed among these groups (P < 0.0001).
• When comparing patients aged 80–89 with those aged ≥90, in-hospital mortality was not significantly different (80.5 % vs. 70.0%; P = 0.44). However, long-term survival outcomes differed significantly. Six-month and one-year survival rates among discharged patients were 80% vs. 33.3 % (P = 0.004) and 70.6 % vs. 0 % (P = 0.002), respectively.
Conclusion
In patients aged ≥80 years with AKI requiring CRRT, short-term survival outcomes did not significantly differ by age group. However, long-term survival was markedly worse in patients aged ≥90 years. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating long-term survival considerations into decision-making when initiating CRRT in nonagenarian patients.

title: #3145 Severe hyperkalaemia: a retrospective study of clinical characteristics, aetiology, and management
authors: Louise Dervan; David Connellan; Ruth Cullen; Brendan Byrne; Denise Sadlier
abstract:
Background and Aims
Hyperkalaemia is common electrolyte abnormality in hospitalised patients with a prevalence of 1.1–10%. It is a life-threatening emergency, often asymptomatic until cardiac arrest, making early recognition and treatment critical. The primary aim of this study was to examine the risk factors for developing hyperkalaemia and to examine whether serum potassium was managed and reduced below 6.0 mmol/L in a timely manner.
Method
A retrospective study was performed of all patients with severe hyperkalaemia (HK) defined as a serum potassium >/= 6.0 mmol/L over a 6-month period across 2023 & 2024. Patients on haemodialysis, outpatient clinic and external hospital samples and haemolysed samples were excluded. Those patients included in further analysis were Emergency Department and inpatients where there is an expectation of prompt treatment of serious hyperkalaemia. Demographic, clinical and laboratory data were reviewed. EGFR was calculated using the MDRD equation. Frequency of monitoring of serum potassium levels and time to achieving serum potassium < 6.0 mmol/L was recorded.
Results
In total, there were over 300 cases of severe HK of which 126 patients met the inclusion criteria. The median serum K was 6.2 mmol/L (Range 6.0–8.2 mmol/L): 73.8% (n = 93) had serum K between 6.0–6.4 mmol/L with 4.8% (n = 6) of patients having a serum K >/= 7.0 mmol/L.
The median age was 71 years (Range 20–91 years), 65.9% (n = 83) of whom were male. The commonest reasons for admission were sepsis (34.1%), active malignancy (19.0%), decompensated congestive cardiac failure (5.6%) and elective cardiac surgery (5.6%). All patients had at-least one co-morbidity pre-admission, the commonest of which were CKD (52.38%), diabetes mellitus (52.4%) and congestive cardiac failure (27.0%).
Renal dysfunction was common in this group with 54.8% (n = 69) had an eGFR < 60 mls/min/1.73 m2 while 37.3% (n = 47) had acute kidney injury at the time of diagnosis of severe hyperkalaemia. Additional diagnostic tests that aid the diagnosis and management of hyperkalaemia were performed in less than 50% of cases including measure of pH (44%), Glucose (44.5%) and creatinine kinase (CK) (23%). In those where this data was recorded the median values were pH 7.321 (range 7.04–7.512), glucose 7.55 mmol/L (range 4.2–54.0 mmol/L) and CK 135 iu/L (range 14–13,659 iu/L).
The median time taken to achieve a serum K < 6.0 mmol/L was 6 hours (range 1–107 hours): serum K < 6.0 mmol/L was achieved within 2 hours in 30.2% (n = 38) of cases, within 6 hours in 32.6% (n = 41) and within 24 hours in 22.1% (n = 28). The remaining 15.1% (n = 19) remained hyperkaliaemic for greater than 24 hours. Risk factors for prolonged HK included known chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus (both insulin requiring and non-insulin requiring), tumour lysis syndrome in the setting of active malignancy and sepsis. Prolonged severe hyperkalaemia was not influenced by age, gender, severity of hyperkalaemia at time of diagnosis or the presence of congestive cardiac failure.
Conclusion
Severe HK is a clinical condition that is commonly seen in hospitalised patients, in particular with sepsis and active malignancy. Timely recognition and management is crucial to prevent adverse outcomes and further research is warranted to refine correction protocols and improve outcomes.

title: #3448 Von Willebrand factor as a predictor of acute kidney injury and hemodialysis requirement in severe leptospirosis: a prospective cohort study
authors: Gabriel Falcão; Renan Gomes Mendes Diniz; Janaína de Almeida; Mota Ramalho; Gdayllon Meneses; Luiz Neto; Gabriela Studart Galdino; Geraldo Junior; Raoni de Oliveira; Domingues Da Silva; Letícia de Araújo; Elizabeth De Francesco Daher
abstract:
Background and Aims
Leptospirosis is a zoonotic disease caused by spirochetes of the Leptospira genus. It is globally distributed, with a higher incidence in the Americas, Southeast Asia, Oceania and East Sub-Saharan Africa. The disease exhibits a broad clinical spectrum, ranging from a nonspecific febrile illness to a biphasic course characterized by an initial febrile phase followed by a severe stage with jaundice, acute kidney injury (AKI), conjunctival suffusion, haemorrhagic manifestations, and mortality.
AKI is a critical complication, with approximately 30% of affected patients requiring renal replacement therapy. The underlying mechanisms of kidney injury in leptospirosis remain incompletely understood. The literature describes multiple pathogenic pathways, including interstitial nephritis due to direct spirochete invasion, acute tubular necrosis and rhabdomyolysis. Recent studies have identified endothelial biomarkers such as Syndecan-1 and Angiopoietin-2 as potential predictors of AKI and the need for hemodialysis, offering new insights into the pathophysiology of renal involvement in severe leptospirosis. This study aims to evaluate the association between von Willebrand Factor (vWF) and AKI in patients with severe leptospirosis.
Method
This prospective observational study was conducted in Fortaleza, Brazil, including hospitalized patients diagnosed with severe leptospirosis. Blood and urine samples were collected at hospital admission to measure von Willebrand Factor A2, Angiopoetin-2 and VCAM-1 levels. Patients were stratified into two groups based on the presence of AKI at admission and followed until discharge or death to assess AKI progression and hemodialysis requirements.
Results
Forty-five patients were included in the study, with a mean age of 39 ± 13 years, of whom 86.7% were male. Acute kidney injury (AKI), as defined by KDIGO criteria, was present at admission in 73.3% of cases, and among these, 69.7% required hemodialysis during hospitalization. Patients with AKI at admission exhibited higher serum levels of Ang-2 (2.9 [1.3, 8.3] vs. 0.7 [0.5, 3.1] ng/ml, p = 0.034), while no significant difference was observed in serum levels of von Willebrand factor (25.3 [3.1, 44.2] vs. 25.2 [3.5, 34.5] ng/ml, p >0.9). In multivariate analysis, serum level of von Willebrand factor (vWF) was independently associated with the need for hemodialysis during hospitalization (OR = 1.01, 95% CI: 1.00 – 1.02, p = 0.003).
Conclusion
Elevated serum von Willebrand Factor levels were independently associated with the requirement for hemodialysis in patients with severe leptospirosis. These findings suggest that vWF may serve as a potential biomarker for early risk stratification and prognosis in leptospirosis-associated AKI and may contribute to the understanding of AKI pathophysiology in these patients.
